en: In the first entry into the systems [of logic],
within the entry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this is the chapter on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
it bestows accomplishment, reveals the reality of all things, is a temple of bliss, and is the sole vessel for all virtues.

The commencement of the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* was also made by this very author [Śrī Vādidevasūri] with the words, "The abode of perfection, the destroyer of great delusion," and so forth; likewise, the venerable Pūjyapāda began the *Jainendra-vyākaraṇa* with the sūtra "Siddhir anekāntāt," employing the letter *sa* at the outset for the sake of auspiciousness. Thus it is said: "The letters *sa* and *ha* bestow happiness and remove burning pain" (*Alaṃkāracintāmaṇi* 1).

For the sake of auspiciousness—The teacher, being one who values auspiciousness, employs the word *siddha* at the beginning for the sake of the auspiciousness of this great flood of treatises (*pātañjala-mahābhāṣya*, p.
Having bowed to the illustrious Lord of Jinas, who is stainless and possesses infinite vigor, I shall proclaim the preeminent *Lakṣaṇapada*.
[This is] an epithet of the Lord of Jinas, as well as the name of the author of the *Laghīyastraya*,
which is also an epithet of the Lord of Jinas.

He is known by name as the author of commentaries on the treatises of Akalaṅka whose intentions are profound, and the commentator on the *Siddhiviniścaya-prakaraṇa*. Thus, it is said: "The stainless speech of Anantavīrya reveals, step by step, the hidden meaning deposited in the unfathomable depths of Akalaṅka’s literary works for those who seek it, like the wick of a lamp [illuminating] constantly" (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 1; likewise, p. 476, first half).
Having reached this exalted middle of the ocean of knowledge, which is adorned with the manifold expansion of the universe,
it shines forth like a collection of diverse jewels, radiant with its own luster.
The treatise on the scriptures, which resembles the illustrious Cintāmaṇi and the beautiful moon,
and whose author of the Nyāyakumudacandra bears the name Prabhendu-bhavana, and so forth— [from] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 1.
May he, the crusher of the pride of fallacious reasoning and the sun for the lotuses of those destined for liberation, be victorious here!
Having explained the incomparable awakening of the state of Māṇikyanandin through logic that refutes fallacious reasoning, this treatise, a treasury of enlightenment, has been composed once again.
The *Parīkṣāmukha* is commenced, which is capable of accomplishing all spiritual attainments and which, at its root, has illuminated the essential reality of the three worlds. 3-vidhe— Ja.
An incomparable awakening, having attained the stainless state, encompasses all objects; by means of that [awakening],
this treatise explains that state which has all things as its object.

Why does the illustrious Gaṇadhara himself, having attained power from the feet of the Lord of Jinas, not explain the incomparable speech of the Lord of Jinas— which consists of all living beings' languages— along with the three concise works together with their commentaries? (4)

And so may the nectar of Your speech protect us—the speech of the Jina, which possesses the nature of all languages (*bṛhatsvaśloka* 96), profound, sweet, most enchanting, free from defects, and beneficial; which is devoid of causes such as the throat, lips, or vocal organs, and does not arise from the obstruction of air; which clearly expresses each desired object, consists of every possible language, and is equal toward those far and near, peerless. May it protect us!
We worship the speech of the Jina, which is present everywhere, eternal, and transformed into all languages.

Regarding those wise ones who desire to cross the great ocean of logic (*nyāyamahodadhi*), and who indeed proclaim us to possess incomparable qualities— by such words [the author] has also remembered the wicked man (*durjana*) in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*. (Kāvyānuśāsana, Śloka 1)

The King of Speakers (Vādirāja) also follows this very point; for instance, he says: "To those whose minds are longing for virtues and who know the essence of things... and so forth (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*):
"This [work], which is equal to the light of the sun and the means for establishing all objects, is commenced for their sake."
But those who are whirled about by the delusions of the waves, ripples, and whirlpools within their own innermost minds—
those who, as stated [in the commentary], are intent on perceiving faults— are not capable of attaining even a single step toward that state. || 5 ||

Since it is impossible for those of unrefined intellect to fathom the glorious *Nyāyamahārṇava*—which contains within it the collection of all jewels of objects of knowledge—the Teacher has composed this treatise (*prakaraṇa*), which resembles a ship for navigating it, in order to provide a concise exposition thereof. At the beginning of the work, the author, desiring the fruit of completing the treatise without obstacles and other such benefits, pays homage to his chosen deity. [He states: "The definition of *nyāya* is the examination of an object by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

Inference based upon perception and scripture is *anvīkṣā*; *anvīkṣā* is the subsequent investigation (*anvīkṣaṇa*) of that which has been examined through perception and scripture. That which proceeds by means of this is *ānvīkṣikī*, the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*), the treatise on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*).
Furthermore, that inference which is contrary to perception, scripture, and [valid] inference is a fallacy of reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*)—thus it is stated in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 6.

In whatever collection of words the establishment of the object to be proven reaches its completion, that collection—consisting of the five members beginning with the proposition—is called "members" (avayava) in relation to the whole.

Among these, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the convergence of authoritative testimony (*āgama*), the reason (*hetu*) is inference (*anumāna*), the example (*udāharaṇa*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the application (*upanaya*) is analogy (*upamāna*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the demonstration of the capacity [of the members] when they converge upon a single object;
this, then, is the supreme method of reasoning (*nyāya*).
The collection of sentences that makes known the probans (liṅga) endowed with all its characteristics—Nyāyabhāṣya, p.
9; Nyāyakusumāñjali-prakāśa, p. 1; Bodhinī, p. 2.

The definition of *nyāya* (inference) according to the path of logic (*nyāyatarka*) is: "A statement that produces a verbal cognition which is the cause of the *liṅgaparāmarśa* (the final consideration of the mark), which is the ultimate cause of inferential knowledge" (*Nyāyapravṛttivṛtti*, Pañjikā, fol. 38); and according to the *Tattvacintāmaṇyāloka*: "A sentence that generates the verbal knowledge which brings about the *liṅgaparāmarśa*, the final cause of inference" (*Tattvacintāmaṇyāloka*, p.
*Veśe* (Upadeśa), p. 329;
*Nyāya-parārthānumāna*, *Nyāyalīlāvatī*, p. 56:
"That by which the reality of things (*vastutattva*), which is both unascertained and uncontradicted, is led [to cognition] is *nyāya*."
*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, folio 15a;
*Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, folio 1; *Prameyaratnālaṃkāra-ṭīkā*, folio 3.
The entire [work] by Bhaṭṭa Akalaṅka;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the avoidance of nihilism, the observance of the conduct of the learned, and so forth are included.
Salutations again and again to the makers of the ford of Dharma, the proponents of *syādvāda*,
from Ṛṣabha to Mahāvīra, for the sake of attaining one's own self. (1) — Vṛṣabha, Laghīyastraya.

The meaning of the verse: *Dharma* is characterized by merit (*puṇya*), consisting of pleasant-feeling karma (*sadvedya*), auspicious lifespan (*śubhāyuḥ*), name-karma (*nāma*), and lineage-karma (*gotra*); or it is the nature of supreme forbearance (*kṣamā*) and so forth; or it is a transformation of the person (*pudgalapariṇāma*) produced by that [dharma] which yields auspicious fruits for the agent; or it is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of entities such as the soul (*jīva*) as they truly exist.

It is not, however, a specific quality of a self (*ātman*) as imagined by others, nor is it characterized by substance, quality, and action (*dravya-guṇa-karma*), nor is it a specific modification of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), nor is it insentient by nature; for these [alternatives] will be refuted in their proper places hereafter.

He alone is the *tīrtha* because he is the cause for crossing over the ocean of *saṃsāra*; or rather, his *tīrtha* is the scripture (*āgama*), because that is the means for plunging into it. To those Blessed Ones, beginning with Ṛṣabha and ending with Mahāvīra, who have performed—that is, practiced—that [scripture] and have taught it, let there be "namo namaḥ. By this repetition of the word, he demonstrates that his own self is intensely engaged in prostration.

Furthermore, from what kind of persons? From the *syādvādins*. The word *syāt* signifies non-absolutism (*anekānta*). Those whose nature it is to speak of reality as being of a manifold nature—such as existent and non-existent, by way of its own form and the forms of others, and so forth—are the *syādvādins*;

to them, for what purpose should there be salutation after salutation? He says: "For the sake of attaining one's own self. One's own self refers to the specific nature of the person offering the salutation, characterized by the avoidance of nihilism and other such defects; [the salutation is made] for the sake of attaining that, which is to say, for the sake of making it known to all people.

Alternatively, for the sake of the attainment—that is, the realization—of one's own self which possesses the nature of infinite knowledge and so forth, there is "attainment" (siddhi), as in the statement: "The realization of one's own self is *sa* [the first letter of *Siddha*]" (*Sa-siddha-bha-ślo-1*). Furthermore, according to the *Tattvārtha Sūtra* (8), "merit" (*puṇya*) consists of the karmas of pleasant sensation (*sadvedya*), auspicious life-span (*śubhāyus*), name (*nāma*), and lineage (*gotra*).

Pleasant-feeling karma (sadvedya), right belief (samyaktva), laughter (hāsya), liking (rati), male gender (puruṣaveda), auspicious life-span (śubhāyuḥ), name-karma (nāma), and lineage (gotra) constitute merit (puṇya).
Tattvārthabhāṣya 8.25.
Supreme forbearance, gentleness, straightforwardness, purity, truthfulness, self-restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possessiveness, and celibacy are the principles of Dharma.
(Tattvārthasūtra 9)

Substantial merit (dravyapuṇya) is the transformation of a specific nature attained by a person (pudgala) as the object of the act of performing [merit], caused by the soul’s (jīva) auspicious transformation;
see *Pañcāstikāya-tattva* p. 196.
— The nature of reality (tattvabhāva)— the Dharma is the inherent nature of things, the tenfold state consisting of forgiveness and so forth;
indeed, Dharma is conduct, and Dharma is that which protects living beings.
And it has been said: "Having established this, [it follows that] there is no prohibition [of pleasure], because pleasure has the self as its locus" (Nyāya-sūtra 4.1.59; cf. Ṣaṭprābhṛta-ṭīkā, p.

Because pleasure (*prīti*) is directly perceived by the self (*ātman*), it has the self as its substratum; likewise, action designated as *dharma* has that very [self] as its substratum, since *dharma* is a quality (*guṇa*) of the self. Therefore, its separation from the self is untenable.
Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 373:

Dharma is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*); it is the cause of what is agreeable, beneficial, and liberation; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*); it is opposed to the cognition of final bliss; it arises from a pure intention born of the contact between the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); it has as its cause specific means prescribed for those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*). Its means, however, are those enjoined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, existing in the form of general and particular [rules] for those of the various castes and stages of life, consisting of substances, qualities, and actions. Without aiming at any visible purpose, these means, depending upon clarity of disposition (*bhāvaprasāda*), result in the production of dharma from the contact of the self and the mind.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 272:

"For human happiness is the highest good; it is to be accomplished through substances, qualities, and actions characterized by Vedic injunctions (codanā); therefore, dharma-ness resides in those alone."
Verse 2 of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra:
Intellect is determination; its attributes are virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.

"This form is sāttvika; the tāmasa is the opposite of this. (SK 23) "In that regard, the sāttvika form of the intellect (buddhi) is fourfold: virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya). — Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti.
The Sāṃkhya [text] (Sāṃkhyakārikā 5.25) states that dharma and the other [qualities] are attributes of the internal organ.

Regarding the various types of volition (cetana), the Buddhists describe the meaning of the term *dharma* as follows: "That volition which restrains oneself, which benefits others, and which is friendly—that is *dharma*; it is the seed for its fruit both in this world and after death."

...this word "dharma" is established in three ways within the teaching: by virtue of the sense of "upholding its own characteristic," by virtue of the sense of "preventing one from going to evil destinies," and by virtue of the sense of "preventing one from wandering through the saṃsāra of the five destinies.

In that regard, by virtue of the sense of "upholding its own characteristic," all phenomena—both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)—are called *dharma*. By virtue of the sense of "preventing one from going to evil destinies," the ten wholesome paths of action and so forth are called *dharma*, according to the saying: "The practitioner of *dharma* sleeps in peace in this world and in the next.
And by virtue of the sense of "preventing one from wandering through the saṃsāra of the five destinies," *nirvāṇa* is called *dharma*.

In the phrase "he goes for refuge to the Dharma," the word *dharma* is intended here specifically in the sense of that which prevents one from going to evil destinies (*kugatigamana-vidhāraṇārtha*). (Mādhyamika-vṛtti, pp. 303–304;
ye te vṛṣa—Bhāṃ.)

In your view, even for the Kevalins, this particle— indicating non-absolutism within sentences and serving as a qualifier with respect to the object to be understood— is [present] because it is connected to the meaning.

The word *ca* is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). While it can occur in many senses— such as in the investigation of the rule of non-absolutism (*anekānta-vidhi*) and so forth— it is here understood to have the sense of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, *Rājavārttika*, p. 181:

Even when that [probans] is employed in every way, the particle "syāt" should be employed to exclude the attainment of [the fault of] being a real entity (*sattva*) and so forth, because it indicates non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
54. Tattvārthaślokavārttika 1.6
The indeclinable *syāt* indicates non-absolutism (*anekānta*)—*Ratnākarāvatārikā* 4.15; see also *Pañcārthabhāṣya*, *Tattvaprakāśikā*, p. 30.
Siddha He [pṛ 1] Syā Ma pṛ 15:
*svarūpapara*— Bhā.

If it is argued that since the purpose of avoiding atheism and so forth is accomplished by paying homage to even a single specific chosen deity, the effort of doing so for all [deities] is useless; this is not so, because the praise of all specific chosen deities without exception serves a purpose: namely, the destruction of all obstacles and the completion of the exposition of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), objects of cognition (*prameya*), viewpoints (*naya*), and categories (*nikṣepa*).

Indeed, the complete exposition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth does not achieve its establishment apart from the destruction of all obstacles; nor does the destruction of all obstacles occur apart from the praise of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

Alternatively, that [act of praise] is performed either to demonstrate that it is the cause for the destruction of obstacles for everyone without distinction, or to indicate the specific magnitude of that particular chosen deity who is distinguished by the aforementioned attributes.

Let this be granted; nevertheless, one might object: "Since the Blessed Ones are by nature oceans of infinite qualities, why is there praise through the medium of only these two qualities? This objection is not valid, because the author of the treatise seeks those specific qualities. It is observed that whoever seeks a particular quality pays homage to that distinguished person endowed with that quality—for example, someone seeking mastery of the science of archery pays homage to one endowed with the quality of such mastery. And this author of the treatise seeks the qualities of being a founder of the ford of Dharma (*dharmatīrthakaratva*) and the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāditva*). (Khila-prabhāvanā-vyākhyā, Āgamodaya Samiti edition, Bombay, Ja.)
—Thus it is said—Commentary:

Compare this with the statement in the *Āptamīmāṃsā* (p. 3): "One who seeks the attainment of a particular quality is seen to pay homage to that which possesses it, as well as to the knower of it and its author—for example, one seeking the attainment of qualities such as the science of weaponry pays homage to those who know that science and its author."

One might object: "Since the Sugata, Īśvara, Kapila, and Brahmā are proponents of the true nature of things as they exist—such as momentariness and permanence—they alone are the founders of the ford of Dharma (*dharmatīrthakara*). Therefore, they alone are to be saluted at the beginning of this treatise, and the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth composed by them are what ought to be explained therein. Anticipating this objection, [the author] speaks in order to clear away the thorns from the path of his own definitions of the means of valid cognition and so forth, stating in the *Śāstra*: "Free from thorns" (*niṣkaṇṭaka*).

If, within the mental continua, there are indeed no momentary cognitions that persist through a causal sequence, then the Buddha— consisting of a false conceptual construction— himself abides out of compassion for the sake of sentient beings, by means of his own and others' mental imputations, as one whose nature is neither real nor caused by a prior fruit.

Just as in the case of [the opponent's] doctrine of permanence, there would be no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for an entity at that time. (Verse 2) The meaning of the verse is as follows: In the continuities (*santati*)—that is, in the streams (*santāna*)—of momentary cognitions that are mutually distinct and lack any underlying substrate (*niranvaya*), how could this be so? In what state are they? They are "non-existent" (*asatsu eva*), meaning they are simply not present. And their non-existence is established because, when examined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are found to be untenable. This untenability will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.

[Objection: "Granted that he may not exist [as a person], yet his mental states will continue to function through a continuous succession of cause and effect. To this, he says: If the Buddha himself remains established by his own nature—while those mental states, whose essence is not that of cause and effect (i.e., whose nature is not characterized by causal relation) in reality (i.e., in the ultimate sense), remain as if non-existent within their own continuums; if he remains established by what? By the conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) of self and other—that is, by the determination that the non-existent are existent. For what purpose does he remain established? He says: for the sake of sentient beings (*sattvārtham*), meaning for the purpose of uplifting those to be trained from suffering or from the causes of suffering. By what means? By compassion. As it has been said:
Even when supreme Nirvāṇa has been attained, for those whose minds are moistened with compassion, there is the resolve—
augmented by meditative cultivation throughout countless, non-conceptual aeons.
"But those for whom there is great compassion remain indeed dependent on others" (Abhisamayālaṃkāra, p.
134). Regarding the phrase "they remain indeed," etc., the second half-verse is found in the *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.160.
199. In its original form, as well as in *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā* p. 386, line 1; *Āptaparīkṣā* p. 43; and *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 25, line 1.
It is found as an introductory citation (*avataraṇa*) in such works as the *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, page 471, and the *Laghīyastraya-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, page 4.
"But those for whom there is great compassion remain indeed dependent on others. Thus it remains, O Jaḍa.

Alternatively—according to the Bhāṣya—the compassion of the Sugatas is threefold: that which has sentient beings as its object, such as toward one's children and wife; that which has phenomena as its object, such as toward the Saṅgha and so forth; and that which is objectless, such as in the case of lifting up a frog caught between two closing hands.

In that regard, the compassion of the Sugatas is great and without objective support because it is independent of both sentient beings and phenomena; thus they remain forever and never enter parinirvāṇa, because they are devoted to benefiting the world through the teaching of the Dharma and because the world is infinite. (Āptamīmāṃsā, p. 43)

Such a Buddha, who—though there is no real entity—possesses a dogmatic adherence to the existence of beings, cannot truly be a founder of a Dharma, because he lacks the quality of teaching the nature of things exactly as they exist, like Īśvara, Kapila, or Brahmā. Rather, he consists solely of false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*); that is, he is essentially composed of that which is false and untrue—the conceptualization otherwise known as conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). How so? Like "permanence" (*nityatva*): just as the permanence of Īśvara, Kapila, Brahmā, and the principles (*tattva*) they have propounded—which is asserted by others—is merely of the nature of false conceptualization and does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), so too is the Buddha.

[Objection: "Since all of this is accepted [by us], there is no fault," says the proponent of the non-duality of appearance (*pratibhāsādvaitavādin*). To him, [the author] says "therein" (*tatra*), etc. "Therein" means in that which is accepted by the proponent of the non-duality of appearance; in what? In the moment (*samaya*)—that is, existing in identity with the manifestation of every single cognition—at that moment, there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), i.e., no experience. For it has been stated: "The final causal efficiency is indeed the production of a cognition having itself as its object"; that [efficiency] does not exist. Of what? Of the entity—that is, of the non-dual reality (*advayapadārtha*).

In some versions, the reading is *vastutaḥ*; even there, it means "in reality" or "from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*)," whereas from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtyā*), it might exist.
Furthermore, how causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is untenable in the absolute positions of eternalism, momentariness, and non-duality will be demonstrated later.

Therefore, like the Buddha and other such [beings], even the non-duality of appearances consists solely of false conceptualization— thus [it is] non-transformative (apariṇāma)— [and is] as if eternal. (Abhāva-bhāṣya)
— by Brahmā— Ā., Ba., Ja.;
— by the Naiyāyikas and others— knowledge— Ba., Ja.
The state of being a proponent [of the Buddha's teaching] in every respect— *buddheṣi* (Ā,
Ba, Ja), *sarvathā* (Ba)—
is the eloquence (*prabhā*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth: at that time, this manifestation is concomitant with all cognitions; in that non-duality of manifestation, there would be no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—that is, no experience—of the non-dual entity, because [the manifestation] is manifold.
(Laghīyastraya-vṛtti, p. 5) [Variant readings:
*nānā*—Ā., Ba., Ja.]

As it has been said: "In this regard, according to the *Tattvārtha-śloka* (p. 195), this causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consists, from the perspective of conventional cognition (*mati*), in the production of a consciousness whose object is itself;
however, in reality—that is, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), depending on the alternative reading—this has been stated."
Laghīyastraya-bṛhaṭṭīkā, p. 5;
arthakriyā—according to the Bhāṣya.

—[The opponent] says: "This treatise is commenced for the purpose of examining the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; however, an examination of that which is non-existent, such as the means of valid cognition, is not possible. And their non-existence [is established] because all cognitions, being devoid of an objective support (*nirālambana*), are equal to dream-cognitions. In order to refute that view, he says: "In that," and so forth. "In that" refers to that doctrine accepted by the opponent. "Equal" (*samaḥ*) means similar, common to both the waking and dreaming states. Regarding the form *ayo* (for *ayaḥ*), the vowel *a* takes the form of the following vowel due to its inclusion in the *śakandhu*-class. What is it? He says: "There is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)."
The mention of "object" (*artha*) is an illustration; by it, "non-object" (*anartha*) is also included.

In this context, the "object" is momentary, partless cognition alone, because it is that which is sought after. That which is other than this is the "non-object," being the opposite. The activity regarding these two—characterized by rejection and acquisition—would not exist. For it will be demonstrated later that it is not logical for all cognitions to be equal in their acquisition of the object and avoidance of the non-object.
How would that [activity] not exist? To this he says: "In reality" (*vastuto vastutaḥ*), that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthena*).
And regarding the reading "vastunaḥ," the meaning is "from the entity characterized as proof or refutation";
by this, even mere illusion is excluded, because the logic is the same for the Mādhyamika.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the methods (*naya*), and the categories (*nikṣepa*) are included;
according to the *vārttika* of Kātyāyana, "in the case of *śakandhu* and similar forms, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) should be stated."
Therefore, between benefit and harm,
that which is not beneficial is the absolute delusion.

[The opponent’s] objection regarding the doctrine of the mental continuum (*santāna*): But surely, it was incorrectly stated that “the mental continua do not exist at all,” because their existence is possible. For instance, the preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness—which proceed in a continuous stream of cause and effect, which perish moment by moment, and whose distinctions are not perceived—are designated by the term “continuum” (*santāna*) and are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

Nor does the consequence of the faults of "the destruction of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*) and "the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) arise, because although mental moments perish at every instant, there is no single self (*ātman*) that could serve as the substratum for the connection between action and its fruit;

for, with respect to the continuum (*saṃtāna*), such a connection is possible, since the connection between action and its fruit is established among the mental moments falling within a single continuum, even though they are momentary at every instant. Thus, there is no occasion for those faults to occur.

Nor does the series (saṃtāna) differ from the members of the series, nor is it non-different; for such an onset of manifold conceptual constructions as these would follow. This is because that [conceptualization] has a real entity as its object, whereas the series is not a real entity. For the sake of conventional usage, the series is a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) consisting of the apprehension of non-difference even among distinct moments. Since it is not a real entity, it is simply inexpressible by means of conceptual constructions regarding difference or non-difference. Whatever is not a real entity is indeed inexpressible by means of conceptual constructions such as difference and non-difference, just like a sky-lotus; and the series—being of the nature of a conceptual construction of non-difference among distinct moments—is likewise not a real entity. —ṇāviśa— Ā., Ba., Ja.
The continuum (*saṃtāna*) and the collection (*samudāya*) are false, like a row or an army.
There exists no such thing as a "continuum" that is a single entity existing in ultimate reality;
what is it then? It is merely a stream consisting of a succession of moments proceeding in a relationship of cause and effect, for nothing distinct from this is perceived.
Therefore, for the purpose of conventional usage, the Buddhas established the convention "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) in order to designate these very moments by means of a single term;
as stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* (p.
334): "Indeed, it is not so; for those moments which possess the continuum are what is denoted by the word 'continuum' (*santati*)."

"They are manifested collectively for the sake of brevity, like the word 'forest' [for trees]. This is not a fault; by the word "series" (*santati*), the very moments (*kṣaṇa*) which are the real entities (*vastu*) constituting the series are manifested collectively and simultaneously for the sake of linguistic convenience, just as the *dhava* and other trees are [manifested] by the word "forest."

This very definition of a continuum (*santāna*) has been cited and refuted in the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, the *Nyāyapraveśabṛhaṭṭīkāpañjikā* (p. 41), the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadvārttika* (p. 1489), the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* (p. 214), the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 443), the *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā* (vol. 2, p. 196), the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* (p. 23), the *Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāvyākhyābhisamayālaṃkārāloka* (p. 165), and so forth.

In the Jaina system, however, the definition of a continuum (*saṃtāna*) is as follows: it is a continuous succession (*anvaya*) consisting of specific excellence (*atiśaya*), which pertains to both cause and effect even when they exist at prior and subsequent times (Aṣṭaśatī on Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p.

186). And that wholesome or unwholesome mind, having arisen and being about to cease, deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*)—characterized by specific formative forces (*saṃskāra*) such as wholesomeness or unwholesomeness—upon the momentary mental state that is its own product.

Furthermore, that [mind], imbued with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by those [actions] and proceeding as a continuum through the uninterrupted succession of subsequent moments conditioned by them, undergoes a specific transformation (*pariṇativiśeṣa*) and produces in the next world a result consisting of the very nature of pleasure and so forth, which is mental in character and corresponds to the specific action. Thus, there is neither the arrival of what was not done nor the loss of what was done to act as an obstacle;
therefore, the connection between action and its fruit is not tenable without a self (*ātman*).
(Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā, p. 472)

In this way, there would indeed be the destruction of what has been done if the cause did not produce the effect; yet this is not accepted, because causality exists through a continuous succession. (538)
There would also be the arrival of what was not produced, if an effect were ever to arise without its cause; this is not so, because of the necessity of causal power. (539)

*Tattvasaṃgraha*: If, indeed, an agent or an enjoyer were intended in an ultimate sense, then by accepting the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and so forth.

However, since this entire universe is merely a collection of causal conditions (*pratyayamātra*), nothing whatsoever is created by any agent, nor is anything enjoyed. How, then, could the consequence of the destruction of what has been done be leveled against us? Just as in the case of seeds sprinkled with the juice of lac and other substances, specific potencies (*sāmarthyaviśeṣa*) deposited by prior actions continue through the continuum (*santāna*); from these, once they have reached full maturity at a later time, the desired or undesired fruit arises.

In the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa, p. 150), the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 443), and other such works, however, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) against the theory of the continuum (*santānavāda*), a refutation of the faults of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*) is made by citing the verse: "But in whichever very continuum the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) is deposited, the fruit arises in that same continuum, just as redness [appears] in the cotton plant."

Since the conceptualization of difference and non-difference has a real entity as its basis, it is logical that things lacking intrinsic nature cannot be designated as being either identical to or different from reality. (340)
Tattvasaṃgraha:
[The section on] the non-apprehension of the object due to the onset of not a few conceptual constructions.
Alternatively,
it is described as being inexpressible in terms of identity or difference.
In that case, activity would be like a continuum and so forth; surely it would be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). (Tattvasaṃgraha 1807)

Just as the person (*pudgala*) is devoid of intrinsic nature because it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from its constituent moments (*santānin*), so too the continuum (*santāna*) is devoid of intrinsic nature;
for if intrinsic nature existed, identity or difference would necessarily follow. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā)

Comparison: Now, if it is argued that the application of conceptual constructions such as difference or non-difference does not apply to the continuum (*santāna*), because those [constructions] have real entities (*vastu*) as their object and the continuum is not a real entity—[as stated in] *Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
1089—"then that [objection regarding] difference and so forth... (*bhāṃ॰*);
"...not by means of a non-aggregated [continuum]" (*ba॰*).

[Objection: "But even so, since a single self that recognizes is not admitted among the mutually distinct moments of consciousness, recognition and the like are untenable. [Reply: This too is incorrect, because such [recognition] is possible through similarity alone, as in the case of a lamp. For just as in the case of lamp-flames and the like—which perish at every moment—there arises the recognition "this is that very same lamp" due to similarity, so it is here as well. (Nanve— Ā., Ba., Ja.)
Furthermore, recognition as a unity based on the occurrence of subsequent similar states—such as in the case of nails and hair that have been cut and grown back again—is free from contradiction;
for this reason, certain specific mental states possess a particular capacity for causal efficacy. (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 133, u.)
Therefore, recollection and the other [mental functions] are everywhere determined and unimpeded. (Tattvasaṃgraha 543)

In whichever continuum a seed for recollection and so forth has been deposited through the production of successively more distinguished moments by means of a powerful experience, therein alone do recollection and the rest arise, and not elsewhere, because the relationship between cause and effect is strictly determined. Furthermore, recognition and other such cognitions, which are preceded by recollection and the like, are produced; thus, there is no contradiction. (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*)

Furthermore, if the self were of a single, eternal nature, it would be non-existent because it could not perform purposeful action (arthakriyā) either successively or simultaneously; how then could it serve as the basis for recognition and other such cognitions? Whatever cannot perform purposeful action either successively or simultaneously is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman; and this same incapacity applies to the self, which is asserted to be eternal and of a single nature.

Furthermore, it is not unestablished that its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is untenable through either succession or simultaneity; for instance, if it exercises causal efficiency successively, does it produce the second effect with the very same nature by which it produced the first, or with a different nature? If it were with the very same nature, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the effects to be accomplished in the second and subsequent moments would arise in the very first moment, because the essential form that produces them would already exist previously.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whenever there exists a cause for the production of something, that thing is established as possessing production at that time, just like the effect intended for that specific moment. Now, the nature of the Self (*ātman*), which is held to be eternal and uniform, is indeed the producer of the effect to be accomplished in the second and subsequent moments, occurring at that very moment. If, however, it produces that [effect] by means of a different nature, then since its previous nature has ceased, its momentariness is established, because the definition of momentariness is the cessation of one's own nature.

Even if it were to perform its causal function simultaneously, then by virtue of having a nature that produces all effects at once, it would produce all effects in the very first moment; consequently, since there would be no effect to be produced in subsequent moments, it would follow—like a horse’s horn—that it is non-existent due to its failure to perform any purposeful action (*anarthakriyākāritva*). Thus, the argument beginning with "by way of succession or simultaneity" is not stated because of a lack of capacity due to the absence of an effect being perceived in the case of non-momentariness, but rather because of the absence of its pervader (*vyāpaka*). For instance, the performance of an effect is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, as there is no other possible mode.

Therefore, since those two—the capacity for causal activity and its pervader—are contradictory in the case of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), when [non-momentariness] is excluded, the causal power (*kriyāśakti*) pervaded by them is also excluded. Thus, non-existence, characterized by the absence of all capacities, entails the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) in the case of non-momentariness, because two contradictory things cannot coexist in one place. Consequently, existence (*sattva*), being excluded from that [non-momentariness], remains only in momentary things and thereby experiences identity with them—namely, "whatever is existent is necessarily momentary" (Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 142).
Because they perform causal efficacy neither successively nor simultaneously, eternal things do not produce effects, as this would involve a contradiction between succession and simultaneity. (76)
Entities are not stable; therefore, they are considered to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). (Tattvasaṃgraha 394)

Does causal efficiency occur through succession or simultaneity? Does it perform the first causal efficiency by means of that same intrinsic nature (svabhāva) by which it performs subsequent effects, or does it do so having acquired a different intrinsic nature?
*Tattvopadeśa*, page 126:
"Just as that which is productive [is not so] because of the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). (*yadutpādakam asti*—Bhāṣya).

Furthermore, you maintain that the self (*ātman*) pervades the successive states (*paryāya*) such as pleasure and so forth; is this [pervasion] held to be by means of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or by many? If it is by a single [nature], then those [states] would necessarily become of one form; for whatever is pervaded by a single intrinsic nature must be of one form, just like the essential nature of a single state. And since the multiple states such as pleasure and so forth are pervaded by the self which possesses a single intrinsic nature, [they would all become identical]. If, on the other hand, it is by many [intrinsic natures], then that [self] possessing many [natures] would itself have to be pervaded by another set of many intrinsic natures, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it were argued that they are pervaded by that single nature, then it would have to be said that here too there is a plurality of natures of the same kind; and in that case, the same infinite regress (anavasthā) would follow, nor is there any other alternative. Therefore, how could a common form (*anvita-rūpa*) of pleasure and the like, which arise sequentially, be established, by means of which the existence of a self (*ātman*) might be proven?
— *syeta*— *ba*, *ja*.
According to the Jaina [view], the modifications such as pleasure and so forth [belong to] the self— Ā॰, ba॰, ja॰.
—It was said by him—:
"by their own nature," [variant: "by themselves"].

Regarding the Jaina position on the doctrine of continuity (*santāna*), the following response is offered: as for what was stated—that there is a relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion; for in the absolute view of momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*), the very relationship of cause and effect is impossible.

In that regard, what is the effect (*kārya*) and what is the cause (*kāraṇa*)? If it is argued that "that which comes into being after having not existed is the effect," then [we ask]: in both its non-existence and its coming into existence, who possesses the status of agent (*kartṛtva*)—is it that very thing itself, or something else? It cannot be that very thing itself, because it is impossible for that which is in every respect non-existent to be a substratum for the property of agency. Whatever is in every respect non-existent is not a substratum for the property of agency, just as the son of a barren woman; and according to the opponent's view, the effect is in every respect non-existent.

For *bhāvanā* (the act of bringing into being) is the appropriation of an essential nature (*svarūpa*), and that is utterly impossible in every respect for that which is non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman;

nor can it belong to something else, because that would entail that very [other thing] being the effect. For that which is the agent both in the absence of becoming and in the presence of becoming is itself the effect. Furthermore, if that [agent] were also entirely non-existent, it could not be an effect, as this would contradict the aforementioned inference (p.

That which acquires its own existence immediately after an effort is indeed something that comes into being after not having existed, such as an effect like a jar; this state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is the property of coming into existence after not having existed. (Nyāyabhāṣya p. 442; Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kiraṇāvalī p. 29)
Because arising consists in the state of having previously been non-existent, there is no other mode of persistence; [Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi, p.

The state of "having come into being after not having been" (*abhūtvābhāvitva*) has been discussed incidentally in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p. 418), in the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 418), and in the *Prameyaratnamālā* (p.
68)—[this applies to the reading] *sattva* in the Ā, Ba, and Ja manuscripts.

In the Buddhist view, does causality consist in being the producer of any effect whatsoever, or in being the producer of a specific effect? In the first case, everything would be the cause of everything; consequently, no one seeking a particular effect would employ a specific material cause.
The second case is also untenable, because it is impossible to qualify the nature of a cause by means of an effect that is as non-existent as a flower in the sky.

Whatever is a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*) is qualified only by a qualifier that is itself existent, just as self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is qualified by its nature of self-awareness. Since causality (*kāraṇatva*) is a real nature, if it were to be qualified by a non-existent effect (*kārya*) such that "this is the producer of that," then the cause would entail the consequence of being non-existent.

For whatever is qualified in every respect by what is non-existent is itself non-existent, just as a pot is qualified by non-existence when one says "the pot is non-existent. And according to the opponent’s view, the cause is qualified in every respect by the non-existent effect.

By this [argument], the claim that the cause is qualified by an effect superimposed upon conceptual construction (*vikalpādhirūḍha*) is also refuted. Indeed, an effect superimposed upon conceptual construction does not abandon its insubstantial nature;
and if the cause were qualified by what is superimposed upon conceptual construction, its status as a real cause would not be established.

A nature that depends upon a qualification superimposed upon conceptual construction is not real, just as "fire-ness" in the case of a young boy. And the nature of being a cause in a cause is likewise dependent upon a qualification characterized by an effect superimposed upon conceptual construction.

Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent in every respect, the activity of the causes would have to be admitted as being without a basis (*nirālambana*). In that case, just as with the production of the intended effect, their activity would necessarily apply to the production of things such as sky-lotuses; consequently, nothing at all would be absolutely non-existent. Alternatively, if they do not act toward those [sky-lotuses] because of their total non-existence, then they likewise would not act toward the intended effect, since there is no difference in their being non-existent in every respect. That toward which causes do not act is that which is non-existent in every respect, such as a sky-flower; and according to your own view, the effect is non-existent in every respect.

Furthermore, if the operation of causes were to occur without any objective support whatsoever, then it would follow that a given cause would operate toward other effects as well as toward its intended effect; consequently, the postulation of other causes would be rendered useless.
(The reading *khapuṣpākhyena* is found in manuscripts *ba*, *ja*, and *da*; [the rest of the phrase is] *danaṃ saṃvi* in manuscript *ba*.)
In the opinion of others, [it is] non-existence; in the opinion of the Avīras, it is *kā* (or *ka*).
For that which... (as in the Bhāṣya).
The state of being [the suffix] -tva— according to the Bhāṣya—
the form of which is -ṇatva—
being present there— according to Ātreya and Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita; according to Jayanta.
—Non-existence— Ā., Ba., Ja.

Or, let it be granted that in your view there exists some nature of being an effect or a cause that is agreeable only so long as it is not investigated; nevertheless, would the effect arise from a cause that has already perished, one that has not yet perished, or one that is in the process of perishing? It cannot be from one that has already perished; for since it is non-existent by its own nature and devoid of all causal capacity, it is impossible for it to function as a cause with respect to that effect.

Whatever is non-existent by its own nature cannot produce anything, just as a son cannot be produced from the child of a barren woman; and according to your doctrine, the cause is non-existent by its own nature.

That it performs an effect while having perished is truly a great marvel! For indeed, the production of a crow’s caw from a dead peacock is impossible; otherwise, how could an effect that arises from such [a cause] be said to have a cause? If, on the other hand, it arises from that [cause] without having perished, then a final farewell has been given to the momentary destruction of entities, since their persistence over multiple moments is thereby established; for they first arise, then exert themselves to perform an effect, and subsequently manifest that effect.

Now, if it is argued that these [causes] manifest their effect at the very moment of their own arising, that is not so; for it would follow that the entire continuum [of causes] must be annihilated, since the effect produced by them would also have to produce its own effect at that very same time. Furthermore, does the subsequent moment arise from a preceding moment that has perished, one that has not perished, or one that is currently perishing? And so forth.

A cause that has perished does not [produce an effect], because it is non-existent, like something that has long since passed away. (Mādhyamika-bṛhaṭṭīkā p. 282; Tattvasaṅgraha ślokas 488–489; Aṣṭasahasrī p. 182).
Does a momentary entity produce an effect while it has perished, while it has not perished, while it possesses both forms, or while it possesses neither form? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 147;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 318;
Syādvādaratnākara p. 777)
Dependence toward the effect—
from that which is non-existent in nature.

Comparison: If the effect were to exist only when the cause exists, then the three worlds would exist in a single moment, because the entire subsequent series of moments would have to arise at the very time of the causal moment; consequently, there would be no such thing as a "series" (santāna).
(*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p.

187) Now, if it is argued that the effect arises from a cause in its state of perishing—that is not so; for for an adherent of an absolute doctrine (ekāntavādin), even the state of perishing itself is logically untenable.

Indeed, when a single entity undergoes destruction in one respect while persisting in another, that is called the "state of perishing. And how could such a state be possible in a doctrine of absolute unity (*ekānta*), given that it implies a nature of manifoldness (*anekānta*)? Furthermore, is this state of perishing existent or non-existent? If it is existent, then it too must possess a momentary nature; what, then, would be its distinction from the entity that possesses it? If, on the other hand, it is non-existent, how can there be causal productivity for that which is embraced by it? For that which is embraced by a non-existent form is not the producer of anything, just like a sky-lotus; and according to your own view, the entity intended to be the cause is embraced by a state of perishing that is non-existent in form.
Momentariness is consistent with its own state of being.
Furthermore, since the possessor of the state (*avasthāvat*) is non-existent in nature,

is this relationship of cause and effect conceptual (*kālpanika*) or real (*vāstava*)? If it were conceptual, then the relationship between action and its fruit would likewise be merely conceptual, leading to the undesirable consequence of nihilism (*laukāyatikatva*), because there would be no real connection between the final moment of consciousness of a previous life and the first moment of consciousness in this life.
Alternatively, [one might argue that] it is real; that is not so, because a real relationship between momentary objects that are absolutely distinct is untenable.

Now, if the causal relation here consists merely of the coming-to-be of the effect and the coming-to-be of the cause—[one might object]: "But surely, that which is the coming-to-be of the effect resides only in the effect, and that which is the coming-to-be of the cause resides only in the cause; thus, there is no connection between these two. Otherwise, the coming-to-be of a jar would also be the coming-to-be of a cloth, and this too would constitute a causal relation; consequently, one seeking a specific effect might take up just any cause whatsoever."

Now, as for the claim that when the exclusion of one thing occurs upon the exclusion of another's own nature alone, the latter exists when the former exists and does not exist when it does not—thus being its effect through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—that is not so; because positive and negative concomitance are unestablished in the doctrine of absolute momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya-ekānta*), since the effect would always be possible even in the absence of a cause.

When a capable cause exists at its own time, the effect arises immediately after; when it does not exist, it does not. This occurrence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is indistinguishable even in the case of something that is ineffective. For just as an effect does not manifest without the intended moment occurring immediately prior to it, so too it must necessarily arise from some preceding moment, some succeeding moment, or some simultaneous moment, since it occurs at a fixed time. It cannot be produced by various other moments belonging to different times—whether before, after, or at the same time—unless they are restricted to those specific temporal relations.

Furthermore, those moments of other continua existing in the same time—whether prior, subsequent, or simultaneous—are not its cause, because they contribute nothing to it; likewise, even the intended moment, because it contributes nothing, would not be its cause even if it existed at a prior time. This is because the causal relation between cause and effect [requires such contribution].
—It is given (dīyate) in the manuscripts Ba, Bhā, and Ā;
"when [the cause] exists, [the effect] comes to be" (sati bhavati) in the manuscript Ā; "only that" (eka-stat) in the manuscript Bhāṃ.

If it is argued that "the subsequent [cognition] is its effect because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [object]," we say no; for that [conformity] is unestablished even in the case of an eternal [object] (*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 182).
—For these two, [the cause and the effect], must necessarily manifest as future entities (bhāvin).

Furthermore, a cause brings about the manifestation of an effect by way of being its material cause (*upādāna*) and auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*); and this relationship is not possible under the doctrine of absolute momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*).

In that context, does "being a material cause" (upādānatva) mean existing at a prior time, or being the producer of an effect that is similar to itself and located in the same place? The first position is untenable, because it would lead to a deviation [in the definition] due to moments belonging to other continua.

The second position is also inadmissible, because the Buddhists do not accept [the concepts of] spatial location or similarity; or, if they were accepted, it would contradict their doctrine of extreme difference and momentariness.

Furthermore, there would be an absence of material causality between the cognition of blue and the cognition of yellow, or between the mind of a non-yogi and the mind of a yogi, due to their extreme dissimilarity.

Thus, if there were an absolute momentariness, the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) would be unestablished, and consequently the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) would also be unestablished, since they are rooted in that [material cause]. Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect, as well as the status of being a material cause, is possible only in an entity that possesses some degree of persistence (*anvaya*). For it is precisely therein that the definition of a material cause is applicable: the occurrence of the assumption of a subsequent form through the non-abandonment of the previous form, which is based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Consequently, one who desires a causal relationship between preceding and succeeding particular moments of consciousness must admit a connection with a single cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*).
The state of being a cooperative cause with grasping—
of that which arises from the doctrine of momentary moments—
ja., bhāṃ.; and of the *pī* [syllable]— ā., ba., ja.

Comparison: Even if that [succession] exists, it is not known which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of which therein? If it is argued that "the cognition of form is the material cause of the cognition of form, and this should be applied elsewhere as well," then it follows that the first cognition of the Buddhist would be without a material cause, because at the beginning there is no such prior material cause; otherwise, how could the state of being a Sugata (Buddha) be established along with its means? (*Siddhi-viṣama-ṭīkā*, p.

197, top). Comparison: And how can there be an establishment of the material and auxiliary causes of a factor if there is destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*)? (*Prameya-kamala-mārtaṇḍa*, p. 147, top).

Comparison: At that time, in the absence of being the material cause (*upādānatā*) for the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), there would also be no status as a causal condition (*nimittatā*), because the status of being a causal condition is pervaded by the status of being a material cause;
for the determination of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārivyavasthiti*) is rooted in the determination of the material cause. (Vaiśeṣika Upaniṣad, p. 145).

Comparison: Because they possess the nature of a single substance, the preceding mode is in some respect the material cause (*upādāna*), and the subsequent [mode] is necessarily the effect (*upādeya*).

*Tattvārtha-śloka-vārttika*, page 38: It has been said— "That which exists throughout the three periods of time, having abandoned and yet not abandoning its own nature, through successive prior and subsequent states, is known as substance (*dravya*) and is called the material cause (*upādāna*)."

That which abandons its own nature and that which never abandons it in any way cannot be the material cause of an object, whether it be momentary or eternal, as stated on page 210 of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*.

Because it is perceived as the material cause (*upādāna*)—being the object of a cognition that involves the continuity of a subsequent form while not abandoning the previous form, and which functions without relinquishing [the former]—as stated in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, page 65: "not abandoning the subsequent material cause...
(variants: ā॰, ba॰, ja॰).
—Just as the relation of cause and effect is impossible [to be established] without a single cognizer, so too the comprehension of that [relation] is untenable without a single cognizer. (Bhāṣya)

For the Buddhists maintain that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established by a pentad of perceptions and non-perceptions (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). First, there is the non-perception of both cause and effect, characterized by the perception of a bare ground; then follows the perception of fire, immediately after which is the perception of smoke; and finally, upon the non-perception of the fire, there is the non-perception of the smoke as well. Thus, through these three non-perceptions and two perceptions, the causal relation between fire and smoke is apprehended.

By means of three perceptions or two non-perceptions—first, indeed, there is the perception of fire and smoke; after that, the non-perception of fire and immediately thereafter the perception of smoke; and finally, upon the perception of fire, the perception of smoke as well—these five entities are brought by this pentad of perception and non-perception into the objective range of a single reflective awareness (*ekasaṃvit-parāmarśa*) by a single cognizer alone.

Furthermore, the manifestation of the single cognizer is precisely the manifestation of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the persisting correlate (*anvayi*) uninterrupted by all other cognitions pervading that duration of time.

For such an operation, consisting of a synthetic conceptualization (*parāmarśa*), is not possible for cognitions that arise and pass away successively moment by moment and are mutually ignorant of one another’s objects.

Even in the case of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), its operation is restricted to the very object of the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); it is therefore not logical [for it] to extend beyond that. For conceptual cognition proceeds only with respect to that blue or other object which has been grasped by the non-conceptual cognition, and not toward an additional object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) because it would be apprehending what has not already been apprehended.
— *Dabhi ga* (Ā., Ba., Ja.)

The determination of the production of that [effect] is also established by the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) through five observations and non-observations (*pratyakṣopalambhānupalambha*). These are: (1) the non-observation of the effect prior to its production; (2) the observation of the effect when the cause is observed; (3) the subsequent non-observation of the effect due to the non-observation of the cause after it has been observed. Thus, there are two non-observations and one observation regarding the effect, and two—namely, the observation and non-observation—regarding the cause. In this way, through these five observations and non-observations, it is determined that smoke exists only when fire exists, and is absent when it does not exist (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 206).
Sarvadaśasamuccaya, page 17— [the portion] beginning with "sā" is missing in the Bhāṣya; it is present in Ā, Ba, and Ja.

—[Objection: Let there be such an operation consisting of this kind of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), or let that [awareness] be its operation; nevertheless, is it momentary or non-momentary? If it were non-momentary, there would be a difference in name only, [for it would be the same as saying] "the self is conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).

Even if things are momentary, there is no distinction [from our position] because of the absence of conceptual construction; for in that case, the cognition of the causal relation between one thing and another would not be possible due to the difference at every moment, since that which is the direct perception of the cause is not the same as that which is the direct perception of the effect.

Granted that for a single person there may be perception of both [cause and effect]; nevertheless, he for whom there is perception of the effect when there is perception of the cause is one person, while he for whom there is non-perception of the effect when there is non-perception of the cause is another. Thus, because there is an absolute difference between the perception and non-perception of even a single cognizer—just as there is between the perception and non-perception of different cognizers—how could the cognition of that [causal relation] arise from them? For instance, two perceptions and non-perceptions that are absolutely distinct from one another do not lead anyone to understand a causal relationship, just like the perceptions and non-perceptions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta; and you yourself accept that the perception and non-perception of the moments of cause and effect are absolutely distinct from one another.

Therefore, if a single cognizing subject is not admitted, neither the causal relationship nor the cognition thereof is possible; how then could there be the activity of those [cognitions] through a continuous stream of that [causal] state?
For conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) has as its function the act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
That non-pervasion— Ā., Ba., Ja.;
perception and non-perception—
Ka., Ā., Ba., Ja.
The nine [letters] beginning with *bha*— namely,
*ja*, *sa*, *gau*, *ta*, *ai*, *kā*, *ra*, *ṇa*, and *yoḥ pra*— are the [causes] according to the Buddhists (*saugatai*). *Bhāṣya*.
— [The term] *bhinnaika* [is explained as] "neither different nor one" (ā॰,
ba॰, ja॰); [it refers to] the preceding and succeeding moments through the continuity of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Furthermore, even if momentariness were established, their activity through a continuous series of cause and effect would be logical; however, that [momentariness] is not established, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove it. The absence of such a means will be demonstrated once non-momentariness is established.

Moreover, even by one who desires the momentariness of objects, the unity of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) must necessarily be admitted; for in its absence, the apprehension of momentariness—characterized by the distinction between preceding and succeeding moments—would be impossible.

For the perception of the preceding form belongs to one cognition, while the perception of the subsequent form belongs to another; therefore, the subsequent cognition, its capacity exhausted by the mere determination of its own object, is not capable of reflecting that "this is distinct from the form of the object grasped by the preceding cognition," because it is in every respect ignorant of any report concerning that [prior] object.

That which is in every respect unacquainted with the report of an object is not capable of reflecting upon the difference of its own object from that object; for example, the cognition of Caitra [is not capable] regarding the object of Maitra’s cognition. And since the subsequent cognition is in every respect unacquainted with the object of the preceding cognition, indeed, when Caitra has seen an object of one form and subsequently Maitra sees an object of another form, no such reflective awareness as "this is different" is observed.
Nor is that—[as stated in the Bhāṣya].
The proof of momentariness— [the word] *abhyupagama* (assumption)— is established by the [authorities] Ācārya, Ba, and Ja;
[the word] *pūrva* (prior) is established by Ācārya, Ba, and Ja.

—[The statement] "the knowledge of Devadatta is the knowledge of Caitra," etc., and that which was further stated—"the preceding and succeeding moments perish at every moment," and so forth—that too is not sound; for since the preceding and succeeding moments do not exist at the time of the present moment, this [present moment], being unconnected with them, cannot logically constitute a continuum (*santāna*). Indeed, in the world, a continuum is well-known to belong only to existing things that are mutually connected, like birds [flying in a line].

Now, if the present moment were a continuum (*santāna*) in dependence upon past and future moments, then what kind of dependence could there be on these two, which—being respectively destroyed and unarisen—are like sky-lotuses? Otherwise, the present moment would also share a single continuum with a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman. Regarding this very point, there are two formal arguments (*prayoga*): The present moment of cognition accepted by the Buddhists does not belong to the same continuum as another moment of cognition intended to be its produced or producer, because it exists, just like a moment of cognition that is not so intended.

Likewise, there is no single continuum for the past, future, and present moments of cognition belonging to those under dispute, because they possess the nature of both existence and non-existence, like the moment of a barren woman's son (pṛ. 6, l. 14), as in the case of the present moment.
By means of the preceding and succeeding moments— that is, by means of the past and future moments— [there is] cognition... [ā॰, ba॰, ja॰]

In this regard— [as found] in the *Syādvādaratnākara* on page 1087, in the editions of Ā, Ba, and Ja— these two formal arguments (*prayoga*) are as follows: the subsequent moment is the produced (*utpādya*), and the preceding moment is the producer (*utpādaka*).

Regarding the statement [in the *Bhāṣya*]: “‘[The moments] are not apprehended as distinct’”; that too is incorrect. For is their non-differentiation apprehended by another cognition, or by themselves? If it is by another cognition, is it one belonging to someone like us, or one belonging to a yogi? Of these, the first position is untenable, because for someone like us, a cognition having past moments and so forth as its object is impossible, since the Buddhists admit that such a cognition has only its own causal moment as its object.

The second position is also impossible, because the cognition of a yogi, being free from the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), cannot be the cause for the apprehension of non-differentiation.

Now, suppose it is from itself alone; that is not so, because since the past and future moments are non-existent, they cannot logically serve as the cause for a recognition of identity. Whatever is non-existent cannot be the cause of a recognition of identity, just as the son of a barren woman [cannot be]; and since the past and future moments of cognition are non-existent, the present moment of cognition also cannot be the cause of a recognition of identity with the past and future moments of cognition, because it is non-existent at those times.

Whatever is non-existent at a given time cannot have with it a cause for a single continuum (*ekasantāna*) based on the conceptualization of non-difference (*abhedaparāmarśa*), as in the case of Rāvaṇa and the universal monarch Śaṅkha. Since the present moment is non-existent at the time of past and future moments, then—given that moments perish at every instant—it would be impossible, according to the aforementioned manner, for there to be a causal relationship or a conceptualization of non-difference among those moments; how, then, could a continuum characterized as described be established? (p. 6, l. 14)

Comparison: From what [source] does the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the non-difference between preceding and succeeding moments arise—from another cognition or from itself? If it is from another cognition, is that [cognition] related to someone like us or related to a yogi? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
108). From the cognition of those [yogis], is there for us—(Ā., Ba., Ja.)—the cause of the reflective awareness? (Ā., Ba., Ja.)
—*marśāhe*— Ā., Ba., Ja.;
*yathā rāvaṇa-śaṅkha-cakravarttibhyāṃ saha* ityādi, Ratnā. pṛ. 1088;
*marśānu* Bhā.

Or let it be granted that [the continuum] exists; even so, would it be existent or non-existent? If it is existent, then is it impermanent or permanent? In the first case, since it would be no different from the members of the continuum (*santānin*), how could it serve as the basis for the regulation of the connection between action and its fruit, such that the faults of the "destruction of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*) and the "acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) would not arise? In the second case, however, there is no dispute over the name or the object, for this is merely the giving of another name to the self (*ātman*) itself by calling it a "continuum."

Now, [if you say] it is non-existent; how then could it be the cause for the establishment of that? Whatever is non-existent cannot be the cause for the establishment of anything, just like a donkey’s horn. And according to your view, the continuum (*santāna*) is non-existent;
therefore, is the continuum existent or non-existent? (Ā., Ba., Ja.)

Comparison: Now, if its substantial existence (*dravyasattva*) is determined, then [the terms] "self" (*ātman*) and "continuum" (*santāna*) are merely a difference in designation; there is no disagreement regarding the object. (Rājaputrīya-bhāṣya, p.
85) For the continuum is also non-substantial; otherwise, let the self be described in that same way. (83)
Tattvāloka, verse, page 23:
"vi" does not exist in Ā., Ba., Ja.; "asat" in Ā., Ba., Ja.

Regarding what was also stated—that the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is indeed inexpressible through conceptual alternatives such as difference or non-difference because it is not a real entity (*avastu*), and so forth—that too is incorrect; for it is impossible for a non-entity to serve as the basis for the establishment of a real entity.
To explain: the continuum cannot be the basis for the establishment of the relationship between action and its fruit, because it is a non-entity, just like a lotus in the sky.
Alternatively, if it is the cause for the establishment of that [continuum], there is a contradiction with its being a non-entity (*avastu*).

For whatever is the cause for the establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) is not a non-entity, just as perception and so forth are; and the continuum (*santāna*) postulated by you is the cause for the establishment of real entities such as karma.

Furthermore, if this [continuum] is a real entity, must it be different from the members of the continuum (*santānin*), or non-different? If it were non-different, then like those [members], it too would perish at every moment, because it is non-different from them, just like their own nature, or like the members of the continuum themselves. Moreover, for that very reason, the consequence of the continuum being differentiated [from moment to moment] follows, just as it does for those [members].

Would that which is distinct be eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, it would be nothing more than a mere difference in name [from the self]. Furthermore, if existence (*sattva*) and so forth were perishable, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) regarding the probandum. On the other hand, if it were non-eternal, then—just like a continuum (*saṃtāna*)—how could it serve as the basis for the specific determination of karma and so forth due to its being distinct? Or else, how could the established system of the five aggregates (*skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*), be maintained, given the consequence of a sixth aggregate consisting of the characteristic of a continuum?
(Page 7, Line 5)
Comparison—because it is impossible for a non-entity to be the cause for establishing an entity (syādvādamañjarī, p. 1089)—is not [the case], O Lord. Bhāṣya.
Or rather, the reason (*hetu*)— as found in the manuscripts of Ā, Ba,
and Ja— is postulated;

[this] objection based on conceptual distinctions such as the continuity (*santāna*) being different, non-different, permanent, or impermanent is seen in other texts as well (as noted in the manuscripts of Bhā and Ja).
For instance: if a distinct continuum (*santāna*) is not admitted, then because the members of the continuum (*santānin*) are impermanent, no agent whatsoever can be found. (37)

However, regarding the non-difference of the continuum, you have stated there by means of another verbal formulation that a non-entity cannot attain the status of being an agent of the continuum. (39)
If the continuum is momentary, then that very [continuum] would be non-momentary; thus there would be a loss of your own tenet, and furthermore, it would become a separate substance. (40)

Furthermore, the continuum would have to be both identical to and distinct from its constituent members, just as the distinction and non-distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject are entailed. (41)
From the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, page 697:
Furthermore, is the continuum (saṃtāna) non-different or different from the members of the continuum (saṃtānin)? It is twofold.
(Verse 633)

If there were no difference [between cause and effect], there would be no attachment to impermanence; if there were a difference, it would follow that they are distinct entities, and the relationship of cause and effect—which you desire—would not exist.

The position that [the cause and effect] are both different and non-different is also not tenable due to contradiction; it destroys one's own established doctrine, nor does it coherently account for the process of origination. (635)
Regarding the conceptualization of the continuity-bearers as being either different or non-different from their own continuum,
the faults that must be stated should be applied accordingly, in accordance with the meaning of "continuum" [as previously discussed].

If you maintain the position that it is "inexpressible," do not say so; for even that is impossible, since, upon imagining it to have the nature of being other, non-other, or both, it would simply be non-existent.
*Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-vārttika*, page 1489:
Now, if that [existence] is established by relying upon the continuum (*saṃtāna*),
it is not so, because the conceptual alternatives of its being either different or non-different are untenable.

In the case of non-difference, conventional usage cannot be established, just as it is not with a momentary entity; however, if there is difference, that [relationship] must be considered whether it is real or unreal.
If it is unreal, the previously mentioned causal efficiency is once again undermined.
If it were real, consider whether it would be stable or momentary:
if the continuum were indistinguishable from its constituent moments, then this aforementioned conventional usage of a "momentary destruction" of the continuum could not be established.

Moreover, if you maintain that there exists an entity called a "continuum" (*santāna*) which is eternal and ultimately real, then rise up, O monk! Your hope has borne fruit; this doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) is now complete.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 464)
Like a moment of a continuum— so long as it exists, it is a continuum;
because it is non-different from that.
— meditation on the non-existence of the connection between action and its fruit, etc., which belongs to the aggregate of form— Vaibhāṣika.
The five aggregates consist of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding this [self], its ineffability through those conceptual constructions is due to its non-existence, the incapacity of the speaker, or ignorance? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; for it has been demonstrated that if the continuum (*saṃtāna*) were non-existent, it could not serve as the basis for the systematic arrangement of karma and so forth.

Or, let us grant its non-existence; even so, since a non-existent form can be distinguished from an existent form, and since it is possible to speak of it by way of such a distinction, how could it be ineffable even while possessing that [non-existent] form? For an object whose nature is non-existent may be impossible to express as having an existent nature, but it is certainly not impossible to express it as having a non-existent nature.
