The second alternative is also untenable, because it would entail the acceptance of the existence of the Sugata’s inconceivable power.
The third alternative is likewise illogical, as it would result in the undesirable consequence that he is not omniscient.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) is a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*)—that is utterly incoherent; for since conventional reality is illusory in nature, it is impossible for it to accomplish seen or unseen purposes.

Furthermore, conventional reality (saṃvṛti) is said to be conceptual construction (kalpanā); and that [construction] does not operate in the absence of a primary [referent], because it would be equivalent to conceptual constructions such as difference, non-difference, and so forth— Ā., Ba., Ja.
Is it inexpressible because of impossibility, or because of non-existence, or because of lack of understanding? (Āptamīmāṃsā 50)
—*syāt*— Ā., Ba., Ja.; even though it has the form of non-existence, p.

Without the primary object, conventional reality would not exist; without the primary, there is no conventionality. (44) Āptamīmāṃsā.

Even that conventional reality is not false by nature, for a figurative designation is never observed to exist apart from a primary referent (pṛ॰ 41). If it is true, how can it be conventional? If it is false, how can there be truth?
Mī. Ślo. pṛ. 218.
For comparison: "Furthermore, *saṃvṛti* is called conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); and that is not possible when the primary [reality] is absent" (Syādvādaratnākara, p.

1090). It is called *saṃvṛti* because by it—through the obscuration of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the manifestation of what is obscured—the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) is concealed (*saṃvriyate*) or covered (*āvriyate*). Thus, it is *saṃvṛti*.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), delusion (*moha*), and perversion (*viparyāsa*) are synonyms; for it is stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā* (p.
352) that "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) is the superimposition of a property well-established in one place onto another.

Furthermore, no form endowed with a primary reality is established for you anywhere that could be postulated as existing through a continuous succession of cause and effect among preceding and succeeding moments;

therefore, even because a continuum of conventional forms would otherwise be impossible, the existence of a single cognizing subject is determined. And this has been cited in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 1090.

And because your recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) would otherwise be inexplicable; for such a synthesis as "I touch now that very same person whom I saw [before]" is not possible without a single unifying subject, since various cognitions arising at every moment lack mutual awareness of each other’s nature and are thus incapable of identifying one another.

That which is ignorant of the respective natures of two things is incapable of the mutual recognition (*pratyavamarśa*) of them, just as the cognitions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta are. And the cognitions of color, touch, and so forth, described in the manner stated above, are ignorant of each other’s natures. Now, if it is maintained that this single cognition consists of the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of both, how then can there be a doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), given that such a cognition would persist for multiple moments? Or how can there be a doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), since that very cognition would be established as the self (*ātman*), being the synthesizer of perception and memory? This is because a single agent who unifies perception and memory has been proven to exist.

Indeed, we do not maintain that the self (*ātman*) is an entity distinct from consciousness (*jñāna*), because we maintain that the self is the continuous consciousness (*caitanya*) that persists through the preceding and succeeding transformations of cognition (*cidvivarta*). For there is no such thing as a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who has never previously experienced anything. What, then, is it? It is the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) which appears in every living being with a sense of "I" (*ahamahamikā*) within the various cognitions that manifest specific objects, and which is the underlying thread (*anvita*) connecting them. If this were not admitted, the very possibility of unification of experience (*pratisandhāna*) would be destroyed.

For it is never observed that when a jar has been experienced by one person, another person can have the recognition "this is that very same jar. Otherwise, such recognition would occur even upon the first sight of it. Now, if it is argued that this recognition occurs only when there is a second sight, is that second sight [the experience] of a single persisting entity or of multiple entities? If it belongs to a single [entity], then our own position is established.

But on the view of manifold selves (*aneka-pakṣe*), because there is no single persisting subject, the unification of experience would be impossible—just as the perception of Yajñadatta does not follow the perception of Devadatta. For Yajñadatta does not unify an object experienced by Devadatta in this way: "I, Yajñadatta, am touching that very same thing which I [Devadatta] saw. However, he might think: "I am touching what was seen by him."

Or, in the view that the mind is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), even that [recollection] would not be possible; for since the preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness exist at different times, there is no mutual perception of objects between them. Indeed, it is only when two people, such as Devadatta and Yajñadatta, exist at the same time and perceive each other's objects that the synthesis—"I touch what was seen by him"—is observed. In all Indian philosophical systems, the permanence of the self (*ātman*) is established precisely through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*);
for instance, because a single object is grasped through both seeing and touching.

"I touch with my sense of touch that which I previously saw with my eye," and "I see with my eye that which I previously touched with my sense of touch"—these two cognitions, having a single object and a single agent, are recognized as being unified. (Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 218)
For it does not occur that "this is the same touch which I saw as having such-and-such a form," nor does it occur that "I see that same form which I touched.
Furthermore, the recognition by Yajñadatta of what was seen by Devadatta is not observed; for it does not happen that Yajñadatta, who saw someone, would think, "I saw him.
What is the reason? Because distinct cognitions have their objects restricted to themselves.

For those who maintain the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*), it is not logical that there can be a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of cognitions which have restricted objects and consist of mutually exclusive forms; therefore, he who is the synthesizer is the self (*ātman*)—this is the reasoning (Nyāyabindu, p.
64). On the contrary, memory and recognition are actually proofs for stability [of the self].
And thus, the teaching that [the world] is merely an illusion because of its rapid perishability, and so forth;
[as stated in] Nyāyamañjarī, p.
444, and [in] Brahma-sūtra 2.1.15, "And because of remembrance."
2.25 Furthermore, how could there be the cognition "How indeed did I see that before? and "I see this now," if there were not a single [subject] who perceives both the earlier and the later?
Moreover, for everyone in the world, it is well known that there is a single agent of both seeing and remembering, as evidenced by the perceptual recognition "I saw this, and now I see it."

If there were a different agent for the two [cognitions] beneficial to oneself, then one would perceive it as "I remember" and "another saw"; yet no one perceives it in that way. Thus, recognizing each successive cognition as belonging to oneself alone, and identifying from the final exhalation until birth all past cognitions as having the single self as their agent, how could the nihilist who asserts momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*) not feel shame? Thus, having cleared away these thorns, the author commences this treatise for the purpose of defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and other categories according to his own system.

Now, it is well known that only those treatises which possess a [logical] connection, a subject matter, a feasible method of practice, and a desirable purpose are respected by discerning persons, and not others.

Therefore, is this treatise being commenced possessed of a subject matter and its connection, or is it devoid of them? If it were devoid of them, the effort of commencing it would be fruitless, as it would be unworthy of respect by discerning persons, like the speech of a madman.

Let it be granted that such a thing exists; nevertheless, must its subject matter be purposeless or possess a purpose? If it were purposeless, then the effort undertaken to begin it would be as futile as an examination of a crow’s teeth, since no authoritative persons could possibly show interest in it.

If, on the other hand, it possesses a purpose, is that purpose one that is desired or one that is undesired? If it possessed an undesired purpose, it would be utterly disregarded, like instructions for marrying one’s mother.

Even if a work possesses a desired purpose, if that purpose is impossible to accomplish, how could anyone find it worthy of adoption? It would be like an instruction on using the crest-jewel of the serpent Takṣaka as an ornament to cure all fevers. To dispel such a doubt, he states the opening verse, which is capable of summarizing the entire unimpaired meaning of the scriptures:

If, however, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) were purposeless, then even the composition of words intended for its comprehension would not be undertaken; just as an investigation into the teeth of a crow is not to be undertaken by a discerning person due to the absence of any purpose. All discerning persons proceed only after seeking out the purpose of their activity. Therefore, the purpose is stated in order to dispel the doubt: "For what reason was this treatise composed by the Teacher, and for what reason is it being heard by the listeners? For if it were not stated, the audience might suspect that the subject matter of this treatise is purposeless, like an investigation into the teeth of a crow.

For the operation of treatises is threefold: enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and examination (*parīkṣā*).
Among these, *uddeśa* is the mention of objects by their names alone;
*lakṣaṇa* is the property that establishes the essential nature of what has been enumerated.

The determination of an object through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as to whether the definition of that which has been enunciated (*uddiṣṭa*) and defined (*lakṣita*) is applicable or not, is *parīkṣā* (examination).

Furthermore, *vibhāga* (classification) is included within *uddeśa* (enunciation) itself; for *uddeśa* is the mention [of an object] by its general name, whereas *vibhāga* is the mention [of it] by names according to its specific divisions.

In this regard, the divisions of the means of valid cognition other than perception, the divisions of scripture, and the "applications of the perspectives" (*nayānikṣepāḥ*)—endowed with the perfection of their definitions, enumerations, objects, and fruits—are the subjects of this treatise. By thus presenting the subject matter of the entire treatise through a brief enumeration, any suspicion that it might be devoid of a subject matter is dispelled. Furthermore, by virtue of that [subject matter], its relationship with this [treatise]—characterized as the relation between the signified and the signifier—is established; thus, any doubt regarding its lack of a relationship is eliminated.

However, the immediate purpose of what is feasible to perform is precisely the understanding of its definition; whereas, indirectly, it is the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

For the activity of the author of a treatise is for the sake of instructing others, and one who composes a treatise devoid of its subject matter and so forth does not instruct another, because such a work would result in the charge of deceiving others.
And that other person intended to be instructed is divided into three types: one who delights in brevity, one who delights in detail, and one who delights in the middle [length].
Furthermore, each of these three types of others is further divided into four: the proficient, the unproficient, the doubtful, and the mistaken.
Among these, the proficient and the mistaken are not to be instructed, because they lack the desire for proficiency (*vyutpitsā*).

Because it would follow that the other means of knowledge would also require establishment through yet another means of knowledge.

If that [universal void] were established without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then everything would be established for everyone; and since that would entail the establishment of the voidness of all things, how could this [voidness] itself possess the status of being expressible and so forth? This is an unconsidered statement; for even by one who accepts the voidness of all things, it is impossible to effect the absence of a means of valid cognition.

To explain: even for the proponent of universal voidness, there exists a means of valid cognition, because otherwise the proof of what is desired and the refutation of what is undesired would be untenable.

Nor does this lead to an infinite regress, because the establishment of what is desired and the negation of what is undesired are well-known to every living being; since there is no dispute among all proponents [of valid cognition] on this point, the dependence upon further means of knowledge is untenable.

Furthermore, the doctrine of universal emptiness will be refuted in detail at the occasion of establishing external objects. Enough of this digression—[otherwise] it would be otherwise, and not so. (Ā., Ba., Ja.)
If a means of valid cognition were established by another means of valid cognition, it would follow that there is an infinite regress of means of valid cognition. (Nyāya Sūtra 2.1.14)

If it is asked, "How then can knowledge dependent on the person (*puruṣa*) be designated as 'perception' (*pratyakṣa*)?", [the answer is: because the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists.

For while dependence on the sense organs (*akṣāśritatva*) is the etymological ground (*vyutpattinimitta*) of the word *pratyakṣa*—just as the act of going is the etymological ground of the word *go* (cow)—its ground for application is rather the quality of being a direct intuition of an object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*), which is characterized by dependence on the senses through their inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*). This is like the word *go*, whose ground for application is the genus "cowness" (*gotva*) as characterized by the act of going.

For the basis for the derivation (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) of a word is one thing, while its denoted meaning (*vācya*) is another. Otherwise, even a cow that is currently moving would not be called "cow" (*gauḥ*), because there is no other basis for its derivation; furthermore, an animal of a different species that is engaged in the act of moving would become the denotation of the word "cow" simply because the basis for its derivation exists [in it].

Or rather, the basis for its derivation is indeed present here as well; for instance, this word *akṣa* applies to the self (*ātman*) just as it does to a sense organ, based on the etymological derivation: "it pierces," "it pervades," or "it knows"—thus, the self is *akṣa*.

For that very knowledge which is restricted to one whose obscurations have been diminished or extinguished, the excellence of the term "perception" (pratyakṣa) is indeed easily established—as [the author] says: "That which is produced by the senses is capable of attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful. (Bhāṣya 1.1.4) Thus he states:
"It is capable of securing the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, being produced by the senses."
That cognition of an object which arises from a specific location is called sensory perception (indriyādhyakṣa) [Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p. 53].
That which is born of the senses and the mind is conventional perception (saṃvyavahārapratyakṣa).

95. Regarding the specific types [of perception]: among them, sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*) is conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*), because it is clear only in respect to a particular location.

The secondary [perception], which is the cause of worldly transaction, has for its object substances that do not encompass all their modes; it arises from the sense organs and the non-sense organ (the mind), and is called "clear" direct perception for those such as ourselves (*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 552). *Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 68.
That which is based on the sense organs and the non-sense organs, and pertains to a specific location, is conventional; this is the definition of perception (parīkṣāmu° 2.5).

Valid cognition (pramāṇa) in its conventional sense consists of avagraha (perception), īhā (speculation), avāya (judgment), and dhāraṇā (retention), which are caused by the sense organs and the mind. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.1)
That which is clear in respect to its domain is conventional;
*Nyāyadīpikā*, p. 9.

In this regard, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which is produced by the senses and determines a single aspect—is divided into two types according to its primary and conventional forms: in the Digambara tradition by Akalaṅkadeva (Jainatarkavārttika, p. 100), and in the Śvetāmbara tradition by Jinabhadragaṇikṣamāśramaṇa in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya*.
The term *sāṃvyavahārika* (conventional) is also seen mentioned in Buddhist texts; for example: "This is the definition of conventional valid cognition" (*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p.

784). Furthermore, the state of not being dependent on the sense organs (*akṣānāśritatva*) is the etymological ground (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) of the word, but not its ground of application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).

However, by this dependence on the sense-faculties (*akṣāśritatva*), the quality of being a direct perception of an object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*) inherent in the same substratum is indicated; and that alone is the basis for the application of the term [pratyakṣa].
Consequently, any cognition that is a direct perception of an object whatsoever is called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, if the basis for the application [of the term] were solely the dependence upon a sense organ (*akṣāśritatva*), then only sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) would be called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), and not mental cognition (*mānasa*) and the rest. Just as the word "cow" (*go*), although etymologically derived from the act of going (*gacchatīti gauḥ*), takes as its basis for application the "cowness" (*gotva*)—which is co-inherent in the same object and characterized by the act of going—so too the word "cow" remains established whether the cow is moving or not moving.
(Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p. 11)

The meaning is that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that cognition which, depending upon a sense faculty (*indriya*), arises as a direct realization of an object; and this is the etymological basis for the word "perception," not its basis for conventional usage—so it is stated in the *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 16. [This is] because of the presence of the factor of clarity and because of its establishment through common practice. (181)
In the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* (p.

182), it is stated that even sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) is conventionally established as perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of its mere clarity (*vaiśadyamātra*). Furthermore, in the *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa* (p. 48, u.), and so forth, it is understood that clarity alone is the basis for the application [of the term "perception"].
—characterized by being characterized as such—ba;
—produced from—ā, ba, ja;
—or of the word—bhā.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, the word *akṣa* denotes a part of a chariot, a legal proceeding, the *vibhītaka* tree, a die, a cart, a furrow, knowledge, the self (*ātman*), and the two Rāvaṇas.
This verse is recorded in the Jaṃ manuscript immediately after the word *indriyavat*:

"It pierces (*akṣṇoti*), pervades, and knows; thus, the *akṣa* is the Self (*ātman*). That which is directed toward that very [Self] when its [karmic] destruction or subsidence has been attained, or when its veils have been destroyed, is *pratyakṣa* (perceptual).
— *Sarvārthasiddhi*, p. 59.
*Tattvārtharāja* p. 38; *Pramāṇaparīkṣā* p. 68;
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-saṭīka* p. 54.

And thus Bhadrabāhu [states]: "The soul is the sense-organ; that which occurs in relation to it is direct perception (pratyakṣa), whereas that which occurs beyond the sense-organ is indirect (parokṣa).
— *Niryukti*, *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī*, p. 15.
The soul is the knower, characterized by the qualities of non-destruction and enjoyment;
that by which it exists is knowledge, which is threefold and direct (pratyakṣa).
In the Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya, it is stated that this perception is indeed of two kinds; what is its specific characteristic? To this he says: "cognition" (vijñāna).

"Vijñāna" (consciousness) is that in which, or that which, possesses a manifold manifestation (*bhāsana*) of knowledge pertaining to both self and other; by this, the extremist position that consciousness is the apprehender (*grāhaka*) of either only itself or only the other is refuted.
Alternatively, "viśiṣṭa" means that which is distinguished, i.e., free from sublation (*bādhavarjita*); this refers to the object of apprehension (*grāhya*).
By this as well, the extremist position that all knowledge of both its own form and the form of another is merely erroneous (*bhrānta*) is rejected.

Alternatively, it should be understood that "of which" or "in which" refers to objects whose forms consist of various substances (*dravya*), modes (*paryāya*), universals (*sāmānya*), and particulars (*viśeṣa*), [all] being the objects of that [cognition]. By this, the extremist position—that cognition is the grasper of either substance alone, mode alone, one of the two (universal or particular) alone, or both forms as mutually distinct—is refuted. Or, it may be explained as follows: that which has something to be depended upon, whether its own nature (*svarūpa*) or the nature of another (*pararūpa*), is described as such.
By this [statement] as well, the absolute position—that its validity (*prāmāṇya*) exists only where it produces that [cognition]—is rejected;
furthermore, the refutation of those various absolute positions will be set forth in detail later on, so enough of this digression.
The prefix *vi-* is understood here as denoting excellence, intensity, duality, and multiplicity.

Siddhivi° Ṭī° pṛ° 3a: Proponents of the theory that cognition apprehends itself— namely, the Vijñānavādins who maintain the non-duality of consciousness, the Advaitins who maintain the non-duality of the Self (puruṣa), and the Mādhyamikas who maintain that cognition is without an external object.

The Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain that knowledge is apprehended by another [cognition] and that knowledge is imperceptible; the Yaugas (Naiyāyikas), who maintain that knowledge is perceived by another cognition; the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain that knowledge is not self-cognizing; and the Cārvākas, who hold that consciousness arises from the elements—all these are proponents of the absolute view of delusion regarding the nature of others and themselves.
Or else, they are diverse:
the Vedāntins are proponents of substance alone,
while the Buddhists are proponents of modification alone.

The Naiyāyikas (Yaugas), who maintain that the two [means of knowledge] are distinct, now describe the second type of means of knowledge, the indirect (*parokṣa*), by means of the term "the rest" (*śeṣa*). [The reading] *syānyonyataramātrasya* in the manuscripts *ba* and *ja* refers to those who assert only one or the other.
Now, he defines the second category of valid cognition, the indirect (*parokṣa*), by the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
That knowledge which, compared to that clear-natured cognition, is of an indistinct nature is *parokṣa*. What is its specific characteristic? To this he says: "cognition" (*vijñāna*).
Its explanation here should be understood as being the same as previously [stated].

And thus, since only two types of specific definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established, it is shown that only two means of valid cognition are established, because all the various distinctions of those [means] are included within these very two; showing this, he says: "The summary is 'the means of valid cognition'"; that is, the summary of the entire subject matter of the treatise is that there are only two means of valid cognition—[as stated]: "Knowledge of an object beyond [the senses] is called 'indirect' (*parokṣa*) with respect to objects. (Ba., Ja., Jaṃ)
*Pravacanasāra*, p.

75: Depending upon external causes such as other sense organs, the mind, light, and instruction, that which arises in the self—which depends upon the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of its obscuring karma—is designated as indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*), namely *mati* and *śruta*.

"Parokṣa [knowledge] is that which arises from the predominance of another, whether it be appropriated or unappropriated," as stated in *Sarvārthasiddhi*, page 59; and "Parokṣa is indirect cognition," as stated in *Tattvārtharājavārttika*, page 38.

That which is turned away from the self (*ātman*) is "indirect" (*parokṣa*). It is called indirect because it is sprinkled (*ūkṣyate*), nourished, and increased by other means such as the sense faculties (*indriya*); thus, it is indirect.
(Tattvārthaśloka, p.
182) Indirect [knowledge] consists of indistinct cognition.
*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, page 69; the other [type of cognition] is indirect (*parokṣa*), according to the *Parīkṣāmukha* 3.1.2.
It is indirect and dependent upon assistants;
[this is stated] in the *Pañcādhyāyī*, verse 696.
Other objects of knowledge are grasped indirectly through the desire for apprehension;
[as stated in] Nyāyāvatāra, verse 4:
"Because the sense-faculties and the mind consist of matter (pudgala), they are external to the self."
That knowledge which is indirect (parokṣa) here [in this world] according to them is like inference (anumāna). (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya 90)
Indistinct, non-contradictory cognition is indirect (parokṣa);
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 595:
"The indistinct is indirect."
Pramāṇatattvāloka 3.1;
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 3.1.

*Parokṣa* is that which is beyond the senses (*akṣāṇām param*), or it exists beyond the senses (*akṣebhyaḥ parato vartate*), or it is perceived by means of something other than the senses, such as [inference] (*pareṇa indriyādinā vā īkṣyate*).
(Ṣaḍdarśanaṭīkā, p. 54)
The explanation of the term *vijñāna* has already been provided previously in the commentary (*ja*).

In this context, the general definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as "that which is knowledge" is supported by the passage beginning with "contact, etc. Contact is the connection between the sense faculty and its object; it is the first among the factors such as the totality of causal conditions (*kārakasākalya*) and the functioning of the sense faculty. Of what nature is [this contact]? It is non-cognitive and insentient; for validity is untenable in that which is not knowledge.

Of what is it like? It is like "something else" (*arthāntara*). An "object" (*artha*) refers to [the causal factors] such as contact (*saṃnikarṣa*); that which is other than this is the object of cognition (*prameya*), such as a jar or the like—this is "that other" (*tadantara*). It is "like that" (*tadvat*).

Now, one might argue: "It could be both a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-cognition (*ajñāna*), since there is no contradiction [between them]. Therefore, because its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is untenable; for validity (*pramāṇatva*) is pervaded by "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*), which is the opposite of non-cognition, and thus the contradiction [of non-cognition] is established therein.

For that by which an object is measured—that is, determined without mediation—by means of excellence characterized by the exclusion of doubt and the like, is *pramāṇa* (valid cognition). How, then, could this be consistent with having contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth as its nature, if they are of the form of non-cognition? Indeed, nothing at all is measured by contact and the like, because it would follow that the postulation of cognition is useless;

therefore, one must accept with the eye of reasoning that cognition alone is *pramāṇa*. [Note: The text contains a corrupted fragment at the end: "ndhaḥ ā– bhāṃ॰", which appears to be a scribal error or corruption.]
Establishment together with ignorance regarding the means of valid cognition—
Āryadeva.
—Regarding "form" (rūpa)—in the *Jaḍa-sannikarṣavāda*, this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika:

It may be your thought that the restriction "only cognition (*jñāna*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)" is untenable, because even non-cognitive things such as sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) are established as means of valid knowledge by virtue of being generators of valid knowledge (*pramā*). To illustrate: while explaining the Sūtra "The means of valid knowledge is that which generates valid knowledge," the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "The means of valid knowledge are the instruments for apprehension" (*Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 18).

In this regard, there is a difference of opinion among commentators: some maintain that sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the apprehension of an object; others, however, hold that it is the totality of causal factors (*kārakasākalya*). Of these, the first view is now established:
for in that case, sense-contact alone is the means of valid cognition because it is the most effective instrument for the apprehension of an object.

For being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) is pervaded by being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), but not by being either knowledge (*jñānatva*) or non-knowledge (*ajñānatva*). This is because [being the most effective instrument] exists in the case of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) regarding the apprehension of an object, just as it exists in the case of doubt and so forth, and like the object of cognition (*prameyārtha*).

Indeed, a cognition cannot arise with respect to an object that is not in contact, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such a cognition arising for everyone with respect to every object.
And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known its existence is precisely the non-perception of an object that is obstructed;

for if the sense organs, such as the eye, were to apprehend an object even when it is not in contact, then why would they not also apprehend what is obstructed? There is no distinction between the two cases. This aphorism is not found in the extant recensions of Gautama’s *Nyāyasūtra*.

Vātsyāyana [refutes] the teacher Uddyotakara, the author of the *Nyāyavārttika*, who states: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of apprehension; that which is the instrumental cause of apprehension is the means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that "the production of valid cognition occurs without an instrument (*akaraṇa*)," [Vātsyāyana replies]: No, because the contact between the sense organ and the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) functions as the instrument, or rather, because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). Thus, there is no logical inconsistency.
Nyāyavārttika, p. 5–6;
Jayantabhaṭṭa, the author of the Nyāyamañjarī, states:
"Thus, knowledge or even non-knowledge, when it is the cause of apprehension, is a means of valid cognition" (Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 22).
The state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*)—
[this applies] everywhere— due to the presence or absence of that [state].
There is no refutation [of the existence of atoms] because they are not perceived when separated by a wall; Nyāya Sūtra 4.2.15.
If the sense organs function without reaching their objects, there would be no non-perception of an object obstructed by a wall;
*Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 255.
Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the apprehension of sensory contact? We reply: it is the non-perception of that which is obstructed.
For if the sense organs, such as the eye, were to grasp an object even when not in contact with it, then an object situated behind an obstruction would also be perceived (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 73).

Furthermore, the sense organ is an instrument (*kāraka*), and an instrument that is not in contact with its object is incapable of producing a result. For instance, a sense organ does not produce a result regarding an object with which it is not in contact, because it is an instrument, like an axe or similar tools.

Moreover, the fact that the tactile and other senses function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*) is quite evident; therefore, based on this commonality, the same should be postulated for the other sense organs as well, since there is no distinction between them.

And this contact, whose nature is thus established, is of six kinds: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in that which is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the state of being a qualifier of the related (*sambaddhaviśeṣaṇabhāva*).

In that regard, there is conjunction of the eye with a substance; there is conjunction-with-inherence with the qualities, actions, and universals inherent in that [substance]; there is conjunction-with-inherence-with-inherence with the universals inherent in the qualities and actions; there is inherence of the ear with sound; there is inherence-with-inherence with the nature of sound (*śabdatva*); and there is the state of being a related qualifier (*sambaddha-viśeṣaṇatā*) with respect to the non-existence of a jar and so forth, and with respect to inherence.

Perception, as it arises, is produced through fourfold, threefold, or twofold contact. Among these, with respect to external objects such as color-form (*rūpa*), perception arises solely from fourfold contact: for the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), the mind with the sense organ (*indriya*), and the sense organ with the object (*artha*).
However, in the case of pleasure and so forth, perception arises from threefold contact alone, because there is no operation of the eyes or other sense organs therein.
In the case of the self, however, for yogis, it arises from the contact of only two—the self and the mind.
Since the sense-faculties function as agents by reaching their objects,
and an agent that is in contact with its object is fit to produce a result, it is a marvel to conceive of an agent that both requires contact and yet functions without reaching its object.
Furthermore, contact is divided into six kinds (Nyāyavārttika p.
31; Nyāyamañjarī p. 72 and 479). Nyāyamañjarī p. 73.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
195: "In that regard, [they are] equal by virtue of [their respective] universal properties such as *guṇatva* (quality-ness), *karmatva* (action-ness), and so forth. (Bhāṣya edition)

Since the space situated within the cavity of the ear constitutes the auditory organ (*śrotra*), and since sound, being a quality of space, inheres therein, there occurs—in the case of "the ground possesses the absence of a jar"—a relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the inherence and the absence, just as in the case where the eye is in contact with the ground and the absence is its qualifier; for [in that instance], the Nyāyavārttika (p. 31) states: "The ground is conjoined with the eye, and the absence is its qualifier."
By this, perceptibility is also demonstrated in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), because we observe the cognition "here" with respect to a cloth connected to its threads; see *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
84; *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 111.
By such statements as these, it is shown that in the Nyāya system inherence (*samavāya*) is perceptible;
however, in the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, on the contrary—as stated by Praśastapāda [in his *Bhāṣya*] (p. 329) and in the *Vaiśeṣika-upaskāra* (p. 296)—it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

By such statements as these, it is established that inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed beyond the reach of the senses, because for the perception of a relation, the perception of all its substrata is a necessary cause; and since inherence is a single entity, it is impossible to have knowledge of all its individual substrates—both past and future—at one time. (Muktāvalī-dīpikā, Rāmarudrī, p. 261)

Regarding substance, first: in the case of a large [substance] possessing multiple constituent substances, when there is the fourfold contact [of the sense organ with the object] along with the manifestation of color and the causal complex such as merit (*dharma*), there is the mere observation of its own form. In the case of sound, which inheres in the auditory organ, there is apprehension by that very [organ] through a threefold contact. In the case of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, there is apprehension through the conjunction of two—the self and the mind. (Praśastapādabhāṣya p.
187; Nyāyamañjarī p.
74) [The following is] the refutation of [this theory of] contact:
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that sense-contact alone is the primary instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion; for it is impossible for that [contact] to be the most effective means in the cognition of an object. Indeed, that in whose presence there is the existence of the cognition, and in whose absence there is its non-existence, is the most effective means in that regard.

Since it is stated that the most efficient instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) is the possession of that [causal capacity] with respect to both existence and non-existence, this [capacity] cannot reside in sense-object contact (*saṃnikarṣa*); for even when that contact exists, valid cognition (*pramiti*) does not arise in certain cases. Indeed, there is a conjunction of the eye with space (*ākāśa*) just as there is with a jar, yet this [conjunction] does not produce valid cognition regarding the former.

Nor is it logical for there to be a distinction in valid cognition despite the lack of distinction in the conjunction of the eye with space and the jar; otherwise, it would follow that valid cognition lacks such a cause.

That which is distinguished despite being non-distinct from another is not caused by that [other]. For example, although atoms are non-distinct, jars and cloths are distinguished; likewise, although sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is non-distinct, the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is distinguished.

Therefore, that which, having arisen, produces its fruit without mediation is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in that regard—just as a lamp is in the illumination of objects situated inside a room. And consciousness, having arisen, produces cognition regarding its own object without mediation; therefore, that [consciousness] alone is the most effective instrument in that case.
And for that reason, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is not, because of the opposite [case]. (Page 28, Line 13) —
*pra* — Ā., Ba., Ja.
For when something exists, there is the state of existence of the cognition, and when it does not exist, there is the state of non-existence [of the cognition] (Aṣṭasāhasrikā p.
276; Pramāṇapaddhati p. 1).
*Nyāyabindu*, p.
4, l. 8: What indeed is the meaning of "the most effective means" (*sādhakatama*)? *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 6: It is the possession of that [effect] in both its presence and absence.

— The consequence [is that] there would be a conjunction of the eye and other [senses] with the substance earth, just as it has [conjunction] with space and so forth; yet that [conjunction] is not the cause of the cognition thereof.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 168:

"For conjunction with space, even though it exists as in the case of a jar [with the eye], is not a producer of valid cognition. All of this has been discussed in this very sequence in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 4–5, and the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 54–61.
Because perception has the conjunction with the eye as its cause,
therefore that [is the case]. (Bhāṣya, Vārttika)

Furthermore, because it lacks the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*), is it mere contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) here that constitutes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it a specific instance of such contact? It cannot be mere contact, for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its validity even in cases such as doubt, since contact is no different there. If it is a specific instance, what is this so-called "specificity" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of it—is it the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*) from a specific cause, or is it the production of a specific valid cognition? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of its validity even with respect to space (*ākāśa*), just as with a jar and other objects, because the acquisition of its own nature from a specific cause is no different in both instances.

And since there is no distinction between them in this regard, why would this [contact] accept qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) or validity (*prāmāṇya*) only with respect to objects such as a jar, and not with respect to space? The second position is also untenable: because it is unestablished that contact possesses the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) toward the production of a qualified cognition, for it lacks such efficacy with respect to valid knowledge; and its lack thereof has just been demonstrated. Or, even if it were established, how could it possess that [efficacy] only with respect to jars and the like while excluding space and so forth, given that there is no distinction between the two cases? It would either produce valid knowledge in both instances equally, or it would not produce it in either at all. [Note: *vaiśiṣṭyam* appears in the variants Ā, Ba, Ja.]
The absence of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) for the production of valid cognition (*pramiti*) on the part of sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*).

Is it not the case that the capacity to produce a distinguished valid cognition exists only in space and the like, since it does not produce a valid cognition there due to the absence of fitness (*yogyatā*), whereas it does so in jars and the like because of the opposite?
Now, what is this so-called "fitness"? Is it a potency (*śakti*), or the removal of obstacles for the cognizer?

If it is a potency (*śakti*), is it beyond the senses (*atīndriyā*) or characterized by the proximity of auxiliary factors (*sahakārisannidhilakṣaṇā*)? Regarding these, the first position is untenable, as it would entail the consequence of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

As for the second position, however, there follows the attachment of all the defects inherent in the position that [the effect arises from] the totality of causal factors (*kārakasākalya*); for the proximity of auxiliary factors does not transcend the very nature of the totality of causal factors.

Furthermore, the auxiliary cause must be either a specific excellence residing in the object, the proficiency of the instrument, a specific merit (*dharma*), the destruction of demerit (*adharma*), or else a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*karman*).

If it is a specific excellence residing in the object, is it the inherence of color and so forth (*rūpādi-samavāya*), or is it visibility (*dṛśyatā*)? It cannot be the inherence of color and so forth, because this [inherence] is not a cause for the arising of valid cognition (*pramā*). Otherwise, how could there be the arising of valid cognition with respect to qualities, actions, and universals, which are devoid of that [color]? Or else, why would there not be the arising of that [cognition] in an atom, since the inherence of those [qualities] is possible there? [For the Vaiśeṣikas hold: "The perception of color occurs in what is large, due to its being composed of multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color" (VS 4.1.6).

Even if this were accepted, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that valid cognition (pramā) would arise from eye-impurities such as collyrium (añjana) and the like, since there is no distinction [between them and clear objects] in that regard.

If, on the other hand, you say it is "visibility" (dṛśyatā), that certainly exists in space (ākāśa) and so forth; otherwise, how could space be perceptible to the perception of God (īśvara)? Furthermore, is the proficiency of the sense organs (karaṇa-pāṭava) defined as being unimpaired by cataracts (kāca), jaundice (kāmalā), and the like, or as being assisted by light (āloka) and so forth? Both of these are indeed possible in the case of space and the rest.
Moreover, a specific property (dharma-viśeṣa) certainly exists as an auxiliary factor when the eye comes into contact with space and the like.

Indeed, there is no contradiction between that [non-existence] and that [the jar]; for if there were such a contradiction, there would be either the non-arising or the destruction of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) when that [jar] exists. Alternatively, if there were a contradiction, the perception of jars and the like would never occur, because upon the arising of that [jar], the specific property—which is its auxiliary cause—could not possibly exist due to the presence of the conjunction with space and so forth, which is contradictory to it.

However, the destruction of demerit (*adharma*) is simply the removal of an obstacle; and if that [destruction] is the cause of knowledge, everything is well-established, since it is precisely that which can be logically shown to be the regulator with respect to valid cognition (*pramā*).

Furthermore, would the substance that acts as a concomitant cause for sensory contact (saṃnikarṣa) have a nature that is eternal and all-pervading, or one that is the opposite? If it has a nature that is eternal and all-pervading, then that [substance] certainly exists even in the contact between the eye and space (nabhas); otherwise, how could direction (dik), time (kāla), space (ākāśa), and the self (ātman) possess the nature of eternal and all-pervading substances? If, on the other hand, it has a nature that is non-eternal and non-all-pervading, then would it be the mind (manas), the eye, or light (āloka)? Any of these three is indeed possible in the case of sensory contact with space and so forth, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Furthermore, would this quality (guṇa) that acts as its auxiliary be located in the object of cognition (prameya), in the cognizer (pramātṛ), or in both? If it were located in the object of cognition, why is space not perceived, given that there is no difference in the presence of qualities [in both]? If it lacks qualities, its status as a substance (dravyatva) is untenable, because a substance is defined by the possession of qualities. Moreover, since it is formless (arūpitva), if it were imperceptible, it would follow—contrary to what has been said—that universals (sāmānya) and so forth would also be imperceptible. If, on the other hand, the quality resides in the cognizer, then either the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) or some other quality certainly exists at the time of the contact between the sense organ and space.

Even in the case of [the action] belonging to both [the object and the sense organ], the faults attributed to both sides would follow as a consequence. Would that action which is the auxiliary cause belong to the object or to the sense organ? First, it cannot belong to the object, because it is not a factor in the production of valid cognition (*pramā*); otherwise, how could there be the perception of stable objects? However, that [action] certainly exists in the sense organ, since the action of opening the eyes and so forth exists during the contact between the sense organ and space.
Therefore, one must accept that fitness (*yogyatā*) consists precisely in the removal of obstacles for the cognizer, because only in that case are all the aforementioned faults impossible.
For whenever and for whomever there is a removal of an obstruction of such a kind, for that person, in that place, a determination of the object of such a kind arises.
Furthermore, the removal of the obstruction will be established on the occasion of the investigation into liberation (*mokṣa*).

Nor does this contradict the thesis that "knowledge is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) because capacity alone is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the determination of an object; for since this [capacity], whose nature is the power to grasp its own object, constitutes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by knowledge that manifests its own object, it is only in the production of that [knowledge] that its status as the most effective instrument is logically established.

[Objection: "But surely, because there is an absence of fitness (*yogyatā*) for the contact of the eye with the sky, it cannot be the cause of cognition. [Reply: This is not more sound either, because it follows that fitness itself is the most effective means of proof (*sādhakatama*).
What, then, is this so-called "fitness" of the contact? (Pramāṇaparīkṣā, p. 51)
Due to error,
there is the manifestation of an effect arising from its own nature as augmented by auxiliary causes.

41), and so forth; thus, in the Nyāya school's view, power is accepted as being of the nature of either the essential form (*svarūpa*) or the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*). Something of this kind—Ā. [Note].
The arising of perception [occurs] through the inherence of color and so forth therein; thus it is established.

In the Vaiśeṣika system, however: "Perception [of a substance] occurs because it is large and possesses multiple substances; perception of color occurs because of its inherence in multiple substances and because of the specific quality of color" (VS 4.1.6).

Furthermore, since it will be established that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with a jar or similar objects. Due to the absence of that [conjunction], there can be no inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) or other such relations with color and so forth.

Consequently, from *saṃyuktasamavāya*, cognition would arise not only regarding color but also regarding sound, taste, and so on—just as it does regarding the sun’s color—and even regarding the action of the sun, because there is no distinction [in the relation].

Furthermore, from *saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*, cognition would arise regarding the generic property of taste (*rasatva*) and so on, just as it does regarding the generic property of color (*rūpatva*). From *samavāya*, it would arise regarding the magnitude of space (*nabhomahattva*) and so on, just as it does regarding sound. And from *samavetasamavāya*, it would arise regarding the generic property of great dimension (*mahāparimāṇatva*) and so on, just as it does regarding the generic property of sound (*śabdatva*).
If fitness (*yogyatā*) is admitted, let that alone be the regulator; enough with the proclamation of the sixfold contact (*sannikarṣa*).

As for the relation of being a qualifier of what is connected (*sambaddha-viśeṣaṇībhāva*), it has already been refuted because relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like are impossible here;
for that [relation] does not apply to an object that is not connected by some other relation, just as the Sahya and Vindhya mountains [are unrelated].

49) — "by proclaiming a set of six," Ā., Ba., Ja.;

By this [explanation of] the state of being a related qualifier, the objection that "if there were apprehension of what is not in contact, cognition would arise regarding everything in respect to every object" is refuted; for only that which is capable [of being perceived] is apprehended.

Otherwise, why would cognition not arise even with respect to every object that is in contact? Therefore, that which does not arise even when something else is present is not caused by it—just as a wheat sprout does not arise even when a barley seed is present—and likewise, the determination of an object does not arise even when sense-object contact is present.

—It is said [by the opponent] that even though there is evidence for the existence of contact, namely the non-perception of objects obstructed by something else, that too is incorrect; because that [non-perception] is unestablished, since objects obstructed by glass, mica, crystal, clear water, and so forth, are nonetheless perceived.

As for the argument beginning with "because it is a causal factor" (*kārakatvāt*) which was stated as a proof for its reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*), that too will be refuted in the section establishing that the eye does not reach its object (*aprāpyakāritva*).

Therefore, the claim that perception arises from a fourfold, threefold, or twofold contact, and so forth, appears like a description of the good fortune of the son of a barren woman; for whether such contact is impossible or even possible, it is not the most effective means [of producing knowledge], since perception cannot be established on that basis (p.

Furthermore, if one accepts that proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is the basis for the validity of cognition, how could even the report of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) be possible? For his cognition—whether mental or sensory—would have to arise from four, three, or two types of proximity only with respect to present objects, not with respect to past or future ones; because since those [past and future objects] do not exist, it is contradictory for their cause, proximity, to exist there.

That which is non-existent cannot be the cause of cognition through proximity, just as in the case of a donkey’s horn and the like; and at the time of the arising of the cognition of a present object, past and future entities do not exist.

Furthermore, when those [objects] come into existence, knowledge of them will arise there through proximity to them. But how could there be omniscience for God even over such an infinite duration of time? Even if his omniscience is accepted on the grounds that he grasps all present objects, how could his teaching possess authority regarding future objects, such that those seeking such knowledge would act upon his teaching because of it? If it is argued that this fault does not apply because his knowledge is eternal, that too is incorrect, as the eternality of that knowledge will be refuted during the section refuting the existence of God.

If sense-contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that subtle, hidden, and distant objects could not be apprehended; consequently, there would be an absence of omniscience, because if sense-contact were the means of valid cognition, there would be no discernment of all things, and due to its absence [in those cases], [omniscience] would be impossible. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 57)

for the sake of the cognition thereof."

Furthermore, how could the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans be established for one who speaks thus, such that inference might occur? For, just as sensory perception functions only with respect to objects in close proximity, so too does mental perception function only with respect to proximate objects; yet pervasion is not restricted by place or time. How, then, could it be cognized through a perception produced by sensory contact? If it is argued: "But pervasion exists in a general sense, and since the capacity for perception produced by that [contact] is possible therein, why should its establishment not follow from that?"—this is also incorrect; for the notion of pervasion in a general sense will be refuted in the section analyzing pervasion.

Therefore, for one who maintains that contact [is the cause of knowledge], it is not possible for contact— which is itself not of the nature of cognition— to possess primary validity; nor is it possible for the totality of causal factors [to possess such validity] for one who asserts that contact [is the cause].—
*kṣasāmarthya*— Ba, Ja.

The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is synonymous with the "completeness of causal factors" (*kārakasākalya*), constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, who maintains that the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, this is his view: the causal totality that produces the apprehension of an object characterized by non-deviation and other such qualities is the means of valid cognition.

Nor should it be argued that because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consists of a collection of causal factors (*kāraka*), and because no excellence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpātiśaya*) exists therein, it is untenable for anything to possess the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). For if the totality of causal factors is accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the status of being the most effective means is logically established.

Indeed, the status of being an instrument in respect to any effect is not perceived in a single part of the complex, such as a lamp; rather, it belongs to the causal totality itself, which is the very nature of the complex. And that [totality] is realized only when there is the existence of both the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Therefore, since the effect does not arise even when the individual causal factors (*kāraka*) that constitute a portion of the totality are present, a single factor cannot possess the status of the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, because the effect necessarily arises when the totality (*sāmagrī*) is present, it is that totality alone which possesses the status of the instrument, as it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) by virtue of being the direct producer (*sannipatyajanaka*).
And the instrument is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the word *pramāṇa* is derived from the sense of "instrument.
Furthermore, apart from this completeness, it is impossible to conceive of the status of the most effective means in any other causal factor.

For if, even in the absence of totality (sākalya), a means of cognition (*pramiti*) were possible in some causal factor (*kāraka*) apart from that [totality], then that factor too would possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). However, such a possibility is not admitted there, because it contradicts experience. Therefore, totality alone is the instrument;

the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it produces the apprehension of an object that is non-erroneous and indubitable.

For its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness, while its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the state of being the means for the apprehension of an object characterized by non-erroneousness and so forth.

Nyāyamañjarī, p. 12: Since the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), and the word *pramāṇa* is derived in the sense of an instrument, for that very reason it is logical that the totality of causal factors (*sāmagrī*) constitutes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for apart from that [totality], it is impossible for any other causal factor (*kāraka*) to ever come into contact with the sense of the suffix *-tama*.

When an effect is being produced through the presence of multiple causal factors (*kāraka*), yet fails to be produced when even one of them is absent, to which [single factor] could it impart a specific excellence (*atiśaya*)? Furthermore, no such excellence can be attributed to any single factor in the production of the effect, because all of them are actively engaged in that process. Moreover, it is impossible to designate that excellence as belonging to any one individual factor within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*); however, it is easily expressed as belonging to the causal complex itself. If the causal complex is present, the fruit is necessarily accomplished; therefore, the causal complex alone possesses that excellence.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 13:

Now, an instrument (*karaṇa*) necessarily depends upon an agent (*kartṛ*) and an object (*karman*); yet, since the agent and the object, being included within the totality (*sāmagrī*), cannot exist apart from their own essential natures [as distinct entities], how can the totality be an instrument in dependence upon them? This is not a point that withstands scrutiny; for its status as an instrument is established precisely in relation to the factors of action (*kāraka*) contained within that very totality.

For totality (*sākalya*) is indeed a property (*dharma*) of the causal factors (*kāraka*); and a property of its own cannot prevail to destroy its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, since the essential nature of the causal factors is recognized even in the state of totality, there is no loss of their essential nature therein. Therefore, with respect to the causal factors included within it, totality—having acquired the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*)—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but knowledge itself is not, because it is the result (*phala*).

Furthermore, it is simply untenable for the result (*phala*) to possess the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for since it is distinct from that [cognition], and because the word *pramāṇa* is etymologically derived in the sense of an instrument—as in "that by which an object is cognized is a means of valid cognition"—it is only the instrument that can logically possess that nature.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that cognition itself is called the means of valid cognition even though it produces a distinct result, that is incorrect; for it would follow as an absurd consequence that words, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth, which are accepted by the whole world as being of the nature of non-cognition (*ajñāna*), would not be means of valid cognition.

Therefore, knowledge (*jñāna*) also attains the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) only when it has entered into the totality of causal factors (*sāmagrī*), just as the cognition of a qualifier does in the perception of the qualified object, just as the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) does in the apprehension of the marked (*liṅgin*), just as the observation of similarity does in analogy (*upamāna*), and just as the cognition of a word does in the cognition of its meaning.

Consequently, the position that the totality of causal factors, whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness, constitutes the means of valid cognition, is the one supported by logic.
As for the question, "In relation to what is the totality a 'instrument' (*karaṇa*)?", we reply: it is in relation to the individual causal factors contained within it.

The causal complex (sāmagrī) of the factors does not entail the loss of their own nature, because even in the state of totality, there is recognition of their own nature. Therefore, the causal complex, having acquired the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to the factors contained within it, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 14;
*tatra teṣām*—Bhāṣya edition).
Indeed, awakening (bodha) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), not the means of valid cognition itself;
[as stated in] Nyāyamañjarī, p. 15: "From the means of valid cognition..."
Regarding the result— the means of valid cognition—

there would follow the undesirable consequence of having to exclude words, logical marks, lamps, sense organs, and so forth, whose natures are known by the entire world to be other than [the nature of] consciousness.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 15:

"Because of the existence of its own nature—[as stated in manuscript *ba*]—therefore, cognition that has entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) attains the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in certain cases of perception, like the cognition of a qualifier; in the ascertainment of the possessor of a mark (*liṅgin*), like the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*); in comparison (*upamāna*), like the observation of similarity; and in the cognition of an object, like the hearing of a word."
Therefore, "the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), whose nature consists of both cognition and non-cognition, is the means of valid knowledge" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

15). This view of Jayanta, who maintains that the causal complex is the means of valid knowledge, exists in this very same manner in the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* (pp. 471–72) and in the *Syādvādaratnākara* (pp. 62–64).

In the *Ratnākara*, however, it is stated: "In that context, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of both conscious and unconscious elements, which brings about the cognition of an object that is free from doubt and sublation, is designated as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That which is invariably concomitant with the production of the result and does not deviate from its own nature is rightly considered the most effective means of accomplishment; it is that [cause], and nothing other than the totality [of conditions].

Because the presence or absence [of the result] depends on the totality [of conditions], the status of being primary or secondary belongs to the agent and the object; thus, there is no deviation from these two.

Because the collection [of causes] is not assisted by the destruction of that which is being collected, there is no perception of what is seen, even though it is designated as "seeing" by means of the totality [of conditions].

The designation of Locanā, Āloka, Liṅga, and so forth by means of the third case [ending] occurs because of the superimposition of their form, just as in the expression "he cooks with a ladle" (darvyā pacati).
And with respect to the factors of action (kārakas) such as the object contained within it,
that [consciousness] is the instrument (karaṇa); for this is a property of the factors of action, not their intrinsic nature.
Even upon entering into the totality [of causes], the essential nature of the agent and the object appears as if possessing a result; thus, the fourfold nature will not be destroyed.

Thus, these seven verses from the *Pallava* composed by Bhaṭṭa Jayanta have been extracted; however, they are not found in the printed edition of the *Nyāyamañjarī*. Furthermore, on page 15 of the *Nyāyamañjarī*, another mode of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is demonstrated: "The causal complex, which is distinct from agent and object, which produces the cognition of an object free from doubt and error, and whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
The refutation of the completeness of the causal complex (*kārakasākalya*) is now addressed here.

As for what was previously stated—that [the causal complex] is qualified by non-deviation and so forth—that is incorrect. For, would the validity of the causal complex be established primarily or figuratively? Indeed, the application of words is understood to be twofold, according to the distinction between primary and figurative usage, as in the expression, "Food is indeed life."

In this regard, it cannot first be considered primary; for since this [means of knowledge], being of the nature of non-cognition, lacks the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the cognition of itself or another, its primary status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable.

Indeed, being the most effective instrument in the cognition of that [object] is invariably concomitant (*vyāpta*) with cognition itself, which is the direct opposite of non-cognition, because in that case there is no intervention by anything else.

However, because it is intervened by cognition (*jñāna*), totality (*sākalya*) is not primary [as the most effective instrument]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is intervened by something else in a given case does not deserve to be designated as the "most effective instrument" (*sādhakatama*) in its primary sense there, just as a blacksmith is intervened by an axe in the act of cutting; and totality, as imagined by others, is intervened by cognition in the production of both self- and other-cognition.

If, however, its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is accepted through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), there is nothing undesirable; for since that [instrument] produces the knowledge which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the ascertainment of oneself and others in its primary form, it too possesses the quality of being the most effective means, and from that, its status as a means of valid cognition follows, due to the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause, as in the expression "food is indeed life. Would its nature be secondary (*gauṇa*) or primary (*mukhya*)? It cannot be secondary, according to the *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa* (p.
29) and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 66).
The denotative property (*abhidhānadharmma*) of this [word] is stated to be twofold: primary (*pradhāna*) and secondary (*bhākta*). (Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, p. 177)
The state of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) for the cognition of both self and other.
Whatever object of cognition (*prameya*) is there separated by another [term], [it is] not [the case] in the *Āgama* (as found in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
MS *ā*, *ba*, *ja*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the suffix *tama* is the excellence (*prakarpa*) of ignorance in its entirety; and excellence is dependent upon that which is inferior (*apakṛṣṭa*). Therefore, as long as there exists nothing else that is either a mere means (*sādhaka*) or a more effective means (*sādhakatara*), it is impossible to speak of "being the most effective means" (*sādhakatamatva*), because that status is dependent upon such a comparison.

Furthermore, a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) has the nature of multiple causal factors, and within the collection of these multiple factors, it is impossible to assert any excellence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpātiśaya*) in any one of them, because there is no difference in the activity of all of them toward the intended effect.

For an effect is perceived as arising when the agent (*kartṛ*), object (*karman*), and instrument (*karaṇa*) are present, and it is not produced in their absence; how, then, can a superiority belonging to any one of them be specified? Furthermore, if there is a desire to express [the cause] in its entirety, since there is nothing else to be depended upon, how can there be "instrumentality in the highest degree" (*sādhakatamatva*)? Indeed, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consists of the entire collection of causal factors (*kāraka*); with respect to what, then, could it possess "instrumentality in the highest degree"? Or, if something else were to be depended upon, it would no longer have that nature, because of the inclusion of other factors—[as stated by] Jayanta.

Is it not the case that, in relation to a mere instrument (*sādhaka*) and so forth, there exists that which is the "most effective instrument" (*sādhakatama*), since excellence (*atiśaya*) has such a nature and the superlative suffix *-tama* has that as its purpose? If so, what then would be this "instrument" and so forth in relation to which [the most effective instrument] would exist? (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p. 29, l. 1)
And furthermore— the characteristic of the determination of an object could not [be established].
—depending on [the context]—ba, ja;
—or its nature would be that of the most effective means (sādhakatama)—bhāṃ. Its nature as the most effective means.

Furthermore, by what is this status of being the "most effective instrument" (*sādhakatamatva*) intended? Is it because something produces the effect through immediate contact, or because it produces the effect instantaneously? If you argue that although an effect is produced by many causal factors (*kāraka*), the activity of these factors proceeds according to intention (*vivakṣā*), and thus the status of being the most effective instrument is attributed to one specific factor alone; [we reply: surely intention is a human desire, and it is not logical to establish the nature of a real entity based on that when there is no actual distinction [in the causal process], for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, as for the production of an effect through conjunction (*sannipāta*), that too is equal for all—the sense organs, the mind, and the objects—when cognition is to be produced, because there is no lack of being a producer through conjunction for any one of them, since this [cognition] arises only when there is mutual contact among them.
If [you argue that] they are distinct... [variant readings: *vailakṣye* (Ā), *vailakṣya* (Ba., Ja., Bhāṃ.)].

[Objection: "The *atiśaya* (excellence) is the state of being a producer through immediate conjunction (*sannipatya-janakatva*). [Reply: No; for even those factors that assist from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*) do not lose their status as causal factors (*kāraka*).

Furthermore, when cognition is produced, what is not a producer through immediate conjunction? Since cognition arises only when all [factors]—the sense organs, the mind, the object, and so forth—are in mutual contact.

Nor is being the producer of an effect all at once what constitutes being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), for that would also apply to action (*karman*); for instance, among a group of women, a woman of extraordinary beauty immediately produces a cognition directed toward herself. *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 13. Nor is being the producer of an effect all at once what constitutes being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), for that would also apply to action (*karman*); for instance, among a group of women, a woman of extraordinary beauty immediately produces a cognition directed toward herself.

The capacity to produce the effect simultaneously [with the agent] belongs to this action (*karman*). Alternatively, excellence (*atiśaya*) consists in the immediate generation of the effect; that too can be predicated of the action, just as it is of the instrument (*karaṇa*), in a certain state. Thus, even when the entire collection of other causal factors (*kāraka*) is present, the perception of the woman does not occur without her; yet as soon as she has arrived, it occurs. Therefore, that factor of action (*karmakāraka*) would also be an instrument (*karaṇa*) because of its possession of excellence.

As for what was also stated—"For a single part, such as a lamp and so forth, does not possess the status of an instrument," and so on—that too is untenable, because it is contradicted by common experience (*pratīti*).

Indeed, neither a worldly person nor an investigator accepts that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the instrument; for if they did, there would be the undesirable consequence of referring to it with the instrumental case-ending, as in "we see by means of the causal complex."

Furthermore, no one ever designates it in this way, saying, "We see by means of a lamp," or "We perceive with the eye," because such a designation is understood to apply only to parts of those [faculties].

Moreover, this designation "instrument" (karaṇa) is dependent upon an agent (kartṛ) and an object (karman), since a specific causal factor (kāraka-viśeṣa) being employed by an agent toward an effect is recognized as an instrument, just like an axe and so forth. (Page 33, Line 11)

Furthermore, the world does not accept that a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) functions as an instrument; for people do not employ the instrumental case-ending for it, such that common speakers do not say, "We see by means of a causal complex," but rather they declare, "We see by means of a lamp" or "We perceive with the eye" (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 13).
But how could this [agent] exist for worldly people? For they do not even know the name "assemblage" (sāmagrī), as stated in the *Ratnākara* (syādvādamañjarī, p. 6).

And if the assemblage is the instrument (*karaṇa*), would the agent and the object be included within it, or would they be distinct from it? In the first case, since they are non-different from the nature of the assemblage, their status as instruments alone is logical, just like the nature of the assemblage itself; moreover, even when they possess the form of instruments, it is not tenable for them to have the form of agent and object simultaneously, due to their mutual contradiction.

For agency (*kartṛtā*) is held to consist in being the substratum of knowledge, desire to act, and effort; the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in possessing properties such as being that which is produced; and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) consists in being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*). How, then, could these be possible in a single locus? Furthermore, in the absence of an object, all cognitions would result in being without a support (*nirālambana*), because the causal factor that serves as the objective support—such as the eye and so forth—is included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Who, then, would now cognize the object of cognition through the totality of causes (*sāmagrī*), since even the cognizer is subsumed within this very same [totality]?

The second position is also untenable; for apart from all the causal factors (*kāraka*), there is no such thing as an agent (*kartṛ*) or an object (*karman*) that exists as a separate entity. Or, if they did exist, there would be no totality of causal factors; for those things which are employed in the production of an effect are what is denoted by the word "totality. If the agent and the object were distinct [from the other factors], how could the remaining ones constitute a totality? [This is because] the agent and the object...

And these [factors], although they possess the forms of agent and object, cannot simultaneously function as instruments due to their mutual contradiction; for, as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 3, u.
