and the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* (p. 473), agency consists in being endowed with knowledge, desire to act, and effort.

Furthermore, at this point, all cognitions would be without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), because the causal factor that serves as the objective basis—such as the eye and so forth—is included within the category of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 202; cf.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 13)
And who cognizes the object of cognition by means of the causal totality? Even the cognizer is dissolved within that very totality (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
13). It is indeed within the causal totality [that he is absorbed].

As for the other argument stated—that its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established only in relation to the factors of action (*kāraka*) included within the totality (*sākalya*), and so forth—that too is incorrect. For this reason: the factors of action assume the state of being an object (*karman*) and so on when they are considered in their individual states, whereas they assume the state of being an instrument when they are considered in their collective state. Thus, when there is the state of being an object and so on, there is not the state of being an instrument; and when that [state of being an instrument] exists, there is not the state of being an object and so on. Consequently, not even a single form would be established, because of their mutual dependence: for the form of the object and so on depends upon the essential nature of the instrument, and that [instrument] depends upon the object and so on.

Furthermore, action (*karman*) and the other factors are engaged in producing the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and they are perceived as the causes of that complex; yet that complex is perceived as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the fruit characterized as valid cognition (*pramiti*). Consequently, since that [complex] is engaged toward the fruit as a single entity, how could it acquire a distinct excellence over the agent and the object already engaged in other respects? Moreover, when the self (*ātman*), being engaged in producing the causal complex, assumes the status of the instrument of that complex, then with respect to the fruit, whose agency would there be? [It cannot be the self’s], because the self is already occupied with the production of the complex. Nor does the self experience agency by first inserting itself into the midst of the causal complex while producing it, and subsequently employing that very complex as an instrument; for such a multiplicity of operations is contradictory for a single nature, and because it is impossible for an entity that is eternal and of a single form to perform an action.

Furthermore, how is this principle [to be understood]: that those very same [factors], when existing separately, assume the state of being objects (*karman*) and so forth, yet when combined, they become the instruments (*karaṇa*)? (Nyāyasaṃgraha, p.
14—as in the Bhāṣya).
— Likewise— :
the state of being an instrument is the essential nature of the instrument.

And thus, when the dharma characterized by totality (sākalya) is produced, the agent and other factors are perceived as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to that [dharma]; and that same [totality], in relation to the fruit characterized by valid cognition (*pramiti*), functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 68; manuscript *ba*, *ja*: "in that [totality]... [The term *sāmagrī* is supplied from the context.]
The definition of being an instrument (karaṇatva) [is] causality;
it is of a single form.

Furthermore, is that "totality" (*sāmagrī*) itself the totality, or is it a property (*dharma*) of the constituent members? Regarding the first position, since all members conform to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to the fruit, we do not know which one possesses the status of the instrument (*karaṇa*). For an instrument is defined as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*); and the sense of "most" (*tama*) is an operation directed toward the effect without any mediation. If that [operation] were equal for all members, then how could the status of being an instrument be established for only some of them? If, on the other hand, it is a property of those members, would it be permanent (*nitya*) or impermanent (*anitya*)? It cannot be permanent, because it occurs only occasionally, like pleasure and so forth.
Now, if it is impermanent, from what would it arise—from that very same [collection] or from something else? It cannot be from something else, because that is not admitted.

If it is from that very same [collection], then this meaning follows: first, the complete collection produces the effect characterized as the collection, and that is the fruit. In that case, since that [collection] is a single unity, with respect to what could there be the status of being the "most effective means" (*sādhakatamatva*) among the causal factors (*kāraka*)?
For is that dharma of theirs eternal or non-eternal? (Ratnākaraśānti, p.

68). And since the causal complex is a single unity and no other distinct establishing factor is perceived, what [additional] excellence (*atiśaya*) could we possibly attribute to it? (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 13).

Furthermore, what is this "concordance" (*sāmagrī*), which is the state of being concordant? By the word "state" (*bhāva*), would it be their existence, their mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), their collection (*samudāya*), their relation (*sambandha*), or their capacity to produce cognition (*jñānajanakatva*) that is denoted, since no other alternative is possible? Regarding these, in the first two alternatives there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for even in a dispersed state, their existence and their mere intrinsic nature continue to be present, which would entail the validity [of cognition] even then. As for the "collection," is it characterized by a single intention, or is its nature to meet in one place? The first position is untenable, because objects, sense organs, and so forth, lack intention.
The second position is also untenable; for it is impossible for the object, such as the moon or the sun, and the sense organ to meet in a single location.

By this very argument, the "contact" (sambandha) position is also refuted, because there is no contact between the eye and the moon and so forth, since the sense organs function without reaching their objects (*aprāpyakāritva*). We shall establish that they function without reaching their objects later on.

Now, if it is argued that the word "existence" (*bhāva*) denotes the capacity to produce cognition, then it would follow that the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) are also means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since there is no difference in their capacity to produce that [cognition]. In that case, the established distinction between them, which is proven by experience, would be destroyed.

Nor is it logical that, despite there being no difference in their capacity to produce [cognition], the status of the cognizer and so forth should be restricted to only certain instances by the power of one's own will; for this would entail the undesirable consequence that everyone could establish whatever reality they desire, since will is unrestrained in all cases.

Furthermore, in this context, "existence" (sattā) must be explained as either the mere essential nature (svarūpamātra), a collection (samudāya), a relation (sambandha), or the capacity to produce cognition (jñānajanakatva), as there are no other alternatives; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 69. (Note: *vyākriyeta* is the reading in the Ānandāśrama edition, while *dhyoyate* appears in the Bhāratīya Ātmānanda Sabhā edition.)
Regarding the establishment of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the knowable (*prameya*):

furthermore, do entities such as the Self (*ātman*), being of a nature that produces those [effects], produce them while remaining eternally of a single form, or are they of a nature that does not produce them? First, they cannot be of a nature that does not produce them, because that would entail the absurd consequence that everything could arise from everything.

Now, if they have the nature of producing that [cognition], why do they not produce it at all times? For those things which are eternal and possess the nature of producing that [cognition] must exist at all times. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that at the moment of the arising of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), all the cognitions produced by them would arise as well.

For it is well known that whenever something is a producer of something else, the latter arises at that time—just as the means of valid cognition intended for that particular moment [arises when its cause is present]. And at that time, the cause considered to be eternal, such as the Self (ātman) and so forth, exists for all the cognitions occurring in both prior and subsequent times.
Even if those [causes] exist, if these [effects] do not arise, they would never arise from them; thus, the entire world would become devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Even though a cause such as the self (*ātman*) is capable of producing them, how can it be established that these [cognitions] are their effects, given that they arise spontaneously at a later time? Whatever does not arise even when its cause is capable, but arises spontaneously at a later time according to its own schedule, cannot be the effect of that cause—just as a cloth is not the effect of a potter, since it does not arise even when the potter is present. And so, even when the self and other such causes are capable of producing them, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not arise [from them].

The claim that “because the Self and so forth possess the capacity to produce those [means of valid cognition] (pramāṇa) in whatever place, at whatever time, and in whatever manner they are about to arise, there is no simultaneous production of all means of valid cognition at once” is likewise an unexamined statement. This is because the differentiation of effects in terms of time and other factors is impossible without a corresponding differentiation in the capacities inherent in their own nature (*svabhāva*).

That which lacks a differentiation in its inherent capacities cannot produce effects differentiated by time and other factors—just like the partless moment postulated by the Buddhists. And such a differentiation in inherent capacities does not exist for the Self and so forth, which are asserted to have a single, eternal nature.

Furthermore, if one accepts a diversity of effects despite there being no difference in the capacity inherent in their nature, then the postulation of distinct causes such as earth-atoms and the like is redundant; let it rather be postulated that a single cause, such as the Supreme Brahman, which is eternal and of a single nature, produces the various effects such as earth and so forth. If it is argued that a diversity of effects is impossible without a diversity of types among the causes, then let there be a diversity of potencies as well, since that [diversity of effects] is impossible even without it. If those [causes] were eternal and possessed a nature of producing those [effects], then there would be the undesirable consequence of those effects being produced at all times. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 3, u.)
Sanmati-Ṭīkā, p. 473: "Having produced [it] on all sides" (samantād utpādya)—this is the reading in manuscript Ja; "the act of producing" (karaṇam) is the reading in manuscript Ā.
— [It is] destroyed;
and since, just as a difference in the effect is not possible without a difference in the genus of the cause, so too [it is not possible] without a difference in its capacity (śakti).
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 3;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, folio 473:
"Supreme Brahman" (parabrahma).

— In the case of the possibility of difference (bhedasaṃbhave), that is, when one accepts a difference in the genus of the causes (kāraṇajātibhedābhyupagame), even without a difference in the causal power (śakti)— that is, even without a difference in the power of the cause (kāraṇaśaktibhedamantareṇāpi).
Furthermore, because a difference in function is impossible:

is totality (*sākalya*) distinct from all its parts, or non-distinct? If it is distinct, why is it not perceived separately like a jar or other objects? Moreover, being distinct, is it connected to them or unconnected? If it is unconnected, how can it be their property? Whatever is not connected to something cannot be its property, just as the Vindhya mountain, being unconnected to the Sahya mountain, is not its property; and this totality is unconnected to the causal factors.

If [the whole] is connected [to its parts], is it by way of inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or the relation of qualification (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*)? It cannot be by way of inherence, because that is unestablished; its non-establishment is proven since it will be refuted in the "Examination of the Six Categories" (*Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*).
Nor can it be by way of conjunction, because conjunction, being a quality (*guṇa*), occurs only in substances (*dravya*), whereas a totality (*sākalya*) is not a substance.
Nor can it be by way of the relation of qualification, because the relation of qualification is impossible in an object that is not already connected by another relation.

Or let it be that something is connected to that very [object]; even so, is it connected simultaneously to all the causal factors (*kāraka*s), or sequentially? If simultaneously, is it one or many? If it is one, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth; and such a nature is not desirable because it is vitiated by the defects inherent in universals and the like. If, on the other hand, it is many, then it would be divided as many times as there are causal factors. If, however, it is sequential, then the property of being related to all the causal factors would not belong to it in its entirety; for at the very moment it is connected with one, it is not yet connected with another.

Now, if that [instrumentality] were non-different from those [factors], then those very factors would not constitute a totality; or else, there would be instrumentality alone for all the causal factors (*kāraka*s), or even that [instrumentality] would not exist, because it depends upon the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), and since these two are thus impossible [if non-different from the totality], whose validity (*pramāṇatā*) could there be? Therefore, since the totality of causal factors, when examined in its own nature, is untenable, it does not possess validity.

Whatever, when examined in its own nature, is not logically tenable is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like a sky-lotus; and the totality of causal factors (*kārakasākalya*) postulated by others is likewise not tenable when examined in its own nature.

Or, let it be tenable; even so, it is not a primary means of valid cognition, because being of the nature of ignorance, it cannot be established as a means of valid cognition except through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this rule regarding logical marks (*liṅga*), words, and so forth; for their status as means of valid cognition is also accepted only through metaphorical designation.
Nevertheless, is this [causal] totality distinct from or non-distinct from all its constituent parts? [Ratnākaraśānti, *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa*, p.
70: "If the totality were indeed distinct from the complete collection of its parts, why is it not perceived?"
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 14—*abhyeta* (ba, ja);
*kathaṃ sa-* (bhā).
Or, let it be connected to them by some relation; even so, is it connected to all of them simultaneously or successively? (Ratnākara, p. 71; *citta* is missing in *ba*, *ja*;
*tat-sākalyam* [the totality of that] refers to the *kārakas* in that very same place).

Even if there were a relation, if that [universal] were related simultaneously to all the causal factors (*kārakas*), it would incur the state of being a universal and so forth, which is corrupted by many defects; as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.

3, upper section): "It would incur the nature of one or another among plurality (*bahutva*), number (*saṃkhyā*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), or generality (*sāmānya*)."
In the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 473:

"When [a universal] exists both as a single nature and through a differentiation of natures, [faults such as] being a universal and infinite regress [would arise]; this is for the sake of [the opponent's] benefit. (bhā.)

But if there were no distinction [between the agent and other factors], then all causal factors would be nothing but instruments (*karaṇa*); consequently, the conventional usage of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) would be abolished (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
— lyam, karaṇa— Ja., Bhā.: [the state of being an instrument] and [the states of] agent and object.

Furthermore, with respect to indeterminate valid cognition (*nirvikalpakapramiti*), would the status of being a means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) belong to the sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) or the totality of causal factors (*kārakasākalya*) by virtue of their producing that cognition, or rather with respect to determinate valid cognition (*savikalpakapramiti*)? In this regard, the first position is untenable; for it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even sense-contact and the like—which produce indeterminate perception that serves as a cause for doubt and other such states—would possess the status of a means of knowledge.

Nor should it be asserted that these [contacts] lack the capacity to produce such [indeterminate perception] in those cases; for if that were so, it would follow that doubt and the like are not instances of fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

The second alternative is also untenable; for when determinate valid cognition (*savikalpaka-pramā*) arises, it is impossible for sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like to be the most efficient instrument (*sādhakatama*), because they are intervened by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). That which is intervened by another in the production of something cannot be the most efficient instrument for its production, just as a carpenter is not the most efficient instrument for the act of cutting when he is separated from the axe. And since sense-contact and the like are intervened by indeterminate cognition in the production of determinate valid cognition, it follows that sense-contact and the like—which are themselves of the nature of non-cognition—cannot in any way be established as having primary validity.
In cases such as doubt, the sense-contact and other factors possess the capacity to produce indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
In whose arising—
[in the arising of which]—
there is no intrinsic nature.
Refutation of the Sāṅkhya position that the functioning of the sense organs (*indriyavṛtti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

Now, although it is true that neither contact (*sannikarṣa*) nor the totality of causal factors (*kārakasākalya*), being of the nature of non-cognition, can logically possess the status of a means of valid cognition; nevertheless, it does not follow that cognition alone is established as the means of valid cognition. For the functioning of the sense organs is established as the means of valid cognition by virtue of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the apprehension of an object, since the "functioning" (*vṛtti*) of the sense organs is their transformation into the form of the object.
Indeed, for them, a specific perception of sound and other objects is not possible apart from a transformation into the specific forms of those sounds and so forth.

Therefore, first, due to contact with the object, the sense organs undergo an assumption of that [object's] form; this is the activity (*vṛtti*) of the sense organ. Subsequently, the mental activity (*manovṛtti*) has as its objective support the activity of the sense organ which has been transformed into the form of the object.

If it is asked: "Why does the mental activity have the activity of the sense organ as its objective support, and not sound and the like?"—the answer is: because [the mind] does not function externally. Otherwise, the postulation of external sense organs would be purposeless.
By this very [argument], the Sāṃkhya who asserts thus is also refuted:
"In regard to form and the other [objects], the function of the five [senses] is held to be mere observation" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 28).

Intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the eye—these four perceive a form simultaneously, [distinguishing] "this is a post" or "this is a person. Thus is the simultaneous functioning of this quartet. And [there is] sequential [functioning]: the functioning of intellect, ego-sense, mind, and the eye is observed to be sequential—the eye perceives the form, the mind conceptualizes it, the ego-sense identifies with it, and the intellect determines it. (Māṭhara-vṛtti, p. 47)

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the modification (*vṛtti*) of the mind, primarily characterized by the determination of the specific qualities of an object—which consists of both general and particular aspects—due to the coloring of the mind by external things through the channel of the senses. (Yoga-bhāṣya on YS 1.7, p.

27). Consciousness itself, reflected in the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*), attains the form of that object by means of the mental modification which takes the form of the object; this [consciousness] is the result.
In this regard, the process is as follows:

through the channel of the sense organs, by means of contact with an object, or by means of the cognition of a logical mark (liṅga) and so forth, a modification (vṛtti) in the form of the object first arises in the intellect (buddhi). (*Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya*, p. 47). *Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya*, *Tattvavaiśāradī*, p. 29. Herein is the method: through the conduit of the senses, by the contact with an object, or by the knowledge of a sign (liṅga) and so forth, first a modification in the form of the object arises in the intellect (*Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya*, p.
Through the connection of the mind with objects by means of the channel of the sense organs, there arises present perceptual knowledge which determines a specific [object]. (23)

The agent of yoga is the pure conscious knower; the means of knowledge is indeed the mental modification (vṛtti), and valid cognition is the reflection of the modifications that take the form of objects upon consciousness.
The *Yogavārttika*, p.

30, states: "Intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed a transformation of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), and the three qualities are insentient (*acetana*); thus, being purely insentient, it transforms into the form of an object through the channel of the senses. That transformation of the intellect which takes the form of 'blue' is called a modification (*vṛtti*) characterized by cognition (*jñāna*). The *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 233, says the same.

If perception is the functioning of the auditory and other senses, then what of the case of those suffering from ophthalmia and similar conditions? Is it not the case that [the cognition] does not function [as a true sense-perception], yet conforms to the defects of those [senses]?
(Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 393)
The statement that "perception is the functioning of the auditory and other senses" has also been examined by this [same analysis];
and when that [functioning] is investigated, its contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established.
36 Tattvārthaślokavārttika, page 187;
Tattvopaplava, page [number].

Since even the activity of the sense organs (*indriyavṛtti*), which is insentient by nature, cannot be established as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the cognition of an object through metaphorical attribution, what then is this "activity of the sense organs"? Would it be their movement toward the object, or their orientation toward it, or their assuming of its form? Among these, the first position is untenable; for the movement of the sense organs toward an object will be refuted in the section concerning the fact that the senses do not function by reaching their objects (*aprāpyakāritva*).

The second position is also untenable, because the orientation toward the object—which is synonymous with "praguna" (favorability)—is the cause of cognition as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the determination of an object; thus, its status as the most effective instrument is established only figuratively.
Furthermore, it is logically impossible for the sense organ to assume the form of the object, because that would contradict experience.

Indeed, the auditory and other sense organs are not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as assuming the form of the object like a mirror or similar things; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of no disagreement whatsoever regarding that matter.

For no one who is not a fool contradicts an object apprehended through direct perception, nor does one do so on the basis of inference; this is because a logical mark (liṅga) invariably concomitant with that [object] is impossible.
Nor should it be asserted that the very apprehension of a specific object is itself the logical mark; for such apprehension is possible even without similarity (sārūpya).
Likewise, its arising will be established on the occasion of proving that consciousness is formless:

"The activity [of the sense organ]—for the auditory or other sense organs are not perceived through direct perception as assuming the form [of the object], like a crystal or a mirror"—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 72.
Without assuming the form of the object, as in the case of a mirror and so forth, [the sense organs] such as the ear and so on [do not perceive].

Let it be that there is the cognition of specific objects even without similarity (*sārūpya*), or let there be some function (*vṛtti*) belonging to them; nevertheless, would this [function] be distinct from them or non-distinct? If it were non-distinct, it would be nothing more than the auditory organ and so forth themselves, and since these exist even during deep sleep and the like, there would follow the consequence of no distinction between one who is asleep and one who is awake, and thus the absence of their respective conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Now, [if it is argued that] it is distinct [from the sense organ]; is it connected to it there, or unconnected? If it were unconnected, how could it be designated as "this is the function (vṛtti) of the ear and so forth"? For whatever is unconnected to something is not designated as belonging to it, just as the Vindhya mountain is not [designated as belonging] to the Sahya mountain; and yet, this function is unconnected with the ear and so forth. If, on the other hand, it is connected; is it by way of inherence (samavāya), conjunction (saṃyoga), or the relation of qualification (viśeṣaṇabhāva)? It cannot be by way of inherence, because its nature is unestablished, and its unestablished nature is well-known since it will be refuted later.

Alternatively, if its essential nature is established as being eternal and all-pervading, and likewise the ear and other sense organs are of such a nature, then it is difficult to maintain that their occurrence in specific locations is merely a manifestation.

Nor can it be through conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for that occurrence would entail the consequence of being a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), since conjunction is not logical between a substance and a non-substance. This is because, as a quality (*guṇa*), it must reside in a substance;
and thus, the admission that occurrence is a property of the sense organ would be contradicted.

Nor can it be through the relation of qualification (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*); for that [relation] is impossible in the case of an object not connected by some other relation, just as in the case of the Sahya and Vindhya mountains. Therefore, since the existence of the sensory function (*indriyavṛtti*) cannot be established when subjected to analysis, how could the mental function (*manovṛtti*)—which has as its objective support a sensory function transformed into the form of the object—be easily established? Since it is untenable for the sensory function to be transformed into the form of the object, it is likewise untenable for the mental function to have that [sensory function] as its objective support;
therefore, it is logical that this [mental function] has only the external object as its objective support.

Nor does it follow that the postulation of external sense organs is purposeless; for we observe that the mind functions toward objects only in dependence upon them, as they serve as mutual auxiliaries in the production of cognition.

Indeed, the activity of the mind in producing cognition is not independent of the external sense organs, because otherwise it would follow that such cognition could arise even regarding an object never before perceived.
Likewise, the external sense organs do not function independently of the mind, because otherwise it would follow that cognition could arise even for one whose mind is directed elsewhere.

Furthermore, it is not tenable for the function (*vṛtti*) to be either distinct or non-distinct from the sense organs (*indriya*), as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 6, upper section) and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p.
73): "The function of the sense organ, such as the ear... (*śrotrāder indriyasya vṛttiḥ*).
This [is] the *si*-form; that too is the *si*-form.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 6, first part.

Since, upon investigation, the occurrence of the sense organ— whether as a conjunction or as a qualifying relation— is thus impossible, how could it be feasible for the mental function to have as its object a modification of the sense-organ that has transformed into the form of the object?
In the *Ratnāvalī*, page 73, it says:
"The mental activity [occurs] only for one who is dependent upon the external sense faculties."
Of the sense-faculties and the mind with respect to external objects—
mutually and together.
The mind and consciousness function toward the arising of consciousness; this is the positive concomitance.
Granted that the external sense organs lack validity because the functions of the senses— along with their causal conditions such as contact— are tainted by the aforementioned defects; nevertheless,
the cognition of the knower is indeed of the nature of an action (*kriyā*), and an action is inferred from its fruit (*phala*), since the fruit cannot be produced without the operation of the knower.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 17.
In the discussion regarding the validity of the operation of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra-prāmāṇya-vāda*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Prābhākara is as follows:
"But [the operation] will belong to the subject (*pārasya*); for without it, the result called the manifestation of the object (*arthaprakāśatā*) would not be accomplished."
For indeed, there is no production of an effect without an operation (*vyāpāra*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the status of a factor as a causal agent (*kāraka*) is established only through its engagement with an action (*kriyāveśa*), according to the etymological derivation that "a causal agent is that which acts" (*karoti iti kārakam*). Otherwise, it would be a mere thing (*vastumātra*) and not a causal agent, since it is stated that "a substance (*dravya*) engaged in an action is a causal agent.
Moreover, a mere thing is not employed by those seeking a result, for they employ only that which accomplishes their intended purpose.

Just as the causal factors—such as rice, water, fire, and a cooking pot—which possess an established nature, combine to accomplish the verbal root-meaning of "cooking" (pāka), which is characterized by an unestablished nature, and having combined, produce the action; so too, when there is contact between the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object, the activity of the knower arises as the cause for the manifestation of the object. Therefore, this [activity] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in producing the result characterized by the manifestation of the object. That which is not a means of valid cognition is not the most effective instrument in that regard, such as mere proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth; and the activity of the knower is indeed the most effective instrument in producing that result characterized by manifestation.

Furthermore, a factor becomes a causal agent (*kāraka*) by virtue of being permeated by activity (*kriyāveśa*); otherwise, it would be merely the essential nature of the thing itself and not a causal agent.
Consequently, it would not be employed by those seeking a result, which would lead to the collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 17)
Neither the substance alone nor the action alone is the *kāraka*;
rather, the *kāraka* is that which accomplishes the action and is conjoined with a specific action.
(*Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 106)
— “That which is distinguished,” [as stated] in the commentary on the verse, “For these four are indeed the methods of meaning (arthanaya),” refers to the mere thing-in-itself (vastumātra).

Therefore, just as causal factors such as rice, water, fire, and a pot—which possess established natures—combine by taking up a single effect to be accomplished, namely the action characterized as cooking, and having combined, they produce that action; so too, when there is contact between the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object, the operation called "cognition" arises (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 17).
Therefore, the very arising of cognition with respect to an object is held to be its operation;
that itself is the form of valid knowledge, and the intellect possessing that [form] is the instrument.

Its very birth is its activity; and because that [birth] has the specific result of manifesting the object, it is a valid cognition (*pramā*). Through its connection with that [activity], the intellect (*dhī*) is called both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and, by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well.
(Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 151)

Alternatively, the mutual relationship between the self, acting as the agent, and the object, acting as the patient—a relationship characterized by the pervader-pervaded (vyāptṛ-vyāpyatva) nature mediated through cognition and action—is apprehended by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and leads to the postulation of consciousness (*vijñāna*). [Śābarabhāṣya, p. 202; Bhāṣya, tatra...]
Refutation of the validity of the cognitive operation, which is insentient by nature—here it is replied:

as for what was stated, that "the validity of the cognitive operation will [be established]," and so forth; that is incorrect. For would its validity be sought when its existence is already well-established, or when its existence is not yet established? It cannot be the latter, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and entail a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*).

For instance—that which has unestablished existence is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as a sky-lotus; and the activity of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) intended by the followers of the Prabhākara school likewise has unestablished existence.

Now, if its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is sought on the grounds that its existence is already established, one must ask: from where is its existence established—from a mere description of its own internal process, or from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? In the first case, since even the contact between sense-organ and object (*sannikarṣa*) would have its existence thus established, it would follow that such contact is itself a valid cognition; how then could the establishment of your position remain unopposed? If it is from a means of valid cognition, would its establishment be through perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or another? If it were through perception, would that perception arise from the contact of the sense-organ with the object, from the contact of the self with the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-sannikarṣa*), or from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because it is accepted that the sense-organs, such as the eye, produce cognition only regarding an object with which they are connected and which is capable of being perceived.

Furthermore, a connection between them and the activity of the knower is not possible; for a connection with these [objects] is possible only through their respective, determined forms such as color and so forth, and because that [activity], being absolutely imperceptible, is incapable of being apprehended.

Or, let us grant that there is a relationship between it [the object] and those [senses], and that it possesses the fitness for apprehension; nevertheless, when this [object] produces a cognition of its own object with the aid of the eye and other [senses], does it produce it assisted by the operation of another cognizer, or unassisted? In the first case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that operation too would entail the production of a cognition of its own object while being dependent on the operation of yet another [cognizer].

As for the second case, it is untenable; for it is impossible for this [object], which is the passive factor (*karman*) and is not assisted by the operation of another, to generate a cognition of its own object.

For instance: the operation of a knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) produces the cognition of its own object only when assisted by another operation of a knower, because it is an action that produces the cognition of its own object, like a jar or similar things.

If such [an operation] were to produce that [cognition] even without being assisted by it, then it would follow that a jar or the like would also produce the cognition of its own object independently of it; thus, enough with the postulation of an "operation of the knower.
By this, the second position is also refuted, since the faults already demonstrated apply there as well without distinction.

Furthermore, perception arising from the contact between the self and the mind is not capable of operating upon an object that is unfit for apprehension, since its operation is observed only in respect to such [objects] as pleasure and the like. Moreover, the self and the mind—which you postulate to be eternal, partless by nature, and respectively all-pervading and atomic—are not established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
We shall demonstrate this lack of establishment in detail during the examination of the substances "self" and "mind" in the investigation of the six categories.

Nor is its establishment through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), because that is not admitted, and because self-awareness is contradictory with respect to that which is absolutely beyond perception; thus, the activity of the knower is not established through direct perception,
but merely from the description of one's own system.

Is that [cognition] indeed perception, inference, or something else? If it is perception, is it self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), produced by an external sense organ, or born of the mind? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 6; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 20). What [is it] from perception? (Bhāṣya).
—Because of the conjunction [of the sense organs with their objects], there is the perception by the sense organs. (Variant reading: ...the apprehension by direct perception...)
If the operation of the knower were itself an operation of the knower,

then action— which is accomplished by the factors of action (kārakas)— would, being an effect, itself have to be produced by factors of action possessing operations; this would result in an infinite regress.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 18:
[This refers to] the operation of the knower, which is distinct from the operation of another knower.
As an object, it is that which produces a cognition of its own sphere, being independent of the activity of the knower and not assisted by the activity of the knower.

Nor [is it established] through inference, because its nature is defined as "the cognition of an object not present to the senses arising from the perception of one part [of a known relation]" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5,
p.

Furthermore, would the apprehension of the relation [between the object and the cognition] arise from perception or from inference? It cannot be from perception; for if the activity of the knower is admitted to be entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), it is impossible to apprehend through perception that the cause—characterized by the manifestation of the object—is related to it. Indeed, the cognition of a relation, such as "this is related to that," is only logical when both natures are grasped, as in the case of fire and smoke.

Nor can it be established through inference, because that would lead to an infinite regress—for that inference, too, arises from a reason whose invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is ascertained, and the ascertainment of that concomitance must come from another inference; thus, if that [concomitance] were ascertained by the first inference, there would be a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*).

By this, the establishment of the operation of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also refuted; for even the object that gives rise to such a presumption can only function as a means of knowledge once its connection with the probandum is established, and not otherwise, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and if that [connection] were established, the aforementioned defects would necessarily follow.

Furthermore, is this activity of the knower produced by causal factors (*kāraka*), or is it not so produced? It cannot be the latter; for instance: the activity of the knower is not unproduced by causal factors, because it is an activity, like the activity of a cook and others.

Moreover, if it were not produced by them, would it be of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*) or of the nature of a negation (*abhāva*)? If it were of the nature of a negation, there would be a contradiction with its producing a result characterized by the illumination of an object;

or, if there were no such contradiction, the search for causal factors by one desiring a result would be fruitless, and the entire world would be destitute, since the desired results of all living beings would be accomplished simply due to the absence of causes.

Now, suppose it is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*). In that case, is it eternal (*nitya*) or non-eternal (*anitya*)? If it were eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everyone would simultaneously apprehend all objects, which would render the search for causal factors such as lamps and the like useless, and it would entail the total cessation of the practical activities of the blind, the sleeping, and so forth.
If, on the other hand, it is non-eternal, that is incorrect; for it is a contradiction for an object whose nature is a positive entity and which is unproduced (*ajanya*) to be non-eternal.
Whatever is a positive entity that is an unproduced object is not non-eternal, just like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth; and this activity of the knower (*jñātṛ-vyāpāra*) is of such a nature.

Or let it be impermanent; even so, does it endure for a period of time or is it momentary? In the first case, the statement that "it is indeed momentary and does not persist for another time" is contradicted.
In the second case, however, since there would be no manifestation of the object after a single moment, the world would become blind and mute.

If one assumes a succession of different activities at every moment, the same defect remains: the impossibility of sleep and so forth, because that which is not produced by causal factors cannot have a fixed determination of place, time, or intrinsic nature.

"Inference is the cognition of an object not present to the senses (*asannikṛṣṭe'rthe*) based on the perception of one part [of a known relation] by one who knows the relation" (Śābarabhāṣya, p. 36). Now, is that relation apprehended through the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or through the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? Regarding the first alternative, is its determination by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or by means of inference (*anumāna*)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 6; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 28).

Furthermore, regarding that activity of the knower which gives rise to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), is it produced by causal factors (*kāraka*) or unproduced? (See *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 7, upper section; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 25). [Variant readings:
*jñāturvyā-* in *ba* and *ja* manuscripts.]

If that which is non-produced is either of the nature of an absence or of the nature of a presence—[as stated in] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 7, l. 1, and *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* p. 25—if it were eternal, then because the substance would always be joined with activity, there would be the undesirable consequence of the constant production of results.

In the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 18), the *Śābarabhāṣya* (p. 32), the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 7, l. 1), the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* (p. 25), and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 122), the reading is "it does not persist for a long time" (*na cirakālam avatiṣṭhate*), whereas in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 7, l. 1) it says: "For that [cognition] is momentary; it will not remain until the time of another cognition."

Now, suppose this [self] is produced by causal factors (kārakas); let that be so. Nevertheless, would it be of the nature of action (kriyā) or of the nature of non-action? If it were of the nature of action, then would that action have the nature of motion (parispanda) or the nature of non-motion? In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable; for since the self is all-pervasive (vyāpaka), it is impossible for it to be the substratum of such an action as motion.
That which is all-pervasive cannot be the substratum of an action characterized by motion, just like space and so forth; and according to your own view, the self is all-pervasive.

Alternatively, if action, which has the nature of motion (*parispanda*), does not reside in a pervasive substance—just as the action of a flag and so forth—and yet the action characterized as the operation of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) has the nature of motion, then it would follow that this operation of the knower must depend upon something other than the knower. In that case, how could it have the form of the knower’s operation, or how could it be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For it would then follow that even operations such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, which depend on things like flags, would likewise be the means of valid cognition.

Regarding the second alternative as well, is "non-vibration" (aparispanda) the absence of vibration or a distinct entity? If it is the absence of vibration, then its capacity to produce an effect is untenable, because it is contradictory for an absence to possess causal efficiency. How this contradicts its causal efficiency will be explained in detail during the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, if it is a distinct entity, is it of the nature of consciousness (*cit-rūpa*) or of the nature of insentience (*acid-rūpa*)? If it is of the nature of consciousness, is it the substratum (*dharmin*) or a property (*dharma*)? If it were the substratum, then it would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the Self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, is dharma distinct from the self or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then since it would be the self itself, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) is untenable. If, however, there is a distinction, then because there would be no connection [between them], the designation "belonging to that" (*tasya*) is untenable. If the designation "belonging to that" is based on its being an effect of that [self], then does its being the cause of that [dharma] occur through another operation or otherwise? If it occurs through another operation, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is otherwise, that is not so; for if one accepts that something devoid of activity can produce an effect, it follows that the postulation of an activity is useless.

Furthermore, would this other entity—which is insentient in nature—be a substratum (*dharmin*) or a property (*dharma*)? If it were the substratum, it would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like a clod of earth.

If, on the other hand, it is a property, of what would it be a property? Of the self or of something else? If it belonged to something else, it could not be a means of valid cognition, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, [if it is argued that the self] is [the agent] of itself; that is not so, because for this non-inert entity, there is a contradiction in its possessing the properties of an inert thing.
Therefore, an operation in the form of an action is not possible.

Even if it were not in the form of an action, would it be of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*) or of the nature of non-consciousness (*abodha*)? If it were of the nature of consciousness, there would be a contradiction with its being absolutely imperceptible (*atyantaparokṣa*), since it is impossible for such a thing to possess the nature of consciousness. And that impossibility will be established when self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is proven.

If, however, it were of the nature of non-cognition, its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be untenable, just like a jar or similar objects; furthermore, there is a contradiction between the conscious nature of the Self and an unconscious operation.
Therefore, since the operation of a knower—when examined by the aforementioned reasoning—is untenable, how could there be validity?
[This applies to] that which has the nature of motion (*parispanda*).
That activity is the operation of the knower, or else it is insentient. (Vyāpaka-ā॰, ja॰, bhāṃ॰; jaḍaṃ vā ba॰, ja॰, bhāṃ॰)
The self alone is the means of valid cognition— [this is] even though it is insentient without an operation— Ā॰, Va॰, Ja॰, Bhā॰.
For that which has an insentient property as its own,
its activity— whether of the nature of consciousness or of the nature of non-consciousness— is indeed devoid of action.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 7, upper section; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, folio 25:
"And the obstruction of that which is absolutely beyond the senses" (*atyantaparokṣasya-rodhaśca*). *Ba.*, *Ja.*, and *Bhā.* manuscripts.

As for what was also stated—that even the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*) belongs to an agent only by virtue of its immersion in action (*kriyāveśa*), and so forth—that is indeed true. For we do not deny the perceptible activity of an agent consisting of motion (*parispanda*), since a variety of activities such as the flickering of flames is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in each respective agent. We merely deny an activity imagined by you that is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because such an activity is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the manner described.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a knower—or anything else—that is eternal, uniform in nature, and unchanging, to perform an action or produce an effect.
Furthermore, that "causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is not tenable in the positions of either permanence or momentariness" will be demonstrated in detail later;

therefore, [the claim] that "the operation of the knower is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it is the most effective instrument for the result characterized by the manifestation of the object," and so forth, attains a status comparable to a description of the good fortune of the son of a barren woman—thus, we shall desist.

Thus, since contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like—which are non-cognitive in nature—are untenable when subjected to analysis, or even if they were tenable, because they cannot be the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the primary cognition of an object, their status as a primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is likewise untenable. Therefore, since it produces a cognition characterized as the most effective instrument for that primary cognition, its validity here must be understood by those skilled in discernment only in a figurative sense.
Thus, it was rightly stated: "The validity of non-cognitive contact and the like is untenable, just like other extraneous things" (p.

For we do not deny the activity that is observed to consist of motion, since such diverse activities as flaming and so forth are perceived directly in each respective causal agent; however, we maintain that there is no activity that is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
18; Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra, Pramāṇaprakaraṇa, verse 8).
Regarding the phrase "in the result" (*phale*),
[it refers to] the attainment (*prāpti*) in the valid cognition of an object (*arthapramiti*).
— O King, even there, its validity should be examined by those skilled in investigation. [Variant: O King, even there, its validity...]. [Variant: O King, even there, its validity...
Indeed, let it be that cognition alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
That [perception] is of two kinds— non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Among these,
the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Buddhist is that the validity belongs only to non-conceptual perception.
Knowledge in the form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), whereas that in the form of inference (*anumāna*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Regarding these, the definition of direct perception is: "Direct perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (*Nyāyabindu*, p.
11). Conceptual construction is a cognition associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpavatī pratītiḥ*); [direct perception] is free from that.

Indeed, it is not possible for perception to grasp an object as conjoined with verbal expression; for a linguistic designation cannot be applied to its object, since that object does not persist from the time of the convention to the time of practical usage. That which does not persist from the time of the convention to the time of practical usage is not assigned a word by those engaged in worldly activity, just as no word is applied to some object that perishes immediately upon arising. Furthermore, the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is restricted to a specific place, time, and form, does not persist across other places and so forth.

Therefore, how could there be a grasping of an object qualified by that [word] through perception, such that it would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*)? Whatever word is not applied to something, there is no grasping of that thing as qualified by it; for example, when the word "horse" is not applied, there is no grasping of the substance "cow" as qualified by the word "horse. And since no word whatsoever is applied to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). As stated in the *Nyāyapraveśa* (p. 7): "That cognition which, regarding an object such as color-form (*rūpa*), is devoid of conceptual construction consisting of name, genus, and so forth..."
Perception is free from conceptual construction and unassociated with name, genus, and so forth.
(Pramāṇasamuccaya, Chapter 1, Verse 3)

Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous; conceptual construction is a cognition associated with verbal expression, consisting in the nature of being a cause for linguistic designation, and not otherwise.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 366:

However, some of our own [Buddhist] colleagues do not accept the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), because even erroneous cognitions, such as the perception of a yellow conch shell and the like, are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*). For instance, that [cognition] is not inference because it is not produced from a logical mark (*aliṅgaja*); and it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvāditva*).
Therefore, the term "non-erroneous" was not included in the definition by the Master Dignāga.
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, page 394:
Now, what is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) like? It is said: it is the association with name, genus, and so forth.
In the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), an object qualified by a name is expressed, such as "Ḍittha."
By means of a genus-word, [one identifies] "this is a cow" through the genus;
by means of quality-words, "white" through the quality;
and by means of action-words, "cook" through the action.
In the case of substance-words, [the cognition] "one with a staff" or "one with horns" occurs by means of a substance; thus it is stated in the *Pramāṇasamuccayaṭīkā*, page 12.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is associated with sensory consciousness and the mental factors of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Furthermore, according to the Yogācāra school, with the exception of the non-dual gnosis of the Tathāgata, all other gnosis is conceptualized as consisting of the grasped and the grasper; others, however, state that mental gnosis associated with universals (*jāti*) and so forth is "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*).
(Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī, p. 21)

For conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—consisting of the mental and verbal discrimination (*vikalpa*) based on universals (*jāti*), substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and designations (*paribhāṣā*)—does not exist in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (Tattvārtha-ratnākara, p. 39)

In that regard, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not expressed by words, because it lacks continuity across the time of the convention, the time of usage, and the intervening period. (872)

And the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not possess the capacity to pervade the times of convention and linguistic usage; therefore, there can be no linguistic convention (*samaya*) with respect to it. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p.
277) These [particulars] do not follow along as the nature of the individual, nor do they [possess] a mutual form.
Due to differences in place, time, action, capacity, appearance, and so forth,
the object perceived at the time of convention is not seen during practical usage.
Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 277: "The object qualified by the word" refers to the word *go* (cow). Ā. [Commentary]

Furthermore, when a cognition arises regarding a present form (*rūpa*) or other object for one who is conceptualizing past objects and so forth through their association with words that denote them, how can that cognition be considered determinate (*savikalpaka*), given that the association of the name with a present object is not perceived at that time? Moreover, since words are impossible in relation to the object and there is no identity between them, how could there be an association of the form of a word—which is not its cause—with a cognition produced by that object? Whatever is not the cause of something does not conform to the form of that thing; for example, a gustatory cognition produced from taste does not conform to the form of color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are not its causes, and sensory cognition is likewise produced from objects such as blue and so forth.
Therefore, that cognition alone which apprehends a word as being conjoined with an object in its capacity as a signifier is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); no other is.

For this very reason, even though the cognition of a yogin manifests many words and objects, it is not conceptual because of the absence of such conjunction. Furthermore, it is non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) because of the absence of grasping an object qualified by qualifiers.
Indeed, the state of being qualified by qualifiers cannot be grasped by perception, since two distinct objects appearing at the same time manifest therein.

Furthermore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified does not exist between two things perceived merely in their own essential natures (*svarūpa*); for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition is engaged in the direct perception of a certain object, that cognition does not possess a conceptual form consisting of the association of qualifiers and the qualified—which are distinct from the object's own nature—just as visual or other sensory cognitions engaged with forms (*rūpa*) and so forth do not possess a form that associates qualifiers such as odor which have not been made objects of that cognition. And such is the case for every cognition engaged with its own respective object.
For words do not exist in the object, nor are they identical with it, because otherwise it would follow that even one who has not learned the linguistic convention would have cognition [of them];
as it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (p. 531) and the *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā* (p.
133): "For words do not exist in the object, nor are they of the nature of that [object], such that when the latter appears, they too would appear."
*Nyāyapraveśavṛtti*, p. 35; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 118; *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, p. 75, u.
Taste-cognition (*rāsanajñāna*)—
that is, cognition [arising from the sense of taste]—

is of such a nature that this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is divided into four types based on the distinctions of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), sensory perception (*indriya*), mental perception (*manas*), and yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*).

In this regard, the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors is *svasaṃvedana* (Nyāyabindu, p. 19); sensory perception arises from the sense organ, the object, and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) (Nyāyabindu, p. 18); mental perception is produced by a sense cognition acting as the immediately preceding condition, assisted by the object immediately following its own [sensory] object (Nyāyabindu, p. 18); and yogic perception is born from the culmination of the intensification of the cultivation of reality (Nyāyabindu, p.
20). Thus, having refuted non-conceptual [perception], the validity of conceptual [perception] is established. To this, we reply:

Regarding what was stated—“free from conceptual construction” (*kalpanāpoḍha*), and so forth—what is this “conceptual construction”? Is it (1) an appearance associated with verbal expression, (2) ascertainment, (3) the delineation of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, (4) an indistinct form, (5) independence from the proximity of an object, (6) not being produced by the senses, or (7) the superimposition of another property? Among these, the first position is untenable; for it is impossible for an appearance to possess verbal expression. Would that [appearance] be so because it has that [verbal expression] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or because it has that as its cause? It cannot be because it has that as its intrinsic nature, since identity (*tādātmya*) is impossible due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) upon the conscious and the unconscious.

There is no identity between two things upon which contradictory properties are superimposed, as in the case of water and fire. Furthermore, since sound and cognition possess the nature of being insentient and sentient respectively, they are characterized by the superimposition of contradictory properties;
therefore, in proving that perception is non-conceptual on the grounds that it is devoid of their intrinsic nature, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Nor can it be [proven] because of being caused by them; for does this mean being produced by them, being the producer of them, or both? If it were to possess them by virtue of being produced by them, then auditory cognition would not be non-conceptual, because it follows that it must possess [conceptuality] due to its arising from verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).
If [it is argued that] the cognition possesses that [conceptual nature] because it produces it, then the perception of roots, suffixes, and so forth would be conceptual;

thus, in both positions, both faults follow, as well as the contradiction of having both forms in a single [cognition]. Therefore, since it is untenable for a manifestation accompanied by verbal expression to be the definition of conceptualization, the argument beginning with "that word which is not applied therein" and so forth is rejected.
Page 46, line 2:
Regarding the term "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*): according to some, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
For them, there would either be an indistinct cognition or a conceptual construction;
there is no other possibility for a determination of its own object when analyzed.
For that [cognition] is either accompanied by verbal expression or is capable of it;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 185.

And what indeed is this so-called "conceptualization" (kalpanā)? Is it the state of being produced immediately after recollection? Or is it being permeated by the form of a word? Or is it the delineation of universals (jāti) and so forth? Or is it having a non-existent object as its domain? Or is it the determination of the nature of an object through dependence on something else? Or is it mere metaphorical designation (*upacāra*)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 18, l.
20–21). [The text continues: ...of the existence [of the object]... (ā॰ –satvasya ja॰)

Now, it may be argued that conceptual determination (*niścaya*) is being asserted [as the nature of perception]; this is true. However, the claim that perception is devoid of such determination is false, because it is impossible for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be non-determinative in nature. To explain: perception is essentially determinative regarding its own object because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference. On the other hand, that which is itself non-determinate in form and non-determinative regarding the object is not a means of valid cognition, just as the cognition of another person or a cognition consisting of doubt and the like.

Indeed, there is no other basis for the invalidity of another person’s cognition or of doubt and the like than their lack of the nature of a determination regarding their own object; and that [invalidity] which others assert in the case of perception entails the invalidity of certainty itself.

For certainty is the ascertainment of the true nature of an object through the exclusion of doubt and the like, and this very character of valid cognition is established by the etymological derivation of the word "pramāṇa" (valid cognition).

For instance: that by which an object is measured—that is, determined—through excellence characterized by the exclusion of doubt and the like, is *pramāṇa* (valid cognition). And since this [excellence] is not possible in the case of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), how could even the word "pramāṇa" apply to it? Furthermore, because it is useless for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), it is not a valid cognition; for that which is useless for practical activity is not a valid cognition, such as the sensation of touching grass while walking. And such is the indeterminate perception postulated by others.

You have extended this investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by accepting conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), as stated in such passages as "Validity [is established] by means of conventional usage" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.5).

However, a non-conceptual [cognition] does not possess the capacity to establish conventional activities such as purposeful action (*pravṛtti*), because it does not ascertain its own object; consequently, like an indeterminate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*), it cannot account for the engagement in action or other such activities on the part of those engaged in worldly practice.
If conceptual construction (kalpanā) is accepted as being the determination of its own object,
then this definition would be entirely impossible in every respect.
But in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 185, it says:
"tat-prabhā-ṇaṃ vā" (or its radiance), [as found in] manuscripts Ba and Ja.
The nature of being non-determinative with respect to its own object—
[this is] perception, which is free from conceptual construction, as defined by [the school of] Śabara, Jaimini, and Bhārata.
— Thus, validity is established by worldly convention; the scripture is for the removal of delusion,
or it is the illumination of an unknown object, or it is for the realization of its own nature.
From the non-conceptual [cognition], Pramāṇavārttika 2.5.

Now, the claim that even non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) attains the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it prompts activity by generating a subsequent distinct conceptualization (*vikalpa*), is mere faith; for since its own nature is not known, it would follow that it is indistinguishable from sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). Indeed, its capacity to prompt activity is established in this manner [through a subsequent concept], yet there is no distinction between the two [contact and perception] based on being sentient or insentient, as the sentience of non-conceptual perception itself is not established.

For consciousness is said to be that which reveals its own nature through independence from anything else; yet even in a dream, non-conceptual perception does not reveal its nature in such a way. How, then, could it be conscious, since it would be distinguished [from insentience] only through contact? Therefore, one who desires to distinguish it must accept that it is of the nature of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*), because for this [perception], which is devoid of activity and whose nature is not experienced [otherwise], no distinction from contact can be established by any other means. Consequently, perception becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when it performs a determinative judgment.

However, if no subsequent determination (*anyavasāya*) occurs, the cognition remains undetermined as having the nature of the awareness of blue; and thus, the nature of the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*), which consists in the apprehension of the object, remains unestablished. Consequently, due to the absence of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*), the cognition would not even be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p.
27) Even non-conceptual cognition possesses the capacity to produce a conceptual determination (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, it becomes a constituent part of all remaining conventional usage by means of that [ultimate reality].
(Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 390)
Contact as well—
produced by that [proximity]—
is independent of anything else.

Even realization (*adhigama*) consists essentially of determination (*vyavasāya*); for if that [determination] does not arise, then even though perception (*darśana*) exists, it is indistinguishable from mere proximity because it depends on other means of accomplishment, like the consciousness of one in deep sleep.
Indeed, proximity is the contact between the sense organ and the object (Aṣṭaśata, Aṣṭasahasrī, p.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the very operation (*vyāpāra*) of perception is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of 'I see'? How then can it be devoid of operation? [Reply: This too is unsound; for it would entail that [perception] is of the nature of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*). Indeed, you do not accept that an operation is distinct from its possessor, since the former is of the same nature as the latter. If you argue that it is distinct because it is the effect of that [possessor], then how can it be its operation? For a son does not become the operation of his father.

Or let it be so; nevertheless—if non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-adhyakṣa*) were not of the nature of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya-svabhāvatā*), then how could that nature exist even in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced from it? For would it accept the nature of determinate cognition by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness (*bodha-rūpatayā*), or by virtue of being produced from a distinct causal complex (*vilakṣaṇa-sāmagrī-prabhavatayā*)? If it were by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness, then since that [nature] exists in perception as well, perception too would have to accept the nature of determinate cognition.

Even though there is no difference between them [in being non-conceptual], that which possesses the direct operation of grasping an object does not ascertain it, whereas that which depends upon that operation does ascertain it; this would be established only if a difference between the two were proven—such as the sharpness of a sword versus the sheath, or their arising from distinct causal complexes—but a nature distinct from conceptualization is not established even in a dream.

For indeed, this single cognition alone—consisting of the determination of its own object and arising from the totality of causes such as the sense organs—is what is experienced. In that regard, neither a difference in intrinsic nature nor a difference in the causal totality ever appears to anyone at any time, except perhaps to the Buddhist whose internal organ is overcome by great delusion.

Otherwise, how could the Sāṅkhya be refuted while thus describing a difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*caitanya*)? For it would follow that a difference between these two is established merely through assertion, even though their distinct natures are not apprehended, just as one might assert a difference between conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptual perception (*avikalpa*).
The claim that there is no perception of difference because of the determination of identity between those two is equally applicable in both cases,
even though there is no distinction in their nature as consciousness, in the case of non-conceptual [cognition].
Conceptualization is the function of non-conceptual [perception];
[this pertains] to both the non-conceptual and the conceptual.

And how could it be that, for the followers of Kapila, the difference between intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*caitanya*), though unperceived, does not exist? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 8; Syādvādaratnākara, p.

79). Furthermore, when both are cognized as distinct in their own nature, the determination of oneness through the superimposition of one upon the other is logical, as in the case of a firebrand and a boy; however, it has been stated that there is never, at any time, or for anyone, a simultaneous cognition of both conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).

And does this determination of oneness arise from one of these two, or from something else? If it arises from one of them, is it from a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or from non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*)? It cannot be from non-conceptual perception, because, being devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it lacks the capacity for the determination of oneness.
Nor can it be from conceptual construction, because that is not the object-domain of non-conceptual perception.

Whatever is not the object of a cognition does not have its identity with that [object] determined by it; for example, a cognition whose object is a jar does not determine its identity with atoms because atoms are not its objects. And since this conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) has the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) as its object, if it were to have the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, then conceptual cognitions would also have the particular as their object—whether from another prior cognition, from a subsequent cognition, from a form associated with [the object], or from the perceiver themselves—due to the determination of identity with that. It cannot be from the prior cognition, because that has already perished at the time [of the conceptual cognition].
Nor does it arise from a subsequent cognition, because at that time those two [the previous and the current cognitions] no longer exist;

likewise, even if both—whether non-conceptual or conceptual—are present, it is not logical for them to be the cause of the determination of their identity, since both faults would follow in either case.
Nor is there a determination of their identity by the perceiver based on a form that persists [through them], because such a [persisting] entity is not admitted by the Buddhists.

Therefore, by one who accepts the establishment of reality based on cognition, perception must be admitted as being one alone—consisting of the determination of its own object as established through experience; for it is through that [perception] alone that there is the discernment of both self and other, and all practitioners of worldly discourse depend upon it.
Thus, in giving it another name such as "non-conceptual" (*avikalpaka*), there is nothing undesirable, since a difference in terminology does not establish a difference in the underlying object.

It is also not contradictory to say that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is the mention of universals (*jāti*) and so forth; for it is logically consistent that the determination (*avasāya*) of universals and the like—which serve as qualifiers and qualificands and are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*)—by way of cutting through delusion (*vyāmoha*), constitutes conceptualization. Indeed, does this unity [of the object] belong to the perception itself, or to the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) arising in its wake, or to another cognition? (From *Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 53; *Prakaraṇapañcikā* [or *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*], p. 9, upper section).
Sanmati-Ṭīkā, p.

500: What is this so-called "superimposition" (adhyāropa)? If it is argued that it is the apprehension of identity between the perceived and the attainable, then this cannot possibly occur through perception (pratyakṣa); for perception is admitted to have as its object only a thing restricted to its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), as stated in Nyāyabindu-vivaraṇa, p. 54, u. 1.
Just as in the case of the atom and prior cognition, at the time of both the non-conceptual and the conceptual [cognitions], so it is for these two as well— ba, ja.
—Hārāṇa—ba, ja:
