Direct perception, which consists in the determination of its own object, does not have as its nature a universal (*jāti*) and so forth; nor is it unestablished that the object possesses such a form directly.
Because all doubts have been destroyed by unimpeded awakening,
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 186.

As for what was also stated—"whatever cognition is directed toward the direct realization of an object," and so forth—in that regard, what is this so-called form of the qualifier, the qualified, and so on, which would be negated in a cognition directed toward the direct realization of an object? Is it a reflection (*pratibimba*) or a mental image (*ullekha*)? If it is a reflection, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we also accept its negation in cognition, since we maintain the thesis that all cognitions are devoid of forms (*nirākāra*).

Now, as for "ullekha" (mental representation); its negation is untenable, because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) illuminates the nature of an object exactly as it exists. Furthermore, the nature of that object—qualified by genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is well-established through such cognitions as "the cow," "white," or "it moves"; indeed, the denial of what is being perceived is not logical, as it would result in a lack of confidence in all things. The existence of genus and so forth, as well as the fact that objects are qualified by them, will be demonstrated in detail in the section on the determination of the object (*viṣayapariccheda*); therefore, enough of this digression.

Page 47, Line 6 – [The opponent argues: "The nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) consists in having an indistinct form (*aspaṣṭākāratā*), and this is established precisely because it is conceptual. For instance: whatever cognition is conceptual is indistinct, such as inference (*anumāna*); and this cognition under dispute is likewise conceptual. This too is incorrect; for the distinctness or indistinctness of cognitions is not established by their being non-conceptual or conceptual, since these qualities are established solely through the specificities of their own causal complexes (*svasāmagrī*).

Otherwise, how could even perception—not being indistinct like inference—be [considered] a valid means of knowledge (*pratyaya*)? Furthermore, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for only if its indistinct form is established can its conceptual nature (*savikalpakatva*) be established, and only if that is established can its indistinct form be established.

Moreover, does this indistinctness arise from its grasping an object qualified by qualifiers, from its reflecting upon unity, or from its delineating an indirect form? Of these, the first two positions are untenable, because the actual nature of the thing itself cannot be the cause of indistinctness.

Indeed, that which is the very nature of a thing cannot be the cause of its lack of clarity, just as blueness and so forth are not. Furthermore, since the nature of a thing consists in its being qualified by attributes and so on, let there be a lack of clarity wherever there is the representation of an object through a remote (parokṣa) form; but it does not exist elsewhere.

For conceptual cognition (vikalpa) does not always operate solely upon a remote object; for we perceive its operation even with respect to a present, immediately present object, by way of the representation of a clear form.

For conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), in grasping an object as having been perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), would grasp it as being fit for association with words. Now, "having been perceived at the time of the convention" means being the object of a cognition that arose at the time of the convention. And just as a cognition that arose previously and has now perished does not exist at present, so too the state of being the object of that previously perished cognition no longer exists for the object at present. Thus, by grasping the object in its non-existent form, because it grasps an object that is not present, it appears indistinctly (*asphuṭābha*).
And precisely because it appears indistinctly, it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*);
[this is stated] by way of its being either conceptual or non-conceptual, *Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 21. *Bhāṣya*.

Nor is independence from the presence of an object the defining characteristic of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for this [conceptual cognition] proceeds by way of "this-ness" only when an object is present before one. Indeed, such a conceptual construction is not possible regarding an object that is not present.
Therefore, even if its characteristic is the presence of an object, if it were not perceptual (*apratyakṣatā*), nothing at all would be perceptual.
Why, then, should it be thought that conceptual construction does not arise from an object? Because it is independent of the presence of an object.

Nor is "not arising from the senses" a defining characteristic of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it is precisely here that one concludes its arising from the senses, since it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the senses; for a non-conceptual [cognition] is never perceived following the operation of the senses.
Furthermore, this [cognition] which directly perceives an object must arise from a sense-organ (*akṣaprabhavatva*);
however, it is impossible for that which is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) to possess such direct perception, because its own nature (*svarūpa*) is itself unestablished.

That whose own nature is unestablished cannot be a direct perceiver of an object, just like the cognition of a barren woman’s son. And the cognition intended to be non-conceptual is unestablished in its own nature.

Furthermore, the superimposition of another property (*dharmāntarāropa*) upon indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is not its defining characteristic. For in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), what [substratum] is there upon which another property is superimposed? If you say it is the indeterminate perception, then what is that "other property"? If you say it is clarity (*vaiśadya*), then why could it not be said that the son of a barren woman is superimposed there? Since that [son of a barren woman] is not established as a locus for that property, how could it be superimposed there? This same logic applies elsewhere as well.

Indeed, even for a person who is authoritative, whose mind is not distracted by anything else, and whose eyes are wide open, that which is non-conceptual is never established as having those [sensory] qualities as its substratum. Therefore, perception must be understood as being produced by the operation of the senses, characterized by clarity, directly apprehending its own object, and consisting of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*).

Consequently, since the definition of perception postulated by you is untenable, the description of its divisions—beginning with "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvedana*) and "sensual" (*indriya*)—is like describing the fragrance of a lotus in the sky; thus, the definition of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is disregarded.

An extensive discussion on the attribution of clarity (*vaiśadya*) by way of a different formulation is to be found in the *Nyāyaviniścayaṭīkā*, pp. 42–47; [it is] not attributed as being accompanied by the son of a barren woman (*vandhyāsuta*). (B, J) Clarity.

In the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Pratyakṣasūtra, verses 86–145, Kumārila engages in a discussion to refute both the Buddhist position— which maintains that only non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is valid on the grounds that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is like the son of a barren woman and cannot serve as a locus for the property of clarity— and the Grammarians' position— which maintains that only conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*) is valid; thereby, he establishes the validity of both non-conceptual and conceptual perception.

That very same discussion is seen to have been elaborated in a different style by Vācaspatimiśra in his *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā* (pp. 133–137), by Bhaṭṭa Jayanta in his *Nyāyamañjarī* (pp. 92–100), and by Śrīdharācārya in his *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī* (pp.
189–194). Generally, the defense of the validity of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-prāmāṇya*) is to be found in the *Prakaraṇapañjikā* (pp.
47–51). Indeed, it is impossible to make known that which is unestablished, even if it were pointed out as being like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Without proof, there is no purpose for a definition; this is true, O Hero, regarding one who hates you"—
by this verse in the *Yuktyanuśāsana*, the definition of non-conceptual [cognition] has been refuted.
The refutation of the position of those who maintain non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*) through various methods is found in the *Tattvārtharājavārttika* (p. 39), the *Anekāntajayapatākā* (p.
607), and the *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā* on *Pratyakṣasiddhi* (p. 32).
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 185; *Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 53; *Prakaraṇapañcikā* (or *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*), p. 8, upper [section].
*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, folio 384a;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, folio 499;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, folio 76.
This is to be seen in the *Ratnākara* (p. 18), the *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā* (p. 156), and other such works.
The commentary explains this very point: "Indeed not," and so forth.
It means that it is certainly not the case that something is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) merely by being called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Why is this so? Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

He demonstrates this very over-extension with the words beginning "saṃvyavahāra" (conventional practice): conventional practice is either correct or consistent—that is, a practice free from disagreement between proponent and opponent, characterized by the rejection or acceptance of what is to be abandoned or adopted, or characterized by cognition and so forth; in that regard, [it would follow that] things which are useless...
Of what? Of knowledge.
Furthermore, of what kind of knowledge? To this he says: "Doubt," and so forth.
The cognition "Is this mother-of-pearl or silver? is doubt.
The cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl, or "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl, is an error (*viparyaya*).
Because its cause is indeed the cause of that [error], there is no contradiction with the existence of that which is useless for it, nor is there a contradiction with its being real.

The meaning is this: just as a cognition that is the cause of doubt and so forth lacks validity because, despite being a cognition, it is useless for practical transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*), so too is the case with the non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) postulated by you.

In this regard, there are conflicting views among the proponents concerning the object of error (*viparyaya*), namely: the theory of non-discrimination (*aviveka-khyāti*), the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asat-khyāti*), the theory of the apprehension of a well-known object (*prasiddhārtha-khyāti*), the theory of self-apprehension (*ātma-khyāti*), the theory of the apprehension of a well-known object [in another form], the theory of the apprehension of an indefinable object that is neither existent nor non-existent (*sadasattvādyanirvacanīyārtha-khyāti*), the theory of the apprehension of an extraordinary object (*alaukikārtha-khyāti*), and the theory of the apprehension of a contrary object (*viparītārtha-khyāti*). Among these—concerning the object of error:
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Prābhākara, who maintains that error consists in the non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekā’khyāti*):
Those who follow the doctrine of Prabhākara maintain that error consists in the non-apprehension of distinction.

For instance, the two distinct cognitions "this" and "silver"—which take the form of perception and recollection respectively—are established as being distinct because they arise from different causes and have different objects.

For it is established that the sense faculty (*indriya*) is the cause of perception (*pratyakṣa*), which apprehends the "this" aspect, while the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause of recollection (*smaraṇa*); thus, there is here an origination from distinct causes.

And for those two things that originate from distinct causes, there is a mutual difference, as in the case of perception and inference. Furthermore, the fact that these two cognitions—"this" and "silver"—originate from distinct causes and possess distinct objects is well known here:
because the cognition "this" has the mother-of-pearl fragment present before one as its support (*ālambana*), whereas the cognition "silver" has as its object the silver situated at a distance.
Where there is a difference in objects, there is mutual difference, as in the cognitions of color, taste, and so forth; and such a difference in objects exists in the cognition "this is silver.

Thus, although memory is distinct from perception, because it is obscured, it does not appear through discrimination; this is what is called "non-discriminative manifestation" (*aviveka-khyāti*), but it is not the case that this is a single cognition. For if it were so, there would be no cause for its arising.

In that regard, what is the cause? Is it the sense organ or something else? It cannot be something else, because it would follow that such a cognition could arise even when the operation of the sense organs has ceased.

Nor is it the sense organ [that errs]; for when that [organ] is in contact with a piece of mother-of-pearl that resembles silver, having produced an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) regarding that very object, it would likewise produce a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) regarding that same object, not regarding silver. This is because [silver] has no connection with the sense organ and is not present [at that time].

Furthermore, what is unconnected and non-present cannot be grasped by a sense organ; rather, only what is connected and present is grasped by the eye and other senses, as stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Sūtra 4, Verse 84.

Otherwise, since even all remote objects would follow as being graspable by that [cognition], the omniscience of everything regarding everything would be established without any means; nor should it be argued that this is the power of defects (*doṣa*), for what indeed is this so-called "power"? Is it an obstruction of the sensory capacity, its destruction, or the manifestation of erroneous cognition? Among these, the first two alternatives are untenable because it would entail the non-arising of the effect; for when the burning power of fire is obstructed or destroyed by a jewel, a mantra, or the like, the arising of an effect such as a blister is never observed.
The third alternative is also untenable; for indeed, it is not observed that defective barley produces a contrary effect.
Therefore, this is a duality of cognitions: "this" is a perception (*pratyakṣa*) grasping an object situated in front, and "silver" is a recollection (*smaraṇa*) of previously experienced silver.

For the cognition having the form of silver has silver as its object and not mother-of-pearl, because it is impossible for a cognition having one form to have a different object; otherwise, if that were possible, every cognition would have everything as its object, resulting in the absurdity that everyone would be omniscient.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition has a certain form, that cognition must have that very thing as its object, just as a cognition with the form of a jar has the jar itself as its object. This cognition, moreover, has the form of silver. If a cognition having one form were to have another thing as its object, then, because it would deviate from its own object, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases; consequently, no one would ever engage in or desist from any activity whatsoever, resulting in the total collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, it must be admitted that a cognition with the form of silver has silver itself as its object.
Furthermore, silver is not present before one; therefore, it is only something past that is being remembered at that time, and thus that cognition is not perception.

This is because it lacks the quality of being produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object (*indriyārthasannikarṣaja*), and because the cognition "this is silver" does not arise for one who has not previously apprehended silver.
For if that [cognition] were perception, it would arise even for one who has not apprehended silver through the operation of the sense organs.
—The *Nyāyavibhākara* states: "These two cognitions are as follows: 'this' is perception, and 'silver' is recollection" (*Bṛhaṭṭīkā*, p. 51).
For it is not possible for a cognition having another object to arise when the eye is engaged with something else, because such a cognition does not arise in a blind person (*Prakaraṇapañjikā*, p.
For that [cognition] is not born of the sense-faculty, because there is no contact with it; and a sense-faculty does not produce cognition regarding that which is unconnected (Bṛhaṭ-ṭīkā, p. 51;
Prakaraṇapañcikā, p.
34), as it must be proximate and present (Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, p. 413).
It is perceived by the eyes and other [senses] (*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p.
45). And if the eye perceives even that which is not [normally] perceptible, by what could the omniscience of everyone be prevented? (*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p.
180) — [the reading "bandhaṃ pradhva" is found in the Ā, Ba, and Ja manuscripts].
And it is logical that being defective implies an incapacity for its own function, but not the capacity for another function;
as stated in the *Bṛhatī* (p.
53): "Weakness is the incapacity for one's own function, not the ability to produce another function."
*Bṛhatī*, page 57:

In the cognition "this is silver," it is silver that appears; therefore, that alone must be the object of knowledge by that cognition, and not the mother-of-pearl, because the latter is not being perceived.
Therefore, the appearance of one thing as another is refuted by mere perception;
for when one thing is appearing, another does not appear.
Furthermore, the cognition of silver does not arise in a blind person; this is explained in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 33.
Therefore, this [cognition] is dependent upon the sense-faculties; and when [the object] is in contact, the sense-faculty produces cognition.
(Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 33)

Now, if past silver is being remembered, then this past object should appear precisely as something past, and not as identical to present silver; this objection, however, is unsound. For even though the silver is past, due to a defect (*doṣa*), it does not appear as such; and the cognition that grasps the present object characterized as mother-of-pearl is incapable of apprehending that object in its true nature as "this is mother-of-pearl."

Because the specific characteristic of being "mother-of-pearl," which differentiates the mother-of-pearl from silver, is not apprehended, the object—presenting itself through its common nature as something associated with silver—becomes the cause for the cognition of the memory of silver, which is devoid of the form "I remember.
This very absence of the form "I remember" constitutes the "stealing" (*pramoṣa*) of the memory.

Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed as "this is silver," and the resulting practical behavior identical to that of a correct perception of nearby silver, are not difficult to account for here; for these are established through the non-apprehension of difference.

Furthermore, the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) is of three kinds: namely, the difference between the two objects manifested is not apprehended, the difference between the two manifestors is not apprehended, and the difference from correct cognition is not apprehended.

Nor should it be argued that if the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) is admitted, then because the cognition of silver would be real, its sublation by a subsequent cognition would be untenable; for that [sublation] is established by the fact that when there is the cognition of difference—namely, "this is mother-of-pearl"—the failure to determine the difference is removed, thereby preventing the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) such as the inclination toward silver praised by the previous impression.

However, for those who do not accept the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) and instead maintain that the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is a case of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), the establishment of external objects becomes impossible; for by that very example, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).

For just as the cognition of silver manifests silver even in the absence of silver, so too all cognitions of external objects manifest such objects [only nominally]. Thus, the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*) would be established.
Therefore, one who does not desire this must admit that in such cases there is indeed a loss of memory.

A cognition that has arisen based on the similarity with another object, without having grasped the distinction [between them], becomes the cause for a memory regarding that similar other object; this is called "devoid of the cognition 'I remember'" (Bṛhatī, p. 51). A fragment of mother-of-pearl is thus perceived, devoid of its distinctness.
Those specific qualities of the mother-of-pearl which are the causes for its distinction from silver are not perceived due to being overwhelmed; rather, it is its generic form that is perceived.
Immediately thereafter, memory arose regarding the silver; nevertheless,
due to a defect in the mind, it was devoid of the reflective awareness of that "this" aspect.
*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 34;
according to Ja, [the reading is] *svasvarūpeṇa*.
In the case of the cognition of silver regarding mother-of-pearl, it is correctly described as a memory-cognition due to the loss [of the original perception], as stated in the *Bṛhatī* (p.
53): "I remember"; these memory-cognitions are devoid of the [present] cognition [of the object].
Furthermore, these two—perception and recollection—are devoid of the manifestation of their distinction. (Bṛhatī, p.
Although, from the perspective of ultimate reality, they are indeed distinct due to the correct awakening to silver,
nevertheless, they are not [perceived as] distinct, because of the equality [of the two cognitions] in their failure to grasp the non-existence of the difference [between the silver and the shell].
And because there is a correct cognition of silver whose object is directly present,
these two— recollection and perception— are not understood to be distinct from one another.
People perceive [the world] solely through a uniform form;
worldly convention likewise proceeds from that very same source.
And because there is an awareness of similarity and a non-apprehension of difference (as stated in *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p.

34), and because there is a non-apprehension of the mutual distinction between the memory of silver and the apprehension of the mere substance present before one— in terms of both their own nature and their objects— the two distinct acts of memory and perception, by virtue of their resemblance to a cognition whose object is actually present silver, give rise to the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "this is silver."
*Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, p. 88; *Bhāmatī*, p. 14 – *hārakatva* – Bhā.
Therefore, it is held that even a subverting cognition possesses the quality of being a subverter,
because it prevents the occurrence of the conventional usage of "silver" that would otherwise result. 39.
Furthermore, it is also logical that there would be the consequence of applying the same conventional designation [to the sublater as to the sublated]; therefore,
because it effects the removal of that [consequence], the sublater possesses the status of a sublater.

Furthermore, because the linguistic usage of non-difference—which is occasioned by the non-apprehension of difference—is sublated, it is also logically established that the corrective cognition "this is not silver" functions as a sublater. (Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 35)
*Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, page 88;
*Bhāmatī*, page 14—
by means of refutation (*nirākaraṇena*).

Because that [theory] is untenable; those who, being hostile to the theory known as *vivekā’khyāti* (non-apprehension of distinction), assert that there is a cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl are not experts in the systems of enumeration (*saṅkhyāvid*). For in this way, the establishment of external objects would not be possible for them. (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
107) — [The reading "rītārthakhyā—" appears in the Bhāṇḍārkar manuscript.]

This very loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*), which is the non-apprehension of reality, is called *akhyāti*. Bhaṭṭa Jayanta, in works such as the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 179), designates this loss of memory by the term *akhyāti*, stating that although these two—perception and memory—are distinct, they are not apprehended as distinct; thus, the non-apprehension of their distinction is *akhyāti*.
This [view] is refuted here by the term "non-apprehension of distinction" (*vivekā'khyāti*) in the *Bhāmatī* and other works by others, headed by Vācaspati Miśra.

As for what was stated— beginning with "because they arise from different causes" and so forth— therein, what is the refutation regarding the non-discrimination known as *vivekākhyāti*, which is synonymous with the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*)? (Page 52, Line 14)

Is the difference in the effect established merely from a difference in the cause, or from a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? In the first case, no single cognition would exist, because it would follow that even the cognition of a jar or similar objects—produced by multiple causes such as light, the sense organ, and so forth—would itself be manifold. The second position, however, is untenable; for a difference in the causal complex is impossible here, since the entire collection of causes, such as the eye and so on, constitutes a single causal complex, and any difference in that complex must be inferred from a difference in the effect, whereas no such difference in the effect exists here.

If it is argued: "Surely, a difference in effects exists here in the form of memory and perception, as in the cognition 'this is silver'; therefore, a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) must be postulated," [the reply is]: No, because this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). For only if a difference in causal complexes were established could the difference in effects—consisting of memory and perception—in the case of "this is silver" be established; and only if that were established could the difference in causal complexes be established. In that regard, do you wish to establish the difference in the effect under discussion based on the difference among the multiple causes included within the causal complex due to its being produced by distinct causes, or rather from the difference in the causal complexes themselves? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 109)
—[This is] merely a verbal quibble.

By this, the inference beginning with "those two which have their origin in different causes" is refuted; for only when their difference is established would their origin from different causes be established, and only when that is established would their difference be established.
And thus, [the statement] "the sense organ (*indriya*) is indeed the cause of perception," which is an exposition of your own system, would be untenable.

Furthermore, if you maintain that there is a difference in the effects here as well—on the grounds that elsewhere the sense organ and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are established as the causes of memory and perception respectively—then even recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) would not possess unity, since there is no distinction in its being produced from both a mental impression and a sense organ. If, however, you argue that because the effect is observed to be one in this case, a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is postulated for it; then the same applies to the other case.

And thus, the claim that "this cognition is not one and the same because of the absence of a cause" and so forth is incorrect; for the causal complex (sāmagrī) consisting of the eye and other factors is precisely its cause.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to suspect the absence of a cause when an effect is perceived, since the very perception of that [effect] establishes the existence of its cause.
Indeed, the production of an effect without a cause has never been observed.
Therefore, its distinction does not arise from a difference in causes; rather,
the existence of the cause is established solely through the cognition of the effect.
Nor is it due to a difference in the object (*viṣaya-bheda*), because the single fragment of mother-of-pearl (*śukti-śakala*) alone is the object of this cognition.
For the eye and other senses, through the onset of defects such as cataracts or opacities (*kāca-kāmala*), present the very fragment of mother-of-pearl situated in front as having the form of silver.

Otherwise, how could the manifestation of that cognition occur independently of the proximity of the mother-of-pearl? Does that [proximity] function there merely as a cause (*kāraṇatā-mātreṇa*), or as the object (*viṣayatayā*)? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; for just as in the case of real silver, if the eye and other senses were absent, so too if the fragment of mother-of-pearl were absent, the cognition of silver would not arise—which would lead to an absurdity.
In the second alternative, however, it is established that the cognition has the mother-of-pearl as its object;

for this single cognition—"this is silver"—is experienced as having a single object. Here, the word "this" (idam) refers merely to the state of being present before one, while the word "silver" (rajata) refers merely to the nature of silver and not to a different object. How, then, could there be a suspicion of difference in this cognition? For such a consequence would apply even to the cognition of real silver, since there is no distinction between the two when only their respective intrinsic natures are manifested. [Thus,] the piece of mother-of-pearl...
— You are the manifestation of knowledge;
for the manifestation of the cognition of silver occurs elsewhere.

And as for the other point—that there is either an obstruction or a destruction of the power of the sense-faculties by defects (doṣas), and so forth—that too is incorrect; because neither an obstruction nor a destruction of that [power] is effected by them. Rather, even in their presence, it is simply the cognition "this is silver" that is produced.
And this indeed is the greatness of defects: namely, that they produce a cognition even with respect to an object that does not exist. (Page 53, Line 4)
Neither the obstruction nor the destruction of the capacity [of a cause] by defects is established; see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 15, l.
1 (variant: "is produced," Ā., Ba.).

Furthermore, as for what was said—namely, "Indeed, [merely] defective barley... and so forth—that too is mere words; because this very nature belongs to that which is defective, namely, the non-production of its effect or the production of a contrary effect, like a corrupt servant. And both of these are certainly present in the case of barley and the like, since it is observed that they do not produce their effect in the form of a sprout, and that they produce contrary effects such as abdominal pain in those who consume them.

Indeed, the objection that it is contradictory for a defective cause to produce an effect has also been refuted by this very argument; for what is contradictory in its case is the production of a non-erroneous effect, but not the production of a contrary effect.

If, however, even the mere production of an effect were contradictory there, then how could the production of an effect characterized as the "theft" (misappropriation) of memory arise from it? Therefore, it is logical that through a defect, a contrary cognition arises having a fragment of mother-of-pearl as its object;
hence, the cognition is not differentiated by a difference in its object.

Furthermore, because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the cognition of the five fingers and so forth, it is indeed impossible for this [cognition] to be divided even when there is a difference in objects; thus, on page 53, line 6, the [opponent's] position is refuted by this [argument]. (Bhāṣya)

Furthermore, regarding the cognition of the five fingers and so forth, as well as the cognition of silver: if the cognition of silver does not have a piece of mother-of-pearl as its object, would it be objectless, or would it have past silver as its object? It cannot be objectless, because there is a cognitive apprehension that delineates an object in the form "this is silver. Nor can it have past silver as its object, because that would entail the appearance of silver there as something past; and if that were so, the activity of those seeking to obtain it from this [present locus] would not occur, since what is past cannot be obtained.

Therefore, that cognition must be understood as having precisely the present, perceptually present fragment of mother-of-pearl as its object, because it is the cause of activity directed toward that very thing; for whatever is the cause of activity toward a particular object has that very thing as its object, just as the cognition of silver has silver as its object when it occurs in relation to real silver; and this cognition is the cause of activity toward the present, perceptually present fragment of mother-of-pearl.

Now, it might be argued that even though this [cognition] has as its object past silver, it serves as the cause for activity toward it because, due to a defect, there is a non-apprehension of the difference between the past silver and the mother-of-pearl. That is not so; for mere non-apprehension of difference cannot logically be the cause of a person's activity. Indeed, the cause of such activity is the manifestation of silver as being present before one, and not the non-apprehension of difference.

If it is argued that even though this appearance of silver has as its object past silver, it nevertheless causes a person to act because it is identical to the appearance of real silver present before one, and that identity consists in the non-apprehension of any difference from it—then, surely, since it is not manifest as present, it is also identical to a cognition that manifests past silver; and by virtue of that identity, it would likewise fail to cause action toward it, for there is no distinction between the two cases.

And likewise, how could this possessor of the cognition of silver act—either engage with or withdraw from—the object present before him, which is actually a piece of mother-of-pearl? For, having fallen into two mutually contradictory actions simultaneously, what would he do? Nor is it reasonable to assert that, despite their being equal in that respect, the cognition prompts its appropriate practical activity in one case but not in the other; for such a claim would lead to the consequence of [the cognition] being invalid.
Therefore, it must be understood that the piece of mother-of-pearl itself is the object of the cognition "this is silver";
thus, there is no difference in this cognition even on account of a difference in objects.

Thus, this is established: the cognition of silver and so forth, which is the subject of dispute, has as its object the thing present before one, because it invariably induces activity toward that [thing] by a person seeking silver, due to its similarity to a cognition that manifests past silver (*Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p.
Due to the extreme similarity,
as in the case of the appearance of real silver present before one and the cognition manifesting past silver— the equality of these two [is established].

Now, if it is argued that their distinction is established there because of the difference in their forms (*ākāra*), that is incorrect; for even a difference in form does not entail a difference in the [cognition], since this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). For the latter, although it is pervaded by multiple forms, is nonetheless one; and the same applies to cognitions such as "this is silver."

Therefore, since no difference whatsoever is established for that cognition, its unity alone must be accepted, because it manifests its own nature in that very way. Whatever manifests its own nature in a certain manner must be accepted as being exactly so; just as in the case of real silver and the like, the nature of the cognition "this is silver," which manifests as a unity, is accepted as a unity, and the nature of the cognition "this is silver" with respect to a piece of mother-of-pearl likewise manifests as a unity.
Indeed, we do not perceive any distinction produced by appearance between the two cases, by which we might understand that in one case there is a single cognition and in the other there are two;

such that it would follow that one is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it grasps the true nature of the object as it exists, while the other is invalid (*apramāṇa*) because it is the opposite— this is the difference in cognition.

Since even a difference in form does not logically entail a difference in cognition—because this is contradicted by the case of recognition (pratyabhijñāna)—[it follows that] by this cognition [and] by that [cognition], it is one and the same. (Syādvādaratnākara, p.
115; B, J: *jñānenānenacā*;
Baṃ, J: *ekamevaṃ raja-*)
The same [object], O King— [namely] silver— in the cognition of real silver and in the cognition of false silver; in the case of the cognition of real silver...

Even if we grant that there are two cognitions in the case of the erroneous cognition of silver, would their production occur simultaneously or sequentially? It cannot be simultaneous, because that would entail the occurrence of simultaneous cognitions, and because it would result in the contradiction of the accepted principle that the sense organ has the capacity to produce cognitions only in succession. Even if production were sequential, would the recollection of silver occur prior to the perception "this," or subsequently? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; for at that time, the awakening cause for the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the seed of recollection, is absent.
Furthermore, memory arises when a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is awakened, not when it is unawakened, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if you claim that the awakening of that impression occurs through non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), then there follows the consequence of the simultaneity of the conceptual cognition and the memory of silver; this is precisely the destruction of your own accepted position.
Moreover, it has already been stated in the *Savikalpasiddhi* that non-conceptual cognition is not established by any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, suppose it arises later; that is not so, because the cognition of silver, which arises subsequent to the perception "this," would arise even when the visual faculty has ceased its operation, and thus one with closed eyes would also experience that cognition.

Furthermore, that sequential arising is contradicted by experience; for there is no perception of a sequence between the cognition of the two—even in a dream—such as "first I grasped the piece of mother-of-pearl standing before me, and afterwards I remembered the silver. This is because, according to the experience of all people, the object standing before one appears all at once as consisting of silver. Otherwise, when a sublation occurs, there would be no negation of that identity in the form "this is not silver," since such an identity would not have been previously presented.
Yet this negation does exist, as evidenced by the perception of the negation of the piece of mother-of-pearl as being silver through the pointing of a finger.

Therefore, whatever is negated in a certain place must have been previously present there, just as a jar might be in a certain location; and since silver is negated in the mother-of-pearl shell lying before one, would that [silver] appear simultaneously or successively? (Ratnāvalī, p.
[Objection:

"But even so, just as in the case of a jar and the ground, there will be a negation of conjunction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver. [Reply: This too is not well-said; for in this case, unlike that, no lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is perceived. Indeed, just as there is a perception of lack of coreferentiality in the statement "there is no jar here," there is no such perception of lack of coreferentiality in the statement "this is not silver.

And where there is no perception of lack of coreferentiality, there is no negation of conjunction, as in cases such as "this is not blue. Furthermore, in the case of "this is silver" and so forth, there is no perception of lack of coreferentiality.

For just as by the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin), who accepts the oneness of the universe, that which is superimposed—namely, the blue nature of what is yellow—is negated by the statement "this is not blue," so too, that identity between mother-of-pearl and silver which was superimposed by the prior cognition is removed by the sublater "this is not silver"; however, neither the "this" aspect nor the "silver" aspect is negated.

And thus, the cognition of the existing fragment of mother-of-pearl as having the nature of silver is a *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension), because it contradicts its established form; it is not, however, a "loss of memory" (*smṛtipramoṣa*).—
*tāpi tasya bhā॰, ā॰*—
[The text reads] *bhā॰, ā॰*— *ktikāśa– bhā॰*.
And as for that [memory], it remains [unexplained].

Furthermore, what is this so-called "loss of memory" (*smṛti-pramoṣa*)? Is it destruction, the determination of identity with perception, the attainment of the form of perception, the non-experience of the aspect "that," or mere disappearance? If it were destruction, then because the memory of the relationship between the probans and the probandum would be destroyed at the time of the cognition of the probandum, there would likewise be a loss of memory in that case as well.

Now, if it is argued that the "non-deprivation" (*apramoṣa*) of this [cognition] consists in the determination of its identity with perception, we ask: from what does this determination of identity between the two arise—from the determination of the identity of the object, or from the determination of the identity of their own-natures? Regarding the first alternative, what is this so-called "determination of the identity of the object"? If it means the superimposition of one object upon the other, would there be a superimposition of the object of perception upon the object of memory, or of the object of memory upon the object of perception? In the first case, the mother-of-pearl would appear clearly in the location of the remembered silver, and not as "this" in the sense of being present before one, because it is being superimposed there. Wherever something is superimposed, it appears in that location, just as water superimposed on a mirage appears in the location of the mirage. And yet, it is the mother-of-pearl—the object of perception—that is being superimposed upon the silver—the object of memory.
In the second alternative, however, the clear manifestation of the mother-of-pearl as "this" would not occur, because that which is being superimposed—the object of memory—is indistinct.
Therefore, it is not logical to determine identity between memory and perception based on the determination of identity between their objects.

What, then, is this so-called "error"? Is it the appropriation of the form of experience, the destruction of the form of memory, the state of grasping a previously apprehended object, the state of being produced by sense-object contact, or the state of not being produced by sense-object contact? (Tattvopaplava, p. 25)

And what is this "loss" (pramoṣa) of memory? Is it the non-existence of memory, or an appearance of something else, or the cognition of a contrary form, or the grasping of a past time as being present, or its arising indistinguishably from the original experience, like milk and water? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
15, u. Are these the alternatives: the non-existence of memory, or an appearance of something else, or perhaps the cognition of another form? (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 28)

Is it a concealment (*pravr̥tti*), or a determination of identity with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through proximity, or perhaps the assumption of the form of direct perception, or else the non-experience of that aspect [of the object], or merely its disappearance? (Syādvādaratnākara, p.
120; the word "jalasya" has fallen into the margin of the manuscript *ba*, *ja* at a certain point in the subject matter).

Nor is it [established] by means of the two [cognitions], because their own nature is not clearly determined; for that [identity] must be established either by those two themselves or by another. It cannot be by those two themselves, because if memory and perception—whose natures are not self-cognized—are incapable even of determining their own mere natures, they cannot possibly possess the capacity to determine identity with something else.

Nor can there be a determination of identity by means of another cognition, because that [other cognition]—being itself of an unreflexive nature—is ignorant even of its own form, and thus it is impossible for it to be cognizant of the determination of identity with anything else.

Furthermore, is the identity of those two determined by that [cognition] when they have been perceived, or when they have not been perceived? It cannot be the case when they have been perceived, because the perception of duality contradicts the determination of their identity.
Nor can it be the case when they have not been perceived, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, it might be argued that at the very moment those two are perceived, there is no determination of their identity—which would entail a contradiction—but rather that after first perceiving those two, they are subsequently determined as one. This is incorrect; because cognition is momentary, its persistence for such a duration is untenable. Therefore, the determination of identity with perception does not belong to memory, nor is there a loss of memory in this case. Thus, [the opponent's] claim is refuted.
—of another who knows [it], others—ba॰, ja॰, bhā॰;
then, not when...
bhā॰—at that very time bhā॰.

It is neither identical to that [perception], nor does it undergo the state of being perception itself; for if it were to undergo that state, it would abandon its nature as memory, and thus it would be nothing but perception and not memory—so how could there be a "loss" (pramoṣa) of it? Otherwise, even in the case of a lump of clay undergoing the state of being a jar, since it would abandon its nature as a lump of clay, it would follow that it remains a lump of clay, and thus there would be a "loss" of the lump of clay as well; the sublation by perception is equal in both cases.

Now, if it is argued that the non-experience of the "that" (tat) portion constitutes the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*), on the grounds that the cognition "this is that silver" is indeed a memory—since the word "that" denotes a past, imperceptible object, and where that [object] is not experienced there, memory is said to be lost—that is incorrect. For it would follow that even the form of "silver" would lack experience; for you maintain that this recollection is a single one integrated with the element of "silver. In that case, if the word "that" were lost, the element of "silver" would also be lost, since it is impossible for a partless entity to suffer a loss of only one part.
For the cognition in the form "that is silver" is a memory, because the word "that" has as its object a remote thing previously experienced;
when that [object] is not experienced there [in the present], it is called "obscured memory. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 121)

Memory is experienced as being associated with a word that denotes a perceived but now absent object, such as "that" (tad), in cases where there is a loss [of memory]—as found in manuscripts A, B, and J.

Furthermore, regarding the term *pramoṣa*, what meaning is expressed by the prefix *pra*? Is it the removal of a part, or the removal of the whole? It cannot be the removal of a part, because its employment would be redundant in that case;

for when thieves steal only a portion of a substance, the word *moṣa* alone is used in common parlance. Therefore, it is logical that its meaning is the removal of the whole: *pramoṣa* means an excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*) theft (*moṣa*).
Furthermore, the height of this deception is that it involves the total removal of the object in its entirety;
and thus there is a contradiction with one's own words: [you claim] "the memory exists, but it is forgotten.
For if it exists, how can it be forgotten? And if it is forgotten, how can it exist?

Furthermore, what meaning is intended by the word *pramoṣa* (deprivation/loss) for one endowed with wisdom—is it the removal of a single part, or the removal of the whole? [Ratnākaraśānti’s] *Sāratamā*, p. 122: "In that case also, if this [consciousness] does not exist, how could it be deprived; and if it is deprived, how could it exist? (*bhāṣya*).

Even concealment (*tirobhāva*) could only be established once the simultaneity of cognitions is proven; yet that is not established by you, as it would entail the fallacy of contradicting your own tenets. Furthermore, what is this "concealment" of it? Is it its non-performance of an effect, its being covered, or its remaining in a state where its nature is suppressed? In the first case, what is its effect such that its non-performance of it would constitute concealment? If it is "determination" (*paricchitti*), that indeed exists there, since the determination of silver is currently being experienced here. The second case, however, is untenable, because it is impossible for cognition itself to be covered.
For it is observed that only an object which persists over time can be obscured; however, cognition has never been seen or accepted by anyone as persisting for long.

Thus, the third alternative is also untenable. For the suppression of the nature of a weaker thing by a stronger one is observed, as in the case of the sun suppressing the cluster of stars. But is this [cognition] weak because its object is past, or because it is being sublated? In the first case, the very possibility of memory would be destroyed; for since all memory has a past object and is thus weak, it would follow that its nature is suppressed by a cognition that perceives a present object.
It has been stated that being subject to sublation is not possible except through the theory of misapprehension (viparītakhyāti);
therefore, setting aside the notion that it is a lapse of memory, that very [theory] must be accepted—[only then] would it be established in the verse. (ba, ja)

As for what was stated regarding the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*)—namely, that if misapprehension is accepted, the existence of external objects could not be established, and so forth—that too is incorrect. For even if unreal cognitions lack a real object as their support, it is well-established that true cognitions do have such a support.
Furthermore, the distinction between true and false cognitions is easily established through the presence of validating and subverting means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And this will be demonstrated in detail in the section on the proof of external objects (*bāhyārthasiddhipraghaṭṭaka*); therefore, enough with this digression.
Thus, since the position of non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekākhyāti*) is in every way untenable when scrutinized, those who are discerning and wise should not maintain an attachment to it (p.

First of all, the term *smṛtipramoṣa* (loss of memory) is employed by the teacher Prabhākara in his commentary on the *Bṛhatī*, page 56, in the passage beginning with "I remember" (*smarāmi*) and "that is equal to perception" (*pratyakṣasammitaṃ tat*).

It appears as the term *vivekāgraha* (non-apprehension of distinction) in the *Brahmasūtra-śāṅkarabhāṣya*, page 15; as *akhyāti* (non-apprehension) in the *Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha*, page 28, the *Nyāyamañjarī*, page 179, and the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, page 89.
A detailed examination of this [concept] in its various forms is found in the *Tattvopaplava*, page 25.

The refutation of the Cārvāka, who maintains the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) regarding erroneous cognition: Others maintain the theory of non-apprehension;
for instance, in the cognition "this is silver," the existence of silver as the objective referent is not present, because otherwise it would follow that the cognition is not an error.
The absence of silver (*rajatābhāva*) also cannot be its objective support (*ālambana*), because this [cognition] proceeds with the affirmation of that [silver] as its primary intent.
For this very reason, even the fragment of mother-of-pearl (*śuktiśakala*) is not its objective support.

Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that the fragment of mother-of-pearl is the objective support under the form of silver; for one thing is never perceived as being grasped in the form of another, just as a cloth is certainly not perceived as being grasped in the form of a jar.

"Therefore, nothing at all appears in this cognition; thus, non-appearance (akhyāti) is established"—this is an unexamined statement, because it would entail the impossibility of specific designation. For by what distinction could a cognition of silver or any other be designated, if nothing at all appears therein? In a cognition appearing as water, the existence of water cannot be the objective support (ālambana), because that would entail the cognition being non-erroneous (*prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p.
13, u.; *syādvādaratnākara* p. 124).

What is this "non-apprehension" (akhyāti) that appears to you—is it the absence of apprehension, or is it a slight apprehension? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of no distinction between the state of error and the state of deep sleep; for it is only through the specific nature of its manifestation that error is distinguished from the state of deep sleep, and not otherwise. If, on the other hand, non-apprehension is a slight apprehension, then what is this "slightness" of apprehension? If you say it is the failure to manifest the object as it actually exists, then this would be an apprehension of a contrary object, and not non-apprehension at all.
Therefore, even the position of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is not tenable;
indeed, there is no such thing as non-apprehension.
[This concludes] the refutation of the proponents of the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), namely the Sautrāntikas and Mādhyamikas, regarding erroneous cognition.
Others, however, maintain the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*).

For instance: Is the nature of the object appearing as "this is silver" a property of cognition or a property of the external object? It cannot be a property of cognition, because it is not the locus of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and because it appears externally as "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Nor can it be a property of the object, because it lacks the capacity for the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that such an object would entail, and because it is sublated by a sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) precisely as being a property of that [object].

Therefore, the claim that "that which appears there is indeed non-existent, and thus it is the cognition of the non-existent (asatkhyāti)" is an unexamined statement; for it is impossible for that which is non-existent—devoid of both appearance and description—to appear, just like a sky-flower. Furthermore, this [claim] is a contradiction: "it is non-existent and yet it appears.
For the very fact of appearing is the existence of objects.
For things that are absolutely non-existent, such as the horns of a hare, do not appear even in a dream;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an absence of variety in error, since its basis would be lacking. For those who maintain the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), there exists neither a variety residing in cognition nor a variety residing in the object, upon which basis the manifold types of error could occur.
Is the entity appearing in the perception "this is silver" the cognition itself, or is it an external object? (Ratnāvalī, p. 125)

—[If it were] devoid [of objects], there would be the consequence of the absence of the variety of error (*bhrānti*), for according to the proponent of the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyātivādin*), there is no variety residing either in the object or in the cognition by which error could take on manifold forms (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 14, l. 1).

As for what was also stated—that [the object] lacks causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*)—in that regard too, is it intended that there is an absence of causal efficacy to be accomplished by cognition, or an absence of causal efficacy to be accomplished by the object of cognition? In the first case, its existence is untenable precisely because it would be a property of cognition alone, and not because it is non-existent in every respect; for one thing does not become non-existent simply because it lacks the causal efficacy to be accomplished by another thing, since it would follow that even a jar would be non-existent when it does not perform the causal efficacy to be accomplished by a cloth.

The second position, however, is untenable. If it is asked, "Since the causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) consisting in the engagement in verbal expression and so forth is possible there [in the water], how can this [cognition] be erroneous? [we reply: because it lacks the causal efficiency for bathing and such purposes.
For causal efficiency is of two kinds: that which is based on the mere object, and that which is based on a real object.
In this context, [cognition] whose form consists of desire and so forth is based solely on the object (*arthamātra*),
whereas that whose form consists of bathing and so forth is based on a real object (*satyārtha*);
therefore, only the cognition that grasps an object capable of performing that function is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), and no other.
Therefore, the position of *asatkhyāti* (the theory that there is cognition of the non-existent) is indeed untenable.
For, on page 60, line 18, it is stated that purposive action (*arthakriyā*) is of two kinds: that which is based on the object in general, and that which is based on a specific object.
The refutation of the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) is found in the *Ratnākara* (p. 126), the *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā* (p.
86), and the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 177).
This is to be seen in such sources as *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 14, first half; and *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 125.
An examination of the Sāṃkhya who maintains that error is the manifestation of a well-known object (*prasiddhārthakhyāti*):

Others, however, have accepted the theory of the manifestation of a well-known object; for instance, it is argued that in erroneous cognition, it is precisely an object established by common experience that appears.

Nor should its non-existence be asserted when it is being investigated; for apart from cognition (*pratīti*), no other investigation is even possible, and because [the object] is not sublated by cognition, an investigation is not appropriate regarding an object already established by that [cognition]. For even an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of one's hand possesses existence solely by the force of its manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), and that manifestation is no different elsewhere.

Now, [the opponent argues that] in the case of a circle of mirages and the like, since the object such as water that appears ceases to appear upon approaching that location at a later time, it is non-existent. This is incorrect; for although that object does not appear at a later time, nevertheless, when it does appear, it certainly exists at that time. Otherwise, even things such as lightning would not have their existence established at the moment of their own appearance. Therefore, this is simply the manifestation of a well-known object (*prasiddhārthakhyāti*). [The author replies: This is charming only so long as it is not investigated, because it would entail the destruction of the distinction between the conventions of erroneous and non-erroneous cognition.

Indeed, given that there is no difference in their grasping objects as they actually exist, it is not tenable to establish a distinction—without any basis—that one cognition is erroneous while another is non-erroneous, for this would result in the arbitrary exercise of one's own will.
Furthermore, even after water and such have ceased to exist at a later time, their signs, such as the moisture of the ground, would still be perceived;
for unlike lightning and similar phenomena, the instantaneous and traceless destruction of water and such is never observed anywhere.
Therefore, even the position that [an object] is the manifestation of a well-known thing is not superior;

nor can this [position] withstand scrutiny, because when examined, its non-existence cannot be established since there is no possibility of anything other than cognition itself, and because it is not sublated by cognition. For even things such as the palm of the hand possess existence only by virtue of their appearance [in cognition]. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 14, top).

This should be observed in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 126; in the *Mīmāṃsā-prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 14, first half; and in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 126, regarding the phrase "na tatpra... [which appears as] "prasiddhārthakhyātau" in the editions of Ba., Ja., and Bhā.
The refutation of the Yogācāra proponent of *ātmakhyāti* (self-manifestation) regarding erroneous cognition— others, moreover, maintain that there is self-manifestation;
for instance, in the case of mother-of-pearl, silver appears as "this is silver," and the appearance of that external [silver] is untenable due to the subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*).
It is certainly not logical to accept that an object exists exactly as it appears, for that would entail the consequence that there is no such thing as error.

Therefore, this form belongs to cognition itself, which—due to the power of the impressions of beginningless ignorance—appears as if external; this is *ātmakhyāti* (the theory that what is known is the self). This is incorrect, because *ātmakhyāti* could only be established if it were proven that cognition is restricted solely to the awareness of its own nature while simultaneously bearing the form of the object; however, that is not proven, since both of these points will be refuted later on.

Furthermore, if all cognitions were to grasp only their own form (*svākāra*), the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions, as well as the relationship between the sublated (*bādhy*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*), would not be possible, because there would be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in any case. Moreover, if the form of silver and so forth were experienced as being of the very nature of the cognition itself, the awareness would occur as "I am silver," residing solely within the self, and not as "this is silver," residing externally.

That which is cognized as having the nature of one’s own self is not cognized therein as being external, as in the case of the very nature of consciousness itself. And in the theory of *ātmakhyāti* (the manifestation of the self), the form of silver and so forth is cognized as having the nature of one’s own self. Now, if it is argued that this [silver] is perceived as being external due to the force of beginningless impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), then how would this not be precisely the theory of *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension), since there is a determination otherwise of the form of silver and so forth, which is non-different from the cognition?
Indeed, it is consciousness itself that grasps itself by means of itself.
Since an external object of apprehension cannot be established when examined, the intellect, while manifesting itself in various forms,
carries out such worldly transactions even though it is devoid of an external object.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 178:

"If both [kinds of cognition] were to grasp their own forms (*svākāra*), then the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous, as well as the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, would not be possible, because there would be no difference in the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in either case."
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
14, top; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
129: "by way of its own nature" (*svātmarūpatayā*). (Variants: *ba*, *ja*, *bhā*)
For if the self of consciousness were to appear [in that way], the cognition would be "I am silver," not "this is silver" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

178). For that [consciousness] presents silver as the locus of the "this-ness" (idam), which is not the locus of the "I-notion" (aham); nor is it internal, for in that case it would be experienced as "I," since it would be non-different from the cognizer's own awareness.

Furthermore, since it is accepted that "that which is internal in the form of an object of cognition appears as if external," this too would be nothing other than *viparītakhyāti* (the theory of erroneous cognition). *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, p. 85; *Bhāmatī*, p. 14.

Moreover, this is indeed an apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), because the external object of cognition does not exist; see Nyāyamañjarī, p. 178; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 14, upper section.
In the *Ratnāvalī*, page 129, [it is stated that] the forms of silver and so forth exist as external realities.
Furthermore, whether in the non-duality of consciousness (vijñānādvaita) or the non-duality of Brahman (brahmādvaita), this would be a manifestation of the self (ātmakhyāti).

In that case, how could there be an error based on the perception of duality regarding the two kinds of non-duality? If it is argued that this is due to the affliction of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), [we ask]: does its own nature (*svarūpa*) appear there, or another form (*anyarūpa*)? If it is its own nature, how can it be an error? If it is another form, how can this be "self-manifestation" (*ātmakhyāti*)? If you say that it is the very nature of the self that appears as another form through the power of error, then this is a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*); for thus, the status of the cognition as an error is established by the appearance of another form, and the appearance of another form is established by the establishment of that [cognition] as an error.

If it is not accepted that cognition has external objects as its domain, then why does that [cognition] not arise through the manifestation of the form of blue and so forth at the very same time it arises through the manifestation of the form of silver, given the absence of any restrictive factor? If you say that the beginningless impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) alone are that restrictive factor; how then could the production of that cognition be restricted by place and other such factors? If you argue that this is precisely the power of ignorance—that it displays even a non-existent restriction of place and so forth within cognition—it is not so, for it would entail the fallacy of the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). Furthermore, for one who maintains the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*), how could there be the perception of cutting, striking, and so forth? This is because such things are impossible if there is only the awareness of the [consciousness's] own nature. Indeed, the perception of those [external objects] is never observed during the awareness of the nature of consciousness itself, such as pleasure and the like.
Therefore, the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) is also untenable;
furthermore, [the state of] being fuel for Brahman— *ā*, *ba*,
*ja*.

And if it is not accepted that cognition has an external object as its domain, then why does it not proceed by delineating the form of blue and so forth, just as it proceeds by delineating the form of silver? For there would be no restrictive factor [to determine otherwise]. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 130; Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 85;
Bhāmatī, p. 14).

This is to be seen in such works as *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 14,
