and so forth.
The refutation of the Advaitin who maintains that erroneous cognition is the manifestation (*khyāti*) of an indefinable object (*anirvacanīyārtha*):
Some, however, accept here the theory of the manifestation of an indefinable object.

To explain: the form of silver appearing in mother-of-pearl and the like must be either existent, non-existent, or of both natures. It cannot first be existent, because that would entail the consequence that no sublation could arise at a later time, and it would follow that such a cognition is not an error.
Nor is it non-existent, because that would entail the absence of any appearance, like a lotus in the sky;

nor is it of the nature of both existent and non-existent, because that would involve the occurrence of both faults and because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory in their essential nature.

"Therefore, this object manifested by the intellect cannot be described as either existent, non-existent, or possessing both properties; thus, it is the theory of the manifestation of an indescribable object (*anirvacanīyārthakhyāti*). This is an unexamined assertion, because it contradicts the very nature of the manifestation of that which appears. For instance, regarding the term "manifestation" (*khyāti*): does it employ the root *khyā* in the sense of "to speak" (*praka-thane*), or the root *khyā* in the sense of "to appear" (*prathane*)? In either case, it is entirely consistent that both the existent and the non-existent are both expressible and capable of appearing.

Indeed, it must be apprehended and spoken of by a sentient being; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even jars and the like are indefinable (anirvacanīya), just as non-existence is defined as non-existence. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence that even the absence of a jar and so forth would be indefinable.
Furthermore, if indefinability were admitted, then the cognition "this is silver" and its verbal designation would simply not arise at all.

For indeed, the very same silver previously perceived, though separated by space and other factors, appears there by virtue of similarity; therefore, the mention of "this is that" is what constitutes being expressible, while the non-mention of it is what constitutes being inexpressible.
Thus, the position of the theory of the manifestation of an indeterminable object (*anirvacanīyārthakhyāti*), even if it were plausible, is neither existent nor non-existent.

—By way of a consequence (prasaṅga), [it is said]: "Therefore, the cognition appearing as water in mirages has reality as its object; and thus, being correct, it would not be erroneous nor would it be sublated. (Bhāṣya & Āloka) [Objection: Is that cognition of the appearance of water in mirages directed toward reality? And if so, being valid, it would neither be erroneous nor subject to sublation.

Truly, it would not be sublated if the mirage were not of the nature of water and one did not perceive it as having the nature of water; but since one perceives it as having the nature of water, how could it be non-erroneous, or how could it be unsublatable?

Alas! The state of being water-natured in mirages—which are in reality of the nature of the absence of water—is certainly not real, for it is impossible for them to have the nature of water-nature without being non-different from the absence of water.
Nor is it non-existent, for the non-existence of one entity is not maintained to be another distinct entity; therefore, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Due to the mutual contradiction between existence and non-existence, the superimposed water in the mirage must be accepted as being truly indefinable (*anirvācya*). (Bhāmatī, p. 13)
The Vedāntins declare that which cannot be reached by the path of investigation through either existence or non-existence individually to be "inexpressible" (anirvācya); thus says Citsukha, p. 79.

Furthermore, regarding the term *khyāti* in the expression "the appearance of an indefinable object" (*anirvacanīyārthakhyāti*), does this [term] employ the root *khyā* in the sense of "to tell" (*prakathane*) or the root *khyā* in the sense of "to appear" (*prathane*)? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
133). Indeed, that [root] is to be stated as *yā*—(Bhāṣya, Ba., Ja.).
An examination of the theory of the apprehension of the indescribable (anirvacanīyakhyātivāda), which [posits] the absence of the intrinsic nature of a jar— Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 87.

This refutation of those who maintain the theory of the manifestation of an unreal object (*alaukikārthakhyāti*) in cases of error should be seen in *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 14, line 8; *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 133; and in other treatises of the dualist (*dvaitavādin*) schools.

Others maintain the theory of the appearance of an unreal object (*alaukikārthakhyāti*); for they say: since other theories of appearance, when examined in the manner described, are untenable, one must therefore accept the appearance of an unreal object—whether internal or external—whose nature remains unascertained.

This is not tenable when left unexamined, for what is this so-called "unworldliness" (*alaukikatva*) of the object? Is it its having a different form, its performing a different function, its being produced from a different cause, or its being produced without a cause? It cannot be "having a different form," because the very same form that appears in the case of the real (*satya*) appears in the case of the unreal (*asatya*) as well; and if it were to appear with a different form, then the appearance of an unworldly object would simply be another name for the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).

Nor can it be the performance of another action; for if one thing were to perform an action that is to be accomplished by another, it would follow that postulating other causes is useless, since all effects would arise from a single cause alone. By this, the position that [the effect] originates from another cause is also refuted. Furthermore, if it were to originate without a cause, would the object have the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) or the nature of non-existence (*asadrūpa*)? If it has the nature of existence, it follows that it must be eternal, because it is impossible for that which already exists to be produced from a cause and yet be non-eternal.

Now, if it is of the nature of non-existence (*asadrūpa*), how can there be a cognition of it in a positive form as "this is silver"? Indeed, even in a dream, a cognition of a jar in a positive form as "this is a jar" is never perceived when the jar is of the nature of non-existence. If, on the other hand, an object that is of the nature of non-existence is nevertheless cognized as being of the nature of existence due to some cause of error, then this would be a case of the manifestation of a contrary object (*viparītārthakhyāti*); it would not be the manifestation of an extraordinary object (*alaukikārthakhyāti*). Therefore, the position of the manifestation of an extraordinary object is also not tenable.
In that regard, it is said in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 187): "That which initiates worldly transaction is called 'worldly' (*laukika*), while the other is 'non-worldly' (*alaukika*).

[The question arises: Is this [otherness] the fact that the object has a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or that it performs a different purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), or that it is produced from different causes, or that it is not produced from causes at all? This is stated in the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 135).

"Arising without a cause" (*akāraṇaprabhavatva*)—this does not exist [in the case of] the manifestation of supramundane objects (*alaukikārthakhyāti*), according to the *Samīkṣā* on the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 187. (Note: Variants *bhā॰* for *nāsti*, *pra–* for *pra–*, *ba॰, ja॰* for *ba॰, ja॰*).
This is to be seen in such works as the *Praśastakanda*, page 181, and the *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 135, and so forth.

Thus, since the other theories of error (*khyāti*) described by others, when examined in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, are found to be untenable, it must be understood that here only the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) is valid. Regarding the objection against misapprehension: "But surely even misapprehension, when examined, is not tenable."

For instance: what is the object (*ālambana*) of that [cognition]—is it silver or mother-of-pearl? If it is silver, then this would be *asatkhyāti* (the manifestation of the non-existent) and not *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension), because the silver there is non-existent.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that the silver existing in another place and time appears there, and therefore there is no fault, that is incorrect; for if that were so, it would follow that the cognition could not arise with the specific verbal reference "this is silver."

Indeed, an ocular cognition cannot arise with respect to silver that is neither in that place nor at that time, nor when it is not in contact [with the senses]; otherwise, because of the consequence that it would arise everywhere, the entire universe would be its object. Therefore, this [cognition] does not have silver as its objective support (*ālambana*), nor does it have the mother-of-pearl; for it arises in the form of silver, and it is not logical for a cognition having one form to have something else as its objective support, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And if its objective support (*ālambana*) were the mother-of-pearl, how could it be an error?

In that case, if silver were the objective support, this would be precisely "the cognition of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*), not "the cognition of the contrary" (*viparītakhyāti*), because the silver there is non-existent;
or else, if it is argued that it exists in another place and time, [then the following applies].
What benefit is there for this [silver], which is not present here, by that [perceived] existence? (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

176). If it is [mere] gold, then this would indeed be the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), and not the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), because of the cognition of non-existent gold. (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 136).
Therefore, this is not a fault. [Bhāṣya:
"But when there is the perception of mother-of-pearl through visual cognition, it is indeed mother-of-pearl and not silver; what here is the meaning of 'error'? [Nyāyamañjarī, p. 177]
The refutation of that [objection] from the *Ratnākara* (p. 137) is as follows: To this, we reply.
As for what was asked—"What is the objective support (*ālambana*)? and so forth—let it be granted that silver itself is the objective support;
yet this does not entail the fallacy of "apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*). For silver exists in another location and so forth.

Indeed, in the theory of *asatkhyāti*, the appearance of an object that is absolutely non-existent is maintained; here, however, [the object] exists in another location and so forth. Thus, there is a great distinction between these two.

Now, one might object: "How can there be an appearance of silver—which is non-existent there and not in contact with the eye—as 'this'? But this too is untenable; for even though it does not belong to that place and time, its status as an object of appearance is possible through its presentation as being proximate due to the influence of a defect (*doṣa*). For this very reason, that cognition is an instance of "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*).

Nor should it be argued that if this [silver] belonging to a different place and time were apprehended, it would follow that the entire universe is apprehended; for we accept that its appearance is brought about by a memory evoked by the perception of a similar object.

Furthermore, the universe cannot be presented by that [consciousness], so how could there even be a suspicion of its apprehension? And what is called "presentation" is the external manifestation of an object flashing forth in the mind; it is not, however, like being brought forward while bound by a rope, as in the case of a sacrificial animal.

Nor, on this account, should this be called *ātmakhyāti* (self-manifestation) or *asatkhyāti* (manifestation of the non-existent); for here an object distinct from consciousness is manifested, and because there is no appearance of an object that is absolutely non-existent. (p. 64, l. 17)
Now, it might be objected here that this must be the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*); but this is not correct, because silver exists in another location and so forth.

For according to the position of *asatkhyāti*, since the object is absolutely non-existent there, what is the use of considering another location? What can we do, given that we observe the apprehension of an object precisely of such a nature [as it appears]?
However, that object which does not exist even in another place or at another time is never perceived, like a sky-lotus and so forth;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 184.
Because it is possible for silver [to appear] due to its production as such. (Ratnāvalī, p. 137) [Variant readings: *yattvopapatteḥ* (Ba, Ja)]
It has been stated here: "What appears here is silver brought to mind by a memory triggered by the perception of a similar object.
And this bringing to mind is not like leading an animal bound with a rope before someone; rather, it is the external manifestation of an object that is flashing within the heart.

Nor should it be said on this account that this is *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension) or *asatkhyāti* (apprehension of the non-existent); for there is the perception of [silver] as distinct from consciousness, and because there is no appearance of an absolutely non-existent object.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 184;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p.

138: "But surely, since cognitions such as 'this is silver' are of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*), they do not depend upon memory; how then can they manifest objects presented by that [memory]? This too is an unexamined statement; for that [cognition] lacks the nature of perception, as its essential character is that of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), consisting in the synthesis of a previously seen object and the one currently being seen, like the cognition "this is that very Devadatta."
Furthermore, since recognition has perception and memory as its causes, its dependence upon them is logical;

nor does the admission that this [cognition] is a recognition entail the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets, because cognitions such as "this is a tree" will be stated later to be of the nature of recognition.

Therefore, that which is established by mindfulness (smṛti) is the object (ālambana) of this cognition: either it is the mother-of-pearl itself, whose own form is concealed and which has assumed the form of silver; for it is "one whose own form is concealed" because of the absence of the perception of specific features such as its triangularity, and it is "one which has assumed the form of silver" because the form of silver has been superimposed through the recollection of silver produced by the sight of similar properties such as its glittering luster.

"How can a cognition having the form of silver have a mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) as its objective support (*ālambana*), since that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?"—this too is not a valid objection; for that which is pointed out by the finger or other means as being the object (*karman*) is called the objective support of the cognition, and that [objective status] certainly exists in the case of the mother-of-pearl. Otherwise, how could it be required by that cognition? For it must necessarily be required by this [cognition]; otherwise, the cognition of it would arise even in its absence.

And it must be considered whether this dependence [of the cognition] occurs by way of being a cause or by way of being an object? It cannot first be by way of being a cause; for, just as in the absence of light, so too in the absence of the mother-of-pearl, the cognition of silver would not arise, and thus one would have to bid farewell to the cognition of real silver. Therefore, since dependence here is untenable by way of being a cause, it is logical only by way of being an object. Now, if the mother-of-pearl appears here in the form of silver, then because silver is non-existent, this would be an "apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*); that is incorrect, because similarity is what is required here.

For this cognition arises in dependence upon a form that is white and lustrous, which is common to silver; however, the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) does not arise in dependence upon similarity, like the apprehension of a sky-flower in the sky.

Thus, since the invalidity of erroneous cognition—which consists in the nature of the apprehension of the contrary (*viparītakhyāti*)—is established, it is well said [in the verse]: "the cause of doubt and error," and so forth.
Therefore, let it be the position that "it is the mother-of-pearl itself that appears here, its own form being concealed and the form of another being apprehended" (Nyāyamañjarī p.
Syādvādaratnākara p. 138).

And because there is no apprehension of specific qualities such as triangularity and so forth, it is said to have its own form concealed; and because of the recollection of the specific features of silver, it is said to have assumed the form of silver—Nyāyamañjarī, p.
185 (variant reading: *śubhā*).

However, there is no fault in defining the objective support (*ālambana*) as that which, being pointed out by the finger with the words "this is it," generates a cognition as its object (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 138).

Commentary on the Exposition:

It is not merely because of the non-contradiction of its existence that knowledge which causes doubt or error is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is also because of the non-contradiction of the existence of such knowledge as that which is ineffective—such as the knowledge of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) or the capacity to attain heaven (*svarga*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even the knowledge of momentary destruction being valid, in which case inference (*anumāna*) regarding it would be useless.
[The opponent objects: "But surely that [knowledge] is not a valid means of cognition because it does not produce certainty. To this, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.

For indeed, the mere cognition of reality—that is, the ultimate truth—is not the means for determining the object as it truly is; rather, it is only a specific [cognition] that serves this purpose, and that alone is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As it has been said: "Only in that case where it produces this [cognition] does it possess the status of a *pramāṇa*. Regarding this, another—such as Diṅnāga and others—offers the following reply:
"By that also," and so forth.

Not only by one who maintains that validity belongs solely to the cognition of reality, but even by that very person such as Dignāga and others, the validity of only that cognition which is of a determinate nature and is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the ascertainment of reality must be established, out of fear of the aforementioned defects. This is because only that [determinate cognition] is the most effective means toward that [ascertainment]; otherwise, its dependence upon it would be untenable. However, validity cannot be established for the mere cognition of reality or for [the causal factors] such as sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), because those are absent [in the case of erroneous cognition].

If it is argued that validity might still be established for that [mere cognition] because it is the cause of that [determinate cognition], the author replies with the words "by the force of the object" (*vastubala*) and so forth.

Experience is established through the power of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as it arises from the force of the real object (*vastu*); the cause of that experience is contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth; and the cause of that contact is specific food, place, and so forth, because in their absence, conceptualization would be impossible. Furthermore, that contact, food, and so forth, arise from the force of the real object; therefore, they are distinct from that experience itself, for it is not only experience that is logically established as its cause, but also [the factors] that produce conceptualization.
How so? He says: "by way of a succession" (*paramparayā*).

For instance: there is the contact with a specific object of food, place, and so forth; from that arises experience (*anubhava*); from that arises conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, since this [conceptualization] is also produced by that [contact], it would follow that it too possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But such is not the case. Thus, he states the conclusion regarding the subject at hand: "Therefore, not... and so forth.

Because it is thus, therefore, non-cognition (*ajñāna*) does not possess the status of a means of valid cognition for itself or for others, because it depends upon another means of valid cognition. "Non-cognition" refers either to non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakadarśana*) or to direct contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like; its status as a means of valid cognition does not exist.

Is it that [valid cognition] does not belong to him at all? To this he says: "Except for figurative usage (*upacāra*), it does not exist primarily (*mukhyataḥ*); it exists figuratively. This is the meaning.
Then, to whom does validity belong primarily? To this he says: "Of knowledge alone," and so forth.
It is of cognition alone, and not of anything else such as indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*), that [this applies].

Of what kind? Of that which is vividly manifesting—that is, which possesses a clear appearance of its own and other natures by not looking toward another source. This is its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) or its nature as the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇatā*). As for anything else, which is not vividly manifesting, there is indirectness (*parokṣatā*) or the nature of indirect means of knowledge (*parokṣa-pramāṇatā*).
Regarding "error" (*viparyāsa*), another Buddhist says here: "Its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) exists only where it produces that [cognition]"; this is the view of Dharmottara.

An exposition of the Cārvāka doctrine that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, since another means of valid cognition distinct from perception is impossible, of what could a "parokṣa" (indirect) nature be predicated? For perception alone is the means of valid cognition because it is non-derivative (*agauṇatvāt*), whereas inference is not, for the opposite reason. To explain: the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a logical reason (*hetu*) is its subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). And the subject consists of a composite of the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*). If that [composite] is not ascertained, how can there be an ascertainment of its being a property thereof? Or, if it is ascertained, inference is redundant.

Therefore, in order to establish the conventional usage of "property of the subject" (pakṣadharma), the word *pakṣa*, although conventionally fixed (*ruḍha*) for the whole [of the three-part collection], must be applied metaphorically (*upacaraṇīya*) to its single part, the locus (*dharmin*). Consequently, the subject (*pakṣa*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), and the reason (*hetu*) is also secondary; for that which is a property of the locus is called "the property of the subject. Thus, because it is of a secondary nature, or because it is produced by secondary causes, inference is secondary.
And so they say: "Because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not secondary, the ascertainment of an object from inference is difficult to obtain" (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 118).
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 179;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 554; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 45, upper section.

Therefore, in order to establish the conventional usage of the "property of the subject" (pakṣadharma) and its "concomitance" (anvaya), the word *pakṣa*—which is conventionally established as referring to the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*)—must be described as applying figuratively (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) to that one part of it, namely the subject alone. Furthermore, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the ascertainment of an object (*arthaniścaya*), yet such ascertainment of an object is difficult to obtain through inference (*anumāna*). To explain: inference is the cognition of another object based on an object already being cognized. Now, would the cognized object be the indicator (*gamaka*) of another object that is either related to it or unrelated? It cannot be the case that it indicates what is unrelated, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, regarding that which is related: from what source is the establishment of that relation—through perception or through inference? It cannot be through perception, because perception, having its range restricted to specific places, times, and forms, lacks the capacity to grasp a universal relation.
Nor can it be through inference, because that would lead to an infinite regress; for even inference proceeds only when a relation has already been grasped.

Furthermore, it is impossible to ascertain with certainty a universal necessary connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) among objects that perform distinct causal functions and possess distinct capacities due to differences in state, place, and time; for even though astringency is observed in the *āmalakī* fruit in thousands of instances, sweetness is also perceived when it is sprinkled with milk and other substances.

As it has been said: "Because of differences in state, place, time, and so forth, the capacities of entities vary; thus, the cognition [of their nature] through inference is extremely difficult to achieve."
