(Vākyapadīya 1.34) Furthermore, would the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*), or the aggregate of the two be the probandum (*sādhya*) in inference? Among these, the first position is untenable; for since the subject is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would follow that the proof is redundant, and there would also be the consequence that the logical reason (*hetu*) lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Indeed, there is no such positive concomitance as "wherever there is smoke, there is a mountain."

Even in the second alternative, would the property (*dharma*) to be proven be of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) or of the nature of a particular (*viśeṣa*)? In that regard, if it were of the nature of a universal, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because there is no disagreement among anyone regarding mere fire. Furthermore, there is no purpose in the cognition of that [universal], for the "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) is not perceived as being useful for burning or cooking, nor is "cowness" (*gotva*) perceived as being useful for carrying loads or milking. Moreover, how could one who acts based on a cognized universal necessarily act only toward a specific direction? For a universal does not possess a fixed direction, as that would entail the consequence of its lack of pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*).

Now, since a universal is not possible without an individual, once that [universal] is cognized, the cognition of the individual occurs through the principle of "otherwise being impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*), and thus activity proceeds according to a specific direction. But is it impossible without a specific intended individual, or with any individual in general? It cannot be with a specific intended one, because the universal can exist even in another individual. And if there is a cognition of an individual in general, another effort must be made for the sake of cognizing the intended individual; and regarding that [second effort], the same objection applies, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, if a specific form (*viśeṣarūpa*) were the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be no positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) for the reason (*hetu*). For instance, in an inference such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," where a specific fire—characterized by being made of *khadira* wood and so forth—is the probandum, the concomitance of the reason with that specific probandum is not possible; this is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and the like with such a specific probandum has never been perceived in the kitchen (*mahānasa*) or other such places.

Moreover, since contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*), the sublation of what is desired (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*), or the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) fallacy could be suspected in every inference, a specific form cannot be the probandum either.
Therefore, even a property (*dharma*) is not the probandum.

Nor is it the collection of those [two]; for that too lacks positive concomitance elsewhere, since the positive concomitance is not perceived in the form: "Wherever there is smoke, there is a mountain possessing fire. As it has been said: "When the subject (*dharmin*) is the probandum, the reason lacks positive concomitance; for the positive concomitance is not 'wherever there is smoke, there is a mountain'."
Furthermore, in inference, would the subject (dharmin), the property (dharma), or their aggregate be the probandum (sādhya)? [Syādvādamañjarī, p. 262]—you say: [Bhāṣya].
It proceeds... [the text] occurs here now... (variants: *pravartate* in Ba, Ja; *tīrtir-di-* in Bhā; *hy-atredānīm-* in Ā, Ba, Ja).
Furthermore, since contradiction with inference and the presence of contradictory reasons are possible in every proof, as well as the case of the non-deviant contradictory (viruddhāvyabhicārin).
Furthermore,

since the contradiction of inference— known by the other name "contradictory with respect to the particular" (*viśeṣaviruddha*), which destroys the intended [conclusion]— or the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), which is a cause of doubt, is possible in every inference due to its subverting the object of the fundamental inference, validity would be difficult to attain (Svārthānumāna-ratnākara, p. 263).

"It brings about the subversion of what is intended [by the proponent] by proving the opposite, even though that intended [point] was not explicitly stated by words"—this is the definition of *iṣṭavighātakṛt* (the subverter of the intended), Nyāyabindu p.

103. "When two reasons, each possessing its own defining characteristic, are presented together regarding a single subject as being contradictory—that is, as proving mutually opposed probanda—this is the *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-erroneous contradictory). This is the definition of the *viruddhāvyabhicārī*, Hetubinduṭīkā p. 204.

The contradictory non-deviant (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," and "Sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). Since both are causes for doubt, these two together constitute a single inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*). As stated in the *Nyāyapraveśaka* (p. 4): "That which contradicts what has been established by another reason, yet does not deviate from it, is the contradictory non-deviant."

Alternatively, it is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves a property that is the opposite of what is established by another means of proof; and it is "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārī*) because it does not deviate from its own probandum. Thus, it is a "contradictory non-deviant" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*). [Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 111] Since both [of these characteristics] are impossible when the subject is to be proven as qualified by a property, smoke cannot first be perceived as having the nature of being a property of the mountain qualified by fire.

Nor can there be such positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—as in the logic [of the Nyāyamukha], "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire on the mountain"—because there is no following through (*anugama*) in the particular case, and because it would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the general case. Since that which possesses [the property] (*tadvat*) is untenable, how can there be any talk of inference? (1)
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 109; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 263:

"If [the probans] resides in the universal (*sāmānya*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); if it resides in the particular (*viśeṣa*), there is a lack of concomitance (*anugamābhāva*). *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 71: "In the universal, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). *Tattvopaplavasiṃha*, p. 88; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 45, upper section; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 554.

In the *Ṭippaṇī* on the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 45, note 20, it is stated: "But inference would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to the absence of certainty; therefore, the completion of the second half [of the verse] is seen in this form, as they say: 'There is a lack of concomitance (*anugama*) in the particular (*viśeṣa*), and in the universal (*sāmānya*), there is the proving of what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*);
thus, the elephants that are the proponents of logic (*vādi-dantinaḥ*) have sunk into this mire of the collapse of inference.'"
Śāstradīpikā, p. 63:

Because it is vitiated by such defects as "the absence of positive concomitance (anugama) in the particular" and "proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā) in the universal," there is no valid inference for us.

To place one's trust in a relationship based on mere concomitance (sāhacarya) is ignorance; for even if that [concomitance] is observed a hundred times, the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra) remains. (2)
In objects whose natures vary according to differences in place, time, and state, a rule of invariable concomitance cannot be easily established. (3) And as stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p.
119): "Even if invariable concomitance exists, it cannot be determined without an examination of all things existing throughout the three worlds. (4)
As long as all individual instances of smoke and fire have not been directly perceived, there may still be room for the doubt that "this smoke might even be from something other than fire.
(5) But for those like you who perceive the entire universe through direct perception—what need is there for inference for those possessed of divine vision?
(6) [The purpose of inference for them: Nyāyamañjarī, p. 119.
Nor is there a certainty of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) even by means of a universal (sāmānya), for no such thing as a real universal exists at all.

(7) Furthermore, pervasion (vyāpti) cannot be established even as something accessible through repeated observation; for even if it is observed a thousand times, deviation (vyabhicāra) may still be ascertained. (8) [Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, p. 119]
Even if the nature of an object has been ascertained as being such-and-such through repeated observation, it may nevertheless appear otherwise due to differences in place, time, and other factors.

(9) Furthermore, while smoke may be understood to be concomitant with fire through repeated observation, the fact that it does not exist where there is no fire cannot be known through repeated observation alone. (10)
Nor is [the concomitant] a prover merely by virtue of being unobserved; for its necessity in that very [locus] is preceded by the absence of anything other than that.
Nor [is it a prover] merely by virtue of being observed. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 119)

In that regard, once the restriction (*niyama*) has been apprehended as a constituent part of inference, it is then realized; and the apprehension of this [restriction] does not occur without the certainty of its non-existence elsewhere. Having apprehended the restriction as a constituent part of inference, it is realized.
"Furthermore, the restriction [of the probans to the subject] is a constituent of inference" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
120); and "it is restricted" (Bhāṣya).

If it is argued that the apprehension of a rule [of concomitance] occurs through observation and non-observation, that too is incorrect; for indeed, the non-observation of smoke in the absence of fire is accepted [by us].

(13) And how much of the entire world is devoid of fire? Non-yogins do not perceive the non-existence of smoke there. (14) Furthermore, everything would be non-fire... [Ratnākaraśānti, *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa*, p. 264]
Or there would be a contradiction with inference, or it would subvert what is desired, or a non-erroneous contradictory [reason] (viruddhāvyabhicārī) would arise easily in every case. (16) [Note:
*iṣṭa-* appears as *iṣṭa-* in the manuscripts b, ja, and the Nyāyamañjarī (p.
120); *viruddhāvyabhicāraḥ* appears in the Syādvādaratnākara (p. 264).]
Or there is the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), as in *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 120.
For this very reason, not seeing the validity of inferences, the wise have said this for the purpose of prohibiting reliance upon them:

"These seventeen [verses] were cited in the *Nyāyamañjarī* on pages 119 and 120 under the heading 'api ca'; however, in the *Syādvādaratnākara* on pages 263 and 264, they are cited with the exception of the second and the final verses."
"Perception alone is the valid means of knowledge because it is non-derivative"— this is the refutation of that [position].
Here, the following rebuttal is offered:

As for what was stated—that perception alone is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—that is an unexamined assertion. Since non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*) is the defining characteristic of a valid means of knowledge, and since that [characteristic] exists in inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, how can the restriction "perception alone is the valid means of knowledge" be tenable? For instance: inference is a valid means of knowledge because it is non-contradictory, just like perception.

Indeed, the validity of perception is not established through anything other than non-contradiction; and this is no different in other cases, because contradiction is impossible regarding an object already understood through inference and the like.

16: "For even in the case of perception, one who maintains that it is a means of valid cognition cannot point to any other basis for establishing its validity than non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*)," *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 428.

Regarding what was stated concerning inference as well—that it is not figurative (*agauṇatvāt*)—from what reason is inference considered figurative? Is it because its nature is indistinct (*aviśadasvabhāvatvāt*), because it depends on another for the ascertainment of its own object (*svārthaniścaye parāpekṣatvāt*), because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādakatvāt*), because it is preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvakatvāt*), because it does not arise from the object itself (*arthādanutpadyamānatvāt*), because its object is not a real entity (*avastuviṣayatvāt*), because of the metaphorical application of the word "subject" (*pakṣa*) to the locus (*dharmī*), because it is sublated (*bādhyamānatvāt*), or because of the absence of a means of valid cognition that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans? In this regard, it cannot first be due to its nature being indistinct; for clarity (*vaiśadya*) is not a defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For if that were the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, since inference and the like would be excluded from it, their validity would be negated along with that exclusion, and thus their invalidity would be established. However, this is not its definition; for even though clarity (*vaiśadya*) exists in the cognition of a double moon and such, validity is impossible [therein]. Furthermore, dependence on another for the ascertainment of its own object is also impossible for this [perception], because, like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is independent of another in ascertaining that object.

The dependence on another for the ascertainment of an object in the case of inference during the stage of non-familiarization (*anabhyāsa*) is equally present in the case of direct perception as well.

Furthermore, its non-conformity [with reality] is untenable; for since non-conformity is impossible regarding an object correctly apprehended by valid inference (*samyaganumāna*), it is logical that if non-conformity occurs regarding an object apprehended by a fallacy of inference (*tadābhāsa*), that [fallacy] alone should be considered secondary (*gauṇa*) and not anything else. Otherwise, because non-conformity is observed in the case of a fallacy of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), it would follow that even true perception (*satyapratyakṣa*) would be secondary. Moreover, the claim that inference is preceded by perception is unestablished, because it will be stated later that inference is preceded by the means of knowledge called *ūha* (presumptive reasoning).

Furthermore, inference arises from the mark (liṅga) alone; how then could its production from perception be possible, since the function of perception consists solely in the apprehension of that mark? Or, let it be granted that its production is indeed from perception; even so, there is no secondary status (gauṇatva) for it, because it possesses the same causal complex (sāmagrī). For if that which arises from its own causal complex were considered secondary, it would follow that perception itself would also be secondary. (Page 67, Line 16)

Now, its lack of authority is asserted—whether because its own nature is indistinct, because it depends on something else for the determination of its own object, because it is preceded by perception, because it does not arise from the object itself, because its object is non-existent, because it is sublated, or because there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans (Syādvādaratnākara, p.

266). For just as perception does not depend on inference or other means for the direct determination of its own object, so too inference does not depend on perception for the ascertainment of the inferable (*anumeya*); [rather, it] conceives [it] independently.

Furthermore, because this [inference] is preceded by the means of valid cognition known as *ūha*, its being preceded by perception (*adhyakṣa*) is unestablished. (Pramāṇaparīkṣā, p. 64; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 266)

Furthermore, if inference were secondary because it is preceded by perception, then perception would also necessarily be secondary because it is sometimes preceded by inference; for we observe that the activity of perception is indeed preceded by inference in the case of one who acts after having ascertained the object to be proven through inference. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 46, top; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 267)

If its secondary status were due to its not arising from an object, then that consequence would apply to perception as well; for it will be demonstrated that perception also does not arise from an object.
Furthermore, its having a non-entity as its object is unproven, because—just like perception—it has as its domain an object consisting of both the universal and the particular.
For the Jains do not accept, as the Buddhists do, that inference has as its object a non-existent *apoha*; for that [notion] will be refuted therein.

Even by virtue of the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the word "pakṣa" (the subject) to the *dharmin* (the locus), its status as secondary (*gauṇatva*) is not established; for that metaphorical usage is intended merely for the sake of brevity in the formulation of the statement.

Indeed, for the authors of definitions who compose their language with concision, the inference does not become secondary merely through the metaphorical application of the word "pakṣa" to the *dharmin*, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, as for being "sublated" (*bādhyamānatva*), is this the case for a valid inference or for a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*)? The first alternative is untenable, because sublation is impossible in the case of an inference of fire and so forth from a valid means of proof such as smoke.

However, when sublation (*bādha*) is impossible for a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*), it is logical that its status as secondary (*gauṇatva*) belongs to that very [fallacy] and not to a valid inference (*samyaganumāna*); otherwise, since sublation is observed in the case of a fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), it would follow that even a valid perception would have to be considered secondary.

Furthermore, the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans is unproven, because such an apprehension is well-established through the means of valid cognition known as *tarka*.

And thus, the argument that perception or inference would function to grasp that relationship has been refuted; furthermore, we shall explain later how its capacity for apprehending universal relationships is established. Moreover, if inference were invalid because it is preceded by perception, then perception itself would also incur invalidity, since some perceptions are likewise preceded by inference (Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 267).
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
46, l. 1: "Like perception, because its object is an entity consisting of both the universal and the particular," Syādvādaratnākara, p. 267.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
45, u.: "of that object"—Ā., Bhāṃ.; "will be refuted"—Ba., Ja.

Even if the terms "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth have been used figuratively by commentators, how can the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) thereby become figurative? For if its definition is stated by means of another word, there is no lapse such as figurativeness;
[as stated in] *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 123, regarding inference (*tarka*).

Furthermore, regarding the understanding of affirmation and negation—such as "perception alone is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not inference"—is this capacity found in perception itself, or in a mark (*liṅga*) such as "non-derivativeness" (*agauṇatva*)? It cannot belong to perception; for that [cognition] arising from the causal complex of the sense organs and so forth is not capable of establishing the point that "I alone am the valid means of knowledge, not inference," since its capacity is possible only for the apprehension of specific forms and other such objects.
Nor is the capacity of the mark "non-derivativeness" and so forth established in that regard, for its validity is untenable if inference is not a valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, for one who establishes [reality] by means of what is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), the consequence follows that he is insane; for it is not logical to establish an object of cognition (*prameya*) without a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Moreover, for one who accepts that "perception alone is the valid cognition," is it perception in its entirety that is accepted as the valid cognition, or a specific instance of it? In the first case, there is the consequence that even the perception of two moons and so forth would possess validity.

But regarding the second position, what is this so-called "specificity" (*tad-viśeṣa*)? If it is said to be "conformity with reality" (*yathārthatā*), then when another person is being instructed that perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when it is conforming to reality and not otherwise, one must first set aside certain individual instances of perception and accept those that are conforming to reality, and then demonstrate: "If perception is of such a kind, it is a valid means of knowledge, but not if it is otherwise. And this cannot be demonstrated without another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), for it is certainly not possible to demonstrate this by means of individual instances of perception that are restricted to objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) existing in the present and located in front of one.

Furthermore, the person to be addressed is ascertained to be distinct from pillars and the like by virtue of possessing intelligence, and is capable of grasping the meaning of what is being communicated; yet, regarding that ascertainment, nothing other than inference has the capacity [to establish it], since perception has the capacity only for the apprehension of objects possessing form and so forth,
having set aside [the case of] that which is present before one.

Furthermore, if inference is not accepted, how can there be a negation of heaven, the unseen force (*apūrva*), deities, and so forth—along with the objects of knowledge distinct from the means of knowledge established by oneself—given that perception lacks the capacity for this? Moreover, if an object of knowledge were established without a means of knowledge, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the denial of inference must be based either on the non-existence of its essential nature or on the absence of its faultless definition. It cannot be due to the non-existence of its essential nature, because that nature is well-known to all the world.

It is not reasonable to deny that nature which is well-known to the entire world, just as one cannot deny the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since the nature of inference (*anumāna*) is likewise well-known to the entire world, this [nature] is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For even women, children, cowherds, and others perceive, without hesitation, the cognition of one object—such as fire—from another object—such as smoke. How could there not be a contradiction with one's own words for one who, while denying its nature, asserts that "direct perception alone is the means of valid knowledge because it is non-derivative"?

And it has been said: "Because the existence of the general categories of valid cognition and its opposite is understood through another cognition, and because of the negation of the existence of any other means of valid cognition, [there is no need for a further means] regarding any object of knowledge" (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 46, l. 1).
*Sammatti-ṭīkā*, p. 554;
*Syādvāda-ratnākara*, p. 268:

Is this merely a rejection of the very nature of inference (*anumāna*), or is it a rejection of its definition as characterized by those logicians? In that regard, the nature of inference is indeed impossible to deny, because it is well-established among all people.
Even women, children, cowherds, plowmen, and others understand that from one certain object another object necessarily follows without doubt;
[this is] the *Nyāyamukha*, p. 120.
According to the *Ratnākara* (p.
268), that is not [the case] because its own nature is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, the claim that there is an absence of a faultless definition [of inference] is also untenable; for a faultless definition of it—such as "inference is the cognition of the probandum from the probans"—will be established later on. Moreover, if the definition formulated by others is faulty, then let one state one's own faultless version instead; however, it is not proper to deny the object of definition (the inferential process) itself out of hatred for that [other] definition. For a discerning person does not discard their clothing out of fear of lice.
Thus, inference is the cognition of the probandum from the probans.
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 400 (first part):

Thus, since it is established by experience, just like the nature of inference itself, the definition of that [inference] composed by the technical experts is unexpressive; let that faultless definition be made known by itself, but it is not proper, out of hatred for it, to deny the object of definition—namely, inference.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 123.

As for what was also stated—"due to differences of state, place, time, and so forth"—that too is mere words; for when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been correctly ascertained through the means of valid cognition known as *ūha*, there can be no subversion [of that pervasion]. It is indeed the fault of the cognizer in that case, not of inference (p. 68, l.
7), because there is no subversion when the pervasion has been correctly ascertained. It is indeed the fault of the cognizer in that case, not of inference.
Nyāyamañjarī, p.
123. They say: "This is the fault of the cognizer who does not perceive the distinction;
there is no defect in inference, for it is non-deviant with respect to the object of cognition."

As for what was stated [in the *Ratnākara*], namely that "there is an absence of concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to the particular (*viśeṣa*)," etc.; that too is incorrect. For, depending on the time of the formulation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the probandum (*sādhya*) differs:

as he will state, in the case of pervasion the probandum is the property (*dharma*), whereas at the time of the formal argument (*prayoga*) it is the locus (*dharmī*) qualified by that [property]. In that case, how could there be an absence of concomitance, or how could there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?
The property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), or in some cases the property qualified by it, [is the object of inference]; *Parīkṣāmukha* 3.1.8.
But in the case of pervasion (vyāpti), the property to be proven (sādhya) alone [is the object], according to the *Parīkṣāmukha*. 3.25.

32. Furthermore, as for that which was stated elsewhere—"because in every inference, contradictions with other inferences and so forth are possible," and so on—that too is incorrect; for when a valid proof is employed, contradictions with other inferences and the like are impossible.

Indeed, when a proof such as smoke is employed to establish that a mountain possesses fire, there can be no occurrence of a contradiction with an inference—such as "this mountain does not possess fire because it is a mountain, like other mountains"—nor of a non-erroneous contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) such as "it does not possess fire here because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen. Nor is there the possibility of a sublation of the intended [conclusion], since the proof of smoke establishes the presence of fire in the mountain just as it establishes the presence of fire in a place devoid of roots and trees, given that this is observed in kitchens and similar locations; for such cases are merely fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*) due to their being contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition.

Indeed, only that which is an unimpeded means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is fit to be either a prover or a sublater of something, and nothing else, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, since it is established that inference and the like are distinct means of valid cognition, it is well said that "the indistinct manifestation [of an object] constitutes its being beyond the senses" (*parokṣatā*).
Thus, because perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the beyond-the-senses (*parokṣa*) possess distinct essential natures, their mutual difference is proven.

Between two things whose natures are distinct, there is a mutual difference, as in the case of water and fire; and since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition (*parokṣa*) possess distinct natures by virtue of being manifest and otherwise [unmanifest], when the probative reason is employed, there is no room for such [objections]. (Page 69, Line 4)
There is neither a contradiction by a specific [property] nor a subversion of what is desired, because the reason is well-established; these [fallacies] are not applicable here. (Nyāyamukha, p. 124)

In the case of inference functioning by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*), a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is not possible; *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 430, commentary.

If it is asked, "What, then, are the clarity and lack of clarity of cognition, by possessing which there would be a distinction between perception and other [means of knowledge]?", it is said in reply:
The manifestation of particulars apart from inference and the rest is considered the clarity of cognition; that which is beyond this is its lack of clarity. (Verse 4)
Clarity (*vaiśadya*) is the appearance [of an object] without intervention by another cognition or as possessing specific characteristics;
*Parīkṣāmukha* 2.4.
"Clarity (*spaṣṭatva*) is the manifestation of particulars through the predominance of inference and so forth," according to *Pramāṇanayatattvāloka* 2.3.
Clarity (*vaiśadya*) is manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantvena*), according to the *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p.
114; [and] the *Jainatarkavārttika-vṛtti*, p. 95.
Clarity is the manifestation [of an object] without dependence on other means of valid cognition; this is the definition of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
(Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1)
Commentary: Among these, conventional perception consists of sensory and non-sensory direct cognition; the primary [perception] is supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*).
That exists because it possesses a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is well-ascertained and free from any possible sublation, just like pleasure and so forth.

Because it is impossible to have complete knowledge of an assembly of all persons without knowledge that pervades the entire range of the knowable, there is no one who knows the reality of that absence [of such omniscience], since such a person is unperceived, like a sky-flower.

Neither Jaimini nor anyone else is a knower of the reality of that absence, because they possess qualities such as being a sentient being, being human, and being a speaker, just like an ordinary man on the street.

If such an excellence in a person were possible, why could he not be a seer of supersensuous objects? To this, [the opponent] replies: "Since you do not accept non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), on what basis would you establish the absence of specific qualities such as omniscience? [The response is: Because there is no difference [between the two cases], doubt arises there due to the absence of both proving and refuting evidence; this has already been answered. Since a refuter is simply impossible, the conventional usage of existence and non-existence is established everywhere by the presence or absence of a refuter. Doubt arises precisely from that doubt regarding the refuter, and for that very reason, the validity of experience is established. Enough of this digression.
Regarding the absence of contradiction— according to the commentary on the verse by Jaḍavṛtti:

that manifestation of particulars, which consist of specific forms such as color and configuration, characterized by the apprehension of objects either as distinct from or superior to inference and other means of knowledge, or in the form of determining an object endowed with a greater abundance of particulars, namely the forms of objects with their fixed locations, times, and configurations— that is intended here as the "clarity" (*vaiśadya*) of cognition.

That which is other than this—namely, the non-appearance of specific details—is "indistinctness" (*avaiśadya*). With respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), however, every cognition is indeed distinct, because the nature of all cognitions appears in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as a perfectly clear form.

As for the external object, however, it appears with a perfectly clear form to some cognitions, but to others in a manner contrary to that; therefore, their distinctness or indistinctness should be understood in relation to that [external object].

Since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), as the cognizer of all [cognitions], can somehow be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), everything is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in relation to it; there is nothing that is a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
(Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 246;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 170)

For the designation of cognitions as "perceptual" or "otherwise than perceptual" is made with respect to the apprehension of external objects; this is because, in that case, clarity or its opposite is possible due to the presence or absence of intervention by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is not, however, with respect to the apprehension of their own nature (*svarūpa*), because in that regard such [intervention] is absent. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
59; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 318).
Laghīyastrayavṛtti, p.
13; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 17; "all knowledge," Ā., Ba., Ja.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation:
This perception, characterized by the definition of clarity, is of two kinds—secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*).
Among these, he explains the secondary as "that which pertains to conventional usage" (*sāṃvyavahārika*), and so forth.
That which is employed in common worldly practice (*saṃvyavahāra*) is "empirical" (*sāṃvyavahārika*), meaning secondary.
What is that? It is sensory and non-sensory perception (*indriyānindriya-pratyakṣa*).

This is the meaning: that partial, clear cognition which is the effect of the sense organs (*indriya*), such as the eyes, and the non-sensory organ (*anindriya*), namely the mind (*manas*), is empirical, secondary perception.

[Objection: But surely, by the statement "perception through the sense-faculties and the non-sense-faculty," the description of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for conventional perception (*sāṃvyavahārika-pratyakṣa*) is improper, because its causes—the self (*ātman*), the object (*artha*), light (*āloka*), and so forth—are not included here. [Response: This is not so; for it is intended here to describe only those causes that are specific (*asādhāraṇa*) to perception. Now, it is impossible for the self or the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to be a specific cause of perception, since they are no different in relation to other cognitions. Nor can the object and light be such causes, because their status as causes of cognition will be refuted later.

Nor can it arise from sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth; for the causality of that [contact] has already been refuted previously, and because it is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), it cannot be its cause. Indeed, there is no contact between the eye and visible form, since the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*).
Furthermore, [contact] lacks universality (*pratyasādhāraṇatva*).
This concludes the presentation of the Naiyāyika position that "sense-object contact is the means of valid cognition" (*sannikarṣaḥ pramāṇam*).

But surely this proposition that [the eye] acts without reaching its object is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For instance: the eye acts by reaching [its object], because it is an external sense organ (*bāhyendriya*); whatever is an external sense organ is established as acting by reaching [its object], just like the skin and so forth; and the eye is an external sense organ; therefore, it acts by reaching [its object].
Nor is this reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*), since it occurs in the subject (*pakṣa*);
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), since it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it does not occur in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) as much as it does in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the mind (*manas*); for if it were stated simply as "because it is a sense-organ" (*indriyatvāt*), there would indeed be a deviation by way of the mind. To exclude that, the qualification "external" (*bāhya*) is employed.
Nor is it "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because its subject matter is not contradicted by perception or scripture;
nor is it "equally balanced" (prakaraṇasama), because there is no other reason that could initiate the investigation of the matter.

Now, it might be thought: "The eye exists only in the location of its physical base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and not elsewhere, because when the base is covered, there is no perception of objects. Whatever does not perceive an object when its base is covered exists only in the location of that base, just like the nose and other organs; and since the eye does not perceive an object when its base is covered, it must exist only in that location. Therefore, how could it have the property of reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*)? This too is not tenable. For what is the meaning of "only in the location of the base"? Does it mean (1) existing in the location of the base, or (2) being non-different from the base, or (3) not existing elsewhere than that? Among these, the first position is incorrect; for existing in the location of the base is not incompatible with reaching the object, since we do not observe a contradiction between the tactile organ (*sparśana*) and others existing in the location of their bases and yet possessing the property of reaching their objects.

The second alternative is also untenable, because the non-difference of the sense organ from its physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not established in any case; indeed, the non-difference of even the tactile organ and others from their bases is not admitted by both parties. The third position is also inconsistent, because it is possible for that [organ] to exist elsewhere than at the base;
for the base is merely the fleshy globe (*golaka*), while rays emanating from it extend as far as the location of the object, like rays issuing from a lamp.

The fact that the eye covers its own substratum and does not grasp objects [in contact] does not negate its *prāpyakāritva* (the property of functioning by reaching the object), because even though this [covering] exists in the case of the nose and other senses, it does not contradict their *prāpyakāritva*.
Furthermore, it is not unproven that the eye possesses rays (*raśmivat*), for there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes this:
namely, the eye has rays because it is composed of light (*taijasa*), like a lamp.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished for that very same reason; for instance, the eye is composed of light (taijasa) because, among color-form (rūpa) and the other [sensory objects], it illuminates color-form alone, just like [the sun]. Thus, since its possession of rays is established here, the objection that "if the eye functions by reaching [its object], there would be the consequence that large objects such as mountains would not be illuminated" is refuted. This is because, like the flower of the *dhattūra*, it is possible for what is initially minute to become large at the end;
therefore, the rays of the eye expand to the extent of the object when they meet with light, since otherwise the illumination of large objects such as mountains would be inexplicable.

Now, one might object: "If the eye functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*), how can there be a simultaneous perception of both the branch and the moon? But this is also trivial; for simultaneous perception is unproven. Indeed, the eye first reaches and illuminates the nearby branch, and only afterwards [reaches] the distant moon. The misconception of simultaneity, however, is based on an illusion, like the rapid piercing of a hundred lotus petals.

Even the conventional usage of "far" and "near" is not difficult to reconcile with the eye's functioning by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*); for since the proximity or remoteness of the visual object relative to the body is logically established, such usage is easily accounted for. If the eye were to function without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāri*), then it would illuminate objects such as a jar or even Mount Meru—even when separated by many hundreds of *yojanas*—just as it does when unobstructed by a wall, because in that case there would be no distinction between proximity and distance. But this is not the case; therefore, it must be understood that the eye functions by reaching its object.

Now, what is the proof for the eye having the property of acting by reaching its object? Its very nature as a sense organ [is the proof]: the eye acts by reaching its object because it is a sense organ, like the nose and so forth.
(Nyāyavārttika, p. 36;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 122)

The eye is not an illuminator of what it has reached, because it does not illuminate objects that are obstructed, like a lamp; and because it is an external sense organ, like the sense of touch (Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kandalī, p.
23). The eye and the ear perceive their objects by reaching them, because they are external sense organs, like the sense of touch.

In the *Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, page 73, some here say: "The eye does not act by reaching [its object], because it grasps objects not connected to its physical base (*adhiṣṭhāna*); this is incorrect, because the reason—'grasping objects not connected to its base'—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of a lamp.
(Śaṅkara’s *Kiraṇāvalī*, page 74).
The perception of that [object] occurs due to a specific contact between the rays [of light] and the object;
Nyāyasūtra 3.1.38.
The perception of those two large atoms occurs due to a specific kind of contact between the visual ray and the object, just as [the perception] of an object by the light-ray of a lamp;
thus it is stated in the Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 247.
The black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra) [eye] possesses rays, because, while being a substance, it is the instrumental cause for the perception of color in a fixed manner, like a lamp;
or alternatively, the eye possesses rays, because, while being a substance and possessing fixity, it illuminates objects obstructed by glass and the like, like a lamp.
(Nyāyavārttika, p. 381)

Its luminous nature (taijasatva), however, is [established] because it invariably manifests color among [the qualities] such as color and so forth, like a lamp; [as stated in] Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p.
525, and Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 40.

That sense organ which, while not manifesting odor and the like, manifests color, is fiery; and its being fiery consists in its manifesting color while not manifesting touch and the like, just like a lamp. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, Vyomavatī, p. 256; Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kiraṇāvalī, p.
73; Vaiśeṣikopaskāra, p. 128)

The eye is composed of light (*taijasa*), because, while not manifesting the touch and other qualities of another object, it manifests the color-form (*rūpa*) of another object, like a lamp (Muktāvalī, p. 176). Furthermore, its capacity to illuminate both the large and the minute is not a valid proof [for its luminous nature], as it is established otherwise; for instance, the dimension of the object arises from the contact of the externally projected visual organ with external light (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.
159), since even the perception of something larger [than the eye] is explained in the same way by the [organ's] having a broad tip (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī, p. 74).
As for the argument that "the branch and the moon are perceived at the same time," that too is not correct, because it is not admitted [by us].

For what person of sound mind would maintain that the branch and the moon are perceived simultaneously? This is a false cognition due to the non-apprehension of the difference between the two, like the [erroneous] perception of a hundred lotus petals being pierced one after another;
thus says the *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 35.
Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 120; Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 23;
Vyomavatī, p. 159.
In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-ṭīkā Kiraṇāvalī* (p.
74) and the *Muktāvalī* (p.

178), some describe the following solution regarding simultaneous cognition: "The visual rays, having become unified with the external light that exists simultaneously pervading all objects, are the cause of simultaneous apprehension."
Regarding this, others raise an objection: "If such reaching [of the object] is admitted, then the apprehension of objects even those extremely distant or obstructed would be unavoidable.
Others, however, say: "Because those rays travel so swiftly, the difference in time is not perceived, and thus there is the misconception of simultaneity.

Yet others do not accept that either, saying: "In the case of objects very close at hand, let us hope that the difference in time is not perceived—just as the piercing of a hundred lotus petals [appears simultaneous]."

Regarding objects situated on the earth separated by many thousands of *yojanas*, as well as the Pole Star (*dhruva*), the failure to determine them due to the difference in time does not satisfy the intellect; however, we say that there is no fault because of the dependence upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Even when the external light has become one with the rays of the eyes, only that portion of it which is acquired as a cause of perception through the power of the unseen force is capable of producing perception, and not the whole; thus, there is no simultaneous perception of everything, nor is there the establishment of seeing [objects] such as the earth and the Pole Star at once. (*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 45).
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that [the cognition of direction and place] arises "from the designation of direction and place"—that too is due to the body being the limiting factor (*avadhi*).
Where the sense-organ and the body are both connected with the object, there is no designation of direction and place, nor does there follow the perception of distance or proximity.

However, where only the sense-organ is connected [with the object], there, taking the body as the limit, for one who considers the lesser or greater number of intermediate contacts (*saṃyoga*) in the series of conjunctions, there arise cognitions of direction and place, as well as cognitions of "near" and "far."
*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 35;
*Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, p. 121:

Because the connection with the sense organ (*indriyasambandha*) is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), the two cognitions of "with an interval" (*sāntara*) and "without an interval" (*nirantara*) are not produced by the presence or absence of that [connection]. Rather, they are produced by the presence or absence of the connection with the body. Where there is the apprehension of an object connected to the body, there is the cognition "this is without an interval"; but where there is [the apprehension] of one not connected to it, there is the cognition "with an interval. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 24.

If the eye were operative without reaching its object (*aprāpyakārin*), then there would be no efficacy for obstructions such as walls or mats, and thus the impossibility of obstruction would follow; yet, there is no perception of objects that are concealed. Therefore, the eye is not operative without reaching its object.
Nyāyavārttika, p. 35;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 121;
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 479.

Furthermore, for those who claim that the eye is an agent, it would be difficult to prevent its grasping of objects both obstructed and distant; just as with a nearby object, even distant and extremely subtle objects would be clearly perceived. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
45; Nyāyamañjarī, p. 479)
[Objection: Why [is it] luminous? [Because] it is an agent (*kāraka*). Whatever is an agent acts by reaching [its object], such as an axe and so forth; and the eye is an agent.

Furthermore, as for the proof stated for its non-contacting agency (*aprāpyakāritva*)—namely, "because it does not manifest objects that are too close"—that is no proof at all because it is indistinguishable from the very point to be proven (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatvāt*).
For in the case of a relative negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*), that which constitutes its non-contacting agency is precisely what constitutes its failure to manifest objects that are too close.
However, a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is not accepted by the Jains, as it would entail the fallacy of contradicting their own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
An instrument, such as an axe, is observed to act by reaching its object, and the sense organs are likewise [instruments]; therefore, they must act by reaching their objects. (Nyāyavārttika, p.
36) It is indeed strange that something should be both an agent (*kāraka*) and yet act without reaching its object.

Because the sense organs function by reaching their objects due to their nature as causal agents (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 479); [and] because they function by reaching their objects due to their nature as causal agents (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 73).
The proof that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), preceded by a refutation [of opposing views]—here it is replied:

as for what was stated [by the opponent], namely, "because it is an external sense-organ" (*bāhyendriyatvāt*); in that regard, what is this so-called "externality of the sense-organ"? Is it (1) being directed toward the apprehension of external objects, (2) residing in an external location, (3) originating from external causes, (4) transcending the essential nature of a sense-organ, or (5) being other than the mind (*manas*)? Among these, in the first alternative, there is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*) due to the mind; for even though the mind functions without reaching its object, it possesses the status of an external sense-organ by virtue of being directed toward the apprehension of external objects.

Even in the second alternative, would the eye—whether in the form of rays or as having the nature of the eyeball (golaka)—be situated in an external location? Regarding the first position, what does its "being situated there" mean: is it being supported [by that location], or is it functioning as an illuminator? In the first case, there is a contradiction with your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*); for you do not admit that the eye in the form of rays is supported by an external location, since you have asserted that the rays have their support in the luminous substance (*tejodravya*) contained within the eyeball.

In the second alternative, however, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the eye as being of the nature of rays, and thus its functioning in external space as an illuminator is unproven.

Furthermore, the absence of such a means of valid cognition will be demonstrated in this very context, and the example is also devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because such a nature of being an external sense organ is impossible in the case of the skin and so forth.

Furthermore, if the eye, which is of the nature of a globular entity (*golaka*), were to reside in an external location, it would be contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*); for this [eye] is perceived through direct perception to exist precisely in a region of the body, not connected to the location of the object. Moreover, its being produced from an external cause is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even with respect to the mind itself; for in relation to the self (*ātman*), the "external cause" is the reality of matter (*pudgalatattva*), and the state of being produced from that exists for the mind just as it does for the sense organs such as the eye, since its material nature (*paudgalikatva*) will be established in the "Examination of the Six Categories" (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*). Furthermore, its being beyond the nature of a sense organ is untenable, as it would entail the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhāntaprasaṅga*).

Even the distinctness of the mind would be established only if the mind itself were established; however, that is not established, because the mind as conceived by you will be refuted during the examination of the six categories.

Or let it be established; nevertheless, "being an external sense organ" is defined as being a sense organ while being distinct from the mind (*manas*). In that case, the qualification "external" is inappropriate for the purpose of excluding the mind, because even the mind functions by reaching its object in all instances—whether in the case of pleasure and so forth, through relations such as inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), or in the case of pervasion (*vyāpti*), by producing that cognition through a relation of relations, just as the eye does in the case of color and so forth. Indeed, in the case of color and so forth, there is no relation other than a relation of relations for the eye and other [external senses] (p.
75, l. 12). [End of section on] the external sense organs. (Bhāṣya)
Is this orientation toward the apprehension of an external object, its existence in an external location, or its production from external causes? (Ratnāvalī p. 328; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
59, l. 1; Ratnākaraśānti p. 55).
—The state of being a substance (*raṇatva*) and the state of being a person (*pudgalavattva*).

For, with respect to the self (*ātman*), there is indeed an external cause consisting of the reality of the person (*pudgalatattva*), and the mind also possesses its origination from that [reality], just like the sense organs such as the eye;
[as stated in] *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 329.
—Regarding this, [the opponent says]: "The mind—" [Bhāṣya:

Is the eye, which is here taken as the substratum of the mind, of the nature of the physical globe (*golaka*), or of the nature of a ray? In the first case, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for the eye, being of the nature of the physical globe, is perceived by direct perception as being unconnected with the object and located in a region of the body itself, having abandoned the location of the object. Otherwise, the region of the eyelashes would be perceived as being devoid of it.

In the second case, however, there is the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmin*), because the eye in the form of rays is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For what could that proof be: perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be perception, because its own nature is not perceived therein as having an object; for rays are certainly not perceived through perception, as that would entail the consequence of there being no disagreement [regarding their existence]. Indeed, when something blue is perceived as blue, no one disputes it.

Furthermore, according to your view, perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises from the contact of a sense-faculty with its object. However, there is no contact of another sense-faculty with those [faculties] existing in the location of the object, such that perception could arise therein, for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For the same reason, can its establishment not occur even through inference (*anumāna*), either from this very [perception] or from something else? If it were from this very [perception], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for once the arising of inference is established, the establishment of perception occurs from it, and from the establishment of perception, the arising of inference occurs. If it were established from another inference, there would be an infinite regress, because it would entail the necessity of establishing the locus (*dharmin*) of that [inference] through yet another inference.

And here, is the eye taken as the subject (*dharmin*) in its nature as the physical orb (*golaka*), or in the form of rays? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 59, Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa p. 397, Syādvādaratnākara p.
In the *Ratnākara* (p. 52),
[it is stated that] "possessing dharma" (*dharmavat*) therein is according to the system of the *Yaugas*, in the manuscripts *ba* and *ja*.

Indeed, O Baṭu and Jaṭu, by this [argument], that inference establishing the rays—namely, "the eye possesses rays because it is composed of light"—is refuted, since the faults stated regarding the aforementioned position apply here without distinction.

Furthermore, is the possession of rays being established for the eye in the form of the eyeball (*golaka*), or for something distinct from it? It cannot be for something distinct from it, because its nature is unestablished and because it would entail the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

If, however, the eyeball (*golaka*) is the subject (*pakṣa*) for proving that [the eye is light], there is sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), because the eyeball is perceived through direct perception as being devoid of radiant light. Now, if it is argued that its rays are invisible because they possess non-manifest color and touch, and therefore there is no sublation by perception for this [position]; how then could it have the capacity to illuminate color? For instance, the eye does not illuminate color, because its color is non-manifest, like fire in contact with water;
nor is any substance of light ever perceived that possesses both non-manifest color and touch.

It is also incorrect to claim that there is a perception of the non-manifestation of both the brilliant color and the hot touch in water and gold; for even in those cases, the non-manifestation of both is not established.

Furthermore, the postulation of an unperceived object must follow what is observed; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that earth and other substances would likewise possess those qualities. For instance: earth and other substances possess rays because they are substances, like a lamp.
Just as being composed of light (taijasatva) is understood to be pervaded by the possession of rays in the case of a lamp, so too is the state of being a substance (dravyatva).
Now, if there is a contradiction with perception regarding their existence in that [human] case, that same [contradiction] applies elsewhere as well.

If, on the other hand, rays are perceived through direct perception in the eyes of cats and the like, how can there be a contradiction in that case? Even if they are indeed perceived there, what does that have to do with another instance? Otherwise, because one perceives yellowness in gold as being pervaded by its nature as gold, the presence of yellowness in cloth and other things would result in the establishment of their being gold—an absurdity that would apply equally elsewhere due to the sublation of perception.

Furthermore, if it possessed rays, there would be no need for it to depend upon light to illuminate objects. For instance: whatever possesses rays does not depend on light to illuminate objects, such as a lamp; and you maintain that the eye possesses rays. If it were so endowed with rays, it would follow that it illuminates even its own adjuncts, such as collyrium; for it is not the case—contrary to common experience—that a lamp, being possessed of rays, fails to illuminate the wick-stick or other items connected to it (p. 76, l. 5).
Is it established that the eyes of all beings are composed of light, like a lamp, because they possess the aforementioned defects? No; this would not prove that the eye is luminous.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 232;
*Rājavārttika*, page 48.
From the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 60a;
from the *Syādvādaratnākara*, folio 319—
[the word] "go" [is derived] from the limb, [manuscripts] ba and ja.
Furthermore, this ocular ray has unmanifest color; therefore, it is not perceived through direct perception.
And a distinction in the properties of light is observed: light with manifest color and touch is perceptible, as in the case of the rays of the sun;
and light with manifest color but unmanifest touch is perceptible, as in the case of the rays of a lamp.
That which has manifested touch but unmanifested color is imperceptible, such as fire in conjunction with water;
likewise, the ocular ray is imperceptible because its color and touch are unmanifested—Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 250.
In the *Nyāyavārttika* (p.
378), it is stated: "In the visual ray, there is no refinement of color (*rūpa-saṃskāra*) nor the manifestation of color;
and in the light of a torch at midday, there is a refinement of color but no non-overpowering of color. Therefore, these [rays] are not perceptible."
In the Vaiśeṣika Upaskāra, page 120: "Light is not observed when both [qualities] are unmanifested, since that is the case with the eye;
if it is argued that this is due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), why is it not the same for every sense organ?"
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 233; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 60a.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.
541: [The soul] possesses rays, because the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures are observed.
Nyāyasūtra 3.1.43:
"The non-existence of the effect [is established] by means of the non-perception of its cause."

Furthermore, if the eye of persons such as ourselves were to function by reaching its object, then one would see the collyrium-stick even when it is applied very close to the eye; and there would be clear perception of distant objects.

*Catuḥśatakavṛtti*, p. 186: The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever possesses rays necessarily illuminates the object with which it is connected, just like a lamp. And the eye possesses rays; therefore, it must necessarily illuminate [defects] such as jaundice (*kāmalā*) with which it is connected. Nor should it be asserted that there is no connection between the eye and these [defects] at all. For is the eye, in its nature as the eyeball (*golaka*), unconnected therein, or in its nature as rays, or in its nature as power (*śakti*)? Regarding the first alternative, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the eye in the form of the eyeball is perceived to be connected with glass and the like.

Even in the second case, its connection with that [object] certainly exists; for it is not the case that rays of light from a lamp situated inside a crystal jar, emerging from it, are not connected with what they contact or do not become illuminators of it.

Furthermore, as for the visual organ (*cakṣus*) in the form of a power (*śakti*), would it occupy a different location from the visual organ in the form of a manifest entity (*vyakti*), or the same location? It cannot occupy a different location, because that would entail the contradiction of it being a power [of that organ] and the consequence of it being without a substratum (*nirāśrayatva*);

for it is not logical that the power of one thing should have another thing as its substratum. Moreover, there would be the consequence that objects would be perceived through the very location of that [power].

Now, [if you say] it is in a location non-different from that [eye], is it connected to it there or unconnected? If it is connected, then like the external object, it would manifest its own substratum as well as the collyrium and so forth connected to it.
Or, if it is unconnected, how can it be called "located" (ādheya)? For that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
At the very least, let the external eye itself be seen, such as the black pupil and so on.
For one who perceives that the object has not been attained, there is sublation by perception due to the contradiction of what was [supposedly] attained;
if it is invisible in its form as potency, then there is sublation by inference.
By means of scripture and by one's own determination that there is no possible sublation [of the object], [the truth is established].

For would that [eye] be accepted as being of the nature of the physical orb (*golaka*), or of the nature of rays? If it were of the nature of the physical orb, then there would be sublation by direct perception (*adhyakṣabādha*), because this [orb] is perceived through direct perception as being devoid of luminous color and hot touch.

There is also sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*), as follows: the eye is not composed of light (*taijasa*), because it lacks radiant color and hot touch; whatever is such [lacking these] is not composed of light, like a lump of clay and so forth; and the eye lacks radiant color and hot touch, therefore it is not composed of light.

Likewise, the eye is not composed of light, because it illuminates darkness; whatever is composed of light does not illuminate darkness, like light; and the eye illuminates darkness, therefore it is not composed of light.

However, since the nature of the eye as consisting of rays is unestablished, its being composed of light (taijasa) is not tenable; indeed, it has already been stated that rays are not established through perception or other means of valid cognition.

[Objection: Surely, in the eyes of cats and other animals, the property of being an eye (*netratva*) is perceived as pervaded by the possession of rays (*raśmivattva*); therefore, in the case of others as well—such as human eyes—the possession of rays is established because they possess the property of being an eye, and from that, their luminous nature (*taijasatva*) is proven. [Reply: If that were so, then in the eyes of cows and other animals, the property of being an eye is perceived as pervaded by blackness (*kārṣṇya*), while in the eyes of men and women it is perceived as pervaded by whiteness (*dhāvalya*). Therefore, without distinction, either blackness or whiteness could be used to prove either their earthiness (*pārthivatva*) or their watery nature (*āpyatva*), since there is no difference [in the logic]. Furthermore, the eye is not luminous (*taijasa*), because it illuminates darkness (*tamaḥ-prakāśakatvāt*).
It would be [as stated in] the *Ratnāvalī*, folio 324— [the portion beginning with] "po" is not found in the Bhāṣya— [and it is] established in the Bhāṣya.

—Even regarding the eyes, [the argument] "because they possess the nature of the eyes of humans and so forth" (Bhāṣya)—and furthermore, that which was stated as a proof for their being composed of fire (*taijasa*), namely, "because among form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], they illuminate form alone"—that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to water, collyrium, the moon, rubies (*māṇikya*), and so on. Nor should it be said: "It is the rays of the eye themselves that, having reached water and the like, illuminate those [objects], and not the water and the like," for this would result in the futility of the observed cause in all cases.

Furthermore, the example [you cite] is unestablished (*asiddhi*), because it would follow that even in the case of a lamp and the like, something else must be the illuminator of that [lamp]. Moreover, there is a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣabādhana*) in both cases, as the experience of color (*rūpa*) is the illuminator of color; is this [experience] the production of a cognition (*jñāna*) regarding it? In the first alternative, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) due to the cognition of color, since the experience of color is possible even though that [cognition] is not composed of light (*ataijasatva*). In the second alternative, however, there is an inconclusiveness due to the form of a jar (*ghaṭādirūpa*) and so forth, because it is admitted that even that which is not composed of light produces a cognition of color.

Even with the qualification "being an instrument," there is an inconclusive [reason] due to light and the contact between an object and its sense-organ, as well as due to the "inherence in the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) relation between the eye and color. Even with the qualification "being a substance," there is an inconclusive [reason] due to the moon and so forth.

Therefore, since the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of the eye cannot be established by any means, how could its possession of rays be established, such that it would possess the property of acting by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*)? (Page 76, Line 6)

The reason—"because it is the illuminator of form alone among [the categories] beginning with form"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to examples such as water, the moon, and rubies (*maṇi*). (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
60; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 541).

Furthermore, if this [eye] functions by reaching [the object], would the object come to the location of the eye, or would the eye go to the location of the object? In the first alternative, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*); for the movement of an object such as a mountain to the location of the eye is not perceived, nor is it seen or accepted by anyone of unimpaired mind.

In the second alternative as well, there is contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the movement of the eye toward the object is not perceived. Furthermore, there is contradiction with inference (*anumāna*): "The eye does not go out and connect with the object, because it is a sense organ (*indriya*), like the skin and other organs.

Even if there were no such distinction [between the eyes], why, rather than bypassing what is observed, do you not accept that for some [organs] there is no connection at all once they have gone there? Enough with this denial of what is actually perceived!

Furthermore, if the eye, having gone out and come into contact, illuminates an object, then—just as it illuminates the form of a distant object such as the sun through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (saṃyukta-samavāya)—it should likewise illuminate action, since there is no difference in the nature of that relation.

Furthermore, for one who maintains such a view, how could there be the perception of objects situated behind glass, mica, clear water, crystal, and so forth? For the eye traveling toward them would be obstructed by the composite whole (avayavin) consisting of the glass and other such materials. If, on the other hand, it is argued that the rays of the eye pass through the glass and other such materials to reach the location of the object, then at the time of perceiving the object thus screened, the glass and other such materials should not be perceived; moreover, the substance contained within them should fall away due to the destruction of its supporting composite whole. Yet this is not the case, as both are perceived simultaneously and without interruption.

The establishment of the Buddhist doctrine [of momentariness] is based on the illusion of continuity—like the flame of a lamp—because when each preceding configuration ceases, another subsequent configuration of that same form arises immediately thereafter. For even though all objects are momentary at every instant, there would otherwise result the undesirable consequence of such an illusion of continuity.

By this, the following view is refuted: that even when the branch and the moon are perceived sequentially, the conceit of simultaneous perception is caused by rapid succession, like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals. As for the other argument stated—that because the object of the eye can be proximate or remote relative to the body, the conventional usage of "far" and "near" is easily established—that too is mere faith; for such usage would be untenable if the object were apprehended through sense-contact. To explain: that which is apprehended through sense-contact does not admit the conventional usage of "far," "near," and so forth, as in the case of taste and the like; and yet, the object of the eye is apprehended through sense-contact (p. 77, l. 3).

Furthermore, if the eye functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*), doubt and error would be impossible; for, just as with universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*) that are in contact [with the sense organ] could also be perceived. Indeed, doubt and error are caused by the non-perception of particulars, and one cannot maintain that—despite the lack of difference in terms of being in contact—the eye perceives only the universal and not the particular, because [otherwise] there would be no particulars at all.
Therefore, it is not logical for the eye to function by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*);

nor does the consequence follow that, if it functions without reaching the object (*aprāpyakāritva*), it would illuminate all objects. This is because it depends upon a suitable location (*yogyadeśa*), just like a magnet. For a magnet, while acting to attract iron even without reaching it, is not capable of attracting every such piece of iron; rather, it attracts only that which is situated in a suitable location.

Or, for example, collyrium, a forehead mark, or a mantra, though they do not reach women and the like whom they attract, are observed to attract only specific women and so forth, and not everyone, because their attraction is perceived only in those specific cases. Thus, [the eye illuminates only what is suitable].

Furthermore, for you as well, why do the rays of the eye, having reached the end of the world, not illuminate form? Or, if the eye illuminates form through the relation of inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), why would it not also illuminate smell and so forth, since its capacity is no different in those cases as well? To this objection, the only refuge is "fitness" (*yogyatā*). If it is argued that in the case of non-contacting action (*aprāpyakāritva*) there is an absence of doubt and error, [we reply] that even in the case of contacting action (*prāpyakāritva*), that [absence of doubt and error] remains no different. The Buddhist prima facie argument that the ear functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), as found on page 318 of the *Ratnāvalī* and page 51 of the *Ratnākarāvatārikā*.

Is it not the case that the statement beginning with "nanu śrotrādau hi" is incorrect? For if it is to be proven that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), it is untenable for the ear to serve as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), since like the eye, the ear also functions without reaching its object; this is because it has been stated that the eye, the ear, and the mind reveal objects without reaching them. Furthermore, if the ear were to function by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*), there would be no such conventional usage regarding its object as "the sound is far" or "the sound is near," yet we do observe such usage here. Therefore, it is only the functioning without reaching the object that is logically consistent for the ear.

And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*): Sound is perceived by its perceiver precisely while being non-contiguous (*asannikṛṣṭa*), because it is perceived through cognitions such as "being at a distance," like a tree or similar objects.

Nor should it be argued: "If sound is perceived while non-contiguous, how can there be an impact upon the ear from it? For even when a brilliant form is perceived while non-contiguous, an impact upon the eye is observed;
however, the distinction here is that luminosity is the cause of impact in the case of light, whereas intensity is the cause in the case of sound.
The eye and the ear do not reach their objects; the other three, beginning with the nose, are considered to grasp objects of equal size [to themselves]. (Abhidharmakośa 1.43)

According to the established tenet [of the Sautrāntikas] that the eye, ear, and mind do not reach their objects, and that sound has as its primary cause both appropriated and non-appropriated [elements], see *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 603;

The eyes, ears, and mind function without reaching their objects (*aprāptārthakāritva*), according to the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 545. However, there is this distinction: here [in the case of light], it is luminosity (*tejasvitā*) that is the cause of impact (*abhighāta*), whereas in the case of sound, it is intensity (*tīvratā*).
Regarding this, the refutation [found] on page 333 of the *Ratnākara* is stated as follows:
here, the following response is given.

As for what was stated—that sound is apprehended by its own grasper even while being non-contiguous (*asannikṛṣṭa*), and so forth—in that case, the thesis is contradicted by perception (*adhyakṣabādhā*). This is because the ear is perceived through direct observation as the illuminator of sounds such as mosquitoes that have entered within the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*); therefore, like the non-hotness of fire, the sound’s state of being non-contiguous with its own grasper is contradicted by perception. Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the example of odor (*gandha*); for although odor is apprehended by its own grasper while being contiguous, it is nonetheless perceived as being graspable from a distance and so forth.

Nor is the conventional usage of "distant" and "near" unestablished when the odor is being perceived in that manner; for such usage—as in "the scent of a lotus is distant, the scent of jasmine is near"—is well-known in the world. [Objection: There would be a contradiction [if this were so], because in the perception of a sound from a remote distance, the sound of a mosquito clinging inside one's own ear would not be apprehended.
