*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 545.

From the observation of the conventional usage, "I smell a fragrance from afar," it would follow that the sense of smell functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), which entails the loss of what is accepted [by the opponent].

Furthermore, is the state of being apprehended by cognitions such as "distant" and so forth asserted on the basis of accepting the position that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra-jñāna*), or the position that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna*)? Regarding this, the first position is untenable; for if one apprehends the form of sound residing within its own cognition, the conventional usage of "distant" and "near" would be impossible.
Indeed, it is only for one whose formless cognition perceives an object located in a different place that it is appropriate to say, "this is distant," or "this is near."

Furthermore, for the proponent of cognition with form (*sākārajñānavādin*), that which is distant and so forth cannot be known by that cognition; and if it is not known, the conventional usage of "distant" and so forth is not tenable. For there is no real-world conventional usage such as "this is distant" or "this is near" for a blind person. Moreover, that which is known by cognition is merely its own internal form, and that is not "distant" and so forth, because it is non-different from the nature of the cognition itself.

Indeed, the nature of cognition, or pleasure and the like, when perceived as non-different from cognition, are never perceived as being subject to the conventional usage of "distant" and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total elimination of the conventional usage of "near" everywhere.

Now, even in this case, the conventional usage of "distance" and so forth is based on the distance of that which imparts the form [to the cognition]; however, the effort to prove that [the sense organ] functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*) is therefore futile. For even when grasping a sound that has entered the auditory canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), the conventional usage of "distance" and so forth is justified by the distance of its underlying cause. Indeed, we observe that even when a fragrance in close proximity to the olfactory organ is perceived, there is a conventional usage such as "the scent of a lotus is far away," based on the distance of its underlying cause.
One must state whether this admission [of the convention] applies to the position of cognition with form (*sākārajñāna*) or to the position of cognition without form (*anākārajñāna*).

[The opponent argues: "Is it that the form [of the sound] is near (ba, ja), or that it is non-different from cognition (ba, ja)? It cannot be by way of its own nature (svarūpataḥ); for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of treating even that which is near as being likewise [distant]."

Furthermore, since this [sound] is fit for the conventional usage of "distant" and so forth by virtue of originating from causes located at a distance and so on, it is not established that it is perceived by its own perceiver while remaining non-proximate; for this has been shown to be inconclusive due to the case of odor (*gandha*). Now, if it is argued that sound is "distant" because it has come from a distant location, this is correct, as its nature is established in that very way, just like odor and the like. For an odor or a sound that has come from a distant region, even when being cognized through the contact of its own sense organ, is perceived as either proximate or remote due to a specific capacity (*yogyatāviśeṣa*), despite its own intrinsic nature [remaining the same]. (Ā., Ba., Ja.)

—Is its nature [of being distant] due to its very essence (*svabhāva*), because it possesses the quality of distance and so forth; or because it originates from causes such as distance; or because it is situated in a place that is distant and so forth? (Syādvādaratnākara, p.

335) If, however, its state of being distant and so forth were due to its being situated in a distant place and so forth, then it would have to be admitted that sounds are perceived by the ears while they remain in the very place where they originated, and not having traveled [to the location of the listener].

And likewise, how could a sound that is not heard even slightly by one standing at a distance in a windless place be heard when there is a favorable wind? And why is that very same sound which is heard by one who is nearby not heard by him when there is a contrary wind—is it because the ear is struck by the wind, or because the sound has been destroyed by it? If it were due to the striking of the ear, then let it be heard by one situated in a windless region;

for it is not logical that the ear, being located precisely where the sound is, should be struck by it [the wind] while the sound itself is absent from that spot—otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that food being cooked in a kitchen would be burned by a fire blazing on a mountain.
If, however, sound were destroyed [upon reaching the ear], then even for one for whom that wind is favorable, it would not be heard, as there is no distinction [in the case of others].

Therefore, since it is impelled toward him by that [wind], it is established that this [sense organ] functions by reaching its object, because it perceives that [sound] once it has reached the auditory organ.

Furthermore, if all sounds were to perish at the very place of their own production, how then could the sound of a flute or the like, as well as the sound of a drum and so forth, be perceived by filling the cavity of the ear? Or how could there be an echo in a white palace or similar structure? For clods of earth and the like are not perceived to produce sound unless they come into contact with a hollow vessel.

Moreover, if a sound were apprehended while remaining only at its place of origin, then even a tiny sound such as that of a mosquito would be perceived without any confusion, since it would not be overwhelmed by the loud sounds of drums and the like located in the same place.

Those things which, while remaining in their own place of origin, are perceived by the sense organ without coming into direct contact with it, do not mutually obstruct one another—whether they be large or very small—just as in the case of mountains, trees, and so forth; and sounds, too, are perceived by the sense organ while remaining in their own place of origin without coming into direct contact with it.

Now, one might object: "A mountain situated at a great distance overpowers trees and other objects and presents only itself; therefore, your example is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). This too is incorrect, because their non-appearance is due to their being unsuitable for perception on account of the remoteness of their location, not due to being overwhelmed. However, in the case of sounds such as those of mosquitoes and the like, there is indeed an overwhelming by sounds such as those of kettledrums even when they are not remote; therefore, these latter are not perceived while remaining in the very place of their own production.

Furthermore, if a sound were perceived by the auditory organ while remaining exactly at the place of its own production and did not travel [to the ear], then how could it be that a sound produced at that very spot is heard with the wind, is not heard against the wind, and is heard only faintly with a gentle breeze? (Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 546). [The word] "gantavyam" is to be supplied; [the reading] "nnena sa eva" is the variant in manuscript Bhā.
Those very [words] are heard by him; thus it is stated in the Bṛhat- and Jaiminīya-śruti.
In a favorable wind,
[he should carry] the vessels,
O Brahmin.

As for what was also stated—that because the ears are struck by those sounds, they are not perceived, just as the subtle [objects] are not perceived because the eyes are struck by a brilliant form—that too is incorrect, because of the disparity between the example and the case to be illustrated. For it is observed that the rays of the sun, having been reflected from a brilliant form and coming into contact with the eye, are the cause of its being struck, since such a striking is not seen when there is no intense light; however, in this case, there is nothing of that kind which, having been reflected from the sound, could be the cause of striking the ear.

If it is argued that sound is air (*vāyu*), then it would not be heard in a windless place, because of the absence of the cause for striking the auditory organ. Furthermore, even here, in the midst of a great clamor such as that of kettledrums and the like, the fainter sounds are not perceived. Therefore, one must admit that there is an overpowering of the smaller sounds by the louder ones through their mutual approach to the same location. Consequently, its distance is established precisely because of its reaching a distant place, just like odors and other things, and not because of a metaphorical attribution of distance to those sounds remaining at their own place of origin; otherwise, the cognition of it would be erroneous, like the cognition of fire in a boy.

Or how could that [analogy] establish the ear's functioning without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), since a metaphorical designation does not establish [the actual] effect? For the metaphorical attribution of "fire" to a young Brahmin (*māṇavaka*) does not establish effects such as burning;
[as stated on page 83, line 7] regarding the sounds of drums and so forth...
In the case of words such as "mosquito" (*maśaka*),
[the perception] would not occur in a place with intense light where their impact is unseen, even in a windless environment; [as stated in] the *Ratnākara*, folio 337.

—like [the case of] cognition, Bhāṣya—of this [word], the prior—Bhāṣya—furthermore, as for that distance of the word in relation to space, would that exist when there is a perception of space, or when there is not? It cannot be when there is not; because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Whatever is a qualifier, only when it is itself perceived can it serve as the cause for the cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*), just like a staff or similar things. And in the cognition of "far" and so forth regarding a word, space is the qualifier.

Likewise, the cognition of distance and so forth regarding sound occurs only when there is the apprehension of a distant location and so forth, because this cognition of distance and so forth is dependent upon that [apprehension]. Whatever cognition of distance and so forth is dependent upon something occurs only when that thing is apprehended, just as the cognition of distance and so forth regarding trees and the like. And this [cognition] regarding sound is dependent on such [apprehension]; therefore, it occurs only when that is apprehended.

For it is well-established that in the case of distant or near trees, the conventional usage of "distant" or "near" occurs only when a distant or near location is apprehended by the eye; therefore, let it be accepted that in the case of sound as well, this [usage] occurs only when that [location] is apprehended.

Likewise, in the case of the [proposed] perception, how is that [sound] apprehended—is it by means of the auditory organ (*śrotra*), or by something else? If it were by means of the auditory organ, it would follow that even the location (*deśa*) is sound, because it possesses the defining characteristics of that [sound].
Furthermore, since there is no possibility of its cognition by another sense organ, there could be no such perception as "the sound is distant" in relation to the location.
Indeed, it is never observed that Yajñadatta perceives a sound as being "distant" in relation to a distant location perceived by Devadatta.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because such a cognition occurs in a conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) arising immediately after the experience of the two sense faculties, then there would have to be a sequential cognition of it—first as devoid of distance and so forth, and then again as possessed of them; but this is not the case, since it is perceived from the very beginning as qualified by distance and other such attributes.

Therefore, just as in the case of odor—which, having undergone transformation through movement, is itself distinguished by the fitness for being perceived from a distance and so forth—it should be understood that sound likewise becomes an object of perception from a distance and so forth. Thus, the fact that the auditory organ functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*) is established; otherwise, how could there be doubt regarding its location and other attributes in relation to its object, as there is with visible form? For when a visible form is being perceived, no such doubt arises as to whether "this form appears in this place or in another, or in this direction or in another," because it is perceived by means of a sense organ that does not reach its object (*aprāpyakārin*) precisely as having a fixed direction and location. If it were the same here [with sound], such a doubt would not exist; yet such a doubt does exist: "Has this sound arisen inside or outside, in the eastern direction or in another?"

Now, if it is argued that because there is doubt regarding the location and so forth, there is likewise doubt in this case, then let odor also be perceived even when not reached [by the sense], since doubt is possible here too for the very same reason of uncertainty regarding location and so on.

If it is further argued that the odor is understood to have been reached because of the observed modification of the olfactory organ, this is equally applicable to sound; for the modification of the auditory organ—such as deafness—is perceived from sound.

Therefore, since it is impossible for anything other than the sense-organ and the non-sense-organ (the mind) to serve as the specific cause for secondary perception (*gauṇapratyakṣa*), it is well said: "Conventional perception is perception by means of the sense-organs and the non-sense-organ."
If it is claimed that the directions and locations are objects of auditory perception, why is this not logically consistent for us?
Or, if they were indeed logical [to be so perceived], how could they not then be of the nature of sound?

In that very context, [the author] establishes the fact that the ear functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), because it is not common to other [senses], in the *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā*, page 87. (Ba, Ja; Ā; Śrotra)
In the *Catuḥśataka*, page 191;

Now he explains the primary [type of perception]: "The primary" means the principal [form of] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as the term continues from the previous context.
What is that? He says: it is supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*) known as *avadhi*, *manaḥparyaya*, and *kevala*.
This is stated as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) against the Mīmāṃsaka, who maintains that an omniscient being does not exist.

But surely, since supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*) or its possessor transcends the scope of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend existing things, their form is swallowed up by the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*); thus, because they do not exist, for what could "direct perception" (*mukhyapratyakṣatā*) be established? Nor is this transcendence unproven, because among the means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), none is possible regarding one who knows supersensuous objects. To explain: direct perception is certainly not its object, because it operates only within the domain of specific [sensory] qualities such as color-form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, perception operates only with respect to an object that is present and in contact [with the senses]; yet one who knows all objects is neither in contact with the sense organs such as the eye, nor is he present [at a specific time and place]. Therefore, how could he appear in a perception produced by those [senses]? Nor is inference the means for knowing him, for inference proceeds only when the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between a mark (liṅga) and the thing marked (liṅgin) has been grasped; and no mark that is invariably concomitant with an omniscient being is ever perceived.

For that [omniscience] must be either an effect (*kārya*) or an essential nature (*svabhāva*). It cannot first be an effect, because no causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) can be established between anything and an omniscient being who is remote [from our senses], since such a relationship is proven through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). Nor can it be an essential nature; for as long as the one who knows all things remains imperceptible, it is impossible to apprehend an essential nature that is non-different from him. Furthermore, could scripture (*āgama*)—whether eternal or non-eternal—be the indicator of the existence of an omniscient being? It cannot be eternal, because an eternal scripture that establishes his existence is simply impossible.

Furthermore, since scriptural passages such as "Hiraṇyagarbha is omniscient" and "He knows all worlds" function as commendatory statements (*arthavāda*) for ritual injunctions, they cannot establish the existence of an omniscient being. Moreover, an eternal scripture (*āgama*) cannot contradict the teaching of an omniscient being who has a beginning in time.

As for an impermanent scripture, would it be composed by an omniscient being or by one who is not omniscient? In the first case, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): the validity of the scripture is established only upon the proof of the omniscient being's existence because it was composed by him, yet the proof of the omniscient being's existence depends upon the establishment of that scripture.

Furthermore, since a scripture composed by one who is not omniscient lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could that [omniscience] be understood from it? Even if it were understood from such a source, why would it not be understood from one’s own words alone, given there is no distinction between them? Indeed, there is no difference between one’s own words and the statement of another whose status as a valid means of knowledge has not been established. Therefore, it is not through scripture (*āgama*) that this is understood, nor through analogy (*upamāna*); for the latter is invariably dependent upon the perception of a similar object, just like the analogy of a cow based on the perception of a gavaya that is similar to a cow.

Furthermore, no one in the world is recognized as being similar to the Omniscient One; since such a person is not perceived, it is logically impossible to perceive a similarity to him. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that for which there is no apprehension of a similar instance is not an object of comparison (*upamāna*), just like the child of a barren woman; and since there is no apprehension of a similar instance for the Omniscient One, he cannot be established through comparison. Nor can he be established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there exists no object cognized by any of the six means of valid cognition that would be logically untenable (*anupapadyamāna*) without the existence of an Omniscient One.

Nor should it be asserted that the omniscience of the Buddha and others is established by the fact that their teaching of dharma and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable; for their giving such instruction is explicable as arising from sheer delusion,
since instruction is of two kinds— that preceded by delusion and that preceded by correct knowledge—
and among these, that preceded by delusion is, for example, the instruction regarding objects perceived in a dream.
Instruction regarding all matters such as Dharma, preceded by right knowledge, is rooted in the Veda, as seen in the case of Manu and others;

for they, having attained pure awakening from the Veda—the source of the arising of knowledge of all categories of things—instructed on the entire multitude of objects such as Dharma. This is not the case with the Buddha and others; otherwise, like the instruction of Manu and others, their instruction would have been accepted by those learned in the three Vedas. Since it has not been accepted by them, it is concluded that it was composed by them out of sheer delusion regarding its subject matter.
Consequently, it is established that the Omniscient One transcends the scope of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend existing things;
and this being established, it proves that his form is swallowed up by the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*).
Since he is thus non-existent, having attained a state resembling a lotus in the sky, for whom could omniscience be sought?
—Because of the non-existence of sentient beings—bhāṣya. Of what [is it the cause]?—bhāṣya.
An omniscient being is not seen at present by people such as ourselves.
Nor is there the conceptualization that "it did not exist," by virtue of a power similar to that of negation.
(Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Sūtra 2, p. 81)
An omniscient being is not seen by people such as ourselves at present, nor does there exist any part [of him] or any logical mark (*liṅga*) that could lead to his inference. (3186)

Nor is it an effect, because the causal relationship is established through perception and non-perception, and since no causal relationship can be proven between anything and an omniscient being who is beyond sensory reach (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā,

Even though it is an essential property (*svabhāva*), a reason does not establish the existence of an omniscient being through remoteness; for if that [being] is not perceived, it is impossible to apprehend an essential property that is non-different from it.
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 831.
Nor can an omniscient being be established through scripture, because that scripture would depend on him; for how could the authority of a work composed by another person be understood?
Nor can such an eternal scripture be found here;
for if it were eternal, it would be a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), and if its purpose were [to convey] that [eternal self], it would itself be non-eternal. (119)
[Objection: But surely there exists one who is omniscient and all-knowing, and so forth; therefore, he says: "If [he were] eternal...
Why then is this a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)? To this he says: "'In that regard' (*tatpare*).
For if scripture were to establish the omniscience of a non-eternal person possessing a physical body, then that scripture itself would be non-eternal.
And there is no eternal scriptural injunction that makes known an omniscient being; for how could he be established by means of something artificial and untrue? (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-ṭīkā, p. 82)

Praise (*stuti*) is that commendation characterized by a statement of the fruit of an injunction, intended for the sake of generating conviction. Censure (*nindā*) is a statement of an undesirable fruit, intended for the sake of avoidance. A statement concerning an injunction performed by another that is contradicted [by other means of knowledge] is a "deed of another" (*parakṛti*). An injunction practiced as a traditional report is a "former practice" (*purākalpa*).
According to the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (p.
156), an *arthavāda* is a sentence whose primary purpose is either praise or censure.

how can there be proof for those two [the words and the Omniscient One], given that they are mutually dependent?

A statement is true because it was spoken by an omniscient one; therefore, how could his existence [be established] without another established basis? How could both of these be proven without such a foundation?
*Tattvasaṃgraha*: But from a statement composed by one who is not omniscient, which is devoid of a [valid] foundation...

For the instruction of the Buddha and others can also be accounted for in another way; thus, *Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 838.
Because of the delusion seen in dreams and the like, and because of the infallible Veda as it is heard,
for those who do not know the Veda, [the cognition] arising from the Veda is impossible.
Therefore, the instruction was given by them solely out of delusion;
whereas Manu and others who are established as authorities are primarily those who know the three Vedas.
Those treatises relied upon by those who know the three Vedas have their utterances originating from the Vedas. (Tattvasaṃgraha 3228)
The three Vedas, known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, are called the Trayī; those who know them are called "knowers of the Trayī" (trayīvidaḥ), referring to Brāhmaṇas (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p.
840). According to Amara, "Ṛk, Sāman, and Yajus are the three Vedas, [collectively] the Trayī."
From the state of omniscience, for the one who possesses immeasurable knowledge, there is valid cognition.

Or, let it be granted that there is an omniscient being; even so, does he perceive the entire range of objects encompassed by past time and the like in their own respective forms, or rather as being present? In the first case, the status of his cognition as perception (*pratyakṣa*) is untenable, because its object would be non-present entities. That which has non-present entities as its object is not perception, just like memory and so forth; and the cognition of the omniscient one has non-present entities as its object, since it has past and future things as its objects.

In the second case, however, it follows that that cognition is erroneous; for it apprehends an object existing in one way as being otherwise. Whatever apprehends an object existing in one way as being otherwise is erroneous, such as the cognition of two moons and the like. And the cognition of the Omniscient One apprehends an object existing in another time—past or future—as being present.
Or rather [as stated in the Āloka]: "By that very [reasoning]..."

Furthermore, in this cognition "this is existent here," do its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) appear along with the existence of the thing itself, or not? If they do appear, then do they appear simultaneously or successively? If simultaneously, then there would follow the designation of it as both unarisen and destroyed at that very same time, which entails the absurd consequence of designating simultaneous birth and death. For whatever appears by way of a particular nature is designated by that very nature, just as blue is designated by its blueness; and for the Omniscient One, every object appears by way of the nature of existence, prior non-existence, and posterior non-existence.
Furthermore, because there would be no cognition of the specific nature of individual objects, his omniscience could not be well-established;

for there is neither simultaneous cognition nor sequential cognition. This is because past and future objects are infinite, and since they cannot be fully encompassed, the knowledge of them would likewise be incomplete, making omniscience impossible.
Now, if those two do not appear [to him] like the existence of real entities (*vastusattā*), then how could he be omniscient?
For one who knows everything— whether simultaneously or in succession— would be accepted as "all-knowing" either by virtue of having a single nature or through a specific capacity (*śakti*).

3248. It is never observed that cognitions of contradictory natures, such as the pure and the impure, occur simultaneously within a single cognition, nor do they ever have different modes of apprehension.
Who could possibly understand, even in hundreds of years, each individual thing— past, present, and future— in its infinite variety, one by one?
By such verses as these, the author of the *Tattvasaṅgraha* (p. 844) presents the view of Sāmaṭa and Yajñaṭa, who are detractors of the Omniscient One;
and that [view] is indeed exactly so, according to the Bhāṣya.
—It is explained in the *Bhāṣya*... By this very method, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the Omniscient One has been set forth in the following texts: *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 830.

The proof of the Omniscient One preceded by the refutation of that [objection]: To this, the following response is given.

As for what was stated—that the non-existence of the supersensuous knowledge, or of its possessor, follows from its being beyond the scope of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend existing things—therein, first of all, its being beyond that scope is unestablished (*asiddha*), because there exists the means of valid cognition known as inference (*anumāna*) which makes known its existence.

He demonstrates this with the words "that very [knowledge]," etc.: that supersensuous knowledge exists, because there is a well-ascertained absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), just as in the case of pleasure and so forth. Thus, this reason (*hetu*) is not "unestablished in its substratum" (*āśrayāsiddha*); for one should not say that the substratum is unestablished by any means of valid cognition prior to the application of the reason, since it is established through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Indeed, there is nothing that does not fall within its range, because its activity is unimpeded everywhere.

Indeed, even in the inference of fire and so forth, the establishment of the locus (dharmin), such as a mountain, does not arise from anything other than conceptual construction (vikalpa); this will be explained later.
Nor is it unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha), because there is no possible means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that could sublate it.

For one who perceives objects beyond the senses (*atīndriyārthadarśin*), what could serve as a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)? Would it be perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, or non-existence (*abhāva*)? If it were perception, would that perception establish the absence of such [supersensible] things in some place at some time, or everywhere and at all times? In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for we have not asserted that their existence occurs everywhere and at all times. However, in the second case, without a perception of supersensible objects, the absence of knowledge of supersensible things everywhere and at all times cannot be established. This is what he indicates with the words beginning "as long as" (*yāvat*).

The connection is as follows: that [supersensory knowledge] exists, because it is impossible to have a complete understanding of the entire assembly of persons—[an assembly] which is "devoid" or empty of that knowledge whose nature is such that it pervades and takes as its object the entirety of all that is knowable—without supersensory knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*).

Indeed, it is not possible to establish the non-existence of one who perceives everything, at all times and in all places, by means of a cognition produced by limited sense faculties; for that [limited cognition] does not have that [omniscience] as its object. Whatever does not have something as its object cannot subvert a contrary property in that thing—just as visual cognition, which does not have sound as its object, cannot subvert the property of being non-audible in sound. Furthermore, a cognition arising from sense faculties is local and has as its object only a specific person or assembly existing at a particular place and time (pṛ. 86, l. 15).
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a verbal cognition common to both valid and invalid means of knowledge. Its...

Indeed, for that which has cognition as its intrinsic nature, there is nothing that is not within its range such that it would not penetrate it—[as stated in] the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, page 49, line 8 (MS: *jñe*; Bhāṃ: *bhāṃ*).
—*laṃ jñā*— Ācārya;
*sakalapu*— Ācārya, Ba, Ja;
because that [object] is not its domain, Bhāṃ.
Visual consciousness is the opposite of that—bhāṃ॰; visual consciousness—ba॰, ja॰;
visual consciousness—bhāṃ॰.

[Objection: It is not the case that the perception of one who sees all things (*sarvadarśin*) is sublated by its own occurrence—just as the perception of audibility in sound is not sublated by its non-audibility—but rather by its cessation. For where there is the cessation of perception, the absence of that object is determined, as in the case of a hare’s horn; whereas where there is the occurrence [of perception], there is the existence of that object, as in the case of color and so forth. Now, even in a dream, perception has never occurred with respect to an object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*); therefore, due to its cessation, the absence of that [omniscient being] is also determined. [Reply: This too is untenable. Because if perception were either the cause or the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of a thing, then upon its cessation, the thing itself would cease to exist; it cannot be otherwise, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For it is observed that when a cause, such as fire, ceases, its effect, such as smoke, also ceases; and when a pervader, such as "treeness," ceases, its pervaded, such as "śiṃśapā-ness," also ceases. However, an object is not the direct cause of its perception, because the perception occurs even in the absence of the object. Whatever occurs even in the absence of something else cannot have that thing as its cause; for example, a horse, which exists even in the absence of a cow, does not have the cow as its cause. Furthermore, an object exists even when there is no perception by a person of limited vision due to spatial or other obstructions.
Nor is it a pervader (*vyāpaka*); for even when that [perception] ceases, [the object] does not cease.

That which does not cease even when another ceases cannot be a pervader of that other; just as, for example, while a jar ceases, a pillar that does not cease is not pervaded by the jar. And even though perception ceases, an object remote in space and so forth does not cease.

Furthermore, it is not logical that the cessation of an object—which is neither its cause nor its pervader—should follow from the cessation of perception—which is neither its effect nor its pervader—lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this principle.
Even that determination of the absence of a cause in some instances due to the absence of the effect pertains only to one whose capacity is unimpeded, and not to a cause in general.
Furthermore, no objects whatsoever possess the capacity toward our immediate perception such that, upon its cessation, it could establish their non-existence.
We do not say that perception establishes non-existence while it is actually operating.
What then? [It is] that which is turning back.
(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 848; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 72).
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, folio 45;
*Syādvāda-ratnākara*, folio 381:
"the absence of that"—Bhāṣya.
In this context, the cessation [of the effect] upon the absence of the cause or the pervader is logical,
because the probans and the pervasion [respectively] consist in origination and identity.
Just as smoke, mango trees, and so forth cease to exist in the absence of fire or trees,
otherwise there would be a lack of causality, and the consequence of manifoldness would follow.
*Tattvasaṃgraha* (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 72, l.
9): Nor is it logical that what does not cease when another ceases should be the nature of that [other], as in the case of a cow and a gavaya.
And it is not logical that the cessation of one thing should entail the cessation of another that is neither its cause nor its pervader, because this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 851)

Furthermore, the non-apprehension of the effect that has been mentioned does not indicate the absence of the cause in general; what then? It indicates only the absence of that whose capacity is unimpeded (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 851).

Moreover, if the relationship of pervaded and pervader were established between the cessation of perception and the absence of the object, then the absence of the object could be ascertained from that cessation; however, this is not established, because the cessation of perception is observed even when an object is present but remote in the three ways [of distance, time, and nature].

Furthermore, does the cessation of your own perception establish the non-existence of the Omniscient One, or is it the cessation of the perceptions of all people? Regarding this, the first position is untenable, because the cessation of your own perception occurs even when an object exists but is hidden by distance and other factors. The second position is also incorrect; for the cessation of the perceptions of all people regarding the subject of the Omniscient One cannot be established without the Omniscient One himself. Indeed, as long as those with limited vision have not directly perceived all cognizers, it is impossible for them to determine that the perception of [the Omniscient One] does not occur in that regard.

[Objection: "In that case, the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) would be abolished everywhere, because even when proving the non-existence of a jar or the like in some location, the aforementioned defect would still follow. [Response: This too is an unexamined statement. For in those cases, the conventional usage of non-existence is established through the perception of another object associated with the same cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*). Indeed, the isolation (*kaivalya*) of one thing is the deficiency (*vaikalya*) of the other. Furthermore, there is no association with any other object within a single cognition for an omniscient being (*sarvajña*), such that by perceiving that [other object], his non-existence might be established; for he is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). Therefore, perception does not constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*) of the omniscient being.
Furthermore, the cessation of perception is not pervaded by the non-existence of an object, such that this non-existence could be ascertained from it;
for even when an object exists—such as one that is obstructed—the cessation of perception is observed (*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 848).
[Objection:

If this is so, how is it that you describe the establishment of the non-existence of a jar and the like in another location as resulting from perception known as non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)? [Response: This is not so; for when two objects are capable of co-occurring within a single cognition, the apprehension of one itself constitutes the establishment of the non-existence of the other (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p.

Furthermore, the co-occurrence of omniscience with anything else within a single cognition has never been ascertained, such that we could determine its non-existence through the perception of that [other thing] alone; for it is always and absolutely beyond the reach of the senses (atyantaparokṣa).
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 849)

Nor is there inference [to prove the non-existence of an omniscient being], because the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and the probans (*sādhana*) are not established. For in the inference that would refute [omniscience], who is intended as the subject: the Omniscient One himself, the Sugata, or all persons? If it is the Omniscient One, then what is to be proven therein—is his non-existence or his non-omniscience? If it is his non-existence, what is the probans—is it non-perception (*anupalambha*), the affirmation of a contradictory (*viruddhavidhi*), or the state of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) and so forth? If it is non-perception, is it the non-perception of the Omniscient One himself, of his cause, of his effect, or of his pervader (*vyāpaka*)? If it is the non-perception of the Omniscient One himself, is that non-perception related to himself or related to everyone? If it is related to himself, is it without qualification or qualified by the condition of being perceptible (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*)? It cannot, first of all, establish his absence if it is without qualification, because it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the mental states of others and similar factors.

Nor can it be qualified by the condition of "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*); for this would entail the consequence that there could be no proof for the non-existence of an omniscient being at any time or place. Indeed, it is not possible for that which is absolutely non-existent to reach the conditions for perception, because reaching those conditions is invariably concomitant with existence at some time and in some place.
For instance: whatever has reached the conditions for perception is not absolutely non-existent, such as a jar or similar objects; and the omniscient being has reached the conditions for perception.
By this, the position regarding all possible relations is also refuted.

Furthermore, the non-perception of all possible relations is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to comprehend them. Indeed, as long as all souls and their respective cognitions are not comprehended, the non-perception of a relation to those [souls] cannot be established by one who is not omniscient. Nor is it logical to conclude the non-existence of an omniscient being based on the non-perception of its causes in a particular location—such as the absence of shade due to the non-perception of an umbrella—because the cause of such omniscience, namely the destruction of karmic veils like *jñānāvaraṇa*, can be apprehended through inference and other means.

And it will be established on the occasion of the exposition of liberation that the manifestation [of omniscience] for one who knows all things occurs through the destruction of the karma-obscuring factors such as the veil of knowledge (jñānāvaraṇa) originating from the Three Jewels.

Would there be, for this first formulation, a proof consisting of non-perception (anupalambha) or a proof by means of a contradictory positive instance (viruddhavidhi)? [Ratnākaraśānti’s *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 382]—the pervasion... [Baṭu]... (Note: The text fragment provided appears to be a commentary or a citation from Ratnākaraśānti’s *Syādvādaratnākara* regarding the logical proof for the existence of an omniscient being (*aśeṣavit*). It addresses two potential types of proof: non-perception and a contradictory positive instance.)
Is non-apprehension intended to be without qualification—by not relying on this qualification, "of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension"—or is it with qualification?

[In either case], even the non-apprehension of the effect is unestablished; for the scripture itself, which teaches all objects such as dharma and so forth, is perceived as its very effect. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 850)

The objection—"How can that scripture be an effect [of a cause], since it is non-personal (apauruṣeya)?"—is also incorrect; for the non-personal nature of scripture will be refuted, and it will be established that the validity of all words depends solely upon having a virtuous speaker. Furthermore, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the pervader of that [non-personality] is perceived through inference.

For that which pervades omniscience is the direct perception of all objects, and not merely the complete knowledge of all objects; for the latter is found even in one who is not omniscient, by means of scripture.

And that [omniscient being] is established through inference; for instance: there exists some self (*ātman*) who is a direct perceiver of all objects, because, while having the nature of apprehending them, its obstructing conditions have been eliminated. Whatever has the nature of apprehending something and has its obstructing conditions eliminated is a direct perceiver of that thing, just as visual consciousness—when the obstructions such as cataracts have been removed—is a direct perceiver of form. And some self has the nature of apprehending all objects and has its obstructing conditions eliminated.

First of all, this reason is not "unestablished in its qualification" (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), because the nature of grasping all objects through the medium of scripture is well-known in relation to the self (*ātman*); nor is it "unestablished in its qualificand" (*viśeṣyāsiddha*), because the state of having obstructions and conditions eliminated will be established later. Therefore, non-perception is not a reason for its absence; this inference exists in such works as *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 70, l. 1), *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 370), and *Prameyaratnakośa* (p. 54), etc.

Nor is it the affirmation of a contradictory [property]; for would the affirmation of something contradictory—either directly or indirectly—establish the non-existence of an omniscient being? In the first case, would the non-existence of that [omniscience] be proven by the affirmation of its direct opposite, non-omniscience, at some place and at some time, or everywhere and at all times? In the former alternative, the non-existence of all-knowing persons in their entirety would not be established.

For where there is the affirmation of that [property], there alone its absence would be established, not elsewhere; indeed, it is never observed that when fire is affirmed in some place at some time, the absence of cold is seen everywhere and at all times. Furthermore, the second alternative is also impossible, because for one who perceives only what is near (an arvāgdṛś), it is impossible to affirm the non-omniscience of someone everywhere and at all times; or, if such an affirmation were possible, it would follow that this person himself must be omniscient. Alternatively, the negation of something occurs only through the affirmation of something else that is directly or indirectly contradictory to it, and not of something non-contradictory, since the latter can coexist with it.

For example, just as there is the negation of cold touch in the statement "there is no cold touch here because of fire," due to the direct affirmation of fire which is contradictory [to cold], so too would there be a negation of an omniscient being through the negation of omniscience. However, this occurs either through the indirect affirmation of something contradictory [to the object to be negated], or through the affirmation of something contradictory to its pervader (*vyāpaka*), whereby there is a negation of the all-knowing one; for instance, just as there is a negation of the touch of frost due to the affirmation of fire, which is contradictory to the cold that pervades the touch of frost; or, through the affirmation of something contradictory to its cause, such as the negation of the effects of cold—such as horripilation—due to the affirmation of a particular fire, which is contradictory to the cold that is the cause of horripilation and the like.
Nor is it a contradictory affirmation (*viruddhavidhi*), because even that would establish its absence either in a specific place and so forth, or in all places? (*Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
382) — [the absence of] knowledge.
—because [the property] is not established—abhāṣya.

Could the affirmation of something that is (1) contradictory to its pervader, (2) contradictory to its cause, or (3) the effect of what is contradictory to it, establish its absence even through a traditional lineage? It cannot be the case that the affirmation of non-perception of all objects, or of perception of only limited objects—which is contradictory to "omniscience" (sarvajñatva) by virtue of being contradictory to its pervader, namely "the direct perception of all things"—is capable of proving the absence of that [omniscience]. For such an argument could only prove the absence of omniscience in a particular place at a particular time—just as the presence of fire, which is contradictory to the coldness that pervades the touch of frost, proves the negation of the touch of frost in a specific place at a specific time—but not everywhere and at all times. This is because the affirmation of something contradictory to its pervader is impossible in that case [of universal absence], since the affirmation of its pervader has already been established in some particular instance of the self.

The affirmation of something contrary to the cause of that [effect] may also establish the absence of an omniscient being only at certain times and in certain places; for example, from the affirmation of a specific fire—which is contrary to the cold that causes goosebumps and the like—there follows the negation of goosebumps and other effects of cold only at certain times and in certain places, but not in their entirety, because the affirmation of something contrary to the cause cannot possibly occur in its totality.

For the cause of omniscience is the destruction of karmas such as the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), while its opposite is their non-destruction; the prescription for this [destruction] applies only to a particular self and not to all, since the absolute destruction of those [karmas] will be established in respect to a specific self.

By this, the prescription of an effect contrary to that [omniscience] is also refuted. For by that [contrary effect], there is the prescription of a certain limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), which is contradictory to omniscience, namely speech whose object is a restricted thing; yet even that is not capable of proving the absence of all-encompassing knowledge in its entirety. This is because its capacity to establish the absence of that [knowledge] is logically possible only where that [contrary effect] is prescribed, just as the prescription of smoke and the like—an effect of fire and such which is contrary to cold and so forth—is possible only in a particular location, and only there is there a negation of the sensation of cold, not everywhere.
Therefore, even the prescription of a contradictory [property] does not establish the non-existence of the Omniscient One,
because the Omniscient One is the opposite of that which is contradictory to His effects.
—[The word] *sparśāni* is missing in Ja, Ba, and Ā;
*aśeṣajñatvābhāvaṃ* is present in Ja, Ba, and Ā; *prasādhaka* is present in Ja.

Nor can [the reason] be "being a speaker" and so forth; for if one accepts the non-existence of such a being, it is logically impossible for him to possess attributes such as being a speaker. Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with one's own words.

Indeed, for one who asserts, "There is no omniscient being, yet he is endowed with attributes such as being a speaker," it is impossible to avoid a self-contradiction. Therefore, the non-existence of an all-knowing being cannot be established by any means of proof whatsoever.

Nor is there non-omniscience [in the Buddha], because the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) is no different in this case as well; for it is impossible that a contradiction with one's own words would not occur for one who says, "The omniscient one is non-omniscient. Furthermore, is it intended as a reason that the Knower of All (*sarvavit*) speaks a meaning contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it merely the fact of being a speaker? In the first case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because such a speaker of contradictory meanings is impossible for the Blessed One. In the second case, however, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the state of being a speaker of meanings not contradicted by what is seen or accepted is possible only when there is knowledge of those [meanings].

Even in the third alternative, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*); for there is no possibility of a contradiction between mere speakerhood and omniscience. By this, the position that the Sugata is the subject (*dharmin*) is also refuted; because the aforementioned defects apply equally in view of the probandum (*sādhya*), such as non-existence, and in view of the probans (*sādhana*), such as non-perception (*anupalambha*).

Furthermore, if the omniscience of the Sugata is denied, the affirmation of it for others necessarily follows, because the negation of a specific instance is invariably concomitant with the permission of the remainder, as in the case of "This man is a Brāhmaṇa" [whereby others are implied to be non-Brāhmaṇas].

Now, if one takes all persons as the subject (*pakṣa*) and seeks to prove their non-omniscience on the grounds of their being speakers and so forth—that is not tenable. For, since the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished, its exclusion from the counter-example remains doubtful; thus, it cannot logically serve to prove non-omniscience. This is because speakership and the like are observed in people on the street and others who are indeed non-omniscient, yet they are never observed in an omniscient being. Therefore, the claim that the exclusion [of the reason from the counter-example] is established is merely a wishful thought; for it has been demonstrated that non-perception pertaining to all souls is unestablished and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

These conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are found in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 73), the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* (p. 45), the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 384), the *Prameyaratnakośa* (p. 57), and other such works; however, regarding the negation of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*), speech and other such criteria remain doubtful.
Having accepted [this], it is asked in the *Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 519, l. 1: "What is established? [The reading] "iti" is found in Ā. and Ka.

If it is argued that since no omniscient being exists at all, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of [the reason] such as "being a speaker" is thereby established; from what, then, is the non-existence of such a being established—from this very [reason], or from something else? If it is from this very [reason], there is the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*), for instance: the non-existence of an omniscient being is established through "being a speaker" and so forth; once that is established, the negative concomitance of this [reason] with it is established; once that is established, its pervasion (*vyāpti*) by "non-omniscience" alone is established; and once that is established, the non-existence of an omniscient being is established from this [pervasion]. If, on the other hand, it is from something else, then this [reason] is redundant; moreover, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends its non-existence.

If it is argued that non-apprehension exists [as proof], we say no; for this [non-apprehension], being related to all selves, is unestablished and inconclusive, and thus its capacity to prove the absence of such a person is untenable. Furthermore, if the absence of one who perceives supersensible objects were established by mere non-apprehension, then why would the absence of even one who knows of that absence not also be established? Since there is no distinction [between the two cases], he says "tadabhāva" (the absence of that) and so forth, regarding the non-existence of the Omniscient One, in reference to the non-apprehension of himself and of everyone else.
The doubt regarding its unestablished nature [arises] because it is not apprehended by those of limited vision;
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 553, first half; commentary on the Vivṛti.

The non-existence of that supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*) is itself the reality (*tattva*). There is no one who knows that [reality], because such a person is not perceived, like a sky-flower. Now, even if such a person among ourselves is not perceived, one might suspect that another such person may exist; anticipating this, he says: "Neither Jaimini nor anyone else is a knower of the reality of that non-existence, because they possess a body, are human beings, and are speakers, just like a man on the street. This is an illustrative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, it should also be understood that [Jaimini] does not know the meaning of the Vedas either, for the same reasons. And thus, for one who desires gain, there would be the destruction of the very root.

To the objection that even though there is no distinction in terms of being a sentient being (*sattva*) or a person (*puruṣa*), Jaimini and others possess a superior knowledge of such persons because they differ from ordinary men on the street, [the author] says: "A person," and so forth.

If an excellence in a person such as Jaimini—characterized by the knowledge of the reality of the non-existence of an omniscient being regarding the meaning of the Vedas—were possible, why would he not be a seer of supersensuous objects? [Objection: It has been stated that this is incorrect, because no one is a knower of that non-existence due to its non-perception; for only the non-perception of a perceptible object is established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and this is not a case of the non-perception of a perceptible object, since the minds of others are imperceptible to those with limited vision. To this, he says: "In this regard," and so forth.

In this context, regarding the proof of non-existence by one who knows the reality of its absence, the Mīmāṃsaka asks: if the very person—such as the author of the Veda and so forth—is the specific subject whose non-existence is to be proven, on what basis could he be considered a means of valid cognition? The meaning is: on no basis whatsoever.

Why is this so? To this he says: because there is no distinction—that is, because there is no difference—it follows that even inference cannot serve as a sublater (*bādhaka*) against one who knows all things.
—[He] says [this] because of [the property of] being a person (*puruṣatva*) and so forth, [as found in] Ba, Ja, Bhā; Ā, Ba, Ja—[the property of] knowing (*jñatā*) and so forth. Ba, Ja.

Nor is there proof by presumption (*arthāpatti*); for there exists no object known through any of the six means of valid cognition that would be inexplicable without the non-existence of such a person [an omniscient being].
Indeed, the authority of the Veda is established only if an omniscient being exists;
for, as will be demonstrated during the refutation of its non-human origin, the authority of a word cannot exist in the absence of a speaker possessed of excellence.
Nor does the non-perception of an object prove that [the person] is omniscient;
*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 849; *Āptamīmāṃsā*, p. 56, verse 102.
Nor is analogy a sublater of that [object of knowledge], as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 73, u. and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 388).

Indeed, that [analogy] arises as having similarity as its objective basis only when both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison are perceptible, as in the case of a cow and a gavaya; not otherwise, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, neither all persons nor an omniscient being have been seen by anyone, such that there could be an analogy like "the omniscient being is like all persons" or "all persons are like the omniscient being. Or, if they were seen, it would follow that the person who sees them must himself be all-knowing. How, then, could the non-existence of an omniscient being be established through analogy? For if that were so, this [following argument] would be plausible: [The text continues: "All persons are non-omniscient, because they possess bodies, just like myself. But since no one has ever perceived all persons, how can this be established? Furthermore, even if one were to say, "I am non-omniscient, because I possess a body, just like Devadatta," this would not prove the non-existence of an omniscient being; for it is possible that Devadatta might be omniscient while you are not. Therefore, since no one has perceived all persons, how can the non-existence of an omniscient being be proven through analogy? Thus, the claim that the omniscient being does not exist because he is not perceived is refuted by the very fact that his non-perception cannot be established. Consequently, the non-existence of an omniscient being cannot be proven through inference either, because the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Nor can it be proven through verbal testimony (*āgama*), because the words of those who are not omniscient are unreliable. And since the existence of an omniscient being cannot be proven by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), his non-existence cannot be established by any means of valid cognition either. Therefore, the omniscient being exists. This is the conclusion.

"Having observed that all men of the present day are non-omniscient, the determination of the remaining [men] as non-omniscient is made through the analogy of similarity"—this is the reading found in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p.
838) with a variant reading, and in the *Sarvajñasiddhi* (p. 136).
"By means of an analogy based on similarity to him, the proof of the remaining [beings] as non-omniscient [is established].

(Verse 1) Furthermore, would the one who knows all things be comparable—on account of having a bodily configuration that is not distinct from the bodily configurations of the bodies of all knowers—by virtue of determining objects through perception produced by the senses, or by virtue of being formless like a donkey’s horn? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; for it lacks the capacity to subvert the existence of an omniscient being, and thus it does not produce anything undesirable for those who maintain the doctrine of an omniscient being.

For those who propound that [theory], omniscience is not held to reside in the physical configuration of the body; for if it were so, then since the body-configuration of an omniscient being would be no different from the body-configuration of other people, he too would be non-omniscient by virtue of possessing such a body. However, [omniscience belongs] to the self (*ātman*), and that [self] is absolutely distinct from that [body]. Therefore, how could there be an analogy for his non-omniscience based on a lack of distinction from that [body]? Indeed, when one thing has similarity with another, it is not logical to apply that [property] to a third thing which is distinct from both and whose nature has never been observed before, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Otherwise,] there would be no distinction [between cases], and [the property] would apply to everything without exception. (Śābarabhāṣya, Pratyakṣa section).
— Even the state of being a knower [is not established], because it resides in the body;

furthermore, since the omniscient one would be equal to all other persons in terms of determining objects through perception produced by the sense organs, he would be subject to comparison (upameyatā).

Now, it might be argued that the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is either the remembered object itself as qualified by its similarity to the object present before one, or the similarity itself as qualified by that [remembered object].
Furthermore, memory operates only with respect to an object previously experienced and not otherwise, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Yet, all persons and their respective mental states have certainly not been experienced by any non-omniscient being, such that they could be remembered.

Nor can any property common to non-omniscience be ascertained regarding those [beings] who have not been experienced, by virtue of which all persons—just like me—could always be seen through their sense organs to perceive only specific objects, or by which I could be compared to all persons on the basis of non-omniscience. Furthermore, even that which is observed in some non-omniscient being, such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, is not a property exclusive to non-omniscience, because existence and the like are not incompatible with omniscience either; otherwise, all persons would likewise be compared to him [the non-omniscient one] as being ignorant of the meaning of the Vedas or as being fools, since there would be no distinction.

And just as no one who is not a fool, upon seeing the properties of a *gavaya* and so forth, would infer the similarity of jars and other objects to a *gavaya*, so too, because all persons are seen to possess properties such as existence (*sattva*) and so on, they cannot be non-omniscient.

By this, the claim that the omniscient being is a subject of comparison—either like a "donkey’s horn" for the sake of his formlessness, or a "donkey’s horn" like the omniscient being—is refuted; therefore, analogy (*upamāna*) also does not constitute a sublation of that [omniscience].
Therefore, that which is remembered, qualified by similarity, would be the object of knowledge for analogy; or else, it is the similarity itself as connected with that [remembered object]. (37)

Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Upamānapariccheda: Even regarding omniscience, there is no scripture [to refute it]. For would such a scripture be of human origin or of non-human origin that could contradict it? First, it cannot be of non-human origin, because it will be refuted in detail during the occasion of examining scripture, and because you yourselves accept its authority only regarding matters of action (*kārya*), whereas if it were authoritative regarding the nature of things (*svarūpa*) as well, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, there is no Vedic statement that establishes the non-existence of an omniscient being, for we repeatedly hear numerous Vedic passages—such as "Hiraṇyagarbha is omniscient"—which indeed testify to his existence.

Now, if it is argued that those [scriptural passages] do not establish the existence of that [omniscient being] because they are intent upon ritual injunctions (*karma*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), then from what source does this intentness upon ritual injunctions follow, rather than their establishing its existence? If it is because of its non-existence, then from what source is that [non-existence] known? Is it from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or because that [other *pramāṇa*] is intent upon ritual injunctions and thus does not establish its existence? Of these, the first alternative is untenable, because any other means of valid cognition that could apprehend the non-existence of an omniscient being has already been refuted.

In the second case, however, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*); for instance, if the non-existence of an omniscient being is established, it follows that the scripture—being intent on ritual injunctions and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—is not proven to inform us of his existence; and if that is established, then the non-existence of the omniscient being is established.

Furthermore, regarding a human-authored scripture (*āgama*), would it be one composed by an omniscient person, one composed by a person who negates the existence of an omniscient being, or one composed by someone else that serves as its sublater? If it were composed by an omniscient person, how could it be a sublater of that [omniscience], given the contradiction? Even in the second case, does the author of the scripture which establishes the non-existence of an all-knowing being perceive the entire world as devoid of an omniscient being, or not? If he perceives it, then the scripture composed by him is valid (*pramāṇa*), but it cannot be a sublater of the omniscient being; for, in perceiving it in such a way, the very author of that scripture is established as being omniscient.

Now, if it is not accepted [that the Veda is the word of an omniscient being], how then can it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it was composed by a person overwhelmed by the great mountain of ignorance, like a scripture composed by an ordinary man on the street? Even in the case where it is held to have been composed by another [an omniscient being], these same two objections must be seen to apply; therefore, scripture (*āgama*) also does not contradict the existence of an omniscient one.
Nor is it the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*); for that will be refuted at length later on.

Or let it be so; nevertheless, you maintain that it consists in the cessation of the five means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest. And is this cessation of theirs of the nature of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) or of the nature of a presuppositional negation (*paryudāsa*)? In the case of the position of non-presuppositional negation, its status as a cause for the determination of an object is untenable because it is formless (*nīrūpa*). Whatever is formless cannot be a cause for the determination of an object, just like a sky-lotus; and the means of knowledge consisting of absence (*abhāva*), being of the nature of non-presuppositional negation, is indeed formless.

For the quality of being a cause of determination (*paricchitti-hetutva*) is a property of existent things (*bhāva-dharma*); how could it belong to non-existence (*abhāva*), which is by nature entirely void, given the contradiction? And in the absence of that [quality], how can there be the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*), since the designation "means of valid cognition" applies to that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the act of determination? Furthermore, because non-existence is of the nature of the absence of a means of valid cognition, its designation as such is untenable;

for whatever is the absence of something cannot be designated by that very term—just as the absence of a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve the designation "Brāhmaṇa"—and yet you claim that the absence of the means of valid cognition, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), is itself the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*).

If non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is described as a mere cessation of [other] means of valid cognition characterized by a simple negation (*prasajya-lakṣaṇa*), then it is neither a cognition of anything, nor is it a cause for cognition.
(Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 850) — *rmaka* — Bhāṣya.

Even in the case of the view that [non-existence] is a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), something other than a positive entity must be denoted by the term "absence of the five means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇapañcakābhāva*). And would that be (1) a self devoid of the five means of valid cognition, or (2) a cognition other than those? Regarding the first alternative, is the self devoid of the five means of valid cognition in every respect, or only with respect to the five means of valid cognition regarding the object to be negated? If it were in every respect, how could there be a determination of the absence of an omniscient being? For it is impossible to determine an object of knowledge (*prameya*) without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, the postulation of means of valid cognition would result in futility.

Even regarding the second position, does your own self establish the non-existence of the omniscient being because it is devoid of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that object, or does everyone [do so]? Of these, the first position is untenable, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the mental states of others.

The second position is also incorrect, because it is impossible for anyone who is not omniscient to ascertain that all cognizers are devoid of those means of valid cognition with respect to that object. Therefore, the position that the self is devoid of the five means of valid cognition does not lead to a secure conclusion.

Nor is the position that it is a cognition of something other than that [omniscience] tenable; for "cognition of something other" (*tadanyajñāna*) refers to a cognition whose object is some limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) distinct from omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), which is what is to be negated. And would such a cognition establish the absence of omniscience in someone, somewhere, at some time, or rather everywhere, at all times, and in everyone? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is admitted that wherever, whenever, and in whomever limited knowledge is established, there and then the lack of omniscience in that person is likewise established.

The second position, however, is accessible through faith alone; for it is untenable to establish that [the omniscient being] possesses limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) when he does not directly perceive living beings situated in the three times and the three worlds, as this would also entail the impossibility of establishing that everyone, everywhere, and at all times, is non-omniscient. Thus, even the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) cannot refute the existence of an all-knowing one. Consequently, it is established that the absence of the production of perception and other means of knowledge is called the "absence of a means of knowledge" (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding the supersensuous direct perception (*atīndriyapratyakṣa*) which directly perceives all objects of the past, future, and present, provided that there is no well-ascertained evidence of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).
"Either the non-modification of the self, or consciousness directed toward another object," [Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika,
Abhāvapariccheda 11].

Regarding the statement that "the omniscient one's cognition sometimes [perceives] the omniscient one," and further what was said— that "an object encompassed by past time and so forth appears in its own respective form," etc.— that too is without substance; because it appears in its very own form.

If it is asked: "How then is the perceptuality of this [object] logical when it appears as non-existent in the present? [The answer is: Because it grasps the object with complete clarity. For the definition of perception is not "the appearance of an object as being in a proximate place and time," since that would lead to the absurd consequence that even the appearance of the existence of a soul in the body of an infant lying on one's lap—[inferred] from signs such as breathing and so forth—would also be perception.

What then? It is the vivid manifestation of the object; if that exists even for an object that is past and so forth, why should it not be considered perception (*pratyakṣa*)? And just as there is no contradiction in the vivid manifestation of sensory perception even when grasping an object spatially remote, so too there is no contradiction in the vivid manifestation of suprasensory perception (*atīndriya-pratyakṣa*) even when grasping an object temporally remote.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the consequence of the past and so forth attaining presentness, because [the past] is graspable by the grasping of a present object, just like a present object; for an object at a distant location would then attain proximity, since it is graspable by the grasping of an object at a non-distant location (just as a proximate object is). (Page 88, Line 10;
in its own form, Ā.)
—of pride, according to the Bhāṣya; —the mention of "pride," according to the Bhāṣya; —the sense of "place," according to the Bhāṣya.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "In the cognition that 'this is existent here now,' do its prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*) and subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) appear, or not? For just as in a perception produced by the senses, an object—whether blue or non-blue, positive or negative—that is qualified by a particular location, appears precisely as qualified by that location; likewise, in the knowledge of the Omniscient One as well, an object—whether positive or negative—that is qualified by a particular place, time, and form, appears precisely with those place, time, and form. Therefore, how could there be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous designations such as birth and death, or the failure to perceive the specific nature of objects, such that his omniscience would not be well-established? For the undesirable consequence of simultaneous designations such as birth and death, and the failure to perceive the specific nature of objects, would occur only if the nature of a future entity were perceived as having the nature of a present entity; but not when it is perceived according to its own time.
This [objection] is also a subverter of the one who knows all things without exception;

therefore, it is established that the existence of an omniscient being is proven by a means of valid cognition that is well-ascertained and free from any possible subverter—[concerning] the object which is the self-restricted nature. (Bhāṣya)
Generally, the proof of the omniscient one should be sought in the following texts along this very same line: *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p.
846; *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, *Sarvajñasiddhi*, and *Āptaparīkṣā*, p. 54.
*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 47;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 13;
*Śāstravārttāsamuccaya*, p. 80.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
70, top; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 53;
Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p. 553.
*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
370; *Prameyaratnamālā*, p. 54;
*Sarvajñasiddhi*, p. 142.

The Naiyāyika’s prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*): Now, it is not the case that the existence of an omniscient being is established merely because there is no well-ascertained subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*); rather, it is established because He is the agent of effects such as the earth and so forth.
Nor is His authorship of these effects unestablished, for there exists an inference (*anumāna*) that proves it.
For instance: the earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent, because they are effects, like a jar.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for it is well known that the earth and so forth are effects due to their possessing parts.
To illustrate: the earth, mountains, trees, and so forth are effects, because they possess parts, just like that [jar].
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it is well-established in the case of jars and the like, which have ascertained agents;
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is excluded from things such as space (*ākāśa*) which have ascertained non-agents;
nor is it mis-timed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because its subject matter is not sublated by perception or scripture.
Nor is it a "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) reason, because there is no other reason capable of initiating the investigation into the matter; thus,

this faultless reason, establishing an intelligent creator by the force of its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā), establishes him as qualified by attributes such as omniscience and the capacity to construct the universe—
(pūrvaṃ ā॰, ba॰, ja॰).
The act of naming is a mark of those superior to us,
because the act of naming proceeds from direct perception;
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.19.
