The four great elements are preceded by a conscious being, because they are effects and because they possess parts, like a jar; Praśastapāda, p. 54.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

301; *Vaiśeṣikopaskāra*, p. 62: That which arises independently of a body is preceded by an intelligent agent, because it possesses a cause—since such an inference is drawn from its being composed of parts among substances, from its being an effect-quality among qualities, and from its being an action itself among actions.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
97; Nyāyalīlāvatī, p. 20;
Nyāyamuktāvalī, p. 23.
God is the cause, because human action is seen to be fruitless;
Nyāyasūtra 4.1.21.

The Lord is another self distinguished by twenty qualities, and the fruit of his dharma and meditative concentration is the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇiman*. His dharma follows his volition and sets in motion the individual occurrences of merit and demerit, as well as the elements such as earth and the rest (Nyāyabhāṣya 4).

Prior to their initial activity, the primary matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and karma function only when presided over by an intelligent cause (buddhimatkāraṇa), because they are insentient, like an axe and other such tools.

This is another reason: the manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, becomes the cause of pleasure, pain, and the like, because it possesses form and other qualities, just like a chariot and such.
Merit and demerit, presided over by an intelligent cause, bring about experience for the person, because they are instruments, just like an axe and such.
The great elements, ending with air, proceed toward their respective functions such as supporting, being presided over by an intelligent cause, because they are insentient.
*Nyāyavārttika*, pp. 457–67:

Bodies, trees, mountains, and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, have an intelligent agent as their creator of the material cause (*upādāna*), because they possess the quality of being produced (*utpattimat*) or because they have insentient material causes; just like a palace or similar structures.

Nor is their possession of the quality of being produced unestablished, since it is established—like cloth and other things—either by their having parts or by their possessing action while being large.
*Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 598;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 194:
"From the arrangement, maintenance, and so forth of effects, from words, from cognition, and from scripture..."
The omniscient and immutable [Lord] is to be established through [His] own words and from the particularity of His friendship;
Nyāyakusumāñjali, Fifth Chapter.

In that regard, he states the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) presented by Aviddhakarṇa for proving the Lord (*īśvara*): "That which possesses a specific configuration of its own constituent parts, etc."— namely,
that which is understood through an intelligent cause is such, as for example a jar and so forth.

That which is perceptible by two sense-faculties, that which is imperceptible, and such a subject of dispute— all these are considered to be preceded by an intelligent agent; thus, atoms are cited as the counter-example (vaidharmya).
The taking up of the threads and so forth must be presided over by an intelligent agent,
because they possess form and other qualities; for instance, as is observed, threads and the like produce their own effects [only when supervised].
*Tattvasaṃgraha*,
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 75, first part.

Praśastamati, however, says: "At the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of persons must have been preceded by the instruction of another, because it is restricted to specific objects for those who are later awakened; just as the linguistic usage of children, who are unacquainted with verbal conventions, regarding cows and other things is restricted to specific objects and is preceded by the instruction of their mothers and others" (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p.
The contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*)—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 75, top; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 101. Bhāṣya.
[The opponent] establishes [this]:

"It might be thought that this reason (*hetu*) is one that subverts what is desired (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*). For instance, [you] accept [the creator] as omniscient, the maker of all things, possessing eternal knowledge, will, and effort, and being bodiless yet intelligent; however, in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), such as a jar, a maker is observed who is characterized differently from that [creator]. And since the understanding of an unperceived object occurs in accordance with the properties observed in the example, this reason is 'contradictory' (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of the property sought to be established."
Furthermore, the example [of a jar] is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because an intelligent agent of that kind does not exist in the case of jars and the like;

this is incorrect. For there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans in terms of specific instances, as that would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.

Rather, pervasion is determined through generalization by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Since these two cannot be grasped with respect to specific instances due to their infinity and the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the pervasion of "being an effect" must be understood solely in terms of "having an intelligent agent as its cause," and not in terms of [the agent] possessing a body and so forth.

Indeed, the body does not enter into the causal complex of agency; for even in its absence, agency is observed in the act of propelling one's own body by virtue of being the locus of knowledge, desire to act, and effort.
If the body were considered a cause merely by its concomitance, despite being otherwise ineffective, it would follow that the tawny color of fire is also a cause of smoke.
Furthermore, even when the body is present, if there is an absence—either collectively or individually—of knowledge and the other factors, agency is not observed even in a potter and the like.

First, indeed, there arises the cognition of the collection of causal factors that produce the effect; from that, the desire to act upon them; from that, effort; and from that, the accomplishment of the result. Since these three alone constitute agency with respect to the effect, they are invariably present in all cases. [Objection: If the probandum is "being preceded by a creator who is the substratum of the knowledge of all knowable objects," then the example lacks the probandum and the reason is contradictory. [Reply: This is not so; for when the probandum is "an agent who is the substratum of consciousness," there is neither a lack of the probandum in the example nor is the reason contradictory.

Nor can it be established here that there is a contradiction of the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) regarding the nature of being the cause of the substratum of awakening and being its effect; for if [the reason] were not a means of proof due to the absence of pervasion in the specific case, it would follow that even smoke would not be a means of proof (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.
302). Furthermore, that which is postulated in accordance with the pervasion is what becomes established.

The creator would be similar to a potter; thus, there would be a contradiction of the specific [attributes]. Possessing activity, non-omniscient, embodied, and beset by afflictions—just as the maker of a jar is, so too would the maker of the earth be.
Furthermore, regarding the proof of a specific [agent], the illustrative example would be devoid of the probandum (*sādhya-śūnya*);
however, once the general nature of the agent is established, how could there be an understanding of a specific [agent]? (p.

191) As for the claim that this [reason] is contradicted by the specific, that too is an unexamined statement, because there is no such fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) as "contradiction by the specific" (*viśeṣa-viruddha*); otherwise, if it were accepted, it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total destruction of all inference.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 198; Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 55: For instance, palaces, staircases, gate-towers, upper chambers, and so forth.
Because it is determined to be preceded by many impermanent cognitions,
for this very reason, it is also accepted as being a subverter of what is desired.
Because it is established that [the world] is preceded by manifold and impermanent cognitions. (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 50)
[The opponent might argue: "It is intended for the sake of creation" (sisādhipita)—this is the reading; "it is intended for the sake of desiring to create" (sisādhiyiṣita)—this is the commentary.

Now, if one admits that God possesses a body by virtue of His intelligence, then by one who so admits it, the body and other such things must necessarily be accepted as being either eternal or non-eternal.

Now, if you postulate that the body and so forth are eternal, even so, what has been postulated is contrary to what is observed; for one who maintains a position contrary to observation, the eternity of the intellect (*buddhi*) must be accepted, since there exists an unafflicted and unimpeded desire regarding all objects, just as [one accepts] the intellect—[as stated in] Nyāyavārttika, p. 465.

And the fact that [the world] is not preceded by a bodiless agent is capable of being proven: every agent first ascertains the nature of the instrument, then desires—"I shall accomplish this by means of this"—then exerts effort, then sets the body into motion, then presides over the organs, and finally acts. One who does not ascertain, does not desire, does not exert effort, and does not set the body into motion does not act. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the body, like the intellect, is an instrumental cause for the production of an effect. This inference that [the creator] is not preceded by a body is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, by the force of that pervasion, it contradicts the intended qualification of bodilessness; thus, it is a "contradictory-to-the-qualification" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) reason. Consequently, it is merely a specific variety of the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reason. This is the summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

To this, the rebuttal is as follows: agency does not consist merely in having a body, for that would entail the absurdity of attributing agency to one who is in deep sleep or is indifferent. Rather, it consists in being the prompter of causal factors whose efficacy has been observed; since the production of an effect occurs when that [prompting] exists, this [agency] is possible even for one without a body, just as it is for the Self in the case of impelling its own body.

If it is argued that even there, the Self possesses that very body acquired through its own past karma, we grant that it exists, but it cannot serve as the means for impulsion, because action upon oneself is a contradiction.

If it is argued that even for the production of desire and effort, the body must be depended upon; let it be so where those two are adventitious. However, where these two exist as inherent, dependence on the body there is useless.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the eternality of intellect, desire, and effort;
for we observe a twofold course among qualities such as color and the like depending on the difference of their substrates, and the same will apply to intellect and the others as well.
Praśastakanda, p. 55; Vyoma, p.
305: "Not the body"—Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, his omniscience is established because he is the agent of the entire multitude of effects. Whatever is the agent of something is necessarily cognizant of its material cause and so forth; for example, the potter who produces a jar is cognizant of the clay, the staff, and other such tools. And this Lord (Īśvara) is the agent of the universe.

For the material cause of the universe consists of the four kinds of atoms; the instrumental cause consists of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth; the enjoyer is the self (*ātman*); and the object of enjoyment consists of the body, the sense organs, and the like.
Furthermore, agency with respect to the earth and other elements is not possible for one who lacks knowledge;
thus, his knowledge and other qualities are eternal, because they are distinct from the knowledge and other qualities of potters and the like.

Nor is it possible for there to be total similarity between the property-possessor (dharmin) of the probandum and that of the example, for that would entail the destruction of all inference; indeed, the fire seen in the kitchen is not exactly the same as the fire on the mountain.
And those [cognitions] belonging to it, such as the cognition of a lump of clay and so forth— Ja.

Is that sovereignty of the Lord eternal or non-eternal? We say it is eternal. But what is the proof for the eternity of His intellect? Is it not this very [argument]: "The atoms proceed only when presided over by an intelligent cause" (Nyāyavārttika, p.
464)? For since His powers of knowledge and action are eternal, His sovereignty is eternal.
And the oneness of the creator of the earth and so forth is established, because the activity of even multiple creators is possible when they are regulated by a single supervisor;
for it is well known that the activity of architects and others in the construction of a great palace or similar work proceeds when they are regulated by a single master builder.

If the occasional nature and diversity of effects do not contradict the fact that God and his qualities, such as will, are uniform and eternal—since, by obtaining occasional and diverse auxiliary factors, the diversity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is established, and thus no contradiction with those [qualities] is possible—[then there is no fault].

[Objection: "If the earth and so forth have an intelligent cause, then even for one who has not observed an agent, the cognition that they were 'made' would arise—just as it does in the case of ruined wells, palaces, and the like. Yet such a cognition does not arise. Therefore, because the reason (hetu) seen in the example is absent from the subject (dharmin), the reason is unestablished (asiddha). [Reply: This too is incorrect. For is this stated with reference to what is accepted by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), or otherwise? If it is the latter, how could there not be a total destruction of all inference, since the fault of being unestablished would follow even in the case of smoke and so forth? But for that which is accepted by valid means of knowledge, there is no lack of establishment, because the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) of "being an effect" with "having an intelligent cause" is well-known in the case of the earth and so forth, just as smoke and so forth are well-known on mountains and the like.

Nor is there a rule that for as many produced objects as there are, that many instances of the cognition "it has been made" must manifest within oneself; for in the case of ground filled by a natural spring, the cognition "it has been made" does not arise in one who has not observed the activity [of its creation].

Furthermore, one should not argue that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) from the rule due to stationary things such as plants, which grow without being cultivated, on the grounds that they are perceived to arise from their own specific causal complexes even in the absence of an intelligent cause; for these are included within the subject of the inference (pakṣa), and if a reason were to deviate within the subject itself, no reason whatsoever would be capable of proving anything, resulting in the total destruction of the science of inference.

Furthermore, you seek to establish the absence of an intelligent cause here based on non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); this is incorrect, because only the non-perception of something perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is logically capable of proving non-existence. Such [perceptible non-perception] is not possible in this case, since the creator of the earth and so forth is invisible.
Moreover, if mere non-perception were to prove non-existence, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), such as the absence of action in ground that has been thoroughly leveled. — Bhāṣya.

—And as for [the objection]: "Is it not a mere fantasy to claim that the Blessed One, being supremely compassionate and acting for the sake of others, would have the world as his motive, yet still face the contradiction of initiating a body and so forth that produce suffering; or, if there were no such contradiction, that his supreme compassion would be untenable?"—this too is merely a wishful thought, because he acts as an agent with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as auxiliary causes. For when merit or demerit serves as the auxiliary cause in the initiation of a body and so forth, he initiates such a body and so on for the sake of experiencing the results in the form of pleasure or pain corresponding to those [causes].

For the Blessed One’s activity is indeed for the sake of benefiting others, with the thought, "I shall liberate living beings from saṃsāra," and their liberation occurs through the exhaustion of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Since that exhaustion is not possible without the experience of the results [of those actions], it is not contradictory for one possessed of compassion to engage in such an arrangement. If it is argued: "If his activity is due to the power of merit and demerit, then let all effects arise from those two alone; what is the use of postulating a Lord (*īśvara*)?"—this is also not sound. For it is only when those two [merit and demerit], being insentient, are presided over by a sentient being, that their engagement in their own effects is logically established.
For instance: merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), being insentient, proceed toward their own effects only when presided over by a conscious agent, just like an axe or similar tools.
Nor is it logical that the self of beings such as ourselves should be the presiding agent; for such a self lacks the cognition of objects such as unseen forces (adṛṣṭa) and atoms (paramāṇu).
Furthermore, there can be no spontaneous activity of an insentient entity; otherwise, it would continue to operate even after the effect has been accomplished, due to its lack of discernment.
dhe ca pa— ā॰ — tvādyanupa— bhā॰, ja॰ na iti ā॰, ba॰, ja॰.

If an intelligent supervisor is what is to be proven, how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of action (*karman*), which is insentient? For that too, being insentient, requires a supervisor. To explain: everything insentient is seen to function only when presided over by a sentient being, just as in the case of threads and so forth; and likewise, action and the like [require such a supervisor].
Nor is the self of beings such as ourselves the supervisor, because it lacks knowledge of those objects.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the self of beings such as ourselves regarding action is not produced by the senses, nor does it have atoms and the like as its objects.
Furthermore, in the absence of that [conscious agent], no impeller for it is observed;
nor is the spontaneous activity of an insentient entity ever perceived.
If there were such activity, it would continue even when the effect was fully accomplished, because of its lack of discrimination.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī*, page 304:
Refutation of God’s (Īśvara) being the creator of the world.
To this, it is replied:

As for the argument stated to prove that earth and other elements have an intelligent cause—namely, their status as "effects" (kāryatva)—does this consist in having parts (sāvayavatva), or the inherence of its own cause in what previously did not exist, or being the object of the cognition "it is made," or perhaps being subject to modification? If it is "having parts," then what does this mean: existing in the parts, being produced by the parts, possessing spatial extension (pradeśavattva), or being the object of the cognition "it has parts"? Regarding the first alternative, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the universal (sāmānya) of parts, for that [universal], though not an effect, exists in its parts.

In the second alternative, however, there is the fallacy of the reason being non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatva*); for just as the "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*) of the earth and so forth is the probandum, so too is their "being composed of parts such as atoms" the probandum.

In the third alternative as well, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, because although space possesses spatial divisions (*pradeśavattva*), it is not an effect; furthermore, its possession of spatial divisions will be established in the section examining the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*). Likewise, the property of "being an object of the cognition 'it has parts'" is also inconclusive by this very same reasoning.

Nor should it be asserted that, even though this [space] is partless, the designation "pot-space" or "cloth-space" is merely figurative because it can be the object of a cognition of having parts due to its conjunction with partite objects such as pots and cloths; for if it were partless, its omnipresence would be contradicted, just like an atom, and thus its omnipresence too would necessarily be merely figurative.

Nor is "being an effect" (kāryatva) the relation of that which was previously non-existent with the existence of its own cause; for since that relation, called inherence (samavāya), is eternal, it cannot logically serve as the definition of an effect. Alternatively, if it were so defined, then effects such as the earth and so forth would necessarily follow as being eternal like that [inherence], and what then could be proven to have an intelligent cause? Furthermore, this definition of "being an effect" will be refuted in detail during the examination of the six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha-parīkṣā).

The state of being an object of the cognition "it has been made" is also not its defining characteristic; for this [cognition] applies even to space—which is not an effect—when one says, "Space has been made by digging and filling," since it extends to that which is not a product.
Furthermore, if being subject to modification were the meaning of "being an effect," then Maheśvara himself would face the consequence of being an effect;

for being subject to modification consists in the alteration of an existing entity, and since that exists in the case of Īśvara as well, he too would have to have another intelligent cause, leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, its capacity to produce an effect is extremely difficult to establish if it is unchanging;
therefore, since the nature of the effect, when scrutinized, is untenable, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (asiddha). (Page 97, Line 16)

Is "being an effect" (kāryatva) the inherence of its own cause's existence, or the state of coming into being after not having existed, or the production of the cognition that it has been made even by one who does not observe the action [of its production], or conformity with the operation of a cause? (Prameyaratnamālā, p.
64). Or is it existing together with parts, or being produced by them, or being the object of the cognition "it possesses parts"? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 75, first part).
— By virtue of its being [an effect],
its existence is characterized by a connection with the existence of its own cause, [which was] previously non-existent. (Bhāṃ, Ba, Ja)

Furthermore, in common worldly experience, an occasional entity is well-known as an effect (*kārya*). However, since the world exists eternally—just like Maheśvara—how can it be an effect? If it were argued that Maheśvara is also an effect because the trees, grass, and so forth contained within him are effects, then by the same logic, Maheśvara and others would also necessarily be effects, because the intellect (*buddhi*) and other qualities contained within him, as well as the color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*) and other properties contained within atoms, are themselves effects. Consequently, this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that Maheśvara must also have another intelligent cause, which results in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and contradicts your own established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*).

Or let it be granted that the world has the nature of an effect in some way or another; even so, is "effect" in general intended here as the reason (*hetu*), or a specific kind of effect? If it is effect in general, how can there be an inference from this to a specific cause characterized by intelligence? Since its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established only with a cause in general, the inference from this would have to be only for that general cause; and in that case, there is no dispute [regarding the existence of a cause], but the reason would be either redundant or contradictory, because when "being preceded by an intelligent agent" is the probandum (*sādhya*), one is merely proving a cause in general. (Note: *akiñcitkaratvaṃ* is corrected from *akiñcitkaratvaṃbuddhi-* based on the context.)

[Objection: "But surely, just as one infers fire in general from smoke in general, setting aside specific details such as whether the fuel is grass or leaves, so too, by inferring an intelligent cause in general from an effect in general, how can there be any contradiction here? [Reply: This too is incorrect; for an inference proceeds only on the basis of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), and that concomitance between an effect in general and a cause in general is established only through the cause itself—just as smoke in general is established through fire in general—and not through an intelligent being.

Nor does even mere smoke indicate the presence of mere fire, because it is inconclusive due to smoke in a room from which the fire has been removed; rather, it is smoke characterized by its rising, thick, and banner-like form that indicates it. Similarly, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) also indicates an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*), but only when it produces the cognition of having been made, not every instance of it.

If being merely similar were sufficient for something to be a means of knowledge (*gamaka*), it would follow that even steam and the like would be means of knowing fire; it would entail that the nature of being a self (*ātmatva*) and so forth would lead to the inference of Maheśvara’s being a transmigrating being, possessing limited knowledge, and not being the creator of the entire world; and it would result in the consequence that because of the property of being a real entity (*vastutva*) and so forth, the world would be preceded by a non-intelligent cause and produced by [atoms], just as in the case of atoms, since the objections and their resolutions are identical.

Just as some distinction is admitted between vapor and smoke despite their similarity in certain respects— by virtue of which smoke, and not vapor or the like, leads one to infer fire— so too, even regarding the "effect-ness" and "configuration" of the earth and other things as distinct from [non-effects],

if the specific kind of effect-ness is the reason, which is ascertained as following the positive and negative concomitance with an intelligent agent, then that reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because such a thing does not exist in the case of the earth and so forth.

Or, if it did exist, there would follow the absurd consequence that even for one who has never seen its production, the cognition that it was "made" would arise, just as it does in the case of dilapidated wells, palaces, and the like.

If it is argued that [the agent] does not [exist] because of superimposition (*samāropa*), why would that [superimposition] not also exist in both cases without distinction? For there is no difference in the fact that the agent is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*) in both instances. Now, if it is claimed that for one who possesses valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), the notion of "having been made" (*kṛtabuddhi*) indeed exists here, then by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the status of being a possessor of valid cognition established for the cognizer—is it by this very inference, by another inference, by scripture (*āgama*), or by worldly consensus (*lokapratīti*)? In the first case, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): for the arising of this [inference] depends on a reason whose qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is already established, and the establishment of the qualification of the reason occurs only upon the arising of that [inference].

Furthermore, there is no other inference whatsoever; or if there were, that too would arise only from a reason possessing a qualification. If that qualification were established through yet another inference, there would be an infinite regress; if it were established from the first inference, there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Would scripture (*āgama*) establish the authority of the knower when supported by reasoning, or even when unsupported? It cannot be the unsupported one, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is it supported [by reasoning], because the very reasoning that could support it is impossible;

and if one were to resort to such reasoning, it would lead to a circular argument (*cakraka*). For, the proof of the inference of "effect-ness" characterized by the production of the notion of having acted even in one who perceives no action depends upon the support of scripture; from that scripture thus supported, the status of the knower as an authoritative person (*prāmāṇika*) is established; and once that is established, the proof of the inference of "effect-ness" characterized by the production of the notion of having acted even in one who perceives no action is established.

Nor is the validity of the worldly consensus that "the world was created by some creator" established, because this consensus is rootless—just like the consensus that "the world was never otherwise than it is now," or like the Mīmāṃsaka’s conviction regarding the non-artificiality of the Veda. For there is no inferential mark (liṅga) for this [consensus], since the very emergence of such an inference is impossible due to the prior absence of any cognition of the relationship between the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin).

Furthermore, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of this [scripture] as being well-founded depends upon the emergence of this inference through the reason having its qualification established; and the establishment of this [scripture] as being well-founded depends upon the establishment of that [inference].

Nor is there any [support from] scripture (*āgama*), because even in that case, the consequence of mutual dependence would follow: for the establishment of this [scripture] as being rooted in a scripture that is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) depends upon the establishment of a transcendent person (*sātiśayapuruṣa*); and the establishment of its being rooted in a scripture that is a means of valid cognition—by virtue of being composed by him—depends upon the establishment of that [person].
Therefore, the perception of the earth and so forth as being artificial, which has come down through a succession of worldly rumors, does not arise from the force of a means of valid cognition.
Or, if there were perception [of activity] therein, then even one who observes no action would form the conviction that it has been performed, as in the case of ruined temples and the like;
thus says the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, fol. 115.
By this other inference, [it is established]. (Ba., Ja.)
—[The remainder is] "because of the existence of...

[Bhāṣya]. Now, it might be argued that there is no such rule that a produced thing must necessarily give rise to the cognition of being produced; for on ground filled with natural depressions, or among artificial gems and pearls, the cognition of being produced does not arise in one who perceives no human action. This, too, is an unexamined statement; for in those cases, the non-arising of the cognition of being produced is logically accounted for by the presence of a similarity to the configuration of non-artificial ground and so forth, which prevents the arising of the cognition of being produced.

Furthermore, even in the case of the earth and so forth, a similarity to an uncreated configuration is not possible, because you yourself do not accept the existence of an uncreated configuration; or, if you were to accept it, there would be the consequence of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Therefore, you must accept that there exists a specific characteristic—namely, the state of being of the same class as wells and other things whose makers are observed—which produces the cognition of "having been made" even for one who perceives no action, and which is impossible in the case of the earth and so forth (such as in old wells). Thus, how is the reason (*hetu*) not unestablished (*asiddha*)? — [Pariṣū-bhāṣya] — p. 105.12–14.

Even if it were established that the form consisting of the configuration of the earth’s surface and so forth is artificial— whether in the Bhāṣya or the Āhnika— it would nevertheless be contradictory, because here [in this argument] what is being proved is an intelligent agent qualified by a body and the like, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Nor should it be argued that this results in the total abolition of all inference, since contradiction would thus apply everywhere; for in the case of inferring fire from smoke and so forth, it is possible to apprehend fire as something common to both the kitchen and other locations.

To claim that here too there is no contradiction because a general "intelligent agent" (buddhimat-sāmānya) is established is also incorrect; for from this [inference], only that generality which has visible particulars as its substratum is established, not one whose particulars are invisible, since such a thing is not perceived even in a dream, just like the generality of a donkey's horn and its substrate.

Furthermore, if that which is not recognized as being pervaded by the cause were to be cognizable [by inference], then there would be the cognition of fire from smoke even when that fire possesses a non-luminous form and a hot touch;

therefore, one who distinguishes the relationship of cause and effect must infer such an effect only from such a cause, just as when the production of smoke possessing all its attributes from fire possessing all its attributes has been established through very firm means of valid cognition, it is only from such smoke that there is an inference of such fire.

Nor can the excellence of the creator be established on the grounds that, just as in the case of effects such as palaces, a gradation of excellence is perceived even in effects such as the earth; for if that were so, it would follow that a creator like ourselves—who possesses excellence—would be established.

[If one argues that] because he lacks the capacity to construct the earth and so forth, a different kind of creator must be established; this too is incorrect, because it would thus lead to the conclusion that there is no creator at all, since a creator of a different kind has never been perceived as being either the cause or the pervader [of such effects].

If that which is non-pervasive were to be cognized, then the pervasive would be uncognized while the non-pervasive would be cognized; this is a great feat of logical skill!—the realization [is] great illusion. (Bhāṣya; Ānandagiri)

Now, by way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), a specific creator (*kartṛviśe�șa*) possessing the excellence of complete knowledge of all causal factors (*kāraka*) through his causality and pervasiveness (*hetuvyāpakatvena*) is established; for one who has not understood the capacities of the causal factors cannot be the creator of an effect, as that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of everyone being the creator of everything.

Furthermore, it is not possible for someone like us to comprehend the capacity of all causal factors, such as the earth and so forth, because atoms and other such entities are beyond the reach of the senses. Therefore, if his agency—defined as the state of being the employer of all causal factors—is established, it is established only as preceded by an excellence consisting in the thorough knowledge of their capacities. This too is charming only when left unexamined; for it is not proven that the status of being an employer is invariably concomitant with the thorough knowledge of capacities, since we observe the employment of the palate and other organs—which are the causes of speech and so forth—even in states such as sleep, intoxication, or madness, despite the absence of any thorough knowledge of their capacities.

Or, let there be that invariable concomitance (between God and the knowledge of all causal factors); even so, the complete knowledge of the powers of all causal factors is not established, because we observe architects and others acting as directors of construction in temples and the like despite their lack of knowledge regarding dharma and other such matters.

And just as architects and others lack complete knowledge of all causal factors—such as dharma—because they do not bring the work they have begun to completion, let it be the same for God as well, since there is no difference in this regard: he too does not bring to completion the effects he has initiated, such as the sprout.

Even if that [divine] knowledge were admitted, let such an arrangement exist for the enjoyer as well, due to the power of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), just as it does in the case of the architect and others; furthermore, the contradiction with common experience (*pratīti*) is equally present in both cases.

Moreover, let it be granted that this [enjoyer] alone possesses that knowledge; nevertheless, it is untenable for a single entity to be the presiding director of all causal factors (*kāraka*), since it is entirely possible for multiple entities to be the directors of various causal factors.

Indeed, there is no fixed rule that every effect must be produced by a single agent alone, or by several agents restricted to acting together; for we observe the production of effects in many ways: sometimes a single effect is produced by a single agent, as a cloth by a weaver; sometimes a plurality of effects is produced by a single agent, as jars, pots, bowls, and so forth, by a potter; sometimes a plurality of effects is produced by a plurality of agents, as jars, cloths, crowns, carts, and so forth, by potters and others; and sometimes even a single effect is produced by a plurality of agents, as an anthill by white ants—for indeed, there is no single presiding agent over them.

Furthermore, in the construction of palaces and the like, it is not the case that activity proceeds only when many architects and others are presided over by a single master builder; for there is no contradiction in their activity even when they have distinct intentions and are not presided over by a single master builder, and because we observe the activity of many architects and others being presided over by a single master builder. If one were to postulate a Great Lord as the sole presiding agent of the world, why would there not also be activity of various individual bodies even without his presiding, given that the validity of both types of observation is indistinguishable?
"You are its accomplished agent"— this is the reading in manuscripts *ba*, *ja*, and *bhā*;
in manuscript *ā*, it is "in the state of being asleep or intoxicated."
Nevertheless, the oneness of the creator is not established because of the demonstration of deviation;
and if a single creator is unproven, what is the basis for his omniscience? (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 57).

It is not so, because a single agent [of such an act] is unestablished due to the non-existence of [multiple] causal factors; furthermore, since the state of having multiple agents is never observed anywhere, there is no doubt [that it is impossible].

For there is no such rule that every effect must be produced by a single agent alone, nor that it must be produced by many agents restricted to acting as one; this is because we observe the production of effects in various ways [Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 367; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.

Furthermore, this reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) due to trees, grass, and so forth that grow without being cultivated (*akṛṣṭaprabhava*). For two kinds of effects are observed: some are preceded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimatpūrvaka*), such as jars and the like; others, however, are the opposite, such as trees and the like that grow without cultivation. Thus, since both [types of effects] are established through the validity of their respective cognitions, [the reason is uncertain].

If there were no deviation [of the reason] because those [counter-examples] are made the subject (*pakṣa*), then even such arguments as "He is dark-skinned because he is his son, like other sons" would result in being valid proofs; consequently, no reason whatsoever would be deviant, since it is possible to make the very object of deviation the subject in every case.

Furthermore, there is deviation with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth of God (*īśvara*); for although these are effects, they do not have an intelligent agent distinct from God as their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

For in the case of examples such as a jar, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" is established not only by its being preceded by an intelligent agent, but also by its being preceded by an intelligent agent distinct from its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Furthermore, if one were to admit the existence of an intelligent agent distinct [from the material cause], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor is it logical for a single entity to be both the inherent cause and the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), since that is not observed in the case of jars and the like. If one were to postulate something not observed in those cases, why could one not likewise postulate that the earth and so forth have non-intelligent causes, given that there is no distinction?

Some describe an inconsistency regarding this [argument] even with respect to stationary objects and the like, which have been made the subject of the thesis, since their status as causes possessing intelligence is established. (38)
We observe this in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 362, in the manuscripts designated as Ba,
Ja, or Bhā.

And this [reason] is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa); for the absence of an agent in the case of sprouts arising without being ploughed and so forth is determined by direct perception itself, just as [the reason] "substantiality" is [mistimed] when proving that fire is not hot.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the non-existence of only that which is visible (*dṛśya*) is established by its non-perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not of anything else? Otherwise, even space (*ākāśa*) and so forth would be non-existent. But this [self] is not visible; how then could its non-existence follow from this? [Reply: This too is unsatisfactory. For, if its existence were established from some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then there would be a non-perception due to its invisibility. And would that existence be established from this very [non-perception], or from another means of valid cognition? In the first case, there is a circular argument (*cakraka*): for if its existence were established from this [non-perception], then its non-perception due to invisibility would be established; once that is established, there would be no fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*); and from that, the establishment of its existence [would follow]. Thus, it is circular.
The second position is also untenable; for there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its existence.

Or, even granting its existence, if it is invisible, is the cause its lack of a body, the power of knowledge and so forth, or a specific class (*jāti*)? It cannot be the lack of a body, because it is impossible for one who is bodiless to be an agent of action.
For instance: God is not the creator of the earth and so forth, because He is bodiless, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*).

[Objection: Surely the body does not enter into the causal complex of agency, for even in its absence, agency is observed in the act of impelling one's own body merely by being the locus of knowledge, desire, and effort. [Reply: That is incorrect; for that impulsion is observed only through a connection with the body. Indeed, the self’s possession of a body consists precisely in such a connection; only when this exists is agency in performing an action—whether toward one's own body or elsewhere—logically possible.

In the absence of a body, even the status of being a substratum for knowledge and so forth is impossible, as in the case of a liberated soul (*muktātman*); for [the body] is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for the production of those [qualities]. If they were produced even in the absence of that cause, it would follow that they could also be produced in a liberated soul; or else, it would follow that the earth and other elements could be produced even in the absence of an intelligent efficient cause. If it is argued that this is not a fault because those [qualities] are eternal, that too is unsatisfactory, since the eternity of knowledge and so forth is not perceived anywhere. Furthermore, it contradicts the following inference: "The knowledge and other qualities of God are not eternal, because they are knowledge and so forth, like the knowledge and other qualities of people such as ourselves."

If there were a transgression of their observed nature, then that [transgression] would apply to trees and the like as well, since there is no distinction; therefore, it must be admitted that cognition and the rest are produced solely by the body. How then can the body be "inefficacious"? For if being a cause consisted merely in being a concomitant, it would follow that even the yellowness of fire is a cause with respect to smoke. Indeed, mere yellowness is not the cause of smoke, because smoke does not arise even when that [yellowness] exists in yellow orpiment and similar substances.

However, there is nothing contradictory in [the claim] that it is fire as qualified [by other factors] that serves as the cause; for just as fire connected with fuel produces smoke and not any other [fire], so too it is yellowness as qualified by fire that is the basis for that [perception], and not anything else. Furthermore, if the power of spells (*vidyā*) and the like were the cause of invisibility, then this person might occasionally become visible; indeed, perpetual invisibility is never observed among those who possess spells or those who hold the *tantras*.

Since this [being] differs from those who possess other sciences (*vidyā*), why, when one seeks to transcend the nature of what is perceived, would one not also seek to transcend that [nature] for the world, given that the world also differs from other effects? If it is argued that a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*), like that of a *piśāca* or similar being, is the cause of his invisibility—this too is unsatisfactory, because a specific genus is impossible for a single entity, as such a genus must reside in multiple individuals.
[Objection: But even though he possesses a body, how is he invisible? Is it due to the power of sciences (*vidyā*) and so forth, or due to a specific genus? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 433)
Because no part of the body is perceived [as such], and because it is impossible for that which lacks a body and sense organs to perform that action.
Because it is impossible for one who lacks that connection [to the world] to be the creator of the universe, just like a liberated soul (*muktātman*), as stated in *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī* p.
271, and *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* p. 119.
For a bodiless presiding agent would be like a liberated soul;
[Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 660].
"The intellect of the Creator is not eternal, because it possesses the nature of being conscious, like any other consciousness";
since this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), the Creator is not the cause of the earth.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 360:

Or let it be that he is invisible; even so, would he be the cause of the earth and other things by his mere existence (*sattāmātra*), or by possessing knowledge (*jñānavattva*), or by possessing knowledge, desire, and effort (*jñānecchāprayatnavattva*), or by activity preceded by those, or by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)? In the first case, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a potter and the like would be its cause, since mere existence is no different in their case as well.
In the second case, however, there follows the consequence that even yogis would be its creator.

Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because yogins do not possess such cognition whose object is the entirety of all things, from what source is this established? If it is said to be from "being the creator of all," that is untenable due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of being the creator of all depends on the establishment of omniscience, and the establishment of omniscience depends on the establishment of being the creator of all.
Furthermore, the third position is also incorrect, because the possession of knowledge, desire, and effort is denied to one who is bodiless;

thus, even the possession of activity is impossible for the bodiless. For activity must be either produced by the body or produced by speech; neither of these two is possible at all in one who is bodiless.
Furthermore, there is no such cognition whatsoever for anyone that "I have been impelled here by the Lord" through either speech or body;
and activity is action, yet that is difficult to establish for him.

For instance, the Lord is devoid of activity because he is omnipresent, like space. If he were possessed of activity, it would follow that he lacks stability, and thus he would be non-eternal; for only an object whose nature does not deviate from its own state can be established as eternal and of a single form.

Nor is there a deviation [of the reason] by means of atoms (*paramāṇu*), for even their impermanence through transformation is accepted; likewise, if God (*īśvara*) were also accepted as being subject to that [transformation], it would entail the consequence of his having another intelligent cause, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Otherwise, there would be a deviation of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth by that very [atom]. Therefore, this is established.

If the omniscience of God is established primarily because He is the instigator of all causal factors (*kārakas*), and His status as the primary instigator of all causal factors—without dependence on any other instigator—is established by virtue of that very omniscience, then how can the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) be avoided? (Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 368; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
78; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 128)

Furthermore, regarding its effectuation, would its activity be partial or total? If it were partial, then there would have to be as many parts of God as there are effects; thus, the thesis of a partless God is abandoned. If the activity were total, then for as many effects as there are, there would follow as many distinct Gods, resulting in the destruction of the thesis of a single God.

Furthermore, does that [entity] perform its one effect by means of that very same nature by which it performs that [effect], and likewise its other effects such as its persistence, or by means of a different nature? If it were by means of that very same [nature], there would be no sequence or diversity among the effects, namely persistence, arising, and destruction;
or, if there were a difference in nature, its impermanence would be lost. (Ba., Ja., Bhā.)

Because, if the intention (*abhisandhi*) of Maheśvara were unitary with respect to the production, destruction, and persistence of all effects, it would follow that they arise and so forth simultaneously, and thus their diversity would be untenable;
as stated in the *Aṣṭaśatī* and on page 279 of the *Aṣṭasahasrī*. (Note: *a-ba-ja* refers to manuscript variants).

Is sovereignty (aiśvarya) knowledge, agency, or something else? If it is knowledge, is it merely the state of being a knower, or omniscience? Regarding the first alternative, he would be merely a knower and not the Lord (Īśvara); for one who knows a particular thing is not called the Lord in that regard, just like any other knower.
As for the second alternative, he would possess only omniscience and not sovereignty, as is the case with the Sugata and others.
If, on the other hand, it is agency, then it would follow that potters and others—who produce various kinds of effects—would also possess sovereignty.

Nor is it anything else, because there exists nothing other than desire and effort that could serve as the basis for sovereignty in God. If it is maintained that those two alone are the basis for it there, then does everything encompassed by them produce [the effect] simultaneously, or only some part? If everything were encompassed, then everything would arise at once.

If you say it is something [distinct], then, since the objects of desire and effort are successive, how could those two possess a single uniform nature? Furthermore, desire arises through the delimitation of the object desired; and without the form of the object of the knowledge produced by the subsequent conjunction of the self and the mind, that [desire] would not be able to apprehend even the self as having a fixed object—[that is,] to take it as its objective domain. Moreover, do this [Lord's] desire to create and desire to withdraw occur simultaneously or successively? If they occur simultaneously, there follows the undesirable consequence of creation and withdrawal occurring at the same time.

If [the Lord] arises sequentially, a cause for that must be stated; and if there is dependence on a cause, his eternality is undermined. Now, if it is argued that even though he is eternal, he produces a variety of effects due to the proximity of various auxiliary factors (sahakārin) such as desire and effort—[we ask]: are those auxiliaries independent of him, or dependent upon him? If they are independent, then by virtue of being effects themselves, they would constitute a counter-example (vyabhicāra) to the claim that everything is an effect of him. If they are dependent upon him, why do they not exist at all times? If you say it is because their own causes are absent, then the same question arises: are those causes also dependent upon him or not? Thus, the refutation remains in its original state, leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā).

Furthermore, do these auxiliary causes (sahakārin) provide assistance to that [entity], or not? If they do not provide assistance, how can they be auxiliaries? For that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). If they do provide assistance, then this [entity] must be subject to transformation (pariṇāmin), because the assistance rendered by them is not distinct from it. If it were a distinct entity (arthāntara), the designation "its [assistance]" would not be possible. Moreover, if another assistance were to be produced by that [first assistance], there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).

It might be argued that the Lord alone is not the sole cause, but rather acts in dependence upon other auxiliary causes such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). This is incorrect; for if some assistance were to be rendered by the auxiliaries, then he would have a dependence upon those auxiliaries.

Since [the Lord] is eternal and thus incapable of having any excellence added to him by others, there is nothing he has to obtain from his auxiliary causes (sahakārin); why, then, would he depend upon such auxiliaries who provide no benefit? Furthermore, even those auxiliaries—since their very birth is dependent on the Lord—are always present together with him. [Objection: But why are they not always in attendance, given that their birth is dependent on His knowledge and so forth? [Reply: If it is the case that their production is not dependent on Him, then the reason "being an effect" (kāryatva) and so forth is inconclusive (anaikāntika) because of those very [auxiliaries].

Furthermore (*kiñca*), does the Lord’s engagement in the creation of the world proceed according to his own whim, through dependence on karma, out of compassion, with the aim of achieving purposes such as merit (*dharma*), for the sake of sport (*krīḍā*), for the purpose of inflicting punishment and bestowing grace, or by his very nature? If it were according to his whim, then at some time there might even be a different kind of creation. *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 122; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 79. U. [Vādidevasūri] states: Moreover, regarding the Lord's activity in the creation of the universe, does it proceed according to his own pleasure, under the subjection of karma, out of compassion, with the objective of attaining goals such as dharma, for the sake of play, for the purpose of administering restraint and favor, or by way of his inherent nature? If it proceeded according to his pleasure, then perhaps a different kind of creation would occur at some point.
Furthermore, if he were dependent on karma, his independence would be lost; for this alone is true independence or lordship (*īśvaratva*)—namely, not looking toward the face of another.
If, however, [he acts] out of compassion, then by virtue of being compassionate, he should simultaneously endow everyone with prosperity; consequently, no one would remain in suffering.

If it is argued that he causes them to experience various karmas with the very intention that they might attain prosperity, this is the logic of discarding a sweetmeat after its impurities have been washed away.

For this indeed is the compassion of the Compassionate One: the constant concern that not even a trace of suffering should befall others. Now, what does the Lord do? It is by their previously accumulated karmas alone that they are so controlled that they experience suffering. If that is so, what is His human effort (puruṣakāra)? For the exhaustion of karmas is established through their very experience.

And if [the Lord] acts as an agent while depending on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), what is the purpose of postulating him? If even this postulated being is dependent upon the unseen force, then let the world itself be dependent on that; what is the use of this internal tumor? Furthermore, if he engages in activity for the sake of purposes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, how could he be one who has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*), given the contradiction of having such purposes? And if there is the existence of play (*krīḍā*), how can he be free from passion (*vītarāga*), like a common man in the street? It is truly a great marvel that the Supreme Person, the Lord, plays like a child or a madman!
Even if he bestows both punishment and favor, how can he be free from passion and hatred? For instance: God must possess passion because he bestows favor, like a king;
likewise, he must possess hatred because he inflicts punishment, just as a king does.

Now, if it is argued that he acts by his very nature—just as the sun illuminates because its nature is luminosity—then since consciousness would be rendered ineffective despite its existence, let the insentient world also proceed by its own nature; what is the use of postulating a presiding controller? For he has existed by his very nature throughout beginningless time.

How could there be a restriction regarding place and so forth for that which is insentient, or how could there be no activity toward an effect even when it has been accomplished? This is the same in other cases as well, since the same defect is demonstrated for God (Īśvara) as well, who possesses a nature such as eternity and so on. Furthermore, for what purpose does this God act when creating? For in the world, those who are agents proceed by aiming at something, thinking, "I shall obtain this" or "I shall avoid this. However, for God there is nothing to be avoided because he is devoid of suffering, nor is there anything to be acquired because he possesses mastery.
Some say it is for the sake of sport (krīḍā).

First, some say that the Lord creates for the sake of sport (*krīḍā*). But this is improper; for sport indeed exists for the sake of pleasure, and the Blessed One does not seek pleasure. Others say it is for the sake of manifesting his own power (*vibhūti*); but this too is just the same. For what purpose, then, does he act? He proceeds from his very nature (*svābhāvya*); thus it is faultless. (Nyāyavārttika, p.
463; Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, 4)
1.21 Nyāyamañjarī, p. 202.
And thus, for one who is dependent, independence is obstructed.
(Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 653)
And because there would be no beings to be pitied, compassion would not arise in him; yet, impelled by compassion, he would create only that which is auspicious. (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 76)

*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 76.

And if these were to engage in play for the sake of sport, their state of having accomplished their purpose would be frustrated. (56)
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, p. 653; *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 77:

Furthermore, would this [Self’s] possession of intelligence be by means of an impermanent cognition or a permanent one? It cannot be by means of a permanent one, because its permanence has been demonstrated to be sublated by both perception and inference.

Now, if [the knowledge] were impermanent, from what would it arise—from the contact of the sense organs with their objects, from a particular state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), from the power of the qualities (*dharma*) arising therefrom, or from mere reflection? Among these, the first position is untenable; for this disembodied internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and any other sense organ are impossible [for a liberated being], just as in the case of a liberated soul (*muktātman*). Or, even if they were possible, there would be no omniscience, because the knowledge produced by them would have only restricted objects.

Furthermore, are the insentient eyes and other organs produced by knowledge when presided over by someone, or without being presided over? If they are without a presider, then let the world also produce [effects] while being insentient and without being presided over by anyone; enough with the postulation of a presider. If, on the other hand, they are presided over, is it by another presider or by that very same one? If it is by another presider, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is by that very same one, there is a circularity (*cakraka*). For instance: being knowers, they are impelled; being impelled, they produce knowledge; and having produced knowledge, they become knowers.

The excellence of meditative absorption (*samādhiviśeṣa*) and the contemplation (*anudhyāna*) are themselves specific forms of knowledge; since that [knowledge] is not yet established, how could there be the arising of something from itself? Furthermore, in the absence of an excellence of meditative absorption, how could the dharma arising from it be possible therein, such that through its majesty the production of knowledge might occur? Moreover, for one who is bodiless, an excellence of meditative absorption and so forth is as impossible as it is for a liberated soul (*muktātman*).

Therefore, since a cause is impossible, the existence of knowledge in God cannot be established; how then could His possession of intelligence be proven? If it is argued that His possession of it is established by means of the generality of "intelligence" (buddhi-sāmānya), regardless of specific distinctions between eternal and non-eternal intelligence, that too is worthless; for a second specific type [of intelligence] is impossible, as no eternal specific instance of intelligence is ever experienced, since only non-eternal intelligence is experienced at all times.

Therefore, if that generality were established, it would be established as being the very basis for the specific cognition of impermanence; yet, since a cause for that specific [cognition] is impossible in the case of God, how could that generality, which is based upon it, be established?
Regarding this, first:

let us grant, for the sake of argument, that he possesses intelligence in some way or another; nevertheless, there would be a collapse of the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge regarding scriptures—every scripture would be valid simply because it was composed by God, just like the well-known scriptures composed by him.

Furthermore, there would be the collapse of the established distinctions between the proponent, the opponent, and so forth, because all beings would be subject to the commands of the Lord. Moreover, since those who carry out commands cannot engage in contrary conduct, there would be the collapse of *saṃsāra*; for prior to the activity of the Lord, there is an absence of bodies, organs, and the like, and consequently, an absence of all personal qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so on. Indeed, it is not logical that souls which have attained absolute purity—given the absence of bodies, organs, and the like, and the absence of specific qualities such as cognition—should remain unliberated.

Is it not a great exercise of foresight to claim that he who is engaged in the process of cyclic existence brings about its cessation? Therefore, since it is impossible for the God imagined by the followers of Yoga to be the creator of the entire world, omniscience is not established on this basis.
The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (2.1.18) contains treatises intended to support the Lord’s status as the creator of the world.
