By this, the omniscience of the Lord (Īśvara) as postulated by the Sāṅkhya is also refuted; for if he is asserted to be the efficient cause of the world, the aforementioned defects follow without distinction. This constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Sāṅkhya regarding the nature of the Lord. *Prameyaratnamālā*, p. 61.

Now, since the Sāṅkhyas describe the nature of the Lord differently, how can the defects stated regarding the position of the Lord as conceived by the Yogins be applicable here? For it is said: "The Lord is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (kleśa), actions (karman), their fruitions (vipāka), and latent dispositions (āśaya)" (Yogasūtra 1.24).
In this context, ignorance (avidyā), egoism (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and the will to live (abhiniveśa) are the afflictions.
Yoga Sūtra 1.24:

"Karmas" are auspicious and inauspicious actions; their "fruits" consist of the experience of the results of those actions; "dispositions" (āśayas) are various latent impressions (saṃskāras) corresponding to those [fruits]. That particular Puruṣa who is untouched by these is Īśvara.

Nor should it be argued that this would result in the undesirable consequence of all liberated souls (muktātman) being Īśvaras, since they are equally untouched by those [karmas]; for it is impossible for them to ever be untouched by bondage.
For He who is eternally liberated from bondage, untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like, is the Lord (*īśvara*);

and the other liberated souls (*muktātman*) are not of such a nature. This is because they possess the three types of bondage characterized as *prākṛta*, *vaikārika*, and *dakṣiṇā*. For the *prākṛta* bondage has the nature of the absence of discrimination between the Self and the non-Self; the *vaikārika* is of the nature of attachment to sense objects; and the *dakṣiṇā* bondage consists of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) that have mounted upon experience.

By these three bonds, the Lord alone remains untouched from the very root; whereas liberated souls have attained isolation (*kaivalya*) only after uprooting all three of these bonds through discriminative knowledge, equanimity, and the experience of the fruits of karma.

But this Blessed Lord is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord; He has no prior limit (*pūrvā koṭi*) as do transmigrating or liberated souls, nor does He have a subsequent limit (*aparā koṭi*) as do yogis who possess knowledge of reality but remain dissolved in *prakṛti*, for they, even after attaining liberation, may again become subject to bondage.

His sovereignty is established through his connection with an intellect characterized by unsurpassed excellence; and the unsurpassed excellence of that intellect is established because he has adopted the scripture whose defining characteristic is instruction and protection.

But if this is so, there is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*): for only when the unsurpassed excellence of the intellect is established is the adoption of the scripture characterized by it established, and only when that [scripture] is established is the unsurpassed excellence of the intellect established. This is an unexamined statement, because in the case of Īśvara, the relationship between the scripture and the unsurpassed excellence of the intellect is possible as being beginningless (*anādi*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of the eternal, the pure, the blissful, and the self in what is non-eternal, impure, painful, and non-self.
Yoga Sūtra 2.6:
Asmitā is the very identity of the powers of the seer and the seen.

The affliction called *asmitā* (egoism) is said to be the attainment of a single nature by these two: the power of consciousness (*puruṣa*), which is the power of seeing, and the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the power of being seen.
When there is an apparent non-differentiation between the power of the enjoyer and the power of the object of enjoyment—which are utterly distinct and utterly unmixed—experience is imagined to occur.
(Yogasūtra Vyāsabhāṣya 2.6)
Attachment is that which underlies pleasure;
aversion is that which underlies suffering.
"Spontaneous clinging (abhiniveśa) is rooted in that same way even for the wise" (Yoga Sūtra 2.9).

Ignorance has five branches— ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live; these very [five] afflictions (kleśas) shall be designated by their own specific names as darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter gloom (andhatāmisra) in the context of the impurities of the mind, in the *Yogabhāṣya* on *Sūtra* 1.8.
The latent deposit of karma, rooted in the afflictions, is to be experienced in the present or future birth. (Yoga Sūtra 2.12)
When the root exists, there is its fruition: birth, lifespan, and experience.
(Yoga Sūtra 2.13)
The latent impressions (vāsanā) corresponding to that [experience] constitute the disposition (āśaya);
Yoga Sūtra, Vyāsabhāṣya 1.24.
And that bondage is threefold: the bondage of nature (*prakṛtibandha*), the transformative bondage (*vaikārikabandha*), and the bondage of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇābandha*).

Among these, the "bondage of nature" is the conceit of superiority regarding the eight constituent natures—namely, intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). The "transformative bondage" is the notion that the states beginning with Brahmā are the highest good.
The "binding of the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇābandha*) refers to the ritual worship consisting of the giving of cows and other gifts; [see] *Sāṃkhyakārikābhāṣya* (Māṭhara) p.
62 and *Tattvayāthārthyadīpanī* p. 81.

Absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) is called the bond of nature (*prakṛtibandha*); that which arises from sacrifices and the like is called the bond of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇābandha*); and experience caused by power and so forth is called the transformative (*vaikārika*). (Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya ad Sāṃkhyakārikā 45; Yogasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇa ad YS 2.41; Tattvavaiśāradī ad YS 2.41).
Sāṃkhyasaṃ [pṛ.

24]: Ignorance and the other afflictions (*kleśa*), wholesome and unwholesome actions (*karman*), their maturation as fruit (*vipāka*), and the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) conforming to those [are] the disposition (*āśaya*).

And these [qualities], while residing in the mind, are designated as belonging to the Puruṣa, for he is the enjoyer of their fruit; just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is designated as belonging to the master. That particular Puruṣa who is untouched by this experience is the Lord (Īśvara).
[Objection: But there are many who have attained isolation (kaivalya); for they too, having severed the three bonds, have attained isolation.
Furthermore, the relationship of the Lord with that [bondage] is neither past nor future;

just as for one who is liberated, no prior limit of bondage is known, so it is not for the Lord; or just as for one merged in primordial nature (prakṛti), a subsequent limit of bondage is conceivable, so it is not for the Lord.
But he is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord.
Is that perpetual excellence of the Lord, which arises from his assumption of preeminent *sattva*, caused by something or is it without cause? Scripture is its cause;
but what is the cause of the scripture? It has preeminent *sattva* as its cause.
The beginningless connection between these two— the excellence of the scripture and the existence of God— subsists,
as stated in the *Yogasūtra* with the commentary of Vyāsa (1.24).
And that sovereignty is eightfold: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, and *yatrakāmāvasāyitā*.
Among these, *aṇimā* is when, having assumed a minute body, one moves through all worlds unseen by any beings;
*laghimā* is when, due to lightness, one moves about like the wind.
*Mahimā* (greatness): that one becomes worshipped by all the worlds and greater even than the great.
*Prāpti* (attainment): whatever one thinks of with the mind, that very thing one attains.
*Prākāmya* (unrestricted will): that one possesses abundant desire; the meaning is that one is able to enjoy sense objects.

Sovereignty (*īśitvam*) is that by which one becomes the lord of the three worlds; mastery (*vaśitvam*) is that by which one brings under control all beings, both stationary and moving, and whose senses are subdued;

and the power of fulfilling desires at will (*yatrakāmāvasāyitā*) is that by which one dwells wherever one desires—whether among the realms of Brahmā, Prajāpati, the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pitṛs, Piśācas, humans, animals, or in other locations.

Sovereignty consists of eightfold lordly power by virtue of being a lord—namely, *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*, *mahimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva*—as stated in the Sāṃkhyamāṭharavṛtti, p. 41.

Among these, *aṇimā* is that one becomes minute; *laghimā* is that one becomes light; *mahimā* is that one becomes great; *prāpti* is that one touches the moon with the tip of a finger; *prākāmya* is the non-obstruction of one's will, such that one emerges from and sinks into the earth as if in water; *vaśitva* is that one becomes the master over the elements and elemental products, while others are not masters; *īśitṛtva* is that one exercises lordship over their origin, dissolution, and arrangement; and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva* is the state of having true resolve, whereby the primary constituents of the elements abide exactly according to one's resolve (Yogasūtra Vyāsabhāṣya 3.45).

Supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), which has transformation as its domain, is of many kinds: *aṇimā* (minuteness), *mahimā* (magnitude), *laghimā* (lightness), *garimā* (heaviness), *prāpti* (attainment), *prākāmyam* (efficacy), *īśitvam* (lordship), *vaśitvam* (control), *apratighāta* (non-obstruction), *antardhānam* (invisibility), *kāmarūpitvam* (the ability to assume forms at will), and so forth. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, Rājavārttika, p.
144; Pūjita, Ma-ba, Ja).

Regarding the power of determining objects according to one's will (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*) and the state of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*): for a yogin who has mastered the efficacy of the *guṇas*, whatever he resolves upon as being for a particular purpose is made fit for that specific utility;
even by resolving that poison shall perform the function of nectar, he can cause someone to live by making them eat it.
In the *Yogasūtra-bhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī* (3.25):
"The divine [birth] is of eight varieties, and that of the animal kingdom is fivefold."
And the human realm is of one kind; briefly stated, the elemental creation is fivefold.
For example—the Brahma, Prajapatya, Aindra, Paitra, Gandharva, Yaksha, Rakshasa, and Paishacha—thus the divine creation is eightfold. (53)
The animal realm is fivefold; here, because they share a common characteristic, it consists of domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and immobile beings.
The human realm is of one kind, because they share a common characteristic, ranging from Brahmins down to Cāṇḍālas (Sāṃkhyamīmāṃsābhāṣya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, p.
—*sa pai*— *ba*, *ja*, *bhāṃ*;
—*cepu tai*— *ba*, *ja*, *bhā*.

And because a gradation (*tāratamya*) is observed among these [qualities] such as knowledge and sovereignty, by way of being more excellent or most excellent, that in which excellence finds its ultimate rest is the Lord (*īśvara*). Thus, He is established through presumptive inference (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*).

For instance—that which is a gradation of excellence must come to rest somewhere, just as the excellence of dimension comes to rest in space; and since there is such a gradation of excellence regarding qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty, the activity of this Lord, whose nature is thus well-established, proceeds solely for the sake of bestowing grace upon all transmigrating beings. For He remains possessed of the vow: "I shall uplift the entire world during the dissolution of the aeons and the great dissolution.
And when meditated upon by those engaged in contemplation, or recited with the *praṇava* and other designations, He grants them their desired fruit.

Furthermore, because he is not limited by time, He is the teacher even of the ancient sages such as the great seer Kapila; for they are indeed delimited by time, such as the *kalpa* and *mahākalpa*, but the Lord is not.
Thus, in Him resides the unsurpassed seed of omniscience.
(Yoga Sūtra 1.26)

There is the attainment of the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāprāpti*) of the seed of omniscience because it possesses degrees of excellence, like [the growth of] a physical dimension; that wherein there is the attainment of the limit of knowledge is the omniscient one (*sarvajña*).

Vyāsabhāṣya: Although there is an absence of benefit for himself, his purpose is the benefit of beings through the instruction of knowledge and dharma, thinking, "I shall rescue the transmigrating persons during the kalpa-dissolutions and the great dissolution."

And so it has been said: "The Blessed One, the Supreme Sage, the Primordial Knower, having empowered a mind of emanation out of compassion, proclaimed the Dharma to Āsuri, who desired to know," as stated in the *Yogasūtra-bhāṣya* on 1.25.
The syllable *praṇava* is the designator of that [entirety];
its repetition and the contemplation of its meaning [constitute yoga].
Yoga Sūtra 1.26–27:
He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time.
Yoga Sūtra 1.26:
For previous teachers were limited by time; he, however, to whom time does not apply for the purpose of limitation—he is the teacher even of the ancients.
Vyāsabhāṣya: The refutation of that— here it is answered.

As for what was stated—beginning with "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth—that is charming only so long as it is not critically examined. For, is his essential nature merely the state of being untouched by afflictions and the like, and when that exists, does he possess omniscience? In the first case, he would be nothing other than a liberated soul (*mukta*), because he is untouched by those [afflictions], just like any other liberated soul, and not the Lord (*īśvara*); for otherwise, the status of being the Lord would follow for the selves of other liberated souls as well.

The claim that "there is no possibility of that [bondage] for them because they are never touched by bondage" is mere faith; for even in the case of God, it is impossible for him to be never touched by bondage, and that impossibility will be demonstrated on the occasion of explaining liberation. Now, if his nature consists in omniscience while being untouched by that [bondage], how is that established? Is it from his being the creator of all, or from his being the locus of sovereignty? Of these, the first position is untenable, as it would entail the same multitude of defects already cast upon the position of the Lord accepted by the Yogas.

Furthermore, if agency is admitted for him, then the definition of the Self—namely, that "it is non-agent, devoid of qualities, and pure"—would be untenable. If it is argued that this definition belongs only to other selves and not to the Lord, because the Lord is distinct from them, and therefore this fault does not apply; [we reply: in that case, since purity and so forth would also not constitute the very nature of the Lord, he would become excessively distinct from them.
(Page 109, Line 8)
Is its nature merely the state of being untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, such that when this exists there is omniscience?
Or is it lordship (*īśvaratva*), due to being the creator of all things or being the locus of sovereignty? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 454)

Or, let it be granted that he is the agent; even so, would he perform his work independently or under the influence of *prakṛti*? If he were independent, then he would not differ from the God postulated by the Yogas, and thus he must be understood as being flawed by the very same defects as that [Yoga] doctrine. If, on the other hand, he were dependent on *prakṛti*, that is not the case, because *prakṛti* itself is unestablished in its own nature; and the non-establishment of that [prakṛti] will be proven later, as it is going to be refuted.

And would its dependence on that [cause] be due to the imparting of a new excellence (*atiśaya*) by it, or because of performing a single effect in conjunction with it? Regarding these, the first hypothesis is untenable, because since it is entirely eternal and unchanging, the imparting of a new excellence to it is impossible.

The second hypothesis is also illogical, because it would entail the simultaneity of all effects; for the two causes known as Īśvara and Pradhāna, whose capacities are unimpeded, are present everywhere and at all times, and thus their causal conditions would be complete at every moment.

Whatever has its complete causal conditions present must necessarily come into being at that time, just as a sprout arises from a causal complex that has reached its final moment. Since every effect is dependent upon two causes—the eternal and omnipresent Lord (Īśvara) and Primordial Matter (Prakṛti)—does He produce all effects independently, or is He dependent on Prakṛti? [Syādvādamañjarī, p. 454]. Their cooperation is postulated because of their acting as auxiliary causes.
That [cognition] would arise either from the imparting of an excellence or from the performance of a single purposeful action; however,
neither of these conceptions is tenable for that which is immutable.
Not [from] a second [cause], because it would entail the simultaneity of effects. (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 59)
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 84, first half;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 554.

Now, it might be argued that although these two causes are always and everywhere present, the effect does not arise at all times or in all places because, in the regulation of the persistence, origination, and destruction [of things], the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—whose functions have become manifest—act as auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) respectively, and because those [auxiliaries] occur in a sequential manner. This too is unsatisfactory; for, between the persistence, origination, and dissolution of Nature (*prakṛti*) and God (*īśvara*), at the time of producing any one of them, do they possess the capacity to produce the others or not? If they do, then even at the time of creation, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of persistence and dissolution, since the causes are complete, just as they are for origination. Similarly, at the time of persistence, there would be the consequence of origination and destruction, and at the time of destruction, the consequence of persistence and origination.
And this is not tenable,
for it is not logical that phenomena such as arising and so forth, which exist through mutual exclusion, should simultaneously reside in a single substratum, because that contradicts experience.

Alternatively, if they lack causal capacity, then among the [four] characteristics— stability and the rest— only one effect would always be produced, since those two possess the capacity to produce that [one], while the capacity to produce any other does not exist for them.
Furthermore, since it is contradictory for these two immutable entities to produce capacity [for action], otherwise their nature as eternal and unitary would be contradicted;
this is stated here: at the time of performing one action, do those two possess the capacity to accomplish another effect, or not?
If even at the time of creation both [subject and object] were to exist as something other [than consciousness], then,
given the existence of one, the other two would follow as a consequence.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 60;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 84, line 102.
Furthermore, regarding the consequence [stated] on pages 455–456 of the *Ratnāvalī*:

"But surely, even though these [qualities] possess that capacity, when the functioning of *rajas* is manifest and it becomes the auxiliary cause, then there is the production of origination; when *sattva* is [manifest], then there is the effect of persistence; but when *tamas* is [manifest], then there is the production of dissolution"—this too is incorrect. For is their state of having manifest functioning eternal or non-eternal? It cannot be eternal, because [origination, etc. occur only occasionally, and because it would entail the simultaneous occurrence of persistence and the other states.

Now, if it is impermanent, from what is it born? Is it from *prakṛti* and *Īśvara* alone, or from something else, or independently? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of its existence at all times, because the cause known as *prakṛti* and *Īśvara*, being eternal in nature, is always present.
If it is from something else, that is not so; for you do not admit any other cause apart from *prakṛti* and *Īśvara*.

In the third case, however, there is a contradiction regarding its manifestation according to the restrictions of place and time, because if it were to exist independently, such restriction would be impossible.

For entities whose functioning depends upon another nature would be occasional, because their existence and non-existence are tied to the existence and non-existence of that [other nature]; they cannot be otherwise, since there would be nothing else for them to depend upon, or else, if such a thing to be depended upon exists, their independent production would be contradicted. Therefore, since agency as it pertains to God is in no way tenable when investigated, his omniscience cannot be established on this basis. To explain: when Maheśvara is joined with *rajas* in its active state, he becomes the cause of the creation of living beings, because *rajas* has procreation as its function.
When it resorts to the functioning of *sattva* that has arisen, then it becomes the cause for the maintenance of the worlds, because *sattva* is the cause of stability.

But when it is joined with the power of *tamas* that has arisen, then it effects the dissolution and destruction of the entire universe, because *tamas* is the cause of dissolution. As it has been said: "To him who partakes of *rajas* at the birth of beings, to him whose nature is *sattva* during their maintenance, and to him who touches *tamas* at their dissolution."
Salutation to the Unborn One, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction; who consists of the three Vedas and whose nature is the three *guṇas*.
(Kādambarī, p. 1; Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 59; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
84, first line).
If that intense form of power were the sole cause,
it would exist at all times, because its cause, being eternal in nature, is ever-present.
Nor is it desired by others to be something else, for that reason it does not come from anything else either; nor is this [cause] independent, because its occurrence is only occasional.
For if an entity exists by itself, it would be causeless, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself;
indeed, it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.
*Tattvasaṃgraha* and *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 84, upper section.
[From the *Ratnākara*, p. 455:

"Therefore, would its existence [arise] sometimes from causes such as Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) or God (*īśvara*), or from another cause, or would it be independent? [From the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 61:

Nor can it be [independent], because it rests upon sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); for when sovereignty itself is examined, it is untenable. For that [sovereignty] must be either inherent in him (*svābhāvika*) or produced by Primordial Matter (*prakṛtikṛta*). It cannot first be inherent, because the Sāṅkhyas admit that it is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*); indeed, they accept that consciousness alone is the inherent nature (*svarūpa*) in the self (*ātman*).

Now, [if it is argued that this] is produced by *prakṛti*; for instance, when *prakṛti* transforms into a modification characterized as the intellect (*buddhi*), then its specific states—such as merit (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and power (*aiśvarya*)—manifest. This is an unexamined statement; for you yourself have established that the Lord lacks such power, since it is not logical for this [power] to belong to one who is distinct from the transformation of the intellect, because otherwise it would follow that even another person (who is not the intellect) could possess it.

Now, if it is argued that because a relationship exists with the intellect (*buddhi*), that [cognition] belongs to that [Self] alone and not to another; well then, what is this relationship between them—is it inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth, or merely the fact of activity directed toward that [intellect]? It cannot be inherence, because it is impossible for the property of one thing to inhere in another; for whatever is the property of something does not inhere in anything other than that, just as the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) does not inhere elsewhere. And since the intellect is a property of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it therefore does not inhere in this [Self], which is a different entity from it.

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) due to the quality of redness and so forth inherent in a crystal and the like; for when a *japā* flower is in proximity, it is the crystal itself that undergoes such a transformation. This will be explained in detail once the emergence of reflection (*pratibimba*) has been established. Furthermore, if one accepts that the Self (*ātman*) likewise undergoes such a transformation through the proximity of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) which has transformed into the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), this would contradict such passages as: "The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is unchanging and non-transmigrating" (Vyāsa-bhāṣya, p. 15).
Therefore, neither an inherence relation nor a conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is tenable;

for the intellect is not a substance, and [if it were,] there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Indeed, a conjunction with that [intellect] exists already for all selves (*ātman*), since they are eternal and all-pervading.
By this, inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) and other such relations are also refuted, as the impossibility and the over-extension apply here as well without distinction.

If it is argued that its connection with Him consists merely in its activity being directed toward Him, that too is incorrect; for such activity on the part of Nature (prakṛti) directed toward God is impossible. It is by virtue of the necessity of fulfilling a human purpose that the modifications, such as the intellect (buddhi) and the rest, manifest when Nature proceeds toward evolution. Since there is no human purpose to be accomplished by God—because He is eternally liberated and has already achieved all that was to be done—how could Nature proceed with Him as its aim? And if it does not so proceed, how can His sovereignty be possible?

For is sovereignty there innate, or is it produced by primordial nature? [Ratnāvalī, p. 455] "Resolve, intellect, virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—this form is characterized by sattva; that which is contrary to this is characterized by tamas."
Among those, the sattvic form of the intellect (buddhi) is fourfold: righteousness (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (virāga), and sovereignty (aiśvarya).
— Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭhara-vṛtti.

Now, what is this relationship between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the Lord (*īśvara*): is it inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or the like; or is it merely the intellect’s activity directed toward the Lord? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
456). The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is unchanging, non-transmigrating, does not display objects [by itself], is pure, infinite, and consists of the quality of *sattva*.
(Yogasūtra with Vyāsabhāṣya, Sūtra 1).
And it was said by her to Pañcaśikha: "For the power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigratory" (Yogasūtra-Tattvavaiśāradī 2.20).

Furthermore, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is defined as the possession of material resources, assistants, and so forth, for the accomplishment of one's intended purpose. If he accomplishes no intended purpose at all and merely knows things as they truly are, how then can he possess sovereignty on that basis? For one who merely knows something is not called its "lord" (*īśvara*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that his knowledge is unconditioned by time, and therefore he is the Lord and no other—surely, being unconditioned by time is an indicator of eternity (*nityatva*), not of sovereignty.

By this, inference based on possibility (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) is refuted; for from that [inference], the supreme excellence of qualities such as intelligence might be established, but not sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Furthermore, in accordance with the fulfillment of the purpose of the *puruṣa*, the intellect (*buddhi*), which proceeds from its primary cause, completes the *puruṣa*'s purpose by bringing about discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) preceded by the complete exhaustion of all experiences; then, once its notions of agency and enjoyership have ceased, it undergoes dissolution into its own cause. Consequently, is this [intellect] considered to have fulfilled its purpose (*kṛtārtha*) with respect to the Lord, or not? If it has fulfilled its purpose, then because the intellect has dissolved into its own cause, the Lord's sovereignty would be lost. If, on the other hand, it has not fulfilled its purpose, then since a trace of bondage still exists, He would be equal to a yogi and not truly the Lord.

Therefore, since the existence of an omniscient being cannot be established through such modes as being the creator of the world and so forth, the establishment of His existence must be accepted solely on the basis of the fact that there is no valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) that can definitively and irrefutably negate it—
this is the explanation of the commentary on the verse beginning with *mānāya ni*.

One might object: "Since there is an absence of a proving means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) just as there is an absence of a subverting one, let there be doubt. Dispelling this apprehension, he says: "Because of the absence of both proving and subverting means of valid cognition," etc. By this passage beginning with "as far as the knowable," the doubt regarding that supersensible perception is refuted and set aside. Why is this so? He says: "Because a subverting [cognition] alone is impossible, not a proving one."
If indeed there is simply no subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), how can this much suffice to establish the existence of supersensible perception? To this he says: "In all cases," and so forth.

In every case—whether regarding an object of perception or any other object—the establishment of the conventional usage of existence and non-existence proceeds from the presence or absence of a subverting cognition. For, by the absence of a subverting cognition, the conventional usage of existence regarding a thing is established; and by its presence, the conventional usage of non-existence is established.
So then, whence comes this doubt? To this he says: "That," and so forth.
Since there is doubt regarding both of these—the sublater and its opposite—there is doubt everywhere.

Now, one might object: "The establishment of the conventional usage of existence does not result from the absence of a sublater, but rather from cognition. Anticipating this, he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth.
That is, precisely because of the absence of a sublater, the validity of experience—that is, the awareness of pleasure and so on—is established. Thus, enough of this digression.

It is incorrect to say that there should be doubt regarding an omniscient being due to the absence of both proving and refuting evidence (*sādhaka-vādhaka-pramāṇa*); because, through the determination of proving and refuting evidence, there is no disagreement regarding existence and non-existence. For [it is stated] in the *Aṣṭasahasrī*, page 49: "Due to the determination of the refuter (*bādhaka*), there is [certainty] regarding non-existence. (In the Bhāṣya edition, it reads: "Because of its existence therein...")
—He said: "In all that is perceived"—Ānandabodha:
"here, because of the absence of sublation"—Bhāsarvajña: "precisely because there is no doubt regarding either the presence or the absence of a sublater."

Now, one might object: "Since sensory and non-sensory perception (indriyānindriya-pratyakṣa) is restricted solely to the present moment, it cannot have as its objects things to be abandoned or acquired; how, then, can it be employed for practical worldly activity (*saṃvyavahāra*)? In response to this doubt, [the author] says: "In the contact between the sense-organ and the object, there is the illumination of existence (*sattāloka*), followed by the cognition that conceptualizes the form of the object. (Bhāṣya)
Avagraha is the initial apprehension; īhā is the desire for specific distinction; and avāya is certainty.
Commentary: Following the contact between the object (*viṣaya*) and the sense organ (*viṣayin*), the first grasping is *avagraha*.

The object consists of things characterized by substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*); the subject consists of the material sense organ (*dravyendriya*) and the functional sense organ (*bhāvendriya*).
The material sense organ (*dravyendriya*) consists of matter (*pudgala*);

the functional sense organ (*bhāvendriya*) consists of attainment (*labdhi*) and application (*upayoga*). Attainment is the capacity for grasping objects, while application is the actual operation of grasping objects.

The apprehension of an object is characterized by its suitability; following that, the perception of pure existence (*sanmātra*) undergoes a subsequent transformation into a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that establishes its own object, which is *avagraha*.

Furthermore, *īhā* is the desire for specific details regarding what has been grasped by *avagraha*, while *avāya* is the determination of those specific details as they have been sought. Although there is some lack of distinction [between these stages], there is a difference in designation due to the differences in their transformations (*pariṇāma*).
The first apprehension occurs immediately after the moment of contact between the object and the subject;
[see] *Sarvārthasiddhi* p.
62, *Tattvārtha-rājavārttika* p. 42.
That apprehension of the differentiation of objects which arises from the contact of the sense-organ with its object—characterized by the grasping of the mere thing—is *avagraha*.
(Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 219)
Non-apprehension is the grasping of an object; likewise, discernment, inquiry, judgment, comprehension, and retention are known as memory (dhāraṇā).

Āvaśyaka-niryukti: Apprehension (avagraha) is the grasping of a general object; investigation (īhā) is the search for its specific distinctions; retention (avāya) is the determination of that [object]; and memory (dhāraṇā) is the non-forgetting of it.
*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*: Among these, *avyakta* (unmanifest) is the perception and ascertainment of objects by their respective sense organs; this is *avagraha* (apprehension).
"Avagraha, graha, grahaṇa, ālocana, and avadhāraṇa are synonymous terms" (Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya, p. 18;
Pramāṇanaya-tattvāloka, 2).

7. When there is a conjunction of the sense organ and its object, the apprehension of the object immediately following perception is the *avagraha* means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). (Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 1.1)
27 –yam ā॰ vi॰ ❀ This reading within the *tāraka* [marginal note] does not exist in the commentary (*vivṛti*) of Ārya.

Ihā is the desire for the specific details of an object that has been grasped through avagraha (perceptual apprehension). [Variants: *avagrahagṛhīta-vi-* (Āvaśyaka-niryukti), *avagrahīta* (Jñātṛ-dharma-kathā-niryukti), *avagrahagṛhīte 'rthe tadviśeṣākāṅkṣaṇam īhā* (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya)].
In the *Sarvārthasiddhi*, page 63;
in the *Rājavārttika*, page 41; and in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 220, regarding the object that has been grasped (*avagṛhīta*).
When an object has been grasped, the subsequent pursuit of the remaining parts of that objective, as well as the desire for specific determination, is called *īhā*.
*Īhā*, *ūhā*, *tarka*, *parīkṣā*, *vicāraṇā*, and *jijñāsā* are synonymous terms;
[as stated in] *Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 18.
*Īhā* is the desire for the specific details of an object that has been grasped; *Pramāṇanayatattvāloka*, 2.8; *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, 1.1.
1.28 Jainatarkapañjikā, p. 116.
*Apāya* is the comprehension of the true nature [of an object] resulting from the specific determination [of its qualities], as stated in the *Sarvārthasiddhi* (p.
63), the *Rājavārttika* (p.
42), and the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* (p. 220).
When an object has been grasped, the removal of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding its qualities and defects through the investigation of whether it is "correct" or "incorrect" is *apāya*.
*Apāya*, *apagama*, *apanoda*, *apavyādha*, *apeta*, *apagata*, *apaviddha*, and *apanutta* are synonyms; *Tattvārthādhigamasūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 18.
Determination of the specific object of inquiry is *avāya*;
Pramāṇanayatattvāloka 2.9.
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.29
*Jainatarka°*, p. 116, Commentary on the Verse:

When there is a connection (*yoga*)—characterized by suitability (*yogyatā*)—between the sense organs (*akṣa*), such as the eyes and so forth, and their objects (*artha*), such as jars and so forth (but not a connection characterized by conjunction and the like, since that has already been refuted), there first arises for the self the "light of existence" (*sattāloka*), which is the perception (*darśana*) of mere existence common to all things to be rejected or accepted. Subsequently, that very same light becomes the cognition of conceptualization (*vikalpa-dhī*) bearing the form of the object.

An "object" (*artha*) is a thing sought by a practitioner either for its rejection or its acceptance. Its "form" (*ākāra*) is a specific sub-genus within the general category of existence, such as "humanity" and so forth. The "conceptualizing cognition" (*vikalpadhī*) regarding that form is an intellect in the nature of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*); the meaning is that perception transforms into that very form.
What is the name of this [cognition]? To this he says: "Apprehension" (*avagraha*).
This too gives rise to a desire for further particulars.

Since nothing else is relevant or heard in this context, it is the specific form of the object itself—the distinction such as "crane" and so forth—that is apprehended. Its "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in its being oriented toward apprehension by way of the cognition that it "must exist.
He names this state "investigation" (*īhā*). This too becomes "determination" (*avāya*), which is the ascertainment of the specific feature that was expected.

Consequently, since it is established that knowledge and its object persist in some manner over a period of time, it is proven that perception—whether produced by the senses or the non-senses—is applicable to practical activity (*savyavahāra*), because it is possible for it to have as its objects things to be avoided or acquired. For if [the object] did not persist at all, such [activity] would be impossible, and thus its applicability to activity could not be logically maintained. Explaining this while commenting on the verse, he says: "The object," and so forth.

If it is asked: "In the *kārikā*, 'perception' (*darśana*) is mentioned first and 'apprehension' (*avagraha*) afterwards, whereas in the *vṛtti* the order is reversed; for what purpose? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of demonstrating that perception—which was posited first in the *kārikā*—is to be inferred from apprehension. For just as a subsequent cognition of particulars is preceded by the grasping of an intermediate genus (*avāntarajāti*), so too is the grasping of the intermediate genus preceded by perception of existence (*sattā-darśana*). And there is no further universal (*sāmānya*) beyond existence, from which an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow.

The object (*viṣaya*) is the jar and so forth; the subject (*viṣayin*) is the eye and so forth. Their "correct contact" (*nipāta*), which generates knowledge in accordance with reality, is their presence in a suitable location and so on. Immediately following that, the first apprehension or cognition is "perception" (*avagraha*). It is the determination of a specific intermediate genus, such as "human-ness.

In this context, by the words "the object" and so forth, [the author] first defines the nature of the object. The word "successively" (*krama*) is used here in the sense of sequence. What is the object? It is the range of perception (*gocara*), the referent (*artha*). Of what nature is it? It consists of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāyātmā*).

In this context, "substance" (*dravya*) is the vertical generality (*ūrdhvatāsāmānya*) which is apprehended through the cognition of the underlying continuity (*anvaya*) existing throughout preceding and succeeding transformations (*vivarta*); therein, the successive transformations are the modes (*paryāya*), and that of which these are the self (*ātman*) or nature (*svabhāva*) is thus described—as its very essence being the modes. (Note:
*ātmā* is read as *bhāva* in the Bhāṣya and Ja versions).
The prima facie argument of the Yogācāra, who maintains the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvedanādvaitavādin*):

Since there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an object distinct from the nature of cognition itself, of what thing—characterized by the nature of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāya*)—is objectivity being described? For it is well-established that every appearing entity is included within the nature of cognition; thus, consciousness alone is the ultimate reality.
To explain: whatever appears is indeed cognition, just like pleasure and so forth, and all entities do appear.

Furthermore, the manifestation of these [objects] from something else is not tenable. For that [manifestation] would have to arise either from what is related to it or from what is unrelated. It cannot be from what is unrelated, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Suppose, then, it were from what is related; is this through identity (*tādātmya*) or through origination from it (*tadutpatti*)? If it were through identity, then objects would possess the nature of cognition, or cognition would possess the nature of being insentient (*jaḍa*), because the essence of identity consists in the mutual appropriation of each other's essential natures.
If objects were of the nature of consciousness, the non-duality of consciousness would be established;

Cognition cognizes that which is without appearance, that which is with appearance, and that which has the appearance of something else; yet cognition never [cognizes] an external object in any way whatsoever. (1999)
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 559:
"—nyarūpa—" (in the Ā manuscript: *jñānarūpatve*; in the Ba, Ja, and Bhā manuscripts: [as above]).

Now, [let us consider] its arising from that: how could anything arise? Would the object arise from cognition, or would cognition arise from the object? In the first case, it follows that the object must have the nature of cognition, because it arises from cognition, just like a subsequent moment of cognition. Alternatively, if cognition arises from the object, does it arise from something simultaneous or from something at a different time? It cannot be from something simultaneous; for there is no relationship of cause and effect between two things existing at the same time, just as with the left and right horns of a cow. Otherwise, it would follow that cognition is also a cause of the object, as there would be no distinction between them.

If that [cognition] were to arise from an object at a different time, it would follow that cognition is causeless, because the object does not exist at the time of the cognition. For that which is non-existent cannot produce anything, just as a peacock cannot produce its cry from a dead peacock; and the object is non-existent at the time of the cognition.

Furthermore, would the object that produces cognition be permanent or impermanent? If it were permanent, it would produce all cognitions simultaneously, since its capacity to produce them would be possible only once due to its eternally uniform nature; otherwise, its eternally uniform nature would be contradicted.
Furthermore, the capacity of something—whether it be non-eternal, simultaneous with [the cognition], or occurring at a different time—to produce that [cognition] has been refuted.

Likewise, would this [object] be of a single nature or of a manifold nature? If it were of a single nature, there would be no distinction between clear and unclear appearances for those who are distant or near. If it were of a manifold nature, then because of its division into atoms, there would be no appearance of a single gross object, whether clearly or unclearly perceived, for anyone.

Furthermore, is this [cognition] apprehended by a cognition devoid of form (*nirākāra-jñāna*) or by a cognition possessing form (*sākāra-jñāna*)? If it were apprehended by a cognition devoid of form, there would be a collapse of the systematic distinction between individual objects; for, in the absence of anything that establishes the specific determination of objects—such that "this is the apprehender of blue" and "this is the apprehender of yellow"—even directed activity toward specific objects would become impossible.

Moreover, if cognition possesses form, the postulation of an external object is redundant, since the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender is fully accounted for within that very [form].

Now, it might be argued that because the occasional form appearing in cognition cannot be accounted for by the perceptible causes, and because the existence of an effect is impossible in the absence of a cause, one must postulate an object as its cause—that which produces such a cognition in that manner. This too is incorrect; for since such a cognition arises from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the existence of an external object is not thereby established. Furthermore, if such a cognition were dependent upon an object, then in cases such as dreams, magical illusions, and cities of the Gandharvas, such cognitions would be impossible in the absence of an object.

For in dreams and the like, there is no external object appearing that could impart its own form to consciousness; therefore, since forms such as those of a city of Gandharvas are not perceived in the absence of cognition, but are perceived when cognition exists, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that this form belongs to cognition itself. Consequently, the entire distinct form, being devoid of the status of an external object due to the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), means that cognition is without an objective support (*anālambana*).

For this very reason, all cognitions are without an object (*anālambana*), because they possess the nature of being a cognition, like a dream-cognition; such is the purification by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapariśuddhi*).
For it is precisely this that constitutes being without an object: namely, the experience of its own form (*ātmākāravedanatva*). (Pramāṇavārttika-alaṃkāra, folio 22).

Furthermore, an object attains the status of being an "object" (*arthatā*) only when it is mounted upon cognition; however, cognition—independently of an object—brings about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) by manifesting even non-existent objects through its own inherent capacity, as seen in dreams and the like. Therefore, the object is non-different from cognition.

Moreover, the recognition that "this [object] is similar to that [cognition]" is logical only when both are perceived; yet an object distinct from cognition has never been perceived, such that one could determine, "This form belongs to the object and not to the cognition."

Therefore, since the manifestation of blue and other objects is impossible from anything external to them, it is established that they are necessarily self-luminous; and from that, it follows that they are non-different from cognition.
For instance: whatever manifests itself is not other than cognition, just like pleasure and so forth; and blue and other such objects manifest themselves.

[Objection: But how can blue manifest its own nature? For objects to be manifested, such as jars, are not their own illuminators by means of a lamp or the like; indeed, an action upon oneself is a contradiction, for a sword-blade is not cut by that very same blade. [Response: This is not so. It is not the case that blue is manifested by something other than itself, because there is no other object to be manifested. Nor is it manifested by another cognition, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, blue must be self-manifesting. And since it is self-manifesting, it is non-different from cognition. Thus, the identity of the object with cognition is established. Furthermore, the nature of cognition is that it is self-manifesting; therefore, the object which is non-different from cognition must also be self-manifesting. Consequently, the identity of the object with cognition is proven. Thus, the conclusion is reached that all things are nothing but consciousness. This is the view of the Vijñānavādins. However, this is not tenable, because the proof for the existence of external objects has already been established. Moreover, the claim that "whatever manifests itself is non-different from cognition" is not proven, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). For it is not the case that pleasure and the like manifest themselves; rather, they are manifested by cognition. Therefore, the reason is unproven. Furthermore, the example cited is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because pleasure and the like are not self-manifesting in the same way that cognition is. Hence, the identity of the object with cognition is not established. Thus, the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins is refuted. Finally, the claim that "the nature of cognition is self-manifestation" is also unproven, because cognition is not perceived apart from the object. Therefore, the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins is untenable. Thus, the existence of external objects is established. This concludes the section on the refutation of the Vijñānavāda. Now begins the section on the refutation of the Madhyamaka. The Madhyamikas maintain that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This is not correct, because the existence of things is established through perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the doctrine of the Madhyamikas is also untenable. Thus, the existence of external objects is firmly established. This concludes the section on the refutation of the Madhyamaka. Now begins the section on the refutation of the Sautrāntika. The Sautrāntikas maintain that while external objects exist, they are not directly perceived, but are inferred from the cognition of their forms. This is not correct, because the form of the object is directly perceived. Therefore, the doctrine of the Sautrāntikas is also untenable. Thus, the existence of external objects is established. This concludes the section on the refutation of the Sautrāntika. Now begins the section on the refutation of the Vaibhāṣika. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that both external objects and cognition are directly perceived. This is not correct, because cognition is not perceived apart from the object. Therefore, the doctrine of the Vaibhāṣikas is also untenable. Thus, the existence of external objects is established. This concludes the section on the refutation of the Vaibhāṣika. Now begins the section on the refutation of the Sammitīya. The Sammitīyas maintain that the person (*pudgala*) exists as a real entity. This is not correct, because the person is merely a designation (*prajñapti*) based on the aggregates (*skandha*). Therefore, the doctrine of the Sammitīyas is also untenable. Thus, the existence of external objects is established. This concludes the section on the refutation of the Sammitīya. Now begins the section on the refutation of the Vātsīputrīya. The Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the person exists as an indescribable (*avaktavya*) entity. This is not correct, because if it were indescribable, it could not be known at all. Therefore, the doctrine of

The rebuttal here is as follows: Just as light is accepted as the illuminator of its own nature because it is manifest through identity (*tādātmya*), so too is cognition the knower of itself; see *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.329.

And because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension: for that which is invariably apprehended together with something else does not differ from it, just as a second moon [is not different] from the single moon perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia; and an object is invariably apprehended simultaneously with cognition.

For, as a rule, simultaneous perception is not observed in the case of difference, such as between a jar and a cloth; thus, difference is pervaded by the non-necessity of simultaneous perception. And the observed necessity of simultaneous perception, being contrary to that [non-necessity], excludes its own opposite—the non-necessity. That [non-necessity], in being excluded, excludes its own pervaded—namely, difference. Therefore, this reason, being excluded from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) of difference—which is pervaded by its own opposite—remains as non-difference alone, since there is no other alternative; thus, the establishment of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is proven.

Likewise, whatever is cognized is indeed non-different from cognition, just like the very nature of consciousness itself; and since blue and other objects are cognized, the non-duality of consciousness is established for this reason as well.
Furthermore, how can an object that is simultaneously cognized be established as something other than the intellect, given that it is invariably [perceived] together with the intellect?

For the object, such as blue and so forth, is perceived simultaneously with the cognition; it is not perceived separately from the cognition. Therefore, how could the object be something other than that perception? It must be that the perception itself is of such a nature, for it has been demonstrated that it is impossible to distinguish [the two]. If it is argued that "there is indeed an appearance of difference"—then this difference would be seen through erroneous cognitions, just as the [apparent] duality in the case of the moon.
In the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, page 91,

with the verse beginning "yatsavedanam" and so forth, [the author] provides a proof for the non-difference between blue and its cognition against the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānavādin*): that whose cognition is necessarily the very cognition of something else is not distinct from it, or it does not differ from it.
Just as the self of the cognition of blue, or as a second moon, [is perceived],
so too this perception of the cognition of blue is due to the perception of the form of blue.

This is what is meant: because it is not separate from cognition, it is non-different from it, just as the cognition of blue is non-different from its own nature, or as the second moon appearing in the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia [is non-different from that cognition]. "And this is the cognition of the sensation of blue"—this is the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*). Here, the subject (*dharmin*) consists of the blue form and its cognition; their non-difference is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); and the reason (*hetu*) is the aforementioned necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*).

In the Master’s syllogism beginning with "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*), this very [meaning] is intended as the sense of the reason (*hetu*), because there is no internal contradiction; *Tattvasaṃgraha* p. 567, Ba, Ja.

Because there is no other possibility (bhāṣya), by this continuous argument the reason characterized as "being an object of cognition" (vedyatva) is established by the Vijñānavādins; and it deserves to be formulated as follows: that which is cognized by a certain cognition does not differ from it, just as the self of a cognition [does not differ from itself].
(*Vidhiviveka*, *Nyāyakaṇikā*, p. 260).
The extensive prima facie argument concerning the non-duality of knowledge is to be found in the *Vṛhatī* commentary on the *Śābarabhāṣya*, at [Mīmāṃsāsūtra] 1.1.1.
Refutation of the Doctrine of the Non-duality of Cognition:
To this, we reply.

As for what was stated—that "whatever appears is cognition," and so forth—in that regard, does the appearance of objects occur by itself (*svataḥ*) or from another (*parataḥ*)? If it is by itself, that is unproven (*asiddha*); for jars and the like are not established for anyone, even in a dream, as having an appearance independent of anything else, except perhaps for a Yogācāra whose mind is overcome by great delusion.

If [the opponent argues that the object exists] from another [source], this is contradictory; for appearing in such a manner is possible only when there is insentience (*jaḍatva*), since insentience is characterized by looking toward another for its own establishment. Furthermore, because the insentience of jars and the like is established through inference—namely: "Whatever does not appear with a form that has reached the conditions of perceptibility is not of the nature of that [form], just as a cloth is not of the nature of a jar's form; and the object such as a jar does not appear with the form of cognition"—the [opponent's position] is subject to the fallacy of *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), as it is employed immediately after the presentation of a thesis that has been sublated by inference.

[Objection: Since an object distinct from cognition is not established by the manner previously stated, how can there be an "appearance from another" (parataḥ pratibhāsa), such that the reason [of your argument] would be contradictory? [Response: That is incorrect; for the difference between cognition and the object is established by perception itself. For by direct perception, an object is apprehended which possesses a clear and distinct form—such as blue, white, and so on—situated in a specific location in space, residing in something other than itself (anātmaniṣṭha). If one were to deny what is being perceived, what confidence could there be in internal self-awareness (*saṃvedana*)? Thus, there would be a denial of everything, for the existence of cognition or of pleasure and so forth is not established through anything other than their own perception.

Nor should it be asserted that the existence of the object is accepted as being of the nature of consciousness; for this [object] appears as something distinct from consciousness. And thus, whatever is not perceived in a certain place despite meeting the conditions for perception does not exist there, just like a jar in a particular location. Furthermore, such a nature of knowledge is not unestablished, because when a jar or the like is being perceived, one experiences an internal locus of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) which is distinct from the external nature of the object that is not the locus of the "I-notion."

Furthermore, whatever experience possesses contradictory forms does not have a single-natured object as its domain, just like the experience of pleasure and pain. And there exists an experience of the forms of the object and the cognition, which are contradictory by virtue of having natures established through mutual exclusion.

For consciousness has the nature of the grāhaka (the apprehender) within, while the nature of the grāhya (the apprehended), such as blue and so forth, appears clearly outside. Nevertheless, if these two were non-different, nothing would be differentiated from anything else; for apart from a difference in appearance and the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), no other differentiator is possible.

Likewise, that which appears as having two forms is in reality distinct, just like pleasure and pain; and since the forms of the object and the cognition appear as two forms, by this inference there is a difference between the two.

Alternatively, if they were non-different, it would follow that if the nature of the cognition were not apprehended, blue and so forth would also not be apprehended. For when the ultimate form of something is not apprehended, that thing itself is not apprehended either—just as yellow is not apprehended when the yellow form of yellow is not apprehended—and yet the nature of the cognition of blue and so forth is not apprehended.

Now, one might object: this [distinction] would hold if blue and so forth were perceived as distinct from the light of consciousness (*prakāśa*); however, they are never perceived as distinct from it. This is incorrect, because what is this so-called "light"? Is it the cognition "I," or is it the visibility of blue and so forth? In the first case, the difference of blue and so forth from that [light] is established; for it is not logical that what is perceived as distinct should be non-distinct, as that would lead to the absurdity of there being no difference even between pleasure and pain. By this, the second case is also refuted; since visibility is dependent upon the act of seeing, its existence is thereby established even prior to that seeing.

On page 117, line 10: "Momentariness, the state of being cognizable by nothing other than itself, and the state of having multiple continua are not established by themselves," as stated in the *Bhrānti* section of the *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 241.
As for that non-duality of consciousness, like the non-duality of the *puruṣa*,
it cannot be established either by itself or by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it would entail the abandonment of one's own desired position.
The examination of the authoritative [source] (*āptaparīkṣā*):
the nature of the object as it is established by its own essence (*svarūpa*).
—[The object] has no intrinsic nature—(bhāṣya);
what is its intrinsic nature? (bhāṣya). Furthermore: "The non-existence of an object is [known] from non-perception, not from anything else; this is the sole reason for negation" (Nyāyabindu, p. 39).
Because of this statement, it is not logical to claim that what is actually being perceived is itself non-perceived, as that would contradict direct experience (*pratīti*).

Nor should it be argued that only the form (*ākāra*) of the cognition present before one is perceived, and thus how could there be perception of an object? For no one has an experience of the object present before them as being the form of the cognition; rather, an experience arises with respect to the object through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that one thinks, "we perceive the blue object."
The fact that consciousness possesses a form will be refuted later; however, even if we grant it for the sake of argument, the form reflected therein must be an effect because it is occasional.
Indeed, whatever is occasional is seen to be an effect, such as a jar and the like; and the blue and other forms of cognition are likewise occasional.

The state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by dependence upon something else (*anyāpekṣā*). And that "something else" which is additional to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of cognition is the object (*artha*), because even when that complex is present, [the cognition] does not arise [without it]. Whatever does not arise despite the presence of [a certain set of conditions] is produced by a cause additional to those; for example, a sprout that does not arise from the causal complex of earth and so forth is produced by an additional cause called the seed. Likewise, since the representation of blue (*nīlākāra*) does not arise even when the eye and other [conditions] are present, that which is additional and productive of it is the object.

If it is argued that the latent impression (*vāsanā*), being superior to the eyes and other [senses], will serve as the cause here, is it so by way of being the objective support (*ālambana*), the dominant condition (*adhipati*), or the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara*)? In the first case, the object itself would simply be stated under a different name. In the latter two cases, however, like the eyes and other [senses], its status as a cause for the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*) is untenable.

If the cognition of form and so forth were to occur without an external object, how could it be restricted to a specific place, time, and cognizer? For, in the absence of a determining factor, it would follow that such cognition would occur everywhere, at all times, and for everyone without restriction. Furthermore, how could it arise for that very cognizer in that very place at one time and not at another? Or how is it that the vision of a mass of hair in the sky occurs only in the mental continuum of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) and not for others; and why is no functional effect produced by those hairs perceived by him, while it is produced by others, even though the non-existence of the object is equal in both cases? If one attempts to account for the restriction of place and so forth based solely on the analogy of a dream while denying the existence of objects, it would entail the establishment of a partless, singular, supreme Brahman, since its appearance as diverse—like the moon reflected in water—is possible through mere manifestation.

And just as this manifold appearance of diversity within the non-duality of consciousness occurs precisely due to the specific determination of the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), so too, within Brahman— which is eternal, partless, and of a single nature— the four conditions (*pratyaya*) are taught, namely: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), due to the specific determination of the power of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
Abhidharmakośa 2.61:
Sometimes it arises— Bhāṣya.
The restriction of place and so forth is established as in a dream;
furthermore, there is no restriction of a continuous stream [of consciousness] in the case of everyone seeing rivers of pus and the like.
The performance of purposeful action is like that in a dream; furthermore, it is like hell in the perception of all the hell-wardens and others, and in being tormented by them.

Furthermore, [the opponent argues that] representation-only (vijñaptimātra) is erroneous, because error arises everywhere from the perception of similarity; for example, the error of water arises in relation to mirages which lack the nature of water. However, for the proponent of representation-only, there is no perception of similarity whatsoever that could serve as the cause for the error of difference.

[Objection: But surely, in states such as sleep, when there is an absence of objects and an absence of the perception of similarity, a delusion of difference is observed; therefore, this [criticism] is not a fault. [Reply: That is incorrect; because even in that case, there is an indirect dependence on external objects. For a dream never arises anywhere regarding an object that has not been experienced. Thus, since the birth of a dream depends upon previously experienced objects, how could it be possible in the absence of objects? [Objection: But knowledge arises even regarding things never experienced, such as the cutting off of one's own head. [Reply: That is not so; even there, the cutting off of another's head has been seen and one's own body has been experienced. There, due to a defect of the mind, failing to perceive the distinction, one imagines the cutting off of the head in one's own body. Therefore, even in that case, the cause is indeed an experienced object.
Indeed, even that knowledge does not arise for one who has never experienced the severing of another's head;

furthermore, even in the case of a perception of a city of Gandharvas, external objects such as clouds exist in ultimate reality and merely appear under some other form. Moreover, if external objects are denied, how can the necessity of universals (jāti) be established? For if the world were mere consciousness, there would be no regulating principle, and thus a human might become a horse, a horse a human, an elephant an ant, and an ant an elephant.

However, if one accepts the existence of external objects, that necessity is easily established: for whatever person has performed karma that serves as the cause for the pleasure, pain, and so forth experienced through the human genus (*manuṣyatva-jāti*), he attains that very genus by virtue of its maturation; likewise, other living beings also attain their respective births through the power of their own acquired common karma. [This passage is missing from the manuscripts *ba*, *ja*, and *pra*, while in manuscript *bhā* the reading is *nacit*, though it was perhaps once *kadācidapyude*.]

Furthermore, is the non-existence of an object asserted merely by one’s own whim, because of the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because of the absence of correspondence (*saṃvāda*), because of the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), or because of the presence of a subverting means of knowledge? If it were by mere whim, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since it would follow that even that very non-duality and so forth would consequently be non-existent.

Nor is it because of the absence of a proving means of knowledge, for perception itself exists as a means that establishes objects such as water—which are not of the nature of the self, which are uncontradicted, and which perform causal functions.

The lack of correspondence (*saṃvādāsattva*) is also unestablished, because in the case of water and such things apprehended through perception, there is the possibility of a corroborating means of knowledge such as inference;
furthermore, the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is untenable, since both external and internal causal efficiency are dependent upon that [perception],
and no subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the object is ever perceived.
Nor is there an absence of objects, because [cognition] arises precisely as that which illuminates external objects, being apprehended by perception; (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
21, top; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 349).

This [cognition] expresses external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the form of "it speaks," "it moves," and so forth, and internal causal efficiency in the form of "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth.

As for the objection raised here—whether [the cognition arises] from something related to the object or from something unrelated—the manifestation of the object occurs precisely from a cognition that is related to it. This relation is characterized by *yogyatā* (fitness), not by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), because both of those are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the existence of relations between] momentary destruction and the like, or between the eye and other [senses] and their objects.
Furthermore, the apprehension of a fit object—whether simultaneous with or at a different time than the cognition—is not contradictory.

"Indeed, the relation between cognition and its object, which is the basis for the relationship of the apprehended and the apprehender, consists precisely in their mutual compatibility (*yogyatā-svabhāva*), and not in identity (*tādātmya*) or any other [relation]," Syādvādaratnākara, p. 163.

Even though there is identity between momentary destruction and cognition, the appearance belongs to the cognition and not to momentary destruction; cognition arises from the eye and other [senses], and its appearance would not [arise] from the cognition itself. (Ratnāvalī, p.

[blank]) If it is asked: "Why is it that for such an object, as long as the cognition is the grasper, the object is not likewise the grasper of the cognition? [The answer is: because of the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāvabheda*).

Indeed, the very nature that belongs to one does not belong to another; otherwise, it would follow that a jar, like a lamp, would also possess the quality of being illuminating. Such a cognition is the same in other cases as well; for an object is not perceived as a grasper in the manner that cognition is.

Or rather, why are blue and other forms not pervasive of this [cognition], just as far as cognition is pervasive? And when it is asked, "Why are these [forms] not pervasive of all [objects] to the same extent that they are pervasive of this [cognition]?", there is no answer other than the perception of a difference in nature (*svabhāvabheda*) even for you.

As for what was also stated—that an object is either eternal or non-eternal, or of a single nature or of multiple natures, and so forth—that too is refuted by the acceptance of the non-absolutism (anekānta) of all objects. For there exists no object, whether external or internal, that is in every respect eternal or non-eternal, or of a single nature or of multiple natures; this will be demonstrated in the proof of non-absolutism (pṛ. 117, l. 21). To explain: first of all, no external object such as earth and so forth exists as its [the cognition’s] apprehended object, because such an object is devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold.
What is the nature of this external object that appears? Does it manifest with the intrinsic nature of atoms, or rather as something characterized by having parts?

Regarding what was stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p. 550)—namely, that "an object attains the status of being an object only when it is mounted upon cognition," and so forth—what is this "mounting" of the object? Is it a formal establishment (*vyavasthiti*) or a dependence (*apekṣā*)? It cannot be a formal establishment; for that [object], which is not of the nature of cognition, which does not illuminate itself or others, and which depends on another for its own illumination, is perceived through perception and other means as established externally, being the object of inert worldly activity. Otherwise, if it were not so, there would be no external acts such as cutting and so forth by way of inert worldly activity.

In the second case, however, there would necessarily be a difference between cognition and its object, because dependence is possible only when there is a distinction, as in the case of a master and a servant; thus, the establishment of the object through dependence on cognition would imply that the object is identical in nature to the cognition, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that the effect is identical in nature to its cause, and thereby result in the doctrine of the non-duality of the cause. For the establishment of an effect does not occur independently of its cause.

Furthermore, as for the other argument stated—that whatever manifests by itself is non-different from cognition—that too is mere faith, since the self-manifesting nature of the object has already been refuted.
Because dependence has already been refuted previously— [this applies] even to the [view that] "the existence" (bhāva) [is established]— Bhāṣya.

As for what was stated—"because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*), and so forth—that too is mere words; for [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*). Indeed, even when the stars Kṛttikās are distinct, there exists a rule of simultaneous apprehension.

Furthermore, [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddhatva*), because simultaneous apprehension is pervaded by difference alone. For the word "together" (*saha*) has difference as its basis, since the meaning of the word "together" is untenable in the case of non-difference; for that very thing cannot be designated as being "together with itself."

Furthermore, this [reason] lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*). To explain: pervasion is to be determined through the existence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the heterologue (*vipakṣa*). Since difference (*bheda*) is the heterologue for non-difference (*abheda*), once the exclusion of "necessarily simultaneous perception" from difference has been shown, and since there is no other possible alternative, the pervasion would be established with non-difference alone. Yet this [reason] is not excluded from difference, for it is observed that even among distinct stars such as the Kṛttikās, there is necessarily simultaneous perception.

Furthermore, this [inference] is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa); for consciousness, the object of consciousness, and the cognizer are perceived by uncontradicted perception as having mutually distinct natures.

Nor is their "uncontradictedness" unestablished on the grounds that they are contradicted by this very [inference]; because when there is a contradiction with perception, it is impossible for this inference even to come into being. And only that which has attained its own existence can be either a prover or a sublater.

This might be the case: although existence in the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) is not certain, it is at least doubtful; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the heterologue is doubtful (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p.
569). Furthermore, that "rule of simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambhaniyama*) which was stated cannot withstand critical analysis.

If the apprehension of cognition and object occurs through their coexistence (*sāhitya*), then this reason is contradictory (*viruddha*) and cannot establish non-difference, because coexistence is pervaded by difference—which is its opposite—and is therefore impossible if there is non-difference. And what is intended here by the term "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*)? Is it the coexistence of two apprehensions regarding two objects, or rather the simultaneous appearance of two objects within a single apprehension?
