furthermore, the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhanavikala*). For in the appearance of two moons, there is no coexistence of two distinct appearances, since perception determines [the object] through a single cognition that delineates both forms.

In the second case, however, there is a contradiction (*viruddhatva*), because the appearance of two objects together in a single perception is possible only if there is indeed a difference [between them]. Now, if it is argued that what manifests within a single cognition is non-different from that cognition—just as the nature of the cognition itself—and since entities such as blue and so forth manifest within that very cognition, this inference does not suffer from contradiction because a manifestation would be impossible if there were a difference; that is not so, for the difference between consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya*) has been established as well-known through perception and other means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, since cognition has the nature of illuminating both itself and others, and since in the absence of an "other" the very nature of cognition—which consists in the awareness of that [other]—is impossible, cognition itself would be impossible; therefore, of what could there be non-difference with what? As for what was stated—that "whatever is cognized is non-different from cognition," and so forth—what here is this "cognizability"? Is it (1) being the object of cognition (*vedana-karmatva*), (2) merely having a relation to that [cognition], or (3) having that [cognition] as its intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*)? If it is "being the object of cognition," then the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*). This is because being an object is invariably concomitant (*vyāpta*) with difference alone; for instance, pieces of wood, which are the objects of the act of cutting, are not perceived as non-different [from the act]. Thus, since action and its instrument are always perceived only when there is a difference, the state of being an object and the action is pervaded by difference itself. Therefore, since it proves a meaning contrary to non-difference, the reason is contradictory when non-difference is the probandum (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, regarding the non-difference (*abheda*) of these two, does the object’s non-difference from cognition arise from cognition, or does cognition’s non-difference from the object arise from the object? In the first alternative, there would be only cognition and no object, because the object has entered into that very [cognition]; thus, the reason "because it is cognizable" (*saṃvedyatvāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

In the second alternative, however, there would be only the object and no cognition; so how could its non-difference be proven? Moreover, since their difference is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the argument is also subject to the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). And since the nature of consciousness is non-dual and thus lacks an object (*akarmaka*), the example [adduced] is devoid of the probandum (*sādhanavikala*).

Now, if "knowability" (*vedyatva*) is merely the state of being related to consciousness (*saṃvit*), even so, there is a contradiction, because relation is possible only when there is difference; for relation has difference as its basis, and in the absence of that [difference], it too would be absent, resulting in the non-establishment of the state of being related to consciousness—and thus [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Alternatively, if "knowability" is intended to mean having the nature of consciousness (*saṃvitsvabhāvatva*), that is likewise unestablished, since it has been demonstrated that the object does not have the nature of consciousness.

Therefore, by one who accepts the determination of real entities based on unimpeded cognition, an external object—though of the nature of non-cognition—must be admitted to possess multiple forms such as blue, white, and so forth, just like that [cognition’s] own awareness (tatsaṃvedana).

The prima facie argument of a certain school of Buddhists, the proponents of variegated non-dualism (*citrādvaitavādin*): "Indeed, it is only cognition that appears as this variegated [reality], inlaid with multiple forms such as blue, pleasure, and so forth; it is not an external object, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. That which lacks a means of valid cognition for its existence does not exist, like the horn of a donkey; and there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the existence of an external object."

Nor is this [argument] unproven; for instance, would the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known the existence of that [object] be formless (*nirākāra*) or with form (*sākāra*)? It cannot be formless, because it is impossible for it to be the basis for the determination of each specific object (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) since it would be indistinguishable in all cases.

However, if it possesses form, then it is established that cognition itself—variegated and singular, yet pervaded by multiple forms such as blue and so forth—is [the object], and not an insentient object distinct from it, because there is nothing whatsoever that could serve as the cause for determining that [external object].
Nor can cognition alone, as qualified by a form, be the cause for determining that [object], because its purpose is fulfilled merely through the experience of its own form.
As it has been said:
"Just as waves, arising from the condition of the wind, proceed dancing upon the rising and setting of the ocean, and no interruption is found;"

*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 163.

18): 'If cognition possesses the form of blue and so forth, what would be the basis for an external object? (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.433)."

Furthermore, would the cognition that establishes the object of knowledge (prameya) exist prior to that object, or posterior to it? In the first case, how could this cognition be produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object, given that it arises even in the absence of the object? Whatever arises even in the absence of an object of knowledge is not born from the contact of a sense organ with an object, just like the cognition of a sky-flower; and the cognition intended to establish the object, which exists prior to the object, likewise arises even in the absence of the object of knowledge.

Regarding the second alternative, however, is the existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*) at a time prior to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apprehended from some source, or not? If it is not apprehended, how can it be the object of the conventional usage of "existent"? For that which is not apprehended from any source is not the object of the conventional usage of "existent," like a sky-lotus; and the existence of the object of cognition at a time prior to the means of valid cognition is likewise not apprehended from any source.

Now, [suppose] it has been apprehended; is this [apprehension] from itself or from another? If from itself, how can there be a distinction between this [object] and cognition, since that very [cognition] is characterized by self-manifestation (*svato'vabhāsa*)? That which is established by itself is not distinct from cognition, just as the nature of cognition itself; and the object intended as a "knowable" (*prameya*), which exists prior to cognition, is established by itself. Now, suppose it is from another; that is not so, because there is no "other" distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could serve as the cause for the determination of the knowable.

Now, it might be argued that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself reveals its occurrence in that [past object]; this is not so. For it is impossible for something that does not exist at that time to reveal it by itself. Whatever does not exist at a certain time cannot be the revealer of that [object], just as a lamp that does not exist at the time when an object existed prior to its own production is not the revealer of that object; and likewise, cognition does not exist at the time of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) as qualified by the past time.

If knowledge and the object of knowledge were simultaneous, there would be an absence of the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender, like that of the left and right horns of a cow. Nor should it be argued that an external object must exist as the colorer [of consciousness], because otherwise the perception of the imprint of blue and other forms within cognition would be inexplicable; for even in the absence of such an object during the state of dreaming, the perception of that imprint occurs. Indeed, there is no external object acting as a colorer in the cognitions of elephants, horses, and so forth that arise in that state, since otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between cognitions occurring in dreams and those occurring outside of them.
Therefore, just as cognition itself—regardless of an external object—is produced here by its own causal complex as variegated by the reflections of diverse forms, so too is it elsewhere.

Now, even if this is so, one might ask: "How is the unity of a single cognition tenable when it appears in the form of diverse aspects? This objection is not valid; for since it is impossible to differentiate [the aspects from the cognition], there is no contradiction in its unity.
And it has been said:

there is an object, O Ārya; blue and so forth are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the cognition of variegated consciousness (*citravijñāna*), not sharing in anything else.
— vijñāno ba, ja, vijñāne syāt, ratnā, pṛ 173,
pramāṇavā.

For one who discriminates with respect to that object which is impossible to perceive falls [into error]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.220) For one situated in valid cognition should discriminate. (Pramāṇavārttika, variant readings:
ba, ja)

On this point, Devendra’s explanation is as follows: In a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), that which appears as blue and so forth is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of cognition, a qualification of cognition—meaning, it is of the very nature of the experience itself. That alone is the single part that possesses non-blindness, because its intrinsic nature is that cognition; it does not relate to any other object, just as the cognition itself does not. Being of such a nature, when it appears in that variegated perception, it cannot be perceived in isolation from the appearance of the other [colors] such as yellow, because while that [blue] is appearing, all others necessarily appear as well, since they too possess the status of being that same cognition.

Therefore, when the cognizer discerns a single form such as blue from others such as yellow by means of another cognition—thinking "this is blue"—at that very moment, while discerning it in that way, he does not reflect upon that [discerning] cognition itself, because that cognition does not possess the nature of that [object]. What then? He falls toward the object; the meaning is that the cognition is directed toward the object itself.

Therefore, even when a single form appears, either everything appears or nothing at all appears. Thus, it would follow that the appearance of blue and so forth is impossible through discernment in perception.
(Ratnāvalī, p. 173)
And this has been cited: *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā* 5.4, *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*, p. 182, first citation:

"Even though it appears as variegated, cognition is indeed unitary, because it is distinct from external variegation; for external variegation can be analyzed [into its parts], whereas the forms such as blue and so forth belonging to cognition cannot be analyzed."

If it is objected: "But in a painted cloth and the like, a variegated form is perceived; how then can that be a property of cognition? [The reply is: Because it is untenable for it to be a property of the object.

To explain: would a single object such as a painted cloth be a partless whole (*avayavin*), or would it be the opposite? In the first case, when the blue portion is perceived, the yellow and other portions could not remain unperceived, because they would necessarily follow as being distinct from it. Whatever is not perceived when something else is perceived is distinct from it, just as the Vindhya mountain is distinct from the Sahya mountain when the latter is perceived; and indeed, when the blue portion is perceived, the yellow portion and so forth are not perceived.

And likewise, it is untenable for the whole (*avayavin*) to possess a single nature (*ekarūpatā*), because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). That which has the superimposition of contradictory properties cannot have a single nature, as in the case of water and fire; and the whole possesses the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by being perceived and not being perceived.
Alternatively, because the blue part consists of the yellow and other parts, if the yellow and others are not perceived, that [blue] would also certainly not be perceived.

Whatever is of the nature of something else, when that is not perceived, it too is not perceived—just as when yellow and so forth are not perceived, their own nature is not perceived; and the blue part is of the nature of yellow and so forth.

But if it were otherwise, then in the case of a variegated cloth and the like, the disappearance of variegation would be established by itself—just as blue, yellow, and other colors residing in different substrata [do not form a single variegated whole]. Therefore, variegation is not a property of the object (*arthadharma*), but rather a property of cognition (*jñānadharma*). When consciousness arises from its own complex of causes, it arises already inscribed with multiple forms, and it is experienced as such.
Consequently, such a single cognition alone is the reality; thus is established the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaitasiddhi*).

Now, if it is argued that because insentient pleasure and so forth lack the nature of cognition, how could cognition alone—appearing as a manifold—be the single reality from which the non-duality of the manifold is established, that too is mere words; for since pleasure and so forth are also produced from causes non-different from cognition, their identity with cognition is logically established.
To explain: pleasure and so forth are of the nature of cognition because they are produced from causes non-different from cognition, just like other cognitions.

This is the refutation of the view of the proponents of variegated non-duality (citrādvaitavādin).
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that whether cognition is with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*), it would serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of external objects, and so forth—in that regard, it is precisely cognition without form that is the means of valid cognition for the existence of those [objects], because the position of [cognition] having form will be refuted later.

Nor is there an absence of a cause for the determination of specific objects (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) on the part of formless awareness due to its lack of distinction in all cases; for it will be demonstrated that even though it is formless, its status as the cause [of such determination] is established through capacity (*yogyatā*).

As for what was also stated—that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists at a time prior to the object of cognition (*prameya*)—that too is an unexamined assertion; for there is no fixed rule regarding the priority, posteriority, or simultaneity of an illuminator.
To illustrate: in some cases, that which exists previously becomes the illuminator of things that arise later, as the sun is of those [beings] coming into existence;
and in other cases, that which arises later becomes the illuminator of objects already existing, as a lamp is of the jars and other objects situated within a room.
In some cases, however, it is the illuminator of co-existent things, as for instance, "producedness" (kṛtakatva) is [the illuminator] of "impermanence" (anityatva) and so forth.

Therefore, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) reveals a real entity (vastu) independently of any restriction regarding prior, posterior, or simultaneous existence, because it is an illuminator, like the sun and other such lights.
(Page 124, Line 13)

Since it will be demonstrated [in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 23, first half] that the determination of objects for each specific cognition is established through a formless (*nirākāra*) cognition alone by means of rejecting the theory of having a form (*sākāravāda*), one might ask:
"If there is no form, how is there a restriction of the object? We reply: "It is due to the restriction of capacity (*śaktiniyama*) itself, which is induced by its own causes."
Nyāyaviniścayaṭīkā, p. 127, l. 1; p.

Because there is no fixed rule regarding the prior, posterior, or simultaneous occurrence of the cause of apprehension and the object that is the content of apprehension, the distinction between them is stated according to how they are observed.

In some cases, the cause of perception occurs first and the object of perception follows later, as with the light of the sun for things coming into existence. In other cases, the object of perception occurs first and the cause of perception follows later, as with a lamp for things already existing.
In yet other cases, the cause of perception and the object of perception occur simultaneously, as with the apprehension of fire by means of smoke.
Nyāyabhāṣya 2.1.11

As for what was further stated on page 174 of the *Ratnāvalī*— namely, that even in the absence of external objects during the state of dreaming, the coloring by blue and so forth is perceived— that too is mere words; for, immediately following this, in the context of examining the Madhyamaka position, it will be established [on page 125, line 15] that dream-cognition has external objects as its domain.

As for what was also stated—that even though cognition appears in variegated forms, it is a single unity because it is impossible to distinguish [its parts]—in that regard, what is this so-called "impossibility of distinction"? Is it (1) non-difference from cognition, (2) the experience of simultaneously arisen blue and other elements by that very cognition alone to the exclusion of other cognitions, or (3) merely the absence of a distinct discernment? In the first case, the reason is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*); for what is being said is that "blue and the rest are non-different from cognition because they are non-different from it," which is precisely what is meant by "because they are impossible to distinguish."

In the second case, however, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). Since the world of moving and non-moving beings arises simultaneously with the Sugata’s cognition and is apprehended by that very cognition to the exclusion of any other cognition, it lacks identity with it; or, if there were identity, the Sugata would be subject to cyclic existence (*saṃsāritva*), or those in cyclic existence would possess the state of being a Sugata. Furthermore, the fact that a single entity possesses both the nature of cyclic existence and its opposite supports the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*).

Moreover, the claim that experience occurs through that cognition alone to the exclusion of other cognitions is unproven, because blue and other objects are experienced even by means of other cognitions.

Since they are of the nature of cognition, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) in establishing that: for their being of the nature of cognition is established only through that very cognition while excluding any other cognition, and once that [cognition] is established, their being of the nature of cognition is established. Thus, even the mere absence of a distinction between them is unproven; for the distinction between the blue object and its cognition is well-established by virtue of their connection with external and internal locations respectively.

Furthermore, it is not logical to deny the distinction between these two when they are thus distinguished, as that would lead to the denial of everything, resulting in the consequence of universal nihilism (*sakala-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, since the internal reality (*antastattva*), even when pervaded by multiple forms, cannot be analytically separated, its unity is not contradicted; for the same reason, let there be no contradiction to the unity of the external reality (*bahir-tattva*)—such as the composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth—as there is no distinction [between the two cases].

The analytical separation of its nature by the intellect is no different in other cases either; for even in the case of a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), there is no difference in the fact that the forms of blue and so on exist by mutually excluding one another’s locations.

And if they were in the same location, it would follow that all forms would enter into a single form alone, because there would be no distinction from it, and thus its variegated nature (*citratā*) would be contradicted.

Whatever possesses parts does not have a difference in its constituent forms, just as a single blue form [is uniform]. And since the blue and other forms within a variegated cognition (*citra-jñāna*) are its parts, it follows that where there is no difference in form, there is no variegated nature, as in the case of a single blue cognition. Furthermore, are these forms connected with the variegated cognition such that they serve as the basis for its designation, or are they unconnected? They cannot be unconnected, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if they are related, is it through identity (*tādātmya*) or through origination from that (*tadutpatti*)? It cannot be through origination from that, because that is impossible for things existing at the same time, like the pair of eyes on a woman's face.
Nor can it be through identity; for since cognition is not distinct from its manifold forms, it would follow that it lacks a single nature.

Whatever has a nature not distinct from manifold forms is manifold, just as the nature of manifold forms is; and the nature of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) is not distinct from its manifold forms.
Furthermore, if multiple forms were not distinct from the single nature of cognition, their multiplicity would be untenable;

for that which is non-distinct from a single thing cannot be manifold, just like the very nature of that cognition itself. And since the forms such as blue and so forth—which are intended to be manifold—are non-distinct from the single nature of cognition, [they must be one].
Moreover, are these forms such as blue, being connected with the variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), the causes for its designation, or are they unconnected? (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 177)

Regarding what was stated—that variegatedness is not a property of the object because it would involve the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by being apprehended and not apprehended—that too is unsound; for an inference cannot operate when there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, the variegated form appears in an uncontradicted perceptual cognition as a property of the external object; it is not logical that it be a property of cognition, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued: "Whatever is perceived as having a certain nature cannot possess a different nature from that; for example, luminosity and heat, being perceived as the nature of fire, are not the nature of water. Since variegation (*citratā*) is perceived as the nature of external objects, how can there be the possibility of perceiving or not perceiving it as such a nature? [The answer is: Because the apprehension of variegation is based upon the apprehension of multiple colors, it is entirely logical that even when the blue portion is apprehended, if the yellow and other portions are not apprehended, the variegation itself remains unapprehended.

Furthermore, even if variegation (*citratā*) were a property of cognition, the contradiction would remain exactly the same. To explain: is cognition unitary and yet possessed of multiple forms, or is it the opposite? The first alternative is not tenable; for since the forms are mutually exclusive, their subsistence in a single partless cognition is impossible. Those things which are mutually exclusive cannot subsist in one partless entity, as is the case with cows, horses, and so forth. And since the forms such as blue and the rest are mutually exclusive, it is not possible for this single, partless [cognition] to have identity (*tādātmya*) with these mutually contradictory forms; otherwise, it would follow that the cognition itself must be as manifold as those forms.

The formal argument (*prayoga*): That which is a single, partless entity cannot have identity (*tādātmya*) with mutually contradictory forms, just as a moment that has already arisen cannot possess both arising and non-arising, or existence and destruction; and yet, you maintain that variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) is a single, partless entity.

Furthermore, if there were identity (*tādātmya*) with those [aspects], even the report of any difference among the aspects would be difficult to find; so how could there be their variegatedness? Now, if it is maintained that the cognition of that [object] is also manifold—just like the aspects of blue and so forth—is this so in some respect or in every respect? If it is in every respect, then because those cognitions are absolutely distinct from one another, the perception of a variegated [object] would not occur even in a dream.

For those things that are absolutely distinct from one another do not have the perception of a variegated [object], just as in the case of the cognitions belonging to different mental continua (*santāna*); and the cognitions of that [object], like the aspects, are absolutely distinct from one another.

If, however, there is some kind of non-difference, then let it be accepted that the external object—just like cognition—possesses a variegated nature (*citrasvabhāvatā*), since it is perceived through means of valid cognition such as direct perception as being in some way identical with its own diverse forms. What is the use of this stubborn insistence on [the distinction between] objection and resolution, given that variegation is the same whether it pertains to the internal or the external?

For instance—is that [entity] one and real with multiple forms, or is it the opposite? (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 177; variants: *syād bahvākāratā*—Ba, Ja; *syād vā*—Ā)

As for what was also stated—that pleasure and so forth are of the nature of cognition because they arise from causes non-different from those of cognition, and so on—in this regard, is their arising from causes non-different from cognition intended in every respect (*sarvathā*), or in some respect (*kathañcit*)? In the first case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for pleasure and so forth are dependent upon causes such as the arising of karma to be experienced as pleasant or unpleasant, garlands, women, and the like, whereas cognition arises from a collection of causes such as the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and the sense organs.

Furthermore, because these [phenomena] possess distinct natures, it is logically untenable for them to be produced by a cause that is entirely non-distinct. Those things which possess distinct natures cannot be produced by a cause that is entirely non-distinct, just as in the case of water, fire, and so forth; and since knowledge, pleasure, and the like do possess distinct natures, this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because pleasure and the like have the form of exhilaration and so on, whereas knowledge has the nature of the experience of the object of cognition (*prameya*).

Furthermore, is it said that pleasure and the rest are produced from a cause non-different from consciousness in relation to their material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), or in relation to their auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)? Regarding the first alternative, what is their non-different material cause: the substance of the self (*ātman-dravya*), or a moment of cognition (*jñāna-kṣaṇa*)? It cannot be the substance of the self, because [such a thing] is not admitted.

Or, if this [non-difference] is accepted, is the non-difference of these [pleasure, knowledge, etc. established with respect to their material cause (*upādāna*), or with respect to their own nature (*svarūpa*)? If it is with respect to the material cause, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because non-difference among pleasure and the rest is accepted from the perspective of the substantial reality (*dravyārthādeśa*) of the conscious substance; yet, from the perspective of the specific modal reality (*paryāyārthādeśa*) of pleasure, cognition, and so forth, their mutual difference is indeed accepted.

However, if non-difference is accepted with respect to their own nature, there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to jars and the like; for there is no non-difference in their own nature among jars, pots, bowls, water-jars, and so on, even though they share the same material cause.

Now, if it is intended that being the material cause (*upādāna*) of a moment of cognition means being produced from a cause non-different from consciousness, that is unproven; for those [moments] have the substance of the self (*ātmadravya*) as their material cause. Indeed, nowhere is it observed that one mode (*paryāya*) serves as the material cause for the production of another mode; rather, it is logical that only the substance (*dravya*), whether internally or externally, functions as the material cause. As it has been said: "That which persists through the sequence of before and after, even throughout the three periods of time, without abandoning its own essential nature or taking on a new one, is remembered as the substance that is the material cause."

The establishment of the self as a substance has already been proven during the investigation into the continuum (*santāna*), and it will be further established during the discussion on the proof of the living being (*jīva*).

Now, if it is intended that pleasure and so forth arise from causes non-different from consciousness due to their dependence on auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), that too is merely an intention, because such a claim has been shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the eyes and other sense organs. Furthermore, if pleasure and so forth were in every way non-different from cognition, then they too would possess the capacity to illuminate objects just like cognition; however, this is not the case here, because they are restricted to illuminating their own nature (*svarūpa*).

For it is well known to every living being that knowledge is invariably characterized by the illumination of both itself and others (*sva-paraprakāśa*), whereas pleasure and the like are invariably characterized by self-illumination alone (*svaprakāśa*). Therefore, due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), how can there be non-difference here? Wherever there is the imposition of contradictory properties, as in the case of water and fire, there is no non-difference; and such imposition of contradictory properties exists between knowledge, pleasure, and so forth.

Thus, since it is not established that pleasure and the like are of the nature of knowledge, the statement that "even the variegated manifestation of blue, pleasure, and so on is a single cognition because it is indivisible" merely indicates an intention and is not true.

The author of the treatise says: "Even in that view, it would not be so"—this is contradictory, namely, that it is both "one" and "variegated. Indeed, there is no basis for the existence of multiplicity and unity other than the two real modes of difference and non-difference; in this regard, if cognition is held to be both manifold in form and yet one in its reality, then the entire universe would become a single substance, and consequently, faults such as simultaneous arising would follow. Therefore, mere consciousness alone, devoid of an objective support (*ālambana-pratyaya*), is the real reality, because all cognitions have the nature of being without an objective support. Furthermore, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can operate upon an object that is distinct from the consciousness of the form of the moment being experienced; for it is impossible for such a [cognition] to function toward that [object], whether it be simultaneous with it or occurring at a different time.
That very [consciousness] is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipat*), the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*), and the emptiness of everything (*sakalaśūnyatā*).
As it has been said: "That itself is the Middle Way, the selflessness of all phenomena."
This very [nature] is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), this very [nature] is suchness (tathyatā), and this very [nature] is emptiness (śūnyatā);
thus,
the state of all phenomena being devoid of intrinsic nature is established because they cannot withstand analysis as to whether they possess a singular or multiple essential form.

For instance: those things which cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many are not ultimately real, just like the horns of a donkey and so forth. And entities such as the *ātman* and others postulated by opponents cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many.

For if those entities like the *ātman*, which are accepted as having a single nature, are admitted to be capable of producing successive effects such as cognitions, their unity cannot be maintained because it would entail a multiplicity [of natures]. As for their multiplicity, however, it is utterly untenable because they are accepted as having a permanent, unitary nature.
Therefore, it is established that as phenomena are investigated in whatever manner, they merely float away; thus, their inability to withstand such investigation is proven.
And it has been said: "The nature by which phenomena are defined does not exist in reality, because neither a singular nor a manifold nature is found in them."

Whatever is experienced by a cognition does not exist as something else; just as there is no other object to be experienced, so it has been explained.
In that case, let there be an experience of another by the cognition; no, for even there, the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper are absent.
Indeed, how can that which is established in its own nature as pure consciousness be an experience of another? Direct perception and the like have been rejected [for consciousness].
Furthermore, if it were to enter into that experience, the two would become one; thus it is established that it is that very [consciousness] which shines by itself, and nothing other than that.

"Because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines forth by itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.327). This is the refutation of the Madhyamaka position thus stated; here, a rebuttal is provided.

As for what was stated—that the appearance of forms such as blue is unreal because it is fashioned by the artisan of ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth—on that point, from what source does this appearance of blue and the like arise from ignorance? Is it because it is sublated, or because its object lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? In the first case, the status of being produced by ignorance would not be established for all appearances of water, blue, and so on; for it is only where such an appearance is sublated that it is produced by ignorance, as in the appearance of water in a mirage or the appearance of silver in a piece of mother-of-pearl. It is not the case, however, that an appearance of water in actual water, or an appearance of silver in actual silver, is produced by ignorance.

Furthermore, regarding the subverting argument here: if the nature of the middle moment is mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), how is that established? If you say it is because appearances such as blue and so forth are unreal, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): for the reality of the middle moment as mere consciousness is established only when the unreality of those appearances is established, and the establishment of such a reality of mere consciousness occurs only when their unreality is established. Moreover, any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) intended to establish mere consciousness has already been refuted.

However, the claim that its object lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is unproven (*asiddha*), because objects such as water and fire—which are the objects of that [cognition]—are well-established as being constantly capable of causal efficiency, such as bathing and drinking. And if that [object] were devoid of causal efficiency, what other kind of causal efficiency could there be? If it is argued that "it is the experience of its own nature," even that exists for the forms such as blue and so forth residing within the cognition; for there is never an experience of mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) in the form of a middle moment that is devoid of form, since only an object possessing multiple forms, whether external or internal, is experienced (p.

From what cause does this appearance of forms such as blue arise based on ignorance—is it because it is sublated, or because its object lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? [In the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
183, it is stated that] there is causal efficiency in actions such as bathing. [Variant reading: *snānādikriyāyām arthakriyākāritve*].
Now, the experience of its own nature would be the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), as stated in the *Ratnāvalī*, page 183: "the nature of consciousness...
(*rūpa saṃvi–*).

Now, if the experience of multiple forms such as blue and so forth is false, then—given that there is no distinction in the appearance of consciousness and the forms such as blue, which possess respectively singular and plural natures—how can one distinguish between what is real and what is otherwise? If the [form] possessing multiple aspects is unreal because it is contradictory with that which possesses a single aspect, why should the [form] possessing a single aspect not likewise be unreal? Since the unreality of multiple aspects is well-established in dream-cognition, if they are unreal even in variegated cognition (*citra-jñāna*), then since the unreality of even a single aspect is well-established in cases such as [the illusion of] hair-tufts, why should the unreality belong to the single aspect alone elsewhere as well? And just as the multiplicity of multiple aspects is contradicted if they are non-different from a single aspect, whereas if they were different, it would entail the consequence of being separate cognitions; so too, if a single aspect is non-different from multiple aspects, it entails multiplicity, whereas if it were different, it would entail the consequence of being a separate cognition.

Furthermore, if a single [cognition] is not admitted to possess multiple forms, then for each form there would be a distinct cognition, as in the case of separate mental continua; and since those forms are not perceived by means of the blue form, they would likewise be non-existent.

Since even the blue portion is divided according to each individual atom, the cognitions of the blue atoms must be mutually distinct; and since those [cognitions] are not perceived by a single cognition of a blue atom, they would be non-existent. Furthermore, that single cognition of a blue atom would likewise have to consist of a triad due to the distinction between the forms of the object (*vedya*), the subject (*vedaka*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*). Moreover, each of these three cognitions of the forms of the object and so forth would require another set of three cognitions of the forms of the object and so forth, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, the desired reality could not be established, and because such a thing is not perceived, it follows that it does not exist; thus, there would be nothing but universal emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Therefore, for those who accept the determination of reality based on cognition, such an object—whether external or internal—must be understood by those skilled in discernment as being either unitary or manifold according to its appearance; otherwise, how could it exist?

If it is argued that even though there is no difference in the appearance of the single and the multiple forms, the distinction between what is real and what is otherwise is established because the single form is contradictory with the multiple form, and since that [multiple form] is unreal, why would the single form itself not be unreal? If it is further argued that since the unreality of the multiple form is well-established in dream-cognition, it is likewise reasonable to postulate its unreality in variegated cognition (*citra-jñāna*), then [we reply]: since the unreality of even the single form is established in the case of [the illusion of] hair-tufts and the like, how could unreality be considered unreasonable in that case? (Aṣṭasahasrī p. 76;
Syādvādaratnākara p. 184)

Indeed, in this way, since there is a distinction for every atom, even the cognition of a blue object must consist of mutually distinct cognitions of each blue atom. Furthermore, even the cognition of a single blue atom must likewise consist of a triad due to the distinction between the object (*vedya*), the subject (*vedaka*), and the consciousness-form (*savidākāra*). Moreover, each of these three cognitions—the cognition of the object-form and so forth—must itself consist of another triad of cognitions, namely the cognition of its own object and so on. Thus, because of the postulation of an infinite regress of successive triads of cognitions, the establishment of a single cognition is impossible for those who oppose the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*).
(Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 77)

Furthermore, as for the other statement—that "all cognitions are without an objective basis" (*nirālambana*) and so forth—that too is charming only so long as it is not critically examined. This is because waking cognitions are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as illuminating objects such as pillars, jars, and the like, which are distinct from their own nature, stable, gross, and common.

Thus, since the reason "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) is employed immediately after stating a thesis that is sublated by direct perception—just like the argument "sound is not audible because it exists"—it is a case of the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

And it is unestablished (*asiddha*); for you do not admit that "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) exists as something distinct from the cognitions themselves. Furthermore, if those [cognitions] alone are the reason, there is the fallacy of the unestablished nature of a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśāsiddhatā*), as well as the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*), because the locus is not established due to the lack of an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*) for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends them.

Moreover, there is the unestablished nature of the essential character (*svarūpāsiddhatā*), because the cognition that apprehends the essential character of the reason is likewise, for this very reason, without an objective basis.

Now, if—desiring to avoid this fault and to establish the [existence of] the subject and so forth—one accepts that the cognition apprehending it possesses an objective support (*sālambanatva*), then by that very fact, the nature of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) becomes both inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and contradictory (*viruddha*). For the status of being a cognition is established only when cognitions possess an objective support; since those by which one’s own form or the form of another is cognized are "cognitions" (*pratyaya*), their state is "the nature of being a cognition. How then could that not be pervaded by having an objective support, which is the opposite of being without an objective support, such that it would not be contradictory?
Because it is [something] that goes; even when there is the external, [it is so]. (bhā॰ satyeva bahi ā॰ ca ba॰, ja॰, bhāṃ॰)

Furthermore, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for even cognitions such as those occurring in dreams possess external objects as their objective supports (*ālambana*), and thus lack the quality of being "without support" (*nirālambanatva*).

Indeed, dream is of two kinds: true and false. Among these, the first is produced by a particular deity or by merit and demerit (*dharmādharmakṛta*); it is certain in its correspondence with reality (*arthāvyabhicārī*). This is because an object perceived in a dream with a specific place, time, and form is established to be obtained in the waking state with that same place, time, and form.

Some, however, [hold that dream-cognition is valid] through a mediated succession (*paramparayā*); for, just like inference, the seeing of kings and such is the cause for attaining results described in dream-treatises, such as the increase of one’s family. Since occasional deviation (*vyabhicāra*) occurs equally in inference as well, even that dream which is renowned as unreal because it is produced by an excess of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and so forth, does not deviate from the object in its mere existence. For no cognition whatsoever deviates from pure being (*sattāmātra*), as that would entail the consequence of its non-arising at all. It is only with respect to a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) that it deviates, and for that very reason it is called "unreal."

Furthermore, since the Buddhist does not admit that cognition exists in dreams and the like, of what could these serve as an example? Or, if such cognition is admitted, then if the cognition grasping the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) were itself without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), it would follow that the example is devoid of both the property to be proven and the proving property. Moreover, if the cognition grasping the example itself were without an objective basis, the example would be non-existent, resulting in a lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).

Alternatively, if the cognitions of the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*), and both were without an objective basis, the thesis (*pakṣa*) would have an unestablished locus, an unestablished predicate, or both unestablished.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the thesis and the reason: if it is to be proven that all cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), then by adducing a reason, one necessarily admits that the cognition of that reason *does* have an objective basis; otherwise, how could this proof establish the thesis?
For dreams are of two kinds: true and false.

In that regard, a dream may be true, being produced by a deity or produced by merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*), manifesting for someone as a direct determination (*vyavasāyātmaka*). This is because an object perceived in the state of dreaming with a certain place, time, and form is determined in the waking state with that very same place, time, and form; thus, some dreams are true and determine objects through a causal chain, since they bring about the attainment of the objects described in dream-omens. As it has been said: "At the end of the night, one sees a king, an elephant, a horse, gold, a bull, and a cow; his household increases."
*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 58; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 186. Note:
prati—he—Ā.
[The term] "erroneous" [is used] because [it occurs] in states such as sleep (bhāṃ॰;
*svāpādau* in *ba॰*, *ja॰*, *ā॰*).

Furthermore, if one accepts that all cognitions are false with respect to external objects based on the analogy of dreams, it follows that they must also be false with respect to their own nature (*svarūpa*).
For instance: whatever appears is false, just like an external object; and the nature of consciousness (*vijñānasvarūpa*) also appears.

Thus, even though there is no difference in their appearing, if you accept that the appearance of its own nature is true based on experience, then why would you not accept—on the grounds of experience—that the cognitions of external objects during the waking state are true, given that there is no difference in their being cognitions? For there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Furthermore, those inferences that were put forward—beginning with "because they cannot withstand an analysis of their nature as being either one or many"—are to be understood as having been refuted by these very same defects of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Moreover, the inability to withstand such analysis is unestablished in every respect; for the entities such as the Self (*ātman*) can withstand an analysis of their nature as being both one and many.

Indeed, the capacity of the Self and so forth to produce effects such as successive cognitions does not prove its diversity, since it is precisely the difference in their functional capacities (*sāmarthya-bheda*) that is established thereby.

Now, [the objection]: "If capacity (*sāmarthya*), which is of the nature of the essence (*svabhāva*), is divided, how is it that the possessor of that capacity is not divided?"—this too is incorrect, because a difference in essence is not a necessary factor for a difference in the entity (*bhāva*). Otherwise, how could there be a single, variegated cognition? Furthermore, if that [difference in essence] were not admitted, the total emptiness [of all things] would have been established long ago.

Or else, how could there be unity in a cognition that possesses a difference in essence, given that it bears indirectness (*parokṣatā*) by way of being distinguished from the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*) and directness (*pratyakṣatā*) by way of being the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*)? —Thus it is unestablished (asiddha).

For even if one does not admit that some [cognition] which persists for a moment possesses a manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpya*) consisting of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, it follows by implication that a single self-cognizing consciousness—which possesses the distinction between the forms of the grasped and the grasper in a manner that is imperceptible (*parokṣa*)—is established as having a manifold nature through its having both perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and imperceptible aspects.
(Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 91)

As for what was also stated—that objects are devoid of properties such as origination and so forth—that too is incorrect. For it is logically consistent that these [objects] possess the properties of origination and so on, being existent in the form of substance (*dravya*) and non-existent in the form of modes (*paryāya*). Indeed, the occurrence of those properties is not possible for that which is either absolutely existent or absolutely non-existent; we shall demonstrate this in its proper place. Furthermore, if properties such as origination did not exist in any way whatsoever, then pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) would follow as being non-existent, because it lacks causal efficacy (*kāryakāritva*), like a sky-flower; or else it would be eternal, because it is existent and lacks a cause, like space (*ākāśa*).

And if these [entities] do not exist, how can they be the objects of a clear manifestation? That which is non-existent in every respect cannot be the object of a clear manifestation, just like a sky-flower; and since the dharmas such as arising (*utpāda*) imagined by you are non-existent in every respect, their being objects [of cognition] would entail the impossibility of their being non-existent in every respect. For that which is the object of a clear manifestation is not non-existent in every respect, just like the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit-svarūpa*); and the dharmas such as arising are indeed the objects of a clear manifestation.
Nor is this unproven, for it is well-established—even among children—that the production of bracelets and so forth from gold and the like falls within the range of clear perception;

moreover, if those [properties] were non-existent in every respect therein, even mere cognition would not occur. For that which is non-existent in every respect in a given place is not cognized there, just as pleasure is not cognized in pain, or a yellow form in a blue form; and thus, the properties such as production and so forth are non-existent in every respect in objects.
(Page 132, Line 7)
That which has no cause is eternal,
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.1.

As for the objection that [the reason] is inconclusive because perception occurs even when water is non-existent in a mirage, this too is incorrect; for in that case, it is impossible for the water to be non-existent in every respect.

For non-existence is said to be absolute non-existence when it pertains to substance, location, time, and form; however, this [non-existence] does not apply to it here, because it exists there in a nature similar to waves and ripples, since otherwise—like wood or stone—the cognition of it would not arise even within that wheel.

Or, let it be granted that there is a cognition even of these non-existent things; nevertheless, would that cognition be primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇa*)? Regarding this, the first position is untenable; for primary cognition is the unique characteristic inherent in the very nature of knowledge itself. How, then, could such cognition belong to production and other factors which are of the nature of non-cognition? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which is of the nature of non-cognition does not possess primary cognition, just like a hare’s horn. And the properties such as production and so forth, as well as the objects characterized by them, are accepted as being of the nature of non-cognition due to their non-existence.

The second position is also untenable; for that which is called "secondary cognition" is simply the production of a cognition manifesting its own form, and this is impossible for non-existent things such as a horse’s horn or production (*utpāda*) and so forth, because non-existence is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity. That which is devoid of all causal capacity cannot have secondary cognition, just like a horse’s horn; and the properties such as production and so forth, which are intended to be non-existent, as well as the objects possessing them, are likewise devoid of all causal capacity. Thus, these [properties] are non-existent. (Bhāṣya)

Furthermore, what is the relationship between arising and so forth and the cognition [of them], by virtue of which they would necessarily be cognized when that [cognition] is being experienced—is it identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*)? It cannot be identity, because that would entail the consequence that they, like the cognition, must also be existent.

Nor can it be origination from that, because if the forms of arising and so forth were formless (*nīrūpa*), then both the state of being produced and the state of being a producer would be impossible.

Therefore, since there is no connection, how can they be cognized by that [cognition]? Whatever has no connection with something else is not necessarily cognized when that thing is being cognized, just as the son of a barren woman is not cognized when the nature of cognition itself is being cognized. Furthermore, there is no connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between cognition and the forms such as arising, which are non-existent entities.

Furthermore, when these [characteristics] are cognized within cognition, they are necessarily cognized; therefore, there must be some relationship between them and that [cognition]. And since this [relationship] is not possible without ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), their ultimate reality is established.

For whatever is necessarily cognized when something else is cognized is related to it and possesses ultimate reality—just as the nature of that [cognition] itself is necessarily cognized when cognition is cognized—and production and so forth are necessarily cognized when cognition is cognized, and objects possess those [characteristics].

If these [objects] were non-existent even while being experienced, it would follow that they are non-existent even in the nature of cognition itself, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of universal emptiness (*sakala-śūnyatā*).

If you argue that this consequence is not a fault because it is accepted [by us], we ask: what indeed is this so-called "universal emptiness" that its acceptance would not be a fault? Would it be the mere absence of all categories of objects, or pure consciousness (*saṃvin-mātra*) devoid of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper? In the first alternative, is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its existence, or not? If there is none, how can it be established? For the establishment of a real entity is dependent upon a means of valid cognition.

Now, [you may ask]: how can there be universal emptiness (*sakalaśūnyatā*) if there exists direct perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as the sense faculties and so forth that produce them, since this would contradict universal emptiness?

[The answer is: "This is the construction of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*); duality does not exist therein, but emptiness exists here, and within that [emptiness] too, it [the construction of the unreal] exists."

Because duality does not exist therein, for the unreal imagination is empty, being devoid of the grasped and the grasper; thus it is not non-existent by way of its own nature in every respect (Madhyāntavibhāga-sūtra-ṭīkā, p. 9).

Furthermore, would this total emptiness (*sakala-śūnyatā*) arise from the absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*), due to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), through analysis (*vicāra*), or by way of reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*)? Regarding the first position, what is this "absence of the means of valid cognition that apprehends them"? Is it cognitions produced by defective sense organs, such as doubt and the like, or is it the non-arising of cognition (*jñānānutpāda*)? The first alternative is untenable; for if one admits the existence of doubt and so forth, it follows that total emptiness is abandoned. As for the non-arising of cognition, does it lead to the understanding of the non-existence of everything when it is itself known, or when it is unknown? It cannot be the latter, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Whatever is an absence, when known, indicates the absence of another, just as the absence of smoke in a certain place indicates the absence of fire; and this [absence] is the non-arising of cognition. Now, if it is known, from what does its cognition arise—from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or from itself? In the first case, due to infinite regress, there would be no comprehension of the original absence. If its cognition were from itself, it would follow that all absences are also cognized by themselves, and thus the absence of a means of knowledge would be redundant.

If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is our loss?", [the answer is: there would be a contradiction with the doctrine of universal emptiness (*sarva-śūnyatā*), because such a thing would necessarily result in being of the nature of both the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Furthermore, it is untenable to claim that "there is a total non-existence (*sarvābhāva*) that cannot be designated by the terms 'means of knowledge' or 'object of knowledge'"; for if its own nature is cognized by itself, there is a contradiction in negating that very nature.
Alternatively, if it were not designated by those terms, it would follow that it is non-existent.

For instance: that which cannot be designated by the terms "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) or "object of valid cognition" (*prameya*) does not exist, just like a donkey's horn; and yet, the non-existence of everything is designated by those very terms.

Furthermore, the emptiness of all things would have to result either from the non-apprehension of the means and objects of valid cognition, or from critical investigation, or from a reductio ad absurdum argument (see *Ratnākaraṇḍāvatāra*, p. 189).
For one whose desired [position] has not been definitively established anywhere, there is no doubt;
in its absence, further objections from others are not applicable.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 80:
The arising of cognitions is the apprehension of their own nature. *Ja*.

Nor can the proof of universal emptiness be established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because of the absence of both the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), and it would follow that you are merely proving what is already established, since you admit the non-existence of things that have been destroyed or those not yet produced.

And there is the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Since the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are not perceived, their existence is refuted by the very means of cognition that would establish them; for if one does not admit their existence, faults such as the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) necessarily follow. How, then, can the proof of universal emptiness be established? If it is argued that because non-perception is a property of absence (*abhāva-dharma*), the fault of the unestablished locus and so forth does not apply—this too is unsatisfactory, because there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for non-perception being a property of absence.

Furthermore, is non-apprehension employed for the cognition of another thing when it is apprehended in its own nature, or when it is not apprehended? It cannot be the latter, because it is a cognizer; for whatever is a cognizer is employed for the cognition of another thing only when it is apprehended in its own nature, as in the case of smoke and so forth, and non-apprehension is the cognizer of all absences. Nor can it be [employed] when unapprehended; for if there were the operation of a means of valid cognition—either perception or inference—to apprehend its own nature, it would entail the contradiction of the total emptiness [of everything].

Furthermore, it is not logical that something which is itself not ascertained as a logical mark (*liṅga*), and for which no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been established in an example, should possess the capacity to prove its own probandum; for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
[Otherwise] one would have to employ means of proof for the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth. (Bhāmatī)

Now, if it is argued that the non-existence of everything is established through investigation (*vicāra*), [we ask]: does this investigation itself exist as a real entity or not? If it exists, how can there be the emptiness of all things? If it does not exist, how could the non-existence of everything be proven? Furthermore, if it is argued that its non-existence is established by means of a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), we say no; for one who maintains the non-existence of everything, the distinction between self and other is impossible, and thus a *prasaṅga-sādhana* itself cannot occur, since such a proof is characterized by the production of an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) based on what is accepted by the opponent.

And how could one who, without accepting the manifold expansion of means and objects of knowledge—which stands firmly established upon the mountain peak of common experience—accept the non-existence of everything that is not perceived even in a dream, be considered an authority (*prāmāṇika*)? If it is argued that this expansion appears as a mere falsehood, just like elephants, horses, and so forth in a dream, then where would truthfulness reside now? If you say it resides in the non-existence of objects such as jars, then from what source does that [non-existence] derive its truthfulness? If you say it is from an appearance free from sublation (*bādhā*), then that is the same in the other case as well.

For just as there is an uncontradicted appearance of objects in some place or at some time despite their non-existence, so too, if objects were non-existent even during their middle state—just as they are prior to and after their destruction—then even at the time of their persistence, there would be no designation of genus, quality, or action, such as "this is a cow," "it is white," or "it moves," because it is impossible to designate what is non-existent.
Yet this designation does exist; therefore, in the middle state, the form of existence must be understood as something distinct from the form of non-existence of objects.

Therefore, there is no such thing as the non-existence of all objects—that is, a "universal void"—because in the absence of any investigation, it is impossible to assert through investigation that anything is untenable. Furthermore, the proponent of emptiness has no settled conclusion whatsoever upon which an investigation could proceed regarding some other unsettled matter, since he is in disagreement with everything.
As it is said in the *Tattvārtha-ślokavārtika* (p. 80, v. 140): "An investigation proceeds elsewhere by relying upon something that has been settled."
But in the case of every contradiction, there is no deliberation;
[the point] would be established in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, page 116. Ārya.

In the middle [of the commentary], the words "padārthā" (in the manuscript *ba* and *ja*) refer to the remainder of the sūtra: "Because of the absence of action, quality, and designation for that which is non-existent, the existent is a different entity."

Now, it may be argued that "she" (the Goddess) is said to be pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) devoid of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhakabhāva*) and so forth. But from what source is such a [consciousness] established—is it by mere assertion (*abhyupagama*), or by perception (*pratīti*)? In the first case, how can there be an establishment of a thesis (*pakṣasiddhi*) that is free from opposition, since it is possible for anyone to establish whatever reality they personally desire? The second case is also untenable; because pure consciousness devoid of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper is never perceived at any time, how could its defining characteristic—that emptiness—be established through perception? Furthermore, one who establishes the nature of things based on perception must accept that an object consists of multiple aspects, whether external or internal, since external and internal objects appear in perception precisely as being occupied by various forms such as the grasped, the grasper, and so on.

And this [cognition] is not false, because there is no sublation; for sublation consists in the apprehension of a contrary object, and that is not present here, since even in dreams there is no apprehension of a mere consciousness (saṃvinmātra) that abides in a middle moment, which would be contrary to it.

Or, if one were to postulate a sublation even by means of what is non-existent, then why would the mere consciousness (saṃvinmātra) abiding in the middle moment not be sublated by the perception of the supreme Brahman—which is eternal, partless, and all-pervading—since there is no distinction [between the two cases]? Therefore, by one who accepts that the determination of reality is based upon cognition, an object consisting of multiple aspects (anekāntātmā), whether external or internal, must be admitted as the domain of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). Thus, it is established that even an external object is within the range of the means of valid knowledge. If the state of being the grasped and the grasper were to exist, then the emptiness of the grasped and its grasper would be the object of apprehension; otherwise, there would be a lack of such emptiness.
Therefore, it is not exclusively an error, nor is it merely a non-existent conventional reality. (Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 81)
Therefore, by the force of the meaning, the praise of a manifold self follows;
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 206, u. 91.

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) of Bhartṛhari regarding the doctrine of Śabdabrahman: By this, even the proponent of the non-duality of Brahman (brahmādvaitavādin), who denies external objects, is refuted, because there is no evidence for the existence of Brahman. [Objection: But of what kind of Brahman is there an absence of evidence for its existence—is it of that which has the nature of sound (śabda), or of that which is the Supreme Self (paramātman)? For Brahman is indeed twofold, due to the distinction between the Brahman of Sound and the Supreme Brahman.

And it has been said: "One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Supreme Brahman" (Brahmabindu Upaniṣad 22). In this regard, the first alternative is untenable; for when the Brahman whose nature is sound exists, there is the presence of both perception and inference as means of valid cognition.

To explain: every perception, whether born of yoga or not born of yoga, appears as being permeated by the Śabdabrahman. This is because this [perception], arising with respect to external and internal objects, arises only as being interpenetrated by sound, since it is difficult to establish the manifestation of cognitions in the absence of contact with that [sound].
For the nature of speech is eternal and reflective; in its absence, no other form remains for them.
As it has been said: "Of the nature of the Self... [bhāṃ]
Two knowledges are to be known: the Brahman of sound and that which is the supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the supreme Brahman.
(Brahmabindu Upaniṣad 22)
There are two Brahmans—the lower and the higher (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
536; Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p.
105)—of cognitions.
There is no cognition in the world that exists without the accompaniment of words;
everything appears as if permeated by them, for all is established in speech.
All knowledge, as it were, permeated by words, shines forth through them.

And when the nature of speech (*vāgrūpatā*) exists, even though illumination has arisen, it does not establish itself as the means for the act of illumination unless it assumes that specific nature of speech; for that nature of speech is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which is conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), and [the nature of speech] is that which brings this about—this is the meaning. (Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī, p. 20)
And that very [word] is the means for the act of manifestation; such is the meaning of Vākyapadīya-Ṭīkā 1.125.
"Indeed, that [light] which possesses reflective awareness would not shine as light. (Vākyapadīya 1.124–25).

Thus, even every worldly transaction is experienced as being permeated by words; for no one at all exerts themselves to accomplish a task for themselves—such as "I shall eat" or "I shall give"—without mentally delineating words, nor does one incite another to act without words such as "Give! and so forth.

The manifestation of the forms of both life and its opposite is likewise dependent solely upon sound (*śabda*). For instance, during the state of deep sleep, because the form of sound is not articulated, one is not distinguished from the dead. However, at a subsequent time, a person awakened by some sound attains life by means of sound itself, through the nature of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*), sustaining the self. From that life sustained by sound, all manifestations of the creative potency of sound (*śabdabhāvanā*)—in the form of "I am," "this," "I perform this," and so forth—evolve. And these, evolving toward various objects, manifest their respective objective referents.
When a word uttered by a person, having manifested, disappears, it then causes its own inherent meaning to disappear as well, just as the moon [causes its] moonlight to vanish.

Now, one might ask: "In a reality that is non-dual in nature, how can there be the appearance of the manifold of difference, characterized by manifestation and disappearance? This need not be kept in mind; for due to ignorance (*avidyā*), the appearance of such [duality] therein is not contradictory, just like [the appearance of objects] in space.

For just as a person whose vision is impaired by cataracts perceives even the pure sky as if it were interlaced with a multitude of various lines, so too does a person afflicted by the cataracts of ignorance perceive the *śabdabrahman*—which is without beginning or end, of undivided nature, and free from the entire manifold of distinctions—as if it were endowed with the manifold of distinctions such as manifestation and the like.
And it has been said: "Just as a person overwhelmed by cataracts conceives the pure sky to be mixed with various measures [of visual distortions]."

In the same way, this stainless Brahman, though changeless, perceives itself as having assumed a state of differentiation— as if it had attained impurity— due to ignorance (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika 3).
Thus.
Upon the dissolution of the entire play of ignorance, however, yogins realize the true nature of that [Brahman] as it is, unassociated with its phenomenal expansion.

Just as a modification of water—consisting of waves, ripples, bubbles, and foam—requires the pure, essential water for its manifestation and disappearance, so too does this gross, empirical diversity of distinct sounds such as "a" and so forth require Brahman, which consists of sound (*śabdamaya*). This Brahman is of the singular nature of mere supreme subtle manifestation, the cause of the production of the cognition of all objects of speech, and possesses an undetermined, single, innate essence.
And it has been said:
That [wisdom] which arises from some source is the Buddha;
it is the binder of all sciences, crafts, and arts.
Through its power, when [a thing] is fully accomplished, every object is differentiated;
this very perception of those wandering in saṃsāra operates both externally and internally.
Even when it has transcended those subtle elements alone, consciousness in all living beings impels every speech regarding purposeful actions for the embodied soul. 127.
Upon its departure, this [body] is seen to be unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall. (Vākyapadīya, Prakīrṇaka-kāṇḍa, Kārikā 128)
And thus it was not clearly reflected in the minds [of those present]: "Just as a person afflicted by cataracts [perceives] the pure sky..."
One perceives it as if mixed with various measures;
one should observe it through its various [aspects].

likewise, "this immortal Brahman undergoes illusory manifestation (vivarta) in a differentiated form" (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 72).
