"But one perceives it as having a differentiated form" (bhedarūpaṃ tu paśyati). [This is found in] Ratnākaraśānti’s *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa*, p. 91; however, the reading in the present text is found in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 12, and the *Nayopadeśavṛtti*, p. 96.

Because it lacks a fixed, singular form— like waves, bubbles, and foam— the speech of those who perceive the essence of words regards the non-dual water of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) as their substance.
And this has been cited—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
91; *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*, p. 237, upper part:

"Even though the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) is thus perceived through direct perception, those whose minds are afflicted by the cataract of ignorance do not accept it as such, but rather fall into error. With reference to them, this is said: 'Whatever things are permeated by the form of X, they consist of that [X]; just as jars, bowls, buckets, and so forth, which are modifications of clay, consist of clay; and all entities are permeated by the form of the Word.'"

Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for it has already been demonstrated that all objects are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being associated with the form of the word, and once that is established, their being composed of that [word] is necessarily established, since they arise solely from it.

Furthermore, because the difference between those two is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); for instance—the object is not distinct from the word, because it is perceived only when that [word] is perceived. Whatever is perceived only when something else is perceived is not distinct from that thing, just as the very nature of the word itself. And the object is perceived only when the word is perceived; therefore, it is not distinct from it. Thus, since the existence of Brahman as the essential nature of the word is established, the existence of perception and other means of knowledge is proven, which constitutes the refutation of the doctrine of the non-duality of the word (*śabdādvaita*).
To this, we offer the following response:

as for what was stated—that "in the existence of Brahman as the nature of sound," and so forth—that is incorrect. For, how might its existence be perceived? Is it through perception arising from the senses, through that which transcends the senses, or through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because you maintain that the Śabda-Brahman has a nature interwoven with a multitude of forms consisting of all objects, places, and times.

Furthermore, would the existence of such a [Brahman] be known through a perception arising from the ear, or through a direct perception produced by another sense organ? It cannot be known through a perception arising from the ear; for since that [perception] operates only within the domain of the mere nature of sound, it is incapable of apprehending that Brahman as being endowed with a multitude of forms (*ākāra*) that lie outside its domain.

Whatever is not the object of a cognition is incapable of apprehending anything as being endowed with that [object], just as visual cognition is incapable [of apprehending] taste; and this multitude of forms is not the object of auditory cognition.

If that [Sound-Brahman] were apprehended as being associated with that [object] even though it is not within its range, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because it would follow that everything could be apprehended as being associated with everything.

By this, the apprehension of it through perception produced by other sense organs is also refuted; for, since it is not within the range of words, those [other senses] are likewise incapable of apprehending it.
Therefore, apart from the specific objects such as form and so forth, no other Sound-Brahman is perceived through sensory perception.
That [permanent entity] is not established through perception, because it does not appear;
nor is there an inferential mark consisting of an effect there, since production from a permanent [cause] is impossible.
There is no establishment of Brahman through any sensory cognition whatsoever.
Because it is false, like a dream and so forth, its [nature] is entirely [known] by itself.
(Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 240)
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 11, uttarārdha;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pṛṣṭha 384;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 98.
Nor can this [non-dual reality] be established through supersensuous perception (*atīndriya-pratyakṣa*), because such perception is impossible in this context.

If it is argued that such perception is possible for yogis through that which is born of yoga (*yogaja*), we say no; for if yogis, yoga, and the perceptions arising therefrom were to exist, it would entail the loss of non-duality (*advaita*).

The claim that "this [Self] does not entail such a consequence because it is self-luminous by nature even in the state of being fit [for liberation]" is merely a wishful thought; for if the three—those states, the forms, and the luminosity—exist simultaneously, non-duality would cease to exist. Furthermore, regarding that state of fitness: is its form manifested prior to that state, or not? If it is manifested, then liberation—which is the manifestation of Brahman whose very nature is light—would be achieved effortlessly for everyone at all times, and this would follow as a logical consequence even during the state of unfitness.

Now, if it does not manifest, then does it exist or not? If it does not exist, how can it be eternal, given its occasional nature? That which is occasional is not eternal, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is not; and since the nature of light (*jyotis-svarūpa*) is Brahman, if that were non-eternal, it would follow that the *Śabda-Brahman* is also non-eternal, because the latter is composed of the former. Consequently, the establishment of duality (*dvaita*) would follow with unimpeded force, for upon the destruction of non-duality (*advaita*), the establishment of duality is inevitable.

Now, if it does exist, why is it not manifest? Is it because of the absence of a grasper (*grāhaka*), or because it is overwhelmed by ignorance (*avidyā*)? Regarding these, the first position is untenable, because Brahman itself is its grasper, and since that [Brahman] is eternal, it exists at all times. If this is so, it must be stated what its nature was prior to the state of non-yoga (*ayogitva*). If it is always of the nature of light (*jyotis*), then there can never be a state of non-yoga, because Brahman is eternally of the nature of the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*);
consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that everyone would attain liberation effortlessly.
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 74;
*Sanmatitarkaṭīkā*, p. 385;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 99.
The second position is also not tenable, because ignorance (*avidyā*), when subjected to analysis, is found to be untenable.

For is it distinct from Brahman or non-distinct? If it were distinct, would it be a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)? It cannot first be a non-entity, because it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), just like Brahman; if it possesses such efficiency, then to call it a "non-entity" while giving it another name would be nothing more than a change in terminology.

Now, if even its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is not admitted, how can it attain the status of a real entity (*vastutva*)? How, then, could such statements as "it has become as if defiled by ignorance" be consistent? Furthermore, in the case of space, cataract (*timira*)—which is the cause of false appearances—is well known to be a real thing; since ignorance, being unreal, cannot logically be the cause of diverse appearances, there is no possibility of similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration. Consequently, even the statement "just as space is pure," and so forth, is difficult to establish.

Nor is it logical that Brahman, which is incapable of receiving or losing any excellence (*atiśaya*), should appear as such [i.e., as manifold] by virtue of that [ignorance], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does a real entity (*vastu*) undergo a change of state due to an unreal thing (*avastu*), for the same reason of over-extension.

If, on the other hand, it is a real entity [that causes this appearance], that is not so; for it would entail the destruction of your own accepted doctrine, and because it would result in the non-existence of non-duality (*advaita*) through the establishment of two entities characterized as Brahman and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, if it [avidyā] were non-different from Brahman, then it would follow that Brahman itself is false, because it would be non-different from avidyā, which is of a false nature—just like the very nature of avidyā itself. Thus, for one who desires gain, there would be the destruction of the root; or else, the consequence would be the reality of avidyā, because it is non-different from Brahman, whose nature is real—just like the very nature of Brahman itself. Therefore, how could this [avidyā] be the cause of false cognition? That which is real cannot be the cause of false cognition, as is the case with Brahman; and avidyā is real by virtue of being non-different from Brahman.

Or, let it be granted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is by its very nature charming only so long as it is not investigated; nevertheless, there can be no suppression of this [Self]—which possesses such a nature—by that [ignorance]. For suppression is observed to occur only when the weak is overcome by the strong, as the host of stars is eclipsed by the sun. But ignorance lacks strength because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like the horn of a horse.
Therefore, precisely because of its non-existence, the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), whose nature is the light of the Self, does not manifest during the state of unfitness.

Furthermore, if that form of it does not exist [in the present], how could it have existence in its potential state (*yogyavasthā*), such that it might be perceived through supersensuous perception (*atīndriyapratyakṣa*)?

For would that [potentiality] be different from or non-different from the *Śabdabrahman*? If it were different, would it be a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)? (Ratnākaraśānti, *Śāstravārttāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*, fol.

Furthermore, since there actually exists in space a real optical defect (*nimira*) which serves as the cause for false appearances, there is no similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
13, l. 1; Syādvādaratnākara p. 99).

Now, even if it is admitted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is distinct [from Brahman], since Brahman is eternal and incapable of having any excellence added to it, it is not logical to say that this [ignorance] does nothing to it; for [it is argued] that it appears as such through the power of ignorance (*tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p.
74; *sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 385).
In this regard, the form [of the argument] is as follows:

by this, even the realization of that [Śabdabrahman] through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is rejected; for this [Brahman], whose nature is the light of the Self (*ātmajyotis*), is not within the range of awareness even in a dream. Or, if it were within the range of such awareness, then liberation would be achieved effortlessly for all living beings; for what you consider liberation is precisely that self-awareness of the Śabdabrahman of such a kind.

Furthermore, neither the word "pot" nor its object possesses a self-cognized nature, such that their concomitance could be established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); for this [concomitance] is well-known to every living being precisely because they lack a self-cognized nature.

One might argue: "That [concomitance] is established by the very perception of self-awareness, because it has the nature of the essence of cognition; for instance, light itself is the essence of sound and the nature of consciousness. This, however, contradicts self-awareness... (*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 73; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 11, upper section).
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p.

384: Furthermore, when there is a relationship between a word and its object, the fact that the object is associated with the word would have to be cognized through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether such a relationship exists or not. It cannot be so when it does not exist, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it follows from the contradiction of an inference: "That which is unrelated to something is not associated with it, just as the Vindhya mountain is not associated with the Sahya mountain; and the word is unrelated to the object. Thus, there would be the consequence of contradicting this inference.

Now, even if a relation exists, what indeed is this relation between the two—is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*), identity (*tādātmya*), the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*), or the relation of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*)? It cannot be conjunction first of all, because they occupy different locations; for there is no conjunction between two things that occupy different locations, as in the case of Mount Malaya and the Himalayas, and words and their objects likewise occupy different locations.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished; for sound appears in the region of the ear, while the object appears in the region in front [of the observer]. Furthermore, if a relation between these two were admitted, it would follow that they are established as distinct substances; how then could the establishment of their non-duality (advaita) occur? Or, even if one were to admit a relation for the sake of [explaining] their connection, the admission of their identity (tādātmya) is also untenable, because they are perceived by different sense organs. Whatever two things are perceived by different sense organs do not possess identity, just like color and taste; and sound and object are indeed perceived by different sense organs.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished; for a jar or the like, which is devoid of the form of sound, appears in visual cognition, whereas sound, which is devoid of that [visual form], appears in auditory cognition.
Even if one were to admit the identity (*tādātmya*) of these two despite their being thus distinct, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, if objects were identical in nature with sound, then even for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), there would be no doubt regarding the object upon the perception of the sound, because—just as in the case of the sound—the object would also have been apprehended. Otherwise, their identity would be untenable.

Furthermore, from hearing words such as "razor," "fire," or "poisonous stone," there would follow the consequence of the ear being cut, burned, or struck; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with its identity [with those objects].

For whatever does not accomplish the purpose to be achieved by something else does not experience identity with it, just as taste does not [experience identity] with color; and sound does not accomplish the purpose to be achieved by the object, such as burning and so forth.

Likewise, there is no identity between a word and its object because they possess different locations, times, and forms. Whatever possesses such [differences] does not have identity therein, as in the case of a jar and a cloth; and the word and its object are of such a nature.
Nor is their difference of location unestablished, since this has been proven previously;
nor is their difference of time unestablished, because objects such as jars are perceived to exist even prior to their respective words.
Nor is there a difference in form, because that [identity] is well-known to all people in that regard.

Now, one might ask: "If identity with that [object] is impossible, how can there be cognition of the object from this [word]? This too is incorrect; for even in its absence, this [cognition] is established through the power of convention (*saṅketa*).

Indeed, the capacity of words—endowed with innate fitness—to bring about the cognition of objects is derived from the tradition of elders, just as the capacity of wood and other materials to accomplish cooking is [derived].

Therefore, identity is not tenable in that case, nor is there identity with the object because the word is perceived as a qualifier of the object; for word and object are perceived in different locations (Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.

Furthermore, if there were identity between word and object, then upon the utterance of words such as "razor," "fire," or "sweetmeat," there would follow the undesirable consequence of the mouth being cut, burned, or filled [respectively] (Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.
386; Śāstravārtā-samuccaya-ṭīkā, p. 237a).
As the venerable Bhadrabāhusvāmin said: "The designation (abhidhāna) may be either different from or identical to that which is designated (abhiheya).

For instance, when pronouncing the words 'razor,' 'fire,' and 'molasses,' there is neither cutting nor burning for the speaker or the listener, nor is there filling; therefore, [the word] is indeed distinct [from its referent]."
[From] the *Mañjarī* on the *Kiraṇāvalī*, verse 14:

Nor is there the state of being a qualifier; for it is impossible for things that are not connected by another relation—such as the Sahya and Vindhya mountains—to stand in that [qualifier-qualified] relationship.

The relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*), however, establishes only the difference between word and meaning, for without that [difference], such a relationship between the two would be impossible. Thus, since no relationship whatsoever—consistent with non-duality (*advaita*)—can be found upon investigation between word and meaning, it is not logical for the meaning to be "conjoined" (*anvita*) by the word. Furthermore, the state of being conjoined with the word is postulated in cognition based on perception; if that [perception] exists elsewhere as well, then that too should be postulated, as there is no distinction. And thus, the statement that "there is no cognition in the world [that is not conjoined with words]" and so forth is incorrect.

Furthermore, it was established in the section on the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-siddhi*) that even in the case of sensory perception (*locanādy-adhyakṣa*), there is the capacity to illuminate its own object despite the absence of contact with words. Enough of this digression.

As for what was also stated—that "all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*)" and so forth—that too is incorrect; for we experience that only verbal activity is permeated by [conceptualization], whereas that which arises from the eyes and other senses is not.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated [on page 140, line 8]—"in the state of deep sleep," and so forth—that too is mere words; for in non-duality (advaita), the very states of "deep sleep" and "awakening" are impossible, since their occurrence would contradict non-duality.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of ignorance (avidyā) in that regard, this is mere faith; for the fact that ignorance is the cause of the appearance of duality has already been answered previously.

As for what was also stated—namely, "those things which are permeated by the form of X," and so forth—that too is without substance; for the state of being permeated by the form of a word (*śabdākārānusyūtatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

This is because a cognizer perceiving blue and so forth through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) perceives them precisely as unconnected with the form of a word; furthermore, its [the word-form’s] non-establishment follows from its being merely imagined (*kalpitatva*).

For even in the absence of an object, those [cognitions] are imagined by you to possess a form associated with the aspect of sound (*śabdākāra*), as they are associated with it; yet how could the ultimate Brahman be established from such a reason? Furthermore, the example is devoid of both the probandum and the probans, because even in the case of jars and other things, being "consisting of one alone" or "associated with one" is unestablished.
Indeed, there is no universal conformity to a single nature among entities, since all objects consist of both similar and dissimilar transformations (*pariṇāma*).

Regarding what was stated— namely, "the object is not distinct from the word," and so forth— in that case, the thesis is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), because the object is perceived through direct perception as being distinct from the word by way of differences in location and so on; furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the object is perceived even when the word is not perceived by means of visual cognition (*locanādijñāna*).

Otherwise, how could a deaf person have the cognition of objects such as color through perception arising from the eye and other senses? Therefore, the existence of Brahman as having the nature of sound is not established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Or, let it be granted for the sake of argument; even so, because the world is a transformation (pariṇāma) of sound, it would follow that the world consists of sound, just as a jar consists of clay because it is a transformation of clay. Or [it might be argued] that it arises from sound, according to the rule that the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied in the sense of "origin" as in the expression "the vital breaths consist of food" (*annamayāḥ prāṇāḥ*)? Of these, the first position is untenable, because transformation itself is untenable in this context.

For Brahman, whose nature is sound (*śabdātmaka*), in assuming the form of blue and so forth, must it do so by abandoning its inherent nature as sound, or without abandoning it? In the first case, there is a contradiction with its being without beginning or end (*anādinidhana*), because its prior nature would have been destroyed.

In the second case, however, at the time of the cognition of blue and so forth, even a deaf person would necessarily experience the cognition of sound, since blue and the rest are non-different from it.

Whatever is non-different from something else is perceived when that thing is perceived, just as the nature of that very blue object and so forth is perceived during the state of perceiving the blue object; and since sound is non-different from the blue object and so forth, if it were not perceived, it would follow that the blue object and so forth would also not be perceived, because there is no distinction in their identity (*tādātmya*).

Otherwise, due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), it would entail its difference from that [blue object]; for it is not logical for a single partless entity to be simultaneously grasped and not grasped by a single cognizer, because of the contradiction.

Furthermore, even if there were the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), it would follow that there is no distinction between the Himālaya and the Vindhya mountains and so forth.

Moreover, as the essence of sound undergoes transformation, does it attain distinction for each individual object, or not? In the first alternative, it follows that the *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman) must be manifold, because its nature would consist of various distinct objects, just like the nature of those objects themselves.

In the second alternative, however, it follows that for all things such as blue and so forth, there would be no distinction of place, time, nature, function, or state, nor would there be any distinction in their manifestation; this is because they are non-different from the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) due to its being a single nature, and thus like its own essence. In this regard, the "consisting of sound" (*śabdamayatva*) of the world is not tenable, whether one intends to prove it here sometimes as "being of the nature of a transformation of sound" (as in the case of the suffix *mayaṅ* in the phrase "the vital breaths consist of food," *annamayāḥ prāṇāḥ*), or as "arising from sound."
In this regard, the first position is not tenable, because transformation itself is untenable.

To explain: when Brahman, whose essence is sound, assumes the form of blue and so forth, does it do so by abandoning its own inherent nature as sound at some point, or without abandoning it? (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 68; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 12, uttara).

Even those who maintain that "it is precisely this [cognition] which, following upon [the object]," must be asked: does this nature of the word abandon its own form and attain the state of being blue and so forth?
Or if it is not so; if the first position is adopted, then there would be a loss of its imperishability due to the destruction of its prior self-nature.

Furthermore, in that case, according to the immediately preceding position, there would also be a clear perception of the nature of sound itself within the cognition of blue and other such objects, even though it is not heard.
By which all that consists of sound is established in its primary sense,
because there is no transformation [of it] apart from the nature of sound.
And since the non-figurative unity of blue and other [objects] is thus established,
how could there not be the cognition of this [object] at the very moment of its own cognition?
For if this [consciousness] were not perceived, there would be no perception even of blue and so forth;
because they are of one essence, if they possessed distinct attributes, an absolute difference [between them] would follow.
For the association with contradictory properties is indeed the defining characteristic of difference among many things;
otherwise, even an imagined [difference] would not constitute a distinction between individual manifestations.

For it is not logical for a single entity to be simultaneously perceived and unperceived with respect to a single cognizer, as that would entail the loss of its oneness (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p.
and if the nature of the word is held to be one yet distinct in each individual object.
If it were a single part common to all, then consciousness would be of a single form;
however, if there were a difference in this [consciousness] for each individual, it would follow that Brahman is manifold.
Because it consists of the nature of many distinct entities, like the difference between individual manifestations; Tattvasaṃgraha 137.
For does that nature of sound, undergoing transformation, undergo differentiation according to each object, or not? (Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā p. 70; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
12; Sanmati-ṭīkā p. 382).

Nor [can it arise] from sound, because that [sound], being eternal, is unchanging; and since it is impossible for that which is unchanging to produce effects sequentially, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all effects must be produced simultaneously.

For effects are delayed only due to a deficiency in their causes, and not otherwise; if that [cause] is complete, what else could they require such that they would not arise simultaneously? Thus, since the evidence for the existence of the *śabdabrahman* and its status as the cause of the construction of the world’s manifold diversity remains unestablished, it is not reasonable to reject an object that is supported by an uncontradicted cognition merely on the basis of accepting that [theory]. Nor is it reasonable to do so on the basis of accepting the *paramabrahman*, for that too is no different, as the [required] proof remains unestablished. Even so, the world is composed of *śabdabrahman* in the form of its effects.
Nevertheless, because it is changeless, no sequential emergence can arise from it.

Even so, since sound is eternal and thus unchanging, the emergence of effects in succession would not be possible; rather, because the cause possesses its full capacity without obstruction, all effects would have to be produced simultaneously.

For effects are delayed due to the deficiency of their causes; if that [cause] is not deficient, what else would they require such that they do not arise simultaneously? (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 71; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
12; Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, p. 382)

The refutation of the theory of Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman) through various methods may be observed in the following texts: Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Pratyakṣasūtra, verse 176; and Nyāyamañjarī, page 531. (Ratnākaraśānti’s *Ratnāvalī*, page 101).

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vedāntins, who are proponents of the Supreme Brahman:

"Indeed, all this is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad), "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad), "They see His grove, yet no one sees Him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad)—from such Vedic statements, the existence of the Supreme Brahman is established; thus, its status as the cause for the construction of the manifold world through the transformation of the sentient and the insentient is logically justified.

For the transformation of this [Brahman], whose essence is action, is conscious; because, through non-contradiction, the concomitance of consciousness is established for all [transformations] therein. As for that which is unconscious, consisting of the great elements such as earth and so forth—it need not be asked how this manifold transformation occurs given the oneness of Brahman; for we observe a diverse transformation into bracelets, curd, and so forth, even though gold, milk, and the like are unitary, since there is the recognition: "This very gold has transformed into the form of a bracelet," and "This very milk has become curd."

It is also incorrect to ask: "If there were identity (*tādātmya*) between milk and curd, why would they not appear simultaneously, as in the case of a bracelet and gold, or like a single object possessing forms such as blue and yellow? This is because only an object whose spatial diversity is manifest is capable of simultaneous appearance; however, that which possesses temporal diversity is constrained by its own inherent sequence, and thus cannot have a simultaneous appearance.
As it is said in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (3.14.1): "All this is indeed Brahman, born from it, dissolved in it, and breathing in it; one should meditate with a peaceful mind."
For indeed, all this is Brahman; indeed, all this is truly Brahman.
It should be perceived by the mind alone through loving-kindness; here there is no diversity whatsoever.
"O Death, he goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19)
This is to be attained by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here.
He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death.
From the Kaṭhopaniṣad (4.11):

"Directly [the scripture teaches] 'One only, without a second; there is not anything here as manifold' and 'O Death, he goes from death to death'"; because of these and many other such statements which negate the world-appearance (*prapañca*) as distinct from Brahman, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the world has consciousness alone as its material cause (*upādāna*), just as a snake superimposed upon a rope has the rope as its material cause.
Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-Bhāṣya, Adhyāya 1, Pāda 1, Sūtra 5.
They see his garden, but no one sees him. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14)

99; *Prameyaratnamālā*, p. 75:
"If it is argued that [the soul is not eternal] because we observe its exhaustion, we say no; for it is like milk."
Brahma Sūtra 2.1.24

Therefore, because even the one Brahman possesses a variety of powers, its diverse transformation is logically possible, just as in the case of milk and other substances (Brahmasūtra Śāṅkara Bhāṣya). Now, [an objection is raised]: how can there be sequence for that which is one? And how for that which is many? For there is no sequence other than pots, cloths, and so forth; it must be either their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or a property (*dharma*). If it were their essential nature, would it belong to each one individually or to the many collectively? If it belonged to each one individually, then sequence would be perceived even in the cognition of a single pot.
If [you argue that the sequence belongs] to many [cognitions], then even for multiple objects appearing simultaneously, there would have to be a sequential perception.

Alternatively, if [the sequence] is a property (*dharma*); does that depend on other causes, or is it dependent upon the conceptual construction of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*)? Of these, the first position is untenable, because in the production of that [sequence], no cause other than cognition itself is perceived.

However, if it is dependent upon the conceptual construction of the cognizer, then even in the case of unity, this [sequence] does not present any contradiction, since the conventional designations such as "these appeared sequentially" or "these appeared simultaneously" are established solely in accordance with that conceptual construction.

If it is objected that the manifoldness of space and time contradicts the oneness of Brahman, or that its oneness is contradicted by such manifoldness, we say no. For even in the case of variegated cloth and the like, oneness is perceived despite the diversity of space and time; thus, even a difference in appearance does not entail a contradiction for a single entity. This is evident from the fact that even a tree, whose oneness is certain, is perceived as the object of different appearances depending on whether it is viewed by a person standing far away or nearby.

Even a difference in capacity does not contradict unity, because even in the case of the single ocean, there is the determination of a difference in capacity when it performs various effects such as waves, ripples, bubbles, and foam—[as stated in] the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (v. 306). [The commentary notes:
"the diversity of place" (*deśacitratā*) [is mentioned in the verse], while "time" (*kāla*) is in the *Bhāṣya*.

For instance, although the foam, waves, ripples, bubbles, and so forth—which are modifications of the ocean—are non-different from the ocean consisting of water, a worldly transaction characterized by their mutual distinction and mutual conjunction is nevertheless observed;

yet, even though they do not attain the state of being mutually identical, they do not become something other than the ocean itself. In the same way here as well, there is no attainment of the state of mutual identity between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
And there will be no otherness from Brahman, the Supreme (Brahmasūtra Śāṅkara Bhāṣya 2.1.13).

Furthermore, if He were a single unity, it would be untenable for Him to carry out a manifold creation—the production of superior and inferior beings, and the infliction of unsurpassed sufferings such as those in hell caused by cruelty; for He acts as a creator only in dependence [on other factors].

Indeed, He brings forth a diverse creation aided by the merit and demerit performed by the *karmātmans* (individual souls), for these *karmātmans* are well known to exist in every living being as the performers of enjoined and prohibited actions.

Although they are transformations (*vivarta*) of Brahman, which is of a single form, nevertheless, through ignorance (*avidyā*), they are made to appear as if distinct; they are determined to be the agents of actions and the enjoyers of their fruits.

Therefore, for this [Brahman], who—having perceived them as endowed with merit and demerit through omniscient knowledge—initiates creation in the manner described, it is not appropriate to level the charge of cruelty or other such faults.
Or rather, by its very nature, like a spider with respect to its threads, Brahman is the cause of the world's diversity, independent of any other cause.
"Neither partiality nor cruelty [can be attributed to Brahman], because it has regard for [the merit and demerit of souls]; for thus Scripture shows.
(Brahma-sūtra 2.1.34)

Because [the Lord] is dependent. For if the Lord were independent and alone to fashion this unequal creation, these two defects—partiality and cruelty—would indeed follow; however, there is no such thing as being a creator while being independent. Indeed, the Lord fashions the unequal creation by being dependent.
If it is asked, "On what does he depend? we reply that he depends on merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

Therefore, since the creation is uneven due to its dependence upon the merit and demerit of the living beings being created, this is not the fault of God; rather, God is to be regarded as being like the rain-cloud. In this way, God is the common cause for gods, humans, and others; however, regarding the inequality among gods, humans, and so forth, the specific and uncommon causes are the very karmas residing in those respective individual souls. Thus the Śruti shows: "For it is He indeed who makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds, and it is He indeed who makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8).
"Indeed, one becomes virtuous through virtuous action and evil through evil action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).
And so it is said.

Smṛti as well demonstrates that the Lord’s role as bestower of grace and his role as restrainer depend precisely upon the specific karma of living beings, as in such passages as: "In whatever way people approach me, in that very same way do I reward them" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.11). If the difference between objects is not produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) but is rather real, then a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that must be stated—would that be perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be perception, because its operation is untenable with respect to a difference consisting of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For this difference is a mutual exclusion, such as "this is not that" or "this is different from that," and that is not an object of perception, since perception has affirmation (*vidhi*) as its object. As the wise have stated: "Perception is an affirmer, not a negator. Furthermore, regarding difference... [the text continues].
"Therefore, scripture is not sublated by that perception regarding [the doctrine of] non-duality," thus [ends] the latter half-verse; see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p.
17, *Nyāyaviniścayaṭīkā* p. 186a.
It contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) [according to] *Syādvādamañjarī* p. 100, *Prameyaratnamālā* p. 74, and *Nyāyamañjarī* p. 526.
As for what some say: they declare [it] to be the creator (*vidhātṛ*). (Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.
273; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 191;
Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya, p. 99).

Furthermore, would the difference between objects be apprehended successively or simultaneously? It cannot be simultaneous, because that [apprehension of difference] depends upon the apprehension of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Nor can difference—which depends on the apprehension of the counter-correlative—be apprehended through the mere apprehension of the object's own nature (*svarūpa*) when the counter-correlative is not apprehended, for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the simultaneous apprehension of the locus (*āśraya*) and the counter-correlative is impossible; because the cognition of the counter-correlative must be preceded by the cognition of the object's own nature which is the locus of the difference, and without that cognition, the cognition "this is different from that" cannot logically arise.

Nor can it be established successively, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): for the cognition of a jar occurs through the exclusion of cloth and so forth, while the cognition of cloth and so forth occurs through the exclusion of the jar.
Thus, difference is not apprehended by perception;
nor is it apprehended by inference, since inference is preceded by perception.

For inference proceeds preceded by the apprehension of a relation (*sambandha*); and it is not logical for the apprehension of a relation to arise from perception regarding that which is not its object.
Furthermore, there is no mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with difference.

Nor is it logical to infer the difference of the self (*ātman*) and so forth on the grounds that the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so on would otherwise be inexplicable; for that [cognition] is of a false nature. Therefore, even difference would be established as merely non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*) for the self and so forth, and not as real (*vāstava*).

Furthermore, is this difference distinct from the entities, non-distinct, both, or neither? If the first position is held, does that [difference] itself differ by its own nature or by another difference? If it differs by its own nature, what fault have the objects committed such that their own inherent difference is not accepted? If it differs by another difference, then there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that [second difference] would also necessarily have a further difference to distinguish it from the objects.
If, on the other hand, it is non-distinct, then there would be either only the object or only the difference.

Nor is it of both natures, because the faults attributed to both positions would follow, and because difference and non-difference, being characterized by mutual exclusion, cannot coexist in one place at one time.
Nor is it of neither nature, because when one of two alternatives—affirmation or negation—is excluded, the other must necessarily be affirmed.

Furthermore, is the difference of all objects one and the same, or is it distinct for each object? If it were one and the same, then because of its non-difference, there would likewise be no difference among those objects.

Now, if difference is distinct for each object, is it intrinsic or through another difference? In either case, the two faults previously explained must be seen. Therefore, abandoning the insistence on difference, one should realize the ultimate reality characterized as the non-dual Supreme Brahman.
This is the refutation of the non-duality of Brahman.
To this, the following response is given:

as for what was stated—that [the soul undergoes transformation] through the transformation of the conscious and the unconscious, and so forth—that is incorrect; for in this case, the very application of the term "transformation" (pariṇāma) is impossible, since transformation consists in the relinquishing of preceding attributes and the assuming of other attributes.

If Brahman, having first abandoned its nature as consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), were to assume the nature of ether and so forth, then its very status as Brahman would have been abandoned by it; for Brahman is said to consist of consciousness and bliss (*cid-ānanda-maya*).
Alternatively, if it transforms into the form of ether and so forth without abandoning its own essential nature, that is not possible, because such a transformation is nowhere observed.

For in that case, he would have produced an effect that is indeed a distinct entity; and thus, another material cause (upādāna) would be established, because [the effect] cannot be accounted for apart from that [other cause]. Consequently, there would be a loss of non-duality (advaita), and there would be a contradiction with one's own statement that "Brahman is the material cause of the world" (p. 147, l. 6). [End of previous section—Bhāṣya, Ā.]

The transformation (*pariṇāma*) of a substance that persists through all states (*sarvadharmāvasthita*) consists in the cessation of a previous property (*dharma*) and the arising of another property (*dharmāntarotpatti*). (Nyāyabhāṣya 3.2.14)
Yoga Sūtra with the Vyāsabhāṣya, Chapter 2, Section 15.
Having avoided [the other options], "Consciousness, Bliss, Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3). ā॰, ba॰, ja॰.

Furthermore, it is observed that the transformation of things such as milk or gold—which are subject to change—occurs only when they depend upon auxiliary factors such as the passage of time or the activity of a goldsmith; yet, since Brahman lacks any such auxiliaries, how could there be any activity toward it, or the accomplishment of its transformation? If such auxiliaries were to exist, the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) would be lost.

Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because that [Self] is distinct from other transformable entities, and that this very fact constitutes its greatness—namely, that it undergoes such a transformation even without depending on anything else—that is not correct. For the postulation of an unperceived object is only valid when it follows from what is already perceived.

On what basis can one postulate that something possesses a nature of transformation that has never been observed in anything at any time? If it is argued that this is because no other material cause (*upādāna*) is possible, we say no; for it is impossible to deny the possibility of such a cause, since milk and the like are perceived to be the material causes of curd and so forth.

Furthermore, even if there is no other distinct material cause (*upādāna*), how could that form of Brahman which is logically untenable be possible? Moreover, if it were to engage in transformation by its very nature, there would be the undesirable consequence of it never ceasing; and its transformation would have to be of a single, constant form.
Furthermore, all purposeful activity of intelligent beings is pervaded by having a specific purpose.

Furthermore, does Brahman have some purpose or no purpose at all in creating the manifold universe? If there is none, then he would not be acting with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*); for one who acts with foresight never engages in activity without aiming at a purpose, except in the case of an insentient being.
Indeed, activity is of two kinds: that of the insentient and that of the other (the sentient).

In that regard, the activity of an insentient entity is always dependent on another; for an insentient thing never engages in any activity unless it is impelled by a conscious being with a specific purpose in mind. Furthermore, the insentience of Brahman cannot be admitted, as this would entail the necessity of postulating another impeller, which would result in the loss of non-duality (*advaita*).

If it is argued that even for a conscious being, activity is observed during states such as sleep even without that [consciousness], this too is an unexamined statement; for that activity is conditioned by the momentum of previous practice and its own inherent purpose. Otherwise, there would be activity even toward objects not previously practiced.
Furthermore, if Brahman possessed a purpose, it would follow that it has unfulfilled desires, and thus its state of having accomplished all aims (*kṛtārthatā*) would not exist;
for a "purpose" is defined as something desired to be achieved, and for one who has in every way accomplished their aim, the absence of anything to be achieved contradicts that definition.

Since the activity of one who acts with foresight is pervaded by having a purpose, it must be stated for what purpose this Person performs such an operation as the creation of the world; [for] the activity of an insentient thing [is not possible]. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 76) Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, is Brahman possessed of parts (*sāvayava*) or devoid of parts (*niravayava*)? It cannot first be possessed of parts, because its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*); for it is impossible for consciousness to have parts, and if such parts were possible, it would follow that it is an effect (*kāryatva*), which would result in the loss of its eternity.

Furthermore, if it were partless, then having undergone the transformation into space and so forth in its entirety right from the beginning, it would follow that it has lost its own nature and thus become inert; for one who desires gain would instead suffer the destruction of the very root, and there would be no transition into any further transformation. For it is not possible for this inert entity, having attained the form of space, to turn away from that state and proceed toward another transformation unless impelled by something else; nor is there any other impeller distinct from it, as that would entail the consequence of duality.

Therefore, this account of the sequence of creation is untenable—namely, that the first transformation of Brahman is characterized as space (*ākāśa*), from which arises air, then fire, then water, then earth; from which arise various kinds of herbs; and from which follows the creation of diverse bodies and objects through the divisions of the womb-born, egg-born, soil-born, and so forth.
Furthermore, if space and the rest were transformations of Brahman, there would be no distinction between them and the selves (*karmātman*) because their cause is non-different.

Indeed, it is not logical for something of a different genus to arise from a material cause (*upādāna*) whose nature is non-different, for that would entail the absurdity of fire arising from water or light.

Furthermore, the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer is untenable for these [elements]. It might be argued that the agents of action (*karmātmānaḥ*) are the enjoyers and the elements (*bhūtāni*) are the objects of enjoyment;

however, since they are non-different from Brahman, two contradictory natures cannot coexist. Or, if such a coexistence were possible, then due to the superimposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), the oneness of Brahman would be lost.

Therefore, it is said: "From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, man" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

As for what was also said—that even though gold, milk, and so forth are unitary, all this is possible here as well, just like the diverse transformations into bracelets, curd, and so on—that too is mere words. For such diverse transformation is only logical if that [gold or milk] possesses multiple natures and undergoes production and destruction in some respect; it is impossible for an object that is absolutely unitary in nature and devoid of the properties of production and destruction, as it would be like a donkey’s horn.
Furthermore, succession is a property of objects that is dependent on other factors and resides in many things.
And that [sequence] is twofold: spatial sequence and temporal sequence.

Among these, spatial sequence consists in the spatial proximity of things that arise simultaneously, as established in such cognitions as "these elders are seated in order. Temporal sequence, however, pertains to objects characterized by temporal proximity, as is understood through such cognitions as "the phonemes arise in succession" or "the stool, the chest, and so forth, arise in succession."

If it is asked: "Why is there not a sequential cognition of multiple objects appearing simultaneously? [The answer is: because of the absence of time as a limiting condition (*upādhi*). For whatever cognition is dependent upon something, that cognition does not occur in the absence of that thing; just as sequential cognition is dependent on space, and this [simultaneous] cognition is dependent on time. Furthermore, even in the case of a variegated cloth, distant and nearby trees, the ocean, and so forth, their absolute identity of nature (*ekasvabhāvatva*) is unproven. This is because they possess variegated forms, because they are the objects of clear and indistinct perceptions, and because a difference is established here through a distinction in capacity (*sāmarthya-bheda*), [occurring] in some respect (*kathañcit*).
On page 147, line 10:

Just as a substance such as a painted cloth, though possessing a single nature, appears in forms distinct from color and so forth due to the diversity of the causal complex of the eyes and other sense organs—and because it conforms to those [perceptions]—let there likewise be a difference in the nature of the object itself, since there is a difference in the appearances for persons situated at distant or near locations who have fixed their various observations upon that same single thing;
see *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 110.

Furthermore, whether Brahman possesses a variegated nature, whether it is the object of diverse appearances, and whether there is a diversity of capacities—would these occur when there is a difference between its states (*avasthā*), or when there is no difference? It cannot be in the case of non-difference, because those [qualities] would necessarily follow even for a single state.

If, on the other hand, there is difference, then in order to establish the mutual difference between those states, even "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*) and so forth must be admitted; thus, non-duality (*advaita*) is perfectly established, since that which is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*) cannot serve as a proof for negation.

Or let there be some kind of mutual distinction among those states; even so, are they distinct from the possessor of the states, non-distinct, both, or neither? If they are distinct, the designation "these are its states" would not be possible, because there is no mutual benefit; or, if there were such benefit, it would lead to an infinite regress.

In the case of non-difference, does the substratum exist as identical with its states, or do the states exist as identical with the substratum? In the first alternative, the unity of the substratum is untenable, because it would follow that it too possesses plurality; for it is not logical that what exists as identical with something distinct should be non-distinct from its own nature, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

In the second alternative, however, the states themselves would not be the states, for what exists as identical with its own nature cannot be distinct from it, since that would entail the distinction of the nature itself. Thus, both faults apply to both alternatives.

The position of being neither [affirmation nor negation] is, however, illogical; for since the affirmation of one of two properties—positive or negative—is necessarily concomitant with the negation of the other, it is impossible to negate both simultaneously in a single locus.

Furthermore, even for one who does not accept that the states (*avasthā*) of a thing possessing states (*avasthāvat*) are distinct entities (*padārthāntara*), how could there not be a difference in the possessor of states due to the difference in its states? Or, how could there not be non-difference among the states themselves, given the absence of their being distinct entities? (Āptaparīkṣā, p. 21)

As for what was also stated—that agency belongs to the "action-self" (karmātman) because it acts as an auxiliary to the actions performed—this too is untenable; for the arising of both the action-selves and the actions is entirely dependent upon that [consciousness], since nothing else is admitted apart from it.

In this regard, does [the Lord] first create the "karmic selves" (karmātman) and then yoke them with actions, or does He first produce the actions and then create the karmic selves? It cannot be the first case, because in the absence of performers, actions cannot be created; and without a connection to action, distinct performers cannot be postulated. Thus, due to mutual dependence, there would be no creation of anything at all.

The claim that "ignorance has produced a semblance of difference" and so forth is extremely difficult to maintain, because the positions of its being either distinct or non-distinct from that [reality] are untenable; furthermore, that untenability has been explained in detail in the section refuting the monism of sound (*śabdādvaita*). Enough of this digression.
(Karmānuṣṭhita, p. 148, l. 9)

Furthermore, ignorance (*avidyā*) has the nature of non-knowledge, whereas Brahman has the nature of knowledge; and no identity whatsoever is observed between knowledge and non-knowledge, which are like existence and non-existence.

Nor should it be asserted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is thus indefinable, because it is logically consistent for a real entity to be examined in terms of its difference or non-difference [from another]; nor is its status as a non-entity tenable, for if ignorance—which brings about the entire manifold of distinctions—were a non-entity, then Brahman itself would likewise be a non-entity.

Furthermore, is the manifestation of ignorance caused by the non-perception of the nature of Brahman, or is the non-perception of the nature of Brahman caused by the manifestation of ignorance? It cannot be the first position, because since Brahman is eternally manifest, the non-perception of its own nature is impossible.

Nor can it be the second, because while that [Brahman] is eternally manifest and shining—like the sun at midday—the manifestation of ignorance, which is as opposed to it as darkness is to light, is impossible.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because ignorance is beginningless, we say no; for even so, the coexistence of Brahman and ignorance is untenable, just as it is impossible for light and darkness to exist together.

Furthermore, if those whose nature is action (*karmātman*) are by their very essence ignorance (*avidyā*), how can this discrimination (*viveka*) consisting of inquiry arise? For that which is of the nature of ignorance is opposed to inquiry, which is of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*). From what, moreover, does it originate—from ignorance itself, or from something else? It cannot be from something else, because nothing other than ignorance is admitted to exist. If it is argued that ignorance itself is the means to such knowledge, that is not so; for there is a contradiction, as darkness is never perceived to be the means for the manifestation of light.

Furthermore, as for the other claim—that Brahman is, by its very nature, the cause of the world’s diversity, independent of any other cause, like a spider with respect to its threads—that too is mere words. For it is observed that in the production of threads, the spider depends on internal and external causes; thus, its independence in that regard is unproven. Consequently, how can it be possible to establish, on the basis of that example, that Brahman is by nature the cause of the world’s diversity while remaining independent? Indeed, that spider is perceived to produce long threads after having encountered an external collection of causes such as bamboo or walls, out of a desire to harm living beings, and by taking up an internal mass of matter in the form of saliva for the purpose of devouring those creatures.

Therefore, one who accepts that Brahman—the material cause (*upādāna*) which does not depend on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*)—is the source of the world's diversity, must simply be disregarded; for this involves both the abandonment of what is observed and the unwarranted postulation of the unobserved (p.
13), as well as the fact that saliva flows from his mouth even at the thought of devouring living beings (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 652).
Even in the case of the spider, its status as the cause of its threads is not admitted to be due to its own nature alone,
since it produces a web of saliva out of a craving for devouring living beings.

As for what was also stated—that regarding difference, either perception or inference would function as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so forth—in that case, difference is indeed cognized through perception itself. This is because in a cognition arising immediately after the operation of the senses, blue and other such objects appear as mutually unmingled; and the very appearance of mutual non-confusion is the appearance of difference.

Furthermore, difference is not the exclusion of one from another, but rather the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity itself; for that [nature] is produced from its own causal series with a character entirely distinct from the three worlds.

And that which is thus constituted—consisting of volition, the locus of the "I," and having the form of the subject—manifests internally; whereas blue and other objects, having the form of the object, manifest externally.
Indeed, apart from these two, no non-duality whatsoever manifests even in a dream for anyone.

If it is objected: "If difference is indeed the very nature of the object, then why is it not perceived at the first contact with the sense organ as 'this is different from that' when its nature is being apprehended? [The answer is: Because it depends upon the apprehension of another object, just like non-difference. For just as non-difference—characterized by existence (*sattāsāmānya*)—though apprehended at the first contact with the sense organ, does not manifest in its inclusive form as "existent, existent" when other objects are not apprehended; so too is the case with difference.

Or let difference be of the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); even so, its perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not contradicted, because objects appear in direct perception both by way of their own nature and by way of the nature of the non-existent. Indeed, it is not only the existence of objects by way of their own nature that appears in direct perception, and not their non-existence by way of another’s nature; for if that [non-existence] were not perceived, there would follow the consequence that the objects themselves would not be perceived either, since the reality of a thing consists in its being produced by the apprehension of its own nature and the exclusion (*apoha*) of others’ natures (p. 149, l. 1).
—Indeed, it proceeds [thus]: Bhāṣya, Śrā., Tadviśvakā—Ba., Ja.

For, without the negation of other forms, even the determination of its own nature is not accomplished; indeed, blue is apprehended as "blue" only when it is distinguished from yellow and so forth, and not otherwise.
And so he said: "That which is delimited by it excludes others"; thus, perception is capable of grasping even non-existence (abhāva), just as it grasps existence (bhāva) (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

529). As for what was further stated—"Is this [difference] grasped successively or simultaneously? and so forth—that too is refuted by this very [argument], because the simultaneous manifestation of difference is possible according to the logic already stated.

The objection that "if the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not apprehended, how can difference, which is dependent upon it, be perceived? is also unsound; for it is the *transactional usage* (*vyavahāra*) of difference alone that is dependent on another, not its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Indeed, that [nature] arises from its own causal complex independently of the apprehension of a counter-correlate. Otherwise, even in the case of non-difference, why would there not be a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*)—namely, that the establishment of a universal depends on difference, and the establishment of difference depends on that [universal]? Furthermore, in the case of fingers that are contracted or extended, a sequential difference consisting of prior and posterior non-existence (*prāk-pradhvaṃsābhāva*) clearly manifests in a successive manner.
6 – For even dependence [is not established], as stated in the Śrāmaṇya-phala-sūtra.

Furthermore, that which was said—that for all objects there is either one single difference or a difference distinct for each object—is also incorrect; because difference is characterized by the contradiction of unity, for wherever there is a contradiction of oneness, there the word "difference" is employed, as in such cases as "yellow is different from blue," and so forth.

The collection of dilemmas such as whether that [dharma] is different or non-different from the substratum (*dharmī*) is also rejected by resorting to the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekānta*); for indeed, neither absolute difference nor absolute identity between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) is possible, as will be explained later.

Furthermore, how could non-difference be established for one who speaks thus, since the investigation into whether they are different or non-different can be applied there as well? For instance: is this non-difference different from differences, or non-different? If it were non-different, then its nature as non-difference would be untenable, because it would follow that it is itself a difference, just like the nature of difference.

Now, [it may be argued that] it is distinct; that is not so, because non-difference is not perceived as distinct from the various differences. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of any disagreement [regarding difference]. For when a cloth is perceived as distinct from a jar, no one disagrees [with that perception]. (p.
150, l. 1, suśakya—MS)

Furthermore, would that [difference] be perceived from that [entity] by perception (*pratyakṣa*) or by inference (*anumāna*)? If by perception, is it by one that grasps the nature of difference itself, or by another? It cannot be by another, because such a thing is not experienced; for a perception that does not manifest the nature of difference—whether internal or external—is never experienced even in a dream, since perception is always experienced as manifesting the nature of differences such as blue, pleasure, and so forth.

Even by that [perception] which grasps the nature of difference, would non-difference be cognized simultaneously or sequentially? It cannot be simultaneous, because there is no cognition of both together; indeed, difference and non-difference, being entirely distinct, do not manifest simultaneously in any perception whatsoever, as will be demonstrated on the occasion of establishing the doctrine of manifoldness (anekānta). Nor can it be sequentially, because perception lasts for only a single moment, and thus sequential cognition of it is impossible. Therefore, the cognition of non-difference through perception is not tenable.

Nor [can it be established] through inference, because in the absence of perception, that [inference] is also untenable, since you yourselves admit that [inference] is preceded by that [perception]. Furthermore, non-difference (abheda) is dependent upon a second [entity]; if that [second entity] is not apprehended, how can this [non-difference] be apprehended? For there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Whatever property is dependent upon something else cannot be apprehended when that thing is not apprehended, just as "being a staff-bearer" cannot be apprehended when the staff is not apprehended; and the property characterized as non-difference is indeed dependent upon a second [entity].

And if one accepts the establishment of non-difference based on how things are perceived, then the establishment of difference must likewise be accepted in that same way. Thus, it is established through perception that there is a difference among selves, just as there is a difference among bodies and so forth, because otherwise the perception of distinct pleasures, pains, and so on would be inexplicable. Nor is this [perception] false, because its nature is non-doubtful and uncontradicted, just like the perception of the self.

Furthermore, if the non-difference of the self were accepted, then when one [self] is happy, the entire world would be happy; and when it is suffering, it would be suffering; when bound, it would be bound; when liberated, it would be liberated; when active, it would be active; and when withdrawn, it would be withdrawn. But this is not the case. Therefore, there is a real difference between selves;

otherwise, it would follow that the very same entity is happy and suffering, bound and liberated, active and inactive—which is not tenable, because mutually contradictory attributes cannot coexist in a single, partless, eternal reality.

Nor should it be argued that all this will be established because there is an imagined difference in the Self, just as there is an imagined difference in space; for while the nature of space is well-established by uncontradicted means of knowledge and its real locations are thus known, the conventional usage of "the space of a jar" or "the space of a cloth" is appropriate. However, since Brahman is not established by any means of knowledge whatsoever, an imagined difference cannot possibly exist in it either, just like a flower in the sky—[as stated in the *Grahādhikaraṇa*]: "Even if [it were] grasped... and "Likewise, if it were accepted... [Śaṅkara-bhāṣya].
Because of its being non-dual,
there would be for us no duality of action, no duality of fruit, and no duality of worlds;
there would be no duality of knowledge and ignorance, nor likewise any duality of bondage and liberation.
26. Āptamīmāṃsā—by Umāsvāti. Śrī.

Therefore, his very self conforms to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form created by ignorance; thus the Lord becomes [conditioned], just as space conforms to limiting adjuncts such as jars and water-pots—
Brahma-sūtra Śāṅkara-bhāṣya 2.3.43.

Furthermore, as for the scriptural authority (āgama) such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" which was cited as establishing that [non-duality], even that establishes only duality because its subject matter is dualistic. Indeed, the existence of the authoritative scripture cannot be maintained if any one among the following is absent: the denoted object, the denoter, the thing to be established, or the establisher.

Furthermore, if the self were one and the same in all bodies, it would follow that there must be recognition [of experiences] even when the body differs; for just as there is recognition within a single body despite the difference in its parts because the self is one, so too would it occur despite the difference between bodies.

Nor does the absence of mutual recollection follow from the difference between individual souls (*jīvas*)—which are themselves imagined—as it does in the case of imagined differences in spatial locations (*pradeśa*); for although there is no mutual recollection among distinct locations, such recollection does exist with respect to the single substratum (*pradeśin*) in which they reside. Likewise, although there is no mutual recollection among the different souls due to their difference, such recollection would occur with respect to the Self (*ātman*) that permeates them all.

Therefore, having abandoned the stubborn insistence on non-duality and other such views, one who has ascended to uncontradicted cognition must accept external objects as they are perceived; otherwise, the consequence would be their lack of epistemic validity.
Thus, the object established as consisting of substance and mode is the subject matter.
To the question "Of what is this the object?", he says: "Of the subject—the substantial and functional sense organ."

Now, what is the substantial sense-organ (*dravyendriya*)? To this he says: the substantial sense-organ consists of matter (*pudgala*). For matter possesses color, taste, smell, and touch; that [sense-organ] consists of that [matter], having as its nature a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) thereof, serving as the means for each respective [perception]. (Śrāvakaprajñapti)

Pudgalas possess touch, taste, smell, and color; this is the fifth category of reality.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika—that the sense organs are composed of earth and other elements which are of an entirely different genus—is refuted as follows:

"Now, it is not tenable that the sense organs are, without distinction, of the nature of *pudgala* (matter), because the manifestation of the sense organs such as the eye—which belong to an entirely different genus—is observed from earth and other elements which belong to entirely different genera.

And thus says the *Nyāyabhāṣya*: 'Because of the existence [of the sense organs] due to the existence of earth, water, fire, and air, there is the state of being the olfactory, gustatory, visual, and tactile sense organs.'"

He supports this very point through inference: the sense of smell is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), because it manifests only odor when color and other qualities are present. Whatever is of such a nature is observed to be composed of earth, as for example the palm of the hand that crushes a *nāgakarṇikā* flower; and the sense of smell manifests only odor when color and other qualities are present; therefore, it is composed of earth. Likewise, the sense of taste is composed of water (*āpya*), because it manifests only taste when color and other qualities are present, like saliva.
The eye is composed of fire (*taijasa*), because when color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities are present, it manifests color-form alone, just like a lamp.

The sense of touch (*sparśana*) is composed of air (*vāyavya*), because when color-form and other qualities are present, it manifests touch alone, just like a portion of air that manifests the cold touch of water.

However, it is utterly untenable that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) has the person (*pudgala*) as its essence; for it is logically established that sound is perceived by a sense organ that possesses a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) belonging to the same genus as itself. To explain: sound is perceived by a sense organ possessing a specific quality of the same genus as itself, because (1) while possessing both generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*), it is perceptible by a single external sense organ, like color (*rūpa*) and so forth; or alternatively, (2) while being perceptible by a single external sense organ, it is not a specific quality of the self (*ātman*). The five elements, beginning with earth, possess the properties of being elemental substances (*bhūtatva*), being the material causes of the sense organs (*indriyaprakṛtitva*), and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) perceivable by a single external sense organ; see Praśastapāda-bhāṣya, p.
22. Likewise, the Nyāya-bhāṣya states: "From earth, water, fire, and air arise the sense organs of smell, taste, sight, and touch."
In the *Ratnāvalī*, page 344, it is stated:
"Because of its abundance and because it possesses fragrance, earth is the primary cause in the cognition of smell;
likewise, water, fire, and air [are the causes] in the cognitions of taste, color, and touch, respectively, due to their lack of distinction [in those qualities]."
Vaiśeṣikasūtra 8.2.5, 6.
The tongue, eye, and skin are the sense organs; [this is] the remainder. [Their] identity with the specific qualities of the primary elements follows from the perception of those qualities;
Nyāyasūtra 3.1.58.

For a rule regarding the manifestation of specific qualities of the elements—such as air and the rest—is observed: air is the manifestor of touch, water is the manifestor of taste, fire is the manifestor of form, and certain substances derived from earth are the manifestors of the smell of other substances. And there exists this rule for the sense organs regarding the perception of specific qualities of the elements. Therefore, because of the perception of specific qualities of the elements, we consider the sense organs to have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*), and not the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) as their material cause. (Nyāyabhāṣya)

Whatever specific quality of an object— such as odor and so forth— is the cause for distinguishing it from other elements, that quality is perceived by whichever sense organ corresponds to its kind; this is the rule [Nyāyavārttika 1.1.4].

[The earth is] an earth-element (pārthiva), because it invariably manifests odor among color, taste, smell, and touch, just like external earth; the meaning is that things such as chicken droppings, which manifest the scent of musk, are earth-elements—Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p.

[this is] the proof for its being an earth-element even though it is a substance, since it manifests scent alone among [the qualities] beginning with color, like ghee which manifests the scent of saffron. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 481; Praśastapādabhāṣyakandalī, p. 35).

—[Reply:

This is not tenable when unexamined; for since earth and the other elements belong to entirely distinct classes, they cannot be established as a single composite substance, and thus it is not established that the individual sense organs are composed of them.
Furthermore, the fact that they are not established as distinct substances will be demonstrated in the section on the determination of objects (*viṣayapariccheda*).

As for what was stated—that the olfactory organ is composed of earth (*pārthiva*)—that too is incorrect; for the reason [adduced] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the rays of the sun and the sprinkling of water.
Indeed, it is observed that the manifestation of fragrance occurs in oil-anointed [objects] through the rays of the sun, whereas in the case of the earth, it occurs through the sprinkling of water.

The claim that "the tongue is composed of water" (*āpya*) and so forth is also incorrect, because the reason [adduced] is inconclusive due to salt (*lavaṇa*); for even though salt is not composed of water, it is well known to be the manifestor of taste alone when color and other qualities are present.

Furthermore, the claim that "the eye is composed of fire" (*taijasa*) and so forth is untenable, because the reason is rendered inconclusive by the light of rubies (*māṇikya*) and the like; for that light, among color and the other qualities, manifests only color, yet it is not composed of fire.

The claim that "the sense of touch (*sparśana*) belongs to air" (*vāyavya*) and so forth is also incorrect; for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason [of being an expresser] due to camphor and the like. For camphor, while color and other qualities are present in water and other substances, is the manifestor of cold touch alone, yet it is not composed of air. Furthermore, since the sense of touch manifests the touches of earth, water, and fire, it follows as a consequence that it must be an effect of earth and the others—just as it is an effect of air because it manifests the touch of air, and just as the eye is an effect of fire because it manifests the color of fire, it would follow that it is an effect of earth and water because it manifests the colors inherent in earth and water.
Furthermore, just as the tongue is an effect of water because it manifests the taste of water, it would follow by the same logic that it is an effect of earth because it manifests the taste of earth.

Likewise, the argument that "sound belongs to that which possesses its own specific quality of a similar class" and so forth is merely an exposition of one's own domestic system; for the status of sound as a quality of space (*nabhas*) will be refuted later.
Therefore, the specific derivation of the sense organs from particular elements is not established, due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
