line 5–dyanupa—
Śrī: All of this exists word-for-word on page 62 of the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* and on page 345 of the *Syādvādaratnākara*.
[The refutation of the Sāṅkhya doctrine that the sense organs are derived from the *ahaṅkāra*:

By this, the Sāṅkhya-imagined derivation of the sense organs from the *ahaṅkāra* is also refuted; for there is no difference in the absence of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for that [doctrine] as well, and because it is contradicted by valid evidence.

For instance: the sense organs are not derived from the *ahaṃkāra*, because they are instruments while being insentient, like an axe or similar tools; or else, because they are sense organs, like the organs of action.
There is no deviation [in the inference] due to the mind (*manas*), since the substantial mind (*dravyamanaḥ*) is admitted not to be derived from the *ahaṃkāra*;
nor is there deviation due to the functional senses (*bhāvendriya*) or the non-senses (*anindriya*), because of the qualifying clause "while being insentient."
Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] regarding pleasure and so forth, because they lack the status of being instruments (*karaṇa*).

Likewise, the sense organs are not derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*), because they are the causes for the designation of specific cognitions, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, or because they illuminate specific objects, just like a lamp.

For just as color-form, taste, and so forth—which are the causes for the designation of specific cognitions such as "cognition of color" and "cognition of taste"—are not derived from the ego-principle, in the same way, the sense organs such as the eye are also [not derived from the ego-principle], because they are the causes for the designations "eye-cognition," "tongue-cognition," and so forth.
Likewise, the sense organs are not composed of ego (ahaṅkārika), because they serve as the substrata for benefit and injury caused by material things (paudgalika), just like a mirror and so forth.

For just as mirrors and the like are not composed of ego but are material, since they serve as the substrata for benefit and injury produced by material things such as ash or stones; similarly, the eyes and other senses, which serve as the substrata for benefit and injury produced by material things such as collyrium and the like, are also not composed of ego.
Furthermore, the mind (manas) is not composed of ego, because its objects are not fixed, just like the self (ātman).

Therefore, it should be understood that the material sense organs (*dravyendriya*) are composed of *pudgala* matter, as they are produced from *pudgala* atoms suitable for specific senses; thus, their nature as *pudgala* is established. Enough of this digression.
Egotism (*abhimāna*) is the *ahaṅkāra*; from it, the twofold creation proceeds:
the group of eleven consisting of the sense organs, and the pentad of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Sāṃkhyakārikā:
But if there were only one ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) as the material cause, then either all [the senses] would have a single object, or all [the objects] would be the objects of all [the senses].
However, from the restriction of their objects, the restriction of their material causes (*prakṛti*) is also inferred (Nyāyakalikā, p.

6). But if [the senses] were composed of the elements (*bhautika*), then because the elements differ and possess a predominance of specific qualities, they would have as their material cause sense-faculties that grasp restricted objects; thus, even when many objects such as color, taste, and so forth are present near a lamp or other light, it is only color that ought to be illuminated.

The same should be stated regarding the other sense-faculties as well. Thus, this restriction of the objects of the sense-faculties is caused by the restriction of their nature; therefore, the sense-faculties are composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*). (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 480).
This complete discussion is to be found on page 346 of the Āloka-ṭīkā on the Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā.

By this, indeed, that which the Sāṃkhyas assert—namely, that the sense organs are derived from the *ahaṅkāra* (ego)—is refuted. He states the reason for this refutation: the word "aikātmya" (identity) is used here in a double sense. According to the established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) of the Sāṃkhyas, the effect is of the same nature as its cause, and since the cause of the sense organs is the *ahaṅkāra*, there would be "aikātmya," meaning they share a single cause. Consequently, there would be "aikātmya" in the sense of identity among the olfactory organ and the others; thus, there would be no distinction between them, as stated in Nyāyasūtra 1.1.12.
Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 223:
"The five sense organs [are distinct] from the soul because the mind is not a sense organ, and because intellect and ego are forms of the soul and are the results thereof."
Tattvārthaślokavārttika 2.15

Regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika, who asserts that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a supersensuous power (*atīndriya-śakti*), [the author] now explains the "actual sense organ" (*bhāvendriya*): the actual sense organ consists of *labdhi* (attainment) and *upayoga* (application); *labdhi* is the capacity for grasping objects.

But surely, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*), how can the functional sense-organ (*bhāvendriya*), which consists of the acquisition (*labdhi*), be established? To explain: a cloth produced immediately after the final conjunction of threads, and the burning that occurs immediately after the contact of a finger with fire, do not depend on any additional cause; for, since these effects strictly follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of those [specific] factors alone, it is impossible for them to have any other cause.

Nor should it be argued that this restriction—that the quenching of thirst comes from water and not from fire, nor does the removal of cold come from fire but from water—is inexplicable without the existence of a supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*), and therefore such a power must be admitted for its sake to be established. For that restriction is explained solely by means of the power inherent in the essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) and the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-śakti*);
indeed, power is of two kinds, distinguished as the power of essential nature and the power of auxiliary factors.

In this context, the *svarūpa-śakti* (intrinsic power) consists of the nature of the threads and so forth, such as their being "thread-ness" (*tantutva*), while the *sahakāri-śakti* (auxiliary power) consists of the final auxiliary condition. For even though threads exist, they do not produce a cloth without the final conjunction of the threads.

Likewise, fire alone dispels cold because of its connection with the property of firehood (*analatva*), and not water, due to the absence of that [firehood]; and water alone removes thirst because of its connection with the property of waterhood (*jalatva*), and not fire, because those two, by virtue of residing in their respective specific universals, lack the capacity to produce each other's effects.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Fire and other such factors possess a capacity characterized solely by the proximity of their own auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), because they produce an effect when no obstruction is present. Whatever produces an effect when no obstruction is present possesses a capacity characterized solely by the proximity of its own auxiliary causes; for example, just as action (*karman*), once the prior conjunction has ceased through disjunction, possesses a power characterized solely by the proximity of its own auxiliary causes to produce a subsequent conjunction—and fire and the like are likewise—therefore, they too are so.

Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of fire producing effects such as a flash of light even when an obstructing magnet or the like is present, because the power characterized by the proximity of its own auxiliary causes exists; for in the production of that [effect], the absence of the obstructing magnet and so forth is also an auxiliary cause, just like the contact between the palm and fire.

Nor is it the case that non-existence, being a non-entity, lacks causality; for our authority is perception (*darśana*). And in the cognition "it does not exist," the absence of both the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is seen to function as a cause—just as the non-performance of obligatory rites is a cause for transgression, and the absence of conjunction is a cause for the action of falling. Furthermore, the sense organ is a positive entity (*bhāva*), according to the *Tattvārtha Sūtra* (2).
Attainment (*lambhana*) is acquisition (*labdhi*).
What, then, is this? It is a specific subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama-viśeṣa*) of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*).
Sarvārthasiddhi 2.18;
Tattvārthasāra, verse 44, page 111.
The specific degree of destruction-cum-subsidence (kṣayopaśama) which is the cause for the manifestation of the sense organs is attainment (labdhi).
— Rājavārttika 2.18.
And acquisition (*labdhi*) is precisely the incapacity for the cognition of one's own object;
*Tattvārthaśloka* 2.18.
Labdhi is the capacity for apprehending objects, consisting in the attainment of the subsidence and destruction of the veils [of knowledge]. (Ratnākaraṇḍa-śrāvakācāra, p.
344; Jaina-tarka-paribhāṣā, p. 114).
It is established [as follows]:
we do not, like the Mīmāṃsakas, accept a supersensible power (*śakti*); rather, it is either the essential nature of the causes or the completeness of their auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
(Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 103)
For it is not possible to postulate another supersensuous power [in a cause] that arises from its own nature and is augmented by auxiliary factors;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 41.
However, power (*śakti*) is precisely the proximity of its own nature as delimited by fitness (*yogyatā*) along with its auxiliary causes;
this very power is said to be twofold: the inherent (*avasthitā*) and the adventitious (*āgantukā*).
The inherent power is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as delimited by [the qualities] such as *sattva*.

However, the adventitious [property] consists in the form of conjunction with the staff, the wheel, and so forth (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 495). It is not that the category of power (*śakti*) does not exist in our system; what then is it? It is causality (*kāraṇatva*).

What is that? It is either the state of having a genus fixed for a previous time, or the state of possessing an absence of effect caused by a deficiency in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). Since the term "power" (*śakti*) is applied even to auxiliary factors due to their similarity in being contributory, [it is said]: "For action such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), once the prior conjunction has been terminated by disjunction and the subsequent conjunction is produced, does not possess any power over and above the power consisting in its own nature—which is characterized by the destruction of the prior conjunction—and the power consisting in the form of the auxiliary factor, which is characterized by that same destruction. (Nyāyakusumāñjali 1.13, p. 63; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 286).

When [the action] has been turned back—[referring to] the production of conjunction—furthermore, even when poison or fire is present, the non-perception of their effect due to the employment of a mantra is not caused by the obstruction of power, but rather has its cause in the introduction of another causal complex (sāmagrī). (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 42)

The non-arising of an effect in the presence of mantras and the like does not necessitate the postulation of an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*). Just as fire, whose capacity is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is the cause of burning, so too is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of obstructing mantras and the like a cause. If it is argued that there is no such thing as an effect produced by a non-entity (*abhāva*), because we observe that an entity is invariably dependent on a causal entity that is itself an entity—this is not so. For from the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises; otherwise, the performance of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) upon the non-performance of obligatory duties would be pointless, as it would be devoid of purpose. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 145)
To this it is replied: Whether it be an entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*), the prevention [of an effect] is considered to be like an effect;
the impediment (*pratibandha*) is the lack of causal completeness (*visāmagrī*), and its cause is the obstructor (*pratibandhaka*).
*Nyāyakusumāñjali*, Chapter 1, p.

43: Either fire and so forth, as qualified by the absence of a [counteracting] jewel and other such things, is the cause of burning and so forth, or rather, the absence of the jewel and so forth alone is the cause independently. Since this alone suffices, it is improper to postulate an infinite number of powers (*śakti*), their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and their subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). *Muktāvalī*, Verse 2:

Furthermore, is this power eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence of the effect being produced at all times, because that power would exist at all times.

"Is it not the case that even if that [cause] is eternal, its occasional production of an effect is logical because its auxiliary causes (sahakārin) are occasional, since it is asserted that it produces an effect only in dependence upon them? This too is incorrect, because it would entail the uselessness of postulating a [distinct] power (śakti); for it is sufficient to maintain that the very nature of the cause itself, when dependent on auxiliary causes, brings about the production of the effect.

If [the effect] occurs in the case of impermanence, is it produced solely by the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity, or is it produced by the power of its own inherent or adventitious characteristics, or is it brought about by some other supersensible capacity (*atīndriya-śakti*)? In the first case, since the essential nature of the entity is eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the constant production of the capacity; consequently, that very entity would always produce the effect continuously.

However, if the capacity were produced by inherent or adventitious powers, then let the effect itself be what is produced by them; there is no need for the postulation of a supersensible capacity that is not perceived in experience.

Even if [the capacity] were produced by another supersensible capacity, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that [second capacity], being occasional, would itself entail the necessity of being produced by yet another [capacity].

Furthermore, if a capacity is admitted, it must be admitted as either eternal like the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity, or as an effect. If it were eternal, there would be the consequence of the effect arising at all times; if, however, there is dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then let that dependence belong to the essential nature itself—what is the use of a capacity? If, on the other hand, the capacity is an effect, would it be an effect of the mere essential nature of the entity, or an effect of the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) such as the auxiliaries? (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 42)
Because of its existence, that [is] she— [the reading] "dyā" is found in Ā, Ba, Ja, and Bhā; [the reading] "dyo'sau" is found in Śra and Bhā.
—[Is the power] to be produced (bhāvyā) or [is it] manifest (bhātyā)?
Likewise, regarding each effect, is the power one or many? It cannot be one, because its differentiation is based on the differentiation of the effects.

Now, if [the power] is manifold, is it distinct from the possessor of power or non-distinct? If there is distinction, there is the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). If, however, there is non-distinction, is the possessor of power non-distinct from the powers, or are the powers non-distinct from the possessor of power? In the first alternative, like the nature of the powers themselves, the possessor of power would also be manifold and beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because it would be divided into as many parts as there are powers due to its identity with them, and because its nature is admitted to be beyond the senses; otherwise, its identity with them would be untenable.

In the second alternative, however, just as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) has a single nature, the powers themselves would necessarily follow as being one; for since they are non-different from that single entity, multiplicity—just like its own nature—is impossible. How, then, could there be the possibility of a diversity of effects? Thus, the refutation of the Naiyāyika, who does not accept multiple powers (*aneka-śakti*).
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that "immediately after the conjunction of the final threads," and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion. For a specific causal relationship is untenable without a supersensuous power (*atīndriya-śakti*). Indeed, a specific cause and effect are observed: cloth arises from threads, not from *vīraṇa* grass and the like; burning comes from fire, not from water and the like. This established order, being untenable on the basis of the intrinsic nature of the perceptible objects alone, implies for its own establishment another distinct property residing in those very objects that transcends them.

Now, one might object: "Is this systematic arrangement not established even apart from that [power], since it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the threads alone possess the capacity to produce a cloth? Even for one who asserts this, power (*śakti*) distinct from the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is the only refuge; for if it were not admitted, then since there would be no difference in the nature of the substance itself, the production of everything from everything would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that "the production of everything from everything does not occur because of a difference in essential nature (*svabhāva*)," then one must admit that one's own nature (*svo bhāvaḥ*), which is the cause for the restriction of effects, is a specific intrinsic form—a manifold and diverse power residing in all things and possessing differentiation.
pṛ॰ 158, l. 11: *prativiniyatam* Ā; *prativiniyataṃ bhyo vī-* Bhā; *prativiniyataṃ bhyo vī-* Śra.
—By what [is it] concomitant?
—The own-nature (svabhāva), not [the own-nature] from its own particulars (svabhedāt). —Bhāṣya; Śrāmaṇya.

As for what was also stated—that [the universal] exists solely by virtue of its own nature and its auxiliary causal powers (*sahakāri-śakti*), and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for the universal persists independently of the effects produced by its own substratum, and because it is common to effects produced by other causes that do not serve as its own substratum, it is impossible for it to establish the restrictive determination of the relation between cause and effect.
Indeed, "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) is of an identical form even with respect to effects produced by causes of a different class, just like the universal "explosion" (*sphoṭa*).

For fire-ness does not belong to fire only in relation to a flash of light (sphoṭa), as father-hood belongs to a father in relation to a son, or master-hood to a master in relation to a servant; rather, fire is fire for everyone.
Indeed, fire does not become a non-fire with respect to other effects; therefore, just like burning, it should also effect the removal of thirst and so forth.

[Objection: Surely it is the unique nature (*asādhāraṇa-svarūpa*) that serves as the basis for the determination [of causal relations]; and such indeed is "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) in relation to fire, because it is the cause of its exclusion from non-fires, and "burning-ness" (*dāhatva*) as well, because it is the cause of the burning's exclusion from non-burning. Therefore, since the restriction of the relation between cause and effect is established by what is observed alone, the postulation of an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) is not tenable. [Reply: That is incorrect. For even if fire-ness does not possess a unique nature insofar as it excludes non-fire, it is impossible for it to be the determinant of the production of a specific effect, because it is common to all effects. Indeed, fire-ness does not lack the quality of excluding fire from non-fires with respect to other effects as well, such that it would not be the producer of them. For the uniqueness of fire-ness is relative to causes such as water and the like, and not relative to effects such as water and the like.

In this way, even regarding water, a fixed rule for its producing coldness and so forth would not be possible; for the cause of that restriction, namely "water-ness" (*jalatva*), is common even to burning and other such effects. Consequently, water might burn, and fire might quench thirst, because there is no distinction [between them]. (Page 158, Line 16) Its own universal "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) has fire as its substratum, and its effect produced from it is [such things as] a crackling sound (*sphoṭa*).
Another cause, such as water and so forth, which does not serve as the substratum for its own nature as fire— [this cause] is,
with respect to the causal relation—
of the nature of a supersensuous power (atīndriya-śakti).
Even though it is unique, fire-ness has an identical form. (Śābarabhāṣya)
The capacity of fire-ness (agnitva) to produce a different effect— while being [fire-ness] itself— [is established]. (ni-bhāṃ)

Regarding the rule of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇaniyama*): [Objection] Now, if burning is produced by fire, then since the universal "burning-ness" (*dāhatva-jāti*) is the basis for its determination, earth and other elements—being non-burning in nature—could not possibly be produced by fire. Furthermore, if coldness and so forth are produced by water and the like, then because that universal is the determinant, how could there be the contingency of burning being produced by water and the like, given that it lacks that universal? [Response] That is incorrect; for although the universal "burning-ness" is not equivalent to coldness and the like, it is equivalent to other causes such as water, and thus it cannot serve as the basis for determining a specific, restricted relationship between cause and effect.

Now, if it is argued that the universal which inheres in a particular thing is precisely what establishes the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) therein—such that "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) does not inhere in water and the like, nor does "the nature of burning" (*dāhatva*) inhere in cold and the like—that too is unsatisfactory. For even so, fire-ness and the like would be incapable of establishing causality and so forth. Indeed, that which is excluded from non-causes and persists among causes establishes causality because of its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*); however, fire-ness and the like are not excluded from non-causes, since they are present even in non-causal things, such as past and future fires or other fires that do not produce an effect.

Nor does the non-existence of the two specific fires—one past and one future—entail the impossibility of their being substrata of the universal fire-ness (*vahnitva*); for if that were so, it would follow that the two cognitions "there was fire" and "there will be fire," delimited by the universal fire-ness, could not arise.

Or, let it be granted that [the universal] has as its locus a particular qualified by a substance (*sattva*); even so, there is still no exclusion of the universal *vahni-tva* (fire-ness) from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*). This is because another specific fire is not the cause of smoke produced by a specific fire intended [as the subject], and another [cause] is not the cause of that which is produced by it; therefore, since *vahni-tva* is observed even in a heterologue that is not a cause, it does not entail being a cause of its own locus, despite the fact that universals such as "coldness" (*śaitya*) are indeed uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
If Agni were not present, or if he were seated elsewhere—bha-bhāṃ, śra. (variant: a-śra.)—śra. (variant: a-śra.).
Even though the conditions are untenable,
and even though it is qualified by truth,
the discernment [remains].

Furthermore, while fire-ness (*agnitva*), by excluding itself from things that are not of the nature of fire, might well preclude those non-fire things from being causes with respect to effects produced by fire, how can it possibly avoid the consequence of a confusion of causal capacities regarding the mutual production of effects among all individual instances of fire? Therefore, some restrictive factor must be stated to avoid this; and would that be a universal (*sāmānya*), a particular (*viśeṣa*), both, or a power (*śakti*)? It cannot be a universal, because it does not persist even in other individual instances [of fire].

Nor is there a "particularity" (*viśeṣa*); for a particularity does not abandon its nature as a particularity when producing an effect that arises from another particularity, nor do both [the cause and the particularity] abandon it. Therefore, one must admit that power alone is the regulator of that [effect]. Furthermore, if the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and the auxiliary power (*sahakāri-śakti*) were the regulators, it would contradict worldly experience; for in the world, even regarding oxen, humans, and the like who possess their own nature and auxiliary powers, there is common usage and perception such as: "this one is capable of this task," "this one is incapable," or "this one has little capacity."

Thus it is established that there exists a causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) distinct from both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the auxiliary power (*sahakāri-śakti*), which serves as their cause; otherwise, this distinction would not exist, and all things would either equally produce an effect or equally fail to produce one.
For how could the nature of fire be excluded [from producing heat]? (Note: *bhāṃ* and *bhā॰* refer to manuscript variants.)
Even in another manifestation, O Mountain,
he does not abandon his nature;
for indeed, O Mountain, [he possesses] the power that effects his own essential form.

Furthermore, O man, do things produce an effect merely through the acquisition of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), or because there is a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) due to that acquisition of auxiliaries? In the first case, even when those auxiliaries are acquired, since the essential nature remains unchanged, a cloth would be produced from a lump of clay just as a jar is; and it has already been stated that a difference in intrinsic nature can only occur when there is a difference in causal capacity (*śakti*).

Furthermore, if it is admitted that fire produces its effect merely through the presence of its own nature and its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then it would follow that it produces its effect even when an obstructing magnet or similar object is present. For at that time, there is neither the destruction nor the alteration of the fire-ness (*agnitva*) or of the auxiliary cause, namely the contact with the fire on the palm; this is because its nature is recognized as remaining unimpaired. Therefore, since the effect does not arise from the visible form of the cause, one must postulate some other instrumental cause distinct from it, and that is what is called "power" (*śakti*). (Bhāṣya on Śābarabhāṣya).

[Objection: Is it not the case that fire is not a cause [of burning] in the proximity of that jewel and so forth, because it fails to produce its effect due to the absence of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), since—as in the case of the contact between the palm and fire—the absence of the jewel and so forth is also a constituent of the causal totality for the production of burning? [Reply: That is incorrect. For what kind of absence (*abhāva*) acts as the auxiliary here—is it the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), or mere absence (*abhāvamātra*) of the obstructing jewel and so forth? If it were the antecedent non-existence, then even while one jewel is present, burning would still occur in dependence upon the antecedent non-existence of another jewel.

If it is argued that this [fire] produces burning only upon reaching its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then burning would not occur either when that [fire] has perished, or even while this [fire] exists if an "enabling gem" (*uttambhakamaṇi*) is present;

by this, the auxiliary role of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is refuted, because there would be the undesirable consequence of no burning occurring when that prior non-existence exists or when the enabling gem is applied.

Nor can it be mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because such non-existence is possible even when the obstructing gem and so forth are present, which would entail the occurrence of burning; furthermore, if the prior and destructive non-existences were possible, there would be the undesirable consequence of burning not occurring.

Furthermore, the status of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) is rejected precisely because it is impossible for such a thing to exist in an obstructing magnet or similar object.

Nor is mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*) a cooperative cause, since "mere non-existence" is itself impossible apart from the four specific types of non-existence. Therefore, the non-existence of an obstructing magnet or the like is not the cause of burning and so forth, because it lacks both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Whatever lacks positive and negative concomitance with respect to something is not its cause, just as a potter is not the cause of a cloth; and this [non-existence of the magnet] is likewise. Therefore, it is so.

Alternatively, because its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is established by other means—as in the case of [the color] *ṣaiṅgalya* and so forth—what kind of absence (*abhāva*) could serve as a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) for the production of an effect? Would it be mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), or mere absence (*abhāvamātra*)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
52; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 288).
In its destruction,
[there is] the non-existence of mutual [dependence],
because it is impossible for [it] to arise.

Furthermore, if the absence of that particular mantra and so forth were the cause of burning, then even when one specific instance of that mantra exists, why would burning not occur, given that there exist absences of other instances of that mantra—past, future, and present—in that same place and at that same time? Nor can it be argued that because the absence of one individual instance does not exist, the absences of other instances should not produce their own effect; for it is not observed that because other positive individuals do not exist, a single positive individual fails to perform its own function. This is a matter of common experience.

Nor can it be maintained that an infinite number [of absences] acting together to produce an effect is ever established anywhere, nor that this absence is a single entity because the genus (*jāti*) of those mantras and so forth is one; for you do not admit the existence of a genus among absences. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that absences would be identical with one of the categories of substance, quality, or action, since the genus is fully contained within those very categories—[as is the case with] obstructing mantras, gems, and the like.

Furthermore, is the absence of the mere jewel and so forth the cause of burning, or is it the absence of the obstructer? Regarding this, the first position is untenable; for burning is not observed when there is merely the absence of the jewel and so forth.
Nor is the absence of a "qualified" jewel the cause, because such qualification—which is only cognizable through the effect—is nothing other than a different name for power (*śakti*) itself.
The second position is also inadmissible; for if one has consumed poison that was neutralized by an obstructer, death would follow once that obstructer subsequently ceases to function.

For in this case, does the obstructing factor produce the absence of rasa, or some other excellence? It cannot be the absence of rasa, because a state of being devoid of rasa is not perceived in poison, since rasa is recognized there.
Nor can it be another excellence, as that would entail the postulation of something unseen (adṛṣṭa).

And if some supersensuous excellence (*atiśaya*) were to be postulated, then what is the aversion to postulating a power (*śakti*)? Consequently, this [position] is refuted: namely, that fire and the like possess a capacity characterized solely by the proximity of their own auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); for, according to the manner described, it is impossible for them to produce an effect based on a capacity characterized merely by the proximity of their own auxiliary causes.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that [the effect] arises from that [Ishvara] by virtue of His possessing the characteristic of being "tall" (or "great"), then it would follow as an absurd consequence that sprouts and other effects could likewise arise from seeds and the like for that very same reason; moreover, it would entail that pleasure and other states arise from garlands, women, and so forth. Consequently, the postulation of an imperceptible Ishvara, as well as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so on, would be untenable. [The word] *dāhādi* occurs in the Bhāṣya and Ānanda-vardhana’s commentary; it is conjectured (*kalpeta*) in the Ānanda-vardhana manuscript.
Furthermore, because this would entail the undesirable consequence of [the cause] being non-existent (*abhāva*), as stated in the *Bhāṣya* and *Āraṇya*:

"And as for what was said—that there is a state of non-causality because of the failure to produce the effect when a counteracting agent such as a magnet is present—what is this so-called 'failure to produce the effect'? Is it being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of the effect, or is it being obstructed (*pratibaddhatva*)? If it were being the counter-positive, then burning would not arise from that [fire], just as it does not from water."
Nor is there dependence [on other factors], because it would follow that the effect would not be produced even when a magnet or similar object is present;
and as for that magnet or similar object— [Bhāṣya, Śrīpura, p.
In this regard,
since there is no possibility of the production of the effect even when the obstructing gem and so forth are present, provided that the counteracting gem and so forth are also present,
the counteracting gem and so forth— relative to the obstructing gem and so forth— function according to the maxim of a wrestler and his rival wrestler. (Bhāṣya, Śruti)

Furthermore, is this power (śakti)—which is being obstructed by an impediment—of the nature of a universal (sāmānya), of the nature of a substance (dravya), or of the nature of a quality (guṇa)? And is this obstruction its destruction (pradhvaṃsa) or its suppression (abhibhava)? In that regard, first of all, an obstruction characterized as destruction is not possible for a power of the nature of a universal, because it is eternal.

Nor is it possible for one of the nature of a substance, because its destruction is admitted to result from the destruction of its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) or from the destruction of its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa).
Nor is it possible for one of the nature of a quality, because its destruction is declared to result from the emergence of a contradictory quality or from the destruction of its substratum (āśraya).

Furthermore, an obstruction characterized by suppression is untenable; for even when an obstructing magnet or similar object is present, the innate causal power (*sahakāri-śakti*) inherent in the nature of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth is perceived as unobstructed.
Moreover, regarding these two powers, are both produced by causes, or is one produced while the other is eternal? The first position is not tenable, as it is not accepted [by our school].
In the second case, however, it is a great marvel that one power destroys the obstructer while another protects it;
therefore, through mantras, medicinal applications, and other means of inconceivable power, the obstruction must be understood as pertaining to the very power that is beyond the senses.
If it is asked, "What then is the obstruction of power? it is either suppression or destruction.

Indeed, does the obstructer obstruct the power by reaching it—characterized as distinct from its own nature and its auxiliary causes—or without reaching it? It cannot be by reaching it; for since the gem, mantra, and so forth do not reach the possessor of the power, it is impossible for them to reach this power [inhering in it]. Indeed, when a cloth is not reached by the hand, it is not possible to reach the color and other qualities residing in it.

Furthermore, if there were an obstruction of that which has not yet reached [the object], then from a single magnet, mantra, or the like, there would have to be an obstruction of the capacity of everything; this too is untenable, because an obstruction by that [agent] occurs only for that which is capable, by virtue of a relationship characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*). Indeed, as in the case of a magnet, the magnet has no relationship with iron other than fitness, such as proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth; nor is there an attraction of what is unfit, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even all the iron existing within the belly of the three worlds being attracted by that single [magnet].

If it is asked: "Once the power has perished, how can it manifest again so that effects such as burning may arise? [The answer is: It arises precisely from a momentary flash of fire (*vahnikṣaṇa*) endowed with another power. Nor does the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) constitute a fault, because—as in the case of the seed and the sprout—the beginninglessness of the stream of cause and effect is accepted.

And such powers of objects exist in manifold forms because they produce multiple effects at every moment; otherwise, how could fire, though its power is obstructed for one person, simultaneously perform acts such as burning for another, or how could poison, whose lethal power is obstructed, effect the alleviation of disease? Nor is there a contradiction in a single entity possessing multiple natures, for that which is established by valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not subject to contradiction. Furthermore, the objection raised against the positions of absolute identity or difference regarding the power and its possessor is untenable, since we accept their identity in some respect (kathañcid).

Therefore, by those who assert the specific determination of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāvapratiniyama*), it must be understood by the discerning that each individual entity possesses a distinct, inherent, supersensuous, and diverse internal form—designated as "power" (*śakti*)—which is to be apprehended solely through its effects.
Thus, the existence of power in entities is established;
consequently, the capacity to grasp objects is logical, being the attainment (*labdhi*) characterized by the subsidence and destruction of obscurations (*āvaraṇakṣayopaśamaprāptirūpā*).
— whatever slight obstruction there may be among entities, Bhāṣya; whatever slight obstruction there may be, Śruti.

—These texts, which aim to establish supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*) through its effects (*kārya*), should be understood as follows: "Since power is always to be inferred from its effect, why is it being questioned? (*nityaṃ kāryānumeyā ca śaktiḥ kim anuyujyate*).
In that case, the only proof understood is the mere fact of its occurring when that [other thing] occurs.

The author of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, however— stating in verse 1607, "In that regard, there is no such thing as 'power' (śakti) distinct from the [entity] possessing power," and so forth— accepts that power is indeed the very nature of the entity (*padārtha*).
Furthermore, its function (*upayoga*) is the operation of grasping an object.

Now, he explains the passage beginning with "the conjunction" (*sannipāta*) by means of the words "capacity" (*yogyatā*), etc.

"Arising immediately after" (*anantaram bhūtam*) refers to those two—the object and the subject; by this, the word "immediately" (*anantara*) is explained directly, while the word "conjunction" (*sannipāta*) is explained by implication.

Indeed, when the conjunction characterized by the presence of suitable place and other factors for those two is impossible, the manifestation of anything immediately following that [conjunction] is not tenable—as in the previous case—due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

What, then, is that which occurs immediately after? He says: "The apprehension of the object" (*arthagrahaṇam*), meaning the apprehension of the object just mentioned, and not merely the form of the object inherent in its own nature; for consciousness possessing the form of the object is not perceived even in a dream.

Since for every living being there is the perception of an appearance through a cognition connected with an internal location, which arises in competition (*ahamahamikayā*) with an object such as a jar that is connected with an external location—surely, if [the cognition] were produced from an object and imitated its form, it would not be so; how then could it be the grasper of a specific object? To this he says: "characterized by capacity" (*yogyatā-lakṣaṇam*).
Capacity is the power to grasp a specific object; that whose characteristic—that is, whose essential nature—is this is described as such.
The transformation of the self caused by that [object], which consists of the apprehension of all objects, is *upayoga*. (Rājavārttika 2.18)

Investigation 2.9:
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Sautrāntika, a proponent of the theory of cognition with images (*sākārajñānavādin*) and a member of one school of Buddhism.

On this point, one who follows the Sautrāntika school says: When cognition becomes the apprehender of an object, does it apprehend that which is connected to it, or that which is unconnected? It cannot be the unconnected, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Suppose, then, it is the connected; is it by way of identity (tādātmya) or by way of origination from that (tadutpatti)? Of these, the first alternative is untenable, because it would entail the position of the Yogācāra school.

Furthermore, its arising cannot occur at the same time [as the object]; for there is no relationship of cause and effect between two things existing simultaneously, just like the left and right horns of a cow. And if they exist at different times, since the object has already perished, its apprehension is not possible without the presence of its form. As it has been said: "If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be the object of cognition, those who know the logic understand that its very nature as a cause is what makes it the object, provided it is capable of imparting its form."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: [Thesis] Cognition possesses the form of the object; [Reason] because it is an effect of the object; [Example] like the subsequent moment of the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.247)

Likewise, whatever is the apprehender of something must have the form of that thing; for example, cognition which apprehends its own nature has the form of its own nature, and cognition is the apprehender of objects such as blue. [Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting one's own established doctrine (*matapratiprasava*). (Bhāṣya, Ātmatattvaviveka)
As it has been said:
"If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be the object of cognition, they [the wise] know its status as an object.
And this has been cited in the *Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā*, page 135, line 135.
"Those who know the reasoning [state that] the capacity to impart its own form to the cognition is itself the state of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). (Prameyaratnamālā, p.
48). "Those who know the reasoning [state that] the very fact of being a cause is the capacity to impart its own form to that [cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.247).

Furthermore, since there is no external object to be grasped in the case of cognitions of past or future objects, as well as in the case of cognitions such as [the illusory perception of] a mass of hair, how could there be a grasping of those [objects] without an internal form? Whatever does not possess the form [of an object] cannot be its grasper, just as the cognition of white is not the grasper of blue; yet cognition is indeed the grasper of the object.

Furthermore, if one accepts that cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), it follows that even its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) would not be perceptible. For a cognition, as it arises, is perceived precisely through forms such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow"; in the absence of such [forms], how could it possibly be perceptible? Moreover, if cognitions were formless, the mutual distinction between them would be extremely difficult to establish. Indeed, the form of blue and so forth is the very characteristic that differentiates one consciousness from another; in its absence, what would be differentiated from what? Therefore, that very form by which the comprehension "this is the cognition of blue" or "this is the cognition of yellow" occurs with a restricted object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this act, because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), and it is that which distinguishes one consciousness from another.
And it has been said: "In that regard, since cognition is of a homogeneous nature,
it must possess that specific character by which it is distinguished for each respective object" (Pramāṇavārttika 3).

302. Thus, if the nature of the object (*artharūpatā*) is absent, the connection of this cognition with the object—expressed as "this is the cognition of blue"—is not possible. Furthermore, since such a cognition would be indistinguishable with respect to all objects, even the systematic determination of each specific object (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) would be difficult to establish. Consequently, if that [cognition] were devoid of form (*nirākāra*) with respect to each individual object and thus lacked internal differentiation, how could it serve as a factor for activity toward a specific object by those practitioners seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), given that it would not be the cause for the perception of a restricted object? As it has been said: "It does not indeed connect this [cognition] with the object without [assuming] the form of the object."

Therefore, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in its having the form of the object of cognition (*meyarūpatā*), because the apprehension of the object of cognition [occurs] through it;

And it has been said: "Just as when children are born from parents who are alike in terms of diet, time, and so forth, the child takes on the form of one of them and not that of anyone else."

It connects this [cognition] with the object, for it cannot do so except by taking on the form of the object;
nor can anything other than its own differentiation—namely, the differentiation of the cognition itself—connect it with the object in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, in the cognition of the object of knowledge, the means of cognition consists in its assuming the form of that object;
as it has been said: "One should connect this [cognition] with the object" (Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, p. 119).
Sanmati-ṭīkā, pṛ. 510; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛ. 28, top;
Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā, pṛ. 126, bottom.

"From that [cognition], because the object of cognition is apprehended, the nature of the means of valid cognition consists in its having the form of the object. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.305). Pramāṇamīmāṃsā p. 33; Syādvādamañjarī p. 136.

"Just as when offspring is born from parents who are identical in terms of diet, time, and so forth, it takes on the form of one of them and not that of any other," as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.369.
— Nāvala—
Śrī [X]: The establishment of the formlessness of cognition preceded by the refutation of the theory of cognitive forms (sākāravāda)—
to this, the following reply is given.

As for what was stated—that cognition is the apprehender of an object, whether it be related or unrelated—and so forth: therein, it is only that which is related that is its apprehender. Furthermore, the relation between cognition and the object is characterized by "fitness" (*yogyatā*), and not by "origination from it" (*tadutpatti*), because the origination of cognition from the object will be refuted later.
Thus, in the argument that "cognition possesses the form of the object because it is the effect of the object," the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, because of the connection with the characteristic of height (*tallakṣaṇa*), there is no contradiction in cognition being the grasper of an object that is either simultaneous or non-simultaneous [with it]; therefore, the objection "how can something of a different time be grasped? and so forth is untenable. Moreover, is the possession of form (*sākāratā*) established by relying on the cognition well-known from your own scriptures (*svāgama*), or is it established by what is well-known through experience (*anubhava*)? Regarding the first alternative, since the non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpaka-jñāna*) well-known from your own scriptures is like a lotus in the sky (*ākāśakuśeśaya*), we have no concern for whether it possesses form or not.

For it is precisely that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), which is well-established through experience from childhood as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the cause for engagement (*pravṛtti*), withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and so forth, that has been undertaken here to be proven as being devoid of form (*nirākāra*).

Indeed, worldly people do not perceive that the object of cognitions is their own internal form; rather, because they are oriented toward an object that is not themselves, those [cognitions] are asserted by them to be the delimiters of objects. Furthermore, it is not logical to establish the nature of objects by transgressing worldly convention; for "validity is established by worldly convention" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.5).

Because of the consequence of such contradictions and the resulting conflict with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge, it is as follows: first, by perception, cognition is experienced as being devoid of the form of the object, grasping jars and so forth for each individual person through a competitive "I-me" assertion; it is not, however, like a mirror or similar surface, overlaid by a reflection.

This is also established by inference: for whatever is perceived by something as an entity distinct from its own self is perceived by that [perceiver] as not having its form, just as the insentience of a pillar and so forth is perceived; and blue and other objects, which are distinct from the cognition's own self, are indeed perceived by that cognition.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because the difference between blue and so forth from cognition has been proven [on page 165,

line 11]. For the relationship between cognition and its object, which constitutes the basis for the state of being the apprehended and the apprehender, consists precisely in the nature of *yogyatā* (fitness), and not in identity (*tādātmya*) or the like.
*ratnāvalī*, page 163:
"unfit for the purpose" (narthayogya) [variant:
*lakṣaṇasambandha*]—Bhāṣya, Āgama.
It is not obstructed (bhāṣya), [as stated in] Śrāvakabhūmi—[referring to] the knowledge of the kalpa.

And what is this so-called "having an aspect" (*sākāratā*) of cognition? Is it its nature as self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpatā*), its essence consisting of clarity (*vaiśadya*) and so forth, the imprinting of the object’s form (*arthākārollekha*), or the state of bearing the object’s form (*arthākāradhāritva*)? Among these, in the case of the first three alternatives, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for all three of those exist in cognition, because if any one of them were absent, the very nature of cognition as cognition would be untenable, since it has the nature of determining itself and others by way of its clarity and other such qualities.
However, it is untenable for cognition to bear the form of an object, because this contradicts the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To explain:

the form of blue and so forth does not transfer into cognition, because it is a property of that which is insentient (*jaḍa*). Whatever is a property of the insentient does not transfer into cognition, just as insentience itself [does not]. And the form of blue and so forth is indeed a property of the insentient.

Nor is there a deviation [from the rule] by the case of existence (*sattva*) and other such qualities; for it is impossible for those to be properties of the insentient alone, since they are possible even in non-insentient things such as pleasure.

What is this "half-aspectuality" (*ardhākāratva*) of cognitions, by virtue of which there would be a determination of specific objects? Is it being inscribed with the aspect of the object (*arthākāra-lekhitva*), or is it bearing the aspect of the object (*arthākāra-dhāritva*)? (Ratnākarāvatārikā 4.47;
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 131)
—Thus, [it is] the manifestation of the object itself; [it is] the manifestation of the object itself;
[it is] the insentience of the object itself.
Furthermore, regarding the non-insentient [cognition]:

is the cognition's similarity to the object in its entirety or in part? If there were similarity in its entirety, then because the object is insentient, the cognition would also necessarily be insentient; for that which is similar to an object in its entirety is itself insentient, just like the subsequent moment of the object, and the cognition is indeed entirely similar to the object.

Furthermore, there would follow for this [cognition] the same contradiction regarding its nature as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as [there was for the object], because it would be imitating the nature of the object of cognition (*prameya*); and this is not tenable, because the means of valid cognition and the object of cognition appear as distinct through their having outward- and inward-facing forms respectively.

Now, if it is claimed that there is a partial similarity [between the cognition and its object] in order to avoid this fault, then, since there is no apprehension of insentience by means of that non-insentient form, how could the object's qualification by that [insentience] be perceived? Whatever is not perceived by something in a certain case cannot be perceived as qualified by that thing in that case; for example, a citron (mātuliṅga) cannot be perceived as qualified by taste when the cognition of color has not apprehended it. And insentience is not perceived by the cognition of blue and so forth through its non-insentient form. If insentience is not perceived, how could even "blueness" be perceived? Otherwise, there would be a difference between these two.

When one thing is perceived even though another is not perceived, the former is distinct from the latter; for example, while a jar is not being perceived, a cloth may still be perceived. Likewise, even when insentience (*jaḍatā*) is not being perceived, "blueness" is perceived.
If this [blueness] is not perceived by the Sugata, how can it have existence? Or, if it does exist, how can he possess omniscience?
For if there were a complete identity in nature (*sārūpya*), knowledge would lapse into non-knowledge.
If there were equality in some respect, then everything would be the cognition of everything.
(Pramāṇavārttika 3.435)
Even in the case of similarity, the refutation of the universal generally applies; [as stated in] Tattvasaṃgraha, verse 2039, and Sanmati-ṭīkā, page 464.
That which has its cognition turned away from that object, which does not possess the form of that [object], yet perceives that object—[this is the definition of perception].
(Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 129, u.)
If the object were to impart its own form to the cognition in its entirety, it would follow that the cognition is insentient (*jaḍatā*), just like a subsequent moment of the object;
if, on the other hand, it were to impart it only partially, it would follow that the object possesses parts (*sāṃśatā*).
(Śāstravārtā-ṭīkā, p. 159).
In the case of an object,
it is as it is; in the case of those two [cognition and its form], it is otherwise than that.

Furthermore, if this [omniscient being] were to possess the forms of others’ passion and so forth when perceiving them, then, by imitating the entire web of another’s conceptual constructions (*kalpanājāla*), how could he be free from passion (*vītarāga*) and devoid of the web of conceptual construction (*vidhūtakalpanājāla*)? If it is argued that even while imitating those forms, this fault does not apply because there is no cognition such as "these passions and so forth are mine," then how can they belong to the other person? If you say, "Because the cognition of them exists in the other," then surely, in imitating the form of that cognition, this very same fault follows.

Now, if—fearing this fault—it is admitted that insentience and so forth are perceived by a cognition that does not possess their form (*atadākāra*), then the form of blue and so forth should likewise be perceived by a cognition that does not possess their form; enough with this stubborn obsession with grasping forms.

Alternatively, if it is held that blueness is apprehended by a cognition possessing its form (*tadākāratayā*), while insentience is apprehended by one not possessing its form (*atadākāratayā*), this is merely following the logic of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*).
For in the perception of other [qualities] such as passion and the like, there arises a correspondence (*sārūpya*) with them.
In the view of those who maintain the existence of apprehension, the presence of obscuration follows.
(Tattvasaṅgraha 2048)
And it would not exist;
[the opponent] understands this through scripture (śruti), as stated in the Bhāṣya:
"For example, people desire half of an old woman, but not the other half."
Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 4.1.78
The aged woman does not desire [him] as a whole, but desires only a certain limb;

O noble one, for the aged woman, like a lamp, only half the face—that is, the face alone—of the old woman is desirable, but not her limbs. This is the maxim of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīnyāya*).
Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-Bhāṣya, Ratnaprabhā, 1.2.8.
For not one part of a bad crow or the like is cooked for consumption while another part is fit for reproduction; [Brahma-sūtra Śāṅkara-bhāṣya, Ānandagiri,
The specific nature of other logical principles (nyāyas), along with references to various instances, should be seen in the *Laukikanyāyāñjali*, page 7.

Furthermore, due to similarity by way of a single part, there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving all objects, just as one perceives a blue object; for this [consciousness] possesses an undifferentiated similarity with everything by virtue of mere existence (*sattva*) and so forth.

If it is argued that even though that [similarity] is undifferentiated, they are not perceived because of their difference in form such as blue and so on; then it follows that all things possessing the same form would necessarily be perceived.

Furthermore, the apprehender would have to imitate the specific form of that very [object] from which it arises, and not merely through similarity; even so, it would follow that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) would be its apprehender, since validity is established by both arising from it and having similarity to it. Moreover, if there were an apprehension [of the object], it would follow that a father would be the valid cognition for his son.
If similarity to that [object] and arising from that [object] were the definition of being cognized,
then a cognition of a similar object and an immediately preceding [cognition] would be cognized.
(Pramāṇavārttika 3)

Furthermore, do atoms each impart their own individual form to cognition in their atomic nature, or as a composite whole? Regarding this, the first position is untenable, because atoms do not appear in their own essential form, whereas there appears instead a whole (*avayavin*) consisting of multiple parts, which is stable and gross—characteristics contrary to those of atoms.
The second position is also incorrect; for even when combined, they do not abandon their own essential nature, and thus it is impossible for them to appear in the form of such a whole.
Indeed, when combined, those atoms do not abandon their atomicity and plurality, as that would entail the consequence of entering into the opponent's doctrine;

nor is it logical for them, being otherwise constituted, to produce a cognition of a different nature, because that contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance: atoms do not represent a cognition in the form of something gross and so forth, because they lack that form; whatever lacks a certain form does not represent a cognition by way of that self-nature, just as blue does not [represent] a cognition by way of the nature of yellow; and atoms are devoid of the form of grossness and the like.
— Renunciation; likewise, according to the Bhāṣya, it is the state of having the same nature as consciousness (vijñānasvarūpakatva),
whereas according to Ātreya, it is the similarity of cognition (jñānasya tatsadṛśatvam).
Furthermore, is the form (ākāra) non-different from cognition, or is it different? If it were different, cognition would be entirely devoid of form;
if they were non-different, one of the two would simply cease to exist;
and if there were a partial difference, it would entail the adoption of another philosophical position.

Furthermore, if a form that is non-different from cognition itself were the object of apprehension, there would be no conventional usage regarding distance, the past, and so forth with respect to the object.

That which is apprehended as non-different from itself does not admit such conventions of distance and so on, as in the case of its own nature (*svarūpa*). Yet mountains, palaces, and the like are apprehended as non-different from themselves;
nevertheless, there is indeed the conventional usage regarding the object, since we perceive unerring expressions such as "the mountain is far," "the palace is near," and "the king is past."

Nor should it be argued that such conventional usage [of "memory"] does not occur because the factor that imparted the form has become long past; for if that were so, it would follow that there could be such usage in the waking consciousness regarding the dream-consciousness, since the latter is also long past.

If you then say that this conventional usage is erroneous because it treats the form of cognition—which is actually extremely proximate—as something otherwise; [we ask] how do you know it is the form of cognition? If you say it is due to its being erroneous, then there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of the fact that it is the form of cognition depends upon the establishment of its error, and the establishment of its error depends upon the establishment of the fact that it is the form of cognition.

Furthermore, if inference, when apprehending the impermanence and so forth of sound and other phenomena, possesses their form, then it would possess the nature of those very phenomena themselves rather than the nature of inference. On the other hand, if it does not possess their form, how can there be an apprehension of them by means of it? Or, if there is such an apprehension, what is the point of the effort to establish "having a form" (sākāratā) in other cases as well? [For] it is merely a form... [bhāṣya].
It is not logical for that [object] to be both manifest and unmanifest based on distinctions such as distance and proximity;

if it were argued that this difference arises from a distinction in the light [reaching it], then whether that light is obstructed or unobstructed, there would be either uniform perception or total non-perception, because no particular subtle part of it exists.
If it is argued that there is a distinction because an object is not seen with dim light, [then we reply:
Pramāṇavārttika 3.408–9.

Furthermore, if cognition were to assume the form of the object, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the conventional distinctions of "distant" and "near" with respect to the object would not exist; see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
27, l. 1. (The reading *prasaṅgaḥ syāt* is found in manuscript A; *abhāvaḥ* is in manuscript Bhā.)

Furthermore, does that very cognition itself perceive its similarity to the object, or is it another cognition? If it is another cognition, does it perceive the similarity after having perceived both the cognition and the object, or without having perceived them? It cannot be without having perceived them, because the perception of similarity is inseparable from the perception of those two; for it is not possible to perceive the similarity between twins without having perceived them.

Now, having accepted [the existence of the object]; from where does that apprehension arise—is it from this very same cognition, from another cognition, or from both? Among these, the first position is untenable, because since the two exist at different times, their simultaneous appearance in a single cognition is impossible.

For two things existing at different times do not appear together in one cognition, as in the case of sunrise and sunset; and the cognition and the object are indeed at different times, for you do not admit that they coexist simultaneously due to their being in a cause-and-effect relationship. Furthermore, it is not unestablished that these two are at different times.
The second position is also untenable, because since the two distinct cognitions are absolutely dissimilar, they cannot serve as the cause for the apprehension of similarity between them.

Those two cognitions which are absolutely dissimilar are not capable of apprehending the similarity of anything, just like the cognitions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta; and the two cognitions regarding the object and the cognition itself are absolutely dissimilar.

Nor is this unproven; for it is well-established that the cognition possessing the form of the object produced from a cognition is absolutely distinct from the cognition possessing the form of the object produced from the object itself, due to their arising from different causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) and having different objects.

Whatever two things arise from different causal complexes and have different objects, they are absolutely distinct, as in the case of the cognitions of color and touch; and the cognitions of the [external] object and the cognition of that cognition likewise arise from different causal complexes and have different objects.

Or, let us grant that there is a cognition of similarity between those two [the object and the cognition]; even so, the similarity between these two—namely, the object and the cognition—must be cognized through something else. And the similarity of that [second cognition] with the cognition of the object and the object must likewise be cognized through something else, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that the very same cognition cognizes its own similarity with the object, that is not correct. Because at the time [of the cognition], the object does not exist. That which does not exist at the time of another cannot, by itself, cognize its similarity with that other, just as a son cannot cognize his similarity with a father who was non-existent at the time of the son's birth. And the object does not exist at the time of the cognition.

Therefore, since the conformity of the cognition to the object (*arthasārūpya*) cannot be established when examined, the [argument] beginning with "whatever does not possess the form of X is not the apprehender of X" is incorrect— [this is stated in the *Śrāmaṇya-phala-sūtra*],
where [the cognition] is distinct from the [object] and different from it. Thus, the two [positions] are refuted.
Because the two cognitions arise from entirely different causal complexes (*bhinnasāmagrīprabhavatayā*),
[they are distinct]; thus it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Āgama*.
Because their causal complexes are distinct and because their objects of cognition are distinct,
[perceptual] cognitions [are not identical with] object-cognitions.
Regarding what was stated by [the opponent]—
namely,

that if cognition were formless (*nirākāra*), it would follow that even its own nature (*svarūpa*) would not be perceptible, and so forth— that too is a mere assertion; for the form of cognition is its capacity to illuminate both itself and others (*svaparaprakāśakatva*), and not a form such as blue (*nīlādyākāra*), since the latter is a property of the object (*arthadharma*).

Furthermore, it is not logical for one thing to be perceived through the form of another, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga); rather, it must be through its own form. And that this consciousness possesses perceptibility by means of such a form is well-established through expressions such as "I perceive blue.

Moreover, the exclusion of one cognition from another occurs precisely by way of its nature as the apprehender of a specific object, and not by way of the nature of blue and so forth, because the latter is a property of the object to be grasped (grāhya-dharma).

For the mutual exclusion of objects is logically possible only through their own inherent properties (svagata-dharma) and not through the properties of another, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Consequently, [the opponent's claim] that "by mere experience" and so forth is untenable;

for even if cognition possesses similarity (sārūpya) to the object through mere experience, a specific distinction occurs for each respective object by way of the particular mode of experiencing that specific object.

Indeed, the nature of apprehending yellow cannot belong to that which has the nature of apprehending blue; and since a connection with each respective object is possible only through such a nature, the claim that "it joins this [cognition] with the object" and so forth is nothing but the play of profound darkness (pṛ॰ 166 paṃ॰ 2 –sya rūpasyā– ā॰).
Direct perception [is that which] arises from the experience of its own [object], such as blue and so forth, produced by [the object] itself.
Furthermore, by what characteristic does it "correspond" (*pratyabhā*)?

Is it by having the nature of grasping a specific object (*pratiniyatārthagrāhakatva*), or is it intended that it "connects" (*ghaṭayati*), meaning it relates [itself] to [the object], or rather that it determines [the object] as being connected with the thing? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; for if the cognition's possession of the form of the object were the cause of its connection to the object, it would follow that there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between them.

The second position is also untenable: that there is no identity between those two things which stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, as in the case of fire and smoke, and that such a cause-and-effect relationship exists between the cognition connected with the object and the form of the object itself; for a connection between the form of the object and the cognition connected with the object is never perceived anywhere.

That which has no relationship with something else never serves as a cause for the ascertainment of that thing; for example, the Sahya mountain, whose relationship with the Vindhya mountain is not perceived anywhere, does not serve as a cause for the ascertainment of the Vindhya. Furthermore, since the relationship between the cognition and the object is not perceived anywhere—given that the "form of the object" [in the cognition] is not established through a cognition already connected to the object—how could this [cognition] bring about the ascertainment of a cognition connected to the object? Nor is any other connection of the cognition to the object possible than the production of a cognition having a specific object; and since that [production] is accomplished solely from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), the effort to establish the "form of the object" is futile.

Does [the form] connect—that is, relate—the intended cognition to the object, or does it determine the cognition’s conformity to the nature of the object? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 28, l. 1). Now, [it may be argued:

"If cognition were formless, then everything would be the apprehender of everything, since there would be no distinction. This too is incorrect; for cognition is restricted by its own causes to the object situated right before it, just like a lamp.
Indeed, a lamp is not perceived as the illuminator of jars and other objects by imitating their form; this is because such a view contradicts direct perception.

Nor does it follow that if cognition were a manifestor devoid of form (ākāra), it would manifest all jars and so forth; for it manifests only those specific objects located within houses and the like, since it acquires a specific capacity by being produced from a specific causal complex (sāmagrī). If you argue that even if one accepts that cognition manifests an object through possessing a form, it would follow that a single cognition of a jar would manifest every jar existing within the belly of the three worlds, we reply that for you as well, there is no answer other than the specific capacity arising from a specific causal complex.

Thus, since the position that [cognition] possesses a form (*sākāratā*) is corrupted by numerous faults, cognition does not have its own form alone as its object. What then? It has an external object distinct from that [form] as its object. This is because it has an appearance distinct from that [form]: whatever cognition has an appearance distinct from something X does not have X as its object; for example, a cognition of taste, which has an appearance distinct from form, does not have form as its object. And the cognition of a jar and so forth has an appearance distinct from its own form.

Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is well-known that the cognition appearing with an outward-turned form, such as [the cognition] of a jar, has a manifestation distinct from the form of the cognition appearing with an inward-turned form.

By this, those who prattle that "everything is known by a single [cognition] due to the equality of the existence of cognitions" are refuted, as [the distinction] is the same in the case of the arising of reflections.
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 127a:
The rule of manifestation does not apply to the cognition of the cause as a reflection.
Even in the absence of such a nature [of identity], the grasped and the grasper exist;
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 139, l. 1.

—O Venerable Sir—this same objection applies even if [cognition] possesses a form (*sākāratva*), because the determination of [cognition] according to each respective object would otherwise be impossible (*anyathānupapatti*). (Sāmānyasammatī-ṭīkā, p. 460).
And since cognition possessing a form is described as being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
why should it not also be the establisher of such states as momentary destruction?
Because that [nature] is its own essential form (svarūpa) due to the exclusion of other particularities (viśeṣāntara), [it is established as the universal].
(Tattvārthaśloka, p. 126)
