—not for the sake of objects, Śrāvakayāna—; for the sake of [all] objects, Śrāvakayāna—; in the meaning of [liberation], Śrāvakayāna.

Or, let there be some mark (*liṅga*); even so, if its invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has not been grasped, it is incapable of inferring a remote cognition, for it is observed everywhere that only a mark whose concomitance has been grasped serves as the inferent of its own probandum. Furthermore, the concomitance between a mark and the possessor of the mark occurs only between two things established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, no such mark that is invariably concomitant with cognition has been established by any means of valid cognition, through which an inference—preceded by the apprehension of the relationship—could proceed.
Therefore, by one who desires inference, direct perception must be accepted as a means of knowledge.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the activity of the Self—which is immediate and self-luminous by nature—to be eternally imperceptible. For instance, that activity of illumination belonging to the Self which is self-luminous is not eternally imperceptible, because it is an activity of illumination, just like the activity of the mass of light emitted by a lamp or similar objects.

Furthermore, when knowledge arises, it is experienced through its own self-awareness as being distinct from the experience of that [object], and the object is experienced precisely by having entered into the state of being its content, as evidenced by the cognition "I know the object.

However, if knowledge were always inferable, both of these would be impossible; for since an object, while manifesting, is common to all, if knowledge were imperceptible (parokṣa), the determination that "it manifests to me" would be without foundation.

Therefore, fearing the aforementioned defects, one who wishes to abandon the stubborn obsession with the mediacy of knowledge must accept its nature as self-cognition (*svasaṃvidrūpatā*)—thus [it is said].
(Variant readings: *pakapra*—Ā., Bhāṃ.;
*ṇatvaprati*—Śra.)
Of the self which is light; of the light—[variant readings: *bhā* (Bhāṣya), *bhā* (Ātman);
*jñānam utpādya* (Ātman)].
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika, who asserts: "Cognitions are cognizable by another cognition, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*)," is as follows:

"Indeed, it is untenable that a cognition is self-cognized, for in this case it is more reasonable that it is cognized by another cognition. Thus, the inference is: cognition is cognized by another cognition, because it is an object of knowledge, like a jar and so forth."
Furthermore, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it exists in the subject (*pakṣa*);
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*);
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it does not occur in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) as it does in the subject and the similar class.

Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) on account of the knowledge of God (*īśvara*), because we admit that [God's] knowledge is cognizable by another knowledge only in relation to the knowledge of beings such as ourselves, and because the knowledge of God is distinct from the knowledge of beings such as ourselves. One does not attain the status of a discerning person (*prekṣāvattā*) by applying a property observed in a specific instance to what is not specific; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all cognitions, like that [knowledge of God], would possess the capacity to grasp all objects. Nor is the reason sublated by a lapse of time (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because its subject matter is not contradicted by perception or scripture.

"Now, surely cognition of an object is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself as having the nature of being self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*); therefore, because this [reason] is employed immediately after a statement of the subject matter that is sublated by direct perception, it is indeed 'mistimed' (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). This too is incorrect; for it is impossible for cognition to have the nature of being self-cognized, since it is established solely by its nature of grasping an object—as expressed in the terms 'grasping of an object,' 'intellect' (*buddhi*), and 'consciousness' (*cetanā*)—and furthermore, its grasping occurs only through a subsequent cognition residing in the same self, and not by itself."

If it is argued that, in this case, there would be a perception of the object and the cognition arising sequentially exactly as they occur; we say no, for even though these two exist in succession, due to their rapid occurrence, there arises the misconception of simultaneity—just as when one cuts through a hundred lotus petals—and thus their distinction is not perceived.

Nor should it be argued that if the cognition of an object were perceived by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress because that [second] cognition would also require perception by yet another cognition; for since the object is established by the second [cognition] apprehending the first and the third apprehending that second, there is no purpose in postulating further cognitions, and thus no possibility of an infinite regress. Indeed, when there is a desire to know the object, cognition arises regarding the object, whereas when there is a desire to know the cognition, it arises regarding the cognition; such is the nature of experience. The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: the cognitions under dispute are known only by another cognition, because they are cognitions.

Whatever conditions there may be, all those conditions must be cognized by another condition; for if they were not cognized by another condition, it would lead to the over-extension [of the principle] that even non-existent things appear. Therefore, one must admit that only what is being known appears.
In that case, if consciousness were self-cognizing, it would result in the contradiction of that very same thing being both its own object (*karman*) and its own action (*kriyā*).
As it has been said: "Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself by itself,
so too knowledge cannot know itself by its own part."

The state of being a condition (*pratyayatva*), which is a real entity pervaded by non-contradiction, is excluded from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) because one observes its opposite—contradiction. Thus, it is pervaded by the property of being cognizable by another cognition; in this way, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.

Similarly, properties such as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), being a quality (*guṇatva*), and existence (*sattva*) may also be employed as reasons for [the conclusion] that it is cognizable by another cognition.
Consequently, it is established that cognition is not self-aware.
As stated in the *Nyāyakaṇikā* (p.
267): "For instance, if [it is argued that] the self, being self-cognized, is perceived through its conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then that is indeed acceptable.

However, if it is claimed that this very same cognition is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the result (*phala*), that is not so; for such non-distinction among the triad is never observed elsewhere, whereas in cases where there is distinction, there are numerous examples such as a staff and so forth."
Therefore, in cognition, there is no identity between the instrument and the object, nor is there identity between the action and the object;
consequently, consciousness is cognizable by another cognition because it is an object of cognition, like a jar and so forth (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 529).
Like a jar,
it is indeed directly perceived;
its intrinsic nature is reality.
*Āptaparīkṣā*, p. 9;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 224—[the word] "sthā" is [corrupted to] "śra" in the manuscript.

However, those who accept that [cognition] has self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*) as its intrinsic nature should be asked: is it "self-cognition" because it is cognized by itself, or because it is cognized by something belonging to itself? If it is by something belonging to itself, then this is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since you accept that a preceding cognition is cognized by a subsequent cognition immediately following it. If, on the other hand, "self-cognition" means being cognized by its very own self (*ātman*), that is incorrect, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. For even a very sharp sword does not cut itself, nor does even a well-trained boy climb onto his own shoulders.
If that were so, this [argument] would be illogical: "Knowledge has self-luminous nature because it illuminates objects, like a lamp.
Furthermore, [the argument is flawed] due to the inconclusiveness [of the reason] by the eye and other [senses].

Moreover, what would constitute having a self-luminous nature? Would it be the state of being of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatva*), or the state of possessing a radiant form (*bhāsurarūpasambandhitva*)? In the first case, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because the state of being of the nature of consciousness is impossible in the case of a lamp.

Now, if [the probandum] is "being connected with a radiant form," since that [radiance] is absolutely non-existent in cognition, how can it be the probandum? Otherwise, there would be sublation by perception; for there is a contradiction in something acting upon itself, just as a fingertip cannot be touched by that very same fingertip, nor can the edge of a sword be cut by that very same sword-edge (Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā, p. 78).
—And [regarding] "luminosity"—[as stated in] Ātmatattvaviveka and Bhāmati:

In that case, if by "luminosity" (prakāśakatva) one intends "having the nature of consciousness" (bodharūpatva), then the example [of a lamp] is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because having the nature of consciousness is impossible in the case of a lamp.

Alternatively, if luminosity means "possessing a radiant form," that does not exist in the cognition [itself]; therefore, the determination of the cognition consists precisely in the arising of another cognition which has that [first cognition] as its object.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 529.

Furthermore, by what very same nature does cognition manifest itself and by that same [nature] the object, or by a different nature? If it is by that same [nature], how can there be a distinction between cognition and the object? For they would be identical in nature, since they are grasped by the apprehension of an undifferentiated nature, just like the essential form of either one of them. If, on the other hand, it is by a different nature, then are those two natures non-different from that [cognition], or not? If they are non-different; then in that case too, is the cognition non-different from those two, or are those two non-different from the cognition? Regarding the first alternative, those two alone would not be the cognition, because the cognition would have entered into them exclusively, just like their own essential form.

In the second alternative, however, there is only cognition and not those two [the object and the self], because they are included within that very [cognition]; and if that were so, how could cognition be the illuminator of its own object and itself? Or, if they are distinct; even then, are they self-cognized or cognized by a cognition residing in their own substratum? In the first case, there would be the consequence of three self-cognized cognitions; and if each of those too possesses a dual nature consisting of both self-illumination and the illumination of another, the same objection applies and there is an infinite regress.

Even in the second case, if there is a cognition of those two which serve as the causes for the manifestation of themselves and others, and it manifests them by means of such a dual nature, then there would be an infinite regress;

if it does not manifest them, then their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is untenable, or else there is a contradiction with their having that nature—thus, "having that nature" involves a contradiction. (Bhāṣya, Śruti)
The establishment of the self-cognition of knowledge preceded by the refutation of its being cognizable by another cognition—here it is replied:

regarding what was first stated as the proof, namely "because it is an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*), is it intended to establish that the knowledge of persons such as ourselves is cognizable by another cognition, or that knowledge in general is so? If it is knowledge in general, then there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara*).
Now, [if it is argued that the qualification] "of our own and others' cognition" [is intended], that is not so; for the qualification "our own and others'" is not perceived here.

If you say, "It is implied within the heart [of the argument]," how is this meaning understood without an oath (kośapāna)? Or, even if it were accepted, would that be a qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*) or of the reason (*hetu*)? If it belongs to the subject, then let the cognition of God (*īśvara-jñāna*) not be the subject; but who can prevent the reason from operating there, such that it would not be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)? (p. 181, l. 16)

It might be argued that [the probandum] is established by the knowledge of the object that is Maheśvara, because the reason is deviant with respect to pleasure and so forth, as stated in the *Pramāṇaśarīra* (p.
60), and because knowability is also deviant with respect to the knowledge of Īśvara.
The cause is therein; Nyāyaviniścayaṭīkā, p. 116a; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 222. (bhāṃ॰)

Furthermore, by what means is the knowledge of God excluded from being self-cognized—is it because it is always imperceptible (*parokṣa*), or because it is always unapprehendable (*aprameya*)? If it is because of its being self-cognized, how is that established for him—through reasoning or merely through his own admission? If it were established merely through his own admission, then everything would be established as desired for everyone.

Now, [suppose it is established] through reasoning (*yukti*); what is the reasoning here? Is it "having the nature of grasping an object" or "being cognition"? Since both of these exist in the cognition of people like us, self-cognizability (*svasaṃviditatva*) would be established for both [external objects and cognitions], or it would not be established for either at all, because there is no distinction between them.

Now, one might argue: "Since the cognition of God is superior to the cognition of those like us, it is only there that self-awareness (svasaṃviditatva) is appropriate, and not elsewhere; for one who applies a property observed in a superior instance to an inferior one does not deserve the title of a discerning person. This too is charming only when left unexamined; for it would entail the undesirable consequence of denying the properties of being a cognition and having the nature of grasping an object—which are observed in the superior cognition of God—to the cognition of those like us.

[Objection: "But if the nature of being cognition (*jñānatva*) and the nature of apprehending an object (*arthagrahaṇātmakatva*) are absent, how could that be cognition? For its very essence consists in those [two]. [Reply: This is the same in other cases as well. Indeed, if the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃviditatva*) were also absent, it would not be logical for cognition to possess the status of being cognition (*jñānatā*); for there is no difference in the fact that its essence is likewise constituted by that [self-cognition]. Indeed, even in the case of the Lord’s (*īśvara*) cognition, the nature of being cognition is never observed to exist without self-cognition, just as it is not observed without the nature of being cognition and the nature of apprehending an object. Thus it is with other cases as well.
Furthermore, it is not logical for an essential nature (*svabhāva*) to be partial, just as light possesses the quality of illuminating both itself and others.

Indeed, the quality of illuminating both itself and others is not the inherent nature of sunlight alone, but rather of the light of lamps and such as well, since that [quality] is perceived without distinction in both cases.

Now, if the cognition of beings such as ourselves were of the nature of determining both self and other—just like the cognition of Īśvara—then it would follow that it too, like His, would manifest all objects. That is incorrect, because only that which is suitable [for manifestation] is manifested, just as in the case of a lamp.

For although a lamp, like the sun, possesses the nature of illuminating both itself and others, it is not observed to illuminate all objects; rather, it illuminates only those objects in specific locations for which it is capable. Likewise, in this case as well, the capacity (*yogyatā*) of all cognitions must be understood as characterized by the varying degrees of the subsidence and destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of their own respective veils (*āvaraṇa*);
for in the absence of that [capacity], the gradation in the apprehension of objects would not be possible for them, as will be established further on.

Therefore, because [cognition] is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvidita*), there is no exclusion of the cognition of God (*īśvarajñāna*) by the qualification "ours and so forth" (*asmadādi*). Rather, with respect to the cognition of ours and so forth, it is established by the reason of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) that the cognition of an object is cognizable by another cognition; consequently, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the cognition of God, since that is distinct from the cognition of ours and so forth.
For one who, having observed a property in a qualified subject, attempts to apply it to an unqualified subject, does not attain the status of a discerning person;
[as stated in] Pramāṇaparīkṣā p. 60 and Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 34. U. [Note: "U. refers to the source of the citation].
It is found in the Ratnāvalī, page 222;
it is joined in Ā [and] Śra;
it is obtained in Bhāṃ and Śra.
This is its own nature;
this is its inherent state—
also [stated] elsewhere in the Śruti.

Nor can it be [known] always, because it would then follow that [the Mīmāṃsaka view] is accepted, for the Naiyāyikas do not admit that any cognition is always beyond perception (*parokṣa*); and if it were always beyond perception, how could God possess omniscience? Furthermore, the claim that "omniscience consists in the grasping of all other objects" is also incorrect, because if cognition itself is not grasped, it is impossible for it to grasp an object.

Indeed, an object cannot be said to be experienced unless it is experienced by its own cognition; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that an object would be perceived even through the direct perception of another person’s mind. For there is certainly no other cause for non-perception than the fact of not being self-cognized (*asvasaṃvidita*).

To claim that "whatever is inherent (*samaveta*) in something is the cause of its perception therein, rather than being self-cognized" is a mere fantasy, because inherence itself is unproven, and thus the state of being inherent is likewise unproven.

Furthermore, if one accepts that [the Lord’s cognition] is always unapprehendable (*aprameya*), it follows that the cognition of the Lord would never exist; for whatever is always unapprehendable is never existent, like a sky-flower, and the cognition of the Lord is always unapprehendable.
Therefore, by one who desires its existence and its apprehension of objects, it must be admitted that its nature is unknown to us. The same applies to other cases.

Now, if you qualify the reason (*hetu*) as "because it is apprehendable while being a cognition of those such as ourselves," then the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because such a qualified reason is impossible in the case of examples such as a jar.
Omniscience follows from that; likewise,
the cognition of Īśvara is accepted as having an unconditioned nature.

— Even that which was stated by others, namely, "the cognition of those such as ourselves is also [an apprehension]," and "cognition is the grasping of an object, consciousness," and so forth— that too is incorrect; for in the absence of a self-cognizing nature, the very apprehension of an object within cognition would be impossible.

For that [cognition] must arise there either from the object (*artha*) or from consciousness (*cetanā*). In this regard, if it is held that the apprehension of the object occurs in cognition because it arises from the object, then let it be admitted for a jar as well, since there is no difference in its arising from objects such as the potter’s wheel and so forth. If, on the other hand, it is due to consciousness, then how is the consciousness of cognition established—is it from the apprehension of the object, or because it originates from a conscious self? If it is from the apprehension of the object, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for the consciousness is established once the apprehension of the object is established, and the apprehension of the object is established once that consciousness is established.

Now, if [it is argued that consciousness arises] because it originates from a conscious self (*ātman*), how indeed is the consciousness of the self established—is it through the inherence (*samavāya*) of consciousness, or by itself? If it were by itself, then let that same [consciousness] belong to cognition (*jñāna*) as well, since there is no distinction [between them].

If, however, it is through the inherence of consciousness; this is another circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for the self would be conscious because of the inherence of consciousness, and cognition would be conscious because it originates from that [self] (p.
For does the nature of cognition as the "grasping of an object" arise from its production from the object, or from its essential nature being consciousness? (Syādvādaratnākara, p.

224) Furthermore, regarding the statement "cognition is the grasping of an object," is it determined that cognition is the grasping of the object *alone*, or that it is [the grasping] of the object *as well*? Of these, the first position contradicts direct perception; for, just as there is the grasping of an object through the mental presentation "this is blue," there is likewise the grasping of the self through the presentation "I," as is experienced in introspection.

Indeed, the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of that [cognition] is not experienced at a time distinct from the cognition of blue and so forth; for it is experienced precisely at the same time as that cognition, appearing with a clearly manifest form within. Therefore, since the cognition of an object has a nature non-different from its own self-cognition, when that [self-cognition] is cognized, the object-cognition is also cognized. This establishes self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). For whatever is of a non-different nature from something else, when that [latter] is apprehended, the former is necessarily apprehended—just as when blue is apprehended, its very own form, such as its configuration, is apprehended. And the cognition of an object has a nature non-different from the cognition of its own form.

If the position is accepted that there is also the apprehension of the object— [the cognition] having the form of the mental representation "I" (*aham*)— then this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not being denied.

Furthermore, if cognition is held to be of a nature that is not self-cognized, then would it be imperceptible (*parokṣa*) or cognizable by another cognition? It cannot be imperceptible, for that would entail the position of other schools [who deny self-awareness], and because there is no contradiction in the perception of an object by means of that [cognition] which is itself not perceived. For instance: that whose manifestation is unmanifested is not manifest, just as some cognition is unknown by someone; and an object such as "blue" has an unmanifested manifestation. Thus, [if cognition were not self-cognizing, it would follow that it is never manifest].

For manifestation is cognition; when that [cognition] is unmanifest, how can the manifestation of the object be established? For it would follow that even from the cognition of another mental continuum there would be a manifestation of the object. Thus, the determination of an object that is the domain of imperceptible cognition would be like something imperceptible itself. (Nyāyabinduṭīkā, p. 97, l. 1).

And if that [object] were also beyond perception, then no object could be established as perceived; therefore, how could there be a determination of knowledge from the cognition of something unestablished? (224)
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 47:

Now, if it is maintained that [the object] is cognizable by another cognition, then in that case too, would it be cognized by a cognition arising simultaneously [with itself], or would it be cognized by a cognition occurring at a subsequent time? Of these, the first position is untenable, because multiple cognitions cannot exist simultaneously; otherwise, the non-simultaneous production of cognitions would not serve as the mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of the mind (*manas*), as stated in *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.16.
Thus, this statement would be contradicted;

the second position is also untenable because there is no appearance of a gap, for one certainly does not experience an interrupted cognition such that first there is the knowledge of the object and subsequently the knowledge of that knowledge.
Consequently, the [view] that the apprehension of the cognition of an object occurs through a subsequent cognition inhering in the same self, and so forth, has been refuted;
this has also been extracted at *Sanmati-ṭīkā* p.
477 and *Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā* p. 117 (Uttara-khaṇḍa).
Furthermore,

at the time of a subsequent cognition, does that preceding cognition persist or not? If it persists, there would be the same consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions, as well as the undesirable implication of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*).

Now, if it does not persist, then whose grasper would that [cognition] be, since the object (*grāhya*) has already perished? Furthermore, sensory perception (*indriyajam pratyakṣam*), when it operates, operates upon an object that is both connected [to the senses] and present. A cognition existing in a past moment lacks the quality of being present, nor is contact with the sense-organ characterized as the mind (*manas*) possible for it. Moreover, it is not logical for a cognition to be perception if it operates upon an object that is unconnected or non-present. Therefore, how could there even be a mention of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) in that case? Furthermore, a cognition produced from an object is the grasper of that object; and that which has perished cannot be a producer, because of its non-existence.
Furthermore, it is logically impossible for that which is non-existent to exercise causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), because of the contradiction involved.

Nor is it reasonable for something in the state of perishing to possess the capacity to produce an effect, for such a thing is never observed to be an agent; indeed, a father who is in the act of dying is never seen to be the cause of his son's birth.

Furthermore, upon the arising of the cognition of an object, does a cognition that apprehends it necessarily arise, or not? In the first case, even in a human lifetime, there would be no transition of the cognition to another object, because the mind would remain occupied from birth with the arising of the cognition of the cognition itself; thus, due to infinite regress (*anavasthā*), neither the object nor the cognition of the object would be established. Moreover, it is not logical for the cognition of the object to be perceived by a cognition of the cognition of the object, nor for the object to be perceived by that [latter cognition], because that would lead to the same consequence [of non-perception] regarding the cognitions of other mental continua (*santānāntara*).

Now, even if that [cognition] arises, it does not necessarily arise [from the desire to know]; for when there is a desire to know an object, cognition of the object arises, but when there is a desire to know cognition, cognition of cognition arises. This too is unsatisfactory, because it is impossible for cognition to be produced by a desire to know it. Just as for one whose horse has been lost, even though there is a desire to see the horse, the sight of the horse does not arise; and even in the absence of a desire to see a cow, the sight of it may arise. Therefore, [desire to know] cannot be the cause. Furthermore, the experience of a cognition turned away from an object is contradictory to its manifestation through another [means].
There would be no movement, no stability, and no distinction between the qualified and the qualifier;
likewise, even the knowledge of knowledge would require another knowledge.
The creeper of the knowledge of knowledge spreads across the entire expanse of the sky.
(Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 110–111)
*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 60;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 42;
*Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā*, p. 7.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 479; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
34; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 94.
Candraprabha 2.57–59:
...or the knowledge of the object whose nature is cognition, Bhāṣya, Śrī.

Furthermore, when there is a desire to know an object, does one apprehend that very cognition as "I have arisen," or another cognition? In the first alternative, the Jaina position is established; for a cognition apprehended in such a manner would indeed be self-cognizing of its own object. In the second alternative, however, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because even in that case, the fact of being produced by a desire to know would have to be perceived by yet another [cognition].

Or, let it be that the non-arising of the third and subsequent cognitions is due to their being produced from that [second cognition]; nevertheless, one must consider whether another cognition apprehends the first cognition as "the cognition of the object is indeed unknown by me, yet it is the determiner of the object," or not? If it does so apprehend it, then, O Lord, it is established that very [first] cognition is the determiner of both itself and the other.

If it does not apprehend [the object], how can there be such an apprehension? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, having apprehended the object and itself, would the cognition of the object apprehend another cognition—thinking "I, who was previously ignorant, now know the object"—or would it do so without apprehending them? In the first case, it follows that this [second] cognition would have three objects.
In the second case, however, there is an over-extension; for then one might also apprehend that "two atoms, while still unknown to me, initiate a dyad."

Furthermore, if one cognition were to be grasped by another cognition, it would result in its very non-cognition, just as light would be non-light if it depended upon another light; for there is no other definition of an insentient thing (*jaḍa*) than this: that it depends on the gaze of another for its own establishment.
(Tīyajñā—*śra* edition;
*cetadeva* — *ā* and *bhā* editions)

Furthermore, the cognition of an object would have to be restricted solely to apprehending the object and itself, [as stated] in the *Yuktyanuśāsana* (p. 9) and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 37, upper).

Furthermore, if the cognition of the object were distinct from the cognition of that [cognition], why would it not be perceived in exactly that same way? If you argue that this is due to rapid succession—just as when one cuts through a hundred lotus petals, there is the misconception of simultaneity—we ask: how could it be that all things are not momentary? For even the Buddhist can assert that here too, the determination of oneness occurs due to the operation of rapid succession. Moreover, in the case of material lotus petals being cut by a material needle-point, cutting in sequence is the only logical conclusion, since simultaneous contact is impossible.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: This cutting, performed by the action of a single person using a material [instrument] upon material lotus petals situated in a sequence of upper and lower positions, occurs only in succession; just like the cutting performed by the action of a single person using a material needle-point upon similar copper plates.

But for the self—which by nature illuminates both itself and others, possesses unimpaired sense faculties, illuminates objects without reaching them, and is formless—what contradiction is there in its simultaneous illumination of its own objects, such that the simultaneous arising of cognitions would not occur? Nor should it be argued that the sense faculties exist in mutual exclusion like a hundred lotus petals, and thus, because the formless mind (manas)—which is like the point of a needle—is incapable of reaching them all at once, such simultaneous arising does not happen; for the "mind" as conceived by you will be refuted during the examination of the six categories.
Because of its rapid movement, a sharp-pointed material object is unable to simultaneously pervade a hundred lotus petals situated one above the other; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 36, top.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.

As for what was also stated—that self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is cognition by means of one's own self—and that this is incorrect because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself (*svātmani kriyāvirodha*), and so forth; even that is without substance, because [the argument] is inconclusive (*anekāntāt*) due to the case of the knowledge of God (*īśvarajñāna*) and the light of a lamp and the like.

For the Lord’s knowledge does not require another cognition for its own manifestation, since it is accepted that the Creator of the world possesses a single, eternal knowledge that illuminates both itself and others.

Nor does the light of a lamp or similar source require another illumination to manifest its own nature, as this would contradict experience. Furthermore, what kind of action is contradictory to knowledge in respect to itself—is it of the nature of origination, or consisting of motion, or having the essence of a verbal root-meaning, or characterized as making known? If it is of the nature of origination, let it be contradictory.
For it is not our position that cognition produces itself, since we maintain that its production arises from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*);

nor is it of the nature of motion (*parispanda*), because motion subsists in substances (*dravyavṛtti*), and thus its existence in cognition—which is non-substantial in form—is impossible. (Page 182, Line 14)

—Thus [it is said]. But what kind of activity is contradictory in the self—is it of the nature of motion (*parispanda*), or of the nature of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*)? *Tattvārthaśloka*, p.
42; is it origination (*utpatti*) or manifestation (*jñapti*)? *Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 59.
Āptaparīkṣā, p. 47; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 35;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 228.

[From *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 93: Is an action—which, though consisting of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), is either intransitive (*akarmikā*) or transitive (*sakarmikā*)—contradictory with respect to its own self? It is certainly not intransitive; for in cases such as "the tree stands" (*vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*), that [action] is perceived as residing in the self [of the agent] alone.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction in this case because it is so perceived, then let there likewise be no contradiction in such intransitive actions as "knowledge shines forth" even with respect to the very nature of knowledge, since perception is indistinguishable in both instances. If, on the other hand, it is said that the transitive action "knowledge knows itself" is contradictory in relation to its own self because the status of being an object is perceived only elsewhere [than the agent], that too is mere words; for then contradictions would follow in such cases as "the self kills itself" or "the lamp illuminates itself," since the metaphorical attribution of the status of an object to the agent (such as the self) is equally applicable to knowledge as well.

By this, the contradiction of the act of cognition within itself is refuted; for no contradiction is established in anything by its own nature, otherwise even a lamp would face a contradiction in illuminating both itself and others, yet such is not the case. Therefore, just as a lamp, arising from its own causal complex with the nature of illuminating both itself and others, does not encounter any contradiction, so too is it with cognition.

If it is argued that the act of informing (*jñapti-kriyā*) is contradictory within itself because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is perceived only elsewhere than in itself, then let the act of illumination (*prakāśana-kriyā*) likewise be contradictory within the nature of a lamp, since its perception is no different [from the former], occurring only elsewhere than its own nature. [Response:

There is no contradiction in that case, because this [lamp] arises from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*) with a nature consisting of the illumination of both itself and others; this is the same for the other case as well.
— in the performance [of the rite],
otherwise also,
by one's own self.
Because there is a specific distinction in cognition regarding the act of illumination as an object.

Furthermore, regarding this diversity: is there a contradiction with its being an object (*karmatva*) in relation to another cognition, or in relation to its own nature? In the first case, Maheśvara would not be omniscient, and there would also be a contradiction with the text stating that "the cognition of an object is to be grasped by a subsequent cognition inherent in the same self."

If there is no contradiction for that [knowledge] with respect to another knowledge, then let there likewise be no contradiction with respect to its own nature; for, like the thousand-rayed sun, it possesses the nature of illuminating both itself and others.

Furthermore, since instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is perceived as being a distinct entity from the action of knowing—just as [the sun is distinct] from the state of being an object (*karmatva*)—there would also be a contradiction for that [instrumentality] in that context. And thus, the cognition "I know the object of the self by means of knowledge" would not occur through the instrumentality of knowledge.

Now, if [it is argued that] knowledge is not self-evident because the nature of knowledge is not perceived when there is the perception of an object, [we ask]: what is the meaning of "like the object"? Does it mean that knowledge is not perceived in the same way as the object is perceived—namely, as connected with an external location—or does it mean that knowledge is directed toward the object and not toward itself? In the first alternative, the argument proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the object such as a jar and its cognition appear as being connected respectively with an external and an internal location.

If cognition were not perceptible because it does not appear as being connected with the location of objects such as a jar, then the object such as the jar would also be non-perceptible because it too does not appear as being connected with the location of the cognition;
thus, the second alternative is also untenable, since all three—“I,” “the jar,” and “I know”—are indeed manifested.
In this case, if two of these manifestations were lost, what confidence could there be in the manifestation of the jar?
—Self-cognition, Ārya;
in the first position, Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, if the nature of cognition as being of the form of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpatā*) does not manifest, how can its orientation toward an object (*arthonmukhatva*) or anything else be established? This is because the apprehension of a relation—such as "this belongs to that"—is necessarily dependent upon the apprehension of the relata. If it is argued that the cognition is first perceived by another cognition and its orientation toward the object is then perceived, then there follows the consequence of an infinite regress (*āvṛtti*) in the apprehension of the object: first, the apprehension of the object would occur in the primary cognition, and then in the subsequent cognition. Otherwise, how could there be the perception that "this [cognition] is oriented toward the object"? Therefore, just as the manifestation of the cognition's orientation toward the object is accepted, the manifestation of its own self-orientation must also be admitted; enough with this denial of the perceptibility [of cognition].

And what is the "own-nature" (*svātmā*) of action, wherein its contradiction is asserted—is it its essential form (*svarūpa*), or is it that which possesses action (*kriyāvad-ātmā*)? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; for the essential form cannot be contradictory, otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence (*anuṣaṅga*) of contradiction in the essential form of all entities, resulting in their being devoid of essential form.
Furthermore, because contradiction resides in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*), it is not logical for there to be a contradiction in the essential form of this [action].

The second alternative is also untenable; for all actions are perceived as residing in that which possesses action. Otherwise, all substances would be devoid of action, and actions themselves would be without a substratum. But this is not the case, since an action residing in the agent is perceived in the agent, and one residing in the object is perceived in the object.
Now, is the nature of an action its own self, or is it the self that possesses the action? (Āptaparīkṣā pṛ. 47; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa pṛ.
35, uttarapakṣa).

As for what was also stated—that luminosity (*prakāśatva*) consists in being of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatva*) or in possessing a radiant form (*bhāsurarūpasambandhitva*), and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; because "the illumination of an object" (*arthaprakāśakatva*) is said to be "the shining forth of an object" (*arthodyotakatva*), and that [illumination] does not involve any contradiction whether it occurs in some cases through the nature of consciousness or in others through a radiant form (p.

The claim that luminosity is derived from scripture—that is, the illumination of an object—and whatever else has been stated, such as "by the very same nature through which cognition illuminates itself, by that very same [nature] it illuminates the object," and so forth, is an unexamined assertion. This is because there is a non-absolutist (anekānta) relationship regarding the difference and non-difference between the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*). For, while there is non-difference between the nature and its possessor in terms of the self-nature of cognition, there is difference in terms of the self-nature consisting of the illumination of both self and other. Thus, since cognition itself is the non-difference and its two natures are the difference, there is no room for the aforementioned fault.

However, regarding the distinction and non-distinction that are merely conceptualized, when one proceeds to refute them, it is only one's own intended position that is negated, not the actual nature of the thing (*vastusvarūpa*). Nor does this prevent the establishment of any desired reality for anyone, since such a procedure is possible in all cases. Furthermore, cognition possesses the nature of grasping both itself and the object, and its capacity to manifest them constitutes its indirectness (*parokṣatā*), because those two [aspects] are inferable from the effect characterized by the manifestation of the object. Thus, there is no room for the aforementioned defects.

That too is incorrect, because of the non-absolutism (anekānta) regarding the difference and non-difference between the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*), as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 38, l. 1. (Note: *tadapyasat* is reconstructed from *tadapyasa-*; *śra-*, though appearing as a corruption, likely refers to the source text).
There is no room for [the objection], because it proceeds in that manner;
[there is] the absence of [the two] faults.
The refutation of the theory that knowledge is cognizable by another knowledge should be sought in the following texts: *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 40;
*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, page 60;
and the commentary on the *Yuktyanuśāsana*, page 7.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 33, upper section;
*Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā*, page 109, upper section;
*Prameyaratnamālā*, Sūtra 6.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 475;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 219.

By this [argument], the Sāṅkhya, who maintains that cognition is cognizable by another cognition, is also refuted; for, due to its insentience (*acetanatva*), cognition is not of the nature of self-determination (*svavyavasāyātmaka*). This is the Sāṅkhya’s prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 95, verse 15)
Objection: Knowledge does not have the nature of self-determination because it is insentient (*acetana*), like a cloth or similar objects;

nor is its insentiency unestablished. For instance: knowledge is insentient because it is a transformation of *pradhāna*, just like [the objects themselves]; furthermore, whatever is sentient is not a transformation of *pradhāna*, such as the Self (*ātman*); and knowledge is indeed a transformation of *pradhāna*.
And its being a transformation of that [Prakṛti] is well-established, because of such statements as "From Prakṛti comes Mahat" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 22).

For when the Pradhāna proceeds toward the construction of the manifold world, first there arises the Great One (Mahat)—singular, all-pervasive, consisting of the determination of objects, and lasting from the beginning of creation until the dissolution—since it is stated that "from the beginning of creation until the dissolution, there is one Intellect (buddhi)."

And that [Self] is by nature imperceptible to those like us; however, the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛttayaḥ*) which emerge through the medium of the functions of the senses and the mind, being distinct for every individual, are by nature perceptible by other means of knowledge.

For, first, the function of the sense organ transforms into the form of the object, and then, through the medium of the function of the mind, the modification of the intellect—having received the form of the object from one side and the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) from the other—establishes the cognition of the object.

Indeed, when there is no transfer of the form of the object into the intellect (*buddhi*), which stands in the place of a mirror, the *puruṣa* cannot perceive the object; for it is stated that "the *puruṣa* perceives the object as determined by the intellect.
"Determined by the intellect" means reflected in the intellect.
From *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); and from that, the group of sixteen.
From those sixteen as well, from five [of them], the five gross elements arise. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22)
From that primordial nature (prakṛti), the Great One (mahat) arises first;

"the Great One," "intellect" (buddhi), "thought" (mati), "wisdom" (prajñā), "consciousness" (saṃvitti), "manifestation" (khyāti), "cognition" (citi), "memory" (smṛti), "Āsurī," "Hari," "Hara," and "Hiraṇyagarbha" are synonyms—
according to the Māṭhara-vṛtti and Gauḍapāda-bhāṣya.
The first effect, called the Great One (mahat), is that mind (manas). (Sāṃkhyasaṃgraha, p.
The first effect, called the Great (mahat), is that mind whose function is deliberation; here, "deliberation" means ascertainment,
and thus the meaning is that the intellect (buddhi) has that as its function.

That which is this expanded seed, consisting of the primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa), is called the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva); it is termed the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva). — Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya 1.61.
That which has the nature of mere existence and is characterized by the thought "I am" (38).

Alternatively, the intellect-principle (buddhitattva) is described as "the Great One" (mahat), characterized by the cognition of self-determination; it is the cause consisting of six primal natures (prakṛti).
And this has been cited in the *Yogakārikāsādhanapāda*— *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, page 29;
*Sanmatitarkaṭīkā*, page 300.
These specific qualities, distinct from one another like lamps, having illuminated the entire object for the sake of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect. 36.

The external senses, having perceived objects, present them to the mind; the mind, having formed a conceptualization, presents it to the ego-sense; and the ego-sense, having produced self-identification, presents everything to the intellect (*buddhi*), which serves as the presiding authority over all.
Since it is the intellect that accomplishes every experience for the *puruṣa*, it is the intellect alone that further discriminates the subtle difference between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*.
For the intellect (buddhi), through its proximity to the Puruṣa and by receiving his reflection, becomes as if of his very nature; it thus accomplishes for the Puruṣa the enjoyment of all objects.
— Sāṃkhyakārikā 36, 37.
Through the channel of the senses, by contact with an object, or by the knowledge of a logical mark (liṅga) and so forth, an initial modification of the intellect arises in the form of the object;
memory likewise [arises]— all these perceptions of objects are reflected in that expansive mirror of consciousness, just as trees on a riverbank are reflected in a lake.
Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya 1.87:

The very transference of the reflection of the *puruṣa* onto the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*) constitutes the *puruṣa*'s state of being the experiencer through the intellect. Thus, the meaning is that sound and the other objects become "objects of sight" (*dṛśya*) when they are conjoined with the intellect that has assumed the shadow of the seer (*dṛśi*).
This [verse] is quoted from the *Yogasūtra-bhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī* 2.20—
see *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 50.
Āptaparīkṣā, p. 41; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 26; Nyāyaviniścayaṭīkā, p. 547, top.
[The Ratnākara] (p.

233) objects: "Since consciousness that is distinct from the intellect is never perceived, how can there be a transfer of the reflection of consciousness into it? This too is incorrect; for although the distinction between these two exists, it cannot be discerned by one who is deluded due to a particular kind of contact, just as [the distinction] between a firebrand and fire [is not perceived when they are joined].

Nor should it be asserted that even in the case of the firebrand and fire there is no difference at all; for their mutual difference is perceived through the perception of specific shapes, colors, and touches that are impossible for each to possess in the other.

When a specific configuration, color, and touch that are mutually impossible for two things are perceived, there is a mutual difference between them, as in the case of a jar and a cloth; and such mutually impossible specific configurations, colors, and touches exist between an iron ball and fire.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*), for the distinction between the non-luminous color and non-hot touch residing in the iron ball and the luminous color and hot touch of the fire is perceived through direct perception itself.

Therefore, just as in this case one is deceived by the contact characterized by the mutual interpenetration of spatial points and thus does not discern their difference, so too it is with the intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*caitanya*).
And it has been said: "Therefore, through that contact, the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 20).
For even though the intellect is insentient, it appears as if it were conscious due to its contact with consciousness.
— Because of the perception of a distinction between color and touch; because of the perception of a distinction, as in the case of [the example] "like here," Bhāṣya, Śruti.

Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient; likewise, although the qualities (*guṇas*) are the actual agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent.

Since the Puruṣa has consciousness as its essential nature, therefore, through union with it, the unconscious *liṅga*—consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest—proceeds as if conscious in its functions such as determination, self-conceit, volition, and perception. What is the illustration? It is as follows: a jar, which is neither hot nor cold, becomes cold when mixed with cold water, and becomes hot when joined with fire; in the same way, the unconscious *liṅga* consisting of the Great Principle and the rest, though being unconscious, becomes as if conscious. (Māṭhara-vṛtti, Gauḍapāda-bhāṣya).
Regarding the establishment of the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of knowledge preceded by the refutation of its insentience (*acetanatva*), while [the opponent] is deliberating,
the following response is provided here:

As for what was stated—that cognition does not have the nature of self-determination because it is insentient (*acetana*)—in that regard, what is this so-called "insentience"? Is it (1) non-self-cognizability, (2) the bearing of the form of an object, or (3) being a transformation of the inert? In the first case, the reason is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).

In the second case, however, the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), for cloth and other such things are not perceived as bearing the form of an object in the manner of a mirror or the like; furthermore, such insentience is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because it is impossible for an incorporeal cognition to bear the form of a corporeal object.

For instance: cognition does not bear the form of the object because it is formless (*amūrta*). Whatever is formless does not bear the form of the object, just as space (*ākāśa*); and cognition is formless. Alternatively, if it were to bear that form, its formlessness would be contradicted. To explain: whatever bears the form of an object is material, such as a mirror and the like; yet cognition bears the form of the object. Furthermore, the fact that cognition bears the form of the object has already been refuted previously in detail. Enough of this excessive elaboration.

The claim that [the intellect] is a transformation of the insentient (*jaḍa*) is likewise unestablished (*asiddha*); for it is a transformation of the Self (*ātman*). To explain: the Self possesses the transformation of knowledge because it is a seer (*dṛṣṭṛ*). That which does not possess such [a transformation] is not a seer, like a jar or similar objects. But the Self is a seer; therefore, it possesses the transformation of knowledge. Furthermore, the proof you offered to establish its insentience—namely, "because it is a transformation of the Pradhāna"—is also unestablished, since we have established that this [intellect] is a transformation of the Self.
Nor does the self incur impermanence due to its transformation into impermanent cognition; for that consequence would apply to the *pradhāna* as well.

Even though there is no difference between the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*), only the manifest is impermanent because it is a transformation, whereas the unmanifest is not [impermanent] because it is the substratum of transformation; this same logic applies elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, if the Self were unchanging, it would follow that it is non-existent—like a horse's horn—due to the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Moreover, the claims that the intellect (*buddhi*) persists from the beginning of creation until dissolution and that it is all-pervading (*vyāpitva*) are utterly untenable; for its transformation contradicts those [attributes].
Thus, the intellect is neither all-pervading nor eternal, because it is a modification of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), just like a cloth or similar objects.

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) due to space and so forth, because it is not established that those are transformations of that [Self]; or, if it were established, then like that [Self], they too would necessarily entail contradiction with that [Self]. If you argue that even though there is no difference in being a transformation of that, some things—such as space—remain pervasive from creation until dissolution while others are otherwise; then, why is it not accepted that even though there is no difference in being a transformation, cognition is self-cognized while cloth and the like are otherwise? For there is no distinction between the two cases.

Furthermore, since the Pradhāna is not distinct from the impermanent Manifested (vyakta), one who perceives the eternality of the Pradhāna must also admit the eternality of the Puruṣa, as it is in no way different from the non-eternal cognition; for there is absolutely no distinction [between them]. (Āptaparīkṣā p. 41;
Syādvādaratnākara p. 235)
The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.
According to the Sāṃkhya school, like cloth and other such things, space as well [is produced].

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with [the principles of] permanence and omnipresence. Moreover, from what would this first transformation of *prakṛti* in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) arise—by its own nature (*svabhāva*), by the necessity of fulfilling the purpose of the *puruṣa*, or by unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)? If it were by its own nature, then it would follow that it must exist eternally, because a nature is possible only as something eternal. That which is inherent does not occur only occasionally, just as the state of consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātmakatva*) [is eternal]; and the first transformation of the intellect of *prakṛti* is indeed inherent.

Now, if it is argued that the cause for the necessity of accomplishing the purpose of the *puruṣa* is that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) transforms into the forms of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, having reflected, "I must bring about the experience of the self"—that too is unsatisfactory; for it is impossible for that which is insentient by nature to possess such a reflection as, "I must bring about the purpose of the *puruṣa*."

For instance—at the time of the first creation, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is devoid of recollection (*anusandhāna*), because its mental modifications (*buddhivṛtti*) have not yet arisen; when its mental modifications have not arisen, it is devoid of recollection, just as in the state when creation has been withdrawn; and at the time of the first creation, primordial nature is one whose mental modifications have not arisen.

When a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) has arisen and the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) has been transferred [to it], there occurs a synthetic connection (*anusandhāna*). However, at the time of the first creation, since *prakṛti* is insentient and the *puruṣa* is devoid of desire, whose would this synthetic connection be—[namely], "I am proceeding for the sake of the *puruṣa*'s purpose"? Furthermore, the transfer of the reflection of consciousness to the *puruṣa* is a reflection [of the *puruṣa*] in the intellect, just as that of a face in a mirror. And it is not logical for this [all-pervading *puruṣa*] to have a reflection anywhere; for that which is all-pervading does not reflect anywhere, just like space (*ākāśa*), and the Self (*ātman*) is all-pervading.

Furthermore, it is appropriate for things such as a face, which possess a non-luminous nature, to be reflected in a mirror, which possesses a luminous nature; but how could the *puruṣa*, whose nature is absolutely luminous, be reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*), which—being composed of the three *guṇas*—possesses an extremely dull nature? That which is luminous by nature does not reflect in that which is non-luminous, just as a mirror [reflects] a face; and since the *puruṣa*, consisting of consciousness, is luminous by nature, if there were a reflection, it would not be perceived by people like us because he remains in a stage inaccessible to our experience.

That which abides in the stage of non-perception cannot be grasped as a reflection anywhere, even if it were reflected, just as an atom [cannot be perceived]. And since the self of those like us abides in the stage of non-perception, if it were so grasped, there would be liberation for everyone at all times due to the discernment of Nature and Spirit—just as [one perceives] the face and the mirror [separately]. Consequently, no one would exert themselves in hearing, reflecting upon, or meditating on the scriptures. Therefore, that transformation of Nature does not arise from the necessity of fulfilling the purpose of the Spirit.

Nor can it arise from the unseen (adṛṣṭa), for that would entail a logical circle (*cakraka*): for the existence of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) permeated by the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) to be established, there must first be the performance of the means to the unseen based on the cognition of the means to happiness; from that performance, the unseen arises; and upon its arising, the existence of such a mental modification is established at the time of the first creation.
Thus, this would only occur in a state where [the self] is not yet known.

Regarding what was stated [in the Śruti]: "Therefore, through that association, the insentient *liṅga* appears as if it were sentient"—in this regard, what is the meaning of the word "association"? Is it reflection (*pratibimbanam*), or is it the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer (*bhogyabhoktṛbhāva*)? It cannot be reflection, because that has been refuted;
nor can it be the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, because the *puruṣa* is devoid of desire (*nirabhilāṣatvāt*).

Furthermore, in this [Self] which is devoid of desire, the state of being an object of enjoyment for primordial nature (prakṛti) or its state of being an enjoyer is not tenable; for in the absence of experience—characterized by the perception of pleasure and pain—in one who is free from desire, the relationship between the enjoyed and the enjoyer cannot logically exist.

And what is the meaning of this statement, "possessing consciousness" (*cetanāvat*)? Does it mean that the unconscious becomes conscious, or that it is permeated by its reflection? Regarding these, the first position is untenable; for it is impossible for one thing to assume the attributes of another through mere proximity to it. Otherwise, due to the proximity of the Self—which is endowed with attributes such as non-agency—the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) would also have to assume attributes such as non-agency, and thus the entire exposition of the cosmic evolution beginning with "from *prakṛti* comes the Great One" (*mahat*) would collapse.

Regarding this very point, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: consciousness (cetanā) is not the cause for the designation [of agency] in the intellect (buddhi), because it is a property of the self (ātmadharma). Whatever is a property of the self is not the cause for the designation [of agency] elsewhere, just as non-agency and so forth are [properties of the self] in primordial matter (prakṛti); and consciousness is indeed a property of the self.

Now, if it is argued that "in the proximity of consciousness (caitanya), the intellect (buddhi) becomes suffused with its reflection," this too is charming only so long as it is not examined; for since that proximity exists at all times, it follows that the intellect—which persists from the beginning of creation until its dissolution—is always suffused with its reflection, and thus there would be constant cognition. In that case, the statement that [the Self] "remains in a stage inaccessible to perception by those like us" would be contradicted.

Furthermore, in the absence of actual consciousness, it is not logical for this [intellect] to possess the power to determine objects; for indeed, a boy’s capacity to produce burning and so forth is never observed through the metaphorical application of the term "fire.

Whatever is used metaphorically does not accomplish its primary purpose in that context, just as fire and the like do not in the case of a boy; and yet, consciousness is applied metaphorically to the intellect (pṛ.
— so says Bhāṃ; — due to the impossibility of [that] arising, so it is designated, according to Śra.

Furthermore, only when a difference between intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*caitanya*) were established—as they are in the case of a face and a mirror—would it be logical for one to be reflected in the other; yet such a difference is not established. This is because the single nature of pure awareness (*saṃvid*), which assumes various forms such as joy and sorrow, is well-known through experience as that which determines objects.
Therefore, these terms—consciousness, intellect, determination (*adhyavasāya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and cognition (*saṃvitti*)—are synonyms.
Thus, consciousness is indeed knowledge, since it is expressed by words synonymous with it, just like "awakening" (*bodha*).
For in common worldly usage, the terms "he intends," "he knows," "he perceives," "he resolves," and "he sees" are employed as synonyms;
and a real difference in meaning does not follow from a mere difference in words, as that would lead to over-extension.
We observe that this very single form of consciousness undergoes various transformations (*vivarta*) in the form of joy, sorrow, and so forth.
Intellect, apprehension, and knowledge are synonymous.
(Nyāyasūtra 1.1.15) [Cited in Nyāyamañjarī, p. 74]
1.15 Praśastabhāṣya, page 171.
Intellect (*buddhi*), it is said, is a transformation of the three *guṇas*, and since the three *guṇas* are insentient, intellect itself is insentient;
it transforms into the form of objects solely through the channel of the senses.
The power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), however, is unchanging and has the nature of eternal consciousness.

Due to its proximity to that [intellect], the intellect—which is like a magnet—attains, as it were, the nature of consciousness by assuming the reflection of that [consciousness]; transformed into the form of the object, it perceives the object.
Therefore, that transformation of the intellect which takes the form of blue is called the *vṛtti* characterized by cognition (*jñāna*).

However, the connection of the reflection of the Self, which has been transferred to the intellect, with the blue form of the intellect is called the "activity" (*vyāpāra*) of the Self; it is designated as the *vṛtti* of the Self, appearing as if it were the Self's own operation.

This very principle of *buddhi*, being insentient by nature like the lunar orb, does not shine by itself; rather, it shines through the reflection of the solar orb of consciousness and illuminates objects. Therefore, to refute that [notion], the following synonyms are set forth: "intellect" (*buddhi*), "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*)—Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā 1.1.1.
Praśastapāda, p.
171: For cognition is indeed determination (adhyavasāya), as well as consciousness (saṃvit) and the act of experiencing (saṃvedana).
"Consciousness" (saṃvitti) and "volition" (cetanā)—these are all designations for sentience. (Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 115)
In the *Sanmati-ṭīkā* (p.
304) and the *Syādvāda-ratnākara* (p. 238), it is stated that [the views] are identical: "The person intends; the intellect knows"—in this case as well, the meaning does not differ (*Nyāyabhāṣya* 3).
2.3 Only he who perceives, knows, and determines also sees and cognizes; indeed, we do not observe any difference in the nature of the object here.

As for what was also stated—that, "deceived by the force of a particular conjunction, one does not discern the distinction between intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*caitanya*)," and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for even in the case of fire and an iron ball, there is no mutual difference, since the substance of the iron ball is experienced as arising as a single entity that, through proximity to fire, abandons its prior form and becomes the locus of specific modifications (*paryāya*) of color and touch, just like a jar-substance which, by abandoning its raw form, becomes the locus of the state of being cooked.

Likewise here too, when a single mode consisting of the nature of self-luminosity and other-luminosity is being experienced, the existence of another [mode] should not be admitted; otherwise, there would be no determination of unity anywhere, and there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all worldly transaction. For even when a single desired object is being experienced, activity and so forth toward it would be impossible due to the suspicion that another [object] exists, were one to avoid the undesirable by [admitting such a suspicion].

Therefore, since there is an uncontradicted appearance of unity, one who desires to establish unity in an object appearing through the exclusion of others must also accept the unity of the transformation of consciousness (*cid-vivarta*), which—though it is the substratum of multiple attributes such as agency and enjoyership established by experience—is itself experienced as a single entity; for there is no other intellect (*buddhi*) distinct from that [consciousness] with which it could be associated.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is not perceived apart from something else should not be accepted as being distinct from it; for example, a jar is not perceived apart from its form consisting of a broad base, a belly, and so forth. And the intellect (*buddhi*) is not perceived apart from consciousness (*caitanya*), because there is no difference between fire and a mass of iron (*vahnya-yogolaka*). (Page 190, Line 8)
And as for what was stated [in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*,
p. 26, u.], beginning with "by means of the functioning of the sense organs and the mind," that too is incorrect, because the functioning of the sense organs and so forth has already been refuted.

Or let it be so; nevertheless, if the mental modifications (buddhi-vṛtti) that extend to each individual soul were cognizable by another cognition, then all the defects mentioned in the [Yoga] system would follow as a consequence, as well as the fact that the Self would possess the form of the object transferred [to the mind]. Does it then perceive this the intellect itself, or the Self? It cannot be the intellect itself; for as long as it does not perceive itself, it is impossible for it to perceive, "I am equal to this [object]. But if it does perceive itself, then its self-cognizability (svasaṃviditatva) is established. (Page 190, Line 1)

Whether by itself or through another cognition, if there is the apprehension of the similarity between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the object, then all the defects already attributed to the Buddhist position follow as a consequence.

Would the self (*ātman*) apprehend that similarity after having apprehended both the intellect and the object, or without having apprehended them? It cannot be without having apprehended them; for if the object and the intellect are not apprehended, the apprehension of their similarity is impossible. Indeed, the apprehension of similarity—that "this is similar to that"—is logical only when the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of both are apprehended, but not when they are not so apprehended.

For instance: the apprehension of similarity is preceded by the apprehension of both [the object and the standard], because it is an apprehension of similarity, like the apprehension of the similarity between a cow and a gavaya. Now, if it is argued that this person apprehends the two objects of cognition (buddhy-artha), is it through itself or by another cognition? If its apprehension were through itself, the postulation of a further cognition would be futile;

yet, since an action cannot occur without an instrument, that postulation must be for the sake of efficacy. This too is mere faith, for it is established that the sense organ and the internal organ alone serve as the instruments in that case.
And if that [object] were apprehended by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, at the time of the initial cognition, there is no other cognition present, since the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions (*jñānayaugapadya*) is not admitted. Therefore, how could there be an apprehension of it by that [subsequent cognition] as well, when it is itself non-existent at that time? Moreover, if the possession of a form (*sākāratā*) is admitted, then the absence of conventional usage regarding things that are far past and so forth—which was stated against the Buddhist position—should be understood to apply here as well.
3–5 Nyāyamañjarī, p. 490;
Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 115.
*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 61; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 26; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 233.

By this, the Cārvāka— who asserts that "cognition is not self-cognized because it is a transformation of the elements (*bhūtapariṇāma*), like a jar"— is also refuted; for if cognition were cognizable by another cognition, all the defects stated in the positions of the Yogas and Sāṃkhyas would follow as consequences,
and its being a transformation of the elements is unproven, since it is a transformation of the Self (*ātman*).

The establishment of the self will be set forth in the section on the determination of objects of knowledge (*prameya-pariccheda*) during the examination of the Cārvāka doctrine; therefore, enough of this digression.
Knowledge is not self-cognized, because it is a transformation of the elements transformed into the form of the body, like bile and so forth. [End of] *Pramāṇaparikṣā*, page 62.
Having thus explained the first part of the verse, the explanation of the latter part is now commenced:
Explanation of the second half of the verse:

Among the specific types of cognition previously explained, such as *avagraha* (perception) and the rest, each preceding one possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the subsequent determination;
each succeeding cognition is the result (*phala*), because it is that which is to be accomplished by the former.
Therefore, just as *īhā* is the fruit when *avagraha* is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too should it be applied to the subsequent stages.

This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsaka who maintains that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇyavādin*): "Granted that the distinction between these [cognitive stages] as means of valid cognition and their fruits may be established in the manner described; however, their validity must be accepted as intrinsic. For if validity were accepted as extrinsic (*parataḥ*), many logical faults would ensue."

For instance—the existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its capacity to determine an object, or its activity is the determination of the object; this validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). It arises from the very same causal complex that produces the mere cognition itself.

Indeed, it does not depend upon any additional factor, such as a "quality" (*guṇa*), either with respect to its own nature or its own operation, beyond the causal complex that produced it; for it is not perceived through a positive form or through its effect, unlike inference (*anumāna*).

Indeed, in the case of inference, no other cause for the production of validity is observed apart from the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) which produces the cognition itself; for it is through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the production of that [validity] is understood to proceed from that very [three-fold character].

Furthermore, validity is the capacity (*śakti*) to determine the actual nature of the object, and the capacities of entities manifest spontaneously (*svataḥ*), not being dependent on the causes that produce them.
As it has been said:
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic;

the Naiyāyikas hold them to be extrinsic; the Buddhists say that the latter is intrinsic while the former is extrinsic; and the proponents of the Veda declare that validity is intrinsic and invalidity is extrinsic.
The followers of Jaimini maintain that validity is intrinsic and invalidity is extrinsic; first,
let this matter concerning all cognitions be considered at all times.
Are validity and invalidity intrinsic or extrinsic?
Let it be understood that the validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic.

In the same way, the capacity of consciousness to discern the true nature of an object does not arise from the eyes and other sense organs—since that capacity is not present in them—but rather manifests from itself alone.

If, however, the determination of validity were to arise from a cognition of correspondence (*saṃvādajñāna*), a cognition of excellence (*guṇajñāna*), or a cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyājñāna*), then the faults of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and so forth would follow: because a cognition of correspondence would require another cognition of correspondence; a cognition of excellence would require another cognition of excellence; and a cognition of causal efficacy would require something other than itself—such that the validity of the first cognition would depend on the second, and the second on the first, resulting in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Since the cognition of correspondence and so forth determines its object independently of further correspondence, what is the basis for this aversion toward the first [cognition] being of that nature? And it has been said: "Just as the first cognition requires its own correspondence, so too must a further correspondence be sought by that correspondence; yet, if this were desired for anyone at all, then validity would be established by itself (*svataḥ*)."

If the first [cognition] is of such a nature, for what reason would there be aversion [to it]? (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sūtra 2, Verse 76).
