Therefore, validity is everywhere inherent in itself; just as the first cognition does not depend upon its corroboration, these three verses are cited in the following works: *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 40 (upper).

Validity is not established through a relationship of mutual dependence;

rather, invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Indeed, in its production, it depends upon another cause called "defect" (*doṣa*), which is distinct from the causes that produce the cognition itself. Furthermore, regarding its own effect, known as cessation [of doubt], the apprehension of itself is required;
for invalidity is threefold, consisting of the distinctions of doubt, error, and non-cognition.

In that regard, since ignorance consists of the mere absence of knowledge, it is established by itself and thus requires nothing else; however, for the arising of doubt and error, the following are accepted as causes according to their respective possibilities: defects of the knower such as hunger and so forth, defects of the mind such as lack of attention and so forth, defects of the sense organs such as cataracts and so forth, and defects of the object such as instability and so forth.

And there is a requirement for the cognition of itself in its own effect, which is called "cessation" (nivṛtti). As soon as a cognition arises, it does not cause a person to desist merely by being perceived in common [with other cognitions], so long as it is not determined to be false through the cognition of defects in its causes and so forth.

Nor does validity depend on any other cause called "excellences" (guṇa) at the time of its production; therefore, that too must be said to be extrinsic (parataḥ). This is because excellences are not established from any source whatsoever, or if they were established, they would have no function in its production, since their purpose is fulfilled solely in the removal of defects.

For such indeed is the nature of entities: that in arising by themselves, they manifest their own opposites; and virtues are the adversaries of defects. Therefore, when those [defects] have been removed by them, the causes, functioning by their very nature, produce knowledge that is indeed valid.
If, however, even when the knowledge has been produced, the capacity to perform its own function did not exist inherently, then its very nature would remain unproduced.

For it is not the case that when fire—which possesses the property of non-illuminativeness—is produced, properties such as illuminativeness are subsequently imparted to it by some other cause. Thus, let it be granted that qualities (guṇas) have a function in producing knowledge that constitutes a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); nevertheless, validity does not exist extrinsically (parataḥ). For validity is indeed the state of being a cognizer (bodhakatva), and if that is established for knowledge at the very moment of its birth, independent of anything else, then the self-evident establishment of intrinsic validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) is proven beyond all obstruction.

And thus, while the intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya*)—characterized by the capacity to produce cognition—is established for all cognitions, it is only in those cases where a sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) or the knowledge of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣajñāna*) arises that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is determined extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
Invalidity is divided into three types: falsity (*mithyātva*), non-cognition (*ajñāna*), and doubt (*saṃśaya*);
however, since two of these [falsity and doubt] are positive entities (*vastu*), they can arise here from a defective cause.
Furthermore, an invalid cognition would, by its very nature, be a grasper of its own object. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sūtra 2, verse 54)
Its cessation cannot occur as long as its falsity has not been apprehended by others.
(Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sūtra 2, Verse 85)

1.5 A demonstration of how validity is both intrinsic and extrinsic in some respect, preceded by a refutation of the theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya-vāda*).
To this, the following reply is given:

as for what was stated—that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the capacity to determine an object—does that nature of validity consist in a capacity that determines the mere object, or one that determines the object as it truly is? In the first case, there is a deviation from that definition in the case of cognitions such as doubt, error, and dreams, because even though these are invalid, the capacity to determine the mere object exists within them.

In the second case, however, there is the establishment of extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*), because validity—characterized by the capacity for the correct determination of an object—is not produced from the causal complex of the eye and so forth that produces mere consciousness alone; rather, only a causal complex endowed with excellences (*guṇa*) possesses the capacity to produce it. [Objection: Since excellences are not perceived either through a positive formulation (*vidhimukhena*) or through their effects (*kāryamukhena*), how can their production depend upon them? [Response: This is an unconsidered statement; for, being witnessed by all people, they are firmly established in common experience.

For one who asserts that there are no such qualities as clarity residing in the eye and other [senses], proximity and steadiness residing in the object, intentionality and so forth residing in the mind, contentment and well-being residing in the self, or vividness and so forth residing in the light, is not contradicted by worldly consensus (lokapratīti). (p. 195, l. 8 – *ārūḍha*—Ā.)
[Objection:

"But clarity (*nairmalya*) and so forth are the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the eye and other [senses], not their quality (*guṇa*). How, then, is it established that they are its nature—is it because [the sense] arises only as conjoined with them, or because it is not perceived apart from them? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; for although a jar or the like arises only as conjoined with them, those [colors, etc. are nevertheless perceived as qualities of it."

And how could the status of being a defect (doṣatā) be established for such things as cataracts (kācakāmala) and the like for one who speaks thus, given that the eyes and other organs arise already endowed with that [defect], as in the case of one born blind? By this, the second position is also refuted; for even though cataracts and the like are not perceived as distinct from the eye, color-form, and so forth, or from pots and the like, they are nonetheless recognized as defects. Furthermore, what is the meaning of the word "intrinsic nature" (svarūpa) here—is it identity (tādātmya), or is it being nothing but that (tanmātratva)? In the first alternative, there is no negation of the quality-status (guṇatva) of clarity and so forth, because identity does not stand in opposition to that [quality]; otherwise, there would be an absence of quality-status even for color-form and the like.
The second alternative, however, is untenable; for even while the eye and so forth persist, this [defect] ceases, and thus it cannot be established that the one is merely the other.

That which ceases even while something else persists is not merely that thing itself; for example, while a cloth persists, the quality of whiteness ceases due to conjunction with blue and so forth. Likewise, even while the eye and so forth persist, the clarity and such of one afflicted by jaundice or the like cease—thus [the opponent argues].
(Śrīdhara)

And if qualities are not admitted in the eye and other sense organs, then the existence of a gradation in their sharpness would not be possible; yet this gradation does exist, as evidenced by such cognitions as "this person has keen faculties" and "this person has even keener faculties."

Alternatively, how can the statement in various places such as *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika* 2.65—"In the absence of the acceptance of excellences (*guṇa*), there is an absence of defects (*doṣa*) due to those excellences"—which proclaims the existence of excellences, be appropriate? Nor should it be argued that "excellence" is nothing at all, since the term is used merely for the absence of defect; for if that were so, it would follow by implication that "defect" likewise does not exist, since one could then say that the term "defect" is used merely for the absence of excellence. The mouth of one who asserts this does not turn back [in shame].

Furthermore, since the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*)—such as *nairmalya* (clarity) and so forth—is not a positive quality (*aguṇatva*), how could there be the worldly convention "this eye possesses excellence" upon seeing it? Moreover, the imparting of an excellence (*guṇātiśaya*) to the eye by means of collyrium and the like is well-established; otherwise, how could one perceive specific forms through the application of ointments from the eyes of tigers and other animals in the middle of a night of dense darkness, or perceive objects hidden by water through the application of ointment made from the fat of a crocodile? Nor can it be maintained that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) because qualities function merely to remove defects and are thus not the cause of validity; for if that were so, it would follow that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is also intrinsic, since defects function to remove qualities and therefore do not produce invalidity.
Therefore, both must be accepted as being either from themselves or from another, because the objections and their resolutions are identical.

Nor is it accepted that validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises for a manifested cognition (*jñānavyakti*) after its production from some other cause—like the redness of a cloth produced by lac and so forth—such that the following objection would find scope: "Since the cognition perishes immediately after its production, upon what would validity depend? For we accept that validity, characterized by the capacity to determine the object as it actually is, arises from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), just like invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), which is characterized by the capacity to determine the object otherwise than it is.
In this regard, there is clarity (*paṭutva*).
The outpouring of Kumārila, the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*,
is like a crocodile—
a specific kind of aquatic creature.
Śiśumāra:
For that very same reason, according to your logic, it can also be said that invalidity is inherently established (*svataḥ prasakta*),
since this is clearly evident even in that case.
Therefore, from those defects, there is an absence of excellences; due to that absence,
there is a non-existence of the nature of valid cognition, whereby the general rule remains unrefuted.
Tattvasaṃgraha 3067: Would it not follow that those cognitions which are non-cognitions would themselves lack the status of being valid means of knowledge?
Precisely because there is no distinction [between them], it is so everywhere and in every way.

Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 243.

As for what was stated—that in the production of the validity of inference no other quality besides the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) is observed, and so forth—that too is charming only when left unexamined. For in its production, the very quality of *sādhyāvinābhāvitva* (inseparable connection with the probandum) exists.

[Objection: But how can the inseparable connection of the reason with the probandum be a "quality," since it is simply the completeness of the reason’s own nature? [Reply: In that case, the absence of that inseparable connection would likewise be a deficiency in the reason’s own nature, rather than a "defect" (*doṣa*). Consequently, invalidity in inference could not possibly arise from defects.

Now, if it is argued that here the defect consists solely in the deficiency of its own nature (*svarūpa-vaikalya*), then let its completeness (*sākalya*) be the excellence (*guṇa*), since there is no distinction [between the two]. Thus, it is established that even in inference, validity arises from excellence (*guṇa*); and in the production of the validity of scripture (*āgama*), the operation of an excellence such as a vision of reality (*yathārtha-darśana*) is well-known, just as the operation of a defect such as an unreal vision (*ayathārtha-darśana*) is known in the production of its invalidity.
On page 195, line 11:

However, for the reason that produces an inference, its quality is precisely its inseparable connection with the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvitva*), whereas its deficiency therein is a fault; as stated in *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 42, section U.

As for what was stated—“But in the acquisition of their own nature (ātmalābha) [the properties of things arise],” and so forth—that too is incorrect; for by such reasoning, the consequence follows that invalidity (aprāmāṇya) would also exist intrinsically (svataḥ). For just as the capacity to manifest an object as it truly is—which is the form of validity—is said to be intrinsic because it arises in the cognition even though it does not exist in the causes such as the eyes, so too should the capacity to manifest an object erroneously—which is the form of invalidity—be said to be intrinsic, since there is no distinction between the two cases; for that [invalidity] also does not exist there [in the causes] in the same way [as validity].

And thus, there would be a contradiction with the verse from the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Sūtra 2, Verse 54: "In this case, because it is a real entity, there is the possibility of two kinds [of error] arising from a defective cause" (p. 195, l.

Furthermore, is the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in its production, in its cognition, or in its own operation? Among these, it cannot first be in its production. For instance: validity must be produced by a causal aggregate distinct from the collection of causes that produce the means of knowledge, because even when those [causes] persist, [validity] is absent; whatever is such [i.e., absent despite the persistence of others] is distinct from them, just as conjunction and the like—which are absent even when a jar persists—are distinct from it; this case is exactly so, therefore it is so. Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for in the case of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), although the awareness that serves as the substratum of validity exists, validity does not arise.
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it does not occur in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) alone;
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), precisely because it is excluded from the counter-example;
nor is it one whose application is mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because there is an absence of perception or other means of knowledge that would establish a contrary object.
Validity is produced by a causal complex distinct from the collection of causes that produce the means of valid cognition;

furthermore, among the meanings of the word *sva*—namely, self (*ātman*), one's own (*ātmīya*), kinsman (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*)—in which sense is it understood here? Since [the meanings of] kinsman and wealth are impossible in this context, only "self" and "one's own" remain.

In that case as well, the meaning would have to be either that validity arises by itself (*svataḥ*) without a cause, from the [cognition] itself; or from the [cognition] itself; or from its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Regarding the first position, since there can be no restriction of place or time for that which is causeless, it would follow that it must exist everywhere and at all times.

In the second alternative as well, does the term "from itself" (*svataḥ*) qualify validity (*prāmāṇya*) or the cognition (*pramā*)? If it qualifies validity, it follows that validity acquires its own existence from validity; and that is untenable. For it is neither perceived nor logically possible for a single entity to possess the properties of being both produced and producer with respect to its own self. To explain: validity is not produced from its own self because it is an effect, like invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) or like a jar and so forth.
[Note: *Sva* means the knower in the sense of "self," the soul in the sense of "in oneself," one's own in all three genders, and wealth when not feminine.]
Amarakośa, Nānārthavarga,
Pramāṇavarga, Śravasvarga.

By this, the second alternative is also refuted: Is that causal complex which produces mere consciousness (vijñānamātra) [consciousness] relative to itself, or is it distinct? If it is distinct, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*), because it is accepted that all objects arise from the specificities of their own respective causal complexes.

And likewise, invalidity and all objects would be established intrinsically (*svataḥ*) in that same manner. Furthermore, the fact that [the causal complex] produces mere cognition has already been refuted by the demonstration of its specific nature (*viśiṣṭatva*).

The claim that it produces "mere cognition" is accessible only through blind faith, because a "mere cognition" distinct from specific instances of valid and invalid cognitions is never perceived at any time or place, just as a "mere tree" distinct from specific individuals such as *dhava* trees is not perceived.

Furthermore, since mere cognition, like a mere tree, possesses the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), and according to your own view it does not arise from anything [specific], how could there be any causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces it? Moreover, if you accept that validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises from the same causal complex that produces mere cognition, then it would follow that validity must also arise in cases of doubt and the like, because that causal complex is no different there either. If you argue that in cases of doubt and the like the pure causal complex for cognition is absent—otherwise, how could they arise?—then in that case, cognition itself would not arise either, because its causal complex would be impure and thus incomplete.

[Objection: Surely the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed complete; however, there is the further intrusion of defects such as cataracts (*kāca*) or jaundice (*kāmalā*). If that is so, then due to the intrusion of these additional causes, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) produced by them should also arise. Validity, however, being born from the causal complex of cognition, would emerge like the cognition itself and be difficult to prevent.

[Response: Now, validity arises from a causal complex qualified by the absence of defects, not from any other. [Objection: In that case, validity is established as extrinsic (*parataḥ*), since its production is well-known to result from a cause called the "absence of defects" which is distinct from the causes of the cognition itself.

For the absence of defects is not the cause of cognition, since the arising of cognition is observed even in the case of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) despite its absence; however, it is indeed a cause for the arising of validity (*prāmāṇya*), because of the occurrence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

If this [absence of defects], whose capacity is established through positive and negative concomitance, were not the producer of validity, then defects would likewise lack the capacity to produce invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
— *na vyati* (Ā), *bhā*.

Furthermore, what is done to the eyes and other sense organs by defects such that they do not produce validity when those defects are present? If it is their power to produce [cognition] that is removed, is that very same power which produces mere cognition also the power to produce validity, or is it something else? If it is the same, then upon its departure, how could they have any function even in producing mere cognition? If, on the other hand, it is different, then why is validity not extrinsic (*parataḥ*)? Therefore, intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is not tenable regarding the production [of cognition].
Nor does it reside in the cognition itself, because since the ascertainment of validity is occasional, it cannot be without a cause.
To explain: whatever is occasional is not without a cause, just like a jar or other such things; and the ascertainment of validity is indeed occasional.
Now, would its cause be its own nature or something else? It cannot be its own nature, because you admit that [the cognition] is not self-cognized (*asvasaṃvidita*).

Nor can it be something else, because that would entail the contradiction of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). And what is this other cause? Is it perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), since nothing else is applicable here? If it is perception, no; for perception operates upon an object connected with the sense organs, and there is no connection between the sense organs and the cognition of the object such that the validity of this [cognition]—which consists in its nature of determining the object as it truly is—could be perceived through perception. This is because the sense organs are connected only to specific objects, such as color-form (*rūpa*), and to the substratum possessing those qualities.
Nor is it cognizable through perception arising from mental activity, because such an experience does not exist;
nor is it cognizable through inference, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*).

If it is argued that the manifestation of the object (*arthaprākaṭya*) is the inferential mark, [we ask]: is it qualified by "being in accordance with reality" (*yathārtha*), or is it without qualification? It cannot be qualified by "being in accordance with reality," because prior to the ascertainment of validity, the qualification of the manifestation of the object as being "in accordance with reality" is unestablished.
If its validity were established through that [cognition], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Furthermore, if this [cognition] were to determine validity without any qualification, it would follow that it determines validity even in the case of false cognition, as there is no distinction between them.
Therefore, it is not logical that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) even in the case of the apprehension [of an object].
Regarding the non-ascertainment of validity (prāmāṇya):
if it has a cause, is that cause intrinsic (svanimitta) or extrinsic (anyanimitta)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 42;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 13).
Alternatively, it might be [argued]:
"Does that result—whether unqualified or qualified by correspondence (yathārthatva)—infer the validity of its own cause, namely the cognitive operation of the knower? (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 168).
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 42;

—It is not a particularity either—[says the opponent]. Nor [is it a particularity] with respect to its own effect (*svakārya*); for what is its effect? Is it human activity (*puruṣapravṛtti*) or the determination of an object (*arthapariccheda*)? In that regard, it is only logical that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the cause of human activity when it has been ascertained, just as invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is the cause of desisting from activity.

For those who act with foresight do not engage in action based on mere desire alone; for even when there is an intense longing, such persons do not proceed to take a medicinal elixir (*rasāyana*)—an efficacious drug endowed with the power to remove old age, death, and so forth—if its efficacy as such has not been ascertained. Indeed, all factors that cause engagement depend upon certainty.

Nor is validity independent of its own apprehension with respect to its own operation called the "ascertainment of the object" (*arthapariccheda*); for is this [operation] merely the ascertainment of an object, or is it the ascertainment of an object as it truly is? It cannot be merely the ascertainment of an object, because that is possible even when there is invalidity.

Furthermore, the ascertainment of an object as it truly is does not arise from a means of knowledge whose validity has not been apprehended; therefore, since only the mere ascertainment of an object—which is common to both valid and invalid cognitions—arises [from the means of knowledge].

Furthermore, there is no consequence of defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the apprehension of that [validity]; because in the state of proficiency (*abhyāsāvasthā*), validity is determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*), and since there is no dependence on corroboration (*saṃvāda*) and the like, infinite regress does not arise. Indeed, a cognition of water regarding water that is embraced by proficiency does not depend on corroboration and so forth for the realization of its own nature as being capable of determining the object’s actual state of affairs. This is because such a cognition—which consists of a decisive ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) that "this is exactly thus"—is well-known to every living being, just like invalidity.

Indeed, in the case of an object well-practiced [through familiarity], such as a mirage and the like, the appearance of water does not depend upon a subsequent realization of its nature as being incapable of determining the object's true state—such as its lack of correspondence—to establish that incapacity. This is because its nature as such is well-established for everyone there by itself (*svataḥ*). Thus, both [the cognition and its validity] must be accepted as established there by themselves.
However, in the state of non-familiarity, validity is established through another [cognition] (*parataḥ*);

yet this does not lead to an infinite regress, because since that [subsequent cognition] has a familiar object, its own validity is established by itself, rendering it independent of further means of valid cognition.

For in the case of an unfamiliar object appearing as water, its validity is ascertained either through the cognition of causal efficiency—such as the croaking of frogs or the fetching of water—or through inference arising from such signs, because it has been repeatedly determined to be invariably concomitant with water.

Thus, for a discerning person, all activity is rightly based on that which is ascertained by means of valid cognition alone; for others, however, activity may sometimes proceed even from doubt and the like.

Not even one of these four positions is accepted by the Buddhists, because the position of non-restriction (aniyamapakṣa) is desired. For it has been previously explained that both of these—namely, that some things [arise] from themselves and some from others—are [part of this view].

In the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, page 811, some have stated directly: "In that regard, through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), validity (*prāmāṇya*) is ascertained by us as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*); but in the absence of repeated practice, it is extrinsic (*parataḥ*)."

And that [establishment] belongs only to the proponents of the "may-be" (syādvādin), because they determine their own objects; it does not belong to those who maintain that all knowledge is devoid of self-determination.
In some cases, because the intrinsic validity [of a cognition] is ascertained through extreme repetition, there is no fault such as infinite regress;

Thus it is established: the successful accomplishment of what is desired [arises] from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while its opposite arises from what appears as such (*tadābhāsa*).
Validity (*prāmāṇya*), however, is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*) through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), whereas otherwise it is established extrinsically (*parataḥ*). (Pramāṇaparīkṣā, p. 63)
—Therefore, [it is] well-known...

Śrī. But surely, even the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*) is seen in the state of dreaming despite the absence of an object; so what is the distinction of this [cognition] from the preceding cognition? This too is not sound, because in the waking state, no such non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) is observed.

Indeed, it is not the case that the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) is perceived independently of the object in the same way that the cognition of an object is perceived during the waking state even in the absence of an object; for if that were so, one might suspect its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) at that time and determine its validity through another subsequent cognition of purposeful action, and based on that state, the investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth would be extended. Therefore, even the slightest suspicion of parity between what is perceived in the waking state and what is perceived in the dream state is not beneficial.

For a person acting with foresight does not consider the waking state to be equivalent to the dream state; otherwise, by that very example, it would follow that all cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of external objects. In such a case, where and for whom could there be validity (*prāmāṇya*) or invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*)?
[Objection: But surely, even in a dream, there exists cognition manifesting purposeful action (*arthakriyābhāsi-jñāna*), yet that [cognition] lacks validity, as does its cause—the first [cognition].
Indeed, that state is not at all erroneous, for it is entirely without an external basis;
in those states, there is no correspondence with external objects.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 43a.
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p.
15: Therefore, there is no equality with that which is perceived in a dream-state.

[Objection: But if the validity of a prior cognition is established by means of a cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), then it would follow that the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel, as well as the cognition of a counterfeit coin, would also be valid. [Reply: That is not so; for by such a cognition of purposeful action, the very invalidity of the prior cognition is established, since a correspondence (*saṃvāda*) with it is impossible.

For while there is a cognition of the jewel when its light is situated in the opening of the keyhole, there is a cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) regarding the jewel itself when it is connected with the interior space of the room; since these two have different objects by virtue of grasping objects at different locations, how could they be non-discrepant (*avisamvāda*), like a cognition of delusion produced by cataracts and the like? Furthermore, in the case of a counterfeit coin, would the cognition of it as counterfeit, the cognition of it as a coin, or the cognition of it as base metal be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Regarding that, in the first two positions, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

The third position, however, is untenable; for it is impossible to verify the fulfillment of the purposeful action (arthakriyā) intended by that [statement], since the attainment of complete consciousness and wealth constitutes the purposeful action for a donkey-driver, whereas the attainment of a few instances of consciousness and wealth does not, especially when the speech is false and deceptive.
*Drama* is a specific type of seal;
*mūlya* is the price;
*karmaṇyā*, *vidhā*, *bhṛtyā*, *bhṛti*, *bharma*, and *vetana* are synonyms for wages.
*Bharaṇya*, *bharaṇa-mūlya*, *nirveśa*, and *paṇa* are synonyms for wages; this is according to the Amarakośa, Śūdravarga 38.
*Kharaka* means "truth," as it is called *khara* in the vernacular.

In some cases, even on a deceptive peak that is [otherwise] high and lofty, because a certain amount of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is observed through knowledge, the knowledge of it as a deceptive peak is indeed a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, the knowledge of it as a non-deceptive peak is not a valid means of cognition, because it lacks corroboration (*saṃvāda*).
For its purposeful activity consists in the attainment of complete consciousness, not the attainment of only partial consciousness (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 43, part 2).

As for what was stated—that "validity is indeed the capacity to inform," and so forth—even there, does validity consist merely in the capacity to inform, or rather in the capacity to inform an object? Regarding these two alternatives, the first position is untenable, because the mere capacity to inform is never perceived in any cognition, since all cognitions are determined precisely by their capacity to inform their own objects, whether external or internal.

As for the second position, would that [validity] consist in the capacity to inform any object whatsoever, or the capacity to inform an object that is non-erroneous? It cannot be the capacity to inform a non-erroneous object, because it has been established that this depends upon a specific collection of causes.

Nor does it consist in merely making an object known; for otherwise, even the cognition of a double moon and the like would entail validity. Consequently, that which is cognized by such [cognition], namely the double moon and so forth, would not be unreal.
Indeed, whatever is cognized by a valid cognition is not false, just as pleasure and the like; and the double moon and so forth are cognized by a valid cognition.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the cognition of a double moon and the like consists precisely in its nature as consciousness (*bodharūpataiva*), this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is not distinct from something else is necessarily concomitant with the mere nature of that thing; just as "treeness," which is not distinct from possessing branches and so forth, is concomitant with that alone; and validity is not distinct from the nature of consciousness.

But surely, the very nature of a cognition that has not been sublated is its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); yet here, a sublation does arise. For this very reason, we accept that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). That too is unsatisfactory: if it is indeed the case that the validity of a cognition exists simultaneously with its own nature, then while that [validity] is present, how could there be any room for extrinsic invalidity?

Others, however, describe the meaning of the proposition differently: they claim that validity consists in being of the nature of cognition (*bodhātmakatva*). This is incorrect, because it is not logical that being of the nature of cognition alone constitutes validity, since it is possible even in erroneous cognition; for external and internal objects... [Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, p. 811].* *Note: The source text fragment provided ends with "bahirantaścārthā–ā॰", which appears to be a citation marker or a partial reference to the Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā.*

If it is argued that the excellence of awakening constitutes validity, then one should not have said: "And that [validity] of cognitions is indeed intrinsic, not produced by qualities" (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 811).
Nor should it have been said: "Of the knower... (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-bhāṣya).

Furthermore, is this invalidity (aprāmāṇya) the absence of validity, or is it a real entity (vastubhūta) as a property? In the first case, the absence of validity would be said to be the very absence of being a cognition (jñānatva), for according to your position, validity is indeed nothing other than being a cognition. Consequently, the claim that a cognition lacks its nature as a cognition due to something external is entirely inconsistent; for that which is determined by a specific form cannot become something of a different form through another cause, just as a jar possesses the form of a broad base and belly. Since a cognition is determined by the form of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), it is not logical for invalidity to arise from a subverting cognition (bādhaka-jñāna).
From defects arises the absence of knowledge; [it has] the form of a reflection. (Bhāmatī) Ba., Ja.
Furthermore, [the opponent claims] that the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is restricted [by subsequent factors].

Moreover, how can the non-occurrence of the knowledge of a defect in the cause or of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) bring about the absence of validity for a past cognition? For that [subsequent cognition] does not exist at the time of the prior cognition, nor does the prior cognition exist at the time of the [subsequent one]. Thus, if its invalidity were produced by it [the subsequent cognition] at its own time, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because it would follow that even the cognition of a jar would be invalid at the time of the cognition of a cloth.
Indeed, nothing other than [valid] cognition is accepted by anyone as being invalid at another time.

Now, if it is argued that the object (dharma) itself is invalidity, then it must be stated: what is this? If you say it is doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*), [we reply]: since those two consist of the nature of cognition, it is not logical for them to be invalidity. For instance: "Doubt and error are not invalidity because they are cognitions, like a cognition that is accepted as valid"—this is the recurring [argument]. (Ā., Ba., Ja.)
In the cognition of the cloth, [the object] is not reached—Ba, Ja.

Furthermore, since validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the general rule for all cognition, how could there be the possibility of qualities characterized by doubt or error? For that [invalidity] must arise from the cognition itself, from its object, from auxiliary factors, from the knower, from the influence of another cognition, from the sense organs and so forth, or from a connection with a substratum. In the first case, it would follow that the cognition would always remain in that state [of invalidity]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever arises from the very nature of a thing never departs from it, just as the blueness of a blue object does not depart from it; and such is the nature of doubt and so forth in the case of cognition.

Even in the second alternative, does the operation [of the sense organ] consist in the production of doubt and so forth regarding the object in its mere generality, or regarding a qualified object? If it is regarding the object in its mere generality, then every cognition would take the form of doubt and so forth. If it is regarding a qualified object, then what is this "qualification" of the object—is it its lack of discrimination, or its being affected by similarity? If it is its lack of discrimination, then the object in its mere generality would have been admitted, and in that case, the aforementioned fault applies.

Now, if it is argued that an object, impaired by similarity, produces a cognition of error through the recollection of a contrary particular, and a cognition of doubt through the recollection of both particulars—that too is unsatisfactory; for since every object necessarily possesses some degree of similarity, such cognitions would arise at all times. If it is claimed that only a perceived similarity acts in this way, then it should do so even when [the object] is present before one's eyes.

If it is argued that the non-apprehension of the specific feature (*viśeṣa*) is also a cause for that [non-production], and since that [non-apprehension] is absent when [the object] is present, it does not produce [the cognition]; [we reply: But from what does the non-apprehension of an existing specific feature arise? If it is due to unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), that is not so; for we do not observe that *adṛṣṭa* acts as an obstacle to an effect when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is complete.

For it may be that, due to the influence of those [adṛṣṭas], sometimes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself does not come together, or even when it has come together, it joins with something heterogeneous, thereby attaining the state of a different causal complex. In this case, since the causal complex consisting of the sense organs and so forth is neither altered nor unjoined, how could there be a non-apprehension of the specific difference? Furthermore, why should the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) not also function in the production of validity (*prāmāṇya*) as well as the non-apprehension of specific differences, such that validity—just like invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*)—would not be extrinsic (*parataḥ*)?
[Objection: Since the ascertainment of validity is spontaneous (*utsargika*), it must arise from the mere presence of those [causes] themselves.
And when that [knowledge] has arisen, doubt and error have no footing; *Tattvasaṃgraha* 2929.
"There is no [defect] in the object, nor is there another [cause]" (variant readings: *ba*, *ja*, *śra*).

By this, the third position is also refuted: that invalidity in the form of doubt and so forth is produced by auxiliary factors such as demerit (*adharma*), whereas validity, which consists in the determination of a non-erroneous object, is produced by merit (*dharma*) and so forth.
Nor is that form produced therein by the cognizer, because it would contradict experience; for no cognizer has such an experience as "May I become one who possesses doubt.

Or, even if such an admission were made, this cognition would not be a cause for the invalidity of the [subsequent] knowledge. To explain: the cognition "May there be doubt for me" is not a cause of invalidity, because it is a cognition, just like the cognition "May I know a jar," and so forth.

Now, suppose this particularity (*viśeṣa*) arises due to the influence of another cognition. In that case too, does it arise from the influence of its own [cognition] or from that of another’s? If it arises from its own, then is this particularity produced by that cognition when it is already existent at its own time, or when it is non-existent? It cannot be the former, because at the time of the subsequent cognition, the prior cognition is no longer possible; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the non-acceptance of two simultaneous cognitions.

And how could that [subsequent cognition] be able to establish this [prior object], given that it is non-existent at its own time? Because they belong to different times, whatever belongs to a different time cannot have its specific qualities established by another; for example, a present crystal cannot be characterized by a *japā* flower existing in the past or future. And since this other cognition belongs to a different time, there can likewise be no arising of doubt or the like from another person’s [cognition], because such a perception does not occur.

[Objection: But surely there exists the cognition among other cognizers that "I am producing doubt in this person. [Reply: That is not so, because it is impossible for the knowledge of other cognizers to be invariably present in every case of doubt.

For whatever is the cause of something must be invariably present in that thing, just as a seed that has reached its final stage is the cause of the sprout; yet the knowledge of other cognizers is not invariably present in the effect such as doubt.
Furthermore, if the sense organs and so forth were the causes of that [doubt], it would follow that doubt and the like would arise in the form of every cognition.

Now, [it might be argued that] its production therein occurs due to a connection with a substratum (*ādhāra*). But is that connection established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or not? If it is established, how could one occupy a substratum known to cause doubt and error, given the consequence that [one's own cognition] would lack validity? If it is not established, how can there be the realization that the nature of doubt and so forth in cognition is produced by that [substratum]?
[In the manuscript, the word *jñāne* appears as *mānaspha-*, *ba*, *ja*.]

Furthermore, O Caitra, is this invalidity in the form of doubt and so forth distinct from the nature of cognition, or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, how can there be a dependence upon distinct causes? If it is distinct, then by that same logic, since the validity consisting of the nature of a correct determination is also established as being distinct from it, it is proven that both arise from causes distinct from the causes of the cognition itself. Enough of this digression;

therefore, it is rightly stated that for apprehension (*avagraha*) and the other stages which have subsequently attained the status of valid cognition, the results are examination (*īhā*) and the rest.

The commentary (*vivṛti*):
In order to refute the view of the Buddhist who does not accept this, he says "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthe*), and so forth.

Because of this statement [in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*], and because the establishment of the result (*phala*) as having the form of the knower is the "attainment" (*adhigati*), according to the dictum "the result is attainment," if that [form] is accepted, then for the "momentary destruction and so forth"—where "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes a category, by which every mode of momentary destruction, such as partlessness and other intrinsic natures, is understood as non-different from the logical mark (*liṅga*)—there would follow the perceptibility, that is, the state of being an object of perception, not only for the reason of existence (*sattva*) but for those as well.
If it is asked, "What fault would there be from that perceptibility? [the author] says here: "Once grasped," and so forth.

Because it apprehends what has already been grasped—that is, what has already been made an object of perception—this inference, such as the inference of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like conventional [perception] or like the conceptual construction that follows upon direct perception.

If it is argued: "Even though momentary destruction and so forth have already been grasped, inference is not invalid because its result is the exclusion of a contrary superimposition (*viparītāropavyavaccheda*)," to this he says: *tat* and so forth.

Between these two—the conventional and the inferential—which are accepted as being respectively invalid and valid, there would have to be a distinct means of knowledge for each, not only for inference over and above direct perception, but also for the conventional over and above those two.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? he says here: because there is no difference in the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*).

For just as, when the distinction of moments is ascertained through inference, the future superimposition does not arise due to the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between the ascertainment and the mind of superimposition—thereby making that [inference] its excluder—so too, when blue and the like are ascertained conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), that [superimposition] which has the form of non-blue and so forth does not arise; therefore, let that [conventional cognition] also be its excluder.
If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault? he says here: "of everything indeed," and so forth.

The validity of all four types of perception would not exist; there would be no validity whatsoever regarding [objects] such as blue or [properties] such as momentary destruction. For what, then, is the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*)? It refers to non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). Of what nature is it? It is that which desires the exclusion of superimpositions (*samāropa-vyavaccheda-ākāṅkṣin*), because it is the cause for the exclusion of superimpositions. Regarding momentary destruction and the like, inference is the means of exclusion; regarding blue and the like, conventional [cognition] is the means. Thus, it is of a nature that desires such exclusion.

The meaning is this: just as in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) dependent upon that [momentariness] lacks authority because only inference (*anumāna*) possesses authority therein, so too in the case of blue and other objects, even there only conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) possesses authority.

By the previous section he showed the absence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); by this [present] section, however, he shows the absence of even the intended means of valid cognition, perception (*pratyakṣa*). [Objection:
But surely it is only the [cognition] that prompts action that is a means of valid cognition, and nothing else, for fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
In the state of practice, non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is the initiator, whereas in the state of non-practice, inference (*anumāna*) is the initiator;
there is no other state in which conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*) could be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being an initiator. To this, he says: "From that," and so forth.
From that non-conceptual cognition, because in the state of practice there is an absence of conventional worldly activity characterized by engagement and withdrawal.

And this similarity to the object (*arthasārūpya*) has been explained in detail on the occasion of establishing determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*). This [similarity] is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is its result; the ascertainment of the object occurs through that very form [of the cognition].
The very form of the object is its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), for by that [form] it is measured;
*Pramāṇasamuccaya* 1.10.

In this context, the apprehension of the object is held to be the fruit of the means of valid cognition; alternatively, self-awareness is the fruit, while the means of valid cognition is either the similarity [of the cognition to the object] or its capacity. (1343)
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, [it is stated that] because the mind of ascertainment and the mind of superimposition stand in a relationship of sublated and sublator, [the former is valid cognition].
(*Pramāṇavārttika* 1)
He desires— ba, ja—
what knowledge does he not [desire]?— ba, ja.

Regarding the passage beginning with "anyadaśā śra" (variant readings *ba*, *ja*), one might think: since all cognitions are admitted to be erroneous, even perception is not admitted to possess validity; how then could even conventional cognition (*saṃvṛti*) constitute a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Would such a claim not appear preposterous? To this, he says: "For one who seeks purposeful action," and so forth.

The term *artha* means that which is sought (*arthyate*) or desired (*abhilaṣyate*), namely the absence of all means of valid cognition (*sakalapramāṇābhāva*). The "activity" (*kriyā*) regarding that [absence] is its apprehension (*upādāna*); for it is one who seeks that [absence] who searches for a means of valid cognition. Why is this? [It is because] he seeks what is non-valid, or as if it were non-valid, meaning as if it were the absence of a means of valid cognition. For, as was stated to the Mādhyamika in the section on the establishment of external objects, the absence of that [means of valid cognition] cannot be established without a means of valid cognition: "For every discerning person seeks a means of valid cognition or a non-valid cognition for the sake of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."

Or rather, the object is that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) and that which is to be adopted (*upādeya*); its "action" (*kriyā*) consists in its attainment (*prāpti*) and avoidance (*parihāra*). For one seeks the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is from that [cognition] that the attainment and avoidance of those two occur, or else one seeks the non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because it is from that that those two do not occur; thus, one investigates.
And since those two do not arise from non-conceptual [perception], this is the intended meaning.
If it is argued that [the cognition] indeed seeks out a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the author says here: "Regarding form and so forth," etc.

That which has form as its beginning—namely taste and so forth—is described thus; likewise, that which has momentary destruction as its beginning—namely partlessness and so forth—is also described thus. Because there is no distinction between the clear and vivid manifestation of these two, validity does not belong to form and so forth alone, nor to momentary destruction and so forth alone. That which depends on something—meaning that which depends on the ascertainment of its own object—or that for which there is dependence upon something—that alone is the result; it is not tenable or logical that the mere attainment [of an object] is the result.

Now, if it is argued that certainty is indeed the result, and that its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists only where it produces that [certainty]—since it has been stated that "that [certainty], moreover, arises from non-conceptual [perception]"—to this he replies with the words "produced by that" (*tatkṛtaḥ*), and so forth.

"Produced by that" means produced by that non-conceptual [perception]. [The certainty] does not exist in reality (*tattvataḥ*), that is, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*); the meaning is that it exists only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
In some places, there is a reading: "In reality, that does not arise from that.
The result of that determination is that [cognition] does not arise from that non-conceptual [perception];
and how it does not arise from that has already been explained in the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*).
Even granting this, [the author] states the following to demonstrate the refutation: "Or, if there were existence," and so forth.

Or, if there were existence—that is, if there were production—from that [perception], the determination (*nirṇaya*), which is the ascertainment of its own object, would occur without fragmentation. Why would it not occur even with respect to momentary destruction and the like, just as it does with respect to color-form and the like? This is because the manifestation is equally clear in both cases. Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Savikalpakasiddhi* that the sharpness of perception and so forth remain undifferentiated for a partless perception in both cases;
for that purpose, indeed, Ācārya... [text fragment].
"Certainty regarding one's own object" (svārtheniścayaṃ), Ā; "in reality" (tattvato), Ā. Where [is this]? Ā. Bhā.
Then, from *ba* and *ta*, [the sound] *ja*— clearly *ti*— [arises]. *Ba*, *ja*.

Now, one might object: "Just as the distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is contradicted in the case of the single ultimate consciousness (*paramārthaikasaṃvit*) because of the forms of the object-to-be-known (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*), so too is it contradicted in the case of apprehension (*avagraha*) and the rest, since even a particular (*viśeṣa*), like the universal (*sāmānya*), is grasped by apprehension alone. Otherwise, there would be two entities with distinct natures—one already grasped and the other not. Furthermore, just as non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) lacks validity because it is not itself perceived, so too do apprehension and the rest, since they likewise lack such perception. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Many, of many kinds," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: there is no contradiction regarding the determination of the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphalavyavasthā*) with respect to that apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth which pertains to the various alternatives and distinctions—namely, those that are manifold, of many kinds, rapid, not yet released, unspoken, and constant, as well as their opposites, such as non-manifold and so on.

If one asks, "Why is this so? the author replies here: "Because of the difference in intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvabhedāt*). This should be understood to mean either because of the difference in some respect of the object to be grasped, which is the "own state" (*svabhāva*)—that is, the specific nature—of apprehension and the rest;
or else, because of the difference in intrinsic nature, meaning the difference in the essential form (*svarūpa*) of apprehension and the rest.
Regarding what was stated— that "there is no perception of that [object]"— he says in response: "Even when there is a difference in appearance," and so forth.

Even though there is a distinction—that is, a plurality—of the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) due to its self-cognition (*svarūpasaṃvitti*), what [follows] from the postulation of the absence of difference in nature (*svabhāva*) among perception (*avagraha*) and the rest? That is, from the postulation of the absence of difference in nature—which is to say, the absence of difference in essence (*svarūpa*)—or the postulation of non-dual cognition (*advayajñāna*)? To this he says: "successively" (*krameṇa*), and so forth. Because those things which function successively—namely, seeing, remembering, and so on, which exist in the form of material causes (*upādāna*) and their effects (*upādeya*)—also possess that state; that is, they exist by way of that same method of postulating the absence of difference in nature, not merely perception and the rest. For this reason, [there is no such non-duality].

From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—from none at all—could a sequence, a causal relationship, or the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth (the word "and so forth" including joy, blue, etc.), be established or determined from the perspective of ultimate reality? The implication is that there would be non-dualism of the Self (*puruṣādvaita*).
— *Advayājñā* (Ā), *bhedabhāva* (Ba, Ja).
Now, one might ask: "If there is a difference in the manifestation of the *avagraha* (perception) and the other stages, how can they be one? To this, he says: "Like simultaneous manifestation.
This means that just as the forms such as blue and so forth, which manifest simultaneously within cognition, are [considered one], so too is that [the case here].

With the words beginning with "tad" (that), he provides a summary of the point already stated: Since it is so, therefore this Buddhist [maintains] that a single, non-different, manifold-aspected—that is, variegated-aspected—momentary cognition, which perceives the middle moment as distinct from the preceding and succeeding limits, [is such] due to some proximity characterized by non-separable acquisition and preservation (*ayoga-kṣema*) or characterized by the impossibility of being distinguished;
[proximity] belonging to what? He says: "of the various appearances."

The various appearances (*pratibhāsa-bheda*) are the specific forms such as blue and so forth belonging to cognition; accepting these, even though they occur sequentially—that is, even though they have the nature of occurring in succession—it is possible to establish their unity by way of the proximity consisting in the impossibility of being distinguished [as separate]. To the question, "Of what things can unity be established through that mode of proximity consisting solely in the security and well-being (*yoga-kṣema*) of non-difference, since this is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to cognitions in other continua (*santāna*]? he says: "of joy, sorrow, and so forth."

Therefore, from this [reason], namely that oneness, the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) is to be understood; this is because of its connection with the word "to be understood" (pratyeya), which will be mentioned later through a transformation of gender in the genus (*jāti*).
[This] introduces [the following]. Śra॰-canapratyā–bhā॰, ba॰, ja॰.
Yoga is characterized by the discernment of objects at every moment, and *kṣema* is characterized by the performance of purposeful action in the form of protection (Hetubinduṭīkā, p.

56). Now, if it is argued that because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) occur sequentially, their identity cannot be established—just as in the case of distinct mental continua—the author replies with the words beginning "pramāṇe" and so forth.

The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is carried over from the previous context. Therefore, according to this reasoning, although there is a sequential occurrence between the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*)—namely, between apprehension (*avagraha*) and inquiry (*īhā*), between inquiry (*īhā*) and perceptual judgment (*avāya*), and between perceptual judgment (*avāya*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*)—there is nonetheless identity (*tādātmya*), that is, a certain oneness (*kathaṃcid-ekatva*).
This constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika, who maintains that the means of cognition and its fruit are entirely non-different (*sarvathā-abheda-vādin*).

Is it not the case that the identity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is untenable due to a contradiction with the means of valid cognition itself? For instance: the means of valid cognition produces an action distinct from itself because it is an instrument (*kāraka*); whatever is an instrument is understood to produce an action distinct from itself, just like an axe or similar tools; and since the means of valid cognition is an instrument, it therefore produces an action distinct from itself.

Likewise: A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) produces a result distinct from itself because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*). Whatever is an instrument is known to produce a result distinct from itself, just like an axe or similar tools; and since a means of valid cognition is an instrument, it therefore produces a result distinct from itself.

Nor is this example deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for an instrument such as an axe is never observed to perform an action upon itself, nor is it logical for something that does not act to be an instrument, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, an instrument must be understood as performing its distinct result either upon the agent (*kartṛ*) or upon the object (*karman*).

Furthermore, it is contradictory for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself to have the nature of its result (*phala*); for it is not possible for a single entity at one time to possess both the nature of an instrument and the nature of a result with respect to its own self, since the simultaneous coexistence of two contradictory properties in a single locus is impossible. Therefore, the distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result is indeed the superior view.

For the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*) is the result (*phala*); how then could there be non-difference between these two? Since difference is established precisely by their arising from distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) and having distinct objects, those two which arise from distinct causal complexes and have distinct objects are different—just as, for example, the cognitions of a jar and a cloth. And the cognitions of the qualifier and the qualified likewise arise from distinct causal complexes and have distinct objects.

Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the contact of the sense organ with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is distinct from the causal complex characterized by the contact of that same sense organ with the qualified substance (*viśeṣya*) and so forth. Furthermore, the difference between the objects of these two cognitions is well-established, since they have as their respective supports (*ālambana*) the qualifier and the qualified, which are mutually distinct. When there is contact, there is the cognition, which is the means of valid knowledge (*pramiti*); when there is the cognition, there is the result (*phala*), namely the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.4:

In that regard, with respect to universals and particulars, perception as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) is the mere observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-ālocana-mātra*); the resulting valid cognition (*pramiti*) is knowledge whose object is substance and so forth. Alternatively, perception as a means of valid cognition is that knowledge which arises with respect to all categories (*padārtha*) through the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa*), which is non-erroneous (*avitatha*) and non-verbal (*avyapadeśya*); the resulting valid cognition is the observation of qualities, defects, and neutrality (*guṇa-doṣa-mādhyasthya-darśana*).
Praśastapāda-bhāṣya, p. 187:

"And every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is, with respect to its own object, a *bhāvasādhana* [denoting the action], as in 'the means of valid cognition is the act of cognizing' (*pramiti*). With respect to another object, it is a *karaṇasādhana* [denoting the instrument], as in 'that by which something is cognized is the means of valid cognition' (*pramīyate 'nena*). If the word *pramāṇa* is a *bhāvasādhana*, what is the result (*phala*), since the object has already been apprehended? It has been stated that the results are the cognitions of avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth.
Nyāyavārttika 1.3, p. 29.

For an instrument (*karaṇa*) is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because [an object] is cognized by means of it; moreover, an action itself never becomes an instrument. Whatever factor of action (*kāraka*) serves to accomplish an action that is yet to be achieved is called an instrument, as in the example: "Caitra cuts a stalk of rice with a sickle. Just as the agent, the object, and the instrument are perceived as distinct from the action, so too here, in the case of "he sees a jar with his eye," it is logical that these [factors] exist as separate from the act of seeing; it is not the case that the act of seeing itself is the instrument.

The statement "valid cognition (*pramā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)" is merely an etymological explanation of the word *pramāṇa* when applied to the result, similar to the expression "the instrument of action" (*kṛti-karaṇam*). Therefore, it is logical that the eye and other sense organs possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) because they produce the act of cognizing, while cognition itself is the result (*phalatva*); such a designation is appropriate. Śaṅkarasvāmin establishes this through the following reasoning: "The means of valid cognition produces an action distinct from itself, because it is a causal factor (*kāraka*), like an axe. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 70). 1353.
*Tattvasaṅgraha*:

When indeterminate knowledge of the universal and the particular is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then determinate knowledge having substance and so forth as its object is the resulting cognition (*pramiti*); this is the meaning.

When even non-conceptual knowledge of the universal and the particular is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*) because it consists in the apprehension of an object, then, at its production, the undifferentiated mere observation (*ālocanamātra*) is the perception (*pratyakṣa*). For the knowledge of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*) is the result of the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), and the knowledge of the qualifier is not the result of another distinct cognition. Thus, when the non-conceptual knowledge of the universal and the particular is the result, the sense-object contact (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); when the knowledge of the qualified is the result, the observation of the universal and the particular is the means of valid cognition. This much has been stated.

Now, regarding the fact that cognitions such as loss (*hāna*) and so forth constitute the result, [the author] states that the cognition of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyajñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 199;
Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sūtra 4, verses 70–73; *Tattvabodhinī*, p. [blank]).
You, however, [hold the opposite].
— “You [assert] that the object,
the means of valid cognition, and the result are established as being somehow identical, preceded by a refutation of their difference in every respect”—
to this, the following response is given.

As for the argument stated—that the difference between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is to be proven because they possess the nature of causal factors (*kārakatva*)—that is incorrect. For, in this regard, is it intended to prove that there is some kind of difference between these two, or a difference in every respect? If it is "somehow" (*kathañcit*): then it is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is because the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*), being a property of the means of valid cognition, and [the acts of] avoidance and acquisition, being its effects, are admitted to be somehow different from the means of valid cognition.
Indeed, the result of a means of valid cognition is twofold: that which is different from it and that which is non-different from it.
Among these, the cessation of ignorance is non-different [from the cognition], because it is a property of that [cognition].

Whatever is a property (*dharma*) is non-different from that which possesses it (*dharmī*), just as the illumination of self and other is non-different from a lamp; and the cessation of ignorance, characterized by the removal of delusion regarding one's own and others' forms, is a property of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the relationship of property and possessor of property is not tenable if there is either total difference or total identity, due to contradiction. To explain: there is no relationship of property and possessor of property between two things that are totally different, such as the Sahya and Vindhya mountains; and you maintain that there is total difference between the property and the possessor of property.

Likewise, where there is absolute non-difference, there can be no relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmibhāva*), as in the case of the essential nature of either the attribute or the substrate itself. Since you [the opponent] maintain that there is absolute non-difference between the attribute and the substrate, the relationship between them is untenable under the doctrine of absolute non-difference; therefore, difference in some respect (*kathaṃcid-bheda*) alone is superior. For the status of cognition as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) consists in its being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama-svabhāvatā*), while its status as a result (*phalatā*) consists in its having the nature of the cessation of ignorance. And this state of being the most effective instrument is precisely its operation of apprehending both itself and the object, characterized by its orientation toward that apprehension.

For knowledge, arising from its own collection of causes, being of the nature of *upayoga* characterized by the operation of grasping its own object, transforms into the form of a determination (*vyavasāya*) regarding that object;
thus, even though there is some degree of non-difference between these two, their relationship as cause and effect is not contradicted.

And thus, the claim that "it is untenable for a single entity at one time to possess both the nature of an instrument and the nature of a result with respect to itself," and so forth, is incorrect; for even a single entity can possess multiple causal forms due to a difference in perspective, as in the cases: "the tree stands," "done by the tree," "departed from the tree," and "look at the tree. Likewise, even for a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its status as a means of valid cognition and its status as a result do not involve any contradiction, when considered with respect to [its] nature of removing ignorance—characterized by the severance of delusion regarding its own form and the forms of others—and its nature of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). (Page 208, Line 10)
Equanimity is the fruit of the first [dhyāna]; for the remainder, it is the cognition of taking up or abandoning, or else the destruction of ignorance regarding its own object.
The fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the direct cessation of ignorance;
for pure [cognition], it is pleasure and equanimity; for the rest, it is the cognition of what is to be acquired and what is to be abandoned.
In the *Nyāyāvatāra*,
equanimity or the destruction of ignorance is the fruit for the sake of all goals. (Sarvārthasiddhi 1)
The fruit of valid cognition is the direct establishment [of the object], which is the ascertainment of its own referent;
*Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, p. 126a.

The fruit of the means of valid cognition is the cognition of what is to be acquired and what is to be abandoned through the determination of reality, or else supreme beatitude; however, there is also indifference toward that which is indifferent. (Nyāyaviniścaya 3)
The experience of loss and so forth is accepted as a distinct result [of cognition] according to valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, that non-differentiation from it is the equal turning away from ignorance regarding one's own object.
(Tattvārthaśloka, p. 127)
The cessation of ignorance, as well as rejection, acceptance, and indifference, constitute the fruit;
it is both distinct from and non-distinct from the means of valid cognition.
— *Parīkṣāmukha* 5.
