An Investigation of the Means of Valid Cognition 1.1
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between action (*kriyā*) and instrument (*karaṇa*) because they are one and the same, this is incorrect;
for while we admit a distinction between their properties (*dharma*), the underlying entity (*vastu*) is held to be non-different.
Furthermore,
in the case of an absolute distinction [between means and result], there could be no understanding of the nature of the means of valid cognition and its fruit.
Just as in another continuum, so too within one's own desired single self, there is no cognition [of the object].
(Tattvārthaśloka, p. 128)
Because that conventional usage would be untenable if there were non-difference,
and because it would likewise be untenable if there were difference— just as in the case of other selves (Parīkṣāmukha 6).
And it transforms by way of its nature of cessation, according to Śrī [and] Ba and Ja.
[The reading] "karaṇatā" [is found in] Ā, Bh;

[the reading] "tā vānupapatteḥ" [is found in] Ba, Ja. Now, [an objection is raised]: "The cessation of ignorance is indeed knowledge itself; and it is not logical for that very thing to be the effect of itself, because of the contradiction. Therefore, how could this [cessation] be the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? This too is charming only when left unexamined, because there is no contradiction in the cessation of ignorance—which is characterized by the transformation into the determination of its own object—being an effect produced by the means of valid cognition in the form of *upayoga*, which is characterized by the operation of grasping its own object; for it is established that the factor of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) is in some way distinct from the other factors.

Furthermore, having accepted either the nature of an attribute (*dharma*) or the nature of a substratum (*dharmin*), would one maintain that the cessation of ignorance is indeed knowledge itself? If it is the nature of a substratum, then with respect to what is the status of being a substratum for the cessation of ignorance postulated—is it with respect to knowledge, or with respect to some other attribute? In the first case, the cessation [of ignorance] would be the substratum and knowledge its attribute; this results in a reversal [of the relationship], and this is not logical, because [the cessation] is dependent upon that [knowledge].

Whatever is dependent upon something else is not observed to have the status of a subject (*dharmin*) in relation to its own substratum, as is the case with pleasure, form, and so forth. Since the cessation of ignorance is dependent upon knowledge, how can it possess the status of a subject? For it is logically established that this [cessation], being necessarily dependent on another, possesses the very nature of a property (*dharma*), since that is its defining characteristic.

Now, if [it is argued that it is so] in relation to another property (*dharma*); then what would this [non-knowledge] have in relation to knowledge? If it is its nature as a property (*dharmarūpatā*), how is it appropriate to state their non-difference by saying "knowledge itself is the cessation of non-knowledge," since it is only the statement of their difference that is logical—namely, that "the cessation of non-knowledge is a property of knowledge"? Indeed, apart from metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), it is not proper to state the non-difference of property and property-possessor (*dharmin*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
In relation to what [is this said]? (Ā. Bhā.)

Furthermore, would this [valid cognition] be something produced (*kāryā*) or unproduced (*akāryā*)? If it were unproduced, it would follow that it exists everywhere and at all times; consequently, everyone would be an omniscient seer. For the spatial and temporal restriction of entities is dependent upon causes restricted by space and so forth, and not otherwise.

Now, if it were produced, from what would it arise—from a cognition regarded as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or from something else? If it were from something else, it would follow that it arises both before and after the production of the cognition regarded as a means of valid knowledge; for it is not logical that something which is not its effect should obtain its own existence only at the time of that [cognition's] existence.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is not an effect of something else does not depend upon the existence of that thing for its own attainment of being (*ātmalābha*). For example, a cloth, which is not an effect of a jar, does not depend upon the existence of the jar for its own attainment of being. And the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*) is not an effect of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it possesses an origination from something other [than itself].

Now, if it is argued that this cessation arises from valid cognition alone, then it is established that it is the fruit of valid cognition; and thus, the claim that the cessation of ignorance is identical to knowledge (*jñāna*) itself becomes untenable.

Or, even if it were easily established, would the cessation of ignorance be mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) itself, or a specific cognition? In the first case, non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) and the like would be dismissed—since the cessation of ignorance, characterized by the cutting off of delusion regarding one's own and others' natures, exists there as well, being a property of mere cognition.

For delusion (*vyāmoha*) has the nature of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) and so forth; how could it find any room within mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), which is embraced by the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*)—the very opposite of such delusion? Wherever the presence of a contrary property is dependent solely upon the existence of something else, there the former cannot possibly occur. For example, in the case of the self (*ātman*), which is embraced by properties such as incorporeality and consciousness that depend solely upon the existence of the self itself, properties such as corporeality and insentience cannot occur. And cognition is likewise embraced by the property of the cessation of ignorance, which depends solely upon the existence of cognition and is opposed to non-determination and the like.

Now, if it is maintained that the nature of distinguished knowledge (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*), one must ask: what indeed is this so-called "distinguishedness" of knowledge? Is it (1) being the cause for severing delusion regarding its own and other forms; or (2) being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*); or (3) fitness for producing a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); or (4) the acquisition of its own essence from a specific collection of causes? In the first alternative, our own position is established, because the followers of Syādvāda accept that a specific kind of knowledge—which is the cause for severing delusion characterized by non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) and the like—is the substratum for the property of the cessation of ignorance.

The latter three alternatives also pertain to our own position, because it is logically consistent for a specific cognition—which severs delusion regarding both its own nature and that of others, which is uncontradicted, and which manifests from a collection of specific causes capable of producing a latent impression—to serve as the substratum for the property of the cessation of ignorance.

Therefore, it is well said: since it is a property of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the result characterized by the cessation of ignorance is non-different from the means of valid cognition; however, [the results] such as rejection and acquisition are different—[this is established] by the force of their existence. (Āloka)
"Merely cognition" (jñānamātra);
"attainment of the self" (ātmano lābhaḥ) [is] capable of producing [it].

If it is asked: "Just as cognition—which is characterized by the application (*upayoga*) directed toward grasping its own object—transforms into the form of the valid cognition of self and other, and into the form of the cessation of non-cognition (*ajñāna*), so too does it transform into the forms of rejection (*hāna*) and so forth; how then can there be a difference in its results? The answer is: because they are mediated by that [cessation of non-cognition]. For when the result characterized by the cessation of non-cognition has arisen, the result characterized by rejection, acquisition (*upādāna*), and so forth arises. Thus, due to being mediated by the result characterized by the cessation of non-cognition, there is a difference [between them]. However, because the cessation of non-cognition is not mediated by anything else—even in a dream—there is no difference [between the primary result and the cessation itself].

Therefore, the absolute difference between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is not established on the grounds of their being "agents" (*kāraka*), nor on the grounds of their being "instruments" (*karaṇa*); for this would entail all the faults already mentioned.
— *Nādikaṃla*, *Ba*, *Ja*.

As for what was stated—that the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the result (*phala*), and so forth—that too is untenable. This is because the qualifier and the qualified do not serve as the objective supports (*ālambana*) for distinct cognitions;

rather, a single cognition alone has them as its support. Indeed, in cases such as "a white cloth" or "a man with a staff," no difference in the cognition of the qualifier and the qualified is experienced, as that would contradict actual experience (*pratīti*).

Nor does the difference in cognition arise from a difference in objects; for even though an object such as a five-fingered hand is manifold, it serves as the objective support for a single cognition. Otherwise, how could the category of "existent and non-existent" be the objective support of a single cognition for someone, given its multiplicity—just like the five fingers—and how could this serve as an example in that context? Furthermore, how could the existence of a whole (avayavin) be established, since there would be the undesirable consequence that the upper, lower, and middle parts themselves would lack the status of being the objective support of a single cognition; for it is impossible to establish the whole by means of its pervading those parts.

Furthermore, that distinct causal complex (sāmagrī) characterized by the contact of the qualifiers with the senses and so forth which was proposed is also untenable, because contact has already been refuted.
Moreover, a difference in causes is only to be postulated when there is a difference in effects; however, it has already been stated that no such difference exists here.
Therefore, it is well said: "Even though the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its fruit (phala) occur sequentially, their identity and their having the same object must be understood."

The Establishment of the Objects (*Arthasiddhi*). [In the *Bhaṣya* and *Ja*, regarding the Vaiśeṣika’s prima facie argument in the doctrine of the six categories:

Now, the six categories—namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*)—which are accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas, along with the seventh, called non-existence (*abhāva*), are indeed well-established through valid cognition as being absolutely distinct from one another, characterized by definitions that are mutually exclusive.

For instance—the definition of substance (*dravya*) does not apply to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, since its definition is "the connection with the universal 'substance-ness' (*dravyatva*)," as well as "possessing action," "possessing qualities," and "being an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (VS 1.1.15).
1.15 Thus, those characterized by such definitions are the nine substances: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.
Among these, earth, water, fire, and air are of two kinds, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal.

Therein, those in the form of atoms (paramāṇu) are eternal because they exist and are not produced by causes; however, those in the form of composite wholes (avayavin), such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth, are non-eternal because they possess the quality of being produced.
Space, time, direction, self, and mind, however, are indeed eternal.

From the knowledge of the true nature of the categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—through their similarities and differences, which arises from specific dharma, there is the attainment of the supreme good. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.4.
Because non-existence (abhāva) depends upon the thorough cognition of existence (bhāva), it is not enumerated separately; Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 20.
Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not taught separately because it is dependent upon existence (*bhāva*), and not because it is non-existent [itself]. As stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (Kandalī, p.

7): "And since non-existence is established in a related system (*samānatantra*) and is not refuted in the *Nyāyadarśana*, its status as a mental sense-organ (*mānasendriyatā*) is not contradicted here either, because it is established by way of a tenet accepted for the sake of argument (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*)."

That which has the nature of being existent and causeless is eternal. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.1. The term *sadakāraṇavat* (existent and having no cause) refers to that which is both real and lacks a cause of production; such a thing is eternal (*nitya*). This sūtra establishes the definition of eternity based on the absence of a cause for its existence. It serves as a foundational principle for the Vaiśeṣika school's ontology, particularly regarding the nature of space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and the self (*ātman*), which are considered eternal because they exist and yet have no prior cause that produced them. The suffix *-vat* here functions as a possessive marker, indicating that the subject possesses the quality of being both existent and uncaused. Thus, the sūtra states: "That which is existent and devoid of a cause is indeed eternal. This definition distinguishes eternal entities from those that are produced and perishable. While some schools, such as the Sāṃkhya, maintain that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is eternal due to its uncaused nature, the Vaiśeṣika restricts this status strictly to those categories that are inherently unproduced. This sūtra thus provides the logical criterion for identifying what constitutes an eternal substance within the system.

1.1 And this definition of substance (*dravya-lakṣaṇa*) is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki-anumāna*), as follows: Substance is distinct from others because of its connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*), or because of possessing action (*kriyāvat*), or because of possessing qualities (*guṇavat*), or because of being an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*). Whatever is not distinct from others is not thus, like qualities and so forth; and this [substance] is such; therefore, it is distinct from others.

Alternatively, that which is the object of dispute to be established in common usage must be designated as "substance" (dravya) for the same reason previously stated; whereas that which is not so designated is not such [a substance], like qualities (guṇa) and so forth; and since this [subject] is thus, it must therefore be designated as "substance."

In the same way, the remaining definitions are also to be understood as follows: earth is [defined] by its connection with earthness (pṛthivītva) (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 20); water by its connection with waterness (aptva) (p. 35); fire by its connection with fieriness (tejastva) (p. 38); and air by its connection with airness (vāyutva) (p.

44). However, since ether, time, and direction are each singular, and thus lack the higher generality (parasāmānya) that serves as their defining characteristic, they are designated by three technical names: ether, time, and direction. These names themselves serve as their definition.

For instance: Space is distinct from others; the substance under dispute should be designated as "space," because it is denotable by the term "space" which has been in use since beginningless time. Whatever is not distinct from others and is not designated as "space" is not denotable by the term "space" since beginningless time, such as color-form and so forth; but this [substance] is denotable by that term; therefore, the stated probandum follows.
In this same manner, the definition of space and time should also be understood.

"Because of its connection with selfhood (ātmatva), it is the self" (Praśastabhāṣya, p. 69); "because of its connection with mentality (manastva), it is the mind" (Praśastabhāṣya, p. 89). Here too, as before, a purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekyanumāna) is to be understood.

In the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*), there is the refutation of eternal substances characterized as earth-atoms and so forth. To this, the following response is given:

regarding what was stated—that earth, water, fire, and air are of two kinds, and so on—that is incorrect, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of those [elements] in the form of atoms.
For when they exist, perception by people such as ourselves does not operate toward them because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*);

nor is there inference, since an inference that makes their existence known is impossible. If it is argued: "The effect, such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), is produced from a cause possessing a smaller dimension than its own, because it is an effect, like a jar," this too is an unexamined statement; for there is no necessary rule that an effect must be produced from a cause possessing a smaller dimension than its own.

To explain: is it merely an effect that is to be established as being produced by that [atom], or is it an effect qualified by substantiality (*dravyatva*)? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to cognition and so forth; for although these are effects, it is impossible to establish a rule that they must be produced from causes possessing a smaller dimension than their own.

In the second case, however, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to ashes and the like; for although ashes possess substantiality and are effects, they are not perceived to be produced from causes possessing a smaller dimension than themselves.

Indeed, there is no universal rule that a substance with a smaller dimension must be the cause simply because the effect has a larger dimension; rather, the universal rule is that an effect cannot exist without a cause, for we perceive substances—whether larger, smaller, or equal in dimension—to function as causes.

In this regard, it is observed that from a large heap of straw and a loosely structured mass of cotton, there arises ash and a densely structured mass of cotton which are smaller in dimension; likewise, from a small-sized seed, there arises a tree and so forth which is large in dimension; and from substances such as milk which are equal in dimension, there arises curd and so forth which are equal in dimension.

Nor is it proper to establish that every effect-substance is preceded by a cause possessing a smaller dimension than its own, simply because some effect-substance is observed to be so; for if one were to observe the momentariness of sound, lightning, lamps, and the like, it would follow that all existing things must be proven momentary.
Even though an example exists, this [argument] cannot be a proof because there is no universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) here; this same point applies elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, since the existence of atoms is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the reason in the argument that "earth and the other elements are eternal because they exist and lack a cause" is unestablished in its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*) (p.

214, l. 7). Likewise, from the effect one infers a constituent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of smaller dimension, and another cause of even smaller dimension for that; thus, it is known that the first effect is composed of atoms possessing a dimension that admits no further reduction.
Because of the impossibility of its being commenced [from] a mass of cotton balls with loose parts, as [in the case of] a heap... (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 224; variants: ba, ja, bhā, śra).
A dense-bodied lump of cotton is produced;
some [lumps] are preceded by minute dimensions as their cause, some are preceded by large dimensions as their cause, and some are commenced by causes of equal dimension.

—[The reason] is unestablished for the opponent; furthermore, there is the unestablished nature of the qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddhatva*) because those [atoms] are preceded by the destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*). "It is incorrect to say that 'division alone arises from the destruction of that [conjunction], and not the atom'; for this would entail the consequence that even the aggregate (*skandha*) is likewise causeless.

Now, it might be argued: "Even though threads existing at a time subsequent to a cloth are preceded by the disintegration of that cloth, those existing at a time prior to it are not so preceded; likewise, some atoms might also not be preceded by the disintegration of a composite (skandha). 27. It is incorrect [to claim] that the division of atoms arises from the disintegration of aggregates, or that atoms do not arise because of their eternity, like the path of the wind.

Because those [effects] are preceded by that [cause],
and because it is well known that even that [cause], such as the thread, arises only from the disintegration of the cotton-wool ball and so forth.

"Now, since you yourselves have established their non-existence due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends atoms, your thesis that they are preceded by the disintegration of aggregates is not superior; this too is untenable. For instance: the gradations of atomic dimension (aṇuparimāṇa) must terminate somewhere, because they are gradations of dimension, just like the gradations of large dimension (mahatparimāṇa). That wherein this [gradation] terminates are the atoms; thus, their existence is not impossible.

Likewise, among the causes of causes of jars and so forth, the state of being smaller and so on must terminate somewhere, because it is denotable by words such as "more" and "most," just like large dimension; that wherein it terminates are the atoms.
The *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p. 224) states:

"The gradation of atomic dimension must terminate somewhere, because it is a gradation of dimension, like the gradation of large dimension. That wherein this [gradation] terminates, beyond which no further atom exists, is the atom. The *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kaṇḍalī* (p. 31) likewise [states this].
It would be [found] in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, page 870, [edition] Ā., Ba., Ja.

Because an eternally uniform nature is itself impossible, for if they possessed such a nature, it would be logically untenable for them to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) either successively or simultaneously. To explain: if atoms were to exist as absolutely eternal by nature, would they be admitted to have a nature that never produces an effect at any time, or one contrary to that? In the first alternative, there follows the absurd consequence that effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth would never exist, because their production from those atoms—which by definition always possess a nature not to produce them—is impossible. For whatever has a nature not to produce something does not produce it—just as a rice seed does not produce a barley sprout—and you postulate that atoms always possess a nature not to produce effects such as dyads.

And in that case, even atoms would necessarily be non-existent, because they do not produce an effect; for whatever does not produce an effect is not existent, like a sky-lotus, and according to your view, atoms are always such that their sole nature is the non-production of that [effect].

Now, if it is admitted that these [atoms] possess at all times a single nature consisting solely in the production of an effect, even then—do you maintain that they possess this nature of producing that [effect] while alone, or when conjoined with auxiliary causes? If they are alone; then the effects produced from them would arise only simultaneously, because their causes would be unimpaired. For those things whose causes are unimpaired arise only simultaneously, just as many sprouts produced at the same time. And all entities intended as the effects of atoms, which possess a nature solely for production, would have their causes unimpaired. Thus, [the consequence follows].
Therefore, even for those things that have become thus, there would follow the consequence of their never arising at all, because there is no distinction [between them and what has already arisen]—
[the reading "vāḥ paramā-" appears in the manuscripts Ba, Ja, while "atra api" appears in manuscript Bhā].
If all gross things were produced from a single cause and were eternal, they would indeed arise all at once;
for there is no dependence on conjunctions and the like, since those [causes] are without distinction.

If it is accepted that the atoms which serve as the causes of gross objects such as mountains are eternal, then, because their causes would be complete and unobstructed, it follows that those gross effects must arise all at once. The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: those things whose causes are fully present and unimpeded arise simultaneously, just as many sprouts arise together when their conditions are equal.
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 186;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
159; *Sanmatitarkaṭīkā*, p. 657.
[From the *Ratnākara*, p. 870]:

Now, is it not the case that the cause operates in the production of an effect in three ways—by way of the distinction between inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes?
For that in which the effect inheres is the inherent cause, just as the two atoms are for a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

Furthermore, that which produces an effect by inhering in the same object as the effect (*kāryaikārthasamaveta*) or by inhering in the same object as both the effect and its cause (*kāryakāraṇaikārthasamaveta*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). For example, the conjunction of threads (*tantusaṃyoga*) in the production of a cloth, and the color and other qualities of the threads in the production of the color and other qualities inherent in the cloth.

As for the rest—such as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), including the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and space (*ākāśa*)—it is claimed that their status as complete causes is unestablished because they lack the necessary factors such as conjunction. This, however, is mere faith; for since atoms cannot have any excellence (*atiśaya*) imparted to them by conjunction and the like, their dependence on such factors is logically untenable.

Now, if conjunction itself is the excellence (*atiśaya*) of these [causes], is it eternal or non-eternal? If it is eternal, there would be the production of the effect at all times, because the conjunction—which constitutes that excellence—would exist eternally. If, on the other hand, it is non-eternal, then what excellence would there be for its own production—conjunction itself, or action (*kriyā*)? If it is conjunction, is it that very same one, or another conjunction? It cannot be that very same one, because its existence is not yet established, and because it is contradictory for a thing to operate upon itself in its own production.

Nor is it another conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for that is not admitted, and if it were admitted, then even upon the production of that [conjunction], there would follow the necessity of postulating yet another excellence of conjunction, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is it an excellence of action (*kriyā*); for even upon the production of that, the previously mentioned fault would persist. Furthermore, since you admit that action arises in atoms from the conjunction of the self and the atom which depends on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then even for the production of the conjunction between the self and the atom, another excellence must be postulated; and in that case, the same refutation applies—thus there is another infinite regress.

It might be argued: "The cause is threefold—namely, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Since the conjunction and other factors required for these are not present, the state of having all causes complete (*samagrakāraṇatva*) is unestablished; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Conjunction and so forth...

For if some particularity were imparted to the atoms by means of conjunction and the like, then they would depend upon it; however, since the atoms are eternal, no particularity can be imparted to them by others. Therefore, how could conjunction and the like be something upon which they must depend?
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 186:

"When action arises in the atoms of air from those conjunctions [of soul and atom] which depend upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) obtained through the functioning present in all souls" (*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

48): "And those conjunctions of the soul and the atoms—which depend upon the unseen forces residing in all souls and obtained through their functioning—from those [conjunctions], actions arise in the atoms of air."

The atoms of air (*pavana-paramāṇu*) are the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); the conjunction of the atom with the self possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭavat-ātman*) whose activity has been attained is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*); and the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p.

52) Furthermore, regarding this conjunction which brings about dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth: does it reside in the atoms, or does it reside in something other than them, or is it non-resident? In that regard, concerning the first position, when it arises, does the substratum arise or not? If it arises, then it follows that the atoms themselves must be effects, because they undergo transformation into the form of conjunction by abandoning their prior state of being non-conjunction.

Now, if it does not arise [simultaneously], how could it be dependent upon that [substratum] at that time? For, due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), it would follow that there is an absolute difference between them. If it is argued that even though it is of such a nature, it is dependent on that because of its connection with it; by what kind of relation is it connected to it—by inherence (*samavāya*), by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or by the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)? It cannot be by inherence, because that does not exist, and its non-existence is established since it will be refuted later.

Nor can it be by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for conjunction is impossible with respect to conjunction itself, since, being a quality (*guṇa*), it must reside in a substance (*dravya*). Nor can it be by way of the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); for atoms lack the status of being causes with respect to conjunction. And that absence [of causality] is due to their lacking any excellence (*atiśaya*);

for if things devoid of excellence were productive, there would follow the absurd consequence of them being productive at all times, as there would be no distinction [between when they produce and when they do not].

Furthermore, if one postulates another excellence (*atiśaya*) [in the conjunction], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because for the production of that [second excellence] as well, one would have to postulate yet another excellence.

If, however, it were to reside in something else, then conjunction could not produce an excellence in the atom, because of the absence of a relationship [between them]. For wherever this [conjunction] resides, an excellence belongs only to that [substratum] and not to anything else, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Yet, its being non-resident is untenable, because it is a quality (*guṇa*); for whatever is a quality is not non-resident, just like color and so forth, and conjunction is intended by you to be a quality.

Alternatively, if it were non-dependent, its status as a quality would be untenable; for that which is non-dependent is not a quality, just like space and so forth. And the conjunction imagined by you in the form of an excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in atoms is [supposed to be] dependent on atoms and so forth—[this is the point]. (Note: *ba*, *ja* read "saṃyoga" [conjunction];
*ā*, *ba* read "na saṃyogasya" [not of conjunction]).

Furthermore, would this conjunction be between them by way of their entire being (*sarvātmanā*) or by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*)? If it were by way of their entire being, the aggregate (*piṇḍa*) would be no more than the size of a single atom.

If, on the other hand, it were by way of a single part, then it would follow that atoms possess parts (*sāṃśatva*). Therefore, it is not tenable for those [atoms] to have, in isolation, a nature solely directed toward producing [an effect].

Nor can it be [produced] by atoms conjoined with auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); for are those auxiliaries merely specific excellences (*atiśaya-viśeṣa*) inherent in the atoms themselves, or are they distinct entities (*vastvantara*)? In the first case, all the aforementioned defects would follow. In the second case as well, do these distinct entities provide assistance to the atoms or not? If they do, is that assistance distinct from the atoms or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then the atoms themselves would possess the nature of the effect.
If it is distinct, then since the production of the effect would arise from that [assistance] alone, the atoms would be rendered non-causal.

Now, if those causal factors (*kārakas*) are assisted by the assistance (*upakāra*) provided by that [other factor], then does this assistance act as an assistant through another assistance, or by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*)? In the first alternative, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because it would follow that even that further assistance must act as an assistant by means of yet another assistance.

In the second alternative, however, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because it would entail that everything could be an assistant to everything else by its mere existence; consequently, since an atom would be simultaneously conjoined with six [other atoms], it would possess six parts (*ṣaḍaśatā*).
Because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom. (Verse 12) [This concludes the section on] the mere-cognition of the visible.

Furthermore, do these auxiliary conditions assist the atoms by way of a relationship of mutual assistance and being assisted, or otherwise? If it is by way of a relationship of mutual assistance and being assisted, then once again the aforementioned host of faults follows, based on the two positions of whether that assistance is different from or non-different from them.

Now, it may be argued that the auxiliary causes do nothing for the atoms, either individually or collectively, because the effect is produced by them only when they are joined together. This too is incorrect; for are the atoms, being already capable individually, performing the action in conjunction with the auxiliaries, or are they incapable? If they are capable, then it would follow that each of them produces the effect individually, which would result in as many distinct effects as there are atoms, and the dependence upon auxiliaries would be rendered useless.

Now, if those [atoms] are individually incapable, then how could they possess capacity when in proximity? If it is argued that [the capacity arises] from the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) themselves, well then, is the capacity produced as non-different or different from them? If it is non-different, then it follows that those [auxiliaries] would be the effect. If it is different, then a relationship between them and that [capacity] is untenable because inherence (*samavāya*) and the like are impossible; consequently, since the effect would arise from those [auxiliaries] alone, the atoms would be non-causal, or else [the same fault would apply] to the opponent.

Or, let it be granted that they possess some capacity in whatever way possible; nevertheless, do the atoms produce another effect in the very same form by which they produce one effect, or in a different form? If it is in the very same form, then it follows that all effects would be one, because they are effects produced by a cause of a single nature. Whatever is an effect of a cause possessing a single nature is one, just like the intended effect; and all those effects considered to be products of atoms are of such a nature.

Now, if [the atom] exists in another form, then at that time, does its previous form cease or not? If it ceases, then there follows the undesirable consequence of the atoms being impermanent, because that [impermanence] is characterized by the loss of one's own nature (svarūpa). For whatever undergoes the loss of its own nature is impermanent, such as a jar or other objects; and at the time of the arising of another form, there is indeed the loss of the previous nature of the atoms.

Now, if it does not cease, then how could there be the emergence of another form in them? Where the previous form does not cease, there the emergence of another form is impossible, just as the form of an extended finger cannot emerge while its previously unextended form has not ceased. And since the previous nature of the atoms for producing an effect does not cease at the time of their producing a subsequent effect, if that [previous nature] were to emerge at that time, then because the capacity to produce all effects simultaneously would be present, the production of all effects would occur all at once.

Thus, since it is logically impossible for atoms to possess causal efficiency if they were strictly eternal and of a single nature, and since a productive nature arises when they have abandoned their prior non-productive nature through transformation into a specific conjunction, their partial impermanence is established.

The formal argument is as follows: those things which are the causes of successive effects are impermanent, just as seeds and the like, which produce successive sprouts and so forth; and atoms are of such a nature.
Therefore, that eternal substance characterized by earth-atoms and the rest, as imagined by you, cannot be established.
Does it perform subsequent effects by the same nature through which it performs the first causal operation, or does it do so having acquired a different nature? (Tattvopaplava, p.
126; *prāktanakārya*, *ba.*, *bhā.*;

refutation in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā* following the rejection of the causal relationship regarding substances such as earth, which consist of composite wholes like dyads produced from those [atoms]).

Nor is it the case that the composite substance, such as a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth, is produced from those [atoms]; for only when the relationship of cause and effect is established can it be asserted that the dyad and so forth are "produced from them. And in your view, that relationship is not established, because this [composite] is found to be untenable here upon investigation.

To explain: according to the followers of the Nyāya school, what indeed is this so-called "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*) of a composite substance such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)—is it inherence (*samavāya*) with the existence (*sattā*) of its own causes, or is it the state of coming into being after not having existed? In the first case, does the effect’s inherence consist in its inhering with its own causes and with existence, or in its inhering with the existence of its own causes, or rather is it that inherence which is conjoined with existence? Regarding that, in the first sub-case, does the inherence of the effect occur when it has already arisen, or when it has not yet arisen, or in both forms, or in neither form? If it occurs when it has already arisen, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for the arising of the effect is established only once its inherence with the existence of its own causes is established, and the establishment of that inherence depends upon the establishment of its arising.

Furthermore, if this [effect] were to arise independently, without depending on inherence (*samavāya*) in that [cause], the postulation of inherence would be useless. For that which is established as independent does not inhere in anything else, just as a jar does not inhere in a cloth; and according to your view, the effect is established as independent. Moreover, any talk of a "cause" here is extremely difficult to maintain, because the status of being a cause is predicated only of a thing that is actively engaged in bringing about the acquisition of the essence of an entity, and not of anything else, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, if its activity were directed toward the production of what is already produced, it would follow that it never ceases, and thus the essential nature of the effect would never be established.

Moreover, since that which is unproduced is like a lotus in the sky (*ākāśakuśeśaya*), how could it have an inherence (*samavāya*) with its own causes and with existence? Furthermore, it is utterly impossible for one thing to be both produced and unproduced at the same time; for two mutually contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single locus at once according to those who maintain absolute [monistic] doctrines.
However, its being neither of these two forms is untenable; for between the two properties of affirmation and negation, the negation of one necessarily entails the affirmation of the other.

As for the claim that "the state of being an effect belongs to the effect because of its inherence in the existence of its causes," what does that have to do with the effect? Indeed, when there is an inherence of a jar in its own existence, nothing happens to a cloth. Some maintain that "the state of being an effect consists in the inherence of existence in that which previously did not exist"; this is incorrect, because that [inherence] is absent in the case of destruction. Therefore, the state of being an effect is the acquisition of its own self-nature dependent upon the cause.

Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 18: What is this so-called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)? It is the connection with the existence (*sattā*) of its own cause, because of the conventional usage that "existence is an effect";
some, however, say it is "coming into being after not having been."
The state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is the quality of coming into existence after having not existed previously; see *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
129; *Praśastapādakiraṇāvalī*, p. 29.

Furthermore, the designation of something as a "cause" occurs only in relation to the nature of an effect; however, we do not perceive any form whatsoever in an effect that resembles a horse's horn, in relation to which this [non-existent cause] could possess causality. And if it lacks causality, how could it be the producer of an effect? Now, if it is argued that the very inherence (samavāya) of the effect with existence is what constitutes its "effect-ness," that is not so; for since the nature of inherence is unestablished, it is impossible for it to serve as a defining characteristic [of the effect]. Moreover, the fact that its nature is unestablished is well-known, as it will be refuted later on.

Or let it be granted that such a thing exists; nevertheless, because it is eternal, like the self (*ātman*) and so forth, it cannot be an effect. If it were an effect, its eternity would be untenable; for whatever is an effect is not eternal, as in the case of a jar or similar objects, and inherence (*samavāya*) is postulated by you to be an effect. Furthermore, if the definition of an effect consists in inherence with existence (*sattā*), then since such [inherence] is uniform everywhere, at all times, and toward all things, it would follow that even ether (*ākāśa*) and other such entities must be effects.

Furthermore, this inherence (*samavāya*) is a relation, and a relation is the effect of its relata and resides in them, as is the case with conjunction (*saṃyoga*). However, since the relatum that is the effect has not yet been produced, it is impossible for inherence to be its effect or to reside in it. Alternatively, if that [relatum] were already produced, they would be separately established (*yutasiddha*), and in that case there would be only conjunction, not inherence; for the logicians (*yogaiḥ*) accept that inherence resides in relata that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*).

Now, if it is argued that this relation exists even when the related entity is unestablished, that is incorrect; for a relation is so called because it relates two related entities, and how could it exist in the absence of a related entity? Otherwise, there would be a relation between a barren woman and her son.
Furthermore, since destruction lacks inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*), it would follow that it is not an effect; consequently, causes such as a mallet would be useless for its production.

—[The opponent says: "Its" (referring to the effect) [is that which has] non-existence followed by existence; this is its being an effect. If it is argued, "To what does this belong? It belongs to that which, having not existed, comes into being," then we ask: in this process of non-existence and existence, who possesses agency? First of all, the effect cannot possess agency because it is like the horn of a hare. For "coming into being" is the assumption of one's own nature, and that is impossible for a non-existent thing. Therefore, the status of being an effect does not coherently belong to anything else.

Nor can it be causality; for that [causality] must consist either in the production of any effect whatsoever, or in the production of a specific, restricted effect. In the first case, everything would be the cause of everything, since the mere production of "that" [an effect] is possible everywhere; thus, no one seeking a specific effect would ever employ a specific cause.
In the second case, however, since the effect is as non-existent as a horse's horn, how could the nature of the cause be delimited by it? For a real form is delimited only by something that exists.

Furthermore, if there were a delimitation by means of what is non-existent, it would follow that the cause itself is non-existent. For example, just as a jar is delimited by the mere conceptual construction "the jar is non-existent," so too would its causality be of that same nature. Indeed, when a delimitation is made by means of a conceptual construct, the real nature of the entity is not established—just as in the case of the expression "the boy is a lion.

Moreover, does the activity of causes proceed with reference to an effect, or without such reference? If it were without reference, they would never cease from activity anywhere, and consequently, even things such as a donkey's horn would come into existence.

If, on the other hand, it has the effect as its objective support, then its existence would have to be admitted, and thus the activity of the cause would be rendered futile. — Ā. (Āloka) states: "is perceived."

Now, it might be argued that the status of things as causes does not depend upon their possessing an operation; rather, when the presence or absence of one thing follows the presence or absence of another, the latter is designated as the "effect" and the former as the "cause. This is incorrect. For if this were so, just as there is no operation residing in the cause in the sense that "it does not exist when that [cause] is absent," so too in the case of "it exists when that [cause] is present," only the mere existence of the cause would be established, and nothing would be shown regarding its efficacy toward the effect.

And how, for one who speaks thus, can the causality of space and so forth be established anywhere? For, due to their eternity and omnipresence, it is impossible for them to possess a negative concomitance (vyatireka) based on place or time.

Furthermore, if there were no relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) between that which is indicated by the word "that" (*tat*) and that which is indicated by the word "arises" (*bhavati*), then the statement "when that exists, this arises" would merely establish the fact of the clay's existence. Consequently, the objects would never be expressed by the second case endings and so forth—which function to denote the status of being an object (*karman*) and so on acquired through dependence on another—and things would be established solely by their own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*) rather than by virtue of possessing functional capacity (*sāmarthyabhāktva*).
[Note: In the phrase *saṃbhavati sati*, the locative case is to be understood.]

By designating the cause and the effect with the same word, the meaning would be that "it becomes that" in the sense of the object characterized as clay—that is, the object remains characterized as clay—and not that "the jar becomes. This is the meaning; [otherwise] there would be the activity of a cognition directed toward something remote.

If, on the other hand, causality consists in being antecedent in time with necessity, then even Mount Meru and the like would be causes of a cloth, as there is no distinction in that regard.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate causality based merely on the fact of existing necessarily at a prior time, even in the absence of an operation (*vyāpāra*), then in the production of the form of a citron (*bījapūraka*) and the like, the tastes and other qualities residing in its parts would also have to be considered causes; likewise, in the production of taste and the like, the form residing in those parts would also be a cause. Consequently, there would be no rule that forms and other qualities invariably give rise to their own kind (*sajāti*).

Thus, since the relationship of cause and effect is untenable when examined according to the opponent’s view, the argument that "earth and other substances, in the form of composite wholes such as dyads, are impermanent because they possess an origin" is incorrect; for the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).

Indeed, "possessing an origin" is said to be "being an effect," and this is entirely unestablished in your system according to the manner described above, and it is also unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because a composite whole such as earth, which is absolutely distinct from its own parts, is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The refutation of the diversity between cause and effect is to be found in the fourth chapter of the *Aṣṭasāhasrī*.

Regarding the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyikas (Yaugas) is as follows: "The part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) are absolutely distinct, because they appear as distinct [to cognition], and so forth."

But surely, from this inference, its absolute distinction from them is established: "The part and the whole are absolutely distinct because they appear as distinct, like a jar and a cloth; for in the case of a jar, a cloth, and so forth, the appearance of distinction is observed only when there is absolute difference; thus, how could that [appearance] being observed in the case of the part and the whole not establish absolute difference? Otherwise, it would follow that this [inference] fails to establish [distinction] in other cases as well.

Nor is it unestablished that these two have distinct appearances; for the appearance of a composite whole, such as a cloth, being different from the appearance of its constituent parts, such as threads, is well-known to all living beings.
Likewise, their difference is established by the attribution of contradictory properties, just like water and fire.

Nor is the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) between these two unestablished; for the cloth is related to the universal *paṭatva* (clothness), performs a distinct purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and is endowed with extreme magnitude, whereas the threads are related to the universal *tantutva* (threadness) and possess attributes such as small dimension. How, then, are they not different from one another? Furthermore, they have different makers, like a jar and a cloth; for here, the threads obtain their own existence through the operation of weaving and spinning, whereas the cloth [obtains its existence] through the operation of the shuttle, the thread, the loom, the pins, and the weaver.

Furthermore, due to their distinct potencies, there is indeed a difference between the part and the whole, like poison and its antidote; and because they exist at earlier and later times, they are like father and son; and because they possess different dimensions, they are like the jujube fruit and the myrobalan. Even if there were no difference between these two, despite the difference in appearance and the superimposition of contradictory properties, there would be a confusion of categories (*padārtha-saṅkara*), because it would follow that the conventional usage of difference would be destroyed everywhere. Indeed, apart from the difference in appearance and so forth, we do not perceive any other basis for that conventional usage; therefore, [the part and the whole] are not non-different. (Śrīdhara)
— because of this [reason], and because they have different agents,
the thread and the cloth are distinct, just as [two things] are distinct due to having different agents, powers, and so forth.

"By virtue of the association with contradictory properties, like the difference between a pillar, a jar, and so forth"— this is stated in the form of a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 189.
We disregard the exclusion of difference (bhedavyavaccheda), which is the basis for conventional usage (vyavahāranibandhana). (Ā.)

Furthermore, if identity (*tādātmya*) between the part and the whole is accepted, then the difference in appearance and so forth becomes extremely difficult to maintain. For identity is said to be oneness; if that exists, how could there be a difference in appearance or the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), given that those two would have distinct objects? And if the whole, such as a cloth, is not an entity other than its parts, such as threads, then the threads too are not entities other than their own filaments, and those [filaments] are not other than their own parts, and so on until one reaches partless atoms (*paramāṇu*). If there were non-difference from those [atoms], then the entire collection of effects (*kāryagrāma*) would be imperceptible.

Therefore, as for the claim that the whole (*avayavin*) must be understood as something entirely distinct from its parts—namely, that there is no whole existing as a separate entity from its parts because the alternatives regarding its mode of existence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) are untenable, like the horn of a donkey—and that this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*): for instance, if a whole such as a cloth were a separate entity, would it exist in its constituent parts such as threads by way of a single part, or by its entire self? It cannot be by way of a single part, because apart from the parts themselves, there is no other "part" of the whole; or if there were, then the same question would have to be asked of those [sub-parts] as well, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it exists by its entire self (sarvātmanā) in one [part], then because it exists by its entire self in that very single part, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the other parts would be devoid of the whole. Or else, there would be as many wholes as there are parts, since it is fully completed in its entirety within each individual part. But this too is incorrect; for, in the refutation of the whole, is this a self-contained proof (svatantra-sādhana) or a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga-sādhana)? If it is self-contained, there is a contradiction between the subject (dharmin) and the predicate to be proven (sādhya), such as "this" and "does not exist";
furthermore, the reason (hetu) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatā), because the whole is unestablished.

Furthermore, existence (*sattva*) is not pervaded by [inherence] as a mode of occurrence (*vṛtti*), because you yourself admit the existence of color and other qualities even while not admitting the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Moreover, when the occurrence of a whole (*avayavin*)—whether in part or in its entirety—is denied, since the denial of a specific case implies the admission of the remaining possibilities, some other mode of occurrence would necessarily have to be admitted; otherwise, one should simply say that "it does not occur at all."

And inherence (*samavāya*) is the mode of existence (*vṛtti*); because it is unitary and partless in all respects, it cannot be the object of the terms "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) or "part" (*ekadeśa*). Furthermore, since the terms "entirety" and "part" have difference as their object, their application to a non-different whole (*avayavin*) is illogical. For "entirety" denotes the totality of something only when there is multiplicity, while "part" denotes a portion of something only when there is multiplicity; these two terms, "entirety" and "part," being understood only where there is difference, are untenable in relation to a single whole.
This is not an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*).
For instance, regarding the statement "it is non-existent because its occurrence is untenable," is this an independent proof or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*)?

If it were an independent proof, then with "the whole" as the subject (*dharmin*), "does not exist" as the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be a contradiction between the words of the proposition (*pratijñā-vākya*), such as "this does not exist."
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), because the subject (*dharmin*) is not established.

Likewise, according to our own system (*svamata*), while form (*rūpa*) and other qualities exist, they do not possess [inherent] subsistence (*vṛtti*). Thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since we do not admit the existence of inherence (*samavāya*).
Nor is existence pervaded by subsistence according to the opponent's view.

Because there is no difference in a single [entity], the application of a word denoting difference is untenable; therefore, the question is invalid. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.34) *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 45.
2.11: Is the whole composite substance present in each individual part, or is it present in only one part? This question is not tenable.

Why? Because there is no differentiation within a single entity, the application of the word "differentiation" is untenable; for the term "entirety" denotes the absence of remainder in a single thing, whereas the term "part" denotes a portion of something that possesses multiplicity.
These two terms, "whole" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*), which have difference as their object, are not applicable to a single composite whole because of the absence of difference;
*Nyāyabhāṣya* 4.2.10.

Now, *prasaṅgasādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) consists in the demonstration of an undesirable consequence for the opponent by means of what is accepted by them. But is the opponent’s acceptance a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is a valid means of knowledge, then the contrary inference cannot arise because it is sublated by that very [acceptance]. Nor can this [inference] itself sublate that [acceptance], because without it, this [inference] lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), and thus its status as a valid means of knowledge is impossible.

If that [reason] is invalid (*apramāṇa*), then one must simply state that "without a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not established"; what is the point of the labor of adducing an inference? If, on the other hand, it is intended as a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) against the opponent by means of the opponent’s own pervasion (*vyāpti*), then that counter-inference (*viparītānumāna*) cannot arise because it is sublated by that very [means of knowledge] through which the opponent has apprehended [the reason]; for it is not sublated by this [counter-inference] itself, since it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) without that [original means of knowledge].

Now, if [the object] is apprehended by a non-valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then one must state that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not established without a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); what is the use of adducing an inference (*anumāna*), since that [inference] is not a valid means of knowledge because its property does not reside in the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*)? [Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p.
46; note: *na cāsyā bādhā* is found only in the editions of Ā., Ba., Ja., Bhā., and Śr.]
In this very manner, the prima facie argument [is found] in the *Tattvasaṅgraha* (p.
189), the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.
155), and the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* (p. 658).
The discussion concerning the distinction between part and whole is found in the *Nyāyasūtra*, *Bhāṣya*, *Vārttika*, and *Tātparyaṭīkā* 2.1 (Ratnaprabhā, p.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 550;
*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 44;
*Praśastapādabhāṣyakandalī*, p. 41.
In such passages as these, the refutation of a permanent, partless whole that is absolutely distinct from its parts is to be observed;
here, the following response is provided.

As for the proof stated—"because of their appearing as distinct"—is it intended to establish that there is some kind of difference between the part and the whole, or a total difference? If it is some kind of difference, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since we also accept that there is some kind of difference between them.

If, however, it is a total difference, then the thesis is contradicted by direct perception (*adhyakṣabādha*), because these two appear in direct perception as having attained a state of identity in some respect (*kathañcittādātmya*).

Whatever appears in an uncontradicted perception must be accepted exactly as it appears, just as blue is accepted as being blue. And since the part and the whole appear in an uncontradicted perception as having some form of identity (*tādātmya*), the qualification "uncontradicted" applied to that appearing perception is not unestablished; for there is no possible means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever that could contradict it (p.
Indeed, perception is not its sublater, because their absolute difference does not appear therein.

Could inference also, having arisen from the fact of distinct appearances (*bhinna-pratibhāsatva*), serve as a sublater of that [thesis], on the grounds of performing distinct purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), originating from distinct causes, existing at distinct times, being superposed by contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharma*), possessing distinct potencies, or undergoing distinct transformations? First of all, an absolute difference between the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) is not established by an inference arising from distinct appearances; for, since it is employed immediately after stating a proposition sublated by perception, it is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), like the argument "fire is not hot because it is a substance. Furthermore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of objects such as trees appearing to persons situated at a distance or nearby.

Nor [is it established] by virtue of performing distinct purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), because this is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a dancer and the like. For even a single dancer performs many distinct actions—such as instrumental gestures, bodily postures (*aṅgahāra*), frowning, and casting glances—as well as various purposeful effects upon the spectators, such as joy and sorrow, which are mutually distinct. Thus, even the property of "arising from distinct causes" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to sprouts and the like, since even a single sprout is perceived to arise from a manifold collection of causes, such as soil and so forth.

Furthermore, the difference of the cloth from the threads is being established on the grounds of their existing at different times: is it from the threads situated in a widow’s basket, or from the threads situated in the state of a cloth? In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we also admit that there is a difference of the cloth from those [threads].
In the second case, however, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for it is impossible for threads in the state of a cloth to exist at a time different from the cloth.
— *antaṃ tadbhe-* (Ba., Ja.)
Because of non-identity (anekānta) [of the cause],

for it is not the case that in a single moment of a dancer or the like, the various effects such as action, cognition, designation, pleasure, and so forth, are unestablished for the spectators whose gazes are simultaneously fixed upon her; whereby, even if there were no difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there would be no diversity of activity.
And if the difference of the cloth from the primary threads is established, then the futility of the proof would be unavoidable. (Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 95)
For those other threads that have arisen in a particular state of attainment,
being capable of a specific purposeful action, are distinct from the first ones.
580 Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 194; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 157, upper section.
—Rabhyu— Ja.

—Even the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the case of] incense, fire, and so forth; therefore, it does not establish their absolute difference. Indeed, even though there is a superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by cold and hot touch upon the hand-held part and the other part [of the same object], there is no difference in the incense, the fire, and so forth.

Nor should it be asserted that the substratum of the sensations of cold and heat belongs only to the parts touched by the hand and other regions, and not to the whole (avayavin) such as the incense-burner; for this would contradict direct perception.

Furthermore, because threads, cloth, and so forth possess distinct potencies and undergo distinct transformations, only a difference in state (*avasthābheda*) is established in some respect (*kathañcit*), but not an absolute difference. In that case, the argument would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Therefore, since even the fact of having different appearances establishes only a partial difference between the part and the whole, the qualification of perception—that it grasps their non-difference in some respect—is proven to be non-sublated.

Whatever is not cognized by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as having a certain form does not possess that form, just as a jar [does not possess] the form of a cloth. And the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) are not cognized as having the form of absolute difference.

For the whole, such as a cloth, which performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) like the removal of cold and so forth, appears as a particular state belonging to its own nature consisting of the parts such as threads; it is not, however, an entity absolutely distinct from them, because such a thing is not perceived even in a dream.
(Variant readings: *vibhinna*—b, ja, śra)
This is well-known;

for instance, some threads, having reached a specific state, become capable of performing a single purposeful action, such as removing cold, while others do not. In that regard, in order to designate those specific threads which are useful for that single purposeful action performed by a woman [weaving], users employ a single conventional term, "cloth" (*paṭa*).
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, page 195;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 157, first part;
*Sanmatitarkaṭīkā*, page 662.

Likewise, its non-appearance must be due to either its having an invisible nature (*adṛśyasvabhāvatva*), or because of inherence (*samavāya*), or because of the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), or because of the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). It cannot be due to its having an invisible nature, for that would entail the contradiction of your own admission that "the perception of the whole occurs when there is the perception of many parts.
Nor can it be due to inherence, because—inherence being distinct from identity in some respect—it will be refuted later during the refutation of inherence itself.
Nor can it be due to the relation of cause and effect, for that would entail the consequence that even a jar and a potter would appear as non-different.

The claim that the appearance of non-difference occurs precisely because the parts, such as threads, are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the whole, such as a cloth, is also unsatisfactory; for since inherence itself is unestablished, the status of being an inherent cause is likewise unestablished. Indeed, there is no other such thing as inherence apart from some form of identity (*tādātmya*), nor is anything else ever established anywhere as an inherent cause apart from the nature of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

Nor [is it established] through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśe�yabhāva*); for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a staff and a person would appear as non-different. For just as there exists a relation of qualifier and qualified between threads and cloth in the case of "threads qualified by cloth," so too does it exist between a staff and a person. Therefore, if the whole were absolutely different from its parts, it would be perceived exactly as it is, since there is no cause for its non-perception; yet it is not so perceived. Consequently, it is not absolutely different from them.

Whatever is not perceived as distinct by way of absolute difference from something else is not absolutely different from it, just as the nature of a whole (avayavin) is not [perceived] as distinct from its parts; and the whole is not perceived as distinct from its parts by way of absolute difference, because it is apprehended through the contact of the sense organ with the parts, assisted by repeated contacts of the sense organ with those parts (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

As for what was said—that [the argument] is either an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*), and so forth—that too is without substance. For whether it be a reductio or an independent proof, what does that matter to you? Furthermore, as for the claim that there is a contradiction between the subject (*dharmin*) and the predicate to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in an independent proof, that too is incorrect. This is because this statement is not made for the purpose of negating the existence of the whole (*avayavin*); rather, it is for the purpose of negating its absolute difference [from its parts].

It has already been stated that a whole (*avayavin*) that is absolutely distinct from its parts is not perceived by anyone. However, that which is established through perception—the specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) that constitutes the very self of the parts such as threads when they have undergone transformation into the states of being stretched lengthwise and crosswise (*ātāna-vitānībhāva*), namely the whole such as a cloth—is not rejected; for the refutations such as the dilemma regarding its mode of existence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) do not apply there.

For a separate entity (*arthāntara-bhūta*) existing [in the parts] would incur defects such as whether it exists in one part or in its entirety; but this is not the case for that which is identical with its own self, because it is a transformation of that very nature.

Whatever exists in something other than its own self must do so either by its entire being or by a part, as for example a *bilva* fruit in a bowl, or Devadatta in various seats; and since a whole (*avayavin*) exists in its parts, which are other than its own self...
[page 224, line 1].

With the words "by way of independence" (*svātantryeṇa*), etc., he anticipates the rebuttal of Śaṅkarasvāmin: "The proof that proceeds by way of an independent reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*)."
For it is only when that [whole] is perceived by itself that [the existence of parts] is logically consistent; however,
a mode of subsistence— whether in its entirety or in part— is never observed anywhere.

Because this [perception] is impossible, substance would be non-existent; and for another reason as well: because if this perception were observed anywhere, it could not be excluded from substance and so forth.
Furthermore, if that difference is not perceived, a question regarding it is not appropriate;
at most, one might say "there is no occurrence [of the universal]," but even that is not the case.
If it is argued that direct perception is established here by the cognition "this is this" through its being joined [with the object],
and if that is not accepted as direct perception, then let some subverting argument be stated.
Otherwise, even for the mind [perceiving] form and so forth, there would be no direct perception at all.
(Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 204)
— either the accomplishment of the mantra (mantrasādhana),
or that which... (as per variants in ba, ja, and bhā pṛ 224,
paṃ 2).
That is incorrect;
for by the words "entirety" (kṛtsna) and "part" (ekadeśa), this meaning is revealed:
does its occurrence [in the whole] consist in its being partless, or is it otherwise?
Just as the bilva fruit and so forth are perceived when situated in a bowl or similar vessel, or as Caitra and others are perceived when seated upon many seats; so too is it here.
621 *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 205; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 162, u.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 668:

A single cognition possessing manifold forms is conceived as subsisting in its own substratum through identity—just like jujube fruits [in a bowl]—provided that there exists a state of distinctness [between the forms and the cognition].
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 481, l.

10: Furthermore, as for what was stated—“the occurrence [of a substance] is inherence,” and so forth—that too is mere words; for since inherence has been root-and-branch refuted, its occurrence anywhere in anything is untenable, like a lotus in the sky.

As for what was also stated—that because the words "entirety" (*kārtsyam*) and "part" (*ekadeśaḥ*) have difference as their object, it is illogical for them to apply to a partless whole (*avayavin*), and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for a single, partless whole, which is a distinct entity, is never perceived as existing within its multiple parts. Furthermore, no mode of existence other than through entirety or through a part is ever perceived;
for whatever exists in something must do so either partially, as a bamboo pole does in its supports, or by its whole self, as curd does in a bowl.

Therefore, if these two modes [of existence] are not admitted, the subsistence of the whole (*avayavin*) in its parts (*avayava*) is untenable, because its pervaders—namely, existence in part (*ekadeśa*) and existence in its entirety (*sākalya*)—are absent. And since that [subsistence] is untenable, there is consequently an absolute absence of difference [between them]. To explain: the whole, such as a cloth, is not absolutely different from its parts, such as the threads, because it does not subsist in them either in its entirety or in part. For whatever is absolutely different from something else does not subsist in it either in its entirety or in part, as in the case of curds and the like in a vessel; yet the whole does not subsist in its parts either in its entirety or in part.

Furthermore, if the whole (*avayavin*) possesses a partless, unitary nature, it is impossible for it to simultaneously pervade multiple parts. To explain: whatever substance has a partless, unitary nature does not simultaneously pervade multiple substances, just as an atom (*paramāṇu*); and the substance that is the whole is likewise partless and unitary in nature.

Nor is there an inconclusive argument (*anekānta*) based on space (*ākāśa*) and so forth; for it is not established that these are partless (*niraṃśa*), since they possess infinite and other such spatial divisions. Alternatively, whatever is a manifold substance is not simultaneously pervaded by a single partless substance, just as mats, walls, and the like are not pervaded by a single atom; and parts are manifold substances. Furthermore, if the whole (*avayavin*) were partless, then when a portion of the body is covered by a loincloth or similar garment, would the entire body be covered or not? If it were covered, then—just like the specific part intended—it would follow that the whole body would be imperceptible.

Now it is said: even when that [the whole] is obscured, there is no obscuration of the body, because the conjunction with the substances that obscure the parts lacks the capacity to obscure it. Indeed, the very same extent of conjunction with the constituent substances that obscures the parts does not obscure the whole, because of its greater magnitude. If this is so, is there an obscuration of it in part, or not? If it exists, it is not so; for since that which is partless lacks spatial divisions (*pradeśa*), such obscuration is impossible. Or, if it were possible, the partlessness would be contradicted due to the association of contradictory properties.
