That which is associated with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsargi*) is not partless, just like water, fire, and so forth; and the nature of the whole (*avayavisvarūpa*) is associated with contradictory properties by virtue of having both covered and uncovered aspects. If there were no difference in this [whole] despite such association with contradictory properties, then all talk of difference would be cut off everywhere, because it would follow that the entire universe, despite its manifold forms, would be a single substance.

Now, if you argue that there is no obscuration even in the spatial parts (*pradeśa*) of the whole (*avayavin*) due to its conjunction with the substance that obscures the parts, then it follows that this [whole] would be perceived even in those obscured parts; consequently, the entire whole would be perceived, since there is no distinction [between the obscured and unobscured parts]. For there is no difference whatsoever in the whole whether its parts are obscured or not, because it is admitted that it remains unobscured in both cases. If it is objected that the application of the terms "entire" (*samagra*) and "not-entire" (*asamagra*) to a single, non-different whole is improper—since these terms refer to distinct objects—this has already been answered previously by demonstrating that the whole exists as a certain kind of distinction (*kathañcid bheda*).

There is a contradiction regarding the subsistence of the whole (avayavin) in its parts, because even when the parts are concealed, the whole is not concealed; for indeed, when something exists in a certain place, it is observed that if that [place] is concealed, the thing itself is also concealed—just as curds are when the bowl is concealed—and yet the whole exists in its parts. Furthermore, when the perception of one thing is preceded by the perception of another, the latter is not perceived in the absence of the former—just as a basket or similar object is not perceived when its triangular shape or other features are not perceived—and the perception of the whole is preceded by the perception of its parts.

Now, if it is maintained that [the whole] is unperceivable in the regions of its constituent parts, how could it have unity? For, due to the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by being perceivable and unperceivable, a certain degree of difference is established. Furthermore, threads, hands, and so forth do not at all inhere in a single whole, because they are multiple, just like mats, walls, huts, and the like.
Alternatively, if the accepted substance were not dependent upon multiple parts,
then the invalidating proof would be the logical inconsistency of its existence as a single unit, just like an atom.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 201;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 665.
If the whole (*avayavin*)—
that is, the gross object— possessed a single nature, then when it were covered by a mere fly’s foot, the entire thing would necessarily be covered, because there is no division [between them].
Furthermore,
if passion were one with the impassioned person, then everyone would be impassioned like that impassioned person;
or else, if they possessed contradictory properties, it would follow that they are distinct entities.
594 *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 198; *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.594.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 663;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 883.

—The syllogism (*śloka-vārttika*): That which possesses a conjunction of contradictory properties is not one, such as an object like a jar; and an object such as a gross blue thing possesses the superimposition of contradictory properties.
Or rather, this [argument] regarding the conjunction of contradictory properties is otherwise... page 78.

For instance: when one part, such as a hand, is covered, the simultaneous occurrence of both the covered and uncovered forms of a gross object indicates its conjunction with two contradictory properties;
this proves the non-existence of the whole (*avayavin*), because even when one part is covered, there is no covering of the whole. (Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, p. 85)
Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kandali, p.
42; Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, 1.1.1.
On page 32, line 383: Even when there is partial obscuration, the whole (avayavin) possesses an unobscured single nature.
*Nyāyalīlāvatī*, page 9:
*śṛṅgāṭaka* etc.; in the vernacular, it is called *siṅghāṅ*.

Furthermore, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by being colored and not being colored; for instance, when a single constituent part such as a thread is being dyed, does the whole (the cloth) become dyed or not? If it becomes dyed, then it would follow that the entire whole would be perceived as dyed.

But surely, the redness of a whole (*avayavin*) is its conjunction with a substance such as saffron, and that [conjunction] is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). For it does not pervade its own substratum like color and so forth, since it is not perceived even when other parts [of that substratum] are perceived. Therefore, how can there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of redness everywhere when there is redness in only one place? This too is incorrect; for it is impossible for a conjunction to be non-pervasive in a partless whole.

Is its non-pervasive existence (avyāpyavṛttitva) defined as not pervading all substances, or as existing only in a restricted location, or as being unperceived in other parts of the whole (avayavin) even when that whole is perceived? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; for it is not accepted that a single substance is the object of the term "all," and if it were partless (niraṃśa), how could there be a non-pervasion of it by its conjunction in its entirety? Furthermore, if such non-pervasion were to occur, it would contradict its partlessness.

The second alternative, however, is tenable only if the whole (*avayavin*) were admitted to occupy a fixed location; yet, if that were admitted, it would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), because the Yogins assert that it is devoid of spatial parts (*apradeśatva*).

By this same reasoning, the third alternative is also refuted; for if its occupying a fixed location were not admitted, it would be impossible for its conjunction not to be perceived when the whole is perceived in another part.

Therefore, its existence as something non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti) is not tenable; or, if that were tenable, the superimposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa) would be established—so how could it be unitary in every respect? If it is argued that even when one part is being dyed, the whole is not dyed, that too is incorrect, because it contradicts both perception and accepted doctrine; for no one has ever seen or accepted that while a constituent part such as a thread is being dyed, the cloth is not dyed.
Nor can a single entity possess uniform dyeing and so forth without falling into the fault of having partial dyeing and so on.
Likewise, a contradiction with both passion and its absence is to be expected;
see *Avayavinirāsa*, p. 87; *Nyāyaviniścaya*, p. 197, l. 6.

Redness is the conjunction with the substance redness, and non-redness is its absence; and both indeed exist in one and the same place, because conjunction is a state that does not pervade its locus (avyāpyavṛtti), as stated in Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī p.
42 and Nyāyalīlāvatī p. 9.

With the words "But surely," etc., he anticipates the rebuttal of Śaṅkarasvāmin: "But surely, because conjunction does not pervade [its locus], redness does not apply to the whole, nor is the whole seen as covered. (600)

In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 199, Śaṅkarasvāmin says here: "The coloring of a cloth is said to be a conjunction with substances such as saffron, and that [conjunction] is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*); therefore, when one part is colored, there is no coloring of the whole, nor is it logical that the covering of one part of the body and so forth should result in the covering of the whole."
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, folio 664:

"If [the opponent means] that it does not pervade all substances—that is the meaning—then that is incorrect, because it is accepted that a substance is not an object of the word 'all' [in this context].
[If they mean] that it exists in one part of its substratum—that too is incorrect, because a 'part' (ekadeśa) is impossible for it."
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 200:

It is understood [from the commentary]: if the whole (*avayavin*) were partless, the perception of a variegated form would be impossible; for it is illogical for blue and other variegated aspects—which possess distinct appearances and are pervaded by contradictory properties—to be one. Indeed, it cannot be said that "blue is yellow"; if even such [contradictory] things were identical, the world would not be manifold.

Now, it might be argued that blue and other such colors are not designated as "variegated" (*citram*) therein, because, due to their distinct appearances, they do not fall within the scope of a single variegated cognition; rather, there is only one color called "variegated," and by its connection with it, the whole (*avayavin*) is variegated, just as something is called "white" through its connection with whiteness. To this we reply: even here, is the "variegated" merely a color devoid of specific qualities like white and so on, or are it the white and other colors themselves when combined, or is it a color distinct from the forms of white and the rest? Among these, it cannot be the mere color [devoid of specifics], because a universal (*sāmānya*) devoid of particularities (*viśeṣa*) is never perceived anywhere.

Nor can it be that blue and the other colors themselves, when combined, constitute the variegated [citrarūpa]; for individually they lack variegation—indeed, blue is not variegated, nor is yellow variegated—and thus each one by itself does not possess the nature of variegation.

It might be argued that this will arise when they are combined; but this too is impossible. For "combined" refers to many things, whereas "variegated" is a single thing. And it is not possible for many things, which have not attained a particular state, to become a single form; otherwise, blue itself would be yellow.
The position is indeed maintained that non-variegated colors, by combining on a cloth, produce a variegated color;
and thus, in this case, nothing is contradicted.
(Nyāyavārttika 4)

We indeed accept that a variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) is produced in the composite whole (*avayavin*) by means of white, green, red, and so forth, which are inherent in its parts and serve as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*).
Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā 4.2.12
Therefore, it is produced by them acting together;

and since that which is being produced conforms to the natures of its various causes, it must consist of black, white, and green components, and is thus designated as "variegated" (*citram*). (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 30)

Furthermore, do these [qualities] such as blue pervade their substratum (*āśraya*) or do they exist in only one part? If they pervade the substratum, then, since the substratum would be occupied by a single blue [quality], there would be no room for others; moreover, it is illogical for them to exist in only one part, for the whole (*avayavin*) has no parts because it is impartite (*niraṃśa*). If, on the other hand, those colors belong only to the parts, then the whole would be colorless; and if that were so, it would not be perceptible. If even that which is colorless were perceptible, it would follow that space and the like would also be perceptible.

Now, if that variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) is distinct from colors such as white and so forth, then there would have to be a cognition entirely distinct from the perceived particulars such as blue and so on; furthermore, the blues and other colors being recognized therein would not appear [as they do]. For when yellow and the like, which are distinct from white and so forth, are appearing, there is no recognition of "white. Therefore, there is a contradiction in asserting that many colors exist in a single earth-substance.
And even granting this, we say:
When many qualities such as white and others coexist in a single locus, do they pervade the entire substrate or do they reside in specific parts? (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.

221). Furthermore, regarding variegated color (*citrarūpa*), are these limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as blue and so forth detrimental to the whole (*avayavin*), or are they beneficial? Of these two positions, the first is untenable, because that which is detrimental cannot logically function as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

In the second case, however, if there is no apprehension of all the contributing adjuncts (*upādhi*), then because the possessor of the adjunct (*upādhimat*) is also dependent upon them for its assistance, it follows that nothing at all would be apprehended. If it is argued that this consequence does not arise because the object is perceived as being assisted by only specific adjuncts, then, since it is perceived as being assisted by those [specific ones], it would follow that it must also be apprehended as being assisted by all adjuncts—given that its nature consists in being assisted by all adjuncts—and thus the consequence of apprehending everything remains.

Now, if it is argued that there is no consequence of perceiving everything because, when this [whole] is apprehended by virtue of being assisted by one particular attribute (*upādhi*), it is grasped only as qualified by that specific attribute and not as qualified by other attributes; then, since a single whole would possess two forms—one perceived and one unperceived—its partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) would be contradicted. For its nature is not merely being assisted by one attribute, but rather being assisted by the complete set of attributes; and that cannot be cognized as long as all the attributes have not been apprehended. If one thing that provides assistance is perceived while another is not seen, then those [other attributes] do not exist [in the sense of being perceived].
For that one [entity] is indeed the benefactor of all; when it is grasped, there is the grasping of everything.
(Pramāṇavārttika 1.56)

As it has been said: "When one thing that provides assistance is to be grasped, there are no other assistances [required] beyond that; for when that in which they reside is seen, those [others] are seen as well. Thus, in the grasping of that [one], there is the grasping of all.
(*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 152).

Now, it might be argued that the powers of that [entity] which are assisted by each respective limiting condition (*upādhi*) are distinct; therefore, even when the possessor of the conditions (*upādhimat*) is perceived as qualified by the power assisted by one condition, it is not perceived as qualified by the power assisted by other conditions, and thus there is no perception of the whole. To this we reply: since the possessor of the conditions consists of all its powers without exception, if that which is endowed with one power is perceived, it follows that that which is endowed with all powers must also be perceived; consequently, because the entire class of conditions would also necessarily be perceived, the perception of the whole is unavoidable.

For by the very same form in which it bears one power, it bears the other; if one were to postulate a different form even in that case, there would be an infinite regress and a destruction of the thesis that the whole is partless.

Furthermore, at the very moment there is a disjunction between the hand and space, there is simultaneously a disjunction between the body and space, as well as a conjunction between the body and space produced by the conjunction between the foot and space. Thus, a single composite whole would be both conjoined with and disjoined from the same single space at one and the same time. How, then, could that which is occupied by two mutually contradictory forms be considered absolutely one? For that which is occupied by two mutually contradictory forms is not absolutely one, just like the nature of fingers that are both extended and otherwise; and the composite whole such as the body is likewise occupied by the mutually contradictory forms of being conjoined with and disjoined from space and so forth.
—[The opponent] places [the objection] thus:

"In the conceptualization of the body, etc., even regarding the pair of contradictory properties characterized as moving and non-moving, one must see the absolute rejection of unity; for when a limb such as the hand moves, there is movement of the embodied whole (avayavin) in that region, while there is non-movement elsewhere."

Therefore, a partless whole (*avayavin*) that is absolutely distinct from its parts should not be understood; rather, the whole, such as a cloth, should be understood as a particular state characterized by a certain degree of oneness through transformation, belonging specifically to the parts such as the threads when they have attained states such as being stretched lengthwise (*ātāna*) or crosswise (*vitāna*). This is because of the cognition: "That very thing which I saw, I now touch," and because otherwise, if there were a separate establishment [of the whole], it would follow that when the hand and other parts move, the whole would undergo birth [or motion] everywhere, which is impossible since contradictory actions cannot coexist in one place.

In that case, when a single part such as the hand is moving, how could the gross object—which is simultaneously perceived as having both a moving and a non-moving form—not possess the conjunction of contradictory properties? (Refutation of the Whole, p. 81)
—In the case of [the cognition] "this is that," there is the recognition of a single [object]; surely [this is so], O Ārya! *ba*, *ja* [manuscripts]. *pratīteḥ*; indeed, O Ārya! *ā*.
The Buddhist's prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, as a matter of course, there exists no composite whole (*avayavin*) distinct from [its constituent] form and so forth.

Now, since a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities] is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can it be appropriate for discerning people to accept it? To explain: would that whole distinct from them be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be through direct perception; for in a cognition produced by the sense organs such as the eye, only form and so forth appear, and no other whole. If one were to designate that very [collection of qualities] as the "whole," there would be nothing undesirable, as the difference is merely one of name.
Nor can it be through inference, because inference does not operate regarding that which is not an object of direct perception.

For if the whole (*avayavin*) were ever perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and if there were some inferential mark (*liṅga*) invariably concomitant with it, then, like fire from smoke, it might be inferred upon seeing that mark somewhere. However, apart from color and so forth, this whole does not appear even in a dream within direct perception. Therefore, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it, its non-existence alone is more reasonable.
That for which no apprehending means of valid cognition exists is non-existent, just like a donkey’s horn; and there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that apprehends a whole.

Indeed, it appears that the word "Buddhist" (bauddha) written in the mirror prior to this point belongs only to the marginal note (*ṭippaṇī*), because the cause for its production is untenable. That for whose production a cause is not tenable does not exist, just like the son of a barren woman; and no cause whatsoever is tenable for the production of a composite whole (*avayavin*).

Nor is this [reason] unproven; for the cause of the production of composite wholes such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) is the conjunction of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃyoga*), and that [conjunction] is untenable either by way of total pervasion (*sarvātmanā*) or by way of partial contact (*ekadeśena*).

For if atoms were to combine with their entire being (*sarvātmanā*), it would follow that the composite whole (*piṇḍa*) would be no larger than a single atom, and thus a final refutation would be offered to the concept of a whole possessing parts.

Nor can they combine by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*); for atoms have no spatial divisions, and if such divisions were possible, their status as atoms would be untenable. Since an atom joined simultaneously with six others from different spatial directions would necessarily possess six parts, atoms must therefore be accepted as being, in ultimate reality, like iron rods (*ayaḥśalākākalpa*).

Nor should it be argued that, if a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is not admitted, there could be no cognition of a single gross form regarding atoms that are mutually unconnected and resemble iron rods; for such a cognition is possible there, just like the perception of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*).

Just as a person with ophthalmia has a cognition of a single gross form even regarding hairs that lack such a form, so too does it occur for us and others regarding atoms; indeed, hairs are never perceived by a person with ophthalmia one by one.

Therefore, the cognition of grossness and so forth is erroneous, because it consists in apprehending something as what it is not, like the cognition of a person in a post; [as stated in] *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* 12: "because of simultaneous conjunction with six [sides]," and so on; or else, if [the atom] were to exist by its entire self, it would follow that it is manifold.
And it is not undesirable [to say] that it is neither one [in part] nor anywhere at all;
this is from the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
—The attainment, Śrāvaka; —the attainment, Śrāvaka.
For those whose forms are joined in succession are indeed like iron rods.
All manifest entities are seen to have a nature mixed with conceptual construction (kalpanā). Furthermore, we maintain that things such as jars are merely an aggregation of atoms.
Tattvasaṃgraha: Just as one suffering from ophthalmia perceives non-existent hairs, moons, and so forth.
20. [The Chapter on] Representation:
Just as there is no delusion regarding a lamp because it arises from a continuous series of identical flames, so too is there no delusion in consciousness.
In the same way, when there is the cognition of many subtle objects existing in immediate succession, [the mind] appears as one. (Tattvasaṃgraha 589)

Furthermore, you maintain that the whole (avayavin) pervades its multiple parts and consists of [qualities] such as color and taste; yet that [whole] can only be apprehended when all its parts are apprehended, and not otherwise.

And would that apprehension occur through a perception grasping the parts situated on the near side, through one grasping the parts situated on the far side, or through a perception grasping both? It cannot be through the perception grasping the parts on the near side, because such a perception is ignorant of the news regarding the parts situated on the far side; nor can its pervasiveness be grasped when the pervaded [parts] are not grasped, as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Whatever appears in a particular form is an object of the conventional usage of existence in that very way; for example, blue, appearing as having the form of blue, is an object of the conventional usage of existence in that very way; and the whole (avayavin) appears as being connected with parts located on its near side.

And thus, since a difference is possible due to the imposition of contradictory properties—namely, that the nature of the whole as related to the parts existing on the near side is distinct from its nature as related to the parts existing on the far side—how could the pervasion of all parts by a single whole be established? For even if there were an imposition of contradictory properties characterized by being related to those [parts], if there were no difference [in the whole], the very talk of difference would be annihilated.

Likewise, when one thing appears and another does not appear, the latter is distinct from the former; for example, when a jar appears, a cloth that does not appear is distinct from it. And when the nature of the whole as connected with the parts situated on the near side appears, the nature of the whole as connected with the parts situated on the far side does not appear. Thus, there is a distinction between these two due to the difference in their appearance.
By this [argument], the claim that perception apprehending the parts on the far side grasps the pervasiveness of the whole is refuted.

Nor can it be perceived by both [types of perception] together, because that is impossible; for a single perception is never observed to grasp the parts situated at the near, far, and middle [surfaces] simultaneously—
[as noted in the Ābhāsa and Bhāṣya commentaries].

By this very [argument], its being composed of color, taste, and so forth is also refuted; for it is not tenable that its apprehension occurs through a perception that grasps color, one that grasps taste, or one that grasps both. This is because visual perception, which grasps color, does not operate upon taste, and gustatory perception, which grasps taste, does not operate upon color; furthermore, a perception that grasps both is not manifested even in a dream.
Thus, the proof of the "whole" (*avayavin*)—which is somehow non-different from its parts and possesses a nature that is both one and many—is preceded by this refutation.
To this, the following reply is given:

Regarding what was stated previously—that [the object] arises from the causal condition consisting of the sense organs such as the eye, and so forth—does that form which is worthy of being designated as a "jar" or the like appear in the causal condition arising from those [senses] as a single transformation characterized by upper, lower, and middle parts, endowed with a specific shape; or rather, as a collection of atoms (paramāṇu) that are distinct from one another and partless? In the first case, how could there be no appearance of a composite substance (avayavidravya) in the causal condition arising from those [senses]? For the very transformation characterized by a specific shape, which consists of those parts, is precisely what constitutes the composite. If you accept its non-existence because there is no appearance of a composite distinct from color-form (rūpa) and the rest, then it follows that color-form and the rest must also be non-existent, since this [composite] does not appear apart from them either.
Indeed, even in a dream, the color and other qualities of a bilva or āmalaka fruit are never perceived as existing apart from the composite substance (avayavidravya) that possesses them.

Whatever appears in an uncontradicted cognition in a certain form must be understood as being exactly of that form, just as blue is understood as having a blue form. And the form of the bilva, āmalaka, and so forth, appears there as the form of a composite substance characterized by unity, transformation, and so on.
Furthermore, the qualification "uncontradicted" applied to the cognition in which that appears is not unestablished, because no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists that could contradict it.
For perception and the other means of valid cognition do not sublate that [unity]; for even when one investigates hundreds of times, objects appear only as having a nature of unity and so forth (p.

But surely, it has been argued that the transformation into oneness and so forth is preceded by the conjunction of parts, and yet the conjunction of parts—whether in its entirety or by way of a single part—is not possible; this is incorrect. For when you say this, do you intend there to be an absence of relation altogether, or do you intend a relation in some other manner, setting aside both "entirety" and "a single part"? Regarding the first alternative, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the relation of objects through their parts is manifest in perception. If that relation did not exist, then when one part of a rope, a bamboo pole, or the like is pulled, the rest would not be pulled along.

That which is unconnected with something else is not observed to be drawn along with it; for example, when a jar is drawn, the wall is not drawn along with it. And according to your own view, the near part of the rope, bamboo, staff, and so forth, is unconnected with its far part.

Now, if it is intended that the mutual connection of parts occurs through another mode, setting aside [the modes of] "in its entirety" or "in part"; that is not tenable. For the connection of objects is observed precisely through the other mode characterized by "smoothness" (*snigdha*) and "roughness" (*rūkṣa*); indeed, in cases such as flour and water, no other mode is perceived as the cause of connection apart from those two, since the occurrence of holding and pulling is explained thereby.
(Nyāyasūtra 2.1.35)

1.35 In the absolute non-difference of cause and effect and so forth, there would be no pushing, pulling, and so on, even when atoms are in a state of aggregation, just as there is none during their separation.
Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 223; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 152, top; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 253.
Bondage occurs due to the qualities of smoothness and roughness;
Tattvārthasūtra 5.33.

Since atoms cannot be related either in their entirety or in part, yet a relation is perceived, the postulation that their relation occurs through some other mode is indeed logically sound (Sanmati-Ṭīkā, p.

252). Furthermore, as for the argument that atoms would necessarily possess six parts; does this refer to the points of contact with the originating [atoms], or to the nature that serves as the cause of conjunction? In the first case, there is a mutual contradiction: namely, that atoms are both [partless] and composed of six parts.

For if they were to begin with parts, it would be possible for them to possess a dimension greater than that of their own constituent parts; how then could they be atoms? For that which possesses the ultimate minimum of dimension is an atom (*paramāṇu*).

The second position, however, is not subject to fault, because it is intended that atoms possess parts characterized by a nature that serves as the cause for conjunction with other atoms, distinguished by spatial divisions (*digbhāgabheda*). Otherwise, how could there be the production of things such as jars, which perform purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) like holding and carrying water? Indeed, atoms are not capable of performing such actions if they were like iron rods [without connection], because they would be mutually unconnected. Those things which are mutually unconnected do not perform purposeful actions such as holding water—just like atoms situated in different locations. And according to your own view, the atoms designated as "jars" and so forth are mutually unconnected.

Now, if it is argued that only those who perform that action are distinguished by proximity to a location, and not others—that is not so; for if a whole (avayavin) is not admitted, proximity to a location is also untenable, since a location itself is also a whole.
(Page 231, Line 21: *hetusva*—ba, ja, bhāṃ, śra).

By this, the position that the nature of jars and the like—which consists of an accumulation of partless atoms mutually distinct from one another—appears in a cognition produced by the senses, is refuted. For atoms possessing the nature as previously described do not appear at all in a cognition produced by the senses; rather, for all living beings, it is an object whose nature is stable, gross, and common that appears therein.

"The appearance of that [hair] there is like the perception of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*); this too is incorrect. For even for one suffering from ophthalmia, hairs that are mutually unconnected are never the objects of perception; rather, it is only when they have attained the state of a collection characterized by a specific conjunction that they are cognized as such objects.
Furthermore, the refutation of the whole (*avayavin*) based on the example of hair is untenable, because the hairs themselves are the wholes. — *Dīrgharūpam*, Śrauta-bhāṣya.
In the cognition of the eye and other senses, that which appears as a single gross form contradicts the doctrine of the absolute distinction between atoms;
for [the object] results from the conjunction, disjunction, and transformation of those multiple entities. (Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 223)
But the aggregate (skandha), which possesses spatial parts, is directly perceived by people on the outside. (Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 481, u.)
In that regard,
it appears as such [to the ear],
just like the perception of a mass of hair by one suffering from ophthalmia; thus is its perception.

The variation in the apprehension of an object by a sense organ—whether it be sharp or dull—is due to the organ’s own state of intensity or dullness without overstepping its proper domain; it does not involve activity toward what is not its object.
(Nyāyasūtra 4.2.10)

Furthermore, if the whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, would the cognition of a jar and so forth be without an object (*nirviṣaya*) or with an object (*saviṣaya*)? It cannot be without an object, because it is experienced as having an object through such mental formulations as "I know the jar," and because there is no evidence for its being objectless. Moreover, any argument intended to prove that all cognitions are without an object—such as "all cognitions are without a basis because they are cognitions, like dream-cognitions"—has been refuted in detail during the establishment of external objects.
Page 135.

Now, [regarding] that which has an object: what is its object? If it is an aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu-samūha*), then what indeed is this so-called "aggregate of atoms"—are they the atoms themselves, or a property of them? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; because atoms, being extremely minute, are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is impossible for them to be objects of perception. Furthermore, if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no perception of anything at all, and thus no empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) based on perception would ever occur. This is because even qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), and so forth, are perceived as objects of perception only when they consist of a composite whole (*avayavin*), as in the cases of "cow," "white," or "moving."

Now, if that property [of conjunction] is of the nature of a conjunction and is denoted by the term "their collection" (tatsamūha), that is not so. For if the conjunction of atoms is admitted, the rejection of the composite whole (avayavin) becomes untenable, as the underlying logic is the same: by the very same logic by which this [conjunction] exists as one in many places, the composite whole would likewise exist.

Furthermore, is this conjunction of theirs real or unreal? If it is unreal, how can it be an object of perception? That which is unreal is not an object of perception, just like a sky-lotus; and yet, the conjunction of atoms intended by you is held to be unreal.

Even if this [atomic conjunction] were real, it would be illogical for it to be an object of perception for persons such as ourselves, because it is a conjunction with a substance of unsurpassed magnitude. Whatever is a conjunction with a substance of unsurpassed magnitude is not an object of perception for persons such as ourselves, just like the conjunction between space and an atom; and the mutual conjunction of atoms is a conjunction with a substance of unsurpassed magnitude. [End of Bhāṣya on the Atom.
In that regard, due to the distinction of spatial divisions, atoms have six parts.
If the aggregate were not even as much as an atom, it would not be an object of cognition for you.
(Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 197)
It is not logical that a single entity, which consists of [the nature of] conjunction, should possess the state of being [both] Śra and Ba, Ja, Bhā, and Śra.
—ṇasaṃyo— Ārya, Baṭu, Jaṭu:

"But surely that conjunction is not an object of perception for people like us; what is it then? It is merely the atoms in a state of aggregation. This too is incorrect, because the position that atoms are perceptible has already been refuted. Furthermore, would this state of aggregation (*sañcitattva*) consist in their spatial proximity or in being characterized by conjunction? In either case, the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) is established; for space itself is a composite, and the same logic applies to conjunction.

And if atoms were the objects of that [perception], then there would be no such cognition as "this is one large jar" and so forth, because they lack largeness and are manifold. If it is argued that [the object] is merely an aggregate (*sañcaya*), we say no; since an aggregate consists of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and because that [conjunction] is beyond the reach of the senses, its apprehension is untenable.
(Nyāyabhāṣya 4)
2.14 Is their "arrangement" (sanniveśa) proximity in space or a particular kind of conjunction? (Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 886)

Now, [the opponent might argue] that this notion arises there just as in the case of an army or a forest; for just as a single notion—“one forest” or “one army”—arises with respect to many parts of an army or parts of a forest whose distinctness is not perceived from a distance, so too, because their distinctness is not perceived when atoms are in extreme proximity, a notion such as “one large jar” arises with respect to those atoms. This is incorrect; for since atoms are beyond the senses and thus unperceived, it is impossible for them to be the objects of such a notion. Indeed, it is observed that only those parts of an army or parts of a forest which are actually perceived—such as chariots and so forth, or *dhava* trees and so forth—are the objects of non-differentiating notions like “one army” and the like, not those that are unperceived.

Furthermore, if the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, the analogy "like the cognition of an army or a forest" does not hold; for if the parts of an army or a forest cannot be established as having a whole, the cognition of an "army" or a "forest" likewise cannot be established.

Furthermore, if there were a single cognition of oneness regarding the parts independent of a single composite whole, then a difference in apprehension would be observed despite the difference in location. For wherever a cognition of non-difference is based solely on the nature of non-difference itself, independent of a single composite whole, a difference in apprehension is seen upon a difference in location, as in the case of the individual components of an army or a forest; and you maintain that the cognition of non-difference among the parts occurs independently of a single composite whole.

For it is well known that among the components of an army or a forest, there is a difference in perception due to the difference in location, since they appear as a unity when far away and as a plurality when near. However, such a variation in perception based on a variation in location does not occur in the case of jars and the like. Furthermore, even in the absence of a single composite whole (*avayavin*) in those components, the cognition of non-difference—such as "one army"—is appropriate because of the existence of a single cause, namely the proximity of locations or the conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). But in the case of atoms, since no single cause whatsoever is possible, how could such a cognition be appropriate?
If it is argued that [the perception of atoms] is like the perception of an army or a forest, we say no; because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.34).
36 –ṅgeṣu dūrā– [iti pra–] ā॰ (according to the reading "dūrā" in the manuscript)

As for the other statement—that the cognition of grossness and so forth is erroneous because it consists in apprehending something as what it is not (atasmiṃstadgrahaṇa), and so on—that too is an unexamined assertion. For the cognition of something as what it is not is impossible without the prior perception of that thing in its primary sense; indeed, the cognition of a man in a post—which is not a man—is never observed by one who has not previously established the primary existence of a man. Furthermore, grossness and the like are not established by you in any primary sense anywhere, since that would entail the establishment of a whole (avayavin) [which you deny]. (p. 232, l. 3)

As for what was stated—that [the whole] is grasped by that which perceives the parts located in the near portion, and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for it is logically possible for the self, aided by perception, memory, and other factors, to grasp the whole as pervading the parts located in both the near and far portions.

Indeed, we do not maintain that only a momentary cognition such as perception is the grasper of the object, such that this fault would arise; rather, it is the self transformed into that [cognition] [that is the grasper], and the existence of that [self] has been established on the occasion of the investigation into the continuum (santāna), page 232, line 5.
Regarding the term *padārtha* (p.
9, folios ba & ja):

If the difference of the whole (*avayavin*) from its parts were to be established—either as some kind of difference or as a total difference—on the grounds of its connection with parts that possess prior and posterior portions, due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*), then: if it is a difference in some respect (*kathañcit*), it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For we do not maintain, like the followers of the Yoga school, that the whole connected to those parts is partless (*niraṃśatva*); rather, we accept that for every relation, the related entity is different in some respect.

In every respect, therefore, if one attempts to prove their difference [on the grounds of contradictory properties], there is an inconclusive reason (*anekānta*) due to the case of a momentary form (*rūpa-kṣaṇa*). This is because, even though that [momentary form] is superimposed with contradictory properties characterized by its capacity as a material cause (*upādāna-śakti*) and its capacity as a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-śakti*) with respect to subsequent moments of color, taste, and so forth, its non-difference [from them] is admitted. For the very capacity of a momentary form to act as a material cause with respect to another momentary form is not the same as its capacity to act as a cooperative cause with respect to a subsequent moment of taste and so forth; otherwise, it would follow that taste and the rest would possess the nature of form. To explain: taste would have the nature of form because it is produced by the material causal capacity of form, just like a subsequent momentary form.
Nor is the auxiliary power itself something other [than the substance], for it would follow that the subsequent form produced by it would also possess the nature of taste.
To explain: the form coexisting with the taste would have the nature of taste because it is being produced by the auxiliary power along with the prior form, just like the taste itself.
Therefore, one who desires to maintain the distinction between form and taste must admit a real distinction between the material cause and the other [auxiliary] powers of the cause.

Now, if it is argued that because [the object] is imagined (*kalpita*), its distinction therein is unreal (*avāstava*), that is not so. For if this were unreal, it would follow that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is also unreal; consequently, inference from taste (*rasa*) to color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth—which is non-deviant—would be impossible. How then could there be the cognition of color-form and so forth, which arise from the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*), as being real? [This is stated in] *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.10. [The term] *pratisambandhin* [is used in the sense of] "related" [in the manuscripts *ba*, *va*, *ja*].
"Even for that which has the characteristic of being unperceived (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*),

[inference occurs] by means of inferring a property of the cause (*hetu-dharma-anumāna*), like the transformation of fuel by smoke"— this is the meaning of the second half of the verse from the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.1).
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, page 417;
*Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, page 162.

As for what was also stated—that [the whole] consists of color, taste, and so forth—that too is incoherent. This is because the whole is established as consisting of color and the rest through the synthetic cognition (anusandhāna-pratyaya) that "I touch now that very same thing which I saw. Indeed, a synthetic cognition is not possible without the apprehension of a single object as the substratum of both color and touch by means of two sense organs; and since color and touch are each perceivable by distinct sense organs, such a synthesis would otherwise be impossible.

Thus, it is not logical to deny the existence of the whole (avayavin), whose reality is well-established; for if that were denied, it would follow that even the mere atom (paramāṇu) must be denied, since apart from the whole, there exists no other means by which those atoms could be established.

Whatever is an effect is produced from causes possessing a smaller magnitude than its own, just as a cloth [is produced from threads]; and since the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is an effect, [it follows that there must be something with a smaller magnitude]. Alternatively, [the existence of the atom is established] because there must be something with a minimum magnitude somewhere, since magnitude is gradable, just like large magnitude. Why, then, could this not be established simply through the existence of composite wholes (*avayavin*)? Furthermore, if the composite whole were denied, how would the entire system of inference not be destroyed, given that for you the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—which possess the nature of composite wholes—would be unestablished? Or, if they were established, how could there be a denial of them, since they are established precisely as having the form of atoms?
Page 232, line 18:
From the error regarding the effect follows the error regarding the atom; for the cause is known through the effect as its logical mark (*liṅga*).
Due to the absence of both [cause and effect], that which resides therein—neither a quality nor a genus—is also non-existent.
*Āptamīmāṃsā*, Aṣṭasahasrī, p.
223; *parakā*—Ā. (Note)

How indeed, O venerable one, could a real pot or the like— an entity consisting of both a unitary and manifold nature— be established as somehow non-different from its own parts, given the [impossibility of] place and time? [This is the meaning of the verse.]

Thus, the composite substance consisting of atoms (*paramāṇu*), dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and so forth—which is imagined by others as being the nature of cause and effect—does not stand [as a valid entity].

Therefore, the claim that "earth, water, fire, and air are of two kinds, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal," and so on, is refuted; for, according to the manner explained above, the substances such as atoms imagined by others are not established.
This concludes the refutation of the definition of substance (*dravya*) as stated by the Vaiśeṣikas within the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*).

Furthermore, by what means would its substantiality (*dravyatva*) be established? If you say it is through its connection with substantiality, [we reply]: surely substantiality is the state of being a substance (*dravyabhāva*). That is known only when the substance is known; yet there can be no cognition of a substance without substantiality, because the Vaiśeṣikas admit that the apprehension of substances and so forth occurs solely through the medium of a universal (*jāti*). Thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).

Moreover, a universal is manifested by some characteristic such as shape, just as "cowness" is manifested by the shape of the dewlap, hump, and so on, or as the nature of ghee and oil is manifested by their smell when heated; however, in this case, there is no such manifesting factor present.

If it is argued that "possession of action," "possession of quality," and "being an inherent cause" exist here [as defining characteristics], is each of these individually the manifestor, or are they collectively? They cannot be individually, because possession of action is impossible in the case of substances such as space (*ākāśa*), and possession of quality is impossible in the case of newly produced things such as cloth. For a composite whole (*avayavin*) becomes an inherent cause for the production of qualities only after its own self has been attained; thus, you yourselves have admitted the absence of qualities in a newly produced cloth. Consequently, there would be no cognition of a substance in that regard for yogins.

Nor is the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) its manifestor; for that too is impossible at all times, since not everything is an inherent cause at all times. Thus, this definition suffers from the fault of being non-pervasive (*avyāpti*) in all cases. Furthermore, when it is a cause, it is not an inherent cause, and when it is an inherent cause, it is not a cause. For in the moment prior to the effect, it is the cause, and at that time the effect does not exist such that it could be the inherent cause of the effect; and when it is the inherent cause of the effect, the effect has already been produced and thus it is no longer a cause. Therefore, the definition suffers from the fault of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).

Regarding the principle that "whatever is possible in a certain case is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that case," even here, the fault of impossibility applies to things such as a jar produced at that very moment (*sadyaḥ-samutpanna*), because no such characteristic is possible therein. Even if one were to claim that the collection [of characteristics] constitutes the definition, this would still result in under-extension (*avyāpti*), since all three [characteristics] are absent in a jar produced at that very moment; furthermore, while action (*kriyāvattva*) exists in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, [the definition fails there too].
If it is argued that "it is a substance (*dravya*) because of its connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*"), that is not the case, for both [substantiality and its connection] are unestablished.
In *Sarvārthasiddhi* and *Tattvārtharājavārttika* 5.2,
"vā" is used in the sense of "iva" (like).

Nor is the definition [of substance] one and the same for all five, such as earth and the rest; for while the definition of substance—"that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause"—applies only to those things possessing action, it does not apply to ether, time, space, and self, which are devoid of action, because they lack the property of possessing action (Āptaparīkṣā, p. 5).

In that regard, the definition of substance (*dravya*) as "that which is the substratum of qualities" (*guṇāśraya*) is not a valid definition, because it is both under-extensive (*avyāpti*) and over-extensive (*ativyāpti*): in the first moment [of its production], a substance lacks qualities; furthermore, [the definition] is observed to apply to qualities and so forth as well. *Ratnākara*, p. 845.

In that context, the definition of substance as "that which is the substratum of qualities" is not a valid definition, because it is neither too narrow nor too broad: in the first moment, there is an absence of qualities [in a substance]; moreover, [the definition] is seen to apply even to qualities and the like.
Because it is accepted that a substance, as soon as it arises, remains for a moment without qualities, there is the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) [to substances];
and because one observes the application of number-qualities such as "there are twenty-four qualities" even to qualities themselves, there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
(Citsukhī, p. 175)
*Khaṇḍanakhādya*, page 579:
"Pervasion (*vyāpti*)—[when]... [is]... when [it is]... (do—ā., śra., yadā tu ja.)

—the definition of these [is as follows]: according to Ārya, Ba, Ja, and Bhā, [it consists] in the possession of action, the possession of quality, and the state of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva) with respect to cloth and so forth. Ba, Ja.
—pyasaṃbhā— bhāṃ

Furthermore, the inference that "whatever substance is distinguished from others because of its connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*)" and so forth, is also incorrect. For an inference proceeds only when there is a subject (*dharmin*)—such as a mountain—that is established for both disputants; otherwise, the reasons (*hetu*) would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Moreover, the example must be one agreed upon by both disputants, while the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), such as fire, exists in the subject of the inference (*sādhyadharmin*) though it remains doubtful; otherwise, the thesis (*pakṣa*) would have an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). And the probans (*sādhanadharma*), such as smoke, must be established in the subject agreed upon by both disputants; otherwise, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, in this case, no subject (*dharmin*) consisting of nine types of substances is established for anyone by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is there a probans (*sādhana*) such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) operating therein, nor is there a property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) called "difference" (*bheda*).

For difference (*bheda*) is indeed mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and that is perceived only in dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, since there are infinite counter-correlates distinct from the substance, one must consider by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) these could be grasped by those who are not yogis? Moreover, when the counter-correlates are being grasped, are they grasped as distinct from the substance or non-distinct? In the first case, since the distinction of the substance from others would already be established by the very means of valid cognition that grasps the difference, this inference would be purposeless.

In the second case, however, since objects are being apprehended as mutually intermingled, the question "of what is there a difference from what? would arise; thus, the thesis would have an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, that is called a purely negative (kevalavyatirekī) reason for which there is only a negative concomitance (vyatireka) while it pervades the subject (pakṣa), and no positive concomitance (anvaya) exists. Consequently, how can the negative concomitance—that where the property to be proven, called "difference" (bheda), is absent, there "substantiality" (dravyatva) is also absent—be ascertained when there is no necessary connection (pratibandha) between these two properties? There remains a doubt: is it because of the absence of difference that substantiality is not there, or because of the non-existence of another entity?

For where there is the apprehension of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), it is logical that in the absence of one, the second does not exist; as, for example, when the causal relation between fire and smoke has been established through means of valid cognition such as perception and non-perception, it follows that in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist.

Furthermore, in this case, because the nature of both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) is unestablished according to the manner previously described, and because their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has not been apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no comprehension of the absence of the prover in the absence of the probandum. Thus, since a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) is not a true inference, it is impossible to establish either its distinction from other types of inference or its practical application (*vyavahāra*).

By this, the purely negative inference such as "because of its connection with earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvābhisambandhāt*) and so forth is refuted; for the aforementioned defects apply here without distinction.

Furthermore, this could only be asserted once it were established that earth and the other elements are absolutely distinct from one another; however, that is not established, because they are in some sense non-different from one another by virtue of having the *pudgala* as their essence.

If earth and the others have the *pudgala* as their essence, there would be no rule regarding their being the substrata for specific qualities such as odor and so forth. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyikas.

Now, if they were of the nature of a single *pudgala*, the restriction regarding their being the substrata for specific qualities such as odor would not obtain; for it is admitted that *pudgalas* are without distinction, consisting of form, taste, odor, and touch. Consequently, if they were of that nature, there would be the perception of odor and so forth without distinction in all four—earth and the others—but this is not the case, since in all four of these, the fourfold set of qualities beginning with odor is perceived only according to their respective restrictions.
And it has been said: "Odor exists only in earth; taste in water; form in fire; and touch in air."

Furthermore, even the connection with specific universals such as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) would be difficult to establish if those [elements] were one; for if they were of an identical nature due to the absence of any difference in essence from one another, then water and the other elements would also, without distinction, possess the connection with "earth-ness" and so forth.

Indeed, it is not the case that for jars, water-jars, bowls, buckets, and so forth, a connection with "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) is not observed despite their being of the same genus without distinction; nor is there a lack of such a connection for them, since the connection with "earthness" is perceived only in earth, and the connection with "waterness" (*aptva*) and so on is perceived only in water and the like. How then are these qualities to be applied? [The answer is: because each subsequent quality exists in each preceding one, the subsequent ones are not perceived in it—Nyāyasūtra 3.1.68.
1.64 The non-existence of reality— Ā.
The demonstration that they consist of a single person (*pudgala*), preceded by the refutation [of the opposing view] regarding the non-existence of other principles (*tattvāntarābhāva*).

To this, the following reply is given: as for what was stated—that [the objection] regarding "the nature of a single substance, the person (*pudgala*)," and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion. For, in that case, would the restriction regarding the substratum of specific qualities such as odor depend upon their existence, or upon their manifestation? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; because, just as in earth, the fourfold set of qualities beginning with odor exists in water and other elements as well, a restriction regarding their being the substratum would be impossible.

If it is asked, "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is their existence therein established?", we reply: "By inference (*anumāna*). For instance: water and the other elements possess odor and so forth, because they possess touch (*sparśavattvāt*). Whatever possesses touch is known to possess odor and so forth, just as the earth (*pṛthivī*); and water and the others do possess touch. On the other hand, whatever does not possess odor and so forth does not possess touch, just like the self (*ātman*) and so forth—this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). [Thus: Water possesses odor, because it possesses touch, just like the earth.
*Sarvārthasiddhi* 5.3:

Now, it may be argued that the specific determination of earth and the other elements as the substrata of qualities such as odor is stated with respect to their manifestation; let it be so stated. Nevertheless, even by that much, the establishment of them as distinct substances (*dravyāntara*) does not follow, because of the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) of fire when it is conjoined with water, gold, and so forth.

For fire in conjunction with water, gold, and so forth—which possesses a non-manifested radiant form and hot touch—is not established by you as a substance distinct from fire characterized by a manifested radiant form and hot touch, since that would entail the fallacy of contradicting the established number of substances.

In the same way, earth and the other elements, because they are endowed with qualities that are not manifested and are non-distinct, are not separate entities by virtue of being absolutely different substances from one another. Whatever is endowed with non-distinct qualities is not a separate entity by virtue of being absolutely different substances from one another, just as the selves (ātman) and so forth; and since earth and the others are endowed with non-distinct qualities such as form (rūpa) and so on, they likewise do not constitute different principles (tattvāntara), just as there is no difference in principle among the selves due to their non-distinction in possessing intellect (buddhi) and so forth, so too there is no such difference in principle among earth and the others due to their non-distinction in possessing form and so forth.

Otherwise, a difference in essence (*arthāntaratva*) would be established. As for what was also stated—namely, that there is a connection with specific universals such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth—that too is charming only when left unexamined; for the connection with a subordinate universal (*avāntarajāti*) cannot in any way establish a difference in essence. Indeed, this [connection] establishes only a difference in individual (*vyakti*), not a difference in essence; otherwise, because of the connection with subordinate universals such as "kṣatriya-ness," even selves (*ātman*) would result in being different essences, which would lead to a contradiction in their number.

Furthermore, if one were to accept an absolute difference between earth and the other elements based on their difference in genus (*jāti*), there could be no relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*). For those things that possess an absolute difference by virtue of a difference in genus, there is no relationship of material cause and effect—just as, for example, between the self (*ātman*) and earth and so forth. Since you maintain such a difference between earth and the others, the qualification "absolute" (*ātyantika*) is added to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the relationship of material cause and effect seen in the case of threads and cloth. Indeed, in that case [of threads and cloth], there is no absolute difference, because the commonality (*sāmānya*) of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth is possible even though it is non-different.

[Objection: "In that case, since non-difference is also possible for earth and the other elements by virtue of their being substances (*dravyatva*) and so forth, let there be that [non-difference] between them. [Reply: This too is incorrect; for in this way, there would be no distinction between the self (*ātman*) and earth and the other elements, and consequently, the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) would obtain. And thus, because of the resulting consequence of the non-duality of the self (*ātmādvaitaprasaṅga*), one would be offering a libation of water to the entire manifold of substances such as earth. (Page 238, Line 18) [The text contains the fragment *sattvabhe*.]

[Answer: That is not so. If an absolute difference between earth and the other elements were admitted, their being [of the same nature] would not be possible. Yet this is the case, because we perceive the production of water from the moonstone (candrakānta), and of pearls and the like from water and so forth.

Therefore, they do not differ as entirely distinct realities in every respect. Those things that stand in the relation of material cause and effect do not differ from one another as absolutely distinct realities, just as in the case of threads and cloth and the like. And earth and the other elements stand in the relation of material cause and effect.

The claim that water and so forth arise solely from substances such as water already contained within moonstones and the like is also untenable. This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish their existence therein, and because if things of a different genus were to arise from things of a different genus, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of the established order of principles (*tattvavyavasthā*). Furthermore, if one accepts that a substance arises only from another substance already contained within it, then one must likewise accept that a jar arises only from a jar already contained within a lump of clay; thus, the Sāṃkhya system is established.

Therefore, since water is not perceived in things such as lumps of clay—just as a jar is not perceived therein—and since it is absent in moonstones and the like, and because the relationship between material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) is untenable if there were absolute difference, the wise should understand that earth and the other elements are distinct from one another through their modal differences (*paryāya-bheda*), yet non-different insofar as they consist of the substance *pudgala*, which is characterized by color, taste, smell, and touch.
Consequently, the fourfold substance consisting of earth and so forth, as postulated by others and possessing an absolute difference in nature such as permanence and the like, cannot be established.

Nor is it the substance of space (ākāśa); for there is no difference in the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the existence of this [space] either, which has a nature imagined by others.

This is because we perceive the production of water from a moonstone, of pearls and the like from water, of fire from wood, and of wind from a fan and so forth (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 163, upper section).
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.

29, in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*: The Vaiśeṣika’s prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that "space has sound as its quality. Now, is there not indeed the means of valid cognition consisting of inference, arising from the mark (*liṅga*) of sound, for the existence of that [space]? For instance: sound is dependent upon something, because it is a quality, like color and so forth.

Nor is its status as a quality unestablished. Sound is a quality because, while being distinct from substance and action, it is related to existence (*sattā*). Whatever is of this nature is a quality, such as color and so forth; and sound is likewise; therefore, it is so.
Nor is its distinction from substance and action unestablished. To explain: sound is not a substance because it inheres in a single substance, like color and so forth.

For some substances are non-composite (not composed of other substances) due to their eternity, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth; others, however, are composed of multiple substances due to their being effects, such as a jar and so forth, but never [is there a substance] that inheres in only one substance.

If it is asked, "How is it established that sound has the property of residing in a single substance? [The answer is: Sound resides in a single substance because, while possessing generality and particularity, it is perceptible by a single external sense organ, like color and so forth. This is the inference.

Now, if only "because it possesses generality and particularity" were stated, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to atoms and the like; therefore, to exclude those, "because it is perceptible by a sense organ" was said.
Even so, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) with respect to jars and the like; to eliminate that, the qualification "single" [substance] was added.

If it were stated simply that "because it is perceived by a single sense organ," there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to the self (ātman); to exclude that, the qualification "external" (bāhya) is added.
Furthermore, to avoid deviation with respect to "color-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth, the qualification "possessing a general property and particularity" (sāmānyaviśeṣavattve sati) is added.
Likewise, this [object] is not an action (karman), because it is not the cause of conjunction and disjunction, just like color and the rest.

For this reason as well, sound is neither a substance nor an action, because while being impermanent, it is invariably perceived by non-visual perception (*acākṣuṣapratyakṣatva*). Whatever is such [impermanent and invariably perceived by non-visual perception] is so [neither substance nor action], just like taste and so forth; and sound is such, therefore it is so. The qualification "while being impermanent" is added to exclude the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by the self (*ātman*). Nevertheless, there would still be a deviation with respect to substances and actions that are perceived by non-visual perception; to avoid that, the qualification "invariably" is added, because in the case of those two (substances and actions), an invariable non-visual perceptibility—such as that of sound—is impossible.

Likewise, sound is neither a substance nor an action, because it inheres in a pervasive substance; whatever is thus [inhering in a pervasive substance] is so [neither a substance nor an action], just like pleasure and so forth, and sound is likewise; therefore, it is so.
Consequently, the qualification "while being other than substance and action" is established.

If it were stated merely as "because of being other than substance and action," there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to universals (sāmānya) and so forth; to exclude those, it is stated "because of being related to existence" (sattāsambandhitvāt).
Sound is dependent on something [as its substratum] because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*), like color and so forth (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

322). Since the possibilities of being a substance (*dravya*) or an action (*karman*) have been excluded, and since it cannot belong to a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, sound remains as a quality alone.

But why is sound not a substance? Because it subsists in a single substance, it is either a non-substance or a substance; for a substance is either one that subsists in a single substance, such as space or an atom, or one that subsists in multiple substances, such as a composite substance like a dyad. Sound, however, subsists in a single substance—namely, space—and therefore it is not a substance.
Nor is sound an action, because it produces another sound;

for an action does not originate another of its own kind, and since it possesses a connection with universals such as "existence" (sattā) and "sound-ness" (śabdatva), it would follow that it belongs to the triad of universals and so forth. Therefore, by the method of elimination, sound is indeed a quality (guṇa).
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 229:
Sound is not of the nature of substance or action, because it is perceptible by the sense of hearing, like the universal "sound-ness" (śabdatva) and so forth;
sound is a quality, because, while being distinct from substance and action, it is related to existence (sattā), like color and other qualities.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
649: "That which does not have substance as its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is 'subsisting in a single substance' (ekadravyaḥ). Śrī [Vallabha].

Sound possesses the genus *guṇatva* (the state of being a quality), because, while existing, it is perceptible by external perception by people such as ourselves but not by visual perception, just like odor;
thus it is so, according to the *Nyāyalīlāvatī*, page 25.
*Tattathā*, Āhnika 1.
[The reading *acakṣuṣya* is incorrect; it should be *aprākṣuṣya*.
Therefore, it is established that sound, by virtue of being a quality (*guṇa*), must reside in something.

And that which is its substratum (*āśraya*) is, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), space (*ākāśa*). For instance: sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of tangible atoms (*sparśavat-paramāṇu*), because it is perceptible to the senses of persons like us, just like the color and other qualities of produced substances (*kāryadravya*).

Nor is this [sound] a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the effect-substances such as earth and so forth; for it arises even when other effect-substances do not appear, like pleasure and so forth; because it does not have the qualities of its cause as its antecedent, like desire and so forth; because it does not persist as long as the substance [endures]; and because, while being perceptible to one person such as ourselves, it is imperceptible to other persons, just like that [pleasure]; and because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum, such as a drum;
for in the case of tangible substances like earth and so forth, qualities are perceived as the opposite of what has been stated.

Nor is it a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) of the self, because it is perceived as distinct from the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra), because it is perceptible by the external sense organs, and because it is perceivable by other selves; for qualities of the self such as cognition (buddhi) and the like are observed to have the opposite characteristics.
Nor is it a quality of the mind (manas), because it is perceptible to people like us, just like color and so forth;
nor is it a specific quality of space or time, because those two are the causes of notions such as "prior" and "posterior."

Therefore, this [sound] resides in a substratum distinct from earth and the other elements, because it is a quality (guṇatva) while there exists a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that sublates its subsistence in them; for whatever is not thus [residing in those] is not so, like color and so forth, and sound is such; therefore, it resides in a substratum distinct from those. And that in which it resides is space (ākāśa), because the inferential mark (liṅga) of sound is non-specific and there is an absence of any specific mark [to distinguish otherwise]. Furthermore, it is established as one and all-pervading (vibhu), and as eternal like an atom (paramāṇu), because it is the locus of a magnitude (parimāṇa) that is unsurpassed.
And because no other effect [of sound] appears, sound is not a quality of things that possess touch.
(Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.25)
Because another effect, which would be of the same genus as the effects of its own parts, does not appear— that is, because it is not perceived—

the point is this: just as in the case of a drum or similar objects, specific qualities such as color and so forth are perceived as being of the same genus as the color and other qualities of their own parts, so too, a sound that is of the same genus as the sounds of its own parts is not observed in a drum or similar objects.

Sound is not a specific quality of tangible substances (sparśavad-viśeṣaguṇa), because, while being perceptible, it does not originate from the qualities of its own causes—as seen in the case of sound produced by the parts of a drum or similar instruments (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Vivaraṇa, p. 90); because it does not persist as long as the substance itself; and because it is perceived elsewhere than in its substratum.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 58:

"The qualities in the inherent causes are the causal qualities (*kāraṇaguṇa*); that quality which has those as its prior cause is 'preceded by causal qualities' (*kāraṇaguṇapūrvaka*), such as the color of a cloth being preceded by the color of the threads.
But this is not the case [for sound], because space, which is the inherent cause of sound, is itself uncaused and thus lacks inherent-cause qualities."
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

323: Sound does not have as its antecedent a quality belonging to its own inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because—unlike the color of a cloth and so forth—it does not arise immediately after the production of its substrate; therefore, like pleasure and so forth, it is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of tangible substances. Praśastakandalī, p. 59.
Sound does not exist as long as the substance [endures], because it perishes even while its substratum, such as a conch shell, still exists. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kandalī p.
59; Praśastapādabhāṣyakiraṇāvalī p. 107)
Even though [sound] is perceptible to persons such as ourselves who reside in its vicinity, it is not perceptible to other persons residing at a distance;
this would be the case if sound were a specific quality of a tangible substance (sparśavad-viśeṣaguṇa), for in that case, the substratum of the sound— such as a conch shell— would have to be stated,
yet that [substratum] is perceived elsewhere, at a distance, in the location of the ear-cavity.

Furthermore, there is no apprehension of a quality belonging to one thing in another; therefore, sound is not a specific quality of a tangible substance, because it is perceived in the ether delimited by the ear-cavity, which is distinct from the conch-shell or other objects considered to be its substratum. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 60)
In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p.

107), the word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) has the sense of "without. Therefore, the meaning is: "because [the object] would be perceptible even without a substratum," which amounts to saying "because it would have an unsuitable substratum.
(*Nyāyalīlāvatīprakāśa*, p. 277).
Because it exists elsewhere [than the body] and because it is perceptible, it is neither a quality of the self nor a quality of the mind.
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.19.

Because it is perceptible by the external sense organs, because it is graspable by other selves, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), [sound] is not a quality of the self.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 58.
— Because of the apprehension [of them], due to their being other than the self (ātmāntaratvāt) — [this applies] to those [cognitions], however, according to the Bhāṣya and Śrī [commentaries].
