Because it is perceivable by the sense of hearing and because it possesses the nature of a specific quality (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*), sound does not belong to space, time, or the internal organ (*manas*) (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

58). Sound has as its substratum a substance distinct from earth, water, fire, air, space, time, self, and mind; for, while there exists valid cognition subverting [its subsistence in those], it possesses the nature of a quality (*guṇatva*).
"Because there is no distinction in the word or the mark, and because there is an absence of a specific mark," Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.19; Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 329.

1.30 Furthermore, the process of the production of sound, which serves as its defining characteristic, is demonstrated as follows: sound is produced from conjunction, from disjunction, and from [another] sound.

In that case, when sound arises from conjunction, space is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the conjunction of the drum and so forth with space is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the conjunction of the drum and the stick is the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).

Because there is no deviation from the rule that the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*), when caused by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), invariably have conjunction as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the specific qualities of all-pervading substances, which are caused by conjunction, have conjunction as their non-inherent cause; because, while being caused by conjunction, they are specific qualities of all-pervading substances; whatever is thus is so, just like cognition (*buddhi*) and the rest; and sound (*śabda*) is likewise; therefore, it is so.

Likewise, in the production of sound from disjunction as well, space is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the disjunction between the bamboo split and space is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the disjunction between the bamboo splits is the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).

Now, one might think: "Since sound is observed to arise after the disjunction of the bamboo segments, it is logical that this [disjunction] is its cause; however, it cannot be the disjunction between the bamboo segment and space, which would be its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because there is no evidence for the existence of such a thing. But this should not be held in mind; for we perceive that the qualities of multiple substances, which serve as the efficient causes (*nimitta*) of sound, give rise to sound when they are endowed with a homogeneous non-inherent cause.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Disjunction (*vibhāga*) initiates sound in conjunction with its own non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) which is of the same class [as itself], because it is a quality of multiple substances (*anekadravyaguṇatva*) while being a producer of sound; whatever is such is so, just like the conjunction of a drum and a stick; and disjunction is likewise; therefore, it is so. Furthermore, regarding the production of sound from sound, ether (*ākāśa*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the preceding sound is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and factors such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) are the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). — Thus ends the section on action (*kriyā*).
The production of sound indeed arises from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound itself.
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.32.
Sound is produced from the conjunction of a drum and space; here too, space is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) [Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p.
Because of the non-existence of the [object], there is no cognition of its being a cause. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kandalī, p. 289) — Śrī — Because of the non-cognition of its being a cause. — Śrī —

The proof of the substantiality of sound— preceded by the demonstration that it lacks the quality of being an attribute of space— and the proof of space as the cause for the simultaneous apprehension of all objects— preceded by the refutation of its being entirely eternal and partless—
are here addressed.

As for what was stated—that sound is dependent upon something, and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion. For, does this inference establish that sound merely depends upon some substrate, or that it depends upon a substrate that is eternal, unitary, and all-pervading? If it is the first position, how can the existence of the substance "space" (nabho-dravya) be established from this? It would follow that only a mere substrate is established. Furthermore, in that case, you are proving what is already established, since we accept that sound, being a transformation of matter (pudgala), is dependent upon such a [material] substrate.

However, if the probandum is "having a single, eternal, and all-pervading substratum and being dependent upon it," then the example is devoid of the probandum; for color and other qualities depend on a substratum that is the opposite of that [i.e., not eternal, not one, and not all-pervading].
Furthermore, its status as a quality (*guṇatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove it (pṛ. 240, l. 6).
If it is being proved in a general sense that these sounds merely possess the quality of being dependent, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*),

because it is logically possible for the person (*pudgala*) and the aggregates (*skandha*)— as single substances— to serve as the substratum of sound; thus, there is the fallacy of establishing what is already proven.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 422; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 164, upper section; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 670.

However, a concomitance that is uniform, pervasive, and like the eternal ether is established for these [reasons], because there is no deficiency in their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, due to their pervasion by non-sequential [succession] and the like.

In the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, although the proof was set forth to establish [the non-substantiality of sound] by the argument: "because, while being distinct from substance (*dravya*), it is related to existence (*sattā*)," even that does not establish it, because the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) is partially unestablished (*ekadeśāsiddha*). For even though sound is distinct from action (*karma*), its distinctness from substance is unestablished; since it is logical for it to be a substance due to its being characterized by the definition of substance, and the definition of substance—namely, possessing qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*)—is present in sound in its entirety.

Therefore, sound is a substance because it possesses qualities and action; for whatever possesses qualities and action is a substance, such as an arrow and so forth, and sound possesses qualities and action.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because there exists valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its possession of those [qualities]. To explain:

sound possesses qualities because it is the substratum of touch, smallness, largeness, dimension, number, and conjunction; for whatever is of such a nature possesses qualities, such as the jujube fruit, the myrobalan, and so forth, and sound is likewise; therefore, it is so.
Page 240, line 8:
"Sound is a substance, because it possesses touch... (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

164, first half). In this regard, its being the substratum of touch is not unestablished; for instance: sound possesses touch, because it is the cause of the impact of another object with which it is connected; whatever is thus is so, like a mallet or similar objects; and sound is thus; therefore, it is so.
Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*); for when there is contact with sounds from bronze vessels and the like, an impact upon the auditory organ is perceived.

Nor should it be argued that the impact here is caused by air accompanied by sound; because [the phenomenon] follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of sound, if one were to postulate another cause even for such a [directly observed] phenomenon, there would be no fixed rule (*pratiniyama*) regarding the relationship between cause and effect anywhere.

If sound were a quality (*guṇa*), it would lack qualities itself and thus lack touch (*sparśa*); consequently, it could not be the cause of impact (*abhighāta*). This would lead to a circular argument (*cakraka-prasaṅga*): for its being a quality would be established only once its non-substantiality (*adravyatva*) is established; that [non-substantiality] would be established only once its lack of touch is established; and that [lack of touch] would be established only once its being a quality is established. Furthermore, its possession of touch is established by the inference: "Sound possesses touch, because it is impacted by objects possessing touch, like grass and so forth.
Thus, this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*), since we perceive its impact by means of things possessing touch, such as a headwind or a wall.
Therefore, its being a substratum of touch is not unestablished;

for sound—which is commonly known to produce a crackling sensation within the ear-cavity, to be generally a cause of resistance, and to cause injury to houses and other structures—dispels the hypothesis that it is intangible (*asparśatva*).
(Aṣṭaśa, Aṣṭasaha, p. 108)
—[Sound] being established [as a substance], that [quality of dimension] is also established.

Nor does it consist in being the substratum of the dimensions of smallness or largeness; because it is the object of the cognition of smallness and largeness. Whatever is the object of the cognition of those [dimensions] is the substratum of those dimensions, just like the jujube fruit, the *āmalaka* fruit, and so forth. And sound is the object of that cognition; thus, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), for it is well-known even among children that "the sound is small" and "the sound is great," by virtue of its being the object of such cognitions.

Even for such a [sound], if one were to deny its being an object of cognition, it would follow that one must also deny its being an object of cognition in the case of jujube fruits (*badara*) and the like; consequently, there would be an absence of dimension in all things, for indeed, the establishment of dimension therein cannot come from anything other than cognition. If it is argued that the establishment of dimension is appropriate for jujube fruits and the like because they are substances (*dravya*), but not for sound because the opposite is the case—that too is incorrect, as it entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for only if the non-substantiality of sound is established can the absence of dimension in it be established, and only if that is established can its non-substantiality be established.

Furthermore, if one does not admit that it possesses such a magnitude, on what basis would there be the cognition of that [magnitude] in sound? If it is argued that this is based on the smallness or greatness of the magnitude residing in its cause, then let that same [cognition] in the case of jujube fruits (*badara*) and so forth also be based on the smallness or greatness of the magnitude of their own causes; and since this would apply elsewhere as well, there would be no instance where the cognition of smallness or greatness were based on a primary magnitude. This contradiction with experience is the same in other cases as well;
therefore, its being the substratum of the magnitudes of smallness and greatness is also unestablished. [Note:
*prasiddhiḥ* is corrected from *ba॰, ja॰, bhāṃ॰* based on the context.]

Nor does it possess smallness or greatness, nor is it dependent on number; for, through the cognition "one sound," "two sounds," or "many sounds," sound is established as possessing number, just like a jar or other such objects.

Now, it might be argued that the cognition of number in sound is merely figurative (*upacāra*). But to what does that number belong which is figuratively attributed there—is it to the cause, or to the object? If it belongs to the cause, is it attributed as residing in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), or as residing in the cause in general? In the first case, the designation "one sound" would always apply, because its inherent cause, characterized as space (*ākāśa*), is unitary.
In the second case, however, the designation "many sounds" would always apply, because those [causes] in their generality are plural.

Furthermore, if the application of numbers were merely figurative with respect to their objects, then words such as *gagana*, *ākāśa*, and *vyoman* would not admit of multiple designations, because their object is one, whereas since cattle and so forth are many, the designation "the single word 'cow'" would be impossible even in a dream.

To argue that the application of numbers is figurative in accordance with what is non-contradictory is also incorrect, because non-contradiction is possible only when [the entity] itself possesses number.

Furthermore, a figurative conception (*upacāra-kalpanā*) would occur only if there were a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) consisting of a contrary perception, as in the case of "The boy is fire" and so forth. However, there is no perception of a word devoid of number such as unity, just as there is no perception of a boy devoid of fire; so how could a figurative conception of that [number] occur therein? Even if one were to conceive of it as being thus, nothing at all would remain non-figurative.

The objection, "How is it that even for you there is the designation of number (*saṃkhyā-vyapadeśa*) such as 'one form' and so forth among qualities? is also untenable. For in the view where number is itself a quality (*guṇatva*), it would follow that because number is impossible therein [in the case of a single entity], there could be no designation of it; this is not our position, however, because we accept it as a property (*dharma*) of those [entities], just like knowability (*prameyatva*) or substantiality (*vastutva*). Furthermore, the existence of properties within qualities and the like is not contradictory; otherwise, it would follow that they themselves would lack knowability and other such attributes.

Otherwise, how could there be designations such as "the six categories" and so forth? Therefore, its being the substratum of number is also unestablished. [The word] *go* (cow) [is applied] to the existence of the dewlap... [text fragment].

Nor does sound possess the status of being a substratum for conjunction with respect to qualities such as number and so forth; for it is struck by air and other elements. Whatever is struck by air and other elements is a substratum for conjunction, just like dust and the like, and sound is likewise struck by them.

Nor is this unestablished; for it is perceived that a sound directed toward Devadatta is turned back by a headwind and the like. Wherever a turning back is perceived by means of something, there an impact exists by that thing, as in the case of dust and so forth; and a turning back is indeed perceived in the case of sound by means of a headwind and the like.

And the cognition of its turning back is determined by the fact that this [sound], while situated in one direction, is perceived by someone situated in another direction; for wherever something situated in one direction is perceived by someone situated in another direction, there a turning back occurs, as in the case of grass and the like; and sound is likewise perceived by someone situated in another direction.

Now, one might object: "When odors and the like approach Devadatta, they are turned back by him, yet there is no conjunction between them and him, because qualities (guṇas) are themselves devoid of qualities. This objection is not valid; for it is the substance (dravya) possessing those qualities that is turned back by him, since it is impossible for the qualities alone—being devoid of action—to come or be turned back. Thus, it is established that sound has conjunction as its substratum; furthermore, this is evident from the perception of the conjunction of phonemes in words such as *kṣa*.

If this were a different category [of entity], then in every case there would follow the consequence of the cessation of the discourse on conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because it would entail that even things such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) must arise as a different category [from the staff]. Therefore, the fact that sound possesses qualities (*guṇavattva*) is not unestablished;
for this reason also, it exists [as a quality]. (Śrāvaṇa-sūtra)

Nor does it possess action (*kriyāvattva*); for it is perceived in another location after having left its previous location. Whatever is thus perceived in another location is seen to possess action, such as an arrow or the like; and sound is likewise perceived there. Thus, this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is universally acknowledged by all people that sound is perceived in the region of the listener’s ear after leaving the region of the speaker’s mouth.
Nor is it inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) due to [the presence of] universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, because this qualification [of the reason] does not apply to them.

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not the case that the very first sound produced from the conjunction of space with the mouth of a conch shell and its inherent, non-inherent, and efficient causes does not reach the ear and become connected with it—such that it would possess motion—but rather, according to the analogy of waves and ripples, each subsequent sound, being entirely distinct and produced from its own set of inherent, non-inherent, and efficient causes such as space and so forth, is something else? Therefore, how can there be any possibility of this [first sound] possessing motion? This too is an unexamined statement; for if this were the case everywhere, it would result in the total abolition of all action. For even in the case of arrows and the like, one who imagines that they are not the same [identical] entities reaching the target region, but rather are produced from preceding moments of the same kind, would have no reason for his face to turn away [from such a position].

Since permanence is established here through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), such an assumption [of momentariness] is not tenable; this is the same in other cases as well. For even in the case of sound, there is the perception of recognition grasping identity, such as "I hear what was spoken by the teacher" and "I hear what was spoken by the pupil. Just as with the series of waves, there is a series of sounds; thus, the sound is perceived once it has reached the location of the ear via that series. Since there is no coming or going between the ear and the sound, there is no perception of something that has not reached [the sense organ]. By process of elimination, the existence of the series is established.

Just as a wave produced by the impact of a large stone or similar object initiates another wave, and that [subsequent] wave in turn initiates yet another, so too are the series of waves; in the same way, there are series of sound. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
288; Praśastapādavyākhyā, p. 650)
In the *Praśastikandali*, page 289, it is stated: "one should meditate" (in the versions of Ba and Ja).

[Objection: But surely, according to your own view, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) arises from the causes of perception and memory; since these are absent here [in the case of hearing a word spoken by a teacher], how can it arise? For indeed, when a word is uttered by a teacher or the like, memory is not possible in the same way as perception, because memory is dependent upon the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by previous perceptions. And it is not logical for an effect to arise in the absence of its cause, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Reply: This too is untenable. Because unity is cognized here by means of the apprehension of relatedness (*sambandhitā*), and since perception and memory can both exist within that relatedness, the arising of recognition is not contradictory.

For instance: having understood through perception and non-perception, or through inference, that sound is related to [the speaker] as its effect, one now recognizes it—arising from the memory of seeing that [speaker]—as being related to him, and thus recognizes it as qualified by identity, just like the case of a fan and the wind. Otherwise, how could there be such cognitions as "I hear what was spoken by the teacher"? For [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition: "I hear another sound, similar to that which was produced by him."

Now, if it is argued that this recognition is based on the production of successive similar [moments], like nails and hair that have been cut and grown again, and not based on identity; then this is the same in the case of an arrow and so forth, and thus the doctrine of the Sugata would be established through the consequence that all objects are momentary—because of their non-permanence.
(Variant readings: *ṇatvāt* for *ba*, *ja*)

[Objection: "But surely sound is perceived as divided into six distinct varieties—namely, the extremely intense, the more intense, the intense, the mild, the milder, and the mildest—whereas arrows and the like are not. Therefore, because the perception of these distinctions in sound would otherwise be inexplicable, its momentariness is postulated; this is not the case for arrows and so forth due to the opposite being true. Thus, how can the Buddhist doctrine be established? [Reply: This too is charming only to the unreflective; for the perception of those distinctions does not prove momentariness. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of air also being momentary, since there is no difference in the fact that even this [air], when produced by a collection of causes such as a fan, is perceived with distinctions such as "extremely intense" by persons situated at varying distances.

Furthermore, this consequence would apply even to an arrow and the like, because it is possible for such an object, when discharged toward a target, to be perceived as distinct by those [perceivers] who possess such [various capacities]. If it is argued that here the appearance of distinction is based on actions characterized by extreme intensity and so forth, then this is the same in the case of sound as well—[whether it be] intense, more intense, most intense, or very faint. (Bāṇa, Ja)
"It is postulated" (Ā), [says] Ba:

"Now, because of the existence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) here, the postulation of momentariness is improper, but not so in the case of smell and the rest, because the opposite is true. But what is the subverting proof here—is it perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? If it is perception, is it one whose object is unity, or one whose object is momentariness? First, it is not one whose object is unity, because that would be concordant with it due to having the same object.
Nor is it one whose object is momentariness, because such a perception is unestablished (*asiddha*) regarding sound or anything else.

Now, it might be argued that inference, having that [permanence] as its object, is the sublater of that [thesis]; for instance: "Sound is momentary, because, while being perceptible to persons such as ourselves, it is a specific quality of an all-pervading substance, like pleasure and so forth. This too is a mere wishful thinking; for the reason is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), just like the argument regarding "origination from a single branch" (*ekaśākhāprabhavatva*). Nor is its being *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* unestablished, because it is employed immediately after the statement of a fact sublated by the perception known as *pratyabhijñā* (recognition).
Furthermore, its being a specific quality of an all-pervading substance is unestablished, since the substantiality of sound has been proven.
Alternatively,
you are indeed the venerable Abhijñānaśrī.

Furthermore, if the production of sound is accepted according to the analogy of waves and ripples, does a single sound first arise from the activity of the speaker, or many? If it is one, how could multiple sounds be produced simultaneously in various directions? Since there is no contradiction in the simultaneous production of multiple sounds in all directions—given that the non-inherent causes, namely the conjunctions of air and space generated by the activity of the palate and other organs in all directions, and the inherent cause, namely omnipresent space, are present—the theory that sound possesses the capacity for origination (ārambhakatva) is untenable.

For just as the first sound is not produced by another sound— since it arises from the conjunction of the palate and other organs with space as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)— so too all subsequent sounds in every direction can arise only from the conjunctions of air and space resulting from the activity of the palate and other organs as their non-inherent causes;
and thus, sound is produced from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound [Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.31].
Thus it floats [in the ether].

Now, among subsequent sounds, the first sound is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because it is similar to them; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the production of subsequent sounds dissimilar to it, due to the absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*). But if this were so, the first sound would also arise from another sound as its non-inherent cause, and that [second sound] from yet another preceding sound, resulting in the consequence of the beginninglessness (*anāditva*) of the series of sounds (*śabdasantāna*).

Now, if the first sound is specific and is produced solely from the specific activity of the speaker, and it initiates other sounds similar to itself, then what is the purpose of postulating the first sound as an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause)? Since it is possible for successive sounds similar to itself to arise from the specific activity of the speaker and from the specific conjunctions of air and space resulting therefrom, a single sound does not initiate another sound.

When sound manifests in space due to contact with the mouth of a conch shell, does it manifest as one only, or as many? (Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 421; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 167, upper section; Syādvādaratnākara p.
In this way, the final sound is perceived by the ear through a process like that of waves and ripples;
however, in that view, many assumptions of the unperceived would result. 90
...it would be from another [source], mī॰ ślo॰ pṛ॰ 753 –ttiḥ syāt ta– bhāṃ॰; ba॰, ja॰.
Nor [can it arise] from many; for it is impossible for multiple sounds to be produced from a single conjunction of the palate and other organs with space.
Furthermore, it is not possible for multiple conjunctions of the palate and other organs with space to occur simultaneously for a single speaker, because the effort [of speech] is unitary.

Without a diversity of efforts, a conjunction of the palate and other organs with space—preceded by the action of those organs and produced by the motion of either one of the two factors—cannot be established, such that there might be multiple sounds.

Or, let us grant for the sake of argument that the initial sound is multiple due to some cause; even so, does it originate other sounds in its own location or in another location? It cannot be in its own location, because that would entail the impossibility of perceiving sound in any other location.

Now, [suppose merit and demerit produce their effects] in another location. In that case, does he produce them in that other location after having gone there himself, or while remaining in his own country? If he produces them while remaining in his own country, then even the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—residing only in the region of the body—would have to effect the attraction of jewels, pearls, and so forth located in a different place. And in that case, there would be a contradiction with the principle that "dharma and adharma initiate action in another substratum conjoined with their own substratum."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that sound either arises in the region of the listener's ear, or that the cognition of it arises [there], which would render the postulation of intermediate sounds and their reaching the ear purposeless.

Furthermore, in cases such as ripples and waves, it is not observed that they initiate [a new effect] without having reached the location of that effect, such that one might postulate the same here as well; for that would contradict direct perception.
If, on the other hand, [the sound] goes to that location, then the fact that sound possesses action (*kriyā*) is established.
—The initial action of fire, which is its upward flaming; of air, which is its horizontal blowing; and of atoms and the mind, is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.14.
2.13 Furthermore, merit and demerit, when inherent in their own substratum, initiate pleasure and pain; however, when residing in another substratum, they initiate action.

Furthermore, if sound were a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), its perceptibility by people like us would be untenable, because space is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). Whatever is a quality of a substance that is absolutely imperceptible is not perceptible to people like us, just as the color and other qualities of atoms (*paramāṇu-rūpādi*); and since sound is accepted as such by the opponent, it follows that if it were perceptible, it could not be a specific quality of an absolutely imperceptible space. Whatever is perceptible to people like us is not the quality of an absolutely imperceptible substance, just as the color and other qualities of a jar (*ghaṭa-rūpādayaḥ*); and so too is sound.
Because a quality that lacks form, like a quality of the self (*ātman*), is not observed to be an object of the senses (see *Tattvārtharāja* p.
48; *Tattvārthaśloka* p. 421).

Sound is not a quality of an incorporeal substance, because a quality and its possessor occupy the same location and are thus cognized by a single cognition; otherwise, even an incorporeal substance would fall into the category of being an object of the auditory sense-organ (Pañcā° Ṭī° pṛ° 185).

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that [sound is a quality] "because it is connected with existence" (*sattāsambandhitvāt*)—is it intended that it is connected with existence as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or with existence as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*)? In the first alternative, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; for although they are connected with such existence while being neither substance nor action, they nonetheless lack the status of being a quality.

The second alternative, however, is untenable; for, as will be refuted on page 240, line 8, during the commentary on the fortieth verse of the fifth chapter, [the claim] that "entities which are non-existent in themselves become existent through an existence that is a distinct entity (arthāntarabhūta), just as objects exist by virtue of their own existence" is to be rejected. Thus, let entities exist in themselves, like existence itself.

And as for what was further stated—"Sound is not a substance because it inheres in a single substance"—in that case, the proof for its inhering in a single substance is unestablished (*asiddha*). For that [proof] could only be established once its quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and its existence through inherence (*samavāya*) in the single substance of space (*gagana*) were established; and since that has been refuted by the aforementioned reasoning, how can its establishment occur?

As for the proof stated for [sound] being a single substance—namely, "Sound is a single substance because, while possessing generality and particularity, it is perceptible by a single external sense-organ"—that too is sublated by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*). For instance: "Sound consists of multiple substances because, while being perceptible to those such as ourselves, it possesses touch, like a jar"; furthermore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to air (*vāyu*), for air, while possessing generality and particularity and being perceptible by a single external sense-organ, nonetheless consists of multiple substances; and this is also the case with the moon, the sun, and so forth, which are perceived by the single organ of sight.

The cognition of that [object] by means of an external sense-organ different from those of people like us is the same in the case of sound as well; the non-perception [of it] here is equal to its non-perception elsewhere (p.
240, l. 13). [Sound is] a single substance (ekadravyam). (Ā.)

As for what was stated—that [sound] is not a substance because, while being impermanent, it is invariably non-perceptible to the eye—that too is incorrect, because it is inconclusive due to air (*vāyu*); for air, while being impermanent and invariably non-perceptible to the eye, is nonetheless a substance (p.

As for what was stated—that [sound is not a quality] because it inheres in a pervasive substance—that too is a mere assertion, because it is unproven (*asiddha*). For its inherence in that [substance] would only be established if its status as a quality were already established; yet that is not established, since it has been refuted by the method previously explained (p.

2). Furthermore, as for the other statement—"Firstly, [it is not a quality] of atoms possessing touch," and so forth—that is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we do not admit that sound is a quality of those [atoms].
Just as there is a contradiction in sound being a specific quality of atoms if it were perceptible to us and others, so too there is a contradiction in its being a specific quality of space;

for the perceptibility of sound to us and others does not exclude only its being a specific quality of atoms, but also its being a specific quality of space, since there is no distinction between the two cases.
For just as color and other qualities of atoms are imperceptible to us and others, so too are magnitude and other qualities of space.

As for what was stated [on p. 241, l. 6]—that "because [sound] is perceived elsewhere than its substratum, such as a drum," and so forth—that too is incorrect; for it is not established that the drum and the like are the substrata of sound, since they are merely its instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*).

Furthermore, the refutation of [sound] being a quality of the self (*ātman*) and so forth does not constitute a valid resolution, as it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*).

The process regarding the production of sound—namely, that space (*ākāśa*) is its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and so forth—is also refuted by this [same argument]; for when the status of sound as a quality of space is denied, it is impossible for space to be its inherent cause.
Alternatively, if space, being partless, were the inherent cause of sound, then, like [space], sound would also necessarily follow as being all-pervasive (*vyāpin*).

For spatial restriction is said to be non-pervasiveness; and that is extremely difficult to establish for space, which is its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), since it lacks spatial parts (*adeśatva*).

Whatever quality belongs to a substance that has no spatial parts does not fail to pervade its own substratum—just as the magnitude of that [substance], or the color and other qualities of an atom. And sound is postulated by you to be a quality of space, which is without spatial parts.

Or, if that [sound] were non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), how could its substratum, space (ākāśa), not possess parts? Who other than one of dull intellect would say that a quality resides in a limited region (pradeśavṛtti) while its substratum is partless? Furthermore, if space were not possessed of parts, then even a sound existing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) would be perceived by people like us—just like a sound inherent in the auditory organ—because it would be equally inherent in the auditory organ characterized as a single, partless space.

Now, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is simply that portion of space (*ākāśadeśa*) enclosed within the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), which has been conditioned by merit and demerit (*dharmādharmābhisaṃskṛta*). Since sound existing in the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) does not have a direct inherence (*asamavāya*) with that [auditory organ], it is not perceived by people such as ourselves. [Objection: Is this not merely a solution that accepts the possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*) according to the maxim of a blind man entering a snake's hole? [Reply: No, because the portion of space that is the auditory organ is distinct from the portion of space that serves as the substratum for the sound residing in the cosmic egg—so says the *Ātmatattvaviveka*, page 242, line 3.

Furthermore, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is a region of space (*nabhodeśa*) known as the cavity of the ear; it is bound by *dharma* and *adharma*, which bring about the experience of the cause of sound.
"Is it not the case that this very admission of having parts would be a solution [to the problem], following the maxim of a blind man entering a serpent's hole? (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 59;
Nyāyaratna, p. 891).

Furthermore, would this non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) be of the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) or of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajya*)? In the first case, it would amount to nothing more than saying that it occurs in only one part (*ekadeśavṛttitva*). For by asserting that sound does not exist pervading space, one would necessarily be admitting that it exists in a single part of it. Indeed, pervasive occurrence means occurrence in its entirety; when that is denied, there must be occurrence in a single part, and as has been stated, that is extremely difficult to establish given that space is partless. In the second case, however, it would merely be a denial of occurrence; but this is not tenable.
Because sound, as a quality (*guṇa*), must reside in a substance (*dravya*), its denial [of such residence] would be contradictory; or, if it were denied, its status as a quality would be untenable.

For that which has its mode of existence (*vṛtti*) denied in every respect is not a quality, just like the son of a barren woman; and since you admit that the inherence (*samavāya*) resides in sound in that manner, there is no fault such as [the question of whether it resides] in one part or in its entirety. This too is mere faith, for that [position] will be refuted later.

Furthermore, if space were partless (*niravayava*), there would be no perception by the ear of a sound that has arrived through the process of a continuous series (*santānavṛtti*); for it is impossible for this sound to be inherent in the auditory organ (*śrotrasamavetatva*) by way of its production in successive locations of space. Indeed, if one assumes the production of sound in successive locations of space according to the analogy of waves and ripples (*vīcītaraṅganyāya*), how could its possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*) not be established? Therefore, it is not at all logical for space to be partless. — Śaṃvyā—Ā. 1.2.9. (Śābarabhāṣya-vyākhyā)

Nor is there absolute permanence [of the substratum], for that would entail the same permanence for sound as well. For its destruction [is supposed to occur] either from the destruction of its substratum, from the manifestation of a contrary quality, or from the absence of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that causes it. It cannot be from the destruction of the substratum, because you assert its permanence in every respect. Nor can it be from the manifestation of a contrary quality; for what is this contrary quality—is it its magnitude (*mahattva*), or is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth? Of these, the first position is untenable, because its magnitude, by virtue of being inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamaveta*), cannot be established as a contradictory factor.

Alternatively, if that [sound] were established [in the drum], it would follow that sound is absent even at the time of hearing, or else there would be no production of sound at all, because its magnitude (mahattva) is always present; thus, the second position is also untenable. Furthermore, since conjunction and so forth are the causes of sound production, they cannot be considered obstructive.

Nor can its absence be due to the absence of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that serves as its efficient cause, because an absolute non-entity (tucchābhāva), being devoid of all causal capacity, cannot be a cause for the destruction of anything—just like a horse's horn.
— also [would be] in every respect impossible;
for then, indeed, there would be the existence of its magnitude.
Even then, because of the existence of that magnitude (*mahattva*), [the argument holds].
Thus, since it is untenable for sound to have space (*ākāśa*) as its cause, one must necessarily accept its nature as consisting of *pudgala* (material atoms). To explain:

sound consists of *pudgala*, because, while possessing qualities and actions, it is perceptible by the external sense organs of beings such as ourselves; whatever is thus is so, like a jar or similar objects; and sound is likewise; therefore, it is so.

Consequently, since sound is not established as a quality of space (*ākāśa*), it cannot be its logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, the existence of that [space] is not proven by this. Now, one might ask: "If you thus deny the substance of space, how would you avoid the fault of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*)? This objection is also baseless; for we reject only that which others have imagined—namely, space as having a nature that is entirely eternal and partless—but we do not reject that which is the opposite of this, because the latter does not fall within the scope of the aforementioned defects. Space is produced from sound, and space is an aggregate of a collection of atoms.
When those [senses] are touched, a sound arises that is inherent and produced.
79. Pañcāstikāya.

If it is asked, "How is the existence of that [space] established even for you?", we reply: "Because of the effect consisting in the simultaneous accommodation of all substances. To explain: simultaneous accommodation of all things requires a common cause, because it is a simultaneous accommodation of all things; whatever kind of accommodation is of such a nature is seen to require such a cause, as in the case of the accommodation of fish and other creatures within the water of a single lake; and this [accommodation of substances] is likewise an accommodation.

[Objection: "But surely, just as there is immersion of honey in ghee, of water in ashes, and of horses and so forth in water, so too will there be the immersion of all objects within light and darkness; therefore, how can the existence of space (ākāśa) be established from this? [Reply: This is also incorrect, because even for these two, immersion would be impossible in the absence of space.
"That which provides an opening for all living beings, for the rest [of the substances], and likewise for all material particles (pudgala), that is what constitutes 'space' (ākāśa) in the world."
By the characteristic of providing space for immersion, it is the astikāya of space (ākāśa).
Vyākhyāyukti-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra 13.4.481
The capacity for accommodation is the characteristic of space (Tattvārthasūtra 5.18).
The space element, because its intrinsic nature consists of light and darkness within the form realm, has a clear meaning;
*Sphuṭārthā*, folio 58.

Now, one might object: "Just as all objects must have their location within space, so too must space itself have its location in another substratum; this would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, space were to reside within its own nature, then it would follow that all objects likewise reside within themselves. How, then, is the existence of space established? This objection is also untenable. Since space is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*), it is logically consistent for it to reside within itself, and thus an infinite regress does not arise. Furthermore, other things, being non-pervasive, cannot reside within themselves; indeed, no object of limited dimension is ever observed to be its own substratum, as we perceive that horses and the like have water and the like as their substrata.

"How can there be such an 'inherence' (*avagāha*) of space, time, and the self within space? Because they are all-pervading (*vyāpitvāt*). This too is incorrect, because their all-pervasiveness is unproven. That lack of proof is established because the substance of *diś* (space) will be shown to be non-existent, and both time and the self will be shown to be non-all-pervasive substances. "But even so, since time and the self are formless (*amūrttatvena*), they cannot fall [into anything]; how then can they have the state of being contained (*ādheyatā*)? This too is illogical; for it is well-established that even formless things, such as cognition (*jñāna*) and the like, possess the state of being contained within the self.
Indeed, [all]—*ba*, *ja*.

If space is self-supported, and phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth are likewise self-supported, then if another support were postulated for phenomena and the rest, another support would have to be postulated for space as well; if that were the case, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If this objection is raised, it is not a fault, because there is no substance larger than space upon which space could be said to reside, for it is infinite in every direction (Sarvārthasiddhi 5).

By this [argument], the claim that space is not the locus of anything because it is formless (*amūrtatva*) is also refuted; for even though the self (*ātman*) is formless, it is perceived as the locus of cognition (*jñāna*).

The claim that because all things exist at the same time, there can be no relationship of container and contained (ādhārādheya-bhāva), otherwise they would have to come into existence after space—this too is incorrect. For even among things existing simultaneously, such as the self and formlessness (amūrtatva) and so forth, that relationship is perceived. Indeed, even the opponent does not admit a temporal sequence (pūrvāparībhāva) here, as that would entail the loss of their eternity.
Therefore, the substance of space (ākāśa-dravya) as conceived by others is untenable. Nor is there a substance of time (kāla-dravya);
for the relationship of container and contained is observed even among things occurring simultaneously, as in "color and other qualities in a jar" or "the hands and other limbs in the body."
Sarvārthasiddhi 5.12:

Generally, the discussion regarding the substance of space (ākāśadravya) according to this very methodology is to be found in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* p. 431, the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 163 upper, the *Tattvārthabhāṣya-ṭīkā* p. 358, the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* p. 670, the *Syādvādaratnākara* p. 941, and so forth.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika is that there exists an eternal, unitary, and distinct entity called Time, based on the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior."

Now, one might object: since the substance of time (*kāla-dravya*) is well-established through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, how can it be said that [the existence of time] is untenable? To explain: the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so on—which are distinct from the cognitions of "prior" and "posterior" produced by direction (*diś*) and space (*deśa*)—must be preceded by a specific cause, because they are qualified cognitions (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*). Whatever is a qualified cognition is seen to be preceded by a specific cause, just as the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth. And these cognitions of "prior," "posterior," "simultaneity," "non-simultaneity," "long duration," and "short duration" are indeed qualified cognitions.

For here, a transposition of "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "nearness" (*aparatva*) caused by direction and location is observed: for when a father is situated in a certain direction and location, "remoteness" arises [in him], yet when his son is situated in that very same direction and location, "nearness" arises; and conversely, when a son is situated where "nearness" has arisen, it is seen that "remoteness" arises in the father situated in that very same place.
Therefore, another cause distinct from direction and location must be admitted as the basis for this cognition, since such a transposition would otherwise be impossible.

Furthermore, it is not logical that the activities of the sun and so forth, or wrinkles and grey hair, should be the cause of cognitions such as "posterior" and "anterior," because those cognitions are of a different nature than the cognitions of cloth and the like;
and thus the Sūtra states: "In relation to what is posterior, there is the notion of 'prior'; simultaneity and non-simultaneity, long and short—these are the marks of time" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.6).

Because there is no distinction in its generic characteristics and because there is an absence of specific characteristics, its properties— such as oneness, eternity, and omnipresence— are to be understood as being like those of space.

And for such a substance as time (*kāla*), when its distinction from other things is to be established, or when the conventional usage "time" is to be proven, the very cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth, serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*). For instance: Time is distinct from other things, or it is to be conventionally designated as "time," because it possesses the logical mark consisting of the cognitions of priority, posteriority, and so forth. Whatever is not distinct from other things, or is not conventionally designated as "time," does not possess the aforementioned mark, such as earth and the like. And time is thus; therefore, it is so.
[The terms *yaugapadya* and *cira* are noted in the manuscripts *ba* and *ja*.]

For it is observed that where "remoteness" (paratva) is produced with reference to a direction, there "nearness" (aparatva) is also produced; and where "nearness" exists, there "remoteness" is likewise produced. This is like the case of gender (liṅga). (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p. 343).
Likewise, in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p.

342): "Time is distinguished from other [substances], or rather, the conventional usage [of 'time'] is established; that which is the subject of dispute is to be designated as 'time' because it possesses such marks as the confusion of priority and posteriority. (*sū– ā॰, ba॰, ja॰*) "Time is distinguished from other [substances], or rather, the conventional usage [of 'time'] is established; that which is the subject of dispute is to be designated as 'time' because it possesses such marks as the confusion of priority and posteriority" (*praśa॰ vyo॰* p. 342).

In the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*), following the refutation of time (*kāla*) as being eternal, unitary, and partless, there is the establishment of its nature as an atom (*aṇu*) and as consisting of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*). Here, a rebuttal is offered to what was stated [by the opponent] beginning with "prior" (*parā*) and "posterior" (*apara*): that is incorrect. For, based on this mark (*liṅga*), would time be established as having the nature of a single substance (*ekadravyasvarūpa*) or as having the nature of multiple substances (*anekadravyasvarūpa*)? Among these, the first position is untenable, because when examined as being eternal, partless, and of a single nature, such [a single-substance nature] is logically impossible.

Whatever, when examined in a certain form, is not logically tenable, should not be accepted as being of that form—just as the world is not [tenable] as being of the nature of non-duality with Brahma and so forth—and time, when examined as being of a permanent, partless, and unitary nature, is likewise not tenable;

thus this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because such a nature is untenable due to the impossibility of accounting for the diversity of effects characterized by mutually distinct notions of "other" and "not-other," and due to the impossibility of accounting for the distinctions within its own forms such as the past and so on.

For it is not possible for an object that is in every way eternal, partless, and of a single nature to produce effects that are non-eternal, located in different places, and possessed of multiple natures; otherwise, even Brahman—being of such a character—would entail the production of various villages, gardens, and so forth, which would result in the contradiction of its non-duality.

Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction in such a [single-natured] entity being the agent of those effects due to the influence of diverse auxiliary causes, as this is no different in other cases, since auxiliaries such as ignorance (avidyā) are possible even in the case of Brahman.
Furthermore, it has been stated in the course of the investigation into God and the atoms that cooperation is not possible for those whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is non-different;

therefore, in this case, there would simply be no arising of cognitions such as simultaneity. For that collection of effects produced at one time is called "produced simultaneously. And if time were of the nature of being eternally one and so forth, then because all effects would be produced by it [simultaneously], the consequence would be that all effects arise at one and the same time, and thus nothing would ever be produced non-simultaneously (pṛ.

Because they possess a partless and unitary nature, succession and simultaneity are impossible; if it is argued that these two [properties] exist due to a difference in their correlates, then surely those two [correlates] are themselves fruitless.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 169b;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, folio 892.

... [of that] — [the reading] *ni-* is found in manuscripts B, J, and Ā.

Furthermore, there would be an absence of the conventional usage of "slow" and "quick"; for that which is done over a long time is called "done slowly," and that which is done in a short time is called "done quickly. And both of these are impossible if time were entirely eternal and so forth in nature.

[Objection: Even though time possesses that nature [of being one], since differentiation is possible through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no absence of cognitions such as "simultaneity" and so forth. As it has been said: "The division of time is like that of a man or a cook, due to the difference of limiting adjuncts. [Reply: That too is an unexamined statement; for in this case, the difference of limiting adjuncts is merely the difference of effects, and that [difference] certainly exists even in the case of "done simultaneously. Why, then, would there not be a cognition of non-simultaneity? If it is argued that the difference of effects occurring in succession is the cause for the conventional usage of the "division of time," then what is this "succession" of his? If it is the non-production [of effects] simultaneously, then what is the meaning of the stated term "non-production simultaneously"? If it means non-production at one and the same time, then this is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*): for as long as the division of time is not established, the succession of effects—characterized by their production at different times—is not established; and as long as such a succession of effects is not established, the division of time based on the difference of limiting adjuncts is not established.

Therefore, a distinction in time must be admitted as existing by its very nature; for only in this way are such conventional expressions as "this is simultaneous," "this has arisen after a long time," or "this has arisen immediately" easily accounted for, and not otherwise.
[Objection: Multiplicity is merely a figurative designation based on the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like a jewel or a cook. [Reply: No. *Ā* (This is the beginning of the refutation).
As stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p.

64): "Just as a gem is metaphorically designated as manifold—such as 'yellow' or 'red'—due to the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) without abandoning its own essential nature; or just as a person is designated by different terms such as 'cook' due to various activities without abandoning his own essential nature, so too is it here," as found in the *Praśastapādavyākhyā* (p. 351).
*Praśamaratiprakaraṇa*, p.

66: By this, the confusion between the remote (*para*) and the proximate (*apara*) is also considered, because in a time that is entirely devoid of the nature of eternity and so forth, even that [distinction] is untenable.

For just as an object is called "remote" (*para*) when it is separated by many parts of the earth or parts of light, and "proximate" (*apara*) when separated by few, so too an object is called "remote" (*para*) when separated by many moments (*kṣaṇa*), days and nights, and so on, and "proximate" (*apara*) when separated by few.
Furthermore, the states of being "much" or "little," like heaviness, magnitude, and so forth, are based on relativity; they would be entirely impossible if time were a single entity.

That which is the cause of the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so on, must be manifold, just as the spatial points of the earth and other locations are; and since time is the cause of the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so on, [it follows that it is manifold].
As for the other argument stated—"because its mark is non-distinct" and so forth—that too is mere words, because that non-distinction is unproven.

For the cognitions of simultaneity and so forth, which serve as its logical marks (*liṅga*), are not inherently indistinguishable from one another; since they are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as distinct from each other in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), a distinction is indeed experienced for each of them individually. For instance, in cases such as "those who ate simultaneously," "those who slept simultaneously," or "those who stood or went simultaneously," there is no lack of distinction among those cognitions, as that would contradict actual experience.

Or, let it be granted that there is no distinction in the cognition of that [time]; nevertheless, if time is accepted as being one on this basis, then because there is likewise no distinction in the cognitions of weight and so forth, it would follow that weight, dimension, and the like must also be one, since the objection and its resolution are identical.
Therefore, just as weight, dimension, and so forth consist of multiple qualities, it must be admitted that time consists of multiple substances (pṛ. 251, l.

Furthermore, if time were of the nature of a single, eternal, partless substance, it would be impossible for objects to possess the states of past, future, and present; for there would be no distinction between the times of past, future, and present. Indeed, it is only when such a distinction exists that objects can be designated as such through their connection with those times, and not otherwise, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is the establishment of such a distinction possible for this [time], because it is conceived by you as being eternal, partless, and of a single form. That which is of such a nature does not admit a distinction of its own character as past and so forth—just as in the case of an atom—and yet time is postulated by you to be eternal, partless, and of a single form.

Or, let us grant that such a distinction exists therein; nevertheless, would this [distinction] arise from itself, from a connection with another past time and so forth, or from a connection with a past action and so forth? It cannot first be from itself, because there is a contradiction between partlessness and having the nature of a distinction.

Nor can it be from a connection with another past time and so forth, because since that [time] is of a single uniform nature, another time is simply impossible; or, if it were possible, it would lead to an infinite regress, since its own pastness and so forth would likewise have to be established through a connection with yet another past time and so forth.

Now, [you might argue that] its status as past and so forth arises from its connection with actions that are past and so forth. But how is the status of actions as past and so forth established—is it through connection with other past and so forth actions, or through connection with such a time? In the first alternative, there is an infinite regress;

in the second alternative, however, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the status of time as past and so forth would be established through its connection with those actions once the pastness of the actions is established, and the pastness of those actions would be established through their connection with time once that [status of time] is established.

For would that [existence] arise from its connection with another past time and so forth, or from its connection with the causal activity of such an entity, or from itself? In the first case, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
145; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 671)

Or, let it be granted that the distinction between the past and so forth is established there from some source; nevertheless, if one asserts the absolute oneness of time, there is a contradiction with one's own words, because by one's own speech the distinction of this [time] is demonstrated through its forms of past and so forth.

There is also a contradiction with common worldly experience, for worldly people certainly do not accept the oneness of time—which possesses the nature of the forenoon, midday, and afternoon, as well as the character of cold, heat, and rain—since they admit its distinction in each respective case.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with inference; for instance: whatever substance is superposed with subtle and non-subtle attributes is manifold, such as earth and the like; and the substance of time is likewise superposed with subtle and non-subtle attributes.

Just as material substances such as earth possess the nature of being multiple substances because they are superposed with subtle and gross attributes by way of their forms as atoms and as non-atoms, and as soul-substances possess the nature of being multiple substances because they are superposed with the attributes of being subtle and gross through the distinctions among soul-substances such as those of the *kunthu* and the elephant; so too, the substance of time (*kāla-dravya*) must be understood as having the nature of being multiple substances, since it is possible for it to be superposed with its own attributes in relation to its specific divisions such as the *samaya*, the *muhūrta*, and so forth.

Furthermore, because of the possibility of the distinction between the primary and the secondary: indeed, the conventional time consisting of moments (*samaya*), series (*āvalikā*), and so forth, is not logically possible without a primary substance of time (*kāla-dravya*). Just as a figurative existence is not possible without a primary existence, so too—despite the established usage of specific names such as "moment" for particular actions being accomplished in a moment, or "cooking" for the act of cooking being brought about over a moment—the designation of "time" applied to these by superimposition—as in "the moment is time" or "the time of cooking rice"—indicates the existence of a primary time which serves as the basis for that designation.
Why? Because the secondary depends upon the primary;
[this is stated in] Sarvārthasiddhi 5.22.

And that primary substance is manifold; for conventional time would otherwise be inexplicable if it were not distinct with respect to each point of space (*ākāśapradeśa*), since the difference between day and so forth in the points of space at Kurukṣetra and Laṅkā could not otherwise be accounted for. Therefore, the differentiation of time is established as being atomic (*aṇu*) in form with respect to every point of space within the world-ether (*lokākāśa*).
As it has been said:

"Conventional time (*vyavahārakāla*) is distinct for each spatial point of ether (*pratyākāśapradeśa*), because otherwise the simultaneous distinction in conventional usage regarding various substances and times would be inexplicable; and because otherwise the distinction between day and so forth at the two locations of the ether of Kurukṣetra and the ether of Laṅkā at one and the same moment would be inexplicable."
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 399:
"If it consists of multiple substances, what is its measure? And it is said: "The spatial units of the world are the atoms of time (*kālāṇu*); they are innumerable substances. (*Sarvārthasiddhi* 5).
39. *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 399; *Bṛhad-dravyasaṃgraha*, Gāthā 22.
There is a difference of opinion among the Śvetāmbaras regarding the substance of time (*kāladravya*); for instance, some maintain that "time [is a substance]" (Tattvārthasūtra 5.38),
while other teachers explain that "time is also a substance."

In the *Tattvārthādhigamasūtra-bhāṣya* (5.38), however, the word "tu" is intended to include a distinction; that distinction is the *naya* characterized by differentiation (*bhedapradhāna*), and by its force, time (*kāla*) is also included. The word "api" has the sense of "and," and they state that time is also described as a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) in the *Āgama*.

"Venerable sir, how many substances are taught? O Goyama, six substances are taught, namely: the substance of motion (dharma-astikāya), the substance of rest (adharma-astikāya), the substance of space (ākāśa-astikāya), the substance of soul (pudgala-astikāya), the substance of life (jīva-astikāya), and time (addhā-samaya).
[From the *Anuyogadvāra*, in the section on the names of substances, qualities, and modes, verse 124; the word "tu" is used in the sense of exclusion.]

Of what [is this] a refutation? It is a refutation of the *dravyanaya* (substance-view) which maintains that time (*kāla*) is a transformation distinct from the five *astikāyas* (existential categories), such as *dharmāstikāya* and so forth. For there exists another sūtra in the Āgama, following its opposing viewpoint: "Is it the case, O Venerable One, that 'time' is spoken of? "Gautama, it is indeed living beings (*jīva*) and non-living beings (*ajīva*). This sūtra was taught by the Tīrthaṅkara to establish that time is not distinct from the five *astikāyas*; the meaning of the sūtra is that time is a modification (*paryāya*) of the substances *jīva* and *ajīva*.
(Tattvārthabhāṣya-ṭīkā, p. 430-32).

The measurement of the spatial units (*pradeśa*) of the substance of time (*kāla-dravya*) has not been stated; however, with the intention of explaining that, it is said here: "It consists of infinite [spatial units]" (Tattvārthasūtra 5.39).
Thus, etc., the infinite number of spatial units (*anantapradeśitva*) of the substance of time (*kāladravya*) is stated in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya-ṭīkā*.

However, Hemacandrācārya follows the Digambara view; for instance: "Those distinct atoms of time (*kālāṇu*) situated in the spatial units of the world-space (*lokākāśa*), which exist for the transformation of entities, are called primary time (*mukhya kāla*)."

For the detailed study of other doctrines mentioned in the *Yogaśāstra*, one should consult the *Dharmasaṃgrahaṇī*, the tenth chapter of the *Dravyānuyogatarka* (verses 10–18), the *Yuktiprabodha* (verse 23),
and so forth.
In each individual space-point of the universe, those which reside one by one are to be known as time-atoms (kālāṇu), like a heap of jewels within the space-points of the universe. Thus [it is said].

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) of those who deny the existence of the substance *kāla* is as follows: "This conventional usage regarding the past and so forth depends solely upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and is not produced by time.

Since the substance *kāla*, when subjected to analysis, is impossible even in its own nature, for what could one establish a state of being multiple substances by rejecting its state of being a single substance?"

Indeed, time divided into distinctions such as past and so forth cannot exist, through whose relation objects would possess their state of being past and so on; for such a distinction is untenable either intrinsically or extrinsically. For if time were past and so forth intrinsically, let that state belong to objects intrinsically as well—there is no need for the postulation of time. If, on the other hand, its state of being past and so forth is accepted as extrinsic—either through a relation with another distinct time that is past and so forth, or through a relation with past and so forth actions—the aforementioned defects necessarily follow.

Therefore, this conventional usage regarding the past and so forth depends entirely upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For an object experienced simultaneously by a means of valid cognition is called "present," whereas that experienced at non-simultaneous times is designated as "past" if it occurred in a prior moment, or "future" if it will occur in a subsequent moment. Thus, cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior" are based on mental attention (*manaskāra*) arising from specific temporal conditions; they do not arise from time (*kāla*) or space (*diś*) themselves.

"Distinguished convention" (*viśiṣṭasamaya*) refers to the linguistic conventions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, applied to objects produced on days such as those preceding or following [a given day]. The mental attention (*manaskāra*) arising from that is the "orientation" (*ābhoga*); since this [cognition] has that as its basis, it is described in that way. For this very reason, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayadoṣa*), because this cognition is based upon the convention for specific objects.
In the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, page 209,
following the refutation of that [position], there is the establishment of real time as a substance consisting of multiple substances;
here, it is refuted.

As for what was stated—"of the substance time," and so forth—that is charming only when left unexamined; for why is its existence impossible by its very nature? Is it because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it, or because of the impossibility of distinctions such as "past" and so on? In this regard, the first position is untenable, because there exists a means of valid cognition that makes known its existence, namely, inference arising from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior."

For those cognitions are not causeless, because they occur only occasionally; nor do they have an undifferentiated cause, because they are specific cognitions; nor do they have direction, quality, or genus as their causes, because they arise with a distinctness from the cognitions produced by those [causes].

To illustrate: in the case of an old, unattractive, low-caste person situated in the "other" (west) direction, there arises the cognition "this one is other"; and in the case of a young, excellent, high-caste person situated in the "further" (east) direction, there arises the cognition "this one is further" (p. 254, l.

Likewise, when one considers a person of inferior birth in relation to another, an elder, by way of spatial direction—observing the proximity of wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth—and taking a person of superior birth who is young as the limit, the cognition arises: "This one is further than that other; this one is remote," [Praśastapādabhāṣya p.
343; Tattvārthabhāṣyaṭīkā p. 429].

Now, if it is argued that the movement of the sun and so forth is the cause of that [distinction], such that for one person there are more revolutions of the sun from birth onwards and thus "remoteness" (*paratva*), while for another there are fewer and thus "nearness" (*aparatva*)—then how could notions such as simultaneity arise? For no cause other than time can be established here upon investigation. Would that cause be the revolution of the sun, a specific action, or the agent and the object? It cannot be the revolution of the sun, because all things are produced even during a single revolution of the sun.

For the revolution of the sun—that is, its circumambulation of Mount Meru by way of counter-clockwise rotation—is designated as "day and night. Even within that single period, the production of objects that are the objects of simultaneous perception is indeed perceived; yet, there is no designation for it as such. For the designation is "simultaneous time" (*yugapatkāla*), and not "simultaneous revolution of the sun" (*yugapadādityaparivartana*).

From birth onwards, for one person there are more revolutions of the sun, which constitutes "priority" (*paratva*), while for another there are fewer, which constitutes "posteriority" (*aparatva*). If it is argued that let the revolution of the sun itself suffice and what is the need for "time" (*kāla*), we say no; because [priority and posteriority] are inferred from cognitions such as "simultaneous" (*yugapat*) and so forth.

Furthermore, cognitions such as "simultaneous" cannot arise from the revolution of the sun alone, since all such cognitions would arise at once, given that the revolution of the sun occurs identically for everyone.
From the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 343:
"And because of the absence of designation [otherwise]; for the designation 'simultaneous time' would not be [possible] as 'simultaneous revolution of the sun.
Nor should it be said that time is simply action; for that would entail the non-occurrence of cognitions such as 'simultaneous' and so forth."

[The *Prasannapadā* on verse 343 states: Is the specific action [of time] of the nature of the revolution of the sun, or is it of the nature of the movement of water in a water-clock (*ghaṭikā*) and so forth? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because it would entail the faults previously mentioned.

The second alternative is also illogical, because that [movement] is merely an indicator of that [time]. For instance, the specific action—the movement of water in such-and-such a water-clock by such-and-such an amount—is the indicator of time; however, that [action] itself is not time.

Furthermore, since that action possesses the nature of an action, it would—like any other action—be a cause for the cognition of "action," but not a cause for the cognitions of "simultaneity" and so forth. Even specific actions such as "the flow of that water simultaneously" or "the flow of that water sequentially" are perceived as being conditioned by time, just like any other action; how then could that very [action] be time? Moreover, if one were to give a different name, "action," to that time which accomplishes the aforementioned effects, it would merely be a difference in name.
If it is argued that time is merely action itself, because nothing is perceived apart from it, we say no; for in the absence of such [action], the designation "time" would be untenable.
(Tattvārtharāja, p. 228:
"that which brings about an effect," Ā., Ba., Ja., Bhā.)
And if action were distinct from the agent and the object, such that it produced a specific cognition, there would be nothing more than a mere difference in terminology (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 343).

Now, if it is argued that the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) alone are the cause for the cognition of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) and so forth—that is incorrect. Why? Because simultaneity is the activity of many agents toward an effect, which is understood through the cognition, "These [agents] act simultaneously"; and the simultaneous acquisition of self-nature by many effects is established by the cognition, "These [effects] were produced simultaneously. Furthermore, in this case, neither the agent alone nor the object alone can be the objective basis (*ālambana*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For even where an effect arises sequentially, since the agent and the object exist there as well, such a cognition [of simultaneity] would occur, yet it does not.
—*pratyayani* (according to *ba*, *ja*); *sama* (according to *ā*, *ba*, *ja*).
The performance of an action by many agents is the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) by many effects.

For instance: it is observed that there is a cognition based on the agent, such as "these [actions] they perform simultaneously," and a cognition based on the effect, such as "these [effects] were performed simultaneously.
Furthermore, in this case, the mere agent is not the object of cognition, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For even where the effect occurs sequentially, since both the agent and the action exist there as well, this cognition would [erroneously] arise.
And it does not exist; why? Because it is known that this consciousness arises depending upon either a specific agent or an effect (Praśastapādabhāṣya p. 343; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
170, upper).

By this, the cognition of non-simultaneity is also considered; for even that [cognition], such as "these do not act simultaneously" or "this was done by them non-simultaneously," does not apprehend anything other than the mere agent and the mere object in their undifferentiated forms, precisely because of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, time must be accepted as a qualifier [of action]; otherwise, how could there even be the conventional usage of "slow" and "quick"? For a single agent performs one task slowly due to distraction or lack of desire, yet performs another quickly due to eagerness; in this regard, the two cognitions—"done slowly" and "done quickly"—because they are distinct, imply a distinct cause. Thus, time is established. To this we reply: that is not so, because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends time; therefore, time is impossible. This is because these [cognitions] do not occur simultaneously... [text fragment] ...Ā, Ja.
Likewise, a single agent performs one effect slowly due to distraction or lack of desire, while he performs another quickly due to a desire for it;
in this case, the cognition that "this was done slowly" and "this was done quickly," being distinct, necessitates a distinct cause (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
