Nor [is it non-existent], because distinctions such as past and so forth are impossible [for a non-entity]; for these distinctions of past and so forth are possible for this [entity] by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Since its own and other natures are restricted to their respective natures as past and so forth, it is illogical for it to depend on anything else in that regard.

Whatever is determined by its own nature in a particular respect does not depend upon another in that respect; for example, a lamp does not depend on anything else for the manifestation of its own and other forms. Time is likewise determined by its own nature regarding the past and other temporal states of things.

One should not argue that, in this way, the distinction between the past and other temporal states of objects should also exist inherently by themselves, because entities possess specific, determinate natures (*pratiniyatasvabhāvatva*).

For it is not logical to attribute the nature of one thing to everything else; otherwise, since a lamp is perceived as self-illuminating by its very own nature, it would follow that jars and other objects are likewise so, and thus the established distinction between the specific natures of individual things would be destroyed. (Tathā prasaṅgaḥ, B, Ja).

As for that which was further stated—"it is dependent upon valid cognition" (*pramāṇāpekṣa*) and so forth—what is this so-called "simultaneous experience by means of valid cognition"? If you say it is "being experienced at the same time as the valid cognition," no; for that would entail a contradiction with your own words. By speaking thus, you have indeed established "time" (*kāla*) through your own statement, since it is impossible to speak of "simultaneity" without accepting it, and because such expressions as "that which existed in a previous moment" (*pūrvakṣaṇabhāvi bhūtam*) would be untenable, given that "time" is merely another synonym for "moment" (*kṣaṇa*).

Therefore, this nature of entities such as "presentness" and so forth is merely conditioned by time (*kālopādhika*) and is designated in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the nature of being "far" or "near" which is conditioned by space (*deśopādhika*). Furthermore, if time were not accepted, there would be a contradiction with worldly experience (*lokapratīti*); for in the world, there exists the actual perception of times such as spring (*vasanta*). Indeed, all those engaged in worldly affairs employ such conventions as "specific trees blossom at specific times," just as the *pāṭala* and other flowers bloom only during the season of spring and so on.

In this way, it should be inferred in other cases as well; for its existence is established through common usage such as "it awaits the time of birth," and through conventions regarding time-units like *samaya* and *muhūrta*.
Therefore, real time (*kāla*) is established as having the nature of a multiple substance.
Consequently, neither the substance of time nor the substance of space (*dig-dravya*) postulated by others is tenable.
On page 254, line 12:

"The blossoming of *pāṭala* and other flowers occurs only during the spring season and not at other times; in this same way, it should be inferred for other effects as well that they depend upon the time of their production. Thus, from the common usage [of saying] "it depends on the time of production," time possesses causality (*kāraṇatva*).
(*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 349).

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika is as follows: "Direction (*dik*) exists as a distinct substance, because it is cognized through the inferential marks (*liṅga*) of notions such as 'east,' 'west,' and so forth" (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 170, top).

[Objection: But since this [direction] is perceived through the mark (liṅga) of notions such as "prior" and "posterior," which are the opposite of notions such as "earlier" and "later" produced by time, how can there be no fixed order? To explain: when one takes a corporeal substance as a limit among corporeal substances, those ten notions—namely, "this is to the east of that," "to the south," "to the west," "to the north," "to the southeast," "to the southwest," "to the northwest," "to the northeast," "below," and "above"—from which they arise, that is direction (dik).
And thus says the Sūtra: "That from which [the notion arises] 'this is from here' is the mark of direction."
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.10:
These cognitions are not without a cause, because they are occasional.
Nor do they have undifferentiated causes, because they are specific cognitions, like the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth.
Nor do they have as their cause substances that are corporeal and mutually dependent; for, due to mutual dependence, there would follow the non-arising of both cognitions.
Since it is impossible for them to be produced by any other cause, these [cognitions] are the inferential indicators of space (*dik*) itself.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: This cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, is based upon a category of entity distinct from corporeal substances, because it is of a different nature than the cognitions of those [corporeal objects], just like the cognition of pleasure and so on. Likewise, the substance of space (*dig-dravya*) is distinct from others, or should be designated as "space," because it has the cognition of "prior" and so forth as its inferential mark (*liṅga*). For that which is not so [distinct] does not have the cognition of "prior" and so forth as its mark, such as earth and the other elements; and this [space] is so; therefore, it is so. Furthermore, its properties—such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*), unity (*ekatva*), and eternity (*nityatva*)—are to be understood as being like those of time (*kāla*).

Nor is the conventional usage of distinctions such as "eastern" and so forth difficult to establish in the case of this [space] being one; for it is easily established through the conjunction of the sun, which revolves clockwise around Mount Meru, with the directional regions occupied by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). With reference to this, [the definition is: having taken a corporeal substance as a limit, that from which the ten notions arise regarding corporeal substances themselves—namely, "this is to the east," "to the south," "to the west," "to the north," "to the southeast," "to the southwest," "to the northwest," "to the northeast," "below," and "above"—is *diś* (direction/space).
"That from which [one perceives] 'this is from that' is the indicative mark (liṅga) pertaining to direction," Vaiśeṣika Sūtra. Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 66.
The reading in the present context, however, is as follows: *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 170a; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p.
669; and likewise, "it is distinguished from others," *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 357.
The eastern direction is so called from the former, future, and present conjunction with the sun; likewise the southern, western, and northern directions.
By this, the intermediate directions are explained.
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.14, 15, 16.

As the Blessed Sun revolves clockwise around Mount Meru, there arise ten specific designations for the directional regions governed by the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), which correspond to their actual meanings according to the divisions beginning with the East (*prācī*). [Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

67] Following the aforementioned refutation of direction as a substance, this establishes that it is solely the linear series of spatial points (*ākāśapradeśapaṅkti*) that serves as the cause for the cognitions of "East," "West," and so forth.
To this, it is replied:

As for what was stated—that [these notions] occur only with respect to corporeal substances (*mūrta-dravya*) and so forth—that is incorrect. For these cognitions, being effects, do they infer a cause in general, or a specific cause characterized as the substance *dika* (space)? In the first case, how can the substance *dika* be established from this, since only a cause in general would be established? Furthermore, in that case, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatā*), because you admit that they are preceded by a cause characterized as space (*ākāśa*). If one merely applies the name "direction" (*dik*) to that very [space], then the dispute is over a name alone and not over the actual object; thus, the substance *dika* is not established as a distinct entity from that [space].

By this, the second alternative is also refuted. For if the substance of direction (*dig-dravya*) were entirely non-existent—like the horn of a hare—how could the cognitions [of direction] be preceded by it, such that they would serve as its inferents? Nor should it be argued: "In the absence of that [substance], how could there be the conventional usage of 'east' and so forth? This is because the conventional usage of 'east' and so forth is established precisely within the series of spatial points (*ākāśa-pradeśa-śreṇi*) by virtue of the rising of the sun and other factors. Thus, these [cognitions] are neither causeless, nor do they have an undifferentiated entity as their cause.

Furthermore, because specific cognitions such as "eastern" and "western" arise in corporeal substances due to their connection with the previously established directions (such as East), corporeal substances themselves cannot be the cause of those [cognitions] based on mutual dependence. For if the "easterness" of one is not established, the "westerness" of the other is not established; and if that is not established, the "easterness" of the first is not established. Thus, due to this circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*), there would be a non-existence of both.

Therefore, if the mere cause is what is to be proven, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); if a specific [cause] is to be proven, there is a sublation of the inference (*anumānavādhā*). (Page 257, Line 15)
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 209;
*Sanmatitarkaṭīkā*, p. 670;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 898.

The directions (*diś*) are also included within space (*ākāśa*), because the conventional usage of "this is here" and "that is there" with respect to the rising of the sun and so forth is possible based on series of spatial points (*ākāśapradeśapaṅkti*),
as established in the *Sarvārthasiddhi* and *Rājavārttika* (5.3).
[From *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
170; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 898]:

If it is asked, "If the series of spatial points (*ākāśapradeśaśreṇi*) is the cause for the cognition of 'east' and so forth with respect to corporeal substances, then what would be the cause for that cognition [of east, etc. with respect to those [spatial points] themselves? We reply: "It is simply their own-nature (*svarūpa*) that is the cause."

Because that spatial direction (dik) is the cause of the notions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, with respect to both its own nature and the natures of others—just as light is the cause of the manifestation of both itself and other forms—otherwise, how could those very notions arise even regarding the spatial divisions? For in that regard, would the arising of the notions of "prior," "posterior," etc., be due to its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), in dependence on another substance of space (*dig-dravya*), or in mutual dependence? If it were due to its own intrinsic nature, then there would be no reversal of those notions. For in whichever spatial division there exists the causality for the notion of "prior," it could not simultaneously possess the causality for the notion of "posterior"; and where that [causality for "posterior"] exists, there could not be the causality for the notion of "prior."

And there is indeed a reversal of that [direction], for in whatever spatial region the state of being a cause for the cognition of "east" is observed in relation to a particular intended location, in that very same region, the state of being a cause for the cognition of "west" is observed in relation to another location.
As it has been said: "That which is the eastern part of Surāṣṭra is the southern part of Mālava;
yet that same eastern part stands to the north of those [Mālavas]."
Thus,

if the cause of that cognition [of direction] were due to the dependence upon another substance of direction, there would be an infinite regress— because for that [substance] as well, the state of being the cause of that cognition would entail its dependence upon yet another substance of direction. Furthermore, if those spatial points were the cause of that cognition through mutual dependence, it would result in the fallacy of reciprocal dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Since the conventional usage of directions such as "east" and so forth is established in the substance of space (digdravya) by the principle that "the sun revolves clockwise around Meru," and since for this very reason the same usage is established even regarding the series of its points, there is no need to postulate a separate substance of direction.

Furthermore, because a reversal of the spatial series is observed— since that which is the eastern direction in one place is perceived as the southern direction in another— it is held that "that which is the eastern part for the people of Surāṣṭra is the southern part for the Mālavas."
"The eastern part of Surāṣṭra is the southern [part] of Mālava"—this has been cited from *Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p.
567a (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 141).
Furthermore, their eastern slope is situated to the north of them.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating a substance called "space" (*deśadravya*), because the cognition "this region is to the east of that," and so forth, would be inexplicable even without a substance of space; and in that case, the enumeration of substances as nine would be contradicted.

It is untenable to claim that earth and the other elements alone constitute the substance of space (*deśadravya*); for since they are the causes of the cognition of "earth" and so forth, it is impossible for them to be the cause of such cognitions as "this is the eastern direction from here. If it is argued that the cognition of "eastern space" and so on with respect to earth and the other elements is produced by the cardinal directions (*dik*), this is merely a fantasy; for, according to the reasoning already stated, it cannot be established that the directions—which are a series of points in space (*gaganapradeśapaṅkti*)—are distinct entities.

Now, one might argue: "If the notions of 'east,' 'west,' and so forth are established even on the earth and other substances—just as they are in rows of spatial points (*ākāśapradeśa*)—solely by virtue of the rising of the sun and such, then the postulation of rows of spatial points is also fruitless. This too is an unexamined statement; for since we observe the conventional usage of locus and located in the form "the earth and so forth are in the eastern direction," the postulation of those rows of points as the substratum for the earth and so forth is indeed fruitful. Furthermore, space (*ākāśa*) has already been firmly established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, enough with this digression.
Because it would follow that even a spatial location (*deśa*) and a substance (*dravya*) would be mere conceptual constructions; see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 170, l. 2;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 899.

By this, the inference beginning with "that cognition of east, west, and so forth" is refuted; for since that cognition is based on a category of object characterized by a series of points in space (ākāśa-pradeśa-paṅkti) distinct from corporeal substances, it is untenable for it to be based on the substance of direction (dig-dravya).

Therefore, since the substance of direction is not established through any means of valid cognition, arguments such as "the substance of direction is distinct from others" are like a description of the good fortune of the son of a barren woman, and are thus to be disregarded.

Therefore, neither the substance of space (dig-dravya) imagined by others nor the substance of the self (ātma-dravya) is established; for even that [self], though endowed with properties such as omnipresence, is not proven by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). (Page 257, Line 23)

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika is as follows: "The self exists and is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), because if it were of the size of the body, logical defects would arise; moreover, it is distinct in each individual body.
[Objection: But this is incorrect; for its possession of those attributes is established here through inference (*anumāna*). To explain:

the self is all-pervasive, because, while not being the locus of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), it is an eternal substance (*nityadravya*). Whatever is thus is so, just like space (*ākāśa*); and the self is thus; therefore, it is so.

Furthermore, it is not unestablished that the Self is not the locus of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). To explain: the Self is not the locus of atomic dimension because it is the locus of specific qualities perceptible by us and others, like a jar and so forth.
Likewise, the Self is an eternal substance because it is a substance devoid of touch, like space;
or alternatively, the Self is eternal because it is the substratum of momentary specific qualities, like space.
Likewise: "The self is a substance because it possesses qualities, like a jar; or else, because it is the locus of qualities," [as stated in] Ba., Ja., Bhā., and Śra.

Furthermore, if the self (*ātman*) were not all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), then the production of Devadatta’s wife’s limbs and of jewels, pearls, and so forth existing in other continents—which serve as benefits for Devadatta—would not occur, because those [benefits] are preceded by his qualities (*tadguṇapūrvakatva*). To explain: Devadatta’s wife’s limbs and so forth are preceded by Devadatta’s qualities, because, while being effects (*kāryatva*), they are beneficial to him, just like food and the like.

Furthermore, a cause that is present at the location of the effect operates toward the production of that effect, and not otherwise, for [otherwise] there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, just as the cause of those [elements] is established at the location where their limbs and so forth appear, so too is the possession of those qualities (*tadguṇasiddhi*) established. And wherever the qualities are perceived, there the substratum of those qualities (*tadguṇin*) is also inferred, because they cannot exist without it.

[The body and so forth] are effects produced by the elements impelled by the specific qualities of Devadatta and are appropriated by him; for, being effects, they are the instruments of his experience, like a house. (Praśastapādabhāṣya with Kiraṇāvalī, p. 149)

Furthermore, it is logical that [qualities] which depend on their own substratum can initiate action in another substratum with which they are conjoined; for instance, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) initiates action in another substratum conjoined with its own substratum, because—while being a single substance—it is a quality that causes motion, like volition (*prayatna*).

Nor is its status as a quality causing motion unestablished; for the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial actions of atoms and the mind are caused by the specific qualities of Devadatta, because—while being effects—they are beneficial to him, like the movement of the hand and so forth. This is established through inference.

Nor does it possess the property of subsisting in a single substance (*ekadravyatva*). To explain: if it were argued that "the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) subsists in a single substance because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), like sound," this would be subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of color and other qualities. To exclude these, it is stated that it is "because it is a quality that causes action" (*kriyāhetuguṇatvāt*).

However, if it were stated merely "because it is a quality that causes action," there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) due to the conjunction between a hand and a club, which—while being a cause of action—is not itself a quality but rather causes action in a pillar or similar object that is not conjoined with its own substratum. To avoid this, the qualification "while subsisting in a single substance" (*ekadravyatve sati*) is added.

If it were stated simply that [gravity] is the cause of action while possessing the nature of a single substance (*ekadravyatva*), there would be an inconclusive fallacy (*anekānta*) due to the magnet, which causes the movement of iron and other metals not conjoined with its own substratum. To exclude that, "because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*) was stated.

Similarly, since merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are qualities of the self, if their substratum were non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of air, and the initial actions of atoms and the mind would not occur; for these depend upon conjunction with their own substrata.

Just as effort in the action of the hand requires conjunction with the self, so too merit and demerit would not produce action without conjunction with the self, because they are qualities of the self; and since there is no other cause in that case, the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) itself is the cause, requiring conjunction with its own substrate. Furthermore, because it is all-pervasive, it possesses supreme magnitude. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p. 411)

Furthermore, if the self were not all-pervading, there would be no simultaneous conjunction with atoms situated in different directions and locations; consequently, there would be no initial action [of the body]. Due to the absence of that [action], there would be an absence of the final conjunction, the body caused by it, and the connection between the two; thus, liberation would be achieved without means for everyone at all times. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 88)

Or let it be that the body arises in some manner or other; even so, as the self enters into each part of the body—which possesses parts—the self itself would become possessed of parts. And if it were possessed of parts, it would follow, like a cloth or similar objects, that it is an effect. If it were an effect, would it be produced by causes of the same class or of different classes? It could not be by causes of different classes, because things of different classes do not originate [composite effects].

Now, [if you argue that the self is produced] by those of the same class (*samānajātīya*); but surely their being of the same class would follow precisely from their connection with the nature of a self (*ātmatva*). And if that were so, it would follow that a self is originated by selves, which is untenable. This is because it is impossible for multiple selves to originate another self within a single body; or, even if such origination were possible, the unification of experience (*pratisandhāna*) would be inexplicable. For one person cannot unify what was perceived by another, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, if the self were originated in this way, it would perish—just like a jar—due to the destruction of its conjunctions resulting from the disjunction caused by the motion of its constituent parts.

Because there is no initial action for the final conjunction [of the soul with the body], the soul would have to be of the same nature as that [conjunction]; furthermore, if the soul were of the same dimension as the body, it would follow that the soul is corporeal (mūrta), and because of this corporeality, its entry into the body would be impossible, since there is a contradiction in one corporeal entity entering another corporeal entity. Consequently, it follows that the entire body would be devoid of a soul.

Or how, if it were of that [limited] size, could that [self], while existing with the dimensions of a child's body, assume the dimensions of a youth's body—either by abandoning those dimensions or without abandoning them? If by abandoning them, then, because it would follow that it is impermanent like the body, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the next world and so forth. If, on the other hand, without abandoning them, that is not possible; for if the previous dimension is not abandoned, the arising of a subsequent dimension in it is untenable, just as in the case of the body.
Furthermore, if the self were of such limited dimensions, it would follow that it would be cut when the body is cut.

Now, if it is argued that the supreme magnitude of the self is unestablished because its size is limited by the body—such that in a small body the self is small and in a large body it is large—then, under this view, since the self possesses the properties of contraction and expansion, the self would perish even in childhood; consequently, in old age, there would be no single self, and thus memory [of past experiences] would not occur due to the difference in identity. Furthermore, as long as the previous dimension has not ceased, it is impossible for a subsequent dimension to arise; therefore, the cessation of the previous dimension occurs only through the destruction of its substrate (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 411).

And thus, if the self were limited by the dimensions of the body, it would follow that the self is non-eternal, like a jar or similar objects; this same defect applies even within a single lifetime across the stages of childhood, youth, and old age. (Brahma Sūtra Śāṅkara Bhāṣya 2.3.19)
2.34 The demonstration that the self has the same dimensions as the body, preceded by the refutation of its all-pervasiveness and other such attributes.

To this, the following reply is given: As for what was stated—that the self is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), and so forth—that is incorrect. Because the reason (*hetu*) is adduced immediately after the presentation of a thesis that is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhita*), it is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

For when the self is apprehended through direct perception such as "I am happy," it is apprehended only within one's own body, not in another's body nor in the space between them. Otherwise, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient, and there would be a confusion of activities such as eating and so forth.

Furthermore, its possession of that [quality] is not tenable, because it contradicts direct perception; for by direct perception, the self is [known as] the object of cognition... (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 171a).
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 142;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 899.

Now, it might be argued that if the self (*ātman*) is understood as non-pervasive, then the thesis (*pakṣa*) would be sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), just as when "non-hotness" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), there is sublation by the perceived hotness of fire. Furthermore, such a [non-pervasive] understanding of this [self] does not exist, because there is an absence of limitation by a fixed location. This is incorrect. For what is this so-called "absence of limitation"? Is it the non-experience of a fixed location, or the non-employment of words denoting such [a location]? Regarding these, the first position is untenable; for the experience of a fixed location is indeed perceived in the case of the self. By the cognition "I am happy," etc., the self—consisting of pleasure and so forth—is experienced precisely in a region of the body, just as by the cognition "this is a jar," a jar with a broad base and belly is experienced in the space in front.

Indeed, it is not possible for perception to experience an object apart from the experience of its specific place, time, and form, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Thus, the second alternative is also untenable; for even if there is no employment of words denoting a specific place, how could there be a non-experience of that [place] by perception? Indeed, being permeated by words (śabdānuviddhatva) is not the essential nature (svarūpa) of perception, such that in its absence perception would lack the capacity to discern the true nature of the object, since the refutation of such permeation has already been established previously.

Therefore, in all cases, the employment of words occurs only subsequent to experience. For when an object has been experienced as being endowed with many attributes, the employment of a word occurs only in respect to that specific aspect for which the recollection of a convention—rooted in the awakening of that experience—is produced, and not elsewhere. How, then, can the absence of such employment prove the absence of the experience of those [other aspects]? If, because of the non-employment of words specifying a particular location, there were no experience of spatial restriction, then there would likewise be no experience of restrictions regarding time or form. Indeed, in external and internal cognitions such as "this is a jar" or "I am happy," there is no employment of words specifying spatial, temporal, or formal restrictions, such as "here," "now," or "of this kind."

Therefore, since there is no manifestation of any specifically determined nature of a real entity (*vastusvarūpa*) in this cognition, it would not differ from the cognition of a sky-flower in any way—unless one argues that the difference here consists in the manifestation of existence versus non-existence. But if you say this, we reply: no, for if the words "existent" and "non-existent" are not employed, even that [distinction] is impossible.

Or let it be so; nevertheless, what would constitute the distinction between this [perception of a pot] and the perception of atoms or space? If you say it is caused by the appearance of clarity (*sphuṭatva*) or lack of clarity (*asphuṭatva*), we say no; for apart from the grasping or non-grasping of a specific place, time, and form, the very appearance of clarity or lack of clarity is impossible.

Therefore, one who desires a distinction between perceptual cognition and other types of cognition must admit that there is an appearance characterized by the restriction of place and so forth, even if the word "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*) is not explicitly used. Thus, the thesis is sublated by perception, and the reason (*hetu*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
—because of the non-exclusion of location—ba, ja; —because of being [the object of] cognition—a, p.
It is experienced (anubhūyate) by Ba and Ja— as awakening (vabodha)— by Ā and Śra— as the awakening to existence (vabhavaprabodha).

Furthermore, "not being the locus of atomic dimension" is the negation of being the locus of that dimension. Would this negation be of the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) type or the *prasajya* (absolute) type? If it were of the *paryudāsa* type, it would function by way of accepting another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*). And what would that other entity be in this context? It would have to be either the state of being the locus of infinite magnitude (*paramamahāparimāṇa*) or the state of being the locus of some intermediate dimension (*avāntaraparimāṇa*). In the first case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished with respect to the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), as in the argument: "Sound is non-eternal, because, while being non-eternal, it is perceptible by the external sense organs."

In the second case, however, there is a contradictory qualification (*viruddhaviśeṣaṇa*), as in: "Sound is non-eternal, because, while being eternal, it is perceptible by the external senses. In the case of the prasajya-type negation, however, there is the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhatva*); for at the time of investigating negation, it will be demonstrated that a negation whose nature is a mere void (*tuccha*) does not fall within the range of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or, if it were established, would this [negation] be of the same nature (*svabhāva*) as the probandum (*sādhya*), or its effect (*kārya*)? If it were of the same nature, then it would follow that the probandum also possesses the form of a void, because it would have a nature non-different from a negation whose nature is a void, like a sky-lotus.

Now, as for the body: that is not so; for it is impossible for this, which is of a void nature (*tucchasvabhāva*), to be an effect. Whatever is of a void nature is not an effect, just like a sky-flower; and the negation of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) postulated by you is of a void nature. Furthermore, if this were an effect, it would follow that it is occasional; consequently, prior to its production, the self would have to possess atomic dimension as its substrate.

Furthermore, what would this "being an effect" (kāryatva) consist of for it? Would it be inherence in the existence of its own cause, or would it be being the object of the cognition "it has been made"? Of these, the first position is untenable; for you do not admit that non-existence has inherence in the existence of its own cause, otherwise it would simply be of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva).

The second position is also illogical; for it is impossible for non-existence, which is by nature void (tuccha), to be the object of such a cognition. How indeed could that which is beyond the scope of any means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) be the object of the cognition "it has been made"? Therefore, when examined, the negation of atomic dimension (aṇuparimāṇa) in the case of the self (ātman) is not tenable.

—[The property of] having magnitude (*parimāṇatva*) [is attributed to it]. Even that proof which was stated for its establishment—namely, "because it is the locus of specific qualities perceptible to those like us"—is also incorrect; for in refuting that [proof], all the aforementioned defects would follow, and there is the consequence of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since we ourselves accept that the self, like a jar or other objects, possesses merely the negation of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the soul’s status as an eternal substance (*nityadravyatva*), is this intended in some respect (*kathañcit*) or in every respect (*sarvathā*)? If it is in some respect, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) with objects such as a jar; for although a jar is not the locus of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) and possesses a kind of eternal substantiality, it lacks omnipresence (*vyāpitva*).

If, on the other hand, it is in every respect, that is unproven; because an entity that is eternal in every respect lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), its very existence is impossible, like the horn of a donkey.

By this, that which was stated to prove the eternity of the self—that it consists of a substance devoid of touch—is also refuted. For, if its eternity is proven in some respect, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*);
if it is proven in every respect, the reason lacks positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), because even space and so forth have been denied absolute eternity.
— *vaddravyaṃ* (Ā., Ba., Ja.)

By this, the argument "because it is the locus of momentary specific qualities" is also refuted; furthermore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the case of] lightning and so forth. For even though it is the locus of specific qualities characterized by momentary, radiant color and so on, its absolute eternity is impossible.

If it is argued that radiant color and the like do not possess the status of momentary specific qualities because they are perceived as non-momentary in fire and other such things, then let it be that cognition (*buddhi*) and the rest also do not possess the status of specific qualities of that [soul], since they are perceived as non-momentary in God (*īśvara*).
pṛ॰ 260 pa॰ 2 –lakṣaṇaguṇā– ba॰, ja॰; –thā’nityatvasambha– śra॰.

As for what was also stated—"the limbs of Devadatta’s wife," and so forth—that too is incorrect. For, are the qualities of Devadatta’s self—namely knowledge, vision, and so on—which are intended as the cause of that [birth], or are they merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)? In the first case, the reason is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*); for knowledge and the rest are perceived through direct perception and other means to exist in Devadatta’s very body, without being operative in the production of the limbs of Devadatta’s wife.

Now, as for merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*): if that is so, we too certainly accept their causal status as the basis for effects such as limbs and so forth. However, we do not accept that they are qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa*), because they are insentient (*acetana*), like sound and other such things.

Nor is there a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason due to pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth; for these lack the absence of sentience, being pervaded by consciousness (*caitanya*) characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the opposite of insentience.
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for instance: those two [merit and demerit] are insentient because they are devoid of the capacity to perceive themselves, like a jar or similar objects.

There is no inconclusiveness regarding knowledge, because its nature as self-apprehending will be established [later], and the materiality (*paudgalikatva*) of karmas will also be proven on the occasion of the investigation into liberation; therefore, enough of this digression (p.
For are the qualities of Devadatta’s self, such as knowledge and vision, or merit and demerit, intended to be the causes of effects such as the limbs of Devadatta’s body? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
171; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 147;
Syādvādaratnākara p. 906)

—Or let it be that those two [the soul and the body] possess the quality of being its [the self's] attributes; even so, their existence is not established at the location where the limbs and so forth manifest.

For there is no rule that every cause must be present at the location of the effect to be active in the production of that effect, since we observe that collyrium, forehead marks, mantras, and the like perform actions such as summoning, even though they are not present at the location of the woman being summoned.

And for what purpose is the qualification "being an effect"? If it is said that it is for the sake of removing the deviation [of the reason] by means of time, God, and so forth; then, since time, God, and so forth—even though they are not preceded by those qualities—are nevertheless beneficial to them, some effects, even if preceded by something else, will likewise be beneficial to them. Thus, because its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), just like "speaking" and so forth when "lack of omniscience" is the property to be proven—[as in the case of] *dravyādeḥ* (in the versions *ba*, *ja*, and *ā*).

Furthermore, the example "like the act of eating" (*grāsādivat*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for in that case, what quality of the self (*ātman*) is intended—merit (*dharma*) and so forth, or effort (*prayatna*)? If it is merit and so forth, then the same undesirable consequence as the thesis follows.

If, however, it is effort, one must ask: what indeed is this thing called "effort"? Is it the vibration of the self or of its constituent parts located in the hands and other limbs? In that case, how can that which is characterized by motion (*calana*) be a quality (*guṇa*)? Otherwise, by extension, even movement and the like would have to be qualities, and the very discussion of action (*kriyā*) would be destroyed.
And this example, "like food and so forth," is devoid of the probandum; for in that case, [the self] is the object of cognition... (Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.

By this, the argument that "the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), having entered [the body], initiates action in another substrate conjoined with its own substrate," and so forth, is refuted; for the unseen force is not established as a quality (guṇa) by the aforementioned method. Therefore, the reason (hetu) is unestablished in its qualificand (viśeṣya-asiddha) and unestablished in its qualifier (viśeṣaṇa-asiddha), because its existence in a single substance (tadekadravyatva) is not proven.

For how could that [perception] arise? Would it be because of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in a single substance, by way of inherence (*samavāya*), or from some other cause? It cannot first be due to conjunction, because conjunction, being a quality (*guṇa*), must reside in a substance, whereas the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is not a substance; otherwise, it would follow that it is a substance itself by virtue of possessing qualities, which would contradict the statement that "it is a quality that is the cause of action.
Furthermore, its existence through inherence could only be established if inherence were already proven, yet that is unproven since it will be refuted later.
As for the third alternative, it is untenable simply because it is not accepted.
Page 260, line 9 – [The term] "vidha" is found in manuscripts *ba* and *ja*.

Furthermore, its status as the cause of action is unproven; for instance, is the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in that portion of the self conjoined with Devadatta’s body the cause of the action in gems and pearls located in another continent which move toward Devadatta, [residing] in that portion of the self conjoined with a substance in another continent, or rather, is it [the cause] everywhere? Of these, the first alternative is untenable; because of the extreme distance, there is no connection between it and those [objects], and thus its status as the cause of action is untenable.

Now, if it is argued that the absence [of conjunction] is unproven because a relation consisting of conjunction with its own substratum is possible, that is incorrect; for since that [conjunction] exists everywhere, it would follow that everything would be attracted. Furthermore, the claim that "only that which is produced by a particular *adṛṣṭa* is attracted by that same *adṛṣṭa*, not everything," is also incorrect; for it would follow that the atoms initiating Devadatta’s body would not be attracted, as they are not produced by that [body’s] *adṛṣṭa*. Even if attraction were to occur despite this, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because of the absence of a [necessary] connection. (Bhāṣya)
Now, that which is produced by the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is the object of cognition (prameya). (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 172;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 143;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 906)

Even regarding the second alternative: just as the wind, moving by itself, is the cause for other things such as grass to move toward it, so too would the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), moving by itself toward that [person], be the cause for others to move toward him; or else, would it reside in a portion of the self conjoined with substances existing in another continent? In the first case, does the unseen force itself move toward that person, or does it do so because of another unseen force? If it moves toward him by its own power, then the same consequence would apply to substances existing in other continents as well, rendering the postulation of an unseen force useless. Furthermore, the reason—that "whatever moves toward Devadatta is drawn by a quality of Devadatta, because it moves toward him"—would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

If its movement toward that [object] were caused by another unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that [second unseen force] would also have to move toward it due to yet another unseen force.

Alternatively, if you argue that the cause for their movement toward that object is simply its being located in a portion of the self (*ātmapradeśa*) conjoined with a substance situated in another continent, we say no; for such a principle is not accepted in the case of other qualities of the self, such as effort (*prayatna*). Indeed, effort residing only in a portion of the self conjoined with the morsel of food is not the cause for the movement of that food toward Devadatta’s mouth, because it would follow that efforts in the intervening space would be useless.

Furthermore, if the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were to operate everywhere, it would follow that it is the cause of action in all substances; yet, if one were to argue that "the unseen force which produces a particular substance brings about action only in that very substance," even in that case, it has been stated that there would be no action in the atoms that initiate the body (see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
172, uttara-pakṣa). Indeed, effort does not reside solely in those parts of the self conjoined with the mouthful of food and so forth.
Sanmati-Ṭīkā, p. 143:

Furthermore, this reason is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because it is employed after the statement of a fact that has been sublated by perception. For the substratum of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is the self, and one perceives the self through the direct perception of self-awareness as being indeed dissociated from substances existing in other continents.

Thus, since the self is perceived as dissociated from those substances, if one were to nevertheless admit a conjunction of the self with those substances, why would there not also be a conjunction of jars and the like with Mount Meru and so forth, whereby the Sāṃkhya system would no longer exist? The sublation by valid cognition is equal in both cases.

Furthermore, the self (*ātman*) is the single substratum for merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the conjunction with other substances. And according to your view, it is partless (*niraṃśa*). Therefore, since its body is embraced in its entirety by merit, by demerit, or by both, there is no room for the conjunction with other substances therein; nor, conversely, can there be [conjunction] in merit and so forth because of that [self]. If, on the other hand, the conjunction with other substances were to occur there by excluding that nature which is embraced by those [merits and demerits], then the self would possess parts (*sāvayavatva*), be composed of constituent parts (*svārambhakāvayavārabhyatva*), and would be non-eternal (*anityatva*), just like a jar or similar objects.

By this, the following argument is refuted: "Animals and the like, as they approach Devadatta, are drawn by the qualities of Devadatta, because they approach him, just like food and such"; for if they were drawn by his qualities, all the aforementioned defects would necessarily follow.

Furthermore, what is intended by the term "Devadatta" here? Is it the body, the self (*ātman*), their conjunction, the body qualified by conjunction with the self, the self qualified by conjunction with that [body], or a portion of the self conjoined with the body? If it is the body, then since animals and others approach it because they are attracted by its qualities, the reason—being attracted by the qualities of the body—would be contradictory when one seeks to prove that [the movement] is attracted by the specific qualities of the self (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*).

Now, as for the self (*ātman*): because it is always connected with the object through its location and time, nothing could approach it. For a woman whose neck is already firmly embraced does not approach her lover again; indeed, an object located in one place approaches an object in another place, just as an arrow and the like approach a target, or an object of one time approaches an object of another time, just as a seed and the like approach a sprout by obtaining successive transformations of power.

Furthermore, since both [of these] are impossible given that the self is eternally and pervasively present everywhere and at all times, the qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaṇa*)— "approaching Devadatta"— and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)— "drawn by the qualities of Devadatta"— would, for the opponent, be nothing but a fabrication of their own imaginative artifice, based on the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*) "because of possessing the quality of approaching him. (Page 260, Line 4)
Regarding this, it is said [in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

173, u.]: "In that case, what is the referent denoted by the word 'Devadatta'? Is it the body? The self? Their conjunction? The body qualified by conjunction with the self? The self qualified by conjunction with the body? Or a portion of the self conjoined with the body?"
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 144; tatprati, ba, ja;
nityatvavyā-, ba, ja.

Furthermore, if the conjunction of the body and the self were denoted by the word "Devadatta," then it would follow that when these [atoms] approach him, they are drawn by his qualities (*guṇa*); yet there are no qualities in qualities, because they are themselves devoid of qualities. If, on the other hand, the body qualified by its conjunction with the self were denoted by that word, the same contradiction should be understood to apply here as well.

If it is argued that the Self, as qualified by its conjunction with the body, is what is denoted by that word [‘Self’], even here the same defect inherent in the position of the Self would arise; for, despite being of such a nature, its presence everywhere and at all times cannot be avoided due to its eternal omnipresence—indeed, space conjoined with a jar is certainly not absent from Mount Meru and other such locations.

Now, if it is argued that the portion of the self (*ātmapradeśa*) conjoined with the body is what is denoted by that term [the word "self"], is that [portion] conceptual (*kālpanika*) or ultimate (*pāramārthika*)? If it is conceptual, then since animals and others are drawn toward the self by the qualities of that conceptualized portion of the self, and because they approach that self characterized by those qualities, one would have to establish that those qualities themselves are also conceptual. Consequently, as in the case of the Buddhist, rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) caused by those qualities would not be ultimate;
for the color-form (*rūpa*) and other properties of a conceptual fire, or its effects such as burning, are never seen to be ultimate.

Now, if it is ultimate (pāramārthika), is it non-different from the self or different? If it is non-different, then since it would be the self itself, the aforementioned fault is not avoided. If, on the other hand, it is different, then the fact that animals and others are drawn by its specific qualities establishes that very [quality] as the self; thus, the postulation of another self is useless. Or, if such a postulation were made, it would follow—as has already been stated—that because it possesses parts, it would be an effect and therefore impermanent.

As for what was also stated—that if the self were not omnipresent, [it could not interact] with atoms existing in other directions and locations, and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for there is no possibility of a rule such as "whatever is conjoined with something moves toward that very thing," since we observe that iron is attracted toward a magnet even though it is not conjoined with it.

Furthermore, for one whose self is omnipresent, since there would be simultaneous conjunction with other atoms that have already begun to form an effect, those atoms—having become oriented toward the commencement of that body in exactly that same manner—would necessarily approach it; thus, I do not know what the size of that body might be.

Now, if it is argued that only those conjunctions which depend upon that *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) produce the initial action in their own conjoined atoms, while others do not—well then, what is this so-called "dependence on that *adṛṣṭa*" of theirs? Is it inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), assistance (*upakāra*), or the simultaneous production of the initial action? Among these, the first position is untenable, because all conjunctions of atoms would possess inherence in a single object with the *adṛṣṭa* residing in Devadatta’s self.

The second position is also untenable; for since there is no relationship between the object of dependence and the dependent, and because this would entail an infinite regress, the very assistance [required] is impossible.

As for the claim that "the first action is produced simultaneously," that too is incorrect; for otherwise, by virtue of there being no distinction, it would follow that such production occurs everywhere. Furthermore, if either of those two—the conjunction with that [object] or the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—possesses the capacity for production independently, then dependence on another is logically inconsistent.

If, on the other hand, it is maintained that the capacity to produce an effect belongs only to the two [the magnet and the iron] when they are conjoined with an unseen force (adṛṣṭa) due to their own causes; then let that capacity be attributed to the unseen force alone, independent of its conjunction with its own substratum.
For it is observed that a magnet, by means of its substratum such as a hand, attracts iron situated on the ground without being in contact with its own substratum (p.

This would indeed be the case if there were a rule that whatever is joined with something moves toward that very thing; however, such a rule does not exist regarding the magnet, because movement toward it is observed even for that which is not joined with it (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 175, uttarārdha; Syādvādamañjarī, p.
62, verse 9).

Furthermore, as for what was stated [by you]—namely, that "the self enters the body which possesses parts," and so forth—that too is mere words; for, by the very fact of possessing parts, the quality of being composed of distinct constituent parts is unestablished even in the case of a jar and the like.

Indeed, a jar or similar object, though possessing parts, is not observed to be preceded by a conjunction of previously established homogeneous potsherds; rather, its production is perceived from the very beginning from a lump of clay endowed with the activity of the potter’s hands and other such factors, appearing already in the form of a broad base, belly, and so forth.

For the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) consists in a substance’s transformation into a subsequent form through the relinquishing of its prior form; and this is indeed experienced internally just as it is externally.

Nor is it logical to conclude that everything is thus [i.e., produced by the conjunction of its own parts], based on the observation that in the case of cloth and the like, the state of being an effect is preceded by the conjunction of its own parts; for if that were so, it would follow that a diamond (*vajra*) must also be so, since the property of being scratchable by iron is observed in wood, yet the sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhana*) is equal in both cases.

Nor does the absence of recognition follow from the admission that the self possesses the aforementioned nature of being an effect, because— as will be explained on page 260, line 22— this [recognition] is established only when there is some degree of impermanence.
Indeed, even though a jar or similar object is composed of parts, it is not preceded by the conjunction of potsherds belonging to the same class as those previously established.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
176, top; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 149;
*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 63, verse 9.

—Thus [it is said]. By this, the argument beginning with "the soul has the dimensions of the body of a child" and so forth is refuted; for even when the soul abandons the dimensions of the body of a child upon reaching the state of having the dimensions of a youth’s body, its total destruction is impossible—just as a snake, upon abandoning its coiled state, assumes an expanded state—and therefore, how can the non-existence of the next world follow? This is because, although it is impermanent in terms of its modes (*paryāya*), it is eternal in terms of its substance (*dravya*).
On page 261, line 8:

Since it is impossible for the self to be utterly destroyed when it relinquishes the dimensions of its childhood body while in the state of the dimensions of its youth—just as a snake [remains] when it produces a coiled state—how can the non-existence of the next world be logically entailed? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
65, Kārikā 9).

As for what was also said—that upon the cutting of the body, there would follow the consequence of its [the self's] own cutting—that too is untenable, because such cutting is accepted in some sense. For the "cutting" of the self consists in the relocation of those parts of the self that were connected with the body to the part of the body that has been severed; and this certainly occurs here. Otherwise, one would not perceive the trembling of a limb that has become separated from the body.

Nor does it follow that the portion of the self which has entered into a severed limb becomes a separate self; for it has entered into that very same [body]. Otherwise, why would signs such as trembling not be observed in a severed hand or similar limb? Nor should it be argued that because it has gone elsewhere, those signs are not perceived there; for since the self is one, it would follow that the remainder of the body must also go along with it. Nor should it be argued that because it remains in its original state, it is destroyed right there and thus not perceived; for since the self is one, it would follow that the remainder of the body would likewise be destroyed.

Furthermore, there is not a plurality of selves within a single continuum; for if there were, it would follow that cognitions appearing as multiple objects could not manifest as being based upon a single knower, just like the experience of objects determined by multiple cognitions residing in different bodies. Therefore, because [the self] does not go elsewhere, because it is not absent there, and because it has not perished, its entry into that very [body] is inferred.

If it is asked, "How can there be a subsequent rejoining of parts that have been severed and unsevered?"—we say no; for we do not admit an absolute severance, since we also admit non-severance, as in the case of a lotus-stalk fiber. Furthermore, due to the power of such unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), their rejoining is entirely uncontradicted.

As for what was also stated—that if [the self] were of the size of the body, corporeality (mūrttatva) would follow, and so forth—what is this so-called "corporeality" that would attach to the self? Is it the state of having the dimension of a non-omnipresent substance, or the possession of color and other qualities? Regarding these, the first position does not entail a fault, because it is accepted; for that which is desired does not become a defect.

However, the second position is untenable due to a lack of pervasion (vyāpti); for there is no invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) such that whatever is non-omnipresent is necessarily possessed of color and other qualities, since this is not possible in the case of the mind, even though the mind is non-omnipresent.

Indeed, even water and other substances, though endowed with corporeality characterized by possessing color and so forth, are not obstructed from entering into ashes and the like; yet it is truly a great marvel that this [entry] is obstructed for the self in that same place, even though it is devoid of such [corporeal qualities]! Therefore, whatever appears in unimpeded cognition (*nirbādhabodha*) in a certain way, that very thing enters into the conventional usage of being ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) in that same way—just as a jar [is real] by virtue of its specific location, time, and form in front of one; and the self (*ātman*) likewise appears in unimpeded cognition by virtue of its specific location, time, and form within the body.
Nor is this reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has already been demonstrated that there is no appearance of it outside the body.

Furthermore, since no subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) for that which is irreproachable is possible in the manner described, there is no lack of establishment regarding the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhatva*).

Likewise, [the following argument is presented]: "The self (*ātman*) is not all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), because while possessing general and particular qualities (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattve sati*), it is perceptible to persons such as ourselves (*asmadādipratyakṣatvāt*). Whatever is of this nature is so, like a jar (*ghaṭādi*) and the like; and the self, while possessing general and particular qualities, is perceptible to persons such as ourselves; therefore, it is not all-pervasive. Thus, even the substantial self (*ātmadravya*) as conceived by the opponents does not hold up.
Nor is the mind-substance (manodravya) [eternal]; for its nature as eternal and so forth is not established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) of the Vaiśeṣika is that because cognitions do not arise simultaneously, there exists a distinct substance called the mind (manaḥ), which is eternal, atomic in form, and different for each individual self. [Response:

But surely, since its being an effect is untenable, the eternality of the mind’s nature is already established; and that unestablishability is well-known because of the absence of any causal material (ārambhaka-kāraṇa) for its production.

For its originating cause would have to be either heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) or homogeneous (*sajātīya*). In this regard, the first position is untenable, because a heterogeneous thing lacks the capacity to originate [an effect], as it has been stated that "heterogeneous things do not originate [a substance].

The second position is also incorrect, because when a mind (*manas*) manifests, only a mind can be its homogeneous [cause]; and thus, if one mind were to manifest, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the existence of multiple minds acting as its causes, since one substance cannot be the cause for the production of another substance. [As the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra states: "Substances originate another substance" (VS 1.1.8).

Because of this statement, there is no existence of multiple minds within a single body, since they exist as one per body respectively; otherwise, the production of cognitions would occur simultaneously for every body.

Furthermore, their conjunction with one another is impossible because each is restricted to its own specific body, nor can those that are not conjoined produce [cognition], as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Now, if it is claimed that because those whose minds are liberated lack the state of being obstructed by that [body], a mutual conjunction is possible, and therefore its production is admitted; that is incorrect. For it is impossible for those [atoms] to produce it when they are not presided over by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Consequently, since its status as an effect is untenable, its eternity is established. — Śrauta-bhāṣya.

The proof of the existence [of the mind] is from the mark of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions; for even when all the sense organs are simultaneously connected to their respective objects, only that one which is impelled by the mind produces a cognition regarding its own object.

Likewise, the sense organs and their objects, though present simultaneously, depend upon a sequential cause for their own effects, because they produce their effects sequentially despite the presence of other causal conditions, like a blacksmith and others who require a hand and so forth.

The eye and other sense organs depend upon sequential causes, because even when all other causes are present, they produce [cognition] only after having been produced [themselves], like an axe or a knife. Furthermore, the cognition of pleasure and so forth is born from the contact between the sense organ and its object, because it is a cognition that is perceptual, like the cognition of color and so forth arising from the eye and other organs. The apprehensions of form and so forth require another supervisor distinct from the eyes and other [senses], because they do not arise simultaneously; just as, for example, various tools such as axes belonging to a man skilled in many crafts, though present together, do not simultaneously perform multiple chariot-making activities because they require a supervisor such as the hand, so too the eye and other [senses] do not produce multiple cognitions simultaneously; therefore, they too require another supervisor. Thus, the sense-faculties such as the eye require another supervisor in their activity, because they do not act simultaneously, like axes and other tools.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 89: Refutation of the substance "mind" (*manas*)—whose nature was previously described and which is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas—in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*: Here, it is replied as follows.

As for what was stated—that its originating cause is either homogeneous (*sajātīya*) or heterogeneous (*vijātīya*), and so forth—that is incorrect. For with reference to what is the consideration of whether a cause is homogeneous or otherwise extended? Is it with reference to a substance such as earth, or to a subordinate universal (*avāntarasāmānya*)? If it were with reference to a subordinate universal, then the relationship of cause and effect would not apply even to threads and cloth, because they do not serve as the substratum for a single subordinate universal that is impossible for both of them to possess simultaneously; consequently, homogeneity could not be established with respect to that. Indeed, cloth cannot be homogeneous with respect to the universal "threadness" (*tantutva*), nor can threads be homogeneous with respect to the universal "clothness" (*paṭatva*).

Now, if it is argued with reference to substances such as earth and so forth, then—just as there exists a causal relationship between threads and cloth because they can be established as belonging to the same genus (*sajātīyatva*) with respect to those [earth-substances]—likewise, there would exist such a relationship between atoms and the mind, since they can be established as belonging to the same genus with respect to the substance *pudgala*.
And thus, the materiality (*paudgalikatva*) of the mind is proven.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the mind is material, because it is a sense organ, like the eye and so forth.

[Objection: "But surely, since the eye and other [senses] are established as the effects of specific elements (bhūta) due to their manifesting specific objects such as form, whereas the mind—because it manifests all forms and so on without distinction—cannot possibly be their effect, how can its being an effect of *pudgala* be established by that example? This too is a mere wishful thought; for the claim that they are effects of specific elements has already been refuted in detail in the section stating that 'the material sense-organ (*dravyendriya*) consists of *pudgala*, and the distinction between the classes of those elements has been rejected during the refutation of the fourfold substances such as earth."

These [faculties], beginning with the eye, are merely synonyms for a single person (pudgala) who possesses form and so forth; therefore, there is no disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration.

If it is maintained that the eye and the other faculties are the effects of specific primary elements because they manifest specific objects such as form, then let it be maintained that the mind is the effect of all primary elements because it manifests all objects such as form, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
(Page 268, Line 20)

In that case, there would also be no relationship of cause and effect between threads and cloth, because they are separated by intermediate universals that are mutually incompatible, and thus it is impossible for them to be of the same class (*sajātīya*) in relation to one another. 911) — *yatakā* — Bhāṣya.
