As for what was also stated—that the existence of a mind possessing a permanent nature and so forth is established by the mark of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions—that too is an unexamined assertion; for it is impossible for a mind consisting of a single atom to exercise control over the eyes and other sense organs. For the eye consists of multiple rays, while the nose and other organs consist of parts of earth and other elements. Is this [mind] controlled by the mind simultaneously, or successively? Of these, the first position is untenable, because it is impossible for a single entity in the form of one atom to simultaneously control multiple locations.

Whatever has the nature of a single atom cannot have multiple presiding agents simultaneously, just like a single atom; and since the mind as conceived by you is of that nature, even in the second position, there would be cognition of near and distant objects only successively.

The claim that "because of its rapid movement, there is an illusion of simultaneous perception even though there is sequential cognition" is also untenable; for it would entail the absurd consequence that the perception of a composite whole (*avayavin*) is also illusory. For even in the case of a single object situated before one, the cognitions produced by each individual ray [of light] would grasp only their respective objects sequentially, and the uniform perception of all parts simultaneously would have to be considered an illusion—just as with the *dhattūra* flower, where what is initially subtle appears large at the end. Such a thing is never observed to occur among atoms that function sequentially.

Furthermore, the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is unproven, because in cases such as eating a long roll of sweets, the arising of the fivefold cognition of color-form and so forth is perceived even simultaneously.

If you argue that although these cognitions occur in succession, they are perceived as simultaneous due to their rapid occurrence, this too is incorrect; for it would entail the consequence that all entities are momentary, since the determination of non-momentariness would everywhere be a result of rapid occurrence. Thus, the sublation by perception is equal in both cases.

Now, since the perception of simultaneity here is erroneous, it cannot be established as a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, it lacks the power to sublate the perception of succession. [Objection: But from what is its erroneous nature established? [Response: If you say it is because simultaneity is impossible given that [the mind] is preceded by a single mind (*ekamanas*), then there is the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka-prasaṅga*). For, the establishment of the impossibility of its being a direct perception depends on the establishment of the erroneous nature of that perception; the establishment of that [impossibility] depends on the establishment of the unsublated nature of the perception of succession; and the establishment of that [unsublated nature] depends on the establishment of a single mind. [Objection: Like the sight of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), that perception [of simultaneity] arises from rapid movement (*āśusañcāra*).
Nyāyasūtra 3.2.60.
In this context, the misconception of simultaneity should be understood as being due to rapid succession, like the misconception that one is piercing a hundred lotus petals at once;
see *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 426 (variants:
ekasmin—ba, ja, bhā, śra).
It is not logical for it to be grasped (*saṃgṛhīta*), because it is currently functioning (*pravarttamānatvāt*). (Variant readings: *na ghaṭate* in Śrī and Bhāṣya; *ba*, *ja*)
Because of its rapid occurrence, [the cognition] arises in the auditory faculty (*śrotra-śraddhau*).

Furthermore, as for that which was stated—"the sense-faculties and their objects," etc.—that too is refuted by this very [argument]; for their status as agents of an effect in a sequential manner is unestablished, since it is demonstrated that they act as the agents of five cognitions simultaneously in cases such as the eating of a long *śaṣkulī* (a type of pastry).

This [reason] is inconclusive with respect to the mind (*manas*). For even when all other causal factors are present, the mind produces its effects sequentially, yet it does not depend on sequential instruments [to do so], because that would entail the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). (Page 269, Line 7) By this, the argument "because it produces what has not been previously produced" is also refuted; for there is an inconclusiveness due to the very mind as accepted by you yourself. Indeed, even though the mind produces what was not previously produced when all other causal factors are complete, it does not depend on other sequential instruments, since that would entail the same fallacies of infinite regress and contradicting one's own tenets.

Furthermore, is its status as the producer of what was previously unproduced intended to occur sequentially or simultaneously? If sequentially, then the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has been demonstrated that even in cases such as eating a long roll of pastry, cognitions arise simultaneously.

If, on the other hand, it is simultaneous, then the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because such productivity depends upon non-sequential operation, like a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces multiple effects known to exist together (p. 269, l.
Because of the inconclusiveness [of your argument] due to the very mind admitted by you, [as stated in] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 36, l.
9: "akramakara... (ja, śra).

As for what was also stated—"the cognition of pleasure and so forth," etc.—that too is a mere assertion; because the reason (hetu) has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). For the perceptuality of the cognition of pleasure and so forth is not established, since, according to your view, perception is dependent upon the sense organs (*indriya*), and there exists no sense organ whatsoever that serves as the cause for that cognition such that its perceptuality would be based upon it.
If it is argued that "the mind (*manas*) exists [as such]," we say no; because its existence is not established from any source whatsoever.

For this very reason, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) in establishing that [the mind]: for if the mind is established, then the cognition of it is established as being perceptual (*pratyakṣa*) because it is dependent upon it; and if that [perceptual nature] is established, then the mind is established through the establishment of the probans (*hetu*) together with its qualification. Furthermore, this [probans] has an unestablished subject (*viśeṣyāsiddha*), because no cognition distinct from pleasure and so forth is perceived as the grasper of them.

For this very reason, this [reason] is also unestablished in its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); for there is no such worldly cognition as that "pleasure and so forth, like a jar or other objects, first arise with their nature unknown, and are subsequently connected with the sense organ, and from that [connection] there is knowledge and apprehension. Rather, immediately upon the experience of a desired or undesired object, the arising of this [pleasure] is cognized as being self-luminous by its own nature (p. 269, l.
10). For [it is not the case that] there is [such a process] of knowledge... [text fragment].

Furthermore, if you accept the position that the mind produces cognition only with respect to that which is inherent (*samaveta*) in the locus where the mind is conjoined (*saṃyukta*), then let that cognition be produced with respect to pleasure and so forth, which are inherent in all selves (*ātman*), since there is no distinction in their conjunction with the mind due to its eternal omnipresence. Consequently, a separate mind for each individual soul would be useless.

Even the claim that "the mind belonging to whichever soul is the cause of cognition in that which is inherent to it" is mere faith, for the very fact of a specific relation to a particular soul is not established here.

For that [cognition] would have to arise either because it is an effect of that [soul], or because it is assisted by that, or because of conjunction with that, or because it is impelled by the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of that, or because it is impelled by the soul itself. First, it cannot be because it is an effect of that; for that would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), and it would also entail a contradiction with its permanence.
Nor can it be because it is assisted by that; for since it is in every way permanent—possessing no excellence that can be added or removed—assistance to it is likewise impossible.

Nor can it be because of conjunction with that; for since this [conjunction] is without distinction everywhere, it would follow that it is related to everything, and thus there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that cognition is produced in all substrates of that [conjunction] without distinction.
For that [unseen force] is indeed an object of cognition because it is an effect of that [agent] and because it is assisted by that [agent].

Nor should it be asserted that whatever proceeds or ceases to proceed impelled by the unseen force belongs to that [agent]; for since the unseen force is insentient, it is impossible for it to impel one toward the desired [state] such as heaven, while avoiding the undesired such as hell. Otherwise, the postulation of a conscious presiding agent called God would be rendered purposeless.

If it is accepted that there is no pointlessness because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) functions as its impeller, then let the mind itself be that impeller; enough with this succession [of causes], for since that [mind] is common to all, a restriction to it is not logical. Nor is a specific restriction established even for the unseen force, because it is absolutely distinct from the self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, the claim that "even though there is absolute difference [between the self and the mind], the restriction [of ownership] is established through inherence (*samavāya*)" is also unsatisfactory, because its nature is unestablished and because it is common to all things.

The argument that "the mind which is impelled by whichever self belongs to that [self]" is also worthless, because that which is unperceived cannot be impelled; and if such [an imperceptible entity] could indeed impel, it would follow that even the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms, and so forth, would be impellers, thereby rendering the postulation of a Lord (*īśvara*) useless.

Therefore, there is no establishment of the mind from any source; or, even if it were established, there could be no conjunction [of the self and the mind]. If the partless self and mind were to conjoin by way of a single part, they would possess parts; if they were to conjoin as a whole, this would result in the contradiction of both.
Thus, for others, the substance of the mind does not stand to reason with the nature described above.
Furthermore, because it would be common to all [selves], there could be no restriction [of its activity] to a specific individual.

In the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 36, u.), the Buddhists indeed maintain that the mind (*manas*) is of the nature of cognition itself, based on such [scriptural] passages as: "That consciousness which has just passed away from among the six is called the mind" (*Abhidharmakośa* 1.17). However, in the Yogācāra system, there exists a mind-element (*manodhātu*) distinct from the six consciousnesses.
The Tāmraparṇīyas also postulate that the heart-base (*hṛdayavastu*) is the support for the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*). (Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya, p.
49). Thus, when the substantial entity (*dravyapadārtha*) imagined by others is examined in this way, it does not withstand scrutiny.

Nor is "quality" (guṇa) a distinct category, for even when examined, its nature as accepted [by others] remains unestablished; thus, the Vaiśeṣika's prima facie position—that "the twenty-four qualities, such as color and so forth, characterized by the general definition of 'residing in a substance and possessing [other] qualities'"—is untenable.

But surely, the nature of the category of quality (*guṇa*) has been accepted by us as being dependent on substance (*dravyāśritatva*) and so forth; and since that is perceived precisely in that way through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be a lack of established order? To this effect is the aphorism defining it: "That which resides in substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not, in conjunctions and disjunctions, an independent cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.16).

That which has substance (*dravya*) as its substratum (*āśraya*) is "substance-dependent" (*dravyāśrayī*), meaning it is dependent on substance (*dravyatantra*). It is "without qualities" (*aguṇavān*), that is, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). It is "not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions" (*saṃyogavibhāgeṣvakāraṇam*), meaning that while these [conjunctions and disjunctions] are to be produced, its causality is dependent [on other factors]. By this definition, those twenty-four qualities—such as color and so forth, which are well-known as distinct entities from substance due to specific cognitions such as "the cloth is white," "the mango is sweet," "musk is fragrant," and "water is cold"—are characterized.

And it has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "Color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognitions, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—these are the qualities" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6).

Thus, seventeen qualities are enumerated in this sūtra, while seven others—gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression, merit, demerit, and sound—are included by the word "and" (ca) [in the sūtra].

By this very [text], the qualities (*guṇa*) are stated: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—these seventeen are explicitly mentioned; and by the word "and" (*ca*), the seven others—gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound—are also included. In that regard, color-form (*rūpa*) is apprehended by the eye; it functions in earth, water, and fire (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

104). Taste (*rasa*) is apprehended by the gustatory faculty; it functions in earth and water (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 105). Odor (*gandha*) is apprehended by the olfactory faculty; it functions in earth.
Tactile sensation (*sparśa*) is that which is apprehended by the sense organ of touch; it resides in earth, water, fire, and air (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

106). Furthermore, these qualities—color, taste, smell, and tactile sensation—are impermanent in the atoms of earth because color and other qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise therein due to contact with fire. In the atoms of water, fire, and air, they are permanent as far as possible, because they do not arise there in any other manner. In the effect-substances composed of earth and so forth, they are impermanent. Taste is that which is apprehended by the sense organ of the tongue (Praśastapādabhāṣya).
The color, taste, smell, and touch belonging to earth and the other elements are non-eternal because their substances are non-eternal;
by this, their eternality in eternal [substances] is stated.
In the case of earth, those produced by heating (pākaja) are preceded by the qualities of their causes.

The process of the production of qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and others through baking (*pāka*) in the atoms of earth is as follows: when a raw substance such as a jar comes into contact with fire, actions arise in the atoms that constitute it, either due to the impact of the fire or its impulsion. From these actions arise disjunctions; from the disjunctions, the destruction of the [original] conjunctions; and from the destruction of the conjunctions, the effect-substance perishes. When that has perished, in the independent atoms, due to contact with fire and depending upon heat (*auṣṇya*), the destruction of the black color and other qualities occurs. Then, again, from another contact with fire and depending upon heat, the qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise.

Immediately thereafter, due to the conjunction of atoms with the self, which depends upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of sentient beings, action arises in those atoms in which qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) have been generated. From their mutual conjunction, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) is produced through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; and therein, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the succession of the qualities of the causes.
[Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 106] In water, fire, and air, these qualities are eternal because the substance itself is eternal.
In impermanent [substances], [qualities] are impermanent because of the impermanence of the substance; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.5.

Because there is no production [of number] from any other cause, number (saṃkhyā) is the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so forth; it is characterized by oneness and the like, and it resides in either a single substance or multiple substances.
In this regard, the number one resides in a single substance, whereas numbers such as duality and so forth reside in multiple substances;

and that [number one] is established through perception itself. Furthermore, because the cognition of specific [higher] numbers depends on other causes, the number one is also established there through inference.
Among eternal substances, the number one is eternal; among effect-substances, it is non-eternal.
Number, beginning with duality (dvitva) and ending with the highest unit (parārddha), is produced by relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) and is everywhere impermanent.
This number is the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so forth;
furthermore, it resides in either a single substance or multiple substances.
In that regard, for that [number] consisting of a single substance, its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of the color and other qualities of atoms of water and so forth.

But the number consisting of multiple substances—beginning with duality and ending with the highest possible count (parārddha)—is indeed produced from unities accompanied by a cognition of multiple objects; its destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi).

111: Dimension (parimāṇa) is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement; it is fourfold: large, small, long, and short.
Among these, the large is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.

Infinite magnitude (*paramamahattva*) is eternal in ether, time, space, and the self; it is non-eternal in substances such as dyads and triads, being twofold according to the distinction between eternal and non-eternal. Atomic dimension (*aṇu*) is eternal in the case of atoms and internal organs (*manas*), characterized by sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*); it is non-eternal only in the dyad.

However, even in the case of large objects such as the jujube (*badara*), the emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and the *bilva* fruit, the conventional usage of the term "minute" (*aṇu*) is figurative, in view of the absence of that [atomic] excellence.
In the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), shortness is non-eternal; in the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, length is non-eternal.

Now, it is incorrect to claim that there is no mutual distinction between the minuteness and shortness existing in the dyad, and the largeness and length existing in the triad and so forth; for there is a well-known distinction between largeness and length for every living being, based on the perception of a difference in conventional usage, such as: "Let the long be brought from among the large," and "Let the large be brought from among the long."
The distinction between atomicity (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), however, is perceptible only to yogis.

Furthermore, this dimension (*parimāṇa*), such as largeness (*mahat*) and so forth, is a distinct entity from color (*rūpa*) and other qualities, because it is apprehended by a cognition different from the cognition of those [other qualities], just like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.
Dimension is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement.

That [dimension] is of four kinds. Now, what is the mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) as they exist in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, and what is the distinction between minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)? In that regard, there is a mutual distinction between largeness and length, because we observe specific linguistic usage such as, "Let the long among the large be brought," and "Let the large among the long be brought. However, the distinction between minuteness and shortness is perceptible to one who perceives them; thus it is stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 130.

and the permanent is permanent.

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the attainment (*prāpti*) preceded by non-attainment; disjunction (*vibhāga*) is the non-attainment preceded by attainment.

Gravity (gurutva), which resides in earth and water and is the cause of the action of falling,
is eternal in the atoms of earth and water, but non-eternal in dyads (dvyaṇuka) and other composite substances.

Viscidity (sneha) exists only in water; it is the cause of the cognition of "smoothness."

Impression (*saṃskāra*) is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental disposition (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*).

Among these, that which is called velocity arises in corporeal substances—earth, water, fire, air, and mind—from motion dependent upon specific effort or impact; it is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction and is opposed by conjunction with tangible substances.

Furthermore, that which is called mental disposition is a quality of the self; it is born of cognition and is the cause of cognition, its existence being inferred from the effects of memory and recognition regarding objects seen, experienced, or heard.

The quality of elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) is a quality of corporeal substances (*mūrtimaddravya*). It is so called because it restores its own substratum—which is characterized by a dense arrangement of parts and has been displaced from its original state through effort—to its former position as it was before. This is observed, for instance, in the case of palm leaves and other materials that have been folded for a long time; when released, they return to their original state due to this *saṃskāra*. Likewise, its effect should be seen in bows, tree branches, garments, and so forth.
Furthermore, although this *saṃskāra* is of three kinds, it is exclusively non-eternal (*anitya*).
Both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are specific qualities of the self (*ātmaviśeṣaguṇa*), and they too are exclusively non-eternal.

Refutation of the category of quality (*guṇa*) and its enumeration as stated by the Vaiśeṣikas in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*:

Here, the following is refuted. First, as for what was stated—that "residing in a substance" (*dravyāśrayī*) and so forth is the definition of qualities—that is incorrect; because the "substance" (*dravya*) imagined by you has been refuted, it is impossible for them to reside in it.

Or, let it be granted that their definition consists in being dependent on those [substances] and so forth; nevertheless, the restriction that "there are only twenty-four qualities characterized by that definition" is untenable, because qualities are heard of in many ways. For in common worldly usage, qualities such as bravery, magnanimity, and the like are heard of in many ways;
furthermore, according to the grammarians' system, it is well known that the substantive is the substance (*dravya*) and the qualifier is the quality (*guṇa*).

Indeed, when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used in denoting that [quality], as stated in Pāṇini’s Mahābhāṣya (5.1.119).
Because of this statement,
in the medical system (vaidyakatantra), however, qualities such as clarity, stability, hardness, and sliminess are well known to possess the status of *guṇa* (quality).

Furthermore, since the Sāṃkhyas maintain that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* possess the status of *guṇas*, how can their number be determined? Moreover, you [the Vaiśeṣikas] accept that these qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, in a single composite whole like a jar, possess a partless and unitary nature; and if that were so, then when a jar or similar object is perceived through an aperture such as a keyhole, there would have to be a perception of the color and other qualities existing throughout the entire substance, both inside and out. Otherwise, the claim of a partless and unitary nature would be contradicted.

Indeed, it is not logical for that which possesses such a nature [to be subject] to the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by appearance and non-appearance, precisely because of their contradiction.

Likewise, if odor were manifested in the earth in some places through the sprinkling of water and so forth, there would have to be a manifestation of the odor belonging to the whole composite (avayavin) of the entire globe of the earth; otherwise, due to the superimposition of contradictory properties—namely, being manifested and not being manifested—there would be no single quality pervading the composite at all. However, regarding the production of color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*) from contact with fire, there is indeed no disagreement, as this is also accepted by us.

The claim that numbers such as duality and so forth arise from relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—as stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 211—is untenable. This is because those [numbers] are established by their own nature within objects, just like oneness; it is merely the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of them that is produced by relative cognition, not their essential form (*svarūpa*). This is just like the conventional usage of "large" and so forth in the case of jujube fruits (*badara*), myrobalans (*āmalaka*), and the like. For just as when jujube fruits and the like have arisen from their own collection of causes as endowed with properties such as largeness, the conventional usage of those [properties] arises from relative cognition, so it is here as well.

Furthermore, no authoritative person asserts that objects arise from enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); for if objects were produced by mere desire, it would follow that everything one intends would be accomplished.
Moreover, how could individual qualities appearing in a single cognition sometimes produce duality and sometimes plurality? For there is no distinction among them in their state of oneness.

Nor should it be asserted that two qualities, each possessing the quality of oneness, produce the number two, while many [qualities] produce the number plurality; for prior to the production of numbers such as duality, neither duality nor plurality can exist within those [qualities].

Furthermore, its status as a quality is not tenable, because it exists even in qualities themselves. Indeed, the existence of number in qualities is well-established through such common cognitions as "one cognition," "two cognitions," "twenty-four qualities," and "six categories";
nor is this cognition figurative, because it proceeds without faltering.
For "stumbling gait" (skhaladgatitva) is the defining characteristic of a figurative cognition, as in the case of the cognition of fire in a boy; that [is not correct], Ba., Ja., p. 273, l.
However, this cognition of "one" and so forth regarding jars arises from the mental attention to conventions established by desire, just as it occurs in the case of cognitions and the like. (639)
Because they lack substantiality, there is no differentiating number among them; therefore, it is not logical for the cognition of that [number] to be figurative, since it is unerring. 640

Furthermore, as for the fourfold dimension—large, small, long, and short—which has been set forth, that too is merely the play of no small ignorance; for since its distinction is impossible apart from specific configurations of objects, of what could it be described as a quality? If even those specific types were described as being of the nature of that [dimension], then by extension, circularity, triangularity, squareness, and so on would also have to be described as qualities, and thus the description of its fourfold nature (pṛ.

As for what was also stated—that the usage of the term "atom" (*aṇu*) regarding jujube fruits, myrobalans, and so forth is figurative (*bhākta*), and so on—that too is incorrect. For there is no one at all who perceives a figurative status in those cases. Indeed, unlike the case with a lion and a boy, where everyone perceives the distinction between the primary and the figurative without contradiction, there is no such perception of the distinction that "minuteness" (*aṇutva*) and "shortness" (*hrasvatva*) are primary only in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and figurative elsewhere.
Furthermore, since the demonstration of a mere theoretical framework is easily found in all treatises, the nature of specific entities cannot be established on this basis.
Furthermore, dimension (*parimāṇa*) is not a quality because it is relative; for relativity is never observed in the case of qualities such as color (*rūpa*) or pleasure (*sukha*).

Even the relative usage applied to "blue" and "bluer," or "pleasure" and "greater pleasure," is based on their intensity (*prakarsa*) and lack thereof (*apakarṣa*), and not on the essential nature of the quality itself.
(Page 274, Line 4)

As for what was stated—that separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause of the conventional usage of abstraction (*apoddhāra*)—that too is not tenable. For the conventional usage of abstraction is indeed the conventional usage of difference, and that is based upon the specific, inherent, and unique differentiating qualities (*bhedaka-dharma*) belonging to each object. What, then, is the point of postulating a further quality characterized as "separateness" in this regard? Otherwise, one would have to postulate another distinct quality called "non-separateness" as the cause of the conventional usage of non-difference, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. Furthermore, the process of "duality-of-separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so forth has already been refuted by the refutation of "duality" (*dvitva*) and other numbers. As for the postulation of "separateness" and the like as the basis for the usage of abstraction—[this is unnecessary].
Is it not considered that, because of its cause, that [consciousness] rests upon a distinct nature,
just as cognition, pleasure, and so forth are mutually distinct? (651)

according to the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (652).

Even conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not perceived as something distinct from objects situated in immediate proximity;
for it is objects transformed by such immediate proximity that come within the scope of the conventional usage of "conjoined.

Furthermore, if conjunction in the form of immediate proximity were a quality (*guṇa*), then proximity and distance would also necessarily be qualities, which would result in a contradiction regarding the enumeration of qualities.

Disjunction, too, is merely the absence of conjunction; it is not the production of a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*) in objects that have become disjoined. Furthermore, the cognition of "disjoined" is observed even in cases such as the Sahya and Vindhya mountains, which are devoid of the quality of disjunction, for that quality does not exist there, since it can only occur in objects characterized by prior conjunction, as stated [in the Praśastapādabhāṣya]: "Disjunction is non-attainment preceded by attainment" (p. 151).

Nor is this cognition figurative, because there is no lack of distinction [between the two types of cognition]; for no difference is perceived between the two cognitions, "two sheep are distinct" and "the Sahya and Vindhya mountains are distinct," since both are equally characterized by unimpeded occurrence. Indeed, when two objects are situated in a state of proximity such that one perceives them and another brings them together, they are of that nature by virtue of their genus (*jāti*).
Tattvasaṃgraha, Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 179a.
This twofold means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) should be stated accordingly even in the case of division, as in the *Sanmati-ṭīkā* (p. 679) and the *Syādvāda-ratnākara* (p. 931).
"And it is not logical for one [entity] to subsist in many; this is the subverting argument" (Tattvasaṃgraha 674).

The refutation of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) should also be understood to be similar to that of number (*saṃkhyā*), because they are alike in being produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

For it is sufficient that proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) alone serve as the causes for the notions of "prior" and "posterior"; there is no purpose whatsoever served by priority and posteriority themselves.

Furthermore, this conventional usage of "remote" (*para*), "proximate" (*apara*), and so forth, also exists in relation to existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and the like. If that [usage] is based solely on the intrinsic nature of things by virtue of convention, let it be the same elsewhere as well; what is the use of the effort to prove that even there it is based on the qualities of remoteness and proximity? Moreover, if this were the case, "mediateness" (*madhyatva*) would also have to be a quality, because we observe conventional usages of "middle" produced by time and space, just like the usages of "remote" and "proximate.
Just as colors such as blue and others are designated as such when established in a temporal sequence—even when distinct from other limiting conditions—so too are others [designated].

"Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to accept even 'middleness' [as a distinct category]," so says Bhūṣaṇa (Sanmati-ṭīkā p. 681; Syādvāda-ratnākara p. 935).

It is incorrect to say that gravity is to be inferred from falling; for even in the case of a lump of gold or similar objects resting in the palm of the hand, there is the cognition, "this is ten palas," or "this is five palas," even in the absence of falling.

Furthermore, what is called gravity is the power of a substance to fall, and powers are manifold for each individual substance with respect to their respective causal functions (*arthakriyā*); how could all those [powers] ever be numbered?

For the six causal powers (*kāraka-śakti*) of objects are indeed primary, and their various subdivisions are infinite; if these are not counted, what is the use of counting "heaviness" (*gurutva*)? Furthermore, if heaviness were a quality (*guṇa*), then lightness would also have to be a quality, as there is no distinction between them. If you argue that lightness is not a quality because it consists of the absence of heaviness, then why should heaviness not likewise be the absence of lightness? If you say, "But if heaviness were of the nature of an absence, there could be no gradation (*tāratamya*)," this is equally true for the other case as well.

Furthermore, the conventional usage of the term "heaviness" (gurutva) does not apply solely to that which performs the action of falling; for we observe the usage of the term in such cases as "my teacher" (*madīyo guruḥ*) with respect to one worthy of veneration, and "the syllable *ma* has three *gurus*" (*mastriguruḥ*) with respect to the properties of phonemes.

Moreover, if heaviness were a quality (*guṇa*), then—given the accepted principle that qualities in the effect are produced by qualities residing in the cause, just like color and so forth—heaviness produced in a cloth by the ten-pala measure of heaviness residing in the threads would have to be greater than the sum of its parts, just as [the size] is in the case of dimension (*parimāṇa*). Consequently, there would be a corresponding excess in the bending of the scale-pan, but this is not the case.
Even when a specific object situated upon the palm of the hand or elsewhere is not perceived to fall, [it is still an object of knowledge]. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
180, upper section; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 938).
The syllable *na* consists of a heavy syllable followed by three light syllables;
it is the eighth [meter] in prosody.
In the *mantriṇī* meter, there is a *magaṇa* (three heavy syllables) followed by a heavy syllable (*guru*);
in the *bhā* and *śra* [varieties], it is observed that the qualities of the effect are preceded by the qualities of the cause.

As for the claim that fluidity (*dravatva*) is the cause of the action of flowing—that too is nothing other than a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*).
For it has been stated that fluidity is simply a particular capacity for the production of that action, and capacities residing in objects cannot be exhaustively enumerated.
Furthermore, the assertion that it subsists in three substances is also incorrect, because it is absent in fire (*tejas*).

Furthermore, the fact that gold and other such substances are composed of fire (taijasa) is unproven; or, even if it were proven, the liquidity perceived therein must be purely earthy due to inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya), just like taste and other qualities.
Moreover, liquidity is not possible in all instances of earth, since it is absent in dry wood and the like. (Page 274, Line 18)

It is untenable to claim that liquidity exists even in earth and fire, as [stated] in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 180, first half. By this, the quality of viscidity (*sneha*) is also refuted; for it is not logical that it is something other than a specific capacity, nor is it a specific quality of water, because it is perceived in earthly substances such as clarified butter and oil, yet is not perceived in water, since no perception of viscidity is observed in a person who has bathed with pure water.
The quality of being a cause of cohesion is observed even in earthy substances such as lac and the like due to their inherent capacity;
furthermore, it is well known in the world and in medical treatises that even clarified butter and similar substances possess viscosity (*snigdhatva*). (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 180, top).

As for that threefold *saṃskāra* [possession, momentum, and elasticity], it too is untenable. Indeed, no quality called "momentum" (*vega*) distinct from the capacity of actions to arise in a continuous stream is perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is asked, "How then is the perception 'he goes with speed' not contradicted?"—the answer is: there is no contradiction in the perception "he goes with speed" provided there is a continuity of rapid actions.

Therefore, because of the cognition [of speed], if a quality called velocity (*vega*) were to exist, then even in such cases as "he understands the scripture with speed" or "the sixty-day rice is cooked with speed," there would have to be the existence of the quality of velocity;
and because of the cognition that "it comes by way of a series," the series (*santāna*) would also have to be a quality.
Furthermore, the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not anything other than the soul's capacity to produce memory.

By this, the *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) impression (*saṃskāra*) is also refuted; for it does not appear as anything other than the capacity to restore an object to its original state, nor does it invariably restore an object to its original state, since when a branch or similar object is being pulled, both its movement and its staying are observed with no fixed direction (p.

Nor is velocity (vega) a distinct entity from action, because the conventional usage of the term "velocity" is established merely for the rapid production of that [action]; see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p.
180, *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* p. 684.

it is stated that even merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) cannot be established as qualities of the self (*ātman*), because there is disagreement regarding them.

For in our own view, those two [dharma and adharma] belong to the person (pudgala); in the Sāṃkhya system, they are qualities of the intellect (buddhi); in the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine, that which is denoted by the word [dharma] is substance and so forth characterized by the capacity to be a means for attaining the highest good (śreyas); and in the Buddhist tenet, it is well known that action is merely a form of potency called "latent impression" (vāsanā) belonging to cognition itself. By this, sound also is refuted as being a quality of space (ākāśa), since there is no distinction among these conflicting views.

For instance: the Jains maintain that it consists of matter (*paudgalika*); the Mīmāṃsakas, that it is an eternal substance; the Śikṣākāras—a specific branch of the Mīmāṃsakas—that it is composed of air (*vāyavīya*); the Sautrāntikas, that it is of the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu-rūpa*); the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*), that its essence is *sphoṭa*; and the Sāṃkhyas, that it is a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti-pariṇāma*).
Thus, even the category of quality (*guṇa-padārtha*) as imagined by others does not hold up when examined.
By this, the category of action (*karman-padārtha*) is also refuted.
And that has been established on page 242;
for in the *Śāstradīpikā*, it is maintained that eternal phonemes (*varṇa*) possess the very nature of substance (*dravyatva*).
And likewise, the authors of the Śikṣā say: "The wind attains the state of sound"; this is not so.

They declare that for the *sphoṭa*, which is devoid of temporal divisions and conforms to the duration of the sounds (*dhvani*), there is a difference in its mode of manifestation due to the differences in the conditions of its apprehension (*vākyapadīya* 1).
Sound, which is included within the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), is a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); for this purpose, Sāṃkhyakārikā 24 should be consulted.
"The five actions are throwing upwards and so forth"—this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika.

But surely, since action is characterized by a definition distinct from that of quality, how can it be rejected by the rejection of the latter? For its definition is: "Action is that which inheres in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.16).

17. Thus, "subsisting in a single substance" (*ekadravyam*) means that it has a single substance as its substratum; "qualityless" (*aguṇam*) means that it does not possess qualities itself, nor is it a quality; and "independent" (*anapekṣam*) means that in performing conjunctions and disjunctions, it does not depend upon any other cause. Action (*karma*), characterized by these definitions, is of five kinds. And so says the Sūtra: "Throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion, and locomotion—these are the actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6).
1.7 Thus,
because of specific cognitions such as "the hand is raised," "the foot is cast down," "the palm is contracted," and "the finger is extended," [action] is a distinct entity from substance.

Among these, throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*) is that action which arises as the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with points in space above and below—such as when an action arises in a limb of the body or in an object like a pestle connected to it, being the cause of conjunction with objects such as space situated in the upward direction and the cause of disjunction from those situated in the downward direction, produced by the force of gravity, effort, and contact; whereas action that is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions in the reverse manner of what was described is throwing downward (*apakṣepaṇa*).

Action that causes the curvature of a straight substance is contraction (*ākuñcana*). For example, when there is disjunction of the distal parts—such as the fingers—of a straight substance like an arm from their respective points of conjunction with space and other entities, and there is conjunction with the proximal parts, that action by which the whole (*avayavin*) becomes curved is contraction.
Conversely, when conjunction and disjunction arise in the opposite manner, that action by which the whole becomes straight is expansion (*prasāraṇa*).
That which is the cause of conjunction and disjunction with objects such as jars in various directions is motion (*gamana*).
The fourfold types of action, beginning with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), have specific directions and locations as their causes;
for this very reason, there are only five kinds of action, since whirling (*bhramaṇa*), gliding (*syandana*), and emitting (*recana*) are included within "going" (*gamana*).

This means that [action] does not depend on any other entity that arises immediately after its own arising. Therefore, even when considering dependence on the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and dependence on the absence of prior conjunction (*pūrvasaṃyoga-abhāva*), the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

In the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*, following the refutation of the category of action (*karma*) as previously described, it is established that action is a modification consisting of motion (*parispanda*), which is the cause for an object’s transition from one location to another. To this, we offer the following rebuttal:

First, regarding the definition of action stated as "residing in a single substance" and so forth—that is incorrect. For, since the "substance" (*dravya*) postulated by you has been refuted, it is impossible for that [definition] to be a valid characteristic of such a thing.

Or, let us grant that such a substance exists; nevertheless, would this substrate of action (*karman*) have the nature of a mover (*gantṛ*), the nature of a non-mover (*agantṛ*), both forms, or neither form? If it has the nature of a mover, then the postulation of an action distinct from it is redundant. Moreover, if one were to postulate such an action even for that which already possesses that nature, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, does it always possess that nature, or only at certain times? In the first case, it could never remain stationary, because it would always have the nature of a mover, like the wind.

Now, suppose at some time [the atom changes state]. In that case, it follows that it would first have the nature of a non-mover and subsequently the nature of a mover. And in this regard, would it assume the nature of a mover by abandoning its prior nature of being a non-mover, or without abandoning it? If it were by abandoning it, then the substance, such as an atom, would fall into the state of impermanence, because impermanence is characterized by the loss of one's own nature (*svabhāva*).

If, on the other hand, it were without abandoning it, that is not tenable; for it is impossible for that which has not abandoned its nature of being a non-mover to possess the nature of being a mover, just like the Himalayas and so forth.

Therefore, it is not tenable for a substance such as an atom (*aṇu*) that has the nature of a mover to be the locus of action, nor is it tenable for one that has the nature of a non-mover; for, like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, it is contradictory for such a thing to be the locus of that [action]. Furthermore, if that which previously had the nature of a non-mover were to possess the nature of a mover at a later time, then the aforementioned fault would follow regarding its being the locus of that [action] (p. 279, l.
If that [goer] were by nature of the form of going and so forth, then going and so forth would always exist; it could not remain motionless for even a single moment.

Nor can it be of the nature of both; for that would entail the defects inherent in both positions. Furthermore, does this nature of being both exist simultaneously or successively? It cannot be simultaneous, because the natures of being a goer and not being a goer are dependent upon different times. There is no simultaneous existence of two things whose dependence on time is distinct, just as there is no simultaneity between the natures of a finger being extended and its being otherwise. And these two natures are indeed dependent upon those respective times.

If that state were to occur simultaneously, then because of the superimposition of contradictory properties upon the atom and so forth, there would follow a distinction [between them], which would contradict their unitary nature. If one accepts that it occurs sequentially, then upon the production of the form of the goer—whether by abandoning or not abandoning the non-going form—there follows the attachment of all the aforementioned defects. Furthermore, a state consisting of neither is not tenable due to contradiction, since when one of two properties—a positive affirmation and a negation—is negated, the affirmation of the other necessarily follows.
Therefore, since action is logically impossible in an entity that possesses a single, uniform nature in every respect, the category of "action" cannot be established for others;
for if it were to exist, this [agent] would at one time be of one form and then again otherwise.
From the connection with natures that are distinct from one another, there would be distinctness. (Tattvasaṃgraha 703)

Or let that [motion] exist; nevertheless, since it is sufficient to define action merely as "the transformation consisting of a revolution (parispanda) of an object which is the cause for its reaching another location from one location," the description of it as being of five types is not tenable. This is because upward throwing (utkṣepaṇa) and the others are already included herein.

Furthermore, if one were to designate even those things included herein as distinct by taking some particularity into account, then whirling (bhramaṇa), scattering (recana), and so forth would also have to be designated separately from this; how then could it be restricted to exactly five types?

An alternative state (*paryāya*) arising by virtue of both types of causes is "action" (*kriyā*), which is the cause for a substance’s attainment of another location; this is established in the *Sarvārthasiddhi* (5.7).
Furthermore (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.

183, l. 1): Moreover, does the distinction between actions such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth depend upon their own nature (*svarūpa*), or upon their genus (*jāti*)? If it depends upon their own nature—is it dependent upon the nature alone, or upon a qualified nature? It cannot depend upon the nature alone; for that alone is indistinguishable across all instances.

If even what is indistinguishable were to function as a differentiator, it would follow that even a single individual instance would be a differentiator, and consequently, the conventional usage of "oneness" would never occur anywhere.

If [the difference between actions] is based on a specific nature (*viśiṣṭasvarūpa*), by what is that specificity produced? If you say it is produced by the universal (*jāti*), then it follows that the distinction between those actions is based on the universal. In that case, would the universal of "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth produce the distinction of that action while being manifested (*abhivyakta*) or unmanifested (*anabhivyakta*)? It cannot be the unmanifested, because that would entail the consequence that it would manifest that distinction everywhere and at all times.

If it is argued that [the universal] is manifested, from what does its manifestation arise—from a particularity of action (*karmabheda*) belonging to that [individual], or from something else? It cannot be from something else; for if things of a different class were the manifestors, it would follow that the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is manifested by white horses (*karka*) and the like. Nor can a particularity of action be the manifestor, because that would involve a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): the difference of those actions is established only when the manifestation of the universals is established, and the establishment of the manifestation of the universals depends upon the establishment of the difference of those actions.

Furthermore, is it the moment of that action (*tatkarmakṣaṇa*) which manifests these [universals], or their collection (*tatsamudāya*)? It cannot be the moment of that action; for the mere moment of that action produced in the first instant is difficult to perceive, and thus it is incapable of manifesting universals such as "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇatva*). Indeed, an action existing for only a single moment—whether "throwing upwards" or "throwing downwards"—is not perceived by people like us, whereby a distinction between those universals could be manifested from it. Because of its extreme subtlety, that [momentary action] is perceptible only to yogins.
Nor is their collection (*samudāya*) the manifestor [of the universal], because since actions are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), a collection is simply impossible.
It is also incorrect to say that such a collection exists as a mental construction (*buddhiparikalpita*); for a conceptual entity lacks the capacity for real causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, it is non-existent because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it, whether it be identical to or different from the object itself in every respect.

Whatever is not cognized by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being entirely distinct from its object should not be accepted as such, just as the intrinsic existence of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth [is not accepted]. And since action (*karman*) is not cognized by any means of valid cognition as being entirely distinct from its object, therefore action—possessing the aforementioned nature alone—must be understood by those skilled in discernment as having ascended to the peak of the mountain of direct experience.
[It may be] either a momentary instance of action (*karmakṣaṇa*) that manifests the genus (*jāti*) such as "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇatva*), or the collection thereof. (Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 950)
In every way, there is the grasping of a different object (*arthāntara*)—that is, the grasping of an object that is distinct [from the self].
*grā-*, Ja; *cārthagrahaṇasya*, Bhā; *śra-*, Śrā; *-thārthānta-*, Ā.
The refutation of the view of the Bhūṣaṇakāra that activity itself is karma:

Now, another [opponent] argues: "Indeed, no action whatsoever is perceived apart from the conjunctions and disjunctions of composite substances with light and so forth. For 'upward throwing' (*utkṣepaṇa*) is merely defined as a series of conjunctions and disjunctions with composite substances such as light in the upper regions; the same should be said for 'downward throwing' (*apakṣepaṇa*) and the rest. This too is unauthoritative, because it denies what is actually perceived. For conjunction and disjunction do not serve as the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the perception "it moves," since those two are the objects of the cognitions "conjoined" and "disjoined. Since a cognition proceeds without error according to its object, otherwise even the cognition of a cloth would have a jar as its objective basis.

Furthermore, if this [notion of motion] had conjunction and disjunction as its objective basis, then the cognition "it moves" would arise even while it is stationary; but such is not the case. Indeed, when a post standing in the middle of a river undergoes conjunctions and disjunctions due to the flow of water or a hawk, no one—even in a dream—has the perception that "the post moves.
Moreover, because a continuous series of conjunctions and disjunctions is observed [in both cases], there would likewise be the perception that the ground moves, just as Devadatta does.

For since there is no difference in the occurrence [of conjunction and disjunction] in both [the person and the ground], it is not reasonable to establish a restriction—without basis—that the cognition of them occurs only with respect to Devadatta and not with respect to the ground, as that would entail the consequence of arbitrary behavior. Now, if it is argued that those two are produced by the action of Devadatta alone and not by the action of the ground, and therefore they produce the cognition of them only there and not on the ground—if this is so, then since the cognition conforms to the presence and absence of the action, it is established that its objective support is indeed the action itself; this is the ornament [of our position].

Furthermore, according to the *Bhūṣaṇa* school and others, since action (*karman*) is a quality (*guṇa*), there is no entity distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as asserted by the author of the *Nyāyalīlāvatī* (p. 94); such is the view of the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*.
"Action is indeed conjunction," according to the view of the *Bhūṣaṇa*, as cited in Muktāvalī (p. 40), Siddhāntamuktāvalī (p. 40), Nyāyakusumāñjali (p.
206), and Tarkabhāṣā-prakāśikā (p. 206).
Furthermore, even when the conjunctions and disjunctions [of a bird] are not perceived, the cognition "the bird moving while traversing the supportless sky" is nonetheless experienced;

for the conjunction between the sky and [the bird] is not perceptible to people like us, because it resides in a substance other than those [objects] that are perceptible, just like the conjunction between the wind and a tree.

Now, it may be argued that space is a pervasive whole consisting of light-particles (*ālokāvayavin*), and therefore its conjunction with a bird is indeed perceptible to people like us; however, this too is unsatisfactory. For it would lead to the absurd consequence that there would be no cognition such as "a firefly moves in the darkness," since no whole consisting of light exists there, which could serve as the basis for grasping the conjunctions and disjunctions [of the firefly] that would produce such a cognition. Furthermore, according to your own view, there is no real entity whatsoever characterized as "darkness," because you admit that darkness is merely the absence of light.
When an earthquake occurs, the cognition "the earth moves" is observed; however, in that case, conjunction and disjunction caused by the earthquake are not perceived.
Therefore, the cognition "it moves" does not have conjunction and so forth as its objective basis; rather, it has action alone as its objective basis.
[Furthermore,] darkness is non-existence, because it possesses characteristics different from those of substances, qualities, and actions.
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.19
However, regarding the absence of light in the *Kandalī*, there is a variant reading of the sūtra on page 10;
therefore, this is a specific kind of form [of darkness], which is the superimposition of darkness everywhere when there is an absolute absence of light—
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, page 9.
The Jains, however, maintain that darkness is the cause of the obstruction of vision and is composed of matter (*paudgalika*), as stated in *Sarvārthasiddhi* 5.24.
The Bhāṭṭas and Vedāntins declare that darkness (*tamas*) is a substance (*dravya*); some followers of the Prabhākara school maintain that it is the absence of light and cognition;

and the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), however, [hold that] due to the omnipotence of the atoms, it functions as both difference (*bheda*) and conjunction (*saṃsarga*). (Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, Aulukya-darśana, p. 229)
Shadow, heat, and darkness undergo transformation through the state of sound.
(Vākyapadīya, Part 1, Verse 111)

Furthermore, would these two—conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*)—be causeless or possessed of a cause? If they were causeless, they would either always exist or never exist at all. If they were possessed of a cause, what would that cause be: the mere nature of the substance itself, or a specific transformation (*pariṇāma*) thereof? In the first case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even in a stable object, conjunctions and disjunctions with various other locations or constituent parts would arise, because the mere nature of that object remains unchanged therein.

If, however, [the movement] has a specific transformation (*viśiṣṭapariṇāma*) as its cause, there is merely a difference in name, because it is simply action (*karman*) itself that is designated by the term "that transformation. This is because, apart from that [action], a specific transformation of entities—which serves as the cause for conjunctions and disjunctions of further and further spatial points or constituent parts—is impossible.

Therefore, action is a distinct entity from conjunction and disjunction, as well as from Devadatta and so forth, because it is apprehended by a different cognition, just like a pot and a cloth. Nor is this unproven; for conjunction and disjunction are perceived as being established in two separate cognitions, whereas action is established in a single cognition.

Likewise, Devadatta is cognized by the notion "Devadatta" in both his moving and stationary states, whereas action, however, is cognized by the notion "it moves" only in the moving state; therefore, it is distinct from him. This is because the determination of difference everywhere is based on a difference in cognition.

[Objection: Since objects last for only a single moment, it is impossible for them to reach another location from one location; thus, even this definition of action is untenable. [Reply: This too is a mere fantasy, because the momentariness of objects will be refuted later.
Therefore, even the category of "action" (karman) as postulated by others does not hold up under scrutiny,
nor does the category of "universality" (sāmānya); for when its very nature is examined, it is found to be untenable,
since actions such as upward throwing and the like are impossible within entities that are momentary.
Because in the place of birth, there is no possibility of attaining anything other than death itself. (Tattvasaṃgraha 692)

The Vaiśeṣika’s prima facie argument is as follows: "Generality (*sāmānya*) is an entity distinct from substance and the other categories, and it is of two kinds, namely the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). Now, generality is that which serves as the cause for a non-sublated, inclusive cognition that is not occasioned by substance, quality, or action. How can this, when examined, be found to be untenable? For its nature will be established as being within the range of perception and other means of knowledge. And generality, possessing such a nature, is twofold: the higher and the lower."

Among these, the highest is that which has a vast scope and is called "Existence" (*sattā*); because it is the sole cause of the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) regarding all substances, qualities, and actions, it is a universal (*sāmānya*) alone and not a particular (*viśeṣa*).

However, the other [universals], characterized by "substance-ness," "quality-ness," "action-ness," and so forth, are called universals because they are the causes of inclusive cognition within their own substrates; yet, since they are also the causes of exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛttapratyaya*) of their substrates from those of different classes, they are designated as "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) even while being universals.

For instance, regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, when this differentiated cognition arises—such as "it is not a substance" or "it is without qualities"—these very factors, namely substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and so on, are perceived as the causes of that cognition, and nothing else.

Nor should it be argued that the status of being both a universal (*sāmānya*) and a particular (*viśeṣa*) for a single entity is contradictory; for there is no contradiction in their status as such, given the difference in perspective (*apekṣābheda*).

And regarding its existence, perception itself is the proof; for this single, recurring [universal] distinct from individual cows and the like appears in the recurring cognition produced by the senses, such as "cow, cow," and so forth.

This [cognition] is not possible without an object consisting of a recurring, unitary form, because otherwise there would follow the consequence of either its eternal existence or non-existence due to being causeless, or else the consequence of its application [of the term] everywhere else, since there would be no restrictive factor, just as in the case of [individuals like] Khaṇḍa and others.

Nor should it be argued that this fault does not arise because [the universal] has individuals as its objective support; for since individuals possess distinct forms, they cannot logically serve as the objective support for a single, recurring cognition of a uniform form.
If a cognition of one form were to have another thing as its objective support, there would be no confidence in anything anywhere, and thus no determination of any specific object would be possible.
That from which [the notion] "existent" arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions is *sattā* (existence).
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.7
—Substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness are universals and also particulars; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.4. Commentary: [These exist] even in the substratum. Ānandagiri.
And because that [exclusion] is also a cause, it is a universal (sāmānya) while simultaneously receiving the designation of a particular (viśeṣa).
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 11,
312 – *vṛtti-pra* – *Śrāmaṇya* – *vṛttatva-bu* – *Śrāmaṇya*.
—Not so—ba, ja.

Likewise, inference also operates as a means of making known its existence; for instance: the specific cognitions and designations of "cow," "horse," "buffalo," "boar," and so forth, occurring in relation to cows and the like, must be based on other causes that are related to their own nature and distinct from the convention (*samaya*), the form (*ākṛti*), and the individual body (*piṇḍa*). This is because, while having cows and the like as their objects, they are specific cognitions and designations distinct from the cognitions and designations of the individual bodies and so forth—just as, in those very same cows and others, the specific cognitions and designations such as "the cow with her calf," "the buffalo burdened by a load," "the boar with a thorn," or "the elephant with a goad" arise from the occurrence of other causes. Furthermore, those which do not have other causes distinct from the nature of the individual body and so forth are not specific cognitions and designations distinct from that [body], just like the cognitions of the individual body itself.

Likewise: whatever cognition is distinct from the form of an object must be based on another cause distinct from that object, just as the cognition of "red" and so forth regarding cloth and other things; and such is this cognition of "cow" and so forth regarding individual bodies (piṇḍa) and the like.
Therefore, the inclusive cognition regarding cows and the like is based on a cause distinct from the individual bodies, because it is a qualified cognition, like the cognition of "blue" and so forth.
Thus, "cowness" (gotva) is an entity different from the individual cow-body, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, like color, touch, and so forth.
Cowness (*gotva*) is a distinct entity from the individual substance (*piṇḍa*), because it is designated as "of that" (*tasya*), just like "the horse of Caitra.

Furthermore, the recurring designation and cognition "cow, cow" are based upon a recurring real entity, because—while being distinct from designations and cognitions of absences or universals—they are recurring designations and cognitions, just like the recurring designations and cognitions "blue, blue" in leather, cloth, and so forth due to their connection with the substance indigo;
by such inference, that [universal] appears as a distinct entity from substance and the other categories.

Regarding this, Bhāvivikta said: "The specific cognitions produced by words such as 'cow' and so forth, with respect to cows, elephants, and so on, have as their cause an object distinct from convention, configuration, the individual substance, and so forth. (716)

For when they have as their object cows and the like, that [cognition] is distinct from the word and the cognition of those [objects], just as in these very cases there are the cognitions and sounds of "with calf" and "with goad. (717)

The qualification [of the subject] and the statement of its essential nature are for the purpose of avoiding deviation through cognitions such as that of a rabbit's horn; this constitutes the example by way of dissimilarity. (718)
In the form of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *Tattvasaṃgraha* states: because it is a specific cognition that expresses the essential nature [of the object],

and because, while having cows and so forth as its objects, it is a cognition expressing a name that is distinct from the cognition that expresses the essential nature of the individual body (*piṇḍa*) and so forth.
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 238:

Just as there is a recurrence of the cognition "blue, blue" with respect to mutually distinct things such as skins, garments, and blankets due to their connection with the substance indigo, so too there is a recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent" with respect to mutually distinct substances, qualities, and actions; and that [recurrence] must arise from something other than [the objects themselves]. *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, pp. 311–12.

That cognition of recurrence observed among cows and the like—which is distinct from the forms of the individual objects—arises from a mark (liṅga) distinct from the individuals, because it possesses a specific characteristic, just like the cognition of blue and so forth. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 238)
Nyāyavārttika 2.2.70
Cowness is distinct from the individual cow, because it is the object of a different cognition, just like the cognitions of color and touch;
thus says the *Nyāyavārttika* (2.2).
Cowness is a different entity from the cow, because it is the object of the term used for designation, like Caitra’s horse;
*Nyāyavārttika* 2.1.34.
The cognitions of the recurrence of "cow" in various individual cows have distinct causes, because they possess particularity, like the cognitions of color and so forth.
Nyāyavārttika 2.2.70
— And because it is primarily concerned with refutation (pratiṣedha)—

[the author] establishes, in the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*), that the universal (*sāmānya*) as described by the Vaiśeṣikas— which is eternal, partless, unitary, and so forth— is in fact of the nature of a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*), preceded by its refutation.
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that [the universal] has substance, quality, and action as its cause, and so forth—that is incorrect. Since substance and the rest as conceived by you have been refuted by the aforementioned method, it is impossible for the universal, which is dependent upon them, to be the cause of the inclusive cognition (anugata-jñāna) regarding them;
for things that are dependent cannot exist anywhere in the absence of a substratum.

Alternatively, if causal efficiency (*kāryakāritva*) were observed [in the universal], it would entail the consequence that it is non-dependent (*anāśrita*). Furthermore, what is the meaning of the statement that [the universal] is the cause of inclusive cognition (*anugatajñāna*)? Does "the cause of inclusive cognition" mean the cause of an inclusive cognition, or does it mean that being inclusive, it is the cause of cognition? In the first case, by what is the inclusion (*anugama*) in the cognition produced—is it produced by its own nature (*svarūpa*), or by a universal (*sāmānya*)? It cannot be produced by its own nature, because otherwise there would be the consequence of objects themselves being inclusive by their very nature, which would lead to the uselessness of postulating a universal.

Now, if [the universal] were produced by the universal itself, then the persistence of cognition would indeed follow from what appears [in it], and not otherwise; in that case, the position that the persisting [universal] is the cause of cognition would be accepted.

In that regard, what constitutes its "concomitance" (*anugatatva*)? Is it the state of being a substratum possessing a nature common to both cognition and the object; or is it the state of existing in multiple locations through a distinct mode of subsistence while remaining eternal and unitary? In the first alternative, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), for although conjunction is concomitant by virtue of having a nature common to both cognition and the object, it lacks the character of a universal (*sāmānya*).

It is not unestablished that by the very same nature through which it is the object of its own cognition, it exists in its own relatum; for, like a universal (*sāmānya*), this [particular] also lacks a difference in nature due to being partless.

As for the second position, however, it is untenable; for even now, the eternal unity of the universal and its existence in multiple locations through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*) remain unproven (p. 283, l.

*Anugatapratyaya*: It is a "conforming cognition" (*anugata-pratyaya*) because it is both conforming (*anugata*) and a cognition (*pratyaya*); or alternatively, it is a cognition regarding a conforming object (*vastu*). (Syādvādamañjarī, p.

For instance, what is this "universal" (sāmānya)? Is it the cause of a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*), or is it that which is established by a recurring cognition as its means of proof? Or is it merely recurrence itself? Or is it recurrence while being eternal? Or is it the state of being eternal, unitary, and inherent in many?
(Citsukhī, p. 190) [Note: *bhāsasyā* in the manuscript is corrected to *bhāsasya*].
By means of that knowledge—ba, ja;
knowledge—ba, ja, śra;
at the time of [attaining]—ba, ja.

—Furthermore, as for what was stated—"And when that [universal] exists, it is indeed perception," and so forth; in that regard, would the perception that determines the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) or conceptual (*savikalpaka*)? It cannot be the non-conceptual, because, being devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it lacks the capacity to reflect upon a recurring entity through the verbal articulation "cow, cow," and so on.

Or, if it were a reality, it would not appear there with the nature previously described—devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables, and possessing an eternal, unitary, and all-pervading essence; for that would entail the consequence of there being no disagreement [regarding it].
Indeed, no one disputes an object when it appears in its own essential form, just as in the case of a particular (*vyakti*).

Nor is it conceptual (*savikalpaka*); since conceptual cognition follows upon non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), it operates only upon an object already apprehended by that [non-conceptual] perception.

And it has been stated that the universal is not apprehended by non-conceptual [perception]; or, if it were apprehended, its lack of validity would be even more extreme due to its grasping what has already been grasped (pṛ.
283, l. 27). In that case, would its apprehension arise from non-conceptual [perception] or from conceptual [perception]?
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
141, u.; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 958:

What is this inclusive cognition (*anugatapratyaya*)? Is it "This cow is that cow," or rather, "This is a cow, and this too is a cow"? The first alternative is untenable; for when a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and a black cow (*bāhuleya*) appear [to the senses], there is no appearance such as "That which is this cow is precisely this cow," because that would entail their identity (*aikya*).

The second alternative, however, is logical; for by the word "this," one refers to a particular such as a *śābaleya* cow which is distinct from others, and by the word "cow," one refers to a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*).

Indeed, it is from its own causes alone that such a form arises which produces a cognition of that kind; there is no universal (sāmānya) existing as a distinct entity with an eternal nature or the like, for if it were so, it would follow that the universal would be perceived even when it is not perceived [in the individual]. For just as a cloth, being distinct from a jar, is perceived even when the jar is not perceived, so too the universal—being distinct from the particular (viśeṣa)—would be perceived even when the particular is not perceived. But since it is not perceived when that [particular] is not perceived, it is therefore not distinct from it.

Is it that "this cow is indeed that very same [cow]," or "is this also a cow? This also is a cow"? Or rather, is it by way of a generality, as in "a cow is a cow"? (Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 952). Indeed, Ā., Ba., Ja. [so read].
— Even in the case of grasping, it is grasped [by] Ārya; [in the sense of] reality, [it is grasped by] Bhāva and Ja.

Now, if it is argued that because they [the individuals] are the manifestors of that [the universal], there is no appearance of it apart from them, then their own appearance should occur first, just as in the case of a lamp or similar objects. But this is not so, because it is accepted that the universal is grasped first and the individual later; furthermore, this would entail a contradiction with the principle that "there can be no cognition of a qualified object (viśeṣya) without the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) having been grasped. Moreover, this reversal [of the order of appearance] refutes the relationship of manifested and manifester between these two; for if the individual were the manifester, then even an individual of a different class would be a manifester, since there is no difference in their status as individuals.

Nor should it be asserted that the manifestor is merely its own individual manifestation (*svavyakti*), because as long as the universal (*sāmānya*) is not established, its own manifestation cannot even be defined. Or, let it be granted that it is indeed its own manifestation; even so, how can there be unity for it if it exists in the form of both the manifestation and that which is other than it?
