Furthermore, if individual instances such as the "broken-horned" cow (*khaṇḍādi*) are its manifestors by virtue of possessing a nature identical to the power of producing it, then the purpose of the universal is accomplished by those alone; what, then, is the use of this [universal] which merely presents what is already established? Moreover, a qualified cognition is desired here, and it does not occur when the qualifier is unknown.
88th verse of the Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda section:
[The view that] the apprehension of the universal— which is the manifested (vyaṅgya)— occurs even prior to the manifestation (vyakti) which serves as its manifestor (vyañjaka).

Furthermore, does the individual manifesting [the universal] do so by performing a service (*upakāra*) for the universal, or without performing one? If it does perform one: what kind of service is rendered to it by this [individual]? Is it the capacity for the production of its cognition, or the cognition itself? If it is the capacity for that [cognition], is that capacity established as distinct from [the universal] or non-distinct? If it is distinct, then by producing that [capacity], nothing at all would have been done to the universal; thus, its non-manifestation would remain as it was.
If, on the other hand, it is non-distinct, then by producing that [capacity], the universal itself would be produced; and in that case, it would follow that the universal is impermanent.

If that [cognition] is knowledge, how can the universal be established from this? For the inclusive cognition arises from the individuals alone. To claim that "this [universal] also functions here with their assistance" is mere faith; for if, in the production of the inclusive cognition, the universal were perceived as functioning while accompanied by the individuals—just as a potter equipped with a staff and other tools is perceived in the production of a jar—then this might be so. But since that is not perceived, how could this [universal] have a function there even with their assistance? Furthermore, if something that performs no action were a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), then it would follow that even an individual of a different class would be a manifestor.
It would follow that the universal is produced by the individual, because it performs an assistance that is non-different from it (the universal).
(*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 139; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 138, upper section).

[Objection: "If a single, pervasive universal (*sāmānya*) is not admitted for individuals (*vyakti*), then how could there be a pervasive cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*) and the application of a single word (*abhinna-śabda-niveśa*) with respect to them? For such [a cognition and application] is not observed in the case of jars, cloths, and so forth, which possess distinct natures. [Response: This too is not well-founded. Even in the absence of a [higher-order] universal among universals, we observe a pervasive cognition—such as "universal, universal"—and the application of a single word.
Furthermore, that which occurs even in the absence of something else cannot be caused by that thing, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, [you argue that] this [cognition of "cow"] regarding universals is based on inherence (*samavāya*). Why is this so? If you say it is because no further universal is perceived therein, then what further universal is perceived in the case of individual cows (*khaṇḍa*) and the like? If that [universal] is perceived precisely from that cognition, then let it be perceived in the case of universals as well.

Furthermore, if inherence is the cause here, then let that very same thing be the cause for the inclusive cognition regarding individual cows and the like; enough with the postulation of a [separate] universal.

For just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) inheres in individuals such as the spotted cow (*khaṇḍā*) by means of that very same inherence relation by which the universal "horseness" (*aśvatva*) inheres in individuals such as the white horse (*karka*), so too, due to this single inherence relation, there would arise a cognition of a universal among universals. Likewise, since the individual spotted cow (*khaṇḍa*) exists in its own parts by means of that very same inherence relation by which the bald cow (*muṇḍa*) and others also exist, the cognition "cow, cow" would likewise be based solely on inherence. How then [could this be avoided]?—[they reply]—in the case of the spotted cow... [text fragment].

Furthermore, does it [the universal] itself serve as the cause for those respective cognitions when [individuals] are similar, or when they are dissimilar? In the first case, since that [cognition] arises from that very [universal], the universal would be established as being present [only] in similar instances;

however, if it were to produce that [cognition] even in dissimilar cases, then the cognition of "cow" would arise even with respect to a white horse (*karka*) and the like, because it [the universal] is all-pervading and its inherence (*samavāya*) exists everywhere.

Furthermore, the state of being common among similar things is "generality" (*sāmānya*). And is this similarity of theirs due to a connection with a generality, or from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? In that regard, the first alternative is untenable; for by this [connection] other things do not become similar; rather, those possessing it would be so by virtue of their own nature.
If it is from their own nature, then they will produce such a cognition from that very [nature]; therefore, enough with the postulation of a generality.

Moreover, if this [cognition] were based on that [generality], it would occur even upon the perception of a single individual instance for the first time, since there is no difference in its connection with the sense organ, just as there is in the case of the individual itself.

Now, if the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals is also part of its causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then it would not appear in the manifestation of the first individual; how, then, could this conceptual cognition (*savikalpapratyaya*), which consists of synthesis (*anusandhāna*), arise, since it does not function with respect to an object that has not been apprehended? — [The opponent replies: "Not so...
[The text continues with the refutation].
Furthermore, is this universal distinct from the individuals or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then, like them, it would follow that it is subject to arising and destruction.
If it is distinct, does it arise when the individual arises or not? If it arises, then, like the individual, it would be impermanent.
If it does not arise, does it exist in the location where the individual arises or not? If it exists there, it should be perceived even before the individual has arisen.

The claim that "because [the universal] depends on the individual, it cannot be perceived in its absence" is also incorrect; for the relationship between locus and located can only exist when there is a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, as in the case of a bowl and jujube fruits.

Indeed, because the jujube fruits possess weight and would fall downward, the bowl serves as their support by performing the function of obstructing that fall. However, since the universal is inactive and lacks falling, no support is possible for it. Thus, because it does not depend [on anything], it should be perceived both before and after [the individual];
or, if it were dependent, it would cease to exist in the absence of its support, just like color and other such qualities.

Now, if that [universal] is not present in that location [where the individual has arisen], but rather comes from another individual upon the arising of a particular individual—surely, as it comes from there, does it come having abandoned its previous individual, or not? In the first case, it follows that the former individual would be devoid of it. If, on the other hand, it does not abandon it; even then, does it come together with the individual itself, or does it remain in that very place with one part while coming with another part? In the first alternative, there would be the cognition "this is a *bāhuleya* (a brindled cow)" even regarding a *śābaleya* (a spotted cow).

The second alternative, however, is untenable; for since it is partless (*niraṃśa*), its occurrence as something possessing parts is impossible. For when something lacks the basis for its occurrence in a certain place, it does not occur there—just as a single atom does not exist in both the Sahya and Vindhya mountains. And since the universal lacks "parts" (*aṃśa*) as the basis for its simultaneous occurrence in individuals located in different places, if it were to possess parts, it would follow that it is non-eternal, just like the individual (*vyakti*), because [the universal] would arise [along with] the arising of the individual. (Bhāṣya on *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* 1.2.18)

For they do not arise together with it because of its eternality, nor do they abide there [previously], since they were not all-pervasive; nor do they come from elsewhere, as they are devoid of action. (807)
The *Tattvasaṃgraha* is cited in the *Āloka*— from the beginning of the *Saṃgraha*.
Because of that connection,
there is no obstruction to its movement either; since it is inactive like a jujube fruit and so forth, it possesses no motion, and therefore no substratum is postulated for it.
Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, Ratnākaraśānti’s commentary, page 963.

It does not go into the substratum, nor was it there before, nor does it exist there afterwards; nor does it leave its former substrate like something with parts— alas, what a succession of calamities!
Pramāṇavārttika 1.155; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 138, section U.
In the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, page 691,
and the *Syādvāda-ratnākara*, page 955, it says "vibhi" (variants).

If it is argued that because it is omnipresent, its existence is simultaneous everywhere—whether this "omnipresence" means being present in all things or being present in all its own individual manifestations (svavyakti)—then, if it were omnipresent in all things, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving "cowness" in the space between individual cows, in a white horse (*karka*), and so forth; for this [universal], being visible, would exist everywhere without distinction. If it is argued that it is perceived only where its own manifestations act as its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), that too has already been answered by the refutation of these [individuals] acting as manifestors.

Even if it were omnipresent within its own manifestations, does it exist in each manifestation in its entirety or by way of a single part? If it existed in its entirety, all manifestations would become one, or else the universal itself would possess multiplicity like the manifestations. Furthermore, existence by way of parts has already been refuted. Therefore, since a universal characterized as eternal and so forth is untenable within individual objects due to these dilemmas regarding its mode of existence and other factors, it does not exist.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever, being capable of being perceived, is not perceived in a certain place, does not exist there—just as a jar does not exist in a certain location. And the universal (*sāmānya*) postulated by others is not perceived in individual entities (*piṇḍa*), even though the conditions for sensory contact are present.
Therefore, it is not logical that the universal has a nature entirely distinct from the individuals, nor does it have a dual nature; for this would entail the defects inherent in both positions.
Therefore, perception does not establish the existence of a universal;
for it would have to be either omnipresent in all things or present only in individual objects.
If it were omnipresent in all things, then even a white horse (*karka*) would possess the nature of a cow.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 299, in the form of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*);
likewise, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 138a: "Is that [universal] omnipresent in all [things], or is it omnipresent only in its own manifestations?"

For a universal cannot be one while residing in the individuals that serve as its substrata, because it would follow that it would be perceived even in the intervals between those individuals; see *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 108; *Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 345.1. *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.

The immeasurable is indeed unattached and immeasurable; even in the case of differentiation, because of the existence of its occurrence and non-occurrence, there is no occurrence through the alternatives of "entirety" or "part," nor is there measurement for that which has an infinite substratum.
Even that which is not of the nature of [the object], *Yuktyanuśāsana-Ṭīkā*, Sanmatitarka-Ṭīkā, p. 689— ba, ja, śra.

Furthermore, as for the inference stated to prove its existence—namely, that "the specific cognitions of the designations 'cow' and so forth [must have a cause other than the individual objects]"—does this prove merely another cause distinct from the individual body (*piṇḍa*) and so on, or does it prove a universal (*sāmānya*)? If it proves merely another cause, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*) is accepted as such a distinct cause.

However, if it seeks to prove a universal characterized by eternality and so forth, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), because a universal as a distinct cause is impossible therein.
Moreover, even in the absence of a [substantial] universal, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it applies to things like the universal of "existence" (*sattā-sāmānya*).
Furthermore, [the reason] is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because the absence of a universal in the subject (*pakṣa*) has been understood through the previously stated reasoning;
and it is also "contradictory" (*viruddha*), because in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) it is pervaded precisely by the absence of a universal.

Thus, even the inference beginning with "whatever cognition is distinct from the form of an object... is not a proof for the existence of a universal, as it is vitiated by these aforementioned defects.

Thus, since a universal (*sāmānya*) imagined by others is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the description of its divisions starting with "it is of two kinds" is equivalent to describing the good fortune of the son of a barren woman; therefore, we shall desist [from further discussion]. (p. 284, l. 6) If, however, it is being proved that these [particulars] are based on a connection with a so-called "universal"—which is distinct from them, eternal, unitary, and pervasive—then the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
As stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 242,
and the *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 956:
"The cognition that 'it exists' which persists with respect to existence (*sattā*) and other such categories..."
If it is caused by the sign of another property, then there too the notion of existence would arise;
and if that [existence] were caused by yet another property, there would be the consequence of infinite regress, resulting in the absence of any foundational property.
Therefore, this reason is held by these [opponents] to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) regarding reality (*tattva*). *Tattvasaṃgraha* 745.
Regarding the contradiction:

in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, within the "Examination of the Category of the Universal" (*sāmānyapadārthaparīkṣā*), there is a refutation of the Buddhist position that the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*) alone is the basis for the recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*). Following that refutation, it is established that this [cognition] is based on a real, similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*).

[The opponent objects: "Let it be then that the exclusion of heterogeneous things alone is the basis for the recurring cognition, since, as previously stated, it is impossible for an eternal, partless, and unitary universal to be its basis."

If it is asked: "How is it that, in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the cognition of 'cow' arises only with respect to [individual cows] such as Khaṇḍa and excludes [others] such as the white horse (*karka*)? We reply: "Because of the exclusion of dissimilar things (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*). For that [exclusion], wherever it exists, produces that cognition only there and not elsewhere.

Now, one might object: "If this cognition does not have an external object as its domain, how can there be purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) toward that object based on this cognition? This objection is not valid; for it is possible because of the determination of identity between the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*).
And this determination of identity consists in the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgrahaṇa*) between the conceptualization arising immediately after perception and that perception itself.

Then, due to the non-apprehension of difference, by setting aside the operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "this has been perceived by me," one acts; and the attainment of the object occurs through a mediated succession because of the connection with the real object. The distinction between the correct and the false also arises from this very fact: for that conceptual construction which arises from the perception of a connection with a real object is true, while any other is otherwise [false].

The single common term [denoting] the white horse, the cow, and the bull arises from the identity of their difference [from others], due to the parsimony of postulation, the impossibility [of multiple causes], and the futility [of assuming otherwise].
This [distinction] was established by the elders based on the exclusion of what is not that effect;
it does not apply to all entities, because each entity is established in its own intrinsic nature.
That form which belongs to the brindled cow and the black cow does not exist [in others]; yet,
the exclusion of what does not produce that effect (atatkāryavyāvṛtti) exists in both of them.
Without non-difference of meaning, non-difference of word is not tenable;
therefore, its being an effect of that [meaning] is accepted, as well as its difference from that which is not its effect. (141)
Pramāṇavārttika 1.139–142; Tattvasaṅgraha, pp. 239, 317.

That too is charming only when not subjected to critical examination; for even if the universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by an eternal nature and so forth does not serve as its basis, it is nonetheless logical that this [universal], which is defined as a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*) and whose nature is established through means of valid cognition such as perception, should serve as its basis.

Indeed, a similar transformation in the form of the possession of common properties is not unperceived among objects through direct perception, since a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is entirely distinct from everything else is not perceived even in a dream.

For the determination of an object occurs everywhere solely through the clarity of the cognition (*pratyaya*); and here, even regarding variegated individuals such as brindled cows and the like, cognition is apprehended in a uniform form as "cow, cow.

Nor should it be asserted that a thing appearing in one form can manifest in another form, for that would entail the appearance of yellow in what is blue, resulting in the collapse of the established order of specific objects. Therefore, because of this uniform manifestation, it must be admitted that the object itself is endowed with a uniform property (*anugata-dharma*).

Furthermore, if this [cognition] had exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) as its object, then its activity would not proceed with a predominance of affirmation (*vidhi*), characterized by the mental expression "cow, cow. Just as the nature of an entity is excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya-parāvṛtta*), so too is it excluded from those of the same class (*sajātīya-parāvṛtta*). Thus, since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising immediately after perception delineate the form of exclusion from the dissimilar, they must—due to the non-difference [of the object]—also delineate the form of exclusion from the similar.
Nor is there any difference between the exclusions of the similar and the dissimilar and the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because both are real entities (*vastu*) and are partless (*niraṃśa*).
Nor is there any cause for specific restriction in the appearance of a universal characterized by exclusion from specific [particulars],

because since both [the similar and the dissimilar] are excluded from what is seen— whether of the same class or of a different class— they would both touch upon that very exclusion; and there is no difference between the exclusion from the similar and the exclusion from the dissimilar,
such that a conceptual construction could be formulated as touching upon only one of them.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

316. Furthermore, homogeneity (*sajātīyatva*), characterized by a common form, is postulated through the exclusion of dissimilar forms. In that case, would this commonality be postulated for that which is itself of a dissimilar form, or for that which is already of a similar form? Regarding the former, how could there be a common form even when excluded from others if it is itself of a dissimilar form? For otherwise, it would follow that a cow and a horse would also have a common form by virtue of being excluded from buffaloes and the like. Moreover, just as cognition is excluded from a material object such as a jar, so too is a cloth; therefore, "materiality" (*mūrtatva*) would be a common property of both.
And there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for uniformity of form arises from exclusion from others, and from that [uniformity] comes exclusion from others;

thus, for something already uniform in itself, the conceptualization of uniformity through exclusion from others is futile. (The reading *lakṣaṇavaiphalyam* in manuscripts *ba* and *ja* means "futility of the definition.")

And as for the homogeneity (*sajātīyatva*) of objects—would it be due to their performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*), their producing a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśajanakatva*), or their being the substratum of a single exclusion (*ekavyāvṛttyādhāratva*)? It cannot be due to performing a single purposeful action; for since actions such as carrying a load or milking differ with each particular instance, unity is impossible. Furthermore, because such an action is occasional, that which does not perform it at a given time would lack homogeneity, and thus there would be no recurring cognition "cow, cow" even when a specific individual is connected with the eye.

If it is asserted that the capacity for performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*) is a single, continuous entity pervading all particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then that very thing is established as the universal (*sāmānya*) residing in all its specific differences.

If it is argued that this [universal] is merely superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpāropita*), we say no; because such a construct lacks a real object and thus does not have an external thing as its domain, it is incapable of superimposing the unity of purposeful efficacy upon those [particulars].

Nor [is it a universal] because of producing a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*); for since both the reflective awareness and its capacity to produce it differ with each individual instance, their oneness is untenable. Indeed, the very same reflective awareness of a "cow" and the capacity to produce it that exists in a brindled cow (*śāvaleya*) does not exist in a black cow (*bāhuleya*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no difference between those two, just as there is none within a single individual.

Nor is it [a universal] because of being the substratum of a single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); for that [exclusion] cannot transcend the alternatives of being either external or internal. If that exclusion were external and pervasive across all individuals, it would follow that it has the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*).

But if it [the cognition] were internal, since it would lack the status of being a substratum for an external object, how could the similarity of the external object to it be established, or how could it appear as having an external form?—
[as stated in the *Āgamānusāriṇī* commentary].

Regarding the point that [the exclusion] resides therein: the claim that it is neither internal nor external is merely a matter of one's own subjective opinion. For is such a nature of exclusion (vyāvṛtti-svarūpa) something or nothing? If it is nothing, how can there be a basis for its being of the same class (sajātīyatva)? If it is something, it must necessarily be either internal or external, and in that case, the aforementioned fault applies.

Now, the objection—"By that very same proximity through which certain entities themselves undergo a similar transformation, why do those [entities] which are not of that nature themselves not appear as such?"—is an unexamined statement. For this would entail the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between the conscious and the non-conscious. Indeed, for a proponent of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaitavādin*) who asserts that "by the very same proximity through which entities assume the natures of the conscious and the non-conscious, they themselves, though not of that nature, appear as such," his mouth would not even turn back (i.e., he would be forced to abandon his position).

Since this [entity] does not exist apart from blue, pleasure, and so forth, how can it appear in such a way? This objection applies equally elsewhere as well, for there is no particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) devoid of similar and dissimilar transformations that could appear in that manner.

Nor is it contradictory for a single thing to possess a manifold nature; for, just as in the case of a variegated form or a conceptual and non-conceptual form, there is no contradiction in a single thing having such a nature.

Therefore, one must accept that the possession of similar and dissimilar natures by an object is real, because an object situated before one, such as a piece of sugar-cane, appears exactly in that way.

Indeed, it is not the case that even between cognition (*jñāna*) and the object of cognition (*jñeya*), there is only the perception of a difference due to their being of the nature of the sentient and the insentient; for they are also perceived as similar by way of [the cognition appearing as] blue, existent, and so forth. Otherwise, one or the other of the two would alone be real, and the doctrine of conformity (*sārūpyavāda*) would be lost.

As for the statement "neither internal nor external," this is merely a clever turn of phrase (*bhaṇitibhaṅgīmātra*). For if that [object] is something of such a kind, or if it is nothing at all, or if it is something, then it must necessarily exist either internally or externally (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 316).
The aforementioned fault [applies] here as well; in the versions of Ā and Bhāṃ, it reads "ātmatvā" instead of "ba, ja."

Nor should it be argued that because the cognition of recurrence (anuvṛttapratīti) is causeless, there is no need to consider causes such as a similar transformation (*sādṛśyapariṇāma*); for if it were causeless, its restriction to specific places and so forth would be impossible. Furthermore, if it were caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there would be no dependence on an external object; for an object whose cause is one thing cannot depend on something else, as that would lead to the absurdity of smoke depending on water. Moreover, even a latent impression arises only with respect to an object previously experienced, and according to your own view, the experience of a universal (*sāmānya*) is impossible because it is absolutely non-existent.

Furthermore, does that [universal] produce such a cognition as its object (*viṣaya*), or merely as its cause (*kāraṇa*)? If it is as its object, then a real entity (*vastu*) consisting of a form of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*) that follows all particulars has been stated under another name as "the universal" (*jāti*) itself. And if it produces it merely as a cause, then an object must be specified; for a cognition without an object is impossible.
Moreover, no other object for that [cognition] is tenable apart from a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*), because the aforementioned defects would follow.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that this [cognition] arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because by whatever means of valid cognition the causality of latent impressions toward conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is perceived, that [means of cognition] itself—being of the nature of a conceptual construction—is incapable of having an external object as its domain; thus, it is impossible to determine that "this conceptual construction arises from latent impressions. Since no other cause is possible, one must accept that this inclusive cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*) has as its cause precisely a similar transformation (*sadṛśa-pariṇāma*). — [The reading] *kāraṇatvam asti* is found in the manuscripts Ā, Ba, and Ja.
But surely, if that [the universal] were the cause, the cognition would be "this is similar," and not "this is that very same cow.

To whom, then, does the cognition "this is that very same cow" belong? For when one who has seen a white [cow] sees a brindled one, the cognition "this is that very same white cow" does not arise; for it is contradictory for a non-erroneous person to have the perception of whiteness in what is brindled.

What then? There is the cognition "cow, cow. If it is asked how even that is not contradictory: it is because the convention for the word "cow" is applied to a specific similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāmaviśeṣa*). For, since the convention for the word "similar" (*sadṛśa*) applies to all common properties, the cognition "this is similar" proceeds by taking that [similarity] as the primary factor. Furthermore, regarding the specific instances of that [similarity], since the conventions for specific words such as "cow" and "horse" are applied, cognitions such as "cow" and "horse" proceed by taking those [specifics] as the primary factors.

Otherwise, how could there be the cognition "universal, universal" with respect to universals, or "category, category" with respect to the six categories? For, apart from a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*)—consisting in an inherent nature that is pervasive in the case of universals, and characterized by being marked by entirely distinct definitions in the case of the six categories—there is no other cause for such application. Furthermore, [your claim] that this application occurs because of the determination of identity between the perceived and the conceptualized is mere faith; for that determination of identity has already been refuted in the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*).
Therefore, neither the category of "generality" (*sāmānya*) imagined by others is tenable,

nor is the category of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*); for in those cases as well, there is an impossibility of both a faultless definition and a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend them,
because of that [lack of proof].
He, it is said, [is] of the nature of existence—Bhāvarūpa (Ba., Ja., p. 289, l.
The refutation of the category of *sāmānya* (generality) by means of various logical arguments (*bhaṅga*) is to be seen in the *Citsukhī*, page 190.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika is as follows: "Ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) reside in eternal substances; they are the causes of the cognition of absolute distinction among eternal substances that possess identical genus, quality, and action."

Is it not the case that there indeed exists an irreproachable definition of the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣas*)? For instance: "The ultimate particulars are those residing in eternal substances" (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

13). Indeed, for eternal substances which possess identical genus, quality, and action, there can be no cause for the cognition of their absolute differentiation other than the ultimate particulars, which serve as the basis for the cognition of their mutual exclusion.
And these [qualities] reside in eternal substances (*nityadravyavṛtti*), because they reside in atoms (*paramāṇu*), ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), space (*diś*), self (*ātman*), and mind (*manas*).

Furthermore, they are "ultimate" (*antya*): for atoms constitute the terminal points of both the destruction and the origination of the world; and liberated selves and liberated minds possess the nature of being the final limit of *saṃsāra*. Thus, they are called "ultimate" because they exist in those [substances]. Moreover, their residence (*vṛtti*) is most clearly perceived in all eternal substances, beginning with the atoms; for this very reason, they are said to "reside in eternal substances. The employment of both terms—“residing in eternal substances” and “ultimate”—is therefore intended to convey this dual characteristic.
And because they serve as the cause for cognitions that are absolutely distinct from one another, they differentiate their own substrata from others and are thus called *viśeṣas* (particularities).

They are infinite, eternal like their own substrata, perceptible to yogins, and inferable by people such as ourselves. For instance: atoms, which possess identical genus, quality, and action, are related to a differentiating property because they are the objects of distinct cognitions, just like a pearl marked with a sign among a heap of pearls.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished; for instance, atoms are the objects of distinct cognitions because they possess a connection with existence (*sattā*), like jujube fruits (*badara*) and myrobalans (*āmalaka*).

Therefore, their non-existence is not established even due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends them, since both perception and inference have been demonstrated to be the apprehenders thereof.
All of this explanation regarding the category of "particular" (*viśeṣa*) should be consulted in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, pages 311–12.

Atoms, which are the substrata of identical genus, quality, and action, are related to particularities (viśeṣa) because they are the objects of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-buddhi*); *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī*, p. 58, 693. Atoms are the objects of the cognition of exclusion because they are substances (*dravyatva*), like cows and so forth.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

693: In the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*, following the refutation of the category of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) as described therein, it is established that the cognition of exclusion with respect to eternal substances is based solely upon their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that the definition of the *viśeṣas* (particularities) is "residing in eternal substances" and so forth—that is incorrect. For is the absolute eternality of the substances that serve as their substrates intended, or is it intended in some qualified sense (*kathañcit*)? In the first case, the definition is vitiated by the fault of being impossible (*asaṃbhava*); for there exists no substance whatsoever that is absolutely eternal, since such a thing has been refuted in the section on the examination of substances (*dravyaparīkṣā*).

Their status as "ultimate" (antya) is likewise impossible because it is unestablished; for neither the total destruction of an existing world characterized by a great dissolution, nor the production from nothing of that which was entirely non-existent, is established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, since atoms would constitute the terminal point of the world’s destruction and its commencement, they could be considered ultimate; and since specific qualities (*viśeṣas*) would exist at that [terminal] state, they too would possess ultimacy.

In the second alternative, however, there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition, because it applies even to a non-specific characteristic that serves as the cause for the cognition of absolute exclusion (*atyantavyāvṛtti*) in objects such as pearls which possess a common genus (*jāti*) and so forth; for it is not unestablished that the substance which is their substratum is in some sense eternal, since every entity is eternal by virtue of its substantial form. Or, let it be granted that substance is eternal in every respect; nevertheless, those qualities that reside therein never abandon the eternal substance.

If they were of the nature of particulars (viśeṣa), there would be a deviation [from the definition] due to the universals such as "selfhood" (ātmatva) and the like, as well as by [atomic dimensions] such as sphericality (pārimāṇḍalya); for these also reside only in eternal substances and do not receive the designation of "particular," yet they certainly possess the quality of being causes for the cognition of differentiation, since they possess the nature of both universal and particular.

[Objection: "But surely there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason] by means of *ātmatva* and the like, because it is asserted that those which reside in all eternal substances possess the nature of *viśeṣas*, whereas *ātmatva* and the like reside only in specific eternal substances. [Reply: This too is entirely incorrect, because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] by means of *niratiśaya-parimāṇa* (ultimate dimension). For that resides in all eternal substances alike, and because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it distinguishes its own substratum from others, yet it does not have the nature of a *viśeṣa*. Furthermore, as for these *viśeṣas* which are imagined to exist as ultimate entities... [page 292, line 3].
Because they exclude eternal substances, those moments as well are impossible. (Tattvasaṅgraha 813)
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 698; p. 217—“tti he”—Ba., Ja.
[The quality of] selfhood, atomicity, and so forth,
exist only in eternal substances— only in those very eternal substances.
Furthermore, [it applies] only to eternal substances (*nityadravya*).

Moreover, since it is established that objects, by their very own nature, produce cognitions that are mutually exclusive, there is no purpose whatsoever to be accomplished by means of "particularities" (*viśeṣa*).

For eternal substances, are they differentiated by their particularities (*viśeṣa*) while already differentiated by their own nature (*svarūpa*), or while not yet differentiated? If they are not yet differentiated, how could they experience differentiation even through connection with something else? For that which is not differentiated by its own nature does not experience differentiation even upon connection with another, just as the nature of a single individual entity; and eternal substances are not differentiated by their own nature.

Now, if they are already excluded [from others] by their own nature, then what is to be accomplished by the particularities (*viśeṣa*)? For that which is excluded by its own nature, there exist no separate particularities serving as causes for its exclusion, just as in the case of the nature of a particular itself. And since eternal substances are excluded by their own nature, if one were to postulate further particularities for these [substances] which are already excluded by their own nature, it would follow that even those particularities—being excluded by their own nature—would require the postulation of yet other particularities, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if it is argued that the exclusion of particulars follows from the exclusion of the object, and the exclusion of objects follows from the exclusion of those [particulars], that too is incorrect; for it entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
[The particulars] would have to be established by one another.
—By those [means], somewhat;
thus Ā., Ba., Ja. and likewise Ā.

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Just as lamps and the like possess luminosity by their very own nature because that is their inherent essence and not due to a connection with jars and so forth—whereas jars and the like possess it due to such a connection—likewise, particulars (viśeṣas) possess the quality of being causes for the cognition of exclusion by their very own nature because that is their inherent essence and not due to a connection with atoms (paramāṇus) and so forth—whereas atoms and the like possess it through association with those [particulars]. This too is an unexamined statement; for, when jars and other entities come into contact with a lamp and the like, they abandon their previous non-luminous nature and arise as something entirely different characterized by a luminous form. Thus, it is logical that they possess luminosity due to that connection. However, this is not possible in the case of atoms and the like, because they are admitted to be absolutely eternal; since they do not abandon their previous undifferentiated nature, they cannot arise in another differentiated form.

[Objection: But surely, since a non-distinct form is impossible in the case of atoms and so forth, of what could they be divested to become distinct? For those [atoms], which are eternal and of a single nature, must always possess a distinct form, as they are always embraced by the category of *viśeṣa*. [Reply: This too is mere faith; for the notion of being eternal and of a single nature has been refuted during the examination of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, as in the case of lamps (A, B, J, Bhāṃ), here a cognition caused by something else occurs with respect to things that do not possess that nature, as in the case of jars and the like due to a lamp; but [this does not occur] in the case of a lamp due to another lamp.
Furthermore,

due to the influence of lamps and the like, momentary objects such as jars and ornaments indeed attain the nature of being the production of cognition (as explained in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 322).
There is no cognition of distinctness among those [atoms] that arises by the power of a specific property under dispute, because they arise sequentially, like pleasure and so forth.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*,
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 182, first half.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, folio 699;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, page 964.

As for what was also stated—"and those [atoms] are perceived by yogis," etc.—that too is incorrect. For is the nature of atoms and so forth inherently unmixed with one another, or mixed? In the first case, how can there be the establishment of distinction from this? Since the cognition of differentiation among them by yogis would be established solely from the mutually unmixed natures of the atoms and so forth. In the second case, however, there follows the consequence that such a cognition is erroneous; for this cognition, which functions as having a differentiated form toward atoms and so forth whose natures are not mutually excluded in their own right, consists in apprehending something as what it is not (*atasmistadgraha*). And thus, those who possess such a cognition would themselves be non-yogis.

It is also untenable to argue that although these [entities] are not excluded from their own nature (*svarūpa*), they are nonetheless apprehended as excluded by virtue of the category called "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), and thus they do not lack connection [with it]. This is because the capacity of particularities to effect exclusion—whether the things are already excluded by their own nature or not—is denied. Furthermore, the arising of that cognition [of difference] from distinct particularities is contradicted by inference. For instance: the cognition of difference regarding the entities under dispute is not based on particularities distinct from those entities, because it is a cognition of difference, just like the cognition of difference regarding the particularities themselves.
Page 292, line 13: The unmixed nature of atoms, space, direction, and so forth, as it exists,
is the defining characteristic that distinguishes them from this [other category].
If, moreover, those two— the self and the other— were to become mixed together,
then even when they are not distinct entities, there would be no unerring perception of their difference.
If it is argued that the perception of differentiation among those particularities occurs through themselves alone, this is not so; for what is your view regarding atoms and the like?
*Tattvasaṃgraha*,
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 181, part U.
sanmati॰ ṭī॰ pṛ॰ 698 –dgrahaṇarū– ba॰, bhā॰, śra॰ –tyanu– ā॰, ba॰, ja॰.
A cognition possessing a distinct characteristic is not based on a particularity other than that [object]; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 182, *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* p.
699, *Syādvādaratnākara* p. 964.

As for the inference stated—namely, that [substances] possess a common substratum for their genus, quality, and action—insofar as it seeks to prove merely that atoms are related to some distinguishing property (*vyāvarttaka-dharma*), it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). However, if it seeks to prove a relation to a distinct category called "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), then all the aforementioned defects necessarily follow.

Therefore, neither the category of "particularity" nor the category of "inherence" (*samavāya*) postulated by others is tenable; for in both cases, there is an impossibility of any faultless definition or any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend them.
"From page 292,

line 13— *dyatallakṣa*— the relation characterized by the definition beginning with 'of things that are inseparably established' (*ayutasiddhānām*) is inherence (*samavāya*); and that [inherence] is one and eternal"— this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika.

But surely, since its definition is faultless—namely, that inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation which is the cause of the cognition "this is here" with respect to things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of substratum and superstratum—the non-existence of that [inherence] is unproven.

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the absence of an interval in the case of the cognition "trees in this village," because that is caused by the apprehension of a [specific] relation;

nor is there such inconclusiveness due to the cognition "a bird in the sky," because that is caused by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), given the qualification "of things standing in the relation of substratum and superstratum. For, since space is all-pervasive, the bird does not exist only below it, as it exists above it as well.

Nor can it be established by the cognition "there is curd in this bowl," because that is designated as a case of things that are "inseparably established" (ayutasiddha); whereas curd, bowls, and the like are "separately established" (yutasiddha), and separate establishment is defined as existing in different substrates and having distinct movements.
This [separate establishment] does not exist in the case of threads and cloth, since the cloth does not exist elsewhere apart from the threads.

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation [from the rule] here because, while "space" is the denoted (*vācya*) and the word "space" is the denoter (*vācaka*), there is a relationship of denoted and denoter between the self and knowledge here by way of the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*); for in this case, there exists the state of being inseparably established (*ayutasiddhi*) and the relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). This is because in both cases [of the word-space pair and the self-knowledge pair], the restriction [of the definition] is maintained, whereas these two [properties] exist even among things that are separably established (*yutasiddha*) and not related as locus and located, such as a jar and the cognition of its word.

[As stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra: "Inherence (*samavāya*) is that [relation] which exists between cause and effect, and between [the whole and its parts] in the sense of 'here' and 'this'. (VS 7.2.29)
2.26 Inherence is that relation between things that are inseparably established and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition "here [is this]."

The apprehension of the relation [of concomitance] consists in the fact that even the non-perception of an interval is a cause for the cognition "here" (*ihapratyaya*). For instance, it is observed that for those who do not see the space between a village and a grove from a distance, the cognition arises: "There are trees here in the village," and so forth. All these functions of the words are explained in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p. 13), the *Praśastapādavyākhyā* (pp. 107–108), and the *Kandalī* (p.
14). Furthermore, this is presented as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the *Āptaparīkṣā* (p. 26) and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 182, u.).
This is to be seen in such passages as these.

Now, one might object: "Even if the restriction 'only of those that are inseparably established' (*ayutasiddhānām eva*) is applied, since there is no deviation [from the rule], the mention of 'those that stand in the relation of container and contained' (*ādhārādheyabhūtānām*) is redundant—just as the mention of 'inseparably established' would be redundant if the restriction were instead 'only of those that stand in the relation of container and contained'. This too is not sound; for even though color, taste, and so forth are inseparably established, they do not possess an inherence (*samavāya*) with one another because they inhere in the same substrate. Therefore, the subsequent restriction is intended to exclude deviation regarding the relation of inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*); for this [relation] does not occur even among things that are separably established (*yutasiddha*), as is the case with the relation between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

Thus, even though there is a restrictive determination (*uttarāvadhāraṇa*), in order to prevent any deviation (*vyabhicāra*)— since it is impossible for things that are in no way related as container and contained to exist through a particular kind of conjunction characterized by the relation of container and contained— it is well said that this definition includes the prior restriction (*pūrvāvadhāraṇa*).

Therefore, this is stated: it must be conventionally expressed that threads, cloth, and so forth, or universals (*sāmānya*) and their possessors (*tadvat*), and so on, are not conjoined (*saṃyukta*). This is because they are invariably inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and exist in a relationship of substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheya*). For those things which are conjoined are not thus, such as a bowl and a jujube fruit; and these [threads and cloth, etc. are likewise. Therefore, they are not conjoined.

Or alternatively: the relation between threads, cloth, and so forth, is not conjunction, because it is invariably an inseparable relation, like the relation of object and subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*) between cognition and the self.

Regarding the existence of inherence (*samavāya*), perception itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for by perception, a cloth is indeed manifested as connected to its threads, and qualities such as color are manifested as connected to the cloth and so forth.

Nor is this [connection] conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because the related entities are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and because causes such as the action of one of the two [relata] are impossible. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 326)

In the Nyāya school, inherence (*samavāya*) is perceptible; for it is said in the *Nyāyavārttika*: "In the case of inherence and non-existence (*abhāva*), there is the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
(Nyāyavārttika 1.1.4)

1.4 Parts and wholes, qualities and possessors of qualities, actions and agents of action, and universals and possessors of universals are experienced as being mutually connected; it could not be otherwise. For otherwise, there would be no such cognition or designation as "the cloth is in the threads," "the cloth is white," "the cloth moves," or "the cloth is a substance."
Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā 1.1.4

Likewise, this [inherence] is also cognized through inference; for instance: the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" and so forth is produced by a relation, because it is an uncontradicted cognition of the form "it is here," like the cognition "curds are here in the bowl.
First of all, this cognition is not causeless, because it occurs only occasionally;
nor is it caused by the threads or caused by the cloth, because that would entail the occurrence of the cognitions "threads" or "cloth" [in place of "the cloth is here in these threads"].

Nor is it caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because that which lacks a cause cannot possibly exist. If you argue that a prior cognition is its cause, then from where would that [prior cognition] come? If you say it comes from a preceding latent impression, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of cognitions and impressions. If you claim this is not a fault because they are beginningless, it is not so; for it would follow as a consequence that there is no establishment of external objects such as blue, nor of other mental streams, nor of one's own stream, nor of the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*). This is because, according to your view, the cognition of blue and its self-manifestation would be possible solely through the power of beginningless latent impressions.

Nor is this [inherence] caused by identity (*tādātmya*); for identity is said to be oneness, and in that case, there would be an absolute absence of relation, since that [oneness] resides in only one of the two. Nor is it caused by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because conjunction is possible only among things that are established as separate (*yutasiddha*). Furthermore, it is not here being proved that [inherence] is preceded by inherence (*samavāya*), which would render the example devoid of the probandum and the reason contradictory; nor is it being proved that it is preceded by conjunction, which would contradict your own tenets.

What then? It is the state of being preceded by a mere relation; and once that is established, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it will be proven that inherence (*samavāya*) alone is its producer.

In the Vaiśeṣika system, however, it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and inferable (*anumeya*); for it is said [in the Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 329]: "Precisely because it is beyond the senses, inherence is inferable from the cognition of 'here' (*iha-buddhi*)."

In such cases as "the cloth is here in these threads," the cognition of "here" (ihapratyaya) is produced by a relation, because it is an uncontradicted cognition of "here," just like the cognition in the case of "curd is here in the bowl" (Praśastapādabhāṣya p.
Praśastakandalī p. 325).

And here, it is not being proved that [the cognition] is preceded by inherence (*samavāya*), for that would entail the fallacy of the probandum being unestablished (*sādhyavikalatā*); nor is it preceded by conjunction (*saṃyoga*). What then? It is merely the state of being an effect of a relation (*sambandhamātrakāryatva*). As for this inference—namely, "this cognition of 'this is here' which is the subject of dispute is not preceded by inherence, because it is an uncontradicted cognition of 'here,' like the cognition 'curd is here in the bowl'"—which is an inference contradicted by a specific property (*viśeṣaviruddhānumāna*), it should not be employed by a proponent of inference, since it would result in the destruction of all inference.

As for what is said—that the cognition "this is here" does not have inherence (*samavāya*) as its objective support—that is true; however, because that cognition has a qualified substratum as its object, the notion "the cloth is here in these threads," for instance, does not have inherence alone as its objective support, since it has the threads and the cloth as qualified by that [inherence] as its object. Furthermore, this relation between the two is not manifold like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because there is no difference in the notion "it is here" and because there is an absence of any specific mark [of multiplicity], just as in the case of existence (*sattā*), where there is no difference in the notion "it exists" and no absence of its specific mark.

Furthermore, being a relation (*sambandhatva*) alone is not a specific probans (*viśeṣaliṅga*), because this is established otherwise; for it is not by virtue of being a relation that the plurality of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is proved, but rather because it is perceived through direct perception to arise successively while inhering in distinct substrates. As for inherence (*samavāya*), if it were manifold, there would be no occurrence of a uniform cognition (*anugatapratyaya*); whereas in the case of conjunction, such plurality could exist due to the property of "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*). This, however, is not possible in the case of inherence, because inherence cannot inhere in inherence; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, since conjunction is a quality (*guṇa*), it can only exist in substances (*dravya*); moreover, the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*) is inherent (*samaveta*) in conjunction itself. Nor is this [nature of conjunction] non-different from a universal (*sāmānya*) simply because it produces a uniform cognition, for it possesses a distinct definition.

Nor does it possess plurality like conjunction, because, like an existent entity (*bhāva*), its inferential mark is non-distinct and there is an absence of any specific inferential mark [to indicate plurality].

Therefore, as with existent things (*bhāva*), inherence (*samavāya*) is one and the same everywhere; thus [states] Praśastapāda-bhāṣya, p. 326. Furthermore, another objection raised against inherence is: "Does inherence belong to two things that are already produced or to those that are not yet produced? It cannot belong to those that are not yet produced, because a relation is impossible when the related entities have not come into existence."

But regarding two things that have already come into existence, their conjunction itself—how is it related to its own relata? Is it unrelated, or is it related? It cannot be unrelated, because that would entail the impossibility of the designation "this is the relation between those two.
If it is related, is it so by itself or through something else? It cannot be by itself, because that would entail the same consequence for conjunctions and the like as well.
Nor [is it established] from another, because that would lead to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, it is not logical for qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth to possess the state of being supported (*ādheyatva*); for they are devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), and a substratum (*ādhāra*) is that which obstructs motion, as in the case of a jar supporting water and the like—yet this too is mere words. For there can be no inherence (*samavāya*) between what is already produced and what is not yet produced; since "production" consists precisely in the connection with the existence (*sattā*) of its own causes, production is not one thing and inherence another, such that there could be a sequence of priority and posteriority.

Nor does inherence have a connection with another relation such that there would be an infinite regress; for we do not observe a relation that is itself connected by a relation possessing the same characteristics [as the first]. Therefore, like the heat of fire, inherence is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*); otherwise, since a relation is never observed in the absence of related entities, inherence could not be tenable.

Now, if the relation between two produced things were inherence (*samavāya*), then there would be separate existence (*yutasiddhi*), because [inherence] is so; otherwise, [it would not be produced]. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 699) — Śrī. [Note: *niṣpa* refers to *niṣpannayoh*]
Therefore, it is precisely the negation of a co-occurrent function that is intended [by Praśastapāda, *Praśastapādabhāṣya* p.
for inherence (*samavāya*), which is indivisible and consists of a function, has no other function; consequently, its function is its own self.
Only this [intrinsic] relation is logical for it, because it possesses the nature of a relation by its very own nature; conjunction and the like are not, because that [nature] is absent in them.
For the nature of one thing does not belong to another; otherwise, since heat is observed in fire by its own nature, it would likewise exist in water and other substances by their own nature alone.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Inherence (*samavāya*) does not require another relation, because it is inherently a relation by its own nature. Those things which do require another relation are not inherently related, such as jars and the like. This [inherence], however, is not something that is not inherently related; therefore, it does not require another relation.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that "because they are devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), they cannot be made to possess [a relation]"—that is incorrect. This is because qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are distinct from substances (*dravya*) that enter into conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for while those substances that enter into conjunction are necessarily active, even though these [qualities] are devoid of action, their status as substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The demonstration that inherence (*samavāya*) is, in some sense, identical in nature, preceded by a rebuttal of the qualification beginning with "of things not established separately" (*ayutasiddhānām*):

here it is replied—firstly, as for what was stated beginning with "of things not established separately," that is incorrect; because if the inherent relata (*samavāyin*) are impossible, it is untenable for inherence to be characterized by such a definition, and that impossibility has already been demonstrated previously.

For you have postulated five categories—substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity—as being inherent (samavāyin). These have already been refuted in detail during the examination of those very categories. Therefore, how could there be the possibility of characteristics such as "inseparable existence" (*ayutasiddhatva*), by virtue of which inherence (*samavāya*)—defined by such characteristics—could be established as a distinct category? Furthermore, is this "inseparable existence" technical (*śāstrīya*) or worldly (*laukika*)? Of these, the first position is untenable, because "technical inseparable existence" is impossible in the case of things such as threads and cloth.

For it is well known in the Vaiśeṣika treatise that "inseparability" (ayutasiddhatva) consists in having a non-distinct substratum; however, that is certainly not the case here. Since it is established that the threads reside in their own parts (aṃśu) and the cloth resides in the threads, they possess distinct substrata; thus, non-distinctness of substratum is simply non-existent.
In this way, one should understand that qualities, actions, and universals likewise lack non-distinctness of substratum.

Furthermore, if inseparability were defined merely as residing in a single common vessel as is commonly perceived in the world, then how could that be a defining characteristic [of inseparable things], since even milk and water—which are separable—exist in the same vessel?
pṛ॰ 294 paṃ॰ 18 –ye talla– Śra:
The five possess the nature of being inherent and manifold.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 16:

"If [it is argued that] inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*) consists in being real, this qualification is not correct, because the two things related by inherence (*samavāyin*) lack the kind of inseparable existence recognized in the treatises."
A substance has its own parts as its substratum, whereas a quality resides in a substance; however,
according to worldly usage, even milk and water may be considered inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*).
Examination of the Authority (*āptaparīkṣā*), *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 184, recto.

"Separate establishment" (yutasiddhi) means separate existence; it is the state of two related things having distinct substrata by mutually excluding one another. Those two in which this does not exist are "non-separately established" (ayutasiddha).
(*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 14).

Now, one might argue: "Just as there are two distinct substrates called the bowl and the curd-parts, and two distinct superstrates called the bowl-whole and the curd-whole, such is not the case with threads and cloth and so forth; for a thread itself is a superstrate relative to its own parts and a substrate relative to the cloth. Therefore, since the definition of 'separate existence' (*yutasiddhi*)—namely, 'subsisting in separate substrates'—is absent in these cases, they possess 'non-separate existence' (*ayutasiddhatva*). This too is incorrect, because it would entail the absurd consequence that space, time, ether, and the self lack separate existence, since they do not possess the quality of being substrates and superstrates in relation to separate substrates.

Furthermore, the characteristic of "separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*)—defined as having separate motions for eternal substances—is impossible in that case; for, due to their all-pervasiveness (*vyāpitā*), it is impossible for them to have either one or both types of separate motion.

Moreover, there is a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*): for only when inherence (*samavāya*) is established can "separate existence"—defined as inhering in separate substrates—be established; and only when that is established can the inherence of those things that lack separate existence (*ayutasiddha*) be established by its negation.

[Objection: "But surely a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) establishes that which already exists by distinguishing it from others; it does not bring about its existence. Therefore, this is not a fault. [Reply: That is incorrect; for in the case of a definition being a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), there is an even greater risk of the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

To explain: as long as "separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*) is unknown, one cannot know the inherence (*samavāya*) of things that are not separately existent by means of its negation. And if that [inherence] is unknown, it is incapable of establishing "separate existence," which is characterized by the inherence of distinct substrata.

Nor is it logical that something unestablished by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be established by its definition alone. That which is unestablished by means of valid cognition cannot be established by its definition alone, just as the non-duality of the Self (*ātmādvaita*) and so forth; and your postulated *samavāya* is likewise unestablished by means of valid cognition.

For once the existence of the thing to be defined (*lakṣya*) is established through some [means], a corresponding definition is recognized, but its establishment does not proceed from the power of the definition alone; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everyone could establish their own preferred reality, since it is easy for anyone to formulate a mere definition at will.

And there is mutual dependence: for only when inherence is established would its definition be established, and only when that [definition] is established is inherence established; for, as stated in the Praśastapādabhāṣya (p. 152), "inherence in separate substrata" is the definition of "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*) for impermanent things.
Furthermore, that [movement] belongs either to both or to one of the two separately; this [other kind], however, belongs to eternal things—Praśastapādabhāṣya p. 152;
Praśastakandalī p. 14.
This [definition] is also not possible in the case of all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*), for that [quality of] having separate motion is of two kinds...
[as stated in] Āptaparīkṣā, kārikās 44–47; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 184, l. 1.
In the *Ratnākara* (p.

965), some raise the following invalid objection: "If inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished, then there can be no inherence in substrates that are separate; this is not a valid objection, because a definition serves to exclude what already exists.
For if a non-existent thing were produced by a definition, this would indeed be a fault; but this is not so, because a definition is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*)."
In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā* (p.

108) and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p. 184, upper), it is stated that in the view of [the opponent] who holds this to be a logical indicator (*jñāpaka*), there is all the more the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Furthermore, "non-separate establishment" (*ayutasiddhi*) is the absence of "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*). Now, by the word "establishment" (*siddhi*) here, is "cognition" (*jñapti*) or "origination" (*utpatti*) intended? If it is cognition, then it would follow that even universals (*sāmānya*) and their possessors (*tadvat*) are separately established, because their own natures can be cognized individually from one another in the form of the inclusive (*anuvṛtta*) and the exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*), and so forth.

Now, if "arising" (utpatti) is meant, then there would be no such thing as "non-separate existence" (ayutasiddhi), for it would follow that it means "arising not separately. That too is untenable, because one accepts that a universal (jāti) is eternal. If, on the other hand, "non-separate existence" is merely the absence of separate existence, and that exists in the case of a universal, then this fault does not apply; [we reply: no, for in that case, even ether and so forth would possess non-separate existence. Furthermore, when a cloth has arisen, its color and other qualities arise quite separately; and since the cloth exists in threads that are already established as separate, there would be "separate existence" (yutasiddhatva) here as well. Moreover, by the word "existence" (siddhi), do you mean cognition (jñapti) or arising (utpatti)?
Furthermore, as for this state of non-separateness (*ayutasiddhatva*), is it non-distinctness of location, non-distinctness of time, or non-distinctness of nature? In no way whatsoever is it tenable.
(Brahmasūtra Śāṅkara-bhāṣya, p. 965)

Furthermore, is this inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*) due to having a non-distinct locus of space, a non-distinct locus of time, a non-distinct locus of substratum, a non-distinct origin from causes, or a non-distinct essential nature? It cannot first be due to having a non-distinct locus of space, because that is unproven (*asiddha*); for the very spaces that belong to the threads are not the same as those of the cloth, since the threads reside in their own parts (*aṃśu*), whereas the cloth resides in them.

Nor [is it identical] by way of having the same time, for this very reason: it is not the case that whatever is the time of the threads is also the time of the cloth, because that would contradict experience and entail the absence of the relationship between cause and effect. For the simultaneity of the effect with its cause could only occur if the effect were already established through some other means; and if it is already established, what could the cause do to make it so? Nor is it identical by way of being based on the same substratum (*dharmin*), because that is impossible here: parts and the whole, and so forth, do not reside in a single substratum anywhere, because that would contradict experience and lead to the fallacy of abandoning one's own tenets.

Is it existence in the same location, simultaneity, having the same substratum, being produced from the same cause, or having the same essential nature? By this [examination], inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*)—even on the grounds of being produced from the same cause—is also refuted. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 965) —[The reading] *asyā āśrayatvena* is in the Asi edition; *asi* is in the Bhāṣya.
By this, inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*) has also been rejected, even by way of being produced from the same cause.

If, however, these two were of an identical nature (*abhinnasvarūpatva*), then with respect to what would there be dependence, and what would constitute their inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*)? Or, where could there be inherence (*samavāya*) of one in the other? Furthermore, does this identity of nature mean that one thing assumes the nature of another, or that it acquires its selfhood through a state of total fusion (*ekalolībhāva*)? In the first case, there is a contradiction with perception; for the assumption by a universal (*jāti*) and so forth of the nature of an individual (*vyakti*) and so forth is certainly not perceived through direct experience. In the second case, however, it is precisely such a transformation (*pariṇati*) of objects that constitutes their inseparable existence, and thus our own doctrine is established.

Furthermore, since such inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*) is possible even for color, taste, and so forth—which reside in a single substance—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they are related to one another by inherence (*samavāya*).

[If you argue] that this consequence does not apply because there is no relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) among them, that too is unsatisfactory; for apart from such a transformation (*pariṇati*), no other relationship of substratum and superstratum is possible even in the case of threads and cloth, whereas such a distinct relationship is possible only in the case of separately established things (*pṛthaksiddha*) like a bowl and jujube fruits.

As for what was also said—that because the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is applied in both cases, and so forth—that too is incorrect; for even when the restriction is applied in both cases, the definition [of a reason] that exists in only a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) remains fallacious (*vyabhicārin*). And it is accepted by everyone that a reason which does not exclude even a portion of the counter-example is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), just as "eternality" is [inconclusive] when "being produced immediately after an effort" is to be proven in the case of sound (p.
5); even with a restriction, [it remains so]. (Ja.)
As for what was stated—namely, that "the threads, the cloth, and so forth are not conjuncts," and so on—that is true; for in that case, identity (tādātmya) is admitted [between them]. (p. 295, l. 14)

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that inherence (*samavāya*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth—that too is mere faith; for its unique nature (*asādhāraṇasvarūpa*) is not established. Indeed, the perceptibility of jars and the like is established only when their own unique natures are established, yet that [perceptibility] is not established for this [inherence].

For would that consist in being a relation of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhasambandhatva*), or merely being a relation (*sambandhatvamātra*)? It cannot be the former, because its [nature as] a relation of inseparable existence is not established in the manner already explained.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to have a nature consisting of a universal (*sāmānya*), because a universal is impossible in the absence of things that are common; this would be like "sky-ness" in the sky.
Nor is mere relatedness the unique nature of inherence (*samavāya*), since it is possible even in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. (Page 295, Line 18)
mere relation, mere relation; ba, ja. mere relation, mere relation; ba, ja.

Furthermore, does this [inherence] appear in the cognition of a relation (*sambandha*) in the form of that [relation] within the experience "this is here," or within the conceptual cognition "this is inherence"? Regarding the first alternative, what is this so-called "relation" in whose cognition it would appear—is it a relation characterized by the universal "relationality" (*sambandhatva-jāti*), produced from multiple substrates, dependent on multiple things, the producer of the cognition of a relation, or the object of that cognition? It cannot be the first, namely, being characterized by the universal "relationality," because it would follow that inherence itself is not a relation; for since no further inherence exists, the universal "relationality" cannot apply to it.

Now, if it is produced from multiple substrates like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then it follows that inherence (*samavāya*) would lack the nature of a relation, because that [conjunction] is not possible given the admission of its [inherence's] eternality; whereas for cloth and the like, that [relation] is possible, and thus they would follow as being relations.
Nor is it dependent on multiple [substrates], because it would then follow that "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are also relations.
Nor does it produce the cognition of a relation, because it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs are also such [relations].

Nor is it the object of the cognition of a relation; for if the relation and the related entities were objects of a single cognition, it would follow that the related entities themselves would possess the nature of that [relation]. Furthermore, there is no difference in cognition for each individual object, as that would entail the impossibility of a variegated cognition (*mecakajñāna*). Is it then determined by the cognition of a relation, or by the cognition of "here" (*iha-buddhi*), or by the cognition of inherence (*samavāya-buddhi*)? (Tattvopaplava, p. 10; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 184, uttara).

Is a relation (sambandha) something conjoined with a genus of relation, or is it produced from multiple substrata, or does it reside in multiple [entities], or is it a specific cognition of relation, or that which produces the cognition of relation, or is it the form of the relation? (*Tattvopaplava*, p. 10; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 184, u.

Now, it might be argued that inherence (samavāya) appears in the experience "this is here"; this is not so, because this [experience] merely delineates the form of a relation characterized by the nature of the locus and the located.
