Furthermore, when an object is being perceived under one form, it is not logical to postulate an object under another form, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if it is argued that since the relation between a bowl and jujube fruits and so forth is observed to be preceded by another relation, therefore this [relation] between part and whole and so forth must also be established as being preceded by another relation—thus proving *samavāya* (inherence)—then indeed there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For, since the relation between a bowl and curd and so forth is perceived to be dependent upon another relation, it follows that the relation between part and whole and so forth must likewise be dependent upon yet another relation.

Now, if it is argued that this [inherence] is perceived through the cognition of inherence (*samavāya-buddhi*), that is not so; for such a cognition is impossible for anyone. Indeed, even in a dream, the triad—“these are threads,” “this is a cloth,” and “this is inherence”—never appears to anyone as mutually distinct. Therefore, inherence is not accessible through perception;
people never cognize it in the form: “this is a thread, this is a cloth, and this is the inherence between these two.”
In the *Tattvopaplava*, page 10:

"If there were an extreme difference [between property and substratum], the relationship of property and substratum would not exist; if it does exist through inherence (*vṛtti*), then the triad [of property, substratum, and relation] would not appear [as distinct].
Furthermore, the cognition 'this is here' would not exist regarding inherence, nor would there be even a figurative difference, which contradicts common worldly experience."
It is not the case that there is cognition [of the cloth] through direct perception, because it cannot be determined apart from the threads of the cloth.
Nor is [the existence of the whole] cognizable through inference (*anumāna*), because even such a faultless inference that would make its existence known is impossible.
As for the inference stated here to make its existence known— namely, "there is a cloth in these threads" and so forth— that too is incorrect, because it is vitiated by numerous defects.

To explain: first of all, the reason (hetu) here is unestablished in its substratum (āśrayāsiddha); this lack of establishment is due to the non-establishment of the subject (dharmin), namely the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" and so forth.

Furthermore, this reason has an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa), because the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" is sublated by cognitions perceived in the form of "threads in the cloth" or "branches in the tree.

It is also unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha), because the quality of being a "here-cognition" (ihapratyayatva) is not experienced in the cognition of the threads and the cloth, since this [latter] is experienced in the form of "this is a cloth" and so forth.

Furthermore, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for here, in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), there is beginninglessness, and in the case of the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), there is the non-existence of the non-existence of destruction. Thus, since the uncontradicted cognition of "here" (*ihapratyaya*) lacks the necessity of being preceded by a relation, one cannot claim that the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is what constitutes it; for that state itself is impossible without some other underlying relation. Otherwise, everything would be both the qualifier and the qualified of everything, because of that state.
The establishment of inherence (samavāya) through such means as "the tree is here in the branches," which cannot be established by any other means— oh, what a world-transcending state!
In the *Nyāyaviniścaya*, Part 1,
page 226 (first edition, page 295, line 20),
he supports that very same [point regarding] the non-establishment of the substratum (*dharmyasiddhi*): "There is no perception of threads, cloth, and so forth as being distinct [entities]."
That by virtue of which there exist such cognitions as "this is here" with respect to those [objects]— Tattvasaṃgraha 829.
"A branch on a tree" and "a goat on a rock"— such is the common worldly understanding. (Tattvasaṃgraha 831)

Furthermore, from this inference, is merely a relationship established between the threads and the cloth, or a specific type of relationship? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) is already accepted.

Now, it might be argued: "If there were identity (*tādātmya*) between the threads and the cloth, then only one of them would exist. And if the two related entities are one, how could there be a relation, since a relation must reside in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*)? This too is incorrect. For while it is logical that a relation which resides in two things (*dviṣṭha*) should be absent in this way, how can there be an absence of that [relation] which is characterized by being their very nature (*tatsvabhāvatā*)? Indeed, the cloth is merely a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) consisting of the threads themselves, not a separate entity (*arthāntara*), because apart from the threads arranged in the form of warp and woof (*ātānavitānībhūta*), it is not perceived through spatial distinction or any other means.

Now, if a specific relation is being established—whether it be conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)? If it is conjunction, there is a contradiction with your own tenets. If it is inherence, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), and the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because inherence is not established anywhere at all.

Now, if it is argued that neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) is being proven, but rather a mere relation (*sambandha*), and that once this is established, inherence is proven by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*); [we ask] what indeed is this so-called "elimination"? If it is said that it is the cause of the cognition of the remainder when the possible [alternatives] have been negated; [we reply: is that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is not a means of valid cognition, how can it be the cause for the realization of the matter at hand? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, on the other hand, it is a means of valid cognition, is it perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be perception, because perception is incapable of establishing the intended object through the negation of the possible alternatives.

Now, if it is argued that *kevalavyatireki-anumāna* (inference based solely on negative concomitance) is *pariśeṣa* (the method of elimination); then the inference under discussion would be redundant, because even when that [negative inference] exists, the intended conclusion cannot be established without *pariśeṣa*. Since *pariśeṣa* alone is capable of establishing that [conclusion] even without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), let that alone be stated; yet it has not been stated. Therefore, how could *samavāya* (inherence) be established?

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that an inference contradicted by a particular (viśeṣaviruddha) should not be advanced because it would result in the destruction of all inference, and so forth—is it not to be spoken because it destroys fallacious inferences, or because it destroys valid inferences? Of these two positions, the first is untenable; for a proponent of inference does not refrain from employing perception and other means of knowledge which destroy inferences arising from reasons that are "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), since that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

The second position is also untenable; for it is not possible to subvert a correct inference based on smoke and so forth—even by a thousand inferences that contradict specific particulars—by means of perception and other means whose objects have already been superseded.

Nor can this [inference] be declared invalid simply because it is an inference contradicting specific particulars; for the status of being an "inference contradicting specific particulars" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) has not been defined as a logical fallacy (*hetvābhāsa*) in the section defining fallacies, like "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and the rest, such that proponents of inference would refrain from employing it just as they do with the unestablished and other fallacies.

Therefore, only that faulty inference which serves to negate a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) should not be stated, such as: "This place does not possess fire by means of the fire located therein, because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen.

For whatever specific qualification is refuted by such [an inference] is perceived by perception itself upon approaching that location; and this is not possible in the case of *samavāya*, since it has been established that this [inherence] is beyond the scope of perception and the other [means of knowledge].
Nor can there be a sublation (*bādhaka*) whose object is not that [very thing], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
"Is it, then, because it eliminates fallacious inference that [it is not] prameya? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 186, first part).

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that "it does not possess plurality like conjunction," and so forth—that too is incorrect, because its oneness is sublated by inference. For instance: inherence is manifold, because it is the cause of the cognition of a relation among objects that differ in place, time, and form; whatever is such [i.e., the cause of the cognition of a relation among diverse objects] is manifold, just like conjunction; and this [inherence] is likewise; therefore, it is manifold.
Indeed, the difference between the conjunction of a staff and a person and the conjunction of a mat and a wall is well known.

If one accepts a distinction in this [inherence] based on the difference in cognitions such as "dense conjunction" and "loose conjunction," then let there also be a distinction in inherence itself based on the difference in cognitions such as "eternal inherence" and "occasional inherence," for there is no distinction [between the two cases].

If the production of those cognitions regarding inherence were due to the eternality and occasional nature of the relata of inherence, then the production of such cognitions regarding conjunction would likewise be due to the density and looseness of the relata of conjunction; it could not be because of the possibility of density and so forth being the inherent nature of conjunction itself. Thus, while one seeks to establish [the unity of inherence], the other [conjunction] falls away. (p.

In various times and contexts, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not non-different from its qualified substratum; for there is no perception of non-distinction between the conjunction of a staff and a person and the conjunction of a cloth and incense. Likewise, let inherence (*samavāya*) be understood as manifold. Just as there are cognitions such as "loose conjunction" and "dense conjunction" regarding conjunction, so too there are [cognitions] such as "eternal inherence" and "occasional inherence" regarding inherence as well.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 19–20; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 186; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 702.

Furthermore, its multiplicity is established by the fact that inherence (*samavāya*) depends upon various things—such as parts and wholes—which are not established apart from one another (*ayutasiddha*), just like number (*saṃkhyā*).

Nor is this unproven; for if inherence did not depend on those [six categories], then the rule that "the six [categories] reside [in others]" would be contradicted, except in the case of eternal substances.
This contradicts [the statement] on page 16 of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*:

"Now, inherence does not possess the quality of being dependent in an ultimate sense, but rather by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). The ground for this metaphorical designation is the cognition of inherence occurring when the inherent substrates (*samavāyin*) exist. For if it were dependent in a real sense, it would follow that it would perish upon the destruction of its substrate, just like qualities and so forth. This too is incorrect, because the cause [of the designation] is the general property of dependence itself.

Furthermore, by this same reasoning, it would follow that even space (*dig*) and the other [eternal substances] must be dependent. For among corporeal substances that have attained the conditions for perception, there exists the cognition of space as a mark—namely, the notion "this is to the east of that"—and the cognition of time as a mark, namely, the notions of priority and posteriority (*paratva-aparatva*).

Consequently, this contradicts the principle that [universals exist] "other than eternal substances," and it entails the undesirable consequence that a universal would be non-dependent, since it would not perish even upon the destruction of its substratum, just like inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, its lack of dependence (*anāśritatva*) is contradicted by inference from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). For instance: [Thesis] Dependence exists in ultimate reality; [Reason] because it has inherence as its relation; [Example] like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.

Since inherence is perceived only when the inherent substrates (*samavāyin*) exist, why is it that direction (*dik*) and the other [categories] do not likewise depend upon corporeal substances (*mūrtadravya*)?
Examination of the Valid Person (*āptaparīkṣā*), *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 186, section U.

Furthermore, the claim that "inherence is one because there is no difference in the cognition 'here' and because there is an absence of any specific indicative mark" is incorrect. This is because the absence of specific indicative marks is unproven (*asiddha*), owing to the existence of the indicative mark just demonstrated.

Moreover, the lack of difference in the cognition 'here' is also unproven; for there is a distinction in the cognition 'here,' as in "knowledge is here in the self" and "color and so forth are here in the cloth. Indeed, the distinctness of a cognition consists in its being colored by a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Nor is the oneness of inherence (samavāya) established by means of a recurring cognition (*anugatapratyaya*); for even though there is no oneness recurring among universals such as "cowness" and so forth, or among the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), the recurring cognition "universal, universal" or "category, category" is nevertheless perceived—just as in the case of "existence" (*sattā*). Thus, the example [provided by the opponent] is deficient in both the probandum and the probans; this is because absolute oneness and the lack of distinction in the cognition of "being" are unproven. And that they are unproven is established because their multiplicity and their distinctions will be demonstrated later in some way.
Thus it is. (Ā.)
pṛ॰ 296-paṃ॰ 16 –ntaraṃpra– bhāṃ॰ –kasya ba॰, ja॰.

The example "like existence" (sattāvat) is also devoid of both the probandum and the probans, because [existence] is in every respect a single entity, while [the subject] is manifold. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 186, l. 9). Bhāṣya.

—And as for what was stated [by others], beginning with "because production is simply the relation of its own cause with existence" (svakāraṇasattāsambandha), that too is an unexamined assertion; for if the acquisition of self-nature (ātmalābha) were synonymous with inherence in the existence of its own cause, it would follow that it is eternal.
Furthermore, the definition of "being an effect" (kāryatva) as inherence in the existence of its own cause has already been refuted; so enough of this digression.
Regarding what was stated on page 297, line 4,
and page 101—

that "it is like the heat of fire," and so forth— that too is mere words; for when the nature of a thing is established by direct perception, it is appropriate to respond with its own inherent properties, as in the case of water and fire.

Furthermore, it is not established by perception that inherence (*samavāya*) is inherently a relation while conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like are extrinsically so; for it has been demonstrated that its own nature is beyond the scope of direct perception, and because this contradicts inference: "Inherence, when being related by another, is not related intrinsically, because it is something being related, like color and so forth" (p.

Furthermore, as for what was stated [by the opponent]—that "inherence does not depend on another relation because it is inherently a relation," and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for the reason (hetu) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Indeed, as long as the very nature of inherence is unestablished, its inherent status as a relation cannot be established therein;
moreover, this is because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which, though being inherently a relation, nevertheless depends upon another relation.

Indeed, if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like do not possess the nature of being related (*sambandha*) by themselves, it is not tenable for them to possess that nature through another; for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since jars and other such things are also related, they too would possess the nature of being relations through another. Thus, it is incorrect to say that "they are not relations by themselves," because it is not logical for this [conjunction] to have a relation by itself.

Nor [is it produced] from another; for from what else could it arise? From conjunction (*saṃyoga*), from another inherence (*samavāya*), from the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*), or from the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)? It cannot first be from conjunction, because conjunction, being a quality (*guṇa*), lacks the possibility of existing in inherence, which is not of the nature of a substance (*adravyasvabhāva*).
Nor can it be from another inherence, because inherence is admitted to be of a single uniform nature; otherwise, its status as a single principle would be lost. (VS 7.2.29)
This would contradict what was explained [on page 297, line 9]:
"Because it is itself an attainment (*prāpti*), there is no other attainment [of it]. If this is argued, it is not so, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Connected, Tattvārtharāja° pṛṣṭha 5, pṛṣṭha 297, line 10; Ā. [manuscript].
Is it by way of the relation of qualifier and qualified, or by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or by inherence (*samavāya*)? (Aṣṭasahasrī p. 215;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 20; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 188a)
It has been explained in the *Ratnāvalī*, page 969; this is the remainder [of the citation] from the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* and the *Upaskāra*, section 7.

Nor [can it be said that the relation is] due to the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*); for this [relation] is observed to function only with respect to objects already connected by another relation, as in the case of "a man qualified by a staff" (*daṇḍaviśiṣṭaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and so forth. Otherwise, everything would be both the qualifier and the qualified of everything else.
Furthermore, it is not possible for inherence (*samavāya*) to be connected to its inherent substrates (*samavāyin*) by means of another relation, because such a thing is not admitted.

Moreover, since the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is also entirely distinct from these [substrates], how could it be restricted to them alone? If you say it is due to inherence, there is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*): for the restriction of inherence would be established only when the restriction of the state of being a qualifier is established, and the restriction of inherence would be established only when that [restriction of the state of being a qualifier] is established.

Furthermore, is this relation of qualification (viśeṣaṇabhāva) different from the six categories, or non-different? If it is different, is it of the nature of existence (bhāvarūpa) or of the nature of non-existence (abhāvarūpa)? It cannot be of the nature of existence, because that would result in the violation of the rule that there are only six categories; nor can it be of the nature of non-existence, because such a thing is not admitted [by you]. If, on the other hand, it is non-different, would it have the nature of substance (dravya) or the nature of qualities and so forth (guṇādi)? It cannot have the nature of substance, because that would entail the consequence that it does not reside in qualities and the like.
For this very reason, it is neither a quality nor an action, because it would follow that it lacks dependence on action,
given the designation "action that is non-action."
Nor is it a universal (*sāmānya*), because that would entail its absence from universals and the like, since a universal subsists only in three categories of entities;

nor is it a particular (*viśeṣa*), because that would entail the absence of the state of being a qualifier in anything other than eternal substances, and because if it were a qualifier of multiple inherent substrates simultaneously, it would follow that it is manifold—whatever qualifies multiple objects simultaneously is manifold, such as a staff, an earring, and so forth; and inherence is likewise; therefore, it is manifold.

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) due to [the property of] existence (sattā) and so forth, because that too is established as having a manifold nature; therefore, it is not connected even by way of being a qualifier, since it is not perceived [as such]. (ba, ja)
Actions are explained by means of actions, and qualities by means of qualities, as they are connected with their respective causes— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.6.
Actions do not possess actions, nor do qualities possess qualities.
Upaskāra: the specific state— such as being a bracelet (kuṇḍalatva) and so forth— is the jāti (genus).

Nor can it be by means of the unseen (adṛṣṭa); for its very nature as a relation is impossible. Indeed, you have accepted that a relation must reside in two things (dviṣṭha). And since the unseen resides in the self, not abiding in both the inherence and the inherent, how could it be "residing in two"? Furthermore, this would contradict your doctrine of six types of relations. Moreover, if inherence were related to the unseen, then qualities, their substrates, and so forth would also be related by that very same means; thus, there is no need to postulate a relation such as inherence even in those cases.
Nor can an inherence-relation (*samavāya*) that is unperceived and unrelated be the cause of a relation, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is related, it must be stated how so. If it is through another inherence, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*);
if it is through something else, it results in the fallacy of abandoning one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Therefore, that inherence is neither connected—
like the [conjunction] of air and so forth— nor is it unconnected, because that would entail a contradiction with the principle that "the six categories are dependent."

Furthermore, regarding the cognition of a relation such as "there is knowledge in this self," this cognition of a relation cannot be preceded by a relation between two things that are themselves unrelated, because it is a cognition of a relation, like the cognition of the relation between a staff and a person; for otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradicting this inference.

Moreover, is this inherence (samavāya) postulated as existing between two things that are inherent, or between two things that are not inherent? If it were between two things that are not inherent, then it would follow that it must also exist between a jar and a cloth.

Now, regarding the two things that are inherent (*samavāyin*): from what does their state of being inherent arise—by means of inherence (*samavāya*), or by themselves? If it is by means of inherence, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of their state of being inherent depends on the establishment of inherence, and the establishment of that [inherence] depends on the establishment of those two. But if they are inherently inherent by themselves, what is the use of inherence? Nor should it be argued that all this is equally applicable to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as well, because such a thing [as conjunction] is impossible, since it cannot exist apart from the objects produced in a state of contact. However, if one maintains that there is a necessary rule governing two distinct conjoined things, then this [criticism] applies equally to that case.

Is this inherence [the relation] between two inherent things or between two non-inherent things? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 188, l. 9). Furthermore, as for what was stated—namely, "because qualities and so forth are distinct from substances that possess conjunction," and so on—that too is untenable. For even if these [qualities, etc. are devoid of motion, they possess the status of being "contained" (ādheyatva) either because of their small dimension, because they are effects thereof, or because of such an appearance. Among these, the first position is inconsistent; for it would entail the undesirable consequence that a universal and a quality of large dimension could not be contained. For this very reason, the second position is also incorrect.

The third alternative is also untenable; for there is no appearance of those [atoms] as being supported [by the atoms], and that absence [of such an appearance] exists because color and other qualities exist both internally and externally within their own substrates.
Indeed, the supported objects, such as jujube fruits, do not exist in that manner within another locus, such as a bowl.

It may be argued that although objects such as color and so forth possess the status of being supported (*ādheya*), they do not appear as being situated above [the support] because they lack separate existence (*yutasiddhi*). This is not so; for since "separate existence" and "non-separate existence" are, according to the manner already stated, not definitively established, they cannot be the basis for such an appearance.

Furthermore, separate existence is not the cause for the cognition of being situated above, since this is absent in the case of bamboo stalks standing vertically or horizontally, and in the case of milk and water.
Therefore, when examined, a relation that is in every respect a distinct entity from its relata is not tenable.
On page 297, line 11:
"Because of the relationship between substratum and superstratum, the inherent entities lack independence"—this is incorrect; that relation is not tenable with respect to the inherent entities.
64. Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) apart from the related entities themselves.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Buddhist, who refutes the mere relation by stating that "the cognition of a relation is not real because no relation exists apart from those [relata]," etc.:

Now, once a relation is established, it would be logical to conceive of it as being either distinct from its relata or non-distinct from them; however, that relation is not established, because its own nature cannot be determined. To explain: must the relation of things be characterized by dependence, have the nature of a formal union, or consist in mutual expectancy? In the first case, does this relation exist between two relata that are already established or those that are not yet established? It cannot be between those that are not yet established, because their very nature is non-existent, like the horns of a hare or the son of a barren woman.
Nor can there be a relation between two such [entities] when they are already established, because, like the Sahya and Vindhya mountains, they lack dependence, and thus a relation is untenable.
As it has been said:
"A relation is indeed dependence; what dependence can there be for that which is already established?"
And this has been extracted from: *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 146;
*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 111; and *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 149, upper section.
Therefore, there is no relation for any entity in reality,
nor is it tenable that its nature is a conjunction of forms; for if the two related entities are dual, their conjunction is contradictory.

If they were identical, there would all the more be an absence of relation, because a relation is impossible in the absence of two related entities, since a relation must reside in both. Now, if it is argued that their relation is mere contiguity (*nairantarya*), we say no; for this contiguity, being merely the absence of an interval, is not ultimately real and thus cannot logically constitute a relation. Furthermore, if contiguity were the relation, then even the state of having an interval (*sāntaratā*) would be a relation, as there is no distinction between them. Moreover, is the contact of these two atoms total or partial? If the contact were total, the entire mass would consist of only a single atom.
If there were contact with them by way of a single part, it would follow that atoms have six parts.

And are those parts non-different from the atoms, or different? If they are non-different, then since those [parts] do not exist [as distinct entities], how could there be contact with them by way of a single part?

If, on the other hand, they are different, then the same objection would apply regarding whether those [parts] also contact the atoms in their entirety or by way of a single part, leading to an infinite regress.
And it has been said: "For relation is indeed the fusion of forms (*rūpaśleṣa*); how could that exist when there is duality?

Therefore, in reality, there is no relation between things that are distinct in their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*). Now, suppose this relation is of the nature of dependence on another (*parāpekṣā*). Let that be so; nevertheless, would an entity depend on another while being itself existent or non-existent? It cannot be the case that it is non-existent; for such a thing, like a horse's horn, is contradictory to being a substratum for the property of dependence.
Nor is it existent, because it is devoid of all dependence; otherwise, it would contradict its very existence.
As it has been said: "For a relation is indeed dependence upon another; how can that which is non-existent depend?
And how can an entity that is existent and devoid of all dependence depend?"
Furthermore, is the relation distinct from the relata, or non-distinct? If it were non-distinct, then there would be either just the two relata or just the relation itself.

Now, if it is distinct [from the relata], then how could the two unrelated entities be connected? Or, let it be a separate entity from those two; even so, what is the connection between the two relata and that single relation? Just as there is no connection between the two relata due to the aforementioned defects, so it is here as well. Furthermore, if one were to admit yet another connection between these two and that [primary] relation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because another connection would necessarily follow for that too.
Therefore, the cognition of a "relation" is not real, since a relation distinct from the [relata] does not exist.

In a sentient being, there are two related entities and the relation itself; thus, all things exist in ultimate reality as mutually unmixed, established in their own respective natures. Even though things are of such a nature, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) displays them as if they were mutually mixed.
And it has been said:
"The conjunction of forms... (*rūpasaṃśleṣa*).
For connection is indeed the fusion of forms; how could that exist when there is duality? And this has been stated [in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 148, and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
149]: "Therefore, in reality, there is no connection between things that are distinct by nature."
Now, another [verse]:

"For a relation is indeed dependence on another; how can that which is non-existent depend [on anything]? This has been cited in *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* p. 148, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 149, and *Syādvādaratnākara* p. 813.
And how can an existent that is entirely devoid of expectation depend upon related things?
If it is argued that there is a relation because of the two being connected to a single [third] thing, then that relation belongs to those two.
And this has been cited: *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 147; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
149, upper section; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 813: "What relation [could there be]? And there would be an infinite regress; likewise, there would be no cognition of a relation."

Then— those two entities and that which is other than them, all these abide within their own selves; thus, the entities themselves are unmixed, and it is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that mixes them,
and so forth.

"Those two entities and everything else distinct from them all abide in their own selves; thus, entities are inherently unmixed, and it is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that mixes them. One should consult this very method in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 149, and the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 812, where the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented.
The establishment of the relationship as being characterized by a transformation into unity in some way, preceded by a refutation [of the opponent's view]—herein we respond:

as for what was first stated, beginning with "dependence" (*pāratantrya*) and so forth, that is incorrect; for dependence characterized by a transformation into unity is impossible to deny, as it is established for objects through means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

That which is established by means of valid cognition, such as direct perception, cannot be denied—just as [the existence of] blue and so forth; and this dependence characterized by unity and transformation is established by those very means of valid cognition for external and internal objects.

The Jains intend by "relation" (sambandha)—which is another name for "dependence" (pāratantrya)—a proximity (pratyāsatti) produced by substance, space, time, and state, whose essential nature is the transformation into oneness (ekatvapariṇati). This relation is evident to everyone, from children onwards, through means of valid cognition such as direct perception; for it is perceived directly that color and other qualities residing in a single external composite substance, as well as knowledge, pleasure, and so forth residing within a single self-substance, appear in a state of fusion (lolībhūta).
Furthermore, the existence of the composite substance and the self-substance has already been established previously; therefore, let us refrain from further prolixity.

Likewise, the dependence based on the field (*kṣetranibandhana*), characterized by the transformation into a single unity through the merging of milk, water, and so forth existing within a single field, is perceived directly.

Similarly, that same kind of dependence based on time (*kālanibandhana*) is also perceived directly, as in the case of the mango juice and so forth, or the growth of the limbs of a body in stages such as infancy and so on.

That [proximity] based on manifestation is indeed perceived in the case of substances and modes that are conjoined, because jars, cloths, and so forth undergo transformation into the nature of conjunction, and because the self, pleasure, and so forth possess the nature of consciousness and the like;

and such a proximity is demonstrated as having each [factor] as primary, rather than through the exclusion of others, since even when proximity is defined by substance and so forth, proximity by field and so forth is not precluded (p. 305, l.

— The relationship of [objects such as] a loom and so forth, whether in terms of substance, location, time, or state, is established for someone through their own proximity, and is made clear by another.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 146;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, page 821.
On pages 232 and 261:
because it is impossible to refute the relationship characterized by proximity in terms of substance, space, time, and state.
For it would follow that nothing could be designated (nirupākhyatva), because there is no relation whatsoever—whether direct or indirect—between anything and anything else;
see *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 111, Ā. edition.
The proximity of the field (*kṣetrapratyāsat*) is as follows:
*Tattvārthaśloka*, p.
147, "residing in the self" (*ātmastha*). (*Ātmasu*—Ā.)

As for what was said—that [the relation] exists between two things that are either already established or not yet established—that is an unconsidered statement. For we admit a dependence (*pāratantrya*) between two related entities in some sense.

Indeed, when a real entity (*vastu*) consists of both substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*), it is logical that a substance which is established in its form as substance possesses dependence upon a mode that is not yet established, because it transforms into that [modal] form.

A cloth, for instance, is indeed established in the form of the substance of the threads, since the persisting substance exists even prior to the production of the transformation into a cloth; however, it is not established in its own specific form [as a cloth].
Even a substance such as thread is accomplished in its own nature, yet unaccomplished in the form of a transformation into cloth;

likewise, a substance such as a finger is accomplished in its own nature, yet unaccomplished in the form of a transformation consisting of conjunction. Thus, it should be understood that every entity is both accomplished and unaccomplished, as it partakes in dependence upon other factors.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of dependence among entities, is a relation pervaded by that [dependence] established anywhere in the absence of such relations, or not? If it is established, how can there be an absence of relation everywhere and at all times? This would be a contradiction. If, on the other hand, it is not established, how can the non-existence of the pervaded be proven from the non-existence of the non-pervader? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
(Page 305, Line 13 – *paryāya* – Ā.)

By asserting that there is no relation between entities due to the absence of dependence, [the opponents] either perceive that relation as being pervaded by that [dependence] in some cases, or they do not;
[as stated in] *Tattvārthaśloka* p. 146 and *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 152.

As for what was further stated—namely, "for there is a fusion of forms," and so forth—that too is a refutation only of those who maintain an extremist position (ekāntavādins), not of us, because we accept that the relationship characterized by the fusion of forms has the nature of the two related entities becoming one in some respect (*kathañcit*).

For the "fusion of forms" of the related entities consists in their being inseparable, while their "non-fusion" consists in their possessing unique, specific characteristics. And this does not contradict their duality, since they are perceived as such, just like the single cognition of a variegated form.
For they (the Jainas) define relation as the attainment of some kind of unity between the relata, which is a fusion of their forms (*rūpaśleṣa*),
as stated in the *Tattvārtha-śloka-vārttika*, p. 148.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 152, uttarārdha;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 824:
"of its own nature, [the contact]... (svarūpaśleṣa).
Furthermore,

regarding what was stated— namely, "whether by its entire self or by a single part," and so forth— that too is a mere assertion; for this [bonding] is accepted precisely through another mode, since it is impossible for it to occur either by way of totality or by way of a single part, yet another mode is possible,
and because the cognition of a relation would otherwise be inexplicable, this [bonding] must be accepted as being based on smoothness (*snigdha*) and roughness (*rūkṣa*) through that very other mode.

For in the view of those for whom two distinct related entities—possessing their own prior and subsequent natures that are neither lost nor newly produced—are joined together with one another, this aforementioned defect certainly occurs. In our view, however, the relationship between flour, water, and so forth is intended to be a transformation (*pariṇati*) characterized by a state of total fusion (*ekalolībhāva*), in the form of being conjoined while abandoning a separate form. How, then, could there be even a trace of an opportunity for the aforementioned defects? Furthermore, if such a relationship were not accepted, how could the establishment of variegated cognition (*citrasaṃvedana*) occur? For no other relationship with multiple forms such as blue and so on is possible for variegated consciousness apart from such a transformation; because if it were related to them either in its entirety or in part, all the aforementioned defects would follow as a consequence.

And such a relation between objects occurs, in some cases, through the mutual interpenetration of all their constituent parts (*pradeśa*), as in the case of flour-meal and water; in other cases, however, it occurs merely through the contact of parts, as in the case of fingers and the like.
Furthermore, for one who maintains that things possess parts—whether internally or externally—the consequence of having parts is not a defect, because it is accepted [as true].

Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because there is no absolute difference between the possessor of the parts and its parts. For if there were such a difference, those parts would themselves require a connection with further parts of their own possessors, which would result in an infinite regress; but this is not the case otherwise.

Because a real entity whose nature is non-exclusive (anekāntātmaka) constitutes a distinct category [of existence] due to its absolute difference from and non-difference from [its attributes], just like a variegated cognition;
see page 305, line 23—
[the reading] "asya vā saṃ— " in the *Bāhulya* and *Jaina* manuscripts.
[Viśiṣṭa:

Objection: "In that case, it would follow that atoms too must possess parts. This is not a valid objection, because here the word *aṃśa* (part) is intended to mean either "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) or "constituent part" (*avayava*). If it means intrinsic nature, there is no fault whatsoever, since a differentiation of intrinsic nature is established to that extent by the fact that the connection [of one atom] with multiple other atoms situated in different spatial directions would otherwise be impossible.
However, the meaning of "constituent part" does not apply there, because since atoms are indivisible, constituent parts are impossible.

Now, [the objection]: "If a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) among atoms were possible, how would the thesis of their indivisibility (*avibhāgitva*) not be contradicted?"—this too is untenable; because their indivisibility is said to mean their incapacity to be divided, and not their lack of intrinsic nature (*nisvabhāvatva*). Does the word *aṃśa* here mean "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) or "part" (*avayava*)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 152, u.; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 824).

—[This objection] is refuted by [the fact that it has already been] answered, as stated in the *Āptamīmāṃsā*, the *Bhāṣya*, the *Jaṭī*, and the *Bhāṣya*: "As for what was said—that dependence on another (*parāpekṣā*) and so forth—that is avoided simply because it is not accepted. For those who follow the doctrine of the Lord of Jinas do not accept a relation characterized by dependence on another, since they accept the reality of a transformation into some form of unity (*kathañcidekatva*)."

The claim that the nature of the relation between objects is false because it depends on something else—that the nature of the relation of objects depends on objects whose nature is non-relational—is merely the play of profound ignorance. For in what respect does it depend on another: in its own acquisition of being (*ātmalābha*), or in the conventional usage of the relation? It cannot be in its acquisition of being; for the acquisition of being of the relation, characterized by the transformation into unity, is perceived from its own collection of causes alone, without depending on anything else.

The fact that its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is dependent upon another does not establish its falsity (*mithyātva*), because it is not the opposite of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*). Indeed, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that wherever a convention is dependent on another, there must be a lack of ultimate existence; otherwise, since the convention of "more vivid" and so forth regarding the Buddha’s cognition is dependent on other cognitions, it would follow that his cognition lacks ultimate existence, which would result in the total destruction of the root for one who desires gain.

And how could the non-relational nature of objects be established as real for one who speaks thus, given that this too is no different from being relative? [The opponent might argue: "That which appears in perceptual cognition is indeed non-relative, but when determined by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following upon that perception, it is relative—and likewise unreal. This is the same in other cases as well; for the relation certainly does appear in direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), such that it would not be non-relative. Indeed, an object that lacks the transformation into oneness internally and externally does not appear even in a dream.
And because the nature of a relation is dependent, it is a false appearance;
*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 148; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 152, u. 1. *Pṛ.* 306, l. 6.
...regard for [the outside], or [the word] "outside" (syād ratnāvalyām pṛṣṭha 825 –pekṣā ā –barhir vā ba, ja).

Regarding what was stated—"because of the connection of two with one," and so forth—that too is a refutation only for those who maintain an extremist (ekānta) position, since they alone admit an absolute distinction between the relation and the related entities. It is not [a refutation] for us, because we do not admit a relationship of "related entity and relation" that exists apart from their state of being merged into a single unity (*ekalolībhāva*). And since such a state has been described as falling within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is incorrect to say: "Entities are themselves unmixed; it is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that mixes them."

Therefore, since the very type of relationship already described is established in the case of parts and wholes and so forth, even the category of "inherence" (samavāya) postulated by others is not tenable.

Thus, since the six categories set forth by Kaṇāda in the Vaiśeṣika system are found to be unstable when scrutinized, the establishment of an object in the extreme of difference (bhedaikānta) as defined by that system is not possible. (Page 306, Line 16)

Let it be that the category of *samavāya* (inherence) is not established there [in the Vaiśeṣika system]; however, its establishment will occur in that system of sixteen categories— such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)— composed by Akṣapāda, because these [categories], being characterized by distinct definitions and thus absolutely different from one another, are logically established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since it is possible to establish the specific definitions of these categories that have been mentioned there in general, he indicates the sixteen categories in the Sūtra by way of enumeration: "The attainment of the supreme good results from the knowledge of the truth regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the objects of valid cognition (prameya), doubt (saṃśaya), purpose (prayojana), example (dṛṣṭānta), tenet (siddhānta), members of a syllogism (avayava), reasoning (tarka), ascertainment (nirṇaya), discussion (vāda), destructive debate (jalpa), cavil (vitaṇḍā), fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa), quibble (chala), futile rejoinder (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna).
— Nyāyasūtra 1.1.1.
Thus, in this context, the means for the determination of an object is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and that is fourfold: perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the valid cognitions.
Because it is stated in the Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3.

Thus, when the [objects] have been taught by means of the four instruments of knowledge (pramāṇa)— namely, those called perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), reasoning (yukti), and verbal testimony (śabda) [Caraka-saṃhitā, Sūtra-sthāna, p.
69]— the objects of knowledge (prameya) to be determined by them are of twelve kinds, beginning with the self (ātman).

And thus says the Sūtra: "The self, the body, the sense organs, the objects, cognition, the mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation are the objects of valid knowledge" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.9).

Thus, in this context, the self (*ātman*) is the witness of everything that serves as a means to pleasure and pain, and it is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) by virtue of being the substratum for all cognitions of pleasure and so forth. Its body is the locus of enjoyment; the sense organs are the instruments of enjoyment; the objects of the senses are what are to be enjoyed; and cognition (*buddhi*) is the enjoyment itself. Since the sense organs are not capable of perceiving all objects, the mind (*manas*) has all things as its domain.
Activity (*pravṛtti*)—consisting of merit and demerit—is the cause of the cessation of the body, sense organs, objects, cognitions, pleasure, and pain.
The defects (*doṣa*) are attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) is the soul’s connection with another set of bodies and so forth, following its connection with the body, sense organs, cognitions, and sensations that have already arisen.
The fruit produced by the defects of worldly activity— the experience of pleasure and pain—
is suffering characterized by affliction (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.21).
And because it must be avoided with effort, it is mentioned separately from the result;
liberation (apavarga) is the absolute separation from suffering, which is divided into twenty-one types beginning with the body.
In that regard, the Self (ātman) is the seer of all, the enjoyer of all, omniscient, and the experiencer of all;

its locus of enjoyment is the body, the loci of enjoyment are the sense organs, the objects of enjoyment are the sense-objects, and the enjoyment is cognition (buddhi). Since the sense organs are not capable of perceiving all objects, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the mind (manas), which has all things as its domain. Activity (pravṛtti), the defects (doṣas), and the cessation thereof are the causes for the production and dissolution of the body, the sense organs, the objects, cognition, and the experience of pleasure and pain. (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.2)

1.9 Nivṛtti—Ārya-śūra’s *Jātakamālā* (The Garland of Birth Stories) 1.9.10. The Story of the Monkey King. Once, when the Bodhisattva was dwelling as a monkey king in a certain forest thicket, he saw a man who had fallen into a pit of glowing embers. Seeing him, the Great Being felt compassion for that man and, out of his great compassion, descended from the tree and entered the pit of embers. Having entered, he took hold of the man by the hand and drew him out. Then, having drawn him out, he led him away from that place to safety. And having led him away, he spoke these words to him: "Friend, do not go back to that same place again; it would be a disaster. But the man, being foolish and lacking wisdom, did not heed those words. He went back to that very same place and fell once more into the pit of glowing embers. Thereupon, the Great Being, seeing that the man had fallen into the pit of embers once again, felt even greater compassion for him than before. And with a heart full of sorrow, he lamented:

"Alas, how much more difficult it is to find one who speaks the truth than to find one who listens to the truth! 1.9.2. The Story of the Elephant King. Once, when the Bodhisattva was dwelling as an elephant king in a certain mountain forest, he saw a man who had been struck down by a poisoned arrow and was suffering. Seeing him, the Great Being felt compassion for that man and, out of his great compassion, went to where the man was lying. Having gone there, he asked the man: "Friend, what is your ailment? The man replied: "I have been struck by a poisoned arrow. Then the Great Being, feeling compassion for the man, went to where the hunter was staying and said to him: "Friend, give me this poisoned arrow. The hunter replied: "I will not give it to you; it is my livelihood. The Great Being said: "Friend, if you do not give it to me, I shall take it by force. The hunter thought: "This elephant is powerful and strong; if I do not give it to him, he might take it by force. Thinking thus, he gave the poisoned arrow to the Great Being. Then the Great Being, having received the poisoned arrow, went to where the man was lying and extracted the arrow from his body. Having extracted it, he applied a medicinal herb to the wound. Then the man, having been cured of his illness, recovered his strength and rose up. And having risen, he bowed his head at the feet of the Great Being and said: "Noble sir, you have saved my life. The Great Being said: "Friend, do not think that I have done something difficult; rather, it is the nature of the compassionate that they act for the benefit of others. 1.9.3. The Story of the Tortoise King. Once, when the Bodhisattva was dwelling as a tortoise king in a certain lake, he saw a man who had been swept away by a great flood and was struggling in the water. Seeing him, the Great Being felt compassion for that man and, out of his great compassion, went into the water and carried the man on his back to the shore. Having carried him to the shore, he set him down on dry land and spoke these words to him: "Friend, do not go back into the water again; it would be a disaster. But the man, being foolish and lacking wisdom, did not heed those words. He went back into the water and was swept away once more by the flood. Thereupon, the Great Being, seeing that the man had been swept away once again, felt even greater compassion for him than before. And with a heart full of sorrow, he lamented: "Alas, how much more difficult it is to find one who speaks the truth than to find one who listens to the truth! 1.9.4. The Story of the Deer King. Once, when the Bodhisattva was dwelling as a deer king in a certain forest thicket, he saw a man who had been struck down by a poisoned arrow and was suffering. Seeing him, the Great Being felt compassion for that man and, out of his great compassion, went to where the man was lying. Having gone there, he asked the man: "Friend, what is your ailment? The man replied: "I have been struck by a poisoned arrow. Then the Great Being, feeling compassion for the man, went to where the hunter was staying and said to him: "Friend, give me this poisoned arrow. The hunter replied: "I will not give it to you; it is my livelihood.
The Great Being
Activity consists of merit and demerit (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
428); its threefold nature arises because passion, hatred, and delusion are distinct entities.
Nyāyasūtra 4.1.3

Rebirth after death (*pretyabhāva*) is the renewed arising of one who has been born, having died in some category of beings; this renewed arising of one who is born and connected [to a body] is rebirth after death. Connection, however, consists of the body, the sense faculties, the mind, the intellect, and sensations.
Rebirth is the connection once again with a body and so forth (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.19).
19. Pretyabhāva (rebirth) is the abandonment of the previous aggregate consisting of the body, sense organs, and so forth, and the assumption of another aggregate;
*Nyāyakalikā*, p. 7.
The object produced by the activity of the senses, their objects, and the cognitions thereof is the result; the experience of pleasure and pain is the result.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.20

The primary fruit is that which consists of pleasure and pain and generates activity and defects; its means, however, is secondary (Nyāyakalikā, p. 7). Although suffering, which is of the nature of oppression, is already implied by the mention of the fruit, it is taught for the purpose of cultivating the realization of its nature as suffering even in that which is conventionally regarded as not being suffering.
For this very reason, although it is indeed a result (*phala*), pleasure (*sukha*) is not explicitly mentioned here [among the sufferings], as stated in the *Nyāyakalikā* (p. 7):
"Sufferings consist of twenty-one items: the body, the six sense organs, the six objects, the six cognitions, pleasure, and pain."
Liberation... (Muktāvalī, p. 42); "Apavarga is the absolute release from that [suffering]" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.22).
1.22 Apavarga is the absolute cessation of suffering; it is the abiding of the self in its own essential nature, divested of all qualities.
*Nyāyakalikā*, p. 7:

Doubt is a deliberation on multiple objects; it is a deliberation requiring specific characteristics due to the occurrence of common or multiple properties, and due to the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception. *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.23.

1.23 According to the statement of the author of the Sūtras, and in the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, that [doubt] is threefold; for it is said: "Doubt is a deliberation requiring further particulars, arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, and from the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception."

Because the common property (*samānadharma*)—namely, tallness (*ūrdhvatā*)—is found or perceived in both the post (*sthāṇu*) and the person (*puruṣa*), and because that perceived common property is not the cause of doubt by itself, but rather depends upon a specific distinction (*viśeṣāpekṣa*) due to the lack of a settled determination between perception and non-perception; for, due to the lack of a settled determination between perception and non-perception, there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish or refute either side regarding the specific distinction. Thus, the deliberation (*vimarśa*) as to whether it is a post or a person is "doubt" (*saṃśaya*).

Likewise, "multiple" refers to both that which is of the same class (*samānajātīya*) and that which is of a different class (*asamānajātīya*). A property (*dharma*) excluded from multiple things is called "multiple-property" (*anekadharma*). Due to the occurrence of such a property, and because there is no fixed determination regarding its perception or non-perception, doubt arises depending on specific characteristics. For example, upon observing that sound is produced by disjunction (*vibhāga*), one wonders: "Is this a quality (*guṇa*), a substance (*dravya*), or an action (*karman*)? For the property of being produced by disjunction does not reside in any quality of the same class, nor in a substance or an action of a different class; therefore, it is a cause for doubt—of what kind of entity is this [sound] that possesses the property of being produced by disjunction?

Likewise, from conflicting opinions and from the lack of a fixed determination regarding perception and non-perception, there arises doubt that requires further qualification; for example, some say "the self exists," while others say "the self does not exist. Since existence and non-existence cannot coexist equally in one and the same thing, there is consequently a lack of ascertainment of the truth as to whether the self exists or does not exist—this is doubt (*saṃśaya*). Doubt is defined as a state of uncertainty regarding objects that are themselves uncertain (Caraka Saṃhitā, p. 264).
The view of both causes [of doubt] is stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, page 709:

"Doubt is a deliberation that depends upon specific characteristics, arising from the perception of common and multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception."
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.23
And here, "deliberation" (*vimarśa*) means "doubt" (*saṃśaya*); this is the general definition of doubt according to the *Tātparya-ṭīkā* (p. 247).

"Deliberation" is the consideration of contradictory objects, as in "Is it a post or a person? By this much, the general definition has been stated, which is common to the five types of homogeneous doubt and which distinguishes it from heterogeneous categories such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, other Buddhists [hold that] doubt is a deliberation arising from the perception of similarity in one who desires to apprehend a specific distinction; see Nyāyabhāṣya, p.
100. Nyāyamañjarī, p. 556.
In that regard, doubt is of only three kinds: arising from the perception of common properties, the perception of multiple properties, and conflicting testimony (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.23).
On page 23, line 87:
In that regard, perception and non-perception do not individually constitute causes for doubt.
Nyāyavārttika, p. 96:
"Dependent [on that], doubt [arises]... This common property (sādhāraṇadharma), when perceived, is the cause of doubt.
Is it alone? No, it is not alone; rather, it is because of the lack of a fixed rule regarding perception and non-perception, provided that perception and non-perception do not remain established.
Is this alone the means [of doubt]? No, it is said:

if there is a desire for a specific distinction, one perceives a common property; perception and non-perception do not remain fixed as "this" or "not this," and when there is a desire for a specific distinction, doubt regarding the object arises (Nyāyavārttika, p. 89).
The means of valid cognition for the proponent—[Śrīdhara]:

Now, what is the meaning of "having multiple properties" (*anekadharma*)? It is a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), because it distinguishes [the subject] from both similar and dissimilar classes. "Multiple" (*aneka*) refers to both the similar class and the dissimilar class; therefore, that which is a distinguishing factor (*viśeṣaka*) among these many is a property (*dharma*), and thus it is called "having multiple properties" (*anekadharma*).
"A property that is the cause of both unitary and manifold cognitions is a manifold property;
because of the conflict [between these], there is doubt" (Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 91).

The meaning of the term *vipratipatti* (contradictory assertion) is the proclamation of contradictory meanings; when one perceives that there is a state of being the object of such a proclamation of contradictory meanings, and when there is an instability regarding both perception and non-perception, and when there is recollection of the specific qualities pertaining to those [objects], doubt arises—thus says the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 96.

According to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, perception and non-perception are distinct causes of doubt, and thus doubt is fivefold. To explain: from the occurrence of perception and the lack of a fixed determination regarding perception and non-perception, there arises a doubt that requires further specific characteristics. For example, water is perceived when it exists, yet it is not perceived in mirages when it does not exist. Now, upon perceiving water somewhere, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine its true nature, the doubt arises: "Is this water real, or is it unreal?"

Likewise, because non-apprehension is possible, doubt arises from the lack of a settled distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension, depending on specific characteristics. For example, there is doubt as to whether a tree-root, a stake, or the like—which exists—is not being perceived, or whether it is something non-existent that has not yet arisen or has already ceased; or even whether a *piśāca* (demon), which exists, is not being perceived now, or whether it is non-existent. This is the case when the common characteristic resides in the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). However, the distinction is that contradiction, apprehension, and non-apprehension reside in the knower (*jñātṛ*). Furthermore, regarding the unsettled state of apprehension: water is apprehended as existing in ponds and the like, while water is apprehended as non-existent in mirages.

Therefore, since no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes reality is perceived when something is being perceived in some cases, the doubt arises as to whether what is perceived is existent or non-existent;
*Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.1.23.

Because non-apprehension is not determinative, that which exists—such as the root of a tree, a wooden pin, or water—is not apprehended; and that which does not exist—such as what is unarisen or ceased—is likewise not apprehended.
Therefore, when something is not apprehended in a certain place, a doubt arises as to whether it exists but is not apprehended, or whether it does not exist at all. Thus, there is doubt.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.23
The property common to many resides in the object of knowledge, whereas apprehension and non-apprehension reside in the knower.
(Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.23)

The author of the Vārttika, however, does not accept that similarity and multiplicity of properties residing in the object of cognition (*jñeya*) are the cause [of doubt]. He says: "We do not understand this either—that similarity and multiplicity of properties reside in the object of cognition;
for here, is it the property (*dharma*) that is the cause of doubt, or is it the cognition (*jñāna*)?"
It has been established in many ways that the property (*dharma*) itself is not the cause of doubt;

rather, it is the cognition of common or multiple properties that is the cause of doubt, and since that cognition resides in the knower, there is no distinction [between the property and its cognition].
(Nyāyavārttika, p. 96)
The purpose (*prayojana*) consists in the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful, as well as the means to achieve them.
That object with reference to which one acts is the purpose;
*Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.24.
From this statement,
it follows that the purpose (*prayojana*) is that object which, having been determined as something to be attained or avoided, one proceeds toward.
And that [purpose] is twofold: primary and secondary.

The primary consists in the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering; the secondary, however, is the means to those, which is called "purpose" (prayojana), for the sake of which undertakings are commenced.

"That object which, having determined whether it is to be acquired or abandoned, one undertakes the means for its acquisition or abandonment—that is to be known as the purpose (prayojana). — Carakasaṃhitā, p.
264; Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.1.
1.24 And that [meaning] is of two kinds, distinguished as figurative and primary.
The primary [goal] is the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering; the means to that is secondary. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 563;
Nyāyakalikā, p. 8)
An example (dṛṣṭānta) is the locus for ascertaining the invariable concomitance (pratibandha);
and thus the Sūtra states: "That object upon which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts is an example" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.25).
Ordinary people have not attained excellence, whether innate or acquired; those who are the opposite of them are the investigators (parīkṣakas).
*Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.1.25.

1.25 An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is an object that serves as a locus for the similarity of cognition between [the proponent and the opponent], either by way of being the subject of the probandum and the probans, or by way of being devoid of them.
In this context, an "example" is that wherein there is a commonality of understanding between the ignorant and the learned.
In the *Carakasamhitā* (p.
263), it is stated that an illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntavacana*) should indeed be uttered when there is a commonality of understanding between ordinary people and noble ones;
for an illustration is of two kinds: the complete illustration (*sampūrṇadṛṣṭānta*) and the partial illustration (*āṃśikadṛṣṭānta*).
*Nyāyamukha*, p.
5: A thesis (*siddhānta*) is an object possessing both general and particular characteristics that is accepted on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
A thesis is the established position resulting from the acceptance of a system (*tantra*) or a specific context (*adhikaraṇa*).
According to the statement of the author of the Sūtras in Nyāyasūtra 1.1.26.

*Tantra* means a treatise (*śāstra*). Those objects which have a treatise as their basis are called *tantrādhikaraṇa*. The established acceptance (*abhyupagama-saṃsthiti*) of these is the *siddhānta*, defined as the rule regarding their specific mode of being.

It is of four kinds, because of the difference in the meaning of the established acceptance of a treatise: the universal (*sarvatantra*), the particular (*pratitantra*), the topical (*adhikaraṇa*), and the accepted (*abhyupagama*)—Nyāyasūtra 1.1.26.
1.27 Therein, an object that is not contradicted by any system and is accepted within a system is a tenet established by all systems (sarvatantrasiddhānta). Nyāyasūtra 1.1.28.

1.28 That which is the object of agreement for all [schools]— such as that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the instruments for establishing objects of cognition (*prameya*), that the sense organs (*indriya*) such as the nose and so forth exist, and that their respective objects (*artha*) such as odor and so forth exist—
is a tenet established in one system but not established in other systems (*pratitantrasiddhānta*). It is well-known in its own school but unestablished in other schools.
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.29:
For example, according to the Yogas, the sense organs are material; according to the Sāṃkhyas, they are non-material.
That, upon whose establishment there is the establishment of another topic, is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on a supporting argument),
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.30.

30. *Adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on the context) is that when, upon the proof of a certain reason, there is the proof of another intended thesis (*pratijñārtha*) being processed; for example, when by means of [the reason] "being an effect" and so forth, the general [conclusion] of an intelligent cause is established regarding the earth and other things, there follows the establishment of another cause capable of producing it—namely, one who is the substratum of eternal knowledge, will, and effort.
*Abhyupagamasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on acceptance) is the examination of specific details arising from an unexamined acceptance.
(Nyāyasūtra 1.1.30)
When some object is accepted without examination and its specific qualities are then examined, that is an *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (a tenet based on provisional acceptance).
For example: "Let sound be a substance; however, is it eternal or non-eternal? Having accepted the substantiality of sound, its specific quality—whether it is eternal or non-eternal—is then examined.

A tenet (*siddhānta*) is that which, having been established by means of various reasons after being examined in many ways by investigators, is set forth as a conclusion; that is a tenet (*Caraka-saṃhitā*, p.
263). A collection of objects that is accepted as being "thus" and "of such a nature" is established (*siddha*); the formal establishment of what is established is a tenet (*siddhānta*).
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.26
"A tenet (*siddhānta*) is the acceptance of an object possessing both general and particular properties," according to the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (p.
103). A tenet is an object that is the subject of an admission based upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and which possesses both general and particular properties.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
565; *Nyāyakalikā*, p. 9: The detailed establishment and determination of the probandum by means of reasons.

He states the definition of this established tenet (*siddhānta*): "How many are the characteristics of the established tenets? To this it is replied: there are four—namely, that which is entirely equal, that which is equal at first and different later, and that which is different at first and equal later (Upāyahṛdaya, p. 6).

*Tantra*—the teaching of a collection of objects interconnected with one another—is a treatise; it is the establishment of an acceptance, the adoption of a meaning not yet determined for the sake of examining its specific details; this is the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (accepted tenet). (*Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.1.26)

Those objects which possess a system (tantra) as their basis (adhikaraṇa) are called "system-based" (tantrādhikaraṇa). The established position of acceptance regarding these, the determination of their mode of being, and the rule of properties (dharmaniyama), constitute a tenet (siddhānta).
What is meant by this? It means that an object which is not established by a treatise (śāstra) cannot be a tenet through its mere acceptance.
The *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 104, states:
"The tenet established by all schools (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*) is as follows: there are causes, there are diseases, there are means of cure, and there are curable [conditions].
The *Carakasamhitā*, p. 263, states the same.
A tenet established by all systems (sarvatantrasiddhānta) is that which is the object of agreement for all;
for example, "the means of valid cognition are the instruments for establishing the objects of cognition" (Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 104).
Just as the sense organs, such as the nose and so forth, and the objects of the senses, such as odor and so forth, [are distinct], Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.4.
That which is taught in one's own treatise and is not contradicted by any other treatise is a *sarvatantrasiddhānta* (a tenet established for all systems),
according to the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 565.
*Nyāyakalī*, p. 9:

"Established in a system" (*tantrasiddha*)—in the *ba* and *ja* manuscripts, this is called "a tenet established in a particular system" (*pratitantrasiddhānta*), meaning that which is well-known within that specific system.
Carakasamhitā, p.
263: The necessary acceptance of the universal (sāmānya), the particular (viśeṣa), and that which possesses them (tadvat) is the tenet established within one's own system (pratitantrasiddhānta);

for example, that the sense organs are composed of material elements (bhautika) according to the followers of Yoga (Yauga), whereas they are not composed of material elements (abhautika) according to the Sāṃkhyas.
*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 105:
"The established tenet (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*) is that when a particular topic is being discussed, other topics also become established;
*Carakasamhitā*, p. 264."
"In the establishment of the meaning of a sentence, that meaning which follows as a consequence is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*," according to the *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 105.

Therefore, when a certain object is being known, those objects which follow as its consequences are known by being included within it; that object, being directly under discussion, is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of its consequences because their establishment depends upon it. Whether that [object] be the subject (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*), it is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* in that form.
First, regarding the thesis: that which is the subject of dispute has an intelligent cause because it is produced, like cloth and so forth.

For here, when the fact of having an intelligent predecessor is being established for earth and the rest by means of their being produced, what is established is precisely their being endowed with omniscience and other qualities that follow as a necessary consequence within its own proof (Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā 1).
1.30 pratikriyā— ba, ja.

The *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (presumptive tenet) is that which [the disputants] accept at the time of debate—an object that is unestablished, unexamined, or lacks a stated reason—just as physicians do (Caraka Saṃhitā, p.

264). In this regard, when some category of object is accepted without examination—such as, "Let sound be a substance; however, is it eternal or non-eternal?"—and its specific quality, such as the eternality or non-eternality of that which exists as a substance, is then examined, that is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta*.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.31
An unexamined tenet (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*) refers to that meaning which is not established in the *sūtras* but is accepted in the treatises (*śāstra*).
For example, for the Naiyāyikas, "the mind is a sense-faculty" (*mana indriyam*); and for the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas, "the ear is space" (*śrotram ākāśam*).

"Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that the 'abhyupagamasiddhānta' (the tenet of acceptance) is an unexamined admission made by a proponent for the sake of examining specific details" (Nyāyavārttika, p. 105;
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 568).

*Nyāyakalika*, p. 10: The members (*avayava*) are parts of the statement of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). There are five [members], which are parts of that collection of words within which the establishment of the object to be proven is fully completed.
And thus says the Sūtra: "The thesis, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion are the members [of a syllogism].
(Nyāyasūtra 1.1.32)
32. Among these, the statement of the probandum is the proposition (pratijñā);
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.33.

The statement that apprehends a subject (dharmin) as qualified by a property (dharma) to be made known is the indication of the probandum (sādhyanirdeśa); for example, "Sound is impermanent" (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1).
The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*).
(Nyāyasūtra 1.1.34)

34. The reason (*hetu*) is the demonstration of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) through similarity with an example (*udāharaṇa*), as in: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced, like a jar. Likewise, [it is demonstrated] through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.35)

1.35 A reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum through dissimilarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-vaidharmya*); for instance: "This living body is not soulless, because [if it were] it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth, like a clod of earth.
An example (*udāharaṇa*) is an illustration that possesses the property of the probandum through similarity with it (*sādhyasādharmya*).

Nyāyasūtra 1.1.36: "Sādharmya" means having a common property (*samānadharmatā*).
