From that [common property], it is "taddharmabhāvī"—that is, possessing the property of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). Here, by the word "sādhya," the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven is understood. Its "bhāva" (state/possession) is the "sādhyadharmabhāva. That example in which this exists is "taddharmabhāvī. For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced, like a pot"—this is an example based on similarity (*sādharmyodāharaṇa*).
The opposite of that is the reverse.
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.23.
37. "Example" (udāharaṇa) is connected with the subject under discussion.

Its opposite—by way of dissimilarity from the probandum (sādhyavaidharmya)—is an instance that does not possess that property; this is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced; for whatever is eternal does not have the property of being produced, such as atoms and so forth.
The application (*upanaya*) is the conclusion regarding the probandum, based on the example, in the form "it is so" (*tathā*) or "it is not so" (*na tathā*).
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.38:

"Dependent on the example" (udāharaṇāpekṣaḥ) means dependent upon the example; in an example that possesses similarity with the probandum (sādhyasādharmya), such as "and likewise sound is characterized by the property of being produced," the fact that the probandum, sound, is characterized by the property of being produced is subsumed [into the conclusion].

In a [statement] endowed with dissimilarity to the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*), however—such as "Substances like space possess the property of non-origination and are eternal, but sound is not so"—the property of having the nature of origination is established by the negation of the application of the property of non-origination. The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) based on the indication of the reason; *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.39.
1.39 When the reason has been applied by way of similarity or dissimilarity as in the example, the restatement of the proposition is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Since the formulation of the statement of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is established, its constituent parts (*avayava*) are logically required.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 569;
*Nyāyakalikā*, p.

9: "In whatever collection of words the establishment of the object to be proved is completed, its five members—beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*)—are called 'members' (*avayava*) in relation to that collection."
And thus the reading "tathā ca sūtram" (and so the aphorism) is found in all manuscripts immediately after the word "avayavāḥ" (the members); however,
in accordance with the Nyāya-sūtras as they have been received, we have placed it immediately after the word "pañca" (five).
A proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of that which is to be proven, such as "the person is eternal" (Caraka Saṃhitā, p.
262); a reason (*hetu*) is the cause of apprehension.
The statement of the mark (*liṅgavacana*) is the reason (*hetu*), according to Carakasamhitā p.
263 and Nyāyakandalī p. 10.

The proof of the property to be established (sādhya-dharma) by means of a general similarity through an example is as follows: having connected the reason with the property to be established and having connected it with the example, the statement of its being a means of proof is the reason, such as "because of the nature of having the property of arising"; for it is observed that whatever has the property of arising is impermanent.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.34

And how can there be proof of the probandum through a reason that lacks similarity to the example? [For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced; that which has the property of not being produced is permanent, such as the substance of the self (ātman) and so forth" (Nyāyabhāṣya 1).

1.35 The commentary states, "The example is: 'Sound is impermanent,'" but we consider this to be incorrect, because it is merely a difference in formulation; for it is only the formulation that differs, not the meaning.
And because there is only a difference in the example (*udāharaṇa*): only the example differs [when one says] "the self is like a jar";
therefore, this example is not logical.
The correct example, however, is: "this living body is not without a self, because [otherwise] it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth."
*Nyāyavārttika* p. 122;
*Nyāyamañjarī* 575:

"Similarity with the probandum" (*sādhyena sādharmyam*) means having a common property (*samānadharmatā*). Because of this similarity with the probandum as the cause, the example is that which possesses the properties of that [probandum].

Its property is *taddharma*. Its [property]—that is, the property of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*)—is of two kinds: either a property qualified by the subject, as in "the impermanence of sound," or a subject qualified by a property, as in "sound is impermanent. Here, the latter is understood by the mention of "its" (*tasya*). Its property is *taddharma*; the state of being that property is *taddharmabhāva*. That example in which this *taddharmabhāva* exists is an example because of its similarity to the thing to be proven; it possesses the state of having that property (*taddharmabhāvī*), and it is intended as the *udāharaṇa* (illustration).
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.36
An example (*udāharaṇa*) is the statement of a correct illustration;
[as stated in] the *Nyāyasāra*, p.
12: "The statement of an illustration is an example."

Where the existence of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the property that proves it (*sādhana*) is made known by way of the relationship between the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*), that is the example based on similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*).
The statement expressing the relationship of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) contained therein is the "exemplification" (*udāharaṇa*).
(Nyāyakalikā, p. 11)

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the subject under discussion; an example that possesses the property of being dissimilar to the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*) because it does not possess that property is the "illustration" (*udāharaṇa*). For instance:
"Sound is impermanent because it has the property of arising; that which has the property of not arising is permanent, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth. (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.36)

The *upanaya* (application) is the statement that, by means of the example, makes known the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) of the probans whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is established in the example.
*Nyāyasāra*, p. 14:
"Dependent on the example" (*udāharaṇāpekṣa*), "governed by the example" (*udāharaṇatantra*), and "under the influence of the example" (*udāharaṇavaśa*)—where *vaśa* means capacity (*sāmarthya*).

In an example that possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), such as "a substance like a cooking pot is seen to have the property of arising and to be impermanent; likewise, sound has the property of arising," the fact that sound, which is the subject to be proven, possesses the property of arising is thereby subsumed.

Furthermore, in an example characterized by dissimilarity to the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*), such as "substances like the self (*ātman*) are seen to be eternal because they do not possess the property of being produced, whereas sound is not so," the property of not possessing the nature of being produced is negated in the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). Consequently, the property of possessing the nature of being produced is concluded; this constitutes the two-fold nature of the conclusion (*upasahāradvaita*) resulting from the two-fold nature of the example (*udāharaṇadvaita*).
(Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.38)
1.38 – [The commentary on] Dharmaka by Ācārya Ba and Ja.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the demonstration of the capacity [of the proof] when all [the members of the syllogism] converge upon a single object;

it is the restatement of the matter under discussion in the thesis (*pratijñā*) once it has been established by all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the purpose of negating the possibility of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*). (Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 9)
The *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 137: "The restatement of the proposition together with its reason, following the application (*upanaya*), is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The *Nyāyasāra*, p. 15.
—Haraṇasā— Ācārya, Bhāṣya, Śrī:

Whether in a statement of similarity (*sādharmya*) or a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), when the conclusion is drawn according to the example, such as "therefore, because it possesses the property of being produced, sound is impermanent," this is the *nigamana* (conclusion).
It is called *nigamana* because the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), and application (*upanaya*) are all brought together (*nigamyante*) into one.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.39
*Tarka* (reasoning) is the cognition of probability regarding one of two possible sides of a doubtful matter, due to the observation of reasons favorable to that side;

and thus the Sūtra states: "Tarka is an inference (*ūha*) for the sake of knowing the true nature of an object whose reality is unknown, based on the logical possibility of its causes" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.40).

Regarding an object whose true nature is unknown and which is thus doubtful—such as the verticality [of a post]—*tarka* (presumption) is the deliberation (*ūha*) that "this must be a person," based on the perception of a supporting cause, namely the presence of a place suitable for a man's amorous play.

If one asks, "For what purpose is this? it is for the sake of knowing reality (*tattvajñāna*), that is, for the sake of the operation of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) known as inference (*anumāna*).

For the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) determine an object that has been distinguished by reasoning (*tarka*). Thus, reasoning—which assists the means of valid cognition—is an inference (*ūha*) for the sake of the knowledge of reality; it occurs when the true nature of a subject (*dharmin*) is not yet known but is known in a general way. Upon seeing a cause favorable to one side, it produces a conviction of probability regarding that [side], appearing as its necessity, while weakening the other side. By thus assisting the means of valid cognition that apprehend that [truth] and facilitating their easy operation, reasoning is for the purpose of the knowledge of reality. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 586)

The followers of Jaimini, however, state that *ūha* is the modification of a ritual application through reasoning; and it is of three kinds, pertaining to the sphere of mantras, *sāmans*, and consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*). *Nyāyakalikā*, p. 13.
As stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

588: "Or, for example, in a place for outdoor recreation and the like, from the perception of a substratum qualified by height, there arises the cognition: 'This must be a man,'" as noted in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 586.
Or, for example, in a place where horses play, upon seeing something upright, there arises a cognitive state of probability (*sambhāvanā-pratyaya*) that "this must be a person";
yet this is not doubt (*saṃśaya*),
because in a place where horses play, the existence of a post (*sthāṇu*) is improbable, just as it is for a person.
In the *Nyāyakalikā* (p.

13): "Reasoning (*tarka*) is not subsumed under the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it a separate means of valid cognition; rather, it serves as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition for the sake of attaining knowledge of reality.
In the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (p. 10).

But how is it that this [inquiry] has the purpose of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), yet is not itself the knowledge of reality? Because it is non-conclusive (*anavadhāraṇāt*). It allows for one or another property through the application of reasons, but it does not determine, "This is exactly so. How, then, is it the purpose of the knowledge of reality? Because from the deliberation (*ūha*)—characterized by the allowance of the object of the knowledge of reality—which has been cultivated and purified, the knowledge of reality subsequently arises through the power of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus it is the purpose of the knowledge of reality. (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.1)
1.40 How, then, does this [treatise] serve the purpose of knowledge of reality? By means of the discernment of the objects of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By this [definition], he distinguishes the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [showing] that "this matter is logical"; for the means of valid cognition, when they operate, cause one to understand the object as it truly is, as distinguished from mere reasoning (*tarka*). (Nyāyavārttika, p. 141) Determination (*nirṇaya*) is the realization of reality born from the proof and the refutation [of opposing views].
And the Sūtra states: "Nirṇaya (ascertainment) is the determination of the meaning through the examination of a thesis and its counter-thesis" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.41).

41. Having reflected—having doubted whether sound is impermanent or permanent—the determination of the object to be proven (*sādhya*) as "this is indeed impermanent because it is produced" is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment). For it is said that the thesis and the counter-thesis (*pakṣapratipakṣau*) consist of the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*upālambha*), based upon the thesis and the counter-thesis. By the word "thesis" (*pakṣa*), the proof concerning the subject of the thesis is expressed; by the word "counter-thesis" (*pratipakṣa*), the refutation of the proof concerning the subject of the thesis is expressed. The ascertainment of the object through those two, namely the proof and the refutation, is *nirṇaya*. (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.41)

1.41 *Nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is the determination of one of the two sides through the examination of the proof and refutation regarding the subject matter of the proponent's position and the opponent's counter-position.
*Nyāyakalikā*, p. 13:
Debate (*vāda*) has as its fruit the determination of the subject matter of a discourse free from passion;

likewise, the Sūtra states: "Debate is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, characterized by the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning, the refutation [of the opponent's position], not contradicting established tenets, and consisting of the five members."
Nyāyasūtra 1.2.1.

The two properties of a real entity (*vastu-dharmau*) that constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) must share a single locus (*ekādhikaraṇau*), be contradictory (*viruddhau*), exist at the same time (*ekakālau*), and be established (*anavasitau*).
These properties of the real entity are specific attributes (*viśeṣa*) of the entity itself, such as "the self exists" or "the self does not exist.

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum (*āśraya*); those two [properties] which have a single locus instigate an investigation, whereas those with different loci do not. Furthermore, they must be contradictory, as in the case of "the self is eternal" versus "consciousness is impermanent."

Even when not contradictory, two properties do not necessitate investigation, as in the case of "substance possesses action" and "substance possesses quality. Even when occurring at different times, two properties are not subject to investigation because both are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of "substance possesses action" and "substance is inactive," which are determined when there is a difference in time; such properties do not necessitate investigation because, after a definitive conclusion has been reached, no dispute remains. These two properties, characterized in this way, constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*). Their "acceptance" (*parigraha*) is precisely the restriction to a specific state, namely: "this property-bearer (*dharmin*) possesses such qualities and does not possess other qualities."

In this context, "debate" (*vāda*) refers to that which one speaks with another, preceded by a treatise and involving contention. Briefly summarized, that debate is of two kinds: *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
According to the *Caraka-saṃhitā* (p.
262), debate is indeed a collection of sentences consisting of various speakers, establishing a proof for each respective position, and concluding with the determination of one of those positions.
Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 11:

Discussion is the undertaking of a thesis and a counter-thesis by a proponent and an opponent; it is of two kinds: discussion among those free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*) and discussion among those seeking victory (*vijigīṣu-kathā*).

Where one who is free from passion engages in proof and refutation together with another who is likewise free from passion for the sake of determining the truth, that is called "discourse of those free from passion" (*vītarāgakathā*), using the technical term *vāda* (Nyāyasāra, p.

15). *Vāda* is defined as a collection of statements consisting of the employment of proof and refutation based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), preceded by the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis by two parties free from passion, and culminating in the determination of one side.
Others, however, such as the followers of Vasubandhu, define debate (*vāda*) as speech for the purpose of establishing one's own position and refuting that of the opponent (Nyāyabindu, p.
150). *Nyāyakalikā*, p. 13.

Two contradictory properties residing in the same substratum constitute a thesis and its counter-thesis because they stand in a state of opposition, as in "the self exists" and "the self does not exist. Two contradictory properties residing in different substrata are not a thesis and its counter-thesis, such as "the self is eternal" and "the intellect is non-eternal" (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2).

Two properties of a real entity (*vastudharmau*) that are contradictory, reside in the same locus (*ekādhikaraṇau*), and exist at the same time (*ekakālau*)—provided they are not yet established as properties of a real entity—are specific features of that entity; however, two properties of a real entity that reside in different locuses do not necessitate an investigation, because both are established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇopapatti*). For example: "Cognition is impermanent; the self is permanent."

The same applies even to those that are not contradictory: it is those that are contradictory which necessitate an investigation, not those that are non-contradictory. For example, "substance possesses action" and "substance possesses qualities" [are non-contradictory] when they refer to the same time; for two things belonging to different times do not necessitate an investigation, as this is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Just as a substance possessing action and one devoid of action are not yet determined when there is a difference in time—since it is those that are undetermined which necessitate an investigation, not those already determined—for after a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), there is no further investigation.

These two properties, characterized by such contradictory qualifications, are the thesis and its counter-thesis; the acceptance of these two is the restriction to a specific state of being, namely: "this property-possessor has this property" and "it does not have that property" (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2).
Two properties that reside in the same locus, are simultaneous, and are contradictory.
The *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 590) states that the "separate graspings" (*pṛthak-parigraha*) are designated as the "proponent's position" (*pakṣa*) and the "counter-position" (*pratipakṣa*).

Furthermore, the grasping of the proponent's position and the counter-position is common to both *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil); therefore, the phrase "establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning" (*pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambha*) serves as its qualification. That [debate] in which there is establishment and refutation by means of *pramāṇas* and *tarka* is thus described.

By the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the members of the argument, such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth—which are rooted in the means of valid cognition—are designated. Consequently, in debate (*vāda*), only the presentation of proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*upālambha*) that are embraced by the cognition of the means of valid cognition are to be employed.

Furthermore, by the term "reasoning" (*tarka*), through the logic of referring to what has occurred in the past, the rule for its formal articulation is obtained, since it makes known that this is a discussion conducted by those free from passion (*vītarāga*).

In that debate, when the opponent employs quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) with the intention of [establishing] valid cognition (*pramāṇabuddhi*) and not with the intention of [inflicting] defeat, they are pointed out [by the proponent] with the intention of warding them off. Our engagement is for the sake of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); and since a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) or a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) is not a cause for the knowledge of reality, their employment is not proper.

If it is argued that "because of hearing the reproach, there would be the consequence of all points of defeat," we say no; for the two subsequent words [of the sūtra] are intended to establish a restriction (*niyamārtha*).

By the phrase "not contrary to the established tenets" (*siddhāntāviruddha*), the point of defeat called *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets) is excluded; by the phrase "endowed with five members" (*pañcāvayavopapanna*), since the number five is specified, the defects of deficiency and excess are excluded; and by the mention of "members" (*avayava*), the five fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are excluded. Thus, exactly eight points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are restricted to formal debate (*vāda*).

If it is asked why? It is because of the debate and instruction with the teacher and others; for this person, desiring to know reality (*tattva*), engages in debate while seeking the threefold fruit characterized by the cutting off of doubt, the comprehension of unknown objects, and the confirmation of what has been determined. Therefore, for one who desires to know reality, the opponent must state the proof (*sādhana*) as long as he does not comprehend that reality, since there is no opposition [from the opponent]—[these are] the non-defective [means]. *Ja* [commentary].

In this context, however, by the term "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa), one does not mean perception and so forth, nor even inference; rather, the members [of the syllogism] which are rooted in the means of valid cognition are denoted. By means of these, proof and refutation are effected (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

593). Because of the inclusion of the term "refutation" (upālambha), there is no mere difference in terminology regarding the contingency of all points of defeat (nigrahasthāna); for the latter two [members] serve the purpose of restriction.

According to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, as stated in the *Nyāyavārttika* (p. 149), the phrase "not contradicted by the established tenet" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) implies that only the contradictory (*viruddha*) fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is permitted [as a type of inconclusive reason], according to the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (1.2).

Furthermore, according to the opinion of the Vārttikakāra, the phrase "not contradicting the tenet" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) permits the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "contradiction of a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*). To explain: by the phrase "not contradicting the tenet," one might think that the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is obtained; however, this is not so. Since the term "five" is used in the expression "obtained from elsewhere as consisting of five members," the defects of deficiency and excess are thereby obtained. Furthermore, since the term "members" (*avayava*) is used, their fallacious counterparts (*tadābhāsa*) are obtained. Thus, to state again what has already been obtained would be like grinding what is already ground.

Now, is this term "not contradicted by the tenet" (siddhāntāviruddha) entirely meaningless? It is not meaningless, because it serves to exclude the fallacy of a non-tenet (apasiddhānta). However, according to the view of the author of the *Nyāyamañjarī*, everything therein is fit for formal application (*prayoga*).

However, this is the distinction: in debate (*jalpa*), the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and so forth may be performed intentionally even in certain circumstances; but in formal discussion (*vāda*), their employment is useless.
Nevertheless, if they are somehow employed through error, they must necessarily be pointed out [as fallacies].
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 593)

According to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, there are three [types of debate], while according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, there are eight, because of the instruction on debate with the teacher and others; for this seeker of truth engages in debate with the teacher and others, desiring the threefold fruit (Nyāyavārttika, p. 149).
Maturation (paripāka), however, consists of the cutting off of doubt, the understanding of an unknown object, and the acceptance of what has been determined; thus [states] the Nyāyabhāṣya 4.2.1.
The three fruits are: the realization of the truth not previously attained, the removal of doubt, and the acceptance of what has been determined;
*Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 316.
—The permission of what has been resolved— (ba, ja);
—The permission of what has been resolved— (bhā); —The cognition of the permission— (śra).

Regarding that, [the commentary] states: "Therefore, for one who desires to know reality, the means of proof must be explained as long as there remains something to be known by him, because of its non-contradictoriness" (Nyāyavārttika, p.
Debate (jalpa) is discourse aimed at victory, having as its fruit the examination of a person's capacity;

and the Sūtra states: "Debate is the employment of means for proof and refutation by means of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, when [the debater] is endowed with what has been stated" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.2).

By the inclusion of the phrase "endowed with what has been stated" (*yathoktopapanna*), only the employment of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) for proof and refutation is indicated, not the entire definition of debate (*vāda*). This is because it is impossible for the latter two terms—"not contrary to established tenets" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) and "endowed with five members" (*pañcāvayavopapanna*)—which serve as the basis for restricting the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), to be connected here; for all points of defeat are possible in the case of contentious discussion (*jalpa*).

[Objection: Is it not improper to say that "the proof and refutation consist of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)"? For since quibbles and the rest are fallacious responses, it is untenable for them to function as proofs or refutations. [Reply: That is incorrect. When proof and refutation are being carried out by means of valid instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), quibbles and the rest serve as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) because they have the purpose of protection; they do not possess the status of proof or refutation in their own right. Indeed, these are not employed independently as proofs or refutations. Rather, when a correct proof has been employed and an opponent opposes it by means of a quibble, a futile rejoinder, or a point of defeat, [the proponent] refutes him by pointing out those very things, saying: "A quibble, a futile rejoinder, or a point of defeat has been employed by you. Once that [opposition] is refuted, one's own position becomes protected.

Alternatively, when an opponent has employed a formal proof (*sādhana*), one might suddenly fail to perceive a flaw and instead counter-argue using a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) and so forth. Thus, the respondent, being overwhelmed by such futile rejoinders and unable to formulate a proper reply, is defeated. Once he is defeated, his own position is established as being without opposition.

Therefore, for the sake of protecting the knowledge of reality—which is grounded in valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and held within the heart—even a dispassionate person may occasionally employ quibbles (*chala*) and other such tactics; otherwise, one of keen intellect might be diverted from the ascertainment of reality by the mere display of refutations devised by wicked logicians.

As it has been said: "Discussion (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds" (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.50).

50. Thus, the speech of those who rely on opposing positions is *jalpa* (disputation). For example, one [person] holds the position that rebirth exists, while another holds the position that it does not exist; when these two establish their respective positions through reasons and refute each other, this is *jalpa*.
In the *Carakasamhitā* (p.

262), it is stated that where one who desires victory engages with another who also desires victory—driven by a desire for gain, honor, and fame, and seeking either victory or defeat—that is "discourse between those desiring victory" (*vijigīṣukathā*). This is designated as *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* in the *Nyāyasāra* (p. 16).
*Nyāyakalikā*, p. 13;
*Nyāyabhāṣya*, p. 1.2.

According to the opinion of the two authors of the *Majjarī* (pp. 594), the phrase "endowed as described" (*yathoktopapanna*) is extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*) to the entire definition of debate (*vāda*).
However, according to the opinion of the author of the *Vārttika*, because the extension applies only to what is possible: that which is connected here is extended by analogy.
And what is it that is connected? It is this: "the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning for proof and refutation" (*pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambha*).

It is not for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because there is nothing to be restricted. Alternatively, when one arrives at the form *yathoktopapannopapanna*—meaning "endowed with that which is endowed as stated"—one elides one of the two instances of the word *upapanna* because its meaning is already understood, just as in the case of *goratha*.
But by what means is this understood? It has been stated: "by implication" (*sāmarthyena*).
For the two terms "restriction" (*niyama*) and "purpose" (*artha*) cannot possibly exist in a [mere] verbal dispute (*jalpa*).
According to the *Nyāyavārttika* (p.

161), the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), the establishment of a position (*sādhana*), and the refutation (*upālambha*)—as well as quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)—function as auxiliary members (*aṅga*) because they serve to protect one's own position; they do not possess the status of independent means of proof (*sādhana*).
But in the case of a refutation, there is also independence [of the opponent];
see Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2.1.
In the absence of [the first] limb, one who is free from passion engages [in activity] either for the sake of favoring others or for the sake of protecting the sprout of knowledge.
"Because even for one desiring liberation (mumukṣu), it is useful in certain contexts," as stated in *Nyāyasāra* p.
16 and *Nyāyamañjarī* p. 595.
The term *bhāṃ* (or *bhāṣā*) is set in motion; *vitaṇḍā* is a specific kind of verbal dispute (*jalpaviśeṣa*).
Thus, the Sūtra states: "That [debate] which is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position is *vitaṇḍā*."
Nyāyasūtra 1.2.3:
That aforementioned *jalpa* (disputation), when distinguished by the absence of a formal establishment of a counter-position (*pratipakṣasthāpanā*), attains the status of *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).

And for the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), his own position is indeed the "counter-position" (*pratipakṣa*) in relation to the proponent's position, according to the analogy of an elephant and a rival elephant. Regarding that counter-position, the caviller does not state a proof; he proceeds solely for the purpose of refuting the opponent's position.
Thus, what is called *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is merely the statement of defects in the opponent's position (Caraka-saṃhitā, p. 262).
*Nyāyakalikā*, p.

2.3 The proponent of the counter-position (*uttarapakṣavādī*), being a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), is called the "counter-position" (*pratipakṣa*) in relation to the position being established by the first proponent, according to the analogy of an elephant and its rival.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 596: Fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are those which, though not being valid reasons, appear as such; there are five fallacious reasons:
the inconclusive (savyabhicāra), the contradictory (viruddha), the counter-balanced (prakaraṇasama), the unproved (sādhyasama), and the mistimed (atītakāla).
According to the statement of the author of the Sūtras: "Nyāyasūtra 1.2.4."
In that regard, the definition of the deviating [reason] is: "The deviating [reason] is the inconclusive" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.5).

5. *Vyabhicāra* means lack of restriction (*aniyama*). That which exists together with that is *savyabhicāra*, i.e., *anaikāntika*. *Aikāntika* is that which occurs in one extreme (*ekasmin ante*); its opposite is *anaikāntika*. For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*).
These are non-reasons (*ahetu*) appearing as reasons due to the absence of the definition of a reason (*hetulakṣaṇābhāva*), as stated in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* on page 72.
Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are those that lack the characteristics of a valid reason yet appear as if they were reasons;
*Nyāyasāra*, p. 7;
*Nyāyakalikā*, p. 14.
The "savyabhicāra" (inconclusive) is so called because it involves deviation (*vyabhicaraṇa*).

Deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is the lack of restriction to one side; that which exists in one extreme is "conclusive" (*aikāntika*), and by contrast, that which does not is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), because it pervades both extremes. (Caraka-saṃhitā, p. 265)
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2.5
What, then, is this deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? It is the occurrence [of the reason] in that which is other than the probandum and its like.
(Nyāyavārttika p. 170;
Nyāyamañjarī p. 597)

"Because it exists at one extreme, it is 'one-sided' (*ekāntika*); because of the opposite of that, it is 'non-one-sided' (*anaikāntika*), since it pervades both extremes"— thus [it is stated] in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.2.2.
The definition of the contradictory (viruddha): Having accepted a tenet, that which contradicts it is the contradictory (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.6).

2.6 Although the term *siddhānta* (tenet) is well-known to refer to a subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*), here it must be understood as referring to the object of proof (*sādhya*). Therefore, that which, having accepted a property to be proven, contradicts it—by establishing its opposite—is "contradictory" (*viruddha*). For example: "Sound is eternal because it is produced. That [reason] which lacks presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and has occurrence in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) becomes contradictory because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven.
*Nyāyakalikā*, p.

14: "Although the term *siddhānta* has been explained as referring to the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by its property (*dharma*), here it is intended to denote the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which is a single part of that [locus]. — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 600.

The definition of the "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) [reason]: That for which there is an investigation of the matter (prakaraṇa), and which is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion, is the neutralized [reason] (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.7).

The *prakaraṇa* consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) being deliberated upon; although its "investigation" (*cintā*) occurs from the onset of doubt until the attainment of a definitive conclusion, here it is understood specifically as the state of indecision (*vimarśa*). And that [indecision] arises precisely from the non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣānupalambha*). When that very non-perception of a distinguishing feature is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion, it becomes the *prakaraṇasama* (the "equal-to-the-issue" fallacy), because it does not transcend that very issue.

For example, when one person has stated, "Sound is eternal because its non-eternal properties are not perceived, like space," a second person replies, "Sound is non-eternal because its eternal properties are not perceived, like a jar. Since it is not logical for objects to possess a dual nature, and since cognizers, failing to ascertain their fixed essential nature, wander and doubt due to the non-apprehension of the specific distinction, a doubt arises regarding the matter: "Is sound eternal or is sound non-eternal?"

That very non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣāgrahaṇa*), when employed as a cause through error, becomes the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*).
According to the *Nyāyakalikā* (p.

15), the two sides—the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*)—are the "point at issue" (*prakaraṇa*). The investigation (*cintā*) of that point, from the onset of doubt until before reaching a conclusion, is the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). When a reason is employed for the sake of a conclusion based on that [desire], it does not transcend the point at issue because it remains equal regarding both sides; thus, the *prakaraṇasama* is not capable of leading to a definitive conclusion.
Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2.7
Nevertheless, it is precisely that which consists of reflective awareness (vimarśa) that is grasped here,
because from that [awareness] it arises.
And why does that [fallacy] occur? Because of the non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣānupalambha*).

If that very non-perception of a distinguishing feature is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion, it becomes "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*), because it does not transcend the state of being a mere point at issue (Nyāyamukha, p.
—because of the impossibility [of it], Ā;
—of these, Bhāṃ, Śra;
—this [is] the ford, Ba, Ja, Bhāṃ.
"But cognizers, being unable to determine their fixed nature, simply wander in error"—

this is the definition of the *sādhyasama* (the "equal-to-the-probandum") fallacy from the *Nyāyamañjarī* (602): "That which is not distinct from the probandum, because it is itself yet to be proven, is the *sādhyasama*."

Nyāyasūtra 1.2.8: That which is employed to prove [a point] against the opponent is the *sādhya* (the probandum); a reason (*hetu*) that is not distinct from that [probandum] is the *sādhyasama* (equal to the probandum).

If it is asked, "In what way is the reason equal to the probandum? [the answer is: because it is itself yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*). For example, for a Mīmāṃsaka, the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot" is called "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*) because, as something remaining to be established, it must be proven just like the probandum;
this [reason] also, being unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*), must be demonstrated in the same manner as the probandum.
Nyāyabhāṣya, Nyāyavārttika, 1.2.8

That which is employed to prove a point for one of the two disputants, being accepted by the other, is the *sādhya* (the thing to be proved). A reason (*hetu*) that is not distinct from that *sādhya* is *sādhyasama* (equal to the thing to be proved). If it is asked how there is equality with the *sādhya*, [the author] says: "Because it is itself something to be proved" (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
606). The definition of the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) fallacy is: "The *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* is that which is 'past its time' (*kālātīta*)."

Nyāyasūtra 1.2.9: The proper time for the application of a reason (*hetu*) is immediately after the adoption of a thesis (*pakṣa*) that is not contradicted by perception or scripture; a reason that is stated after having passed beyond that time is "stated when the time has elapsed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
For example: "Fire, as a composite whole, is not hot because it is produced, like a pot"; or "Wine should be drunk by a Brahmin because it is a liquid substance, like milk.
This is called *atītakāla* (mistimed), wherein that which ought to have been stated first is stated later; because of this mistiming, it becomes ungraspable.
(*Carakasamhitā*, p. 267)

For the time for the statement of a reason (*hetu*) is that which is characterized by doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*). And whenever there is a contradiction with perception, inference, or scripture, all such cases transcend the time characterized by doubt through a contrary determination based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, when a reason is stated after this time has passed, it is called "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) (Tattvārtha-ṭīkā, p. 347). The time for the application of a reason is precisely the occasion of adopting a thesis (*pakṣa*) that is not sublated by perception or scripture; for example: "The composite whole of fire (*tejo'vayavī*) is not hot, because it is produced, like a jar."
"A Brāhmaṇa may drink liquor because it is liquid, like milk or water" (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
612) is a [reason] contradicted by perception and scripture, and is therefore "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

For a reason that is sublated by a more firmly established means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is one that is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), as in: "Wine should be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa because it is a liquid substance, like milk" (Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p.
340). (Nyāyakalikā, p. 15)
*Nyāyasāra*, p. 11:
"Quibble (*chala*) is the subversion of a statement through the fabrication of alternative meanings.
And likewise the Sūtra: "Quibble is the subversion of a statement by means of the application of an alternative meaning."

*Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.10: "The obstruction of speech is not by means of covering the mouth, but rather by means of the introduction of an alternative meaning for the purpose [of the speaker]. The general definition is that the quibbler (chalavādī), having superimposed upon the speaker's statement a meaning not intended by the speaker, effects its negation through a fabricated construction."
That [quibble] is threefold: quibble regarding speech, quibble regarding a general term, and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (Nyāyasūtra 1.2).
11. That *chala*, characterized by its general definition, is of three kinds according to the divisions of *vākchala* (verbal quibble) and so forth.
*Chala* is defined as that which is deceptive, appearing to have meaning while being meaningless, consisting of mere words—thus says Caraka, p. 266.
Quibble (*chala*) is the obstruction of another’s speech when they are speaking, the suppression of their expression; see *Nyāyamañjarī* p.
613 and *Nyāyakalikā* p. 16.
What is the use of covering the mouth and so forth? He says "no," because [the opponent acts] by means of the occurrence of a conceptual construction of the meaning (*arthavikalpopapattyā*).

Having superimposed upon the words spoken by the speaker a meaning not intended by him, the quibbler (*chalavādī*) negates that [meaning], through the fabrication of a conceptually constructed object (*vikalpyamānārthaghaṭanayā*), according to the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 613.
That [quibble] is of two kinds: quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) and quibble regarding a general term (*sāmānyachala*). Regarding these, as defined in the *Caraka-saṃhitā* (p.
266): "Quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) is the postulation of a different meaning for a statement whose meaning has been expressed without qualification, contrary to the speaker's intention."

Nyāyasūtra 1.2.12: When a word is used without a specific distinction being stated—i.e., when it is employed in a general sense—*chala* (quibble) consists in denying the meaning intended by the speaker and imagining another, and then making a statement to negate that [imagined] meaning, while speech serves as the instrumental cause. This is *vākchala* (verbal quibble).

For example, when it is said, "Devadatta has a new blanket" (*navakambalo devadattaḥ*), the compound term is indistinguishable in its two possible meanings: either "a new blanket belongs to him" or "nine blankets belong to him. In this case, setting aside the speaker’s intended meaning—the connection with a brand-new blanket—which is supported by valid evidence, and instead superimposing a connection with the number nine, an opponent objects by negating that [intended meaning]: "Where are his nine blankets?"—this is *kalpa* (or *vākchala*). Similarly, *vākchala* (verbal quibble) occurs, for instance, when someone says: "This physician is *navatantra* (possessed of nine systems)."
The physician should say, "I have not studied nine treatises; I am one who has studied a single treatise.

The other should say, "I do not say that you have [studied] nine treatises, but rather that your treatise has been practiced nine times. The physician should reply, "My treatise has not been practiced nine times by me; my treatise has been practiced many times over."
This is *vākchala* (verbal quibble);

as for what is called *sāmānyacchala* (generalization quibble), it is as follows: when it is said that "medicine is for the alleviation of disease," another might say: "You have stated that 'the existent [is for] the alleviation of the existent. For the disease is existent and the medicine is existent; and if the existent is for the alleviation of the existent, then since cough is existent and consumption is existent, by virtue of this commonality of existence (*sattva-sāmānya*), your [medicine] will result in the alleviation of consumption."
Carakasamhitā, p.
266: For example, someone says, "This new woolen blanket (*navakambala*) was worn by me. Here one might state the refutation: "That which was worn by you is but a single garment; how can it be 'new'?
To this one should reply: "I said 'nine' (*nava*); thus it is a nine-fold blanket (*nava-kambala*), not [merely] 'new' (*nava*)."

Here, one might object: "Why 'nine'? Since it is made from nine hairs, it is called 'nine'. To this, the opponent would say: "In reality, the hairs are infinite; why then is it said to have 'nine hairs'? To this, he replies: "I previously said 'nine,' but I did not say 'not-nine' (na va).
The objection here is: "That cloth belongs to you alone; why is this not stated?
The answer to this is: "I said 'nine' (nava), but I did not say 'not-nine' (na va)."

The refutation here is as follows: "It is a matter of direct perception that a blanket is clothing your body; how can it be said that 'this is not a blanket' is a fallacy of reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? Furthermore, there is another kind of quibble of words (*vākchala*): for example, when it is said 'the mountain is burning,' the refutation is: 'In reality, only grass and trees are burning; how can it be said that the mountain is burning?'"
This is called verbal quibble (*vākchala*), as stated in the *Upāyahṛdaya* (p.
15): "The usage [in question] is 'this young brahmin has nine blankets.'"
Nyāyabhāṣya, Nyāyavārttika 1.2.12
*Nyāyasāra*, p. 16; *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 614;
*Nyāyakalikā*, p. 16.
The quibble concerning the general (sāmānyachala) is the postulation of a non-existent meaning based on the application of an overly broad generality to a possible fact;
Nyāyasūtra 1.2.14.

An "overly extensive" universal is an "excessive universal" (*atisāmānya*). Because of its connection with such a universal, when a certain object is possible in one individual (*vyakti*), and its production is conceivable in another individual, there occurs an opposition based on the imputation of a non-existent meaning to that which has been stated by the speaker; this is called "quibble based on the universal" (*sāmānyacchala*) because it is caused by the universal.

When it is stated that "the perfection of knowledge and conduct is possible in a Brāhmaṇa," the caviller (*chalavādī*) says: "No, because of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of the *vrātya*. That is incorrect; for [Brāhmaṇahood] was not put forward as the logical reason (*hetu*) for the perfection of knowledge and conduct.
What then? This is a statement of praise (*praśaṃsāvāda*).
And when a certain property (*tattva*) is connected to one individual (*vyakti*), [it does not necessarily follow] in another individual... [fragmentary].

An overly extensive generality is an "over-generalization" (*atisāmānya*). Because of its connection with that [generality], or because of its occurrence therein—namely, when some specific manifest object is possible and its production is being anticipated, yet there is a conceptualization of a non-existent meaning regarding that which has been stated by the speaker—the resulting opposition based on that [conceptualization] is quibble based on a generality (*sāmānyacchala*), as it is caused by a generality.
(Nyāyamukha, p. 615;
Nyāyakandalī, p. 16)
Therefore, in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* and *Nyāyavārttika* (1.2.7), the following objection is raised:

"Aha! Indeed, that Brāhmaṇa is endowed with knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*). If the perfection of knowledge and conduct is possible in a Brāhmaṇa, it would also be possible in a *brātya*. The rebuttal to this is as follows: when the cause is not intended to be expressed, there is a restatement of the subject for the sake of praise; thus, being a Brāhmaṇa is the object of the perfection, not the cause of the perfection. (*Nyāyabhāṣya*, *Nyāyavārttika* 1.2.7).
Furthermore, quibble (chala) is of two kinds: that which is based on what precedes (pūrvavat) and that which is based on a general property (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).

When it is stated that "conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty like space," the following refutation arises: "If both are empty and non-existent, then phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and equal to space. This is a *sāmānya-chala* (quibble regarding generality), as defined in the *Upāyahṛdaya* (p.
15): "The denial of the actual existence of the referent when there is a description involving a distinction of properties is *upacāra-chala* (quibble regarding metaphorical usage)."

*Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.14: "Dharma" refers to shouting and so forth; its "vikalpa" (conceptualization) is metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). When a statement is made using such [metaphorical] designation—as in the expression "the beds are shouting and singing"—there occurs a negation of the actual existence of the object, which is a negation of the primary meaning: "How can insentient beds shout? What then? It is the persons situated there who shout, not the beds. This is *upacāracchala* (quibble regarding metaphorical usage), which is a form of quibble based on metaphorical usage.
And that is incorrect; because it does not refute the speaker’s intention, for in common usage, the employment of expressions is well known to be both figurative and primary.
Thus, to raise an objection by imagining a primary meaning when a figurative expression is used is "quibble regarding metaphor" (*upacāracchala*), according to the *Nyāyasāra* (p.
Nyāyakalikā, p. 16:
"kṛte'rtha—" (corrected from "kṛte'rtha" in Ā., Ba., Ja., Bhā.)—they [attain] the human...
Ā., Ba., Ja., Bhā.

In this regard, when a linguistic usage is established through conventional consensus (*samādhi-prasiddha*), the affirmation or negation of the word and its meaning is not a matter of arbitrary whim (*chandata*) for the speaker, but follows his intention. The usage of both the primary word and the secondary, figurative word is established in the world. When a usage is thus established, the word and its meaning must be affirmed or negated according to the speaker's intention, and not by whim; if the speaker employs a primary word, its affirmation or negation must likewise follow that reality and not be arbitrary.

If, however, it is subordinate, then it belongs to that which is subordinate; but where a speaker employs a word in a subordinate sense while intending it as primary, and thereby negates another, that negation is based on his own whim and does not constitute a valid censure of the other—
so says the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (1.2).
*Jāti* (the futile rejoinder) is an objection that consists primarily of a reflection based on a [false] cause;
and thus the Sūtra says: "An objection consisting of similarity and dissimilarity is *jāti*."
Nyāyasūtra 1.2.18: This is the general definition of all classes (jāti).

*Pratyavasthāna* (counter-position) is an opposing position; that counter-position which, by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), consists primarily of a reflection upon the reason (*hetu*), is *jāti* (futile rejoinder).

Their twenty-fourfold classification is as follows: *sādharmyasama*, *vaidharmyasama*, *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *avarṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, *sādhyasama*, *prāptisama*, *aprāptisama*, *prasangasama*, *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*, *anutpattisama*, *saṃśayasama*, *prakaraṇasama*, *ahetusama*, *arthāpattisama*, *aviśeṣasama*, *upapattisama*, *upalabdhisama*, *anupalabdhisama*, *nityasama*, *anityasama*, and *kāryasama*.
(Nyāyasūtra 5.1.1–4)
1.1 According to the statement of the author of the Sūtras,
*pratyavasthāna* is an opposing position.
Nyāyabindu 1.2.18
In that context, "jāti" (a futile rejoinder) is a reason employed against a probans used as a *sthāpanāhetu* (a proving reason) which is incapable of counteracting it.
(Nyāyabindu 5.1)
Whatever kind of counter-position is formulated by way of the path of the reflection of a reason, that is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder);
Nyāyamukha, p. 619.
"When a reason has been adduced, a *prasaṅga* (reductio) is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) when it is intended as a means of leveling [the opponent's position]. — *Nyāyakalikā*, p.
17; *Nyāyasāra*, p. 17.

If this refutation (khaṇḍana) is endowed with the threefold defects—namely, perverse refutation (viparītakhaṇḍana), baseless refutation (asatkhaṇḍana), and contradictory refutation (viruddhakhaṇḍana)—then it constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Perverse refutation is of ten kinds: refutation by similarity (sādharmyakhaṇḍana), refutation by dissimilarity (vaidharmyakhaṇḍana), refutation by alternative (vikalpakhaṇḍana), refutation by non-distinction (aviśeṣakhaṇḍana), refutation by reaching or not reaching (prāptyaprāptikhaṇḍana), refutation by lack of reason (ahetukhaṇḍana), refutation by perception (upalabdhikhaṇḍana), refutation by doubt (saṃśayakhaṇḍana), refutation by non-statement (anuktikhaṇḍana), and refutation by difference of effect (kāryabhedakhaṇḍana).

Page 12: The refutation of the non-existent (*asatkhaṇḍana*) is threefold: the refutation by means of the unmanifested indicator (*avarṇya-vyañjaka-khaṇḍana*), the refutation by means of the indicator through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti-vyañjaka-khaṇḍana*), and the refutation by means of the indicator of a counter-observed object (*pratidṛṣṭārtha-vyañjaka-khaṇḍana*).

Page 24: The refutation of the contradictory (*viruddhakhaṇḍana*) is threefold: the refutation of non-arising (*anutpatti-khaṇḍana*), the refutation of eternality (*nityatā-khaṇḍana*), and the refutation of what is contradictory to one's own purpose (*svārthaviruddha-khaṇḍana*).

Page 28: The correct refutation (*samyakkhaṇḍana*) is fivefold: the sublation of the intended object (*iṣṭārthadūṣaṇa*), the manifestation of the unintended object (*aniṣṭārthavyakti*), the manifestation of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgavyakti*), the manifestation of an inconsistent object (*viṣamārthavyakti*), and the manifestation of the attainment of the establishment of all principles (*sarvanyāyasiddhilābhavyakti*).

The essence of these twenty types is twofold: similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). 1.2 Having stated a proof by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), when the proponent of the proof has made a conclusion regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) intended to be established, the opposition that counters it by establishing the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) through similarity is the "counter-argument based on similarity" (*sādharmyasama*).

For example, when a reason is employed through similarity—such as "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort; whatever follows immediately upon effort is impermanent, like a jar"—the proponent of a futile rejoinder (jātivādī) counters by means of similarity alone: "Sound is permanent because it is partless; whatever is partless is seen to be permanent, like space. Yet, in this case, there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other]: that sound is impermanent due to its similarity to a jar in following immediately upon effort, rather than being permanent due to its similarity to space in being partless.

Or one may object by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "Sound is eternal because it is partless; for whatever is non-eternal is observed to have parts, as in the case of a jar. There is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other] such that sound is non-eternal due to its similarity to a jar—namely, being produced immediately after an effort—and not eternal due to its dissimilarity to a jar—namely, being partless. Thus, when a conclusion is drawn through similarity, the refutation that establishes the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of similarity alone, being indistinguishable from the original argument, is the "balancing of similarity" (*sādharmyasama*) refutation.

Now, [the fallacy of] "balancing the homogeneity" (*sādharmyasama*) is as follows: "A clod of earth is seen to possess action and to be endowed with the qualities that cause action; likewise, the self possesses those [qualities]. 1. [The first chapter] of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* on the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is concluded. The second chapter, on the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), begins. First, the summary verse (*uddeśa-kārikā*) is stated: "Having paid homage to the Mother of the Buddhas, who possesses the ten powers, I shall explain the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, which is the ornament of clear realization. In this context, "the Mother of the Buddhas" refers to the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). She is called the "Mother" because she gives birth to the Buddhas through the production of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). She "possesses the ten powers" because she is endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, such as the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). "Ornament" means that which beautifies; it is so called because it adorns the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) by way of their characteristics, divisions, and so forth. "Clear realization" refers to the direct, non-conceptual comprehension of the objects of knowledge. It is called "ornament" because it is the cause for the attainment of Buddhahood. Now, regarding the meaning of the homage (*namaskāra*): it is performed for the purpose of removing obstacles to the composition of the treatise and for the sake of generating merit. Furthermore, the homage is expressed by way of the object of worship, the nature of the worship, and the purpose of the worship. Here, the "object of worship" is the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom. The "nature of the worship" is the act of bowing down with body, speech, and mind. The "purpose of the worship" is to indicate the excellence of the subject matter and to inspire faith in those who hear it. Next, the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) of the summary verse follows. Therein, the first section concerns the knowledge of all aspects. This is divided into three parts: the basis (*ādhāra*), the objective (*ālambana*), and the practice (*abhyāsa*). Among these, the "basis" is the lineage (*gotra*), which is the natural disposition of the Bodhisattva. The "objective" consists of the two truths: conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The "practice" is the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) and so forth. Regarding the "knowledge of the paths," this refers to the thorough understanding of the paths of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, as well as the path of the Buddha. This knowledge is necessary because one must know the paths in order to lead sentient beings to liberation according to their respective capacities. Finally, the "knowledge of all aspects" is the omniscience of the Buddha, which perceives all phenomena in all their modes without exception. This is the final goal of the Mahāyāna practitioner. Thus, the entire structure of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* is established upon these three types of knowledge. This is achieved through the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). These are practiced within the framework of the three doors of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) and the perfection of wisdom, ensuring that they are free from the conceptualization of subject and object. And these are of twenty-two kinds: loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), abandoning the proposition (*pratijñāsannyāsa*), shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), shifting the subject (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), the incoherent (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*), neglecting to censure when censurable (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), censuring when not censurable (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), deviating from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsāḥ*). Therein, the definition of the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) is: "The admission of a property belonging to the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) in one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*) is the abandonment of the thesis."
Nyāyasūtra 5.2.2:

When the proponent has stated a proof for the sake of establishing his thesis and the opponent has offered a refutation thereof, if the proponent, while at his third speech-act, admits the property of the counter-example into his own example, then his thesis is lost; this is "abandonment of the thesis" (pratijñāhāni).

For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," the opponent objects: "Since the universal (sāmānya) is seen to be perceptible by the senses yet eternal, this reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika). To this, the proponent of the proof says: "If the universal is perceptible by the senses and eternal, let the jar be so as well.

When the opponent opposes with a property contrary to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), the proponent abandons the thesis by admitting the property of the counter-example into his own example; this is "abandonment of the thesis" (pratijñāhāni), Nyāyabhāṣya 5.2.4.

In the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra, there is a difference of opinion from that of the Vārttikakāra; for instance: "We do not understand how, in this case, the thesis (pratijñā) is abandoned. When the opponent has pointed out the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of the reason by means of a general example, [the proponent], without stating a rebuttal to that fault of inconclusiveness, establishes permanence through his own example."

Furthermore, because the realization of permanence is unestablished, there is a flaw in the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*). This [flaw] constitutes a point of defeat (*nigraha*) due to either a flaw in the example or a flaw in the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*), and not a "relinquishment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*). How then is this Sūtra to be understood: "The relinquishment of the proposition in one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*) by admitting the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*)"? It is called an "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) because it is both seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and established at the end (*ante vyavasthita*). It is called "one's own example" (*svadṛṣṭānta*) because it is both one's own (*sva*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); by the term "one's own example," the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is denoted. By the term "counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), the opposing side (*pratipakṣa*) is meant; it is called a "counter-example" because it is both the opposing side (*pratipakṣa*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

When a refutation has been made by demonstrating the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason—such as "being perceptible" (*aindriyakatva*)—with respect to the subject of the proposition (*pratijñātārtha*), such as "sound is impermanent," and the proponent fails to remove that defect, he instead engages in a shift of attributes (*dharmavikalpa*). He asks: "Is this sound non-omnipresent like a jar, or is it omnipresent like a universal (*sāmānya*)? If it is non-omnipresent like a jar, then let it be impermanent just like that. By thus making a new proposition—"sound is non-omnipresent"—while having previously proposed that "sound is impermanent," he is defeated because he has failed to understand the actual power of his own proof.
"Sound is impermanent" is the first proposition (*pratijñā*); "it is not omnipresent" is the second proposition, which is a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*).

How is this a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? A different proposition is not a means of proving the original proposition; rather, the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are the means of proving the proposition. Therefore, this is the employment of what is not a means of proof and is thus useless; it is a point of defeat because of its uselessness.

As previously stated, the five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—characterized by the aforementioned definitions, namely: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*)—constitute points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
This is just as the three types of fallacious reasons—the unestablished, the inconclusive, and the contradictory—were previously explained in the *Tarkaśāstra*, page 40.

A detailed exposition of these points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is to be found in the respective commentaries (*bhāṣya*, *vārttika*, and *tātparyaṭīkā*) on the Nyāyasūtras, in the *Nyāyasāra* (pp. 23–28), in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (pp. 638–659), and in the *Nyāyakalikā* (pp. 22–27). The detailed refutation of the sixteen categories, and the establishment of *dharma* and *adharma* as distinct substances due to their being the common causes of motion and stability—herein we respond to what was first stated, beginning with "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and so forth: that [position] is charming only so long as it remains unexamined; for when the sixteen categories such as the means of valid cognition, as postulated by you, are investigated according to their true nature through the means of valid cognition, they are found to be untenable, and thus the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) through the knowledge of their respective realities is impossible.

Whatever, when examined by means of valid cognition according to its own nature, is not logically tenable, the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) does not result from the knowledge of that reality—as is the case with the knowledge of the nature of two moons [seen by one with cataracts]. And the sixteen categories (*padārtha*) postulated by you are not logically tenable when examined by means of valid cognition according to their own nature.

Nor is it unestablished that these [categories], when examined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to their own nature, are untenable. To explain: first of all, as for the category of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which was propounded by you at the outset because it is the most important of all categories—that is not tenable when examined by valid cognition according to its own nature. This has been explained in detail during the occasion of defining the nature of the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), and it will be explained in detail in the section defining the natures of the means of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth (page 309, line 17).
[Note: *yadbhava* and *ba*, *ja* are manuscript variants.]
As for what you [have stated]—that because it is the most important of all categories, [the category of existence] comes first (*syād-ratnākara*, p.

Therefore, since the category of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) as imagined by you is not established, how can the reality of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), such as the self (*ātman*), be established as being determined by that [means]? Just as the self, imagined by you to have the nature of being eternal, all-pervading, and so forth, is not established, so too has it been demonstrated in the section examining the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha-parīkṣā*) that the body is refuted as being an entity distinct from its constituent parts, precisely because the "whole" (*avayavin*) has been rejected.

The view that the sense organs are material and function by reaching their objects, that the intellect (*buddhi*) is cognizable by a subsequent cognition, and that the mind (*manas*) is atomic—this triad has already been refuted.

Furthermore, since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), as postulated by you to be qualities of the self (*ātman*), are themselves unestablished, activity (*pravṛtti*) characterized by them is likewise unestablished. This lack of establishment regarding these two as qualities of the self was demonstrated during the investigation into the substance of the self.

Furthermore, rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) has been rejected on the grounds that the self (*ātman*) is all-pervasive; the defects (*doṣa*), results (*phala*), and sufferings (*duḥkha*), which are qualities of the self, have been refuted during the investigation into the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*);
and liberation (*apavarga*), as conceived by you, will be refuted in the section defining the nature of *mokṣa*.
Therefore, that twelvefold object of cognition does not remain [as such],
