Furthermore, does the determination that this [world] consists of twelve kinds result from the completion of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from the completion of the purpose? Regarding these, the first position is untenable; for the operation of the means of valid cognition is observed even with respect to the manifold (*prapañca*) of space, time, ether, earth, and so forth, yet it cannot be asserted that this manifold is included within these [twelve] alone, because it is absolutely distinct from them.

Whatever is absolutely distinct from something else is not included within it, just as fire is not included in water; and since entities such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are absolutely distinct from the twelve kinds of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) postulated by you, if these too were included therein, then because all things would be included within the Self alone, the postulation of sixteen categories would be sublated by the consequence of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*).

Even regarding the second alternative, for what purpose would there be completion right here—whether for a worldly purpose, for the purpose characterized as liberation (*apavarga*), or for purpose in general? It cannot be for a worldly purpose, because things that accomplish such purposes—such as pots, cloth, crowns, carts, food, and drink—are not included here.

Nor can it be for the purpose characterized as liberation, because the means that produce that purpose—such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), austerity (*tapas*), and meditation (*dhyāna*)—are not included here.
Nor can it be for purpose in general, because a "purpose in general" distinct from both worldly and non-worldly purposes is impossible.

Therefore, this is incorrect: "That knowledge which leads either to liberation or to worldly existence, whether correct or incorrect, is intended here as the object of cognition (*prameya*), and not merely the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 427). This is because it is impossible to include within the twelvefold categories of objects of cognition the entire mass of objects cognizable by both true and false knowledge.

Moreover, the determination that it consists of twelve types would be due either to the completion of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at that point, or to the completion of the purpose; otherwise, there would be the conceptualization of a further object. (Ratnākaraśānti, *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa*, p. 976).
Because there is no inclusion of those who establish that [knowledge] in the manuscripts *ba*, *ja*, *bhā*, and *śra*, [the text reads]: "O *ba*, *ja*,
*bhā*, knowledge (*jñāna*)— whether correct or incorrect— that leads either to liberation or to worldly existence."
In this context, that which is intended as the object of cognition (*prameya*) is not merely the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For if one were to enumerate categories of objects (*padārtha*), there would be the undesirable consequence of also enumerating doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*), and indecision (*anadhyavasāya*), since these too are factors for the operation of reasoning (*nyāyapravṛtti*). Furthermore, if only those [factors] are enumerated, there would be the undesirable consequence of also enumerating the desire for favor, the wish to overcome others, gain, honor, fame, and so forth, because there is no difference in their being factors for the operation of reasoning. *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 427. Regarding the enumeration of categories of objects, and in the enumeration of doubt: there is the contingency of also enumerating error and indecision, because they too are factors for the operation of reasoning. If only those [factors] are enumerated, there is the contingency of also enumerating the desire for favor, the wish to overcome others, gain, honor, fame, and so forth, because there is no distinction in their being factors for the operation of reasoning.

Furthermore, the ancient Naiyāyikas have declared five other members [of the syllogism] in addition to the five beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), namely: inquiry (*jijñāsā*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), feasibility (*śakyaprāpti*), purpose (*prayojana*), and the removal of doubt (*saṃśayavyudāsa*).
Among these, why do you accept only doubt and purpose?

Moreover, since error (*viparyaya*) and indecision (*anadhyavasāya*) are perceived as distinct entities from the sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [why are they not included]?
Also from the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 189a;
and from the *Syādvādaratnākara*, folio 976—
[the word] "gaṇa" is in the Āgamodaya [Sanskrit Series edition].
Some Naiyāyikas enumerate ten members in a syllogistic statement: inquiry (jijñāsā), doubt (saṃśaya), feasibility (śakyaprāpti), purpose (prayojana), and the removal of doubt (saṃśayavyudāsa)—
thus [it is stated] in the Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.1.
In the *Nyāyamañjarī*,

page 570, there is a mention of inquiry (*jijñāsā*), purpose (*prayojana*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and the attainment of the object (*arthaprāpti*) as being of the nature of categories (*padārtha*) to be understood through knowledge of the paths of debate; this is also seen in the *Carakasaṃhitā*, page 262.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not distinct from the instance (*udāharaṇa*);
therefore, if it were stated separately, there would follow the undesirable consequence of stating all the members [of the syllogism] separately, as there is no distinction [between them].
Furthermore, the tenet (*siddhānta*) is not something other than the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Therefore, providing a separate definition for this [apasiddhānta] is useless; for all authors of treatises hold that one who asserts a non-tenet (apasiddhānta) is defeated, yet they do not provide a definition of tenet (siddhānta) distinct from the proposition (pratijñā), since it is universally well-known as being the very nature of the proposition. Furthermore, if the members of an argument (avayava) were enumerated among the categories of things (padārtha), it would follow that inference (anumāna) should also be enumerated separately.

Since it is included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not enumerated separately; likewise, because the members (*avayava*) are also of the nature of inference (*anumāna*), they too would not be enumerated separately.

Furthermore, since inference, as the primary element, is not mentioned separately because it is included within the means of valid cognition, yet its constituent members are mentioned separately—this is a great display of deliberate reflection. Moreover, determining their exact number is improper, for only as many as are required to bring about the understanding of the intended object should be employed, and that [understanding] occurs through some number in certain cases.

Does the role of reasoning (*tarka*) consist in purifying the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is to say, removing that which obscures it; or in ascertaining it by way of excluding doubt and the like; or in merely discerning the nature of the means of valid cognition for one who has already set out to employ it? In the first case, there is a contradiction with experience; for we do not perceive that darkness or other such obscurers of a jar and so forth are removed by reasoning.

Even in the second and third positions, would this [inference] be of the nature of non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) and thus perform that ascertainment and mere discrimination, or would it be of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It cannot first be of the nature of non-valid cognition; for it is impossible for the purification of the object of a valid cognition to be effected by something whose nature is non-valid cognition. That which is non-valid cognition does not purify the object of a valid cognition, just like false knowledge or an object of cognition itself; and yet, you postulate that inference is non-valid cognition.

Alternatively, if it were a purifier of that [object], it would follow that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for whatever purifies the object of a means of valid cognition is itself a means of valid cognition—just like inference (*anumāna*) and so forth—and since you have postulated that reasoning (*tarka*) purifies the object of a means of valid cognition, let it then be of the nature of a means of valid cognition. If this is argued, we say: no, because it would entail a contradiction of the established number [of means of valid cognition], namely that there are only four.

And what is this [nature of] ascertainment (*nirṇaya*)? Is it the removal of that which obscures the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or its determination through the exclusion of doubt and the like, or merely the discernment of the nature of the object by the means of valid cognition as it proceeds toward its apprehension? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.

977) Furthermore, ascertainment is the fruit of the means of valid cognition, and since it necessarily occurs when the means of valid cognition exists, there is no purpose whatsoever in mentioning it separately. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of mentioning even avoidance (*hāna*) and acquisition (*upādāna*) separately, as they too are not different from being fruits of the means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, the definition of debate (*vāda*) as "that which concerns one who is free from passion" (*vītarāga-kathā*) and so forth is also untenable, because it is impossible for it to have one who is free from passion as its subject. To explain: debate does not concern one who is not seeking victory (*avijigīṣu*), because it possesses points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), just like *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.

Nor is its possession of points of defeat unestablished, since the eight points of defeat—characterized by the five fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*) along with deficiency, redundancy, and departure from tenets (*apasiddhānta*)—are present therein.

It is also incorrect to claim that these [fallacies] do not constitute objects for one seeking victory (*vijigīṣu*) in a formal debate (*vāda*) because they are not pointed out with the intent to suppress them; for if that were so, it would follow that even in *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, they could not be objects for one seeking victory, since they too would not be pointed out in such a manner.

If it is argued that because the employment of *chala* (quibble) and other such fallacies is possible therein, there is no absence of their exposure [in debate], then we ask: why is there an absence of their employment in a formal debate (*vāda*)? If you say it is because [debate] lacks the purpose of protecting the determination of truth (*tattvādhyavasāya*), then [we reply]: since *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* do indeed have that purpose, their employment occurs only in those two and not in *vāda*. But this too is the manifestation of profound ignorance; for since *chala* and the rest are "unreal rejoinders" (*asaduttara*), they cannot logically serve as causes for the protection of the determination of truth.

The claim that "the reason those [fallacious replies] are causes for the opponent’s silence is because they serve as the basis for that silence" is also incorrect; for in that way, the opponent’s silence is impossible, since fallacious rejoinders are infinite.

Furthermore, the assertion that debate lacks the purpose of protecting the determination of reality is unestablished, because it is precisely debate that is logically shown to have that protective function.

For instance: debate (*vāda*) alone is for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth (*tattvādhyavasāya*), because—given that it possesses the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) as its proof and refutation, is not inconsistent with established tenets (*siddhānta*), is endowed with the five members (*pañcāvayava*), and involves the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis—it is like that which is not so; whereas that which is not so is not like that, such as verbal abuse and the like. And since debate possesses the aforementioned qualifications, it is for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth. Debate belongs only to those who desire victory, because otherwise [the determination of truth] would be impossible, and because it possesses points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
(Tattvārthaśloka-vārttika, p. 279)
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 194, line 8:
“-ṇārtharahi-” (ba, ja);
“tadadhya-” (bhā, śra).
Debate itself is for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality;
[as stated in] *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* p. 278, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 195, first part.

Likewise, [the opponent might object]: "But this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). [To this we reply: Debate (*vāda*) is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, consisting of the establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning, which is not contradictory to established tenets and is endowed with the five members [of a syllogism] (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.1).

2.1 Because of the statement "since it involves the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis," if this were stated alone, it would follow that *jalpa* (wrangling) also possesses those characteristics; thus, there would be a contradiction with the intended restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). To avoid this, the qualification "consisting of proof and refutation by means of valid means of knowledge and critical reasoning" (*pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambhatva*) is added.

For that [debate] does not occur in *jalpa*— namely, "debate (*jalpa*) is the establishing of proof and the refutation of an opponent by means of equivocation, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat,
as previously defined" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.2).

Because of this statement, it does not follow that [this] is *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), for *vitaṇḍā* is merely a form of *jalpa* (disputation); "that [disputation] which is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position is *vitaṇḍā*" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.3).

Because of this statement, and because the qualification of "employing means of valid cognition and reasoning for proof and refutation" is absent in *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* due to their lack of the formal adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, it is established that only *vāda* has the purpose of protecting the determination of reality.

For the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of reality is indeed certainty (*niścaya*); its "protection" (*saṃrakṣaṇa*) consists in the removal of all subverting factors (*bādhaka*) through the power of logic (*nyāya*), and not merely in some way silencing one who raises a subverting factor against it. This is because even the humiliation of such a person by means of sticks, slaps, and so forth would entail the consequence that it is for the sake of protecting the determination of reality.

Furthermore, it is not possible to effect the removal of all subverting factors through *jalpa* (disputatious debate) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), since these two are intent upon employing quibbles (*chala*) and other such tactics, thereby giving rise to doubt (*saṃśaya*) or misconception (*viparyaya*).

For even when there is a determination of reality (*tattvādhyavasāya*), if one proceeds with the intent of turning others away from it, the judges may doubt or be mistaken regarding it— wondering whether this person possesses a determination of reality or not, or whether he does not possess it at all— because activity directed solely at turning others away is observed even in one devoid of a determination of reality, as in the case of the proponent of the dissolution of reality (*tattvopaplavavādin*).

Therefore, it is *vāda* alone—a specific type of discourse whose fruit is the preservation of the determination of reality and which serves as a cause for gain, honor, and fame—that should be accepted in the treatises on the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), and not *jalpa* or *vitaṇḍā*, because they are the opposite of that.
This has been explained in detail in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*; it should be seen here [in this work] after reaching a firm conclusion (*avasāya*). (Ja., Śr.)

If it is argued that for the sake of protecting the truth, the virtuous must indeed employ quibbles (*chala*) and the like against those seeking victory, then one must also say that they may likewise employ scratching with the nails, slapping with the palms, striking with weapons, setting fires, and so forth. Therefore, this method of protecting the truth is not superior;
[it is] the logic of debate (*vādanyāya*). (p.
71) [The reading *tannyakaraṇa* is found in the manuscripts *ba*, *ja*, *bhāṃ*, and *śra*.]
"It is not possible," says Ācārya Śrāddhācārya;

for even in the case of engaging in an action, one observes activity on the part of someone who lacks such a resolve, provided it is merely directed toward turning another away [from error], as in the case of the proponent of the *tattvopaplava* (the sublation of all principles).
From the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 279;
from the *Āptamīmāṃsā*,
page 194.
In the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* as well (p. 278), it is stated: "Here [the arguments] are set forth with elaboration" (bhāṣya:
"it is explained with elaboration," ā॰, ba॰, ja॰).

The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are indeed accepted by us; however, they serve no purpose in the treatise on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of having to mention fallacies of perception and the other means of knowledge as well, which would result in the destruction of the fixed number of sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśapadārtha*).

Since the fallacies of perception and so forth are already understood by the very power of mentioning the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as perception, let them not be mentioned; and since the fallacious reasons are also understood by the very power of mentioning the members of the syllogism (*avayava*), let them likewise not be mentioned, as there is no distinction between the two cases.
However, quibbles (*chala*), which are mostly like children's play, are not fit to be relied upon by authoritative persons seeking the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

As for the "classes" (*jāti*)—such as *chala* and so forth—which are merely fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), why are they mentioned separately since they are already subsumed under the fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? Furthermore, it is impossible to determine their exact number, because even you yourself admit that they are infinite.

As for what the author of the Bhāṣya said—"Even though universals (*jāti*) are infinite, twenty-four types are mentioned with the intention of providing unmixed examples; no restriction to this number is intended" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

622)—and [the claim] that their inclusion is for the sake of illustration through mutual distinction, that too is incorrect; for even if those that are included serve as illustrations through mutual distinction, it is impossible for those not included to be so illustrated.

And when formulating a definition for the purpose of indicating a few instances of that type by means of their distinction from others, the definition should be formulated as follows: "A futile rejoinder (jāti) is a false reply" (Nyāyaviniścaya 2.202), because this [definition] pervades all its individual instances.
Thus it is said in the Ātmatattvaviveka, the Bhaṭṭikāvya, and the Jayamaṅgalā.
They are not refuted here because of the infinity of false rejoinders (*mithyottara*), or because they have been explained in detail in the treatise;
nor is the "futile rejoinder" (*jāti*) elaborated upon here, as it is equivalent to [the fallacies of] similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth.

527: "From its various classifications, there is a multiplicity of *jāti*s and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*s)."
Nyāyasūtra 1.2.20
This sentence is not found in the Bhāṣya;

however, in the Nyāyamañjarī (p. 622), it is stated that although universals (*jāti*) are infinite, their twenty-fourfold nature has been described with the intention of providing unmixed examples, but no restriction to that number was intended. Thus, there exists therein a "futile rejoinder" (*mithyottara*) which is a "point of defeat" (*jāti*), as in the case of those who hate the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
Because it would follow that curd, camels, and so forth are non-different [from one another], there is a single injunction; Nyāyaviniścaya, p. 526, uttarapakṣa;
Pramāṇasaṃgraha, chapter 6.
This much alone constitutes its definition.
Likewise, because the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are infinite, it is impossible to determine their exact number;

and you yourselves have accepted this infinity, as stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "Although there are many varieties of misconception and non-comprehension, twenty-two points of defeat are demonstrated."

Furthermore, the refutation of each of the quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been elaborated in detail in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* and should be consulted there.
Thus, since these sixteen categories, when examined, lack any fixed stability, a restriction to sixteen categories—just as the Naiyāyikas maintain a restriction to six categories—is not tenable;
nor is this statement found in the *Bhāṣya*.
With respect to the general [classification], there are two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*);
however, when one intends to describe the details of their divisions, there are twenty-two types.
Furthermore, because these divisions are merely illustrative, they are actually infinite.
Nyāyavārttika 5.2.1

And the enumeration of twenty-two varieties is intended to provide unmixed examples; however, in terms of their internal subdivisions, they are indeed infinite, just like the [twenty-two] classes (*jāti*), as stated in *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 639, pp.

The refutation of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* (pp. 281–311) should also be consulted in the *Vādanyāya* (pp. 78–142); for this purpose, the chapter titled "Establishment of Debate" (*jalpasiddhi*) in the *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā* should also be examined.

If it is asked, "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the existence of the two substances, *dharma* and *adharma*, established as entities distinct from those [other categories]? we reply: "By inference (*anumāna*). To explain:

all movements occurring simultaneously, which have as their substrata all living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*), depend upon common external causes, because they are movements occurring simultaneously, like the simultaneous movement of many fish and other creatures in the water of a single lake.

Likewise, the states of existence of all souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) depend upon common external causes, because their states occur simultaneously, like the simultaneous existence of many jujube fruits resting within a single bowl.
That which is the common cause is *dharma* and *adharma*; for without these two, the effects of motion and rest would not arise.
Thus, the assistance provided by *dharma* and *adharma* consists in the facilitation of motion and rest.
Just as in the world, the rising of fish is helpful for their movement; (Tattvārthasūtra 5.17).
Likewise, understand the substances of living beings, matter, and dharma;

The medium of motion (dhammatthikāya) is that by which the coming and going, speech, expansion, mental activities, vocal activities, bodily activities, and whatever other such mobile states of living beings (jīva) exist—all these proceed by means of the medium of motion; for the medium of motion has the characteristic of motion.
(From the Prajñāpanā Sūtra, Chapter 13).
Just as it is with the substance of Dharma, know that substance to be the foremost of substances.
Furthermore, it is like the earth, serving as the cause for those endowed with the activity of stability.
Pañcāstikāya.
"By what does the *aham-atthikāya* (the soul-substance) function?

O Goyama, by the *aham-atthikāya*, the standing, sitting, reclining, and mental unification of living beings occur; whatever other such stable states there may be, they all function through the *aham-atthikāya*, which has the characteristic of stability."
Vyākhyāprajñapti 13.4.481
Because it is untenable:

if objects that are themselves subject to the transformations of motion and rest were mutually the causes of one another, this would not be the case; for it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). For only when the motion of moving objects is established by means of stationary objects can the rest of those stationary objects be established; and only when that [rest] is established can the motion of the moving objects be established.

If it is argued that the movements and states of all objects are indeed devoid of a common cause, because they are preceded by their own specific, individual causes; then how could God (*īśvara*) be the common cause for the production of effects such as sprouts, or how could a moment in a dancer’s performance be the common cause for the arising of various cognitions of her in all the spectators? If you say this is impossible without such a common cause characterized by those features, then this [objection] applies equally elsewhere: for even the movements and states of all objects occurring simultaneously cannot be established without a common cause characterized by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), because they are effects that occur simultaneously. Whatever effect occurs simultaneously cannot be established without a common cause, just like a sprout and the like; and these movements and states of all objects are of that same nature.

It is also incorrect to say that Īśvara alone is the common cause of these [motions and rest]; for motion and rest are impossible in Him, whereas they are observed in the earth and so forth. If it is then argued that He alone is their cause because they are seen in the earth and such, this too is untenable; for motion and rest belonging to objects situated in the sky are impossible in Him.

If it is then argued that space (*nabhas*) is the common cause of these, since it is possible everywhere, this too is unconvincing; for space is established as being the cause of immersion (*avagāha*).

If that single [ether] alone were the cause of multiple effects, there would be the undesirable consequence of the uselessness of postulating multiple all-pervading categories; for the cognition of simultaneity and so forth regarding the effects of time, self, space, generality, and inherence, as well as the cognition of intellect and other qualities, the cognition "this is to the east of that," the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and the cognition "this is here"—all these would be possible due to ether alone, since it exists everywhere and at all times.

If it is argued that since the distinction between causes such as time and so forth is established by the specific nature of the effect, let the distinction between causes such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) also be established from that very same source— because in every respect there is no difference—

and if it is further argued that the earth, water, and so forth alone are capable of producing those effects and thus there is no need for merit and demerit, we say: no, because it has been specifically stated that [the body] has a common substratum (*sādhāraṇāśraya*).

If it is argued that the assistance provided by dharma and adharma to all objects is logically attributed to space because of its omnipresence, that is incorrect; for such assistance exists for other things as well.
By this,
their having the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as their cause is also refuted; furthermore, because the unseen force is impossible for *pudgalas*.

If it is argued that those persons who are the enjoyers of a particular body have their motion and stability caused by the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) belonging to that very self, then the *adṛṣṭa* would be the non-common cause of those motions and stabilities. This is because it is well-established that the *adṛṣṭa* of a specific self is the cause for the motion and stability of a specific substance, and this is not undesirable; for, just like the earth and so forth, it is accepted that *adṛṣṭa* is also a non-common cause. However, the common causes of those motions and stabilities are *dharma* and *adharma*. Thus, the existence of these two is established through the distinction in their effects.
If it is objected: "Motion and stability are caused by *adṛṣṭa*," we say no, because [such a cause] is absent in the case of insentient objects (*pudgala*).
*Tattvārtharāja*, 5.17, p. 215.

Therefore, since the categories postulated by the followers of Yoga, when examined through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding their essential nature and their numerical limits, are found to be untenable, the establishment of an object is not possible within the extreme doctrine of difference (*bhedakānta*) imagined by them;

nor is it possible within the extreme doctrine of difference imagined by the Cārvākas, because there is no distinction in the fact that even those principles they postulate are equally untenable when examined regarding their essential nature and their number.

"The principles are earth, water, fire, and air; from these arises consciousness," and so forth—thus the Cārvāka's prima facie argument: "There is no self distinct from the elements transformed into the form of the body that could be a traveler to the next world."

Now, in the Cārvāka system, only four principles—earth, water, fire, and air—are indeed established; these are characterized by mutually exclusive definitions, are capable of performing the purposeful actions (arthakriyā) defined as body, sense-faculties, and objects, and have their natures apprehended through the means of direct perception (pratyakṣa). This is because it is stated that "earth, water, fire, and air are the principles, and the designations 'body,' 'sense-faculty,' and 'object' apply to their collection"; there are no principles beyond these, as there is a lack of evidence for their existence.

Indeed, perception does not operate regarding the existence of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, because its operation is observed only with respect to objects possessing form (*rūpa*) and the like, as well as those substrates thereof; nor is this possible in the case of space and so forth, since it is accepted that these are formless substances (*arūpidravya*), and because inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Therefore, its existence is not established even by that [inference]. This has been cited from the *Tattvopaplava*, page 1.
Śāṅkara Bhāṣya on the Bhāmatī, 3.3.54.
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, page 520;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 28;
*Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā*, page 73.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 30, upper;
Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, pṛṣṭha 454, upper;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 186.

Now, one might object: "In the absence of a self as a grasper (grāhaka), how can the existence of even the four principles (tattvas) be established, given that the determination of the objects of knowledge (prameya) depends upon the knower (pramātṛ)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Regarding these [principles], some maintain that consciousness is manifested (*abhivyajyate*) here, while others hold that it emerges (*prādurbhavati*). Therefore, the soul (*jīva*) postulated by others, or the beginningless stream of cognition (*jñānasantāna*), is rejected as the knower of those [principles], because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their existence."
And since the property of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is established as being inseparable from the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) alone, consciousness itself will be the cognizer;
from those [elements] alone, knowledge is either produced or manifested. (1859)
Regarding the statement in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* that "consciousness arises from them," some commentators explain that consciousness is produced from them, while others maintain that it is manifested;
see *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 520.
Brahmasūtra-śāṅkara-bhāṣya 3.3.53
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

30; *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, Cārvākadarśana: "But how is it not contradictory for consciousness—bearing manifestation or appearance—to be non-different from the distinct [elements] such as earth and so forth? To this he says: "Consciousness is like the power of intoxication."

For just as a specific state characterized by the power of intoxication arises from the ingredients of liquor, such as fermenting agents (*kiṇva*), depending on particularities of place, time, and condition, so too, from earth and the other elements, when they reach a certain specific state, there arises a distinct, determinate cognition that perceives a specific object such as a jar;
thus [it is stated in] the *Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-Bhāṣya* 2.3.3.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 437:
"And consciousness is like the power of intoxication."
*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 146:

Even regarding its specific variations, since the diversity of effects such as specific pleasure and pain is untenable without a regulating factor, and since that regulating factor—*adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) acquired in a previous existence—is established, the existence of its agent, the *ātman*, is proven even in the previous existence; for living beings are like bubbles in water.

For just as bubbles, possessing diversity by virtue of the inherent power of things, arise in the ocean and so forth without a guiding agent or unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), so too do living beings (*jīva*) possess the diversity of pleasure and pain; they are not, however, eternal or of any such nature distinct from the elements transformed into the form of a body, because there is a lack of evidence for their existence as such.

In that regard, does a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—either perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna)—operate? First of all, perception does not operate with respect to the existence of a self distinct from those [objects], because perception functions within the range of color-form and so forth associated with specific sense organs, and thus its operation upon a soul (jīva) characterized differently from them is untenable.

Nor should it be asserted that in the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) such as "I know the jar," the self appears as such by virtue of being the agent of knowledge; for even that [notion] is logically explained as having the body as its object, just like [the notions] "I am fat" or "I am thin."
Indeed, that cognition does not have the self as its objective support (*ālambana*), because properties such as grossness and so forth are impossible therein;
likewise, this is true for cognitions such as "I know the pot. For even in a dream, no self distinct from the body—such as the one postulated by you—is perceived as an objective support.
If one were to postulate something that is not perceived, there would be the fault of conceptual over-extension (*kalpanā-gaurava*) and the absence of a fixed determination of specific objects.
Furthermore, agency is not logical for that whose existence is not perceived, because that would entail the same status for things such as a sky-flower.
Therefore, since its nature is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is only the body that is logically the agent with respect to consciousness.

This is also because consciousness follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the body; for whatever effect imitates the positive and negative concomitance of something else, that is the product of the latter—just as a jar is the product of a lump of clay—and consciousness indeed imitates the positive and negative concomitance of the body.

For everywhere the relationship of cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two are present here: when the body exists, there is the perception of consciousness, and in its absence, there is no perception. Therefore, the self is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as it lacks a determining factor (*niyāmaka*). [Bhaṭṭa Jayanta]

They assert that the body itself is the conscious self, and they state the reason: "because it exists when the body exists. For whatever comes into being when something else exists, and does not come into being when that thing is absent, is determined to be a property of that very thing (*brahmasūtra-śāṅkarabhāṣya* 3.3.54).
3 53 –rekeṇa sa– bhāṃ.
Nor [is it established] by scripture (śruti),
because scripture is not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa); nor by inference (anumāna), because this [inference] lacks validity.

Alternatively, if the reason (*hetu*) were valid, it would be "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is employed immediately after stating a thesis that is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitapakṣa*). For the thesis of a self distinct from the body is sublated by perception itself;

nor is there any mark (*liṅga*) or invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with its own probandum established anywhere for it, since the apprehension of pleasure and so forth, being effects of the elements, can only have invariable concomitance with those very elements.

Therefore, since no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists for the existence of a self, what wise person would have faith in its eternity and other such qualities, which would then be like the fragrance of a sky-flower? Consequently, consciousness must be understood as either the very effect of the elements beginning from the embryo and ending with death, or as something manifested by them.

Now, one might object: "If consciousness is manifested by earth and the other elements, then it should also be manifested in jars and the like, just as it is in the body. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The non-manifestation of consciousness in jars and the like is due to the absence of other necessary causes, just as the power of intoxication is not manifested in husks and the like [due to the absence of fermentation]."

For the cause of the manifestation of consciousness in earth and other elements is their transformation into the form of a body, just as the manifestation of intoxicating power [in liquor] results from the transformation of flour, water, and the properties of dhātakī flowers and so forth. This [transformation] does not exist in jars and the like; therefore, there is no manifestation of that [consciousness] therein, just as there is no manifestation of the power of intoxication in sand and such things due to the absence of the transformation of flour and the like. Nor should it be argued that, because the transformation is equally present, consciousness would likewise be perceived in a dead body; for its non-perception there is logically established by the deficiency of the necessary causes.

For the cause of the persistence of consciousness is a specific transformation of skin, bone, flesh, blood, and so forth; when this [body] is impaired by the stroke of a weapon, disease, or the like, consciousness does not persist and is thus unperceived, just like a specific bodily form. And since consciousness, possessing a specific form, is thereby established as a property of the body, it follows that because there is no one who goes to another world, there is no other world.

For he who has a connection with the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures, their practice, and the enjoyment of their results is one who belongs to the next world; and since such a person is not established by the aforementioned method, the negation of the next world is indeed established without effort—due to the absence of the manifestation of capacity. This is cited from the *Tattvopaplava*, page 58.
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 523;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
30, top; *Sanmatitarkaṭīkā*, p. 71.
"Because [the reason] is unestablished due to the word ‘kāra’ (in the Śruti),
following the refutation thereof, there is the establishment of the Self— which is distinct from the body and so forth and characterized by the unique attributes of cognition and so on.
To this, the following rebuttal is offered:

As for what was stated—that earth, water, fire, and air, and so forth—that is incorrect. For the restriction that "there are only four principles" could only be established if the non-existence of other principles were proven, yet that non-existence is unproven. This is because the existence of another principle characterized as the living soul (*jīva*) is established through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), and the existence of space and so forth is established through scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Furthermore, the validity of these two—scripture and inference—was demonstrated on the occasion of refuting the position that "perception alone is the single means of valid knowledge."

"Now, is it not the case that the soul’s status as a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) is unproven, since this entity characterized by consciousness is included within the elements themselves—just like a jar or other objects—because it is an effect of the elements? This is an unconsidered statement. For the causal relationship between the elements and consciousness is untenable.
To explain: consciousness is not an effect of the elements, because even when those [elements] exist, [consciousness] is absent, just like its perpetual non-perception.

Indeed, just as [sound] is not an effect of earth and the other elements because it is not perceived at all times despite their presence, so too is consciousness, for there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Indeed, although the elements (bhūta) exist eternally in various distinct states such as clay, bodies, jars, and so forth, consciousness (caitanya) is not always perceived [within them], as is the case with threads and cloth. Furthermore, because there is no relation of priority and posteriority here, there is an absence of the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva). For a body—which is a transformation (pariṇāma) of those [elements]—is never first perceived devoid of consciousness, followed by consciousness; rather, since these two are perceived as co-existent (sahasiddha), like water and fire, there is no causal relationship between them.
(Page 341, Line 16)

It is self-cognizable; it cannot be seen by another, nor can it be seen by another. How could it be pointed out? That person perceives himself, yet he is unable to show it to another. (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5)
The self arises as something to be known by the notion of "I.
(Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Ātmavāda 107)

The self is established as eternally real by virtue of self-awareness, because it is free from sublation; for its manifestation as earth and so forth is untenable within the nature of the Self itself. (96)
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 26;
*Śāstravārttāsamuccaya*, verse 79:
"The negative concomitance [is established] because [the effect] does not exist when that [cause] is absent, but it is not like [the case of] perception."
Brahma Sūtra 3.3.54
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p.
525; *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 30:
"In the presence [of the object], there is non-existence" (satsu abhāvaḥ).
Because there is no distinction [between them], they are included therein;
[the reading] "always" (sarvadā) is found in the manuscripts Ba, Ja, and Bhā, while "existent" (sadvā) is found in Ā.
Is the [material cause] of things such as cloth or jars the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) or rather the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)? (Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, p.

526). Let it be so; nevertheless, would the elements (*bhūta*) be the cause of consciousness by way of being its material cause, or by way of being its auxiliary cause? It cannot be by way of being its material cause, because even when they undergo transformation, this [consciousness] remains untransformed.

That which does not undergo modification even when another thing is modified cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of that thing; for example, a horse is not the material cause of a cow. And since consciousness (*caitanya*) does not undergo modification even when the elements transformed into the form of the body do undergo modification, this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*). This is well-known from the fact that even when the body undergoes transformation through the stroke of a weapon or other causes, there is no modification of consciousness in those whose minds are directed elsewhere and who are as indifferent to pain as to pleasure (like the "axe and sandalwood"). Furthermore, because the body itself undergoes modification even while consciousness remains unmodified, it is just like that [example].

Nor is this [argument] unproven; for even when the prior states of the body, such as its lack of clarity, have not perished, one observes transformations such as joy arising in consciousness upon the proximity of a desirable woman.
Therefore, it is not tenable that those [bodily states] produce consciousness by way of being its material cause (*upādāna*).

But if they produce it by way of being auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then does something other than them exist as its material cause, or not? If it does not exist, how could there be the production of this [consciousness], which lacks a material cause? That which lacks a material cause has no production, just like a donkey’s horn; and yet, consciousness is conceived by you to be without a material cause.

Now, if it exists, is that [effect] of a different class from consciousness or of the same class? In this regard, the first position is untenable; for if something of a different class were produced from something of a different class, it would follow that water and so forth could produce fire and so forth, which would entail the non-existence of the four fundamental principles (tattvas).
If, on the other hand, it is of the same class, this is logical, since it is established that in all cases only that which is of the same class can serve as a material cause (upādāna).

For instance: whatever is the material cause (*upādāna*) of something must be of the same genus as that thing; for example, a lump of clay is of the same nature as a jar which possesses color and other qualities. And you yourselves accept that some reality (*tattva*) is the material cause of consciousness (*caitanya*), whose nature is self-awareness. Therefore, it is logical that this [reality] is distinct from earth and the other elements and is of the very nature of that [consciousness]; thus, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is established. Are the elements the material cause of consciousness or its auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)? (Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 78; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 30, upper section).

Furthermore, it is not logical that something which does not undergo modification even when another thing undergoes modification should be its effect, for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); because even when a reality is cognized, it remains uncognizable [in its essence], since modification is non-modifying.

Because there is no decrease or increase [in the body], whereas in the case of the intellect there is decrease and increase due to its being stronger or weaker— and because the opposite occurs when this is reversed— it follows that pleasure and the like are not transformations of the body.
Nyāyaviniścaya, chapter 2, verses 73–74,
page 459, part U.
In the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*,
page 528, it is stated: "That which, even when there is no modification of the cause, can undergo the production of a modification, is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [effect]."
Nor do those causal factors become auxiliary conditions for consciousness,
because that [consciousness], being devoid of its own material cause, does not arise from them.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 28:

"And [the state of] being without appropriation (*anupādāna*) is imagined by you"—in the manuscript *Śra*, it says "and [the state of] being without appropriation"; in the manuscripts *Ba* and *Ja*, it says "and [the state of] being without appropriation is intended and imagined by you as consciousness (*caitanya*), which has the nature of self-cognition."

Is the subtle element (sūkṣmabhūta) heterogeneous or homogeneous with consciousness? (Tattvārthaśloka p. 29; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 30a). Furthermore, do the elements, in their undifferentiated state, attain the status of being causes for consciousness, or in their differentiated state? If they are undifferentiated, it would follow that they produce it everywhere and at all times.

Now, if [you claim] they are distinguished, from what does their distinction arise—is it from the collection (*samudāya*), from the transformation into the shape of a body (*kāyākārapariṇati*), from a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*), or from another auxiliary cause (*sahakāryantara*)? If it were from the collection, then consciousness would result even from [the mere act of] placing [rice] on the stove and so forth, just as the cooking of rice occurs, because there is no difference in that collection [of elements] in those cases.

If it were from the transformation into the shape of a body, then how did that very transformation come about for them? Would it be without a cause (*nirhetuka*), arising from its own nature alone (*svarūpamātraprabhava*), or caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭanimitta*)? If it were without a cause, it would have to exist eternally or not exist at all.

If their production were due to their own nature alone, there would be the undesirable consequence of them arising everywhere and at all times, because their own nature is undifferentiated everywhere and at all times.

Suppose, then, that they are produced by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit). Would that *adṛṣṭa* have its origin in that very birth, or would it have its origin in another birth as its cause? Regarding the first alternative, there is the consequence of a logical circle (*cakraka*): for consciousness arises only when the body has arisen; once consciousness has arisen, *adṛṣṭa* arises from the performance of means to achieve *adṛṣṭa* preceded by the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful; and from that *adṛṣṭa*, the body arises again.

Furthermore, if it were established that the one who goes to the next world arises from a different state of being, then the claim that "because there is no one who goes to the next world, there is no next world" would be inconsistent.
[Objection: But even here, would these [states] be undistinguished or distinguished?
(Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 1082)

Or, let there be some kind of transformation of the elements into the form of a body; even so, if this [body] were the cause of consciousness, it would follow that consciousness would arise even in a dead body, since there is no difference [between the two states]. If it is argued that a specific state [of the body] is also a cause of that [consciousness], and thus there is no such consequence in the case of a dead body because that [specific state] is absent—on the grounds that the elements transformed into that form must possess a specific state to function as its cause—[we reply:]...

Now, what indeed is this so-called "being characterized by specific states" in those [elements] of such a kind—is it being endowed with consciousness, being conjoined with specific unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), being augmented by specific constituents (dhātu), or being associated with specific stages of life (vayas)? It cannot be "being endowed with consciousness," because that would entail the consequence that they lack the status of being causes for the initial production of consciousness, since at that time they would not yet be endowed with it.

Now, if it is maintained that even at that time they possess that [consciousness], would that be by means of that very consciousness or by one prior to it? If it were by that very same [consciousness], there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of their being qualified by that [consciousness] would depend on the establishment of the initial consciousness, and the establishment of the initial consciousness would depend on the establishment of their being qualified by it.

Now, regarding the point [of the opponent] previously stated: how can there be a denial of one who exists in the next world, given that consciousness would necessarily follow as a continuum even prior to the consciousness of the embryo? If it is argued that their state of being "qualified" consists in their being conjoined with a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), then why does that qualification not exist in the clay body? Is it because of the absence of consciousness, the absence of the performance of actions that establish it, or because it was acquired only for a limited duration? In the first case, the conjunction with a specific *adṛṣṭa* cannot be the establisher of consciousness, because it follows that consciousness itself must be the establisher of that [conjunction].

By this, the second and third positions are also refuted; for the performance of rituals that produce a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is of such a duration, and the state of having acquired [consciousness] depends upon a particular consciousness.

Furthermore, it is not logical that their [the elements'] accumulation of specific constituents or their being characterized by specific states [constitutes consciousness], because even when the body is so accumulated during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), no arising of consciousness is perceived.

The claim that "being endowed with a specific age" constitutes that "distinctiveness" is also refuted by this very argument; for even though the body in the state of deep sleep and a dead body are endowed with specific ages such as childhood and so forth, they do not produce consciousness.
Nor does the distinctiveness of the elements arise from another auxiliary cause, because no auxiliary cause other than the four principles is admitted;

or, if one were to admit such a cause, it would contradict the restriction that there are "only four principles," and it would also result in the establishment of a self (*ātman*), since that [auxiliary cause] itself would be the self.
And because [the soul] does not exist when [the body] has died, [there is no rebirth]. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
69; Śāstravārtāsamuccaya, verse 65)
And in the first [case], because it is not established for the opponent (śrauta-prasiddheḥ). (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p. 454, line u; manuscript reading: śrauta-).
Furthermore, every effect possesses a substratum; therefore, if consciousness were an effect, some substratum for it must be stated.

Would that be the body, the elements, the sense organs, the mind, or the object? First, it cannot be the body, because—like a jar—it is composed of the elements (*bhautika*), perceptible by the external senses, and possesses form (*mūrta*). By this, the status of the elements as the substratum of consciousness is also refuted, because it would follow that consciousness would exist everywhere and at all times, since those elements constituting its substratum exist everywhere and at all times without exception.

"Let it be then that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are its substratum, since through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it follows that it is preceded by them"—this too has not been abandoned by him, because the contradiction with the inference [of their] being material (*bhautika*) and so forth remains the same here as well. Furthermore, would they be its substratum individually or collectively? If individually, then there would follow the consequence of multiple streams of consciousness (*cetanā-santāna*) in a single body; and even within a single stream, there would be an absence of synthetic recollection (*anusandhāna*), just as there is between different streams.

Furthermore, how could there be recollection of form and so forth in the blind and others when their sense faculties have perished? How could there be cognition of form, taste, and so forth during states such as dreaming? And how could there be cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth when the sense faculties are impaired by diseases such as paralysis? Moreover, that which does not undergo modification when another thing is modified cannot be the effect of that thing, for this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

By this very argument, the position of "totality" (sāmastyapakṣa) is also refuted; for totality is not possible upon the loss of even a single sense faculty, and thus, in the case of the blind and others, not even a trace of cognition would arise.
For it is not observed that when any one of the [elements] such as earth is absent, there is either the totality [of causes] or the production of a sprout;

nor does consciousness belong to the body, senses, or mind because they are insentient; nor is there consciousness in the body because, like a jar or other things, it is an effect of the elements and because it is impossible once [the body] is dead. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 69)
Because it ceases to exist when the body is present; [see] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 394; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 29. U. (Uttarapakṣa).

Consciousness is not a quality of the body; why? Because it does not persist as long as the body exists, because it does not pervade the entire body, and because it possesses characteristics contrary to those of the qualities of the body.
Nyāyasūtra 3.2.49, 52, 55

The body does not possess the conjunction with knowledge and so forth, because it is subject to transformation, because it possesses form and other qualities, because its nature consists of a collection of many parts, because it is characterized by a specific configuration,
and because its properties differ from those of the self (*nyāyamañjarī*, p. 439).
Brahmasūtra-śāṅkara-bhāṣya 3.3.54

It does not [arise] from the sense organs, because they are instruments; for it is observed that recollection occurs even when the organs are impaired or when the objects are absent (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
69). Nor does it arise from the sense organs and their objects, because cognition persists even when those two have perished.
Nyāyasūtra 3.2.18
— Because it is well known [from scripture],
the denial of consciousness in the elements and the sense organs is established,
as they are subject to transformation through their collective and individual combinations and their distinct separations.
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Ātmavāda:
"And would those atoms be the causes individually or collectively? (*Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā*, p. 527).

If it is argued that—since mental cognitions do not arise even when there is a deficiency of a single organ such as the nose, and since mental cognition remains unaltered even when the bodily sense-faculties are impaired by diseases such as paralysis—it must therefore be the mind (*manas*) that is the substratum [of consciousness], because knowledge in the form of internal conceptualization continues to manifest even when the sense-faculties have ceased to function; [we reply: would that [mind] be eternal or non-eternal? It cannot be eternal, for that would entail a contradiction with the enumeration of the principles (*tattva-saṃkhyā-vyāghāta*) and the consequence of falling into the position of the opponent’s school.
Now, if it is impermanent, does it have the elements as its cause or some other cause? It cannot have another cause, because that is not accepted.

If it has the elements as its cause, then—given the previously mentioned inferences regarding its being composed of the elements and so forth—it is impossible for it to be the substratum of consciousness.
Nor can it be the mind, because if it were independent of any other cause, there would be the consequence of simultaneous perception and memory, and because the mind itself is an instrument (karana).
… [as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 69; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
30, upper section: "Let it be then that cognition is a quality of the mind (manoguṇa); and because objects of knowledge are not perceived simultaneously, [it is not the case that] the mind..."
Nyāyasūtra 3.2.19

Furthermore, does that mind, being conscious, produce the appearance of objects independently of other causes, or is it dependent upon them? If it were independent, then because of the consequence that all objects would appear simultaneously, everyone would be omniscient.

If, on the other hand, it is dependent on other causes, what is that other cause—is it the mind itself, or something else? If it is the mind, is that [mind] conscious or unconscious? It cannot be unconscious, because it is asserted to be conscious by virtue of being the substratum of consciousness; otherwise, the first [mind] would also necessarily be unconscious.
If, on the other hand, it is conscious, then this too would produce the appearance of an object by depending upon another cause, leading to an infinite regress;
nor can it be something else, because for one whose sense organs have ceased [to function], there is no activity of other sense organs;
nor can the object be its substratum, because that would entail the occurrence of the defects already raised regarding the position that the body and sense organs are the substrata.

Therefore, it must be admitted that the self alone, which is distinct from the body, is the substratum of cognition; thus, it is established as a separate reality, being neither the instrument nor the object of the instruments.
Therefore, for this very reason, even the object does not possess consciousness.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kandalī, p. 72)

Otherwise, how could the desire and other factors that serve as the basis for the activity of a newborn infant toward the breast and so forth be established? Nor is it unproven that this [activity] has such [desire] as its basis; for instance: the activity of a newborn infant toward the breast and so forth is preceded by desire, because it is an activity, just like the activity of one in middle age.

Desire, too, is preceded by recollection, and recollection is preceded by experience, because it is such, just like that [middle-aged activity]. And since no such experience and so forth exists in the womb or at birth, the existence of experience in a previous life is established.

For he, being afflicted by hunger, recollects the breast and so forth as a means to pleasure—the opposite of that [affliction]—and proceeds toward it out of desire; failing to obtain it, he begins to weep; and having obtained it, his weeping ceases and he drinks from it. Furthermore, fearing the recollection of the pain of falling and such, a young monkey child clings tightly to its mother’s lap and avoids the place of falling. Indeed, those who have not experienced the results of desired or undesired means would not invariably seek to acquire or avoid them, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

And for that which has established its experience through previous existences—that is, the self (*ātman*) as a distinct reality—its "birth" is its connection with new bodies, sense-faculties, and so forth; it is not, however, the manifestation of something previously non-existent. Likewise, its "death" is the cessation of that [connection], not total annihilation.
This is known from the persistence of memory regarding previous experiences, as evidenced by the fact that a newborn exhibits joy, fear, and sorrow.
Nyāyabhāṣya 3.1.19
Because there is agreement among those who remember their past births, the persistence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is established;
otherwise, one who imagines things differently merely transcends the world.
There is no desire without memory, nor is that [memory] possible without perception;
for this [desire] is not observed even in one just born, as it arises from a previous birth. (Nyāyaviniścaya 2)
On pages 79 and 80 (pūrvapakṣa 463):

By means of which [cognition] one seeks the means of pleasure, such as the breast and so forth, and begins to weep when not obtaining it; and having obtained it, the newborn infant—even that of a monkey or other species—ceases its crying and, fearing death due to the pain arising from falling down a precipice, clings intensely to its mother's lap and avoids places such as precipices.

As for the statement in the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* (532) that "consciousness is like the power of intoxication," that too is incorrect; for since the power of intoxication is perceived elsewhere than in the transformation of the ingredients of liquor—such as in the *dhattūra* plant or *kodrava* grain—it is not contradictory for that power to arise from a specific transformation of the elements (*bhūta*).
However, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is not perceived even in dreams within specific transformations of the elements such as a jar, which contradicts [the analogy].

O wise one, just as the components of liquor manifest a distinct power when combined, so too is this non-divine creation; alas, those who are satisfied with nourishing their own bodies, genitals, and bellies, being shameless and fearless, have been utterly deceived!
Yuktyanuśāsana,
page 342, line 7.

Furthermore, as for the other claim that living beings are like bubbles on water, that too is incorrect; for there is no possible similarity between the example and the thing illustrated. Since bubbles of water do not differ essentially from water, it is logical that they are caused by it, and thus their diversity is justified. However, because matter (*bhūta*) and consciousness (*caitanya*) are absolutely distinct, a causal relationship between them is impossible. Therefore, without the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), neither the diversity of pleasure and pain nor the diversity of bodies and so forth is logically tenable. Otherwise, how could it be that among those who exert equal effort in service, agriculture, or the like, or who study equally, some obtain results while others achieve nothing? Thus, since visible causes are seen to deviate [from results], the existence of an unseen cause is established; and it is proven that the diversity of pleasure and so forth arises from the diversity of the unseen force.
Therefore, having accepted the relationship of cause and effect, it is not possible to deny the existence of a future life;
for just as there is an action that is the cause for the production of a body, so too is there an action that is the cause for the production of conjunction.
By this, the [doctrine of] restriction is refuted;
*Nyāyasūtra*, Bhāṣya 3.2.10.
Nor can there be a relationship of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), because such a relationship would be conducive to the establishment of the next world.

To explain: would the manifestation of consciousness (*caitanya*) pertain to that which already exists, to that which does not exist, or to that which is of the nature of both existing and non-existing? In the first case, the establishment of the next world is beyond dispute, since it follows that consciousness must exist even prior to the elements having transformed into the form of the body.

Manifestation (*vyakti*) of that which was previously non-existent is contradicted by experience; for manifestation is well-known to be merely the making manifest of an existing thing, such as a jar, by means of a lamp or similar instrument, but not of something non-existent.

Now, if it is argued that it belongs to that which is both existent and non-existent, is this in every respect (*sarvathā*) or in some respect (*kathañcit*)? It cannot be in every respect, because that is a contradiction. If it is in some respect, then the Jaina doctrine is established; for the Jainas maintain that consciousness—which is existent in its substance (*dravyataḥ*) and non-existent in its modes (*paryāyataḥ*)—is manifested from the atoms of earth and other elements transformed into the form of a body. Thus, it is proven that this self (*ātman*) is beginningless and endless.

Would they manifest the power of consciousness as something already existent, or as something previously non-existent, or as both existent and non-existent? (Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 75; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 30, upper section; Lokatattvanirṇaya, Śrī [Haribhadra]).

Regarding what was stated—"because there is a lack of evidence for its existence," and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for there exists direct perception as proof for the existence of the self (*ātman*). To explain: a self-evident cognition arises in every living being, such as "I experience pleasure," which delineates the distinct objects of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing.
And this is not false, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against it.
Nor is it doubtful, because there is no contact with both alternatives;
nor is it logical for such a cognition to be without an object (*anālambana*), since that would entail the consequence that even cognitions of form (*rūpa*) and so forth would be without objects.

Nor does it have the body as its object, because it arises through the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) independently of the external organs; for the body is not known by the "I-cognition" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) in this manner, as it is an object of the external organs.

Therefore, one must admit that there exists some conscious entity distinct from the body which serves as its objective support (*ālambana*), since knowership is logically possible only for such an entity and not for the body, because the body is composed of the elements (*bhūta*), like a jar or other objects. Indeed, knowership is never observed in the case of jars and the like, which are composed of the elements.

Nor should it be argued that even though there is no difference in being composed of the elements, the body alone will be the object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*); for this would lead to a fallacy, as the dead body does not possess such a notion.

Even the cognition "I am stout" and so forth, which arises with respect to the body because the body is beneficial to the self, is metaphorical—just like the cognition "this is I myself" directed toward a servant who is extremely helpful (pṛ.
14). Furthermore, the perception "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I have desire" is observed; nor is this a case of erroneous knowledge, because it is not sublated.
Nor is it a cognition of doubt, because its specific form is not experienced (*praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

391); nor does it have the body as its objective support, because it arises through the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). For instance, the body cannot be delimited by the internal organ, because it is an external object (*praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 391).

In the cognition "I am happy," there is a connection with happiness, not in the body; for if it were in the body, it would follow that it is perceivable by external organs, nor even in the sense organs themselves.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 32:

Just as in the case of a servant, it is appropriate that the cognition "I" with respect to the body is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Since a figurative usage does not proceed without a cause (*nimitta*), the body's status as a benefactor to the self is postulated as that cause.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 391; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 29; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 86.
Likewise, the self is also cognized through inference: "The cognition of color and so forth must be dependent upon something, because it is a quality, like color itself;

cognition, pleasure, and so forth must be preceded by a material cause, because they are effects, like a jar. Nor should it be argued that this proves what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), on the grounds that dependence upon and having as its material cause the body are already accepted; for such dependence upon and material causality by the body have already been refuted at length in the preceding section.
Likewise, the living body is presided over by an agent possessing effort, because it is the substratum of actions that conform to will, like a chariot;
and the auditory organ and the rest are instruments employed by an agent, because they are instruments, like an axe and the like.
Furthermore, the validity of this [inference] has already been established previously.

Thus, since the substance of the self (*ātman-dravya*) is established as a distinct principle from earth and the other elements, how can the restriction that "there are only four principles" be justified? Furthermore, since their mutual status as distinct principles was already refuted during the occasion of denying these four kinds of substances—earth and so forth—that restriction is all the more untenable.

[For the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra states: "Inhalation and exhalation, closing and opening of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, and the modifications of the other sense organs, as well as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, are the marks of the self" (VS 3.2.4).
Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self.
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.10
The cognition of sound and so forth is dependent on something, because it is a quality; [see] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 393; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 29. U. (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa).

The state of being preceded by an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is established for [the object] because it is an effect, just like color and so forth; [as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 393. Note: *upādānapūrva* is the reading in the *ba* and *ja* manuscripts.

Just as the movement of a mechanical statue indicates the existence of an operator, so too the activity of inhalation, exhalation, and other vital functions establishes the existence of a self that possesses action; *Sarvārthasiddhi* 5.19.
"By means of the activity of the chariot, like a charioteer, the presiding agent of the body is inferred through [the presence of] breath and so forth" (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
69). "The living body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is the locus of actions that conform to desire, like a chariot."
In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p.

402), it is stated that the self is apprehended through the instruments—the ears and so forth—which are inferred from the perception of sound and other objects; for we observe that instruments such as axes are employed by an agent, and thus, based on the well-known application [of instruments] to sound and the rest, the one who accomplishes the action is inferred (*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 69).

The establishment of the substance of the self (*ātma-dravya*) should be examined in detail in the various texts indicated in the notes, such as the *Aṣṭasahasrī* (p. 63) and the *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, Chapter 4, and so forth.

Consequently, since the absolute distinction (*bhedai-kānta*) postulated by the Yogas and the Cārvākas—when subjected to analysis—is untenable like a lotus in the sky, even the report of the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-siddhi*) does not apply to it.

Just as the establishment of that [causal efficiency] is not tenable in the Buddhist-imagined extreme of difference, so it will be demonstrated in the following verse; therefore, the accomplishment of causal efficiency is not possible in the extreme of difference,
nor in the extreme of non-difference, because the monistic extreme of Brahman-advaita, which consists of absolute non-difference, has already been refuted.

—But [the opponent objects]: "However, regarding the Sāṅkhya who describes twenty-five principles starting with 'From Primordial Matter (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat)' and so forth, there is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa):

'Surely, while there may be no establishment of causal efficiency (arthakriyā-siddhi) in an absolute non-dualism that is imagined as being entirely incapable of withstanding analysis, such will exist in the case of the form of Primordial Matter (prakṛti), because that is capable of withstanding analysis.'"

The Sāṃkhyas indeed declare that *pradhāna*—which resembles a great ocean without waves—is the cause for the construction of the manifold world (*jagat-prapañca*). It is called *pradhāna* because "in this, the transformations (*vikāras*) are deposited. In brief, that [cause] is threefold: power (*śakti*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and effect (*kārya*); thus the world exists in these three ways.

Since it is stated that "the effects are the organs, the voids, and the power, which is the triad of qualities," there is no manifold world (jagat-prapañca) existing apart from effects, organs, and power.
In this system, the effect (*kārya*) is of ten kinds—designated as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*mahābhūta*).

The instrument (*karaṇa*) is of thirteen kinds, distinguished as the sense organs of cognition, the organs of action, the internal organ, the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Furthermore, power (*śakti*), whose nature is not directly perceived, is the single primordial material cause (*prakṛti*).

The proof for its existence, however, is the fivefold reason stated in the *Sāṅkhyakārikā* 15: "Because of the finiteness of distinct objects, because of their commonality, because of activity proceeding from a power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the resolution of the manifold universe [into a single cause]."

For finiteness is understood to belong only to that which is preceded by a single cause, as in the case of a jar, a bowl, a water-pot, and so forth, which are all preceded by a single substance; and this manifest world is finite—there is one intellect (*buddhi*), one ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), eleven organs (*indriya*), and five gross elements (*bhūta*).
Therefore, that which is the single cause is indeed the Pradhāna; thus is its existence established.

And because of homogeneity (*samanvaya*): for whatever is endowed with a certain genus (*jāti*) is the effect of a cause consisting of that [genus]. Just as particular objects such as jars, being endowed with the genus "clay," are effects of a cause consisting of clay; so too, this manifest world beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), being endowed with the genera "sattva," "rajas," and "tamas," [is the effect of a cause consisting of those].

For the effect of *sattva* is clarity, lightness, exhilaration, joy, and so forth; that of *rajas* is distress, emaciation, stimulation, agitation, and so forth; and that of *tamas* is despondency, dejection, loathsomeness, heaviness, and obscuration.

Furthermore, in the Great One (mahat) and the other evolutes, effects such as serenity, distress, and despondency are observed; therefore, the existence of the Pradhāna is established through its presence [in the effects] and through activity from power (*śakti*). For whoever applies himself toward a particular object is capable in that regard, just as a weaver is capable in the making of cloth; and the Pradhāna applies itself toward the production of the manifest (*vyakta*). Therefore, it possesses a power by which it produces the manifest, and since that power cannot exist without a substratum, the existence of the Pradhāna is established.
