And because of the distinction between cause and effect; for indeed, without a cause, the distinction of effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth is not possible, just as a jar and the like are not possible without a lump of clay. And this distinction exists; therefore, from the observation of the effect, the existence of the cause is established.

And because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe (vaiśvarūpya); for the manifold universe is designated as the expansion beginning with the Great Principle, and that at the time of dissolution goes to a state of non-distinction in a certain place: for the gross elements dissolve into the subtle elements (tanmātra), the subtle elements and the sense organs into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), the ego-principle into the intellect (buddhi), and the intellect into primordial nature (prakṛti).

Thus, primordial nature (prakṛti), whose existence is established by means of valid cognition, proceeds toward the creation of the principles (tattva) in this sequence: "From prakṛti comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five of that group of sixteen come the five gross elements" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 22).

First, from Prakṛti arises the Great One (Mahat), which is single, all-pervasive, consisting of the determination of objects, and enduring from the beginning of creation until its dissolution; it is of a nature imperceptible to those like us. From that, however, emerge the various modifications of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) for each individual, which are of a perceptible nature.

And from that, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)—which is like an ocean—spreads forth for every living being through various specific waves of ego-sense such as "I am gross," "I am handsome," and so on. That ego-sense first spreads forth in two forms: the *vaikārika* (the sattvic) and the *bhūtādi* (the tamasic).

In that regard, from the *vaikārika* [tattva], which is dominated by *sattva*, there arises the elevenfold group of organs (*indriya*) characterized by luminosity (*prakāśa*). These consist of the five cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*)—namely, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—which are called "organs" because they function as instruments for the sake of cognition (*buddhi*), in order to manifest it. There are also the five active organs (*karmendriya*)—known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—which are called "organs" because they function as instruments for the sake of action (*karman*), in order to manifest it. And there is the mind (*manas*), whose nature is volition (*saṅkalpa*); its function is volitional determination, such as: "I am setting out for the village; there will be the acquisition of gold or wealth," and so forth. This is the mind.

From the *bhūtādi*, however, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arise, which possess the nature of being eternal and so forth; from those, in turn, the gross elements (*mahābhūtas*) arise in the same manner—thus it is established that the world exists in a threefold way: as power (*śakti*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and effect (*kārya*).
The cause is the body;
the effects are the elements; the instruments are the sense organs; the power is the three qualities (guṇas), which are [the constituents] of the body.
The cause of power (śakti) is the thirteenfold instrument (karaṇa), which performs the functions of grasping, maintaining, and manifesting.

And its effect is tenfold: that which brings forth, that which sustains, and that which illuminates. That which brings forth is characterized by the sense organs; that which sustains is characterized by ego-consciousness (abhimāna); and that which illuminates is characterized by the intellect (buddhi). — Sāṅkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti, verse 32.

"Because of the finite measure of specific effects, because of their commonality, because of activity proceeding from power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe [it must have a single cause]. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 15.
Thus, it is precisely that which has not yet come into being... [fragmentary].

Sattva is held to be a single material substance that is buoyant and illuminating; rajas is supportive and mobile; and tamas is heavy and obscuring. Their functioning occurs for a purpose, like a lamp.

According to the Sāṅkhya, the *upaṣṭambhaka* (supporting factor) means the stimulator, namely the *unnāḍī*. Just as an intoxicated bull becomes excited upon seeing another bull, so too when the heavy elements (*bhūtāni*) prevail and the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*) become sluggish and incapable of grasping their respective objects, then one should consider that this *tamas* exists in a state of predominance.

In that regard, O Māṭhara, sattva, because of its purity, is illuminating and free from affliction; it binds [the self] through attachment to happiness and, O sinless one, through attachment to knowledge.
Know that passion consists of attachment; it arises from thirst and clinging.
O son of Kuntī, it binds the embodied soul by means of the attachment to action.
Know that darkness, O Bhārata, is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings; it binds them through negligence, laziness, and sleep.
In the Bhagavadgītā, Chapter 14: Indeed,
from *sattva* arise serenity and lightness.
*Tattvārtharājavārttika*, page 12;
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, page 21—*avaṣṭambha*: Ba, Ja, Bhāṃ, Śra.
The three worlds merge indistinguishably into the five great elements; the five great elements [merge] into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
According to the *Māṭhara-vṛtti* (p.
27): "From primordial nature (*prakṛti*) comes the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the I-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); and from that, the group of sixteen."
"From that group of sixteen, from five [of them], the five gross elements arise" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 22). Here, *prakṛti*, *pradhāna*,
*brahman*, *avyakta*, *bahudhātmaka*, and *māyā* are synonyms.

From that primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the one Great One (*mahān*) arises—synonyms for the Great One are intellect (*buddhi*), understanding (*mati*), wisdom (*prajñā*), consciousness (*saṃvitti*), manifestation (*khyāti*), awareness (*citi*), memory (*smṛti*), the demoness (*āsurī*), and Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha.

From that [Great One] comes the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); its synonyms are the modified (*vaikṛta*), the passionate (*taijasa*), the elemental-originary (*bhūtādi*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and the sense of "I" (*asmitā*).

Whatever is expressed by the intellect through the sixty-four phonemes, beginning with the vowels and ending with the *vaikharī* speech, all that—by grasping the two letters *a* and *ha* at the beginning and end, adorned with the *bindu* which resembles a globule situated above according to the method of *pratyāhāra*—is designated as *ahaṅkāra*. (Māṭhara-vṛtti, p.
[blank]). Here he says: "The *ahaṅkāra* is threefold; we shall explain it."

In this regard, from which *ahaṃkāra* do the sense organs arise, and from which do the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arise? To this it is said: the group of eleven consisting of *sattva* proceeds from the *vaikṛta* *ahaṃkāra*; the subtle elements proceed from the *bhūtādi* [which consists of *tamas*]; and from the *taijasa* [which consists of *rajas*], both proceed. (25)
When *sattva* becomes predominant in the *ahaṅkāra*, and by that *sattva* both *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome, then it is called the *sāttvika* *ahaṅkāra*.
The ancient teachers have given this *sāttvika* [type] the designation "vaikṛtika.

Having become *vaikṛtika*, the *ahaṅkāra* produces the eleven organs. From the *ahaṅkāra* named *bhūtādi*—which is designated as such by the ancient teachers because *tamas* is in abundance there and *sattva* and *rajas* are subordinate—the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with sound, is born.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: from the *rājasa* ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), designated as *taijasa*, which has overcome the darkness of the *sattva* quality and is characterized by active function (*pravṛtti-karman*), there arose both that which consists of luminosity—the eleven organs—and that which consists of delusion—the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Indeed, within the *rājasa* *taijasa* ego-sense alone resides the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*);
for *sattva*, being inactive and solitary, is unable to produce [effects] on its own.

And because darkness (*tamas*) is characterized by delusion, it is inactive and incapable of producing creation without the quality of passion (*rajas*). Therefore, both goodness (*sattva*) and darkness (*tamas*), when assisted by passion regarding the sphere of creation, generate the two groups consisting of the sense organs and the subtle elements; this is the intended meaning of Sāṃkhyakārikā 25 according to the Māṭharavṛtti.
They call the sense organs of cognition those known as the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; and the organs of action, speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ.
The term *sākhyakāḥ* means "objects"; those which run toward these objects are the *indriyas*.

Those which perceive sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the *buddhīndriyas* (cognitive faculties). Those which perform actions and cause actions to be performed are the *karmendriyas* (action faculties).
Māṭhara-vṛtti: For the sake of clarity, the Bhāṣya states: "In this context, the mind is of a dual nature; it is both the faculty of volition and a sense organ, due to its common characteristics."
Due to the diversity of the specific transformations of the gunas and due to the difference in the objects to be grasped, [the cognitions are diverse]. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 27)

In this context, the mind possesses the nature of both; among the organs of action, it is an organ of action, and among the organs of cognition, it is an organ of cognition (Māṭhara-vṛtti). Such is the case for those [organs], according to the Śruti.

Thus, having established the creation of the principles (*tattva-sṛṣṭi*), when *prakṛti* proceeds toward the creation of the elements (*bhūta-sṛṣṭi*), first there is the manifestation of Brahmā. From his *mahat-tattva*, an intellect (*buddhi*) measuring a hundred *yojanas* emerges; from the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*), the ego and the eleven sense organs emerge; and from the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the elements that constitute the subtle body (*sūkṣma-deha*) emerge. Above that, from the abundant gross elements, the gross body—which stands like a surrounding wall—is produced instantaneously, without the natural sequence of the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*. This is likewise the case for Manu and others.

However, for others, the body is composed of subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*) and persists from the beginning of creation until its dissolution; whereas for humans and the like, it stands in the place of a surrounding wall (i.e., is gross), being born of mother and father, while for gods, denizens of hell, and minute creatures, it is of spontaneous birth (*aupapāduka*).

Furthermore, this manifold expansion beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) exists within primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and merely manifests from some cause—because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is a grasping of a material cause, because there is no production of everything from everything, because the capable [cause] produces only what it is capable of producing, and because the effect is of the same nature as the cause; therefore, the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkārya*).
This is understood from the fivefold reasoning [of the Sāṅkhya-kārikā, verse 9]:
for if the effect were non-existent in the cause, then, being formless like a sky-flower, it could not be produced;

and if the effect were indeed non-existent, there would be no restriction regarding the material cause (upādāna). For just as the jar is non-existent in the threads, so too is it non-existent in the lump of clay; consequently, one seeking a jar would take up the threads just as one takes up the lump of clay. The previous fault was with respect to the effect, whereas this one is with respect to the cause.

Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent, then everything would arise from everything because there is no distinction in their non-existence; consequently, a jar and a cloth would be produced even from a lump of clay, and they would also arise from threads. This is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with respect to the cause.

Moreover, it is logical that a capable cause produces what is possible for it to produce; however, a non-existent effect—like a lotus in the sky—cannot be produced, nor can a cause possess efficacy toward it. And this is the fault with respect to the properties of the cause and the effect.

Furthermore, the effect exists [prior to its manifestation] because it has the nature of being the cause; for "having the nature of the cause" means being a cause, and that [status], due to being eternally related, requires a relation with the effect. Now, there can be no relation whatsoever between a cause and something non-existent, such as a sky-lotus; therefore, the effect exists within the cause through identity (*tādātmya*). If this is so, how can there be a distinction between the two? If you ask this, [we reply]: The manifest (*vyakta*) is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composite, and subordinate; the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the opposite.

Because of the difference in definition stated in Sāṃkhyakārikā 10, [the manifest] is clearly "possessing a cause"—that is, it has a cause (hetu) or a producer (kāraṇa). For the intellect (buddhi) possesses Pradhāna as its cause; from the intellect comes the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from the ego-sense comes the group of sixteen; and from the five subtle elements (tanmātras) come the five gross elements (mahābhūtas). However, Pradhāna does not possess a cause, because no cause for it exists.

The Puruṣa, being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), cannot be the cause of that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) because of their absolute dissimilarity. That [insentient state] is the most subtle condition (*sūkṣmatarāvasthā*) of insentient things; there is no other state more subtle than this. Therefore, since neither the insentient nor the sentient can be the cause with respect to the Pradhāna, its state of having no cause (*ahetumattva*) is established.

For this very reason, it is eternal (*nitya*); by contrast, the Mahat and other effects are non-eternal. Furthermore, an effect must be smaller in dimension than its cause; thus, in comparison to its cause, the Mahat and others are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), while by contrast, the Pradhāna is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*).

Action consists of vibration and belongs only to that which possesses form, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest; thus, that [the Manifest] is active. By contrast, the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) is inactive. However, action in the form of transformation exists for both. If there were many Lords (*īśvara*), their mutual disagreement regarding the commencement of an effect would result in the non-attainment of the effect—just as when several cooks are involved—so too would it be with many Primal Natures. Therefore, that [Primal Nature] is one. The Manifest, however, is manifold due to the distinctions of the Great Principle and the rest.
Furthermore, the Manifest is dependent, because whatever is produced from something else is dependent upon that source; the Unmanifest, however, is not so, because it is not an effect.
And [the mark is] the *liṅga*. It is called *liṅga* because it makes known its own subtle cause (*līnaṃ sūkṣmaṃ svakāraṇaṃ gamayati*), or because it goes to dissolution (*layaṃ gacchati*).

The manifest (*vyakta*) possesses parts (*sāvayava*) due to its connection with constituent parts that have become condensed, and due to its connection with parts that stand in the relation of quality and qualified (*aṅgāṅgibhūta*) such as *sattva* and the other *guṇas*. The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is partless (*niravayava*) because it is the opposite of that.
Furthermore, the manifest is dependent (*paratantra*) by virtue of having a cause (*hetumattva*) and being supported (*āśritatva*), whereas the unmanifest is not so.

Nor is there an absolute difference between these two, because their non-difference is also established due to the lack of distinction in their defining characteristics, as stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (K. 11): "The manifest is composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive; so too is the Pradhāna. The Puruṣa is the opposite of that, and likewise [the same] in certain respects."
Because both consist of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, they are equally composed of the three *guṇas*.

These *guṇas*—*sattva* and the others—cannot be distinguished from one another, such that one could say, "this is the manifest" and "this is the unmanifest"; therefore, both are non-discriminative (*aviveki*).

Furthermore, both are objects (*viṣaya*) because their nature is to be experienced as objects of enjoyment; they are called "objects" because they bind the senses by means of being objects of experience.

And the *sāmānya* (the commonality) is insentient because it is to be enjoyed by all persons, like a house or a field, and precisely because it is an object (*viṣaya*); for it is impossible for a sentient being to possess such a nature. Furthermore, both [the *sāmānya* and the *viśeṣa*] possess the quality of productivity (*prasavadharmi*); "productivity" means the generation of effects, and this is their inherent property. For instance: the *pradhāna* produces the intellect (*buddhi*); the intellect also produces the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego-sense produces the eleven sense organs and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and the subtle elements produce the gross elements (*mahābhūta*).

The Puruṣa, however, is similar [to the Pradhāna] by virtue of the common property [of being a cause], but dissimilar by other properties; for just as the Pradhāna is common to all enjoyers by way of being an object of enjoyment, so too the Puruṣa is common to all objects of enjoyment by way of being the enjoyer.
"My womb is the Great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings comes to be."
Bhagavadgītā, Chapter 3:

My own being—my *māyā*, which consists of the three *guṇas* and is *prakṛti*—is the womb (*yoni*) of all beings. Because it is greater than all effects and because it sustains its own transformations, it is called the "Great Brahman" (*mahad brahma*); thus, the womb itself is further specified.

In that great womb, which is Brahman, I place— that is, I deposit— the seed of the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, the seed that is the cause of the birth of all beings; Bhagavadgītā Śāṅkara-bhāṣya— Ribhu-bhāṣya, Jaḍabharata-bhāṣya.
Among humans, there are three kinds of distinctions: the subtle, those born of mother and father, and those arising together with the primary elements.
Of these, the subtle ones are constant, while those born of mother and father cease.

First, there are the five subtle *tanmātras* belonging to the Sāṃkhya; by means of these very [elements], the subtle bodies (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) of the three worlds were initiated at the beginning of creation.

That subtle body, composed of those [elements], enters the mother's womb at the time of conception; this subtle body, having been initiated by them, descends into this gross body— Māṭhara-vṛtti on Sāṃkhya-sūtra 3.1.2.
However, for those [beings], it is *aupapāduka* (spontaneously born). *ba*, *ja*, *śra*. *aupapādukam* (*ba*, *ā*).

The effect exists [prior to its production], because what is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because all things do not arise from everything, because an efficient cause produces only that for which it is capable, and because the effect is of the same nature as the cause. — Sāṅkhyakārikā 9.
If [the letter] *ka* can be perceived like [the letter] *kā*,
[then it follows that] *śra*.
That [composite]—
which is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative— is produced at that time.

"The manifest is composed of parts and is dependent; the unmanifest is the opposite. (Sāṅkhyakārikā 10). Thus is the nature [of the elements]. The eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*)... [are the manifest].

"Non-agency, consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive—such is the manifest (vyakta) as well as the primordial matter (pradhāna); and the Spirit (puruṣa) is the opposite of that. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 11.
A detailed commentary on the Sāṅkhya verses presented in the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument) is to be found in the *Māṭharavṛtti* and the *Tattvakaumudī*.

Here, a refutation is provided, which consists of a detailed critique of the Sāṅkhya-accepted theory of creation—the very essence of their doctrine—following a rebuttal of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
Herein it is replied:

As for what was stated—the fivefold set of reasons beginning with "because of the limited magnitude of the various effects" as evidence for the existence of *prakṛti*—that is untenable because it is vitiated by the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). This is because *prakṛti*, being by nature imperceptible, is unestablished in its own form, and because [the reason] is unestablished due to a difference in substratum (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*); for while the probans, such as "limited magnitude," resides in the various effects (*bheda*), the probandum, "existence," resides in *prakṛti*.

Now, if it is argued that here the fact that the various categories beginning with *mahat* (the Great One) are preceded by a single cause is being established—and thus the two aforementioned faults do not apply—that is not so; for there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and *puruṣa* (the self). For although they are limited by the numbers one and many respectively, and by their great magnitude, it is impossible for them to be preceded by a single cause. Furthermore, what contradiction would there be if something were limited yet not preceded by a single cause? Moreover, if there were such a single cause, it would be either God, time, or some other factor; thus, [the reason] remains contradictory.
The example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*); for it is impossible for a jar or the like to be preceded by a single cause.
Indeed, no single thing is perceived as a producer, because effects arise from auxiliary causes and other causal factors.

Furthermore, even a lump of clay does not possess absolute unity, as it consists of a collection of many parts. Moreover, even the substance of clay is distinct in each of its various states (*paryāya*).

Therefore, because being limited is pervaded by the fact of having multiple causes as its antecedent, [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*)—*kaṃsādhanaṃ* (the proof of *kaṃsa*)—p. 350, l. 15. (Ā.)
Because of the non-exclusive nature [of the argument] regarding primary persons (pradhānapuruṣa), there would be...
[of the jewel... and its... [from the Śrāvakabhūmi, folio 986].

Likewise, the various modifications such as pots and so forth do not possess a single genus; they are established through multiple causes due to their distinction from the lump of clay and other factors. (43)

Even though they possess consciousness and other qualities, it is not admitted that persons have a single prior origin; if that [single origin] is considered secondary, why is it not the same in this case as well?
*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 306;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 986.

The argument that "because of the homogeneity (*samanvaya*) of the parts with the whole" is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for even in the absence of a single prior cause for *prakṛti* and the *puruṣas*, a homogeneity is possible through properties such as eternity and omnipresence, and for the *puruṣas* through properties such as being the enjoyer. Furthermore, it is difficult to establish that things of different classes, such as water and fire, originate from a single material cause (*ekopādāna*), because the difference in the class of entities is incompatible with the unity of their cause.

This [argument] is unestablished (*asiddha*); for there is no proof that the entire aggregate of elements (*bhūtagrāma*) is connected with *pradhāna* by virtue of being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion. This is because pleasure and the rest appear as having the nature of internal consciousness (*saṃvid*), and it is therefore untenable that external objects consist of them. Indeed, no one perceives an external object such as a garland or sandalwood paste as "pleasure" itself; rather, it is well-known even among children that these things are so designated because they produce pleasure.
Furthermore, authoritative persons do not accept a non-figurative identity between cause and effect.

Furthermore, since the primary principle (*pradhāna*) itself remains unestablished even now, how is it coherent to say "it exists" on the grounds that "it proceeds from its own power"? Otherwise, one could also say "the sky-flower exists because it proceeds from its own power.

Moreover, since it is logically untenable for power to be either entirely distinct or non-distinct [from the possessor of power], how can anything proceed from it? Furthermore, the establishment of the existence of *pradhāna* based on the distinction between cause and effect merely drags along the absurdity of establishing the existence of a donkey's horn; indeed, unlike a donkey's horn, the existence of *pradhāna* is not established by any means whatsoever.

Furthermore, since the time of dissolution (pralaya) is not established, the aforementioned mode of non-distinction of the manifold universe (vaiśvarūpya) is likewise unestablished; therefore, the existence of primordial matter (prakṛti) is not proven by the stated reasons,
[as argued] regarding suffering and the rest— [Bhāṣya].
For it is not possible to establish a pervasive connection between external and internal objects on the basis of their consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion;
this is because pleasure and the like are perceived as internal, whereas sound and the like are perceived as not having that nature (Brahmasūtra Śāṅkarabhāṣya 2.2.1).
2.1 Let it be collected. (Ba, Ja)

By the phrase "proceeding from power" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteḥ*), if what is being proved is merely a cause endowed with non-distinct powers, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
However, if [the cause] is a single, eternal cause endowed with distinct and diverse powers, then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*). (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā 39)
Prameyakaṇikā, page 84, first part;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, page 306;
Prakṛtasi—Ja.

Or, let it be granted that [the desired conclusion] is established from that; nevertheless, when primordial nature (*prakṛti*) proceeds toward the creation of the principles (*tattva*) and the creation of the elements (*bhūta*), does it proceed by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), or by depending on some cause? If it proceeded by its own inherent nature, there would be no regularity in its activity nor any cessation of activity, because such a sequence—namely, "the creation of the principles shall extend only this far" and "this [creation] shall be beneficial to this [soul]"—is impossible for that which is devoid of consciousness and lacks the capacity for reflection.

And what could the cause be: the impulsion of the Puruṣa, or the necessity of fulfilling the purpose of the Puruṣa? It cannot first be the impulsion of the Puruṣa; for since the Puruṣa is desireless and indifferent, there is an absence of the reflective awareness that "this arises from that," and thus an impulsion toward a specific act of production is impossible.

Nor can it be the necessity of fulfilling the purpose of the Puruṣa; because the Puruṣa is desireless, the very existence of a "purpose" is impossible, and because Prakṛti is insentient, the reflective awareness "I am accomplishing the goal of the Puruṣa" is untenable.

Indeed, there is no such thing as a human goal that is not desired by a person; for in the world, having ascertained from his own words or from some other source that "this is what he desires," one engages in action with the underlying intention: "I shall accomplish what he desires, so that he may be satisfied with me. This is how activity is observed to occur.

Now, if it is argued that her very nature (*svabhāva*) is such that she brings about this manifold world (*viśvaprapañca*) in this manner—even though she is not prompted by anyone and is devoid of the thought "I shall fulfill her desire"—then surely this doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*) is tenable only regarding an object established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of fire and space having the natures of burning and non-burning respectively. But if it were accepted even for what is not so established, why would one not also accept an inherent nature for the son of a barren woman and the like in the production of the world's diversity? Consequently, since the expansion of the transformation of *pradhāna* is untenable, the description of the sequence of its expansion—beginning with "from *prakṛti* comes the Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth—is incorrect.
And does that primordial matter (pradhāna) alone proceed by depending on something else, or independently? [Prameyaratnamālā 4.1]— what is stated there?
Let it be so—[as you say] "it does not act" (ba., ja., ā.).

Furthermore, is this manifold expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest different from *prakṛti*, or non-different? If there were non-difference, then because there would be no distinction between the two, both would possess either the status of being an effect or the status of being a cause. Consequently, [your established position] that *prakṛti* alone is the cause, the group of sixteen characterized by the elements and the sense organs is exclusively the effect, and that intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are both effects and causes depending on what precedes or follows them, would be contradicted.
If that were so, this would be inconsistent:
for it is not logical that what is non-different from something else should be its cause or its effect, because cause and effect possess distinct characteristics;
therefore, your assertion that the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) possesses only causality [is untenable].
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, folio 22;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 81;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, folio 296.
"In relation to other forms, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both evolvents and evolved;
the group of sixteen is only evolved; and the Spirit (puruṣa) is neither evolvent nor evolved. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 3.

Furthermore, regarding the proof presented for the existence of the manifestation beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) within primordial nature (*prakṛti*), such as "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced" and so forth: in this case, what is the subject (*dharmin*) and what is the probandum (*sādhya*)? If the effect is the subject and "existence prior to production" is the probandum, then the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*). For while the probandum—existence—resides in the effects such as the Great Principle, the reason—"because that which is non-existent cannot be produced"—resides in non-effects such as a sky-flower. Alternatively, if "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced" is understood to mean "because that which exists is produced," then there is the fallacy of the probandum being identical to the reason (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatva*).

Now, if "being in the process of being made" (*kriyamāṇatva*) is the reason [for the existence of the effect prior to its production], such that "the effect exists prior to its production because it is in the process of being made," and if "because what is non-existent cannot be made" is stated as the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, "that which is non-existent is not made, just like a sky-flower"—that too is charming only so long as it is not scrutinized. For there is a contradiction in the making of that which already exists; for that which has been accomplished and is independent of anything else with respect to its own existence is called "existent. How, then, can there be the making of such a thing? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: that which exists in its entirety cannot be produced by anyone, just like *prakṛti* or the *puruṣa*; and according to the opponent's view, the effect exists in its entirety [prior to production].

Therefore, it is logical that only that which is unestablished (*aniṣpanna*) is produced, because for an extremist (*ekāntavādin*), the coexistence of two contradictory properties—establishedness and unestablishedness—is impossible within a single substratum (*dharmin*). Consequently, this reason (*hetu*) is contradictory, since the state of being "in the process of being produced" (*kriyamāṇatva*) is possible only when there is non-existence (*asattva*). [As stated: "That which exists in every respect is not produced by anything, such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) or consciousness (*caitanya*). *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 25.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 298:

Furthermore, if the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (asatkāryavāda) is not accepted, how could properties such as "having a cause" (hetumattva), which do not exist in the cause, possibly come to exist in the effect? Indeed, they do not exist in the unmanifest (avyakta) in the same way that they exist in the manifest (vyakta).

And [the reason] is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because the thesis is sublated by perception; for indeed, prior to its production, an effect is not perceived as either independent or consisting of its cause. For if curd and the like—which possess specific forms, structures, tastes, and so forth—were already present in the milk and such, they would necessarily have to be perceived, and there would be activity toward the milk and such by one seeking curd and the like.

Now, if it is not the case that the state of curds and so forth is established there as something directly manifested, but rather that the curds and so forth existing there in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) become manifested—well then, what indeed is this so-called "state of being a potentiality"? Is it the existence of the curds and so forth in a subtle form, or is it the capacity of the milk and so forth to produce them? Regarding these, the first position is untenable; for a thing does not possess two forms, gross and subtle. Indeed, the completion of a thing is its attainment of its own nature (*svarūpa*); if that exists, what is the use of the distinction between gross and subtle? As for the second position, the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is not supported, for it is not logical that the capacity itself is the effect.
For those seeking curd (dadhi)— whether they be Āryas, Bāhikas, Jains, or Śrāvakas— if curd and the like already exist within the nature of milk and so forth,
then since they are already present, what remains to be produced for those things whose nature is identical to their causes and so on?
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, [verse on] the capacity for producing that [effect]. *Śrī*.

Furthermore, what is this so-called "effect"? Is it the manifestation of something non-existent, the attainment of the relationship between parts and whole, or the acceptance of another property by a substratum through the relinquishment of its previous property? In the first case, there is a contradiction with your own doctrine.

But in the second case, what is the meaning of the relationship between the subordinate (aṅga) and the principal (aṅgin)? If it means the relationship of the secondary (guṇa) and the primary (pradhāna); for instance—where *sattva* is the principal and *rajas* and *tamas* are subordinate, there the transformation is of the nature of *sattva*, consisting of pleasure, such as garlands, sandalwood, and so forth; where *rajas* is the principal and *sattva* and *tamas* are subordinate, there the transformation is of the nature of *rajas*, consisting of pain, such as snakes, thorns, and so forth; where *tamas* is the principal and *sattva* and *rajas* are subordinate, there the transformation is of the nature of *tamas*, such as darkness and so forth—this is untrue, because the fact that garlands, sandalwood, and the like are essentially pleasure and so forth has already been refuted.

Furthermore, would the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgitā*) between existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities occur when there is a difference from their prior form, or when there is no difference? If there is no difference, would it be the state of being the whole or merely the state of being a part? If, however, there is a difference, then the relinquishing of the substance's (*dharmiṇaḥ*) previous property and the assumption of another property must necessarily be admitted; for by abandoning the subtle form of existence and assuming a gross form, the previous property is abandoned. And if that previous property is abandoned, there is either its destruction (*nāśa*) or its concealment (*tirobhāva*). If destruction is accepted, there is a contradiction with your own doctrine.

Furthermore, concealment (*tirobhāva*) is not possible without the destruction of non-concealment (*atirobhāva*); and if that [destruction] is admitted, then let the destruction of the previous property itself be admitted—what is the use of this internal quibble? Thus, there is an entry into the position of the opponent (*paramata*).

Is the acceptance of another property also its production (*utpāda*) or its manifestation (*abhivyakti*)? It cannot be its production, because that would entail the collapse of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

Furthermore, would this manifestation be a property of cognition or a property of the object? If it were a property of cognition, what would happen to the object by virtue of which it too would be manifested? Moreover, if it is a property of cognition, is that cognition produced at that same time [as the object], or was it already present at an earlier time? If it were present at an earlier time, there would have been perception of it previously as well;
and if it were produced at that time, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be utterly destroyed.

Even if it were both the object and its nature (*dharmatā*), since the object exists at all times, it would follow that this [manifestation] must also exist at all times; consequently, the object would be eternally manifest. Alternatively, if it were non-existent [at other times], it would follow that this is the theory of the non-existence of the effect prior to its production (*asatkāryavāda*), which entails entering into the position of the opponent.

Furthermore, just as a thing is incapable of other actions such as burning prior to its manifestation, so too it is incapable of manifestation; how then could that [manifestation] be possible? And how could the manifold of entities (*bhāvaprapañca*), which is perceptible by nature, arise from *pradhāna*, which is imperceptible by nature; or how could that which possesses form arise from that which is formless by nature? If the manifold of entities possessing form can arise even from this formless source, why would the insentient world-manifold not likewise arise from the sentient Self (*ātman*), whereby the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) would fail to be established? Even when manifested, [the world remains distinct] from the sentient Self... [fragmentary text].

Furthermore, in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there can be no efficacy for causal factors (*kāraka*), because it is impossible even to designate something as a "causal factor" if it does not produce anything that was previously non-existent. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which has no non-existent objective to accomplish is not a causal factor, just like consciousness (*caitanya*); and according to the opponent’s view, the entity intended to be a causal factor likewise has no non-existent objective to accomplish. Nor is their activity directed toward manifestation (*abhivyakti*); for in that case too, the operation of an instrument is impossible whether one assumes the manifestation is already existent or non-existent. Indeed, it is not logical to produce what is already existent, as that would entail the absurd consequence of the instrument never ceasing its activity.
Furthermore, if one acts upon that which is non-existent, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be lost.

Moreover, causal factors (*kāraka*) are distinguished by their various types, such as the material cause (*upādāna*) and auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); in that case, where could the effect—such as a jar—which exists in an unmanifested, subtle form, reside? If it resides in the material cause, such as a lump of clay, then the staff and other instruments would not be causal factors.
If the effect already exists in every respect, it ought not to arise anew.
And the postulation of transformation is a complete subverter of [the doctrine of] eternalism.
(Āptamīmāṃsā, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 181)
Furthermore, regarding that manifestation (*abhivyakti*), does it exist prior to its occurrence or not? The same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before applies; see *Nyāyavārttika* p.
444 and *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* p. 26.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 493;
Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p.
144; Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī, p. 545.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 82, upper section;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, folio 298: "pot, etc. (*ghaṭādi*). [Manuscript variants: *ba*, *ja*, *bhā*, *śra*.]

By this, the argument "because of the grasping of the material cause" (*upādānagrahaṇāt*) is also refuted; for the defects such as the lack of common locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) and unestablished nature (*asiddha*) apply here as well without distinction.

Furthermore, the relationship between cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); and whatever is seen to arise from something through positive and negative concomitance is what is grasped by those seeking that result, not everything. Thus, the admission of the existence of the effect prior [to its production] is futile.

If that were accepted, it would follow that there is no grasping of material causes at all from the very beginning; for no one grasps a material cause for the sake of establishing an already existing thing. Moreover, [the Sāṃkhya view] is rejected because it would entail the necessity of grasping material causes even for the sake of establishing *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*.
Indeed, it is only when production is established that the consideration of material causes arises.
But for one who exists, that very [self] does not exist; so what is the use of considering its substratum? (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
495; Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 26)
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 302:
"Because of the consequence of [everything arising from everything]...

by this, the absence of the possibility of everything is also considered. For the absence of the possibility of everything is said to mean that what is restricted arises from what is restricted; and that is difficult to maintain under the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda)."

Furthermore, necessity is understood precisely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): for how could that which is determined by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to arise from a specific cause arise from another? This has already been answered by the principle that "the capable [cause] produces what is possible" and by the nature of causality itself.

And for what purpose is the composition of this treatise and the presentation of reasons directed toward your disciples? If it is said that it is for the sake of destroying doubt and producing certainty, then if those two—doubt and certainty—already exist in their own nature within the intellect of the disciple, how can there be their destruction and so forth? Or, if by that [treatise] only the concealment of doubt is effected and not its absolute eradication, [then we reply: "There is no non-existence of that which exists" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.16).

16. Because of this admission, [the claim] that even certainty is merely a manifestation is likewise a mere fantasy; for there would follow the consequence of the re-emergence of doubt, and thus a final farewell would be given to *samprajñāta-yoga*, since the absolute eradication of doubt would be impossible for anyone.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that manifestation—whether of something existent or non-existent—is not possible.

Now, if for the sake of making the application of the means prescribed by the scriptures effective, you accept the production of the non-existent and the destruction of the existent, then, by that very fact, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the principle that "what is non-existent cannot be produced," and so forth.

Thus, since the existence of *pradhāna* and the existence of the *mahat* and other principles therein are not established from any valid reason, the process of the creation of the principles (*tattva-sṛṣṭi-prakriyā*) under discussion is like a description of the fragrance of a sky-flower, along with the process of the creation of the elements (*bhūta-sṛṣṭi-prakriyā*), and is therefore disregarded.
Consequently, this remains established: because neither absolute difference nor absolute non-difference is perceived, the establishment of an object occurs through non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
Thus, doubt and error are never eliminated, as they persist at all times.
Nor does it arise from certainty; therefore, everything [in that regard] is in vain. (Tattvasaṃgraha 24)
Samprajñāta [samādhi] arises from the accompaniment of the forms of vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, and asmitā (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 82; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 979).
Yogasūtra 1.17;
"kvacid api" in manuscripts Ba and Ja.
—[This view] is disregarded by Ārya[-deva]:
"The intellect is devoid of the object of consciousness and is insentient; space and so forth are born from the subtle elements such as sound;
and there is neither bondage nor liberation for the *puruṣa*. How much that is contradictory has not been composed by the dull-witted!
13. From where does this [doctrine of *syādvāda*] come? To this he says: "Neither internally nor externally," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) imagined by the followers of Sugata, and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) imagined by the Advaitins such as Brahmā and the Sāṃkhyas, are not the objects of cognition (*prameya*).
Where [is it then]? Whether internal or external, that which is imagined by the Naiyāyikas would be the object of cognition; to this he says: "mutually non-identical" (*parasparānātmaka*).

The connection is that neither the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) nor the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which are mutually and absolutely distinct, is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
To the question, "How is it not an object of cognition? he says: "In whatever way," and so forth; that is, in whatever manner it is conceived by others.

In response to the objection that, since nothing other than absolute difference or non-difference is possible, there would be no object of knowledge (*prameya*) at all, he says: "Substance," and so forth.

Since the substance (*dravya*) and the mode (*paryāya*), which possess the characteristics already described, constitute the nature (*ātman* = *svabhāva*) of an object, and since they appear in cognition—such as perception and the like—it is established that these alone are its objects of knowledge. This counters the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika (*yauga*), who describes absolute difference by asserting: "Substance and mode are entirely different, because they appear as distinct."

Now, one might object: since substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) are absolutely distinct from one another—due to their having different appearances and so forth—how can an object that consists of both be an object of valid cognition (*prameya*)? To explain: substance and mode are absolutely distinct because they have different appearances, like a jar and a cloth. For it is only when there is absolute difference, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, that the possession of different appearances is observed. How then could this [difference] observed in the case of substance and mode not establish their absolute difference? Otherwise, it would follow that this [reason] fails to establish [difference] in other cases as well.

Nor is it unestablished that these two have distinct appearances; for the appearance of substances such as threads is well-known to all living beings as being different from the appearance of modes such as cloth.
Furthermore, due to the imposition of contradictory properties, there is a difference between these two, just like that between water and fire.

Nor is the superimposition of these two [the cloth and the threads] unestablished; for the cloth is experienced as being related to the universal *paṭatva* (cloth-ness), as performing a distinct purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and as possessing an exceeding degree of magnitude, whereas the threads are related to the universal *tantutva* (thread-ness) and are endowed with properties such as small dimension. Thus, how could they not be different? Furthermore, identity is said to be oneness; and when that [oneness] exists, neither a difference in appearance nor the superimposition of contradictory attributes can occur, because those two [appearance and attribute] would then have different objects.

Likewise, if there were identity between the threads and the cloth, the distinction of designation as "the cloth is the threads," the distinction of grammatical number, the genitive case in "the state of being cloth (paṭatva) belongs to the cloth," and the derivation of secondary nominal suffixes would not be possible.

Likewise, if there were identity (*tādātmya*) between them, the *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva* compounds would also not be possible; for the *tatpuruṣa* is observed only when there is a distinction, as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) or "the cloth of threads" (*tantūnāṃ paṭaḥ*); and the *bahuvrīhi*, as in "one who has variegated cows" (*citraguḥ*) or "a cloth having threads as its cause" (*tantukāraṇakaḥ paṭaḥ*); and the *dvandva*, as in "the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees" (*plakṣa-nyagrodhau*) or "threads and cloth" (*tantu-paṭau*).—*antabhi*—*bhāṣya*; *ghaṭādi*—*bhāṣya*.
If there is a distinction [between the two], it would be a *tatpuruṣa* compound, as in the *Bhāṣya*:

"Furthermore, regarding the term *tādātmyam*, what is its analysis? Is it that 'the state (*bhāva*) of those threads whose self (*ātman*) is that cloth is *tādātmyam*'; or is it 'that cloth whose self is those threads'; or is it 'that whose self is both those [threads] and that [cloth]'? In that regard, in the first alternative, because the cloth is one, it follows that the threads must also be one; otherwise, their identity with it (*tattādātmya*) would be untenable. In the second alternative, however, because the threads are many, it follows that the cloth must also be many; otherwise, there could be no identity between them.

The third alternative, however, is charming only so long as it is not critically examined; for there is no entity possible apart from those [two], since there exists no other distinct thing apart from the threads and the cloth to which the nature of being both thread and cloth could be attributed.
Thus, the identity (*tādātmya*) of substance and mode is untenable.

By this, the identity of quality and the qualified, of action and the agent, of universal and particular, and of existence and non-existence is also rejected; for the reasons that subvert such identity—namely, the fact of appearing as distinct and the attribution of contradictory properties—are no different in these cases as well.

Furthermore, even if there were a plurality of forms among qualities, the qualified, and so forth, yet no mutual plurality between them—whether external or internal—the very discourse of plurality would be cut off.

Moreover, the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) is one, eternal, partless, and all-pervading, whereas particulars (*viśeṣa*) possess a nature contrary to that. In that case, if the nature of the entity is accepted as being that of the universal, how could it possess the form of a particular? Because of the contradiction. If, on the other hand, its having the form of a particular is accepted, then in that case it could not have the nature of a universal for that very same reason.
Furthermore, it is utterly impossible for objects to possess the nature of both existence and non-existence simultaneously, as these are as contradictory as shadow and light.

Moreover, the very essence of non-existence consists in the negation of existence; therefore, if the nature of existence were swallowed up by it, then only the nature of non-existence would remain there, and even the name of "existence" would not be heard.

Furthermore, the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed everywhere only when the subsequent term has been determined, as in the case of "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) and so forth. If a single-sided certainty were established anywhere, how could everything be of a manifold nature (*anekāntātmaka*)?

Furthermore, if objects were of that nature (identical with consciousness), defects such as doubt and the like would arise; for instance, there would be doubt as to by what essential nature threads and cloth are distinct, and by what they are non-distinct.

Likewise, there would be contradiction, since where there is non-difference, difference is opposed, and where there is difference, non-difference is opposed—just as the sensations of cold and heat. Moreover, there would be a lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), since non-difference, whose nature is unity, has one substratum, while difference, whose nature is plurality, has another.

Likewise, the fault that follows from absolute monism—characterized by the absence of multiple natures—and the fault that follows from non-absolutist monism—characterized by the absence of a single nature—apply here as well; thus, there is the fault of both. Furthermore, by whichever nature an object possesses a single nature, there follows the consequence of its possessing multiple natures, and by whichever [nature] it possesses multiple natures, there follows the consequence of its possessing a single nature; this is the consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*), which is the simultaneous occurrence of all [contradictory attributes].
Because it is stated thus, by that same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through which there is plurality, there follows unity; and by that through which there is unity, there follows plurality.
This "intermixture" (*vyatikara*) is the mutual entering into each other's domains.

Because of this statement, there would be a lack of finality (*anavasthā*): in whatever form there is difference, there must be some degree of difference; and in whatever form there is non-difference, there must likewise be some degree of non-difference.
Consequently, for the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādins*), the non-existence of reality would follow due to the impossibility of its being apprehended.
In this way, even if one accepts [the existence of] existence (*sattva*) and so forth, these same faults must be seen;

likewise, in the case of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), one who is liberated would be unliberated, or one who is unliberated would be liberated, otherwise there would be a destruction of non-absolutism,
because [contradictory properties] cannot coexist in a single entity.

For it is not possible for contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to coexist simultaneously in a single substratum (dharmin), just like cold and heat. These seven categories that have been determined—namely, that there are exactly these many and they are of such a nature—must either be exactly so, or not be so at all. Otherwise, if they were both so and otherwise, then knowledge whose form is undetermined would be invalid, just like doubtful knowledge. Furthermore, they would be called "inexpressible" (avaktavya) while yet being expressed; to say they are both "expressed" and "inexpressible" is a contradiction. Moreover, it would be contradictory to say of them that they are both determined to be exactly so and not determined.

Likewise, there exists right vision (*samyagdarśana*) which has the result of such ascertainment: "Does it exist or does it not exist?"—for it is inconsistent with the Jaina doctrine that contradictory properties, such as existence and non-existence, could coexist in a single substratum (*dharmin*) like the soul (*jīva*) or other categories; for if existence were present in one property, another property such as non-existence could not exist, and if non-existence were present, existence likewise could not exist. (Brahmasūtra Śāṅkara Bhāṣya 2.2.33).

Furthermore, if it is argued that because substance and mode are commingled, like the man-lion (narasiṃha), they possess a single variegated form and are thus said to have two forms—that is incorrect, because the variegated nature of the man-lion is unproven. And it has been said: "Indeed, the duality of form belongs to the entity because of its nature as both substance and mode;
even though those two are of one essence, there is a distinction due to the difference in designation and so forth."

And that [subject] would indeed possess the status of a subject (dharmitva) because it is dependent upon them; yet no other [subject] is perceived by means of that. Therefore, this debate is devised by a fool.
Hetubinduṭīkā, pp. 151–57;
Tattvopaplava, pp. 95–96.
If the universal and the particular were mutually identical in nature, there would be a confusion between them; therefore, this twofold nature is not logically tenable in reality. 1722
Even if these two lack mutual intrinsic nature, their distinctness remains a consequence; furthermore, even if they were entities, a dual nature would not be tenable. (1723)
Furthermore, the existence of that [nature] and the non-existence of that [nature], due to their mutual contradiction, cannot in any way be conceived within a single entity. (1729)
For prescription and prohibition, being mutually contradictory, cannot be established by anyone with a sound mind in a single instance. (1730)
For instance, since permanence and impermanence consist of affirmation and negation, they cannot exist in a single substratum; likewise, this applies to existence and non-existence as well.
Thus, even in liberation, non-absolutism (anekānta) does not cease to apply, and it would follow that "the liberated one is both liberated and not liberated."

And this being the case, it follows that the very same person is both liberated and a transmigrating being; such is the fault in the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) when one accepts [the existence of] non-absolutism itself—see Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 20.

Thus, following the refutation of others, the proof that substance and mode are essentially characterized by both difference and non-difference in some respect, as well as the removal of defects such as doubt regarding non-absolutism (anekānta),
is now addressed here.

As for what was stated—that substance and mode are absolutely distinct because they appear as distinct, and so forth—does "appearing as distinct" mean being apprehended by distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or appearing with distinct forms? In the first case, there is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*) due to the self (*ātman*) and other such entities; for even though these are apprehended by distinct means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest, their actual difference is impossible.

Even in the second alternative, do you intend for those two to appear as having different forms in some way, or in every respect? If it is in some way, then their difference would be established only in that limited sense, because an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is possible only through that very [partial] difference, and not in every respect, since the opposite would be the case. Furthermore, in such a case, the reason (*hetu*) would be contradictory, as it would prove the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), and it would also be a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we ourselves accept a difference in some way.

In every way, however, the proof of their difference is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), because it is employed after the statement of a fact that has been sublated by perception—just as in the case of "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance. Or rather, it is because it is employed after the statement of a thesis sublated by inference: "Whatever is not perceived through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a certain form should not be accepted in that form, just as a jar is not [accepted] in the form of a cloth; and substances, modes, and so forth are not perceived through a means of valid cognition in the form of absolute difference" (p. 359, l. 5).

Thus, in that regard, [the question is]: is it because they are apprehended by different means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or because they appear with different forms (*ākāra*)? [From the *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 738]—[this refers to] the distinction between the mind and its objects. *Śra.* (Śrīmad-Ācārya) [notes: *cittadbheda*].

Furthermore, there is inconclusiveness due to [the case of] distant trees and so forth; for even though there is a difference in appearance for observers situated in distant or near locations by virtue of their cognitions being apprehended as indistinct or otherwise, no actual difference in the object itself is possible.

But surely, in this case, there is indeed a difference in the object due to the difference in its cognition; for instance, initially, the cognition of one standing at a distance has the universal of "uprightness" as its object, whereas at a later time, upon approaching that place, it has the particulars such as "branches" as its object. This too is charming only so long as it is not scrutinized; for if a difference in objects were thus admitted, there would follow the impossibility of the determination of identity in the form: "The tree which I saw while standing at a distance, that very same one I see now. This is because cognitions appearing with varying degrees of clarity would have different objects—by virtue of having universals and particulars as their respective objects—just like the cognitions of a jar and a cloth.

Now, if it is maintained that they have a single object of cognition with respect to the tree as a whole, but a difference of objects with respect to the general and particular aspects; how then would the acceptance of absolute [difference] not collapse, since in the case of substance and mode (dravya-paryāya) as well, such difference and non-difference are established in some sense? Or, if it is intended that they appear in entirely different forms; that is unproven, because substance and mode, which are in fact related through identity in some sense, are perceived together without contradiction in direct perception.

Whatever appears in uncontradicted perception must be accepted exactly as it appears, just as blue is [accepted] as being blue; and since substance and mode appear in uncontradicted perception as having some form of identity, [this is established] from mere consciousness. (Note: *ū* is for *ūrdhva*; *ba*, *ja*, *ā* are manuscript variants).
—[The opponent says: "The state of being an object of poetry (*kāviṣayatva*) is what is distinguished [in the definition]. [The author replies:

This is not so; for it is not unestablished that the direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) in which that [object] appears is non-sublated, since no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever exists that could sublate it.
Perception is not its sublater, because an absolute difference from it does not appear therein.

Could inference also be its sublater—either this very same [inference] or another? It cannot be this very same one, because it is impossible for it even to arise, since its object is sublated by perception.

If it is argued that there is no sublation of its object by this [inference] because it is erroneous, from what does its error arise? If it is argued that it arises from being sublated by this [inference], there is the consequence of a logical circle (*cakraka*), for instance: the sublation of perception by this [inference] occurs when the latter arises with an uncontradicted object; once that sublation exists, the error of perception follows; and once that error exists, the latter arises with an uncontradicted object.

And how could there not be the application of the [inference] "fire is thus non-hot because it is a substance, like water," since its object is likewise uncontradicted? For here too, there is no difference in that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), just as in the case of [the reason] "having a different appearance" (*bhinnapratibhāsatva*). Since the subject (*pakṣa*) is contradicted by direct perception, its lack of probative force (*agamakatva*) is identical in the other case as well; therefore, this inference does not contradict it at all. (Ta-ba, Ja)
Indeed, perception is not its sublater, because an absolute difference between them is not manifested therein (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
739). If it were sublated by another inference, this [perception] would be redundant, since the probandum would already be established for that very reason.

Nor is there any sublater of that [perception] appearing between them; for would that sublater arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*) characterized by its performance of a different purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), its production from a different cause, its occurrence at a different time, or its being superposed with contradictory properties? Among these, the first position is untenable, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of a dancer and so forth; for even a single dancer performs many mutually distinct purposeful actions characterized by gestures, bodily movements, frowns, and glances, as well as joy, sorrow, and other states in the spectators.

The state of arising from different causes is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to sprouts and the like, because it is observed that even a single [effect], such as a sprout, arises from a collection of multiple causes such as earth and so forth. Now, if it is argued that what constitutes difference is arising from different material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and not merely arising from different causes in general—and since that [specific condition] does not exist here, this fault does not apply—then how could there be a distinction between qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) and so forth? For even in those cases, arising from different material causes is impossible. —[End of citation from] Piṇḍanartakī. Ā. [Note: *pi* is likely a scribal abbreviation for *piṇḍanartakī*.]

Furthermore, on account of their difference in time, would the difference of the cloth be established from the threads characterized by a prior state when they have not yet reached the state of being a cloth, or from those that have reached the state of being a cloth? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for it is admitted that all entities differ between their prior and subsequent states. Indeed, the prior state of an object cannot be the same as its subsequent state, since the arising of a subsequent form is perceived only through the abandonment of the prior form.

In the second case, however, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for it is impossible for the threads in the state of being cloth to exist at a time different from that of the cloth—[since] the cloth [is not distinct from them].

Furthermore, the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to incense, fire, and so forth; indeed, even when there is an attribution of contradictory properties characterized by cold and hot touch in different parts of the hand held [there], no distinction is perceived in the incense, the fire, and so on.

Nor should it be asserted that the substratum of the sensations of cold and heat belongs only to the parts of the hand that are touched and not to the whole (avayavin) such as the incense-burner, for that would contradict direct perception.

Therefore, it is absolute difference (*atyantabheda*) alone that is incompatible with identity (*tādātmya*); thus, cessation [of the object] occurs through the superimposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), but not in the case of partial difference (*kathañcidbheda*). This is as seen in the examples of the knots on a rope, the contraction and expansion of the hand, and the coiling of a snake.

For the distinction between entities is accepted on the basis of their cognition; if that [cognition] exists even when there is some degree of difference between the state and that which possesses the state, then why is this [distinction] not also accepted? Nor is it a royal decree that a single entity cannot possess a nature consisting of multiple states.

If even a single entity were to persist through successive states by way of identity according to the method described, then how could there be any contradiction whatsoever regarding its unity? For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must accept an object exactly as it reveals the nature of that thing: where it reveals absolute difference, there is absolute difference, as in the case of a jar and a cloth; but where it reveals difference in some respect, there is difference in some respect, as in the case of a rope and its knots.

Thus, because it is vitiated by numerous defects and because the probans—such as "appearing as distinct"—is untenable as a proof for the absolute difference of substance and its attributes, the example is also devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for even in the case of jars, cloths, and so forth, absolute difference is impossible. This impossibility is well-established through their mutual non-difference by virtue of existence (*sattva*) and other common characteristics;

furthermore, this [example] is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), since for one whose eyes are wide open, the appearance of jars and other objects is possible even within a single act of perception.

Furthermore, one should not admit a difference in consciousness for each respective object, because that would entail the non-establishment of the whole (avayavin), since it is equally easy to imagine such a difference in its upper, lower, and middle parts here as well; and the contradiction with actual experience has not been devoured by crows elsewhere either.

And if it is claimed that because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [reason] is observed in the example through absolute difference, it is therefore accepted as a prover even when proving the absolute difference of substance, mode, and so forth; then one must also accept as a prover such arguments as "sound is non-audible because it exists, like a jar," since there is no distinction here either, as the connection of existence and the like with non-audibility is understood in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) such as a jar. If it is argued that this [latter argument] is not a prover because the subject (*pakṣa*) is sublated by perception, then that lack of being a prover is no different in the other case as well, due to the absence of [the required conditions]. (Abhayadevasūri’s *Tattvabodhavidhāyinī*, A, B, J, Bhāṃ)

Regarding what was stated— that there is a difference in designation (saṃjñābheda) such as "threads" and "cloth"— because that is easily refuted by [the principle of] non-difference (akṣe), and because that [distinction] is based solely on a difference in state (avasthābheda), it is merely a verbal assertion; therefore, this [argument] establishes only that [difference of state], but not an absolute difference (atyantabheda).

Furthermore, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for in cases such as "the sky" (*gagana*) and "space" (*ākāśa*), although there is an absence of absolute difference between the things, there is still a difference in designation (*saṃjñābheda*). On the other hand, in cases such as "water" (*jala*) and "waters" (*āpaḥ*), both a difference in designation and a difference in grammatical number (*vacanabheda*) are possible. Indeed, a difference in designation and so forth establishes an absolute difference between things only when it pertains to objects that lack a common substratum (*ananvayavastu*), and not otherwise; for otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: A difference in name and so forth regarding an object whose underlying substance (*anvaya*) is not abandoned does not establish absolute difference, just as the difference in names such as "water" and "fluids" [does not establish that they are distinct substances]. And this difference in name and so forth—such as "threads" and "cloth"—pertains to an object of such a nature.

If it is objected: "In that case, would it not follow that terms like 'thread' and 'cloth' are synonyms (*paryāya-śabda*), just like 'gagana' and 'ākāśa'? [The response is: This is indeed so, because those words denote specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the same substance.

For threads produced by the manual activity of women and others are incapable of removing cold or serving other such purposes prior to the activity of the weaver and others; they receive the designation "threads. However, after that activity, having attained a specific state and becoming capable of those [purposes], they receive the designation "cloth" (paṭa).
(Page 359, Line 14: *saṃjñābheda*—Ā.)

Furthermore, as for the other statement—"the existence of the cloth" and so forth—that too is incorrect; for in cases such as "the existence of the six categories" or "the group of the six categories," we observe the occurrence of the genitive case and so on even in the absence of any difference [between the relata], yet you certainly do not accept that "existence" and the like are entities distinct from the six categories.

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Existence (sattva) is the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition that makes an existent known; it is intended as a distinct property (*dharmāntara*) called 'being an object of a means of valid cognition that apprehends the existent,' which constitutes the existence of the six categories. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) by this [reason]. This too is untenable, because it would entail the contradiction of the number of the six categories, since that property of existence would be an entity distinct from them.

[Objection: Surely those entities that are of the nature of substrata (*dharmin*) have been declared to be the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), whereas those that are of the nature of attributes (*dharma*) are indeed admitted to be distinct from them. Thus, the *Padārthapraveśaka* text states: "In this way, the substrata alone have been indicated without their attributes" (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 15).

[Response: Let it be so; nevertheless, what kind of relation exists between an attribute such as existence (*astitva*) and the six categories, by virtue of which it could be an attribute of them—is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)? It cannot be conjunction, because conjunction, being a quality (*guṇa*), must reside in a substance (*dravya*).
Nor is it inherence (*samavāya*), because that is held to be unitary;
if this [quality] were related to inherence by means of another inherence, it would follow that inherence is manifold, which contradicts the intended position.
Furthermore, if one were to accept the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) without a [real] relation, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
*sajjñāpaka*—ba, ja;
*ṣaḍjñāpaka*—śra.
Now, is it not the case that existence (*sattva*) is the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes [something] known? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
157, line 2; see also *upalambha-pra-* in the B and J editions).
Thus [it is stated in] Anu-;
this is also cited in Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 192, and Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 157.
This is to be accepted from the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, folio 661, and the *Syādvāda-ratnākara*, folio 878— thus it is desired by Jaḍa.

Furthermore, since there is no existence other than [the primary] existence, how could there be a case-ending based on distinction (vyatireka) therein? If another existence is admitted even in that case, then there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). Moreover, because existence and the like would result in being of the nature of a substratum (dharmin) through the successive addition of further attributes, the claim that "there are only six substrata" would be contradicted; for those very things which are of the nature of substrata are determined to be six. This argument is also baseless, as it would entail the non-enumeration of quality (guṇa), action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya).

For these [qualities] do not possess the nature of a substratum (*dharmin*) alone; since they can also exist as attributes (*dharma*) by virtue of being dependent on a substance, so too, in cases such as "the state of space" (*khatva*), where there is no difference [between the base and the attribute], the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is observed; thus, that [formation] does not rely solely on the position of difference.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—"it is a *tatpuruṣa*," etc.—that is merely a conventional designation, because a *tatpuruṣa* is seen even when there is no difference, as in "an army of elephants" (*senāgaja*) or "trees in a forest" (*kānanavṛkṣa*), and a *bahuvrīhi* is seen in cases such as "an army consisting of rutting elephants and heroic men" (*mattagajā vīrapuruṣā senā*).
pṛ. 359, l. 16 – *vṛkṣaḥ* (MS:
