*śra*) Regarding what was stated—"In the case of 'identity' (*tādātmya*), is that cloth the self (*ātman*)? and so forth—the analysis (*vigraha*) there should be seen as follows: "The two selves (*ātmānau*) of that entity (*vastu*)"—namely, substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*), or the properties (*dharma*) of existence (*sattva*) and non-existence (*asattva*)—"are its two selves" (*tadātmānau*), because the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the entity. The state of being those two (*tayorbhāvaḥ*) is identity (*tādātmya*)—that is, having the nature of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*).

For difference (*bheda*) is merely the nature of a mode (*paryāya*), while non-difference (*abheda*) is the nature of substance (*dravya*). Indeed, difference and non-difference have the very essence of substance and mode; for a real entity (*vastu*) is neither substance alone nor mode alone. This is because a real entity is a collection consisting of both aspects. Substance and mode, however, possess neither the status of being a complete entity nor the status of being non-entities, but rather the status of being a single part of an entity. Just as a portion of the ocean is neither the ocean nor a non-ocean, but a single part of the ocean, so it has been said:
"The wise declare that a part of an entity is neither an entity nor a non-entity."

Just as it is said in the *Tattvārthaśloka* (p. 118): "Neither that which is not the ocean, nor the ocean itself, is the one who possesses the ocean," so too there is no fault in the analysis [of the compound] as "those whose self (*ātman*) is that cloth"; for, with respect to a particular state, the oneness of the threads is accepted.

If it is argued that, in the analysis "the cloth is that which has those threads as its self," the multiplicity of the threads would entail the multiplicity of the cloth; we ask: what is this so-called "multiplicity" of it? Is it being composed of multiple constituent parts, or is it the consequence of such multiplicity for each individual thread? In the first case, you are proving what is already established, since the cloth is indeed composed of multiple constituent parts such as the threads arranged in length and breadth (*ātāna-vitāna*).
As for the second case, it is untenable, because such a transformation is impossible for each of them individually.

For the cloth is a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of those [threads] characterized by their being stretched lengthwise and crosswise; and that [transformation] is perceived only when these [threads] are combined, not otherwise. And such states of theirs are called the "self" (*ātman*) of the cloth.
For the transformation of a substance is twofold: in its individual state and in its collective state, as in the case of milk and the like [becoming] curd and the like.

Thus, just as with substance and mode, the identity of qualities and the qualified, and so forth, must be understood in some sense; for it has been established on page 359, line 19 that the difference in appearance and the attribution of contradictory properties do not prove absolute difference. "Its two selves" means its two natures; the state of being those two selves is identity, which is the nature of both difference and non-difference.
Āptaparīkṣā, p. 22; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 158a:
"This is neither a real entity nor a non-entity; it is described by the wise as having the nature of a partial entity."
Regarding the variant reading "yata yathocyate," it is said:
"Just as the ocean is neither non-ocean nor ocean, nor even a part of the ocean" (Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 118).

And as for that which was further stated—"even though there is a plurality of forms in the case of qualities, the possessor of qualities, and so forth"—that too is not tenable. Since it is impossible to apprehend all objects through a nature that is somehow both distinct and non-distinct—just like the relationship between a quality and its possessor—the distinctness of one thing from another is established.

For their distinction and non-distinction consist in the difference in their identity and form; and apprehension in both ways is simply the appearance [of them] as such. Since that [appearance] does not exist elsewhere, how could the discussion of multiplicity, whether external or internal, be eliminated? (Page 359, Line 26)

As for what was also stated—that [the universal] is one, eternal, and so forth—that too is mere faith; for it has been established that the nature of the universal consists of being manifold, non-eternal, composed of parts, and non-pervasive.

Therefore, like the modification into specific particulars (*viśeṣapariṇāma*), the modification into the universal characterized by similarity (*sādṛśyalakṣaṇasāmānyapariṇāma*) is also distinct for each individual object.

Furthermore, since these [particulars] are perceived through direct perception as the substrata of such similar and dissimilar properties (*dharma*), how could the acceptance of their nature as universals (*sāmānya*) contradict the acceptance of their nature as particulars (*viśeṣa*)? Moreover, the relationship between property and substrate (*dharma-dharmin*) is not tenable if they are either entirely different or entirely non-different, like the Sahya and Vindhya mountains, or like the individual nature of either one; rather, it exists through a certain degree of difference. For while there is indeed difference between the property and the substrate, their non-difference is characterized by the impossibility of conceiving them as separate substances—that is, their indivisibility (*aśakyavivecanatva*).

Indeed, it is not the case that for these two [substance and mode], as it is for jars, cloths, and so forth, the characteristic of being incapable of being distinguished is impossible; for although the substrata such as jars are mutually distinct, they are nonetheless permeated by a single substance such as clay throughout all their properties—including similar and dissimilar transformations—and thus there is a difference of the substratum-substance from its other properties such as taste in the form of color and so forth, while there is non-difference in the form of the substance itself. (Page 359, Line 28)

In the same way, it should be inferred that the whole (*avayavin*) is non-different from its parts in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), yet it is different from one part in relation to other parts. In this regard, just as even contradictory natures such as long and short—though they appear contradictory—are accepted as non-contradictory in a single locus due to a difference in perspective by the force of perception, so too should it be understood for difference and non-difference, since there is no distinction in their being perceived.
(Śāstradīpikā 1)
1.5 The forms of the mouth and so forth belonging to the self cannot be separated from one another because they can never be led into another self; therefore, they are indivisible.

Because of mutual exclusion (*mitho-bheda*), according to Bhā[ṭṭa] and Śrī [Harṣa], if one were to admit an absolute difference between the substratum (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharmas*), it would follow that they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); for even intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is a property, and thus, by being different from the substratum, it too would lack existence. And thus, this [substratum] would be non-existent.
Whatever is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is non-existent, just like a sky-lotus; and yet, the subject (*dharmin*) intended by you is [alleged to be] devoid of intrinsic nature.

Consequently, there would be the non-existence of all phenomena (*dharmas*) as well, because it is impossible for them to exist without a substratum. Thus, a state of universal emptiness (*sakalaśūnyatā*) follows even for the opponent who protests so loudly.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is devoid of intrinsic nature to serve as a substratum, for if it were, it would follow that even things such as a donkey’s horn could be a substratum.

The claim that "even though the nature is distinct, there is no lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) because it inheres in the substratum (dharmī)" is also unsatisfactory; for it has already been established that inherence (samavāya) does not exist. Furthermore, even if the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmī) were absolutely non-distinct, it would follow that they possess the nature of only one of them, resulting in the non-existence of both;
for if they were entirely identical, there would be either only the property or only the substratum, and thus the nature of one or the other would be absent.

To claim that "since its existence is merely imagined, its non-existence does not constitute a fault" is likewise an unexamined statement; for an imagination that is without a basis (nirbīja) is itself untenable, and its lack of a basis is not unestablished, since if an entity—whether external or internal—possessed an absolute, unitary nature, it would be impossible for it to function as a cause.

Indeed, it is not logical for that which possesses an absolutely unitary nature to be the seed of manifold conceptual constructions; for it is impossible for something devoid of distinct capacities to be the cause of diverse effects. Whatever is devoid of distinct capacities cannot be the cause of diverse effects, just like an entity considered to be eternal; and the entity considered to be a *svalakṣaṇa* (particular) is likewise devoid of distinct capacities.

Therefore, how could this [exclusion] be the cause of the two effects characterized by the conceptualization of property and property-bearer? To claim that "the production of distinct effects from a single nature—even one devoid of distinct potencies—is not contradictory, by virtue of the exclusion of distinct intrinsic natures," is an unexamined statement. This is because that [exclusion], being distinct from that [nature], is impossible; and since it is of the nature of a non-entity (*avastu*), its possession of a distinct intrinsic nature is untenable, just like a donkey's horn. Alternatively, if such a nature were possible, it would not be a non-entity. This will be explained during the investigation of *apoha*.

And if there is a difference in that [exclusion], let the difference reside in the entity itself, since it is not contradictory for it to be there; for it would be quite extraordinary to claim that the non-entity is divided while the entity is not.

Furthermore, if one accepts a difference in exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), then a difference in properties (*dharma*) is established, because exclusions themselves are properties—this follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). — *Asaj-jñāna* (Commentary on the *Jaina-nyāya*).

Regarding what was stated— that [an entity] consists of both existence and non-existence, and so forth— even though there is a difference between those two distinct natures, that too is incorrect; for since their being of such a nature is perceived in objects, the contradiction is not established.

For contradiction is established through non-apprehension, as in the case of a suckling infant in a barren woman. However, when a thing exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth, there is no non-apprehension of its non-existence by way of another nature (*pararūpa*) and so forth.

Indeed, the very existence of a thing is not its "own-nature" (*svarūpa*) in every respect; for if it were, it would follow that it exists even by way of another’s nature, which would entail that everything possesses the nature of everything else, resulting in a monism of existence (*sattādvaita*). And this [monism] has already been answered previously.

Nor is it non-existence alone; for if it were so, there would be the consequence of its non-existence even in its own nature—just as in the case of another's nature—which would entail its being like a sky-flower. Furthermore, this would entail a universal void, resulting in the cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), since there would be no engagement in anything whatsoever.
Moreover, that [notion of] emptiness has already been refuted previously; therefore, enough with further prolixity.
(Page 360, Line 1)
[Objection: But how can the two contradictory [qualities], difference and non-difference, exist in one and the same thing? [Reply: There is no contradiction, because they are perceived together.

For if difference and non-difference were perceived through mutual exclusion—like "this is silver" and "this is not silver"—then there would be a contradiction; but their perception is not through mutual exclusion.
The two cognitions, "this is a cow," appearing simultaneously, establish that a single object possesses a dual nature.

For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) brings about non-difference, while non-synonymy brings about difference; therefore, there is no contradiction due to the force of perception and because of the difference in perspective. Thus it is said in the *Śāstradīpikā* 1.1: [text follows].
Pramāṇakhaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 158:
Who would not accept that everything exists, by virtue of its fourfold nature consisting of its own form and so forth?
If it were not that what is non-existent appears as such due to cognitive distortion, then [the object] would not be established; thus, [the object] is authoritative (āpta). 15.10a-b.
An entity, which consists of both existence and non-existence in relation to its own nature and that of others, is not perceived erroneously;
for it is eternally composed of existence and non-existence by virtue of its own form and the form of others. (Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 135)
12. *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Chapter on Non-existence (*Abhāvapariccheda*): Existence [is established] by its own [nature].

If [an entity] were existent by virtue of another's form just as it is by its own form, then consciousness and so forth would result in being non-conscious and so forth, just like their own self; if it were non-existent by virtue of its own form just as it is by another's form, then total emptiness (śūnyatā) would follow;
and if it were existent by virtue of another substance just as it is by its own substance, there would be a contradiction with the specific determination of substances (*dravyapratiniyama*).
(Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 131)

Nor should it be asserted that existence itself [of an object] in its own nature and so forth is non-existence in the nature of another, and that non-existence in the nature of another is itself existence in its own nature; for there is a distinction between them based on the difference of the respective causes to be considered. Indeed, existence is established in an object with reference to its own substance and so forth as the cause, whereas non-existence is established with reference to the substance of another and so forth. Therefore, because they are dependent upon distinct causes, there is a difference between existence and non-existence.

That which has its basis in distinct causes possesses difference, as is the case with numbers such as unity and so forth; and existence and non-existence have their basis in distinct causes. Thus, this reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has been proven by the method already stated;

nor is there a deficiency in the probandum or the probans (*sādhyasādhanavaikalya*) in the example, because it is well-known that within a single substance, the number "duality" and so forth—which depends on another substance—has a basis in distinct causes and possesses difference compared to the number "unity," which depends solely on the substance's own nature.

If there were absolute non-difference between these two, their being based on distinct causes would be untenable; for that which is absolutely non-different cannot have its basis in distinct causes, just as in the case of existence (*sattva*) or non-existence (*asattva*). Furthermore, you yourselves maintain that there is absolute non-difference between existence and non-existence;

therefore, it is impossible for these two to function as the objects of their respective restricted cognitions of "existent" and "non-existent. For that very reason, if they were based on a non-distinct cause, your accepted principle—that a difference in causes everywhere results in a difference in effects—would be contradicted.

Furthermore, there would be a collapse of the established order of specifically determined entities if existence and non-existence were entirely non-different. For just as a jar exists by way of its own substance and so forth, it would not exist by way of another’s substance and so forth, because non-existence is not distinct from that existence. Consequently, if it were non-existent [by way of another], it would also have to be non-existent by way of its own substance and so forth, because existence is not distinct from that non-existence. Therefore, since the specific nature of individual entities would not be established, the collapse of the established order of specifically determined entities is proven.

To claim that the very existence of a thing (*vastusattva*), when qualified by its distinction from others, is the cause for its determination [as distinct], is merely to follow the maxim of a blind man entering a snake’s hole; for this is nothing but giving a different name to non-existence itself.

Therefore, all entities must be understood as having the nature of both existence and non-existence in terms of their own and other forms, because otherwise the determination of their specific forms would be impossible, or else the performance of their specific effects would be impossible.

This is because, through the dependence on the fourfold [consideration] of own-form, other-form, and so forth, there is a difference in their essential nature, whereby the distinction between existence and non-existence is logically established within a single entity.
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 132; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 158, l.

And those two [do] not exist; thus, "not"— *ba*, *ja*.

Now, if it is argued that the determination of those [categories] will occur by virtue of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), we ask: what is the nature of this mutual non-existence—is it independent (*svatantra*) or a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*)? It cannot be independent, because such a thing will be refuted later on.

Now, regarding the property of existence (*bhāvadharma*): of what entity is this property? Is it of the jar, of the ground, or of both? If it belongs to the jar, is it a negator of the jar’s own nature or not? If it is a negator, does it negate it in the jar itself, or on the ground? In the first case, how can this be a property of the jar, given that the substratum (the jar) itself is non-existent? Or else, why would there be the cognition "the jar is not on the ground" when, according to you, that cognition would logically apply to the jar itself? In the second case, however, our own position is established, because we accept that the absence of the jar—which is indeed a property of the jar—functions as the negator of the jar’s own nature on the ground.
Now, if it is not a negation [of the jar], then because the nature of the jar would logically follow even for the ground, the postulation of non-existence (abhāva) would be useless.

If, on the other hand, it is a property (dharma) of the ground, that is not so; for, due to the occurrence of the cognition "the jar is not" through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), its being a property of the jar is established here just as in the case of existence. For just as existence is a property of the jar based on the coreferential perception "the jar exists," so too is non-existence.

If there is no contradiction in non-existence being a property of the substratum even while maintaining grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which is supported by it, then let there likewise be no contradiction in existence also being such a property. Consequently, an object such as a jar, being devoid of both properties, would not differ from a sky-flower. By this, the view that non-existence possesses both properties is also refuted, because it would entail the absurd conclusion that existence also possesses those same properties. Furthermore, as for this [alleged] existence in its own location and non-existence in other locations, this is indeed accepted, since the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) between them is admitted.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 20, line *ḍa*: "And thus, [it is] cognition," *sā*— *Bhaṭṭa*, *Jaṭā*.
It is qualified by that which is to be contained—this is what is meant by "it is distinguished" (viśiṣyati) in the versions of Ba, Ja, and Śra.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—"the nature of being (bhāvarūpatā) is swallowed up," and so forth—what is this so-called "swallowing up" by way of the nature of non-being? Is it the removal of its own essential nature (svarūpāpahāra), or the negation of its single substratum? It cannot be the removal of its own essential nature, because since existence and non-existence possess equal force, it is impossible for them to remove each other’s essential nature.

Nor is there a negation of a single substratum; for it has been established that existence and non-existence, by way of their own and other forms, both exist even in a single substratum (pṛ॰ 360, l. 3;
abhāvarūpa—MS).

And as for what was further stated—that it is the meaning of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha*), and so forth—that is true; for it is accepted that the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed only with respect to an absolute (*ekānta*) determined through a *naya*. Nor does this contradict the fundamental tenet that "everything is of a non-absolute nature" (*anekāntātmaka*), because that declaration of everything being of that nature is made in reference to the domain of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, in reference to the scope of a *naya*, even that which is of an absolute nature is accepted; thus, even non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is itself non-absolute, being established by both *pramāṇa* and *naya*.
For it is stated in the *Bṛhat-svayambhū-stotra*, verse 103,
that "the substratum possesses multiple forms, but the attributes do not [possess them] in any way whatsoever."

"Non-absolutism [is established] from valid cognition (pramāṇa), while its absolutism [is established] from the applied standpoint (naya). This is the second half of the verse.

If it is argued that there is no pervasion (avyāpti) because that [non-absolutism] is absent in non-absolutism itself, we say no; for it is established even there, as stated in the *Tattvārtharājavārttika*, p. 25.

As for what was stated—that if [an object] were of that nature, defects such as doubt would arise—that too is a mere fantasy; for when a thing is perceived as having a manifold nature consisting of existence, non-existence, and so forth, doubt is untenable.

Whatever is perceived as having a certain nature, there can be no doubt regarding its being of that very nature, just as there is no doubt regarding the nature of a post and a person when they are perceived as possessing their own respective characteristics. And all entities are indeed perceived as having a manifold nature consisting of existence, non-existence, and so forth.

Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has already been demonstrated that [the object] is perceived as having that very nature; nor is the example deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because even in a dream, when the property of being a post (*sthāṇutva*) and so forth is perceived, no doubt regarding the post and such is perceived, since it is only when that [property] is not perceived that doubt is observed there;
and doubt is a wavering perception, whereas perception as having the nature of existence (*sat*) and so forth is not so.

Indeed, for anyone whose mind is unimpaired, the cognition of an object as having the nature of existence and non-existence by way of its own and other forms does not waver; yet, even though such doubt is not actually arising, you here forcibly impute it. But if this were so, the determination of any specific form would not be possible for anything, because it would be easy to impute such doubt everywhere—for instance, regarding a jar or the like, the question would arise whether its nature as a "jar" belongs to an impartite whole (*avayavin*), or to momentary atoms (*paramāṇu*), or to a collection of cognitions (*jñānapracaya*), or to the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and so forth; thus, nothing would be established.

Therefore, by one who desires the determination of the specific form of a jar or similar object, doubt must necessarily be admitted here, even if it has not yet arisen. Thus, it is not logical for there to be doubt regarding an entity that consists of both existence and non-existence, nor is there any contradiction; for existence and non-existence are based on different causes in that case. There is no contradiction between two things in a single substratum when they are based on different causes, as in the case of unity and plurality, or subtlety and grossness. And existence and non-existence in a single substratum are indeed based on different causes.
Furthermore, contradiction is everywhere established through non-perception (*anupalambha*).

Indeed, when something that meets the conditions for perceptibility is not perceived in a certain place, it is contradictory to it there—just as a horn is contradictory to the head of a horse. However, since there is no non-perception of non-existence by way of another form while existence is being perceived of a thing by way of its own form and so forth, if one were to admit a contradiction between these two even while they are both being perceived, then because of the consequence of a thing being contradictory even with its own nature, it would result in the loss of its intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

If the nature of both affirmation and negation were contradictory in a single locus, then how could a universal-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa) possess a dual capacity consisting of the causes for inclusive and exclusive cognitions? Or how could a variegated object (mecaka) possess a nature that is both one and many? And how could a single entity possess the nature of both man and lion, or the nature of both Umā and Īśvara? because many varieties can coexist in a single location— like a variegated gem (*mecaka*) and so forth— [it is established].

"There is neither absolute difference nor non-difference between affirmation and negation, because of the aforementioned faults";

"By way of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), Narasiṃha is proclaimed; it is not because he has the form of a man-lion, nor is he 'not a man'—he is simply a man. "From the perspective of conventional cognition, [the categories] emerge and submerge like waves in water—distinct from one another yet non-different from their own substance. (Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 174; cf. Bhāṣya on Anekāntavādaprameyaratnākara, p. 15).
Furthermore, contradiction is determined by the non-existence of one thing when it possesses its complete causes but another is present, as in the case of cold and fire;
however, the non-existence of non-existence (asattva) when existence (sattva) is present, or the non-existence of existence when non-existence is present, is never experienced at any time.

Furthermore, would this contradiction between these two be characterized by non-coexistence, by the nature of existing through mutual exclusion, or by the form of a slayer and its victim? It cannot first be characterized by non-coexistence, because existence and non-existence are perceived in a single substratum without being mutually excluded; for there is no such contradiction between two things that are perceived in this way, as is the case with color and taste, and existence and non-existence are indeed perceived in this manner.

Contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, however, would only be possible between two things that are both possible together in one place—such as form and taste in a mango fruit—and not between two things that are impossible together, like a hare’s horn and a horse’s horn, nor between a possible and an impossible thing, like a barren woman and her suckling child. For contradiction among entities is indeed twofold: either it is understood through the fact that when a thing whose causes are unimpaired occurs, another is absent, as in the case of cold and hot touch;
or it is understood through the characteristic of existing by way of mutual exclusion, as in the case of existence and non-existence.
Nyāyabindu, p. 96–98; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 158;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 131.

Furthermore, is this contradiction between two properties (*dharma*), or between a property and its substratum (*dharmin*)? In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because such is the very definition of properties;

nor is there a contradiction regarding their having a single substratum when they are pervaded by such a contradiction, since these [properties], even in such a state, are perceived as having that same substratum, just like color and other qualities in a citron fruit.

If there were a contradiction between the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*), there would be no cognition of the properties at all within the property-bearer; yet this is not the case, because they appear as established by uncontradicted cognition.

Furthermore, even a contradiction in the form of mutual destruction—like that between a snake and a mongoose—is not to be suspected here, because the existence and non-existence [of the properties] possess equal force, whereas in the case of the strong and the weak, the weak is perceived [as being overcome].

Or, let there be some contradiction; even so, would it be total (*sarvathā*) or partial (*kathañcit*)? It cannot be total, because even the sensations of cold and heat, for instance, do not establish a contradiction in their nature as such, since they are not excluded from the essential nature of existence (*sattva*) and so forth. Whatever does not exclude the essential nature of something is not contradictory with it in that form, just as a jar and the like are not contradictory with respect to their jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*). And the sensations of cold, heat, and so forth do not exclude the essential nature of existence and the like.

And because they are perceived as having a single substratum; for that which is perceived as having a single substratum is not in every respect contradictory, just as color, taste, and so forth [coexist], or as the lowering and raising [of the ends] in a single balance scale. Furthermore, cold and hot tactile sensations and so forth are perceived as having a single substratum in things such as incense-burners; thus, while there may be some degree of contradiction, this is equally the case even for color and the rest. Consequently, just as a single entity could possess the nature of both existence and non-existence, it would also follow that it could not have the nature of color and so forth; but this is not tenable, because it contradicts direct perception. And thus it is said in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*: [text fragment].

Furthermore, is contradiction (virodha) distinct from entities or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, how can it be called a "contradictor," since, being identical with its own nature, it would be like the very essence of those entities? If, on the other hand, it is distinct, even so it cannot be a contradictor for that very reason, just like any other separate object. If it is argued that although contradiction is a separate entity, it is a contradictor because it serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of entities, whereas other separate objects do not because they lack this quality—that too is incorrect. For contradiction is a non-entity (*abhāva*) consisting of a mere void; if it were a qualifier of two substances such as cold and heat, then it would follow that those two could never be perceived.

Even if it were a qualifier of only one of the two, this same objection would apply, and that very thing would be the contradictory factor—namely, that which is its qualifier and nothing else. Furthermore, contradiction cannot reside in only one of the two, because it must be shared by both; otherwise, it would follow that contradiction would exist everywhere and at all times.

Now, although contradiction resides in both the agent and the object in relation to the states of being contradicted (*viruddhyamānatva*) and contradicting (*virodhakatva*), it is nevertheless designated as "residing in both" (*dviṣṭha*) because, in relation to contradiction in its general sense (*virodhasāmānya*), it serves as a qualifier for both. But if this were so, would it not follow that even color-form (*rūpa*) and the like would be contradictors? For there is no difference in their general nature (*sāmānya*) also residing in both. Furthermore, if this [contradiction] were of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), the relationship between universal and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣabhāva*) would be untenable; and if it were of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*) and so forth, its status as a qualifier of qualities and the like would be untenable. [The opponent replies: Contradiction resides in itself... (*virodhaḥ svā-śra*)... [text fragment].
—Thus, always, [it is] due to the non-existence of the six categories...

[Śra]. Furthermore, if contradiction (*virodha*) is accepted as a specific category distinct from the six categories, residing in multiple things, and established through the specific cognitions of the contradictory and the non-contradictory; even then, would this [contradiction], being unconnected, function as a qualifier for substance and so forth, or would it be something connected? First, it cannot be unconnected, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and because a staff and so forth are not perceived as such when unconnected with a person. Indeed, a staff that is unconnected with a person is not perceived as its qualifier; if that were the case, the same would apply here as well.

Now, if it is related, by what means? Is it through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the relation of qualification (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*)? It cannot be through conjunction, because, being non-substantial (*adravya*), it cannot be the locus of conjunction. Nor can it be through inherence, because, being distinct from substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity, it lacks the nature of an inherent cause (*asamavāyitva*). Nor can it be through the relation of qualification, because that is impossible in the case of an object not already connected by some other relation; otherwise, such a relation would exist even in the case of a staff and a person, despite the absence of conjunction or other relations. Therefore, enough with this laborious attempt to postulate relations such as conjunction.

Therefore, since contradiction, when examined, is untenable, it is not appropriate for [existence and non-existence] to reside in the same locus, nor is it a case of different loci; for they appear together in an uncontradicted cognition as having a single substratum.

Nor does there follow the consequence of both defects, because the entity consisting of those two is of a different genus, like a person who is neither a thief nor an adulterer [is distinct from both a thief and an adulterer].

Indeed, those who follow the doctrine of the Lord of Jinas do not maintain the identity of existence and non-existence, or of difference and non-difference, as being mutually independent, such that this fault would arise; for they accept them only as being dependent upon one another, and because they are perceived in that way, there is no confusion or intermixture either, since both are perceived in their own respective natures within the object. Nor is there an infinite regress, because further attributes (dharmas) cannot exist for attributes themselves; for while the substratum (dharmin) possesses manifold forms, this is by no means the case for its attributes.
Because of this statement,

the fault of non-existence is indeed cast far away; for an object whose nature consists of the manifold indeterminacy of being, non-being, and so forth, is established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception,
since it constitutes a distinct category, just as a person who is neither a thief nor an adulterer is distinct from both a thief and an adulterer.

The avoidance of the eight defects, beginning with doubt (*saṃśaya*), should be observed in the following texts: "The establishment of difference and non-difference regarding an existent characterized by origination, persistence, and dissolution occurs through the distinction and non-distinction of its manifestations and so forth, because it transforms in that way due to its own inherent connection; [this] surpasses the mutual non-discrimination of perceptions involving doubt, contradiction, lack of common locus, the consequence of both defects, infinite regress, confusion, and the postulation of non-existence" (Pramāṇasaṃgraha, p.
Nor does this [position] incur the faults of contradiction, confusion, or infinite regress, as explained in the *Nayacakra* (p.

58, u.). Furthermore, even when a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is perceived, there is no consequence of multiplicity, contradiction, confusion, or infinite regress, just as in the case of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender within the mind, as stated in the *Aṣṭasahasrī* (p. 206).
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 435; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 158, upper section; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 451.
*Ratnākara*, p. 741; *Prameyaratnamālā* 4.1.
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 44; *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 197; *Saptabhaṅgītaraṅgiṇī*, p. 81.

As for what was also said—that one who is liberated is yet unliberated, and so forth—that too is the manifestation of no small darkness; for non-absolutism (anekānta) is indeed twofold: non-absolutism of simultaneity (akramā'nekānta) and non-absolutism of succession (kramā'nekānta).
Among these, non-absolutism of simultaneity pertains to the various simultaneous attributes such as knowledge, bliss, and so on, because they are possible even simultaneously in a single self.
Non-absolutism of succession pertains to the various successive attributes of being liberated and otherwise, because they occur only in succession.

And thus, it is not at all contradictory that the very same self which was previously unliberated becomes liberated at a later time, nor does this entail the destruction of non-absolutism (anekānta). Furthermore, if the self were of a single uniform nature, there would be an absence of both bondage and liberation; for liberation belongs to one who was bound, and it is not logical for that which is entirely uniform in nature to possess two distinct states due to their inherent contradiction.

Therefore, abandoning this stubborn adherence to extremist dogmas, one must accept that the nature of reality, as established upon the mountain peak of direct experience, is characterized by non-absolutism (anekāntātmakatva).
Therefore, this is established: "Substance and mode," etc. (p. 361, l.
1); for here [it is] twofold, indeed. (Ā.)
For non-absolutism (anekānta) is indeed twofold;
[as stated in] Pramāṇakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
93, l. 10: "tatsaṃ... [in the Śrāvaṇa edition].

Thus, because there is no presentation of an object characterized by absolute [categories] such as permanence to perception—since it cannot be grasped by direct perception—it is not possible to have a direct realization [of it].

By the words "not only" (*na kevalam*) and so forth, he indicates another refutation regarding this very point, saying: "Not only is direct realization—that is, apprehension through perception—not possible in the case of the absolute [view] of permanence (*nityatvaikānte*) nor in the absolute [view] of impermanence (*anityatvaikānte*); rather, [it is impossible] precisely because direct realization is impossible. (Bhāṣya/Ācārya)

Causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is not tenable in the positions of either permanence or momentariness, for it is considered the defining characteristic of entities by virtue of occurring either successively or simultaneously.

Commentary: Having accepted that "that which is capable of causal efficiency is ultimately real" as your own position, how can you, without being insane, yourself refute causal efficiency? Furthermore, why would one reject causal efficiency—which is nothing more than its own manifestation—even in the case of the opposing view, or why would one reject false conventional usage? Even though there is no difference in consciousness itself, it is only the aspect of the object (*viṣayākāra*) that serves as the means of establishing the object, and not any other aspect.
Then:
"That which is capable of causal efficiency is here the ultimately real" (Pramāṇavārttika 3).

Explanation of the *kārikā*, and the proof that in the case of an eternal [entity], there is an absence of causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) by virtue of its inability to act either successively or simultaneously—
neither the action nor the performance of an object, a cognition, or anything else would be tenable or possible.
Where? In the two positions of permanence and momentariness.

This is what is meant: since the direct perception of an object is not possible in either extreme [position], for that very reason the causal relationship established through perception and non-perception is also not possible.

Furthermore, purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; yet neither succession nor simultaneity is possible in the extreme of permanence or the extreme of momentariness. To explain: performing one effect first and then performing another is "succession" (*krama*); therefore, it is not logical for a permanent entity to be an agent of effects.

For if that [permanent entity] produces the subsequent effect by the very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which it produced the prior effect, then both effects would necessarily exist at one and the same time. Consequently, the subsequent effect would also exist at the very time of the prior effect, because it is produced by an intrinsic nature that generates the prior effect. Whatever is produced by such an intrinsic nature exists at the time of the prior effect, just like the effect considered to belong to that [prior] time; and the subsequent effect of a permanent, unitary entity is indeed produced by an intrinsic nature that generates the prior effect.

Now, if it performs the subsequent effect by the very same nature by which it performed the prior one, then the prior effect would also have to exist at the time of the subsequent effect, because it is produced by that same nature which produces the subsequent effect, just like the subsequent effect; or else, [if you say] there is a different activity or instrument (bhāṣya,
śruti), then by whatever nature it performs the first causal efficiency, by that very same [nature] it must perform the subsequent effects, since no other nature has been acquired.
*Tattvopadeśa*, p. 126:

Now, even though there is no difference in being produced by that which has the nature of producing it, if you maintain that the sequence of effects therein arises from the sequence of their respective auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then that effect must be produced solely by those auxiliaries.

If you argue that this fault does not apply because the eternal entity is also present there, [we ask]: what is the use of the presence of something that performs no function? Otherwise, since a donkey is also present when a jar is produced, it would follow that the jar is produced by the donkey as well.

Alternatively, if it were to contribute something [to the effect], there would be the undesirable consequence of its being subject to change (*kācapacya*). For a permanent entity would desire to produce the effect at the earlier time alone, whereas the auxiliary causes exist at a later time.

Now, if it produces that [effect] at the earlier time by one nature and at the later time by another, well then—does that duality of natures always exist for it, or would it be successive like the effect? In the first case, that same fault remains: the later nature would exist at the time of the earlier effect, or the earlier nature would exist at the time of the later one.

Regarding the second position, however, are those two natures non-different from it, or different? Even if they are non-different, is the pair of natures non-different from the eternal entity, or is the eternal entity non-different from them? In the first alternative, there follows the consequence that the entity is eternal, because its nature is non-different from what is eternal; for whatever has a nature non-different from the eternal is seen to be eternal, just like the eternal self, and the pair of natures has a nature non-different from the eternal.

In the second alternative, however, there follows the consequence that the eternal would be non-eternal, because its essential nature is non-different from the non-eternal; for whatever has an essential nature non-different from the non-eternal is understood to be non-eternal, just like the very self-nature of the non-eternal; and the entity intended to be eternal has an essential nature non-different from the two natures of the non-eternal.

Now, if it is maintained that the two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct from [the entity] itself, then this fault does not arise; yet, how can there be the designation "this is its twofold intrinsic nature" given the impossibility of a relationship, since [relationships such as] inherence (*samavāya*) have already been refuted? Therefore, it is not possible for an eternal entity to produce an effect sequentially.
[The manuscripts read *tatsahabhāva*, *tatkārya*, etc.]
Since stable entities do not perform their respective functions either sequentially or simultaneously, they are therefore considered to be non-existent.
He demonstrates that it is not logical for a stable entity to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) sequentially: "For effects are delayed due to the absence of their causes;
when a capable cause is present, by what could their postponement be caused?"

Now, with the words "But even if" (*athāpi*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's reply: "But even if there exist successive auxiliary causes for the eternal [entity], depending upon which it produces this collection of effects in reliance upon succession."

He responds with the words beginning "Well said" (sādhu): "This is well; however, do those [auxiliaries] become its auxiliaries by virtue of being causes in a suitable form, or by virtue of performing a single purpose?"
If that which is capable were the cause, then that entity would be created by them; however,
since its own nature is eternally established, it cannot be produced.
Or, if [the capacity] were produced, its eternal nature would be lost;
for if that excellence is distinct [from the entity], how could it be the causal agent?
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (verse 399): Because that which is eternal is independent, sequential production is contradicted.
Pramāṇavārttika 2.267; Hetubinduṭīkā, p. 218.

Nor can it be simultaneous; for if all effects were to arise in a single moment, then in the second and subsequent moments, that entity would lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), resulting in its non-existence like a sky-lotus. Therefore, since a permanent entity cannot perform causal activity either successively or simultaneously, it follows that it is nothing but a non-entity.

That which does not perform a causal function either successively or simultaneously is not a real entity, just like a sky-lotus. And an eternal entity such as the self or an atom does not perform a causal function either successively or simultaneously in any way; therefore, it is not a real entity. He shows this by stating that simultaneity is also not accepted, because its effects are observed to perish [one after another]: "And simultaneity is certainly not desired, because its effects are seen to cease" (413).
If that entity, whose nature is causal efficiency, returns after having performed all its effects simultaneously, then its momentary destruction is established.

*Tattvasaṅgraha*: Furthermore, does this [cause] possess the nature of performing its function at all times, or only occasionally? In the first case, there would be the production of all effects at all times, because their causes would always be unimpeded.

Whatever has its causes complete at a given time is established as being subject to production, just like many sprouts that arise simultaneously. And all effects are held to have their causes always complete by virtue of being produced by an eternal entity whose nature is to produce effects.

Therefore, it follows that if [an effect] were to arise only occasionally, then that which was previously of a nature incapable of producing an effect must subsequently become of a nature capable of it.

In that case as well, at the time of its production, does that [entity] abandon its nature of incapacity or not? If it does not abandon it, then there follows the undesirable consequence that the effect would never be produced. For indeed, that from which an incapacity for producing something has not been abandoned cannot produce it—just as a rice sprout is not produced from a barley seed—and the entity regarded as eternal possesses, at the time of production, the same unabandoned nature of incapacity for producing the effect as it did previously.

Now, if it is argued that it abandons [its former nature], that is not so; for, because it is eternally of a single form, it is impossible for it to abandon its prior nature which was incapable of producing that [effect].

Alternatively, if such abandonment were possible, its status as eternally of a single form would be contradicted; for that which has abandoned its prior nature is not of a single form, just like a finger and so forth, and yet the entity in question is intended to be eternally of a single form while having abandoned its prior incapacity.

Therefore, how can it possess the nature of being eternal and uniform? For its very capacity for transformation is established, since the adoption of a capable nature through the abandonment of an incapable nature is impossible without that [transformation]. Indeed, the relinquishment and acquisition of prior and subsequent forms are not compatible with an entity that is eternal and uniform; where there is the relinquishment and acquisition of prior and subsequent forms, that is transformative, such as a snake or similar object encompassing states other than its coiled form. And these—namely, the relinquishment and acquisition of prior and subsequent forms characterized by incapacity and its opposite—exist in the entity intended to be eternal.

Even one who asserts that an object, though eternally of a single nature, produces an effect only when accompanied by auxiliary causes and not at all times, has in fact established its very mutability (pariṇāmitva), because it abandons the state of non-accompaniment and assumes the state of accompaniment; thus, it must be understood that an object, consisting of multiple attributes either successively or simultaneously, alone possesses causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva).

Having performed all its effects simultaneously, does that nature of his which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) cease, or does it persist? In that regard, if the position is that it ceases, then its momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgitva) is established. But if that very form persists, it would produce the effect again;
for how can efficacy be attributed to a form that is incapable of acting?
Because they are devoid of all causal efficiency, like a lotus in the sky, all non-momentary things are non-existent; for power is the defining characteristic of a real entity. (416)
Or rather, its hearing of the reality is always indeed [present], O Ba, Ja.
For whom indeed would there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)?

Furthermore, it should be understood that for the self (*ātman*), eternal substances (*nityadravya*), and primordial matter (*prakṛti*), which are unchanging (*apariṇāmin*), there is likewise an absence of causal efficiency.
Just as it is impossible for such entities to possess that capacity, this has been explained in detail in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā* and the *Prakṛtiparīkṣā*.
Therefore, for an eternal entity, the performance of purposeful action (arthakriyākāritva) through either succession or simultaneity is not possible;
even under the absolute position of eternity, transformation is not tenable,
let alone the absence of causal factors— where then is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and where is its result?

How can one who asserts that purposeful activity—characterized by the relinquishing of a prior nature and the acquisition of a subsequent nature—is possible even in the case of immutability (*kauṭasthya*), not be insane? (Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 179)

Nor can it belong to that which is momentary; for it lacks both the relinquishing and the assuming of prior and subsequent natures, and it is devoid of multiple powers at a single moment. (Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 76; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 147a)

Whatever is of such a nature—that is, that which is devoid of the relinquishment and acquisition of prior and subsequent intrinsic natures due to its existence for only a single moment and its partlessness, and which is simultaneously devoid of multiple powers—is not capable of causal efficiency through either succession or simultaneity, just like a donkey’s horn. Furthermore, an entity conceived by others as being exclusively momentary has already been refuted on the occasion of the refutation of the *santāna* (continuum), and the capacity of an entirely momentary thing to perform causal efficiency will be refuted further below.

Furthermore, the determination of the objects of knowledge (prameya) is established by means of the instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇa); yet there is no instrument of valid cognition for momentariness.

Moreover, even on the absolute position of momentariness, rebirth and so forth are impossible due to the absence of recognition and the like; thus, there can be no commencement of an action, much less its fruit.
41 Āptamīmāṃsā, Aṣṭasahasrī 181,
Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 77.
From the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*,
page 147,

line 10: The Buddhist's prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that all entities are momentary due to reasons such as existence (*sattva*), and that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible only therein, not in what is eternal.
Now, this [argument] exists: "Whatever is existent is all momentary, like a jar; and entities are existent.

For existence (*sattva*) consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). And causal efficiency is pervaded by succession and simultaneity. That [efficiency] is not possible in a non-momentary entity, because its two pervaders—succession and simultaneity—are impossible therein. This impossibility [of the pervaders] follows from the fact that such an entity is always of a single uniform nature; therefore, causal efficiency must either be performed by it at all times or never at all, since there is no distinction [in its nature].

If it is possible for this [entity] to perform purposeful action sequentially, does it produce the second effect by the same form with which it produces the first, or by a different form? If it is by the same form, then it follows that the effect to be accomplished in the second moment would arise in the very first moment, because its productive nature exists even previously.
If it is by a different form, then since the previous form has ceased, [the entity] is momentary.

Now, [it may be argued that] the eternal [entity] produces each respective effect by depending on the proximity of various successive auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). But do those auxiliaries provide some benefit (*upakāra*) to it, or not? If they do, is that benefit distinct from it or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then it follows that they are merely producing that very [entity] itself; and since that [entity] has already been established previously, nothing at all would be produced by the auxiliaries.

On the other hand, if it is distinct, then there would be no designation of it as "belonging to that" (*tasya*), because of the lack of a relation; and if one were to postulate another relation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, that which is non-momentary does not produce an effect sequentially— [this is the meaning]—
in the case of non-momentariness.

That causal activity is not performed sequentially, nor is it simultaneous; for, by virtue of having a nature that produces all effects at once, all effects would be produced in the very first moment. Consequently, since there would be no effect to be produced in subsequent moments, the consequence would follow that it is non-existent—like a horse's horn—due to its failure to perform any purposeful action (*anarthakriyākāritva*).

Furthermore, for one who has already produced the entire collection of effects, does this nature of his cease or not? If it does not cease, then, because that nature remains unceased in the second and subsequent moments just as it was in the first moment, there would follow the production of everything that has already been produced; thus, the consequence of "grinding what is already ground" (piṣṭapeṣaṇa) would ensue.

If it does cease, then upon its cessation, that [entity] would also cease, because it is non-different from it; therefore, how could this [entity] be non-momentary? Or, if it were different from it, the designation "its" would be untenable due to the absence of a relationship; or, if such a relationship were to exist, there would be an infinite regress, as it would necessitate the postulation of yet another relationship for that [relationship] as well. Furthermore, at the time of producing the effect, do those [entities] abandon their previous form and nature or not? If they do not, then as before, there is the undesirable consequence that no effect would be produced even then.

If [it is argued that] they exist, then there is momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), because at every moment there is the destruction of the previous nature and the arising of the subsequent, which constitutes difference.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which perform an action without having previously performed it are not of a single uniform nature at every moment, just like seeds and the like; and those entities intended to be eternal likewise perform actions without having previously performed them.

Thus, since their status as produced (*kṛtakatva*) is established, momentariness is also established from that. For instance: whatever is produced is momentary, such as lightning, a lamp, and so forth; and the entities under dispute are indeed produced.
For being produced from a cause is indeed the state of being created (*kṛtakatva*), and that is necessarily restricted to having a perishable nature.

For entities, as they arise from their own causes, arise as being necessarily restricted to having a perishable nature. Therefore, just as in the case of *śiṃśapā*-ness and tree-ness, the identity (*tādātmya*) between being created and impermanence is established.

Nor should it be argued that even though there is no difference in their arising from the efficacy of a cause, some entities will be eternal and others impermanent, and thus their identity is not established; for there is no distinction in the causal efficacy [of the respective causes], just as in the case of fire and so forth.

Indeed, it is not the case that some collection of causes producing fire generates a fire accompanied by the sensations of light and heat, while another generates its opposite; thus, a difference in their capacities (*sāmarthyabheda*) is not within the range of our perception. If such were the case, one might imagine a difference in the capacities of causes here as well, based on their generating entities with either a permanent or impermanent nature.

Therefore, when entities manifest an entity, they manifest it precisely as having the nature of destruction. Thus, the identity (*tādātmya*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) is established;
otherwise, there would be the fallacy of their being distinct entities (*anyatvāt*). (Bhāṣya)
In this regard, all those entities that are produced are momentary,
because they all exist without dependence regarding their destruction.

*Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā*, p. 213: Having thus established—by means of the impossibility of dependence on other factors for destruction due to [the resulting] incapacity and futility—that existence characterized by being produced (*kṛtakatva*) lacks a cause for its destruction as demonstrated by the former teachers, he says the following, showing how that [existence] encounters a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the opposite [position]: "Therefore, there is no cause for destruction... (*tasmād vināśahetubhiḥ*).
[The text] "uṣṇaprakāśasa—" [is found in] Ā, Ba, Ja, Bhā;
"kalpeta" [is found in] Ā, Ba, Ja, Bhā.

Now, even if objects possess a perishable nature, their destruction does not occur merely by persisting for a single moment; for that destruction will happen precisely when the encounter with its cause occurs. This too is incorrect; because if there is no destruction at every moment even for that which is perishable, then destruction would be impossible at any other time as well, since there is no difference [in its state]. Indeed, it is never observed that light lacks luminosity at every moment, or that it regains luminosity at a later time after having been non-luminous.

Furthermore, since the destruction of objects is observed, if luminosity were subject to destruction, its destruction—like its luminosity itself—would be established as following from its very nature alone without delay, because there would be no distinction [between its beginning and end] even at the outset.
Now, if it is argued that for that which has escaped death, let its first moment remain for even hundreds of aeons due to its nature of being indestructible; [we reply: no.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 448: ...tve prakāśakasya (bhā., ba., ja., śra.); ...tve prakāśatva (ā.)...
Like luminosity (bhāṣya),
because of being a luminator (vārttika); it is concomitant (jaṭa)— (bhāṣya).

Furthermore, does an entity whose nature is to endure for a hundred thousand moments remain exactly as it was in the second and subsequent moments after having arisen in the first moment, or not? If it remains so, then because it would follow that it exists in the same way even at the final moment, its destruction could never arise; or, if it were to abandon that nature at that point, its momentariness is established, since its characteristic is a difference in nature at every moment.

Furthermore, non-momentariness (akṣaṇikatva) means that an object possesses an existence persisting through multiple moments; and its connection with multiple moments is difficult to comprehend if those temporal characteristics are not apprehended.

Furthermore, perception—which arises through the power of the connection between the sense faculty and a present object—is not capable of apprehending the extension of an object across multiple temporal phases apart from its connection with the present time. For if the object were simultaneously connected with multiple temporal phases, then perception, arising through that power, would apprehend such extension; however, that simultaneous connection is impossible, because preceding and succeeding temporal phases occur sequentially.
Nor can that [momentary nature] be established through recollection or recognition, because those are not valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

As for what was said—that it will perish when a cause of destruction encounters it—does that cause of destruction destroy an entity that is perishable by nature, or one that is imperishable? In the former case, even if a hundred causes of destruction were to encounter it, the destruction of the imperishable is impossible; for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities cannot be altered.

Furthermore, if destruction is perishable, then its causes would be useless; for the operation of another entity toward an object that has already acquired its own nature from its own causes cannot be fruitful, as this would entail the absurd consequence of that operation never ceasing (p. 376, l.
13). [The text reads *nāśayati* in Ā., Ba., and Ja.]

For this reason as well, it must be stated that causes of destruction are incapable of producing any effect; for instance, when an entity arises from its own cause, does it arise by its very nature as something inherently perishable, or as something imperishable? If it is perishable, there is nothing whatsoever for a cause of destruction to do. On the other hand, if the position is that it is imperishable by nature, even then the cause of destruction is entirely ineffective, because it is impossible for anything to bring about a change in its essential nature (*svabhāva*). (Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, p. 140)

Furthermore, is destruction distinct from the entity, or is it non-distinct from the cause of destruction? If it were non-distinct, then the entity itself would be produced by those causes; however, since that entity arises from its own causes, and because it is impossible to produce what has already been produced, those causes would be redundant and the distinction between their causes would be untenable.

Now, if it is distinct [from the entity]; then would it exist at the same time as that entity, at a time prior to it, or at a time subsequent to it? In that regard, if they were co-existent, there would be the perception of existence and non-existence simultaneously due to their lack of contradiction; or, if there were contradiction, because the entity would be encompassed by non-existence, its perception and its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) would not occur. If it existed at a time prior to the entity, then since the entity itself would not yet exist, to what would this [non-existence] belong? For destruction belongs to that which exists; and it is a great marvel indeed that there could be the destruction of that which has not attained existence. (Svabhāvabhaṅga, Ja.)
For thus, a cause that destroys is not logically the producer of a destruction that is non-different from the entity itself, since the entity is produced by its own cause. (358)

*Tattvasaṃgraha*—[The word] "tu" means "therefore. [If it were] non-different from that, [it would be] without cause (*nirhetukatva*). That it attains its own nature immediately after the arising of the entity is illogical. In this regard, there are five possible positions: its existence prior to the arising of the entity, simultaneously with it, immediately after it, at another time, or its non-existence.
*Tattvopadeśa*, p. 128; *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 136:
"having embraced each respective state," *ba.*, *ja.* edition.

If the jar and other objects were to exist at a time subsequent [to their destruction], what would happen to them such that they would not perform their purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) characterized by their own perception and so forth? For surely, when a cloth has arisen from threads and the like, no one can prevent the jar from performing its own purposeful activity. Now, it might be argued that because the cloth is not an incompatible factor, the jar does not lack the performance of its own purposeful activity upon the production of the cloth; however, for non-existence (*abhāva*), the opposite is the case, and thus [the jar] would indeed lack it.

Now, what is this so-called "contrariety" (*virodhitva*)? Is it the state of being a destroyer (*nāśakatva*), or the state of being destruction itself (*nāśarūpatva*)? If it is the state of being a destroyer, then, like a mallet or similar instruments, this [contrariety] must uproot the jar or other object by way of producing a destruction; and if there were yet another destruction, the same objection would apply, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is the state of being destruction itself, then how can this [contrariety], being a distinct entity, be the destruction of that [object]? Otherwise, a cloth might as well be the destruction of a jar! If you say it is due to contrariety, then a circular argument (*cakraka*) follows.

Furthermore, since there is no distinction in their being distinct entities (*arthāntaratva*), how could this [connection] belong to the pot alone? Since there is no distinction, why could it not be said to belong to another as well? Nor should it be asserted that "this belongs to that with which it is connected," because since the difference [of being distinct entities] is the same everywhere, it would follow that the connection exists in all cases.

Now, if it is argued that by means of a hammer or other instrument, another form called "fragility" (bhaṅguratva)—distinct from the previous form—is produced in a jar or similar object, and for that reason it is said to "belong to it"; then, is this [new form] produced while the object remains in its own nature in that very same form, or while it has already perished? In that regard, it is not logical for another form to belong to something remaining in its own nature, because of contradiction; for while the state of being blue remains, the state of being yellow cannot be produced.

Furthermore, since that which has perished is non-existent, how could there be the arising of another form? It would be like the horn of a hare. Moreover, there would be the consequence of a logical circle (*cakraka-prasaṅga*): if a jar or the like has perished, there is the arising of another form; if that [arising] exists, there is the connection with destruction; and if that [connection] exists, there is the state of having perished. Furthermore, a positive entity (*bhāva*) whose nature is a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) cannot be the locus for the property of being an effect, because it would then entail the status of being a real thing (*vastu-rūpatā*).

For the nature of an entity consists in its existence arising from a causal complex and its capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*). If non-existence were also produced from that same complex and were to perform purposeful action characterized by the uprooting of another, then what would distinguish it from existence? Furthermore, since non-existence in the form of a mere void will be specifically refuted in the section on the refutation of non-existence, enough of this over-elaboration here.

But if it is a relative negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*), then if the shards and so forth—which are other than the jar and so forth—constitute its non-existence, by whom has its having a cause been denied? For we admit that hammers and the like function toward the production of a dissimilar continuum; however, jars and the like, being by nature unstable immediately after their own moment of origination, arise solely from their own causes and do not persist into another time. [Note: The variants *bhāṃ* and *śra* read *tantvādeḥ* instead of *ghaṭādeḥ*.]
But when the name "destruction" is applied to an entity that is distinct from the thing itself, nothing at all is produced in that entity by other causes. (360)
Therefore, as before, the consequences regarding perception and its effects follow;
and because it remains in that same state, it is not logical for this [consciousness] to be obscured either.
It is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "For him, it will come to pass... [The manuscript variants are: śra° for śrute, i° for iti, and ba°, ja° for the respective readings].
Now, if this is a negation of action, then indeed it does not produce any entity; nevertheless, the lack of a cause is established, because the agent loses its status as a cause. (363)

For instance: in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), because the negative particle is connected with the verb "to do," it results in the negation of action—namely, "one does not produce non-existence" or "one does not produce existence. Thus, non-agency is established as the cause for the destruction [of the self]. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p.
136; *kāryadha*... *ba*, *ja*).

— From this [perspective], non-existence is established by way of affirmation (*vidhi*) through the basis of exclusion (*paryudāsa*); thus, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding difference (*vyatireka*) and so forth that occur therein are once again [addressed].

For, by the power of intention (*vivakṣā*), a positive entity (*bhāva*) itself is designated as "non-existence" (*abhāva*) when it is distinct from some other entity; and in that case, the aforementioned fault recurs regarding the conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) such as exclusion (*vyatireka*).
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 135)

Therefore, the following is established: whatever is independent of anything else with respect to a certain state is necessarily of that nature; for example, the final causal complex is independent with respect to the production of its own effect. And all entities are independent with respect to their destruction. From this inference as well, it follows that entities do not persist beyond their moment of arising.

Likewise, it must be accepted that whatever appears in a certain way exists in exactly that way; for example, a blue water-lily, appearing as blue, exists in that very form. And all entities appear in a form encompassed by a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Thus, even from the standpoint of inference, the apprehension of presentness is said to be the apprehension of momentariness. And this [apprehension] exists in perception, for it has been stated previously that entities cannot be apprehended through perception or other means by means of a self-nature encompassing prior and subsequent times. Therefore, with respect to an entity, that which does not depend on any other cause [for its existence]...
In that case, it should be known as certain because it arises from its own causes in that manner;
for just as a causal complex (sāmagrī) is independent when producing its own effect, [so too is the certainty of the result]. 354
Furthermore, all produced things are independent with respect to their destruction.
(Tattvasaṅgraha 355)
Hetuviṭīkā, folio 213:
"Its own nature" (*tatsvabhāvaḥ*), as in Bhāṣya;
"the apprehension of the means of knowledge" (*mānagrahaṇam*), in Ba and Ja.
Regarding the detailed refutation of the Sautrāntika who, as described above, explains momentariness both externally and internally:
here it is refuted.

Regarding what was stated—namely, "that which exists," and so forth—what is this so-called existence (*sattva*)? Is it a relation with *sattā* (the universal of being), being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? In the first case, there is the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*bhāgāsiddhatva*), because the relation with *sattā* is impossible in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like;
furthermore, it would constitute a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), since the Buddhists do not accept existence as defined by that [relation with *sattā*].

Furthermore, does the status of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviṣayatva*) differ for each individual entity, or not? If it differs, then—like the intrinsic nature of the objects themselves—it would possess a distinct nature for each; consequently, it could not be the object of a single [unified] cognition. Thus, due to a lack of continuity (*ananvaya*), it could not function as a logical reason (*hetu*).

If, on the other hand, it does not differ, is it perceived or not? If it is not perceived, how can it exist? If it is perceived, then "being an object of a means of valid cognition" is merely another name for existence (*sattā*) itself. And if there is a relation with that [existence], the aforementioned faults would follow.
Moreover, if the status of being an object of a means of valid cognition were to exist independently of that [existence], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If things possess existence by themselves (*svataḥ*), let that [existence] belong to objects (*artha*) as well by themselves; what is the use of postulating that [cognition]? Moreover, this is contradictory: for existence, characterized as being the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is established as having all non-momentary things as its domain, and that very [existence] establishes non-momentariness itself (p. 375, l. 7). [Objection: Because it is the nature of the object, there is no single cognition [of both]. (Ā.)
The lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) is the reason.

Furthermore, even the definition of existence as "the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākāritva*) is not sufficient to prove momentariness, because it is vitiated by the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Among these, first, regarding its being unestablished: causal efficiency is said to be the state of being a cause of purposeful action; and that is difficult to comprehend when the purposeful action itself is non-existent.
For it is not possible to grasp, merely by observation, that entities endowed with various kinds of powers possess the capacity to produce their respective effects;
this is because you yourselves have admitted that even when "fitness" (yogyatā) and "momentariness" (kṣaṇikatva) are grasped, the actual existence of the thing cannot be ascertained.

But surely, it is through mere possibility that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is understood here, for it is possible that "this [entity] will perform this causal function. But surely, on what basis does even this possibility proceed? If you say, "because the causal efficiency of something of the same class has been observed," then the same objection applies there as well: if the capacity to produce that [effect] is understood from observing the causal efficiency in something of the same class, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, in your system, because objects are absolutely distinct, even the report of their belonging to the same class is difficult to find; this was stated in the section on the examination of the universal (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*).
Therefore, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is indeed unestablished—this can be [understood].

And it is contradictory [to claim that a non-momentary entity lacks causal efficiency], because the performance of an action through either succession or simultaneity is possible only for a non-momentary object.
