Indeed, a momentary object is not capable of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) successively, because a succession produced by differences in place, time, or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is impossible for it. For it is logical that a single entity, having performed one effect and subsequently acquiring another capacity through the proximity of required auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), performs a different effect through a succession of places and times; however, if an object endures for only a single moment, such successive causal activity is untenable.

Because it is partless, it lacks the nature of possessing multiple powers simultaneously; therefore, its simultaneous production of multiple effects is also extremely difficult to achieve. This has been explained in detail during the refutation of the *santāna* (continuum).

Consequently, since succession and simultaneity—which are the pervaders of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—are contradictory in a momentary entity, it is established that whatever performs causal efficiency through either succession or simultaneity is necessarily non-momentary. Thus, [the reason] is shown to be both contradictory (*viruddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even in a non-momentary object, the performance of causal efficiency through either succession or non-succession is possible when the respective auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are present.
Because of the impossibility of momentariness (kṣaṇika), [there is] proximity (sannidhi). Ba, Ja; Ā. reads "proximity."
Page 9:

With the words "Even in the case of momentary entities," etc., he raises the objection regarding the view of Bhadanta Yogasena: "But how can there be causal efficiency (arthakriyā) even in things that are momentary?"
For those initial auxiliary causes, which produce mutual distinctions,
perform purposeful activity both successively and simultaneously.
Therefore, for them, [the doctrine of] momentariness becomes useless.
For he (Dharmakīrti) said: "Even if things are momentary, there is indeed a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by way of either succession or simultaneity."

Are they [the auxiliary causes] themselves capable or incapable? Regarding that which was stated—that the auxiliaries either do or do not provide an assistance to that [cause], and so forth—that is incorrect; for we admit that only those things which provide assistance are auxiliaries, because an excellence (*atiśaya*) arises in them through their mutual proximity.
Indeed, it is not logical that those in whom no excellence has arisen should produce an effect, since they would not differ from their previous state.

There is a distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*) by way of their being property and possessor, yet despite this distinction, it is not the case that the possessor lacks causal efficiency because only the [property] possesses it; for an absolute difference between them is unestablished. Indeed, their distinction consists in their being property and possessor, while their non-distinction consists in their being incapable of being separated, just like the cognition and its form.

Furthermore, that which is postulated for the sake of something cannot be its own sublater, because this would entail the consequence that cognition lacks the capacity to grasp an object, and [it would instead] imply that the mental form (ākāra) alone is what grasps the object.

Now, as for the objection: "If each of these possesses its own causal capacity, what is the need for dependence on anything else?"—this too is untenable. For one determines the causality of as many factors as are present when the effect is perceived and absent when it is not; since the presence or absence of the effect is determined by the presence or absence of the causal capacity of those factors. (Page 375, Line 15)
—The venerable [opponent] asks:

How, in this way, is causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) possible for that which is momentary? For is it capable of producing an effect while depending on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), or is it capable independently? If it is independent, then even a momentary seed-syllable (*bījakṣaṇa*) situated within a granary should produce a sprout. If, however, it is argued that only the final momentary seed-syllable—which has acquired a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) through a succession of preceding moments of earth and so forth—is the producer of that sprout, then it is established that this [momentary entity] possesses productive power only by depending [on others]. In that case, let the same apply to the eternal [entity] as well, since there is no difference [between the two cases].

Now, if it is argued that this [entity] requires auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*) only for its own production and not for the effect, that is not so; because even its own production is an effect of others, it too must arise toward its own effect without depending on them, and likewise for those others as well. Consequently, there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a seed remaining in a granary would produce a sprout. Furthermore, since everything would arise independently at the very moment of its existence, there would be the destruction of the entire continuum (*saṃtāna*).

If it is argued that there is no annihilation of the effect because it arises even when the cause has perished, [we reply]: In that case, how could that be its cause? For it is impossible for something to be the cause of another if the latter does not arise when the former is present, yet arises when it is absent. Therefore, those who are skilled in discernment must understand that a cause produces its respective effect only when the respective collection of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) is present.

To this, it is said: existence (*sattva*) is not a probans for proving momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), because it is either inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) or because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

For instance—existence is pervaded by succession and non-succession; therefore, by the non-perception of those two, it is excluded from the non-momentary. Likewise, that same existence is pervaded by dependence and independence; therefore, by the non-perception of those two, it is excluded from the momentary as well.
Do the seeds of earth, air, water, and fire, when reaching their final moment, produce [the sprout] independently of one another, or dependently? (Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā 3.2)
Page 14,
Praśastapādabhāṣya, Kirāṇāvalī, page 144.
Even for a momentary entity, there is no existence at all;
for it is incapable of producing an effect either successively or simultaneously.
What kind of succession can there be for a momentary thing, and what [succession] in its simultaneous productions?
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 453:
"But surely it does indeed depend [on something]; however, it depends on that for its own production, and not for its own effect;
in that regard, its independence is accepted with respect to its own production, but not with respect to its own production."

But surely, even for its own production, it is the preceding moment alone existing within its own continuum that is active, being independent; thus, each preceding moment, falling within its own continuum, is active in producing [the effect] without dependence. In this case, the farmer would be successful merely by placing the seed in the granary; what need would there be for his labor of cultivation?
(Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā 3.2)

As for what was stated— that the effect to be accomplished in the second and subsequent moments would arise in the very first moment, and so forth— that too is incorrect; because the causal complex (sāmagrī) differs, for the causal complex of the second moment and so on is not the same as the causal complex of the first moment.
Furthermore, the capacity to produce an effect through a single nature is unestablished, because without a difference in the natures of the causes, a difference among the effects is impossible.

Nor should it be argued that this would entail a difference in the possessor of those natures for each individual nature, which would result in momentariness; for there is no contradiction in a single, continuous entity possessing multiple natures.

Nor does the mere attribution of contradictory properties necessarily contradict the fact that a single entity possesses multiple natures; for contradiction is established through non-perception (*anupalambha*), and there is no such non-perception of multiplicity in a single thing, since even a single instance of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) is perceived as having multiple natures. Furthermore, by virtue of the presence or absence of auxiliary factors, even a single momentary form (*rūpa-kṣaṇa*) is revealed to possess multiple natures.

Indeed, a form does not produce a moment of taste by the very same nature through which it produces a moment of form; for if it did, it would follow that the taste is itself a form, or conversely, that the form possesses the nature of taste.

If that [effect] is produced by means of a different intrinsic nature, then it is established that even when contradictory properties are superimposed, a single entity can consist of multiple intrinsic natures;
since this is not contradictory here due to the distinction based on dependence, let that [multiple-naturedness] belong to the non-momentary as well for this very reason—
[in the second moment]— ba, ja, śra.
For, without a difference in the power of the cause, a multiplicity of effects is not logical, just as in the case of the cognitions of color and so forth (Aṣṭaśata,
Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 183).
Furthermore,

if that very form by which matter (*rūpa*) is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) with respect to [another] matter were also the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) with respect to taste (*rasa*), then once again there would be no distinction between matter and taste. On the other hand, if the status of being the material cause of matter is by one nature and the status of being an auxiliary cause for taste is by another, then there is a plurality [of natures] due to the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-bheda*).
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 455:

"And if there is no contradiction in a single [entity] possessing multiple natures simultaneously, let there be no contradiction even in succession, since there is no difference in the uninterrupted cognition.
Thus, this reason is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), because the position of momentariness is sublated by perception, just like the thesis 'sound is not audible'."

For one whose eyes are unblinking indeed apprehends objects as being non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), yet even by this [apprehension] a single moment is not experienced, because there is no discernment of preceding and succeeding moments. It should not be asserted that there is a cognition of non-momentariness therein; for no interruption in experience is perceived, since his determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) of the object is experienced as having an uninterrupted form while persisting through multiple moments.

Indeed, there is no rule that knowledge must necessarily exist for only a single moment; for that [knowledge] must arise from the very perception of its object in such a way, and not from anything else. And that [perception] remains the same even if [the knowledge] persists for multiple moments. Nor should it be argued that stability is untenable because a distinction [of the object] could arise therein due to its connection with different times; for time is one, as it persists through all the perceptions belonging to a single experience.

Likewise, the sublation of the thesis of momentariness by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is even more evident; for this [cognition], which functions in the form "this is that very same [thing]," has as its objective manifestation an object encompassed by both past and present time.

But is it not the case that, because past space and time are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), there is no contact with the sense organs; how then could the object be perceived as qualified by them? This objection is also incorrect, because recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) cannot possibly be born from the sense organs, since it arises from both memory and perception. Therefore, because memory—which is capable of grasping the past—is present here, it is entirely logical that the cognition "that" occurs with the past as its object. And because perception—which is capable of grasping the present—is present, the cognition "this" occurs with the present as its object. Thus, even though space and time are past, there is no contradiction in perceiving Devadatta—who is related to them—as being connected to the present space and time.

Even the difference characterized by past and present times does not, in every respect, differentiate the essential nature of Devadatta; for there is the cognition of the identity of his nature, in the form: "That very same Devadatta whom I previously apprehended is now being perceived.
Moreover, recognition shines forth everywhere; while it exists, who could assert that entities are subject to momentary destruction?
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 458)

Furthermore, this entire proof for momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because there is a subsequent cognition of that which has already been cognized by the direct perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*); [as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 80: "[of that which is] present... [Ātmatattvaviveka].

Furthermore, if the object were non-persistent from the moment of perception up until the moment of recognition, recognition itself could not occur; for there is no occurrence of the cognition of blue in the absence of blue. Yet this [recognition] does occur; therefore, the persistence of objects is established. Otherwise, even the establishment of blue and so forth would not result from the cognition of blue. Moreover, its validity will be demonstrated later.

If the pervasion of an object by time and space is not perceived, does its non-existence follow from that alone? For it is the cessation of perception by an all-seeing being (*sarvadarśin*) that establishes the non-existence of an entity, not the cessation of perception by one of limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

An object, existing in its own nature, cannot be altered by cognition; for cognitions possess no power to either transform an object into something else or to establish it as it truly is, since their function consists solely in the illumination of the object's own form.

For if cognitions arising from a determinate causal complex are incapable of determining an object in its entirety, then this is the fault of those very cognitions and not of the object; indeed, it is not the fault of the taste, nor is it its non-existence, that a lamp does not illuminate it, due to the defect of the cognition's failure to engage with it. 56

Āptamīmāṃsā (Aṣṭasahasrī), p. 202: Furthermore, if the existence of objects were to derive from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), then how would the existence of that causal efficiency itself be established—by another causal efficiency or by itself? If it were by another causal efficiency, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it were by itself, then let that [existence] belong to the objects themselves as well; what is the use of postulating that [efficiency]? Moreover, is existence merely the capacity for causal efficiency, or is it [defined] by means of causal efficiency? In the first case, because there is no distinction, that which is capable of causal efficiency is itself the ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

Thus, there would be no relationship of defined object (*lak�śya*) and defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) between existence (*sattva*) and causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), because such a relationship is only possible when there is a distinction [between the two].

If, on the other hand, existence is defined by causal efficiency—meaning that whatever performs that [efficiency] possesses existence—then it follows that causal efficiency is one thing and existence is another. And if that were so, the statement "existence is indeed causal efficiency" would be contradicted. Furthermore, if a further causal efficiency were required to establish the existence of the initial causal efficiency, [an infinite regress would ensue].
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 148;
Sanmati-ṭīkā, pṛṣṭha 402:
"That alone is ultimately real."
Because a real entity is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya), [Nyāyabindu 1.14,
Pramāṇavārttika 3.3; Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 144.
"The other is said to be conventionally real; those two are the universal and the particular characteristic"—this is the second half [of the verse], *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* p.
121, *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-āloka* p. 547.
For in that case,
the example would be devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikala), since it is not established that jars and the like endure for even a single moment.

Let there be no example; what is the use of it? For the probans (*hetu*) is established as a means of cognition because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). But does this subverting proof make known the non-existence of the counter-example, or does it establish the exclusion of the probans from that [counter-example], or does it establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)? In the first case, regarding the subverting inference: "Non-momentary things do not exist, because they lack causal efficiency through either succession or simultaneity, like a sky-flower," the probans would suffer from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*).

There is no reason whatsoever for that which is mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍha*) to serve as a locus (*āśrayatva*); it would be a case of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), since such establishment is impossible in every instance.

Nor can its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) be established by means of it, because when the subject (*dharmin*) is not apprehended, it is impossible to grasp its exclusion from that locus. And if its exclusion were ever apprehended through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would be proper to establish it by seeing a mark (*liṅga*) invariably concomitant with it, as in the case of fire and smoke; yet there is no such apprehension of it from any source whatsoever.

Could that [non-existence] be known through perception or through inference? It cannot be known through perception; for since non-existence (*vyatireka*) consists of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is a non-entity (*avastu*) and thus lacks causal efficiency (*ahetutva*). Consequently, it cannot be an object of perception;

or, if it were an object of perception, it would follow that it possesses causal efficiency, which would entail its being a real entity (*vastutva*). In that case, the definition of existence as "the capacity for purposeful action" (*arthakriyākāritva*) would apply even to the non-momentary, resulting in the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
Indeed, you yourself do not accept momentariness for exclusion, because you maintain that it belongs only to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Even if that [invariable concomitance] were understood through inference, this very same objection would apply; nor can the necessary connection (pratibandha) be established through a subverting proof (bādhaka).

Furthermore, the connection between existence (sattva) and momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) is itself preceded by the apprehension of the negative instance (vyatireka); and it is not possible to apprehend its absence from the counter-example (vipakṣa) if the counter-example has not been apprehended, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, once [the two] are grasped, a necessary connection between them would be difficult to establish;
moreover, if momentariness were accessible through inference, it would not be a real entity, because inference has exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) as its object, and that [exclusion] is not a real entity.

Furthermore, does this momentariness exist as something distinct from the blue object, or not? If it does not exist [as distinct], how can that [blue] possess momentariness? If it does exist [as distinct], does it subsist in the blue, or not? If it does not subsist, how is there no difference between this [momentariness] and the blue? If it does subsist, then that too would be merely the blue; thus, the established order of things (*vastuvyavasthā*) would be destroyed.

Nor is this fault equal in the case of a tree and a *śiṃśapā* (e.g., "this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*"); for one who maintains that things possess parts, the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the tree and so forth from the *śiṃśapā* and so forth in some form is logically established.

Furthermore, there are specific divisions of time such as *kṣaṇa*, *lava*, and *muhūrta*; however, since time is not accepted by the Buddhists, the qualification [“momentary”] is unestablished (*asiddha*). How, then, could the meaning “that which has a moment” (*kṣaṇaḥ asya asti*) be “momentary” (*kṣaṇika*)? Moreover, momentariness through a merely imagined (*parikalpita*) moment would not be real. And if momentariness is unreal, then non-momentariness alone must be real, because no other alternative is possible. This is because time is accepted by them as a mere designation (*saṃjñāmātra*), and it is not proper for a mere designation to serve as a real qualifier of an entity (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 142).

And if [the state] were imagined (parikalpita), there would be [the consequence that] the momentariness of the moment immediately following [the first] would be real; and if there were [such a thing as] the moment immediately following the moment... [text fragment].

Furthermore, what is this "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvam*)? Is it the state of persisting for a moment, or is it non-existence immediately after a moment? If it is the state of persisting for a moment, then that exists even in a non-momentary entity, for even that persists for a moment; otherwise, it would not be non-momentary at all. If, on the other hand, it is non-existence immediately after a moment, then it is not the meaning of the word [“momentary”]; for non-existence immediately after a moment is not denoted by the word “moment,” whereby the thing could possess that property. Moreover, it has already been stated that the non-existence of objects immediately after a moment is contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition. Thus, it is not... [the text ends].

Likewise, regarding that which was stated—"of one for whom the entire collection of effects has been produced," and so forth—therein, once the effect has been produced, its nature as a producer of that [specific] effect indeed ceases, because it assumes a nature for the production of another effect.

Yet, this does not entail its momentariness; for even though there is a difference in natures, it is established as non-momentary because it remains the object of a cognition of identity (*abhedapratyaya*) despite that difference in natures.

By this, [the objection] beginning with "those who perform [an action] without having performed [it before]" (p. 375, l. 22) is refuted, because [the action] is a condition (pratyayatvena). Ā. [notes].

And as for that which was stated as the proof for the fact that being produced implies momentariness; there too, defects such as those pertaining to the thesis (pakṣa) and so forth are to be understood as before.

And "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is said to be "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). Furthermore, since the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) has already been refuted on the occasion of denying the continuity (*santāna*) in the case of the absolute doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayaikānta*), how could that [causal relationship] be established? Or, even if such a relationship were to exist there, even so, in this context, does one effect arise from one cause, or one from many, or many from one, or many from many? Among these, the first position is untenable, because we observe the arising of multiple effects—such as the burning of wicks, the drying of oil, and the dispelling of darkness—from a single cause like a lamp.

The second position is also untenable. According to your view, it is impossible for a single effect in the form of a composite whole (*avayavin*)—produced by a multitude of constituent parts—to arise from a collection of multiple causes such as color-form (*rūpa*), light (*āloka*), and so forth. This argument is also flawed because, due to the association with a plurality of natures brought about by the diversity of its causes, its unity cannot be established. For, by the object (*artha*), the aspect of blue and so forth is imparted to the cognition; by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvid-rūpatā*); by light, clarity (*spaṣṭatā*); and by the eye and other organs, the restriction to color-form and so forth is imparted to the cognition. Thus, [the cognition] is not one.

If its unity persists even when there is the superimposition (adhyāsa) of various contradictory properties upon it, why should its unity not persist even when it exists across multiple times? For there is no distinction [between the two cases]. By this, the third position is also refuted: for a single entity producing multiple effects through different natures—whether as auxiliary causes (sahakārin) or otherwise—their unity is untenable due to the superimposition of contradictory properties. Or, if that unity were maintained, then let its unity be established even when it is connected to multiple moments, since there is no difference [in the reasoning];

for even in the theory of momentary destruction (kṣaṇakṣaya), causality is not directly possible for anything anywhere, because there is no activity whatsoever, just like an immovable soul (acalātman).
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 77:
Furthermore, if momentariness were the case, the relationship between cause and effect would not be tenable.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.

401: "In the case of momentariness, it must be examined whether one arises from one, or one originates from many, or many are produced from one, or many come into being from many" (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 453).
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 400;
Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 761;
Abhidhāna-āloka, p. 548.
Regarding the burning of the tip of a wick:
[the objection] that for you, as for us, there is no effect in the form of a composite whole (*avayavin*) constructed from a multitude of many parts.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

454: For a consciousness appearing as blue, its state of having the form of blue arises from the blue object, which is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); its nature as cognition arises from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), namely the prior consciousness; its clarity regarding the object arises from light, which is the auxiliary condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*); and the restriction to the apprehension of color-form arises from the eye, which is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). (*Brahmasūtraśāṅkarabhāṣya*, *Bhāmatī* 2).
2.21 First of all, its very oneness is contradicted by the connection with a plurality of natures brought about by the difference in causes.
Nyāyamañjarī, p.
454: "If unity is admitted even when there is a conjunction of contradictory properties, then let it be accepted that an entity remains one even when it is conjoined with multiple moments."
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 454:

Now, if the fourth position is adopted—that the preceding causal complex (*sāmagrī*), which consists of a collection of moments such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, proceeding by way of a continuous stream (*saṃtāna*), produces a subsequent causal complex of its own nature, whereas when heterogeneous causes intervene, it produces one of a different nature—this too is not tenable. For is that causal complex non-different from the individual members of the complex, or is it different? It cannot be different, because that would entail the consequence of contradicting your own established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*).

Now, if they are non-distinct, then that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is itself a single complex; and in that case, when the subsequent complex is initiated by the preceding complex, would each individual constituent within it produce its corresponding constituent individually, or would all of them together produce it? Of these, the first position is untenable, because the production of one from one has already been refuted, and because it would entail the contradiction of the thesis that multiple things are produced from multiple causes. Furthermore, even if [the complex] were of the nature of an accumulation (*pracaya*), [the same difficulties would apply]. (A, B, J)

Now, what is this so-called "assemblage" (*sāmagrī*)? It is not distinct from the individual members of the assemblage, because it is not perceived separately; yet, if it were not distinct [from them], then the assemblage would be nothing other than the members themselves—each one individually. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 454) [Variant readings: *ekaikaśa eva* for *ekaikaśa eva*; *ba*, *ja* manuscripts.]

In that regard, when a subsequent aggregate is initiated by a preceding aggregate, does one [cause] produce only one constituent within it, or do they produce it collectively? According to the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p.
454), "one would produce each one individually, or all together. According to the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 766), "would each one produce each one individually, or would all together produce it?"

The second position is also untenable; for, in the production of each individual constituent, would all the constituents function sequentially or simultaneously? In the case of sequential functioning, there is a loss of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*); for those five or six momentary constituents that exist there, having produced one [constituent], they would produce another, and then yet another—thus, because they persist for that duration of time, how could they be momentary? If, on the other hand, all [constituents] function simultaneously in the production of everything, then the effect, being a composite aggregate, would arise from a cause that is itself a composite aggregate. Consequently, due to the absence of a restrictive rule regarding the differentiation of causes, there would be no differentiation among effects such as "this is form" and "this is taste"; rather, everything would be either form or taste, since it arises from a single composite particular.

Furthermore, even though one aggregate arises from another aggregate, there is no consequence of a confusion of the intrinsic natures of form and the other [sensory objects], because the preceding moments of form and so forth, acting as material and auxiliary causes, produce the subsequent moments of form and so forth that constitute the later aggregate.

For if a moment of form were the material cause (*upādāna*) for a subsequent moment of taste and so forth, then there would be the transformation of taste into form; but that too is incorrect. This is because the relationship between material cause and auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) is only possible when there is a distinction between the capacities of the material cause and what is other than it, and such a distinction is impossible in a partless particular (*niraṃśa-svalakṣaṇa*), as has already been stated. Furthermore, in the production of a collection of individual effects, would [the cause] operate upon every member of the collection sequentially or simultaneously? (Nyāyamañjarī p. 454; Syādvādaratnākara p. 766)
For those five [elements] which, as a collection of fifteen, exist there for a moment; see Nyāyamañjarī, p. 454.

In that case, since [the effect] would arise from a cause that is merely a mass (nikurumba), there would be no distinction between form, taste, and so forth, due to the absence of a restrictive rule regarding the differentiation of causes (Nyāyamañjarī p. 454; Syādvādaratnākara p.

Furthermore, since the nature of form (*rūpatā*) [is not established], and because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable in the absolute doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayaikānta*), "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) therein.

Nor is there a rule that what is produced must perish immediately after its own moment of existence; for it could be produced and yet perish at a later time, as there is no contradiction [in this]. Thus, the reason is inconclusive due to doubt (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*).

"It is not the case that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced) does not deviate from *anityatva* (impermanence) due to their identity (*tādātmya*). This too is unsatisfactory; for even if there is non-deviation from impermanence, there may be non-deviation from an impermanence that occurs at a later time, but not non-deviation from an impermanence that occurs immediately after production. Since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of *kṛtakatva* is possible through mere impermanence, the proof of the identity of *kṛtakatva* and *anityatva*—and so forth—is thereby refuted.

Furthermore, how is the establishment of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) between these two [the cause and the effect] achieved? It cannot be through perception (*pratyakṣa*), because perception is non-investigative (*avicāraka*) and has only proximate objects as its domain; thus, it lacks the capacity to grasp a universal relation.
Nor can it be through inference (*anumāna*), because an inference capable of proving such a relation is itself impossible.
As for the claim that this relation is established through a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*), that has already been answered previously.
It is not established that there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva); thus, [the reading] "nāsti" does not exist in the Ā, Bhāṃ, and Śra manuscripts;
[the term] "andhaprasiddhi" is found in the Śra manuscript.

As for the other argument stated—namely, "because there is no difference in the capacity of the causes" and so forth—that too is mere words; for, does the non-difference in the capacity of the causes pertain to the production of entities whose nature is merely perishable, or to the mere production of objects that are by nature unable to endure after their arising? In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*), since whatever is produced by causes is accepted as having a nature characterized solely by impermanence.
However, the second case is untenable, because we do not perceive that which has acquired its own existence through the operation of causes to be incapable of enduring immediately after its arising.

For the causal complex is indeed diverse: some brings forth a state such as lightning, which is characterized by destruction that occurs immediately after its arising and is accomplished without effort; another, however, [brings forth] a form such as a jar, which is embraced by non-existence at a later time and is accomplished through effort; yet another [produces] things such as mountains, whose destruction cannot be attained by people like us even with a thousand efforts over a vast period of time.

Indeed, the non-existence of lightning and the like immediately after its appearance is not established by anything other than cognition; and since that [cognition] occurs elsewhere as well, why should it not establish their existence? For certainly, the non-existence of a jar and the like prior to the operation of a mallet or similar instrument is not cognized.
(Page 376, Line 8) — *bhedaiḥ* (variant readings: *ba*, *ja*).
The interval between the arising [of the effect]—
in the cause, there is the absence of [the effect]. — *adhyabhāva*— in *ja*, *ba*.

As for what was also stated—that because destruction is perceived at the end, and so forth—that too is incorrect. If the property observed at the end is admitted to exist at the beginning as well, then since the cessation of the continuum is observed at the end, that cessation would have to occur at the beginning too. Furthermore, since the exhaustion of ignorance and craving is seen at the end, it would follow that this is already established at the beginning, rendering the practice of the Sugata’s path useless. Moreover, if an entity has arisen from its own cause with destruction as its inherent nature, then it should appear as such independently of the striking of a mallet or other such instruments.
For a lamp or the like, having arisen as something whose nature is illumination, does not manifest as such by depending on anything else;

nor is the destruction of a jar or the like perceived even in a dream in the absence of a blow from a mallet or similar instrument. Therefore, being occasional, this [destruction] is established through positive and negative concomitance as having the mallet and so forth as its cause.
Indeed, it is not logical for that which is occasional to be without a cause, just like arising.
Nor can it be said that whatever arises from something else is not caused by it, for that would entail the impossibility of establishing the fixed relationship between specific causes and effects.

Furthermore, one should not assert that the function [of the cause] is fulfilled solely by the production of a dissimilar continuum; for if a jar were not destroyed, a continuum of shards could not arise. Indeed, as long as the jar exists, a continuum of shards is not perceived; therefore, that continuum arises only through the destruction of the jar. Since both [the jar and the shards] equally follow the presence and absence of that [cause], let it be granted that even destruction is produced by it.

"Because destruction is necessarily present in produced things, they do not depend on another cause [for their destruction]; this [argument] is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the series of potsherds, for that [destruction] is necessarily present, yet it does not lack dependence on other causes such as a mallet, etc.
(p. 376, l. 16). [The reading *vināśasadbhāvabhā* is found in the manuscripts *ba* and *ja*.]

The supreme opponents [argue] that even for that which is causeless, there is no contradiction because it may persist for a certain period of time. *ba*, *ja* read *paramapakṣā*; *bhā* reads *bhāsate*.

Nor is causelessness logical, because, just as in the case of an existent entity, the operation of a cause is observed in the case of a non-existent entity as well through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) [Praśastapādabhāṣya p. 399;
Nyāyamañjarī p. 458].
That [cause] is the reason;
[it is] non-occurrence (anupapatti) according to Śrī., while according to Ba.
and Ja.—even when the production and destruction [of the cause] have ceased, that which is produced by it remains, according to Ba. and Ja.
Even if [it were] independent,

and even if its continuum were one, and even if it were causeless— would this [entity] always exist like space and so forth, or would it be non-existent like the son of a barren woman? In the first case, there would be the simultaneous perception of existence and non-existence, because their coexistence is possible due to the absence of contradiction between them.
Alternatively, if there is a contradiction [between existence and non-existence], the perception of an entity would become impossible, because its contradictory non-existence is always present.

In the second case, however, the jar and so forth would have to be eternal, because their destruction—being causeless—would never exist. Furthermore, it is not tenable for non-existence to have an entity as its cause, because we perceive a difference in their causes: indeed, the hammer and such are one thing that is the cause for the destruction of a jar, while the lump of clay and such are quite another that is the cause for its production.

Furthermore, if non-existence were caused by an existent entity, then non-existence would also occur at the very time of the existence [of its cause]; and in that case, the perception of the existent would be impossible, just as it was before.

Or, if it does not occur then, it could not have an existent entity as its cause; for it is never observed that things produced from a single cause arise sequentially in time. If you argue that its manifestation does not occur at that very moment because it depends on the second moment, how then can it be causeless? For dependence itself constitutes the nature of a cause; indeed, that which is causeless depends upon nothing at all.

One who asserts that "there is no cause for destruction" should be questioned: Is it because of the absence of a cause that destruction does not exist, or is it because of the absence of a cause that destruction is eternal? If destruction were eternal due to the absence of a cause, then there would be the fault that the production of an effect could not occur, as it would coexist with destruction. Alternatively, if destruction were non-existent [even though it has no cause], then likewise everything would be eternal due to the absence of destruction. (Nyāyavārttika 3.2.10)
14 pṛḥ 414 –[such as] a blow with a sword and so forth— Śra.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "This entity is produced by causal factors with such an intrinsic nature (*tathābhūtasvabhāva*) that it exists immediately after the existence of the [prior] entity. But is its existence something that perishes immediately after the moment [of its production], or is it endowed with another form? In the first case, there is sublation by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādibādhā*), because the existence of the entity is perceived through perception and other valid cognitions even in the second and subsequent moments.

But in the second case, how can objects be momentary? For the destruction that occurs immediately after an existence persisting through multiple moments is logically possible only if [the object] is non-momentary. Nor is there any other "mere existence" (*sattāmātra*) which could be that which exists immediately after [the object]; for would this [existence] be conjoined with a single moment or pervade multiple moments? (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 389)
–vino’sattvasya ja;
–vinoṃ’śasya ba;
–vino vināśasya śra.

—[The opponent asks: "Is its being causeless because it occurs immediately after the arising of the object, or because its being produced by that [object] is impossible due to the dilemma of whether there is a distinction or non-distinction [between them]? It cannot be because it occurs immediately after arising, for that would entail the faults already mentioned.
Furthermore, through the dilemma of distinction and non-distinction, its lack of causality by the hammer and so forth might be established, but not its occurrence immediately after production."

For when that [destruction] is perceived, it is logical to accept it as being causeless; yet, the destruction of jars and the like is not perceived prior to the operation of the hammer and so forth, nor is it reasonable to assert that it exists even while unperceived—since the determination of the nature of things is based upon perception. Furthermore, for one who does not admit the arising of destruction from the operation of a cause at a later time, but instead accepts its causelessness immediately after its appearance despite it being unperceived, there would be a great lack of circumspection!

Furthermore, is the fact that entities perish immediately after arising determined by something other than the alternatives of [the destruction being] different or non-different from the entity, or by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.

145, l. 1). And thus, the investigation into whether destruction is distinct [from the entity] and so forth, which is undertaken by the wise with respect to the object destroyed, is indeed entirely futile.
Following the meaning of the treatise (śāstravāda), [there is] the manifestation (bhā-). Śra.
Even its being causeless is accepted by Śrāvakas and others; its being caused by birth is also accepted by Śrāvakas and others.

And how could arising (*utpāda*) itself not likewise be without a cause? For that [arising], whether it is itself arising or not arising as an effect, cannot be produced by causes in such a way that it is either distinct or non-distinct from it—just as the non-existence of a jar or the like cannot logically result from a mallet and so forth. Furthermore, even if it were to exist by its own nature, it would not escape the following alternatives: whether it is itself perishable or imperishable, or whether it is distinct or non-distinct [from the entity].

Just as that which is perishable is independent of destruction, so too that which is stable is independent of stability; because the cause [of stability] is incapable of acting [upon it], since it neither produces something distinct from nor non-distinct from it—thus all [this] is the same [as the argument regarding destruction].
(Aṣṭasahasrī p. 185;
Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā p. 169, uddhṛta).
This same prattle applies equally even regarding origination; see Nyāyamañjarī, p. 458; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 146, first part.

Now, it might be objected: "In our view, nothing happens to an entity; rather, that which has the nature of existing for only a single moment, having arisen from its own respective causes, is merely designated as 'not existing' in the subsequent moment. As it has been said: "Nothing happens to it; it simply does not exist" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.281).

Now, does the word "destroyed" (naṣṭa) have some meaning at all, or not? If it has none, what is the point of its being uttered? If it does have one, is it different from existence (sattva), or non-different? The position of difference is untenable, because there would be no relationship [between them] and because such a relationship is not admitted.
If, on the other hand, it is non-different, then the words "existent" (asti) and "non-existent" (nāsti), as well as the cognitions produced by them, would become synonyms.

And thus, since entities perish moment by moment and are destroyed without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśa*), such specific statements as "nothing happens to it," or "it simply does not exist," would not denote any object distinct from existence itself; consequently, their utterance would be useless, because there is no disagreement regarding existence. Therefore, just as an entity that has acquired its birth from its own causes possesses a nature of existence (*sadrūpatā*) determinable by valid cognition, so too does it possess a nature of non-existence (*asadrūpatā*) in the subsequent moment. (Ā., Ba., Ja., Śr.)
And this has been extracted from: *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasāhasrī* p. 200;
*Hetubindu-ṭīkā* p. 120;
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā* p. 400.

Is there any meaning for the word "naṣṭa" (destroyed/perished), or not? [Syādvādamañjarī, p. 788] — [The answer is: There are various types of statements... [Syādvādamañjarī, p. 790]. Śrī. [End of citation].

And what kind of destruction is intended by this term "causeless"? Is "destruction" (vināśa) the act of perishing, which is mere non-existence in the form of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or is it that which "perishes," being the nature of a non-enduring entity in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*)? First of all, this [destruction] cannot be causeless if it is in the form of a simple negation, because you yourself do not accept the existence of such a non-existence. Nor can it be so if it is in the form of a relative negation, because no one accepts that the nature of a non-enduring entity is causeless.

Therefore, the independence of entities with respect to destruction is unestablished, because they depend upon the mallet and other such factors for that [destruction]. Furthermore, the principle that "whatever is independent with respect to the occurrence of something" applies equally even in the case of non-perishability.

And likewise, Trilocana states in the *Prakīrṇaka*: "What is it that perishes? Is 'destruction' (vināśa) the nature of a non-enduring entity, in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*), or is 'destruction' the act of perishing, being mere non-existence in the form of an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)? It cannot be the first alternative; for the nature of a non-enduring entity is unestablished (*asiddha*), since no one accepts it to be causeless. (*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 788: "of the nature of being causeless...")
An entity would have transformation as its intrinsic nature because it does not depend [on anything else] in that regard;
this is the cause of causal efficiency (arthakriyā), even without a lack of continuity (niranvaya).
— *Nyāyaviniścaya* 2.120.2.

Furthermore, in this case, is the reason merely "independence from others," or is it "independence from others while possessing that specific nature"? In the first alternative, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to barley seeds and the like; for even though these are independent of other factors at the time when the causal complex for producing a rice sprout is present, they lack the necessity of having that [rice-sprout-producing] nature.

In the second case, however, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished with respect to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because it is demonstrated that even if things possess that nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*), they lack independence (*anapekṣatva*) regarding destruction.

Furthermore, it is partially unestablished with respect to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), namely "independence while possessing that nature," because substances (*dravya*) and so forth lack the nature of being subject to destruction.

Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*); for it is impossible for the final causal complex (*antyakāraṇasāmagrī*) to be independent of a second moment in the production of its own effect. Indeed, even though the final causal complex has the nature of producing its own effect, it does not produce that effect independently of a second moment, because such a claim contradicts experience (*pratītivirodhāt*). Moreover, the reason (*hetu*) is not merely independence from others, but rather independence from others while possessing that specific nature (*tatsvabhāvatve sati*), as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 145, first part.

As for what was said—that [the object] persists for a hundred thousand moments—that too is incorrect; because it has been stated [at Śrāvakabhūmi, p. 376, l. 18]: "An object produced from its own complex of causes, persisting for a hundred thousand moments from the first moment until the final moment, does not abandon that very nature even in the second and subsequent moments, up until the final moment."

As for what was also stated—"In whatever manner something appears," and so forth—that too is a mere assertion, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For a blue object appearing does not appear as being momentary; otherwise, there would also be a mental apprehension (*ullekha*) that "this is momentary" just as there is the apprehension "this is blue," since you accept that only that which is grasped by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, the appearance of blue is not itself the appearance of momentariness, because the two cognitions are distinct.

Even though it is distinct from that [other cognition], if its nature is the manifestation of momentariness, let its nature also be the manifestation of non-momentariness, for there is no distinction [between them]. Indeed, one form is not capable of determining another, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is the apprehension of presentness itself the apprehension of momentariness; for it has been demonstrated (p. 378, l. 17) that even for one whose eyes do not blink, there is an apprehension of presentness despite the absence of momentariness.

Since momentariness, when thus examined, is untenable, the Sautrāntika position—that form, taste, smell, touch, and sound atoms, as well as cognition, perish at every moment—is refuted. Likewise, the Yogācāra and Mādhyamika positions—that reality is mere cognition characterized by momentary existence—are also rejected. Since the refutation of each of those views has already been specifically established previously through the proof of external objects and the proof of other principles such as the self, it is not stated here again.
The Vaibhāṣika position, although already refuted by the rejection of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), is now specifically refuted by demonstrating its methodological framework as follows:
the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaibhāṣikas, who assert the diversity of the universe while accepting the twelve-linked dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Those who study the *Vibhāṣā*, a specific treatise that elucidates the True Dharma, are the Vaibhāṣikas. They, accepting dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), explain the manifold variety of the universe. For instance: when from certain aggregates other aggregates arise—depending on one another, making each other their cause, relying upon various collections of conditions, and existing through the nature of causes and conditions, independent of any creator such as Pradhāna or Īśvara—that is dependent origination.

And its twelve members are established in the nature of cause and effect; that is to say: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming is birth (*jāti*); and conditioned by birth are old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
In this regard, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition contrary to the nature of phenomena—which are momentary, selfless, impure, and suffering.

Formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are of three types—meritorious, non-meritorious, and neither—and are the causes for performing virtuous, non-virtuous, or mixed actions; they consist of various forms such as attachment and so forth.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the conceptual designation of objects, and it is of six kinds, distinguished as the five sensory consciousnesses and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Those who sport with or practice according to the *Vibhāṣā* are the Vaibhāṣikas; alternatively, those who know the *Vibhāṣā* are the Vaibhāṣikas (*Sphuṭārthā*, p.
12). Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the arising of the aggregates and so forth, having depended upon and relied on causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*).
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, page 15: Regarding that, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained in the *Śālistamba Sūtra*:

"In that regard, what is the causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) of internal dependent origination? It is as follows: conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), up to: conditioned by birth (*jāti*) are aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)."

That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and so forth arise.

In this context, what is ignorance (*avidyā*)? It is that various forms of non-knowing regarding these very six elements (*dhātu*), such as the notion of unity, the notion of a whole, the notion of permanence, the notion of stability, the notion of eternity, the notion of pleasure, the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), the notion of a living soul (*jīva*), the notion of a creature (*jantu*), the notion of a human (*manuja*), the notion of a youth (*mānava*), and the notions of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṅkāra-mamakāra*). This is called ignorance.

When ignorance exists in this way, passion, hatred, and delusion arise toward sense objects. Among these, those passions, hatreds, and delusions directed toward sense objects are called the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) conditioned by ignorance.
The specific representation of an object is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The four great elements and the derived matter constitute form (*rūpa*); the four non-material aggregates (*skandha*) that have consciousness as their nature constitute name (*nāma*). That is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
The sense faculties based upon name-and-form are the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The coming together of the three factors is contact (*sparśa*).
The experience of contact is feeling;
attachment to feeling is craving;
the expansion of craving is grasping.
Action produced from grasping that generates renewed existence is becoming;
the manifestation of the aggregates caused by becoming is birth;
and the maturation of the aggregates manifested through birth is old age.
"The destruction of the aggregates is death" (Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā, p. 386;

Abhidharmakośa, Third Chapter:
Consciousness is the distinct discernment of each object. Abhidharmakośa 1.16.
The four aggregates characterized by form, sensation, perception, and mental formations constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Among these, the aggregate of form is elevenfold: the five sense faculties, their five objects, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

In this context, *avijñapti* (non-intimation) is that which serves as the substrate for the bodies of living beings; it arises from the performance of virtuous, non-virtuous, or neutral actions and is like a cloak. Because it is imperceptible to those who are not yogis, it is called "non-intimation" according to its literal meaning. Its constituent elements—earth and so forth—exist and manifest themselves through the nature of benefit or harm; thus they are called *bhūtāni* (elements).
Space (*ākāśa*) is an aperture, and since that is nothing other than light and darkness atoms, it is not counted separately.

And these also acquire other designations such as "the earth element" (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and so forth, because they are the locus of arising, like the mineral ores of copper and the like. Feeling (*vedanā*) is threefold, consisting of the experience of pleasure, pain, and that which is neither pleasant nor painful. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the discernment of the signs of things (*nimitta-udgrahaṇa*), such as: "it is form (*rūpa*) because of its transformation (*rūpaṇāt*)," "they are elements (*dhātavaḥ*) because of their supporting (*dhāraṇāt*)," or "it is a jar (*ghaṭaḥ*) because of its connection to purposeful action (*arthakriyāyām ghaṭanāt*). Thus, there are many such varieties.
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are also of many kinds due to the distinctions of passion and so forth.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), however, although denoted by the term "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), is also spoken of by the word "aggregate" (*skandha*); for there is no difference among all five in their being a heap. For instance: form (*rūpa*) is a heap consisting of eleven [bases], feeling (*vedanā*) consists of three [types], perception (*saṃjñā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) consist of many [types], and consciousness (*vijñāna*) consists of six [types]; thus, "name" (*nāma*) refers to the formless aggregates.
The four aggregates distinct from form— designated as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— are conventionally designated by the term "name" (nāma). (Abhidharmakośa 3.30)
Form consists of the five sense faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter alone. (Abhidharmakośa 1.9)

When these same things function as causes, they are the "origin" (*samudaya*). Those very [factors] free from outflows (anāsrava) are the Path;
Cessation (nirodha) is of two kinds: analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

Among these, that cessation which is attained through a specific wisdom by means of which the Noble Truths, beginning with Suffering, are analyzed and determined as they truly are—that cessation, which is the eradication of ignorance and so forth, is analytical cessation.
Apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha (cessation not through deliberation), which consists of meditative concentration and attainment, acts as an absolute obstacle to the arising of passion and other afflictions.

The sense bases (*āyatana*)—the eyes and the other faculties—are so called because they extend (*tanvanti*) the arrival (*āya*); the meaning is that they are the means for everything that comes [into experience].
Contact (*sparśa*) is the meeting or conjunction of the object, the faculty, and consciousness, as in "I see a form with the eye," and so forth.
When there is contact, there is experience, which is feeling; from that comes greed, which is craving;
and the expansion of craving is grasping.
Existence (bhava) is characterized by karma that produces renewed existence;
birth (jāti) is the manifestation of previously non-existent aggregates;
and old age and death (jarā-maraṇa) are characterized by the maturation and destruction of the aggregates born of that birth.
In this way, the wheel of existence (bhavacakra) revolves;
and here, by the word "existence" (bhava), the three realms known as Kāma, Rūpa, and Ārūpya are designated.
Among these, the Kāmadhātu consists of the abodes beginning with the hells.
The realm of form consists of the forms of meditative absorption;
the formless realm consists of the nature of the pure continuum of mind.
Thus, conditioned phenomena—both with outflows and without outflows—are those that exclude the Path.
They are with-outflows (sāśrava) because the outflows (āśrava) adhere to them;
the truth of the path (mārgasatya) is without-outflows (anāśrava), as are the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta). Abhidharmakośa 1.4.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is that disjunction which is distinct for each [defilement] and is the absolute prevention of grasping (*upādāna*). The other cessation is by means of non-deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā*).
Discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is indeed wisdom (*prajñā*); because this cessation occurs by means of that [wisdom] acting as its cause, it is "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

That other [cessation], which is an absolute opposition to the arising of phenomena and consists in a dissociation from their own nature, is "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 1)

To this, the following response is given:

As for what was stated—that [the Buddha taught] "dependent origination" and so forth—that is incorrect. For, within dependent origination, the twelve factors beginning with ignorance were presented because they are useful for those seeking liberation; however, is it the case that only these many exist? It cannot be determined that there are only this many, because the world, in its synonymous variety, is pervaded by infinity.

Nor are these alone sufficient for those seeking liberation; for false view (*mithyādarśana*) and conduct (*cāritra*), which—like ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by false knowledge—are respectively of the nature of perverse faith and practice and are causes of *saṃsāra*, must be abandoned, while right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and the others, being causes of liberation, must be adopted.

Furthermore, it will be established in detail during the examination of liberation that the triad of [right] knowledge and so forth, when in an incorrect form, is the cause of *saṃsāra*, whereas in its correct form, it is the cause of liberation.

Nor should it be asserted that these [defilements] are included within ignorance (*avidyā*) alone; for, because they are absolutely distinct from it, their inclusion therein is impossible. Whatever is absolutely distinct from something else is not included within it, just as fire is not included in water; and since false views (*mithyādarśana*) and the rest are absolutely distinct from ignorance, if they were included therein, the teaching of the twelve enumerated limbs (*dvādaśāṅga*) would be untenable. As for the statement that "the latent dispositions (*saṃskāras*) are passion (*rāga*) and so forth," that is utterly inconsistent. For is the nature of passion and the rest as latent dispositions asserted because they are well-known as such in both worldly and non-worldly [contexts], or merely by way of etymological derivation? In this regard, the first position is untenable, because in both the world and the scriptures, *saṃskāra* is well-known only as having the nature of momentum (*vega*) and the like.

The second position is also untenable; for by the mere etymological derivation that "those which are refined are *saṃskāras*," it would follow that all objects whatsoever would be *saṃskāras*, just like attachment (*rāga*) and so forth. Consequently, since all objects would arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) itself in that form, the previously demonstrated process of their distinct causes would collapse, and their classification as types such as merit (*puṇya*) and so on would become utterly impossible. Indeed, the designation of attachment and the like as "merit" and so forth is nowhere well-known in the world or in the scriptures, for that term is established there only for dharma and other factors that are the means to pleasure and the like.

The claim that they too are designated as such because they are the effects of those [defilements] is also incorrect; for merit and so forth cannot possibly be the causes of passion and so forth, since merit is based on specific types of conduct, and while it may be indirectly based on them, if it were designated by their name, it would follow that ignorance and other factors would also be so designated, resulting in the collapse of the established order of specific distinctions. As for the statement that "consciousness has formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition," that too is the manifestation of no small darkness; for since passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] are the opposites of consciousness, it is impossible for them to arise from formative forces which possess the characteristics of that [consciousness]. And that they are indeed its opposites has been stated by others as well: "This great blindness is blindness; one who is blinded by sense-objects has his vision destroyed.
One who is blind by means of the eye does not perceive, but one who is blinded by sense-objects perceives nothing at all" (Ātmanuśāsana, verse 35).

And its sixfold nature is like a flower in the sky; for the cognition produced by the senses and the conceptual cognition postulated by you have already been rejected in the proof of [the existence of] determinate cognition (savikalpaka) (p. 390, l.
6). This person is a great blind man, blinded by objects, though his eyes have been opened.

"One who is blind with the eye does not know, and one who is blind with regard to sense-objects does not know by any means" (Ātmanuśāsana, verse 35). As for what was stated—that "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition"—that too is most extraordinary, because it is impossible for name-and-form, characterized by the four aggregates beginning with form, to originate from consciousness; rather, it is logical that consciousness itself originates from that [name-and-form]. For is that [consciousness] produced by this [name-and-form] in the capacity of a material cause (*upādāna*), or in the capacity of a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*)? It cannot be in the capacity of a material cause, because since the sense organs and their objects are entirely distinct, it is impossible for them to be its material cause.

That which is absolutely distinct from something else cannot be its material cause (*upādāna*), just as fire is not the material cause of water; and since the sense faculties and so forth are absolutely distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*), they cannot be its cause even in the capacity of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). This is because it is observed that consciousness itself arises from the sense faculties and so forth, and this is accepted by everyone. Furthermore, since it is possible for all the constituent factors (*aṅga*) to arise from consciousness by way of being auxiliary conditions, it would follow that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) alone could not be the condition for consciousness.

Since the verse is easy to understand, the author does not provide a word-by-word commentary; instead, under the guise of mocking others, he supports the statement beginning with "of entities" (*bhāvānām*) and says "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*), and so forth.

The "action" (*kriyā*) of an object—whether it be its own cognition or another effect such as burning—is its "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*). That which is capable (*samartha*) or fit for that [accomplishment] is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Whatever performs purposeful action is alone ultimately real.

Having thus accepted and affirmed [the position] regarding his own side, and then subsequently, by stating "everything is incapable" in that very same context, the Buddhist himself negates causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by his own hand; how could he not be insane, given that his speech is contradictory from beginning to end, like one intoxicated by liquor and the like?

Regarding the *dohā* and so forth, another [author] says here: "The performance of a function (*arthakriyā*), characterized by the production of a subsequent effect, is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of an entity, because of contradiction;
for one thing cannot be the defining characteristic of another, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."
Therefore, he states that the "attainment of its own nature" (*ātmalābha*) for self-cognized consciousness is "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*)—beginning with the words "its own" (*sva*), etc.

By the word "own," non-dual self-cognition is referred to; its "becoming" (*bhūti*) is the attainment of its own nature, which is precisely that [consciousness] alone—not a subsequent effect. How could even that very thing be excluded as purposeful action, even in the opposing view of the doctrine of the non-duality of the *puruṣa*? Not at all; for there too, it is no different.

[Objection: But in the doctrine of the non-duality of the *puruṣa*, how is there the conventional usage of distinctions such as cities and villages? [Response: How is it in the case of the non-duality of consciousness? The point is the same.

If it is argued that "this [worldly activity] is false" in that case, he says that the same applies elsewhere: "false," and so forth. How could that which is false—the delusive worldly activity concerning cities, villages, and so on—be excluded from the counter-position? Therefore, since there is no causal efficiency whatsoever in the positions of either permanence or momentariness, how could cognition—whether with form (*sākāra*) or otherwise—be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein? Or, even if such [cognition] were to exist there, he states the refutation: "from consciousness," and so forth.

Even though consciousness (*saṃvitti*)—that is, the cognition possessing the form of an object—is non-dual and partless, it is only the form of the object, such as the form of blue and so forth, that serves as the means of establishing the object; that is, it is that which determines the object such as blue. It is not some other form, distinct from the form of the object and so forth, such as the form of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), that serves as the means of establishing the object. The sense is that this [status of being the means] applies everywhere, as there is no distinction [in its nature].
Therefore, because only the form of the object serves as the means of establishing the object—[it follows that] even consciousness [is subject to] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Because it is the means of achieving that [result], there is no contradiction even in the absence of difference; or rather, modification is indeed modification itself.

The commentary states: Even though the ultimate reality is one, due to the distinctions in false conventional usage, the appearances of cognition—which perform various purposeful actions and mutually cognize their objects—establish the nature of reality as consisting of both difference and non-difference.

Commentary on the Verse (*kārikāvivaraṇam*): The particle *eva* is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the word *na*. The word *vā* has the sense of *iva* (as if). Consequently, the following meaning is established: even in non-difference—that is, even in unity—it would not at all be contradictory.

What is this? It is transformation (*vikriyā*), which is modification (*vikāra*); it is the transition to a subsequent form while not abandoning the previous form, occurring through a process of non-abandonment (*ajahadvṛtti*).
What is it like? He says: "Like a modification" (*vikriyeva*). "Modification" (*vikriyā*) means various (*vividhā*), manifold kinds of activity or the performance of an action; it is like that.

Alternatively, there is a reading in some places as "or indeed non-modification" (*avikriyaiva vā*). In that case, the meaning is this: even though it is changeless, it would not be contradictory [to appear as such]. This is the sequence. (Ānandagiri)

The commentary on the *Śrī-vivṛti* explains the passage beginning with "Even though there is oneness in the ultimate sense" up to "or indeed modification," because the remainder is easy to understand.

Even though, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is oneness—that is, even though it possesses an undifferentiated nature—of what? Of cognition (*jñāna*). Of what kind of cognition? That which performs manifold purposeful actions (*anekārthakriyākārin*); "manifold objects" refers to blue and so forth, and their "action" is the determination (*paricchitti*) thereof; [cognition] is that which performs such action. Why is this so? Because of the differentiation of false conventional usage (*mithyāvyavahārabhedāt*). "False conventional usage" is a usage constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*), characterized by the postulation of a universal form such as "blue" through the exclusion of forms such as "non-blue"; because of its "differentiation," that is, its manifoldness.

This is what is meant: that very cognition which, by the exclusion of non-blue (*anīla-vyāvṛtti*), possesses the form of blue and thereby determines it, is the same cognition which, by the exclusion of non-yellow (*apīta-vyāvṛtti*), possesses the form of yellow and thereby determines yellow and so forth. Thus, what do its [various] manifestations accomplish? He says: the manifestations—the forms of blue and so on—establish reality as being of the nature of both difference and non-difference. In what manner? They are "mutually cognizant of each other's objects," meaning they grasp one another's referents.
For instance: that very manifestation which perceives blue also perceives yellow, red, and white; likewise, that which perceives yellow also perceives blue, red, and white.

This should be applied to other cases as well, otherwise the cognition "I perceive blue and so forth simultaneously" would be untenable. And for this reason, it has been stated that [the object] performs multiple causal functions (*arthakriyā*).

Therefore, it is established that the manifestation grasping a present object is also the grasper of past and future objects, and the grasper of those [past and future objects] is the grasper of the present object, with respect to its own pervading cognition (*jñāna*).

And likewise, if the past and the future were graspable by the apprehension of the present, then they would be nothing but the present, because they are graspable by that same apprehension, just like a well-known present object. This [position] is refuted; for it would follow that yellow and other colors, which are graspable by the apprehension of blue and other colors, would themselves be blue and so forth. To explain: yellow and the rest would be blue, because they are graspable by the apprehension of blue, just like the intended blue. An objection to this proof is equal in both cases;
thus, there is no such thing as "that which grasps them."
