Indeed, existence (*sattva*) is not accepted by the followers of Yoga (the Vaiśeṣikas) as belonging to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth merely through their connection with existence; for that would entail a contradiction of their established tenet (*kṛtānta*) that "existence is that which makes the three categories existent."

Nor can it be asserted that the existence of substance (*dravya*) and so forth is distinct from that [primary] existence (*sattva*), and therefore only that [existence]—and nothing else—is the basis for the connection with the category of existence (*sattā*). For what is this so-called "distinctness" of that existence? Is it being apprehended by a distinct cognition, being unsublated, or being figurative (*gauṇatva*)? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because there is no cognition of it as being apprehended by a distinct cognition even in a dream.

Indeed, it is not the case that the existence of universals and so forth is established through individual cognition in the same way that the distinctness of a buffalo from a cow and other animals is well-known to every living being by virtue of being apprehended through a differentiating cognition; for you, however, such a cognition is based on the obsession with the tenets of your own school and is not produced by the power of perceiving the actual object, just as [the claim] that a jar or similar object is of the nature of non-duality with the Self is not.

The second alternative is also untenable; for there is no distinction between the two cases regarding the fact of being unsublated (*abādhitatva*). Indeed, existence (*sattva*) in substances (*dravya*) and so forth is not sublated by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the existence of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, because that would entail the consequence of their non-existence.

If it is argued that the "secondary nature" (*gauṇatva*) of the existence of universals and so forth constitutes its difference from the existence of substances and so forth; [we ask] how is this very secondary nature established? If you say it is due to the absence of a distinct qualifying attribute (*bhinnaviśeṣaṇa*); [we reply] that existence in substances and so forth is caused by a distinct qualifying attribute characterized as "Being" (*sattā*), whereas such is not the case for universals and so forth.

Nor is it logical for that which has non-distinct qualifiers to possess primacy, because it is stated that "that which has distinct qualifiers is primary, while that which has non-distinct qualifiers is secondary. This too is incorrect, because it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of its being secondary depends on the proof that existence as a general property (*sāmānya*) and so forth lacks the basis of having qualifiers distinct from the definition of "existence" (*sattā*); and conversely, the proof that it lacks such a basis depends on the establishment of its being secondary. The reading "sattāviśeṣa" in manuscripts *ba* and *ja*, and "asat" in manuscripts *ā*, *ba*, and *ja*, implies that the primacy of existence (*sattva*) in substance (*dravya*) and so forth has also been considered [and rejected]; for there is no difference in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To explain: if the primacy of existence in substance and so forth were established, then the establishment of its being based on a distinct qualifier characterized by existence (*sattā*) would follow; and once that is established, the establishment of its primacy would follow. Thus, there is a circularity.

Furthermore, no one who is not a fool would think that existence based on its own nature (*svarūpa*) is metaphorical (*upacarita*), while existence based on a separate entity (*arthāntarabhūta-sattā*) is primary (*mukhya*). For no discerning person thinks that being a staff (*yaṣṭitva*) is metaphorical in relation to a staff, but primary in relation to a person. Moreover, is existence itself existent (*satī*) and thus the cause of existence for another, or is it non-existent (*asatī*)? If it were non-existent, how could it be the cause of existence for another through its own connection? That which is non-existent cannot be the cause of existence for another through its own connection, just like a donkey's horn; and existence is [alleged to be] non-existent.

Now, regarding existence (*sattā*): is it intrinsic, or does it arise from a connection with another existence? If it is intrinsic, then let the reality (*vastu*) itself also possess existence intrinsically; what is the use of the laborious effort of postulating existence through a connection with that [other existence]? Whatever exists does so by means of an existence that is its very own self, just as universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) exist; and substances (*dravya*) and the rest do indeed exist.
If, on the other hand, it arises from a connection with another existence, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, it may be argued that because the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) acts as a subverting factor, existence is held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in the case of universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*), whereas it is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, since that [infinite regress] does not occur there. For indeed, an infinite regress does not descend upon the extrinsic existence of substances and the like—since the existence of substances and so forth derives from "Being" (*sattā*), while the existence of "Being" itself is intrinsic. This too is charming only when left unexamined; for it has already been demonstrated that if the existence of substances and the like were also extrinsic, it would be contradicted by the inference: "Whatever exists, exists only through an existence that is its own essence," and so forth.

Furthermore, there would follow the fallacies of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), futility (*vaiyarthyam*), and contradiction with the definition (*lakṣaṇabādha*). To explain: for that which exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa sat*), would existence (*sattvam*) arise from a connection with "Being" (*sattā*), or for that which does not exist? It cannot be for that which does not exist, because of the fallacy of over-extension; for there is no connection with "Being," nor existence resulting from such a connection, in the case of a sky-lotus, which is non-existent by its own nature. Moreover, this would result in a contradiction with inference, since substance (*dravya*) and so forth—which are accepted by others as existing—would be claimed by you to be non-existent by their own nature.

If, on the other hand, it exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then the relation with existence (*sattā*) is redundant; for that which is itself existent does not possess existence through a relation with existence, as is the case with existence itself. Furthermore, since every object is already existent even prior to its relation with existence, if one were to postulate existence for that which is already existent by virtue of such a relation, it would follow that one must likewise postulate it for existence itself—thus resulting in the very same infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if it is not existence itself that resides there, but rather existence arises only through a relation with existence—well then, does existence arise in that object through a relation with that very same existence, or without it? If it is through that very same [existence], then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the relation with existence would be established only when its existence is established, and its existence would be established only when that relation is established. Furthermore, if its existence were established through a different [instance of] existence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To explain: even if a relation with another instance of existence were established, it would only be established once the object’s existence is established; and the establishment of that existence would, in turn, depend on a relation with yet another instance of existence.

Therefore, the existence (*sattva*) of objects does not result from a connection with an existence (*sattā*) that is a distinct entity—because of the refutation by the fault of redundancy (*vaiyarthyabādhaka*).

For if one accepts that substances, qualities, and actions possess existence by their own nature (*svarūpasattva*), then the inherence of existence (*sattāsamavāya*) is redundant, just as in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; or else, it would follow that universals and so forth must have a connection with existence, just like substances and so forth.

If their existence as intrinsic natures (*svarūpasattva*) is not admitted, there would be no distinction from [non-entities] such as tortoise-hair, which would result in the contradiction of valid inference (*anumāna*) as stated in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* (p. 221), etc. (Ba., Ja.).
Nor [is it established] from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because that [efficiency] is distinct from them.

Whatever is distinct from something else does not have its existence established by that thing, just as a cloth is not established by a pot; and it is not unestablished that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is distinct from objects, because its distinction from them is well-known due to its occurring at a time prior or subsequent [to the object],
for an entity already established is what engages in some causal efficiency.

Furthermore, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): for the existence of the object to be established first, its subsequent establishment [as causal efficiency] must occur; and upon that establishment, the existence of such an object is established.

By this, its existence based on causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is rejected; because causal efficiency is said to be the state of being a cause of purposeful action, and that is logical only for what is already existent—thus, there is a circular dependency: for existence to be established, the establishment of causal efficiency is required, and from that, the establishment of existence follows.

Furthermore, the capacity of objects to perform causal functions (*arthakriyākāritva*) in the event of their being subject to destruction without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśitva*) has already been refuted at length previously; this was established by the former master Śrīsiṃha.

By this, the capacity for that [causal] action is also refuted in the case of perishability; for if an object perishes at every moment, it is impossible for it to perform a causal function, and thus the capacity for such action is utterly impossible. Furthermore, does the causal function and so forth—which is supposed to be the cause of another's existence—exist itself, or not? In either case, the faults already stated regarding the positions of existence and non-existence are to be observed.

Therefore, the existence of objects is not established by their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, nor by their connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for this [connection] applies to non-existence (*abhāva*) just as it does to existence (*bhāva*), and consequently, it would follow that non-existence, like existence, possesses the nature of being real, since there is no difference in its connection [with the means of cognition].

Now, even if there is no distinction [between objects], it might be argued that only that whose existence is made known through a connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is real, and not anything else. But how can such a connection with a means of valid cognition be the definition of existence? Furthermore, if the existence of objects were established even prior to that connection, then this defense would hold; but it is not so established. For otherwise, the postulation of the existence of objects through their connection with a means of valid cognition would result in futility, and there would also be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): existence [would depend] on the connection with a means of valid cognition, and the connection with a means of valid cognition [would depend] on that which exists.
However, existence is held to be that which is apprehended by a non-sublated, positive cognition (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

453). Furthermore, is that relation itself existent or non-existent? If it is non-existent, how could the existence of anything follow from such a relation, given the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle? If it is existent, is it so by itself, through a connection with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from some other source? If it is by itself, what wrong have the objects (*padārtha*) done that their own existence is not likewise admitted to be intrinsic? But if their existence were due to a connection with another means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Could its existence [be established] from something else—from a connection with an object of cognition (*prameya*) or from another cause? If it were from a connection with an object of cognition, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If, however, it were from another cause, then let that very non-deviating [cause] be the reason for existence in all cases; what is the use of postulating a connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? And that [existence] cannot be anything other than being endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence, as it is characterized by itself. (Bhāṣya, Śrīmad-Yogabindu)
Is existence itself [the object]?

No. Furthermore, it is logical that the existence of objects is established through their connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of perception and so forth; yet that establishment of the means of cognition would arise from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of the sense organs, the objects, and so on. In this way, there is the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*): for instance, when the means of cognition such as perception are established, the existence of the sense organs and objects is established through their connection with them; when that [existence] is established, the establishment of the causal complex of the means of cognition—consisting of the connection between the sense organs and objects and so forth—occurs; and when that is present, the means of cognition such as perception are established.

Furthermore, is the existence of objects produced by their connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it made known? It cannot be produced, because even prior to that [connection], objects have already attained their own self-nature (*ātmalābha*). For that which has already attained its own self-nature prior to something else, its existence is not produced by that thing—just as a father who has already attained his own self-nature prior to his son does not have his existence produced by the son—and objects such as jars and the like have already attained their own self-nature even prior to the means of valid cognition.

Now, it is being made known: there is nothing undesirable [in this], because the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, the determination of the object of knowledge is not tenable without valid cognition, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, since existence cannot be established for an entity through any other means, its existence must be understood precisely as being endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence.

Furthermore, origination and the rest are not distinct from the entity, such that they too would have to possess existence through connection with further origination and so forth—which would result in an infinite regress—because they are established as being identical in essence (*tādātmya*) with it.
—Thus, from what has been heard:

substance (*dravya*) is indeed eternal, while form (*ākṛti*) is non-eternal. Gold, when endowed with a certain form, becomes a lump; having destroyed the form of the lump, earrings (*rucaka*) are made; having destroyed the form of the earrings, bracelets (*kaṭaka*) are made; having destroyed the form of the bracelets, swastikas (*svastika*) are made. When the gold lump returns again, joined with yet another form, it becomes two earrings resembling acacia-wood coals; the form changes from one to another, but the substance remains the very same. Through the destruction of the form, only the substance remains.
(Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 1)
1.1 Yoga-bhāṣya 4
13. A person experiences grief, joy, or indifference based on causes, such as the destruction, arising, or persistence of a jar, a crown, or gold.
59. And when a vardhamānaka vessel is broken by an expert [artisan], a rucaka is fashioned from it.

Then, there is sorrow for one who desires the former, and joy for one who desires the latter; but for one who desires gold, there is indifference. Therefore, an object consists of these three natures.
There is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising,
and no equanimity without stability; therefore, there is a common permanence [in all things].
23rd verse, page 619.

Now, some may argue that if [the characteristics] were distinct, then each individual characteristic—such as persistence (sthiti) and the rest—would necessarily possess all three characteristics; otherwise, they would lack those characteristics. Furthermore, because this would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the desired conclusion could not be established. However, such a person has failed to consider the nature of entities (*padārtha-svabhāva*), for both positions are somehow acceptable. In that regard, if one accepts their non-difference in some sense (*kathaṃcid-abheda*), then it is understood that: from the power [of the underlying reality], persistence itself arises, and by implication, it perishes; destruction itself persists, and by implication, it arises; and origination itself perishes, and by implication, it persists. Thus, since persistence and the other characteristics are non-different from the entity possessing the three characteristics—such as the living soul (*jīva*)—it is established that they themselves possess the three characteristics.
By this very [argument], it has been stated that even when their difference is admitted, the establishment of the three-fold characteristic (*trilakṣaṇatva*) is proven; see *Aṣṭasāhasrī* p.
112 and *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā* p. 169.

But why is it that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists precisely of things characterized by manifoldness, such as origination and so forth? To this he says: "Because an absolute [nature] is not perceived; since this is so, therefore the object (*artha*) has a manifold nature. This concludes the summary of the meaning of the determination.

May that illustrious and peerless Lord Jinendra, the Sun without blemish, be victorious—he by whom the darkness of the delusions of all fallacious reasoning has been uprooted, and the vast, bottomless multitude of false doctrines has been entirely dried up; and by whose incomparable rays of the Syādvāda doctrine the entire world is pervaded on every side. By him the darkness of the delusions of all fallacious reasoning was uprooted, and the vast, bottomless multitude of false doctrines was completely dried up.

May that illustrious Lord Jineśvara, the peerless sun Akalaṅka, be victorious; he who pervades the entire world from all sides with the incomparable and abundant rays of the *syādvāda* doctrine, and who is free from obstruction. 1.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, an ornament to the *Laghīyastraya*, composed by Prabhācandra.
[Page 4300] The third chapter, the examination of the indirect (*parokṣa*), in the *Pramāṇapraveśa*.
Having established perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its true nature, along with its definition, result, and its relation to its own object;

Now, that scripture which was heard is being explained by those whose vision is overcome by the darkness of evil intellects; it is indistinct and devoid of the comprehension of its clear meaning, yet they maintain its authority.
O you of dull intellect, has water not indeed been poured by them for the sake of knowing an object that is remote? (1)
Now, for the sake of certain knowledge that transcends the senses and for the purpose of defining the nature of the imperceptible, he says:
"Knowledge is the first; [it consists of] mati, saṃjñā, cintā, and ābhinibodhika.
By this verse, [the author] aligns with the meaning of the *Tattvārthasūtra* (1.13), which states: "mati, smṛti, saṃjñā, cintā, and abhinibodha are not different in meaning."
Comparison, intellect, memory, and so forth do not occur without the application of words; therefore, it is not an absolute rule that they would otherwise be confounded.

Furthermore, under the assumption of such an absolute rule, they would not occur anywhere at all, because the recollection of their names would be impossible, leading to infinite regress and other such fallacies—Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 100A.

According to the view of teachers such as Anantavīrya, Vidyānanda, and Abhayadeva, because of the application of words [to objects], those [mental states] occurring prior to that time—namely *mati*, *smṛti*, and so forth—are included within *mati-jñāna*; however, those occurring subsequent to that time are included within *śruta*. Thus, their texts state: "Now, since everything beginning with *mati* perceives its own object only by means of a verbal designation (*abhidhāna*), this [perception] is included within *śabda-śruta* alone; and thus, when that [śruta] is reflected upon, reflection on this will also occur. Therefore, reflecting upon it separately here is useless. To this, he replies: "The application of words," and so forth.

The meaning is that there is no such absolute rule (*ekānta*) that mental factors such as intelligence and memory do not exist without the application of words, but rather exist only when such application occurs—by virtue of which [rule] they would necessarily be included therein;
or, taking *yataḥ* as an objection, they would not be confused at all.
He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposite position: "In that absolute case," and so forth.
That [consciousness] is also "exclusive" (*ekānta*); if that were accepted, then cognition, memory, and so forth would never exist, either externally or internally.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of the application of that name," and so on.
That by the application of whose name cognition, memory, and so forth arise is called "that name"; because memory of that [name] is impossible [in such a state].
—Siddhiviniścaya-Ṭīkā, p. 100A.

Now, he examines the work of Akalaṅka, which establishes the nature of *śruta* (scriptural knowledge), preceded by a restatement [of the opponent's view]: "On this point, some declare that *śruta* is established because it is conjoined with words and is preceded by them; otherwise, it would contradict what is desired."

If it is said that "scriptural knowledge" (*śruta*) arises solely from the application of words, then auditory-cognitive knowledge (*śrotra-mati-jñāna*) would not exist; nor would it exist in the cognition of others.
If, however, you maintain that for them scriptural knowledge is conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*), [then...]

Thinking that there should be no sublation of one's own desired [position], they agree [with this]; or rather, it was stated by them here in order to refute the absolute [claim] that "there is no cognition in the world which is devoid of the accompaniment of words."

The first [type of] knowledge is memory (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), reflection (*cintā*), and perceptual-cognition (*abhinibodhika*); the remainder is scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) because it is conjoined with words. Regarding this, Ākalaṅkadeva says: "The first [type of] knowledge is memory. In this regard, the following is investigated: Is there a restrictive determination that everything from the first, *mati*-knowledge, up to *abhinibodhika*, is "only the remainder" because it is conjoined with words? Or is it that "scriptural knowledge alone is [so] because it is conjoined with words"? If the former restriction—that scriptural knowledge alone is so because it is conjoined with words—is intended, then there is no contradiction, as it excludes the possibility of non-scriptural knowledge being conjoined with words.

If the rule were that "śruta" (scriptural knowledge) arises solely from the application of words, then there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine, which holds that śruta is preceded only by auditory cognition and not by visual or other sensory cognitions.

However, if this restriction is made with respect to what is conventionally termed "śruta"—namely, verbal knowledge—then there is no subversion of our desired position, because we accept that even knowledge preceded by visual or other sensory cognitions is ultimately śruta for the sake of understanding one's own system. Or, as it is said: "There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words."

"Everything appears as if permeated by sound, for everything is established in speech"—this statement is intended to refute the extreme [view] that [perception] occurs prior to the application of names; however, one should follow the complete explanation that it is not [the case] that [perception] is mixed with names. (Page 239–40) But this [cognition] follows upon the application of words, just like auditory cognition and sensory perception.

The cognition of existence and non-existence is presumptive knowledge (*arthāpatti*), and likewise inference; for this cognition is proclaimed to be of an unconfused nature. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever for those who enjoy the nectar of *syādvāda*.
Regarding this, the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* (p.

243) states: "And here, that which functions prior to the association with words—such as memory and so forth—and is capable of accomplishing non-contradictory worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is *mati*; however, everything that arises from the association with words is *śruta*. This is the distinction.
The *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā* (p. 553) likewise provides this analysis.
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, Bṛhatṭīkā, folio 84B:
"bādhinī" (ba), "bodhakam" (ba, śra), "bodhanam" (mu, Laghīyastraya).

Prior to the application of names, the remainder [of the text] was heard; following the application of words, it is now being properly refined by Mahendra, who delights in knowledge, having adorned it with traditional lore (*aitihya*) and other means, as the latter portion of the *Nyāyakumudacandra*. 1.

Commentary: Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of the fruit, which is non-contradictory memory (*smṛti*). Memory is the cause of recognition (*saṃjñā*), which is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*); recognition is the cause of reflection (*cintā*), which is reasoning (*tarka*); reflection is the cause of discernment (*abhinibodha*), such as inference and so forth, prior to the application of words. The remainder is scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*), which has many subdivisions.

Cognition (*mati*), which consists of comparison (*tulanā*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*), is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of the fruit, which is non-contradictory memory (*smṛti*). Memory is also [a means of valid cognition] because it generates the fruit, which is recognition (*saṃjñā*) characterized by the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of such [an object]. Recognition is also [a means of valid cognition] because it generates the fruit, which is reflection (*cintā*) characterized by reasoning (*tarka*) regarding such [an object]. Reflection is also [a means of valid cognition] because it generates the fruit, which is determinate cognition (*abhinibodha*) characterized by inference (*anumāna*). And that [inference] is also [a means of valid cognition] because it generates the cognition of rejection (*hāna*) and so forth.
— *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 553; *Ṣaḍdarśana-samuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, p. 84B.

Comparison—some maintain that prior to the application of words this is sensory cognition (*matijñāna*), while the remainder, which arises from the application of words and is indistinct, is scriptural cognition (*śruta*); [as stated in] *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p.
553; *Ṣaḍdarśana-samuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, p. 84B, commentary on the verse.

Regarding what was stated in the first verse—that "the remaining [cognition] is indistinct knowledge" (*aviśada-jñāna*)—what is that? Because of the expression "heard [knowledge] is indistinct conceptualization" (*śrutam avispaṣṭatarkaṇam*), one might ask: is only that indistinct knowledge which arises from the application of names (*nāma-yojanā*) called *śruta*, or is there something else as well? To this he says: that indistinct knowledge which arises prior to the application of a name—that is, before the application of a designation (*abhidhāna*)—is *śruta*. The intention is that this is so because of its similarity to the indistinct knowledge of an object produced by the application of a name.

Regarding the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [it is] thought" (*cintā ca*), this particle is to be understood as occurring after the word "from the application of words" (*śabdānuyojanāt*), because it follows that term. By this, it is included that not only is that indistinct cognition which arises prior to the application of names called "heard" (*śruta*), but also that which arises from the application of words is likewise "heard.
To the question "What is that? he says: "the designation," and so forth.

Regarding the word "ca" (and) in the term *cintā*, it should be understood as having a different scope (*bhinna-prakrama*) and serving to conjoin *smṛti* (memory) immediately after *mati* (sensation);
thus, it is stated that knowledge which is not clear, such as memory and so forth, is *śruta* (scriptural knowledge).
However, sensory-born *mati-jñāna* is called conventional perception (*sāṃvyavahārika-pratyakṣa*), because clarity exists to some degree (*deśataḥ*).

What is the cause of that *śruta*? He says: "The primary cause is knowledge. What indeed is this [knowledge]? He says: "It is *mati*. And there is no contradiction with the scripture, for it is stated in the *Tattvārthasūtra*: "Scripture is preceded by *mati*" (1.20).

Because of this statement, [the author] provides an additional verse by means of the line "If each preceding one were a valid cognition, the subsequent ones would be the result" (*laghī॰ kā॰ 7*) and explains it with the words beginning "non-contradiction" (*avisaṃvāda*), etc.:
that which has no contradiction is "non-contradictory," and that which is such is also "recollection" (*smṛti*); [it refers to] that [recollection].

Of what kind [is it]? Because it is the cause of the fruit, which has become the fruit itself, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is retention (*dhāraṇā*), which is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
[The reading] "knowledge of sound" (*śabdajñāna*) does not exist within this [passage] in the Ā [manuscript]. The Śrā [manuscript] reads as follows.

This has been extracted—Siddhiviṣaraṇa-ṭīkā, fol. 101B. For comparison: "Therefore, that which is preceded by mati should be known as śruta, characterized by indistinct reasoning"—Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p.
237; Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, fol. 504B.
—They also—Ā., Ba., Śr.; —“born from a yojana”—Śr.
(and this is not present in Ā., Śr.).

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Buddhists and others who maintain that memory is invalid (*aprāmāṇya*). The [text] reads *śadajñānaṃ* (Ā), *śra* (Śrā), and *prabhavamati* (Ba). Memory... [is thus addressed].

Now, since memory, when examined both in its own nature and in relation to its object, is found to be untenable, for what could one seek non-contradiction? To explain: is the referent denoted by the word "memory" the knower or the cognition? Of these, the first position is untenable, because no knower whatsoever is possible apart from preceding and succeeding cognitions.

Even in the second alternative, would that which is denoted by the word "that" (tat) be mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), or cognition whose object has been previously experienced? In the first case, since even perception and other means of knowledge would result in being of the nature of memory, the discourse regarding the distinctness of valid means of knowledge such as perception, apart from memory, would be destroyed.
In the second case as well, there would follow the consequence that the perceptual or other cognitions of Yajñadatta regarding an object experienced by Devadatta would be of the nature of memory.

Now, if it is argued that memory is a cognition arising at a later time with respect to that very same object previously experienced in that very same place, that too is a mere assertion; for it would follow that even a continuous stream of perception (*dhārāvāhi-pratyakṣa*) would be memory, since the aforementioned process is equally present there as well. (The commentator Yauga says:
"the expressed meaning"—*vācyārtha*—in manuscript *ba*).

Comparison: Now, what is the referent denoted by the word "recollection" (smṛti)? Is it mere cognition, or is it a specific cognition whose object is a previously experienced thing? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 336. [Note: "The word recollection" — Ā.
Ti.; "recollection" — Ā. Ti.]

Regarding the phrase "in the case of an experienced object" (anubhūte 'rthe)—as noted in the Āloka-ṭīkā—even in the case of continuous perception (*dhārāvāhika-pratyakṣa*), by what is it cognized that [the cognition] arises with respect to an experienced [object]? Is it by means of experience (*anubhava*), by memory (*smṛti*), or by both? It cannot be by means of experience, because at that time, memory is simply impossible.
Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot be made an object of cognition, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Whatever is non-existent cannot be made an object of cognition, just like a donkey’s horn; and since memory is non-existent at the time of the [original] experience, it cannot arise there without being made an object of cognition, and thus it is impossible to maintain [its existence], precisely because of the consequence of over-extension.

The notion that "that which is not made an object by something, in a certain place, through a certain means, does not arise in that thing, in that place, [by that means]" is logical—just as, for example, in the case of a waking person's cognition regarding objects such as blue or pleasure that were not made objects by one who is asleep; and just as memory regarding a past object is not made an object by experience.

This is not so, however, because such a notion arises neither from experience nor from memory; for if both the experience and its object were not made objects [of awareness], it would be impossible to cognize via the thought, "I have arisen with respect to what was experienced."

Furthermore, if the state of having been experienced were accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then memory (*smṛti*) would also know: "I arose with respect to what was experienced," since memory follows upon that experience.
However, that state is not accessible through direct perception, because such perception terminates in the mere fact of being currently experienced;
therefore, it is not cognized by memory either.
Nor can it be by both, because that would entail the defects already assigned to both positions;
therefore, memory does not withstand examination when its nature is investigated.

[Tulanā: Now, by what could it be cognized that [memory] arises regarding what has been experienced? Not by the experience itself, because at that time memory is simply non-existent. (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 336)
By means of direct perception—[Ācārya’s Commentary];
therein—[Bhāva’s Commentary, Śrī’s Commentary];
for comparison: because it would be impossible to have such a cognition if the past experience and the object were not made into objects [of that perception].
—The state of having been experienced through memory (smṛtyā anubhūtatā) — Ā. Ṭī. (Commentary on Pramāṇavārttika, Prameyakhaṇḍa, p. 336).
The cognition "it is arising in what has been experienced" belongs to perception,
[distinguished] from both memory and [ordinary] perception.

Nor [is it] from the perspective of its object (*viṣaya*). For what is the object of that [memory]? Is it the mere object (*arthamātra*), or is it the object as qualified by the state of having been experienced (*anubhūtatā*)? It cannot be the mere object, because that would entail the consequence that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are memory.

Nor can it be [the object] as qualified by the state of having been experienced, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of classifying Yajñadatta’s cognition of an object previously experienced by Devadatta, as well as continuous cognition (*dhārāvāhivijñāna*), as memory.

Furthermore, if this [memory] had as its object an already experienced thing, it would lack validity because its object is no longer present. Whatever has a non-existent object is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the cognition of a mass of hair in the sky; and since memory-cognition is intended to have as its object an already experienced thing, its object is non-existent.
If such a thing were nonetheless considered valid, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition of validity.
Furthermore, regarding memory which has a non-existent object:
it is well known that for those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which brings about the attainment of an object capable of such action;
and since this is not possible in the case of memory because its object is a non-existent thing, how can it be a means of valid cognition?

Comparison: In the world, one who causes a person to obtain an object previously indicated is called "reliable" (*savādaka*); likewise, a cognition is also called "reliable" when it causes the obtaining of the object it has itself indicated.
Furthermore, the capacity to cause one to obtain an object is nothing other than the capacity to induce activity toward that indicated object.
For instance, a cognition does not cause the obtaining of an object by producing the object itself; rather, it causes the obtaining of the object by inducing a person to act toward that object.

Even "inciting" (pravartakatva) consists solely in indicating the object of activity; for consciousness cannot compel a person to act by force. Furthermore, those who seek purposeful action (arthakriyā) search for a cognition that serves as the cause for attaining an object capable of such action;
and precisely that which they seek is what is investigated in this treatise.
Therefore, right knowledge (samyagjñāna) is that which indicates an entity capable of purposeful action.
*Nyāyabinduṭīkā*, pp. 5–6:
The capacity to bring about an object capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsamartha*), preceded by the refutation of that [opposing view], is the establishment of the distinct validity of memory.
To this, the following reply is given:
as for what was stated—that "it is either the knower or the knowledge," and so forth—that is incorrect, because we maintain that only knowledge is denoted by the term "recollection" (smṛti).
Nor does it follow that all knowledge is recollection, since being recollection is not invariably concomitant with knowledge alone.
Indeed, memory is defined as a specific kind of cognition that arises from a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*), possesses the form "that," and has as its object an experienced thing.
Furthermore, it is distinguished from other cognitions by differences in cause, nature, and object.

Among these, the difference in cause consists in the fact that memory has a potent mental impression as its cause, whereas perception and the other types of cognition have the eye and other sense organs as their causes.

There is a difference in their essential nature: because recollection is characterized by the mental projection "that," whereas perception and the other means of knowledge are characterized by projections such as "this.

There is also a difference in their objects: because recollection has as its domain an object previously experienced, whereas perception and the others have as their objects present and other [temporal] things (p. 405, l. 11).
Memory occurs only when there is an object of knowledge [present];
cf. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9: "Memory arises from a particular conjunction with the self and from a mental impression (saṃskāra)."
2.6 Memory is the non-losing of an experienced object.
—Yogasūtra 1.11; Sāṃkhyatattvāloka, p. 16.

Memory (*smṛti*)—which has past objects as its domain and is the cause of subsequent determination (*anu-vyavasāya*), desire, recollection, and aversion regarding things seen, heard, or experienced—arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind that depends upon the desire to see, observation, recollection, and so forth, and from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by intense, repeated, or respectful cognition.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 256).
Memory is a cognition whose object is the connection with that [past experience], occurring when perceptual cognition has ceased.
—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 366, 431.
Memory (*smṛti*) also, like desire, is a cognition similar to a previous cognition or having the object of a previous cognition; it is called memory—*Śābarabhāṣya*, p. 65.
Furthermore, memory (*smṛti*) is said to be a cognition produced solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous cognition—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 42;
*Tantrarahasya*, p. 2.
And *smṛti* (recollection) is defined as knowledge arising solely from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—Śāstradīpikā, p.
153; recollection is *smṛti*—Sarvārthasiddhi, 1.1.4.

That cognition which remembers an object such as form (rūpa) and so forth— delimited by those very same sense-faculties— even though it has perished after some time, is *smṛti-jñāna* (memory-cognition).

It has a past entity as its objective support (*ālambana*), possesses a single agent, and is, in short, a mental cognition (*manojñāna*) whose essential nature is a transformation of consciousness (*caitanya-pariṇati*).

"Recollection is a cognition having the form 'that,' which is based on the arousal of a latent impression"— *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* 1.13; "Recollection is a cognition having the form 'that,' which is caused by the arousal of a latent impression"— *Parīkṣāmukha* 3.109.
3 Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.2
Memory is a cognition having the form "that" (tad) and having as its object an experienced thing; it is characterized by conceptualization (*vitarka*). (Pramāṇapaddhati, p.
69) And memory is characterized by conceptualization.

"Recollection (smaraṇa) is a cognition that arises from the awakening of a mental impression (saṃskāra), has as its object a previously experienced thing, and takes the form 'that' (tad). — *Pramāṇanayatatvāloka* 3.1.28. "In that regard, recollection is a consciousness that is produced by the awakening of a mental impression, which has as its object a thing previously experienced, and which possesses the cognitive form 'that'. — *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 99.
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, Bṛhatī, fol.
84B: Memory is knowledge produced solely by experience.
—Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 8. Compare:

"From the causes of application, connection, repetition, characteristic marks, similarity, possession, the supported and the support, relation, immediate succession, separation, a single effect, opposition, excellence, attainment, intervention, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, fear, seeking, action, passion, merit, and demerit" — Nyāyasūtra 3.1.24.
2.43 This refers to the mention of "this" (idam).

As for what was also stated—that the fact that "there is memory regarding what has been experienced" is not cognized by either the experience, the memory, or both, and so forth—that too is devoid of even the slightest light; for it is possible for that [fact] to be cognized by a cognizer who persists through the three times.

To claim that there is no cognizer distinct from the preceding and succeeding cognitions is also incorrect; for such a distinct [cognizer] has already been established in detail during the refutation of the [theory of] the continuum (*saṃtāna*).

[Objection: "But in this way, when the cognizer experiences the state of being experienced (*anubhūyamānatā*) regarding an object through perception, there would also be an experience of the state of having been experienced (*anubhūtatā*), since there is no difference in the existence of that [cognizer]. And thus, because it grasps what has already been grasped, memory lacks validity. [Reply: This too is incorrect. Because it is tied to a past time, the state of having been experienced cannot possibly exist at the time of being experienced. Furthermore, the mere existence of the cognizer is not a factor for the apprehension of that [state]; for the cognizer, aided by memory, apprehends the state of having been experienced regarding an object, whereas aided by perception, he apprehends the state of being experienced (p. 405, l. 19).
[The existence] of a cognizer distinct from the preceding and succeeding cognitions... [p.
9]—compare: "And there is no experience of the state of being experienced by perception" (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 336).
Even experience occurs within the existence of the subject;
[therefore] the existence of the subject is real.
The apprehension of the experienced nature of the object already grasped.

Thus, although memory may be distinguished from perception and other means of knowledge by differences in its cause, its nature, and its object, one must state the reason for its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). That reason would have to be either: (1) grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*); (2) the absence of a specific determination (*paricchitti-viśeṣābhāva*); (3) functioning toward an unreal past object; (4) not being produced from the object itself (*arthād-anutpadyamānatva*); (5) being non-concordant (*visaṃvādakatva*); (6) not excluding superimposition (*samāropa-avyavacchedakatva*); or (7) not accomplishing any purpose (*prayojanāprasādhakatva*). In the first case, of which already-grasped object is there the grasping by memory? Is it the cognition (*jñāna*), the object of cognition (*jñeya*), the object qualified by the cognition, or the cognition qualified by that [object]? It cannot be the cognition, because in memory there appears an object distinct from that [cognition].

Now, as for the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), let this be granted; nevertheless, memory does not lack validity merely because it apprehends an object already apprehended. For if that were so, there would follow the consequence that even direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) occurring at a later time regarding fire already apprehended by inference would lack validity. Furthermore, there would follow the consequence that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and inference would also lack validity, since it is possible for them to apprehend an object already apprehended in some respect.

Now, even in the case of the apprehension of an object already apprehended, validity (*prāmāṇya*) exists here because it is possible to apprehend a previously unknown aspect of the object. How then can memory (*smṛti*) be invalid? For in that case as well, since there is the apprehension of an object already apprehended under the limitation of the present time by way of its apprehension under the limitation of past time, the apprehension of a previously unknown aspect of the object is established. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Memory is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because even regarding an object already cognized by another means of knowledge, it determines a previously unknown aspect of that object; whatever is of such a nature is a valid means of knowledge, just like perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth with respect to an object already apprehended by inference (*anumāna*); and memory is likewise. Therefore, it is a valid means of knowledge.

Comparison: From what source would one manifest the invalidity of this [cognition]? Is it because it grasps an object already grasped, because there is an absence of a specific determination, because it operates upon an unreal past object, because it does not arise from the object, because it is non-concordant, because it does not exclude superimposition, or because it does not accomplish a purpose? (Syādvādaratnākara, p.
486) Since it is dependent on another, this determination of its validity is not established by itself; however, the alternative of its invalidity is refuted by its very firmness.

Cognition whose object is the object of a previous cognition is called memory; without that previous cognition, its validity cannot be determined—*Tantravārttika* 1.1.4. The term *smṛti* (memory) refers to a cognition whose object is the object of a prior cognition. Without that prior cognition, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of such [memory] cannot be ascertained.
3.1 In that regard, the validity of that prior cognition is accepted.
"Merely by bringing that [object] to presence, memory fulfills its purpose;
since it has already operated upon what was cognized, memory possesses no status as a means of valid cognition. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 396)

"Because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, that which is conventional is not accepted [as a valid cognition]" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.5). "The conventional is not accepted because it apprehends what has already been apprehended" (Ślokavārttika, Śabdanirṇaya,
verse 104).
"That which apprehends what has already been apprehended is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like memory. (*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p.
388) "Memory is not a valid means of cognition because it depends upon a prior apprehension. (*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 388)
For memory, arising as the thought "that," conforms to a prior cognition and does not determine its object independently; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
— *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 42;
*Tantrarahasya*, p. 2.

Nor is memory a means of valid cognition (*pramā*). For the relationship between a word and its meaning is determined by worldly convention, and the world describes as a valid cognition—characterized by non-deviation from the object—a perception distinct from memory, which arises solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
(Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 21)

For this very reason, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because in determining an object by demonstrating that its object was the domain of a previous experience, it is dependent upon that prior experience in the delimitation of the object.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, *Kanda*, p. 257.

This is what is meant: all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth bring about the apprehension of an object not previously apprehended, either in its general form or in its specific mode; memory (*smṛti*), however, does not transcend the limits of a previous experience—it has that same object or a lesser object, but never an object greater than that. —*Yogabhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī* 1.1.4.

Regarding past objects, the authors of the *Jainatarkavārtika* indeed maintain that memory lacks validity because it lacks an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with its object; for the author of the *Vārtika* considers as follows: the validity of a cognition is appropriate only when it is inseparably connected to an object, but not in the case of memory, since it occurs even in the absence of an object.

Since the causes for the non-deviation of perception and the other [means of knowledge] have been stated, there is no fault even if some [instances] deviate; however, there is no cause for the non-deviation of memory at all. Furthermore, because unconfused memory is the fruit of a prior perception, it possesses no separate validity—Jainatarkavārttika-bṛhaṭṭīkā, p. 99.
"From the object [arises] existence; from its absence, [there is] non-existence"— Pramāṇavārttika 2.375.
"How can memory, which arises from experience, possess the form of blue and so forth if it occurs in the absence of the object? (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, Manorathanandin, 2.375).
Or rather, why is it not accepted that memory is produced by the object itself? Because it arises even when the object has perished.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the cognition which has arisen as an experience qualified by a particular place and time should have that very [object] as its objective support;
for at the time of recollection, since that [object] no longer exists, it lacks the status of being an object.
Moreover, because the external sense organs individually fail to produce recollection, the operation of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is determined [to be the cause].

Furthermore, since it is impossible for that [cognition] to operate upon an external object independently, it is logical that it is indeed produced from what is not an object; therefore, it is simply devoid of an object. Thus, the invalidity of memory is not caused by its grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitā*). (Pramaṇaviniścaya-vyākhyā, p. 621)
Moreover, being produced from a non-existent object (*anartha*) is the cause of its invalidity.
But how can memory be produced from a non-existent object? For at the time [of recollection], the object mounted upon it does not exist—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 23.

If it is asked why recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), we reply: because it is erroneous (*bhrāntatva*), like the cognition of a snake in a rope and so forth.
(*Nyāyasāra-ṭīkā*, p. 68). [The portion beginning with *nāsādha* is missing in manuscript *ba*.]

If it is argued that memory lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, then by what [reasoning] would the continuous stream of sensory cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-kṣavijñāna*) not also be [denied that status]?
For even in that case, there is no superior utility (*upayoga*). If [memory] is nonetheless considered [to be a *pramāṇa*], then so too must the others.
In the absence of that [perception], let memory also possess the status of a means of valid cognition for us, just like sensory perception;
for once one has determined one's own object by means of memory and acts upon it, one is not sublated,
and thus the activity of a discerning person is not prevented.
—*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 189;
“of that which is distinguished from the object of knowledge” — Ā. Ṭī.;
[meaning] distinct from cognition.

—Regarding the comparison with the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) that is devoid [of intrinsic nature]: because it would follow that even the perception occurring at a time subsequent to the fire already apprehended by inference would lack validity—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 486; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
—by the power of comprehension, Ā., Śr.;
—and because of the attachment to [the notion of] reality, Ba.;
now, upon the comprehension of the object, Ā., Śr.
Of recognition and inference—the former [is based on] perception and so forth. *ba* (variant). *pratyabhijñānānumānayoḥ*—the former [is based on] perception and so forth.
*ba*. *pratyakṣādi*.

By this, the position that the object of knowledge is qualified by the knowledge is also refuted; for even here, partial validity would still result. Furthermore, what is this so-called "qualification of the object by knowledge"? Is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*)? Among these, the first two positions are untenable: conjunction is impossible because knowledge is not a substance residing in the object, and inherence is also impossible because [knowledge] does not inhere in the object as it does in the self.
In the absence of those two, the state of being a qualifier is also difficult to establish, since it presupposes them.
Indeed, in the case of a staff-bearer and so forth, their existence is not observed to be independent of relations such as conjunction;

however, the position that [the object] is a cognition qualified by the knowable is not tenable, because the manifestation of such [an object] is impossible even in memory or in a dream. For no one accepts that a cognition—whether unqualified or qualified—manifests in memory; rather, it is the external object itself that is perceived as manifesting there for every living being.
Therefore, memory is not invalid because it apprehends what has already been apprehended;
for [memory] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its exclusion from the category of objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). (Āryadeva, *Śataśāstra*)
— Or [it is] the wind or the particular; because of the absence of connection,
[there is] self-inherence.
—In the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth, there is a relation through the *anupala* [non-apprehension] of the cowherd’s wife. *Ba*. (Fragment)
The state of being a qualifier does not exist for that which appears as a cognition qualified by an object of knowledge,
because it [the qualifier] is not present.

Nor is it a mere appearance of memory (*smṛtibhāsa*), because there is no absence of a specific determination (*paricchitti-viśeṣa*); for in the case of things deposited, whispered, or studied, that specific determination exists within memory.
[Tulanā: In the case of things deposited, whispered, or studied, since a specific determination—which is the cause for rejection or acceptance—exists within the memory...

Nor is there a specific determination [of the object], because it functions with respect to a past object that does not exist; for is the non-existence of the past object at its own time, or at the time of the memory? It cannot be at its own time, because it exists at that time.

However, at the time of recollection, the non-existence of that which is grasped by it is not a factor for invalidity, because that would entail the invalidity of perception as well; for there is no difference in the fact that even the object grasped by perception is non-existent at that [time of recollection]. If it is asked, "How can an object belonging to a different time be grasped?", they [the Buddhists] understand "being grasped" [in this sense].

Because this would entail a contradiction with the statement in *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.247: "Those who know the reasoning [of causality] hold that only the state of being a cause is capable of imparting its form [to the cognition]."

Therefore, even perception would lack validity because it does not function when [the object] is absent—is this because the past object was non-existent at its own time, or at the time of recollection? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 487).
In the past time,
there is neither existence nor non-existence of that which is to be grasped by memory. — Śrāvakabhūmi.

If it is asked, "At the time of perception, how can that which is to be grasped by perception be grasped when it exists at a different time?", those who know the reasoning (the experts) understand its state of being grasped as that which is capable of imparting its form to the cognition.
Explanation: Those who know the logic [of the system] understand that the object's status as an object of cognition consists in its capacity to project its own form into the cognition.

If it is asked: "How can an object existing at a different time be apprehended because it arises earlier?"—those who know the principles of logic understand that the very capacity of a cause to impart its own corresponding form to a cognition is what constitutes its status as an apprehended object (*grāhyatā*).
For the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) between cognition and the object is not like that of a pair of tongs and a glowing iron ball;
rather, that which a cognition imitates in its form is said to be the apprehender of that apprehended object.
"—it is logical that it [the object] possesses the very nature of being a cause for cognition" (Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s commentary 2.247;
cited in the following texts). "The very nature of being a cause for cognition... (Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 153).
Vidhiviveka-ṭīkā, p. 198; Sphoṭasiddhi-ṭīkā, p.
233; Hetutvameva ca vyakter jñānākāraḥ, Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, p. 36.
Capable of imparting its form to cognition—*Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, p.
17; *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 20; the present reading: *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 135B.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 487; Prameyaratnākara, 2.7.
Those who know reasoning [hold that] only the state of being a cause is capable of imparting its own form [to the cognition]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.247) ...

Furthermore, the fact of not being produced from an object is no different even in the case of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), because the causality of an object with respect to cognition will be refuted later.
The claim that recollection does not arise from an object is unproven, because it arises from the very object that constitutes its own domain (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
Furthermore, the lack of correspondence in recollection is unproven, because it is non-contradictory with respect to the object as it was apprehended by itself.

Whatever is non-contradictory (avisamvādaka) in a given respect is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) therein, just as perception and other means of knowledge are with respect to their objects. Furthermore, memory is non-contradictory regarding the object it has apprehended; for non-contradiction consists either in the attainment of the apprehended object or in the operation of another means of knowledge. Both of these exist indeed in the case of an object such as a substance that was previously grasped and is now apprehended by memory.

But where there is contradiction, that is a semblance of memory, like a semblance of perception and so forth. [Objection: "Comparison is a valid means of knowledge because it is non-contradictory; it is false because it is the opposite of that, since it apprehends what has already been apprehended. [Response: No, because there is a difference in its purpose.

Even perception possesses validity because of its non-contradiction (*avisavāda*), and not because of its conformity to the object (*arthānukāritā*), for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, if it were to characterize validity as belonging to the recollection of what was previously experienced, [the opponent objects]: "This is incorrect, because in conceptual cognition (*savikalpa*) there is no determination of an unapprehended object. [We reply: No, because of a specific purpose; for in some cases, such distinct forms [of cognition] do not contradict validity in that very way.

Otherwise, since one does not accept that even the apprehension of an object not previously known constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to differences in time and other factors, if the recollection of the probandum— the possessor of the mark— were established from the very beginning through the mark by way of complete pervasion, it would not be a specific type of valid cognition.
–Siddhiviṃśatikā-ṭīkā, folio 146B; Pramāṇasamuccaya, page 99:
"And that [inference] is a means of valid cognition because it is non-discrepant, just like perception" –Pramāṇaparīkṣā, page 69.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
337; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 553;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 487.
*Prameyaratnāvalī*, p.
31; *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 33; *Nyāyadīpikā*, p. 17.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 9:
"Non-contradiction is the establishment of causal efficiency" — Pramāṇavārttika 1.3.
And non-contradiction [consists] in the fact that [cognition] arises from an object and does not deviate from the object—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 273—
and that non-contradiction is characterized solely by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

And non-contradiction consists in the capacity to bring about an object capable of performing the desired causal function, but not in the actual bringing about [of that object], because obstacles and the like are possible— *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*,

When the object has already been apprehended, there is no further engagement with another [cognition]; and its validity is logical, for one who acts after having determined the object by means of that [cognition] is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

The claim that "recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not exclude superimposition (*samāropa*)" is also incorrect; for, since no contrary superimposition can enter into an object already grasped by that [recollection], its exclusion is possible.

That which excludes superimposition (samāropa-vyavacchedaka) is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as inference; and memory regarding an object already apprehended by oneself excludes superimposition. Therefore, because memory and inference are equal in their exclusion of superimposition with respect to their own objects, the status of memory as a means of valid cognition is not precluded in any single instance.
— *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 189; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 338; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 487.

The claim that memory lacks authority because it does not accomplish a purpose is also unsound; for there exists a purpose to be accomplished by it, namely the operation of inference. For inference proceeds from a reason (*hetu*) that is connected with the probandum (*sādhya*), and this connection with the probandum is a factor for its operation merely by its existence—whether it be known or subsumed within memory? In the first case, even a person born on an island of coconuts who has never apprehended the relationship between fire and smoke would attain the cognition of fire upon seeing smoke.

In the second case, however, there would be the undesirable consequence that even one who has previously apprehended the relationship between fire and smoke during childhood, but has subsequently forgotten that relationship upon reaching adulthood, would still cognize fire upon seeing smoke.

As for the third case, how can you deny the validity of memory, given that it is a necessary factor for the operation of inference? Whatever is a factor for the operation of inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just as perception is; and such is memory; therefore, it is a valid means of knowledge.

Thus, since memory is established as distinct from perception and the other means of knowledge due to differences in its cause, nature, and object, and since its non-contradiction with respect to its own object is well-established, it is rightly said: "Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of the result, which is non-contradictory memory.
Likewise, memory is a means of valid cognition because it is the cause of the designation "non-contradiction.

He states a synonym for this: "recognition" (*pratyavamarśa*), such as "this is that very same [thing]" or "this is similar to that. Recognition is the synthesis of objects based on identity or similarity.
— Not unproven—
Ācārya Śrī; for inference is indeed to be established by memory.

Regarding the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between that which is inseparably connected with the probandum (*sādhya*)—is it the cause for the operation of inference by its mere existence, as in the case of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), through the perception of that [relationship], or through the recollection of it? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 338.

And is the invariable concomitance (pratibandha) of the reason with the probandum a factor for the operation of inference by its mere existence, or by being fully cognized, or by being brought within the range of memory? — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
488: "In the operation of inference, it is that which has been made the object of memory."
For the inhabitants of this island sustain their lives by eating only coconut fruit and drinking its water; therefore, fire and smoke have never been seen by them for the purpose of cooking.

As for the analogy regarding the relationship between fire and smoke—who indeed, having accepted inference based on memory, would then reject it? For such a rejection would entail the rejection of inference itself.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
338; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
488; *Prameyaratnāvalī*, p. 32.
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, page 34;
*Syādvādamañjarī*, page 208;
*Ratnākara*, verse 3.
That knowledge which is non-discrepant regarding the object of inference... [or] regarding the object of verbal testimony... [Śrauta].
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the connecting cognition regarding an identical object, such as: "I knew this object previously; I know it now"—*Nyāyabhāṣya* 3.2.1.

Recognition (pratyabhijñāna), indeed, is the third perception—preceded by memory—which occurs upon the cessation of the first perception and the seeing of a second [object], when the latent impression (saṃskāra) previously deposited is manifested.
— Nyāyavārttika, p. 400.

Some maintain that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is a cognition produced by the sense organs assisted by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), which grasps the coreferentiality between what is being remembered and what is being experienced.

Others, however, consider it to be a mental recognition even in the case of pillars and the like; for since it grasps an object qualified by a previously known [state], and because it is impossible for that qualifying object to be grasped by the external senses, it must be mental.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 224)
These two views are accepted by the author of the *Mañjarī*; it should be observed (in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 461):
"Recognition is knowledge directed toward [an object].

For in common worldly usage, when an object has been brought before one through a synthesis such as "This is that very Caitra," the resulting knowledge is designated as "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*).
–*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p.
193: *sañjñāna* means *saṃjñā*. –*Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.13:

What is called "cognition through recognition" (*saṃjñājñāna*) is that which, having previously perceived an object with those very same sense faculties, perceives it again and recognizes it thus: "This is that very same thing which I saw in the forenoon. This is cognition through recognition.
— Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā 1.13:
Recognition (pratyabhijñāna) is a synthesis caused by perception and memory.
"This is that very thing," "this is similar to that," "this is different from that," "this is the counter-correlative of that," and so forth—
*Parīkṣāmukha* 3.5.
*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, page 69;
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* 1.2.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a synthetic cognition (*saṅkalanātmaka*) caused by experience and memory, which has as its object horizontal and vertical universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; *Pramāṇanaya* 3.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 9:
"Recognition lacks validity because of the superimposition of contradictory properties, the absence of a cause, and the absence of an object"—this is the Buddhist prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).

Now, an objection is raised: at the occasion of defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is improper to define recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); for its very nature is impossible due to the superposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and the absence of a cause, and because its validity cannot be established due to the non-existence of its object. To explain: recognition is the knowledge that "this is that very same [thing]" regarding what was previously known at another time. However, unity is not tenable for this [recognition], because of the superposition of contradictory attributes. Where there is a superposition of contradictory attributes, there is no unity, as in the case of water and fire; and such a superposition of contradictory attributes exists in recognition.

Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*); for its presence there is well-known by virtue of its being pervaded by the natures of the "clear" and the "otherwise. To explain: in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the aspect "that" (*saḥ*) is indistinct because it consists of memory, whereas the aspect "this" (*ayam*) is distinct because it consists of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). Furthermore, it is not logical that there be non-difference even when there is the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized as "distinct" and "otherwise"; for if it were, then direct perception and inference would also result in being non-distinct.
The Buddhist replied:

"The cognition 'this is that very same [thing]' which arises is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for identity, because identity is not being apprehended; rather, it is simply the perception of that which was previously seen.
For it is only when identity with the former [moment] is apprehended that identity enters the scope of dispute."

If mere presentness were the single entity, that would be a case of proving what is already established; moreover, because it has been grasped by each preceding cognition, there is no further [presentness] beyond that, and by the preceding cognition, this [object] is grasped precisely in its state of perishing as being "prior."

Furthermore, when it is being synthesized, it must be synthesized exactly as it was grasped or as it truly is; and since this [subsequent cognition] is a grasping of what has already been grasped, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), like any other subsequent recollection. As for its correspondence with reality, that is due to its performance of a causal function (*arthakriyā*).
Nor is there an efficient causal activity to be accomplished by oneness, since [the effect] arises from the mere capacity of the thing itself;
therefore, this is merely a pair of cognitions: "this is that very same [thing].
— *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 51.
By the word "that" (*sa*), an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) connected with a prior time is made the object;
by the word "this" (*ayam*), one connected with the present time is made the object.

And there is no difference whatsoever between these two, nor is there non-difference, because a real entity possesses a single intrinsic nature consisting of both its present state and its future form.

Therefore, since it is precisely difference (*bheda*) that appears when there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), how can this [recognition] subvert the inference of momentariness? Or rather, it has been stated that the object’s connection with a previous time is simply non-existent now, because that previous time no longer exists; or, if it were existent, it would necessarily be connected only with the present time and not with the previous time, due to their mutual contradiction. Consequently, that cognitive aspect which apprehends the non-existent connection with the previous time must be erroneous; otherwise, it would clearly apprehend the object in its various states such as childhood and so forth, yet it does not do so.

Therefore, how could there be sublation by inference from that erroneous cognition which, through the superimposition of a previously perceived form, thinks "this is that very same thing"? However, since you have already conducted an extensive analysis of the refutation of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, it should be understood from that very work—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 78.
For instance, first of all, the recognition arises in the form: "This pot is that very same one."

Is that [recognition] a pair of cognitions consisting of memory in one part and experience in the other; or is it a single cognition that is memory in one part and experience in another; or is it memory alone; or is it experience alone? (Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya, p.
156) — Or rather, this cognition of recognition is indeed erroneous because it lacks a real object.

And the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: that cognition which is a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) does not, in reality, have a single object, just like the case of grass and so forth that has been cut and grown again; and this cognition "this very same blue [object]" is a recognition—this is the perception of a property pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
— *Tarkabhāṣā*, p. 29.
[The reference to] the previous cognition is from the *Śruti*.
— Nor is there recognition;
for in the case of recognition, the superimposition of contradictory properties is well-established.
— “That [is] established,” Āgamānusāriṇī; in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*,
“distinct from the tree,” Śrī.

Furthermore, do these two aspects—“this” and “that”—appear there through mutual interpenetration or without interpenetration? In the first case, only one aspect would appear, because the second aspect would be inseparable in nature from the first; for whatever is inseparable in nature from something else does not appear as distinct from it, just like the very nature of that thing itself. And since the nature of the second aspect is inseparable from the nature of the single aspect, [the same result follows].

In the second case, however, there would be the consequence of two mutually distinct appearances, because the two forms would exist without mutual interpenetration; for whenever two things exist without mutual interpenetration, they have mutually distinct appearances, as in the case of color and taste, and such is the case with these two forms [of "this very same thing"].

Nor should it be asserted that these two appearances share a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*); for it is logically impossible for two appearances—one of a remote form and one of a non-remote form—to have a single substratum. Otherwise, all cognitions would result in having a single substratum, which would establish the non-duality of the self (*puruṣādvaita*).
Therefore, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), this cognition cannot be accepted as a single entity.
Consequently, how could recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) be possible?
In recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),
there is either the aspect "that" (*sa*) or the aspect "this" (*ayam*),
as in the case of [mistaking] a post for a person (*sthāṇu-puruṣa*). (Bhaṭṭa, Śrī)

However, the point is that these two cognitions are distinct: because the cognition in the form "that" (*saḥ*) is of the nature of recollection, while the aspect "this" (*idam*) is of the nature of perception;

furthermore, this is due to the absence of [a single] cause. To explain: its causes would have to be either the sense organ, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous experience, or both. It cannot be the sense organ, because that produces the manifestation of a present object;
nor can it be the latent impression, because that is the cause of recollection.
