Nor is it both, because that would entail the faults of both [positions];
nor is any other cause perceived.
Therefore, the possibility of recognition does not exist.
— Or let it be that [the object] is the gnosis-being (jñānasattva) of the sense-faculty; even so, it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because of the absence of an object.

For its object—must it be the very same entity that appeared in the preceding cognition, or something distinct from it? In the first alternative, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, like a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*). In the second alternative as well, by what is its "distinctness" constituted—is it constituted by a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), by a connection with two different times, or by the perception of identity despite that connection? If it were constituted by a difference in essential nature, then, since a difference in essential nature would be established for the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) at every moment just as for the cognition itself, it would follow that the Buddhist doctrine (*saugata-mata*) applies to recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Furthermore, when the object for which the action was performed has already come into being, it is not logical for this [cognition] to be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) has been lost— just as in the case of forgetfulness and the like.

For that alone which is the most excellent instrument (*prakṛṣṭam upakaraṇam*) in the accomplishment of the act of cognition is called the "most effective factor" (*sādhakatama kāraka*) and is termed the means of valid knowledge.

And if recognition were to have as its object that thing already grasped by a previous means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, since it would not contribute anything further toward the activity directed toward an object for which the act of cognition has already been accomplished, how could it possibly attain the status of a *pramāṇa*? Otherwise, even memory would possess the status of a *pramāṇa*—[as stated in] *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 159, regarding the object.
—[This is] the entry into the [opponent’s] position.

Now, if it is argued that [the identity of the object] is established by its connection with two points in time, that too is incorrect; for such a connection with two points in time is possible even when there is a difference in the object, since it is not the case that the connection with two points in time is unestablished in the instance of a difference in objects such as nails and hair that have been cut and grown back again.

Now, it may be argued that when Devadatta is related to two points in time, his identity is perceived; therefore, because the object appearing in the prior cognition is apprehended as possessing an additional attribute through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), it is not invalid on the grounds of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*). This too is a mere assertion; for what is this so-called "identity"? Is it the number one (*ekatvasaṃkhyā*), or is it persistence (*sthāyitva*)? If it is the number one, then since that has already been understood previously, how can there be a determination of an additional attribute by recognition? If, on the other hand, it is persistence, is that distinct from Devadatta’s own nature or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then like his own nature, that too would have been apprehended by the prior cognition itself.

Whatever is non-different from something else is also perceived when that thing is perceived, just as its own essential nature (svarūpa) is; and the persistence of an object, intended as the referent of recognition, is non-different [from the object itself].

Now, suppose it is distinct [from the previous cognition]. Does that [distinctness] have already arisen previously, or does it arise only at the very moment of recognition? If it has already arisen previously, then since it would have been determined by the previous cognition alone, how could there be a determination of its superiority by means of recognition? Or, if one accepts that its superiority is determined through some specific aspect, then due to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the fundamental reality in question cannot be established.

If, on the other hand, recognition arises at the very moment of its occurrence, then since that [object] was not previously apprehended, how can it be the object of recognition? For it is accepted that the object of recognition is an object previously apprehended which is grasped again at a later time.

Furthermore, if a cognition that makes known a different object not apprehended by a prior cognition were considered recognition, then it would follow that the cognition of a cloth appearing immediately after the cognition of a jar would also be recognition.
At that time, since the production of stability would entail momentariness, how could objects qualified by it be non-momentary? This concerns the connection with both the past and present times.
— regarding the related deity— ba॰
— the designation "it is necessary" (ṇyam) is merely a verbal expression— ba॰— at the very time of direct perception.
The permanence of the intended object is also like the nature of Devadatta— Ā, Śra.
If there were no going of the state of persistence, there would be an infinite regress.
Is that part distinct or non-distinct from the nature of the entity? If it were non-distinct, it would be perceived even earlier, just like the nature of the entity itself.

Regarding the difference [between the two cognitions], does this [recognition] arise prior [to the perception], or does it arise at the very moment of recognition? In such a manner, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) consisting of the repetition of the text; thus, in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the establishment of the determination of excess and the state of having been accomplished—Ā॰.
—[The term] *jñānavi* is found in the manuscripts *ba* and *śra*;
[the term] *tipannānantarāvabodhaka* is found in manuscript *ā*;
[the term] *jñānatve* is found in manuscript *śra*.
The consequence of that:
the consequence of [the cognition] being a recognition at the time of recognition.

The meaning is that because objects qualified by a duration produced at that specific time are indeed non-momentary only insofar as they are qualified by a duration that persists across the three periods of time; thus,
following a refutation of that [opposing view], the independent validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is established separately.

To this, the following response is given: Regarding what was stated—that [the self is not one] because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), and so forth—is there a contradiction between the properties and the substratum, or among the properties themselves? It cannot be with the substratum, because those properties are perceived therein; for whatever is perceived in a thing is not contradictory to it, just as the forms of blue and so on are not contradictory within a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*). And in recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), both aspects—namely, "that very same" and "this"—are perceived; therefore, they are not contradictory therein.

Furthermore, that which is contradictory in a certain locus is never perceived there—just as a horn is not found on the head of a horse. Yet, in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the two aforementioned forms are indeed perceived.
Therefore, it is not logical for there to be a contradiction between the properties (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).

As for mutual contradiction among the properties themselves, what does that have to do with the substratum, such that one would seek a distinction of the latter based on the imposition of contradictory properties? For when a contradiction characterized by the mutual exclusion of properties is possible, it is logical that the distinction belongs only to those properties themselves.
pṛ॰ 411 pa॰ 8 –ghyāsa i– ā॰ dharmiṇi [superimposition on the locus]
–cidupala– Ā., Śra.

Compare: “In that case, even if there is indeed a contradiction between the two forms characterized by perception and recollection, what does it matter to the subject, namely recognition, such that its difference [from them] would be sought on the grounds of the superimposition of contradictory properties? — Syādvādamañjarī, p. 492.
—sparavirodhaḥ (ba); it is requested that there be no mutual contradiction among them (śra). (ba, śra)

Furthermore, regarding the distinction [of recognition]: would the difference of recognition be established by means of its two constituent causes—the forms of seeing and remembering—due to their being superimposed with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), or by means of those that constitute its own nature (*svabhāva*)? In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for the proponents of the doctrine of manifold aspects (*syādvādin*) do not maintain that the very nature of the cause is in every respect the same as the nature of the effect.

Even in the second alternative, would that difference be established in some way (*kathañcit*) or in every respect (*sarvathā*)? If in some way, then it is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we accept that the form (*ākāra*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) are different in some way.
However, difference in every respect is untenable, because it would entail the consequence that those two lack the nature of being related as [form and] its possessor.

Whatever is the nature of something, there can be no absolute difference between it and that which possesses it—just as, for example, the blue form is not absolutely different from the variegated cognition; and the nature of this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is precisely the two forms: "this is that very same [thing]."

For that [recognition], arising from the causal complex of perception and memory, arises as having two embraced forms, just like a single variegated cognition arising from the causal complex of a painted cloth and so forth, or like a single conceptual cognition possessing both non-conceptual and other (conceptual) forms arising from the causal complex of perception and so forth. [Objection: Would the difference of recognition not be established by its two contradictory constituent parts—the forms of seeing and remembering—whether these are taken as its causes or as its own inherent natures? [Response: No, because the difference between cause and effect is accepted. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 493; Āloka-ṭippaṇī).
The distinction of recognition (*pratyabhijñānabheda*): according to the Ācārya’s commentary (*ā॰ ṭi॰*),
recognition consists of the two natures (*svabhāva*) of the aspects of perception and recollection.

— By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the causal complex consisting of conceptual construction, latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), linguistic convention (*śabda-saṃketa*), recollection (*smaraṇa*), and so forth is to be understood,
just like the nature of a single cognition itself. — Āloka-ṭīkā.

Comparison: If the cognition that reflects upon prior and subsequent states were to differ due to the distinction between the attributes of mediacy and immediacy, then—alas!—even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "that" would have to differ;
for that too is both mediate and immediate, both conceptual and non-conceptual:
it is mediate and conceptual with respect to the object, yet non-conceptual and immediate with respect to itself.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the objects are different, [we reply]: "Well then, here too, there is no contradiction; for that very same single cognition is indirect (*parokṣa*) with respect to one object's connection with a prior place and time, and direct (*aparokṣa*) with respect to its connection with another place and time—what contradiction is there? (Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p.

140). For according to the Buddhist doctrine, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) with respect to its own nature, and conceptual (*savikalpaka*) with respect to the nature of the object.

As for what was also said—"Do the two forms appear through mutual interpenetration? and so forth—what is this so-called "interpenetration"? Is it the commingling of their respective natures, or their occurrence in a single substratum? The first alternative is untenable, because it contradicts experience; for the two forms as described are not perceived even in a dream with their natures mutually commingled.
Regarding the second alternative, however, there is nothing undesirable, since those two forms appear in an unimpeded perception within a single cognition known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Whatever appears in an uncontradicted cognition must be accepted exactly as it appears; just as blue is accepted as being blue, so too a single cognition appears in such a cognition as being endowed with two forms.

Furthermore, a collection of false conceptual constructions is not capable of affecting the nature of a thing established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for if it were, it would follow that even the emptiness of all things could be established.

And how can there be the establishment of variegated cognition (*citra-jñāna*) and the like for one who speaks thus? For if the appearances of blue and so forth were to interpenetrate one another, it would follow that all of them possess a single form; how then could there be variegation, as in the case of a cognition having the single form of blue? If they do not interpenetrate, then their absolute difference is established—just like the appearances of blue and so forth belonging to different mental continua—and thus there is an utter lack of variegation. Since they are perceived through direct perception as having a single cognition as their locus, there is no room for the aforementioned faults; this remains the same even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Therefore, it is not logical that there be an absence of recognition due to the imposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa),
as stated on page 412,
line 4— [beginning with] "it appears"— in manuscript *ba*.

Comparison (*tulanā*)—the mutual confusion of essential natures (*parasparasvarūpasāṅkarya*) or the coexistence (*ghṛti*) [of them] in a single substratum—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 493; *paraspara-sva-* [variant reading].
Nothing exists in the form of seeing or remembering,
due to its being of the nature of water.

For the Buddhist who asserts that the two forms consisting of perception and recollection appear either through mutual interpenetration or non-interpenetration by way of their very reality—how, for one who speaks thus, can the establishment of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) be possible? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 342)

Just as the cognition of blue in Devadatta, the cognition of yellow in Yajñadatta, and the cognition of red in Indradatta—though appearing as blue and so forth—are absolutely distinct from one another and do not attain the nature of a single variegated form, so too [is it in this case]. (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 493)

Nor can it be said that the appearances of blue and so forth lack a cause, because their cause— characterized by perception and recollection— is present. If it is asked how these two, which have distinct objects and distinct forms, can have that as their cause, [the answer is] that they conform to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that cause.

Whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something is caused by that; for example, a sprout follows the positive and negative concomitance of a seed and so forth, and thus it has that as its cause. Recognition likewise follows the positive and negative concomitance of perception and memory.

Indeed, there is no basis other than this following of positive and negative concomitance for the seed being the cause of the sprout, or for the variegated cloth and so forth being the cause of the cognition of variegation. Therefore, its non-existence due to the absence of a cause is not logical.
Comparison—Nor [is it] due to the absence of a cause (Syādvādaratnākara, p.

494). As for what was stated—that because of the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and the association with contradictory properties, the unity of the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is untenable—that is incorrect. This is because the conjunction (*samprayoga*) and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) together constitute a single causal complex. Nor is there an impossibility of their being the cause of a single cognition elsewhere, on the grounds that conjunction and impression are causes individually and independently of one another; for elsewhere, the joint operation of the mark (*liṅga*) and the sense organ, though independent of each other, is observed in relation to a specific inference.
Therefore, since the validity of the cognition of recognition is possible through its unity— *Citsukhī*, p.
214— [the text reads] *ṇatatkā-* [in the Ānandāśrama edition].
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the synthesis caused by perception and memory, as stated in the *Parīkṣāmukha* (3.5).
For perception has as its object the present mode (*paryāya*), whereas memory has as its domain past transformations.

For perception delineates this [object's] form, while recollection delineates that [past object's] form—such as that of a variegated cloth and so forth (as stated in the *Bṛhat-ṭīkā* and *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, this recognition is an effect; and an effect, when perceived, makes known the existence of its cause. Therefore, how could the absence of its cause be more tenable? For instance: whatever is an effect is preceded by a cause, such as a jar and the like; and this recognition is an effect.

Regarding what was stated—"Even though recognition exists, it lacks validity," and so forth—that too is an unexamined assertion. For would its lack of validity arise from the absence of an object (*viṣaya*), from the fact that it grasps what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), or from being sublated? It cannot be due to the absence of an object, because its object—namely, a single substance persisting through prior and subsequent modifications—is actually present;
furthermore, since recognition differs in nature from perception and other means of knowledge, a difference in its object must necessarily be admitted.

For whatever has a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*) from another, it also possesses a difference in its object (*viṣaya*) from that other; as, for example, memory differs from direct perception. And it is well-established that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) possesses a difference in its own nature [from perception and memory]. Indeed, because direct perception and memory differ in their own nature—by virtue of being respectively clear and otherwise, and by virtue of having present and past objects as their respective referents—they possess a difference in their objects as delimited by the times of the present and the past. The same applies here as well.

For the object of perception is delimited by the present time, whereas the object of recollection is delimited by the past time; however, the object of recognition is a specific substance delimited by both times. It should not be argued that because all things are momentary (kṣaṇika) at every instant, no specific substance whatsoever is possible, and therefore whose status as its object one could seek; for the existence of substance has already been established in detail previously through the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga). Thus, its invalidity cannot be maintained on the grounds of the absence of an object.
Page 413, line 1:

*asya prāmā–* (Ba). For comparison: "Is its invalidity due to its grasping what has already been grasped, or due to its occurring immediately after recollection, or due to its bearing the form of a word, or due to its being sublated? (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 343).
Of recognition— [in the case of] that which exists within a cavity— [it must necessarily be admitted]...
Śrauta.
In this context, the distinction is that while perception and recollection occur individually, here they occur simultaneously— this is the marginal note (ā-ṭi).
Even in the case of recognition (pratyabhijñāna), [the object] is perceived as momentary— this is the commentary (dra-ba).

For comparison: In the refutation of the theory of forms (ākāravāda), it is argued that through the sense organ assisted by the recollection of impressions produced by prior experience, a cognition arises that refers to both [the past and the present], namely "this is that very same [object]";
and because this cognition conforms to the presence and absence of the object, it is incorrect to claim that it is without an objective referent (nirviṣaya).

"In this [cognition], an object qualified by past time and delimited by present time appears"—Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 397; "In this [cognition], an object qualified by past time and delimited by present time appears"—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 459.

First of all, from this cognition, a single reality delimited by prior and posterior time is perceived; yet it is contrary to experience to claim that even this [reality] is not its object. Furthermore, grasping and recollection do not take a single object as their support. Therefore, on the strength of this perception, one must accept that this very single cognition has both as its objects—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 80.
Nor can it be said that [the cognition] apprehends what has already been apprehended, because its object cannot be apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For how could it be apprehended? By perception (*pratyakṣa*), by recollection (*smaraṇa*), or by another means of valid cognition? It cannot be by perception, because perception operates only within the range of the present moment, and thus lacks the capacity to apprehend a substance (*dravya*) that exists throughout past and present moments.
Nor can it be by recollection, because recollection has as its object only past modes (*paryāya*) and is therefore incapable of apprehending that [substance].

Nor can it be established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because no means of valid cognition other than recognition—which has as its object the substance persisting through both transformations—is possible.
If it is argued that there exists a conceptual cognition produced by the impressions of those two [transformations], we say no, because that very [cognition] is what constitutes recognition.

Comparison—Indeed, there is no single substance that is the object of both recollection and perception such that recognition, operating upon it, might be considered to grasp what has already been grasped. Even though the substance possesses some degree of novelty (*apūrvatva*) because of its identity with the past and present manifestations (*vivarta*) grasped by those [two cognitions], recognition, as having that [substance] as its object, is not invalid; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) that inferential cognition and the like would also be invalid, since even they are not established as being entirely novel in every respect.
(Pramāṇapaddhati, p. 70; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
Syādvādamañjarī, p.
495; Prameyaratnākara, p.
33; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 35.

In the case of grasping a substance that persists through past and present modes (*paryāya*), [the cognition] has as its object the manifestation (*vivarta*)— according to Ācārya and Śrāyaka— and the substance that manifests (*vivartti-dravya*)— according to Śrāyaka— or the manifesting substance (*vivartin-dravya*)— according to Bhaṭṭa.

If it is argued that there exists a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) produced by the recollection of the past and the perception of the present— namely, a comparison— [we reply: no, for we ourselves accept that very [cognition] as being recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
[Śāntarakṣita:

"Indeed, [the opponent argues: if substance (*dravya*) is not the object of both perception and recollection, then how could it be produced therein by those two? For that which is not the object of something does not produce a cognition regarding it, just as the eye [does not produce cognition] regarding taste; and oneness (*ekatva*) is not the object of perception and recollection. This too is incorrect, because there is an inconclusive instance (*anaikāntika*) with respect to non-conceptual direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), which produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for it is observed that even though such [perception] has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its range, it produces a conceptual construction regarding that universal.

The response—that [perception], aided by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), produces that [recognition] even with respect to its own object—applies equally elsewhere as well; for even perception, when aided by memory, is observed to produce recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding unity, since the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) is inconceivable.

Otherwise, how could the cognition of one who is not omniscient, aided by a specific kind of practice (*abhyāsa*), generate the cognition of an omniscient being? Furthermore, the fact that perception has unity as its object has been established in the proof of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*).
Otherwise, this [cognition] would be entirely devoid of an object, since absolute impermanence is never perceived at all;

rather, by means of that [perception], oneness is perceived in the object by virtue of its being the substratum for a specific present modification (*paryāya*). However, the distinction is that through recognition—which arises from perception aided by memory—the object is perceived as the substratum for both remembered and currently experienced modifications.

Therefore, since its object is in some way unprecedented (*apūrva*), it does not possess the character of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), which would otherwise result in its invalidity; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of invalidity for inference and other means of knowledge as well, because it is impossible for them to have an entirely unprecedented object. This is because the specific individual fire characterized by place and so forth—which is the object of that [perceptual] cognition—is established as being in some way not different from the general property (*sādhyasāmānya*) that was the object of the cognition grasping the [original] relation; thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding a substance is valid.
In that regard,
according to the Buddhist (Saugata) doctrine, conceptual cognition arises from non-conceptual perception;

and since non-conceptual perception is produced by the specifically characterized particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which exists in the ultimate sense, it is established as having a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, whereas conceptual cognition, because its domain is the universal (*sāmānya*) constructed by the intellect, has a non-entity as its object.

The point is this: just as non-conceptual perception, even while not cognizing a universal (*sāmānya*), gives rise to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has a universal as its object, so too should perception and memory—though not cognizing the identity (*ekatva*) residing in both past and present transformations—give rise to a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) having that [identity] as its object.
[Comparison: "Because there is an inconclusive reason (*anekānta*) due to perception which produces conceptual construction"—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 495.
—Having performed [the analysis], [one understands that] non-conceptual [cognition] occurs with respect to the universal (sāmānya). (Śra. 1.23ab.

Even in a case where recognition arises from the unity [of an object] through perception and memory, specific instances of repeated practice (*abhyāsaviśeṣa*) and so forth serve as auxiliary causes— Ānandagiri’s Commentary.
But in the case of direct perception (pratyakṣa), [there is] recognition (abhijñāna) — Ā., Śra.
Of the object of inference—
the fire located in a place such as a mountain— [the means is] tarka (reductio ad absurdum).

Because the object of inference—the particular characterized by place and time, which is in some way non-different from the universal such as the probandum (sādhya) that is the object of the cognition grasping the relation through comparison—is indeed the object of that [cognition].
(*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p. 70; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

The claim that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is therefore invalid because it is sublated (*bādhyamānatva*) is also incorrect, since no such sublator is possible. For what could possibly sublate it—either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be perception, because perception does not operate within its domain. Whatever does not operate upon a certain object cannot be a sublator of that [object’s cognition], just as the cognition of taste is not a sublator of the cognition of form. And perception does not operate within the domain of recognition.
Nor is it inference, because that [inference] does not operate upon its object; or, if it were to operate, since it would be consistent with reality, it could not serve as a sublater of it.

If it is argued: "But surely in cases such as nails and hair that have grown back after being cut, that [recognition] is clearly seen to be sublated; therefore, how can it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?"—[we reply: even if it is indeed perceived as such in those specific instances, what follows for other cases? Otherwise, since the perception of the appearance of silver in a fragment of mother-of-pearl is observed to be erroneous, it would follow that this same perception must also be erroneous in the case of real silver. Therefore, the denial of the recognition of identity is not tenable.
Comparison— namely, the certainty that there is no contradiction— is indeed present everywhere in recognition, just as it is directly in perception;
for there is never any direct perceptual sublation of that cognition.

Nor is it correct to say that recognition is not a valid means of knowledge because it has an object distinct from that [of the sublater], like the cognition of another world, on account of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*); for such a sublater is impossible.

For perception cannot be its sublater, because it is impossible for it to function with respect to that object; for sublation is contradictory to [perception's] status as a means of valid cognition, just as [it is contradictory to its] status as a prover—*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p. 70;
*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 280.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 344;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 496;
Prameyaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 36.
And this is incorrect;
[it applies] to the object of recognition (pratyabhijñā), that is, to the object of the act of recognizing.
An examination of inference as well:
"Nor is recognition everywhere devoid of an object, like [the case of] nails and hair that have grown back after being cut" (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 342; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
The recognition of identity, "This very [object] is the nail and so forth," is sublated in cases such as nails and hair that have been cut and grown back again,
where the recognition "This very nail and hair" is contradicted.
The sense is: how can the recognition that "this very same nail or hair is that [same one]" be sublated?
For, since sublation is observed in one instance, if one were to accept that it is sublated everywhere, then even the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the appearance of silver would be sublated.

Nor can it be based on the recognition of similarity, for that would entail the impossibility of inference arising. For it is only for one who previously perceived fire accompanied by smoke that the subsequent production of an inference of fire is logical upon seeing smoke similar to the previous smoke, and not for another person upon seeing something else. Furthermore, without recognition, the cognition "this is similar to that" is not possible, because the former object—such as the smoke—is not apprehended by the latter perception, nor is the latter object apprehended by the former perception.
Furthermore, it is not possible to perceive similarity—which resides in two things—without perceiving those two things, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Whatever resides in two things is perceived only upon the perception of those two, just as a relation [is perceived]. Since similarity resides in two things, it follows that recognition, which manifests both unity and similarity, is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
The word "denial" (*apahnava*) is to be connected with the preceding term "is appropriate.
Regarding comparison—recognition based on similarity—it has been examined by this very [same method]:
it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its correspondence with its own object, and it is not a valid means of knowledge otherwise.
And how could there be the operation of inference if recognition were abolished? For it is by means of that very [recognition]—as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

343—that [inference proceeds], since otherwise the non-arising of inference would follow; for it is by means of that very [recognition] that smoke was previously [seen] in relation to fire—as stated in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 496.
Smoke has been seen by the cognizer as being accompanied by fire.
Because people perceive [objects] such as jars and smoke.
Comparison with the subsequent perception of smoke— [the objection] that "there would be no [comparison] if the two were not apprehended" (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
496)— is not [valid], for it does not exist.
He states this very point: "The designation [is] of the consideration of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it is the cause of the result"—this is the connection.
He states a synonym for this: "of reasoning (tarka).
If it is asked, "What, then, is this so-called reasoning? [the answer is: it is the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti).
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the probandum and the probans;

the cognition that grasps this is designated as *tarka* (reasoning). This is because it alone possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*) therein, whereas other cognitions lack the capacity to grasp it and thus cannot be established as valid in that regard. Furthermore, through the cognition of reflection (*cintājñāna*), the very accomplishment of the future object occurs, and not otherwise. Just as the attainment of supreme bliss occurs only when one is endowed with those three—knowledge and so forth—and not otherwise, such a cognition of reflection is indeed the "mental knowledge" (*manojñāna*).
—Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 78:

"That by means of which one proceeds after having ascertained the relationship between objects through pervasion (vyāpti) is *tarka* (reasoning); because it is consistent with reality, it is understood to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that regard."
"Reasoning (*ūha*) is the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which has as its cause perception and non-perception. (Tattvārthaśloka p. 194; Pramāṇaparīkṣā p. 70)
"This exists only when that exists, but does not exist at all when that is absent"— this is the investigation (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 3.11,
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.2.5

Tarka— also known by the name ūha— is a cognition whose object consists of the relationship between the probandum and the probans as determined across the three times through the occurrence of apprehension and non-apprehension, and which takes such forms as "this occurs only when that exists," and so forth.
(Pramāṇanaya 3.5)
"Knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti) is tarka"—Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 10; "Tarka is knowledge of pervasion"—Nyāyadīpikā, p. 19.

Tarka (reasoning) is the reflection upon the cognition of pervasion—established through positive and negative concomitance and based on perception and memory—which serves as the basis for non-apprehended recognition; it is an inquiry into the true nature of an object whose reality is unknown, for the purpose of attaining knowledge of that reality by means of the logical justification of its causes.
(Laghīyastraya-abhaya-vṛtti, p.
29). Tarka is an instrument for the sake of knowing the truth regarding an object whose essence is not yet understood, proceeding from the application of reasons.
— Nyāyasūtra 1.1.40

When the true nature [of an object] is unknown, yet its locus (*dharmī*) is known in a general sense, the appearance of a possibility—a cognition of "it must be so"—arises from observing a reason favorable to one side. This [cognition], by weakening the opposing side and assisting the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends that [object], facilitates the easy engagement [of the mind] for the sake of the knowledge of reality; this is *tarka* (reasoning).
(*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 586;
*Nyāyakalika*, p. 13)

When one property is accepted, the second is necessarily obtained; this is *tarka*. (Nyāyaliṅga, p. 54). *Tarka* is the mental imposition (*āhāryāropa*) of the pervader upon that which has been determined to be devoid of the pervader, through the mental imposition of the pervaded—for example, from the imposition of "absence of fire," the imposition of "absence of smoke" [follows].
"If it were without fire, it would be without smoke"—
Nyāyasūtravṛtti 1.1.5.
And reasoning (*tarka*) is rooted in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*āpādya*) and the probans (*āpādaka*). — *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, folio 131.
The followers of Jaimini, however, state: "Modification (ūha) is the determination of the application through reasoning,
and it is of three kinds, pertaining to mantras, sāmans, and ritual preparations" (Śābarabhāṣya 9).

1.1– Definition: Tarka (presumptive reasoning) is the cognition of something imperceptible based on a relationship that has not been previously perceived; this is the definition [from Nyāyamañjarī, p. 508].

"The relation intended here [in this context] is pervasion (vyāpti), [which is] the restriction of the property of the mark (liṅga) to that which possesses the mark (liṅgin)" — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p.
300; "The Mīmāṃsakas [hold it to be] of the nature of a restriction" — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Anumāna, v. 4; *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 56.
"In the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 68:

'Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).'—In the *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, page 570: 'Pervasion is the inseparable concomitance of the probans with the probandum by virtue of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*)."
—*Nyāyasāra*, p. 5:
"But that 'association' (*sāhacarya*) is the relation is not convincing to our hearts;
for [the relation] consists in occurring only when that [other thing] exists, and not occurring without it."
This very [relation] is inseparable connection (avinābhāva), necessity (niyama), and concomitance (sahacāritā)—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 121;
Nyāyakalika, p. 2.

Therefore, whatever that relation may be, it is only logical that the one which possesses it as inherent and necessary is the signifier (*gamaka*), while the other related term is the signified (*gamya*)—as stated in the *Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 165.
"Inherent" means being devoid of external conditions (*nirupādhi*).
—Tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 691; Nyāya-līlāvatī, p. 54;
*anaupādhika-sambandha* (unconditional relation), Praśastapāda-bhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī, p. 217.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a relation that is not adventitious (*anaupādhika*), or alternatively, pervasion is the co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such a way that it is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence that co-occurs with the probandum— *Vaiśeṣika-upaskāra* 3.1.15.
1.14 Commentary on the Reality (Tattvavaiśāradī)

The relation free from limiting conditions (*upādhi*)—as stated on page 7 of the *Sarvada*—and the statement of the necessity of the probans (*sādhana*) with respect to the object to be proven (*sādhya*) constitute the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
As it has been said: "Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) there, and the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only there" (*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 3).
Thus— according to the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā*, p. 64—
this pervasion (*vyāpti*) is twofold, by way of being the property of the pervader (*vyāpaka-dharma*) and the property of the pervaded (*vyāpya-dharma*).

In this context, pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) when the pervaded (*vyāpya*) exists, and the existence of the pervaded only when the pervader exists. By these two, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are respectively expressed;
for the rule that the pervader must exist when the pervaded exists is the nature of positive concomitance.
And because the absence of the pervaded [the effect] in the absence of the pervader [the cause] is of the nature of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—
*Pramāṇavārttika*, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 3.1.
Of that which exists as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is understood through the relationship of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
When it is intended to be expressed as the property of the pervader, then the connection is: "the very existence of the pervader, which is the object to be known.

Here, the locative case in the word *tatra* primarily signifies the sense of "in relation to" rather than the sense of a physical substratum, because one property cannot be a separate entity from another property.

Therefore, this is the meaning: wherever the pervaded (vyāpya) exists in a given subject (dharmin), there the pervader (vyāpaka) must necessarily exist; thus, pervasion is the property of the pervader.

However, it is not restricted in such a way that "only the pervader exists there," for that would entail the consequence that the logical reason (hetu) could never exist [as a pervaded property]. This is because non-pervading properties, such as corporeality (mūrtatva) and the like, also exist there.

Nor is it restricted to mean "it exists only there," for that would result in properties such as being produced immediately after an effort (prayatnānantarīyakatva) failing to function as a valid reason.
Furthermore, [the reason] would be a "common" (sādhāraṇa) reason, because it exists only among those things that are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), which are [in fact] eternal.

However, when the intended meaning of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that the property to be pervaded (*vyāpyadharma*) [is present] only where the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is, then the presence of the pervaded occurs only in that locus (*dharmin*) where the pervader exists, and not elsewhere.

Even in this case, the restriction that "the pervaded exists only there" is not accepted because it would entail the non-existence of the reason; for even that which is not pervaded might exist there.

Nor is it determined that the pervaded (vyāpya) must necessarily exist there [in the subject], for if that were so, a reason that exists in only a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣa) would fail to be a valid reason, and furthermore, the common property (sādhāraṇa), such as "knowability" (prameyatva), would become a valid reason because it necessarily exists in eternal things.

By the statement "the pervader (vyāpaka) exists there," the positive concomitance (anvaya) is implied; and by the statement "or the pervaded exists only there," the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is implied. — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 3.129.3–5.
1. *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 180;
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 38;
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.2
In the apprehension of pervasion, tarka alone [is effective], not perception and the other means of knowledge.
The Cārvāka’s prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is no validity for *tarka* because, in the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the very nature of pervasion itself is impossible.

But surely, since the very nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, how can *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding it? To explain: pervasion is a relation between things, and would that [relation] exist between some thing and another either spatially or temporally? It cannot be spatially, because smoke is in the sky, fire is on the ground, rain is in the upper region, and the swelling of a river is in the lower region. Nor can it be temporal, for at the time of rain there is no swelling of the river, nor at the time of the rising of the constellation Kṛttikā is there the rising of Rohiṇī. Thus, the nature [of pervasion] is impossible. (Śrāvaṇa 1)

Regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*): is it to be defined as spatial, such that "wherever there is the probans, there is the probandum"; or as temporal, such that "whenever there is the probans, then there is the probandum"; or does it possess the nature of both simultaneously?—[as discussed in] the *Hetubindu*, folio 4B, concerning the probans or the probandum.

Regarding comparison by way of the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*): if one accepts mere spatial pervasion (*deśavyāpti*), then how can the conceited person avoid being led onto a wrong path even regarding the inference of smoke, which is universally esteemed as valid among all waking authorities? For in that case, there is no possibility of perceiving spatial pervasion even in a dream; for instance, where is the spatial pervasion when smoke hangs from the surface of the sky while the fire is on the low slopes of a mountain?
—In the inference [stated in] *Hetubindu*, page 4B: "The cloud has rained above, because a flood of the river is seen below."

Consider the following instances of inference: "The moon has risen in the sky because the reflection of the rising moon is seen in the water"; "There was rain in this region previously because such a flood of water is observed later on"; "There will be a downpour of water because such clouds are appearing"; "Rohiṇī will rise because Kṛttikā has risen"; "The sun will rise tomorrow because the sun is seen rising today"; "Pūrvāphālgunī rose three hours ago because Uttaraphālgunī is now observed to be rising. In all these cases, there are numerous types of causes—such as the effect, the cause, the antecedent, and the subsequent—which are spatially, temporally, or both spatially and temporally remote from the object of inference. Since no pervasion (*vyāpti*) can be established between these causes and their respective objects in terms of space, time, or both, they would consequently result in being non-causes (*ahetu*).

Furthermore, of what is this invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) with what—is it of the universal (sāmānya) with the universal, or of the universal with particulars (viśeṣa), or of particulars with particulars? In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), because the universals "fire-ness" (agnitva) and "smoke-ness" (dhūmatva) are well-established as being connected to all places and times due to their eternity and omnipresence.

Even in the second case, is the invariable concomitance of the universal with the mere particular unconditioned by place and time, or with that which is so conditioned? If it is with the unconditioned, then there is simply the proving of what is already established.
Now, if [the relation] is restricted by place and time, then there is a lack of universal concomitance (*anugama*);
for there is no concomitance between the smoke-universal located in the kitchen and the specific fire located on the mountain, nor between the fire on the mountain and that in the kitchen.

Furthermore, there can be no restriction of particulars by particulars; for such a restriction would have to be either (1) of perceived [particulars] with perceived [ones], (2) of unperceived [particulars] with unperceived [ones], or (3) of perceived [particulars] with unperceived [ones]. If it were (1) of perceived [particulars] with perceived [ones], then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), and inference would be impossible upon the perception of a previously unknown individual instance.

Now, [the relation] cannot be between unperceived things and unperceived things; for even in that case, how could there be inference, given the absence of a grasp of the connection and the absence of any concomitance? Nor can it be between perceived things and unperceived things, because that would entail the same faults mentioned previously.

Furthermore, from this perspective as well, the apprehension of the relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is untenable: is the determination of the connection between two universals (*sāmānya*), or between two particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*), or between a universal and a particular? (Tattvopaplava, pp. 65, 83)

For instance, there are five possible positions regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*): does it occur between two individual instances of the probans and the probandum; or between the universals (*jāti*) of "being a probans" and "being a probandum"; or between the possessors of the probans and the possessor of the probandum; or between the possessors of the universal "being a probans" and the universal "being a probandum"; or between the states of possessing a probans and possessing a probandum? (Hetubindu, p.

4A). To explain: do you maintain that pervasion exists between two individuals, or between two universals, or between the two specific possessors of those, or between the states of possessing the probandum and the probans?

It [the relation] does not exist between two individuals because of their infinity; nor between two universals because that is impossible; nor between the possessors of those [universals] due to the aforementioned defects; and there is no fourth [option] because it cannot be defined. — *Citsukhī*, p. 233.
Furthermore, there is no [distinction] between particulars by means of particulars;
for in the view that [substance] is eternal and all-pervading, there is no spatial [limitation].

If there were a comparison based merely on the specific nature of fire and so forth, without regard for locations such as mountains or kitchens, or for times such as the past or present—then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because fire and other specific entities unconditioned by space and time are already well-known. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 505)
Comparison—Furthermore, having provisionally accepted inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states that in reality it is not a valid cognition:

"In the case of a particular (*viśeṣa*), there is a lack of concomitance (*anugama*); in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Because it is thus vitiated by such defects, for us, there is no inferential cognition (*anumiti*) that is a valid cognition.

Is the pervasion (vyāpti) between two individuals, or between two universals, or between two particulars pervaded by those [universals], or between "smokiness" and "fire-possessiveness"? It is not the first, because a universalization over all instances is unestablished. It is not the second, because of the difference in their own-natures and the difference in their substrata.
It is not the third, due to the aforementioned fault.

Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because no property based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-dharma*) that is distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) can be established—*Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya-vārttika*, p. 1401; *Nyāyakumudacandra*, p.
69, note 5.

Even if an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between two things established by perception were established, there would be no result whatsoever, because both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) would be perceptible; and thus, the implication is that inference would lack validity. Furthermore, since there is no apprehension of invariable concomitance regarding a previously unperceived individual (*apūrvavyakti*), inference does not operate.

Furthermore, it does not exist [as a universal], because it is impossible to grasp an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) with that which is imperceptible; even if such grasping were possible, there would be a lack of positive concomitance (*anugama*).

Moreover, inseparable relation is a connection, and a connection is preceded by the perception of its two relata; since the relata are two distinct particulars (*viśeṣa*), how then can pervasion (*vyāpti*) be grasped by means of a synthesis of all instances?

Furthermore, the relation would only be grasped between those two related entities—the smoke and fire of a kitchen—that are objects of direct perception, and not between all individual instances of the probandum and the probans.

Moreover, this term "inseparable connection" (avinābhāva) expresses the absence of the probans when there is an absence of the probandum; thus, it denotes only the negative concomitance (vyatireka), not the [positive] relation.
Furthermore, in the statement "smoke is not possible in the absence of fire," the absence of fire is a qualification of the non-occurrence of smoke.
That [pervasion] must be either ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real.

If it were ultimately real, then because smoke is non-existent [in the ultimate sense], the pervasion dependent upon it could not be apprehended; for it is impossible to apprehend that which depends on a substratum when the substratum itself is not apprehended, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If, however, it were not ultimately real, then since the smoke conditioned by that [pervasion] would be untenable, the pervasion itself—being conditioned by it—would also be not ultimately real; and thus, it follows that inference (*anumāna*) itself would likewise be not ultimately real.

Now, if it is argued that the existence of smoke would be impossible if there were an absence of fire, because the absence of fire is pervaded by the absence of smoke—that too is untenable. A pervasion (*vyāpti*) that is both existing and apprehended is a constituent of inference, not one that is merely contingently possible, because such a [contingent] pervasion is not ascertained even in its existence; this is merely a cognition of possibility (*saṃbhāvanājñāna*), and it does not determine the reality of the object. For example: "If the earth did not exist, mountains would not fall"—the remainder of the phrase being "of the absence of fire" (as noted in the Ācārya’s commentary).
Residing in smoke,
it is perceived in its own locus,
which is characterized by smoke.
The nature of pervasion (vyāpti) is the limiting adjunct (upādhi), [namely] the qualification consisting in the absence of fire (agnyabhāva). Śra., Ba.
Because it is beneficial, [the word] *dhū* [is used].
This reading is not included within this [text] in the Ā. manuscript; [it refers to] that which is qualified by the absence of fire (*agnyabhāva*).
— there would be [the fault of] non-reality (anarthikatva) because of the [opponent's] position;
this is what is being considered.
Even the existence of the pervasion that is being considered remains uncertain.

Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned cognition—"If there were an absence of fire, the presence of smoke would be impossible"—is it the case that smoke is not possible in the absence of some particular fire, or in the absence of all fires? It cannot be the former, because even in the absence of that [particular] fire, the presence of smoke is possible in the case of another fire.

Nor can it be "of all" [fire], because the apprehension of a universal (uṣahita) is impossible without the apprehension of its limiting adjunct (upādhi), and because smoke would otherwise be unaccounted for. The limiting adjunct here is simply the absence of *all* fire; however, this cannot be apprehended as long as not all fires have been apprehended, since the apprehension of an absence depends upon the apprehension of its counter-positive (pratiyogin) and its locus (āśraya).

The point is that even if there were the absence of some single fire, the apprehension of a qualified entity in the form "the absence of smoke is qualified by the absence of all fire" would be impossible.

[Commentary on the term *viśiṣṭa*: According to Ācārya-ṭīkā, that whose absence is being established by means of a qualifier consisting of the non-existence of all fire is the *pratiyogin* (counter-positive); for example, when the non-existence of all fire is to be established, "all fire" is the *pratiyogin*. That in which the absence is established is the *āśraya* (locus); for example, when the non-existence of all fire throughout the three times and the three worlds is under discussion, the "three times" and the "three worlds" are the *āśraya*.

For it is stated [in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Abhāva section, verse 27]: "Having apprehended the existence of the locus and having remembered the counter-positive, a mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the senses.

Furthermore, in some cases, even in the absence of the non-existence of fire, the presence of smoke is seen to be contradictory to the absence of smoke; therefore, the non-existence of fire is not the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the contradiction with the presence of smoke, but rather the absence of smoke itself.

Therefore, when examined, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not tenable; how then can there be validity for the reasoning (*tarka*) that apprehends it, or for the inference (*anumāna*) produced from it? Or, let us grant that pervasion exists; nevertheless, even though invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is present, the redness of fire is not inferred from smoke, because it is fire itself that is inferred by means of smoke.
Likewise, although there is no difference in their being equally restricted [to fire], smoke alone is the indicator (*gamaka*), and not its properties such as blackness and so forth.

Comparison: Furthermore, when the cessation of one thing occurs only upon the presence of another, there is a contradiction between them by virtue of that [presence]. In this case, since the cessation of smoke is observed only when there is an absence of smoke, its contradiction is with the absence of smoke alone, and not with the absence of fire;
for even in a state such as glowing embers where fire is absent, the cessation of smoke is perceived despite the non-existence of the absence of fire. — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 505.

In a place containing fire in the state of glowing embers (*aṅgārāvasthā*) where there is no smoke—even though the absence of fire is absent (that is, fire is present)—there is still the presence of smoke.

For if the absence of fire were the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the absence of smoke, then according to the logical principle that "in the absence of the condition, the conditioned entity must also be absent," the absence of fire would not exist in that place containing fire in the state of embers; consequently, the absence of smoke would also have to be absent there. Yet, the absence of smoke does not exist there, as it is actually characterized by the presence of smoke.
Therefore, the absence of fire is not a qualifier of the absence of smoke; rather, it is simply the cessation of smoke,
even though it has been brought forth by the force of the pervasion grasped through *tarka* from the smoke.

Even though the connection is the same in that manner of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), the establishment of the separate validity of *tarka* (presumptive reasoning) following its refutation [of other means of knowledge] is addressed here: to this, the following rebuttal is offered.

As for what was stated—beginning with "of the nature of pervasion" (*vyāptisvarūpasya*) and so forth—that is incorrect; because pervasion is asserted to be non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) as necessitated by the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of the terms], how could that [nature] be impossible? For the nature consists of fire-ness (*agnitva*) and smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*), which are endowed with their own respective sets of attributes belonging to the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). Indeed, having distinguished these from other [factors] such as place, time, and form, it establishes a connection within itself with excellence.

"Understand the pervasion as depending solely upon me; understand, understand"—by thus establishing the pervasion as being related specifically to himself, he makes the cognizer understand a pervasion that is his own formulation (pṛ.
420, l. 1). Compare:
Because it is asserted that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) inherent in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the probans]—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 506;
*Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 10.

As for what was also stated—that "invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is not possible either spatially or temporally"—that too is refuted by this very [argument]; for the invariable concomitance of that which possesses [the property] with that which possesses it is established as a manifestation grounded in uncontradicted cognition.

Indeed, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is characterized by non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*), and yet spatial and temporal [locations] do not possess such non-deviation; because smoke and the like are perceived even in the absence of the specific space and time intended [as the locus].
[Page 420,
Line 2] By means of smoke and so forth, which possess universals and particulars (sāmānyaviśeṣavat) — [Ācārya’s Commentary];
by means of fire and so forth, which possess universals and particulars — [Ācārya’s Commentary].
Comparison— For smoke is apprehended in a general sense as "wherever [there is fire]," and it is not intended in such a way that it is restricted to "on a mountain," "in a forest," or "in a house"—
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 111.

For, having transcended place and time, the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of smoke and the like with fire and the like is established upon an unimpeded cognition by virtue of their own essential nature alone—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 506—for those who move [within this system]. *Śrāvakabhūmi*.

Comparison—whatever is determined in a certain way, by a certain means, and of a certain kind, that [means] indicates that very thing, in that same way, as being of that same kind, in another instance. (Nyāyamukha, p. 57)
The passage contained within this [text] does not exist in Ā [manuscript].

Furthermore, as for what was stated—“Whose pervasion (vyāpti) is there by what?”—in that regard, whatever has an invariable concomitance (avyabhicāra) with whatever, it has pervasion by that. And since smoke and the like, which possess both general and particular characteristics, have an invariable concomitance with fire and the like, which likewise possess general and particular characteristics, it is by those very [characteristics] that they have pervasion. Consequently, there is no room for the aforementioned fault;
for the pervader (vyāpaka) is that which is to be understood (gamya), while the pervaded (vyāpya) is that which makes [the pervader] known (gamaka).

Furthermore, the universal and the particular are not experienced in isolation as the forms of the signifier and the signified, because it is only a distinct entity (*jātyantara*) consisting of both natures that appears in that form (p.
420, l. 6). Compare: "The pervaded is held to be the signifier, and the pervader is the signified."
Whatever [entity] may be equal to or even inferior to another in terms of place and time, that is the pervaded (*vyāpya*); the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is either equal to or superior to it.
Therefore, when the object that is the pervaded is apprehended, its pervader is also apprehended.
For otherwise, this relationship of pervaded and pervader between those two would not exist;
[this applies] only to a different genus. *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Anumāna-pariccheda, verses 4–6. *Bādarāyaṇa*.

In every respect, that which was stated— namely, that the relationship is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and that such a relationship is preceded by the apprehension of the related terms, and so forth— refers to that which is of a dual nature in some way, consisting of a genus (*jāti*) distinct from both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). This [objection] is also refuted by this very [point], because pervasion (*vyāpti*) between a particular characterized by a universal is possible only through a universalization of all instances.

For in that case, defects such as infinite regress find no footing, because [the relation] pertains to the individual instances of smoke and fire as qualified by the universals *dhūmatva* and *agnitva*. (Page 421, Line 6)

Comparison—Since it is accepted that there is an apprehension of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) between the possessors of the universals (*sāmānyavat*), although specific fires and specific smokes exist in infinite variety, nevertheless, the universals of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) and "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*) residing within them act as the subsumers (*upagrāhaka*). By virtue of these subsumers, and through the force of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the apprehension of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between fire and smoke is established, even when there is deviation regarding place and other factors. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 570; Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 210)

In whatever manner smoke arises, whether at another time or in another place, it arises only from fire and never from what is not fire; this kind of comparison—pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases—is [defined] in the *Tarkabhāṣā* (Mo. p.
19) as being free from non-concomitance, spatial deviation, and so forth.

As for what is said—that the term *avinābhāva* (inseparable relation) denotes mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and not a general relationship—that too is a mere assertion; because the term *avinābhāva* does not terminate in mere negative concomitance, as that would entail its application even in the absence of a jar or similar objects. Rather, it refers to a necessary rule (*niyama*), and that rule is established through two modes: "possibility otherwise" (*tathopapatti*) and "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). Therefore, both of these are expressed by the term *avinābhāva*: "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," and "where fire is absent, there smoke is also absent."

If it is asked, "How is it known that where there is no fire, there is also no smoke? [the answer is: because smoke is invariably not perceived in the absence of fire, it is necessarily concomitant with its existence; otherwise, just as fire might be observed in some cases even in the absence of smoke, so too smoke might be observed in some cases in the absence of fire.

That which does not have an impossibility of occurrence in the absence of another is not necessarily concomitant with it; for example, fire, which can occur even in the absence of smoke, is not necessarily concomitant with smoke. However, since smoke has an impossibility of occurrence in the absence of fire, it is therefore necessarily concomitant with it.
(Page 421, Line 8, regarding the general category of non-existence)
Comparison: "The restriction (niyama) is indeed the inseparable relation (avinābhāva), because [the reason] does not occur without the probandum"—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p.
70. Comparison: "The formulation of the reason may be by way of its occurrence in that manner, or otherwise."
The establishment of the probandum may occur through either of the two [types of reason]—
*Nyāyāvatāra* 17;
*Parīkṣāmukha* 3.
95 Pramāṇanaya° 3.28
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 2.1.4
If the existence of smoke were not necessarily concomitant with the existence of fire, or if fire were not necessarily concomitant with the existence of smoke,
as in the case of a heated iron ball and the like.

As for what was also stated—that if the absence of fire were ultimate (pāramārthika), then because smoke would be non-existent [therein], the pervasion (vyāpti) residing therein could not be apprehended—that too is incorrect; for, in whatever place or time there is a real absence of fire, it is only there that smoke is non-existent, not everywhere. How, then, could the pervasion residing therein be impossible to realize? (Page 421, Line 11, regarding large lakes and so forth).

As for what was said—that smoke is untenable either in the absence of a single fire or in the absence of all fires—that too is incorrect. For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is understood by including all cases: "whatever smoke there may be, all of it is untenable in the absence of fire. It is not, however, by specifying each individual locus (*dharmin*)—such as "smoke on a mountain, in a house, or in a forest is untenable in the absence of fire"—that it is so understood.
Otherwise, even in an infinite amount of time, the comprehension of pervasion would never occur, because the loci (*dharmiṇaḥ*) are infinite.

Furthermore, it would follow that inference is redundant, because at the very time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), all subjects (*dharmin*) possessing fire and smoke have already been grasped—just as in the case of fire and smoke [as previously discussed].

On page 421, line 19, compare: "In that regard, we say 'of all' (*sarvasya*); for the non-occurrence of smoke is perceived by implication of everything—that whatever smoke there may be, all of it is impossible in the absence of all fire" (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 506).
—*Gharmolle*— [The word] *ba* [is used].

When the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is cognized through the indication of a specific individual locus (*pratiniyatadharmin*), infinity (*ānantya*) is a subverting factor; he states this with the words "tathā" (so).

Nor should it be argued that because smoke is impossible where no fires have been apprehended, its absence—which serves as a qualifier—is impossible to apprehend; for that absence has the nature of other places and so forth, since absence has the nature of another entity (*bhāvāntara*), as an absence whose nature is a mere nothing (*tuccha*) will be refuted later.
And that location and so forth, devoid of all fire, is perceived through direct perception itself.

For it is only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that depends upon the apprehension of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), not the cognition of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*). Otherwise, how could even a jar or similar object be cognized? For its own nature, too, being distinct from the three worlds, would entail the consequence of non-cognition whenever the three worlds are not cognized. [This refers to] the absence of fire—Ānandajñāna’s Commentary.

It is possible to apprehend [it]—in the absence of fire (agnyabhāva)—because non-existence has the nature of another entity, namely, the nature of that which is other than the place where fire exists and so forth. (Compare: since non-existence of fire has the nature of another entity, such as a place other than that [where fire is present]).
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 507.

Therefore, that which has the nature of apprehending something other than the intended object—such as fire—is [the cognition of] a mountain and so forth, like a great lake and so forth. —Āloka-ṭippaṇī.

If even the cognition of the essential nature of the conventional usage— such as "there is an absence of a jar here" or "there is an absence of fire here"— were dependent upon the apprehension of the counter-positive, then...

As for what was also stated—that even in the case of the nature of a jar, a contradiction is observed in that the presence of smoke sometimes occurs despite the absence of fire—this too is a mere assertion; for since the presence of smoke necessarily ceases when there is an absence of fire, it is logical that the absence of fire, just like its own absence, serves as the cause for that contradiction.

Whatever necessarily ceases when something else is present has that as its cause of opposition, just as cold touch [ceases] when hot touch exists. And since the presence of smoke necessarily ceases in the absence of fire, therefore this [absence of fire] is the cause of the opposition to smoke.

[Objection]: But surely, the fact that smoke necessarily ceases in the absence of fire is unestablished, because in cases such as the "cowherd’s pot" (a smoky chimney), smoke is perceived even in the absence of fire. [Reply]: This is not so; for even in those cases, the presence of smoke is possible only when there is indeed the presence of fire.

For the existence of smoke is its acquisition of selfhood (*ātmalābha*), and that occurs only when fire is present; so how could there even be a suspicion of the presence of smoke there in the absence of fire? If that were so, then smoke would indicate fire even in a cowherd’s water-pot as it does on a mountain and the like; but this too is incorrect, because this [smoke] differs from the smoke on a mountain and such.

For the smoke on a mountain and the like is experienced as having an existence simultaneous with the fire, possessing a nature that appears like a thick banner; but this [smoke] is not like that, and therefore it lacks the capacity to infer fire.
(Page 422, Line 2)
Just as the absence of smoke follows from the contradiction of smoke with that which has a nature opposed to it— namely, the absence of fire—
so too does the absence of fire follow from the contradiction of fire with smoke.

—The comparison for this very point is as follows: "Therefore, that in whose presence something invariably ceases must be contradictory to it; and since smoke invariably ceases when fire is absent, it is contradictory to that [fire] just as it is to the absence of smoke. For instance, that in whose presence something invariably ceases... (*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 507).
In the absence of fire—in such things as a magic pot or a Gopāla-jar—[the inference fails]. (Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā, p. 571).
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 507:
"Because smoke is perceived even in the absence of fire"— in the absence [of fire], its [smoke's] existence— *śra*, *ba*.
The existence of fire alone [is the cause] of smoke in cases such as a jar produced by sorcery.
Regarding "of smoke indeed"— according to the Śrīkrama,
this refers to the comparison with the smoke produced from cow-dung cakes; for this [smoke] differs from the smoke of mountains and the like.
For smoke on a mountain and the like is experienced as having an existence simultaneous with that of fire, its very nature being manifest like a thick banner—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 507.

As for what was also stated—that even when invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) exists, yellowness (*paiṅgalya*) is not inferred from smoke, and so forth—that too is inconsistent; because inference is performed in accordance with pervasion (*vyāpti*), and pervasion is determined solely by way of the properties of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) and "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*), and not by way of properties such as yellowness, since those are infinite in number and subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

For yellowness (*paiṅgalya*) is observed to deviate [from fire] in yellow orpiment, gold, and so forth; luminosity (*bhāsuratva*) in the sun, stars, lightning, and so forth; substantiality (*dravyatva*) in all nine substances; and upward motion (*ūrdhvagatitva*) in whirlwinds and so forth. Thus, there is a deviation among the properties residing in fire, and likewise among those residing in smoke. For instance: blackness (*śyāmatva*) is seen in blue collyrium and so forth; pungency (*kaṭukatva*) in the "three pungents" (*trikaṭuka*) and so forth; causing irritation to the eyes (*akṣivikārakāritva*) in mustard oil and so forth; sticking to the throat (*kaṇṭhagrāhitva*) in unripe rose-apple fruit and so forth; and upward motion (*ūrdhvagatitva*) is observed as common to steam and so forth.

Therefore, that single form by which the individual instances of fire, the individual instances of smoke, and their properties existing within the belly of the three worlds are subsumed—that very form establishes pervasion (vyāpti) as a rule; and that [form] cannot be anything other than fire-ness (agnitva) and smoke-ness (dhūmatva), for fire-ness and smoke-ness are certainly not like yellowness and other qualities that are common to other distinct entities.

And when the word expressing that [object] is uttered, the hearer grasps the object—fire in the case of smoke—as being distinct from the three worlds and endowed with its own collection of properties; thus, it is established that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans occurs by means of that [word]. (p.
422, l. 5) For comparison: "Since inference is performed according to pervasion, and pervasion is determined precisely by way of fire-ness and smoke-ness" (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 507).
In the vernacular, *vātyā*, *vātūla*, *vavaṇḍara*, and *ādhī* refer to the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), collyrium (*añjana*), and so forth.

The combination of the three pungents—ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), black pepper (*marīca*), and long pepper (*pippalī*)—is called *trikaṭuka*; the triad of ginger (*viśva*), long pepper (*upakulyā*), and black pepper (*marica*) is also designated as *trikaṭu*.
The three pungents (kaṭutraya), however, are called trikaṭu, vyūṣaṇa, and vyoṣa—
Bhāvaprakāśa 5.60.
By means of a single form, that [substance] is one; for example, yellow orpiment, gold, and so forth are distinct entities.
Regarding the nature of fire and smoke:
[it is established] by means of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that demonstrates fire and smoke.

If it is asked: "But if there is indeed a real pervasion (*vyāpti*) between these two by way of the properties of 'fire-ness' and 'smoke-ness,' why does it not manifest at the time of the first observation? [The answer is: Because of the absence of a grasper (*grāhaka*).

At whatever time a grasper of something is absent, that thing does not appear at that time, just as taste does not appear at the time of seeing a color. And at the time of the first observation of fire and smoke, the cognition that grasps the pervasion is absent.
And at that time, the absence of a grasper of that [invariable concomitance] is established due to the absence of its causes;
for the causes of the cognition of pervasion are perception and non-perception,
and these two do not exist at the time of the first observation.

Nor does the absence of the perceiver at that time entail the absence of the pervasion, because the absence of the perceiver at that time is established otherwise (anyathāsiddha). Otherwise, at the time of seeing a form from a distance, there would also be an absence of taste, as there is no distinction [between them];
and if the pervasion were absent at that time, how could it manifest later, like a sky-flower? [This applies to] fire and smoke...
