At the time of perceiving smoke and fire, there is no inferential knowledge called "tarka" (reductio ad absurdum), according to the first [view] in the *Bhāṣya*.

The comparison of reasoning—the cause of the knowledge of pervasion—is indeed perception and non-perception; however, these two do not exist at the time of the first observation. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 508)

At that time, during the first moment of perception, the cognition whose object is the existence of the probandum and the probans is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and the cognition whose scope is the absence of the probandum and the absence of the probans is non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Because it is not a valid reason:
if the non-existence of a thing were to follow from the absence of a perceiver, then [the earth] would also be non-existent due to the absence of gustatory perception, which perceives taste.

If it were to manifest at the time of the first perception, or subsequently after repeated observation, by virtue of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then is it produced or made known by those two? It cannot be produced, for those two are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and a means of valid cognition does not produce its object (*prameya*).

Now, it might be argued that [the pervasion] is made known (*jñāpyate*). Even in that case, is it made known while existing at that time, or was it already existing previously? If it exists at that time, no; for there would be no cause for its existence at the very time of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) when the pervasion is present.

If, on the other hand, it is made known as having existed previously, then it is established that the pervasion exists even at the time of the first observation. How then could its existence and the reasoning (*tarka*) that apprehends it be denied? If even what is being perceived were denied, then one would have to deny either color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, or the cognition that apprehends them.
Therefore, it is established that reasoning is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It appears [as such] through perception and non-perception;
this is the pervasion (vyāpti).

In this context, by the words "positive concomitance" (*anvaya*) and "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*), it is precisely perception and non-perception that grasp positive and negative concomitance which are intended; for the property of the subject [the cognition] is metaphorically attributed to the object [the external thing].
At the time of positive and negative concomitance—this is the *tarka* (reasoning)—Śra., Ba.

He states this very point regarding perception such as visual perception: "Cognition (*cintā*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is the cause of its fruit, which is determinate cognition (*abhinibodha*).
He states a synonym for this: "of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth."

What indeed is this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized as having been described? To this he says: "It is scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*). Why is this so? Because the rest is indistinct (*aspaṣṭa*). Since the phrase "due to the application of words" (*śabdānuyojanāt*) is placed in the middle [of the definition], it connects with both [parts]: that which was previously indistinct prior to such application, and that which remains indistinct due to its application. Therefore, all of that is scriptural knowledge.

And that [cognition] is manifoldly divided because of the infinity of the distinctions among the manifestations of cognition— whether accompanied by the association of words, otherwise, or indistinct—
as indicated by the remaining word "anyena" (by another).

[The opponent] might object: "But surely, the acceptance of tarka as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by its own definition for the sake of realizing pervasion (*vyāpti*) is untenable, since that realization is established either through perception or through inference. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says, refuting it: "No inferential mark (*liṅga*) whatsoever is perceived by a non-conceptualizing cognition. (11)

Since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is not established through non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), it is directly known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Because it has not yet attained its own existence prior to the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti),
the mark (liṅga) known as reasoning (tarka) consists in the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) between the probandum and the probans.

Not even the slightest thing is perceived—that is, it is not known in its entirety—by what? By non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpadhī*), namely by the non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) intended by the Buddhists; for [such perception] is devoid of the conceptualization that "whatever smoke there may be, all of it is produced from fire alone and is never produced from non-fire," since otherwise it would result in being conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

Nor can it be established through inference, because that very [inference] is unestablished; for the arising of an inference is preceded by the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and if the determination of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) in that case were to depend on another inference, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is argued that the determination of pervasion in the second inference comes from the first inference, this is the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

Therefore, even inference does not grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, one must admit another means of valid cognition called *tarka* (reasoning), which is direct, ultimate, and not of the nature of false conceptualization; otherwise, the validity of inference would be impossible. [Laghīyastraya-vivṛti, p. 30]—For perception is not capable of performing such extensive operations as determining that "whatever smoke there may be, in any other time or place, is the effect of fire alone and not of anything else," because it arises from the power of its proximate object and is non-discursive (*avicāraka*).
Nor is it another form of inference, because there would be no distinction in all cases;
for if the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) with the thing to be marked (*liṅgin*) is not established, there can be no such thing as inference anywhere.

Therefore, it is incorrect to say that non-perception (*apratyakṣa*) is a means of valid cognition distinct from inference, since the apprehension of the mark constitutes a separate means of valid cognition.
Comparison— As it has been said: "This [cognition] is not capable of performing so many functions"—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.41.

For indeed, a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its entirety can never occur for anyone at any time or place, because it arises through the power of a proximate object and is devoid of conceptual investigation (*avicāraka*).
— *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, fol. 156a;
*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 119.
As they have said: "For this [sensation] is not capable of performing so many operations, because it arises by the power of a proximate object and is non-discursive"—Śāṅkhya-bhāṣya, Bhāmatī, p.
766; Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā, p. 137.
Thus,
since [it is] from the individual (jaḍa-viśeṣa)— namely, the pervasion (vyāpti) ending in the suffix -anum— [there is] the individual (jaḍa-viśeṣa).
This has been extracted from *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, page 101.

For comparison: "For one who desires to establish near and distant objects either as 'this' (*idantā*) or as 'not this' (*nedantā*) in their entirety, reasoning (*tarka*) is the ultimate refuge" — *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, page 293A.

For a *liṅga* (logical mark) is defined as the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the probans with the probandum, since it is only when that [concomitance] exists that the status of being a *liṅga* is established for the mark.

Is the cognition of that [concomitance] derived from perception (*pratyakṣa*) or from inference (*anumāna*)? If it were from perception, would it be the perception belonging to persons like us, or to a yogi? Regarding the first alternative, would it be cognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), through the sense organs (*indriya*), or through mental perception (*mānasa*)? It cannot be from self-awareness, because its scope is limited to its own nature alone and it is ignorant of external objects.

Could the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) be apprehended through perception (*pratyakṣa*) arising from the senses and the mind—whether conceptual (*savikalpa*) or non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; for the Buddhists do not accept the validity of conceptual perception, and even if they did, such perception is not capable of establishing that [concomitance]. Thus he says: "Not perception," and so forth.

The perception defined as mental or sensory, as imagined by the Buddhists and the followers of Yoga, is not capable of performing such functions as [determining] that "whatever smoke there may be, in another time or another place, is the effect of fire alone and not of anything else.
Why is this so? Because it arises through the power of a proximate object;

that is, because it arises from the strength—the causal capacity—of a proximate object, meaning one that is not remote in space or time, characterized as a specific instance of the probandum and the probans, such as fire and smoke.
By this, it should be understood that even non-conceptual [perception] is not capable of that [inference] for that reason.

On this very point, he states another reason: "because it is non-investigative" (*avicārakatvāt*). This means that the investigative reflection (*parāmarśa*)—to the effect that "whatever smoke there may be, all of it is the effect of fire alone and not of anything else"—is absent from that non-conceptual perception; because of its existence, that is, because of its being such [a state].
The word "ca" (and) here should be understood as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

If it is asked how this [perception] is non-investigative (*avicāraka*), [the answer is]: because for some [objects] they are beyond the senses (*parokṣa*); for another, because they would be cognizable by another cognition, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); and for yet another, because like momentariness, they are ineffective (*akiñcitkara*) with respect to the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is apprehended through conceptual perception (savikalpaka-pratyakṣa) in the grasping of invariable concomitance.
Perception—
[Āloka-ṭīkā: arising from the power of a proximate object]—
in the apprehension of pervasion— [Āloka-ṭīkā].

And because of the reality [of this], the word "ca" (and) [is used]— [this refers to] the Mīmāṃsaka according to Ānanda, and to the Naiyāyika who holds that [cognition] is produced by the senses or the mind, according to the marginal note of Ānanda.
In the Buddhist view—

[as noted in the Āloka commentary]— just as non-conceptual perception, though it has arisen regarding the momentary aspect, does not ascertain it, and thus non-conceptual perception is ineffective regarding the momentary aspect; likewise, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Yogins is that the comprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) regarding the blue aspect and so forth occurs through perception alone.
On this point, the followers of Yoga (Yaugas) say: the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) between the probandum and the probans is perceived by perception itself;

for even in the very first perception, smoke appears precisely as being connected with fire, and thus the restriction inherent therein is also perceived. Furthermore, there can be neither doubt nor error—such as "is it from this [fire] or from another? or "it is from another alone"—because this [smoke] is determined precisely as being connected with that [fire], in the form "this belongs to fire alone."

Thus, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended by the first perception, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), being observed repeatedly, produce firmness for that very cognition;
or else, a perception produced by the sense faculty, assisted by the positive and negative concomitances understood through repeated observation, apprehends the pervasion.

If it is asked: "If the pervasion is indeed apprehended by the first perception alone, then why does the cognition of pervasion in the form 'this is necessarily [concomitant] with this' not arise at that very time?"—the answer is: because of the absence of the necessary causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is delineated through synthesis (*anusandhāna*),
and synthesis consists in the apprehension of one thing together with another on one occasion, followed by the apprehension of that very same thing together with yet another;
and this [synthesis] arises only from repeated observation and non-observation.
Furthermore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are indeed appropriate for the purpose of dispelling doubt regarding the causal factor (*prayojaka*).

For when one observes many co-occurring properties, a doubt arises as to whether this invariable rule is caused by "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), or rather caused by properties such as "being produced from grass" (*tārṇatva*) or "blackness" (*śyāmatva*).

In that regard, while properties like "being produced from grass" are variable (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to the relationship [with fire], properties like "blackness" depend upon smoke; thus, it is "smokeness" alone that is the causal factor for smoke’s connection with fire.

Since, while that [fire] exists, the nature of being fire never deviates [from smoke], this knowledge of pervasion is indeed a perception—just like the specific cognition of a "man with a staff" and so forth—because it arises in a manifest form for one who has observed the positive and negative concomitance many times, whose eyes are wide open, and whose sensory operation has not ceased.
Thus, the initial perception is the observation of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin). (Nyāyavārttika, p. 44;
*bhāsamānāt* from manuscript *ba*).

In that case, it is not from something else; rather, it is from that very thing itself—this applies even to smoke. (Note: *tatrā-śra* is a corruption for *tatra nānyataḥ*; *tatrānyatopyanyata eva* is a corruption for *tatrāpyanyata eva*).
Is this smoke produced from fire, or from some other cause? This is doubt (*saṃśaya*).
"This smoke has been produced from some cause other than fire" is misconception (*viparyaya*), because [smoke] is indeed connected with fire.

Furthermore, the pervasion (vyāpti) of smoke, which is understood through repeated observation, is known as a relation between two general properties by means of abandoning their specific differences; and in some cases, it is also known between two particulars.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Anumānapariccheda, verse 12:
For "the impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) is not cognizable through perception;
rather, it is cognizable through the non-deviation of the effect [from its cause].
And non-deviation is preceded by repeated observation—Bṛhatī, p. 111;
Bṛhatīpañjikā, p. 96.

Through the force of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the apprehension of non-deviation between fire and smoke is established even when there is deviation [of the two] with respect to place and so forth—*Nyāyaprakāśa*, p. 70; *Nyāyamālāvistara*, p. 72; *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 570.

Therefore, we consider it logical that the sense organ itself—accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—is what grasps the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) between smoke and so forth with fire and so forth, just like the discernment of the true nature of a gem of noble origin.

In this same way, regarding those things whose relations are known through other means of knowledge, one should infer that those very other means of knowledge, assisted by repeated observation according to their respective domains, are the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping natural connections.
(Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 167)

Tātparya-ṭīkā, page 697: By this, it is shown that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone, accompanied by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), are the means for grasping [the relation];
for "repeated observation" refers to the sense organ together with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the knowledge thereof.

And here, the true nature of the distinction between gems (*maṇi*) serves as a clear illustration. For instance: those subtle particularities (*sūkṣmaviśeṣa*) by which a gem becomes the object of various transactions—being elevated [as such] and producing their respective fruits—are inferred by the examiner through repeated observations. Likewise, in this case as well, first there is the exclusion of mere chance (*kākatālīya*); then, the determination of the specific upward movement that is constant; and finally, the removal of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vivaraṇa*, p.

295: By means of the final perception—which has its power to oppose [the contrary] removed and is assisted by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from the observation of concomitance—one ascertains the concomitance of the smoke-universal with the fire-universal as being dependent solely upon their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-mātra*), and thereby ascertains the rule (*niyama*) that "this is invariably connected with that.
Although concomitance was indeed grasped even at the first observation, nevertheless, the grasping of the rule did not occur then.
For the restriction [of concomitance] does not arise from mere coexistence, but rather from unconditioned coexistence;

and its being unconditioned is to be known through the repeated practice of frequent observation. Thus, by means of a conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) born from the power of grasping frequent coexistence, that [restriction] is determined.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 209.
The cognition that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a certainty (*niścaya*) consisting of the observation of concomitance accompanied by the absence of knowledge of deviation;

and that [certainty] may be accompanied by doubt in some cases due to suspicion of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and in other cases due to the observation of a common property accompanied by the non-observation of specific features.

And its absence [of the probans] in the counter-example is established either by a reductio ad absurdum (*bādhakatarka*) against the contrary case, or it is self-evident (*svatasiddha*). — *Tattvacintāmaṇi-anumāna*, p.
210; [as noted in the Āloka commentary: "by the fire of the kitchen hearth."
The connection of smoke with fire at a crossroads.
Positive concomitance (anvaya) — marginal note; negative concomitance (vyatireka) — marginal note:
because [the property] exists even in things such as mats made of grass.
Regarding the specific [objection]— namely, the separate establishment of the validity of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) for the purpose of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) preceded by its refutation—
it is here replied:

As for what was stated—that invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is apprehended by perception itself, and so forth—in that regard, would it be sensory (*aindriya*) or mental (*mānasa*) perception that operates in its apprehension? It cannot be sensory perception, for that [perception] illuminates only that object with which the sense organ is in contact—namely, one restricted by specific place, time, and so on—but it does not illuminate pervasion (*vyāpti*). This is because pervasion exists by encompassing objects extending across the entire range of places and times; for when it is apprehended, it is apprehended through the synthesis of all objects—past, future, and present—residing within the belly of the three worlds.

Since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the act of pervading (*vyāpana*), it consists in the inclusion of all individual instances of the pervaded and the pervader by way of their respective natures as the pervaded and the pervader.

However, neither the contact of the sense organ with them nor its capacity for apprehension is possible therein; for such [contact and apprehension] are possible only with respect to a specific, present object. Furthermore, not all individuals existing within the belly of the universe are connected with that [sense organ], nor are they present. Therefore, how can there be an apprehension of pervasion in that regard through perception?
Page 428, line 3.
For comparison: "In that regard, does perception—whether sensory or mental—operate in the apprehension of pervasion? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 510).
Comparison—First of all, perception [is not capable of this], because it is restricted to objects existing in a proximate place and at the present time.

For by whatever means of valid cognition the relation of smoke and so forth with fire and so forth is understood in all places, by that very means their necessary connection is understood; and perception is not capable in that regard.
—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 68; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, p. 43; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 346.
Syādvādamañjarī, p.
510; Citsukhī, p. 238;
by way of universal inclusion.
Pervasion (vyāpti) is possible because of the capacity to grasp the relationship among all individual instances of the pervaded and the pervader.

Furthermore, regarding the individual instances of the pervaded and the pervader that exist throughout the universe, does mere perception alone suffice for the apprehension of pervasion, or is it perception aided by repeated observation, or perception assisted by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? It cannot be mere perception alone; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of one who has merely arisen from the bedchamber perceiving pervasion upon seeing the very first instance of smoke and fire.

Regarding what was stated—that even in the first perception, since smoke appears precisely as being connected with fire, the invariable concomitance (*niyama*) residing therein also appears, and so forth—this too is an unexamined assertion. For, when smoke is perceived before one’s eyes, would it appear there as being connected to a specific fire, or as being connected to all fires without exception? In the first case, how could there be a comprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) upon the first observation? This is because pervasion is impossible in relation to a single, restricted individual, as it must culminate in the inclusion of all [instances].

But in the second case, let alone the first perception, even by means of hundreds of perceptions, pervasion cannot be apprehended; for since those [perceptions] function only within the range of connected and present objects, they lack the capacity to comprehend the inseparable relation (avinābhāva) by encompassing all [instances], such as "whatever smoke there is, all that is in fire," with respect to the kitchen and so forth when they have come before one's eyes. (p. 428, l. 3)

Comparison—since smoke would have to appear in the first perception either as being related to the fire currently seen before one's eyes, or as being related to all fires—[this is impossible] for those who hold that pervasion is perceived [by the senses]. (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 510)
"It exists only when [the other] exists, but never at all when fire is absent"—this must be supplied as the ellipsis.
By this, the position that "the initial perception, aided by repeated observation, apprehends pervasion" is also refuted (p. 428, l.

Nor is that [perception], even when assisted by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), capable of apprehending that [pervasion]; for, even if it were assisted a thousand times, its apprehension of that [pervasion] would only occur where it itself functions, and not by way of a universal induction such as "wherever there is smoke, there is fire" and "where fire is absent, smoke is also absent. And in that case, the apprehension of pervasion would be futile.

For that [perception] is intended for the sake of inference; but once the specific individuals of the probandum and the probans have been apprehended by perception, what is the use of inference? Furthermore, does its being "accompanied by positive and negative concomitance" (anvaya-vyatireka-sahakṛtatva) mean that it functions toward another object by overstepping its own object, or that it confers an excellence upon that which is functioning within its own object? In the first case, there is a contradiction with perception, because such a form of auxiliary function—characterized by functioning toward another object by overstepping its own object—is never observed anywhere.
Indeed, the eye assisted by a lamp is never observed to be functioning toward taste and so forth.

Furthermore, the imparting of an excellence (*atiśaya*) to perception while it is operating upon its own object could only be established if it were proven that perception has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its object;
however, that is unestablished, because perception has as its object only things that are connected and present.
Nor does any enhancement arise in sensory perception even when assisted by that [excellence], by which it might apprehend objects even by overstepping its own domain.
Pervasion is directly perceived thousands of times, even by perception assisted by positive and negative concomitance.

Regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to specific instances of smoke and fire that have become objects of perception, the comparison is as follows: Does the assistance provided by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) consist in the perception’s activity extending toward another object beyond its own domain, or does it consist in the conferring of excellence upon the perception as it operates within its own domain? — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 511.
In its own domain,
the object of pervasion belongs to the supervisor.

By this [argument], it has been refuted that perception—arising from the sense organ aided by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*)—apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Furthermore, is pervasion apprehended by a perception produced from that [sense organ] because of its existence within the domain of the sense organ, or because it is the object of that [perception] itself? It cannot be because of its existence; for if it were, it would follow that taste and so forth are also visible, since their presence in smoke and other such objects is no different from that of pervasion.
Nor can it be [known] through its own object, because it is impossible for that [perception] to have that [invariable concomitance] as its object;
for invariable concomitance has an unrestricted scope, so how could perception—which arises from the senses and has a restricted scope—comprehend it? (p.

Comparison: Furthermore, is the pervasion (vyāpti) apprehended through a perception produced by that [sense organ] because the [object] exists within the range of the sense organ, or because it is its own object? — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 511.

Just as there is pervasion in the case of smoke and so forth, which are produced by the sense organs, so too is there the state of being [possessed of] taste and so forth in the case of mangoes and the like. — *Ācārya-ṭippaṇī*.
Because pervasion (vyāpti) cannot be established as an object of perception—[as] comparison [states]:

"Since pervasion has an indefinite range of objects, how could it be apprehended through perception, which arises from the sense organs and has a definite range of objects? — *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 511.

As for what was also stated—that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is delineated through mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and that this [synthesis] arises only from repeated observation and non-observation, and so forth—that is indeed appropriate, because we have set out to establish the capacity of a cognition produced by apprehension and non-apprehension alone for the comprehension of pervasion.
However, its nature as perception (*pratyakṣa*) is untenable, because its object belongs to a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

For that [perception] is well-known to possess the totality of causes such as the sense faculties and to have as its object a related, present thing; since this [cognition] is not like that, how could it attain the nature of perception? (p. 428, l. 10) [This is the] connection.
It would arise, O Ārya;
[it is] the light of perception,
O Ārya— of that which is called reasoning, according to the commentary of Ba.
For the Jainas, inference born from perception and non-perception is [subsumed under] direct perception.

Now, as for the claim that inferential knowledge (*tarka*)—since it is the means for apprehending the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*), and since that [concomitance] is connected with the sense organ and is present—is not perception: this too is charming only when left unexamined. For, is the concomitance of the universal with the universal, or rather, is it the concomitance of the particulars indicated by that [universal] with the particulars indicated by that [universal]? Regarding the first alternative, there is no purpose whatsoever in the apprehension of concomitance, because it would result in the futility of inference due to proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding the universal.

But since the specific instances characterized by those [universals] are infinite, how could there be a connection with the present such that the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be perceptual? [This is not so], because of the existence of the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*): for when fire and smoke are conjoined with the eye, the universal of fire-ness (*agnitva*) and the universal of smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) both inhere in them.

Since the universals of fire and smoke, as characterized by their general properties, are established through perception precisely in places such as the kitchen, it is only the particular [fire] that remains to be proven— [Āloka-ṭīkā].

By this, the argument beginning with "the repeated observation of positive concomitance" (*bhūyodṛṣṭānvaya*) and so forth is refuted. For it is logical that the cognition of a specific person possessing a staff (*daṇḍin*) and the like is perceptual, because it operates within the range of a related and present object; however, this is not the case for the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it is the opposite of that. This has been stated repeatedly.
Now, if it is asked: "If this [knowledge of pervasion] is not perceptual, how can there be a dependence on the sense organs? We reply: "Because it is the cause of the cause thereof.
For the causes of the knowledge of pervasion are perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), and the sense organ is the cause of those two.
Therefore, perception produced by the sense faculties is not capable of apprehending pervasion (vyāpti),

because it lacks the capacity to have as its object all individual instances of the probandum and the probans, owing to its restriction to objects that are connected and presently existing. (Page 429, Line 6)
Nor is the cognition of pervasion mental, because the mind, being independent of the external senses, does not function toward external objects,
as it is stated that "the mind is not autonomous with regard to external things."

Furthermore, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is an external object because it is a property of an external object; whatever is a property of an external object is an external object, just like color and so forth. Since pervasion is a property of an external object, and since the "mind" (*manas*) postulated by you is non-existent—having been refuted in the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*)—how could that which arises from it be recognized as perception?

Alternatively, it is not possible for this [mind], which has the nature of an atom, to be simultaneously connected with all objects without exception; for that which has the nature of an atom is not simultaneously connected with all objects, just like an atom, and the mind imagined by you is of the nature of an atom.

Now, it might be argued that even though there is no direct connection between the mind and all objects, such a connection will exist through a causal chain (*paramparā*); for instance, the self is directly conjoined with the mind, and all specific instances of the probandum and the probans—such as fire and smoke—are conjoined with that [self]. This too is unsatisfactory, because it would entail that everyone is omniscient, since there exists a connection to every object through the mind, just as there is a connection to every specific instance of the probandum and the probans.
Regarding this, some maintain that mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is the grasper of the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*).

Having perceived smoke through both perception and non-perception as being accompanied by fire and as being excluded from what is not fire, one understands with the mind that "smoke is invariably concomitant with fire.

And who would not accept that the mind has all things as its object, since it is capable of determining even an object not present [to the senses], having ascertained the co-occurrence of presence and absence?
For the knowledge of invariable concomitance is established by the mind once this co-occurrence of existence and non-existence has been determined; so, enough of this persistence.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 121, 123:
Its apprehension occurs through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) aided by direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

Having perceived with the sense organ that smoke is concomitant with fire, and having known through non-perception that it is excluded from non-fire such as water and so forth, one determines by means of the mind: "Smoke does not deviate from fire."
—*Nyāyakalika*, p. 3.

For comparison: "If those for whom perception is the means of knowledge [claim that] it knows the relationship between the mark and the marked through pervasion, what can they do regarding an object that is beyond the senses?"
Wherever the sense-faculties operate, there the mind operates;
it does not exist elsewhere, for otherwise it would follow that all embodied beings would be deprived of their sense-faculties—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 179.

Nor is it logical that there is a mental synthesis (*saṅkalana*) of past and future individuals by means of the mind, because if the mind were independent regarding external objects, it would follow that there is no such thing as being blind or deaf;

for if the mind were to operate toward external objects without depending on other causes, then everyone would be an all-seeing seer (*sarvadarśin*), since there would be no distinction [between them]. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 210)
—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 69;
*Bṛhatī*, page 95;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, page 58.

351; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 511. Compare: "The dependent nature is external and mental."
—Cited from *Vidhiviveka*, p.
114; *Laukikanyāya*, third part, p. 82;
and *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 511.
The [view] imagined by the followers of Yoga,

The knowledge of mental existence is the connection with the mind.

By virtue of the conjunction and non-conjunction with the self— which pervades [the body]— if one postulates a connection of all individual instances of smoke and fire with the mind, such a connection is possible through a mediated relationship (*paramparāsambandha*): the mind is conjoined with the self, and by that [self], all objects are conjoined.

Furthermore, even that relation of relations could exist for the mind only with real objects, not with unreal ones; so how could there be a comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) therein? Nor is the all-pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) of the self established, since it has been refuted in detail during the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*); therefore, how could there be even a scent of a relation of relations? Consequently, you must comprehend the pervasion between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) itself; and thus, inference cannot arise, because the pervasion of the reason by the property to be proven is not ascertained in the subject (*dharmin*) where the probandum resides.
Thus it is established that, according to neither the Buddhist nor the Nyāya school, whether sensory or mental perception is a factor for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [Comparison:

Furthermore, even this "relation of the related" (*sambaddhasambandha*) [of inference] occurs only with existent objects, not with non-existent ones such as those past or future; so how can there be an apprehension of pervasion in that regard? — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 512.
[Note: *sambaddhasamba* refers to the term *sambaddhasambandha*.]
"By means of past, future, space, time, and entities"— this refers to the omnipresence of the Self (ātman),
as noted in the Ācārya’s commentary on page 261.

By this [argument], the status of yogic perception as a factor for the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is also rejected; for it too, being non-discursive and having its range restricted to a specific, proximate object that serves as its cause, is no different in its inability to perform these many functions.

Or, let it be granted that from that [perception] there is the comprehension of that [pervasion]; nevertheless—would the yogi, having comprehended the pervasion through direct perception, perform inference for his own sake or for the sake of others? First of all, not for his own sake, because since all specific instances of the probandum and the probans have been clearly comprehended through direct perception, such [inference] would be fruitless.

Inference is not fruitful regarding that which is apprehended with complete clarity through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), just as it is not fruitful regarding the nature of perception itself. And all particular instances of the probandum and the probans are apprehended by yogins with complete clarity through direct perception;

therefore, one must not claim that inference is indeed fruitful even regarding those things thus apprehended for the sake of excluding superimposition (*samāropa*), because for a yogin, due to having shaken off the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*), superimposition itself is impossible.

Now, regarding the yogin’s inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*): must the other person for whom it is intended have already grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), or must the yogin establish it through inference for others without their having grasped the pervasion? If it is one who has already grasped the pervasion, from where was that pervasion grasped by him? It cannot be by means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), sensory consciousness (*indriyajñāna*), or mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it has been established that these do not have that [pervasion] as their object.
Nor can it be by means of the yogin’s own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that would entail the uselessness of inference.
Furthermore, it is impossible to establish [the pervasion] for someone who has not grasped it, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans cannot be apprehended through any direct perception whatsoever.
[Tulana: Others, however, maintain that at the time of grasping the pervasion, the cognizer possesses knowledge of all objects, as if he were a yogin;
for otherwise, there could be no recollection of the pervasion in the form, "All smoke does not exist without fire."
And because it does not appear as distinct due to its being expressed as identical [to the object], just like an individual grain of rice cast into a heap of grain—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
As for that which Prabhākaragupta considers, namely, that the knowledge of the yogin is the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

It is also difficult to maintain that the pervasion (vyāpti) is established through the yogic perception of the comparison— that whatever smoke there may be, all of it is born from fire and not born from non-fire—
because there is an absence of inferential knowledge regarding all things for every yogi.
Furthermore, its operation toward inference for the sake of others is not tenable;
for it is useless both for non-yogis who do not themselves know the pervasion,
and even for yogis, just as in the case of inference for one's own sake.
Because there is no distinction in superimposition, for yogins in all cases—*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 179; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 351.
Because inference is so clear,
it applies even to those specific instances of the probandum and the probans known through the direct perception of a yogin.
As previously stated by the Yogin, that [cognition] consisting of meditative cultivation appears clearly to them, with the web of conceptual construction shaken off— Pramāṇavārttika 2.283.

Because its object is the true nature of reality, it has shaken off the web of conceptual construction; and because it is non-conceptual, it manifests clearly as the very form of a distinct object of knowledge— Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī 2.281.

Comparison—In that case, would the yogi demonstrate to another [a subject] for which the pervasion has been grasped or for which the pervasion has not been grasped by means of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*)? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 351.
Because it would follow that [the reason] would not be the object of pervasion by another [instance] to be established, and that [the statement] would be purposeless. (Śrī.)
Because both the entire object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) have become clearly manifest,

immediately following this, the verse beginning with "by means of non-conceptual cognition" (*avikalpaghiyā*) is also written in manuscript *ba*; here follows the commentary on both the verse and its exposition:
Therefore, it is well said: "by non-conceptual cognition," and so forth.

That which has no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—namely, the determination of self and other—and which is also a cognition (*dhī*), by means of that [cognition] which is indirect (*parokṣa*) and consists of the ascertainment of the experience of another cognition, no sign (*liṅga*) whatsoever—whether its object be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or an effect (*kārya*) and so forth—is perceived, nor is there any inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*).

To the objection that "it is then cognized through inference," he replies: It is not cognized through inference—that is, through a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the cognition of the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*). For instance, is the first inference capable of determining the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the reason, or is it another inference? Of these, the first position is untenable, because that inference is itself unestablished. Precisely for this reason, there would be circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) in its establishment: for if the invariable concomitance of the reason is established, then the establishment of its production from that [concomitance] follows; and if that [production] is established, then the invariable concomitance of the reason is established.

Nor can there be another inference; for that too arises from a reason whose invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been established. And would the establishment of that [concomitance] occur through perception or through inference? Regarding the first position, he states the refutation: "In all cases," and so forth. Because there is no distinction between the second inference and the first, the same fault applies—namely, that it is not perception—and because the fault is identical, it would follow that its establishment must also occur through inference. Would that establishment occur through that very same [inference], or through another? If it were through that very same one, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

If, on the other hand, [the connection] is established from something else, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that which establishes it would itself have to be apprehended through another inference, and so forth.
Thus, for an opponent, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) cannot come from anywhere.
[The opponent might ask: "Let it not be so; what is the use of it? To this, he says: "For indeed," and so on.

Indeed, if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) by the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) were not established in its entirety, then—whether in some case where impermanence or fire is the probandum, and whether in conventional or ultimate reality—there would be no such thing as inference, whether produced from a mark of essential nature (*svabhāva-liṅga*) or from a mark of effect (*kārya-liṅga*). This is the intended meaning here: just as nothing to be proven (*sādhya*) is established without inference, and thus inference is accepted for that purpose, so too that [inference] is not established without the establishment of the pervasion between the mark and the possessor of the mark; therefore, let that [pervasion] also be accepted, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. What follows from this? To this he says: "That is not so," and so forth.

Since this is so, the claim that "therefore there is no means of valid cognition other than inference—neither non-perceptual (parokṣa) nor distinct from inference—but rather inference itself" is incorrect. This is because the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*), which is the apprehension of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) known as *tarka*, constitutes a separate means of valid cognition. Since it arises from something other than a mark and possesses an indistinct nature, it is not included within the two [accepted] means of valid cognition. Therefore, it is well said: "Reflection (*cintā*) is a means of valid cognition, because it is the cause of inference and the rest.
What kind of inference is that? To this he says:
In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, [it is] the manifestation of its own nature; in the view of the Naiyāyikas, [it is] the apprehension of the object.

There is no inferential mark (liṅga) regarding objects such as the effect (kārya) and so forth, because the nature of the inferential mark under discussion— the inseparable relation (avinābhāva)— has not yet acquired its own form prior to the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti).
When the establishment of inference is accomplished— that is, when the logical reason (hetu) is established— there arises inference.
And the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established because it is common to other forms of inference;
for when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, inference arises, and when inference has attained its own existence, there is the apprehension of pervasion.
Inference is also the apprehension of pervasion that gives rise to another inference.

The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which serves to establish inference, is itself a form of comparison (*tulanā*); for where can there be an unhesitating assent when doubt persists despite reasoning, consensus, and discussion?
The statement by the Buddhist beginning with "Therefore, it is not non-perceptual" (*tattvārthaśloka*, p.
195) consists of the forms of inference and perception.
From the mark (liṅga), which is characterized solely by the certain cognition of its inseparable connection with the probandum (sādhya).

Commentary: What is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called inference (anumāna)? It is the cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin); that is, the knowledge of the probandum (sādhya). This is the meaning.

The term *liṅgin* (the possessor of the mark) is derived from the analysis (*vigraha*) that it is "that which has a connection of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the mark (*liṅga*). He states the cause of its arising: from the mark (*liṅga*), which is the means of proof (*sādhana*) characterized solely by the certain cognition of inseparable concomitance with the probandum (*sādhya*). "Inseparable concomitance" (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum—which consists of being desired (*iṣṭa*), uncontradicted (*abādhitā*), and not yet established (*asiddha*)—is the rule of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). The "certain cognition" (*nibodha*) of this, meaning its determination through universal application across space and time, is the "sole" or primary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, its essential nature (*svarūpa*)—of which [the mark] is thus described. The meaning is that inference is the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgidhīḥ*) arising from such a mark.

[Objection: "But since this [inference] is the fruit of reasoning (*tarka*), how can it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Anticipating this, he says: "Its fruits are the cognitions of avoidance and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), taking up (*upādāna*) and indifference (*upekṣā*) are included. The cognitions—that is, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—of these [three] are the fruits of that inference. Therefore, because it is the cause of the fruit, inference is a means of valid cognition, just like perception; such is the intended meaning. (Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra, p. 31)

That which is connected with the object of inference, which is well-known to exist in what possesses that [object], and which is absolutely absent in its absence—that alone is the inferential mark (liṅga) that brings about inference.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 200.

The reason (*hetu*) is the means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*), and likewise through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). — *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.34.
The reason has three characteristics—Nyāyapraveśa, p. 1.

A reason (hetu) is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that is pervaded by a portion of that [subject]; it is of only three kinds due to the necessity of inseparable connection (avinābhāva). Others than these are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
— *Hetubindu*, *Prakaraṇa*.
Pramāṇavārttika 3.1; Tattvasaṃgraha Kārikā 1362
The reason (*hetu*) has three characteristics— according to the Sāṃkhya school (Sāṃkhyakārikā-bhāṣya,
p. 12)— and the statement of the mark (*liṅga*) that makes known the state of being a means of proof (*sādhana*) is the reason.

"The definition of a logical reason (hetu) is stated as 'being otherwise impossible' (*anyathānupapannatva*)," [as stated in] *Nyāyasāra*, p. 5; "The definition of a logical reason is stated as 'being otherwise impossible'," [as stated in] *Nyāyāvatāra*, verse 22.
The proof is untenable in the absence of the subject under discussion—*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 102;
*Nyāyaviniścaya*, kā. 269;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 214.
And thus it was stated by the venerable Kumāranandi: "The logical mark (liṅga) is understood as having only one characteristic: its impossibility otherwise (anyathānupapatti)."

"A reason has the single characteristic of being ascertained as otherwise impossible" (Pramāṇanayatatvāloka 3). "A reason has the single characteristic of being ascertained as otherwise impossible" (Pramāṇaparīkṣā, p. 72).
A statement of the means of proof (hetu) is a word expressing a means of accomplishment (sādhana), ending in a case-ending that manifests its status as a means of accomplishment. — Nyāyasūtra 1.1.32.
1.12 Inference is the cognition of the inferential mark (liṅgin); its results are the cognitions of avoidance and so forth.
That which arises from the observation of a mark (liṅga) is inferential (laiṅgika). [Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
200] Inference is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] based on the observation of one part [of a known relation] by one who knows the connection.
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5
Inference is the knowledge of that which is to be inferred, based on the perception of an invariable concomitance— Sāṃkhyasūtra 1.100.
Inference (*anumāna*) is a measurement (*māna*) following after (*anu-paścāt*) a mark (*liṅga*) that has been measured (*mita*). (Nyāyavārttika, p.

28). Among these, inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is the knowledge regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*) which arises from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa-liṅga*).
— Nyāyabindu 2.3:
Inference is the means for the experience of that which is beyond the senses by means of a correct invariable concomitance.
—Nyāyāvatāra, p. 5:
"Inference is known to be that which ascertains the probandum from a mark (liṅga) that is inseparably connected with the probandum;
it is non-erroneous because it is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), just like direct perception."

"Inference is the cognition of the probandum from the probans" (Nyāyāvatāra, verse 5); "Inference is the cognition of the object to be proven through the means of proof" (Nyāyabindu, chapter 1, verse 67;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, page 107).
*Pramāṇaparīkṣāmukha*, page 70, verse 3.14.

2.7 Nyāyadīpikā, p. 20.

Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 12. For comparison: "In that context, the perception of the mark (liṅga) is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the resulting cognition of fire is the valid knowledge (pramiti);
or else, the cognition of fire itself is the means of valid cognition, while the perception of its qualities, defects, or neutrality regarding the fire is the valid knowledge."
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

206, *Vivṛti*: Indeed, identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) cannot be known without the reasoning of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*); for even without those two, the establishment of the single characteristic [of proof] occurs, since a tree and the like are neither the nature (*svabhāva*) nor the effect (*kārya*) of its shadow and the like.
And there is no contradiction here— this is the explanation of the verse from the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* (Vita-vṛtti).

From what kind of mark (*liṅga*) or reason (*hetu*) [does this follow]? To this he says: "By that which has as its sole characteristic... and so forth. "Inseparability" (*avinābhāva*)—that is, pervasion (*vyāpti*)—with the probandum (*sādhya*), which is qualified by the attributes of being intended, uncontradicted, and not yet established; the "thorough understanding" (*abhinibodha*) of that, meaning its complete ascertainment (*niścaya*), is the "sole" (i.e., primary) characteristic of which [the reason]. Thus, the meaning is: from that which has as its sole characteristic the certainty of the rule of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) well-ascertained.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition (*dhī*)—that is, knowledge (*jñāna*)—arising when the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), namely the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), is either being employed or is being understood. [The definition continues:

"The subject, well-known in the world, which is intended by oneself as the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*) as being qualified by a well-known qualifier, and which is not contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition"—this is the completion of the sentence (from the *Nyāyapraveśaka*, p.
"A thesis is that which is intended by [the proponent] himself in its own form and is not refuted" (Nyāyabindu, p.

79). However, in the *Nyāyamukha-prakaraṇa*, the reading is "A thesis is that which is intended by [the proponent] himself as something to be proven, which has a non-contradictory meaning, and is not refuted" (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, Chapter 4).
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is the acceptance of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), provided it is not sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition (Nyāyāvatāra,
verse 14). "What is to be proven" (*sādhya*) is that which is intended, capable [of being established], and not yet established (Nyāyaviniścaya, verse 172).
The probandum (*sādhya*) is that which is desired, uncontradicted, and unestablished— *Parīkṣāmukha* 3.15;
the probandum is that which is not already known, not refuted, and intended— *Pramāṇanayatatvāloka* 3.1.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended to be established and is not sublated; [this is] the definition of the thesis (*sādhya*).
— *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* 1.1.2.12.

2.13 [The reason] is established either by the force of the statement of the application (*upanaya*) or by the demonstration that the reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), as it follows from the sense [of the argument].
The refutation of the Buddhist who does not accept the formal employment of a proposition (*pratijñā*):

Is it not the case that [the statement] "when the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is employed" is incorrect? For, since there is no purpose for the thesis (*pakṣa*), its employment is untenable; because the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) is established everywhere simply through the means of proof (*sādhana*), even when this [thesis] is already understood. If it is argued that its employment is not impossible because there exists a purpose characterized by the communication of the meaning of the probandum, we say: no, because it is impossible for that [thesis] to communicate that [meaning].

Does that [thesis] alone convey the object to be proven, or is it accompanied by the presentation of a reason (*hetu*)? If it is alone, then the presentation of the reason is useless, because the comprehension of that [object] arises from the mere employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself.

If, on the other hand, it is accompanied by the presentation of the reason, then since the capacity for that [comprehension] resides in the reason alone, what is the purpose of employing the [thesis]? [The thesis is] qualified by the object to be proven...

The statement of that [proponent's] position is not a direct means of proof for the thesis, because it merely communicates the speaker’s intention and thus gives rise to doubt; nor is it sufficient as an indirect means, since it expresses only the [thesis] itself. For, indeed, if the subject matter were not made known, the application of the reason would be impossible.
If it is argued that its capacity [to prove the point] is established merely by making the object known,
it has been stated in this regard that even without such [a formal statement], when it is said, "All things produced are impermanent," the cognition of their destruction would arise by implication.

Even if the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not stated, because its establishment is not obstructed, the failure to state any one of the three [characteristics] alone is declared to be "deficiency" (*nyūnatā*)— *Pramāṇavārttika* 4.126.

16–23 *Hetubindu*, Chapter on Refutation: Alternatively, the inclusion in a proof-statement of that which is not a constituent part of that very proof— such as the thesis (*pratijñā*), the application (*upanaya*), the conclusion (*nigamana*), and so forth— is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent, because it constitutes a futile statement.

But is it not the case that the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), although not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*), must nevertheless be employed for the purpose of indicating the object? No; because it is redundant. Even in the absence of the statement of the thesis, the establishment of the desired object occurs precisely from the statement of the proof as described; therefore, its employment is useless. (Vādanyāya, pp. 61–65) In the employment of both of these [the reason and the example], the indication of the subject (*pakṣa*) is not necessary.

Since the means of proof (*sādhana*) must be understood as being connected to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) through either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) in both types of formal argument (*prayoga*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) need not necessarily be stated. Now, if the thesis is not to be stated, why was its definition provided? Its definition was not stated because it is a constituent part of the statement of proof; rather, some have understood what is not to be proven as being to be proven, and others have understood what is to be proven as not being to be proven. Therefore, the definition of the thesis was stated for the purpose of refuting such misconceptions regarding what is to be proven and what is not to be proven—*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p.
The thesis is useless because it is not a constituent part of the proof—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 418;
*Sāmarthya-prakaraṇa*.
Because the comprehension of the object to be proven is a form of cognition,
[it occurs] in the comprehension of the object to be proven.

To this it is replied: Is the non-employment [of the *pakṣa*] because it obstructs the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), because its establishment follows from the context (*prakrama*), because it does not accomplish the purpose, or because it accomplishes that purpose only when dependent on the presentation of the reason (*hetu*)? It cannot be because it obstructs its establishment; for when the proponent correctly employs a means of proof (*sādhana*) and performs the task characterized by the establishment of his own position, the employment of the *pakṣa* cannot be an obstruction, since it does not establish the opposite of that [probandum].

When a certain action is being performed, that which does not establish its opposite is not an obstacle to it, just as firewood and the like are not obstacles to smoke. Furthermore, when the action characterized by the establishment of one's own position is being performed through a correct means of proof, the employment of a thesis (*pratijñā*) does not establish its opposite; for [the thesis] merely indicates the position. [Śāntarakṣita’s] *Tattvasaṃgraha* (TS) 1425: "Is its non-statement [considered a fault] because it obstructs the establishment of the probandum, or because of a lack of purpose? [Tibetan: When an effect is being produced, that which does not bring about its opposite is not an obstacle to it, just as wood and so forth are not obstacles to smoke. And when an effect characterized by the establishment of one's own position is being produced through a correct means of proof, the formulation of the thesis (*pratijñā-prayoga*) does not bring about its opposite, because it is merely the indication of the position. [Note on the citation: Regarding that [thesis], is its non-utterance [a fault] because it obstructs the establishment of the probandum, or because of a lack of purpose? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 373.

But why, then, is this not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*)? Is it because it is entirely useless in arguments, or because, although useful, it is included in a different manner? [Answer: Because the employment of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*). (PRAŚASTAKĪRAṆA, p. 335)
The purpose is the establishment of the probandum, because [the reason] does not prove what is contrary to one's own position.

Furthermore, its establishment by way of context is no different for the reason (*hetu*) and so forth than it is for the thesis (*pratijñā*); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of not employing those [reasons and examples] either.
For when the impermanence of sound is being asserted as a thesis, the reason such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and the example such as a pot do not fail to be established through context.
If even such things are stated, what offense has been committed by the subject (*pakṣa*) that its statement in such a manner is not accepted?

Since the reasons and so forth are also established through the context itself, therefore— [it is not] from what is already well-known; even that which is established from the context [is not a valid reason].

Furthermore, the claim that [the thesis] does not accomplish the purpose is unestablished; for there exists a specific comprehension by the person to be instructed, which is the very purpose to be accomplished by it.
Indeed, among those to be instructed, some possess dull intellects while others possess sharp intellects.

In this regard, for one of dull intellect, a specific comprehension of the subject matter at hand is not possible without the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*). Nor is it [possible] for one of sharp intellect who has not mastered the convention, even though they have mastered the convention used in the five-membered syllogism of the Naiyāyikas and others.
Because he states a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) by not employing that [member], the other [argument] is deficient even by one [required member]; Nyāyasūtra 5.2.12.

Because of this statement, for one of sharp intellect, since the comprehension of the subject matter under discussion is observed to occur through the mere statement of the reason (*hetu*) even without the application of that [proposition], the [proposition] would be useless; and if it were useless, the application of the reason itself would also be useless. For we see that some people comprehend the subject matter under discussion from the mere application of a proposition—such as "There is fire here"—derived simply from the words of a person who is certain and non-deceptive. [However, this is not the case here] because when that [proposition] is applied, there exists the purpose of producing a specific comprehension in the person being instructed.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
373; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 550; [from] *niyāmaka*, etc., manuscript *ba*.
When the Naiyāyika does not employ the proposition (*pratijñā*), [the opponent] employs the proposition.

Comparison of the employment of the thesis (*pratijñā*): Even from the mere word of a person determined to be non-deceptive, such as "there is fire here," the object of cognition is established in some cases; therefore, it would follow that even the logical reason (*hetu*) lacks the status of a means of proof, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established even in its absence—*Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 47.
The claim that "for one of sharp intellect and faith who requires the presentation of a reason, [the thesis-statement] serves to accomplish the purpose" is also refuted; for there is no such rule,

since it is observed that in some cases, even without the employment of a reason, the mere employment of the thesis-statement alone accomplishes the purpose characterized by the specific understanding of the person to be instructed.
In this regard as well, Śrā [Śāntarakṣita] says:

"Furthermore, Bha [Bhāviveka], if the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the objective domain of the reason, is not specified, the fallacies of the reason—such as being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—will necessarily follow; for without that [subject], it is impossible to distinguish between real merits and defects therein."

For just as when an archer shoots an arrow without specifying the target, his excellence appears as a defect and his defect appears as an excellence to the onlookers due to their confusion; yet when that target is specified, his excellence—characterized by skill in hitting the mark—and his defect—characterized by the opposite—are perceived by them exactly as they are, so too, when the subject (*pakṣa*) is not specified, even a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) becomes "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) because it is tainted by the suspicion: "Does this reason reside only in the probandum (*sādhya*), or in its absence? And because the contrary suspicion—that it might reside only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—is not removed, it would even become "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

However, in the statement of the thesis (*pakṣanirdeśa*), which is the statement of the object to be characterized (*lakṣyanirdeśa*), there is no fault whatsoever, because—just like an archer—one is able to correctly perceive its qualities and defects. A comparison should be made here: the application [of the thesis] serves to illuminate the scope of the reason (*hetu*); otherwise, it would cause confusion regarding the scope of the reason intended by the proponent.
A reason for that which is to be understood may be one suspected of being contradictory, as in the case of an archer who is being observed by spectators for his skill;
when he is shooting without a target being specified, there is doubt regarding whether it is his skill or something else [that causes the arrow to hit].

Furthermore, due to delusion, one might assert a "contradictory" (viruddha) fallacy, thinking that even though the reason is valid, it exists only in the counter-example (vipakṣa). However, by stating the thesis (pakṣa), this fault does not arise, because the scope of the reason is thereby determined. The intended meaning is as follows: just as when an archer shoots an arrow without specifying his target, the merits and defects perceived by an observer appear inverted—where merit appears as defect, or defect as merit—likewise, when a proponent presents a reason without stating the thesis, the merits and defects characterized by the capacity or incapacity to prove the intended probandum appear inverted even to the judges, the opponent, and others. This is the essential point.
–*Nyāyāvatāra* 14–16, *Ṭīkā*, p.
48–49: The skill of an archer is [demonstrated] in the designation of the target.
For the spectators,
there is the accurate description of merits and defects, characterized by the capacity or incapacity of the means of proof (sādhana) to establish the intended probandum (sādhya).

As for what was also stated—that if the subject (*pakṣa*) alone has the capacity to establish the probandum (*sādhya*), the adducing of a reason (*hetu*) is useless—that too is a mere assertion; for a single cause is never observed to produce an effect on its own.
Indeed, it is not seen that a seed or the like has the capacity to produce an effect such as a sprout when it is solitary;
nor does the capacity of one [factor] therein imply the uselessness of others.

And how could it be that, if the reason alone possesses the capacity to establish the probandum (*sādhya*), the corroboration of that reason and the application (*upanaya*) and so forth would not be redundant? It is also unseemly to argue that because the subject (*pakṣa*) depends upon the reason for the establishment of its object, it is not the basis for that establishment; for this would entail the undesirable consequence that even your postulated non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-adhyakṣa*) would lack the status of being a basis for the establishment of its object, since that perception depends upon conceptualization (*vikalpa*) for the establishment of its object.

If it is argued that conceptualization merely establishes the object already apprehended by the thesis (*pakṣa*), then one might as well say that the logical reason (*hetu*) merely establishes the object already presented by the thesis, and another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) merely corroborates what has been established by that [reason], for there is no distinction between the two cases.
Furthermore, this is the very nature of the thesis: its function is to make the object intelligible in dependence upon the reason.

This is because of the etymological derivation of the term *pakṣa*: it is "cooked" (*pacyate*)—that is, made tender—by the reason, and brought to clarity for those of delicate intellect by way of its being endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Thus, it is called a *pakṣa*.
pṛ॰ 436 paṃ॰ 1 –kāryakāraṇe ā॰ [refers to] the effect and cause, or the seed as the cause.

Regarding the comparison between the production of a sprout (or the establishment of a probandum) and the employment of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and other factors—such as earth, water, and so forth, on the one hand, and the thesis, the application, and so forth, on the other—the objection raised there, namely, "In that case, since the capacity [to produce the result] resides in the reason alone, what is the use of stating the thesis?", is incorrect. For if it were so, then even the statement of the reason would not be necessary, since the reason, when dependent upon support, is established as the cause for the proof of the probandum. Thus, the statement of that [reason] would likewise not occur.
—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
550; *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 47: establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*).
— The basis for the establishment of the object [is] the Buddhist [system].
And that which is established by a non-conceptual perception and demonstrated by a reason apprehended by a non-conceptual [perception].
Because there is no distinction even in the expression "having the nature of a justification," this alone is the position— A, Śra.
Etymological analysis (tulanā): It is called a *pakṣa* because it is "cooked" (*pacyate*).
The root *pac* means "to manifest" (*vyaktīkaraṇe*); that object which is cooked—that is, manifested—is the *pakṣa*.
—*Nyāyapraveśaka-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, p. 13;
*Nyāyasāra-ṭīkā*, p. 101. Thus, the [proponent's] position (*pakṣa*) does not exist in manuscript B.

Furthermore, if the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not accepted, how then could there be the determination of similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), since that determination is preceded by it? And in the absence of those, even a reason (*hetu*) possessing the three characteristics would be untenable, resulting in the abolition of inference,
because the determination of similar and dissimilar instances is preceded by the thesis.

Furthermore, if there were no distinction between similar and dissimilar instances (sapakṣa and vipakṣa), and if the thesis (pratijñā) were unfit for formal employment, then it would not be employed even at the beginning of a treatise (śāstra) and so forth, since there would be no difference;
yet this is not the case, because its employment is observed there.

Indeed, a thesis (*pratijñā*) is not absent from treatises (*śāstra*) or even in informal discourse, for statements such as "there is fire here because of smoke" and "this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*" are observed therein.

Since the authors of treatises are engaged in the task of favoring others and their intellects are dependent upon making the subject understand the point being taught, the employment of a thesis at the beginning of a treatise is entirely logical, as it is useful. If it is accepted that this is so, then let it also exist in formal debate (*vāda*), since the authors there too are of the same nature.
[Otherwise,] if the thesis were useless, it would not be stated even in treatises and the like, as there would be no distinction [between them and other types of discourse].

It is not the case that a thesis (*pratijñā*) is never mentioned in a treatise (*śāstra*), nor is it absent from informal discussion (*aniyata-kathā*); for we observe statements such as "there is fire here because of smoke" and "this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*" in treatises, and we see the employment of thesis-formulations such as "this reason is contradictory" or "this [reason] is unestablished" in informal discussion—(Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī p. 83; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
In the *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, page 551:
because there is no difference in their being unfit for formal application at the beginning of a treatise.
In the treatise or in a good discussion regarding the treatise.

[Objection: "If it is argued that for the authors of treatises—who are engaged in benefiting others and whose intellects are dependent upon making the subject matter understood—the employment of a thesis (*pratijñā*) at the beginning of a work is indeed logical because of its utility; [Response: Then let it also exist in formal debate (*vāda*), since they are of the same nature there as well, for even in debate the teachers are engaged in making their points understood to those seeking victory" (Aṣṭasahasrī p. 83; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 551, it is stated: "In debate (*vāda*) and discussion (*bho-vāda*),
let there be the formal employment of the thesis (*pratijñā-prayoga*)."
For even in debate,
the authors of treatises are motivated by the desire to benefit others.
The justification for the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣaprayoga*) by way of another method is to be seen in the following texts: *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā* p.
601; *Nyāyamañjarī* p.
571; *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* p. 275.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 235;
Praśastapādabhāṣyakiraṇāvalī, p.
335; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 51.

The demonstration that the triple characteristic of the mark—consisting of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—is preceded by the rejection of those three characteristics as the definition of a mark, and that its sole characteristic is inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*):

"Now, it is argued that it is improper for the mark to have inseparable connection from the probandum as its sole characteristic; for since it possesses the triad of characteristics such as being a property of the subject, it cannot possess a single characteristic.
Moreover, if it did not possess those [other] characteristics, the logical reason would be subject to defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*)."

For, in the absence of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), it is impossible to exclude its being unestablished (*asiddhatva*); in the absence of presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), it is impossible to eliminate its being contradictory (*viruddhatva*); and in the absence of non-existence in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it is impossible to negate its being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*).
And thus it has been said:
"The reason (*hetu*) possesses three characteristics."

What, then, is the threefold nature (*trairūpya*)? It consists of: [the reason's] being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and its absence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣe cāsattvam*)—*Nyāyapraveśaka*, p. 1. Furthermore, the threefold nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is as follows: its existence in the object of inference (*anumeya*) alone; the *anumeya* has the definition that will be stated later; in that [object], the certain existence of the mark is the first characteristic. By the mention of "existence" therein, [reasons] such as "being visible to the eye" (*cākṣuṣatva*), which are unestablished (*asiddha*), are excluded.

By the use of the particle *eva*, the reason that is unestablished with respect to only a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is excluded; for example, in the argument "trees are sentient because they sleep," when trees are made the subject, the sleep characterized by the closing of leaves is established only in some parts [of the subject],
