for not all trees close their leaves at night, but only some do.
By the word "only" (*eva*), which follows the phrase "existence in the subject" (*sattva-vacanasya paścāt-kṛtena*), the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is excluded;
for if one were to state "existence only in the inferable object" (*anumeya eva sattvam*), then "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) itself would become a [valid] reason.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*), all doubtful-unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*) reasons are excluded.
Existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). The similar class has its definition to be stated later; existence in that alone, ascertained, is the second characteristic.
Here too, by the inclusion of the term "existence," the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is excluded, for it does not exist in the similar class at all.

By the particle "only" (*eva*), the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is excluded—for example, "Sound is impermanent because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*); for this [reason] exists neither in the similar class alone, but in both [the similar and dissimilar classes].

By the use of the term "existence" (*sattva*) and by placing the restriction first, it is stated that even that which exists pervasively in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), such as "being produced immediately after effort," can function as a logical reason (*hetu*).

However, if the restriction were placed last, the meaning would be: "That which has existence only in the similar class is the reason"; in that case, "being produced immediately after effort" would not be a reason, as it does not exist in all similar instances. By the use of the word "ascertained" (*niścita*), the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) with doubtful positive concomitance (*sandigdhānvaya*) is excluded—for example, "someone is omniscient because he is a speaker. For the property of being a speaker is indeed doubtful in the similar class, namely, in the case of an omniscient being.

And its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is definitely established. The dissimilar instance has the definition that will be stated; its non-existence therein is definitely established—this is the third characteristic. By the inclusion of the term "non-existence" (*asattva*), the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is excluded, for the contradictory reason exists in the dissimilar instance.

By the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*), the common reason (*sādhāraṇa*) that occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instance is excluded, as in: "Sound is eternal because it is produced, like space."

For when "being produced immediately after effort" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "impermanence" exists in one part of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as lightning, but does not exist in others, such as space; therefore, its exclusion by necessity [from the entire counter-example] would follow from the statement of its non-existence [in the counter-example]. If the restriction were placed first [as "that which does not exist only in the counter-example"], the meaning would be this: that which does not exist *only* in the counter-example is the logical reason (*hetu*). In that case, "being produced immediately after effort" does not exist even in all cases within the similar example (*sapakṣa*); consequently, it would not be a valid reason. Therefore, the restriction was not placed first.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), the inconclusive [reason] whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) is doubtful is excluded—Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p. 31–33;
Vādanyāya, p. 60.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 404:
"It is possible" (iti); because of this reason, the determination regarding all three aspects has been described by him (*ba*).
"From the opposite of the unestablished, the contrary, and the deviant [reasons]" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.14).
The meaning is "due to their absence," according to the Āloka commentary.

This is indeed being explained: for that reason, by that cause, the ascertainment (*niścaya*) regarding all three forms—the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—was described by the Master Dignāga in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other works through such statements as "but the unestablished (*asiddha*) [reason] is a proof for both [sides].
To the question "By the exclusion of what? he says: "The unestablished," and so forth.
Because it belongs to the group beginning with "ādi," the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case; thus, the meaning is "by means of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)."
In that context, the certainty of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) by means of the non-existence of the unestablished (*asiddha*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) has been described;

the contradictory (*viruddha*) is the opposite of that meaning. The certain positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) by means of the counter-example of that [contradictory] is the deviant-uncertain (*vyabhicāryanaikāntika*). The certain negative concomitance (*vyatirekaniścaya*) by means of the counter-example of that [deviant-uncertain] is [the valid reason].
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, Syādvādaratnākara, p. 518.
Therefore, since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) must necessarily be accepted, [it applies] to the reason in all three cases—*Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī*.
This has been extracted from: *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.
203; *Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 72;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 354.
By this, [the author] reaches a conclusion—*Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya-vārttika*, p. 1521; *Syādvāda-ratnākara*, p. 518.

Here it is said: The three-fold nature consisting of "presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth is not the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*), because it also exists in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Whatever exists even in the counter-example cannot be a definition, just as "existence" (*sattva*) is not a definition of fire. Furthermore, the three-fold nature consisting of "presence in the subject" and so forth exists even in the counter-example, which is the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

For it is precisely that unique nature which is exclusive to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) that is renowned in the world as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), such as the possession of a brilliant form and hot touch in the case of fire.

This triad of forms—namely, being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—is not of such a kind, because it occurs even in fallacious reasons (*tadābhāsa*), such as "being the son of that man," just like the five forms (*pañcarūpatva*) and so on.

Now, [the opponent claims] that the definition of the triple characteristic (*trairūpya*) is not merely the three features themselves, but rather the three features as possessing the rule of "non-occurrence otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti-niyama*); and since such a [rule] does not exist in that which merely appears to have those features, [they argue] that [the opponent's position] is also inconsistent. This being so, it would follow that the conceptualization of the triple characteristic is useless, because its capacity to produce cognition is established solely by that very rule; for even in a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*), there is the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its absence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).

Some say that the three characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*) consist in its existence only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), [existence in the dissimilar instances, and non-existence in the dissimilar instances]; however, this is not correct, because these [characteristics] can also occur in fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*),
and because the definition would not be contradicted even if the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) were excluded.

For the unique nature (*asādhāraṇa-svabhāva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of an entity because it is non-deviant, like the heat of fire; however, the three-fold form (*trairūpya*) is not unique, since it arises even in its cause and in what merely resembles it. (Tattvārthaśloka, p. 198). For comparison: "Indeed, that very essential nature which is unique to the object to be defined is recognized in the world as the defining characteristic because of its non-deviance, just as the possession of a brilliant form and a hot touch is [the characteristic] of fire."
—In the world, the characteristic is likewise uncommon to the opposite side by virtue of having that as its characteristic. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 518; Ātmatattvaviveka, p. 518; Śrāvakabhūmi).

Comparison: Furthermore, the definition of a probans (*sādhana*) is not merely its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), and its absence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); for this is established even in the case of a fallacious probans, such as "He is dark-complexioned because he is his son, like that other son of his."

For it is well-established that the probans, "being his son," which is pervaded by "darkness," exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*)—namely, in another son of his—and that there is the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), because "being his son" exists in the disputed son who has been made the subject; furthermore, because "being his son" is absent in some other son who is not dark in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), there is the mere absence [of the probans] in the dissimilar class.
And yet, by that much alone, the probans does not possess the status of being a means of proving the probandum.
(Pramāṇapaddhati, p. 70)
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 590; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 518; Prameya-ratnamālā, 3.
15 Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 40;
Nyāyadīpikā, p. 26.
The three-fold nature [of the reason] possesses the rule of inseparable connection;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of meaninglessness,
because it is precisely from the rule of "impossibility otherwise" [that the reason is established].
Indeed, in the inference of the rising of the constellation Śakaṭa from the rising of Kṛttikā, the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) does not actually exist.

If, however, it is argued that the property of the subject is stated here as follows: "The time, space, and so forth, possess the future rising of Śakaṭa, because they possess the rising of Kṛttikā, like previously observed times and spaces," then no reason would ever lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject. For even in the case of the blackness of a crow, when the whiteness of a palace is to be proven, it is easy to imagine the property of the subject by taking the entire world as the subject; for instance: "The world possesses the whiteness of the palace, because it possesses the blackness of the crow."

Likewise, [the argument] that "that [mountain] possesses fire because it possesses smoke from a kitchen, like the world previously perceived" contradicts common experience (*lokavirodha*); this [contradiction] is no different in other cases as well,
and thus the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is not a factor for the probans being indicative.

Comparison: For the rising of Kṛttikā is not present in the subject (dharmin), namely the wagon, when its rising is the property to be proven (sādhya); because that [rising] is a property of Kṛttikā, it therefore lacks the status of being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva). — *Pramāṇapaddhati*, p.
71; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 354.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 519; Prameyaratnākara, 3.15.

"Even so, in such formulations as 'the sun will rise tomorrow because [it rose] today,' or 'there has been an increase in the ocean because the moon is seen rising,' we observe that the reason functions as a means of cognition (*gamaka*) despite the absence of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Therefore, the property of being a characteristic of the subject is not the defining characteristic [of a valid reason]. — *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 591. *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 40.

If it is argued that, just as there is no inference of the rise of the ocean from the rise of the moon—because that would entail inferring it both before and after the moonrise—and rather the inference of it occurs only at the time of the moonrise since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped only then; if this is so, then the connection with that specific time is itself the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). In that case, that very time becomes the locus (*dharmin*), and the inference of the probandum occurs only therein; and since the moonrise is connected to that [time], how can there be the property of being a characteristic of the locus (*pakṣadharmatva*)? — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.3.
Regarding the comparison [of time] with the rising of the Kṛttikās and so forth, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the conceptualization of properties such as time;
*Pramāṇasamuccaya*, p. 104.

If, however, it is held that space or time is the subject (*dharmin*), and that "possessing a cart about to rise" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) while "the rising of the Pleiades" is the probans (*sādhana*) which is indeed a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), then in that case, let "possessing smoke from a kitchen" be the probans for proving "possessing fire supported by the great ocean" with respect to the subject "the earth. And thus, kitchen-smoke would lead to the inference of fire in the great ocean; consequently, there would be no reason (*hetu*) whatsoever that is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). — *Pramāṇapaddhati*, p.
71; *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 200.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 591; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 519; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 12.

If visibility were to possess the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) because of the conceptualization of time and so forth based on the rising of the Pleiades, the full moon, and so on, then why would it not exist in sound? — *Jainatarkavārttika-vṛtti*, p. 140;
*Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 35.

Nor does [the reason] exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), for we perceive that [reasons] such as "sound is impermanent because it is audible" and "everything is momentary because it exists" are indicative even in the absence of existence in the similar class;

since internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is established through the force of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), the postulation of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is useless for its being indicative, precisely because its status as an indicator is thus established in all cases.

Therefore, neither "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) nor "presence in the similar instance" (*sapakṣasattva*) is the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*). For example: [The inference] "the living body is possessed of a self because it possesses breath and so forth" [is valid] precisely because of the impossibility of its being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).
Because this reason, which is devoid of presence in similar instances (sapakṣa), has been supported,
the wise certainly conclude that concomitance (anvaya) is not a characteristic of a valid reason;
for it is established that existence itself is not pervaded by momentariness.

Furthermore, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, there is no proof for momentary destruction; for it is observed that [the property of] being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*), which is absent from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), serves as a means of cognition when the non-eternality of sound is to be proven. (Tattvārthaśloka, pp. 201–202)
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

355; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 519: Internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is the pervasion of the probans by the probandum only within the subject (*pakṣa*), whereas external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) occurs elsewhere.

Just as an object consists of multiple aspects (anekāntātmaka) because its existence is established in that very way— just as "this place possesses fire because it possesses smoke; whatever is thus is so, like a cooking place"—
*Pramāṇanaya* 3.36.

Since for a *sattva* (existence) or a *śrāvaṇatva* (audibility), the very certainty of its non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)— which is the essential nature of the certainty regarding the rule of inseparable connection with the probandum— is itself internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), let that alone be the primary definition of a logical reason; enough with any other definition.

Nor does the absence of presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) entail a lack of positive concomitance (ananvaya) for the reason, because there exists a positive concomitance (anvaya) characterized by internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), which consists in the logical possibility [of the probandum] given the reason, just like negative concomitance (vyatireka), which consists in the impossibility [of the reason] otherwise.

Indeed, it is not tenable to maintain the restriction that positive and negative concomitance must be established only in the subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin); for if that were so, it would follow that properties such as existence (sattva) could not serve as reasons for proving the momentariness of all things.
For momentariness is never established anywhere without positive concomitance, since there is even disagreement regarding sound, lightning, lamps, and so forth.

Comparison: Let that very certainty of non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), where the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent, be the *avinābhāva* (inseparable connection) itself; for it is of the nature of the reason (*hetu*). And thus it has been said in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 203:
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 356;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 521:
"Non-existence in the counter-example alone."
The definition [of the reason] is its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*);

for there exists the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) consisting in "being possible in that way" (i.e., being present in the similar class), which is the very nature of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), just as there is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consisting in "not being possible otherwise."
—Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
356; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 520: Likewise, the establishment of the means of proof occurs only when the probandum exists.
Otherwise, there would be no non-occurrence of the probans in the absence of the probandum;
for, according to the Śruti, even sound and the like are accepted as being eternal by virtue of their substantial nature (*dravyārthatā*).

As for what was also stated—that in the absence of the three forms such as "presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), the fallacies of the reason, such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), would necessarily follow—this too is an unconsidered assertion. For the avoidance of fallacies such as being unestablished is established precisely because this [reason] is characterized by the certainty of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). It is impossible to ascertain the rule of "inexplicability otherwise" for that which is itself unestablished, just as in the case of contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons.

Nevertheless, because the properties such as "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva) involve a proliferation of inseparable relations (avinābhāva), there would follow the undesirable consequence that one must state [additional features]: "certainty" (niścitatva) as another form [of the reason] in order to exclude cases such as the "unestablished" (asiddha); "having an unsublated object" (abādhitaviṣayatva) and so forth in order to exclude cases such as the "sublated object" (bādhitaviṣayatva).
Therefore, the three-fold definition of the reason consisting of "being a property of the subject" and so on, as conceived by the Buddhists, is not tenable.
(Page 438, Line 12)

Comparison (*tulanā*) is established by the very ascertainment of the rule that the reason cannot otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapattiniyama*), since this alone effects the avoidance of the three types of fallacies. For it is impossible to ascertain the rule that the reason cannot otherwise be accounted for if the reason itself is unestablished; rather, such ascertainment consists in the rule that the reason can be so accounted for. Furthermore, this [ascertainment] is impossible in the case of an unestablished, inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), or contradictory (*viruddha*) reason.
—*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 72;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 203; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 354.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 521; Prameyaratnākara, 3.15.
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), page 40; according to the commentary (ā॰ ṭi॰) on the reason (hetu):
"famous through the [logical] removal" (hāraprasi–), Śra॰, Ba॰.
Even though the unestablished (*asiddha*) and other fallacies lack invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*),

since the three forms of the *tulanā* (examination) are present therein, why is that [triple] statement not [sufficient], provided there is also the fourth statement consisting of the nature of certainty?

If, among the three forms [of a valid reason], the form of certainty is not present in the proof, then the reason would not suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished for the opponent; this is the meaning of the verse on reality in the *Tattvārtha* (p. 203).
*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p. 72;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 521.
"Non-cognition" means not being established; its state is "thatness"—Ācārya’s commentary.
The refutation of the five-fold definition as conceived by the Yogins.

Nor is the five-fold nature postulated by the Naiyāyikas [valid], because the three-fold nature consisting of *pakṣadharmatva* (presence in the subject) and so forth has already been rejected; furthermore, apart from the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), other factors such as "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) are impossible. Therefore, let that alone be the primary definition of a logical reason (*hetu*); what is the use of imagining a five-fold nature? For in cases such as "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance, like water," nothing other than the absence of inseparable connection is perceived as "having a contradicted object"; indeed, there is a contradiction between having a contradicted object and inseparable connection.

The existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*dharmin*) only when the probandum (*sādhya*) exists is "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*); and the occurrence of it there only in the absence of that [probandum] is "sublation of the object" (*viṣayabādha*). In this context, the remote object is "indicated" (*liṅgyate*), meaning it is known by means of this; thus it is called a "mark" (*liṅga*). And that [mark] possesses five characteristics.

What, then, are the five characteristics? They are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in similar instances (*sapakṣadharmatva*), exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*), non-sublation of the object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and the absence of a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*).

The subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to establish is the *pakṣa*; its meaning is "the state of being a property of that [subject]," which is to say, "being dependent upon it.

A different subject known through its connection with the property to be established is the *sapakṣa*; "existence therein" means contact with the property to be established. A subject devoid of contact with the property to be established is the *vipakṣa*; "exclusion from that" [is the required characteristic].

The non-sublation of the object to be inferred by either perception or scripture constitutes the "uncontradicted nature of the object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*); the state of not being undermined by a counter-inference employed as a seed of doubt constitutes "the absence of a rival argument" (*asatpratipakṣatva*). A logical mark (*liṅga*) endowed with these five characteristics becomes an inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*).
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 170;
Nyāyakalikā, p. 2;
Nyāyasāra, p. 6.

The inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the reason is fully established in either five or four members; therefore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) serves to indicate the two characteristics of being unsublated (*abādhitatva*) and having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣitatva*). (Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p. 302) Consequently, for the purpose of excluding these two—namely the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) and the "neutralized by an equal counter-argument" (*prakaraṇasama*)—the properties of having an unsublated object and having no counter-argument, as found in the same treatise (*samānatantra*), are to be inferred [as implied]. This is because the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated.
(Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā, p. 565)

Comparison—because apart from the state of being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvitva*), other [criteria] such as having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) are impossible—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 357.
Inseparability itself—comparison: "What is achieved by the five forms [of the reason] other than the state of being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapannatva*)?"
"What is accomplished by the five forms [of the reason] that consist in 'the impossibility of being otherwise'?"—*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 72; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 527.
—Other than that which is inseparable from the *dāva* (fire), according to Ā; other than that which lacks inseparability from the *dāva*, according to Śra.
For a comparison: because there is a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and inseparability (*avinābhāva*), it is thus:

those who, while admitting the aforementioned inseparability, consider the possibility of sublation, state another form [of the reason] consisting in "having a subject not sublated" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). However, this supposition of theirs is not possible, because sublation and inseparability are contradictory by virtue of their definition as being unable to coexist.

Establishing that very contradiction, he says: "For *avinābhāva* (inseparable connection), etc. Indeed, the inseparable connection of the reason (*hetu*) is said to exist only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists; however, there is sublation (*bādhā*) of it when that [property] is absent. For if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to operate against its absence while that [property] is actually present, then because of its erroneous nature, it would simply not be a valid cognition; so how could there be sublation? Therefore, that reason, possessing those characteristics and being inseparably connected to the property to be proven, would exist in the subject (*dharmin*). And in this case, why would the property to be proven not exist, such that there would be room for sublation?

Therefore, there is an impossibility of coexistence between invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhā*); for that which is established by invariable concomitance and its absence are contradictory—characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion—and thus cannot reside in a single locus (*dharmin*).
(Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 195b;
Vādanyāya-ṭīkā, p. 138)
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 448; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
357; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 41.
The existence of the logical reason (hetu) in the subject (dharmin), which is the very absence of the property to be proven (sādhyābhāva), constitutes the counter-example (vipakṣa).

Furthermore, would the characteristic of a logical reason (*hetu*) be "having a subject matter that is not sublated" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), either as something certain or uncertain? It cannot be uncertain, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and moreover, that which is unknown cannot be a constituent part of a probative reason. Nor can it be certain, because the basis for such certainty is impossible. For what could be the basis for that certainty? Non-perception (*anupalambha*), correspondence (*saṃvāda*), or something else? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because non-perception pertaining to all persons is unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The second alternative is also untenable; for prior to the operation of inference, the correspondence [of the object] is unestablished.

If it is admitted that this correspondence is established subsequent to that [operation], there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). To explain: the establishment of correspondence occurs through the operation of inference, and the operation of inference occurs because the non-sublation of its object is established. Alternatively, is there some other factor? Is that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) regarding that object, or is it the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)? In the first case, if the non-sublation of the object is apprehended from some other means of valid cognition, the reason (*hetu*) would be redundant, since the probandum (*sādhya*) would already be apprehended by that very same means.

For when the existence of the probandum (*sādhyasadbhāva*) is not cognized, the absence of its sublation (*tadvādhāviraha*) cannot be ascertained. If it is argued that this cognition [of the probandum] arises from the cognition of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), that is not so; for according to those who maintain that invariable concomitance is fully realized only in a reason possessing the five characteristics (*pañcarūpa*), the cognition of invariable concomitance itself is impossible if the "unsublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) is not cognized. Consequently, since the "unsublated object" remains unestablished, it is not logical to define the reason by means of that [absence of sublation].

Comparison: Is the uncontradicted nature of the object (abādhitaviṣayatva) the definition of a logical reason (hetu), whether it be ascertained or unascertained?—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 358. Regarding the ascertainment of the uncontradicted nature of the object, the comparison is: for that [ascertainment] must be based either on non-perception (anupalambha) or on corroboration (savāda).
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 358.
For comparison: "The non-perception of all [things] is doubtful, while one's own non-perception is inconclusive;
for even when dūrvā grass and the like are not perceived in a hole in the Vindhya mountains, they nonetheless exist."
The doubt regarding the non-apprehension of both [the object] itself and everything else is unestablished— *Nyāyabindu*, verse 4.6; *Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 65.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 13; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 18; *Ātmatattvaviveka*, p. 94.
In the *Tarkabhāṣā* (Moḷi edition), page 22, and the *Nyāyalīlāvatī*, page 22:

Non-perception (*anupalambha*) pertaining to all [persons] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible to know it without being omniscient (*sarvajña*). However, non-perception pertaining to oneself is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) due to [the existence of] specific mental states (*cetovṛttiviśeṣa*) in others and so forth.
If one accepts the establishment of correspondence immediately following the operation of inference,
then when purposeful activity (arthakriyā) occurs, correspondence— characterized by the stability of purposeful activity— is established.
Comparison—the determination that there is no sublation of that [object]—is already established by the means of proof; what then is the use of the reason?
Just as when there is a certainty regarding the existence or non-existence of sublation of the object of the reason.
(Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 205)

Even then, the reason is ineffective; for just as a reason is ineffective because it is incapable of proving its object when the existence of a sublation (bādhā) of that object is ascertained, so too, when the absence of sublation is ascertained from some source, the existence of that object is established. Thus, for one who proceeds to prove that [existence], there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
526. [This is] indeed from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
To determine [the validity of a cognition]—
[this requires] the realization that its object is unsublated (avādhitaviṣayatva)— [is the view] of the Naiyāyikas (yauga). (Āloka-ṭīkā) (Āloka-ṭīkā)

In these five characteristics, inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is fully established—*Nyāyakalika*, p. 2. Furthermore, if its existence is not understood, there can be no absence of a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatvam*). For would a counter-argument be refuted as being of equal strength or of unequal strength? If it were of equal strength, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) would be untenable.

Between two things that possess equal strength, there can be no relationship of the sublated and the sublator, as in the case of two kings; and since the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) are of equal strength, what causes their lack of equal strength? Is it caused by the presence or absence of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, or is it produced by the sublation of the inference? The first alternative is not tenable, because there is no difference between the two regarding the property of being a predicate of the subject and so on;

for when "foolishness" is to be proven, it is not the case that "being his son" and the like cannot be a predicate of the subject, nor is it the case that only the mark consisting of the interpretation of a scripture can be such a predicate.
The second alternative is also untenable; for the sublation of the inference remains unestablished even now.

Indeed, when two [arguments] are indistinguishable regarding their presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and other criteria, it is not logical for one to be sublated while the other is the sublater, since that consequence would apply equally to both.

Furthermore, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): namely, that sublation by inference occurs only when there is a disparity in strength, and such disparity in strength exists only when there is sublation.

Therefore, the following statement is well-said: "Inference is the cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) from the mark (liṅga) as it has been described. This is because the counter-argument (pratipakṣa) may be either of equal strength or of unequal strength—[as stated in] the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 359.
Therefore, he says: "For when the characteristic is equal," and so forth.

This means that when there is a perception of a characteristic that is equal to the counter-reason (*pratihetu*) being suspected—namely, one whose nature of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is based merely on observation or non-observation—in such a case, the possibility of a counter-reason acting as a sublater (*bādhaka*) is observed; this [possibility] gives rise to a doubt regarding the existence of a counter-reason even in those cases where a counter-reason with an equal characteristic is not seen.
What is the reason? Because there is no distinction between one whose counter-positive is unobserved and one whose counter-positive is observed;

for there is indeed no difference between that [unobserved case] and the other [observed case] such that the possibility of its [counter-positive] occurrence could not be suspected. Now, if it is maintained that the certainty of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—which is characterized by a specific restriction—is required for the case where the counter-positive is observed, so that the suspicion regarding the possibility of the counter-positive may vanish, then, even if such a distinction exists, that very distinction must be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the logical reason (*hetu*).
—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, fol. 204A.
[The reading] "pakṣayoḥ" is found in manuscript *ba*;
for it is also possible that [the reason] "this person is not a fool because of his exposition of the treatise" might apply to both sides—Ācārya’s note.

"Is it not the case that since this [process] is fruitless, what is the point of the effort to define its nature? For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be fruitful, and not otherwise, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To dispel such a doubt, he says "its fruit," etc.

The fruit of that inference is "rejection" (*hāna*), which is the first of a series beginning with rejection, such as acquisition (*upādāna*) and so forth; the cognitions (*buddhi*) of these constitute the result.

Now, the claim that "there is no real means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor its fruit, other than specific latencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanāviśeṣa*)," is likewise charming only so long as it remains unexamined; for the existence of both of these as something real has been explained in detail in the *Laghīyastraya-kārikā* (verse 7), where it is stated: "The preceding [cognition] would be the means of valid cognition and the subsequent one the fruit. This is because inference has been thoroughly established [in that work].
Because there would be the undesirable consequence of having to investigate even such things as the teeth of a crow (p.

and because inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is restricted solely to identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), the Buddhist's prima facie argument is that this [inseparable connection] is established only in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

On this point, the Buddhist says: "As for what was stated—that there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), and so forth—that is well said; for it is solely by the power of inseparable connection that the logical reason (*hetu*) is understood as a means of cognition in all cases. The inseparable connection with existence (*satva*) is restricted only to the reasons of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*), because it is necessarily determined by identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*). For the inseparable connection of the reason of essential nature is fully established through identity, while that of the reason of effect is established through origination from that.
Furthermore, there is no other mark (*liṅga*), since even non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is included within the reason of essential nature."

For the absence of a jar and so forth has as its nature the ground and so forth as distinguished from the jar and so forth; and the non-perception of that [jar] is the perception of the ground and so forth as distinguished from it.
This occurs solely by virtue of the power of invariable concomitance with the probandum (sādhyāvinābhāva). Thus, what was said is incorrect.

And that necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the mark (*liṅga*) with the object to be proven (*sādhya*) exists because [the mark] is in reality identical with the object to be proven or arises from it;

for that which does not have the nature of X or does not arise from X lacks a nature that is necessarily connected to it. Furthermore, since those two—identity and origination—belong only to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*), it is through these two alone that the real entity (*vastu*) is established.
—Nyāyabindu, p. 40–42:

"The rule of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is established by either the relation of cause and effect or by essential identity (svabhāva) as the regulating factors; it is known through perception, not through non-perception."

Precisely because [the reason] is indicative by virtue of a necessary connection—whether that be the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which acts as the regulator by establishing the non-deviation between the probandum and the probans, or the essential nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) which acts as the regulator—the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the effect or the essential nature as a logical mark means that its existence does not occur without the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.33;
Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 6B)

The proponents of logic state that only that which is ascertained as being related through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is a valid means of proof for establishing [the probandum]— *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 429.

By the statement "through the existence of the effect" (*kāryasadbhāva*) [in the case of] the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*), all these ten applications of non-perception, beginning with the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), are included within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). — *Nyāyabindu*, p. 55.
However, non-apprehension is included within intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

since the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature is included within the reason of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvahetu*), its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is characterized solely by identity (*tādātmya*). (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 431)

As for the non-perception of the pervading cause (*vyāpakakāraṇānupalabdhi*), it establishes the absence of the pervaded and the pervader precisely through the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—Hetubindu-ṭīkā, p. 7A. For when two things are conjoined within a single cognition, the perception of one is itself the non-perception of the other; and that non-perception is itself the perception of its absence, since if [the other] were present, its non-perception would be impossible.

As it has been said: "When all other causes are present, existence is apprehension because of its non-deviation from that [object]; non-existence is non-apprehension due to the absence of that; and non-apprehension is the apprehension of something else.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.5)
The non-perception of a jar is the perception of that which is devoid of a jar.

And the understanding of that [invariable concomitance] arises from inferential knowledge (*ūha*); this too is mere faith, because the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is understood through the fivefold method of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).

To explain: even when objects such as the ground are perceived apart from fire and smoke, there is first one non-perception, namely of both fire and smoke; then follows a pair of perceptions—first the perception of fire, and then the perception of smoke; finally, there are two non-perceptions—first the non-perception of fire, and immediately after, the non-perception of smoke. Thus, by means of this pentad of perceptions and non-perceptions, the causal relation is understood even in a single instance: smoke is the effect of fire, and whatever is the effect of something is necessarily restricted to it.
If it were not determined by that [cause], then, due to its independence, it would either always exist or never exist;
and that which is determined possesses a regulator, for in the absence of such a regulator, the consequence of its perpetual existence or non-existence would follow again due to its autonomy.

Consequently, this meaning is established: whatever is observed to arise from something even once arises from that alone and not from anything else; for if its arising were without a cause, everything would arise from everything. Thus, through the fivefold method of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) and the two types of essential identity as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is apprehended, as well as the realization of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
This and more is also stated in the *Bṛhat-ṭīkā*.
Comparison—Nyāyaku. p. 12, note 3:

"The first non-perception of smoke in a place distinct from fire; then, after that, the perception of fire and subsequently the perception of smoke—this constitutes two perceptions; and afterwards, the non-perception of fire and immediately thereafter the non-perception of smoke as well—these constitute two non-perceptions. Thus, the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises from this pentad of perception and non-perception. This is the established doctrine. As it has been said: 'The cognition of fire is dependent on the cognition of smoke; the cognition of smoke is dependent on that [cognition of fire]...'"
"By means of perception and non-perception"—thus [it is established] through five [steps]. (Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p.
11). The causal relationship is established by means of perception and non-perception.
—*Hetubindu*, p. 53B.
The word "perception" (*upalambha*) is to be supplied as the remainder—[reading] *upalambhānanta-* in Ānandaśrī’s edition.

"Smoke is invariably concomitant with fire because it is its effect"; [this implies that] smoke must either always exist or never exist in relation to fire, since the reason does not depend on anything else.
For it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible—
*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.36.
Smoke is the determiner of fire because it is invariably concomitant with it by virtue of being its effect;
the word "arises" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
[This occurs] in the form of being a determiner of the aforementioned invariable concomitance—Ānandajñāna’s Commentary (Ā-ṭī).

The two previously mentioned reasons—namely, necessity and the character of being a regulator—are established for the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) by means of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). For instance, as existence is [established] through momentariness; that is to say: existence is characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and causal efficiency is pervaded by succession and simultaneity. These two, when excluding the non-momentary, exclude causal efficiency which is pervaded by them, and that [causal efficiency] is existence.
If it is asked: why is there an exclusion of succession and simultaneity from that which is non-momentary? It is because of its manifold nature (*nānārūpatva*).

For succession is a temporal priority and posteriority, while simultaneity is the opposite of that; thus, these two are manifold in form. Non-momentariness, however, is a single uniform nature (*ekarūpatā*). A single uniform nature and a manifold nature are contradictory when residing in one substratum. Therefore, existence (*sattva*), by excluding itself from the non-momentary, remains only in the momentary, since no other alternative is possible;
for there is no third category distinct from the momentary and the non-momentary in which its occurrence might be suspected.
"Sound is either produced or whatever exists is impermanent, such as a jar and so forth.
Herein is the demonstration of the subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the contrapositive of the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*):

if everything that exists or is produced were not subject to momentary destruction, then because successive and simultaneous causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would be impossible for a non-momentary entity, it would be excluded from the definition characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency; consequently, it would be a non-entity (*asad*).
For that which is characterized by an absence of any description of causal capacity is indeed "indefinable" (nirupākhyam)—*Vādanyāya*, p.
7; *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 143.
Hetubindu-ṭīkā, folio 143A;
Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi, page 20; Nyāyakuñjara, page 8, note 1.
Succession and simultaneity [are the defining characteristics of] causal efficiency—
[which excludes] simultaneity.
Succession (*krama*) is defined as a sequence characterized by the non-simultaneity of other effects, or the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the sprout and so forth;

simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is its association with other effects such as the seed and so forth; and a different mode is the sprout and so forth being otherwise even in the absence of those two states. Furthermore, it is the state of being produced from a cause—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 143b—wherein [the effect] is both unitary and... [fragmentary].
There is no single uniformity (ekarūpatā) [of existence] in the third moment, which is distinct from both the momentary and the non-momentary; rather, existence exists in another mode.
Furthermore, all non-perception (anupalabdhi) is included within the non-perception of essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi),

and the non-perception of essential nature is itself an essential nature reason (svabhāvahetu). Since its necessary connection (pratibandha) consists precisely in identity (tādātmya), there is no need for a separate investigation into its connection.

Demonstrating that even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), there is the possibility of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and thus reasons such as smoke and sunrise possess probative power—this is now addressed:

regarding what was first stated—that "invariable concomitance is restricted by identity and causality," and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion. For identity is not the cause for the restriction of invariable concomitance; because when identity exists, there is an absence of difference, and in the absence of a distinction, a relation cannot exist, whereby invariable concomitance would be untenable, since a relation has difference as its locus.
Furthermore, for one who maintains that [the reason] does not have a non-essential nature (*anaśārthavādin*), neither identity (*tādātmya*) nor difference (*bheda*) is even slightly tenable.

For identity is the state of having that as one's own nature; it is the oneness of the probans with the probandum. And where there is oneness, difference is impossible; or where there is difference, there is no oneness. Therefore, how could a *śiṃśapā* tree indicate a "tree" by way of identity? Moreover, if the indicator functions through identity, then because the probandum is already understood at the very moment the reason is apprehended—due to its being non-distinct from it—inference would lack its efficacy.
For a sign (*liṅga*) that has not been apprehended does not produce a cognition whose object is the bearer of the sign (*liṅgin*).

If the probans (*liṅga*) and the cognition [of it] are apprehended, but the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) does not appear, then how can there be identity (*tādātmya*) between those two? If, however, it does appear, then the futility of inference is established, as well as the fallacy of the reason being a mere part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).

If you argue that its efficacy lies in its purpose of excluding contrary superimpositions (*viparītasamāropavyavaccheda*), then we ask: would such a superimposition occur when its own nature is already cognized, or when it is not cognized? In the former case, what occasion is there for a contrary superimposition? For indeed, when the specific features such as the head and hands are perceived, the superimposition of a post (*sthāṇusamāropa*) does not occur.
But if its own nature is not apprehended, what talk can there be of the superimposition of something contrary? (p.

444, l. 10). For comparison: likewise, there is no relation of identity between "tree-ness" and "śiṃśapā-ness," because it would follow that the relationship of probandum and probans could not be established.

For instance: "If the locus (*dharmin*) is perceived, then because of its identity with that [property], both would be perceived; how then could there be the relationship of the probandum and the probans?
(*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 571).

Furthermore, if there were identity (*tādātmya*), how could there be the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer? For it is not logical that the very same thing should be both the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*), since that relationship depends upon difference.

"Nor is the relationship of the signified and the signifier possible in a case of identity, because it is impossible for a single thing to be both known and unknown at the same time. (Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, p.
163; Bṛhatīpañjikā, p. 95)

Furthermore, the inference that [is based on] identity (*tādātmya*) is not at all sound; for the mark (*liṅga*), the object to be proven (*sādhya*), and the object known through the mark (*laiṅgika*) must be established [as distinct]. Identity between that which is already established and that which is yet to be proven is not tenable—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 67.

Moreover, the determination of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamakabhāva*) is not logical in the case of identity, because that relationship is grounded in difference (*bheda*).

If the tree is not apprehended when the *śiṃśapā*-ness is being apprehended, where is the identity (*tādātmya*)? If it is apprehended, where is the inference? — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 207. Furthermore, if identity is intended as the basis for the capacity to indicate, then because there would be no distinction between the probandum and the probans, there would be an absence of a relation, and thus the impossibility of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 533. (The Buddhist view).

Regarding the comparison: first, in the case of identity (*tādātmya*), since the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) are non-distinct, the very relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is difficult to establish.
Indeed, a sign (*liṅga*) that has not been apprehended cannot produce the cognition of the signified (*liṅgin*).

In that regard, when the cognition of the sign arises, does the sign and the signified appear therein or not? If they do not appear, then since the signified is not grasped by that cognition, how can it be identical with it?

If, however, the object is directly perceived within the manifestation itself—just like the logical mark (liṅga)—then what is the use of inference? (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 113). Furthermore, if the [mark] functions as a means of cognition through identity (*tādātmya*), then since the probandum (*sādhya*) would have already been cognized at the very moment the reason (*hetu*) is apprehended, inference would lack its efficacy.
(*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 353).
Because it is non-different from its cause through identity (*tādātmya*),
the word *gṛhīti* takes the locative singular case even when there is the apprehension of gender (*liṅga*), since the particle *ca* has the sense of "also" (*api*).
When there is a cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), and when the probandum (*sādhya*) appears,

[it is understood that] in the case of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*) and the *śiṃśapā*-ness (*śiṃśapātvatva*)— which constitute the probandum and the probans respectively— the very tree-ness that is the probandum and constitutes a part of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is identical with the *śiṃśapā*-ness which is the reason (*hetu*). Thus, the meaning is that because the probandum is unestablished (*asiddha*), the reason is also unestablished.

If it is argued that inference is for the sake of excluding a contrary superimposition (*viparīta-samāropa-vyavaccheda*), we say no; for when the true nature of an object is apprehended, there is no opportunity for a contrary superimposition to arise.

Indeed, when the specific features such as a head and hands are perceived, the superimposition of a post (*sthāṇu*) does not occur. In that case, [the exclusion] might be possible because of the difference between them—for a head and hands are not themselves the person—and thus even upon perceiving those [features], the superimposition of a non-person might still occur. But here, since "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness" are non-different, once "śiṃśapā-ness" is apprehended, what talk can there be of the superimposition of something other than a tree?
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 113)
In the nature of the reason—such as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* tree or existence—[the probans] may [be absent from the dissimilar instance]. (Āloka-ṭīkā, p. 535)

For when the nature of the reason (*hetu*)—characterized as *śiṃśapā*-ness—is established, since it is non-different from that [tree], "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is also necessarily perceived; how then could there be a superimposition (*āropa*) of its opposite, namely "non-treeness"?

Furthermore, while the superimposition of "non-śiṃśapā-ness" might occasionally occur upon the apprehension of treeness due to the apprehension of a general property (*sāmānya*) and the non-apprehension of the particular (*viśeṣa*), the superimposition of "non-treeness" cannot occur when *śiṃśapā*-ness is apprehended;
for if one's perception of *śiṃśapā*-ness is direct, one's perception of treeness is not indirect.

Comparison—Furthermore, when a tree is perceived, because its general properties are apprehended while its specific qualities remain undetermined, there might occasionally be the superimposition of "non-śiṃśapā-ness"; however, it is not logical for there to be the superimposition of "non-tree-ness" once *śiṃśapā*-ness has been apprehended. For it is not at all common in the world that one who has the *śiṃśapā*-ness within the range of perception should have the "tree-ness" beyond the range of perception.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 114.
How can "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) be perceived through perception? [The opponent replies: "It is not imperceptible.

Furthermore, if there is no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), then just as tree-ness is inferred by means of *śiṃśapā*-ness, why is it that *śiṃśapā*-ness is not likewise inferred by means of tree-ness, since there is no difference in their identity (*tādātmya*)? If you say that *śiṃśapā*-ness alone is restricted to tree-ness, but tree-ness is not restricted to *śiṃśapā*-ness, then the capacity to indicate [the object] does not arise from identity, but rather from inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) alone.
Therefore, there is no necessity of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) in identity (*tādātmya*).

For example: "Even though there is no difference in the identity of both [the tree and the *śiṃśapā*], just as a tree is cognized by way of being a *śiṃśapā*, the cognition of *śiṃśapā*-ness by way of being a tree would also [absurdly] occur"—Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā, p.

Furthermore, because there is no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), just as "tree-ness" is inferred from "śiṃśapā-ness," so too "śiṃśapā-ness" would be inferred from "tree-ness," since there is no difference in their identity (*tādātmya*).

Consequently, the distinction stated between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "being immediately preceded by effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*)—based on whether they pervade the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or not—would be lost.

Now, it may be argued that the relation (*sambandha*) is one thing and the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is another: a relation resides in two terms (*dviṣṭha*), whereas a necessary connection is characterized by dependence upon another.

In that case, the state of being a *śiṃśapā* (a type of tree) is restricted to [the category of] "tree-ness," but "tree-ness" is not restricted to "being a *śiṃśapā*"; likewise, the property of "occurring immediately after an effort" is necessarily concomitant with "impermanence," but "impermanence" is not [necessarily concomitant] with it. This is true; however, if this were asserted, it would be an admission of mere restriction (*niyama*), not identity (*tādātmya*).

For if there were identity (*tādātmya*), just as a *śiṃśapā* tree is never seen without being a *śiṃśapā*, so too "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) would never be seen devoid of a *śiṃśapā*. Yet, tree-ness is observed in the *khadira* tree and elsewhere even when devoid of a *śiṃśapā*; and impermanence (*anityatva*) is perceived in lightning and other such things even when devoid of the property of "following immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*). How, then, can there be non-difference? To say that this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists without the proving property (*sādhanadharma*), and yet is its very self (*tadātmā*) despite being distinct from it—this is a mere deception.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 114)
Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 67;
Syādvādaratnākara, p.
535—[as] a counter-argument due to its being [a state of] destruction. Śrauta.

—then it is not [established] by way of essential identity (*tādātmya*), nor by way of origination from that (*tadutpatti*); for even among the properties of smoke produced from fire, such as blackness and so forth, an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is not observed.

Furthermore, the relation of cause and effect does not exist between two universals, but rather between two particulars. And those two [particulars] whose relation of cause and effect is known in places such as a kitchen do not possess the relation of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*); whereas those two situated on the mountain which possess the relation of the signified and the signifier, their relation of cause and effect is not known.
Furthermore, when that [invariable concomitance] is not cognized, it is impossible to grasp the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between those two;
nor can that ungrasped relation serve as a factor for inference at that time.
If, however, it were grasped, then since the cognition of the probandum would have already arisen at the very moment of understanding the reason, what would be the use of inference?

Comparison—The effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is also not possible; for according to you, the relation of cause and effect must exist either between two moments or between two continuums (*santāna*). If smoke were to lead to the inference of fire because it is its effect, then it would also have to be an indicator of fire by virtue of such properties as being pungent, dirty, or moving through the sky.

Yet, it is not logically tenable for smoke to be both an effect of that [fire] in some respect and not an effect of it in another respect, because that which possesses a complete nature arises only by following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [cause].
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 116)
In the case of smoke and fire, which stand in the relation of effect and cause, their causal relationship [is established].

While there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between smoke and fire situated on a mountain, at the time of the application of inference, one must accept that the invariable concomitance between cause and effect is being apprehended.

—[The opponent] objects: "If the restriction of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is based on identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), then how can there be the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between the rising of the Pleiades (*kṛttikā*) and the rising of the constellation Rohiṇī (*śakaṭa*), or between the rising of the moon and the swelling of the ocean, since identity and causality are absent in those cases?

[Response: In all such cases, that which is inseparably connected with another in terms of place and time is the sign (*liṅga*) of the latter. The mention of "effect" (*kārya*) and so forth in the treatise is for the sake of illustration; it is not intended as a definitive restriction.
Why? Because of the observation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For example: the *adhvaryu* priest’s call for attention (*ośrāvaya*) is a mark of the *hotṛ* priest who is spatially separated; the rising of the moon is a mark of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lotuses; and the clarity of the water in autumn is a mark of the rising of the star Agastya.
All such cases are established by the statement "this belongs to that."
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
562; *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 117:

Furthermore, if one were to accept only those constraints characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), then there would be no inference of touch from the perception of color, no cognition of sunrise from [the observation of] sunset, and no inference of Rohiṇī from the rising of Kṛttikā, because identity and causality are absent in these cases.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 571.

Furthermore, inferers infer a form other than taste as being simultaneous with the taste; yet between these two there is neither a causal relationship nor identity. Moreover, there is no causal relationship or identity between today’s rising of the sun and yesterday’s rising of the sun, nor between the rising of the moon at the same time as the swelling of the ocean, nor between the rising and setting of the eighth lunar mansion and the observation of the middle mansion; and yet, a relationship of indicator and indicated is observed [in all such cases].
—*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 161–163;
*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 67;
*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī*, p. 209.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 199; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 593; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 536.

Regarding the statement concerning the cause of the rising of Kṛttikā and so forth—that "the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is apprehended by the fivefold method of perception and non-perception" (*pratyakṣānupalambhapañcaka*)—that too is incorrect. This is because perception is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), and non-perception likewise consists in the perception of another object; thus, even if these were to operate a hundred times, they lack the capacity to grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Indeed, non-conceptual perception is not capable of performing such operations as "this occurs only when that exists" and "otherwise it does not occur at all," because it arises through the power of a proximate object and is devoid of deliberation; this has been stated immediately above.
Nor can the conceptual construction arising from it [perform these], since you do not admit its validity (prāmāṇya).
(Page 444, Line 16)
By way of non-conceptuality— [Ārya-ṭīkā; see page 427,
line 2, regarding the absence of the probandum].
The Buddhist maintains that conceptualization is produced by non-conceptual [perception],
and that the relationship of probans and probandum exists between two real entities through their exclusions.

Furthermore—“Moreover, how can this be consistent: that two exclusions (vyāvṛtti) stand in the relation of sign and signified (liṅga-liṅgin), that there is a necessary connection (pratibandha) between them, and that they are apprehended by conceptual constructions (vikalpa) as real entities?
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 117.

For that which is accepted as the essential nature of the relation—namely, identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)—is it a property of a real entity (*vastu*), or a property of a form superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? In this regard, it cannot be a superimposed property; for a real entity is produced by a real entity, and a real entity must possess the nature of a real entity.
Therefore, the relation is a property of a real entity, yet a real entity is not touched by conceptual constructions, while their relation is nonetheless determined.

This is a strange thing you have said yourself: that the relation of a real entity consists of identity and so forth, and that the status of being the signifier and the signified belongs to two exclusions (*apoha*) superimposed by conceptual constructions.

Thus, it is all a deception that the connection is in one place, the means of grasping it in another, the cognition in another, and the activity and attainment in yet another—[as stated in] *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
34. Who other than a Buddhist would say that its grasping occurs through conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)? [As stated in] *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 117.

As for what was stated— that the pervasion of the probans by the probandum is cognized through a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the heterogeneous instance (*vipakṣa*) of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)— that too is mere words; because the subverting proof regarding the heterogeneous instance, characterized as the non-perception of [the probandum] either successively or simultaneously,

is itself an inference, and an inference is capable of establishing its own probandum only when its own pervasion is already established, otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, in that case as well, is the pervasion (vyāpti) apprehended by another inference or by the first inference? If it is by another inference, there is an infinite regress (anavasthā);
if it is by the first inference, there is mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).

Therefore, you who accept inference must admit that reasoning which grasps pervasion is a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara), because its apprehension is impossible through either perception or inference.
pṛ. 445, l. 11 – "The definition and inference (anumāna)...
[Ba]: Inference (anumāna) is that by which something is inferred; it is the logical reason (hetu).

Regarding the statement, "That which is eternal is devoid of causal efficiency because neither succession nor simultaneity is observed," the explanation of the commentary (*vivṛti*) concerns the impossibility of apprehending the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
He says this very thing: "Not indeed," and so forth.

That which has the self (*ātman*) as its probandum (*sādhya*)—the state of that is "identity" (*tādātmya*). From that probandum, the acquisition of one's own nature is "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). Furthermore, these two form a *dvandva* compound characterized by mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).

Now, since the word *tadutpatti* ends in a vowel, does it not follow that it should be placed first according to the rule? It is not so; for according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Jainendra Vyākaraṇa 2.2.35), [the word denoting the cause takes precedence].
2.104 Thus, because of this lack of invariable concomitance (*anaikāntikatva*),
those two— identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)— cannot possibly be known at all.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Without," and so forth.

*Anyathānupapatti*—the impossibility or non-occurrence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the manner of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—is that which is related to it by way of being its apprehender; this is *tarka*. Without that [tarka], even though identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth exist between "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapātvādi*), it has been established that only "śiṃśapā-ness" and the like possess the capacity to indicate "tree" and so forth, and not "tree-ness" and the like for "śiṃśapā" and so forth, solely by virtue of the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Now, demonstrating that the capacity to indicate exists even in the absence of those [logical reasons] by the force of that [invariable concomitance] alone, he says: "By those two," and so forth.

Establishing this very point, he says "not indeed," and so forth; for (hi) because—without those two, namely identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—there is the establishment, accomplishment, or determination of the single-characterized inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), taste and so forth are included.

Regarding "shadow and so forth" (*chāyādi*), here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes color-form (*rūpa*) and the like. The intended meaning is that [the relationship is one of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because of the spatial distinction between the tree and its shadow, or [one of] effect (*kārya*) because of their coexistence. Because it ends in *ścy*, the technical term *su*—which is used in place of the Pāṇinian technical term *dhi* for the sake of brevity—is employed according to the Jainendra Vyākaraṇa.
In a dvandva compound, [the final vowel of the first member] becomes *su*.
In a *dvandva* compound, that which ends in *s* should be placed first— Jainendra-vyākaraṇa 2.4.105.
Regarding the grammatical rule *dvandve su*, although the word *hetu* here ends in the suffix *su*, it does not undergo *pūrvanipāta* (prior placement); thus says [the author] in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Even in the case of trees and the like, although there is an absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*),
[the inference occurs] solely by virtue of the power of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).

For the shadow of a tree and so forth does not have [the tree] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because of the difference in location and other factors; nor is it an effect (*kārya*), because of their coexistence—[Āloka-ṭīkā].
[Variant readings: *deśādibhe* (Śrā., Ba.)].

Now, it might be argued that from the taste being tasted, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is inferred, and from that, there is an inference of the color and the shadow through "inference of the inferred" (*anumitānumāna*). This too is incorrect; for such a conventional usage does not exist. Indeed, a practical agent does not infer the causal complex from the taste being tasted, because that would entail the non-perception of the present color and so forth. Consequently, neither the inference—"this mango fruit has such-and-such a color because it has such-and-such a taste"—nor the inference of the simultaneous hot touch from seeing the color of fire, nor the subsequent activity of one desiring that [touch] toward it, would be possible.

Furthermore, you extend your investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), since you state [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: "Validity [is established] by way of convention" (PV 2.5). Moreover, if one were to infer form from its causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there would follow the fallacy of inferring an effect from its cause, which would result in a contradiction regarding the number of logical marks (*liṅga*).

From that, it is established: the inference of shadow and so forth from a tree and so forth—which are neither its effect nor its essential nature—will then involve deviation (*vyabhicāra*). To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.
And there is indeed no non-conformity or deviation in the inference of shadow and so forth from a tree and so forth, because that [shadow] is perceived upon reaching [the object].
On this very point, he states another illustration:

"The cognition of color and so forth, which depend on the same causal complex, occurs through the inference of a causal property from taste, just as [fire is inferred] from the transformation of fuel by smoke."

And as for the cognition of color and so forth from taste—starting with sweet and the rest—the word "and so forth" (ādi) including odor and touch—which [cognition] depends on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) as the taste and other qualities, how does that occur? He says: by means of the inference of the properties of the cause. The property of the cause of taste is its being the producer of color and so forth, which coexist with the taste; by the inference of that [property], there is the cognition of color and so forth from the taste. For the effect, the taste, does not exist without a cause, and its cause is the producer of color which acts as a concomitant to the taste, because of the production of a complex from a complex (*puñjāt puñjotpatti*).
Therefore, when that [cause] is inferred, color is indeed inferred, just as in the case of smoke and the transformation of fuel.

By means of inferring the property of the cause from smoke, there is an inference of the transformation of the fuel, such as charcoal, or of that which coexists with the smoke— *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 3.8.

Therefore, this meaning is determined from the taste: that [the cause] produces a form coexisting with that [taste]. Indeed, its status as a producer of a form coexisting with the taste is determined only if there is also a determination of the form coexisting with it; thus, for things belonging to the past and to the same time, there is only one way of knowing, namely that born from the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgaja*). — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 3.126.
8. Hetubinduṭīkā, folio 54A: sāmāgryānu– (variant: sāmagryānu–) in manuscript Ba; sāmagryānu– in manuscript Śra.
Inference through inference—[as found in] Ātmatattvaviveka and Bhāsarvajña’s Nyāyasāra—compares:

"Because the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer is observed between two moments that are simultaneous; for instance, from the moment of color (*rūpakṣaṇa*), the touch (*sparśa*) of the same time-period is inferred, not one belonging to a prior time. In that case, because they depend on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), there is no proof whatsoever for the existence of a mutual causality in the production of color and touch, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of one with the other are not perceived."
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
571: Furthermore, for worldly people, there is an inference of form from taste;
yet these people with fleshy eyes do not determine the mutual difference between moments.
And those who do not ascertain [the cause] are not able to infer the cause of the taste by means of the capacity of the material cause of the activity—[Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p.
163]—because such [an inference] is not perceived by the world; rather, it is from the taste that the world understands the color.
And worldly consensus must be followed even by investigators—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 67; *Yuktibhāṣya*, p.
The meaning is that it does not attain [the object]; rather, this very fruit is directed toward the cessation of craving (*vairāgya-agra*).—Ārya-ṭīkā.
For one who desires the sensation of heat, there is no engagement with form and so forth; rather, [there is engagement] with the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).—Ārya-ṭīkā.
And the Buddhist [position] regarding practice is as follows:

from taste, which is the effect, its cause—color—must be inferred; and from that color, which is the cause thus inferred, its effect—color simultaneous with the taste—must be inferred. Thus, inference of an effect from a cause is something other than [inference based on] identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*); therefore, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) does not occur through those two alone.
—Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 162; Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 67; Bṛhatī-pañjikā, p. 94.

By those who desire the inference of color through the inference of a single causal complex consisting of taste and so forth, it is indeed accepted that a cause is a reason only when there is no deficiency in other causes capable of obstructing its efficacy—
*Parīkṣāmukha* 3.60.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 593; Pramāṇanaya-tattvāloka, 3.66.
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, page 43:
