If the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the cause and the color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are the effect, then there would follow the undesirable consequence of three types of logical marks—namely, the essential-nature mark (*svabhāva-liṅga*), the effect mark (*kārya-liṅga*), and the cause mark (*kāraṇa-liṅga*). [Āloka-ṭippaṇī]:
And there are only three logical marks.
"And non-apprehension [is a means of proof] regarding the essential nature and the effect"— this is stated in the *Nyāyaviniścaya* (p.
35) for the purpose of establishing the causal reason (*kāraṇahetu*).
Inference is like the cognition of the moon and so forth from the reflection of the moon and so forth in water.

(13) That which has the moon as its beginning—such as the sun and so forth—is "candrādi"; from that which serves as the cause, there arises the cognition—that is, the apprehension—of the moon and so forth, namely the reflection of the moon and so forth, in water, that is, in clear water. This is to be understood as inference because it is non-deviant.
Like what? Just like the cognition of a cause from an effect.
—Laghīyastrayāloka, p. 32. Compare: "The moon in water and the like is also of that same nature there;
and the shadow of a tree and the like is also [of that nature] there at certain times."
—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.
201, *Vivṛti*: Indeed, the moon and so forth are neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor the effect (*kārya*) of the moon reflected in water and so forth.
The commentary on the verse and its gloss:

"That which has the moon as its beginning" refers to the sun and so forth; from that [it follows]. "That which has the moon-in-water as its beginning" refers to the sun-in-water and so forth; that too is described in the same way. Its "cognition" (*pratipatti*)—by way of a method that would otherwise be impossible (*anyathānupapatti*)—is "inference" (*anumā*); that is, inference.
Or, it should be explained as: the cognition of the moon and so forth by means of the moon-in-water and so forth.
He explains this very point with the words "for not," and so forth:

for indeed, the moon or the like is neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor the effect (*kārya*) of the moon reflected in water and the like; nevertheless, because of this, a non-deviant cognition (*avyabhicāriṇī pratipattiḥ*) is perceived therein—[this occurs] even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—as noted in the Āloka-ṭīkā.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, who maintains that there is no such thing as a reflection: "The reflection of the moon and so forth does not exist in the water and so forth, nor does the sun and so forth exist in the moon and so forth; rather, it is the sun and so forth situated in its own location that appears there."

Now, it might be argued that no distinct entity called a "reflection" can exist in water and the like; for if such an entity were possible, it would follow that it should be perceived there even before the proximity of the original object (*bimba*). If it is then claimed that the reflection arises only upon the proximity of the original object—and thus the aforementioned consequence does not apply—then we ask: upon that proximity, does it arise as a quality (*guṇa*) or as a substance (*dravya*)? It cannot be a quality, because it appears as a substance.

Now, as for its nature as a substance (*dravya*): is it the nature of a partless substance or the nature of a substance with parts? Of these, the first position is untenable, because parts are perceived therein;

nor is it [a substance] with parts, because it is impossible to perceive a tactile sensation of that [air] separately from the tactile sensations of water and so forth. Therefore, air is not a substance distinct from water and the rest.
In water— [according to the] commentary (ṭīkā)— the perception of a reflection is a "reflection" (pratibimba).
In the reflection present when the original object is near—
the [reflection of] the hands, feet, and so forth— (Āryaṭīkā).

If the reflection were partless (*niravayava*), [this would be acceptable]; however, if the reflection were possessed of parts (*sāvayava*) and produced in the water as a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhūta*), then it would necessarily have to possess distinct touch and other qualities. But this is not possible, because the touch and other qualities of the reflection consist of the very same nature as the touch and other qualities of the water. Furthermore, atoms that possess touch are the initiators (*ārambhaka*) of substances possessing touch; in this case, are the initiators of this [reflection] the atoms of the water and so forth themselves, or some others? It cannot be the latter, because it is impossible for those [other atoms] to be its initiators in a location occupied by a tangible composite whole (*avayavin*).

Now, if it is argued that the atoms of water and so forth are themselves the originators of that [reflection], that is not so; for this [reflection] does not appear as consisting of water, and its distinctness from the nature of water is perceived—since white is the color of water, and that [white color] is not present in the reflection of the face and so forth.

Nor should it be asserted that the form of the original object (*bimba*) alone is its originator; for the color residing in an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), which exists in a separate location, does not originate the color of the effect-substance.
Furthermore, it is impossible for two things possessing parts to occupy the same location in space;
moreover, there would be an increase in the size and weight of the supporting substance, such as a mirror, which does not occur.
Therefore, it is not logical that a reflection is some distinct entity.

Now, [the objection] that "if that [reflection] does not exist, how is there the appearance of the reflection of the sun and so forth in water and the like? is also untenable; for the appearance of that [reflection] is impossible therein, since it is the sun and so forth, situated in its own location, that appears there as a reflection of a substance possessing touch.
The producers of others— the white form (śukla-rūpa)— [are] the [causes]. (Ārya-ṭīkā)
–For that which is situated [in the cause], the effect– ba:
for the color residing in the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is indeed the producer of the color of the effect-substance; –the producer of color– śra.

Now, [the author] states that the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), having arrived there, brings it about: "Because the efficient cause and the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) cannot both exist together in one place, the reflection is not a real entity. (Āloka-ṭīkā)
If its status as an effect is argued to be ultimately real,
that is untenable because of the non-existence of two things in one place;
for it is in the very same location where the form of the mirror is seen that the reflection is also perceived.
Furthermore, two forms cannot coexist in a single location because they possess resistance; therefore, the simultaneous existence of two forms in one place is impossible.
Consequently, this is an illusion, and thus there is no such thing as a reflection that exists as a real entity.
—Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, folio 418, 697; or *vā* in manuscript *ba*;
reflection (*pratibimba*).
The reflection of the sun and so forth in water and other such media— this is the reading in the *Pratibimba* (commentary), while in the *Āgama* it is [different].

Regarding this, some proponents of the theory of the arising of reflections (*pratibimbodayavādinaḥ*) raise an objection: "If the sun is perceived as situated in its own location and not as reflections, then why is it not seen directly above? For an object situated elsewhere cannot be seen elsewhere, as that would lead to the absurd consequence of such a perception occurring at all times;
nor can it be observed below in wells and the like without the existence of a reflection."

And how could one who is facing east, while looking into a mirror, be facing west? If the sense organ, having gone outside, were to perceive the object right there, then this might be so; however, it is that [reflection] which is perceived within the body. And it has been said—on this point, some raise an objection: [Śābarabhāṣya 2.1.35]... Śāstradīpikā... Śābarabhāṣya... Śābarabhāṣya... Śābarabhāṣya... Śābarabhāṣya... Śābarabhāṣya... Śābarabhāṣya... The Jains and others [assert that it exists] in space, water, and so forth.
The vision of the sun and so forth would occur only in water and such; therefore,
the sun and other [elements] are the Puruṣa.
Having gone to the location of the object, the sun and so forth appear there even while one remains in one's own country— this refers to the sense organ, the eye (indriya-cakṣu).— Āloka-ṭīkā.
Others, however, who desire the arising of a reflection (*pratibimba*), raise an objection here: "If that very [object] were perceived, why is it not seen above [the water]?

Commentary: Thinking that the reason stated as being subject to deviation—namely, that "even though the sun is one, it is seen as having a manifold nature in water and so forth"—is unestablished (*asiddha*), those who maintain that the reflection is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) raise this objection.

If that very same sun were being seen and not its reflection, why would it not be seen above? For its perception would occur in that way only if it were grasping the object's actual form as situated in its own location, and not otherwise; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle. Furthermore, how could the sun and other objects situated far below in wells and the like be perceived if no reflection had been produced there? For the sun does not exist in such a position there.

Moreover, how could one looking into a mirror facing east become facing west? For it is not observed that at that time a face turned toward his back has arisen for him; rather, he perceives it as such [only because of the reflection]. If the sense organ, having gone outside, were to perceive the sun, then this might be the case—that one would see only what is above and not what is below. However, since it is maintained that the sense organ is the perceiver only within the body, which is governed by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), it does not perceive what is situated above.
—Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 614. How could one perceive a reflection here [in a well] from below? And how could one, seeing a mirror facing east, become facing west?
If it were the case that [the cognition] would arise from the perception of a reflection—

[as stated in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*]— "if the sense organ were to go outside and cognize the object right there"— then this [reflection] might indeed be the cognizer within the body. However, that [is not the case].
Regarding the verses on the sense-faculties (*indriya*)—
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, verses 183–186 of the *Śabdanirṇaya*—
these have been cited [from] the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, page 614.
Regarding this, it is said [in *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 408]: For those who perceive the sun and other objects in water, the eye always functions in two ways—one upward and the other downward.

In that case, the self does not apprehend the sun as illuminated by the upward ray, because the locus [of the eye] is not straight; however, through the downward function, one perceives it as it is presented in succession, because the locus is straightened, and one conceives of it as if it were actually downward.

Because its upward movement is of a single nature, for that reason the sun is perceived as being below and at a distance. Likewise, the visual ray, struck by a mirror or similar surface, turns back and presents one's own face to the forward-moving ray; and thus the perceiver, cognizing the face through the upward movement of the visual ray, understands what is presented by that upward movement to be "backward," thinking "it is backward.
As it has been said:
By those who negate the reflection—Ā.
Ṭi.; he [perceives it] because of the oneness of the upward and downward rays—Śra. Ṭi.

...he perceives; and it has been said by the one who beheld the sun in the water: "The eye always functions in two ways—one upward and one downward—and that which is illuminated by the upward portion [perceives the sun]."

Commentary: Just as a single eye functions in two ways—downward and upward—like a snake hanging with its neck craned, the Self is not perceived because the body revealed by the upward function is not straight. Why, then, is it perceived? To this he says: "By means of a succession... (pāramparyeṇa).
The upward movement offers itself to the downward movement, and that [downward movement] to the Self.
Now, what is the connection between the upward movement and the downward movement by which it offers itself? To this he says: "Upward," etc.

For since these two belong to one and the same [entity], there is an identity of the upward movement with that [downward movement] in terms of the nature of the substratum (*dharmirūpa*). Thus, being perceived through the downward movement, and because of its conformity to that, it is as if the head thinks itself to be downward.
Regarding the objection raised—namely, that when one facing east looks into a mirror, how is it that he appears facing west—the author replies with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

Even there, the face revealed by the inward-turned mental mode (*pratyag-vṛtti*) is not perceived as such by the self (*ātman*) because the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not straight; rather, the inward-turned mode presents [the face] to the outward-turned mode (*prāg-vṛtti*), and being cognized by that outward-turned mode which has been presented [to it], the self perceives it as "facing west" in accordance with that [presentation].

[Objection: But surely, in this case [of a mirror], it is the face itself situated within the mirror that is perceived, and not as being below with an intervening space as in the case of water-vessels; for what reason is that? [Response: Even here, that which is manifested by the inward-turning [reflection] along with its intervening space is handed over to the outward-turning [perception], and thus it must be grasped in that very way. It is said: there is no fault, because the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*) is not subject to questioning.

For in metallic objects such as mirrors, the face is perceived as being situated therein, whereas in water it is perceived with an intervening space—what is there to be asked about this? (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 776–77)
For those who see both the water and the sun in a vessel of water, the single eye of those observers of the solar reflection in the water functions in two parts, one upward and one downward.
Therein, the self as the person does not perceive the sun illuminated by the upward part;
why? Because the substratum is not straight—that is, because the substratum of the visual organ is not situated directly facing it at that time.
However, by means of a solar radiance transmitted through a succession of functions (*vṛtti*), one perceives the sun via a downward function that serves as its cause.
For indeed, it is said that the solar radiance imparts itself to the radiant function, the function to the eye, and the eye to the self; such is this successive transmission from the radiant sun.
Thus, one regards the upward-moving sun, situated above, as if it were situated below, facing downwards.
Who? The Self;
and not something else below [the sun].
Why? Because of its oneness—that is, because that sun is non-different [from it].

Others say it is due to the eye; therefore, by the very function of the eye just described, the sun is seen below in wells and the like with an intervening space, and differently according to the various vessels containing water and so forth—otherwise, how could there be a non-differentiated perception? It is said that first the rays of the eye emerge taking the face with them as far as the location of the mirror and such; this is called the "forward-bent" (prāṅnatā) function.
And those [rays], being obstructed there by the mirror or other surface, return and reach one’s own face exactly as it is situated;

and that inward-turning [reflection] there transmits the forward-directed reflection to the inward-turning [reflection], and the inward-turning [reflection] to the self. Then the self, perceiving what has been transmitted by the inward-turning reflection, thinks through delusion: "I am going toward my own face."
The meaning is that the very diversity in the functioning of the eye is the seed of error—*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 615;
the eye is twofold—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*.

In that case, because its upward rays are obstructed by the physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and because it is not situated straight [with respect to that basis], the self does not perceive the sun. Rather, it perceives [the sun] as it is presented through a succession [of rays] by means of a downward function, since the self is not situated straight with respect to the physical basis— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Tattvasaṃgraha*.

Because of its upward orientation and its unity, [the sun] is perceived as if it were below; therefore, the sun is perceived as being at a distance from below. (Tattvasaṃgraha-vṛtti, Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika)
"Because of its upward movement... (*Tattvasaṃgraha*); "Because of its upward movement... (*Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*). [Commentary:

Because the upward-moving rays are identical with the downward-moving rays—[Āgamānusāriṇī Ṭīkā]. Thus, by means of an upward movement, one who perceives a face presented by a backward-turned [mirror] understands erroneously that it is facing backward.
By a previously arisen error— Ślokavārttika, Bhāṣya, Tattvasaṃgraha.
"bhrānte –prameyaka॰ mī॰ ślo śabdani॰ ślo॰ 186-190" — these [verses] are cited from *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 614.

Furthermore, if the reflection were a distinct entity produced from the original object (*bimba*), then why would it necessarily move when the original moves, and remain stationary when it remains stationary? For it is not observed—and indeed it is not the case—that when a staff moves or remains stationary, a jar that is a distinct entity from it necessarily moves or remains stationary accordingly.
Yet, it is perceived that whenever the original object moves or is stationary, the reflection necessarily moves or is stationary; therefore, it is not a distinct entity from it.

And if it were a different entity from that [the face], then why is it not perceived when the original object (bimba) has disappeared from the mirror and so forth? If you say it is because it has perished, we say no; for the perishing of an effect is never observed upon the disappearance of its efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa). Indeed, even in a dream, the destruction of an effect such as a jar is never perceived upon the disappearance of its efficient cause such as a staff. Or, let us grant that its destruction occurs upon the disappearance of that cause; even so, there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving the parts of the reflection separately upon its destruction, just as one perceives the shards upon the destruction of a jar. But this is not the case.

Therefore, one must not accept that the reflection in water and so forth is real; rather, it must be accepted that the rays, struck by that [surface], turn back and present the very image of the face and so forth within the water and so forth.
Thus, how could even that be a reflection? Ārya.
From the staff comes the reflection; from the reflection [comes the original object].
This reading is not present in manuscript Ā;
[it states that] there is no reflection in the absence of the original object (*bimba*), which is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*).
Regarding the disappearance of the reflection which is an effect:
indeed, when the reflection is destroyed, its constituent parts are not subsequently perceived as fragmented fragments.
Regarding the demonstration that the reflection, following its negation by means of a water-mirror and the like, is in ultimate reality of the nature of a person (pudgala),
the following rebuttal is offered:

As for what was stated—that no distinct entity called a reflection exists in water and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion. For its non-existence would have to be due either to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it, or to the absence of causes for its production? Of these, the first position is untenable, because perception (*pratyakṣa*), the foremost of all means of valid cognition, is available there as the indicator of its existence; for the cognition "I see the reflection of the moon and so forth in clear water and the like" is well-established for every living being.
Indeed, the cognition "I see this moon" arises in such a form, nor does it arise as [the cognition of] water;
what then? It is the reflection (*pratibimba*) of the moon and so forth.
Furthermore, this cognition is not erroneous (*bhrāntā*), because it arises everywhere, at all times, and for everyone in exactly the same form.

That which arises everywhere, at all times, and for everyone in one and the same form is not erroneous, such as the cognition of a jar and so forth; and this perception of a reflection is of such a nature, therefore it is not erroneous—for it is impossible for an erroneous cognition to arise in such a form.

For an erroneous cognition of silver and so forth regarding mother-of-pearl and the like does not arise for everyone, at all times, and everywhere in one and the same form; rather, its arising is perceived only by those persons whose sense organs are impaired, since it does not occur for those whose sense organs are unimpaired (p.
For that which is impossible for someone... [text fragment] (MS: *yasyāsambhava*).
—The opponent’s position— Venerable [Śāntarakṣita]: "For indeed, nothing more excellent or weightier than what is perceived is accepted"—*Aṣṭaśata*, *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* p.
80; "For indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) more weighty than what is perceived"—*Nayacakra-vṛtti* p. 18.
And there is no means of valid cognition more authoritative than direct perception—
*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, folio 87A, line on water and so forth.
"Reflection" (pratibimba) means the cognition (pratīti) corresponding to each [object].

The thought "I see" arises with respect to form; this is the remainder [of the statement]. It is not by that [thought] that it (the object) is seen. (Āryadeva’s *Catuḥśataka*, commentary on verse 16).
—in manifold forms—ba; —in manifold forms—ba; —by means of that which is seen as a single form—śra.

Furthermore, regarding persons, that cognition in which a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) or a cognition of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇa-doṣa-jñāna*) arises is erroneous; for example, the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
However, in the perception of a reflection in a mirror or the like, a subverting cognition of the form "this is not so" never at any time manifests.
Nor should its erroneous nature be asserted even in the absence of a sublater, for that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga);

furthermore, since no defect in the cause is perceived, the perception of it cannot be erroneous. Indeed, the cause of the perception of a reflection consists of the self, the mind, the eyes, and so forth, and no defects are perceived therein.

Indeed, hunger and the like are not defects of the self, nor are sleep and the like defects of the mind, nor are cataracts and the like defects of the eye; for these are perceived only when their respective cognitions arise. This is because even for a perceiver who is well-satisfied, whose mind is unafflicted by sleep, and whose eyes are clear, the perception of a reflection is still observed to occur. Thus it is established that this non-erroneous perception proves the reflection to be a distinct entity from the original object. As it has been said: "Therefore, that cognition which has a defective cause and that cognition which is recognized as false is alone an incorrect cognition, and no other."
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5
For the cognition of a reflection does not [arise] with respect to the self, the mind, the eyes, and so forth;
indeed, it is not from the eyes and so forth. (Śra., Ba.)
Those whose minds are struck by the perception of a reflection [do not perceive] the connection.
Likewise, there is indeed an inference that establishes this [reflection] as being a distinct entity from both its substratum (*āśraya*) and the original object (*bimba*).

For instance: whatever is apprehended by a cognition distinct from something else is different from that thing, just as a counter-seal is different from the seal; and the reflection of the moon and so forth is apprehended by a cognition distinct from the original object, the moon and so forth.

Nor is this unproven, for a reflection is that which exists facing toward the original object (*bimba*) by way of imitating the form of that original object, just as a counter-seal imitates the form of the seal.
And if that [reflection] is perceived, how could it be unestablished that this [reflection] is grasped by a cognition distinct from that [original object]?

Nor should it be asserted that "this is merely the perception of the original object itself," for we observe the perception of the reflection of the moon and so forth even by one who has not seen the original object after casting their gaze upon water and the like.

Nor can it be said that "even though a distinct cognition is being experienced here, it does not establish its difference from that [original]," because that would entail the destruction of all talk of difference everywhere, since in every case [the notion of difference] is based on a difference in cognition.
Therefore, a reflection must be admitted as something distinct from the original object (bimba).

Otherwise, how could there be a cognition of that reflection when the object—never perceived at any time—is itself unobserved and obstructed, even in the absence of anything covering that original object? Since perception, recollection, or recognition of that original object is in every way impossible, the reflection cannot exist due to the impossibility of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to apprehend it.

A reflection, such as that in water, is distinct from both its substratum— the water— and the original object— the moon— because it is apprehended through a cognition that perceives it as having characteristics different from those two.

Comparison: Likewise, whatever is apprehended by a cognition that perceives it as having a distinct characteristic from something else is different from that thing, just as an impression is different from its seal (Syādvādamañjarī, p.

863). And in the case of a cognition that conforms to the form of a reflection, [there is a difference] between the reflection of the moon and so forth, and the other surface such as water which serves as its locus.
For a person, there is the perception of reflections such as the moon and so forth in water and other media.
Because the reflection is seen within the mirror,
[it is] of the reflection.
The basis for this report of difference is the perceived difference [of the reflection] from its substratum and from the original object.
In that aforementioned object called the *bimba*,
although it is concealed (*vyavahita*), [it is perceived].

If there were an obstruction of the original object (*bimba*), then the reflection (*pratibimba*) would not arise at all; therefore, he says: because recollection and recognition are rooted in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because direct perception is dependent upon immediate proximity, [the reflection arises] neither due to a lack of productive causes—since both the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) are present here—and nor due to the absence of an obstructor of the original object.

For in the production of a reflection, water and the like are the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), whereas the moon and so forth are the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); this is because, taking the moon suspended in the sky as the efficient cause, the water and other substances undergo such a transformation, according to the *Syādvādaratnākara*.

Page 865. The refutation of this, along with its supporting arguments, is as follows: As for what Prabhācandra has stated—that in the production of a reflection, water and the like are the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) while the moon and so forth are the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), because the water and such undergo a transformation in that manner by taking as their efficient cause the moon suspended in the sky—this is merely a manifestation of extreme naivety. For just as the shadow-particles (*chāyā-pudgala*) of leaves and the like, depending on the absence of light, transform into the form of a substance called "shadow" upon a substratum such as the earth; likewise, if the shadow-particles of a face or other object, depending on the collection of clear substances such as a mirror, were to transform into the form of a reflection, then what indeed would be lost? For even this [reflection] possesses the specific nature of being a shadow.

And thus says the scripture: "The shadow that arises at dawn is bright; that which is dark at night is likewise [bright] here, possessing a radiant appearance and the color of its own body. It should be understood that the limbs of the body are like those of a mirror."
The attainment [of that] occurs for them there through the conjunction with light, and not for others;

as the author of the *Prakaraṇacaturdaśaśatī* also states in the *Dharmasāraprakaraṇa*: "For indeed, the reflection of a woman's face cannot possibly occur in a mirror except by means of its excessive penetration [into it]," and so forth—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 865.

And this must be reflected upon: for according to the opinion of the venerable Ācārya Vādidevasūri, the shadow-particles (*chāyā-pudgala*) of the reflection of the face and so forth, emerging from the face, originate the reflection in the mirror and other surfaces by virtue of a collection of conditions such as transparency; however, in our own view, the reflection arises in a mirror or similar surface that is itself transparent when, due to the proximity of the object, the shadow-particles residing in it are transferred—since he himself has stated [this] in the *Syādvāda-ratnākara* (p. 864).

In this regard, the following must be considered: what is the basis for the emission of shadow-particles (*chāyā-pudgala*) from the mouth and other such parts? If it is their inherent nature that they always issue forth, then how can the emission of rays from the eye—as asserted by the Naiyāyikas and others—be rejected?

For if the emission of shadow-particles from a non-luminous mouth or a jar and the like is considered to be established on the path of logic, then the emission of rays from the eye, which possesses luminous form, would certainly be even more consistent with reason and experience.

Therefore, for those who reject the emission of rays from the eye and yet accept the emergence of a shadow-person from a reflection such as a face, it appears as nothing other than raising a weapon for one's own destruction.

On page 698 of the *Ratnākara*, however, it is clearly stated by those very same [authors] following the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*: "Indeed, due to a specific degree of transparency, water, mirrors, and the like come to possess transformations in the form of reflections of faces, the sun, and so forth. And since the emission of rays from the eye is refuted in this very context, it is understood that in that particular treatise Vādidevasūri follows Prabhācandra both in substance and in wording; yet here, with a desire to refute him, they do not even notice the contradiction between earlier and later statements—this is truly strange!

As for what was also stated regarding its having the form of a reflection—that in its proximity, either a quality-form or a substance-form would arise there, and so forth—that too is incorrect; for it is accepted that it is precisely a substance-form that arises there in its proximity [p.
The reflection of the original object in water and so forth.

As for what was stated—that it must be either of the nature of a partless substance or of the nature of a substance with parts—that too is mere words; for the partlessness of a substance perceptible by the senses of people like us is unproven (p.
6), since that reflection is admitted to be composed of parts such as hands and feet.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that it is not possessed of parts because it is impossible to perceive its touch separately from the touch of water and so forth—that too is incorrect. For the perception of its touch separately from the touch of water and so forth would only occur if water and the like were a substance that exists as a distinct entity in the form of a reflection; however, when water and the like transform in such a way [into a reflection], since it is impossible for it to be a separate entity from that [water], how could there even be a suspicion of perceiving its touch separately? (Page 451, Line 7) [In the form of a reflection].

By this [explanation], the question of whether the atoms of water and so forth themselves are the originators (*ārambhaka*) of a reflection, or whether they are something else, and so on, has been answered; for it is asserted that the atoms of water alone, in the manner described, are the originators of that [reflection].

The objection that "since the reflection is perceived as having a form distinct from the form of the water, how can those [water particles] be its constituent causes? is also untenable; for when the causal complex for the transformation of matter (*pudgala*) into various forms and so forth is present, such a transformation into various forms and so forth is logically established.

Indeed, even in the case of a face or other object acting as a prototype (*bimba*), a diverse transformation of form is observed when that complex is present, since we perceive the face and so forth transforming into redness through anger, blackness through shame, or great radiance through joy.
Therefore, the diverse transformation of form and so forth in water and the like upon the presence of a prototype such as a face or the moon does not involve any contradiction.
Page 451, line 9: By means of the proximity of the original object (*bimba*), through the process of water and other substances transforming into the form of a reflection,
the white color [of the mirror] appears as a dark-colored reflection in the water and so forth.
"Water and so forth" refers to the proximity of the causal complex that excites various forms of anger and the like.

By this [explanation of] "variegated form" (*vicitrarūpa*), the following objection is also refuted: that it is impossible for two composite substances to occupy the same portion of space, and that there would be an increase in the size and weight of the supporting substance, such as a mirror. This is because two composite substances cannot exist in the same place here; rather, it is a single substance, such as water, which undergoes such a transformation by virtue of its specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Furthermore, occupying the same portion of space is not contradictory even for composite substances, since it is observed in the case of water and ash, or wind and sunlight, despite their being composite.

Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding the excellence of size or weight for two things that possess parts; for this is not perceived in the case of fire and so forth when combined with water, gold, and the like (pṛ.
14), as in the instance of the production of a reflection.
Because it is limited by having the form of a reflection;
comparison—“That too is subject to deviation due to wind and sunlight spreading through the same location”—Syādvādaratnākara, p. 861.
The sense is as follows: because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the mixture of gold and mercury—compare *Syādvādamañjarī*, p.

861—in hot water, although both water and fire, which possess parts, come to occupy the same location, there is no increase in their size or weight; likewise, even when heated gold and fire, which possess parts, are in contact, no such increase in those two is observed.
Because that is not established—since neither the magnitude nor the weight [of the eye] is perceived (Ā.

Ṭī.). Furthermore, as for what was stated: "For those who see the sun in water, the eye always functions in two ways," and so forth; that too is charming only so long as it is not scrutinized, because the existence of the eye in the form of rays is not proven by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.
Therefore, that [position] is unestablished; for the non-reach-based functioning (*aprāpyakāritva*) of the eye has been explained in detail on page 452, line 15.

Compare: "Since the perception of the sun as being located in its own region is not established, the claim that visual light travels against the current is utterly inconsistent, due to a lack of valid proof (*pramāṇa*)."...
Furthermore, the claim that ocular light is turned back against its current [of flow] is utterly inconsistent, as there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*);
for it is not established through perception or any other means of knowledge that the ocular rays, having come into contact with water, proceed once again toward the sun.

And just as there is no activity of the visual rays toward an object, so it has been established in the section concerning the fact that the eye functions without reaching its object; enough of this digression—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 698—the non-establishment of the [existence of] the eye... [Ba].
Folio 75–82:

Now, an objection may be raised: "In the view of those who maintain the arising of a reflection, the reflection ought to conform to the original object (*bimba*); how then can there be a perception of the reflection with the left and right reversed? This too is not a valid objection; for [the reflection] arises from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*) precisely as having the nature of being left and right reversed.

For a reflection must face its original object (*bimba*); and this facing cannot occur for it except through the reversal of left and right. Therefore, its arising in that very manner is logical; otherwise, the designation "reflection" would be untenable, since it is precisely by way of the reversal of left and right that it is compared [to the original]. This has already been answered by the etymological derivation of the word "reflection" (*pratibimba*) itself; yet, due to your false attachment, you do not perceive it.
A reflection is said to be an image of the opponent;

and its "oppositional nature" consists in its standing directly in front by assuming all the specific features of that [original], such as its ornaments, tilaka, the knitting of its eyebrows, its frown, and so forth.

And this is not possible for it except through the reversal of the left and right sides; thus, its production in that very manner is established. Otherwise, the very designation "reflection" would be untenable for it.

Furthermore, in the view of those for whom the reflection is a distinct entity, the inversion of left and right is indeed an excellence; precisely because it possesses properties contrary to those of the original object, it is therefore different from that.

Furthermore, if the reflection were not something distinct [from the face], then since the visual rays, having been struck by the mirror and other such surfaces, would turn back and manifest the face itself within the mirror through a reversal of location, why would those same rays—having been struck by a wall or similar object—not also turn back and manifest the face upon that wall? For there is no difference [between the two cases]. Nor is transparency of any utility here, as its utility consists merely in the striking of the rays; and that [striking] is indistinguishable in both instances. On the contrary, a more intense striking is produced by a solid substance such as a wall; therefore, there ought to be a corresponding intense manifestation [of the reflection] therein.

For an excellence in the effect is observed to result from an excellence in the cause; for example, due to an excess of bile (*pitta*), there is an excessive appearance of yellowness in objects such as conch shells.

In our view, however, a reflection arises only when a mirror or similar object is present—provided it is stainless and transparent—and not on a wall or similar contrary surface; therefore, there is no appearance of that reflection upon the latter. Furthermore, in the view where the reflection is considered a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), the inversion of the left and right sides is indeed an advantage.
Precisely because there is a conjunction with properties contrary to those of the original object (*bimba*), for that very reason this [reflection] is distinct from it—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 682.

In clear substances such as the surface of a mirror, the shadow of the face and so forth is perceived as transformed according to its color and other qualities; elsewhere, however, there is merely a reflection (*pratibimba*).

Here it is asked: "How is it that for one facing east, a shadow facing west is seen? [The opponent replies: "It occurs due to a specific transformation of a clear substance. To this, an objection is raised: "The existence of a shadow on the surface of a mirror and such is not possible; what then? It is the perception of one's own face by means of a ray of light that has gone out from the eye, struck against a solid object, and returned. This is incorrect, because it would entail the absence of any perception of inversion, it would lead to the over-extension [of the principle] to walls and other such objects, and there would be an absence of the capacity for such perception.

First, there would be the undesirable consequence of an absence of erroneous perception: if the visual ray were to grasp only one's own body upon its return, then for one facing east, only that which faces east would be perceived, because of the absence of any cause for error;
or else, there would be an over-extension [of the principle] to walls and such, since the obstruction of the visual ray exists there as well—*Rājavārttika*, p. 233.
*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, folio 567B:

But how is it that in the surface of a mirror and the like, the reflection of the face and so forth transforms into the form of a shadow facing [the observer] itself, and not turned away? Or how is it that *pudgala* particles, having emerged from the face by piercing through the hard surface of the mirror-disk, bring about the reflection? As for what was said—that the reflection arises facing [the observer] and not from another direction as the face [does]—in that case, such is the transformation of those *pudgala* particles; for it is not possible to direct an inquiry into that object. (*Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 364; my own marginal note).
For the Jaina,
the opposite is the case: the reflection possesses qualities.

Comparison based on the reflection: If rays [of light] reflected from a mirror or similar surface illuminate the face, then those [rays] reflected from a stone slab or similar surface should also illuminate it, as there is no distinction [between them]. — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 864;
*Darśanādi*, Ba. edition.
In the case of mirrors and the like, as well as walls and the like, there is merely an obstruction to the manifestation of the reflection upon its turning away [from the object].
— Not by means of cloth, walls, or substances, but by the appearance of the reflected image.
In the Jaina doctrine,
with respect to walls and such things which are non-transparent and do not allow one to see through them.

Furthermore, if rays of light, being reflected by a mirror or similar surface, turn back and illuminate the object itself, then there would be the undesirable consequence that a large elephant or other object would be perceived without exceeding its own actual dimensions; thus, the perception of [apparent] smallness would not occur,
yet such is not the case.
Therefore, one must admit that it is precisely a reflection that arises there and appears in such a manner.
For a reflection is produced by a mirror or similar medium in accordance with its own dimensions; thus, the perception of a large object as small is not contradictory.

Furthermore, if those [rays] were struck by a substrate such as a sword or glass and, turning back, revealed the original object (bimba) itself, then there would be no perception of a face that is elongated or dark.
In our view, however, because the substratum (āśraya) is elongated and dark, it is logical that the reflection produced from it should also possess elongation and darkness.
But because water and the like are extremely clear, the production of a reflection therein occurs only by conforming to the shape of the original object (bimba).

For comparison: in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving a large elephant or similar object without its exceeding its own dimensions, and thus its lightness would not be perceived.
— from the hand and so forth, in a mirror and so forth (syāt, ra, pṛ 864; ā, hastādau, darpaṇādau).
Endowed with a small form and possessing swift reflection— compare:
"Moreover, if those [rays] were struck by a glass mirror or a sword and, turning back, revealed only the original object, then there would be no perception of a face that is elongated and dark."
— In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 864: "The rays [are emitted] from the *śyāmaka* grain and so forth."

As for what was said regarding the sword, glass, and so forth—namely, that "if a reflection were a distinct entity produced," and so on—that too is an unexamined assertion; for even if this [reflection] were a distinct entity produced, its possession of action would necessarily be established through its invariably conforming to the action of its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), just as in the case of the light of a lamp or the shadow of a parasol.

For just as when a lamp or a parasol moves, the light and the shadow necessarily move, while they remain stationary when [the lamp or parasol] is stationary; likewise, when the original object (bimba) moves, the reflection (pratibimba) necessarily moves, and when it stands still, it stands still.

However, one should not conclude that the conformity to the activity of the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) is not observed in every case—such as in the case of a jar—merely on this basis, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of denying it even in the case of the light of a lamp and so forth.

And likewise, even luminous color and so forth are not perceived in a jar; therefore, let that [perceptibility] be denied in the case of the light of a lamp and so on as well, since there is no distinction [between them]. The contradiction with experience is the same elsewhere too. (Page 453, Line 5)

Comparison: Even when another object arises, because it necessarily conforms to the activity of the cause of transformation, motion occurs when that [cause] moves, and stability occurs when it remains; thus, the reflection of a face or other object [appears] there. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 862)
When an action such as [striking] with the mouth and so forth exists, there is the inference of an action [such as striking] with a staff and so forth; [variant reading:
the prescription of an action [with a staff and so forth].
Even in the case of a reflection, there is conformity with the activity of the efficient cause;
this is conformity with the activity of the efficient cause.
Just as a staff or similar object, which serves as a non-inherent instrumental cause (nimitta-kāraṇa), [is not perceived when it is not manifest], so too should white color and the like—
not even in a lamp or similar case—

be excluded from its own illumination, just as the luminous color and other qualities of the lamp, which serve as its non-inherent instrumental cause, are [not perceived] in the illumination of that [lamp].

As for the further objection stated—"because the disappearance of the effect is not perceived upon the disappearance of the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)"—and so forth; that too is the manifestation of no small darkness. For, when the efficient cause such as a lamp or an umbrella disappears, the disappearance of light and shadow is indeed perceived (page 453, line 10).
Comparison: "It is certainly not the case that the destruction of a jar or similar object is not observed upon the removal of its clay or other material" (Syādvādaratnākara, p.

863). By this, the argument that "upon the destruction of a reflection, there would follow the perception of its parts separately," and so forth, is refuted; for even when a lamp or similar object is destroyed, those [parts] are not perceived.
Indeed, even upon the destruction of substances such as lamps or lightning, their constituent parts do not at any time or place ever enter the path of anyone's perception—*Bimbaprakāśa*, p.
Comparison: Even when substances such as lightning or a lamp are destroyed, their constituent parts are not perceived separately—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 863; [note on *āvaśyaka-ṭīkā*:
perception of the parts].
Since that [perception] occurs through hearing,

the understanding of past things belonging to a single time is possible, but not of future things due to the risk of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Refuting this [position] from *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.12,
he demonstrates yet another reason that is distinct from the effect (*kārya*) and so forth:
Regarding the phrase "of the past and those of the same time" (*atītānāmekakālānām*) in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-vyākhyā*:

even there, in the case of inferring color and so forth from taste and so forth, the "cognition" (*gati*) refers to the past [factors] that exist at the same time as the material cause of the taste, and to those of the same time that coexist with the taste which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*). It does not refer to future [factors], because an inference based on a present logical mark would be fallacious; for a future factor may indeed fail to occur, as it might be obstructed by other causes and thus subject to a deficiency in its causal conditions (*pratibandhavaikalya*).

Furthermore, the inference of tomorrow’s sunrise from today’s sunrise is not a valid inference because it lacks a determining mark (*liṅga*); it is like inferring tomorrow’s sunrise from seeing a donkey today—
[Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.12].
This has been extracted from: *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, folio 311A;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 381;
and *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 590.

One might act on the basis of what is to come, such as [predicting] that a cart will arrive because of the rising of the Kṛttikās, or that the Rohiṇī constellation will rise tomorrow, or that there will be an eclipse of the sun. || 14 ||

"The constellation Śakaṭa (the Wain) will rise at the end of the Muhūrta because Rohiṇī is rising"—this is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Why? "Because Kṛttikā is rising"—this is the proof (*sādhana*).

Indeed, the rising of Kṛttikā is neither the effect nor the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the rising of Śakaṭa; nevertheless, everyone would understand and accept that it certainly indicates its own successor by the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Likewise, one would understand and accept: "The sun, Āditya, will rise tomorrow morning because the sun has risen today."

Likewise, one might understand that "the eclipse by Rāhu will occur tomorrow" based on the desire for such a result, because there is no deviation [from the truth] in all such cases—*Laghīyatrayatātparyaṭīkā*, p.
33. Compare: "Just as, having observed the rising of Kṛttikā, one determines the proximity of Rohiṇī"—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, p. 351.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
571; Pramāṇapārāyaṇa, p. 71; Parīkṣāmukha, 3.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 591; Pramāṇanaya-tattvāloka, 3.71.
80 *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, page 41;
*Jainatarkabhāṣā*, page 16.

In the enumeration of the types of necessary connection (*pratibandha*), what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the statement "the cart will rise [in the east] because of the rising of the Kṛttikās"?—this is the meaning of the verse, which refutes both the enumeration of necessary connections and the enumeration of means of valid cognition regarding this non-discrepant knowledge concerning a future object.
*Vivṛti*: This very [point] shows that non-discrepant knowledge concerning a future object contradicts both the enumeration of necessary connections and the enumeration of means of valid cognition.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
How could people act toward something that is yet to be? From what [cause] would the cart [be known]? From the rising of the Kṛttikās.

Similarly, one might resolve that "the sun will rise tomorrow morning," yet it is understood as "from today until sunrise"; or one might resolve that "there will be an eclipse," based on some desire for a particular result and so forth. (Āpadyeta) [End of citation].
Regarding the calculation on a wooden board or a tablet— referring to the counting of numbers written with one's own chalk and so forth—
the commentary on the sub-commentary (*ārya-ṭīkā-vivṛti*),
demonstrating the intended meaning of the *karikā*, says: "That," and so forth.

Therefore, from this reason which possesses a single characteristic, it is established that there exists a non-erroneous cognition whose object is the future—having as its domain such things as the rising of a cart in the future. What does this [cognition] do? He says: it subverts the enumeration of the [two types of] necessary connection (*pratibandha*), because identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are impossible here. Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because the rising of the Pleiades (*kṛttikā*) and so forth is an effect of the rising of the cart and so forth; that is not so, because it would follow that there could be no cognition of the past rising of the Pleiades and so forth from the rising of the cart.

If they were mutually causal, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, what else does it do? He says: it also obstructs the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For even in the absence of the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, as well as the "invariable concomitance" (*pratibandha*) postulated by others, inference such as that from the rising of Kṛttikā still occurs. Therefore, the restriction of the number of inferential means of knowledge among the Buddhists—that inference arises only from the three types of evidence consisting of effect, essential nature, and non-perception—is not established, because it is proven that inferences arising from the aforementioned types of evidence are distinct from those [three].
Comparison of the inseparable relationship between the rising of the Pleiades (*kṛttikā*) and the rising of the constellation *Śakaṭa*:

there is neither identity (*tādātmya*) nor causality (*tadutpatti*) between that which precedes and that which follows, because such [relationships] are not perceived when there is an interval of time.
— Examination [of the means of knowledge], Chapter 3, Verse 61;
*Pramāṇanayatatvāloka*, Chapter 3.

Prajñākaragupta, the proponent of future causality (*bhāvikāraṇavādī*), stated that Prajñākaragupta’s view regarding the indicator of future causality is as follows: "An entity is indeed characterized by another entity even when it is yet to come; for instance, there is the worldly convention that 'an omen of death has been manifested.'"

If death were not to occur, such an omen (ariṣṭa) would not have come to pass; therefore, it is logical that even a future event can function as a cause because of its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Thus, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is established: "The rise of the Kṛttikās has occurred [as an effect] from the rise of Rohiṇī. (Āloka-ṭippaṇī).

The Buddhist [position] is that once the inference of the rising of Kṛttikā is established, the inference of the rising of the cart follows from that, and from that, again, the inference of the rising of Kṛttikā [occurs], which would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Of the reflection,
[namely] of the cause consisting of the three aspects of the relationship such as identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth.
Since inferences produced by causes such as the rising of the Kṛttikās are based on the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*),
this refutes the restriction of the number of inferences to five as postulated by the Naiyāyikas; for the aforementioned types of inference are not included within those five categories of inference.
"Only the fivefold [reasons]—namely, cause and so forth—are the indicators," such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣika.
For it is said: "That this is the cause of that, the effect, the conjoined, the inherent, and the contradictory—this is inferential knowledge" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.18).

Thus, these five reasons alone mentioned in the aphorism constitute the constituent parts of inference (*laiṅgika*), since the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is fully established right here. Therefore, how could the Naiyāyikas' fixed number of types of inference not remain established? Here, there is inference of the effect from the cause; for example, from seeing burning fuel, one infers: "There will be ash.
There is inference of the cause from the effect; for example, from the observation of a river's flood, [one infers] rain.
From the perception of that which is conjoined, there is the inference of that which is conjoined; for example, from the perception of smoke, there is the inference of fire.
From the perception of that which is inherent, there is the inference of that which is inherent; for example, from sound, there is the inference of space.
From the perception of that which is inherent in the same object, there is the inference of that which is inherent in the same object; for example, from color, there is the inference of taste.
The inference of one contradictory [object] from the perception of another contradictory [object] occurs, as for example, the knowledge of a nearby snake from seeing a hissing mongoose.

As for the effect: since it is observed to be preceded by a cause, that which is being perceived serves as a means of cognition, just as, for instance, from the observation of a specific rise in a river, one concludes that it has rained upstream.

And likewise, since a river-flood characterized by the carrying away of abundant foam, leaves, wood, and so forth has previously been perceived as the effect of rain, when such a flood is perceived again, an inference is appropriate: "This river-flood is caused by rain, because it is a specific type of river-flood, like a river-flood previously perceived [as such]. Now, this "flood" is the contact of water pervading both banks;
that, through a causal series, is the effect of rain.

A "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is that which, having been previously perceived as the producer of an effect, is now perceived as its mark (*liṅga*); for example, the rising of specific clouds is a mark of the act of raining. Likewise, smoke—whether in conjunction with or inherent in fire—indicates the presence of fire, as does hot touch in the case of fire residing in water. And there is the "contradictory" (*virodhin*), such as a hissing snake, which serves as the mark for the presence of a mongoose.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
572; *Praśastapādakiraṇāvalī*, p. 302:
"Because one [of two things] inhering in the same object is perceived, the other exists. *Ba* does not have this.

Following that rebuttal, there is a demonstration of how even reasons such as the rising of the Kṛttikās—which serve as antecedent indicators (*pūrvacara*) and so forth—function as independent means of cognition.
Here, the following is replied:

as for what was stated—that only the five types of reasons mentioned in the Sūtra constitute the constituent members of inference (*laiṅgika*) and so forth—that is an unconsidered assertion; for it has been established that reasons such as the rising of the Kṛttikās, which are distinct from those [five], also function as its constituent members.

Indeed, the status of a logical reason (*hetu*) as a constituent part of inference is due to the power of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), and not merely by its being a cause or similar factor; for the latter is neither all-pervasive nor free from over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Since inseparable connection, however, pervades the entire range of valid reasons and is excluded from fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), it must be understood that the capacity of a reason to produce cognition arises solely through its power.

For apart from that, the capacity of a reason to produce cognition is never perceived anywhere, since in every case, the capacity to produce cognition is established only when inseparable connection exists.

Furthermore, since the relationship of cause and effect has been refuted in detail during the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), the marks (*liṅga*) of cause and effect are unestablished according to the opponent's view;
likewise, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) have also been rejected therein, the marks of being conjoined and being inherent are also unestablished.

Even in the case of opposites, one opposite can lead to the inference of another opposite precisely because of their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and not otherwise, for [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
pṛ. 460, l. 19: tadavyatiri– [ba.]; compare:
because inference is observed even in cases such as the rising of the ocean, despite the absence of the aforementioned relationship.
However, conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) are not causes for the arising of inference;
for there is no inference of a student from his water-pot, nor an inference of earth from its color and so forth, nor an inference of taste from its color.

Furthermore, the claim that the act of raining—which is the example of a contradictory inference—indicates the conjunction of wind and clouds which has not yet occurred, and likewise that the act of raining indicates the conjunction of wind and clouds which has already occurred, is untenable. For in this case, there is a relationship of indicator and indicated between existence and non-existence, and no contradiction exists between those two. Therefore, only relationships such as cause and effect are [valid]; that whose connection with another is fixed and non-deviant is the logical reason (*hetu*). (Prakaraṇapañcikā, p.
68; Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 164;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 532)
*Laghīyastrayāvatārikā*, p. 34:

[The definition of] being merely the nature of a cause and so forth lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) because it does not apply to causes such as the rising of the Kṛttikā star; and it suffers from over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because it exists in things like fire, which are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) since they deviate with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*) such as smoke, even in the absence of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
In the Vaiśeṣika system, in the examination of the six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha), pṛ॰ 297.

The establishment of the distinctness and probative capacity of reasons such as the antecedent (pūrvacara) and others, which differ from the seven types of reasons—such as the part and the whole (mātrāmātrika)—imagined by the Sāṃkhyas:

As for that which was stated by the Sāṃkhyas—that inference is sevenfold, namely: the part and the whole (mātrāmātrika), the effect (kārya), the contradictory (virodhin), the concomitant (sahacārin), the master and the servant (svasvāmin), the slayer and the slain (vadhyaghāta), and so forth;
therein, the inference of the part and the whole (mātrāmātrika) is, for example, the inference of consciousness from the eye.
Inference of a cause from an effect, as for instance, the cognition of a cause upon seeing lightning;
inference of one contrary thing from the perception of its opposite, as for instance, "the cloud will not rain" because it is joined with a contrary wind;
and inference of an associate, as for instance, the knowledge of the second of a pair of ruddy geese (*cakravāka*) upon seeing one of them.

Inference from the perception of one's own [attendant] is the inference of the master, such as the inference of a king from seeing a particular kind of parasol, or the inference of a killer from seeing a executioner; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there is also inference from association, such as the knowledge that "a snake has been killed by this person" upon seeing a joyful mongoose, or the knowledge that "this is a wandering mendicant" when, amidst a group of people, there arises the doubt "Who is the wandering mendicant? and one sees his triple staff.

This too has been refuted by the very same [argument], because there is no distinction in these causes—such as the rising of the Kṛttikās and so forth—being "different from the object" (*arthāntara*) compared to the reasons postulated by the Naiyāyikas;

and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the seventh type of inference, that of the "possessor of connection" (*sāṃyogika*), is included—as noted in the Ācārya’s commentary: "Because lightning is occasional, it must be an effect, and therefore it must have some cause."
The [term] *pratikṛti*—compare:
"By this, the sevenfold relation is refuted" (Nyāyavārttika, p.
57). By this very [means]—[namely] by means of the measure (*mātrā*), the cause (*nimitta*), the conjoined (*saṃyogin*), the contradictory (*virodhin*), and the co-existent (*sahacārin*).
Inference is sevenfold for the Sāṃkhyas, [namely] through the relations of owner and owned, killer and killed, and so forth; *Nyāyaviniścaya-tātparyaṭīkā*, p.
165; *Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 424A.
Even in the case of the reason postulated by the Sāṃkhya (laghī॰ tā॰ pṛ॰ 34),
because there is no specific distinction from other things (arthāntara) [it is not a valid reason] (śra॰).

Now, rejecting the restriction that only the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is a means of cognition (*gamika*) and not any other because others are causes of doubt, he says: "The establishment of a negation also [proceeds] from only the aforementioned non-perception, because such [non-perception] is impossible when a thing exists; otherwise, in the case of objects remote in space, time, or nature which meet the conditions for non-perception, there is no certainty of absence due to the mere cessation of one's own perception. (p. 42) Non-perception regarding remote objects, characterized by the cessation of perception and inference, is a cause of doubt, because even when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased, the absence of the object is not established.

The meaning is that [the reason] is not indicative [of the probandum] because non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) serves as a cause for doubt; see *Nyāyabindu* p. 59 and *Vādanyāya* p. 18.
Ordinary people understand the non-existence of such things as the invisible minds of others; [Vādanyāyaṭīkā, p. 19; Hetubinduṭīkā, p. 162A].
"Know"—who? Even worldly people; the word "api" (even) is to be understood here, meaning that even worldly people such as cowherds and others know it, let alone investigators.

What do they know? Non-existence (*abhāva*), that is, absence. Of what? Of the invisible mind of another and so forth; "paracittādi" refers to the mind and consciousness (*caitanya*) of other persons, which is the beginning (*ādi*) of that [category]; being both invisible and the mind of another, it is called "invisible mind of another and so forth. They know this.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [conditions such as] elemental spirits (*bhūta*), planetary influences (*graha*), diseases, and so forth are included. Why does that [cognition] have a subtle nature? To this, [the text says] "of that" and so forth: because of the impossibility—that is, the non-occurrence—of the modification (*vikāra*), i.e., the alteration (*anyathābhāva*) of its effect, namely the form (*ākāra*) characterized by heat, touch, and so on, which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvī*) with that [object] such as another's mind; and because of the impossibility of [concomitant effects] such as specific speech or health.
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 34)

Because the occurrence of changes in its form and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable. (15) Commentary: Due to the non-perception of the unobservable, not only is the non-existence of another’s mind not established in the case of absolute skepticism, but even the existence of one’s own mind is not; for that reality which is partless is by nature unobservable. Thus, how can the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of an ultimately real entity be established? It could only belong to that which is the opposite of such [an entity], namely, that which is characterized by non-difference (*abheda*).

It is incorrect to claim that non-existence is established through the non-perception of the imperceptible, because this would lead to doubt regarding the cessation of another's consciousness and result in the absurd consequence that those who perform consecrations (*saṃskartṛ*) would become sinful; for there are many instances where the cessation of diseases and the like is determined even when they are not perceived.
— *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī* p. 52; *Laghīyastrayālaṃkāra* p. 35.
—Examination of Accomplishment (Siddhiparīkṣā)— Jaṭāpaṅkti-viṭṭoka:

Regarding the meaning of the verse—He is invisible and consists of the minds of others and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of spirits, seizing demons, and diseases. Worldly people know his non-existence.

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of its form," and so forth. "Its form" (*tadākāra*) refers to the form characterized by heat, touch, and so on, which resides in the body and coexists with that invisible mind of another (*paracitta*). "Change of that" (*tadvikāra*) means its alteration or transformation, which is the primary feature of a particular verbal expression. Because such [verbal expression] would otherwise be impossible (*anyathānupapatti*), the operation belongs solely to the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), and not to the positive forms of perception and the rest. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsaka, who maintains that non-existence possesses a distinct and independent status as a means of valid cognition.

Now, an objection is raised: in every case of determining a non-existence (*abhāva*), it is the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) alone that functions; and since the non-existence of another's mind is itself a non-existence, it must therefore be determined by non-existence alone.

Furthermore, this *abhāvapramāṇa* is distinct from perception and the other means of knowledge, because it arises from a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), possesses a distinct object, and accomplishes a distinct result. Whatever is characterized by such distinctions as arising from a distinct causal complex is distinct from that [other means], just as inference and so forth are distinct from perception; and since this [non-existence] is of such a nature, it is therefore distinct from perception and the others.

Nor is it unestablished that this [cognition] arises from a causal complex distinct from that [of perception]; for instance, the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) cannot arise from a causal complex such as perception, which consists of the contact between a sense-organ and its object. This is because there is no contact of the sense-organs with non-existence; for in that case, a contact characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is impossible, since non-existence is not a substance (*adravyatva*).
Nor is it characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), because it is distinct from substances, qualities, motions, universals, and particulars.
In the absence of those two [conjunction and inherence], their subdivisions—such as conjunction-cum-inherence (saṃyuktasamavāya) and so forth—are cast far aside;
even the state of being a qualifier of what is conjoined (saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇabhāva) is impossible, because the absence of a jar does not qualify a particular spot of ground.

For a qualifier must be either conjoined with or inherent in its qualificand, as in the case of a staff or a quality respectively; however, it has already been stated that absence is never conjoined with or inherent in anything.
And it has been said:
"Non-existence also [is a means of knowledge] through the absence of a means of knowledge, regarding an object not in contact [with the senses], such as 'it does not exist'" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5).

Because it is denotable by the word "non-existence," non-existence as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is distinct from perception and the other [means of knowledge], just as it is distinct from the objects of knowledge (prameya) that are non-existent.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 54:
Because they have different objects, there is no perception of that [non-existence] through its means... [Bhaṭṭa].
And because of the conjunction between substance and substance,
only substances, qualities, actions, universals, and particulars possess inherence;
[these two] are the substrata of conjunction and inherence.

If it is argued that the eye is in contact with the ground, and since non-existence is a qualifier of that [ground], it should be perceived through the relation of being a qualifier of what is in contact (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatva*), rather than through contact itself—that is not so; for without a [primary] relation, there can be no status as a qualifier.
If it is argued that such a relation certainly exists, then what is it? It cannot be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because non-existence is not a substance (*adravyatvāt*).

There is no inherence (*samavāya*), because that is not accepted [by you], or if it were accepted, since perception would occur solely through "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), its status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) would be inexplicable; thus,
for you there is no such sense-object contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), whereas for us there is indeed "inherence in what is conjoined."
Nevertheless, we shall explain precisely why it is not a matter of sensory perception—
*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 479— the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*).
"It is to be understood as, for example, a jar"—*Bhāṣya*:
"First of all, this cognition that 'it does not exist' is not produced by the sense-faculties. *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*.
"For the sense organ has a connection with the aspect of existence alone, due to its capacity. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 18). "Conjunction... (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 580).

"Either the non-modification of the self or consciousness [is the nature of negation], or another entity. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 11). and that [absence], having the non-existence of a jar or the like as its object, does not exist, and because it does not produce a cognition, it is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), unlike the sense organs and so forth. —*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-nyāyaratnākara*, p. 475.
