152), the production of that [non-existence] from the totality of its defining characteristics is well-established, because it cannot occur if even one of those [characteristics] is absent;

for if there were no non-perception of an object that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), then even when the locus, such as the ground, is perceived, the cognition of absence would not occur.
Furthermore, if there were no cognition of the locus, such as the ground, then there could be no cognition of the absence of a jar or other object as delimited by that ground;
for it is not logical for something unknown to function as a qualifier, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does a cognition of the absence of a jar arise in a general manner, but rather [it arises] with respect to the ground.
Likewise, if there were no recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*), then the cognition would take the form "it does not exist" rather than "the jar does not exist.
Therefore, it is established that the means of valid cognition regarding non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) arises from a causal complex distinct from the causal complex for perception,
and thus the production of non-existence [is distinct].

In the case of "the absence of a jar on this ground," there is the apprehension of the locus— the ground— characterized by its specific location, as well as the non-apprehension of the object to be negated and the recollection of the counter-positive; among these, it is the apprehension of the ground that serves as the basis.

Likewise, it cannot arise from the causal complex of inference (*anumāna-sāmagrī*). For its causal complex consists of the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, and there is no mark that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with non-existence.

If it is argued that "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) is such a mark, [we reply]: would this non-apprehension lead to the inference of non-existence by having its pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped, or without its pervasion being grasped? It cannot be without its pervasion being grasped, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can it be with its pervasion being grasped; for the grasping of pervasion, as in the case of smoke and fire, must be preceded by the grasping of both properties.

Furthermore, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), how is the apprehension of the property called non-existence (*abhāva*) achieved—is it from this very inference, or from another? If it is from this very one, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); for instance, if non-existence is established by this inference, then the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of non-apprehension with non-existence is established, and once that is established, non-existence is established by this inference.
If it were established by another inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Moreover, in this case, its status as an inference is not even perceived, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
"Surely the non-existence of an entity would be the probans at that time, because [the object] is not being apprehended—[Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, p.
But the non-arising of perception and so forth shall not be the probans."

And if it is argued that this [absence] cannot be apprehended unless its logical mark (liṅga) is already known, then that [mark], being itself an absence, would have to be apprehended by another absence,
and that [other] would have to be apprehended by yet another; for only when it has been apprehended does it function as a logical mark.
For its apprehension would have to occur through another inferential mark (liṅga), and thus there would be an infinite regress;

likewise, in the absence of a mark, it would remain unestablished. Therefore, it must certainly possess the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) somewhere, even without being an inferential mark.
—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, p. 486–88;
*Śāstradīpikā*, p. 335.
[The property] consisting of both the form of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*)—[Ānandabodha’s] marginal note.
— for it is through inference—
whether from the effect or from the cause.

Furthermore, the mark known as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is also of the nature of the absence of apprehension; therefore, even in the cognition of its own form, the aforementioned defects persist.
Moreover, if non-apprehension itself is not grasped, it is extremely difficult to establish the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between non-existence and non-apprehension.
Consequently, the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) does not originate from the causal complex of inference.
—Khyali— Ācārya Śrī:

Nor does it arise from the totality of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), analogy (*upamāna*), or scripture (*āgama*); for the previously established totality of the means of knowledge consisting of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is in every respect distinct from the totalities characterized by presumptive testimony and so forth—which involve an object that cannot otherwise be accounted for, the apprehension of similarity between the object of comparison and the thing compared, and words—and thus it is not unestablished that the means of knowledge consisting of non-apprehension arises from a totality of causes distinct from perception and the other means of knowledge.

Nor can it be said that they have different objects. For instance, regarding the cognition "there is no jar on this ground," this cognition is certainly not directed toward a positive entity (*bhāva*), because it is experienced by every living being as distinct from a positive entity. If its object were a positive entity, would the jar be the object, or the ground, or the relation between them? In the first case, even when the jar is present, the cognition of non-existence would arise just like the cognition of the jar's existence, since the objective basis (*ālambana*) would be present.

In the second case, however, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a cognition of non-existence occurring even on a ground where a jar is present, because the ground, which is the object, would still be existing.

Nor can it be its conjunction (*saṃsarga*); for then there would be the undesirable consequence that even when a jar is joined to the ground, one would have the cognition "the jar is not here. Suppose, then, that the object of this [cognition] is the ground as distinguished from the jar. But is this distinction merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the ground, or something distinct from it? If it is merely the essential nature of the ground, then there would be the undesirable consequence of that cognition occurring even while the jar is present.

If, on the other hand, it is distinct from it, then only the name differs, not the meaning, since by the word "distinction" (*viviktatā*) it is simply "absence" (*abhāva*) itself that is being designated.

Therefore, it is established that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the object of determination for the means of valid cognition of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) alone, as a distinct entity from existence (*bhāva*); for perception and the other [means of cognition], having existence as their domain, lack the capacity to range over the sphere of non-existence—[this is] unestablished because [non-existence] is distinct from the cognition of existence (Ā. Ṭī.).
The ground is not the object of the jar, because [otherwise] it would follow that [the ground is the object] even when the jar is present—*Śāstradīpikā*, p.
325; *viṣayabhūtalasya* (of the ground which is the object), variant reading *ba*.
Regarding the cognition "the jar does not exist" directed toward the locus (bhūta) which has become the object,
what is this "exclusion of the jar" (ghaṭaviveka)? If it is simply the nature of the ground itself, then the [cognition] would also apply to a place where a jar is present.
If you say that the absence of connection with a jar [is what is perceived], then you have admitted non-existence (abhāva).
— *Śāstradīpikā*, p. 327.

Regarding the term "devoid of the cognition that 'it does not exist'" (nāstīti-pratyaya-vivikta-śabdena):

if non-existence were determinable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could it be determined by a sense faculty when there is no contact with it? For instance, when a certain person has perceived a room in its own form, but because he lacks the desire to know, he has not ascertained that "Devadatta is not here"; later, having gone to a distant place, when he is asked by someone, "Was Devadatta there or not?", he then provides the answer "He was not" after recollecting that place and realizing the absence of Devadatta.
Since there is no sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) there, how could perception (*pratyakṣa*) be possible? Therefore, absence is not something to be determined by perception;

for even after seeing only the nature of the locus itself and subsequently remembering something else, when one is asked about the non-existence of that other thing there, one understands it at that very moment.

For instance, suppose someone has stayed in a certain place in the morning; having seen no tiger or the like there, and because he did not remember them, he did not even apprehend their absence. Having merely seen the place and then gone to another location, he is asked at midday: "Did a tiger, an elephant, a lion, or a king arrive in that place this morning?

At that time, although he remembers that place because he knows it, he then apprehends for the first time the absence of other things such as tigers in that place, which he had previously not apprehended.

Furthermore, at the time of midday, it is not possible for the absence of the morning [object], which is not in sensory contact, to be apprehended by perception; for that [perception] has as its object only that which is present and in sensory contact—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Nyāyaratna, p.
483; *Śāstradīpikā*, p. 339.
The answer: for that [cognition] occurs even in the absence of Devadatta in that place.
Nor is it determinable through inference and the like, because of the impossibility of a mark (liṅga) or similar evidence that is invariably concomitant with it;
and as for non-perception (anupalabdhi) and so forth, an answer to them has already been given immediately following the discussion of those marks.

Therefore, by the method of exhaustion (pāriśeṣya), non-existence (abhāva) is indeed the object of the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (abhāvapramāṇa); thus, the fact that their objects are distinct is not unestablished.
And it has been said:
"Nor is it inferable, because it is impossible to grasp the relation of any logical mark (liṅga) with that which is unknown"—*Śāstradīpikā*, p. 340.
Just as non-existence is indeed accepted as an object of cognition, so too should it be accepted as a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Just as there is no status of being a means of cognition for non-existence when the object of cognition is of a positive nature, likewise there is no status of being a means of cognition for a positive entity when the object of cognition is non-existent.

Alternatively, non-existence is measured by a means of valid cognition corresponding to its own nature, because it is an object of cognition, just like existence; therefore, it is distinct from that which consists of existence—
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Abhāva section, verses 45, 46, 55.

"Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object"—thus Umbeka has explained [in his] *Vyākhyā*: "When, with respect to an object called 'jar,' the five [means of cognition], beginning with perception, which grasp existence, do not arise, its non-existence is the object of the means of valid cognition consisting in the absence (*abhāva*) whose locus is the ground. (*Śābarabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.

279). In that case, when an object is established as having a dual nature consisting of both existence and non-existence, it is with respect to that aspect of the object's nature called "non-existent form" that the five means of valid cognition, up to and including presumption (*arthāpatti*), do not arise.
For what purpose? For the sake of awakening to the existence of a real entity;

in that regard, regarding the object of cognition which is the portion consisting of non-existence, non-existence itself functions as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). — *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 470.

Nor does it establish a distinct result, for the result characterized by the cognition of absence is established solely through the grace of the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*).

Therefore, one must admit that the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence—which is distinct from perception and the other [means], which arises from the causal complex beginning with the apprehension of the locus of the object to be negated, and which has the cognition of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as its result and the meaning of the negative particle as its object—is a separate means of knowledge.
Furthermore, it is not invalid because its object is a non-entity (*avastu*), since it is untenable to claim that absence is a non-entity when it is being determined by a means of knowledge.

Whatever is determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not a non-entity (*avastu*), just like an existent thing (*bhāva*). Since non-existence (*abhāva*) is also determined by a means of valid cognition, its status as a non-entity would make its differentiation impossible; for that which is a non-entity has no differentiation, such as the case of a sky-flower and the like. Yet, there exists a differentiation of non-existence into prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth. If it were thus a non-entity, there would be a confusion (*sāṅkarya*) of objects, because in the state of milk and the like, the prior non-existence of curd and so forth—being a non-entity—would lack the causal capacity to prevent such confusion. Consequently, the practice of specific, determinate linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed.
As it has been said: "The term 'unestablished' (asiddha) should also be applied here"— this is the commentary (ā॰ ṭi॰)—
because [the reason] is established by scripture (śra॰).
The jar is the object to be negated; its substratum, such as the ground,
must be apprehended, as must the recollection of the counter-positive and the non-perception of the counter-positive, for the sake of the negation.

And it is said in the *Śruti*:

"This worldly convention would not exist through the distinction of cause and so forth, if non-existence were not differentiated by the distinctions of prior non-existence and the rest. Commentary: That which, having previously not existed, comes into being in the form of curd, is the effect (*kārya*) as the material product (*upādeya*); and that which, having existed previously in the form of milk, no longer exists subsequently, is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). This is the distinction between effect and cause.

Likewise, such conventional usages as "a cow is not a horse," "a horse is not a cow," and "a rabbit is devoid of horns" would not be possible if the non-existence [of an entity] did not possess internal distinctions such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 474.
The prior non-existence of the effect is the cause—Ātreya’s *Ṭīkā*.

Alternatively: "Since this [absence] is grasped by cognitions of both inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it should therefore be accepted as a real entity (*vastu*), like a cow and so forth, and because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*).
Commentary: For indeed, there is an exclusion of absence in the form of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so on, and an inclusion in the form of absence itself.
Regarding that very point, he states another reason: "because it is an object of knowledge" (*prameya*). (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 475)

The thesis is that "non-existence is a real entity" (*vastu*); the two reasons are "because it is apprehended by cognitions of inclusion and exclusion" and "because it is an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*); the example is "like a cow and so forth. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p.
473). [The word] "non-existence" is [the subject], according to the Āloka commentary.

[Objection: These distinctions, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, cannot belong to a non-entity; therefore, it [non-existence] possesses the nature of an entity (*vastutā*). That which is the existence (*bhāva*) of the cause, such as milk, is precisely the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the effect, such as curd; and that which is the existence of the effect, such as curd, is precisely the non-existence of the cause, such as milk. This is the nature of non-existence as a real entity (*abhāvavastutva*). — *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 473.
"That which is non-existence by virtue of possessing differentiation, such as a cause, etc. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika); "That which is existence by virtue of a cause, etc. (Tattvasaṃgraha).

The establishment of the non-confusion of entities is dependent upon its validity. That which does not exist in milk, such as curd and so forth, is called prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

Commentary: Although a jar or similar object is cognized by perception and other means of knowledge as having the nature of existence, it is the object of cognition for non-existence (*abhāva*) in its nature of non-existence; "non-confusion" (*asaṅkara*) means, in short, the nature of non-existence as non-existence.
(Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 473)
Based on the authority of that [text], the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika* commentary states:
That which is perceived in the world as "the effect characterized by curd, a jar, and so forth does not exist in its cause, such as milk or clay," is called prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
For if prior non-existence did not exist, the effect, such as curd, would indeed be present in the milk and so forth.
Thus, the non-existence of that which is called milk in curd is what is termed "posterior non-existence" (pradhvaṃsābhāva). Otherwise, milk would indeed exist in the curd.
The absence of a horse and so forth in a cow and so forth is called "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva);
because the other form—the nature of a horse and so forth—does not exist in that cow and so forth, therefore the mutual non-existence of those two is stated.

Otherwise, horses and the like would exist in cows and such if mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) did not exist. As for absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*): the parts of a rabbit’s head are concave, not elevated, and devoid of growth and hardness; they do not exist in the form of horns and so forth at all, and this is called absolute non-existence. If, however, absolute non-existence did not exist, there would certainly be horns on a rabbit.
—This is quoted from *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 472; see also *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
65, and *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 81B.

The non-existence of milk in curd is characterized as *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (non-existence through destruction). The absence of a horse and so forth in a cow is called *anyonyābhāva* (mutual non-existence). As for the case of a rabbit's horn: the parts of a head that are sunken, devoid of growth and hardness, are designated by the form of a "rabbit's horn" and so on; this is called *atyantābhāva* (absolute non-existence). Now, when the parts are elevated, possessed of growth, and hard, they are designated as "horns. And when the parts of a rabbit's head are sunken, not elevated, and devoid of growth and hardness, then those very parts are fit to be designated by the form of the "absence of a horn."

In that case, milk would become curd, and curd would become milk; a cloth would become a jar, and a horn would exist on a rabbit; consciousness would reside in earth and the other elements, and form would reside in the self;

fragrance would be in water, and both fragrance and form would be in fire; and both touch and form would be in air; and both taste and fragrance would be in space—if this [Veda] were not authoritative.
The state of being in contact is "contact-ness" (*saṃsparśitā*), which means "contact" (*sparśa*); they are the "contactors" (*saṃsparśaka*). (Tattvasaṃgraha, Syādvādaratnākara, Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā).

The demonstration that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not apprehended by any one of the means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), preceded by a rebuttal thereof—herein it is replied:

as for what was stated, namely, "the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence is distinct from perception and the others," etc.; that is an unexamined assertion, because since its object is determined by perception and the other means, its distinction from them is untenable.
For non-existence is of two kinds: that which relates to a remote object and that which relates to a non-remote object.

Among these, that non-existence which relates to a non-remote object—such as place and so forth—is determined by perception itself, since immediately following the operation of the sense organs, there arises the cognition "the ground is devoid of a jar," and so on.

And as for the non-perceptibility of absence (*abhāva*), is it because it is not connected with the sense organ, because it lacks form (*arūpitva*), or because it has the nature of non-existence (*asadrūpatva*)? It cannot be because of a lack of connection; for that would entail the consequence that even visible form (*rūpa*) would be imperceptible, since form is apprehended by the eye—which does not reach its object—despite being unconnected. [Objection: But if absence were apprehended by the eye even while unconnected, then there would be the consequence of apprehending absences located in other places as well, since there is no distinction [between them]. [Response: This too has already been answered by the case of form.
For even if that [universal] were apprehended while being unconnected [to the sense organ], the apprehension of it as existing in all places and times is not observed.

Now, if it is argued that its lack of connection is unproven because the relationship of *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) exists between the eye and color-form (*rūpa*), that is not so; for the fact that the eye acts without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*) has already been established. Furthermore, if it were apprehended by means of such a connection, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) of taste (*rasa*) and other qualities also being apprehended, since there is no distinction in that regard.

Since it is not apprehended due to its unsuitability [for perception], let there likewise be non-apprehension of absence residing in another place and so forth, for there is no distinction [between them]. (p.

463, l. 8) Absence, too, is indeed inference; just as an effect that has arisen is a mark for the existence of a cause, so too an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of a cause.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

moreover, the apprehension of an absence depends upon the apprehension of its locus, and a locus is apprehended only when it is present [in contact with the senses]. Therefore, how could there even be the possibility of apprehending an absence located in another place or elsewhere? Thus, it is logical that this [absence] is not perceptible because it is not connected with the sense organ.

Comparison: Nor should it be suspected that there is a perception of the non-existence of everything in other locations and so forth, simply because the lack of connection [to those places] is no different; for the cognition of non-existence depends upon the perception of its locus (*āśraya*), and the locus is perceptible only when it is present—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 52.
The locus is the ground and so forth.

Nor can non-existence [be perceived], because it lacks form (*arūpitvāt*); for that [absence of form] is not a factor for perceptibility. Indeed, the possession of form is not a necessary factor for perceptibility, since atoms (*paramāṇu*), despite possessing form, are not perceptible; furthermore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and universals (*sāmānya*). For instance, the quality of color and so forth, the action of moving and so forth, and the universal such as "cowness" do not possess form, yet perceptibility exists in their case.
The nature of being material (rūpitva) is materiality (rūpatva);

even its having the nature of non-existence does not contradict its perceptibility. For it is untenable that what has the nature of non-existence should be perceived as having the nature of existence, but not [untenable] that it be perceived as having the nature of non-existence, since there is no contradiction in objects being perceived by way of their own intrinsic nature.

For it is not logical that because a jar’s perceptibility is contradicted when it is conceived as having the nature of a cloth, its perceptibility should likewise be contradicted in its own nature; for that would entail the undesirable consequence of abolishing the practical usage of perception everywhere.
Therefore, one who desires this [perceptibility] must admit that non-existence, like existence, is perceived by way of its own intrinsic nature.

If it is asked: "Even so, how can non-existence be perceptible? It is a contradiction," [we reply]: "How is existence [perceptible]? If you say it is because it is graspable by perception, then the same applies to the other case."

For instance: when the eyes are open, both the ground and the absence of a jar appear, whereas they do not when the eyes are closed. Therefore, since the occurrence [of the cognition] is equally dependent on that [state of the eyes], how can the restriction be justified that the cognition of the ground alone is perceptual, while the cognition of the absence of the jar is not? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever conforms to the presence or absence of the eye is perceptual, such as the cognition of the ground and so forth; and the cognition of the absence of a jar and so forth likewise conforms to that [state of the eye]. Furthermore, if this [cognition of absence] were non-perceptual, its dependence on light would be extremely difficult to establish, for light is well known to be an auxiliary factor specifically for the eye.

Furthermore, if it is not admitted that the cognition of the absence of jars and so forth arises from the visual faculty assisted by that [light], then such a cognition would arise even for a blind person;
this would contradict its status as perception and its designation as perceptual activity.

If it is perceptible, how can it be non-existent? If it is non-existent, how can it be perceptible? Thus there is a contradiction; [this applies] even to non-existence, as noted in the *Cakṣu-ādi-ṭīkā*.
The cognition of the absence of a jar and so forth is established [as being] the negation of the existence of a jar and so forth.

[Objection: "Surely, in the cognition of the absence of a jar or the like, which is assisted by light, the conformity to the presence and absence of the eye (*locana*) is *anyathāsiddha* (established otherwise), just like the experience of touch that occurs immediately after the cognition of color. For just as the conformity to the presence and absence of the eye in the experience of the hot touch belonging to a blazing flame situated at a distance—which occurs immediately after the perception of its form—is *anyathāsiddha*, so too is it in the case of the cognition of the absence of a jar, etc., which occurs immediately after the perception of the ground. [Reply: This also is incorrect, because the difference between the cognition "the jar does not exist here on this ground" and the perception of the ground itself is not established.

For it would be appropriate to claim that the conformity [of the cognition] to the presence and absence of that [object] is established otherwise only if a difference between cognitions were proven—as in the case of the cognitions of color and touch—but no such difference exists here. This is because, just like the cognition "there is curd in this bowl," even a single cognition such as "the jar is not here on the ground" is perceived by an observer whose visual activity has not ceased, as it rests upon both parts [of the relation].

Or let there be a distinction between them; nevertheless, since both are perceived without difference due to their conformity with the presence and absence of the sense organs (*indriya-anvaya-vyatireka-anuvidhāyitva*), how is it appropriate to claim that one is perceptual while the other is non-perceptual? For such a claim would result in the fallacy of acting according to mere whim. [Note: *anvaya-vyatirekā* (variant reading) — *anumayā* (Ānandagiri’s commentary)]

When an effect can be accounted for by something whose prior existence is necessarily established as fixed, anything other than that is "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*)—*Muktāvalī*, Kārikā 19–20.

For comparison: Nor is this [causal relation] "otherwise established" merely because it occurs when that [other thing] is present, like the inference of touch preceded by the sight of the form of a distant fire. For in that case, the eye has been repeatedly determined to be devoid of skill regarding the perception of touch, and another cause, the sense-organ of touch (*tvagindriya*), is known to be the determiner of touch.

Furthermore, since it was previously observed that such color and touch are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitā*), it is logical that this touch is merely to be inferred; thus, in that case, the operation of the eye is established as being otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddhatva*). However, in the present instance, no such mode of occurrence exists—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 51.

As for the claim that the dependence of the cognition of absence on the sense organs is otherwise established because the senses are utilized only at the moment of perceiving the location of the ground, that is untenable; for indeed, two cognitions arising in succession are not experienced in this way: first, a sensory cognition of the location of the ground, and then, upon the recollection of the counter-positive, a mental cognition of non-existence that is independent of the senses.

Because a single cognition that apprehends a patch of ground devoid of a jar or the like is experienced as apprehending an absence, and because you yourself have admitted that such a cognition is produced by the sense organs, the dependence of the cognition of absence upon the senses is not established otherwise [than through the senses]—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 310. (Tadā, Śrī.)
The division of this knowledge:
the sense-faculties of knowledge.

Regarding the comparison with the cognition "there is no jar on this ground": just as the single cognition "there is curd in this bowl" has both [the bowl and the curd] as its object for one whose visual operation has not ceased, so too here, the cognition "there is no jar here" likewise has both as its object. In that case, why is there this division—namely, that the knowledge of the bare patch of ground alone arises from the eye, while the knowledge of the other [the absence] arises from another means of valid cognition?
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 51)
The absence of a jar on the ground— both of these are cognitions;
[there is] a distinction between cognitions.
Both the ground and the absence of the jar belong to both the ground and the absence of the jar.

If the cognition of the absence of a jar and so forth were not perceptual because it occurs subsequent to the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*), then one would be offering a funeral libation to determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) itself.

For that [determinate perception], having arisen immediately after indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) upon the recollection of the relationship between word and object, takes such forms as "this is a jar. If even such [determinate perception] is considered perceptual because it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs, then let the same apply to the cognition of the absence of a jar and so forth as well, since there is no distinction between them.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of tactile sensation—which occurs immediately after the perception of form—also being visual; for the eye lacks the capacity to grasp touch, whereas the sense of touch alone possesses the capacity to grasp it. Otherwise, even one whose tactile faculty (tvag-indriya) is impaired would experience the cognition of touch.

Therefore, this cognition is indeed inferential (*ānumānika*), because it arises through the power of a reason whose invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been established both generally and specifically—namely, that "whatever possesses such form possesses such tangibility," or "whatever possesses such a kind of form possesses such a kind of tangibility. Whatever arises in this manner is indeed inference, just like the cognition produced from a reason whose invariable concomitance is understood, such as "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," or "whatever possesses such a kind of smoke possesses such a kind of fire"; and the cognition of tangibility that occurs immediately after the perception of form arises precisely through the power of a reason whose invariable concomitance has been established.
Therefore, this is established: the absence of an object related to a place and so forth that is not remote is determined by perception itself;
[this is] for the sake of [refuting] the recollection of a jar as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—Ācārya’s Commentary.
Conceptual [perception]— the marginal note (ā॰ ṭi॰) states:
even of conceptual perception which occurs immediately after recollection— [this applies] even to direct perception (śra॰).
It is perceptual because it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organ in the same way as the apprehension of touch.
When there is the apprehension of touch by means of the eye—

[according to the Ācārya’s commentary] as in the case of deafness or disease— and for a man whose tactile organ is void of its function due to a disorder of the shoulder-blades and so forth— [according to the Ācārya’s commentary].

The cognition of touch that arises immediately after the perception of form is inferential in nature, because it arises through the power of a reason whose invariable concomitance has been established both generally and specifically;
this is the general pervasion,
and this is the specific pervasion.

The absence of a relation with an object that is remote in terms of space and so forth—whether in general or in particular—is established through inference and other means. In this regard, the absence of blooming and so forth in a lotus from a distant location is inferred from the absence of the rising of the sun;
and the absence of the rising of a constellation such as Śakaṭa at the end of a muhūrta is understood from the rising of Aśvinī when [the object] is remote in time.
Furthermore, the absence of consciousness—which is remote by its very nature—in a corpse is inferred from the absence of specific activities, speech, and forms;
indeed, such an absence cannot be apprehended through any other means than such a mark (liṅga).

Comparison: Furthermore, even that which is to be inferred (anumeya) may exist in a remote location as a non-existence (abhāva). For example, when it rains and the roots of crops are being drenched by streams of water in deep darkness, the absence of contact between clouds and wind is inferred; or as illustrated in the context of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), the absence of Caitra outside is postulated based on his presence in the house. Moreover, the ascertainment of non-existence sometimes arises from authoritative scripture (āgama), such as the knowledge of the absence of thieves and the like among travelers derived from a reliable person.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 54;
at the end of the muhūrta of the Rohiṇī and other lunar mansions, Śra.
And by this,

that which was stated— namely, "If non-existence were determinable by perception, how could the non-existence of Devadatta and others, who are not in contact with the sense organ, be determined in a room and so forth?"— is also refuted; for the cognition "Devadatta was not in the room" is a memory, just like the cognition "There was a jar there," because by the perception grasping the room, the absences of objects not present there are apprehended simultaneously, just as the presence of objects present there is.

And at a subsequent time, through the power of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the cognition that arises regarding the existence or non-existence of that [object] does not forfeit its status as memory (*smṛti*).

Nor should it be said that there would be a sudden recollection of all objects and non-entities experienced at once; for the mere fact of having been experienced is not the cause of recollection. For even among all things—whether positive or negative in nature—that have been experienced, recollection of whichever specific form arises occurs when the causal complex for the awakening of its latent impression (saṃskāra), such as a question and so forth, is accomplished. It is determined [in this way]: "This was there," or "This was not there.
Ā., paricchedyate).

Comparison— although, because this [cognition] is of the nature of memory, a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) such as "there is no elephant here" had not previously arisen, nevertheless, a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) regarding the temple as qualified by the absence of elephants and so forth had indeed arisen;
otherwise, following the question, "When you saw the temple, did you not see the elephant standing near it?", there would be no recollection.

That [non-existence] is indeed perceived when, regarding an object whose prior non-existence was not delimited, one remains silent after another person's question—such as "Was Devadatta there, or was there an elephant?"—and does not determine its non-existence at that moment. Therefore, since the non-existence of the elephant and so forth was already cognized previously, this recollection is logical: "I did not see an elephant there," and so on.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 593;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 53;
*Praśastapādabhāṣyakandalī*, p. 227.
—Because [the cognition] is devoid of [the specific forms of] Devadatta and others, there is an absence of their names due to simultaneous apprehension; in that case, [it is] *bahu*.
—*pra-ā*, *śra* [indicate] the absence of names for Devadatta and others because they are apprehended simultaneously; in that regard, it is *bahu*.

There is a comparison between the existence of those objects whose presence is in the room and the non-existence of those things such as Devadatta and others, by way of their being present or by way of their being absent. Now, one might object: "If all absences were grasped by a single cognition of 'darkness' (mecaka-buddhi), would not the memory of all absences arise all at once? This is not so; for he remembers only that for which there exists a cause of recollection, such as a question or the like, and not everything, since there is no cause for the recollection of what is not present.

But in other cases, even when the phonemes are perceived simultaneously, there will be a recollection immediately following the experience of the final phoneme; in yet other cases, even though [the phonemes] are perceived simultaneously, the recollection will occur sequentially. Thus, there is no such defect in the case of the "cognitive apprehension of a variegated color" (*mecakabuddhi*). — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 53.

As for what was stated—that the causal complex for the arising of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa) consists in the apprehension of a locus such as a floor—this too is insubstantial, because the apprehension of a locus is no different even in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Indeed, the perception that "there is no jar on the floor" is not possible without the apprehension of the floor; nor is there a rule that the apprehension of non-existence must be preceded by the apprehension of a locus, since the cognition of the absence of a lamp in darkness arises even without the apprehension of a locus.

Nor should it be asserted that darkness alone is the substratum; for you maintain that it is merely the absence of light, and that very absence is the non-existence of the lamp. Thus, there is no apprehension of any substratum distinct from that [absence] therein. Likewise, the cognition "there is no odor" also arises independently of the apprehension of a substratum; for even in one whose eyes are closed, the cognition of the absence of odor arises immediately following the operation of the olfactory faculty.

Furthermore, in that case, it is not possible for the substratum of the substance to be apprehended by the olfactory faculty, because the apprehension of a substance is possible only through seeing and touching. Likewise, the cognition of non-existence occurs through the operation of the auditory faculty alone, independent of the apprehension of a substratum;
for it is not possible for the substratum of sound to be apprehended by the auditory faculty, since that [substratum], being entirely beyond perception, is determined only through inference.
Therefore, that apprehension of the locus enters into the causal complex of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence—[it is] of the nature of apprehension... (Śābarabhāṣya, p.
— because it is established by scripture (śruti) that darkness exists for the Vaiśeṣika.
Darkness is non-existence, because it possesses characteristics different from those of the production of substance, quality, and action.
— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.19.
The absence of light is indeed nothing other than the absence of the lamp.
Even in the cognition of the absence of a lamp— the nose, space.

Or let it enter [the cognition]; nevertheless, regarding the apprehension of the locus (*āśraya*), is it [apprehended] together with the absence of the negandum, or alone? Regarding the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) as well, is it [recalled] as being pervaded by absence, or as its opposite? In that regard, if one were to accept that the apprehension and recollection of the locus and the counter-positive—qualified by absence and having entered the path of cognition—are the causes [of the knowledge of absence], then it would amount to saying that the knowledge of absence arises from the knowledge of absence itself; and it is not logical for anything to be established based on itself, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, there is the fallacy of circularity (*cakraka*): for the production of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) depends upon the cognition of the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*); the cognition of that [absence] depends upon the cognition of the locus (*āśraya*) and the counter-positive as qualified by it; and the production of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence occurs only when that [cognition of the locus and counter-positive] exists. Moreover, if the cognition of non-existence were to occur while the locus and the counter-positive are being perceived independently of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence, then the cognition "there is no jar on the ground" would arise even with respect to a ground that actually possesses a jar, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Therefore, since the aforementioned collection [of conditions] is untenable when analyzed, one must admit that the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa) arises from the very collection of the eye and other factors, and that its object is things such as jars, which possess the nature of existence and non-existence from the perspectives of themselves and others.

[Objection: "Surely, the non-existence of a jar and so forth, when cognized through the nature of another, would not be apprehended as its own nature (*svātmatayā*). And how can that which is not apprehended as its own nature be its form? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Reply: This too is not sound; because even though non-existence is cognized through the nature of another, it is the non-existence of the jar and so forth that is cognized, not that of the other. For in the case of "the jar is not a cloth," it is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) that is thus cognized, and not [the non-existence] of "the cloth is not a cloth."

Therefore, although the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is perceived through the medium of another entity (*parātmanā*), it is perceived as belonging specifically to the jar or the like; thus, it is designated that "the non-existence of that [jar] alone exists in that form" (*tasyaiva tadrūpeṇāsattvam*).

For comparison: "In that regard, is the locus of the negation perceived as conjoined with another entity which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), or as unconjoined? And is the recollection of the counter-positive itself one that is conjoined with another entity, or unconjoined? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
203; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 24).
Jainatarkavārttika-vṛtti, p. 93; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 311:
of the ground.
Of the pot together with the absence of the pot,
[in relation to] the ground and the pot...

Regarding its being the cause for the cognition of non-existence— it has been stated that there is no such thing, because when something is cognized in relation to itself, it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*svātmāśrayatva*).
Because it would follow that fire is established by fire itself,
and thus everything would be established for everyone— [in] that [case], that [would be] its [establishment]— Ā॰, ba॰.
"Of the two things characterized by non-existence"—
thus it would be;
*sva*— *āśra*.
But it is not that the cloth is not [the cloth]; rather, it is the jar itself appearing in the form of the cloth.
—[The opponent says: "It is 'thatness' (tattva)," thus [it is] distinguished.

Furthermore, as for what was said: "Is the state of being distinct from the jar merely the intrinsic nature of the ground, or is it something different from it? and so forth—that too is incorrect. For, when that state of being distinct from it is questioned, is it asked as being somehow different from it by virtue of being its attribute (*dharma*), or as a separate category of entity (*padārthāntara*)? In that regard, it is logically tenable that it is somehow different precisely by virtue of being its attribute, but not as a separate category of entity.

For do entities arise from their own causes as characterized by mutually non-confounded intrinsic natures, or otherwise? In the first alternative, it is established that they possess an intrinsic nature unmixed with anything else precisely from the collection of their own causes; therefore, the postulation of a separate entity called "non-existence" (abhāva) is useless. For where an entity is already distinct by its own nature—as in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth—the postulation of a separate non-existence is not fruitful. And since entities arise from their own causes with an intrinsic nature distinct by its very essence, [the postulation of non-existence is redundant].
The second alternative, however, is untenable; for since objects are not distinct in their own nature, it is impossible to effect a distinction because no separate entity exists [to provide it].

That which is by its very nature non-distinct in essence cannot have a distinction effected through the absence of something else that constitutes a different object, as in the case of a single individual entity; and according to the opponent's view, categories (padārtha) are by nature non-distinct in essence. (Page 465, Line 20)

By way of the nature of the jar and the nature of the ground, there is a twofold isolation between the jar and the ground: isolation in the form of property and property-bearer to some extent, as in the case of knowledge and the self; and isolation in the form of distinct categories altogether, as in the case of a jar and a cloth.

Comparison: For all entities abide in their own essential nature and do not mix themselves with another, because that would entail the consequence of [the entity] becoming non-other. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1.42) Nor can a distinction be produced among these [entities] which are mutually non-different by means of non-existence, because such [non-existence] is incapable of effecting a distinction between what is different and what is non-different.
Furthermore, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not possible for things that are non-distinct,
nor is difference produced by the non-existence of mutually distinct things, since they arise as distinct from their own causes alone;

nor is the conventional usage of "difference" produced [by such non-existence], because the very arising of entities in their own essential nature and as their own properties constitutes their inherent difference, and it is precisely through the manifestation of this in perception that the conventional usage of difference is established.
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.6:

Since entities, having arisen from their own complex of causes with their respective natures established, do not mix themselves with another, because that would entail the consequence of [the entity] becoming non-other (i.e., losing its identity)—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 208.
"Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 588; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 581: 'Mutually unmixed in their own nature' means they are distinct."

And in this regard, it has been stated [in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*]: "The state of having a distinct nature does not exist in prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), nor in cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*), and so forth."
Of the solitary one, from the state of being distinct— therefore, from the solitary... [fragmentary]

Furthermore, Vivikta: if there were no non-existence (*abhāva*), and the distinction (*viveka*) of positive entities (*bhāva*) were impossible without it, how could there be a mutual distinction among non-existences or from other positive entities? If, in that case as well, another non-existence is postulated as the cause of that [distinction], an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

If, on the other hand, the distinction of this [non-existence] from others occurs solely due to its own unique nature (*vilakṣaṇasvabhāvatva*) even without another non-existence, then the conceptualization of a separate entity in the form of non-existence is useless; for the exclusion of jars and so forth from others is already established through their very own unique natures.

For instance: the exclusion of a jar or the like from others is based solely upon its own distinct nature (*vilakṣaṇasvabhāva*), because it is an exclusion from others; whatever is an exclusion from others is based solely upon its own distinct nature, as in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*); and since the jar and so forth are excluded from others, [the inference holds]. Furthermore, the difference between existence and non-existence cannot be based on non-existence, for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If, on the other hand, difference exists by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then that same [difference] should apply to existent things as well; what, then, is the use of postulating a non-existence?
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.6:

"If a jar were to be excluded from a cloth and so forth by virtue of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), then would that mutual non-existence itself be excluded from existence, from other non-existences such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and so on, either by itself or by something else? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 208.
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 581: "In the absence of difference,
prior non-existence is distinct from posterior non-existence."
Since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is distinct from the jar and so forth,
there is also a basis for differentiation among absences in the form of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
Non-existence is distinct from existence, such as that of a jar, and from other types of non-existence, such as prior non-existence.

The cloth is not the jar, and the ground is not the jar; thus, the exclusion of the jar from the ground occurs solely through mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and solely through their distinct intrinsic natures (*vilakṣaṇasvabhāva*), and not through [some other] non-existence—this is the meaning (Āloka-ṭīkā). Therefore, [the distinction] is based solely on the distinct intrinsic nature, and not based on non-existence—this is the meaning (Āloka-ṭīkā).

Furthermore, mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) does not differ according to the difference of its substrata, because it is accepted as being one and the same everywhere. Consequently, the exclusion of a jar from mutual non-existence cannot be based on that very non-existence; for in that case, would the basis be mutual non-existence itself or another type of non-existence? If it were mutual non-existence, would it be that very same one or another? It cannot be that very same one, because [if it were], the jar and so forth would not be excluded from it.

When something is excluded from a certain thing, its exclusion does not consist in that very thing; for example, the exclusion of a jar from a cloth does not consist in the cloth itself. Now, if the jar is excluded from mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), then by accepting another mutual non-existence [to account for this], there would be a loss of its unity and an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if it is argued that another absence (*abhāvāntara*) is the basis for its exclusion from that [other thing], that is not so; for it is untenable that mutual exclusion (*itaretaravyāvṛtti*) should have another absence as its basis. Or, if it were tenable, the postulation of four absences would be redundant, since the cognitions "this was not here before," "that is not there," and so forth, are accounted for by a single absence alone. If, on the other hand, the exclusion of a jar from mutual absence is simply not admitted, then how can this fault be avoided? In that case, the jar itself would become mutual absence.

That which has no exclusion from something else has no difference from it, just as a jar has no difference from its own nature; and since a jar has no exclusion from mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*),
there is no second non-existence of mutual non-existence.
Regarding the state of being based on non-existence— according to the Ācārya’s commentary:
from this first mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva),
the exclusion of the pot and its mutual non-existence is not based on that [same] mutual non-existence, because it is from that very [first one] that the latter is excluded.
Exclusion from [the category of] being measured— Ā॰;
however, [it is] precisely from the three worlds— Ā॰ Ṭi॰—
of mutual non-existence.

The absence of a cow in a horse and the absence of a horse in a cow is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). This is one and eternal everywhere; even when an individual instance (*piṇḍa*) is destroyed, it is recognized in another individual instance just like a universal (*sāmānya*).

Just as a universal is connected with a newly produced individual instance by the force of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and its eternity is established by its very nature, so too is mutual non-existence—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 230.
In order to exclude a second mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), a third mutual non-existence must be postulated; and to exclude that as well, a fourth is required.
Thus, there would have to be some other distinct non-existence—such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth—that is different from mutual non-existence and belongs to the jar.
Mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) [is] like that of a cloth [and its threads].
(Note: *prāgabhāva* refers to prior non-existence.)

Because it does not exclude itself from being of the nature of a jar, which is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), that which was stated regarding the substantiality (*vastutva*) of non-existence is also established only as a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*), and not as something whose nature is entirely void; for such a thing cannot logically possess substantiality.
That which is entirely of a void nature is not a real entity, just like a sky-lotus; and non-existence is accepted by others as being entirely of a void nature.

Or, let it be granted that this [non-existence] has the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*); even so, by what means would it be apprehended—by the means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), or by another means of valid cognition? In the first case, is that "nature of a real entity" a positive existence (*bhāva*) or a non-existence (*abhāva*)? If it is a positive existence, how could it be apprehended by "non-existence," since it is not admitted that [non-existence] has that [positive existence] as its object? Furthermore, there is a contradiction in a non-existence whose nature is insubstantial (*tuccha-svabhāva*) being the locus of a "nature of a real entity" which is positive in character.

That which is insubstantial in nature cannot be the locus of a "nature of a real entity" that is positive in character, just like a rabbit's horn; and non-existence, as conceived by our opponents, is insubstantial in nature.

Now, if it is argued that it is non-existence (*abhāva*), that is not so. For if the nature of being a real entity (*vastutva*) were of the nature of non-existence, then it would follow that even blue and other such things are of the nature of non-existence, which would result in the total abolition of the discourse regarding existence (*bhāva*). If it is argued that it is apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), that is not so either; for if one does not admit that other means of valid cognition have the capacity to apprehend non-existence, it contradicts the admission that they have the capacity to apprehend the reality residing therein. Thus, when examined, neither the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) nor the object (*viṣaya*) of the means of valid cognition known as non-existence can be established.
The reality of non-existence.
Non-existence is not a real entity in every respect because its nature is void;
the state of being a real entity belongs to that which has the nature of existence.
Non-existence has non-existence as its object;
non-existence is not the locus of substantiality because its nature is insubstantial (*tuccha*).
— [Commentary on] the *Pari* [chapter].
Since the nature of non-existence is not a real entity,
that [objection] does not apply.

Nor is reality a result residing in non-existence, because it has been established that the result characterized by the comprehension of non-existence exists even through perception and other means of knowledge.
Furthermore, once its own nature is established, it is appropriate to speak of the determination of its cause, object, and result;
yet that [nature] of this [consciousness] is not established.

Now, as for the objection: "Since the nature of the means of knowledge known as non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), characterized by the non-arising of the five means of knowledge that apprehend an existent, is well-established for every living being, how can it be denied?"—this too is untenable. For what is this "non-arising"? Is it the absence of modification in the self (*ātman*) due to its not taking the form of a cognition whose object is the thing to be negated, or is it the cognition of another object? In that regard, since non-modification is itself of the nature of non-existence, how could it possess the capacity to produce such a cognition? Or how could it have the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*)? For the status of a valid means of knowledge is established for that which delimits (determines) an object of knowledge (*prameya*). And how can that which is in its own nature nothing at all be the delimiter of anything? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). That which is in its own nature nothing at all is not the delimiter of anything, just like the son of a barren woman; and the non-existent means of knowledge imagined by others is in its own nature nothing at all.

For the quality of being a delimiting factor (*paricchedakatva*) is a property of cognition; this is extremely difficult to establish for the absence of perception and other means of knowledge, which is like a horse's horn.

Consequently, there is a contradiction between the two terms of the proposition: "the absence of a means of knowledge" and "is a means of knowledge. It is just as in the case of "this exists" and "it does not exist," [which contradict] when the nature of the object is already established.
It is logical that the non-arising of the five means of valid cognition constitutes non-existence.
That which is to be negated is another entity consisting of the locus, such as the ground, by virtue of being the cognition whose object is the jar and so forth.

Comparison: For that which is formless, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not tenable if it lacks the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), because the definition of a means of valid cognition is the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*). That which does not have the nature of the comprehension of the object of cognition is not a means of valid cognition, just like a jar or similar objects; and non-existence (*abhāva*) is devoid of the comprehension of the object of cognition—this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
—*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 478:

Since the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself formless (*nirupākhyatvāt*), how could it determine the absence of the object of cognition (*prameya*)? For determination (*paricitti*) is a property of consciousness (*jñāna*). —*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 205.
Because non-existence is itself a form of existence (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 310; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 578).

In this case, regarding the production of a cognition in the form "there is no jar here," there would follow the undesirable consequence that even things such as a donkey's horn would be objects of determination by that cognition.

The non-existence (abhāva) consisting of the soul’s lack of modification (*apariṇāma*) cannot be a determiner of an object of cognition (*prameya*), because in its own nature it is a mere nothingness; thus, there is a contradiction: on the one hand, the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*)—being of the nature of the non-arising of perception and so forth—is itself an absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*); yet, on the other hand, by virtue of determining non-existence, it is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that serves as the substratum for the property of being a determiner (*paricchedakatva*).

The proposition is the acceptance of [non-existence] as having the nature of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*). Regarding its description as being of the nature of a means of valid cognition by virtue of its being a determiner:

even in the view that it is a cognition of another object, would this cognition be a determiner of non-existence with respect to any other object whatsoever, or with respect to the locus of the jar’s non-existence? In the first case, there would be a cognition of the non-existence of anything at any place whatsoever. If, on the other hand, it is the cognition of the locus of the jar’s non-existence; well then, this would only be established once the non-existence of the jar is established, yet that is not established according to your position.
Or, for anyone [perceiving] on the ground or elsewhere, there is no cognition of absence (abhāvajñāna).

Regarding the section on "the non-existence of established entities" (*siddhabhāvava*), the opponent—the Buddhist—states: "There is no such thing as non-existence (*abhāva*) distinct from the nature of an entity (*bhāvasvarūpa*) that is apprehended by perception or inference.
To this, the followers of the Sugata’s doctrine reply: "No non-existence whatsoever, distinct from the nature of an entity, is cognized either through perception or through inference."

For that which is the object of perception must, while being a producer [of cognition], also impart its form; however, it is extremely difficult for non-existence (abhāva) to possess both productivity and the capacity to impart a form.

That which is of the nature of non-existence cannot be the producer of anything nor impart its own form, just as a sky-flower [cannot]; and since non-existence is accepted by you as being of the nature of non-existence, if it were to produce a cognition by imparting its own form, it would necessarily be of the nature of an existent entity (bhāva).

Whatever produces a cognition by imparting its own form is indeed an entity (*bhāva*) by its very nature, such as a jar or the like; and since non-existence (*abhāva*) likewise produces a cognition by imparting its own form, it is therefore called the essential nature of an entity.

For that which arises from something, appears in a certain form, and performs some purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), is designated as the nature of an entity. This is what is intended: so-called "non-existence" does not exist at all; rather, it is simply the perception whose object is a positive entity that causes the conventional usage of "non-existence" for another thing.
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.6:

"The non-apprehension intended here is the apprehension of another object associated with the same cognition; it is distinct from apprehension, like [the concepts of] 'that which is not to be eaten' or 'that which is not to be touched. That itself is non-existence (*abhāva*), because there is no non-existence other than that which possesses a corporeal form."
— Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 2.3:
Therefore, non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), which consists of the nature of a cognition of apprehension, is an apprehension that has a different object, namely another real entity (vastvantara).
But how can perception itself be called non-perception? To this he says: "The intended," and so forth.

Just as in the section concerning what is edible and what is inedible, a village cock—though edible—is called "inedible" because it is other than the intended edible food; and just as in the context of what is touchable and what is untouchable, a *caṇḍāla* or similar being—though touchable—is called "untouchable" because he is other than the intended touchable object, so too should non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) be understood as apprehension itself. Therefore, that which is other than the object to be negated, such as a jar—which is capable of producing a cognition of its own object—and which is indeed capable of producing an apprehension (but not of the specific object in question), namely the form of the place devoid of the jar and possessing a nature contrary to that [jar], is what is here designated by the term "non-apprehension."
—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 163A.

That which is the isolation (*kaivalya*) of that other, solitary region—namely, its state of being alone (*ekākitva*), its lack of companionship—that very thing is the deficiency (*vaikalya*) or non-existence (*abhāva*) of another counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar.

Therefore, it is said by the followers of the Sugata that what you intend as "the non-existence of that" (*tad-abhāva*) is merely the existence of the other (*anya-bhāva*), a portion of existence (*bhāvāṃśa*); it is not a separate, distinct property (*dharmāntara*) apart from that [existence] which constitutes the portion of non-existence of the counter-correlate.

For there is no non-existence whatsoever that possesses a physical form such that it could be directly perceived; rather, it is something to be dealt with through conventional usage—*Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*, p. 65; *Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, fol. 179B.
First of all, a non-entity (abhāva) is not the producer of anything, nor does it impart its own form [to cognition], because it is of the nature of a non-entity.

Non-existence (abhāva) must indeed have the nature of a positive entity (bhāva), because it produces knowledge while imparting its own form; furthermore, if the form of non-existence were to enter into cognition, it too would result in being non-existent—how then could anything be perceived? Nor should it be asserted that the perception "there is no jar on this ground" is a means of valid cognition for the existence of that [non-existence], because this [cognition], arising through association with words, is conceptual in nature and thus cannot be perception; and conceptual cognitions lack validity regarding the object, since they do not touch the actual thing.

Therefore, the establishment of non-existence is not through perception, nor is it through inference; for that [inference] arises by the power of a mark (liṅga) that is invariably concomitant with the probandum (sādhya).

And is this invariable concomitance between the probandum and the probans cognized through perception or through inference? It cannot be through perception; because non-existence, as shown above, is not within the scope of perception, it is impossible to apprehend its invariable concomitance with any mark through it.
If that [invariable concomitance] were cognized through inference, there would be an infinite regress, because it would follow that even in that case, it must be cognized by another inference;
thus, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) cannot come from anywhere.
And a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose connection is unestablished is not capable of proving the probandum (*sādhya*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
— Because there is no experience of non-cognition, even in the case of cognition, due to the experience of their simultaneous apprehension, one thinks, "I do not perceive this."
The arising of the conceptualizing cognition [expressed as] "I perceive" or "I cognize"—
*Pramāṇavārttika* 4.270.
—of the perceptions associated with conceptual constructions—Ā. Ti. (Ba. Pratyakṣasya Ā. Ti.)
For inference indeed [proceeds] by means of the inseparable relation (avinābhāva). —
Āryadeva’s *Jñānasārasamuccaya* 21ab.
From perception—
[Ārya-ṭīkā]— of non-existence—
[Ārya-ṭīkā]— also in the second inference.
The cognition of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-pratīti*)— the mark (*liṅga*) based on the necessary bond—

and the subsequent establishment of non-existence (*abhāva*), which is a real entity (*vastusat*) consisting of another positive existence (*bhāvāntara-rūpa*), preceded by the refutation of that [opposing view].
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not distinct from the nature of existence (*bhāvasvarūpa*)—that is an unexamined assertion. The distinction [of non-existence] is established because of the difference in cognition, the difference in essential nature, the difference in causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), and the difference in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Whatever has a difference in cognition and so forth from something else, that is distinct from it, just as a cloth is distinct from a jar; and since there is a difference in cognition and so forth between existence and non-existence, [they are distinct].

And this [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*); for instance, the difference in cognition between existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed well-known: "this is here" and "this is not here.

Indeed, it is not proper to deny the cognition of non-existence even when it is being cognized in this way as distinct [from existence], because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of denying the cognition of existence as well.

Now, the claim that "by the power of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the two conceptualizations 'this is here' and 'this is not here' arise, yet the determination of the object does not depend on them because concepts lack validity regarding the object"—this too is mere faith; for since the validity of non-conceptual perception has been refuted upon the establishment of conceptual perception, it has already been demonstrated that only conceptual perception possesses validity as the determiner of an internal or external entity. Therefore, if the absence [of an object] is not established through a conceptualization of absence produced by the power of that [non-conceptual perception], then the establishment of the presence [of an object] is likewise extremely difficult to achieve.

Now, if the establishment of existence is derived from perception alone, then what has been devoured by crows regarding the establishment of non-existence? For first, perception—arising from the causal complex of the sense organs and so forth—apprehends the possessor of attributes as being inlaid with the various limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of both existence and non-existence. Subsequently, the cognizer, having grasped the necessary connection between word and object, recollects the specific words expressive of whatever object he intends to speak of after the perception of the object, and thus demonstrates the operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form: "This is here," or "This is not here."
Furthermore, if those specific absences were not apprehended through perception, then even the recollection of the counter-positive would be impossible;
for it is not logical to have a recollection of a jar as a counter-positive when the absence of the jar has not been perceived, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, since the recollection of a specific counter-positive cannot otherwise be accounted for, the apprehension of a specific absence must be understood as occurring through perception.
Page 476, Line 10:
Non-existence is distinct from the nature of existence, because of the difference in cognition, the causal complex, and purposeful action.
For comparison: "First of all, it is observed that two cognitions arise as witnessed by all living beings: 'The jar is here' and 'It is not here.'"
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 58; *vikalpavaśāt*—Ā. note;
*prāmāṇyāt*—also Śra. manuscript.
Of an object that is conscious in nature internally and unconscious in nature externally (pṛ॰ 47,
Nirvikalpaka— Ā॰ Ṭi॰).

Comparison: In that regard, whatever is asserted—such as "it is the mere awareness of conceptual construction," "it is without an object," or "it has itself as its object"—is the same whether it concerns the cognition of non-existence or the cognition of existence. Therefore, let there be validity for both, or let there be no validity for either.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 58). And because of the absence... (Śrauta-bhāṣya).
"It is non-existence"— this is non-conceptual direct perception [arising] from the conceptualization of existence— Ārya-ṭīkā.

"Various non-existences"— various existences and non-existences are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) or qualifiers; that which is inlaid, variegated, and painted by them is the object possessing those adjuncts, the substantive (*viśeṣya*),
for which a convention has been grasped.
Demonstration: That whose absence exists is the counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
Furthermore, it is not logical for a qualified cognition—such as "there is no jar on this ground"—to occur without its qualifier.

Any qualified cognition is not possible without a qualifier, just as the cognition "one who possesses a staff" and so forth; and here, the cognition "there is no jar on this ground" and so forth is indeed a qualified cognition.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "The basis for the cognition of existence and non-existence is therefore that very thing which will serve as its qualifier; and thus nothing desired by you would be established. This too is incorrect, because: is the entity being negated, such as a jar, accepted as the basis for this [cognition], or is it the locus, such as the ground? The first alternative is untenable, because the distinction between the cognitions of existence and non-existence—which are perceived as uncontradicted—cannot be accounted for except through a distinction in their objects.

The distinction between two cognitions that are perceived as being free from sublation must be preceded by a distinction in their objects, just as there is a distinction between the cognitions of color-form (*rūpa*) and other such objects. Furthermore, the fact that the cognitions of existence and non-existence—which are perceived as being free from sublation—are distinct is not unestablished; for there is no sublater whatsoever of those [cognitions], and they are experienced as having mutually unmixed natures.
No one who is not a fool would understand an entity itself as being non-existence, for the cognition of an entity is indeed different from the cognition of non-existence.
If an entity were itself non-existence, then at the very moment and location of that entity's existence, there would have to be a cognition of its non-existence;
but this is not the case, for no one can possibly apprehend the existence of an entity—restricted as it is to its own place and time—as being non-existence.
The cognition "there is no jar on this ground" is preceded by the apprehension of a qualifier, because it is a qualified cognition; thus,
even the cognition of non-existence is [in fact] existence itself— Ācārya-ṭīkā.
When there is the cognition of non-existence, such as "there is no jar here on this ground," the locus of the non-existence of the jar is the ground.

The difference between the cognitions of existence and non-existence is preceded by a difference in their objects, because there is a difference in their unimpeded cognitions. For comparison: "Indeed, without a difference in the object, there can be no arising of a distinct cognition, nor is a distinction in practical activity possible" (Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 229).
— The non-existence of consciousness (cidabhāva)— is,
by virtue of having mutually distinct natures, precisely existence (bhāva) appearing as non-existence. —
The non-existence of consciousness— by virtue of having mutually distinct natures— is, [in reality], precisely existence appearing as non-existence.
If an entity [exists] at the moment of the existence of that entity,
in the location of that entity.
