Now, if it is intended that the entity consisting of the ground and so forth—which serves as the locus for the pot and other objects being negated—is the basis for the cognition of their absence; even in that case, is it the mere ground that is the basis for the cognition of the absence of the pot, or is it the qualified ground? In the first alternative, there would be the conventional usage of "absence of a pot" even on a ground where a pot is present, because there is no difference in the nature of that [mere] ground.

Even in the second alternative, by what is its specific character (vaiśiṣṭya) produced—is it produced by its own nature (*svarūpa*), or by the absence of contact with a jar? It cannot be produced by its own nature, because it would follow that there would be a cognition of non-existence even on a floor where a jar is present, since the existence of its own nature is equally present there as well. If, however, it is based on the absence of contact with a jar, then there is no dispute over the name, for the non-existence of a jar is designated by the term "the absence of contact with a jar"—[and] by the phrase "having a jar, etc., as its locus" [in the commentary].

Comparison: Then they must be asked, what is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition "it does not exist"? If it is nothing at all, then you are handing over the very hand of proof to the Mahāyānists who assert that consciousness is without an objective support (*nirālambana*).

Alternatively, if the ground is the objective support, then even on ground possessed of thorns and the like, the cognition "there is no thorn" and the resulting activity characterized by walking back and forth without hesitation would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that the cognition "it does not exist" has as its object the bare ground alone, and that when a thorn is present, that bareness ceases, resulting in the absence of both cognition and activity [regarding the bare ground], then we ask: is this bareness the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the ground, or is it a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*)? First, if it is its nature, then since that nature does not change even when a thorn or the like is perceived, the same fault remains—namely, the non-cessation of cognition and activity. On the other hand, if it is a distinct attribute, then a separate category of reality (*tattvāntara*) is established. (Pramāṇasamuccaya-vṛtti, Praśastapādabhāṣya-khaṇḍana, p. 229)
[In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-ṭīkā-kiraṇāvalī*, page 329: Since the mere ground exists there as well, what is [the purpose] of this [mention]? Ba.
Of the ground—
taken away, taken away.

Even regarding a jar on the ground, one should not say: "This conventional usage of 'it does not exist' is mere conceit (abhimāna), because such [usage] is possible only when there is no occurrence of the conventional usage of 'existence'"; for if this [jar], which is being perceived and is free from sublation, were merely a matter of conceit, then it would follow that even the conventional usage "it exists" and so forth would likewise be a matter of conceit.

Furthermore, if the non-occurrence of the conventional usage of "existence" were the sole basis for the conventional usage of "it does not exist," then the usage "it does not exist" would also apply during deep sleep, since the non-occurrence of the conventional usage of "existence" is equally present there as well.
Thus, since the distinction between the cognitions of existence and non-existence—being unobstructed—is established, the real difference between existence and non-existence is proven.

For the Prābhākaras, non-existence (*nāstitva*) is simply the state of not being cognized (*apramīyamāṇatā*), and nothing else; yet this non-cognition itself is not an object of cognition (*prameya*). This is because the non-cognition of an object consists in the self’s possession of an experience that is not associated with that object; and that state of the self is indeed self-known (*svasaṃvidita*).

Therefore, no object of cognition (prameya) remains—*Bṛhatpañjikā*, p. 119–20. Consequently, it is precisely the non-occurrence of the means of valid cognition that apprehend positive entities (*bhāva*) which brings about the comprehension of non-existence (*abhāva*) (p. 119). However, since there is no comprehension of a specific nature for non-existence itself, the absence of an object of cognition is not something other than the absence of a means of valid cognition. Furthermore, the absence of a means of valid cognition is not distinct from the non-comprehension of another nature; and since the comprehension of another positive entity is self-luminous in nature, it does not itself undergo the status of being an object of cognition. Thus, an object of cognition designated as "non-existence" is not logically tenable.
And it is established that because the object of cognition (prameya) does not exist, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) can be postulated;
for the non-existence of the means of valid cognition is understood through their very non-arising, since the apprehension of non-existence cannot occur anywhere without them. (Page 124)
Because the non-arising of a valid cognition capable [of apprehending the object] is accepted as the cause [of non-perception],
even the fault of over-extension finds no occasion—
*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 129.
*Nayaviniścaya*, p. 162; *Tattvārtharahasya*, p.
17; *Prabhākaraviniścaya*, p. 57.

If [the world] were merely conceptual, then in the absence of a cognition of comparison there would be no error regarding cognition, and in the absence of linguistic usage there would be no error regarding usage—just as there is no error regarding darkness when light is not seen. This is not so, because it would entail such a consequence even in states like deep sleep; furthermore, an error is impossible with respect to that which is not cognized, just as in deep sleep and similar states.

—Furthermore, even if it is said out of impudence that "cognition and linguistic usage exist, though not in reality, because there is no perception of Caitra," [and thus] the knowledge "Caitra does not exist" is an error, and the absence of the linguistic usage appropriate for Caitra is an error regarding that absence—[the author] provides this very illustration: "like the error of darkness when light is not seen. He refutes this as follows: "No; because it would follow [absurdly] in states such as deep sleep. For if there were an error regarding those two [cognition and usage] in their absence, then the same would follow in states such as deep sleep."
For at that time there is neither cognition nor conventional usage, since the state of deep sleep and so forth is characterized by the withdrawal of all consciousness.

He states another reason: "And because error is impossible regarding what is not cognized. For, as established in the *Vibhramaviveka*, an error consisting of superimposition occurs only with respect to a cognized object upon another cognized object, and not with respect to an unapprehended form of cognition, nor with respect to non-existence; this will also be maintained here.
Furthermore, the absence of the cognition and its subsequent linguistic usage have never been previously perceived;
or, if they were perceived, what is the point of introducing an error here?
Therefore, since error is impossible regarding that which has not been cognized, this [position] is incorrect—this is the meaning.
—*Vidhiviveka*, *Nyāyakaṇikā*, p. 73–74 — and of that [group] beginning with *daya* — *ba*;
in that case, *anirbā* — *śra*.

And because of the difference in their essential natures (*svarūpa-bheda*): for the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) is the negation of existence (*bhāva*), whereas it is not so for the other.

If there were no difference between these two despite their difference in essential nature, it would follow that the very discourse on difference is destroyed; for in all cases—such as a jar and a cloth—the mutual difference is not established through anything other than a difference in essential nature.

(Compare: "Because a difference in essential nature is logically established; for just as color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, arising from their causes, are distinguished from one another by a difference in essential nature, so too is non-existence distinguished from existence."

Furthermore, the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) consists in its being uncharacterized by the six categories such as substance (*dravya*) and its being apprehended as dependent upon an existent (*bhāva*); this is because of the distinction [between existence and non-existence]. (Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā, p.
400). Or [it is so] because of the difference [of non-existence from existence]. (Bhāṣya).
Of these two, existence and non-existence, there is no existence of an entity.
Furthermore, the distinction between these two is well-established due to the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

For instance, one who desires to produce an entity such as a jar employs a causal complex consisting of a lump of clay and so forth, which is conducive to its production; whereas one who desires to destroy it employs a causal complex consisting of a hammer and so forth, which is of a different nature. Thus, there is a distinction.
[Note: *bhedādvā* appears to be a scribal error for *bhedādvā na* or similar.]
And likewise, that distinction—
the distinction in the causal complex—
is distinct from the causal complex of production.

Now, it might be argued that the causal complex consisting of the hammer and so forth operates only toward the production of shards that are mutually unconnected, and not toward non-existence; nor should it be said that the absence [of the jar] will likewise arise from this very same cause just as the production of those shards does. For every distinction among effects is pervaded by a distinction among causes, and there is no distinction among causes in the case of the distinct effects characterized as "absence" and "shards," since only a single cause—the hammer—is perceived.

Furthermore, the claim that it is illogical for a single entity to produce two mutually contradictory effects due to their opposition is also incorrect, because it would entail a contradiction with empirical experience.

For instance, immediately after the operation of a mallet or similar instrument, both common people and others have the cognition: "The jar has been destroyed by this," but they do not have the cognition: "The shards have been produced.
Nor is an intention such as "I am producing the shards, which are the destruction of the jar" ever experienced, even in a dream.

Indeed, when one intent on killing an enemy with poison or burning a cloth with fire has no further intention (*anusandhāna*) such as "I am producing something else there besides the destruction of the enemy or the cloth," nor do bystanders have the perception that "something else has been produced by him," but rather all people perceive that "only that destruction was performed by him," and he himself is satisfied only with that destruction.

There is no purpose whatsoever served by the production of parts for that [destruction]. Now, one might argue: "Since entities are by their very nature restricted to the nature of destruction, destruction is causeless; therefore, the mallet and such things cannot be its cause. This too is unsound, because the claim that they are restricted to that nature has already been refuted in the proof of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*). Therefore, it is better to maintain simply this: wood and the like cease by their own inherent tendency (*svarasataḥ*), whereas from fire and the like, the production of charcoal and so forth occurs.
—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 83a:

This is the summary of the meaning here: immediately after the operation of the mallet, two things are perceived—the cessation of the jar and the potsherd—and these two are likewise perceived as having the nature of destruction.
Regarding this, he will state that because the cessation of the jar is formless (nīrūpa), it is not an effect;

therefore, the cognition of it as an effect is nothing but an error. Alternatively, if it were an effect, it could not consist of the cessation of the jar, because it would be produced in relation to the jar; furthermore, there would be no cognition of it as having the nature of destruction, since the jar would still exist.

However, if destruction were causeless, the jar would simply cease by its own inherent nature; yet, since the jar is assisted by the hammer and other factors in producing shards—and because it does not initiate subsequent similar moments—it is logical for those of dull intellect to conclude that the cessation of the jar immediately following the operation of the hammer and the existence of the shard constitute destruction, and thus that destruction possesses a cause.

The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: those things that are independent of the presence of something else are necessarily restricted to that state; for example, a causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) that lacks any obstruction is restricted to the production of its effect. And since a produced entity (*kṛtaka bhāva*) is independent of anything else regarding its destruction, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.196–97.
Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 3.269–70;
Tattvasaṃgraha, page 132.
The destruction of the jar also [occurs] precisely from the operation of the mallet and so forth; [this is] because of the operation of the mallet and so forth.

Comparison regarding the characteristics of the destruction of the jar and the arising of the shards: Therefore, the arising and destruction of cause and effect are neither with-cause nor without-cause, because they occur simultaneously, like [the simultaneous perception of] taste and so forth;

and because, following the operation of the mallet and other instruments, just as the effect arises, the destruction of the cause is also perceived, due to the existence of two conventional usages: "the jar is destroyed" and "the shards have arisen."
—Aṣṭaśa°, Aṣṭasahasra° p. 200; *pravṛtta* is found in the manuscript (ba), while *pratīte* is in the Ā [manuscript].
And for the person— the spectators and those who observe.
By a person who bestows poison or who destroys cloth,
the necessity of having destruction as its inherent nature [is established],
page 386.

As for what was also said—that "the difference in effects is pervaded by a difference in causes," and so forth—that too is mere words; for there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) such that a single cause produces only a single effect, since even a single thing like a lamp is perceived to produce multiple effects.
Therefore, destruction is established as having a cause.

Consequently, since a difference is established between the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces the absence of a jar and the causal complex that produces the presence of the jar, the difference between existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) is established.
The existence of [the lamp] as a jar and so forth consists in the burning of the wick’s tip, the drying of the oil, the production of soot, the destruction of darkness, and so on— ba॰.
Furthermore, there is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) between that which consists of the striking with a mallet and so forth,
and that which consists of the lump of clay and so forth, which produces the jar;

for the difference in causal efficiency characterized by engagement and withdrawal regarding existence and non-existence is well-established, since the presence of water and such is the cause for the engagement of one who desires it, while its absence is the cause for withdrawal.

Furthermore, there is a distinction between these two due to their capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) such as joy and so forth; for instance, the destruction of an enemy—whether accomplished or merely heard of—induces supreme joy, whereas its actual existence causes dejection. Indeed, in this case, no cause for joy or dejection is perceived other than the presence or absence [of the object]; as it is said: "The arising of pleasure and pain occurs in the absence of enemies and friends."
"Having observed the absence of thorns, a footstep is placed on the path;
what conscious person, seeing an absence, would indeed deny it?
— *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 59.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that if even non-existence (*abhāva*) were to arise from something and perform some causal function (*arthakriyā*), then it would be nothing other than an existent (*bhāva*)—that too is incorrect. For "existence-ness" (*bhāvatva*) consists in being an object of the cognition of an existent, and not in the performance of causal functions and so forth.

Indeed, non-existence arises from its own complex of causes with a character distinct from that of an existent; and while performing a causal function, it is cognized as a functional entity (*padārtha*), but not as an existent.
pṛ॰ 477 pa॰ 2 – it arises;
[it would be] existence itself, Ā॰, Bhā॰, Ba॰.
Comparison: "For an entity is held to be cognizable through a positive condition (*sat-pratyaya*), whereas a non-entity is cognizable through a negative condition (*asat-pratyaya*)" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

59). And as for what was further stated—"If non-existence were to impart its own form to cognition, then cognition itself would possess the nature of non-existence," and so forth—that too is unsound, because it rejects the fact that cognition reveals an object by virtue of taking on the form of that object.

For it has been stated in the section on the exposition of perception (p. 477, l. 4) that cognition, being indeed formless, reveals an object that is suitable and situated in a suitable location by virtue of its own capacity, characterized by the destruction-cum-subsidence of its own veil (svāvaraṇakṣayopaśama).

One should not say, "Since non-existence (abhāva) is not a real entity (avastu), what is the use of the effort to establish it? For its status as a real entity is established by proving that it is cognized through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For instance: non-existence (abhāva) is a real entity (vastu), because it is cognized through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); whatever is cognized through a means of valid cognition is a real entity, just like existence (bhāva), and non-existence is likewise cognized through a means of valid cognition. Furthermore, whatever arises from a cause is a real entity, such as a jar or the like, and non-existence likewise arises from a cause. Moreover, whatever performs a causal function (arthakriyākārin) is a real entity, such as a lamp, and non-existence likewise performs a causal function.

Likewise, that which is differentiated by internal subdivisions is a real entity (*vastu*), such as color, taste, and so forth; and non-existence (*abhāva*) is also differentiated by internal subdivisions such as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest.
Therefore, it is established that non-existence, like existence, is a real thing, a property of real entities, and an object of cognition (*prameya*).

However, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that delimits it—called "non-existence"—is not established as a real entity distinct from perception and the other [means of knowledge], since its delimitation is accomplished even through perception and the rest.

Where an object is determined by another means of valid cognition as well, there is no restriction to a specific means of valid cognition, as in the case of fire and so forth; and since non-existence (*abhāva*) is also determined by another means of valid cognition, [there is no such restriction].

On the other hand, where an object is not determined by another means of valid cognition of a particular kind, there is a restriction to that specific kind of means of valid cognition, as in the case of color, taste, and so forth—this is what is being cognized.
Non-existence has lamps and the like as its objects;
and that is of two kinds: prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva).

Others say it is fourfold: mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); others say those two together make six types; and others say there are four: relative non-existence (*apekṣābhāva*) and incapacity (*sāmarthyābhāva*). (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 63)
Non-existence (abhāva), however, is of two kinds, distinguished as relational non-existence (saṃsargābhāva) and mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva).

Relational non-existence is further held to be threefold, consisting of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), destruction (dhvaṃsa), and absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva). Thus, it attains a threefold classification.

—[The verse] *muktā* [states]: "There is no separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called 'non-existence' (*abhāva*) as a delimiting factor, because that [non-existence] is delimited even by other means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. —[The commentary] *niyama* also says: "Just as in the *Bhaṭṭa* [school]..."

Just as taste is not determined by visual perception which grasps color, and therefore there is a restriction for gustatory perception to grasp it, so too, when non-existence (*abhāva*) is being determined by perception and other means, there is no restriction regarding its being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, the following is well said: "The absence of even an imperceptible particular state of another's mind [is known] because its facial expression, change of color, and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable.

For in all cases, the capacity to prove [a conclusion] exists solely by virtue of the principle of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*); and since that principle exists even in the case of the non-perception of the imperceptible, how could it not have the capacity to prove [the conclusion]?—[as stated in the Āptamīmāṃsā]: "It exists in the case of non-perception."

The commentary (*vivṛti*) explains the verse by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), beginning with the words "invisible" (*adṛśya*): If doubt alone is accepted as the consequence of the non-perception of the invisible, then for the Buddhist (*saugata*), not only is the absence of another's mind not established, but even the existence of his own mind is not established.
Why is this so? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

Regarding that reality of one’s own mind which is devoid of [other] entities, differentiated from both similar and dissimilar things, and which is the nature of the middle moment—since that is by nature imperceptible, what follows from this? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.

And thus, by that aforementioned manner in which the existence of one’s own mind is unestablished, how could there be a proof of the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of an entity that exists in the ultimate sense? For the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth, are all unestablished.

Indeed, if the partless reality—whether external or internal—is not established because its nature is imperceptible, it is not logical for the subject (*dharmin*) and other factors to be established; and if those are not established, how could there be the establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth? To whom, then, would the establishment of momentary destruction belong? He says: "That," etc. Therefore, the establishment of momentary destruction would belong to that which is the opposite of the partless reality—that is, to the reality characterized by parts (*sāṃśa*), which consists of multiple natures either simultaneously or successively—and not to anything else; such is the meaning of the particle *eva* (only).
The passage beginning with "tad" and so forth does not exist in Ā [manuscript] and Ba [manuscript].
In Ba [manuscript], there is "sajātīyavyā—
" [and] "tena svaci— " in Ā [manuscript].
Because the existence of one's own mind is established through inference of an existing entity,
[the objection] that it is unestablished due to its invisible nature is refuted.

This means: of a substance (*dravya*) characterized by non-difference, which is pervasive because its form is followed through various modes; or alternatively, of an aggregate (*skandha*) characterized by non-difference, which is pervasive because it possesses some degree of identity with its many parts.

Now, one might object: "Since the reality characterized by non-difference is apprehended in its entirety by determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), what is the use of inference regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth in that regard? To dispel this doubt, he says:
"Having observed the non-observation of the atomic sphericity (*aṇu-pārimāṇḍalya*) and momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)," and so on.

That which is visible is that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*). Its atoms are subtle parts; their *pārimāṇḍalya* is their spherical nature; their mutual distinction is their momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), meaning their dissolution at every instant.

That which begins with this—namely, the capacity of cause and effect and so forth—is described as such. The visibility of the atomic sphericity and the momentary destruction and so forth is stated as such; the non-seeing of that is its non-perception by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which constitutes incapacity.

Indeed, momentary destruction and so forth are not perceived by conventional perception (*sāṃvyavahārika-pratyakṣa*), because that [perception] perceives only a stable, gross, and common form; rather, it is only yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*) that has the capacity to perceive them—this is the meaning. Since reasons such as "because of existence," "because of being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*), and "because of performing a causal function" (*arthakriyākāritva*) are pervaded by attributes such as being manifold and impermanent in some respect, their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established.
He states an example for the subject at hand: "self-awareness," and so forth.

Self-existence (*svasattva*) means self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Its "separation from the form of an object"—that is, its exclusion from forms such as those of jars and the like—is the non-perception of that [separation], which is its non-apprehension by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Just as, when the nature of cognition itself appears, the exclusion of the form of an external object does not appear even though it exists—because for the Buddhists (*saugata*), cognition lacks such capacity—likewise, atoms and sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*), whether external or internal, do not appear through direct perception because they lack such power.
Therefore, the meaning is that inference is fruitful only within the framework of the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekāntavāda*).
—Laghīyastrayāvatāraṇī, p. 36:

"Just as there is no perception of a distinction between the self-cognition and the form of the object. Commentary: Since a single gross entity, which is of the nature of the perceptible, is not perceived at its prior and posterior limits, its non-existence is established; thus, its impermanence is proven. Just as in the case of cognition, the distinction between the forms of the cognized and the cognizer possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), whereas [the existence of] circularity and so forth does not, just like the partless essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Nor is there ever a self-apprehension of momentariness, circularity, and so forth, or of the reality of non-differentiated cognition, because they do not appear in that very manner;
therefore, if their nature were to appear in some way, the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta)—namely, "it may be visible"—is achieved. —Jaini-vṛtti.
The meaning of the verse:

That which is to be observed is a gross, single object that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). The "non-observation" or non-apprehension here refers to the sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*)—that is, the roundness—of its atoms (*aṇu*), which are exceedingly subtle parts; and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, as well as the capacity of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇasāmarthya*).
To illustrate this, he says "its own," and so on.

The distinction—that is, the cessation—of the objective form (viṣayākāra), such as the gross form and so forth, from one's own self-awareness (svasaṃvit), which is the partless cognition (niraṃśabuddhi) imagined by the Buddhists, is like its non-perception.

For when that [self-awareness] is manifesting, the distinction from the objective form does not manifest; otherwise, it would follow that there is an absence of the error regarding the gross form and so forth.

Whenever and wherever a real form is perceived, there is no perception at that time of a form contrary to it, just as when blue is being perceived, yellow is not. Yet, the distinction from the objective form is indeed perceived in the consciousness (saṃvit) imagined by the Saugatas.

The eternal [dimension] of jars, cloths, and so forth, as well as atoms and minds, is atomicity (*pārimāṇḍalya*); "atomicity" is its name. For instance: atoms and minds are spherical (*parimaṇḍala*); their state is atomicity, which is simply that dimension itself.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya, Vyomavatī, p. 473)
"Sphericality" (*pārimāṇḍalya*) refers to the most minimal dimension—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
133; "sphericality is the dimension of the atom"—*Saptapadārthī-ṭīkā*, p. 49.
The instrument for attaining heaven and so forth— [Muktāvalī, Kārikā 15]— Bhaṭṭa; Ācārya’s commentary.
–ddhaparika– śra॰ savidi –ā॰ ṭi॰:
the state of being devoid of the form of an object of apprehension.

For if the aspects of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth were to appear within consciousness, only then could one conceive of those appearing gross aspects as being erroneous. But when consciousness exists entirely devoid of the aspects of the apprehended object and so forth, how could a gross aspect appear therein even as something erroneous? There is no appearance of a gross aspect within consciousness even as an error, because what appears there is the actual state of being devoid of the aspects of the apprehended object and so forth—thus [it is] explained in the *Vivṛti*. (Bhāmatī)
The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation: Expounding the meaning of the verse, he says "of the gross," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: the impermanence of that which is gross—that is, large, unitary, and pervading successive and non-successive manifestations—is established in the manner already set forth, and only of that which has a perceptible nature—that is, whose very essence is observable—and not of anything else.

Why is this so? Because of the reason of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), the non-existence of that very [middle moment] at the prior and posterior limits is established. Thus, that which was stated by the opponent—"Whatever, being capable of being perceived (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is not perceived there, does not exist there, just as a jar is not found in a certain particular place; and the middle moment, though capable of being perceived, is not perceived at the prior and posterior limits"—is incorrect. For, if its non-existence there were to be proven in some way, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

In every way, if that [momentariness] were to be established, there would be a subversion of the thesis (*pakṣabādha*) by perception and a lack of proof for the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), because its non-perception is unestablished in that case.

Anticipating the objection— "Let it be that an object possessing a gross nature and so forth is impermanent, but it does not possess ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), since it is non-existent like the water in a mirage and the like"— he says "of the cognition" (*buddheḥ*), etc.,

meaning that the ultimate reality of the very object as described is [demonstrated], just as [the reality of] the distinction between the forms of the cognized and the cognizer in cognition [is established].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which possesses a manifold nature (*aneka-svabhāva*) is ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*), just like consciousness (*saṃvit*), which has a manifold nature consisting of the object of cognition, the subject of cognition, and so forth; and the entity accepted by the Jains, whether internal or external, possesses a manifold nature.
Nevertheless, by the example of the water in a mirage, since there is no distinction [between them], if this [entity] were non-existent, it would follow that consciousness too is non-existent.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that impermanence or ultimate reality belongs not to an object with a manifold nature, but rather to atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like? To this, he says: "But not again," and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not the case that an atom is spherical simply because of its connection with something spherical; rather, he states the demonstration of the impermanence and ultimate reality of that which is so described—namely, the composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth imagined by the followers of the Nyāya school—as being "like consciousness" and so on:
just as the partless reality, the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), of consciousness is [ultimate], so too is that [the atom].

Now, the followers of the Yoga and the Buddha schools maintain that since only a partless reality (*tattva*) is perceived both externally and internally, that alone possesses ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*); and because it is not perceived at the prior and posterior limits [of time], its non-existence is established. To this, he replies with the words "nor even," and so forth:

nor indeed is there ever—at any time whatsoever—the perception of that which consists of partless atoms (the *paramāṇus*), which are spherical, and so on, or of that which begins with the composite whole (*avayavin*), namely, of the reality of undivided consciousness (*avibhāgavijñānatattva*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "in that very way," and so forth.

In the same way, because [the object] does not appear in the manner imagined by others, one might argue: "Even if the external and internal reality does not appear as having a nature that is momentary, partless, and so forth, there is no fault here because it does appear in the form of being existent, conscious, and so on. To this, he replies: "In some way" (*tatkathañcit*), etc.

If it is admitted that the appearance of that external and internal reality occurs in some way—and not in its entirety—as the appearance of its own nature in the form of existence, consciousness, and so on, then the proof of non-absolutism (*anekāntasiddhi*) follows, because a single entity would be established as having both a perceptible and a non-perceptible nature.
According to the Buddhist,
there is an absence of a middle moment between the preceding and succeeding moments.
In every respect,
the apprehension of that [object] between the preceding and succeeding moments is unestablished; thus says the Vaibhāṣika.
In the Buddhist view regarding the middle moment— according to the Ācārya’s commentary—
the object (*artha*) whose nature is gross and so forth is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it possesses a manifold nature.

As it is said in the *Āryaratnāvalī*: "If one who has gone there thinking 'this is water in a mirage' should grasp at that water when it is not there, he is indeed a fool; so too is one who grasps at this world as existing, for it is like a mirage."
The notion "it does not exist" is also delusion; as long as there is delusion, one is not liberated.
Previously imagined through ignorance, when one later determines the true nature of reality and finds no existence at all, then where can non-existence be found?
Thus,
since all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how could they be established in the manner described?

Therefore, having accepted worldly misconception, the establishment of conventional entities— which are like water in a mirage— occurs solely through the acceptance of their being "mere conditionality" (*idampratyayatāmātra*), and not otherwise.
—*Mādhyamikavṛtti*, p. 188: because of the example of the water in a mirage, an entity that possesses a manifold nature such as grossness and so forth [is not ultimately real].
Various, manifold, circular, spherical, and so forth.

—In your view, O Nihilist (Nirātman-vādin), there is the perception of the self (*ātman*) as partless, indivisible, and all-pervading; yet, according to the Buddhist (Saugata) view, there is the non-existence of the external object because its partless, undivided specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not perceived in the preceding or succeeding moments, and it exists only for a single middle moment. Thus, [in both cases] there is only momentary existence.
—Because [the existence] of entities and so forth is established.

Having thus refuted the non-perception of the opponent, he now says, while refuting the reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth: "It is partless, both externally and internally, because it does not appear as such."

That which is imagined by the Buddhists as external and insentient, internal and sentient, partless (*niraṃśa*), and devoid of the divisions of substance, space, time, and state—how can that partless [entity] be non-perceptual, being outside the scope of perception?
Because it does not appear; because that partless reality (*niraṃśatattva*) does not appear and is not experienced.

Indeed, a reality whether conscious or unconscious, devoid of the divisions of substance and so forth, does not manifest in perceptual cognition, since in that [cognition] an object is cognized as pervading multiple parts such as permanence, impermanence, and so on.

Therefore, for that partless [entity] which is not established through perception, what nature or property could serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*)? The meaning is: none at all, because that which is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be a reason.

Furthermore, how could its effect be a reason? Since a partless and unchanging entity is incapable of producing an effect, from what [effect] could an inference arise? This is a statement of an objection, meaning: from nothing whatsoever.
Therefore, in the Buddhist doctrine, inference does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge because it is untenable—[as stated in] Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra, p.
37: "What could be its essential nature as a logical reason (hetu), or what could be its effect, from which an inference [could arise]? (17)

Commentary: For an entity that is partless (*niraṃśa*) and whose nature cannot be directly manifested, there is no possibility of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) in its inference, because its nature is remote (*svabhāvaviprakarṣāt*);
for the same reason, there is no possibility of a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*), since cause and effect are nowhere perceived.

Furthermore, in this case, there is no capacity established by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), nor is there a causal power characterized by the exclusion of the effect (*kāryavyatireka*).
That acceptance [of the relationship] is untenable without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

for if [the cause] were perceived by itself but not perceived before or after [the effect], its impermanence would be established due to its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and not otherwise. Thus, the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 73:
"When one thing exists, the other exists; and when that [first] thing exists, the existence [of the second] is brought about.
Thus, the relationship of cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception."
The meaning of the verse [from] *Sambandhaparīkṣā-prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 510;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, page 818.
Regarding that partless reality (tattva) imagined by the followers of Yoga and Saugata: where is it? Is it external or internal?
It is not perceived; why is it not graspable by perception? To this he says: "Because of its non-appearance," meaning because that partless reality is not cognized.

What happened then? To this he says: "Who is that? and so forth. Who [is there]? None at all; for what nature (*svabhāva*) could be the cause of that partless [entity]? Or is nothing its effect, which would then be the cause? Of that partless [entity], nothing [could be the cause].

The mention of "effect" (kārya) is an illustration; by this, the exclusion of those things distinct from the probandum—such as the conjunct (saṃyogin) and the inherent (samavāyin)—is established. Therefore, no logical mark (liṅga) whatsoever is possible according to the opponent's view, from which an inference could arise.
Is it the reason of effect (kāryahetu), which is not perceptible? Or [the other types]?
— Inference (anumāna) would be [the case], Ārya; inference is the detailed exposition (vivṛti-vyākhyāna).
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Directly," and so forth.

For an entity that does not directly manifest its own nature (*svabhāva*), which is its essential form (*svarūpa*), when an inference is being made regarding its partless reality—that is, its essential form—why is a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) impossible? To this he replies: "Essential identity," and so forth.

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is the essential form (*svarūpa*), is remote and thus invisible, there is a non-apprehension of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) for that very reason of its remoteness.
Why is this so? He says: "In the case of the effect," and so forth.
Furthermore, because cause and effect are not perceived—that is, are not seen—either externally or internally in all cases;

moreover, the comprehension of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is only logical once the causal relationship has been established, yet that [relationship] does not exist here. Thus he says: "And not," etc.
And not indeed—in this absolute position (*ekānta*) imagined by the Yogācāras and Sautrāntikas—is there a means of proof consisting of perception and non-perception; such is what is meant.

What is this "origin" (*prabhava*)? It is the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), based on the etymological derivation that "it originates" (*prabhavati*) or "it originates from this" (*asmāt*). And just as such an origin is not tenable in the case of an imagined monism, so too has it been explained at length in the section on the objects [of cognition]. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that origin is not everywhere established by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), but rather, in some cases—like the power of the sense organs—it is also established through the negative concomitance of the effect (*kāryavyatireka*)? This [latter method] might apply here. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the effect," and so forth.

The absence of the effect (*kāryavyatireka*) is its non-arising even when there is a completeness of causes other than the intended cause; or, the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position characterized by that [absence].
The connection is: "the causal capacity is not present here."
The intention is that when cause and effect, being partless, are not perceived even at their root, the exclusion of the effect based on the exclusion of the cause cannot be established.
Furthermore, he states—beginning with "the acceptance of that"—that it is not logical to accept the power of a cause without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The acceptance of that, namely the admission of the existence of the causal power through the exclusion of the effect, is untenable without another means of valid cognition, specifically without the means of cognition called *ūha* (presumptive reasoning).
For the postulation of a causal capacity (*kāraṇaśakti*) would occur only when the relationship of cause and effect is already established through the absence of the effect;

however, it has been stated that perception and inference lack the capacity to apprehend such relationships as causality—[as in] Laghīyastraya-kārikā 11: "No inferential mark (*liṅga*) is perceived by a non-conceptual cognition.
How, then, can that [causality] be accepted, since nothing is logically untenable without it? To this he says: "By itself," and so forth.

The non-apprehension of that very thing which was previously apprehended by oneself and seen in its intermediate state—namely, its own subsequent non-perception or disappearance—is what establishes its "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), that is, its being an effect; from this, the impermanence of sound and so forth is established, and not otherwise, nor by any other means. Since neither perception nor inference is capable of cognizing it in such a manner, it is held that the function here belongs to *ūha* (presumptive reasoning) alone. The mention of "producedness" and "impermanence" is illustrative; it applies to all reasons and their respective probanda.
"Show its own nature"—Bhaṭṭa says "this," while Śrīkaṇṭha says "here. [The commentary] states:

the etymological derivation of "effect" (*kārya*) is "that from which an effect arises"; the etymological derivation of "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is "the cause from which an effect arises"—Ātreya’s Commentary (*Ātreya-ṭīkā*).
"From this it originates"— thus [it is] *vyu-* (expanded/elaborated), as stated on page 220 and page 384 of the *Śrī-bhāṣya*.
Or rather, the acceptance of the causal power of the atoms cannot occur without the means of valid cognition known as *ūha*.
—And there exists a causal power in that [seed], because otherwise the production of the effect would be impossible.

Now, if it is argued: "Is it not the case that this entire relation of cause and effect, or the relation of means of inference and object of inference, is constructed by the artifice of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and is not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*); therefore, how can there be the application of another means of valid cognition?"—this too is untenable; for if conceptual cognition were established, then this entire worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) constructed by it would come into being.
And he demonstrates that its establishment—whether by itself or from another—is not tenable:

"In this way, this entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference is indeed constructed by the intellect, through the distinction between property and property-bearer as mounted upon the intellect.
He states "In this way" and so forth, indicating that this was also said by the Master Dignāga.

"All [of these] indeed" means that even in cases where there is a real distinction between the probandum and the probans, such as fire and smoke, because it is impossible to engage in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) by means of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is a conventional usage regarding them—namely, the inferential mark (*liṅga*), which is "that by which something is inferred" (*anumīyate 'nena*); the object of inference (*anumeya*), which is the subject possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*); and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). This conventional usage takes the form of a diversity [among these]. That is to say, the distinction between the property and the subject is established by means of a distinct form that has ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*); the meaning is that the conventional usage of distinction occurs through those distinct forms residing within the appearance of the intellect (*buddhipratibhāsa*). — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.1.1.204.1–3.
The intellect that accomplishes conceptualization has both conceptual and non-conceptual natures; how much more so, then, regarding that which is external and internal?

What, then, would be established? The meaning is that it would not be established. What is this "intellect" (*dhī*)? It is characterized as being of the nature of certainty; the meaning is that it is inferential cognition (*anumāna-buddhi*).

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is said to have the nature of both conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*). Conceptualization is determination (*vyavasāya*), while non-conceptualization is non-determination (*avyavasāya*); that which has these two as its natures is so described. Where [is this]? Both externally and internally. Here, the connection should be made according to the respective order: externally, with respect to objects such as jars and the like, it has the nature of conceptualization; internally, with respect to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it has the nature of non-conceptualization. Why would this not be established? Because of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself; for since that [self-awareness] is non-conceptual, it is not an object of conceptualization.
Because of the statement that "the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors is *svasaṃvedana*," it is established not only by itself (*svataḥ*), but also from another;
however, what more could be established? The meaning is that it is not established even from another conceptual cognition (*vikalpāntara*).
Why?

Because that [inference] is not established by itself, as it is not its own object; rather, it would be established through another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Since another conceptual construction must be postulated for the sake of establishing that one as well, there is no cessation anywhere.
Therefore, since inference is unestablished, how can the restriction on the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) imagined by the Buddhists be tenable? This is the point.
*Laghīyastrayāvatārikā*, p. 38:
"The nature of certainty would be established either by itself or by another; [but] because of the consequence of infinite regress [if it were by another], [certainty cannot be established].

*Commentary (Vivṛti)*: If the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of all cognitions is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*) free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), then since no certainty whatsoever is established by itself, and because the postulation of a further certainty leads to an infinite regress, how can the establishment of practical transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) with respect to that [cognition] be possible? Therefore, even regarding its own object, a single cognition must be understood as having a dual manifestation—being in some way capable or incapable of association with verbal expression—just like its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
All minds and mental factors have self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
The mind (*citta*) grasps the mere object, while the mental factors (*caitta*) grasp specific states such as pleasure and so forth.
All of these together constitute "all minds and mental factors" (*sarvacittacaitta*).
The term "all" is employed to dispel the doubt that pleasure and so forth alone—because they are clearly experienced—are self-cognized, while other states of mind are not.
There is no state whatsoever of mind in which the self's own cognition would not be perceptual;
for in whatever form the self is known, that very form constitutes the perception of the self's own cognition.
—Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā, p.
19—“Non-conceptual” (īśvarabindu).

For comparison: “If conceptual cognitions were determined by themselves alone, then even a conceptual cognition would have the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as its object; if [determination] were by another, there would be an infinite regress, resulting in non-apprehension.”
—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, p. 170. Meaning of the verse:
*Dhīḥ* means intellect (*buddhi*). Of what nature is it? It means the conceptualizing intellect whose essence is ascertainment (*niścayātmā*).
Furthermore, of what nature is she? To this he says: "conceptualization," and so forth.

Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is discursive determination (*vyavasāya*); non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*) is the non-discursive (*nirvikalpaka*). She whose two natures (*ātman*) are these is described as such.
Where? Both externally and internally; that is, her nature is conceptual externally and non-conceptual internally.
What is that? To this he says: What, then, would be established? It would not be established at all.
Why? Because of its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

That which is grasped by a non-conceptual [awareness] is not established, such as momentary destruction, the capacity to attain heaven, and so forth; and yet, the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is grasped by the non-conceptual.
"In that case, it will be established through another conceptual construction (vikalpa)," [to this he replies] with "from another" and so forth.
Not only from itself, but even from another—that is, from another conceptual construction—what could possibly be established? The connection is: "it would not be established.

Why is this so? He says: "because of infinite regress" (anavasthiti); because of the lack of finality, since there would be the consequence of yet another conceptual construction being established by a further one.
Non-conceptual;
from what [source]—from oneself;
accompanied by knowledge.
The nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is unestablished, because it is apprehended by non-conceptual [cognition] (*nirvikalpa*),

such as the momentary destruction in the case of blue and so forth, and the capacity to bring about heaven in the moment of non-violence— this is the form of conceptual construction (*kalparūpa*). (Śrī.)
Furthermore, there is no [reading] "it would not be established for us" (vika– ā॰ no siddhyet iti nāsti ā॰) in the *Śrī-vivṛti* commentary.
Explaining the verse, he says: "All," and so forth.

If it is maintained that the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the grasping of itself by all cognitions—both conceptual and non-conceptual—is perception (*pratyakṣa*) that is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*, i.e., *nirvikalpaka*), then here is the refutation: "ascertainment" (*niścaya*), and so forth.

Not only for non-ascertainment, but even for some form of ascertainment that serves as the cause for the conventional usage of inference and the object of inference, there is no ascertainment *per se*—that is, through self-cognition alone—because of the absence of ascertainment [in that case].

Now, if it were argued that ascertainment comes from something else, the author says "ascertainment," etc.: another ascertainment distinct from the ascertainment under discussion; because if one were to postulate such a thing, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Why? From nothing whatsoever; therefore, the intended meaning is that the establishment of conventional practice—characterized by the relation of cause and effect and so forth—is impossible because that very [convention] is unestablished. If it is argued, "Let it be then that cognition, being of the nature of ascertainment, exists both externally and internally," he says: "From that," and so on.

Therefore, even regarding its own object (*svārtha*), that is, the external particular (*bahiḥ-svalakṣaṇa*) which is the apprehended object of one's own cognition—there too, not only in the case of a universal, but in some way and not in its entirety—it is associated with two types of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*): namely, the word (*śabda*) and the universal (*jāti*), etc., [respectively] expressed by "it is expressed by this" and "this is expressed. The association (*saṃsarga*) of these two is the conjunction [in the form]: "this is the designator of this," or "this is the designated of this. Buddhists must admit a single common cognition (*jñāna*) that manifests both the capable and the incapable [aspects] of that [association].
Regarding this, he provides an example: "like its own nature" (*svarūpavat*), meaning just as it is with its own nature (*svarūpa*).
If it is accepted that [the mind] is dependent upon feeling, and that [feeling] is likewise [dependent].
Alternatively, it does not exist [there],
because of the absence of infinite regress; even in another [case], there is no [infinite regress].
Thus, "expression" means the word; that which is expressed by expression consists of [the categories] such as genus (*jāti*), and so forth.
The phrase "svarūpavat" does not appear in manuscripts Ā and Ba.

Having thus established for the opponent other means of valid cognition such as *tarka* (reasoning) and so forth, [the author] now states—refuting the restriction that *upamāna* (analogy) is a distinct means of valid cognition:
"Analogy is the means of establishing the object to be proven through its similarity to a well-known object."
In this context, the word "yat" (if) is supplied.

If that which arises from similarity (*sādharmya*)—that is, from resemblance—to a well-known object determined by a recognized means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the form of a cow, and which serves as the proof for the object to be established (*sādhya*) characterized by that resemblance, namely the knowledge "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," is accepted as a distinct means of valid cognition called analogy (*upamāna*), then what would be the status of that knowledge which arises from dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—that is, from the lack of resemblance to a well-known object—and which serves as the proof for the object to be established, namely the knowledge "the buffalo is different from a cow"? What would be its name? This is the objection.
For that [object] is not itself the means of comparison, because it lacks the defining characteristics of such a means;
nor is it perception and the like, because their objects are distinct and they arise from different causal complexes.
Furthermore, the communication of the named object involves a synthesis by way of its being the referent of the intended name, as in the thought, "This is a tree."
It is objected: "In that case, what indeed would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Certainly, the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the named object is not invalid, for that would entail the destruction of the validity of scripture (*āgama*), and it would also entail the invalidity of analogy (*upamāna*).
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 39)
Comparison (upamāna) is the means of establishing what is to be established through its similarity to an object of well-known meaning—
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.6.

Due to its dissimilarity to that, how could the communication of a name [of an object] be a means of valid cognition? || 19 Comparison—And upon the perception of a gavaya, one proceeds toward a horse and so forth.
Is that cognition of dissimilarity not another means of valid cognition?
Just as similarity [is a means of valid cognition], so too would dissimilarity follow as being a means of valid cognition. (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 450)
— Nyāyakusumāñjali 3.9:
If similarity were the object of cognition, why is dissimilarity not likewise?
—This is cited from *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 76; see also *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 498, and *Ratnākarāvatārikā*, 3.
4. Objects of Cognition (prameya), section 3.5.

*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*, p. 35, *Vivṛti*: If the similarity to a well-known object is determined to be otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapanna*), then it is nothing other than a logical mark (*liṅga*); from that, the cognition [of the object] arises, for otherwise it would not be tenable. For, in the case of a perceptible object, the cognition of the relationship between a name and the named thing constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, the cognition "this is a tree" for one who perceives a tree would be a distinct means of valid cognition, just as the cognition "this is a gavaya" is for one who perceives a gavaya; however, this is not so, because there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity to a well-known object.

Just as one who has heard "the gavaya is like a cow" and then sees a gavaya attains the cognition of its name, what indeed would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the subsequent ascertainment that among other animals perceived directly, this very one is *not* a non-gavaya? It ought not to be a non-means of valid cognition, since it results in the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference; for it would be logical [to consider it so], as stated in the *Jainaviśeṣa*. Among others, that very [cognition] is indeed [valid]. *Īśvaraviśeṣa*.

—Thus ends the meaning of the verse from the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*: A well-known object is the "cow"; the similarity or resemblance that the gavaya bears to it is the means of establishing—i.e., the proof of—the probandum, which is either the particularity qualified by similarity, or the similarity qualified by that [particularity]; this is the instrument of knowledge called analogy (*upamāna*).
The word "yadi" (if) should be understood here.
He states the refutation in this regard: "tat" and so forth.

By that well-known object, there is a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), a lack of resemblance, in the case of buffaloes and the like; from that, there arises the cognition that "these buffaloes and others are distinct from cows," which constitutes the proof of the probandum (*sādhyasādhana*). Is that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? What is its designation? One must assign some name to it, since it is not included among perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [accepted] means of valid cognition.

And likewise, because it would follow that there is a seventh means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be a contradiction of the established number [of six], namely that "there are only six means of valid cognition.
[The text reads: *prasiddhārtho* śra॰ –ṇaṃ kiñci– ba॰.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsaka is that comparison (*upamāna*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

"But if the means of valid cognition called comparison is not accepted, how can there arise in the mind a cognition of an object not present [to the senses] upon seeing a *gavaya*? For consider one who has perceived a cow but not a *gavaya*, and who has not heard the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), 'A *gavaya* is like a cow. While he is wandering in the forest, after seeing a *gavaya*, there arises in him a cognition of similarity regarding the cow—which is beyond his senses—in the form: 'The cow is similar to this. That is comparison."

And in this case, regarding the perception of similarity that is remote, it is stated that the proximate similarity is the instrument; and it has been said: "the cognizer... [Ātmatattvaviveka, Bhaṭṭa].

*Atideśa* is not [that]; *atideśa* is the connection elsewhere of that which has been heard in one place—*Vyutpattivāda*, Ga. The instruction (*ādeśa*) for the application of the properties of one thing to another—*Vācaspatyam*.
The extension [of a rule] is the principle that "this must be done in the same manner"—*Śāstradīpikā*, p.
277. Analogy (*upamāna*) also produces a cognition regarding an object not present to the senses through similarity, just as the sight of a *gavaya* produces the recollection of a cow.
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5

Comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition arising from the perception of similarity that has similarity as its object; for example, when a person who has previously seen a cow sees a *gavaya* (wild ox) similar to it, the cognition regarding the cow as being similar to the *gavaya* is comparison—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p.
110: "That which arises with respect to the counter-correlative [the cow] based on the perceived [similarity]."

Cognition whose object is similarity is called analogy (*upamāna*)—*Bṛhatīpañjikā*, p. 109. Analogy is the cognition of the similarity between an object currently being perceived and an object previously seen that is now being remembered; for example: "The cow that was seen by us in the city is similar to this one."
—*Śāstradīpikā*, p.
258; *Nayavīthī*, p. 146; *Tantrarahasya*, p. 13.
The remote cow is the instrument (*karaṇa*)— the most effective means— for [cognizing] the similarity residing in the proximate gavaya; thus says the Āloka-ṭīkā.
When a cognition arises with respect to something other than that which is being perceived— such as [the cognition of] a cow based on a gavaya— [it is called inference].
"By those who know it, analogy is remembered as [a means of knowledge] arising from the condition of similarity"— this was extracted from the *Āptaparīkṣā*, page 53,
and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 185.
From the *Tattvārtha-sarvajña-mati-ṭīkā*, page 575:
Its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) arises from its capacity to apprehend an object not previously apprehended.

Although the cow was perceived by him previously, and similarity is now seen in the gavaya through direct perception itself, nevertheless, because there was no prior realization that "the cow is similar to the gavaya," it possesses the quality of apprehending an object not previously apprehended.

Now, the claim that this [cognition] apprehends what has already been apprehended—because at this very moment the cow is apprehended through memory and the similarity through perception, and because there is no further object of knowledge—is also incorrect. This is because the state of being qualified by that [similarity] is not apprehended therein by those two;

for even though the similarity is cognized by perception and the cow by memory, nevertheless, since the individual cow as qualified by similarity is not perceived either by memory, by perception, or by both, the means of knowledge called comparison (*upamāna*) possesses validity, as it apprehends an object not previously apprehended.
For even in inference, there is no basis for its validity other than this;

for even in the case of perception, when the locus such as a particular spot has been apprehended and fire has been cognized through memory, it is by virtue of having as its object a place qualified by fire that inference possesses validity. It is the same for analogy as well;
thus it has been said:
The comparison [is made] by means of a person, like memory— Ārya-ṭīkā.
The similarity of the object of comparison (*upamāna*)— [as noted in the Āloka commentary]—
is [established] by those two. (Ba)
In the case of a cow,
[the cognition] has a qualified object by virtue of being both recollection and perception.
Because its object is distinguished [from others], such as a mountain (as noted in the Āloka-ṭīkā),
therefore that which is remembered becomes the object of knowledge for comparison (upamāna), either as qualified by similarity, or as the similarity itself conjoined with that [remembered thing].
Therefore, it is seen [as follows]: "The determination of similarity" (Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā, p. 19)—[this is] the marginal note (Ā. ṭi.).
*Commentary on the Tattvasaṅgraha*:

Since there is no object of cognition for comparison (*upamāna*) whatsoever in the case of the perceived gavaya, therefore it is the remembered cow itself— qualified by similarity to the gavaya— or the similarity qualified by that [cow], which is the object of cognition for comparison.
[Objection: Is it not the case that when similarity is perceived in the gavaya, the cow is remembered; what else remains to be compared? To this he says: "By perception...
He provides an example for that very point in the words: "In perception... (*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 445).

Even when similarity has been perceived and the cow has been remembered, comparison (*upamāna*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the specific [cognition] cannot be established through any other source. As it is said: "Because the specific [object] is not established through another... (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
345). Just as even when the place is perceived and the fire is being remembered, inference is not invalid because its object is specific.
These [verses]—from the *Bhāvanākrama*, the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika* (Upamāna section, verses 37–39)—are cited here:
*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 445.
The first two—Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 345; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 576; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 497.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 10:

Now, let it be granted that analogy (upamāna) is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); however, it is not distinct from perception (pratyakṣa) and the others, because its nature is included within one of those [categories]. This too is untenable, because its nature as being any one of those cannot possibly exist therein. For instance, it is not of the nature of perception, since it arises even in the absence of sensory contact with an object when the cow is beyond the senses (parokṣa).
Nor should it be asserted that this [cognition] is merely recollection (*smaraṇa*); for recollection arises only with respect to an object already apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, at the time of perceiving a cow, since the gavaya is not apprehended by that same perception, its similarity cannot be cognized through any one of the means of knowledge, such as perception.

This [cognition] in the case of the object of comparison is indeed an inference (*upamāna*) and not perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it arises when the cow is concealed and beyond the reach of visual contact;
nor is it memory (*smṛti*), because for one who has not previously perceived the cow at the time of seeing the [similar] object, there can be no experience of its similarity.
—Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 111.
Compare: "And this is not merely memory, because there is the possibility of an excess of objects of cognition;
for the similarity with the *gavaya* was not previously ascertained."
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 146: "The similarity to a gavaya [is known] through the direct perception of a cow."

Even if it is held that similarity is the connection with further common parts, its cognition [does not occur] until the counter-correlative has been apprehended; for its cognition occurs when that counter-correlative is perceived.

Since it is stated [in the Nyāyamañjarī, p. 146] that "the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of the similarity to a gavaya is the gavaya," this [cognition] does not have the nature of inference either, because it does not arise from a logical mark (liṅga).

In this case, would the probans (*liṅga*) be the similarity (*sādṛśya*), or the gavaya that is being perceived? If it were similarity, would that similarity residing in the cow or the similarity residing in the gavaya be the probans? First, it cannot be the similarity residing in the cow, because prior to the perception of the gavaya, that [similarity] is unestablished (*asiddha*); and that which is unestablished cannot function as a probans, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and the fallacy of the probans being a mere part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatva*). For the similarity residing in the cow is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and yet you claim that very same thing is the probans.

If it is argued that, "In that case, let that [similarity] residing in the *gavaya* be the logical mark (*liṅga*), because the two aforementioned defects do not apply here," we say no. For even in this case, there would be the fallacy of being unestablished due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*).
And that which is unestablished due to a different locus cannot be a means of cognition, just as the blackness of a crow [cannot prove the mortality of Devadatta].

[Objection: But surely, the state of having a known relation (*jñātasambandhitā*) is the same; and that is the definition [of a logical mark] here, whether it resides there [in the subject] or elsewhere. What does this distinction matter? [Response: It matters greatly. For in that context, the definition is "from the perception of one part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*), and "having a known relation" (*jñātasambandhasya*) is the qualifying attribute. Thus, the location of the relation is indeed relevant.

Therefore, the similarity residing in the gavaya is not [the means of] the cognition of the similar; furthermore, the cause of inference is that which has its relation observed repeatedly and which depends upon exclusion from what is not of the same class. Since neither of these two conditions exists here, it is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
— *Bṛhatī*, p. 108.
Prakaraṇapañcikā, page 111;
Śāstradīpikā, page 287;
[it is] imagined (parikalpate).
Because of the consequence that similarity to a cow would [apply] to a non-cow, the cow is the probandum.

For similarity residing in the cow is the probandum (*sādhya*), while similarity residing in the *gavaya* is the logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, [the reason] is unestablished due to being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*), just as in the case of [arguing] "the palace is white because the crow is black. (Āloka-ṭīkā)
By this, the status of the *gavaya* as a logical mark (*liṅga*) is also refuted, because there is no difference in the fact that they reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*).
And it has been said:

"For the *gavaya* resides in the forest, while the similarity is to be proven (*sādhya*) in the cow; thus, there is the fallacy of being unestablished due to residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhatā*)."

Nor can this [comparison] be considered inference, because the conditions such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) are impossible. Prior to [the cognition], the similarity of the object of knowledge is not apprehended as a property; nor is it [apprehended] subsequently. *Commentary:* However, those Buddhists who maintain that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or the Sāṃkhyas who maintain that there are three, who consider this [comparison] to be included within inference—against them he says: "Nor... and so forth.

He demonstrates the impossibility [of this] with the words "prior" (*prāk*): the similarity residing in the cow (*gau*) is not the probans (*liṅga*), because prior to the comparison (*upamāna*), that similarity has not been apprehended as a property of that [cow].
Thus he says, "in the gavaya," meaning that even the similarity residing in the *gavaya* is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) when the cow is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Furthermore, that which resides in the cow cannot be a logical mark (*liṅga*) because it constitutes only a portion of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). For that very thing residing in the cow is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), as he says: "the proposition.

Moreover, even the gayal (*gavaya*) characterized by similarity is not a logical mark precisely because it lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); thus he says: "in the gayal. Now, one might object: surely "being a property of that" (*taddharmatva*) consists merely in having a relation to it, and does not require only conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*); the gayal has a relation to the cow, for it is similar to it. In that case, how can there be a lack of *pakṣadharmatva*? To this he replies: "similarity."
Granted that the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) might somehow exist, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For the similarity of a gavaya residing in the gavaya has never been seen to be concomitant with the similarity of a cow residing in the cow; for it is only now that the similarity of the gavaya is apprehended.

[Objection: But surely, for one who perceives both the gavaya and the cow simultaneously—or any two other mutually similar objects—it is indeed possible to grasp the concomitance, thinking: "That which is similar to what is similar to X is itself similar to X. [Reply: Therefore, it was said [in the text]: "by everyone" (*sarveṇa*).
It is true that the universal concomitance (*anvaya*) is not grasped by everyone merely upon seeing a *gavaya* and apprehending its similarity [to a cow];

however, there is indeed the case where even for one who has not seen two similar things, upon seeing only a single cow and then seeing a second animal, a *gavaya*, in the forest, there arises at that very moment a cognition characterized by similarity. Thus he says: "In one... (*ekasmin*)—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 447.
Prior to seeing the gavaya— [as noted in the Āloka-ṭīkā]—
it is not perceived;

and that which is being apprehended in the gavaya cannot be the inferential indicator (liṅga) for the cow, because it is a part of the very subject of the thesis (pratijñārthaikadeśatva), and thus the property residing in the cow lacks the status of a logical mark.

The gavaya is not a mark for the inference of a cow because there is no [inherent] relationship; nor is its similarity [to a cow] previously perceived as concomitant with it, because they reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*). For it is only when a relationship exists that a signifier makes the signified known—Āloka-ṭīkā.

Furthermore, the similarity residing in the *gavaya* which is concomitant with that [similarity in the cow] was not previously perceived; rather, it arises for every cognizer at the very moment of seeing the *gavaya*. By this, the seed of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of comparison (*upamāna*), which consists in its being a means of apprehending an object not yet apprehended, has been made known. (Ānandajñāna’s Commentary) — When one sees a second object in the forest while one [object] has already been seen, the cognition arises regarding this [second object] together with the similarity. (Bālakṛṣṇa’s Commentary) "Together with one... (sahaikasmin—) *ba*.
Together in one place—these [quotations] are cited from *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 577; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
187; and *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 577.
Comparison is not inference because the three characteristics [of a valid reason] are untenable; nor can it be established here as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) or the like in any way,
for similarity residing in the cow is not apprehended as a property [of the gavaya].

And that which is perceived in the gavaya cannot be an inferential mark for cows, because it is a part of the very subject of the proposition; nor can the cow possess the status of a logical mark for the gavaya, due to the lack of a necessary relationship between them.
Furthermore, the gavaya itself does not attain the status of a logical mark for the cow, as there is no connection [between them].
—Tattvasaṅgraha, kārikās 1539–41.
Nor is this [cognition] verbal (śābda), because it could occur even for a cognizer who has not heard the sentence of extension (atideśavākya).
Nor is it presumptive (arthāpatti), because it does not depend upon a perceived or heard object that would otherwise be inexplicable (anyathānupapadyamāna).
Nor is it non-existence, because it does not depend on the cessation of means of valid cognition and objects of cognition; thus,
