the word "ba" [is used], and since it is a statement of extended application (atideśavākya) based on what was heard, it is not of much practical utility.
For even those who have not heard that specific statement, this [cognition] arises—[Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Upamāna, verse 10]. Compare:
"Presumption (arthāpatti) does not exist, because it does not depend on a perceived or heard object that cannot otherwise be accounted for."

It is not non-existence, because it does not depend on the cessation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the objects of valid cognition (prameya); for otherwise, there would be the consequence of [the impossibility of] its occurrence, since it cannot be established otherwise. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p.
450). Anyathānupapattiḥ. (Ā.)

Regarding the refutation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the demonstration that analogy (*upamāna*) is included within recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) based on similarity: here, the following response is given.
As for what was stated—namely, "the cow is similar to this" and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion, because such a cognition is simply impossible.

To explain: a city-dweller who has not heard the sentence of instruction (atideśavākya) while wandering in the forest, upon seeing an animal never seen before that is similar to a cow, perceives and says, "There is some animal that is indeed similar to a cow," but at that time no one possesses either the cognition or the verbal expression, "The cow is similar to this.
Or, even granting that such a thing exists, since it is of the nature of recognition (pratyabhijñā), it does not constitute a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).

[Objection: "Recognition (pratyabhijñā) occurs only with respect to an object previously experienced, because it is based upon both perception and memory. Now, the individual cow was not previously experienced as having the limiting condition of similarity delimited by the gavaya standing before one; for as long as the gavaya is not perceived, it is impossible to perceive the individual cow as qualified by a similarity delimited by that [gavaya]. [Reply: This is incorrect. For, of what is there the absence of experience—the delimitation by the gavaya, or the similarity? In the first case, even such cognitions as "this is that very same [person]" would not be considered recognition, because the delimitation by the subsequent instance had not been experienced previously.

Now, in this case, even though there is no prior experience of the delimiting factor—the subsequent state—there is recognition because of the experience of the delimited substance, which is the associated entity; that is the same elsewhere as well: even when the gavaya, the delimiting factor, is not apprehended at that time, there is apprehension of the similarity, which is the delimited factor.

If it is asked, "How can the gavaya, which is not yet cognized, serve as a qualifier for similarity?"—when is it not cognized? At the time of seeing the cow, or at a later time? In the first alternative, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even a subsequent mode (paryāya) could not qualify a substance, because at the time of cognizing the preceding mode, that [subsequent] one is also not cognized. If, on the other hand, it is argued that it qualifies it when it is cognized by a subsequent perception, this is no different in other cases as well. Therefore, there is no lack of experience regarding the delimitation of the gavaya.
16. For comparison: "Because such a cognition does not exist, the similarity of an unknown thing is indeed understood through that which is well-known."
But the reverse—that the cow is like the body of the gavaya—is not logical.

For instance, a city-dweller who has not heard the description [of a gavaya] while wandering in a forest, upon perceiving a living being previously unseen that resembles a cow, thinks and says: "Oh, what a creature this is that resembles a cow!

At that time, no one possesses either the cognition or the expression, "A cow is like this [creature]. Therefore, since there is no such valid cognition at all, what is the point of investigating the means of knowledge?
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 146;
*nāgarika* (variant reading:
*paśyan maivam*).

Comparison—because the cognitions of oneness and similarity do not transcend the nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), since they consist of a synthetic cognition (*saṅkalanajñāna*)—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
345; *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 19.
Syādvādamañjarī, p.
497; Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, p. 35; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 10.
— Because it is not so; nor indeed,
O venerable one, is there recognition [of the cow] as being qualified by a specific similarity residing in the gavaya.
[This refers to] the form "this similarity resides in the gavaya," and [the form] "this oneness resides in the subsequent synonym, namely, this very gavaya."

Regarding the recognition of identity (*ekatvapratyabhijñāna*), it has been demonstrated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* and other works that the comparison (*upamāna*) favored by the Mīmāṃsakas is actually included within authoritative testimony (*āgama*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*). For instance, since the instruction regarding the gavaya—which is not previously known—is conveyed by a reliable person through its similarity to a cow, this comparison is nothing other than authoritative testimony;
thus says the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 576.

Furthermore, analogy (*upamāna*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its nature is that of memory; rather, it is properly classified as a type of memory, just like any other memory. In this regard, certain parts of the body of a *gavaya* are the causes for a cognition of similarity with the parts of the form of a cow.
Thus, when a *gavaya* is seen, a memory arises in the observer regarding that [similarity].
—Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 448:
"Granted that this cognition [arises] in the form 'the cow is similar to this'; nevertheless, because it is a memory, it is not the fruit of a means of valid cognition" —Nyāyamañjarī, p. 146.

Therefore, when the gavaya is perceived, the cognition of similarity—which relies upon the absent individual cow—is merely a memory produced by a latent impression (saṃskāra) manifested by the sight of the similar object; it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 221.

Furthermore, this is the sequence in the arising of the cognition of similarity: first, one perceives directly in the cow the similarity [of the gavaya] such as its possession of horns; subsequently, after seeing the gavaya, one remembers—“This similarity of horns and so forth which was perceived by me in this individual body is the same that was perceived in the cow”; immediately after that, there arises the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of the similarity of horns and so forth, namely, “The cow is similar to this individual body. And since this cognition is thus of the nature of memory (*smārta*), how could it be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)? — *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 582.
Even in the case of recognition based on similarity—
such as the instance of recognizing identity in the form "this is that very same thing"— the subsequent momentary state [of the object] is also involved.

The intended meaning is that here the similarity residing in the cow and the gavaya is meant to stand in the place of a substance (*dravya*) that is already perceived; for even in this case, it is possible for the similarity perceived through the direct perception of the gavaya to function as a qualifier of the cow—this is the underlying purport. (Āloka-ṭippaṇī)

Nor can it be due to similarity itself; for is that similarity not perceived because it is not present, or because of the existence of an obstructing factor? It cannot be because of its non-presence, since its presence is not established, given that it subsists in the object currently present.

Nor is its non-perception due to the existence of an obstructing factor, for no such obstructor is perceived at all when similarity is perceived, just as there is none when an individual cow is perceived.

Now, one might object: "Since similarity resides in both [the object and its counterpart], how could there be its perception at the time of perceiving only one individual, without the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)? This too is not sound; for since this [similarity] is fully present in each [individual] separately, its perception is logically possible even without the apprehension of the counter-correlate. Otherwise, how could this [following] be tenable regarding similarity: [The verse: "Just as a face is perceived through a mirror, so is similarity perceived through its counterpart. If similarity were not complete in each individual, how could it be perceived in that way? Therefore, it is established that similarity is complete in each individual. Thus, the perception of similarity does not depend upon the apprehension of the counter-correlate. Furthermore, the cognition of similarity arises from the recollection of a previously perceived object and the perception of the present object; it is not produced by the sense organs alone. Hence, there is no fault. Thus, it is proven that similarity is a distinct category (*padārtha*). It is not merely a collection of common attributes, because it is cognized as a single entity, like a forest or an army. Nor is it a mere non-existence (*abhāva*), because it is perceived as a positive entity. Nor is it a substance, quality, or action, because it is perceived as distinct from those. Nor is it a universal (*sāmānya*), because it is perceived as residing in two substrates. Nor is it a particularity (*viśeṣa*), because it is perceived as common to many. Nor is it inherence (*samavāya*), because it is perceived as having a cause. Therefore, similarity is a distinct category. Thus ends the section on similarity. Now begins the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*). Non-existence is of four kinds: prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Prior non-existence is the state of a thing before its production; it is the cause of the cognition "it will be," and it is destroyed by the production of the effect. Posterior non-existence is the state after destruction; it is the cause of the cognition "it has been destroyed," and it is beginningless but has an end. Absolute non-existence is the negation of a thing where it never occurs, such as "there is no water in a desert"; it is eternal and devoid of beginning or end. Mutual non-existence is the negation of identity, such as "a horse is not a cow"; it is beginningless, endless, and eternal. Among these, prior and posterior non-existence are not real categories, because they are merely specific states of the substance itself. Absolute non-existence is also not a real category, because it is merely the absence of a thing's own nature. Mutual non-existence is also not a real category, because it is merely the difference between things. Therefore, non-existence is not a separate category. Thus ends the examination of non-existence. Now begins the examination of the six means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The means of valid knowledge are sixfold: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, presumption, and non-apprehension. Perception is the direct cognition arising from the contact of the senses with their objects. Inference is the cognition of an object through its mark (*liṅga*). Verbal testimony is the cognition arising from words. Comparison is the cognition of an object through its similarity to a known object. Presumption is the assumption of a fact to account for another perceived fact. Non-apprehension is the cognition of the absence of an object. These are the six means of valid knowledge. Thus ends the examination of the means of valid knowledge. Now begins the examination of the objects of valid knowledge (*prameya*). The objects of valid knowledge are twelvefold: the self, the body, the senses, the objects, intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), activity (*pravṛtti*), defect (*doṣa*), rebirth (*pretyabhāva*), fruit (*phala*), pain (*duḥkha*), and liberation (*apavarga*). The self is the substratum of cognition and the agent of experience. The body is the locus of the senses and the seat of experience. The senses are the instruments of cognition. The objects are the fields of the senses. Intellect is the determinative faculty. Mind is the internal organ that coordinates the senses. Activity is the effort toward an object. Defects are attachment, aversion, and delusion. Rebirth is

And like a universal, similarity is fully realized in each individual instance; therefore, it is perceived even when the counter-correlative is not seen. Thus, that [perception] is logically established—*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*; thus, it is perceived—*Nyāya-mañjarī*, p. 147.
This has been cited from: Nyāyamañjarī, p. 147; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
346; Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 221.
Comparison— since similarity, like a universal, is fully present in each individual, it is perceived even when the counter-correlative is not seen— Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 445.

For it is the very linguistic convention of similarity—expressed as "this is similar to that"—which depends upon the apprehension of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and not the cognition of its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

Indeed, having perceived a *gavaya*, the cognizer reflects with an attentive mind upon the specific configuration of the body of a cow previously experienced, and thereby initiates and synthesizes the linguistic convention of their similarity, thinking: "Previously, I already apprehended a cow whose configuration was equal to this living being"; then, recollecting that equality of configuration, he employs the convention of similarity, thinking: "Therefore, I am employing the convention of similarity."

Therefore, that cognition which consists of synthesis is indeed recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), just as the cognition "this is that very same [thing]," and the cognition "a cow is similar to this" also consists of synthesis.

For synthesis is the reflective discernment (*pratyavamarśana*) of two objective forms apprehended at earlier and later times, by virtue of their connection with a single property or their connection with properties such as similarity;
and this nature exists here, because a reflective discernment is possible due to the cow and the gavaya being endowed with similar properties.
He synthesizes:
the cognition "this is similar to that cow" consists of recognition, because it is synthetic in nature.
Or, through the connection with a single property (*ekadharmayogitayā*), there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same [thing].

[Objection: But if this is indeed recognition, does it not follow that it must arise from memory and perception, since it manifests only from their causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? And that [complex] is not present here, because its production occurs solely from the causal complex of the perception of the *gavaya* and so forth.

Nor is it logical that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a cognition produced by a heterogeneous causal complex (*vilakṣaṇasāmagrī*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); this too is incorrect, because such a causal complex exists even in this case. To explain: does the perception of a *gavaya*, depending upon memory, produce such a cognition, or does it do so independently? If it were the producer independently, then this [recognition] would occur even for one who has never previously perceived a cow.

Now, if its capacity to produce [recognition] depends upon recollection, then in that case too, does it depend upon recollection in general, or upon the recollection of a specific cow-individual (*gopiṇḍa*) to produce that [recognition]? If it depends upon recollection in general, then it would produce that [recognition] even upon the recollection of a horse or other such animals. If, on the other hand, it depends upon the recollection of a specific cow-individual, then in that case too, does it depend upon the mere recollection of a cow-individual, or upon the recollection of a cow-individual as delimited by similarity (*sādṛśya*)? In the first alternative, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would produce that [recognition] even upon the recollection of a buffalo or similar animal, because there is no perception of similarity and because there is no distinction between the two cases.

If, however, it were required that there be a recollection of the cow-individual as delimited by its similarity to a *gavaya*, then the prior experience of that similarity would already be established; for if that [experience] were not established, such a recollection would be impossible due to the absence of a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, if that [similarity] had not been experienced previously, a careful examination regarding the specific configuration of the cow-individual would be entirely useless;
for even if there were merely a recollection of the individual, it would follow that a cognition of remote similarity could arise by the force of seeing a nearby similarity.
Furthermore, for one who merely recollects the individual substance (*piṇḍa*) without determining its specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*), the cognition of similarity does not arise;
therefore, we consider that this recollection is produced by the experience of the cow’s individual substance as delimited by its similarity to the *gavaya*.

And it is established that the perception of the *gavaya*, aided by such a recollection, generates the knowledge "the cow is similar to this," and thus its origin from both recollection and perception is proven.

Therefore, analogy does not differ from recognition, because they arise from an identical causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Whatever arises from an identical causal complex is non-different, just as the inference of the nature of an effect and so forth, which is produced from a reason characterized by the mark of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). And the pair of cognitions characterized as recognition and analogy likewise arises from an identical causal complex consisting of memory and perception.

Comparison—In this regard, does the sense organ itself produce the cognition by depending on memory, or without depending [on it]? If it were a producer of cognition without dependence, then this [cognition] would occur even for one who has no memory of the cow's body. If, on the other hand, it depends on the memory of the body in general, then it would occur upon remembering the bodies of horses and so forth. If it depends on the memory of that which is delimited by similarity to a *gavaya*, then, if it depended merely on memory [of similarity], it would occur even upon remembering elephants and the like.

Now, if it is argued that [the cognition] depends upon the recollection of the cow-individual (*gopiṇḍa*), even then, does it depend on the recollection of the cow-individual alone, or on the recollection of the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya*? If it depended on the recollection of the cow-individual alone, it would occur even when there is a recollection of the body of a horse or other animals. If, however, it depends on the recollection of the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya*, then a prior experience must be asserted; for without that, no latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises, and consequently, the recollection itself would be non-existent. Therefore, even in the absence of a determinate cognition (*savikalpajñāna*), a prior experience regarding the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya* must be admitted.

For if, upon the arising of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), there were a cognition from memory such as "this *gavaya* is similar to my cow," and if previously the individual cow delimited by similarity to a *gavaya* had been established through experience, then why would there not also be the memory: "my cow is similar to this"? Thus, when questioned, one says, "I perceived something similar to this," but does not point to another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 588.

"The cow is similar to this"—this is the perception of the gavaya, [arising from] a cognition of such a kind—[Ānandajñāna’s] Commentary; [the reading] "cognition of such a kind" is in manuscript *ba*; [the reading] "cognition of such a kind" is in manuscript *śra*.
The perception of the gavaya.

For just as in the perception of a gavaya, similarity to a cow is not perceived when there is recollection of a buffalo or other animals, so too, even upon the mere recollection of the individual cow, there is no apprehension of similarity—
provided that [recollection] does not depend on [the perception of the gavaya].
The cognition arising from the power of existence is precisely the recollection of similarity— thus [it is stated] in the Śrauta and Bāhya [traditions].

As for what was stated—that "in the cognition of a remote similarity, the proximate similarity is the instrument," and so forth—what constitutes this instrumentality of the proximate similarity? Is it its being an inferent (*anumāpaka*), its being a cause of recollection (*smāraka*), or its being an analogizer (*upamāpaka*)? In the first case, there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows: for previously its status as an inferent was denied, whereas here it is accepted. In the second case, however, since the proximate similarity is merely a cause for the recollection of the remote similarity, it cannot logically be the cause of analogy (*upamāna*), because recollection itself cannot constitute analogy.

But that [similarity] would be the cause of that [recognition] only when accompanied by the memory of it, not by itself; and thus, the statement "that which is other than what is being seen" and so forth is difficult to establish.

By this, the third position is also rejected; for mere similarity cannot possibly be the indicator of that [object], nor is it possible for similarity to produce cognition, since the capacity of an object to produce cognition will be refuted later on.

Therefore, it must be admitted that comparison (*upamāna*)—which is synonymous with recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and which discerns the similarity between a cow and a gavaya—is produced by perception and memory directed toward similar objects.

If it is objected: "Even if the cognition of an object arises through other means, why would *parārthānumāna* (inference for others)—such as 'this mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen'—not be included within *āgama* (verbal testimony), given that you admit *upamāna* (analogy) is included therein? We reply: Because it is both the effect and the cause of inference.

For, although it takes the form of speech, *parārthānumāna* does not lose its status as inference, since it is the effect of the proponent's own *svārthānumāna* and the cause of the listener's own *svārthānumāna*.
This [status] is not possible in the case of the *upamāna* postulated by you.

Indeed, for you, there exists no other well-known means of cognition called *upamāna* apart from the comprehension of an object through the method characterized by the similarity (*sādharmya*) that has been taught; nor is there any [other] which, by virtue of being an effect of its cause, could constitute the status of *upamāna* even for this [cognition] arising from instruction.
This is because the convention is understood from the sentence itself;
for instance, the meaning of the statement regarding similarity is simply this: "That which is similar to a cow is to be designated as a *gavaya*."
And he, having apprehended the convention from the sentence and perceiving an individual delimited by similarity, employs it in discourse toward another, saying, "This is a gavaya.
As for comparison (*upamāna*), it is first the sentence, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya"; the cognition produced by that is simply scripture (*āgama*). (Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā, p. 589)
—from the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī*, p.
39; the *Vaiśeṣika-upaniṣad-bhāṣya*, p. 337:
"from the knowledge of the similarity to a well-known individual object as understood through a statement of analogy (*atideśavākya*)."
In the *Āgama*— according to the *Āgamānusāriṇī-ṭīkā*— even that statement [is authoritative] because it has that as its cause; thus it is stated in the *Parīkṣāmukha*, 3.56.

The intended meaning is that it is logical for this [comparison] to be included within scripture (*āgama*), because of the relationship between the name and the named entity—this is the purport of the marginal note (*āṅka-ṭīkā*). By this, the definition of comparison (*upamāna*) stated by the older Naiyāyikas—namely, that "comparison is simply the sentence of transfer (*atideśavākya*) which establishes the similarity between the well-known and the other"—is also refuted; for since this [transfer sentence] consists of scripture by its very nature, it cannot logically function as comparison.
If, by taking some slight distinction, one were to accept that this [cognition] has a nature not based on scripture (*anāgamatva*), then all the faults previously explained would necessarily follow.

Therefore, those who are discerning should understand that, primarily, it is only the cognition consisting of the reflection upon the similarity between a cow and a gavaya that is rightly termed "analogy" (*upamāna*), and nothing else; for in this case, there is no possibility even of a trace of the aforementioned faults.
pṛ॰ 497 pa॰ 9 –taḥ pramāṇaṃ yuktaṃ ba॰ –vāditi ba॰. From this point onward, it is logical that [this] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), according to the manuscript *ba*.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) provides an explanation:

showing that even though it was not explicitly stated in the verse (*kārikā*), a refutation is well-known, he says—“If the similarity to a well-known object is determined as being otherwise impossible, that is, in the form of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), then it is indeed a logical mark (*liṅga*), because that is the definition of a logical mark.
Now, if it is not determined as such, he states the refutation therein: “Therefore,” and so forth.

Therefore, comprehension—the realization of the probandum—arises from the similarity with a well-known object; otherwise, it would not be tenable in the absence of a determination of the "inseparability" (*anyathānupapannatva*) [of the reason].

He explains the first half of the verse beginning with "pratyakṣe" (in perception): when an object characterized as a *gavaya* has been made the object of a visual perception (*darśana*), there is the name "gavaya"; that object characterized as a *gavaya* is the "named thing" (*saṃjñī*). The relationship between these two, characterized by the nature of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*), is the connection. Regarding the cognition "this is a *gavaya*"—that is, the awareness (*saṃvitti*)—if this were admitted to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), he states the refutation: "vṛkṣa" and so forth;
the cognition "this perceived entity is a tree" would [absurdly] be a separate means of valid cognition—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To the question "Whose is that knowledge?", he says: "of one who sees the tree. Here he provides an illustration: "the gavaya," and so forth.

Just as the cognition "this is a gavaya" belonging to one who sees a gavaya is a distinct means of valid cognition called analogy (*upamāna*), so too would this present case be another [distinct] means of valid cognition.

If it is asked, "Why is this not considered *upamāna* (analogy)?"—to this he replies: "Because of the absence of that [analogy], which is the establishment of the object to be proven (*sādhya*) through similarity to a well-known object (*prasiddhārtha-sādharmya*). If it is further asked, "How then does that cognition arise as a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?", it is said: When someone who is ignorant of trees asks another, "What is a tree like?", the latter replies to him, "A tree possesses branches and so forth."
Due to that statement, the questioner, having formed a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), perceives an object possessing branches and so forth and recognizes it as "this is a tree.
By this, the meaning has been explained through its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to that [previous case] and the distinctness of that recognition;
for comparison: "The cognition that 'this word *gavaya* is the designator of what is similar to a cow' is also nothing but inference (*anumāna*)."

For whatever word is employed by the elders for a certain object, that word is its designator provided there is no other mode of application, just as the word "cow" is the designator of cowness; and since the word "gavaya" is employed for that which resembles a cow, it is the designator of that very thing—thus, the knowledge thereof is indeed inference (*anumāna*).
(Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, p. 40; Nyāyalīlāvatī, p. 56)
Because its defining characteristic is "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*),
[it is not] otherwise— *ā॰*.
That is well-known—ba; "from direct perception," etc.—āśrama; "this is a tree," etc.—āśrama.
Comparison—“This is a tree,” and so forth—*Parīkṣāmukha* 3.10; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 347.
"This is a gavaya"—
this [cognition] is a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*),
not, however, one consisting of analogy (*upamāna*). (Ānandagiri’s Commentary)
"Tree-cognition" (vṛkṣajñāna), "tree-sacrifice" (vṛkṣayajña);
and by that [reasoning],
Ācārya [states] that because of the dissimilarity in the case of the buffalo and so forth, there would follow the consequence of it being a separate means of valid cognition— Ācārya’s Commentary.
It is explained that, in order to bring about another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the opponent, [the author] says "like a cow" and so forth.
This is its meaning: when a certain forest-dweller is asked by a city-dweller, "What is a *gavaya* like?", he replies, "A *gavaya* is like a cow."
Then, just as for that city-dweller who wanders about and sees a gavaya after hearing the statement "the gavaya is like a cow," there is the comprehension of its name;
so too, the gavaya seen by means of that word is referred to, and the comprehension of its name as "gavaya" is precisely what is meant by "it is like that."

When other animals such as buffaloes—which are perceptible, have been made objects of visual perception, and are dissimilar to well-known objects—are seen by one who has previously heard the statement "a *gavaya* is like a cow," what indeed would be the name of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the subsequent ascertainment that "this is not a *gavaya*"? The term "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is used in a general sense to include both the non-verbal ascertainment belonging to the Mīmāṃsakas and the verbal ascertainment belonging to the Naiyāyikas; thus, the explanation provided for the Mīmāṃsaka is also included. Otherwise, he would have said, "the ascertainment of the name 'non-*gavaya*'."

Now, if it is argued that the cognition of a *gavaya* is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the author provides the following reply: "The result [of the cognition of a *gavaya*] is the apprehension of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference" (*hānopādānopekṣāpratipattiḥ phalam*). That cognition of a *gavaya*, whose fruit is such an apprehension, cannot be invalid; rather, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge. Thus, there is a contradiction regarding the limited number of valid means of knowledge. [This is stated by one] who has seen [the animal], saying "it is a *gavaya*. (*śra*) *Note: The final character "śra" appears to be a scribal or typographical error for "Śrī" or a similar honorific, or perhaps part of a citation marker.*
The statement of the [opponent’s] apprehension—[Āloka-ṭīkā]:

Just as there is for you the comprehension of that name through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too, when a gavaya is seen, the comprehension of the object would result in yet another *pramāṇa*; such is the sense. [Āloka-ṭīkā]: [This concerns] the investigation of non-similarity. [Variant reading: *asādṛśyamīmāṃsā*]. [Bāla-ṭīkā].

For the Mīmāṃsakas describe the cognition of similarity as analogy (*upamāna*); therefore, for them, analogy does not consist of verbal testimony (*śabda*). However, the Naiyāyikas describe the cognition of the relationship between a name and the object named as analogy; thus, according to their view, it consists of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
Otherwise, [the reading would be] *gava*—
[as noted by] Ācārya Akalaṅkadeva in his commentary on the Sūtra (Ācārya Bhaṭṭa’s marginal note).
—[This is] the fruit of giving and equanimity.

Furthermore, demonstrating another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is undesirable for another, [the author] says: "For one who understands the relationship [between words and objects], there is dependence on other perceptible objects."
From what [source] does it arise? From knowledge (*jñāna*).

What is it? It is the "comprehension of the relationship" (*sambandha-pratipatti*), that is, the cognition of the relationship consisting of the signifier-signified (*vācya-vācaka*) relation. How is it qualified? It is "dependent upon another object perceived by direct perception" (*pratyakṣārthāntarāpekṣā*). An "object other than the one under discussion" (*arthāntara*) is an object different from the object characterized as the word; and that which is both "perceived" (*pratyakṣa*) and an "other object" (*arthāntara*) is a "perceived other object" (*pratyakṣārthāntara*), such as a tree and so forth—that is what was stated. That [comprehension] which has dependence upon such a thing is "dependent upon another object perceived by direct perception."

If that knowledge were not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how could all the *upamāna* (analogy) postulated by the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others be a means of valid cognition? For there would be no distinction;

it is not the case that the knowledge of a relationship based on similarity is a means of valid cognition while the knowledge of the relationship between the denoted and the denoter is not. Consequently, the synthesis of the name and the named would also have to be a distinct means of valid cognition; so how can there be a fixed rule regarding the number of means of valid cognition? — *Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra*, p. 40.

If that [cognition] were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could all analogical cognition (*upamāna*) be so? Commentary: For one who has acquired a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) through scripture and who perceives the object, the comprehension of its name—whether taken as a complete valid means of knowledge or not—is not merely analogical cognition. For example, for one who has previously acquired a latent impression that "this eastern, western, northern, or southern village-hub bears this name," and who perceives it again, the comprehension of that name [is not analogical].

And what is this certainty? Why is it that only that which establishes the correspondence between a name and the named object is considered a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a perceptible object, whereas that which establishes the cognition of number and so forth is not?

[Otherwise]—as in the cognitions "this is before," "this is after," "this is long," "this is short," or "this is large"—it would follow as an undesirable consequence that these too would be [distinct] means of valid cognition.
—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 450;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 242 — "O you who destroy that [ignorance]! — *Īśvarapratyabhijñāviveka*.

The term *saṃjñāsamprajanya* refers to that [cognition] which possesses a dependence (*apekṣā*) upon both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and its object as something distinct (*arthāntara*). Thus it is so described.

"What is that? he asks. [The answer is: "The apprehension of the relation"—that is, the apprehension of the relation between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*). The ellipsis "from which" (i.e., from which it arises) is to be supplied. That is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He states the refutation should that not be accepted: "If not," and so forth.

If the analogy (*upamāna*) postulated by all the Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas is not a means of valid cognition, why? It is not a means of valid cognition for any reason whatsoever; such is the connection. Likewise, in that manner, by way of its lack of validity— *Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary argument concerning the status of analogy (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition.*
From which it is known that this [work] was composed by him; from where [is this known]? From the [colophon]. Ārya. Ba. Ā.
The analogy—
[as noted in] the Āloka commentary and the Vivṛtivyākhyāna— while explaining the verse, he says: "The scripture," and so forth.

A person who is non-deceptive regarding something is an *āpta* (reliable authority) in respect to that thing; his word is *āgama* (scriptural testimony). For one who has been impressed by that [word] with a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and who perceives its object—that is, perceives the meaning of the scripture—there is the apprehension of its name. This apprehension of the name of the object of the scripture, which consists in the apprehension of the designation for the meaning of the scripture, whether it be complete or partial, whatever such apprehension of the name there may be for one who perceives that object—is that a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? The word "it might be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied here. If it were a valid means of knowledge, there would be a contradiction in the number of valid means of knowledge.

Now, if [inference] were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then analogy (*upamāna*) would also be invalid, as there is no distinction between them; therefore, that same contradiction regarding their number remains.

Anticipating the objection that "the cognition of that [object] by means of it is indeed analogy, and that is accepted as a valid means of knowledge, so there is no room for the aforementioned fault," he says: "But not... and so forth.
"But not" means that it is certainly not the case that the cognition of that [object] is simply analogy—this is how the phrase continues.
However, the intention is that there exists another [type] besides that;
regarding this, he states an example, beginning with "Just as," and so forth.

The word *yathā* is used here to indicate an illustration. From this city or other location, there is a village headquarter (*grāmadhānaka*)—this is a designation for a particular village, meaning that its name is such-and-such, though not explicitly specified. For a person who has formed a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) in this way, when he sees it again, the cognition of its name—that is, the cognition of the name "village headquarter"—occurs in one whose disposition is such that he perceives what was previously described by the words "from this" and "village headquarter.
The word *ca* (and) should be understood here [to imply the cognition of the object itself].

By the word "from this" (*etasmāt*), that which depends [on perception]—namely, another object of perception—is stated; however, by the words "previously" (*pūrvam*) and so forth, that which depends on it—the primary cognizer—is indicated.
For this very reason, there is a distinction between them.
If it is asked, "Let this be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); what is the fault?", he says here: "And what," and so forth.

And what is this? Nothing at all; for when another person states a certainty—that is, an inevitability—one asks, "What is that? To which he replies: "It is precisely the means of establishing the correspondence between a name and the named object regarding a perceptible thing, and not a means of establishing [abstract categories] such as number and so forth. However, the underlying intention is that even that [means of establishing number, etc. might exist. Demonstrating this very point, he says:
Those who are liberated from passion and darkness through the power of austerity and knowledge,
whose stainless knowledge is always unimpeded throughout the three periods of time— they are the *āptas*, the disciplined, the awakened; their word is undoubtedly authoritative.
They will speak the truth; why [should they not], for they are free from passion and darkness?
— *Carakasamhitā*, Sūtrasthāna 11.18–19.
An authoritative person (āpta) is indeed a teacher who has directly realized the dharma and is motivated by the desire to communicate the object exactly as it was perceived—
*Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.1.7.
Sāṃkhyakārikā, Māṭharavṛtti, Kārikā 5;
Yuktidīpikā, p. 46.
"One must be an authoritative person (āpta) whose defects have been eliminated, who is omniscient, and who seeks the scriptures—*Ratnakaṇikā*, verse 5.
He who is non-contradictory regarding a particular subject is authoritative regarding that; anyone other than him is non-authoritative."
—Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p.
236: For one who perceives the meaning of the scripture, there is the realization of its name.
The comparison—whether it be a mountain, a city, or the like—[is the object of perception]. (Śrī. Ā. Ṭī.)
And then—due to the absence of well-known similarity and so forth—this very [reason] of his... [Ba, Śra;
Āṭi].
The apprehension of names—[Āloka-ṭīkā:

the apprehension of designations]—and the apprehension of duality and so forth, since they too are produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), would entail the consequence of being distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the intended meaning—[Āloka-ṭīkā].
Whether [an object] is small or large, distant or near, tall or not—
such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding an object present before one arises from comparative expectation;
this is another means of knowledge (*sādhanāntara*), that is, another instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

What is it? It is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). He states its specific manifestation: "This is smaller than that," "This is larger than that," "This is closer than that," "This is faster and longer than that," or "This is not as fast as that. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates mutual conjunction.
In what? In an object that is present and perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).
Why? Because of dependence (*vyapekṣā*); for there is some kind of non-abandoning of the function [of cognition] due to the dependence on a contrary opposite (*viruddha-pratipakṣa*).
Thus, the synthesis of smallness, largeness, and so forth also subverts the restriction of the number of other means of valid cognition (*parapramāṇa-saṃkhyā-niyama*)—this is the meaning.
—*Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra*, p. 40.

For comparison: "For those who have formed the latent impressions [of the words] 'the rhinoceros has one horn' or 'the *saptaparṇa* has seven leaves,' what kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would their recognition (*abhijñāna*) be when they subsequently see such things? Likewise, for one who has heard the characteristics of a woman and so forth, the recognition upon seeing her, as well as the comprehension of numbers and so on by those observing from before and after, and the application of names—all these, like analogy (*upamāna*), would be distinct means of valid cognition.
—*Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 150B.
Examination [of the means of knowledge], Chapter 3,

This verse is cited in the *Prameyaratnākara* (p. 498) regarding the meaning of "in the presence of" (*samakṣa*).
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, page 35.

Commentary: Regarding perceived objects, the cognition of smallness, greatness, and so forth—characterized by mutual dependence—as well as the cognition of lower, higher, and so forth, the cognition of numbers such as duality, and other such cognitions, are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they are non-contradictory, just like analogy (*upamāna*).

Whether presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a means of valid cognition distinct from inference (*anumāna*), or not—what is the point of such inquiry? For everything is included within the indirect (*parokṣa*).

Thus, it is consistent that there are only two means of valid cognition: the direct (*pratyakṣa*) and the indirect (*parokṣa*); otherwise, their number would be indeterminate due to mutual exclusion. Regarding the cognition of smallness, largeness, and so forth—compare the *Īśvarapratyakṣavivṛti*: "The cognition of numbers such as 'two' and so on is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). It should be understood that for a person to be instructed who possesses the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the verbal statement of a number from one skilled in calculation, the subsequent perception of substances qualified by numbers such as 'two' among those very objects leads to the realization of the relationship between the name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha-pratipatti*); this is the fruit of the means of valid cognition consisting in the cognition of numbers such as 'two'."

Likewise, the cognition of upper and lower [positions] regarding staircases and the like, the cognition of grossness regarding joints and the like, the cognition of largeness regarding one's own lineage and the like, the cognition of configuration regarding triangles and the like, and the cognition of curvature and straightness in certain cases—these have arrived as distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
— *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 242. (The passage contained within this is not found in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāviveka*.)

Comparison—some maintain that inference, analogy, verbal testimony, postulation, probability, and non-existence are also means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); how is this so? To this it is replied: all these are included within sensory perception (*mati*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), because they are caused by the contact of the sense organs with their objects—Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra, Bhāṣya 1.12.
Because analogy, presumption, and so forth are included within this very category— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.11—
presumption and the like, although distinct from inference, are nonetheless included among the types of indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*).
—*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, p. 281. The meaning of the verse:

the word "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) is connected with each [term]. There is the conceptualization that "this is small"; there is the conceptualization that "this is large"; there is the conceptualization that "this is distant"; there is the conceptualization that "this is near"; there is the conceptualization that "this is tall. Likewise, there is the conceptualization that "it is not small," the conceptualization that "it is not large," the conceptualization that "it is not distant," the conceptualization that "it is not near," and the conceptualization that "it is not tall."
The word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative position.
From what does this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arise? To this he says: "from relative dependence" (*vyapekṣātaḥ*).

For example, a *bilva* fruit is large in relation to an *āmalaka* fruit, while a mountain and so forth are distant in relation to a well near Devadatta; the same should be applied in other cases as well.

The mention of "this is small," and so forth, is an illustration; by it, the apprehension of distinctions such as inferior and superior, as well as distinctions such as duality and so on, is included.
Where does this [apprehension] arise? To this he says: "In an object present before one.
To the question "What is that? he says: "Another means, another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."
Having thus composed [the verse], he now provides an exposition by commenting on the *kārikā*, beginning with the words "In those things seen," and so forth.
That which is characterized by mutual dependence (*vyapekṣā*) with respect to objects perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is so described.
What is that? It is the cognition of smallness, largeness, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), distance and the like are included.
Likewise, it is the cognition of lower, upper, and so forth; here too, by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of the cognition of middle and other such positions is intended.

The cognition of numbers such as duality, etc.—here too, by the word "etc.," the inclusion of the cognition of numbers such as triad and so forth is intended—furthermore, the cognition of priority, posteriority, and so on; what is that? He says: it is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Why? Because of its non-contradictory nature (*avisaṃvādakatva*).
To what is it like? He says: "Like comparison" (*upamānavat*).

Having thus examined the convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasamplava*) according to the Naiyāyikas and Mīmāṃsakas—which undermines their restriction on the number of accepted means of valid cognition—he now reflects upon the *arthāpatti* (presumption) asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas and says: "Presumption," and so forth.

That presumption (*arthāpatti*) which has been defined by the Mīmāṃsakas as: "When an object known through the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being otherwise impossible, leads one to postulate another unseen [object], that is cited as presumption" (Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Arthāpatti, v. 1)—is this a distinct means of valid cognition from inference (*anumāna*), or not? What is the point of such inquiry? The intention is this: since the object that gives rise to presumption necessarily lacks logical consistency in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), it is characterized by the nature of an inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); therefore, its status as a logical mark (*liṅga*) alone is established.
And since the knowledge arising from that [scripture] is nothing other than inference,
therefore: perception, inference, verbal testimony along with comparison, presumptive testimony, and non-existence— these are the six means of valid cognition according to Jaimini.

Thus, for Kumārila speaking [in this way], there is a contradiction regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃkhyāvyāghāta*); and for Prabhākara, who asserts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a specific kind of perception, there are five means of valid cognition.
This is seen in the passage beginning with "dṛṣṭa" etc., which compares it to the sight of a row of trees and so forth: "Upon seeing a row of trees and the like, from the sight of a single tree..."

The ascertainment that "this is that same [tree]" arising from the cognition of a second tree would entail another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because it does not depend upon similarity or other such factors—
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 450.
Regarding this,
Ba and Śrā say:
the convergence (*saṃplava*) [of means of knowledge] is the operation of many means of knowledge upon a single object of cognition.
—[Commentary on] *Niṣkramaṇavināśa* by Śrī [Śālikanātha]:
"When an object, known through the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be otherwise [accounted for]...

Explanation: When an object delimited by the six means of valid cognition—namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*)—with respect to a particular place, time, and so forth, is not possible otherwise [if it were not as it is], that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) concerning an imperceptible object which thinks, "If such an object did not exist," is cited by Śabarasvāmin as the means of valid cognition called presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
"One might postulate another [cause] for what has not been perceived; this is cited as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 456). This [verse] is quoted from:
"It could not be otherwise" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Arthāpatti, v. 1).
Praśamaratiprakaraṇa, p. 590;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 216; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 578.
It postulates another [entity]—Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 456;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 578; present reading—Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 187.
Sya-ra-pṛ 276; Ratnākarāvatāra 2.1.
If it is not [as] imagined by oneself—*ba* and *śra* read "na cet" (if not);
*ā*’s commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "of fatness."
In the absence of eating at night— according to the Ācārya’s commentary—
the means of valid cognition consist of perception arising from the [sensory] marks, inference, verbal testimony, along with comparison.

Presumption (arthāpatti) and non-existence (abhāva)—these are the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) according to Jaimini. (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, verse 72). For comparison: "Perception, inference, verbal testimony, along with analogy, presumption, and non-existence—these six are the means of establishing what is to be proven."

—Because presumption (*arthāpatti*) is included within inference (*anumāna*), there would be a reduction to five [means of knowledge]—[Ā. Ti.]—the particularity of perception and so forth [is not established], b., śra. *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 450. Note: The commentary (Ā. Ti. points out that if presumption were not distinct, the number of means of valid cognition would be reduced to five. Furthermore, it notes that the specific forms of perception and other means are not established as separate categories. The manuscript variants *ba* and *śra* refer to different recensions of the text.
In this regard, the teacher’s view is that there are five kinds of valid cognition: perception, inference, as well as scripture, comparison, and presumptive testimony—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 127.

The connection is "the contradiction regarding the number of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasaṃkhyāvyāghāta*). There would be only four [means of valid cognition]—this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsaka who asserts that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a means of valid cognition distinct from inference (*anumāna*). (Āloka-ṭīkā)

But surely, since presumption (*arthāpatti*) is established as distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge due to differences in its essential nature and so forth, how can there be a contradiction regarding the number of means of knowledge? Accordingly, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Presumption is a means of knowledge distinct from perception and the others, because it has a distinct essential nature; for whatever has a distinct essential nature from something else is a distinct means of knowledge from that thing, just as inference is distinct from perception; and presumption has an essential nature distinct from perception and the others.
Nor is its distinct nature unestablished; for instance, its nature is as follows: "The postulation of an unseen object because a seen or heard object is otherwise inexplicable.

Here, "seen" means perceived by the five means of knowledge beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*); "heard" means understood from either worldly or Vedic statements. The postulation of another object (*arthāntara*) based on that which is thus inexplicable is *arthāpatti*.
And it is of six kinds, according to the distinction of its causes, such as perception and the rest.

Among these, the postulation of the burning power of fire based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the effect known as burning—which is apprehended through direct perception—is presumption preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā arthāpatti*). The postulation of the sun’s power of motion based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the sun’s movement, which is inferred from the mark (*liṅga*) of its arrival at another location, is presumption preceded by inference (*anumānapūrvikā*).

Likewise, the postulation of a cow’s power to be grasped by that cognition based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the individual cow-essence qualified by its similarity to a gavaya, as understood through the cognition of comparison (*upamāna*), is presumption preceded by comparison (*upamānapūrvikā*).

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also the postulation of a fact when a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for; for example, when Devadatta is known to be alive, the perception of his absence from the house leads to the postulation of his unperceived presence outside—
*Śābarabhāṣya* 1.1.5.

Presumption (arthāpatti), however, is a mental construction that leads one to perceive an unobserved object by showing that an observed object would otherwise be inexplicable without it, even in the absence of conceptualization.

When there is no other possible explanation for a perceived fact, the postulation of another fact that renders that perceived fact otherwise inexplicable is *arthāpatti*—as stated in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p.
"Having observed that a known object is inexplicable without another object, the postulation of that other object for the sake of its explanation is *arthāpatti*."
—*Śāstradīpikā*, p. 290; *Nyāyaviniścaya*, p.
152; *Tantrarahasya*, p. 13.
As seen on page 53 of Prabhākara-vi.,
the cognition arising from scripture (*śrutodbhavā*) is stated to be distinct even from these five [types of valid cognition],
because, by virtue of its grasping authoritative testimony (*pramāṇa*), it is dissimilar to the preceding ones.
—In the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Arthāpattivāda, verse 2:

although the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) refers to anything merely perceived, nevertheless, due to its proximity to the word "heard" (*śruta*), it refers to that which is distinct from what is cognized through verbal testimony, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).
—*Bṛhatīpañcikā*, p. 117.
Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 450; Sphoṭa—Ānandajñāna’s Commentary: similarity (sādṛśya).

The cognition of similarity (upamānajñāna) [arises] from a cow-individual qualified by similarity, which possesses the capacity to apprehend that [similarity]— [Ācārya’s] Commentary (ā. ṭi.), the capacity to grasp that knowledge (tajjñānagrāhakaśakti)— [Śrīdhara].

These aforementioned presumptive cognitions (*arthāpatti*) constitute a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because they have as their object a power (*śakti*) that transcends the senses.
Indeed, powers cannot be determined by perception, since they are supersensible;
nor can they be determined by inference, because inference does not operate upon what is not an object of perception, being dependent upon the latter.
For inference operates only when a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since power (*śakti*) is beyond the senses and thus not an object of direct perception, it is not logical for its connection with any inferential mark (*liṅga*) to be apprehended [through perception].

Nor can that connection be apprehended through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because such concomitance cannot even occur regarding an object that is not within the scope of direct perception.

Nor can the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) arise from inference; for would that inference proceed toward the apprehension of that connection by means of this very [inference], or by means of another? It cannot be by means of this very one, because it would lead to a circular argument (*cakraka*): for the operation of inference occurs when the apprehension of the connection exists; the apprehension of that [connection] occurs when there is the apprehension of capacity (*śakti*); the apprehension of that [capacity] occurs when the inference operates; and both that apprehension and its operation occur when the apprehension of the connection exists.

Now, if it is argued that the cognition of that necessary connection (*pratibandha*) arises from another inference; but surely that [second inference] also functions only when the necessary connection has been cognized. And in that case, would the cognition of the necessary connection arise from the first inference or from yet another? In the first alternative, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): for once the second inference is established, the establishment of the first inference follows from its well-known mark (*liṅga*) whose connection is already proven; and once the first is established, the establishment of the second inference follows from its well-known mark whose connection is already proven.

In the second case, however, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in one inference would itself have to be established by another inference, and that [second inference] cannot succeed in establishing its own probandum without the apprehension of a connection. Furthermore, there is no possibility at all of apprehending the capacity [of a word] through verbal testimony or comparison (*upamāna*); for the apprehension of that [capacity] is perceived even without the mediation of words or similarity.

Therefore, it is logical that the scope of capacity belongs to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone; moreover, the capacities of entities— which are established by presumptive testimony based on their effects—
are recognized as ultimately real and are determined for each respective effect.

— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śūnyavāda, verse 254: Therefore, in this case, there is a precedence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), where the existence of a power in a cause is understood from the non-perception of its effect.
Surely, the effect cannot serve as a logical mark (liṅga) because it does not depend on a [prior] relationship;
for this capacity is understood only after one has perceived its state of being related, and not otherwise,
since at the time of that perception, perception and other means of knowledge are impossible.

The validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would exist even without the three characteristics [of a valid inference]; furthermore, the postulation of a capacity (*śakti*) is also nothing but presumptive testimony. Thus he says, "Where... and raises the objection with the words, "Of the effect... (*kāryasya*).

He refutes the claim that "power (śakti) is postulated because [the effect] possesses a cause, and the cognition of the cause arises from the effect, which is thus an inference," by saying "no," and provides the reason: "because of the relation..."

Because the production of a sprout is observed when a seed exists, the seed's status as a cause is understood; yet, even when that seed exists, if it has been smelled by a mouse, the sprout is not produced, and thus its lack of causality is also understood. Desiring to avoid this contradiction between being both a cause and a non-cause, one postulates a "potency" (*śakti*). Furthermore, this is not an inference because it does not depend on the knowledge of a relation. To show why it is not an inference, he says [in the verse] beginning with *dṛṣṭvā* (having seen) for one and a half lines: for the apprehension of a relation is preceded by the apprehension of the relata; however, the direct perception of potency is not possible. Therefore, at the very moment of apprehending the relation, the apprehension of potency must necessarily be admitted.
For presumption (arthāpatti), being devoid of the three characteristics [of a valid reason], is capable of apprehending them—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Arthāpatti; *Nyāyaratna*, p. 462–63;
*Śāstradīpikā*, p. 306.
Because inference is preceded by direct perception,
[it depends upon] inseparable connection (avinābhāva) – Ārya-ṭīkā.
From perception— according to Ānandagiri’s commentary—
[it follows] the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
From one inference,
another inference arises for the sake of apprehending causal power.
Therefore, there is no [such thing].

Likewise, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), having understood the expressive power of a word through the fact that the comprehension of its meaning would otherwise be impossible, one postulates its eternity because that too would otherwise be impossible; this is "presumptive testimony preceded by presumptive testimony" (*arthāpattipūrvikā arthāpattiḥ*).
[Variant readings: *arthapratītyanya-* (Śrā), *ba*.]

Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is the postulation of [Devadatta’s] eating at night upon hearing the sentence "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," because the expressive power of the word would otherwise be inexplicable.

This sentence, merely as it is being heard, is not the basis for that comprehension; for since the words "fat" and so forth are intent upon conveying their own primary meanings, they lack the capacity to convey the meaning characterized by eating at night.
Nor can that comprehension arise from the collection of words, because this collection is intent upon conveying a different meaning altogether.

For when a collection of words such as "the fat Devadatta does not eat during the day" is heard, it conveys only the prohibition of eating during the day in the absence of elixirs and the like; it does not, however, convey a prescription for eating at night. This is because injunction and prohibition are mutually exclusive by nature, characterized by their opposition as mutual negations, and thus lack any coexistence.
Furthermore, a collection of word-meanings that is not syntactically connected (ananvita) is neither observed nor accepted as the meaning of a sentence, as this would contradict cognition.
Nor, in such a collection of words, does there exist either the denotative power (*abhidhā*) or the purposive power (*tātparya*).

Therefore, since the matter characterized by eating at night is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) itself, *śrutārthāpatti* is established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As it has been said:
"Some maintain that this object is indeed the meaning of the very statement that was heard."
However, for others who maintain that the meaning [of the Veda] is subverted by those [reasons], this meaning is not accepted even for another sentence that is being heard;
for it is not logical for a single sentence to possess multiple expressive meanings in that manner.
For the meaning of a sentence is indeed understood through the connection of word-meanings;
however, the word-meaning "night" is not conveyed by the sentence concerning the day,
nor is the nocturnal meal the connection of the word-meanings such as "day."
There is no difference [in the word] by which that sentence could be the expresser of it;
and because it is occupied with another meaning, there is no postulation of a second meaning.
Therefore, this [meaning] is understood through another sentence present in the mind.
One must state what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) applies to it among direct perception and the others;
for when a sentence has not been uttered, it is not accepted as being within the scope of direct perception,
nor is it [within the scope of] inference, since it has never been observed in association with anything else.

If, however, the status of being a logical mark (liṅgatva) were admitted even when the relationship [between word and object] is unperceived, then every utterance would result in the cognition of everything.

Regarding this, some imagine that the very word as it is heard is the conveyor of that [object], while others maintain that it is another word entirely that conveys it; therein, he refutes the latter position with the words "not, first of all" (na tāvat).
He states the reason: "For not...
Furthermore, if a sentence were expressive, there might indeed be multiple meanings; however, a sentence is not expressive, as he says: "Expressiveness...
How, then, is the cognition of the sentence-meaning produced? To this he says: "The meaning of the words..."
"Why is it that eating at night does not constitute the meaning of the sentence concerning the day? To this he says: "Not at night.

For the referents of words such as "night" are not denoted by the words of the sentence concerning the day; how then could they become the meaning of that sentence through a process of mutual connection?

Even if eating at night were either a combination or a distinction of the words "day" and so forth, it would still be the meaning of that very sentence; however, that is not the case, and thus he says: "Not by day."
Even though a word may have multiple meanings, nevertheless, when it is employed in a single instance, another meaning is not possible; thus he says, "of another meaning.
Therefore, he says "therefore," meaning that this is the meaning of an imagined distinct sentence, and not of the one actually heard.
He then says "of that," indicating that the means of knowledge for that sentence must be investigated.

And as for that [entity] which is a distinct object, although it is based on scripture because it is the meaning of a sentence and thus not without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, one must consider what the means of valid cognition for that very sentence is;

therefore, in order to state that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone is the means of valid cognition in this case, [the author] says "for not... (*na hi*)—*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Arthāpatti* section, *Nyāyaratnākara*, pp. 464–65.

Since the statement "he does not eat during the day" is intended to convey a prohibition, [the opponent] asks: "Let there be no contact; what is the fault? To this he replies: "Of that which is devoid of contact. (Ā. Ṭī.)
Likewise, in such words,
when they are intent upon conveying another meaning,
there is a direct power (*sākṣāt-śakti*).
In that regard, from the burning perceived directly, the power to burn is known in fire; and from the inferred motion of the sun, its possession of that power [the power of movement] is known. (Note:
*śaktatā* means the capacity for movement.)
From its power to burn is inferred the capacity for burning in fire; from its movement, the suitability for that capacity [of motion] is inferred in the sun— Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika.
This is cited from page 278 of the Syādvādamañjarī— Tattvasaṃgraha, page 457;
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 188.
In the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p.

579: "The capacity of the cow, which has been compared to the *gavaya*, to be apprehended by that [corresponding] cognition is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for the sake of establishing its designation. In the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*: "The cow that has been compared to the *gavaya* is held to possess the state of being apprehensible by the cognition of that [cow]."
The capacity for being apprehended— this is cited from Syādvādamañjarī, page 278—
in *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 188,
and in *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 579.
Comparison— the capacity of a cow to be apprehended by the cognition of that [cow] which has been compared to a gavaya— is understood through the power produced by the force of comparison—
Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 459.

"Because of the capacity of the word as a signifier, its eternity and its status as an object of knowledge [are established]; otherwise, denotation would not be possible; thus, the power of signification resides in the word. — *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*. "Because of the capacity of the word as a communicator, its eternity is postulated. — *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*.
The state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*)—that is, the state of being determinable—of that sound [is established] by virtue of its eternality. (Cited from *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
188; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 579).

Since denotation could not otherwise be established, one must first understand the expressive power [of a word] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and then, because there is no other way, [one understands] that [power] as being non-different from it.
The capacity to denote [an object] is understood precisely through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)— *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 459.
It is understood precisely through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—as stated in the *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 278;
the reading in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
188, is as follows: "Denotation" (*abhidhāna*) means denoting (*abhidhā*), that is to say, the communication of meaning.

Since that [meaning] could not be established without the word’s capacity to denote it otherwise, one understands—that is, realizes—the word’s capacity to convey meaning; and since there is no other recourse for that conveying capacity except for the eternity of the word, the eternity of the word is ascertained once again by means of another *arthāpatti*. (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 459)

The capacity [of the word] is indeed to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there is no way to understand it as being other than that or non-other than that. Furthermore, the ascertainment of the permanence of the word occurs precisely through another presumptive testimony;
for after the cognizer has understood the expressive power through one presumptive testimony, he would ascertain the permanence of the word through another. (Ānandajñāna’s *Ṭīkā*)

This will be explained under the [sūtra] "Because perception is for the sake of another" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.4). In the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, in the section on Arthāpatti, verses 3–7 state: "When such statements as 'The fat man does not eat during the day' are heard, the resulting cognition of his eating at night is called *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard)."
—From the scripture (śruti); [this] is called verbal presumption (śabdārthāpatti) —Syādvādamañjarī, p. 278;
this is quoted in Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 457.
The definition of presumptive testimony based on non-existence (abhāvārthāpatti) is as follows— [Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 188; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 579].

The proof of Caitra’s existence outside the house, which has been shown and described here as being based on the house qualified by Caitra’s absence as determined by the non-operation of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*)—this [proof] is cited from *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 460; it is also quoted in *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 189.

*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 579; *Syādvāda-ratnākara*, p. 278. Explanation: By means of the absence—determined and ascertained through the non-existence (nivṛtti) of valid cognitions such as perception—of Caitra, the house is qualified [as "the house where Caitra is not"]. From this [qualification], namely "Caitra is not here in the house," there arises the establishment of his being outside while he is alive, in the form of the certainty that "Caitra exists outside. This is what was described by Śabarasvāmin in this commentary (*bhāṣya*). The point is that this example was cited as an illustration for other types of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

"Just as when Devadatta is alive, the existence outside [the house] is postulated based on his non-perception inside the house"— this is the illustration of another presumption (arthāpatti) arising from non-existence (*abhāva*), as stated in *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* p. 460 and *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Arthāpatti section, verses 8–9.

When one perceives the absence of the living Caitra from his house and, through the impossibility of that [absence] being otherwise accounted for, postulates his existence outside, this is presumption (*arthāpatti*) preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*).
If it is argued that this is merely inference because the unperceived is established through what is perceived, that is not so, because the causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) for inference are absent.

For it is well known that inference is the cognition produced by the totality of conditions, such as the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); yet that [totality] does not exist here.

To explain: when Caitra qualified by his absence from outside, or the external location qualified by Caitra, is the object of inference, what could serve as the logical reason (*hetu*)? Is it Caitra qualified by his absence from the house, or the house qualified by the absence of Caitra, or the absence of Caitra in the house, or the non-perception of Caitra in the house? Among these, not even one can function as a valid reason, because they lack the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
Indeed, these are neither properties of Caitra nor properties of his being outside.

For while he is living, the collection of factors such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is indeed distinct from inference, because it lacks the constituent parts of the subject-property and so forth.

When the object of knowledge (prameya) is either an external location qualified by [the person] or that person qualified by the location, how can the absence from the house— which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma)— be a property of that [person], who is qualified by the absence [from the house]? Indeed, it is not a property of anything at all.
At that time, Caitra is not perceived as qualified by the absence from the house;
rather, the house is perceived there, and Caitra is not perceived.
Furthermore, non-perception (*adarśana*) is not the cause here, as will be explained in the case of [the definition of] non-existence (*abhāva*).
Therefore, the reason "because it was not seen in the house" is not postulated;
for when the non-existence [of the object] is determined through non-perception,
the cognition of its existence outside [the house] does not have that non-perception as its cause.

He first refutes the view that the absence in the house is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—namely, that the absence of Caitra in the house is the cause [of his being outside]—by stating "outside.

For the absence residing in the house is not a property of Devadatta, nor is it a property of the external location; rather, he says "the absence in the house" because a house qualified by absence is not a property of anything at all.

To the question, "How is it that 'this Devadatta' or 'the external region' [is perceived]? he says, "It is cognized. Here, the mention of Caitra is illustrative; it is only the house that is cognized, not Caitra or the external region.
Furthermore, since the cognition of a property (*dharma*) is not possible without first cognizing the subject itself,
if it is argued that the non-perception of Caitra is the logical mark (*liṅga*), [the author] replies with "na ca" (and not).

For just as the status of being a logical mark is impossible for non-existence when non-existence itself is the object of inference, so too here, it is because the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is absent.
For this reason as well, non-perception is not a cause [of knowledge]; thus he says: "Because of non-perception" (*adarśanāt*).

Once non-existence has been understood through non-perception, the subsequent cognition of external existence cannot have non-perception as its cause.
