Therefore, non-existence is not a logical mark (*liṅga*), nor does it possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Thus he says: "Of Caitra’s non-existence" (*caitrābhāvasya*)—*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Nyāyaratna*, p. 454–55.
Comparison—Nyāyamañjarī, p.

37: "There is no [cognition] of Caitra's absence in the house with respect to Caitra's specific external existence" (Śāradā manuscript); "or [there is no cognition] of Caitra's absence in the house" (Ānandāśrama edition).
With respect to the first two reasons—[Ācārya’s Commentary];
with respect to the second two reasons—[Ācārya’s Commentary].

Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of [the cognition] entering into the object of knowledge (*prameya*), this is not inference (*anumāna*). For instance, the presence outside of Caitra, whose life is known through scripture, is postulated on the basis of his absence from the house; otherwise, there would be an inconclusive deviation (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of one who is dead.
Furthermore, it is the apprehension of non-existence (*abhāva*) that makes known the external existence [of the person], not its non-apprehension, just as smoke [makes known fire].
And the apprehension of non-existence is preceded by the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend an existent;

however, in this case, there certainly exists a means of valid cognition that apprehends the existent, namely the scripture (*āgama*) called "life. While that [scripture] exists, how could the apprehension of non-existence proceed? Indeed, this very means of valid cognition that apprehends the existent establishes a distinct object [of knowledge] as it proceeds.

For "living" is existence; that which is apprehended of it in a general way through scripture is restricted by the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that determines its absence from the house to something other than its own object—namely, "its existence is outside, while its absence is in the house. Thus, since the cognition of the probandum characterized as existence outside is established as being preceded by the cognition of the probans characterized as the living person's absence from the house, the entry [of the probans] into the object of knowledge (prameya) is established. Therefore, this is not inference.

For in the inference of fire and so forth, the cognition of the object to be inferred (the probandum) is not perceived at the time of grasping the mark (liṅga), such as smoke, since that cognition is perceived only after the grasping of the smoke and so forth has occurred.

[Objection: But is not the fault of the inclusion of the object of knowledge (prameya-anupraveśa) equally present in presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) as well? [Reply: That is indeed true; nevertheless, presumptive testimony—which functions to establish the existence and non-existence of a single entity presented by two means of valid cognition—necessarily takes both objects of knowledge into account, for otherwise their synthesis would be impossible.

Therefore, that very cognition which previously arose from scripture as the awareness that "it exists somewhere" due to its location being unspecified, becomes this cognition that "it exists outside" once the absence in the house has been apprehended.
Because of this difference in character, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not inference;
for in the case of presumption, the knowledge of the object to be proven (*sādhya*) enters [into the cognition] at the very time the reason (*hetu*) is apprehended.
In this case, the absence from the house while alive is postulated as the property of the subject (pakṣadharma);
and the cognition of that [absence] does not arise without first cognizing his existence outside. However, the possession of smoke is perceived independently of the possession of fire.
For at the time of perceiving that [absence], nothing whatsoever depends upon fire;
however, the mere absence of the house, being pure and devoid of the quality of existence,
is seen even among the dead, because it occurs externally, and thus it is not a prover [of the person's absence].
By this cognition of the absence of Caitra in the house— which is conjoined with his existence— Caitra is indeed inferred to exist outside the house;
for it is merely the state of being absent from the house that is cognized independently.
It is not by that much alone that Caitra’s external existence is determined; rather,

once his existence is established through the cognition of his presence elsewhere, the fact that he is absent from the house implies that his being, having departed from the house, must reside outside.
Therefore, for that [cognition] which is independent, there is deviation by means of death and so forth;
however, from that which possesses non-deviation, nothing other than that is cognized.
Consequently, when Caitra is absent in the house, his absence is indeed established through perception.
That very cognition of existence which occurs when [the object] is known is itself situated externally;
it is introduced into the external state for the sake of acquiring the nature of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
That [external object], as qualified by that [cognition], would be the inferable (*anumeya*) through the property of the subject, positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and so forth.

If the cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth were to occur through external awareness, and that [external awareness] were necessarily to be known by those [cognitions], there would inevitably be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśrayatā*).
However, in the case of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), there is rather an entry into the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Since [the absence] is cognized precisely as having that same nature [as the cognition], no fault appears; for that external existence by which Caitra would be qualified so as to be inferred has already been introduced at the very moment of its perception in order to establish the self-nature of the absence as a property of the living Caitra who is the subject (*pakṣa*).

If, despite this being the case, one still wishes to maintain that it is an inference, then it is clearly a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*); thus he says: "Because of the property of the subject, etc. (*pakṣadharmādīti*).

But surely this same defect applies to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as well; for there too, the mere absence from the house is compatible with death and does not necessitate the postulation of being outside. Only when it is conjoined with the fact of being alive could it lead to such a postulation, yet that conjunction cannot be known so long as being outside is unknown. Furthermore, what is unknown cannot be the object of a postulation, and once that [being outside] is known, there would be no further object of knowledge (*prameya*). To this, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).

This means that in the case of another means of knowledge consisting of the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), the entry of the object of knowledge—namely, being outside—occurs at the very moment of the cognition of the absence from the house conjoined with being alive; thus, there is no defect.
Why? Because it is known precisely through its own form (*tādrūpyeṇa*).

For this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is of such a nature that, having observed an impossibility due to mutual contradiction with another object for which it exists, one avoids that contradiction by postulating another object; it is for this very reason that its status as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntaratva*) based on a different causal complex (*vilakṣaṇasāmagrī*) is untenable, and thus the contradiction with another object is stated regarding that which has already been understood—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Nyāyaratnākara*, pp.
Śāstradīpikā, p. 297; cf.
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 37:
"If external existence were to be inferred solely from the absence [of the person] in the house..."
And that [is] ... (ā॰), ... (ba॰) ... graspable by the living being ... (ā॰, ba॰) ... present ... (śra॰).

The means of valid cognition known as scripture, which is to be grasped through the authority of life, cannot indeed be a means of valid cognition without an object; and thus, since only a positive entity (bhāva) is apprehended and not a non-entity (abhāva), how can that be the reason? For, like the positive entity itself, it remains yet to be proven—[as noted in] the Āloka-ṭīkā regarding Caitra.
By means of the pramāṇa of non-existence,
[he perceives him] outside of the house characterized by its interior.
The external entity, which is the object to be established,
is fire; this [notion] is indeed false.

"Caitra is alive" is the means of valid cognition known as scripture (*āgama*); "he is not in the house" is the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*). For the sake of supporting these, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) operates in the form "he must be outside," for otherwise the operation of these two means of valid cognition would not be possible—[Āloka-ṭīkā]. Indeed, by the means of valid cognition that is scripture, the existence of Caitra is made its object, and by the means of valid cognition that is non-existence, his non-existence [in the house] is made its object. Therefore, presumptive testimony operates to establish the lack of contradiction between the existence and non-existence regarding Caitra; and it refers to the two objects of knowledge: "Caitra is not in the house" and "he is outside."
Because, without presumptive testimony (arthāpatti),
the conjunction— that is, the non-contradiction— of existence and non-existence would be impossible, resulting in the fallacy of non-existence.

Furthermore, because there is no apprehension of a relationship through verbal testimony (*śabda*), existence and non-existence cannot be cognized simultaneously as being connected within a single sensory perception, as is the case with fire and smoke. For if the absence from the house were the pervaded (*vyāpya*), then presence outside would be the pervader (*vyāpaka*); and that [presence outside] cannot be directly perceived by those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), since it subsists in infinite locations.

[Objection: Is it not the case that someone standing at a door perceives the presence and absence of another person, such as Devadatta—namely, that when he is absent from this house, he is present elsewhere—and thus, after the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the existence of Caitra outside is ascertained because of his absence from the house, given that his life is certain? [Reply: True; nevertheless, there is a distinction between this and inference (*anumāna*). For in that case (inference), once the relation has been grasped with a pervader (*vyāpaka*) in a general sense—that is, one whose location is not fixed—at the subsequent time of ascertaining its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the pervader is cognized as having a fixed location. Here, however, the reverse is the case.
For Caitra is not perceived as being restricted to a specific location simply because of his absence from the house; indeed,
just as he was perceived at the time of grasping the pervasion, so too at the time of the formal application (prayoga) is he perceived as being unrestricted by location—
this is because there is no absence of the absence of [his] apprehension.
This is not inference; this is the connection with what has been stated previously:
the absence from the house and the presence outside are not perceived [simultaneously], nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their necessary concomitance.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Arthāpatti section, verse 31. Compare: Nyāyamañjarī, p. 37:
"But he who, standing at the door of the house, should conceive of an external existence..."
When [a thing] is not present in one location, it does not follow that it is absent elsewhere;
even then, its non-existence is not perceived everywhere,
nor will there be pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason simply because of its absence in one location.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Arthāpatti section, verses 34–35:
If [it is argued that] because of the existence and non-existence [of Devadatta] in his own house... Śābara-bhāṣya.
For in inference, at the time of formal application, [the reason] of fire...
By virtue of being located on a mountain or elsewhere— according to the Ācārya’s commentary (Ā.
Ṭī.), even in the case of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), [the object] exists externally in an unrestricted manner, that is, somewhere or other.

Furthermore, if the relation between the absence of Caitra in the house—while he is at the door—and his presence outside is grasped, then how could there be a grasp of the relation when one seeks to prove his absence outside by means of his presence in the house? As it has been said:
"The grasp [of the relation] while standing at the door... and "...the grasp of Caitra in the house... (Baḍarāyaṇa).
It does not exist in the house [according to Ācārya], and it has been stated by Bhaṭṭa: "But surely there is indeed the apprehension of the connection for one standing at the door of the house."
Let it be so; [it applies] to one standing at the door of the house— [Nyāyamañjarī]—
to one standing at the door (vārttika).
But if non-existence is established by means of existence, how will this [non-existence] come to be? (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
38). If existence is established by means of existence—how indeed [could it be]? (*Nyāyamañjarī*). (*Śrāvakabhūmi*).

Indeed, the relation [of concomitance] is not established in this way: when Caitra’s presence in his house leads to the determination of his absence in other places because his presence elsewhere would otherwise be inexplicable, the apprehension of a relation between his presence in the house and his absence in other places cannot occur through direct perception (*adhyakṣataḥ*), because those other places are infinite. If it is asked, "How then can there be a certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of smoke with non-fire?", what is the purpose of such an apprehension? For when the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between smoke and fire is possible to apprehend, there is no possibility of intent toward apprehending the negative concomitance.

For those whose minds have attained satisfaction through the realization of the probandum—realization brought about by the knowledge of the rule (niyama) easily obtained through repeated observation—is there any further purpose served by the certainty regarding the absence [of the probans] where fire is absent? No, because the realization of the probandum has already been accomplished. In this case, however, it was stated at the very time of understanding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that the property to be understood (*gamyadharma*) is difficult to ascertain, because it resides in infinite locations.

Now, if it is argued that its ascertainment occurs through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), that is not so; for it is impossible to ascertain the absence of that [property] in all locations other than one's house by means of a non-perception restricted to a specific location.
"Having gone to various other regions, [the absence of the object] is established through non-perception; this too is not correct,
because [there is a relationship between] that which is pervaded and that which pervades."
But surely, even in the absence of fire and so forth, since things other than smoke and the like do not go to that place, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not clearly established;
for one whose object of cognition is the non-existence of another entity, this [proof] fails.
"O friend, my companions are such that they understand [the truth] merely by seeing you.

Indeed, this is a fault only for one who seeks to establish inference through the ascertainment of the absence of the mark (*liṅga*) in all other heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*). We, however, having understood the concomitance of smoke with fire in two, three, or four cases, infer the companion fire from smoke based on the mere non-observation of it in heterogeneous instances; we do not seek the ascertainment of the absence of smoke in all heterogeneous instances, nor do we require the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of fire in all things possessing smoke."
—*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Nyāyaratna* p.
460; because non-fire locations are infinite—Ā. Ṭī.;
"ascertainment" means ignorance—Śra.
— nivṛttace—
for those who understand through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
The comprehension of the positive concomitance (anvaya)—[as noted in] Ba and Śra;
the existence outside [the locus of the probandum]—ĀṬ;
where it is not perceived, there it does not exist, such as Caitra—ĀṬ.
The determination of the relationship is by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Now, in this case as well, the relationship is established through non-perception,
since the absence of Caitra has been observed in the presence [of Maitra].

In the case of literary works, because [the coexistence] is limited in scope, and in the case of fire and smoke, because their negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not observed, their capacity to indicate [the other] is postulated; here, however, this very coexistence belongs to one thing that exists together with another.
First of all, it is not tenable [that the universal exists] because it resides in infinite locations—
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Arthāpatti, verses 1–43;
[the universal exists] by virtue of being restricted to specific locations (*niyatadeśatayā*)— *Bhaṭṭa*, *Śālikanātha*.
Regarding those [objects], [the reading] "deśāntara" [is found in] Ā॰ and Śra॰.
Now, it is indeed through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) that non-existence here is understood;
and since that [non-perception] is accomplished without effort, it establishes [the object's absence] while one remains in one's own place.
The non-existence of an object here is not cognized by this non-perception, because one has not gone to that place; for such [non-perception] exists even when things are present but at a distance,
whereas [only] after having gone repeatedly to those places is an object not perceived.
Therefore, because there is no other cause for its non-perception, it is understood to be eternal— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Arthāpatti section, verses 36–38:
"Even though you have gone again and again to those places, you do not know its non-existence."
I know—[from the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
38]—that because you have departed from Kauśāmbī, they [the people there] suspect you of entering it; [the *Nyāyamañjarī* reads "suspecting [him] of entering," etc.]—*Nyāyamañjarī*.
Therefore, this is not the domain of those who lack omniscience;

consequently, because the existence of a person whose body is perceived in a restricted location and possesses a limited size cannot otherwise be accounted for, there is an ascertainment of his non-existence in all other places precisely through *arthāpatti* (presumption), whereby his absence therein is determined. Thus ends [the section].
Non-apprehension—
[of] Caitra [while he is] in the house.

The determination of Caitra’s absence outside [the house] and the demonstration that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is included within the means of valid cognition known as inference (*anumāna*).
To this, the following response is given:

Regarding what was stated—“seen or heard,” and so forth—does the object that is seen or heard lead to the postulation of something else when it is connected with its own probandum, or when it is unconnected? If it is unconnected, how can it be the cause for its postulation? For one cannot postulate just any object upon seeing anything whatsoever, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if [the relation] is connected (*sambaddha*); then the cognition arising from this is indeed inference (*anumāna*). For instance: cognition of another object arising from an object that has been seen or heard is indeed inference, because it arises by the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Whatever arises by the force of invariable concomitance is indeed inference, just like the knowledge of fire from smoke; and the cognition intended as "presumption" (*arthāpatti*) arises by the force of invariable concomitance—[as stated on page 505, line 18:
"by means of eating at night," etc.—Ānandagiri’s Commentary].
Comparison, when examined, does not differ from inference;
for without an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), one thing cannot cause the cognition of another thing,
and no one perceives anything upon merely beholding some object.
Even a counteracting factor does not become a cause for cognition if it is unknown;
likewise, cognitions do not arise in newborn infants and the like,
where the possibility of knowing a universal does not exist through its specific nature.
Even in that case, there is indeed the apprehension of it in a general form—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 41.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also included within inference alone, because it establishes the cognition of an object through the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
When it is stated that "it is not possible otherwise," it is understood that "it is possible only thus";
this very [relationship] is the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)—*Nyāyasāra*, p. 22.

Is the object that gives rise to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) something not yet understood as being otherwise inexplicable, or is it something already understood that serves as the basis for the postulation of an unseen object? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 193; Syādvādaratnākara, p.
283). [The marginal note states: "from an object seen or heard."]

"Inference from implication (arthāpatti) arises from an object intended for the purpose of comparison; it is indeed a contradiction [of the perceived], and from hearing it, there is inference based on an inference" — *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, Kanda p.
223; *Praśastapādavyākhyā* p. 590.

There is no refutation [of the means of knowledge] because tradition (aitihya) is not distinct from verbal testimony (śabda), and because presumption (arthāpatti) and possibility (saṃbhava) are not distinct from inference (anumāna).
— Nyāyasūtra 2.2.1.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an unperceived object that is connected to a perceived one; likewise, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), possibility (*saṃbhava*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are also [inferences].
Presumptive testimony is simply inference, consisting in the apprehension of an unexpressed meaning through its opposition to the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 2.2.2
How is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) subsumed under inference (*anumāna*)? Because the negation of one of two things has as its object the affirmation of the second.

Wherever, between two entities, one entity is negated, there the affirmation of the second is observed; for example, from the statement "he does not eat by day," it is understood that "he eats at night" (Nyāyavārttika, p.

"Nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) distinct from inference, because there is no example in the world where it is unmixed with that [inference], and because there is no other mode [of cognition]" — *Nyāyakusumāñjali* 3.1.2. (Cf. *Nyāyalīlāvatī*, p. 57).

For the established inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is indeed the source of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); and that which is the reason for probability (*sambhava*) and the like does not differ from the inferential mark (*liṅga*).

It has also been explained that the inferential mark (liṅga) is independent of an illustrative example; therefore, the cognition of an object through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and so forth does not arise from a separate means of knowledge (māna) distinct from inference.
— *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 217.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 193;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pṛṣṭha 585;
Jaina-tarkavārttika, pṛṣṭha 77.
Sya-ra-pṛ 283; Ratnākarāvatāra 2.1
—The cognition of another [object]—[as stated by] Śrāmaṇera—[is] the consciousness of fire.

Furthermore, would this [object], though connected to that [consciousness], be the cause for the conceptualization of it (the object) while being known in its own form, or while being unknown? It cannot be the former, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of even children and others conceptualizing unseen objects based on this [consciousness].

Now, suppose it is known. Even in that case, is it known at the time of the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) as being connected with it, or previously? Regarding the first alternative: is it known at that time as being connected with it through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from that very same [means]? Of these, the first option is untenable, because at the time of that comprehension, another means of valid cognition capable of grasping its connection is impossible; or, if such were possible, since the probandum would be established by that very means, what would be the use of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? [As stated: "An object seen or heard... [Āloka-ṭīkā:
...in the form of being connected... [Āloka-ṭīkā].

Or is it a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—a comparison (*tulanā*)—based on the impossibility of its being otherwise (*anyathānupapadyamānatva*), [derived] from scripture (*āgama*), from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) itself, or from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 193; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 284.

Let it be that at the time of the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), this [cognition] arises from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) which grasps the relation; nevertheless, it does not differ from inference (*anumāna*). To explain: presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is indeed inference, because it arises from a reason whose connection with the probandum has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition. Whatever arises from a reason whose connection with the probandum has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition is nothing but inference, just like the cognition of fire from smoke; and the cognition intended as presumptive testimony arises from a reason whose connection with the probandum has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition.

Now, if it is known from that very [evidence] as being connected with the probandum (*sādhya*), then there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): for only when presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is established is the cognition of the object that gives rise to it established as being connected with it; and only when that is established is the presumptive testimony established. Furthermore, if it was previously known as being connected with that [probandum], was it known in the very subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) or in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*)? In the first alternative, presumptive testimony would be useless, because its probandum would have been already established. Moreover, since we do not admit [the presence of the evidence] even in the subject of the example, it cannot be known there as being connected with that [probandum].
— from that which is unconnected,
from that which is unconnected— O Ātreya;
[from] corpulence, the absence of a house, etc.— Ātreya’s commentary.
This is even more established for the Śruti-Mīmāṃsakas,

who do not admit the apprehension of a relation in an example within the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between presumptive testimony and inference;
furthermore, in this context, the state of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*) is only then postulated.
"Simply because it was not previously ascertained, this [capacity] is not the cause," according to the statement in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Arthāpatti section, verse 30.

Furthermore, regarding the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*), if the object has already been perceived or heard, then what relevance does that have for the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmī*)?

Moreover, in that case, would this [capacity] be understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) as being connected with the probandum (*sādhya*), or through non-perception in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), or through another presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? It cannot be from repeated observation, because since capacity (*śakti*) is beyond the senses, repeated observation is impossible.

Nor [is it established] through non-perception in the counter-example (vipakṣa), because that too serves as the cause for the cognition of a relation only with respect to objects that are capable of being perceived.
Nor is it from another presumption (arthāpatti), because that would lead to an infinite regress.

If it is asked, "How then, according to you as well, does the cognition of the relation between the probandum and the probans occur?", [the answer is: from another means of valid cognition called "inference by elimination" (ūha).

If it is asked, "What is the fault in our accepting that [power]?"—the fault is the contradiction of the established number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as the contradiction with such textual passages as: "For inference proceeds once the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been apprehended through perception," and so forth. This is because the apprehension of the relationship is universally well-known to arise solely from the means of valid cognition called *ūha* (presumptive reasoning); indeed, there is no object whatsoever that is beyond its scope. Consequently, since the power is supersensible (*atīndriya*), the relationship between it and any indicative mark (*liṅga*) cannot be apprehended; thus, there would be no apprehension of it through inference in the case of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*).

Comparison—Now, if that [invariable concomitance] is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is it through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) or non-perception in the counter-example (*vipakṣe'nupalambha*)? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 194; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 284)—[the word] *sambaddha* is missing in manuscript *ba*, while in manuscript *śra* it reads *sādhyasya sambaddha*.

For the counter-examples (vipakṣa), such as places where there is no fire and so forth, are indeed infinite—[Āloka-ṭīkā]; [this is] due to the inference (ūha) regarding the cause with respect to the connection—[Āloka-ṭīkā]; from this—[Bālapriyā].
Pervasion is to be understood through repeated observation; [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-vārttika] Anumāna-pariccheda, verse 12.

Furthermore, regarding the definition of presumption based on perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikārthāpatti*) which was stated as "by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the effect called burning perceived through direct perception," etc., the nature of that "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) must be explained: Is this impossibility the non-existence of the bursting [of the seed] and so forth in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), or is it a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*)? In the first case, the statement "it is not possible without that" expresses a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). And since a negative concomitance, when perceived, implies a positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—namely, that it *is* possible when that [probandum] exists—and since both positive and negative concomitance are properties of a probans (*liṅga*) alone that serves as a means of cognition, how could presumption be distinct from inference? Even a contradiction with a means of valid cognition is nothing other than the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).

And likewise, when there exists a relationship of sublation and sublated between two cognitions—one grasping silver and the other grasping its absence—in relation to mother-of-pearl, there would follow the postulation of another object on the grounds that silver is otherwise inexplicable; for here too, as there is no difference [from the previous case], the definition [of presumption] applies because of the inexplicability [of the fact], just as in the case of the power of fire (p. 506, l. 4).

"Comparison—'Without that, it is not possible'—this is a statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). And negative concomitance, being perceived, implies positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the form 'when that exists, it is possible. Since both positive and negative concomitance are properties of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which brings about cognition, how is *arthāpatti* not inference?
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 41).
[The reading "due to the consequence of conceptual construction" (*kalpanānuṣaṅgāt*) appears in the *ba* and *śra* manuscripts.]

Furthermore, regarding the definition of contradiction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*): presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) operates when two means of valid cognition stand in mutual opposition, and those two must be stated.

Now, what is there to be said here? [It is] because it is well-established. To explain: first, the nature of the *sphoṭa* is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet no visible cause for it is possible, nor is any other cause perceived. Furthermore, the absence of an effect is observed when there is an absence of its cause; therefore, from the inference arising from the mark (*liṅga*) known as the "absence of a cause," its non-existence would follow. Thus, when these two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) appear to conflict, *arthāpatti* (presumption) operates by reconciling them and demonstrating a distinction between their respective objects.

The claim that the cognition of *sphoṭa* has *sphoṭa* as its object, while the inference of the absence of causes has as its object the absence of an effect whose causes are otherwise observed, is also incorrect. For, in this case, the absence of the cause serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the determination of the absence of the effect. Is this [absence] determined or undetermined to be that mark? It cannot be undetermined, because it would follow that even steam and the like, when suspected of being smoke and so forth, could function as a logical mark.

Now, [you claim] it is certain; from what does that certainty arise? If you say it is from the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), is that the non-perception of a perceptible object (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) or the non-perception of an imperceptible object (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*)? If it is the non-perception of an imperceptible object, how can non-existence be established from that? For there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) due to atoms, *piśācas*, and so forth. If, on the other hand, it is the non-perception of a perceptible object, then since the absence of the cause is established from that, how could there be validity for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) which indicates the existence of the cause? Furthermore, the absence of the cause cannot serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) because it would lead to a circular argument (*cakraka*). To explain: once the relationship between effect and cause has been grasped, the inference called "absence of the cause" proceeds; the grasping of the relationship occurs only when the cause has been grasped; the grasping of the cause occurs through presumptive testimony; that presumptive testimony occurs only when there is the inference of the absence of the cause; and that inference occurs only when the relationship has been grasped. Thus, it is circular.
Nor is the existence of a cause for the *sphoṭa* and so forth established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone; for it is established even by inference (*anumāna*).

To explain: the *sphoṭa* and so forth are preceded by a cause, because they are effects; whatever is an effect is preceded by a cause, just like smoke and so forth; and this *sphoṭa* and so forth is an effect; therefore, it is preceded by a cause—thus proceeds the argument of the speaker.
The visible cause is the form of fire—
the form of power— according to Ācārya’s commentary.
Regarding the *sphoṭa*:

first, the existence of the *sphoṭa* is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, the non-existence of the *sphoṭa* is inferred through an inference based on the absence of a cause in the form of a capacity (*śakti*). Thus, perception and inference are in conflict regarding the *sphoṭa*. Therefore, *arthāpatti* (presumption), by demonstrating the difference in their respective objects, acts as a reconciler—serving as the mark for certainty (*niścayaliṅga*). (Ānandajñāna’s *Ṭīkā*)

By this, the two types of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by inference and comparison are also refuted; for since they also have capacity (*śakti*) as their object, all the defects already assigned to the position of presumption preceded by perception (p. 506, l. 5) follow as well. Compare: "But since comparison is not distinct from memory, presumption preceded by it is nothing but inference, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) was previously apprehended."

And likewise: "A cow-individual delimited by similarity is capable of carrying loads and so forth, because it is a cow-individual, like a previously perceived cow-individual of this same kind" (PRAŚASTAPĀDABHĀṢYAVYĀKHYĀ, p.

590). Furthermore, that which was stated as an "inference based on presumption preceded by presumption" (*arthāpattipūrvikārthāpatti*) for the purpose of establishing the eternity of sound is also untenable; for even if sound were non-eternal, its capacity to function as a signifier (*vācakatva*) would still be possible, and we shall establish its non-eternality later on.
On page 507, line 9,

regarding the statement "because the speaker is possible" (vācakasyopapatteḥ): even that "presumption based on what is heard" (śrutārthāpatti) which was mentioned, such as "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," is nothing but inference, because it is a cognition of the cause through its effect.

For, in the absence of the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like, corpulence is known to exist both in oneself and elsewhere as an effect of eating. This [corpulence], when ascertained through the testimony of a reliable person (*āpta-vākya*) regarding a specific subject named Devadatta by means of a prohibition of eating at a particular time, makes known the existence of its own productive cause during a time other than the prohibited one. Indeed, the arising of an effect without a cause is not possible, because that would entail the consequence of it being either eternally existent or eternally non-existent due to its lack of a cause.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Devadatta is one who eats at night, because, in the absence of the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like, and while being devoid of eating during the day, he is corpulent; for whoever, in the absence of the use of elixirs and the like, and while being devoid of eating during the day, is corpulent, is one who eats at night—just like a nocturnal prowler (*naktañcara*); and Devadatta is corpulent while being devoid of eating during the day and in the absence of the use of elixirs and the like; therefore, he is one who eats at night.

Therefore, it was incorrectly stated that the sentence alone is the basis for the cognition of that [fact], because the cognition of that fact arises from the very mark (liṅga) characterized by corpulence—which is distinguished by the aforementioned qualifiers—precisely through this sentence; and the establishment of the cognition of eating at night follows from that mark once it has been cognized. (Bṛhatī, p.

Comparison—Even the wretched presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) does not differ from inference, because the postulation of a partial statement is untenable and the fact (*artha*), which serves as the effect-sign (*kāryaliṅga*), exists.

Just as you, upon observing smoke residing on the slopes of a mountain, infer its cause, fire; so too, having ascertained from scripture the effect known as corpulence, one should likewise infer its cause, eating. What is the difference here? (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 45).
A person connected with eating at night is thus cognized.
Because one who is fat despite abstaining from eating during the day is fat only when eating— just like others—

it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that fatness occurs when there is food; thus, the cognition of the object arises from a thing that is in fact connected to it.
—Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 465;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 587;
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 306.

The postulation of eating at night upon hearing the sentence "The fat man does not eat during the day" is an inference based on an inference (anumitānumāna), because one infers the cause—eating at night—from the fatness which has itself been inferred from the sentence acting as a logical mark (liṅga):
"Devadatta eats at night, because he is fat while not eating during the day. (Pramāṇakhandana, p. 223)
— Vaiśeṣika Upaniṣad 9.2.5
When a large person is being prevented [from entering] during the day...

The existence of the cause that brings about its own production— [the reading] *svotpādakasya* in manuscript *ba*, *śra* [manuscript], and *pīnatvopapādakasya* according to the commentary (*ā॰ ṭi॰*)— is not [perceived]. Manuscript *ba*.
The examination of food: Existence is indeed constant, because it does not depend on any other cause;
whereas the occasional occurrence of entities is possible only through dependence.
— Pramāṇavārttika 3.34— of the [consequence]... śra.
pṛ॰ 507 paṃ॰ 12 "Due to the absence of the use of elixirs and so forth" etc.—Ācārya’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.); "from what [would there be] its counter-"—Manuscript Ba.
Regarding "understanding from what is understood through a statement":

even that presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) which is preceded by non-perception is nothing but inference (*anumāna*), because the existence outside [the house] of the living Caitra is understood through the mark (*liṅga*) of his absence from the house.

For instance: Caitra, who is alive, possesses external presence because he is absent from his house while living, because he is a living person absent from his house, like a previously observed case of such absence from a house; just as smoke possesses fire because it is smoke, like previously observed smoke.
Therefore, the rejection of the house and so forth as being logical marks (*liṅga*) is mere verbal ostentation, as it does not touch upon a portion of our own position;
for that [external presence] is indeed inference itself, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been grasped.

For instance: "Devadatta is connected with the outside, because, while being alive, he is not perceived in the house, like Viṣṇumitra"—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī*, p. 591. Even then, his connection with the outside is ascertained by the non-perception [of him] despite the visibility [of the space].

Therefore, in that case, external existence is determined solely from the mark (liṅga). For a person who is not connected with the house is necessarily outside; he is like a man seen standing in the courtyard of the house by those stationed at the door.
Even the counter-position (vipakṣa) in this case is included within the locus of existence;
therefore, this is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), and it does not differ from inference—Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 470.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
203; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 586;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 308.

"The absence from the house of Caitra is the subject (*dharmin*); that he possesses [existence] outside [the house] is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), because of his being absent from the house while alive, like the previously perceived absence from such a house"—this too is indeed inference (*anumāna*). For when a person exists in one place, he is not in another; or when a non-pervading entity exists in one place, he is not in another. Thus, the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is easily accomplished with respect to one's own body alone. (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 43)

And thus, the perception of his being outside is an inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of perceiving his absence from the house while he exists—*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 438; *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī*, p. 44.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
223; Nyāyakusumāñjali, 3.19.
Praśastapādabhāṣya, kiraṇāvalī, p. 324;
Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra, 9.2.

Furthermore, as for the objection stated regarding the entry [of the probans] into the object of cognition (*prameya*), that too is not tenable. For what is intended here by "object of cognition"? Is it mere existence, or existence qualified by an external location? In that regard, mere existence is already understood from scripture alone and thus does not depend upon being an object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
However, existence qualified by an external location is indeed an object of cognition; yet, at that time, there is no entry [of the probans] into it.

For the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends Caitra’s absence in the house precludes the very means of valid cognition that indicates his presence in that same place; it does not, however, concern itself with an investigation into his existence or non-existence outside [the house] (pṛ.
509, l. 8). Compare: "What is intended here as the object of cognition (prameya)? Is it mere existence, or is it existence qualified by a specific external location?"
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 43; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 309; tat-pramā—Ā.
Immediately thereafter, [the following is] the rule: for one who has died right at home, or for one who remains alive but far away, or even for one standing in the courtyard.

For there is no difference in the determination of Caitra’s absence from the house whether he is virtuous— according to the *Nyāyamañjarī*— or deceased, or alive and standing far away or even in the courtyard.
"There is no difference whatsoever in the determination of the absence from the house" (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 309); "in the determination... (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
43). [Variant reading: *paricchedana-*.]
However, when this [absence] is apprehended as qualified by life, it attains the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) precisely because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Nor is the apprehension of the qualifier itself the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*); for life is one thing, and the object of cognition called "external existence" is another.
And this [absence] is qualified... [fragmentary].
[The opponent says: "The absence of the house" (gṛhābhāva)—[as noted in the Āloka commentary]—is the apprehension of a specific [absence];

now, it may be thought that the very cognition of the absence of the person from the house, qualified by his being alive, is itself the cognition of his being outside. That too is charming only when left unexamined; for while the cognition of his being outside arises from the cognition of the absence from the house qualified by his being alive, the cognition of his being outside is not identical to that [prior] cognition.
For it is not observed that the cognition of smoke as residing in a locus of fire is itself the cognition of the fire;

rather, since the fire is distinct from the smoke, a difference in their cognitions is appropriate here. This is the same in the other case as well: since the absence from the house and the [person's] being alive are distinct from his being outside, how could there be non-difference between those two cognitions? And just as, because the mountain and the fire are already established, only the possessive relation (*matvartha*) is accepted there as the novel object to be inferred, so too here, let only the external location be the novel object to be inferred.

If, however, that additional object of cognition (*prameya*) is not accepted here, then since the absence from the house and the [person's] being alive are already ascertained by their own respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), presumption (*arthāpatti*) would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, because there exists another object of cognition which is not included [in those two], there is no fault whatsoever.
Moreover, this same fault applies equally to presumption itself, for even there, it is admitted that one thing is postulated on the basis of another thing.

Regarding the conventional usage that "there is the cognition of that [object] from that [evidence]," in such a case, the fault of its [the object's] necessarily entering into that cognition follows; for, as in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the establishment of the [object] occurs through the establishment of the cognition thereof, rendering any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) redundant. For example, when there is the cognition of the absence from the house qualified by life, the cognition of being outside does not consist in that very cognition [of absence].

For the cognition of smoke as being in the locus of fire is not itself the cognition of fire; rather, fire is something other than smoke. Likewise here, external presence is something other than both the absence from the house and living. Since the mountain and the fire are already established, only the possessive sense (*matvartha*) therein is the novel thing to be inferred. Similarly, here too, only the connection with an external location is the novel thing to be inferred. (Nyāyamañjarī p. 43; Syādvādaratnākara p. 309)
The cause such as burning, etc.—Śra;
by that, its [non-existence]—Śra;
the absence from the house and the existence outside for one who is living—Ā; Commentary (Ṭīkā).
The form "the mountain possesses fire" is established by the very fact of [the person's] being alive— [Ānandagiri’s] Commentary (Ā-ṭī);

for the means of knowledge that apprehends absence is the cognition of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), whereas the means of knowledge that apprehends being alive is scriptural testimony (*āgamapramāṇa*).

Regarding the comparison with external existence: this same fault applies even to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there too one accepts the postulation of another object based on a given object, as the text itself establishes: "Presumptive testimony is the postulation of an object because a perceived or heard object would otherwise be inexplicable."

If there is a cognition of that [object] from that [word], then there is linguistic usage with respect to it; is it then inexpressible? If there is a cognition of that [object], its inclusion [in the word] is indeed a fault, because—just as in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—the object is established by the establishment of the cognition of it, rendering any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) redundant.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 44)
"From that means of proof, there is the cognition of that which is to be proven"—this linguistic usage exists in presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) just as it does in inference (*anumāna*). (Ā. Ṭi.
"Cognition" (*pratipatti*) is the reading in Śra. (Ā. Ṭi.)

Just as in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), once the cognition of a tree has arisen through the very cognition of a *śiṃśapā*, there is no need for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); so too here, since the state of being outside is understood by the mark (*liṅga*) of the absence from the house alone, there is no need for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).—Ānandajñāna’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.), Siddhi (Ā., Ba.).

But surely, non-existence (abhāva) will be the certain mark (liṅga). And how can there be certainty regarding that when two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which grasp existence and non-existence, are in contradiction? Therefore, as long as it is not understood that the scripture has as its object [the person's] being outside, there is no certainty of non-existence within the house alone. If there were such certainty, there would be the fault of the object of cognition (prameya) entering into the means of cognition (pramāṇa); for presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) operates only when there is a contradiction between two means of valid cognition—so how could it enter into that? This is an unconsidered statement; for since the cognitions of existence and non-existence do not have the same object, their contradiction is not established.

For by means of scripture (*āgama*), the existence of Caitra—unrestricted by any particular location—is established, whether he be inside or outside the house; whereas by perception (*pratyakṣa*), the absence of Caitra as restricted to the house is established.

Since the two have the same object, the knowledge arising from scripture is sublated by perception—which is not otherwise accounted for—just like a false cognition; thus, it cannot serve as a basis for postulating another object, but rather [indicates] the absence [of Caitra] everywhere. (Ānandajñāna’s Commentary)

The very certainty of Caitra’s absence from the house based on his being alive is itself the certainty of his presence outside; therefore, the meaning is that the reason known as "absence from the house" has entered into the object of cognition known as "presence outside"—Ānandajñāna’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.). Compare: "For instance, either mere existence is contradicted by Caitra’s absence from the house, or his existence in the house [is contradicted] when he is elsewhere."

First of all, there is no contradiction between the existence of a person anywhere and his non-existence in the house, because they do not have the same objective domain (*viṣaya*). It is the absence delimited by the house that is negated by the presence in the house, as it is contradictory to it; however, mere existence is not negated, because the latter is indifferent (*audāsīnya*) toward it. Therefore, it is logical that the existence of the person outside is inferred from the established absence in the house. By this, the position regarding the scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—which attempts to resolve the contradiction between two conflicting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through a restriction of their domains—is refuted, because there is no contradiction between that which is delimited and that which is undelimited.
(Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 439)
In the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī*, page 44:

"There is no lack of reason for that which is not governed, nor is there a lack of a governor as its establisher; there is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition, or even if [the object] is well-known, this [contradiction] is the same."
— Perception is established precisely as having a restricted spatial object; — Āloka-ṭīkā on Nyāyakuṃjara 3.19.
Regarding these two, otherwise:

[the Vaibhāṣika says] "Knowledge arising from scripture (*āgama*) is not authoritative because its object is not restricted to a specific location" (Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Auto-commentary, p.

402). Now, the following view may be held: in inference, the qualifier of the prover (*gamaka*) is "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*), as in "smoke is not possible without fire"; however, in presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the reverse is the case: "the probandum (*gamya*) is not possible without the prover."

"It is argued that external existence is what is to be known (*gamya*), and that this is not possible without the absence from the house while one is alive; thus, since the relationship between the known and the indicator (*gamaka*) is otherwise untenable, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) from inference (*anumāna*) because of this reversal. This too is inconsistent. For the definition of inference is: 'Inference is the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgin*) from a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with it.

And this [definition] certainly applies to presumption, for the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the object that gives rise to it with the probandum is not unestablished; otherwise, it would follow that its establishment is impossible."

Furthermore, this invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), which is synonymous with "the impossibility of being otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*), must reside in both [the probans and the probandum]; therefore, it may be a qualification of the indicator (*gamaka*) or a qualification of the indicated (*gamya*). It is not on this account that a distinction exists between presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*). Otherwise, the following would constitute a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "The sun possesses the power of motion because its actual movement is otherwise impossible"—which would be a presumptive testimony accompanied by the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—as opposed to the presumptive testimony devoid of it: "Fire possesses the power of burning because the bursting of a blister is otherwise impossible. If that were so, there would be a contradiction in the established number of means of valid cognition.

Since there is no distinction between the two insofar as both involve the comprehension of another object from a restricted object, and since there is likewise no distinction here in that one comprehends another object from an object that is inseparable from its own probandum, how could there be a difference between inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)?

For the Prabhākara, if X cannot be accounted for without Y, then X alone would be the means of cognition; however, in this case, it is precisely that which is not accounted for which is what is cognized.
And what is it that is not tenable here? Since one observes the absence of a living person from his home, his absence elsewhere is not tenable.
What follows from that? It is not the absence that is being cognized here;
rather, what is it then? It is the presence [of the person elsewhere] that is being cognized.
And this [inference] is not established by the observation of absence from the house;
indeed, it is certainly not established,
for the existence outside is not established without the observation of absence from the house.
— Śābarabhāṣya on Bṛhatī 1.1.5
That [cognition] which leads to the conclusion that a perceived object is otherwise inexplicable without a postulation is indeed a postulation (arthāpatti); for instance,
the existence of a person at home cannot be accounted for by the perception of his absence from the house without the postulation of his being outside.

Just as the impossibility of an external object being cognized is postulated here through conceptual construction— without which there would be a contradiction with other means of knowledge characterized by the occurrence of doubt— so too is the impossibility [of the internal] to be postulated.
For an entity is never observed without its location;
even if established without an entity, your [position] incurs doubt.
Therefore, the conceptual construction that proceeds is for the purpose of dispelling that doubt.
This presumption (arthāpatti) is traditionally defined as arising from a fact that gives rise to doubt;
however, in inference, the indicator (gamaka) is understood through its absence in the counter-example (vipakṣa),
whereas inapprehensibility (anupapannatva) is understood only in the absence of the object to be inferred (gamya).

It is certain that these two means of valid cognition, known as presumption (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*), are distinct from one another due to the difference in their respective causal complexes— *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p.
Comparison—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 44:
"Because of the reversal of the means of knowledge" (*mānaviparyayāt*).

Comparison—this too is merely an attempt to establish a discrepancy in the text, not the discovery of a new distinction; for as long as the object to be understood (*gamya*) is not apprehended, how could its inconsistency (*anupapadyamānatva*) be determined? But once the object to be understood is apprehended, what is the use of apprehending its inconsistency, since the probandum (*sādhya*) has already been established? — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 44.
In the case of presumption based on a real entity (*tattvārthāpatti*), the probandum is [the object] other than the entity that gives rise to the presumption.

[The opponent argues: "In the case of fire, there is the capacity [to burn] accompanied by the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), whereas in the case of the *sphoṭa* (the sound-unit), it exists in the palm of the hand and so forth; thus, the *sphoṭa* lacks the status of being a predicate of the subject. [The author replies:

"If there is no difference between two presumptive arguments (*arthāpatti*)—one possessing the status of being a predicate of the subject and one lacking it—then let the same hold true for inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive argument as well. (Āloka-ṭippaṇī)

There would be a contradiction regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by asserting that there are only six, because a seventh is established; for even in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there are two types: that which possesses the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and that which lacks it.

Furthermore, the status of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) as a qualifier of the object to be known (*gamyaviśeṣaṇatva*) is unestablished here. For it is possible for it to be a qualifier only in cases such as when Caitra’s absence in the house is the means of cognizing his presence outside;
indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in its being a qualifier of that [object], such that one would have to assume it to be a qualifier of the object to be known.

Moreover, the status of inseparable concomitance as a qualifier of the object to be known is not possible in every instance of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because in presumptive testimony arising from perception and other means, it is the indicator itself—such as the *sphoṭa*—that can possibly be qualified by inseparable concomitance.

Indeed, in that case, it is not possible for the capacity of the signifier (*gamikā śakti*) to be inexplicable (*anupapatti*) without the *sphoṭa*, because its existence is admitted even in the absence of that [sphoṭa];
for the qualifier of the signifier is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
(Ānandabodha’s Commentary) Regarding inseparable concomitance:
If it is a qualifier of the indicator (*gamaka*),
then, even without the *sphoṭa* and so forth, there is no logical necessity (*arthāpatti*) for the former.

As for what was further stated by Śaṅkara—that there is a distinction from inference because at the time of ascertaining the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), the probandum is not perceived here as being restricted to a specific location, and so forth—that too is mere words. For the existence outside is perceived through the delimitation of the locus called "absence from the house"; indeed, it is the locus itself that is denoted by the word "location," and since such delimitation exists here [in the case of absence], there is no distinction from that [inference]. (p.
The cognition [arising] from presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is [the understanding] that there is fire outside.

As for what was stated, beginning with "and because there is no apprehension of the relationship," that too is not correct; for it has been said that in all cases, the apprehension of the relationship is established solely through the grace of the means of valid cognition called *ūha* (presumptive reasoning).

Consequently, the argument that "because other locations are infinite, there can be no apprehension of the relationship there as being non-existent" and so forth is incorrect, since that [means of cognition] has the nature of apprehending the relationship between specific instances of the probandum and the probans without restriction.

Otherwise, how could there be a certainty regarding smoke’s exclusion from non-fire, since this same defect applies equally in that case as well? Nor is it logical for this [smoke] to be a prover by means of mere positive concomitance (anvaya) understood through repeated observation, because that which lacks a certain negative concomitance (vyatireka) cannot be a cause for the ascertainment of the probandum. Nor does it serve as its cause by its mere existence, because, just like positive concomitance, it is only when negative concomitance is ascertained that it can properly function as a constituent of inference. (p. 510, l. 15)
That too is incorrect, because [in the Śruti], in the context of defining reasoning (*tarka*), on page 426, it says:
"the grasping of the relation," etc. (*sambandhagrahaṇamityādi*).
Regarding the comparison with *ūha*: what recourse do you have concerning smoke when its exclusion from non-fire is ascertained?
Whatever account applies there will apply here for us as well.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to say—as in the *Ślokavārttika*, Arthāpatti chapter, verse 40: "But for one whose [non-existence] of another thing is to be known solely on the basis of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) understood through repeated observation, that very person is at fault; for me, however, the concomitants are indicators by mere non-perception"—because there can be no certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) for one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain. Thus, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), as well as positive and negative concomitance, are factors of inference (*anumānāṅga*) only when they have been apprehended.
—The smoke is the reason (hetu) [as stated] in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 45. —Śrī Dhūma.

Furthermore, since a non-pervasive substance such as Caitra exists in a restricted location, its absence in other specific locations is established through perception, and in non-specific locations through inference. How, then, can the aforementioned fault be imputed? That inference is as follows: "Other locations are devoid of Caitra, because they are distinct from the location occupied by Caitra, like the space immediately adjacent to it."

Nor should it be argued that this [inference] is sublated by a counter-inference (*praty-anumāna*) such as: "The various other locations are not conjoined with Caitra, because they are distinct from the location adjacent to him, like the location occupied by Caitra himself"; for that position is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge. Thus, since it is not established that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a category of evidence distinct from inference, the opponents' violation of the fixed number of means of knowledge is proven.
Comparison (*tulanā*): For a non-omnipresent substance that exists in a restricted location, the determination of its non-existence in other locations occurs without difficulty.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 45;
*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 43.

This has been observed: "A substance that is non-pervasive exists in one place but not in another; just as the sun, being perceived in one location such as the east, is not present in another such as the west—it is determined in this way by the force of observation alone."
—[From] *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, *Kandalī* commentary, p.
223: "Because [sound] exists in a limited space" (parimitadeśavṛttitvāt)—this is the reason;
[it applies] to that which is restricted to a different location (*tadanyadeśe*) and to the subsequent [moment]. (anu-va.)

It is strictly determined [as follows]: compare—“The other regions are devoid of Caitra, because they are distinct from those regions occupied by Caitra, like the region in his immediate vicinity”—Nyāyamañjarī, p.
But surely it is perceived by Caitra himself as being empty of another location,
because it is distinct from that location, just like a location situated nearby;
for its status as a non-erroneous contradictory [reason] is understood in exactly that same way.
Because they are distinct from the proximate location, like the location occupied by Caitra.

What is meant by this is as follows: first of all, the reason—that "other locations are devoid of Caitra because they are locations distinct from the location conjoined with him"—is not possible, because it is doubtful; for it is precisely this that is being investigated: whether or not those other locations are also conjoined with him.
How, then, can their distinction from the location conjoined with him be established?

If it is argued in this way—that [Caitra] is currently occupying that specific part of the room because it is distinct from other places—such a reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). For otherwise, one could equally argue: "The place occupied by Caitra is distinct from the place near him, because it is a different location, just like the place he previously occupied.
(Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Arthāpatti; Nyāyaratna, p.
461–62). Furthermore, the counter-argument (*pratipakṣaprayoga*) is merely a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), as it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition.
— Nyāyamañjarī, p. 45 —
because [the reason] is not established for the Mīmāṃsakas.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that you too face an equal contradiction regarding the fixed number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the various means of cognition such as comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth—which have been explained—do not differ from direct (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*) cognition in being distinct categories? In order to dispel this doubt, [the author] says: "Of all," and so forth.
Because all the aforementioned varieties of means of cognition, such as comparison and the rest, are included within indirect cognition (*parokṣa*), we have no fault whatsoever.
If it is asked, "Why are they included therein? [the answer is]: "Because they are characterized by the definition of that [indirect cognition]."

Whatever possesses the characterization of a particular definition is included within that [category]; for example, the cognition of form, pleasure, and so forth is included in perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the cognition characterized by the definition of the indirect (*parokṣa*) is included in analogy (*upamāna*) and the rest. For just as the cognition of form and the cognition of pleasure, though distinct from one another due to the difference in their objects and the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), are nonetheless considered "perception" because they are characterized by the definition of perception—namely, the nature of clarity (*vaiśadya*)—so too, analogy and the rest are considered "indirect" because they are characterized by the definition of the indirect—namely, the nature of non-clarity (*avaiśadya*). This is the view of the Jains as well.

The five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-pañcaka*)—namely, comparison (*upamāna*) and the others—are included within the indirect (*parokṣa*), because they are characterized by the definition of the indirect. The analogy is as follows: that which is characterized by a single defining characteristic remains one and the same despite differences in individual instances; for example, sensory perception such as that of the eye is characterized by the single defining characteristic of clarity (*vaiśadya*), while verbal testimony and the like are characterized by the single defining characteristic of non-clarity (*avaiśadya*).
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
192; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 595;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 283.
The characteristics of form and so forth, pleasure and so forth,
the eye and so forth, and the mental faculty and so forth, are mutually distinct.

[Objection: Even so, since indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*) is enumerated as being divided into recollection (*smṛti*), recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), reasoning (*tarka*), inference (*anumāna*), and verbal testimony (*āgama*), how can comparison (*upamāna*) and the like be included therein? Or, if they were included, would there not be a contradiction with that enumeration? [Reply: This is incorrect; for since comparison and the like take the form of recognition and so forth, their inclusion does not contradict that enumeration.

For recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is defined as a synthesis (*saṅkalana*) caused by both perception and memory; this cognition of analogy (*upamāna*) and the like is also caused by perception and memory, and has the nature of synthesizing similarity and so forth. Therefore, how could it be distinct from recognition? Whatever is caused by perception and memory and has the nature of synthesizing similarity and so forth is indeed recognition, just like the well-known instance of recognition; and analogy is likewise caused by those [perception and memory] and has the nature of synthesizing similarity and so forth.
In the verse "The first [work] is the Laghīyastraya, its knowledge is memory" (Kārikā 10), and in *Parīkṣāmukha* 3.2 and *Pramāṇanaya* 3.
2 Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.2
And there is a comparison regarding these [passages] in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 193.

The conceptualization [of similarity] (syā° ra° pṛ° 283) is indeed of the nature of analogy and recognition, because, while having perception and memory as its causes, it has the essential nature of synthesizing similarity and so forth.
— The synthesis of causes— Ā., Śra.:
"This very person is Jinadatta"— this recognition of identity has similarity as its cause, Ba.

With the words beginning with "tad" (that), he provides the conclusion regarding the subject at hand: since comparison (*upamāna*) and the other [means of knowledge] are included within the indirect (*parokṣa*), therefore it is "samañjasam," that is, logically established, that there are only two means of knowledge, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the indirect.
To the question, "Why is this so? he says: "Otherwise," and so forth;
otherwise, by another way, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*) of those means of knowledge.
Having completely incinerated the vast heap of straw consisting of six types of fallacious arguments,
this commentary has now been composed in their absence by means of the great rays of correct reasoning.

—O Great Sage! Victorious is that stainless Teacher, the Jina, whose inconceivable majesty is radiant; for by him was granted the abundant awakening of all the lotuses of valid cognition. || 6 || cha ||
— “This does not conquer that which is beyond perception”—
In the fourth chapter on scripture (*āgama*) within the *Pramāṇapraveśa*, having explained all means of valid cognition— both direct perception and its others— along with their fallacious forms,
the present undertaking is now commenced to demonstrate the nature of that [scripture].
For one whose intellect is utterly deluded by falling into the great, single-minded darkness-well of false pride,
who indeed other than the sun of Syādvāda would be clearly skilled here in pointing out the path of truth? (1)

Now, demonstrating that even a cognition well-known as a pseudo-means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is in some respect a semblance of that [valid knowledge] and not in every respect, he says: "A cognition established as such, though appearing as perception, might in some respect be a valid means of knowledge, such as that which arises from ophthalmia and the like. (*ba. pratyakṣābhaṃ kathaṃcit syāt pramāṇaṃ taimirādikam*)

What might it be? It would be "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), meaning an appearance of the means of valid cognition that is perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is based on the etymological derivation:

*akṣa* refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) and the non-sense organ (*anindriya*); *prati-niyata* refers to that which is restricted to them; thus, *pratyakṣa* is simply knowledge (*jñāna*). That which appears as if it were that [perception] is so designated.

What is its specific characteristic? It is that which arises from conditions such as *timira* (ocular disorder); "taimira" refers to that which originates from *timira*, and it is so described because it is preceded by rapid whirling and the like.

How could such a cognition be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? In some respect—either with respect to the objective entity as a state (*bhāva*) or as a substance (*dravya*)—it is not entirely a mere semblance of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), because while there is a discrepancy regarding the object consisting of the external form, there is no discrepancy regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*).
Here, he demonstrates the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the words beginning "that which" (*yad*):

that cognition which is non-discrepant (*avisavādi*)—discrepancy being the deviation from the object grasped, and non-discrepancy being its absence—in whatever manner it cognizes its objects, to that extent, in that manner of cognizing its objects, that cognition is considered and accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by investigators.

For instance—every instance of doubt and the like is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own nature or with respect to its substance, because it is non-contradictory (*avisavādin*) therein; for whatever is non-contradictory is a valid means of knowledge therein, just as the cognition of taste is a valid means of knowledge regarding taste. And since doubt and the like are non-contradictory with respect to their own nature or their substantial form, they are therefore in some sense valid means of knowledge therein.

This is because the principle that contradiction alone is the basis for invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) and non-contradiction is the basis for validity (*prāmāṇya*) is agreed upon by all disputants, and because a pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is entirely devoid of such logical principle.

Because of the statement in the *Āptamīmāṃsā* (verse 83), "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) depends upon an external object of cognition (*prameya*)," knowledge is not contradictory regarding its own nature, since that is established by the self-awareness (*ahaṃpratyaya*). Furthermore, how could that which operates toward a well-established object be invalid?
*Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra*, p. 42.

Regarding this verse, Dignāga and others have described pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) such as that caused by ophthalmia; [the author] demonstrates how that is indeed pseudo-perception in some respect.

The texts of Dignāga and others that demonstrate the nature of pseudo-perception are as follows: "Erroneous cognition, conventional cognition, conceptual cognition, inference, and that which is derived from inference..."
Recollection and verbal expression are semblances of perception accompanied by visual impairment (*sataimira*).
Furthermore, because of the conceptualization of water and so forth in relation to mirages and the like, erroneous cognition is a semblance of perception;
for conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is indeed a semblance of perception, since it superimposes another object upon itself and thereby conceptualizes its own nature as that [other] object.
Inference and its result are not perception, because they involve the conceptualization of a prior experience; [this is stated in] Pramāṇasamuccaya, Vṛtti 1.8.
