There are four kinds of pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*): three kinds of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) arising from the affliction of the basis (*āśrayopaplava*), and one kind that is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
Regarding the three kinds of conceptual cognition as pseudo-perception: there is the erroneous cognition that determines water in a mirage.

That which is obscured by a conviction that contradicts reality is knowledge obscured by a veil; and that which functions through the conceptualization of identity with what was previously seen, such as the knowledge of an inferable object from a logical mark (*liṅga*), is non-conceptual—both of these are semblances of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). Of what sort are they? They are those whose origin is from an impairment of the basis—the sense organ—such as the affliction of cataracts (*timira*) and so forth. Thus, there are four kinds of semblances of perception.
But surely perception is non-conceptual; therefore, since this [other cognition] is conceptual, is it not a pseudo-perception?
Indeed, it is an erroneous cognition, such as the apprehension of water in a mirage, or the cognition of substance and so forth from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

Inference is the cognition of the mark (liṅga), and that which is based on inference is the cognition of the bearer of the mark (liṅgin); these are the divisions of conceptual construction (vikalpa) described as mnemonic and as associated with verbal expression, as stated by the teacher Dignāga.
—*Pramāṇavārttika*, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 2.288.

For comparison: “However, cognition regarding yellow conch-shells and the like is not indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because there is an absence of the fulfillment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) accordingly. When the fulfillment of purposeful action consisting merely of the [perceived] shape is established, another cognition—namely inference—is the valid means of knowledge. Therefore, this pair of cognitions, [the first being] inference and [the second] the subsequent doubt regarding the shape, consists of both the valid means of knowledge and the non-valid.”
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, First Chapter:

"In whatever way a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory, it is considered to be [valid] in that very way. (22) Compare: "In whatever way [an object] is clear in a certain respect, in that very way it is perception (*pratyakṣa*)."

Just as there is validity where there is non-contradiction, so too, in every case—whether regarding an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or an extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*)—there is validity only in some respect (*kathañcit*) and not in every respect (*sarvathā*).
(Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 86A)
To the extent that there is non-contradiction, to that same extent there is validity therein—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.
170; *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, p. 69B.
For it has been stated by the venerable Akalaṅkadeva as well: "In whatever way there is non-contradiction, in that very way there is validity"—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 163:
"Whatever is non-contradictory in a certain manner, that is considered valid in that manner."
And that [cognition] which is non-contradictory is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding both perception and the beyond-perceptible—
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, folio 595, *Vivṛti*:

"Just as a cognition affected by an impairment such as cataracts is a means of valid cognition when it is non-contradictory with respect to the moon and so forth, yet it is not a means of valid cognition because it is contradictory with respect to its number and other attributes, since the definition of what is a means of valid cognition and what is otherwise consists precisely in that [non-contradiction or contradiction]."

For even that cognition which conforms [to what has been previously perceived] is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein, because it requires the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*);

otherwise, how could there be the operation of another means of knowledge regarding what has already been seen? This is because it is impossible to perform what has already been done, and because that would entail the abandonment of its absolute uniqueness, since one does not desire its performance in any other way.
Furthermore, this [cognition] may be non-concordant (*visaṃvāda*) due to the appearance of a non-entity, whereas appearances of entities such as the moon and so forth are non-discordant.
Comparison: Validity is defined in relation to the specific mode by which reality is determined.

Accordingly, one should generally infer that the status of validity and its opposite is conflated even in the case of perception and its semblance (*pratyakṣatadābhāsa*), because even for one whose vision is renowned and unimpaired, there occurs the appearance of non-existent forms—such as spatial proximity—in the case of the moon, the sun, and so forth.
Likewise, even for those whose sense organs are impaired, although there is a discrepancy regarding [the number] two and so forth, because the true nature of the moon and such is perceived,
the determination of designation is made in relation to its excellence, just as in the case of fragrant substances and the like—
*Aṣṭaśata*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 277.
For those whose vision is unimpaired, there is the perception of the moon and so forth;
[likewise] there is pleasure and so forth in relation to friends and the like, not merely due to proximity and such—*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 170.
This entire commentary has been extracted from *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, page 595. Regarding the meaning of the verse:

"resembling perception" (*pratyakṣābham*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, that which resembles inference (*parokṣābham*) is also included. The intended meaning is that whatever is established as such exclusively by disputants or by the world may, in some sense, be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not [simply] a fallacy thereof in an absolute sense.
What is that? To this he says: "caused by ophthalmia, etc. (*taimirādikam*).
That which arises from ophthalmia is "taimira"; this refers to that [cognition] of which rapid whirling and so forth are the beginning.
Why is this so? To this he says: "in whatever manner," and so forth.
Since a cognition is intended to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that very form in which it is non-contradictory,

so too [is it defined] in the *Nyāyabindu* (1.4) as "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," and in the *Nyāyasūtra* (1.1.4) as "arisen from the contact of sense-faculty and object and non-deviating."

In this context, and in such [sūtras] as Jaimini’s *satsamprayoge* (JS 1.1.4), the inclusion of qualifiers such as "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is for the purpose of excluding erroneous cognition; if that [erroneous cognition] were to be excluded altogether because it is not perception at all, then there would be a contradiction with the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If, however, it were somehow [the case that the object exists], then it would follow that there is a total loss of certainty; for what has been stated regarding those who maintain extremist views—
that the darkness before the eyes is a disorder of the visual faculty— is a cause of error residing in the sense organ itself.

Regarding the rapid whirling of a firebrand (*alāta*) and the like: for if the firebrand and such were whirled slowly, the illusion of a wheel (*cakra-bhrānti*) would not arise; therefore, the whirling is qualified by the term "rapid. Furthermore, the cause of error residing in the object is the agitation of the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*; for when the *vāta* and the other humors become agitated, the illusion of a flaming pillar and so forth arises. This is the cause of error residing within the self (*adhyātma-gata*).
And by all these causes of error—whether residing in the objects of the senses, in the external, or in the internal—the sense faculty itself must be affected.
Because there can be no error of the sense-faculties when the faculties are unaltered,

by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," those residing in the sense-faculties such as cataracts and jaundice are included, as well as those residing in the objects, such as the rapid bringing near or taking away [of an object].

For when the rapid movement and non-movement [of an object] are being performed, as in the case of a whirling firebrand (*alāta*) and the like, there arises the error of the appearance of a staff colored like fire;

external bases such as riding an elephant and so forth, and internal bases such as severe blows to the vital organs and so forth, are understood to be the causes of such delusion—*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p. 16–17.
If that knowledge—
[that is,] if that knowledge— is perception; this is the ellipsis.
Perception is knowledge arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature. — Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4.

When there is contact of a person's sense organs with what is existent, the arising of cognition is perception; it is not a means [for knowing Dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is currently present— Jaimini-sūtra 1.1.4.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), those [perceptions] produced by non-deviant contact with an existent object are included.

"Erroneous"— according to the commentary (ṭīkā), the connection is that by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) and so forth, [the definition] excludes that which is not perception because it is erroneous.
[The author] provides a detailed commentary on the verse by explaining it with the words beginning "timira," etc., [stating that there is] a partial loss [of the object].

The erroneous cognition (*upaplavajñāna*) that has as its object two moons and so forth—which is the effect of [defects] such as *timira*—is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the moon and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), whiteness, roundness, and the like are included. Why is this so? Because it is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvādaka*) regarding that particular aspect. To provide an illustration for this, he says: "Just as," and so on.

Anticipating the objection—"Just as that cognition affected by defects such as cataracts is invalid because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādaka*) regarding number and so forth, or duality and stability, even if it is indeed of that nature, does this necessarily mean that [all] cognition will possess the form of either valid or invalid?"; he says: "Valid cognition" and so forth.

Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite, invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), are established by their respective definitions; that is, they are defined by concordance (*saṃvāda*) and non-concordance (*visaṃvāda*).
If it is asked, "But how is it logical that the same thing is both a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and something else, given the contradiction?"—to this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.

For (*hi*), because the cognition imagined by you—that is, non-conceptual awareness (*nirvikalpaka-vedana*)—even though it exists, the word "even" (*api*) is used here in the sense of concession; for, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), the assumption of the form of the object (*arthākāratā*) is impossible in cognition. And that impossibility is established, since it has already been refuted at length previously.

Even having granted this, it is said: "The aforementioned cognition, even though it conforms to an object—that is, takes on its form—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object; however, it is not [necessarily] so," is the connection [of the words]. But rather, it may also be an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); such is the meaning of the particle *eva*.
Why is this so? He says: "Because of the requirement for the exclusion of superimposition" (*samāropa*), and so forth.
Superimposition is the cognition of non-momentariness in what is momentary; its exclusion is its removal, and because there is a requirement for that [exclusion].
He states the refutation [of the opponent] for not accepting that [position]: "How otherwise," and so forth.

How could there be the operation of another means of valid cognition—namely inference—with respect to momentary destruction and the like, which have already been perceived, in the manner of having no further expectancy? The meaning is: not at all.
For its fruit is nothing other than the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*).

Now, if its engagement with that [object] is not for the purpose of negating superimposition, what then? It is for the purpose of apprehension. To this he says: "Because of the impossibility," and so forth. Because it is impossible to apprehend—that is, to grasp—what has been done by experience, such as momentary destruction which has already been experienced, through inference; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress, since there would be the consequence of having to apprehend this [inference] as well by means of another inference.
Because it is characterized by correspondence and non-correspondence— [Āloka-ṭīkā];
that cognition is not [the same as] the self-awareness of the knower— [Bhāṣya].
pṛ. 167: Therefore, it is established that [the opponent] accepts... (ba, śra); thus it was stated (śra).
Regarding this, Śrā[maṇya] says:

"Non-conceptual [perception] is not a means of valid cognition because it does not apprehend momentariness and so forth; for if momentary destruction and the like were indeed apprehended by non-conceptual perception itself, then for what purpose would inference be employed to prove that?"—this is the point of the commentary (Āloka-ṭīkā) on inference.
Because it is impossible for [the momentariness] to be apprehended by non-conceptual perception (nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa), [the opponent might argue]:

"Now, by means of the perception of the object, only blue and so forth are apprehended, not momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) and the like; therefore, this fault does not apply. To this, he says: "That," and so forth.

That [position] is one-sided (*ekānta*), for it has been made one-sided; because of the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.42), "of a single nature of an object," etc., whatever has been established remains established as such. Since its abandonment would entail the abandonment of that very [established fact], how could there be the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)? From what, then, would its abandonment arise? To this, he says: "In some way" (*kathañcit*), and so forth.

Because it is not accepted that there is a grasping of an object in some way as having the form of blue and so forth, but not in the form of momentary destruction and so forth—otherwise, a single thing would possess both a grasped and an ungrasped nature—he states another refutation under the guise of a summary: "Therefore," and so on.
Since this is so, for this perception of the form of the object, there is even non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) or even deception (*vipralambha*), and not merely some kind of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the appearance of a non-entity" (*avastunirbhāsāt*).

The sense is that, since according to your own view there is an appearance—meaning a representation—of a gross form which is in fact non-existent, whether external or internal, perception would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Even if validity were granted on the basis of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), the Buddhist’s desired establishment of reality (*tattvasiddhi*) is not achieved.

Now, [the opponent] argues that even if there is no imitation of the nature of objects such as those that perish without leaving a trace (*niranvayavinaśvara*), there is validity because of the imitation of the nature of objects such as blue and sentient beings; to this he says: "The moon, etc. and so forth.

That which is both the moon, etc., and an object—its validity would belong to its appearances, namely the manifestations associated with the cognition of a deceptive [object]. Here, the word *pramāṇa* (valid cognition), which follows from the preceding context and has acquired the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), is connected [to the subject].
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of non-contradiction" (*avisaṃvādakatvāt*).
Indeed, the cognition of an optical illusion such as the moon does not fail with respect to its whiteness, circularity, and so forth;

thus, that which was described by the opponent as a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*)— the sensory cognition of those afflicted by ophthalmia and the like— has been established in some way as being perception itself, [even] in the case of the absolute momentariness (*kṣaṇaikānta*).

For whatever object exists, it is grasped by non-conceptual [cognition] as having been made [known] in its entirety; thus, since the nature of a single object is directly perceived in an absolute sense,
what other part of it could possibly remain unseen that would need to be examined by means of valid cognitions?
—This has been cited from the *Pramāṇavārttika*—in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 93, and in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā-nāma* (Abhidharmakośa-āloka), p. 152.
Siddhibiṭīkā, folio 71A;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, page 405; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 236.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 507; Nyāyaviniścaya-vivaraṇa, p. 496B;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 534.
And there is no deception regarding the moment, nor is there any [such thing] at all. (Śāstravārtāsamuccaya, Yaśovijaya, p. 158b)
Even in the case of non-apprehension— [as noted in] the marginal note (ā॰ ṭi)—
and regarding the sense-faculties afflicted by cataracts and so forth [as noted in] the commentaries (śra॰,
ba॰)— he now states [the following], establishing that even what is called "conceptual cognition" (kalpanājñāna) by the opponent, which appears as such, is indeed perception:
It should be observed— page 521, note 4—
that for conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*), there occurs a self-cognized vivid manifestation of the object.

What is it? It is "self-cognizable" (*svasaṃvedya*), meaning that which is to be cognized or grasped by itself through its nature as the knowledge of reality; the sense is that its essential form is knowledge, because there is no contradiction in the two aspects of the known and the knower within cognition, otherwise [cognition] would result in being a non-entity. What is it qualified by? It is "the manifestation of a clear object. The manifestation, the making known, of an object that exists in the ultimate sense is "object-manifestation"; "clear" means distinct, and that which is both that and object-manifestation is described as such.
Of what? Of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), such as the certain cognitions "this is a jar," "this is a cow," "this is white," "this is a singer," and so forth.

Why? Because of the manifestation of conceptual construction; for "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) means that which is accompanied by conceptualization—the cognition of forms such as genus (*jāti*) and so on—and because of its manifestation, that is, its experience.

When? In the state where all thought has been withdrawn; that state in which all thoughts, such as memory and the rest, have been withdrawn—that is, destroyed—is thus described, and [it occurs] therein.

The meaning is that because the perception of specific forms such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth is unimpeded in the cognition of the eye and other senses, it is therefore incorrect to claim that conceptual knowledge (*vikalpajñāna*) is a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
For [conceptual knowledge] appears as conceptual even when all thought has been withdrawn. (23) *Laghīyastrayavivaraṇa*, p. 43.

Commentary: Having withdrawn thought from all sides, even one who stands with a tranquil inner self perceives through the eye a form consisting of configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which is gross in nature, yet possesses a manifold subtle essence; however, he does not perceive the unique, absolute particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). This is because when the mind emerges from that withdrawal, there is no recollection of it in that same way. Therefore, indistinct non-conceptual cognition is merely a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

Furthermore, there is no absolute difference in the objects of distinct and non-distinct conceptualizations, since perceptions of objects that are near or distant are established as having the same object.
As Dharmakīrti has stated: "The perception of form by the eye that occurs through a tranquil mind is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*);
and in that [perception], the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form—consisting of momentary atoms (*paramāṇu*)—appears.
For instance: 'Having withdrawn all thought from every side, with an inner self made motionless...'"

"Even while remaining [stationary], one perceives form with the eye; that is cognition born of the senses" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.124). The author of the treatise refutes this: "Even in that state, it is experienced that cognition is indeed conceptual (*savikalpaka*), as it grasps objects that are stable, gross, and so forth."

Comparison: Having withdrawn the mind from all sides and remaining with an inwardly tranquil self, even while looking with the eye, one clearly discerns both form and oneself—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 186.

Comparison: Indeed, we never perceive a form that is without a companion, because it is not determined in the manner it is described; for jars and the like, which consist of various parts such as color and so forth, are perceived externally as having many constituents, but not as being merely an accumulation of atoms—*Siddhiviṣaraṇī*, *Ṭīkā*, p. 36B.
[The text contains the fragments *pratisaṃhāraṃ* and *vyu-*.]
The meaning of the verse:
"Self-cognizable" means graspable by the direct perception of self-awareness.
Of what things? He says: "of conceptual constructions."

"What is that? he asks. He replies: "The manifestation of a clear object. Why is this so? He says: "In which all thoughts have been withdrawn," and so forth; because even in that state in which all thoughts have been withdrawn, there is still the manifestation of only conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*).
Therefore, as for what was stated by the opponent— “That which is permeated by conceptual construction cannot have a clear manifestation of the object” (Pramāṇavārttika 2.283),
and so forth— it is established by perception itself that perception is free from conceptual construction.
And [the argument] beginning with Pramāṇavārttika 2.123 is refuted, because it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣa-bādhita*) and because [perception is] non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). (Śrāvakabhūmi)
For that which is bound by conceptual construction, there is no manifestation of a clear object;
for knowledge that is bound by conceptual construction and accompanied by verbal praise, there is no manifestation of a clear object—
*Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 2.
This has been extracted from *Tattvopadeśa*, page 34,
and *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, pages 28B and 95A.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 120; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 502; *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 77A.

For one who is bound by conceptual construction—*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, Yaśovijaya, p. 157B—the object does not appear clearly to one who is bound by non-conceptual [cognition]—*Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī*, p. 35. Perception is free from conceptual construction; it is established by perception itself.

The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) common to all, which is based on names and is personally realized within oneself—that which is well-known as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*)—should be understood as being devoid of conceptualization; that is to say, it is free from the object of conceptualization. And this very [nature] is established by perception itself, namely, by self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Because the nature of an object that is free from conceptual construction is directly perceived,

if this [perception] were of the nature of conceptual construction, it would manifest in that very way, since conceptual construction is directly perceived. For indeed, conceptual construction— which relies on names and is associated with words— is personally experienced by all living beings.
If it were to exist, it would necessarily be perceivable—
*Pramāṇavārttika*, *Manorathanandin* 2.123.
This has been extracted from: *Anekāntajaya* p.
207; *Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā* p. 154; *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā* folios 17A and 31A.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛ. 32;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pṛ. 503; Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, pṛ. 45A, 83B, 495A.
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 82,
and in the *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya* by Yaśovijaya, page 157B,
[the word] "ba" does not exist.

This is another explanation: that form which is self-cognizable, meaning graspable by self-awareness—of what? Of conceptualizations, that is, of mental cognitions such as inference and so forth. What is it? It is the manifestation of a clear object; the meaning is that it is non-conceptual and non-erroneous.
When? When all thoughts have been withdrawn.
In what form? By means of that which is self-cognizable; this is the connection, with the case ending changed [from the instrumental to the locative].
Having done what? Having relied upon that manifestation, because of the appearance of conceptual construction—this is the meaning.
Therefore, the point is that those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are somehow non-perceptual (*pratyakṣābhā*).
Regarding the explanation of the commentary (*vivṛti*):
while commenting on the verse (*kārikā*), he says "from all [sides]" and so forth.

Having withdrawn from everything—both from what is of the same class and from what is of a different class—and having abandoned what? Thought; that is, the intellect of deliberation—even while remaining [in the world], the practitioner [is thus situated].
In what manner? He says: "Stimiteṇa" (by the steady), and so forth. "Sthimitaḥ" means having become steady, motionless; "antarātmā" refers to the mind (*manas*).
What does it do with that? He says: "Cakṣuṣā" (with the eye), and so forth.

The mention of the "eye" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the ear and other senses; thus, one sees form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the mention of "form" is also an elliptical expression for taste and the other objects.
Of what nature is it? It consists of shape (*saṃsthāna*), having as its essential character qualities such as roundness and so forth.
Again, of what nature is it? It consists of grossness (*sthūla*), having a gross nature, and is a single [entity].

Furthermore, what are its specific characteristics? It is said to have a subtle and manifold nature (*sūkṣmānekasvabhāvam*); that is, it is that which possesses a subtle and manifold intrinsic nature.

Now, one might object: "Are not [qualities] such as shape (*saṃsthāna*) properties of a substance (*dravya*) and not of form (*rūpa*), since this [form], being a quality itself, is devoid of further qualities? This too is an unconsidered statement. For in the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), there is no contradiction in form also possessing the attributes of a substance, by virtue of the presentation of the non-difference between substance and quality. Now, one might argue: "When form is perceived by the eye, it is perceived only as a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) consisting of a nature of multiple, mutually distinct, partless atoms, and not as a gross (*sthūla*) or similar nature. To this, he says: "But not... and so forth.

The word "again" (*punar*) refers to the stage of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). One does not perceive a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Of what nature is it? It is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). "Uncommon" means that which is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes, being singular and without companion; its ultimate property (*anta-dharma*) is thus described.
Why is this so? He says: "In reabsorption," and so forth.

*Saṃhāra* is the absence of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), while *pratisaṃhāra* is the recurrence of conceptual construction. One who has that [state] as their basis is called "one whose mind has emerged" or "awakened. For such a person, because there is no recollection—that is, an absence of recollection—of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in that very same uncommon and exclusive manner, there is therefore never a perception of it. Rather, because there is always recollection of that which has the nature of the gross and so forth, there is always perception of that;
thus, what is it? It is only the form of the particular characteristic of the essence.
There is nothing uncommon; that which is unique is excluded from others,
and it is precisely that [unique thing] which is recollected.

—Because of this [he says], with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he states the conclusion: since non-conceptual cognition, which is intended by the opponent to be perception, never appears as having a clear nature, therefore the non-conceptual is indeed indistinct and a mere semblance of perception.

Now, one might object: "Since cognitions that are clear and those that are otherwise have distinct appearances, they must have distinct objects; therefore, it is logical that [the former] does not perceive a form whose nature is gross and so forth. For whatever two things have distinct appearances, they have distinct objects, as in the case of the cognitions of color and taste. And since there is a distinction in appearance between perceptual and non-perceptual cognitions, it follows that the clear-natured perception has the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, whereas the non-clear-natured conceptualization (*vikalpa*) has the gross and so forth as its object. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not... and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no absolute distinction between the objects of clear and non-clear conceptualizations—such as those beginning with *avagraha* (perception) and ending with *smaraṇa* (recollection)—in the sense that a clear conceptualization operates upon an ultimate reality (*paramārtha-vastu*) while a non-clear conceptualization operates upon a mentally constructed object (*kalpita*). Rather, the very object of a clear conceptualization is itself the object of the non-clear conceptualization.

As for the argument stated previously—that [the two differ] because they possess distinct appearances—that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as he demonstrates by saying: "proximate," and so forth.

Even though there may be a difference in the appearance of clear versus unclear forms for those direct perceptions whose objects are respectively near and not near, it is nonetheless possible for them to have the same object,
because the difference in appearance among the direct perceptions of trees and so forth by persons situated at a distance or nearby is not unestablished,
nor is there a difference in their object; for the single tree and so forth is indeed the object of both.
Non-conceptual [cognition] is superior;
because cognitions other than direct perception have distinct objects and distinct appearances, it is not so in this case.
—Regarding the [passage] beginning with "of the non-conceptual" (*avikalpakasya*), the portion starting from "proximate" (*pratyāsanna*) and so forth does not exist in Ā;
this should also be applied to the phrase "unestablished" (*asiddha*) in Śra and A. — Ā-Ṭīkā.

As for what is also said—"In perception there are no conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*), because those that meet the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) are not perceived; for whatever meets the conditions for apprehension and is not perceived in a given place does not exist there, just as a jar in a certain particular location; and such real conceptual constructions are not perceived in perception"—and as for the claim that "the fact of their meeting the conditions for apprehension is not unestablished, since these conceptual constructions do not arise and perish entirely unnoticed, whereby they might be real yet unobserved," [the author] states the following in order to refute that:
They exist through direct perception (pratyakṣa), as it has been said: "Nor do these conceptual constructions arise and perish entirely unperceived;
nor can it be imagined that, in their apprehension, there is a superimposition of their form or any doubt by following a logical mark (liṅga). — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.1.46.
Even though they exist, conceptual constructions have their arising and passing away clearly perceived; even though they exist, they are merely mental constructs.
What would not be perceived or distinguished? What [would be] conceptualization or mental construction?
In what? In direct perceptions, such as self-awareness and the like.
What are they qualified by? They are existent (*satya*), meaning they are present.

Furthermore, of what nature are they? Their arising and passing away are individually perceived. "Arising" is the acquisition of self-nature; "passing away" is the cognition of non-existence. Those [entities] whose arising and passing away are "individually perceived"—that is, apprehended in every living being—are so described. Indeed, existence is never experienced without possessing arising and passing away, for otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is asked: "What is the reason for the non-perception of existing conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) in perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣabuddhi*)? we reply: "It is due to the incapacity of the cognizer and a lack of focused attention. To this, he provides an illustration, beginning with the words "that" (*tat*), etc.:

"The *svalakṣaṇa* (specific characteristic) of those conceptual constructions is their own nature (*svarūpa*); the 'differentiation' (*bheda*) of that is its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from similar and dissimilar things; 'like that' (*tadvat*) means possessing that [differentiation]."

The meaning is this: just as the perceived arising and passing away [of objects] is not observed despite the conceptual exclusions (*svalakṣaṇavyāvṛtti*) of their specific characteristics, because that [exclusion] is established solely through inference; so too, conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) are not observed within perceptions.

If it is asked, "How then is the existence of those [constructions] established there when they are unobserved?"—the answer is: no, for they are established by the fact that otherwise the recollection of their objects would be inexplicable.

For the state of perceiving a cow while one is conceptualizing a horse is a state in which all conceptualizations have been withdrawn; even in that case, the perception of the cow consists essentially in a determination (*niścaya*), because otherwise the subsequent recollection of its object would be inexplicable.
—*Laghīyastrayāloka*, p.

44. For comparison: "Indeed, forms such as 'many' or 'of many kinds' do not arise or pass away within consciousness while remaining entirely unknown to itself, such that they might be unperceived even though they exist, like conceptual constructions"—*Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, fol. 98A.

They would not be perceived in their perceptible states, just like the difference between their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Commentary: Due to the deception caused by the arising of successive similar [moments], one who does not perceive their distinction fails to ascertain [the truth]; this is an unexamined assertion. Since similarity in every respect is not admitted, it must be considered whether the doctrine of absolute reabsorption (*pratisaṃhāraikānta*) is possible or not.
And how could all perceptions, which are entirely free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), subsequently undergo conceptualization?

Because they arise from their own causes in such a way that momentary existence is their very nature, even one of dull intellect—who, despite seeing this nature, always suspects its continued existence due to the apprehension of "being" (*sattā*), or who is deceived by the production of successive similar moments—does not ascertain it.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1)

Furthermore, even while perceiving that impermanence, one of dull intellect does not ascertain it— either because they are constantly deceived by the apprehension of existence and the resulting suspicion of its continued presence, or because they are deceived by the production of successive moments that are similar to one another.
(Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, Chapter 1, page 237)

Those [cognitions] whose arising and passing away are individually cognized by each living being are described as such; even though they exist in that manner and are not merely non-existent, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) would not be perceived within the direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), the plural number being used for the purpose of including all four types of direct perception.

Nor is it contradictory that there should be non-perception of something existent which possesses manifestation and destruction that are clearly perceived; in order to support this point, he presents a well-known illustration and says: "like the differentiation of their own specific characteristics" (*tatsvalakṣaṇabhedavat*).

This means: the *svalakṣaṇa* (specific characteristic) of those conceptual constructions is their own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*); its "differentiation" (*bheda*) is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from both homogeneous and heterogeneous entities; "like that" (*tadvat*) means possessing that [differentiation].

This is what is meant: just as the distinction between arising and ceasing, though present, is not perceived in conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) because they are cognized [simultaneously]—otherwise, the inference of momentary destruction would be purposeless—so too, even though conceptual constructions exist within direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), they are not perceived.
This is because [the perception] is distinguished from its own kind by the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of the sense-faculties, the mind, and the yogi.
Thus it has been said:
momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*) and the distinction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpabheda*);
[this is] the explanation of the commentary (*vivṛti*).

Having demonstrated the opponent’s argument along with its refutation through the words "similar" (*sadṛśa*) and so forth, he concludes the meaning of the verse with the words "the absolute [view] regarding the withdrawal" (*pratisaṃhāraikānta*) and so forth: The production of something similar—that is, identical—again and again causes a delusion, like the visual confusion of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakravat*). Therefore, for the Buddhist who does not perceive those specific features—that is, one whose nature is such that he does not see the aforementioned specific feature characterized by the exclusion of what belongs to the same class (*sajātīyavyāvṛtti*), unlike a fire-brand wheel—the failure to ascertain, which is the non-perception of difference, is an unexamined assertion. Why is this so? To this he says: "In every way" (*sarvathā*), and so forth.

The intention is this: since similarity among those conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) cannot be established in any way—whether through difference, non-difference, both, or neither—it would follow that they are merely characterized by their mutual distinction.
But this is not the case; therefore, just as their distinction exists yet is not perceived, so too do conceptual constructions exist within perceptions despite being [unperceived].

Thus, one must reflect upon and carefully examine whether the absolute exclusion of all conceptual construction from perceptions—the absolute negation (*pratisaṃhāraikānta*)—is possible or not; the meaning is that it is not possible.
[Objection: "Since their individual characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are distinct, it is possible for those [characteristics] to exist there even if they are not perceived;

for even if their distinction is not perceived, nevertheless, the appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsargayogya-pratibhāsa*), which does exist, ought to be perceived. Yet it is not perceived.
Therefore, because this is not perceived, its non-existence is established, and thus the absolute withdrawal (*pratisaṃhāraikānta*) is proven. To this, he says: "And how... and so forth.

And how could it be that perceptions of external objects are not in any way at all free from conceptualization? The plural number is used for the purpose of including all perceptual cognitions without exception. In every respect, like their own nature (*svarūpa*), they would be non-conceptual even regarding external objects; "again" (*punar*) is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*): [if one were to argue] that they might be conceptualized—that is, they would consist of conceptualizations regarding the external—this is because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the object] being manifold (*anekānta*). Alternatively, those cognitions, being entirely non-conceptual and real, how could they not subsequently be conceptualized—that is, produce conceptual constructions?

For it has been stated in the section establishing the existence of conceptual cognition (*savikalpasiddhipraghaṭṭaka*) that a conceptual construction cannot arise from a non-conceptual experience, just as [a conceptualization of] an object [cannot arise] from the object itself.
Then, demonstrating the established meaning, he says: "Thus, Ā. uvāca? (Ā. said).—Ā. Ṭī. (Commentary)
There is no such thing as "in every way" and so forth regarding that distinction; [the manuscript] lacks this.
Because similarity is not admitted [by us],
the objection that there would be non-difference between those two should be carefully considered; this does not exist.

This is the definition of conceptualization (*kalpanā*) among conceptualizations; for it is said: "Conceptualization is the cognition of a representation that is capable of being associated with a verbal expression" (*Nyāyabindu* 1.5).
Therefore...
Because there is the establishment of a manifestation capable of being associated with verbal expression—this is the opponent's [position];
"in what way? and so forth is the [author's] response.
Furthermore, how is it that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) arises only from conceptualization?

Just as a conceptualization associated with words does not arise from a momentary object that is devoid of the genus, quality, action, and so forth denoted by verbal expression, in exactly the same way, a conceptualization consisting of words should not arise even from non-conceptual experience, which is itself devoid of words.

By means of sensory perception (akṣadhī), memory (smṛti), recognition (saṃjñā), reflection (cintā), and discernment (abhinibodhika),

Because of that connection, the fact that *akṣa*, *dhī*, and so forth are in the nominative case is due to the principle that "the transformation of case endings occurs according to the requirements of the meaning. Non-contradiction in practical activity [is the criterion]; its semblance is otherwise.

(25) Commentary: Because non-contradiction is established through perception, memory, recognition, inference, and so forth, these possess validity regarding objects; otherwise, there would be a classification of their semblances. In the same way, there is a classification of scriptural knowledge and its semblance.
The meaning of the verse:

Intellect (*dhī*)—that is, cognition (*buddhi*) consisting of apprehension (*avagraha*) and so forth—is the effect of the sense organs (*akṣa*), such as the eye. That [intellect], along with memory (*smṛti*), perception (*saṃjñā*), reflection (*cintā*), reasoning (*tarkeṇa*), and inferential cognitions (*ābhinibodhika*)—the plural number is used in reference to individual instances—all of these, whether taken collectively or individually, constitute non-contradiction in worldly practice; therefore, they possess validity (*prāmāṇya*). Otherwise, in the manner imagined by proponents of extremist views (*ekāntavādin*), it would be a mere semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

For in the world, the non-contradiction of practical activities such as purposeful action is not well-known to occur through the modes of recollection, recognition, and reasoning postulated by the proponents of extremist views (ekāntavādin)—which deny the validity [of these], nor through the mode of inference arising from signs such as "unconceptualized sensory cognition" (*avikalpākṣajñāna*) and "the effect" (*kārya*), which are enumerated [by them];
[this is established] by those possessing *abhinibodhika* [knowledge]. (Bhagavatī Sūtra 8.2.10; Āvaśyaka Niryukti 453) — Commentary and Explanation.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Perception," and so forth.

Because non-contradiction is established through perception, recollection, recognition, inference, and so on, these—perception and the others—possess validity (*prāmāṇya*) with respect to objects such as jars; otherwise, there would be a classification of fallacies (*tadābhāsa*) and a classification of pseudo-validity according to the manner imagined by proponents of extremist doctrines (*ekāntavādin*). Extending this very principle to verbal testimony (*śabda*), he says: "In the same way," and so forth.

Since another [type of] heard [knowledge], such as recollection (*smaraṇa*), has already been mentioned, the term "heard" (*śruta*) here refers to verbal knowledge (*śābdam śrutam*); likewise, the distinction between that [valid] knowledge of what is heard and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) is established precisely through the modes of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) and non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) with worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), just as in the case of indirect (*parokṣa*) [perception]. Regarding the term *parokṣa*—[as noted in the] marginal note (ā॰ ṭi॰)—it refers to a mode of verbal testimony (savādaprakāre) [according to the commentary] (śra॰).

Now, one might raise the objection: "But since scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) is not itself a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can its establishment [as such] be possible? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Scripture (*śruta*) is established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding objects in other continents and so forth; the phrase "non-contradiction in worldly practice" carries over [from the previous definition].

Scriptural knowledge is the cognition of an object preceded by intelligence, based on the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) and so forth; and that is indeed established as a means of valid cognition.
If it is asked, "By what is it established? it is said: "Because of the non-contradiction of its practical application (*vyavahāra*)," just like perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge.

In regard to what objects? In regard to objects of cognition (*prameya*). Of what kind? Such as those belonging to other continents (*dvīpāntara*) and so forth. Jambūdvīpa is the subject under discussion; other than that, there are the other continents such as Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and others, which are preceded by [those separated by] time and nature—this is what is meant by "in those [objects] remote in space, time, and form. This is the meaning.

For one who proceeds after having determined the object from what has been heard is not deceived regarding the application of elixirs and the like, nor in matters such as seizing [a target] or reaching places like Malaya;
therefore, why would investigators not place their trust? Because of its occasional deviation in certain cases.
In some cases, such as when sweets (*modaka*) and the like are offered on a riverbank, there is a deviation or contradiction of that which was heard;

therefore, one should not suspect a lack of validity for all knowledge simply because of a lack of validity in a particular instance, for if that were so, it would follow that even perception and other means of knowledge would likewise be invalid, resulting in the collapse of all worldly activity.
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 46)
One should not entertain doubt anywhere because of its possible deviation.

Commentary: Scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even regarding objects other than the speaker’s intention; otherwise, how could one comprehend—without hesitation or contradiction—the nature, effects, and locations of islands, regions, rivers, mountains, and so forth, which are situated in distant lands according to their spatial divisions and whose intrinsic natures and effects have never been perceived? (Ca and Na are not present in the *Īśvaravāda*, *Jainavāda*).
The meaning of the verse:

"Scripture" (*śruta*) is the subject (*dharmin*); "is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam*) is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). The reason (*sādhana*) following this is "because its non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*) is established. By this, it is stated that not all scripture is a means of valid cognition, but only that which is non-discrepant. To the question, "In what respect is such scripture a means of valid cognition? he says: "With regard to objects" (*artheṣu*), and not merely with regard to the [speaker's] intention (*abhiprāya*).

In what kind of cases? To this he says: "In other continents, etc."—that is, established in another treatise or well-known in the world. Now, since words are observed to function even in the absence of an object, how can they be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard? To this he says: "They would not cause lack of confidence," and so forth. "Lack of confidence" (*anāśvāsa*) means the absence of trust. They would not cause such lack of confidence in certain cases, such as "a herd of hundreds of elephants resides on the tip of a finger," because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of what is heard—that is, by relying on the fact of deviation. The intention is that for this very reason, the same would apply even to sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), as it would result in its [the word's] status [as a means of knowledge].
—Where has such a thing been seen? In what scripture or in the world?
In the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* and other works, or in the treatises of the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and so forth?

Regarding the meaning of what has been heard, this is the comparison: "What other person, possessing a sense of shame, would dare to say that there exists a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass—something never seen before? This is the Sāṃkhya beast.

That [inference] is fallacious because, in certain cases such as the cognition of two moons, a deviation of visual perception is observed; consequently, there would follow a lack of confidence even regarding the cognition of a single moon, resulting in a state of total distrust.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣikas and Buddhists, who do not accept that scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinct from inference (*anumāna*):

[Objection: But surely, since the distinction of *śruta* (verbal testimony) from inference (*anumāna*) is not established, and because its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is proven only through the establishment of that [inference] itself, the claim that "verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition regarding objects" and so forth is incorrect. To explain: verbal testimony is not distinct from inference, because its object is non-different from that [of inference], and because it is endowed with a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) non-different from that [of inference]. Whatever is of such a nature is not distinct from inference, just as one inference is not distinct from another inference; and this verbal testimony is of such a nature.

Nor is its having the same object as that [inference] unestablished; for both verbal testimony and inference operate within the domain of the universal (*sāmānya*) without distinction, and both serve as causes for the cognition of a related object. Indeed, a word does not convey an unrelated object, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and in conveying a related object, it would not transcend the status of being a logical mark (*liṅga*) of that object.

Nor is its possession of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) non-different from that [of inference] unestablished, because, like smoke and so forth, a word depends upon the recollection of a relation for the cognition of an object.

Furthermore, because it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): for whatever word is observed in the world to apply to a particular meaning, that word is its designator; whereas where it is not so observed, it is not its designator.

Moreover, it is endowed with the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). To explain: the intended word possesses a meaning, because it is a word, like a previously perceived word; just as this smoke possesses fire, because it is smoke, like previously perceived smoke;
and just as fire is cognized upon seeing smoke through direct perception, so too is its meaning cognized upon hearing the word.
Furthermore, the independence from examples is common to both of these in the case of a familiar object—
since [the cognition of] sound and so forth is also included within inference due to having the same method of operation.

"Just as inference regarding supersensuous objects arises for one who knows the convention [of linguistic signs] through the perception of an unmistakable mark and the recollection of its established connection, so too does it arise from words and the like. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

For a person for whom the convention (*samaya*)—that is, the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*)—is well-known, inference regarding a supersensible object occurs through both the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of that well-known [relation], namely, the recollection of the established rule that "where there is smoke, there is fire. He states the reason for this: because they possess the same rule (*samānavidhitva*), that is to say, because they share the same cause of operation (*samānapravṛttikāraṇatva*) and are not subsumed under the definition of a different class.

Because it serves as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the apprehension of the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) when that desire is intended;
for just as every sound is an inference for the apprehension of space (*ākāśa*), so too is the effect of the desire to speak [an inference] for the apprehension of that very desire.

578: The establishment of the validity of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) as distinct from inference (*anumāna*) and other means of cognition, preceded by a refutation [of opposing views]—herein it is replied:
As for what was stated—that "verbal testimony is not distinct from inference," and so forth—that is incorrect, because the identity of their objects is unestablished;
for the object of verbal testimony is the mere thing (artha-mātra), whereas the object of inference is the subject (dharmin) as qualified by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).

Furthermore, how could there be non-difference of object between these two? Would it be by virtue of their having as their range only the universal (*sāmānya*), or by virtue of having as their object only that which possesses it (*tadvanmātra*), or by virtue of being the cause for the cognition of a related object? Regarding the first position, what is this so-called "universal"? Is it something permeating all individuals, endowed with properties such as eternity and unity, or is it of the nature of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)? Both of these positions are untenable, because a universal of either form has already been refuted on the occasion of the examination of the universal, and because the view that these two have as their object merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) will be refuted later.

If these two [perception and inference] had as their object a universal (*sāmānya*) whose nature is eternal and so forth, the Buddhist would be entering the position of the Mīmāṃsakas; and that is untenable, because the fact that they have such an object will also be refuted later.

Now, if it is intended that there is no difference in their objects because both have merely that which possesses the universal (*tadvanmātra*) as their object, then surely perception would also follow as being inference, since there is no distinction here either regarding that non-difference, given that it has been established on page 530, line 13 that all means of valid cognition have as their object an entity consisting of both the universal and the particular.
The scope of comparison is seen to be different; furthermore, he will establish that the word has a universal as its object,
and it has already been proven that the subject (liṅgin) is the substratum (dharmin) qualified by its attributes (dharma).
"Indeed, there is no inference as long as its object is not [known]"— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Śabdanirūpaṇa*, verses 55–56.
For the object of a word is the mere thing (*arthamātra*), whereas the object of inference is the substratum (*dharmī*) as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 620: First of all, the objects denoted by the word and the logical mark (*liṅga*) are indeed dissimilar;
likewise, it will be established that the meaning of the word consists solely in that which possesses the property (*tadvanmātra*).
Inference, however, has the meaning of a sentence as its object; for instance, in the cognition "there is fire here" or "the mountain possesses fire"—[Nyāyamañjarī, p. 153;
Śabdānumāna, B].
In the printed edition there is a reference to a footnote but no footnote.

Comparison of *anumāna* and *śabda*: "Moreover, would the non-difference of the scope (*gocara*) of these two [means of knowledge] arise from their having as their object merely a universal (*sāmānyamātra*), or from their having as their scope merely that which possesses it (*tadvanmātra*)? — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 620.
—Also for form (*rūpa*), there is the examination of the universal (*sāmānya*)...
[in] Śabara-bhāṣya, page 285; page 289, [concerning] verbal testimony and inference (*śabdānumāna*).
Because even the state of having a universal— such as "eternity" and so forth— as its object would entail, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view,
that it has an external object possessing a universal as its domain.

By this [argument], the status of verbal testimony as inference has also been refuted on the grounds that its object is not distinct from that of [inference], since it too has as its object a thing possessing a universal (sāmānyavat), and because it is a cause for the cognition of a related object. For otherwise, even perception would entail the consequence of being an inference, since perception also is a cause for the cognition of a related object;
indeed, it is only when it is related to its own object that it is a cause for the cognition of that object, and not otherwise, lest there be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Now, although this [word] is connected with its object and is indistinguishable from inference in its capacity as a cause for comprehension, it differs from inference due to a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). If that is so, why would there not also be a difference between verbal cognition and this [inference], given that they are indistinguishable in that respect? That is not correct; for it is logical that verbal cognition is not inference because its object is non-distinct [from that of perception], whereas perception has its own unique object.
Nor [is it established] through inference, because the distinction between causal complexes (sāmagrī) is the same;
nor by virtue of being endowed with an identical causal complex, since that is impossible in the case of sound.

For the causal complex in inference consists of the three forms, such as the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and that is not possible in the case of verbal testimony. To explain: first of all, it is not possible for a word to possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject; because here no subject whatsoever is possible.

For in this case, would the subject be the word or the object? It cannot be the word; because if the word itself were the subject and the word itself were the reason, it would follow that the reason is merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatva*).

Now, if it is argued that "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*), and thus it does not constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatva*); [we reply: no, because according to your own view, sound-ness—which is by nature a universal (*sāmānya*)—cannot exist as an ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). Even if it were to exist as a conceptual construct (*kalpita*), it would lack the capacity to prove [the conclusion], for you yourselves have admitted that "it is the object (*artha*) that makes the object known. As it has been said: "Therefore, in the case of verbal cognition, there can be no inference, just as in the case of perception."
Because it lacks the three characteristics [of a valid reason], such an object is excluded—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdanirṇaya, verse 98; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 620.
Comparison: Now, why is the word not postulated as the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of its possessing meaning?
For in that case, it would follow that the reason (*hetu*) is merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*);
yet, in the case of smoke as the subject, a universal (*sāmānya*) is accepted as the reason.
"In this case, 'soundness' (śabdatva) is the indicator; the specific term 'cow-sound' (gośabdatva) will not be negated.
Since the individual instance (vyakti) alone is the qualificand, it follows that there is only one reason. — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdapariccheda, verses 62–64.

[Objection: But was it not said that just as in inference the subject (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma) is the probandum (sādhya), so here the word qualified by its object should be the probandum? [Reply: Not so; because the word is the reason (hetu), and the reason itself cannot be the subject (pakṣa).
— *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 153.
In the Buddhist doctrine (syād-ratnākara, p.
620), [the universal] is of the nature of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).
For you yourselves have accepted that "an object indeed makes an object known"— *Syādvādamañjarī*,
p. 620 (reading *bhavat* from *śra* and *ba*).
By this very [argument], the Buddhist inference that "sound possesses meaning" and so forth is refuted.

Or, let it be granted that "the nature of being sound" (*śabdatva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*); even so, what is being proven (*sādhya*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), namely sound—is it its "being qualified by an object," its "possessing the capacity to convey an object," or its "being qualified by the cognition of an object"? Among these, the first position is untenable; for, as in the case of a mountain and fire, the relationship of subject and attribute (*dharmidharmabhāva*) is impossible between sound and its object. An attribute must be dependent, and the object is not dependent upon sound, because they occupy different locations.

Whatever occupies a different location from something else is not dependent upon it, just as the Vindhya mountain is not dependent on the Sahya mountain; and since the object occupies a location distinct from the word, there is no relationship of substratum and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva) between them.

Where such a relationship of substratum and superstratum does not exist, there can be no relationship of attribute and substrate (dharmadharmibhāva), as in the case of Citrakūṭa and Kaśmīra. Furthermore, since the relationship of substratum and superstratum is absent between the word and its object, no one who is not a fool would consider the word to be qualified by the object, for the object is well-known to everyone down to children as being entirely distinct from the word.

Comparison—Is it the fact of being qualified by an object that is being proved of the word, which is the subject (*dharmin*), or its being qualified by the capacity to convey [that object], or its being qualified by the cognition of the object? —*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 153; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
620. (The reading *acalānila* is from the Ānandāśrama edition.)
Comparison: because there is no relationship of attribute and substrate between word and meaning, as there is none between a mountain and fire—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
153; because the relationship of attribute and substrate is impossible between word and meaning, as it is between a mountain and fire.
—In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 621:
"The property of both word and object... (*ba*);
"the object is not [existent] at all" (*ba*).
There is no relationship of attribute and substrate between word and meaning, because there is no relationship of locus and located.

If it is argued that what is being established is the fact that the word possesses the capacity to convey the meaning, that too is incorrect; for it is impossible to employ a word for the sake of that [capacity].
Indeed, a word is neither employed nor heard for the sake of establishing that capacity, but rather for the sake of establishing the meaning.
For the purpose of perceiving the capacity to convey meaning, there is the following comparison: A word is neither spoken nor even heard for the sake of establishing a capacity;
rather, people hear and speak it solely for the sake of understanding the meaning.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.

154; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 621. Now, if it is argued that what is being proved is the state of being distinguished by the cognition of the object (*arthapratītiviśiṣṭatva*), that too is incorrect, because the dilemma of whether [the distinction] is already established or not established (*siddhā-siddha-vikalpa*) is untenable.
For if the cognition of the object is unestablished, it is illogical for the word to possess that [object], because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
But if this [cognition] is established, what else could possibly be inferred? Since there is no contradiction in this [cognition] which has self-cognized nature, this inference is futile.
Nor should it be said that this same fault applies equally to the inference of smoke and so forth; for in that case, there exists a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Indeed, fire is not produced by smoke, but rather it is cognized; however, the cognition of an object is produced by the word. Therefore, it is only in this [cognition] that the alternatives of "established" or "unestablished" can apply. Consequently, it is not tenable for the word to function as the subject (*dharmin*), because the alternatives of being established or unestablished are inapplicable—just as in the case of comparison (*tulanā*).
Even if [the word] were unestablished, how could it possess that [quality] by virtue of the cognition of the object?
Or, if that [cognition] is established, what else is inferred from its perception?
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 154)
Now, the cognition of an object must arise either from a word or from something else— [as stated in] *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 621,
regarding the cognition of an object.
Regarding the term "defect" (doṣa): compare this with the following—“In that case, fire is not produced by smoke, but rather [fire] is cognized;

however, in this case, the cognition of the object is produced by the word. It is precisely in relation to this [production of cognition] that there is occasion for the alternative options of being established or unestablished.
Nor [is it a property] of the object, because you do not admit a relationship between the word and that [object]. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 154; Siddhiviniścaya, Ātmatattvaviveka).

For the Buddhists do not accept a relationship between word and object characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or by origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because that would entail a contradiction with such statements as: "Words do not exist in the object, nor are they identical to it.
Nor can a word, even if unrelated to an object, be a property (*dharma*) of that object, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if it is argued that this [property] belongs to the word because it is the cause of the cognition of the object, we say no, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): for the status of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is established only when the word’s status as the cause of the cognition of the object is established, and the latter is established only when the former is established. Furthermore, if its status as a property of the subject were based on its being the cause of that cognition, then the eye and other sense organs would also be established as properties of the subject; consequently, the cognition arising from them would also have to be inferential. Therefore, the status of being a property of the subject is not possible in the case of the word.
Regarding the object (*artha*) consisting of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),

it has been stated by the Buddhists: "For words are neither identical with the object nor do they possess its nature, such that when that [object] appears, those [words] would also appear," and so forth.
—*Nyāyapraveśaka-bṛtti*, p. 35:

Just as smoke exists in relation to fire through a connection of produced and producer by way of posterior occurrence, so too words do not exist in relation to an object through a connection of produced and producer by way of posterior occurrence;
by this, he explains that there is no causal relationship (*tadutpatti-sambandha*) capable [of establishing the connection] between word and object.

Those words whose essence (ātman) is that very object are "tadātmānaḥ" (of that nature). By this, he states that even the relation of identity (tādātmya-sambandha) does not exist; thus he says, "in that [object]. The intention is as follows: when the object appears—that is, when it is determined by direct perception (pratyakṣa)—if words were to appear or shine forth [simultaneously], [it would be untenable]. For according to the Buddhists, there are two kinds of relations: characterized by identity (tādātmya-lakṣaṇa) and characterized by origination (utpatti-lakṣaṇa).

In that regard, neither of the two types of relation—namely, the one characterized by identity (tādātmya), as between "tree-ness" and "śiṃśapā-ness," nor the one characterized by origination from that (tadutpatti), as between fire and smoke—is possible for the word and its object. To explain:
first of all, it is not a relation characterized by identity.
For if there were identity (*tādātmya*) between word and object, it would have to be either the word or the object, but not both.

Likewise, if there were identity between word and object, then upon the utterance of words such as "razor" (*kṣurikā*) or "sweetmeat" (*modaka*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the mouth being sliced open or filled; yet this is not observed.
Furthermore, [the relation] characterized by origination (*tadutpatti*) is also untenable.

What, then, is this so-called "origination from that"? Does it mean the origination of the object from the word, or the origination of the word from the object? If the origination of the object were from the word, then the entire world would be without poverty, since gold and other things would originate merely from the utterance of their words.
Nor does the word originate from the object, because we observe its origination from a collection of causes such as the palate and other vocal organs—*Nyāyapraveśavṛtti*, p. 76.
And it has been said by Dharmakīrti: "For words do not exist in the object, nor are they identical with its nature, such that they might appear as that [object].
(This is cited from *Anekāntajaya*, p. 119; also cited in *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, p. 118).
*Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, folio 75B;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, page 621;
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccayavṛtti* (Bṛhatī), page 16.

For words do not exist in the object, nor are they identical with it; for if that were so, even one who has not mastered the language would engage in linguistic usage just like one who has—this has been stated (*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p.
133)—because this [usage] is a property (*dharma*) [of the speaker].

This [relation] would be a property of the object (*arthadharma*), yet it is understood through the comparison of words; and if its status as a property were established by its being a signifier, and its being a signifier were established by its status as a property, there would indeed be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, this hypothesis is not tenable either.

—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdaparikṣā, verse 77: If it is asserted that [the reason] possesses that property by virtue of being a producer of cognition, then, as before, there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*):
cognition occurs through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth, and only when cognition exists is the status of being a property of the subject and so forth attained.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 154;
Syādvādaratnākara, p.
621: [This refers to] the word.

Nor can [the relationship] be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) produced by the eyes and other senses, because there is no co-occurrence (*anugama*) of the word and its object in either space or time;
for the word is perceived in the mouth, while the object is on the ground (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5).
This is because you yourselves have admitted this;

nor do those engaged in worldly transaction possess a determinate cognition of its concomitance. Indeed, it is not the case that whenever people hear a word such as "pīṇḍakhajūra" (a specific kind of date), those engaged in transaction thereby apprehend the actual existence of the object, the pīṇḍakhajūra, and so forth.

For wherever there is smoke, fire is necessarily established as its concomitant by virtue of its existence; however, such a spatial or temporal concomitance does not exist between a word and its object. Indeed, it is not the case that wherever a word exists at a certain time, its object must necessarily exist there. For words such as "Rāvaṇa" or "Śaṅkhacakravartin" are present [in speech], yet their objects are past or future. How, then, can objects be the concomitants of words? And in the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), there is also an absence of negative concomitance (vyatireka), since the latter is preceded by the former.
Comparison—the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a word with its object of cognition is not established;
for the agency of all [means of knowledge] is understood through their operation.
Where there is smoke, there is fire—thus the positive concomitance is clear.

However, there is no certainty that wherever the word exists, the object also exists; for at that place or at that time, the object is not perceived— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdapariccheda, verses 85–86.
Positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are also difficult to establish for it, because there is no co-occurrence of word and object in either space or time;
for where there is a word, there is not necessarily its object, as the Vedic scholars have said: "We perceive the word in the mouth, but the object on the ground."
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 155;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 612, by the Buddhists and others.
Wherein there is neither the state of a lump nor even the state of non-existence,
nor the state of differentiation.

As for what was also stated regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, "for whatever word is observed in whatever meaning," and so forth—that too is incorrect. This is because we maintain that the capacity to denote that [meaning] is established through such positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, one should not claim that this constitutes inference merely by virtue of such positive and negative concomitance, for otherwise it would follow that even perception (*pratyakṣa*) is inference, since that mere [concomitance] is no different in the case of perception as well.

For where the existence of a jar is present, there it is perceived; but where it is not present, there it is not perceived—this is the meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "the word refers to an object seen," etc. (p. 531, l. 5).
For the Jaina, even in the case of direct perception, there is [the cognition] of the word.

Comparison—[the establishment of] positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—is present even in perception, as in: "wherever there is a jar, there is the cognition of a jar; where it is not, there is its absence" (Nyāyavārttika, p.

261). As for what was said—that [comparison] depends upon the recollection of a relationship—that too is untenable, because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since this [dependence on recollection] exists even in non-inferential cognitions such as doubt and analogy; and that analogy and the like are not inference has already been established.

Page 531, line 4: As for the claim that inference is [merely] verbal because it depends upon recollection (*smṛti*), that is not so, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntāt*). Dependence upon recollection exists even in non-inference (*ananumāne*), as in the case of doubt (*saṃśaya*), as in the case of reasoning (*tarka*), and as in the case of comparison (*upamāna*).
—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 260;
on the dependence upon the recollection of the relationship, p. 495.

Furthermore, as for the other statement—that sound is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) and so forth—that too is the play of no small darkness; for its validity will be refuted in detail in the passage beginning at page 532, line 10, where it says: "In that regard, letters, words, and sentences declare meanings not intended [by the speaker]," as stated in Laghīyastraya-kārikā 64.
Regarding the speaker’s intention:

Therefore, verbal testimony (śabda) is not inference, because its object is distinct from that [of inference] and because it is connected with a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), just like perception. For this reason as well, it is not inference: because when it is employed by persons according to their will, it serves as the cause for the cognition of an object. Whatever is inference is not thus [employed at will], such as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth; and verbal testimony is thus; therefore, it is not inference.

Nor should it be argued that this example lacks the negative concomitance (*avyatireka*) of the probans; for when [verbal testimony] is employed by them in that manner, it does not produce the cognition of the probandum.

For "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is not the cause for the cognition of that [permanence] simply because it is employed by one desiring to prove permanence; nor is "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) and so forth the cause for the cognition of that [fire] simply because it is employed by one desiring to prove water and so forth. Otherwise, no reason would ever be contradictory.
