Likewise, sound is not inference, because it generates non-deviant knowledge solely through being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). Furthermore, whatever is inference does not generate such [non-deviant] knowledge in that manner—like "producedness" and so forth—yet sound does generate it.

For in the case of a proof such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), the sole cause for generating a non-erroneous cognition regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); it is neither the fact that the word was spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) nor that it was spoken by an unreliable person. However, in the case of verbal testimony, it is precisely the fact that it was spoken by a reliable person [that serves as the cause]. Thus, due to this difference in the object and the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is established that verbal testimony is distinct from inference, just as it is from perception—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 155.
Comparison— Because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is conventional and because there is no fixed rule regarding specific universals,
the employment of words by seers, Aryans, and barbarians proceeds according to their own desire for the purpose of conveying meaning. (Nyāyabhāṣya 2.1.56)
Even that cognition which arises from a word through its application according to one's desire [is not the true meaning].

"Not from smoke and so forth"—this refers to *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdapariccheda, verse 19. Regarding the reason such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), compare: "The cognition of an object from a word occurs through the power of authoritative instruction."

Regarding objects that are not perceptible—such as heaven, the *apsarases*, the Northern Kurus, the seven continents, the ocean, and the structure of the world—there is no cognition from the mere word alone; rather, there is conviction because "this word was spoken by trustworthy persons (*āpta*)," for in the absence of such [trustworthiness] there is no conviction. However, this is not inference. — *Nyāyabhāṣya*, *Nyāyavārttika*, 2.1.68.
Likewise, its producer is also [to be understood] from scripture.

The Buddhist prima facie argument is as follows: "Verbal testimony is not produced by a reliable person (*āpta*), and because it is generated solely from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it does not touch upon the actual object; for this very reason, it lacks validity.

The response is: True, this verbal testimony is indeed not of the nature of inference (*anumāna*) because it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); for if it were a means of valid cognition, the effort to include it within inference would be fruitful.

And this [relation] does not belong to it, because a relation with a real entity is impossible. For if a relation between word and object were to exist, would it be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or by the nature of being produced from that (*tadutpatti*)? It cannot first be characterized by identity, because the two are perceived as occupying different locations; for the word is perceived in the mouth, while the object is on the ground. And if they were identical, it would follow that upon the utterance of the words "razor" or "sweetmeat," one’s mouth would be cut or filled.

Nor do words have the nature of arising from [external] objects, because words such as "a hundred herds of elephants are on the tip of a finger" are perceived as arising even in the absence of an object, and because they originate from the effort of the articulatory places and organs (*sthāna-karaṇa-prayatna*).

Therefore, since words do not touch upon external objects, they are incapable of producing a cognition regarding an external object; how then could they possess validity? For these [words] arise dependent solely upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and, by their own power, produce cognitions that exclude external objects—just as in the case of "a hundred herds of elephants are on the tip of a finger"—because there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) between words and real entities.
"Therefore, there is no establishment of the object from them, for they indicate the speaker’s intention.
Now, he states that these [words] do not possess validity regarding an external object, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth.

Because there is an absence of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), that is, a necessary connection, between words and things—that is, specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*)—there is no establishment of the object, nor is there any determination of an external entity, from those words; this is because they indicate the speaker’s intention.
— Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 3.212:
"Or what connection could there be with words even regarding external objects?"
By establishing those [causes], this [cognition] would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
for it does not arise from a single identity due to its being apprehended by different sense organs and so forth,
nor is it appropriate for another [cause] to be non-deviant, since deviation occurs.

For there is no connection between words and the objects denoted by them—neither characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) nor characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—by virtue of which these words, while expressing those objects, would possess validity.
In this regard, first of all, there is no connection characterized by identity, due to reasons such as their being apprehended by different sense organs;
therein, "apprehension by different sense organs" means apprehension by distinct sensory faculties.
For instance: sound is apprehended by the auditory faculty, whereas the object is apprehended by the visual faculty and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the distinctions in the causes of the appearance of time, place, and manifestation are included—*Tattvasaṅgraha* p. 440;
*Nyāyapraveśavṛtti-pañjikā* p. 76.
Comparison: "For we perceive the word in the mouth and the object on the ground"— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5.
And because of the non-perception of weighing, filling, burning, and splitting, there is an absence of relation—
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.34.
If there were a connection with the object, then upon the utterance of the words "razor" and "sweetmeat," the mouth would be cut and filled respectively.
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5
*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, verse 645;
*Anekāntajayapatākā*, folio 42A;
*Nyāyakumudacandra*, page 144, note 3.

Cognitions arise there having as their object only that which is superimposed, produced by the latencies of conceptual construction; they do not have external objects as their domain. Produced—that is, arisen—from that latent power (vāsanā-śakti) deposited by beginningless conceptual constructions of a similar kind, these cognitions have as their object those forms such as space and so forth that are superimposed according to tradition; they appear as those very [forms] and arise with respect to those things like space which are imagined as being external.
But those cognitions do not have external objects as their domain, nor do they have the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so forth as their objects—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.288.

"—that this [capacity] belongs to the faults of the person (*puruṣadoṣa*) and not to the words themselves; this too is incorrect. For even in the case of a faulty person such as a mute who has not uttered any sound, such a capacity for producing false cognitions is impossible. Furthermore, even in the absence of any corruption in the person's heart, sentences such as 'the finger [is broken]' when uttered by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) certainly produce those [cognitions].
Therefore, this is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of words alone, and not of the speaker's faults."

It is incorrect to argue that authoritative persons do not employ such statements, or that those who do employ them would not be authoritative; for even so, the claim that defects in the speaker are the cause of the arising of non-correspondent cognition remains unproven, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished.

For if these very same statements were employed in the absence of defects in the speaker and yet did not produce non-correspondent cognitions, then—through both positive and negative concomitance—it would be established that verbal cognition is produced by defects in the speaker.

Regarding those [other means of knowledge], when they are not employed by trustworthy persons (āpta), it is doubtful whether the non-arising of false cognition is due to the absence of words or rather to the absence of defects; thus, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is uncertain. In the case of verbal testimony, however, it is certain: even when defects are present, if the word is not uttered, false cognition does not arise. Furthermore, being a trustworthy person is not contradicted by the utterance of such a sentence; for even when there is the utterance of such a word, since there is no defect in the intention (āśaya), it is impossible for the speaker not to be trustworthy.

For instance—an authoritative person (āpta) may instruct someone else, saying: "You must not employ a sentence whose object has not been experienced by you, such as 'A herd of hundreds of elephants resides on the tip of a finger.
Therefore, this is the power of the word itself, not of the speaker's defects.

[Objection: If it is argued that here too, this is the power of the person's defects and not of the words; [Response: Not so, because even for a defective person such as a mute who has not uttered any words, there is an absence of such skill in producing such a cognitive distortion (viplava).

Moreover, even in the absence of any impurity in the speaker’s heart, sentences such as "the tip of a finger [is a mountain]" produce error simply by being uttered; thus, this is the inherent nature of words themselves, not the fault of the speaker—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 157; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
Thus,
[the term] "deceivers" (pratāraka) and so forth refers to false cognitions that are devoid of external objects.

[Objection: "If one were to argue that trustworthy persons do not employ such statements, or that those who do employ them would not be trustworthy—this too is unsatisfactory. For even so, the fact that defects in the speaker are the cause for the arising of non-correspondent knowledge remains unestablished, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished. — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 701.
[Examples of such statements include: "A hundred herds of elephants reside on the tip of a finger," and so forth. (*Śra.* = Śrutasāgarasūri)
And there is the non-existence [of the object] due to a defect in the eye.

Compare what Umbeka has said: "Even when a reliable person instructs someone, he should not employ a statement whose subject matter is an object not experienced by him, such as 'a hundred herds of elephants are on the tip of a finger'; in that case, the deviation from the actual object is evident."

Furthermore, even when a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) arises, a word still produces false knowledge; it does not remain indifferent like a sense organ. Therefore, it is established that words do not touch upon [external] objects and have their origin dependent solely on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
As it has been said:

Comparison: Moreover, the visual faculty and the like do not cease their activity when a subverting cognition arises; for in cases such as the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl, where a contrary experience is produced, we observe the disappearance of the error.

Words, however, even when subverted a hundred times, produce a false conceptualization exactly as they were uttered—such as "a hundred elephants stand upon the tip of a finger"—and thus generate a conceptual construction of that very same nature once again. Therefore, because their birth is dependent upon conceptual construction, this very quality of words—namely, their lack of contact with the actual object—is established.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 158)
Words have conceptual construction as their source, and conceptual constructions have words as their source;
in their mutual relationship—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
158—in their absolute relationship—*Nayacakravṛtti*, L. p. 167A.
Because of their mutual relationship, there is a causal relation between them—*Siddhibiṭīkā*, folio 365B, 484B; "Words do not touch even the objects [of those relations]"—*Nyāyāvatāraṭīkā*, folio 44;
*Ratnākarāvatārikā*, folio 9.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 175;
Prakṛtapāṭha— Syādvādaratnākara, page 701 (first half)— Anekāntajayapatākā, page 37.
*Anekāntavāda*, p. 47; *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 260B;
*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-yaśovijaya*, p. 402A.
"The mutual relationship between them [is such that] these words do not touch upon objects"—
in response to this, we shall first offer a rebuttal and then establish that words denote ultimately real objects and possess individual validity.
Here, the following rebuttal is provided:

As for what was stated—that because a relation is impossible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*) and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion. For in that case, the non-existence of such a relation is impossible, since a word reveals its object only when it is indeed related to it, because it is the cause of a specific cognition regarding that object, just like the eye.

Alternatively, the verbal cognition is produced by both the word and the object which are related to each other, because it is a specific cognition, just like the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*).

Now, the objection that "since the relationship between word and meaning—characterized as identity (*tādātmya*) or origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*)—has been rejected, how can there be a relationship? is also untenable; for even in the absence of those two, a relationship characterized as *yogyatā* (fitness) is possible between them. Nor should it be asked, "How could that [fitness] exist in the absence of those two?"; for we observe such a relationship between the eye and color-form even in the absence of identity, origination therefrom, or conjunction, since the Buddhists do not accept that the eye has identity with, is produced from, or is in conjunction with the form of a jar and so forth, as this would entail a contradiction with experience and the undesirable consequence of destroying the doctrine of non-contact (*aprāpyakāritva*).

Nor is it the case that in the absence of that [object], there is an impossibility of its possessing an essential nature related to the capacity for manifesting form; for otherwise, like the ear and other senses, it would follow that even this [eye] lacks the capacity to manifest that [form] (pṛ.
Regarding the object:
The meaning is "absence of connection"—
thus [says] Ācārya.
In the absence of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*)— (Ānandagiri’s commentary)—
compare: "Because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is conventional" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.55).
And that [conceptual cognition] is precisely the knowledge of the convention based upon the signified and the signifier.
–*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
585: "Or, such a denotative word is that in which a convention resides" – *Nyāyaviniścaya*, Kārikā 432.

Others, however, assert as follows: "There exists a connection between word and meaning characterized by the signified and the signifier; through the cognition of that [connection], [the meaning is understood] from this or that"—*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, verse 652.
For words and so forth are the causes for the comprehension of objects by virtue of the convention of innate fitness—
Parīkṣāmukha 3.100.
"Sound is the cause for the cognition of meaning through both its inherent capacity and convention"—
*Pramāṇanaya* 4.11.
The relationship between word and meaning,
characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*),
exists even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
Comparison [is established] because it is perceived even in the absence of the form of the eye in some cases—Syādvādamañjarī, p.
702; with the eye (cakṣuṣā)—Bhaṭṭa, Śrī.
If one accepts the conjunction of the eye and visible form,
[the fault arises] because of the non-existence of the eye— [as noted in the] commentary (āṭīkā).
In the absence of identity and origination from that—[Āryaṭīkā: of the eye—Āryaṭīkā:
with regard to form—Āryaṭīkā].

Now, one might object: "If a word denotes its meaning by virtue of its capacity (*yogyatā*), why should the meaning not likewise denote the word? This is also incorrect, because entities possess specific, restricted powers.
For the capacity between word and meaning is the power of the signifier and the signified, just as there is a power of the cognizer and the cognized between knowledge and the object known.

Nor should it be asserted that the restriction between cognition and the object of cognition arises from a causal relationship rather than from capacity (*yogyatā*); for that causal relationship will be refuted in detail in Laghīyastrayakārikā 54, where it states: "If the object were the cause of cognition through positive and negative concomitance... Furthermore, how could there be a restriction regarding the relationship of illuminator and illuminated between the eye and form, or between a jar and a lamp? This is because, in those cases, no other restrictive factor such as causality is possible apart from capacity.

Comparison (*tulanā*) is the innate, natural fitness (*yogyatā*) between word and meaning, which is the power of the signifier and the signified, just as there is the power of the knower and the known between knowledge and the object of knowledge—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 428; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
The specific restriction between the object to be known and the means of knowing consists in the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the cognition and its object;
[this is] the basis for that [restriction].

The comparison between the eye and form, and between a jar and a lamp [is made] otherwise; for otherwise, the restriction that "cognition alone is the illuminator and the object of cognition alone is the illuminated, and not cognition [as both]" would be untenable—
Syādvādamañjarī 702.
Regarding the restriction between the illuminated and the illuminator:

if it is argued that a word conveys its meaning only by virtue of its inherent capacity (*yogyatā*), then it would follow that it should convey it even to one who has just arisen from a house on the earth, since there is no difference [in the word's capacity] for such a person. This objection is also unsound; for we accept that the word conveys that meaning by virtue of its capacity as aided by convention (*saṅketa*). And since this [aided capacity] does not exist with respect to one who has just arisen from a house on the earth, there is no contingency of it conveying that meaning to him.

Convention (*saṅketa*) is indeed the application of the signified and the signifier in the form: "this is the signified of that," or "this is the signifier of that. A word conveys its own meaning only for one who possesses such [convention], and not for anyone else. Otherwise, even a means of proof such as smoke would cause this person to understand the fire and so forth which are to be proven, because there is no distinction; for inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is the factor that enables a means of proof to make known what is to be proven, and that exists for everyone at all times.

If it is accepted that a probans is the indicator of a probandum only for one who has grasped the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between them, then it must likewise be accepted that a word denotes its object only for one who has grasped the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) between the word and the object, since there is no difference [in the logic]. Let the word convey the object accordingly.

Because it is accepted that a word possesses the capacity to denote its meaning—a comparison [is made]: what, then, is this "convention" (*samaya*)? It is the application of a rule governing the relationship between the signifier and the signified, such that "this collection of meanings is the denotable object of this word. When that [convention] is employed, the cognition of the word's meaning arises.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 2.1.55
The convention (*samaya*) is said to be the application of the restriction between the signifier and the signified;
[as stated in] *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
241: "The statement that 'this [word] is the designator of this object' is the convention."—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, 1.1.1.
The desire— either "may this word convey this meaning" or "this meaning is to be understood from this word"— is [the cause of the convention]. (Tattvacintāmaṇi, Śabdapariccheda)
In the case of the injunction,
there is the expression of the inexpressible for the person [who acts].
For a person who has arisen from the increase of the elements, abodes, and existences, there is the accomplishment of the means for what is to be accomplished.

Now, one might object: "Convention is created by human will, and it is not logical for the determination of reality to depend on such will, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, why could the object not be the signifier and the word the signified? For that will is unrestrained. This too is unsound, because that convention is based upon innate fitness (*sahajayogyatā*), just as [the relationship] between smoke and fire is.

For just as the relationship between smoke and fire is indeed an innate inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), yet for the sake of understanding it, one relies on causes such as repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), so too the relationship between word and meaning is indeed natural, consisting of the power of the signifier and the signified; yet for the sake of understanding it, convention (*saṅketa*) is relied upon.

Furthermore, if there were a transgression of the innate power of the object, there would also be a transgression of the power of illumination and the illuminated even in the case of the eye, color-form, and so forth;
and consequently, the eye, the lamp, and the like would become the objects to be illuminated, while jars and the like would become the illuminators.
The contradiction with empirical experience has not been devoured by crows even elsewhere;
he clarifies this very point of over-extension:
"For that [word] is a convention made by a person, and a restriction on the nature of things cannot be established by human will, because the scope of such will is unimpeded."
Why is it that the object (artha) does not also become the signifier?
It is not so; for even a person who does not desire fire does not fail to cognize it from smoke, nor does one who desires water fail to understand it from that [smoke].

In this regard, just as there is an innate relationship between smoke and fire known as "invariable concomitance" (avinābhāva), yet for its cognition one relies on causes such as repeated observation, so too there is an innate relationship between word and meaning consisting of "potency" (śakti), yet for the acquisition of that [knowledge] one relies on the established usage of elders.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 241:
Because convention is based upon innate fitness, just as there is indeed an intrinsic inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between smoke and fire—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 703.
For the purpose of grasping invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*),
"reasoning" (*tarka*) is to be understood by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*); it is for the sake of its production— thus [it is said] in the Ācārya-bhāṣya.
In the sequence of the eye,
ear, and lamp, and also in the case of word and meaning, there is the indication of the signified and the signifier.

Now, is the inherent power of a word for the communication of a single meaning, or for the communication of multiple meanings? If it is for the communication of a single meaning, then even by means of hundreds of conventions, no cognition of another object would arise from it, just as smoke does not produce the cognition of non-fire.

If, on the other hand, it is for the communication of multiple meanings, then there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous cognition of many objects from it, and thus there would be no application toward a specific, restricted object. This too is an unexamined assertion, because it is possible for all words to possess the power of communicating all objects.

Otherwise, how could there be doubt when a word whose relationship [to its meaning] is unknown is employed—namely, the doubt: "For which object was this word employed by him? Nor should it be argued that, because all objects would then be apprehended simultaneously, there would be no activity toward a specific object; for it is established that those words convey specific objects by virtue of their specific conventions (*saṅketa*).

For even in the case of a single word, a convention restricted by differences of place and so forth is observed; for example, the word *karkaṭikā* is seen to denote a particular kind of fruit among the Mālavakas and others, but a female organ among the Gurjaras and others.

Furthermore, it is observed everywhere that although the eye is capable of manifesting form, it produces cognition of a form not present due to the influence of near cataracts, yet of a form present due to the influence of distant cataracts; and through the power of specific collyrium and the like, it produces cognition even of a form hidden in darkness, while through the power of glass, jaundice, and so forth, it does so even when the intended form is absent.

Just as the eye, though capable of manifesting various forms, produces cognition of specific distant forms and so forth due to the influence of specific auxiliary conditions such as distance or cataracts, so too it is not contradictory that a word, though capable of conveying multiple meanings, conveys a specific meaning due to the influence of a specific convention (*saṅketa*). Comparison: "If words were restricted to a single meaning, there would be no comprehension of other meanings; if they were connected to multiple meanings, there would be the possibility of contradictory manifestations."
— Pramāṇavārttika 3.228;
likewise, Bhaṭṭa.

Comparison (*tulanā*)— a restriction is established regarding either the object, which has the capacity to be delimited in all its aspects, or the expressive word, which is capable of bringing about the cognition of the object in all its aspects— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, p. 202.
Since all words possess the capacity to convey all meanings, linguistic usage occurs in a particular place with a particular meaning;

for this very reason, when a word is heard whose relationship [to a meaning] has not been previously apprehended, doubt arises as to which meaning this word might have been employed to convey—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 242.

In this context, there is a dependence on convention (*samaya*) because [the capacity for denotation] exists as the agency of that [convention] only when its destruction or subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) has occurred; however, for a yogi, such dependence does not exist,
because words possess diverse powers due to their being the denotators of all things.
"And likewise, there is no restriction of the denotable [meaning] elsewhere even at that time" (Śāstravārtāsamuccaya, verse 663–64).

Thus, all words generally possess the capacity to denote all meanings, and all meanings are endowed with the capacity to be denoted by all words; they function in various ways through the conjunction of auxiliary factors such as diverse *kṣayopaśama* (subsidence-cum-destruction of karma), and so there is no contradiction whatsoever—(Anekāntajayapatākā, p. 36A).
Because it is established that every word possesses a diversity of capacities for conveying all objects,
and because every entity possesses a manifold capacity of being denotable by all words—
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 143.

Although a word possesses an innate capacity to convey multiple meanings, its function as a conveyor of a specific meaning is established through the power of a fixed convention; thus, how could there be [confusion regarding] the object? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 703). How [could there be confusion regarding] the object? (Śrāvakabhūmi).

The comparison of words with words is as follows: the word *yava* is used by the Āryas for the object that has long awns, for they understand the object with long awns from the word *yava*; however, the Mlecchas understand the *priyaṅgu* plant [from it].
Thus, the sages employ the word *trivṛt* to refer to a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses, whereas the Āryas use it for a specific creeper—Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 420.

For even a single word is observed to have a fixed convention depending on differences of region and so forth; as, for example, the word *cora* means "thief" in Gurjara and other regions, but "boiled rice" in Draviḍa and other regions.

And it is observed everywhere that even for the eye, which is capable of illuminating form, there is the production of cognition regarding a form that is not proximate due to the influence of nearby cataracts (*timira*), and regarding a form that is proximate due to the power of distant cataracts; furthermore, through the influence of special ointments and the like, there is the production of cognition even regarding a form hidden by darkness, and through the force of defects such as *kāca* (cataract) or *kāmalā* (jaundice), even in the absence of the intended form. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 703).
In the same way, words such as *karkaṭī* should be understood as denoting a womb (*yoni*) and so forth, depending on the respective context.
—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 178;
*Mālavādi* (in the Mālava region etc.), *Bālakrīḍā*; *śanayogya* (suitable for the planet Saturn), *Śrāvakabhūmi*.

If it is argued that even in the absence of a yellow form, the conch-shell possesses the capacity to produce the cognition of yellow—just as the eye and other sense organs do—given that a relationship characterized by "fitness" (*yogyatā*) exists between the word and its object, then, like those [senses], the cognition of the object would occur without depending on convention (*saṅketa*). But this too is inconsistent; for since it is a communicator (*jñāpaka*), it is only when dependent upon convention that it can logically serve as a factor in the cognition of the object.

Whatever is a communicator produces a cognition of the thing to be communicated only when its connection (*pratibandha*) has been established, just as smoke and the like do; and the word is indeed a communicator.
However, because the eyes and other sense organs are *kārakas* (producers), it is logical that they produce [cognition] without depending on the apprehension of a relation to their own objects.
For that which is itself being perceived and serves as the cause for the perception of an unperceived object is called a "cognizer" (*jñāpaka*).
This nature belongs only to words and the like, not to the eyes and so forth; therefore, only the word conveys its own meaning once the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been established.
Power, however, is inherent; just as the eye and other senses possess the power to manifest color-form, so too does the word possess the power to manifest its object,
just like the eye,
from the word itself.

Regarding the comparison of words: the connection between word and meaning is indeed characterized by the relationship of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*). For instance, it is argued that meanings have the nature of the signified and words have the nature of the signifier; thus, according to the doctrine of their manifestation, why is it that they are not understood from that [connection] even without a convention (*saṅketa*)? It is said in reply: because of the absence of such a specific subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) [of karmic veils].

For even a lamp, though its nature is to illuminate form, does not illuminate it when the eye is absent; and the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣayopaśama) is like the eye, being produced by convention, ascetic practice, meditation, and so forth, as is observed [in experience].
This is because a word is a communicator [of meaning]—*Anekāntajaya* folio 36A.

The nature of an indicator, such as smoke and the like, is that its status as an indicator of what it makes known depends upon the apprehension of a relationship [with that object]. However, factors such as its fitness do not depend upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), because they are included within the causal complex of perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*). But capacity (*śakti*) is innate; just as a lamp and the like possess an inherent power to illuminate form, so too does a word possess an inherent power to convey its meaning.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 241:
"The cognition of the object accompanied by the apprehension of the convention... (*Śra.*).
Therefore, that very [nature] is of the form of a signifier,
such as sound and so forth.

As for what was stated—"Therefore, words do not touch upon objects," and so forth—that too is an unexamined assertion; for is it being proved that a word uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) does not touch upon its object, or one uttered by an unreliable person, or words in general? Regarding the first position, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), because from a sentence uttered by a reliable person such as "There are fruits on the riverbank," a cognition arises that is not set aside regarding the external object, and one who acts upon it attains that object.

Now, if it is [the case] that [this lack of contact with the object belongs] to that which is composed by an untrustworthy person; then it is logical that this very [lack of contact with the object] belongs to that [untrustworthy composition] alone and not to anything else. Otherwise, since a lack of contact with the object is observed in the case of perception produced by an eye impaired by defects such as cataracts, that same [lack of contact] would also belong to perception produced by a flawless eye (pṛ.
536, l. 12). For comparison: "Why should there be a lack of contact with the object for a word uttered by a trustworthy person? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 703).
Objection: This might be so if words never produced a cognition that corresponds to reality;
for in that case, one would understand that its very nature is to be in contact with the object.

However, from a sentence spoken by a person possessing excellence—such as "There are fruits on the riverbank"—there arises a cognition corresponding to reality that does not disregard the external object, because one who acts upon it attains that object.
—From the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
158: "Because of the cognition of the object for one who has already acted [on the basis of] the word spoken by a reliable person (āpta)."
The meaning is that even for that which appears as white during the bright fortnight,
there would be a lack of contact with the actual object despite its appearance as white, and consequently, it would be false.

By this, the third alternative is also rejected; for there is no such thing as "mere speech" distinct from words uttered by either a reliable or an unreliable person. Now, one might argue: "Since we observe the arising of erroneous cognition from statements such as 'pointing with a finger' uttered by a reliable person, this is a power of the word itself and not of the speaker's defects. This too is an unexamined assertion; for even reliable persons do not employ such statements—[if they were so employed] by those [reliable persons], [the cognition would be erroneous].
(Variant readings: *prayuktād* / *śra*)
The capacity of a statement such as "a herd of hundreds of elephants stands on the tip of a finger" to produce a cognition that disregards external objects is [the definition];
for comparison: those possessed of virtue lack the frivolity of uttering such statements.

—"By the authoritative [persons], such a statement is not employed"—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 158; "Even an authoritative person teaches something to someone"—this and so forth was stated in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 704. Regarding that, since this [statement] has negation as its primary purport, it is indeed true to the facts (*yathārthatā*); for even a portion of a sentence, when intended as an illustration, is taken as referring to the word itself by being delimited by the particle *iti*, and thus, through its syntactic unity with the negation, it is indeed true to the facts.
If, however, words were intent upon their objects, they could not form a single syntactical unit with a negation;

therefore, because words composed by a reliable person lack non-correspondence with reality, words do not inherently fail to touch upon their objects, but rather [do so] due to the influence of human defects. (p.

Comparison: As for the case where even a reliable person (āpta) might occasionally instruct, "Do not say a statement with an unreal object, such as 'there are a hundred elephant-herds on the tip of a finger-ring,'"—in that instance, because the phrase delimited by the particle *iti* is employed as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) as being subordinate to the word itself, it possesses truthfulness (*yathārthatva*) by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with the prohibition.
However, if it were intended to refer to the actual object, there would be no single syntactical unit with the prohibition at all.

Therefore, since there is an absence of non-correspondence to reality (*ayathārthatva*) in the words of a reliable person, words do not inherently fail to touch upon their objects; rather, this distortion is caused solely by the attachment of human defects.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p.
158; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 704: [This refers to] the authoritative instruction that prohibits the employment of sentences such as "the finger" (*aṅguli*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "A herd of a hundred elephants stands on the tip of a finger," even if such a sentence is not uttered by authoritative persons (*āpta*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful: is the non-arising of false cognition due to the absence of the word, or due to the absence of defects in the speaker? This [objection] is also not convincing upon examination; for even when a word is not uttered, a person who possesses defects is perceived as a deceiver through hand gestures and the like. Nor should it be asserted that hand gestures and so forth lead to the inference of a word, from which a false cognition arises; for there is no such perception.

Furthermore, when a certain cognition has arisen from a sentence such as "The river [is flowing]," a person who follows the riverbank without obtaining the expected fruit reproaches only the person, saying, "I have been deceived by this wicked man," and not the word.

Now, one might argue that the function of a person—whether endowed with qualities or defects—consists merely in the utterance of the word, whereas the comprehension of the meaning is dependent solely upon the word; therefore, in the case of a misconception, the fault lies with the word itself, not with the speaker's defects. This too is incorrect, because when a sentence uttered by a qualified speaker, such as "There are fruits on the bank of the river," gives rise to a true cognition, the function would likewise belong to the word alone, since the speaker’s role is fulfilled merely by its utterance.
Consequently, how could it be an absolute rule that the very nature of a word is its non-contact with the object?
Comparison: Even a person who has not uttered a word produces a misconception through means such as hand gestures and the like—Nyāyamañjarī, p.
Syādvādaratnākara, p.

704. For comparison: When a cognition has arisen from a sentence such as "There is a river" regarding something not previously perceived, and a person who has acted upon it—having followed the bank of the river but not obtained the fruit—is met with a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), he reviles only the person, thinking, "Alas! I have been deceived by that wicked soul," and not the word itself. And when he has obtained the fruit, he praises only the persons, saying, "Excellent, excellent! It was well-taught by him. Thus, because [the validity of the cognition] conforms to the presence or absence of the faults of the person, the non-arising of error among trustworthy persons (*āpta*) when they remain silent is caused precisely by the absence of those faults; therefore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not doubtful.

The distortion [of meaning] arising from words is caused solely by defects in the person [who uses them], and is not based on the inherent nature [of the words themselves]. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 158; Syādvādaratnākara, p.
Regarding the counter-argument concerning the failure to comprehend the meaning:

"Alas, in that case, even when there is a correct cognition such as 'there are fruits on the riverbank' while the speaker is possessed of excellence, since the operation belongs to the word alone and the person's role is exhausted by mere utterance, it is not the case that the non-contact with the object is the absolute nature of the word" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

Furthermore, regarding the nature of form (rūpa): since the causal operation of as many factors as are perceived to exist simultaneously with the arising of a cognition of error is established, and since such [a cognition] is not observed here in the utterance of a word in the absence of the speaker’s unreliability, there is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) wherein both the word and the speaker’s intention (*āśaya*) operate therein.
The production of erroneous cognition;
[this refers to] the operation [of the cause] in the production of erroneous cognition by one who does not intend [to deceive].
Comparison—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.

407: Furthermore, the essential nature of a word is merely the illumination of an object, like the eye and other sense organs; it is not, however, the illumination of an object as it truly is (*yathārtha*) or the illumination of an object as it is not (*ayathārtha*), for those depend upon the presence of qualities (*guṇa*) or defects (*doṣa*).

For when a quality such as clarity exists, the eye illuminates an object correctly; but when a defect such as a cataract (*kāca*) exists, it illuminates it incorrectly. In the same way, a word also illuminates an object in its true or false form depending upon the qualities or defects of the speaker.

For this very reason, even when a statement concerning a hundred elephants based on the tip of a finger is sublated, yet repeated again and again, there arises a delusion regarding its luminosity; for that essential nature [of luminosity] does not depart even upon the onset of a hundred sublaters. Furthermore, the eye and so forth—compare:

"And it is logical that, like a lamp, the essential nature of a word is merely luminosity, and not either truthfulness or untruthfulness, because even when the object is contrary, the lamp's luminosity does not cease."

However, this is the distinction: while a lamp possesses the quality of illumination independently of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), a word possesses it in dependence upon such convention. Since a word, being of the nature of illumination, has its truthfulness or otherwise dependent on the virtues or defects of the speaker, an illusion may arise even when a statement—such as "a hundred elephants are situated on the tip of a finger"—is sublated, provided it is repeated again and again; this is because the nature of illumination does not depart from the word. Yet, this is not a defect of the word itself.
"But for one who prattles on without considering the connection between word-meanings, this is merely the speaker's error; the word itself is not at fault here"—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 159.
The nature of sound is the non-manifestation of reality as it is (yathārtha). *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 704; *Śabdapramāṇa*, p.
312. *Yathārthāprakāśa*—Ā. (Ācārya) [Note: This refers to the commentary or authorial gloss].
Regarding the quality of revealing what is real or unreal, as in the statement "a hundred elephants sit on the tip of a finger," [this applies] to the nature of the words themselves.

As for the further claim—that the sense organ does not remain indifferent—that too is mere words; for even when a subverting cognition arises, the sense organ is still perceived to be the producer of the false cognition whose object is the two moons.

Nor can it be asserted that upon the occurrence of that [subverting cognition], the sense organ no longer produces the cognition having that [dual moon] as its object, because that would contradict experience.
(Page 537, Line 14)
When a subverting cognition arises,
the sense organ [is engaged] with the object, the moon— Ārya-ṭīkā.

As for what was said—that words have their origin in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth—that is disregarded because it has already been answered in the proof of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*).

Therefore, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is the cause for the apprehension of objects, just like perception and the other means; and because it is capable of establishing one’s own position and refuting the positions of others, just like correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); and likewise, because it is the cause for the cessation of all misconceptions regarding reality, just like the knowledge of a yogi.

Indeed, the cessation of misconceptions regarding all objects—however remote they may be in terms of space, time, or nature—is not possible through anything other than verbal testimony, since no other means for that purpose exists.
If it is argued that there exists some other inferential mark (*liṅga*) as a means to that [knowledge], we say no; for no such mark invariably concomitant with that [object] is ever apprehended.
Therefore, one must admit that the word itself possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) in that regard, by virtue of its relationship characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*). Thus ends the section.
Page 537, line 16;
page 47:
[The example] of Mount Meru, the king of mountains, Rāmarāvaṇa, and so forth, as well as atoms and the like.
The means for the realization of remote objects— namely,
objects remote in terms of place, time, and nature (as stated in the *Ārya-ṭīkā*).
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsaka is that because a permanent relationship between word and meaning is possible, there is no convention created by a person. [Objection:

Granted that there is a relationship between a word and its object, but would that be non-eternal or eternal? Of these, the first position is untenable; for it is impossible to create a non-eternal relationship, since a convention, when being made, must be established either for every individual person, for every individual word, or for every individual object at the beginning of creation—since no other alternative is possible.
And it has been said:
"By this much, the fortunate sequence has been stated here"—[Ānandagiri’s commentary: the *samaya* [occurs] either for every mortal or indeed with every recitation.

[The opponent objects: "Is this convention—that 'this is its name'—established by someone at the beginning of the world, once and for all; or is it established for each object or for each person; or for each person alone, for each utterance or for each performance; or else, at the beginning of the world, at the time of the creation of the universe, is it established once and effortlessly by some creator such as Īśvara? These are the three alternatives. *Vyākhyā:* This is the convention (*saṃketa*), namely that "this is its name. Would it be made for each object, or for each person; or indeed for each person, for each utterance, or for each performance; or alternatively, at the beginning of the world, at the time of the world's creation, would it be made once and for all, with ease, by some creator such as Īśvara? Thus there are three options.
—Cited from *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 622; *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* 1.230.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 622;
*Jainatarkavārttika*, p. 31;
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verse 13.

Regarding the first position: when a relation is being established by a person with each individual object, is it one or many? If it is one, how can it be produced (*kṛtaka*)? For its existence is established even previously, and thus its non-produced nature (*akṛtakatva*) is proven;
indeed, the birth of an existing entity from a person is not logical, since its manifestation alone is thereby accounted for.

If, on the other hand, it is many, how could there be a connection to a single meaning? Just as the referent of the word "cow" is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, while the referent of the word "horse" is that which possesses a mane and so forth.
Alternatively, the relation might be distinct for each [individual] or it might be one;
if it were one, it could not be produced, and if it were distinct, there would be a cognition of difference.
Regarding the case of oneness, first of all, it could not be something produced, for it is impossible for a single thing to be created by many; thus he says, "If it were one."

–In the view of unity, because it would follow [the universal] like a genus (*jāti*) across differences of place and time, it would not be produced; that is to say, it would be eternal. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 622) — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Nyāyaratnākara, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verse 14.

It has been established [in the Śrāmaṇya] that for the ether, a single atom, and so forth, oneness is invariably concomitant with permanence; for oneness is indeed the state of having a single nature, and that perishes when being produced— [Āloka-ṭīkā on the relation].
Furthermore, regarding the human activity [involved] in the Keśarā [convention]:

in establishing a connection for each individual, is there one creator of that convention, or many? If there were one, how could he establish a convention for those situated in other regions? If it is argued that he does so by going to each respective place, then its establishment would be impossible even within a human lifespan, because those [regions] are infinite.

Now, suppose one person makes an agreement while many others are present, and those who have made the agreement will communicate it to others, and they in turn to others; in this way, practical usage (*vyavahāra*) would be established everywhere. This is not so, because since they lack any motive, it is impossible for them to travel everywhere; therefore, wherever they do not go, practical usage cannot be established there.
Furthermore, if many people are the makers of the agreement, then the uniformity of the agreement across all places and times would not be achieved, due to the absence of a cause for such uniformity.

Nor should it be asserted that all of them, having come together or deliberated, establish a single convention at one and the same time; for it is impossible for those who act independently and without mutual regard to establish such a convention in that manner.

For instance, how could many people acting as correlators in all difficult places agree upon the fact that in this region the word "cow" applies only to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth? One person alone would not be able [to do so].
Therefore, there is no creator of the relationship— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5.
The impossibility of establishing a convention regarding other locations.
And they establish a convention for other men.

If the nature of the connection were uniform, then even when the relationship has been established by many, a single [person] would not be the one who causes it to be understood— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 644.
Nor is their conjunction perceived in common usage among persons— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verse 17.

Since there would be no purpose in establishing a convention by combining [the words], would the convention be made after pronouncing each individual word, or without pronouncing them? It cannot be without pronouncing them, because that would entail the consequence of it being without a basis;
and a relation without a basis is not logical, as it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can it be established by utterance, because even in the course of a human lifetime it is impossible to establish such a connection—
[this refers to] the refutation of the view that the convention [of meaning] is established by utterance. (Śrāvakabhūmi)

Furthermore, when pronouncing each word again and again, is a new relationship being established, or is it the very same one as before? If a new relationship is being established, how can its capacity to convey meaning be understood? And if that capacity is not understood, the act of establishing a relationship is untenable.
On the other hand, if it is the previous relationship, since it already existed previously, its establishment is likewise untenable.

For it is the cognition (*jñapti*) of a single object that recurs repeatedly, not its production (*utpatti*). Consider this comparison: when there is a re-utterance (*pratyūccāraṇa*), is it the very same [act] as before, or is it new? If it were being made anew, how could its capacity to convey meaning be understood? And if that capacity were already understood, what would be the purpose of making it again? Since that which was previously made is not [then] unmade, its repetition is illogical. Thus, it is the cognition of a single object that recurs repeatedly, not its production.
"The production [of a word] at every utterance is not tenable from the perspective of linguistic usage" (Tattvasaṃgraha, verse 2274; Nyāyamañjarī, p.
In the absence of a thorough knowledge of the power to convey meaning for a new convention— that is, a novel convention— of that convention.
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish a connection with each individual object repeatedly, because objects are infinite and remote.

Even at the beginning of creation, it is illogical to posit a simultaneous establishment of the relationship [between word and meaning], because at that time all denotable words and meanings do not coexist,
and because a period of time devoid of linguistic usage of words and meanings is impossible;
therefore, the relationship between word and meaning must be accepted as being eternal.
Because it exists at a remote time;
For at the beginning of creation there is no activity, since such a time is not admitted.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verse 42;
Śāstradīpikā, page 418;
Tattvasaṅgraha, page 627.
Nyāyamañjarī, p.

242: "Because of the absence of non-occurrence at once" (sakṛtsaṃbhavābhāvābhāvāt), Ā; "because of occurrence at once" (sakṛtsaṃbhavāt), Ba—[and] of the conceptual construction (vikalpasya ca kā–), Ā.
But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate— Jaimini-sūtra 1.1.5.
By "autpattika" (inborn), we mean "eternal";
for "origination" (utpatti) is used figuratively to denote "existence" (bhāva),
and the relationship between word and meaning is an existence that is inseparable.
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5
The relationship between a word and its meaning is not of human origin— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5.
"Verbal testimony attains the status of a means of valid cognition when its relationship [to its object] is non-human (apauruṣeya)" —
*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 161.
The relationship between word and meaning is eternal— Vākyapadīya 1.23.

And that comprehension is accomplished by means of the three instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To explain: when one person communicates to another who has already grasped the convention, saying, "Devadatta, drive the white cow here with a stick," then another bystander who has not yet mastered the convention perceives the word and its object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, by observing the listener’s activity—such as the act of throwing—pertaining to that object, he understands the cognition regarding the cow and so forth through inference (*anumāna*). And because that cognition would otherwise not arise, he postulates a denotative power (*vācikā śakti*) residing in the word itself.
As it has been said:

The three means of valid cognition consisting of perception, inference, and presumptive testimony are apprehended by the auditory perception of the word and by the visual perception of the object; this is established through the position that they have those as their respective objects. (Śrāvakabhūmi)

In the case of Devadatta, the hearer whose object is a cow and so forth, upon hearing the sentence "Devadatta, bring the cow," there arises a cognition directed toward the throwing of the cow; for immediately after hearing that sentence, the physical act of throwing the cow occurs, as it could not otherwise be accounted for. Thus, comprehension is produced.

In the sentence "Devadatta, drive the cow," there exists a capacity [in the word] to express the act of throwing with respect to the cow and so forth; because that cognition would otherwise be inexplicable,
one perceives here through direct perception the word, the elder (the speaker), and the object denoted, all pertaining to the act of throwing directed toward the cow.
And [the objects are] the word, the elder, and the denotable object—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā* 1.228;
*Nyāyamañjarī* p. 245.
"By perception itself [the speaker knows the hearer's understanding], and by inference through [observed] activity,
he knows— by way of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability)— the capacity residing in both [the word and its meaning]. — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra 140–41.

And by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for [the cognition], they understand the capacity of the intellect which rests upon both [the word and the object]—thus the relation has three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*). —*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, p. 680.
"He knows the twofold power"—Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.228; Nyāyamañjarī, p. 245.

Commentary: This principle regarding the comprehension of the relationship between a word, its usage by elders, and the denoted object was described by Kumārila as follows: First of all, one perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) both the word and the elder who employs it, as well as the denoted object which is the thing to be expressed. Thereafter, one perceives—that is, determines—through inference (*anumāna*) based on the mark (*liṅga*) characterized by purposeful activity (*ceṣṭā*), that the listener has understood [the meaning].
Purposeful activity is called "inference" by treating it as the instrument (*karaṇa-kāraka*).
Following that, one knows through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) the capacity (*śakti*) residing in both, namely, that which resides in the word and the object.

However, because they understand [the meaning] directly through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it is said that "they understand through presumptive testimony" (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 709). For instance, children who are listening to elders engaged in discourse for their own purposes are seen to comprehend the object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5

Furthermore, this is the final resort for beginners: it is not necessarily through a sentence that explicitly states the relationship that children acquire the understanding of that relationship from elders; rather, when elders—who already possess a well-established knowledge of the relationship—engage in linguistic activity for the sake of their own purposes, the children who listen to them acquire the understanding of the relationship.

For when someone says "Bring the cow" and another brings an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, a nearby child understands: "Because this person has been made to understand this meaning from this sentence. Thus, the capacity to convey meaning is first apprehended in a general form. Subsequently, through repeated usage and by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the individual components of the sentence—namely the words—and the components of the words—namely the bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*)—are distinguished from their respective parts of the sentence-meaning, namely the word-meanings. Therefore, the relationship [between word and meaning] is not of human origin. (Śāstradīpikā, p.
463; cf. Buddhiprakaśa, p. 677).

Now, following the refutation of that [position], the following response is provided here regarding the argument that words convey meaning solely by virtue of human-made, impermanent conventions: [The text continues: *nu ā*, *ba*. Regarding the demonstration that words possess the capacity to convey meaning only through the power of human-made, impermanent conventions, this is the rebuttal.

As for what was stated—that [the relation] is either impermanent or permanent, and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion; for when that relation is investigated as being of a permanent nature, its permanence is untenable because it cannot be logically established.

Whatever, when investigated as having a certain nature, is not logically tenable, should not be accepted as having that nature, just as the world is not accepted as being of a non-dual nature. And the relation between word and meaning, when investigated as being of a permanent nature, is not logically tenable.

Nor is its untenability when examined as having that nature unestablished; for instance, would the permanence of its connection be due to its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or due to the permanence of the connection? If it were due to its own intrinsic nature, then it should illuminate the object for everyone at all times, because it is illuminative by its very essence.
For it is not observed that a lamp, while being illuminative of form by its own nature, illuminates it for some and not for others.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "This [word] is manifested by convention (*saṅketa*), and it is that which illuminates [the object]; therefore, this fault does not apply. [The reply is: How can this [word] have a permanent, uniform nature (*nityaikarūpatā*)? For the consequence follows that there would be a distinction [in its nature] due to having both manifested and unmanifested forms. Indeed, if an entity that is permanent and uniform were manifested, then it would be manifested at all times, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-different [from itself].
(Page 542, Line 16: Regarding the relationship between word and meaning.)
Comparison—like the word and its meaning—is not [a separate means of knowledge], because that third [means] is not apprehended by perception or any other means of valid cognition (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
243). The relation between word and meaning is not eternal, because it is untenable when examined as having an eternal nature.
By virtue of its nature as being eternal, [it arises] from its own-being;
by virtue of its own-being as co-arising, [it arises] from the sacred word.

Because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, there is a comparison: either this [word], being eternal, would manifest the object by its own nature, or [it would do so] through the manifestation of convention (*saṅketa*). (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 701). Compare: "If the relationship were not of human origin, there would be comprehension even for one who does not know [the convention]. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 701).

Even if the non-human origin of the relationship [between word and meaning] were accepted, there would be no cognition of meanings for a person who lacks awareness—that is, for one in whom the cognition of convention (*saṅketa*) is absent.

If the relationship between word and meaning were not conventional (*sāṅketika*), consisting of the signified and the signifier, but rather inherent (*svābhāvika*), then even one who has not grasped the convention would understand the meaning upon hearing the word. — *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 3.197–198.
And since the capacity to illuminate the meaning is always established,
the understanding of that meaning— which is caused by it— would also occur for everyone at all times.
–Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 710:

For if that state were established by its own nature, then the comprehension of meaning from a word would occur—just as from a lamp or from anything whatsoever, whether it be something previously employed such as error and so forth, or something entirely new—just as from a lamp.
–Nyāyamañjarī, p. 243.
One should illuminate the relationship between word and meaning;
[the scripture] reveals its true nature and that which illuminates it.
The form is the connection that illuminates the word and its meaning.

Comparison: "If that [relation] is manifested through convention (*saṅketa*), then the conceptualization of another non-existent object is certainly not [justified]. Even if a relation exists, it is not the cause for the cognition of an object unless it is manifested;
indeed, it is convention that manifests it. In that case, why is something that merely presents what is already established maintained as a cause? — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.327.

229. If it is argued that just as a lamp, though capable of illuminating an object, requires the sense organ [for its perception], so too does a word require a sense organ, and likewise a word also requires a convention (*saṅketa*), we say: no. For while it is appropriate for there to be mutual dependence between the lamp and the sense organ—since neither can illuminate an object in the absence of the other—it is not so for the word’s capacity and the convention; because the cognition of the object arises from the convention alone. Therefore, a word is not inherently capable of conveying meaning. Thus, verbal testimony lacks validity by virtue of its very origin (*utpatti-lakṣaṇam aprāmāṇyam*). — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.189.1–3.
Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s Commentary,
Chapter 3, Verse 227.

If it is postulated that the capacity [of a word] depends upon convention (*saṅketa*) with respect to that [object], then surely it would depend upon something that is assisted; yet that [capacity] is unchanging and cannot be assisted.
(Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 710)

Now, if it is manifested through convention (*saṅketa*), how can its nature as eternally uniform be established? For, by virtue of having both manifest and unmanifest forms, the consequence of difference would follow—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
709; *Prakāśaka*: Ka–Ba.
Furthermore, regarding the relationship between word and meaning— which is eternal and uniform—

the convention (saṅketa) depends upon human beings; and since such a person lacks knowledge of supersensuous objects, they might establish a convention in the Veda otherwise [than it actually is], whereby its lack of authority would result from the characteristic of falsity.

Comparison—For convention (*saṅketa*) is the cause for making the meaning of words known, and it depends upon persons. Therefore, even if [the Veda] were not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the possibility of falsity remains; for what is the use of its being non-human? Since the comprehension of meaning arises from convention, that convention is of human origin and could be erroneous. For instance, there is the statement regarding heaven as the result of practicing moral conduct (*śīla*); otherwise, one might subvert it through a different convention, since it is possible for it to reveal something that does not correspond to reality.
— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.228:
Because there is no cognition of meaning from a sentence, even one that is non-human (apauruṣeya), in the absence of convention (*saṅketa*).
In this context, a convention (*saṅketa*) must be accepted as the cause for making meaning known; and since that convention is created by persons, it is dependent upon persons.
Therefore, because convention is dependent upon persons, even if words were not of human origin, the possibility of falsity remains, for speech expresses its meaning by virtue of convention.

And since that [scripture] is produced by a person who is the locus of defects, there is no removal of the suspicion of its being erroneous, just as in the case of human speech; thus, the postulation of its being authorless is useless— *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 3.226.

And because convention, which serves to illuminate meaning, depends upon human beings, there is the possibility of falsity even in a capacity produced by something other [than that convention]. — *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 710.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 430:
[The view] of the Puruṣa-veda.

Furthermore, by virtue of its eternal connection, would a word be restricted to a single meaning or restricted to multiple meanings? If it were restricted to a single meaning, would it do so partially or in its entirety? If it were restricted to a single meaning in its entirety, there could be no comprehension of another meaning from the Veda; consequently, the Veda would possess the lack of authority characterized by ignorance. Or, how could the word *caura*, which is conventionally established for a "thief" due to an eternal connection, denote boiled rice when used by southerners (*dākṣiṇātyaiḥ*)?

Now, if that [Veda] is restricted to a single part, is that part restricted to a desired object or restricted to an undesired object? If it were restricted to an undesired object, the Veda would possess the characteristic of falsity and thus lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). If, however, it is restricted to a desired object, does this arise from a person or from its own nature? In the first case, the effort to establish its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) is futile.

For a person is indeed set aside [as unreliable] due to being blinded by passion and other defects; therefore, if even a single portion of the Veda were to establish a restriction to a specific meaning, what would be the point of its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*)? If there were a restriction to a single intended meaning by its very nature, then the distinction between meanings such as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and so forth would be untenable.

On the other hand, if the Veda were restricted to multiple meanings, then because it would be common to all possible meanings, how could an author of a convention (*samayakāra*) establish a convention for only a specific intended manifestation?

[Comparison: Furthermore, does the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācaka-sambandha*) of speech exist with one meaning or with many? If speech were restricted to a single meaning, there would be no comprehension of another meaning.

When there is a connection with multiple meanings, and words are restricted to being denotative of a single meaning, it would follow that—due to the force of convention—they could not convey another meaning; yet, we observe that they do express multiple meanings according to the speaker's intention. Furthermore, when there is a connection with multiple meanings as denotative, there would be the possibility of the manifestation and cognition of even a contradictory meaning.
If it were even determined that the Agniṣṭoma is not a means to heaven,
then there would be no engagement at all on the part of one who desires heaven—
[as stated in] Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s commentary, verse 3.
That power must be either restricted to a single object or restricted to multiple objects—
Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 710.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 430:

If it is further asked, "What is the fault if the word possesses an inherent capacity (*yogyatva*) toward the object itself, such that a convention (*saṅketa*) must be required for it?"—it is replied: Is that [capacity] universal in its scope or restricted in its scope? In the first alternative, because of the consequence that all objects would be cognized simultaneously, there would be no activity or other engagement with a restricted object; thus, linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed.
Therefore, he says: "Universal capacity is not tenable, if restriction [of the word's application] were due to convention."

He states the fault in the second alternative: "If there were a restriction of the relation, then even if the convention were elsewhere, [the word] would not apply [to its own object]" (Nyāyabindu-kārikā 4.31).
And from that follows the consequence of ignorance... [Āloka].
Just as in common worldly usage the word "thief" (cora) may signify something edible,
so too in the Tantra certain words have that very same meaning.
As it is said in the *Jñānaśrī* (p.
75): "Just as the word 'caura', which denotes a thief, is used by Southerners to refer to boiled rice"—as stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 242).
Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 215:
"In the case of the word *udana*, it is restricted to a specific portion of the meaning."

Comparison (*tulanā*): There is indeed doubt as to whether the very same thing that, according to the actual state of affairs, is a means to attain heaven, is expressed by the word "fire-sacrifice" (*agnihotra*) and so forth by the author of the convention, or whether—due to intellectual dullness—it is something else entirely that is contrary to the means for attaining heaven.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.230)

Regarding the comparison with the Veda: the word "this" is not restricted as a denoter for all things; rather, its restriction to a specific meaning is understood from a person, that is, from human convention.
And that person might establish a convention even for a contradictory meaning.
And thus, not only would there be the possibility of a contradiction,
but this postulated authorlessness of the Veda, which is desired [by you], would also be rendered useless— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.

Now, even though a word denotes multiple meanings, it is restricted by a person through convention to denote only the intended meaning; therefore, the postulation of its being non-human (apauruṣeya) would be useless,
and a reason must be stated for the fixed determination of the relationship between distinct [words and meanings].
—Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 3.229. Compare:
"Because it could not be further refined by people, it would be entirely useless."
If one were to resort to mental constructs (*saṃskāra*), this would be like the "bathing of an elephant" (*gajasnāna*);
*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.230.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 430.

For comparison: If it is argued that Vedic words are restricted to their intended meaning by their very nature (*prakṛti*) or essence (*svabhāva*), and therefore no defect is introduced by human refinement (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), then, this being the case, they would not require instruction for the manifestation of their meaning; yet they do require it, because there is no cognition of meaning from them by themselves.

If words were restricted to a single meaning by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), then once they had been applied to a particular object at some time, they could never again, through convention (*saṃketa*), manifest another meaning in any other way; yet they do manifest such meanings. Therefore, they are not by nature restricted to a single object.

Furthermore, if there were a natural restriction to a single meaning, the various alternative explanations of Vedic sentences by commentators and the differences between successive interpretations would not exist, because of that fixed restriction to one meaning; however, such variations do occur. Consequently, like human utterances, Vedic words are not restricted to a single meaning by their inherent nature.

The sense is that there would be no difference in interpretation regarding the subject matter of the Vedic meaning among the Bhāṭṭas, Vedāntins, and Prābhākaras, [if it were] in the form of an injunction (*vidhi*) consisting of a mandate (*niyoga*), as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.230.
Comparison— Why is there a restriction that a capable word everywhere indicates only a single object?
(Pramāṇavārttika 3.326)
For indeed, a single sound possesses the capacity to illuminate various meanings; however,
objects such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice are not applicable to all purposes,
because it is possible for them to illuminate even meanings contrary to what is intended.
"Your postulation of an eternal relationship between word and meaning is useless"—*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 711.
Therefore, regarding the Vedic revelation: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra."
"One should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice"—
"one should eat dog-meat"— in such cases, what is the authority for saying that this is not the meaning? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.318)

"By that [explanation]" means: since the meaning is not fully understood, what is the proof (*pramā*) for the claim that regarding the Vedic statement "one desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," the meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat," but rather some other intended meaning? There is no proof at all—[Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.320].
"Agni" means "one who kills"; thus, Agni is the dog. One should offer its meat here as the *hotrā* (oblation);

or else, "Agni" means "that which goes" (*agati gacchati*), and the dog is called *hūyate* because it is eaten; that which is the *hotrā* (food) of Agni is the *agnihotra*. A twice-born man desiring heaven should offer—that is, eat—that dog-meat, the *agnihotra*.
(From the *Prameyaratnamālā-ṭīkā*, p. 134).
This has been cited—*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, verse 605;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, page 405;
*Nandimālā*, page 19.

Therefore, the relation is not eternal by its own nature, nor is it eternal because of the eternity of the related terms; for what here is the eternally related term—the word, the object, or both? It cannot be the word, since its impermanence will be established later;
nor can it be the object, since objects such as jars and the like are perceived through direct perception and other means to be impermanent.

Now, if it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the referent of the word and that it is eternal, and therefore the relationship residing in it is also said to be eternal—that is incorrect. For it is untenable for the universal to be the referent of the word, since it will be established later that "the referent of a word is precisely that which possesses [the universal]" (*tadvān*), and because the universal postulated by others has already been refuted. Thus, even the position of both [parties] is untenable, as it is entangled with the defects attributed to both positions. As it has been stated: "Because the relata are non-eternal, there is no eternity in the relationship."
—Pramāṇavārttika 3.231:
"That which possesses an eternal connection. (Ātmatattvaviveka)

The object which is the referent of the word— that is, the object that constitutes the domain of the relationship with the word— [is what is meant by] "the meaning of the word" (śabdārtha). (Ārya-ṭīkā)
One who relies on universals and possesses universals is precisely the Mīmāṃsaka, Naiyāyika, and so forth.

[Page 285]—Because of this...
