[let us assume] that there is some eternal relation; even so, would it be perceptible by the senses (*aindriya*), supersensible (*atīndriya*), or cognizable through inference (*anumānagamya*)? It cannot first be perceptible by the senses, because that which has an eternal nature does not appear in any sense organ whatsoever.

Now, if it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), how can it be an auxiliary to the comprehension of an object? For there is a contradiction in something being a communicator (*jñāpaka*) when it is itself unknown, since it has been stated that "that which is unknown cannot be a communicator. Furthermore, if it were a communicator by its mere presence, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would follow. Nor is it accessible through inference (*anumāna*); for if the relationship (*sambandha*) is not perceived, inference—which is preceded by such perception—cannot operate in this case.
For no mark (*liṅga*) that has not had its invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) grasped can bring about an inference, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, even if this [concomitance] is not perceived, its grasping will occur through inference; but surely, does that grasping arise from this very same inference, or from another? If it were from this very one, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of the grasping of the concomitance depends upon the establishment of the inference, and the establishment of the inference depends upon the establishment of that grasping. If it were established by another inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because the grasping of the concomitance in that case too would have to be established by yet another inference.
Furthermore, there is no mark (liṅga) here for comparison;
moreover, this relation must be either perceptible by the senses, supersensible, or cognizable through inference—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 430.

Comparison—Furthermore, a permanent relationship between word and meaning is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as such [a relationship] is not experienced; and in its absence, it cannot be established even by inference (*anumāna*), since the latter is admitted to be preceded by the former.
— *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 436, regarding the relationship between word and meaning.

Comparison [is not the means of knowledge] because it lacks a super-sensuous relationship; for from such a super-sensuous relationship, the consequence would follow that the object could not be apprehended.
Why? Because that which is unestablished—that is, not ascertained in its own form—is not a communicator [of knowledge].
Indeed, it is not logical that there be a cognition of one thing by means of another with which its relationship has not been grasped.
Now, he says that a relation, even if unknown, makes the meaning known just like a sense faculty: "By mere proximity," and so forth.

If it were admitted that the relation makes the meaning known by its mere proximity—that is, by its mere existence—then even those who are unlearned regarding the relation between word and meaning would have the realization that "this is the designator of this meaning.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1)
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 712;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 430.
This has been extracted from the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 124 and 206,
concerning the relationship between word and object based on its being preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvakatva*).
The necessary connection, which is the relation of inseparable concomitance,
[is established] for the relation between word and meaning through another inference.
In the apprehension of inseparable relation (avinābhāva),
there must likewise be another inference for the apprehension of that inseparable relation.
In the comprehension of the relationship between word and meaning, understanding does not arise from inference;
why? Because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Indeed, there is no inferential mark (liṅga) whatsoever that establishes the relationship; nor is the cognition of the object a valid mark, because an example is unestablished—
for nowhere has the cognition of an object as an effect of the relationship been apprehended in any instance.

What is the reason? Because even in that case where [the example] is presented as an illustration, one must rely on a means of proof (*sādhana*) due to the fact that the relationship is beyond the reach of the senses;
yet no such means of proof exists there either, because the example remains unestablished. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1)

For what could be the mark (*liṅga*) of an eternal relation: the cognition of the object, the object itself, or the word? It cannot be the cognition of the object, because as long as the relation is unestablished, that cognition cannot be determined to be its effect.

Nor can it be the object, because the relation with it remains unestablished; for identity between the relation and the object is impossible, as it would entail the consequence that the relation—like objects such as a jar—is non-eternal.
Nor can it be produced by that [word], nor can it be a conjunction or the like, because such things are not admitted;
nor is the word itself the logical mark (liṅga), because it would be subject to the same defects attributed to the position that the meaning is the object of inference.
Therefore, since an eternal relation cannot be established from any source, one must admit that this relation is indeed non-eternal.
For is its indicative mark (liṅga) the cognition of the object or the word?—[as stated in] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
430. For when the relationship has been apprehended, its effect, which is the cognition of the object, is ascertained; yet that [relationship] is not yet established—[Āloka-ṭippaṇī].
Compare: "If it is argued that the word and the object are the indicative mark," he says: "Not so," etc.
For in that case, neither the form of the word nor the object is a logical mark (*liṅga*) for a specific relation;
what is the reason? It is because both the word and the object are everywhere capable:
every word is capable of being a denoter with respect to every object, and every object is capable of being denoted by every word.

And the cause for the cognition of a specific object is a specific relation; and since that relation, which is the basis for the cognition of a specific object, cannot be conveyed by the word and the object when they are indeterminate— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.238.

As for the objection raised regarding the relationship [of words] with their objects— that it would be impermanent and thus require a new relationship for each person, and so forth— that too is an unexamined statement; for the linguistic usage of words is beginningless.

For neither the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), characterized by the total eradication and destruction of an already existing world, nor Creation, characterized by the acquisition of self-existence for what was non-existent, is established for either us or you, such that the resort to the appearance of a previously non-existent creation—on which [theories] such as "for each moment" or "for every person" are based—would be appropriate.
Furthermore, even if [the world] were eternal, one must admit that the manifestation of its relation is non-eternal; therefore, this same objection applies equally there as well.
Moreover, how could the relation between fire and smoke be established for one who speaks thus? For the aforementioned alternatives apply equally in that case as well.

Now, it might be argued that since the universals of "fire" and "smoke" are eternal in their nature, their relationship can also be eternal, and thus there is no room for the aforementioned alternatives in that case. This too is unsatisfactory; for the relationship between two bare universals has already been refuted in the section on the investigation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the eternity of a universal was likewise refuted previously.

Therefore, just as by means of the cognition of pervasion there is an inclusion of the infinite particular instances of the probandum and the probans—though they are characterized by similarity and have similarity as their primary feature—so too must there be an inclusion of the particular instances of the signified and the signifier.

Therefore, the relation has three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*). Regarding what you have stated: it is correct that "one perceives here through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the word, the elder, and the object denoted";

and it is also reasonable that "the listener's comprehension is known through inference (*anumāna*) by means of [their] activity. However, the claim that "one knows the power residing in both through the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*)" is untenable. This is because, if the relation is called a "permanent power," there is no such thing as "impossibility otherwise" [regarding its existence]. Even if the power residing in the word and the object were impermanent—just like the power [of causality] between fire and smoke—the listener’s comprehension of the meaning would still be possible.
Whether for the Jains or for you, O Śrāvaka, [the same applies]. (Page 543, Line 13)
For the Mīmāṃsakas—

[as noted in the Ānandagiri-ṭīkā]— therefore, even today, the conception of creation and dissolution here is not established through the destruction and birth of all things, as it lacks any basis in valid cognition.
— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verse 113ab: “Even in the case of manifestation—
the proponent [says] that smoke and fire are also [perceived by] the ear.”
For one who maintains that there is an eternal relationship between word and meaning, the point is this:

it is not the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the universals "fire-ness" and "smoke-ness" that is apprehended in the case of the relationship between fire and smoke; rather, it is the invariable concomitance of smoke as qualified by the universal "smoke-ness" with fire as qualified by the universal "fire-ness" that is apprehended.
Page 423, Page 285:

Even though the individual instances of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) are infinite, they are nonetheless subsumed by the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to their similarity; likewise, the individual instances of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) are also subsumed by that [cognition] on account of similarity. For here too there is indeed similarity: "This is denotable by the word 'jar' because it has the form of a broad base, belly, and so forth, like other jars previously perceived."

—Ācārya’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Compare this with the following: "Therefore, as for what you assert—that the relationship [between word and meaning] is established by three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—that is not accepted by us.

It is true that one perceives here the word, the elder, and the object denoted through direct perception (pratyakṣa); and it is also true that the listener's comprehension is known through inference based on purposeful action (ceṣṭā)."

However, the claim that "one knows the power residing in both [the word and the object] through the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability)" is not true, because it has already been stated that this is accounted for otherwise—
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 245— by the Mīmāṃsaka Kumārila Bhaṭṭa.

Just as the power of the signified and the signifier between fire and smoke— though impermanent— is the cause for the comprehension of the object to be inferred, so too is the power of the denoted and the denoter between word and meaning.
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted:

"The word, its meaning, and their relationship are eternal; this has been declared therein by the great seers who were the authors of the Sūtras, along with their Anutantras and Bhāṣyas" (Vākyapadīya 1.23). [Note: This refers to the Vākyapadīya together with its commentaries. (Ā. Ṭi.)
The *Anutantravārttika*— in the *Vākyapadīya*, page [blank], commentary:
"When the word, the object, and the relationship are established," meaning when the word, the referent, and the connection between them are established.

—Pāṇini, Mahābhāṣya, p. 55: "The word is eternal, the meaning is eternal, and the relationship [between them] is eternal; this is the established doctrine of the treatise (śāstra) as proclaimed therein by the great seers (maharṣi), the authors of the Sūtras and other works."
It is precisely those who are the authors of the *sūtras* and so forth who are designated as the "expounders" (*vyākaraṇa*).
In that context, from the very commencement of the *sūtras*, the eternality of words is intended;
for if words and such were non-eternal, there would be no purpose whatsoever in the undertaking of this treatise.

"For this is merely conventional usage and devoid of ultimate meaning; the great learned ones (śiṣṭas) ought not to follow it. Therefore, the treatise on traditional grammar (smṛti-śāstra) operates with respect to words whose correctness is already established—Vākyapadīya, Hari-vṛtti 1.23.
This has been cited—Siddhiviṣaraṇī-ṭīkā, p. 505; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
429—as stated in the Viddhaśālabhañjikā.

Because the impermanence of the relationship has been established, and because both the word and its referent will be demonstrated to be impermanent later on, and because it has been shown that an absolutely eternal entity lacks causal efficiency (arthakriyā) through either succession or simultaneity—how, for one who speaks thus, could the Vedic injunction (codanā) possess authority regarding a task to be accomplished (kārya), given that the task itself is impermanent? Therefore, it is established that the scripture conveys its meaning by virtue of a relationship characterized by a certain degree of impermanent fitness; hence, it is well said: "Scripture is a valid means of knowledge because it is consistent with reality."
Six at the beginning;
[Bibliotheca Indica edition, page 372].
For those who maintain that there is an eternal and necessary connection [between word and meaning]—
[as stated in the commentary]— because the sacred tradition (āmnāya) has action as its purpose; Jaimini-sūtra 1.1.2.
"An injunction (codanā) is said to be a statement that impels one toward action"— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2.
1.2 Of ritual action in the form of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma.
The Buddhist’s prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the fact that a word denotes only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*):
"But is it not the case that the non-contradiction of what is heard [in verbal testimony] is unestablished? For words are perceived even in the absence of an object;

indeed, those very same words which are seen to have a real referent are also seen in its absence. Therefore, since it is untenable for words to denote an object through the mode of affirmation (*vidhi*), it is only logical that they denote merely the exclusion of others."
And it has been said: "A real entity is not indicated by affirmation through either word or a logical mark.

This is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Whatever appears therein is its object; for example, in a sensory perception, the nature of the object—such as blue and so forth—which appears with perfect clarity, is its object. And in a cognition arising from a word or a logical mark, only the intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) devoid of the reality of an external object appears; therefore, that alone is its object.

Furthermore, it is not unestablished that, in the causal condition of its production, [cognition] has as its nature the manifestation of the mere intrinsic form that does not touch upon an external object; for this is established because it is impossible for words and logical marks (liṅga) to have an external object as their domain. To explain: if an external object were the domain of a word, it would have to be either of the nature of a particular (svalakṣaṇa) or of the nature of a universal (sāmānya). Of these, the first alternative is untenable, because words cannot function with respect to it due to the absence of linguistic convention (saṅketa).

For a convention is established for an object whose essential nature persists through the time of the convention and the time of its practical application; however, such a nature is not possible for a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because, being restricted by place, time, and form, its nature does not persist. That which does not persist through the times of convention and application is not the object to which words are conventionally assigned by those engaged in linguistic practice—just as one does not assign a word to an object that perishes immediately upon arising. Furthermore, a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and the like do not persist from the intended place and so forth to another place and so forth;
nor would there be the fault of the word having a false referent with respect to things past or yet to be born.
"Of any [such] speech"— this [verse] is considered to have as its object the referent of a cognition (bauddhārtha).
— Pramāṇavārttika 3.207.
It is bound to the conceptual reflections that are based upon those [external objects];
therefore, because it is based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to perform the exclusion of others.

At the time of convention, [the word] is bound to the forms of conceptual reflections—which are established as the objects of linguistic usage through being determined as entities excluded from others—because these conceptual reflections have as their nature the exclusion of external things and thus serve as the objects of linguistic usage. For this reason, because it is based on the exclusion of others, the word is said to perform the exclusion of others.

Because it generates conceptual cognitions with forms excluded from others and because it causes engagement with things excluded from others, a word is said to perform the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

Now, [an objection is raised]: "In verbal cognition, the object of apprehension is perceived precisely as something external, not as a form within the cognition. To this he replies: "That reflection of the object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct [from the cognition itself]—even that is not the actual nature of the object; it is an error arising from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)."

The meaning is that, just as with the hairs seen by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), even though the form of conceptualization is merely an external error, there is nevertheless an external conventional usage due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*)— *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 2.164–65.

In this regard, that non-different form which appears to objects through a conceptualizing cognition that imposes [a universal] is called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoḍha*) because it arises from the force of experiencing objects as excluded from others, because it manifests itself as being excluded from others, because it is determined by the deluded as being one with the object excluded from others, and because its fruit is the comprehension of an object excluded from others.
Therefore, it is well known that exclusion (*apoha*) is the meaning of a word—*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 274.

Apoha is the form superimposed as being external, so called because "by this [mental construction] something is excluded" (*apohyate 'nena*), or else it is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, so called because "in this [particular characteristic] something is excluded" (*apohyate 'smin*). Therefore, the external object is not grasped by conceptual cognitions in its own nature, but rather the external object is grasped only as unified with its own [mental] form; and since that [unified object] is unreal, it is called *apoha* because "by this [cognition] something other is excluded. — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.48.

Now, what indeed is this so-called *apoha*? The external object itself, such as a jar, is designated as *apoha* in accordance with its determination (*vyavasāya*), on the grounds that "that which is of a different class is excluded (*apohyate*) from it.
Alternatively, the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*) as it appears is *apoha*, on the grounds that "the heterogeneous is excluded—that is, set apart—within this cognitive form.

Or, *apoha* is the mere exclusion (*nivṛttimātra*) according to reality, consisting of a simple negation, on the grounds that "it is the act of excluding (*apohana*) and not non-exclusion (*anapoha*)."
—This is cited from *Tarkabhāṣā*, Moḍha Paṇḍita, fol. 26; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, p. 140;
and *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 180.

Comparison— how is it understood that this very exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is conveyed by word and logical mark (*liṅga*) through affirmation (*vidhi*), and not the nature of a real entity?— [is addressed] by the Teacher (*ācārya*) when he states that exclusion (*apoha*), which has as its object the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is conveyed by word and logical mark. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1.44)
— Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 3.133:

The objects of the cognitions arising from words and logical marks are merely their own intrinsic nature (svarūpa), devoid of external objects, because it is only the intrinsic nature itself that appears therein.
It is said: there is no object whatsoever for these mental cognitions (*dhī*);
rather, their basis is the seed (*bīja*) residing within the internal dimension (*antarmātrā*).

For instance, we maintain that the cause for these [cognitions] is the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*), but not an external object; because the preceding verbal cognition is erroneous, it is devoid of an object.
"Established within the internal measure" means, in other words, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) established within consciousness.

Demonstrating this very point through scripture, he says "of whatever," and so forth: "For whatever object is expressed by whichever word, that [object] does not exist at all; for such is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of things."
—Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 275 — [The object] whose nature is devoid [of conceptual construction]...
because the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), the universal (jāti), the connection with that [universal], and likewise the possessor of the universal (jātimat) [are all excluded].
The form of cognition does not, in reality, fit within the referent of the word—*Tattvārtha*, p.
there, the first position is [as follows]—*Bāhyārthasiddhi*.
Words express that which is conventionally designated for the sake of practical usage;
since that [designated object] does not exist as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) at that time, there is no convention regarding it. — *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.169–170ab.
91. At that time, during the occasion of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist upon which a convention (*saṅketa*) could be established;

for because even a single particular characteristic is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), there is no persistence of it in the same form at another time. Or, if it were not momentary, there would be no persistence of its being the object [of cognition] at another time simply due to the absence of the cognition of the convention; how much less so in the case of particular characteristics differentiated by place and time? For that reason, a convention is not made with respect to those particular characteristics.
— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*.
In that regard, first of all, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not communicated by words,
because it lacks pervasion across the time of the convention and the time of practical usage.

This is what is meant: a convention (*saṃketa*) is indeed established for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), not out of mere habit; therefore, it is only appropriate for speakers to employ a convention regarding that which possesses the quality of pervading the time of both the convention and its subsequent usage, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not possess the quality of pervading the time of the convention and its subsequent usage; therefore, no convention can be applied to it.
These [particulars] do not follow one another in their own nature,
because they differ according to distinctions of place, time, action, capacity, appearance, and so forth;
therefore, the object perceived through convention is not seen in actual usage.
And one who has not grasped the convention [regarding it] cannot understand its nature, which is of such a kind, any more than [one can understand] other sounds. (*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 207).

The meaning is that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not pervade other locations, times, or forms, because it consists of the form of a single atom, lasts for a single moment, and is partless;

for it does not extend across differences of place and time. "Of that" refers to what was perceived at the time of the convention; it does not extend across, nor does it follow through, differences of place and time such as those occurring during the state of linguistic usage.
For a difference observed in one place cannot possibly exist elsewhere.
— Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.94:
There is no linguistic convention regarding the particular (svalakṣaṇa), because it does not persist from the time of the convention to the time of its practical application.
For that which exists in the intended location is one thing, and that which moves to another location is another, because of momentariness—[Āloka-ṭīkā].

Furthermore, in that cognition in which the relation "this is the designation of this" appears, there is no appearance of the specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*) of word and object, which are the respective domains of their corresponding sense organs;
nor is it logical for that [cognition] to establish a relation between those two which do not appear therein, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If two things do not appear in a cognition that establishes a relation such as "this belongs to that," then no relation can be established by that cognition between them; for example, when the relation between the word "cow" and its object is being cognized, the word "horse" and its object—which do not appear in that cognition—cannot have their relation established by it. Furthermore, the intrinsic natures of the word and the object, which appear in their own respective sensory cognitions, do not appear in the cognition that establishes the relation "this belongs to that. And a word whose relation has not been established with an object is not capable of signifying that object, precisely because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

That which has not established a connection with something else does not convey that object, just as the word "cow" does not convey the meaning of a horse because no connection has been established between them;

and since all words have no established connection with the particular (svalakṣaṇa), if verbal cognition were to have the particular as its object, it would follow—just like a cognition produced by the senses—that it must possess a clear manifestation, yet this is not the case, as it contradicts actual experience.
Thus it has been said:
The ear and the eye [function] through the cognition of the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of sound and objects, respectively.

Regarding the word and its object— the commentary notes that the relation between the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word and the specific individuality of the object is not grasped by the cognition apprehending their relation, because they do not appear within that cognition which apprehends the relation of the word "cow" and its object.

In one's own sensory cognition—[as noted in the Āloka commentary]—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object appears in visual cognition, and sound appears in auditory cognition (Āloka-ṭīkā).

This is what is meant: if a word were to convey an object for which no linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) has been grasped, then even the word "cow" would convey a horse, and the act of establishing a convention would be rendered useless. Therefore, the consequence of such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) serves as a refutation.
*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 277:

A word does not denote a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because no convention has been established for it. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things for which no convention has been established in reality with respect to a certain object do not, from the perspective of ultimate truth, denote that object; for example, the word "horse" when no convention has been established for it regarding an individual possessing a dewlap and so forth. And all sounds have no convention established in reality with respect to every object. [This is so] because of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*); for denotative capacity is pervaded by the state of having a convention established.
And it has been said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 276: "Furthermore,
that which is perceivable by the senses is one thing, while the object of sound is another."

Commentary: The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as color-form, which is perceivable by the sense organs, is one thing; let it be understood that the range and object of a word is something else entirely.
One whose eyes have failed understands through words in a manner different from how one with intact vision perceives—that is, not as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Alternatively, if they had the same object, then even for a blind person, just as for one who is not blind, the comprehension from a word would necessarily be non-mediated (*aparokṣa*).

If that were the case, then just as there is a connection with the fire of the sense organ and so forth, the meaning of "burning" would be understood even from the word "burning. To this he says: "In quite another way"—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyomavatī*, p. 584. The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) graspable by the senses is one thing, while the object of a word is another, namely the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Why? Because through words, even one with different senses understands [objects] such as a jar, whereas one with eyes does not perceive it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

He explains this very point: otherwise, due to the connection with burning experienced through a clear perception, one would consider oneself burnt by the contact of the sense organ with the object; yet the person does not know it in that way. Otherwise, for one who does not clearly experience it himself, the meaning of "burning" is understood by the ear through the word "burning"—as stated in the *Śāstravārtā-ṭīkā*, verse 666–67:
"One whose eyes are closed understands from the sound, but does not perceive it directly."
"With eyes burst open"— this refers to the wound.
This [passage] beginning with "anya-śabdasya" has been extracted from the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, page 384,
and the *Nyāyamañjarī*, page 31.
*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, verse 666;
*Anekāntajayapatākā*, page 45; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 446.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 260; Dharmasaṃgraha-vṛtti, p. 149; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 710.
"One who is burned perceives the burning from contact with fire in one way [only];

[the commentary explains: "it is understood for the sake of burning and so forth—if the external object were conveyed by the word exactly as it is, then why would that object, brought into proximity by the word, not perform that causal function? Since, however, one who is burned experiences the burning differently from the contact with fire, and understands the burning differently through the word 'burning,' it must be understood that there is no real correspondence whatsoever between the word and its object. (*Vākyapadīya-puṇyarāja-ṭīkā*)
This has been cited—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
584; *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 31; *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, verse 667.
It is elucidated in the *Anekāntajaya* (p.
45), the *Nayacakravṛtti* (Lithograph, p.
44B), and the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (p. 280).
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 447;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pp. 177, 260;
Syādvādaratnākara, p. 710.
Comparison: The cognition of heat and so forth that arises from words such as "heat" does not appear with such clarity as the sensory cognition of those objects;
for just as the sensory cognition whose object is the thing—such as heat—is experienced as having a vivid manifestation, the cognition arising from the word "heat" is not so experienced.

For those whose eyes, tongues, noses, and so forth are impaired do not experience the color, taste, and other qualities [of an object] upon hearing words such as "mātuliṅga," just as those with unimpaired eyes and other senses experience them through sensory cognition (TS, p.
280). Otherwise, as it is said: "By the word 'burning,' the object 'burning' is understood" (VP 2.425).

Furthermore, a single entity cannot possess two forms such that the indistinct form inherent in the object itself would appear in a verbal cognition; for it is a contradiction for one thing to have duality. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not appear in a cognition produced by something else cannot be the object of that [cognition], just as taste is not the object of a cognition produced by visible form; and the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear in verbal cognition. Moreover, if words had real entities as their objects, then—given the diversity of philosophical views—it would be impossible for them to denote different meanings.

And it has been said: "If words were directed solely toward the ultimate reality (paramārtha), their application toward objects that differ according to various conventions would be impossible" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3).
206. Thus, it is not tenable that the object of a word is the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇasvabhāva*);
nor can a single entity possess two forms, one clear and the other indistinct.

Otherwise, it would follow that the very same form of an object, which is indistinct, is expressed by words; for it is contradictory for one thing to possess two forms—distinct and indistinct—which are mutually exclusive, such that one should appear in sensory cognition while the other appears in conceptual construction. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 281) Indeed, there cannot exist two mutually contradictory forms, distinct and indistinct, belonging to a single entity, whereby one might manifest in sense-perception and the other in conceptual thought.
That being the case, since difference would belong to the thing itself— [as stated in] the *Apohasiddhi*, p.
7— the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of verbal cognition, because it does not appear in verbal cognition.

The connection of that [particular] with that word is not logical; nor does the object appear when the cognition produced by it occurs, just as taste does not appear in the cognition of form. For that which does not manifest in the cognition produced by something is not its object, just as taste is not the object of a cognition produced by form. And the particular (svalakṣaṇa) does not manifest in the cognition of the word; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). — *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 280.

With respect to the condition of form (*rūpa-pratyaya*), when there is a state of being exclusively directed toward the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-ekatānatva*), the explanation of words would be without basis— meaning that when there is that state of being directed toward a single point in the ultimate particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the activity of words would not occur without a basis, as they would be devoid of a foundation in ultimate reality regarding objects that differ according to various philosophical systems (*darśana*) and are distinguished by differences in tenets (*siddhānta*).
— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.209:

If words were directed solely toward the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-ekatānatve*), that is, if they were focused exclusively on the ultimate, there would be no basisless— that is, devoid of any foundation in the ultimate— application of words toward objects that differ according to philosophical systems (*darśanāntara-bhediṣu*), since each system accepts different conceptual distinctions such as permanence, impermanence, or being composed of the three qualities (*triguṇīmayatva*).
For indeed, many mutually contradictory properties do not exist in one place— *Pramāṇavārttika*, Manorathanandin’s commentary, 3.206.
"There would be no engagement with objects that differ according to different conventions" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.206);
[this refers to] "those that differ according to other systems of thought" (Pramāṇavārttika-śāstravārttika,
verse 647).
Anekāntajaya° fol. 35A;
Prakṛtapāṭha—Aṣṭasahasrī fol. 168;
Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā fol. 268A.

Therefore, there can be no engagement with objects that differ according to different conventions, nor can there be such engagement with a universal form; for a real universal is impossible, and its impossibility is well-established because, like a horse’s horn, it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Indeed, it has already been stated during the refutation of the universal that causal efficiency—whether successive or simultaneous—is not possible for that which is eternal and of a single nature.
Therefore, words do not have external objects as their domain; rather, they have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their domain.
Even though [the word] has the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), a person would act only after having cognized those things capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).
For the purpose of accomplishing that [goal], expressive words are applied to objects;

however, it is certainly not the case that the world would suffer from not employing words without having established a convention regarding a universal (*jāti*) that is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
If it is asked, "What then of one who has fallen into calamity?"— the answer is that every undertaking is indeed to be undertaken for the sake of a result,
since an undertaking that is fruitless is to be disregarded; therefore,
when employing words in some context, it is proper to expect some specific result.

If all that [is meant by the Veda] consists of the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, then one would attend to an injunction— thinking, "Therefore, having determined what is and is not a means to the desired and undesired, I shall engage in or desist from it, or cause another to do so"— or else one would employ words [with such intent], for otherwise they would be objects of indifference;
in that case, a universal (*jāti*) is incapable of purposeful action.

For a universal (jāti) is never present for tasks such as carrying or milking, nor is there the employment of words in worldly transactions in the absence of such contexts— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.169.
Of the universal,
page 285.

And that [exclusion] consists of four and a half aspects (*ardhapañcamākāra*). To explain: neither the universal (*jāti*) nor the individual (*vyakti*) can be its object, due to the faults previously mentioned;

nor can it be the cognition (*jñāna*) or its form (*tadākāra*), because these too, in their own nature, are particular characters (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since a particular character cannot be the object of a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), it is impossible for them to be the domain of words. Rather, it is that very form of cognition which, having unified the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*), is superimposed (*adhyasta*) as an external form; this is the "four-and-a-half-aspected" exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
For its "externality" constitutes the "half-aspect."

These—namely, the universal (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*), the cognition (*jñāna*), and its form (*tadākāra*)—are these five [factors] plus half; that is, four and a half forms. As for the "half-ness," it is because the object of perception (*dṛśya*) is real (*satya*) while the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is unreal (*asatya*).
[This refers to] the status of being the object of words (*śabdaviṣayatva*). (Āloka-ṭīkā)
Only those who explain the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition do so by means of its nature as knowledge; indeed, it is not for the sake of conventional users [of language].
But they, considering only their own objective support to be fit for causal efficiency, proceed by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object;

for while establishing the object as it actually exists, they discern that "the appearance in conceptual cognition is one thing, and the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is another," yet it is not the ordinary users of language who perform this discernment.

But those who engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahartṛ*), considering that which appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which has its own objective support (*svālambana*) and is alone capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāyogya*)—to be the nature of an external particular (*bāhya-svalakṣaṇa*), clarify this very point: they proceed toward an object that performs causal efficiency by being convinced that "the visible object is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)," while "the conceptualized object is the appearance of a universal (*sāmānya-pratibhāsa*"); having unified these two, [they think] "this very particular is made the object of conceptual cognition and is impelled by words. It is on account of their intention—that is, on account of the intention of those engaged in transaction—that it is said: "conceptual cognition arises with respect to entities that are [in fact] distinct."

By stating that "activity proceeds by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized [image]," it is not being said that there is a superimposition of the external upon one's own internal form (*svākāra*); otherwise, activity would necessarily follow toward the internal form alone, as in the case of one seeking water who acts upon the superimposition of water onto a mirage.

Nor is there a superimposition of one's own form upon the external; otherwise, activity would necessarily follow solely out of a desire for the fruit of what is being superimposed, as in the case of one desiring water acting upon a delusion of water.

When an object is experienced, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises in its form through the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that experience; this conceptual construction determines its own form to be non-different from the external, but it does not actually make them non-different.
Therefore, because the object of conceptual construction is determined as having the nature of the perceptible, the unification of the perceptible and the conceptually constructed is spoken of—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.72.
And *apoha* is negation, and it is of two kinds: *paryudāsa* (exclusion) and *prasajya* (absolute negation).
*Paryudāsa* is also of two kinds: consisting of cognition (*buddhyātman*) and consisting of the object (*arthātman*).
In this context, the "nature of cognition" (*buddhyātmā*) refers to the appearance within cognition that is determined as having a single, continuous form across various objects;

the "nature of the object" (*arthātmā*) refers to the intrinsic nature of the object, namely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object which is excluded from what is heterogeneous. Regarding these, the specific definition of the nature of cognition is as follows: based on objects that are by nature mutually distinct yet perform a single function through having a common cause, there arises a cognition whose nature is a reflection of the object and which consists in a single unifying conceptualization (*ekapratyavamarśa*); this [cognition] is designated as *apoha*.

The aspect of conceptualization (*vikalpākāra*), which is a shadow of a portion of a real entity (*vastubhāgacchāya*), being delineated by conceptual thought and imagined as external, is *apoha* because it uproots the aspect contrary to its own [true] aspect; it is called *apoha* because "by means of this" (*anena*) [the contrary is] excluded (*apohyate*). It is called *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) because it manifests itself through its distinction from the aspect residing in other conceptualizations, and thus "it is excluded from another" (*anyasmāt apohyate*). This indeed is what is primarily denoted by the term *anyāpoha*.

However, it is metaphorical for three reasons: either because the properties of the effect are superimposed upon the cause, or because the properties of the cause are figuratively attributed to the effect, or because of the determination of identity with the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as excluded from heterogeneous things? For the effect is the attainment of the object excluded from others, which is the aforementioned apoha; therefore, by virtue of being its cause, the property of the effect—namely, exclusion from others—is superimposed there [upon the cause].

Either the property of the cause exists in the effect, or [the term "exclusion of others" is applied] because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is unmixed with others, is the cause of that conceptual reflection whose nature is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) through a single unifying cognition; for that [reflection] is produced by the experience of that [particular characteristic]. Furthermore, since the exclusion of others exists in the particular characteristic which serves as the cause, it is metaphorically attributed to the conceptual reflection which is its effect. Alternatively, it is described as "exclusion of others" because the form appearing in the conceptual reflection is determined as one with the particular characteristic that is excluded from those of a different class. Thus, exclusion (*apoha*) has been explained in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*);
for indeed, exclusion is of two kinds: by way of relative negation and by way of absolute negation (*niṣedha*).
Exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is also twofold, distinguished as being of the nature of cognition (*buddhyātman*) or of the nature of the object (*arthātman*).
Among these, that which is of the nature of cognition is the appearance in cognition, determined as a single, pervasive form with respect to objects;
that which is of the nature of the object is the intrinsic nature of the object, meaning the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object excluded from what is heterogeneous.
—*Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā*, p.

316. For comparison: "For exclusion (*apoha*) is indeed threefold: first, the excluded particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself; second, that in which something else is excluded, as stated [in the verse]: 'Because they partake in exclusion from both their own nature and other natures'; this is merely a negation (*vyavacchedamātra*), being called 'the exclusion of others' (*anyāpohana*) or 'exclusion of others' (*anyāpoha'). Third is the appearance in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi-pratibhāsa*), so called because it is by means of this that [the object] is excluded. And this [third type] is accepted as the basis for the word. —*Anekāntajayapatākā*, p. 37A.
—bhāsānu— ba;
—ṣvavyavasthita śra; then the self ba.

In this regard, demonstrating the essential nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), he says: "The causes of a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) previously stated— objects such as 'fearlessness' and so forth— are by their very nature distinct from others."
Relying upon those [individuals], when knowledge arises, there appears a reflection of the object;
even though that conceptualizing cognition lacks the nature of the object itself, it is determined as "these are the objects.

Just as many things such as *harītakī* and others perform a single effect characterized by the pacification of fever and so forth even without a universal (*sāmānya*), so too will objects such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others—despite their difference—by their very nature become causes for a single uniform reflective awareness, even without a real, substantial universal. Thus, there is no need for a real entity called a universal.

"Equal to *abhayā* and so forth" means they are equal to *harītakī* and other such fruits by virtue of performing the same function; "relying upon those" means relying upon those objects that are equal to *abhayā* and so forth, taking them as the cause. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: in that conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*) which arises through the power of experiencing those [objects], there appears an appearance of the object—an image of the object—in the form of the object itself; it is with respect to this [appearance] that the designation "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is stated, because [the exclusion] exists in identity with it.
"Conceptualizing" (*kalpaka*) means "conceptual" (*savikalpa*), that is to say, within conceptual cognition.

And this [phrase] "etacca jñāne" (and this in cognition) is in grammatical apposition [with the subject]; "even in the absence of the nature of an external object" means even in the absence of the nature of an external object.
"Ascertained" (niścita) means determined (*adhyavasita*)—*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 317.
A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a cow and so forth is distinct from a conceptual construction of a horse and so forth—*Āloka-ṭīkā*.
Now, as to how this designation "its exclusion" (apoha) is applied, he says: "Because of the difference from another appearance," and so forth.

This is because, by way of a thing that is not conjoined [with others], there is the attainment of a thing excluded from others due to its difference from another appearance, and because it serves as the cause for such attainment.
The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the fruit [of inference] because it is excluded from those of a different class;

or rather, due to the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [particular] as being identical with this [conceptual image], which is a cognitive distortion (*vipluta*), this designation "this is another thing" is said to have a basis in reality.

It is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) for four reasons: primarily, because it manifests itself as distinct from other appearances superimposed by other conceptual constructions; secondarily, because it is that which is excluded (*apohyate*); and figuratively, according to the etymology "exclusion from another" (*anyasmād apohaḥ*), which is "other-exclusion" (*anyāpoha*). However, [the term is used] through three [of these reasons].

1—Either because the properties of the effect are superimposed upon the cause, as it is said: "by virtue of being the cause for the attainment of the object excluded from others"; or 2—because the properties of the cause are metaphorically attributed to the effect. He demonstrates this by saying: "even because of the cognition [of the object] by means of an unconnected object.

"Unconnected" (*aśliṣṭa*) means not related to anything else; that is to say, excluded from others. That very object serves as the "door" (*dvāra*), meaning the means, since a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that same kind arises through the force of the experience of that [object].
The fourth reason is that it is determined by deluded cognizers as being identical with the referent of the term "exclusion of the dissimilar" (vijātīyāpoha);
he demonstrates this with the words beginning "vijātīya...
and "asya."

"Having a basis" (*sanibandhanā*) means that it exists together with its basis (*nibandhana*), namely the fourfold [basis] previously described as difference and so forth from other appearances, regarding the reflection of an object mounted upon the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*).
— *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 317.
The cause is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha); the effect is the attainment of the object as excluded from others—[Āloka-ṭīkā: "apohe" means "in the cause"]. This is the effect.
The reason for this—[Āryaṭīkā];
[the exclusion of others]—[Āryaṭīkā]; in the nature of the exclusion of others—[Āryaṭīkā].
Alternatively, because it is not established [as a positive entity],

the word must be accepted as denoting only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which— being of the nature of a negation (*prasajya*) such as "this cow is not a non-cow"— culminates in mere exclusion, according to the mode already described.

Furthermore, the relationship between the signified and the signifier is not other than the relationship between cause and effect; for since the reflection residing in the intellect is produced by the word, it is the signified of that word, and since the word produces it, it possesses the status of being the signifier— thus,
there is also the case of absolute negation, as in "this cow is not a non-cow."
This exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is indeed understood with extreme clarity—*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p.
318. Having thus explained the threefold nature of apoha, he says "In that regard, this... and so forth, applying it to the subject at hand, namely, the meaning of words (*śabdārtha*).
In this regard, this is the first [type of] apoha by which it is understood through words,
because a cognition that determines an external object arises from a word;
"the first" refers to that whose nature is a reflection of the object as previously described.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "of that which determines external objects," and so forth.
For it is logical that only that which appears in verbal cognition is the meaning of the word;
however, in this case, there is no determination of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), nor is there an appearance of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as there is in sensory perception.
What then? A purely verbal cognition arises that determines an external object;

therefore, it is that very reflection of the object which is rightly considered the "meaning of the word" (*śabdārtha*) because it appears directly in verbal cognition as having that [external object] as its essence, and nothing else—this is the sense.
Thus, it has been shown that exclusion (*apoha*) characterized as a reflection is the primary meaning of a word, since it is produced directly by words.

Showing that even for the remaining two types of exclusion (*apoha*), the description of their being figurative meanings of words is indeed not contradictory, he says: "When this very form is thus established directly, even the non-affirming negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is understood by implication,
because of the connection [of the word] with things as 'not having that nature' or 'having another nature'."
The comprehension of the excluded object also occurs by implication;
therefore, this too is figuratively designated as the word's own meaning (svārtha), but it is not directly verbal. Thus, apoha is said to be twofold.
And thus,
showing why a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is understood by implication through its being produced, he says: "It is not of that nature."

Considering that the nature (ātman) of that reflection of a cow and so forth is not the nature (svabhāva) of another reflection, such as that of a horse and so forth, he has thus established that the denotation of a word is figurative (*gauṇa*) because exclusion characterized by negative concomitance (*prasajyalakṣaṇāpoha*) is necessarily perceived. Now, demonstrating that this applies to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as well, he says: "When there is a connection," and so on.
In this context, the "connection" is the bond (*pratibandha*) between the word and the real entity, characterized by a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) through a mediated succession.

First, there is the experience of the object as it actually exists; then the desire to speak; then the movement of the palate and other vocal organs; and then the sound. If, through such a succession, there were a connection between the word and external objects such as fire, then—given that connection—the object, even though it is excluded from things of a different class, would be apprehended by means of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, both types of negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and exclusion (*apoha*), which consists in the nature of the object as excluded from others, are metaphorically designated as the "meaning of the word" (*śabdārtha*). By the word "this," [it refers to] that which consists of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and by the word "also" (*api*), [it includes] that which consists of simple negation (*prasajya*).
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, Pañjikā, pp. 318–19:

Now, since the Buddhists maintain that the relation [between things] consists solely of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), why is the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) also accepted here? To this he says (Āloka-ṭīkā):

"And as for that well-known relation of a word with its object, characterized as the state of signifier and signified, it does not exist apart from the relation of cause and effect; rather, he shows that it is essentially of the nature of cause and effect," beginning with the words "of the reflection of that form" (*tadrūpapratibimbasya*).
When a cognition arises from a word through the medium of such a reflection,
this relationship of signifier and signified (vācyavācakabhāva) comes into being as one consisting of cause and effect:
the word is called the "signifier" because it generates the reflection, and that reflection is the "signified" because it is produced by the word.
—Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 318–19.
Therefore, by that word, its reflection (tatpratibimba) possesses the status of being the denoted (vācyatva)—Āloka-ṭīkā.
This is the demonstration, preceded by the refutation of the Apoha theory, that a word denotes an object consisting of a universal and particular that are ultimately real.

To this, the following reply is given: as for what was stated—that exclusion (*apoha*) [is apprehended] by means of words and logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth—that is incorrect. For it would be logical that something is the object of those [means of knowledge] only if it is established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); yet this [exclusion] is not established by any means of valid cognition. To explain: would exclusion be established through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be established through perception, because the latter has only the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
nor can it be established through inference, because there is no logical mark (*liṅga*) invariably concomitant with it.
Indeed, there is no logical mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with the exclusion of the non-existent or the exclusion of the non-cow,
for according to your own view, invariable concomitance is established through the two modes of essential identity (*tādātmya*) and causal origination (*tadutpatti*);
and neither essential identity nor causal origination is possible between the exclusion of another and anything else.

To explain: the exclusion of non-produced-ness (*akṛtakatva-vyāvṛtti*) is "produced-ness" (*kṛtakatva*). Would that be of the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), or would it be of the nature of impermanence (*anityatva*), which consists in the exclusion of permanence? First, it cannot be of the nature of a particular, because it is not a real entity (*avastu-rūpa*); for whatever is not a real entity is not of the nature of a particular, like a donkey's horn, and produced-ness—by virtue of being the exclusion of non-produced-ness—is not a real entity.

Nor can it be of the nature of impermanence, which consists in the exclusion of permanence; for since both [the exclusion and the excluded] are devoid of form (*nīrūpa*), there is no relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) between them.

Between two things that lack intrinsic form (*nīrūpatva*), there can be no relationship of identity (*tādātmya*), just as between a sky-flower and the son of a barren woman; and since producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) are by nature the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti-svabhāva*), they lack intrinsic form.
Therefore, identity is not possible between these two, nor is causality (*tadutpatti*), precisely because they lack intrinsic form.

For instance: that which is formless (nīrūpa) is neither produced by anything nor productive of anything, just like a donkey’s horn; and the two types of exclusion (apoha) under discussion, intended as the probandum and the probans, are formless—[as stated] on page 551, line 9.
Regarding exclusion (apoha):

The scope of words and logical marks [is restricted to what has been perceived]. For example: "Apoha is not first determined by the sense organs; nor does the function of a word apply elsewhere. Having seen what, then, would it be employed?"
By the aforementioned argument, no inference exists here;
therefore, even the experience of its connection is not at all established.
An exclusion (apoha) denoted by a word cannot be a means of communication in any way if it has not been apprehended;
perception is incapable of that [apprehension], nor do the inferential mark (liṅga) and the expressive word exist [to provide it].
Since its apprehension would [otherwise] occur, and since there would be no fixed rule regarding the postulation of inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth,
it must be stated that this is impossible without being rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*).
107 – Apohasiddhi, verses 78–79; 106–7, Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 435.
The object of cognition (prameya) [is] that which is inseparably connected with exclusion (apoha).
In the Buddhist tenet, that which is invariably concomitant—
namely, "being produced," which consists in the exclusion of "not being produced"— is not of the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is of the nature of a non-entity.
—How so?

Because there is no identity between "producedness," which has the nature of the exclusion of non-producedness, and "impermanence," which has the nature of the exclusion of permanence; for both producedness and impermanence, being of the nature of the exclusion of other things, are devoid of intrinsic form (nīrūpatvāt).
"Producedness and impermanence"—Ā. Ṭi.

[Objection: But even in the absence of an external object, that very reflection which arises in the form of an object is itself the *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), and since that is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), inference regarding it is useless. [Response: This too is an unexamined statement, because the fact that cognition bears the form of an object has been refuted in order to establish its lack of form. [Objection: But the form of the object... [Ā.]
Thus [it is stated in] the *Asamīkṣya* (Śrīmad-Ācārya-bhagavat-pāda’s work), page 167:

"Or let that be so; nevertheless, what is reflected here—is it the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) or the universal (*sāmānya*)? First of all, it cannot be the particular, because its form is differentiated (*vyāvṛtta*)."

And since the reflection intended [by you] is one that conforms to a single form (*anugataikarūpa*), namely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), therefore the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) must also be of such a nature.

For instance, whatever the form of a reflection is, that very thing itself must have that same form, just as in the case of a face, the moon, and so forth. And the reflection of the particular characteristic in cognition is a form that conforms to a single [excluded] aspect.

Now, if it is claimed that the reflection occurs in the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*); that too is incorrect, because it is impossible for that which is non-existent (*asat*) to produce a reflection.

That which is non-existent is never reflected, just like a sky-flower; and since the universal (*sāmānya*) is non-existent according to your own position, if you nevertheless accept its reflection [in cognition], it would follow that prior to the arising of the reflection, those two distinct forms would be perceived separately from one another.

For wherever something is reflected, those two are perceived as mutually distinct prior to the emergence of the reflection, as in the case of a face and a mirror; and yet, the form of the universal is reflected in cognition.
It has no reflection that conforms to a single form.
For whatever [object],
its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is followed by a single form; because it is reflected in the form of that single following form,
the universal (*sāmānya*)— being of the nature of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and lacking causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)— is non-existent.
A universal does not appear as a reflection in cognition, because according to the Buddhist view, it lacks existence within cognition.

The point is this: the two distinct intrinsic natures— the cognition which is the substratum of the reflection and the universal which is the reflected object— would appear as distinct from one another.
And both [the object and] the cognition would be perceived as distinct, because [the object] is being reflected therein— [it] is mirrored (*bimbate*)—
and [the cognition] is mirrored (*bimbate*).

Alternatively, it might be argued that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, by virtue of performing a single purposeful action such as carrying or milking, possesses a recurring aspect and is thus the universal (*sāmānya*); therefore, there is no room for the aforementioned fault. This is incorrect; because that which does not perform a single purposeful action lacks the capacity to perform it, it would follow that there is an absence of reflection (or manifestation). Furthermore, since purposeful action is occasional, the arising of that [recurring aspect] would also occur only occasionally, resulting in the fault characterized by the absence of reflection.

Furthermore, regarding the universal: if it is admitted that the capacity for performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*) is one and the same within the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), then let that [particular] itself be the object of appearance by virtue of the power of the manifestation perceived as appearing externally; what is the use of grasping at a reflected image?

Furthermore, if verbal conceptualization were to consist merely in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its own internal reflection, then how could there be any activity toward an external object on its basis? If you argue that it is due to the determination of an object within what is not an object—namely, one's own reflection—we ask: what is this so-called "determination of an object"? Is it the grasping of the external object, its production, its conjunction, or its superimposition (*samāropa*)? In the first case, the position of the opponent is established; for the Buddhists do not admit that verbal cognitions grasp external objects.

The second alternative is also untenable; for cognitions lack the capacity to produce external objects, since they arise from their own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*); otherwise, there would be the unimpeded accomplishment of all objects for everyone.
Nevertheless, even so, the activity directed toward an external object by one who desires it would not occur on the basis of conceptual construction—Nyāyavārttika, p. 485.
For in this way too, activity toward an object would be impossible from that [cognition];
as stated in the *Anekāntajayapatākā* (p.
35B): "And when there is cognition of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), how could there be engagement with the object?"
"From [the mere] word, this person's [knowledge] would be established in every respect, because of the over-extension [of the consequence]" (Tattvārthaśloka p. 109; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
Ratnākaraśānti, folio 4, line 11:

"No, because the unification of those two is not established; for the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized object (*vikalpya*) are absolutely distinct, a commonality (*sādharmya*) between them is impossible, and since there is no single experiencer of both, at that time the conceptualization of seeing or not seeing the two is untenable."
—*Anekāntajaya*, fol. 35B.

If it is argued that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), while not projecting its own form externally, determines an external object, and thus has as its object something external to its own form—as it is said: "Activity proceeds by determining an object within one's own manifestation, which is not an object"—then what is this "determination" (*adhyavasāya*)? Is it grasping, or production, or conjunction, or superimposition (*samāropa*)? Among these, how could conceptual construction grasp or produce its own manifestation, which is not an object, as if it were an object?
For it is not possible for even a hundred artisans to apprehend yellow as blue;
nor can a conceptual construction (vikalpa) associate its own form with a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) that has not been apprehended,
and it has already been established that the particular characteristic is not the object of conceptual construction.
—Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 485;
*dhāraṇa* according to the Jaina doctrine.

If the production of objects were to occur through the mere cognition of them, then from the mere knowledge of an incalculable number of silver coins, an incalculable amount of silver would be produced, and the entire world would be wealthy.
Alternatively, if it is argued that conceptual thought joins its own internal form with an external object—that is incorrect; for such a perception is impossible.

For no one has such a cognition as: "This form of mine is qualified by an external object. This is because, due to the absence of any relation between one’s own form and an external object, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is untenable. Nor should it be asserted that there exists for this [form] a relationship of "arising from that" (tadutpatti) through a mediated succession; for it has been refuted that an object with a distinct (vyāvṛtta) form can be the cause of the reflection of a continuous (anuvṛtta) form. [End of fragment] svākāravikāśa-... [fragmentary]
— Because of the non-existence of the form of conceptual construction (vikalpākāra) [in the absence of its object], according to the marginal note (ṭīkā) of Ārya;
[this refers to] the own-form (svākāra) and the external object.

The external object has the nature of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); from that arises non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), and from that arises conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*). Thus, there is a relationship of origination between the conceptual and the object through this succession—Āloka-ṭīkā. For indeed, a continuous form does not arise from a differentiated form—Āloka-ṭīkā. Now, if it is argued that conceptual cognition superimposes the external object onto its own form, that too is incorrect; for superimposition would occur only if both [the object and the cognition] were apprehended, or if neither were? It cannot be the latter, because superimposition is preceded by the apprehension of both.

Whatever is a superimposition (*samāropa*) is preceded by the apprehension of both [the object and the locus], just as the superimposition of "cow" upon a *vāhīka* (a person from the Punjab). Furthermore, the superimposition of an external object occurs upon the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*);

thus, this illustration is not deficient in respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). For it is precisely one who has experienced both the cow and the *vāhīka* who, having ascertained such properties as the carrying of heavy loads in the *vāhīka*, superimposes "cowness" (*gotva*), thinking, "The *vāhīka* is a cow."

Now, if there were a grasping of both, there would be superimposition (*āropa*). But surely, this grasping of both must occur either through conceptualization (*vikalpa*) or through non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*)? It cannot be through non-conceptualization, because since its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is impossible for it to function toward the form of a conceptual construction whose nature is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Nor can it be through conceptualization, because the latter is turned away from the apprehension of external objects. Therefore, how could it superimpose the external upon its own form, or its own form upon that [external]?
For superimposition consists in one thing being placed upon another.

The superimposition of an external object upon the form of conceptual construction does not constitute a [true] superimposition, because it is preceded by the apprehension of both [the internal and the external]; for example,
there are those called Śrāṇartikas who are Vāhīkas, and their conduct is thoroughly censured.
—Mahābhārata, Karṇaparvan, Chapter 200:
In the vernacular, the word *jāṭa* is used;
just as the word "cow" (*go*) has as its referent the Vāhīka person, based on qualities such as dullness (*jāḍya*).
— Mahābhārata, Prathamaparvan 1.1.15

Comparison: If it is argued that "who indeed determines that the object of perception is nothing but conceptual construction? It is conceptual construction itself," we say no, because a universal (sāmānya) appears therein; otherwise, its status as a conceptual construction would be untenable.
If it is argued that "it is something else," we say no, because that would entail the doctrine of a self (ātmavāda), and because there is no basis for such a determination [of an external object].
Even the determination of oneness never touches the perceptible object; otherwise,
the conceptual construction would directly possess the quality of touching the perceptible.

"Indeed, perception determines that unity; the subsequent determination, or another cognition, follows it"—*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p. 53. "That is to say, perception determines that unity; the determination arising after it, or another cognition [does so]"—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 109.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 31;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pṛṣṭha 500;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 82.

Because non-conceptual [cognition] has a non-entity as its object— [Ānandajñāna’s] Commentary (ā॰ ṭi॰)— since it is oriented toward the prior reflective awareness (parāmarśa).— [Abhinavagupta’s] Explanation (śra॰)

Let it be that conceptual construction (vikalpa) apprehends both [itself and the external object]; nevertheless, does it first experience its own appearance as a non-object and subsequently superimpose the object upon it, or does it simultaneously experience its own appearance and superimpose the object? Or rather, is it the case that what is meant by "experiencing its own form" is precisely what is meant by "determining the object"? It cannot be that there is first an experience of its own nature and subsequently the superimposition of the object, because cognitions cannot persist for two moments; otherwise, the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) would be undermined.

Now, if one simultaneously experiences one's own appearance and superimposes the object upon it, then, while the nature of conceptual construction—which consists of the forms of the grasped and the grasper—is being experienced, the object being superimposed exists at the very same time as that self-experience as something external to the nature of the conceptual construction itself. How, then, could this [conceptual construction] superimpose what is not an object (anartha) as an object? Furthermore, if the superimposition of the object is merely the experience of its own form, that too is unsatisfactory, because there is a difference between that which is to be experienced and that which is to be conceptually constructed.

For a nature conjoined with words must be conceptualized, whereas a nature unconjoined with words must be experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); how, then, can there be identity between these two? [Comparison:
Nor does the cognition superimpose its own form—which is not the object—upon the object;
for it is impossible to superimpose a form that has not first been apprehended, and thus the apprehension of that form must be admitted.
Does one grasp [the object] and then superimpose [the conceptual construction], or does one grasp it and superimpose it at the very same moment?
It cannot be the first alternative, for a conceptual cognition, being momentary, is incapable of performing the two successive acts of grasping and superimposing.

As for the second alternative, since the conceptual construction being superimposed lacks the status of "I" (anahaṅkārāspada), whereas the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of the conceptual cognition—which possesses the form of that conceptualization—is the locus of "I," it is impossible to apprehend them as non-different, because the superimposed conceptual construction is not within the range of that [self-awareness].

Nor can it be apprehended as identical with the external particular (*bāhya-svalakṣaṇa*) by conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), because the external particular does not appear [in that cognition]—*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 485; [referring to] the previously appearing object—*Śrāmaṇya*.
The meaning is that the very experience of its own form (*svākārānubhavana*) is the determination of the object (*arthādhyavasāya*).
[Otherwise,] there would be the consequence of a total collapse of all logical categories.

If, at the very moment when a conceptual construction (vikalpa) experiences its own appearance—an object that is not real—it simultaneously superimposes [that appearance] upon the real object, then, because the conceptual construction is occupied with experiencing itself, the object finds no opportunity and remains entirely outside the nature of that construction; it does not transfer into the construction. Therefore, how could the form of the conceptual construction superimpose an object upon itself when it is itself non-existent? This is the intended meaning—*ā॰ ṭi॰*; the meaning is "upon itself, which is non-existent."

By this, the argument that "the perceived and the conceptualized are unified and superimposed as having an external form," and so forth, is refuted. Furthermore, is this unification effected by that very same cognition, or by another cognition? It cannot be by that very same cognition, for it does not perceive its own form and the perceived object separately and then realize their identity, since such a perception does not occur; moreover, because of [the cognition's] momentariness, it cannot be by another cognition either. For would that other cognition be one or many? If it were many, how could it realize identity? For the nature of the cognition is perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), whereas the perceived object is perceived through the act of seeing (*darśana*).
