But if it perceives two as one, how can there be unity? Or if it perceives unity, how can there be duality, given the contradiction? (p.
555, l. 5). For comparison: "This is not [the case] by means of unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object through their distinction..."
And because there is no single cognizer, those two [subject and object] are not established as real entities—
Śāstravārttika 1.10.
Because it is impossible to superimpose non-existence upon that which has passed away by virtue of its being of that nature—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p.
320; *pramityabhāva*, manuscript *ba*.
Furthermore, due to momentariness, nothing exists [to be apprehended].

Moreover, is this exclusion (apoha) perceived as belonging to an entity within another entity, or is it perceived alone? Regarding the first alternative, is the cognition of the two entities derived from the word itself or from another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? It cannot be from the word itself, because it is not admitted that this [word] functions with respect to anything other than the exclusion.

Or, if you do accept this, do you hold that the exclusion (*apoha*) is perceived by depending on two positive entities (*bhāva*), or that the two positive entities are perceived by depending on the exclusion? Regarding the first alternative, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) cannot be the primary meaning of a word, because the meaning consists primarily of the two positive entities themselves; for the exclusion of others is understood only through implication (*sāmarthya*) after the [entities] have been perceived—just as one understands the exclusion of the non-blue upon perceiving "blue. If one were to maintain that the perception of the blue occurs by depending on the perception of the exclusion of the non-blue, then that perception would be faltering.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the blue is perceived from the word just as it is from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, as being essentially the exclusion of the non-blue.

In the second alternative, however, there is a contradiction with experience; for indeed, there is not even a dream-experience of anyone to the effect that "first the mere exclusion (*apoha*) is cognized from the word, and afterwards the two entities. By this, its cognition through any other means of knowledge is also rejected; because even in the case of their cognition through that [other means], the aforementioned defects would apply without distinction. Or, let it be granted that there is some way for this [exclusion] to be cognized; nevertheless, if exclusion is cognized as distinct from the two entities, how could it have a relationship with those entities? For a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is impossible between existence and non-existence.

Comparison: "And as for this exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which is the meaning of the word 'cow'—namely, that 'it is not a non-cow'—is that a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negation (*abhāva*)? (Nyāyavārttika, p. 329). [The marginal note *āṭi* explains:
This refers to the case where the word functions toward a positive entity distinct from the exclusion (*apoha*).

Since "being" (bhāva) is primarily the meaning of the word "existence" (bhāva)— according to the Āloka commentary— its specific, unique nature is indeed constituted by the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti).
The cognition of the exclusion of non-blue, because it is dependent upon the cognition of the exclusion of other [things]. (Note: *anyavyāvṛttipratīti* = the cognition of the exclusion of others.)
The cognition of a person engaged in worldly transaction (vyavahārin), according to the Bhaṭṭa school; there is cognition, according to the Śrāvaka school;
[there is] the cognition of both existence and non-existence.
—[The opponent asks: "What is the purpose [of the suffix] -tiḥ?
— [The author replies: Because there is no contradiction with the connection (anuṣaṅga) of the exclusion (apoha). Ba. [This is the reading of manuscript Ba.]

This position—that a mere exclusion (apoha) is cognized as an exclusion—is also refuted by this very same argument. Furthermore, if a mere exclusion were cognized from a word or a logical mark (liṅga), then all words would become synonyms, because the mere exclusion, being indistinguishable, would be expressed by every word without exception.

Consequently, distinctions such as those between qualifier and qualified, distinctions of time such as past and so forth, distinctions of gender such as feminine, masculine, and neuter, and distinctions of number such as singular, dual, and plural would be impossible.

Furthermore, the distinction between the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin) would be utterly discarded; for that which is denoted by the word "sign"—namely, mere apoha—would also be what is denoted by the word "signified.
Consequently, all words expressing distinct universals as well as those expressing particulars would become synonyms, provided that apoha is the denotable object.

Furthermore, according to your view, words such as "cow" (*go*) and others which denote distinct universals (*sāmānya*), and words such as "Śābaleya" and others which denote particulars (*viśeṣa*), would become synonyms because there is no difference in their referents, just like the words "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and "peda-pāda" (*pādapa*). (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda, verse 42; Nyāyamañjarī, p. 304)
—Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
433; Prameyaratnakośa, 3.101.

Thus, [if] it is accepted that in words such as "blue lotus," which denote variegated objects, there is the denotability of mere exclusion (*apoha*) alone— [this is the view of] Viśeṣa and Śrā. (Compare with the corresponding passage).

The establishment of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, as well as co-referentiality, is not possible; for when "non-blue" is excluded, there is no exclusion of "non-lotus"— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Apoha section, verses 115–16.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 436.
Compare: "The relationship of gender, number, and so forth does not exist for the *apoha*;
because the individual (*vyakti*) is inexpressible, that [relationship] does not exist even by means of it."
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda, verse 135.
Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because a distinction among exclusions (*apoha*) is admitted, that is incorrect, because such a distinction is unestablished.

For its distinction would have to arise either from the distinction of the excluded objects (*apohya*), from the distinction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), from being produced by different causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), from performing different functions, from a distinction of substratum (*āśraya*), or from a distinction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). It cannot first be due to the distinction of the excluded objects; for since words such as "all" (*sarva*) and "knowable" (*prameya*) lack a distinction of excluded objects, they would consequently become synonyms.

For nothing that is non-all exists apart from the aggregate of all things, nor is there anything immeasurable by which "all" and so forth could be established through exclusion (*apoha*). Furthermore, how could the reason (*hetu*) such as "existence" or "being produced" be established? Indeed, there is nothing in the world that is non-existent or unproduced by means of whose exclusion the proof of existence and so forth could be established. Moreover, if the distinction between exclusions depends on the distinction between the objects to be excluded (*apohya*), there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): for the distinction between exclusions is established only when the distinction between the objects to be excluded is established, and the distinction between the objects to be excluded is established only when the distinction between the exclusions is established.
Therefore, there is no differentiation of the exclusion (*apoha*) based on the differentiation of the objects to be excluded,
nor is it based on a differentiation of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), because that differentiation of impressions is itself untenable;
for a differentiation of impressions is necessarily grounded in a differentiation of experience, and since the exclusion is of a single uniform nature, a differentiation of experience is impossible.

Nor can there be a distinction between exclusions (*apoha*) based on their arising from distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), because it is logically impossible for this [exclusion]—being of an imagined nature—to manifest from a specific causal complex.

Whatever is of an imagined nature does not arise from anything, just like a horn on the head of a horse; and since, according to your view, the exclusion is of an imagined nature, if it were to arise [from a cause], its status as an imagined nature would be contradicted.

Whatever arises from some cause is not of an imagined nature, just like a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and yet, exclusion (*apoha*) arises from a particular causal complex (*sāmagrīviśeṣa*).
[The opponent’s] comparison is as follows: "But surely, because exclusions are distinct, this consequence is not tenable;
if you posit a universal-exclusion (*sāmānyāpoha*), then for you it would be the same as a mere entity (*vastumātra*)."
Because they are my own entities, universals are mutually distinct and possess unmixed natures; they do not extend a state of oneness,
for their essence is free from the conceptual constructions of either combined unity or plurality.
Since exclusions (*apoha*) are non-entities, how could there be any difference between them for you? — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Apohavāda, verses 43–45.
Regarding exclusion (*apoha*).
Because they arise from distinct causal complexes, there is no [intrinsic] connection.
Cf. *Anyāpohaśca śabdārtha ityayuktam*, because it is not universally applicable (*avyāpakatvāt*):
where a duality exists, there the one is cognized through the negation of the other; as in the word "cow," when the cow is cognized, the non-cow is being excluded.
Furthermore, this [term] "all" does not exist as a distinct entity; for there is nothing whatsoever called "non-all" that could be excluded by the term "all"—*Nyāyavārttika*, p.
329. But surely, the distinction of exclusion (*apoha*) will be established through the distinction of its objects of exclusion?
Its distinction is not intrinsic, nor is it extrinsic; it is merely figurative.
But how could there even be an object of negation for words such as "the knowable" or "the cognizable"?
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda section, verses 47 and 144; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 434; Prameyaratnakośa, 3.

Comparison: Although other words may have something to be excluded (apohya) as their referent, for the word "existent" (sat), nothing distinct from what is called non-existence (abhāva) is intended to be the exclusion.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda, verse 98:

"Or else, if there were difference, another [exclusion] would [be required]; [furthermore], the postulation of a distinction among the things to be excluded (apohya) could not occur because there is no difference among absences."
If it is argued that the distinction between those [exclusions] arises from the distinction between the exclusions themselves, then a mutual dependency is reached:
because the universal "cow" is distinct, the term "non-cow" is distinguished; and by means of the distinction of the term "non-cow," the universal "cow" is distinguished.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda, verses 65–66; Nyāyamañjarī, p. 304. Compare:
"Nor [is there] a distinction [of the universal] due to a difference in mental impressions (vāsanā), nor even its existence as a real entity."
Exclusion (apoha) cannot be conceptualized, for there is no latent impression (vāsanā) regarding a non-entity;
nor does it possess the capacity for connection with another operation, except through memory.
Therefore, it does not produce a cognition of one kind regarding an object of a different kind.
Even a difference in words caused by that [exclusion] cannot be found by you—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Apohavāda, verses 100–2; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 439.
Even the experience of that distinction [is untenable],
because the distinction between latent impressions (*vāsanā*), being of the nature of non-existence, would have a single, void essence.
Because the distinction of exclusion (*apoha*) is imagined; because the manifestation of exclusion is impossible.
In the Buddhist view, exclusion (apoha) does not arise from anything because it is of an imagined nature; [this would be the case] if exclusion were produced from a causal complex.
Apoha is not imagined because it arises from a cause;

by this, its distinction [from other things] based on performing distinct functions is refuted. For it is impossible for that which is not ultimately real to perform distinct functions, like a sky-flower;
or, if it were to perform such functions, its lack of ultimate reality would be untenable, just as in the case of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, from what source is the difference between cause and effect established, such that—on account of that difference—the difference of the *apoha* might be established? Is it through a difference in the *apoha*, or by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*)? If it were through a difference in the *apoha*, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for only when the difference between cause and effect is established could the difference of the *apoha* be established, since the *apoha* is produced by and caused by them; and only when that [difference of the *apoha*] is established could the difference between cause and effect be established. Moreover, if that difference were established by its own nature, the conceptualization of the *apoha* would be useless, as the difference of the *apoha* [would be redundant].
And regarding the capacity for causal efficiency, there is no other [distinction] than the difference between effects.
By virtue of arising from distinct causes,
by virtue of being their effect,
and by virtue of performing distinct functions.
Or, if the distinction between cause and effect were established,

[one might argue] that the exclusion (apoha) differs due to the difference in its substrata; that is not so, because it is impossible for this, which is non-substantial in nature, to be dependent upon anything whatsoever.

That which is of the nature of a non-entity is not dependent upon anything, just as a sky-lotus; and since apoha is of the nature of a non-entity, if it were indeed dependent, would it be distinct with respect to each individual instance or non-distinct? If it were distinct, then it would have to be accepted as being one of the forms of substance, quality, or action, because it is impossible for anything other than these to be dependent upon each individual instance.
If, on the other hand, it were non-distinct, then it would simply be the nature of a universal expressed by another name. Thus, in both cases, the nature of apoha as a distinct entity is untenable.
Comparison: Even by means of that very difference in substratum, its differentiation is not tenable;

for even in the case of a real entity, differentiation is not admitted on the basis of a difference in its relata, much less in the case of a non-entity which is unconnected and not excluded from anything else.
"Since no specific excellence has been attained, it is something entirely undetermined"—
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Apohavāda, verses 48–49.
"Apoha is not dependent on anything, because its nature is that of a non-entity."

Substances, qualities, and actions alone must be the substrata of the universal that is the nature of exclusion (apoha), because the universal resides in these three categories— substance and the rest—
and so does exclusion.

Now, if it is argued that the exclusion (*apoha*) is differentiated by a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*), that is not so; for if it lacks ultimate reality (*aparamārthasat*), a difference in its own nature is untenable. Whatever lacks ultimate reality has no difference in its own nature, as in the case of a sky-flower, a donkey’s horn, and the like; and since exclusion is [claimed to be] lacking ultimate reality, if it were to possess a difference in its own nature, it would follow that it possesses ultimate reality, just like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
There is no difference in the essential nature of exclusion (apoha) or non-exclusion, because this [exclusion] lacks ultimate reality.
The comparison of *apoha*: "Or rather, because it is differentiated, like the unique [particulars] of a real entity;
for if it were a non-entity, there would be no plurality"—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Apoha section, verse 46.

Furthermore, would the *apoha*—whether in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) or an absolute negation (*prasajya*)—be denoted by words as something distinct in its own nature? If it were in the form of a relative negation, then it must be admitted that it has the nature of another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*).

And that other entity would have to be either a particular (*viśeṣa*), a universal (*sāmānya*), a particular characterized by that [universal], or the collection of those two. Thus, in all four of these positions, the meaning of the word would be a positive injunction (*vidhi*) alone, not an exclusion (*apoha*).
Now, if it is of the nature of a *prasajya* (absolute negation), then only a mere negation would be expressed by words; and that is improper because such is not how [the object] is perceived.

For the employment of words is for the purpose of communicating to another; and the other person, seeking blue, does not desire to know a mere negation of non-blue. Furthermore, for one who communicates what has not been sought to be known, there follows the consequence of acting without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakāritva*).

Moreover, when the universal called *apoha* is stated as the denotable meaning, would it be stated as having the character of a *paryudāsa* (relative negation) or the character of a *prasajya*? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 432.
It is designated as the object of cognition (prameya). (Prameyaratnāvalī 3.101) [Variant readings:
ba, śra]
Just as a jar, being distinct from a cloth by its very nature, is a different entity—[as noted in the *Āloka-ṭīkā*: "A comparison:

'The universal consisting in the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago-nivṛtti*) which is postulated by some as the denotable object—by them, it is clearly stated that "cowness" (*gotva*) is indeed a real entity (*vastu*), though expressed by the term "exclusion of the non-cow" (*agopoha*).']"
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Apohavāda, verse 1; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 432. For comparison: "But surely, in your position, it has been described that a word effects the exclusion of others (anyāpoha)."
In this case, mere negation is not understood in the manifestation;
rather, verbal cognition proceeds by determining a positive form through words such as "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," "tree," and so forth.
In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 910–11;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 432;
[the text] desires to know (*jijñāsati*). *Ba*.

Furthermore, if [the words] were to denote mere exclusion (*niṣedhamātra*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "blue" and "lotus" would not be established. For the word "blue" would have its purpose exhausted merely by the exclusion of what is non-blue, and the word "lotus" likewise by the exclusion of what is non-lotus;
yet these two exclusions cannot be related to a single substratum (*dharmin*), because a relationship such as identity (*tādātmya*) is impossible between existence and non-existence.
Nor can those two words have a single substratum as their object, since—unlike the words "pot" and "cloth"—it is not admitted that these two have a single substratum as their object.
Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of two words with distinct causes [of application] in a single substratum—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.64.
For comparison: "And for one for whom the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it must be explained how the exclusions of 'non-blue' and 'non-lotus' can be co-referential."

Furthermore, for one who maintains that the meaning of a word is something being enjoined, a substance qualified by genus and quality is denoted by the two words "blue" and "lotus"; the genus and the quality reside in the substance, and not in the exclusion of the non-blue and the non-lotus. Therefore, there is no such thing as co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
— *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 331;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 305.

Furthermore, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two exclusions (*apoha*) because they are distinct; nor is this [coreferentiality] accepted on the basis of their referents. What kind of "inherence" could there be for those two?
Moreover, neither a unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-vastu*) is perceived, nor does anything else exist for you.
Of what use is the identity of meaning between two words when it is not being understood?
— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Apohavāda, verses 118–19; *Anekāntajayapatākā*, p. 40.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 436:
The subject (*dharmin*) is of the nature of existence, while the exclusions (*vyavaccheda*) of non-blue and non-lotus—namely, "blue" and "lotus"—are of the nature of non-existence.
These are the words [denoting] "the blue lotus."
“The object is the jar” (ā॰).

For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the application of two words with different bases of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single referent (ā॰ ṭi॰). Furthermore, it is only the negative particle (*nañ*) that functions either as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or as a simple negation (*prasajya*); however, this [word] “cow” (*gaur*) is not a negative particle. Therefore, how could the word “cow” function through the exclusion of a non-cow? This is because it operates solely in the form of an affirmation, as in “This is a cow.”
Therefore, one must accept that the object of a word is a referent (*artha*) consisting of both the universal and the particular; there is no point in denying this established perception.

Furthermore, since it is well known that such a referent persists through the time of the convention and the time of its practical application, making a convention regarding a *svalakṣaṇa* (particular) of this nature would be futile.
As for the *svalakṣaṇa* imagined by you, it has already been refuted in detail during the examination of the Sugata’s doctrine; thus, making a convention with respect to that is indeed fruitless.

Therefore, [the argument] beginning with "that which does not follow through the times of convention and usage" and so forth should be disregarded, because it proves what is already established (siddhasādhanatva)—
[the reading] "the application of words" (śabdapravṛttiḥ) [is found in] Ba and Śra, while [the reading] "or its occurrence" (vāsya vartta-) [is found in] Ā.
The convention regarding an object that consists of both the universal and the particular is fruitless with respect to that which consists of both the universal and the particular.
Regarding the momentary particular (kṣaṇika-svalakṣaṇa) imagined by the followers of the Sugata, page 379.

The establishment of the convention (saṅketakaraṇa) and the relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakayoḥ sambandha) are cognized through the means of valid cognition called inference by presumption (ūha), because the cognition of the relationship everywhere depends upon that [presumption].

Therefore, the following statement is also incorrect: "In the cognition that establishes the relation 'this is the name of this [object],' there is no manifestation of the word and the object, which are the respective domains of specific sense faculties. This is because it is logically consistent for the word and the object—which consist of both the universal and the particular—to be the objects of specific sense faculties; so how could there be an absence of their manifestation in the cognition that produces that [relation]? (See *Ūha*, p. 553, l. 4).

"Furthermore, regarding the maker of conventions, since we observe the occurrence of activity even in the absence of an object for words referring to past or future things—and for expressions such as 'there are heaps of sweetmeats on the riverbank'—how can a necessary connection with an object be established for them? This too is an unexamined statement; for we do not maintain that all words are invariably concomitant with an object, but rather only those whose authors are well-ascertained and trustworthy.

Nor is it logical to conclude that all words are deviant from their objects simply because some words are seen to be so; for if the non-validity of perception—which manifests water and the like in a mirage—is observed, it would follow that even this same perception, when manifesting real water and the like, must be non-valid. To argue that the non-validity belongs only to the perception manifesting water in a mirage because a sublater (bādhaka) exists there, and not to the other, applies equally elsewhere as well.
Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between perception and verbal testimony regarding their having ultimate reality as their object.
The Jains [hold that] there is no obstruction of those sounds.
Comparison—We do not indeed accept the validity of all words; rather, we accept that validity only for those whose authors are well-ascertained and trustworthy.
We do not perceive any difference between perception and verbal testimony regarding that validity.
—*Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 6.
The state of being invariably concomitant with the object belongs to the cognition of water produced by those who are not untrustworthy authors.
Therefore, this [argument] is refuted: "The object of the senses is indeed something else," and so forth.

For a difference in appearance does not establish a difference in the object, since such a difference is possible even when the object is non-different, due to the specificities of its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), as in the case of people looking at an object situated at a distance or nearby with their vision.

For just as a tree or similar object, though itself undifferentiated, becomes the object of distinct appearances due to the specific conditions of distance, proximity, and so forth, so too, although verbal and perceptual cognitions have the same object, the difference between their indistinct and clear appearances—arising from the difference in the causal complexes of word, sense-organ, and so on—does not entail any contradiction. Therefore, since a difference in appearance is logically established for both the blind and the sighted even regarding the same object due to the difference in their causal complexes, it is incorrect to say: "One with impaired vision cognizes [the object] through words, but does not perceive it directly."

Comparison: Nor does the difference in appearance between the perception of the apprehender and its memory imply an absence of non-difference in the nature of the object, just as in the case of the objects of the cognitions of two persons—one situated near and the other distant—both directed toward the same single object at once.

For just as when two persons, one near and one distant, simultaneously direct their vision toward a single object such as a tree, there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that tree despite the difference in the clarity and lack of clarity of its appearance in their respective cognitions—since it does not deviate from its oneness—so too, although there is a difference between the two apprehending [cognitions], namely the appearances of perception and memory, there is no difference in their object because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is admitted to have a single nature;
for the difference in the two modes of apprehension arises from the difference in the instruments [of cognition]. (Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 124)
For from sound, a cognition whose object is form arises for one who is blind, but not a visual cognition;
and he who possesses immediate visual cognition is not blind—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 586.

Furthermore, the distinction in the appearance of an object as clear or unclear is not contradictory, given the difference in the causal complex [of cognition], just like the appearance of an object connected to the senses at a distance or nearby—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 446;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 259.
*Syādvādamañjarī*, folio 715;
*Pratibhāsabheda*, folio 553, line 10.

Furthermore, as for the other statement—that the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) is not distinct from the relationship between cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*), and so forth—that too is untenable. For, if there were a reflection (*pratibimba*) associated with the intellect, then that reflection would be the signified because it is produced by the word, and the word would be the signifier because it produces it. But that is not the case, since this [reflection] has already been refuted at length.

Furthermore, if the relationship of denoter and denoted were simply the relationship of cause and effect, then even though a word appears in auditory cognition, it would indeed be the cause of its own appearance; consequently, that [appearance] too would be a denoter.

Moreover, just as a word is the cause of a conceptual construction (vikalpa), so too is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) indirectly its cause; therefore, that [particular characteristic] too would be a denoter.
Thus, the established order of the specific relationship between denoter and denoted would be destroyed.

Therefore, whatever appears in an uncontradicted cognition in a certain manner, that must be accepted as being exactly so in that context; just as pleasure appears in its aspect of refreshing gratification, so too does an external object such as a jar appear in an uncontradicted verbal cognition as having the nature of both universal and particular (sāmānya-viśeṣātmaka). (Chap.

By this much, it is established that for the reflection residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), the effect is the signified and the cause is the signifier— [this is] the reflection in the intellect (*buddhau pratibimbam*). (Ānandajñāna’s Commentary)
—The manifestation in cognition (*jñānapratibhāsa*).
According to the Śrāvakas and Vaibhāṣikas, sound is the cause of non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpakapratyakṣa*); for they accept that "that which is not a cause is not an object.

For comparison: if the relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) were nothing other than the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), then since sound appearing in auditory cognition is indeed the cause of its own manifestation, that [sound] would also be the denoter of that [manifestation].

And just as the word is the cause of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through a traditional succession, so too is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, that too would be expressive—[as stated in] the *Ratnākara* (4.11).
[The particular characteristic is the cause] of its own appearance—[Ārya-ṭīkā].

For, according to your view, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the cause of the expressive word, since the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) that grasps the word arises from the particular characteristic, and from that [non-conceptual cognition] the conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) arises; or else, since the non-conceptual cognition arises from the particular characteristic and from that the conceptual cognition arises,
the particular characteristic itself would be expressive by virtue of being a cause.
Since it follows that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be denoted,

an object appears in verbal cognition precisely as consisting of both the universal and the particular; for in that case, it is the object of an uncontradicted cognitive apprehension exactly in that manner, [as stated] in the *Śabda-pratyaya* (Śrā., Ba.).
Comparison: "The denotatum of a word may be manifold or unitary"—*Bṛhatsvavṛtti*, verse 44;
"The denotatum is necessarily either manifold or of a single nature, and the denoter is likewise of a dual nature"—*Anyayogavyavacchedadvātriṃśikā*, verse 14.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsaka—that a word denotes only the universal (*sāmānyamātra*)—is as follows:

It is unestablished that an external object such as a jar appears in verbal cognition by virtue of having the nature of both the universal and the particular; for since words function solely within the domain of the universal, it is logical that the cognition produced by them should have only that [universal] as its object.

For the object of words is indeed only the universal (*sāmānyamātra*), because it is possible for that which has been apprehended in one instance to be the referent of a convention everywhere due to its uniform nature; however, particulars (*viśeṣa*) are not [the object], because they are infinite and thus impossible to perceive in their entirety, making it impossible for them to be the referents [of conventions]. If it is argued that a convention is established only for as many [particulars] as are perceived, then, since a convention would be impossible regarding other particulars, linguistic usage (*śābdavyavahāra*) would be untenable.

Furthermore, for a non-yogi cognizer, the perception of every single particularity in its entirety—whether simultaneously or sequentially—is impossible, as that would entail the contradiction of being a non-yogi.
As for a yogi, since they are the subject of dispute, their perception is set aside entirely.

And when those [particularities] are unperceived, it is impossible to establish a convention characterized by the rule of understanding the signifier and the signified—namely, "this is the signifier of this" and "this is the signified. In the absence of such a convention, the comprehension of meaning upon hearing a word is untenable; thus, the cessation of verbal communication is established.
Therefore, by one who desires that linguistic usage, a convention must be admitted with respect to the mere universal; consequently, that alone is established as the meaning of a word.
As for the configuration (*ākṛti*), however, it is [the object of the word] because it serves the purpose of action—Jaimini-sūtra 1.3.33.
But the word "tu" (but/however) excludes other positions; [the view that] the meaning of a word is the generic form (*ākṛti*)—Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5.1.

3.33 According to the Mīmāṃsakas, by the word *ākṛti* (form), only the genus (*jāti*) is intended; for it is said: "They call the genus itself the form (*ākṛti*), by which the individual (*vyakti*) is formed."
And that generality is the basis for the single cognition of individual objects;
whatever serves as its cause is the object of the word "generality."
Let it be designated as the universal (sāmānya), the form (ākṛti), the genus (jāti), or the power (śakti).

If a single entity indeed possesses multiple forms, then a word expressing it in such a way would not be expressive of the universal alone; therefore he says: "And not," meaning that no word whatsoever is capable of expressing it in such a manner. (63)
"Having extracted the universal, every word functions"— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Ākṛtivāda, verses 3–4, 18,
63; for prior to the cognition of the universal, a variegated cognition does not arise.

From the sentence "Bring the cow," because one accepts [the meaning] according to one's preference, it is understood that when the word "cow" is uttered, the universal (*sāmānya*) is first cognized even before the individuals have been grasped; subsequently, after the cognition of that form has arisen, the individuals are cognized. Therefore, since there is no other cause for the cognition of the form, and since the cognition of the individuals is caused by the universal previously perceived, it is determined that the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of the word.

Furthermore, if the individuals were the denotable objects, then because their specific forms—such as being variegated, hornless, or shorn—would be grasped, the cognition upon the utterance of the word would be manifold.

However, since it arises with a single form, it is determined that the *ākṛti* (form) is the meaning of the word; for when one is commanded, "Bring a cow," in the absence of any specific purpose or context, one brings some individual (*vyakti*) endowed with the universal (*sāmānya*), but not every individual, nor a specifically distinguished one.
And if the individual were the denotation, then because all individuals would be denoted simultaneously, either all of them would have to be brought,

or else only that single one which is denoted would be brought; however, since they are brought without distinction as being merely connected with the universal, it is thereby understood that the universal is the word-meaning—
*Tantravārttika* 1.3.33.
3.33 Because of non-occurrence and non-deviation, there is the fault of having multiple potencies.
Because of doubt, because of the final cognition, because of the absence of a variegated cognition,
and because of the perception of a single form through positive and negative concomitance,
it is that very *ākṛti* which is denotable by the first cognition.
Furthermore, because the individual and the form are non-different, their utility for linguistic usage—
such as the connection with gender and number, and the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality—
is entirely consistent for one who maintains the doctrine of the manifold nature of reality (*anekāntavāda*).
— Śāstradīpikā 1.3.35
Existence itself, being differentiated according to its various relata in cows and other things,
is called a "universal" (jāti); all words are established as denoting that [existence]— Vākyapadīya 3.1.33.
Originating from sound—[Ācārya]Ṭīkā;
by way of being the object—Baṅga.
Of that universal— [as indicated by] the marginal note (ā॰ ṭi॰)—
in a particular individual.
This applies even to infinite individuals—
because it is established that [the universal] is the object of the word; such is the connection.
For it is not possible to comprehend the state of being denotable with respect to infinite individual instances— *Śāstradīpikā* 1.3.1.3.
Together with the *Saṅketābhismaraṇī-ṭīkā*,
in sequence, manuscript Ba.
The sense is that if there were perception of every individual instance, there would indeed be omniscience;
for the Mīmāṃsaka does not accept an omniscient being—
[this refers to] the perception of its [the universal's] instances (ā॰ ṭi॰).
Regarding particulars— [Ācārya’s Commentary]—
the expression "to be denoted" [in the root text];
[Śrīdhara’s Commentary]— in the absence of convention characterized by the fixed rule of the understanding of the signifier and the signified— [Ācārya’s Commentary].
The object of verbal expression is well-known to be the universal alone— Ācārya’s Commentary (ā॰ ṭi॰), Sub-commentary (sāmānyameva— Ācārya’s Commentary), and Śrī [Vimalaprabhā] (śra॰).

Furthermore, for those who maintain that the meaning of a word is a particular qualified by a genus (*jāti*), does the word denote the individual after having denoted the genus, or without having denoted it? It cannot be the former; for since its capacity would be exhausted solely in the cognition of the particularity characterized by the genus, the consequence follows that it could not convey the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
And it has been said: "In the cognition of the characteristic... (*lakṣaṇapratipatti-*)... [fragment].
—*Lakṣaṇaviśeṣaṇapra* [śastā]. Quoted in *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 191;
*Kāvyaprakāśa*, p. 44.
*Muktāvalī*, p.
373; *Kāvyānuśāsana*, p. 25:
*Abhidhā* is the power of the word; it does not go to, that is, it does not reach, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
To address the doubt as to why this is so, he says: "kṣīṇa" (exhausted).
After the phrase "the power of the qualifier is exhausted," the word "sat" (being) should be supplied.

Thus, the final meaning is that since the power of the word is exhausted—meaning its capacity is spent—upon reaching the qualifier, the denotation (*abhidhā*) does not go to, nor reach, the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
"The denotation [of a word] cannot proceed to the qualified object once its power is exhausted with respect to the qualifier;
therefore, that is the primary meaning, and the primary function of the word toward it is called 'denotation' (abhidhā)."

Nor can it be said that [the word] does not denote [the universal], because this would entail the consequence that it does not denote that which possesses the genus (*jātimat*), since it would be conveying only the particular (*viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, one must not argue that if only the general property (*sāmānyamātra*) were denoted by the denotative words, then activity toward the particulars would not result from the word for one seeking a purpose, because that mere [general property] which is apprehended from it does not accomplish the purpose. This is because the apprehension of the particulars is possible through the fact that the apprehension of that [general property] would otherwise be inexplicable.

For initially, only the universal (*sāmānya*) is cognized from the word; subsequently, by the principle of "presumption based on what is otherwise inexplicable" (*arthāpatti*), the specific individual (*piṇḍaviśeṣa*) is cognized through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because a universal without a substratum is impossible, like a horse's horn.
And it has been said: "The denotation... [fragment of verse].
From the word—
[according to the Āloka commentary]— of the universal alone— [according to the Āloka commentary]— by virtue of the impossibility of the cognition of the universal otherwise.
For if "cowness" (gotva) were not denoted, the restriction of usage to the individual cow (*govyakti*) alone could not be established by means of it as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*);
since that [cowness] is indeed denoted, it is proven that the word's meaning is the form (*ākṛti*).
— *Tantravārttika* 1.3.9.10.
For it is not possible to denote an individual by way of its belonging to a certain class without first denoting that class.
Consequently, what results is merely the denotation of a qualified entity through a different mode of expression, rather than the denotation of the pure [entity] itself.
And when there is the denotation of a qualified entity, the qualifier must be denoted first;

and since the cognition of the individual, which is absolutely inseparable from it, is established by that very [denotation of the qualifier], there is no occasion to postulate a denotative power for that [individual].
— Śāstradīpikā 1.3.35
Regarding indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he says: "Therefore, in the case of the individual (*vyakti*) indicated by that [universal], the injunction of the connection with action,
or the non-difference between the universal and the individual, is intended in the meanings of sentences."
— Śāstradīpikā 1.3.35

The nature of indication (lakṣaṇā) is as follows: "When the primary meaning is obstructed, yet there is a connection [between that meaning and another], another meaning is indicated—either by convention or for a specific purpose; this transferred operation is indication. (Kāvyaprakāśa, p. 40).
Sāhityadarpaṇa 1.9:
Because the literal meaning has no logical connection with the sentence-meaning...
The definition is stated by way of the positive concomitance (anvaya) obtained through the force of that connection: *Prakaraṇa-vākyārtha*, p. 13;
as it was said in the *Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya*.
"The cognition of that which is inseparably connected with its own denotation is called indication (*lakṣaṇā*)," as stated in *Tantravārttika* 1.4.23; thus,
the application [of a word] to that which is inseparably connected with its denotation is accepted as indication— *Tantravārttika* 1.4.23.
This has been extracted from the *Abhidhāvṛttimātṛkā* (p.
50): "The operation [of words] is called indication (*lakṣaṇā*)," and from the *Kāvyaprakāśa* (p. 204).
In the *Padārthadīpikā* (p.

31), it is stated that "indirect indication by indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) occurs when the cognition of specific purposes such as carrying or milking— which cannot otherwise be accounted for— arises from the cognition of a particular object, such as a cow, which has been indicated [by the primary meaning].

Where, however, there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of an indirect connection with the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) that has been characterized in a general way, it is called "signification of the signified" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

For example, in words such as *dvirepha*, the connection with two *repha* sounds is known to exist in the word *bhramara*, and the connection of the word *bhramara* with the bee is known; in that case, there is *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*.
— Muktā° pṛ° 389:
Refutation of that [position] followed by the establishment of the fact that a word denotes an object consisting of both a real universal and a particular—
herein it is replied:

As for what was stated—that "the object of words is merely the universal" (*sāmānyamātra*) and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion; for the denotative capacity of a word is established by following convention (*saṅketa*), and this convention is understood to apply precisely to that which possesses the universal (*tadvat*), and not to the universal alone. This is because verbal usage is impossible with respect to the universal in isolation—since it is not the locus of activity and the like, and lacks the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) such as carrying or milking—and because the apprehension of a convention regarding such a bare entity would be fruitless.

For the person to be instructed has been made to grasp the convention by the one establishing it only between a signifier and a signified that have undergone a similar transformation—namely, that "from such a word, such a meaning is to be understood by you," and "for such a kind of meaning, a word of such a kind is to be employed"—[this being] with respect to a particular possessing a universal (sāmānyavati viśeṣe). (Ā. Ṭī., p. 566, l. 7)
For it is extremely difficult for there to be a manifestation of the individual based on a convention regarding the mere genus in that which has entered [into usage]— Śabdashatakārikā 19.

Comparison: In that regard, a universal (*jāti*) is incapable of purposeful action; for a universal is never present in activities such as carrying or milking, nor is there the use of words in worldly transactions in the absence of such contexts.
The universal (*jāti*) is not capable of performing functions such as carrying or milking;
therefore, for one who seeks such functions as carrying or milking, an injunction regarding the universal is fruitless, and thus no person employs a word for that purpose.

Furthermore, even if a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by one's own cognition is attributed to the universal, a person does not act for its sake, because that [cognition] is already established through the very employment of the word.
If it is argued that the use of a word will be for the purpose of conveying the mere universal (*jāti*), he says "no" and so forth.
This is because it has already been stated that such a use of a word—referring to something like a universal—is to be disregarded when it is fruitless in contexts such as "bringing" or "milking.

Furthermore, if the universal were the denoted object, there would be no comprehension of the sentence-meaning in the sentence "Bring the cow," because the universal "cowness" cannot be connected with an action.
— Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.95:
Indeed, a universal cannot be denoted in its entirety, because its cognition is useless with respect to purposeful action.
For the nature of a cow (gotva) is not useful for tasks such as carrying loads or milking—Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 139;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 102.

As for the argument that because particulars are denotable, they cannot be apprehended in their entirety due to their infinity, and so forth—that too is incorrect. For just as with individual instances of the probandum and the probans, even though the individual instances of the signifier and the signified—which have undergone similar transformations—are infinite, they can nonetheless be understood in their entirety through inferential knowledge (*ūhājñāna*).
This has been explained in detail in the refutation of the eternal relation between word and meaning and in the refutation of *apoha*; therefore, we shall desist.

And thus, the argument that "it is not possible for a non-yogi perceiver to perceive every single particularity— either simultaneously or successively," and so forth, has been refuted; for it has been demonstrated on pages 567, line 1 and page 550, line 11, that even for a non-yogi, the perception of all particularities is possible by means of the method described.
...is said, [as found in] manuscript Ba, page 564,
line 14.

Regarding what was stated [on page 567, line 3]—namely, "Does the word, having denoted the universal (jāti), denote the individual (vyakti)? and so forth—that too is incorrect; for it is possible for the universal and its possessor to appear simultaneously in a single cognition. (Ā. Ṭī. [Page 567, Line 3]. By the aforementioned method, by the aforementioned means known as *ūha*—(Ā. Ṭī.)—even that which was said—"Does the word, having denoted the universal, denote the individual? and so forth—that too is improper; because the appearance of both the universal and its possessor together in a single cognition is possible.

Nor should it be argued that if two things are objects of a single cognition, there could be no fixed determination of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), or else there would be a reversal—since it would follow that even the qualifier would take on the form of the qualified. For, even when a staff and a person appear simultaneously in a single cognition, we perceive a fixed determination of the qualifier-qualified relationship between them. Indeed, despite the lack of difference in their appearance, that by which something is qualified as perceived is the qualifier, and the other is the qualified. Certainly, there can be no other status of being a qualifier for a staff or the like than the production of a qualified cognition regarding the person.

Just as in visual cognition there is no contradiction regarding the specific restriction [of attributes] because the staff and the person, having entered into the relationship of qualifier and qualified, appear simultaneously, so too it is with the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*). For here it is not merely the staff or merely the person that appears; rather, both are presented simultaneously as having entered into the relationship of qualifier and qualified. Therefore, just as from the word *daṇḍin* a person qualified by a staff appears, so it should be understood that from the word "cow" (*go*) a physical body (*piṇḍa*) qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*) appears.

Now, it might be argued that because no specific instance such as a *śābaleya* cow is perceived upon hearing the word "cow," the specific instance is not the meaning of the word. This is not so; for even when those specific instances are not perceived, a particular object possessing a hump and other features—conjoined with the universal—is indeed perceived from the word "cow. However, the specific instances such as the *śābaleya* are perceived from words such as "*śābaleya*";
yet, on this account alone, it is not logical to maintain that the universal alone is the meaning of the word, since both appear in the cognition in the relationship of primary and subordinate.

In injunctions such as "Bring the cow," since the cognition of the connection with actions like bringing arises for an object possessing a universal (*sāmānyavat*), that which possesses [the universal] alone is the meaning of the word (p.

567, l. 9). For comparison: "In perception, both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are objects of the sense faculty; for when the sense faculty operates through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*) toward the universal, it takes the qualified object as its object just as it does the qualifier."
For there is no such conventional usage as "the universal is perceived, while the particular is to be inferred.
If that were the case, the possessor of a quality (*guṇin*) would have to be inferable by the sense organ that grasps the quality-ness (*guṇatva*). But this is not so;

therefore, it is logical that perception extends up to the particular (*viśeṣa*), and likewise, the word also has that same object and does not rest upon the universal alone, just as the operation of a sentence is held to extend to the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*).
In the same way, let it be accepted that the operation of the word extends as far as the individual (vyakti)— as stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī*, pp.
324–25— such that the staff alone is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the person alone is the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
Even though [the object] appears in a single cognition,
in the verbal cognition "this one is possessed of a staff,"...

Regarding the simultaneous [perception] of both [the universal and the particular], [compare: "Now, since one does not perceive particulars such as the *śābaleya* upon hearing the word 'cow,' the particular is not the meaning of the word. This is true; however, what then? An object conjoined with the universal is perceived, but not the particular such as the *śābaleya*; and that [particular] is perceived precisely from words such as *śābaleya*. Yet, it is not on this account that the universal alone is the meaning of the word, because both appear in the relationship of primary and subordinate. Likewise, in usages such as "Bring the cow," the object possessing the universal is connected with actions such as bringing.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 192:

Even though the particularity (viśeṣa) consisting of the form of a brindled cow (śābaleya) and so forth does not appear, [there is no contradiction] in the case of a non-brindled cow (aśābaleya). [Note: *aśābale* is a scribal error for *aśābaleyādi*.]

The comparison characterized by "cowness" (gotva)— namely, that the individual, the configuration, and the genus constitute the meaning of a word— the word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of specification; what is it that is specified?
The status of a word-meaning (*padārtha*) is not fixed as being either the primary or the subordinate factor;

for when there is an intention to express distinction and a comprehension of particulars, then the individual (*vyakti*) is primary while the genus (*jāti*) and the configuration (*ākṛti*) are subordinate. But when distinction is not intended and there is a comprehension of the universal, then the genus is primary while the individual and the configuration are subordinate. This is the case in the majority of usages.
But the predominance of the form (ākṛti) is to be inferred—
Nyāyabhāṣya 2.2.67.
*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 329;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 325.
For comparison: "But in other applications, such as 'Give me a cow' and so forth..."
Because causal efficiency belongs to that which possesses it, only that [particular] has the status of a real entity (*padārtha*)—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
323; "possessing universals and particulars"—Āloka commentary.

Furthermore, as for the other statement—that "the denotation does not reach the qualificand" (*viśeṣyaṃ nābhidhā gacchet*), and so forth—that too is unsound. For it is not accepted that a word functions by ceasing after first conveying the qualifier and then subsequently conveying the qualificand; rather, its operation in conveying both the qualifier and the qualificand is shown to occur simultaneously. Moreover, the claim that its power is exhausted is untenable, because power is to be inferred from its effect. Indeed, the observed effect—characterized by the cognition of the qualifier and the qualificand—infer the existence of its power in that regard.

And this objection would apply to the relationship of qualifier and qualified between two things that are the objects of distinct cognitions, but not to those that are the objects of a single cognition.

For you as well, this objection is equally applicable: since a word can only convey a meaning after it has been perceived, its capacity is exhausted in the perception of itself; therefore, even for the sake of conveying a meaning characterized by a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it would be unable to do so. Thus, for one who desires gain, there would be the destruction of the very root (pṛ. 567, l. 12).

One might go on to ask: does [the cognition] first apprehend the mere universal (*jāti*) alone, and because that apprehension is not yet complete, subsequently apprehend the particular (*viśeṣa*); or does it apprehend the universal as already containing the particular within itself? Not the first, because cognitions do not function by pausing after one operation to engage in another.
(Citsukhī, p. 263)
The absence of activity after ceasing [the operation] of sound, cognition, and action is [the definition of cessation] according to the proponents themselves—
Sāṃkhyadarśana, Chapter 5, on Sound.

Regarding the comparison with sound: it was indeed stated that a word whose power is exhausted would not denote the qualified object; however, since that power has as its domain the effect, and the effect—characterized by the cognition of the qualified object—is observed just like the cognition of the qualifier, it serves to establish the existence of that power.

Now, if one were to assert the non-existence of the effect itself, by so speaking he would contradict even self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because [self-awareness] consists in the awareness of the qualified object— [as stated in] the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
192— in the apprehension of both the qualifier and the qualified.
This is also the same for the Mīmāṃsaka,
because he accepts that it is the perceived sound that conveys the meaning; and since [the sound] is exhausted in its own apprehension, it could not convey a universal.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 192:

"Now, if it is argued that because the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) is observed [to arise] from a word, there is no exhaustion of its capacity in that regard, then since the cognition of the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣya*) is likewise observed to arise from it, how could there be an exhaustion of its capacity in that case as well?"
In the case of the cognition of a universal,
[it arises] from a word, [which itself arises] from a word.

As for what was stated regarding the exhaustion of the word’s power—namely, that it is due to the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition [of the individual]—that too is a mere assertion. For if only the universal is cognized from the word, then what has happened to the individual such that the word indicates it? If it is argued that because there exists a relationship between the universal and the individual, the universal, being cognized, indicates the latter; then what indeed is this so-called relationship between them—is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), origination from that (*tadutpatti*), or identity (*tādātmya*)? It cannot be conjunction, because [the universal] is not a substance.
Nor is there inherence (*samavāya*), because that would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets;
for this very reason, its arising (*tadutpatti*) is also untenable.

However, if identity (*tādātmya*) is admitted between the universal and the particular, such that they have attained identity and are perceived from the single word "cow" and so forth as having the form of qualifier and qualified, then how can it be appropriate to say that the meaning of the word belongs to only one of them? For that would entail the consequence of the other being unauthentic (*aprāmāṇikatva*).

Page 567, line 16. For comparison: If it is argued that because the individual (*vyakti*) cannot be directly enjoined, the universal (*jāti*) is expressed through "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), [the opponent asks: even if there is a connection with that which is not directly enjoined by the word, how could one act? For when someone says, "Cut the staff," no one cuts the person holding the staff; such is the objection regarding indication of the indicated, etc. (para).

Truth is that neither the universal (*sāmānya*) performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), but rather only the individual (*vyakti*). Because it is impossible to enjoin an individual directly, a word applied to a universal indicates that universal; and through its connection with the universal thus indicated by the word, the individual is also indicated. For when the word "cow" is uttered, it is not the "cowness" (*gotva*) that is cognized, but rather the cow itself that is determined.
Even so, it is nevertheless said [that the word denotes the universal].
Regarding the passage beginning with "not prompted by a word" (*aśabdacodita*),

even if there were a relationship between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), how could [the word] apply to a specific individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*) that is not prompted by a word? For even though a relationship exists between a staff and the bearer of a staff, no prudent person, when told "cut the staff," cuts the bearer of the staff, because he is not what was prompted by the word.
The meaning is that, when the universal (jāti) has been indicated, it is not logical for there to be an application [of a word] to the individual (vyakti)—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.95.

The function [of a word] by way of indication based on what is indicated (lakṣitalakṣaṇā) would not occur in the case of non-identity, because no other relation is established, as in the case of a bow and so forth—Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī p.
139; Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 102.

Furthermore, even if it is granted that the universal (*jāti*) is understood from the word, what has occurred regarding the individual (*vyakti*) such that the former causes the latter to be cognized? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 412;
*Śabdasāmānya* [fragment].
The universal [is understood] from the word as a particularization of the universal.
Because conjunction occurs only between two manifested substances, and since conjunction is a quality (guṇa) it must reside in a substance;
for the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept the category of inherence (samavāya).

Precisely because it would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets; for there is no relationship of producer and produced between word and object— [in the case of] those [words] which have attained identity with their respective objects.

Furthermore, is the relationship characterized by these two [the word and the individual] apprehended at the very time the word is uttered, or previously? It cannot be at that very time; for the individual is not perceived at the time of the word's utterance, and if it were already perceived, what would be the purpose of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? Moreover, how could its perception at that time occur—through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or from the word itself? It cannot be through direct perception; because the individual is remote in terms of place, time, and nature, it is impossible to perceive it through a perception produced by the senses, as there is no contact between the sense organs and that object.

Nor can it be established through inference, because no inferential mark (liṅga) invariably concomitant with it is observed. If, however, that [universal] is cognized from the word itself, then it is proven that the individual (vyakti) is also the meaning of the word. Now, if it is argued that the relationship between the universal and the individual, characterized by identity (tādātmya), was previously apprehended—even if that relationship was seen between those two on that occasion, it does not follow that they must exist as such everywhere and at all times. Otherwise, since the identity of a cloth with its white color is observed in some cases at some time, it would follow that they exist as such everywhere and at all times.
At the time of the utterance of the word, is the relationship of comparison between the universal and the individual perceived then, or previously?— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 412.

The cognition of a relationship characterized by identity occurs when there is a cognition of the identity between the universal and the individual produced by the contact of the sense organ with the object.
For it is not possible to grasp a relation residing in that [individual] even when the individual itself has not been apprehended; thus, for that reason,
[the relation] is always [grasped] through the word (*śabda*).
Because of its connection [with a cause],
it exists only at certain times— never always.

Now, this very state of residing in individuals (*vyaktiniṣṭhatā*) is the nature of the universal’s identity with whiteness. But surely, would that nature belong to it if it were omnipresent in all things (*sarvasarvagatā*), or if it were omnipresent only in its own individuals (*vyaktisarvagatā*)? Regarding this, the first position is untenable; for it would entail the non-existence [of the universal] in the intervals between individuals, since its nature cannot exist there.

However, if one accepts that nature for the universal as being omnipresent only in its individuals, then—just like the individuals—the universal would also be established as manifold. Consequently, because there would be no distinction between the two, either both would be the meaning of a word, or neither would be.

Or, let it be granted that this [universal], whose nature has not been investigated, has as its inherent property residing in those [individuals]; even so, would it be perceived through perception or through inference that "this resides in all individuals at all times"? If through perception, is it simultaneously or successively? Of these, the first position is untenable; for since all individuals are not apprehended simultaneously, it is impossible to apprehend the universal simultaneously as residing in them.

In the second case, however, because it is impossible to comprehend an infinite succession of individuals even over the course of a thousand yugas through gradual apprehension, it is extremely difficult to establish that [the universal] resides in them;
therefore, its subsistence in them cannot be established through perception.

Nor can it be established through inference, since you yourself admit that inference is preceded by perception, and in the absence of the latter, the former cannot operate there; furthermore, no mark (liṅga) invariably concomitant with its subsistence in them is possible.
Consequently, if the word denotes the universal (*sāmānya*), the denotation of the individual (*vyakti*) becomes impossible; for it would follow that the very nature of the word—
which was previously stated to consist in its subsistence in the individual— would be non-existent.
Because the nature called "residing in individuals" is impossible to conceive in the interval between individuals—

for indeed, in the absence of individuals, that nature called "residing in individuals" cannot be established— and because of this absence of nature, there is also the absence of the universal which possesses that nature.
—because of its possibility;
arising from hearing;
born from the Āgama.
Once the acceptance of its own nature, termed "residing in the individual," has occurred, [it is] residing in the individual.

Jāti—Commentary: Compare: "Furthermore, is it perceived through direct perception or through inference that a universal (jāti) always resides in an individual (vyakti)?"—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 412. Of the infinite...
When perception is absent according to the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
When inference also has brought about the understanding that the universal (jāti) is grounded in the individual (vyakti).

Furthermore, does a word denoting a universal express it when it has been conventionally assigned (*saṅketita*) to it, or when it has not been so assigned? It cannot be the latter, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is the former—that it is conventionally assigned—then is this convention established with respect to a universal that is already apprehended, or one that is not apprehended? If it were with respect to one that is not apprehended, there would again be an over-extension.

Now, if [the universal] is apprehended, from what does that apprehension arise? It cannot be from perception or inference, because these two have already been rejected on the occasion of the examination of the universal, since they grasp only the generalities of intrinsic natures such as permanence.

If, however, it were to be cognized solely through the authority of verbal testimony, there would follow the faults of infinite regress and mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To explain: if the very same word that is conventionally designated for the universal is the means of its apprehension, then there is mutual dependence—since the convention for that word is established only once the universal is apprehended, and the apprehension of the universal occurs only once that convention is established.

If that [universal] were established through another word, there would be an infinite regress; for a convention regarding that other word would also occur once its universal is apprehended, and the apprehension of that [second universal] would likewise depend on yet another word. Furthermore, if the universal itself were cognized from a word, then verbal cognition (*śābda*) would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it would be grasping what has already been grasped. For the universal has already been grasped by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the relationship between the word and its object—namely, perception and inference.
pṛ॰ 285 [The word's] establishment from that— Ā॰.

When the universal is established through repeated observation and so forth, that very universal which was grasped at the time of apprehending the relationship between word and meaning is indeed the same one grasped at the time of uttering the word—Ā. Ṭī. (Commentary).

Furthermore, does the universal, as it is perceived from a word, prompt a person toward that which is undifferentiated (*nirviśiṣṭa*) or toward that which is differentiated (*viśiṣṭa*)? It cannot be the undifferentiated, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is the differentiated, by what is its differentiation produced—is it produced by identity (*tādātmya*) with a particular instance (*vyakti*), by its being the cause for activity toward that very [instance], or by the cognition "this belongs to this"? Among these, the first position is untenable; for since it possesses identity with all its own instances, it is impossible for it to have identity with only a particular instance.

Now, if it is argued that its particularity (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consists precisely in its identity with its own entire unique individual (*viśiṣṭavyakti*), then indeed, because of this, there would be the undesirable consequence of a person's activity occurring toward every such individual; consequently, there would be no activity toward a specific individual restricted to a particular instance.

Furthermore, when the universal "cowness" alone is cognized from the word "cow," activity toward any specific individual is not tenable, because that individual has not been apprehended in any way whatsoever.

When X is perceived, that which is not perceived in any way at all cannot be the object of activity based on the perception of X; for example, there is no activity toward fire based on the perception of water. Since only "cowness" (gotva) is perceived from the word "cow" (go), and specific individuals such as Khaṇḍa and others are not perceived, [the word] refers only to the universal (sāmānya) as residing in a specific individual.
Because only the universal of cowness (*gotvasāmānyamātra*) is apprehended— [as noted in] the Āloka commentary.

Even when the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is cognized from the word, there is no application [of the word] toward individuals such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*), because even when that [universal] is cognized, those [individuals] have not been apprehended in any way whatsoever. Now, if it is argued that the "cowness" being cognized from the word "cow" is cognized precisely as connected with the individual cows; how then could the universal alone be the meaning of the word? For both the universal and the particular, standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified, are cognized from it.

Now, it might be argued that from the word "cow" (go) only the universal "cowness" (gotva) is directly perceived, while the individual is perceived only through the impossibility of its otherwise being accounted for (*tadanyathānupapatti*). This too is unsatisfactory; for in this way, it would follow that the word's meaning is the universal alone, while the individual remains accessible only through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). Consequently, it would be difficult to establish that a word conveys a particular (*viśeṣa*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Now, it may be argued that this internal operation of the word itself is such that, having conveyed the universal (*sāmānya*), it—acting as a cooperative factor for that cognition—also causes the individual (*vyakti*) to be understood through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is incorrect; because only that which functions with the recollection of its relationship [to the word] is the object of that word, and not everything else that might be cognized through another means of knowledge by virtue of being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*) with that object. Otherwise, fire established through the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of smoke perceived by perception would itself have to be considered directly perceived (*pratyakṣasiddha*).
Therefore, its possession of a specific attribute (*vaiśiṣṭya*) cannot be established through identity with a qualified individual;
for it is indeed the individual that is cognized from the word. (Śābarabhāṣya-vṛtti)
By the word, indeed, the universal (sāmānya) is grasped; the particular (viśeṣa), however, is [grasped] through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)— what need is there for indication (lakṣaṇā)?—
[this is] the comprehension of the universal (sāmānyapratipatti).
—The auxiliary [factor]...
[ba, śra], that too is incorrect...
[śra, ba], the recollection of the convention.

The universal must be rejected either on the grounds of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) or through inference (anumāna). Ba, Śra. [Note: This refers to the two schools of thought mentioned in the source].
Nor is it caused by its being the reason for activity toward that very [particular] itself; for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

To explain: only when the generality’s qualified nature is established is the status of being the cause of activity toward those very qualified particulars established; and only when that is established is the generality’s qualified nature established. Thus, activity toward that very [particular]... [Ba., Śr.]

The third [position] is that there is the establishment of its being a cause. According to Ātreya, when that [cognition] exists, there is the establishment of its being the cause for the occurrence of that very [cognition].

However, in the third position, a circular argument (cakraka) is incurred: for only when the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the universal is established is there the establishment of its being the cause for the cognition of specific particulars; when that is established, there is the establishment of the cognition "this belongs to this" (*asyedam*); and when that is established, there is the establishment of the qualification of that [universal].

Therefore, for one who desires the determination of reality based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whatever appears in whatever manner from whatever source must be accepted as its object by virtue of having a form that is either similar to or different from it—just as color and so forth, appearing with the form of blue and so forth, are the objects of the cognition produced by the eye and other [senses]; and since the entity such as a cow appears from words such as "cow," therefore that very [entity] is the object of those words, and not merely a universal (*sāmānya*).
This is the third alternative: that [the object] is established by the cognition "this belongs to that."
Regarding the doctrine of injunction (*vidhivāda*), there are various prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*):
by this, the view of the proponents of injunction (*vidhivādins*)—that injunction alone is the meaning of a sentence—is also refuted.
For they assert: "Injunction alone is the meaning of a sentence, because its essential nature consists in impelling one to act who has not yet acted."
As it has been said: "The definition of an injunction (*vidhi*)—both primary and secondary—is simply this: the instigation of one who has not yet acted.

Regarding that injunction which possesses such a definition, there is disagreement among disputants. For instance, some maintain that the word itself, in the form of a sentence, is the injunction because it is that which instigates action.
Others hold that its operation is *vidhi*, synonymous with *bhāvanā*;
others that it is *niyoga*;
and some that it consists of *praiṣa* and so forth.
Others say it is merely the occurrence [of action] when those conditions have been set aside;
others say it is the fruit itself because of its capacity to impel;
and some say it is simply the longing for the fruit.
Others say it is action itself;
others say it is the cognition of the self's connection with an activity not yet attained;
some say it is the dharma known as the means to the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhanatva*).
Some say it is instruction;
others say it is simply the comprehension of what ought to be done;
some say it is intuition alone.
Some say it is devotion alone;
others say it is desire alone;
and some say it is effort alone.
The view [of the opponent] is rejected;
for an injunction (vidhi) impels persons toward a subject matter that is to be performed.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Vākyādhikaraṇa, verse 274;
"In that context, the portion of the Veda which makes known an unknown object is the injunction" (Arthasaṃgraha, p. 29).
The object of the causal cognition that prompts the desire to act is the injunction (*vidhi*).

According to Śabara-bhāṣya on Jaimini-sūtra 1.1.2, that which is taught as something not previously known by means of the injunctive suffixes *liṅ*, *loṭ*, or the *kṛtya* suffixes, is an injunction (*vidhi*).
—Yuktidīpikā, p. 20. [The definition of injunction:
