But surely they say that the definition of an injunction (*vidhi*) is simply this: the impelling of one who has not yet acted.
"An injunction does not consist in making known what is already known, because that would lead to the fallacy of over-extension"—
this is the view of the Bhāṭṭas (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 340).
The Prābhākaras [hold that] the *preṣaṇa* (impulsion) and so forth are [the meanings of verbal suffixes],
with the specificities such as the person (*puruṣa*) abandoned— Ānandabodha’s Commentary.
Thus say others;
thus say some.

In this regard, those who maintain that the word itself is the injunction (*śabdavidhivādinaḥ*) declare: "The capacity to incite action is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); and since these two are not established otherwise, they lead one to understand that the capacity to incite action belongs to the word alone. Therefore, that [word] itself is the injunction."
If the meaning were an injunction, it would contradict the *Śābarabhāṣya* (1.1.2), which states: "An injunction is a statement that prompts action."

If speech functions as an instigator by means of conveying an object that prompts action, its status as an instigator would be merely figurative (*aupacārika*), whereas its primary (*mukhya*) status as an instigator is established there in accordance with the actual nature of things; thus, in this view, that [instigating power] of speech must be understood as being independent of the object itself.

Even in the position that it acts as an instigator through a particular excellence of operation (*vyāpārātiśaya*), there is no loss of the word’s primary status as an instigator, because everything brings about the intended object precisely by relying on such an excellence of operation.

Indeed, even when firewood and the like depend upon intermediate operations such as flames, there is no contradiction in designating them as the primary causal factors (*kāraka*) with respect to cooking;

and although the capacity to incite activity (*pravarttakatva*) is generally attributed to speech, it is nevertheless appropriate only for words ending in the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), and gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes, since other types of words are not observed to be causes of activity. Thus [Śabara] determines.
In the case of the word *pra-*, there is the predominance of the action with respect to the sound.
The capacity to incite action is the word's power to incite action.
—The position (*pakṣa*) is also correct—Ā. Pañcamī—Ā. Ṭī.
The meaning is the fifth *lakāra*, namely *liṭ*, *loṭ*, and *tavya*—[variant: *loṭ* and *saptamī*]—this is the sense. (Ānandagiri’s and Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita’s commentaries)
The meaning is that this refers to the seventh verbal suffix (*lakāra*).

Here, others—unable to tolerate the fact that a word functions as an injunction (*vidhi*) because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because activity occurs without [prior] restriction, and because it relies upon knowledge—point out contradictions with such reasoning as follows: First of all, its status as a means of valid cognition is difficult to establish if it were to cause activity *per se* (independently) without first making known an object that prompts action, for it would then be like wind and so forth; since it is impossible for something that is merely a causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*) to be a means of valid cognition, such a status is possible only for that which makes [an object] known.

Now it might be argued: "This activity of the self, which consists of consciousness and is of a nature similar to desire and so forth, is distinct from the activity of the elements produced by air and other factors; it depends upon the cognition of an object and is brought about by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like. That is not so; for, insofar as they are causal factors for the activity, the validity [of the words] cannot be established—just as with other causal factors—and even if validity were granted merely on the basis of making something known, it would follow that this would apply even to sentences containing the *laṭ* suffix and others used to denote the present time, which do not incite action. Therefore, in this treatise, an injunction (*codanā*) is defined as a sentence that incites one to act (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra, verse 3).
This is a contradiction;

therefore, since the validity of a word ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is established solely by its capacity to convey an object characterized by the activity of sacrifice and the like, which possess the nature of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the word does not possess the character of an injunction (*vidhi*) by its own form alone— so [argue] Maṇḍana Miśra and others.

Because it is a means of valid cognition, because there is no restriction regarding engagement, because it relies on consciousness, and because it is uttered in grammatical coordination with [the object], the word is not an injunction, since the action is understood from the result.
— *Vidhiviveka*, p. 5.

In that regard, if sound were to function by its own nature like the wind, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be undermined; furthermore, it would cause one to act without restriction.
— *Nyāyasūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 26.

For verbal testimony is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and a means of valid cognition is that which makes something known. In this regard, a word attains the status of a means of valid cognition as an injunction (*codanā*) when it makes one understand some specific excellence of an object that serves as a cause for activity. However, if it were itself an agent of activity, it would forfeit that status of being a means of valid cognition; for a cause that is an agent is not a means of valid cognition, but rather a means of valid cognition is that which makes something known. Indeed, it is declared that "Dharma is an object characterized by an injunction."
And a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which produces a cognition of an object that is uncontradicted, not already known, and free from doubt;
however, the status of being a cause of activity—even for an invalid cognition—would not forfeit its status as a means of valid cognition.

[Objection: Why then is the cause of activity, even if it is invalid, not considered a means of valid cognition? To this he says: "For a cause that is merely a producer is not a means of valid cognition."

Let it not be that seeds and the like, which are the producers of sprouts and so forth, possess validity; what then is valid? He says: rather, it is the indicator (*jñāpaka*), because such is the case with the sense organs and so forth—*Vidhiviveka*, *Ṭīkā*, p. 5.
For this very reason, even a word does not impel action by its mere form, as that would entail the consequence of it being equivalent to wind and the like.

If a word were an impeller in the same manner as wind, a demon, or a wicked king, then even one who has not understood the relationship between a word and its meaning would be impelled to act simply by being subject to hearing it; but such is not the case.
Therefore, a word is an impeller only insofar as it generates the cognition of an object.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth can be the instigator [of action] merely by denoting the instigator;
for although a word differs from causal factors such as the eye in its being a communicator (*jñāpaka*), its status as a cause in the production of cognition is unavoidable.
And a cause is an agent (*kāraka*); moreover, an agent is incapable of accomplishing its own effect without an operation. Thus, an operation necessarily belongs to it. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 342)

The optative suffix and so forth [are authoritative] in their capacity as causes of activity (pravṛttikāraka), but lack authority in their capacity as causes of cognition (bodhakāraka)— this is the marginal note (ā॰ ṭi॰).
[The reading is] "parakāraṇā" in Ā॰ and Śra॰.
"But validity [belongs] only by virtue of making a specific cognition known" — [this is the] Ācārya’s gloss.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the Veda] makes its object known, we say no; for that alone is common to other [means of knowledge] as well, which would render the accepted principle that "Dharma is a matter characterized by the Vedic injunction" (codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ) purposeless. He refutes this with "No."
Why? Because that alone [the agent] is equally present even in other cases where there is a statement of an existing state, such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*);
for indeed, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is not unperceived there.

If it is argued, "Let there be equality; what loss is there to us?", he says: because it would result in the futility of the accepted principle that "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*).

The nature of being an *codanā* (an injunction) consists in its being a motivator; it attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) by making known some specific excellence of an object that serves as a cause for activity, and not merely by denoting a mental disposition (*bhāvanā*), because that [mere denotation] is common to other [types of words] as well. Therefore, in the form in which it possesses validity, it is not an *codanā*; and in the form in which it is an *codanā*, it does not possess validity, because in that latter case it functions as a causal factor (*kāraka*) toward activity—*Vidhiviveka-ṭīkā*, p. 6.
— In cases such as "the Kalinga and so forth" (ba॰), "present" (varttamāna) (ā॰ ṭi॰), and "Caitra cooks" (caitra pacati) and so forth.
Because of the attainment of validity [of such injunctions] as "one should perform the Agnihotra," which end in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

Likewise, because activity would proceed without restriction: for if the word were an injunction by its very nature, independent of the comprehension of its object, then even a conscious person would be compelled by force against their will—like one agitated by a mantra and rendered helpless—and their activity arising from the word would not differ from activity produced by wind or other such causes. Furthermore, since such activity would occur solely through compulsion, it would follow that the scriptural prescriptions regarding penance for the fault of non-performance of what is enjoined—which presuppose human autonomy—are rendered devoid of subject matter; thus, what was stated is incorrect.

And if the word were independent [of human intent], there would necessarily be activity [even against one's will]; and thus, the scriptural injunction "one who does not perform the prescribed duty" would be rendered devoid of object.
For at that time, just as for one being driven by a powerful torrent of wind and water, even the person's own desire is not the governing factor regarding the activity—*Vidhiviveka*, p. 6.
— of non-distraction itself; according to the reading in Śra, as if by force (haṭhāt) in an activity not preceded by desire, due to the influence of sound.
In your view (*bhavatyām*),

when human autonomy (*puruṣasvātantrya*) exists, there may be expiation (*prāyaścitta*) due to the non-performance of prescribed acts such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*); however, when a person lacks autonomy regarding their engagement in action, how could they incur expiation through its non-performance?

—Oblations— [Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.20.9] Commentary: A person who fails to perform prescribed duties and instead practices what is censured, being constantly attached to the objects of the senses; who does not perform the obligatory rites such as the *saṃdhyopāsana* (twilight worship) nor the occasional rites such as bathing after touching a corpse; and who likewise persists in prohibited acts like violence while maintaining extreme attachment to both the un-prescribed and the prohibited—he, being merely a human being, deserves expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
"A man who becomes addicted to the objects of the senses incurs the need for penance. (Manusmṛti 11.44) Thus [it is said].
Likewise, because it depends upon cognition (*saṃvit*), a word is not the causal factor for activity.

For it is never observed that seeds and the like perform their own effects while depending upon cognition; rather, it is only in the case of an indicator, such as smoke, that dependence on that [cognition] is perceived. Furthermore, an indicator requires a cognition whose object is the relationship between its own form and its function; yet the form of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the causal factor for activity. Consequently, it would follow that even a person who lacks the cognition of the word's own form, its function, and their relationship would still engage in activity.
—Vidhiviveka, p. 7:
"The seeds [of cognition] depend upon self-awareness."

Furthermore, in sentences such as the *viśvajit* sacrifice where no fruit is heard, there would be the necessity of supplying (adhyāhāra) both the fruit—such as heaven—and the qualified agent—such as one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*). Moreover, in the case of the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites, since words like "heaven" function as subordinate members of a compound referring to another object, it would be necessary to determine that heaven and so forth are the fruits; thus, connecting the word with such meanings would be redundant. This is because it would follow that the word itself, without depending on a connection to a fruit or other factors, could serve as the cause for action, just like the wind and other physical forces.
Therefore, the word is not the injunction (*vidhi*).
In sacrifices such as the Viśvajit, the fruit of heaven and so forth is not explicitly stated in the scripture; therefore, the fruit in the form of heaven is supplied there in a general sense.
Thus it has been said in the Jaiminīya Nyāyamālā: "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, is there no fruit, or is there one? It is not [explicitly] heard."
The fruit [of an injunction] must be postulated with respect to the object to be cultivated, for the sake of inducing a person's activity;
this is to be seen in the Śābarabhāṣya and the Śāstradīpikā (4.3).

Furthermore, in cases where no fruit is heard [explicitly stated], there is the superimposition of a fruit; in some cases, such as with the *samidh* offerings, there is the postulation of assistance to the sacrifice (*kratu-upakāra*); and even in the case of those fruits that are heard, such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, there is the determination of their status as a fruit. Thus, this entire majesty belongs to the injunction (*vidhi*). This would be untenable in the absence of that [injunction]. Moreover, in rites such as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* where no fruit is heard, there is the superimposition of fruits like heaven; in some cases, such as with the *samidh* offerings, there is the postulation of assistance to the sacrifice; and even in the case of those fruits that are heard, such as heaven and so forth, there is the determination of their status as a fruit by virtue of being qualifications of the person. Thus, this entire majesty belongs to the injunction.

That [result] is untenable as a positive injunction when the sound exists and the injunction exists—in the case of *jita* and so forth, there is no fruit (*phala*). (Vidhiviveka, Ṭīkā, p. 14; Ā., Ba.)

For indeed, the person qualified [for the ritual] has been stated as the object of the Vedic injunctions, but not the fruit; and that fruit—namely "heaven"—is determined to be the result within the compound word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), which defines the qualified person, by virtue of its status as the first member (*pūrvapada*) and thus being subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*).
If it is argued that [the injunction] is the motivator, we say no; for even that [motivator] can be accounted for like the wind and so forth, without requiring a causal factor in the form of a fruit.
Therefore, neither the injunctive word nor its operation constitutes [the motivator].

He objects: "If it is argued that [the injunction] is the motivator (*pravartaka*), [we reply: indeed, it is the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth that are the motivators of persons; and these are not capable of motivating a person toward something fruitless. Therefore, the postulation of a result follows from the impossibility of that [motivation] otherwise.
He refutes this meaning by stating that even for that [suffix], the status of being a motivator is possible, just as it is in the case of the wind and so forth.
The meaning is that not every agent who initiates [an action] expects a result, for it is observed that even those such as the wind who initiate [actions] do not depend upon one;
thus [it is stated in the] *Vidhiviveka-Ṭīkā*, p. 14.

However, those who maintain that the operation of words (*śabdavyāpāra*) is the injunction (*vidhi*) argue as follows: since, immediately after hearing words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), one observes in the linguistic usage of elders an effect called "initiation" (*pravṛtti*), there exists a causal operation of the word—distinct from spells, the wind, and so forth—which serves as the cause of initiation. Therefore, the aforementioned defects do not apply.
As it has been said by Bhaṭṭa Kumārila and others:
"In all cases, the meaning of a sentence is indeed the efficient force (bhāvanā), because it is present wherever there is a verbal suffix."
"Though colored by objects that produce various qualities, classes, and so forth,
it is grasped by a single cognition that possesses a variegated form"— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 139.

In that context, the second type of *bhāvanā*, which consists of the verbal element (*śabdadharmā*) and is of the nature of expression (*abhidhātmikā*), refers to the instigating activity (*prayojakavyāpāra*) of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) toward a person; this is called "injunction" (*vidhi*).
— *Tantravārttika* 2.1.1.
"By means of mantras and so forth" (matravacanādi)—in the Ā [manuscript]; "by means of the recitation of mantras and so forth" (matrapaṭhanādi)—in the Ba [manuscript].
As for example, someone who has been brought under subjection by means of a mantra for malevolent purposes (abhicārika) and the like, proceeds even against his will—Ā [manuscript] commentary.

The authors of the *Tantravārttika* (2.1.1) state: "Those beginning with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) express a distinct *abhidhābhāvanā* (the productive urge of denotation), which is not preceded by [the meaning of] a word."

Commentary: Accepting that the word *abhidhā* (denotation) refers to "sound" (*śabda*)—either through an etymology based on the agent (*kartṛ-vyutpatti*) or an etymology based on the instrument (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*)—the meaning is as follows: the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) of the sound that is *abhidhā*, which constitutes the general form of the activity of instigation (*pravartanā*), is expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth. Since a general property cannot exist without particulars, and since the particularities observed in the world such as "command" (*praiṣa*) are attributes of persons and thus impossible in the impersonal Veda, and because it is observed that the general property of instigation resides in the operations of those who instigate such as commands, and because it is determined that in the Veda the optative suffixes themselves are the instigators, [the optative suffixes] cause [the *bhāvanā*] to be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is the sense.
—Nyāyasūtra 5.1.59; Jaimini-nyāyamālāvistara, p. 75;
Tantrarahasya, p. 47.
*Mānameyodaya*, page 272;
*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, page 156;
*Muktāvalī-dinakara*, page 515.

"Abhidhā" (denotation) is that which is denoted; it is either the instigation (*pravartanā*) or the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*). And since that very [denotation] brings about the activity of the person, it is called "bhāvanā" (productive operation); thus they say "they call that bhāvanā. Alternatively, the "bhāvanā" of the word's denotation is "abhidhā-bhāvanā"; even though that very instigation resides in another [the person], when the word causes the person to act, it is said to be denoted for the sake of accomplishing that [activity], and is thus called the "operation of the word" (*śabda-vyāpāra*); thus they say "they call that.

Alternatively, "abhidhā" is the denotation of the fact of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatā*); that itself, by the etymological derivation of "vidhi" as "that which ordains" (*vidhāna*), is called "vidhi" (injunction).

And that very [capacity], when it attains the state of being the agent of the act, is the operation of the word which prompts the activity of the person; they call this *bhāvanā*—as stated in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*, p.
53, and the *Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, p. 181.
This has been cited: "They say that the nature of sound is the creative contemplation (bhāvanā)"—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p.
19; *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 262;
*Vidhiviveka*, p. 15.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 343;
*Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika-ṭīkā*, p. 590;
*Abhidhānabhāvanā*—*Nyāyakuṃjalaprakaraṇa*, 5.
13 *Mīmāṃsārthaprakāśa*, page 8;
*Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, page 181.
Śāstradīpikā 2.1.1
*Nyāyaratnamālā*, p. 47;
*Mīmāṃsābālaprakāśa*, p. 75:

"The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are the expressers of that *bhāvanā*—which is the causal operation of the word itself toward the production of a person's activity—which belongs to the word as its own instigating function."

The operation of the producer (bhāvaka-vyāpāra) has as its object that which is to be brought about (bhāvya), and this is the verbal productive energy (śabda-bhāvanā). Furthermore, the object to be brought about by this verbal productive energy is either the activity of the person or the person himself as the agent of that activity. Moreover, without the expression of commendation (prāśastya-abhidhāna), the injunctive power (vidhi-śakti), even if it has attained the status of a cause, is not capable of inciting one toward action.
For even if one were told a hundred times, "Buy this cow," no one would proceed to buy it unless there arises a cognition of its excellence, such as "it has a full udder" or "it yields abundant milk.
Therefore, the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*), accompanied by the cognition of excellence produced by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), is the factor that prompts action.
And that [verbal productive energy] becomes complete with its three components: *what* [is to be done], *by what means*, and *how*.
What is to be brought about? Heaven.
By what means? By the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
How? [The text] indicates the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), which consists of the performance of the *prayāja* and other such rites.
The verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā), when complete in its three constituent parts, impels the person toward the productive energy of the result (phalabhāvanā).

Although desire, memory, and so forth are causes for the person's activity, they do not receive the primary designation of "impelling" (pravartanā); rather, it belongs primarily to the verbal productive energy, because it is the fundamental cause by virtue of its function of bringing about the comprehension of what is to be accomplished (sādhya).

Regarding the term *śabdabhāvanā*: because it is designated as a property of the word by means of the word "word" (*śabda*), just as the designation of the king as the "giver" when land and so forth are granted is primary, whereas for the staff-bearers and others who act in accordance with the king's command it is secondary (metaphorical), so it is here as well. This has been stated: [in the Bhāvanāviveka].

Therefore, those who know *bhāvanā* say that *bhāvanā* is the instigating action (*prayojaka-kriyā*) of a real entity (*vastu*) which has attained the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to various results (*bhūtiṣu*). (Tantravārttika 2)
1.1 For here, in sentences containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, two types of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) are understood.
It consists of both the word-essence and the object-essence.

In that context, the instigating agency (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*) belongs to the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc.), while the person is the one to be instigated (*prayojya*). Therefore, when there is an expectation of "what [is to be done]?", it is connected with "the instigation of the person. Alternatively, by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*), the action within the scope of the optative suffixes is expressed as "one should instigate"; then, when the expectation of "what [is to be done]? arises, it is connected precisely with "the person."

Now, when the question "by what [is one impelled]? arises, it is connected with the answer: "by the knowledge of the injunction (vidhi-jñāna) which depends upon the experience of a prior relationship. To the question "how?", the answer is: "by that which is assisted by the knowledge of excellence (prāśastya-jñāna). Why is this so? For persons who act with deliberation do not engage in an action as long as they do not perceive that "this is excellent"; in such a case, the injunctive suffix falters, and it is the knowledge of excellence that sustains it.
And since that [performance] regarding the portion consisting of the fruit—which is the human goal—occurs spontaneously for everyone, it is well known and thus does not require arising from the Veda;
however, because the person has not yet been impelled toward the means and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the scripture itself is required to establish their excellence (*prāśastya*).
2.1 Nyāyamukha, p. 32–...
For *bhāvanā* is an activity capable of bringing about that which is to be produced (*bhāvya*)— as established in the *Bhāvanāviveka* (p.
6)— since it is well known that *bhāvanā* is an activity conducive to the production of what is to be produced.
– *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 31:
"Meditation (*bhāvanā*) is a specific activity of the meditator that is conducive to the becoming of that which is to become. – *Arthasaṃgraha*, p. 11.
The *bhāvanā* is a specific operation of the agent (*bhāvaka*) that is conducive to the coming-into-being of that which is to come into being (*bhavituḥ*).
[Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa, p.
2]. The distinction is this: the operation conducive to activity (*pravṛtti*) is *abhidhā*, while the operation conducive to the fruit (*phala*) is *bhāvanā*.
—*Mīmāṃsārthaprakāśa*, p. 8:
"Bhāvanā is the activity of the agent (bhāvaka) which culminates in the object to be brought into being (bhāvya).

For the object to be brought into being is the fruit, such as heaven, because it is that which is being accomplished; and the human activity which culminates in that [fruit] and produces it is *bhāvanā*. It is expressed by the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*)."
That which is the agent of the root *bhū* (to become) in its primary sense—namely heaven and so forth—becomes the object (*karman*) of the causative form (*ṇyanta*).

However, the agent of this [causative] is the instigating person (*prayojaka-puruṣa*). The meaning of the suffix *ṇic* is the activity of the instigator expressed by *ṇic*; for a person brings about (*bhāvayati*), that is, accomplishes, an object such as heaven through his own activity. That activity which accomplishes it is called "productive operation" (*bhāvanā*). — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 335.
The nature of *bhāvanā* (productive operation) consists in possessing an activity that causes something to come into being (*bhavitṛ*).

In this regard, the definition applies to *arthabhāvanā* because it is the causal activity that brings about heaven and other results which are the things to be produced (*bhavitṛ*). It also applies to *śabdabhāvanā*, because it is the causal activity that prompts a person’s inclination toward action, which is itself the thing to be produced—Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā, p. 20.

Therefore, there exists a verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) which has the activity of a person as its result, the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth as its instrument, and the knowledge of the excellence of the object—produced by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—as its procedure; it consists essentially of an instigation (*preraṇā*). Furthermore, although it is characterized as a denotation (*abhidhāna*), this verbal productive energy is an operation [of the word], just like the operation of Devadatta and others (see *Bhāvanāvivaraṇa-ṭīkā*, p. 94). In that context, the verbal productive energy is a specific operation of the producer [the word] that is conducive to the activity of the person.

And that [efficient force] impels one toward action precisely upon hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*), because it is invariably cognized as "possessing an operation conducive to the agent's engagement.

Whatever is invariably cognized from a word is its denotation; for example, in the sentence "Bring the cow," the denotation of the word "cow" is "cowness. This specific operation is, in worldly sentences, a particular intention residing in the person [who utters the command]; however, in Vedic sentences, due to the absence of a person, it resides solely in the optative suffix and the like.
For this very reason, it is conventionally termed "verbal efficient force" (*śābdī bhāvanā*).
—*Arthasaṃgraha*, p. 11–13;
*Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, p. 3, 178;
*Mīmāṃsārthaprabodha*, p. 8.
—Or [if it were] merely active, [then] a person... by this much, let there be no authoritative status for the explanatory (arthavāda) statements. —Ānandagiri’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.).
"You have approached" (tvamupāga);

[the commentators] state that "pravṛtti" is the cause of engagement, and they call the property of the instigator (*pravartayitṛ*) which serves as the cause of engagement "pravartanā" (Vidhiviveka, p.
243). Thus, *pravartanā* is the property of the instigator that functions as the cause of engagement.
—*Mīmāṃsābālaprakāśa*, p. 75;
*Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, p. 180 — *ghaṭedhv iṣa* (variant: *ghaṭādiṣu*) — *Ba*; *Śra*.
O venerable ones, please consider these well-known worldly statements:
for example, "This cow belonging to Devadatta is to be purchased."
"For she is one who yields much milk, has many offspring, and whose progeny does not perish"—
Śābarabhāṣya 1.2.1.

Therefore, that cultivation depends upon a triad: the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). [One asks: what should one cultivate, by what should one cultivate it, and how should one cultivate it?

In that context, when there is an expectancy for an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the objective efficient force (*ārthībhāvanā*)—endowed with the three factors to be described later—connects as the thing to be accomplished. Although number and other grammatical features are understood through the same suffix (*ekapratyayagamyatva*), they do not connect as the object to be accomplished because they lack semantic fitness (*ayogyatva*).

When there is an expectancy for a means (*sādhana*), the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth connects as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Its status as an instrument is not due to its producing the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), since that force already exists in the word even prior to it; rather, it is due to its making the efficient force known, or by way of accomplishing the object of the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*).

When there arises an expectancy for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*), the excellence (*prāśastya*) made known by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) connects as that manner of performance—*Arthasaṃgraha*, pp. 16–18;
*Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, p. 3.
The instrumental portion consists of the knowledge of the procedure; what part is the instigation of the person?
And here, the "manner of performance" (itikartavyatā) is indeed the praise of the explanatory passage (arthavāda).
— *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya-vārttika*, p. 590.

Even in the case of verbal expression (*abhidhā*) which results in activity, the three factors consisting of the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are required; otherwise, because its nature and result would be unknown, there would be the undesirable consequence of no activity occurring.

In that context, the knowledge of the injunction (*vidhi*) expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth connects as the instrument (*karaṇa*), just as the sacrifice does in the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*);
and activity itself connects as the goal (*sādhya*), just as heaven does in the objective efficient force.

The knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya*) produced by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like functions as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) within the objective-efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*), just as the collection of subsidiary rites such as the *prayāja* does. As it has been said: "The denotation by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is itself the verbal-efficient-force (*śabdabhāvanā*); its objective (*bhāvya*) is the activity of the person;
the cognition of the relationship [between the two] is the instrument (*karaṇa*); and the incitement (*prarocanā*) toward that [activity] is employed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*)."

That by which [a person] is incited is *prarocanā* (incitement); it is the knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya-jñāna*), and it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that assists the result, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. (Mīmāṃsābālamanoramā, p.
81; Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā, p. 18)

In this regard, when there arises the inquiry as to "what is to be produced," "by what means is it to be produced," and "how is it to be produced," the expectation is fulfilled by establishing the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—namely, "one should produce heaven," "one should produce it by means of sacrifice," and "one should produce it by accomplishing auxiliary services through such acts as the placing of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*), and the threshing (*avaghāta*). Thus, because it fulfills these expectations through the support of the object, the instrument, and the procedure, the entire collection of words recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*), which is an expansion of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) that expresses *bhāvanā*, is called the "objective *bhāvanā*" (*arthabhāvanā*) characterized by its three components, beginning with the object to be accomplished.

That entire verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*)—which has that which is to be brought about as its object, the optative suffix and so forth as its instrument, and the praise accomplished by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as its procedure—is understood solely through the optative suffixes and the like.
It has been stated that the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) is understood by all verbal suffixes: Jaimini-Nyāyamālāvistara, p. 76.
The specific sacrifice performed on the new moon day is the *darśa*, and the performance of the sacrifice prescribed on the full moon day is the *paurṇamāsa*.
How so? How so? [This refers to] that which has become established as a duty; specifically, the particular duty to be performed in the sacrifice—[Ānandagiri’s commentary].

The *prayāja* and other such rites are forms of remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) toward the objective efficient force (*arthībhāvanā*), like a staff-bearer [who assists indirectly]—*Nyāyaratnamālā*, p. 120; *Ānandajñāna’s Commentary*, marginal note.
The meaning is that they are like gatekeepers; this is the designation for the setting in motion of desire, mindfulness, and so forth.
The causal operation (*hetuvyāpāra*) that brings about the gatekeepers and others who carry clubs and staffs within the context of the injunction (*vidhi*) is called *śabdabhāvanā*.
The operation of the reason,
which is explained as being a property of the word, has its existence indicated by the effect; this is the state of the operation of the reason [as] the probandum.
Its existence is indicated by its effect, which is in the form of a person—[Ānandajñāna’s] Commentary (Ā.

Ṭī.). And thus, the objection asking what proof there is for the existence of the verbal *bhāvanā* is untenable; for just as the denotative operation (*abhidhā*) of a word is postulated because the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be inexplicable, so too the instigating operation (*pravarttanā*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is postulated because human activity would otherwise be inexplicable. Therefore, in the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), two types of *bhāvanā* are perceived: the verbal one, consisting of the impelling of the person, and the objective one, consisting of the activity of the person.
In that context, the general meaning of the letter *la* is the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*), as it has been said:
"The [meaning] consists of the act of denotation" (*abhidhānātmaka*). (Bhaṭṭa, Śālikanātha)

The verbal suffix (*ākhyātavibhakti*)— according to the *Ākhyāta-ṭīkā*— denotes the *ārthībhāvanā*, which is the activity directed toward an action produced by the desire for a purpose. This is expressed by virtue of its being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*), because the general category of verbal suffixes denotes activity (*vyāpāra*).

That [injunction] also requires three factors: the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—namely, "what should one bring about?", "by what should one bring it about?", and "how should one bring it about?

Among these, in response to the requirement for a goal, the fruit such as heaven (*svarga*) is connected as the goal; in response to the requirement for a procedure, the collection of subsidiary rites such as the *prayāja* offerings is connected as the procedure.
(Arthasaṃgraha, pp. 19–23)
And activity (*pravṛtti*) is indeed the efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*)—as stated in the *Mīmāṃsārtha* (p.
9)—which is the effort directed toward sacrifice produced by the desire for heaven;
that very [effort] is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

Upon hearing the verbal form "he sacrifices" (*yajate*), there arises the cognition that "one should strive toward the sacrifice"; therefore, effort (*prayatna*) itself is the objective efficient force (*arthībhāvanā*). As they say in the *Nyāyasudhā* (p. 579): "But an objective efficient force distinct from effort cannot be asserted here, as it is the one under discussion that is denoted by the verbal suffix; thus we desist."
"But this [other] one, which pertains to all meanings, exists in all verbal forms" (Tantravārttika 2.1.1); this is the *ārthī bhāvanā*.
But another [kind of] mental cultivation regarding the object is understood in all finite verbs—
Tantravārttika 2.1.1.
1 Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya-vārttika-ṭīkā, p. 590; Śāstradīpikā 2.
1.1 Nyāyaku[mu]daprakaraṇa 5
13 Jaiminiyanyāyamālāvistara, page 75; Mīmāṃsābālaprakāśa, page 75.
The scope of all verbal expressions—*Mīmāṃsārtha* p. 8;
original reading—*Aṣṭasāhasrikā* p. 19;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika* p. 262.
But the other [type of] cultivation has the object as its essence; it is everywhere within the domain of the verb.
(Tantrarahasya, p. 47;
Mānameyodaya, p. 272)
And that [is the meaning] of the verb—*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, p.
156; *Muktāvalī*, p. 515.

Commentary: In order to indicate that the *bhāvanā* (productive operation), which is to be enjoined, culminates in the *bhāvya* (the object to be produced) that constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and to suggest its origin in desire, the term "one who desires" (*arthin*) is derived from the root *arth* preceded by the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—that is, from *arthayati*. By forming the word *arthin* through the addition of the suffix *ac* according to the rule *erac*, the person desiring is designated by the word *artha*. Since the *bhāvanā* is a property of the person, and because there is no absolute difference between a property and its possessor, one may intend their identity; thus, the analytical compound (*vigraha*) should be formed as: "this *bhāvanā* is of the nature of the object (*artha*)."

By the word "anyām" (another), it is indicated that the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) depends upon the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*). For, since human activity exists everywhere in relation to an object, all objects constitute the objective productive energy; this is present in all verbal forms, such as *yajate* (he sacrifices), *ayajata* (he sacrificed), and *ayaṣṭa* (he sacrificed).

Indeed, in those cases, a verbal productive energy in the form of an impulsion toward a person is not experienced, because what is experienced is the established human activity, which is synonymous with the objective productive energy.

Regarding the domain of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, such as in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), two things are experienced: first, that a person, desiring their own goal, engages in their own activity characterized by the injunction to perform the sacrifice—this is the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*); and second, that the optative suffix impels that person—this is the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*). (As noted in the Ānandagiri-ṭīkā regarding the past tense and so forth.)

For when the *bhāvanā*—which follows all verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), is denoted by the root *kṛ*, and consists in the activity of a person—is understood, then its specific forms—denoted by particular words distinct from the general term "verbal suffix"—are perceived as injunctions, prohibitions, the past, the future, the present, and so forth.
And thus, in every case, the general meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) is understood:
"What does he do? He cooks."
What has he done? He cooked. What will he do? He will cook.
What should he do? He should cook.
"What should one not do? What should one not cook? — *Tantravārttika* 2.1.1.13.
When there is a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) expressing an accomplished agent and action (*siddha-kartṛ-kriyā-vācin*).

The meaning of "doing" (karoti) is understood through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); therefore, verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), which denote the activity of an agent whose self-nature has been established, possess the meaning of "doing"—

2.1 This view of the proponents of *bhāvanā* is untenable. For, would "verbal *bhāvanā*" (*śabdabhāvanā*) mean the *bhāvanā* of the word, or that the word itself is the *bhāvanā*? In the first case, the *bhāvanā* of the word would be its capacity to impel; and since that [impulsion] consists of commanding or entreating, which are attributes of a conscious person, how could it possibly exist in a word without being metaphorical? Indeed, such [impulsion] is possible in the word only because it is employed by a person upon whom those attributes have been superimposed, and not in a primary sense.
This is not the essence [of the matter], because [the agent] cannot be determined through formal application (prayoga), because it would be purposeless, because of the aforementioned defects,

because there is no activity when there is no engagement, because of the lack of connection with the fruit, and because of the scriptural statement regarding the nature [of the agent's] operation (*vidhiviveka*, p. 16).
Because of non-existence and because of the absence of activity, even the designation [of a cause] is not more significant;
since the subverting argument is equal, the method of elimination (pariśeṣa) is also difficult to establish.
— Nyāyaku. 5
*Preṣaṇa* (commanding) is the act of directing preceded by a formal designation; the meaning is that it concerns an inferior object.

On the other hand, *adhyeṣaṇā* (requesting) is when one directs a person of superior status; the meaning is that it concerns a superior object. *Prabodhana* (informing) likewise concerns a superior object.
—Vākyapadīya, Part 1, Chapter 3, Verse 9, p. 257: An action being communicated by a superior speaker with respect to the person to be prompted is designated as "command" (praiṣa);
when [communicated] by an equal, it is "invitation" (āmantraṇa).
"Commanding by means of an inferior [means]"— as stated in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 180—
it is not the case that the operation (*vyāpāra*) of a word is determined to consist of commanding or permitting, because that [operation] is a property of a person (*puruṣadharma*).
For the operation of a word—characterized by commanding, requesting, or permitting—is not established as its function;

yet, since that [operation] is understood immediately after the utterance of the word, one might ask: "How is it that the application of a word characterized by commanding and so forth is not established? To this he says: because that [operation] is a property of the person (puruṣadharma); while it is true that it is perceived immediately after the cognition of the word, [it is not the word's own function].

But this [injunction] does not belong to the word, because it consists of a difference in intention; for since instigation and the like are impossible in a word due to its insentience—*Vidhiviveka*, *Ṭīkā*, p. 16.
Since sound is insentient, [functions] such as commanding, which consist of human intention, can only be considered metaphorical and not primary;
for a person characterized by the properties of commanding, requesting,
and so forth is not possible in sound— [the reading *na hi tacchabde* is supported by the manuscripts *sa* and *ba*].
Furthermore, it takes the form of sending and requesting;
moreover, the activity of both the impeller and the impelled is not fruitless,

for it is well known that some impeller and impelled act with a specific purpose in mind, such as the attainment of a benefit or the avoidance of a harm, whether directed toward themselves or another.

Furthermore, since intention (*abhisandhāna*) is impossible in the case of an insentient word, how can it possess the capacity to impel? If it were to impel despite lacking intention—just like a powerful wind—then all the defects attributed to the position that words are injunctions (*śabdavidhi*) would descend upon it. A person would not act, because even if the word were to impel, it would not be something to be obeyed; for the wise do not act toward every impeller, but only toward one who is to be followed.
Furthermore, there is no cause in the word [itself] that conforms to the attainment of a desired object or the avoidance of an undesired one, as there is in the case of a master and so forth;
for if activity were to proceed from the result [alone], the [word] would be useless.
(Vidhiviveka, p. 18)
Furthermore, an insentient word does not possess the deliberation regarding purposes such as the attainment of what is beneficial or the avoidance of what is harmful.

It might be thought that the optative suffix (*laṅ*) and so forth impel the person, just as the wind and so forth [impel objects]. That is incorrect, because the designation [of the operation] would be useless; because, like the wind and so forth, it would be an impeller by its very nature even if its operation were not perceived; and because the aforementioned fault would ensue—for when a word is a causal factor (*kāraka*) with respect to activity, even if its operation is designated, that designation is not a contributing factor, since it is a causal factor even when its operation is not designated, as a causal factor does not depend upon being known—*Vidhiviveka*, p. 18.
The futility of expiation regarding the word—Ācārya’s Commentary:

Furthermore, what is the proof for the existence of this [apūrva]? Is it the activity occurring immediately after hearing words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), or the word itself, such as the optative suffix? It cannot be the activity, because since that activity is dependent upon it (the apūrva), it has never been observed elsewhere [independently].

For whatever basis for activity is observed in the world, it is proper to infer that very basis upon seeing such activity; however, it is not possible to infer a previously unperceived specific operation of words, as this would entail the consequence of its being unauthoritative.

Nor is the word itself—such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard, because a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped is non-expressive.
And the failure to grasp that [word] is established by the fact that its correlate—the specific operation characterized by it—is not determined.
For the cognition of a relation is not possible when the relatum has not been determined, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This [is the case] regarding the existence of the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*).

If it is argued that when an activity occurs, the activity itself—occurring immediately after words such as the optative suffix—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for an activity is never observed elsewhere to be based on that [activity itself].

Indeed, an activity is observed to be based on something else, and having seen that very thing, one is able to infer [the cause]; but one cannot infer a specific operation of a word whose status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) has not been previously established.
—the meaning of the sentence, page 27; verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā), Ānandajñāna’s commentary (Ā. ṭī.); inference, manuscript Ba.

Furthermore, the claim that the word itself— specifically the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which is called "verbal cultivation" (*śabdabhāvanā*)— is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is reckless; for a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been apprehended is not expressive.
For when the relatum is not determined, there is an absence of the cognition of the relation— [Prakaraṇapañcikā, p.
172]— therefore, the word [is used] there (ba), or the words are used there (śra).

Furthermore, there is the non-apprehension of a relationship: does the word produce its own operation depending upon the cognition of the injunction (*vidhi*), or independently? It cannot be independent, because it is admitted that the cognition of the injunction serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the impelling of the person. If, on the other hand, the word first produces the cognition of the injunction and then—aided by that instrument—begins its own operation in the form of impelling [the person], this is unprecedented (*alaukika*). For in the world, it is not observed that the self-cognition of any object is the cause of its own production.

If a word performs its own operation and expresses [its meaning], does it express that operation after having produced it, or does it produce it and express it simultaneously? In this regard, the first position is untenable; for no one other than a credulous person would accept that a word, having produced its own operation, subsequently expresses it.
The second position as well is contrary to experience, for no authoritative person accepts that a word uttered once can be both the producer and the speaker of its own operation.
For when an object is already established, the operation of a word is understood to be preceded by the comprehension of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*);
[this] verbal activity is of the nature of human engagement.

It might be thought that, because it is an instrument (*kāraṇa*), the word, having produced the knowledge of the injunction, initiates its own operation in the form of an impulsion (*preraṇā*) aided by that instrument; thus, there is no lack of instrumentality, since instrumentality exists precisely in the accomplishment of an action. But this is unworldly (*alaukika*); for it is not observed that the self-knowledge of any object whatsoever is the cause of its own production—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 173.
The instrument consisting of knowledge of the procedure,
its cause being the impulsion of the person.

Regarding this activity which is both performed and denoted: is it first denoted and then performed, or is it first performed and then denoted later, or are its performance and denotation simultaneous?

It cannot be that it is first denoted, because denotation is impossible for that which has not yet arisen; for one does not perform the naming of a son who is not yet born, and [otherwise] the word would fail to touch its object.

For that very reason, both [production and denotation] do not occur simultaneously, because [the word] has not yet been produced and would not cease [to exist], and because it would entail the consequence of excessive effort; nor does denotation occur after having first produced [the word], because no awareness of an operation following a pause is perceived.
— *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 345.
The word is not the denoter [of the injunction].

[Objection: But surely, since immediately after hearing a word such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), an effect known as "activity" is perceived through the realization "I am being impelled," how can it be said that there is no perception of the word's agency in that regard? [Reply: That is incorrect; for activity is perceived to be of two kinds: one belonging to one who is under the power of another, and the other belonging to one who acts with deliberation.

In that regard, according to the first position, let the activity of even a Buddhist or others in rituals such as sacrifice be brought about by the word through force (*haṭhāt*), since there is an absence of human autonomy; for indeed, is it not observed that one impelled by powerful water or wind acts through force due to the absence of autonomy? For there is the recognition: "Even though I do not desire it, I am set in motion, impelled by the wind and so forth. But according to the second position, as long as a person acting with foresight does not deliberate—asking whether the word by which I am impelled is fit to impel or not—one does not undertake the activity.

One does not rely on a word merely because it has been uttered, thinking "I must necessarily act upon this," for that would entail the contradiction of [the word] being dependent on that [act of utterance].

Therefore, how could anyone's engagement [with an action] arise from an authorless word that is like the cry of a crow? For it is only in the case of a human word that the capacity to incite action is established; since one can ascertain the reliability of its author through some means, engagement without hesitation becomes possible for a person acting with foresight, just as from the instruction of a skilled physician or similar authority.

Therefore, since the activity of a person is not a constituent factor in the non-human (apauruṣeya) nature of a word, the position that the word's capacity to impel toward action is "word-efficient-force" (śabdabhāvanā) does not hold; for [in such a case], there is no activity in the word itself— [Ānandajñāna’s] Commentary.
—Non-understanding [of the object].
Śrā.—A person who acts with foresight [does not act] otherwise; for if there were reliance on the mere word, it would contradict the state of being one who acts with foresight.
Next, [the opponent] says:

"The word itself is the *bhāvanā*. This too is incorrect; for if the mere nature of the word were the essence of *bhāvanā*, then the consequence would follow that even words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) would be *bhāvanās*, since their mere nature is no different in this case as well.
Thus, the injunction (*vidhi*) is that which is signified by the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), and the suffixes of the future passive participle (*tavya*).
Thus, this statement is contradicted;

for, since the nature of verbal *bhāvanā* (word-efficient-force) remains unsettled when examined in this way, how could it bring about the objective *bhāvanā* (objective-efficient-force)? For it would only be well-established that *bhāvanā* is the activity of an agent directed toward an object to be produced (*bhāvya*).
Furthermore, the description of its twofold nature does not differ from a description of the fragrance of a sky-flower.
Therefore, even an injunction in the form of a productive operation (bhāvanā) is not tenable.

Now, if it is thought that the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth have as their meaning the denotative function itself as the productive operation, to this it is replied: because [the denotation] would either apply everywhere or, due to the consequence of its being established through the nature of the task (*kārya*), it would fail to be restricted.

Because it lacks a locus and because there is no cause for its restriction, it follows that denotation itself is not an injunction (*vidhi*). If denotation were the injunction, then since the existence of that [denotative capacity] would reside in the respective objects denoted by all words, it would follow that activity [toward those objects] would arise even from words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), as there is no distinction in this regard.
—Vidhiviveka, p. 21:
"The meaning of the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), and the suffixes *tavya* and the fifth verbal suffix (*pañcamalakāra*) is injunction (*vidhi*) as the mere form of the word."

"The verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā) resides solely in the suffixes liṅ, kṛt, loṭ, and tavya" — *Nyāyasudhā*, p. 560; "by means of the verbal productive energy" — *Jaimininyāyamālāvistara*, p. 75.

Comparison: As for what was stated—that the operation of the word (*śabdavyāpāra*) is the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*); in that regard, is that operation distinct from the word or non-distinct from it? (Aṣṭasahasrī p. 31;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 262).

Furthermore, the ingenious theory of the followers of Kumārila, which holds that the verbal productive energy itself is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, is refuted by its contradiction with actual experience and other such grounds.
For a person who hears an injunctive sentence does not conceive that "I must proceed" by means of the verbal suffix *liṅ* expressing its own operation;

thus, it is entirely illogical for the denotation (*abhidhā*)—which is the object of the cognition produced by the *liṅ* suffix and so forth—to be the instigator of action independently of the knowledge that [the act] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). (Nyāyapariśiṣṭa, p. 398; Tantrarahasya, p. 48)

—*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, p. 157—Others, however, declare that the injunction (*niyoga*) itself is the *vidhi* (prescriptive rule), because it is the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*). Furthermore, [the text reads] "even having the form... (*rūpāpi*) in the Śrauta manuscript, and "the rule having the form... (*rūpo vidhiḥ*) in the Bhaṭṭa manuscript.

And regarding this, there are various disagreements: some maintain that the meaning of verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) is an injunction (*niyoga*). They argue that since the injunction is understood as a pure entity and as having the nature of a task (*kārya*), it is considered here to be a pure task.
Because it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, page 29,
others, however, maintain that the injunction (*niyoga*) is simply the state of being an instigator.

A comparative analysis according to the school of Prabhākara: What is this so-called *niyoga*? The word *ni-* signifies "without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*), and the meaning of *yoga* is "joining" (*yukti*). Thus, *niyoga* is a joining that is without remainder, because there is not even the slightest absence of connection [to the action]. Indeed, *niyoga* is the state of being necessarily to be performed (*avaśyakartavyatā*).
For those who regard *niyoga* as the authoritative means of knowledge proceed solely on the basis of the comprehension of *niyoga*.
As stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (p.

14): "I am enjoined by this sentence"—this is *niyoga*, which is *yoga* (connection) without remainder; for in that case, there is no possibility of even the slightest suspicion of non-connection (*ayoga*).
—Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 261; Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 5.

Furthermore, as for the view that "the meaning of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is an injunction (*vidhi*), which is not the object of other means of valid cognition, has as its objective support the word alone, is to be individually experienced as 'I am enjoined' like pleasure and so forth, and is untouched by the three times."

—*Vidhiviveka*, p. 48. For comparison: "For some, the meaning of suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) is a pure *niyoga* (an injunction) in the form of a task (*kārya*), independent of anything else"—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 6.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 261:

"Since the meaning of the suffix and the injunction (*niyoga*) are perceived as pure and in the form of an action (*kārya*), therefore this [injunction] is considered here to be a pure action. *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 29.
For just as other words are derived for their respective meanings through the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa), so too,

upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (liṅ) and the like, one infers the cognition of a specific task (kārya) from the resulting activity— which occurs only when that [sentence] is present— and thereby determines that the sentence is the cause of that cognition.

Even there, when one analyzes which part of the meaning is expressed by which part of the word, since the comprehension of the *kārya* (the "to-be-done") is observed upon the insertion of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like, and is not observed when they are removed, it follows that these [suffixes] alone bring about the comprehension of the *kārya*. Thus, as with other words, the established linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) is that the optative suffixes and the like denote the *kārya*. Indeed, the *kārya* alone is the single cause for all activity, because activity is never found to deviate from it; therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth is designated as such. Furthermore, because the *kārya* is the primary element, it is logical that it constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). (Page 179)
"For that very sentence indeed expresses [the meaning] as connected with the object of the injunction"—[Prakaraṇapañcikā, p.
Therefore, the entire Veda is authoritative only insofar as it has *kārya* (what is to be done) as its primary purport.

This very task, because it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is called "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*); and as it enjoins the person toward its own self, it is termed "enjoining" (*niyoga*).
As stated in the *Tantrarahasya* (p. 66):
"The meaning of the sentence, understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, is the enjoining (*niyoga*), which consists of an impulsion in the form of a task."
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 355;
*niyoga* — Ānandagiri’s commentary (*Ā. ṭī.*). Compare: "Since the meaning of the suffix and the *niyoga* are perceived as pure [in themselves]..."
And because it has the form of an action, that which is pure action is considered here to be the object;

however, whatever else is perceived as a qualifier of that [action] is not properly the meaning of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*), but rather the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), like "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).

However, as for that quality of being an instigator which is here intended as its qualification, because it is not denotable by the suffix, there is the status of a *niyoga* (an injunction) toward the pure task—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p.
6; *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 261.
The intention [of the author] is that for others, a pure instigation is *niyoga*—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 29; cf.
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 6.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 261:

In that context, according to the view that "an injunction (*niyoga*) is a pure instigation (*preraṇā*"), since instigation consists in the state of being one to be enjoined (*niyojyatā*), the primary cognition is: "The one who desires heaven is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) with respect to the sacrifice.

Then, through the implication of the enjoiner (*niyojaka*) by the person to be enjoined, a second cognition arises—derived from the act of taking up (*aupādānika*)—concerning the *apūrva*: "The enjoiner [is one] whose object is the sacrifice and who belongs to the one desiring heaven," and so forth; this is how it should be understood.

"In this context, 'injunction' (*niyoga*) is understood everywhere as nothing other than instigation (*preraṇā*), for no one undertakes what has been enjoined unless they have been instigated. — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 29; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, Yaśomitra, fol. 49A.
It awakens by itself—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*.
Others, however, consider that an injunction (*niyoga*) is an action accompanied by an instigation;
that is, when there has previously arisen the cognition: "This is my duty."
Let alone actions in the world such as going and coming;
even that action which has satisfaction as its result, such as the drinking of breast milk by an infant.
As long as it was not determined that "this is my duty," so long did I never engage in it— Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 177.
"For the sake of establishing itself preceded by knowledge—*Tattvārthaślokavārtika*, p. 261; *Sarvaśāstra*, p.
[missing]; it must be that which impels its own establishment, otherwise it would not be established—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 30."
Others say that *niyoga* (an injunction) is an instigation (*preraṇā*) accompanied by a task (*kārya*).
And [they hold that] a person is never instigated here without a task.
Comparison: *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, folio 30a;
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, page 6;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 261.
And thus, instigation (*preraṇā*) is said to be the injunction (*niyoga*) conjoined with the task; [as stated in] the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.

30: "Others hold that the injunction (*niyoga*) is the causative force of the task itself through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). The task is the object of the instigation, and it is not inherently the instigator."
Not indeed [is it] pre-... nor is this pre-...;

rather, the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is metaphorically attributed to the object of cognition (prameya). *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 30. "The state of being an instigator" (*pravartakatva*)—Ānanda’s Commentary.

Others hold that the relationship between the task (*kārya*) and the instigation (*preraṇā*) is the mandate (*niyoga*). For instigation, without a task, does not instigate anyone at all, nor is a task joined with instigation; therefore, the mandate is accepted [as their union]. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 30)

Some maintain that *niyoga* is the conjunction of the task (*kārya*) and the instigation (*preraṇā*), which is its applicability (*viniyojyatva*)— as stated in the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*— and that it is the collection of these two.
"These two are perceived as mutually inseparable:
the injunction (*niyoga*) and the aggregate; therefore, it is considered to be both the task (*kārya*) and the instigation (*preraṇā*). (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p.
30). Some maintain that the *niyoga* is the nature of the Supreme Self, being free from the nature of those two.
—The supreme state of complete liberation; for the one Brahman, which is eternally consciousness, is established by the sacred tradition (āmnāya). (Ānandajñāna’s Commentary and Ṭīkā)

[Objection: It is known—[as stated in the] *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 30—that because [the object] is already established, it cannot be the motivator for its own effect; how much less so could that [injunction] be? Others, however, maintain that the injunction (*niyoga*) is mounted upon a machine (*yantra*).

The meaning is that "mounted on a mechanism" (*yantrārūḍha*) refers, by way of illustration, to the conceit of being mounted upon an object; it is an injunction. From the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the understanding is that the one desiring heaven possesses the conceit of being mounted upon the sacrifice.
(Aṣṭasahasrī Yaśovijaya, p. 49B)
"Wherever there is a certain person who has a desire, he proceeds toward that [object], considering himself as having ascended to the object. (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p.
30). Others hold that "the *niyoga* is of the nature of the object of enjoyment."
Thus say others: "This is mine to be enjoyed"—in this way, the object of enjoyment is perceived. And through the sense of "mineness," consciousness is established in the enjoyer alone.
For that in which the enjoyer has the conceit of ownership—that alone is to be known as the object of enjoyment; that alone is defined as "one's own."
That very [relationship]—the state of owner and owned—is indicated; [it is] defined as "one's own" (*sva*). (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra-ṭīkā)

That by which [an object] is perceived as "this is mine" through its state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpatayā*) is designated as one's own (*sva*) by means of that form which is to be accomplished;

for an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) that exists in an already established state (*siddharūpa*) does not, by that much alone, constitute an injunction (*niyoga*). Here, the nature of an injunction belongs to the object of enjoyment because it acts as an impeller precisely through its state of being something to be accomplished.
"Those [qualities] belong to the person," say some; others maintain that "the person alone is the agent.
The person always thinks, "This is my duty to be done."
"The excellence of the agent’s action is the *niyoga*, and it is its denotation. (*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p.

30). Thus, when the accomplishment of the task has occurred, the person endowed with that [task] remains always [in the state of] *niyoga* whose reality is uncontradicted. (*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*).
"The person [who has attained this] would be one who has accomplished [his goal]; this alone is said to be the meaning of the sentence" (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 30;
Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 6).
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 262:
[The opponent claims] that for the person to be enjoined (*niyogya*), [the *kārya*] is [the *niyoga*].

That too is charming only so long as it is not examined; for is the nature of the *kārya* as a *niyoga* admitted as being independent of the instigation of the person to be enjoined, or as dependent upon it? Of these, the first alternative is untenable, because a mere *kārya* independent of that [instigation] cannot logically be a *niyoga*, since it would not be a cause for activity.

But if the *niyoga* (the mandate) is dependent upon that [trio], how can the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) alone possess the nature of the *niyoga*? For since all three are causes for activity, it would follow that they all possess that nature. By this, the view that "the *niyoga* is an instigation (*preraṇā*)" is also refuted, because an instigation independent of the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined) and the other factors is a mere babble, as it cannot logically constitute a *niyoga*. Nor is it correct to say that "the *niyoga* is the *kārya* accompanied by an instigation," because in the absence of a *niyojya*, the *niyoga* itself is impossible.
By this, the view that "the *niyoga* is the instigation accompanied by the *kārya*" is also rejected.

The claim that "niyoga" is simply the causative power of the task (*kārya*) itself through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is also unsubstantial. For it is impossible to metaphorically designate as a "causative agent" something that is independent of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and other such factors. Furthermore, does the relationship between the task and the instigation (*preraṇā*) attain the nature of *niyoga* by being either distinct from its correlates or non-distinct from them? It cannot be distinct; for since such a distinct relationship is impossible, it is illogical for it to have the nature of *niyoga*.
Even if the relationship were of the nature of its correlates, it would still be impossible for it to have the nature of *niyoga* if it were independent of the person being instigated.
The theory of *niyoga* as a collective injunction (*samudāyaniyogavāda*) has also been refuted by this very [argument].
However, an *niyoga* that is devoid of the impelling of an action relies upon the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*), and that has already been answered previously.

Furthermore, as for the claim regarding an "injunction mounted on a machine" (*yantrārūḍhaniyoga*), wherein a person desiring heaven, upon the existence of an injunction from a sentence such as the *agnihotra*, considers himself to have entered the objective sphere characterized by sacrifice and thus proceeds—that too is unsatisfactory; for the status of being an instigator (*niyoktṛtva*) in a non-human (Vedic) sentence has already been rejected and will be rejected further.
The *niyoga* as something to be experienced (*bhogyarūpa*) is refuted precisely by the rejection of an injunction whose nature is a fruit;
however, if the *niyoga* were of the nature of the person (*puruṣasvabhāvatva*), there would follow the consequence of its being eternal, because of its eternity— therefore,
[it is] independent.
For one who does not require the instigation of an injunction (*niyojya-preraṇā*)—[Ā.
Ṭi. compare: "An action devoid of instigation, which is not undertaken by an *niyojya*, is not called an 'injunction' (*niyoga*) for anyone."
When the application of the word "niyoga" (injunction) is held to refer to a pure *kārya* (task), by what can its status as an injunction be prevented on the grounds of mere nomenclature? However,
it is logical [to maintain that] a person is enjoined only where a *kārya* is not already perceived.
If it is argued that this *niyoga*— which, like the cognition of the past and so forth,

belongs to the instigator— is a duty recognized by the world and is therefore the very thing to be accomplished (*kārya*), [we reply: because it is already established (*siddha*), it lacks the nature of something yet to be achieved (*sādhya*).

If it is argued that this injunction (niyoga) is designated as something to be accomplished (sādhya), that is merely a figurative application (upacāra) of that status to its object; for how can that which is unestablished possess the nature of an impeller?

If it is claimed that its status as an impeller consists in its being understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then how can one and the same thing be accepted as both the "to-be-accomplished"— which is unestablished— and the "understanding"— which is of the nature of an established entity? These two are mutually contradictory.
If its cognition as something to be accomplished were the impeller [of action],
that would be a cognition of an injunction, not the reality of the injunction itself—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 323b.

Since an injunction (*niyoga*) is impossible for one who is devoid of both the impeller (*preraṇā*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), if such an injunction were to be made, it would merely be a case of giving one's own blanket a different name, "the jumper" (*kūrdālikā*).
— *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 265.

The nature of the *niyoga* [is that] of the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the instigation (*preraṇā*), and the action (*kārya*)—[Ā. Ti.]; the state of being a *niyoga*—[Ā. Ti.]. *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 9.
Because an instigation that is devoid of a person to be enjoined and a fruit for the person to be enjoined is mere idle chatter—
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 265.
Because an injunction is contradictory in the absence of one who is to be enjoined—
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 10.
*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 266:
"In this case as well, because there is no person to be enjoined—[Ācārya’s] Commentary:

because it is impossible to metaphorically attribute the status of an instigator to an *kārya* (duty/task) that is independent of the person to be enjoined and so forth, since such [instigation] is never observed in that manner in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) anywhere."
—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 266; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 10.
For it is impossible for a relation that is distinct from its relata and independent of them to function as a necessary connection (*niyoga*).

Furthermore, the claim that "the nature of a relation consists in its being an injunction" is also difficult to maintain; for it is untenable that the nature of an injunction belongs to two related entities independent of the person being impelled, since an injunction must incite toward action.
(Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 10;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 266)
Of that which is distinct from the two related entities—
see page 150 for comparison— it is said that the relationship between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer exists by virtue of their being mounted upon a machine (yantra).

There is no connection with the nature of the object of enjoyment, nor is the person established at that time; for at the moment of cognition, everything lacks its own essential nature because it is yet to be accomplished.
If that [cognition] were its very nature, then the state of being "to-be-accomplished" would be lost.
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 34.

That too is not contrary to the doctrine of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because it states that "necessity" (*niyoga*) is merely the conceit of the person (*puruṣābhimāna-mātra*), and because that [conceit] is based on the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*).
—*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 10.

Furthermore, what is this "niyoga"? Is it that which enjoins (*niyuṅkte*), or is it the act of enjoining (*niyukti*), or is it that by which one is enjoined (*niyujyate*)? Among these, the first position is untenable; for since the status of being an agent in the act of enjoining cannot possibly exist within a *niyoga* whose nature is merely an effect or the like—given that such a status requires discernment—it is not possible for one who lacks the reflection, "I shall enjoin this person for this purpose," to possess the role of an enjoiner. This is because the notion of being an enjoiner is perceived only in cases such as a master, where such reflection exists. *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 266. What is more, is this *niyoga* that which enjoins, or is it the act of enjoining, or is it that by which one is enjoined? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; for the status of being an agent in the act of enjoining is impossible in a *niyoga* whose nature is an effect and so forth, given that this status belongs to one possessing discernment. Indeed, the status of being an enjoiner is not possible for one who has no such consideration as, "I shall enjoin this person for this purpose"; for this perception [of being an enjoiner] is found only in the case of a master and the like, where such consideration exists.
Furthermore, if [the injunction] were an instigator according to the analogy of water and wind, the previously mentioned defects would follow;
for no one engages in action merely through the existence of an instigator, so long as they do not realize their own subordination to that [instigator].
