Nor is it tenable to define "injunction" (*niyoga*) as "that by which one is enjoined" (*niyujyate 'nena*), because the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) necessarily depend upon an agent (*kartṛ*) and an object (*karman*); and since those two [agent and object] are impossible [in this case], the abstract state and the instrument are also impossible.
For there exists no one here who can enjoin [the word],
and the capacity of a word to act as an injunctive agent has already been refuted; thus, the status of being an injunctive agent is untenable for the word.
Regarding the state of being an instigator (*niyoktṛtā*):

just as the wind, though devoid of intention, impels water, so too might there be the state of being an instigator even for one who lacks intention; to this objection, he replies [with the argument] beginning with "the futility of expiation" (*prāyaścittavaiyarthyāt*), etc.—Ānandagiri’s Commentary (*Ā-Ṭī*).
—[it] would fall [into error]; —iti cettya— Śrī., —iti itya— Ācārya.
Compare also: "Furthermore, an injunction (*niyoga*) is the operation of the one who enjoins; it is not possible without the one who enjoins."
Nor can it have an origin, because its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) is accepted—*Vidhiviveka*, p. 60.

Furthermore, is this *niyoga* (impulsion) of the nature of a verbal operation, of the nature of a human operation, of the nature of both, or of neither? In the first case, the defects already assigned to the position of *śabdabhāvanā* (verbal productive energy) would follow as a consequence, since a verbal operation is by definition the form of *śabdabhāvanā*.

In the second case, however, the same refutation stated for the position of objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) would follow, because the human activity is of the nature of objective efficient force; thus, in both positions, the defects introduced for both positions would persist. As it is said: "And in every sentence-meaning there is an eightfold distinction—is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) the injunction (*niyoga*), or rather is it the object of knowledge (*prameya*)?"
Or it may be devoid of both, or again, it may have the form of both; or it may consist of the operation of the word, or the operation of the person,
or the operation of both, or indeed the non-operation of both.
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 31; *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 262; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 10.
—[The group of] refutations:

[Objection: Both faults would follow. [Response: Even in the case of neither [being the nature], would this *niyoga* (the mandate) have the nature of the object (*viṣaya*), the nature of the fruit (*phala*), or be without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? If it has the nature of the object; then does that object, such as the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, exist at the time of the enjoining sentence—"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *agniṣṭoma*"—or not? If it does not exist, then the *niyoga*, having that as its nature, also does not exist; how then could it be the meaning of the sentence, like a sky-flower? If that which is yet to come and is mounted upon the intellect were the meaning of the sentence, there would be the consequence of following the Buddhist doctrine.
Now, even if that [niyoga] exists at that time, the *niyoga* (the mandate) still cannot be the meaning of the sentence, because it exists for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice and so forth.

Furthermore, if there were identity between these two, it would be illogical for the self to be the producer of its own self due to contradiction, and because it is contradictory for an already accomplished sacrifice or the like to undergo further accomplishment, as in the case of a person who already exists. If it is argued that the *niyoga* has some unaccomplished aspect and the mandate is for the purpose of accomplishing that, then since the *niyoga*—being of that nature—is itself unaccomplished, how can it be the meaning of the sentence? If something merely ascended upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) were to be the meaning of the sentence, that would be a lapse into the Buddhist doctrine.

It is also untenable to claim that the nature of the *niyoga* (the mandate) is the fruit [of action]. For it is not logical that the *niyoga* itself be the fruit such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, because that would entail the necessity of postulating yet another fruit, since a *niyoga* devoid of a fruit is impossible. Furthermore, for those who maintain that the *niyoga* has the fruit as its very nature, if that [first] fruit were to become a *niyoga*, then in postulating a further fruit for it, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, since the fruit is not present at the time the sentence is uttered, the *niyoga* whose nature is that fruit is likewise not present; how then could it be the meaning of the sentence? If it is argued that what is mounted upon the intellect (*buddhyārūḍha*) is the meaning of the sentence, then one falls into the position of the opponent’s doctrine.

The claim that "an injunction is devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) has also been refuted by this [very argument], because such a thing, being devoid of intrinsic nature, does not transcend the status of being a mere exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). As the comparison states: "If an injunction is held to be a property (*dharma*) belonging to the object being enjoined, the agent enjoining, or both, then in all cases it does not abide as the meaning of the word."
For if the nature of that [object] were to consist in being something to be enjoined, how could its status as something to be performed be established?
Even if it were established, if it were still to be performed, there would be no cessation of performance—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 16.
Is that [object] also of the nature of the object (*viṣaya*), or of the nature of the result (*phala*), or devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? — *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 8;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 262.

Compare: "Even if it were the property of the object, since the object itself is not established and lacks its own essential form (*svarūpa*), how could it be cognized from a word? — *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 17.
*The nature of the object*:
[this refers to] the future object, such as a sacrifice (*yāga*), which is yet to come.
Accordingly, at the time of employing the sentence— [as stated in] Pra., Ā.,

or Ba.— if that [injunction] exists at the time of the sentence, then the injunction is not the meaning of the sentence, because its purpose is the accomplishment of the sacrifice and so forth, and it is impossible to accomplish again what has already been accomplished.
—*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 8;
[the compound] *niyoga-viṣaya-niyogayoḥ* (of the injunction and the object of the injunction)—Ārya-ṭīkā.
Now, what of [the case of] sacrifice and the like?

Even in the second alternative, that is not an injunction (*niyoga*), because since the fruit is something yet to come into being, it cannot constitute an injunction; furthermore, at that time, it is not present.

If that [sentence] were the meaning of the statement, then because one would have to resort to the doctrine of words being without a basis (*nirālambana-śabdavāda*), how could the system of Prabhākara be established? (Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p.
262; Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 8; Sugatamata).

Furthermore, is this *niyoga* (an injunction) of a nature that impels one to action, or is it of a nature that does not impel? In the first case, it would impel even the followers of the Buddha and others, just as it does for the Prabhākara school, because its nature is to impel in every respect.
If you argue that it does not impel them because they are mistaken (*viparyāsa*), we say no; for it could equally be said by you that it impels [us] because you are mistaken.
Now, if its nature is non-impelling, then it is established that it lacks the quality of being a cause for activity, and that [lack] proves its lack of status as a sentence-meaning.

Furthermore, in sentences such as "The Agniṣṭoma," there is no word whatsoever expressive of a *niyoga* (an injunction) that stands between the object and the fruit—either as an intermediary or as a bystander—distinct from the words denoting the constituent elements of the object and so forth, by virtue of which even that [injunction] might attain the status of a word-meaning like the object and the rest.

Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence cannot be something that is not the meaning of its constituent words; for the meaning of a sentence is defined as a collection of word-meanings that are mutually dependent and independent of other words.
Therefore, even an injunction (*niyoga*) cannot logically constitute the meaning of a sentence.
For would that [cause] have the nature of being an initiator (*pravartaka*), or would it not have that nature? (Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 264;
Aṣṭasāhasrikā p. 8). Compare: "If [it is argued that] cessation occurs by means of what is appointed [to cause it], then it would follow for everything."

Because of having that as its intrinsic nature, space is not non-space; for nothing whatsoever has an intrinsic nature. If it were perceived otherwise due to error, then who would establish the distinction between error and non-error?
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 15: "Thus, the [command] of the Tathāgatas... [Sanskrit fragment]: *śra-niyogasya*.

— A comparison with the Buddhists and others regarding intrinsic nature (svabhāva): If it is argued that [the world] does not proceed from them because of their error, then let it be that [the world] proceeds even for others because of their error.
For one might indeed say: "The Prābhākaras act upon the injunction of words because they are deluded, whereas others do not, because they are not deluded";

yet to claim that the Buddhists and others are deluded because their doctrine is subverted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the Prābhākaras are not, is mere partiality, since there is no difference in the fact that their doctrine is likewise subverted by valid cognition.
(Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 9)
"According to the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 264,
it should be stated that this applies to the Prābhākaras as well" (Ānandāśrama edition).
Comparison—The meaning of a sentence is indeed the meaning of the words themselves, and it is not something beyond their scope;
for since the meaning of the sentence consists precisely of the meanings of the words as qualified by their relations to other word-meanings, it would be untenable if they were not word-meanings.
(*Vidhiviveka*, p. 49)

Even those who maintain that "injunction" (vidhi) is the property of an agent—characterized by commanding, requesting, or permitting—and well-known as a cause for activity, are ignorant of the truth. For in Vedic sentences, which are devoid of any connection to a person, it is impossible for commanding and the like to exist as properties of a person; thus, the assumption that they constitute an injunction is untenable.

Or, if one were to assume them to exist there, the consequence would be their human authorship, making the assumption of their non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) impossible. Thus, while seeking to join one thing, another falls away.

For instigation (*vyāpāraṇā*) preceded by disrespect is called *preṣaṇā* (commanding), whereas that preceded by respect is *adhyeṣaṇā* (requesting); and *abhyanujñā* (permission) is the conduct of not opposing what another desires. Since all these—commanding and the rest—are essentially specific states of intention residing in persons, they do not apply in the slightest degree to the Vedic sentences, which are not of human origin. In that context, an injunction (*vidhi*) is an instigation; it is the impelling of a subordinate person, such as a servant.

*Nimantraṇa* is the performance of an assignment; its meaning is the urging [someone] regarding what is necessary. *Āmantraṇa* is permission to act according to one's own will. *Adhīṣṭa* is an activity preceded by a formal invitation of respect.
—Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa, p. 142—The Naiyāyikas also [state] the purpose of the definition... Ācārya.

A *vidhi* is a prescriptive statement; that which prescribes and impels is a *vidhi*. A *vidhi*, moreover, is either an injunction (*niyoga*) or a permission (*anujñā*), as in "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice," and so forth.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 2.1.63
A sentence which enjoins, "One should do this," is an injunction (*niyoga*);
that which authorizes an agent to perform an action is an authorization sentence (*anujñāvākya*)—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 269.

The injunction (*vidhi*)—namely, the intention of the speaker—is denoted by the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. in relation to activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth; however, the status of being a means to what is desired by the agent (*kartṛ-iṣṭābhyupāyatā*) is what is inferred.

The phrase "in relation to activity and so forth" uses the locative case of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*); thus, the meaning is that the meaning of the optative is the intention of a reliable person (*āpta-abhiprāya*) with respect to the objects of activity and cessation (*nivṛtti*).

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply the cognition that [an action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), which functions as the instigator (*pravarttaka*); however, it is the intention (*abhiprāya*) of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) [that constitutes the meaning], because of parsimony (*lāghava*). This is the sense [of the author of the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*, *Prakaraṇa* 5.15].

In that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the injunction (*praiṣa*) and so forth—which are attributes of a person—are not possible. For in the world, it is well-known that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is an excellence of intention characterized by commanding, entreating, or permitting, and this is an attribute of an agent. If it is argued that while such [an intention] is impossible in the case of Vedic sentences which are not of human origin, it is possible in what is known [to be of human origin], we say no; for that would entail their being of human origin.
—Vidhiviveka, p. 23; "But [an injunction] such as 'the command' (ājñā) and so forth cannot be the meaning of the Veda, as it is not appropriate for it to be a duty of the individual (pudharma).
—Nyāyasudhā, p. 37.
In the Veda,
the nature of the *praiṣa* (commands) and other such forms, which consist of the intention of a person,
is to be observed— page 580, note 4.

Others, however, maintain that because each of the specific forms such as *praipa* (command) is subject to deviation [from its intended function] and because it would involve the fault of postulating multiple powers (*śakti*), there must be a single "impulsion" (*pravartanā*) alone—which is non-deviant in all cases—that constitutes the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*). They too have not correctly examined the reality, because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible;

for just as a universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) cannot exist if it is empty of particular instances like the brindled cow (*khaṇḍa*), so too an "impulsion" in general cannot exist if it is divested of its particular forms such as *praipa*.

Furthermore, if the Veda is accepted as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), then since specific injunctions (*praiṣa*) and other such particulars— which are by nature dependent on the particular intentions of a person— are impossible, how could there even be the possibility of "instigation" (*pravartanā*) in general?

The Mīmāṃsakas, Grammarians, and others maintain that the denotable meaning is "instigation" as a universal (*jāti*) inherent in these four [types of verbal suffixes], because this is more parsimonious (*lāghava*).

And it has been said: "There exists a form of instigation (pravarttanā) permeating all four [means of knowledge]; it is precisely there that the optative suffix (liṅ) should be prescribed. What is the purpose of intending to express a distinction?
Whether for the sake of explaining the underlying logic, or for the sake of elaboration."
The four [factors] beginning with injunction (*vidhi*) have been presented at the outset;
thus, "being an instigator" (*pravarttakatva*) consists in being the delimitor of the objecthood of the cognition that produces activity.
Since this property belongs to "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), that alone is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*).

And since specific instances such as commands (*praipādi*) are not denotable due to their variability, it is understood that the general property of instigation (*pravartanāsāmānya*), which pervades all of them, is what is denotable—*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, p.
145. And therein, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), one determines the injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) residing in instigation—*Nyāyasudhā*, p. 30.

An activity conducive to engagement is "incitement" (*pravartanā*), and since that activity takes various forms such as commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth, it is impossible for each individual form to be denoted by the word "injunction" (*vidhi*). Therefore, one concludes that only the general category of incitement (*pravartanāsāmānya*) is what is denoted by the word "injunction"—as stated in the *Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, p. 180: "Command and the rest... (*preṣaṇādyā*).

Nor is it tenable that the meaning of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth in common usage is merely "instigation" (*pravartanā*)—indeterminate and devoid of an agent. For even if one holds this view—that because of the fault of postulating multiple potencies and because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), commands (*praiṣa*) and the like are not denotable, whereas mere instigation is non-deviant and thus its application in the Veda is also justified—this too is unconvincing. This is because a universal cannot exist without particular instances, and because an activity cannot be established in the absence of an agent.
For neither are particular instances such as commands possible [in the case of the Veda], nor is any other particular instance demonstrated.
Alternatively, if it were for the sake of demonstrating that [activity], the mention of a "universal" (*sāmānya*) at this juncture would be useless;
for such a universal, from which all particular distinctions have been discarded, would be like the caste of Brahminhood when its specific divisions such as the Kaṭhas have been abandoned.

Furthermore, activity (*pravartanā*) is the operation of one who instigates; it does not shine forth without him, because of the absence of a person and because the capacity of a word to instigate has been refuted. Thus, there is an absence of an instigator.
—Vidhiviveka, pp.

25–26: As for what was stated—"because [the injunctions] such as *praiṣa* (command) are fallible," and so forth—that is incorrect; for we accept that they function as motivators (*pravarttaka*) according to their possibility and according to their own nature.

For when [an action] proceeds from an injunction (*preṣaṇā*), then that [injunction] possesses the quality of being the instigator; but when it proceeds from a request (*adhyeṣaṇā*), then that [request] does so.

It is not the case that long threads of a white nature and so forth are the producers of a cloth at one time, while short threads of a red nature and so forth are [the producers] at another; for on this basis alone, it is not logical to attribute the status of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) toward the production of a cloth to some other entity distinct from the threads, as this contradicts empirical experience.

The meaning is as follows: if *preṣaṇā* (command) were the injunctive force (*vidhitva*), then *adhyeṣaṇā* (request) would not possess the injunctive force; conversely, if *adhyeṣaṇā* were the injunctive force, then *preṣaṇā* would lack the injunctive force. Thus, there is mutual inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, the implication is that it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a distinct potency (*śakti*) for each of these, such as *preṣaṇā* and the others.
—This is appropriate according to its respective [context].

Others, however, say: "The fruit (phala) is the motivator; its activity is 'instigation' (pravarttanā). For every person who acts with foresight acts for the sake of a fruit; therefore, the fruit possesses the quality of being the motivator."

"The nature of pleasure (*prīti*) is its activity (*vyāpāra*) in regard to engagement, and that very [nature] is the instigation (*pravartanā*), which is the injunction (*vidhi*). This too is inconsistent; for it is untenable that the fruit (*phala*) is the cause of engagement, since even a known fruit is not a cause of engagement without a desire for it (*arthitā*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of everyone engaging everywhere.

Desire for the object (*arthitā*) is not itself an operation (*vyāpāra*); rather, because it consists of the cognizer’s wish, it is a property of that [cognizer]. Since a wish does not arise unless the object—the result—is of the nature of pleasure (*prītyātmaka*), the property of being of the nature of pleasure—which belongs to the result—serves as the cause of activity by way of producing that wish. [Objection: Even so, since the state of being of the nature of pleasure resides only in the result, the self’s activity would occur toward that [result] alone, and not toward the action (*karman*), because the two are distinct entities. [Response: ... [The remainder of the argument follows].
For it is not the case that activity occurs toward one thing when something else is desired, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that there is no such over-extension because activity occurs only toward the action itself since it is the means for achieving the intended result—since indeed those who act with foresight do not abandon the means and instead engage with what is not a means or what does not accomplish the goal—then how can the result itself be the motivator? For that would entail that the motivator is actually the means to that result.
Thus say Jayanta Bhaṭṭa and others.
Seeing that only the fruit being desired possesses the power to impel,
it is held [by us] that neither an injunction nor the word with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth has the capacity to cause a person to act;
for even the operation belonging to these, known as the "denotative productive activity" (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*), is not capable [of such a task].
The state of being a means to the highest good does not reside in the object of the injunction, nor does it reside in passion and the like;
therefore, the stainless-minded author of the Sūtras, the impeller [of inquiry], has declared that the desired fruit is the motivator—
sometimes expressed directly by a word, and sometimes arrived at through the context.
In some cases the fruit is obtainable through mere observation, yet it is understood to be present everywhere;
therefore, because the fruit is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and because it is not excluded from all [actions],
and because actions and so forth exist for its sake, it is accepted as the meaning of the sentence.

Alternatively, due to its preeminence, the fruit constitutes the meaning of the sentence; for the effort of the wise is directed toward that [fruit], and it is precisely that which the author of the Sūtras has taught as the motivator—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 362–65.

If it be thought that the fruit (*phala*) is the instigator (*pravartaka*), and that its operation (*vyāpāra*) is the instigation (*pravarttanā*), because a person desiring a fruit engages in the means to achieve it and would otherwise not do so—[and thus] no specific operation is the instigation, but rather any operation whatsoever capable of producing engagement is the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*), as seen in such instances as "alms cause one to dwell" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) or "the kārīṣa fire causes one to study" (*kārīṣo 'gnir adhyāpayati*)—that is incorrect. For what is the basis for the restriction (*niyama*) that a person's activity (*vyāpṛti*) must be directed toward the fruit? The status of being a means to the fruit (*phalasādhanatā*) is to be determined in relation to the action (*karman*); when, then, is the status of being the end to be achieved (*sādhyatā*) [determined]?
—Vidhiviveka, p. 26; because it is a property of the self (puruṣadharman), according to the Āloka commentary.

If the desire for a fruit (*phalārthitā*) is the cause of engagement (*pravṛttihetu*), then—whether it be that desire itself, its connection [to the agent], or its inherence [in him]—it is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*), according to the rule: "In compounds, *kṛt*-derivatives, and *taddhita*-derivatives, the relation is expressed by means of the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal*" (*Pāṇini 5.1.119*). Thus, the fruit is not the activity (*vyāpṛti*). — *Vidhiviveka*, p. 27. Alternatively, if the nature of the fruit as consisting of pleasure (*prītyātmatā*)—which is the property of the fruit that serves as the cause of engagement by way of presenting that [desire]—is the instigation (*pravarttanā*), then that too resides only in that [fruit], and not in the action (*karman*).
And if it were to proceed by means of the operation of the fruit, it would proceed everywhere, because there would be no cause for restriction—
[Vidhiviveka, p. 27]— by way of generating desire.
The Sage— [commentary]: "In the fruit itself,
from the fruit"— [commentary].
The fruit of action— [Ānandagiri’s commentary notes:
"in action," such as sacrifice (yāga) and so forth].

Because it is the means to that [result], one engages only in action, not everywhere; for that very reason, the cause of engagement in action is its being the means to that [result], and since that [means-ness] does not exist in the form of the result itself, but rather inheres in the action, the action would be the motivator. He objects: "Because it is the means to that, one engages only in action, and not everywhere, because not everything is a means to the result. He replies: "Precisely because of that—that is, precisely because engagement occurs when there is the state of being a means to that."

"Let it be, then, that the cause of activity toward the action is its being a means to that [result], and not its being of the nature of the result; what is the fault? To this he says: "And therefore, since it would be inherent in the action and not inherent in the result, the action itself would be the motivator. (Vidhiviveka-Ṭīkā, p. 27-28)

The sacrifice itself, as the means for accomplishing the fruit, would be the motivator; for it is observed that activity occurs only when the sacrifice is ascertained to be the means for that [fruit]. Now, one might argue that since the state of being accomplished by a specific action—which inheres in the fruit—is the cause of activity, the fruit itself is the motivator, and thus activity toward the specific action serving as the means is not contradictory. But what is this "state of being accomplished by that" (*tatsādhyatā*)? Is it the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the fruit, or a distinct power (*śaktibheda*)? If it were the essential nature, then because that is indistinguishable everywhere, activity would occur even toward other things, just as it does toward the specific action.
For satisfaction does not occur merely in relation to the food consumed, nor in relation to the fire; thus, one who desires satisfaction must also engage with the fire.

Furthermore, would this difference in capacity (śaktibheda) belong to the fruit at the time of its own existence, or at the time of its non-existence? Of these two alternatives, the first is untenable, because that difference in capacity is postulated for the sake of the production of a specific fruit from a specific action alone; moreover, a capacity belonging to what has already been produced is of no use in determining its production.
Indeed, that which has already arisen does not arise again by virtue of a power, because that would involve a contradiction;
thus, the second alternative is also untenable. For an effect that is non-existent—resembling a sky-flower—cannot be the locus of a specific power known as "the capacity to be produced" (*sādhyatā*).
If it were such a locus, its non-existence would be contradicted, since the definition of the non-existent is the total absence of all powers.

In that case, then, being something-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatā*) is the cause of activity, and since that resides in the fruit (*phala*), there is no fault. For instance, because things such as satisfaction—which are intensely desired—are accomplished through a specific action, activity occurs toward that [action] alone. But what is this "being something-to-be-accomplished"? If it were the nature of the fruit itself, there would be the undesirable consequence of activity occurring everywhere. What is meant is this: although "being something-to-be-accomplished" resides in the fruit, because its determination is dependent upon the means (*sādhana*), it also encompasses the means; however, it does not encompass what is not a means. Therefore, due to that very distinction, it impels one toward the means alone, and not toward everything.

He refutes this as follows: "What, then, is this 'being-to-be-accomplished' (sādhyatā)? If it is the nature of the result, then, since that [result] does not depend upon the means for its definition, one would not be prompted to act toward the means; or else, one would be prompted everywhere, because there is no difference in its being something other [than the means]. (Vidhiviveka-ṭīkā, p.

28). The point is that the state of being produced by sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma inheres in the result, such as heaven; therefore, if the fact of being accomplished by the sacrifice were actually the cause of activity, it would follow that the result itself is the motivator.
—Engagement by way of being something to be accomplished;
the state of being accomplished through specific actions and their capacity. —Śrī.
In the case of cow-slaughter and the like, [the result] is not of the nature of heaven as a fruit, unlike the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices— Ā. Ṭī.
For indeed, a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣa*) does not [exist] at the time of its own existence, [as stated in] Śra., Ba. (Variant readings: bhu-Śra., śra.-Ba.)

But when is this distinction of capacity (śaktibheda) said to be something to be accomplished? Certainly not at the time of the existence of the result, because that would be redundant and because it would not be a cause for activity. Indeed, a capacity that produces what has already arisen is not purposeful;
nor does anyone engage in the means to achieve a result that is already established.
—Because there is a contradiction between that which has already arisen and arising; for it is only that which has not yet arisen that is seen to arise.
Even at the time of non-existence, how could that which is non-existent possess causal power? It would be like a sky-flower.—*Vidhiviveka*, p. 29.
Regarding the capacity for being a probandum (*sādhyatāśakti*):
[it consists] either in being the locus of a specific capacity in the form of being a probandum,
or in the existence of that substratum.
The sense is that if the fruit were the locus of power, it would necessarily exist.

Furthermore, does this fruit impel the person while being present, or while being absent? If it is present, for what purpose does it impel him? For a person engages in activity because he desires the fruit; if that fruit already exists, there is no need for such activity.

For it is not observed in the world that one who already possesses something engages in activity for the sake of that very thing, as this would lead to the absurd consequence of the cessation of activity never occurring.

Nor is it correct to say that one engages in activity to establish a connection with oneself even regarding a result that already exists; because a result consists of pleasure and the absence of pain, and both of these, when they arise, arise as being already connected to the self.

Now, a person desiring heaven proceeds to act in order to bring about the connection of the self with the fruit of heaven and so forth, which already exists; but what then is the case regarding those who desire a son and the like? For it is not possible for the fruit such as a son to exist at that time, because that would contradict perception.
Therefore, the fruit is heaven and so forth.

Even when the fruit has been accomplished, there would be no cessation of activity; for instance, in the Putreṣṭi sacrifice performed with the desire for a son, the son does not exist [prior to birth] in the same way that heaven and such do. Furthermore, is this fruit a cause for activity by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*), or as qualified by the state of being something to be achieved (*sādhyatā*)? In the first case, there would be a cause for human activity even when the fruit is already established, since mere existence is no different in that regard.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable for prudent persons to engage in an activity for the sake of what is already established, as that would entail the consequence of never ceasing from it.

If it is argued that the fruit as delimited by its state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatāvacchinna*)—and not the fruit alone—is the cause of engagement, that too is untenable; for it would follow that even one who does not desire the fruit would engage in it.

For if a fruit, perceived as qualified by its state of being to-be-accomplished, prompts the cognizer to act, then it would prompt even one who does not desire it, since there is no distinction between them in that regard.
Therefore, it is not logical for this [Self] to be an impeller when it exists,
nor when it does not exist; for it is impossible for that which is non-existent to be an agent, and there is a contradiction in saying "it is both non-existent and an impeller."
Because it would entail the consequence of never ceasing activity; [the text] "devoid of a petitioner" (arthitā-rahitam)—[variant reading in Ānandagiri’s commentary:
"of a petitioner" (arthino’–)].
One should also satisfy the seeker by means of the fruit delimited by the state of being the probandum (sādhyatāvacchinna).
Ā॰, yedaviśe– śra॰, ba॰.
— of pride, [there is] no impelling— Oṃ;
because that which lacks a fruit does not exist.

The sense is that if [an impulse] were the motivator, it would necessarily be a real entity (*sattva*). As for those who assert: "The desire for a result residing in the person to be impelled is the injunction (*vidhi*) because it is the motivator; for no activity is observed in one who lacks such desire. Indeed, even without a verbal expression, it impels a desiring person toward an object they long for," their words are also unexamined. This is because desire, being non-pervasive, cannot logically be a constituent factor of activity.
Its non-pervasiveness is well-established by its impossibility in the case of the activity of infants.

For instance—a certain boy, prompted by his teacher while performing some task, being asked by someone about its purpose, replies: "I do not know what purpose there is in doing this; I am simply acting because I am prompted by my teacher. Thus, since human activity is observed even in the absence of a desire for a result, the desire for a result is not all-pervasive (avyāpaka) across all instances of instigation.

Others, however, maintain that action (*karman*) alone—residing in the person—is the injunction (*vidhi*) because it accomplishes the intended object; yet even that view is inconsistent, because it is impossible for action to have the nature of an injunction simply by being the object of an injunction.
For in common worldly usage, action is well known as the *object* of an injunction, not as its *nature*; therefore, there must be something else here that acts as the motivator.
Indeed, it is not logical for something to be an instigator for the sake of its own self-establishment, because that would be a contradiction.

Let it be, then, that the object (*karman*) is the instigator; its "instigation" (*pravartanā*) consists in being the means to a desired end, since it takes the form of a cause for activity. No; because it is the object (*viṣaya*).
He refutes this [objection] by stating: "Not so, because that [object] is the object; the instigator is that which prompts the agent of the activity."
And that [agent] becomes established;
for if the action were already established prior to its commencement, then the object of cultivation would not exist before the cultivation begins,
and the sky can never be an object to be cultivated by this [cultivation].
If the object (*viṣaya*) is the action (*karman*), then since it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*), how could it be an instigator? This is the meaning [of the *Vidhiviveka*]. (Commentary, p. 35).
For it is not logical that a pot, in its capacity as an object of cognition, should possess the nature of cognition itself. (Author’s Note)
The nature of the ritual (*vidhisvabhāva*) in actions such as sacrifice (*yāga*). *vidhirviṣa–* (Śrī. / *vidhiviṣa–* (Bā. [is the reading].

Furthermore, does the arisen karma impel the person toward the establishment of the self, or the unarisen? In that regard, since the nature of the arisen has already been established, its impelling of the person is useless;
as for the unarisen, it is impossible for it to be an impeller.
For only something existent can be an instigator for someone, not something non-existent such as a donkey’s horn, because it is impossible for such a thing to function as a causal agent;

and since no relationship with this non-existent entity is possible for the authorless Vedic word, how could it be conveyed by the Vedic sentences, such that—by being the cause of human activity—it would constitute the meaning of those sentences?

Now, if it is argued that action (*karman*), while existing in a general form, impels a person toward the accomplishment of its specific form—that is not so. For that aspect by which it exists [already] cannot be accomplished by a person; and that aspect by which it is to be accomplished cannot be the denotable object [of the word], because a relationship [between them] is impossible.

Indeed, if one accepts the eternality of the relationship, the denotable object, and the denotation itself, then even the possibility of an eternal relationship occurring with respect to a non-eternal specific action is not feasible.

As for the claim that there is comprehension of it through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that too is incorrect, because such [comprehension] has been refuted along with that [view] during the examination of the word and its meaning.

Because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to possess the nature of an agent— that is, the capacity to instigate— within the activity of its own manifestation, [it cannot be so] by means of an object.
"Along with the human sacrifice"—Ā.
Ṭi.; "of cow-dung and so forth"—Ā. Ṭi.
That which is to be expressed by a Vedic sentence, whether in a general form— according to Ānandagiri’s commentary— or in a specific form— according to Ānandagiri’s commentary.
Of conventions, objects, and words.

Now, one might object: since it is accepted that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth constitute the sentence of an injunction (*vidhi*), and since [the injunction] is unestablished prior to the utterance of those suffixes, it is impossible for them to have [an injunction] as their denotation because the relationship [between word and meaning] has not yet been grasped; therefore, it is improper to claim that they have that as their primary object (i.e., the injunction) even before the utterance of the *liṅ* etc. Anticipating this objection, [the author] argues as follows: By denoting the general category of "incitement" (*pravartanā*)—which persists through operations such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*) or entreating (*adhyeṣaṇa*) and serves as the cause for the activity that arises immediately after hearing the words—the specific form of that incitement is required. Since in the impersonal Veda, human attributes such as commanding are impossible, the specific form called "injunction" (*vidhi*), being distinct from those, is understood through implication (*lakṣaṇā*) by process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Because this [implied injunction] does not depend on the grasping of a relationship [between word and meaning], it does not require prior establishment; thus, its status as the function of the word is not contradictory. (Nyāyasūcīnibandhana, p. 559; likewise, p. 30)
Mīmāṃsānyāya-prakāśa, p. 180:
[The definition] of injunction (vidhi).
Like a relation, page 570.

Now, if it is argued that an injunction (*vidhi*) is the cognition of the self’s connection with an action not yet attained—because it prompts activity—for people in the world are observed to act after understanding their connection with an action upon being told, "This is your duty," that too is incorrect. For in the world, activity is not observed to arise from the mere cognition of a connection with an action; rather, it arises through conformity to that [action]. Otherwise, it would follow that everyone would act merely by the cognition of a connection with a duty, such as "This is your duty. Consequently, even conformity to that [action] would result in being an injunction, simply because it prompts activity.
Or rather, that [intention] is not even possible; for, as in the case of a master’s statement, it is impossible for such an intention to exist in a Vedic statement.
Indeed, having understood the intention of a master from a command such as "Do this," one proceeds by conforming to it and not transgressing his will;
but this is not possible in the case of a Vedic statement, because there is no speaker.

As for the following justification: "Activity occurs through the cognition of the self's connection with an action that has not [previously] attained a relation, as in the worldly usage 'This work is yours today';

therefore, the injunction (*vidhi*) is the connection between an agent and an unattained action, consisting of the making known of what was unknown and the impelling of one who has not yet acted, by way of negating both types of attainment"—this is merely the belching out of those who profess to know injunctions.
—Vidhiviveka, p. 40;
Śrīdhara: "That very same [objection regarding] action [is not valid], because...
This is not the core point, since: "In the world, there is no activity of the intellect regarding yoga, because [people act] from the perception of intention."
O Desire, it would be false; why then does this person exert himself in vain?

Let him determine from the word that "this is the application of action for the self," and if it is so, let him conclude "it is thus"; if it were otherwise, he would conclude "it is not so. But why does he proceed [to act]? In the world, however, upon hearing the statement "This is your duty today," one who has understood the speaker's intention and who conforms to that intention is fit to proceed; otherwise, everyone would simply act [at random].
—Vidhiviveka, pp. 41–42:

Since activity occurs in accordance with the intention of the person who utters the sentence, provided there is no contradiction [with other means of knowledge], the sense is that compliance with intention alone must be the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Thus, since there is no agent who performs the action and consequently no conformity to intention, even those who claim that "the injunction (*vidhi*) is the cognition of *dharma*— known as the means to the highest good (*śreyas*)— which, being the cause of engagement, leads one to think, 'We shall engage in this because we perceive the meaning of the verbal root as a means to a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of its being a means to achieve results such as heaven,'" they too do not understand the meaning of the word; for in common worldly usage, the status of being a means to the highest good is not established as the nature of an injunction, whereas commands (*praiṣa*) and the like are what are so established.
For an injunction (*vidhi*) is that which is denoted by words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*);

however, the state of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*) is not well-known in the world as being denoted by that word, such that it could constitute its nature as an injunction. And the determination of word-meanings follows worldly usage;
"those very words which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.3.30).
From such statements as these, Maṇḍanamiśra and others [hold this view].

Maṇḍanamiśra indeed maintains that the very cognition "this is the means to my welfare" is the cause of activity; and thus it has been stated by him: "For a person, there is no other motivator for actions than the fact that they are the means to what is desired. And they declare that the 'incitement' (pravartanā) is the property that is the cause of activity.
For incitement is a certain excellence of being capable of producing activity, which is designated as an 'operation' (vyāpāra)."
And that very [status] of actions as being the sought-after means is precisely what is meant; for no one engages in them without first apprehending them as such.
Even engagement arising from commands and the like is based, in some way, upon their status as sought-after causes, since otherwise it would not occur.
—Vidhiviveka, p. 243.

And so it has been said: "When the fact that the meaning of the verbal root is the object to be accomplished is indicated by the direct denotation (*pada-śruti*) of the word, then by the direct denotation of the injunction (*vidhi-śruti*), the *bhāvanā* is established as having the human goal as its objective."
For it is said [in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, p. 49]: "Indeed, this status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) is eternally understood from the Veda.

Therefore, the meaning expressed by the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is precisely the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). Consequently, in the case of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) associated with that [suffix], the fruit alone is the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), while the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*). (p. 46) Thus, just as the operation of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*) is denoted as "instigation" (*pravartanā*), the word denotes the state of being a means to what is desired in the form of instigation, and not in its own intrinsic nature; therefore, there is no contradiction with our cognition.
This very point is also the intention of the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra, who says: "Because [the act] is not desired as a means by the person, there is no other motivator for actions;
they declare that the property which is the cause of activity is indeed the impelling force (*pravartanā*), and the cognition of such [impelling force] is the condition for activity," and so forth.

That very expression of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), which consists in the instigation produced by the word as its agent, is what is called "word-bhāvanā" (*śabdabhāvanā*)—*Nyāyaratnamālā*, p.
47, 53–54. The essence of injunction (*vidhitattva*) is precisely this being a means to a desired end—*Tantrarahasya*, p. 45.

And thus, in accordance with its nature as an instigation, even the injunction (*vidhi*) has as its meaning nothing other than being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth— *Muktāvalī*, p.
516— in the case of sacrifices such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* in the world.

This has been extracted from the Tautātita (Tarkapāda), page 134: as the nature of an injunction— which is synonymous with being a means to the highest good— it consists in being a means to what is desired.

Furthermore, to what does this status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) belong—to the *bhāvanā* or to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)? It cannot belong to the *bhāvanā*, because its essential nature is unestablished according to the manner previously stated.
Nor can it belong to the meaning of the verbal root; for sacrifices and the like, which primarily involve the slaughter of animals, cannot logically be means to the highest good.
Indeed, violence is not a means to the highest good, since that would entail the same status for the killing of Brahmins and so forth.

Since it is the performance of what is enjoined that constitutes its being a means [to a goal], then even such injunctions as "one should kill a Brāhmaṇa" would entail being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) simply because they involve the performance of what is enjoined;

furthermore, their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) would be no different in the Veda than in the case of the *ṭhak*-suffix rule. For comparison: moreover, those [who hold this view] maintain that the capacity to be a means to the highest good residing in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is what prompts action, and it is not proper for that [capacity] to be denoted separately [from the productive urge itself].
Since meditation has three aspects, at the time of understanding its essential nature, the relationship of means and end between this [meditation] and the sacrifice for heaven is established;
for otherwise, it would follow that [the sacrifice] were merely a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 361)
Regarding the performance of what is enjoined:

[The opponent] says that since sacrifice is enjoined in the Veda, it is therefore a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). To this, the following comparison is offered: If it is argued that the reason [given by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because the slaughter of animals and so forth, when preceded by an injunction, lacks the status of being a cause of harm due to its being the performance of what is enjoined, then let there likewise be no status as a cause of harm for the slaughter of living beings by the *Khārapaṭikas* when preceded by an injunction, on the grounds that it is the performance of what is enjoined; thus, let the statement "heaven results from the slaughter of living beings" be the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). (Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 12)
Because it is established by the treatises of the Cārvākas,
others, however, maintain that "instruction" (upadeśa) is the injunction (vidhi);
and by the word "instruction," both the object [of the injunction], such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and its denotation (*abhidhā*) are expressed.

In this context, "instruction" (*upadeśa*) refers to that which is taught or made known; thus, the *viṣaya* (the object), such as a sacrifice and so forth, is the instruction. Alternatively, "instruction" refers to that by means of which something is taught; thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are the instruction. Furthermore, "instruction" is defined as the act of teaching, the expression, or the utterance. This too is inconsistent, because it would follow that even the technical suffix *-ṭhak* would constitute an injunction (*vidhi*), since according to your own postulated method of analysis, the status [of being an instruction] would be equal in cases such as "one desiring prosperity should kill a Brahmin" just as it is in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma. Therefore, "instruction" is the utterance of a specific word—[Śābarabhāṣya 1].
1.5 "But has not the authority of *codanā* been asserted? How then is it established for *upadeśa*? To this he says: *codanā*, *upadeśa*, and *vidhi* are synonymous terms.
—Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika 5.11:

"Instruction" (upadeśa) is the impulsion of one who has not yet set out toward an action that serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined; it is well-known [to occur] in cases such as teachers and physicians, and it is not imagined to be absent even in the case of obligatory (nitya) rites.

Although in the Veda, command (*ājñā*) and entreaty (*abhyarthanā*) are untenable, instruction (*upadeśa*) is appropriate; yet even that, being of the nature of instigation, is recognized as a fourth [type] in common worldly usage.
For indeed, command and entreaty direct the agent toward an action whose fruit has not been secured for the one being enjoined.

Instruction (*upadeśa*) has the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) as its purpose, whereas permission (*anujñā*), although it may be similar in some cases, does not have that as its scope because it concerns a person who is already engaged in action.
The wise declare that instruction is the incitement of one who has not yet begun to act toward an action within the domain of what is to be enjoined.

For there is no cognition of an instruction such as "Bring the cow," "Teach the boy," or "Do as you please," nor is there a cognition such as "If you wander for alms" or "One who has a fever should eat wholesome food. Furthermore, this [instruction] is most commonly recognized in the world among human compositions, such as treatises on erotics and economics, as being unadulterated by commands and the like; and it is also found in the words of cowherds and others intent on describing a path, such as "Go by this way," which is intended for demonstration. Therefore, the term *upadeśa* (instruction) denotes the knowledge of the expression, utterance, and so forth of the word's meaning, established through the grammatical relations of object, agent, and instrument.

For by them [the teachers], like [the authors of] injunctions and so forth, the objects and other elements are indicated according to their intended meaning. He introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): It is said—“Instruction” (*upadeśa*) is appropriate, because it is possible even in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), for he will state later that this [instruction] does not have the function of a compeling agent (*niyojaka*), whereby it would have a conscious being as its author; nor is it non-worldly or non-exhortatory in nature, whereby it would not be an injunction (*vidhi*). He says: “That too, just like that [injunction], is known in the world as the fourth [type of speech], consisting of exhortation (*preraṇātmaka*), just like a command (*ājñā*).”

This is what is meant: commands (*ājñā*), entreaties (*abhyarthanā*), and instructions (*upadeśa*) are equal in their nature as instigations (*preraṇātmatā*) because they bring about activity toward an action by making that action their object.

Among these, the action made the object of a command or an entreaty is understood to serve the purpose of the one who issues the command or the one who makes the request, since the agent to be enjoined (*niyojya*) disregards his own purpose.

However, action (*karma*) is the domain of instruction (*upadeśa*), which—disregarding the purpose of the instructor—is intended solely for the sake of the matter to be instructed. This constitutes the distinction between instruction and [the other two means, namely] command (*ājñā*) and entreaty (*abhyarthanā*), as well as its nature as instigation (*preraṇā*). The construction of the words is as follows: that instruction whose action is for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and not for the sake of the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*) is described in that way. The instigation (*codanā*) is the setting forth of a person who has not yet set out, one who has not yet engaged in activity. Now, is instruction (*upadeśa*) the same as injunction (*vidhi*)? It is; and it is a word that expresses a distinct purpose. Thus, in some places it speaks of the mere utterance of a word, saying "the utterance of the word."

In some places, it is stated that [the Veda] has a single syntactical unity with the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*); in some places, it is said that "codanā" is the word that impels one toward action; in some places, it is defined as knowledge—namely, the cognition of an object not present to the senses arising from the comprehension of the words of the scripture—and the author of the *Vārttika* states that they speak of the "denotative productive energy" (*abhidhābhāvanā*), referring to it as "abhidhā."
Therefore, he says: "And this [statement] that 'the word is the injunction' (*vidhi*) is for the sake of illustration;

hence, by means of the grammatical derivation (*sādhana*) as object (*karman*), agent (*kartṛ*), or instrument (*karaṇa*), the knowledge of the meaning, the word, the denotation, the utterance, and so forth, is expressed by the term 'instruction' (*upadeśa*) as appropriate. (Vidhiviveka-Ṭīkā, p. 238–241).
This refers to the successive [applications] among those derived as object, instrument, and agent.
And even in the technical sentences of the grammatical treatises, that which is beyond the scope [of ordinary usage] is called "utterance" (uccāra).
Furthermore, "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is well known as the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*) who is engaged in the act of favoring others;

yet no such person exists in the case of the Veda, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of its being non-authoritative (i.e., not authored by a person). Therefore, how can this [Veda] possess even the status of instruction? Indeed, instruction is never perceived apart from an instructor;

for it is only when an instructor—such as a teacher or a physician—is present that instructions such as "go about begging for alms," "practice meditation and study," "one suffering from fever should drink medicine," or "one should eat wholesome food" are recognized.

Nor should it be asserted that the word alone is the instructor; for otherwise, it would follow that even one who is unlearned in linguistic conventions would understand the meaning from it. If you argue that it teaches reality only in dependence upon the learner’s mastery of the relationship between word and meaning, then from where does that mastery come? If it comes from a distinguished person, then let that person alone be the instructor—what is the use of this intermediate step? Furthermore, its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) will be refuted later on; so, enough of this digression.
Regarding the injunctive statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma," which is directed toward another [the agent], [it is said]: "Then the herb... [ĀpŚS 1.4.1].

—Regarding the understanding of the instruction (upadeśa): [Objection] Was it not stated that "instruction" is the utterance of a specific word? If this is so, then it would follow that even one who is unlearned (avyutpanna) would act;
to this it is said: he teaches the means for the pure human goal (puruṣārtha), which is specific.

When a particular human goal is desired by a person through a specific means, the word "Veda" is said to be distinguished by its excellence because it makes known that means of attaining the human goal which was previously unknown; otherwise, since every word is distinct from other words, there would be no such distinction. Therefore, one does not engage [with the Veda] until its meaning has been understood.
—Vidhiviveka, p. 240: [the statement] that the Veda is a means to the goals of human life.

Furthermore, those who maintain that the very cognition of the "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) regarding an object is itself the injunction (*vidhi*) because it impels one to action—arguing that no one ever engages in an act without first apprehending, "This is to be done by me"—are also speaking without due reflection. For is this cognition of "to-be-done-ness" the cause of engagement when it is unqualified, or when it is qualified as being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*)? The first position is untenable, because it would entail the consequence that everyone would engage in every activity merely through the cognition of its "to-be-done-ness. In that case, you would have to engage even in the killing of Brahmins and the like, simply by virtue of the cognition that such killing is "to be done."

Now, if it is argued that it is that [activity] qualified by being a means to the desirable (*śreyaḥsādhanatā*) which is the cause of engagement, then "being a means to the desirable" itself would be the injunction (*vidhi*), because it is the cause of engagement, and not "the state of being something to be done" (*kartavyatā*), since the former does not incite activity without the latter. But even this is not tenable, because the status of "being a means to the desirable" as an injunction has already been rejected previously.

Comparison—Regarding the claim that "activity arises from the cognition that 'it ought to be done,'" some who pride themselves on their tradition say: "Activity arises from the cognition that 'it ought to be done'";
the underlying intention here is this: these [lingual suffixes] such as the optative (*liṅ*) indeed have their activity inferred from the observation of purposeful action.
Furthermore, an activity characterized by purposeful engagement is observed among elders immediately following their hearing of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers;
and because this activity is preceded by cognition and is an independent undertaking, it is like our own activity.

Moreover, that cognition is inferred to range over the same object as the cognition that is the cause of our own activity, because it is a cognition that causes activity, just like the cognition that is the cause of our own activity.

Regarding its object, having ourselves opened our eyes and set aside the "blindness" (ḍiṇḍikarāga) of those who are afflicted by intellectual blindness, we reflect and understand that it is precisely the "state of being what ought to be done" (kartavyatā), rather than the operation of the word, the intention of the person, or the means to that intended end.

For instance, even in the case of suckling at the breast, we do not act merely because it is a means to a desired end; rather, it is because of the hearing of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth that the subsequent activity occurs with the thought, "This is what ought to be done. This very fact establishes that the optative suffixes and the like denote "what ought to be done.
Thus, since their relationship [to this meaning] is known, the optative suffixes and so forth denote that same thing even in the Veda.
—Vidhiviveka-Ṭīkā, p. 244 — *adya* Śra., Ba.; *ukta* everywhere Ā.

Comparison: Now, one might object that even if it were stated a hundred times that something "must be done," it would not lead to activity unless it is understood as a means to a desired end; therefore, he says: "For how could one who understands it in such a way not proceed to act? First of all, the word, having its conventional relation known, makes known the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*);
likewise, when this [state of being something to be done] is perceived in the case of occasional injunctions (*naimittika*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*), it cannot be said that it does not exist.
— *Vidhiviveka-ṭīkā*, p. 245.
In the case of prohibited actions such as the killing of a Brahmin,
there arises the cognition of their being something that ought to be done, once that [erroneous] cognition of their being something to be done has occurred.

The nature of an injunction consists in the cognition of a duty qualified by being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), because [an action] possesses the status of being a means to the highest good; this is the definition of an injunction. (Ba., Śra.)
According to the opinion of others, intuition (*pratibhā*) alone is the injunction (*vidhi*), because it is that which prompts action;

for apart from intuition, even the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers does not impel a person to act—following the analogy of powerful water and wind—since otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of everyone acting [simultaneously].
Nor is it merely the comprehension of the object [of the injunction], for the same reason.

Therefore, whatever activity there may be, it is all preceded by a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*) consisting of the determination of the appearing form; for as long as, even when an object appears, the intuition that "this is a means to happiness" does not arise, no one engages in action. Thus, when a particular means is presented, the vivid manifestation of a specific action is intuition (*pratibhā*).

And it has been said: "Pratibhā is the wisdom (prajñā) conducive to the cognition of an action not delimited by specific means" (*Vidhiviveka*, p. 246). That too is without substance, because the nature of *vidhi* could only exist once the essential nature of *pratibhā* is established;
yet the nature of *pratibhā* as propounded by you is not tenable.

For it is well known that *pratibhā* (intuition) is a cognition that arises from the causal complex of the mind alone, independent of external causal complexes such as the sense organs, and which reveals the actual state of an object—as in the thought, "My brother will come tomorrow," and so forth; it is not merely the form of a determination of the appearing aspect. Otherwise, even conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), which occurs subsequent to non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpaka-adhyakṣa*), would necessarily be classified as *pratibhā* due to possessing that same nature, and thus the very discussion of conceptual perception would be abolished.
Furthermore, for the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), all words are traditionally held by others to be the cause of *pratibhā* through repeated practice.
In the case of conveying the meaning as it truly is to children and even to animals,
when objects are perceived through their distinctness, a different kind of intuition (pratibhā) arises.
They say that the meaning of a sentence is that [cognition] which is brought about by the meanings of the words;
it cannot be described to others in any way as "this is that."
Established as an internal mental process, it cannot be defined even by its agent; though itself unexamined, it brings about, as it were, a connection with objects.
Having attained, as it were, the form of all things, it exists as an object,
whether produced directly by the word or through the accompaniment of mental cultivation (bhāvanā). 147
No one transgresses that [authority] regarding what ought to be done;
everyone in the world regards it as a valid means of knowledge.
"Even among animals, purposeful undertakings are observed to occur by virtue of that [past action].
(Vākyapadīya 2.149)

Because it would follow that everyone who hears [a word] would engage [with its meaning], *pratibhā* is the determination of the form appearing [in consciousness]; such is the nature of *pratibhā*. (Ārya-ṭīkā)

Comparison— [is] not that which proceeds when the distinction of intuition (*pratibhā*) has not yet arisen, thinking "this must be done by this person in this manner," even regarding an object already apprehended through perception and other means;
for in such cases, the function of the means of knowledge is completed [by those means],
whereas the world relies upon intuition as its eye when striving toward courses of action (*itikartavyatā*).
—In the ritual procedure, folios 247–48;
in the sacrifice and so forth, Ācārya’s commentary;
with reference to a specific means of accomplishment, when one has resolved to act, Ācārya’s commentary.

A specific action does not impel a person [to act], because it would follow that everyone would be impelled to act; as for "vibration" (*parisphuraṇa*), the explanation is: indeed, those who are possessed of intuition (*pratibhāvin*) do not describe intuition as being non-determinative in nature while accompanied by cognition, for that [would be] doubt.

We have studied that *pratibhā* (intuitive insight) is the cognition "this is to be done," which is conducive to the comprehension of an action delimited by its goal (*sādhya*), its means (*sādhana*), and its procedure (*itikartavyatā*); it acts as a cooperative factor when that action, characterized as a duty to be performed, is to be executed.
As stated in the *Vidhiviveka-ṭīkā*, p.
247: "Pratibhā is the cognition conducive to the comprehension of an action delimited by specific means" (*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 286).

When it is established—[as follows]—the knowledge that arises from the contact of the self and the mind, due to the excellence of merit (*dharma*), which reveals objects as they truly are, regarding supersensuous matters pertaining to the past, future, and present, whether they are connected with *dharma* and so forth or recorded in texts; this they call *ārṣa* (sage-knowledge).
That, moreover, occurs extensively among the divine sages (*devarṣi*).
Sometimes, as among worldly people, a girl might say, "My brother will come tomorrow; my heart tells me so"—as stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
258—this is the means of valid cognition known as *pratibhā* (intuition), which is observed in the form: "My brother will come tomorrow."
"Intuition (pratibhā) is a flash of insight; its absence is [the state of] non-intuition"—Yogabhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī on YS 3.33. Nyāyamañjarī, p.
Intuition (*prātibha*) is knowledge arising from one's own innate insight, not derived from instruction—
*Yogabhāṣya* 3.33.
In that regard, *pratibhā* (intuition) is the capacity for the sudden manifestation of objects—whether concealed, remote, past, future, subtle, and so forth—even without a perceived cause;
[as stated in] the *Yogasaṃgraha*, p. 55:
"That manifestation of an object which occurs in the absence of sense organs, logical marks, and the like, is *pratibhā*"; [and as stated in] the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 258.
His intellect is a creative intuition (*pratibhā*) characterized by the manifestation of ever-new waves of wisdom;
it is a discerning cognition (*ālocanājñāna*). (Cf. *Dhī-alaṃk.*, p. 2; *Ācārya-ṭippaṇī*).

As for the manifestation of a specific action within a particular means of accomplishment by way of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*), does that arise through the force of previously deposited mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), in accordance with the operation of means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), from a Vedic injunction (*codanā*), or merely from the mind alone—as in the thought, "My brother will come tomorrow"? Among these, the last alternative is untenable, because for one who has not heard the words of an injunction, a specific action regarding a means such as sacrifice does not manifest even in a dream.

However, in the case of the three previous alternatives, the nature of *pratibhā* would be contradicted; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anuṣaṅga*) that even memory and other cognitions produced from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth would possess the nature of *pratibhā*, and thus that alone would be the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For an injunction (*codanā*) is indeed a sentence that prompts action, such as "One should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice."

—Because there is no manifestation [of the object]... by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the terms "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and "operation" (*vyāpāra*) are to be understood, corresponding respectively to the terms "recollection" (*smṛti*), "inference" (*anumāna*), and "verbal testimony" (*śabda*). —Ā. Ṭīkā.
Some declare that what is called *pratibhā* (intuitive insight) is itself the injunction (*vidhi*), because it is that which impels action;

for indeed, without *bhakti*— which is synonymous with *śraddhā* (faith)— neither engagement in the hearing, reflecting upon, and meditating on the Supreme Self, nor in sacrifices and the like, is possible.
As it has been said:

"But some [hold that] even when [the root] *bha* or *bhū* is present, if it is asked what meaning is grasped by the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes, [the answer is: since the meaning of the verbal root (prakṛtyartha)—such as sacrifice, which consists of the propitiation of a deity, as expressed in the rule 'yaj devapūjāyām'—is established through linguistic convention as being achievable through the agent's activity (*kartṛvyāpāra*), the optative and other suffixes denote this; thus, nothing is untenable."

"Devotion (bhakti), however, is indeed a specific kind of knowledge characterized by a lack of thirst for everything other than that which consists of unsurpassed bliss and the beloved as its sole purpose"—*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p.
344; *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, p. 225.

The touch of uninterrupted fullness [is attained] not without devotion; and even the distinction of the scripture from the royal edict exists only through the non-entry of a portion of devotion. (Vedārtha, p. 152)
For that [state] is indeed devoid of internal devotion, because only the fear of the king and similar concerns manifest within;
and it has been said:
"The governance of a kingdom."

For men, that scripture would become empty, serving merely as a teaching, unless it were distinguished by faith and a portion of devotion, just as [the authority of] a king's command is distinguished in the world by royal decree. Thus.

That alone is devotion, not scripture—and even that [scripture] is not the primary cause; for once devotion has arisen, it would be the motive for engagement. And its arising is either from the Word or from a particular person capable of both restraint and grace? It cannot be from the Word alone, as in: "This Self is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4).

Because it would follow that devotion toward the Self and so forth would arise in every single cognizer who hears such words, and consequently they would engage in the contemplation of that [Self] and so on; yet, even though there is no difference in hearing those words for everyone, such devotion does not arise in all of them. Therefore, that [devotion] is not caused by those words alone.

That which does not arise despite the absence of any distinction is not caused by that [distinction] alone; for example, a sprout does not arise even when the seed is undifferentiated. Likewise, devotion toward the Self and so forth does not arise in all those who hear that sound, even though the sound is undifferentiated. Now, if it is argued that such devotion arises for those who desire the desired fruit from a particular Person capable of both punishment and favor—this is reasonable, since it is well known that this very [devotion] is what is designated by the term "bhakti. However, the claim that the Veda is impersonal (apauruṣeya) is untenable, because its being the work of a person is established in this manner.

Furthermore, since the Self endowed with the attribute of uninterrupted fullness has been refuted in the section on the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaitapraghaṭṭaka*), how could there be devotion toward it for anyone—whether from another such person or otherwise—any more than there could be toward a donkey’s horn? [And] what is the cause for its engagement (*pravṛtti*)? Śaṅkara.

"Verily, the Self, my dear Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Indeed, when the Self is seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, all this is known. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5.
Devotion to the various words used for the vision, hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption regarding the Self.

Devotion based solely on the hearing of the word does not have the mere hearing of the word as its sole cause, because it does not arise even when there is hearing of the word; [this is] the fruit of the Śruti.
Because that very propitiation of the Lord, which is capable [of accomplishing the goal], is not prohibited.

If the Veda were to enjoin devotion (*bhakti*) in the form of worship of God, then even regarding *dharma*, God alone would be the source of authority; and in that case, there would be a contradiction with the Veda’s lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), for it would follow that God is the author of the Veda just as He is the agent of punishment and grace.
This is the sense [of the objection] concerning Brahman, who is characterized by being prior and free from conditions (*nirupādhi*).
pṛ॰ 150– [The distinction] in Brahman from Īśvara.
Or rather, regarding Vedic statements and the like—
just as in the case of [the injunction for] the *vaṣaṭ* call and so forth— the devotion mentioned in the Śruti,

as well as desire, effort, and so on, must be rejected by the very same method previously stated; for since these too lack the capacity to cause a person's engagement when they are independent of an object, a result, and so forth, their status as injunctions is untenable.

If, however, those [factors] dependent upon it (the injunction) were the cause of its activity, how could they alone possess the nature of an injunction? For that consequence would extend even to the object (*viṣaya*) and other such factors. Therefore, since an injunction whose nature is postulated by others is untenable when subjected to analysis, it is not logical for it to be the meaning of a word.

Consequently, it is well said: "The means of knowledge is the heard [word] regarding objects," and so forth; thus, one must accept that the meaning of a word is precisely that which possesses [the capacity for action].

Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not "being a means to what is desired" according to the method of the logicians, but rather, as stated previously, it is the very desire that impels action—[Bhaṭṭarahasya, p. 8]—thus [the suffixes] such as the injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth... [Ākhyāta-viveka].

Comparison: Others, however, declare that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is what they call "exertion" (*udyoga*), which is a particular vibration of the self (*ātmaspandaviśeṣa*) arising upon hearing words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*). But we do not know its true nature; for what is this so-called "vibration of the self"? Is it cognition (*buddhi*), or effort (*prayatna*), or one of the two—desire (*icchā*) or aversion (*dveṣa*)?
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 365).
The subject matter concerns sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma*.
Even desires for results such as heaven and the like, as well as efforts and so forth, are dependent upon objects, results, and other factors.
This is because it would follow that desire, effort, and so forth themselves would possess the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), and that [consequence] has already been refuted previously.
The commentary and explanation—that the object itself consists of both the universal and the particular—is as follows:

by means of the verse beginning with "śrutajñāna," he explains [the text]: "śrutajñāna" is verbal cognition; it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding an external object, even when that object differs from the speaker's intention, and not only regarding that intention itself.
He states the refutation for not accepting that [position]: "How? and so forth.

How? Not in any way; otherwise, in the manner of there being no validity regarding external objects, neither the Buddhist nor anyone else can possibly apprehend such things as islands, regions, rivers, and mountains. Why is this? He says: [because they would be unapprehendable].
