Of what nature is it? Its nature and its effects are unperceived; the meaning is that its own form is neither perceptible nor inferable. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is situated in another location;
in what manner? By way of spatial division (*digvibhāga*).

Regarding the objection that "even in the absence of an object, since scriptural revelation (*śruti*) is generally seen to function, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere," he says in response:
*Śruti* is knowledge derived from scripture (*āgama*).
If, due to frequent contradictions with scripture, those who do not perceive a necessary connection were to have no confidence—
that is, no trust— what then? What would happen?
Where? Everywhere, regarding the authority of the non-contradictory scriptures.

Of whom? Of the Sugatas (Buddhists), who do not perceive an obstruction—that is, who do not see the relationship characterized by the innate fitness between word and meaning. Why? Because of contradiction.
Of what? Of the scripture (*śruta*), that is, of the traditional authority (*āgama*).
How? "For the most part," meaning "only occasionally" or "at some time.
At that time, that lack of confidence is equal—that is, identical—to [the lack of confidence regarding direct perception].

Of what? Of cognitions produced by the senses and the logical mark (*liṅga*). The meaning is that [the charge of non-reliability] would apply even to those cognitions (*jñāna*) produced by the two—namely, the sense-organ (*akṣa*) and the cause that is the logical mark (*liṅga-hetu*)—because one observes occasional discrepancies in some cases. If there were a lack of confidence in all instances, that would be the same for the cognitions produced by the senses and the logical mark. (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 47) || 27 ||

Commentary: Sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) cannot be considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without the qualification "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) or "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārī*), because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If such qualifications are required [for sensory cognition], why should there be dissatisfaction with them in the case of scriptural cognition (*śrutajñāna*)? Just as the cognition of a wagon from the star Kṛttikā and so forth occurs without an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), in the same way, a cognition that expresses an object whose connection is not perceived is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvādaka*);
for indeed, nothing is impossible when it is actually observed.

If there is no confidence because of the possibility of deviation in some cases, how could there not be a lack of confidence even regarding the speaker’s intention? For even there, the possibility of deviation exists. Likewise, since one might utter words such as those of the Vedas—which are flawed by being imagined without desire—one employs the qualification "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the definition of sensory cognition; thus the Buddhists state: "Perception is that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (Nyāyabindu 1.4).
Because of this statement,
the qualification "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*) in the definition of perception should be understood from the perspective of the Naiyāyikas:

"Perception is knowledge that arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object, which is non-verbal (*avyapadeśya*), non-erroneous (*avyabhicāri*), and of a determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*)."
Because it has been stated in Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4.
The non-erroneous cognition of an object qualified by such attributes as being non-erroneous and so forth.
Comparison: "When an intrinsic nature is established through perception, others may raise an objection;
in that case, this answer must be stated: 'There is no inconsistency in what is perceived.'"—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, p. 68.
For there is no inconsistency in what is perceived—*Dhavalā-Ṭīkā*, p. 320. Compare: "A sentence produced by the speaker's intention is not obstructed with respect to its own meaning."

For how could the determination of reality be established by means of a mark (liṅga) indicated by that [sentence], when one objects without distinction that sentences indicate only the speaker’s intention? Thus, one would not understand reality even through a traditional succession;
nor do they indicate the speaker’s intention with absolute certainty, since defects in the audition (*śruti-duṣṭa*) and so forth are established from other sources alone.
—Siddhiviniścaya, p. 264; Śrutakalpa, commentary on the verses of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāviveka.

If, due to the frequent (prāyas) or general (bāhulyena) non-correspondence of scripture—that is, of the word or its cognition—there is a lack of confidence (anāśvāsa) even regarding all true scripture, for whom?
For the Buddhists (Saugatas), who do not perceive [such correspondence]?

To this he says: "The connection" (pratibandham)—that is, the relation (sambandha) existing in the form of capacity (yogyatā) as an inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva). That lack of confidence everywhere is equal to that regarding the cognitions of the senses and logical marks (liṅga), because those too are generally seen to be non-correspondent; such is the intended meaning.
—of this knowledge, [there is] a connection with hearing;
Ārya—exhalation; of those too, [there is] hearing.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) provides an explanation by way of negation (*vyatireka*), beginning with "nahi" and so forth: "nahi" means indeed not;
sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

By what [qualification] is it led? He says: without the qualification "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) or "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārin*), how can it be established that it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when those qualifications are present? He says: because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for there would be the consequence of even the cognition of a double moon and so forth being valid.
Indeed, if one were to accept the validity of mere cognition without qualifications, it would be impossible to exclude the validity of the cognition of a double moon and so forth.
Now, if that qualification is indeed present, then it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, this fault does not apply. To this, he says: "In that way," and so forth.

If the qualification of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) by way of being non-erroneous and non-deviating is accepted, what dissatisfaction is there regarding scriptural cognition (*śrutajñāna*)? Let its validity also consist precisely in its being characterized by those same qualifications. [Objection: Surely, because sensory cognition is an effect of the object, its non-erroneousness or non-deviation is appropriate, but not so for scriptural cognition, because the opposite is the case. To this, he says: "Just as," and so forth.

Just as, by whatever mode of fitness, the cognition of a cart and so forth arises from the constellation Kṛttikā and the like, that [cognition] exists without an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*). By the term "essential connection," both the connection of identity (*tādātmya*) and the relation of origination (*tadutpatti*) are understood, based on the etymological derivation: "one's own nature" (*svo bhāvaḥ*) [is the cause]. Without such a connection, a non-contradictory cognition of the expression of an object whose connection—such as identity—is not perceived is "of that very kind"; that is, it is a cognition of the expression of an object in which no connection such as identity has been observed. Such a cognition is non-contradictory.
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies with the words beginning with "na hi" (for not).

For (*hi*) since it is not the case that [the validity] is unestablished when there is non-discrepancy with what is heard regarding visible phenomena such as eclipses of the planets and so forth—because if it were, it would follow that [validity] would also be unestablished even when there is non-discrepancy with sensory cognition.

Showing that because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is generally observed regarding external objects, there would be no confidence (*anāśvāsa*) anywhere, and thus there would be no validity even regarding the speaker’s intention (*vaktrabhiprāya*), he says "In some cases" (*kvacit*), and so forth. If, due to deviation in certain restricted objects, a lack of confidence is admitted for the scripture (*śruti*) in its entirety—not only regarding external objects but also regarding the speaker’s intention—how could there not be a lack of confidence in its entirety? Indeed, there would be exactly such a lack of confidence. Why is this so? He says: "Even in that case," and so forth.

In that case as well, since deviation (vyabhicāra) is possible even with respect to the speaker’s intention, he says "tathā" and so forth to demonstrate this very point: by means of such a manner—as when one strikes another and then rests [the blame] on the other by saying, "For by whom you were loved," and so forth—and likewise by saying, "He is a man of valor," and so forth, which is *śrutiduṣṭa* (defective in hearing) and *kalpanāduṣṭa* (defective in conception); in that same manner (*tathā*), even for one who does not intend it—that is, for one devoid of such an intention—there is [the occurrence of] *śrutikalpanāduṣṭa* and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of "slipping of the name" (*gotraskhalana*) and the like is intended; [this occurs] from the utterance, that is, from the speaking.
Furthermore—
[in the case] of being accompanied by qualifiers such as "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) and so forth, [there is] a specific style (rīti)— Ācārya.
Sensory cognition and so forth belong only to a sense organ that is qualified by attributes such as being non-erroneous.
Because we observe the use of words even in the absence of an object, as in the case of the past, the future, and so forth— [as stated by Dharmakīrti]:
"For it is only when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) that one object can cause another object to be understood."
Because for that which is not connected [to it], there is no rule of non-deviation from it—*Nyāyabindu*, p.
40—[the word] *pratibandha* [is used]. *Bā*. (variant reading)
—The state of being a proponent of that [view]—; according to Śra., it is "that knowledge of what was heard" (taj-jñāna-śruta). According to Ba.
and Śra., it is "of what was heard" (śrutasya).

Comparison: "Moreover, since another word is observed even when there is no intention to express something else, and because there is deviation even when such an intention exists, there is a lack of confidence in all cases; how then could those words indicate a specific intention?
(Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 266).
[The reading *prāye* appears in the Ā and Śra manuscripts.]
—He said: For by which, indeed, through its own nature...
[he] heard... [he] spoke.
"Defective in hearing" (*śrutiduṣṭa*), "harsh to the ear" (*śrutikaṭu*),
or "harsh to the ear" (*śrutikaṭu*) refers to that which is defective due to its form consisting of harsh phonemes—
*Kāvyaprakāśa*, p. 267.

In the phrase "yā bhavataḥ priyā" (she who is dear to you), occurring in the context of describing the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), the harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭutva*) should be understood as arising precisely from the employment of the letter *ra*, which is prohibited here.
In the word "priyā," the conjunction of the letter *ra* is indeed evident.
Furthermore, this is a defect of conception (*kalpanā-duṣṭa*), to be understood as being characterized by either a contradictory conception or an inappropriate conception.

Regarding the phrase "having struck another" (*para-prahṛtya*): when a powerful man, having struck another, becomes specifically exhausted and fatigued immediately after the blow, then his description as being powerful is indeed inappropriate.
For if he is exhausted immediately after the blow, how can he be powerful? This is because exhaustion and power are contradictory;
this is a case of a contradiction between what is heard and what is imagined (*śruta-vikalpanā*). (Ācārya Śrī)
—The grasping and the being grasped by the quarters [of space] (Śrīmad-Ācārya):

Since there is no ascertainment of external objects through either authoritative scripture or reasoning, how can there be a distinction between truth and falsehood, and from where could there be the status of a means of proof or its opposite? || 28 ||

This is the meaning: since there is no determination of an external object based on the statement of an authoritative person (*āptokti*), how can there be a distinction between the truth and falsity of the words of the Sugata and others, given that they are equally devoid of an objective referent?

Furthermore, because of the doctrine of causal reasoning (*hetuvāda*), if an external object is not determined, how can there be a distinction between a means of proof (*sādhana*) and its opposite, since they are equally characterized by the absence of an external object?
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 48)

For the distinction between truth and falsehood is based solely on the attainment or non-attainment of an external object; as it has been stated in the *Āptamīmāṃsā* (Kārikā 87): "The status of cognition and words as valid means of knowledge is possible only when an external object exists, not when it does not;
for the distinction between truth and falsehood is logical only in relation to the attainment or non-attainment of the object.
This is comparable to the statement that there is no difference among sentences in general, even those expressing what one intends.

The distinction between truth and falsehood does not arise from the perception of reality and unreality; rather, it is considered that a statement has a false meaning due to the cognition of a false perception—Siddhiviniścaya, p. 502.

Commentary: Indeed, intentions regarding human goals do not invariably fail with respect to their objects; otherwise, since the absolute non-deviation between words and objects would be impossible, how could there be any inference [of an object] from speech when there is a discrepancy between the speaker’s intention and [the object]? Since one relies oneself upon some means of establishing the distinction between an authoritative person (*āpta*) and one who is not, or between a valid and an invalid member of a proof, [words] indicate what the speaker intends without distinction, but not the reality of the object itself—how, then, can you be so confident? [The text ends with: "all objects," etc. (*sarvārthān jaṃ viṃ*).
Because words lack an inseparable connection with real entities, no objective reality is established through them; therefore, they merely indicate the intention of the speaker. (3.212)
The object that appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker’s activity—
that is where the validity of the word resides; it does not depend upon the actual state of the external object.
Whatever is designated by speakers as a signifier, regardless of whether it depends upon an external object, is considered a signifier in that very capacity.
1.67 – Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā (Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra)

And it has been stated that words do not convey [objects] directly, because they are devoid of any necessary connection with external objects; rather, these [words] are indicators of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
— *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 702.
As it has been said: "Words may indicate the speaker's intention" (*Tarkabhāṣā*, p. 4).

Even the utterance of one word when another is intended to be spoken is observed, as in the case of Gotraskhalana (slip of the tongue), where, for instance, Yajñadatta is uttered when Devadatta is intended.
Commentary on the Verse:

One who is not a deceiver of another is an *āpta* (reliable authority) for that person. If it is accepted that the determination of external objects does not arise from their speech—that is, from the words of such an authority—nor from logical reasons—that is, from the statement of signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, then what would be the distinction between the word of the Sugata, which is true, and the word of Kapila and others, which is false? None at all; everything would simply be false.
Consequently, there would be no engagement whatsoever even with the word of the Sugata.

Likewise, from where does the distinction between "means of proof" (*sādhana*) and "other" arise? Statements regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth constitute the means of proof; the other is the statement of its refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). From where does the existence of these two states (*tattā*) come? It could not exist at all.

And thus, because [statements such as] "whatever exists is momentary" would lack the status of being a member of the means of proof, they would become points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); this is the intended meaning.

An authoritative person (*āpta*), indeed, is one who has directly perceived the nature of things (*dharmā*) and is an instructor employed by the desire to communicate an object exactly as it was seen.
The realization of an object is attainment; one who acts by means of that is an *āpta* (an authoritative person)
— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.7.

*Āpti* is the direct attainment of an object; it exists as the apprehension of an object exactly as it is. Thus, one who has directly realized the *dharma* is an *āpta*. Through the attainment of the object as it truly is, one grasps the meaning of what has been heard; for scripture (*āgama*) is the word of an authoritative person (*āpta*). Because of the destruction of defects, an authoritative person is one whose faults have perished; such a wise person would not utter a false statement, as the cause [for falsehood] is absent.
One who is devoted to his own duty, free from passion and hatred, and is always honored by those of like nature—such a person should be known as an authoritative teacher (āpta).
—Sāṃkhyakārikā-bhāṣya, Māṭhara-vṛtti, p. 13.

That which is non-contradictory in a particular respect is authoritative (*āpta*) therein; the other is non-authoritative (*anāpta*). Non-contradiction consists in the demonstration of reality through the knowledge of its object—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p.
236. In this context, the statements regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth constitute the proof (*sādhana*)—*Nyāyapraveśa*, p. 1.

Refutations (*dūṣaṇāni*) are the pointing out of defects in a proof (*sādhanadoṣodbhāvanāni*). [In the] *Nyāyapraveśaka*, page 8, the commentary on the sub-commentary explains the meaning of the verse by means of the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*), beginning with the words "for not" (*na hi*).
Indeed, human intentions and human purposes do not fail to correspond with their objects in all cases.
Why is this so? He says: "Otherwise," and so forth.

This is because, otherwise—that is, in the manner of their failing to correspond—there would be the possibility of an absolute deviation between words and their objects; that is, there would be the possibility of an absolute deviation of words from their external objects or from anything else.
When there is a discrepancy between speech and intention, how [could there be inference]? From nothing at all could that intention be inferred.

Now, demonstrating that the opponent’s behavior is like the conduct of a madman, [the author] says, beginning with “The Sugata,” etc.: For one who lives by himself—either by relying on the establishment of the Sugata as an authoritative person (*āpta*) based on his teaching of the Four Noble Truths, which is non-contradictory and lacks any other source of instruction or inferential mark; or by relying on the establishment of Kapila and others as non-authoritative due to their teaching of principles such as *pradhāna*, which are contradictory; or by relying on the establishment of the limbs of proof and non-proof, namely, the establishment of the statement of a three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) as the limb for proving its own probandum, while the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth is established as the limb for failing to prove it—he, Dharmakīrti and others, speaking thus—that words indicate the speaker’s intention but not the reality of the object without distinction—is he not confused and deranged? To this, the Buddhist replies: “Even if there is no validity (*prāmāṇya*) of speech regarding the speaker’s intention, let it be so; what is lost for one who maintains the doctrine of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since we accept its validity therein only out of conformity with worldly convention (*vyavahāra*)? Anticipating this, [the author] says:

In the same way, the Blessed One is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because he is non-deceptive regarding the Four Noble Truths as they have been taught, and because he reveals those very truths which were previously unknown to others— *Pramāṇavārttika*, Manorathanandin’s commentary 1.9.

Furthermore, the Blessed One, the Sugata, possesses authority because of his quality of being a protector (*tāyin*); for instance: he does not speak untruth because there is no purpose in teaching a path he has not himself realized;
and because of his compassion, he speaks for the sake of others, being devoted to all undertakings for their benefit.
Therefore, he is authoritative either by virtue of being a protector, or by virtue of illuminating the Four Noble Truths.

Teaching (*deśanā*) is the proclamation of the path that he himself has seen as the means for turning back the cause of suffering; it is called "protection" (*tāya*) because of the metaphorical application of the effect to the instrument, for by means of it he protects sentient beings. Because he possesses this [path], he is a protector (*tāyin*); and since it would be fruitless, he does not speak what is false.
Someone speaks untruth out of a desire for their own pleasure and so forth, or out of ignorance;
however, for one who has abandoned the view of self and has directly realized reality, both of these [motivations] are absent.

In particular, he states that compassion alone is the cause for speaking the truth: "And because of his compassionate nature, and because of his application toward the welfare of others—through his exertion in undertaking everything such as the practice of the path—he attained perfect enlightenment solely with the aim of benefiting others. How, then, could there even be a suspicion of his deceiving sentient beings by speaking falsely?"
Therefore, because he is a protector (*tāyin*), the Blessed One is an authority (*pramāṇa*);

for to speak of an object exactly as it has been perceived is indeed to be reliable (*saṃvāditva*). Thus, by virtue of possessing the first definition of an authority, his status as an authority is stated by this [term].
He also states his possession of the second definition: "Or, *tāya* is the illumination of the Four Truths."

*Tāya* is the illumination of the four truths unknown to others; because he possesses that, the Blessed One is *tāyin*. He has been stated [by Dharmakīrti] as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.147–48), as cited by Manorathanandin.
Therefore, those possessed of intelligence call the Sugata alone the Omniscient One;
and they call him the supreme physician, for he knows the primary goal of human existence—*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 878.
Because they are not taught [as such], there are four noble truths, namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—*Dharmasaṃgraha*, p. 5.
The four truths have been stated: suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path; their sequence follows the order of their realization—*Abhidharmakośa* 6.1.

Or else, *sādhana* is that by which an object not yet understood by others is established; it is a collection of statements consisting of the three-fold reason (*trirūpahetu*). Its *aṅga* (component) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth. Or, it is that which is not a component of that very *sādhana*, such as the thesis (*pratijñā*), application (*upanaya*), conclusion (*nigamana*), and so on—*Vādanyāya*, p. 61.
Or rather, [it is] the state of the word in accordance with the intention of the speaker.

If speech were to deviate from its meaning due to the diverse intentions of a person—given that, because of such diversity of intention, there is a confusion of activity, verbal expression, and so forth, and since no excellence can be determined anywhere, what purpose would there be in seeking a distinction? For even one who possesses knowledge may be in error; where, then, could we find confidence?
(*Aṣṭaśata*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 71).

If speech were the word of a trustworthy person (*āptavacana*), why would it be subject to deviation from its meaning—that is, non-correspondence with external objects? Because of the speaker’s diverse intention (*citrābhisandhi*)—that is, because of the various intentions, purposes, or desires for expression consisting of truth, falsehood, and so forth;
for whom? For the person who is the speaker, since it is said that "even those possessed of passion act as if they were free from passion."
In that case, it would be non-contradictory for an effect to be observed even from a cause of a different genus;

therefore, how could that [effect] possibly possess the nature of distinguishing—that is, of setting itself apart from what is of a different genus—on the basis of its own specific acquisition which is restricted to its particular cause? It could not do so at all; this is the meaning, because there would be no contradiction in its arising from just anything whatsoever.

Indeed, an effect produced by an indefinite cause does not indicate a distinction between causes; for when an incapable [cause] is observed to produce an effect, can that effect possibly differentiate the cause from one of a different class? (Laghu-tantra, p. 49) || 29 ||

The commentary on the *Īśvaravivṛti* regarding the perception of the effect (*kāryadṛṣṭa*) states: If it is argued that, although scripture frequently does not contradict external objects, there is no confidence in its meaning everywhere because its connection to that meaning is unestablished—since [scripture] follows the intention of the speaker—then it has been stated in this regard: that there is non-contradiction in the cognition of an imperceptible object even without identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).

Furthermore, how can there be confidence in such [inferences] as "this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*" or "there is fire here because of smoke"? Since creepers, mango trees, and the like are sometimes observed, there is no contradiction even if a *śiṃśapā* were itself not a tree; and since smoke produced from wood, smoke produced from a collection of causes such as gems, smoke produced by lightning, and smoke produced from other substances are all entirely consistent with the nature of fire, why is there this restriction that smoke is produced only from fire and not from other things? It is precisely because of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) that there is confidence in the inference "there is fire here because of smoke."

When there is the cognition of an imperceptible object through the impossibility of its being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), the validity of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) is established because its non-contradiction in certain instances is itself impossible to account for otherwise, given that it does not possess a perceived identity with or origination from [the object] itself. [The opponent’s] critique: For a proponent such as this, there is no such thing as inference (*anumāna*) at all; for even among those who lack intentional design, a restriction regarding the nature or effect [of things] is frequently not observed. This is because, while something is observed in the presence of a specific causal complex such as wood and so forth, it is generally not observed in their absence—even when a collection of causes such as a jewel and the like is present.

If it were the case that "whatever is observed to be of a certain nature [must arise] from something of that same nature," then because such a restrictive rule is difficult to establish, how could the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) even be determined for smoke, comets, and the like? Since trees are sometimes seen to be *śiṃśapā* trees and sometimes to be creepers, mango trees, and so forth, what would a discerning person have grounds for being confident in saying, "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*"? (Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p.
72; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 266, commentary on the verse).

Because it is stated that "the intention of a person is diverse, such that even those possessed by passion act as if they were free from passion," therefore, if speech (*vāk*) were to deviate from its object—meaning if the observed effect could arise even from a different class of cause, while excluding the intended causal class—then what would follow? To this he says:
"It is possible" (*śakyam*), etc. It is not at all capable of indicating a specific difference in the cause (*kāraṇabhedi kāraṇaviśeṣaṃ gamayitum*). This is the meaning.
The mention of "effect" (*kārya*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "essential nature" (*svabhāva*); therefore, the intention is that inference (*anumāna*) as well would be non-existent.

For comparison: "From mental states [arise] correct or false activities; these are to be inferred from the bodily and vocal behaviors produced by them, which transcend the senses. And such behaviors can generally be performed otherwise than with conscious intent, because they proceed from human will and because those [wills] have diverse intentions."

Therefore, how could one who does not ascertain [the truth] due to the confusion of signs (*liṅga-saṃkara*) arrive at a conviction? He explains this by saying, "because of the difficulty of understanding," "because of the difficulty of attainment," and "because of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determine the qualities and defects of others.
"Arising in the mind" (*caitasāḥ*) refers to qualities and defects.

From mental qualities—such as the causes of compassion, dispassion, and awakening—there arise "correct activities," meaning activities that accord with reality. From mental defects, such as attachment and so forth, there arise "false activities," meaning activities that are contrary to reality.
Furthermore, the virtues and faults of others' mental states are beyond the reach of the senses because they are properties of the mind; therefore, they are not accessible through direct perception.
Rather, they must be inferred from the effect-sign (*kāryaliṅga*) of bodily and vocal actions, which originate—that is, arise—from those virtues and faults.
And that [inference] does not exist.

Because conventional practices (*vyavahāra*), characterized by bodily and vocal actions, are for the most part preceded by cognition (*buddhipūrva*), they can be performed otherwise through deliberate discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*).
For instance, even those possessed of passion (*sarāga*) may present themselves as being free from passion (*vītarāga*), and those free from passion may appear as if possessed of passion.

What is the reason? It is because conventional practices proceed according to the will of persons, and because those persons possess diverse intentions (*abhisandhi*) and diverse purposes (*abhiprāya*); therefore, conventional practices proceed according to their desire. Consequently, there is no certain determination (*vivekaniścaya*) regarding conventional practices that arise from virtues or faults.

Therefore, for this reason, how could this person who infers—failing to ascertain [the object] due to the deviation of the mark (*liṅga*) from its mark-possessor (*liṅgin*)—accept the author of scripture as one whose defects have been exhausted? The conclusion is that he certainly could not; thus it must be understood.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.222)
Just as one who is attached speaks, so too does one who is detached;

it is not from mere words, nor even from specific [external] characteristics, that there is a comprehension [of the internal state], because intention is difficult to ascertain and because all [indicators] are fallacious due to the confusion of worldly practice—for the detached person behaves like one who is attached, and the attached person likewise behaves like one who is detached; thus, the intention is difficult to know. (*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1)

"Even though he has realized the characteristic [of reality] with all obscurations exhausted, he might teach otherwise due to various underlying intentions; thus there is the possibility of deception"—*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p.
116; *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 71.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 9; *Sūtrakṛtāṅga-ṭīkā*, p. 384; *Laghīyastraya-āloka*, p. 49.

The *Vivṛtivivaraṇa*—explaining the verse, he says "of the scripture" (*śruteḥ*), etc. [This means: although there is frequently (*bahulam*) and abundantly (*prācuryeṇa*) no non-correspondence with external objects in the case of scripture—that is, sound—it is not merely due to the absence of that [correspondence], but because of the reason that a connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*) with that object, namely the external object, is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
He asks: "Of what kind of scripture? and says: "That which conforms to the intention of the speaker.

He asks: "Where? Why? and says: "Everywhere there is a lack of confidence in its objects; that is, a lack of confidence in external objects. If this is so, he says here: "It has been stated," and so forth;
the answer to this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) has already been stated.

He asks, "What is that? and says: "Because there is non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) of the scripture even without identity (*tādātmya*) or causal origination (*tadutpatti*), since there is comprehension of an imperceptible object.

Furthermore, with the words "api ca" and so forth, he applies that same refutation to the opponent's position as well: "Moreover, why is there no confidence at all in this inference which is currently being observed—such as 'this is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*, or there is fire on this mountain because of smoke'? Why is this so? He says: "In some cases," and so forth.

In certain specific regions, because of the perception of creepers, mango trees, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) including such things as creepers and *badarī* trees—[the existence of rain is inferred].

And likewise, since there is no contradiction even if a *śiṃśapā* tree were itself not a tree, how could there be any confidence? For fire produced from wood is distinct from fire produced by the causal complex of a gem (*maṇi*) and so forth, and similarly, fire produced by lightning is distinct from that produced by wood. If, despite this difference in origin, one were to accept that there is no contradiction in their nature as fire in its entirety and without exception, then why would there be this restriction—that smoke is produced only from fire and not from other things—by virtue of which, through the non-deviation of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), one could have confidence in such inferences as "there is fire here because there is smoke"?
Now, it is said that a well-discriminated cause-and-effect relationship is not subject to deviation;
regarding this, he says: "Of something," and so forth.

When the cognition of an imperceptible object is accepted as occurring through the impossibility (*anupapatti*)—in the form of the absence of the probandum—of some specific nature or effect in any other way, then for one who has heard [the reason] but has not himself perceived its identity (*tādātmya*) or its origination from it (*tadutpatti*), [the inference would fail], just like the aforementioned person with the crow's footprint (*vokṣkapuṣpa*). (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa 5)

Therefore, because the absence of neuter gender in certain cases— such as the word *dvīpa* and others— is not otherwise possible without [the Veda] being non-contradictory, its validity is established.
In the absence of the six [senses], by that [means] there is no perception of external [objects]. (Ā, Ba,
Śr)
In some places, *kimi*—
[Śrauta-pṛṣṭha 435];
in the state of direct perception— Ācārya.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), [actions such as] rubbing grass and the fire-drill should be understood.

As for the comparison: if it is argued that an effect examined with effort does not transcend its cause, then this is merely praising what has already been established—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭamahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya*, p.
72; *Prameyaratnamālā* 3.
101. *Laghīyastrayāloka*, p. 49:
Now, according to the principle that a well-discriminated effect does not deviate from its cause...
—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 266.
Regarding the phrase "in the beginning" (*bhāvau vā ukta*), the variant *ba* reads *bhādau cokta*.

The meaning is as follows: that whose identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are not perceived is "that which has unperceived identity and causality"; this refers to scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) whose nature, such as its own essence (*svabhāva*) or its effects (*kārya*), has not been grasped.

Here, because the word *adṛṣṭatādātmyatadutpatti*—which is heard [in the compound]—functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is employed in the masculine gender according to the rule *bhādau* (Pāṇini 7.1.19) and others, which states that when a neuter stem ending in *imac* or *umac* follows a word beginning with a consonant (*bh-*) or a vowel other than *a* (*aj-*) within a *sup*-inflected form, it optionally takes the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*). However, in the neuter gender, after the addition of the augment *num*, the resulting usage would be *adṛṣṭatādātmyatadutpattinaḥ*; such is the intended meaning of what was heard.

May that Lord of Jinas be victorious—he who is the sun that dispels the darkness of fallacious reasoning, the ocean of Nyāya, and the moon to the exquisite night-lotuses of the hearts of living beings in the world; he by whom *pramāṇa* (valid cognition), along with its fallacies (*sābhāsa*), objects, results, and enumerations, has been proclaimed here in a few words that are both lucid and profound. Thus, uprooting the pride of the lordly elephants of all rival schools with the firm blows of his stainless intellect, the lion Akalaṅkadeva—whose form is fierce with hundreds of manes of the *syādvāda*—triumphs on earth as a five-faced lion.
*Pramāṇa*, along with its fallacies, objects, results, and enumerations, has been explained here...
In this work,
the author Pabhācandra has spoken with a few words that are both lucid and profound.
May that Lord of Jinas prevail— he who is the sun to the darkness of fallacious reasoning (*dustarka*), the ocean of logic (*nyāya*),
and the moon to the exquisite night-lotuses of the hearts of the world’s living beings.
[Chh] By this epithet, *Nyāyakumudacandra* and its author, Prabhācandra, are indicated.

Victorious on this earth is Akalaṅkadeva, the five-faced lion, whose form is fierce with hundreds of manes of the *syādvāda* doctrine; he who, like a lion, utterly uproots the pride of the lordly elephants of all rival philosophical schools with the firm blows of his stainless arguments. || Cha ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, an ornament to the *Laghīyastraya*, composed by Prabhācandra. [End of the fourth chapter.

The extent of the text is 1,130 [units]. Here ends the fifth chapter on the systems (*nayapariccheda*) within the second section on the introduction to the systems (*nayapraveśa*).
The emergence of the power of knowledge regarding all objects existing within the belly of the three worlds—
the path to the stainless god Akalaṅka, which is difficult to attain— has been reached here through the rise of merit;
it has been reached here, O venerable one.
May that path of Akalaṅkadeva— which has been repeatedly practiced and analyzed hundreds of times through the teachings of Anantavīrya—
bestow the attainment of its realization upon me, whose mind is fixed on the method of right vision. || cha ||
Now, having examined the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by Prabhācandra, he begins the examination of the viewpoints (*naya*):
"Regarding the object of knowledge, which consists of both difference and non-difference, there are intentions [of apprehending] difference and non-difference."
This has been extracted—thus Ākalaṅka said: "Since difference and non-difference are perceived and ascertained through dependence and independence... (Avaśyakaniryukti-malaya-vṛtti, fol. 370B;
Gurutattvaviniścaya, fol. 16B).
They are perceived and determined.
What are *nayadurnayas*?
They are *nayas*, *durnayas*, and fallacious *nayas* (*nayābhāsas*).

By what means are they so classified? By *apekṣā* and *anapekṣā*. *Apekṣā* is the desire for the attributes of the opposing perspective; *anapekṣā* is the opposite of that, namely absolute one-sidedness (*sarvathaikāntatā*). By these two [they are distinguished].

Of what nature are they? They are the intentions (*abhisandhi*) regarding difference and non-difference. "Difference" (*bheda*) means particularity, mode (*paryāya*), and distinction; "non-difference" (*abheda*) means generality, unity, and similarity. The compound *bhedābheda* means both difference and non-difference; the "intentions regarding difference and non-difference" refers to the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of one who possesses scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñānin*). With respect to what? With respect to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the object of cognition (*prameya*), such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth. Of what nature is that [object]? It is said to be "consisting of difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedātmake*), meaning that whose essence or nature (*ātmā/svabhāva*) consists of both difference and non-difference.
—Laghīyastrayāvatāraṇī, p. 50:
"Those which are characterized by dependence and independence are [respectively] *naya* and *durnaya*.
(30) These [are from] the *Mukhāgama* on the *Laghīyastrayāvatāraṇī*.

"Taking sides" (*pakṣapāta*) is dependence; "not taking sides" (*apakṣapāta*) is independence (*nirapekṣatva*). The rejection of a contrary property is "taking sides," while indifference (*upekṣā*) is dependence.
— *Aṣṭaśahasrikā*, *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 290.

Therefore, all viewpoints (*naya*) are false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) when they are bound to their own side and not dependent on one another; however, when they are mutually dependent, they possess the true nature of right view (*samyaktva*).
Views that are independent [of other perspectives] are false; those that are dependent [on others] are the reality that accomplishes the purpose. —Āptamīmāṃsā 108
"Standpoints (*naya*) are relative, while fallacious standpoints (*durnaya*) are absolute; this is established even from the worldly perspective.
As it has been said: "The cognition of an object that possesses multiple aspects is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
a standpoint (*naya*) is the cognition of one of its parts, while a fallacious standpoint (*durnaya*) is the rejection of the other attributes. (*Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, folio 537B)

—Because [the categories] are characterized by the acquisition of other properties, indifference, and abandonment; because no other mode is possible for valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), right perspective (*naya*), and fallacious perspective (*durṇaya*); and because through valid cognition there occurs the comprehension of that [object] as having such-and-such a nature, the comprehension of what it is not, and the exclusion of what is other than that. —Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 290.

That which exists must exist as "existent" (sat); thus, an object may be cognized in three ways by means of fallacious reasoning, pseudo-reasoning, and valid cognition—*Anyayogavyavaccheda-dvātriṃśikā*, verse 28, *Vivṛti*: Reality (*tattva*) is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), consisting of substance and mode (*paryāya*), and endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence. It is precisely therein that the distinction between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its semblance (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is established in some respect.
*Naya* is the intention of the knower; it is twofold:

*dravyārthika* (substantive) and *paryāyārthika* (modal). That which moves (*dravati*), will move (*droṣyati*), or has moved (*adudruvat*) is *dravya* (substance); that for which this very substance is the object (*artha*) is *dravyārthika*. It is based on non-differentiation. — *Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya* 1.1.58.

*Nyāyakumudacandra*, p. 401, note 6.
For comparison: "Whether arisen, or perished, or permanent"—*Sthānāṅga*, Sthāna 10.

Or, as for "existent substance" (saddavva)— according to Vyākhyāprajñaptiśataka 8.309, the category of the door of existent states (satpadadvāra)— it is characterized by existence and endowed with the threefold nature of arising, passing away, and persistence.
Or rather, that which is called "the substratum of qualities and modes" by the Omniscient One—
[as stated in] Pañcāstikāya-gāthā 10— is endowed with the nature of arising, passing away, and permanence, while not abandoning its own inherent essence.
That which possesses qualities and modes is called a substance—
*Pravacanasāra* 2.3.

The definition of an existent substance: "That which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence is existent" (Tattvārthasūtra 5.29, 30). Substance is devoid of modifications, and modifications are not separate from substance.
Arising, persistence, and dissolution are the characteristics of substance—
thus [says] the *Sanmati* (Gāthā 1.12).
In the absence of arising, abiding, and ceasing, there would be the three cognitions— [as stated in] Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 619—
the inherent connection of arising, abiding, and ceasing with intrinsic nature.
Because its causes lack such capacity, it consists of three natures—*Siddhiviniścaya*, p.

167. For comparison: "The means of attainment (*prāpaka*), the agents (*kāraka*), the accomplishers (*sādhaka*), the effectors (*nirvartaka*), the manifestors (*nirbhāsaka*), the perceivers (*upalambhaka*), and the revealers (*vyañjaka*) are not different in meaning."

The *nayās* are so called because they lead toward, reach, cause to be accomplished, establish, bring about, manifest, cause to be perceived, and reveal the categories of existence, such as the soul (*jīva*) and others— *Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya* 1.35.
Naya is that which manifests the specific distinctions of objects analyzed through the doctrine of manifold aspects (syādvāda).

According to the *Āptamīmāṃsā* (verse 106), naya is the application of a logical reason toward an object characterized by non-absolutism (anekāntātman), which, by presenting the reason without contradiction, is inclined toward establishing the true nature of the specific property to be proven.
— Sarvārthasiddhi 1.33:
"Indeed, the standpoints (nayas) are the intentions of the knowers with respect to substance and mode."

The *naya* is considered by the knower to be the perspective; the *nayas* are those which describe the specific distinctions of objects revealed by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, folios 517A, 518A)
— Rājavārtika 1.33:
Because, by means of restriction alone, one [predicate] is established for a thing that possesses manifold properties.

Then, by way of the principle of vision (naya), that [cognition] becomes sevenfold; for it is called a "naya" because it leads [the object], and it is a substance characterized by many qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*). (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, gāthā 2676)
"White with its true nature undestroyed amidst differences of transformation, place, and time"—*Dhavala-ṭīkā*, p.
11; "A mode of cognition (*naya*) is the determination of a portion of an object whose reality is grasped by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)"—*Dhavala-ṭīkā*, p. 83.

In the *Sārasaṃgraha* as well, it was stated by Pūjyapāda: "When it is necessary to comprehend one particular mode (*paryāya*) of an entity that consists of infinite modes, a faultless application based on a valid reason (*jātihetu*) is *naya*.

This was also declared by the venerable Prabhācandra in the *Dhavalā* commentary on the *Vedanakhaṇḍa*: "A *naya* is an intention (*praṇidhi*) inclined toward the exposition of a specific object that has been brought under control through the conceptualization of transformation (*pariṇāma*) based upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

"Nayas" are so called because they lead, bring about, or cause one to reach meanings; that is, nayas consist in the exclusive adoption of one or another among the multiple natures of a real entity (*vastu*). As it has been said: "Nayas are the determination of one or another single nature of a substance (*dravya*) which possesses multiple natures, because they lead to only a single part [of its full reality]. (Nayacakra-vṛtti, p. 526A).
– *Nayacakravṛtti*, folio 6B:
"They lead," thus [are called] *nayas*; they determine an object consisting of multiple properties as being exclusively eternal or exclusively non-eternal by means of a single property.
Tattvārthasiddhi 1.6
"For a *naya* is traditionally defined as the determination of one part of its own object" (Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 118);
"Indeed, that by which a portion of the meaning of scripture is led—that is, understood—is a *naya*" (Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p.

"Naya is the intention of the knower which grasps a particular aspect of an object while not rejecting its opposite" (Nayavivaraṇa, verse 4); "Naya is the intention of the knower which grasps a portion of the thing, without setting aside its counter-position" (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.

That which is the grasping of objects through the divisions of scripture as expounded by the possessors of knowledge is here applied according to the *nayas*; moreover, the possessors of knowledge [proceed] by means of various *nayas*.
— *Nayacakra* Gāthā 2.

Or, *naya* is so called because it leads (*nayati*) or causes one to reach (*prāpayati*) an object toward a single intrinsic nature by excluding it from various intrinsic natures— whether this be a conceptualization based on what has been heard or the intention of the knower; thus,
it is a discourse concerning *naya*.

The *naya*— which, having entered through that [door of *pramāṇa*], is intent upon establishing the meaning of the object as resting in multiple properties (*anekadharmaniṣṭha*), and which proceeds by way of accepting, rejecting, or setting aside the remaining properties— is, according to the *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā* (p.
82), the means for manifesting the nature of an entity (*vastu*) that possesses infinite properties (*anantadharma*).

That which leads to one part [of an object] is known as *naya* in its various forms—*Tattvārthasāra*, p. 106. That specific intention of the cognizer by which, while an object has been made the domain of the means of valid cognition called scripture (*śruta*), one part is directed toward while remaining indifferent to other parts, is *naya*.
—Pramāṇanaya° 7.1; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 310.

Nayas are specific types of cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya-viśeṣa*) that grasp one part of an object determined by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which consists of infinite properties, while not rejecting the remainder of its aspects—according to the *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 21. A naya is a specific type of cognitive determination that grasps a particular aspect of the subject matter at hand while not rejecting the other aspects.
—*Nayarahasya*, p. 79; *Nayapradīpa*, p. 97B.

According to the opinion of Ācārya Malayagiri, all *nayas* are indeed false (*mithyā*). To explain: a *naya* is that specific intention (*abhiprāya-viśeṣa*) of the knower by which the intellect of the person to be instructed is led—that is, brought—to a single property, such as permanence or another, following the determination of an object consisting of multiple properties. It is this specific intention of the knower that constitutes a *naya*.

For here, that *naya* which apprehends an object marked by the word "syāt" (*syātpada*) through its dependence on other *nayās* grasps the object in its ultimate sense as complete, and thus it is included within valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, that *naya* which intends to determine an object by means of only its own intended attribute, preceded by a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) due to independence from other *naya*-doctrines, is [merely] a *naya* because it grasps only one part of the object (Āvaśyakaniryukti-malaya-vṛtti, fol.

369A). And that [object] is fourfold: namely, the substantialist (*dravyāstika*), the matrix-word-orientated (*mātṛkāpadāstika*), the origination-orientated (*utpannāstika*), and the mode-orientated (*paryāyāstika*).
— Tattvārthādhi° Bhā° 5.31.
Thus, the Dravyāstika and the Mātṛkāpadāstika constitute the Dravyanaya.
The mode of perspective (paryāyanaya) consists of the existent-in-origination (utpannāstika) and the existent-in-modification (paryāyāstika)
— Tattvārthahari 5.31.
The substance-aspect and the mode-aspect are the two [primary] viewpoints; all other variations are included within these. (Tattvārthasiddhi 5.31)
—Sanmati 1.3:
The standpoint (naya) is of two kinds: that which has substance as its object (dravyārthika) and that which has modification as its object (paryāyārthika).
—Sarvārthasiddhi 1.6:
There are two fundamental divisions: the Dravyāstika and the Paryāyāstika.
Alternatively, there are the substantialist (dravyārthika) and the modalist (paryāyārthika)—
as stated in the *Rājavārttika* (1.33)—
wherein these two fundamental viewpoints (mūlanaya) have substance and mode as their respective objects.
Falsehood exists in the absence of partiality, while rightness exists in its opposite—Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, p. 521A.
For the substantialist standpoint, it is the substance; for the modal standpoint, it is the mode.

—[Regarding] those remaining scriptures: "In brief, there are two primary divisions of the *nayas*: the substance-view (*dravyārtha*) and the mode-view (*paryāyārtha*); their subdivisions are the *saṃgraha* and the others.
— *Nayacakra-vṛtti*, p. 526A.
Dhavalā Ṭīkā, page 83;
Pramāṇanayatatvāloka, 7.5.
"Paryāyārthika" means that which has synonyms as its meaning or purpose— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.6.
"Paryāya" means that which goes toward or reaches differentiation;
"paryāyārthika" refers to that whose meaning or purpose is precisely this paryāya—*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 84.
It flows.
(Jaṃbū-vyākhyā) For comparison: "Alternatively, that whose essential nature (*tattva*) is not destroyed even when other qualities (*guṇāntara*) manifest is a substance (*dravya*).

What, then, is this essential nature? It is the non-existence of that [other quality]; it is the essence. For example, although qualities such as redness or yellowness manifest in fruits like the *āmalaka*, they remain simply 'the *āmalaka*' or 'the *badara*']" (Tattvārthasūtra 5.37).
Furthermore, the etymological derivation is indeed meaningful: "substance (dravya) is a confluence of qualities (guṇasandrāva). — Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 5.1.120.
That which moves and goes through various modifications of its own nature is called "substance" (dravya), for it is non-different from existence (sattā).
— The five existents (pañcāsti), Gāthā 9:
Those things which are called "substances" (dravya) because they are perceived or perceive according to their respective modes (paryāya),
Sarvārthasiddhi 5.
It flowed, it flows, and it will flow— whether as a single or multiple modification of itself.
— Nyāyaviniścaya, Verse 114.

Substance (dravya) is that which possesses qualities (guṇas), is devoid of modifications (paryāyas), and is the substratum of qualities; it is the potentiality for becoming (bhavya) and that which is fit for the state of being (bhūta-bhāva).
— Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, Gāthā 28.

It flows (*dravati*), it will flow (*droṣyati*), it has flowed (*dudravat*), and it has flowed away (*adudravat*); thus it is *dru*. A modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) of wood (*dru*) is *dravya*. [Nyāyakandalī, p. 99B]: "A modification of wood is *dravya*, or a part of wood is *dravya*; and since *dravya* is that which is capable of becoming (*bhavya*) or comes into being (*bhavati*), *dravya* is 'that which is to be' (*bhavya*); it is *dravya* because it flows (*dravati*), or it is *dravya* because it is flowed through (*drūyate*); or *dravya* is the confluence of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*) due to the flowing of qualities."
– *Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 441B: "It will flow; it has flowed; it flows—by way of these states it is a substance (*dravya*)" — *Dhavalā-ṭīkā*, p.

*Dravya* is that which flows (*dravati*) or moves through various modes (*paryāya*), or that by which one is moved or gone through those modes; thus it is called *dravya*. (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa, Ālāpapaddhati, p. 26).
That which has substance (*dravya*) as its object (*artha*) or purpose (*prayojana*) is the substantialist (*dravyārthika*)— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.6.

The statement "the generality of worship exists for one who stands from the perspective of substance" is the remainder; the entire method of discourse consists of the consideration of modes along with their opposites.
— *Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa*, Gāthā 1.
*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 83:

"The object by means of substance is 'substance-object' (*dravyārtha*); or, that for which substance is the object; or, alternatively, 'substance-aimed' (*dravyārthika*)—that for which substance alone is the aim is this 'substance-object' (*dravyārtha*)."
—*Nayacakravṛtti*, folio 4B. Explanation of the verse:

"Difference" (*bheda*) is particularity (*viśeṣa*), and "non-difference" (*abheda*) is generality (*sāmānya*). That which has these two as its nature (*tadātman*) is an entity (*vastu*) that possesses such a nature in some respect (*kathañcit*). [This refers to] an entity, not one imagined by the Naiyāyikas and others, since that has already been refuted.
He states what that [object] is like: "in the knowable," meaning that which is to be delimited by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This qualification should also be understood as applying to the proof (*sādhana*);

therefore, it is understood that every entity consists of both difference and non-difference because it is knowable, just as when it is said, "it is existent and impermanent," [the reason] is "because of existence" (*sattvāt*).

Nor is this reason inconclusive or contradictory; for whether there is total difference or non-difference, the capacity of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine its object has already been rejected.

In that regard, the intentions of persons concerning difference and non-difference—those which have generalities (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*) as their objects—are designated and determined as "standpoints" (*naya*) and "pseudo-standpoints" (*durnaya*). By what means? He says: by "regard" (*apekṣā*) and "non-regard" (*anapekṣā*); through regard they are standpoints, and through the other [non-regard] they are pseudo-standpoints.
In the second chapter, "The Determination of Objects," all [cognitions] are ascertained by means of direct perception.
And [the author], in commenting on these two [verses], says—beginning with "In substance"—while explaining the *kārikā*: "In substance," etc. (ba॰ vivṛtivivaraṇam).

In this context, the subject (*dharmin*) is the reality of the thing (*vastutattva*), and the probandum (*sādhya*) is that it is qualified by specific attributes such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.

If one asks, "For what purpose is the inclusion of the term 'reality' (*tattva*)?"—it is for the purpose of precluding the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). To explain: the living being (*jīva*) and so forth are neither illusory, nor empty, nor merely imagined; rather, they are reality (*tattva*), existing in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*).
Furthermore, the ultimate existence of the entity consisting of the living being and so forth has already been established previously. Enough of this digression.

"Let it be so; nevertheless, that [reality] will be of a uniform nature," he says—referring to "substance" and so forth—that which has as its constituents (ātman) substances and modes (paryāya) whose characteristics are to be described later is thus designated.
Why is this so? He says: "because it is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence."
Since it has production and so forth as its nature, it is of such a kind;
but why is it even of this kind? He says: "existent" (*sat*), because that which is existent is that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*).
To the question, "How does that [object] possess the capacity to produce an effect? he says: "Because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*).
Since the entity consisting of the living being (*jīva*) and so forth is an object of cognition, it therefore performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

For it has already been stated previously that it is not possible for that which is postulated by the Sāṃkhyas—the Self (*ātman*)—to be an object of cognition if it does not perform any purposeful action.

One might object: "If a single reality is being perceived, how can the various intentions of cognizers be established as *nayas*, given that distinct appearances are impossible? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that very [object]," and so forth.

In that very object—namely, the moon and such, whose nature was just described—there is a distinction between the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends it in some way through its existence, whiteness, and so on, and the appearance (*tad-ābhāsa*) which apprehends it in some way through its duality and so on; because of this distinction, there is a perception of difference.
And since this has already been established previously, it is cited here as an illustrative example.

Therefore, since different modes of apprehension are possible even with respect to a single object, *naya* is defined as the intention of the knower based on a specific partial description (*vikalādeśa*).
He states its divisions with the words beginning "That [naya]," etc.:
that *naya* is either *dravyārthika* (substantive) or *paryāyārthika* (modal).

Therein, he first explains: "Substance" (*dravya*) means that which has flowed, will flow, or has flowed; thus it is *dravya*. That very thing is the object (*artha*), and he who holds that [object] as existing is the *dravyārthika*.
Why is he such? He says: because he relies upon non-differentiation (*abhedāśraya*).
That whose self (ātman) consists of the discernment of objects is [the self], according to Ārya and Bhaṭṭa; [it is] ultimately real (paramārthasat).
pṛ॰ 191: In that regard, [the reading] "śra॰ –ṣṭe dravati" is found in Ā॰ and Ba॰.
"Since it is dependent upon difference...

[the opponent objects]: "But surely, because all entities are absolutely distinct in terms of place, time, and form, there is no such thing as non-difference (abheda); therefore, how could this [Reality] be the substratum of non-difference? To dispel this doubt, he says: "That in which the various divisions of the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva) are dissolved—that exists as the Real."
What is it that exists, is found, and is perceived? It is *sat*, the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*).
Of what nature is it? "That which," and so forth; that within which [all things] are internally contained, that is, included.

What are they? They are the categories of *jīva* (living beings) and *ajīva* (non-living things). A *jīva* is characterized by consciousness (*cetanā*); *ajīva*, on the other hand, is its opposite, consisting of *pudgala* (matter) and so forth. Their sub-divisions include the further distinctions of mobile (*trasa*) and immobile (*sthāvara*) beings, and so on. These are what were described as "the *jīva* and *ajīva* and their sub-divisions.

Indeed, neither a substance (*dravya*) nor a mode (*paryāya*) can be designated as something distinct from existence (*sattva*), for that would contradict one's own words and lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is asked, "How can a single entity be the pervader of multiple categories such as *jīva* and the rest? the author replies with the verse beginning with "one" (*ekam*).

Just as a single cognition possesses its own manifestations—namely, the blue and other forms which are its own cognitive nature appearing within it—as in the case of a cognition having a variegated cloth or the like as its object; and just as a single soul (jīva) is not contradicted when it is pervaded by its own modes (paryāyas)—that is, by its own conscious modifications such as passion and so forth, and is thus established in the realm of experience—in the same way, existence (sattva) also is not contradicted when it is pervaded by the various distinctions of souls and so forth. This is the meaning. (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 52)
Just as a single cognition is not undermined in its unity by the various manifestations of itself, so too is the soul (jīva) [not undermined] by its own modifications (paryāyas).

Commentary: Just as the various manifestations within a cognition do not contradict the unity of that cognition—whether it be of a soul or a non-soul (ajīva)—in the same way, the soul’s own qualities and modifications do not contradict its unity. Likewise, the various categories of existence, such as soul, non-soul, and so forth, do not contradict the unity of reality (sattva).
Thus it is:
Jīva and so forth—*Jaṃ-vi-kārikāvyākhyānam*:
Jīva and ajīva; their subdivisions (prabhedāḥ) are intermediate distinctions which are contained within, that is, which have entered into, that [Reality] which exists, which is present.
He asks, "What is that? and says: "Being" (sat) refers to the generality of existence (sattāsāmānya).
In what manner is it one, and so forth?

One's own manifestations (*svanirbhāsa*) are the appearances of forms such as blue that do not reside in another cognition; that which possesses these is "cognition with its own manifestations," meaning a single, variegated cognition (*citraikajñāna*).
Just as [the object] exists in the manner of its manifestation and so forth, so too does the subject under discussion exist. This was stated from the perspective of the Buddhists;
however, from the perspective of others, he says: "The soul (*jīva*) [exists] through its own modes (*paryāya*)."

The mention of "living beings" (jīva) is an illustration for the entire category of non-living principles (ajīvatattva). Therefore, it is established that just as a living being and so forth exists as one when conjoined with its own modifications (paryāyas), so too does "existence" (sat) exist as one—meaning it is knowledge (jñāna).
[Śrāvaṇa reads "āste," while Bhaṭṭa reads "asti"].
— That which is the living being... by this [is meant] the commentary on the Vivṛti.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Just as," and so forth.

Just as—by which very manner of inseparable union and security (*abhinnayogakṣema*) in which the various manifestations (*nirbhāsabheda*), such as the forms of the apprehended blue and so on, belong to the cognition or to the nature of the self (*ātman*)—those do not contradict its unity; neither that of the living being (*jīva*), the self, nor that of any non-living thing (*ajīva*) such as a jar, which is well-known to all people, [nor] that imagined by the Naiyāyikas and others, since that has already been refuted.
The connection is: "just as the qualities and modifications (*guṇaparyāya*) of their own [substance] do not contradict its unity."
In that very same manner, he asks: "What are the divisions of *sattva*, the universal property of existence?
He replies: "Living beings (*jīva*), non-living beings (*ajīva*), and so forth. [The opponent asks: "Do these not contradict its oneness?
[The author] says: "If that [oneness] exists, what has been produced? He replies: "Thus, in this way..."
When that sentient being exists in the manner thus described, consisting of both the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva)—
for it is impossible to separate [the two], since the forms such as blue within a single unitary cognition cannot be transferred to another cognition;
and "yoga" is the persistence of properties not yet acquired.
The persistence of the attained dharma is security—
Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā 1.24.

Yoga is the attainment characterized by the discernment of an object not yet attained; security is its preservation, characterized by the performance of its purposeful activity—*Hetubindu-ṭīkā*, p. 55.
The *saṃgraha* intends pure substance because of its non-difference from that [substance].
Who apprehends [it], that is, makes it an object? It is the *saṅgraha* (comprehensive) standpoint.

Why? Because the pure substance, which is the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), can be considered "pure" insofar as it is devoid of any other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); for the standpoint whose object is that [pure substance] is indeed the *saṅgraha*.

By bringing together, through non-contradiction with its own genus (*sajātīya*), various modes (*paryāya*) whose differences are not overridden, into a single unity, one grasps them all; this is the etymological definition of *saṃgraha*.

Why? Because of their non-difference from that—that is, because of the non-difference from that pure substance (*śuddhadravya*) characterized by existence (*sat-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which is present without distinction in all living and non-living entities.

Now, one might object: "Since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like are distinct from existence (*sattva*), how can there be non-difference from it? Anticipating this doubt, he says: Among the various specific instances of existence (*sad-viśeṣa*), such as the different categories of living beings (*jīva*) and so forth, not even a single instance—whether it be a living being, a mode (*paryāya*) thereof, or anything else—is of the nature of non-existence (*asad-ātmā*) or possesses a non-existent form (*asat-svarūpa*); such a thing does not exist, nor is it found.

From the standpoint of contradiction: if it has the nature of both existent and non-existent, how can it exist? If it exists, how can it have the nature of the non-existent? Because this is unestablished due to self-contradiction, one must therefore accept—on the strength of empirical cognition—that its prior absence and so forth are in some way of the nature of the existent alone.
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 52)
"Comprehension and summary of the meaning; they say that the language of comprehension is, in brief, [the means of understanding]—
Anuyogadvāra 4, Dvāra Āvaśyaka Niryukti, Gāthā 756."

The *Saṃgraha* (Compendium) is the inclusion of all objects or a portion thereof. And it is said: "That which is a statement of inclusion pertains to the universal, to a part, or to the particular. (*Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya*, Gāthā 2699).
One who knows the method of the rule of right knowledge (*vidyānaya*) and the method of the rule of conduct (*nayavidhi*), which is determined by the means of grasping that [knowledge]—
this is the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*). (Tattvārtha-sūtra-bhāṣya 1.35)
*Tattvārthahari*, *Tattvārthasiddha* 1.35:

It is called "comprehensive" (*saṃgraha*) because it grasps all things collectively without distinction, by bringing various modes (*paryāya*) together into a single unity without contradicting their own nature, while not overriding their differences.
— Sarvārthasiddhi 1.33;
Rājavārttika 1.33.
*Sagraha* is either the determination that "only affirmation (*vidhi*) is reality" because no negation (*pratiṣedha*) apart from affirmation is perceived, due to the grasping of the whole;
or it is the determination that "only substance (*dravya*) is reality" because no mode (*paryāya*) apart from substance is perceived.
The *Dhavalāṭīkā* (p.
84) states: "It intends a pure substance, being intent upon the apprehension of pure existence (*sanmātra*);
and it maintains a state of perpetual indifference toward all particularities (*viśeṣa*) here."
—Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 70; Nayavivaraṇa, verse 67; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 677.
"Depending upon pure substance, there is the 'with-grasping' [view] due to its impurity"—Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.
272, 311; *Nayacakra*, gāthā 34;
*Tattvārthasāra*, p. 107.
Pramāṇanaya° 7.13; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 311.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 22:

"Among the various distinctions, there is not even a single distinction that is non-existent by nature, because of contradiction. Commentary: "Everything is one, because of the lack of distinction in its existence"—this is the *saṃgraha* [view].
And because the unity of existence is not contradicted by the existence of various natures,

there is no distinction whatsoever that is non-existent in essence, for that would involve a contradiction; indeed, no cognition, being of the nature of existence, can apprehend a distinction without first cognizing the substance as existent.
Comparison— just as everything is one because there is no difference in its existence—
Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.35.
Alternatively, "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*) refers to that which is grasped as the essence of its own substratum and is distinct from others;
it is described as a generality that is non-different from all particulars in every respect— *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, gāthā 2701.
"The universe is one reality because there is no distinction," as stated in *Pramāṇanaya* 7.16.
Commentary on the verse:

It intends to, that is, takes as its object, pure substance characterized by existence (*sattā*), and not even the specific attributes such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth. As to what this is, he says: it is the *saṃgraha*, the *saṃgrahanaya* (the inclusive perspective).

To the question "Whence is this so?", he says: "Because of its non-difference from that"—that is, because that *sattva* (Being) is without distinction among all particularities (*viśeṣa*). To the question "Whence is even this so?", he says: "Among the particulars," and so forth. The connection is as follows: among the particulars (*bheda*), such as the specific distinctions of living beings (*jīva*) and so on, there is not even one particularity (*viśeṣa*) that is of the nature of non-existence (*asad-ātman*) or has the nature of non-being (*asat-svabhāva*), nor indeed many; rather, [all] exist solely as having the nature of Being (*sad-ātman*).
He asks, "From what [reason] does it not exist? and says: "Because of contradiction.
For instance: if it is non-existent, how can it exist; and if it exists, how can it be non-existent?

By this, the fourfold negation (*abhāva-catuṣṭaya*) has been examined. To explain: if that [entity] is cognizable by the notion "it exists," how could it be of the nature of non-existence? Because even in its own nature, it would possess the character of existence.
Now, if it is of the nature of non-existence, then it cannot be known through cognition; how, then, can its existence be established?
If you ask, "How does it exist?"—[the answer is: it exists as the object of all [cognitions].
The fact that even the fourfold non-existence is apprehended by the cognition "it exists" establishes the actual existence of the fourfold non-existence.

The Vivṛtivivaraṇa, explaining the verse, says: "All," and so forth. All things—whether sentient or insentient by nature—are one and non-different, based on the non-distinction of existence (*sattā*); such is the summary.

Anticipating the objection that "since existence is non-distinct even though those things possessing it are established as distinct, it is incorrect to say that 'everything is one,'" he says: "And of existing things," etc. This means: because there is no sublation of the unity of existence—that is, the unity of the nature (*svabhāva*) of existing things, which are the properties of being (*bhāvadharma*)—there is no negation of the unity of existence. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For not," etc.
For this reason, there is no such thing as a non-existent essence—that is, a particular or distinction among substances and so forth that has the nature of non-existence.
Why? He says: "Because of contradiction," meaning because of opposition.
Furthermore, demonstrating that there is no such distinction whose nature is non-existent, he says: "Indeed not," and so forth.

Without having understood—that is, without having grasped—the existent nature (*sadrūpa*) or the essence of existence (*sattvasvarūpa*) of some cognition, whether it be perception or inference, one does not indeed grasp the distinction (*bheda*), the particularity (*viśeṣa*), or the substance (*dravya*)—the mention of "substance" being an elliptical indication for qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. To the question "What [does one not grasp]?", he says: "one does not grasp at all."

Therefore, this [position] is refuted: that substance and so forth are not existent by themselves, nor are they non-existent, but become existent through a relation with "existence" (*sattā*). For this [argument] would hold if there were a perception of substance and so forth devoid of the nature of existence, and of the nature of existence itself devoid of their own essence; yet such a perception does not occur, because both are always experienced as having both natures. This is the distinction: the former [passage] points out the contradiction in the opponent's position, while the present one establishes, through direct experience, that difference consists in the nature of existence. (The term *dravyasvarūpa* occurs in both manuscripts *ba* and *śra*.)
Because, for that which is devoid of an intrinsic nature such as substance and so forth,
existence depends upon the particularity of substance and so forth, while substance depends upon the qualification of existence.
By the explanatory statement beginning with "for [it] does not have a non-existent nature," and by the portion beginning with "for there is no cognition whatsoever."

Here the Buddhist says: "As for what was stated—that just as the internal manifestations and distinctions of cognition do not contradict its unity—that too has been said [incorrectly]; because you accept a partless, unitary cognition, this entire appearance of pillars and so forth, being superimposed with contradictory properties, is an illusion like water in a mirage. How, then, could the desired reality be established by means of that illustration? The proponent of the non-duality of the Self (*puruṣādvaitavādin*) also says: "The reality is the waveless, pure Self alone; the distinction between living beings and the non-living is a mere delusion. Therefore, [distinctions] such as 'of a living being' or 'of a non-living being' are also untenable. Anticipating this, he says:
By the illustration of variegated cognition—
the various divisions and sub-divisions of the individual soul— ignorance regarding duality, both external and internal, exists as the very nature of reality.
One should teach, praise, and explain—what is the meaning? Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is clear sensory and non-sensory cognition.
