Just as the components of a lamp [flame], the activity—the action—of the qualities which are the components of the intellect (*buddhi*) is flickering; at every moment it becomes one thing and then another. It is not the case that the qualities remain devoid of activity. (Yoga-bhāṣya, Yoga-vārttika 2.15)

Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya position, the object consists of the three *guṇas* and is mobile, for such is the nature of the *guṇas*: "The activity of the *guṇas* is mobile" (Yogasūtrabhāṣya 4.15);
"The activity of the *guṇas* is mobile and eternal" (Yogakārikā 3).
Consciousness is the essential nature of the Puruṣa—Yogabhāṣya, p. 37, commentary on the Kārikā.

Let objects—substances and so forth—exist by themselves, that is, through their own nature; let them be present, possessing existence (*sattā*), which is the highest generality (*para-sāmānya*). The mention of "existence" here is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, one should understand that they possess intermediate generalities, inherence, and particularities as well. Why is this so? He says: "By existence," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is this: Are objects inherently existent (*svataḥ santaḥ*) by virtue of inhering in existence (*sattā-samavāyāt*), or could they be otherwise? In the first case, regarding those objects whose nature is "being" (*sat-ātmanām arthānām*), what [is done] by existence (*sattayā*)? The ellipsis to be supplied is: "nothing at all is produced by existence. For their own-nature existence (*svarūpa-sattva*) is not produced by that [existence], since it occurs spontaneously (*svata eva*) and because it is impossible to produce what already exists; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor [is there any need for] the designation "existent" and so forth, since even that is possible solely through the existence of their own-nature.

Now, regarding the claim that things which are non-existent in themselves become possessed of existence through inherence (*samavāya*) with that [existence], the author replies with the words "non-existent" (*asad*), and so forth:
In those things whose self-nature (*ātman*) is non-existent—that is, not present—this existence postulated by others could not exist.
Why? Because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for it would follow that this [existence] would also apply to such things as the horns of a donkey.
And the existence of objects has been analyzed in detail from the perspective of their being (*sattā*) during the examination of the six categories; thus, enough with this over-elaboration.

[This concludes the discussion of] intermediate generalities (*avāntara-sāmānya*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), earthness (*pṛthivītva*), and so forth, which belong to those things that are existent (*sad*). (Ā., Śr.)
Of those whose nature is impermanent,
not of those whose nature is eternal.
Even though existence by its own nature is already existent,
if it were to be produced, there would be an infinite regress consisting in the non-cessation of causal activity.

Even for those entities that exist by their own nature, the verbal expression "existent" or the cognition "existent" would have to be produced by means of [their] existence (sattā); therefore, he says "nor even... and so forth, because the verbal expression "existent" or the cognition "existent" arises from the inherence of existence (sattā-samavāya).
If it were non-existent, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the term] "existence" (*sattā*).
Folio 285– Vivṛtivyākhyāna:
In order to explain the *kārikā*, he says "yathā" and so forth.

Just as those other categories such as *sāmānya* (universality) exist by themselves—that is, through their own nature—and not by means of inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*), and yet they possess existence; in that very same manner, let substances, qualities, and actions alone exist by themselves, and not things like the horns of a donkey. What is the use of inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) regarding those substances and so forth? Why is this so? He says: "By themselves," and so on.

For would the existence of substances and so forth—which are either inherently existent or non-existent—result from their inherence in *sattā* (existence)? Regarding this, the first position is untenable: for if they were already inherently existent, the inherence of *sattā* would be redundant; and if they were inherently non-existent, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since it would follow that even things like a sky-flower would possess existence through the inherence of *sattā*.
Extending this very same refutation to other cases, he says: "In this way," and so forth.
The objection just mentioned should be applied in this manner according to the method stated:
where? Even in the intermediate classes, that is, even in the generalities such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth.

For instance—just as "existent substance," "existent quality," and "existent action" are so by their own nature, so too are "substance," "quality," and "action" substances, qualities, and actions by their own nature; likewise, a female buffalo is a buffalo and a white horse is a horse by its own nature. What, then, is the use of the inherence of "substance-ness" and so forth there? Because it would be redundant for substances, qualities, and actions [if they already exist] by their own nature, and because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) for things that are not substances, qualities, or actions.

For [a universal] does not become such [i.e., manifest] through connection with another unless it has already been transformed; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence (prasaṅga) that even a sky-lotus would possess that nature.
Showing another refutation here, he says: "of cowness, etc.

Here, by the word "etc.," horsehood and so forth are included. If all-pervasiveness is admitted, there would be a confusion of cognitions—that is, a confusion of the cognitions of cowness and the like; consequently, just as in the case of a spotted cow (khaṇḍā), the cognition of a cow would arise even in respect of a white horse (karka).

This is an elliptical expression; by it, the confusion of verbal usage is intended. And when such confusion exists, its status as a subordinate genus (avāntarajāti) is extremely difficult to maintain.
Furthermore, a genus that is specifically eternal and omnipresent was refuted during the examination of the universal (sāmānya); therefore, enough of this elaboration here.
Now, demonstrating the refutation of the universal (*jāti*) under the alternative position that it is not omnipresent (*asarvagatatva*), he says: "Otherwise," etc.

Otherwise—that is, by the other mode of being non-omnipresent—there would be no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) based on intention for a motionless entity such as "cowness" (*gotva*) which does not pervade the location where an object (*artha*) is about to arise; thus, the object would not function as the qualifier [and consequently], there would be no prior placement of the word "about-to-arise" (*utpitsu*). Furthermore, it is illogical for a partless (*anaṃśa*), i.e., indivisible entity, to have an occasional existence in multiple substrates.

To demonstrate the absence of faults in his own system, he says: "In the mutual identity of quality, qualified entity, and so forth, there is nothing contradictory. This has been explained in detail in the section on the establishment of non-absolutism (*anekāntasiddhi*); therefore, enough of this digression. Now, regarding the three categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*), he states their common characteristics: "Of generality and the others... [and so on].

The very self is the existence (*sattva*), which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of universals (*sāmānya*) and the others; that alone is their existence, not existence through connection with the category of "Being" (*sattā*).
By this, it is meant that the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of these three—universals and so forth—is their being devoid of a universal.
How is this so? Because there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*).

Existence (*sattā*) does not reside in the universal (*sāmānya*), because that would lead to an undesirable consequence; nor does it reside in the particulars (*viśeṣa*), because if the universal were present in the particulars, doubt would still be possible, and even if one pursues the particulars for the sake of certain determination, there would be an infinite regress.

Furthermore, if existence were admitted to reside in inherence (*samavāya*), the very admission of inherence as the locus where it resides would result in the same undesirable consequence—this is the refutation [found] in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, Kanda, p. 19.

For in the case of the primary [universal], there arises the sublation [of its existence] by such defects as infinite regress; thus, the summary of the sublaters of a universal is: non-difference, equality, confusion, infinite regress, loss of form, and lack of connection (Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā, p. 142).
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, *Kiraṇāvalī*, p.
33 — just as existence (*sattā*) [is not perceived] by itself;
for [it is] from itself, indeed. (Ā. Ha.)
Because of the inherence in existence—
[from the commentary]—
in substance and so forth.
Nor [is it] excessive— [as stated by] Śrīdhara—
because of the redundancy of substance-ness, quality-ness, action-ness, and inherence;
for that which is not inherently such cannot possess suchness through inherence.
—From the *Āptamīmāṃsā*, verse 72:

Because [the universal] would possess existence through inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*), there would follow the consequence that it possesses existence; therefore, the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva-pratyaya*) [arises from the individual]. From the *Śruti*.

Even in the case of a white object (*karka*), whether there occurs the verbal usage "this is a cow" or the cognition "this is a cow," the nature of cowness (*gotva*) would be difficult to ascertain; for if cowness were present everywhere—including in horses and so forth—just as whiteness is, then it would be a *mahāsāmānya* (the highest universal) alone, and not a subordinate universal (*avāntarasāmānya*). This is the intended meaning.
pṛ॰ 258–ṇa asarva– ba॰, śra॰; ni kriyasya ba॰, ā॰
Comparison— In that regard, when an object appears in another location, it is not understood how they (the universals) are seen there or how they participate in its activity;
for they do not arise together with it because they are eternal, nor do they abide [in that place].
In that regard, because they were previously non-pervasive, they do not come from elsewhere; for there is no absence of activity [in what is to be produced]. (Tattvasaṃgraha 806–7) — Śrī.
— *Cit-varttana*—
[Ba] Furthermore, in order to show another semblance of the *naigama* [view], he says "of the qualities" (*guṇānām*), and so forth.
The "functioning" (*vṛtta*) or "operation" (*varttana*) of the qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas— is "mobile," characterized by appearance and disappearance.

He explains this very point with the words "This alone is happiness," and so forth: for the function (*vṛtti*) of *sattva* is characterized by happiness and the like, that of *rajas* by suffering and the like, and that of *tamas* by ignorance and the like.
To the question of what the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *puruṣa* is, he says: "Consciousness" (*caitanya*), and so forth;
consciousness, which is perception (*darśana*), is the own, personal, and unique form of the *puruṣa*.

Since it is stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (verse 3) that "the Puruṣa is neither nature (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*"), what is its nature? It is immovable, devoid of manifestation and disappearance.
The word "iti" serves to conclude the refutation of the opponent's position.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "This too," and so forth.
This refers not only to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine but also to the Sāṃkhya doctrine; it is likewise a mere semblance of reasoning (*naigamābhāsa*).
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "That," and so forth.

Regarding those two—the Puruṣa and the functioning of pleasure and so forth—there is no "difference in object" (arthāntaratā), because "difference in substance" (vastvantaratva) is unestablished and thus uncertain.
In this very context, he states another fault: "And in this way, there would be an over-extension.

The sense is that even though the Puruṣa and the functioning of pleasure and so forth are non-different in the ultimate sense, if a difference were accepted by others in the manner of their own dogmatic adherence to their views while they are still being perceived, there would be an over-extension; the implication is that nothing at all would remain as a single entity.

The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the preceding faults. Now, one might object: "Surely their being different objects is established because of the contradiction between them. To this he says: "In the absence of their difference," and so forth. The meaning is that if there were non-difference—that is, oneness—between those two states of the person (*puruṣa*), then no contradiction would exist; for there would be an absence of contradiction, whether defined as the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), consisting in the nature of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*), or consisting in sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*).

Now, if it is thought that when the nature of the immovable Puruṣa enters into the movement of the active [Guṇas], there would be either mobility or immobility for both, and thus a contradiction arises—to this he says: "Of the Guṇas," and so forth.

When it is accepted that the Guṇas—characterized as Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—are of the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest (dṛśya-adṛśya), being manifest from the perspective of the evolved effects (vyakta) and unmanifest from the perspective of the primal source (pradhāna), then it is logical and established that the Puruṣas themselves possess that nature of being both manifest and unmanifest; for it has already been demonstrated by means of the entire treatise that the Self consists of the transformations of pleasure and the rest. Enough of this digression.
What happened after that? To this he says: "Done," and so forth.

"Done" means sufficient; the intention is that [the effort] is enough through the postulation of qualities (*guṇa*) or the postulation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), because [the world] has that as its nature.
Furthermore, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) has already been refuted in detail in the section examining *prakṛti*; therefore, we shall desist.
He explains the perception of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*:

"Consisting of pleasure, pain, and dejection. Here, the compound is as follows: pleasure (*prīti*), pain (*aprīti*), and dejection (*viṣāda*)—those qualities whose essence (*ātman*) or nature (*svarūpa*) consists of these are "consisting of pleasure, pain, and dejection" (*prītyaprītiviṣādātmakāḥ*). Their characteristics are now stated; therein, *sattva* consists of pleasure.
Why does the word "self" (ātman) refer to intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? Because it is characterized by happiness.

For whenever anyone experiences joy anywhere, one should understand that *sattva*—consisting of uprightness, gentleness, truthfulness, purity, modesty, intelligence, forbearance, compassion, knowledge, and so forth—is present there.
Why is *rajas* characterized by lack of pleasure? Because its defining characteristic is suffering.

For whenever anyone, anywhere, at any time, experiences a lack of pleasure, there arise hatred, malice, envy, censure, arrogance, longing, deceit, fraud, imprisonment, and acts of mutilation; that should be recognized as *rajas*.
Why is *tamas* characterized by despondency? Because its defining characteristic is delusion (*moha*).

For whenever anyone perceives delusion anywhere, there one finds ignorance, intoxication, laziness, fear, dejection, incapacity for action, atheism, despondency, sleep, and so forth; that should be understood as *tamas*.
—Sāṃkhyakārikā, Māṭharavṛtti, Jayamaṅgalā, Kārikā 12;
Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa, p. 106 — [The state] beyond the functions and the Puruṣa. Ā.
— [The reading] "tāmavalastvantā" in manuscript *ba* is [corrupted];
in manuscript *śra* and *ba*, it is "[the reading] 'tadabhedavirodhe' by the Kāpilas."
Regarding pleasure and the self,

there are two kinds of contradiction among categories: first, the cognition of contradiction based on the absence [of one thing] when another exists, despite the cause being unimpaired, as in the case of cold and hot sensations.
Or [it is like] existence, by virtue of having a characteristic that exists through mutual exclusion—Nyāyabindu, p.
Introduction to the Two [Truths], Āloka.
—He said: It is logical that [the object] consists of both the visible and the invisible, and is characterized by manifestation.
Ārya.
Page 191: The examination of the qualities of the Puruṣa. Śrī. Puruṣasya.

Because they consist of pleasure and so forth, [and] because there is currently a lack of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), he says the following in order to demonstrate that those two are merely semblances thereof (tadābhāsatā): [pṛ. 354]
— By [the author] who illuminates [this],

the validity of the appearance of the *sagraha* (with grasping) and the appearance of the *naigama* (global) is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), for that [validity] would not exist in reality (*tattvataḥ*) for those two.

Commentary on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): A means of valid cognition, which is the basis for establishing what is desired or refuting what is undesired—whether it be perception or something else—must be accepted by everyone, otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
and that [means of valid cognition] arises from conventional practice (*vyavahāra*).
The meaning is: "relying upon that" refers to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which consists of the systematic removal, distribution, differentiation, and conceptualization [of objects].

And that [transaction] would not exist in reality—that is, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—where? In those two: the semblance of inclusion (*saṃgrahābhāsa*) and the semblance of the synthetic view (*naigamābhāsa*).

Indeed, in the extreme view of absolute non-dependence (*nirapekṣa-bhāvaikānta*), there is no conventional usage of the distinctions between means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, because such usage has been refuted; nor is there any conventional usage of the means of knowledge and its result (*phala*) in the extreme view of absolute difference (*bhedaikānta*), because of the absence of a relationship.
If it is argued that "there exists a figurative (*aupacārika*) usage of the means of knowledge and its result therein," he replies with the words beginning "false" (*mithyā*):

if a figurative usage of the means of knowledge and its result is admitted in the extreme view of falsity—that is, in the extreme view of non-reality—then what distinction or difference is there? The meaning is: none at all.

What is the body [of the argument]? It consists of one's own position and the opposing position; "one's own position" refers to the doctrine of Brahman or the doctrine of duality, while the "opposing position" refers to the doctrine of momentariness or the doctrine of non-duality—the meaning being that because of the consequence of their mutual contamination, some form of conventionally real discourse must be accepted in some way. (Laghīyastrayālaṃkāra, p. 60)
The determination of validity is by means of practical activity—
Pramāṇavārttika 1.7.
In the case of an absolute falsehood, what distinction would there be between one's own position and its opposite?

Commentary: For one who establishes a substance as pure or impure, or a mode as collective or individual, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought to prove that; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the validity of that [means of cognition] is established solely through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, that [notion of] difference based on synthesis is purely false;

how then could it surpass its opposite, like the nature of truth versus its opposite? Even though there is no distinction in their being exclusively false, establishing such a distinction is improper, because the perception of both has a non-false nature. Otherwise, like within a dream, there would be no valid cognition at all due to contradiction.

Even in the *naigama* [view], the claim that "the activity of qualities is mobile" and "consciousness is eternal" is merely a display of a doctrine fabricated according to one's own whim, as it is not established by worldly usage (*vyavahāra*).
For there is no authority [for the claim] that "the supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision,
whereas that which has reached the range of vision is merely illusion and utterly insubstantial," nor that the whole (avayavin) exists in its own parts by way of inherence (samavāya).
The worldly convention that "the cow is in the horn" or "the tree is in the branch" would be contradicted by this [view], because it is the opposite:

how could a self whose nature is inherently ignorant become a knower through the inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge? For such is not the true nature of that which has not undergone transformation, as it would entail the absurd consequence that even *samavāya* itself is a knower.

If you argue that there is no inherence of knowledge belonging to *samavāya*, then how can that [self] exist or function while being devoid of its own inherent nature, given that there is no other *samavāya* [to connect it] and that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)?
— vya vya— īśvara vijñāna
— sta vya—
jagat vijñāna bala īśvara vijñāna
The supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision;
he cites scripture as authority for this stated meaning: "And so," meaning that which is supreme, ultimate, and eternal.

"Like an illusion" means like worldly illusion, momentary and subject to destruction; therefore, it is "utterly void" (*sutucchaka*), meaning extremely void and of little substance due to the absence of any stable hope.

Here, by the word *su* (well/extremely), the voidness even of the *guṇas* is indicated by virtue of their being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). The *guṇas* themselves are void in comparison to the immutable eternal (*kūṭastha-nitya*) because they are subject to transformation; and the visible effect of the *guṇas* is void even in comparison to the *guṇas* themselves. Therefore, it is "utterly void" (*sutuccham*).
— *Yogavārttika*, p. 414.

The supreme form, the primordial form, in its unmanifest state, does not come within the range of vision; that which has become manifest and reached the path of vision, consisting of the forms of the *guṇas*, is as utterly void as an illusion (*māyā*), just like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) displayed by an illusion—thus it is said. This verse is cited in the following texts: "And so is the instruction of the scripture regarding the *guṇas*... [Yoga-sūtra-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa, p. 414].
— Yogabhāṣya 4.13: The instruction of the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* treatise concerning the *guṇas*.
—Yogabhāṣya, Tattvavaiśāradī 4.13; Yogabhāṣya, Bhāsvatī; Pātañjalayoga-rahasya 4.13.
The Blessed One [spoke] of the qualities of Vārṣagaṇya—
Śāṅkara Bhāṣya on the Bhāmatī, page 352.
*Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 43A;
*Tattvopaplava*, p. 80; *Sāṃkhyatattvāloka*, p. 6.
The nature of the qualities is exceedingly great—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, Chapter 4, p. 33;
*Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, p. 74B.
"A thing that has come within the range of vision is that illusory object, which is utterly void"—Jayamaṅgalā, p.
63: "But that which has come within the range of vision is indeed illusion itself, being utterly void."
These expressions, such as "as a cloth is in its threads," were composed by [the author] himself;
for in common worldly usage one would say "a horn is on the cow," whereas "the cow is in the horn" is unworldly.
(Pramāṇavārttika 3)
The notion that "there is a branch on the tree" or "there is a goat on the rock" is a worldly cognition,
arising from the perception of the proximity of the remaining parts known as "rocks."
Furthermore, that knowledge regarding those [energies] is said to transcend the worlds— *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 267— it should abide there, *Īśvarapratyabhijñā-vivṛti*.
Commentary on the verse:
Validity [is established] from worldly practice (*vyavahāra*); that is, by relying upon worldly practice. The particle *hi* has the sense of restriction;
the meaning is that it is from worldly practice alone, and not by relying on non-duality of cognition and so forth.
If it is argued, "Let that [conventional usage] be exactly so; what is the fault?", he says here: "That," and so forth.
That conventional usage would not exist in reality—that is, from the perspective of the ultimate truth—of those two, namely the semblances of *saṃgraha* and *naigama*.
Now, if their conventional usage is not real, one might think, "Let it be non-real; however, it will still exist. To this, he says: "The absolute false," and so forth.

The intended meaning is this: where conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) is false, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based upon it is also exclusively false. If that absolute falsity is accepted, what distinction or difference (*viśeṣa*) would there be? None at all—of which two? Of one's own position (*svapakṣa*) and the opposing position (*vipakṣa*).
Therefore, the implication is that for both, there would be either proof (*siddhi*) or non-proof (*asiddhi*).
The word "vā" has the sense of the word "api"; the authority is [from] Devajñāna.
From non-duality of knowledge—ba;
then from that—śra; as it is for those two—ba.
Now,
as for the *āsravas* (influxes), they are not real entities; this is the explanation of the commentary on the single authority (*pramāṇa*).
In order to explain the *kārikā*, he says: "Pure," and so forth.
Pure substance (*dravya*) devoid of modes (*paryāya*) is [the concept of] Brahman and the like; pure mode devoid of substance is the form of momentary, partless atoms (*paramāṇu*);
and impure substance is that which possesses modes.
He states the qualification of this immediately following [verse], which concerns the impure mode (*paryāya*) possessing substance (*saddravya*): "separate," and so forth.
"Separate" means mutually independent; by this, the view of the Naiyāyikas is shown.

The whole is mutually identical; by this also, the Sāṃkhya system is illuminated, since the Sāṃkhyas establish the identity (*tādātmya*) between the modification and the modifier. This [point] is to be connected with each [of the preceding arguments]. Their proof—that is, the proof for those two, namely the pure and impure, discrete and collective substance and mode—is to be sought and investigated.
And that [naya] cannot be anything other than a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it has no authority other than in the determination of objects such as perception and so forth;

otherwise, if its determination were established by way of the absence of a search for a means of valid cognition, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), resulting in the undesirable consequence that everything would be established as every object from every perspective.

Nor should it be asked: "In the context of explaining the fallacious *saṃgraha* and *naigama*, why is this irrelevant 'pure mode' (*śuddha-paryāya*) being introduced? For it is intended as an illustration.
Just as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought by the Buddhist when establishing a pure category, so too must it be sought by anyone else when establishing another;
or rather, this must necessarily be stated later regarding the semblance of the *ṛjusūtra* [naya], and thus it has been stated here:
"If it is argued, 'In that case, a valid means of cognition must indeed be sought,' to this he replies: 'That... and so forth.

The validity of that which establishes such [distinctions] is established by conventional usage alone, and not by the mode of ultimate reality imagined by others, because that [ultimate mode] is unestablished therein;
and that convention is entirely false within the summary [of the system], not being true even in the slightest degree—this is the meaning of the particle *eva*.
Why is this so? He says: "Because it is based on difference."
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he says here: "From that," and so forth.

How could the *saṃgraha* (the inclusive school) surpass the *pratipakṣa*, which is the absolute view of difference (*bhedaikānta*), on account of that false conventional practice regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth? Not at all;
for even there, because of the existence of a false conventional practice regarding the means of valid cognition and so forth, [there is no superiority]. [Prāmāṇya-vyavahāra, Pramāṇavārttika 1].
Because of such statements as these, one might object:

"The *sagraha* (clinging to existence) consists of non-duality, whereas the *apratipakṣa* (non-opposition) consists of duality; how then does the latter not surpass the former? To this he says: "True," and so forth.
"True" (*satya*) means non-false; "the other" (*itarat*) means false. That which possesses both those [qualities] and their respective natures (*svarūpa*) is "possessing that" (*tadvat*).

This is an adverbial modifier: "the synthesis (*saṃgraha*) should excel in such a way that it possesses the nature of truth, and the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) should be in such a way that it possesses the nature of the other [falsity]. The meaning is that, like the counter-position, the synthesis would also be false. To the question, "What is the fault in that? he says: "False," and so forth. Even in the case of the lack of distinction between the synthesis and the counter-position—let alone in the case of their actual distinction—it is improper to establish that synthesis as being [true].
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," and so forth.

Since that is so, therefore, because both are perceived—namely, the inclusion and its opposite—and because they possess a non-false nature, that is, a true intrinsic nature, how could it (the former) surpass its counter-position? This is the connection.
He states the refutation regarding its non-false nature: "Otherwise," and so forth.
Otherwise, because it lacks the nature of being non-erroneous— just like other dreams or specific dream-states— it is non-concordant; therefore, nothing [such as] substance,
mode, or pure substance (*śuddhadravya*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By this [statement],
the authority of the proponent of the non-duality of Brahman and so forth is established.
And it is said here [in the *Bhāṣya*]:
"Conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) proceeds by relying upon difference; therefore, from the perspective of the *saṃgraha-naya*, which grasps non-difference, it is indeed false."
This has been extracted from: *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.
173; *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, folios 18A, 232B, 294B, 305B, 324, 520B;
and *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, pp. 217, 383.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 111, 497; Nyāyaviniścaya-vivaraṇa, p. 38; Śāstravārtā-samuccaya-yaśovijaya, p. 258b.
—The root is *tad-vitha*—Śra.
Yo. Vi. Ba., Ā.
Its application—Ā.

Having thus demonstrated the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding the semblance of inclusion (*saṃgrahābhāsa*), he now says "In the case of the Naigama [view] as well," etc., while demonstrating that same [absence of valid cognition] regarding the semblance of the Naigama.
This is not only the case in the *saṃgraha* [naya], but also in the *naigama* [naya] there is no proof whatsoever;
he states this very point with the words "unstable," and so forth.
"Unstable" means characterized by appearance and disappearance.
He asks, "What is that? and says: "The functioning of the qualities," and so forth.

The functioning (*vṛtta*) of the qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the others, is their transformation (*pariṇamana*) into the forms of the Great One (*mahat*) and so on; [they claim] consciousness (*caitanya*) is eternal. This is merely a presentation of a philosophical system (*darśana*) constructed according to their own fancy.
Why? Because it is not established by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For indeed," and so forth.

For (*hi*) because the supreme form of the qualities (*guṇas*)—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—characterized as *pradhāna*, does not come within the range of vision; whereas that form which has reached the range of vision, such as the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, is utterly void like an illusion (*māyā*). Such is the proof, since perception and other means of knowledge do not apply here.
[The reading] *nityacaitanyaṃ śra* [is found in manuscript Śra], while *nityacetanā* [is found in manuscript Ba].
"That is merely an illusion"—
enough of this digression.

Having demonstrated the absence of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the pseudo-Sāṃkhya and pseudo-Naiyāyika systems, he now states "by way of inherence" (*samavāyena*) and so forth, demonstrating that same absence in the pseudo-Naiyāyika system.

There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that a whole (*avayavin*) exists in its own parts by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). If it is argued that the cognition "the cow is in the horn" or "the tree is in the branch" serves as such a means of valid cognition, he replies with the words beginning "in the horn":

whatever means of valid cognition there might be for the notions "the cow is in the horn" or "the tree is in the branch" would transcend worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), because such a cognition does not actually occur in those cases.

To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of the opposite," since in common worldly usage there is the established perception that "there is a horn on a cow" and "there is a branch on a tree.
Here he states another objection: "By itself," etc.

How could the self, being by its own nature ignorant and insentient (*acetana*), become a knower or sentient (*cetana*) even when there is an inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge? For it is not logical that the state of being a knower belongs to that which has not undergone transformation (*pariṇata*) into the form of knowing.

Whence is this [conclusion]? Because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even *samavāya* (inherence) possesses the nature of a knower. With the words "Certainly not" (*na vai*), etc., he raises the opponent’s objection: "Certainly not; there is no inherence of *samavāya* with cognition. Therefore, how can it follow that it possesses the nature of a knower? To this, he replies: "In what way," etc.

In what manner (*kathaṃ*)—by what means—is there an inherence? It is by none at all, because the proofs that establish [the existence of] *samavāya* have been refuted in detail during the examination of *samavāya*.
Furthermore, this [inherence] does not exist because it is devoid of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For its intrinsic nature is the state of being an inseparable relation (*ayutasiddhasambandhatva*), and that has already been refuted in detail in that very context.

Moreover, how is it logical for this [inherence] to have an inseparable relation with its substrates when it does not reside within them, like a horse's horn? Or, if it were indeed to reside there, to this he replies: "Or it would reside," and so forth.

Thinking that the refutation characterized by its being a "knower" has been stated here, he states another refutation: "Or how could it exist, since there is no other inherence (samavāya), because of its oneness?
If it is argued that "it exists by way of being a qualifier," he says "that," and so forth.

If another inherence (*samavāya*) were postulated for inherence itself, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow; consequently, how could that [inherence] reside anywhere? This is the intended meaning: for fear of infinite regress, the opponent does not postulate another inherence for inherence. And this [regress] is no different in the case of postulating a "qualifier-state" (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*), because the necessity of postulating a further relation remains the same here as well. For it has been stated in the section refuting inherence (*samavāyaniṣedhapraghaṭṭaka*) in the *Naigamābhāsa* that a qualifier-state which is unconnected cannot be the cause for inherence’s subsistence in its substrates (*samavāyin*).
The absence of a means of valid cognition does not exist,
neither in the world nor in worldly convention.
— The cognition of the necklace— ba, śra; nor by this much alone is there [cognition] of inherence (samavāya) by means of knowledge— ba.

Now, in order to demonstrate the conventional perspective (*vyavahāranaya*), he says: "The perspective that is non-contradictory to worldly convention is a valid perspective (*naya*); otherwise, it is a fallacious perspective (*durnaya*).
— *Mūla-laghuīya-vivaraṇa*.
Explanation:
What might it be? It is a perspective (*naya*) characterized by such things as inclusion (*saṃgraha*), which holds that "external objects exist."

From the word "iti" [it follows that] there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), and so forth. Being of what nature? It is "non-contradictory with worldly practice" (*vyavahārāvisaṃvādī*). Worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) is the systematic arrangement of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth; non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). That which possesses this is so described. For if worldly practice is based on sound reasoning (*sunaya*), then the establishment of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth, which depends upon it, will occur; otherwise, if it were contradictory to worldly practice, it would be a fallacious reasoning (*durnaya*).

Of what kind? It is "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*); that is, consciousness alone is the reality, and nothing else is empty; the very sublation of all knowledge and objects of knowledge is the reality.
The word "iti" (thus) expresses a manner; it indicates such modes as "existence alone is reality," "delusion alone is reality," and so forth.
—*Laghīyastrayāloka*, p. 61. Compare:
"The conventional usage proceeds with its meaning determined regarding all things"—*Anuyogadvārasūtra*, Chapter 4.
In the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti* (gāthā 756) and the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya* (gāthā 2708),
it is stated that *vyavahāra* is similar to worldly convention, consisting mostly of metaphorical usage, and having an extensive scope.
And it is said: "One should understand that worldly discourse is established by conventional usage" (Tattvārthasūtra-bhāṣya 1.35).
*Tattvārtha-hari* (Tattvārtha-siddha 1.35):
*Vyavahāra* is the systematic extraction (*avaharaṇa*) of meanings implied by the inclusive perspective (*sagraha-naya*), preceded by the method of affirmation (*vidhi*).
— Sarvārthasiddhi 1.33;
Rājavārttika 1.33.
The meaning is that the *vyavahāra-naya* (the conventional standpoint) is dependent upon linguistic convention; — *Dhavalā-ṭīkā*.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 271; *Nayavivaraṇa*, 74; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 677.

"Let it be understood that [a cognition] which possesses a division into substance and mode superimposed by conceptual construction is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas any other is determined to be a semblance thereof (*tadābhāsa*)."
—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 271; *Nayavivaraṇa*, 76; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 678.

Commentary: Even the validity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is dependent upon worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

How, then, does that [transaction] consist of the object, the designation, and the cognition? It is as follows: existence is characterized by origination, destruction, and persistence; a substance (*dravya*) possesses qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*); and the soul (*jīva*) has consciousness (*caitanya*) as its intrinsic nature.

Non-contradiction consists in scripture not being sublated by other means of valid cognition and in its internal consistency between earlier and later parts; this is the correct perspective (*naya*) which depends upon that. How, then, would it be a fallacious perspective (*durnaya*) otherwise? Even externally, having accepted that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is real because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), one might reject that and establish that "mere consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*) is the internal reality. Yet, when even that is scrutinized with subtle analysis, it is found incapable of withstanding examination. Thus, one who prattles confusedly—proposing the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nairātmya*) as a proof for what cannot be proven—would find no stable ground, being addicted to contradicting both himself and others, and thereby conflicting with perception and other means of knowledge.

Since one or another of these is intended [by the author], enough with further idle chatter; see *Rājavārttika*, p. 17: "The three categories [of word, object, and cognition] are distinct because of the difference between the object, the denotation, and the cognition"—p.
605, note 7.
Comparison: Substance is the locus of qualities; qualities reside in a single substance;
but the characteristics of the modes (paryāyas) reside in both.
— Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.28.
That which is characterized as substance (dravya), endowed with the threefold nature of arising, passing away, and persistence, and which is the substratum of qualities and modifications—
that is what the Omniscient One calls it.
– Substance possesses qualities and modes (Tattvārthasūtra 5.38). There are five [kinds of substance] (Pañcāstikāya 10).

Know that substance is that which is endowed with qualities and modifications; know that qualities are co-existent, while modifications are said to be successively produced. — *Paramātmaprakaraṇa*, Gāthā 57.
Nyāyaviniścaya, verse 111; compare: "The soul is characterized by cognition" — Bhagavatīsūtra 2.

"and contradiction between what precedes and what follows is inconsistency"— Īśvarapratyabhijñāviveka.
That which is capable of causal efficiency is here the ultimately real— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.3.
All this is representation-only, appearing as non-existent objects,
just as one suffering from ophthalmia sees non-existent hair, moons, and so forth—
*Viṃśatikā-vijñapti*, verse 1.

Furthermore, by teaching these three mutually contradictory doctrines— external realism, idealism, and nihilism— the Sugata has clearly demonstrated his own state of incoherent prattle, or else he harbors malice toward the people [thinking], "Lest these people become deluded by grasping at contradictory meanings"—
*Śālistamba-bhāṣya* 2.

Commentary on the Verse:

Conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is the systematic arrangement of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth; a *naya* would be that which is non-contradictory to it, whereas otherwise, by way of being contradictory to it, it would be a *durnaya*, a pseudo-*naya*.

Regarding this, he provides an example: "The external object exists," and so forth. This is an illustration of the *naya* (perspective); the remainder is an illustration of the *durnaya* (fallacious perspective).
By taking the apprehension of an external object as an illustration, all *nayas*—such as "valid cognition exists" or "the relationship of cause and effect exists"—are thereby subsumed.
The view that "the reality is representation-only" or "the reality is emptiness" would constitute such a false doctrine—
this is the explanation of the commentary on all [the verses], O Śrāvaka.
Explaining the verse, he says: "Even of perception," and so forth.

Not only of inference and the like, but even the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perception depends upon conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, [the definitions] such as "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" and so on, are established by way of convention; whereas the definition "the illumination of an object not previously known" is [only] valid from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This latter position is incorrect, because an ultimate reality distinct from conventional usage is impossible.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "That," and so forth.

That which is required by way of validity is, moreover, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), consisting of object, designation, and cognition; for there is no other possibility whatsoever that could be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is the intended meaning. Although both object and designation are objects in this context, the term "object" (*artha*) is used here by intention to denote their referent (*viṣaya*), because if any one of these were absent, worldly transaction would be impossible.

Regarding the objection that there would be no distinction from a dream, [the author asks]: "How could there be a determination of various streams of consciousness, a determination of error, or any other [determination]? This was stated in the section on the establishment of external objects (*bāhyārthasiddhi*).
The question of the opponent is: "In what way?
By what manner does the nature of the conventional reality of the object itself remain established? He provides the answer, beginning with "arising" (*utpāda*), etc.
That whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and essential nature (*svarūpa*) consist of origination, cessation, and persistence is described as such.

What is that? He says: it is the existent (*sat*), such as a jar and so forth, which is an object of cognition (*prameya*) and has been established; furthermore, the fact that objects have the nature of origination and destruction was established against the Sāṃkhya in the "Examination of Primordial Matter" (*prakṛti-parīkṣā*).
He states how permanence is established for the Buddhist: "The qualities," and so forth.
Co-existent qualities (*guṇa*) are pleasure, cognition, vigor, and so on; sequential modes (*paryāya*) are pleasure, pain, and so on; and the substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses these.

This argument by reductio (*prasaṅgasādhana*) should be explained specifically against the Buddhist as follows: if the mind—or whatever else—is admitted to consist of various co-existent properties, then it must also be admitted to consist of multiple sequential properties.
If not, then even in the case of simultaneity, it should not be accepted as being thus, because there is no distinction [in the underlying principle].

Furthermore, against the Naiyāyika, it is argued as follows: if the inherence of qualities such as desire is admitted for something, then its nature must be admitted as consisting of successive states (paryāya); if not, then that inherence of those qualities would be impossible.

If it is asked, "Who realizes that substance (*dravya*), which possesses qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*), is existent (*sat*) precisely because it is characterized by origination (*utpāda*), disappearance (*vigama*), and persistence (*dhrauvya*)?"—to this he replies: "The soul (*jīva*).

That is to say, the soul, the self (*ātman*), realizes that the object of knowledge (*prameya*), such as a jar, is existent in the form of origination and so forth; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Because it is possible for that [self] to possess the capacity for such realization due to its nature of being without beginning or end,

the self has been established as a distinct reality and as having a nature without beginning or end, both in the *Cārvākamataparīkṣā* and on the occasion of the refutation of the continuum (*santāna*).
Now, if this [self] realizes that [object] by its mere existence, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that [the soul] perceives through perception and other means, then there would be a lack of capacity [in the soul itself]; to this, he says: "Because its nature is consciousness" (*caitanyasvabhāva*).

Since its nature is consciousness—that is, its essential form consists in the apprehension of both self and other—it, while undergoing transformation through the modes (*paryāya*) of perception and so forth, cognizes those objects.

Thus, the conventional reality (*vyavahāra*) consisting of the object is established as having the character of an entity characterized by origination and so on; the conventional reality consisting of cognition is characterized by the cognition of that object; and the conventional reality consisting of speech is characterized by the words that describe it.

Comparison: Therefore, that which was stated—“valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge,” and so forth—is the definition of valid cognition in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); whereas “the illumination of an unknown object” is [the definition] in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because self-cognition, which is the appearance of non-duality as an object unknown by other means of cognition, is designated in this way. (Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, fol.
9B) This is the definition of this conventional valid cognition: “valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge.”
—Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 774; he indeed... [i] ...śra... —hārārthābhi... ā.
Regarding those two particulars (*tadviśeṣa*), [the object] is the domain of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or the domain of a designation and a cognition;
