If the self were of the nature of being an object of cognition such as arising and so forth,
there would be the undesirable consequence of it being an object of cognition even during states such as deep sleep.

If one knows by means of perception and so forth, then it follows that the self itself lacks the capacity for the cognition of its own object of knowledge; therefore, he says "of the nature of consciousness" (*caitanyasvabhāva*). Even in the earlier fragmentary manuscript, the reading was simply "then there is incapacity," and the phrase "of the nature of consciousness" does not appear in manuscript Ā.
—Thus, consciousness is the intrinsic nature; the absence of consciousness is [the state of] self and other.
(Śrīmad-Āgama) Śrī Ātman.

Regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*), one might ask: in a linguistic transaction consisting of words, what constitutes non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) and what constitutes contradiction (*visaṃvāda*)? To this he says: "Of the scripture," and so forth.
Non-contradiction is the non-sublation (*abādhanam*) of the scripture—that is, the expression—by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding the question of how there can be non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) with respect to an object that is entirely beyond the senses, since it is impossible to apprehend either the non-sublation by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or any other [criterion], he says: "The former," and so forth. Non-contradiction is the non-opposition between a statement that precedes and one that follows; it is not merely the absence of sublation by other means of valid cognition. And this [non-contradiction] exists in the scripture marked by the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness). For example: "One should not harm any living beings whatsoever" (*Manusmṛti* 5.40), and "Animals were created for the sake of sacrifice by the Self-existent One himself" (*Manusmṛti* 5.39).
39. Thus says the scripture: having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, Nīlaparvata, and the holy site of Kanakhala, one may not be born again;
yet a wicked mind that has entered within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords.
Even if washed a hundred times with water, it remains impure like a liquor jar; thus says Jābāla (4.54).
Thus, it has been stated that there is no non-contradiction in such scriptural passages because of the existence of internal contradictions between earlier and later parts;
this refers either to the non-contradiction of the *śruti* itself or to non-contradiction in the form of the stability of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
Or rather, that which is to be said is:
"For the prosperity of the sacrifice and of all; therefore, in the sacrifice, killing is non-killing"—this is the latter half [of the verse].
This has been extracted: "Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, Nīlaparvata, and the sacred site of Kanakhala, one shall not be born again. (Yaśastilaka Udayasundara, p. 91, 357)
A mind that is corrupt within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
even if washed hundreds of times with water, it remains as impure as a wine-vessel, O wise one. (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4.54)
These two [verses] are cited—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra*, Chapter 4, p. 140:
"The mind is defiled within; it is not [purified] by bathing at sacred fords" (*Jābāla Upaniṣad*).

The injunction of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), "One should not harm," is contradicted by the slaughter of animals in sacrifice. Furthermore, the injunction regarding bathing at sacred fords such as Gaṅgādvāra is contradicted by the demonstration of the futility of bathing at sacred fords through the statement, "One is not purified by bathing at sacred fords."
Having thus demonstrated conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), he speaks—beginning with the words "dependent on that" (*tadapekṣa*)—to demonstrate the method (*naya*) which is its basis:

this method called conventional usage, established in the world, is "dependent on that," meaning it depends upon that [conventional usage]. Otherwise, in the manner of lacking such dependence, it is a fallacious method (*durnaya*).

Surely, that [view] alone is a *durnaya* (a fallacious doctrine), because it relies upon a worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) rooted in what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); it is not anything other than that, since it takes as its basis the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of partless moments.
He says this very thing: "How?"—the connection is that it is in no way a *durnaya* other than that.
To this, he states the following reply: "Even externally," and so forth.

Not only internally, but even externally, he accepts that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—defined as momentary, partless atoms, and capable of causal efficiency—is real (*sat*, i.e., existent). Having thus established this, he then rejects and refutes that specific characteristic, asserting that the internal reality is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and not the self (*ātman*) or other such entities. Having thus repeatedly re-established his position, he then scrutinizes and reflects upon that very representation-only with subtle analysis and finds that, like [theories of] permanence and so forth, it cannot withstand critical examination. Thus, while prattling in a confused manner about the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanairātmya*), which is itself devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), the Buddhist—being devoid of both the probandum and the probans—would find no footing anywhere, whether internally, externally, or in total emptiness; for it has been said that a fallacious argument (*durnaya*) is only such when it is dependent upon that [very position it seeks to refute]. This would indeed be a fitting conclusion.

Now, if it is asked: "Is it not said that the selflessness of intrinsic nature (svabhāvanairātmya) is neither the probandum nor the proof, since in this case the proof is merely investigation? To this he replies: "By [the work] composed for oneself and others," and so forth. "Self" refers to the Buddhist; "other" refers to the Naiyāyika and others. Their "disagreement" is the failure to realize reality; their "affliction" is the suffering of being cast into the river of saṃsāra. With respect to these, the subsequent "needless chatter"—that is, irrelevant speech—is sufficient and adequate. Thus, there is no need for further elaboration.

To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of contradiction with perception and the rest. This means because of contradiction with that which has perception as its beginning—namely, inference, worldly consensus, and so forth—or because of contradiction with those [means of knowledge] themselves.
Now, [the opponent might argue] that there is no fault here because perception and the rest are not accepted; to this he replies: "Among those," and so on.

The intention is: because among those [means of knowledge] such as perception and the rest, at least one is desired—that is, accepted—by the Buddhists; otherwise, how could they establish their own positions or refute those of others? Such is the meaning.
To demonstrate this, he says:
"Of that which depends upon it," [the] Buddhist (saugata).
And that [criticism] is based on indifference toward that [momentariness]; indeed, it is indifference toward it.

[The opponent] relies upon worldly conventions imagined through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that are not established, whereas we rely upon momentary objects established by means of valid cognition.
For one who seeks [it],
that [is] in the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa-kṣaya*).
In the destruction of the afflictions, patience (*kṣānti*)— [this is] the root.
—The proof of what is already established (prasiddhasādhana), as far as that [point] is concerned; —the *tārtti* is in Ā. (i.e., the commentary).
In the case of his defeat through contradiction,
there is no conflict for him [in the view] that perception and so forth are not accepted— [variant reading: there is conflict for him].

Having thus explained the method of conventional usage (*vyavahāranaya*) along with its fallacies according to the Buddhists, [the author], now demonstrating the *ṛjusūtranaya* along with its fallacies, says:
"Now, having explained that of the *ṛjusūtra* naya... [Ā॰, ba॰]
For the *Ṛjusūtra* [naya], the mode (*paryāya*) is primary.

Explanation: That which is straight (*ṛju*), characterized by the present mode, and which threads (*sūtrayati*) or determines (*nirūpayati*) [the object] is the *Ṛjusūtra*. What would be its primary subject? It is the mode (*paryāya*), that is, the present transformation (*vivarta*).

Since the past is non-existent due to its having perished and the future is unestablished due to its not yet being realized, they are useless for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*); for it is said that "a *naya* is that which does not contradict conventional discourse. If it is argued that a single variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) possessing multiple forms might be useful for conventional discourse, the author replies with the words beginning with "citra": "Variegated" (*citram*) refers to consciousness (*saṃvit*). This is because it is an aggregate (*samūha*) of conscious atoms (*cetana-aṇu*); "consciousness" (*cetana*) means knowledge (*jñāna*), and its "atoms" (*aṇavaḥ*) are its parts (*aṃśāḥ*), namely its indivisible units (*avibhāga-praticchedāḥ*). It is a "tattva" (reality/principle) because it is an aggregate (*samudāya*) or collection of those parts. A variegated consciousness is not the object of the *Ṛjusūtra-naya*.
Indeed, an aggregate consisting of various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, is not useful for specific conventional discourse.
If it is asked, "In that case, why is the difference not perceived there?", he says here: "Because of the non-perception of difference.
One must supply the phrase "due to the delusion caused by the production of successive similar [moments].
Thus, it is explained that because of the non-perception—that is, the non-observation—of difference or plurality, the intellect becomes deluded by the production of successive similar [moments].

The meaning is this: just as the distinction between modes (*paryāya*) existing in an iron ball or similar objects is not determined by one whose intellect is deluded, so too the distinction between modes existing in consciousness (*cit-saṃvid*) is not perceived. Alternatively, it should be explained that for the *Ṛjusūtra* [naya], the mode that is inseparable from substance (*dravya*) is primary, because a mode that is entirely independent of substance is a non-entity; and the absolute momentariness devoid of continuity (*niranvaya-kṣaṇikaikānta*) is a fallacy of the *Ṛjusūtra*.
—*Laghīyastraya-tātparya-vṛtti*, p.
62. For comparison: "The method of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint should be understood as grasping the present"—*Anuyogadvāra-sūtra*, chapter 4, verse 2.
According to the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti* (gāthā 757) and the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya* (gāthā 2718),
the thorough knowledge of the designations of present objects is considered to be *ṛjusūtra*.
And it is said: "One should know, in brief, that the Ṛjusūtra-naya apprehends only the present object" (Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya 1.35).
*Tattvārthahari*, *Tattvārthasiddhi* 1.35:
It is called *ṛjusūtra* because it threads (*sūtrayati*) or extends (*tantrayate*) that which is straight (*ṛju*) and direct (*praguṇa*).
–Sarvārthasiddhi 1.33; Dhavala-Ṭīkā, p. 86.
The *ṛjusūtra* [naya] is like the laying down of a measuring line;
— *Rājavārttika* 1.33.
It is called *ṛjusūtra* because it draws out and leads [the object] straight and correct, like the laying down of a measuring line; thus it is called *ṛjusūtra*. (*Nayacakravṛtti*, p.

The *Ṛjusūtra* [naya] delineates that which is momentary and substantially real as "straight" (*ṛju*), because it emphasizes the primary [factor], while the substance is subordinated and not presented as being existent [in a permanent sense]. — *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 271.
*Nayaviniścaya*, folio 77; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 678;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, page 311.
*Nayacakra* 8;
*Tattvārthasāra*, p. 107; *Pramāṇanaya* 7.
*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
312; *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 22.

"Because it is an accumulation of subtle volitions (*cetanā*), there may be a non-perception of its differentiation. (43) Commentary: Just as external atoms, when arranged together, present a single, gross, and unreal form, so too do the atoms of consciousness (*saṃvit*).
That [consciousness] is not a single, multiform reality that is devoid of sequence; for if it were to establish itself as having sequence, it would contradict its own non-differentiation (*abheda*).
In some cases there is indeed multiplicity; otherwise, it would not exist.
A perspective that takes into account other factors is a valid standpoint (naya), whereas one that disregards them is a fallacious standpoint (durnaya).

Establishing a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) based on a difference in appearance, one ought indeed to recognize non-difference based on their non-difference, since there is no distinction [between them];
for in the absence of either one, the object would not be perceived— this is the meaning of the verse.

For the *ṛjusūtra* perspective, or for one who holds that intention, the mode (*paryāya*) is primary; because the word "primary" is a relative term, substance (*dravya*) is secondary to it. [Objection: But surely even that [substance] has a manifold, unitary consciousness (*saṃvit*); so how can the mode be primary? To this he says: "Because a manifold consciousness consists of an aggregate of atoms of consciousness, there is no single, manifold consciousness"—this is the meaning. Now, if it is thought that if this were merely a mode, it would be perceived in exactly that same way [as a constant], and therefore the inference of difference at every moment would be useless, to this he says: "It may be," and so forth.
There may be a non-perception or non-determination of difference—that is, of manifoldness—due to the deception caused by the successive arising of similar [moments], like a whirling firebrand;
thus it "goes around" or "reaches" [the state of being perceived as one], according to the *Paryāyadhavalāṭīkā*, p. 84.
To this, Ba and Śra say:
"It is with sensation; it is variegated cognition."
Only in the form of differentiation—
*golava* (Ā), *golakṣaṇava* (Śra)—
is the explanation of the commentary.
Explaining the verse, he says "yathā" and so forth.

Just as—in the manner of demonstrating the example of hair that is distant and sparse—the external atoms (bahiḥ-paramāṇavaḥ), which are insentient atoms, being arranged in a particular configuration and situated in a specific order, display a gross form alone and not a subtle one; and they display a single form and not many, even though that form is unreal and non-existent; in that very same manner, the atoms of consciousness (saṃvit-paramāṇavaḥ) do likewise. The point is that, just like external atoms, the atoms of consciousness also do not appear by way of their own intrinsic nature. He states the conclusion with "tat" and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore, that single, non-different reality cannot possess multiple forms;

furthermore, how could such a reality—which is established as being without succession (akrama) and non-momentary (akṣaṇika)—be logically consistent with the Jain who would seek to prove it to be successive (sakrama)? This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of the contradiction between difference... and so forth.

Because difference—that is, plurality—is in contradiction with non-difference—that is, unity—therefore, whether internally or externally, there is only multiplicity, which is to say plurality; otherwise, in the manner of the absence of contradiction between difference and non-difference, such [multiplicity] would not exist.

Having thus demonstrated the general nature of the *ṛjusūtra* [naya], he now states its divisions while demonstrating them, beginning with "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*), etc.: the *ṛjusūtra-naya* is that which exists together with dependence upon something other than its own object; that which is independent (*nirapekṣa*) is a false doctrine (*durnaya*).
To the question "Why is this so?", he says "difference in appearance" (*pratibhāsabheda*), etc.

A system or a proponent who establishes a difference in intrinsic nature—that is, a plurality of the essential form of things—based on a difference in appearance, ought indeed to understand non-difference, that is, the unity of the entity, based on the non-difference of that appearance; for surely, there exists a distinction between those two appearances consisting in one being real and the other unreal, and therefore reality cannot be established from the appearance of non-difference any more than from the appearance of difference? To this he replies: "Because of the absence of distinction.
This means that because there is no distinction, that is, no difference characterized by being real or unreal, between the two appearances, both are equally real.
Regarding the refutation of the denial of the cognition of either one of those appearances, he says "tataḥ" and so forth:

if, between those two appearances of difference and non-difference, the disappearance of either one is admitted, then because the object—the real entity—would not be perceived as lacking that one appearance (i.e., because there would be an absence of perception), and because it is always perceived as possessing both natures, one must indeed accept that [the object has both natures]. This is comparable to the delusion caused by a lamp, which arises from the production of similar flames.
Regarding the cognition of many subtle objects existing in uninterrupted succession as if they were one:

just as in the case of a lamp and the like, because of the occurrence of successive flames that are similar to one another in uninterrupted succession, there arises an illusion of unity despite the existence of difference; so too, from the perception of many extremely subtle objects in uninterrupted succession, this illusion of unity occurs—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 197.

Furthermore, what was stated here by Prajñākaragupta—"The establishment of such an object from two things that are not of that nature, because such a [cognition] is seen even in the case of distant, sparse hairs which do not possess that nature" (Siddhiviṣṭi-ṭīkā, p.
100b)—is a manner of illustration; for the atoms of vision [are the basis].
Only its own part (svakīyāṃśa),
because of the contradiction with oneness; there is no multiplicity (nānātva), otherwise.
— Whichever proponent [asserts] that either of the two objects appearing as distinct or non-distinct is [the case].
Now, explaining the *śabda*, *samabhirūḍha*, and *evambhūta* nayas— which do not involve the conceptualization of internal reflections— he says:
"Due to the differences in tense, agent, and gender, the word brings about a difference in meaning."

What is this method called *śabda* like? It is "that which effects a distinction in meaning" (*arthabhedakṛt*). It effects—that is, it intends—the distinction or plurality of the object (*artha*), which is the thing to be known (*prameya*).
Why? Because of "distinction," that is, because of its specific particularity.

Of what? Of tense (kāla), grammatical relation (kāraka), and gender (liṅga); this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), meaning that it also includes number (saṃkhyā), means of accomplishment (sādhana), and voice (upagraha).

Furthermore, the method called Abhirūḍha is that which creates a distinction in meaning through synonyms—that is, through words that are synonymous yet functionally distinct—such as "Indra" from the act of ruling (indana), "Śakra" from the act of being powerful (śakana), and "Purandara" from the act of shattering cities (pūrdāraṇa).

Indeed, in the absence of a distinction between the properties such as ruling (*indana*) and so forth, it would be impossible to employ words such as "Indra" and the like; otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). In the *Nirukta*, the term *abhirūḍha* is explained as that which is established or well-known by way of its own primary meaning. Furthermore, this kind of method (*naya*)—which is based on action and makes the intended action primary—creates a distinction in meaning. For example, one is called "Indra" only at the very moment he rules; he is not [called] Indra when he is consecrating or when he is worshipping. Otherwise, if that [action] were present even in other states, there would be no restriction regarding the employment of action-words.
—Laghīyastrayāloka, p. 63.

Compare: "The word, indicating the distinction of objects through differences such as gender and so forth, is used in its conventional sense (*abhirūḍha*) by means of synonyms; however, it is based on the action of a thing as it is (*itthambhūta*)."
—*Pramāṇasaṃgraha*, p. 126. For comparison:
"The cognition of sound accepts it as even more specifically qualified as present"—*Anuyogadvāra*, chapter 4.
Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Gāthā 757;
Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, Gāthā 2718:
A word that denotes its object according to reality.
And it is said: "The Śabdanaya is that which consists of words qualified by knowledge and according to their true meaning" (Tattvārthādhigamasūtra Bhāṣya 1.35).
The word *tattvārthahari* and *tattvārthasiddha* (1.35) refers to that which aims at the cessation of fallacies regarding gender, number, means of accomplishment, and so forth.
A word (śabda) is that which causes one to understand by signifying its object, calling it forth, and making it manifest. *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.33.
— Rājavārttika 1.33:

The *śabdanaya* is inclined toward grasping the meaning following the word, because it is intent upon the exclusion of deviation regarding gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), case-role (*kāraka*), person (*puruṣa*), and voice (*upagraha*).

That which demonstrates the difference in meaning based on distinctions such as time and so forth is here called the *śabdanaya*, because it is predicated upon the primacy of words. (Ghavalāṭī, p. 86)
—Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 272; Nayavivaraṇa, 84; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 678.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 312;
Nayacakra, gā. 40;
Tattvārthasāra, p. 107.

A word whose difference in meaning is understood through the distinction of time and so forth— such as "Sumeru existed," "exists," or "will exist"— is a *śabda* [as a means of valid cognition]. — *Pramāṇanaya* 7.126.10–11.
32, 33 *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 313; *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 22.
That which has ascended [to a state] through synonyms is "thus-constituted" (*itthambhūta*), serving as the locus for an action. (44) [Commentary on *laghīyastraya-vivṛti*:
First, due to the difference in time, there are [the forms] "it was," "it is," and "it will be."]

Due to the difference in grammatical roles (kāraka), there is [the distinction between] "he does" (karoti) and "it is done" (kriyate); due to the difference in gender (liṅga), [there is the distinction between] Devadatta and Devadattā;
likewise, due to the difference in synonyms (paryāya), [there is the distinction between] Indra, Śakra, and Purandara.

Likewise, these [categories]— the verbal (śabda), the conventional (samabhirūḍha), and the etymological (evambhūta)— are based on action; for the etymological [category], agency belongs only to one who is currently acting.

When [the cognition] does not act, then, because agency is impossible, how can verbal cognition apprehend an object distinct from the intention to speak? And why is it not so? Because there is no necessary connection [between them]; for it has been refuted that what is not a cause of cognition is its object, as determined by the analysis of consciousness regarding future objects. [In this regard, the comparison is: according to the *samabhirūḍha* [naya], it is "substantial" (*vastutaḥ*) when there is action, but "non-substantial" (*avastutve*) otherwise.
The Samabhirūḍha [naya] is the non-transference [of meaning] among the six categories; [Anuyogadvāra 4, Dvāra, Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Gāthā 758].
–Tattvārthādhi° Bhāṣya 1.35; Tattvārthahari°, Tattvārthasiddha° 1.1.

Whatever conventional designation one expresses, one adheres strictly to that very thing; because one turns away from the referent of the convention, one is therefore called "Samabhirūḍha" (the one who has ascended to the specific).
—*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, Gāthā 2727:
It is called *samabhirūḍha* because it ascends to various distinct meanings;
or else, it is *samabhirūḍha* because that which is established (*abhirūḍha*) in a particular [meaning] ascends (*ārohaṇāt*) toward it by meeting (*sametya*) it directly (*abhimukhyena*).
—Rājavārttika 1.33;
Dhavalāṭīkā, p. 89.

The *samabhirūḍha* [naya] is precisely that which, through the unification of meanings, regards each individual object—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—as being one and the same in its direct presentation;
for it ascends to the distinct meanings of objects according to the difference of synonymous terms (*paryāya-śabda*). (From the *Samabhirūḍha-nayacakravṛtti*, folio 483B)
The Samabhirūḍha [naya] would be as before; and its definitive [nature] is as stated in the *Tattvārtha-śloka-vārttika* (p.
273) and the *Nayavivaraṇa* (92).
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
680; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 313; Nayacakra-gāthā, 41.
*Tattvārthasāra*, page 107;
*Pramāṇanaya*, 7.36.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 314;
Jaina-tarkabhāṣā, p. 22. For comparison:
"The *evaṃbhūta* [naya] distinguishes [the word] according to its denotation, its referent, or both."
— Anuyogadvāra 4, Dvāra, Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Gāthā 758:
*evambhūta* refers to both the phoneme (*vyañjana*) and the meaning (*artha*).
— Tattvārthādhi° Bhāṣya 1.35; Tattvārthahari°, Tattvārthasiddha° 1.1.
It is "thus-occurred" (evambhūta) because it determines by means of that very nature through which it has come to be;
or else, it determines by means of that very knowledge through which it has become transformed.
–Savarthisi 1 33 Rājavā 1
One distinguishes the meaning by means of the word, and both [word and meaning] by means of the word;
just as the word "pot" indicates its activity, so too does that [meaning] by means of that very [word].
— As stated in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka-gāthā 2743:
"In the case of difference, because [the words] exist as such [separately],
there is no compound of words, since there is a contradiction in the oneness of those that exist at different times and reside in different meanings."

Nor is there even mutual dependence among words that are distinct by virtue of their phonemes, meanings, number, tense, and so forth, because it is impossible for distinct words to depend upon one another; therefore, it is established that even a sentence does not exist.
Consequently, the determination that a single word is the denoter of a single meaning is the *evambhūta-naya*. (Ghaṭāvalī, p. 90)

In this very manner, according to this system, there is no compounding (*samāsa*) of words by their own nature, because there is a contradiction in the unity of things that are distinct due to differences in time.

There can be no compounding of words existing at a single time, because it is impossible for those that arise sequentially and perish in each moment to possess such a state. Nor is there compounding in the sense of a single referent (*ekārtha*), because it is impossible for distinct words to function with a single referent.
Nor is there even a combination of phonemes (varṇa-samāsa) there, because that would entail the same faults already mentioned regarding the combination of words;

therefore, only a single phoneme denotes a single meaning. Thus, the *evambhūta-naya* holds the intention that the meaning of a single phoneme within a word is itself the single meaning [of that word].
(*Jaya-dha.* p. 29)

"Because it is certain that the object is the transformation of that very activity, [the word] should be understood as *evambhūta* (denoting the state of being thus), being turned away from other activities"—
from the *Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 274.
*Nayavivaraṇa* 94; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 680;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 314.
*Nayacakra*, verse 43;
*Tattvārthasāra*, page 107;
*Pramāṇanaya*, verse 7.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 315; Jaina-tarkabhāṣā, p. 23.
Because agency is untenable—this is the meaning of the verse from the *Nyāyakumuda*:

because of the difference between time and so forth, the word "śabda" refers to the Śabdanaya; it is called "tadbhedakṛt" (the maker of its distinctions) because it effects—that is, demonstrates—the distinction of the object (*artha*), such as the living being (*jīva*) and so on.
Furthermore, the explanation in the Vivṛti is as follows: "One who has ascended to the method [of analysis] creates a distinction in meaning through synonyms—
that is, through words that are synonymous— being thus constituted by the differentiation of action-words, which creates a distinction in meaning."
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says "time," and so forth.

The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence. First, the distinction of objects based on the distinction of time—that is, based on specific times—is illustrated: a soul (*jīva*) and so forth "has been" (*abhūt*) by way of its mode as past experience and the like; it "is" (*bhavati*) by way of its form as present recollection and the like.

Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) should be observed here: because it "is," therefore it "has been," for it is impossible for something to "be" without a transforming material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna-kāraṇa*).

"It will come to be" means it will arise by way of its nature as a future state; here too, since it "comes to be," therefore it "will come to be," for otherwise, if it were not to come to be, there would be non-existence due to the absence of the effect—this is what is intended.
The word *iti* serves to conclude the position regarding the distinction of entities based on the distinction of time.
To provide an illustration of the [distinction] based on the distinction of causal factors (*kāraka*), he says: "the causal factor," and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is that "because of the distinction among the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, the word effects a distinction in meaning. An example here is "he makes" (*karoti*) and so on;
for when Devadatta is intended to be expressed as independent with respect to an effect such as a jar, then the expression "Devadatta makes a jar" (*karoti ghaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*) occurs.

But when that very same [agent] is intended as being assisted by another, then one says, "Devadatta is made," and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the six factors of action (*ṣaṭkārakī*), such as "place Devadatta" and "other than Devadatta.
Likewise, due to a difference in gender, a word creates a difference in meaning, as in "Devadatta" (*devadattaḥ*) and "Devadattā" (*devadattā*).
The experience of the relationship between the letter *kā* and the letter *ba*, occurring in succession,
arises... [fragmentary].
The state [of a word] is dependent on its usage (vato bhāvaḥ), as indicated by the words "ādi" (beginning with) in the manuscripts Ā and Ba;

and just as the word *yathā* creates a difference in meaning due to differences in time and so forth, so too does the conventional term (*abhirūḍha*) create a difference in meaning through different synonyms, such as *indra*, *śakra*, and *purandara*.
In this way, according to the very manner previously stated, these two—namely, *śabda* and *samabhirūḍha*, which were just mentioned—are explained. [The text says: "In this way" (*evam*).
What kind of thing is *itthambhūta*? To this he says: *itthambhūta* is that which has action as its basis (*kriyāśraya*).

Now, one might object: "When the description of a thing's nature as it actually is (*itthambhūtasvarūpaprarūpaṇa*) is under discussion, what is the connection between that and the statement of 'being thus' (*evambhūtābhidhāna*)? This is not correct, because this term "being thus" (*evambhūta*) is merely another name for that which is "as it actually is" (*itthambhūta*).
To explain why this [agent] is the substratum of action, he says: "Because the status of being a *kāraka* belongs only to that which acts.
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "When," and so forth.

When, at a certain time, the Lord of Śacī (Indra) does not perform his functions such as ruling and so forth, then, due to the impossibility of agency, the designation "Indra" and so on would not apply. To this, the Buddhist says: "All three of these perspectives understand the object through the word; therefore, since there is a difference in the object resulting from the difference in time and other factors, how can that verbal cognition apprehend a real entity (*vastu*)—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is distinct from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*)? To this, the Teacher asks him: "And how is it that it does not apprehend [it]? This is the connection [of the sentence].

He states the following reply: "Because of the lack of a necessary connection with that object" (*tadapratibandhāt*) means because there is no necessary connection with that real entity (*vastu*), due to the absence of a necessary connection based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—this is the syntactical connection regarding verbal cognition (*śabda-jñāna*). If it is argued that "even in the absence of such a connection, it [the cognition] cognizes that [object]," he says here: "Certainly not" (*na hi*), and so forth. For it is certainly not the case that a real entity in the form of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is not the cause of a cognition produced by words can be its object; for a cause is that whose positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are not unreplicated, and it has been stated that "that which is not a cause is not an object."
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Here he states the refutation: "This," and so forth; that which was stated by the opponent has been countered and rejected.

He asks "By what? and says: by the determination that consciousness has future objects as its domain. And this determination that it has future objects as its domain has been established [in the Laghīyastrayakārikā] by such passages as "One would perceive the future" (Laghīyastrayakārikā 14), etc.
"This" refers to one who is thus disposed—[the text here appears to contain scribal variants: *āśraya* for *evambhū*, and *praṇapra-stu* for *prastu*].

there is nevertheless verbal cognition (*śabdajñāna*).

Now, it may be argued that words express only a conventionally designated object and no other, for otherwise there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, a convention is not possible for word-meanings that have not been made objects of cognition, since that would result in their being without a referent (*nirviṣayatā*).

Nor can they be made objects of cognition by perception, because a verbal perception does not function toward its own denotation, nor does a perceptual cognition of the denotation function toward the word.

Nor can it be apprehended by memory, because that [memory] lacks an object; having raised this doubt, he says: "[of] auditory perception and of visual and other perceptions which grasp the denotable object."
And [the opponent might argue]: "If sensory cognition knows a past object, how could there be memory?
If it is held that the cognition produced by the senses—namely, knowledge—is such that it knows a past object and that which is denoted by its own cause, namely the word; if this is so, then...

For in the Buddhist doctrine, because an object is the cause of cognition, and a cause is said to exist in the moment preceding the moment of the effect, then from what cause would memory not also know a past object? Rather, it certainly does know it—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "In that case, how can memory be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it apprehends what has already been apprehended? Anticipating this, he says: "By perception," and so forth.

"Even with respect to that single, undivided, common object—the referent characterized as the word-meaning—because there is no difference in its being past, memory is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Why? Because of the distinction in manifestation (*pratibhāsa-bhidā*). There is a distinction in the manifestation, which is the reflective awareness of the past form; for by perception, that which is experienced as 'this' is later made the object of memory as 'that' through its past form."
Regarding this point, he provides an illustration: "dūretyādi" and so forth.
"Dūrāsanna" means that which is both distant and near; regarding such an object, like the cognition of the eyes (akṣabuddhi) with respect to a tree or similar thing.
The meaning is that just as the validity of perceptual cognitions is established through the distinction between clear and unclear manifestations, so too is it for memory.
—*Laghīyastrayāloka*, p.
65: "In the case of a single object, there is a difference in appearance, just as in the cognitions of the eye [perceiving] from far and near.
For comparison: "Even when speech, the senses, and direct perception have a single object as their domain, [a difference in appearance] is appropriate."
"The distinction in appearance [is like] the perception of a single object as distant or near" (*Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, fol.

470A). The *Vivṛti* explains: It has been stated that, given the necessity of the causal relationship between a momentary sensory cognition and its object, perception would be without an object; for its cause, being past, does not constitute the essence of that [present cognition], since there is no difference between non-existence and the two types of absence—prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and subsequent absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—as well as between immediate succession and mutual destruction. Furthermore, because the production [of the effect from the cause] and the similarity [of form] are impossible and because of [logical] deviation, it remains to be explained which [cognition] is the cognition of what.

If, however, one somehow perceives a past object directly, why would memory not be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? To claim that it is not so because it does not arise immediately from the object and lacks its form is mere audacity; for even when arising through mediation, we observe a reproduction of that form, as seen in dreams of perceived objects. Thus, the argument that memory and direct perception do not have the same object because their appearances differ is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for instance, two perceptions of the same object—one distant and one near—have different appearances yet share the same object. Furthermore, knowledge of an object by someone with impaired vision (due to distance) would not be direct perception because of its error; it would instead have to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

For there is no absolute lack of correspondence when one acts after having determined the object from that [cognition], such that it would render it invalid. Therefore, having combined the word and the object through memory, one subsequently understands that object upon the cognition of the word during the convention. Since even memory and recognition have the ultimate reality as their object, the cognition of the word and its object occurs even in the absence of that [particular] object—just like perception—because the convention is possible with respect to the real entity itself.
One is always deceived when, having formed a conceptual construction (*saṃkalpya*), one engages [with an object] through that very conceptual construction (*īrṣyā-vikalpa*).
Commentary on the Verse:

If the cognition (*buddhi*) which is the effect of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), such as the eye and so forth, perceives—that is, takes as its object—a past object, then for what reason does memory not perceive that same past object? Indeed, it does perceive it. If this were the case, there would be no difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*) between the sensory cognition and the memory, because their objects are identical, just like two cognitions of blue. To this, he says: "The appearance," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the sense-faculty and cognition" (*akṣabuddhi-smṛtyoḥ*): although they refer to a single object (*ekārthe*), this designation emphasizes the state of being (*bhāvapradhāna*).
The connection is as follows: "Memory has a distinct appearance; because its appearance is indistinct, it knows the object through a distinction from other appearances.
To illustrate this, he provides the example beginning with "far and near," and so forth.

For it is well-established that, even when the object is not different, there is a difference in manifestation— namely, clarity or lack thereof— in the cognitions of the senses regarding distant or near things, because a single tree appears in such a manner;
[this would not be possible] if the cognition called "blue" and the eye-cognition had the same object.
The commentary provides a clear and detailed exposition;
in order to explain the verse, he says: "momentary," and so forth.

Both of those—the sense-born cognition and its object—are momentary. If their relationship as cause and effect is accepted in that specific order, then direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be without an object and without a basis.
Why is this so? He says: "That," and so forth;
[it refers to] that entity which is the cause of that direct perception.

Of what nature is it? It is that which has passed away (*atīta*). Because it does not possess that [present] nature, it is said to be "that whose nature is such": namely, that for which the object of perception is non-self, being of a nature that is not its own self.

Due to the existence of that [past state], since this [object] has perished in its entirety at the time of perception, its status as an object of perception is not tenable due to the absence of its own essential form (*svarūpa*).
Because it exists at its own time, it possesses that [past object] as its object. Why would memory lack an object? For its object, too, there is no difference in terms of existing at its own time.
This refutation was stated while accepting that the past is a cause with respect to sensory cognition;
now, showing it without accepting that, he says: "The prior non-existence," and so forth.

Therefore, regarding "tadutpatti-sārūpye" (in the case of arising and similarity from that object which is considered the object), what fear is there? In the rule *jainendravyākaraṇa* 1.3.32, *bhībhiḥ*, the augment *sa-* is applied due to the separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) by means of the word *kā*.
Alternatively, the particle *tat* functions in the sense of *tasmāt* (therefore);

that is, "because of the impossibility of those two," [one asks] what—whether perception or something else—is the apprehender (*grāhaka*) of the cognition of whichever object is intended as perceptible or some other object; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Or, regarding the question "From where does this [distinction] arise? he says: "Previously," and so forth.

Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is non-existence prior to production; destruction-non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is the loss of the essential nature of that which has already attained its self-nature. Since there is no distinction between these two in terms of being non-existence—that is, because they are identical as non-existence—the following is the intended meaning: when an effect does not exist despite the presence of its cause, or exists when the cause is absent, this indicates that the absence of the thing considered the cause is the cause [of the non-existence of the effect]. Consequently, since that absence is indistinguishable even during the beginningless time of its prior non-existence, the production of the effect would necessarily occur [at that time as well].

Now, if it is argued that it is only the *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (the absence following destruction) of the cause that produces the effect, and not its *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence), to this he replies with the words "immediately subsequent," and so on: the destruction of the cause that arises immediately prior to the production of the effect is "immediately subsequent" (*samanantara*), whereas the other [destruction] is "distantly arisen" (*itarah*) in the beginningless past; and because there is no distinction between these two types of destruction, [the argument fails].

The intended meaning is this: if, despite the lack of distinction in their status as non-existence (*abhāvatva*), only the *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (non-existence by destruction) produces an effect and not the *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence), then the beginningless and endless past and future *pradhvaṃsābhāvas* would also produce effects; and in that case, it would follow that the effect itself is beginningless and endless.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that only the destruction of the specific cause produces the effect and no other [destruction does], this rebuttal is untenable because we do not accept that *pradhvaṃsa* alone is the cause.

Nor should it be asserted that only the immediately preceding destruction is its producer and no other; for if space and time are not admitted, even this solution is difficult to establish, since immediacy is indeed a proximity produced by space and time. Furthermore, demonstrating the question "Whose cognition is which?", he says: "And because of deviation, whose cognition is which? This has been explained in detail in the proof that cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), and thus is not stated here.
That which is not the self (nātmā) [is the object]; thus,
the object possesses the status of being a perceptual object.
Even for a past object that has become the content of memory, there is the state of being an object of perceptual cognition;
this is [the view of] Akṣapāda.
In the old manuscript, the reading for the word *pratītasya* appears as *bhībhi*;
what does *bhībhi* mean?

A word ending in the fifth case (pañcamī) that expresses fear (*bhī*) forms a *ṣaṣ* tatpuruṣa compound with words ending in the first case (*subanta*) that denote the cause of fear. For example: *vṛkebhyo bhīḥ* becomes *vṛkabhī*, *vṛkabhayam*, or *vṛkabhītaḥ*. Furthermore, by analysis, those who protect others from enemies are called *paritrāḥ*.
In the *Jainendra-prakriyā*,

when there is a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), the meaning of the rule *kābhībhīḥ* would be as follows: just as a compound occurs with words expressing fear (*bhaya*) following a word ending in *kā*, so too a compound— specifically a *tatpuruṣa* compound— would occur with other words following a word ending in *kā*.

In the Jainendra-vyākaraṇa, the term *sa* is the designation for a compound (*samāsa*): "The word *abhi*, when it has a correlative, [forms a compound with] a word ending in the sixth case. (*Śabdānuśāsana*)
The phrase “ity adhyāhāraḥ” (thus [the word] is to be supplied) is to be connected [to the text].— [The state is] obtained as a positive entity (bhāva),
The effect exists in the form of its cause.
Likewise, at the time of the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the cause— which is beginningless— meaning, during the state of the absence of the cause,
there is the non-existence of the cause.
The antecedent non-existence of the cause arises in the immediately preceding moment; [the effect] arises after a long time. *Śruti*.
Because there is no distinction in the form of non-existence,
[the capacity] of those things that are beginningless and endless is [unimpeded].
In the Buddhist doctrine, which maintains that effects arise from causes that are without beginning or end and have passed away,
no spatial or temporal contiguity is possible between the moments designated as cause and effect, because they lack a common location and a common time.

For in their view, the place and time of that which is considered the cause are one thing, and those of that which is considered the effect are another; this is because both space and time are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Furthermore, they do not accept space or time as real entities (*vastubhūta*), since space is merely an aperture (*chidra*) and the designation "time" is applicable only to the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth (p.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that neither perception nor any other [cognition] has as its object, in reality, something past or otherwise distinct? That which is said to be so is merely by way of conventional usage. Anticipating this, he says: "If, however," and so forth. The connection of the words is as follows: if perception, in some way—whether by way of conventional usage or by another method—knows or takes as its object a past thing, then why would memory not exist [with respect to] that past thing? The opponent replies: "Directly," and so forth.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: because it is direct (*sākṣāt*), that is, immediate (*avyavadhānena*); because it does not arise from that [object], since there is no arising from a past object; and because memory lacks that nature, and because similarity with a past object is impossible, "it" (memory) "would not cognize that" (the past object).
To this, the reply begins with "iti ādi" (and so forth).
Thus, "shamelessness" (*vaiyātyam*) refers to the state (*bhāvaḥ*) of one who is shameless (*viyātaḥ*), meaning one who is wickedly clever (*durvidagdhaḥ*), belonging to the opponent.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of the manifestation of the form of that [object] which is remote," and so forth.

An object that is remote—that is, separated—by means of direct experience; from that [experience], there is the production of memory through a causal series. Even in that [memory], because one observes the imitation of the form of that remote object, he provides an illustration here:
"In the case of a perceived object," and so forth.
Whatever object is seen in the waking state is [considered] "seen"; its dream is just like that in that very same place— thus it is from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ).
The Buddhist Smṛti and its commentary (Tatsavi)— Vaṅgīya edition.

The Buddhist might hold the view that perception and memory do not have the same object because they possess different appearances, like the cognitions of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; to this, he says: "In perception," and so on.

Because the word *pratyakṣa* (perception) is more venerable, it is placed first in the compound *pratyakṣasmṛtyoḥ*. As for the opponent’s claim that there is no identity of object between perception and memory because of the difference in their appearances—that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it falls within the scope of an inconclusive reason. This very point is established through the example of "distant" and "near," and so forth: those two [cognitions] are perceptions of the same object, even though one is distant and the other is near.
Of what nature are they? Even though their appearances are distinct, they have the same object as their domain because they have the same distant or near object as their domain.
[Objection: Is it not the case that for those whose senses are at a distance, the cognition of the object is not perception, but rather non-perception?
Why? Because there is an error; one perceives indistinctly and yet attains something distinct—thus says the opponent.
To this, he states the following reply, beginning with "pramāṇe" (as a means of valid cognition):

that cognition would be a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and inference, because, due to its lack of clarity and its not being produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*), it is not included within the two [accepted] means of valid cognition.

If it is objected: "But surely, because it is non-concordant (*visaṃvāda*), it is not a means of valid cognition at all; so how can it be distinct from them?"—to this he says: "nahi" (for not), and so forth.

Indeed, it is not the case that when one acts after having determined an object such as a tree by means of that cognition of a distant object, there is an absolute lack of correspondence; for even if there is a lack of correspondence due to its indistinct form, there is no such lack [of correspondence] with respect to the form of the tree and so forth. Therefore, that cognition of a distant object is not invalid in an absolute sense, from which the Buddhist's [proposed] attainment would follow. (Śrā.)
The Buddhist [maintains that] the cognition of objects at a distance is characterized by perception and inference.
He states the summary of the subject at hand— that there is another means of valid cognition— because of the absence of contradiction, beginning with the words "That," and so forth.

Since, in the manner described, it is established that memory—just like direct perception—has a real entity as its object, therefore this Buddhist practitioner, having integrated and recognized through memory acting as the instrument those two—the word and the object—which were previously apprehended by perception, at the time of the convention thinks: "An object of this kind is denotable by a word of this kind"; and subsequently, at the time of linguistic usage, when there is the comprehension of the word, he correctly understands—that is, takes as his object—the meaning by integrating it through memory.
This [phrase] "by integrating through memory" should also be connected here.

[Objection: But since memory and the like have non-existent things as their objects, the convention and the comprehension thereof must also pertain to non-existent things. To this he says: "Memory," etc.;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), inference (tarka) and so forth are included. This is because not only perception, but these as well, have ultimate reality (paramārtha) as their object.
[Objection: If words have ultimate reality as their object, then in the absence of such a thing, there could be no cognition of it through those words. To this he says: "That," etc.

The meaning of that word is "tadartha" (the object of that). Even in the absence of that [object], not only when it is present, there occurs the cognition of the word's meaning; for instance, the cognition of an object resulting from a word—such as "the material cause of the world-manifold," "God is the cause," or "Brahman is the cause"—is the effect of the word.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "like perception" (*pratyakṣavat*).
Just as perception occurs even in the absence of an object such as a double moon, so too does that [verbal cognition] occur.
If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says here: "Even with regard to a real entity," and so forth;
for by the word "even" (*api*), it is indicated that convention is possible even with regard to a non-real entity (*avastu*). Furthermore, [the text continues]:
*ba*.
One understands the object through verbal testimony (*śabda*);
[this occurs] even in the absence of an object, such as when there is verbal cognition regarding an object existing in past, future, or other times.
—Thus he said. Ba says:
"That too—from what [source]?
Śrī says: "Even the cognition of sound."
Now, one might object: "If that cognition were to occur even in the absence of an object, then all verbal cognition would be invalid.
To this objection—formulated as the formal argument: "The cognition of the word-meaning under dispute is invalid because it is a [verbal] cognition, like the cognition in question"—the author says:
"Verbal cognition..."
— The cognition [in question] is not [a valid means of knowledge], because it is a cognition based on words, like the cognition of that [same object] under discussion. (Ba)

The cognition of the meaning of the word "akṣa" is equal [to the cognition of the word "hare's horn"] because it is non-discrepant, like the cognition produced by words such as "hare's horn," etc.; [this is stated] from the perspective of the word (*śabda*), not from the perspective of the sense faculty (*akṣa*).

What is equal and of the same measure? It is the cognition of the object produced by the sense organ (*akṣa*) and the word (*śabda*). The sense organ is the faculty; the word consists of phonemes, words, and sentences, which are sounds. From these two arises the specific cognition or apprehension of the object—which is a reality consisting of both the universal and the particular—free from doubt and other such defects. Why? Because it is non-contradictory, as it does not deviate from purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Just as knowledge of an object produced by the senses is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory, so too is that produced by words.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that sensory knowledge is a *pramāṇa* because of its clarity, whereas verbal knowledge is not, due to its lack of clarity? Anticipating this, he says: "Though unclear.
Even though the knowledge produced by words is unclear and indistinct, it must be accepted as a *pramāṇa* for the very same reason: non-contradiction.
For clarity or lack of clarity is not the basis for validity or its opposite, because those two are based on correspondence or its opposite;
like what? Like inference—*Laghīyatrayatātparya-vṛtti*, p. 66:
"An indistinct verbal cognition is a valid means of knowledge, like inference. (46)

Commentary: Even though there is deviation from the definitions such as "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) or "similarity to that" (*sārūpya*), verbal cognition of an object is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is related to that [object] by way of determining its nature, just like direct perception; for verbal cognition itself is non-contradictory. Unlike inference, which lacks a fixed rule of relation, speech conveys the reality of the object independently of the speaker's intention.

For even a relationship characterized by the signified and the signifier is observed to be a cause for the cognition of external objects—[the syllables] ṇaṃ vya— (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā-vimarśinī, Viṣamapadoddyota); compare: "If similarity to that [object] and origination from that [object] are the defining characteristics of what is cognized..."
If it were to have the same object, then the subsequent cognition would be immediate [to the preceding one]—
*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.323.
Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 240; Pramāṇanayatatvāloka, 4.47.
"That is so," [as stated in] Ja and Vi;
the meaning of the verse is: the sense organs and the sounds, and the cognition of their objects, are simultaneous.

To the question "By what [is it so]?", he says: "Because of non-contradiction" (*avisaṃvādataḥ*). Just as sensory cognition (*akṣajñāna*) is non-contradictory, so too is the cognition of the meaning of words.

This is the intended meaning: just as it cannot be asserted that all sensory cognitions are invalid simply because some sensory cognition is seen to be contradictory—just like the cognition of two moons (*dvicandra-jñāna*), for instance)—on account of its nature, so too it must be with the cognition of the meaning of words.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the distinction between this and perception (*pratyakṣa*)?", he says here: the cognition of words is indistinct and unclear, whereas sensory cognition is distinct; this is the distinction between the two.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the proof for that [scriptural knowledge]? the author replies here: "The proof is the cognition of the word, just like inference;
here too, it should be connected with the phrase 'because of non-contradiction'.
This is the explanation of the commentary.

Now, one might object: "Since sensory cognition possesses both the arising from the object and its similarity to it (sārūpya), its non-contradictoriness is logical; however, this is not the case for verbal cognition because the opposite is true. Therefore, the statement beginning with 'akṣa' (sensory) is incorrect. Anticipating this objection as a critique, he explains the verse, beginning with "tadutpatti" (arising from that): [The author] says: "Arising from that... and so forth.

Therefore, that which has its origin from the object and its similarity [to it], etc., is what is called "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*). That alone is the definition of validity (*prāmāṇya*) or non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*), because even when there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from those [three], there is still the production of that [ascertainment] by means of the eye and so forth; of similarity, by means of a subsequent cognition having the same object; and of that ascertainment, by means of the perception of water in a mirage, which is the cause for the ascertainment of water therein. [And] by means of a subsequent yellow-cognition produced from the cognition of yellow in a white conch-shell. He says "yadartha... etc., to address the question: "What happens when there is not merely non-deviation?"
Because of the employment of two instances of the word *tat* later on, a second instance of the word *yat* should be understood here as well;

from this, the following meaning arises: that cognition which has the characteristic of determining a particular object—that is, whose nature consists in the apprehension of that object—is [the means] of that object.

This is what is meant: in that regard, by whatever proximity—despite the lack of distinction among sentient beings—only a certain thing is the cause for a certain other, and not everything for everything; and despite the lack of distinction in their causality, a certain thing assimilates a certain form [into itself], and despite the lack of distinction in that [assimilation], it determines a certain [object]; thus, even though it lacks that production and so forth, it possesses the determination of that [object].

In this way, even if there is deviation [between the cognition and the object], because of the relationship between the cognition and its object, verbal cognition also possesses validity—not only other [cognitions]—by virtue of its own non-contradiction, just like direct perception (*pratyakṣavat*).

"Granted that this may be a valid means of knowledge, but only with respect to the speaker's intention (vivakṣā). To this he says: "The speaker's intention," and so forth. Does it cause one to understand—that is, to cognize—any external reality or the nature of the object apart from the speaker's intention? He asks: "What is that? and answers: "The cognition of the meaning of speech," which is the cognition of the object that has arisen as the effect of the words.
What is it like? He says: "Like inference.
Just as inference makes known an object distinct from the speaker's intention, so too does the knowledge of word and meaning;
why is this so? He says: "Because of the absence of a fixed relation."
This is because the restriction—that the relation [of a word] exists only with the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) and not with an external object—is impossible;
or else, because the restriction regarding relations—that a relation consists only of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) and nothing else—is absent.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "The denotable," and so forth.
Not only [is this true] of other things, but even of the relationship characterized as signifier and signified, for it is observed to be the cause for the comprehension of external objects.

This is the intended meaning: another relationship also is said to exist only when it is observed to produce that comprehension, and not otherwise, because [otherwise] there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Likewise, let existence belong to the subject under discussion as well, provided it is observed.
And its existence has been established in detail at Laghīyastraya-kārikā 26, where it says, "The means of valid cognition is heard regarding objects. Therefore, enough with further digression.
The reading between "purassarā kā–ba" and "purassara kā–ā" does not exist in manuscript Ā.
From the eye and other [senses], the cognition of a jar arises, yet that [cognition] does not become a grasper of the eye and other [senses].

Regarding an identical object, such as a sesame seed, the second cognition of the sesame seed that arises immediately after the first cognition possesses a similarity (*sārūpya*) with that first cognition of the sesame seed; yet, the second cognition does not apprehend the first, for according to their established doctrine, one cognition is not the regulator of another cognition.
Furthermore, the arising of a favorable conceptual construction (*anukūla-vikalpa*) constitutes "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*);

the perception of water occurring in a circle of sunbeams (*marīci-cakra*) produces a conceptual construction in the form "this is water," which is favorable [to the object], yet that [perception] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The reading contained within this [manuscript] does not exist in Ā [the manuscript]. [For otherwise],

there would be the undesirable consequence that validity would apply to the preceding cognition— namely, the yellow-cognition arising immediately after a yellow-cognition produced by the white conch— which, due to the triad of [its] arising from that, its similarity to that, and the determination of that, conforms to the form of that [conch] and produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the form "this is a conch corresponding to that."
And this is not the case, because it would entail the collapse of the rule that one cognition does not determine another cognition;
for where there is [the qualification of] existence... [fragmentary].
Regarding the phrase "even though there is no distinction in the imitation of the letter 'a'," Ba and Śrā state that this is because such [imitation] is impossible.
— because it is not the cause of that [cognition]— ā॰; — the state of being its cause through origination from that [object], etc.— ba॰, śra॰.
Of the relationship between the signified and the signifier—
[the reading] "exists" (astīti) is found in the Śrā [manuscript];
[it refers to] the state of being signified and signifier.

Now, since time and the other [factors] do not exist because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to apprehend them, and even if they did exist, they would be non-different from one another;
if their difference were due to a difference in time, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā);
and if their difference were due to a difference in objects, there would be mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
Having raised the objection that what was said— namely, that time is the agent (*kāraka*) and so forth— is incorrect, he says in response:
"Because there is no difference [in time itself],

once a distinction such as 'past' and so on has been established among objects, it is therefore the time that possesses the status of being past and so forth, and from that [status of time] the objects themselves possess the status of being past and so forth."
The definition of time and so forth should be examined in detail elsewhere as it has been scrutinized;

what is to be examined—that is, to be observed—is the definition of time and so forth? Time and so forth refers to those things beginning with time, such as grammatical relations (*kāraka*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), means (*sādhana*), and voice (*upagraha*); their definition is their unique essential nature (*asādhāraṇa-svarūpa*).
How is it distinguished? It has been examined and investigated in detail (*nyakṣeṇa*) by masters such as Svāmī Samantabhadra and others.
Where? In other works, such as the *Tattvārthamahābhāṣya* and so forth.

What is its qualification? It is that whose nature (*ātman*) consists of substance, modes, generality, and particularity—namely, *dravya* (substance), which is the vertical generality (*ūrdhvatā-sāmānya*) pervading prior and subsequent transformations; *paryāya* (modes), which are the successive transformations occurring within a single substance; *sāmānya* (generality), which is the horizontal generality (*tiryak-sāmānya*) characterized by similar transformations; and *viśeṣa* (particularity), which is the differentiation existing in distinct entities. That which is established, fixed, and essentially identical with that object (*artha*) consisting of substance, modes, generality, and particularity is what is meant.

For it is only in such a case that causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is possible, since that [efficiency] is contradicted by the extreme of independence; [thus, reality] is established as an object consisting of substance, mode, universal, and particular. (47) [Laghiyastraya-tātparya-vṛtti, p. 67]

—The commentary of Jayanta Bhaṭṭa: A single, absolute characteristic of existence cannot belong to time, because from such [an absolute nature] the distinctions of past, future, and present could not arise, since purposeful action (arthakriyā) would be impossible.

Nor can the definition of an agent (*kāraka*) be "substance," "power" (*śakti*), or "both"; for if there were an absolute difference between power and the possessor of power, no relationship could be established, which would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
If there is an absolute non-difference between them, the verbal formulation "the power" and "the possessor of power" is empty;
therefore, the sixfold set of factors (ṣaṭkārakī) does not hold under such an absolute [non-difference].

Furthermore, how could there be a fixed gender for any one among the word, the object, or the cognition—such as: "she is called *strī* (female) because the embryo *styāyati* (coagulates) within her; he is called *pumān* (male) because he *prasūte* (begets) his own offspring; and it is *napuṃsaka* (neuter) when both are absent"? Likewise, for a single object, Indra is so called because of his *indana* (sovereignty), Śakra because of his *śakana* (power), and Purandara because he *purandārayati* (shatters cities). Thus, a difference in meaning for the words denoting them due to a difference in synonyms is simply impossible, because of the contradiction between absolute identity and absolute difference (*vyatireka*).
For that very reason, the impossibility of [distinct] action and agent in that regard should be understood.

The proof of its non-absolutism [is established] because it expresses its objects through both affirmation and negation; thus, there is no absolutism of non-existence. Why? Because the objection regarding the impossibility of its expression, logical marks, and so forth, would follow the doctrine of *syādvāda*. As it is said: "Time is characterized by succession" (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28).
The revolution of time— *Pravacanasāra* 2.42.
Time (kāla) is that which is devoid of color, taste, smell, and touch; it is neither heavy nor light, is immaterial, and is characterized by persistence (vartanā).
— Pañcāstikāya-gāthā 24.

Substance (dravya), according to Gāthā 21; and duration (vartanā), transformation (pariṇāma), activity (kriyā), priority (paratva), and posteriority (aparatva) belong to time (kāla) — Tattvārthasūtra 5.20.

22. Bhartṛhari and others are proponents of the theory that the causal factor is power (*śakti*); for they maintain: "That which possesses the capacity to bring about the accomplishment of actions—whether inherent in its own substrate or likewise in another substrate—is known as the means (*sādhana*)."

"When the activity has ceased, the capacity of the substance is established as the instrument; 'by this, the action is accomplished'— thus the authors of the Bhāṣya and others maintain," as stated in the *Vākyapadīya*, Tṛtīyakāṇḍa, verse 173 (Iśvaravimarśinī).

Comparison: "Neither is the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) merely a substance, nor is it merely an action; for the word *kāraka* applies to that which accomplishes an action and is connected with a specific action" (*Nyāyavārttika*, p.

6). "In this context, the *kāraka* is that which is the meaning of a nominal suffix (*subartha*) and serves as a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)" (*Śabdakaustubha*, Kārikā 67).
According to their own established doctrine, Śakti and Śaktimān are to be understood as the *styāna* (the state of being dissolved) and the *prasava* (the act of procreation), respectively.
In common usage, the female is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) and the instrument (*sādhana*), for it is said that "the womb is dissolved within her."
And the person (puruṣa) is both an agent and an instrument;

[the term] "person" is used as feminine when there is no intention to express procreation, as masculine when there is an intention to express procreation, and as neuter when there is an intention to express both— Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 4.1.3.
1.3 In the absence of both of those, one is a *napuṃsaka* (neuter). *vi.* [Commentary]
—*Kāntaraya’s Jaṭāpāṭha-vivaraṇa on the Kārikā*:

That of which time (*kāla*) is the first [factor], such as the *kārakas* and so forth, is described as "that" (*tathokta*). Its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), which is its essential nature (*svarūpa*) or its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has been examined (*parīkṣita*) and investigated (*vicārita*) elsewhere, such as in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* and other works. It is to be scrutinized (*īkṣya*) and sought after (*anveṣya*) by oneself (*ātmanā*) in its entirety (*nyakṣeṇa*). This is because of the etymological derivation: *nyakṣa* is that which has been previously determined (*niścita*) and established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, *nyakṣa* refers to the senses (*akṣa*) that have been fixed.
Regarding the phrase "in detail and extensively," he asks: "In what manner is that object to be perceived by it? He replies with the words "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth.

Substance is the generality of verticality (*ūrdhvatā-sāmānya*). Its manifestations (*vivarta*), which occur both simultaneously and successively, are the modes (*paryāya*). Similar transformation is generality; dissimilar transformation is particularity (*viśeṣa*). That object whose very nature consists of these [generality and particularity] is "established therein"—that is to say, it is of that nature.
Therefore, this [objection] is refuted: since time and the other factors are themselves non-different, how could a difference in them produce a difference in objects?

This is because, like the causal conditions (*sahakārin*), the material cause (*upādāna*), and the continuum (*saṃtāna*), there is no contradiction in the mutual transformation and manifestation of time and the others.

Furthermore, if it is held that the transformation of one object depends on time, while the transformation of time itself depends on its own nature—just as the illumination of a jar or similar object is dependent on a lamp, whereas the illumination of the lamp is dependent on itself—then there is no possibility of infinite regress or mutual dependence.

Alternatively, the meaning is that "niṣṭhita" refers to that which has its own nature established by means of that [prior] object serving as a mark (liṅga); thus, "tanniṣṭhitam" means characterized by that, i.e., having that as its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For instance, the cognition—"this object exists prior to, after, or together with this"—is preceded by an object distinct from the objects themselves, because it is a cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth, just like the cognition: "this object is in a location prior to this," "this is a subsequent location," and so on.
And that which is the cause of such [cognition] is time.
The same should be applied to the agent (*kāraka*) and so forth; for instance:
the cognition "he does" (*karoti*) or "it is done" (*kriyate*) is based on objects possessing distinct potencies, because it is a distinct cognition, like the cognition of water and fire.
Likewise, the cognition "Devadatta" or "Devadattā" is based on objects of distinct natures, because it is a specific cognition, like the cognition of a jar and a cloth.
It is to be examined;
thus it is born as a stream.
*ārya*, *ba* (manuscript variants).

The word "bhavati" (it exists) is preceded by an object distinct from the meanings of its own diverse constituent parts; it is the cause of the cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth—[this is] the effect. (Nyāyāvatāra)
The commentary (*vivṛti*) provides an explanation by way of negation (*vyatirekamukhena*): "For [it is] not absolute," and so forth.

For this reason (*hi*), in the case of an absolute [view] such as momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikānta*), there can be no functioning (*varttanā*) of time itself through its modes (*paryāya*) which have the three times as their domain, with respect to entities that exist [in those times]. Since [this] characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) would be the cause of the distinction between past, future, and present time, it cannot be possible. Thus, the differentiation of time and so forth into past, future, and present would not occur.

The word "yataḥ" (since) is used either as a challenge (*ākṣepa*) or to indicate that from which its distinction would arise; [the author] says "it could not exist at all," asking "why is this so?"— [he replies] with "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*), etc.,
connecting it to "in the case of an absolute [position]" (*ekānte*), because the production or accomplishment of the action of an entity and so forth is untenable.

And just as the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) of time in its isolated state—such as [its being] past and so forth—is untenable, this has been specifically examined during the investigation of time (*kālaparīkṣā*).
Thus, it is said: "Indeed, the activity of all entities is not a functioning that depends upon time."
"Vartanā means origination, subsistence, and movement; it refers to that which is based on the first moment"— this is the meaning of Tattvārthabhāṣya 5.22.

From the root *vṛt* with the causative suffix (*ṇij*), the feminine noun *vartanā* is derived either in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the abstract state (*bhāva*) by means of the suffix *yuṭ*. Thus, *vartanā* signifies either the act of turning or the mere process of existing.

Since substances such as *dharma* and the rest exist by their own nature alone with respect to their own modifications (*paryāya*), and since they lack such activity in the absence of external assistance, time is defined as that which is characterized by the impelling of those substances. Therefore, *vartanā* is the service rendered to time.
–Sarvārthasiddhi 5.22:
Vartanā is the experience of its own existence, wherein each substance and each modification internally contains a single moment of time.
— Rājavārttika 5.22, page 225.

Having thus refuted the causal efficacy (*prayojakatva*) of time with respect to present entities by means of its one-sided definition, he states the following—beginning with "And not..."—in order to refute that [causal efficacy] in the case of the agent (*kāraka*):
"And not even the definition of an agent.
