To the question "What is that?", he says: "Substance, power, or both of these. This [definition] must also be connected here [to the previous argument], because the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is untenable in those cases through a one-sided [definition].
He states another objection: "In the case of power," and so forth.

If an absolute distinction between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is admitted, the relationship between them cannot be established, just as [there is no relationship] between the Sahya and Vindhya mountains.

If, on the other hand, even in that case of absolute distinction, the establishment of a relationship is desired on the basis of a mutual beneficiary-benefactor relationship (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*), like that of a king and his servant, he says in response: "Because it would entail an infinite regress (*anavasthānuṣaṅgāt*)."

The intention here is as follows: if, just as there is a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between a king and his servant, such a relationship were to exist between power (*śakti*) and its possessor (*śaktimat*), then another power would have to be postulated for each of those two, and the same objection would apply to that as well, resulting in an infinite regress. By this, the inherence (*samavāya*), the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇībhāva*), or any other distinct relation between these two has been considered.
Refuting the absolute non-difference (*abhedaikānta*) of those two, he says: "In the case of the absolute non-difference [of power from its possessor]," and so forth.

If an absolute non-distinction—that is, an absolute identity—is accepted between these two, namely the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), then that verbal formulation of yours, "power" and "possessor of power," becomes empty and meaningless.

For if that were the case, there would be only power; yet it is not logical for your opponent to maintain that [power] is without a substratum, as this would entail the futility of postulating substances and so forth.
Alternatively, there would be only the possessor of power; but even that is untenable in the absence of power.

Nor should it be asserted that power (*śakti*) is nothing other than substance (*dravya*) and so forth, because in the *Śaktiparīkṣā*, it has been established that power is distinct from those [categories], having refuted their definitions. Furthermore, [this is supported by] Śrī... and Śrī... [and] Śrī... [the author of the *Śaktiparīkṣā*].
If it is established that [the cause] exists, then the establishment [of the effect] is desired; thus, there is the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary (upakāryopakārakabhāva).
The Mīmāṃsakas and others [assert] that power and the possessor of power [are distinct].
Even that which possesses power [is] powerless.
Concluding the discussion on substance (*dravya*) and so forth, he says: "That," etc.

Since the relationship between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is not tenable in the absolute positions of either difference or non-difference, therefore the aggregate of the six factors of action—the collection of the six *kārakas* beginning with the agent—cannot be established in an absolute [monistic] position; for the intention is that in the absence of the *kārakas*, their aggregate cannot exist.
Likewise, he states another point that has been reached, beginning with "From where?"— the phrase "not from anything else" is intended to indicate yet another refutation.

Regarding the "establishment of gender"—the stability of genders such as femininity and so forth—whose is this not? To this he says: "Of any one [of them]. Of which ones? He says: "Of word, object, and cognition."

Since the grammarians accept the determination of gender for those very three [categories] according to possibility, one might ask: "If there is no fixed rule for the *kārakas*, what does that have to do with the lack of a fixed rule for gender, such that the latter would also not exist? To this he says: "It thickens," and so forth.
It is called *strī* (female) because the embryo *styāyati*—that is, it becomes aggregated (*saṅghātībhavati*) within it.
One is a male (*pumān*) because he produces his own offspring (*svān ātmīyān paryāyān*);
when both [of those] are absent—that is, in the absence of both the state of being solidified (*styāna*) and the state of procreation (*prasavana*)—one is a neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
From what, then, does such a definition arise? It is thought that since the determination of gender is dependent upon causal factors (*kāraka*), it cannot exist in their absence.
In this very same context, in a certain secluded place, he states another objection beginning with the words "tathā" (in that way):

"In that manner," meaning by that mode of the absence of causal factors (*kāraka*), for a single, non-different entity characterized as the Lord of the Gods (*surapati*)—such as [the designation] "Indra" because of ruling (*indanāt*), "Śakra" because of being powerful (*śakanāt*), or "Purandara" because of shattering cities (*purandārayati*)—there is a distinction of synonyms (*paryāya-bheda*) due to the distinction in transformations such as ruling (*indana*), or else, due to the distinction of synonymous terms such as "Indra" and so forth; and having relied upon that distinction, that [nature] which has been accepted by the opponent...
What is it? He says: "the state of having different meanings," that is, the state of having manifold meanings.
Of what things? He says: "of those words expressing them"—that is, of words denoting a single object such as Indra and so forth.
What is that [state]? He says: "it is simply not possible"; the meaning of the particle *eva* is that there is not even the slightest possibility of its occurrence.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because of the distinction," and so forth.

Between that single entity characterized as the Lord of the Gods (Indra) and [the action] such as "shaking" (*śakana*), there is an absolute distinction (*vyatirekaikānta*), meaning an absolute difference; and between these two, there is also an "other absolute," meaning an absolute non-difference (*abhedaikānta*). There is a contradiction regarding those two absolutes because, in the case of an absolute distinction, a relationship cannot be established and an infinite regress would follow; thus, contradiction is proven in the case of absolute distinction.
[Opponent: "But surely that [agent] is established because the oneness of Indra and so forth is established in isolation.

For neither substance (*dravya*), nor power (*śakti*), nor both together constitutes the definition of a *kāraka*; rather, a *kāraka* is a substance permeated by action (*kriyā*). To this, he says: 'Precisely for that reason,' and so forth.

Precisely for that reason—namely, from the contradiction just mentioned—the impossibility of action and *kāraka* must be understood therein: action being characterized by placing [fuel on the fire] and so forth, and the *kāraka* being the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. This impossibility applies to that false monism (*mithyaikānta*)."
The six powers of others are eternal, endowed with both difference and non-difference,
and reside inherent in objects for the sake of accomplishing actions, like a genus [in individuals]—
Vākyapadīya, Sādhanasamuddeśa, verse 35.

The reading contained within these brackets does not exist in the Ā [manuscript]. For comparison: it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "the marks [of gender] are to be understood as contraction and procreation. Thus, the mark has been explained, and so he says: "In contraction, from the root *styai* comes *strī* (female) with the suffix *ṅīṣ*; in procreation, from the root *sū*, comes *pumān* (male).
Contraction (*styāna*) is the gathering together; procreation (*prasava*) is the accumulation of form and other qualities, such as the *sattva* and other *guṇas*.
She in whom the embryo coagulates (*styāyati*) and attains consolidation (*sahananam āpadyate*) is called *strī* (female), based on the locative sense of the verbal root *sū* (to bring forth).

When the suffix *ḍumsun* is applied to this root in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*)—meaning "procreation" or "growth"—and the letter *s* is replaced by *p*, the form *pumān* (male) is derived.
As it has been said: "In the word *sa-bi-ti*, there is the replacement of the letter *s* by *p*. This is the meaning.
And by this manner, he indicates that the function [of the neuter] occurs in the sense of a substance (*dravya*);
the state consisting of the equality of both genders is, by implication, stated to be the neuter—Vākyapadīya, Liṅgasamuddeśa, p. 436.

Depending on the causes or their distinction, it is asked: for whom does [the state] of having gone [to them] exist? It is said: for whom does the state of having different meanings exist? For whom? For the Vaibhāṣikas.
He says that there is not even the slightest possibility of [their] mutual contact.

Established by contradiction (virodhasiddhaḥ) Ā; establishment of contradiction (virodhasiddhiḥ) Śrā; because [contradiction] is established in the extreme of non-difference (abhedaikānte)—established Śrā.
It is well known that a substance qualified by action is a *kāraka* (grammatical factor) when it is engaged in an action.
— *Yuktyanuṣaṅga-ṭīkā*, p. 28— [Regarding] "hearing"— in the *Bāhyārthasiddhi*, he states the conclusion beginning with "that" (*tat*), etc.

Since the characteristic of being the agent of death is not tenable in an absolute sense (ekānta), therefore the establishment of non-absolutism (anekānta) follows, because it is only there that this [characteristic] is tenable. By what two means is its establishment? He says: by affirmation and negation—that is, by existence and non-existence in relation to the fourfold aspects of self-nature, other-nature, and so forth. And this has been demonstrated on the occasion of establishing non-absolutism; enough of this digression.

If it is argued that, since a word-meaning distinct from the manifold (anekānta) is impossible, there would be an impossibility of logical marks (*liṅga*) and so forth in all cases, the author replies with the words beginning "that" (*tad*): because that object, which possesses a manifold nature, is denoted— that is, presented—
here too, the connection should be made with the phrase "by means of affirmation and negation" (*vidhipratiṣedhābhyām*).

Why? Because there is no ground for the objection that its expression, its indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth are impossible; for "its expression" refers to the statement that communicates that non-absolutist object, and by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of [its] indicative mark and other such factors is intended. The impossibility of these constitutes the objection. Why would this not apply? It applies to one who follows *syādvāda*, the doctrine of non-absolutism.

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Since entities do not exist in any way whatsoever, the expression of their meaning is unestablished. To this, he says: "There is no absolute non-existence, nor an absolute void."
And how that [agent] does not exist has been examined in detail in the section on the determination of objects (*viṣayapariccheda*),
in the *Ekāntakāraka* [chapter],
page 366.
—The word *rikta*—ā॰;
its *ākānta*—ā॰;
there too—ā॰.
The attainment of injunctions and prohibitions is manifold— Śrauta, p.
And since there is no such censure against the non-absolute (anekānta), therefore— there is no such [censure] against the absolute (ekānta).
Therefore, it does not exist.

Since a single entity encounters multiple causal complexes (sāmagrī), which [of these] could be conceived or function at every moment? "The hexad of factors" (ṣaṭkārakī) refers to the collection of the six factors (kāraka).
Of what? Of even a single entity such as a soul (*jīva*), by supplying the word "even" (*api*) from the context.
How? At every moment; a *kṣaṇa* is a unit of time, and "at every moment" means at each successive instant.

Why? Because of the convergence of multiple causal complexes (*aneka-sāmagrī-sannipātāt*); "multiple" (*aneka*) refers to the collection of external and internal causes, and "convergence" (*sannipāta*) is their coming together or presence. Therefore.

For instance: at the very moment Devadatta is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the jar due to the proximity of the wheel and other tools, he is simultaneously the object (*karman*) because of the proximity of the onlookers; he is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the sense of "causing Devadatta to act" with respect to the purpose; he is the recipient (*sampradāna*) in the sense of "giving to Devadatta" with respect to the gift, the action, and the substance; he is the point of departure (*apādāna*) in the sense of "departing from Devadatta" with respect to the separation; and he is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the sense of "the earring is in Devadatta" with respect to the substance situated therein. Since there is no contradiction in such a cognition, there is indeed no contradiction in what is being perceived.

Likewise, just as [the six factors] are simultaneously [imputed], so too would there be a sequence—a distinction of time, place, and form—due to the difference in time and so forth; by that sequence as well, the sixfold set of factors (*ṣaṭkārakī*) would be conceptualized, for it is brought about by the force of such cognition as "Devadatta did," "he does," and "he will do. Or else, just as the sixfold set of factors is conceptualized for a single [agent], so too would time and the rest be conceptualized.

Why? Because of differentiation; for there is some degree of differentiation in the object, since if it were entirely non-different, the distinction between all the various factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth would be untenable—*Laghīyastrayāvatāra*, p. 68.

In the same way, a set of six factors (*ṣaṭkārakī*) might be postulated based on the distinctions of time and so forth. [The commentary] explains: although a set of six factors may arise because various causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) converge at every moment and for every object, just as a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) remains one because its own-nature and effects do not differentiate it, so too it remains one despite the distinctions of time and other factors.

The rejection of that [other aspect] is a fallacious method (*durnaya*); a method (*naya*) is that which is dependent upon it. Even when its own object is predominant, it is subordinate to that [other aspect]; therefore, knowledge whose object consists of both is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as stated in the *Jainaviśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*.

Comparison: Thus, these standpoints—the verbal (*śabda*), the conventional (*samabhirūḍha*), and the etymological (*evaṃbhūta*)—are correct when they are mutually dependent; however, it should be understood that they are false when they do not depend upon one another. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
680) The absolute plurality of words alone, without a corresponding difference in meaning, is a fallacy (*tadābhāsa*).
— Prameyaratnāvalī 6.7.4
In this way, those who maintain that objects are in every respect non-different from sound and so forth are proponents of fallacious viewpoints (durnaya)—
as stated in the *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 90—
and one who maintains that very same [non-difference] by means of their difference is a pseudo-proponent of such a viewpoint (tadābhāsa).

"Just as the words 'Sumeru existed,' 'exists,' and 'will exist'— which belong to different times— denote distinct objects because they are words belonging to different times, like other established words of that kind," etc.—
*Pramāṇanaya* 7.34, 35.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 24:
"The statement of distinctions such as Indra and so forth, even in the absence of a plurality of modes (paryāya), is a fallacy thereof" — Prameyaratnākara, v. 6.

One who maintains that synonymous terms possess only different denotata—that which appears as such [is the fallacy]—argues, for example, that words such as *indra*, *śakra*, and *purandara* have indeed distinct denotata because they are distinct words, just like the words *karin*, *kuraṅga*, and *turaṅgama*. And so forth.
—Pramāṇanaya [tattvāloka] 7.38, 39; Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 24.
Because it is independent of action, the conventional usage among words expressive of action is merely conceptual; it is a semblance [of reality]. — *Prameyaratnāvalī* 6.74.
An "appearance" (*tadābhāsa*) is that which rejects an object not currently engaged in an activity by way of its being denotable by a word;

for example: "The object called 'pot,' when devoid of specific activity, is not denotable by the word 'pot,' because it lacks the activity that constitutes the ground for the application of the word 'pot,' just like a cloth," and so forth.
— *Pramāṇanaya* 7.1.12.
In the *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, pages 42–43: "Knowledge regarding the object" (*arthe jñānam*). Ja. Vi. (Jayasimhasūri’s commentary).
Commentary on the Verse:

Regarding "of a single entity," the word *api* (even/also) is to be understood here; therefore, he asks, "What [nature] could be postulated even for that which is manifold? and answers: "the sixfold set of factors" (*ṣaṭkārakī*).

Why is this so? He says: "Because of the convergence of multiple causal complexes. Multiple means various; a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the totality of causes that produce a manifold effect. Because of the convergence (*sannipāta*) of such a complex, how is it conceptualized? He says: "Moment by moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*); that is, it is conceptualized in such a way as it occurs at every single instant.

For instance: at the very moment Devadatta is the agent (*kartṛ*) because of his performing the making of a jar through the proximity of the wheel and other tools, he is simultaneously the object (*karman*) due to the proximity of the perceptual conditions such as place; he is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to other objects; he is the recipient (*sampradāna*) in relation to the goods being given to him; he is the point of departure (*apādāna*) in relation to the things being drawn away from him; and he is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in relation to the purpose for which he is stationed there.

"In that way," meaning by such a manner, "due to the distinction of time and so forth"—that is, due to the distinction of time and other factors such as place—the construction of the sixfold set of kārakas (the six grammatical relations) would be possible for a single entity; this is the connection [of the sentence].
For example: "Devadatta, whose nature is that of an agent (*kartṛ*) and so on, existed, exists, or will exist.
In the same way, it should be applied to other cases as well.
It would be conceived;
it would be conceived;
at every moment, moment by moment.
In every moment there is no [self];
it would be conceptually constructed by way of dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*).
Because of its non-difference from that,
it would be conceptualized— [this is the] commentary on the *vivṛti*.
Demonstrating the meaning of the verse, he shows here the distinction between right method (*sunaya*) and wrong method (*durnaya*) with the words beginning "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*).

"At every moment" means at each and every moment; "with respect to each object" (*pratyartham*) means with respect to each individual object. Although the sixfold set of factors (*ṣaṭkārakī*) is possible due to the convergence of various causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), its rejection—that is, the denial of that sixfold set—is a wrong method (*durnaya*). To the question, "How is its possibility [established]? he replies: "Just as a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)," meaning that just as a single unique particular is established, so too is its possibility [established]. Thus, even though it exists in that manner, [its denial is a wrong method].

[Objection: "If it were possible for a single *svalakṣaṇa* to have multiple intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and multiple effects, then that possibility might exist elsewhere as well; yet it does not exist, because if such [multiplicity] were possible, there would necessarily be a difference [in the *svalakṣaṇa*] itself. To this, he says: "Intrinsic nature," etc.
Because differences in intrinsic nature and differences in effects do not differentiate that [single entity], i.e., they do not differentiate the *svalakṣaṇa*;
indeed, there is no difference in the *svalakṣaṇa* whether there is a difference among its effects—whether of the same or different class—or a difference in the intrinsic nature of its cause.

Thus, demonstrating that even though the sixfold set of factors (*ṣaṭkārakī*) is possible when there is a distinction of time and so forth, the denial of that [distinction] is a false doctrine (*durnaya*), he says: "In the same way," and so on.

The connection is as follows: just as when there is a distinction of causal totality (*sāmagrī*), although the sixfold set of factors is possible for a single [entity], its denial is a false doctrine; likewise, even when there is a distinction of time and so forth, although the sixfold set of factors is possible—this is the link.
Here too, the phrase "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth should be supplied.

What, then, is *naya*? To this he says: "*Tadapekṣo nayaḥ*" (naya is that which depends upon that). That is, *naya* is that which has dependence (*apekṣā*) upon those six factors of action (*ṣaṭkāraka*). Why is it called *naya*? To this he says: "*svārtha*," and so forth.

When an object being made the focus of cognition is predominant, yet because its subordinate qualities are not excluded—since those qualities remain present even though they are not intended to be expressed—if such a method [of cognition] occurs, then what kind of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it? To this he says: "That," and so forth.
That is, the cognition of an object whose nature consists of both intended and unintended qualities, wherein [the intended] is not subordinate, is valid cognition.

By this, the statement from the *Tattvārthasūtra* (1.6), "The comprehension [of reality] is by means of the instruments of knowledge and the methods of reasoning," is subsumed within the categories of sound and so forth.
Moment by moment,
in whatever way it may be, that [state] becomes supportless.
The meaning is that it is one in such a manner that it remains one and the same even when distinctions such as time and so forth are possible.
The occurrence of an effect with multiple intrinsic natures;
in the case of the occurrence of an effect with multiple intrinsic natures.
Regarding the phrase "of the object" (arthasya) and "its instrument" (tatkaraṇa)— the reading *tad* etc. is found in the Śrā [manuscript].
The refutation of the six factors; its quality—
[namely] the knowledge of the object.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that every *naya* is a mental construction (*vikalpa*), and since a construction is devoid of an object—just like constructions such as 'primordial matter' (*pradhāna*) and so forth—how could there be the comprehension of anything by means of it? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states: "Indeed, a *naya* is not [devoid of an object] because it is a construction," thereby demonstrating the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason "because it is a construction" by means of *tarka* (logical reasoning) and other arguments.
By means of the method (*naya*), one clarifies the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) by the probandum (*sādhya*); without reflection (*cintā*), there is no perception in a single place—
it neither clarifies nor manifests it.
What [is it]? It is the observation (*dṛṣṭi*)—meaning perception (*pratyakṣa*)—of the probandum and the probans in one place, such as a kitchen (*mahānasa*).
What [does it establish]? Pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Of what? Of the reason (*hetu*), that is, the probans (*sādhana*), such as smoke.
With what? With the probandum (*sādhya*), such as fire and so forth.

With what [else]? With completeness (*sākalya*). What is completeness? It is the state (*bhāva*) of all individual instances of the probandum and the probans that are separated by space and time. How [is this known]? The meaning is that without reflection (*cintā*), there would be an absence of the means of valid cognition consisting of inference (*ūha*).

For the observation of the relationship between the probandum and the probans in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is not capable of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its entirety, because that would entail the futility of inference and would imply that the observer possesses super-knowledge (*abhijñatva*). If it is asked, "Then what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) clarifies it?"—it is replied: this is *tarka* (reasoning), which clarifies the pervasion between the probandum and the probans in its entirety; and that very knowledge is what is universally recognized by all logicians as *tarka*. Now, one might object that it lacks the status of a valid means of cognition because it apprehends what has already been apprehended; anticipating this, he says: "its object is unapprehended" (*anadhigataviṣaya*).

Of what nature is it? It is characterized by right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), for it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object; likewise, recollection (*smaraṇa*) or memory is also a valid means of cognition. Of what nature is it? It is non-contradictory with respect to the object already apprehended; that is, the object is one previously experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and "non-contradictory" means being free from contradiction regarding that object.
And in what case does this constitute valid cognition? It is when there is validity—that is, when there is the status of being a means of valid cognition—of what?
Of inference, that is, of the inferential process.

Where? In a portion of the object established by that [reasoning]. The meaning is that the object established (*kṛta*)—that is, ascertained—by that reasoning is the "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*); and in a portion of that, namely the probandum (*sādhya*), there exists the validity of inference because the validity of memory and reasoning is inseparably connected to it.
Alternatively, recognition (*saṃjñāna*) and re-cognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they are indistinguishable in their non-contradiction.

Not only is this conceptual (*vikalpātmaka*) cognition a means of knowledge regarding the remote (*parokṣa*), but all perception (*pratyakṣa*) as well is a conceptual means of knowledge, since it alone is useful for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), whereas the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) is of no use anywhere.

Therefore, for this reason, just as in the case of reasoning (*tarka*) and so forth, the thorough comprehension—the correct understanding and determination of the principles of living beings (*jīva*) and other categories—occurs through the modes of knowledge (*nayadṛṣṭi*) which consist of conceptualization (*vikalpātmaka*).

Of what nature are they? They are called "sevenfold" (*saptadhākhyaiḥ*), meaning those whose designations (*ākhyā*) are of seven kinds, namely the seven types beginning with the *naigama*. — *Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra*, p. 70.

In its entirety, this reasoning has for its object that which has not yet been apprehended; and regarding the validity of inference with respect to a portion of the object established by that [reasoning], all recollection is non-contradictory with respect to an already apprehended object— [as stated in] Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Vyāpticarcā*.
And valid cognition is the thorough comprehension [of objects] and so forth; therefore, it is attained through the sevenfold categories of the excellent systems of viewpoints (naya). (49) —yo yai Ā.
Commentary on the Verse:

It does not clarify—that is, manifest—the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the reason (*hetu*), the mark (*liṅga*), with the probandum (*sādhya*), the marked (*liṅgin*). What is it that [does not do so]? Perception (*dṛṣṭi*), that is, observation (*darśana*), occurring "in one place" (*ekatra*); this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which perception occurring "at one time" (*ekadā*) is also included. Thus, it is perception in its entirety that would manifest [the pervasion], and in that case, the intention is that inference (*anumāna*) would be useless.

He asks, "In the absence of what? and answers: "In the absence of *cintā* (reflection). The sense is that when accompanied by it, [the *pratyavamarśa*] manifests clearly; therefore, it would constitute a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
He asks how it does not manifest it in its absence, and answers: "In its entirety" (*sākalyena*), that is, in its totality.

If it manifests [the object] only partially, then let it manifest it so; however, since inference does not arise in that manner, who then manifests it in its entirety? To this, he says: "This," and so forth.

This is the mental, indistinct conceptualization (*aspaṣṭa-vikalpa*) which is reasoning (*tarka*), established through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in every living being.

Of what nature is it? He says: "having an unapprehended object" (*anadhigataviṣaya*). That is so-called because its object (*viṣaya*) has not been apprehended—that is, not determined—by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). What is it? He says: "it is indeed cognition" (*saṃjñānameva*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the particle *eva* (indeed). For this very reason, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, how it is entirely a revealer of pervasion (*vyāpti*), how it has an unapprehended object, and how it is cognition—all this has been explained in detail during the examination of the knowledge of pervasion; therefore, enough with this digression.

From this, the following is established: when "because it is conceptual" (*vikalpatvāt*) is adduced as a reason to prove that a system of logic (*naya*) lacks a real object (*nirviṣayatva*), that reason is shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) by means of both reasoning (*tarka*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*). Thus he says, "recollection," and so forth;
the connection is that all recollection is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Of what nature is it? He says: "Non-contradictory with the object apprehended. That is, non-contradictory with the object that was itself apprehended through recollection; or alternatively, non-contradictory with the object apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Under what condition? He says: "When validity exists. Of what [validity]? Of inference (*anumā*).

Where? To this he says: "established by that," and so forth. An object established—that is, ascertained—by that reasoning, characterized by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), [is found] even in a single part (*ekadeśa*) which serves as its substratum, namely in the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*). The word *ca* (and) is used in a different syntactical order and has the sense of the particle *api* (even). What results from this? To this he says: "comprehension," and so forth.

Therefore, from this reasoning— which establishes that [the opposing] systems lack a valid object— there is the attainment of knowledge regarding the soul and other entities through the means of logic, tradition, inference, and cognition; and through the multitude of viewpoints known as the sevenfold *nayās*,
there is the vision of the Omniscient One in the state of universal perception (*sakaladṛṣṭi*).
Without vision, there is no seeing for them.
When the pervasion is grasped by means of a single part,
[one perceives] the pervasion.
Tarka (reasoning) through reflection,
page 423.
—[The word] *miprasa* [is a corruption of *atiprasa*;
*anaikāntikatvam* [is the intended term; the word order is inverted in the manuscript (śra).
"—*tiriti*," and so forth.
By these [means], once their realization has been attained, he shows what has resulted: *nayai*.
Homage to you, the omniscient proponent of *syādvāda*, whose cognition is free from sublation regarding the objects of existence such as the soul;
for one who is not a knower of all things could not be a perceiver of all substances and modes throughout the three periods of time.
Who? An extremist, such as the Sugata (Buddha) and others.

What doing? Not perceiving—that is, not knowing—what? Reality (*tattva*). Of what kind is that [reality]? It is "possessing manifold aspects" (*anekāntabhāk*); that is to say, it possesses or makes its own the nature of manifoldness (*anekānta*), which consists of substance and modes (*dravyaparyāyātmatā*). Thus, it is called "possessing manifold aspects."

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "capable of being examined" (*śakyaparīkṣaṇa*), meaning that which can be analyzed by means of the exclusion of doubt and other such factors; the sense is that it is even within the scope of worldly perception.
How so? By means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Having done what? Having cultivated (*abhyasya*) or meditated upon it.

What? One's own doctrine (*svamata*). The meaning is: how can those [others] possess omniscience, since their minds are not capable of attaining the reality of non-absolutism (*anekāntatattva*), as they are occupied with the cultivation of views of absolute one-sidedness (*sarvathaikāntadarśana*), such as the doctrine of destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*)?

For that reason, O Akalaṅka—O you who are free from the stains of knowledge-obscuring karma and the like—to whom shall I offer salutation? To you! Of what nature are you? Omniscient. Furthermore, how qualified are you? You are so described because your intellect (*dhī*) is "one whose obstructors have been cast out" (*nirastabādhakā*); that is, it is one whose two types of obscuring defects—the obstructors—are separated [and eliminated] by the power of the cultivation of the principle of non-absolutism (*anekāntatattva*). To such a one as you, I offer salutation.
Furthermore, to what kind of person? To the proponent of *syādvāda*.

Not only do I alone pay homage to you, but every discerning investigator also seeks refuge in and resorts to you alone. Because your speech proceeds from the desire to express the eternal truth, what is your name? Vīra, the last Tīrthaṅkara, Vardhamāna.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is the *Jina*, so called because he conquers (*jaya-ti*) the "conquerable" (*jina*), namely, the evil deeds that cause one to wander through various kinds of treacherous and dense [existences]. (Laghīyastrayāloka, p.
72) He perceives directly that reality which partakes of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), even while practicing his own doctrine;
therefore, the Omniscient One (*sakalavit*) is capable of investigating the truth, whereas the proponent of absolutism (*ekāntavādī*) is not.
The discerning one, free from blemish, goes for refuge to you alone, the heroic Jina. (50) —
[In the Pāli language,
the word *jina* is derived from the verbal root *jināti*, thus it is established that "he who conquers" is a *jina*.]

Immediately following this verse, the manuscript *Ja-Vi* records the following verse at the conclusion of the chapter; however, because it has not been commented upon by Abhayacandra, the author of the *Tātparya-vṛtti*, nor by the author of the *Nyāyakumuda-candrodaya*, and because it appears inconsistent with the context and subject matter, it seems to be an interpolation: "Thinking, 'Neither I nor another shall ever again be bound hereafter by actions, nor shall [anyone] ever be an enjoyer of the fruit of action,' a person whose vision is thus perverted pays homage to the *caityas* and other objects with various austerities and an uplifted mind."
Or rather, what austerity is there in that? These fools have been deceived solely by rogues.
This verse is also established in the form of a citation on page 257 of the *Yaśastilaka-campū*, in its latter part (*uttarabhāga*), as the meaning of the *kārikā*: [text follows].

From that aforementioned attainment, it is understood—this is the ellipsis—that Sugata and others, being proponents of an extremist doctrine, are not omniscient (*sakalavit*) or all-knowing (*sarvajña*).
What are they doing? Not perceiving (*alakṣayan*), that is, not ascertaining (*aniścinvan*).
What is this? It says: "the reality (*tattva*) of the soul (*jīva*) and so forth."
Of what nature is it? He says: "possessing manifold aspects" (*anekāntabhāk*), meaning having a manifold nature (*anekāntātmaka*).
Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "capable of investigation. The word "also" (*api*) is to be understood here;
that which is capable of investigation—namely, the discernment of its own nature through the exclusion of doubt and the like—is thus described.

The meaning is that even that which is characterized as being within the scope of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), meaning it is also graspable by direct perception; here too, the word "even" (*api*) is to be understood.

Having done what does one fail to perceive it? He says: "having practiced" (*abhyasya*). What [did one practice]? He says: "one's own doctrine" (*svamata*), which is "extreme" (*ekānta*); or rather, "well-imagined ignorance" (*suṣṭhu amata*), namely the reality of momentariness and partlessness (*niraṃśa*).
By this, the reason for defining the principles (tattvas) such as the soul (jīva) has been stated.
If one asks, "What is the purpose of defining them?", he says here: "The discerning person" (*prekṣāvān*), and so forth.

Here too, the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is to be understood; thus the meaning established is this: therefore, from that knowledge, the discerning investigator—the world (*loka*)—becomes stainless (*akalaṅka*), faultless (*nirdoṣa*), and free from the practice of what is not the truth (*atattvābhyāsa*).
He goes for refuge to you alone—of what nature are you? You are the Hero (Vīra), the deity who is the final Tīrthaṅkara named Vīra;

or alternatively, you are the assembly of Tīrthaṅkaras known as Vīra, because they bestow (rāti) the distinguished (viśiṣṭām) glory (īm)—consisting of both internal and external characteristics—which is not shared by other people.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is the *Jina*, the uprooter of the wheel of karma that causes one to whirl within the eddies of the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
This discerning person does not merely go for refuge to You who possess the aforementioned attributes, but also pays homage to You.
By what attribute? To this he says: "To the Omniscient One" (*sarvajñāya*), the knower of all things.

Of what nature is he? He says: "To him whose intellect has cast aside sublation" (*nirastabādhakadhiye*). This means either that his intellect has cast aside the intellects of the one-sided proponents (*ekāntavādin*) who act as sublaters; or, that his intellect is such that its sublation has been cast aside; or, that his sublating intellect has been cast aside—to such a one, and furthermore, of what nature? To you, the proponent of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvādin*), let there be salutation (*namaḥ stāt*); let there be an offering of homage.
The latter three words should be construed by changing the case endings as "to the stainless one, to the hero, to the Victor"— this is the analysis;
[the phrase] "in the cutting" refers to its own [contextual] dependence.
Even more than that is the goal:
from that knowledge—
what is the "Akala"?— Śrī.
To you, named Vīra,
[the assembly] of the wise— [at the sacred ford]—
the multitude of the learned.

O Lord, for you who are like the fierce sun of the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness), which illuminates the entirety of all objects even in part, these seven *sannayas* (modes of analysis) have been declared as a partial reflection of that [sun]. Is the sun, capable of illuminating everything, able to dispel even the thickest darkness by its rays without [the aid of] a mirror? || 6 ||
Since the fierce sun of *syādvāda* illuminates all objects even partially, were these seven systems of right reasoning (*sannaya*) merely spoken for the sake of reflecting its form?
Is not the sun capable of illuminating everything, even the tip of a hair, with its full intensity?
Is it possible to illuminate [the world] by dispelling dense darkness with raised hands?
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, an ornament to the *Laghīyastraya*, composed by Prabhācandra. Thus ends the work of the venerable master Prabhācandra.
—daḥ is completed.
Thus, the second chapter, the *Nayapraveśa*, consisting of five sections beginning with *prakrānta* and *pratyakṣa*, is completed.
*ekānta*—ba.
In the third entry into the teaching,
the sixth chapter on the teaching:
[The Ocean], whose water is the clarity of the truths, which contains a multitude of excellent jewels, and whose surging waves are sublime knowledge.

The crooked course of the Śruti, which delights the people, has a sequence of fierce and formidable crocodiles in the form of evil doctrines whose true nature is destroyed by the whirlpools of reason; its body is vast, unfathomable, and profound, and its path is incomparable.
This ocean of *syādvāda*, when properly cultivated, shall grant the fruit desired.
Now,
having defined the nature of *pramāṇa* and *naya*, he begins to define separately the nature of *āgama*, which is a specific type of *pramāṇa*, because there exist various disagreements regarding it.
At the beginning of this treatise, he recites a hymn to the specific qualities of his chosen deity, which serves as the intermediate auspicious invocation:

"Having prostrated before the Great Hero, whose seven eyes are the Syādvāda"—the *syādvāda* is the doctrine consisting of the sevenfold predication beginning with "it may be that it exists," and the *īkṣaṇasaptaka* (seven eyes) is the group of seven eyes; he is so called because this [doctrine] serves as the seven eyes for those to be instructed. He prostrates before him who possesses the sevenfold perspective of the Syādvāda. This is the meaning.
Indeed, one who provides no benefit is not worthy of salutation by a discerning person, as that would lead to an over-extension [of the principle].—*Laghīyastrayālaṃkāra*, p. 74.
I shall now describe the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the perspectives (*nayāḥ*), and the categories (*nikṣepāḥ*) according to the tradition. (51)
Regarding the meaning of the verse:
having prostrated—that is, having bowed down—to whom? To the Hero (Vīra), the last Tīrthaṅkara, or to the entire assembly of Tīrthaṅkaras.
Of what specific nature is it? It is "possessing the sevenfold vision of *syādvāda*.
*Syādvāda* is the doctrine consisting of the sevenfold predication beginning with "in some sense it exists" (*syād asti*). That which possesses this sevenfold vision is so described.

Now, is this designation of "vision" applied to *syādvāda* primarily or figuratively? It cannot be the first alternative, because the primary application of that term is well-established only for the eye.

The second position is also untenable, because in the world it is well known that the eye is the cause for the apprehension of form and so forth, and *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness) is not the cause for the Blessed One’s own apprehension of those objects; how then can he be designated metaphorically as "seeing"? If it is argued that he is so designated because he causes others to understand by means of this [doctrine], and thus it is the cause for their apprehension; then that "sevenfold seeing" would belong only to the other person, not to the Blessed One, since it is illogical for one person to have an apprehension based on something belonging to another. That is incorrect, because of a different interpretation.
It is *syādvāda* itself that is the "sevenfold vision" (*īkṣaṇasaptaka*); because it possesses this for those who are capable of liberation (*bhavya*), it is so described.
Alternatively, *syādvāda* is like a sevenfold vision, and thus it is called "that which has the sevenfold vision.

If one asks: what is the similarity between *syādvāda* and that group of seven, such that it is spoken of in this way? It is its capacity to generate knowledge of an object without depending on instruction and the like.

Just as the cognition of form and other objects arises from mere observation, independent of the instruction of others or the positive and negative concomitance of logical marks (*liṅga*), so too does the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) arise from the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*).

Having prostrated before that particular deity who is thus characterized, I shall expound the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the viewpoints (*naya*), and the modes of categorization (*nikṣepa*), which are defined by the characteristics to be described hereafter. How? In accordance with the scriptures (*āgama*), without transgressing the scriptures.
By this, his own independence in that regard is refuted; where [is there] a hero, [or] the assembly of the final Tīrthaṅkara? Or [where is there]...?
The designation of "seeing" would apply to the cognition of form and so forth according to the Syādvāda.
—Now, according to Rāmaṇa—Ā; now, according to the opinion of others—Ba; [the Blessed One] by means of the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects).
The designation "observation" (īkṣaṇa) refers to the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda); thus it is stated in the Bādarāyaṇa [Sūtra].
By the sevenfold contemplation—
by what would it be?—
by this [contemplation] of the Self. (Ātma-śruti)
There, the author, setting forth the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth in brief, says:
"Cognition is the means of valid cognition; it is held to be the instrument for [the knowledge of] the self and other [objects]."
It is accepted—that is, it is admitted—because all opposing views have already been refuted.
What is it? It is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Of what nature is it? It is knowledge (*jñāna*). Knowledge is so called because it knows, that by which something is known, or because it is mere consciousness (*jñapti-mātra*); for when one intends to express the difference or non-difference between substance and its modes (*paryāya*), the grammatical derivation as agent and so forth is appropriate.

Of what? It means that which grasps its own object, namely the self and so forth; "self and so forth" (*ātmādi*) refers to that external object for which the self (*ātman*)—its own essential nature—is the beginning.

Alternatively, "self" refers to the substance of consciousness (*ciddravya*), while by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are included the internal and external causes—the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) and destruction (*kṣaya*) of the veils (*āvaraṇa*), as well as the sense organs (*indriya*) and the non-sense organ (*anindriya*, i.e., the mind). [The phrase] "arising from that" is to be supplied [to the sentence], and thus it is accepted.

Who? [The speaker. What is the nature of the method? [It is the means of knowledge. What is the intended meaning? [It is the desire to speak. Of whom? [Of the knower who possesses scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñānin*).]
What is intended in this way? It is the "deposit" (nyāsa).
Of what kind is it? It is the "means" (upāya), which is the cause for realization (adhigama-hetu), consisting of names and so forth.
Anticipating the objection—"Since the object is established by itself, what is the use of these means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and so forth?"—he says "by reasoning" and so on:

the apprehension and determination of the object, such as the soul (jīva), occurs only through reasoning, the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), the viewpoints (naya), and the modes of presentation (nikṣepa), and not by itself.
(Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra, p. 75)
"Comparison (tulanā) is knowledge; it is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), so say the Nayas; this is the opinion of the Knower"—Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, fol. 518A;
Pramāṇasamuccaya-vṛtti, p. 127.
This has been cited: "They say that knowledge is the means of valid cognition" (Ghaṭaṭīkā, p. 17).
It is said: "The Jaina view (nayavāda) is the intention of the knower, the apprehension of an object through reasoning. (52)

Comparison: "The viewpoints (*nayas*) are indeed the intentions of the knowers with respect to substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*); therein, substance is the locus of infinite modes, and modes consist of differentiation"—Siddhiviniscaya-ṭīkā 517A.

Commentary: Knowledge is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is untenable for a cause that is insentient to possess the status of a means of valid cognition, just like a sense organ when it is not in contact with its object.

"This comparison is flawed because that which is not in contact [with the sense organ] cannot be its cause"; this is without substance. For the object is not the cause of that [cognition], since it [cognition] is caused by both the sense organ and the mind (*manas*), and the object is merely its domain.
Indeed, an object to be determined does not assume the status of being the cause of its own determiner, just as a jar or similar object is not the cause of a lamp. As the analogy states:
"Valid cognition is knowledge, not ignorance; it arises from the contact of the sense organs with objects, and so forth" (Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī, p. 3).

By the restrictive emphasis "cognition alone" (*jñānam eva*), the exclusion of sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) and other factors—which lack a conscious nature—is established; [Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, p. 518A]. *Laghīyastraya-ṭippaṇī*, p. 132.
Comparison and the light of a lamp are not causes [of perception], because they are objects to be delimited, like darkness.
— *Parīkṣāmukha* 2.6.
Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.25
The meaning of the verse: in every instance, such restrictive determinations as "cognition alone" or "valid cognition alone" are to be understood;
of what [is that valid cognition]?
Thus he says: "Of the self, etc.";
by the word "etc.," the inclusion of the *pudgala* and so forth is intended.

If it is asked, "Since a relationship such as identity (*tādātmya*) between cognition and its object is impossible, how can it be said that 'this belongs to that'?", we reply: no, for even in the absence of those [other relationships], a relationship characterized as the state of being the object and the subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is possible.

The objection, "In the absence of that [object], how could even that [cognition] exist? is also trivial; for even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) between cognition and its object has been established, just as there is a relationship of illuminator and illuminated between a lamp and its object. Furthermore, the claim, "Since the self (*ātman*) and so forth do not exist, he has no cognition at all," is mere faith, because his discernment of objects has been proven through our treatise. Alternatively, "self" refers to its own nature (*svarūpa*), and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the object (*artha*) is included; thus, the meaning "of itself and its object" is established.

Furthermore, that cognition consists of the determination of both self and other has already been established at length in the proof of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); therefore, there is no need for further effort in proving it.
Now, what is "deposition" (*nikṣepa*)? To this he says: "The means," and so forth.
The means is the cause; the deposition (*nyāsa*) consisting of names and so forth of [objects such as] the self and the like is intended as "deposition" (*nikṣepa*).

*Naya* is the intention (*abhiprāya*) of the knower; it is the intention of the knowing subject regarding one specific aspect of an object that has been made the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [The author] asks: "What is the fruit of describing their essential nature? He replies: "The apprehension (*parigraha*), that is, the acceptance (*svīkāra*), of the object through reasoning (*yukti*) characterized as the means of valid cognition and so forth.
This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); by it, the avoidance of what is not the goal (*anartha-parihāra*) is also included.
"Knowledge of the object"— thus [it is said] in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*.
In the absence of a relationship such as identity (tādātmya) and so forth, even the relation of object and subject would not exist for the Self and other entities.
Page 343, Page 176.

For comparison: "In this context, what is the purpose of the exposition of the *nayas*? Whatever object is not fully perceived through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the *nayas*, and the *nikṣepas*..."
"The appropriate appears as inappropriate, and the inappropriate appears as appropriate"—
this is the explanation of the *Dhavalāṭīkā*, folio 16.
Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "Knowledge is the means of valid cognition" (*jñānaṃ pramāṇam*), and so forth.

Here, "knowledge" is the subject (*dharmin*) and "being the means of valid cognition" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). The reason (*hetu*) to be understood here is "because its being a means of valid cognition would otherwise be untenable.

Now, one might object: this reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) because of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and other factors; for even though they are not themselves of the nature of knowledge, they can still be considered means of valid cognition since they produce knowledge that is non-verbalizable (*avyapadeśya*), non-erroneous (*avyabhicārin*), and determinate (*vyavasāyātmaka*). To this, he replies: "Even of the cause," and so forth.
Even for a cause—such as sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth—which produces the aforementioned cognition, validity is untenable because it is insentient.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "like non-proximate sense-objects" (*asannikṛṣṭendriyārthavat*).

"Proximate sense-objects" (*sannikṛṣṭendriyārtha*) refers to that which is proximate (*sannikṛṣṭa*), the sense-organ (*indriya*), and the object (*artha*). Those other than these intended [proximate ones] are "non-proximate sense-objects"; "like them" (*tadvat*) means like those.
Alternatively, [the compound may mean] "like those two, namely the non-proximate sense-organ and object";

or rather, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which has entered the scope of dispute, such as sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*), is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because it is insentient (*acetanatva*), like unintended sensory contact and so forth;
and just as the validity of insentient sensory contact and the like is untenable, this has been established in detail in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*).
Comparison: "Right knowledge is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because its status as a means of valid cognition would otherwise be untenable" (*Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, p. 51; *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 41;
Prameyaratnakośa,
This [is the view] of Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, page 2 et seq., and also of Bhaṭṭajñānaka.
Comparison: "For an insentient object is not an instrument in its own cognition, like a jar or similar things"—*Pramāṇapaddhati*, p.
Here the opponent says: "It is dissimilar," and so forth.

The illustration in the form of an example is not similar to the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*). He demonstrates that very dissimilarity with the words beginning "of that which is not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭasya*).

Because that object characterized as a sense-object, being non-proximate, is not its cause—that is, it is not the cause of the intended cognition—this is what is meant: if the Naiyāyika and others accept validity in some cases on the basis of sentience, then just as there is an absence of validity in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) due to the absence of sentience, so too would it be in the case of the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*).

However, since that [object] is accepted as the cause of cognition, and although that causality does not exist in the example, it nevertheless exists in the case of the subject of the argument, its validity is established.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "This is not sound," and so forth.
This [position] that validity consists in being a cause of knowledge is not sound.
Why is this so? He says: "Of the object," and so forth.
Because the object—the jar or other thing that is the objective domain of cognition—is not its cause, since it does not produce the cognition that apprehends it.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Of that," and so forth;
because that cognition of the jar and so on has the sense-faculties and the non-sense-faculties (the mind) as its causes.

If it is asked why [the object] cannot be the cause of the [cognition], he says here: "Because the object is the objective domain (*viṣaya*), because it is that which is to be determined (*paricchedya*).
Now, one might ask: what contradiction is there between something being both an object and a cause? To this he replies: "Indeed not," and so forth.

For (*hi*) since the object is not that which is determined by that cognition, it could not appropriate for itself the state of being its cause—that is, the status of being the cause of the cognition.
In this regard, he states an example well-known to the opponent: "Like a jar and so forth, in relation to a lamp.

The intended meaning here is as follows: just as a jar or similar object, which is illuminated by a lamp, does not assume the status of being the cause of the lamp, yet it is nonetheless illuminated by the lamp; likewise, even though this [object] does not assume the status of being the cause of cognition, it is nevertheless illuminated by that [cognition]. By this, the rule postulated by the opponent—that an object cannot exist without being a cause—is refuted, since we observe that objects such as jars, though not causes of the lamp, are nonetheless the objects of its illumination.

The validity [of cognition] is not accepted on the basis of being conscious, nor on the basis of being unconscious; such is the sense regarding the contact of the object—its invalidity [is thus established]. (Śra.)
A lamp, etc., does not possess the status of being a cause for the cognition of objects such as a jar, etc.
O Saugata, let that [object] be illuminated by cognition;

however, for one who accepts the principle that "that which is not a cause is not an object," is it intended that "only a cause is an object," or that "a cause is necessarily an object"? In the first case, the self-cognition of the nature of consciousness would be untenable.
Indeed, an entity's own nature cannot be its own cause, because it is contradictory for an action to operate upon itself.

In the second case, however, it would follow that even the eyes and other sense organs would be objects [of cognition], since there is no difference in their status as causes. Furthermore, would this restrictive rule be postulated once the fact that the object is a cause of cognition is established, or while it is not yet established? It cannot be while it is unestablished, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Now, if [the object] is established, from what does its establishment arise—from that very cognition, or from something else? It cannot be from that very [cognition], because we state that being the cause is what is meant by "being the object," and not a [separate] relation.
For instance, an object such as color becomes the "object" when it functions as a cooperative condition for the arising of visual consciousness.

And that meaning of "cooperation" is twofold: either mutual assistance, as [in the case of the eye and light], or the performance of a single purpose, as when one perceives a form merely by opening the eyes. In both cases, it is specifically the cause of consciousness that is called the "object" (*viṣaya*).
— *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 683.

Comparison—To explain: is the object only the cause, or is the cause only the object? In the first case, the eye and other [senses] would also become objects for the cognition of color and so forth. In the second case as well, the future rising of Rohiṇī would not be an object for this inference—"the rising of Kṛttikā [indicates] the past night"—because the future rising of Rohiṇī is not its cause (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p.
510). Furthermore, there would be self-cognition of the nature of consciousness only if the nature of consciousness were the cause with respect to its own self-cognition.
And this is not the case;
for even if one were to imagine it thus,
"this is the meaning," one would know the cognition, but not its production from the object.
One should know—that is, one should understand—what? Knowledge;
how? That this is the meaning.
Furthermore, one would not know what? One’s own birth—the thought "I have arisen from this"—from what object? From an entity such as a jar.

And this [fact that cognition arises from the object] is established by the very nature of the apprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Otherwise, if cognition were known to arise from the object by its own nature, then there would be no dispute between the proponent and the opponent regarding whether or not cognition arises from the object. Why? Like the case of a pot and the potter; just as there is no dispute for anyone when the production of a pot from a potter and so forth is established by perception, so too there should be no dispute regarding the production of cognition from the object. Yet, such a dispute exists among the proponents of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvādin*) concerning the production of cognition.
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 76)

Otherwise, there would be no dispute, as in the case of a pot and its maker, such as a potter. Commentary: A cognition that determines an object necessarily indicates another, distinct cause for itself;
for the determination of that object does not occur while [the cognition] is still occupied with acquiring its own nature, because it has not yet arisen.
Even for that which has already arisen, there is no further operation upon the cause, as in the case of instruments and the like.

If consciousness were to determine the relationship between cause and effect regarding the self and its objects, then no one would be able to disagree concerning the agent, the instrument, and the object— this is the meaning of the verse.

For cognition that apprehends an object such as a jar would know the object itself through the mental representation (ullekha) "this is a jar, characterized by [specific] place, time, and form"; it would not know the object's arising or its acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*).
If it is said that "it knows that [arising] from that," to this he replies with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth:
otherwise, by some other mode of cognizing that [arising], there would be no dispute.

When the arising of something from something else is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no dispute regarding its arising from that; as, for example, the case of a jar from a potter. Since there is a dispute regarding the arising of cognition from an object, one should understand that its [the object's] arising from that [cognition] is not perceived through direct perception. Thus, [it follows that] cognition is [not produced by the object].
That is to say, its arising—
from that [is known] from scripture (śruti).
The arising of knowledge.

Now, if it is argued that its status as the effect of that [object] is cognized through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—well then, would that [means] be of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or of the nature of inference (*anumāna*)? If it is of the nature of perception, would it have cognition as its object, the object as its object, or both as its object? Among these, in the first two alternatives, the cognition of the causal relation between the two is untenable, because each is grasped by a cognition having only one of them as its object. Where two things are grasped by cognitions having only one of them as their object, there is no cognition of a causal relation between them, as in the case of color and taste, or smoke and fire. And such is the case with the object and the cognition.

Now, [it might be argued that] the cognition of that [object] arises from a perception whose object is both [the object and the cognition]. That is not so, because such a perception is impossible for people like us. Furthermore, is the cognition perceived as being the effect of the object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)? If it is through direct perception, is it through that very same [perception of the object] or through another perception? Now, if its status as the effect of the object is cognized through another means of valid cognition, would that [cognition] have the cognition as its object, the object as its object, or both as its objects? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 232) [Regarding] cognition and the object.

Furthermore, does the perception whose object is those two [cause and effect], having arisen from them, cognize their relationship as cause and effect, or does it do so without having arisen? It cannot be the latter, because it would follow that even the first cognition, if it did not arise from the object, would nonetheless grasp the object.

If, on the other hand, it has arisen [from them]; then its arising from them must be cognized by another cognition produced from it, and that [cognition’s] arising by yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If the cognition of that [causal relation] arises from the second based on the first, and from the first based on the second, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).

Therefore, the fact that cognition is an effect of the object is not established by another means of knowledge in the form of perception, nor by inference characterized by its conformity with the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the object; for that [inference] will be refuted in the immediately following verse.
From both of these— knowledge and the object—
it arises from those two, namely, from the knowledge of the meaning as heard.
Regarding the cognition of the arising of that from both,
the explanation of the commentary is as follows:
Explaining the verse, he says: "The object," and so forth.

A cognition that determines an object such as a jar indicates another cause for itself—an additional cause characterized by the eye and so forth—which is indeed distinct from the other cause characterized by the "object" as postulated by others.
Why is this so? He says: "For not," and so forth.

For this reason, [it is] not [the case]. Why? Because for that which is exerting itself toward the acquisition of its own nature—that is, for that which is seeking the attainment of its own form—how could there be a determination of that object, i.e., a determination of the object? He says: because it has not yet arisen.

That which, being unarisen, acquires its self-nature from something at a certain time, cannot at that time be the determiner of that [object]; just as, for example, a son is not the determiner of his father during the state when he has not yet acquired his own nature. And cognition, being unarisen, acquires its self-nature from the object at the moment of its arising.
Now, if it is argued that once cognition has arisen, it will possess an activity (*vyāpāra*) in the grasping of the object; to this he replies: "Even when arisen," and so forth.

Not only in the case of what is unarisen, but even for cognition that has already arisen, there is no activity—characterized by the grasping of that [object]—toward its own cause, which is its producer. He provides an illustration for this: "like the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth."

The "instrument" (karaṇa) refers to the eye and so forth, as well as the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and other such factors. The application [of the argument] is that the object is not the cause of cognition, because it is delimited by that [cognition]; for whatever is the cause of that [cognition] is not delimited by it, just like the eye and so forth. And since the object is delimited by cognition, it cannot be its cause.
Nor is there an inconclusive [reason] due to light; for the status of light as a cause of cognition will be refuted later.

If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the son—since even though he is produced from the father, he is the cognizer of that [father]—this too is incorrect. For it is the body of the son alone that is produced from him, and that [body] is not the cognizer; rather, it is cognition (*jñāna*). And that [cognition] is not produced from him, since it is produced precisely from the eyes and other [senses].

How, then, can it be established as an example in the previous application? This objection is not to be raised; for its establishment is possible by considering merely the absence of being a cognizer in that which has not yet acquired its own existence either from the body or from the cognition qualified by it. Indeed, from whom... [Ba. (Note: The fragment "na hi yasmāt ā॰, ba॰" appears to be a scribal or editorial marker indicating a break or a reference to a source text.)

Of the son of Śra, whose function is solely that of thorough knowledge.
Because it delimits the father, and because the father [is delimited] by that— Śra., Ba.
The body of the son is the knowledge that distinguishes the father.
In the formal argument, "That which is not produced is existent," and so forth, regarding the knowledge of the father.
Of the son,
who has not yet arisen either in the form of a body or in the form of knowledge qualified by a body.

Because the example of the son is applicable: for just as a son who is not yet produced—either in the form of a body or as a specific cognition—is not a determiner of his father, so too cognition, while unproduced, is not a determiner of its object.

[Objection: But cognition, by being the effect of the object, cognizes itself; therefore, because it is employed immediately after the mention of the action that contradicts it, the reason "because it is being determined" is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed). To this, he says: "If," and so forth.

If cognition were to determine the relationship of cause and effect between the self and the object—namely, the status of the self as the effect and the object as the cause—then no one would be able to disagree.
Where? To this he says: "Among the agent, the instrument, and the object; the object is the agent, the eye and so forth are the instruments, and cognition is the object; among these."

Where the relationship of cause and effect appears within unimpeded consciousness, no one disputes the triad of agent and so forth, as in the case of the potter and the jar; yet the Jains and others do dispute it regarding the agent and so forth in the case of the object and its cognition.

Therefore, following the formal argument whose probandum is sublated by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), [the author] says: "In that regard... (*tatrādhi-*) [or *tadādhi-*].
—immediately following the application—ā॰, ba॰; having determined—ba॰; of its own cognition—jñānasya.
Because it produces knowledge, the object is the agent;
because it arises from the object, knowledge is the action.

Now, is it not the case that everywhere the relationship between cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two are indeed present here as well—since knowledge arises only when the object exists, and does not arise in its absence?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something is its effect, just as smoke is the effect of fire; and cognition conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of the object. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Cognition is the effect of the object because it follows the positive and negative concomitance of the object;
for if, through positive and negative concomitance, the object is the cause of cognition..."
If it is asked what the cause is, it is "ka" (the letter Ka); for what is the object?
For "vida" (knowledge).

By what means? By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Positive concomitance is existence when [the cause] is present; negative concomitance is non-existence when [the cause] is absent. By these two, it is thus:
"Cognition has the object as its cause, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance of that [object].
In that case, how could it be *kautaskuta*? *Kautaskuta* means "from where has it come? (*kutaḥ kuta āgataḥ*).

What is this? Let those who advocate that [theory] reflect within their own minds and consider thus: the arising of doubt and so forth means the production of knowledge consisting of doubt or error. Even in the absence of an object, doubt and the like arise;

for neither an object consisting of a post or a person, nor an object consisting of a mass of hair, exerts any causal efficiency (*vyāpriyate*) toward the production of the cognition thereof. Therefore, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of knowledge with an object is unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddha*).
—*Laghīyastrayāloka*, p. 76.
Herein is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): The fact that an object produces knowledge is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For instance, when someone seeking Devadatta goes to his house, [he perceives him].

Having gone there, he does not see Devadatta even though he is present; yet, in another moment, as he returns, he perceives him. Thus, through the presence and absence of that person, his intellect understands the reality of the situation accordingly.

When Devadatta has not yet arrived, the knowledge of Devadatta does not arise; once he has arrived, that knowledge arises. Since [the knowledge] exists only when [Devadatta] exists, its being produced by him is determined—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
544. Let it be observed: from where could the production of doubt and other such cognitions possibly come? (54)

—*Dichidutpāda*— Commentary (Āvivṛti): It is only the cognition that is erroneous, not the object. How could that which conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an unerring object itself be erroneous? Consequently, knowledge such as doubt would be without a cause.
If [the error] were caused by factors such as cataracts, rapid spinning, or the agitation of a ship, then one must investigate what object it is that the [erroneous] cognition is nourishing.

Even in the case of true cognition, the absence of cataracts and the like, which reside in the sense organ and the mind, is a cause; therefore, it is well said: "The sense organ and the mind are the causes of cognition, while the object is its domain.
A cataract is a disorder of the eye; this is a cause of error residing in the sense organ.

Regarding the rapid whirling of a firebrand (*alāta*) and the like: for if the firebrand and such were whirled slowly, the illusion of a wheel (*cakrabhrānti*) would not arise; therefore, "whirling" is qualified by the term "rapid.
Furthermore, this refers to the cause of delusion residing in the object, as in the case of traveling by boat (*nauyāna*).

For one standing on a moving boat, the illusion of moving trees and so forth arises; thus, the mention of "motion" (yāna) is included. Furthermore, this refers to the cause of delusion residing in external supports, as well as the disturbance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
For when the [humors] such as wind (vāta) become disturbed, an illusion of flaming pillars and so forth arises;
this is the cause of internal delusion—Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā, p. 16.

For what purpose was this extracted from the *Arthaviniścaya*? Because of the statement: "The sense-faculties and the mental object are the causes of consciousness" (*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 32A).

Therefore, even those who are free from error [hold that] the sense-faculty and the mind are the causes of cognition, and not the object as well—the meaning of the verse on page 330 of the *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*—is as follows:

"Presence when the object exists is positive concomitance (*anvaya*); its absence when it is absent is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). If, by these two, the object were the cause of the knowing cognition; [then it would be a cause].
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Doubt," and so forth.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) provides an explanation:
in order to explain the verse, he says "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*), and so forth.

The deviation (*vyabhicāra*) belongs to the intellect alone—characterized by the apprehension of an object qualified by one place and so on as being in another place and so on—not to the object. This is the connection [with the word] "deviation."
For he indeed produces a cognition by causing the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) to follow, whether they correspond to reality or not;
this is because of the accepted principle that "all knowledge has an objective support" (sālambana),
since even the cognition of a mass of hair-threads and the like is based upon the eyelashes and so forth.
The first half has been explained; now, explaining the second half, he says: "How," and so forth.

In what manner (*kathaṃ*)—by what means (*kena prakāreṇa*)—could a cognition that conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an object that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) possibly deviate (*vyabhicaret*) from that object? It could not deviate at all.
For if one were to apprehend an object exactly as it is established, then there would be no error, since non-deviation is characterized by the attainment of its own nature;
yet, [perception] does deviate.

Therefore, just as there is the apprehension of a property (*dharma*) connected to another place and so forth even though it is non-existent, so too the apprehension of the substratum (*dharmin*) is possible even when it is non-existent. Thus, the position that it is "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) is not the best option, because it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being "apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*). This is the intended meaning.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "From that," and so forth.

From that—namely, from the deviation of cognition—doubtful and other such cognitions would be causeless, being devoid of the object-characterized cause; for even a non-existent subject (*dharmī*) could appear, just like its property (*dharma*).
Indeed, it is observed that even when the eyelashes and so forth have been removed, a person with ophthalmia (*taimirika*) still has the cognition of a mass of hair and the like.
— There is no other knowledge of what remains— ba; — [there is] no [such] knowledge— śra.
Thus [it is said]:
