"Just as for one who has risen after being fatigued by long-term study and the like, something called a 'tuft of hair' (*keśoṇḍraka*), characterized by qualities such as blue or red, appears vividly before the eyes; or else, that state of a mass of hair which occurs when the rays of the eyes are pressed by the hand is the 'tuft of hair'—*Śāstradīpikā*, *Yuktisnehaprapūraṇī*, p. 99."
There are birds called *keśoṇḍuka* which pull out the roots of hair—[as stated in] the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, p.
70—and just as for those with ophthalmia there is the appearance of *keśoṇḍuka* and so forth even in the absence of an external object, [so it is here]—[as stated in] the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, p. 15.
"Just as a mass of hair is falsely perceived by people with cataracts"—
*Laṅkāvatāra*, p. 274—
[the phrase] "beginning with the fortnights," etc., [is cited].
The causal relation is not observed [to be] auditory; for it is seen that even when the eyelashes and so forth are removed, [the cognition occurs].

[Compare: For one whose eye is afflicted by jaundice (*kāmalā*) and the like, the object does not function as a cause in the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*). In that case, is the operation [of the cause] that of the mass of hair, or of the eyelashes and so forth, or of the jaundice and so forth? Since there is no other alternative, it cannot be the first option; for that cognition does not arise only when the object characterized as a mass of hair exists, because that would entail the absence of error.

If the eyelashes and other such parts were the cause [of that perception], it would follow that they themselves would appear; however, there would be no appearance of them as suspended in the sky, as being in front, or as having the form of a mass of hair. For one thing cannot be perceived elsewhere in another way.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that the very hairs of the eye appear there in that manner even though they do not exist, then there would be an absence of such an appearance even for one with jaundice who is devoid of those [eyelashes].
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
233: Now, it may be argued that the cognition of a mass of hair and the like arises even in the absence of an object because it is erroneous, whereas other cognitions do not for the opposite reason;

and that the error of one does not entail the error of another, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This too is an unexamined statement. For the nature of cognition is its self-luminosity and luminosity of others, independent of anything else; it is not, however, its truth or falsity.
And in that regard, just as cognition regarded as true has the nature of illuminating both itself and others, so too does the cognition of a mass of hair and the like;
however, this is the distinction: some [cognition] makes something real known because it is possible for it to be corroborated, while some makes what is unreal known because it is non-corroborative.

Nor does their difference as distinct classes of entities, nor the absence of deviation (vyabhicāra), follow merely from this much; otherwise, in an inference such as "sound is produced immediately after effort because it is created, like a jar," there would be no deviation with respect to lightning, forest flowers, and the like—which are not produced immediately after effort—since a sound or a jar generated by the palate or a stick is different from its opposite, namely lightning and the like. Furthermore, if one thing’s deviation implies another’s deviation, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Nevertheless, if there is deviation here in the present case, let it be so even in the case at hand, for there is no distinction between them.

Nor is there any deviation [from this definition] for anything else—for cognition is characterized by the grasping of both self and other. In that regard, just as a cognition considered true grasps both self and other, so too does the cognition of a mass of hair and the like;
the only difference is that one grasps something real because it possesses correspondence (*saṃvāda*), while the other grasps something unreal due to its lack of correspondence.
— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 235:
"Truthful knowledge is that which illuminates both its own nature and other things. (*svarūpaparaprakāśaṃ satyajñānam*)
False knowledge arises from contradiction;
it occurs merely through the apprehension of what pertains to the non-existent as pertaining to the existent.

With the words "the darkness regarding the knowledge of the true and the untrue," etc., he raises the objection of the opponent's view: *timira-ādi* is a *dvandva* compound; furthermore, by means of the word *ādi*, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and the word *ādi* is connected with each [member] individually.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in one instance, there is the inclusion of all defects of the sense organs, such as jaundice (*kāmalā*); in another, the acceptance of severe blows and the like; in yet another, the employment of horse-vehicles and so forth; and elsewhere, the taking of *kodrava* grain and the like.

If these are accepted as being the causes [of the cognition], then one must investigate what purpose or what benefit the object serves—meaning, what utility does the object nourish? The point is that there is none at all.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Even when there is true knowledge," and so forth.

Not only in the case of false cognition, but even in the case of true cognition, the absence of cataracts and the like is a cause; for what kind [of absence]? Because the absence of cataracts residing in the sense organ, the absence of agitation and the like residing in the mind, and the absence of rapid rotation and the like residing in both the sense organ and the mind are the causes [of true cognition]. Furthermore, it is held that the sense organ and so forth themselves, when devoid of those [defects], constitute that absence, because absence has the nature of being another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*).

The intention of the Master is that just as a cognition such as doubt, which arises from something else, apprehends an object that is non-existent and lacks a [corresponding] cause, so too does true knowledge apprehend an existent object. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore," etc.:

because, in the manner described, it is not tenable for an object to be the cause of its own cognition, therefore it is well said—"The sense-faculties and the mind are the causes of cognition; the object, such as a jar, is the domain, that which is delimited."
In cases of darkness, rapid spinning, or traveling by boat.
In the absence of agitation,
there is nothing— Ā; in the absence of contraction and so forth— Śra.
"Free from cataracts and the like" means the absence of cataracts and so forth due to defects of the sense organs and the like.

Comparison [of this definition]: Due to the deviation caused by the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka-jñāna*) and by doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*), [the object] does not exist even when that [cognition] occurs; for otherwise, it would entail non-erroneousness (*abhrāntatva*), and because it is impossible for the two objects characterized as a post and a person—which constitute its objective domain—to coexist in a single location. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 234)
Regarding the apprehension of objects—according to Akalaṅkadeva:

Now, one might raise the objection that even when the sense organ and the object are present, cognition does not arise in the absence of their contact, whereas it does arise when that [contact] exists; therefore, since contact alone is logically established as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) therein, the sense organ and the mind are not its cause. To dispel this doubt, he says:
Because of the proximity of the sense organs and their objects to the cognition itself, [the former] are established through positive and negative concomitance.
What is that which is determinative and decisive? It is cognition (*buddhi*), which is indeed knowledge.

To whom does it belong? [It belongs] to someone. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it applies not only to the object (*artha*), but also to proximity (*sannidhi*) and even to contact (*saṃnikarṣa*).
Of what? Of the sense organs and their objects—the sense organs being the eye and so forth, and the objects being form and so forth.

It is not merely from their proximity, but also from their positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—that is, from the presence and absence of contact—and likewise from the relationship between cause and effect.
The effect is proximity; the cause consists of the sense organ and so forth. And it is cognition alone that possesses the power of determination (*adhyavasāyinī*);

therefore, that [cognition] alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not proximity and the like, because the latter is itself an object of cognition (*prameya*). — *Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra*, p. 77.
"And the intellect is also the determiner of both cause and effect.

(Verse 55) Commentary: Contact and the other factors are determined by the intellect produced from other causes; nor does the intellect [determine] them prior to its own determination. Otherwise, for what purpose would there be a search for the intellect? The contact of the self, the mind, the sense organs, and the objects—which are themselves beyond the senses—is difficult to perceive.

How is it to be considered that there is an acceptance [of the object] in the arising of that consciousness? Before the arising of consciousness, not having cognized the object, how could they speak of it as either a cause or a non-cause? For it is consciousness once arisen that is the determiner of the object, not its causality;
even light is not the cause, because it is what is to be determined, just like the object—as stated by Buddhapālita (Ja-vi).

How could those who, before the arising of cognition, do not perceive the object—whether it be a cause or a non-cause—of the self, the mind, and the supersensory organs, which are difficult to understand, declare [anything]?

And how could they, once cognition has arisen, acknowledge the instrumentality of that [object] in the production of cognition? On the other hand, how could those who, after the arising of cognition, do perceive the object, declare it to be either a cause or a non-cause? [This applies to] those for whom [cognition] has already arisen.
Because it is the cause of that [cognition],
even though it is produced by light, it is not accepted as an object (*ālambana*)— there is no distinction here—
but rather merely as the reinforcement of the power of the sense faculty (*indriya-bala-ādhāna-mātra*).
—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 218:
"The light [of consciousness] and the object are not the causes [of cognition], because they are objects to be delimited, like darkness;
for there is an absence of conformity to their presence and absence, as in the case of the cognition of a mass of hair or the cognition of a night-stalker."
[From] *Parīkṣāmukha* 2.6, 7:
Neither the object nor light is the cause [of perception], because there is no exclusion [of them from the case of non-perception].
— Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.25
Regarding the meaning of the verse:

the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of both cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇayośca*) is to be understood as following immediately after "proximity" (*sannidheḥ*). From this, the following sense arises: cognition is determinative not only of the object (*artha*), but also of proximity—that is, of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*).
To the question "Of what [is it determinative]?", he says: "of the sense-faculties and objects" (*indriyārthānām*).
Likewise, the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāyinī buddhiḥ*) arises from the presence and absence of the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
this applies not only to these two, but also to cause and effect. Either the contact is the cause and the sense organ etc.
is the effect, or else the cognition is the effect and the contact is the cause; and with respect to these two as well, there is a determinative cognition.

This is what is meant: even when there is the presence of contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, as long as cognition (*buddhi*) does not arise, there can be no determination of its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), of the relation of cause and effect, or of anything else, because it would follow that the postulation of cognition is futile. But once it has arisen, the determination of reality occurs without depending on anything else; therefore, that [cognition] alone, being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not contact and the rest. — *Avyavasā* (Commentary).
The effect of proximity is immediate;
[this is] the reading of Śrī Ācārya.
So long as there is no [observation of] positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) between that sense-object contact and the cognition of the contact.
In the intellect, there is the cognition of the causal relationship between the sense faculty and its contact, or between the contact and the resulting cognition.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation:
Expounding upon the *kārikā*, he says "sannikarṣa" and so forth.

Those things of which "contact" (*sannikarṣa*) is the first—namely, positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and the rest—are referred to as such. They are determined by a cognition (*buddhi*) produced from other causes characterized as the sense organs and the mind (*indriya-manas*).
Nor is cognition determined by those [factors] such as contact;
why is this so? He says: "Prior," etc.—because prior to the arising of cognition there is no determination, since contact and the other factors lack the determination of the object of cognition.
He states the refutation for not accepting that [position] with the words "Otherwise," and so forth:
otherwise—that is, by some other mode of prior determination—there would be a search for the purpose of cognition;
for, just as in the case of cognition, everything else would also be established from contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like alone.
But this is not so; therefore, the intention is that validity belongs to cognition alone, because it is the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*) in all cases.

As for the statement—"The self is joined with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object" (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 74)—to that he says: "Of the self with the mind," and so forth;
[meaning] of the self with the mind, of the mind with the sense organs, and of the sense organs with the object.
Of what nature [are these]? They are *atīndriya*, meaning they transcend the senses. That contact (*sannikarṣa*) is difficult to comprehend and impossible to know;

therefore, in what manner or by what means can that contact be accepted as the cause for the arising of cognition? Thus it should be considered: whatever cannot be known from any source whatsoever must not be accepted as a cause for the arising of cognition by a discerning person, just like a donkey's horn; and contact and so forth cannot be known from any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as it has been demonstrated in detail in the *Pratyakṣapariccheda* that this [self] cannot be known through any means of valid cognition whatsoever,

and just as it has been explained in detail in the *Viṣayapariccheda* that the self, mind, sense-faculties, and objects imagined by you— being partless in nature and so forth— are logically untenable;
therefore, what could have contact with what?
If contact and the like were capable of determining an object even without the arising of cognition, then other [means of knowledge] would also [be so];
and this perception proceeds from the contact of four, three, or two [factors].

In that regard, with respect to external objects such as form (*rūpa*), cognition arises from the contact of four factors: the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), the mind with the sense organ (*indriya*), and the sense organ with the object (*artha*).
However, in the case of pleasure and so forth, cognition arises from the contact of three factors, because there is no operation of the eyes or other sense organs therein.

As for the self, in the case of a yogi, cognition is produced solely from the conjunction of the two—the self and the mind—because a third factor, whether an object of perception (*grāhya*) or a perceiver (*grāhaka*), is absent there.
—This is cited from *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 74; see also *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 140 (ba).
The reason why sense-contact and so forth are not the cause of the production of knowledge is that it is impossible to know this from any means of valid cognition whatsoever.
(Page 20)

Having established through the passage beginning with "The Naiyāyikas imagine that the production of doubt and so forth [occurs in this way]" that there is no negative concomitance (vyatireka) of cognition when the object is absent, he now says "Previously," etc., in order to demonstrate the absence of apprehension of the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the object:

"Previously"— that is, prior to the arising of cognition— the Naiyāyikas and others, not perceiving the object, would say nothing at all regarding whether the object is the cause or the non-cause of the arising of cognition.

This is what is meant: just as the perception of smoke follows immediately after the perception of fire, if the perception of cognition were to occur immediately after the perception of the object, then that cognition would be the effect of the object; but this is not the case.

[Objection: "Surely, prior to its arising, because there is no perceiver, there can be no apprehension of the distinction between cause and non-cause; however, once it has arisen, such an apprehension will occur. To this, he says: "Having arisen," and so forth.
For a cognition that has arisen—that is, one which has attained its own existence—is clearly the determiner of the object, and not [the indicator] of its status as a cause.
Now, refuting that light is a cause of cognition, he says: "Light also," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: not only objects and the like, but light also is not the cause for the arising of consciousness.
Why is this so? He says: "Because it is an object of discernment."
He states the previously established example:
"like an object" (*arthavat*), meaning "possessing an object" (*artha* + *vat*)—as in the case of the production of consciousness (*cidutpāda*). (Śra., Ba.)
Cognition [arises] with respect to an object when there is the production of the cognition that has become the apprehender.

[The opponent] objects: "If light were not the cause of its [visual cognition's] arising, then why would visual cognition not arise even in the absence of that [light]? Anticipating this doubt, the Buddhist, who maintains that light is the cause, says: "And thus, in his own commentary on the *Pramāṇavārttika*, he states: 'Just as the sense organ, light, and mental attention—or the self, the sense organ, and mental attention—jointly produce a single cognition of form. (*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1)
Even in the absence of light,
they perceive that which obstructs darkness and is not itself veiled by darkness.
Who specifically behold—that is, see—in the form of blue and other colors? Who? Visionaries, that is, people possessing sight. What? Darkness, which is a mode (paryāya) of matter (pudgala).
Of what nature is it? It is obstructive, concealing other objects of cognition.
Furthermore, what do they not perceive? Other things such as jars and the like.
Of what nature is it? It is covered, that is, enveloped.

By what? By darkness (*tamas*). [Objection: How then can there be light (*āloka*), which is the cause of knowledge, given its absence? [Response: Because that [knowledge] arises even in the absence of that [light].

Regarding this point, he provides an illustration: "Just as observers see things such as walls, yet do not see jars and the like when they are concealed by walls and so forth, in the same way, they perceive darkness, but do not perceive that which is other [than darkness] because it is veiled by it. (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 77). This is cited in the Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 187b.
Upon the cessation of darkness, jars and other objects are perceived; see *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 544. (Ā.)
Observers do not see things such as walls as if they were concealed by walls and the like.
[Verse 56] Commentary: Darkness is certainly not an obstructor of visual cognition, for that would entail the non-existence of the cognition of darkness itself.

If it is argued that elsewhere it is the cause for the absence of cognition; then light, too, being the cause for the absence of the cognition of darkness, would—like darkness—be a cause for non-existence.
Since one who perceives only the near portion lacks the discernment of the far portion, that [near portion] would also be subject to the cessation of cognition, like darkness;
for cognition is determinative only in relation to the removal of obstructions specific to each object,
and thus an obstruction such as cataracts is not itself an object of determination, unlike the object itself.
—Regarding knowledge—Jaṃ. Vi. Knowledge-contradiction—Ī. Vi.
The meaning of the verse—
People perceive *tamas* (darkness) as *andhakāra* (obscurity); they see it specifically because it is not obstructed or because its form is clearly manifest.
How is it? To this he says: it is "obstructive" (*nirodhi*) and "concealing" (*pracchādaka*).

Furthermore, if that cognition arises even in the absence of light, how could it be its effect? That which arises even in the absence of something else cannot be the effect of that thing; for example, the cognition of taste, which arises even in the absence of the eye, is not the effect of the eye. And the cognition of the form of darkness and so forth arises even in the absence of light.

Now, if it is thought that "if light were not the cause of the cognition of those [objects], then objects such as jars situated in darkness would be perceived," that is incorrect, because light is obstructed by that [darkness].
He says this very thing in the verse beginning with "by darkness" (*tamasā*):
they do not perceive the external object, such as a jar, which is covered—that is, concealed—by *tamas*, meaning by darkness.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "a wall and so forth," and so on.
The word "iva" (like) is used in the sense of "yathā" (just as);
that is, just as observers do not perceive a wall and such things [as solid reality].

Of what nature is it? It is concealed by a wall or the like, meaning it is obstructed by another object such as a wall; likewise, "the subject at hand" refers to the knowledge of darkness that is not sublated by any particular [perception].
The effect of light is the cognition of darkness; it is not the effect of light, because it arises even in the absence of light,
and therefore it is not caused by that.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of Śālikanātha is that at the end of darkness there is no object "darkness" distinct from the non-arising of cognition regarding walls and the like; and the view of the Naiyāyika (*yauga*) is that darkness is merely the absence of light.

But surely, since no other darkness is possible apart from the non-arising of cognition, what could it be that is suppressed by it? For that which is non-existent cannot be a suppressor of anything, as this would lead to the absurd consequence that even things like a horse’s horn could be so. Nor is it unproven that nothing else exists apart from the non-arising of cognition; for even in a well-lit inner chamber or similar place, when a perceiver comes from outside, the perception of darkness is observed despite the absence of actual darkness, provided there is a non-arising of cognition. Furthermore, if this were a distinct substance, the eye would not require light to illuminate it.
For it is light alone that the eye illuminates when independent of external light, and not some other substance.
[Objection: But if darkness were not a distinct substance, there would be no perception of shadow as something distinct from the umbrella or other objects;
yet such a perception of it does exist. Therefore, like a sprout from a seed, it is established as a distinct substance.

If it is argued that this [shadow], being thus established, proves that darkness (*tamas*) is a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), that is incorrect. For although it cannot be a distinct substance because its nature is the absence of light (*ālokābhāva*), its perception as such is nonetheless possible due to the force of delusion (*vibhrama*). To explain: in whichever other region light, obstructed by an obscuring object such as an umbrella, does not reach, there shadow is perceived; however, when the obstructing object such as the umbrella is removed, light is perceived in its own form. Thus, shadow is simply the absence of light.
If, however, it were a distinct substance, then even upon the disappearance of that [darkness], there would be the perception of it as coexisting with light;
for never has any substance been perceived to be non-coexistent with another substance—
Śālikanātha.
Furthermore, as for that blueness which is perceived at night, it does not belong to the sky;
to whom, then, does it belong? To no one.
But how can it be a quality if it belongs to no one? True; this is indeed a quality, though it is unestablished [as belonging to anything].
If it were established by the force of cognition itself, then only that [cognition] would be established; however, that [cognition] is not established due to the absence of a cause.

But surely the eye is the cause? No, because the eye does not illuminate when independent of the assistance of light. Therefore, this delusion of cognition in the dull-witted occurs precisely where there is no cognition.
For this very reason, there is no perception of darkness during the day; otherwise, the eye aided by the solar rays would manifest the blueness of the sky even more clearly.

Since the production of darkness is impossible [as a distinct entity], darkness would have to be a substance possessing color (*rūpavat*); and being composed of multiple substances, it would be perceptible to the eye.
However, such constituent substances do not exist; if they did exist, they would have to be produced even during the day.
It has been stated [in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 143] that the conceit of blueness belongs to the sky itself, as in the case of the blind:
"Darkness is not a distinct substance; it is merely the conceit of blueness on the part of the blind."
— *Tantrarahasya*, p. 21 —
by one intent on [the state of] *tti*, the concealment of jars and other objects [is achieved].
From darkness arises the non-arising of knowledge; from darkness [arises] darkness.
Regarding the phrase "tamaḥprakāśane," in the old manuscript (pū॰ pratau) where that substance (taddravyā) was missing, the reading "tamaso 'dravyā— " appears as the very same text.
From the umbrella, distinct from the shadow [produced by] the umbrella.

As for this which is said— that shadow is indeed darkness, and that it is a real entity possessing qualities such as mobility and immobility, largeness and smallness, distance and proximity— this too is worthless, precisely because it is untenable.
As for the qualities such as mobility and immobility that were proposed, those too are based on superficial observation;
for instance, when light is obstructed, a shadow is also perceived.
Therefore, a shadow is not seen as a distinct color (rūpa) separate from the existence of the ground or other objects from which the light has been excluded.
Therefore, we consider that shadow is precisely that portion of the ground and so forth from which light has been excluded—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p.
144: "Shadow is merely the portion of the ground and so forth from which light has been excluded."

"Regarding the absence of the knowledge of light, this is the view of a certain faction of the Prābhākaras" (*Tantrarahasya*, p. 21); "the absence of the knowledge of light" (*Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, p. 229).
For, in the case of a shadow, there is indeed the cognition of it as being a distinct entity from the umbrella, by means of which [cognition] the location— *pradeśa*— is [distinguished].
Darkness is non-existence (abhāva), because it differs from the production of substance, quality, and action.
— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.19.
Darkness is that which possesses manifested color and so forth, up to the absence of contact with light—
*Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-upaskāra* 5.2.19.
2.20 Even when the parasol and other [ornaments] have disappeared.

By this, the argument that shadow (*chāyā*) is a distinct substance because it possesses motion—due to its reaching from one location to another—is refuted. For instance, wherever the contact of light with an obscuring object such as an umbrella is prevented, there a different and distinct shadow is perceived; it is not the same shadow previously perceived in the former location that appears elsewhere. Thus, the perceiver, superimposing the action residing in the obscuring object onto the shadow, understands that "the shadow moves," just as one mounted on a horse superimposes his own action onto a tree and perceives that "the tree is moving."

Furthermore, regarding its arrival at another location, is it a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with that other location, or an inherence (*samavāya*)? If it were conjunction, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of its being a substance would depend on the establishment of the conjunction, and the establishment of the conjunction would depend on the establishment of its being a substance.
If, on the other hand, it were inherence, that too is untenable, because it is impossible for a substance that inheres in one place to inhere in another;
moreover, light is obstructed by other substances.
— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.20

The reason "because it possesses motion" (*dravya-cchāyā-gatimattvāt*) is not distinct from the probandum; for what is this? Does the shadow move like a person, or rather, as the substance that obstructs moves, a continuous absence of light is perceived due to the continuity of the obstruction? Indeed, as the substance moves, the very absence of those successive portions of light that are covered by it is perceived as being delimited [by the moving object].
(Nyāyabhāṣya 1.2.8)
When a substance that obstructs light spreads, that substance which is perceived as characterized by the absence of light is called "shadow" (chāyā)
— Nyāyavārttika 1.1.4.8.
2.8 Because shadow is of the nature of the absence of light.
— Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
46: Shadow is not included within [the categories of] generality, particularity, or inherence, because it is impermanent;
nor is it action, because it lacks the status of being a non-inherent cause of conjunction or disjunction.
It is not a quality of substance because it does not inhere in substance;
it is not a quality of the mind, space, or time because their qualities are imperceptible;
nor is it a quality of the self because it is perceptible by an external sense organ.
Nor does it belong to space or air, because their qualities are not perceptible to the eye;
nor to fire, because of its opposition [to cold] and because no other quality coexisting with it is perceived;
for the same reason, it does not belong to earth or water either.
Furthermore, its quality of visibility cannot be perceived without light, whereas shadow is perceived even without it; yet it is difficult to maintain that it is not perceived when light is present.
Nor is it a substance, for it would have to be one of the [four] beginning with earth, or else a tenth [substance];
it cannot be any of those, because their qualities are not perceived therein.

Nor is it logical that it has another form like color, because it is impossible for that which is not a substance (*adravya*) to be perceptible; since it lacks touch, it does not initiate [composite substances] and thus lacks the state of being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*).
Therefore, it is established that shadow is indeed non-existence (*abhāva*), and not a real entity.
—*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p.
345; *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kiraṇāvalī*, p. 19. However, Śrīdhara accepts darkness (*tamas*) as being of the nature of a specific superimposed form (*āropitarūpaviśeṣātmaka*).
Therefore, this particular form of color, when there is an absolute absence of light, is perceived as "darkness" due to being superimposed everywhere;
and we shall explain later that during the day, there is an appearance of blueness above the eyeball.
However, when the absence of light occurs in a specific location, then the perception of "shadow" arises regarding the blueness superimposed upon that location.
For this very reason, when a blackness pervading that space is perceived, there arises the conceit that "the shadow is long," "short," "large," or "small" (*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 9).
To explain: wherever the proximity of light is obstructed by an obscuring substance, there the conventional usage "shadow" occurs.

One perceives that "the shadow moves" by superimposing the action residing in the obstructing substance onto the absence of light; otherwise, there would be no dependence upon the action residing in the obstructing substance (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p.

47). As for the fact that a substance which obstructs light—such as a body—moves in such a way that light is simultaneously released and obstructed, it is the shadow that appears to move as if it were moving; otherwise, even when the body moves, why would the shadow also move? For there would be no cause for it.
— Prakaraṇapañcikā, page 144:
It is negated, O Ātreya, in the absence of light.
The word "proceeds" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
As for this quality of reaching another location belonging to the shadow, is that a conjunction with another location? For that too is yet to be proven.

For instance: if substantiality (*dravyatva*) is established, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established; if conjunction [is established], substantiality [is established]. Thus, there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 47).
Furthermore, if [conjunction] were the inherence (*samavāya*) in reaching another location, that too is unestablished.
For that which inheres in one place does not inhere elsewhere;
however, shadow, though perceived as connected in one place, is perceived again in another location.

Furthermore, its possession of action is not established by its inherence in another location, because that [possession of action] also exists only among things that are inseparably connected (ayutasiddha).
— Regarding the proof that darkness and shadow possess the substantial nature of *pudgala* (matter), as found on page 47 of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*,
the following response is provided here.
As for what was stated—that there is no darkness other than the non-arising of cognition and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion, because it contradicts experience.

For the distinct cognition of light and darkness as mutually different by their own nature is well-established through direct perception for every living being. Furthermore, it is not logical for a difference in cognition to exist apart from a difference in its object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of establishing the non-duality of the person and so forth, which would lead to the total destruction of the doctrine of duality.
If one does not accept this, then the difference between cognitions must be understood as being preceded by a difference in their objects.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that difference between cognitions is preceded by a difference in their objects, because it is a difference [of cognition], just like the difference between the cognitions of a jar and a cloth.

[Objection: This is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since the cognition of light and darkness is accepted as being preceded by a difference in objects consisting of existence and non-existence. [Response: This too is charming only when left unexamined; for since darkness possesses color and other qualities, it cannot logically be of the nature of non-existence, just like light.
Or, if it were of that nature (i.e., the nature of light), it would contradict its possession of color and other qualities;
for whatever is an absence does not possess color and other qualities, just like the absence of a jar or the like, and darkness is intended to be of the nature of the absence of light.
Nor is its possession of color and other qualities unestablished, because their existence is perceived there just as it is in light.

For just as a shining form and a hot touch are well-known in the world in the case of light, so too in the darkness of shadows and the like, there is a black form and a cold touch; therefore, darkness is a substance because it possesses qualities (*guṇavattvāt*). Whatever possesses qualities is a substance, such as light and so forth, and darkness likewise possesses qualities. Not only is its possession of qualities well-known in common worldly experience regarding shadows and the like, but it is also established in the medical treatises (*vaidyaka-śāstra*).
As it has been said [p. 666, l. 16]:

"For this very reason, there is no absence of light-cognition; for since non-existence is necessarily perceived by the same sense organ that perceives its counter-positive (pratiyogin), it would follow [absurdly] that it must be mental."
—“Nor can there be an illusion of cognition when there is no cognition at all, because the linguistic usage [based on that illusion] would be impossible without the cognition of it.
—Citsukhī, p. 29.
— thus, in its own nature—
O Puruṣa, non-duality; light and darkness are merely a difference in appearance.
The Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others [assert that space] possesses the nature of black color, cold touch, motion, and so forth, or else that it is of the nature of non-existence.
Darkness does not possess form and so forth, because its nature is non-existence;
even in darkness,
there is a luminous form.

Indeed, the Jains accept that darkness consists of the substance of *pudgala* (matter); for it is said: "O Gautama, by day there are beautiful *pudgala*s and a beautiful transformation of *pudgala*; at night there are unwholesome *pudgala*s and an unwholesome transformation of *pudgala*" (*Bhagavatīsūtra* 5.9).
Sound, light, darkness, brilliance, shadow,
and heat, as well as color, taste, smell, and touch— these are the characteristics of *pudgala* (matter).
— Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.12;
Navatattva Gāthā 9
And they possess sound, bondage, subtlety, grossness, configuration, division, darkness, shadow, heat, and light—
Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.24.

Sound, subtle and gross, configuration, division, darkness, shadow, light, and heat— these, together with others, are the modes (paryāyas) of the substance of matter (pudgaladravya). — Dravyasaṃgraha, Gāthā 16.
The grammarians accept that atom as being of such a nature: "Atoms, because they possess all powers, function through differentiation and conjunction;
they undergo transformation into the form of shadow, heat, darkness, and sound.
(Vākyapadīya 1)
Other philosophical systems also accept that darkness (*tamas*) has the nature of a substance (*dravya*). Regarding the perception of darkness, it is the perception of the shadow of the earth.
But what among substances and so forth is darkness? Is it not indeed a substance, because it possesses the quality of blackness (*kālimā*) and because it possesses motion (*spanda*)?
For instance—only blackness is perceived as its color, just as whiteness is for water and fire;

likewise, number such as oneness and so forth, and dimension, which is fourfold, [are perceived], since by inference the atoms of darkness are established just like the atoms of earth and the other elements; furthermore, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and the five kinds of action are all observed through direct perception.

As the venerable author of the Vārttika has said here: "Indeed, the status of darkness as mere absence is not accepted by the elders, because in the Purāṇas it is heard that 'blackness' (kārṣṇya) belongs to shadow, which is a quality of earth;
the meaning is that blackness, being a quality of earth, is heard of in scripture as a distinct substance [in the form of] shadow."

A shadow that follows the movements of the body— such as a lamp placed near or far— and which becomes large or small, moving or stationary according to whether the lamp is close or distant, cannot exist without being a real entity that conforms to the body.
Thus,

since it is none of the [elements] beginning with earth, and since there is no sublation [of its existence], it is established that shadow (*chāyā*) is a distinct substance, the eleventh, possessing nine qualities; for it is not non-perception when there is perception, nor is it an absence, as it is perceived even when memory is absent.
Because of the existence of means [such as color] in relation to form, there is the following of one substance by another substance—*Vidhiviveka-Ṭīkā*, p. 76–79.

What is this thing called "darkness"? The followers of Kaśyapa (the Vaiśeṣikas) hold that darkness is the absence of light, because it differs from the production of substances, qualities, and actions; however, in that case, the cognition of "blue" would be without a cause, since non-existence lacks blueness.
Furthermore, there is nothing—neither a perceiver nor a recollector—that apprehends a non-existent blueness;

yet, through the mere observation of light, that delusion occurs even in a portion devoid of it. Therefore, this is a distinct substance possessing the quality of blueness, like air; the distinction being merely that air possesses the nature of touch, whereas this possesses form but lacks touch.

Alternatively, those atoms of earth (*pārthivātrasareṇu*) which are seen moving everywhere through the openings of windows—the blue quality belonging to those [atoms], when its blue form is perceived, appears as if pervading the entire universe because other qualities, other substances, and the space between them are not perceived; furthermore, it is accepted on the strength of observation that there is no dependence on light (*āloka*) for the perception of this blue form. —*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-nyāyaratnākara*, p. 740.
When the unimpeded and clear cognition of [an object] as dark as a *tamāla* tree is manifest, why is darkness—a distinct substance—suddenly denied? —*Citsukhī*, p. 28.
Being intangible yet possessing supreme form,
that black color— which is perceivable solely by the organ of sight, revealed by the absence of light,
and possesses a luster as tender as a blue lotus— is exceedingly beautiful to behold for those with eyes.
One should understand darkness (*tamas*) as black, as established by scripture;

because of the existence of its qualities, actions, and so forth, it appears as "it exists," and because its counter-positive is not remembered, darkness is certainly of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*).
In the world, people perceive that sunlight is pungent and rough, while shade is sweet and cool. (Mānameya, p. 159)
Sunlight is pungent and dry; it brings about perspiration, fainting, and thirst, and produces burning sensations and discoloration while aggravating eye diseases.
Shade, however, removes burning, fatigue, and perspiration; it is sweet and cooling.
Moonlight is astringent and sweet; it destroys burning sensations, hemorrhaging, and pitta;
it causes fear from darkness and is bitter, yet it opposes the power of vision. —Rājanighaṇṭu 5.109–110.
Sunlight pacifies the three *doṣas*, while moonlight causes all diseases— [Rājanighaṇṭu,
cited here]— sunlight is pungent and dry, whereas shade is sweet and cool.
–*Praśamaratiprakaraṇa-vṛtti*, p. 46; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 855; the shadow is sweet and cool – *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 672.

Moonlight is astringent and sweet, and it removes all diseases and darkness. [In the *Rājanighaṇṭu*] then the following view is held: in that case, qualities such as sweetness are merely figurative (*aupacārika*), because there exists an obstacle to their being primary;
for instance, the perception of sweetness in milk and the like occurs through the operation of the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*), but it does not occur in the same way with regard to moonlight.

Therefore, the intent of the medical science (*vaidyaka-śāstra*) is that whatever qualities and defects are observed from the consumption of substances such as sweet ones are the very same as those resulting from exposure to shade; thus, the claim that "the possession of qualities in shade and the like is unestablished" is merely the play of great ignorance, because since it appears as an uncontradicted cognition, its figurative nature (*aupacārikatva*) is untenable.

Whatever appears as established by non-sublated cognition is not figurative in that respect, just as luminosity and so forth are not figurative in fire. And since the existence of qualities such as coolness is perceived in shadows and darkness as being established by non-sublated cognition, if such [qualities] were also considered figurative here, then let there be no primary establishment of qualities even in moonlight and sunlight, for it would follow that qualities such as pungency are also merely figurative therein, since the previously mentioned medical system could easily be applied to those cases as well.

Therefore, by one who regards common consensus as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it must be admitted that just as in the case of moonlight and the like, the existence of the quality [of coolness] in shadow—even in darkness—is established in its primary sense. Thus, its status as a substance (*dravyatva*) is proven because it possesses qualities.
Furthermore, as for this sweetness or coolness of the shadow mentioned in scripture, that too is figurative (*upacāra*);
for those qualities which belong to a sweet substance or a cool substance arise from the resorting to the shadow, and it is so called because it performs their function.
–Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 47: In shadow and so forth, [there is] sweetness and so forth.
Comparison: "Even shadow [is material] because it possesses coolness and nourishment, like water, wind, and so forth" (Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p.
363). Since metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) proceeds only when the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) is contradicted, and such contradiction does not exist here.

— In the case of reflections and the like, sweetness and so forth are not merely figurative, because they possess a manifestation established by uncontradicted cognition; this remains true even though they are objects of uncontradicted manifestation.
The comparison [of sweetness] with respect to shadow and so forth is the same even for that light.
—Sanmati-ṭīkā, p.
672; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 856: "Because it is a quality (guṇatvāt), [the manuscript reads] ba."
Comparison— Nor is it unestablished that darkness is composed of matter (pudgala), because its visibility would otherwise be inexplicable, just like the light of a lamp;
and since it possesses color, it is also inferred to possess touch, as it produces the cognition of a cold sensation— Syādvādamañjarī, Kārikā 5.
Darkness possesses touch because it possesses color, like the earth;
nor is its possession of color unestablished, because there is the appearance of a black form [in the cognition], "This darkness is black" (Ratnākarāvatārikā, p. 69).

As for what was also stated—that even in the absence of darkness, such as in an inner chamber (*garbhagṛha*) and so forth, when cognition does not arise, "darkness" is perceived, and so on—in that case too, is it the total non-arising of cognition that is the cause for perceiving that [darkness], or is it [the non-arising] regarding the objects existing within it? In the first alternative, there is a contradiction with one's own words, like saying, "My mother is barren. Indeed, for one who asserts the total non-arising of cognition, the perception of darkness is not tenable; nor, if there is the perception of that [darkness], can there be the total non-arising of cognition.

In the second case, however, an observer whose vision is impaired by an excessive amount of light is unable to perceive the objects situated there correctly; instead, like a circle of mirage-rays [appearing] as water, he perceives the light itself as being of the nature of darkness. Yet, it is not logical to equate a perception of false darkness with a perception of non-false darkness, because that would entail the consequence of equating a perception of real water and so forth with a perception of unreal water and so forth, which would lead to the collapse of the established order of reality. Therefore, [the opponent claims] the cause of the cognition of darkness is...

Comparison—Is it then that knowledge does not exist during the state of darkness? If so, how is there the cognition of darkness? If there were cognition even without that [knowledge], then the postulation of knowledge would be useless in other cases as well.
Furthermore, the claim "cognition does not exist" is a contradiction of one's own words, because the very fact of being cognized constitutes knowledge. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 238)
The ellipsis "are not contradicted in the cognition of darkness" refers to objects such as cloth situated within the interior of the darkness.

Furthermore, if one does not admit a "darkness" (tamas) distinct from the non-arising of cognition, then let there also be no admission of a "light" (āloka) distinct from the arising of clear cognition.

For even in the absence of light, during the night of thick darkness, objects appear clearly illuminated to nocturnal creatures and to those whose eyes are treated with collyrium when vivid cognition arises;
thus, the contradiction with common worldly experience is equal in both cases.

For just as there is a common worldly perception that people are unable to go outside at midday because the light is too intense, so too there is the perception that they are afraid to go outside at night when there is thick darkness. Therefore, since this appears as an uncontradicted cognition, if one accepts the substantiality of the substance of light (*āloka-dravya*), one must also accept the substantiality of the substance of darkness (*tamaḥ-dravya*), as there is no difference between them. If this were so, then even light would be non-existent, because nothing other than a clear cognition is perceived in its case either.
But its conventional usage in the world consists merely in the arising of clear cognition— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 238—
[not] due to beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*).
For people,
all objects are perceived as such;
substance [is perceived] as shadow, darkness, and so forth, because it obscures jars and other things, just like a screen or curtain.
Furthermore, because it possesses motion, it is a substance (*dravya*), like an arrow and so forth;

nor is its possession of motion unestablished. This is because its possession of motion is well-known to every living being through the common experience that "the shadow moves swiftly" or "the shadow moves slowly," and this is established both by such universal recognition and by inference. For instance: the shadow possesses motion, because it reaches from one location to another, just like an arrow and so forth.

Comparison: Darkness is indeed a transformation of matter (pudgala), because it obstructs vision like a wall, and because it is an obscuring agent like a cloth; [as stated in] *Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 363:
"Darkness is of a positive nature (bhāvarūpa), because it obscures jars and other objects, like a screen."

Nor is its quality of being an occluder of jars and other objects unestablished; for, like that very [jar], it obstructs the operation of the eye as it proceeds toward the object, and thus its status as such is established—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 851: "Shadow is a substance because it possesses action, like a jar."
— The shadow possesses motion (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 853).
It is also to be established by inference, as follows: "Shadow possesses motion because it reaches another location, like Maitra" (Syādvādamañjarī, p.

853). As for what was stated—that reaching another location is either conjunction with another location or inherence, and so forth—in that context, what is intended by its "reaching" or connection with another location is precisely conjunction.
Nor does this involve mutual dependence; for we do not establish the substantiality of shadow [as a premise].

Rather, its possession of motion is established from its reaching another location, and from that [motion], its substantiality is established. Thus, one should not claim that this results in a logical circle (*cakraka*), because the nature of that reaching [of another location] is already well-established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For if its reaching [of another location] were to be established by means of proving its substantiality (*dravyatva*), and its possession of motion (*gatimattva*) were thereby established, then there would be a circular argument (*cakraka*).

Otherwise, how could there not be the occurrence of faults such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) even in cases such as: "The sun possesses motion because it possesses the attainment of reaching another location"?
(Page 668, Line 3)
Since here the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is defined as the shadow's reaching another location,
or where there is the raising of the objection regarding mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), that is due to a lack of reflection on that [point];

for we are not endeavoring to establish its substantiality (*dravyatva*) on the grounds of its possessing the reaching of another location, but rather its possession of motion (*gatimattva*), and from that, its substantiality.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 854: the connection [is established] through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which consists in reaching another location.
And because it possesses motion,
it is a substance (*dravya*).
But even so, you have fallen into a very great circularity (*cakraka*).

For instance: [it is argued that] because of conjunction with another location, there is possession of action; because of possession of action, there is substantiality (*dravyatva*); and because of substantiality, there is possession of conjunction with another location. This is merely the ravings of one in a dream, because when reaching another location is directly perceived, the true nature of shadow is already established.
If indeed the reaching of another location were to be established by means of proving its substantiality, then that objection would hold;

however, since the reaching of another location is established through direct perception, the substantiality of shadow is established from its possession of action, which is itself established by that very fact.
— In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 855, the attainment of another location (*deśāntaraprāpti*) is established. (Ā.)

Furthermore, as for the other argument—that because action residing in the obscuring substance is superimposed upon the shadow, one perceives that "the shadow moves," and so forth—that too is untenable. For if the shadow were non-existent, the superimposition of motion residing in the obscuring substance upon it would be impossible;

indeed, only when a tree or similar object exists does a person mounted on a horse superimpose his own motion upon it, not when it is absent. Therefore, since such a superimposition would otherwise be inexplicable, the real existence of the shadow is established.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Shadow is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it possesses a superimposed motion (*adhyāropyamāṇagati*). Whatever possesses a superimposed motion is ultimately real, such as a tree and so forth; and shadow possesses a superimposed motion. Therefore, darkness is not merely the non-arising of cognition. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 668, l. 2)
In the case of non-existence,
[there is] action in the shadow— [this is the reading of] Āśvalāyana and Baudhāyana.
Because the superimposition of motion upon the obscuring substance in the tree and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable,
shadow is of a positive nature, since it possesses the motion of that which is being superimposed, just like the tree.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 854, *Vivṛtivyākhyāna*:

Now, an objection is raised: "Even if darkness were established as a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), the statement that it obstructs visual cognition—namely, 'they see darkness as an obstruction,' and so forth—is incorrect. This is improper, because one must ask: does that [darkness] act as an obstruction to itself, or to something else? Regarding the first alternative, he states the refutation with the words "nahi" and so on: "Indeed, darkness is not at all an obstructor of visual cognition with respect to itself"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies:
"Because it would follow that there is an absence of the cognition of darkness, yet that cognition does exist; therefore, darkness cannot be its own negator.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is not the object of a cognition cannot be the negator of that cognition with respect to itself, just like a screen or a cloth; and darkness is indeed the object of visual cognition.

If it is argued that light is not non-existent in other things such as a jar, but rather within itself, and therefore it is the cause for the absence of the cognition of darkness; then light, too, being the cause for the absence of the cognition of darkness, would—like darkness—be a cause of non-existence.
[For] the "absence" of visual cognition is either its non-arising or the destruction of what has arisen; light would thus be the cause or reason for that.

Consequently, in the formal argument: "The eye is composed of light (*taijasa*), because among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], it illuminates only color-form, just like light," the example provided is deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*).

Now, if it is maintained that light is the cause for the absence of the cognition of darkness and the cause for the cognition of objects such as jars by its own nature, then darkness too should be maintained to be the cause for the cognition of its own object and not the cause for the cognition of objects such as jars, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. If it is argued that light is the cause of that [cognition] because the cognition of color arises for some only when light exists and does not arise in its absence, then darkness too would be the cause of that [cognition], since the cognition of it does not arise for some in the absence of darkness and arises only when it exists.

And thus, among [the qualities] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, this reason—"because of being the illuminator of color-form and so forth"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to darkness (*tamas*). For even though darkness is not luminous (*ataijasatva*), it is the illuminator of color-form; it is the cause of obstruction to vision and is opposed to light. (Sarvārthasiddhi, Rājavārttika, Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā 5)
24 – Unobstructed by knowledge – Śrauta Sūtra edition.
Darkness, which obstructs cognition within itself and negates cognition regarding itself,
does not obstruct visual cognition [of other objects], because it is itself an object of visual cognition.

Even regarding the argument that darkness is perceived even in light— namely, that the eye is composed of fire (taijasa) because, like a lamp, it illuminates only color (*rūpa*) among the [five] objects such as color, while removing the darkness that obstructs the form of a jar— it should be understood that this is refuted by the fact that the example lacks the probans (*sādhanavikalatva*). (Śrī Tulanā)
—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 544; *Nyāyakumuda-candrodaya*, p. 76, n. 2:
"For light is not the illuminator of the form of darkness; therefore, because it is the illuminator of form alone among [the objects] such as form and so forth, the proof [of your claim] is void."
The form of one's own light, called "radiant," which is the cause of the cognition of jars and other objects, is not [perceived] due to the darkness of ignorance. (Ā, Ba)
Light for those like us regarding the domain of darkness.
For some, the cause of the cognition of form is the cognition of darkness.
Even darkness is a cause for the cognition of form within darkness.
Likewise, regarding the form [of darkness]— specifically its own black color—
he states the refutation of the claim that darkness obstructs the cognition of that [form], beginning with the words "for one who perceives only the near side" (*arvāgbhāgadarśinaḥ*).

For one who has the habit of seeing only the near side (*arvāgbhāga*) and thus perceives it, because there is no delimitation of the far side (*parabhāga*), not only darkness but even that near side would be an obstruction to knowledge; by the force of the context, it is considered here that it would be an obstruction to visual cognition.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "like darkness" (*tamovat*), meaning just as [darkness is an obstruction], so too [is that near side].
And likewise, by that same logic, it would follow that the near-side portion [of an object] would also be invisible; thus, for one who does not see everything, there would be nothing but blindness.

Furthermore, whatever obstructs visual cognition cannot be apprehended by that cognition, just as darkness does; and the near-side portion obstructs visual cognition—therefore, it [cannot be apprehended by its own cognition].
(Ba)
The visual cognition is the non-verbal portion;
it is indeed consciousness.
No, O honorable Parabhāgavat; or rather, like darkness,
the near-side portion is not graspable by the visual faculty, because it is obstructed by visual cognition.

[Objection: "Granted that darkness (*tamas*) may not be the object of perception, but surely [obscuration] such as cataracts (*timira*) will be. To this, he says: "With respect to each object," and so forth. "With respect to each object" (*pratyartham*) means for every individual object. Because cognition possesses the quality of delimitation (*paricchedakatva*)—that is, the quality of grasping an object—in dependence upon the absence or cessation of obscuration, namely the karma that obscures knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya-karman*), [darkness] is not an obscuration that veils cognition.
What is it? He says: "Timira and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), conditions such as jaundice (kāmalā) and others are included.

For it is specifically the *jñānāvaraṇīya* karma that invariably obscures [knowledge], because when that exists, knowledge lacks the capacity to determine its object; whereas timira and the like do not have this power, since even when they are present, the perception of forms occurs in a true dream.
For this reason as well, he says that it is not an obscuration: "Because it is an object of discernment.
Here he provides an illustration: the formal argument (*prayoga*) is "like an object" (*arthavat*).
That which is an object of discernment is not an obscuration, just like an object; and cataracts and the like are objects of discernment.

If it is argued that the Master’s statement—that "if darkness and the like were not obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), then that cognition which is erroneous regarding its own object would be obstructed, just as visual cognition whose domain consists of two moons and so forth; and such is the cognition of those with false views"—would contradict his own accepted position, we say no. This is because the Master’s intention is otherwise: his view is that darkness, cataracts (*timira*), and the like do not constitute an obstruction independently of unseen causes (*adṛṣṭa-kāraṇa*), but they certainly do constitute one when dependent upon them; for they are what conceal cognition.

Only when there is the arising of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇakarma*) does an obscuration such as cataracts exist, because it is something to be delimited; thus, visual cognition is [obstructed], [as is] auditory cognition.
The rising of the *jñānāvaraṇa* karma is to be understood by the term "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the self has knowledge as its intrinsic nature, and because it possesses the nature of grasping all objects everywhere, at all times, and in every way, it would follow that it is omniscient; therefore, there is no need to postulate any obscuration. To dispel this doubt, he says: "At all times, regarding all objects... [Śrāvaṇa 1.2.3].
Just as the manifestation of a gem pierced by a thread occurs in many ways through its grasping in every respect,
so may it be.
What is it? It is the manifestation—the emergence of brilliance—of a gem pierced by impurities, such as a ruby or similar stone that has been perforated by stains, black streaks, and the like.

How does this occur? By means of various modes; that is, by depending upon many diverse ways, such as the distinctions of clarity or lack of clarity, and whether the light is manifested from afar or nearby.
In this manner, it may be so.

What is it? It is the cognition (*vijñapti*) of the self (*ātman*) as pierced by karma. "Karma" refers to the veils of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and so forth; "pierced" means bound or connected with them. That which is both this [karma] and the self is the "self-pierced," and its cognition is the apprehension of objects. How [does it arise]? "In manifold ways" means by depending upon various and diverse particularities of the manifestation of objects—whether perceptible or otherwise, distant or near—as well as particularities of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veils. However, when those specific veils are completely removed, the cognition of all objects indeed becomes possible for the self, because its intrinsic nature is knowledge.
—Cited from *Laghīyastrayāloka*, p. 78; *Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā*, fol. 193A;
*Āvaśyakaniyukti-malaya-vṛtti*, p. 17.
*Nandi* (Malayagiri’s commentary), p. 66;
*Iṣṭopadeśa-ṭīkā*, p. 30;
*Karmagrantha-ṭīkā*, p. 8.
Comparison: Just as the manifestation of a gem covered by impurities is seen to be of many kinds, why should the various capacities of the self, which is veiled by karma, not likewise be manifold?
(Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 191)

The representation of the self, pierced by karma, manifests in manifold ways. (57) Commentary: Depending on the respective destruction or subsidence of karma, the instrument and the mind are the causes of cognition, not external objects and the like.

It is the prattle of fools to say that what does not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is not a cause, and that what is not a cause cannot be an object. For instance, nocturnal birds perceive forms in the dark due to the removal of an obstruction; conversely, because that obstruction is not removed, doubt and other types of cognition arise even when light is present.
Since cognitions of yellow and other forms arise in those whose sense faculties are impaired by glass and the like regarding objects such as conch shells,

and since even when an object is present, those about to die have contrary perceptions as the case may be, it is established that the object and so forth are not the cause of cognition— [as stated in] the *Jainavijaya*:
"by one's own karma."
It should be observed—see p. 640, note 2—the meaning of the verse:

Just as the manifestation, that is, the appearance, of a gem pierced and bound by impurities occurs through a certain process of refinement (*viśrasopayoga*) in various ways—in a manner that is more or less subtle, whether partial or complete, and whether it involves the illumination of what is situated nearby or at a distance, and so forth.

Or else, by relying on another [cause] characterized by the deprivation of objects and so forth; in that manner, there occurs the cognition (*vijñapti*)—defined as the illumination of objects—of the self (*ātman*), which is the living being (*jīva*) pierced and obscured by karmas such as those obscuring knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya*). This occurs in manifold ways, depending on whether it functions through the senses, the non-senses, or the super-sensory; whether it illuminates all or only a portion of objects, those nearby or those distant; whether it illuminates its own nature or the nature of others; or whether it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or otherwise.

"But surely there is no self whatsoever distinct from the preceding and succeeding moments of cognition, nor distinct from the four elements transformed into the form of the body; so for whom would there be this manifold representation?"—thus argue the Buddhist and the Cārvāka. Yet they are prone to forgetting what has already been established: for at the occasion of refuting the [doctrine of] *saṃtāna*, a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) was established as distinct from the preceding and succeeding moments of cognition and as being without beginning or end; and in the examination of the Cārvāka doctrine, [the self] was established as distinct from the four elements transformed into the form of the body. Enough of this digression.
