The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation:

Expounding upon the verse (*kārikā*), he says "according to their respective [karmas]" (*yathāsvam*) and so forth; "according to their respective [karmas]" means not transgressing that which is one's own (*svam*), that is, the individual karma (*ātmiya-karma*) which is the obscuration of a particular cognition.

Since the senses and the mind depend upon the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of karma, these—the sense-faculties and the internal organ—are the causes of cognition, and not external objects and the like; this has been explained immediately above. Furthermore, it is observed that the sense-faculties and the mind, depending upon the subsidence-cum-destruction of their own obscuring veils such as dust and mist, are the causes of the cognition of trees and other things;
and from what is seen, the existence of the unseen is established.

With the words "not imitated" (*nānanukṛta*) and so forth, he raises the objection of the opponent's view: that which has positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) not imitated by the effect is not a cause; rather, only that which has imitated positive and negative concomitance is a cause. And that which is not a cause is not an object of cognition. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the opponent's position. To this, he states the refutation: "the babbling of a child" (*bāliśagītam*), and so forth.

He asks, "Whence is this song spoken by the foolish and undiscriminating? and answers: "The perception of forms by nocturnal birds occurs when darkness exists due to the removal of an obstruction, not from light; such is the intended meaning.
Likewise, because that [obstruction] is not removed—that is, due to the absence of the removal of that obstruction—doubtful cognition and the like can arise even when light is present.
For this reason as well, he states that its perception does not arise from light—beginning with the words "glass" (*kāca*) and so forth:

"The term 'glass' refers to a specific eye disease; that which has 'timira' and others as its beginning is thus described. For those whose sense faculties are impaired by such [conditions], there arises a cognition of yellow and other forms regarding white objects such as conch shells. Therefore, the connection is that [the claim of perception] even when light is present is merely the babble of fools."

Likewise, for living beings on the verge of death, because there exists a contrary apprehension even when the object is present—provided that this occurs according to possibility and without overstepping what is possible—it is established that objects and so forth (the word "and so forth" including light and the like) are not the cause of cognition.
This was previously stated in consideration of the Naiyāyikas; the distinction is that this [view] belongs to the Saugatas.
As for the covering... [text fragment].
— That which is [the view] of the non-establishment of that [self], according to the Ārya and Śrāvaka [traditions], is the Buddhist doctrine (saugata-mata).
— That which is the light of truth for consciousness,
O seekers of liberation, [is] the [true] light.
Page 663.
Regarding the section on "pratibhāga," he states another refutation right here:
Neither its birth, nor its form, nor its ascertainment [is the cause] with respect to validity in this cognition, when aiming at the status of being a means of valid cognition.
They do not possess the status of being a cause or a causal condition;

rather, what does he say?—“arising from that”: arising (*janma*), that is, production (*utpatti*), [is not established] because its occurrence is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the collection of sense organs.

Nor is there “conformity to that” (*tādrūpya*): conformity (*tādrūpya*) is the state of having a form (*rūpa*) or aspect (*ākāra*) like the form of that object, and that is subject to deviation by means of a cognition that is simultaneous with and has the same object.

Nor is there a determination (*vyavasiti*) regarding that object; for "determination" (*vyavasāya*) means ascertainment (*niścaya*), and that [ascertainment] is subject to deviation due to the determination of a double moon and so forth. How so? Neither individually—that is, each one separately and specifically—nor collectively, do those [factors] possess the status of being causes of validity.

"Because there is a deviation [of the definition] even with respect to those three, due to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) which, though belonging to the pure series, generates a cognition having the form of yellow"—this is from the *Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra* (p.

79). Buddhist texts that determine the triad beginning with its birth as the cause of validity state: "The very form of the object (*viṣayākāra*) is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for by it [the object] is measured."
— Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.10:
Therefore, visual cognition arises in dependence upon both the eye and visible form.
If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be the object of cognition, the wise reply: its status as an object of cognition [is established].
Those who know the reasoning [of causality] maintain that the very nature of being a cause is the capacity to impart its own form [to the effect];
for even though an effect may have multiple causes, it arises imitating one of them,
and it is said that because of this, the form of that [specific cause] is apprehended therein.
It connects this [cognition] with the object, for it does so without abandoning its own objective form;
therefore, in the apprehension of the object of cognition, the means of cognition consists in having the form of the object— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.308.
For it is that [cognition] which, possessing a sensation, establishes the object according to its form— as "blue" or as "yellow"—
(Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 2).

For what purpose, then, is similarity (sārūpya) accepted as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It serves as the basis for the determination of the action and its object in the world; otherwise, through similarity, there would not be the cognition of a blue object as "blue" or a yellow object as "yellow. Thus, it is accepted for the sake of the specific restriction of action and object.
(Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 119).

Furthermore, the arising of a conforming conceptual construction (*anukūlavikalpa*) is itself the determination (*adhyavasāya*); for even non-conceptual perception possesses the power to produce a conceptual construction.
Because it serves as a constituent part of all remaining conventional discourse through that door—
[Tattvasaṃgraha Kārikā 1306]—
or else, each [of these] here functions as a cause with respect to validity. (58)
Commentary: An object is not the cause of cognition, because it ceases to exist without reaching the time of its effect, like something that has already passed away;
nor is cognition its effect, because cognition exists only when the object is absent and is absent when the object is present, like something yet to come;
furthermore, cognition does not possess the form of the object, because it is immaterial.

For it is observed that only corporeal objects, such as mirrors and the like, serve as the substrata for the reflections of corporeal things like faces; an incorporeal object does not bear the reflection of a corporeal one. Furthermore, cognition is incorporeal because it lacks the properties of corporeality;

indeed, the object does not exist within cognition, nor is it identical with its nature, such that when cognition manifests, the object would manifest within it—just as [an object] does not appear in a word.
Consequently, there could be no determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [object].

How could this triad, being non-existent, be helpful toward the validity of knowledge by way of being its definition? For it is impossible for that which does not reach the time of the effect to function as a cause, just like something that has long since passed away—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 89.
—[The opponent] who acts thus [says]:
"O Master, in the case of the manifest and the unmanifest...

[Commentary: A comparison—just as there is no designation for an object within the range of the senses, so too there is no object within sense-perception itself; therefore, even though it appears therein, it would not appear [as an object].
—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, p. 118.

Meaning of the verse: Therefore, in this world, birth from that object—that is, its arising—does not serve as the cause for the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the cognition; nor does "conformity" (*tādrūpya*)—the state of having a form like the form of that object—serve as the cause for it. This is the connection [of the sentence].

"Its determination" means the determination or ascertainment of that object; "not toward that" means it does not partake of that [determination]. Regarding the terms *saha* (together), *yugapat* (simultaneously), *pratyekam* (individually), or *ekamekam* (one by one)—the word *vā* being used as a conjunction—there is first of all no [determination] individually, because the group of sense organs (*karaṇagrāma*) that produces it is fallible; nor is there [determination] simultaneously, because of the deviation caused by a subsequent cognition of the same form (*tādrūpya*) regarding an identical object; nor is there [determination] through the determination of that [object], because of the non-exclusive nature of the erroneous cognition of yellow in a white conch-shell due to the cause of such an illusion.
In the Truṭi-pūrva manuscript, the reading is simply "bhajatīha";
however, because of the agent [of the action] in the phrase "tajjanma," the reading "bhajati" alone is appropriate, as there is no such meaning [in the other]. (Ā)
They serve as the cause for validity, according to the Śruti.
Regarding the word *bhajanti*:
according to Śrā, there is no *vā* or *nāsti* in Ba; [the meaning is that] birth and so forth do not individually possess the status of being a cause for validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Comparison—by what is there the cognition of that object? [If you say] "because of its having that form" (*tādrūpyāt*), that similarity to the object is fallible; for the forms of the cognition of two moons, floating hairs, or a net of hair exist even in the absence of an object.

Furthermore, showing that the claim that similarity to the object is the basis for experience is untenable, he says: "By what do those atoms produce a similar appearance, since they appear as gross? (*sarūpayanti tatkena sthūlābhāsañca te'ṇavaḥ*)?
Therefore, its possessing the form of an object— which does not deviate from a real object—
is not capable of establishing the state of being a cognition of that [object].
Therefore, for a cognition that is similar [to its object], there is no actual form of the object;
or, even if the form of the object were real, it would be fallible, as in the case of the cognition of two moons and so forth.
Furthermore, in establishing that the state of being a cognition of an object consists in its being a cognition of that object, that "form of the object" (artharūpatā) alone is not sufficient;
for the status of being a cognition of an object does not arise from mere similarity to the object (*sārūpya*) such that there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

What then? It arises from both similarity and origination from it (*tadutpatti*). And these two [conditions] do not exist in the case of cognitions such as that of two moons, because of the non-existence of a second moon and because of the impossibility of its originating from such a thing.

He says this very thing: "If similarity to that [object] and arising from that were the definition of being cognized, then a cognition of a similar object would be cognized immediately following [it]. (323)

If it is accepted that the definition of self-cognition consists in its similarity to the object and its arising from that [object], then even so, the immediately preceding cognition would be cognized by the subsequent cognition as having the same object— that is, as having the same apprehended content— because of the possibility of both similarity to it and arising from it. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 2.320–23)

Furthermore, if that from which and in whatever form a cognition arises were its objective support (*ālambana*), then in the case of a stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*), each preceding one would be the objective support for each subsequent one, because it produces it and because it possesses a similar form. However, this definition—characterized by being produced from that and having a similar form—is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*), as it occurs even in cases of different streams directed toward the same object; and so too does its status as the cause for the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that object.
(Bṛhatī Pañjikā, p. 79; Siddhiviniścaya-Ṭīkā, p. 566)
The arising of perception occurs not only through the power of the object, but also through the capacity of the eye and other sense organs.

If it is argued that the object appears therein because the perception imitates the form of the object, whereas the instrument [the sense organ] does not appear because it does not imitate its form—then, like the object, the instrument ought to be imitated. Yet it is not so, because there is no distinction [between them]. Even though there is no distinction in the perception’s being produced from that [object], the claim that it has the external object as its domain on the basis of a determination (*adhyavasāya*) is without substance; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of determining even the material cause (*upādāna*), such as the atoms of color and so forth.
(Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 118)
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
108; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 510; Prameyaratnakośa, 2.

Furthermore, would these two be the causes of apprehension individually or collectively? If individually, then the first moment of the potsherd and so forth would become the apprehender of the final moment of the jar, or the moon in the water the apprehender of the moon in the sky, because of [their] arising from that and having its form.
If, on the other hand, they are collective, then it follows that the moment following the jar would be the apprehender of the preceding moment of the jar.

If it is argued that these [mental factors] are the cause of apprehension because they possess the nature of cognition (*jñāna*), then it would follow that a cognition of a similar class must apprehend its immediately preceding cognition—*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* p. 20; *Pramāṇanayatatvāloka* 4.
Even when combined, those factors beginning with the birth of that [text] do not possess causality toward validity; thus,
commenting on the verse, he explains it with the words "nārthaḥ" (not the meaning), etc., while refuting this triad by means of the fault of impossibility (*asambhava*).

"How can an object be the cause of consciousness for a follower of the Sugata? To this he says: "Because [the object] ceases—that is, perishes—without reaching the time of its effect," namely, the time of its own cognition.

Regarding this, he states an illustration: the formal argument (*prayoga*) is "like an object that is extremely past. An object that has just passed away is not a cause of cognition, because it is in every respect non-existent at that time. Whatever is in every respect non-existent at a given time is not its cause, just like an object that is extremely past; and an object that has just passed away is in every respect non-existent at that time. By this, the causality of even a future object is also rejected.
And just as the object is not the cause of that cognition, so too that cognition is not its effect.

Why is this so? He says: "Because of that," and so forth. Because that cognition arises only when the object imagined by others is absent, and because it does not arise when that [object] is present; otherwise, there would be a cessation of the continuum.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "as in the case of the future. Furthermore, the causal efficiency of cognition has already been refuted at length previously; therefore, enough of this further digression concerning its threefold production and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: [it would follow that] because of its arising from that very [object], if the cognition, which is the effect, were to arise at the very same time as the object, which is the cause, then—due to the consequence of the cause and effect being simultaneous—the object, which is the cause, would exist at the time of its own cause, and that [cause] too at the time of its own cause; thus, all subsequent moments would exist at the time of the first moment, and since destruction occurs in the second moment, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total annihilation of the entire continuum (*saṃtāna*).

Comparison: If the effect were to exist only when the cause exists, then the entire threefold world would exist in a single moment; for at the very time of the causal moment, the entire subsequent series of moments would come into being, and consequently, there would be no such thing as a "series" (*santāna*).
— *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasāhasrī* p. 187; [the term] *sajjñānoccheda* is in manuscript *ba*.
To negate its similarity [to the object], he says: "Not the object," and so forth.
Consciousness does not possess similarity to the object;
why? Because it is formless (*amūrtatvāt*).

If it is asked, "But could that which is formless (amūrta) also be a bearer of reflection? What is the contradiction here?", he says in response: "Only those things that are formed (mūrta)," and so forth.
For it is observed that only formed objects such as mirrors and the like are bearers of reflections of formed things such as faces;
if it is argued that something formless is also seen [to bear a reflection], he says in response: "Nothing formless is seen to be a bearer of the reflection of a formed thing."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: cognition does not bear the reflection of an object, because it is formless (*amūrta*). Whatever bears the reflection of an object is not formless, such as a mirror and the like; yet cognition is formless. If it is asked, "How is its formlessness established? [the answer is: because of the absence of the properties of form (*mūrti*). For those properties consist in being insentient while possessing color, taste, smell, and touch; and these do not exist in cognition.

Furthermore, its similarity [to the object] has already been refuted at length in the section establishing its formlessness; therefore, enough with this effort, for [the claim that it possesses] the properties of a material thing— [is impossible],
since the properties of a material thing...
—*Kārasiddhi*, Āgamapṛṣṭha 167.
Refuting the determination of that [object], he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.

For this reason: since an object such as a jar does not exist within cognition as its substratum, but rather exists externally—or else the object is of the nature of that [cognition] or has cognition as its own essence—this is the connection [of the argument], because similarity [between object and cognition] is denied and because [the object] appears elsewhere.
This is what is intended: by which [means] it might appear in that consciousness while appearing there either as existing or as being of that nature;
for if one asks, "How is it that the object is not there, or how is it not of that nature?", he says here: "like sound," meaning "just like sound" (*tadvat*).
What happened after that? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

Since there is no appearance of the word and its object as being either contained within or identical to that [cognition] even when the nature of cognition itself appears, there would be no determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that object;

for determination is a cognition accompanied by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), and such a thing is not possible without the experience of those two [word and object], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

In detail, the refutation of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [object] by means of non-conceptual [cognition] has already been set forth in the establishment of conceptual cognition; therefore, we shall desist from further elaboration.

Thus, demonstrating how the result is established, he says: "How can this triad—which was stated by the opponent and is non-existent, characterized by its arising, similarity, and determination—be of assistance to the validity of cognition? Not in any way. In what form would it be of assistance? It would not be so at all. To this he replies: "By way of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatvena*)."
The intended meaning is that this [object] has the characteristic of being impossible,
because the object appears externally, in places such as the ground, rather than within cognition.
Or, by the reason of having the nature of cognition,
[the object] is in the cognition.
For he who [shows] by means of "consisting of knowledge" and so forth, [the nature of] knowledge—
[variant reading: for he who is not...].
Even conceptual construction is not devoid of verbal expression,
because it possesses the nature of verbalization.
Comparison— page 46, note 2:
verbal cognition [arises] from the word and its meaning.
pṛ॰ 48 atrasi— śra॰;
asambhavati lakṣa— śra॰

Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is impossible for cognition to possess those three [characteristics] arising from that [object], how can it be a grasper of the object? This would lead to over-extension. To this, he says: "Just as an object, though produced by its own causes, is determinable by itself..."
What [is it]? A jar or the like.
How could it be qualified? As something to be delimited or known.
How so? By its own nature alone, not by arising from cognition or the like.

Even though it is produced by its own cause— that is, even though it is generated and brought into existence by its own cause, the causal complex such as clay and so forth— how could cognition, which consists of determination, be of the nature of grasping an object?
[It cannot be], because it arises from its very own nature, and not from the production [of the object] or other such factors.

Of what specific nature is it? It is "arisen from its own cause" (*svahetūttha*). Its internal cause is characterized by the destruction-cum-subsidence of obscuration (*āvaraṇakṣayopaśama*), while its external cause consists of the sense organs and the mind (*indriyānindriya*). That which has its arising (*utthā*) or production from these is described as such; this is the meaning. (Laghīyastraya-tātparya-vṛtti, p.
80). This verse is cited in the following works: Siddhi-ṭīkā, p. 10B.
Likewise, cognition, arising from its own causes, is by its very nature determinative [of its object] intrinsically. (Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p.
33A) —[This concerns] the state of being a cause, [as explained in] the Jaina-viniścaya.

Commentary: Only when both the object (*artha*) and the cognition (*jñāna*) have attained their own existence from their respective causes does the relationship of the delimited (*paricchedya*) and the delimiting (*paricchedaka*) arise, not when they have not yet attained their own existence, just as in the case of the nature of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*).

Therefore, even in the absence of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), the relationship of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) would be established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvataḥ*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of systematic order (*vyavasthābhāva*). — *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vivaraṇa* (or similar commentary).
The meaning of the verse:

Even an object such as a jar, though produced by its own cause, is determinable by itself through its own nature, because it arises from its own cause with that very intrinsic character. For an object is not made to possess that [cognitive] nature by the cognition; otherwise, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the establishment of such an object would depend upon the establishment of the cognition, and the establishment of the cognition would depend upon the establishment of that object.

In whatever manner there is a capacity for such [cognition], so too is knowledge— arising from its own causes, produced by its own causes characterized as the instrument (karaṇa) and the mind (manas), consisting of determination, and having the nature of apprehending an object— not [produced] by itself through the production of the object and so forth;
even when produced, it is [known] by virtue of its own determinable nature, like a jar.
The nature of an object is its own essence (ā); the object has its own essence from itself (svataḥ) (ba);
it arises from its own form and cause (śra).
The commentary (*vivṛti*) provides an explanation:
in order to explain the verse, he says "of the object and the cognition," and so forth.

Only those [object and cognition] that attain their own existence from their respective causes—and not from each other—possess the relationship of the perceived and the perceiver according to their respective order; this is not the case for those that have not attained their own nature, nor for those that are entirely eternal or momentary.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "like the nature of agent and object.

Just as the nature of agent and object belongs only to these two when they have attained their own existence from their respective causes—neither for those that are absolutely existent nor for those that are non-existent—so too is the case with the subject under discussion.
For the sake of the conclusion, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Since that state of things is established for those two as they arise from their own respective causes, therefore, even without arising from that object, the relationship of apprehended and apprehender between the object and the cognition would be established.
Why? By way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that is, through their own specific capacity;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence of the absence of any systematic determination by any other means.
In the case of knowledge and its object— as in "one knows the jar"— there is the status of agent for the knowledge and the status of object for the jar; thus,
there is also the relationship of the apprehended and the apprehender.
Thus, there is no relationship of agent and object between cognition and its object.

Now, even if its existence as a distinct entity is established by its own nature, its fruit must be stated; and regarding that, some say it is mere apprehension (*adhigati-mātra*), others say it is the apprehension of the [cognition's] own nature, while still others say it is the apprehension of the object itself. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Regarding the state of the grasped and the grasper, the Buddhist masters..."
In both cases, that very cognition is the fruit [of the means of knowledge], because its nature is that of realization (*adhigama*)—
*Nyāyapraveśa*, p. 7—
and that same perceptual cognition is the fruit of the means of knowledge, because its nature is the apprehension of the object (*arthapratīti*).
—*Nyāyabindu*, p. 25;
*Tattvasaṅgraha*, verse 1343: "And its fruit is self-awareness."
The fruit [of valid cognition] is self-awareness. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.8)
— the Naiyāyikas and others— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.366.
Valid cognition (pramiti) is knowledge whose object is substance and so forth— [as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 187—
it is held to be determinate knowledge that apprehends the self and its objects.

What is the nature of that which is desired, liked, and known? What is the essential form of knowledge? It is said to have "determination" (*vyavasāya*) as its essence; that is, determination—meaning the ascertainment of a particular object through its forms such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is its very self, its essential nature. Thus it is described.
By this, the [definition] "perception is free from conceptual construction" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham*) has been refuted.

Furthermore, what is its specific qualification? It is "the grasper of itself and its object" (*ātmārthagrāhakam*). It grasps—that is, it determines—the nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*) and the external object (*artha*), such as a jar; thus, it is the grasper of itself and its object. By this, the two extremes are discarded: namely, that cognition is exclusively a grasper of the object and not a grasper of its own nature, or that it is exclusively a grasper of itself and not a grasper of the object. For that reason, what does it pervade (*aśnute*) or partake of (*bhajati*)? Grasping (*grahaṇa*), which is the agent, [pervades] cognition.

What is its nature? Its nature is the determination of its own object; this is the meaning. What is it that becomes the object [of the definition]? Validity (*prāmāṇya*), which is the state of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Of what kind is it? It is primary (*mukhya*) and does not follow [the characteristics of] inference, because sense organs, marks (*liṅga*), and so forth are considered means of valid cognition only by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), since they are causes of cognition.
—Laghīyastrayāloka, p. 81.
"Apprehension is determination; by means of that, it attains primary validity.
[Laghu-vṛtti] "Primary validity"—Jaṭā-vṛtti.
Commentary: There is no attainment of that which results in non-determination, because such a thing is logically untenable when investigated.

Furthermore, non-contradiction (avisaṃvādakatva) is dependent upon determination (nirṇaya), since it is absent when determination is absent and present when determination is present. Thus, it is established that knowledge whose result is ascertainment (vyavasāya) is the primary means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Since that which is inherently non-determinative cannot be a factor in the production of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), its fitness for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogyatā*) must not be denied if it is to be a factor in the production of that construction; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of conceptual construction.

When there exists a primary cognition consisting of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) which governs all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*), how can one be considered sound-minded who asserts that this [perception] is unperceived, ineffective, without means, and without an object?
—of the attainment of the fruit—ī॰ vi॰; even by itself, the final determination—ī॰ vi॰;
the meaning of the *kārikā*—.
"Vyavasāya" means determination; that whose essence (ātman) or nature (svabhāva) is this is "tadātmakam," meaning its essence is the fruit of determination.
By this, the view that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which produces the mere apprehension (*adhigati-mātra*) distinct from indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is rejected.
And what is the means of valid cognition that has such a fruit as its essence? He says: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*).

By this [argument] as well, the claim that the eye and other [senses] are instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is refuted, because there is a contradiction in their being of the nature of that [instrument]. Furthermore, it has been established in detail at *Laghīyastrayakārikā* 7—that the fruit (*phala*), which consists of the determination of self and object, is in some way non-different from the instrument of knowledge—and that each preceding [cognition] would be the instrument while each succeeding one is the fruit.
Now, he asks again: "Of what nature is that? and says: "It is the grasper of the self and the object; it is the knower of its own form and the form of others."
It is held that [cognition] is known through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-adhyakṣa*).

The fact that cognition grasps itself has been established in detail in the proof of self-awareness, and its fact that it grasps objects has been established in the proof of external objects; enough with this over-elaboration.
What, then, is established by this? To this he says: "The apprehension," and so forth.

For that reason— namely, because determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka-jñāna*) grasps both the self and its object— for that very reason, apprehension (*grahaṇa*), which is the ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) of the attainment of its own object, attains the status of primary, non-figurative validity (*prāmāṇya*); it is not the case for indeterminate [cognition] or the eye and other [senses], nor for the means of achieving the result of ascertainment (*nirṇaya-phala-sādhana*).
The nature of the eye and other [senses] consists in having the result of determinate cognition (vyavasāya) as their essence— or rather, not [having it as their essence].
pṛṣṭha 209;
pṛṣṭha 176–pṛṣṭha 119–
Regarding the mention [of this] by him, which is the explanation of the commentary (*vivṛti*),
he says— beginning with "of that which has non-determination as its result"— in order to explain the verse (*kārikā*) by way of its contrapositive (*vyatireka*).

The meaning is that there is no "attainment"—that is, no experience—of that which has the result of non-determination, being devoid of the result of certainty, namely, the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Why is this so? He says: because it is untenable when subjected to investigation. Whatever is untenable when investigated cannot be experienced, just as is the case with principles such as non-duality (*advaita*) or emptiness (*śūnya*). Furthermore, the non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakadarśana*) is likewise untenable when investigated; how this investigation renders it untenable has been explained at length in the establishment of the conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Now, if it is argued that non-conceptual [cognition] possesses validity because it is non-discrepant, to this he says: "Non-discrepancy," and so forth.

Non-discrepancy is the state of the apprehended object being exactly as it was grasped; that [validity] is dependent upon that [non-discrepancy], which in turn is dependent upon a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

In the absence of such a determination—whether in the perception of momentary destruction and so forth, or in the perception of a mirage and so forth, which produce doubt—there is an absence of non-contradiction; whereas in its presence—that is, when there is the existence of a determination—there is the existence of non-contradiction. Thus, it is established that knowledge whose fruit is ascertainment (*vyavasāya*) is the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the conclusion (p. 47).
Or, [if it is argued that] there is doubt regarding the vision of destruction and so forth, and since there is the presence of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), [it is not indeterminate].

If it is argued: "Let it be that the non-conceptual [cognition] itself is not of the nature of determination; nevertheless, it may be its result because it generates it," to this he says: "Intrinsically" (*svataḥ*), etc.
Since that which is itself non-determinate (*avyavasāya*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) is incapable of being a factor for the production of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*),
and since this has been explained in detail in the proof of the existence of conceptual cognition, it is not discussed here.
Alternatively, he states the refutation regarding its being such a factor, beginning with "that" (*tat*), etc.
With respect to the arising of that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the capacity for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa*)—which is itself non-determinative—is not to be denied.

"Verbal expression" (*abhilāpa*) refers either to that by which something is expressed or to that which is expressed; it consists of the genus of sound (*śabda-jāti*) and so forth. "Association" (*saṃsarga*) is the relationship characterized by the signifier-signified (*vācya-vācaka*) relation. "Capacity for that" (*tasmai yogyaḥ*) means fit for that [association]; its state (*tattā*) is what is not to be denied.

For just as the cognition’s possession of that [object’s] form is inferred from the observation of even a slight trace of the object’s form in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), so too should its capacity for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogyatā*) be inferred from the observation of that [capacity] in the conceptual construction; for there is no difference between the two cases. Why then is this distinction made—that such capacity belongs to the conceptual construction but not to the object’s form within the cognition? In refuting that [distinction], he states the fault with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth: because otherwise, by way of negating that capacity, it would follow that conceptual constructions could not arise at all. The connection is that "that [capacity] is not to be negated."

[Objection: "Surely, conceptual construction arises solely from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction; perception (*darśana*), however, is merely its awakener. Therefore, this is not a fault. To this, he says: "When [it] exists," and so forth.

When there exists a primary cognition that consists of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), which is independent of anything else and establishes itself and others—furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "entire," and so forth.

How can the Buddhist be at ease while asserting that the entire range of worldly activity—characterized by the experience of objects, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), their awakening, recollection, recognition, reasoning, inference, and purposeful action—is governed by that [non-conceptual cognition]? What does he assert? He says: "Cognition.

Of what nature is it? It is "inefficacious" (*akiñcitkara*), "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*), and "unperceivable" (*asaṃvedya*). It is "unperceivable" because it is not perceived; or, it is so called because for it there exists no perceivable object (*saṃvedya*) to be grasped. For this very reason, it is "without means" (*anupāya*) and "not to be attained" (*anupeya*); such is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

Because it generates conceptual constructions characterized by determination (*vyavasāyātmaka-vikalpa*), the prima facie position is as follows: therefore, perception becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when it performs determination; for if determination is not performed, the cognition remains undetermined in its nature as the awareness of blue—*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p. 27.
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* on verse 1306:

"This is not a fault [of perception], because it is the cause of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)," says the Buddhist; this is an unexamined statement, because in that [perception] there is an absence of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).
(*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasāhasrī*, p. 118)
And regarding this, [Śrīdhara, p.
47] states:
"For the Buddhists accept that perception consists of a non-conceptual nature; therefore, they deny that perception possesses the capacity for association with words."

And so it has been said: "Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the cognition of an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression; that which is devoid of this [is perception]"—*Nyāyabindu*, p. 13, etc.
(Śrīdhara).
— Or rather, [it is] because one observes that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form "this is blue" possesses the aspect of blueness.
The non-perception [of the object]— that is, the non-conceptual direct perception— possesses the form of blue.

The non-conceptual [cognition] has the form of blue; for otherwise, the appearance of the form of blue in the conceptual cognition arising from it would be inexplicable. This being so, [it follows that] the conceptual [cognition]... [is based on perception].

The capacity for association with verbal expression exists in non-conceptual [perception], because otherwise the capacity for association with verbal expression in the conceptual cognition produced from it would be inexplicable.
This is the case for conceptual cognition.

The point is this: if the capacity for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogyatā*) is impossible in direct perception (*darśana*), yet possible in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then even though the form of blue (*nīlākāra*) is impossible in direct perception, it would exist in conceptual construction. Consequently, since the conceptual construction of "blue" would directly have the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue as its object, this would contradict the established tenet that "conceptual construction has the appearance of a non-entity" (*avastu-nirbhāsa*). For comparison: just as there is an absence of verbal expression regarding color and so forth, so too is there an absence of it in direct perception, because the latter is free from the conceptualization of verbal expression and arises through the causal efficiency of an object whose nature is non-verbal.

If it is assumed that perception performs a determinative function even in the absence of that [conceptual content], why would perception not itself determine the particular (svalakṣaṇa), even though it is devoid of verbal expression?

How can it be a well-established statement that the cause of determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) is perception itself and not form (*rūpa*) and so forth? If, however, it is held that even from non-conceptual perception the production of determinate cognition—which is conceptual in nature—occurs, just as the production of soot and the like occurs from a lamp and the like since effects are seen to arise even from causes of a different genus; then let such perception, being conceptual in nature, likewise arise from its object for that very same reason.

If it is asked: "How can perception, which consists of the conceptualization of universals and so forth, arise from an object that is devoid of the conceptual constructions of universals, substances, qualities, actions, and designations?"—then the same objection applies: "How can a conceptual construction consisting of the conceptualization of universals and so forth arise from a perception that is itself devoid of them? (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā-vyākhyā, p. 118).
[The manuscript reads *vikalpotpa* for *vikalpāt*.]
The latent impression of conceptual construction (*vikalpavāsanā*) is the object of inference (*anumeya*).
Thus, having established that cognition which is determinate in nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a general sense, he now speaks while showing its divisions:

In this context, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which consists of right knowledge, is of only two kinds; it is indeed of two types. Those two types are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition (*parokṣa*). This applies to all cognitions other than [self-awareness].

One might object: "But surely, the enumeration of the distinctions among the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as inference and so forth, could also be conceived. To this he says: "In this regard," and so on.
Why are they not tenable? Why are they impossible? They are the "restrictions" (niyamāḥ), namely, the propositions asserting numbers such as two, three, and so forth.
Of what kind are they? They are "conceived by others," meaning constructed or fashioned by others such as the followers of Sugata (Buddhists) and so forth.
Why are they not tenable? Because of their inclusion—that is, because of their subsumption—within what? Within other cognitions, namely inferential and other types of knowledge.
Where? Right here, within the very inclusion of the perceptible and the imperceptible... — Laghīyastrayālaṃkāra, p. 81:
"Because they are included herein, the restrictive rules (niyama) imagined by others are not tenable. [61]

—Now, Jaṭāsiṃhanandin’s *Vivṛti*: Sensory cognition (*indriyārthajñāna*) is clear perception (*pratyakṣa*) characterized by apprehension (*avagraha*), speculation (*īhā*), perceptual judgment (*avāya*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*); it is capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, yet remains limited (*prādeśika*).
Non-sensory perception (*anindriyapratyakṣa*) consists of recollection (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), deliberation (*cintā*), and discernment (*abhinibodha*).
Supersensuous perception is of the nature of determinate cognition, extremely clear, non-erroneous, supersensuous, unobstructed, supramundane, and has the self and its objects as its domain;
it exists because there is no valid means of knowledge that can subvert it with absolute certainty, just like pleasure and other such experiences.
Scriptural testimony is indirect, expresses the extent and nature of all means and objects of knowledge, and is a valid means of knowledge free from contradiction.

In this system, presumption (*arthāpatti*), inference (*anumāna*), analogy (*upamāna*), and so forth are included [within the two primary means of knowledge]. Since the refutation of other means of knowledge postulated by others has been discussed elsewhere, it is not stated here. Regarding the comparison: accomplishment is based on knowledge; "accomplishment" consists of the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the acquisition of what is to be adopted.
Therefore, it may be said that the establishment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted consists in their respective rejection and acceptance—*Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*, p.
8—for valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful; thus, it is knowledge itself.
— Examination of Perception 1.2; Valid Cognition and Perspectives 1.1.
Conventional perception (*sāṃvyavahārika-pratyakṣa*). Comparison: *Laghīyastraya-ṭīkā*, p. 132, l. 10.

It is equal to the definition; this much is the distinction: it has the entire range as its object, is beyond succession and causal instruments, and is stainless for the most eminent beings—Nyāyaviniścaya, Kārikā 168.

The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that the cognition established as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is of the nature of ascertainment, is of exactly two kinds—it is not of one kind, nor of three or more kinds.
How is it of exactly two kinds? He says: "Perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*).
The word "iti" should be understood here; thus, [it is] in this way, and not by way of perception and inference alone.

[Objection: But since inference, analogy, and so forth are distinct from those [two], how can there be the restriction that [valid cognition] is of only two kinds? To this, he says: "In this regard," and so on.

In this context, because other correct cognitions are included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*parokṣa*), there are only two kinds; and this inclusion has been examined in the section on non-perception.
And for this reason, the restrictive rules (niyama) imagined by others, such as the followers of Sugata and so forth, are not tenable;
for those who know the Veda, there are only two [types of knowledge].
The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation:
Expounding upon the verse (*kārikā*), he says "the sense-faculties," and so forth.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is knowledge that is the effect of the sense-faculties—such as the eye—and which apprehends an object such as a jar, but not [an object] such as the water of a mirage. It is direct perception.

Of what nature is it? It is clear (*spaṣṭa*), distinct (*viśada*), non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), indirect (*parokṣa*), or direct perception through another cognition (*jñānāntarapratyakṣa*). To the question of how it might be so, he says: "Beneficial" (*hita*), etc.

"Beneficial" (*hita*) means happiness (*sukha*) and its means; "unbeneficial" (*ahita*) means suffering (*duḥkha*) and its causes. Capable (*samartha*) means fit (*yogya*) for the attainment of the former and the avoidance of the latter.

Furthermore, non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) and the like lack the capacity for that [subsequent cognition], because, as stated in the section establishing conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*), they lack the capacity even for the apprehension of the mere object.

Now, one might object: "Since the object is grasped in its entirety by conceptual perception, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should function with respect to it. To this he replies: "Partial" (*prādeśika*);
all perception belonging to people such as ourselves is restricted to only a certain part [of the object].

Just as in the vision of two moons and so forth, there is the non-perception of oneness and other qualities by the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), or just as in the perception of blue and other colors, there is the non-perception of momentary transformation,
[the author] now demonstrates the self-cognizing direct perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) of sensory cognition, saying "of the senses," etc.:

the effect of the senses is the knowledge of the nature of the self's cognitions, which is clear, capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, localized, and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
What is the difference between those two? To this he says: [it is] that which consists of *avagraha*, *īhā*, *avāya*, and *dhāraṇā*.

The commentator has explained *avagraha* and the others in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pariccheda*). That cognition whose nature consists of these is the agent; [it is] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). B.

If it is asked, "But surely sensory knowledge is also indeed an effect of that which is not a sense-organ; how then is this distinction [justified]?"—the answer is: because of the relationship between the primary and the secondary.
For in sensory knowledge, the sense-organs are the primary factor, whereas here it is the non-sensory [mind]; thus, the distinction is appropriate.
"What is its nature? To this he says: "It consists of memory, conception, reflection, and discernment.

Now, one might object: since memory and the others were previously established as being indirect (parokṣa), how is it appropriate to establish them here as direct (pratyakṣa)? This would lead to a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. This objection, however, is an unexamined statement; for they are established as direct precisely in that aspect where they possess clarity.

Indeed, their clarity exists only in their own essential form (svarūpa); therefore, they are direct in that very respect, because of the connection [of the term] with "knowledge of the self" (ātmajñāna).
Regarding external objects, however, because this [cognition] is indistinct, its status as indirect (parokṣatā) entails no fault;
here too, the phrase "for one's benefit" and so forth is connected,
and the mention of "memory and so on" is an illustration (upalakṣaṇa), by which "consisting of pleasure and so forth" is also included.

[the portion] "śra" refers to predominance and its opposite.

Comparison: Sense-perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*) arises from the predominance of the senses and the support of non-sensory power; non-sense-perception (*anindriya-pratyakṣa*) arises solely from the non-sensory, depending upon purification—*Prameyaratnāvalī* 2.4.

Thus he said;
now, for the purpose of defining supersensuous perception (*atīndriya-pratyakṣa*), he says "supersensuous" and so forth.

Supersensuous perception is that which transcends the sense organs (*indriyebhyo 'tikrāntam*). Of what nature is it? It is of the nature of determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmakam*); by this, the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) [perception] postulated by the Sāṃkhyas and the Sautrāntikas is refuted.
Most clearly, through our own direct perception, it is more distinct and unerring than in its entirety regarding its own object;
by this, O monks, I have also rejected [the notion that things are real], saying: "I too am like an illusion, like a dream."
Establishing its transcendence of the senses, he says "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*) and so forth.

"Beyond the senses" means not produced by the operation of the senses. Why? Because it is "unobstructed," that is, devoid of obstructions such as spatial distance and the like. Whatever is unobstructed in its own object-domain is not produced by the operation of the senses, just like the cognition of a true dream.

And since supersensuous perception is likewise unobstructed in its own object-domain, the argument that "the Lord’s cognition is born from the contact of sense-organ and object because, while being a perception, it is a cognition, like other cognitions" is thereby refuted.

Since it has been established in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*) that if such knowledge were produced by the sense faculties, it would not have all things as its object, [the author states] "supramundane" (*lokottara*), meaning superior to the entire world, and having the self and the object as its domain. By the phrase "having the self as its domain," the Lord's direct perception (*īśvarādhyakṣa*), which is not self-cognized, is refuted;
for it has been demonstrated that if it does not have the self as its object, it is logically impossible for it to have the object as its domain.
By the phrase "having an object as its domain," however, the [opponent's] claim that "there is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.327) is refuted;
for if the intellect did not have an object as its domain, its very nature as intellect would be untenable, since its essential character consists in the determination of both itself and others.
Furthermore, the external object has been established in detail during the occasion of proving the existence of external objects.

Now, one might object: "Is this not like describing the beauty of the son of a barren woman? For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known the existence of supersensible perception (*atīndriya-pratyakṣa*), and thus it is non-existent, like a flower in the sky. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That exists," and so forth.
That supersensible perception exists because there is no means of valid cognition that can definitely establish its impossibility, just as in the case of pleasure and the like.

Furthermore, the fact that this [argument] possesses a well-ascertained absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been established at length in the section on the Proof of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña-siddhi*); therefore, enough with the effort of proving it again.

The non-returner is like an illusion, like a dream; the fruit of non-returning is like an illusion, like a dream. The Arhat is like an illusion, like a dream; Arhatship is like an illusion, like a dream. Even a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha) is like an illusion, like a dream;

Showing the distinction between what is heard regarding the imperceptible and such things as probability and tradition, he says:
What are the two types of application known as *syādvāda* and *naya* that belong to sacred scripture (*śruta*)? The two applications are its functional operations.

Of what? Of *śruta* (scriptural knowledge). That which is heard is *śruta*; it consists of the words of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*) and takes the form of phonemes, words, and sentences as a substance (*dravya*). Or, according to the etymological derivation (*nirukti*), *śruta* is that which is heard, namely *bhāva-śruta*. How many are there? Two. What are their names? They are designated as *syādvāda* and *naya*. *Syādvāda* is a statement made in some way (*syāt kathañcit*) in relation to its counter-position. *Naya* is the leading (*nayana*) toward a specific attribute of an object intended for expression. Both *syādvāda* and *naya* together are *syādvādanayau*; those two whose designations (*saṃjñā*) and expressions (*vyapadeśa*) are thus [defined] are described in that manner.

He defines those two by their characteristics: What is called *syādvāda*? *Sakalādeśa* is the comprehensive statement (*ādeśa*) or description of an entity possessing manifold attributes (*anekadharman*). For example, the six categories—living beings (*jīva*), matter (*pudgala*), motion (*dharma*), rest (*adharma*), space (*ākāśa*), and time (*kāla*)—are further [classified] according to the *naya*.

What is it? It is a discourse on a partial [attribute] (*vikalasakathā*). A discourse (*kathā*) is the presentation of a single intended attribute (*dharmā*) of that which is partial, in relation to its correct counter-correlate (*pratipakṣa*), such as "the soul (*jīva*) is indeed a knower (*jñātṛ*) and indeed a seer (*draṣṭṛ*)" (Laghīyastraya-tātparya-vṛtti, p.

83). Compare: "It has been said: 'There are two types of application (*upayoga*) for the scripture (*śruta*), distinguished by the categories of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and viewpoints (*naya*')."
—Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, folio 4A.

Syādvāda is the comprehensive statement (sakalādeśa), while [other] doctrines are partial descriptions. Syādvāda is the expression of the intended property, joined with the particle *syāt*, which indicates all other remaining properties distinct from the property being currently specified.
—*Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā*, p. 93;
*Nyāyakumuda*, p. 3, note 10.

Commentary: Syādvāda is the statement of objects as having a manifold nature (anekāntātmaka); for example: soul (jīva), matter (pudgala), merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), space (ākāśa), and time (kāla).

In this regard, the soul (*jīva*) is characterized by non-common attributes such as knowledge, perception, energy, and bliss; by common-and-non-common attributes such as formlessness, having innumerable spatial points (*pradeśas*), and subtlety; and by common attributes such as existence, knowability, relative weight (*agurulaghutva*), being a substratum (*dharmitva*), and possessibility (*guṇitva*). Thus, the soul is manifold (*anekānta*).
The doctrine of conditional predication (*syādvāda*) constitutes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that soul through its various perspectives (*ādeśa*).
Likewise, other categories should be applied according to the supreme scripture (*paramāgama*).
"The soul (jīva) is a knower because of its experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth"— such is the *nayavikalādeśa* (the partial presentation of a perspective).

Completeness (*sākalya*) consists in having an infinite nature of attributes (*anantadharmātmakatā*), whereas deficiency (*vaikalya*) is one-sidedness (*ekānta*) resulting from the non-intention of expressing other attributes.

In that regard, when the word "jīva" is uttered, the term "jīva"—which relies on its own fitness, possesses beginningless convention, and functions to signify its own referent through the exclusion of others by its very nature—would denote the mere jīva alone by completely setting aside all counter-positions. However, through the employment of the word *syāt* (in some respect), and by the abandonment of absolute exclusivity (*ekānta*), the jīva is expressed as qualified by the fourfold attributes such as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth; thus, our desired conclusion is established. Likewise, the *naya* (perspective) is also correctly an exclusive standpoint (*samyagekānta*).

When it is said, "Syāt jīva eva" (In some respect, it is indeed a jīva), the word *syāt* has for its object non-exclusivity (*anekānta*). When it is said, "Syād asty eva jīvaḥ" (In some respect, the jīva exists indeed), the word *syāt* has for its object exclusivity (*ekānta*).

Through the employment of the word "syāt" (in some respect), there is the cognition of those qualities that are unique to [the soul], such as knowledge, perception, and bliss; those that are common to the astikāyas of dharma, adharma, space, and matter, characterized by formlessness, innumerable spatial points, and subtlety; and even those that are common to all categories of existence, such as existence, knowability, being a substratum, and possessibility of qualities—Āvaśyaka-niryukti-malaya-vṛtti, folio 170A.

Although there is generally a consensus among all [scholars] regarding the essential nature of *sakalādeśa* (the complete predication) and *vikalādeśa* (the partial predication), certain teachers such as Akalaṅka and others maintain that, among the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), all propositions (*bhaṅga*) take the form of *sakalādeśa* when they establish an object consisting of all its attributes through the medium of a single attribute; however, at the time of expression, when one attribute is primary and other attributes are secondary, they accept them as being of the nature of *vikalādeśa*.

And some, such as Siddhasena Gaṇi and others, consider the three modes (bhaṅgas) consisting of existence, non-existence, and the inexpressible to be of the nature of complete predication (sakalādeśa), while they regard the remaining four modes as being of the nature of partial predication (vikalādeśa). This is according to the texts of Akalaṅka and others; as it has been said: "Complete predication is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), whereas partial predication is dependent upon the viewpoints (naya).
— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.6.18.

Where and when there is simultaneity, that is the *sakalādeśa* (complete predication), because it encompasses the entire nature of the object through the medium of a single attribute; thus it is called *sakalādeśa*.
In that regard, by virtue of the specific instruction (*ādeśa*), there is a sevenfold division for each word;

however, when there is a sequence, then there is a partial instruction (*vikalādeśa*). Even for that which is partless (*niraṃśa*), there is the conceptualization of parts due to the distinction of qualities; this is partial instruction, and therein likewise there is a sevenfold division.
—*Rājavārttika*, p. 181; *Nayacakra*, p. 348B:

For the comprehensive statement (*sakalādeśa*) presents an object consisting of all its attributes simultaneously as non-different from [the subject] through time and other factors, either by way of non-difference (*abheda-vṛtti*) or by means of metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), because it is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Partial predication (vikalādeśa), however, occurs either through sequential [predication], through metaphorical attribution of difference, or through the predominance of difference—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 136; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 682.
Divided into seven parts, page 32;
*Pramāṇanayatantra*, 4.44, 45.

"This sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*)—in each individual proposition—is of the nature of both a complete assertion (*sakalādeśa*) and a partial assertion (*vikalādeśa*).
— *Pramāṇanaya*, 4.
