Regarding the other [standpoints], the author now demonstrates the *naya* (perspective), saying "the knower," and so forth.

"The soul" (*jīva*) is the designation of the subject (*dharmin*). "A knower, whose nature is consciousness" is the thesis (*sādhya*). "Because of the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth" is the reason (*hetu*). Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated. That which has as its beginning the word "impermanent" and others is described as such. And that is the *naya*, which is the indication of a partial property (*vikala-dharma*) that is independent of other properties.

Now, one might ask: what is this "completeness" (*sākalya*) and what is "incompleteness" (*vaikalya*) of a statement, such that *syādvāda* could be called a "complete statement" (*sakalādeśa*) as a perspective (*naya*), while [other views] would be called "incomplete discourse"? To this, he says: "Completeness," and so forth. "Completeness" (*sākalya*) is the state (*bhāva*) of a complete entity—that is, its nature consisting of infinite attributes (*anantadharmātmakatā*).
The word is used in this way because the term for the object (*viṣaya*) is applied metaphorically to the subject (*viṣayin*), namely the statement that expresses it.
The state of being incomplete (*vaikalya*) is the deficiency (*vaikalya*) of one part; that is called "one-sidedness" (*ekānta*).
Why is it so designated? To this he says: "Because of another property," and so forth.

A property other than the intended property is "that other" (*tadantara*); because of the non-intentionality regarding that [other property], and not otherwise, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a fallacious standpoint (*durnaya*).

[Objection: "Since there is no relationship between a word and its referent, activity [of the word] is impossible; therefore, the exposition of all complete and partial standpoints (naya) is not tenable. To this, he says: "In that regard," and so forth.

In that regard, while reality is established as possessing infinite aspects (*anantātman*), or rather, when that very nature of the *syādvāda* and *naya* has been thus described, if one says "jīva," the word "jīva" would denote merely the jīva itself, devoid of internal distinctions.
Of what kind? He says: "Capability," and so forth.

*Yogyatāpekṣaḥ* means that which has a dependence on fitness (*yogyatā*), or that which depends upon fitness. *Anādisaṅketaḥ* refers to that whose convention (*saṅketa*) is beginningless. By the term "fitness" (*yogyatā*), [the author] demonstrates the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word and meaning even in the absence of a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), and even in the absence of a permanent, uniform relationship; this is because a relationship consisting of the very nature of fitness is possible. This has already been explained in detail previously.
Regarding the phrase "kalyavādeśa":
by the word *sākalya*, that which is denoted— namely, the totality consisting in the nature of having infinite attributes— is intended.
In the Syādvāda, which expresses all aspects, there is no rejection of other properties; this is not the case for the Buddhist.

If reality (*tattva*) consists of infinite natures, then surely, even on the basis of fitness (*yogyatā*), there would be the simultaneous comprehension of multiple meanings from a single word, since it is possible for every word to possess the fitness to convey every meaning; this [consequence] is untenable. By the term "convention" (*saṅketa*), he shows that even though the fitness to convey multiple meanings exists, the comprehension of a specific meaning is established by virtue of a restricted convention.
And this has been explained in the *Laghīyastraya-kārikā* (verse 26) under the heading: "This is the means of valid cognition, namely, scripture (*śruta*)."

If it is objected: "When the word *jīva* denotes its object, there is no prior convention (*saṅketa*) at that time; how then can it be the cause for the cognition of a fixed meaning, since it depends upon such a convention?"—we say: No, because the convention consists in the mind’s [determination] that "this is the denotable" and "this is the denoter," and because that [convention] exists even at that time. Nor is this merely an intermediate conceptual construction; he shows this by the term "beginningless" (*anādi*). Now, it might be argued that it is incorrect to say [the word] "denotes the mere living being" (*jīvamātra*), because the meaning of a word is either the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), or the universal (*jāti*), or both of these [exclusion and universal] which are mutually distinct. To this, he says: "Its own nature" (*svabhāva*), and so forth.

That which has exclusion (*apoha*) from everything else as its inherent nature—that is, non-existence in the form of another—is so described. And that very thing is the "own-object" (*svārtha*), meaning its own denotation; the word "jīva" is the communicator of that. What would it denote? It would denote that alone. Having done what? Having excluded what? The opposing view, characterized by the claim that [the word] denotes mere exclusion and so forth.

How so? In detail—that is, in its entirety—it has been demonstrated at length in the *Laghīyastraya* (verse 26) that the theory of exclusion (*apoha*) and the like cannot logically constitute the meaning of words, as explained in the passage beginning with "The means of valid cognition [is established] regarding objects" (*pramāṇaṃ śrutamartheṣu*).

Therefore, by that reasoning, through the employment of the term *syāt* (in some sense), there is the abandonment—that is, the rejection—of absolute monism (*sarvathaikānta*) such as "the soul exists alone," "it does not exist alone," "it is only of the nature of substance," or "it is only of the nature of modification. Thus, the soul, characterized by the fourfold qualifications beginning with its own nature (*svarūpa*), and qualified by its own substance, space, and so forth, is denoted by the word "soul"; this establishes the soul as having the desired nature of non-absolutism (*anekāntātman*). [The objection that] "the expression of all meanings by the word 'all' (*sarvaśabda*) is untenable"—this is refuted by the following verse: [Verse 12: "That which is restricted... (*yāṃ niyata-*)... [Aṣṭasāhasrī].
The former [is] *saketa* (convention); if that word "jīva" depends upon a beginningless convention (*anādisaṅketa*), then [it is] because of that convention.
The Buddhists [hold that] it is of the mind; the Mīmāṃsakas [hold that it is] of the self.
The two [types of] yoga, as well as the Śrauta and Āgama.

Having thus presented the statement of valid cognition (*pramāṇavākya*), he now says "the perspective (*naya*) also," etc., in order to demonstrate the statement of perspective (*nayavākya*). Not only is there the statement of valid cognition, but the statement of perspective as well—only by means of the aforementioned method of employing the term *syāt*—would it be a correct partial truth (*samyagekānta*), having a correct partial truth as its object; otherwise, it would have a false partial truth as its domain. Now, demonstrating the utility of employing the particle *eva*, he says "syāt," etc.

The term *anekāntaḥ* (non-absolutism) is understood here as being carried over from the previous context; therefore, this meaning is established: "In some respect (*kathañcit*), the soul alone (*jīva eva*) is non-absolutistic by virtue of its attributes—knowledge, vision, bliss, and power—and nothing else. This is the sense of the particle *eva*.

When such a statement is thus employed, the word does not have an absolute scope, but rather has a non-absolute scope; the sentence "it is in some respect the soul alone" possesses a non-absolute form because it expresses that very thing which is of a non-absolute nature.

When it is stated, "The soul (jīva) exists indeed," the word "syāt" (perhaps/maybe) becomes one whose object is non-absolute, having as its range the correct non-absolute; that is, the sentence "syād asty eva" (perhaps it exists indeed). This is because it primarily establishes the non-absolute nature of that existence. The same should be said for the subsequent propositions (bhaṅgas) as well;
[otherwise] there would be no perspective (naya).
There is also no sentence of the *nayavākya* type— [that is],
one joined with the word *syāt*— in the absence of the employment of the word *syāt*.

Regarding the [objection] that in cases such as "the soul might exist" or "it does not exist at all," ordinary people do not employ the particles *syāt* and *eva* in every sentence— since their usage is seen otherwise, and therefore this [rule] is not tenable— the author speaks in order to dispel such a doubt:

They employ [the particle *syāt*]; there would thus be a rule regarding the application of the word *syāt*. Even if not employed everywhere, the particle *kāra* (the suffix *-ka*) is understood from the sense of the meaning.
What is cognized or understood? It is the word *syāt*, an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Where? Everywhere—in the treatises or in the world.
In what subject matter? In an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding existence (*sattva*) and so forth, which is to be established (*sādhya*).
Not only in the case of a positive injunction, but also in the case of a prohibition— even when non-existence and so forth are the probandum,

or even in other cases such as restatement (*anuvāda*) and extended application (*atideśa*)— it may occur even if unqualified and even if unstated, as in the case of [the phrase] "the living self exists."

If it is asked, "Then from what is this understood? he says here: "From the sense," that is, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), if [the listener] were skillful, meaning if they were awakened regarding linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
Who? The instigator (*prayojaka*) and the communicator (*pratipādaka*).
—Cited from *Laghīyastrayāloka*, p.
86— "In the case of affirmation, [it occurs] through negation, and likewise elsewhere"—*Āvaśyakaniyukti-malaya-vṛtti*, fol.
369B; *Gurutattvaviniścaya*, p. 16A.
Comparison: Even when not explicitly employed due to the speaker's intention, every meaning is understood here;
a sentence has exclusion as its result, just as in the cases: "Caitra is an archer," "Pārtha is an archer," or "The lotus is blue."
— Pramāṇavārttika 4.191–92:
And by virtue of its capacity, even when [the particle] *eva* is not employed, the meaning would certainly be understood.
—Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 507b; Nyāyaviniścaya, kā. 453:
Even if not explicitly employed, that [reason] is understood everywhere by those who know it through implication (ārthāt).
Just as the particle *eva* has the purpose of excluding non-connection and so forth—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 137;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 718.
*Ratnākarāvatāra*, page 61;
*Saptabhaṅgītaraṅgiṇī*, page 31;
*Syādvādamañjarī*, page 279.
*Nayapradīpa*, folio 96A:
"Even when the method [of proof] is joined, if one is skilled in negation elsewhere, he is the prompter; even in the case of the *Mukhya-laghu* [system], [this applies]. (63)

Commentary: In some cases, those who do not wish to employ the term "syāt" (perhaps) would have to accept absolute monism (ekānta), because even in the absence of an explicit restriction (avadhāraṇa), the exclusion of non-absolutism (anekānta) necessarily follows; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the identity of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the viewpoints (naya).

What need is there for further elaboration? It is well known even to children that in sentences involving affirmation, negation, restatement, or extension, in grammatical factors such as the agent and so forth, in the meanings of nominal stems such as the primary sense and so forth, and in statements regarding proof, refutation, and their fallacies, there is no establishment of the subject matter without the doctrine of "syāt."
—Regarding the necessity of accepting [the doctrine of] formlessness—the meaning of the verse in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāviveka* is as follows:

the particle "syāt" (perhaps/maybe) would not only be employed where it is explicitly used, but would occur everywhere in every sentence; this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which the particle "eva" (only/alone) is also understood.
Why is this so? He says: "By implication" (arthāt), that is, by force of context (*sāmarthyāt*).
To illustrate: when it is said, "Bring water," if the bringing of both water and something else were intended by worldly people, then the inclusion of the word "water" would be redundant.
Conversely, if non-bringing were intended, then the mention of "bringing" would be useless.
And since there is the apprehension of both [the positive and the negative], the cognition of the particle *eva* occurs;

where? In both affirmation and negation. Furthermore, the word *api*, though occurring at a different point in the construction, is to be understood as following the word *anyatra*—that is, even in other cases such as restatement (*anuvāda*), extended application (*atideśa*), and so forth.
Now, if that [universal] were perceived everywhere, then even in such cases as "a hundred herds of elephants reside on the tip of a finger," it would be so perceived;
and thus, since everything would possess both forms, there would follow the faults mentioned in Pramāṇavārttika 3.181 and elsewhere. To this, he says: "The skillful," and so forth.

Just as a person who has understood an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be a skillful communicator who explains it exactly as it was understood and not otherwise— provided that he is one who employs words— it follows from this very [fact] that he is not [merely] a speaker.
The removal [of the vowel] should be observed in manuscript *ba* and manuscript *śra*;
compare this with other instances as well— in explanatory, extended application, and similar statements.
—Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Malayagiri commentary, folio 369B;
page 530, note 3;
page 620, note 5.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation:
Explaining the verse by way of its contrapositive (*vyatireka*), he says "in some cases" and so forth.

In certain affirmative or other types of statements, those who do not accept the term *syāt*—the proponents of absolute positions (*ekāntavādin*)—would have to accept an absolute position (*ekānta*) in every respect, both with regard to the property (*dharma*) and with regard to the substratum (*dharmin*), or else, just as they do with regard to the substratum, so too with regard to the property; that is, an absolute position in every respect. And in that case, there would be a contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the intended meaning.
Therefore, one who wishes to avoid contradiction with that [doctrine] must accept the term *syāt* (in some sense) everywhere.
Having thus established the use of *syāt* everywhere by way of negation (*vyatireka*), he now says—"In the absence of restriction," etc.—establishing the use of *eva* (only/alone) in the same manner.
The connection is as follows: even in the absence of the restrictive particle *eva*, not only in the absence of *syāt*, would an absolute monism (*sarvathaikānta*) be accepted.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because the refutation of non-absolutism (anekānta) is inevitable.

To explain: since the soul (*jīva*) alone is defined by the functional application (*upayoga*) of cognition (*jñāna*) and intuition (*darśana*), if one does not accept non-absolutism for that which is characterized by these very definitions—thereby excluding its association with anything else—then even a non-soul (*ajīva*) would possess those same characteristics. Consequently, the established order of external objects would collapse, and with that collapse, all conventional discourse regarding the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their objects (*prameya*) would be lost.

If one does not accept the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) by stating "it possesses that very characteristic," then even form (*rūpa*) and so forth would possess this characteristic, and consequently, there would be no distinction between the living being (*jīva*) and what is other than it.
If there is no restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) such as "it certainly possesses it," then there would be the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).
Likewise, from the perspective of [the self] and from the perspective of its attributes (*dharma*), there would be an absolute [confusion]. (Śrāvakabhūmi)
— By means of the [word] "mouth" (mukhena), [the author] says: "In the absence [of that], there is nothing," [as stated in] manuscript Ba.

The particle *eva* when connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) indicates the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). For example, in the statement "Pārtha alone is the archer," the exclusion of connection with anything else means the exclusion of identity and so forth with that which is different from the qualificand.
In this case, by means of the particle *eva*, the absence of identity with anyone other than Pārtha is understood in relation to the archer.
And thus, there is the cognition: "Pārtha is non-different from an archer who possesses the absence of identity with others.
(Saptabhaṅgī, p.

26). In that context, in cases where the [predicate] resides in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), such as "Pārtha alone is the archer," the meaning is the exclusion of identity with others (*anyatādātmyavyavaccheda*).
And otherness is relative to the meaning of the word co-uttered [with it];
thus, the cognition is: "Pārtha is non-different from an archer who possesses the absence of identity with others than Pārtha" (Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra, p. 370).
Alternatively, in another [instance], the quality of being an excellent archer is excluded from Pārtha—
Vācaspati, Nyāyakaṇikā, p. 191.

The sense is that if the word "eva" (only) were absent from the phrase "jñāna-darśana-upayoga-syāt," then even a non-living entity (*ajīva*) might possess knowledge and so forth; consequently, since everything would attain the nature of consciousness, there would be a total absence of external insentient matter.

For if external objects were denied, there would be no established order of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; for it is only in dependence upon external objects that the conventional usage of "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and its "semblance" (*tadābhāsa*) occurs in relation to knowledge, since it is stated [in the *Āptamīmāṃsā*, Kārikā 83]: "In dependence upon an external object of knowledge (*prameya*), there are those two: the valid cognition and its semblance. That soul (*jīva*) which possesses those characteristics such as knowledge and vision is "characterized by them.
The particle "only" (*eva*), conjoined with this qualification, indicates the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), just as in the expression, "The conch is white only."

Exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is defined as the state of not being the counter-positive of an absence that is co-extensive with the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). (Saptabhaṅgītaraṅgiṇī, p. 25).

In cases where it is connected with a qualifier, such as "The conch is indeed white," exclusion of non-connection is understood because it conveys the negation of the absence of inherence of whiteness, delimited by the nature of being a conch (*śaṅkhatva*).
—*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, p. 370:

Here, either the exclusion of non-connection with whiteness (*pāṇḍuratvāyogavyavaccheda*) is understood as delimited by the nature of being a conch (*śaṅkhatvāvacchedena*), or else the exclusion of non-connection with whiteness is understood as residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), namely, the conch.
—Mañjūṣā-prakaraṇa, p. 1; Nyāyakoka, p. 191.
This would be the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of this living being (jīva)—it would be momentary (kṣaṇika). Ācārya.
The soul indeed possesses the characteristics of the functional application of knowledge and perception;
the particle "eva" (indeed) is conjoined with the action to indicate the exclusion of absolute non-connection, just as in the expression: "A blue lotus exists indeed.
— *Saptabhaṅgī*, p. 26.
In the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, page 370, it is stated:
"In the lotus, the absolute non-connection with blueness is excluded"—
*Vākyārthavivaraṇa*.
*Nyāyakośa*, p. 192:

Now, it is argued that the cognition of the particle *eva* alone—whether directly employed or understood through implication—is appropriate, because its result, namely the exclusion of the impossibility of what is to be established, is possible in every sentence; the particle *syāt* (the optative suffix), on the other hand, would be fruitless.
And it has been said:

The exclusion of connection with others, connection with [others], and absolute non-connection, which are to be established by the particle *eva*— namely, non-connection with [the subject] and connection with [other objects].

Non-connection (*ayoga*), connection with others (*yogam aparaiḥ*), and absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*)—the particle *eva* is [respectively] an excluder (*vyatirecaka*) and a restrictor (*niyāmaka*). In some cases, it excludes non-connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*);
in some cases, it excludes connection with others, that is, with things different from the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); and in some cases, it excludes absolute non-connection.

[Objection: But surely a particle (*nipāta*) is not itself expressive (*vācaka*), but rather indicative (*dyotaka*); how then can this distinction of meaning belong to it? [Response: It is said: "When uttered together with the qualifier, the qualificand, and the action..."

The meaning is as follows: because it is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), a particle (*nipāta*) uttered together with a qualifier excludes non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*); when uttered together with a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it excludes connection with another (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*); and when uttered together with a verb (*kriyā*), it excludes absolute non-connection (*atyanta-ayoga-vyavaccheda*). Thus, while the exclusion of non-connection and so forth are denoted by the words "qualifier" and so on themselves, they are indicated (*dyotya*) by the particle uttered along with them—*Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 4.167.
Comparison—Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā, fol. 507A. As for the determination: "Non-yoga with others [is] yoga"—Ṣaḍdarśana-samuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā, fol. 14.

As it has been stated in the *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī*, page 17: "The particle *eva* is considered to be threefold, as it excludes non-connection (*ayoga*), connection with something else (*anyayoga*), and absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*) of a property."

"The particle [eva] which excludes [the property] distinguishes the attribute. (Kāvyaprakāśa-ṭīkā, p. 88). "The particle 'eva' is the distinguisher; it is the excluder. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.190). The particle 'eva' is the distinguisher; it is the excluder, that is, the negator.

In the statement "Caitra is indeed an archer," there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). To explain: a sentence employed for the sake of another's understanding excludes only that which is suspected by that other person due to delusion. Since Caitra is not perceived in the world as an archer, the sentence "Caitra is indeed an archer" is employed to establish his status as an archer by excluding the suspicion that he is not an archer.
In the case of "Pārtha alone is the archer," there is an exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).

Indeed, no one harbors any doubt regarding Pārtha’s status as an archer, since he is universally renowned among all people for his skill with the bow; therefore, it is the possibility of an archer possessing a degree of excellence that is suspected as being common to other men. To exclude that [possibility], the statement "Pārtha alone is the archer" is employed.

In the statement "A lotus is indeed blue," however, there is an exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). For when it is well known that a lotus is devoid of the color blue, and a doubt arises that it lacks blueness, then the sentence "A lotus is indeed blue" is employed to exclude that [doubt]. Thus, the particle *eva* functions as an exclusory (*vyatirecaka*) [marker].
This is because where the existence of a property in a given subject is doubted, the exclusion of non-connection is logically established.

An illustration of this is as follows: regarding the statement "Caitra is an archer," since there is doubt as to whether Caitra possesses archery or not—asking "Does he have it or not?"—the statement "Caitra is an archer" excludes the alternative possibility of his being a non-archer which has been brought to mind by the listener's expectation. In this case, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is what is logically established.
—From the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p.
15: Because of the doubt regarding Caitra’s being an archer, the exclusion of mere non-connection (*ayogamātra*) is effected by the qualifier. —*Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 4.

Thus, in another case—just as in the expression "Pārtha is the archer," although this word "archer" is a general term, by the force of the context and so forth, it functions here to denote one of preeminent quality; for since the status of being an archer is already established in Pārtha, there is no suspicion of non-application (*ayoga*).

When there is a doubt on the part of the listener as to whether such excellence exists elsewhere or not—such as when it is said, "Pārtha is the archer"—then it is understood that Pārtha alone is the excellent archer and no other;
thus, in this case, the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is logically established.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p. 15)

While the status of being a bowman is indeed well-known in the case of Pārtha (Arjuna), when there is doubt as to whether such a status belongs to anyone else as well, a qualification that results in the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is employed— *Pramāṇavārttika-manorathanandinī* 4.192.

In the case of "blue lotus" (*nīla-saroja*), it is certainly not the case that everything is a blue lotus, such that there would be an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); nor is it the case that only a lotus is blue, such that there would be an exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).
Rather, when there is a doubt regarding absolute non-connection—namely, whether a blue lotus is possible or not—it is precisely that [non-connection] which is excluded by the qualifier.
—*Pramāṇavārttika*, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 4.192:

That is an unexamined statement, because the affirmation or negation of the desired and the undesired is untenable without the use of the term *syāt*. For instance, when it is said, "Arjuna alone is the archer," the absence of archery in all other persons at all times and in all places is understood; and in that case, there is a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition.

Now, if what is intended to be negated among other persons is not merely the state of being an archer, but rather a specific [quality] restricted by particular place and time, then this fault does not apply. But surely, this meaning can be understood from the force of the particle *eva* alone; since that is its very purpose, how could it be fruitless? For otherwise, there would be no comprehension of this [restriction] in every sentence—whether it is directly expressed or understood through implication. And thus, in such cases as "Caitra is indeed an archer" (*caitro dhanurdhara eva*) or "The lotus is indeed blue" (*nīlaṃ sarojaṃ bhavaty eva*), when there is an absolute exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga*) and absolute exclusion of connection (*atyantāyoga*), there would result only one of the two: either Caitra or the state of being an archer, or the blue or the lotus.

Now, [it might be argued that] the exclusion of non-connection and absolute non-connection between these two occurs precisely without abandoning their own respective natures, and not by assuming each other's nature; therefore, this is not a fault. That is not so; for it is impossible to comprehend this meaning without the term "syāt" (in some sense). This is incorrect, as in the case: "The archery skill possessed by Pārtha is not such as is found elsewhere."

Comparison: Even where the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is intended, it is a specific type of connection (*yogaviśeṣa*) that is excluded, not connection in general (*yogasāmānya*). As it is said: "The archery possessed by Pārtha does not exist in the same way elsewhere"—*Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 409.
[This pertains to] the term *syāt*.
—of that which possesses the property of being a noble one;
of that which possesses [the property of] hearing; everywhere, *ba*;
comparison—by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), indeed, connection with "existence" is intended.

And is that conjunction (yoga) conveyed as being existent in a general form, or in a specific form, or in both forms? In every case, there would follow the same fault mentioned previously: would it be the exclusion of the non-conjunction with existence in general, or the non-conjunction with a specific existence, or the non-conjunction with both? [For] when the non-conjunction of Caitra with the bow is excluded, the conjunction would be established; otherwise, the application of the statement "Caitra is indeed an archer" would be untenable. (Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 409)

Would that [non-existence] be in every respect or in some way? In the first case, when the non-connection of Caitra with the bow is excluded, neither the state of being Caitra nor the state of possessing a bow would be established.
To whom [would this apply]? He says: "to those who hate the *syādvāda*," meaning to the proponents of absolute positions (*ekāntavādins*).
— *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 508B.

Even in the case of the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*), there are two alternatives: either that there is no absolute non-connection and that connection exists in every way, or that it sometimes exists and sometimes does not exist; in both cases, the same aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) must be applied. Regarding what was further stated—that the particle [‘eva’], when uttered together with the action, excludes absolute non-connection and is a separator (*vyatirecaka*)—he states the refutation thereof with the words beginning “prāptam,” etc. (Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā, p. 409).

If it is argued that "the lotus is indeed blue," then, if it were so, this world would have to be perceived as having the single form of a blue lotus, manifesting as blue eternally and at all times on every side. This is the intended meaning: does the lotus become blue in every respect or in some way? In the first case, this fault arises; in the other case, there is non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
— *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 510A.

[Objection: From the exclusion [of others], Caitra—[and] now, from its own nature—[it follows]. Furthermore, in sentences such as "Caitra is an archer," if the particle *eva* (only), while effecting the exclusion of non-connection with archery and so forth, were to effect the cessation of non-archery and the like—even though they are not directly denoted by the word—on the grounds that they are other than that [archery], then let [the cessation] of qualities such as bravery and magnanimity also be effected, since there is no difference in their being other than the archery and so forth directly denoted by the word.

Now, it might be argued that when a property is predicated of a subject, only its opposite is excluded therefrom: for instance, when "archery" is predicated of Caitra, "non-archery" is the contradictory; when "extraordinary archery" is predicated of Pārtha (Arjuna), "archery common to the entire world" is the contradictory; and when "the possibility of blueness" is predicated of a lotus, "its impossibility" alone is the contradictory. Therefore, only that [specific opposite] is excluded, but not properties such as "bravery" and so forth, because although they are different from those [other properties], they are not contradictory to it. This argument follows the maxim of a blind man entering a snake's hole; for such a distinction is untenable unless one accepts the doctrine of *syādvāda* (the theory of manifold aspects).

If it is objected: "Even if that [exclusion] is accepted, since there is no difference in the fact that words do not denote [positive entities], why is it that only the contradictory is excluded and not everything?"—[we reply: It is because of such capacity;

for the employment of a word is for the purpose of conveying its own object, not out of mere whim, and that object—which consists of both existence and non-existence—appears in the word just as it does in perception.

Furthermore, the conventional usage of "existence" and "non-existence" is based on the dependence upon a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) that possesses its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). And it is not logical for that which is non-contradictory [with itself] to function as its own counter-positive; therefore, how could there even be a suspicion of the cessation of everything? Consequently, the statement beginning with "it remains fixed" (*avadhāraṇe*) and so forth [is justified], because of his being like a master archer.
If it is prescribed [in the Śruti],
let cessation be prescribed—
this is what is intended.
The status of being an archer is nothing more than the mere impossibility of being blue, because of the particle "eva" (only).
—Because of its occurrence; [the opponent says: "But, Ācārya, even though there is a difference from being an archer..."
There is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that one may be both an archer and brave and noble;
for [the objection] consisting of the nature of self-interest (*svārtha-svabhāva-ātmaka*) is [refuted by] the inquiry (*praśna*).

There is a requirement for both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); the linguistic usage of existence (*bhāva*) depends on the essential nature, while the linguistic usage of non-existence (*abhāva*) depends on the counter-correlative—[Ācārya’s] Commentary (*ā. ṭi.*). [Objection: Even when one is capable [of speaking], if it is said "the soul exists," then existence is understood therein; if it is said "it does not exist," then non-existence is understood; since both are perceived by means of both statements, restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is not logical, and so forth. To this, he says: "Otherwise," etc. (*anyathā* etc.).

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: because the exclusion of non-absolutism (anekānta) would necessarily entail the absence [of any distinction], otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of there being no difference between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the standpoint (naya); for this reason, absolute monism (sarvathaikānta) would have to be accepted.

Since, in the absence of such a restriction, there would be the consequence of non-absolutism applying to the attributes (dharma) just as it does to the substratum (dharmi), [the author], showing that even other [doctrines] perish without the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda), says: "What more need be said," and so forth.
What? The ellipsis to be supplied is: "nothing [is established] by much speaking.

This applies to sentences consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), restatements (*anuvāda*), and extensions (*atideśa*)—whereby the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes sentences of restrictive rule (*niyama*) and so forth; to the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and others; to the meanings of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as the object and others—whereby the word "etcetera" includes gender (*liṅga*) and so forth—and to sentences establishing or refuting [a thesis] or appearing to do so. The word "and" (*ca*) here should be understood as having a conjunctive sense.
The connection is: "without the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects), there is the non-establishment of the subject under discussion."
Thus, this is well-known even among children; that is to say, it is not a mere fabrication by one's own whim.
When it is said "it does not exist," the exclusion of non-absolutism (anekānta) necessarily follows—this is the meaning according to the *Anvaya-ṭippaṇī*.

The statement "the soul must indeed exist" is a *naya*-sentence. If the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) were not applied here, then just as there is non-absolutism (*anekānta*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), the soul, when it is devoid of such restriction, so too would that [non-absolutism] apply to the attribute (*dharma*) called "existence. This is because this is the nature of a *naya*: non-absolutism regarding the subject and absolutism regarding the attribute (as noted in the Ācārya’s commentary). Now, one might object: "Since every word is dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), it conveys that intention alone and not the actual object; therefore, it is incorrect to say 'when the word "soul" is uttered there... Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The Buddhists say that letters, words, and sentences convey meanings that are not intended;
they express them.
What are they? Phonemes (*varṇa*) such as the letter *ga* and so forth;

likewise, words (*pada*) such as *go* (cow) and so forth; and likewise, sentences (*vākya*) such as *gām ānaya* (bring the cow) and so forth. What [do they denote]? Objects (*artha*), that is, the denotable meanings.

What kind of things [do they not express]? Unwanted and unintended objects such as the earth and so forth, and even desired and intended objects such as those possessing dewlaps and so forth, they do not express in certain cases when the audience consists of those of dull intellect, because for them there is no comprehension of the meaning from such [expressions]. Such a conventional usage (*prasiddhi*), known as *rūḍhi*, which is well-established among all people and is of this diverse nature, must be accepted by those engaged in practical discourse, since it is precisely in this way that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is possible.

For those who speak and assert according to their own whims and at will—transcending and disregarding established consensus—it is appropriate and logical for the Buddhists; how is this a statement of censure? [The word] "śabda" indicates or denotes [the meaning].

Of what? Of the mere intention of the speaker—the speaker being the instigator; "mere" meaning only the intention, the purpose, or the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), and not of an external object. This is understood as a rhetorical objection: "Oh, how wonderful! [This is because] an external object consisting of both general and particular aspects is cognized through the employment of words, and that alone constitutes its referent, whereas an intention is not cognized from it even in a dream (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 87).
"Or perhaps it does not go to those desired [objects] in some cases; such is the established rule.
For one who speaks by his own will, having transcended that [rule], it is appropriate that his speech be indicative merely of what is intended by the speaker. (64–65)
Comparison—As it has been said: "For words arise from the intention to speak; they indicate that very [intention]" (Tattvopaplava, p.
Thus, Ādi and Muni [state] in the *Laghīyastraya*.
Commentary: The denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of phonemes, words, and sentences is to be understood according to their respective traditional authorities (*āgama*).
Words are the denoters of objects distinct from the speaker’s intention, because otherwise the distinction between truth and falsehood would be untenable.
This point has been explained at length elsewhere, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
If words were to deviate from their meanings, how could deviation from the intended meaning be excluded? For we observe the activity of speech even during deep sleep and so forth;
moreover, corrupt words and the like are uttered even by those who do not intend them, while even those of dull intellect who do intend to speak fail to produce the words of the scriptures.
Since there is thus deviation in both cases, words are not the denoters of anything at all—this is a non-worldly intuition.

For the world establishes the distinction between truth and falsehood regarding the attainment or non-attainment of an object, but not regarding a mere intention; for in that latter case, there is an absence of extensive linguistic usage.

It would be appropriate for those who, disregarding uncontradicted cognition, establish the nature of the means and objects of knowledge according to their own whims—but how is it understood from the *Jñānaviśeṣa* that words indicate merely what is intended?
Comparison: "The activity of speech is sometimes observed even without the intention [to speak];
or else, speakers of treatises do not wish [to speak] because of their dull intellects" (Nyāyaviniścaya, Kārikā 354).

Those of dull intellect, desiring that the merits and defects of speech arise from the merits and defects of consciousness, do not [recognize] the speakers of the treatises— [as established by] Pramāṇasaṃgraha, Kārikā 16.
Pramāṇasaṃgraha-ṭīkā, p. 173, l. 23. Compare: "The status of cognition and words as means of valid knowledge [is established] when an external object exists, not when it does not exist;
thus is the distinction between truth and falsehood possible regarding the attainment or non-attainment of the object."
—*Āptamīmāṃsā*, verse 87:
"The non-attainment of the object" (*arthasyānāpti*).
In this regard, without transgressing the established conventions of linguistic usage, [one acts] according to one's own will. (*Īśvaravāda*) *Jainaviśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*.
Transcending the uncontradicted cognition,
Jaḍavīra explained the meaning of the *kārikās*—
namely, letters, words, and sentences— and what did they express? Objects such as jars and the like.

Of what kind [are these things]? They are those not desired, which have not been made objects of desire, and those desired, which have been made objects of desire—namely, the subjects of scriptural exegesis and so forth. Regarding some beings of dull intellect, they do not speak [of these things]; such is the established fact, this worldly consensus witnessed by all people, which is so diverse.
To state the fault in not accepting this, he says: "By their own whim," and so forth.

For the Sugatas, who speak by their own will—that is, merely according to their own intended method—transcending that very [conventional] consensus, what is appropriate? To this he says: "But speech is indicative of only what is intended by the speaker"—thus is the proof (śruti).
Now, regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain the eternity of sound:

"Is it that letters (*varṇa*), and so forth, being non-eternal, convey the intended meanings, or are they eternal? Of these two positions, the first is untenable; for if they were non-eternal, they would perish immediately upon arising, and thus, because they would not persist until the time of convention (*saṅketa*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it would be impossible for them to convey those meanings."

The second position, however, is tenable; for since those [sounds] are eternal, it is logical that they follow [the sounds] and thus serve as their indicators, and because their very eternity is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: first of all, the eternity of words is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), such as "this is that very same letter *ga*."
Nor does it possess invalidity characterized by ignorance, since it is experienced by every living being;
nor is it of the nature of doubt, because it rests upon a single aspect—
for a cognition that rests upon both aspects is a doubt— and this [cognition] is not like that.
Nor does it have the nature of falsity, because it is not sublated;

for only that cognition which is sublated is established as false, such as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. And this [cognition] is not sublated even in other places, times, or persons.
Nor is its invalidity due to its arising from defective causes, because there is no certainty regarding the defectiveness of its causes.

Nor [is it established] because of being both the object attained and the attainer; for the *ga*-sound and so forth, as delimited by qualifiers such as being remembered or being presently experienced, were objects of previous cognitions.
As it has been said: [citing the *Pratibandha*...].
Or rather, there is no [validity] in scripture (śruti),
because the communication of meaning is impossible;
for when a word is momentary, it is incapable of determining its meaning.
For the apprehension of a relationship is not possible for that which is momentary—*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Śabdanityatā, verse 3; *Nyāyaratna*.
In the view of Kumārila, sound is eternal, of the nature of a substance, perceivable by the sense organ of hearing alone, and possesses the universal (jāti) "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*).

In Kumārila’s view, substance (*dravya*) is considered omnipresent and eternal; it is both the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyo*). Furthermore, in Prabhākara’s view, sound (*śabda*), although eternal, is a quality (*guṇa*) of space (*ākāśa*) and not an independent substance (*svatantra-dravya*).

It should be observed: "Space possesses sound," and that very [space] is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), while sound is its quality (*guṇa*)—[as stated in] the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, *Nyāyamañjarī*, and *Nyāyaśuddhiprakaraṇa*. Because it pervades both the time of the initial convention and the time of subsequent usage, we indeed recognize it; it is not due to any weakness of the sense organ. Likewise, others also recognize it. If they recognize it as "this is that very same one," then just as we do, others too ought to be able to say that it is not something else.
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.20

It has been stated in the *Bṛhatī* (1.1) that persistence over a period of time is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) alone, and that this persistence over a period of time is cognizable through perception accompanied by recognition.
Sound also is understood to exist prior [to its perception] because of recognition— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdanityatā, verse 33.
*Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi*, p. 26:

This is what is meant—by the force of the specific cognition known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which brings about the understanding of the identity between the *ga* sound of yesterday and that of today, permanence is postulated. Therefore, this recognition is established on the basis of a universal such as *gatva*.

This being the case, since there is a difference between individual instances, the universal exists; whereas in the absence of such [identity], one must simply say that no universal exists. Thus, the permanence of the word-sound is established by means of recognition.
—*Śāstradīpikā*, p. 540, 568;
*Tantrarahasya*, p. 26; [regarding] recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
The invalidity of recognition consists in its falsity;
[this applies to] recognition and the causes of recognition, such as the sense faculties and so forth.
Recognition is stated to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of the firmness of the sense faculties— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdanityatā, verse 372;
"This is that very same [person]"— Ānandapūrṇa’s Commentary.

It may be argued: "Surely that part which was previously perceived and previously understood is not being cognized here; how then can there be validity [in this cognition], since what has already been grasped is being grasped again? To this, he says: "yaḥ" (that which...).
"In that case, let there be no validity [of the cognition]; rather, validity depends precisely upon the expectation of a connection with another time not previously grasped" (*Nyāyaratna*).

[Objection: But is it not the case that not only something additional is cognized, but also what was already understood before? How, then, can there be validity? To this he says: "That which was previously... and so forth.

For in determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*), the nature of the word, the object, their relation, and the temporal relation manifest; therein, since the aspect consisting of the word and so forth is the object of memory, let it not be the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the present existence of the thing (*vastu-sattā*) was not ascertained previously, so there is an occasion for a means of valid cognition regarding that. Thus, its status as a valid cognition is established.
Furthermore, because it conforms to the operation of the sense organs, it possesses the character of perception (*pratyakṣatva*).

And this [determinate cognition] should be understood as having as its causes both the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous cognition and the presently existing sense organ and other factors.
"The destruction previously cognized is indeed not [that same one]" — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
339; "The destruction previously cognized is indeed that" — *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 319.
"That part which was previously apprehended here is indeed [the object] for us"—*Nyāyaratnākara*, p.
675 (second half); *Tattvopaplava*, p.
27; *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 77.
"The present existence has indeed not been apprehended by the previous cognition" (Tattvasaṃgraha, p.
159; Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa, vv. 233–34).
And its status as perception is well-established because it conforms to the presence and absence of the auditory faculty;

nor is it logical that this [hearing] should not be perception simply because it is preceded by memory, for even when preceded by that, its status as perception is justified by its being born from the contact of the sense with an existing object.
And it has been said:
Regarding the recognition that "this very sound is that [same sound]," even for a cognizer who remembers the relationship between the word and its object in that instance, there is [the following].
"Because it arises from the synthesis of objects previously apprehended by the intellect,
this [cognition] produced when an object is in contact with the eye would not be non-perceptual"—
Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa, verses 229–30.
*Satsaṃyoga*:
[The compound] *sat* and *saṃprayoga* is a *karmadhāraya*. Thus, it means "when there is a connection (*saṃbandha*) between the sense organs and their objects.
For comparison: "What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? We say it is perception (*pratyakṣa*)."

Because it is produced by a sense organ in conjunction with the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) generated by a prior experience, this single cognition consists of both perception and recollection—*Śāstradīpikā*, p.
568. Indeed, there exists no such statement, whether royal decree or common worldly saying, that "that which precedes recollection is perception. 1.

[Objection: But surely this [subsequent cognition] has an object that exceeds [the previous one]; since it occurs after recollection, how can it be perception (*pratyakṣa*)? For this characteristic is not observed in non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*). To this he says: "No" (*na hi*). For being prior to recollection is not the definition of perception; rather, it is being produced by the sense-faculties (*indriyajatatva*), and that remains unchanged here as well—this is the point. If the very operation of the sense-faculty were obstructed by recollection, then it would be defective; consequently, the conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*) arising at a time subsequent to that might indeed be [non-perceptual], but this is not the case. Thus he says: "And not" (*na ca*).

Since memory neither contradicts nor corrupts the sense faculty, therefore, one must accept that all cognition arising from the contact of a sense faculty with its object—whether prior to or subsequent to memory—is perception. Thus he says, "Therefore" (*tena*). [The *Kāśikā* explains: "That which occurs after recollection is not perception"—this is the meaning of the *Ātmatattvaviveka-ṭīkā*.
Whether royal or Vedic—these [verses] are cited from the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 319 (as noted in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*), as well as from the *Prameya-kamala-mārtaṇḍa*, p.
Nor is the subsequent operation of the sense-organ prevented by anyone from recollection, nor does it become impaired at that time. (Syādvādamañjarī 499; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 319)
Therefore, let it be understood that all cognition which arises from the connection between a sense faculty and its object— both prior to and subsequent to memory— is perception. (Pramāṇavārttika,
Pratyakṣa, verses 234–37).

Thus, since the eternity of sound has been established from this [reasoning], the utterance of a word at any other time—just as it is now—is not its producer but rather its manifestor. Therefore, this is stated: even at another time, whatever is the utterance of a word, that is its manifestor, because it is an utterance; whatever is an utterance is a manifestor, just like the utterance characterized by the present time; and the case in question is likewise; therefore, this too is so, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
If we can establish the eternity of sound by means of a clear reason, then, by the force of the cognition of its eternity, it will follow that it is manifested through effort— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.6.13.
1.12 Effort alone is postulated as the cause of sound.

And since that [sound] has been established as a manifestor through the force of recognition during the perception of the second and subsequent instances, it is a manifestor even at the time of the first perception; therefore, because it exists without a cause, sound is eternal like the sky and so forth, and it does not possess impermanence—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 170; *Bhaṭṭacintāmaṇi*, p. 26.
Thus it is established that the utterance of a word is not its cause but its manifestor;
and since no cause other than utterance is possible, the word is not an effect. Precisely for this reason, because it does not perish, its eternity is established—*Śāstradīpikā*, p. 590.

Sound is manifested by effort, because, while not being produced by it, it is perceived immediately after it; for whatever is perceived immediately after something, without being produced by it, is manifested by that—just as a jar is perceived immediately after a lamp. (Tantrarahasya, p.
26; Mānameyodaya, p. 221)

— likewise, the audibility of sound is the subject under discussion; or else, the time under dispute is connected with speech and so forth, because it is time, just like the time connected with the word already established.
Therefore, its eternity is established even through inference;

it is established by this further inference as well: "Sound is eternal, because it is audible; whatever is such [audible] is so [eternal], just like the universal 'sound-ness' (śabdatva); and this [sound] is such; therefore, this too is so.

Furthermore, cognitions of individual instances of the word "cow" (gośabda), though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, have a single word "cow" as their object and do not have multiple objects as their domain, because they arise as the cognition "cow," just like the cognition of the word "cow" arising at the present moment.

If it were stated simply as "cognitions of the individual manifestation of the word 'cow' (*gośabdavyaktibuddhayaḥ*)," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is admitted that a single cognition of the individual manifestation of the word 'cow' has a single object. To exclude that [possibility], the plural number is used. Likewise, to refute the view that "similar cognitions arise based on the word 'cow' solely with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*"), the term "individual" (*vyakti*) is employed. Furthermore, to preclude the consequence of proving what is already established—that the cognitions of many knowers regarding the word 'cow' in a single place or time have as their domain a single individual manifestation of the word 'cow'—it is stated that they are "distinguished by place, time, and so forth."
Either the word "cow" uttered yesterday continues even today, because it is cognized as "cow," like the word "cow" uttered today;
or else the word "cow" uttered today existed yesterday, because it is cognized as "cow," like the word "cow" uttered yesterday;
or else a word is expressive and persists for a long duration, because it generates the cognition of an object through the force of its relationship [with that object], like the generality of smoke.
However, that which is unstable does not cause one to cognize the object by the force of its relationship, because it is dependent on immediate conditions, like the light of a lamp or lightning;
thus,
this quality of being audible is the reason, just as "being sound" is.

Alternatively, the fact of being perceived by auditory perception (*śrotrapratyakṣatva*) is the reason here; for that, by means of the example of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), is capable of proving eternality. Thus he says: "perceived by hearing" (*śrautra*)—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Nyāyaratnākara*, *Śabdanirṇaya*, verse 393.
And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: sound is eternal, because it is audible (*śrāvaṇatvāt*), like sound-ness.
—*Śastradīpikā*, p. 585:

"Alternatively, all cognitions of 'cowness,' though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, must be produced by a single word 'cow,' because they are cognitions of a cow, like a single cognition [of a cow]."

In the same way, cognitions of the word "cow" should also be conceived as having the single word "cow" as their object by virtue of having that word "cow" as their content, just like a single cognition;
for by the cognition of the word "cow" from yesterday, this word "cow" was revealed.

Just as this [subsequent cognition] cognizes its object by way of being the object of the word "cow" produced at the very first moment, so too must it be due to that same cause as the preceding cognition;
or else, both [cognitions] would have a single object, like a single cognition.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā, verses 418–21.

Compare: "And all cognitions of individual instances of the word 'cow', though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, have the same object; they do not, therefore, have various objects as their domain."
Because they arise as "cow," the cognitions regarding individual instances of the word "cow"—

which are distinguished by the appearance of differences such as place, time, fast, medium, or slow [utterance]— have a single object as their domain and do not have multiple objects as their domain, because they arise while grasping the form "cow," just like a present cognition of a cow.

Alternatively, whatever cognition has the word "cow" as its object has today’s word "cow" as its object, because it has the word "cow" as its object, just like a cognition of the word "cow" produced this morning.
The cognition of the word "cow" yesterday has the word "cow" as its object; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Alternatively, the subject (*dharmin*) is the cognition of the word "cow" today (not belonging to yesterday), and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is having the word "cow" of yesterday as its object; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it has the word 'cow' as its object," and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the cognition of the word "cow" yesterday. Alternatively, both the cognitions of yesterday and today have a single object because they have the word "cow" as their object, like the cognition of a single word "cow.

Alternatively, all cognitions of "cowness," though differentiated by differences of place and so forth, are produced by a single word "cow" because they are cognitions of a cow, like the cognition of a single cow.

The distinction is as follows: previously, the cognitions having the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) as their object were the subject (*dharmin*), and having a single object was the property to be proven (*sādhya*); now, however, the cognitions having the universal "cowness" (*gotva-jāti*) as their object are the subject, and being produced by the single word "cow" is the property to be proven. (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 592; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 676)

But if the word "cow" is eternal, having been previously heard uttered many times with reference to other individual cows, it will—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—make known that it denotes the generic form (*ākṛti*); therefore, for this reason as well, [the word] is eternal. (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.6)
Therefore, the word "cow" uttered yesterday still exists even today,
because it is accessible through the cognition of the word "cow," just as one says today, "This is that same cow."
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā, verse 416:

Because it is devoid of a cause for destruction, like a universal, space, or time; because it is independent. 1.1.11.

Even among those substances whose origin is not perceived and whose mere existence is observed, the impermanence of some is understood when a cause of their destruction is apprehended; for example, having seen a new cloth and not having perceived it being made, one nevertheless understands its impermanence upon seeing its very form.

One understands that this [cloth], produced by the interlacing of threads, perishes either from the destruction of the interlacing of the threads or from the destruction of the threads themselves; however, no cause whatsoever for sound is perceived from whose destruction it would be understood to perish— Jaimini-sūtra, Śābara-bhāṣya 1.1.6–23.
1.21 Thus, for a sound that remains [in this state], at a moment subsequent to the time of its audition, [it is perceived].

And its being devoid of a cause for destruction is established by its stability for some time;
for as long as it remains unimpeded during the period of establishing the connection, by what could it be removed even afterwards? (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 676)

And this [comprehension] is established neither otherwise nor in any other way; for if sound were impermanent, it would be impossible in every respect, since the comprehension of meaning from a word occurs only through a recognized connection (*pratibandha*), and not otherwise, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, once a connection has been recognized, its persistence at a later time is not possible if the sound is impermanent, because it perishes at that very moment.
As it has been said:

Why? Because perception is for the sake of another. "Perception" here means utterance; it is uttered for the sake of another, that is, to convey a meaning to another.
For if a word were destroyed as soon as it was uttered, no one else would be able to convey the meaning to another; therefore, it would not be uttered for the sake of another.
If, on the other hand, it has not perished, then it is logical that there is comprehension of the meaning because it has been perceived many times— Jaimini-sūtra, Śābara-bhāṣya 1.1.5.
However, because the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible, its very permanence is logical;

for it is not possible that a different word produced at each utterance could convey the meaning, since the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] would be impossible, and what has not had its relationship apprehended cannot convey meaning.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one word to convey the meaning of another when the relationship [of the former] has been grasped;

for if its failure to establish oneness is due to the absence of oneness in these cases, that is equally true elsewhere as well.

Now, the objection that—since the causes of oil and so forth are observed to perish later on, and since lamps and the like are established to be different at every moment, their lack of oneness is logical, whereas this is not the case for sound because the opposite is true—is also untenable. For in the case of sound as well, its causes, characterized by the conjunction and disjunction of the palate and other organs, are perceived to perish later on; thus, its difference at every moment is established, and the non-existence of its oneness is logically proven.

If you accept that the conjunction and disjunction [of the vocal organs] are the cause for the production of the air that manifests that [sound], but not the cause for the sound itself, then you must also accept—since there is no distinction—that the contact between the wick, the oil, and the flame is the cause for the production of the air that manifests the lamp, but not the cause for the production of the lamp itself; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with perception, and this [fault] would not have been "eaten by crows" elsewhere either.

Ācārya-ṭīkā: Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the perceptual nature of recognition is also incorrect, because in the section on perception (*pratyakṣa-pariccheda*), it is established that only knowledge whose intrinsic nature is vivid (*viśada-svabhāva*) possesses the status of perception.

Now, while it is logical in some cases to perceive the absence of a jar or the like based on the perception of another object associated with the same cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargi*), the perception of the absence of sound is not [so] logical, because in that case there is no possibility whatsoever of anything being associated with the same cognition. [Reply: This too is not a valid objection; for when there is the perception of the absence of the intended sound, another sound itself is indeed possible as something associated with the same cognition.

If it is argued that [the perception of the absence of all sounds] is impossible in a soundless place because of the cognition of the non-existence of all sounds, we say no; for even there, the self-awareness of the nature of the self—which is associated with that same single cognition—is possible.

Just as there is a co-occurrence (*saṃsarga*) of a jar, the ground, and so forth within a single cognition, so too is there such a co-occurrence of one's own form and the form of another, since all cognitions have the inherent nature of manifesting both their own and other forms.

Nor does this entail the consequence that the absence of color and so forth would likewise follow from the absence of sound, because those [sensory objects] are grasped by specific sense organs, and thus their absence is established only through those specific sense organs.
For whatever is perceivable by a particular sense organ, its absence is also determined by that very same sense organ;

for when the self, having employed a particular sense organ, does not perceive an object that has reached the conditions of perceptibility at a certain place and time, it then understands the absence of that object there at that time— thus [says] the *Bhūtalāṭīkā*.
Regarding the cognition of the absence of sound on the ground and so forth,

the comparison is as follows: when there is the perception of the absence of a specific intended sound, it is possible for another sound, which is related to it through the same act of cognition (*ekajñānasamsargin*), to be present.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 682.

Compare: Even in that case, since the nature of the self is possible as being associated with that single cognition, for a self whose very nature is to manifest both its own form and the form of others, when there is an object situated in a suitable location, there would not only be the self-awareness of its own nature; indeed, all those objects whatsoever that are situated in a suitable location together with the object intended to be negated necessarily appear, and they are all associated with that single cognition.
In that case, in the instance of a jar and so forth, the object to be negated is the ground and such, which is in contact with the same cognition as the locus itself;
however, when sound is the object to be negated, in a location containing sound, there is another sound and the locus itself, whereas in a soundless location, there is merely the locus itself.
Alternatively, let there be no other distinct entity in contact with the same cognition; rather, it will be apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Just as when, in the case of something within the range of memory—such as a shrine or a house—if non-existence is apprehended by you through the means of knowledge consisting of non-apprehension (abhāvapramāṇa), [there is the cognition] of the shrine, the house, and so forth, on the ground and other locations. (Śrāvakabhūmi, p.
682) [Variant readings: bhūpradeśādīnām ba°; śra°].
The meaning is: since there is no distinction in their being "other," just as the absence of sound is known, so too should the absence of form be known—this is the point of the Ācārya’s commentary.
[This applies] to forms and the like, from any cognition whatsoever that grasps its own or another's nature.

According to the statement in the *Kiraṇāvalī*: "Whatever [organ] the apprehension of X requires, that same [organ] is required for the apprehension of the absence of X," and according to the rule: "The absence of whatever entity is apprehended by a particular causal complex is apprehended by that very same complex" (Ānandajñāna’s *Ṭīkā*), and because of the principle:

"By whichever sense-organ an object is apprehended, by that same organ its genus residing therein and its absence are also apprehended"—if sound were eternal, why would it not be perceived prior to its utterance? Would it be due to the absence of the sense-organ, the non-proximity of the sound, or its being obstructed? It cannot be due to the absence of the sense-organ, because sound is perceived immediately after its utterance.
Nor does there occur at that very moment the manifestation of a sense organ that was previously non-existent, because that would contradict experience;
nor [is it due to the absence of the word], because the word, being eternal and all-pervading, is always present everywhere;
nor is it due to its being obscured, because it is impossible for it to be obscured given its nature as eternally one.

Indeed, it is not possible for sound to possess the property of being concealed (*āvṛtatva*) unless it abandons its visible nature and assumes an invisible form; for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Whatever does not abandon its own nature at any given time cannot simultaneously possess a nature contrary to it; just as in its unobstructed state, there is no possibility of an invisible nature for that which does not abandon its visible nature, so too, in its obstructed state, sound does not abandon its visible nature. Therefore, if it were to abandon that nature, its impermanence would be established, because its very essence consists in the difference between its own states.

[Objection: "But surely, even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of jars and other objects, we observe that they are obscured by darkness and the like. [Reply: This too is incorrect, because even in that case, obscuration is logically possible only when there is a difference in the intrinsic nature;
for it is impossible for anything that does not impair the intrinsic nature to function as an obscuration.
Having stated that "prior to its utterance, the sense organ—the ear—did not exist, but at the very time of utterance, it arises together with the sound," he says: "And not... (na ca).
Because of its permanence and pervasiveness— [according to the Ācārya’s commentary]— of sound, [it would follow that] it [is eternal].
In the manuscript *ba*, it reads *tasya* (of it).

In the state of being covered, it is not possible for the sound to have an invisible nature, because it has not abandoned its previous nature. [Comparison: "Whatever does not abandon its own nature at any time... (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 682).
In the state of being covered... (Ā, Ba).

Regarding the abandonment of its perceptible nature during the state of being veiled, the comparison is as follows: "If this [sound], even while abandoning its audible nature produced by the operation of the palate and other organs and attaining a contrary nature, were eternal, then nothing would be non-eternal"—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 107.

Even though there is no difference in the essential nature of impermanence, [the opponent] might argue: "Just as darkness is an obscuration of a jar or similar object without destroying its own nature, so too it is for sound. This is incorrect; for even in that case, the destruction of the object's own nature is admitted, since darkness is established as an obscuration by virtue of destroying the visible nature of the object, thereby proving that everything is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).

Even by darkness, since a jar or the like is not destroyed, why should its perception not occur as before? For it is not destroyed by that [darkness] even in its capacity as an object of perception—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī* p. 105; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 421.
If it is argued that [the external object] is not perceived at all because it is obstructed by still air, he says: "Nor... and so forth.
For that external object, which is of a perceptible nature and visible, no obstruction to its perception is possible.
Because there is no proof for its establishment;

or because even if an obscuration were to exist, it would be impossible for it to suppress the capacity [of the word] without damaging its own nature—that is, without displacing the eternal nature of the word—since it is impossible to obstruct the power that produces cognition.
For in that case, nothing designated as an "obscuration" could be said to perform any function if it did not produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) within the nature of the word.
And what object could possibly be an obscuration? That is to say, what else could obstruct knowledge? In other words, that which is ineffective cannot be an obscuration at all.
Stating that even something ineffective is seen to function as an obscuration, he says: "Walls and so forth," etc.

Do walls and the like produce some excellence in jars and such things, or do they destroy some excellence of capacity, by virtue of which they are desired to be obscurations? [The answer is that they do neither.]

Therefore, he refutes [the objection] with the words "we do not say" and so forth, intending to show that just as those [walls, etc. are accepted as being an obstruction for jars and the like without producing any excellence (atiśaya) in them, so too there will be some kind of obstruction for the eternal sound. He explains:
"We do not say that those walls and such things produce some excellence in the jar or the like—that is, they bring about a distinct intrinsic nature (viśiṣṭasvabhāva)."
If so, why are they called "obstructions"? To this he says: "But not all," and so forth.

Not every moment of a jar is the cause of sensory cognition for every person; rather, it is the object, the sense organ, and the light, when combined with one another, that become causes of consciousness because they produce subsequent distinct moments through mutual interaction. And these factors—the object, the sense organ, and so forth—are mutually supportive provided they are not obstructed by a solid barrier such as a wall. When there is an intervening wall, however, the subsequent moment that was capable of arising does not arise due to the absence of the aforementioned causes; thus, there is a deficiency in the causal conditions. It is on account of this deficiency in causes that consciousness does not arise regarding jars and other objects obstructed by walls and the like, and it is for this reason that walls and such things are called "obstructions. This is not, however, because they prevent a jar or similar object from being previously capable of generating consciousness. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p. 361–62)
Thus [it is said]:
Furthermore, by way of apprehension and non-apprehension,

if the existence of sound were established through some means of valid cognition prior to the operation of its manifestor, then its obscuration could be established— just as darkness is established in the case of a jar perceived by tactile perception— but that [existence] is not established.

The claim that its existence is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is merely a wishful thought, since it has been demonstrated that such recognition does not prove unity. As the comparison states: "A manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is considered to be a cause of another's cognition regarding an object already established by one's own cognition, like a lamp; otherwise, what difference would there be between it and a producer (*kāraka*)?"

In the world, a manifestor—such as a lamp—is established as the cause for the cognition of another [object] by means of the cognition of itself; if that [manifestor] were already established beforehand, it would be established by way of its own homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*). For that very excellence which is the cause of cognition constitutes its causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
However, those things whose apprehension is not [already] established are merely producers, like a potter with respect to a jar.

When is an object considered a manifestor (vyañjaka), serving as the cause for another cognition by means of its own cognition? If that object were unestablished prior to being manifested, what distinction would there be between this manifesting cause and a producing cause (kāraka)?
— *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.264:

Since the existence of sound would have to be established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) before its obscuration could be established, just as darkness [is perceived] in a jar already apprehended through tactile perception (*spārśana-pratyakṣa*).
—Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 421; Ācārya’s Commentary (Ā.

Ṭī.): Or, let it be granted that there is some kind of obscuration of those [faculties]; nevertheless, would that [obscuration] be visible, invisible, eternal, non-eternal, pervasive, non-pervasive, one, or many? It cannot first be visible, because there is no cognition of it through the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Consequently, when that [object] is cognized, there is an absence of disagreement;
for no one disagrees when blue is being cognized as blue.

Now, [you might argue that] it is invisible; but how can it exist? For that would lead to an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*). [Objection: Since there is no other possible cause for the non-perception of the eternal sound prior to its utterance, one must postulate an invisible covering (*āvaraṇa*) as the cause of that non-perception.
