[Reply: This too is not tenable, because it entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the non-perception of this eternal sound prior to its utterance is established only if a covering of the sound is established, and the covering is established only when that non-perception exists.

Now, the claim that because identity-recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) establishes the permanence of sound, there can be no cause for its non-perception prior to its utterance other than an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), is nothing more than mere faith; for the capacity of identity-recognition to prove the permanence of sound has been refuted, and furthermore— [as stated in the *Śruti*]—
"of sounds" (Śrauta commentary).

Comparison: Nevertheless, regarding that obscuration, there are eight alternatives—whether it is visible or invisible, eternal or non-eternal, pervasive or non-pervasive, or singular or manifold—because there is no perception of an obscuration; *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 683.
—Because of the impossibility of [that], [the cognition] is not [a case of] direct perception of blueness. Śrī. Pratyakṣataḥ nīlatāyāḥ pra- Śrī.
The obscuration of the word is non-apprehension— Ārya-ṭīkā.
If sound were eternal, there would be a constant non-perception of sound due to its obscuration; however,
if it were non-eternal, then once it has been destroyed, since there would be no cause for its re-arising, it would follow that everything would be perceived at all times.
For no specific cause for the arising of a specific obscuration is perceived in the case of an obscuration— such as [the obscuration] of sound.
Each individual phoneme has its own respective obscuration—(Ānandajñāna’s Commentary).
Furthermore, its all-pervasiveness is extremely difficult to establish, because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).
To explain: the air (vāyu), which is intended as the obscuration, is not all-pervasive, because it is a substance possessing touch, like a clod of earth.

Furthermore, if it were all-pervasive, then since both the object to be covered and the coverer would be omnipresent, which of them could be the coverer of the other? Indeed, space is not perceived to be a coverer of things such as the self; however, if it were not all-pervasive, then the covering of sound by it would be even more untenable, because [the coverer] exists in the middle of it, in its location, and at its sides. On the contrary, sound itself would be the coverer of it; otherwise, even a mustard seed would be a coverer of a jar.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because we observe that even such space as the ether is covered by earth and other elements, that too is incorrect; for it is admitted that only a particular portion (*pradeśa*) of it is covered by those things.

Furthermore, if it were admitted that a portion of sound is also covered by air, then sound would necessarily possess parts and be non-eternal, [which is contrary to your doctrine].—Because of the absence [of such a portion], [the ether is not covered]. (Ātmatattvaviveka)
Comparison: Wind, which is intended [by you] as an obscuration, is not all-pervasive, because it is a substance possessing touch, like a fragment of stone. (Syādvādaratnākara, p.
683; sparśanadravya, Śrāvakabhāṣya)

Regarding the comparison with the obscuration: if it is argued that, like that [space], the obscuration is also omnipresent, then it is not an obscuration at all; for space is not an obscuration of the self and so forth—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 421.
"By means of sound-still air through another's intention"—Ācārya’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.). Syādvādaratnākara, p. 683.
vāyo—ā॰ ṭi॰: by means of the wind—ā॰ ṭi॰: in the midst of the wind whose nature is obscuration.
By virtue of its pervasiveness— [as noted in] Ācārya’s commentary— [and] by virtue of the wind— [as noted in] Ācārya’s commentary—
if even an object of small dimension were to be an occluder of a large [object], then...
Even though it is all-pervading— [according to] Ācārya’s commentary— it is only a portion of space that is covered by the earth.

Since the Jainas assert that space consists of infinite points (*anantapradeśitva*), if a single obscuration were postulated for all sounds alike, then it would follow that when one is perceived, all would be perceived; for upon the removal of that obscuration, all would likewise be unobstructed.
Alternatively, if that [one] sound is not perceived, then the intended sound would also remain unperceived, as there is no distinction between them.

Now, [the opponent might argue that sound] is distinct [in each instance]; that is not so. Because all sounds, by virtue of being pervasive, occupy the same location and are apprehended by the same sense organ, it is impossible for there to be a distinction in their concealment or a distinction in their manifestors. To explain: sounds are neither concealed by specific concealers nor manifested by specific manifestors, because they occupy the same location while being apprehended by a single sense organ. Whatever is such [occupying the same location and being apprehended by one sense organ] is thus [not subject to specific concealment or manifestation], just like the universal, number, color, dimension, action, and so forth residing in a single jar. And these sounds are likewise; therefore, they are thus.

If it were stated merely that "because they occupy the same location," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to color, taste, and so forth; for even though these reside in a single substance, they are perceived by their respective specific manifestors. Therefore, it was said "because they are perceptible by a single sense-organ.

If that alone were stated, there would be an inconclusive argument (*anekānta*) due to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like residing in pots and other objects situated in different locations. To exclude those cases, it was specified "because they occupy the same location.
Consequently, since it remains unestablished through this inference that words are manifested by specific manifestors, what was stated [by the opponent] is incorrect.

It might be conceived that, upon the removal of an obstruction, there is the perception of a single sound; this is comparable to an eye whose range of vision has been gained upon the removal of a curtain.
Just as one perceives every object in that location upon the stages of a theater,
so too, when the wind from the spreading movement of the *sāṃrodhi* [breath] has cleared away [obstructions], the ear will become a grasper of all sounds in that location.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 221:

"In some cases, if there were a manifestation of the word, it would be perceived by persons situated in all locations because of its pervasiveness; for there is no difference in its pervasiveness when it is unobstructed. —*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 684.
Just as in the case of a single word, when the obscuration of the intended word among all words is destroyed— Ārya-ṭīkā.
In the case of the non-perception of all sounds,
[the reason] "because there is no difference in their being unobstructed" applies to all sounds.

Furthermore, there would be no restriction regarding the manifestation [of sounds], if multiple sounds were to exist simultaneously in space; and thus, whatever manifestor is employed would manifest all [sounds] occupying the same location. Consequently, when a lute is played, the sound of a donkey would also be heard.
For no restriction is observed among manifestors regarding those things that are perceptible by the same sense organ and occupy the same location.
If it is argued that "only that which is the manifestor of a particular thing manifests that thing," this is not so, because such a restriction is never observed.

Now, if you think that when multiple sounds come together, the manifestors differ, and individual manifestations arise for each sound following the differences among those manifestors—that is not so, because it is not observed.
For a lamp does not fail to illuminate multiple objects grasped by a single sense-organ when they have come together simultaneously—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 288.
Nor should it be argued that the air, impelled for the purpose of manifesting the word "cow," does not manifest the word "horse"; for no such restriction is observed among manifestors.
Just as a lamp produced for the purpose of manifesting a jar manifests other objects situated in the same location and perceptible by the same sense organ. (Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 446)

For instance: the auditory organ is not something to be manifested by a specific manifestor, because it reveals objects that are graspable by the same sense organ and situated in the same location, just like the visual organ;
or, the sounds under dispute are not manifested by specific manifestors, because they are graspable by the same sense organ and situated in the same location, just like jars and other such things.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 648)

Furthermore, it is not observed that entities which possess the same instrument of cognition and are perceptible by the same sense organ have mutually restricted manifestors and manifested objects; for instance,
a lamp brought by a householder into a house to see a jar of curd illuminates the cakes located in that same place as well.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 212:

First of all, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is not something whose substrate is modified by a specific conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) for the purpose of perceiving objects that possess the same properties, occupy the same location, and are perceivable by the same sense organ; because it is a sense organ, like the visual organ (*cakṣus*).

Alternatively, sounds are not things whose substrate is modified by a specific conditioning factor, because, while possessing the property of being perceivable by the same sense organ, they are simultaneously connected with the sense organ, like a jar (*ghaṭa*) and other such objects.
—*Nyāyasaṃgraha*, p. 30.
Now, regarding the claim that "the restricted audition is produced by a restricted manifestor," he says: "For not... and so forth.
For it is not logical that this restriction of manifestors should apply to things that occupy the same location and are objects of the same sense organ.

—Because for those [sounds] produced by the same articulatory effort (*samānakaraṇa*), a restriction regarding their manifestation would be impossible; consequently, there would be a simultaneous hearing of all [sounds] everywhere and at all times.
—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 105.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 423; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p.
36; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 683.
Prameyaratnāvalī, folio 3;
Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā, page 378A.
Just as the air, impelled for the sake of one [articulation], does not produce another, so too that which is capable of refining (*saṃskāra*) one phoneme will not produce another. (1)
"Anyārtham" means for the sake of producing another phoneme;

"anyavarṇasaṃskāraśakta" means capable of the refinement of another phoneme. That refinement of the auditory organ which is for the sake of the cognition of another phoneme is expressed by the term "anyavarṇasaṃskāra," but it does not refer to the refinement of the phoneme itself, because the refinement of the auditory organ is the subject under discussion.
"Nānyaṃ kariṣyati" means that it will not refine another phoneme by way of refining the auditory organ.
And he says: *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, p. 608;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
684; he does so—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 608.
The reading in the present context: *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 423;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 36.
O Jains—Ā. Ṭī. (Editorial Note).

"If one [sound] is perceived, it would follow that all [sounds] are perceived"—this is the rebuttal to such an objection stated by the Mīmāṃsaka (Ānandabodha’s *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-ṭīkā*, Śabdanityatā, verse 80). And so forth:
if the palate and other organs, or the articulated sounds (*dhvani*), were the manifestors of words, then their perception would not necessarily occur whenever those [organs] function.
For this is the operation of a producer (*kāraka*): namely, the necessary bringing about of the effect’s presence when it is in proximity; it is not the operation of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

Indeed, it is not the case that wherever a manifestor such as a lamp exists, there the presence or perception of the manifested object such as a jar necessarily occurs, for that would entail the non-distinction between a producer and a manifestor, and would result in the uselessness of the operation of [producers like] the potter’s wheel and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that because a jar and the like are not all-pervading (*asarvagata*), they do not necessarily possess proximity or become perceived when the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is present, whereas for sound this is the reverse (i.e., it does). However, that too is an unexamined statement; for its all-pervasiveness is unproven.

To explain: sound is not all-pervading, because while possessing both generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*), it is perceptible by an external sense organ (*bāhyendriyapratyakṣatva*), like a jar and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no difference between sound and jars etc., one must accept without distinction that both are either produced (*kāryatva*) or manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*).

Comparison [establishes the nature of an effect]: because perception arises from the operation of all causes taken together, and because the status of being an effect is necessarily tied to that; for such [causal operation] is impossible in the case of a manifestor.

Indeed, when the instruments are functioning, there is never a non-perception of sound. Furthermore, the operation of a manifestor does not invariably cause the object to be perceived, as in some cases a jar is not perceived even when light is present.
There must necessarily be the perception of sound due to the operation of that [cause] when it arises;
for it is impossible for that [perception] to be established even through the operation of a non-agent.
Furthermore, because sound is invariably perceived from the operation—characterized by vibration and so forth—of the complete collection of instruments, it follows that sound is an effect.

What is the reason? Because that [manifestation] is impossible in the case of a manifesting cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*), since it is impossible for the manifested object (*vyaṅgya*) to be perceived with necessity—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.265.

When the manifestor is active, there would be no restricted cognition of the manifested; nor would there be a rule of necessary concomitance resulting from the utterance of the audible sound. Therefore, there is no specific reason why the palate and other organs are manifestors, while wheels and the like are not.
Those [factors] are indeed the causal agents (*kāraka*) of a jar and the like, but not so for sound, even though the palate and other organs are involved;

for the operation of a manifestor does not necessarily bring the manifested object into proximity, whereas the operation of the palate and other organs does necessarily bring sound into proximity. Therefore, sound is not manifested by the palate and other organs, just as a jar is manifested by a wheel and other such tools.
–Aṣṭaśa°, Aṣṭasahasra pṛ. 103;
and if the palate and so forth, or the sounds, are its [the auditory organ's]—Prameyakamala pṛ. 415; Syādvādaratnākara pṛ. 684.
Vāyava-ā° Ṭīkā:

A manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is that which effects the refinement of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an already existing causal factor (*kāraka*), whereas a producer (*kāraka*) is that which brings about the essential nature of what was previously non-existent.
–In the production of a jar and so forth, the goal is accomplished by the lamp and such alone – Ā. Ṭī. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 116).

Comparison: Sounds are pervasive and eternal; therefore, because sounds are pervasive and eternal, they are perceived everywhere due to the operation of the manifesting instrument [the vocal organ]. However, jars and the like are neither pervasive nor eternal; thus, they are not necessarily perceived through the operation of a manifesting agent. If this is so, what confidence or certainty can there be now regarding jars and the like—that they are neither eternal nor pervasive? For it may well be that they too are pervasive and eternal. (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p. 385)

"The objection that 'this is not a fault because phonemes are omnipresent' is also false; for it lacks support from the authority of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and [if it were true], it would entail the same state of affairs elsewhere as well" (Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 103; Syādvādaratnākara, p.

The qualification was stated for the purpose of excluding [the category of] the universal (sāmānya) — [Āloka-ṭīkā]. Compare: "And it is not tenable here that the phoneme (varṇa) is omnipresent, formless, eternal, and unitary, because its nature is to be perceivable by the external sense organs, like a jar or similar objects."

Sound is not omnipresent, because, while possessing both generality and particularity, it is perceptible by a single external sense organ, like a jar and other such objects. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.

Because, while possessing both generality and particularity, it is perceptible by the external senses—like a jar and so forth; [it does not exist]—Syādvādamañjarī, page 684 (gha); [it does not exist]—Āptamīmāṃsā.

Furthermore, from what source are these sounds apprehended, such that the hearing of the word-sound would be dependent upon them—is it through perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? If it is through perception, is it by means of auditory perception or tactile perception? It cannot be by auditory perception, because there is no such cognition; for sounds do not appear in the auditory faculty in the same way that the word-sound does, as that would entail the consequence of there being no disagreement [regarding their presence]. Moreover, if one were to admit their appearance therein, the postulation of a separate word-sound would be useless, because it would follow that the sounds themselves, having an auditory nature, are the word-sounds.

Now, as for the claim that sounds are perceived by tactile perception—since one who speaks with his mouth covered by his own hand perceives them through the touch of that hand—that too is incorrect; for, like air, there would be the undesirable consequence that they are merely manifesters of sound because they are perceived as droplets immediately following the activity of the palate and other organs.
If it is argued that this is not so because they perish right at the region of the speaker’s mouth and do not travel to the region of the listener’s ear, then the same applies elsewhere:
indeed, even the air particles are certainly not perceived as traveling there by means of direct perception.
However, the cognition [of air] is equal in both cases because it cannot otherwise be accounted for by the perception of sound;
and just as there is no perception of droplets from one who speaks softly, so too there is no perception of air,
and the postulation of a "stilled" state is equal in both instances.

By this, the following is also refuted: the claim that one perceives sounds through inference because one observes the impelling of cotton and the like situated at the tip of the mouth of a speaker; for by that same logic, there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving droplets [of saliva] from that [mouth] as well. (Tulanā: *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 418; *Syādvādaratnākara* p.
By means of the ear [one perceives] sound; by means of the sense of touch [one perceives] sound;
therein, the sounds possess the quality of sound.
In the auditory organ, it is only specific sounds (*dhvani*) in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are expressive;

there exists no distinct entity called "word" (*śabda-rūpa*) separate from them that expresses a different object, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its existence. This [notion] is far too much to be believed.

What is the reason? Because we do not perceive non-expressive sound (*dhvani*) and the expressive word (*śabda*) as having distinct natures, such that the latter would be of the nature of pure form while the former is not; therefore, it is a specific sound itself that exists in the form of *a*, *kāra*, and so forth, which is called a "phoneme" (*varṇa*). (Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p.
368). Since it is a specific sound itself that is designated as a phoneme.

Therefore, a specific sound uttered rapidly is called a rapid manifestation of the letter *ga*; one uttered at a medium pace is a medium manifestation; and a specific sound uttered slowly is a slow manifestation of the letter *ga*. However, no letter *ga* appears as something other than the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*).—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 382.
Compare: because phlegm and the like are also perceived immediately after the operation of the palate and other organs, just like air, it would follow that they too are manifestors of sound.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
418; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
684: "of the droplets... [Ā.]

Whatever is perceived immediately after the operation of the palate and other organs is a manifester of sound, just as air is; and such are the droplets (*vipruṣaḥ*)—[Ānandagiri’s Commentary (Ā-Ṭīkā):
"of those," i.e., of the droplets, the specks of phlegm].
Even in the case of *dhvani*, the capacity to manifest sound is established through direct perception and through its exhaustion.
Just as in the region of the listener's ear,
the perception of droplets is equally present even within the phlegmatic humors, like wind. (Āryadeva)
"Stimitakalpa" (as if motionless) — [referring to] the winds — [according to the] commentary (ā॰ ṭi॰);
"even of the droplets" (vipruṣām api) — [according to] Ācārya (ā॰).
"Because moisture is observed on a cloth held before the mouth, droplets emerge from the mouth"—this is the inference [stated in the Ācārya-ṭīkā].

For indeed, droplets are seen upon the cloth held at the front of the mouth and so forth. Now, sounds (*dhvani*) are apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); for instance, since sound is eternal, it is not produced; rather, only its manifestation (*saṃskṛti*) is effected. And that specific manifestation would not be possible if sounds did not exist.
And it has been said:
"There are sounds (dhvanis), because otherwise specific refinement (saṃskṛti) would be impossible;
for there are sounds that manifest the word (śabda), because otherwise the comprehension of the word would be impossible."
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.

605: Because the production of sound has been refuted, the arising of a specific refinement [of the auditory organ] from the sounds (dhvanis) is determined through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*). [Variant reading: *...from them it is ascertained*].

Now, if there is no distinction [between the two cases], why is it that only the production of a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is accepted, and not the production of a specific sound? To this he replies: "Sound...

Because the perception of a sound that was previously unarisen but subsequently arisen would otherwise be impossible, something must necessarily be postulated; and since the production of sound is denied by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is more reasonable to postulate a mental impression alone—so says the *Nyāyaratna*.
It is determined from the sounds—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
418; *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 611;
*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Śabdanityatā, verses 126–27. Thus.

That too is not tenable; for what is this so-called "specific embellishment" (viśiṣṭā saṃskṛtiḥ)—is it an embellishment of the word, an embellishment of the auditory organ, or an embellishment of both? For the Mīmāṃsakas accept three kinds of embellishment: that of the sense organ alone, that of the word alone, or that of both. [This is also stated in the Āhnikam:
"The embellishment belongs either to the sense organ alone, or to the word alone, or to both."
Three theories are advanced by the proponents of manifestation (abhivyaktivādins) regarding [the nature of] sounds—
Vākyapadīya 1.79.
For that [cognition] would indeed arise from the refinement of the word "syāt," or of the sense faculty, or of both; thus it is said: "syācchabda" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Tattvasaṃgraha, p.
This has been extracted in this very form—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 419:

"That manifestation of sound, when occurring, must arise either from the refinement of the sound through conjunctions and disjunctions of air, or from the refinement of the sense organ, or from the refinement of both the sound and the sense organ"—*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 599.
Regarding the refinement of the senses:
through the removal of the steady breath, his refinement occurs;
for breath is indeed of two kinds—steady and unsteady.

In this regard, that which exists as a stable [entity] obscuring sound like darkness—conjunctions and disjunctions are produced by the air arising from the effort of the speaker; and by those conjunctions and disjunctions, the removal of that stable air is effected. This alone is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sound, and nothing else such as the nourishment of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is eternal and thus uniform in nature.
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 601)

In that regard, concerning the first position, what is this so-called "manifestation of the word" (*śabda-saṃskāra*)? Is it the perception of the word; some excellence (*atiśaya*) inherent in it; the exclusion of non-excellence; the nourishment of its own nature; inherence in the individual (*vyakti*); the state of being perceived in dependence upon the perception of that [individual]; the mere proximity of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*); or the removal of an obscuration? If it is the perception of the word, how can this be brought about by the sounds (*dhvani*s), since that perception arises solely from the word and the auditory organ? Even so, if one were to postulate another cause for it, there would be an infinite regress of causes.

Whether [the effect] be some excellence (*atiśaya*) that has become identical with the self, or the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of non-excellence—in this case too, excellence is nothing other than the very nature of being perceptible, and the exclusion of non-excellence is simply the negation of the nature of being imperceptible. Are these two established as distinct from that [nature], or as non-distinct? If they are distinct, then by producing them, nothing at all would have been done to the word; thus its state of being inaudible would remain as before.
If, on the other hand, they are non-distinct, then it follows that the word itself must also be an effect, which entails its impermanence.

For when something has an identical nature with another, the production of that [other] entails the production of this as well—just as in the case of the specific nature consisting in the exclusion of both excellence and non-excellence. And since sound has an identical nature with those two, the comparison holds:
whether it be the possession of excellence by the word arising from its causes, or its manifestation, or the removal of an obscuration, or cognition, there is no other alternative possible.
Therefore, manifestation of the word does not occur from its causes; rather, there is only its production.

Alternatively, manifestation (*vyakti*) from the perspective of its causes would be threefold: either manifestation of the sound would consist in its possessing excellence through the abandonment of its prior state; or it would be the removal of the obstruction to its perception; or it would be the cognition that has the sound as its object. This is because there is no other possible way apart from these three modes.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p. 386; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
What is this "refinement of sound" (śabdasamskāra)—is it the imparting of a new excellence, the removal of a lack of excellence, or the disappearance of an obscuration? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
685; Ratnākarāvatārikā 4.9)

In the perception of sound, [the cognition] is distinct from both the sound and the auditory organ—[Ācārya-ṭīkā]. For comparison: "In that case, there is no production of an excellence [in the object], because that would entail impermanence, since such [production] is characterized by the loss of a prior form and the arising of a subsequent one."
— Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1.265:
Even the imparting of a specific quality to this [object] is not perceived as its manifestation.
Because the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) is contradictory for that which is eternal, just like the destruction of its own self—*Tattvārtha-śloka-vārttika*, p.

238—an excellence is nothing other than the visible nature [of the thing] itself, whereas the exclusion of non-excellence is simply the negation of the invisible nature. If these two were different from the [thing] itself, then even when they are produced, nothing at all would have been done to the sound; thus, it remains in its original state, and there is no hearing of it.
If, on the other hand, they are not distinct, then sound too, by virtue of being an effect, would necessarily follow as being impermanent—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
419; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 685.

Being invisible, it becomes visible when an excellence [of cognition] arises— [Ārya-ṭīkā]; however, the activity [of that excellence] is either different from or non-different from those two— [Bhaṭṭa, Śrāvaka].
The exclusion of excellence and non-excellence [is understood] from the word—Ānandagiri’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.). Compare: "For that specific refinement is not distinct from the word."
Consequently, sound would also become unknowable; therefore, even sound arises [as an object].
— *Tattvasaṅgraha*, Verse 2570.
They are distinct. — Ārya.
Whether it be in the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) or in the exclusion of what lacks excellence (*anatiśayavyāvṛtti*),
[the word and its referent] are non-different— Ārya’s Commentary.

Just like the exclusion of excellence and non-excellence— because the word *kṛti* possesses a nature non-different from the two exclusions of excellence and non-excellence, both in terms of being an effect and having the form of an effect.

Furthermore, regarding its cause: would the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of this [sound] be produced by the sounds in the region of the ear alone, or everywhere? In the first case, the sound would be of that limited measure only and not all-pervading;

for if it were to exist elsewhere in a form contrary to that [limited state], there would follow the consequence of its being both visible and invisible, which would contradict its partlessness (*niraṃśatā*).

Furthermore, the doctrine of Brahman is supported by the fact that a single entity can possess both visible and invisible forms; for there is no contradiction in a single thing existing in such a way as to have both conscious and unconscious aspects.

Moreover, it would follow that even a jar or similar object must be all-pervading, for one who asserts that "it is visible in the region where it is perceived and invisible elsewhere" would not have his mouth twisted [in embarrassment].

Furthermore, if its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) were present everywhere, it would be perceived everywhere and at all times; otherwise, it would never be perceived anywhere at all, since there would be no distinction between the two states.
In this way, the [suffix] śraṇ is applied to the word āśraya.
Furthermore, if sound were produced only in the region of the ear, it would be merely of that size and could not be all-pervading— [as stated in] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 419,
regarding sound.
Other than the location of the ear,
it would exist either as an invisible form or as a non-sound form— this is not seen. (Śrāvakabhūmi)
Just as sound has the quality of being both visible and invisible, so too is the heard sound [perceived]. Śra.
[Śābarabhāṣya] on Sound.

Furthermore, the development of its own nature (*svarūpaparipoṣa*) is also untenable, because it is impossible for that which is eternal to undergo a change in its intrinsic nature; or, if such a change were to occur, it would entail the faults associated with the position that [the entity] possesses adventitious excellences (*atiśaya*).
Nor is there inherence in an individual [manifestor], because that is not accepted; otherwise, it would follow that sound would have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth.

For this very reason, its apprehension does not depend upon the apprehension of that [individual], nor is it merely the proximity of the manifestor; for otherwise, it would follow that all sounds would be apprehended by all perceivers at all times and in all places.
If, however, that latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consists in the removal of obstructions, then there would be the simultaneous perception of all sounds;

[if you argue] that this fault does not apply because they are manifested by specific manifestors—that too is a mere wishful thinking, since their being manifested by those has already been refuted. As the comparison goes: "If they were all-pervasive, there would be the perception of all of them simultaneously."
And if there is perception of the conditioned, who is the conditioner of that which is unchanging?
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.153–54.
Sound also inheres in individuals— [Ānandajñāna’s Commentary];
if sound were to inhere in individuals, then it would be a universal, for it is a universal that inheres in individuals— [Ānandajñāna’s Commentary].
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), multiple categories such as conjunction (saṃyoga) and others are to be understood;
this follows from the very same [logical] contingency regarding universals (sāmānya), forms (rūpa), and so forth—[as noted in the] Āloka-ṭīkā.
[The capacity to produce its own cognition] is defined in relation to the apprehension of the individual instance (vyaktigrahaṇa).
If, during the refinement of sound, there is the weighing [of it] and the manifestation— which is the disappearance— of those veils that conceal its form,
then why would the capacity of the collection of sense organs not exist with respect to non-existence?
—*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.266:
"In that case, let it be that manifestation is not the refinement of the word; rather, it will be the refinement of the sense organ."
As it has been said: "Even if there were a refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*), that [refinement] would occur only in the location of its physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna-deśa*);
therefore, the ear would not hear sound, because the concha (*śaṣkulī*) would remain unrefined."
Because the sound has not reached the location of the ear, there is no refinement of the auditory organ;
therefore, the restriction of refinement is established by means of the distinction between the physical bases [of the senses].

[The opponent claims: "As stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Śabdanityatā-adhikaraṇa, verses 69–71; that too is charming only so long as it is not examined. For even on the view that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is refined (*saṃskṛta*), there would follow the consequence that the auditory organ, once refined, would simultaneously manifest all sounds.

Indeed, we do not observe a restriction such that the eye, refined by collyrium (*añjana*) and the like, sees some of its proximate objects—such as blue or white—and not others; nor do we observe a restriction such that the ear, refined by *balātala* and the like, hears certain phonemes like the letter 'ga' and not others, on account of which one might postulate the same [restriction] in this case as well."

Therefore, this is incorrect: that just as a lamp or similar object is held to be the manifestor of a jar or the like through the very assistance it provides to the eye, so too would sound [be the manifestor] through the refinement of the auditory organ;
nor is there a valid objection here as to in what form this refinement occurs.

"Because the same [objection] applies even to its production, the capacity there too is beyond the senses" (Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Śabdanityatā, verses 42–43). For, just as one with eyes aided by a lamp and so forth perceives many objects such as jars simultaneously, it would follow that the ear, aided by sounds (*dhvani*), would perceive multiple words at once.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the auditory organ does not have a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) as its object for the purpose of perceiving objects situated in different locations that are to be grasped by a single sense-organ, because it is a sense-organ, like the eye.

Therefore, even the modification of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) cannot be the manifestation [of sound]. For even if it were a modification of the sense organ, that [modification] would occur only in the location of its physical substrate; consequently, the auditory organ would not hear the sound, as its ear-cavity would remain unmodified.
The substratum is the ear-cavity;
through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that [cavity], there is the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra*), not of the organ alone.

Therefore, because its substratum has not been refined, the auditory organ of those who are situated at a distance, or whose minds are elsewhere, or who are asleep or in a state of fainting, does not hear.

That whose ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is described as such; the suffix *-tas* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*adhiṣṭhāna-deśataḥ*). Although the sounds (*nāda*) that produce the conditioning of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) or the conditioning of the sense organ located in that place do so only when they have reached [their object], they nevertheless effect the conditioning upon the entity that is the locus of conditioning only when they have reached it, not when they have not reached it. Therefore, there is no conditioning of the substratum and so forth belonging to all persons. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, p. 606)
Seventh [note]: The meaning is that the fifth case-ending is used in the sense of the seventh;
therefore, "he will not hear"—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 685.

Because the sound does not reach the region of the ear, there is no refinement of the auditory organ [by it]. Therefore, the restriction of the refinement is established by way of the distinction of the physical locus.
(Verse 2) [Commentary: For whomsoever the sound reaches the region of the ear, for that person alone is there a refinement of the auditory organ—Ā.
Ṭī. Because the sound does not reach the region of the ear, there is no refinement of the auditory organ by the sound—Syā. Ra. p. 686.
The stability of the determination of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-niyama-sthiti*)—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Prameyakhaṇḍa, p.
424; the stability of the determination of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-niyama-sthita*)—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 606.

[If] there were a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense faculty, it might hear all of that; however, because [the faculty] is differentiated by various refinements, there would be a restriction to a single object, if indeed [such a thing were possible]. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 686; cf.)
How can there be auditory perception of a collection of many sounds in a cacophony?
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.255–56.
For them as well, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ consists either in the removal of its obstructions or in the production of a capacity for perceiving sound.
As stated in the *Tattvārthaśloka* (p. 5):

"It is observed that the refinement of a sense organ—such as by opening [the eyes] or by light—produces a refinement conducive to the perception of all objects simultaneously that are capable of being connected with the organ; likewise, the air too would impart a single refinement to the auditory organ conducive to the perception of all sounds, and thus there would be the perception of all sounds."
"But even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving all sounds, for when the auditory organ is refined, all [sounds] are present [to it]. — *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, Śabdakhaṇḍa, p.
405; *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 648.

It is observed as a rule that the auditory organ, when refined by *valā-taila* and other such means, perceives certain sounds such as the letter *ga*, but not others; see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 424;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 36.
The rule "he hears" (śṛṇoti) [is stated] in the *Śāstravārttāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*, folio 377B, and in the *Syādvādamañjarī*, folio 686.
Ā., Ba.

Just as a lamp or similar object is accepted as the manifestor of a jar or other such things by means of assisting the eye, so too shall sound be [the manifestor] through the refinement of the auditory organ. But what is the nature of the manifesting power of sounds? He shows this with the words "just as":

just as a lamp, by providing nourishment and assistance to the visual light, becomes the manifestor of visible objects such as jars, so too the articulations (dhvanis), by effecting a refinement of the auditory organ, will become the manifestors of the word-sound (śabda).
—These two [verses] are cited in the *Nyāyaratna* (p. 424), the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.
602), and the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p. 602).
Due to the assistance provided by the refinement of the auditory organ, sound is the manifester of the word-sound (śabda)—[Ānandagiri’s] Commentary.

Nor should there be an objection here as to "in what form does the refinement [occur]?", for this is equally applicable even in the case of [the theory of] production; in that case too, the capacity must be regarded as transcendental (atīndriyā)—Page 708, Note 18.
Let it be, then, that manifestation is the embellishment of both; for in that case, the aforementioned faults do not apply.

As it has been said: "But regarding the position that there is an embellishment of both, the statement concerning the two faults is futile, because due to the deficiency of either one, everything is not perceived by everyone."
[The opponent claims: "As stated in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Śabdanityatā* section, verses 86–87;

that too is incorrect, precisely because it is subject to the faults already mentioned. To explain: when the auditory organ, having been refined (*saṃskṛta*) so as to perceive a single phoneme (*varṇa*), perceives that refined phoneme, it would then have to perceive all the phonemes present therein. Furthermore, since the refined phoneme exists everywhere and at all times, otherwise its perception would not occur at all, because [the phoneme] is of that very nature. As for the position that there is refinement of both [the organ and the object], the statement regarding these two faults is redundant; for due to the deficiency of either one, everything is not perceived by everyone."

It is not heard by all persons due to a deficiency in the auditory faculty (*śrotra-saṃskāra*), nor is every sound [heard] due to a deficiency in the sound itself (*śabda-saṃskāra*); for both [factors] together constitute the cause.
For if each were a cause individually, there would be a twofold fault—*Nyāyaratna*.
But on the view that there are two types of refinement (*saṃskāra*), those two defects are indeed futile; for, due to the deficiency of either one, sound is not perceived—
namely, because sound is not perceived when there is a deficiency of either the auditory refinement or the object-refinement.

For instance: even when there is refinement of the word, the deaf person does not perceive the sound due to the deficiency in the refinement of the auditory organ; likewise, even for one who is not deaf, there is non-perception of the sound when it is unmanifested.
In some readings, the phrase "the speech regarding these two defects is false" appears—*Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, p. 612.
The statement regarding the two faults is false—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdanityatādhikaraṇa, p.
687; the reading in the present context is from the Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 611.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

424: "The refinement of the word (*śabda-saṃskāra*) is the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*)"—Ācārya’s commentary. Compare: "For instance, the auditory organ and the phonemes are refined by their respective manifestors (*vyañjaka*) from before..."
"They are not lost when the transition [to another state] occurs; therefore, all [sounds] are heard by everyone"—*Tattvasaṃgraha-kārikā* 2573.
When the auditory organ, having been refined, perceives a refined phoneme by virtue of its capacity to grasp a single phoneme, it would then perceive all the phonemes present therein.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
425; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 687: Because all phonemes exist in that region of space by virtue of being pervasive and eternal.
And always,
O Śrī, if one does not know the phoneme (varṇa) as being eternally present everywhere and at all times, then [it would follow that it is] by virtue of having a form that is eternal and pervasive.

Therefore, since it is impossible for sound—which is by nature eternal and uniform—to stand in the relation of the veiled and the veil, or the manifested and the manifestor, its non-perception prior to utterance cannot be caused by an obstruction.

Consequently, because it is perceived immediately after the operation of the palate and other articulatory organs, and is not perceived in their absence, it must be admitted that it is indeed an effect of those organs.

[Objection: But the ether (*ākāśa*) is perceived after digging and the like, and is not perceived in their absence; yet it is not an effect of those actions. Therefore, your reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
And it has been said: "First, the inconclusiveness of the reasons is stated here:

'The observation [of sound] immediately following effort is not contradicted even if [sound] were eternal' (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā, verse 19). For even space, though eternal, when covered by earth and water..."
That [object] is manifested by means of digging, filling, and so forth;
since cognition occurs there as well immediately following effort,
the reason you stated— that "it is seen there"— is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"Now, it is inferred that even though this [sound] is concealed, it certainly exists;

likewise, sound is understood to exist prior to its perception because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā, verses 30–33). That too is unsatisfactory, because the state of having a single nature (*ekasvabhāvatva*) is unestablished even in the case of space (*ākāśa*).

For that [object], being of such a nature, must either have as its sole essence the production of a cognition of itself as its object, or it must be the opposite of that. If its sole essence were the production of that [cognition], then its apprehension would not occur immediately after digging and so forth, but rather it should have occurred even previously;
however, if its nature were the opposite of that, there would never be any apprehension at all due to the absence of any distinction.
Or, if there were a distinction, there would be a contradiction of its having a single uniform nature.
Furthermore, since there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the prior existence of sound is established; and this same argument applies even to nails and hair that have been cut and grown back again.

How then could the prior existence of phonemes (*dhvani*) not also be established? For there is the cognition that "the very same phoneme which previously manifested the letter *a* is the one that manifests it later as well. Consequently, since the existence of the manifestor would be established everywhere just like the manifested, the activity of the palate and other articulatory organs would be rendered useless, and the manifestation of the object would occur at all times and in all places.

And [the Sūtra] says: "Because it is not perceived prior to its utterance, and because no obstruction or other [cause for non-perception] is perceived prior to its utterance, sound does not exist prior to its utterance. (Nyāyavārttika 2.2.13)

Why? Because regarding that which exists, non-perception due to such causes as concealment is not tenable; why? Because the causes of non-perception, such as concealment and the like, are not apprehended.

Because of this [obstruction], sound is not perceived; due to the intervention of something not in contact with the sense organ, and so forth—such causes of non-perception are not apprehended. Thus, this [sound] which was not uttered is [said to be] "non-existent. Therefore, its non-apprehension is not due to the absence of a manifestor, but rather due to its very non-existence. Consequently, when it is being uttered, it is heard; and while being heard, it is inferred that it comes into existence after having not existed.
Because it is not heard after being uttered upward, it exists and then ceases to exist; because it no longer exists, it is not heard.
How so? It has been stated that this is due to the non-perception of its obstruction and so forth.
Therefore, sound possesses the properties of arising and disappearance.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 2.2.18

Sound is impermanent because it is the effect of an utterance consisting of the activity of the palate and other organs, since it follows immediately upon the effort consisting of the activity of the palate and other organs;
nor is that [reason] unestablished.
Regarding the reason: "The act of digging the sky [is non-existent] because it follows immediately upon effort."

First, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reasons (*hetu*) is stated here. The phrase "perception immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantaraṃ dṛṣṭiḥ*) is not contradictory even in the case of an eternal entity;
by the word "first" (*tāvat*), its lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) will also be expressed. Thus, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness of the reason "because it is perceived immediately after effort":

perception indeed indicates existence therein, but it does not exclude [existence] at another time. Therefore, since existence at another time is possible even in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), perception therein is inconclusive.
–*Nyāyaratna*:
"perception immediately following effort" – *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*; "apprehension" – *Āloka-ṭīkā*.

Even though space is eternally existent, when it is covered by earth and water, its cognition occurs following effort—such as digging and draining—through the removal of those [obstructions]. Therefore, the reason [you] stated there—that the cognition of space [proves the point]—is inconclusive (anaikāntika). —Ārya-ṭīkā.
It is observed—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *darśana*; "knowledge arising immediately after effort"—*Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 640;
"from observation"—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Tattvasaṅgraha*.
Now, it is inferred that this [sound] exists even when concealed; likewise, sound is understood to exist prior to its utterance due to recognition,
just as space exists prior to its manifestation even though it is covered by the earth and other elements.
These verses have been extracted: the first from *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 422;
the second and third from *Syādvādaratnākara*, page 689;
and the second and third from *Tattvasaṃgraha*, page 640.
Comparison—the uniformity of space is also unestablished—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 422; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 689; [text fragment] "of the entity... space" (*bhāvasya ākāśasya*).
The point is that if space were of a single eternal nature,

it would follow that its nature of not producing a cognition of itself at the time prior to digging— when it was unperceived— and its nature of producing a cognition of itself after digging would not constitute a single, eternal form for space. Thus, its eternal oneness would be lost.
Just as in the case of the word "prācyatvasi," the palate and other organs are employed only for the production of the sound; and these [organs] exist at all times.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "Even at other times, that which is the utterance of a word is its manifestor, because it is an utterance," and so forth; for this [reasoning] applies equally to sound (dhvani) as well.
To explain: even at other times, that which is the utterance of sound is its manifestor, because it is an utterance, just like its utterance now. (p. 699, l. 5)
That which manifests the sound is not its producer;
by this [argument], who indeed could destroy this [sound], which remains stable for that duration, afterwards?

This [objection] from the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Śabdanityatā-adhikaraṇa*, verse 366, is also refuted; for since sound is also recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) as persisting through both prior and subsequent times, its destruction by anything later is untenable.
This was cited in the *Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 254; compare with the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, p. 955.

As for what was also stated—“The time under dispute is connected with sound (*gādi*) and so forth, because it is time”—that too is a mere assertion. For since sound and the like, which meet the conditions for perception, are not perceived at other times, their non-existence is established. Consequently, any inference intended to prove their existence therein is unconvincing, as its subject (*pakṣa*) is sublated and its reason (*hetu*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

Furthermore, by this same logic, even lightning and such things would be eternal. To illustrate: the time under dispute is connected with lightning and so forth, because it is time, just like a time connected with lightning and so forth.
The contradiction with common experience (*pratīti-virodha*) is no different in other cases as well;

for this very reason, [the argument] "sound is eternal because it is audible" (*śrāvaṇatvāt*) and so forth is also incorrect. Furthermore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to properties of sound (*dhvani-dharma*) such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others, for you yourself have asserted that these are non-eternal despite being audible. If they were not themselves audible, they could not be perceived by the ear as properties belonging to sound; for that which is not itself of an audible nature cannot be perceived by the ear as a property of sound, just like blueness and the like. And the properties of sound, such as the acute accent and others, are indeed not themselves of an audible nature.
Likewise, there is inconclusiveness due to the sounds of the lute and so forth, because even though they are impermanent, they are audible (pṛ. 699, l. 9). Compare:
"Because it has been established that [sounds] such as 'ga' perish immediately after their utterance, as is perceived by direct perception" (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 689).
Even in the case of sound, immediately after its utterance at a later time, page 699,
line 11.
Comparison: [The reason] is inconclusive because of properties such as being high-pitched (*udātta*), for those are not accepted by you as eternal even though they are perceptible by hearing;
however, if they were imperceptible by hearing, they could not be apprehended by the ear, just like blue and other colors.
There is also inconclusiveness due to the sounds of lutes and the like, because although they are audible, they are impermanent;
by the word "and" (ca), contradiction with experience is conjoined. (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 690)
The perception of those [qualities], such as the acute accent (udātta) and so forth, through hearing—according to your own view—[is not possible]. (Ā. Ṭī.)

Furthermore, as for the other argument stated—that "the cognitions of the individual instances of the word *go* are differentiated by place, time, and so forth," and so on—that too is not sound. This is because the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the cognition of the written form of the word *go*; for that cognition arises as "this is a cow" (*gauḥ*), yet its object is not identical to the object of the currently arising cognition of the spoken word *go*. Moreover, such a difference in objects is never established anywhere, as it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all cognitions have an identical object.

To illustrate: cognitions of objects differentiated by place and time must either have one object or multiple objects, because they are cognitions of objects, just like the cognition of a jar arising at this very moment.
Furthermore, if all cognitions of objects were to have as their object a single entity characterized as a jar, there would only be the cognition of a "jar," and not the cognition of the word "cow."

Therefore, how can the cognitions of individual instances of the word "cow" (go-śabda) as distinguished by place and so forth possess the status of the subject (*dharmin*)? Or how could "being a cognition of the word 'cow'" (*go-śabda-buddhitva*) be the logical reason (*hetu*), or how could the example "like a present cognition of the word 'cow'" be established, such that an inference might proceed? If it is argued that because the difference between objects such as cows and horses is established by perception, the reason "because it is a cognition of an object" (*vastu-buddhitvāt*) is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by lapse of time) when proving that those cognitions have a single object—just as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is [a reason] for proving that fire is not hot—then, if this is the case, since the difference between individual instances of the word "cow" is also established by perception through the difference in properties such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth, the reason "because it arises as 'cow'" (*gor ity utpadyamānatvāt*) would likewise be *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* when proving that those cognitions have a single object.

Page 699, line 12. For comparison: because the reason [stated] by means of the cognition of the word "cow" and its script is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for that [cognition] arises with the mental reflection "this is a cow," yet it does not have a single word "cow" as its object, since the words "cow" and their scripts differ according to place, time, and so forth.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
690: "The cognition of the letter *g* is indeed one thing, while the cognition of the word 'cow' (*go*) is another. —Ānandagiri’s Commentary (Ā. Ṭī.).
Comparison: Otherwise, all cognitions would have a single object,
and there would be a contradiction regarding their sequential occurrence even when the efficient cause is present— Tattvasaṅgraha, Verse 2466.
Syādvādamañjarī, page 690: "—distinct entity—" Śra; "nor manifold—" Śra.

As for what was stated—"the word 'cow' from yesterday persists even today," and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for since the difference between the word "cow" from yesterday and that of today is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the attempt to prove their non-difference is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time).
Otherwise, how could there not also be oneness between the flashes of lightning from yesterday and today?
For it might indeed be argued: "The lightning flash of yesterday continues even today, because it is a lightning flash, like the lightning flash of today.

However, since the lightning flash is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having distinct natures by way of its possessing qualities such as intensity—being intense, more intense, or most intense—an inference that seeks to establish its identity is not a valid means of cognition. This applies equally elsewhere: for even the word "cow" appears in auditory perception as endowed with qualities such as intensity.

If that property were adventitious (*aupādhika*) in this case, then let it be so for lightning as well, since there is no distinction [between them]. If it is argued that because pure lightning is never perceived, that property cannot be adventitious in its case—this is no different in the case of sound, for even in a dream, that [sound] does not appear devoid of its properties.
By this, the claim that "the cow-sound of today existed yesterday too," and so forth, is refuted, because the underlying logic is the same.

Page 700, line 6: For comparison— All these cognitions of the word "cow" occurring yesterday and today do not have a single object, because they arise sequentially, like the cognitions of color, smell, and so forth.
— Tattvasaṃgraha, verse 2465 (Śāradā edition, page 690)—
[in the] heart, Śrī., Ba.
It proceeds with the intensity of lightning;

[this is] through the direct perception of the ear—[variant: "through the direct perception of the ear," *śrotrapratyakṣeṇa*]. This is because the principle of determining intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), which is well-known here and there, is equally applicable here as well.

For there is no means of knowledge other than perception to establish that coldness and fluidity in water, or luminosity and heat in fire, are intrinsic; likewise [there is none] for the properties such as the acute accent (*udātta*) in sound. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 690)
In the lightning of the emptiness of all phenomena, such as those that are intense, more intense, and so forth.
Free from qualities such as the acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) accents, it is pure and distinct; it exists even in deep sleep and even in dreams— this is the Śruti.

As for what was also stated—that sound is expressive and persists for a long duration, and so forth—that too is inconclusive because of [the example of] gesture (*ceṣṭā*); for although that [gesture] is a cause for the cognition of an object by virtue of its connection [with a convention], it lacks persistence for a long duration.
(Page 700, Line 8)

In cases such as summoning, [the cognition arises] through gestures performed with a finger and so forth—[Āloka-ṭīkā]. Compare: "Because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to gesture"—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 692. By this, the argument that "whatever is unstable does not cause the cognition of an object by virtue of the force of a conventional relation," and so forth, is refuted; for even if a gesture causes the cognition of an object by virtue of the force of a conventional relation, it is possible for it to have its causal efficiency at that very moment.

Therefore, this [argument] is incorrect: "Sound is stable for some time and must be stable for all time because it is devoid of a cause of destruction, like a universal (sāmānya), space, or time. For, when you say "stability for some time," do you intend stability during the time of its perception, or stability throughout past and present time? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even things such as lightning and the like would be stable for all time, since there is no difference in their possessing such stability for a certain duration.

Furthermore, its persistence through past and present time is not established from any source; as has already been stated, the reason (*hetu*) here is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible for sound—which is occasional—to be devoid of a cause of destruction.
Whatever is occasional is not devoid of a cause of destruction, just like lightning and so forth; and sound is occasional.
[The opponent] objects:
"If sound is stable for some time, is it also stable for all time? (Vādavidhi, p. 700, l. 9).
Because it is devoid of a cause for destruction at a prior time, like the universal ether or time;
that which is perceived immediately after its utterance is the "time of perception"— Ānandajñāna’s Commentary (ĀṬ).
Regarding the comparison with sound: "And because [the property] is occasional, it is unestablished in the case of sound" (Syādvādaratnākara, p.
692). As for what was stated—that the time under dispute is not devoid of sounds such as 'ga' and so forth—that too is incorrect, as it applies equally to lightning and other such phenomena.

For instance—it has been stated by [Bhāsarvajña] that "the time under dispute is not devoid of lightning and so forth, because it is time, like a time endowed with their existence"; the sublation by perception is equal in both cases. (Vādidevasūri, *Syādvādaratnākara*)
Page 701, line 3.
For comparison: "That too is untenable because it is the same in the case of lightning and so forth"—Syādvādaratnākara, page 692;
[this applies] to sound and to lightning and so forth.

As for what was also stated—that sound is eternal because the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible—this too is charming only so long as it is not examined. For even though it is impermanent like smoke and the like, its capacity to convey meaning is established through similarity.

Indeed, there is no rule that the comprehension of meaning must be produced by that very same [sound] which was perceived at the time of the convention; for the cognition of fire is observed from mountain smoke that is merely similar to the smoke seen in the kitchen.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the two individual instances of smoke existing on a mountain and in a kitchen to be identical, because this contradicts experience and would entail the absurd consequence that everything is omnipresent.

Now, if it is the generality of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) that possesses the capacity to signify here, why should the generality of words (*śabdasāmānya*) not possess the capacity to denote elsewhere? [Objection: But if the generality of words is the denoter, what does that have to do with the individual word? [Reply: Then, if the generality of smoke is the inferential indicator, what does that have to do with the individual smoke? If you say that because the generality is non-different from the smoke, when it is the indicator, the smoke is also the indicator; then, since the generality is also non-different from the word, when it is the denoter, let the word also be the denoter, as there is no distinction between the two cases.

Now, if there is no universal (sāmānya) at all in the case of sound, how can its status as a signifier be asserted? In that case, it would not exist in smoke either; so of what could its status as a signifier be asserted? If [it is argued that] because its distinction is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—since we observe an unambiguous, non-sublated, and recurring cognition in the form "this is smoke, this is smoke"—the universal exists there, then this is the same in the other case as well.

[Objection: "But surely, since the difference between individual word-sounds (*śabda-vyakti*) is established through perception, the universal 'word-ness' (*śabdatva*) is indeed accepted there. However, because *ga* and other sounds each consist of a single individual and thus lack internal difference, a universal such as 'ga-ness' (*gatva*) is not possible therein; consequently, that universal cannot function as the expressive [signifier] there. [Reply: This too is incorrect. For even those [sounds like *ga*] can possess multiple individuals due to differences such as acute (*udātta*) and so forth, which makes the existence of universals like *gatva* logically consistent. Furthermore, the claim that "acute and the rest are merely properties of the manifesting sound (*dhvani*)" is a mere fantasy, since we have already provided the answer to the point that they are not properties of that [sound].

Therefore, since the comprehension of meaning from a word is thus possible even on the view that [the word] is non-eternal, its eternality cannot be established even through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Consequently, what was stated—namely, "And this presumptive testimony has been stated" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika)—is incorrect.

Furthermore, it was established during the examination of the eternal relationship [between word and meaning] that the capacity to denote belongs to the word precisely when it is non-eternal; so, enough of this digression.

p. 701, l. 4: For comparison—Even though [the sounds] are impermanent, because the comprehension of meaning occurs when there is the grasping of similarity, in those cases where you perceive such a sequence of the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga (*ḥ*), there the meaning qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*) is to be comprehended and to be communicated. Thus, once the convention has been grasped, one who perceives a word of that kind comprehends and communicates that meaning.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 649:

"Just as in the case of smoke and so forth, it is possible for even a non-eternal sound, once its relationship [with its object] has been understood, to convey meaning through similarity"—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 409.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 33; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p. 692; Prameya-ratnamālā, 3.
If the very same individual instance of smoke perceived in the kitchen were also present on the mountain, then [there would be] the universal of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*).
Of the generality of sound, namely "sound-ness" (śabdatva); [the text] "the generality of sound" is missing in Ā; "smoke also" is missing in Śra.

Since individual instances of smoke—such as those from a kitchen or a mountain—are manifold, there exists therein a pervasive universal called "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*); however, the word "sound" (*śabda*) is one. Therefore, with the intention that the non-difference of the individual would preclude a genus, he raises an objection with the word "atha": [how can there be] "soundness" (*śabdatva*) there, since a genus is established through difference? Śra. [1.1.6] 20.17-21.4: *athocyeta* (Now it might be said). The word *atha* introduces an objection. The opponent argues: "The universal called 'smokeness' is established because its instances are differentiated; however, the word 'sound' is a single entity. Therefore, how could there be a universal called 'soundness' (*śabdatva*) in it? For the non-difference of the individual is a subverter of a genus. This is the sense of the objection. To this, the author replies: "It is not so, because difference is established. The word *tu* ("but") indicates the refutation of the objection. It is not the case that the universal called "soundness" does not exist. Why? Because difference is established. That is to say, even though the word "sound" is a single entity, its individuals are nonetheless differentiated by their locations, such as the ear, the throat, the palate, and so forth. Since these differences are established, the universal "soundness" is indeed established. This is the meaning. Alternatively, the word *atha* may be interpreted as introducing a further objection. The opponent says: "Even if the universal 'smokeness' is established through the establishment of difference, the universal 'soundness' cannot be established in the same way. Why? Because the individuals of sound are not differentiated. For instance, when one utters the word 'cow' (*go*) repeatedly, the individual sounds are not perceived as distinct. Therefore, due to the non-difference of the individuals, the universal 'soundness' is not established. This is the sense of the objection. To this, the author replies: "It is not so, because difference is established. Since these differences are established, the universal "soundness" is indeed established. This is the meaning. Alternatively, the word *atha* may be interpreted as introducing a further objection. Because the individuals of sound are not differentiated. For instance, when one utters the word 'cow' (*go*) repeatedly, the individual sounds are not perceived as distinct. Because the individuals of sound are not differentiated. For instance, when one utters the word 'cow' (*go*) repeatedly, the individual sounds are not perceived as distinct. Therefore, due to the non-difference
— In the case of [the universal] katva, there are differences; [this applies] also to the individual instances (vyakti) such as g and others within the [universal] gatva and so forth.

Furthermore, as for that other argument stated regarding the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth—that similarity, when investigated, is untenable, and so on—that too is merely the play of no small ignorance; for since similarity is the object of uncontradicted cognition from childhood onwards, it cannot be denied.

Indeed, when one thing undergoes a certain transformation due to its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the very same kind of transformation in another thing constitutes their similarity, just like the case of twins.

Furthermore, that [universal] is both distinct from and non-distinct from individuals, as has been explained in detail in the section on the examination of universals (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*); therefore, enough with further digression.

Consequently, whatever is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a certain form should not be accepted as having that form—just as the world is not accepted as being of the nature of non-duality (*advaita*). And since sound is not perceived in any way as having an eternal nature by any means of valid cognition, it must be accepted as having that [non-eternal] nature, because there exists a means of valid cognition for its having the nature of impermanence.
For comparison—since the transformation of one thing from its own cause is exactly like that of another, there is similarity, but not identity;
and that [similarity] is both different from and non-different from the individual instances.
As it is said in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 411, line 289:
"And just as the world... [śra].
Even if sounds were eternal, there would be simultaneous hearing of them all,
because they would be omnipresent and established as being equally accessible to the sense organs.

For one who makes for himself the benefit produced by that [sound], because of the restriction to its occurrence in that specific location, it is not possible for the eternally unchanging [word]—even if it were omnipresent—to be heard as the intended single word;
*Siddhiviniścaya*, p. 554.
If words were independent [of phonetic manifestation], effort would be useless,
because it would contradict [the functions of] the individual manifestation, the removal of obscuration,
and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), since the entire stream of vowels such as *va* and so forth would be perceived simultaneously.
If it is argued that there is no possibility of grasping [the sound] gradually because its simultaneous perception is an illusion,
then if this sound is produced by the proximity of the palate and other articulators,
what fault is there by which its eternity might be inferred from anything?
—*Nyāyaviniścaya*, Verse 42224.
From what [source]? From valid cognition (*pramā*).
And that valid cognition is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar; and this [sound] is produced."

Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*); for instance: sound is produced (*kṛtaka*), because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of its causes; whatever is thus is thus, like a jar; and sound is likewise; therefore, it is so.

Nor is this also unestablished, because its acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) is observed only when the operation of causes such as the palate is present, and it is not observed in their absence—just as the acquisition or non-acquisition of the self-nature of a jar is observed according to the presence or absence of the operation of causes such as clay and a staff.

Nor should it be asserted that the manifestation itself acquires its own nature through that operation, while the word does not, for that [position] has already been refuted at length previously; thus ends the comparison, with "the word is non-eternal" being the response.

How so? "Because it has a beginning, because it is perceptible by the senses, and because it is treated as something produced; for that from which a beginning [is taken]—namely, the source or cause—is seen to be non-eternal, like that which possesses a cause."
And sound, being produced by conjunction and disjunction, is non-eternal because it possesses a cause.

What, then, is this explanation of the meaning of "because it possesses a cause"? It means that sound is non-eternal because its nature is to arise; having come into being, it ceases to exist, for it is subject to destruction.

This is a point of doubt: are conjunction and disjunction the causes of the production of sound, or are they the causes of its manifestation? To this he says: "Because it is perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyakatvāt*); that which is grasped through the proximity of the sense organs is "perceptible by the senses."

Is this [sound] manifested by the manifestor while occupying the same location, like color and other qualities? Or, when a series of sounds arises from a sound produced by conjunction, is it perceived once it has reached the vicinity of the ear? Since sound is perceived even after the cessation of the conjunction, it is not perceived as being in the same location as its manifestor. For instance, when wood is being cut, once the conjunction between the wood and the axe has ceased, the sound is still perceived by one standing at a distance; yet, the manifestation of the manifested does not occur in the absence of the manifestor. Therefore, conjunction is not the manifestor. Furthermore, sound is produced, not manifested, because it is treated as something created (*kṛtaka*).

"Intense" and "mild" are applied metaphorically to what is produced— namely, intense pleasure, mild pleasure, intense pain, and mild pain— and the terms "intense sound" and "mild sound" are likewise applied metaphorically. — *Nyāyasūtra-bhāṣya* 2.2.61.

"Sound is impermanent because it has degrees of intensity (loudness and softness), like suffering; because it is treated as being produced, like a product"—by this sūtra, the entire category of proofs for universal impermanence is subsumed. The mention of "being produced" is for the sake of illustration, [as in]:

"because it possesses general and particular properties and is perceptible by the external senses of persons such as ourselves"; "because, while being perceivable, it is not perceived when the causes for non-perception are absent"; "because, while existing as a quality, it is perceptible by the external senses of persons such as ourselves," and so forth.
—Nyāyavārttika, p. 290.
Thus, because they are distinguished by differences such as intensity and so forth, sounds are impermanent, like pleasure and other such experiences.
Furthermore, since their coming into being after not having existed is perceived when their manifesters are not perceived, they are impermanent due to being effects, like a jar and other such things.

Likewise, because it possesses the specific qualities of a pervasive substance while being distinct from the qualities of the supreme self (paramātman), like pleasure and so forth—[as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p.

649—it follows that for *pudgalas*, there exists no such thing as a nature consisting of phonemes produced by effort, which is perceived in the middle of hearing [speech], either before or after; therefore, the transformation of sound (*dhvani*) is only of that much [duration].
"Sound is subject to transformation, because its status as a real entity would otherwise be untenable"—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 6; *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 108.
