Sound is impermanent because it is endowed with qualities such as intensity and dullness, like pleasure, pain, and so forth— *Ratnākarāvatāra* 4.9.

Therefore, sound (varṇa) is neither eternal nor non-eternal, because it exists and is produced; or because, while being perceptible by external sense organs such as those of ourselves, it possesses a genus (jāti); or because it is a quality directly perceived by ourselves; or, in the view that the self is unitary and perceptible, because it is a specific quality perceived [by the self]; or because it is a specific quality perceived as inherent in a pervasive substance; or because it is a quality perceived as belonging to what is not the self; or because it does not exist pervasively; or because it is a quality that serves as the cause for the regulation of external sense organs; or because it is a quality perceived as belonging to the elements (bhūta); or because it possesses a genus that is the ground for the application of the terms "increase" and "decrease"—and so forth.
–Tattvacintāmaṇi-śabdakhaṇḍa, p. 460: “As it is in Ba, so it is in Śra.”

When the activity of the palate and other articulatory organs is established as the human origin of sounds, then the human origin of words and sentences is established without effort, because they consist of those [sounds].
If it is argued that while those [words] may be established for worldly people, they are not so for Vedic people, we say no; for no absolute difference between them is perceived,
since the very words that are worldly are the same as those that are Vedic (Śābarabhāṣya 1.3).

30. Furthermore, because this would entail a contradiction with one’s own admission, and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*); nor is that absence unestablished, since the means of valid cognition establishing it would have to be either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or something else. It cannot be perception, for perception fulfills its purpose merely by grasping the specific form of the sound, and thus it is impossible for it to grasp whether that [Veda] is of human or non-human origin, since words and sentences consist of phonemes (*varṇa*).

Comparison: "And when even the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves are not eternal, then what [to say] of words, which consist of a collection of phonemes qualified by a sequence and so forth dependent on the speaker’s intention? How much less, then, of sentences, which consist of a collection of such words; and how much less still of the Veda, which is a collection of such sentences? — *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, *Śabdakhaṇḍa*, p. 464. This establishes the human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) of words and sentences.
This has been extracted from the *Tautātita* (Śābarabhāṣya), page 134, and the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, page 39, concerning worldly and Vedic words and sentences.

Furthermore, the authoritativeness [of the Veda] consists in its being non-human (apauruṣeya) by virtue of having existed from time immemorial; how, then, can this be determined by perception arising from the senses? Since the senses operate only within the restricted domain of form and so forth, they have no connection with that which has existed from beginningless time; and because it lacks a connection even with an entity existing at that [present] time, it cannot be a cause for the cognition thereof.
(Compare: "And how can authoritativeness, consisting in existence from time immemorial, be determined by perception arising from the senses?"—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 391).
Because, from beginningless time, it has the nature of being sentient beings and is not a cause for the cognition of authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*).
Regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsakas, who accept the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda:
"Granted, its non-human origin may not be established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, it shall be established through inference (*anumāna*).
And that inference is as follows: the Veda is non-human-originated because, while its author would be capable of being remembered, no author is remembered, just like space (*vyoman*)."

Nor is this [reason] unestablished; for since there is never any recollection by anyone of an author of the Veda, and since those who perform its rites at the time of practice have not ascertained its authority, there would have to be a recollection [of an author] in order to establish that authority.

For those who engage in the performance of a particular purpose necessarily remember its author; for example, those desiring to perform the *aṣṭakā* and other rites remember Manu, their author. And prudent persons engage in the performance of duties prescribed by the Veda, characterized by rituals such as the *agniṣṭoma*, which are accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort. Therefore, they have a great need to remember the author of that [Veda].
For they would otherwise engage in these actions whose fruits are unseen without doubt, provided they possessed a certainty regarding the truth of those matters.
Furthermore, that [authorship] is not possible in the absence of a recollection of its instructor, as is the case with the instructions of a father or others.

For just as one performs even those actions whose fruits are unseen by remembering the father or other instructors—thinking, "This was instructed by my father and others; therefore it is performed"—so too, if Vedic rites were performed, there would be a recollection of the author on the part of the performer.

Yet, such recollection does not exist even among those of the three higher castes who are experts in the performance of the meaning of the Vedas. Therefore, it is certain that no such author exists therein.

Since the relationship [between word and meaning] is established as being non-human (apauruṣeya), how is it understood that this relationship is indeed non-human? Because there is no person who could be its creator; and why does such a creator not exist? Because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as direct perception (pratyakṣa), and because the other [means of knowledge] are preceded by that [perception].
But surely, because it occurred long ago, it would not be an object of perception for those of the present day;
for that which has occurred long ago is not remembered.

Nor can there be a lack of memory regarding [the Vedas], as there is in the case of wells, groves, and so forth on the Himalayas and other mountains, since in those cases there occurs a separation from human beings due to the destruction of the region or the destruction of the lineage.
Nor is there a dissociation between word and meaning for human beings.

It might be argued: "Those who deal with the mere relationship [of words and meanings] might forget it, disregarding the remembrance of an author because it serves no purpose. That is not so; for if a person were to create the relationship and then employ it in practice, he must necessarily remember it at the time of usage.
For when there is agreement between the creator and the user, the purpose is accomplished; it is not accomplished when there is disagreement.
For indeed, by the word "vṛddhi," those who do not follow Pāṇini or who do not accept Pāṇini’s composition would not understand *ā*, *ai*, and *au*;
likewise, by the letter *m*, one who does not follow Piṅgala or who does not accept Piṅgala’s composition would not understand a triad consisting entirely of heavy syllables.
Thus, with respect to that [term], both the author and the user reach a common understanding.
Therefore, by those who employ the Veda in practice, the author of the relationship must necessarily be remembered;
and because of that fact, we understand that the Vedas were not composed by anyone for the sake of linguistic usage after having first established the relationship.
Consequently, the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-human (apauruṣeya).
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5
Bṛhatī, p. 177:
And when a word conveys its meaning because it has been composed by a reliable person (āpta),...
If that state of being authoritative is not apprehended by its own power, why is it not remembered?

For when someone, having established the relationship between words and their meanings, composed Vedic sentences to expound *dharma* and *adharma*, it must necessarily be remembered by those who understand that the creator of that relationship is the very same person who employs the linguistic practice consisting of the composition of Vedic sentences with those words; thus, for those who comprehend the meaning from a sentence, the reliability (*āptatva*) of the sentence’s author must necessarily be remembered by the perceivers, because the ascertainment of the meaning is dependent upon him. However, those who comprehend the meaning from the Veda are not seen to remember the creator of the convention (*samaya*) along with the oneness of the Veda’s author and his reliability.

Let it be so regarding what is perceived, or let it not be; however, Vedic usage cannot exist without the recollection of an author. Even in cases such as "Bring the cow," let there indeed be no mutual agreement between the maker of the convention and the user of the expression; yet even in the Veda, let its validity be established through mere comprehension, even in the absence of such mutual agreement.

As for worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), which consists of the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, it has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and is based solely on verbal testimony (*vākyaikapramāṇaka*). This would not be established if there were no recollection of an authoritative author of the texts; for, since the author of the Vedas and their relations [to meaning] must necessarily have been remembered, and since such an author is not remembered, his non-existence is determined through the non-perception of a suitable object (*yogyānupalambha*). Thus, the eternity of the Vedas and their relations is established. As it is said: "The perceived... (*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Nyāyaratna, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verses 123, 130).
But how is the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas established? It is because no human author is remembered.
—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 140;
"And because no author is remembered, [the Veda] is not of human origin"—*Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, p.
33; *Nayaviveka*, p. 279.

Since the author—who, despite being capable of being remembered, is not remembered—is excluded by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible, inference regarding such an author is impossible; furthermore, since a designation (*samākhyā*) is based on oral transmission (*pravacana*), the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
— *Śāstradīpikā*, pp. 69, 616;
[the word] *cit* [is used] because it occurs occasionally (*kadācitkatvena*). *Śābara-bhāṣya*.
The performers at the time of performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma for the author of the Veda.
The specific *pitr-śrāddha* performed on the three eighth days of the dark fortnight following the full moon of the month of Āgrahāyaṇī;
likewise, there is the statement of Manu: "And one should worship the ancestors on the *aṣṭakās*" (Manusmṛti 4.150).
Furthermore, because its root has been severed, there is an absence of recollection regarding an author therein;

for experience is the root of recollection, and such [experience] does not exist in the Veda with respect to an author. Therefore, how could even the suspicion of the possibility of such recollection arise? Nor should it be argued that because its root is not severed—since the existence of an author is well-known here due to its being a composition, like the *Mahābhārata* and other works—the Veda must have an author; for the composition of the Veda is distinct from compositions preceded by an author.

Furthermore, it is not logical to infer an author merely from the perception of composition here, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of proving [the existence of] an intelligent cause for the entire world through the same inference. Therefore, one must accept that only such a composition as is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with an author can lead to the inference of an author. How, then, could even a suspicion of inferring an author from the Veda be possible? Consequently, the Vedic composition is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), because it is distinct from compositions whose authors are observed, just like space (*ākāśa*).

Likewise: "All study of the Veda is preceded by study under a teacher, because it is denoted by the term 'Vedic study,' just like the present study" (Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Vākyādhikaraṇa, verse 366). [And: "The past and future times are devoid of a creator of the Veda."
Because it is time, just as the present time is observed;
for this reason also, its lack of human authorship (apauruṣeyatva) is established.
If it is asked, "In the absence of being composed by a reliable person (āpta), how could it possess authority? we reply: precisely because of its lack of human authorship.
Since the lack of authority of a statement is established precisely through the intrusion of human defects, it has been said:
"Because of the memory of its author... (tatkartṛsmaraṇāt).
Furthermore, experience shows that some conviction indeed wavers due to a statement made by a human being; however, there is no evidence whatsoever for the falsity of the Vedic word.
[Objection: Having observed that human speech is false in general, one understands this [Veda] to be false as well because of its similarity to speech. [Reply: No, because it is different.
For when one thing is false, it does not follow that another thing must also be false, precisely because they are distinct;
for Devadatta’s being dark-skinned does not imply that Yajñadatta must also be dark-skinned— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2.
The claim that [the Veda] is of human origin because it is a sentence is refuted by the non-perception of such an author.

And because there is a counter-reason that contradicts it, the [Veda] is therefore unauthored (*akṛtrima*). For a mere collection of words belonging to someone, in some particular instance, is not sufficient to infer authorship by a person. This is because the capacity to compose sentences concerning the subject matter of the Vedas is impossible [for humans]. Indeed, authorship is observed only in those collections of words that can be composed by persons; thus, the inference of authorship does not apply to those things which cannot be composed. (Śāstradīpikā, p. 615)

Nor is it the case that the nature of being composed of words and phonemes is not possible without human authorship; for it is by virtue of utterance that words attain the state of being combined together—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 98–99;
*Tantrarahasya*, p. 43.
— [The inference] regarding that agent— Śrī:
From the mere fact of being a composition,
the study of the Veda is preceded by the study [of it] by a teacher.
"But it has been stated that [the Veda] is preceded by speech;
we have already stated that for students, the Veda is preceded by speech" (Jaiminisūtra, Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.27).

1.30 By such reasons as the non-remembrance of an author of the Veda and the fact that the meaning of the Veda transcends the senses, it is established—on the grounds of its being uncreated—that the Veda was not set in motion by anyone after having been conceived, but rather exists as preceded by sound and preceded by other utterances, having been transmitted by reciters since beginningless time; for this reason of its being uncreated has been stated [in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya, p. 78].
And [the argument] "because it is a statement" is accompanied by a counter-proof:
that which is the subject of dispute, namely the study of the Veda, must be preceded by a prior study of the Veda, because it is a study of the Veda, like the study of today.
Regarding this, the author of the Sūtras says: "But it has been stated that [the Veda] is preceded by speech."
Here, by the word "recitation" (*śabda*), what is meant is study produced by [the hearing of] sound.

Thus, the meaning is this: the study of all persons is preceded by another study; for everyone desires to learn exactly as it was studied by the teacher, and there is no first student of the Vedas who could be their author acting independently. Therefore, the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). (Śāstradīpikā, p. 617)

The following arguments are presented as counter-evidences (*pratihetu*) and contradictions: "The study of the Veda has as its subject a student who is dependent on [another] for the study of the Veda, because it is a study of the Veda, like the study [of the Veda] that is commonly accepted"; and "Being a self does not reside in an individual who is the author of the Veda, because it is a universal (*jāti*), like cowness. Furthermore, "the nature of being a sentence" is cited [as a reason]. (Source:
*Mānameyodaya*, p. 173; quoted from *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 338).
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 233;
preceded by the study of that—Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 237;
Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 643.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛ. 396;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pṛ. 137;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛ. 627.
Based on the study of that [treatise], *Viśvatattvaprakāśa*, page 33; *Prameyaratnāvalī* 3.99.
Because it is expressed as the study of the Vedas, just as there is study now, [so there was in the past]. Ratnākara, verse 4.9.

The past and future times are devoid of an experiencer and a creator; being dissociated from an experiencer and a creator, because they are time, just like [the present]. — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 338.
*Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 643;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
398; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 31.
*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
627; *Viśvatattvaprakāśa*, p. 34; *Prameyaratnāvalī*, 3.
99 Ratnākarāvatāra 4.9

Because it is time; for example, just as time is observed as the present—[the text reads] "tvā" (you), "yathā" (as), "ā," "śra," "tvam" (you)—is it not indeed [so]? [The manuscript reads] "nanvā" (surely).
The passage contained within these brackets does not exist in Ā;
nor [is there] "in the absence of a time when it was composed by a trustworthy person" in Ba and Ve.

For indeed, a certain conviction may be subverted by a statement made by a human being, but there is no evidence whatsoever for the falsity of the Vedic word—*Śābarabhāṣya*, p. 17. It is established that the arising of defects in a word depends upon the speaker; the absence of such [defects] occurs in some cases due to the presence of a virtuous speaker.
The word "śabda" [is established as] "ā" — Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Syādvādaratnākara, p. 627.
Ratnākara’s reading (p. 4, l.
9): *prakṛtapāṭha* — Nyāyamañjarī, p. 167.
*Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*, p. 78;
*Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 406A; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 397.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 19; Prameyaratnākara, 3.99.

— Because [the defects] are produced by the speaker (vaktṛtva), it is impossible for them to transfer into the word when they are inferior to its qualities; or rather, due to the absence of a speaker, the defects would not exist, being without a substratum,
since there can be no transfer into the word.

Nor should it be asserted that the validity of a word arises solely through the transfer of the qualities of a trustworthy person (*āpta*), and that because the Veda is not composed by a trustworthy person, such a transfer is impossible and thus it lacks validity; for here, validity does not arise from the transfer of a trustworthy person's qualities, since the latter’s function consists merely in the utterance of the word. Rather, the word itself is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when, by its own power, it brings about a non-erroneous comprehension of the object.

Nor should it be asserted that even for an untrustworthy person, because their activity consists merely in the utterance [of words], the word—producing the cognition of the unreal by its own power—is invalid. For defects such as being composed by an untrustworthy person have no purpose other than the production of invalidity, whereas qualities such as being composed by a trustworthy person function only to remove those defects. Thus, since the Veda lacks both the state of being composed by a trustworthy person and the state of being composed by an untrustworthy person, it possesses neither validity nor invalidity. This too is incorrect. For where the sequence of words is produced by a person, validity or invalidity would depend upon that [person]; however, because the sequence of the Veda is eternal, it makes the meaning known through its own inherent capacity, and thus its validity is independent of any such [human] factor.
For no one is capable of creating such a sequence other than through its manifestation from a previously established sequence; moreover,
it is impossible for anyone to exercise independence in creating a sequence that was not previously established,
and if one were to do so, they would be restrained by the students of that [text] or by others.
And it has been said:
"In verbal cognition, there is no dependence on the qualities of a trustworthy person."
Therefore, due to the qualities of the authoritative person (āpta), there is an absence of defects; because of that absence,
the two forms of invalidity are non-existent, and by this, the general rule remains unrefuted.
In that regard, the Vedas are more easily freed from the charge of invalidation because they lack an author; therefore, they do not even give rise to the suspicion of being non-authoritative.
Consequently, since their authority does not depend upon an author, they are to be revered for that very reason.

This is not tenable; for if its lack of authority were being postulated, there would be a desire for that [authority], and consequently, the fact that it was not composed by a reliable person (āpta) would not constitute a fault here— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Codanā, verses 65–70.
"But in the case of a statement by Pausheya, it must have another means of valid cognition as its basis;
for in the absence of that [other basis], it would be faulty, whereas this [Vedic statement] is never so. — *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Codanā-sūtra, verse 71.
Because it is not a cognition,
it is independent of the qualities of the person (*puruṣa*).
— here too, in the manifest [word],
there is a sequence distinct from the prior sequence (*pūrvānupūrvī*).
"A distinct sequence of words cannot be established by others;
furthermore, if it were altered by someone else, there would be opposition from many [authorities]. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra, verse 150).
Prevention by many [means]—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, original reading; Syādvādamañjarī, p. 628.
The refutation of the claim that the Vedas are not of human origin:

Here, we offer our response to what was stated—that [the Vedas are eternal] because, while their author would be capable of being remembered, no such author is remembered, and so forth. That is incorrect, because what is this so-called "not being remembered as having an author"? Does it mean the absence of remembrance of an author, or does it mean the non-existence of an author? In the first case, the reason is unestablished due to a lack of common locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*); for the absence of remembrance of an author resides in the self (*ātman*), whereas the quality of being of non-human origin resides in the Veda.

And it is unestablished because it is unknown, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend it. Perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not apprehend it, because perception operates only within the domain of specific [positive] entities such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; it is impossible for it to function with respect to non-existence (*abhāva*), or if it were possible, the postulation of a separate means of valid cognition for non-existence would be useless, since that which is to be established by it is already proven by perception and the other [means of knowledge].

If, however, its establishment is through the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), then the cause for its arising therein must be stated, since the emergence of an effect without a cause is untenable. Having apprehended the existence of the object and having remembered the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
the mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the sense organs.

If it is argued that its cause exists—as stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Abhāva-pariccheda, verse 27—[we reply: Well then, does this non-existence (*abhāva*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having arisen from that [cause], establish that absence [of something] as being without a substratum (*nirāśraya*) or as having a substratum (*sāśraya*)? It cannot be without a substratum, because of the statement: "having apprehended the existence of the object.

For by this very statement, Bhaṭṭa, in declaring the apprehension of the object which is the locus of the negandum, has indeed indicated the substratum for the absence of the negandum. Otherwise, the establishment of the absence of the memory of an agent through its occurrence in a specific instance would be extremely difficult to achieve.

That which is without a substratum does not have a restricted occurrence, just like space; and the absence of the recollection of an agent, which you intend to establish through the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), is itself without a substratum (pṛ.

721, l. 5). For comparison: "What is this so-called 'non-recollection of an agent'? Is it the absence of the recollection of an agent, or is it the state of having no agent being recollected? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 392).
In the formal argument "The Veda is not of human origin because no author is remembered," the reason suffers from the fallacy of being misplaced (vyadhikaraṇatva);

for in that case, the property of having an unremembered author is unestablished (asiddha), due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to apprehend such an author. (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 41).

— *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 629: when the knowledge of non-existence produced by the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) establishes the absence of recollection of an agent...
In the arising of the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa),
having apprehended the existence of the object and remembered its counter-correlate (pratiyogin)— Ni kā— Ā॰.
It should be observed— page 464, note 1—
that a mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the senses. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 27) [This refers to] the absence of recollection of an agent.

Now, it may be argued that non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*abhāvapramāṇa*), having thus appeared, would establish that absence only by having apprehended the existence of a real entity (*vastusadbhāva*), because of the statement [in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
629]: "having apprehended the existence of a real entity," which is the latter half of the verse.

The locus of the negandum (niṣedhyāśraya) is the substratum of the non-existence of that which is to be negated; this is established through the means of valid cognition consisting of non-perception (abhāvapramāṇa).

Now, suppose it is argued that this [Veda] is established as having a substratum; but what is its substratum—is it one’s own self, or all cognizing subjects? If it is one’s own self, [the argument being] "there is no memory of the author of this [Veda] within my own self," what is established by this much? There is no memory here of many categories of objects, yet their non-existence is not thereby established. [If you say,] "this [author] must necessarily be remembered by me, the performer, and when he does not enter the path of memory, then he is non-existent"—this too is worthless; for the non-existence of an object is not established merely by the absence of your memory.
[Your argument is] inconclusive because even when an object such as a substance—which was deposited by oneself and must necessarily be remembered—is present, its existence [is not perceived];

likewise, medicine being administered by a sick person is not remembered even though it was taken by oneself despite great need, yet its non-existence does not follow from this, and thus there is an inconclusiveness. Furthermore, if you mean "all cognizers," then surely all cognizers existing within the belly of the three worlds do not remember the author of the Veda; therefore, for one who is not omniscient, the knowledge of the Veda is impossible.
Alternatively, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the self] must experience everything at the time of rebirth.
Furthermore, regarding the absence of recollection by the agent:
is it intended here as the cause that all people lack recollection, or rather the absence of recollection by only a few individuals?

If [the reason] is "because it is not remembered by all people," then it is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible for those who know only the front portion [of a thing] to ascertain [this]. Or, if they were to ascertain it, then they themselves would be omniscient and could no longer be considered knowers of only the front portion.

If, on the other hand, [the reason is] "with respect to a few individuals," then the logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even in the case of things that have an existing author, the author is not remembered by some people.
—Its substratum is its own self, or all subjects—*Syād-ratnākara*, p. 629; [it resides] in my own self—*Tattvopaplava*, p. 117.
In my practice, he [the author] should be remembered— [as stated in the *Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
629]— "If the author of the Veda were indeed the father of the grandfather, yet does not remember his own father or mother, nor their parents, then there would be an absence of them."
— *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 629: [This refers to] the absence of one's own recollection regarding a substance such as a medicinal herb that has been held by oneself.
[Objection:
But surely, for the sake of certainty—how do you know that all persons do not remember the author of the Veda? [Response: This is a comparison. How do you know this?
For the hearts of all people are certainly not perceptible to you, as that would entail the consequence of your being omniscient;
nor is it logical to claim that what you do not know, another person also does not know, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 237.

Furthermore, having gone to all the locations of every cognizer and having questioned them, would the absence of memory be perceived there, or otherwise? It cannot be otherwise, because that would entail a contradiction with the statement [of the Mīmāṃsā school]: "Having gone to those various places... (Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Arthāpatti, verse 38).

If [it is argued that one] goes there; well then, even when those [people] are questioned and they give the reply, "We do not remember," what confidence can there be in the words of men, given that the actual state of affairs cannot be established due to the lack of authority in human testimony? Nor is there a realization of the reliability of all [those people], by virtue of which authority might arise there through the transfer of their qualities; for such a realization is impossible for one who is not omniscient, whether simultaneously or sequentially. Furthermore, having gone to all the places of all cognizers and having questioned them, would the absence of memory regarding the author be perceived there, or otherwise? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 630)
"O All-knowing One!
O Śrī! Having gone again and again to the experience of those who do not know all—that is, those who do not remember [the truth] regarding all knowers—[one attains it]."
Having gone again and again to those places, if the object is not perceived,
then, due to the absence of any other cause, it is understood to be non-existent.
—This is cited from Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, p. 22;
and Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pp. 23, 321.
When it is stated by them [the opponents] that [a cognition] exists among all cognizers in another location, the reply given is: "We do not remember it."

Furthermore, the operation of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa) occurs where the fivefold set of means of knowledge that cognizes the existence of a thing does not operate; that is to say,

when the fivefold set of means of knowledge does not arise with respect to a certain form of an object for the purpose of cognizing its existence, there the status of non-existence as a means of knowledge applies.
Since it is stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Abhāva section, verse 1,

"And since there exists in the Veda a declaration of the existence of a creator of the Self, how could its [the Veda's] authority arise? For that Rudra is the one who first creates Brahmā as the author of the Veda and imparts the Vedas to him."

Likewise, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.18) and elsewhere, the Veda is heard of in various ways as revealing the existence of an author, such as in the passage: "Prajāpati created King Soma; thereafter, the three Vedas were created."

Furthermore, this reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), for the Paurāṇikas remember that Brahman is the author of the Veda: "In every Manvantara, indeed, another Śruti is ordained" (Matsya Purāṇa 145.58),
and subsequently, "the Vedas issued forth from his mouths."
Because of this statement,
the followers of Yoga [assert] that it was composed by Rudra, while the Jains [assert] that it was composed by Kālāsura;
[it is that] wherein the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of the object.
In that regard, non-existence is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the purpose of awakening to the reality of things; [this is stated] in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Abhāva section, verse 1.
Read "sadbhāva" [as the subject]; see page 464, note 4.
He himself, O Rudra, is the author of the Veda; indeed, he is the one upon whom the means of knowledge for the non-existence of the Veda operates.
"He who, O Brahmanas, ordained [the world] in the beginning and sent forth the Vedas" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18).
Likewise, Prajāpati created King Soma, and after him the three Vedas were created; this has been extracted—Syādvādamañjarī, p. 630.
Furthermore, the non-human origin [of the Veda] is asserted because its authors are not remembered. (Ratnākara 4.9)
"There are also those who recite this [Veda]"—fie on you, O all-pervading darkness!
For this reason, this proof is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). With reference to its being unestablished, he says "For instance" (*tathāhi*), and so forth:
the Buddhists remember the authors of the Veda, such as Aṣṭaka and others; by the word "others" (*ādi*), [he refers to] Vālmīki, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and so forth.

The Vaiśeṣikas, followers of Kaṇāda, maintain that Brahmā, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, is the author of the Veda; therefore, the non-remembrance of an author is unestablished. — *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.269.
[Objection: This reason is unestablished, because the followers of Kaṇāda indeed remember [the world] having a creator.
Likewise, even many worldly people commonly say, "The Vedas were composed by Brahmā"— (Tattvopaplava, p. 117)—
yet this is not so for all men, because such a tradition is not established.
For the followers of Kaṇāda remember the Four-faced One (Brahmā) as its cause;
the Jains [remember] Kālāsura; and the Buddhists always [remember] all the Aṣṭakas.
— *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 238.
Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 237; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 393; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 40.

As for the argument that [the Veda is eternal] because its author is not remembered, that is unproven (*asiddha*), since the author is indeed remembered through the very sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this [universe]; there was neither day nor night; he performed austerity; from that austerity the four Vedas were born" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.5.1). Furthermore, the argument is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to such things as dilapidated wells.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 216)
Because from the time of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Gautama, and their disciples up to the present day, the remembrance of the Veda’s having an author is observed— *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, *Śabdakhaṇḍa*, p.
371— and because "In every Manvantara, indeed, another Śruti is ordained" (*Matsyapurāṇa* 145.58).
This has been extracted from the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p.
236), the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.
392), and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p. 630).
*Nyāyapariśiṣṭa*, p. 383;
*Tattvacintāmaṇi-śabdakhaṇḍa*, p.
373: "Immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths."
agency— ba, śra—
agency ba, śra

Furthermore, how could the various Vedic recensions (*śākhā*) such as the Kāṇva, Mādhyandina, and Taittirīya—which are marked with the names of sages like the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*—be considered to have no remembered author? For instance, are these [recensions] marked by those names because they were composed by them, because they were seen by them, or because they were revealed by them? Regarding the first alternative, how could there be any claim of their being authorless (*apauruṣeya*) or having no remembered author? As for the latter two alternatives, if a lost recension was seen or revealed by Kaṇva and others, then how could there be an uninterrupted tradition (*sampradāya*) of it, and how could there be a rejection of those who perceive supersensuous objects? If, on the other hand, that [recension] was seen or revealed by an uninterrupted tradition, then why would it not be marked by the names of all those teachers by whom it was seen or revealed, since there is no distinction between them?

Comparison [is established] because we observe a fixed arrangement of multiple words—such as birth, death, the name of the seer, lineage, conduct, and so forth—which serve as the causes for the engagement or withdrawal of persons seeking results; furthermore, since there is scripture (śruti), the scripture [of the Vedas] is indeed composed by a person, just like the *Manusūtra*—[Ślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, v.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 392;
Syādvādaratnākara, page 630; Prameyaratnakośa, 3.

Comparison of the Kāṇva, Mādhyandina, Taittirīya, and other branches: These [branches] are designated by those names because they were composed by them, or because they were seen by them, or because they were revealed by them.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
392; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 630; *Ratnākarāvatārikā*, 4.
9 – Severed,
scattered, or forgotten.

There is also the designation "branch" (*śākhā*) for the branches themselves; for specific designations such as "the Kaṭhaka" and "the Kālāpaka" are traditionally remembered as referring to specific branches, and these could not exist without an original teaching.

Furthermore, these [authoritative scriptures] cannot be based merely on the fact of being spoken, because speakers are infinite; nor can they be based on the excellence of the speech, for even in the case of teachers (*upādhyāya*), there is rather the fault of possible error, and since no excellence exists in the mere imitation of their recitation, who could be the determiner as to how many speakers have been excellent throughout the beginningless cycle of existence?
—*Nyāyakusumāñjali* 5.17.

Now, it might be argued: "The Naiyāyikas and others do indeed have a tradition of remembering the author of the Veda, but this memory is unreliable because there is disagreement regarding the specific identity of that author; therefore, it is not a valid means of knowledge. This too is a mere assertion; for if the memory were invalid solely due to disagreement regarding the specific identity of the author, then it would be the memory of that *specific* author which is invalid, not the memory of the author *in general*. Otherwise, since there is also disagreement regarding the specific authors of works such as the *Kādambarī*, the memory of their authors in general would likewise be invalid. Consequently, the reason [of yours]—"having no remembered author"—would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it would apply to those cases as well.

Now, just as there is disagreement regarding a specific author of the Veda, there is likewise disagreement regarding an author in general; therefore, even the mere recollection of such an author is not authoritative. However, in the case of works like the *Kādambarī*, there is disagreement only regarding the specific author, and thus that [recollection] is authoritative. Consequently, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). But surely, since Buddhists and others remember an author for the Veda while the Mīmāṃsakas do not, there is disagreement regarding an author in general. If, on that account, that [recollection by Buddhists] is unauthoritative, then why should their non-recollection of an author not also be unauthoritative? For the disagreement is no different.
Thus, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For even those who maintain that [these texts] are of human origin are likewise unable to state that there is a remembrance of a specific author for them through tradition; rather, having inferred an author by means of general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), they project their own preferred author upon it—some [assigning it to] Īśvara, others to Hiraṇyagarbha, and still others to Prajāpati.
And this manifold dispute would not be possible at all if an author were remembered through tradition, as in the case of Manu and others;
for no one disputes the specific author of the *Mānava*, the *Bhārata*, or the Śākya scriptures.

Therefore, since there is no recollection [of a creator] despite his being something that ought to be recollected, the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), which is sublated by the non-perception of a perceptible object, is unable to establish a creator—*Śāstradīpikā*, p.
617; *naṃ kartṛ*—B. edition.
Even in the case of Rudra, there is dispute— [as noted in] the Ācārya-ṭīkā— regarding the Brahmin— [as noted in] the Śruti.

Comparison: "But surely, since there is disagreement regarding the specific author, it would be the memory of that specific [author] alone that is invalid, not the memory of the author in general"—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
393; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 42.
This reading is not found within the text of Syādvādamañjarī (p. 630), Śāstravārtāsamuccaya (Yaśovijaya edition, p. 384A), or Śrī [Vivaraṇa].
The text contained within these brackets does not exist in the Ānandāśrama edition of the *Kādambarī* and elsewhere;
furthermore, there is a dispute regarding the specific author, as even the mere fact of an author is disputed. *Ba*.

Comparison: Now, just as there is disagreement regarding a specific author of the Veda, there is likewise disagreement regarding the mere existence of an author; therefore, even the tradition concerning that [author] is not a valid means of knowledge—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 393;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 42;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 630.

[Objection: There is only a recollection of an author—[this is] from the Buddhist [view]. For instance, the Buddhists and others remember an author for the Veda, whereas the Mīmāṃsakas do not; thus, since there is disagreement even regarding a mere author, if the recollection of an author were false, then the state of having no remembered author would also be unreal, because the disagreement is no different. And so, the reason (hetu) remains unestablished once again.
—Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 42; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 393; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 631.
The mere recollection of an agent is like the recollection of an agent;
it is the non-recollection of an agent.

It is also contradictory because of the state of having an unremembered author; for since "having a remembered author" and "having an unremembered author" are properties of effects, they exist only in the counter-example (vipakṣa). Indeed, some effects are seen to have a remembered author, such as a jar, while others are seen to have an unremembered author, such as a dilapidated well.
Consequently, the Veda is a product (created), because its author is not remembered, like an old well and the like;
for no eternal entity has ever been established as having either a remembered or an unremembered author, but rather as being without an author at all.
Furthermore, this argument is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time), because it is employed immediately after a proposition that has already been sublated by Śruti and Smṛti.
Therefore, the state of having an unremembered author—characterized by the absence of remembrance of an author—is not tenable in the case of a human and impermanent work.
For instance, in the case of an eternal entity, it is neither recognized as having a remembered author nor as having an unremembered author; rather, it is simply without an author.
Nor is it characterized by "the state of having no author" (*akartṛkatva*), because that is not the meaning of the word;
for neither in common worldly usage nor in the treatises is the meaning of the word "having no author" established as "the state of having an unremembered author."

Whether its establishment is equivalent to the probandum itself, or whether "not being remembered to have an author" is something so subtle that it has not been investigated—even so, would this be a reason (hetu) pertaining to the proponent, the opponent, or everyone? If it pertains to the proponent, then it is inconclusive (anaikāntika); for [the principle] "at every banyan tree dwells Vaiśravaṇa" and so forth exists even in cases where an author is present, since Mīmāṃsakas do not remember the authors of such works due to a lack of necessity.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that in the Veda, the reason [for its eternity] is the absence of a remembered author preceded by the non-existence of an author? And since that [non-existence of an author] does not exist here [in the case of the Purāṇas], because it is preceded merely by the non-perception of an author, how can there be inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva)? [Reply: This too is a mere wishful thinking, because from what source is the establishment of the non-existence of an author here—either from another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara), or from this very [text]? If it is from another means of valid cognition, then this [reason] is redundant (ānarthakya).

If that is the case, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for if the non-existence [of a creator] is established by means of this inference, then "the state of having no remembered creator" (which is preceded by that) is established; and if that is established, then the non-existence [of a creator] is established by means of this inference.
Furthermore, if it is intended as a reason belonging to the opponent (*prativādin*), that is unestablished (*asiddha*), for in that case the opponent certainly remembers the creator.

By this, the non-remembrance of everything is refuted; for how could one who is devoid of knowledge and cognition of the self of all [beings] understand the non-remembrance of a creator for everything? Therefore, this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is unknown; even if it were existent, it could not be known by one who is not omniscient. Since "non-human authorship" (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the word is the probandum (*sādhya*), and that very thing is "lack of a creator" (*akartṛkatva*), the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is characterized as being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) because the probandum itself is unestablished.
Comparison: Furthermore, for the proponent who maintains that [the Veda] has an unremembered author, this would apply to everything—[as stated in] *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
395; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 30.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 631; Prameyaratnākara, 3.99.
Furthermore, is it intended here that the cessation of the memory of all people is the reason, or rather the cessation of the memory of only a few persons? (Tattvopaplava, p. 117; cf.
*anaikāntikatvam apy āha*—*dṛśyante ca*, etc.)

Those [words] for which there is a tradition of oral instruction (*upadeśapāramparya*), a tradition of interrupted ritual practice (*sampradāya-vicchinnakriyā*), and a tradition of human authorship (*puruṣakṛtatva-sampradāya*)—such as the words "Vaiśravaṇa" and so forth used in every banyan tree—are thus described.
By this, he states that they have no remembered author; and [consequently], they are both produced (*kṛtaka*) and of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
Therefore, since the non-recollection of an author also occurs in the case of human speech, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā* 1.242.

If [the opponent] says that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it exists in cases such as "May she be well-pleased with you," where there is an existing agent (*kartṛ*), [the response is: *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
Because of its existence in sentences such as "In every banyan tree there is a hearer," [the Self] possesses the nature of being an agent (*kartṛtva-bhāva*).
Its [existence] is [established] by that.

A comparison regarding the state of having an unremembered author in the Veda: "From what [source] is the absence of an author established here—is it from another means of valid cognition, or from that very same [Veda] itself? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 631).
When the absence of an author in the Veda is established by the reason of its having an unremembered author,
and when the state of having an unremembered author is established...

The state of having an unremembered author—compare: if that [non-remembrance] were the cessation of memory for all people, then it would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible to ascertain; and if it were ascertained by those who know only the proximal portion [of time], then they alone would be omniscient and could not be considered knowers of only the proximal portion.
— *Tattvopaplava*, p. 117;
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 237;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 395.
In the matter of the Veda,
there would be ignorance; [this is] the reading of the manuscript (śrā).

As for what was also stated regarding the non-remembrance of any related author—that "those who engage in the performance of a certain purpose necessarily remember the author of its scripture," and so forth—that too is the play of no small ignorance, because there is no such rule.

For, from statements such as "one who is virtuous in dharma," we observe that practitioners engaged in the performance of those purposes do not possess remembrance of their author; indeed, even without that, we perceive engagement in the performance of purposes such as virtue—which are conducive to the great goals of man and are causes for the absence of fear in both this world and the next.
Furthermore, there is no such rule that at the time of performance, people must proceed only after recollecting the author of that [text]—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
395; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 43.

For, from such statements as "one who is virtuous in accordance with the Dharma," there is no recollection of an author for those practitioners who proceed to perform that meaning; even in the absence of such [recollection], their engagement in the performance of the meaning of virtue and so forth— which is conducive to the goal of a great person and is the cause for the absence of fear in this world and the next— is observed.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 631;
—*ṇam* (as in) *Ba*;
—in the cause of the door consisting of the triad, *Ba*.

Regarding the reason for the non-existence of the triad [of causes]—and that which was further stated, beginning with "because its root is severed" (*chinnamūlatvāt*)—that too is unsound. For is its root severed there because of the absence of experience by perception (*adhyakṣa*), or by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If it is by perception, is it by a perception belonging to you, or one belonging to everyone? If it is by a perception belonging to you, then since your own perception does not function to apprehend the existence of an author even in other scriptures, the memory of an author would have its root severed; thus, the reason "having no remembered author" (*asmryamāṇakartṛkatva*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).

Now, if it is argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because others accept the existence of an author even though our own perception does not operate there as a grasper of such an author—that is not so. For the acceptance of another person is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) for you; otherwise, since others also accept the existence of an author for the Veda, the reason "because its author is not remembered" would be unestablished (*asiddha*), if it were intended to apply to all persons.

Furthermore, if it refers to all persons, that reason is unestablished, because it is impossible for one with limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*) to ascertain that [the absence of a remembered author] for everyone.

Now, if it is argued that there is an absence of experience [of such a creator] by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that is not so; for it has been established therein that scripture (*āgama*) makes known the existence of a creator, and because there exists the inference based on the possession of composition (*racanāvattva*) and other such reasons which proves that [existence].
To explain: the Veda is of human origin because it possesses composition, like the *Mahābhārata* and similar works; or else, because it consists of words and sentences, like those same works.

Likewise, Vedic sentences, which possess the status of being objects of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*); because they are sentences that are valid, whatever is thus [is] so, just like the speech of a father or others; and these [Vedic sentences] are likewise; therefore, they are so.

(Page 722, Line 9) Since there is no experience of that [object] by one who does not possess direct perception (*avyakṣa*), it is there cut off at its root either by another means of valid cognition or...
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
393; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 42;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 631.
The recollection of an author for the Veda is subject to doubt; the non-perception by everyone is uncertain, while one's own non-perception is inconclusive.
Because of the existence of dūrvā grass and other things in the caves of the Vindhya mountains, even though they are not perceived—Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 65;
Nyāyaviniścaya-ṭīkā, p. 167, l. 3.
Nyāyalīlāvatī, p. 22: "In that regard, the author—" [referring to] the recollection of the authors of other Āgamas.
The Mīmāṃsaka’s [position] regarding the non-attainment of that [object] in another scripture (āgamāntara).
The existence of an author for that which consists of the Vedas and Smṛtis [is asserted] by the Jainas and others.

Comparison— The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence: the composition of sentences, that is, the arrangement of sentences, is preceded by intelligence, meaning it is preceded by the speaker’s knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence, because it is an arrangement of sentences, like the arrangement of sentences by people such as ourselves, for example, "There are five fruits on the riverbank" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra,
Upaskāra 6.1).

The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence, because it is a composition of sentences, like the composition of sentences admitted by both [parties]— *Pramaṇaviniścaya-vyākhyā*, p. 581.
And likewise: "The Vedic compositions are preceded by an author, because they are compositions, like worldly compositions" (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 232). Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 217.

Therefore, those [Vedic texts] which are not distinguished from the verbal compositions fashioned by humans are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), just as ancient wells, palaces, and so forth are not distinguished from the construction of new wells, palaces, and so forth; and the Vedic word is not distinguished from the verbal compositions fashioned by humans—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 402.

Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 39. For comparison: Furthermore, because they possess phonemes; for worldly sentences possess phonemes and are non-eternal, and likewise are the Vedic sentences; therefore, those too are non-eternal.
And furthermore, because, while possessing universals and particulars, they are perceptible by the sense of hearing, like worldly sentences.
Furthermore, because they consist of words, like worldly sentences—*Nyāyavārttika*, p.
272: "The Vedic sentences are non-eternal, because they are sentences, like the sentences admitted by both parties."

"Nor is the collection of syllables non-human (apauruṣeya), by virtue of which the Veda would be intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*); for that [status] would then follow for other treatises as well, since there is no distinction [between them]. — *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, p. 406B.

The words and sentences of the Veda are of human origin, because they consist of words and sentences, like the words and sentences of the *Mahābhārata* and other such works—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
391. Scripture is of human origin, because it consists of phonemes and so forth, like the *Kumārasambhava* and other such works.

—As for what was stated [in the *Ratnākarāvatārikā* 4.9]: "Because the composition of the Veda is distinct from compositions preceded by an author," and so forth—in that regard, what is this so-called distinction of it from those? Is it its difficulty of pronunciation (*durbhaṇatva*), its difficulty of hearing (*duḥśravaṇatva*), the arrangement of words in a manner distinct from those well-known in worldly grammar, its being composed in unprecedented meters (*chandas*), its propounding of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*), or its being joined with mantras endowed with great power? All of this is not difficult for men, since the operation of speech depends upon the proficiency of the instruments of cognition.

The fact that mantras possess great power is established precisely by their being composed by a person; for when mantras are employed in whatever language by a person of unsurpassed power who has intended, "From this mantra, let such-and-such a result arise for that person," then their capacity to perform such purposeful action is conceivable solely through the power of their author.
Indeed, even today, we observe the eradication of fevers and the like, as well as the neutralization of poisons, resulting from the command of a practitioner of mantras who possesses great power (pṛ.
Comparison: For qualities of the Veda such as being difficult to pronounce, lack of accentuation, obscurity, and unmelodiousness are indeed observed even in the words of atheists and others;
and whatever else, such as the removal of poison or the attainment of prosperity, is seen [in them], [is likewise found elsewhere].
This [fault] is indeed observed even in the recitation of mantras such as those of Vainateya;

it consists of being difficult to pronounce (*durbhaṇatva*), improper articulation (*durabhidhāna*), lack of proper accentuation (*anudāttatva*), unpleasantness (*amanojñatva*), being strained (*kliṣṭa*), or interrupted (*vyavahita*). Unpleasantness to the ear (*aśravyatā*) is the state of being ill-suited to hearing (*śrutidurbhagatā*);
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of pauses between words (*padaviccheda*), protracted vowels (*pluta*), acute accents (*udātta*), and so forth is intended.

The removal of poison (*viṣāpagama*) is *bhūti*, meaning power (*sāmarthya*) or majesty (*prabhāva*); alternatively, it is a compound of "removal of poison" and "prosperity" (*bhūti*), where *bhūti* means manifestation (*vibhūti*) or sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the possession by spirits or planets, subjugation, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and so forth are included.
"Truth" means non-contradictory; by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "Vainateya etc.," the inclusion of the mantra-doctrines of the Buddhists and others is intended—
*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 739.
Because all [qualities] such as being difficult to pronounce and so forth, as well as the potencies of mantras and the like, are common [to all]. —
*Pramāṇavārttikamanorathanandinī* 3.242.

Because [qualities] such as being difficult to pronounce or difficult to hear, which are perceivable by people like us, can be produced through other superior degrees [of effort] even in the case of the other [Vedas]—*Aṣṭaśata*, *Aṣṭasahasrī* p. 237; *Syādvādaratnākara* p.
Ratnākaraśānti, folio 4.9:
"Furthermore, we observe that the claim 'these mantras are not of human origin' is contradictory."

For instance: if mantras were based on convention (*samaya*), it would be logical for them to accomplish some purpose, provided that these mantras were someone's convention—just as, for example, when one employs a sentence composed by me which is intended to convey a specific meaning, thinking, "I shall connect this with such-and-such a meaning"—either out of a commitment to the welfare of others or for some other reason; then the accomplishment of a result from the application of a mantra would be logical, as in the case of readers [understanding a text] through a poet’s convention (cf.
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1).
Furthermore, that which is called "mantra" is not something other [than truth];
rather, it is as follows: "truth," and so forth.

Speaking according to reality is truth (*satya*); the subduing of the senses and the mind is austerity (*tapas*). The power (*prabhāva*) of these two is the capacity for such feats as paralyzing poison and so forth. Those persons who possess this [power] are "those endowed with the power of truth and austerity. For such persons, the means of accomplishing a desired object is indeed a mantra; that speech possesses the definition of a mantra. Why is this? Because even today, among men, we observe the manifestation of the power to paralyze poison, fire, and the like, through the force of their respective foundations in truth.
Likewise, even today, certain Śabaras who abide by their own traditional rules are still able to compose non-Vedic mantras due to the cause of possessing the power to remove poison;
and because we observe the *mantrakalpas*— the ritual manuals for mantras— of the non-Vedic Buddhists and others (indicated by the word "etc."), such as the Ārhata, Gāruḍa, and Māheśvara traditions,

it follows that mantras are syllables of knowledge (*vidyā*), while the instructions for the methods of accomplishing them are the *mantrakalpas*, and these *mantrakalpas* of the Buddhists and others are indeed produced by persons.
—Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p. 342:
"O Lord, even those who are knowers of mantras and compose certain mantras possess that power [of success] because they act in accordance with the principles taught therein."

"Mantras that are produced and composed by persons must be spoken by one who desires the result"— by this very [statement], the claim of those men who hold that [mantras] are incapable of being effective means has been refuted.
(Pramāṇavārttika 3)

309–10 Since the power of mantras is observed even in those that are imperceptible, it cannot be asserted that the efficacy of mantras is found only in those of the Atharvavedins and not in those of the Buddhists and others, for such a claim would be contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The efficacy of mantras and the like is also clearly evident even among the Śabaras. (Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 237; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 633)
Even though it is well-known in the entire world, it is nevertheless not infallible— Śāstravārtā 10.44.
If it exists in a language that is either refined (saṃskṛta-rūpā), vernacular (prākṛta-svarūpā), or Pāli,
then there is no [fault].
Furthermore, the specific arrangement observed here excludes only an agent incapable of producing it, but not an agent in general.

For a specific arrangement perceived in things such as old wells or palaces is not understood to exclude the mere existence of an agent; rather, by that arrangement, only a craftsman incapable of its production is excluded. Indeed, properties that follow the positive and negative concomitance of an agent cannot be accounted for in the absence of an agent.

Therefore, the inference that "the Vedic composition is authorless" (*apauruṣeya*) and so forth is untenable; for, as explained above, the quality of being distinct from compositions with observed authors is impossible in its case, or, even if it were possible, it would not preclude the existence of an author in general. Consequently, it was incorrectly stated that "if an author is inferred merely from the fact of being a composition, it would entail the inference that the world has an intelligent cause," and so on; this is because the Vedic composition is not established as being distinct from compositions preceded by an author, whereas the composition of the world is so established.
The refutation of that [position] has been elaborated at length in the section on the denial of God (*īśvara-nirākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, a comparison with the Veda has been stated: "Moreover, since this structure is of such a distinct nature, an agent of a similarly distinct nature must be inferred; it is not, however, reasonable to deny him."
"Moreover, the specific arrangement observed here excludes an agent incapable of producing it, but not an agent in general. — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
236; also *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 634.
—The measure and its instrument— Śrī.
Objection: Ācārya, is it not merely the agent?
Likewise, in the Veda, by means of a specific arrangement [of sounds].
Page 722, line 12 –ddhetutvānu– Ā.:

Because the state of being distinct from compositions preceded by an agent is established; for indeed, in the case of things whose agents are present, the cognition that "it has been made" arises even in one who has not observed the act of making, but this is not the case with the earth and so forth.

Regarding what was also stated—"All study of the Veda is preceded by the teacher's own study," and so forth—in that regard, would the state of being denotable by the word "study" without qualification establish authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*), or with qualification? In the first alternative, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because this [property] exists even in the *Mahābhārata* and other works whose authors are definitely known.

But in the second case, what is its qualification? If it is "the Veda," then is study qualified by the Veda alone a reason, or is it so by being qualified by another qualification? If it were by that much alone, then it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its presence could possibly occur even in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) without contradiction; for only a qualification that is contradictory to the counter-example excludes the reason from it, and nothing else, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the qualification "of the Veda" is not contradictory to the counter-example characterized by having an author, because there is no contradiction even if the study of the Veda—just like the study of the *Mahābhārata*—is possessed of an author (see page 722, line 17).

For comparison: "Moreover, in this case, does the property of being denotable by the word 'study' without qualification establish the lack of human authorship, or [the lack of authorship] as qualified by the non-remembrance of an author? (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 369).
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 41; *Syādvāda-ratnākara*, p. 634.

For comparison: since this is so, if one were to prove that "study is preceded by another study, just like other studies," the logical mark (*liṅga*) "because it is a study" would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), because the property of being a study exists even in the case of the study of the *Mahābhārata* and similar works, which are of human origin.
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 345:
"For it is not tenable that its being denotable by that word constitutes its beginninglessness;
moreover, this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it can be stated in this same way regarding the *Bhārata* as well."

"All study of the *Bhārata* is preceded by study under a teacher, because it is designated as 'study of the *Bhārata*', just like the study of the *Bhārata* at the present time" (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 233; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

For otherwise, it would follow that there is no speaker even for the *Sanmati-ṭīkā* (p. 41), the *Syādvāda-ratnākara* (p. 634), and the three baskets (*piṭakatraya*) and so forth, precisely because of that same reason.

If it is established that the study of anything else, like the study of the Vedas, is always preceded by prior study, then the mouth does not become distorted [in its logic]; for even in the case of something having a known speaker, the fact that "being denoted as study" exists would not render the reason inconclusive—*Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p.
237: "The study of the *Mahābhārata* is all preceded by the teacher's study."
Because it is denotable by the study of that [Veda], the current study is likewise; as stated in the *Prameyaratnākara* (3.99): "Just as..."
Because this [word] exists even among the Bhāratas (ba), and because it is denotable by the word "study" (adhyayana) (śra)— this is the reason.

"If it is argued that [the fault does not apply] because of the qualification by 'Veda'—that is, there is no fault because the deviation applies only to mere study and not to study qualified by 'Veda'—this is the intention [of the objection]. But who is this person? and so forth, says the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādī*).
What excellence (*atiśaya*) does the study of the Veda possess such that, having performed that study otherwise [i.e., independently], one would be unable to study it?
There is no excellence whatsoever;
therefore, since there is no contradiction in the fact that there could be study of the Veda without it being preceded by [another] study, that very [reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).

For the qualification "being a Veda" is not incompatible with the contrary [of the probandum], namely "not being preceded by another recitation. Therefore, it does not exclude the reason from that contrary.

Why? Because the two—being a Veda and being preceded by another recitation—are possible together in a single Vedic sentence; for what contradiction is there here in that something might be a Vedic recitation and yet not be preceded by another recitation?

Therefore, the qualification "being Vedic" does not add excellence to the reason "study"; it does not confer a distinction, because—due to the absence of contradiction with the contrary—it does not exclude [the reason] from the contrary class. Thus, even though it is employed, the qualification is equivalent to one not employed at all. (*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 345; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 397).
On page 634 of the *Syādvādaratnākara*,
regarding the study preceded by non-study— that is, the quality of being the object denoted by the word "study" as a qualification of the Veda which possesses an author— ...
From the opposite side, [it is] characterized by the absence of the characteristic of agency— variant *ba*—
or characterized by the absence of that [agency], variant *śra*.

Furthermore, is it observed that the study of persons who are of such-and-such a nature is preceded by study, and is that [reason] established as such for persons of exactly that same nature, or for those of a different nature? If it is for those of that same nature, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
If, however, it is for those of a different nature, then the reason—like "arrangement" (*saṃniveśa*) and so forth—is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) regarding the world's having an intelligent cause.

Now, if it is argued that for those very persons who are such [i.e., omniscient], that [omniscience] is established as such, and that this is not a case of proving what is already established—because all persons lack the capacity to perceive supersensible objects, and thus lack the ability to compose an injunction (*preraṇā*) that communicates supersensible matters—that too is unsatisfactory. For the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of an injunction in communicating such [supersensible] objects is unestablished;

and that non-establishment is well-known, because in the absence of a speaker possessed of excellence (*guṇa*), its defects (*doṣa*) are not neutralized by excellences, and thus they exclude its validity.

Moreover, since even those devoid of the power to perceive supersensuous objects are capable of composing such an injunction, how can the fact that all persons are of this nature [i.e., lacking such power] be established on the grounds of their incapacity to compose such an injunction? For, if that were so, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Now, if it is argued that the removal of invalidity in the case of a word occurs not merely through its being spoken by a virtuous author, but because it is also possible for this [removal] to occur through its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), and therefore this fault does not apply—that too is incorrect; for is its authorlessness established from some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from this very same [scripture]? If it is from another, then this [scripture] is redundant.

If it is argued for this very reason, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): for only upon the establishment of the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) through inference would the validity of the *preraṇā* (impulsion) be established; and only upon its establishment would the fact that all persons are of such a nature [as not being authors] be proven by the incapacity of all persons to compose such an impulsion.
Therefore, the mere study of the Veda is not the probans for us and others who are of limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*).

Comparison—Furthermore, is it observed that for persons of such a nature, study is preceded by [prior] study, and that the state of being denoted by the word "study" establishes that very state of being preceded by study for those of that same nature, or for those of a different nature? —*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 398;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 41;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 634.
Preceded by the study of the Guru— the study of the Vedas as previously observed— Ā., Ba.
Or [the cognition] of persons such as ourselves, who possess the vision of supersensible objects preceded by the study of the Vedas.

Comparison (*tulanā*): Just as it is observed that for one who is unable to perform a study by themselves, there exists another cause for that study—namely, a prior study—so too [the case in question] would be preceded by another study. When the specific instance is understood as being caused by that [prior study] rather than by innate capacity (*śakti*), then by abandoning that specific instance characterized by self-performed study, one might attempt to grasp the general property of "Vedic study" (*vedādhyayanatva-sāmānya*) common to both the capable and the incapable, arguing: "All Vedic study is preceded by another study, because it possesses the general property of being Vedic study. However, such an argument is indeed fallacious (*vyabhicārin*).

What is it like? It is like the state of being a white substance [serving as the probans] for the proof of fire—that is, for the proof of the existence of fire—[as stated in] Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, page 346.

The established principle is this: whatever kind of configuration or similar feature is observed in objects such as pots—which, even for one who has not seen them being made, gives rise to the cognition that they were "made"—that very same kind [of feature] in an old well or the like leads to the inference that they have an intelligent cause; however, a feature dissimilar to that, which does not produce the cognition of being "made" for one who has not seen it being made, does not do so. Nevertheless, if one were to infer that the earth and other elements have an intelligent cause based on the commonality of their configuration, then by the same reason of being a modification of clay (*mṛdvikāratva*), an anthill would also have to be the work of a potter. Therefore, just as the commonality of configuration and so forth is irrelevant for establishing that the world has an intelligent cause, so too it is appropriate to prove that the study of only those persons—such as ourselves—whom we observe to be preceded by prior study in another instance, is indeed preceded by study in a different place or time; it is not appropriate for others who perceive supersensible objects (*atīndriyārthadraṣṭṛ*), because in their case, the property of being denotable by the word "study" (*adhyayana-śabdavācyatva*) is an irrelevant probans (*aprayojaka*). This is the intended meaning.
For those of us who perceive only what is near at hand,
study is preceded by [prior] study.
Otherwise, because the Veda is possessed of limited vision— just like ourselves and others— due to the impossibility of there being a person who perceives supersensuous objects.

Others declare: "Since the qualities that serve as the causes for the truth of speech regarding supersensuous objects reside in a person, why should that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) not be false?"
— Pramāṇavārttika 3.225:
To the extent that, in the absence of a speaker possessing [excellent] qualities, validity there is subject to exception because it is not excluded by those qualities and is set aside by faults.
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
397; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 41;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 634.
Because the validity [of a cognition] has been refuted by the qualities of the speaker— thus it was stated by Ācārya [Prajñākaragupta].
Since the authority of the Vedic injunction has been established by the removal of non-authoritativeness, it has become authoritative.

Is its lack of human authorship (apauruṣeyatva) established from some other means of valid cognition, or from that very [scripture] itself?—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 397; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 41; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
[The opponent might argue: "Its status as having limited vision (*arvāgdarśitva*) is established, just like that of ourselves and others.

Now, if [the Veda] is qualified by another attribute, what then is that attribute—is it the non-remembrance of an author, or the non-interruption of the tradition? It cannot be the non-remembrance of an author, because it has been demonstrated that this is vitiated by numerous defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor can it be the non-interruption of the tradition; for is this [non-interruption] restricted to oneself, or does it pertain to all people? It cannot be restricted to oneself, because even if this [Veda] were of human origin, such [non-interruption] would be possible, just as in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and other such works.
