Nor does it apply to all people in the world, because even if such a person existed, he could not be known by one who is not omniscient; furthermore, there is no contradiction even if this [Veda] were of human origin, as in the case of sayings like "In every banyan tree dwells Vaiśravaṇa.

Regarding the reason consisting of "being called the study of the Veda," what is the qualification therein—is it "non-remembrance of an author" or "uninterrupted tradition"? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 635)
Is the non-interruption of the tradition also inherent in the self, or does it pertain to all people? — *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 635;
*Sarvagata* (in *ba* and *śra* manuscripts);
[regarding] the non-interruption of the tradition.

Furthermore, the determination of an object arises from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as does the non-interruption of the tradition. Is this [tradition] an independent means of valid cognition, one of the others such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), or included within them? It cannot be independent, because that would entail the contradiction of the established number of six means of valid cognition. Nor can it be one of the others, such as perception, because it arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) distinct from theirs, like a succession of commands.
For this very reason, it is not included therein;
like the succession of Yakṣas at a banyan tree, this [Veda] merely generates doubt and is not inclined toward the establishment of the true nature of reality.

Furthermore, its non-interruption is accessible through faith alone; for while even those things that have a beginning—such as costumes, ornaments, and childhood games—are observed to be subject to total eradication, it is impossible to conceive of the non-interruption of the beginningless Veda through any means other than mere faith.
The non-interruption of the tradition is included within perception and the other [means of valid cognition] precisely because it arises from a unique causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Therefore, for one who possesses a lineage of compassion based on direct perception, the determination that this [scripture] has such-and-such a meaning arises solely from the fact that it is intended to be spoken by one who knows with certainty; thus, the very act of generating [knowledge] through the study of the tradition (*sampradāya*)—
which consists in the non-interruption of the tradition— is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the comparison with the Veda: moreover, even for the entire collection of scriptures that has a beginning, there is an interruption of the tradition; yet for the Veda, which is beginningless, such an interruption does not exist—what faithful person other than you would accept this? (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 635)

— Established— Venerable [Author]: Regarding what was also stated— "the past and future times," and so forth— that too is an unexamined assertion, because there is no distinction between this [view] and other scriptures.

Furthermore, is time—whether past or future—as it is currently perceived as being either associated with a person incapable of acting as an agent or devoid of such an agent, to be proven as such because it is time? Or is it to be proven as something otherwise? If it is proven as such, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
If, however, it is proven as something otherwise, then the reason is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), like the [fallacious] argument regarding the conjunction of the three humors (*sannipāta*).

Now, if it is being proved that time, while being exactly as it is, is devoid of that [change], there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), because otherwise [if it were not so], time in its altered state would be impossible. But from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it understood that "time in its altered state does not exist"—from this very [inference] or from another? If it is from this very one, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*): for the establishment of the absence of time in its altered state would depend on the establishment of its being devoid of that [change] through this inference, and the establishment of that [absence] would depend on the establishment of the absence of time in its altered state.
If that [authorlessness] were established from something else, then this [Veda] would be purposeless, because authorlessness itself would be established from that very same source;
therefore, since no means of valid cognition whatsoever exists to establish the authorlessness of the Veda, how could it be authorless? (p.
In the case of [the reasons] such as "being time" (*kālatva*) and "being a person" (*puruṣatva*), there is a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*),
because— as in the previous case— the capacity for action is not established for humans due to their lack of mastery over the instruments [of action].
— *Tattvasaṅgraha-kārikā* 2799.

Comparison: Is the time now perceived as being either endowed with a person capable of composing the Veda or devoid of such a person—whether past or future—established as being of that nature because it is time, or otherwise? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 399; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 31; Syādvādaratnākara p.
"Capable of composing the Vedas"—*ba*;
"by a person who has not seen that [Veda]"—*ba*; "devoid of a person who is its author"—thus it does not exist—*ā*.
Because it is devoid of a person who is its author,
the remainder [of the argument] is that it is "devoid of a composer of the Veda";
[the opposite case would be] "endowed with a person who is its author."
It is indeed accepted that time, being devoid of a person who composes the Veda, is itself free from a composer of the Veda;
or rather, [the argument applies] to that which is either endowed with a person capable of composing the Veda and accompanied by such a composer,
or else to that which is truly devoid of a person who composes the Veda.
The absence of an author for the Veda is [established] by means of the possibility that time might be accompanied by a person who is its author.

Comparison with the author of the Vedas accompanied by [the argument]: "But from what source of valid cognition is it understood that there is no time that is otherwise [than eternal]?"—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
399; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 31.
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 635, the reason "because of being time" (*kālatvāt*) is accompanied by the agent of creation (*vedakartṛsahita*).
In the proof of the non-existence of time as something otherwise transformed, because it is devoid of a knower and a maker, the reason is "because it is time."

Or let it be so; nevertheless, would this [Veda] produce comprehension of its own meaning when explained, or when unexplained? It cannot be when unexplained, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is explained, from where does that explanation come—from itself or from a person? Not from itself, because the Veda does not itself establish that "this alone is the meaning of my words and sentences, and not that other," for otherwise there would be no diversity of interpretations.

If [it is argued that authority comes] from a person; how then could the suspicion of error be removed when the understanding of the meaning arises from an explanation produced by a person? For persons, being subject to passion and other defects, are seen to explain even a contrary meaning. Furthermore, if validity were accepted on the basis of correspondence, the postulation of the Veda’s non-human origin would be useless, since validity would be established for the Veda even if it were of human origin simply through correspondence.

Moreover, there is no correspondence among the various explanations, because mutual contradictions are observed among the explanations of meditative realizations (*bhāvanā*), injunctions (*niyoga*), and so forth.
Comparison: Is the Veda, which propounds Dharma, explained by someone, or is it unexplained? — *Āptaparīkṣā*, Verse 110; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 400; *Syaḍdarśanasamuccaya-ṭīkā*, p. 636.
Prameyaratnākara 3.99:
Compare— “For this [object], even while existing, does not produce cognition.”
As long as it has not been illuminated by persons who act as lamps,
then its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) cannot be postulated as the cause for knowledge of the true meaning; for this knowledge proceeds from the explanations of [learned] men.
Therefore, even if this authorlessness of the Veda were true, it would be useless;
for if its desired fruit depends upon knowledge based on a person,
then in this case, persons are independent and the interpretation of the Veda would be according to their own whims.

Those who act thus cannot be restrained by anyone from the defects of delusion, pride, and so forth; therefore, it is suspected that these people, being corrupted, might even provide a distorted interpretation of the sacred scripture (*śruta*).
—Tattvasaṅgraha, verses 2366–71. For comparison: "Words do not say, 'This is the meaning, this is not the meaning';
nor is this meaning to be conceptualized by persons, for they are possessed of passion and other afflictions."
The Veda, being devoid of a human author, does not always express its meaning by itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.312)
The explanation called "Pūrva" is like a staff for a blind man; it requires that very [explanation] for its own support, and being dragged by it, it might even fall onto a wrong path.
Therefore, it is not logical for the Veda to be the eye, like light.
—Tattvasaṃgraha, v. 2374–75; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 400; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 636.

Alternatively, this Veda does not itself explain its own meaning, because if it did, it would follow that everyone would understand it.
—*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 195.

For comparison: "An explanation of that which is non-human (apauruṣeya) is not tenable because there is no means of valid cognition [for it], and because its correctness and so forth cannot be ascertained due to mutual contradictions."
—Śāstravārtāsamuccaya 10.31.
For comparison: "Now others explain [it differently]; do they possess a thorough knowledge of that object, or not?"
In the first alternative, would he be omniscient or non-omniscient?—*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 159. Is the expounder possessed of passion and so forth, or free from passion?—*Āptaparīkṣā*, verse 110;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 8.

99. Furthermore, is this commentator of that [text] a seer of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadraṣṭṛ*), or is he the opposite? In the first case, there is a contradiction with the refutation of one who perceives supersensuous objects.

Furthermore, since its validity regarding dharma and other matters is established, the restrictive determination that "codanā alone is the means of valid cognition regarding dharma" would be untenable.

Alternatively, if it were the opposite [i.e., not valid], how then could there be a correct understanding from its exposition? For that would be impossible due to the suspicion that it might express what is not true to reality.
(Compare: Now, others explain it thus; for them, does there exist a thorough knowledge of the subject matter of that [Veda], or not?
In the first alternative, would he be omniscient or non-omniscient?—*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 159. Is the expounder possessed of passion and so forth, or free from passion?—*Āptaparīkṣā*, verse 110;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 8.

Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 636; Prameyaratnakośa, 3.

Comparison: If it were admitted that there is someone who knows supersensuous objects, then the possibility of non-scriptural knowledge regarding an object that is absolutely beyond perception would arise.

If it were possible for Jaimini and others to possess knowledge—entirely independent of scripture—regarding objects that are absolutely beyond the senses, such as the connection with heaven, then it would be accepted that there exists someone who perceives supersensible objects; in that case, the rejection of such a person would not be logical.
However, if no one perceives supersensible objects, then: "One who possesses passion and other defects does not know the meaning by himself, nor from another source;
the Veda itself does not make it known. How, then, can there be any comprehension of the Veda’s meaning?"
— Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s Commentary 3.316–17:
[the one] who perceives objects beyond the senses.
Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction—
Jaimini-sūtra 1.1.2.
It has been established regarding Dharma that "injunction alone is the means of valid cognition"— Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Codanāsūtra, verse 4.
Whatever is a dharma is characterized by an injunction; the injunction alone is its defining characteristic—
*Śāstradīpikā* 1.1.2.
This has been extracted from Āptaparīkṣā, page 57,
and Tattvārthaślokavārttika, page 12.
Because a cognition corresponding to the object of knowledge is not possible [as explained in] Pramāṇakhaṇḍana, p. 401; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 636.

Comparison—Moreover, even regarding the claim that the Veda or its commentary, when being taught by one person to another, continues to follow an unbroken tradition, even here an oath is the only refuge;

for there is the possibility of a different arrangement due to the arrogance of those who cause the ruin of the tradition, or out of hatred for that philosophical system, or out of the malice of those who have adopted it to disparage it, or through the vice of trickery, or from some other cause whatsoever.

Moreover, in this matter, out of attachment to his own doctrine, you have surely forgotten your own facial expression—that a person overwhelmed by passion and other defects might even speak untruth, and thus his word is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Why, then, is this not considered here as well:
whether it is possible or not that the very same teacher, due to such affliction, might teach the Veda or the meaning of the Vedas otherwise?
For it is heard that certain other recensions (*śākhāntara*) were recovered from among those that had been lost by some men; even now, some of them have only a few students.

Similarly, since even those with many students could, at some time, somehow suffer destruction, and because there is the possibility of their becoming numerous again based on the trust placed in persons who recover them, the possibility of their reaching abundance once more exists.

Furthermore, since those persons who propagate [the teachings] might at some time have forgotten what they studied, or—due to the fear of losing their reputation and so forth—might teach otherwise, and because their followers accept it without inquiry based on trust in them; and because, even among many students, one frequently observes acceptance [of errors] from a person whose reliability has been assumed;
and because, for that reason as well, deception is possible in some way.
Furthermore, we hear from you as well that in this case there is merely a limited succession of explaining persons;
among them, there might even be someone who is hateful, ignorant, or deceitful—thus, there is no confidence.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1)

Nor can there be a correct understanding of the truth through the explanations of Manu and others, simply because they possessed superior intelligence; for their possession of superior intelligence remains unproven.

For would their excellence of intelligence arise from itself, from the repeated study of the Vedic meaning, from unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), or from Brahman? If it were from itself, then it would belong to everyone, as there is no distinction between them.

If it is argued that [the validity of the Veda] arises from the repeated study (*abhyāsa*) of the meaning of the Veda, then must that study of the Vedic meaning be of something already known or of something unknown? It cannot be of what is unknown, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is of what is already known, then from where does that knowledge arise—by itself (*svataḥ*) or from another (*anyataḥ*)? If by itself, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): for the repeated study of the Vedic meaning occurs only when there is self-evident knowledge of it, and that self-evident knowledge occurs only when there is the repeated study of its meaning.

If, on the other hand, it is from another, then the knowledge of that [other source] must also come from another; thus, in the absence of the admission of a seer of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadarśin*), a determination of the truth based on a succession of blind men (*andhaparamparā*) is untenable.

Even the unseen (adṛṣṭa) does not establish excellence of knowledge, because it exists even in other persons. If it is argued that such an unseen force is possible only in Manu and others because of its occurrence there, then from what source does its occurrence in them arise? If it is due to the specific performance of the meaning of the Veda, then would he be a performer of the Vedic meaning known or unknown? If it is of the unknown, then there is an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If it is argued that [the excellence of knowledge] is known [through inference], there follows the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka-prasaṅga*): for only when the excellence of the knowledge of the Vedic meaning is established can the excellence of the performance of its prescribed rites be established; and only when that is established can the excellence of the resulting unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) be established; and from that, the excellence of that knowledge is established.
Thus, even if the knowledge of the Vedic meaning were established for Brahmā, only then could the excellence of Manu and others’ thorough knowledge of that same meaning be established on that basis.

And from what is this [excellence] established for him? If it is from a particular merit (*dharma-viśeṣa*), then that very same circular reasoning (*cakraka-prasaṅga*) follows: for only when an excellence in the thorough knowledge of the Vedic meaning is established would a particularity in the performance preceded by that [knowledge] be established; from that, a particular merit produced by it would be established; and upon the establishment of that, the excellence in the thorough knowledge of the Vedic meaning would be established. Therefore, if one does not accept a seer of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha-darśin*), the comprehension of the Vedic meaning is simply impossible.

[Objection: Whence does he have such an excellence of wisdom? [Reply: If you say it is from an excellence in the study of the meaning of the Vedas (*śruti*), then whence is that? If you say it is from the practice of Vedic study in a previous birth, then is that [practice] due to himself or to another? If it is due to himself, then it would belong to everyone. If you say that the practice of the Vedas is naturally appropriate for him alone due to the power of his unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), while it is not so for others because they lack it; then, whence does he alone possess such a specific unseen merit? If you say it is from the performance of the meaning of the Vedas, then is he a performer of the meaning of the Vedas which he has known by himself, or of that which he has not known? The latter position is not tenable, as it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that [the Veda] is known by itself, then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If it is argued that for Manu and others, the study of the Veda comes from something else, then what is that "something else"? If it is argued that it is Brahman, then from where does he have knowledge of the meaning of the Veda? If it is argued that it is from a particular merit (*dharmaviśeṣa*), then that very same mutual dependence remains.
(Tattvārthaśloka, p. 9)
Because it is not perceived (adṛṣṭatvāt). (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 401; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 636) Śra. [Note: This is a citation.]
“If [the self] exists by itself, then it would be other”— compare Ānandagiri’s commentary:
“Because not even a single person among them is considered to be one who perceives with supersensuous vision,
this [tradition], though beginningless and imagined, is therefore a succession of the blind.”
A blind man led by a blind man certainly does not find the right path; nevertheless, this beginningless conceptualization of his is not fruitless. (Tattvasaṃgraha, kārikā 2379–80)
Even if there were no contradiction, there would be a blind tradition for that which is eternal,
because of the absence of anyone who perceives its object— just like the linguistic usage of barbarians and the like.
(Nyāyaviniścaya, Kārikā 417)
*Aṣṭaśata* (Aṣṭasahasrī), p. 239; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 401; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
Tattvacintāmaṇi, Śabdakhaṇḍa, p. 369: [Regarding] the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) that causes excellence of wisdom, such as that of Manu and others...
For the sake of the accomplishment of specific qualities of dharma for each respective Brahmā.

Now, one might argue that through the study of grammar and other sciences, once the meaning of worldly words and sentences is understood, the understanding of the meaning of Vedic words and sentences—which are not distinct from them—would also be established, just as in the case of previously unheard poetry and the like; therefore, there would be no need for a seer of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadarśin*) to understand the meaning of the Vedas. This, however, is unsound. For even though worldly and Vedic words are identical, they are established as having multiple meanings; thus, it is impossible to restrict the meaning to the specific one intended for exposition while excluding all others.
Nor can that restriction be established by means of context and so forth, because those too function in manifold ways, as in the case of the *Trisaṃdhāna* and other such works.

And if the Vedic word "fire" and so forth conveys its meaning because it is indistinguishable from the worldly word "fire" and so forth, then why should this [Vedic word] not also be human-made (*pauruṣeya*), since it is likewise indistinguishable from that which is human-made? For the meaningfulness of the worldly word "fire" and so forth is pervaded by its being human-made. In that case, how can this Vedic word "fire" and so forth abandon its status as human-made and yet grasp that very same meaning? It must either accept both [properties] or reject both.

Furthermore, there is no other distinction between worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*) words such that the former would be non-human (*apauruṣeya*) while the latter are human (*pauruṣeya*), given that they are identical in their essential nature, equally dependent upon the apprehension of convention (*saṅketa*) for the communication of meaning, and equally unhearable by a person when not being uttered. Therefore, those [Vedic words] which are indistinguishable from compositions fashioned by humans must be of human origin, just as ancient wells, palaces, and the like are of human origin because they are indistinguishable from the compositions of newly built wells, palaces, and so forth; and the Vedic words, phrases, and sentences are likewise indistinguishable from compositions fashioned by humans. Thus it is established.
Comparison: Doubt regarding the determination of the meaning of a word is indeed produced by its very common usage, because it is observed that words function with multiple meanings;
since there is no possibility of it being otherwise, the sound possesses multiple potencies of its own accord.
For those who perceive no regulating factor, doubt must necessarily arise; since everything is capable of signifying any object, how can there be a restriction to a single meaning?
Or by whom could supersensuous intentions be known, other than through speech?
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.323, 24, 26; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 402.
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 637, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and so forth are to be understood;
as it has been said: "Conjunction, disjunction, coexistence, and opposition..."
Context, indicative mark, proximity of another word,
syntactic capacity, expectation, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth,
serve as causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined.
— Vākyapadīya 2.317–18:
Restriction to the intended meaning.
There is also a comparison with the *prakaraṇas* and so forth— since these too proceed in manifold ways, like the *dvisandhāna* and other such works— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 402.
Because their occurrence also involves multiplicity, like the three joints and so forth—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
637. (The *ā* in *ātte* is a scribal error for *i*).
Therefore, even by means of the perception of authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*),
[the word] is a worldly word (*laukikaśabda*).
The purport of Vedic words and their human authorship are not [found] in worldly [words]. (Ānandagiri, Bhaṭṭa)
Now, it might be argued that there indeed exists a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between these two; to this he says: "And here," and so forth.
Here, in this world, we do not perceive any difference in the intrinsic nature of worldly and Vedic sentences.

In the absence of such a difference in their own form, since only a commonality—the identical form characterized by the sequence of phonemes—is observed in those worldly and Vedic sentences, a person who, while discerning the dharma of one [type] of sentence—whether worldly or Vedic—would establish its status as being authored by a person (*pauruṣeya*) or not authored by a person (*apauruṣeya*) through a distinction, would be making an argument that is impossible to avoid error.
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 341:

"Furthermore, since there is no difference in the nature of the words between worldly and Vedic speech, and since both require the apprehension of convention (*saṃketa*) for the communication of meaning, and since they are equally not heard by a person when they are not being uttered, no other distinction exists on account of which the Vedic [words] might be considered non-human (*apauruṣeya*). — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 402.
Syādvādamañjarī, p. 637;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p.
39—[and] those which are produced by man—ba.
It should be seen— page 729, note 14—
the definition of *tara-cana*— in the Ārya and Bhaṭṭa [traditions]— is the definition of word and sentence.
If it is asked, "What then is a *pada* (word) and what is a *vākya* (sentence)? it is said: A *pada* is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are mutually dependent yet [as a whole] independent;

a *vākya*, however, is a collection of *padas* that are mutually dependent yet [as a whole] independent. [Objection: But if this is so, how does this syllogistic statement (*sādhana-vākya*) hold together—"Whatever is existent, all that is subject to transformation, like a jar; and sound is existent"—since there is an expectancy for the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) to be "subject to transformation," and it is not accepted that something possessing expectancy can be a complete sentence? [Reply: This is not a valid objection; for it is possible that for a certain cognizer, that expectancy does not arise.

For that cognizer for whom the expectation regarding the phrase "it is therefore subject to transformation" is satisfied, that sentence is [complete] in relation to him, because the defining characteristics of a sentence as previously stated are present; it is not so in relation to another. Indeed, the state of being free from expectation (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) is a property of the cognizer that is superimposed upon sentences, but it is not a property of the words themselves, since they are insentient.

If the cognizer understands the meaning by that much alone, why would he require anything further? For if there were a requirement for the statement of the conclusion (*nigamana*) even when the meaning is understood from a proof-statement ending with the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of requiring yet another [statement] even when the meaning is understood from a five-membered statement ending with the conclusion; thus, the state of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) would never be established. And consequently, due to the absence of a complete sentence, no one would ever attain the understanding of the meaning of a sentence.

One who desires this [definition] should understand that the status of a sentence (*vākyatva*) is established for as many mutually dependent words as are required for a collection to become free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*).

By this, it should be understood that the status of a sentence is established even for a collection of heard words that depends on other words to be understood through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, provided that the collection itself is free from expectancy—just like the word "Satyabhāmā" (which implies "Satyabhāmā alone"). For comparison, see Pāṇini’s *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra* 1.4.14: "A word (*pada*) consists of that which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṄ*)."
4.14 Those [phonemes] ending in an inflectional suffix constitute a word— Nyāyasūtra 2.2.60.
2.59 Nāṭyaśāstra 14
Furthermore, a word (pada) is a collection of phonemes (varṇa)—Nyāyavārttika, p. 1;
Nyāyamañjarī, p. 367.
A meaningful word (*pada*)—
*Muktāvalī*, verse 81.
"Letters (*varṇa*) that convey a single connected meaning and are fit for usage constitute a word"— *Tarkadīpikā*, section 2.

A word is that which is determined by the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), and its denoted meaning is that which is indicated by etymological treatises (*nirukta*) and glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*); these two constitute the "word" (*pada*). — *Kāvyamīmāṃsā*, p. 21.
A *pada* (word) is an independent collection (*samudāya*) of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are mutually dependent—Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
458. That is, the independent aggregate of mutually dependent phonemes is a *pada*; a collection of *padas*, however, constitutes a sentence (*vākya*).

—*Pramāṇanaya* 4.10. For comparison: it should be stated that "a verb (ākhyāta), along with indeclinables (avyaya), along with case-roles (kāraka), or along with the qualifiers of case-roles, receives the designation of a sentence (vākya). Another says: "A verb, together with its qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), [is sufficient]."

For it must be stated that all these qualifiers [form] a single finite verb; indeed, that which consists of a single finite verb receives the designation of a "sentence" (vākya)— Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya 2.1.1.
A sentence is either a collection of verbal and nominal endings, or it is an action accompanied by its factors (kārakas).

"A sentence is that which, depending on the recollection of the preceding word, produces a cognition of the final word; being joined together through the assistance of memory, it is the cause for the comprehension of a specific meaning" (Amarakośa). "A sentence is that which, depending on the recollection of the preceding word, produces a cognition of the final word; being joined together through the assistance of memory, it is the cause for the comprehension of a specific meaning" (Nyāyavārttika, p. 16).
A sentence consists of as many words as are required for the completion of the meaning—
a collection of words is a sentence— *Vādanyāya*, p. 108.
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 637;
*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 434.

Now, in this context, as an incidental discussion, he states [the following] in order to demonstrate the definition of a Mīmāṃsaka sentence by way of its meaning: "That which has expectant parts, yet whose words do not require expectation of anything else when there is a distinction..."
A sentence is held to be that which has action as its primary element, possesses qualities, and has a single unified meaning—
Vākyapadīya 2.4.
A sentence is a collection of words that are mutually dependent [on one another] yet independent [of others]—*Aṣṭaśata*, *Aṣṭasahasrī* p. 285; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 458.
A sentence is a fourfold arrangement of mutually expectant words. (Pramāṇanaya° 4.10)
A collection of suffixes ending in nominal (*suP*) or verbal (*tiṅ*) endings is not [the definition of a sentence] because it would entail faults such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Rather, a sentence with respect to a given meaning is simply that collection of words (*śabdastoma*) among which there exists a mutual expectancy (*parasparākāṅkṣā*) conducive to the production of a cognitive synthesis (*anvayabodha*) whose object is a specific meaning corresponding to those words—
*Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā*, verse 13.
A sentence is a collection of words endowed with semantic competency, expectancy, and proximity—
Sāhityadarpaṇa 2.1.
A sentence (*vākya*) is a composition or arrangement of words whose intended meanings are interconnected—
this is poetry (*kāvyam*, *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* p. 22)— a sentence being a collection of distinct words.

As it has been said: "A sentence is a collection of words that are mutually dependent; let the grammatical constructions therein be formulated as appropriate afterwards" (Nyāyāvatāra-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī, p. 8).

One might object: "If a sentence is a collection of mutually expectant words that is itself free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), then this [following] proof-statement would not be a sentence at that time: 'Whatever exists is all subject to transformation, like a jar; and sound exists'; for it would be expectant of the word 'therefore, it is subject to transformation. Since we do not accept that something expectant can be a sentence, this objection should not be raised; because it is possible for some cognizer to have no such expectancy. For 'freedom from expectancy' is a property of the cognizer that is superimposed upon sentences, and not a property of the word itself, since the word is insentient."
If the cognizer understands the object to that extent, why does he expect a remainder? — *Aṣṭaśatī*, *Aṣṭasahasrī* p. 85; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 458; *Syādvādaratnākara* p.
For the Buddhist,
in relation to another Buddhist, and in relation to the Naiyāyika who maintains the five-membered syllogism.
The dharma of the thesis (pratijñā) [is established] through the application (upanaya),
which depends upon the sixth member [of the syllogism].

In some cases, where there is no completion of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is no finality of the sentence; nor is there a departure from the definition of a primary sentence when the meaning is understood through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, which function like a constructed sentence. This is because a collection of heard words that is free of expectancy—even if it depends on other words to be understood through context and the like—is established as a sentence, just as in the case of the word "Satyabhāmā" [which implies her husband].
(Aṣṭaśatī, Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 285)
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 458;
Syādvādaratnākara, pṛṣṭha 642:
"tadvākyatvam" (the state of being its statement).

By this, it has been established that there is no [other definition]; for some have stated another definition of a sentence (*vākya*) as follows: "A verb (*ākhyātaśabda*), a collection (*saṅghāta*), a genus (*jāti*) residing in a collection, a single partless word (*ekonavayavaḥ śabdaḥ*), or a sequence (*krama*) synthesized by the intellect (*buddhyanusaṃhṛti*)."

"The first word, the last word, and the word that is dependent [on another]— thus the views of those who know the principles of logic regarding what constitutes a sentence are manifold. (Vākyapadīya 2)

1–2 Thus [it was argued], but that has been refuted. For would a verb (*ākhyāta-śabda*) be a sentence when independent of other words, or when dependent on them? Of these, the first position is untenable; for since this [verb] is a word (*pada*) when independent of other words, its status as a sentence is impossible, otherwise there would be no such thing as a verbal word at all. As for the second position, is this [verb] independent in some cases or not? In the first case, our own doctrine is established, because the definition of a sentence stated by us is thus accepted.

The second alternative, however, is untenable; for even if this [word] depends on other words, if it lacks independence in some respect, it cannot constitute a sentence because the intended meaning remains incomplete— just like a half-sentence—
according to the definition of a sentence provided by grammarians such as Bhartṛhari and others.

The verbal form, the aggregate, the genus residing in the aggregate, the single partless word, the sequence, and the mental synthesis—these are the eight alternative definitions of a sentence according to the teachers.
Among these, in the view that the sentence is indivisible (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), there are three definitions: the genus residing in the aggregate, the single partless word, and the mental synthesis.

In the *khaṇḍapakṣa* (the view that the sentence is divided), there are five definitions: the verb (*ākhyātaśabda*), the sequence (*krama*), the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), the first word (*padamādyaṃ*), and every word taken separately as being expectant (*sākāṅkṣam*).

Here too, the division is as follows: under the *abhihitānvaya* view, there are two definitions—namely, the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) and the sequence (*krama*); whereas under the *anvitābhidhāna* view, there are three definitions—namely, the verb (*ākhyātaśabda*), the first word (*padamādyaṃ*), and every word taken separately as being expectant (*sākāṅkṣam*). Thus, there are exactly eight alternatives regarding the sentence.
It should be understood that they are established according to different philosophical views—
Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā 2.1–2.
A verbal expression (ākhyāta) is a collection of words—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 860;
it is the synthesis by the intellect (buddhyanusaṃhṛti)—Vākyapadīya, Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, p. 860; Syādvādamañjarī, p.
The original reading: *Aṣṭasahastrī*, p. 284;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 427; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 459.

Regarding the definition of a sentence (*vākya*), the views of those who know the principles of logic (*nyāyavedin*) are manifold: some hold that it consists of the first word and the last word, while others maintain that it is even a single word that is dependent on others; furthermore, it is also held that every individual word, when possessing expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*), constitutes a sentence—*Vākyapadīya*. *Nayacakra*, folio 168A. The first word and the final word, as well as a word that is dependent [on others], are considered a sentence; the opinions of those who know the logic [of grammar] regarding the sentence are diverse in many ways. It is also said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "The first word, or every word individually, when it possesses expectancy, [constitutes a sentence]."
"The first word is distinct from all other words and is dependent," as stated in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Nyāyaratnākara* (p. 860), and *Syādvādaratnākara* (p.
647). The reading in the present text is found on p. 284 of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*.
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 427; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 459; Nyāyavādins—Vākyapadīya.

For those who perceive logic (*nyāyadarśin*), as stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, the *Nyāyaratna*, the *Syādvādamañjarī*, the *Aṣṭasahasrī*, the *Tattvārtha-śloka-vārttika*, and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*:
the nature of a declarative sentence (*ākhyātātmakavākya*) is that wherein a specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is understood when a verb (*ākhyātaśabda*) is present.
That too is called a single sentence whose meaning is a compound—

just as when it is said "it rains," the sense is complete through the implication of the agent and object that "the god [is] water," so the expression "the god rains water" is a sentence; likewise, even a single word whose meaning is a compound and whose sense is complete is designated as a sentence—
*Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* 2.

Because that [word], being independent of other words, possesses the nature of a word (*pada*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of any verbal form (*ākhyāta*).
Furthermore, even for a word dependent on others, if it lacks independence in some instances, its status as a sentence (*vākya*) is contradicted, because the intended meaning would remain incomplete.

However, for that which is free from expectancy, its status as a sentence is established because it possesses the defining characteristics of a sentence—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 285; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 459.
In the Jaina doctrine,
regarding the statement that "a sentence is a collection of verbalized words" (*ākhyātapada*),
would the sentence be a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) or a collection of words (*pada*)? In the first case, the word itself is offered a libation of water [i.e., discarded].

In the second alternative, however, would the collection (*saṅghāta*) of words be spatially constituted or temporally constituted? Of these, the first position is untenable, because since those [words] arise successively and perish immediately, they cannot coexist simultaneously in a single location; thus, a spatially constituted collection is impossible.

As for the second position, is this [collection] distinct from the words or non-distinct? It cannot be a partless entity distinct [from them], because such a thing is never perceived, and because, like other phonemes (*varṇa*), it would contradict the very nature of a collection.

Now, is this [sentence] non-different from those [phonemes] in every respect or in some respect? If it were in every respect, how could it be a "conglomeration" (saṅghāta) while possessing the same nature as the individual phonemes? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that every single word would be a conglomeration; yet a single word cannot be called a conglomeration, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). If, on the other hand, it is non-different in some respect, then the consequence is the Jaina doctrine. This is because the definition of a sentence as stated by the Jainas—that it is a collection of phonemes that have attained the state of a group of words which are mutually dependent and free from further expectancy, and whose conglomeration consists in their temporal proximity—is not exceeded [by your position]. Thus, the conglomeration, being in some respect different from the phonemes, falls within the scope of the Jaina view.
However, if those [words], which are expectant yet mutually independent, were to constitute a sentence, they would be subject to the defects previously explained.

As for the nature of the aggregate: they say that whatever meaning is expressed by a word alone is the very same extent of meaning that the expressive unit [the sentence] conveys when situated within a sentence.
When a relation exists, that which arises as an additional element, resting upon many words, they call the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
A word, even when situated within a sentence, expresses only that meaning which it alone is capable of denoting.

Therefore, when there is a mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) of words in a collection (*samudaya*), that which is the "excess" (*ādhikya*) resulting from the force of the word-meanings (*padārthavaśāt*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*); that is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
And it has been said: "That which is the excess here is the sentence-meaning.
By the phrase "residing in many words," it is shown that a collection (*saṅghāta*) is the sentence.
— as stated in the *Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* (2.42):
"Just as phonemes, though possessing parts, [do not exist] without some denotable object..."
A collection of meaningful [words] is also accepted as a sentence— Vākyapadīya 2.55.

Comparison: Regarding the statement "a sentence is a collection [of words]," is it a collection of words that are mutually dependent or independent? In the first case, if they are free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), our own position is established; if they possess expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), there is a contradiction with the definition of a sentence.
In the second alternative, there is the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). — *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 285.
There might be a collection of phonemes produced by space or produced by time—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
459; *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 644.
Regarding words:

a composite [of phonemes] that is distinct from the phonemes does not enter the path of cognition, because it would contradict its status as a composite, just like other phonemes. This is because [such a composite] is unproduced and impossible. (Ārya, Bhaṭṭa)
Nor is the aggregate (saṃghāta) merely non-different from those [individual letters], because it would follow that there is an aggregate for each individual letter;
and yet a single letter cannot be an aggregate—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 426; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 459.
— of that which is not perceived from the dharmas, somehow [there is] the [non-existence] of words.

If there is a requirement for other words [to complete the sense], there is no completion of the sentence; however, if the words are independent of one another, they would merely be individual words and not constitute a sentence. By this, the view that "the universal (jāti) residing in a collection [of words] is the sentence" is also not rejected, because a sentence can be established as consisting of a universal characterized by a similar transformation (sadṛśapariṇāma) which resides in a collection of words that are mutually dependent and free from expectancy, and which is in some way non-different from that collection; otherwise, all the defects mentioned regarding the position that the sentence is the collection itself would follow.

Now, in order to clarify through the presentation of an illustration even the *jāti-sphoṭa* which was indicated as "residing in a collection of universals" (*jāti-saghāta-vartinī*), he says: "Just as a difference in action is not perceived despite a difference in the speed [of its performance], yet the universal (*jāti*) is manifested in repetition; so too, in the case of phonemes, sentences, and words, the auditory perception is identical when the manifesting conditions (*upavyañjana*) are equal, [even though the actions such as rotation differ]."
Even when there is absolute difference, a reality is perceived as if it were identical;
for example, the genus of action characterized by "whirling" is manifested here by a specific projection produced by a particular effort, and because it is fully present in each individual instance,
it is not perceived by a bystander.
In the case of the repetition of revolutions (of the breath), that [auditory perception] is indeed grasped by the cognizer with respect to each revolution.

Regarding letters, words, and sentences, the auditory perception—the manifesting sound—is perceived as if it were of the same form as the reality characterized by the *sphoṭa* of letters, words, and sentences, even though it is absolutely distinct from it. What is it like, even while being ultimately different? It is "possessing a similar manifestor" (*tulyopavyañjanā*).

That [speech-sound] whose characteristics consist in having equal and similar secondary qualities (*upavyañjana*), places of articulation (*sthāna*), and modes of formation (*karaṇa*) is thus described;
therefore, it should be understood that this *jāti-sphoṭa*, manifested by a sound produced by a distinct effort, is indeed distinct [from the individual phoneme].
And this is logical.
Just as for this partless *sphoṭa*, the distinction between prior and posterior parts is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and not by its own nature, because it is eternal—
*Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* 2.20, 21.

Comparison [is established] because the status of a sentence is constituted by a genus (jāti) characterized by a similar transformation, which resides in a collection of words that are mutually dependent and devoid of expectancy—Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 285; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
The claim that a single, partless sound produced from a collection [of phonemes] constitutes a sentence is merely a wishful thought, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it;
and its lack of such a means of valid cognition is well-established, since the proofs for apprehending the *śabda-sphoṭa* will be refuted later.
And *sphoṭa* is of two kinds: external and internal.

The external is also twofold, through the distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). Among these, for that characterized as genus, the genus resides in a collection; for that characterized as individual, it is a single, partless sound.
"But for the internal [perceiver], there is the withdrawal into the intellect"— this is the statement of the summary (uddeśa-vākya) [from the *Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* 2.2].

The commentator, considering this very position to be logically sound as it accords with the intention of the author of the Sūtras, and desiring to explain in sequence that the sentence is indeed the *sphoṭa*—which is of the nature of consciousness, consisting of word and meaning, and being either external or internal and partless—begins by first presenting the analogies of variegated cognition and variegated form. To present the analogy of variegated cognition, he says: "Just as a single cognition of all objects is differentiated according to the appearance of various visible distinctions, so too is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning."

Just as a single, variegated entity is designated by distinct names such as "blue" and so forth through indications of its diverse aspects characterized by different definitions, in the very same way, a single sentence that is entirely free from expectancy is likewise designated.
The designation [of a word] by other words is followed by those that are expectant;
there is no division within the word itself, so how could there be one in its meaning?
It is only the ignorant who, through divisions, arrive at a difference in grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*).
— Vākyapadīya 2.7–9, 13:
"If one postulates the eternality of either the wholes or the genus..."
They say that a sentence has only a single meaning which is non-deviating— *Vākyapadīya* 2.157—
because that [meaning] does not appear in the auditory cognition, and because there is no mark (*liṅga*) bound to it— *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* p. 285.

The view that "sequence is the sentence" does not surpass the position that the collection [of words] is the sentence; therefore, it should be seen as being flawed by the very same defects [as that position].

To explain the position of sequence, he says: "It is the real distinctions themselves, which are established within the word-meanings, that are followed according to sequence; the sentence is not the expressive agent."
It is said that apart from sequence, there is no word-essence nor any sentence that expresses meaning;
for there is no other word denotative than the mere sequence of sounds,
and since sequence is a property of time, therefore no sentence exists [as a real entity].

The designation "word" (*pada*) and the designation "sentence" (*vākya*), which reside merely in the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*), are not accepted as being the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). These two [designations] are either meaningless because they are merely means [to an end], or they possess meaning through the meaning of the word-constituent (*padārtha*).
They say that words uttered in succession constitute the meaning of a sentence, which possesses distinct characteristics—
Vākyapadīya 2.50–52, 56.

Comparison: "The sequence of words is a sentence, just as the sequence of phonemes is a word"—*Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Vākyādhikaraṇa*, verse 53. If it is argued that a sentence is the sequence of specific phonemes that have attained the status of words, [we reply: if that sequence consists of mutually dependent [phonemes] that are free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), then it is simply a collection (*samudāya*). This is because a collection is established only for those things that exist simultaneously through spatial contiguity, whereas for those arising sequentially, they constitute a collection precisely through temporal contiguity.
If, on the other hand, it is expectant [of further words], then it is not a sentence, being like a half-sentence;
for if a mere sequence of mutually independent [words] were considered a sentence, there would be an over-extension of the definition—aṣṭasahastrī, p. 285.
That [statement] is faulty; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 460; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 644. (Śra., Ba.)

Regarding the statement "the sentence is cognition" (*buddhi*), would that be a sentence as a state (*bhāva-vākya*) or a sentence as a substance (*dravya-vākya*)? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for we also accept a sentence as a state consisting of cognition—which, having been produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the cognitions of each preceding phoneme in the self, has transformed into the apprehension of the sentence-meaning and serves as the cause for the understanding of the sentence-meaning immediately after hearing the final phoneme.
As for the sentence being a substance in the form of cognition, what wise person would believe in that, given its contradiction with experience?

Now, regarding that which has been proclaimed as the indivisible reality of sound (*śabdatattva*), which consists of word and meaning, is partless, and is of the nature of consciousness within—that very thing, when manifested outwardly by *nādas*, the teachers call "sentence" (*vākya*). Having thus indicated that "the subsequent engagement of the intellect" (*buddhyanusaṃhṛti*) is what follows, he speaks in order to explain it: "But that reality of sound which is manifested as one within by means of *nādas*, others call 'word' (*śabda*);
likewise, its unity within the sentence [is established], and by means of the portions of meaning, their internal object is revealed."
Word and meaning are two inseparable manifestations of the one Self; they exist as the illuminator and the illuminated, and as cause and effect,
within that essence of the Word which is always the inner dimension of the Self.
—Vākyapadīya 2.30–32; compare:
"And the sequence cannot be extracted by the intellect and then brought together."
For it is indeed the words themselves that possess those [meanings], just as in the case of auditory cognition;
yet, within those very same words, one sequence and another are perceived,
whereby a difference in the sequence of the sentence-meaning would result.

Furthermore, while it might be possible for the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) to constitute a word (*pada*), since that sequence is instrumental in the comprehension of meaning—given that meaning is not comprehended when the sequence is otherwise—how could the sequence of words (*padakrama*) constitute a sentence (*vākya*), given that it is not instrumental in the cognition of the sentence-meaning? Or, if it were so instrumental, there would be a difference in the sentence-meaning whenever there is a difference in the sequence. Thus he says: "In so many... (*tāvatsu*)—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Nyāyaratnākara*, *Vākyādhikaraṇa*, verses 53–55.

In the case of the statement "cognition is the sentence," is it a sentence denoting a state (*bhāvavākya*) or a sentence denoting a substance (*dravyavākya*)? — *Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 285; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 460. — [The reading] "dhīti" is a corruption. — *Bhāmatī*.

By this, the view that a sentence is a synthesis (*anusaṃhṛti*) has also been considered; for what is intended is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the "sentence of being" (*bhāvavākya*), which flashes forth in the mind as a synthesis of the aforementioned words.

When the entire sequence has been withdrawn into a single [unit] that occupies the locus of instruction—this very reality of speech (*śabdatattva*), which is designated as the "inner self" (*antarātman*) or the "inner controller" (*antaryāmī*) and resides within every living being—the synthesis (*anusahāra*) of this [reality] occurs through successive parts that possess sequence, even though they are not [ultimately] such [as they appear]. This synthesis is produced by cognitions (*buddhi*) grasping each preceding part, and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) generated thereby leads to a recollection (*smaraṇa*). By the force of this recollection, at the same time as the apprehension of the final phonemic part, that [synthesized whole] is the sentence (*vākya*). (Syādvādamañjarī, p.

Because the comparison—the mental manifestation of the statement of existence consisting of the aforementioned sequence of words—is desired [as the object of cognition]—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 285; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

Furthermore, his [definition]—that a sentence is either the first word, the last word, or any other word in relation to another—is not distinct from the sentence already mentioned; for it is well known that a collection of words that are mutually dependent and free from expectancy constitutes a sentence. Otherwise, even the very mention of a "word" would be abolished, since a specific action to be accomplished depends upon its specific means.
By its mere presence, the restriction (*niyama*) becomes manifest:

the means (*sādhana*) and the end (*sādhya*) are indeed mutually restricted; it is simply by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth that, when other word-meanings are present, the restriction, though already existing, becomes manifest. Thus, words alone—having other words implied—are the sentence (*vākya*), and word-meanings are the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This is the position of the non-distinct aggregate (*avyatirikta-saṃghāta-pakṣa*); for in that case, expectancy operates as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāvena*).
As things to be accomplished, the causal factors require a verbal root—
Vākyapadīya 2.48–49.

Comparison: Thus, if one conceives of all words, from the first to the last, as being produced separately, there can be no status as a sentence (*vākyatā*) among the words because they lack mutual assistance;
for if the first word were to be completed by all [the others], it would be particularly so.

In that case, there would be that very same sentence, yet another illuminating factor would be a mere quality (*guṇa*); thus, in all subsequent instances, sententiality (*vākyatva*) is not perceived at all among things that are separate, distinct, and independent.

—The statement from the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, verses 49–51, does not differ from the words spoken by Akalaṅka, because a collection of mutually dependent words that is free of expectancy is established as a sentence (*vākya*). —*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 385.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 460;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, folio 646;
*Padavārttika*, manuscript A.

—It is said [in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Vākya-adhikaraṇa, verse 111]: "Even those who think that words themselves, by first conveying word-meanings (*padārtha*), bring about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) and thus receive the designation 'sentence'—for them, the primacy of word-meanings is accepted because the [sentence-meaning] exists when they exist. Therefore, this sentence-meaning is established as being preceded by word-meanings."

This is because of the statement in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, verse 336: "Do those [words] which are intended [to convey meaning], being mutually dependent and not requiring other words, constitute the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, or rather their opposites? In that regard, the latter alternative leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
however, according to the first alternative, the Mīmāṃsakas must simply follow the definition of a sentence as stated by us, like the maxim of a blind man entering a snake's hole."
A sentence is not established as having a distinct meaning independently of the word-meanings;
why? Because there is a lack of evidence. Indeed, there exists no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which we might ascertain this.

For a final phoneme of a sentence, if it disregards its constituent word-meanings and is devoid of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, lacks the capacity to function toward a meaning distinct from those word-meanings.
Indeed, words, having denoted their respective word-meanings, cease their operation;
it is then the word-meanings, once they have been understood, that bring about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

How so? For when a quality such as "white" or "black" is perceived, it indeed produces a cognition directed toward the possessor of that quality. Therefore, those who desire a cognition of the possessor of the quality utter the mere word expressing the quality; thus their intended purpose will be accomplished, and there will arise a cognition of the qualified object.
And the meaning of a sentence is the cognition of a qualified object—
Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.25.
25. Although the phonemes directly effect the communication of the meaning of objects, they do not terminate in this [process], for it would otherwise be fruitless.
The communication of word-meanings is an inseparable concomitant of their activity toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning,
just as fire is for wood in the process of cooking— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Vākyādhikaraṇa, verses 342–43.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is conveyed through the meanings of the words denoted by the individual words, by means of indication (lakṣaṇā) – *Śāstradīpikā*, p. 604.
Thus, neither the sentence nor the words produce the cognition of the sentence-meaning directly; rather—
"It is established that this [sentence-meaning] is indicated by the word-meanings denoted by the individual words themselves" (Nyāyamukha, p.
"Furthermore, the status of being the root of word-meanings is accepted because [the sentence-meaning] exists when they exist" (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Vākyādhikaraṇa, verse 111).

He states the final conclusion: "In this regard it is said: although there may be other roots, the status of being a root is not observed in words; since [the meaning] exists when that [word] exists, it is real. A sentence is not established as the denoter of the sentence-meaning."

Although neither individual words nor their collection is directly the source [of the sentence-meaning], and although the knowledge of the relationship between the genus (jāti) and its relata consists of sentences that have parts as well as those without parts, nevertheless, the word-meanings conveyed by the words—aided by semantic competency (yogyatva) and dependent upon proximity (pratyāsatti)—will constitute the source, because in their absence there is no cognition of the sentence-meaning.
(Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratnākara, Vākyādhikaraṇa, verses 110–11). This is cited in the *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 743.
For one who possesses the cultivation of that—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 461;
from that state—*Śrāvakabhūmi*, p.
461. Therefore, this meaning of the sentence is established as being preceded by the meanings of the individual words; *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Vākyādhikaraṇa, verse 336.

If there were mutual independence [of the words], there would be merely the status of a *pada* (word) and not that of a *vākya* (sentence); or, if there were a requirement for other *padās*, the sentence would remain incomplete. These [arguments] are like a blind man entering a serpent’s hole—see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

461. Furthermore, is the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) different from the meaning of the words (*padārtha*), or non-different? If it is non-different, then it is simply the word-meaning and not the sentence-meaning.
In that case, if the sentence-meaning were merely the act of naming, then the name "kūrdālikā" would have been given to one's own blanket.

Alternatively, if that [sentence-meaning] is something else, consisting of the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasamsarga*), then is such a thing eternal or non-eternal? If it is non-eternal, is it produced by the very word-meanings intended to be expressed, or by other word-meanings? If it were produced by other word-meanings, there would be a contradiction with your own established doctrine.

If the intended objects were produced [by the words], then those very [words] would be both the producers and the indicators; in that case, do they first indicate and afterwards produce, or do they first produce and subsequently indicate? In the first alternative, since the sentence-meaning—the object of cognition—does not yet exist, where could those [words] produce that cognition? Or even if they were to produce it, that cognition of theirs would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its object would be non-existent, like the cognition of a mass of hair [in the air].

Now, if they maintain that they present even that which is non-existent as something to be done, then this is not a fault. But what is the nature of this so-called "obligation to act" (*kartavyatā*)? Is it positive in nature, negative in nature, both, or neither? If it is positive in nature, then it follows that the injunction (*codanā*) has for its object an existing thing; yet its authority (*prāmāṇya*) in that regard is not accepted, because that would entail the establishment of what is undesired, and the obligation to act toward an existing thing is a contradiction of one's own words.
Even in the case of its being of the nature of non-existence, this same objection applies; for since it too is non-existent by its own nature,

there is a contradiction in the possibility of performing that which has such a form— just like a donkey's horn— and furthermore, the authority of an injunction is not admitted in the case of a non-entity.
By this very [argument], the state of being both is also refuted.
Furthermore, if there were a challenge regarding the state of being neither, it would result in a lack of authority (aprāmāṇya) because there would be no object [for the cognition].

Moreover, the state of being neither is not possible for a single thing at one time, because when one of the two properties—affirmation or negation—is negated, the affirmation of the other necessarily follows.
If they first produce [the cognition] and subsequently make it known, then, because its object would already exist, its validity in that regard is untenable;
by this, the position that the meaning of a sentence is eternal is refuted, since there is no difference in the consequence of invalidity arising from having an existing object as its domain.

Comparison: If that [sentence-meaning] were non-different from the word-meanings, then it would be merely the word-meaning itself and not the sentence-meaning; and in that case, how could it be cognized through word-meanings? Alternatively, if the sentence-meaning—consisting of the connection between action and its factors—is a distinct entity from the word-meanings, then if it too were impermanent, would it be produced by the factors of action or produced by the word-meanings? (*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 742). It would be nothing more than giving one's own blanket a different name, such as "kūrdālikā.
(*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 9).
Even if [the object] is produced by the word-meaning, if those very things that are its producers are also its indicators, then it must be stated: were they indicators first, or producers?
— *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 742 (Śrī).

For it is *bhāvanā* alone that constitutes the sentence-meaning everywhere, as it possesses the status of the expressed meaning in all cases, consisting of the connection between the action and its factors (*kāraka*).

The synthesis of the cognitions of words and word-meanings— which are colored by the meanings of the causes such as multiple qualities, genus, and so forth, and which arise from a variegated mass produced by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by those word-meanings— is dependent upon that [synthesis].
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, verse 330–33.

If it is argued that this [cognition] informs you of that [object] as something to be done (*kartavyatā*), we say no; for even in that case, one cannot transcend the conceptual alternatives of existence, non-existence, both, or neither.

In the first alternative, since the duty to perform that [meditation] would have the nature of an existing entity, the injunction would have as its object a sentence-meaning that already exists; and thus, because it would be established as having an existing object of perception and being born from contact with what is real, meditation, like direct perception, would not have a [non-existent] entity as its object.
— *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 742.
Then, regarding the meaning that exists— [as indicated by] *śra* and *ba*— there is an injunction (*codanā*) with respect to that existing object.

Because it would involve the apprehension of something already existing, it would follow that [the cognition of] non-existence is produced by a contact with an existent thing, and thus it would be nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, since non-existence is a mere nothingness (*tucchatā*), it cannot be an object to be brought about; even if it were not a mere nothingness, it would exist in its own form, and thus it would be impossible for it to be something to be accomplished.

Moreover, the authority of an injunction (*codanā*) over an object that is non-existence is not admitted by others, and because non-existence is the province of the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*), if an injunction were to have that as its object, it would be a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*), leading to the undesirable consequence of its lack of authority.
—Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 742: "Even of non-existence, that which is non-existent..."

Because an injunction (*codanā*) would have as its object an already existing thing, it would fall within the domain of objects already apprehended by perception and other means of knowledge, which results in the consequence of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). (Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 742) Now, if it is argued that the eternal sentence-meaning is conveyed by word-meanings; [we reply: in that case, the injunction would indeed have as its object an already existing thing, and thus there would be a contradiction of the accepted tenet that an injunction produces a cognition whose object is an action (*kārya*) characterized by being devoid of the three times.

The sense is that because [the sentence] is included within perception and the other means of knowledge, and because it lacks the capacity to provide cognition of an object not previously known, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is untenable.

Furthermore, it is only reasonable to assert that the meaning of a word or a sentence is manifested through the meanings of the individual words, provided that such a word or sentence is already well-known; however, that [sentence] is not well-known.

For is that [sphoṭa] distinct from the phonemes, or non-distinct? If it were non-distinct, then it would be merely the phonemes themselves, or else there would be only the two—namely, the word and the sentence.
Furthermore, even if it were distinct, would it be perceptible or imperceptible? If it were imperceptible, no cognition of meaning could arise from it;

for if a meaning were cognized from something unknown, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of [cognition arising] from anything whatsoever, as well as the consequence that cognition would never cease.
Nor is it visible, because nothing distinct from the phonemes is perceived;
for among the phonemes such as "devadatta," we do not perceive a single, partless word or sentence that is distinct from them.

Even in the case of those [reasons] which are not indicators (*jñāpaka*)—according to Ācārya—and which do not cause one to know (*ajñāpaka*)—according to Śrī—[they would be] excessively pervasive (*atiprasaṅga*) even with respect to that [object].
According to Bhaṭṭa.
According to Śrī.
There would be a cognition of meaning even for one who does not know the word, such as one who is asleep or in a swoon;

for if the cognition of meaning were to arise from that which makes known what was previously unknown, then even when the meaning of one word has been cognized, there would follow a further cognition of meaning from another unknown word— thus, the cognition of the word would never cease.

Furthermore, is that word or sentence perceived independently, or by way of the phonemes? It cannot be perceived independently, for otherwise it would follow that even one who has not heard the phonemes would have the perception of the word or sentence.

Furthermore, would this [word] be perceived as having parts by way of its constituent phonemes (*varṇa*), or as being partless? If it has parts, then the very definition of words and sentences previously stated must be accepted; for it is established that only a collection—characterized by temporal proximity among mutually dependent phonemes that do not depend on other words—can constitute a word or sentence with parts.

Now, if it is partless: is it perceived from all the phonemes and words taken together, or from them individually? It cannot be from all of them together, because since those [phonemes] perish as soon as they are uttered, their totality is impossible.

Nor can it arise from the letters individually; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the entire word or sentence at the very moment the first letter or word is heard, which would render the utterance of the subsequent letters or words useless.

Now, if it is maintained that the determination of the sentence occurs through the cognition of the final letter accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of all the preceding letters—well then, is this cognition a memory (*smaraṇa*) or a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? It cannot be memory, because it apprehends the final letter which was not previously grasped [as a memory];
nor can it be direct perception, because its object consists of the preceding letters which no longer exist.

Now, it may be argued that a single conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) is produced by the recollection of the preceding phonemes and the perception of the final phoneme, and that through this [cognition] there is ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*). But is this a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or not? If it is a means of valid cognition, is it one of the [accepted] types such as perception and so forth, or is it a different means of valid cognition? It cannot be a different one, because that would entail the fallacy of contradicting the established number of means of valid cognition.
Nor can it be one of those types such as perception and so forth, because its status as being one of those has already been refuted during the investigation into recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Now, if it is argued that this is merely conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) and not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how then can reality (*tattva*) be established from it? For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, because the sentence would consequently be merely conceptual, its reality (*vāstavatva*) would be untenable.

Therefore, one must accept that the word or the sentence possesses the very definition [of validity] as previously stated, since it appears in recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), whose validity has already been established. Thus it should be understood.
By means of the final cognition of the phonemes of either a word or a sentence.

Because it apprehends the final phoneme which has not been grasped by the cognitions of the preceding phonemes, this [cognition] does not have the nature of memory; and because memory follows upon a prior experience while perception apprehends an object currently present, it is a perception.
By means of conceptual cognition— that [is] darkness;
therein, [it is] most intense.

In a recognition (pratyabhijñāna) that consists of a conceptual cognition (vikalpajñāna) produced by perception and memory, there is the nature of being either perception or one of the other [means of knowledge]. (Page 416)

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and others is as follows: "The meaning is conveyed by the *sphoṭa* alone— which is produced by the recollection of the preceding phonemes (*varṇa*) and the perception of the final phoneme— and not by the phonemes themselves."— Vedamapra— Śra.

Is it not the case that the formulation of definitions for letters (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*) is untenable, since they lack the capacity to convey meaning? For it is the *sphoṭa* alone that conveys meaning, and not the letters; for would those letters convey it individually or collectively? If individually, then since the cognition of an object such as "cow" (*go*) would have been produced by even a single letter, the utterance of the second and subsequent letters would be purposeless. If, on the other hand, they act collectively, that is not so, because it is impossible for them to exist simultaneously, given that they arise in succession and perish immediately after arising.

Furthermore, it is not logical to postulate a "collection" (*samudāya*) of those [phonemes] produced simultaneously in a single moment; for, from the perspective of a single person, their simultaneous production is impossible, as they arise from efforts directed toward specific places of articulation (*sthāna*) and instruments (*karaṇa*).

Nor is it observed that a collection of *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya* uttered by different persons conveys meaning, because verbal cognition is perceived as occurring only after the perception of a fixed sequence of phonemes (*varṇa-krama*). — Vākyapadīya 1.84. *Note: The text provided contains a fragment of the commentary on Vākyapadīya 1.84.*

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the word (*pada*) is to be grasped by an intellect accompanied by the synthesis of sounds (*nāda*"): since phonemes (*varṇa*) cannot arise at a single moment and are by nature mutually independent, they appear and disappear without touching or establishing a word; thus, each one is said to lack the essential nature of a word.

Furthermore, each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), though possessing the capacity to denote all things, attains a state of manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*) through its relation to other phonemes acting as its counterparts. Thus, the preceding phoneme is established in a specific distinction by the succeeding one, and the succeeding one by the preceding. In this way, many phonemes, following a sequence and delimited by the convention (*saṅketa*) for meaning, manifest their full range of denotative capacities. These—namely, the *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya*—illuminate the object characterized by a dewlap and so forth. Therefore, that single mental image (*buddhinirbhāsa*) which arises from these phonemes—delimited by the convention for meaning and having the sequence of sounds withdrawn—is the word (*pada*) that is designated as the denoter of the denoted object.
