That [word] is a single unit, the object of a single cognition, projected by a single effort, partless, without temporal sequence, and devoid of phonemes; it is mental, brought forth by the operation of the cognition of the final phoneme, and—by means of the phonemes themselves being uttered and heard by listeners with the intention of communicating it to another—is perceived through the worldly intellect permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless linguistic usage, as if it were an established reality.
— *Yogabhāṣya* 3.17.
According to the proponents of *sphoṭa*, neither a sentence nor a word consists of multiple constituent parts (*tattvavaiśāradī*, *bhāsvatī*, *yogavārttika* 3.17).
This reality of the word, in which all difference has been cast out— *Sphoṭasiddhi*, Kārikā 29,
36: First of all, the word is something additional to the phonemes, apprehended by a single uniform cognition.
"In words such as ‘cow’ (gauh), the cognition [of the word] is clearly one; it is the sphoṭa. — *Sphoṭasiddhi*, Bhartṛhari’s commentary, p. 1;
*Sphoṭanirṇaya*, p. 1.

In reality, however, one must accept that the sentence itself— called *sphoṭa*, which is partless like the embryo within a peacock’s egg, undivided, and the cause for the cognition of distinct meanings—
is what constitutes the sentence-sphoṭa; thus, as stated in the *Sphoṭaprakaraṇa*, the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa, in which the divisions of phonemes and words have vanished, is indeed superior.
— Therefore, it is established that the reality of *sphoṭa* is such that the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa, consisting of a single phoneme, is the signifier;
thus ends the section on *sphoṭa*.
Those who know [the truth] declare that *sphoṭa* is the eternal word, which is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), manifested by the phonemes, and the conveyor of meaning.

For this very reason, they explain the meaning of the word *sphoṭa* in two ways: it is called *sphoṭa* because it is "burst forth" or manifested by the phonemes (*sphuṭyate vyajyate varṇaiḥ*), thus it is manifested by the phonemes; and it is called *sphoṭa* because the meaning "bursts forth" or becomes manifest from it (*sphuṭati sphuṭībhavaty asmād arthaḥ*), thus it is the conveyor of meaning. (Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, p. 300)

Although the established position of the doctrine is that "the sentence-sphoṭa remains when one reaches the ultimate refinement"—and thus there are eight positions established as the final conclusion, namely: the letter-sphoṭa, the word-sphoṭa, the sentence-sphoṭa, the indivisible word-sphoṭa, the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa, and the three types of generic sphoṭas (jāti-sphoṭa) distinguished by letter, word, and sentence—the mention of the "sentence" [alone] would otherwise be both purposeless and redundant. Nevertheless, that [sentence-sphoṭa] is mentioned in order to demonstrate the unreality of all others besides the sentence-sphoṭa; for this very reason, he says: "at the ultimate refinement" (*atiniṣkarṣe*).
(Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa, p. 294)
The word, which is manifested by such a middle sound (*madhyamā-nāda*), consists of *sphoṭa*, has the nature of Brahman, and is eternal—
*Paramalaghumañjūṣā*, p. 28.

Since each [phoneme] individually lacks the power to convey meaning, and since there is no simultaneous existence [of them], and because it is impossible for those occurring in a fixed sequence to act together simultaneously, and because no cognition [of meaning] is observed from phonemes uttered by different speakers, nor when the sequence is reversed or when they occur simultaneously—it follows that the cognition of meaning, which cannot arise from the phonemes themselves, postulates a cause distinct from the phonemes: the sphoṭa (Sphoṭasiddhi, p.

Do these phonemes produce the cognition of the object either individually, like pegs supporting a hanging basket, or collectively, like stones supporting a cooking pot? It cannot be the first alternative, because a comprehension of the meaning does not arise from a single phoneme; or, if it did arise, there would be the consequence that the second and subsequent phonemes need not be uttered.

Since phonemes lack simultaneity, they cannot stand in a relationship of mutual assistance; therefore, even when combined, they do not produce the cognition of the object. — *Yogabhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī* 1.1.70.
If each of the phonemes were individually expressive, it would follow that the utterance of the second and subsequent phonemes would be purposeless;
however, if they are individually meaningless, then according to the theory of their individual production, they cannot possibly be produced simultaneously.

But on the view that [sounds] are manifested (*abhivyakti*), since there is no simultaneous totality due to their manifestation occurring sequentially, if those [sounds] mounted upon a single memory were the expressive agents, it would follow that there is no difference in the comprehension of meaning in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*. Therefore, the sphoṭa—distinct from those [sounds] and manifested by the sounds (*nāda*)—is the expressive agent. (Mahābhāṣyadīpikā, Vol. 1, p.
16) In that regard, first of all, the cognition of the denotable object does not arise from each individual phoneme, such as the letter *ga*.

If it is argued that [the word] arises as soon as it exists, then by the utterance of the very first phoneme, such as *g*, the meaning of "cow" (*go*) and so forth would already be expressed; consequently, the utterance of the second and subsequent phonemes would be purposeless.

The capacity for that [articulation] does not reside in each individual [phoneme]; therefore, the cognition of meaning arising from them is impossible even in the case of a collection of phonemes known in a sequence,
nor is such a cognition of meaning observed to arise from phonemes uttered by different speakers.
Even if [the letters] were simultaneous, nor even if their order were reversed, would the sphoṭa [be manifested]; *Nyāyamañjarī* p. 2; *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* p. 299.

Nor is it the case that the final phoneme, assisted by the preceding phonemes, conveys the meaning when the phonemes arise in a temporal sequence, because it is impossible for the preceding phonemes to assist the final phoneme.

For that [capacity] of theirs must be either the state of being the producer (*janakatva*) of the final phoneme, or the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) in the arising of the cognition of meaning. It cannot first be the state of being the producer, because there is no production of one phoneme from another, since that [production] is accomplished by specific places of articulation (*sthāna*), organs (*karaṇa*), and so forth; and because the production of the initial phoneme is perceived even in the absence of [the preceding] phonemes.

Nor can it be the state of being a cooperative cause in the arising of the cognition of meaning—that is, their being a favorer (*anugrāhaka*) of the final phoneme—because it is impossible for non-existent things to possess the status of a cooperative cause.

And just as the preceding phonemes do not attain the status of auxiliaries with respect to the final phoneme, so too do the cognitions produced by them and the latent impressions (saṃskāra) originating from them; for they, like the preceding phonemes, lack the capacity to assist, since there is no difference in their non-existence at that time.

Furthermore, where is this assistance from preceding phonemes prior to the arising of a [subsequent] phoneme, given that at the time of the *visarjanīya* there is no perception of another phoneme? Indeed, assistance consists in activity toward an effect, and there can be no activity of what is non-existent at that time.

Furthermore, even at its own time, the operation [of a phoneme] ceases at that very moment; therefore, it cannot be the cause for the production of a present effect. [Sphoṭasiddhi, p. 33] Since the preceding phonemes are non-existent at that time, how could there be an operation?
If assistance were possible even for non-existent phonemes,
then the cognition of the meaning would occur even when only the final phoneme is employed— this is the sphoṭa (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 4).
The cognitions produced by the preceding phonemes, as well as the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from the experiences produced by those preceding phonemes,
do not produce the cognition of the object; nor does the capacity for that [cognition], nor the cognition born therefrom.
For that unprecedented conceptual construction (kalpa), there is no result that acts as its producer or creator—Sphoṭasiddhi, Bhāṣya, p. 18;
for them, that [is] the time... Ā.
Furthermore, at the time of the final phoneme, the cognitions produced by the preceding phonemes and the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from them [do not suffice];

for mental impressions produced by a cognition are causes of memory regarding the object of that very cognition which produced them, but they are not capable of producing a new cognition regarding a different object.
Indeed, it is never observed that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of a jar produces a memory of a cloth;

nor is it logical for memories produced by those impressions to have mutual assistance, because they do not arise simultaneously, and because it is impossible for things that have not arisen simultaneously to coexist.

Furthermore, a single memory arising from the totality of all impressions is impossible, as this would entail the consequence that even impressions produced by the experience of various mutually contradictory objects could generate a single memory.

Furthermore, in the case of the word "go" (cow), the final phoneme alone does not convey the meaning independently of the other phonemes; for that would entail the uselessness of the utterance of the preceding phonemes, and it would also lead to the absurd consequence that this same final phoneme—even when situated at the end of the word "ghaṭa" (pot)—would convey the meaning of a hump and so forth.
Therefore, it is impossible for the phonemes, whether taken collectively or individually, to be the conveyors of meaning.

Furthermore, there is the cognition of meaning from words such as "cow" (*gavādi*). Therefore, since this [cognition] would otherwise be inexplicable, one must admit the existence of the *sphoṭa*, which is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*) and is the cause of the cognition of meaning; for it is that very [sphoṭa] which appears through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Indeed, while the phonemes possess distinct bodies, it is direct perception—conforming to the presence and absence of the auditory organ—that manifests the existence of the *sphoṭa* alone in its undifferentiated form.

For that [perception] does not have the phonemes as its object, because the phonemes, having mutually exclusive forms, lack the capacity to produce a direct perception that manifests an undifferentiated form.

Nor does it have a universal as its object; for among the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga, no other universal besides "phonemeness" (*varṇatva*) is possible, and "phonemeness" itself cannot logically function to convey a specific meaning characterized by a hump and so forth.
Furthermore, this cognition is not erroneous, because it is not sublated.

Nor is it logical that the *sphoṭa*—even though it is not the object of a sublated cognition—is non-existent; for if that were so, it would follow that even composite substances (*avayavidravya*) and the like would be non-existent.

Indeed, when mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of a cognition manifested by the appearance of a certain real entity, a cognition regarding that object is not [arbitrarily] imagined based on something other than that.

Indeed, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), whose nature is conditioned by the apprehension of a particular object, manifest cognition only with respect to that very object when they have acquired their awakening through a specific cause; they do not [manifest it] with respect to another object.
For an impression produced by the cognition of perceiving a cow never brings about the recollection of a horse—*Sphoṭasiddhi*, p. 44.

However, the latent impression (saṃskāra), inferred from the production of the fruit that is memory, is restricted to the object of its own cause—the experience—and is not capable of producing a cognition regarding another object; otherwise, having experienced just anything at all, everyone would know everything.
(Yoga Sūtra Tattvavaiśāradī 3.17)

If it is argued that the cognition of the object arises from the final phoneme conjoined with the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the apprehension of the preceding phonemes—that too is not correct; for we do not observe that an impression produced by the apprehension of one thing can generate the cognition of a different thing.
(Sphoṭasiddhi-bhāṣya, p. 16). [The word *ghaṭa* originates from *śra*.]
Nor can a whole arise from the ascent of a single memory,
because simultaneous memory is impossible regarding the letters perceived in succession;

and even if such simultaneity were possible, it would follow that a single cognition of "cow" (gauh) would arise even from those same letters, such as *ga* and so forth, when they appear in a reversed order.
—The *Sphoṭa* (Nyāya, p.

1). Others, however, maintain that [the cognition of meaning] arises from the seeds of all latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) based on the perception of all the phonemes, simultaneously reflecting the forms of all the phonemes, occurring immediately after the direct perception of the final phoneme, and consisting solely of recollection (*smaraṇa*). To claim that there can be no simultaneous recollection of those whose natures have been apprehended sequentially is also false. (*Sphoṭasiddhi*, p. 61).

Nor is it tenable that the phonemes—ascending upon the surface of a memory born from the aggregate of latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the experience of each individual phoneme, and thus attaining simultaneity—are the expressive agents; for there would follow the undesirable consequence that they produce the cognition of the meaning without distinction, regardless of whether they were experienced in a specific sequence, without sequence, or in a reversed sequence.
(Yogasūtra-bhāṣya-tattvavaiśāradī, p. 322)
Even if there were a difference in prior perceptions, the object would still be perceived;
for when there is a single perception, no difference whatsoever is observed among these [letters].

Indeed, prior perceptions—which possess a specific sequence, which have adopted a desired order or its opposite, and which are either sequential or non-sequential regarding the phonemes uttered by a single speaker—do not differentiate the nature of the phonemes as they recur later in a single perception that manifests all the phonemes together.
—[The *Sphoṭasiddhi*, p.

65: "In that case, then, a single memory produced by all the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), which grasps all the phonemes, would be the cause of the cognition of the meaning. That too is not [correct]; because with the disappearance of the sequence, there would follow the consequence of no difference in meaning between words such as *jarā* and *rāja*. —[The *Sphoṭasiddhibhāṣya*, p. 18]

Because simultaneity is equal [in all cases], no distinction between cognitions of objects would then appear in words such as *saroruha*, *nadī*, *dīna*, *jara*, and *rāja*—[this is what the proponent of] the sphoṭa [would claim].
(Sphoṭasiddhi, Nyāyamañjarī, p. 10)
Nor is there a perception of the preceding connection for the final phoneme alone,
because the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has passed beyond the path of the senses; it does not belong to that [final phoneme].
For words whose associations are known reveal their respective meanings,
yet one does not apprehend the final phoneme alone as being connected with the meaning prior to [the others]— [as explained in the *Sphoṭasiddhi*, p. 105].

Whether in the expression "gauraśva" or in the mere utterance [of the word], what difference is there in the *visarjanīya* such that it causes a difference in meaning, as well as the presence or absence of a cognition? — *Sphoṭasiddhi*, p.
33, concerning the *visarjanīya*.
Among these, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed well-established: when the word "cow" (*gauh*) is uttered, there arises a single cognition of a unitary form, namely, "this is one and the same word.

This [cognition] cannot have the individual phonemes alone as its object, because it is impossible for those [phonemes], being distinct, to be the objects of a non-erroneous cognition of a single form.
Nor is this [cognition] erroneous, because there is no cause for error.
—Sphoṭasiddhi, Bhāṣya, p. 1: The manifestation as distinct or indistinct is restricted to perceptual cognition;
in other means of knowledge, there is either apprehension or indeed no apprehension at all.

For the sense organs are the cause of a cognition that appears either manifest or unmanifest; for instance, in the case of perception from a distance or the discernment of subtle objects, signs, words, and so forth, produce a cognition whose nature is determined as being uniform, or rather, they do not produce it at all. In that regard, the distinction between the cognitions of the manifest and the unmanifest pertains to the object, which is determined by verbal cognition, whereas the essence of the *sphoṭa* is to be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, [the position] is faultless.

—Sphoṭasiddhi, p. 169. Nor do we understand the meaning from a word with the intention of conveying a comprehension of the object based on the phonemes as they ascend into a synthetic cognition; nor do we understand it with the intention of [conveying] the word-genus (śabdajāti). For instance, it is not observed that word-genera participate in a collective aggregate (samudāya).
For they declare that it is either the genus (*jāti*) or the individual (*vyakti*) as conjoined with the genus [that is denoted]. However, this does not intend the genus of the word itself;

for there is no comprehension of the meaning from the genus of the word, because in the case of words such as "cow" and "horse," since that [genus of the word] is indistinct, it would follow that there is no distinction between their denotata.

Nor does it intend to refer to individual word-sounds (*śabdavyakti*), because they are distinct; for if that were the case, the use of the singular number in the phrase "from the word 'cow' (*gośabdāt*)" would be untenable.
Furthermore, this [word] must be accepted as eternal. (Sphoṭasiddhi, p. 73)

If [the word] were impermanent, because that which was experienced at the time of the convention would have perished at that very moment, there could be no cognition of an object possessing a hump and so forth upon hearing the word "cow" at another time or in another place;
for it is impossible for a cognition of an object to arise from a word that has not been subjected to a convention,

or if such a possibility did exist, it would follow that even one who had come from another continent would understand the meaning of "cow" from the word "cow," and thus the making of conventions would be rendered useless.

Now, one might object: "In sentences such as 'Devadatta, bring the cow,' verbal cognitions are indeed experienced even during the intervals [between words]; therefore, in those cases too, a *baddha-sphoṭa* (manifested sphoṭa) must be postulated, and thus there would be a contradiction with your own doctrine, since that [sphoṭa] is established there as being partless and unitary. This objection is not valid, because the intervening cognitions serve as causes for the manifestation of the sphoṭa and are thus unfit to be distinct sphoṭas themselves.

For just as a section of a recitation (*anuvāka*) or a verse (*śloka*), when recited again and again, can be easily grasped through repetition—but not when recited only once and then the repetition has ceased—so too this word characterized as *sphoṭa* is manifested by the intervening cognitions, which are like true appearances and serve as means conducive to its apprehension;
for it is grasped as it flashes forth in the intellect, wherein impressions have been deposited by the preceding sounds along with the final sound.
And it has been said:
The reality of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahmatattva), which is without beginning or end and is imperishable— Vākyapadīya 1.1.
And there would be purposefulness [in the effort], for each one of them individually manifests the complete nature of the *sphoṭa*.
Nor is the other [subsequent] sounds useless, because there is a difference in their manifestation.

For this reason: the preceding sounds produce a manifestation that, for a cognizer whose mind has not yet acquired a specific mental impression (*bhāvanā*), grasps the form of the word indistinctly; this manifestation sows the seeds of the mental impressions conducive to the arising of the determination of the subsequent distinct [sounds]. But the final sound, assisted by all the seeds of the mental impressions produced by the indistinct determinations based on the preceding sounds, brings forth an extremely clear cognition, as if it were the reflection of the *sphoṭa* firmly established therein.

Just as for a gem-examiner who is examining a gem, the true nature of the gem (*ratnatattva*) shines forth in the final moment of consciousness—within a cognition that has been infused with a specific refinement through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by cognitions of an indescribable form arising from the attainment of the first moment (Sphoṭasiddhi, p.
129; Sphoṭanirṇaya, p. 20).
*Sphoṭasiddhi*, Bhartṛhari’s *Vākyapadīya-bhāṣya*, p.
21: Even the first manifesting sound manifests the *sphoṭa* indistinctly; through the sequence of successive manifestations, it becomes distinct, more distinct, and most distinct.

Just as a Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) is not grasped when read only once, but its clear apprehension comes through practice; or as the true nature of a jewel does not shine clearly upon the first perception, but is manifested correctly in the final moment of consciousness.
—*Sarvadā*, p.
303—“The foremost of speakers”—Amara states: “The collection of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas].”
"Vedaviśeṣa" refers to the *Śabdakalpadruma*, as stated by Subhūti; it may be called "Śra" by one [manuscript] and "Ba" by another. (Śra॰, Ba॰)

Just as an *anuvāka* or a verse reaches a state of being mastered through repetition, yet the text itself is not analyzed anew with each repetition; [the commentary explains: "Being mastered" means becoming the object of a single unitary cognition (*ekabuddhiviṣayatva*). In this way, the sounds (*dhvani*), produced by specific efforts and having letters, words, and sentences as their objects, repeatedly manifest the *sphoṭas* known as letters, words, and sentences, and superimpose them upon the cognitions. However, it does not follow from this that there is an infinity of *sphoṭas*, just as there is no infinity of verses and the like despite their repeated recitation.
He says that very thing: "But it is not the case that that text, consisting of a collection of verses, is defined through a return [to the beginning] by way of division"—this is the meaning.

In that regard, that which is properly established in the intellect by the final resonance (*dhvani*), and that which, not being grasped as a specific detail, has not yet entered the intellect, remains indeed unperceived.
For by that [ultimate reality], no linguistic convention whatsoever is established— Vākyapadīya, Puṇyarāja’s Commentary; Vākyapadīya, Vṛtti.

"Anuvāka" is a Vedic term; "soḍhatva" (endurance) means the state of being capable of being endured, of being approachable by the intellect, and of being accepted, such that it may be recited at one's own will.

The word "āvṛtti" is used in the singular to denote the class [of repetitions]; even a single repetition is useful for imparting successive distinctions, otherwise endurance would be achieved through only a single repetition. For just as an *anuvāka* or a *śloka* can be easily mastered through repeated recitation.

Furthermore, upon each individual recurrence, no such cognition arises there as "this has been grasped, this has not," yet when there is a multiple recurrence, the manifestation of the verse and so forth is clearly experienced; in exactly the same way, this very essence of the word (*śabdātman*), which consists of the *sphoṭa* manifested again and again, is determined [as a whole], and upon each individual manifestation, no such cognition arises as "this has been grasped, this has not";
or rather, upon multiple manifestations, the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* is clearly experienced.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
650: An *anuvāka* is Vedic, whereas a *śloka* is worldly; "endurance" (*soḍhatva*) means "conquest" (*jitatva*), that is to say, "subjugation" (*vaśatām*). —*Sphoṭasiddhi-ṭīkā*, p.
132: [The reading] *sphoṭatva*. —Ā., Ba., Śra.
Is it not so?
[Vākya-paṃ., Pratyāvṛtti-ni., Vākya-paṃ. Brahm., Sphoṭasiddhi;
the reading in the present text is from Syādvādaratnākara].
The return [of the cognition] is defined as follows: *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 359:

"When the word has been manifested by sounds that are themselves inexpressible yet conducive to apprehension, its own form (*svarūpa*) is determined. *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 576B. The return is explained: "By means of cognitions that are inexpressible and suitable for apprehension, the intrinsic nature of the word, once revealed by the sounds, is ascertained."

Just as a verse, when recited once, is not grasped, yet becomes capable of being grasped upon a subsequent recitation, and is finally mastered through repeated recitation; so too, a sentence, though not manifested by the preceding sounds, is not yet grasped. Nevertheless, through the mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) deposited by the manifestation of each preceding word-sound—which serve as causal conditions for the apprehension of the sentence—the sentence is grasped at the time of hearing the final phoneme. Therefore, it is indeed logical that the manifestation of the sentence, which is itself devoid of sequence, occurs through the phonemes that possess a sequence.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, p. 359)

Conforming to the apprehension of the manifested form (*vyaktarūpa*), these cognitions—which possess an indefinable character because that [form] which has ascended into the intellect cannot be described as "this is it"—are numerous and serve as means; they arise when the word is being revealed by sounds and become the causes for the grasping of the word's own nature (*śabdasvarūpa*).
(Vākyapadīya-vṛtti; Dhvanyāloka-ṭīkā 1).

The reading of the present context—*Sphoṭasiddhi*, *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, *Syādvādaratnākara*, *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*: "In the intellect, whose seed has been sown by the sound and which has reached maturity through repeated practice, the word manifests together with the final phonation."

Thus, by means of non-deficient sounds (*nādaiḥ*) which illuminate the essence of the word (*śabdātmānam*), seeds of the cultivation of latent impressions (*saṃskārabhāvanābījāni*) conducive to the discernment of the manifest [word] are deposited with progressive excellence. Thereafter, the final particular sound (*antyo dhvaniviśeṣaḥ*), through its assistance, causes the form of the word’s own nature (*śabdasvarūpākāra*) to be established in the intellect (*buddhau*), whose capacity has reached full maturity through the acquisition of the functioning of the seeds of the cultivation of latent impressions for discernment. — *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti*

Vākyapadīya, Puṇyarāja’s Commentary, Nādairāhita—Vākyapadīya, Sphoṭasiddhi, Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā, Syādvādaratnākara, Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha; original reading—Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 722, Pañjikā, p. 636.

"Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛ. 456: 'That whose maturation has been turned back'—maturation (*paripāka*) is the specific acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) with respect to the production of an effect (*kāryotpādana*)—[as stated in] the Vākyapadīya-bṛhat-ṭīkā].

That [seed of impression] whose maturation has been turned back (*āvṛtta*) or practiced (*abhyasta*) is so described. By the first sound, some seed of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is deposited; by that, a certain maturation—a specific capacity for producing an effect—is produced; and likewise by the second."

Although the ripenings (paripāka) are distinct, nevertheless the expression "repeated" (āvṛtta) is used by relying on their common genus (*jāti*), just as one says, "the Brahmins have eaten eight times.
Another explanation of the term *āvṛtta* is: "that in which the ripening of the impurities (*kaṣāya*) occurs through repetition (*āvṛtti*) or by means of repetition.
In some places, however, the reading is *āvṛttī*.

The meaning is that the word is apprehended within the internal organ (antahkarana) along with the final sound; when the final sound is apprehended, then the word "cow" (gauh) is also apprehended—*Sphoṭasiddhi-ṭīkā*, p.
132. (*Āvṛttapari-vākya-paṅkti*: *Vākyapadīya*, *Sphoṭasiddhi*, *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 722).
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 435; Sphoṭatattva, p. 9;
Āvṛttiparīkṣā, Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, p. 636.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 456;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, folio 650;
*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, folio 576B.
The word is ascertained— Vākyapadīya, Sphoṭasiddhi, Pramāṇavārttika with its own commentary (Svavṛtti-ṭīkā).
*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā-syādvāda-ratnākara-sarvadurgabhañjana* (The Jewel-Mine of Syādvāda, which Shatters All Difficulties: A Commentary on the *Tattvasaṃgraha*)
The reading in the present context: *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 722; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*; *Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*.

In the *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, following the refutation of the *sphoṭa* theory, there is the demonstration that phonemes alone are the conveyors of meaning; to this, the following response is given.

As for what was stated—that "the *sphoṭa* alone [is the cause]," and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion; for since the comprehension of meaning is logically established as arising from the final phoneme as qualified by the destruction of the preceding phonemes, it is untenable for the *sphoṭa* to be the conveyor of meaning.

Nor is it the case that the causal efficacy of a non-existence (*abhāva*) has not been observed; for we see that the absence of contact between the stalk and the fruit produces the action of falling due to unimpeded gravity. Likewise, an action qualified by the prior absence of conjunction is perceived as producing a subsequent conjunction. Furthermore, the conjunction of fire with an atom is seen to produce redness in that atom when assisted by the destruction of its previous color. Or else, the final phoneme—qualified by the absence of the cognition of the preceding phonemes, or dependent upon the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by those cognitions—is what generates the comprehension of the meaning.

Now, one might ask: "How can a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produce knowledge regarding a different object? This too is not a valid objection; for it is precisely in this manner that the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is observed to occur.

Furthermore, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of the preceding phonemes assists the final phoneme through a serial process. To explain: first there is the cognition of the initial phoneme, and by that, a mental impression is produced; then follows the cognition of the second phoneme, and by that—conjoined with the impression deposited by the cognition of the preceding phoneme—a distinct mental impression is produced. This should be applied similarly to the third and subsequent phonemes, until the final impression is assisted by the final phoneme which generates the comprehension of the meaning.

Alternatively, due to a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that serves as the cause for the apprehension of word-meanings, the preceding cognitions and their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), remaining undestroyed, produce the impression of the final phoneme;
or rather, the final phoneme, depending upon the memory produced by such impressions, is the cause for the comprehension of the word-meaning.
This same principle should be understood to apply to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning as well.
Furthermore, the demonstration that one phoneme does not produce another phoneme is merely a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Thus, since the comprehension of meaning is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to arise from the final phoneme in dependence upon the aforementioned auxiliary causes, the postulation of *sphoṭa* is entirely useless. Since the comprehension of meaning is possible through the manner already described even in the absence of *sphoṭa*, the argument of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) is discarded.
Indeed, when an effect arises from a visible cause, it is not logically sound to postulate an unseen intermediate entity, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Page 745, line 11. For comparison: Others, however, maintain that even past phonemes and their cognitions possess the status of auxiliary causes for the final phoneme, because this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
To explain: the causality of a present [factor] is indeed known through positive and negative concomitance; so too is that of a past [factor].

Or rather, the destructions of the preceding phonemes and the destructions of their cognitions, being proximate, act as auxiliaries for the final phoneme—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 595; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

In this regard, the preceding phonemes, though past, will provide assistance, while the final phoneme is present; thus, this collection of phonemes—just like an imagined collection of moments of action—is what conveys the meaning.
However, the comprehension of the meaning arises from the final phoneme as it is being perceived, as qualified by the destruction of the preceding phonemes. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 376)

Nor is it contradictory for a non-existence to possess the status of a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*). Just as the absence of the contact between the stalk and the fruit is a cooperative cause in the production of the action of falling by gravity when it is unobstructed, and just as it is observed that an action, while producing a subsequent conjunction, is characterized by the absence of the prior conjunction, and the conjunction of fire with an atom, being qualified by the destruction of the previous color residing in that atom, produces redness—[as stated in] *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 433—the status of being a cooperative cause [is established].
Whether it be the black color residing in atoms,
or the final phoneme being perceived as qualified by the absence of the cognition of the preceding phonemes, it attains the nature of a word and generates the comprehension of the word-meaning—
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 433.
"The final phoneme, accompanied by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the conveyor [of meaning]"
— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5.20.

1.5 Indeed, while the phonemes constituting a sentence are being uttered, there is first of all the auditory perception of each individual phoneme; having heard one or more phonemes, one synthesizes them into the form of a word, and having performed this synthesis, one determines the word.

Through the determination of words by means of memory, one understands the word-meanings; through the synthesis of the collection of words, one determines the sentence; and having grasped the related word-meanings, one understands the sentence-meaning—Nyāyabhāṣya 3.2.12.
The cognition of the meaning arises from the cognition of the final phoneme, depending upon the cognition that synthesizes the preceding phonemes—
Nyāyavārttika, p. 310–16.
Because the final phoneme, assisted by the preceding phonemes and aided by its own perception, brings about the comprehension of the meaning— *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 595—
or else, because the final phoneme, dependent on either the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes or the recollection (*smaraṇa*) thereof, is the conveyor of meaning.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 270;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
453; or [it is] dependent upon the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of the preceding letter—*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 433.

Because the cognition of the meaning is established by the perception of the final phoneme itself, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each preceding phoneme, which serves as its manifestor— thus [ends] the section on the word in the *Muktāvalī*.

The point is this: according to the rule that a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) directed toward a particular object produces a memory only of that very object, an impression whose object is sound would produce only the memory of sound, and not the cognition of meaning.
For comparison: "Even though it is established that the function of a mental impression is to cause memory..."
Its capacity for other effects is not denied;
but how can there be capacity for another effect in a cause? To this he says: "Even though...
For it is possible for even a single thing to have capacity in multiple respects, as in the case of an action [which has capacity] for both conjunction and disjunction.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Nyāyaratna, p. 536:

Since, in accordance with the cognition of each object, impressions (*saṃskāra*) having phonemes as their objects are deposited by individual experiences, they are deposited precisely as possessing powers distinct from the impressions that cause memory; for it is only such [impressions] that are apprehended through their effect. —Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī, p. 271: And the impression deposited by cognition... [Ātmatattvaviveka].

Comparison—And thus, when one phoneme is cognized, an impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced by it; then, when the second phoneme is cognized, another impression is produced by that [cognition] as well, with the impression of the preceding phoneme acting as its auxiliary. In this sequence, there occurs the cognition of the final phoneme. From that, when the recollection of all the remaining phonemes is manifested by the prior impressions, the comprehension of the meaning arises from the final phoneme. (PRAŚASTAPĀDABHĀṢYAVYĀKHYĀ, p. 595; PRAMEYAKAMALAMĀRTAṆḌA, p. 453)
In the *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, page 433, it is stated:
"All words, once they have ascended into memory, will cause the meaning of the sentence to be understood;

and in that regard, this conceptualization [is as follows]: first, through the sequence of phonemes, there arises the cognition of the first word, and simultaneously, the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) occur."
For the simultaneity of two cognitions is prohibited in the treatise, but not that of a cognition and its latent impression (saṃskāra).

From that [first word], there arises the cognition of the word-meaning, and from that, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Again, through the sequence of phonemes, there is the cognition of the second word, followed by the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); and by means of that [recollection] together with the previous impression, a more intense impression is produced. Again, through the sequence of the preceding phonemes, there is the cognition of the third word, the recollection of the convention, and—dependent on the previous impressions—a still more intense impression. Again, through the sequence of the preceding phonemes, there is the cognition of the third word, the recollection of the convention, and—dependent on the previous impressions—a still more intense impression. In this manner, when a robust impression produced by the cognitions of the words and a similar impression produced by the cognitions of the word-meanings are established, then immediately after the cognition of the final word-meaning, there occurs a recollection of all the words due to the impression of the words, and a recollection of the word-meanings due to the impression of the word-meanings; thus, by the sequence of impressions, two recollections arise in succession.

In that regard, a collection of words ascended upon one recollection (*smṛti*) is the sentence (*vākya*), and a collection of word-meanings ascended upon the other is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Alternatively, setting aside the conceptualization of recollection, immediately after the cognition of the final word-meaning, there will arise a mental after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is the entirety of the words and word-meanings—standing in the place of the cognition of "a hundred" and so forth.
The words ascended upon that [after-cognition] are the sentence, and the word-meaning ascended upon that is the sentence-meaning.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, pp. 394–95 — [The cognition] by means of the phoneme... by that [cognition], the cognition of the preceding phoneme; by that, the specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced.
[The process continues] up to the final mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

For comparison: others, however, hold that the impressions produced by the experience of preceding phonemes, as regulated by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which brings about the enjoyment of the word and its meaning, initiate a single recollection regarding those preceding phonemes; and with that as its auxiliary cause, the final phoneme constitutes the word.
Alternatively, [they hold that] the impressions initiate a single, diverse [collective] impression, and from that, a single recollection of the preceding phonemes arises.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 595; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 433.
Comparison: Alternatively, that final cognition of all the phonemes which occurs after they have been previously known in sequence through perception is the cause of the cognition of the meaning;
this [cognition] arises even when the final phoneme is cognized, brought about by the impressions (saṃskāra) of the preceding [phonemes].

Others maintain that there is simultaneity in the recollection of all [objects]; for all proponents of [mental] cognition, a mental cognition that synthesizes all [objects] is accepted regarding all such matters, even though the cognitions occur in succession.
If that were not admitted, then indeed the perception of the aggregate [of sounds] in the form of "hundred" and so forth would never arise among those things perceived sequentially; therefore,
it must occur through the ear and the mind in respect to the phonemes, even though they appear in succession.
But subsequently, there occurs a simultaneous recollection [of the phonemes] preceded by prior cognitions;
the phonemes mounted upon that [recollection] are not far from the comprehension of the meaning. Therefore, the cognition of the meaning from the word is so designated by worldly people.
—*Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, *Sphoṭavāda*, verses 109, 112–116;
*Tattvasaṅgraha*, verses 2720–25:
"Alternatively, the final phoneme, depending upon the recollection produced by such formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), is the cause for the comprehension of the word-meaning."

"Therefore, the impressions of memory produced regarding the preceding phonemes, together with the final phoneme being perceived, brings about the comprehension of the meaning"—*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 433; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
It should be observed—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 376, note 6 on p.

750—that even when the phonemes are perceived sequentially, there arises a mental synthetic cognition (*saṅkalanājñāna*) in the form of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that takes all the phonemes as its object; this will serve as the means for the communication of meaning.

Even though there is a simultaneous recollection of all the phonemes, just as ants ascend to the cognition of a "line" only while following a specific order, so too will the phonemes ascend to the cognition of a "word" only while following a specific order;
thus, although the phonemes themselves remain unchanged, the apprehension of distinct words produced by a specific sequence is not contradicted.

In the linguistic usage of elders, these phonemes, being assisted by their sequential order and having acquired specific relationships with meanings, appear in exactly the same form within the intellect—which reflects upon them as a whole immediately after the apprehension of each individual phoneme—even during one's own subsequent usage; thus, they will cause that respective meaning to be understood without error. This is the simpler hypothesis for those who maintain that the word is composed of phonemes (*varṇavādinaḥ*). — *Brahmasūtra-Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* 1.3.28.

For those [perceptions], having been previously experienced and being released from the sequence of their individual experiences, ascend into a single cognition and are thus able to produce the cognition of the object—
*Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā*, p. 470.
Furthermore, the demonstration that one phoneme does not arise from another phoneme is merely a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Indeed, it is precisely by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that it is ascertained that the comprehension of meaning arises from the final phoneme when it is dependent upon the aforementioned auxiliary causes; this [ascertainment] refutes the postulation of *sphoṭa*. Since the comprehension of meaning is possible through the manner already described even in the absence of *sphoṭa*, the "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) [which was cited as a reason for its existence] is discarded. For when an effect arises from a visible cause, the postulation of an unseen intermediary is not logically consistent, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
– *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 433; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 454.
[The reading] "buddhiḥ saṃgatā" is found in manuscript Ba; "yuktiḥ saṃgatā" is found in manuscript Ā.

Furthermore, if the perceived phonemes (*varṇa*), whether taken individually or collectively, are incapable of generating the comprehension of meaning, then they would likewise be incapable of manifesting the *sphoṭa*.
To explain: they do not manifest the *sphoṭa* collectively, because—as already stated—their simultaneity is impossible;

nor do they manifest it individually, because that would entail the uselessness of pronouncing the subsequent phonemes, since the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* would have been accomplished by the first phoneme alone.

Nor should it be asserted that its utterance is for the purpose of excluding the cognition of another word-meaning; for even when that [other word] is uttered, the possibility of that [other] cognition necessarily arises.

For just as the meaning of the word "gauḥ" is cognized from the utterance of the phoneme *ga*, so too the meaning of the word "auśanasaḥ" is cognized from the utterance of the phoneme *au*; and thus, from the word "gauḥ" alone, both meanings—*gauḥ* and *auśanasaḥ*—would be cognized.

Or there may be a doubt: "Is the utterance of multiple phonemes such as 'g' and so forth for the sake of manifesting the *sphoṭa* of a single word by means of excluding the *sphoṭas* of other words, or is it for the sake of manifesting the *sphoṭa* of multiple words?

Nor should it be argued that, because the preceding phonemes produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *sphoṭa*, the final phoneme is its manifester, and thus the utterance of the other phonemes is not useless; for in this case, a refinement distinct from manifestation itself is simply untenable.
Indeed, no momentum (*saṃskāra*) called "velocity" is produced therein by those [sounds], because such a thing is possible only in the case of corporeal substances;
nor is it of the nature of a latent impression (*vāsanā*), because the *sphoṭa* is insentient, or else, if its sentience were admitted, there would be a contradiction with one's own school's tenets.
Nor is it of the nature of *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity), because that too resides only in corporeal substances, whereas the *sphoṭa* is admitted to be incorporeal (*amūrta*).
Thus, [as stated in] Ātreya and Bhaṭṭoji:
"The partless *sphoṭa* is manifested by the cognitions of the phonemes."
Even this [position] is not liberated by such an inquiry;
for there too, a word-sphoṭa is not perceived in each individual phoneme, nor is it manifested part by part, and in the absence of that, no cognition [of it] arises here.
If they are individually incapable, they are also incapable in combination— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, Sphoṭavāda, verses 91–93:
"It is not manifested by all [the phonemes] together, because a composite whole (*samudāya*) is not admitted."

Not by the individual [letters] separately, because if the manifestation were achieved by one alone, it would follow that the utterance of the remaining [letters] is useless—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p.

595. Is the word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*), which is eternal, partless, all-pervading, and formless, a cause for the comprehension of meaning only when unmanifested, or when manifested? In the first case, the utterance of phonemes (*varṇa*) would be purposeless.
But in the second alternative, is the word-sphoṭa manifested by each individual phoneme or by the collection of phonemes? — Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā p. 96;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika p. 426; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 454.
For, according to the *Sanmati-ṭīkā* (p.
433), even from the utterance of one phoneme following another, there would be the unwanted consequence of the cognition of a different object.

For just as the meaning of the word *gauh* (cow) is understood from the utterance of the sound *ga*, so too the meaning of the word *auśanasaḥ* would be understood from the utterance of the sound *au*; since the *sphoṭa* of the word *auśanasaḥ* would be manifested by the first *au* just as the *sphoṭa* of the word *gauh* is manifested by the initial *ga*,
it would follow that the meaning of the sentence *gauḥ auśanasaḥ* (the cow of Auśanasa) would be understood from the word *gauh* alone.
Or there might be doubt—as [stated] in the Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 96, and the Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
454: "Just as a cow... (yathā gauḥ).
Then it is understood from Śrā [that] this reading is not present in Ā.
Comparison: Because no nature of impression (*saṃskāra*) distinct from manifestation can be established;
for instance, first of all, no impression called "velocity" (*vega*) is produced therein by them, since that exists only in corporeal things;
nor is it of the nature of a latent disposition (*vāsanā*), because [the soul] is insentient. — *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 433.
In the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 454, regarding the *sphoṭa* and the phoneme (*varṇa*).

Furthermore, since the *sphoṭa* is insentient, is this impression (*saṃskāra*) the *sphoṭa* itself, or a property (*dharma*) of it? Regarding this, the first alternative is untenable, because it would entail that the *sphoṭa* is produced by the phonemes (*varṇa*).
The second alternative is also impossible, because the conceptual alternatives of being either distinct or non-distinct [from the *sphoṭa*] are logically inadmissible.

For if it were non-different from the *sphoṭa*, then upon its production, the *sphoṭa* itself would be produced; and since that would entail its impermanence, there would be a contradiction of one's own tenets.

If, however, it were different, the relationship [between them] would be untenable because [the manifestation] provides no assistance [to the *sphoṭa*]. Or, if it were to assist it, then for that assistance as well, the dilemma of whether it is different or non-different from the *sphoṭa* would arise; and in that case too, the previously mentioned fault leading to an infinite regress would result.

Moreover, even if a distinct property exists, it is not possible for the *sphoṭa*—without abandoning its unmanifested nature—to be the cause of the comprehension of meaning as it was before, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Alternatively, if it were to abandon that nature, the consequence of its impermanence would follow.
Furthermore, is this impression (*saṃskāra*) the very nature of the *sphoṭa* or a property of it? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 455;
Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 434).
Or rather, the dharma [is the cause] of the non-duality of the *sphoṭa* according to the Śābdikas, and of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) according to the Bhaṭṭas.

Comparison: Furthermore, would that manifestation (*abhivyakti*) be produced by the sounds (*dhvani*) as something non-different from the *sphoṭa*, or as something different? — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
662: "This is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *sphoṭa*."
If the latent impression (saṃskāra) is a benefactor of the sphoṭa, then the benefit produced by that latent impression [must also be considered].
From the *sphoṭa*—
the non-termination of defects—
[in the *Śruti-bhāṣya*,] because of the abandonment of its unmanifest nature.

Furthermore, regarding the embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the *sphoṭa* produced by the phonemes (*varṇa*), would it be performed partially or in its entirety? If it were performed partially, then the previously mentioned defects would follow for both the positions that those parts are either different from or non-different from the whole. However, if the embellishment were performed in its entirety, then there would be comprehension of the meaning for everyone, everywhere, and at all times.

Furthermore, as for the comparison: is the initial sound-phoneme, which constitutes the nature of the word, the manifestor of the whole [word] or of a single part? If it were the manifestor of the whole, other sounds would be rendered useless;
if it were the manifestor of a single part, its partlessness would be lost.
— *Rājavārttika* 5.1.69.
24 *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 455;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 434.

Furthermore, regarding the manifestation (*sphoṭa*), is the impression (*saṃskāra*) of the manifestation a cognition having the manifestation as its object, or is it the removal of an obscuration? If it is the removal of an obscuration, then when the obscuration is removed once in one place, it would be perceived at all times by everyone situated in all locations; for, due to its eternity and omnipresence, this [manifestation], being free from obscuration, has the nature of being perceivable everywhere and at all times.
Alternatively, if its nature were unperceivable, it would never be perceived by anyone, anywhere, at any time.

Now, if the removal of the obscuration is effected only partially, then, because it would possess parts due to being both obscured and unobscured, it would follow that it is a product and impermanent. Alternatively, if it is accepted that because it is indivisible, it is unobscured everywhere simply by being unobscured in one place, then the consequence remains that it would be perceived by those situated in all locations simultaneously. And just as it is unobscured everywhere because it is partless and thus unobscured in one place, so too, being obscured in one place, it would be obscured everywhere and thus not perceived even slightly.

Now, [it might be argued that] the production of a cognition whose object is the *sphoṭa* is the impression (*saṃskāra*) [of the letters]; this too is untenable, because—just as the letters lack the capacity to produce the comprehension of meaning—they likewise lack the capacity to produce the comprehension of the *sphoṭa*, the logic being the same.
Furthermore, does the impression of the *sphoṭa* consist in the production of a cognition whose object is the *sphoṭa*, or in the removal of an obscuration? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.
455; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā p. 434)
The sphoṭa never exists [as a real entity], according to Ātreya;
certainly not, according to Śabarasvāmin; and likewise not, according to Bādari.

Now, it may be argued that there is no fault [in our position] because the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of the word-sphoṭa and so forth occurs for the self (*ātman*), which has been infused with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) by the cognitions of hearing the preceding phonemes, immediately after the cognition of hearing the final phoneme. This too is unsatisfactory; for if the comprehension of the meaning of a word were established in this very way, the postulation of a *sphoṭa* would be useless.
Furthermore, it is impossible for this [sphoṭa], as a distinct reality separate from the conscious self (*cidātman*), to possess the capacity to illuminate the meaning.

Let that very conscious self (cidātmā), characterized by specific capacities, be the *sphoṭa*; for it is called *sphoṭa* because "in this [self], the meaning bursts forth" (*sphuṭati*) or becomes manifest. Thus, the conscious self characterized by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*), energy-obstructing karma (*vīryāntarāya*), and the rest, with respect to word-meanings, is the *pada-sphoṭa*; whereas the conscious self characterized by the subsidence-cum-destruction of the knowledge-obscuring karma, energy-obstructing karma, and the rest, with respect to sentence-meanings, is the *vākya-sphoṭa*. This is because there is no contradiction in applying such designations to the self when it is transformed into the state of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) from the perspective of its actual nature (*bhāvataḥ*). [The rest of the passage concerns] other phonemes... [fragmentary].
In the same way, since the comprehension of word-meanings is established [otherwise], the postulation of a *sphoṭa* is useless;
for apart from the conscious self (*cidātman*), it is impossible for a separate reality called *sphoṭa* to possess the capacity to illuminate meaning.
Therefore, let that very conscious self, possessing specific powers, be the *sphoṭa*.
That in which meaning "bursts forth" (sphoṭati) or becomes manifest is the *sphoṭa*, namely the conscious self (*cidātmā*).

Specifically, the *pada-sphoṭa* is the conscious self characterized by the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of the knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and energy-obstructing (*vīryāntarāya*) karmas pertaining to the knowledge of word-meanings; the *vākya-sphoṭa* is the conscious self characterized by the destruction-cum-subsidence of the knowledge-obscuring and energy-obstructing karmas pertaining to the knowledge of sentence-meanings.

Thus, the *sphoṭa* is well-known as the conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) pertaining to chapters, sections, books, scriptures, and so forth—whether included within the limbs [of the teaching] or external to them—because there is no contradiction in applying such designations to the self when it is transformed into the knowledge of scriptural content (*bhāva-śruta-jñāna*).
—Yuktyanu॰ ṭī॰ pṛ॰ 97;
Tattvārthaślo॰ pṛ॰ 427;
Prameyaka॰ pṛ॰ 456.
Comparison: For the proponent of *sphoṭa*, however, there would be the abandonment of what is perceived and the postulation of what is unperceived;

namely, that these phonemes, being apprehended in succession, manifest the *sphoṭa*, and that *sphoṭa* in turn manifests the meaning—this would be a more cumbersome postulation. (*Brahmasūtra-śāṅkara-bhāṣya* 1.3.28)
3.28 It bursts open. (Śra)

The term *sphoṭa* is so called because "the meaning bursts forth (*sphuṭati*) and is manifested (*prakāśate*) in this"; thus, the claim that the winds (*vāyavaḥ*) manifest the *sphoṭa* in the form of word-*sphoṭa*, sentence-*sphoṭa*, and so on, is also untenable. This is because, just like the manifestation of sound (*śabda*), the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* cannot logically result from them.

If these [air-currents] were the manifestors of those [phonemes], the postulation of phonemes would be futile; for they would be of no use either in the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* or in the comprehension of the meaning.
Furthermore, if one were to postulate that air-currents are the manifestors, it would follow as a consequence that the phonemes themselves are useless.
(Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 434)
And the sounds do not manifest the *sphoṭa*, because it is not an object of visual perception, just like odor—
*Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* 5.1.67, p. 446.
This passage does not exist within the Ārya-varṇas.

By this, [the objection] beginning with "in that cognition in which the seed has been deposited by this sound" and so forth is refuted; furthermore, it has already been demonstrated on page 749, line 7, how the comprehension of meaning occurs even without [the word] being eternal. (Compare:

"The apprehension of a sentence by means of the final cognition endowed with the impressions of all the phonemes" is also false, because nothing that is untouched by the form of the phonemes is ever perceived.)

Furthermore, since phonemes cannot be apprehended out of their sequence, how could there be such a thing as a "non-sequential" entity graspable by a single cognition? Nor do we perceive any other partless essence of sound subsequent to the apprehension of the final phoneme—
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.274.

Furthermore, only if the existence of the *sphoṭa* were established prior to the production of the phonemes or the air-currents would it be logical for the phonemes or the air-currents to function as its manifestors; however, its existence is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And even if the existence of the *sphoṭa* were established prior to the utterance of the phonemes, one might then postulate that the phonemes or the air-currents are its manifestors.
And its existence is not known from any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) [Sanmati-ṭīkā p. 434; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p.

As for what was stated—that "it appears as that very thing through perception," and so forth—that too is mere faith; for in words such as "ghaṭa" (pot), apart from the phonemes characterized by their mutual exclusion and temporal proximity, no entity in the form of a *sphoṭa* that reveals the meaning is perceived within the range of direct experience (*adhyakṣa*).

Nor is it logical to establish the meaning based merely on a non-differentiated appearance; otherwise, there would be an establishment of unity in a dense cluster of trees seen from a distance due to the appearance of non-difference.

Now, because this [sphoṭa] is subject to sublation, it cannot be established as a single entity; that is the same in other cases as well, since even in the manifestation of the sphoṭa, various sublaters have been demonstrated (pṛ.

748, l. 1). For in words such as "ghaṭa" and so on, a single sphoṭa-nature—distinct from the mutually excluded multiple phonemes and capable of conveying the meaning—is not perceived as an object of sensory apprehension (*adhyakṣapratipatti*) (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 435).
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 457.

For comparison: "The perception of density in a sparse object situated at a distance is sublated by a subsequent, powerful cognition of its sparse nature; therefore, let the density established there by virtue of that perception be unreal. But as for the appearance of the constituent parts such as color and so forth, we do not perceive any sublation whatsoever occurring at a later time."

As for the other point that was stated—namely, "just as an *anuvāka* or a *śloka*, etc."—that too is mere words; for there is a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

For in the case of a text such as an *anuvāka*, there is perception through direct sensory experience (*pratyakṣa*), and when it is recited again and again, its ascertainment is experienced through repetition with ease; therefore, such a postulation is appropriate in that case. However, the *sphoṭa* is not perceived even in a dream; how, then, can the postulation that it is manifested by the intervening cognitions be considered superior?
Page 749, line 5. For comparison: "Since the *anuvāka* and the *śloka* must be either with parts (*sāvayava*) or without parts (*niravayava*). In the first case, there is a discrepancy;

for since the *anuvāka* and so forth possess parts, a clear and indistinct manifestation is appropriate, whereas in the case of the *sphoṭa*, because it is without parts, those two [manifestations] are not possible."

Furthermore, this position entails the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), as there is an inequality: for even the *śloka* and *anuvāka*, which are accepted as being of the nature of the *sphoṭa*, are accepted in your own treatise as being partless (*niravayava*).

However, in the second alternative, just like the sentence-sphoṭa in the example "Devadatta, bring the cow," these two [the *śloka* and *anuvāka*] would also appear more clearly even in the first occurrence within the cognition of the final sound, due to the specific impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the manifestations generated by each preceding sound. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 660)

As for the second example cited—that just as a *śloka* or an *anuvāka*, though initially grasped with an incomplete arrangement, becomes more clearly defined through the practice of other arrangements, so too the *sphoṭa*, though manifested by the first phoneme, will attain an even more intense manifestation through subsequent phonemes—that too is not a comparable example, because it is impossible for a *śloka* or an *anuvāka* to be non-eternal (*anaśvara*).

Some parts, whether consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) or words (*pada*), do not manifest in the first cognition; rather, they become manifest in that cognition which has acquired excellence through repeated practice. However, since the *sphoṭa* is partless like a single phoneme, what excellence could there be for the cognition regarding it? Therefore, this example as well is not appropriate.
(Nyāyamañjarī, p. 309;
not found in Ā.)

Likewise, the conceptualization of manifestation in the form of "more clear," "clearest," and so forth, occurs through the imagination of that very self-nature; this is what is perceived. (tathāvatkalpa—ā॰, tadātmanatkalpa—śra॰; pratīto'ta ba॰, śra॰)

Furthermore, if it is asserted that the word-sphoṭa is manifested by the phonemes or by the cognitions thereof, then one must also assert a lamp-sphoṭa manifested by a lamp or by the cognition thereof, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Moreover, because this would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition, the word-sphoṭa should not be accepted for that very same reason if it is not accepted in the other case.
Furthermore, there exists a subverting inference: the phonemes do not manifest the sphoṭa, because they are manifestors [of something else].

Alternatively, the cognition of meaning arises from letters, words, and sentences because it occurs only when they are present, just as the cognition of fire arises from smoke and the like; [therefore] neither the *sphoṭa*,
nor the letters, nor even the sounds (*dhvani*) constitute the word or the sentence.

For proofs such as "they manifest by way of being manifestors, like the light of a lamp and so forth" or "because they exist, like a jar and so forth," are indeed employed according to one's preference regarding an object imagined apart from worldly convention.

The sphoṭa is not the designator of the meaning because it is distinct from the phonemes, just like a jar or other such objects; nor is there a contradiction with what is perceived, because the locus [of the property] is unestablished— *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Sphoṭavāda, verses 131–33.

Or rather, this cognition of meaning arising from the phonemes occurs immediately after the knowledge of them; for whatever [cognition] arises from such [a cause] arises from that, just as the cognition of fire arises from smoke and so forth— Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-vārttika, Sphoṭasiddhi, verse 135.
*Tattvasaṅgraha*, Verse 2731:
Furthermore, if a word-sphoṭa distinct from phonemes and the like is accepted as being for the purpose of cognizing meaning, then a fragrance-sphoṭa and so forth must also be accepted.

For just as a word is the cause of comprehension for someone who has grasped a convention regarding a particular object, so too are odor and the other sense-objects. For those who have grasped a convention such that "having smelled such an odor, touched such a touch, tasted such a flavor, or seen such a form, you must comprehend such an object," it is well known that upon the subsequent perception of such an odor and so forth, there arises a comprehension of the corresponding object. Therefore, let there be a *sphoṭa* of odor and the rest, manifested by specific odors and so on, just like the *sphoṭa* of words and the like manifested by specific phonemes;
for it is appropriate to accept the *sphoṭa* of odor and the rest in this manner.
Just as a word, through the speaker's convention, is the cause for the comprehension of a certain meaning, so too are odor and the rest, since there is no difference in their nature.

Having smelled a fragrance of such a kind, one grasps a convention (*samaya*) such that "having perceived a fragrance of this very kind, an object of this sort is to be understood"; or having touched a tactile sensation, tasted a flavor, or seen a form, one grasps a convention that "having perceived a form of such a nature, a state of being (*bhāva*) of this kind is to be understood. Furthermore, because the determination of such an object is established through the subsequent perception of a similar fragrance or other [sensory data], the *sphoṭa* of the word for fragrance and so forth is logically established as the cause for the cognition of the meaning of that sentence, belonging to the self (*ātman*) which has been infused with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) by the cognitions of the fragrance and so forth. Likewise, because the cognition of the object to be understood—which is reached through the aggregate of specific fragrances and so forth—is the cause for the understanding of the meaning of the sentence regarding fragrance and so forth, the *sphoṭa* of the sentence regarding fragrance and so forth is constituted in the self which has been infused with latent impressions by the prior cognitions of the specific fragrances and so forth, immediately following the perception of the final specific fragrance and so forth.
—Having observed [this], *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* p. 427; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 457—ba, śra.
By this, the sphoṭa of the aṅgahāras and so forth, which have the hands and feet as their sole instruments, should also be understood to be established.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that there is only the *pada-sphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) and not the *hasta-sphoṭa* manifested by specific actions of its own parts—such as the movement of the swan’s wings; nor the *pāda-sphoṭa* characterized by the *vikuṭṭita* and other such gestures; nor the *karaṇa-sphoṭa* characterized by the coordination of hands and feet; nor the *mātritṛkā-sphoṭa* consisting of two *karaṇas*; nor the *aṅgahāra-sphoṭa* characterized by a collection of *mātritṛkās*. For even these must be admitted, as they too are manifested by their respective constituent parts and serve as causes for the cognition of the meanings to be represented.

Alternatively, upon its refutation, the persistent attachment to the apprehension of a word-sphoṭa must be abandoned from afar, because the objections and their resolutions are identical in both cases;

since the nature of the sphoṭa, when investigated, is found to be untenable, it should not be accepted by those discerning in their inquiry as the cause for the comprehension of word-meanings, but rather words such as "cow" and the like should be accepted as that cause— otherwise, the joining of hands and feet would be the means of performing a dance.
— Nāṭyaśāstra 4.30:
There are two dance gestures (nṛttakaraṇa), which constitute the matrix of dance (nṛttamātṛkā).
The *mātṛkā* is the source of origin for the dance (*nṛtta*) and its bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*).
— *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.31.
The manner of bringing the limbs to a suitable location is *aṅgahāra*; this is the application of the "necklace" (*hāra*) of Hara. An *aṅgahāra* is a necklace formed by the limbs;
it is of thirty-two types, distinguished by *sthirahasta* and others, and is performed with two, three, or four *mātṛkās*.
With three [verses] there is a *kalāpaka*, and with four it becomes a *maṇḍaka*; there should be five *karaṇas*, which is known as a *saṅghātaka*;
likewise, it may consist of six, seven, eight, or nine.
When combined here with the *karaṇas*, they are proclaimed as *aṅgahāras*—
Nāṭyaśāstra 4.31–33.

It is only the word-sphoṭa (*padādisphoṭa*) that is logically consistent; however, the notion that the hand-sphoṭa—such as the *hasapakṣma* gesture, which is manifested by specific movements of its own constituent parts—is the cause for the comprehension of its denoted meaning, is merely the display of one with limited intellect.

By this, one who claims that the *sphoṭa* of the limbs (*vitkuṭṭitādi*), the *sphoṭa* of the gestures (*karaṇa*) characterized by the clapping of feet and the joining of hands and feet, and the *sphoṭa* of the *aṅgahāras* consisting of thousands of triplets (*mātrikā*) of two gestures, are not possible, should be understood as having stated something meaningless; for even these, being manifested by their own respective parts and serving as causes for the comprehension of their own denoted meanings, cannot be refuted.
(Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 427;
Pakṣādi, Śrāvaṇa).

[The opponent says: But surely, according to the view that a sentence consists of parts (*sāvayava*), [the objection does not apply]; however, if on the other hand the sentence is indeed one and partless (*anavayava*), then—even though it is a single entity—since there is no possibility of sequential movement within that which is undivided, a distinction in time is simply not tenable.

For it is not logical that the comprehension of a single [sentence] occurs sequentially; because there is no distinction between what has been grasped and what has not yet been grasped, the comprehension of a sentence is observed to occur sequentially. This is because the time required for the hearing and recollection of all the words—completing which takes a succession of many moments and eye-blinks—is not perceived as a single word-soul (*śabdātman*) that transcends the form of the phonemes and appears in a single cognition, since it is the sequence of the phonemes that is actually perceived.

Even though there is no difference [in the nature of the letters], the cognition of the sentence occurs as possessing a sequence because the sentence is produced by a sequence; for if it did not depend on the assistance of the sequence of letters, then any sentence whatsoever might be cognized even when those letters are uttered in any arbitrary order, or even without those letters possessing a sequence,
since it is impossible for that which lacks sequence to receive assistance from a sequence,
and because it is impossible to engage in linguistic usage through what is without sequence.
And because there is no other possible state [for it]:
*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti* 1.253.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsakas, Grammarians, and others is as follows: "Only *saṃskṛta* words are correct and expressive of meaning, whereas *apabhraṃśa* and other such forms are not.
[Objection: Granted that these [words] are based upon those [original forms]; however, this applies only to *saṃskṛta* words and not to *prākṛta* ones, because the latter are incorrect (*asādhutva*).

Indeed, only words such as *go* and so forth, which are established by grammar, are correct; therefore, it is logical that only they possess the capacity to express meaning, and not forms such as *gavya* or *agāvya*, since they lack that quality.

For in the linguistic usage of elders, the relationship between signifier and signified is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be established otherwise; and if those two [concomitances] are accounted for by postulating a power (*śakti*) in the single word "go" toward a single object characterized as "cowness," then they do not postulate such a power in the second word, "gāvī," toward that same object.

For the postulation of those two occurs through non-occurrence (*anupapatti*): that which cannot establish its own existence without another is "non-occurring" in relation to that [other], and thus it postulates that [other] for the sake of its own occurrence; however, that which can occur even without another does not postulate that [other], because the non-occurrence that serves as the basis for postulation has ceased. "A single word, correctly understood, consistent with the treatises, and well-employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world" (Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya 6).
Therefore, a Brahmin must not speak like a barbarian nor use corrupt speech; for such a person is indeed a barbarian when he uses an incorrect word.
—Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśāhnika:
"If the instruction of words is given, then when 'go' (cow) is taught, it is understood that 'gāvī' and other such forms are incorrect words. —Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśāhnika.
Therefore, that which those who are engaged [in the inquiry] teach as "this alone is correct" should be understood as correct—
Śābarabhāṣya 1.3.1.
Words established by tradition from the learned are correct (sādhavaḥ) and are the means for accomplishing dharma;
those which are the opposite, when there is no difference in the communication of meaning, are incorrect (asādhavaḥ).
— Vākyapadīya 1.27:
The reality of a word is its integrity, its correct form when it has not lost its linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*).
But others, being employed with the desire to employ that [correct word], would be deficient or corrupt—
Vākyapadīya, Svavṛtti 1.13.
"He is a correct speaker whose linguistic refinement is understood through grammar and is unimpaired; those which are impaired by it are corrupt forms"—
Vākyapadīya, Puṣpikā-ṭīkā 1.
Therefore, no one— neither from common worldly usage nor from the Vedas— is able to know, as they truly are, those expressive words that are free from corruption, except through grammar.
—Tantravārttika, p. 278:
"In that way, by means of what is called grammar, the correct form is regulated;
otherwise, there would be establishment [of forms] without distinction, in the absence of the grammatical tradition."

"Correctness is the capacity to denote [meaning] as qualified by conformity to the characteristics of grammar"—Tantravārttika, p. 287; "Correctness is the capacity to denote [meaning] as qualified by conformity to the characteristics of grammar"—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 423.

It is remembered as correct by the most authoritative scholars, such as Indra, Pāṇini, and others, without any contradiction; thus it is determined that "this is correct and the other is incorrect" (Nyāyavārttika, p.
714). Correctness (*sādhutva*) is the distinct form of a word which possesses an innate power of expression with respect to a particular meaning.
