And that very nature of correctness (*sādhutva*), which is established for a word by means of grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) through the analysis of roots, suffixes, and so forth, is indeed perceived even more clearly by modern people through auditory perception assisted by grammatical tradition—excluding incorrect words—as being the form of correctness itself. Thus, there is a restriction regarding the nature of correct words: "Only *go* and the like are correct, not *gāvī* and the like. (Tautātita-pṛṣṭha 128)
— Śāstradīpikā 1.3.27
One should employ only correct forms; "only *go* and so forth are correct"—
this restriction exists because they are rooted in successive prior grammatical explanations—
Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.25.

And thus, since the capacity [of words] is established only in the case of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and since the function (*vṛtti*)— which consists in the relationship between the capable [word] and its referent— also exists only therein, that alone is grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).
In reality, correctness (*sādhutva*) does not consist in having a [grammatical] function (*vṛttimattva*), but rather in being produced by grammar (*vyākaraṇaniṣpādyatva*);
whatever word is derived in grammar is correct in that context—*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, p. 249.
"Non-corruption, beginninglessness, fitness for prosperity, manifestation through grammatical analysis, or some kind of universal (*jāti*)— these are what constitute correctness (*sādhutā*) here"—
Śabarakau, p. 25.

Regarding "gavyādi" (the *gavya* group): the corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word "cow" (*gauḥ*), such as *gāvī*, *goṇī*, *gotā*, *gopotalikā*, and so forth— [as stated in] the *Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya*, *Paspaśāhnika*.

The capacity of all entities is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). When a single capacity has been established for an object, multiple capacities are not thereby obtained; furthermore, a name is accepted for an object solely for the sake of conventional usage.
Since the purpose is accomplished by that one alone, a second and so forth would be fruitless—
Tantravārttika, p. 1.3.

Furthermore, that which is called the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) is subtle and can only be understood by resorting to the presumption of a logical necessity (*arthāpatti*); it cannot be understood from any other source when it is weak.

And this [power], being capable of being established otherwise, becomes weakened in the linguistic usage of conveying meaning from words such as "cow" (*go*) and so on. Since the assumption of a power in those [corrupt forms] is rendered unnecessary, the presumption itself establishes that "cow" and its synonyms are the locus of the expressive power, and not words such as *gāvī*.
—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 421.

And here, because Sanskrit is one and the same in all places, the expressive power resides in it alone; whereas because vernacular languages differ from place to place, they cannot possess that power, as they would otherwise result in being mere synonyms for Sanskrit words—*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, p. 248.

Since the cognition of that meaning is established by means of the primary expressive power (*śakti*) in one case and through the superimposition of it upon another, the expressive power resides in only one [word], due to parsimony (*lāghava*), because the meaning of a word is precisely that which cannot be obtained otherwise.
And that expressive power resides only in the *saṃskṛta* [language], because it is one and the same in all regions—*Tattvacintāmaṇi*, Śabdakhaṇḍa, p. 641.
For positive and negative concomitance are not established here;
indeed, this reading is not present in manuscript B. Ā. [does not contain it].

It should not be argued that [the word *gāvī*] is a denoter because the comprehension of meaning is possible even from the word *gāvī* through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For in that case, positive and negative concomitance are established otherwise;
for although the word *gāvī* is not itself a denoter, its positive and negative concomitances are consistent with the comprehension of meaning by means of the recollection of the denoting word *go*.

Moreover, it is observed that even when an incorrect word (*asādhuśabda*) is employed, the comprehension of meaning occurs through the recollection of the correct word (*sādhuśabda*). For example, when a child intends to address someone with the vocative "Mother" (*amba*), being unable to utter it due to a deficiency in the articulatory organs (*sthāna*), the points of articulation (*karaṇa*), or effort (*prayatna*), or due to negligence, he mispronounces it as "ambiti. Upon hearing that sound, the mother proceeds [to act] and thinks: "This child intended to say 'Mother,' but instead uttered 'ambiti' in its place. Thus, from the incorrect word "ambiti," she recalls the original correct word "Mother" and proceeds accordingly.
Similarly, when the word *khaṇḍaṣaṇḍha* is intended to be uttered, the usage of the word *saṃḍha* is observed among the Easterners.

Upon hearing that sentence, the speaker who subsequently acts understands that "this person, desiring to utter the original word, has pronounced the word *saṃḍha* either due to inability or through negligence. Thus, having recalled the word *ṣaṇḍha* from the word *saṃḍha*, he comprehends the meaning and proceeds to act.

Thus, by recollecting the correct form *go* as the source of the incorrect form *gāvī*, the speaker understands the meaning from it; however, because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established otherwise in this case, they lack the capacity to determine its status as a denoter (*vācaka*).
For it is only where those two are ascertained that they cause one to understand the rule of denotation;
and since those two are not ascertained for the word *gāvī* in the manner described, they do not cause one to understand that rule.

However, since both disputants agree upon the word "go" (cow), those two [the word and its meaning] are certain; therefore, the restriction that this very word is the denoter in the cognition of cowness is established. Furthermore, because the word "go" is perceived as performing its function of communication in a uniform manner across all places, times, persons, and ancient Vedic texts, it is logical that the restriction of denotative power belongs only to this word when supported by the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), and not to the word "gāvī," because the latter is perceived as a cause for communication only in restricted regions and so forth.

Indeed, those words such as *gāvī* and the like that originate from other regions and for which the relationship [between word and meaning] has not been grasped do not establish linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) for them.

Therefore, by means of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), whose status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is understood, those words such as *go* and the like which are taught are established as correct (*sādhavaḥ*), but not words such as *gāvī*.
Regarding the word *gāvī*:

Now, as for what was said—that the meaning is understood from words such as *gāvī*, and therefore their connection with the meaning is also beginningless—that is understood as a case of incapacity (*aśakti*).

When someone desiring to utter the word *go* utters *gāvī* due to incapacity, another person understands that the one intended to be expressed is the animal possessing a dewlap and other characteristics; thus, desiring to utter *go*, he utters *gāvī*.
Then, having learned from that, others also utter "gāvī" when they intend to speak of an animal possessing a dewlap and other such features;
by means of this, an animal possessing a dewlap is understood from "gāvī" and similar forms, for "gāvī" and the like are indeed analogous to the word "go."
In this way, from the perception of "gāvī" and similar forms, there arises the recollection of the word "go," and from that, an animal possessing a dewlap and other such features is understood—
Śābarabhāṣya 1.3.10.
Just as when the word *gāvī* is employed in the sense of the word *gauḥ*, it conveys the object possessing a hump and so forth;

nor is the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of words useless, for by means of this [corrupt] word one first understands the word *go*, and from the word *go* one understands the object possessing a hump and so forth.

"But those [sounds], by means of the reflection of their similarity to the phonemes, produce the recollection of words such as 'cow' and thereby become the cause for the comprehension of their meanings" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
*Nyāyavārttika-tātparya-ṭīkā*, p. 714; *Tattvacintāmaṇi-śabdakhaṇḍa*, p. 643:

Nor should it be argued, "How can there be comprehension of meaning from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), since they lack denotative power? For there is no subverting evidence against those who possess a misconception regarding the expressive power [of such forms].
However, those who perceive the specific [phonetic] distinctions are of two kinds: those possessing specialized knowledge of the Sanskrit words expressive of those [meanings], and those lacking it.
Among them, for the former, there is comprehension of the meaning through the mediation of the recollection of the correct form (*sādhu*);

for the latter, however, when there is a recollection of another word expressive of a related meaning connected to the intended object, comprehension occurs from that [recollection] by means of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

This should be understood accordingly—either through the recollection of a universal name (*sarvanāma*), or through the recollection of a correct word (*sādhu*) in the form of a signifier of that meaning, or by resorting to the position of supplying an implied meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*). (Śabarakau, p.
32): "Words such as *asva*, *goṇī*, and so forth, are correct (*sādhavaḥ*) in other contexts."
Due to the difference in their forms, correctness is established everywhere;
they serve as the causes for the arising of cognition regarding correct words through inference, manifesting the word-meaning as if they had attained identity with it.
Those correct forms are not followed by the learned, just as grammatical variants are not;
therefore, according to the Smṛti-śāstra, it is directly non-expressive,
just as a child learning to speak utters "ambāmbā."
That [corruption] is unmanifest to those who know it; thus, there is indeed certainty regarding the manifest form.
When a corruption is employed instead of a correct word (*sādhu*) that ought to be used, a certain meaning is expressed by means of that correct word which has been obscured.

Regarding words such as *gāvī* and the like, because they lack the capacity for repeated utterance, corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) convey their meaning by following the intended original word (*mūlaśabda*) when that original is intended; however, when it is not intended, they do so solely through a misconception of the expressive word. (Vākyapadīya 1.149–53)
—Tautātita-pṛṣṭha 130;
Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi-pṛṣṭha 95;
"anviti" Āhnika.
In that place,
the word "cow" is perceived [by the ear], according to the manuscripts ba and ā.
All these words are indeed employed in various regions throughout different countries— *Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya*, Paspaśāhnika.
Words such as "gāvī" and so forth are not [denotative] of persons, however.

Furthermore, because the restriction regarding their denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is understood in that very context, only words such as *go* (cow) possess correctness (*sādhutva*). To explain: when it is said, "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), there arises the comprehension of bringing an object qualified by the possession of a dewlap and so forth.

In that case, just as it is determined that the meaning of the word *go* is the object characterized by the dewlap and so forth, so too is the restriction determined that this specific meaning belongs to the word *go* alone.
Furthermore, once the rule [of linguistic usage] is understood, it excludes the denotative capacity of anything else.

Thus, let it be granted that the determination of the denotative capacity belongs only to words such as "cow" (*gavādi*) and so forth; nevertheless, that capacity will arise for them through the usage of elders alone. Therefore, the commencement of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) for the purpose of establishing their correctness is useless. This is incorrect, because it is impossible to determine the denotative capacity of all words from the usage of elders alone, independent of grammar.

For the mass of words is infinite; even in an infinite amount of time, it would be impossible to grasp the expressive power (*vācakatva*) of every single word through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).

However, by means of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), which provides definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) characterized by both general and specific features, it is indeed possible with very little effort to understand the expressive power of all words that are thus indicated.
Therefore, the knowledge of their correctness (*sādhutva*) is derived from grammar alone.
For instance, by the single sūtra *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), many words such as *kumbhakāra*, *kāṇḍalāva*, and *vedādhyāya* are characterized as being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*).
Therefore, since correctness can be easily ascertained through worldly usage supported by grammar, grammar serves a useful purpose.

Now, one might object: "Since this [grammar] is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), how is it appropriate to ascertain the correctness of certain words from it? This too is incorrect; for if it were invalid, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a total confusion among the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) such as the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).

Indeed, without grammar, it is not possible to achieve a definitive understanding of the grammatical factors (kārakas), such as the object and the agent, by means of the analysis of roots and suffixes; for no other cause for that definitiveness is possible.
Therefore, the very fact that this definitiveness is observed establishes grammar itself as its own regulating cause.
Let it be so, indeed. (Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, *Śabdakaustubha*)

The determination of denotative capacity—[is established] by the operation of [words] independently [of etymology]. The purpose [of grammar] is the removal of obstacles, the understanding of Vedic tradition, brevity, and the absence of doubt; and grammar should be studied for the sake of brevity. It is said that words must necessarily be known by a Brahmin.

Furthermore, without grammar as a concise means, words cannot be known; therefore, a rule (*lakṣaṇa*) characterized by both general and particular [applications] must be set forth, by which one may comprehend vast masses of words with little effort.
What, then, is that? It is the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*).
A general rule (utsarga) must be formulated, as must an exception (apavāda); the general rule should be stated first, such as "the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after a verbal root" (*karmaṇyaṇ*),
while the exception for it is stated specifically, such as "after a root ending in long *ā*, when no prefix is present" (*āto’nupasarge ka*).

—Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśāhnika; according to the *Kāśikā*, p. 1: [this is done] by means of a definition possessing general and particular characteristics through the conceptualization of the division into roots (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

In that regard, by means of a definition possessing commonality through the conceptualization of divisions such as *prakṛti* (base) and so forth, one arrives at a great mass of words such as "potter," "arrow-reaper," and "reed-reaper"; but by means of a definition possessing particularity, [one arrives at] "heel-protector," "cowherd," "blanket-giver," and so forth—*Nyāsa*, p.
The [words] *sarvada*, *pāṇini*,
*ghyāya*, and so forth,
are [considered] *śrauta* because they consist of many phonemes (*śabdabahugādhutvena*).
For it is through the two— worldly usage and grammatical instruction— which are combined, that the establishment of the speaker who is unerring [in his expression] is achieved;
thus says the *Tantravārttika* (1.3).
Furthermore, without grammar, it is not possible to understand either the primary derivatives (kṛt) or the secondary derivatives (taddhita).
"Without grammar, there is no comprehension of the true nature of words"— Vākyapadīya 1.24. Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśāhnika.
Likewise, if grammar were not authoritative, there would be a contradiction with both common worldly practice and the treatises.
Regarding that, first, there is the contradiction with worldly practice: because all cultured people (śiṣṭas) accept its authority.
There is also a contradiction with the treatises (*śāstra*); for if those were invalid, it would follow that all treatises are abolished.

Indeed, all treatises consist of fixed linguistic forms, and since such restriction depends upon grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), how could that be possible if grammar were invalid? Even by one who does not accept the validity of treatises, the employment of proofs and refutations in order to convince others must necessarily be accepted as establishing their validity.

If that [authority of grammar] were not accepted, it would follow that the entire elaboration of proofs for one's own position and refutations of the opponent's position would vanish; for it is impossible to communicate with others through mere mental constructs or bodily gestures alone. Therefore, by one who wishes to avoid the aforementioned faults, the authority of grammar must not be denied. Thus, its authority is established for the sake of proving the correctness of words, and because the instruction of words (śabdānuśāsana) is intended for all people.

— Haimaśabdānuśāsana-bṛhad-vṛtti, p. 2— This very tradition of grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) has as its object the knowledge of the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those [words] distinguished by their specific [phonetic] forms.
"This composition of the Smṛti is based on the uninterrupted tradition of the learned"—
Vākyapadīya 1.143.

Now, as for the objection: "Since the correctness (*sādhutva*) of words is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can grammar possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) to establish that?"—this too is an unexamined statement; for that correctness is established through perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself.

For instance: to one whose mind is refined by grammar, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of a word appears in auditory perception just like the form of the phonemes themselves; because when words taught by grammar are being uttered, there arises the cognition, "This person speaks correctly" (*sādhu*); whereas when they are uttered otherwise, there arises the cognition, "This wicked person speaks incorrectly," or "He uses corrupt forms" (*apaśabda*). Thus, the distinction between correctness and incorrectness is determined through direct perception itself.

Now it is argued: "If correctness (*sādhutva*) were something distinct from the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*), then it too would have appeared prior to the refinement by grammar (*vyākaraṇa-saṃskāra*), just like the nature of the phonemes themselves, because the connection with the auditory organ—the cause for its appearance—was already present before that time. This is merely a statement; for the auditory organ, which depends upon the refinement of grammar, was not present previously, and it is logically established that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect. Indeed, the auditory organ has the capacity to grasp the nature of the phonemes even when alone, but for the grasping of correctness, it must be assisted by grammar.

Just as the eye, aided by the refinement provided by the treatises on gems and the like, is capable of perceiving the distinctions among them but not when deprived of that aid, so too is grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) not perceptible by the senses; yet it possesses a logical mark (*liṅga*),
this very subject matter of the treatise, and its application is also non-confused.
Because it is admitted that [the correctness and incorrectness of words] are perceivable by the sense of hearing aided by the assistance of grammatical instruction—

just as the universal *brāhmaṇatva* (brahminhood) and others, though perceptible by the sense of sight only in dependence upon instruction, do not lose their status as being accessible through perception— so too, correctness (*sādhutva*) and incorrectness (*asādhutva*), though perceived by the sense of hearing with the aid of instruction from those expert in grammar, do not transcend the realm of perception.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 422; Tautātita, p. 128; *śrautrapra*—Ā., Ba.
—*vatsādhṛ* — *ba*, *ā*; —*śiṣṭeṣūccārya* — *ā*, —*śiṣṭeṣu śabdoccārya* — *ba*;
—*bdānukaroti* — *ā*.
Just as experts recognize rubies and other gems when they are mixed with glass and crystal, while others do not, so too [is the case here]. (pūrvasadbhāva) Ā, pūrvasadbhāva Ba.

Just as the characteristics of the genuineness or spuriousness of a gem are determined by its examination, so too is the determination of correct words established through grammar— *Tantravārttika* 1.3.24.

[Objection: "But since the totality of words (*śabdarāśi*) is infinite and thus beyond the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those [words] be established from that? [Reply: This too is incorrect; for although this [totality] is not within the scope of perception, its correctness is established through inference (*anumāna*). To explain: words whose usage is not currently observed are correct, because they are taught by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), just like the words *go* and so forth which are currently observed.
Likewise,
correctness is established by scripture as well, through such passages as: "Therefore, this refined speech is uttered by the virtuous" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 6.4.7).

Likewise, correctness is understood through analogy (*upamāna*); for just as the words employed by the authors of the Sūtras, the Bhāṣya, and the Vārttika are correct, so too are those employed by others who follow their lead equally correct.

Furthermore, correctness is determined through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), characterized by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the fact that words serve as the means for the cognition of meaning through beginningless and endless positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be established otherwise. Thus it is concluded.
Even for a mass of words that is not within the range of direct perception,

the instruction of the science of grammar— accompanied by the comprehension of meanings understood through linguistic usage occurring after hearing specific words— will serve as an unerring mark (*liṅga*) for determining their true nature, consisting of bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), augments (*vikaraṇa*), elision (*lopa*), insertion (*āgama*), substitution (*ādeśa*), and so forth.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 423;
Tantravārttika 1.3.1.
27–Because its non-existence is not established; this is extracted from the *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 423.
Nyāyavārttika-tātparyaṭīkā, p. 714; Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa, p. 252; Tattvacintāmaṇi-śabdakhaṇḍa, p. 640.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should speak with virtuous people about virtuous things.
— Vākyapadīya 1.141
Therefore, this has been explained: *Tantravārttika* 1.3.27.
Bhāṭṭaciṃtāmaṇi, p.

98: According to the Sūtrakāra and the Vārttikakāra, there is first of all a determination of grammatical correctness (sādhutva) obtained through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), based on the fact that words possess denotative power as established by the cognition of worldly meaning.
— Tantravārttika 1.3.27
Regarding the establishment of the expressive power [of words] by proving the correctness of Apabhraṃśa, Prākṛta, and other vernacular words—it is replied here:

as for what was stated, namely, that "only words such as *go* (cow) are correct, because their expressive power alone is logically tenable," and so forth—that is charming only so long as it is not critically examined; for the relationship between the signifier and the signified is indeed to be understood through worldly convention (*loka-vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, the world is observed to function by means of words such as *gāvī* and the like;
for even those who know the refined (*saṃskṛta*) language are seen to abandon refined words at the time of practical usage and instead employ words such as *gāvī*.

Thus, since the linguistic practice of those who know both the refined and other forms is observed to occur solely through words such as *gāvī*, it is determined—by means of positive and negative concomitance—that these alone possess the capacity to denote meaning.

Furthermore, it is not observed even in dreams that words such as *gāvī* convey their meaning in dependence upon the recollection of [correct] words like *go*, by virtue of which one might claim they are non-expressive because their cognition of meaning could be accounted for otherwise. Indeed, no mediated cognition of meaning is experienced such that one first recalls a Sanskrit word from Prakrit words and only then cognizes the meaning; for, just like Sanskrit words, the cognition of meaning is perceived directly from them as well. Otherwise, in places where those who know Sanskrit do not exist, there would be no cognition of meaning from vernacular words.

Therefore, because it is always perceived that words such as *gāvī* convey their meaning independently of the recollection of other words—just like the word *go* and others—their status as direct denoters (*vācakatva*) is established.

For just as the word *go* is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to denote the object "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth without depending on the recollection of words like *gāvī*, so too do words like *gāvī* denote their objects without depending on the recollection of words like *go*.

And thus, since both [the correct word and the corrupt form] are equal in their capacity to convey meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), if the status of being a denoter (*vācakatva*) is to be attributed to only one, it would be better to attribute it to words such as *gāvī* and the like; for the linguistic usage of all people is understood through those very forms alone.
However, this linguistic usage proceeds from the established convention among elders (*vṛddha-prasiddhi*).
"By means of the conditioned"—that is, by all words, like the sounds of various languages—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 290.
"The unconditioned"—Ā.
The words such as *gāvī* and so forth are established precisely in this manner;
[this occurs] at the first instance.

Since it can also be said that the determination of meaning occurs from Prakrit words through comparison, inversion, or even from corrupt forms (apaśabda) and so forth— given that such is observed and there is no distinction whatsoever in this regard— [the same applies here].
—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 290; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 668. Compare: "Because for women and Śūdras there is an absence of the cognition of both [the Veda and its meaning]."
Indeed, only one who knows both the correct word (*śabda*) and the corrupt word (*apaśabda*) can comprehend [the meaning];

but how could one who knows only the indistinct sound (*nakamukka-śabda*) and not the nasalized sound (*nāsā-śabda*) comprehend the correct word from the corrupt word, and thereby comprehend the meaning? Furthermore, it is observed that comprehension occurs even for one who knows neither.
(Vādanyāya, p. 103)

Since barbarians (mleccha) and others lack knowledge of correct words, how could there be a traditional rule (smṛti) concerning them? In their absence, how could the meaning of "cow" be understood? — Tattvopaplavasiṃha, p. 124.
— just as in the case of "cow" and so forth— [the cognition] occurs through the very medium of words such as "gāvī," which have an identical referent.

Furthermore, because we observe the opposite case—that in the world people are seen not to understand the meaning from correct words (*śabda*), but rather acquire knowledge through corrupt words (*apaśabda*) alone—the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*) is useless.

For instance, when "tree," "fire," or "lotus" are uttered, children whose intellects are untrained remain stuck at the beginning of their inquiry, asking such things as, "What is this tree? and so forth.
And since there is no other means of linguistic instruction [available], they are instructed by means of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) themselves—such as *rukkha*, *aggī*, and *uppala*.
Thus, in this case, it is observed that the opposite is true: only the incorrect forms are expressive, while the correct forms, even though they exist, are not.
— *Vādanyāya-ṭīkā*, p. 105.
Furthermore, recollection becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when there has been an original experience, because it conforms to that experience.

Now, the expressive power (*vācakatva*) of words such as "go" was not experienced through its own natural function at the very outset of the linguistic usage regarding cows; rather, at that time, it was precisely words such as "gāvī" that were experienced as having that power.

Therefore, to claim that those whose expressive power was previously experienced are remembered in a usage based on them while their expressive power was not [previously] experienced—this is a great feat of logic!
— First, those very [sounds] are the modes (*vṛtti*) of the phoneme (*svara*),
because one experiences their denotative function (*vācakatva*) in words such as *gāvī* and so forth. — Ārya.
—Furthermore, it is certainly not the case that words such as *gāvī* lack denotative power.

As for what was said—that when the word *go* was intended to be uttered, the word *gāvī* was instead uttered by a child due to incapacity or negligence—that too is incorrect. For if a child, with the intention of uttering the word *go*, were to utter the word *gāvī* because of incapacity or negligence, then, having abandoned his childhood state and become awakened, he would realize, "This was employed by me through incapacity or negligence," and knowing this, he would abandon that [word] and engage in linguistic usage using only the word *go*.
And even though its expressive capacity is impaired, it does not abandon the word *gāvī* and instead employ the word *go* alone in linguistic usage.

But surely, it cannot be that linguistic usage with words such as "cow" (*go*), which are *saṃskṛta*, can be carried out together with those of unrefined intellects (*asaṃskṛtamati*), because for them—due to the absence of a thorough knowledge of grammatical characteristics—it is impossible to possess a thorough knowledge of *saṃskṛta* words. Therefore, since there are many of such unrefined intellects, even corrupted usage (*apabhraṣṭavyavahāra*), which arises from incapacity and negligence, has reached the highest degree of conventional currency, such that even a person who is capable and knows the true nature of words uses only that very [corrupted form]. This too is refuted by the same [argument]; for if the usage of words like *gāvī* were produced by negligence and incapacity, the aforementioned defects would necessarily follow.
"Page 759, line 6,
etc."— this [reading] is found in the manuscripts designated as Śra and Ba;
and this [is the reading] in Śra.

Regarding the grammatical aphorisms (*vyākaraṇasūtra*), for those whose minds are unrefined, these [Sanskrit words] would be corrupt because they do not accomplish the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). This is because there is no cognition of them as being one and the same—uninterrupted at all times and in all places—as they are supported by the tradition of grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*). Or else, it might be argued that they denote meaning through convention (*saṅketa*). In this regard, the first position is untenable; for the entirety of the goals of human life, such as dharma and artha, is established precisely through the usage of vernacular (*prākṛta*) words.
Indeed, there is no human goal whatsoever in which its application would not occur, whether directly or indirectly.

Even for those Sanskrit words employed with the desire to convey that very meaning, the sense is demonstrated most clearly by means of Prakrit words themselves; how then could the usage of such [words] fail to accomplish the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), such that they would be considered corrupt (apabhraṣṭa)? In the second alternative, however, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the grammatical correctness of such expressions as "one desiring prosperity should kill a Brāhmaṇa who possesses wealth," because this too would not differ in its cognition, since it is everywhere and at all times identical as being sustained by the grammatical tradition (vyākaraṇasmṛti).
Because it has not been accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), its cessation in that regard is the same even in the case of scriptural injunctions for animal sacrifice and the like;
for the scriptural injunction "one should sacrifice a white goat" is not respected by those whose mental dispositions are moistened with compassion and who prioritize critical investigation.

Furthermore, the third position is also untenable; for, just like vernacular words (*prākṛta-śabda*), even Sanskrit words possess the capacity to convey meaning only when aided by convention (*saṅketa*).

Because there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to express what is not conventionally established or not previously denoted, and because no distinction can thus be made between Sanskrit and other words, the correctness or incorrectness of both must be understood without distinction— [for] that which is not fixed... [is not established].
The linguistic usage of those operations is not [the case],
O Ārya; rather, the linguistic usage of words in Prakrit and other vernacular languages is for the purpose of communicating human goals.
Furthermore, [the status of] being an object of perception is [accepted] by the Jains, Buddhists, Vaiṣṇavas,
and others; moreover, when correctness is established by its very nature, it is appropriate to apply either an injunction or a prohibition in certain cases.
Nor is that [correctness] established by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

For what would this "nature" be? Would it be (1) denotative capacity (*vācakatva*), (2) beginningless usage (*anādiprayogitā*), (3) being a means for accomplishing dharma (*dharmasādhanatva*), (4) being composed by a distinguished person (*viśiṣṭapuruṣapraṇītatva*), (5) expressing a specific meaning (*viśiṣṭārthābhidhāyitva*), (6) being free from contradiction (*bādhārahitatva*), (7) being corroborated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntarānugṛhītatva*), (8) being perceptible by unimpaired sense organs (*anupahatendriyagrāhyatva*), (9) being unobstructed (*anāvṛtatva*), or (10) having a form established by grammar (*vyākaraṇasiddhasvarūpatva*)? If it were denotative capacity, then that exists in words such as *gāvī* just as it does in words such as *go*; for, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is demonstrated that those [corrupt forms] also convey meaning. Therefore, they would possess correctness (*sādhutva*).
— [This] form is favored by the venerable [author], [as found in] manuscript *ba*. Or,
if it is argued that the word *gāvī* cannot function as a denotative term (*vācaka*), that is incorrect, because cognizers frequently employ the word *gāvī*.

Regarding the *Tattvopaplava* (p. 124): Is this "beginningless usage" asserted with reference to the continuity of the stream (*pravāha*), or with reference to its eternity (*nityatva*)? In the first case, there would be no distinction between the words *go* and *gāvī*, since beginningless usage is possible for both; consequently, both would be either equally correct or equally incorrect without distinction.
Furthermore, if correctness were based on beginningless usage, then only vernacular forms such as *gāvī* and the like would be correct, because it is precisely for those that such usage is possible.

For *prākṛta* is simply *prakṛti*, and *prakṛti* is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is logical that correctness (*sādhutva*) belongs only to forms such as *gāvī* and the like—which are of the nature of *prakṛti*, which reveal the true form of the object, and which are fit for usage from time immemorial—and not to refined forms (*saṃskṛta*) such as *go* and the like, because their being used from time immemorial is untenable. For refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the attribution of another quality to an existing entity, and that [refinement] is necessarily something that has a beginning. Consequently, it is determined that prior to the refinement designated as "refined" (*saṃskṛta*), there exists something else that is its *prakṛti*.
And that [word] is indeed natural (*prākṛta*); thus, by virtue of its being employed from time immemorial, it has attained the status of being correct (*sādhu*).
For it is through that [naturalness] that it is correct, since [otherwise] the possibility of its being employed from time immemorial would not exist. (Śra.)

Regarding the term *prākṛta*: *prakṛti* refers to the innate activity of speech belonging to all beings in the entire world, which is not produced by the refinement [imparted] through grammar and other sciences; that which arises therein, or that which is identical to it, is *prākṛta*.

Alternatively, because of such statements as "The speech of the Āryas is established, and the gods' speech is half-Māgadhī," it is called *prākṛta* because it was made (*kṛta*) previously (*prāk*). It is said to be the speech that serves as the foundation for all the languages of children, women, and others.

Like water released from a cloud, it possesses a single uniform nature; yet, by acquiring specific qualities due to particular regions and the application of refinement, it attains subsequent divisions such as *Sanskṛta* and the rest.

For this very reason, the author of the treatise has first pointed out the Prakrit, followed by the Sanskrit and others; it is called "Sanskrit" because it is refined (*saṃskṛta*) according to the definition of words taught in the grammars of Pāṇini and others— Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti (Rudraṭa’s commentary on Nami-sādhū), 2.2.2.
And it is not the case that "prākṛta" is simply "prakṛti"; what then? It is that which arises from *prakṛti*.

Now, what indeed is this so-called *prakṛti* (original nature), from which [language] might be called *prākṛta*? Is it the inherent nature (*svabhāva*), the collection of verbal roots (*dhātugaṇa*), or the essential form of Sanskrit words? In the first alternative, the very position that "the *prakṛti* itself is the *prākṛta*" would be accepted; for it is through words such as *gāvī* and others—which have acquired their own existence from the inherent nature of the *prakṛti*—that the linguistic usage of all people is established.

In the second alternative, however, there would be the undesirable consequence that even words such as *go* (cow) and others would be considered *prakṛti* (original forms), since their own forms are established from the list of verbal roots (*dhātugaṇa*) without distinction; thus, a funeral libation would be offered to the very practice of *saṃskṛta*. Furthermore, it is untenable for the form of a *saṃskṛta* word to be a *prakṛti*, because it is itself a *vikāra* (modification).

For when a real entity undergoes refinement (*saṃskāra*) through the addition of other qualities, it exists in the state of a modification; how then could it attain the status of being an original form?

That which exists in the *prakṛti* (the source language). For comparison: "That which exists in or has come from the *prakṛti* [Sanskrit] is *prākṛta*" — Hemaṃdraprākṛtavyākaraṇa, Prākṛtasarvasva, Prākṛtacandrikā, and Vāgbhaṭālaṃkāra-ṭīkā 2.
This very same [speech], when inverted and devoid of the quality of *saṃskāra*,
should be known as *prākṛta* recitation, consisting of various internal states.
— Nāṭyaśāstra 17.2:
"In this context, however, the Prakrit is considered a modification (vikṛti) of the Sanskrit."
— In the *Ṣaḍbhāṣācandrikā*,
it is stated that for Prakrit, Sanskrit alone is the source (*yoni*); thus, [it is called] *Prākṛtasaṃskṛta*.

Regarding the subject at hand, we shall now declare the characteristics of this Prākṛta—which arises from both the established and the to-be-established [Sanskrit]—as they conform to the usage of the literary examples (*lakṣya*):
*Bhāṣāvṛtti*, p. 1.
Thus it is said:
because the collection of verbal roots (dhātugaṇa) is established by its own nature, it is not subject to modification. Śra.
Furthermore, the relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) is observed only when there is a temporal sequence of prior and posterior;
however, that is not the case here, because the opposite is perceived: for *saṃskṛta* has a beginning, whereas *prākṛta* is beginningless.
Thus, regarding *saṃskṛta* and *prākṛta*...

Now, suppose it is thought: "Refinement (*saṃskāra*) is not the imparting of another quality; rather, it is of the nature that the meaning inherent within a word—whose own form is undivided but whose object has not been correctly apprehended—is revealed by means of the division into base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth. This too is inconsistent, because explaining the meaning by means of the division into base, suffix, and so forth constitutes an *exegesis* (*vyākhyāna*), and thus cannot logically be considered a "refinement";
for no such refinement is ever observed in the case of cloth and the like.
What then? It is characterized by the imparting of another quality.
Nevertheless, if this were designated as a *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement), it would be like giving one's own blanket the name "kūrdālikā" [a term for a specific type of cloth].
This has been seen by the wise (*ciddṛṣṭam*).
Now, we do not accept the *saṃskāra* of certain words unless we perceive a superior quality (*guṇātiśaya*) in them—[as stated in] the *Vādanyāya*, p. 107.

By this, the alternative view—that *saṃskāra* (refinement) is the stabilization of a word whose form is indeed unchanging by means of protecting it from corruption through the agency of the speaker’s capacity—is also refuted. This is because the stabilization of a form as something unchanging is never perceived anywhere as being the nature of *saṃskāra*. Furthermore, would this stabilization of words in an unchanging form be in relation to their similarity, or in relation to an eternal, single form? If it were in relation to similarity, then it would follow that even corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and the like would possess the status of being refined (*saṃskṛta*), since there is no difference in that regard.

Now, [if it is argued that] correctness is established by reference to a single, eternal form—that is incorrect, because the eternality and singularity of forms of words have already been refuted in the preceding treatise.
Therefore, correctness of words cannot be established by reference to a continuous stream (*pravāha*), on the grounds of their being employed from time immemorial.

Furthermore, if one were to accept correctness based on that [stream], it would follow that even the practices of barbarians (*mleccha*)—such as "when the father has gone to heaven, the mother must be married by the eldest son"—would be correct; for there is no difference in those cases either, as they too involve employment from time immemorial through a continuous stream.

Now, if it is argued that the correctness of those words is established because they have been employed since beginningless time on account of their eternality—that too is mere talk; for the eternality of words is not supported by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the lack of such support has already been explained in detail in the demonstration of the non-eternality of these words. Enough of this digression:
therefore, even "employment since beginningless time" is not the defining characteristic of their correctness.
For the sake of protecting the Vedas from errors in usage, grammar must be studied;
for one who knows [the rules regarding] elision, augmentation, and the modification of phonemes will properly preserve the Vedas.
— Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya Paspaśāhnika— [regarding] the nature of the *liṭ* [tense], according to the state of its form (*rūpatā*), according to Ba and Śra.
— Incidentally,
that [is established] by virtue of its being employed from time immemorial (ba॰ pṛ॰ 703).

And even among the ignorant, there are certain practices of barbarians—such as marriage with one's mother and so forth, as well as festivals of passion and the like—which are beginningless; and there are also the words of atheists, which deny the existence of the unprecedented [karma] and the next world.
(Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti 1)

Nor can they be the means for accomplishing dharma, for would that be direct or indirect? It cannot be direct, because it would follow that the performance of vows and so forth, which are intended for that purpose, would be rendered useless.
However, their status as a means to that [dharma] through traditional succession is no different for Prakrit words than it is for Sanskrit words;
for when the use of words prompted by meaning occurs in common worldly usage, the scripture establishes a restriction regarding dharma,
stating that "the meaning must be expressed by the word itself, not by an incorrect word (apaśabda)."
When performed in this way, it leads to prosperity; that which is equal to this is [indicated] by the word of the Veda—*Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya*, Paspaśāhnika;
"The correct [words] are the means for accomplishing dharma"—*Vākyapadīya* 1.127.
Comparison: There is no status as a means to dharma; demerit arises even from the incitement to false conduct, since merit arises from the opposite even in other cases.
Thus, the statement that heaven and joy result solely from the correct application of words is mere talk.
Those who know logic do not respect such scriptures,

nor does anyone’s face become contorted at the words of one who claims that falling from a mountain occurs merely through the correct employment of words, devoid of any injunction regarding the means for accomplishing dharma such as generosity and the like—
*Vādanyāya*, p. 106.

And likewise: "From a true word, merit arises; from another [word], demerit would arise. When there is truth, there is merit; when there is untruth, there is demerit. What then is the fixed rule regarding merit and sin? (Tattvārthaśloka-vārttika, p. 290).
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 668:
From the word arises the cognition of the object to be performed; from that, the performance [of the action]; and from that, the production of *dharma*.

Thus, being composed by an authoritative person (*viśiṣṭapuruṣapraṇītatva*), denoting a specific meaning (*viśiṣṭārthābhidhāyitva*), being free from contradiction (*bādhārahitatva*), being corroborated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntarānugṛhītatva*), and being perceptible by unimpaired sense organs (*anupahatendriyagrāhyatva*)—all these qualities are indeed identical in both cases.
Furthermore, the state of being unobstructed cannot coherently apply to sound even if preceded by a state of being obstructed, because sound lacks permanence;
for it is only a permanent entity that can possess the properties of being obstructed or unobstructed,
and the permanence of sound has already been refuted.

Comparison: "For we do not perceive in these [words] any refinement such as wisdom or extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*), nor is there any absolute quality of being worth hearing, nor any excellence in conveying meaning; if it is argued that 'refinement' is simply the usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*'), then who are the learned? They are those endowed with qualities such as being knowable."
Furthermore, what is this stubborn adherence to falsehood, disregarding the excellence of qualities, that they employ only these very words and not others?—*Vādanyāya*, p.
107—[The term] *aṣṭābhidhā* [is used];
[the reading] *anāvṛtatva* is not tenable. *Bāhyam*.
Furthermore, the quality of having a form established by grammar exists for Prākṛta words just as it does for Saṃskṛta words;
for just as words are derived through the analysis of stems and suffixes by means of Saṃskṛta grammar, so too are they by means of Prākṛta.
If this [Prākṛta] were not a grammar, what confidence could there be in anything else?

There certainly exists a Prākṛta grammar, as has been stated elsewhere—that "Sanskrit speech is uttered," and so forth. Even in that case, at what time should this [Prākṛta] be spoken—at the time of ritual action (*karmakāla*) or at the time of study (*adhyayanakāla*)? If it is at the time of study, at whose time of study? That of Prākṛta or that of Sanskrit? It cannot be that of Prākṛta, because at that time the Sanskrit speech has not yet been expressed; otherwise, its study would be impossible.

Now, regarding the refined language (*saṃskṛta*): how can the Prakrit language be considered incorrect simply because it is not studied at the time of studying that [refined language]? If something were deemed incorrect because another [language] is used at the time of study, then the Vedic speech would also be incorrect, since it is not employed at the time of studying the Purāṇas.

Or, if you mean "at the time of ritual action" (*karmakāla*), why should Prakrit not be spoken then? Is it because it does not convey the meaning, because it is a corrupt word (*apaśabda*), or because it is a cause of demerit (*adharma*)? Among these, the first position is untenable, because it is clearly observed that those who know both the refined and other languages obtain a perfectly clear comprehension of the meaning from words such as *gāvī* and the like (p.
Speech arises—
at the time of [the recitation of] the *Āraṇyaka*, or at the time of studying the *Prākṛta* texts.
If it were not denotable,
then that [nature] would be Prakrit, not Śrauta.

Regarding the phrase "saspaṣṭārtha" (of clear meaning): [is it] because the meaning is not understood, or because words such as *gāvī* and so forth are ungrammatical (*apaśabda*) merely by their own form, or because they are not derived from grammar? If it were merely by their own form, then the consequence would be that even the word *go* would be ungrammatical, since there is no difference between them in that regard.

Furthermore, would the non-formation [of a word] result from grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇa*) out of either the refined language (*saṃskṛta*) or the vernacular (*prākṛta*)? It cannot be from the vernacular, because in that case their own forms are already perceived as being fully formed. Nor can it be even from the grammatical derivation of the refined language; for does the word *gāvī* fail to be formed in its mere phonetic form, or with respect to a specific meaning? It cannot be in its mere phonetic form, since [the rule] states: "The substitute *gu* occurs for *yat*, etc.
(Jainendra 1.2).

114. Thus, while there is respect [for the word], since it is well-known that this word *gāvī* is derived merely by its own form according to the grammatical process (*prakriyā*), and because the word *gāvī* is not established [by derivation] in the specific sense of "cowness" (*gotva*), it is called a corrupt word (*apaśabda*). That too is incorrect, because it is not taught [in that sense] therein; for it is only Prakrit grammar that teaches the word *gāvī* in the sense of "cowness," and nothing else.

Furthermore, if [the word *gāvī*] were considered a corrupt form (*apaśabda*) because it is not produced by [Sanskrit] grammar, then the word *go* would also necessarily be a corrupt form; for there is no distinction, as even *go* is not produced from Prakrit grammar. Therefore, since both the words *go* and *gāvī*—which are established by their respective grammars (Sanskrit and otherwise)—function to denote the same object characterized as "cowness" (*gotva*), how can this restriction be maintained that only the word *go* is the denoter of cowness and not the word *gāvī*? Just as *vṛkṣa*, *taru*, and *pādapa* are synonymous terms whose status as denoters is determined by equal means of valid cognition, so too are *go*, *gāvī*, and the others.

For instance: words such as *go*, *gāvī*, *gauṇī*, and *gopotalikā* are denoters of "cowness" (*gotva*), because they are used by elders without disagreement in that regard, just like [the words] *gauḥ*, *uśrā*, *usrā*, and so forth. Likewise, words such as *gāvī* and others have been in use for "cowness" since time immemorial, because no limit to their usage can be discerned, just like [the words] *gauḥ*, *uśrā*, *usrā*, and so forth; this is established in the *Prākṛta-vyākaraṇa*.
Thus it is said:
"In that which follows *tya*, the word-form beginning with *tya* is designated as *guṇa*.
— Śabdārṇava.
The term *gu* is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) corresponding to the technical designation *aṅga* in Sanskrit grammar, with respect to the meaning characterized as "cow-ness" (*gotva*).
Because the word *gāvī* functions as a denotative term— compare: "Therefore, because it is a synonymous term, [the word] *gāvī* and so forth [are valid], like the word *taru* for a tree."
The fact that [the Veda] is to be employed according to established practice is not refuted by those who abide by the scriptures—
Tantravārttika 1.3.1.
24—Because of [its] nature as a tree—ba;
comparison: words such as *gāvī*, *goṇī*, and so forth, all denote the universal "cowness" (*gotva*).
Because it has been employed there by the elders, just like [the word] *gosra* and so forth
— *Tantravārttika* 1.3.10.
24 –gauṇātali– śra॰ reads *gorūpatvetyā*, while ba॰ reads *gorukṣetyā*.

Regarding the phrase "because it has the form of a cow" (*gorūpatvāt*), etc.: [The opponent asks,] "Now, if this [language] is incorrect because it is a cause of demerit (*adharma*), when exactly does it become a cause of demerit—at all times, or at the time of performing rituals such as sacrifices? If [it were a cause of demerit] at all times, there would never be an occasion for merit (*dharma*). For even at the time of performing obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, since Prakrit words denoting clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, and so forth, as well as those denoting gifts of cows, land, and so on, would be employed, it would follow that they are causes of demerit alone.

Furthermore, at the time of performing sacrifices and other such rites, there is a great majesty to that ritual by which it causes the production of demerit (*adharma*) during its own existence, even though it does not produce demerit at other times. Moreover, the rule that Prakrit speech is invariably a cause of demerit would only be established if there were a corresponding rule that Sanskrit speech is invariably a cause of merit (*dharma*). And if such a rule were accepted, then actors, soldiers, hunters, leather-workers, and others who speak refined Vedic words would produce far greater merit than those who speak Prakrit, such as women observing month-long fasts and the like.

If it is argued that this merit belongs only to the Brahmin who utters those [mantras] and not to anyone else, we say no; for Brahminhood is not established by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.
(cha – caruṭa – Ā॰, ba॰)
The Pulindas, Nāhalas, Niṣṭhyās, Śabaras, Varuṭas, Bhaṭas,
Mālas, Bhillas, and Kirātas— these are all specific tribes of Mlecchas.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Mīmāṃsakas and others is that the caste of Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇyajāti*) is based on a womb (*yoninibandhanā*), endowed with properties such as being eternal, partless, and unitary.

Now, is it not the case that Brahminhood is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone? For, when one has opened one's eyes, among groups of Kṣatriyas and others standing before one, there arises—by way of its distinction from them—a cognition of a uniform, recurring form, "This is a Brahmin, this is a Brahmin," within the group of Brahmins. Thus, Brahminhood is apprehended as a recurring, uniform entity distinct from humanity (*manuṣyatva*) and other such generalities.
Furthermore, this cognition is not doubtful, because it lacks contact with both alternatives;
nor is it erroneous, because it is produced by causes free from defects and is devoid of any subverting cognition.
Moreover, if brahminhood were not perceptible, then there would be no specific manifestation such as "this person is a Brahmin."

For here it is a person qualified by the affection for Brahminhood that appears; it is not, however, a mere person devoid of that [qualification] which appears. For if that were what appeared, the appearance would be "this is a person," and not "this is a Brahmin," since Brahminhood is something distinct from the person.
Furthermore, a cognition of a qualified object is not possible when the qualifier has not been apprehended, as this would lead to an over-extension.

Furthermore, there is no consequence of the universal (jāti) appearing even upon the first perception of a Brahmin who possesses such [specific] qualities, provided those qualities are possible; for a universal is manifested by its own specific particulars (*viśeṣa*). And these particulars, appearing while excluding other universals, manifest their own universals by excluding other universals, just as in the case of cows, horses, and so forth. Therefore, although the universal is perceived there, it does not delineate itself because the difference between the manifestors is not grasped. And this non-apprehension of the difference between the manifestors is established due to the extreme similarity of the parts, just as in the case of an extremely similar cow and a gavaya.

Furthermore, it is observed that for those who examine substances—such as jewel-examiners who distinguish between genuine and counterfeit gems—the distinction between the genuine and the counterfeit, or the genuine gem and glass and so forth, occurs only when there is the presence of a totality of conditions consisting of natural and acquired intuition (*pratibhāsa*) in one who possesses attentiveness. In the same way, here too, for one born from an unimpaired Brāhmaṇa father and an unimpaired Brāhmaṇa mother, the manifestation of the distinct cognition "this is a Brāhmaṇa" occurs only when there is the presence of a totality of conditions characterized by the knowledge of the Brāhmaṇahood of the mother and father, based on traditional instruction.

Alternatively, a cognition grasping the caste of Brahminhood—namely, "this person is a Brahmin"—is produced by the sense faculty assisted by the instruction "this is a Brahmin," independent of any knowledge of that Brahminhood itself.

Nor is it reasonable to say that what does not appear [to consciousness] does not exist due to a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the absence of impairment is ascertained from the absence of reports concerning one's parents.

For deviation is pervaded by popular report; therefore, as the popular report ceases, it causes the deviation to cease, because it is contradictory for the pervaded not to cease when the pervader has ceased.
[If] this is a Brāhmaṇa, this is a Brāhmaṇa—such is the inclusive cognition regarding a Brāhmaṇa... [text fragment] ...if a Brāhmaṇa... [Ānandagiri]
The passage contained within this is not found in Ā—
nor, again, is it merely a person devoid of Brahminhood according to Śra and Brā.
In the appearance of a mere person devoid of Brahminhood,
there is the [cognition] "of a Brahmin," [the cognition] "of a Brahmin," "of a Brahmin."
Even though it was promised to other kinsmen and men, Āryā; Śrāmaṇerī.
— Because of the non-existence of the causal complex—
*ba*, thus taught— *ba*, thus explained— *śra*; one born from a Brāhmaṇī by a Brāhmaṇa would be a Brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt.
It should be exactly the same for a Kṣatriya woman, and indeed also for a Vaiśya woman— Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana-parvan 47.28.
Gold is undoubtedly distinguished from its form as copper and so forth;
melted ghee is distinguished from oil by its smell and taste;
and fire covered by ashes is perceived by touch.
And when a horse or the like is at a distance, certainty arises through its own sound;
[certainty regarding] "pot-ness" and so forth arises from its shape, "Brahmin-hood" and so forth from birth,
and sometimes also from conduct that is properly maintained by the king.
—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Vanavāda, verses 27–29.
How, then, is this well-known to the world? We say: by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But why is it that those who are ignorant of the relationship between mother and father do not recognize [the fact] among men who are in contact with their eyes, even when it has not been told to them? Because of a lack of capacity (*śaktyabhāva*), just as [one does not recognize] "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) prior to the acquisition of linguistic proficiency (*abhidhāna-vyutpatti*).

Therefore, just as light, the sense organ, the integration of multiple aggregates, the recollection of words, manifestation, magnitude, proximity, specific forms, and so forth are causes for the apprehension of another genus (*jāti*), so too in this case is the recollection of the producing genus [the cause].

Furthermore, this relationship between the produced and the producer is perceptible only to the mother; for others, however, it is known through inference and authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) as the cause.
Nor is Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) a collection of austerity (*tapas*) and other qualities, nor is it the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by them, nor is it the genus manifested by them.
What then? It is manifested by the knowledge of the birth of one's mother and father, and is to be apprehended through direct perception— Tantravārttika 1.2.6.

Therefore, even though the individual bodies may appear identical in form, the universal such as "Brahmin-ness" (brāhmaṇya), which is cognized through a distinct cognition of "Brahmin," cannot be denied—
*Tantravārttika*, *Nyāyasudhā*, pp. 10–15.

Just as the universal (jāti) such as Brāhmaṇahood, although perceptible by the sense of sight depending upon instruction, does not forfeit its status as being cognizable through perception; and just as another cause for the cognition of the universal such as Brāhmaṇahood has been stated—namely, "also from conduct, when there is proper protection by a king"—so too, in a region where the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) are protected by a capable monarch who follows the faultless path shown by Manu and others, and where the deviation of Śūdras is observed through their suspiciously feigned dress and actions, the universal such as Brāhmaṇahood is cognized even through specific conduct (*viśiṣṭācāra*)—[Nyāyamañjarī, p.
422]—provided there is knowledge of the Brāhmaṇahood of one's mother and father.
However, he himself will state that this relationship is difficult to discern due to the transgression of women;
yet its status as perception is not lost by that alone,
for it is not the case that what is apprehended after climbing a mountain peak is therefore not perceptual.
Nor is it logical to assume that all women are unchaste simply because infidelity is observed in some cases, for such an inference would contradict worldly experience and be impossible; indeed,

women of noble lineage protect themselves with great effort, and for this very reason, kings and brahmins have instituted communal registers in order not to forget the succession of their own fathers, grandfathers, and so forth.
And thus, from the recollection of qualities and defects as being favorable or unfavorable, activities of engagement and withdrawal corresponding to them are observed—
Tantravārttika 1.2.1.2.
The word "kalpanā" (conceptual construction) in the inference is intended to indicate that femininity is both deviant and non-probative;

nor is worldly cognition invalid due to being rootless, for it is possible for it to have a basis in the non-perception of the fit [object] despite diligent search. To demonstrate this, he says: "For by a qualified... etc.

For men of noble lineage, the protection of their wives is indeed the protection of themselves, because of the traditional teaching that "when the wife is protected, the self is protected. Alternatively, it is stated that women belong to great families in order to show that being born of a low family is the cause of a proclivity toward infidelity, rather than womanhood itself. He confirms this very certainty regarding the absence of infidelity through the practice of experienced elders with the words "by this very [means]."

The point is that if there were no certainty regarding the absence of deviation [from the truth], then the collective document consisting of the recording of the lineage of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth would be useless because it would lack a foundation.

He confirms this very point by means of the contemporary practice of marriage and other transactions preceded by an examination of the family, stating "and likewise" (*tathā ca*)—*Tantravārttika*, *Nyāyasudhā*, p. 12.

Wherever the causal complex for perception is present, even if there is no observed deviation among those [factors], it follows that there is indeed no deviation; this is established by worldly authority (*lokapramāṇaka*). Furthermore, women must be guarded against negligence; in their case, there is simply no room for the possibility of suspecting deviation. However, as for those [women] where such suspicion exists, let there be no certainty regarding the descent of their offspring from that specific lineage.
Yet, it is not logical to conclude that because certainty is impossible in some cases, it must therefore be non-existent even in those cases where it is possible.
—*Prakaraṇapañcikā*, Pañcamasthāna, p.
31 — *cāraṃ vini* (variant: *ba*).

Furthermore, if the word "brāhmaṇa" did not have the caste (*jāti*) of a Brāhmaṇa as its meaning, then it would be meaningless; yet this is not tenable, because the cognition of a meaning is observed to arise immediately after the utterance of this [word].

Furthermore, since the linguistic usage based on that [universal], such as "Feed the Brāhmaṇa," is well-known, unambiguous, and uncontradicted, even among those bearing the marks of the Pāśupatas and others, we observe linguistic usages—such as names, insignia, conduct, and instruction—that correspond to the universal of Brāhmaṇahood and so forth. Therefore, because of the observation of such firmly established linguistic usage, the universal of Brāhmaṇahood exists as an entity distinct from the individuals; it is well-established through perception as the basis for the application of the word "Brāhmaṇa."

Likewise, [the existence of the universal is established] through inference as well; for instance: in the absence of an obstructing factor, whatever cognition has a certain form is caused by an object possessing that form, just like the cognition of blue and so forth. And in the absence of an obstructing factor, there occurs a uniform, single-form cognition such as "this is a Brāhmaṇa, this is a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, [this cognition] is caused by the universal "Brāhmaṇahood," which is distinct from the individual bodies.

For whatever is the form of the cognition, the object must also possess that very same form; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that a cognition of blue would have a non-blue object, which would entail the collapse of the established order of specific entities. Likewise, the cognition "this is a Brāhmaṇa" is based on a *brāhmaṇya* (Brāhmaṇahood) distinct from the physical body, because—in the absence of any impediment—it arises with the form "this is a Brāhmaṇa. Similarly, the word "Brāhmaṇa" is connected to a single denotable cause distinct from the individual, because it is a word, like the word "cloth" and others.
And this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it exists in the subject (*dharmin*);
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it does not occur in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) alone;
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it does not occur in the counter-example any more than it does in the subject or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is the example deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because the property of being a word (*padatva*) exists in words such as "cloth" (*paṭa*);

nor is it deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because in those cases, since there is no connection with a single denotable object distinct from the individuals, it would be impossible to grasp the relationship [between word and meaning] even in an infinite amount of time due to the infinity of individuals,
in the case of words such as "cloth."

Just as there is a single cause called "cloth-ness" (paṭatva) which is distinct from the individual pieces of cloth, so too the cognition "this is a Brāhmaṇa" is based on a cause distinct from specific color, study, conduct, the sacred thread, and so forth; this is because that cognition is of a different character than the cognitions of cows, horses, and the like.
Furthermore, the caste of Brāhmaṇa is well-established through such scriptural injunctions as, "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," and "A Brāhmaṇa should be fed."

Furthermore, this [creation] is well-known from the Vedas, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas; for one hears there many statements establishing that very point, such as: "In the beginning, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇa from his mouth, the Kṣatriya from his arms, the Vaiśya from his thighs, and the Śūdra from his feet.
Thus: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth, the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms, what was his thighs became the Vaiśya, and from his feet the Śūdra was born."
*Ṛgveda Puruṣasūkta 12*:
Of this Prajāpati, the person distinguished by the caste of Brāhmaṇa was the mouth; the meaning is that he was produced from the mouth.
That which is the Rājanya, distinguished by the caste of Kṣatriya, was made the arms; the meaning is that he was brought forth as the arms and produced from the two arms.
At that time, from the thighs of this Prajāpati, one of the form of a Vaiśya was produced—meaning he was generated from the thighs;
likewise, from his feet—that is, from the two feet—a Śūdra, a person belonging to the Śūdra caste, was born.
And this origin of the Brāhmaṇas and the others from the mouth and other parts [is described] in the Yajurveda Saṃhitā, section 31.

In the seventh book, at the beginning of the passage starting with "He fashioned the *trivṛt* from his mouth," it is clearly stated— according to the words of Sāyaṇa’s commentary— that [the *trivṛt* was created].
Thus says Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara Miśra.
Regarding the argument that, in this context, Brahminhood consists solely in the nature of a corresponding transformation of speech and is not based on birth,
the following response is provided:

As for what was stated—that Brahminhood is perceived by perception itself, and so forth—that is incorrect. For, is that [perception] which perceives it produced by the sense-faculties alone, or is it produced by the sense-faculties assisted by something else? In the first case, is it perceived by that [perception] produced as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) or as conceptual (*savikalpaka*)? It cannot be by the non-conceptual one, because there is no appearance of genus (*jāti*) and so forth therein; or, if there were such an appearance, its status as non-conceptual would be contradicted. Otherwise, how could this be tenable? (p. 768, l. 18)
Comparison—In that regard, would the apprehension of that [object] arise from non-conceptual cognition or from conceptual cognition? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 482; Syādvādaratnākara, p.
Or rather,
that [is established] by non-conceptual perception produced by the sense faculties.
For there exists an initial non-conceptualizing cognition of mere observation, which arises from the pure object itself and is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others.

Commentary: To one who cannot tolerate the word "also" (api) and believes that all cognition is exclusively conceptual because it is permeated by words—thinking that no non-conceptual cognition exists at all—the author says: "There exists... (asti).

Just as for children, so too for us who are untrained, immediately following the conjunction of the sense-organ with the object, there first exists a non-conceptual perception established by experience—an immediate awareness (*ālocanavijñāna*) whose object is the pure thing-in-itself. For in its absence, the recollection of words would be without cause;
and for one who has not recollected the word, a conceptual construction permeated by language is impossible.
Thus, he explains that it is "born from the pure thing": "At that time, neither the particular nor the universal is perceived."

However, it is the individual (vyakti) itself that is determined as the substratum of those two; others, moreover, call it the "great universal" (mahāsāmānya) and say it is a real substance (dravyasat) — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, Nyāyaratnākara.
This has been cited: "If primordial cognition is non-conceptual" (Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 385; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
482; Prameyaratnakośa, p.
Syādvādamañjarī, verse 13;
Hyālocanajñāna— Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā, page 11.
Furthermore, that cognition by which an object is subsequently determined through properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth is also accepted as being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore,

according to the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika* and the *Nyāyaratnākara*, that cognition which grasps an object by conceptualizing it through genus and so forth at a time subsequent to the non-conceptual [perception] is indeed direct perception itself.
This has been extracted from the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p. 385), the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.
482), and the *Syādvādaratnākara* (p.

Nor can it be apprehended by determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*), because such cognition cannot function with respect to that which is not the object of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); or, if it were so possible, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, for one whose eyes are wide open, there is no manifestation of a single, inclusive property of "Brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇya*)—distinct from "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) or "masculinity" (*puṃstva*)—which persists across all its own individual instances, in the same way that "cowness" (*gotva*) or "horseness" (*aśvatva*) is perceived in various individuals like a humpbacked or hornless cow, or as "whiteness" (*śuklatva*) is perceived in various human individuals.

If it is asked, "How can there be such a case where a continuous cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*) occurs, being attached to the state of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇatva*)?"—it is by virtue of convention (*saṅketa*). For just as there is a single continuous cognition in the form "cow, cow" with respect to mutually distinct things like cows and vajras—even though there is no single universal (*sāmānya*) in the form of "cowness" (*gotva*)—so too, despite the mutual distinctness of individual human beings, there will be a single continuous cognition in the form "this is a Brahmin, this is a Brahmin."

If, however, [the cognition] were produced by the power of the real entity (*vastu*), then it would occur even with respect to individuals for whom the convention has not been grasped, simply through the perception of that [entity] alone—just like the non-erroneous cognition of a "cow" [with respect to a cow]. But this is not the case;

for indeed, just as the universal "cowness" (*go-jāti*) appears with a distinct difference when one encounters a herd of buffaloes and the like, and as a quality or an action appears within its own group, so too Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) never appears as something distinct.

For Brahminhood does not appear as something differentiated from "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*), which is manifested by the form of hands, feet, and so forth, in the same way that the universals such as "masculinity" (*puṃstva*) appear.

Would that [universal] be perceived by that non-conceptual cognition produced by a sense-faculty assisted by something else, or by a conceptual cognition? In both cases, the aforementioned defects would follow, because it would entail the absurd consequence that even from conceptual constructions such as daydreams, the reality of an object would be established.

For instance, when one with wide-open eyes perceives individual instances before him—such as a humpbacked person, a bald man, or a white horse—one does not perceive any "Brahmin-ness" distinct from the universals of "humanity," "manhood," and so forth, just as one does not perceive a universal of "cow-ness" or "horse-ness" in those individuals.
— syā॰ ra॰ pṛ॰ 958 because of being a human male— ā॰, ba॰ — from the [state of] vyati– śra॰.
In the case of a Brahmin— [as found in] Ā, Śra,
and Ba— among individuals who have attained [the state of] a Brahmin, this person is a Brahmin because he is not distinct from humanity and masculinity. Śra.
And by the mere perception of the object itself, there arises the cognition: "This is a cow," or "This is a Brahmin."
Humanity (manuṣyatva) indeed pervades both women and men within their respective classes, such as queens and so forth; however, manhood (puruṣatva) exists only in men.
—The universal (jāti) is [perceived] by means of perception, [as it is] distinct from [the individual] "you" and so forth. Śra.

Brahminhood; the state of being a Brahmin.

Furthermore, when the sense faculties produce direct perception of their respective objects, what else is intended as their auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*)—is it being born from parents who are Brāhmaṇas, the instruction that one's parents are untainted, a specific conduct, a specific sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), Vedic study, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, or origination from Brahmā? Among these, the first position is untenable; for if the Brāhmaṇahood of the parents were already established, then the son’s Brāhmaṇahood would be established by virtue of being born from them. And that [Brāhmaṇahood of the parents] would have to be established either because they were born from parents who were Brāhmaṇas, or because they produced a son of such a nature. In the first case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

"Because the stream of cause and effect is beginningless, like that of a seed and its sprout, this infinite regress is not a fault"—this too is incorrect. For while the causal relationship between a seed and its sprout is cognized through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as independent of the apprehension of any prior seed-sprout causal relationship, here, in the absence of the realization of each preceding Brahminhood, it is impossible to bring about the realization of each subsequent Brahminhood; therefore, there is not even the slightest similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration.
