In the second case, however, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for only when the Brāhmaṇa-status of the father is established can the son’s Brāhmaṇa-status be established by virtue of being born from a father who is a Brāhmaṇa; and once that is established, the father’s Brāhmaṇa-status is established because he is the progenitor of a son who is a Brāhmaṇa. Now, what is it that is intended here as the auxiliary factor for the sense organs: being born from one's own father who is a Brāhmaṇa, an uncorrupted instruction regarding the father, a specific conduct, a specific sacrament (*saṃskāra*), the study of the Vedas, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, or origination from Brahmā? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
958; *janmatvaṃ* is read as *baṃ*).
Regarding that, [the opponent asks]:

"Is the knowledge of the Brāhmaṇahood of one's father and so forth a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid one? Furthermore, would that [Brāhmaṇahood] be established because the father was born from a Brāhmaṇa mother, or because he produced a son who is such [a Brāhmaṇa]? (See *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 483; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 959).

The establishment of Brahminhood [depends on] the state of being a Brahmin; the establishment of the son's Brahminhood [depends on] that [state]; and upon the establishment of that, there is the establishment of the Brahmin. (Variant readings: *brāhmaṇyabhūta* for *brāhmaṇyabhāve*; *putrabrāhmaṇyasiddhiḥ* for *putrabrāhmaṇyasiddhiḥ*; *brāhmaṇa-* for *brāhmaṇya-*)

The claim that "one born from an unimpaired Brāhmaṇa father and an unimpaired Brāhmaṇī mother is a Brāhmaṇa" is merely a matter of faith, as the instruction regarding such unimpaired parents cannot be established as factual through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Where something is not cognized by any means of valid cognition, no factual instruction can exist regarding it—just as there can be no factual instruction concerning the voidness of all things. Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇahood you have postulated is not cognized by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.

Now, if it is argued that the instruction as stated is enjoined only after Brahminhood has been perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that is incorrect, because it entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). For only when the direct perception of Brahminhood is established can the aforementioned instruction, which serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), be established; and only when that [instruction] is established can the direct perception of Brahminhood be established by the sense organ aided by such an instruction.
Thus, the status of being twice-born (*dvija*) and so forth does not indeed fall within the range of the objects of valid cognition.

Is it characterized by the connection with birth, or by the characteristic of lineage (*gotra*), or by the possession of an excellence in the capacity for action? Instruction based on the authority of another's teaching is not logical regarding an object of direct perception;
for instruction among people proceeds even otherwise—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 22.
Nor is it apprehended by perception with the aid of instruction, because it is illogical for there to be a dependence on instruction regarding an object of perception;
or, if such dependence were possible, the operation would belong to the instruction alone, and thus it would be manifested by instruction alone—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p.

Furthermore, there can be no instruction regarding Brahminhood because it is not perceived through any real means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, if the perceptibility of the genus "Brahminhood" were established, then the aforementioned instruction could be established as a cause for that perception; and if that [instruction] were established, then its perceptibility would be established—thus there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 483)

Furthermore, regarding the state of being unimpaired (*avipḷutatva*), is it intended with respect to a specific father, or with respect to the stream of fathers from beginningless time? If it is with respect to a specific father, then even in that case, is the state of being unimpaired intended for these two [the father and son] in that particular birth, or throughout beginningless time? If it is in that birth, by whom would that state be perceived there—by the son, or by others? It cannot be by the son, because even at the time of his own birth, he lacks the capacity for such discernment.

Nor can it be known by other means. For would that [causal relation] be cognized by them through perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)? It cannot be through perception, because an object of the nature "this has arisen from this" cannot be perceived by one whose vision is limited to the present.
Nor can it be through inference, because you do not admit inference where there is no object of perception, and inference arises only from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, there is no mark whatsoever for the state of being "unconfused" (avipluta) regarding the parents.

For in that regard, would the mark consist in a specific quality such as a concealed appearance on the part of the parents, or rather in the lack of distinctness among the offspring? The first position is untenable, because even those who are of immoral conduct are seen to have extremely concealed appearances.

The second position is also unconvincing; for if a distinct appearance were established among the offspring born of confused versus non-confused parents, then the non-confusion of the parents could be determined from the perception of offspring lacking such distinctness. However, that [distinctness] is not established.

Indeed, no difference whatsoever is perceived—even in a dream—between offspring born of a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, as there is between offspring of a mare from a donkey and a horse; nor can the non-corruption of those two [castes] be established through scripture, whether it be of non-human (apauruṣeya) or human (pauruṣeya) origin. It cannot be established by means of non-human scripture, because such a scripture that could establish it is simply impossible.

Even a human-authored scripture attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when its author is understood to have established the non-corruption of these two [the Veda and its author] through another means of knowledge; however, it has been stated that there is no such understanding from any source whatsoever.
Therefore, at the time of its production, the non-corruption of these two cannot be ascertained from any source.
As for the "purity through comparison" (*tulanā-śuddhi*), it occurs when both lineages are pure—that is, when the purity of the parents of each [author] is individually established.

"In that case, due to the fault of having an endless number of lineages, what caste could be free from fault? And who among those associated with the class of women has not had sin transferred to them?
— *Naiṣadhacarita* 17.17.

And by what is "non-deviation" (aviplutatva) intended: with respect to a specific father, or with respect to the stream of fathers from beginningless time? If it is with respect to a specific father, then is their non-deviation intended in that particular birth, or throughout beginningless time? If it is in that birth, then by whom would it be perceived there—by the son or by others? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
959; *tajjanya-vipluta* MS).

Regarding the claim that there is non-defilement in that birth with respect to the intended father, there is no evidence whatsoever for the non-defilement of the parents. For what could that be? Is it a specific feature such as a concealed form, or is it the lack of distinction [in appearance] among the offspring? (Syādvādamañjarī, p.
959; variants: *pitṛviplu-* in Ā, B).
Comparison—Furthermore, no distinction is observed among the offspring of fathers who are either corrupted or otherwise;

indeed, just as no distinction is observed among the offspring of a mare produced from both donkeys and horses, so too no distinction is observed among the offspring of a Brāhmaṇī woman produced from both Brāhmaṇas and Śūdras. (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 483)
And it is not the case that conception occurs anywhere through a man who belongs to a different caste with a woman; rather,
[conception] occurs for those of the Brahmin and other castes.

If it is argued that there is no possibility of a birth from a mare by means of a donkey, we say no; for he would not belong to an entirely different species, due to the similarity of their bodies, such as the presence of hooves and so forth.
Or else, just like that [case], the offspring of the two would be dissimilar.
Since it is not observed to be so here, the establishment of the castes is therefore based on qualities—
Padma Purāṇa 11.196–98.
Since differences in color, form, and so forth are not observed in this body,
and since the initiation of conception by Śūdras and others occurs among those designated as Brāhmaṇas and so on,
there is no distinction among human beings based on caste, just as there is none between cows and horses.
Therefore, because [the universal] is grasped as a form, it is conceptualized otherwise—
*Uttarapuṭa* 74,
—Regarding the state of being born from a father:
the comparison is that among offspring whose other origins are obscured, there is a distinct form;
yet there is no Vedic statement whatsoever that establishes [the status of] being twice-born (dvijāti).
"A statement regarding a universal with respect to a particular is indeed equivalent to what was not stated at all"—
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, folio 25b.2.
That which is established by scripture is not relied upon by the Śrāvaka; rather,
there is the realization of its being uncorrupted.

By this, the apprehension of those two [parents] as being untainted throughout beginningless time is rejected; for it is truly a great marvel to claim that the untaintedness of two individuals—who cannot even be apprehended as such in their current birth—is apprehended throughout beginningless time! By this, the assertion of untaintedness with respect to a lineage of ancestors stretching back to beginningless time is also refuted.

Furthermore, because women are always observed to commit adultery in this very life due to their passion for men, it is impossible even for Brahmā to know what they might have done throughout beginningless time;

thus, the claim that "adultery is pervaded by public rumor" and so forth is incorrect. For even in the absence of public rumor, adultery is possible for those who are extremely secretive lovers, and therefore it is logically untenable for it to be pervaded by such rumors.

Therefore, since the purity of one's parents cannot be established from any source whatsoever, their instruction does not function as a cooperative cause for the eye in the manifestation of the direct perception of Brāhmaṇahood. As they say: "In this beginningless saṃsāra, where the god with the fish-banner is difficult to resist and the family is rooted in women, what is the point of imagining caste?"
In this beginningless lineage of clans, there has been no lapse on the part of a woman.
Thus, how can this be knowledge? For women are always afflicted by desire;
since Brahminhood was established previously, the possibility of belonging to that lineage would have arisen then.
Since that was not established, how can this lineage be anything other than a blind tradition?
—*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 25:
"A great deal of time has passed, and women are exceedingly fickle;
therefore, even though [the lineage] exists, it is impossible to ascertain Brahminhood."
Indeed, there exists no one whatsoever who knows supersensuous objects;
nor has even the eternal Veda declared the purity of your lineage—Tattvasaṃgraha, v. 3579–80.

Since women are generally observed to commit sexual misconduct even in this very life due to negligence and the affliction of desire, how can there be any certainty regarding Brahminhood based on the womb?

Furthermore, in the beginningless succession of lineages (*gotrapaddhati*), because women are always subject to the affliction of desire, it is possible for any one of them to deviate; therefore, how can there be a certainty that the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and the study of the Vedas (*adhyayana*) are unerring, given the lack of certainty regarding Brahminhood based on the womb? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 482)
—Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 698; Syādvāda-ratnākara, p.
"There is never a state of pure conduct for either a Brahmin or a non-Brahmin."
In the beginningless lineage, where does no transgression ever arise?
— *Dharmapada* 17.28.

Nor is it a specific practice (*ācāraviśeṣa*); for that [practice], such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), is unique to the Brāhmaṇa. However, it cannot be the cause for the perception of that [Brāhmaṇa-hood], because of the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For there would be under-extension, since the designation [of "Brāhmaṇa"] would not apply even to those Brāhmaṇas who are devoid of officiating at sacrifices and so forth. Furthermore, there would be over-extension, because the entire practice of officiating at sacrifices and so forth is observed among Śūdras as well, which would result in the undesired consequence of their being Brāhmaṇas.

Now, if that specific conduct is false in this case, how could it be true elsewhere? If you argue that it is because Brahminhood is established [by it], there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for Brahminhood is established only when the truth of the conduct is established, and the truth of the conduct is established only when Brahminhood is established. [The Creator] ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, officiating at sacrifices, performing sacrifices, as well as giving and receiving gifts.

—Manusmṛti 1.88. For comparison: "Now, [caste] is known through specific actions such as study and so forth, not from mere instruction alone"; that too is incorrect, for action is to be accomplished by one who is already of the twice-born caste; it is not through action that one becomes twice-born.
Nor is its cognition from verbal testimony non-contradictory—
[as stated in] *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 23—
since those rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) which are well-known [in the world] are like anything else.
"For those [who possess] conduct are indeed possessed of concealment even regarding artificial things"— *Tattvasaṃgraha-kārikā* 3578.
For this very reason, neither the specific activity of study nor its accompaniment is established as being [the cause].

For it is observed that even a Śūdra, through the loss of his own caste, becomes a Brāhmaṇa in another land and performs the study of the Vedas and the rites prescribed therein—[Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
485]; because of the consequence of both under-extension and over-extension—[Syādvādaratnākara, p. 960].
In that regard, there is the conduct [of others] toward Śūdras and so forth;

furthermore, if one accepts that Brāhmaṇahood is established through conduct, it would follow as an absurd consequence that one is not a Brāhmaṇa prior to the investiture with the sacred thread (vratibandha).
Therefore, conduct (*ācāra*) also is not a limb for the perception of that [Brahminhood], just as it is not a limb for the perception of Brahminhood itself;

by this, the status of specific sacraments (*saṃskāra*) as limbs thereof is also rejected, since the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) are no different in this case as well.
In that regard, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), because it would follow that even a Brāhmaṇa would not be a Brāhmaṇa prior to a specific consecration (*saṃskāra*);
furthermore, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because even one who is not a Brāhmaṇa would incur the status of being a Brāhmaṇa once consecrated in such a manner.
By this, the status of Vedic study, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth as being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of that [Brāhmaṇahood] is refuted.

Furthermore, if being born from Brahmā were a constituent factor [of Brahminhood], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because all living beings are born from him, which would result in the absurdity that everyone is a Brahmin. As for the comparison: "By this, the view that specific sacraments (*saṃskāra*), Vedic study, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth, act as auxiliary causes for [the perception of] the eye is refuted; for here too, the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remain no different. — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 961.
—because the two [types of] pervasion are impossible there—; because of the impossibility of being a property [of the subject], it is not a means of proof for the state of being a cow.
In the case of "gatve," [the reading is] "ba."
If being a Brāhmaṇa were based on direct perception,
then by the mere fact of being the offspring of a Brāhmaṇa, one would follow as a Brāhmaṇa;
yet no one is ever found anywhere who has been born from a non-Brāhmaṇa body.
If there were a distinction of birth in the interval, how could it be without a cause?
Since there is no distinction of action in the interim, caste serves no purpose for anyone.
Now, if you maintain that the distinction among the castes of the twice-born and others is beginningless;

How indeed could it be known? Since there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because that [lineage] is not fully understood, it follows that there would be no activity at all;
furthermore, the non-interruption of the lineage cannot be established.
If it is argued that "charioteers, bards, and outcastes are known by those who know them to be exactly as they are; how else could they be so?"—we reply that there is no such rule (niyama).
(Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra, p. 24)
Furthermore, regarding the fact that [the Brāhmaṇas] originate from Brahmā:

does Brahman possess the quality of being a Brāhmaṇa or not? If it does not, how can there be the birth of a Brāhmaṇa from him? For the birth of a human from a non-human is not observed. If, on the other hand, he does possess it, is it present everywhere or only in the region of the mouth? If it were everywhere, it would follow that there is no distinction between living beings.
If [the Brahminhood] resides only in the region of the mouth, then because it would follow that he is a Śūdra elsewhere, his feet and other parts would not be objects of veneration for Brāhmaṇas.

For instance: "Furthermore, does Brahminhood exist in a Brāhmaṇa or not? If it does not exist, how can a Brāhmaṇa be produced from him? If it does exist, does it exist everywhere or only in the region of the mouth? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 484; Syādvādaratnākara, p.
From the non-Brahmin, the Brahmin-status is understood (ba), or rather, the state of being a Brahmin is understood (śra) everywhere among the limbs of the body, from the face down to the feet.
Furthermore, regarding Brahmanas among the four castes:

is it that only one who is already a Brahmana is born from his mouth, or is he born from his mouth precisely because he is a Brahmana? In either case, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for if Brahmanahood is established, then his birth from his mouth is established; and if his birth from his mouth is established, then Brahmanahood is established.
Furthermore, the qualification of "being born from Brahmā" is not perceived by anyone at the time of the direct perception of Brahminhood;
nor is it possible for an unperceived qualification to produce a cognition of the qualified object, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Whatever is a qualification produces a cognition of the qualified object only when it itself is perceived, just like a staff or similar attributes. And since the quality of being born from Brahmā is the qualification in the perception of Brahminhood [it must likewise be perceived].
Comparison: Furthermore, O Brahmin, if he is born from his very mouth, would he not be born from the mouth of that [Brahmin] alone?—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
484; and indeed, he [is born] from the Brahmin alone. [Ā., B.]

By this, the inference—beginning with “whatever cognition has such-and-such a form, provided there is no impediment”—which seeks to establish the existence of Brahminhood, is refuted; for it has been demonstrated in many ways (pp. 769, l. 8) that impediments do indeed exist.

Furthermore, the inference stated as "the word *brāhmaṇa* [denotes a single cause]" and so forth is also incorrect; for the subject (*pakṣa*) is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣa-bādhitatvāt*). For, in the case of individual *brāhmaṇa*s such as those of the Kaṭha and Kalāpa lineages, the word *brāhmaṇa* is perceived through direct observation to be devoid of any relation to a denotable object that is a single cause distinct from the individuals themselves, just like the property of being non-audible (*aśrāvaṇatva*) is absent from sound.

Furthermore, the thesis has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*); for indeed, neither for the Mīmāṃsaka nor for us is the state of being connected with a denotable object that is a single cause distinct from the individual ever established anywhere, since both parties accept a universal (*sāmānya*) that is both distinct and non-distinct [from the individual].

Moreover, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for even in the absence of connection with a denotable object that is a single cause distinct from the individual—as in the case of the words *sattā*, *ākāśa*, *kāla*, or words such as *advaita*—the property of being a word (*padatva*) still exists.

In this case as well, if one assumes that [the word] is connected to that [universal], it would contradict both the universal's lack of further universals (*niḥsāmānyatva*) and its subsistence in multiple individuals (*anekavyaktivṛttitva*). Furthermore, since non-duality (*advaita*), total emptiness (*akhilaśūnyatva*), and so forth would possess a universal, they would necessarily follow as being ultimately real (*paramārthasat*); how then could there be an establishment of a thesis without opposition? Moreover, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because it is not established that words such as "cloth" have a single cause distinct from the individual objects.

It has been explained during the refutation of an eternal relation (on page 769, line 13) how the relationship between infinite individual instances of the signified and the signifier is established even without a single, eternal universal (*sāmānya*). For instance,

if it is argued that the object of this cognition is established as being merely a cause distinct from the individuals and so forth, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we accept that the collection— which is in some sense non-different from its constituent members— is the object of that cognition.

Now, if it is asserted that [the universal] resides completely in each individual and is entirely distinct [from them], then the thesis is contradicted by its counter-thesis; for in the case of individual Brāhmaṇas such as those of the Kaṭha and Kalāpa lineages, the cognition "Brāhmaṇa" is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being devoid of any cause in the form of a universal distinct from the individuals and so forth, just like the sound [which is perceived] as distinct from its quality of being non-audible (i.e., being audible).
(Syādvādamañjarī, p. 961; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 4)
Now, [the following] is not accepted by the Jains.
[The opponent] accepts a universal that is distinct [from individuals], which is in some way both different and non-different from the individuals— [this is] accepted by both [parties].

If the Mīmāṃsakas and Jains were to accept a relation between individuals and universals such as existence (*sattātva*), etherhood (*ākāśatva*), temporality (*kālatva*), and non-duality (*advaitatva*), which are distinct from the individuals themselves, then [the category of] generality (*sāmānya*) would be established. — Ābhoga.
Because this would entail the proof of both non-duality and the voidness of all things (p. 546),
the inference beginning with "due to the specific nature of the phonemes" and so forth is thereby refuted, as the aforementioned defects apply here without distinction.

Furthermore, the cognition [of "city" and so forth] is non-conclusive because, even in the absence of a basis consisting of a cause distinct from the individual [constituents], one perceives a difference in cognition based on specific colors and other such factors.
Indeed, in cognitions such as "city," "army," or "forest," there exists nothing whatsoever distinct from the individuals that serves as the basis for the recurring (anuvṛtta) notion.

For that [basis] would have to be either a substance (*dravya*), existence (*sattā*), or a particular kind of proximity (*pratyāsatti-viśeṣa*). Regarding the first position: is the substance in that case the city and so forth themselves, or something else? It cannot be the city and so forth themselves, because it is impossible for them to be substances.
A city, an army, or any such thing cannot exist as a substance, because it is impossible for them to originate from things that are unconnected and heterogeneous.
If it is argued that there is a conjunction among a few houses, we say no; for since those houses themselves consist of conjunction, they cannot be the substrata of further conjunction.
Furthermore, because they are of the nature of qualities (*guṇa*), they cannot originate a substance, as it is impossible for substances to be originated by qualities.
Page 769, line 18. For comparison: Just as in the case of the cognition of a city and so forth, such a cognition is somehow possible even in the absence of a distinct external basis;

for even in the cognition of a city and so forth, there exists no other distinct substance that could serve as the basis for a uniform cognition. This is because it is logical that the very materials, such as timber and the like—which through some proximity serve as the basis for the conventional usage of "palace" and so forth—serve as the basis for the conventional usage of "city" and so forth. Otherwise, one would be forced to postulate a separate entity even in cases such as "the city of six" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*).
—Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 697; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 485; Syādvādaratnākara, p.
— Even in the absence of a formal connection (nibandhana), because the conjunction of houses, being a quality (guṇa), is dependent upon a substance (dravya)— Ā, Śra.
Substances of houses originate another substance, and qualities [originate] another quality; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8.

10. Thus, by this rule, even in the case of [the cognition] "existence is a city" and so forth, would this [existence] produce that cognition either as qualified by houses and the like, or as unqualified? First, it cannot be unqualified, because there would be the undesirable consequence of that cognition arising even in a location devoid of houses and such. Nor can it be qualified by houses and the like, because it is impossible for that which is immutable and eternal to be qualified, and because that which effects nothing cannot be a qualifier.
Or, if [Being] were to perform some action, its immutability (*kūṭasthatā*) would be compromised.
Furthermore, how could a collection be possible in the case of "the city of six" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*), given that Being is of a single nature and thus a collection cannot be established?
Being.
The cognition "city" [arises] from existence, from existence.
Regarding the phrase "because of [the production of] houses, etc.":
if houses and so forth produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) in existence (*sattā*), then...
The eternal and uniform nature of *sattā* (Being) would be contradicted;

furthermore, by what specific proximity (*pratyāsatti-viśeṣa*) could anything be designated as a "city" or the like, and with what? If it is argued that houses and so forth [are so designated] because of their relation to other houses and so forth, then what is this relation—between them and those others—is it inherence (*samavāya*) or conjunction (*saṃyoga*)? It cannot be inherence, because since they are established separately (*yutasiddhatā*) and lack the relationship of container and contained (*ādhāryādhārabhūtatva*), inherence is impossible there.
Nor can it be conjunction, because houses and so forth, being themselves of the nature of conjunction, cannot be the substratum of conjunction.

Furthermore, from words such as "city" (*nagara*), no one is observed to have cognition, activity, or attainment regarding a single specific proximity characterized by a minimal degree of conjunction through conjunction (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*);

rather, those [cognitions and so forth] are perceived with respect to multiple objects—such as houses and the like—from the word "city," horses and the like from the word "army" (*senā*), and *dhava* trees and the like from the word "forest.
For that which is understood through cognition and the rest when a word is uttered is the meaning of that word, according to the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).

The claim that houses and the like, when qualified by proximity to a location and so forth, receive the designation "city" and so on, is also refuted by this [very argument]. For regarding the proximity in a location—whether it be their inherence (*samavāya*) or conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—the aforementioned fault remains equally applicable.

How, then, could such a designation as "city" occur for you? This objection is not to be raised; for we accept that the designation applies to palaces and the like when they are qualified by proximity to a location.

Furthermore, in this context, proximity to a location should be understood as characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since for us, palaces and the like are accepted as being composite wholes (*avayavin*).

The objection that "how can it possess the nature of a composite (avayavin), since its production from heterogeneous materials such as wood and bricks is impossible," is also untenable; for we observe the production of composites such as bodies even from heterogeneous elements like earth and so forth.

Furthermore, the rule that production must be from homogeneous materials was refuted during the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*) on the occasion of denying that earth and the other elements are distinct ultimate realities (*tattvāntara*).

Consequently, according to your own view, since the cognition of a city and the like lacks a basis in any cause distinct from the individual objects, this [reason you provide] is proven to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, there is no other mark of Brahminhood from which its establishment could follow.

In the case of houses and so forth, one house is conjoined with another, and that [second] with yet another; thus, due to this conjunction of what is already conjoined (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*), there is a state of being smaller, namely, the quality of occupying a smaller space. In that regard—
— The proximity of the suffix *ṇa*— is for the sake of a person's comprehension, engagement, and attainment.

Comparison: Since it is established that from the word *senā* (army) there arises, in multiple instances, cognition, activity, and attainment regarding objects such as elephants and so forth, and since from the word *vana* (forest) there likewise arise cognition, activity, and attainment regarding multiple objects such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees—
wherever these [three] are understood from a word, that is established as the meaning of that word through the usage of elders—

and yet, from words such as *senā* and *vana*, cognition, activity, and attainment are not experienced with respect to a specific proximity [of parts], such that [that proximity] would be its meaning.
— [This is] the authoritative [view], kārikā 4
— through the realization of that very [truth], according to the Jains.
Regarding the designation of a "city" and so forth as a distinct palace:
a city is a collection of palaces, gateways, persons, and so on.
—*Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, p. 127:
[concerning] the whole-substance (*avayavidravya*) of the Jains.
In the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others—[as stated in] the *Ktanimbandha*, p. 239. Ā. [Note: *Ā* indicates the end of a citation.]

Or, let there be some mark (liṅga) present there; nevertheless, if its invariable concomitance (pratibandha) has not been grasped, it cannot be a factor for the cognition of that [Brahminhood], because of the consequence of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, the grasping of such concomitance is impossible when Brahminhood itself is not cognized, again due to the consequence of over-extension;
and the cognition of that [Brahminhood] through perception has already been refuted.

If that [Brahminhood] were understood through inference, there would be the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*): for only when Brahminhood is established by means of inference is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the mark (*liṅga*) with it established; once that is established, the inference is established; and from that, Brahminhood is established—thus, the mark [would depend on Brahminhood].

Regarding the cognition of being a Brahmin, would its apprehension arise from scripture (āgama), whether that scripture be non-human (apauruṣeya) or human (pauruṣeya)? First of all, it cannot arise from a non-human source, because such a source has authority only regarding matters that are to be accomplished (kārya), whereas Brahminhood is not something to be accomplished since it is held to be eternal. Nor can its apprehension arise from a human source, because that depends upon other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and such [other] means are impossible in this case.

Nor can it be established through scripture (*āgama*), because that [scripture] must be either of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) or of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*). As for the former, [it is said]: "Because the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) has action as its purpose"—the transmitters of the tradition record these sentences in order to declare how an action is to be performed.
— Jaiminisūtra, Śābarabhāṣya 1.2.1.

Since the validity of the scripture authored by him is established only when the speaker’s knowledge of the subject matter to be communicated is proven to be valid, and since such [knowledge] is impossible in this case, there is no [validity]. Ā. [1.2.3]
Nor can that [Brahminhood] be apprehended through analogy (*upamāna*), because analogy has similarity as its objective basis;

and since Brahminhood has not been apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could the similarity of anything to it be perceived, such that from seeing that [similarity] one might apprehend Brahminhood?
[This would require] seeing an object similar to a Brahmin.

Nor can its cognition be achieved through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); for no object whatsoever, known through the six means of valid cognition, is perceived as being logically inexplicable apart from the universal of Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇyajāti*).

Therefore, because it transcends the scope of the five means of valid cognition that apprehend existing things and is thus swallowed up by the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), Brahminhood does not exist—just like a sky-lotus.

Consequently, since the very existence of the universal of Brahminhood is impossible, the argument that "the universal, though appearing at the first sight, does not manifest itself due to the non-apprehension of the difference in its manifestors" and so forth is refuted.

As for what was stated—"of those who examine substances," and so forth—that too is incorrect, because gold is not merely yellowness, nor is a substance merely a transformation consisting of various engraved lines, nor is a gem merely its circular shape; for such would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
What then? It is a specific excellence (*viśeṣa*) of those qualities.

And that [caste] is not perceptible, because it would follow that burning, cutting, washing with husked rice-water, questioning by others, and so forth, would be useless; for if even those [actions] were aids to its cognition, then some such aid must be stated for its production—would that be "being born from parents who are Brāhmaṇas" and so on, or a specific form? Since all of this has already been answered previously, it does not function as an aid to its cognition.

Therefore, it is incorrect to say: "And that which does not appear due to the absence of the causal complex [of perception] does not exist," and so forth; for the causal complex for the appearance of that [universal, etc. has already been refuted in its entirety, including all its specific features (p.

768, l. 7). For comparison: when there is a doubt regarding the unreality of an instruction concerning gold and the like, that doubt is removed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, the reality of an instruction concerning a genus (*jāti*) and so forth is not established by direct perception in the form of grasping the nature of the genus.

For in the case of gold and the like, because a specific quality of form exists, there is no harm whatsoever to the observed worldly convention that "gold is precisely of such a nature," since that convention reaches its completion [there]. But here, however, the claim that "Brahminhood is precisely of this kind" does not provide protection by being a mere stretching of the legs—since gold is not merely yellowness. (Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, p. 22; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 484)

[The removal] of the husks and chaff from the opposing position, through burning, cutting, washing with water, and so forth—Ārya; [the removal] of the husks and chaff from the opposing position, through burning, cutting, washing with water, and so forth—Śrī;
and from the opposing position, through burning, cutting, washing with water, and so forth—Ba.
In the apprehension of gold and so forth, would there be a specific form of that [object], or rather an act of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and the like?— as stated in *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 484,
regarding the apprehension of Brahminhood.
Page 768, line 13:
"In its entirety" (aśeṣataḥ) [is the reading in manuscript *ba*].

Now, [an objection might be raised]: "If you do not admit universals such as 'Brāhmaṇahood' (*brāhmaṇatva*), how could there be for you the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-vyavasthā*), or the practical conduct (*vyavahāra*) of austerity, charity, and so forth, which is based upon that? This too is not a valid objection; for the system and the practical conduct thereof are established in relation to a particular individual (*vyakti-viśeṣa*) characterized by specific actions and marks such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).

Therefore, the Brahminhood characterized by an eternal nature (*nityādi-svabhāva*) as imagined by you is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, it is logical that this conventional usage of "Brahmin" and so forth is based solely on specific actions.

Otherwise, how could there be an absence of Brahminhood and even censure for Brahmin women who have entered brothels and the like? For [according to you] caste (*jāti*) is the cause of purity; and according to your view, because it is eternally uniform in nature, it would remain exactly as it was. Otherwise, even the caste of "cowness" (*gotva-jāti*) would be inferior to Brahminhood.

For it is accepted by the learned that even cows and other animals, though they have lived for a long time in the houses of *caṇḍālas* and others, may be taken up [as property], but not so the wives of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇī*).

If it is argued that their censurability and the refusal to take them up is due to the failure of ritual acts (*kriyābhraṃśa*), then what is the use of this superfluous assumption of "Brahmin-ness" (*brāhmaṇya*)? Even having assumed it, one must admit that venerability and the designation "Brahmin" depend solely upon specific ritual acts; thus [says] the Blessed One... [Śrīmad-Bhāgavata].
The Jains offer this comparison: "One does not become a brahmin by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth;
he in whom there is truth and dharma—he is pure, and he is a brahmin."
And I do not call one a brahmin, O disputant, merely because he is born from a womb and possesses a motherly origin; rather, he who is truly free from possessions,
who is without anything, and who is without grasping— him I call a brahmin.
—Dhammapada, verses 393, 396:
By action one becomes a brahmin; by action one becomes a kshatriya;
by action one becomes a vaishya; by action one becomes a shudra.
Therefore, the establishment of the social classes (varṇa) is based on qualities (guṇas). Uttara-tantra 25.33.
The Brahminhood of the sages, Śṛṅga, and others among human beings is proclaimed on account of their possession of specific qualities, and not because of their birth from a particular womb;
this is just as the fourfold caste system and other distinctions such as the Caṇḍāla and so forth are established.
Everything that has become established in the world through the diversity of conduct—
The human race is but a single genus, arising from the emergence of a name;
yet it attains a fourfold division here through distinctions established by differences in livelihood:
Brāhmaṇas by virtue of their initiatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and Kṣatriyas by the wielding of weapons.
Merchants [attain it] through the righteous acquisition of wealth, and Śūdras by resorting to a humble mode of livelihood—
Ādipurāṇa 38.45–46.
The postulation of a distinction between castes is based merely on a difference in conduct;
there is no fixed, real caste such as "Brāhmaṇī" anywhere, for none of the four— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and the rest— exists in reality.
The human species is but one; it is distinguished by conduct and perfected by virtues. A species falls into ruin through the destruction of its virtues.
—Dharmapada 17

In the Mahābhāṣya as well, the position that words such as "brāhmaṇa" and others denote qualities (guṇavācin) has been presented; for it says: "Alternatively, all these words—brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra—refer to collections of qualities."
— Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 2.2.6

Since the designation and conventional usage of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are established upon that specific distinction characterized by specific actions, sacrificial threads, and other such marks, this conventional usage of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth is based solely on specific actions and the like— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*,
That is not tenable for you; [it is] based on action. (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 962; B. edition: kriyānibandhana).
Comparison—Therefore, Brahminhood is established merely through conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*).
*Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*, p. 26.
If the conventional designation of "Brahmin" and so forth were not based on specific actions, then...
Comparison: Otherwise, how could there be a loss of Brahminhood for Brahmin women who have entered the quarters of prostitutes and the like? (Syādvādaratnākara, p. 962; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
486; Brāhmaṇānām, manuscript B).
Otherwise, according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas, Brahminhood would be inferior even to the genus "cowness" (gotva).
—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 486: [The case] of Śruti-knowing Brāhmaṇī women in the houses of Cāṇḍālas and others.

The internal appendage (*antargaḍu*)—the "māsa-piṇḍa" (lump of flesh) situated between the neck and the head—is [an example of] Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*), [as defined in] the *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*, page 168; [it is] the exclusion of non-Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇyavyatireka*). (*Ā. and Śra.*)

Furthermore, the cessation of the caste *brāhmaṇya* would follow from the cessation of ritual action (*kriyā*), provided that action were its cause or its pervader (*vyāpaka*); otherwise, this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Yet, nothing is accepted as its cause or its pervader;
nor does a modification of that caste occur through the failure of ritual action, because it is declared that caste is non-different within distinct individuals, eternal, and partless.
Furthermore, the cessation [of a nature] that is unmodified is not possible, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Thus, since the "Brahmin-hood" imagined by you has an unestablished essence—like a lotus in the sky—it is not logical that dharma arises solely from a Brahmin’s use of refined words; rather, it should belong to all people without distinction. But such is not the case.

Therefore, one must accept that the correctness (*sādhutva*) of a word consists precisely in its expressing a non-false meaning, and nothing else, because of the persistence of the aforementioned defects.

And such a quality belongs equally to the Prākṛta word as it does to the Saṃskṛta word; therefore, both of these possess correctness (*sādhutva*). Consequently, it was rightly stated: "Phonemes, words, and sentences express intended meanings," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the cessation of action—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 487.
O witchcraft, born of Brahmanhood,
born of Brahmanhood!
This has been cited— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 487: "Dharma [arises] from the utterance of Sanskrit words."
The commentary explains that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is characterized by the expression of an unerring meaning;
explaining the two verses, he says: "the phoneme," and so forth.

The denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of letters, words, and sentences—that is, their ability to convey meaning—is to be understood from scripture (*āgama*) according to each [unit] without overstepping its own respective object, since this has been explained in detail for each one therein. [Objection:
But how can words be denoters of anything other than what is intended by the speaker? To this he says: "From the intention of the speaker," and so forth.

From what [source] do words derive their status as denoters of external objects such as jars, which are distinct from the speaker’s intention? To this he says: because otherwise the distinction between truth and falsehood would be untenable.

Wherever there is a distinction between truth and falsehood, that [cognition] must have as its object an entity distinct from the speaker’s intention, just as in the case of perception and so forth; and such a distinction between truth and falsehood exists in the case of words.

Furthermore, this consequential argument—characterized by the impossibility of establishing the distinction between truth and falsehood without the existence of external objects—has been explained at length elsewhere, such as in Laghīyastraya 2.26, where it says, "The means of valid cognition [is established] regarding objects through what is heard," and so forth; therefore, it is not elaborated upon again here in this section.

Now, one might object: "Since words are observed to function even in the absence of an object, how can they be considered denoters of that object? To this, he replies with the verse beginning "Of words," and so on:

If it is admitted that words deviate from their objects, then from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could their deviation from the intended object be removed or refuted? From none whatsoever.
Why is this so? To this he says: "In deep sleep, etc. By the word "etc.," states such as intoxication are included. [The phrase] "because of the observation of the activity of speech" [is used];
the word "not" (nāsti) does not exist [in the original].
Regarding that, he says "tadvācakam" (its designator) [in the text] "śra" [of the manuscript A],
while [the manuscripts] B and Su read "suṣuptādīnām" (of deep sleep and so forth), and [the text] reads "suṣuptyādau" (in deep sleep and so forth).
Now, it might be argued that the word which arises in the absence of that [intention] is indeed different from the word produced by the speaker's intention;

and that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) of one thing because of the deviation of another, for such would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga), since a well-defined effect never deviates from its cause. But this same point applies equally to words whose acquisition of their own nature is dependent upon the presence or absence of a specific object.

Even when those [external objects] are equal, words are determined to be distinct based on whether they arise from the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) or otherwise; they do not derive their existence from being tied to the presence or absence of specific external objects. This is merely an attachment to one's own philosophical view.

Furthermore, if these [words] have only the speaker’s intention as their domain, it is impossible for them to be the cause of activity toward external objects, because they do not have those as their objects. Whatever does not have something as its object cannot be the cause of activity toward that thing—just as the cognition of color, not having taste as its object, is not the cause [of activity] regarding taste—and according to your position, words do not have external objects as their domain.
And this is not tenable, because it contradicts experience;
for the cognition, activity, and attainment regarding external objects from words is well-established, like perception, even among children.
Therefore, it is logical that these [words] have those [external objects] as their referents.

Whatever is the cause of activity and so forth with respect to something has that thing as its object; for example, the cognition of taste has taste as its object because it is the cause of activity and so forth regarding taste. And words are the causes of activity and so forth regarding external objects; thus, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For, just as from perception—dependent on a totality of conditions such as the practitioner’s focused attention—there arises the cognition of the perceived object, which is well-known to all people, so too from a word—dependent on a totality of conditions such as linguistic convention—there arises the cognition of the word-meaning.

Nor should it be asserted that the word is non-instrumental toward the object because the person desiring the object acts solely out of their own desire; for if that were so, it would follow that perception and other means of knowledge are likewise non-instrumental, since one's activity toward their objects is also observed to arise solely from desire. If it is argued that these [perceptions] are instrumental indirectly, then let the same apply to the word as well, as there is no difference, provided there is an intention to speak (*vivakṣā*).
The acquisition of its own nature by another [is impossible],
because it does not have external objects as its domain.

Sound has the external object as its domain, because it is the cause of activity toward the external object and so forth—[as stated in] the *Tattvasaṃgraha*—for the cognition of the external object is established through sound, just as it is through perception and other means of knowledge.
(Compare: *pratyakṣādiva śabdād bahirarthapratītisiddheḥ*).

For just as the cognition of a perceptible object arises from perception—which depends upon the totality of conditions such as the cognizer’s mental orientation—so too the cognition of a word’s meaning arises from the word itself, which depends precisely upon the totality of conditions for linguistic convention; this is well-established among all people, because otherwise it would be impossible for there to be cognition, purposeful activity, or attainment regarding external objects based on that [word].

Nor is it correct to say that because a person seeking an object acts toward that object solely from the cognition of the object itself, the word is non-instrumental in prompting action; for if that were so, it would follow that even perception and other means of knowledge are non-instrumental, since everyone acts toward their objects solely out of desire.
(Aṣṭasahasrī p. 21; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 449)
Even when an object has already become an object of direct perception, there is the designation of "inducing activity" with respect to that perception.
Regarding the status of being an originator through tradition:

what is this so-called "intention" (*vivakṣā*)? Is it merely the desire to utter a word, or is it the intention: "By means of this word, I shall communicate this meaning"? In the first case, the activity of both speaker and listener in composing or listening to a treatise would not be possible;
for surely no one who is not insane would proceed to compose or listen to a treatise or another sentence merely for the sake of communicating the mere desire to produce a sound.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of all sentences being indistinguishable from such statements as "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) and so forth, because they are all equally indicative of the mere will that produced them. If it is argued that *vivakṣā* (the intention to speak) is the speaker's resolve, "I shall convey this specific meaning by means of this word," and that all words indicate such an intention by virtue of being its indicators—this too is untenable, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
For parrots, starlings, the insane, and others do not utter sentences with such an intention.

And what is this so-called "intention to speak" (*vivakṣā*)? Is it merely the desire to utter a word? [Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 450] Or is it something like the act of hearing or opening one's eyes? Furthermore, does a word convey such an intention independently of convention (*samaya*), or dependent upon it? In the first alternative, no one would ever be ignorant of any language, because it would follow that everyone would understand the meaning of words without distinction.
But why should a word, which depends upon convention (*samaya*), not convey the object itself? For this [word] does not fear the object such that it would not apply to it directly. [Objection:

"The word does not convey the object because a convention cannot be established for it. This too is an unexamined statement; for it follows that [the word] would likewise fail to convey the speaker's intention (*abhiprāya*), since there is no difference in the fact that a convention cannot be established even for that. Furthermore, its incapacity for a convention is unproven; for in the verse *pramāṇaṃ śrutamartheṣu* (Pramāṇasamuccaya 2.26), its capacity for a convention has been demonstrated in detail.

Comparison—Furthermore, does a statement independent of context convey such an intention, or one dependent upon it? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 450). Not only is the deviation of speech from its intended meaning not removed by the observation of vocal activity during states such as deep sleep; but for what other reason is that deviation removed? To this he says: "Of those who do not intend [to speak]," and so forth.

Because even for those who do not desire it—those devoid of the intention to utter corrupt words (*apaśabda*) and the like—the occurrence of speaking corrupt words and so forth still exists; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [faults such as] *śrutiduṣṭa* (phonetically defective) are included.

Likewise, because even for those who do desire it—those of dull intellect—there is an absence of being speakers of the scriptures, how can that [corruption] be removed? Here the opponent says: "In both cases," and so on.

Because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in both cases—regarding the object (*artha*) and the intention (*abhiprāya*)—words are not the denoters (*vācaka*) of any object or intention whatsoever. The particle "iti" marks the end of the opponent's position.

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Supernatural intuition" (*alaukika-pratibhānam*) means a cognition that occurs subsequent to [pure] intuition; "supernatural" (*alaukika*) and "intuition" (*pratibhāna*) together mean that which is contradicted by the world.
Why is this so? To this he says: "For the world," and so forth;
for (*hi*) because the world maintains the distinction between truth and falsehood based on the attainment or non-attainment of objects.
Of what? Of words.

For if words were not the designators of anything at all, then since objects such as jars would not be cognized from them even in a dream, no one in the world could establish the distinction between the truth of certain words and the falsity of others based on the attainment [of their referents] or its opposite; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object that even if they only express an intention, people would still maintain that distinction; to this he says: "No," and so forth.
The connection [of the argument] is: "If the meaning of a word were merely the speaker's intention, the world would not adhere to its established conventions.
Why is this so? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

The sense is that in such a case, there would be an absence of extensive linguistic usage (*śabdavyavahāra*) based on that [intention] alone; for even when such usage occurs in some instances, one frequently observes external usage (*bahir-vyavahāra*) [corresponding to the object].
In deep sleep and so forth,
[the mind] is withdrawn; there is no utterance of sound and so forth.
But not "abhi-ā," as stated in Ba; regarding that, he says "tanmātre" in Ba; regarding this, he says "tatra tanmātre" in Ā;
regarding that, he says "cittatattva" in Śra.

"An object is indeed understood from a word merely through the speaker's intention, even for one who is not omniscient; however, when that [understanding] is scrutinized, it does not hold up, because the word lacks a relationship with that [intention] and thus cannot be a means of communication. To this, he says: "Unsublated," and so forth.

The intention here is as follows: whatever meaning a particular word has been conventionally designated to express in one place, it remains the denoter of that same meaning in another place and at another time by virtue of the relationship characterized as fitness (*yogyatā*); there is no contradiction in this matter, as stated in the *Laghīyastrayavivaraṇa*, verse 62: "The beginningless convention depends upon fitness."

Therefore, for the sake of those followers of the Sugata who—transcending the cognition arising from words that is uncontradicted and has as its object an entity consisting of both the universal and the particular—maintain by their own whim, without relying on such cognition, that the nature of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists only of perception and inference, and not scripture (*āgama*) and so forth; and who maintain that the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists only of the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) cut off at its prior and posterior limits for perception, while for inference it is merely the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*); what is it that they claim? It is the capacity to indicate whatever is intended.
Of what things? Of words (*śabda*).
Regarding external objects, the word is such that it has been conventionally established (saṃketita) with respect to its object as being of such a nature.
And at another time there is no [destruction];
"akṣa" is beginningless—
this has been explained in the root verse as "knowledge is the means of valid cognition for the self and so forth."
Now, desiring to explain that "naya" is the intention of the knower, he says:
"The nayas are sevenfold due to the divisions of *naigama* and so forth.
Explanation: These nayas are those whose characteristics were previously stated.
Who are they?
They are the divisions or alternatives of *śruta*, which is the *sakalādeśa* (the complete description), namely the *āgama*.
How many are there? Seven.
From what [perspective] is it distinguished by the divisions such as *naigama* and so forth? What is its specific characteristic? It is rooted in substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*).
Regarding that, he states the nature of substance: "Substance is the universal.

What is its specific characteristic? It is "that which follows a single continuity" (*ekānvayānugam*). A single thing (*eka*) and a continuity (*anvaya*) are "single-continuities" (*ekānvayau*); that which follows, i.e., pervades, these two is "that which follows a single continuity" (*ekānvayānugam*).

In that context, "verticality" (*ūrdhvatā*) refers to the state of following a single object, which is a generality (*sāmānya*) pervading both the preceding and succeeding [moments]. Furthermore, what characterizes the "horizontal generality" (*tiryaksāmānya*), defined by similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*), as it follows through continuity (*anvaya*)? It is of the nature of certainty (*niścayātmaka*). That whose essence (*ātman*) is this certainty—wherein "certainty" (*niścaya*) means the absence of confusion with other modes (*paryāya*)—is so described.
Moreover, there is yet another mode, namely, particularity (*viśeṣa*).

What is its specific characteristic? It is "possessing differentiation and separateness" (*vyatirekapṛthaktvaga*). It is so called because it moves toward—that is, transforms into—the identity of both differentiation (*vyatireka*) and separateness (*pṛthaktva*). In this context, "differentiation" refers to successive modifications (*paryāya*) within a single substance, while "separateness" refers to dissimilar transformations occurring in relation to other objects.

Furthermore, what are the two fundamental standpoints (mūlanaya) upon which the definitive standpoint (niścaya) and the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra) depend? [The answer is: the definitive standpoint depends on substance;
that is to say, it is the substantial standpoint (dravyārthika).
The conventional standpoint (*vyavahāranaya*) is based on modalities; this means it is oriented toward the aspect of modalities (*paryāyārthika*). — *Laghīyastraya-tātparya-vṛtti*, p. 88.
Compare: "Seven root standpoints (*mūlanaya*) have been proclaimed."
Namely: the Naigama, the Saṃgraha, the Vyavahāra, the Rjusūtra, the Śabda, the Samabhirūḍha, and the Evambhūta.
— Syādvādamañjarī 7.19.
The *anuyoga* [states]: "The *nayās* are the *naigama*, *saṃgraha*, *vyavahāra*, *ṛjusūtra*, *śabda*, *samabhirūḍha*, and *evaṃbhūta*. — *Tattvārtha-sūtra* 1.6.
The fundamental viewpoints (mūlanayas) are to be understood as: the Naigama, the Saṅgraha, the Vyavahāra, the Ṛjusūtra, the Śabda, the Samabhirūḍha, and the Evambhūta.
—Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Gāthā 754:
The viewpoints (nayas) are Naigama, Saṃgraha, Vyavahāra, Ṛjusūtra, Śabda, and so forth;
the first two terms [Naigama and Saṃgraha] each have two divisions.
—Tattvārthādhi° 1.34, 35. Siddhasena Divākara, however, accepts six *nayās*; according to his view, the *naigama* is included within the *saṃgraha* and the *vyavahāra*.
It should be observed: "They [the categories] are rooted in substance and mode; substance is that which persists through a single continuity. (Sanmatitarka 1.4, 5; Dravyasaṃgraha 66)
The other [type of cognition] is also of a determinate nature, consisting of the apprehension of difference and non-difference;
however, determination and conventional usage rely respectively upon substance and mode. (Laghīyastraya 67)

Commentary: The *nayas* are not merely varieties of cognition (*mati*), because they have as their object multiple substances and modes (*paryāya*) across the three periods of time, whereas cognition grasps only a present object;
and even mental cognition—consisting of memory, recognition, deliberation, and inferential knowledge—has as its object an entity already delimited by the primary cognition.
In this regard, the two root *nayas* are the substantialist (*dravyārthika*) and the modalist (*paryāyārthika*).

Substance (*dravya*) has the nature of a single continuity (*ekānvaya*); it possesses unity because it does not transform into what it is not, and because its essence consists of a generality (*sāmānya*) characterized by similar transformation.

With respect to [qualities] such as "humanity," which possess a continuous nature, we infer—despite the presence of an excellence of both similar and dissimilar transformations—that those things whose nature consists of multiple continua nonetheless have the status of being the object of an unerring, uniform, and singular cognition, due to the absence of confusion or intermixture in their state of continuity.

For instance: a *skandha* (aggregate) is the unity of its own qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*), whereas a person (*puruṣa*) is a common transformation (*samānapariṇāma*). Furthermore, while multiplicity pertains to all categories of objects, according to the *niścayanaya* (the standpoint of ultimate reality), the soul (*jīva*) is one when free from karma; yet according to the *vyavahāranaya* (the standpoint of conventional practice), it is possessed of karma.
Succession (paryāya), distinctness (pṛthaktva), and differentiation (vyatireka) constitute distinctness.
Differentiation refers to the distinction between qualities, actions, universals, and particulars within a single substance,
as well as the dissimilar transformation occurring in a different continuum.

Anger and the like are the conventional (vyavahāra) modes of the transmigrating soul; knowledge and the like are the ultimate (niścaya) modes of the pure [soul], each manifesting infinite internal distinctions at every moment. According to the ultimate standpoint (niścayanaya), the substance of matter (pudgaladravya) is one, even though it appears in various forms such as earth and so forth; for despite these differences, it does not abandon its nature of possessing color, taste, smell, and touch, whether that nature is manifested or unmanifested. Likewise, although there are distinctions between the modes of aggregates (skandha) and atoms (paramāṇu), the substance does not relinquish its possession of color and the other qualities.

Indeed, conditions (*avasthā*), space (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), and refinement (*saṃskāra*) do not utterly destroy corporeality, for that would entail the absurd consequence of destroying incorporeality as well. Furthermore, it has already been stated—and need not be repeated here—that living beings (*jīva*) and so forth are distinctions within existence (*sattā*).

Even for the proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*), how could they deny that cognition is a single entity which, in a single moment, assimilates itself into multiple forms? Therefore, one must determine that the *dravyārthika* and *paryāyārthika* standpoints are the primary exponents of the specific syntheses of the words of the Tīrthaṅkaras;
for there is no third alternative, since any such thing would necessarily be included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself.
There is no intention to assert the identity [of the two] because the *naigama* [viewpoint] is not considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The comparison is as follows: sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) grasps objects that have arisen and not yet perished, having the present time as its domain; whereas scriptural cognition (*śrutajñāna*) has all three times as its domain, grasping objects that have arisen, those that have perished, and those not yet arisen.
(Tattvārthādhigamasūtra Bhāṣya 1.25)
20 –*Matibhinnārthavi–ī॰ vi॰* (Commentary):
*Tulanā* (Comparison) is the transition to another object, which is a dissimilar transformation (*visadṛśapariṇāma*), such as [the comparison] between a cow and a buffalo.
— Examination, verse 4.9—
Corporeality— Jaina-viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya.

Comparison—The Tīrthaṅkara’s speech consists of the compendium (*saṃgraha*), the detailed exposition (*vyavasthāna*), and the root-exposition (*mūla-vyākaraṇa*); it is based on the substance-viewpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*) and the mode-viewpoint (*paryāya-naya*), while the remaining [viewpoints] are merely its variations.

Comparison: It is incorrect to say that this [cognition] consists solely of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it grasps both [the object and its form], since in the case of consciousness (*jñapti*), there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate status between them.
It has been explained in detail that perception (*vedana*), which apprehends an object consisting of both [aspects] primarily, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and nothing else;
see *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 269.

The meaning of the verse: What are the "divisions" (bhedāḥ), that is, the specific varieties, of the sacred scripture (āgama) that has been heard, and not of sensory cognition (matijñāna)? They are the "standpoints" (nayāḥ), which are the intentions of the recipients [of the teaching]. How many are there? Seven.
Why? Because of the divisions such as *naigama* and so forth.
To the question "What is their basis?", he says: "In substance," and so on.
Those [divisions] for which substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) are the root—that is, the substratum—are described as such.
"What is the nature of substance (*dravya*)? To this he says: "Substance," and so forth.

This word *eka* (one) has the state of being (*bhāva*) as its primary sense; thus, *ekatva* (oneness) and *anvaya* (continuity)—the latter being a similar modification (*sadṛśapariṇāma*)—it follows (*anugacchati*), that is, it extends toward, its own modifications and other substances respectively.

By the term *tadanugama* (following that), which is explained as *ekatvānugama* (following through oneness), there is a negation of the absolute view of difference (*bhedakānta*). By the term *anvayānugama* (following through continuity), however, there is a rejection of the oneness of all substances (*sarvadravyaikatva*).
Regarding the point that such a substance would be indefinable by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "of the nature of certainty" (*niścayātmakam*).

Certainty is the act of grasping an object of knowledge (*prameya*) characterized by the exclusion of doubt and other such states; that which has this as its essence or intrinsic nature (*ātman/svabhāva*) is so described.

It is not only the substance (*dravya*) that is of the nature of certainty, but also the other—the mode (*paryāya*)—is of the nature of certainty; thus, the term "of the nature of certainty" is connected [to both] through a change in grammatical gender (*liṅga-pariṇāma*).
Furthermore, of what nature [is it]? To this he says: "It goes toward distinction and separateness" (*vyatirekapṛthaktvagaḥ*).

It "goes toward distinction" (*vyatirekagaḥ*) because, in relation to its own substance and other modes, it goes toward distinction—that is, mutual exclusion—without abandoning its single substance. It "goes toward separateness" (*pṛthaktvagaḥ*) because, in relation to the modes of another substance, it goes toward separateness—that is, the state of residing in a different substance.

Now, if the *naigama* and other *nayas* have substance and mode as their basis, then upon what are the two root *nayas*, characterized as the substantialist (*dravyārthika*) and the modalist (*paryāyārthika*), based? To this he says: "Certainty" (*niścaya*), and so forth.

The perspective or determination that relies upon the nature—whether of a conscious or unconscious entity—which exists and never perishes, is the *dravyārthikanaya* (substantial standpoint); this is the meaning.

The conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) that relies upon the nature which does perish is the *paryāyārthika* (modal standpoint). The word "both" (*tau*) is used in the sense of "also" (*api*), indicating that they both rely upon substance and mode.

And he will state there: "The two fundamental standpoints (*mūlanaya*) are those concerned with substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)," and so forth—[the former] consisting of the speaker (*vaktr-abhiprāyātmaka*), while the latter is a separate object of knowledge (*dravya-meya*) consisting of certainty (*niścayātmaka*). However, [according to the *Śrī* commentary...]
The commentary (*vivṛti*):
therein, explaining the first part of the first verse by way of its contrapositive (*vyatireka*), he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
It is not that there are differences of opinion (*mati-bheda*), but rather differences of scriptural tradition (*śruta-bheda*). Which are these? They are the *nayas*.
From where is this [known]? To this he says: "In the three times," and so forth.

The connection is made by changing the case ending: because of the existence—that is, the reality—of those *nayās* (perspectives) which have as their object (*viṣaya*) those many substances and modes (*paryāya*) whose scope (*gocara*) consists of the three times.

"Will the intellect (*mati*) also be like that? To this he says: "Of the intellect," and so forth. The connection is as follows: because the intellect produced by the senses (*indriya-janitāyāḥ*) grasps a present object—that is, because it grasps an object consisting of substance and modes (*dravya-paryāya-ātmaka*) within the domain of the present time—the nayas are not distinctions of the intellect. [Objection: In that case, let those distinctions belong to that [intellect] produced by the non-senses (*anindriya-janitāyāḥ*), since that has as its object substances and so forth within the domain of the three times (*trikāla-gocara*). To this he says: "Of the mental intellect," and so forth.

The connection is that these distinctions are not only of sensory cognition (*indriyamati*), but also of mental cognition (*manomati*). Of what specific nature is this [mental cognition]? To this he says: "consisting of memory, recognition, reflection, and discernment" (*smṛti-pratyabhijñāna-cintā-abhinibodhātmikāyāḥ*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "because of its cause," and so forth.

The intellect (*mati*) that is clear and unerring is called "causal intellect" (*kāraṇamati*) because it is the cause of mental cognition (*manomati*). Since the object delimited by that [intellect] is the domain of mental cognition, and since that very object is apprehended by the latter with some degree of additional clarity, it is described in this way regarding the intellect.
Thus he says:
"The cognition produced by the sense organs [is the apprehension] of the object itself, which has become the domain of the sensory cognition."

By way of the following of one object by another object, he says "In that regard," etc., showing the distinction of the *nayās* within the *manomati* [cognition], because its nature is that of investigation.

Since the systems of viewpoints (*nayāḥ*) are thus established as being divided by their respective scriptural traditions, [the author] asks: "Which two among the *naigama* and others are the root view-points (*mūlanaya*) and the causal view-points (*kāraṇanaya*)? He replies: "They are those whose objects are substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*). That is to say, they are so called because they possess, respectively, those two objects—namely, substance and mode.
Therein, he explains the term "substance" (*dravya*) with the words beginning "substance" (*dravyam*).
Oneness and continuity have been explained; that which has these two as its nature is "of that nature" (*tadātmaka*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says "oneness," etc.;
the word "substance" (*dravya*) is understood to follow.

How can there be unity for that? To this he says: "That," and so forth. That which is intended [to be expressed] is "that" (*tat*), and that which is not intended is "not-that" (*atat*). These two are *tadat* (that-and-not-that); those two are the transformations (*pariṇāmau*), and that which possesses them is "possessing the transformations of that-and-not-that" (*tadatatpariṇāmi*). Alternatively, that which has the nature of transforming into those two is "that which transforms into that-and-not-that" (*tadatatpariṇāmi*). Because of its state of being such—that is, because of its reality—it is now established as "that" (*tat*) consisting of persistence (*anvaya*). The connection is: "the substance is persistent (*anvayi*), meaning it is a substance that follows along with other substances."
Why is this so? He says: "That," and so forth—because [the universal] consists of a commonality characterized by a similar transformation (*sadr̥śapariṇāma*).

Here the Buddhist objects: "Certain entities are postulated as having a similar transformation in relation to what is dissimilar, or as having a single transformation in relation to what is neither material cause nor effect; this is not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because a property produced through dependence is not ultimately real. To this he replies: "The Person," and so forth.

This is its meaning: [it refers to] moments that occur simultaneously or successively, which possess the nature of multiple continua, the nature of diverse continua, or the nature of a single continuum;

the "human-ness" (puruṣatva) or "horizontal universal" (tiryaksāmānya)—the word "etc. including specific substances—which is conceptually constructed based on them, that is, from the aforementioned dependence; even though there exists a distinction in similar and dissimilar transformations—that is, a preeminence in similar transformation, a preeminence in dissimilar transformation, and a preeminence in the transformation of unity—[this conceptual construction occurs].

If it is argued that because the word *itara* denotes a meaning opposite to what has been stated, "other than" (*itara*) from a similar transformation (*samānapariṇāma*) can only mean a dissimilar transformation (*visadṛśapariṇāma*), and not a preponderance of the transformation of unity (*ekatvapariṇāmātiśaya*), this is indeed so; nevertheless—since both the similar transformation and the preponderance of the transformation of unity are the subject under discussion here, "other than" the similar transformation refers specifically to the transformation of unity.

Even when that [transformation of unity] exists, [the substance] is "continuous" (*anvayi*) because it possesses unity through its non-transformation into that which is other [than itself], and because its nature consists of a generality characterized by a similar transformation; such is the connection [of the words].

For that [entity] does not exist as untransformed in relation to another, because that would involve a contradiction; otherwise, even though cognition is itself formless (*amūrta*), it would become possessed of form (*mūrta*) by being distinguished from another formless cognition. If it is argued that this is incorrect—on the grounds that unity and so forth are untenable because, upon investigation, neither a transformation into that nor a transformation into non-that is possible for the entity, nor is a universal characterized by similar transformation established, and because there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its having an undesired form just as it has its intended form—then he says here: "In that way," and so forth.
