Thus, by means of that specific mode of excellence, because of the absence (vyatireka) of those two—namely, confusion (saṅkara) and intermixture (vyatikara)—we infer through reasoning (anumāna), on account of the expansion of the aforementioned logic which serves as the basis for inference, that the concomitant universals (*sāmānya*) which do not undergo transformation into those [particulars] possess, in their entirety, the nature of being the objects of a single, unerring, and uniform cognition, characterized by a manifold continuum. This is the intended meaning.
In that very context, [the text] is designated as having distinct scriptural divisions;

"substance" (*dravya*) and so forth—the word "substance" is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) from the previous section—or rather, the phrase "substance and so forth" is understood to carry over.
—O similar one— Ā., Ba.
—dependent on one— Ba.
—and of those occurring simultaneously and sequentially, of those occurring simultaneously and sequentially, of the moments— Ā.

In the case of an excellence in similar transformation (*samānapariṇāmātiśaye*), there is no [such thing]—in Śra [the manuscript]; in the case of a pre-eminence in similar transformation (*samānapariṇāmaprakarṣe*), there is none—in Ba [the manuscript]. For fire does not become fire by depending on that which has not been transformed into fire, with reference to the exclusion of non-fire; for otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even water and the like would be fire simply through the exclusion of non-fire—this is the intended meaning. [The text continues: "by way of form" (*rūpeṇa*), etc., in Śra [the manuscript], [referring to] an excessive [transformation].

Alternatively, if a Vaiśeṣika or other proponent says: "In relation to *puruṣatva* (the nature of being a spirit), there is an excellence of similar transformation among multiple selves; and in relation to the inherence of qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*), there is an excellence of unitary transformation in a single self, but not in an ultimate sense," then [the author] replies with the words "of *puruṣatva* and so forth. That which has *puruṣatva* as its beginning—namely, the inherence of cognition and so forth, and the conjunction with the three *guṇas*, etc.—is what is thus described. From that dependence, even though there exists an excellence of similar and dissimilar transformations, of whom? He says: "of the selves belonging to multiple and single continua."
"Those [entities] are manifold, yet they belong to a single continuum, and those are their selves"—the rest is as before.

Now, one might object: "Let there be a transformation into a common unity with the self, but not for jars and the like, because in their case only a common transformation is possible. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For instance," and so forth. That is to say, by that manner of being the object of a non-erroneous, uniform, and unitary cognition, the aggregate (*skandha*)—namely, the composite whole such as a jar—is what? He says: "Unity."
Of what things? He says: "one's own" (*sva*), and so forth.

By the word "one's own," the aggregate (*skandha*) is referred to. Its qualities (*guṇas*) are form and the rest; its modes (*paryāyas*) are newness, oldness, and so forth. Their "oneness" is not a common transformation (*samānapariṇāma*), because they are the objects of a single, uninterrupted cognition—this is the intended meaning.

Now, the Buddhist might object: "Let there indeed be a common transformation even for those belonging to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), just as there is for those belonging to different continua (*bhinnasantāna*)."
Regarding this, he says: "And the person (*puruṣa*)"—the connection is that not only the aggregates (*skandha*) but the person as well is the unity of its own qualities and modes (*guṇaparyāya*).

Now, if it is argued: "Just as the person is the unity of happiness and other states that occur sequentially, let that [person] likewise be the unity of selves (*ātman*) that occur simultaneously," to this he replies with the words beginning "similar" (*samāna*).
The word *api* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

It is precisely the common transformation (*samānapariṇāma*) that extends to all objects, not oneness (*ekatva*) that extends to all objects of the Person (*puruṣa*). This connection is established by changing the case-ending [of the words].

By this, the passage beginning with "the state of being thus" (*tathābhāva*) and so forth is supported, and the quarter-verse of the *Kārikā*, "Substance is the following-on of a single continuity" (*dravyam ekānvayānugam*), is explained.

From the perspective of the *niścaya-naya* (the standpoint of ultimate reality) and the *dravyārthika-naya* (the substantial standpoint), the soul (*jīva*) is one and undivided; yet, with respect to its common transformation of consciousness, that very same soul is shown to be twofold from the perspective of the *vyavahāra-naya* (the standpoint of conventional reality). Demonstrating this, he says: "Karma," etc.
The soul is either free from, or possessed of, karma—namely, the *jñānāvaraṇīya* (knowledge-obscuring) and other types of karma.

Why? From the perspective of the conventional standpoint (*vyavahāra-naya*) and the standpoint of modal reality (*paryāyārthika-naya*), the distinction between those with one sense organ and so forth is likewise to be considered;
by this, the second half of the second verse is explained.
The Buddhist [teacher] holds that there is no self consisting of a single or multiple continua, such as cognition and so forth.
And likewise, according to him, even for continua (santāna), the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin) [holds this]. Baḍ; likewise, according to him, Ārya—Baḍ; even for continua, Advaitavādin.
May the person become of the nature of Brahman—Ga: multiplicity, Ā:
that substance—Śra.
From the certainty [of this],
even though there is a distinction between the senses (*indriya*),
he says "paryāya" and so forth, stating the synonym (*paryāya*).
What is the synonym? He says: "distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*) and "differentiation" (*vyatireka*).
Therein, he explains the term "distinctness": distinctness means the existence, in some way, of qualities, actions, universals, and particulars within a single substance through mutual exclusion.
He elucidates the term "differentiation": differentiation is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Who [is it]? He says: a dissimilar transformation occurring in another continuum, such as the transformation into a cow, a buffalo, and so forth.
Demonstrating therein the modifications (paryāyas) residing in the soul, he says "the conventional" and so forth;
the meaning is that these are the conventional modifications, which are the modifications according to the *paryāyārthika-naya* (the perspective of modifications).
What are they? Anger and the like, because they occur only occasionally. Of what kind of soul are these modifications? To this he says: "of the transmigrating soul" (saṃsāriṇaḥ).
What are the modifications of the liberated soul? To this he says: "in the ultimate sense" (niścaya), and so forth.
The connection is as follows: the modes (*paryāyas*) that constitute the scope of the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthika*) are the modes of the pure soul (*jīva*).

What are they? They are knowledge and so forth. Why are they such? Because they are not occasional (*akādācitkatvāt*). And how are they characterized? To this he says: "And they [are those] whose infinite distinctions are assimilated to the self at every moment."

It is not only that there is non-difference for the *jīva* alone according to the substance-view (*dravyārthika-naya*), but rather that there is non-difference even for the *pudgala*-substance; thus he says: "From the perspective of the ultimate" (*niścaya*), etc. From the perspective of the ultimate, which is the substance-view (*dravyārthika-naya*), the *pudgala*-substance is one and undivided. Under what condition? He says: "even when there is a division into earth and so forth."
Doing what does that one [substance] do? To this he says:

"not abandoning" (*ajahat*), meaning not relinquishing. What is it? He says: "the state of possessing color, taste, smell, and touch. This is because of the statement in the *Tattvārthasūtra* (5.23): "Pudgalas possess color, taste, smell, and touch."
Of what nature is that? He says: "Its nature is both manifest and unmanifest.

On earth, its nature is manifest; in water and so forth, its nature is unmanifest, because of the non-manifestation of odor in water, of odor and taste in fire, and of color, taste, and odor in air. Thus ends the section on the synonyms.
—Infinite regress— Śrī.
Cows, buffaloes, etc.—Śrī. Ba.
Particles (pudgala) possess touch, taste, smell, and color.
*Tattvārthasūtra*:

"But surely, regarding color, taste, smell, and so forth—since the existence of smell and the rest in water and other elements is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their non-manifestation is logical; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything would be unmanifest everywhere, which would lead to the position of the Sāṃkhya system. If this is argued, it is replied: Water and the other elements possess smell and the rest, because they possess touch (*sparśavat*). Whatever possesses [the qualities] in this manner possesses [those qualities] in that manner, just like earth. And these [elements] possess touch and the rest; therefore, they possess smell and the rest.

Furthermore, that which does not possess odor and so forth is not tangible, just as the self (*ātman*) and other such entities; this and more has been explained in detail here during the occasion of establishing that earth and the other elements are not distinct ultimate realities (*atattvāntara*), within the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*.
What, then, is it doing? To this he says: "The aggregate," and so forth.

The aggregates (*skandhas*), jars and so forth, atoms (*paramāṇu*), and persons (*pudgala*) are merely synonyms, because they manifest from one another: for indeed, aggregates arise from atoms, and atoms arise from them. Even when these are divided, they do not abandon their possession of form and other qualities; this is stated as a single illustrative example. Therefore, just as that atomic form, while becoming an aggregate or assuming the nature of an aggregate, or while the aggregate assumes the state of an atom, remains one without abandoning its possession of form and other qualities—so too is the case with the subject under discussion. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For not... and so forth.

For this reason—namely, that state (*avasthā*), place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), and refinement (*saṃskāra*) utterly and thoroughly differentiate *mūrttatva* (corporeality), which is the state of possessing form and so forth, because of the definition "a form consisting of form and so forth"—they differentiate the distinctions of earth and the other elements, as well as the distinctions of the aggregates (*skandha*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*).
From what [source] is this known? To this he says: "immaterial," and so forth.
The connection [of the argument] is as follows: because of the consequence that there would be a distinction—namely, a specific individual—that is formless and devoid of color and so forth;

and just as states and the like do not absolutely differentiate that which possesses color and so forth, so too the distinctions of existence (*sattābheda*), such as souls (*jīva*) and the rest, do not absolutely differentiate existence itself. This has already been largely stated in the verse *laghīyastrayakārikā* 31: "That within which the various divisions of soul and non-soul are merged," and thus it is not repeated here.

One might object: "Since no substance such as the soul (*jīva*) or any universal such as existence (*sattā*) is possible, the statement 'the soul is one' according to the *niścaya-naya* is incorrect; and even if such a thing were possible, its oneness could not be maintained because the superimposition of contradictory attributes due to differences in states and so forth would entail a difference at every moment. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Difference," etc. How could even those Buddhists—who assert that a thing is entirely different [at each moment] due to the superimposition of contradictory attributes—not refute [this very point]? What is that? Knowledge. Of what nature is it? It is one.

Doing what? Appropriating for itself its own manifold forms—variegated forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth; or forms that are perceptible and imperceptible, being either distinct from or identical to the nature of the grasped and the grasper—at what time? At a single moment;
for if those were refuted, there would be total nihilism.
And that [objection] has already been refuted in detail in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pariccheda*); so enough with further digression.

Therefore, just as a single cognition is not contradictory even when there is the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmādhyāsa*) simultaneously, so too is a substance such as the soul (*jīva*) [not contradictory] when [contradictory properties] occur successively; thus says the Vaiśeṣika.
Comparison— page 238, note 4;
page 238, comparison— *rūpa* means *mūrti* (form).
What is matter? Matter is the transformation consisting of the configuration of form and so forth— *Sarvārthasiddhi*, *Rājavārttika* 5.5.
Or rather,

there would be a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*): [the meaning is] because of the consequence that this specific distinction (*bhedaviśeṣa*) would be non-existent, which implies the consequence that it would have the nature of being unreal (*asadrūpatva*).
According to the Sugata,
in that context,

cognition is either variegated knowledge (*citrajñāna*)— which is accompanied by the experience of multiple forms such as the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*)— or it is experience consisting of both the perceptible and the imperceptible, in comparison with the experience devoid of such forms as the apprehended object.
The emptiness of all things (sakalaśūnyatā) [is] manifold in form, such as pleasure and so forth. (pṛ. 133)

He states the summary of the meaning already explained—beginning with "therefore" (*tataḥ*) and so forth: since the soul (*jīva*) and other categories are established as consisting of modifications such as pleasure and so on, therefore they are the objects of the Tīrthaṅkara’s speech—the preaching of *syādvāda*—because the *nayās* are subdivisions of scripture (*śruta*). Among those, what are to be understood as the two primary originators—the root-explainers—of the expansion and detailed exposition of their arrangement, namely the *saṅgraha* and the *viśeṣas*, which are the various divisions of the *vyavahāra* and other *nayās*? He says: the *dravyārthika* and the *paryāyārthika*.
If it is asked, "Why is there no other [alternative]? he says here: "Not indeed," and so forth.
For (*hi*) there is no third alternative, nor any other system of logic (*nayāntara*).
Why is this so? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.
The connection is that "that [Naigama] does not exist" because it is included within *pramāṇa* itself, and not within *naya*.

If it is argued that Naigama should also be a *pramāṇa* because it is an intention directed toward the objects of generality and particularity—which are essentially mutual and constitute the primary [subject matter]—the author says here: "No," and so forth.
It is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—of what? Of the *naigama* [view].
Why is this so? He says: "Because of identity," and so forth;

the meaning is that there is an absence of the intention to express it as having the nature of a means of valid cognition through identity, because there is the presence of the intention to express it as a *naya*.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says here:
"The statement of *syādvāda* is the expansion of the sacred tradition (*āgama*)."
The term *prakārabhūtā* [is used] in connection with the knowledge (*jñāna*) of one who possesses intention (*abhiprāyavataḥ*). [This applies to the readings] *pra-ā॰* and *śra-ā॰*.
The explanation of two properties in a single substratum by way of their subordinate and primary status—
what would that be? It is the *naigama* perspective.
What is it? It is the intention (vivakṣā), that is, the purpose (abhiprāya). Of which two properties? Of oneness and manifoldness.
By what means? By the relationship of subordinate and principal (guṇapradhānabhāva).

Where? In a single substratum (*ekadharmiṇi*). A single, non-different substratum is a substance (*dravya*); in that [substance], there would be its "form" (*ākṛti*), meaning the appearance (*ābhāsa*) of that *naigama* [view].

What is it? It is the expression of absolute difference (*atyantabhedokti*). Absolute difference is independence (*nirapekṣa*) and plurality (*nānātva*); the expression of that—that is, the statement—is the intention of the Naiyāyikas and others; the meaning is that this is a semblance of *naigama*.
—*Laghīyastrayāloka*, p. 90:
"The Naigama [standpoint] consists in the expression of absolute difference according to one's intention; its form is as follows.

Commentary: When defining the true nature of the soul (*jīva*) through its primary function (*pradhānavṛtti*), such as "the soul is existent, formless, an agent, subtle, a knower, a seer, consisting of innumerable spatial units (*pradeśa*), an enjoyer, subject to transformation, eternal, and distinct from the elements such as earth," qualities like pleasure and so forth are rendered secondary (*guṇībhūta*).

Alternatively, when defining the essential nature of pleasure and so forth, the intention that the self is absolutely distinct from them is a semblance of the *naigama* [view]. In the *naigama*, there is no desire to express identity (*tādātmya*) regarding qualities and the possessor of qualities, parts and the whole, actions and their agents, universals and their instances, and so on; rather, there is the intention to express qualities and the possessor of qualities, or attributes and the substratum, in terms of a subordinate and a principal relationship. The distinction is that in the *saṃgraha* and other [standpoints], there is the intention to express only one [of these].
The name Jaṅgīva Bhūtāvī in the Nigama of Jaṅgīva.
Commentary on the Verse:

The intention (*abhisandhi*) of the cognizer—the desire to express two properties, one primary and one secondary, in their principal and subordinate forms, upon a single substratum (*dharmin*)—is the *naigama* [standpoint]. How could that [intention] attain the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is a substratum possessing the nature of both properties as primary? He states its fallacious appearance: "The statement of absolute difference between two properties in a single substratum" is the connection [of the verse]. "It would be of that form" means it would be a fallacious *naigama* (*naigamābhāsa*). This is the connection. (Āvaśyakaniryukti-bhāṣya)
The object assumes the form of whatever its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) may be—
this is the explanation of the commentary on Āgama and Śruti.

Explaining the verse (*kārikā*), he says: "The soul (*jīva*) is existent, formless, subtle, a knower, a seer, an agent, possessing innumerable spatial points (*pradeśa*), an enjoyer, subject to transformation (*pariṇāmī*), eternal, and distinct from the elements such as earth. Thus, when the definition of the soul's own nature is being undertaken—that is, when the description of the soul's essential form is being performed—the attributes of pleasure and so forth are secondary.

Or rather, when the essential nature of pleasure and so forth is being defined primarily—as pleasure having the form of delight, pain having a nature opposite to that, and knowledge having the inherent character of apprehending its own object—the self (*ātman*) becomes secondary. This is the connection [of the text].
Explaining the semblance of the Naigama (naigamābhāsa), he says: "That," and so forth.
The intention of absolute difference between those two—the self consisting of pleasure and so on—is the semblance of the Naigama.
He provides an example: "Of qualities and their possessors, parts and wholes, and universals and their instances," and so forth.
The connection is that "the intention of absolute difference is a semblance of the *naigama* [viewpoint].
By this, the intention of absolute difference between consciousness (*caitanya*) and pleasure (*sukha*), etc., as held by the followers of Kapila (*kāpilīya*), is also considered.
To the question, "Why is this a semblance of the *naigama*? he says: "Because of identity," and so forth.

Since this [cognition] proceeds for a cognizer whose mind is perverted by the impressions of his own false tradition (*durāgama-vāsanā*), disregarding the identity (*tādātmya*) that actually exists between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*), it is therefore a semblance of the *naigama* (the collective).
This mention of "property and property-possessor" is intended as an illustration; by it, the parts and the whole, action and agent, and the universal and its instance are also included.

Since in the *naigama* there is an intention to express the relationship of subordinate and principal between two properties, the intention to express absolute difference is what constitutes its semblance—this is the intended meaning.
"How, then, is there a distinction between *saṃgraha* and the others? To this he says:

"*Saṃgraha* etc. That of which *vyavahāra* and the rest are the beginning is so described. In that regard, because there is an intention (*vivakṣā*) to speak of either a single quality (*guṇa*) or the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the distinction of *saṃgraha* and the others arises from *naigama*.
"The cognition of the object of knowledge as having the form of pleasure and delight" — [Nyāyaviniścaya].
It should be observed—[as stated in] Akalaṅkagrantha, Chapter on the Soul, page 58—that the self (ātman) is related [to the body]. (ba = sambandhiḥ; śra = śrāmaṇya).
"Vetyādi" etc.;
since [the text] is from the Āvaśyaka-niryukti and the Naigama-naya, he says the following while demonstrating the nature of the Saṃgraha [naya] along with its counter-position:

The *saṃgraha-naya* [is so called] because it collects [all things] into a single unity through their non-difference as "Being" (*sat*). Commentary: Because it collects—that is, grasps by way of simplification—all particularities of living beings (*jīva*) and non-living beings (*ajīva*) into a single unity, that is, into oneness. Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a simplification of the manifold?", he says: "Because of non-difference as Being. This means: relying upon that which is both "Being"—the generality of existence (*sattvasāmānya*)—and "non-difference" (*abheda*).

It is not logical to say that nothing exists as distinct from existence (*sattā*), because that would involve a contradiction; what would then be a semblance of the synthesis of bad systems (*durnayasaṃgrahābhāsa*)? It would be the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*), which is the non-duality of existence (*sattādvaita*).

Why? Because its essential nature is not attained. Its essential nature—that of the Brahman postulated by others as being pure existence (*sanmātra*) devoid of the manifoldness of difference—is not attained; that is, it is not reached through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is not so perceived through perception or other such means (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 90). Thus, the doctrine of Brahman would be a false system (*durnaya*), because its essential nature is not attained. (69)
Commentary: "Everything is one because of the lack of distinction in its existence"—this is the *saṃgraha* perspective (*naya*).
Its fallacious counterpart (*tadābhāsa*) is the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*). Since there is no means for its realization, it cannot be the goal either, just like a donkey's horn.
Regarding its status as the goal (*upeyatva*):

the aphorism of the *Jaṃbūdvīpaprajñapti* states that because the entire manifold of the specific categories of living beings (*jīva*) and non-living things (*ajīva*) is subsumed through their unity, the *saṃgraha* perspective (*naya*) proceeds; this is the supplementary explanation (*upaskāra*).

To the question, "Whence is the inclusion of the unity of all? he says: because of non-difference from *sat* (Being), even the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*) includes the unity of all by relying on its non-difference from *sat*; thus, that too would be an inclusion. To this, he replies with the words "bad method" (*durnaya*), etc.:
the doctrine of Brahman would then be a bad method, a mere semblance of inclusion.
Why is this so? To this he says: "That," and so forth.

Because of the non-attainment—that is, the absence of the acquisition—of that nature of Brahman which consists of pure existence (sattāmātra) with the entire manifold of difference (bheda-prapañca) negated; by one [means], A, B.
Thus says the *Śrī-vivṛti-vyākhyāna*.

Explaining the *kārikā*, he says: "All," and so forth. "All"—meaning the entire collection of entities consisting of both sentient and insentient forms—is "one" because there is no distinction in their existence; in this manner, the *saṃgraha-naya* (the synthetic perspective) proceeds.
The appearance of that [is] the appearance of the collection; why is this called the "Brahma-doctrine"? To this he says:
"That," etc.—because there is no means for its acceptance, that is, because there is no valid proof for the acceptance of the Brahma-doctrine.
The intention is that an acceptance based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indeed true;

he states another fault with the words "nor also," etc., connecting them as follows: nor can that Brahman be accepted—that is, adopted—as the goal (*upeya*), because there is an absence of a means (*upāya*).
That which lacks a means [of proof] cannot be established, just like the horn of a donkey; and since there is no means for Brahman,
as has been considered in detail on page 150 during the occasion of refuting the non-duality of Brahman, no means whatsoever is applicable to it.
Demonstrating the *vyavahāra-naya* (the conventional standpoint), he says:

"The validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) is due to their conformity with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). Due to conformity with worldly practice—whereby worldly practice consists of both inclusion (*sagraha*) and differentiation (*bheda*), and its conformity is non-contradiction—it is for that very reason [that they are valid].

The meaning is that *vyavahāra* (conventional discourse) is a *naya* because it serves as the basis for establishing what is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and what is otherwise among contradictory cognitions such as doubt and the like; otherwise, it is a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of that [naya]. — *Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra*, p. 91.

This has been extracted: "The validity of means of knowledge is established in accordance with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), and not otherwise; for if they were subject to sublation, that [validity] would follow as a consequence.
(*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 271).

Comparison: Validity [is established] through worldly practice—*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.5—for otherwise, there would follow the consequence that even those cognitions which are sublated [would be valid]. (70)

Commentary: It is well known even among children that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arises from non-contradiction with practical activity (*vyavahārāvisaṃvāda*); otherwise, the validity of doubt, error, dream-cognition, and the like would be unavoidable. Thus, determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is a valid means of knowledge because it does not contradict practical activity.

That which possesses origination, destruction, and persistence is existent; a substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*); the soul (*jīva*) has consciousness as its nature—statements such as these possess validity because they are not sublated by other means of knowledge and because they admit of consistency characterized by the absence of contradiction between preceding and succeeding parts. Furthermore, they possess validity because they are conducive to practical activity (*vyavahāra*) consisting of objects, designations, and cognitions. Conversely, the doctrines of external objects, mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*), and emptiness are "bad standpoints" (*durnaya*) because they contradict practical activity, according to the *Jainendra-vyākaraṇa-bhāṣya* on the *Śruta-jñāna*.
Comparison—The three categories [of object, designation, and cognition] are distinct due to the difference between the object, the designation, and the cognition—*Rājavārttika*, p. 17;
*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 251;
*Mātre śūnya*—*Jainaviśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*.

The meaning of the verse: The validity (*pramāṇatā*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*adhyakṣa*) and the rest, which is asserted by the Buddhists and others, is established solely through its conformity with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), and not otherwise—that is, not in a manner that contradicts worldly practice. Why is this so? To this he says: "being sublated" (*bādhyamāna*), etc.

This refers to the consequence (*prasaṅga*) that those cognitions whose objects are things like a second moon or total emptiness—which are sublated and do not conform to worldly practice—would also result in being valid.
Otherwise, there is no [explanation];
[the commentary] provides an exposition of the *vivṛti*:
he says "of the means of valid cognition," etc., in order to explain the *kārikā*.

The validity—meaning the non-erroneousness—of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and the rest, is established because they do not fail in their practical application (*vyavahāra*), which consists in the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired; this is well-known even among children. Otherwise, if their validity were not based on the absence of failure in practical application, then the validity of doubtful cognitions, erroneous cognitions, dream-cognitions, and so forth would also be unavoidable, since they too possess that lack of failure. Furthermore, regarding the claim that those who hold that non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*) is invalid because it lacks failure in practical application have said: "Perception," and so forth.

The connection is with the statement that "conceptual perception (savikalpaka) would be a valid means of knowledge" (pramāṇa). Why is this so? To this he says: "Because it does not contradict practical activity (vyavahāra), and not because the non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) does so," such is the intended meaning.
Now, demonstrating that scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) possesses validity precisely for that reason, he says: "Arising," and so forth.

That which has arising, disappearance, and persistence as its *lakṣaṇa*—that is, its defining characteristic or essential nature—is this very reality, such as the soul (*jīva*) and other substances. This establishes the validity of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*)—such as "substance possesses qualities and modes" or "the soul has consciousness as its intrinsic nature"—even when it is not accompanied by clear reasoning (*aspaṣṭatarkaṇa*). This is the connection with what precedes.
Why is this so? To this he says: "By another means of valid cognition," and so forth.

Other than scripture (*śruta*), there are other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); the non-sublation by these, as well as the non-contradiction between preceding and succeeding scriptural statements, constitutes the characteristic of that corroboration (*saṃvāda*) which is possible in this very case.

Regarding this point, he states another reason, beginning with "the object" (*artha*) and so forth: the connection is that the validity of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) follows from its conformity with that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) whose nature consists of the object—the living being (*jīva*) and so on—the designation—the word "living being" and so on—and the cognition—the knowledge having that [object] as its domain.
Demonstrating the fallacious reasoning regarding conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), he says: "External objects," and so forth. [The meaning is:
both external objects and mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*)—that which is empty of these two, and the fallacious nature of the words that propound them;

namely, the words propounding the emptiness of external objects, the words propounding the non-duality of mere cognition and so forth, the words propounding the emptiness of that [mere cognition] alone, and the words propounding the emptiness of everything.
Why is their doctrine considered "bad logic" (durnaya)? To this he says: "Because it contradicts worldly practice" (*vyavahāravirodhitvāt*).

For it is not logical that there should be no contradiction regarding worldly practice—characterized by the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired—in those doctrines; for such non-contradiction exists only when there is the actual existence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
Demonstrating the *Ṛjusūtra-naya*, he says:
— Mārabāla Śramaṇa:
because the conventional usage of the Sugatas is non-contradictory.
Thus says [the author]; it should be seen in *Ba* and *Śra*, p. 605, note 7. Compare:
"Substance is the substratum of qualities; qualities reside in a single substance."
But the characteristics and the aspects are both to be understood as being on both sides—
*Uttarādhyayana* 28.6.
That which is characterized by substance, endowed with the nature of arising, passing away, and permanence,
and which is the substratum of qualities and modes— that is what the Omniscient Ones call "existence" (astitva).
— Pañcāstikāya Gāthā 10.
Substance possesses qualities and modifications— Tattvārthasūtra 5.38;
Nyāyaviniścaya, Chapter 1, Verse 111.

That indeed is substance (dravya), which is endowed with qualities (guṇa) and modifications (paryāya); know that qualities are co-existent (sahabhū), while modification is said to be successively born (kramabhū).
— *Paramātmaprakaraṇa*, verse 57.
The Ṛjusūtra-naya is considered to be that which primarily seeks the distinction between consensus and worldly transaction therein.

By "primarily" (*prādhānyataḥ*), meaning by way of being principal, the sense is that it also requires substance (*dravya*) as secondary; however, it then becomes a semblance of that [non-substance]. What is its specific characteristic? It is "that which distracts from unity" (*ekatvavikṣepī*); that is, it has the nature of distracting from—that is, negating—unity, which is substance.

How? In every way, both primarily and secondarily. Furthermore, what is its specific characteristic? It is *alaukika*. "Loka" means worldly convention; that which has this as its purpose is *laukika*, and its opposite is *alaukika*—this is the meaning of "from the non-worldly. For atoms, which are momentary and perish at every instant, and which are excluded from being either similar or dissimilar to one another, are not treated as objects of conventional discourse by investigators; for if they were, there would be no fallacy of a *naya* regarding them. (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 91)
The appearance as a single entity in every respect is indeed extraordinary (*alaukika*).

*Commentary:* Just as external atoms, when accumulated, manifest a gross object that appears as a single form though it is not real, so too do the atoms of consciousness (*saṃvit-paramāṇu*) manifest as a single variegated form. Therefore, there is no reality that is both unitary and multiform, partless yet appearing with parts, or non-sequential yet appearing as sequential; for difference contradicts non-difference. Otherwise, there would be no such thing as multiplicity anywhere.
A standpoint (*naya*) that takes into account [other factors] is valid, whereas one that disregards them is a fallacious standpoint (*durnaya*).

By establishing a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) based on a difference in appearance, it necessarily recognizes non-difference when there is no difference [in the underlying reality], because the object cannot be established if either of those two [aspects] is absent.
In the Buddhist view, atoms aggregated together are themselves the causes for the perception of gross forms. For instance: "Other atoms arise through connection with other objects."
For it has been said: "These [atoms] are accumulated; they indeed constitute the cause for the arising of cognition" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.195).

The meaning of the verse is as follows: one who seeks the distinction of everything from every perspective primarily, and who formulates and describes only the straight, straightforward, present mode (*paryāya*), is considered the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint (*naya*). Furthermore, because the word "primary" (*pradhāna*) is a relative term, substance (*dravya*) is its non-primary correlate.
He states its appearance: "In every way," and so forth.

"In every way" means by way of the presence or absence of the relationship between quality and the qualified. "Dissolving unity" means that which negates unity; this is the appearance of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint.
The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "because"; for this acceptance of difference is non-worldly, transcending worldly convention.

Indeed, it is not by way of a total rejection of oneness that the conventional usage of difference is established in the world regarding such things as a pillar, a sheath, or a granary, or regarding a child, a youth, and so forth.
[The term] *Ṛjusūtra*— derived from the sense of "that which straightens and strings together" (*ṛju praguṇaṃ sūtrayati tantrayate*)— is explained in the *Sarvārthasiddhi* and the *Rājavārttika*.
33 –sya samba– ā॰:
Acceptance of momentariness in every respect.
The commentary (*vivṛti*) and explanation: Expounding upon the verse, he says "externally" and so forth.
External atoms manifest—that is, they produce—a gross cognition of a single form. Of what nature is it? It is unreal, having as its object that which is not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*).

Of what nature are they? They are accumulated, meaning they have become a mass; being of such a kind, they manifest a corresponding cognition in that manner. In the same way, the atoms of consciousness (*saṃvit-paramāṇu*) are also of such a nature. Of what nature [is that cognition]? It has a variegated form (*citrākāra*), consisting of many forms such as blue and so forth, which are objects of apprehension, yet it is one. For this very reason, he states the conclusion—that it is "unreal"—beginning with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

Since a cognition of a single form has for its object that which is not ultimately real, therefore it is not logical that a single reality—such as the entity of the *jīva* and so forth—which is of an undifferentiated nature, should be non-sequential (i.e., simultaneous) and possess multiple forms; this is the supplementary explanation (*upaskāra*). [The phrase] "that which would establish itself as having a sequential nature"—meaning being differentiated by distinctions such as pleasure and so forth—is used either as a rhetorical objection (*ākṣepa*) or to indicate that it simply would not establish itself at all.
From what is this known? To this he says: "Because of the contradiction," and so forth.

He states the subverting argument for the opposing position: "Otherwise," and so forth—namely, that difference (*bheda*), which is manifoldness, is contradicted by non-difference (*abheda*), which is unity.
Otherwise, by some other mode that does not contradict it, there would be no plurality at all in certain things such as jars and cloths;

with this intention, [the author], demonstrating both its nature as a *naya* and its nature as a *durnaya*, says: "dependent," and so forth. A *naya* is "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*) because it functions in dependence upon its opposing property (*pratyanīkadharma*).
That which has departed from or cast aside dependence is "independent" (*nirapekṣa*); such is the "wrong view" (*durnaya*).

Now, one might ask: since non-difference is not established anywhere due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be a "view" (*naya*) that depends upon it? To this he says: "From the appearance," and so forth. By establishing the difference in intrinsic nature—the multiplicity of the forms of sentient and non-sentient entities—based on the difference in appearance, that is, the aspect of the perception of direct experience and so forth, the Buddhist indeed arrives at non-difference based on the non-difference of that appearance; for there is no distinction [between the two].
And this [notion] that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not tenable in the positions of either permanence or momentariness has been explained in detail in Laghīyastrayakārikā 8.
Regarding this very point, he states another supporting argument, beginning with "that" (*tat*):

because, between those two—difference and non-difference—upon the removal of either one (whether difference or non-difference), the subsequent effect or the cognition would be untenable; thus, a perspective that takes account of both is a valid standpoint (*naya*), whereas one that disregards them is a fallacious standpoint (*durnaya*).
They produce [it], because there is no [cognition] of a different kind due to the absence of differentiation.
One should establish [it as such], because there is no difference in appearance; and for that which is non-existent, there is no... [subsequent establishment].
Now, among the seven *nayās*, which ones have meaning as their primary focus and which have words as their primary focus? To this he says:
"These four are indeed *artha-nayas* because they rely upon the meanings of 'living beings' (*jīva*) and so forth.
Explanation: These...

Which ones? The four previously mentioned *arthanayas*—namely, *naigama*, *saṃgraha*, *vyavahāra*, and *ṛjusūtra*—are those in which the object (*artha*) is predominant. Why? Because they rely upon objects such as living beings (*jīva*) and non-living beings (*ajīva*); that is, because they take as their support (*ālambana*) the categories of *jīva*, *ajīva*, and so forth.
The remaining three—the *śabda*, *samabhirūḍha*, and *evaṃbhūta*—are *śabdanayas*, in which the word (*śabda*) is predominant.

What is its specific characteristic? It is "based upon the science of true words" (*satyapadavidyāsamāśritā*). "True words" (*satyapadāni*) are those not sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which denote distinctions such as tense and grammatical case; the "science" (*vidyā*) of these is the treatise on grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*). The meaning is that it is "based upon" (*āśritā*) that [science], because it relies on grammar. (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p.
92). For comparison: "The remaining three [types of objects] are based on words. (Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 92)
—Siddhiviṃśatikā-ṭīkā, p.
517B. Among these, the *arthanayas* (meaning-standpoints) are the Saṅgraha, Vyavahāra, and Ṛjusūtra; the remaining ones are the *śabdanayas* (word-standpoints)—Rājavārttika, p.
186. "The excellent meaning, the word, the object of perception, and the straight thread (*ṛjusūtra*)."
Regarding the abandonment of words and the attainment of the goal, they say: "The remaining [nayas]... (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-gāthā 2753).
Among these, four nayas ending with *ṛjusūtra* are considered *artha-nayas*.
The remaining three verbal standpoints (śabdanayas) have as their domain the objects expressed by words—Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 274; Nayavivaraṇa, p.

Among these, four are "meaning-standpoints" (artha-nayas) because they are inclined toward the determination of meaning; the remaining three, however, are "word-standpoints" (śabda-nayas) because their domain consists of what is expressed by words—
*Pramāṇanaya* 7.44, 45.
This is cited from the *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 23, and the *Nayapradīpa*, p.
104B: "Because of the definitive determination of the objects, such as the soul (*jīva*)."
—Āvaśyakaniryukti, folio 381B;
Sūtrakṛtāngāgama-ṭīkā, folio 426A.
"The three verbal nayas rely upon the science of true words. (72)

—Relying on the arrangement [of letters]— Jaṭāpāla-vivṛti: Due to differences in tense, grammatical case, and gender, a word produces a difference in meaning, as in *abhūt*, *bhavati*, *bhaviṣyati*; *karoti*, *kriyate*; or *devadattaḥ*, *devadattā* due to the difference in number (gender). Due to the difference in synonyms, a word produces a difference in meaning, as in *indraḥ*, *śakraḥ*, *purandaraḥ*.
The locus of action is thus constituted: agency belongs only to one who is acting,
because when one does not act, the status of being an agent is untenable.

But how does verbal cognition apprehend an object distinct from the speaker's intention? And why not? Because there is no necessary connection [between them]. For it has already been refuted that something which is not a cause of a cognition can be its object; since a cognition can determine even what is yet to come.

Upon seeing the rising of the Kṛttikās, there will be the rising of the Śakaṭa constellation; such a cognition is non-erroneous. [Examples include: "The sun will rise tomorrow," "There will be an eclipse of the sun and moon," "Threads will become cloth," "A lump of clay will become a jar," "Rice grains will become cooked rice," and "Grains will become rice grains. Because there is an infinity of such non-erroneous cognitions concerning future objects, verbal cognition is also established as grasping an object distinct from the speaker's intention, because—just like sensory perception—it has the inherent nature of conveying that object even without a [perceptual] connection.

Time has the characteristic of continuous occurrence (*varttanā*); a substance engaged in action is a *kāraka*; gender (*liṅga*) has the general characteristics of solidity (*styāna*), productivity (*prasava*), and the absence of both; a mode (*paryāya*) also effects a distinction in meaning because it distinguishes the nature of a thing in some respect, as it is perceived accordingly;

even a single word, though its etymological derivation is based on action, does not denote that [action] when it is absent; thus, one is called "Indra" only while experiencing supreme sovereignty and not at other times; therefore, a distinction in action is established, as in the case of "cook," "reader," and so forth.

For a treatise that explains letters, words, and sentences cannot be false when it provides the means for attaining the ultimate word-meaning; just as a *naya*—which consists of the intention of the knower—does not incur falsity while revealing an ultimate, non-absolutistic object by extracting a single absolute, conventional aspect through the analytical division of conventional processes such as verbal roots (*prakṛti*), yet remains a means for its comprehension. This is because only that which is entirely independent [of other perspectives] is false.

It is established that the correctness or falsity of the *nayās* consists in their being independent when non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is not rejected, and dependent when it is not rejected; otherwise, this is not the case. — This is the meaning of the verse from the *Jainavijaya*.

These four—known as Naigama, Saṃgraha, Vyavahāra, and Ṛjusūtra—whose natures have been clearly explained, are indeed *artha-nayas* (meaning-aspect standpoints), for they are primarily concerned with meaning (*artha*).
Why? It is said: because they rely upon objects such as living beings (*jīva*), that is, because they take recourse in objects such as living beings.
The three—Śabda, Samabhirūḍha, and Evambhūta—are *śabda-nayas* (word-aspect standpoints), for they are standpoints primarily concerned with words (*śabda*).
"How is it that they are such? To this he says: "In truth," and so forth.

"Truths" means those words which are non-false and devoid of the nature of corrupt speech (*apaśabda*), which express distinctions such as tense and grammatical case; the "science" (*vidyā*) of these is grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), wherein they are etymologically derived. Having relied upon that [grammar], and because they rely primarily on the meaning of words such as "living being" (*jīva*), they are "word-primaries" (*śabdapradhāna*). There is no [contradiction] in the Śruti... [text fragment].

Regarding the verbal perspective (*śabdanaya*), there is no [separate] commentary or explanation, because the first half of the verse has already been explained immediately following [the previous section]. Therefore, explaining the second half, he says: "Time," and so forth.
How is it that the verbal perspective (*śabdanaya*) effects a distinction in meaning? It is due to differences in tense, grammatical case, and gender;
this very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "as follows" (*yathā*).
In that regard, due to the difference in time, there are [the forms] "it was," "it is," and "it will be";
due to the difference in agent, there are [the forms] "he does" and "it is done"; and due to the difference in gender, there are [the forms] "Devadatta" and "Devadattā."
The *abhirūḍha* [naya] arises from a distinction of synonyms (*paryāya*) and effects a distinction in meaning, as in "Indra," "Śakra," and "Purandara," which are based on action (*kriyā*).
Why is this so? He says: "of one who acts" (*kurvataḥ*), and so forth.

The opponent asserts: "The status of being an agent belongs only to the Lord of Śacī (Indra) while he is actually performing actions such as ruling; when he does not act, his agency is untenable. To this, [the author] replies with "How? and so forth.

How? Not at all. Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used here in a sense of challenge. The cognition of the word is the effect of the word; that which is the cognition of the object (*artha-jñāna*) apprehends—that is, takes as its object—the external particular characteristic (*bahiḥ-svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
The master asks further: "And how is it not so?

Being thus questioned, he replies: "Because of its lack of connection to that object; that is, because of the impossibility of a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between the cognition of the word and that object."

If it is argued that even though there is no causal connection between them, the cognition nevertheless apprehends that [object], to this he says: "Certainly not," and so forth. For (*hi*) since it has been refuted that the object is not a cause of cognition but rather its cause—how is this known? To this he says: "Because of the determination of the future by consciousness."
Because there is the possibility of determination through the determination of a future object—which, having not yet attained its own existence, is not yet a cause—for instance:

upon seeing the rising of the Kṛttikās, the cognition that "the cart will rise" is non-contradictory; likewise, [cognitions such as] "the sun will rise tomorrow," "there will be an eclipse of the sun and moon," "threads will become cloth," "a lump of clay will become a jar," "rice grains will become boiled rice," and "paddy will become rice grains"—because there is an infinity of such non-contradictory cognitions regarding the future.

Then, concluding the subject at hand with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*) and so forth, he says: since it is established that cognition has the future as its object, therefore verbal cognition—let alone perceptual and inferential cognition—is established as apprehending an object distinct from the speaker’s intention.
[Objection: But since there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between a word and its object, how can that cognition apprehend the object? To this, he says: "The connection," and so forth.

Even without a restriction—that is, even without the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—it is established that the cognition grasps that [object] because of the word’s own nature, which is characterized by its capacity (*yogyatā*) to signify it.
Regarding this, he states an example: "like cognition" (*vijñānavat*).

Since the cognition of the word is the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the term "cognition" (*vijñāna*) here refers specifically to that perception (*pratyakṣa*) which was previously established as not being produced by an object; "like that" (*tadvat*) means similar to that.
The cognition of sound [arises] such that one understands the various realities of the Sugata, or as it is said in Śrā: "one understands the various realities right now."
There is indeed a purpose,
but there is no [other] cause; it will occur at the rising of the cart— both readings (bhavi-āṃ and bhavi-śraṃ) are acceptable.
Regarding the object,
verbal cognition [arises] from verbal cognition.

[Objection: It is not evident [from scripture]. Surely, it has been established that the *śabda-naya* (the perspective of words) differentiates objects based on differences in time and so forth; however, the definition of time and the other factors has not been stated. And it is not logical for those whose forms are uncharacterized to be the cause for the cognition of a difference in objects, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Anticipating this doubt, he states their definitions, beginning with "varttanā" and so forth:
Time is that which has as its characteristic the causality of the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of all categories of entities. This is the meaning of "that which has such a characteristic."
A substance (*dravya*) endowed with and engaged in action (*kriyā*) is a *kāraka*; the meaning is that a substance performing an action is a *kāraka*.
Gender (*liṅga*) is threefold, distinguished as feminine, masculine, and neuter;
therein, the feminine gender has the general characteristic of being "stiff" (*styāna*).
The general characteristic of the generative [male] is defined solely by the capacity to produce offspring; the general characteristic of the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*) is that.

The general characteristic of the neuter (*napuṃsakaliṅga*) is defined solely by the absence of both [the generative and the non-generative], namely the absence of both the solidified (*styāna*) and the generative.
Thus, this aforementioned triad—time and so forth—should be understood as somehow differentiating the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, because they are perceived in such a manner.
Nor is there a form characterized by the absence of characteristics;
[there is] no distinction in the action regarding the object.

—The moment (*kṣaṇa*) has as its general characteristic the absence of both stagnation (*styāna*) and production (*prasava*). [Objection: But is it not improper to say that "the distinction between synonyms (*paryāya-bheda*) effects a distinction in meaning," because a synonym does not differentiate the object? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "synonym" and so forth.

Not only time and the rest, but even a synonym—such as *indra*, *śakra*, *purandara*, and so on—is in some way a differentiator (*bhedaka*) of the object, such as the Lord of Śacī, bringing about a certain degree of distinctness, because it is perceived in that manner; this is connected with what follows immediately.

As for what was stated—that [the word] is based solely on action—even in that case, why is it a cause of differentiation through the difference in action even within a single synonym? To this he says: "Because of the difference in action," etc.

Because of the difference in action—that is, the difference in actions such as *indana* (ruling) and so forth—a single word, though appearing as a synonym such as *Indra*, has its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) based on action; due to the absence of that [action], there is an absence of the etymological derivation based upon it. For this reason, it does not denote that object—such as Indra—and thus, only while experiencing the action of supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*), namely *indana*, is one "Indra," and not at other times, such as at the time of consecration (*abhiṣecana*).

Thus, Śakra [is so called] only at the time of his being capable, and Purandara only at the time of his shattering the city, because he is not perceived as such at other times; this is the connection with what has been stated.

Since an entity, having undergone a particular action, is denoted by words whose etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is based on that specific action only at that very time and not at other times, it follows that the difference in action is the differentiator of entities, just as in the case of "cook," "reader," and so forth.
He explains [it]; otherwise, [there would be] such terms as "purifier," "cooker," "reader," and so forth. (Ā: ...pāvakapācakapāṭhakādi-; Ba: ...pāvakapāṭhakādi-)

—Regarding the reading and so forth: [The author] says "Not indeed," etc., in order to refute the views of some who claim that words are derived by grammar based on action, and that this is false; and others who claim that only the phonemes (*varṇa*), or only the word (*pada*), or only the sentence (*vākya*) are real. He states:

"Not indeed" means that the science characterized as grammar, which derives phonemes, words, and sentences, is certainly not false, because it is the means for attaining words in their ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

Indeed, if grammar were not authoritative, there would be no possible means for the cognition of correct words through the exclusion of corrupt words (*apaśabda*). [Objection: But surely the distinction between correct words and corrupt words will arise from the tradition of usage among elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra-paramparā*); therefore, it is improper to rely upon grammar for that purpose. [Reply: This too is charming only when left unexamined; for it is impossible to effect the distinction between them word-by-word for all words through the mere usage of elders alone, due to their infinite number.
However, by relying on grammar, it is easy—even with very little effort—to effect their distinction through definitions characterized by both general and specific features;
for instance: *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1).

Thus, by means of a single sūtra alone, many words such as *kumbhakāra*, *kāṇḍalāva*, *śāstrādhyāya*, and so forth, are correctly characterized. Therefore, since the distinction between correct and incorrect words can be easily made based on worldly usage as aided by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), grammar is indeed useful.

Nor should it be asserted that it is useless for that distinction because it lacks authority (*apramāṇa*); for if it lacked authority, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a total confusion regarding the manifold of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and others. And yet, such a confusion does not exist.
Therefore, this very absence of confusion (asamplava) validates grammar for its own establishment, since such a systematic determination cannot be achieved through any other means.

For it is only through grammar—by means of the analysis of stems and suffixes—that the comprehension of the manifold of factors (kārakas), such as object, agent, and so forth, which are mutually distinct, is appropriate; it cannot be achieved otherwise, because no source other than that exists for such comprehension.

[Objection: Since phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*) are partless (*niraṃśa*), what is the point of explaining them by resorting to such divisions as *prakṛti* (base) and so forth? Even for those [phonemes, etc. which are partless, if one were to explain them by postulating such divisions, that treatise would be entirely false, because it would not touch upon their true nature (*svarūpa*). To this, he replies with the words "vyāvahārika" and so on: That which exists in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)—meaning either in the exposition of the distinctions of the *vyavahāra-naya* (the conventional perspective) or in the linguistic practice (*vaiyākaraṇa-vyavahāra*)—is the analytical procedure (*prakriyā*) consisting of *prakṛti* and the rest. The distinction (*pravibhāga*) or division thereof is the means by which the ultimate, real word (*paramārtha-vāstava-śabda*)—which takes the form of phonemes, words, and sentences—is [revealed].

For in common usage, phonemes (*varṇa*) are established as real entities through distinctions such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth; words (*pada*), however, through the distinction between nominal and verbal endings; and sentences (*vākya*) likewise through the distinction of being an independent collection of mutually dependent words, and so on.

Just as the existence of phonemes, words, and sentences as eternal, partless, and so forth is untenable, so too has this been explained in detail in Laghīyastraya-kārikā 64: "Phonemes, words, and sentences convey meanings that are not [ultimately] desired," because they serve as the means for attaining [the ultimate] and as the cause for understanding the true nature [of reality].
The connection is that "the treatise which elucidates that [language] is not false.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is a means for attaining what is ultimately real is not false, just like a *naya* (perspective), which consists of the intention of a cognizer; and the treatise that elucidates phonemes, words, and sentences is a means for attaining language, which is ultimately real. He explains this example—namely, "like the *naya* consisting of the intention of a cognizer"—with the words beginning with "just as" (*yathā*). In whatever manner (*yathā*) something would not experience falsity, what is that? It is the *naya*, the intention of a cognizer.
What is he doing? Illuminating. What is that? Exclusivity (*ekānta*).

Of what nature is it? A portion of that, being a single part of an object whose nature is non-exclusivity (*anekānta*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? Conventional (*vyāvahārika*), having practical utility as its purpose.

Furthermore, what are its specific characteristics? It is the means for attaining that [reality]; "attaining" refers to the attainment of that object which consists of multiple aspects (anekāntātmaka), and it is either that attainment itself or the means by which it is attained.
How does it reveal this? By extracting—that is, by isolating it—from what?
From the [inherent] meaning.
From what kind [of cause]? From that which has a manifold nature (*anekāntātmaka*).

Is this from such a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)? To this he says: "from the ultimate" (*pāramārthikāt*), meaning from that which exists by way of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is the non-conceptualized form (*akalpitaṃ rūpaṃ*). It is because [the effect] arises from that.

"How could one who has become thus not experience falsity? To this he says: "Of the independent," and so forth. One from whom dependence on contrary properties (*pratyanīka-dharma*) has departed is "independent" (*nirapekṣa*); for such a person alone, and not for one of the aforementioned type, does falsity exist. Now, of what is there independence, and of what is there dependence? To this he says: "From the rejection of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), there is independence; from the non-rejection thereof, there is dependence."
Thus it is established that the correctness or falsity of the *nayās* occurs precisely through this manner of being dependent or independent, and not otherwise;
for it is they alone who, through a traditional lineage,
serve to distinguish between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*).
The specific [definition] should be seen in the commentary on each quarter— page 760, note 1— [reading] "lakṣa" instead of "vallakṣa. Ā.
—The method of the treatise—Śrī.
Therefore, Śrī.
the necessity of the causal factors (kārakas) such as the agent (kartṛ) and so forth.
By means of the science of grammar (vyākaraṇaśāstra), the [correctness] of phonemes, words, and sentences is determined.
Because there is no comprehension of the nature of phonemes, words, and sentences— due to the absence of form and because it is not amenable to linguistic usage.
Is it that sound does not exist? Or that of sound there is no [existence]? What is it that does not exist? In what manner does it not exist?
The state of being a means of conventional practice does not exist separately from that. (Variant readings: *vyavahā-śra-pāyatvaṃ ta-śra-pṛthakkṛtya nāsti* [Śrī, Ba]).
Because of existence,
the dharma of the Śrāvakas belongs to that which is dependent.

—O venerable one, may that lake known as the Jaina Āgama endure; it has reasoning for its clear water, well-understood meanings for its lotuses, and the collection of the seven *nayās* (standpoints) for its waves. It is profound, filled with the protection of all truths, and teeming with the swans of the virtuous and the good. It is endowed with the spreading sound of the birds that are the most learned teachers of the Lord of Wisdom, and it destroys the thirst of the heat of miserable rebirths.
[It has] reasoning for its clear water, well-understood meanings for its lotuses, and the collection of the seven *nayās* for its waves.

Profound, filled with the swans of the virtuous and the good, and endowed with the spreading resonance of the birds that are the preeminent scholars who are masters of wisdom; Ārya Pārikali— [this is] the ocean of the *Pāramitāsamuccaya*.
May the lake known as the Jaina scripture prevail, which destroys the thirst of the heat of miserable rebirths.

[In the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, the commentary on the *Laghīyastrayālaṅkāra* composed by Prabhācandra, the sixth chapter is completed. [The reading "tāpavṛddhihanana" is found in manuscripts Śra and Ba.]
Thus ends the sixth [chapter], the seventh section on the Nikṣepas, from the work of the venerable teacher Prabhācandra.

The lotus of the scripture has appeared within the lake of consciousness that illuminates all objects— a lotus possessing an expansion of mature petals in the form of all objects, and mature [wisdom] regarding the objects of knowledge.

O friends, let this field of Lakṣmī be cultivated for the sake of obtaining the abundant and excellent nectar of the deposit [of truth]—a field rich with the filaments and pericarp of the principles of valid cognition! [Chandaḥ:
O friends, let it be cultivated by us... [Śruti: O friends, let it be cultivated!

Now, having first described the fruit resulting from the completion of the study of the scriptural injunctions, [the author], while elucidating the nature of the *nikṣepa* (deposition), says: "Having understood the non-absolutistic meaning from the scripture through various intentions... [Commentary: Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is "one whose karma has been worn away by austerity" (*taponirjīrṇakarmā*). By means of austerity—characterized by *yathākhyāta-cāritra* (conduct as it is called)—specifically the white meditation (*śukla-dhyāna*) of the stage of "cessation of activity" (*vyuparata-kriyā-nivṛtti*), his karmas, such as those of knowledge-obscuration (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and so forth, in both their substantial (*dravya*) and modal (*bhāva*) forms, have been worn away and uprooted; thus he is so described.
By this, the two-fold propitiation of conduct (*cāritra*) and austerity (*tapas*) is indicated.

Furthermore, what is he like? He is "one who knows the principles (*tattva*) of the stages of living beings (*jīvasthāna*), the stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*), and the stages of inquiry (*mārgaṇāsthāna*). By this, the propitiation of knowledge (*jñāna*) is made known.

Again, how is he qualified? He is "one whose firm conviction (*abhiniveśana*) has increased," meaning one whose firm conviction—namely, right vision (*samyagdarśana*)—has specifically increased and is transformed into the nature of the destructive (*kṣāyika*) state.
By this, the propitiation through right vision (*darśanārādhanā*) has been described.

Since it is thus established that this very fourfold propitiation constitutes the path to liberation, one might ask: "Having done what did [the author] become possessed of such deep conviction? Anticipating this, he says: "having investigated" (*anuyujya*), that is, having questioned.
Which substances?
Of what kind? Those beginning with the soul (jīva).
By what means? By the "anuyogas," that is, by questions themselves.
By what [qualifications] are they distinguished? By those consisting of "indication" (nirdeśa) and so forth.

Among these, in response to the inquiry "What?", there is the "indication" (nirdeśa), which is the statement of the essential nature of a thing; for example: "The soul (jīva) is characterized by consciousness.
In response to the inquiry "Of what?", there is the "ownership" (svāmitva), which is the statement of lordship; for example: "Of itself."
By "by what" is the question asked; by "by oneself" is the instrument defined as the means;
by "in what" is the locus established as the substratum in response to the inquiry;
and by "for how long" is duration described as infinite time.

In response to the inquiry "of how many kinds [is it]?", having first performed—meaning having composed and established—the statement of its mode as "of one kind" due to the generality of consciousness (*caitanya-sāmānya*), [the author asks]:

of what? Of the distinctions consisting of object, speech, and cognition; that is, those distinctions—which are linguistic usages (*vyavahāra*)—whose natures (*ātman*) or essential characters are the object, the speech, and the cognition.

In this context, there are two types of distinction: the substantial (dravya) and the modal (bhāva), which consist of the object and the self respectively, since these are the attributes of the object.

Furthermore, conventional usage (vyavahāra) consists of "name" (nāman), which is verbal in nature, and "representation" (sthāpanā), which is conceptual in nature, because it takes the form of mental construction.
Of what nature are they? They are "established by scripture" (śrutārpitān), meaning conceptualized through scripture (śruta) as non-absolutism (anekānta).

By what means? By "depositions" (nikṣepa) that follow the "standpoints" (naya); that is, by depositions or placements that follow, or conform to, the standpoints whose objects are substance (dravya) and mode (paryāya). Of what kind are these [depositions]? They are "means" (upāya), that is, causes.
Where? In the determination of the distinction between primary and secondary [meanings] regarding the cognition of difference; that is to say, by means of the distinctions among causes.
Having done what first? Having examined—that is, having investigated—by what? By intentions (*abhisandhi*), meaning by the perspectives (*naya*) of the knower.

What did he do previously? Having attained—that is, having known—what object? The object of knowledge, such as the soul (jīva) and so forth. Of what nature is it? It is characterized by manifoldness (anekāntātmaka).
Why? From the Śruta, that is, from the Syādvāda—[as stated in] Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, pp. 95–97. —[End of] commentary. —ba.
Having examined those various worldly dharmas through methods that follow right policy, by means of deposits, stratagems, and the discernment of dissension—
*vedana* (in the Ā and Ba manuscripts).
Having formulated the distinctions consisting of meaning, word, and cognition as presented by scripture, and having investigated them according to the distinctions of meaning, word, and scripture...
[74]... [variant readings: *vicāryārthavāk-śra॰-bhedācchrutā-* (Ś) and *vicāryārthavāk-śra॰-bhedācchrutā-* (Ba)]
Through inquiries and further investigations, which have reached various distinctions such as explanations and so forth—
having reached these distinctions— one who possesses an increased attachment [regards] substances, beginning with the soul (jīva), as the self. || 75 ||

—Having known the stages of the soul (*jīvasthāna*), the stages of spiritual qualities (*guṇasthāna*), the points of inquiry (*mārgaṇāsthāna*), and the principles (*tattva*), and having worn away his karma through austerity, this one, being liberated, attains bliss. Thus [ends the verse]. 76.
These have been extracted—thus say the venerable Bhaṭṭākalaṅkadeva: "From scripture, for the sake of meaning... due to increased attachment"—*Anagāradharmāmṛta*, Chapter 6, Verse 169, Commentary:

Scripture (*śruta*) is beginningless with respect to the continuum [of its transmission], but it has a beginning with respect to its proof (*sādhana*). It is the determination of categories such as all living beings (*sarvajīva*) which fall within the scope of the three times; a *naya* (perspective) is the intention (*abhisandhi*) inclined toward the examination of a portion of that meaning.

From those two, there is the comprehension of ultimate and conventional objects; or rather, for those objects thus comprehended which have attained the status of being denotable, there is the presentation of distinctions among their denoters, which is "Nyāsa.
This is, at minimum, fourfold: by way of name, representation, substance, and state.
In that context, "naming" (*nāma*) is the act of designation (*saṃjñākarma*) that does not depend on other causes;
and because there are many acts of designation that do not depend on causes such as genus, substance, quality, action, or characteristic, it is manifold.
"Establishment" (*sthāpanā*) is the determination of a substance to which various names have been assigned, according to its nature of existence or non-existence.
Substance (dravya) is that which has turned its face toward a specific future transformation;
it is twofold, through the distinction of scripture (āgama) and non-scripture (no-āgama), while the modal designation (bhāva-nikṣepa) is characterized by functional application (upayoga).

Because it removes irrelevant matters and elucidates the relevant matter, the Nikṣepa (classification) is fruitful; by means of it, all categories of entities (padārtha) that have been set forth are further investigated through inquiries such as "nirdeśa" (description) and "sattva" (existence), and having been thus investigated and applied, they are fully examined. Nevertheless, there are specific expositions regarding the category of the soul (jīva), namely the *jīvasthāna* (stations of the soul), *guṇasthāna* (stages of spiritual development), and *mārgaṇāsthāna* (modes of seeking).

Thus, having comprehended all categories of existence through the methods of epistemology, logic, and systematic classification, and having understood the reality of the self with even greater firmness by means of the stations of the soul, the stages of spiritual development, and the types of inquiry, the self—possessing right vision characterized by deep-seated conviction, its karma exhausted through austerity, and liberated from all karma—attains a bliss that is free from affliction, uninterrupted, infinite, and beyond the senses.

For the self is not insentient due to the destruction of its qualities, nor is it a void due to the destruction of qualities and the qualified; it is not a non-enjoyer because of the absence of objects of enjoyment, nor does it lack attainment, nor is there any possibility of its being afflicted.

The subject (*dharmin*), such as the body and so forth, does not possess the nature of the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and the like; this is the thesis (*sādhya*), because even when that [obscuration] exists, the arising of knowledge is possible. For comparison: "Scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) is held to be without beginning or end through the presentation of its general nature as substance and so forth; for it has never been imagined by any person, anywhere, at any time, or in any way."

With reference to their specific distinctions, it is said that they possess a beginning and an end; yet, with respect to the continuum (*santāna*), they are without beginning or end, just as a sprout is preceded by a seed, while that [seed-continuum] is itself without beginning or end.
— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.20.
—Regarding the examination: Jaṭādhara-vivaraṇa.
For comparison: "The *nyāsa* (or *nikṣepa*) is for the purpose of comprehension [of reality] through detailed definition and classification"—*Tattvārthabhāṣya* 1.1.29.
"It is deposited in the determination and the discernment"—this is *nikṣepa* (deposition), and it is sixfold: name, representation, substance, space, state, and auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
"That which here is an implication of qualities (*guṇākṣepa*) and is merely metaphorical (*upacarita*), that alone is the figurative designation (*nikṣepa*).
— *Pañcādhyāyī*, verse 741. (Cf. *Dhavalāṭīkā*, fol. 10).

The *nikṣepas* (modes of presentation) are specific arrangements of words and meanings intended for their application in their proper places by means of context and so forth, in order to exclude non-comprehension and other such defects—*Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 25. Compare:
"And wherever one may know [something], one should present it in its entirety through the modes of presentation (*nikṣepa*)."
Even where one might not know [the specific location], one should deposit [the requisites] at a quadrangle (*caukka*).
There, the *āvaśyaka* is explained as being fourfold, namely:
the *āvaśyaka* of name (*nāmāvaśyaka*), the *āvaśyaka* of representation (*sthāpanāvaśyaka*), the *āvaśyaka* of substance (*dravyāvaśyaka*), and the *āvaśyaka* of state (*bhāvāvaśyaka*).
—Tattvārthasūtra 1.5: "Its [the soul's] placement is by way of name, representation, substance, and state. (anu0 sū0 8)
The Nikṣepa (classification) is of four types at minimum; it serves as the basis for the exposition of the subject matter at hand,
is the cause for the knowledge of the meaning of reality, pertains to the two nayas (perspectives), and functions to sever doubt.
—In the *Siddhiviniścaya*, Chapter 12;

in the *Mūlācāra*, Chapter on the Six Essentials (*ṣaḍāvaśyaka*), verse 17, the classification (*nikṣepa*) of *sāmāyika* is stated to be sixfold: by name, representation, substance, location, time, and state (*bhāva*).

In the *Āvaśyakaniryukti*, verse 129, the classification is described as sevenfold, through the distinctions of name, representation, substance, location, time, speech (*vacana*), and state (*bhāva*).
"Karma characterized by indifference is called *jīva-vīrya* (the vitality of the soul);
this is the designation for karma immediately following [the discussion of] its meaning"— from the *Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya* 1.5.
The act of naming (*saṃjñākarma*), which consists in applying a person's form to an object that does not possess those qualities for the sake of conventional usage, is "name" (*nāman*)—
*Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.5.
*Rājavārttika*, page 20;
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, page 18;
*Pañcādhyāyī*, verse 743.
