The application of a name to any [object] whatsoever, without specifying its particularities and without depending on other causes, is what is called "establishment" (*nāma*). As it is said: "That which is not denotable by synonyms, which remains fixed in another object, and which is independent of that object's specific meaning... (*Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, fol. 574A).
Generally, [the categories] are indeed those that are produced and those that are non-produced—
[this is the specific point], Jaina-tarka-bhāṣā, p. 25, verse 25.
Consciousness that is independent of objects, whether sentient or insentient,
and which does not depend on mental representations (*sthāpanā*) and so forth, is called "pure consciousness" (*kevalasañjñā*).
— *Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya*, Gāthā 12.
In that context, "auspiciousness" (maṅgala) is the designation for that which is independent of names, signs, and causes.
Therein, the sign (nimitta) is fourfold: genus, substance, quality, and action—*Dhavala-ṭīkā*, p. 17.

That which is established as a "living being" (jīva) in objects such as wood, cloth, paintings, ritual implements, or dice is *sthāpanā* (representation), like images of deities— such as Indra, Rudra, Skanda, or Viṣṇu. (Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra-bhāṣya 1.5)
"Representation" (sthāpanā) is the establishing [of an object] as "this is that very thing" in relation to wood, cloth, paintings, dice, and so forth—
*Sarvārthasiddhi*, *Rājavārttika* 1.5.

Furthermore, when an object is fashioned with such a form— or even without a form— for a short or long duration, with the intention that it be empty of its actual substance, that is *sthāpanā*. (Pañcādhyāyī, Śloka 743)
—*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, Gāthā 26: "Establishment (*sthāpanā*), moreover, consists of [representations] such as this [statue of] Kumāra and so forth;
it may be temporary or permanent, whereas establishment by name (*nāmasthāpanā*) lasts as long as one's life."

"Restriction [is established] by means of establishing existence, or by means of non-existence, such that it is not of that nature, like a pillar and Indra"—*Nayacakra-vṛtti*, p. 381A. *Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya*, gāthā 13.
In the *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā*, folio 474B,
and the *Jainatarkabhāṣā*, page 25, it is stated:
"The establishment [of a thing] as being something else, such as a snake, even though it is not a snake, is called 'designation' (*sthāpanā*)."
That [establishment] is of two kinds: establishment by way of existence and establishment by way of non-existence—for instance, *Dhavalāṭī*, p.
19: "Establishment is considered to be the fixing of a name that has been applied to an object."
Due to the non-contradiction with reality, there are two types based on the distinction between existence and its opposite—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 111.

A "substantial soul" (*dravyajīva*) is said to be a soul established by cognition as being devoid of attributes and modes, yet endowed with its beginningless, transformative state (*anādipāriṇāmikabhāva*).
— From the *Tattvārthādhigama-bhāṣya* 1.5:
A substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses qualities (*guṇa*), or that by which qualities are possessed.
— Sarvārthasiddhi 1.5:
A substance that has assumed a state of orientation toward a specific future transformation.
Or, it is not that [the effect] arises from that—[as stated in] Rājavārttika, p.
20; Siddhiviniścaya, p. 474.
Dhavalāṭīkā, p.
20; Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 111;
Pañcādhyāyī, śloka 744.
Regarding substance (*dravya*), however, it is the acquisition of that [knowledge] by one for whom it has passed away or will yet come to be,
or even by one who, though not currently engaged in it, describes its qualities here—
*Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya*, Gāthā 14.

A substance (dravya) is a modification (vigāra) characterized by the loss of one state and the acquisition of another; it is the substratum (sadbhāva) of qualities (guṇas), the potentiality (bhavyatva) for future states, and the actualization (bhūtatva) of past states, according to its specific fitness (yogya-viśeṣa). — Gāthā 28.
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 25:
"For that which is the cause of an entity, whether past or future, is called 'substance' (dravya) by the knowers of reality; it is declared to be both conscious and unconscious."
— Āvaśyaka-niryukti, Malayagiri commentary, folio 6B.
Substance characterized by its present mode is *bhāva*
— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.
Rājavārttika, page 21;
Siddhiviniścaya, page 474.
Ghavalāṭī, p. 29;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 113;
Pañcādhyāyī, śloka 745.
But he who is truly engaged in accordance with the meaning, knowing the subject matter even of this [text] which is the essence of the pure viewpoints, and being intent upon it—
*Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya*, Gāthā 15.

Indeed, an entity is defined by the omniscient ones as being joined with the experience of the intended action— just like Indra and others here [are so called] because of their experience of actions such as ruling (indana)—
[as stated in] Āvani-malaya, folio 9A.
Comparison— for what purpose? For the exclusion of what is irrelevant and for the determination of what is relevant—
*Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.5.
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 98:

Now, if it is asked, "Why is this method of exposition (*nikṣepa*) employed? it is said: there are three kinds of listeners—the unlearned (*avyutpanna*), those who have understood all the intended meanings, and those who have understood the intended meanings only partially.
Among them, the first does not determine the meaning of the intended term because of his lack of proficiency.

The second [opponent] lies down in doubt, thinking, "What is the meaning of this word under discussion? Taking up a meaning other than the one currently under consideration, he either contradicts it or acts like the second [opponent]. Likewise, the third also lies down in doubt or contradicts. In that case, if [the respondent] is unlearned, the method of *nikṣepa* (deposition) serves to provide instruction to the unlearned and to refute what is irrelevant.

Now, regarding the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthika*), by means of that, all the modes of designation (*nikṣepa*) are stated for the purpose of explaining the subject at hand; for without the determination of the property of distinction (*vyatireka-dharma*), the determination of the positive rule (*vidhi*) is impossible. The statement of all the modes of designation serves to destroy doubt concerning the second and third [standpoints], and the mode of designation is established for the sake of ascertaining the subject matter for those two who might otherwise be mistaken.

For it has been said: "The exposition is for the purpose of warding off misconceptions, for the purpose of providing an explanation, for the purpose of destroying doubt, and for the purpose of ascertaining the true meaning" (Dhavala-ṭīkā, p.
This statement has been cited—*Jainatarkabhāṣā*, p. 25: "In the *Niddesa*, it is asked: 'What is the cause of a person? Wherein? In what? At what time?
Of how many kinds?'—*Anuyogadvārasūtra* 151."
By way of exposition, ownership, means of accomplishment, locus, duration, and classification—
Tattvārthasūtra 1.7.
By whom, for whom, where, for how long, of what kind, and what is its nature?
[These are] the six doors of non-obstruction— *Mūlācāra* 8.15.

The exposition of the sixfold [analysis] consists of: the exposition of existence, the sequence of substance, the sequence of space, the sequence of contact, the sequence of time, the sequence of intervals, the sequence of states, and the sequence of relative magnitude—thus it is taught in the *Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama*, Sūtra 7.
What is this "sequence" (*anugama*)? It is declared to be of nine kinds.

Namely: the exposition of the hundredfold [categories], the measure of substance, space, contact, time, interval, part, state, and the degree of smallness and greatness—[as stated in] Aṅguttaranikāya Sutta 80:
"And by means of number, enumeration, space, contact, time, interval, state, and smallness and greatness."
— Tattvārthasūtra 1.8:
"They are indeed subtle-bodied and gross-bodied, and they are further divided into those that are fully developed (paryāpta) and those that are not fully developed (aparyāpta)."
The Jinas have declared that one-sensed beings are of four types;

they exist as both developed (paryāpta) and undeveloped (aparyāpta). Two-sensed beings are of six types, likewise as developed and undeveloped; the remaining [three, four, and five-sensed beings] are also [of six types], being either with mind (saṃjñin) or without mind (asaṃjñin).
—Root [text], Section on Synonyms, Verse 152–53;
Gojīva, Verse 72;
Karma-grantha 4.
One should know [the stages] as follows: wrong view, the state of subsidence, mixed, non-abstention, partial abstention, the heedless, and likewise the heedful.
From this [point], there are the stages of *apūrvakaraṇa*, *anivṛttibādara*, *sūkṣmasāmparāya*, *upaśāntamoha*, *kṣīṇamoha*, the *sayogakevalijin*, and the *ayogin*—
Mūlācāra, Paryāya-saṃgrahaṇī, Gāthā 154–55.
Chakkhaḍā Sūtra 9–23;
Jīvājīvābhigama Sūtra 9–10;
Karmagrantha 2.

2. [The fourteen guṇasthānas are: wrong belief (mithyātva), mixed belief (sāsādana), right belief with delusion (miśra), right belief with partial delusion (avirata-samyagdṛṣṭi), right belief with complete restraint (deśavirata), right belief with complete restraint and activity (pramatta-saṃyata), right belief with complete restraint and some activity (apramatta-saṃyata), right belief with complete restraint and effort toward spiritual progress (apūrva-karaṇa), right belief with complete restraint and subduing of passions (ani-vṛtti-bādara-samparāya), right belief with complete restraint and subtle passions (sūkṣma-samparāya), right belief with complete restraint and freedom from passions (vitarāga-chadmastha), right belief with complete restraint and omniscience (sayoga-kevalin), right belief with complete restraint and cessation of all activity (ayoga-kevalin). [The fourteen jīvasthānas are: beings with one sense-faculty (ekendriya), beings with two sense-faculties (dvīndriya), beings with three sense-faculties (trīndriya), beings with four sense-faculties (caturindriya), beings with five sense-faculties (pañcendriya); those with fixed destiny (trasa); those with mind (sa-manaska); those with activity of speech (vacanayoga); those with activity of body (kāyayoga); those with activity of mind (manoyoga); those with female gender (strīveda); those with male gender (puṃveda); those with neuter gender (napuṃsakaveda); those with passions (kaṣāya);

those with knowledge (jñāna); those with self-restraint (saṃyama); those with right vision (darśana); those with thought-coloration (leśyā); those destined for liberation (bhavya); those with right belief (samyaktva); those with consciousness (saṃjñin); and those who take food (āhāraka). — *Chakkhaṃḍāgama*, Sūtra 4.
Gati, indriya, kāya, yoga, veda, kaṣāya, jñāna, saṃyama, darśana, leśyā, bhavyatva, samyaktva, saṃjñin, and āhāra— [these are the fourteen guṇasthānas].
— Mūlācāra, Chapter on Paryāya, Verse 156.
Go-jī-gā 141; Karma-grantha 4,
Free from affliction, beyond the senses, incomparable, liberated from merit and demerit, devoid of returning again, eternal, immovable, and without support— this is the rule. (Gāthā 177)

Those purified by the vision [of the Buddha] worship that which is auspicious, undecaying, free from disease, inexhaustible, unassailable, devoid of sorrow, fear, and doubt— the stainless manifestation of the power of knowledge and the ultimate bliss. (Ratnagotravibhāga, verse 40)
*Sarvārthasiddhi*, page 1;
*Tattvārthādhigamasūtra*, verse 242.
For comparison: "They know liberation to be the attainment of the self through the destruction of the internal impurities of the soul."
Neither non-existence, nor insentience, nor a purposeless sentience—Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 384; Yaśovijaya Upanibandhana, p.
At that time, for the person whose karma has been exhausted and who abides in his own true nature,
there is neither non-existence, nor insentience, nor is sentience purposeless. — *Tattvānuśāsana*, verse 234.

—From [the relationship of] quality and possessor of quality (guṇaguṇin)—Jaḍaviṣaya commentary on the meaning of the kārikā: This self, who is either the author or the student of the treatise, attains happiness; that is, he becomes composed of happiness.
Being characterized by what? He says: "liberated" (vimukta), meaning specifically liberated, being entirely free from all karma.
Being liberated, moreover, in what state would he be? He says: "one whose karma has been worn away by austerity" (taponirjīrṇakarmā).
He is so described because his karmas have been worn away and uprooted by *tapas*, characterized as the conduct of one who has attained the [right] name (*yathākhyāta-cāritra*).

Furthermore, being of what nature would he be liberated? To this he says: "In the states of the soul," and so forth; that knower of reality (*tattvavit*), who knows the true nature of the soul and other principles, [is liberated] through each of the fourteen states of the soul (*jīvasthāna*), the stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*), and the modes of seeking (*mārgaṇāsthāna*).
Furthermore, being characterized by what would he be liberated? To this he says: "increased," and so forth.

He is so described as one whose *abhiniveśana*—that is, right vision (*samyagdarśana*)—has increased, having specifically grown to its highest excellence in the form of the state of destruction (*kṣāyika*).
In some places, the reading is *vivṛddhābhiniveśataḥ*.

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: through the intensification of firm conviction (*abhiniveśa*), this self becomes a knower of the principles such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth, and its karma is worn away by austerity, because right knowledge and conduct are preceded by right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

By this passage, the causal complex for liberation—consisting of right vision, knowledge, and conduct—is elucidated; for that [liberation] cannot occur if even one of these is absent, and the impossibility of its occurrence in the absence of any one of them will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
Having done what does he become one whose dogmatic adherence has increased yet who is a knower of reality? To this he says: "having questioned," and so forth.

The word *anuyoga* applies both to a question and to a reply. For example, in the phrase, "Even though you have been questioned (*kṛtānuyoga*), you say nothing and remain silent," the word *anuyoga* is well known in the sense of a question.
However, in the phrase, "Even though you have given a reply (*dattānuyoga*), you ask again and again," it refers to the response to what was asked.

Therefore, this meaning is established: having examined the nature and other attributes of the substance of the soul and so forth, and having asked about them out of a desire to know them—by what means?
By means of *anuyogas* (inquiries) alone; the particle *ca* (and) here has the sense of *eva* (only/exclusively).
By what characteristics [is it distinguished]? He says: "Nirdeśa" and so forth.

The meaning is: by those which have reached the various divisions of those things—such as ownership and so on—which have "nirdeśa" as their first; that is, by the forms of the distinctions beginning with *nirdeśa*.
(Śā-ba)
Even though liberated, [he is] Śrī;
[he is] one whose [defilements] are exhausted and uprooted—Ārya;
[he has] attained the state of being drawn out—Śrī.
Regarding "vimukte," the lexicon *Amara* states: "praśnaḥ, anuyogaḥ, pṛcchā" [mean question]; and this also occurs in the *Bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, there is no [intrinsic nature] such as substance and so forth;
thus they were questioned by Śrāvaka.

At the beginning of an exposition, there are two possible approaches regarding a question: either, when the name is already known, the question is for the purpose of determining its definition; or, when the definition is already known, the question is for the purpose of ascertaining the name.

In the former case, the question is: "What is the definition of a substance such as the soul (jīva)? and the answer is: "Its definition is consciousness (upayoga), etc. In the latter case, the question is: "What is the name of the category whose definition is consciousness, etc.? and the answer is: "It is named 'soul' (jīva), etc."

If it is asked, "What, then, are 'indication' (nirdeśa) and the others? it is said: in response to the inquiry "what?", the statement of the essential nature of a thing is "indication" (nirdeśa); in response to "of what?", the manifestation of its sovereignty is "ownership" (svāmitva);
and in response to "by what?", the revelation of the instrument is the "means" (sādhana).
The designation of the locus is "in what" (kasmin);
the determination of the state established by time as to how long [it lasts] is "duration" (sthiti);
and the statement of the variety of types is "mode" (vidhāna).
In this regard, the interrogation (*anuyoga*) takes the form of questions such as "What is here?", "Whose?", "By what?", "In what?", "For how long?", and "Of how many kinds?";

whereas the response (*prativacana*) consists of the description of the nature of the entity, the manifestation of its sovereignty (*adhipatitva*), and so forth— thus it is established in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.

Regarding the question "What is the definition? (lakṣaṇaṃ kiṃ), the answer "of the living beings, etc. (jīvādīnām) is the designation [of the subject]. "Intrinsic nature" (svarūpa) is the naming [of the essence]; "ownership" (svāmitva) is sovereignty; "means" (sādhana) is the cause of origination; "substratum" (adhikaraṇa) is the locus; "duration" (sthiti) is the delimitation by time; and "mode" (vidhāna) is the manner.
–Sarvārthasiddhi 1.7–; commentary on the word "tva" by Śrī [Haribhadra].
"What is it?"— this is the inquiry in the form of a reply; thus,
the explanations and so forth have been understood.

If it is asked, "Let 'being' (sat) and the others be defined," it is replied as follows: The term *sat*—which is the root for the comprehension of all categories and has as its objects substance (*dravya*), mode (*paryāya*), quality (*guṇa*), universal (*sāmānya*), and particular (*viśeṣa*)—is the basis for the category of "collection" (*saṃgraha*) because it is a complete predication (*sakalādeśa*); or it is the basis for the category of "practical usage" (*vyavahāra*) because it is a partial predication (*vikalādeśa*).
"Number" (*saṃkhyā*) is the enumeration of distinctions.
The field is the commonality of dwelling in the present;
that same [field] is contact when it has the three times as its object; and time is characterized by the present and so forth.

The "interval" (*antara*) refers to a period of separation occurring within the continuum (*santāna*) of a certain [being], or it refers to a state such as the subsided (*aupaśamika*) and so forth; even when there is certainty regarding one of the categories such as "countable" (*saṃkhyāta*), "fewness" (*alpatva*) and "multitude" (*bahutva*) serve as the cause for perceiving their mutual distinctions.

Having performed what kind of inquiry (*anuyoga*) through the aforementioned modes of exposition and so forth, does this self (*ātman*) inquire into substances such as the soul (*jīva*)? To this he says: "having composed" (*viracayya*), meaning having specifically fashioned or arranged; what [has been composed]? He says: "objects," and so forth—namely, the distinctions consisting of those very things:
objects (*artha*), speech (*vāk*), and cognition (*pratyaya*).

For differentiation consists of three aspects: that which has the nature of meaning—namely, substance and mode; that which has the nature of speech—namely, name and form; and that which has the nature of cognition—namely, representation.
What are these like? To this he says: "placed by scripture" (*śrutārpitān*), meaning those intended as presented by scripture.
By means of what, and having fashioned them how? To this he says: "In the methods" (*nayeṣu*), etc.

When the methods (*naya*s), which describe the various aspects of reality, have proceeded, those "subsequent" (*anu*)—meaning those that follow or proceed after them—are the "modes of presentation" (*nikṣepa*s).
By what kind of things? By "means" (*upāya*s), that is, by those which serve as the causes.
Where? In the cognition of distinctions—that is, in the cognition of substances such as the soul (jīva) that are distinct by nature through their names, representations, and so forth.

If it is asked, "How is it established that these [cognitions] follow the *nayās*? [The answer is: Because they operate upon those specific aspects of reality (*vastvaṃśa*) as determined by the *nayās*.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Having examined," and so forth.

Having examined—that is, having investigated—those various [categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*), as well as their attributes (*dharma*), which are parts of objects consisting of manifold aspects (*anekāntātmaka*); of what nature are they? They are manifold (*aneka*).
Furthermore, of what kind are they? They are "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*), meaning those that accomplish the purposes of worldly transaction.
By what means are they examined? To this he says: "by intentions" (*abhisandhibhiḥ*), that is, by the intentions (*abhiprāya*) of the knower.
Having done what? Having realized what? What object? Of what specific quality? Non-absolutistic (anekānta).
Why [is it] "having realized"? He says: "from hearing" (*śrutāt*). The term *sad* indicates existence (*astitva*).
The counting of the divisions of friendship and residence in the field pertain to the present time;
that same touching pertains to the three times.
Time is twofold: primary and conventional;
the internal [time] is characterized by the states of disjunction, existence, subsidence, and so forth.
The relative smallness or greatness [of categories] is the comprehension of their specific distinctions through mutual comparison—
*Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.8.
The continuum of worldly discourse involving the planets is not even a matter of certainty.
The state of being followed by the instruction of speech; the commentary is an exposition.
Explaining the four verses according to their sequence, he says: "The heard," and so forth.

What is the nature of that which is "heard"? It is the word of a trustworthy authority (*āpta*). How is it [without beginning]? With respect to the continuum (*santāna*) and with respect to the substance (*dravya*).

If it is asked, "How then can a substance (*dravya*) be denoted by the word 'continuum' (*santāna*)? [The answer is: because of the etymological derivation that it is that which possesses a "stretch" (*tāna*), meaning an expansion (*vistāra*) that is correct and follows all modes (*paryāya*) functioning throughout the three periods of time. If so, how then is it "beginningless"? To this he says: "The means of accomplishment," and so forth. That which is accomplished or brought about is the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*), namely the modes such as phonemes and words; or alternatively, that by which something is accomplished or demonstrated. The connection is that "the scripture (*śruta*) is beginningless in relation to that."

By this, it has been refuted in every respect that "it is either eternal or non-eternal," and this has already been explained at length previously; so, enough with further digression. Why is such scripture a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? He says: "In the three times," and so forth.

It has as its object the three times (*trikāla*), all modes (*sarvaparyāya*), and the categories of existence such as the soul (*jīva*); it is an exposition (*nirūpaṇa*) of these, which means the illumination of their nature as it actually exists; and because it is inclined toward and expert in this [exposition], it is therefore a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is inclined toward the exposition of the categories of existence such as the soul, along with all their modes throughout the three times, is a valid means of knowledge, just like the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of an omniscient being; and the scripture (*śruta*) described in the aforementioned manner is of such a kind.
What kind of thing is *naya*? To this he says: "A part of its meaning," and so forth. What is this *naya*? It is *abhisandhi*, which is the intention (*abhiprāya*) of the knower.

Of what nature is he? He is "intent upon the investigation of the aspects of its meaning. Its meaning is the object of that sacred teaching (*śruta*), which consists of the categories previously mentioned, such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth. An "aspect" of that is a property (*dharma*), such as permanence and so forth. He is "intent" upon—that is, skilled in—the investigation of those [aspects].
Through these two, namely *śruta* and *naya*, there is "comprehension," meaning certainty.
Of what things? To this he says: "of ultimate and conventional objects," which means of substances (*dravya*) and modes (*paryāya*).
With respect to substance, there is no [such thing as] activity or cessation; this is what has been heard from the Āgama.
"It may be," he said;
"is it impermanent or permanent?
"It has been heard," [he replied].

"And those living beings" (ca te jīvāḥ) [in the *Bhagavatī* and *Śrutasāgara* commentaries], because they are intent upon defining all categories of existence such as living beings (*jīva*) along with all their modes (*paryāya*) throughout the three periods of time;
therefore, "living beings are like modes" (*paryāyavaj jīvāḥ*). *Bhagavatī*.

Now, having demonstrated that the *nyāsa* (depiction) follows the method [of the scriptures] by means of the passage beginning with "tadadhigata" (those things attained), he explains its essential nature: The term *tadadhigatānām* refers to those things—such as the *jīva* and so forth—which have been attained through the *śrutanaya* (the scriptural method), which exist in the form of substances (*dravya*) and modes (*paryāya*), and which have come to possess the state of being denotable (*vācyatā*) while possessing a common nature. For particular modes of meaning (*arthaparyāya*) do not attain the state of being denotable unless they possess a common nature. The *nyāsa*, or *nikṣepa*, is the presentation—that is, the exposition—of the meanings such as the *jīva* and so forth within their denoting words (*vācaka*) like "jīva," etc., without confusion (*saṅkara*) or intermixture (*vyatikara*). This is what is meant by "depiction."
How many types does it have? To this he says: "He," and so forth.
That placement (*nyāsa*), whose nature has been described, is at least fourfold in its concise form.
How so? To this he says: "Name," and so forth.

The *nikṣepa* (method of classification) is divided into four types by way of name (*nāma*), representation (*sthāpanā*), substance (*dravya*), and actual state (*bhāva*). He explains these with the words "therein" and so forth: among those modes of *nikṣepa*, namely name and the rest, what is "name"? He says: "the cause," and so forth. If it is asked, "What, then, is the cause of a name, or what is another cause? we reply: the speaker’s intention is its cause, while genus (*jāti*) and so forth are other causes.
That act of naming, which is the making of a designation independent of [external objects] and occurring by the power of one's own will, is called a "name" (*nāman*).
To define its specific limit, he says: "And that," and so forth.
And that name, whose nature has been described, exists in many ways—that is, in many varieties.
For instance: some names denote a single living being, such as "Ḍittha"; some denote many living beings, such as "yūtha" (a herd);
and some denote a non-living thing, such as "ghaṭa" (a jar).
Some names denote many living beings, such as "palace" (*prāsāda*); some names denote one living being, such as "doorkeeper" (*pratīhāra*);
and some names denote both one and many living beings, such as "porter" (*kāhāra*).
One should understand that there are various types [of names], such as those denoting many living beings and non-living things, for example, "city" (*nagara*), and so forth.

Why is it of indefinite form? He says: because names (*saṃjñākarma*) are manifold and indefinite when they do not depend on causes characterized by genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*); for it is only in the case of words that depend on fixed causes such as genus and the rest that fixity is logically established.
For those words that apply to substances and so forth by way of a genus (*jāti*) are genus-words (*jātiśabda*), such as "cow," "horse," and so on.
However, those that function by way of a substance (*dravya*) are substance-words (*dravyaśabda*);
and these are of two kinds: substance-words for things joined by conjunction (*saṃyogidravyaśabda*) and substance-words for things joined by inherence (*samavāyidravyaśabda*).

In that regard, words denoting substances through conjunction (*saṃyoga*) include such terms as "one who has earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*); words denoting substances through inherence (*samavāya*) include such terms as "one who has horns" (*viṣāṇī*).

Furthermore, those words which apply to a substance by way of its qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*karman*) are to be understood as quality-words (*guṇa-śabda*) and action-words (*karman-śabda*), respectively—such as "white," "blue," and so forth, or "goes," "comes," and so forth.
For those [beings] attained through the Śruta-naya, there is no [such distinction].

The sense is that "confusion" (*saṅkara*) is the simultaneous occurrence of all [categories], while "intermingling" (*vyatikara*) is their mutual transgression into one another's domains; [the state of the categories] exists as distinct from these two, by virtue of abiding in their own specific, determined natures—just like a possessor of qualities (*bhāvavat*).
As for the phrase "how many," etc., it means "of how many kinds," and so on; [this distinction] does not exist among names and the like.
Comparison has as its cause other factors—namely, genus, substance, quality, and action—as stated in the *Siddhiviniścaya-ṭīkā* (p.
474a): "The speaker's intention is said to be the common cause of the name."
Therefore, something other than that—namely, another cause such as "genus" (jāti) and so forth—is accepted; [this refers to] that which exists independently of it. (Tattvārthaśloka, p. 99, line b).

For that which pertains neither to a single soul nor to non-soul, nor to multiple souls nor to multiple non-souls, nor to both [soul and non-soul] taken individually or collectively—this being established by virtue of its application to individual and collective subjects, whether soul or non-soul—as in the case of the application to an individual soul, such as "This lump of flesh is Devadatta; this is Devadatta," and as in the case of the application to a collective of souls, such as "All these are Gargas and so forth. (Aṇu-sūtra 9)

Because it is possible for it to have a single living being (*jīva*) as its object— just as in the case of "O Abhaya, O Purudeva"— and because it is possible for it to have multiple living beings as its objects— just as in the case of "This is Ḍittha, this is Ḍavittha, this is Jinadatta," which refers to four distinct types of living beings—
and likewise because it is possible for it to have individual non-living things (*ajīva*) as its objects— as in the case of "That is *tya*, that is *kya*," and so forth.
Because it is possible for it to have all living beings as its object, like the rule "bhū-ādayo dhātavaḥ";
because it is possible for it to have a single living being as its object, like "ākāśa-kāla-dharma-adharma";
and because it is possible for it to have many living beings as its object, like "tau satīva."
—Siddhiviniścayaṭīkā, p. 474A.
The substratum (ādhāra) of that auspiciousness (maṅgala) is eightfold, as follows:

a single soul (jīva), multiple souls (jīvāḥ), a single non-soul (ajīva), multiple non-souls (ajīvāḥ), a single soul and a single non-soul, multiple souls and a single non-soul, a single soul and multiple non-souls, or multiple souls and multiple non-souls.
—Dhavalāṭī, p. 19:
For some names refer to a single living being, such as *ḍittha*; others refer to many living beings, such as *yūtha*.
Some names denote a single living being, such as "jar"; some names denote many non-living things, such as "palace";
and some names denote both a single living being and non-living things, such as "doorkeeper."
Some names denote one living being and many non-living beings, such as "kāhāra"; some names denote one non-living being and many living beings, such as "maṇḍura";
and some names denote many living beings and non-living beings, such as "nagara."
—*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 98: The staff-bearer is the gatekeeper; therein, one is the non-living staff and the other is the living gatekeeper, as stated in the Āvaśyaka-niryukti.

There is one living being, the fisherman, and many non-living things, such as jars and the like, employed for the purpose of fetching water. This is the analogy: in arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*), a specific object is expressed by its name, as in "Ḍittha";
in genus-words (*jāti-śabda*), it is expressed by its genus, as in "this is a cow."
In the case of quality-words, [the relation is] by means of a quality, as in "white";
in the case of action-words, by means of an action, as in "cook";
and in the case of substance-words, by means of a substance, as in "staff-bearer" or "horned one."
—*Pramāṇasamuccaya-ṭīkā*, p. 12:
"In that context, 'name based on birth' refers to [terms such as] cow, human, jar, cloth, pillar, or wall;
'name based on the substance of conjunction' refers to [terms such as] 'staff-bearer,' 'umbrella-bearer,' or 'millet.'"
A name based on a collection [of qualities] is, for example, "Galagaṅga" (Long-necked) or "Kāṇa" (One-eyed);
a name based on qualities is, for example, "Black" or "Red";
a name based on activity is, for example, "Singer" or "Dancer."
—*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 18:
"For a word functions toward substances and so forth by way of a universal (*jāti*);
that [word] should be known as having a universal as its cause, like the words 'cow' or 'horse'."
A usage based on the predominance of a quality, which has a substance as its substratum and is caused by a quality,
is understood [in this way], such as in the words "white" or "pale red," and so forth.
Because karma is predominant there, it is understood that karma is the cause; it moves and flows like someone [carrying] something—this is most certain.

The term "substance by conjunction" (sayogidravyaśabda) would be like words such as "the one with earrings," while the term "substance by inherence" (samavāyidravyaśabda) is established as being like "the one with horns."
9 – *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 99 – *suvartta*— Ā, Ba.
Regarding the term *sayogin*—now, what is *sthāpanā*? He says: "placed," and so forth.

That which is established (*sthāpyate*) is *sthāpanā*, meaning a representation (*pratikṛti*). And that is the formal establishment (*vyavasthāpanā*) of a substance (*dravya*) such as Indra, whose name has been applied—that is, whose name has been superimposed—by means of the intention (*abhisandhāna*) "this is he."
By what nature is its establishment? To this he says: "Existence," and so forth.
Therein, the establishment of existence is that which is equal to the primary Indra and others who are being superimposed;
however, the establishment of non-existence is that which is devoid of the primary form.
It is established (*sthāpyate*) as an "establishment" (*sthāpanā*), which is a representation;

and because it is the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of a real entity such as Indra through the superimposition of its true nature upon that which has not yet been given a name, it is the formal arrangement of another [entity] by means of the connection "this is truly [that]. This is because of the statement: "Establishment is merely the act of establishing.
(*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 111).

By this designation—compare: "Whether in woodwork, bookwork, painting, plasterwork, or in a knotted form, a wrapped form, a filled form, or a composite form; or in dice, or in cowrie shells; whether one or many, whether an installation of reality or an installation of unreality—it is necessarily established as an 'installation' (ṭhavaṇā). That is the 'installation-necessary' (ṭhavaṇāvassaya).
— Anuyoga Sūtra 10.

In that regard, concerning the object of reverence (*āgāravatā*), there is the establishment of existence (*sadbhāvasthāpanā*); its opposite is the establishment of non-existence (*asadbhāvasthāpanā*).
[The *Dhavalā* (p.

20) states: "Those such as wood, cloth, and paintings are of the nature of the establishment of existence; likewise, those such as the casting of dice are of the nature of the establishment of non-existence. [See *Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā* 1.]

In that context, an image that is equivalent to the actual entity (bhāva) such as Indra being superimposed upon it is "establishment in existence" (sadbhāvasthāpanā), because for one who perceives the primary object, the cognition of that [image] as the primary object arises due to the presence of some degree of similarity.

On the other hand, an image that is a mere physical thing devoid of the form of the primary object is "establishment in non-existence" (asadbhāvasthāpanā), because the conviction "this is that very one" arises therein only through the instruction of another.
—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 111.
Now, what is the definition of substance (*dravya*)? He says: "The future," and so forth.

But is it not the case that the definition of substance—"substance is that which has assumed an orientation toward a specific future modification"—is incorrect? [For the *Tattvārthasūtra* states: "Substance possesses qualities and modes" (TS 5.38).

38. Some [opponents] claim that this contradicts scripture; however, they too are ignorant of the author of the Sūtras’ intention. For when the author of the Sūtras states, "Substance possesses qualities and modes," he is declaring that substance is the substratum of infinite successive transformations occurring throughout the three periods of time. Furthermore, when a substance is oriented toward a specific future transformation, it is determined to be both occupied by its present mode and having relinquished its previous mode; otherwise, its orientation toward a future transformation would be impossible, like the horn of a donkey.

Merely because of the primacy of the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) in its verbal expression, the author of the *Sūtra* stated the definition of substance (*dravya*) in the section on the "Deposits" (*nikṣepa-prakaraṇa*) as: "Substance is that which follows past modifications while being oriented toward future modifications. However, by means of the exclusion of other doctrines (*paramata-vyavaccheda*) and through the application of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he formulated the [definitive] aphorism: "Substance possesses qualities and modes" (*guṇaparyayavad dravyam*). This is because the manifold nature of succession and simultaneity (*kramākrama-anekānta*) is established in that manner.
And this substance, characterized by such a definition, is divided into two kinds based on the distinction between scriptural knowledge (*āgama*) and non-scriptural knowledge (*no-āgama*).

In that context, the self (*ātman*) is one who knows the *prābhṛtas* such as the *jīva* and so forth in their true nature; however, when not currently engaged in the cognitive activity (*upayoga*) characterized by reflection or teaching to others, that [self] is non-scriptural substance (*noāgamadravya*). This is divided into three types based on the distinctions of the knower’s body (*jñaśarīra*), the future [knower’s body] (*bhāvī*), and that which is distinct from those (*tadvyatirikta*). Among these, non-scriptural substance characterized as the knower’s body (*jñaśarīra*) is also threefold, pertaining to the three periods of time through the divisions of the future, the present, and the past.
When a future soul, situated in another state of existence and facing the attainment of human birth,
does not yet know the *jīvaprābhṛta* (the treatise on the soul) but will know it in the future, that is *bhāvināgamadravya* (potential scriptural substance).
Apart from that, *noāgamadravya* consists of the divisions of karma and nokarma.

In that context, the eightfold karma beginning with knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) is [karma], while the taking up of matter suitable for the completion of the body is *nokarma*— this is the view of the author of the Sūtras, Ācārya Umāsvāti.

Comparison: He too is ignorant of the meaning of the Sūtra; for when the author of the Sūtra states, "Substance possesses qualities and modes," he means that substance is the substratum of infinite successive transformations within the scope of the three periods of time.

And when it is oriented toward a specific future transformation, it is then determined to be both occupied by a present mode and having abandoned its previous mode; otherwise, being oriented toward a future transformation would be impossible, like a donkey's horn.
(Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 112)
—by way of a synonym— Ā., Śr.; —in such a manner— Ba.; —by way of a synonym— Ā., Śr.
With respect to successive states, there is the non-exclusive nature of succession; with respect to co-existent qualities, however, there is the non-exclusive nature of non-succession.

What is that which is the substance-necessity (*dravyāvaśyaka*)? It is declared to be twofold, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of what is other than scripture (*no-āgama*).
— Anuyogadvāra-sūtra 12.
*Sarvārthasiddhi*, *Rājavārttika* 1.5;
*Dhavalāṭīkā*, page 20.

He who has not learned [the word] "āvassaē" (it must be done)—whether it be recited by another or not applied by himself—has not mastered that term; it is not established, not conquered, not measured, not fully mastered, not equal in name, not equal in sound, with deficient syllables, with redundant syllables, or with misplaced syllables. He is not fit for recitation, questioning, rehearsing, or preaching the Dharma there, nor for reflection. Why? Because he considers non-application to be a substance (dravya).

"One who knows the *jīvaprābhṛta* or one who knows the *manuṣyajīvaprābhṛta*, yet whose self is not currently engaged [in that knowledge], is a *dravyajīva* according to the scripture"— *Sarvārthasiddhi* and *Rājavārttika* 1.5.13.

According to scripture, one who is not attentive [to the meaning], even if reciting words permeated by auspicious sounds and endowed with the attainment of knowledge regarding them, is not [truly] attentive; therefore, he is a substance [word].
—[Regarding] the specific [types], Gāthā 29:

therein, according to scripture (āgama), a "substance-auspiciousness" (dravya-maṅgala) is one who knows the treatise on auspiciousness (maṅgalapāhuḍa) but is not currently engaged in it, or the words and jewels of the treatise on auspiciousness, or the meaning, the installation, and the letters of that [treatise].
—*Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 21.

What, then, is non-scriptural (no-āgama) substance-essential-duty (davvāvassaya)? It is declared to be threefold, namely: substance-essential-duty as the body of the knower (jāṇayasarīra-davvāvassaya), substance-essential-duty as the future body (bhaviya-sarīra-davvāvassaya), and substance-essential-duty distinct from both the body of the knower and the future body (jāṇayasarīra-bhaviya-sarīra-vatiritta-davvāvassaya).

[Aṅgavijjā Sūtra 15] Non-scriptural substance-living-being (no-āgamadravyajīva) is established as threefold, through the distinctions of the body of the knower, the future body, and that which is distinct from them.

In this context, that body which belongs to the knower and pertains to the three periods of time is the "body of the knower" (*jñāyaka-śarīra*). From the perspective of generality (*sāmānya*), there is no "living being destined for existence" (*bhāvijīva*) because the general state of living (*jīvana-sāmānya*) is always present;

however, from the perspective of particularity (*viśeṣa*), it does exist—for instance, a living being established in another state of existence who is oriented toward attaining a human birth is a "living being destined for human existence" (*manuṣya-bhāvijīva*).
Distinct from that is the conceptualization of karma and nokarma—
Sarvārthasiddhi 1.5.
*Dhavalāṭīkā*, page 21:

"Or rather, for the *bhavya* (capable soul), even that soul itself is not [the scripture] according to the *āgama*; it is called 'substance-scripture' (*dravyāgama*) because it is devoid of the [actual] scripture.

As it has been said: "The body of one who knows the auspicious categories (*mangala-padārtha*), or else the soul of the *bhavya*, is the substance-scripture (*dravyāgama*), because it is devoid of the [actual] scripture."
Alternatively, that which is not [established] through direct observation (*deśa*) nor through scripture (*āgama*),

but is the cause of something past or future, and which exists as a body distinct from the knowing subject (*jñāyaka*) and the body destined for experience (*bhavya-śarīra*), is here considered "substantial auspiciousness" (*dravya-maṅgala*).
"Performing that auspicious activity while being non-attentive"—*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, verses 44–46.
Now, what is "state" (*bhāva*)? To this he says: "In that manner," and so forth.
Likewise, what is it? It is *upayoga*, which is activity (*vyāpāra*) in the intended manner;
or rather, it is the state of being engaged (*upayuktatva*), the disposition (*bhāva*) of the soul (*jīva*) by way of being either scriptural (*āgama*) or non-scriptural (*no-āgama*).
Consequently, just like substance (*dravya*), disposition (*bhāva*) must also be understood as twofold, based on the distinction between scriptural and non-scriptural.

In this regard, the self (ātman) engaged in the application of consciousness toward objects such as the "gifts" (prābhṛta) of living beings and so forth is the state of scripture (āgamabhāva); the self engaged in the modes (paryāya) of living beings and so forth is non-scripture (noāgama).
Thus, the fourfold method of classification (nikṣepa), beginning with name (nāma), is established as it has been described.

Anticipating the objection that "for what purpose is this [method] elaborated, since it would be fruitless," he says: "Because of the setting aside of the irrelevant subject," and so forth. Because the primary, irrelevant subject—such as Indra—is set aside (apākaraṇāt) or rejected, and because the relevant subject—the nominal or conventional Indra—is explained (vyākaraṇāt) or elucidated, the method of *nikṣepa* (classification/definition) is fruitful and meaningful. And by means of such a *nikṣepa*, the categories (*padārthāḥ*) such as living beings (*jīva*) and so forth, having been classified and elaborated in the manner described, are "investigated" (*anuyujyante*). That is, they are subsequently joined with [inquiries into] their essential nature and other attributes; they are questioned out of a desire to know them.
By means of what? By means of the *anuyogas*.

Of what kind are they? They are characterized by exposition (*nirdeśa*) and so forth—namely, exposition, ownership (*svāmitva*), means (*sādhana*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), duration (*sthiti*), and mode (*vidhāna*). Not only by these alone, but also by [the categories] beginning with existence (*sat*), namely: existence, number (*saṃkhyā*), field (*kṣetra*), contact (*sparśana*), time (*kāla*), interval (*antara*), state (*bhāva*), and relative magnitude (*alpabahutva*).

Although all categories (padārtha) are investigated through such inquiries, nevertheless, there are fourteen stations of living beings (jīva-sthāna), fourteen stations of qualities (guṇa-sthāna), and fourteen stations of the paths of inquiry (mārgaṇā-sthāna) which describe that specific excellence of the nature of the category of the soul (jīva) as distinguished from other categories.

When the substance of the soul (jīvadravya), whose excellence of nature has been described by these, is known as it truly is, the three jewels (ratnatraya)—which are the constituent factors of liberation—become complete for those seeking liberation; it is not otherwise.
This very point is stated in the verse beginning with "evam" (thus).

Having understood all categories of existence through the aforementioned methods of comprehension—namely, the means for realizing the nature of things consisting of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the perspectives (*naya*), and the modes of predication (*nikṣepa*)—and having further ascertained the reality of the person (*puruṣatattva*) with even greater firmness by means of the stations of the soul (*jīvasthāna*), the stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*), and the objects of inquiry (*mārgaṇāsthāna*), [the author] has thereby described right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) as a limb of liberation for the seeker of emancipation.

Furthermore, by the phrase "possessing right vision characterized by intensified resolve" (*pravṛddhābhiniveśātmakasamyagdarśanaḥ*), he has described right vision (*samyagdarśana*); and by the phrase "one whose karma is exhausted through austerity" (*tapasā nirjīrṇakarmā*), he has described right conduct (*samyakcāritra*).
And by means of that triad beginning with right vision (*samyagdarśana*), having exhausted his karma and being liberated from all karma, this self attains bliss; it becomes composed of bliss.

What is the nature of that bliss? It is free from affliction (*bādhārahita*), devoid of obstruction; uninterrupted and eternal; infinite, being beyond all limitation of measure; and supersensuous, arising solely from the pure self.

Now, the Vaiśeṣikas raise an objection: since in the liberation of the self there is the total cessation of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, how can it be said to be "composed of bliss"?
The Buddhists [say] that [the self does not exist] because of the absolute cessation of the mental continuum, since that very [continuum] is impossible;
the Sāṃkhyas [say] it is because [the self] is not an enjoyer.
To this, he replies: "Not indeed," and so forth.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: it is *not* the case that through the destruction of qualities—that is, the annihilation of qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth—the self (*ātman*) becomes inert (*jaḍa*), like a stone, in liberation; nor is it the case that through the destruction of both quality and the possessor of quality, the self becomes void (*śūnya*). "Qualities" refers to cognition and the rest; "the possessor of qualities" refers to the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*). Through their destruction—that is, through their absolute annihilation—the self does not become void, meaning it does not become entirely devoid of its own essential nature. Furthermore, because of the absence of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and because the seer then abides in its own true nature, the self is not a non-enjoyer (*abhoktā*) of pleasure and the rest; this is the connection [of the words].
Why is this so? To this he says: because there is no apprehension of such [a self] and because its sublation is impossible.

Just as in the case of liberation, there is an impossibility of apprehending such a nature of the self through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and likewise an impossibility of its sublation, so it will be explained in detail later on. What is that "substantial reality" (*bhāvāvaśyaka*)? It is declared to be twofold, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*no-āgama*).
— Anuśaya-sūtra 22;
Sarvārtha-siddhi 1.5.
One who knows [the scriptures] and is attentive—this is the essential act (āvaśyaka) from the perspective of scripture (āgama).
— Anuyogadvāra-sūtra 23. Dhavalāṭīkā, p. 29.

In this context, the self that is occupied with the object of the *jīvaprābhṛta* or endowed with the cognitive application (*upayoga*) regarding the object of the *manuṣyajīvaprābhṛta* is the *āgamabhāvajīva*— [as stated in] *Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.5.
One who is engaged in the auspicious scripture (*sūtra*) becomes an auspicious being (*bhāvamangala*) according to the *Āgama*—*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, gāthā 49.
*Āgama* means the established doctrine; [one] who knows the *Mangalapāhuḍa* from the *Āgama* and is devoted to it.

The self (ātman) endowed with the life-mode (*jīvanaparyāya*) or the human life-mode (*manuṣyajīvanaparyāya*) is the soul as a substance of scripture (*āgamabhāvajīva*)—*Sarvārthasiddhi*, *Rājavārttika*, *Tattvārthaślokavārttika* 1.1.5.10. *Dhavalāṭīkā*, p. 29.
Regarding auspiciousness of state (*bhāva-maṅgala*), it is twofold: "engaged" (*upayukta*) and "transformed into that" (*tatpariṇata*).
Without the scripture (*āgama*), one who is engaged with the meaning is "engaged."
"Transformed by the transformation of the sequence of the auspicious (māṅgalaparyāyapariṇata), it is transformed by that"—this is well known from the *Dhavalāṭīkā*, folio 29a. Śra. [Citation].
They are being questioned,
they are being engaged [in inquiry],
[regarding] "the soul" and so forth.
—by means of which [cognition]...
—ā॰ —perceived (dṛṣṭa) pleasure (sukha), delimited (avacchinna) by [that] cognition (śra॰)... śra॰.
The self itself has no self;
thus he said— Bhaṭṭa.

Regarding the nature of the obscuration of that which is distinct from pleasure and so forth— whether it be the void (*śūnya*) or that which consists in the state of being a non-experiencer (*abhoktṛtva*)— the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of others is as follows:

"Indeed, once the existence of karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) is established, it is appropriate to state that 'one whose karma has been worn away by austerity' [is liberated]."
Furthermore, the existence of such [an obscuration] is not established.

For that [obscuration] would have to be either the body, passion and so forth, or space, time, and so on. Among these, the first two alternatives are untenable; for even when the body and passion and so forth exist, the arising of the cognition of an object is possible.

That which, despite its presence, allows for the arising of cognition, cannot be of the nature of an obscuration to knowledge (jñānāvaraṇa) and so forth—just as the eye and other sense organs are not. And since the arising of the cognition of an object is possible even when the body and so forth exist, it follows that they are not of the nature of an obscuration to knowledge and so forth.
If its nature were that [of being an obstruction], then, as in the case of a screen or the like, the perception of it would not be possible even when it exists;

in that case, let space, time, and so forth be of that nature. For it is well known that in the case of Mount Meru and the like, distance of place acts as an obstruction; in the case of Rāvaṇa and the like, distance of time acts as an obstruction; and in the case of atoms and the like, their subtle nature acts as an obstruction; likewise, the earth and so forth act as obstructions in the case of roots, stakes, water, and so on. This too is incorrect, because even for a yogi, the absence of those [obstructions] is impossible to bring about;
indeed, even by a yogi possessing extraordinary supernatural powers (*sātiśayarddhi*), the non-existence of space and the rest cannot be established.
Nor is any other obscuration perceived;

or, even if it were to exist, it would nonetheless be of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) and not composed of matter (*pudgala*). For it is illogical that something corporeal should obscure knowledge and the like, which are incorporeal; otherwise, it would follow that the body and so forth would also be obscurations, since [according to some] karma is a quality of the self and thus not composed of matter. Others maintain this view.

"Let it be that this [karma] is personal (paudgalika) or has undergone transformation; nevertheless, its complete exhaustion (nirjarā) is not possible anywhere, because it proceeds as a stream of cause and effect and is beginningless (anādi), and because that which is beginningless cannot be destroyed, just like the self (ātman) and so forth"—thus say others. [The commentary notes: "Exhausted" (nirjīrṇa)—in the manuscript *Śra*, there is the absence of that [word]; in *Ba*, it is present.

Comparison—For that [comparison] would be either passion and so forth regarding the body, or [the consideration of] place, time, and so on—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 241; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 356.
The body, attachment, and so forth are not of the nature of an obscuration, because knowledge arises even when they are present;
therefore, the body and the rest do not constitute an obstruction to this [knowledge].
For him, there is no possibility of perceiving knowledge as long as the existence of the body and so forth persists.
The nature of an obscuration consists of a tree root, a stake, water, or the like located within the ground;
or the state of being at a remote place, a remote time, or having a subtle nature; or the non-existence of the ground itself.
Therefore, the Vedāntins must accept that the nature of this obscuration is indeterminable ignorance (anirvācyāvidyā);
it is not proper to deny it merely because it is difficult to define, since its existence is established by inference.

To explain: there exists, among the ignorant alone, the conventional usage that the reality of the Self—which is well-known to the wise as transcending hunger and other such states—does not exist and does not manifest. This usage regarding the Self must be caused by a positive obscuration (bhāvarūpāvaraṇa), because it is a usage contrary to "it exists" and "it manifests," even when the full causes for such [positive] usages are present. That which is not so [caused by an obscuration] is not thus, just like the usage "the jar exists and manifests.
Nor is the completeness of the causes unestablished; for here, apart from eternally established self-luminous consciousness (caitanya), there is no dependence on anything else.

Nor can it be established otherwise; for it is impossible to provide a locus for a corporeal substance that constitutes an additional obscuration within the self, which is partless and all-pervading—[as stated] in the *Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha*, p.
21, regarding karma consisting of matter (*pudgala*).
The [term] *yaugā* is to be seen— page 3, note 5—
or rather, *pau*— manuscript *ba*.
Jayantabhaṭṭa and others maintain that karma has the nature of ignorance and so forth.

Comparison: Others, however, maintain that because of the absence of the auxiliary conditions for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by false knowledge, even existing karmas do not initiate a body in another birth—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.
20b. Since there is no fault in the karmas' failure to initiate [a new existence] due to the deficiency of auxiliary conditions, just like seeds remaining in a granary.
And this very state of not initiating effects is their destruction.

[Objection: But surely, since their essential nature is undestroyed, they might at some point initiate an effect just like seeds in a granary; therefore, it would be better that they simply be annihilated. [Reply: Why then should we now strive to annihilate even the eternal self? (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
523) — This establishes that karma consists of matter (*paudgalika*) and proves the existence of *saṃvara* and *nirjarā*.

To this, the following reply is given: as for what was stated—that "the existence of karma such as knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) and so forth is established," and so on—in that regard, do you disagree regarding the mere existence of karma in general, or regarding specific types of karma such as knowledge-obscuring and the rest? Of these, the first alternative is untenable, because the existence of karma in general, as distinct from the body and other such things, is established through inference.

For instance: the extraordinary attachment of the self—which has as its sole nature the cognition of objects of knowledge (prameya) belonging to both itself and others—to inferior wombs, abodes, bodies, sense-objects, and so forth, must be preceded by causes distinct from that [self], because it is a specific state, just like the extraordinary attachment of a woman of noble lineage toward a despicable stranger arising from the use of aphrodisiacs (*tantra*) and the like.

Furthermore, the second alternative is also untenable; for even the specific karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), which is distinct from that [self], is established precisely through inference.

For instance: the knowledge of pervasion (vyāptijñāna) that "whatever is existent is multiform in nature" and so forth is obscured (sāvaraṇa), because it is indistinct regarding its own object. Whatever is indistinct regarding its own object is obscured, just like the cognition of a cluster of trees hidden by dust, mist, and the like; and this [pervasion] knowledge is indistinct regarding its own object.

Thus, for those with false vision (mithyādṛśām), the erroneous cognition regarding every entity whose nature is multiform is obscured, because it is a false cognition, just like the cognition of gold in a piece of clay for one who has consumed the *dhattūra* plant (pṛ.
Comparison: For one who possesses consciousness, the arising of delusion has another related factor as its cause, just like wine and so forth;
how is this established?

It is established through the following inference: "The subject under dispute, the arising of delusion in the living being, has another related factor as its cause, because it is an arising of delusion, just like the arising of delusion caused by wine."

—Aṣṭaśa°, Aṣṭasaha° p. 49: The transmigrating being is bound because of his dependence, like an elephant tied to a tethering post; he is dependent because of his occupation with inferior states, like a Vedic Brahmin who is dependent on the excess of sensual desire due to his occupation with inferior states.
—Āptaparīkṣā, p. 1; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 242: distinct from the body and so forth.

The non-functioning of the self— which is distinct from the body and so forth and possesses the nature of knowing all objects of knowledge— with respect to its own object, is caused by its connection with a specific substance, just as a person whose heart is filled with yellow pigment does not perceive his own object.
And that substance which acts as an obstruction to knowledge is the real entity consisting of *pudgala*, known as *karma*, such as the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*).

"That which does not function with respect to its own object is obscured; for example, the visual cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia regarding a single moon. And our cognition regarding all objects characterized as its own domain does not function [correctly] with respect to its own object. — *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 357. "Whatever is non-functional regarding its own object is possessed of an obscuration (*sāvaraṇa*); just as the ocular consciousness of one afflicted by cataracts is [non-functional] regarding a single moon. And the cognition of people such as ourselves is non-functional regarding its own object, which is characterized by the totality of things.
— *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 736.
Knowledge is obscured because, despite its clarity, it does not bring about the cognition of its own object— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 240, line 9.
—[Regarding] "insult" and so forth: Śrā.

Thus, that which is a cognition of error regarding this entire reality consisting of manifold aspects (anekāntātma), by one whose faculty of discernment has been obscured by the veil of falsity (mithyātva)—that [cognition] is accompanied by obscuration because it is false knowledge (mithyājñāna). —Syādvādara.

Regarding what was also stated—that it will be of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) and not something pertaining to the person (*pudgala*), and so forth—that too is mere words; for it is impossible for that which is formless (*amūrta*) to be obscured by that which is likewise formless. If it is asked: "Since we observe that even a material thing (*mūrta*), such as wine and the like, can obscure formless things such as knowledge (*jñāna*), how could the body and so forth not be its obscuration? We reply: because there is no contradiction [between them].

For even though there is no difference in their being corporeal, only that which is incompatible with knowledge can logically be its obscuration, and nothing else; otherwise, since there is no difference in their being incorporeal, it would follow that space and so forth—just like ignorance—and other cognitions would also be obscurations.

Furthermore, the incompatibility of that [knowledge] with [the obscuration] is ascertained from the cessation of knowledge—which proceeds in a continuous stream through the emergence of karma consisting of matter (paudgalika)—just as in the case of wine and the like.

For instance: the soul's false cognition and so forth are caused by its connection with a particular *pudgala* (matter), because their nature consists in a transformation of its own essence, like intoxication and the like produced by someone such as a madman.

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to another false cognition produced by a false cognition, because that too occurs only when there is the arising of successive *pudgala*-based karmas, just as a continuous stream of intoxication and the like produced by one madman [occurs] when the substances of successive madmen are present.
(Page 809, Line 3)
Because of the observation of being overcome by liquor—Rājavārttika, p. 81; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 243; Prameyaratnakośa, p.
Of that knowledge which is not composed of matter (paudgalika), there is no [obstruction] from karma such as the veil of knowledge (jñānāvaraṇa).

Because of the concealment of this [nature] by knowledge, it is determined that the self’s false cognition and so forth—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 243. (Note: The variants *śra* and *ba* indicate textual differences in the reading *niścī*.)
Because of its non-existence— [the reading] *u* is in Śra., while *rasadbhāve* is in Ba.—

by this, the claim that actions (*karma*) are not composed of matter (*paudgalika*) because they are qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*) is also refuted; for if they were qualities of the self, the cause for their dependence [on the self] would be untenable, which would entail the perpetual liberation of the self.

Whatever is a quality (*guṇa*) of something does not serve as a cause for its dependence on another, just as color and other qualities do not cause earth and so forth to be dependent. Furthermore, it is not tenable that action (*karman*), known as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), is accepted by others as a quality [of the self]. This is because the self is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being dependent; for instance: this self is dependent, because it possesses the appropriation of inferior states, just like a distinguished person who, under the influence of intoxication, appropriates an impure place.
The body is indeed a lowly state because it is a cause of suffering for the self, like a prison; and that the transmigrating being (saṃsārī) possesses such a body is well-established for all.

Nor is there a lack of pervasion in the [logical] subject (*pakṣa*) due to the absence of that [body] in the case of a divine body, for even that is established as a cause of suffering at the time of death.

Furthermore, that which this [being] is dependent upon is karma; thus, its status as not being a quality of the self (*anātmaguṇatva*) is proven, and therefore its nature as consisting of matter (*paudgalikatva*) alone is logical.
The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: Karma is a product of the person (paudgalika), because it is the cause of the soul’s state of dependence (pāratantrya), just like shackles and the like.
Nor is there a deviation [in the reason] due to anger and so forth; for those are transformations of the soul itself, possessing the very nature of dependence.
Indeed, the transformation into anger and so forth is the soul’s own dependence, rather than being the cause of dependence.
Therefore, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as a quality of the self (*ātman*) is refuted, because it is impossible for it to be the cause of *saṃsāra*— Sarvārthasiddhi 8.5.809.5.

If actions were qualities of the self, it would be impossible for them to be caused by dependence on something else; consequently, bondage of the self could never occur, leading to the absurd conclusion that liberation is perpetual. — Āptapañcāśikā, Verse 113.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 243;
Syādvādaratnākara, page 1101;
Yoga.
—“Not occurring in a place unsuitable for the tantras”—ba;
compare: “Birth is a transition to an inferior state due to the power of false cognition and the volition arising from the thirst born thereof”—*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.275.
An inferior state is the body because it is a cause of suffering for oneself, like a prison for some person—Āptaparikṣā pṛ. 1; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa pṛ. 243.
It may be so, because karma lacks the nature of being a cause of suffering.

And these [karmas], consisting of the transformation of the person (pudgala), are like shackles and so forth, because they are the cause of the soul's (jīva) dependence on others—Āptaparīkṣā p. 61; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa p. 243.

Furthermore, as for the other statement—that "nowhere is the possibility of total *nirjarā* (dissipation of karmic matter) found," and so forth—that too is the play of no small ignorance. For even though the succession of the stream of karmas is beginningless, their total destruction is logically possible when there exists, in some instance, the supreme intensity of its opposite (*vipakṣa*).

Whatever possesses the supreme intensity of its opposite in some place, that undergoes total destruction therein, just as the sensation of cold does. And since the supreme intensity of its opposite—characterized by right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth—exists in some soul, [total destruction is possible].

Nor is this example devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for it is not observed that even an infinite continuum of cold touch does not undergo total destruction when there is the presence of an excellence of its opposite, namely hot touch; nor is it observed that the beginningless continuum of seed and sprout, through the flow of cause and effect, continues when its seeds have been burnt by a fire acting as its opposite, or when its sprouts have been consumed.

Furthermore, the existence of the ultimate excellence of the counteragent is established through inference. For instance: knowledge and other qualities reach a state of ultimate excellence somewhere, because they are subject to degrees of excellence (*prakṛṣyamāṇatvāt*), like magnitude (*parimāṇavat*).

Or, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) should be made regarding the total destruction of karma: the destruction of the veils of knowledge and so forth reaches a state of ultimate excellence in a certain particular person, because it is subject to degrees of excellence, like the magnitude in space (*nabhas*).

Nor is the reason (*sādhana*) unestablished here; for the destruction of the veils is subject to degrees of excellence, because it is a destruction of veils, like the destruction of the veils of rubies and other gems.

Alternatively, karma such as that which obscures knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) is destroyed from its very root in certain cases, because it is endowed with the causes for total destruction, just like cataracts and other defects in the eye.

For the causes of the destruction of that karma are indeed restraint (*saṃvara*) and shedding (*nirjarā*), because the destruction follows their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance of something is its cause, just as smoke is the effect of fire; and the destruction of that [karma] follows the positive and negative concomitance of restraint and shedding.
When restraint exists, future karma does not arise; restraint is the cessation of the influx (*āsrava*) of previously non-existent karmas (Tattvārtha Sūtra 9).
Because of this statement, that which has been accumulated is dissolved through *nirjarā* (dissociation), according to the teaching: "The shedding of acquired karmas is *nirjarā*.
Furthermore, that *nirjarā* is twofold, distinguished as *aupakramika* (induced) and *itarā* (natural).

In that regard, the [karma] resulting from external assault (*aupakramikī*) is to be exhausted through the twelvefold austerity (*tapas*); however, the non-assault-related (*anaupakramikī*) would belong to the transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*) according to its own time. (See Prabhācandra’s *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 809, l.
6). For comparison: "Because all [entities] possess opposites, they are subject to decrease and increase."
Through the internalization [of that knowledge] and through its repeated practice,
the outflows (āsravas) may at some point be abandoned.
— *Pramāṇavārttika* 3.281.
And those things which are subject to diminution undergo absolute diminution when their counteragent is present, just like the impurities on gold and so forth.
— Tattvasaṃgraha, Verse 3416:
Through the internalization [of the antidote], when the existing fault that is the adverse side is destroyed,
there is the non-adherence of karma and the cessation of those [actions] already set in motion that yield fruit.
— Nyāyaviniścaya, kārikā 443:
He is the destroyer of the mountain of karma through the excellence of its opposite,
just as in this world someone destroys cold through the excellence of heat.
—Āptapa° kā° 110; Aṣṭasaha° pṛ° 54:

When there is a proportional decrease of one thing corresponding to a proportional increase of another, then upon reaching the ultimate limit of that increase, there occurs the absolute destruction of the former, just as the cold touch is destroyed by the increasing intensity of heat. And since there is a proportional decrease of ignorance, passion, and so forth, corresponding to the proportional increase of knowledge, dispassion, and so forth...
—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 737:

"In that case, because of the excellence [attained] regarding its opposite (*vipakṣa*), the destruction of karma is established, even though it is beginningless by virtue of being a continuum (*santāna*) in form."
For even a beginningless continuum [of suffering] would not exist, as it has been reached by the touch of cold; (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 245; Syādvādaratnākara, p.
—approach [the following]: Śrā° [states that] its seed is burnt by the fire of its opposite; Āptapa° p.
59 [states that] its seed is burnt by the fire of its opposite; Prameyaka° p. 245 [states that] its seed is burnt by the fire of its opposite.
Comparison: There is a reaching of the ultimate limit for the seed of omniscience, because it possesses excellence, like [the growth of] a measurable object—
Yogabhāṣya 1.25.
Furthermore, that excellence is established in the Supreme Self, because the excellence of gradation is proven there, just as heat reaches its maximum degree—
[Āptaparīkṣā, Kārikā 112].
Aṣṭasahasrī, p. 55; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 245; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 358.
Purity reaches its highest excellence in a certain self because it is subject to progressive increase, just like the purification of gold and other substances—
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 315.
The destruction of defects and obstructions is complete because of the possibility of excellence,
just as the removal of external and internal impurities occurs in some cases through their respective causes;
[Āptamīmāṃsā 4].
The removal of obscurations being intensified [is so] because it is a removal of obscurations, like the removal of obscurations from rubies and other gems— *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*,

In some cases, the obstruction to knowledge is destroyed from its very root, because it is the cause of the complete destruction [of that obstruction], just as cataracts and the like are in the case of the eye. (Syādvādamañjarī, p. 359)
—*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 15—...
in some places—Śra.—“the causes of destruction”—Ba., “the causes for destruction”—Ā.

For those who are still subject to rebirth, the restraint of adverse factors is considered [the means]; but for those who have accumulated [merit] through austerity, the wearing away of the mountains of karma is [the means].—
Āptapañcāśikā 111.
The cessation of influx (āsrava-nirodha) is restraint (saṃvara)—Tattvārthasūtra 9.1; Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p.
This has been extracted: "Nirjarā is characterized by the partial destruction of karma" — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, folio 245;
*Sarvārthasiddhi* 1.1.1.
Nirjarā is the partial destruction of accumulated karma when it is brought into proximity with specific forms of austerity— Rājavārttika 1.4.1.
But that shedding [of karmic matter] which occurs through the ripening of karma or through austerity is *nirjarā*— Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā, Tattvārthahari-bhāṣya 1.4.
The abandonment of previously accumulated karma is *nirjarā* (exhaustion of karma) — *Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 483.
It is of two kinds: that which arises from fruition (*vipākajā*) and that which is other than it.

Among these, *vipākajā nirjarā* is the cessation of karma that has begun to bear fruit—karma that has entered the stream of the sequence of experiential manifestations after reaching the time of its gradual maturation within the great ocean of saṃsāra, which is tossed by the various distinctions of many births across the four states of existence, and consists of both auspicious and inauspicious types.

That karma whose time for fruition has not yet arrived, which—by the power of a specific forceful action—is forcibly aroused and, having been forcibly aroused, enters the sequence of emergence and is experienced like the ripening of mangoes, jackfruits, and so forth; that is *nirjarā* (dissociation) born of non-fruition (*avipākajā*). — *Sarvārthasiddhi*, *Rājavārttika*, *Tattvārthabhāṣya-vyākhyā* 8.23.
It is of two kinds: incurable and curable.
Among these, the former occurs at its destined time for one wandering in saṃsāra; the curable, however, is accomplished through twelvefold austerity—Āptapañcāśikā 111.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛ.
244; Syādvādaratnākara, pṛ. 357: Karma is of two kinds—maturation of life-span (āyur-vipāka)—namely, sopakrama and nirupakrama.

In this regard, just as a wet cloth spread out would dry in a shorter time, so is [the karma] with effort (*sopakrama*); and just as that same cloth, when folded together, would take a long time to dry, so is [the karma] without effort (*nirupakrama*). Furthermore, just as a fire set to dry grass and joined by wind on all sides would burn it in the shortest time, so is [the karma] with effort; or just as that same fire, placed gradually upon the parts of a heap of straw, would burn it slowly, so is [the karma] without effort. — *Yoga-sūtra-vyāsabhāṣya* 3.22.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Sāṃkhyas regarding the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), the bondage of karma, and so forth:
