Here the Sāṃkhyas say—True; the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is not a quality of the self (*anātmaguṇa*), because it is a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), since it is stated that "the transformation of primordial nature is action (*karman*), which is white and black."
For action is performed by nature (prakṛti); therefore, that transformation belongs to it and not to the self (ātman), because the self is not the agent.
Indeed, the very nature of the self consists in its being a witness and so forth, not in its being an agent;
as it has been said:
It should be observed— page 3, note 7—
that its effects are dharma and so forth— Sāṃkhyasūtra 2.14.
Comparison: Indeed, this fourfold class of karma consists of the black, the white-and-black, the white, and the neither-white-nor-black—
Yogabhāṣya 4.7.
The karma of the seeker of liberation, the yogi, and the ascetic is neither white nor black; for others, however, karma is of three kinds— black, white, and mixed—
[Yogakārikā 4].
This has been extracted: "The transformation of primordial matter (pradhāna) consists of white and black karma"— Āptaparikṣā, page 61.
The transformation of the Pradhāna results in white and black karma—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 244, 285. "All actions performed in every way by the Gunas of Prakṛti... [Bhagavad Gītā 3.27].
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer"—
Bhagavad Gītā 3.27.
"The witness, the cognizer, alone and devoid of qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
Because of its dwelling in the city (puri-śayana), because of its being the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and because of its filling (pūraṇa), it has the nature of the Puruṣa.
And he is beginningless, all-pervading, conscious, devoid of qualities, distinct, the seer, the enjoyer, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), stainless, and free from the nature of procreation;
he is subtle, eternal, indeed without beginning, middle, or end.
—Sāṃkhyatattvavivaraṇa, p. 10.
And from this very inversion, the witness-status of this Puruṣa is established;
that is, from the reversal of the aforementioned threefold qualities (guṇas).

The Puruṣa is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), discriminative (vivekī), and the enjoyer (bhoktṛ); from this aforementioned inversion of the qualities with respect to the Puruṣa, it is established that the Puruṣa is the witness (sākṣitva) while sattva, rajas, and tamas are the agents. This is the one who has been introduced in relation to plurality: the qualities alone act as agents and proceed, whereas the witness neither proceeds nor desists. Furthermore, there is isolation (kaivalya)—the state of being alone (kevalabhāva); "isolation" means otherness (anyatva), for he is alone and distinct from the three qualities.
The state of neutrality: like a wandering mendicant, the Puruṣa stands as a neutral observer.

Just as a certain wandering mendicant remains solely neutral while villagers are engaged in agricultural labor, so too the Puruṣa does not engage while the Guṇas are active. Therefore, because he is neutral, he is the witness; because he is neutral, the Puruṣa is the non-doer of those actions.
The three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—function through the relationship of action and agent, but the Puruṣa does not;
thus, the existence of the Puruṣa is established.
(Gauḍapāda-bhāṣya, Māṭhara-vṛtti, Sāṅkhyatattvakaumudī, Jayamaṅgalā, Kārikā 19)
This has been cited—Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa, p.
546A; Viśvatattvaprakāśa, p. 140A.
"Isolation, neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the state of being a non-agent" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 19).

By the phrase "the state of being a non-agent," he relies upon a sevenfold non-agency: for this [Puruṣa] does not exercise determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding objects through the proximity of its own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);

nor does it, by means of its own characteristic of consciousness (*caitanya*), assume the status of a subordinate factor (*aṅga-bhāva*) toward the qualities such as *sattva*, which do not function through mutual assistance characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint; nor does it assume the status of a principal factor (*aṅgi-bhāva*).
Thus, like a woman or a young boy, it does not perform any action together with the *guṇas*.

It does not perform a stationary operation like the driver of a chariot, cart, or machine; nor like a lump of clay [acting upon itself]; nor from another, like a potter; nor by command, like a magician; nor from both, like a mother and father. (Yuktidīpikā, p.

100) And therefore, from that very reversal of the three *guṇas*, the nature of the Self as witness (*sākṣitva*) and so forth is established. To explain: first, the witnesshood of the Self consists in its presiding over the activity of the *guṇas*, because it is itself devoid of *guṇas*. For since this [Self] is a distinct entity from pleasure and the rest, it is therefore the witness over their activity.
Likewise, its isolation (*kaivalya*) is also established from that very state of being distinct;
for since this [Self] has become separate from the *guṇas*, it is therefore solitary (*kevala*), and does not exist in association with them.
Similarly, its neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) is also established because of its being the subject.

For since objects possess equal strength and can occur in varying degrees of intensity, mutual obstruction and assistance among them are logically possible; however, this [subject] is the perceiver, and therefore it is not subject to deficiency or the like. For this very reason, the other two [qualities] are untenable in its case. Likewise, its status as a seer is established because its essential nature is consciousness (*caitanya*). Indeed, *sattva* and the other qualities are modifications of *prakṛti*; therefore, having extracted consciousness from them, the *puruṣa* alone is established. Consequently, the *puruṣa* alone is the seer, because its essential nature is consciousness.
And it has been said: "The nature of the Puruṣa is consciousness" (Yogasūtra 1.9);
here, the genitive case is used in the sense of non-difference.

For the person (*puruṣa*) is indeed consciousness alone; the word "form" (*rūpa*) here denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This very thing—namely, that which is called consciousness—is the self's own form, its own nature. Since manifestation and non-manifestation are impossible for it, its state of being a non-agent is likewise established, because it lacks the quality of productivity (*aprasavadharmitva*). Since vibration and transformation, which have the sense of "production," do not exist in the self, it is therefore a non-agent.

—By the phrase "witnesshood in that [state]" (*tatra sākṣitvam*), [the author] declares the lack of independence of the *guṇas* in their activity, because the activity of the *pradhāna* is dependent upon that [purpose].
— *Yuktidīpikā*, p. 100.
From the activity of the qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas— or from the activity of the quality that is the Pradhāna,
[the world arises] for the sake of the Puruṣa.
By the term "isolation" (kaivalya), [the author] negates the status of the self as a property of transmigratory existence;
for the soul's relation with those [guṇas] is not like the conjunction of sattva and the others, which depend upon one another for properties such as illumination—(Yuktidīpikā, p. 100).

By the term "separateness" (*pṛthaggata*), [the author] shows that since neither excess nor deficiency is possible, it is impossible for the Puruṣa to experience either obstruction or favor from the Guṇas; furthermore, it demonstrates his impartiality toward their engagement in their own respective effects—
*Yuktidīpikā*.
In the case of rebirth,
there is no contradiction regarding the forms of obstruction and favor— [as stated in] Śra and Ba.

—The form of consciousness is the essential nature of the Puruṣa—so says Śrī [Bhāskara], while Ba[ṭuka] says it is "the form of consciousness. Śrī [Bhāskara] says: "Consciousness is the essential nature of the Puruṣa."

When consciousness alone is the person (puruṣa), then what is designated here by what? And yet, designation occurs through a functional relationship, as in the expression "Caitra’s cow" (Yoga-bhāṣya 1.9).
This has been extracted from *Sarvārthasiddhi*, p. 1; *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p. 547A:

If it is asked, "But if [the qualities] such as *sattva* are the agents, how is the cognition of agency in the self—as in the expression 'the person performs merit'—justified? [The answer is: It is by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). For just as the intellect (*buddhi*), though itself insentient, is metaphorically designated as "sentient" due to its association with sentience, so too the self, though itself a non-agent, is metaphorically designated as "an agent" due to its association with the primary agent, *pradhāna*.
As it has been said:

"Since these two—enjoyment and liberation—are produced by the intellect (*buddhi*) and reside only in the intellect, how can they be attributed to the *puruṣa*? Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master, for he is the enjoyer of that result; so too, bondage and liberation, though occurring only in the intellect, are attributed to the *puruṣa*, for he is the enjoyer of their results."
The non-termination of the purpose of the Puruṣa within the intellect itself is bondage; the determination that its purpose has been fulfilled is liberation.

By this it is meant that grasping, retention, reasoning, rejection, and the inclination toward knowledge of reality, though existing in the intellect, are superimposed as having existence upon the Puruṣa, for he is the enjoyer of their fruit—Yoga Bhāṣya 2.18.
Likewise, here [it is said]:
"Therefore, due to its association with that [Prakṛti], the insentient [Prakṛti] appears as if sentient; thus is the mark (liṅga) here."

Therefore, through that conjunction, the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient; because the *puruṣa* is by nature sentient, through conjunction with him, the insentient *liṅga*—consisting of the *mahat* and the rest—proceeds as if it were sentient in its functions such as determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), volition (*saṅkalpa*), and perception (*ālocana*). What is the illustration? Just as a pot, which is neither hot nor cold, becomes cold when touched by cold water and becomes hot when joined with fire, even so the *liṅga*, though insentient, becomes as if sentient. Therefore, it is the *guṇas* that perform the determination regarding effects and so forth.

For example, just as a person who is not a thief is perceived as a thief by others due to the fault of association with a thief, so too the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are the agents; and although the *puruṣa* joined with them is itself a non-agent, it becomes an agent through association with the agent, appearing as if it were the agent. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, the *puruṣa* is a non-agent (*Māṭhara-vṛtti*, Gauḍapāda-bhāṣya, Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, Jayamaṅgalā, Kārikā 20). Therefore, the nature of being an object of perception belonging to the cause and the nature of being an agent belonging to the *puruṣa*—which, through contact with another related entity, are perceived in one thing as belonging to another—must be understood figuratively (*bhaktyā*), and not in an ultimate sense.
And it has been said: "The intellect (buddhi), presided over by consciousness, is perceived as if it were conscious;
and the Self (ātman), though situated among the agents, is characterized as the enjoyer, as if it were the agent" (Yuktidīpikā, p. 104).
This has been cited—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 489; "here [it is] like that which possesses consciousness," *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p.
67; *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, fol. 59A.

"Even though consciousness is the agent of qualities, it remains indifferent, as if it were the agent itself. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 20) — *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 234. — "Consciousness, consciousness... — Ātmakhyāti.
Therefore, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) must be accepted as unchanging, non-transmigrating, having objects presented to it, pure, and infinite.
Nor should it be argued that if one accepts the existence of attributes such as agency in *pradhāna*, the postulation of the *puruṣa* is useless;
for he is the seer, and a visible object is not possible without a seer, because these two are mutually dependent, like the lame man and the blind man.

For just as a blind man, lacking the power of vision, cannot reach his desired destination without the instruction of a lame man who possesses that power, and likewise a lame man, devoid of the power of action, cannot do so without association with a blind man who possesses that power; so too, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), even though it has produced an effect, is not capable of seeing it without the *puruṣa* (spirit); and the *puruṣa*, despite possessing consciousness, would not be a seer in the absence of the *pradhāna* because of the lack of an object to be seen.

The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is unchanging, non-transmigrating, has objects presented to it, is pure, and is infinite. Impurity consists in being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; even pleasure and delusion are treated as forms of pain by the discerning one, and therefore, like pain, they are to be abandoned. Furthermore, even that which is exceedingly beautiful causes affliction because it is finite; thus, for the discerning one, even that is to be abandoned. This impurity and finitude do not exist in the power of consciousness, the *puruṣa*; therefore, it is said to be "pure" and "infinite."

[Objection: But if [the consciousness] is conscious of sound and other objects which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, having assumed their form, how can it be pure? And if it both assumes and avoids those forms, how can it be infinite? To this it is said: "having its object shown" (*darśitaviṣayā*).
That for which the object—sound and so forth—is shown is thus described.

This would be so if the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) were to assume the form of the object like the intellect (*buddhi*); however, it is the intellect alone that, having transformed itself into the form of the object, presents the object to the power of consciousness which does not possess that form. Therefore, it is said that "the Puruṣa is conscious."

Now, one might ask: how can there be cognition of an object by the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) when that consciousness has not itself ascended to the form of the object? Or, if it does ascend to the form of the object, why does it not undergo transformation into that form? To this it is said: "non-transmigrating" (*apatisaṅkramā*).
"Transmigration" (*pratisaṅkrama*) means movement; the meaning is that such movement does not belong to consciousness.
Why, then, does it not have this [movement]? To this it is said: "unchanging" (*apariṇāminī*).

The power of consciousness (citi-śakti) does not possess even the threefold transformation— namely, that characterized by properties (dharma), characteristics (lakṣaṇa), and states (avasthā)— by means of which, being transformed into the form of activity, it might undergo transformation through conjunction with the intellect (buddhi).
(Yoga-bhāṣya, Tattva-vaiśāradī, Bhāsvatī 1.2)
Since it is unchanging, the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) is therefore non-transmigratory—that is, it does not move.
Just as the intellect (*buddhi*) goes toward an object for the purpose of grasping it, consciousness does not do so because it is inactive.
Alternatively, "non-transmigratory" means that which has no *pratisaṅkrama*—that is, no attachment (*saṅga*) to objects; in other words, it is untainted (*nirlepa*).

[Objection: But if the Self is unchanging (apariṇāmin), since it lacks the form of the object, how can there be the manifestation of the object? To this he says: "to which the object has been shown" (*darśitaviṣayā*). The analysis of the compound is: that to which the object has been shown—that is, presented—by the intellect (*buddhi*). For one who contemplates that the modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), having reflected in consciousness (*citi*) along with the objects, appears [therein], [the Self] is unchanging; and for that very reason, it is pure (*śuddhā*) and infinite (*anantā*).
— *Yogavārttika*, *Pātañjalarahasya* 1.2.

Comparison—As it has been said by Pañcaśikha: "The power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigrating; yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it follows its modifications" (Yogasūtrabhāṣya 2.20). "The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he perceives the mental modifications. (Tattvavaiśāradī)
"For the sake of the Puruṣa's perception, and likewise for the sake of the isolation (kaivalya) of Pradhāna," — Yoga Sūtra 2.20.
The union of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man; from that [union] arises creation...
In that same way, as in the case of the lame man and the blind man, the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* are to be viewed:
the *puruṣa* is to be viewed as being like the lame man, and the *pradhāna* as being like the blind man.
The Puruṣa possesses the power of vision, while Pradhāna possesses the capacity for action— Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti, verse 21.
The analogy of the six-limbed bond, however, is intended to demonstrate their necessary concomitance.

Just as a cripple does not become capable of purposeful action through his power of sight without the blind man, and the blind man likewise does not become so without the cripple; even so, *pradhāna*—though it possesses the capacity to perceive the effects produced by the *puruṣa*—does not cease its activity because it lacks a specific motive for doing so, proceeding without limit.
Similarly, although the *puruṣa* possesses consciousness, he cannot become a perceiver in the absence of an object to be perceived without *pradhāna*; thus, he depends upon *pradhāna*.
—Yuktidīpikā, p. 107: "Because of the absence of purpose for the Puruṣa and Pradhāna, which have become the seer and the seen"—this is the reading in the Śrā. manuscript.

Now, one might ask: "Since the *puruṣa* is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), how can he experience the fruit situated in *pradhāna*, which is the cause for the continuous flow of transmigratory existence? This is not a valid objection; for although he is of the nature of consciousness, because he is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance (*ajñāna-tamas*), he imagines the fruits such as pleasure—which actually reside in *prakṛti*—to reside within himself, and thus his status as an enjoyer of them is established. However, when knowledge dawns upon him, [realizing]: "This [nature] is the cause of suffering; it is not mine; association with her is not fitting," then, through discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), he no longer experiences the fruit of action produced by that [nature]. And she too, having been recognized as having a different nature, thinks: "I am not his property; he must not enjoy the fruit of my action," and thus, intending to produce it no longer for his sake, she withdraws from him like a leprous woman.
Therefore, liberation is attained through the discernment of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.

The *guṇas*, such as *sattva* and the others, are insentient, exist for the sake of another, and consist of both *prakṛti* and its transformations; whereas I am other than them—not *prakṛti* and not a transformation—but the *puruṣa* (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3). This cognition of distinction is the discernment of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*; from that, liberation is attained. For the *puruṣa*, while situated in *prakṛti*, experiences the *guṇas* born of *prakṛti*.
The cause of this [bondage] is attachment to the qualities; that leads to births in unworthy wombs.
— Bhagavad Gītā 13.21

The cause of the conjunction between the conscious self and its own intellect is ignorance (Yoga Sūtra 2.24). Thus it has been stated here by Pañcaśikha: "Having perceived either the manifest or the unmanifest as the Self, one rejoices in its prosperity, thinking it to be the prosperity of the Self; one grieves over its adversity, thinking it to be the adversity of the Self. All such a person is unawakened."
— Yogabhāṣya 2.5 —
the state of being the enjoyer— Śruti.
The means of liberation is the undisturbed discriminative discernment of prakṛti; this is the discriminative discernment— Yoga Sūtra, Vyāsa Bhāṣya 2.26.

Thus, from the practice of the principles (tattva), through that very practice, there arises for the person a vision of reality—namely, "I am not these, these are not mine, I do not belong to these"—without remainder. From such practice, the understanding arises in the person: "The principles are not I; the principles are not mine; I do not belong to the principles; rather, these are the products of primordial matter (pradhāna)."
From that, knowledge arises; the meaning of "thus and so forth" is that it is exhaustive and leaves nothing remaining.
What is this knowledge? It means it consists of the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.

Here it is asked: what does the person (*puruṣa*) do with that knowledge? To this it is replied: by means of that [knowledge], the person—remaining established like a spectator and self-abiding—beholds *prakṛti*, which has ceased its procreative activity and, by the force of the purpose [of liberation], has desisted from its seven forms. (Sāṅkhyakārikā, Māṭharavṛtti, 63–64)
It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than primordial nature (prakṛti),
which, once seen by the Puruṣa, does not present itself for sight again, thinking, "I have been seen."
Just as a certain virtuous woman of good family, standing at the door of her house, is suddenly seen by a man who has arrived unexpectedly; she, immediately feeling bashful, quickly enters her home,
thinking, "I have been seen by him," and does not come into the sight of that man again,
while the man departs when she has withdrawn.
—Sāṃkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti 61; Tattvāmṛta p. 194;
Sāṃkhyatattvaprakāśa p. 177.
"I have seen [him]," thus the one [Puruṣa] remains indifferent; "I have been seen," thus the other [Prakṛti] ceases. (Sāṃkhyapravacana 3.69, 70)
Even though there is a conjunction, there is no further purpose for creation;

just as a spectator, having seen this dancer on the stage while she remains in all her various states, leaves the stage thinking "I have seen her," so too does Nature (prakṛti) cease, thinking "I have been seen by him. She is one, the primary cause even of the three worlds, and there is no second Nature.

The dancer also ceases from her dance, thinking, "I have been seen by him"; likewise, the Puruṣa also ceases like a spectator, thinking, "This Prakṛti has been seen by me through the eye of knowledge. This means he attains liberation (*mokṣa*). (Sāṅkhyakārikā with Māṭharavṛtti, verse 66).
It is stated in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "Though she possesses transformations and has been enjoyed for a long time by the one whose nature is the *guṇas* due to ignorance..."
"Once its faults have been known, this primordial nature (prakṛti) desists as if out of shame"—Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya, p. 111; "of consciousness," manuscript b.
For the sake of attaining enjoyments,
[one resorts to] a woman with leprosy;
however, the male person (puruṣa) is neither the primal nature (prakṛti), because he does not produce, nor is he a transformation (vikṛti), because he is unproduced.
The meaning is that it is neither a cause nor an effect— this is the view of Māṭhara; therefore, [there is] attainment— this is the view of Āryadeva.
The demonstration that action (*karman*) is a property of the person (*pudgala*), preceded by a refutation [of opposing views]:

here, a rebuttal is offered regarding what was first stated— namely, "the transformation of primordial matter" (*prakṛti-pariṇāma*) and so forth— that is an unexamined assertion, because the investigation of attributes is only possible once the subject (*dharmin*) has been established.

Furthermore, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not established as a real entity (*dharmin*) by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the proofs intended to establish it have been refuted in detail during the examination of primordial nature.

Therefore, how can the description of actions as being transformations of that [nature] be tenable? Or, let us grant that it exists; even so, would it transform in such a way depending upon the person (*puruṣa*) as a cause, or without depending upon him? It cannot be without depending upon him, for then there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would likewise transform to produce a body and so forth even for a liberated soul (*muktātman*).

Now, regarding that which is depended upon: what is it that is depended upon—is it the non-perception of distinction (*vivekānupalambha*), or is it the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)? It cannot be the non-perception of distinction; for, since that consists in the absence of the perception of distinction, it is possible even in the liberated self (*muktātman*).

Furthermore, no distinction whatsoever can exist between its non-arising and its destruction, because there is no difference in their nature as absences (*abhāva*). As for dependence on the unseen force, if it were to transform in such a way [due to that force], there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for only when the unseen force is established is the transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) into white and black karma established through dependence on it; and only when that is established is the unseen force established.

"This is not a fault because the stream [of karma] is beginningless—first, depending on unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), another transformation of that [nature] occurs, and from that, yet another. This too is untenable, because such a transformation would necessarily occur even in a liberated soul (*muktātman*) for the sake of producing a body and so forth. [If you say: "In that case, there is no such necessity because its [karmic] mandate has ceased," this is also trivial, because it would follow that even in one who is not liberated, there would be no such transformation for the sake of producing those [bodies].

The claim that "there is no fault here because [the Pradhāna] possesses the capacity for both activity and cessation" is merely a matter of faith; for it is in every respect contradictory for a single, partless Pradhāna to simultaneously possess the two attributes of having the capacity for activity and the capacity for cessation. Or, if there were no such contradiction, its being single and partless would be untenable in every respect (p. 812, l.

Comparison: If the Pradhāna were to proceed without depending on any external cause residing in the Puruṣa, it would proceed toward the production of bodies and so forth even for a liberated self, because there is no distinction [between the two states]. — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 20; *Dharmottarapradīpa*, p. 316.
In the present context, the object of cognition (prameya) [is as follows].

[Objection: "If it is argued that [the activity of the *pradhāna*] depends on non-perception (*adarśana*), for indeed, the *pradhāna* acts toward one for whom the discernment (*viveka*) of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* is impossible to achieve, and not toward a liberated self (*muktātman*). [Reply: That is not so; because even in the case of the liberated self, since the discernment has perished, it would follow that the *pradhāna* would act [toward him]. Furthermore, we do not perceive any distinction between non-arising and destruction in terms of being "non-perception. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 20, fol. gha.
In the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 316,

it is stated that there is no difference in terms of non-existence, because in the state of saṃsāra there is the non-arising of discernment (*viveka*), whereas in the state of liberation there is the destruction of discernment even though it has arisen;
let this [distinction] be based on *adṛṣṭa*.
In the case at hand, when [the self] has undergone transformation into the form of action,
that [transformation] is its... [fragmentary text].

Regarding the comparison with the transformation of karma as white, black, and so forth in the present context: if it is argued that [the process] proceeds in dependence upon the unseen (adṛṣṭa), that is incorrect, because even that [unseen], being established in the primary cause (pradhāna) in the form of a potentiality, is indistinguishable in both cases—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 20, section Gha.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛ.
316: Although [karma] has perished with respect to one who has achieved their purpose in the form of white, black, and other types of karma, it is not destroyed because it remains common to others.
—Even though an object has perished—that is, has reached destruction—for one person whose purpose has been fulfilled, it is not destroyed for others because it is common to other persons;

even though it has reached destruction for virtuous persons, it is not yet fulfilled for non-virtuous persons. Thus, for their vision, having entered the domain of the object of action, it indeed acquires its own nature through the form of another.
—Yoga Sūtra Bhāṣya 2.22.
The consequence of the transformation into the form of karma for the sake of producing a body and so forth, [applies] to the transmigrating self.

Comparison: Indeed, it is not logical for the same single entity to be the locus of both the state of having ceased its function (*nivṛttādhikāratva*) and the state of being engaged in its function (*pravṛttādhikāratva*) simultaneously, because of their contradiction, just like [the states of] being destroyed and not being destroyed—*Āptaparīkṣā*, p.
83; *pravṛddhavinivṛttā*—MS reading.

Is this "engagement in its office" (pravṛttādhikāratva) of the Pradhāna toward the non-liberated self—namely, being connected to it, or being the producer of the body, pleasure, and so forth? It cannot be "being connected," because that has already passed for the liberated self; for since both the Pradhāna and the self are eternal and omnipresent, they would necessarily be in contact everywhere and at all times.

Now, if [it is argued that the Veda] produces physical pleasure and so forth for the body, then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): for only when the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for its application toward an unliberated self is established can its capacity to produce those [pleasures] for that very self be established; and only when that [capacity] is established can the eligibility for its application toward that self be established. Thus, [the relationship between] being a connection (*sambandhatva*), being eternal (*nitya*), and being universal (*sarva*)—[these attributes would be undermined]. (Ba., Śrā. *Note: The text fragment "ba॰, śra॰ nityaṃ sarva– ba॰" appears to be a scribal or editorial marker indicating the end of a section or a reference to specific manuscript readings.*
Furthermore, with respect to the unliberated self (*amuktātman*) itself:

is some benefit conferred upon it by the body and so forth produced by that [body], or not? If no benefit is conferred, how could it be designated as "belonging to him" (*tasya*), since that designation would then absurdly apply even to a liberated self (*muktātman*)? If a benefit is conferred, is it distinct from [the self] or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then because the person (*pums*) would also be subject to being an effect (*kāryatva*) through the production of that [benefit], its eternity (*nityatva*) would be undermined.

Now, if [the self] were distinct [from the action], then nothing would be performed by the person, and the designation "his" (tasya) would not be applicable because there would be no connection between them. Furthermore, if another benefit were produced by that [action], it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Consequently, since the primary substance (*pradhāna*) lacks existence by its own nature, or even if it did exist, the transformation into action (*karmapariṇāma*) would be untenable. One must therefore accept that action in its substantial form (*dravyarūpa*) is a transformation of matter (*pudgala*), while action in its modal form (*bhāvarūpa*) is a transformation of the self (*ātman*), because the existence of matter and the self, as well as their capacity to serve as the substratum for diverse transformations, have already been established.

Nor is it a fault that the self would incur impermanence upon undergoing transformation through the impermanence of karma; for such impermanence is accepted in some respect, since it has been established in the proof of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) that all entities possess the nature of being both permanent and impermanent in some respect. Furthermore, the consequence of impermanence would apply equally if the primary cause (*pradhāna*) were to undergo transformation.

Comparison with that which is produced by *pradhāna*—for does this modification of *pradhāna*, such as the *mahat* and so forth, which exists for the sake of the *puruṣa*, perform some benefit for the *puruṣa* or not? If it performs one, is it something different from the *puruṣa* or not different? — *Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā*, p. 29;
[concerning] the transmigrating self.
In the case of performing a benefit that is non-different from the transmigrating person's body and so forth, by means of that benefit...
That karma which is transformed even by the assistance rendered through the body and other means of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the acceptance of the nature of impermanent karma as being the self, that which was stated—namely, that "the state of being a witness (sākṣitva) is the self's presiding over the activity of the qualities (guṇas)," and so forth—that too is a mere fantasy. This is because the activity of the qualities characterized as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* has already been refuted in the examination of *prakṛti*; and because a self whose nature is entirely eternal, all-pervading, and so on, has been rejected in the discussion regarding the measurement of its own body. Therefore, what could be the presider of what? (p. 813, l. 5)

Regarding what was stated [on pages 354–266], namely that "the state of being a non-agent also follows from the property of not producing [effects]," that too is charming only so long as it is not examined; for if one were to admit that the person (puṃs) is in every respect neither an effect nor a cause, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that the person lacks reality (avastutva).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The person (*puruṣa*) postulated by you is not a real entity (*vastu*), because it is in every respect neither an effect nor a cause, like a sky-lotus (page 814, line 6).

Furthermore, as for the claim that he is designated as "non-agent" because the two functions of vibration (*praspandana*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*)—which have the sense of producing [effects]—do not exist in the self (*ātman*); that too is untenable, because the existence of vibration and transformation in the self has been established in the cognition of one's own body.

Furthermore, if the self were non-agential (*akartṛ*), its status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) would be contradictory; for one is called an "enjoyer" only when performing the act of enjoying, just as one is called a "goer" when performing the act of going. One that does not undergo modification cannot properly receive such a designation, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Moreover, since the suffix *tṛc* cannot arise from a non-agent, the designation "enjoyer" for the self would be impossible.

[Objection: "Surely, because of the observation of the triplet [of words] beginning with 'the enjoyer' (*bhoktṛ*), agency is not established as real, since the conceptual construction of agency follows from verbal cognition and is devoid of a real object. [Reply: This too is unsatisfactory, because it would follow that the attributes of being an enjoyer and so forth are likewise unreal for the Self. And if one accepts that, then the Puruṣa as a "cognizer" (*cetana*)—defined by the thought "he cognizes"—would not be established in the ultimate sense, because there is no difference in the fact that even the conceptual construction following the word and cognition of "cognizer" is devoid of a real object. If, out of fear of this fault, one maintains that the enjoyer is the agent, then there is a contradiction with the doctrine of non-agency.

Since it does not accomplish another action that is to be accomplished by the primary [agent], if [the self] were a non-agent, it would follow that the primary [action] itself is also a non-agent; for even that [self] does not accomplish the other action characterized as "eating," which is to be accomplished by the person (puruṣa). Therefore, if the person is a non-agent, there is necessarily an absence of being an enjoyer.
The formal argument is: the transmigrating self is not an enjoyer of pleasure and so forth, because it is a non-agent of dharma and the rest, like the liberated self.
pṛ. 814, l. 6. For comparison: Therefore, if the Puruṣa is the agent, his being the enjoyer is logically real;

otherwise, how could there be enjoyment for one who is indifferent and does not perform the act of enjoying? For enjoyment consists in the experience of pleasure and pain, and being the substratum of that is what constitutes being the enjoyer.
—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p.

523: If the self is the enjoyer, let it be the agent as well, since there is no contradiction between those two; but if there were a contradiction between them, how could the enjoyer possess agency? For that which is an enjoyer would [otherwise] lack the state of being an agent.
—Āptapañcāśikā, Verse 81:
The Self (ātman), as the agent who experiences the fruits of its own karma, is not a real entity in the manner imagined by the Sāṃkhya school, because it lacks agency, like a flower in the sky.

Furthermore, the Self is accepted as the experiencer (bhoktṛ); does it perform the act of experiencing or not? If it performs it, then what wrong has been done by other actions? On the other hand, if it does not even perform the act of experiencing, how can it be called an "experiencer" at all? It is thus eternally [inconsistent].
— *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, Bṛhatī, verse 49:
"For the sake of which [the root] *bhṛj*— " [referring to] the suffix *āna*.
[The definition of] conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): "That which follows upon verbal cognition and is devoid of a real object" (*kartṛvi-ā॰, śra॰*).

Verbal cognition is the knowledge produced by words; that which has the habit of following after that is "that which follows upon verbal cognition. That determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) which does not depend on the actual state of the object is called conceptual construction.
—Yogasūtra with Bhoja’s Commentary 1.9.

For comparison: [If it were so,] there would result the unreality of the attributes of being an enjoyer and so forth for the Puruṣa; and if that were accepted, the Puruṣa as a conscious being (*cetana*) who "cognizes" would not be established in reality, because the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following the word and cognition "conscious" is devoid of a real object, just like the conceptual construction following the word and cognition "agent," "enjoyer," and so forth.
— According to the *Āptamīmāṃsā*, verse 81,
even by means of the primary [cause],
it does not exist. Śrī.

Comparison: The transmigrating self is not an enjoyer because it is not an agent, like the liberated self—*Ṣaḍdarśana-bṛhaspati-śloka* 48. Furthermore, if one were to accept that a non-agent is an enjoyer, there would follow the faults of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). For action is performed by *prakṛti*, yet she has no connection with its fruit; thus there is the destruction of what has been done. And since that [action] was not performed by the *puruṣa*, yet he is connected with its fruit, there is the acquisition of what has not been done.

Furthermore, regarding the connection of the fruit with one who is not the agent, the objection that this would also apply to the liberated self (*muktātman*) because the self is conscious—even if it is not the agent—is refuted by this very [argument]: for by that same reasoning, the connection with the fruit would necessarily follow for the liberated self as well; or else, the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātman*) would likewise not have such a connection, since there is no distinction [between them].
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the transmigrating self does not possess a connection with the fruit, because it is conscious, like the liberated self.

Likewise, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is not the agent of actions or their fruit, because it is not an enjoyer, like the liberated self; [it is] a non-agent and non-enjoyer—compare: "Bondage and liberation belong to primordial matter, while the person experiences its fruit," for that would entail the fallacy of the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done.

For if bondage and liberation were produced by *pradhāna*, yet its experience of the fruit [of those actions] does not occur, there would be the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*); whereas if those two were not produced by the *puruṣa*, yet he experiences their fruit, how could the [charge of] the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) be avoided? — [As stated in] Āptapa° kā° 114, Ṣaḍda° bṛha° ślo° 48, 52.
Thus [says] Ācārya [Haribhadra].
Even for one who is liberated, there is the consequence of experiencing the fruits of karma produced by *pradhāna*—
as stated in Āptapañcāśikā, verse 114— precisely because of [the soul's] sentience (*caitanyatva*).
Just as in the case of one who is liberated, there is no connection with the fruits of action;
for qualities such as "agency" cognize houses and so forth in every respect,
yet they do not cognize the "enjoyer"— what could be more illogical than this?
One does not know how to produce [it], such as its name, primary parts, or secondary characteristics.
And he does not understand what is improper beyond this—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 300—as has been stated:

"For just as the intellect (*buddhi*), though itself insentient, [becomes so] through association with sentience," and so forth; that too is mere words, because a distinction between the intellect and sentience is impossible, for "intellect," "sentience," and "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) are synonyms of consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone.
Furthermore, the impossibility of that [agency] for the Sāṃkhya has been explained in detail in the proof of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Therefore, how could agency belong to the Self even figuratively on the basis of that example? Consequently, one must accept that its agency—as established by uncontradicted cognitions such as "the person performs merit" or "he performs meditation"—is indeed non-figurative (*anupacarita*).
(Page 814, Line 8)
It should be observed— see page 193, note 2,
page 193—
by means of the illustrative example of the intellect (buddhi).

By this, the claim that "the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is unchanging" and so forth is refuted; for it is impossible for anything that is unchanging to possess substantial reality, just like a sky-flower. [Objection:

But surely you yourselves accept that the liberated self, though pure and unchanging, possesses substantial reality. [Reply: This too is the manifestation of no small ignorance; for even that [liberated self] is asserted to undergo transformation at every moment. Since the object of perception (dṛśya) undergoes transformation at every moment, it is impossible for the perceiver (draṣṭṛ) to remain unchanging. Nor should it be asserted that the object of perception is a real entity while remaining entirely unchanging; for the Sāṃkhyas themselves admit its capacity for transformation.

Now, if it is argued that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is called unchanging because it does not undergo transition (*apratisaṅkrama*), that is not so; for when its object is presented with respect to each particular object, a transition necessarily occurs. To claim that such a transition belongs only to the intellect (*buddhi*) and not to the power of consciousness is also untenable, because it would follow that the intellect likewise lacks transition, and it would further follow that the transition belongs to the object itself.

If it is asked: "Since there is the possibility of the reflection (*pratisaṅkrama*) of an object being determined by the intellect (*buddhi*), how can that [reflection] be impossible for the intellect?"—then, when there is the reflection of the intellect which reveals the object, how could there be no reflection for the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) which perceives that very object? For just as the intellect, showing a specific object to the power of consciousness, undergoes reflection, so too the power of consciousness, perceiving it in succession, must likewise do so; since there is no distinction [between them], how otherwise could this [power] have objects shown to it in succession?
Therefore, [Śrī...].
Because, by abandoning the state of having no perceived object and adopting the state of having a perceived object, its very persistence as a transformation (pariṇāmitva) is established—
Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 30.
For even the liberated self,

being omniscient, perceives all objects only by undergoing transformation through the relinquishing and assuming of prior and subsequent natures, and not otherwise; because if that which is perceived changes at every moment, it is impossible for the perceiver to remain unchanging,
and he is not capable of asserting that the perceived object is unchanging, since he himself accepts its transformability, which would entail the abandonment of his own established doctrine.
—Yuktyanuṣaṅga-ṭīkā, p. 30—“The state of being a cause... only transformation,” Ātmaparīkṣā, Śrāvakabhūmi.

If it is argued that, because the object of perception appears as an object for each respective sense-organ, it is the intellect (*buddhi*) alone that undergoes such transference (*pratisaṅkrama*) sequentially and not the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), we say no; for this would entail the consequence that the intellect itself cannot undergo transference, and it would instead entail the consequence that the object alone undergoes transference.
— This [statement] from the *Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā*, page 30, is also incorrect,
because it would entail the consequence that the object itself undergoes transference; thus, "it does not exist" (*nāsti*) is not present in manuscript *ba*.
In the process of withdrawal,

just as the intellect (*buddhi*), manifesting objects as specifically determined, transfers [its impressions] to the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), so too does the power of consciousness, perceiving in succession, transfer [them] because there is no difference [in its nature];
otherwise, how could it perceive objects in succession?
—*Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā*, p. 31:
"The object of specific determination" (*pratiniyamaviṣayaṃ*) [is] the object (*viṣayam*).
The ellipsis of the sentence is "it penetrates," [referring to] the power of consciousness (cicchakti).

Furthermore, when an object is presented to the intellect (*buddhi*) by the consciousness, does it [the consciousness] then abandon its previously unmanifested nature or not? If it does not abandon it, how could it be one that has manifested an object at that time, just as it was before? If, on the other hand, it does abandon it, how can it be unchanging (*apariṇāminī*), given that the abandonment of the state of having an unmanifested object is inseparable from the assumption of the state of having a manifested object—which is itself a modification (*pariṇāma*)? Now, if it is argued: "The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) possesses a single, undivided nature such that whatever object is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) by the intellect in a particular place and at a particular time in a certain manner, she perceives it in that place, at that time, and in that manner; therefore, even though there is the manifestation of objects, there is no difference in her own nature for each individual object, which would otherwise entail change,"—that too is incorrect, because it would follow that the intellect (*buddhi*) likewise possesses a single, unitary nature.

For it could indeed be argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) is a single entity whose nature is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of multiple objects occurring in succession; thus, whatever object exists in whatever place at whatever time in whatever state, the intellect determines it as being there, at that time, and in that way.

Likewise, by this logic, it would follow that the sense organs, mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, would also possess a single nature consisting of the perception, conceptualization, and self-conceit of their respective objects; consequently, no distinction in nature would ever be established anywhere for these [faculties] themselves.
The nature of the Seer is consciousness-power;
[it is] consciousness-power.
Likewise, it would follow that cognition (*buddhi*) too must have a single nature;

for one could indeed say that cognition has but a single nature consisting of the determination of multiple objects occurring in succession, by which it determines an object according to its time, place, and mode. Thus, nothing possessing a manifold nature would be established—*Yuktyanuṣāsana-ṭīkā*, p. 32.

As for the argument that the non-transference of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is established because of its purity—that too is incorrect. For while the transference of impure modifications into a pure self is indeed contradictory, the transference of pure modifications is not.

[Objection: But surely the power of consciousness is non-transferring even through pure modifications because of its infinity. [Reply: This too is unsound, because [the reason] is inconclusive due to *prakṛti*; for even though it is infinite, the Sāṃkhyas admit the transference of modifications such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) into it.

Even for one whose self is pure, because there is no contradiction in the non-transference of one's own pure modification (*pariṇāma*), the transference of an impure modification therein is simply impossible;
[this is so] because of deviation from the nature [of purity], as stated in the *Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā*, p. 31.
For that [continuity] too is infinite; even if it were finite, there would be a contradiction with its permanence—Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 31.

As for what was also stated—“like the lame man and the blind man,” and so forth—that is utterly incoherent, because of the disparity between the illustration and the subject illustrated. For in the case of the lame man and the blind man, since they possess consciousness, it is logical that they act in mutual dependence after deliberating, “This very thing will accomplish our desired goal in this manner. However, this is not the case for *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, because the opposite is true (as stated on page 815, line 2).
Compare: if the insentient *pradhāna* were the unbridled binder, there would be no liberation at all.

"Since Prakṛti does not bind even a man who knows the truth, what is her restrainer? Because the conjunction [between Puruṣa and Prakṛti] is equal [to that between others], according to the analogy of the lame man and the blind man" (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 491).
This very point is desired by Ātreya and Bādarāyaṇa.
There would be a reversal.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—"even for this [Self] whose nature is consciousness, because it is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance," and so forth—therein, is ignorance itself the darkness, or are both ignorance and darkness [separate]? In the first case, why would even a liberated soul, while abiding in *prakṛti*, not perceive the fruits such as pleasure as residing in the Self, and why would he not be their enjoyer? For even that [liberated soul], due to the absence of [empirical] knowledge, would be no different in being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance. In the second case, however, what is this thing called "darkness" that is distinct from ignorance? If you say it is passion (*rāga*) and so forth, we say no; for since those are attributes of *prakṛti* which is entirely different from the Self, it is impossible for them to shroud the Self.

Even if it were such [an entity], if it were to conceal that [Self], then even the liberated Self would be concealed, since there is no distinction [between them]. Now, if you say that this concealer belongs only to the *adhikārī* (the qualified one) and not to the liberated Self; well then, what is this so-called state of being an *adhikārī*? If you say that he toward whom Pradhāna has set forth its activity is the *adhikārī*; no, for the answer to the state of having an activity directed toward Pradhāna has already been given previously (p. 815, l. 8).
For is it that ignorance alone is darkness, or is it that both ignorance and darkness [exist]— even for the liberated self? (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, Bṛhatī, verse 52).
In the state of liberation, knowledge perishes; therefore, even for them, there certainly exists ignorance consisting of the destruction of that knowledge.
Furthermore, by means of passion and so forth—which consist of the attributes of *prakṛti* that are absolutely distinct [from the self]—the qualified seeker alone [is affected].
The liberated self does not possess passion and so forth; if there were one who possesses them, [it would not be liberated]. (Ācārya Śrī)

As for what was also stated—“from discriminative discernment” (*vivekakhyāti*) and so forth—in that regard, what is this so-called discriminative discernment? If you say it is the manifestation of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* as they abide in their own respective forms, then of whom does it belong? Of *prakṛti*, of *puruṣa*, or of some other entity distinct from them? It cannot belong to some other entity, because the Sāṃkhyas do not admit of anything else apart from *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
Nor can it belong to *prakṛti*, because she resides in the stage of non-consciousness (*asaṃvedya*), because she is insentient (*acidrūpa*), and because such a capacity is not admitted of her.
Nor does it belong to the *puruṣa*, for he too remains in the stage of non-perception (*asaṃvedyaparvan*).

Therefore, since both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* abide in the stage of non-perception, the manifestation through discrimination (*viveka-khyāti*) of their mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*), which is not otherwise apparent, is exceedingly difficult to achieve. For in the case of objects such as a jar or a cloth, which abide in the stage of perception by virtue of their own nature, discrimination is observed to occur through the power of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that reveals the object as it truly exists, when—due to some cause of error—the object is not initially perceived discriminatively. But this is not the case here.

In that regard, what is this so-called *khyāti*? If it is said to be "the manifestation as distinct [of] Nature (*prakṛti*) and Spirit (*puruṣa*), which abide in their own respective forms," then of whom does it belong—of Nature or of the Spirit? (Ṣaḍdarśanabṛhaṭṭīkā, verse 52).
Of whom... (vi-)? (Variant reading: keṣāṃ vi-).

In the present context, [it is not included] among the categories of the unknowable because it resides within the stage of the non-self-cognizable, because it is insentient, and because it is not admitted [as such].
—The state of being "beyond" (atīti) is difficult to establish within the sphere of the knowable; thus [it is said] in the *Bṛhat-ṣaḍdarśana-samuccaya*, verse 52. Ārya.
It is difficult to establish [the state of being beyond] within the limits of the knowable.

Furthermore, manifestation through discrimination (*viveka-khyāti*) is the ascertainment of that [discrimination]; and since, according to your view, it is a property of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), it cannot possibly exist in the *puruṣa*.

Or, if it were to exist there, would it be distinct from him or non-distinct? If it were non-distinct, then, because it would follow that it too is eternal like the self (*ātman*), the consequence of never being liberated would arise.

If it is distinct, let it be so; nevertheless, is it eternal or non-eternal? If it is eternal, is it connected or unconnected [to the self]? If it is unconnected, how could it be designated as "belonging to that"? For if it were designated as belonging to that despite being unconnected, it would follow that it belongs to everything, and thus no one at all would experience transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). If, on the other hand, it is connected, this is not the case; for between two eternal things that do not mutually benefit one another, no kind of connection is possible. Or, if such a connection were possible, since that connection too would be eternal, it would follow that liberation would occur for one whose nature is eternally [bound].

Now, discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is impermanent. But being impermanent, is it produced (*janya*) or unproduced (*ajanya*)? In that regard, since it is impermanent, its status as unproduced—like a jar or similar objects—is untenable.

Even if it were produced, would it be produced by the Self (*ātman*), by primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or by something distinct from those two? It cannot be by something distinct, because nothing other than primordial nature and the Self is admitted to be its producer.
Nor can it be by the Self, because the Self is not admitted to possess the capacity for agency (*janakatva*).

Or, if it is admitted [that discriminative discernment is produced], would it be produced by that [Self] as dissociated from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or together with it? In the first case, there follows the fallacy of a vicious circle (*cakraka*): for only when the producibility of discriminative discernment is established is the dissociation of primordial nature and the Self established; and only when that [dissociation] is established is the producibility of discriminative discernment by the Self as dissociated from it established. However, if it were produced by the Self together with [nature], then everyone everywhere would always be liberated, because it would follow that [discriminative discernment] would arise everywhere, at all times, and without distinction—even regarding discriminative discernment itself.
In the designation "of the person" with respect to discriminative discernment,
there is also [the implication of] a relationship.
The manifestation of discernment (viveka) is not the producer of this [world], nor is it its non-producer.
And for the self,
discriminative discernment.
Indeed, this is not the case at all;

for even that which was stated— “I am one who has cognized the form,” and so forth— is an unexamined assertion, because such cognition is impossible in the case of the primordial matter (prakṛti) due to its insentience.

Indeed, an insentient object such as a jar is never observed to experience for itself, "I have been cognized by this [consciousness]; therefore, I shall not provide a fruit for it," because that would entail the confusion of the essential natures of the insentient and the sentient. For the nature of the insentient is its dependence on another for the apprehension of its own form, whereas the nature of the non-insentient is its independence from such [another]. Thus, there would be a confusion of these two through the cognition of the object. (Vijñānādvaitavirūpaṇa)

pṛ॰ 816, l. 2. For comparison: "Because of insentience; for instance, since the *pradhāna* is insentient, it lacks consciousness such that it could think, 'I have been seen by this person' or 'I have been recognized as faulty. Thus, in the absence of consciousness, its activity remains no different from before. Enough of this over-elaboration. — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 20, manuscript Gha.

If it is argued that she desists [from further action] because she has already been seen, let it not be so; for she is not like a courtesan who, having been seized by the firm grip of the vow of a devoted wife, yet possesses the fortune of being enjoyed by men as friends, and thus ought not to engage in [sexual] intercourse according to fixed rules—let this matter rest—for it is impossible for such consciousness to arise from primordial nature (prakṛti) due to its insentience. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 492)
–*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, *Bṛhatī*, verse 52;
*jaḍatvarūpaḥ* (in manuscript *ba*);
*tasyai phalam* (in manuscript *ba*).

Furthermore, even if the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is a knower, it would—just as in the state of *saṃsāra*—continue to function by its own nature in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*) in order to bring about experience for the self, because that nature remains present at that time due to its eternity.

For wind, which has activity as its inherent nature, does not cease from that nature merely because it is perceived by someone in an altered state; therefore, how could there be liberation? Alternatively, if that [activity] were non-existent at that time, the eternality and uniformity of *prakṛti* would be untenable, because it is contradictory for it to abandon a prior nature while assuming a subsequent one; such [transformation] is only non-contradictory in the case of that which is eternal through modification (*pariṇāminitya*).

Furthermore, if the transformation-permanence (*pariṇāminityatva*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is accepted, then that same [permanence] must also be accepted for the self (*ātman*). This is because it too abandons its prior nature as an enjoyer of pleasure and so forth, and assumes a nature as a non-enjoyer; and because it relinquishes its unliberated nature and adopts a liberated nature.

Once its transformation-permanence is established, its state of being subject to transformation through modifications such as pleasure and so forth must also be accepted. Thus, it is proven that even in liberation, the self possesses a nature consisting of pure knowledge and the like.

Comparison: Because this [prakṛti] lacks consciousness and thus the capacity for deliberation, just as it proceeds toward sound and other objects even after they have been perceived, so too will it proceed toward that end [of liberation] even after discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has been achieved, since its inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is indestructible. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya-kandalī*, p. 4.
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, verse 52:
because of its nature as a motivator (*pravartakasvabhāva*), it is [perceived] as having a distinct form (*virūpatayā*).

And since its nature as an agent is established, and its permanence is through transformation (*pariṇāminityatva*), it must be admitted that it undergoes transformation even through transformations such as pleasure and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of liberation (*mokṣābhāvaprasaṅga*).
(Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā, verse 52)
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Naiyāyika is that liberation consists in the destruction of the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

Now, it may be argued that it is untenable for the self to possess the nature of pure knowledge and so forth in the state of liberation, because that state consists in the destruction of specific qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) and the rest.

For when the nature of the self is apprehended through means of valid cognition such as perception, and when cultivation preceded by mental concentration reaches its highest degree, true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) comes to fruition; at that point, upon the absolute cessation of the nine specific qualities of the self, the self abides in its own essential nature—this is liberation.
And the proof for its cessation is as follows: the continuum of the nine specific qualities of the self is absolutely cut off, because it is a continuum, like the continuum of a lamp and so forth.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), since it occurs in the subject (*pakṣa*);
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), since it exists in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as lamps.

Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because—just as in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—it does not occur in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Nor is it mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*) that could establish a contrary meaning are impossible here.
Nor is it counterbalanced (*satpratipakṣa*), because there is no possible inference that could establish a counter-argument.
—The nature of cessation—*Bhāṣya*: "Liberation is the absolute destruction of the nine specific qualities of the self"—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 638.

Apavarga is the absolute cessation of suffering; it is not a cessation that is limited [to some]. This is because the word "all," referring to all the qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*) by implying the two kinds of suffering, and through the inclusion of the term "absolute," expresses the disjunction from them in their entirety. Thus, it is stated that apavarga is the eradication, root and branch, of the nine qualities of the self: cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
As long as all the qualities of the self, such as latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, have not been destroyed, an absolute cessation of suffering cannot be conceived.
— *Nyāyamañjarī*, p.
508: "But in that state, what kind of self remains? Its own nature alone remains as its foundation, having abandoned all qualities. — *Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 508.
The final beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*) is simply the abiding in one's own true nature, characterized by the total eradication of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.
furthermore, it is the absolute cessation of suffering—*Praśastapādabhāṣyakiraṇāvalī*, p. 6.
Thus it is established: liberation for the person is the absolute cessation of suffering characterized by this eternal, ever-present bliss—*Nyāyasāra*, p. 41.

The continuum of the nine qualities of the self is absolutely cut off, because it is a continuum; whatever is a continuum is seen to be absolutely cut off, just as the continuum of a lamp; and this [continuum] is likewise a continuum; therefore, it is absolutely cut off.
"The continuum of suffering is absolutely severed because it is a continuum, like the continuum of a lamp," so say the Ācāryas—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 20; *Kiraṇāvalī*, p.

[Objection: But surely, even if liberation consists in the cessation of the continuum [of the self], some cause must be stated, since it is not accepted that destruction occurs without a cause; [Response: This is not to be doubted, because the knowledge of reality itself is its cause, for that very knowledge is the cause of the supreme good through the process of eliminating erroneous cognition.
And it is observed that right knowledge possesses the capacity to eradicate false knowledge regarding such things as mother-of-pearl;
and when false knowledge has ceased, passion and the other afflictions rooted in it cease, because an effect does not arise in the absence of its cause.
Furthermore, in the absence of passion and the rest, the activity of mind, speech, and body—which are their effects—is turned away.
Upon their cessation, there is the non-arising of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

However, as for those actions whose effects—body, sense organs, and objects—have already begun, they are exhausted through the experience of their fruits, such as pleasure and so forth. Even those whose effects have not yet begun, though currently existing, are likewise exhausted only through the experience of their fruits.
Thus says the traditional scripture (*āgama*): "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons unless it has been experienced."
Regarding this very point, there is an inference: prior karmas are exhausted solely through experience, because they are karma, like the karma of the body already begun (*prārabdha*).

Nor does the non-cessation of *saṃsāra* follow from the necessity of other karmas arising once those [prior ones] are exhausted through experience; for it is logically established that *saṃsāra* is cut off for one who has attained knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) by the power of *samādhi*, who—having understood the capacity of karma—has simultaneously obtained all experiences through the medium of all bodies produced by that capacity, and who, through the exhaustion of acquired karma, lacks the mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) born of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), which is the cause for the production of future karma.

For attachment and aversion are indeed "pursuit" (*anusandhāna*), based on the etymological derivation that the mind which has gone [into the past] is pursued by these two. [Objection: Is it not the case that their continuity... [text fragment] ...is without cause? [Variant readings: *tatsantā* (Ba, A); *nirhetuvinā* (Ā)]
There, knowledge is not to be cherished.

However, when action is performed preceded by knowledge and without a desire for its fruit, it results in birth in a pure family for one who desires to know the means of removing suffering. Having approached a teacher and attained knowledge of the reality of the six categories, upon the cessation of ignorance, he becomes dispassionate. Due to the absence of passion, hatred, and the like, there is no production of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are their effects; and through experience, previously accumulated [karma] is extinguished. Having produced the happiness of contentment and the dissolution of the body, and having brought about the absolute merit characterized by cessation—which consists of the happiness born from the vision of the ultimate truth—upon the cessation of passion and the rest, that merit ceases.

Then, through cessation, the self becomes seedless and there is the withdrawal of the body and so forth; when the body and so forth do not arise again, liberation is tranquility, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed—Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 644.

The knowledge of the true nature of the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—by way of their similarities and differences, is the cause of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
"From the knowledge of reality comes the attainment of the supreme good" (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 20; Nyāyasūtra 1.1).
Upon the successive removal of suffering, rebirth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the removal of each preceding one, resulting in liberation (*apavarga*).
— *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.2.
These factors, beginning with false knowledge and ending with suffering, proceeding in an uninterrupted succession, constitute *saṃsāra*.

But when false knowledge is removed through the knowledge of reality, then upon the removal of false knowledge, the defects are removed; upon the removal of the defects, activity is removed; upon the removal of activity, birth is removed; upon the removal of birth, suffering is removed; and upon the removal of suffering, there is absolute liberation, which is the highest good—Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.2.
For thus, it has been observed that correct knowledge possesses the capacity to eliminate false cognition in cases such as mother-of-pearl [mistaken for silver]—Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p.
20a. And when false cognition has ceased, passion and the like perish because they are rooted in it; for in the absence of a cause, an effect does not arise.

And in the absence of passion and the like, activity—which is their effect—is turned away; and in the absence of that [activity], there is no production of merit and demerit, while those whose effects have already begun are exhausted through experience—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, p. 20a.

or Ba— [there is no] inconsistency: "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons."
This has been cited—as it was said: "Karma does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
the performed action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 20, section kha).

308; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 105.

351; *Dharmabindu-ṭīkā*, p. 13: 'One must necessarily experience [the result]'—this does not exist in the manuscript (MS)."

Past karmas are exhausted solely through experience, because they are karmas; whatever is karma is exhausted solely through experience, just like the karma that has already initiated the present body; and these [past] karmas are likewise; therefore, they are exhausted solely through experience—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, fol.

20b. For one who has produced knowledge of reality by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), having understood the purpose to be accomplished by karmas, creates bodies simultaneously and [exhausts them] through experience—*Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, fol. 20b.

—[The opponent says: "Since all experience has been taken up [by the soul], it is impossible for one who possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*) to have even a desire to experience that [karma]; therefore, its experience is untenable. This is not so, because without experiencing that [karma], the exhaustion of *karman* is untenable. Thus, even though the knower of reality lacks a desire to experience it, his engagement in that [experience] is tenable due to his seeking the exhaustion of *karman*, just as a patient takes medicine according to the instruction of a physician.

For just as in the case of a sick person, there is engagement in the administration of medicine even though it is not desired, because the destruction of the disease cannot occur otherwise, so it is here as well.

The subject under dispute is that upon the cessation of the body and so forth, the self is devoid of all pleasure and pain pertaining to sense-objects, because it is devoid of all merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). For whatever possesses pleasure and pain pertaining to sense-objects does not lack all merit and demerit, as is the case with the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātmā*); yet the liberated self (*muktātmā*) is devoid of all merit and demerit; therefore, [the liberated self] is devoid of all pleasure and pain pertaining to sense-objects. This is established by inference. For it is said: "Verily, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12).
Thus, from scripture, it is established that at that time he is devoid of that [object];

nevertheless, even while knowing this, he still proceeds with a desire for it, just as a patient acts upon the administration of medicine according to the instruction of a physician— *Prajñālaṃkāra-vyākhyā*, folio 20b.

And for that embodied being—who, identifying "these external objects" as "mine," experiences pleasure and pain caused by the conjunction and disjunction with external objects—there is no removal, destruction, or cessation of those two which exist in a continuous stream.

However, when that [identification] is removed through the knowledge of one's true incorporeal nature, the lack of discriminative knowledge arising from the conceit of a body ceases; and being thus bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him.

The term "touches" (*spṛśati*) is connected with each [of the two]. Thus, there are two statements: "he does not touch what is pleasant" and "he does not touch what is unpleasant. For those two are the effects of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), whereas bodilessness (*aśarīratā*) is his very nature; since merit and demerit are impossible therein, the state of being their effect is all the more remote. Therefore, pleasure and pain do not touch him—this is quoted from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* Śāṅkara Bhāṣya (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 509).
Brahma-śānti-bhāṣya 1.1.4

Syādvādaratnākara folio 1110;
Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhasaṃgrahaṇī verse 52.
