The demonstration that liberation— following the counteraction of those [obstacles]— consists essentially of knowledge and other [virtues], being devoid of merit and demerit which cause worldly pleasure and pain in the state of bodilessness.
To this, the following reply is given:

As for what was stated—that [the series] is a continuum (*santāna*) and so forth—that is incorrect. For is it being proved that the continuum of the specific qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*), which are entirely distinct from the self (*ātman*), is subject to cessation; or [is it] those that are non-distinct, or those that are distinct in some respect? Regarding the first position, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); because it has already been demonstrated that those specific qualities of the self, being absolutely distinct from it, do not exist at all, the substratum—their continuum—is therefore unestablished.

Likewise, because you admit that they are not self-cognized, and because if they were cognizable by another cognition there would be the consequence of faults such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and because it is impossible for things to exist if they are not known—these reasons also render the self (*ātman*) unestablished as a substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Furthermore, if those [mental states] are in every way non-different from it, then in proving them, there follows the consequence of its own absolute annihilation; who then would possess this liberation? Moreover, a partial non-difference between them is not admitted by your opponents, as that would entail the fault of contradicting their own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Nevertheless, even if that [annihilation] were accepted, its annihilation in every respect would not be established, because in this way its non-annihilation in some respect (*kathañcit*) is also established (pṛ. 824, l. 1). For comparison: "Is it the continuum of qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) that are entirely different from the self, or those that are non-different, or those that are different in some respect (*kathañcit*), whose annihilation is being proved? — *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, pṛṣṭha 317: [The view that] the qualities such as cognition and so forth always belong to the Self (buddhyādiguṇānām).

Comparison: Likewise, since specific qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth are not admitted by the opponent to be self-cognized, or else—if they were graspable by another cognition—the faults of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the like would follow; thus, they are non-cognizable. Consequently, because their existence is not established when unperceived, the reason—namely, "being a continuum" (*santānatva*)—is once again unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
(Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 156; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p.
According to the Vaiśeṣika,
just as there are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of impure things, so too does the self possess them.

In some manner of differentiation, is the continuum (*santānatva*)—which is the probans—of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) or of a particular (*viśeṣa*)? If it is of the nature of a universal, then the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because such a universal, being entirely distinct from the individuals, has already been refuted in the "Examination of the Universal" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*).

Or, let us grant that it exists in that form; even so, would it be of the nature of a higher universal (*parasāmānya*) or of the nature of a lower universal (*aparasāmānya*)? In the first case, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to space (*ākāśa*) and the like, because the reason of "continuum"—which is synonymous with "existence" (*sattā*)—is present there even though there is no absolute cessation [of the series].

Now, as for the nature of a lower generality (*aparasāmānya*): since a genus (*jāti*) is dependent upon specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), [the property of] being a continuum (*santānatva*) would be such. In that case, because it is impossible in the lamp, which is a particular substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*), the example is deficient in its probans (*sādhanavikala*).

If "continuum-ness" intended as the reason is meant to be a generality, then—since no lower generality exists apart from the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) in the case of specific qualities like cognition and so forth, as well as in the lamp, which is a substance of light—the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).

Or, if the nature of being a continuum (*santānatva*) consists in the common form of existence (*sattāsāmānyarūpatva*), it would only be the cause for the cognition "it exists, it exists" (*satsad iti pratyaya*), and not the cause for the cognition of a "continuum" (*santāna*). — *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 156; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

Even so, in that [particular] form, there is existence here; yet, even in the absence of existence here, there is the supreme existence [of the universal]. Now, what is this specific form? Is it a specific form characterized by moments of cognition and so forth, which stand in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*), or is it merely a stream of preceding and succeeding moments of the same genus? In the first case, the nature of being a continuum (*santānatva*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) because of its lack of commonality, since this definition does not apply anywhere else.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with their own tenets (*abhyupagamavirodha*), because the Yogins do not accept the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) between the moments of cognition and so forth; otherwise, there would be no absolute cessation of that continuum, since even in the state of liberation (*muktāvasthā*), it would follow that subsequent moments of cognition and so forth must arise from preceding moments of cognition and so forth acting as material causes.

In the second alternative, however, there is an inconclusive instance (*anaikāntika*) due to the color and other qualities of atoms produced by heating (*pākaja-paramāṇu-rūpādi*); for although such a continuity exists in those cases, an absolute cessation is impossible.

Comparison: Does [the continuity of existence] consist in proceeding by way of a series of the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*), or proceeding by way of a series of the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), or merely the production of successive distinct entities? — *Ratnākarāvatārikā* 7.57; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 317.

Now, what is this "continuity" (santānatva)—is it independent, or merely the arising of successive distinct entities, or the arising of successive [entities] based on a single substratum? (*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
83). Is it an operation by way of the relation of cause and effect, or the arising of another [entity] based on a single locus? (*Nyāyasāraṭīkā*, p. 287).
The "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason] is that which is excluded from all similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
"But in that case, since such a thing does not occur elsewhere, it would be an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), and there would also be a contradiction with one's own tenet"—

Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the nature of a continuum (*santāna*), characterized as a flow of causal moments, is impossible under the absolute positions of either permanence or impermanence; for it has been demonstrated that the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) exists only in the case of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
Moreover, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because an absolute cessation of a lamp or similar object is impossible, since it persists in another form.

Nor does the admission that even an extinguished lamp persists in another form entail a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), for if that were so, it would follow by the same logic that fire situated in water must also possess its radiant form.

Now, since the sensation of heat is impossible in the absence of a luminous substance (tejas) which serves as the substratum for its radiant form, one might postulate that this [heat] exists there in an unmanifest state. If that is so, then even in the case of a lamp and the like, just as their production occurs without a [perceptible] material cause, one must likewise postulate the non-interruption of the ultimate continuum—given that existence, being produced, and other such properties would otherwise be untenable without the lamp serving as the basis for successive transformations from one final state to another. This is because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. The formal argument is as follows: a lamp and the like possess transformation characterized by the relinquishing of a prior nature and the acquisition of a subsequent nature while persisting, because they possess existence and other such properties, just like a cloth and the like.

Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*) is subject to a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*). For instance: the continuum of cognition and so forth does not possess absolute cessation, because such cessation is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Whatever is of such a nature is not to be accepted as real, just like the continuum of color and other qualities of atoms produced by heating (*pākaja*); and this [continuum of cognition] is likewise. Therefore, it does not possess absolute cessation.

Nor should it be argued that the property of "not being perceived by any means of valid cognition" is unestablished (*asiddha*), on the grounds that the cessation of the continuum is actually perceived through the very inference under discussion; for it has been demonstrated that this [inference] is not a valid inference due to its being corrupted by numerous fallacies.

The second alternative, however, is untenable; for if those [qualities] beyond the senses were absolutely ceased, no one whatsoever would engage in activity toward liberation.

For everyone seeking liberation acts solely out of a desire to attain unsurpassed happiness, knowledge, and so forth, and not out of a desire for the annihilation of all specific qualities such as cognition and the rest, because such annihilation is not desired by anyone. Indeed, no discerning person exerts effort toward the destruction of their own excellent qualities, since it is observed that one’s exertion is directed precisely toward their enhancement. For if, in the state of liberation, a person were to become like a fragment of stone, with even a trace of the experience of happiness vanished, then liberation would be of no use at all.
Let it be that we remain in saṃsāra itself, where there is even a slight experience of pleasure, despite its imperfections;

let this be considered: is the experience of a small amount of pleasure better, or is it the total eradication of all pleasure? Therefore, the desire of anyone to go toward a liberation conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas—which is characterized by the destruction of all qualities and is like a stone—is not logically tenable.

Furthermore, is the cessation being established for those qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) that are produced by the senses, or for those that are beyond the senses? However, those who proclaim the cessation of the two [qualities], namely tranquility-bliss (*praśamasukha*) and infinite knowledge (*anantajñāna*), which have the destruction of karma as their cause, are not sound, because it contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that in liberation there is the cessation of specific qualities such as cognition in some respects, while in other respects there is no cessation.

"Better would it be to desire the state of a jackal in the delightful Vṛndāvana than for Gautama to seek the specific liberation [of the Vaiśeṣikas]. Furthermore, regarding liberation, is the absence of specific qualities such as cognition due to the absence of their cause, their lack of purpose, or their contradiction? In the first case, which cause is absent there: the eyes and so forth, or the removal of their obstructors? If it is the eyes and so forth, then only the cognition and other qualities produced by them would be absent there, not others; thus, you are merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Now, one might object: "Since all cognition and so forth arise dependent upon a collection of causes such as merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), the body, and the sense organs, and since these would be impossible in their absence, how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established? This too is not sound; for it would entail the consequence that the knowledge and other attributes of Maheśvara do not exist.

To claim that this is no fault because his knowledge and so forth are eternal is an unexamined statement, as the eternality of that [knowledge] has already been refuted in the section on the rejection of Īśvara.

Therefore, even in the absence of the eyes and other sense organs, one must admit that for the Lord, knowledge and other qualities arise from the removal of obstructions. Likewise, this applies to the liberated souls as well, because they possess that same nature;
and it is not logical for that which possesses a certain nature to remain once that nature has disappeared, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If it is argued that for the liberated soul there is an absence of knowledge and so forth in liberation due to the lack of purpose—since he has accomplished all that was to be done—that is not so; for the very nature of the self, when freed from obstructions, is of such a character, and thus its being "without purpose" is unproven.

Furthermore, the fulfillment of one's purpose (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) for the self consists precisely in the attainment of distinguished qualities characterized by infinite knowledge and so forth, and not in the annihilation of all qualities; for even in the world, the usage of the term "one who has accomplished his purpose" is understood to refer only to the excellence of qualities.
Thus, [the claim that] liberation is [the destruction of qualities] is also untenable.

If it is argued that the non-cessation of those qualities belongs only to others and not to Him—since that [non-cessation] is the definition [of *saṃsāra*], and therefore the consequence of His being a transmigrator does not follow—this too is mere faith, because it involves following the logic of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*), for the unique nature of an entity is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

If, therefore, its non-cessation constitutes the characteristic of *saṃsāra*, then it would follow that wherever this [non-cessation] exists, there must be *saṃsāric* status; for this would be incompatible with the nature of one who is liberated. However, in the second case, our own position is established, because we accept that *saṃsāra* is the attainment of one existence after another due to the power of the karma acquired by oneself, and not for living beings other than Maheśvara.
Therefore, this characteristic of saṃsāra belongs to this Maheśvara.

What then? It belongs to one who possesses perfect right vision, knowledge, and conduct; enough with this dispute, for even as liberation while living arises from a cause consisting of these three, so too does supreme liberation arise from a cause consisting of these three. For the cause of saṃsāra consists of the triad beginning with false vision (mithyā-darśana); therefore, its remover must also consist of a triad, since it cannot be removed by a single form, such as right knowledge alone.

For right knowledge—accumulated through the correct vision of the essential nature of the self, which is distinct from erroneous attachment, and augmented by conduct characterized by the cessation of external and internal activities—is indeed threefold in nature and alone capable of preventing the arising of future karma and destroying accumulated karma; this is like the capacity of heat to prevent the arising of future cold touch and to destroy the cold touch already present (pṛ॰ 825, pa॰ 8). Although, during the state of saṃsāra, the Self does not manifest as the nature of supreme bliss because its true form is veiled by ignorance (avidyā), nevertheless, upon the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), it manifests by itself, through its own self-luminosity, as the very nature of supreme bliss—[Siddhāntabindu, p.
450]. Regarding the proof of the existence of eternal cognition and so forth in the state of liberation, the following is the rebuttal:

As for what was stated—that the self has happiness as its intrinsic nature (*sukhasvabhāva*)—in that regard, what is this so-called "having happiness as its intrinsic nature"? Is it the state of being connected with the universal (*jāti*) of happiness, or is it the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of happiness? It cannot be the state of being connected with the universal of happiness, because that [universal] exists only in a quality (*guṇa*); for no single universal is observed to be common to both substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), such as the self and happiness.

Nor can it be the locus of happiness, because one cannot escape the dilemma of whether that [happiness] is eternal or non-eternal. For if the self is the locus of that happiness, is that happiness eternal or non-eternal? It cannot first be non-eternal, because that would entail the non-eternality of the self as well, since it would possess that very nature. Indeed, it is not logical for that which possesses a certain nature to persist in the absence of that nature, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Now, if it is eternal, is it so in some respect (*kathañcit*) or in every respect (*sarvathā*)? If in some respect, then the Jaina doctrine is established; for the proponents of *syādvāda* accept that pleasure exists in the self as a modification (*paryāya*), which is eternal in its substantial form (*dravyataḥ*) but impermanent in its modal form (*paryāyataḥ*), characterized by occasional manifestation and concealment, just like the modifications of cognition and so forth (p. 831, l.

5). In that regard, if "having the nature of pleasure" means being connected with the universal (*jāti*) of "pleaseness" (*sukhatva*), that is not possible in the self, because this [quality] is observed only in a quality (*guṇa*).

For there is no other genus (jāti) commonly perceived in substances and qualities, such as [the genus] "I-consciousness" (ahaṅkāra) and so forth; nor is it the state of being the substratum of pleasure. That is not the case, because the dilemma of whether it is eternal or non-eternal is untenable—Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 20, line 8.
The reading "of being connected with the genus of pleasure" does not exist within this [text], as found in Ā and Śr,
because [pleasure] has the nature of impermanent pleasure.
One might object:

"If it is admitted that in liberation there is the manifestation of successive modifications such as pleasure and so forth, then their cause must be stated, for the manifestation of a modification cannot occur without a cause. This should not be held in the mind, because it has already been established previously that the self itself—when endowed with the removal of its obstructions—is the cause thereof.

For it is the very self, when endowed with the removal of karma such as delusion which obstructs happiness and so forth, that serves as the cause for such happiness, knowledge, and so on in the state of liberation. Just like a momentary lamp-flame that has been freed from the obstruction of a jar or similar object, if one asks: "In producing its own and others' illumination, what does that [lamp] depend upon at that time to generate them?", we reply: "It depends precisely upon the removal of those obstructions."

For one who has become such [a state], since it possesses the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of producing that [result], dependence on anything else at that time is untenable; for whatever has the inherent nature of producing something at a certain time does not depend on anything else for its production at that time, just as the final causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) in its final state does not depend on anything else for the production of its own effect. And so too, in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), the self (*ātman*), being endowed with the removal of obstacles to the production of supersensuous pleasure and the like, possesses the inherent nature of producing them.

For it is observed that even during the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), those who are like the axe and the sandalwood—equanimous toward all things and established in distinguished meditations and so forth—experience a supreme joy that is not produced by the activities of the sensory body and its organs.
This very experience, by virtue of successive distinctions in cultivation, attains higher and higher states until it reaches its ultimate limit; thus, everything is well-established.

Therefore, since there exists some cause for the manifestation of its modal transformation (*paryāya*) even in that state, one must admit that the modal transformation consisting of pleasure and so forth is in some sense impermanent.
In the state of liberation, by virtue of being the cause for the manifestation of states such as bliss.
Likewise, happiness for oneself and for others— Śrī.

—Indeed, at that time, for the production of that [experience], it is dependent on something else. For comparison: And an experience in the form of supreme bliss, which is not produced by the activity of the body and senses, is observed in one who seeks liberation (mumukṣu), who is like unto the axe and sandalwood [equanimous toward friend and foe], whose conduct is uniform toward all, and who is established in distinguished meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth; and for that very person, as they reach higher and higher stages through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even the attainment of the ultimate limit is possible. —*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 161. —[The term] "produced by activity" (*vyāpāra-janya*) is found in manuscript *ba*.
Due to the power of subsequent cultivation (*uttarabhāvanā*),
there is a successive [progression] from that;
therefore, at the time of that sound— *ā*.

Furthermore, since no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever exists that can apprehend its permanence—whether that apprehending *pramāṇa* be perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)? If it were perception, would it be sensory, mental (*mānasa*), or self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; because the senses have their range restricted to specific objects such as form and so forth, it is impossible for the perception arising from them to function toward anything other than those.
The second alternative is also untenable; because the mind, independent of the external senses, cannot possibly function with respect to anything at all.

If it is argued that because it is stated that "the external mind is not independent," its activity occurs only externally and not internally when it is independent of that [object], we say no; for even in that case, whether it is connected or unconnected, since its self-cognition is established, the denial of its capacity to produce cognition therein is refuted.
Thus, the third alternative is also untenable, as there is no such perception.

For in self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), there is no experience of a nature of bliss that is eternal, partless, and follows through the three times, with its entire collection of spatial and temporal divisions undivided; this is because it contradicts actual cognition. Therefore, perception does not in any way grasp eternal bliss, nor does inference; for there is no possible mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with its being eternal in every respect.

Nor is there scriptural authority (āgama); for even that [scripture] which purports to establish the permanence and bliss of the self is not perceived in any way. To illustrate: since there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the existence of the self's eternal bliss, direct perception (pratyakṣa)—first of all—does not have the power to establish this point for people like us or for anyone else; what then can be said of other [means of knowledge]?
Inference, too, is not possible, because not even a trace of a logical mark (liṅga) is observed—Nyāyamañjarī, p. 509.
Would its grasper be perception, inference, or scripture?—Syādvādaratnākara, p. 1115.
It should be observed— page 432, note 1—
that [this refers to] the mind independent of the external sense-faculties.
Even regarding internal pleasure and so forth, [the proof] of the mind...
page 185.

—[Objection: Let there be a collection of time-moments (*kālakalāpa*). Or, let us grant that for some reason there is a cognition of its permanence; nevertheless, is that from which that cognition arises permanent or impermanent? First, it cannot be impermanent, because it is contradictory for a permanent thing to arise from such [an impermanent source], and how could its production occur? For it is impossible for an impermanent thing to lack the property of being produced. Furthermore, if one accepts that it is produced from the sense organs and so forth, it does not follow that it has pleasure as its object, as was just stated.

Now, if it is argued that the conjunction of the self and the mind itself produces that [knowledge] by depending on *yogaja-dharma* (the merit born of yoga), one might ask: since *yogaja-dharma* is impossible in the state of liberation (*mukti*), how could that [conjunction] depend upon it such that its production would occur there from it? Or, if it is argued that the initial conjunction of the self and the mind produces knowledge by depending on *yogaja-dharma*, and that subsequent knowledge is produced by depending on that [initial knowledge], this too is incorrect, as it would entail the consequence of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

For it is not your established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) that knowledge independent of a connection with a body is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for the conjunction [of the self] in the production of that [knowledge]; rather, it is precisely that [conjunction] which depends upon it that is described as the auxiliary cause for its production in your final conclusion (*kṛtānta*). Because the experience of that eternal bliss arises from a specific cognition, that cognition must exist. To illustrate: Is that infinite bliss in liberation of a cognizable nature (*savedya-svabhāva*) or of an incognizable nature (*asavedya-svabhāva*)? If it is cognizable, then the establishment of that infinite cognition follows; otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding the self-cognizability of infinite bliss.

If, on the other hand, that [bliss] were indeed imperceptible, then how could it be called "happiness"? For happiness is recognized as such only through the perception of a pleasant sensation (*sātasaṃvedana*)—*Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, p. 69.
Is that bliss experienced in liberation or not? If it is not experienced, then even though it exists, it does not differ from what does not exist, because it cannot be enjoyed.
If it is experienced, then the cause of that experience must be stated—*Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

286. If it is argued that eternal happiness is manifested, what is the meaning of "manifestation"? If it is "cognition," then the conceptualization of it as either eternal or non-eternal is untenable—*Nyāyavārttika*, p. 85.
Or let there be some such grasper; nevertheless, is it eternal or non-eternal? [Sya° Ra° p.
1116] Because it is experienced as non-eternal, its eternity is not perceived—[Ba°].
The statement of the reason for impermanence— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.22.

Regarding the acceptance of the arising of sensation, the comparison is as follows: the cause of the conjunction of the self and the mind is [the presence of] merit (*dharma*) along with other auxiliary causes; this is the statement of the cause of merit.

If merit is an auxiliary cause, then its own cause must be stated—that from which it arises? Since merit born of yogic concentration is opposed to the cessation of its effects, when it is exhausted, sensation ceases entirely. If merit born of yogic concentration were the cause, then upon its exhaustion—due to the opposition between that merit and its effects—sensation would be absolutely eliminated.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.22
Nyāyavārttika, page 85;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, page 240:
by means of the conjunction of the self and the mind.
In liberation, knowledge arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, which depends upon dharma produced by yoga.

Comparison: [The opponent might argue that] consciousness arises from the first consciousness produced by the contact with merit (*dharma*), and a subsequent consciousness arises from that, and so on, forming a continuum (*santāna*). This is not correct, because there is no proof for it.

Furthermore, it is not observed that consciousness itself—without depending on a connection to a body—is the required cause for the contact between the self (*ātman*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 20, Ga. edition.
Now, that conjunction produces primordial knowledge, depending upon the dharma born of yoga; [Syādvādamañjarī, p.
1116] "primordial yoga" (ādyayoga) refers to knowledge which has become the object of action (karmabhūta).
The first cognition is the conjunction of the self and the mind;
[it arises from] the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Cognition dependent on a relation; cognition dependent on another relation;
[this refers to] the conjunction of the self and the mind, which depends precisely upon its connection with the body.

If the conjunction of the self and the mind were eternal, then it would follow that there is no distinction between the states of liberation and non-liberation; for since pleasure and its perception are eternal, they would exist identically in both states,
and because this [pleasure] is experienced in association with sense-born pleasure during the state of transmigratory existence, there would be the perception of two types of pleasure simultaneously.

If it is argued that its non-perception at that time is due to its being obstructed, by what is it obstructed—is it by the body, by ignorance (*avidyā*), by the experience of sensual pleasures and the like, or by attachment to external objects? It cannot be by the body, because since the body is the means for achieving pleasure, it is impossible for it to be an obstruction;
for that which serves a particular purpose cannot be an obstruction to that very thing, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument.
Indeed, an obstruction is defined as that which hinders the production of an effect.
Furthermore, the body is not an obstacle to pleasure, because pleasure arises only when the body exists.

That in the presence of which something else comes into being cannot be an impediment to it, just as a seed is not an impediment to its sprout. Since pleasure arises only when the body exists, the body cannot be its obstacle; if it were, then the act of harming one who destroys that obstacle would not result in the fruit of violence, for in common worldly experience, that which removes an impediment is known to be beneficial.
Nor can it be through ignorance (*avidyā*); for, being of a void nature (*tuccharūpa*), it is impossible for it to possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) characterized by obstruction.
Whatever is of a void nature is not causally efficient, just like the water of a mirage, and ignorance has been accepted by you as being of a void nature.
Furthermore, the obstructive capacity of ignorance has already been refuted at length in the section on the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaitapraghaṭṭaka*); so enough with this further digression.

Nor [can it be established] through the experience of worldly pleasure and the like; for by that, an obstruction—characterized either as non-arising or as destruction—of eternal bliss or its experience would not be logical, since both are admitted to be eternal.

Nor can it be due to attachment to external objects; for by that, would there be an obstruction to the knower (*pramātṛ*) or to its adjuncts such as the sense organs? Both of these positions are untenable. For the "attachment" of the self, the knower, consists in the non-arising of cognition regarding another object while a cognition is arising regarding an object such as color; and the non-production of cognition regarding another object when a sense organ is engaged in producing a cognition regarding one object is also impossible here, because—just like pleasure—that cognition [of the self] exists at all times.

Comparison: If it is argued that pleasure is eternal, then there would be no distinction between one situated in saṃsāra and one who is liberated. Furthermore, if this were admitted, the coexistence and simultaneity with the fruits of dharma and adharma would have to be accepted—that is, the fact that the fruit of dharma or adharma, whether pleasure or pain, is experienced alternately in various places of birth, and the simultaneous occurrence of that [alternating experience] with an eternally existing consciousness of pleasure would have to be accepted;
for there would be neither an absence of pleasure nor a lack of its manifestation, since both would be eternal.
(Nyāyabhāṣya, Book 1)
And consequently, the accompaniment of this eternal happiness by pleasure and pain— the fruits of merit and demerit— would be experienced.
—Nyāyamañjarī, p.
510; Syādvādaratnākara, p. 1116: [of] eternal happiness.

In the state of saṃsāra, by what is its bondage [to the body] determined—is it by the body, by ignorance (avidyā), by the experience of sensory pleasures and the like, or by attachment to external objects? —Syādvādaratnākara, p. 1116;
[regarding] the body.

Objection: The connection with the body and so forth is the cause of obstruction [to the experience of eternal bliss]. Response: No, because the body and so forth exist for the purpose of experience (*upabhoga*), and there is no inference to the contrary. It might be thought: "The connection with the body and so forth for one in the state of *saṃsāra* is an obstructer of the cause for the experience of eternal bliss; therefore, there is no lack of distinction [between the liberated and the bound]. This is incorrect. The body and so forth are for the purpose of experience; it is illogical that they would act as an obstruction to experience. Furthermore, there is no inference that a bodiless self possesses any experience whatsoever.
— Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.22
Nyāyavārttika, page 86;
Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, page 240;
Nyāyamañjarī, page 510.
An obstacle is defined as that which causes the obstruction of an effect; however, the non-arising of eternal bliss is not possible—[as stated in] Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 20, line 8:
"of the body."
The fruit of violence would not belong to one who removes that [obstacle] by way of being an impediment;
for it is observed that one who destroys an impediment is indeed a benefactor.
Indeed, there is no absence of the fruit of violence for one who destroys the body and so forth, which are impediments to the experience of eternal bliss—enough of this.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

20; Gaṅgeśa, Syādvādamañjarī, p. 1117: Because it is impossible for light to be obscured by that which is insubstantial (tuccha), even clouds are distinct from the sun and are real in their own nature.
"But that which is inconceivable as being either identical to or different from reality is not capable of veiling through ignorance" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
Because of the connection between eternal bliss and its experience, [there is] the predominance of that;
for since experience itself is eternal in the case of eternal bliss, distraction is impossible.

For instance, when the self produces a cognition of an object such as color, the non-production of a cognition regarding another object is indeed "inattention" (vyāsaṅga); likewise, when a sense faculty is engaged in producing a cognition of one object, its failure to produce a cognition of another object is "inattention.

However, this is not the case for the self: when it produces a cognition of an object such as color, there is no non-production of a cognition regarding eternal pleasure, because that cognition [of pleasure] is also eternal.

Furthermore, just as in the state of liberation (*muktyavasthā*) that which is eternal is postulated by transcending impermanent pleasure and knowledge, so too should the body, the senses, and so forth—which serve as the substrata for the property of eternity—be postulated, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. [Objection:

But how could the body, which is an effect of merit (*dharma*) and so forth, exist in the absence of those [merit and demerit], given the contradiction with empirical experience (*pratīti*)? [Reply: That is the same in the other case as well.

If it is argued that there is no fault because that bliss is distinct from the bliss of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), then the body too must be distinct from the body of worldly existence; for in that case, there would be no distinction [between them]. Furthermore, the transgression of what is observed is equal in the case of the body and so forth:

just as one abandons observed impermanent pleasure and desires eternal pleasure, so too, having transcended the observed impermanent body, senses, and intellect, one must postulate eternal body, senses, and intellect for the liberated one.
— Nyāyabhāṣya, Vārttika, Tātparyaṭīkā 1.1.22.
Just as pleasure and knowledge, so too should his body, sense organs, and so forth be conceived as eternal; in this way, liberation would become more delightful—*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 510.

Furthermore, if knowledge were admitted to exist in liberation like pleasure, then since the capacity for that [knowledge]—characterized by the cessation of contrary obsession—and for *darśana* would be established by their inherent efficacy, the attainment of liberation characterized by the acquisition of the nature of the four infinites (*ananta-catuṣṭaya*) would result, thereby establishing the Jaina doctrine through the abandonment of the absolute [monism] that "bliss is the form of Brahman. *Note on variants:* – *ba*: karaṇadehendri–; *ā*: tadbhāve tatra; *ba*: tadabhāve tata prasave tatra. *kiñca*, *sukhavat*, *jñānasya*, *muktāvabhyupagame*, *tacchakteḥ*, *viparītābhiniveśanivṛttilakṣaṇadarśanasya*, *sāmarthyasiddhatvāt*, *anantacatuṣṭayasvarūpalābhalakṣaṇamokṣaprasiddheḥ*, *jainamatasiddhiḥ*, *syāt*, *ānandaṃ brahmaṇo rūpam*, *ekāntatyāgāt*.
Therefore, the probandum characterized by having happiness as its intrinsic nature does not hold in your system when examined,
because it involves the abandonment of infinite power (*ananta-śakti*), which is employed for the maintenance of infinite knowledge (*ananta-jñāna*). (Śrīmad-bhāṣya)

Furthermore, the two reasons—that it is the object of the notion of being extremely dear and that it is appropriated for its own sake and not for the sake of anything else—are non-conclusive and thus not valid proofs; for they exist even in the case of the absence of suffering.

Moreover, the quality of being appropriated for its own sake and not for the sake of anything else is unestablished (*asiddha*); for the self is not appropriated for the sake of something else, since it is appropriated for the sake of pleasure and so forth.
Likewise, the quality of being the object of the notion of being extremely dear is also unestablished; for even when one is in pain, there still exists the notion that [the self] is not dear.

The fact that [pleasure] is not apprehended for the sake of anything else is unproven, because it exists even in the absence of suffering; its being the object of an absolutely dear cognition is also unproven, because it is apprehended for the sake of pleasure; and the fact that it is the object of a cognition of "unpleasant" when one is in pain is also unproven, because a cognition of "unpleasant" also occurs toward suffering itself.
—[Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā, p. 20, Ga.

As for what was stated: "The self has happiness as its intrinsic nature, because, while being a real entity, it is the object of the primary notion of 'dear'"; that too is refuted by this [very argument]. If it had happiness as its intrinsic nature, then all the defects previously mentioned would follow as consequences; thus, its being the object of the notion of 'dear' and its being denotable by the term 'dear' in its primary sense are unestablished, since that [notion] is absent when [the self] is occasionally suffering.

And it is also "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*). For while there might be an absolute absence of suffering for the self in liberation, those two means [of attainment] do not have happiness as their intrinsic nature;
thus, they are contradictory, because what is established here is precisely the nature of the absence of suffering, which is the opposite of having happiness as its intrinsic nature.

To explain: this self consists of the absence of suffering, because, while being a real entity, it is the object of the primary notion of "dearest," or because it is denoted by the term "dearest" in its primary sense, just like the absence of sensual suffering for those possessed of passion.
pṛ॰ 831 paṃ॰ 6 –In the *ciducitā*,
[this is] because of the absence of the state of being beloved (*preyastva*).

Regarding what was stated—that "the effort of those seeking liberation is for the sake of a desired object," and so forth—that too is unsound, because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), due to the non-existence of the nature of pleasure (*sukhasvabhāva*). *Note on variants:* Regarding the phrase *sukhasvabhāvaviparyayābhāvād iti*, the reading *viparyayābhāvād iti* is found in manuscript Ā, while *viparyayābhāvād iti* is found in manuscript Ba. The meaning remains consistent: because there is no absence of the opposite (i.e., the presence) of the nature of pleasure.

For the effort of discerning people is not directed solely toward the accomplishment of a desired object, since effort is observed even on the part of those afflicted by specific diseases for the sake of the cessation of what is undesired—as it has been said regarding those seeking liberation (mumukṣu)—Ā.,—"regarding the desired object for those seeking liberation"—Ba., p.
Objection: Activity is for the sake of attaining what is desired. Reply: No; because it is for the sake of ceasing what is undesired—Nyāyabhāṣya, Book 1, Chapter 1.

22. For it is observed that even the virtuous, when afflicted by disease, strive for the cessation of what is undesirable, since the ultimate purpose is not merely the cessation of what is undesirable.

"Furthermore, since this burden of the suffering of saṃsāra is exceedingly difficult to bear, those who strive for its cessation do not exert themselves without purpose; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive. — Nyāyamañjarī, p. 509.

Furthermore, what is denoted here by the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*): is it happiness, or merely whatever object is intended? If it is merely whatever object is intended, how could the soul's nature as happiness be established from this? Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous establishment of numerous mutually contradictory forms of liberation, since even for seekers of liberation who follow the doctrines of Kapila and others, their exertion would result in the attainment of that specific object of desire characterized as their particular liberation.

If it is argued that because effort (*prayatna*) is qualified by the term "possessing discernment" (*prekṣāvat*), there is no establishment of multiple contradictory exclusions (*apavarga*), we say: no. This is because such a distinction cannot be made. Indeed, it is impossible to distinguish between those who follow your own doctrine and those who follow the doctrines of Kapila and others by saying, "these are discerning, while those are not. For, by accepting a reality whose nature is entirely eternal and so forth—a position subverted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—all [the opponents] are established as lacking discernment. Furthermore, if "pleasure" (*sukha*) is expressed by the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*), then the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

Indeed, the effort of farmers and others toward agriculture and so forth does not have happiness as its direct purpose, because that effort is for the sake of accomplishing the fruits of agriculture and the like. If it is argued that since that [effort] has happiness as its purpose only through a mediated succession (*paramparayā*), then let the effort of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) likewise have that same purpose [only mediately].

But surely, if those seeking liberation do not have an effort aimed at happiness as its direct purpose, then their effort would be entirely purposeless, since no other purpose to be accomplished by it is possible. This too is unsound; for there exists a purpose to be accomplished by that effort, namely the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra.
For this burden of the suffering of saṃsāra is indeed difficult to endure; therefore, those who strive for its destruction cannot be said to be making a fruitless effort—
[as established by] the *āgama* following the [scriptural] tradition,
and not contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That [arises] from that;
then, from that, through a succession.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "the gradation of pleasure, which results from the effort of one seeking liberation, must eventually find its rest somewhere," that too is a mere assertion; for it is inconclusive due to [the case of] "remoteness" (*paratva*) and so on.

Indeed, the excellence of "remoteness" and the like, which is attained through the progressive intensification of the cognitions of "remote," "less remote," and so forth, is what is denoted by the term "gradation," yet it does not come to rest anywhere.

Nor is there anything [to prevent this], for even in the case of suffering, the same consequence of reaching a supreme limit follows: the gradation of suffering must rest upon some point, because it is denoted by the term "gradation," just like the gradation of magnitude;
yet a supreme limit of suffering is not accepted by you. Thus, by this argument as well, [your reason] is inconclusive.
Regarding the gradation of suffering (*duḥkha-tāratamya*)—

as for the scriptural authority such as "Bliss is the nature of Brahman" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo rūpam*) which is cited as proof for the soul’s nature as happiness in liberation (*mokṣa*), that is utterly inconsistent; for its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is impossible.
For the authority of a statement indeed depends upon its being spoken by a virtuous speaker,
yet you do not accept this for the Veda,
since you maintain its authority is due to its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*); this too is mere faith, because that authorlessness has already been refuted.

Or, let it be granted that this [scripture] possesses such authority; nevertheless, just as it establishes that the Self is of the nature of bliss in liberation, so too does it establish its absence: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12).
Because of such statements as these, the "tiger-on-the-cliff" logic has befallen you: "Where, then, is its authority?"

Now, if this scriptural statement is explained otherwise—namely, that because of the context of "one who possesses a body," pleasure and pain belonging to transmigratory existence, which arise from the perception of agreeable and disagreeable objects, do not touch the bodiless Self in liberation—that too is a mere fantasy, for it is equally easy to explain the passage "Brahman is bliss" in another way; for here the word "bliss" (ānanda) refers to the absolute absence of the suffering of saṃsāra, and not to the subject of ordinary happiness.

Furthermore, the application of the word "pleasure" (sukha) is observed in the absence of suffering; for example, when one burdened by weight or afflicted by long-standing diseases such as fever or headache is freed from them, those who were long distressed by that suffering perceive it as a manifestation within themselves, thinking, "We are happy today.
(Page 831, Line 11) — [The reading] *kartṛtvena* is found in Ā and Śrā.
Page 724:
This might be so if this were the only scriptural statement heard; however, another statement is also heard: "Verily, no.

Indeed, the scriptural statement you have cited can also be explained otherwise: because of the introductory phrase "of one who possesses a body," the meaning is that while worldly pleasure and pain—resulting from the perception of agreeable and disagreeable objects—are possible, at that time [of liberation], they do not touch the bodiless Self.

Well then, Ānanda, even the Vedic statement you have studied— that "Brahman is bliss"— will be explained as referring to the removal of suffering precisely because it occurs within a section concerning the method for avoiding the suffering of saṃsāra;
for indeed, there is no subject beyond the Lord's capacity for explanation,
and we observe the use of the word "bliss" (sukha) in reference to the cessation of suffering.
Afflicted by the suffering of diseases such as chronic fever and headaches, they strive for their removal, thinking, "We are happy today"—
*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 509.
There is a precipice ahead, and my family is dear to me; you too, O friend, are dear. What shall I do? My mind is divided: on one side is the tiger, on the other is the riverbank.
— Pariśiṣṭa 3.166;
Laukikanyāya-tṛtīya-bhāga.
"On this side is the riverbank, on that side is a tiger; what recourse can there be for a living being?
(Yaśastilaka Udayasundara, p. 138).
[The word] "samāyātaḥ" (arrived) is not in manuscript Śra.
The statement beginning with "na havai" (it does not exist),
on page 831, line 8,
involves no contradiction even with the scriptures, because the term "happiness" is used in reference to the absolute absence of the suffering of saṃsāra.

Even if there were some scripture stating that "the liberated one has ultimate happiness," this would be logically consistent because the word "happiness" is employed to denote the absolute absence of suffering;
for the use of the word "happiness" in reference to the absence of suffering is frequently observed in common worldly usage.
— Nyāyabhāṣya, Book 1, Chapter 1, Sūtra 22.
For since an obstacle arises to its primary sense, it is used in a figurative sense;
thus, this word "bliss" (ānanda) is seen to be applied to the absence of suffering,
just as the word "pleasure" (sukha) is applied to the absence of suffering, as in the case of a porter burdened by a load when that load is removed.

Regarding what was stated [in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā*, folio 20, Gaṅgeśa]: "Because eternal bliss is unmanifest due to being veiled during the state of saṃsāra, it is not perceived," and so forth—that too is mere words. This is because the status of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like as its veil is refuted, and because it is impossible for a self that is eternally of a single nature and self-luminous to be veiled. Indeed, the veiling of an entity is only logical if it is subject to modification (*pariṇāmin*), since it would involve the abandonment of an unveiled form and the assumption of a veiled form in some respect.
Therefore, it must be understood that in liberation the self possesses, in some sense, the nature of eternal knowledge and so forth; thus [it is stated] on page 832, line 2.

"Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, its manifestation [is possible]"— this is the Buddhist's prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that liberation consists in the arising of pure cognition through the cultivation of selflessness (nairātmya).

Now, since no other self (ātman) is possible apart from the stream of momentary cognitions existing in the relation of cause and effect, for whom could the nature of cognition and so forth be established in liberation? Furthermore, liberation is utterly excluded for one who perceives a self.

For one who perceives the self as having a stable and other such forms, affection for the self—caused by the perception of qualities such as stability—is inevitable. And from affection for the self, being intensely thirsty for the pleasures of the self, one disregards the defects in those pleasures and their means, and instead superimposes qualities upon them. Seeing qualities and being intensely thirsty, one appropriates the means to pleasure, thinking "this is mine. Therefore, as long as there is the perception of a self, there is only saṃsāra;
as it has been said: [the self is] the agent... [Āptamīmāṃsā].
He who perceives a self develops a permanent attachment toward it, thinking "I am this. From that attachment, he craves pleasures; and through craving, he conceals his own faults.

He who perceives a self within that [body] develops a permanent and indestructible affection for it, thinking "I am this. Due to that affection, he craves pleasures; being possessed by craving, he disregards and conceals the defects—such as impurity and so forth—of those objects determined to be means of pleasure. By concealing these defects, seeing only their qualities, perceiving purity and desirability, and becoming intensely thirsty for them, he becomes greedy, thinking "this is mine" and "this is my pleasure," and thus takes up the means of that pleasure, such as entering the womb and so forth.

Because it is rooted in the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*), as long as there is attachment to a self regarding birth and so forth, for that long one is a "viewer of a self" and remains in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—not merely a continuity of births, but also all its defects are present. Thus he says:

when there is a self, there arises the notion of "other" (*parasaṃjñā*) and the cognition of "other" (*parabuddhi*) with respect to what is different from it; consequently, there arise, respectively, grasping (*parigraha*) and attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) toward oneself, and aversion (*dveṣa*) and rejection toward the other.
All faults—attachment, envy, jealousy, and so forth—are produced as bound up with these two: attraction and repulsion.
(These [quotations] were extracted from the *Pramāṇavārttika* and the *Manorathanandin-ṭīkā*: see *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā*, p. 492.)
*Anekāntajaya* pṛ. 28; *Yaśastilaka Upaniṣad* pṛ. 252; *Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa* pṛ. 581A.
"He who perceives the self, for him [the realization] occurs within the self" (Siddhiviṣṭara-ṭīkā, p. 55B). *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* (Bṛhatī), verse 52; *Jñānavimśikā*, p. 147A.
When there is a self—one is satisfied (Abhidharmālokā p. 67; Praśastapādabhāṣya p. 279).

Seeing qualities and thirsting for them, one grasps at the means of happiness with the thought "this is mine. As long as there is this attachment to a self, so long is there cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
While there is a self, there is the notion of "other"; from the division of self and other arise grasping and aversion. All faults are produced when bound by these two.

Therefore, one who desires liberation should contemplate their own nature, as well as sons, wife, and so forth, through the cultivation born of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*), [realizing them to be] non-self, impermanent, impure, and suffering. For one who contemplates in this way, because of the absence of attachment toward those things, detachment (*vairāgya*) arises through the excellence of practice; consequently, liberation—characterized by the cessation of *saṃsāra*, which is defined as the continuum of the mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)—is attained.

For since there is an adherence to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*) through the superimposition of unity upon momentary mental states (*cittakṣaṇa*) which perish without leaving a trace, the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantāna*)—designated as a "living being" and accompanied by love for a self—is set in motion toward the means of achieving worldly happiness, thereby perpetuating the stream of the contaminated mind (*sāsravacittasantāna*).

Therefore, an effort characterized by the practice of selflessness (*nairātmyābhyāsa*) and so forth must be made in order to eliminate this adherence to the unreal; for even though there is no self that is eternal, partless, or an agent of liberation, it has been said:

In that regard, the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*)—which arises from the statements of inference-for-others (*parārthānumāna*) being heard, and which attains the designation "heard" (*śruta*) as it reaches its highest excellence—is brought forth by reflection (*cintā*) characterized as inference-for-oneself (*svārthānumāna*). This gives rise to the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintamayī*), which then initiates meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is passion (*rāga*). (Āptapāda-kārikā 83ab)

In this context, ignorance and the other factors are considered to exist in the relationship of cause and effect; bondage is held to be their presence, while liberation is desired as the cessation thereof, which is the stainlessness of the intellect.
As it has been said: "The mind itself, when permeated by the afflictions such as attachment and so forth, is indeed saṃsāra."

That very [state], when liberated from those [characteristics], is called the "end of existence" (*bhavānta*)—*Tattvasaṃgraha*, Pañjikā, p. 184; in the section on the characteristics of the mind, Śrī.
—conformity; prā—ba; regarding validity; śra—ba;
because of this—nai—ba.
Therefore, O seekers of liberation, uproot the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi), which has its seed in a homogeneous stream of existence that is beginningless— *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.176.

Furthermore, what is this so-called "selflessness" (nairātmya), which is not to be taught when [the listener] is non-existent, but is to be taught when they exist? It is said: Selflessness is called the unique door to peace, terrifying to those with wrong views, and the objective domain of all Buddhas.
In this context, "self" (ātman) refers to that which has a nature and essence independent of anything else; the absence of that is selflessness (nairātmya).
And this is established as twofold through the distinction between phenomena (dharma) and the person (pudgala):
namely, the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and the selflessness of the person (pudgalanairātmya).
In this context, a "person" (*pudgala*) is that which is designated in dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*); yet, when sought in five ways within those aggregates, it is not found.

On the other hand, "phenomena" (*dharma*) are the entities designated by the terms aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Since both these phenomena and the person have their arising dependent on their respective causes and conditions, and are designated in dependence [upon parts], they lack any form that is independent, not derived from others, innate, or unconditioned. Thus, the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) is established for both the person and the phenomena.
Furthermore, for that object whose own nature (*svarūpa*) is not established, by what other essence could it possibly be established?

Therefore, entities whose characteristics are entirely unestablished exist either through being perceived or grasped by an incoherent self on the part of foolish people, and thus become objects of attachment for those of deluded intellect.
However, when dharmas and *pudgalas* are correctly contemplated according to their true nature by those with right vision (*samyagdarśana*), they lead to the complete destruction of attachment.

The complete destruction of attachment is the cause for attaining nirvāṇa; for one who has realized selflessness and whose attachment to all things has been utterly destroyed, there is no longing whatsoever for anything, so how could there be the perception of signs? Thus, this selflessness alone is the peerless gateway to the auspicious. (p. 151) It is only for one who possesses the conviction that "selflessness is the reality" that [liberation occurs].
"From its existence, whence can there be joy? From its non-existence, whence can there be fear? — *Catuḥśataka*, p. 151, 156; *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 866.
From whatever source fear may arise, if there is indeed nothing at all, and if I myself am nothing, to whom will fear belong? — *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 9.26.

The cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmyabhāvanā*)—the cultivation, that is, the repeated practice, of selflessness which is the absence of a person (*pudgala*) and so forth—is "excellent," meaning supreme, because it is the cause for the cessation of the egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) that functions through the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*).
For, by reaching the ultimate limit of the excellence of that cultivation, one directly perceives selflessness, and thereby the opposing view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is turned back.
And upon the cessation of that [notion of continuity], because no single persisting entity is observed, there is only the observation of a mere moment devoid of prior and subsequent forms.

Consequently, due to the absence of superimposing a "prior" and "subsequent" onto it, one does not perceive anything belonging to oneself as a means for future happiness; thus, attachment toward any object does not arise in him, nor does aversion toward its opposite, precisely because of the absence of clinging.
Furthermore, he does not perceive a person who causes harm as an occasion for retaliation, since both [the harmer and the harmed] lack a second moment of existence.
Furthermore, it is not fitting for a discerning person to seek vengeance against one party when the harm was committed by another; nor is it fitting for the perpetrator himself to do so,
since once passion and the like have ceased, other afflictions and secondary afflictions arising from them no longer arise,
and in reality, no one ever inflicts harm upon anyone else.

Or rather, it is from seeing dependent origination—that "this arising, that arises"—that the view of a self-identity ceases through the emptiness of the person; and because its root has been severed, the afflictions no longer manifest, as it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*: "Śāntamati, it is just as when the root of a tree is cut, all its branches, leaves, and foliage wither."

In the same way, Śāntamati, through the pacification of the view of a self-identity, all afflictions are pacified; therefore, the cultivation of selflessness is superior—Bodhicaryāvatāra, Chapter 9, p. 492–93.

"The effort for the sake of abandoning false superimposition— characterized by [the realization of] selflessness and so forth— is [necessary], even though there is no liberator," as stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.194. (See *Nairātmyapariccheda*, folio 12).
Effort is exerted for the sake of abandoning false superimposition—the determination that one is a transmigrating being—even though there is no such thing as a "liberated self" or the like;
for worldly convention follows not only the actual state of things, but also the determination [of them].
Thus, even a rope becomes an object of avoidance when it is the object of the determination that it is a snake.
"In this way, through the superimposition that 'I alone am bound' and 'I alone shall be liberated,' one exerts effort for the sake of liberation"—
this [verse] was extracted from the *Pramāṇavārttika* (and the *Manorathanandin-vṛtti*), as cited in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 183.
Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 321; Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, pp.
162, 418—[reading] *dhyānop-* [in place of] *śra*.

However, in the absence of effort characterized by the practice of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth, because the clinging to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*) does not cease, and because it is impossible to prevent the notion of "mine" (*ātmīyabuddhi*) regarding the sense faculties and other factors—which are grasped as the basis for experience—dispassion (*vairāgya*) cannot arise; thus, liberation is effectively offered a funeral libation.
As it has been said: [the verse beginning with] *ṇaprayatnā*... [Śloka-vārttika, Ātma-vāda 16].
When the sense organs and so forth have been grasped as the basis for experience,
the abandonment [of attachment] occurs here through the loss of the notion of "mine" regarding them, but not otherwise.
Because they serve as the basis for experience, the notion of "mine" regarding them is abandoned; however, this is not the case in the opposite situation, where the notion of "mine" still exists.

For when the senses and other factors are apprehended as the basis—that is, as the cause—of experience, by what reason could the cognition of ownership, the thought of "mineness," be warded off? Since it is warded off by someone, how then can there be detachment toward those very instruments of experience which constitute one's own body, such that they might be renounced?

Therefore, that which is abandoned is so only through the loss of the notion of "mine," and there is no such loss of the notion of "mine" regarding affection and the like, by which this [affection] could be abandoned—
*Pramāṇavārttika*, Manorathanandin’s Commentary.
This has been cited—*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p.
581B: "By whom could the cognition of ownership be warded off? Whence indeed would there be detachment from that? [The reading *khalvadhī* is noted as a variant for *svatvadhī*.]
Thus, it does not exist.

Now, it might be argued: "This affection for what belongs to oneself (*ātmīyasneha*) does not arise from the notion of ownership (*svatvabuddhi*) based on the perception of the senses and so forth as the locus of enjoyment—which would lead to this fault—but rather it is based on the perception of their qualities (*guṇadarśana*). Therefore, since that [affection] ceases upon perceiving the defects which are contrary to those qualities, the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*) and liberation (*mukti*) is possible. This is incorrect, because this [affection] arises precisely from the notion of ownership based on that [perception of qualities]; for even among children, cattle, and the like, who lack the examination of qualities and defects regarding their own eyes and other organs, affection manifests there due to the notion of ownership based on the perception of them as the locus of enjoyment.

Furthermore, since this [affection] exists even when one perceives defects such as being wrinkled, blind, or lame in those things considered "one's own," yet it does not exist even when perceiving virtues in things belonging to others;

and since affection is absent even toward one's own past limbs or those fallen from one's body despite seeing virtues in them once the notion of "mine" has been abandoned—it must be admitted that this [affection] arises solely from the notion of ownership (*svatva*) based upon that [notion of "mine"].
Therefore, it is appropriate to practice the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth in order to exclude that [notion].
[The objection that] it is unreasonable [to say] "because of the existence of sentient beings" (nibandhanasattvabu) is not correct; rather,
[the reason is] because they are the means for the attainment of enjoyments (bhogasādhanatvanibandhana).
Because of its absence, [there is] the absence of affection for the intellect which is the basis [of the self].
— Even upon seeing this, there is non-existence— Śrī.
Affection is based on its being the locus of experience.

Now, one might argue that even in the absence of such cultivation (*bhāvanā*), liberation will occur through the total exhaustion of all karma by means of austerity (*tapas*) characterized by bodily mortification; but that is not so. Since bodily mortification is itself a fruit of karma—just like the physical torment experienced by those in the hells—it cannot properly be considered austerity. Furthermore, karma possesses diverse potencies because it is otherwise inexplicable that it yields such diverse fruits; how then could that [karma] be exhausted merely by the torment of the body? For if it were so, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

Now, if it is argued that because austerity (*tapas*) is by nature destructive through the intermingling (*saṅkara*) of the powers of various actions, the destruction of action occurs even from a single form of austerity which possesses diverse powers—[we reply: in that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that even a single fast (*upavāsa*) or similar minor affliction would destroy all action without remainder, since the intermingling of powers could not otherwise be accounted for. And it has been said:
"Now, this state... (*atha-etad-bhāva-*) [Śrāvakaprajñapti].
Through austerity, there is both shedding and the destruction of karma— Tattvārthasūtra 9.3. — ba.

Furthermore, because a diversity of fruits is observed, a difference in the potencies of actions is inferred; therefore, there is no exhaustion of actions through the affliction of asceticism, as that is of a single form. Because a variety of fruits is seen—namely, a manifold manner of experiencing pleasure and pain accomplished by various instruments to be enjoyed across diverse states of existence—a difference in potency, that is, a plurality of capacities, is inferred. Thus, due to this cause—the capacity to produce fruits of many kinds—there is no exhaustion of actions through a single form of fruit, such as the affliction of asceticism.
— Pramāṇavārttika 1.277:
"Moreover, even if [it were possible] through the power of asceticism, by means of the mixing or the destruction of powers..."

One might be deprived of [the fruits of] all actions due to some affliction (*kleśa*), provided there is not even a trace of affliction remaining; yet, through the power of austerity (*tapas*), by means of a blending of powers that results solely in the exhaustion of the heat of affliction, those [actions] are exhausted—
either through the power of austerity or through the destruction of karma— and thus there is an absence of rebirth.

And whatever [karma] is undifferentiated is exhausted through some affliction, such as the plucking out of hair; and from the exhaustion of karma, liberation occurs. To this, he replies: "It would be lost entirely without even a trace of affliction. If the exhaustion of karma were achieved through austerity, then all karma would be lost without affliction—that is, without the suffering of plucking out hair and so forth—because karma would have been exhausted.

Just as the suffering of hell-beings and the like does not occur, so too even the slightest [suffering] should not exist; for even if there were a confusion of capacities, karma would be exhausted through mere slight distress and affliction, and the continuity of saṃsāra—which entails further suffering—would not persist for the ascetic.
If that which is desired [by you] is something other than affliction, then it is not truly austerity; if it is indeed affliction, [then it is merely suffering].

Because that [asceticism] is the fruit of karma, there can be no confusion of powers (*śakti-saṃkara*) and so forth arising from it. Furthermore, the increase or destruction of power through asceticism can only be asserted if asceticism is something other than affliction (*kleśa*);

otherwise, if that asceticism were simply affliction, then since asceticism of that nature is the fruit of karma, it would be improper to claim that confusion of powers and the like could result from such asceticism, which is itself a product of karma.
From the word "etcetera" (ādi), complete destruction [is also implied]—
Pramāṇavārttika, Manorathanandin’s commentary, 1.278–79.
In the case of *saṃkaraṇa*, there is the destruction [of karma];

liberation results from the destruction of karma, and that [destruction] results from austerity (*tapas*), which here would not be the cause of destruction if it were merely the physical torment of the body.
"Furthermore, the mixing of those powers causes destruction"—*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhadvṛtti*, verse 52;
"also, it causes the destruction of the mixing of those powers"—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 1118.
[Objection: Since it is the fruit of karma, how could that be austerity, like the suffering of hell-beings?

Furthermore, that which is of a single form could not be the cause for the destruction of that diversity; and as for the statement that "it brings about the destruction of the mixture of those powers," that too is merely words.
Since it would follow that all [defilements] would be destroyed even when a small portion is diminished without effort,
this is the justification for liberation (*mokṣa*) as being the nature of a continuum of pure consciousness together with its lineage (*sānvaya*).
To this, the following reply is given:

as for what was stated—beginning with "the cause and effect," and so forth—that is an unconsidered assertion; for the existence of a self distinct from the stream of moments of cognition existing in the relation of cause and effect has already been established in detail during the refutation of the *santāna* (pp. 838, l.
—The stream of the characteristics of knowledge—Śrā.:

As for what was further stated—"He who perceives a self with a stable form," and so forth—that is indeed well said. However, an ignorant person, not perceiving that the means to happiness are unaccompanied by suffering, engages in the worldly means to happiness which are accompanied by suffering due to attachment to the self (*ātmasneha*).

One who knows how to distinguish between the beneficial and the harmful, however, abandons women and other such things that are means to immediate pleasure, and out of attachment to the self, engages in the path to liberation, which is the means to ultimate happiness.

Just as a patient, unaware of the distinction between what is wholesome and unwholesome, consumes curd and similar substances—which are the means for immediate pleasure but serve as causes for the increase of the disease—whereas one who knows the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome abandons those and engages in drinking water and other such things that bring about health;
and it has been said (p. 838, l.

Comparison: That is indeed well said; however, an ignorant person, perceiving the means to happiness as being accompanied by suffering, engages in those worldly means to happiness that are accompanied by suffering due to self-attachment, just like a foolish patient [engaging] with unwholesome food and the like—*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 1118.
pṛ॰ 9 –seeing the means, ā॰ –but discernment, ā॰
"But as for discernment: the ignorant person becomes attached to things known only for their immediate pleasure;
however, those who investigate thoroughly pursue only what is truly beneficial. Thus [it is said].
This has been cited—*Nyāyaviniścayavivaraṇa*, p.

581; *Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 1119—as follows: "Furthermore, that which was stated—that one who desires liberation [should contemplate] one's own nature, wife, children, and so forth—has also been refuted by this [very argument]; for since the cultivation of [the notions of] being entirely impermanent, selfless, and so on, is devoid of a real object, it is of a false nature, and thus, like the cultivation of [the notions of] being entirely permanent and so on, it cannot logically be a cause of liberation."
And that [cognition] has as its object that which is not distinct from the self, because the establishment of the self and the refutation of momentary destruction have already been proven.

Furthermore, it has been stated in the section on the refutation of the *santāna* (continuum) that even the process of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not possible without a single synthesizing subject who persists through different points of time.

For it is well known in the world that liberation occurs only when there is a single substratum—that is, when one who is bound by shackles and the like possesses the intention and the activity of fully understanding and practicing the means for their own liberation; thus, the distinction between bondage and liberation is established only upon such a common locus. However, in this case [of the Buddhist theory], one moment is bound, while another has the full knowledge of the means for its liberation, and yet another has the intention and the activity of practicing them. Because of this lack of a common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), everything is untenable.
(Page 839, Line 4)

Comparison: Because meditations on momentariness and so forth are false in nature, and because false cognition cannot be the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—as stated in Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.

20; and because meditation, being conceptual in nature and consisting of what is derived from hearing (*śrutamayi*) or reflection (*cintāmayī*), has non-entities as its object, it is contradictory for it to give rise to the knowledge of a yogi which has real entities as its object.
Because a cognition whose object is reality is not apprehended from any conceptual cognition whose object is non-reality—Āptamīmāṃsā 83;
Tattvārthaślokavārttika, p. 21.

*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52: "Bondage and liberation do not exist for one who contemplates [the self] as eternal and so forth; bondage and liberation cannot reside in that which is a single momentary consciousness. That is to say, if the mind is a single momentary entity, then bondage and liberation could not exist within it.

In the view of absolute momentariness (*kṣaṇikaikāntapakṣe*), since the mind that is bound perishes without leaving a trace (*niranvayapraṇāśāt*), it follows that the subsequent mind—which is unbound—would itself be liberated; thus, liberation would belong to one thing while bondage belongs to another. Therefore, both bondage and liberation must reside in a single, continuous mind (*ekacittasaṃsthau bandhamokṣau*). (Yuktyanuśāsana-ṭīkā, p. 41)

Furthermore, everyone who acts with prior reflection proceeds by means of a synthesis [anusandhi], thinking: "From this, such-and-such will accrue to me. As for the reading *anyatrānuṣṭhā* in the Bāṇa manuscript and *vyāpā* in the Ānandaśrama edition, [the correct reading is as follows]. Moreover, everyone who acts with prior reflection proceeds by means of a synthesis, thinking: "From this, such-and-such will accrue to me."
