And here, what kind of entity, while engaging in the practice of the path, would conceive: "May liberation be mine"? Is it the momentary instant (*kṣaṇa*) or the continuum (*santāna*)? First, it cannot be the momentary instant, because, due to its duration of only a single moment and its non-conceptual nature, it is incapable of performing such extensive activities.

Nor can it be the continuum, because the Buddhists do not admit a continuum as something distinct from the members of the continuum, and because [the continuum] has already been refuted in the refutation of the continuum.
Furthermore, everyone who acts with prior intelligence engages in action through the deliberation: "By this means, may such-and-such a result accrue to me."
— *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52
— previously, the present continuum (*santāna*) was refuted by [Vasubandhu] (ba); [this is] the citation (śra).

And as for that which was further stated—"in those things which perish without leaving a trace," and so forth—that too is mere words; for if a self (*ātman*) is not admitted, it is impossible to superimpose unity upon such momentary mental states (*cittakṣaṇa*), and that impossibility has been explained in detail in the section on the refutation of the continuum (*santānabhaṅga*).
Furthermore, if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish without leaving a trace, any effort toward liberation would be futile.

For in your view, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the cessation of passion and the like, and that cessation is a destruction. Since that [destruction] is causeless, it would be established without effort; therefore, the exertion involved in performing practices for its sake would be entirely fruitless.

For by such [exertion], would there be produced the destruction of the preceding moment of the mind characterized by passion and so forth? Or the non-arising of the future one? Or the exhaustion of the power that produces it? Or the cutting off of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), or its non-arising? Or the arising of a continuum of mind free from outflows (*anāsrava*)? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; because destruction is causeless in your view, it is contradictory for it to arise from anything at all.

For this very reason, the second position is also untenable: for non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the absence of arising; since it is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), how could it arise from anything? This would entail the consequence of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Furthermore, the effort directed toward the destruction of its potential is also inconsistent; because that destruction too is of the nature of a non-entity, it is impossible for it to acquire its own being (*ātmalābha*) from anything.

The claim that such effort is for the sake of the annihilation of the continuum (*santāna*) or for the sake of its non-arising has also been refuted by this; for, just like the annihilation and non-arising of a moment, the annihilation and non-arising of that [continuum]—being of the nature of non-entities—cannot logically arise from anything.
(Page 839, Line 7)
And the impossibility of planting [seeds] occurs because of the continuity of those wandering in saṃsāra;
for since destruction is causeless, the cause of injury is not the injurer.
And liberation would be the destruction of the mental continuum, not having the eightfold path as its cause; [this is stated in] Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 52.
Furthermore, if the object were accidental and of the nature of dissolution, the path would not be appropriate, and there would be no destroyer.

And thus, the path—characterized by the cultivation of selflessness—which is the cause for liberation (defined as the cessation of all outflows) or for the peaceful nirvāṇa (consisting in the destruction of the mental continuum), would not be logical; for there is a contradiction with anything that causes destruction.
Since destruction is causeless, effort [toward a means] would be futile, because it would be accomplished without exertion. (*Yuktianuṭīkā*, p. 40).
– *Praśamaratiprakaraṇavyākhyā*, folio 20, ḍa:

Furthermore, by the performance of austerities and so forth—that is, by that practice for the sake of liberation—is the destruction of a prior moment of passion and the like effected; or is it the non-arising of future [moments]; or the exhaustion of the capacity that produces them; or the cutting off of the continuum, or its non-arising; or the arising of a mental continuum devoid of a basis? — *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccayabṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52.
The severance of [the cycle of existence] is the mind without support;
this is the doctrine of the Sugatas.
— The doctrine that [things] arise without a cause is produced; the meaning is that the nihilistic view (abhāvavāda) collapses regarding the cessation and non-arising of the continuum (santāna).

Since it is impossible for a continuum (*santāna*) to obtain its own nature from any source whatsoever, such an effort toward its cessation or non-arising would be logical; yet that [continuum] is not established. Furthermore, such an effort toward its cessation or non-arising would be logical only if a real continuum were established; however, it is not established as such, because you do not admit a real entity distinct from the momentary instants (*kṣaṇa*), and because it has already been refuted in the refutation of the continuum.

Comparison: Furthermore, since a real continuum (*santāna*) is not admitted, what is the use of this effort toward its cessation and so forth? For the killing of one who is already dead is never observed anywhere—*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52.
Moreover, if the final cognition does not act as the producer of another cognition, there will be the cessation of the continuum.

And why does that [entity] not produce [the effect]? Is it because of its existence, or because it lacks the capacity for its production? If you argue that even though it has the capacity, it does not produce [the effect] due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), this too is an unexamined statement; for the absence of those [auxiliaries] cannot act as an obstruction. For by what means would there be an obstruction to the entity's arising, or to its status as a producer? Regarding these two alternatives, the first is untenable; for according to the Buddhist position, the absence of other causes—being of the nature of non-existence and characterized by the lack of all causal power—is not capable of obstructing the arising of an entity.

That which is by nature devoid of all causal capacities cannot be an obstacle to the production of anything, just as a rabbit’s horn; and since the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*) in the Śākya doctrine is of such a nature, this second alternative is also refuted by this [argument]. For an "obstacle" to being a producer consists in the removal of the existence of a thing that produces an effect, and that is impossible in the case of an absence that resembles a horse's horn—[this applies] when there is no intervening agent.
If [the effect] arises from existence (sattva),
then there is the absence of auxiliary causes for that state.
Due to the absence of auxiliary causes,
there is an absence of the absence of the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*), by virtue of its being of the nature of a non-absence.
For, according to the position of the proponent (*sādhyamata*), [the cause] is indeed the producer (*vyutpādaka*) as stated by Śrī; for if it were the producer (*utpādakatva*),
there would be no auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*).

Furthermore, if the final moment of consciousness were incapable of performing a causal function, it would follow that it is not a real entity; and if that is so, then by extension, its producer [the preceding moment] would also not be a real entity. In this way, it follows that the entire continuum of consciousness is unreal.

Now, it might be argued that although a moment of cognition existing within its own continuum does not produce [another], because the cognition of a yogi existing in another continuum is produced by it, the entire continuum is not unreal. This is incorrect; for it would entail the absence of non-deviant inference from taste and so forth toward color-form and so forth occurring at the same time, since—just like the final moment—it is possible for color-form and the rest to produce effects of a different class while failing to produce effects of their own kind.

If form and taste, by virtue of depending on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), necessarily initiate two effects, then other things would also have to initiate two effects, since there is no difference in their dependence on a single causal complex even in the case of the final moment and the cognition of a yogi.

If, however, it is maintained that the final moment lacks the capacity to produce an effect belonging to a different continuum—just as it possesses the capacity to produce an effect within its own continuum—then, being entirely devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), it would be a non-entity (*avastu*) like a lotus in the sky.

If such a thing were indeed a real entity (*vastu*), then even a non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*) thing that is entirely devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would possess the status of a real entity. Consequently, properties such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth would not establish momentariness, because they would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the position that liberation—characterized by the cessation of the continuum—is to be accomplished through the exertion of practicing its causes is not conducive to well-being, given the absence of causal efficiency.

Objection: Since the final moment, being incapable of producing anything, would result in its non-substantiality, it would follow that all preceding moments are also non-substantial, leading to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the total absence of the entire continuum (saṃtāna). If it is argued that this is not the case because the cognition of a yogin produces [an effect] even though lightning and the like do not produce their own kind, [we reply: no, for then it would follow that the material cause (upādāna) of color (rūpa), which exists at the same time as the taste being tasted, would be a cooperative condition (sahakārin) for taste even if it does not produce color; consequently, there could be no inference of color from taste. (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 161)
In the *Syādvādamañjarī*, page 112,
and the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 497:
[it refers to] the penultimate moment that produces the final moment.
—[Regarding] "the mind without remainder"—Ārya [Vimuktisena]:

For when a certain omniscient yogi cognizes that final moment, then that final moment becomes the producer of the yogi’s cognition by way of being its cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), because of the established tenet that an object is not something that lacks a cause;

therefore, even though the final moment does not produce a subsequent homogeneous moment, it is indeed a performer of purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*) because it generates the yogi’s cognition through its status as a cooperative cause.

In the Buddhist view, for a taste existing in the second moment, the taste existing in the first moment is the material cause (*upādāna*), while the form existing in the first moment is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*).

For the form existing in the first moment, having produced a form of its own kind (*sajātīya*) in the second moment, acts as an auxiliary cause for the heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) taste existing in the second moment.

For if the final moment of cognition, even without producing another subsequent moment of cognition of its own kind, were to act as a cooperative cause for a heterogeneous cognition belonging to a different continuum—namely, the cognition of a yogi by way of being its object—then likewise, a preceding moment of form would also act as a cooperative cause for a heterogeneous taste existing in the second moment, even without producing another subsequent moment of form of its own kind existing in the second moment.
And in that case, there could be no inference of form from the taste existing in the second moment; such is the intended meaning.
(Antakṣa—Ā.)
Even though it produces taste,
it is impossible for it to produce something of its own kind,
because it is possible for it not to produce another moment of the same substance.
The yogic knowledge of the final moment [is produced] by the performance of its own cause— variant (ā): *svakāraṇānuṣṭhāna*— variant (ba).

The position that liberation is characterized by the arising of a mental continuum free from outflows (*anāsrava-citta-santati*) and is to be accomplished through effort toward that end is the superior one.

However, it must be stated whether that mental continuum possesses a causal continuity (*sānvaya*) or lacks it (*niranvaya*). In this regard, the position of its possessing a causal continuity alone is logical; for liberation is possible only within such a mental continuum. Indeed, it is the bound who is liberated, not the unbound.
Furthermore, in a mental continuum that lacks causal continuity, the liberation of the bound is impossible, because in that case, one person would be bound while another would be liberated.

If it is argued that even here liberation belongs only to one who was bound because of the identity of the continuum (*santāna*), [we reply: Well then, does the referent "continuum" exist as an ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) or as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*)? If it exists as an ultimate reality, then it would be the self (*ātman*) itself stated under a different name. If, on the other hand, it exists as a conventional reality, then since there is no single entity existing as an ultimate reality, it follows that one is bound and another is liberated; and in that case, there would be no engagement for the sake of the liberation of the one who was bound, as there would be no basis for it. (Note: *nirāśraya-cittayā* in the Ātmatattvaviveka manuscript; *nirāśraya-cittayā* in the Śrāvakabhūmi manuscript.)

Because it is established that the moments of consciousness in the mental continuum are substantially concomitant, and because the annihilation of the continuum is logically untenable—*Aṣṭasahasrī*, p. 69; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, p. 162:
It must be stated whether that mental continuum (*cittasantati*) is with a causal substratum (*sānvaya*) or without a causal substratum (*niranvaya*).
In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because liberation is possible within such a mental continuum itself.
— *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52:
Even in the position that [things] are momentary and without continuity (*niranvaya-kṣaṇika*),
since the continuum (*santāna*) is also not a real entity, let the self (*ātman*) be described in that same way.
Because a continuum is impossible without some form of identity with a substance—
*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 23—
if the meaning of "continuum" were ultimately real, then it would simply be the self (*ātman*) itself expressed by the word "continuum."

Now, if [bondage] were conventional (saṃvṛti), then because that which is ultimately real (paramārthasat) would be non-existent, one [person] would be bound and another would be liberated; consequently, there would be no engagement for the sake of the liberation of the bound—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 162; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 321.

Now, even if moments are absolutely distinct, one might act with the intention, "I shall liberate myself who am bound," because of the determination of their unity due to their extremely firm form. How, then, can there be the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), from the practice of whose cultivation liberation would arise? If that vision arises through the influence of scriptural refinement, then the determination of unity cannot be of an unerring nature; thus, for one who seeks to join one thing, another falls away.

Therefore, from where could there be an exertion for the sake of the liberation of one who is bound? For how else would the statement in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.194)—"effort is for the purpose of removing false superimposition, even though there is no liberator"—be appropriate? [The opponent argues: "The bound self..."

"In that case, there would be no vision of selflessness; how then could liberation, which is based upon it, exist? For as long as the cultivation of selflessness is not of an unshakable nature, there is not even the possibility of the conviction of oneness—namely, 'I shall liberate the very self that is bound. (Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 162; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 321).

When the demonstration of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is being carried out, the determination of [the self] as a unity—which was stated [by you] as "because it is the basis of experience" and so forth—is likewise charming only so long as it is not investigated. For one who knows what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted regards as their own the basis of experience that is the means for attaining ultimate happiness, and not the means for attaining momentary happiness. To explain:
As for what was also stated [at] Baḍarāyaṇa-pṛṣṭha 840, line 5:

those who know what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted indeed regard as their own that which is the means for attaining ultimate happiness, the basis for enjoyment, and the substratum of the self, and not that which is the means for immediate happiness.
—*Syādvādaratnākara*, p.
1119: *upayogāśraya-*, Ā; *upayogāśayamā-*, Ba.
For it has been said in the Prakrit verse:
"I alone am my eternal self, characterized by knowledge and vision" (*ego vaṃ ego me sassado appā nāṇadaṃsaṇalakkhaṇo*);
"I alone am my eternal self" (*eko me sāsado appā*)—from the *Niyamasāra*, verse 102.
My one eternal self is characterized by knowledge and vision;
all other external phenomena are characterized by conjunction,
rooted in conjunction, and have been acquired by the soul as a succession of sufferings.
Therefore, I renounce all that is connected to the self in three ways;
all remaining external states of mine are characterized by conjunction.
The succession of sufferings experienced by the soul has its root in association;
therefore, one should renounce all connections of association through the three modes of action.
"Union with a wife causes humiliation; kinsmen are a bondage; and the objects of the senses are poison.
This verse is included in the *Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra*.
Alas, people! What is this delusion of yours? That you hope for friendship with those who are your enemies, and harbor enmity toward those who are your friends.

For the discerning person who contemplates in this way, even though there exists in those entities related to conjunction—which are causes of suffering—the quality of being means for attaining slight pleasure, how could they have the notion of "mine" regarding them when they perceive at other times the Three Jewels as the means for absolute happiness, such that they would not desist from them? [Objection: Surely, desistance from them would occur through the notion of "mine" only if they were exclusively causes of suffering; but this is not so, because here the possibility of their being causes of pleasure even to a slight degree exists. Therefore, despite their being causes of suffering, due to affection for what is "one's own," one considers the senses and so forth to be beneficial to oneself insofar as they possess the aspect of being causes of pleasure, and thus does not abandon the notion of "mine" toward them. [Reply: This too is incorrect; for even if they are means for a slight pleasure, since there exists another means for absolute happiness, they can be abandoned—just as food mixed with poison is abandoned when food without poison is available.
— In relation to [the causes of] suffering,
1. Comparison—In that regard, first of all, there are three jewels, namely: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. (Dharmasaṃgraha, p. 1)
Because among the means for immediate pleasure, such as women and so forth, there exists here the state of being the means for immediate pleasure, such as women and so forth.
— [in] this case, of one's own Three Jewels
— its non-existence — ba.

Because there is no distinction [between the two] due to the existence of that [object], it is possible for one to abandon only the defective [part]; as for what was also stated—"even when defects such as being blotchy, one-eyed, or crippled are observed," and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for we do not maintain that affection arises from observing qualities such as beauty, but rather from observing the quality known as being the basis for enjoyment.

Furthermore, for the discerning person who perceives the absolute defect—in the form of being the cause of the suffering of saṃsāra characterized by the continuous succession of birth, old age, and death—in those entities associated with yoga, there is no perception of the quality known as being the basis for enjoyment. When attachment based on that [quality] has ceased, how could the perception of defects not be the sublater of attachment?
(p. 840, l. 11; *sārūpyādi*—MS)
— In the absence of relations,
there is the perception of qualities (śra॰), according to Ba and Ā;
[there is] the exclusion of affection (sneha), according to Ba.
Obstruction by unctuous substances (snehabādha) — Chapter 60.

[Objection: "Granted that for one who perceives those faults, although the mind—which was previously attached—may waver at that time, nevertheless, he should not be regarded as being entirely dispassionate toward it, because attachment can arise again through the perception of its qualities. [Reply: This too is incorrect. For it is logical that an ignorant person becomes dispassionate by perceiving a temporary fault known as the cause of immediate suffering, and becomes attached again by perceiving a temporary quality known as the cause of immediate pleasure. However, one who knows the truth of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted becomes dispassionate by perceiving the ultimate fault known as the cause of the continuous stream of suffering characterized by birth, old age, and death; he does not become attached again by perceiving a temporary quality known as the cause of immediate pleasure, but rather by perceiving a quality known as the cause of ultimate happiness.
And since that [state] is not observed among those things related by conjunction, he fully internalizes therein that dispassion characterized by equanimity.

Now, if it is argued that one becomes dispassionate toward that [body] because it is a cause of suffering characterized by such continuity, then one should likewise become dispassionate toward the self (*ātman*), since the state of being a cause of such suffering is no different there as well. Or, if there is no dispassion toward that, then one would not be dispassionate toward anything else either, due to the absence of any distinction. To this, we ask: is this said with reference to an ignorant person regarding the self, or its opposite? If it refers to an ignorant person, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for you yourself admit that dispassion toward the self exists in one who lacks knowledge of the truth regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, even though that self is a cause of such suffering.

But when that [mind] possesses the knowledge of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, there is no dispassion [arising from mere aversion], because such a mind lacks the cause for that kind of suffering;
even if the intellect is momentarily shaken by a fault in one object, it is not truly dispassionate toward that object, just as a lustful man is not dispassionate toward another woman.
— Pramāṇavārttika 1.241–42:
[She] became free from passion.
Thus,
because of the observation of the quality called "causality" (hetutva) [in the case of] another... [Ba, Śra].
The knower of reality [experiences] longing for women and other objects associated with the union of sexual contact. (Śrīmadbhagavadgītā-bhāṣya)

A comparison [is made] even with regard to women and others, concerning their being the cause of the continuous succession of birth, old age, death, and so forth: whatever is a cause of suffering must be abandoned, and that which is accompanied by limiting conditions (sopādhi) is likewise [to be abandoned].
If it is argued that even the attributeless [Self] should be abandoned, we say no; for it is impossible to do so, and because there would be no purpose in doing so—*Ātmatattvaviveka*, p.
106, regarding the Self.

As for what was stated—that bodily affliction is the fruit of karma, and so forth—that too is the play of no small ignorance. For even if bodily affliction that augments the *vrata* (vows) characterized by the abstention from violence and the like is indeed the fruit of karma, there is no contradiction in its being austerity (*tapas*).
Indeed, bodily affliction that does not contradict the vows is designated as austerity because it is a cause for the shedding of karma (*karmanirjarā*).

Nor does this imply that the bodily affliction of hell-beings and others is also austerity; for since that [affliction] is primarily characterized by an immersion in violence and the like, it is impossible for it to be non-contradictory to the vows.
Therefore, how is it appropriate to establish for discerning people an equality between that [asceticism] and bodily mortification performed by one seeking liberation?
(Page 841,

Line 2) For even though bodily mortification— which serves to augment the vows consisting of abstention from violence— is indeed a form of karma, there is no contradiction in its being asceticism (*tapas*).
— *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*, verse 52 — [The definition of] conduct (*vṛtta*) is [stated] because of the absence of non-contradiction with the vows (*vrata*).

As for what was stated regarding the theory of the commingling of potencies (*śaktisaṅkara*)—namely, that even by a very slight [effort] through the affliction of hellish states and so forth—that is well said; for when there is a commingling of the potencies of karmas capable of yielding diverse fruits, their destruction is admitted to occur without affliction and with very little effort, in the form of supreme white meditation (*parama-śukla-dhyāna*), at the final moment of one whose delusion is exhausted and at the final moment of a non-yogi. Otherwise, neither liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) nor supreme liberation (*paramamukti*) would be possible.

However, since that mixing of those capacities is achievable only through a great deal of hardship, it is logical that there should be the exertion of performing various kinds of difficult bodily austerities, such as fasting and so forth; for without that, the mixing of them cannot be established.

Therefore, those who are discerning and wise should understand that the continuum of cognition, when somehow unimpeded, is liberated through the performance of various kinds of difficult and arduous penances.
That is well said; [it is stated] that there is no confusion of the potencies of karmas capable of yielding diverse fruits—*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-vṛtti*, verse 52.
The continuum of the body, which undergoes various kinds of suffering due to verbal afflictions,
is manifold.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Vaiśeṣikas and others is that there is no cognition in states such as deep sleep.
[Objection: But it is incorrect to say that the continuum of cognition is uninterrupted, because even in states such as deep sleep, its limitation is perceived;
for one is said to be "asleep" precisely when not cognizing anything at all, since if cognition were present therein, such non-cognition would be impossible.

If there were the existence of cognition (*jñāna*) in that state [of deep sleep], then there would be no distinction between the waking and the deep-sleep states, because in both cases there would be no difference regarding the existence of cognition that manifests itself and others. If it is argued that although cognition exists there [in deep sleep], it is suppressed by sleep, whereas in the waking state it is absent—and therefore there is no lack of distinction between these two—[we ask]: what indeed is this so-called "suppression" (*abhibhava*) of cognition by that [sleep]? Is it destruction (*nāśa*), or is it concealment (*tirobhāva*)? If it is destruction, how can there be the existence of that [cognition] therein, since destruction is contradictory to its existence?

Now, as for the claim that it is merely concealed (*tirobhāva*), that is not so; for if one accepts that cognition is of the nature of illuminating both itself and others, even that [concealment] is untenable.
Therefore, since cognition—which meets the conditions for being perceived—is not perceived during states such as deep sleep, its non-existence alone is the more reasonable conclusion.
"But at the time of deep sleep, because knowledge is not produced by the mind which has left the skin and resides in the *purītat*— [as stated in] Muktāvalī Kārikā 56—
and because that [mind] is not [then] obstructed..."

If knowledge were present in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there would be no distinction from the waking state, because in both cases there is no difference in the existence of self-cognized knowledge—*Praśastapādabhāṣyavyākhyā*, p. 20d. If it is argued that the distinction lies in being overcome by sleep in deep sleep, this is incorrect; for since sleep is a property of that [self], it is impossible for it to act as an overcomer through identity with it.
If, however, there is a distinction [between the cognition and its object], then since only the entities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth exist, their own nature must be defined;
and if destruction were [the nature] of that [object], it would not belong to consciousness, nor would destruction be causeless.

Alternatively, if [you claim it is] disappearance, that is not so; for if one accepts that the existence of consciousness is itself the perception of that [object] due to its existence, then that [disappearance] is untenable.
–*Praśnavyākaraṇa*, folio 20: [the destruction] by means of sleep.

In response to this, the proof for the existence of knowledge even in states such as deep sleep is now addressed, on the grounds that [the opponent's position] contradicts the actual state of affairs.

As for what was stated—"for one who does not discern anything at all," and so forth—that is incorrect. This is because in states such as deep sleep, there exists the experience of sleep itself and the experience of that pleasure;

for if cognition were not admitted therein, it would follow that upon waking, one could have neither the recollection of the pleasure of sleep—such as "I slept happily"—nor the recollection of the sleep itself—such as "I slept continuously for this long" or "I slept with interruptions for this long. This is because such recollections, having as their object a known thing, are invariably concomitant with a distinct cognition whose object is that very thing.

Whatever is a recollection is invariably concomitant with another cognition of its own object, just like the recollection of a jar or the like; and the experience of the pleasure of sleep and so forth by one who has awakened from sleep is a recollection.

If this [recollection] were to manifest even without another cognition of its own object, then the recollection of a jar and the like would also manifest without it; therefore, how could even the experience of that [sleep] be established? Consequently, that experience by which the recollection of the pleasure of sleep and so forth is manifested during states such as deep sleep must be admitted to have that [pleasure] as its object (pṛ. 847, l. 18).

And therefore, upon waking, all three—the bliss experienced during deep sleep, the Self, and the positive entity that is ignorance—are recollected by one who has arisen, as in: "I slept happily; I was not aware of anything. —*Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha*, p. 60.
[The phrase *svapnādi-śra* refers to dreams and so forth.]
There is no consciousness of the experience of that pleasure; therein, there is no sleep of consciousness.

And herein is the determination of the meaning of the definition of sleep— based on the realization through recollection that "I slept uninterruptedly for this much time" and "I slept with interruptions for this much time"— as stated in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 323,
regarding memory.

Since self-recollection is of the nature of experience, this establishes the existence of cognition even in states such as intoxication and fainting. For one who has emerged from that state, there is the recollection: "At that time, nothing was experienced by me. On the basis of this recollection, that experience by which the self is perceived as being devoid of all other experiences must be admitted to exist in that state; for without that experience, such recollection would be impossible.

Nor should it be asserted that the pleasure of sleep or its cognition is non-existent in states such as deep sleep because there is no determination of it as "this is thus"; for this would be inconclusive due to the case of an infant born on that very day, who experiences pleasure and its cognition produced by breast-milk placed in his mouth—yet that pleasure is certainly not determined by him as "this is thus," and yet it exists. Furthermore, the application of the word "pleasure" here is not figurative based on the absence of suffering, since it has been established during the investigation of negation (*abhāva*) that the nature of a negation consists in the presence of another positive entity which serves as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

—based on what [is it established], by which [it is known] that the mind does not exist in states such as sleep and fainting? From where is your certainty [regarding this]? If you say it is because of the absence of sensation (*vedanā*), then from where has that [absence] come?
If such a certainty as "I do not know the mind" arises in you regarding those states, then the existence of a mind is established. Furthermore,
if in those states such as fainting and so forth, the certainty "I do not know the mind" arises in you, then by that very certainty thus arisen, the existence of a mind is established.
If it is not admitted that the mind exists in states such as dreaming or fainting—[as stated in] *Tattvasaṅgraha*, Pañjikā, p. 540; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 323.
In that case, there would either be death at the time of origination, or indeed an absence of death;
for it is impossible for a self devoid of all experience to possess memory (Tattvasaṃgraha, p. 541).
[Objection: "But surely, [the opponent might argue], if consciousness exists in these states such as deep sleep (suṣupta), why would there not be a memory of that form for one who has awakened?"
That [memory] would not function at all because of the impossibility of factors such as proficiency, just like the mind of a newborn infant;

for if memory were to occur merely by the fact that something was experienced, then this might be so. However, even when there is experience, memory does not occur due to the deficiency of proficiency, repeated practice, desire, and so forth, as is the case with the mind that has experienced something during the state of being a newborn infant.
—Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, page 540; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 325;
there, by that [author], Śrī...

As for what was stated—that because the ground and other such entities are distinct from their counter-correlates (pratiyogin), they possess that [absence] as their very nature—and that "even when there is the existence of cognition" and so forth; that too is an unexamined assertion. For even when cognition exists, the distinction between the waking and deep-sleep states is logically established.

Indeed, that state wherein cognition—unoverpowered and adept at investigating external and internal objects—is present is the waking state; whereas that state wherein cognition is the opposite due to being overcome by sleep and the like is the state of deep sleep and so forth.

"Due to a specific causal complex such as drowsiness (*middha*) and so forth, there exists in states such as deep sleep a distinct cognition that is indifferent to the apprehension of the manifold properties of external and internal objects—comparable to the cognition of the touch of a blade of grass while walking; otherwise, it would follow that even the flow of cognitions during the waking and alert states would be non-existent.
(Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā, p. 163)

As for what was stated [in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 323]—namely, "What is this suppression (*abhibhava*) of cognition by sleep and so forth?"—and the further argument: "In that case, its being deprived of the investigation of external and internal objects due to the influence of that [sleep] is the suppression; but since its nature is to illuminate itself and others, how can it be deprived of that?"—this too is untenable, because it is contradicted by the perception of the touch of grass while walking; for even though that [perception] has that [self-illuminating] nature, it is observed to lack the capacity to determine it.

It is not by its mere possession of that intrinsic nature alone that cognition has the capacity to determine an object; for such capacity is possible only when it is unobstructed in every respect. We consider it logical that just as the perception of the touch of grass being brushed against while walking is obstructed by one's lack of attention, so too the perception of dreams and the like is obstructed by sleep and so forth.

Furthermore, how could the obstruction of fire by a gem or a mantra, or of a lamp by a bowl, be established for one who speaks thus? For an "obstruction" cannot consist in the destruction of one thing by another, as that would contradict direct perception.
Nor is there concealment (*tirobhāva*), because even such concealment is impossible for that which is capable of producing its own effect;
the admission here—consistent with our perception—that there is an obstruction to the capacity of its own nature is the same in other cases as well (p.
By virtue of cognition alone having the nature of illuminating both itself and others.
The experience of deep sleep and so forth [is established],
because it is the same even when fire and the like are obstructed by gems, mantras, and so on, or when lamps and the like are obstructed by bowls and the like—
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 322.
The perception of fire or a lamp by means of mantras and the like, or by means of a shallow bowl and the like.
Even when knowledge is overwhelmed by sleep, there is no destruction of the assembly of one's own body.

Furthermore, who is it that perceives the absence of cognition in states such as deep sleep—the self itself, or someone standing nearby? If it is the self itself, is this perception due to that very [absence of] cognition, due to its non-existence, due to its non-apprehension, or due to another cognition occurring during the state of waking or awakening? It cannot be due to that very [absence], because it is non-existent; for that which is non-existent cannot be the cause of anyone’s perception, just as the son of a barren woman [cannot be]. And you maintain that cognition is non-existent in states such as deep sleep.

Nor can it be due to the absence of that [object], because the quality of being a determiner (*paricchedakatva*) is a property of cognition; therefore, in the absence of that [cognition], such a determiner cannot possibly exist. Otherwise, it would simply be a matter of renaming the absence of cognition itself. As for the comparison: at that state, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of apprehending the absence of consciousness.
To explain: one who is actually asleep does not perceive the absence of consciousness at that state, because consciousness is not admitted to exist at that time.
And since that very [cognition] is itself the knowledge when there is the comprehension of that [object], there is no absence of it in that state;

nor does another person standing nearby perceive its absence, because in this case the non-perception of causes, pervaders, or essential natures, or the affirmation of the contradictory, have no operation, and it is impossible for anything else to manifest its absence—*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 90.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 323:

Even on the basis of the non-perception of that [knowledge], would the cognition of its absence there be due to something existing at that same time, or something existing at another time? In the first case, how can there be an absolute absence of knowledge there, given that the non-apprehension-knowledge which grasps that absence is itself present there?
Nor can it be [an absence] occurring at another time, because that cannot serve as the cause for the cognition of that [absence].
For non-apprehension at one time is not the cause for the cognition of an absence belonging to another time, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension; and an absence can only be grasped when it depends upon the perception of its locus and the recollection of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), since it cannot be grasped in the absence of that perception and recollection due to its dependence upon them.

Therefore, one who desires non-perception (*anupalambha*) therein must first determine the self as its substratum and remember the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); how then could the total absence of cognition in states such as deep sleep be established? Thus, even by means of non-perception, the absence of cognition in states such as deep sleep cannot be proven.

The meaning is that because time is the counter-correlate (*pratihetu*) of that [non-existence], there is indeed knowledge of the self (*ātman*), which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the entity, as well as the recollection of the knowledge that serves as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the absence of knowledge.

Nor can it be established from another cognition occurring during the state of waking, because in relation to that [waking cognition], the cognition of deep sleep and so forth cannot possibly meet the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), and because no other cognition existing at that time which could grasp its absence is ever perceived.

As for the claim that the cognition occurring at the time of waking—expressed as "nothing was known by me while in deep sleep"—is indeed perceived as grasping that absence, this too is untenable; for from this very statement, the existence of that [cognition] at that time is precisely what is perceived.

For this [cognition] has the nature of memory, and memory is not possible at that time without another cognition that apprehends the absence of that [object], as was just stated; therefore, in states such as deep sleep, that very self is not capable of cognizing the absence of knowledge, [thinking] "I did not know anything" during a dreamless sleep, or "I knew nothing. (Variant readings: *mayā na kiñcit* [B], *mayā na kiñcit* [Ā], *mayā kiñcijjñānam* [Śrī]).
The absence of knowledge in the state of deep sleep is precisely due to that [absence of the self].

Nor is [the mind] situated on the side [of the body], because of the non-perception of its cause, its own nature, or its pervader, or because of the impossibility here of a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with its absence through the affirmation of the contradictory.

Nor should it be argued that the impossibility of a mark invariably concomitant with its presence is equally [applicable] there, for in this case we do perceive marks invariably concomitant with its presence—such as the specific forms of inhalation, exhalation, bodily heat, and so forth—which are ascertained to be invariably concomitant with it within their own substratum. Furthermore, even in the waking state, no other mental activity is apprehended from any other source apart from that [perceived mental activity].

Comparison—because there arises a cognition through inference due to the existence of a mark (liṅga) perceived at that time, such as the specific forms of inhalation, exhalation, bodily heat, and so forth, which are ascertained within oneself as being invariably concomitant with self-cognized consciousness (*svasaṃvidita-vijñāna*)—*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p.
90; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 324.
The meaning is that, because it is invariably concomitant with knowledge, knowledge is inferred from the very existence of inhalation, exhalation, bodily heat, and so forth.
Now, one might object: here, the vital breath and its like are of two kinds—that which originates from consciousness, and that which originates from the vital breath and its like.

In that regard, [it might be argued that] consciousness is the source of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth in the waking state, whereas the vital breath and so forth are the source in states such as deep sleep;

therefore, in the waking state, it is logical to infer consciousness from the vital breath and so forth which have consciousness as their source, but not [to infer it] from the vital breath and so forth which have the vital breath as their source.

For indeed, one does not observe the inference of fire from smoke produced by a cowherd’s water-clock (or a mechanical device), since such an inference is observed only from smoke produced by fire. This too is incorrect, because no distinction in the vital breath and so forth is perceived between the states of deep sleep and those other than it.

For just as one who is in deep sleep breathes, so too does the other; otherwise, there would be no doubt as to whether this person is asleep or awake. Furthermore, if these [functions] were not produced from the consciousness of one in deep sleep, then such functions could not possibly arise even in one who is awake but remains under the guise of being asleep with the intent to deceive others. Indeed, smoke produced from fire cannot be generated from anything other than smoke even by hundreds of efforts, nor can fire be produced from smoke.
Moreover, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth of this person are observed to be exactly like those of one in deep sleep;
therefore, these do not originate from different causes.

Furthermore, just as one distinguishes the vital breaths and so forth—which arise from something other than consciousness—from those that arise from consciousness, let one likewise distinguish activities and so forth, which arise from someone free from passion, from those that arise from someone who is not.

And thus, even those possessed of passion act like those free from passion, and those free from passion act like those possessed of passion; therefore, it is impossible to ascertain the distinction between those free from passion and others.

Is it not the case, then, that there are two kinds [of activity] here—the one arising from consciousness during the waking state, such as breathing and so forth, and the other arising from breathing and so forth during states such as deep sleep? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 324)

For just as one who is fast asleep breathes, so too does the other; otherwise, there would be no doubt as to whether this person is asleep or awake. Furthermore, if these [functions] were not derived from the consciousness of the one in deep sleep, but rather derived from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, then such functions would not occur in one who is awake but remains under the guise of being asleep with the intent to deceive others—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 324.
While asleep,
[there is the experience] only of those things originating from the vital breath— namely, the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth— for one who is asleep.
One should examine this—see page 603, note 1.

Furthermore, how could the first [state], such as breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, arise from deep sleep and the like? If it is argued that it arises from the waking breath and so forth which act as concomitants for waking cognition, we say no; for it is impossible that breath and so forth should occur immediately after a single instance of waking cognition, while the cognition of awakening occurs at a different time.

Indeed, it is not logical for two effects occurring sequentially to arise from a single specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*); otherwise, even from a permanent [cause], which is itself non-sequential, there would be the production of two sequential effects, and this would contradict the principle stated in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.45: "Entities that are sequential do not arise from what is non-sequential."

Therefore, it must be admitted that the emergence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth occurring at that time arises from the very cognition existing in the state of deep sleep; how, then, can the absence of cognition be established therein? Consequently, since a cessation of cognition is impossible at any time, an uninterrupted stream of cognition is established. And through the performance of the means for liberation, upon the exhaustion of obstructive karma, the attainment of the nature of the four infinities (*ananta-catuṣṭaya*) constitutes liberation—this applies to states such as deep sleep and so on.

Because it is impossible for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which occur immediately after a single waking cognition, as well as the cognition of awakening, which occurs at a later time, [to exist]—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 325—the [existence of] the future vital breath and so forth is not possible. (Śra.)
—Because of the establishment of the non-arising of the duality;
see p. 619, note 10;
from Śrāvakabhūmi.

Furthermore, those who intend for the Blessed One—who has attained omniscience (*kevalajñāna*) and so forth upon the destruction of the destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*)—to possess the enjoyment of liberation (*muktibhukti*), have effectively offered a funeral libation to the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). This is because the four infinities (*anantacatuṣṭaya*) would be impossible [in such a case].

For solid food (*kavalāhāra*) is taken only when the sensation of hunger arises; and since the suffering of hunger occurs when that sensation arises, how could the Blessed One possess infinite bliss? For liberation while living must be characterized by the attainment of the nature of the four infinities, and there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to indicate that such enjoyment exists therein.
How is infinite bliss [attained] by the Śvetāmbaras and the Yāpanīyas? Ācārya [Śubhacandra].

Regarding the claim that "some Kevalins" (kevalini-kaṃ kañcit) are "consumers of solid food" (kavalāhārin), this is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) of the Śvetāmbaras and of Yāpanīya Śākaṭāyana.

Is it not the case that this is so: when experience (*bhukti*) has its causes complete, it necessarily occurs, as in the state of one still possessed of veils (*chadmasthāvasthā*); and such is the case in the state of the omniscient with vibratory activity (*sayogikevalyavasthā*).
For there are two kinds of causes for experience: external and internal.
Of these, the external consists of food and the like, which remain entirely intact; there is no dispute regarding this.

The internal [karmic manifestation] also— characterized by the emergence of the *paryāpti*, the *vedya*, the *taijasa*, and long life— is entirely unimpaired in the Blessed One; for that which effects the completion of the body, sense organs, and so forth is *paryāpti*,
while *vedya* is the karma that brings about pleasure and pain.
The *taijasa* body consists of internal heat (*tejas*), which is the bodily warmth from which the digestion of consumed food and so forth occurs;
thus, it is the karma that causes long life and prolonged existence.
From the arising of this [karma], the sensation of hunger arises, and since such an arising exists in the Blessed One, his eating is established.
Or, if that [existence of hunger] is not accepted, then the absence of hunger therein must be understood through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And would that *pramāṇa* be scripture (*āgama*), or something else? It cannot be scripture, because no scripture exists that establishes the absence of hunger in a *sayogakevalin* as an established fact, whereas there is scripture establishing the existence of eating by a *kevalin*, just as there was in the past.
The emergence of the faculties, experience, the radiant body, and long life is not the cause;

the karmas have not been destroyed; there is no lack of excellence; and the qualities such as knowledge are not contradictory to the Victor. Is it then that the state of cyclic existence does not exist?
—*Kevalibhukti*, verse 1–2;
*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 612;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, p. 474.
Internal [page 63B]:
There is enjoyment for the Kevalin because the complete causal complex is present, just like his previous enjoyments;

and this causal complex for the consumption of food consists of: the state of being fully developed (paryāptatva), the arising of karma to be experienced (vedanīyodaya), the fiery body (taijasaśarīra) which is the cause for digesting food, and long life (dīrghāyuṣkatva).
—Sūtrakṛtāṅga-śīlāṅkācārya-vṛtti, p. 345;
Yuktiprakaraṇa, p. 153:
"Only that which is produced by conjunction" (ba).

Since the cause for the occurrence of solid food (kavalāhāra) is twofold—external and internal—the external, such as eating and so forth, certainly exists; there is no dispute among anyone regarding that.
The internal, however, is characterized by the manifestation (udaya) of the life-faculties (paryāpti), the capacity for sensation (vedya), the luminous body (taijasa), and longevity (dīrghāyuṣṭva).
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 475.
The passage contained within this is not found in the Āptamīmāṃsā.

Furthermore, would the negation [of omniscience] arise from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), or from something else? It cannot first be from the non-perception of its own nature, because the nature of a *kevalin* (one who possesses absolute knowledge) is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, the non-perception of the nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) of an entity that is spatially remote is not logical, because such non-perception is defined as the perception of another object that is associated with the same cognition.

Would the negation of that [remote entity] occur through something else being affirmed or through something else being negated? If it were through something being affirmed, then that thing must be contradictory [to the remote entity], for the affirmation of what is not contradictory does not establish non-existence.
And yet, nothing is perceived in the *kevalin* (the omniscient one) that is contradictory to hunger.

Nor should it be asserted that knowledge and other such qualities are themselves the opposites of hunger in that case; for is the opposition between hunger and knowledge merely that of knowledge in general, or of a specific degree of it? If it were knowledge in general, then as those qualities increase, there ought to be a corresponding decrease in hunger through varying degrees, just as darkness diminishes as light increases. But this is not the case, for in children and others, when knowledge and so forth are deficient, hunger is not found to be increased; rather, from that point onward, as knowledge and so forth increase in varying degrees, a corresponding decrease in hunger is observed.
Therefore, it is not the case that mere knowledge and so forth are in contradiction with hunger.

If it is argued that only those qualities such as knowledge belonging to a Kevalin—which have reached the ultimate limit of excellence—are in contradiction with hunger, that is not correct; for it is impossible to establish this in such a way.

Indeed, it cannot be established by one of limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*) that the knowledge and other qualities of a Kevalin contradict hunger, because those qualities are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
In the case of existence, there is nothing to be heard—
because of the absence of injunction;
like darkness in the increase of light, there is no gradation in [the development of] knowledge and the other qualities.
In this state, hunger diminishes, yet there is no perception of contradiction regarding knowledge and the other [perfections].
Since there is the presence of the complete cause and the absence of anything else, one might think "this is contradictory to that"; however, such a cognition does not exist in the Kevalin.
—*Kevalibhukti*, verse 3–4, Syādvādamañjarī, p.
"He is not non-omniscient by virtue of possessing solid food (kavalāhāra), because there is no contradiction between the consumption of solid food and omniscience."
–Pramāṇanaya [tattvāloka] 2.27: In the case of the diminution of knowledge, [there is no attainment].

Furthermore, the apprehension of contradiction arises when something whose causes are complete fails to exist upon the presence of another, as in the case of the sensation of cold when fire is present;
however, this is impossible here, because since the qualities of the Kevalin are beyond the senses, it is untenable to have the cognition that "hunger does not occur in his presence.
Therefore, the absence of hunger there cannot be established through the negation of anything whatsoever.
The cognition of contradiction arises because that which exists when its causes are complete does not exist when another [thing] is present;
this is the understanding of contradiction (*virodhajñāna*). (Nyāyabinduṭīkā, p. 96)
When it is said,

"The entity is negated by the Blessed One," would that entity which is being negated be the effect, the cause, or the pervader of that [negation]? If it were the effect, then that [negation] would imply the cessation of only that specific cause which is capable of producing its own nature and is complete in its causal factors, but not of the cause in general, because there is no contradiction in the existence of a cause even when its particular effect is absent.
A cause, when ceasing, causes its effect to cease—just as fire [ceases] smoke—or a pervader, when ceasing, causes its pervaded to cease—just as a tree [ceases] a *śiṃśapā*.
However, in this case, there is no cessation of any cause or pervader of hunger;

nor does the absence of the four types of karma, such as *mohanīya*, result in the absence of hunger, because it is impossible for hunger to be either the effect or the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of those [karmas].

Hunger is not the effect of those four types of karma; for it arises from external and internal causes as previously explained, and because it cannot be averted by the cultivation of its opposite, it is impossible for it to have delusion (*moha*) as its nature. For that which has delusion as its nature is averted by the cultivation of its opposite—just as anger and the like are averted by the cultivation of forbearance and so forth—and yet you maintain that hunger has delusion as its nature.

And thus, for the purpose of counteracting the sensation of hunger, the treatise would have taught only the cultivation of the antidotes (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), and not the practice of alms-gathering (*piṇḍaiṣaṇā*), which obstructs the study of meditation that abounds in afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, because hunger is equal to the affliction of cold and heat, it does not have delusion (*moha*) as its intrinsic nature; otherwise, the affliction caused by those [cold and heat] would also have to be of the nature of delusion, as there is no distinction between them.
Moreover, whatever entity is prohibited must be either the effect, the cause, or the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of that [prohibited state].
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 473. When this is the case, would the pervasive cause, the effect, or the concomitant of physical food (kavalāhāra) be subject to contradiction by omniscience?
—*Ratnākarāvatārikā*, 2.
27. Internal [suffering], verse 5: hunger.

If [hunger] were an effect, then its cessation would lead one to understand the cessation of only that hunger which is capable of producing itself, but not of hunger in general; for there is no contradiction in a cause existing even in the absence of its effect—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 473; "capable of producing itself" (*ātmanivarttanasamartha*), *Śrāvakabhūmi* (variant reading).
When there is the presence of the mere cause in its favorable form,
there is the existence of the effect, such as the karma of knowledge-obscuration arising from the [karmic matter] that obscures knowledge.
Hunger is of a different nature from that [delusion]; it does not even possess the status of being its auxiliary cause—
[as stated in] *Kevalibhukti* verse 10—
for hunger is not an effect of deluding karma (*mohanīya*), since it arises from feeling-producing karma (*vedanīya*).
—Sya-ra-pṛ 473: There is no ripening of delusion (*vimoha-pāka*) which cannot be averted by the cultivation of its antidote;
for indeed, every ripening of delusion is averted by that [cultivation].
—*Kevalibhukti*, verse 7; *Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
474; *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*, p. 393B.

Internal [hunger] (ādhyātmika) is not of the nature of the fruition of delusion (moha-vipāka), because that fruition is averted through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) by means of cultivating its antidote; for instance, the passions (*kaṣāya*) are averted by cultivating their opposites. However, hunger, being a fruition pertaining to the living soul (*jīva*) and the matter-particles (*pudgala*), like disease, cold, or heat, is not averted merely by contrary mental impressions (*pratīpa-vāsanā*). Therefore, hunger does not have the nature of the fruition of delusion. — *Sūtrakṛtāṅga-niryukti*, p. 346A.
Yuktiprabheda, p. 150:
It is produced;
[it is] like hunger, cold, heat, and wind, as well as the desire for its remedy.
"For the deluded person, due to delusion, there arise intense afflictions such as cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth; for these are indeed to be experienced"— *Kevalibhukti*, verse 8.13.

[Syādvādamañjarī, p. 474] Now, it may be argued that if hunger is admitted in the Blessed One, there is a contradiction with his omniscience and other attributes; for when hunger arises, just as in our own case, there would be a diminution of knowledge, vision, and physical activity. This is incorrect, because even when hunger has arisen upon the destruction of the *jñānāvaraṇa* (knowledge-obscuring) and other karmas, a diminution of knowledge and so forth is impossible. Indeed, the diminution [of faculties] is caused by the manifestation (*udaya*) of karmas such as *jñānāvaraṇa*. Therefore, while in our case a greater diminution of those [faculties] is logical due to the intensity of their manifestation, in the Blessed One, however, because of the complete removal of all such obscuring karmas, there is no diminution of knowledge and so forth, even though hunger exists.
For smoke does not arise even when fuel is present if fire is absent;

and if hunger were produced by those four types of karma, there would be a contradiction with the scripture which states that the eleven afflictions (parīṣaha), such as hunger and thirst, arise from the karma of feeling (vedanīya) in the case of a Jina. Furthermore, it is not possible for a *sayogakevalin* who dwells for nearly ten million pūrvas at the maximum duration of his bodily existence to remain without food for such a length of time.

If it is argued that because of his infinite vigor (*anantavīrya*), his [existence] persists even without that [food], then by the same logic, its persistence would follow even without the life-force karma (*āyuṣkarma*); consequently, there would never be any departure of the body and so forth, and thus a final farewell would be given to liberation (*mokṣa*). Alternatively, if its persistence depends upon the life-force karma, then let it also depend upon food, since there is no difference between the two in their being causes for that [persistence]. Furthermore, he possesses infinite bliss accompanied by qualities such as knowledge.
Hunger and other such afflictions do not trouble one who is full; rather, there is great exaltation. (30.11)
Jainatarkabhāṣā, p. 8:
"Due to the rise of knowledge-obscuring [karma]—[the portion] 'until its destruction'—Ba."
Then, in that [state] possessing the excellence of the exhaustion of knowledge, the fourfold karma— Śra., Ba.

In the Jina, for whom the four destructive karmas (*ghātikarman*) have been cast off, the eleven afflictions (*parīṣaha*) exist because of the presence of the karma of experience (*vedanīyakarman*); or rather, one should supply the remainder of the sentence as "the eleven [afflictions] do not exist in the Jina"— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 9.11.

Thus, according to such scriptural authority (*āgama*), the fact that the Kevalin dwells for nearly ten million *pūrvas* as stated in the Sūtra is established; otherwise, liberation would not have a fixed duration of time.
—*Kevalibhukti*, verse 24;
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 613;
*Sūtrakṛtāṅga-śīlāṅkācārya-vṛtti*, p. 346B.
*Syādvādamañjarī*, folio 480;
*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya-ṭīkā*, folio 395A— [the portion] beginning with "pūrvakoṭi-viha— " [is found] in manuscript B.
Just as food is the cause of life, so too would enjoyment be joined [to the self] even without being consumed, like the duration of one's lifespan.
Let it be that one remains with infinite vigor; even without life-span, one might remain for a duration of time.
However, the application of vigor is not like that of knowledge; rather, through the destruction of karma, there is attainment.
In that regard, just as food is required for life-span, so too is it required for vigor, yet there is no obstruction therein.

—*Kevalibhukti*, verses 20–21, *Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 480. Furthermore, the body is comparable to the flame of a lamp or a stream of water; just as the lamp-flame does not persist when the oil is exhausted, nor does a stream of water persist without the influx of more water, so too the body cannot maintain its existence in the absence of food.

Just as a lamp does not remain when its oil is exhausted, nor does a stream of water persist without the arrival of more water, so too the body cannot endure without the application of food— Kevalibhuktiśataka, verse 31.
In that regard, as in the case of the absence of food for a person (*ārya*), [the same applies]. *Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
as in the case of the absence of food for a noble one (*ārya*).

—[If it is argued: "There is no sitting," then eating would be a fault, since the renunciation of fasting and so forth is practiced [by Arhats]; yet a fault is contradictory in the case of one who is faultless (kevalin). If that were so, then sitting and walking would not be possible for the Arhat, because sitting and such are renounced through the yoga of standing and so forth; and speech would not be possible, because he is observed to be observing a vow of silence. Furthermore, eating would be a fault, since one fasts [to avoid it], and yet there is no fault in the case of one who is faultless.
Thus it has been stated that sitting is appropriate for an Arhat, but not standing or other postures—
*Kevalibhuktiśloka*, verse 28;
*Syādvādaratnākara*, page 480.
Regarding the fault concerning eating:

if it is argued that how can there be eating for one who knows everything and perceives [the impurity of] meat and so forth, since an obstacle (*antarāya*) would arise? That is incorrect, because it is not invariably so in the case of the supreme sages (*paramarṣi*) possessing clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*). For they perceive the entire three worlds and yet they eat. Likewise, the Kevalin also [eats];

for an obstacle exists only with respect to the objects of the senses and nowhere else. Otherwise, there would be an obstacle even during the state of being a non-omniscient (*chadmastha*), since at that time too the Blessed One directly perceives all things through clairvoyant knowledge.

For one who has attained the ultimate limit [of knowledge], even as a *chadmastha* (one still in the state of spiritual obscuration), there can be no obstruction even in the perception of all objects; otherwise, it would not be so even previously. (*Bhukti-kevalibhu*, verse 32).
[Syādvādamañjarī, p. 480] "By the great sages and non-sages... [Bhagavatīsūtra].
Nor does the Kevalin have an attachment to sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) upon eating, because sensory cognition does not arise merely from the contact between a sense organ and its object.
What then? It is when there is a connection with that [object] and a subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of sensory cognition (*matijñānāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, since this [connection] does not exist in the *kevalin* (the omniscient one) for whom all veils have been entirely destroyed, there is no consequence of such cognition [arising]. Otherwise, even when there is a connection of the sense organs—such as the ear—with the sound of divine musical instruments, with the forms of the *gaṇadharas* and other deities, with the fragrances of scented flowers, incense, and perfumes, and with the touch of the wind and the lion-throne, sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) would necessarily follow, just as it occurs upon the attainment of an object by the senses during eating.
It is excluded by the attainment of those [objects]— namely sound, smell, form, and touch— [as stated in] *Kevalibhūṣaṇa* verse 33 (*Syādvādamañjarī*, p.
If gustatory sensory cognition were to arise through food, then olfactory cognition would likewise arise through the satisfaction of smelling flowers—
[Dvātriṃśikā 30].

In the morning and in the afternoon, for three-quarters of a watch (*prahara*) during the very time of teaching the Dharma, that Blessed One remains seated upon the lion-throne. For the remainder of the day, however, having gone to the divine abode called Devacchandaka— which is beyond the reach of other humans and animals except for the *gaṇadhara* gods, situated within the second enclosure of the assembly hall (*samavasaraṇa*) in the northeastern direction— he remains at ease on a couch or a seat.
And there, knowing that the food brought by the Gaṇadhara deities was purified of all defects, he accepts it when the sensation of hunger arises;

they see the food placed into his hand, but they do not see how he eats it, because the eating and digesting of food by an omniscient one is beyond the range of perception of humans and animals. Thus it is said.
He enters the assembly hall through the eastern gate; then,
having circumambulated [the central shrine], he sits upon the eastern lion-throne with his feet placed upon a footstool, having performed salutations to the Tīrthaṅkaras.
The Lord, with his profound and sweet voice, provides the teaching—
Kālaloka 30–32.
And in the forenoon, within the second enclosure wall, in the northeast direction, there is [the place] measuring three-quarters of a pāda.
They fashioned the celestial abode for the sake of their master’s repose—
Thus, when the bali-offering ritual was completed, the Victors descended from the first enclosure to the northeast corner of the second enclosure.
Having reached Devacchada, they dwell happily with the denizens of heaven—
Kālaloka 30.68–69.

For instance, that Blessed One remains seated upon his lion-throne only during the time for teaching the Dharma—specifically from the forenoon until one-quarter of a *prahara* remains in the afternoon; the remainder of the day he spends as he pleases in the divine abode named Devacchandaka.
There, when the sensation of hunger arises, he partakes of food brought by the *gaṇadhara* deities, knowing it to be entirely free from defects.

Those with the "moon-eye" (*māsa-cakṣus*) behold the food placed in his sprout-like hands, yet they do not see how he eats, because the intake and removal of food by an omniscient being is beyond the scope of those with the moon-eye.
—*Syādvādamañjarī*, p. 469.
Therein, the *Gaṇadhara* establishes that the omniscient one (*kevalin*) possesses non-material food (*nokarmāhāra*), preceded by the rejection of material food (*kavalāhāra*).

To this, the following reply is given: As for what was stated—that because of the existence of external and internal causes characterized by the rising of karma such as that to be experienced through food (*āhāra-vedya*), hunger arises, and thus the Blessed One’s eating occurs with its causes unimpaired, and so forth—that is incorrect. For, given the existence of those [causes] and the resulting arising of hunger, would you establish merely "eating" (*āhāra*) in the case of a Kevalin, or "morsel-eating" (*kavalāhāra*)? In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since we accept that souls who are *sayoga-kevalins* (omniscient beings still engaged in physical activity) are consumers of food.

For six kinds of nutriment are well-known in the teaching (pravacana), as stated in the Bhāvaśataka-gāthā 110: "Non-karmic nutriment, karmic nutriment, morsel food, and adhesive food, as well as mental and volitional— nutriment is to be known as sixfold in sequence."

And in that case, even in the absence of solid food (*kavalāhāra*), because there exists another form of nourishment characterized by the taking in of *karma* and *nokarma*, the Blessed One’s state of being a consumer of food (*āhāritva*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, it is not logical to maintain that the state of being a consumer of food for living beings consists solely of solid food; for if that were so, it would follow that one-sensed beings, egg-born creatures, gods, and those non-human beings who do not eat, as well as humans who do not eat, would be non-consumers of food. However, in the second position (that the definition of eating applies to all), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the gods and others; for although hunger arises in them due to the emergence of *vedanīya* and other karmas, they lack solid food.

Now, if it is argued that the manifestation of that [karma] establishes it even for the Kevalin despite its being characterized by darkness (*tamas*), then this is the great majesty of the Kevalin: namely, that while the manifestation of that [karma] is incapable of establishing solid food (*kavalāhāra*) among living beings who are overwhelmed by the malignant planets of sense-objects, it becomes capable of doing so in his case!
852, l. 1). Here, is it merely food that is established, or is it specifically solid food?—*Ratnakaṇikā-ṭīkā*, p. 5.
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*,

page 300: "Because of that state— from those beginning with one-sensed beings up to the omniscient with activity (*sajogakevalin*)"— here, having set aside material food, physical warmth, and mental-karma food, non-material food (*nokarmāhāra*) is to be understood.
From the stationary body up to the last stage of the soul with yoga, it is an eater— Jīvakāṇḍa, Gāthā 697.
Non-karmic food, karmic food, mouthful food, plaster food,
and even mental food— food is to be known as sixfold in sequence.
Non-karmic and karmic food belong to living beings who have entered the four states of existence.
Mundane beings have solid food as their nourishment; trees have sap as their nourishment;

birds have air as their nourishment; and for those dwelling among the immobile [plants], there is mental nourishment. Among the gods, there is a fourfold [nourishment], but none of these exists for the Kevalin.

The inclusion of non-karma and karma is stated regarding him in a figurative sense for the sake of his self; it is not, however, in an absolute sense, because he too is indeed supreme among those free from passion—
*Bhāvaśataka*, verses 110–113.
This is cited from Bhāvasena’s *Śloka* 226—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
300; *Pravacanasāroddhāra-ṭīkā*, p. 28.

In the Śvetāmbara scriptures, three kinds of food are described: *Ratnakaṇḍa-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī*, folio 5, states: "Food is of three types: *ojas*, *loman*, and *prakṣepa*. Food as *ojas* is [ingested] by the body through touch; food as *loman* is [ingested] by the skin."

Furthermore, it should be known that food is of two kinds: morsel-food (*kāvalika*) and subtle-essence-food (*oyāhāra*). All organisms in their incomplete stage (*apajjattaga*) should be understood as taking subtle-essence-food;
those in their complete stage (*pajjattaga*) should be known to take both subtle-essence-food and morsel-food.
There is no rebirth for the one-sensed deities and the denizens of hell; there is rebirth for all other living beings remaining within the cycle of existence—
Sūtrakṛtāṅga-niryukti, Gāthā 170–73.

In the *Bauddhadharmasaṃgraha*, food is explained as being fivefold: meditative food (*dhyānāhāra*), morsel food (*kavalīkāhāra*), withdrawal food (*pratyāhārāhāra*), contact food (*sparśāhāra*), and conscious food (*sacetanikāhāra*)—*Dharmasaṃgraha*, p. 15. [The five types of food are:
non-karmic food, karmic food, morsel food, and adhesive food.
Non-physical food,
physical food, and mental food are each to be known as sixfold in sequence. (Bhāvasaṅgrahaṇī,
Gāthā 110) [It is] stainless, free from the suffering of old age and disease, and devoid of the influx of karmic matter.
There is no mucus, saliva, or sweat, nor is there any loathsome odor;
[this is] the yogin, bound to the *nokarma* body, who is most divine at every moment. (Bodhapāhuḍa Gāthā 37)
Bound by its own duration, it binds with a remaining lifespan that has dwindled to a mere fraction—[Labdhisāra, Gāthā 614].

Because of the complete elimination of all obstacles to attainment (*lābhāntarāya*), those Kevalins who have abandoned the activity of solid food intake receive, at every moment, infinite, supremely pure, subtle *pudgala* particles—uncommon to other humans—which serve as the cause for sustaining the strength of their bodies; this is "attainment" (*lābha*) resulting from destruction (*kṣāyika*).
— Sarvārthasiddhi 2.4:
[This refers to] the Arhat who takes in food consisting of non-meritorious and meritorious *nokaṣāya* karma.

That the body persists is a point we also accept— this being the first position [of the opponent]. However, in that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because it is admitted that even liberated souls (*siddha*) and those who have attained the state of isolation through yoga (*ayogakevalin*) are living beings who take food.
—Ratnakaṇḍa-ṭīkā, p. 5; Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 300:
Therefore, with respect to non-material (nokarma) food, the omniscient ones (kevalins) possess the state of being eaters.
—Pravacana-sāroddhāra-ṭīkā, p. 29:
"In one-sensed beings (*ekendriya*), no *lepāhāra* (nutritional intake by absorption) arises. [Note: The manuscript reading *na kava* is corrected to *na kvāpi* based on the context.]

Since mental food exists among all the hosts of gods, it cannot be said that the maintenance of the body of the Lord of Jinas is preceded by the consumption of solid food— Bhāvasaṃgraha, verses 230–31.
