In the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 300, there is a deviation [of the reason] due to its presence in the body of a god; in the *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali-ṭīkā*, page 5, it says:
"upon whose arising... (yadudaye), Ā. and Ba. editions.
That which, among the gods and others, is edible food (kavalāhāra) within its respective domain— [it is] uneven (viṣama)— Ā.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that the rise of karma such as *vedanīya* is capable of producing solid food (*kavalāhāra*) in a *kevalin*: from what is this established—that its rise therein is capable of producing that [food]? Is it from mere assertion (*abhyupagama-mātra*), or from valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? If it were from mere assertion, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because it would follow that everyone could establish whatever reality they desire.

Now, regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): what is the proof here—is it perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)? If it is perception, is it sensory (*aindriya*) or supersensory (*atīndriya*)? It cannot be sensory, because it is admitted that [the Kevalin] is beyond the range of all intake and discharge of food; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scripture stating, "The food and discharge of the Kevalin are concealed. As for the claim that supersensory perception operates therein, one must resort to the "drinking of the vessel" (an oath) to prove it, since [sensory perception] is incapable of establishing the existence of solid food intake (*kavalāhāra*).
When the taking in and the casting out of food are concealed and invisible to the physical eye,
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) [is the means] for the direct realization of the consumption of all knowledge;

as for inference (*anumāna*), what is the logical mark (*liṅga*) here—is it the very arising of that [knowledge], being human, or the state of having a body? It cannot be the very arising of that [knowledge], because its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is demonstrated by [the case of] the gods (*tridaśa*) and others;
nor can it be being human, because of the inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) due to the *ayogakevalin*.

Now, since he has transcended the nature of a human being, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikānta) on his account; however, in that case, the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha), because even a *sayogakevalin* possesses that [transcendence], having likewise transcended it.
As it has been said:
"There is no inconclusiveness" (nānekānta, Ba; na tenānekānta, Śra).

Because he has transcended the nature of ordinary men who are not yogis, he has passed beyond the human condition; and since he is a deity even among deities, he does not possess the state of being dependent on a physical body. For instance, regarding the argument: "The Blessed One’s maintenance of a body is preceded by food, because it is a maintenance of a body, like the maintenance of the bodies of people such as ourselves"—in this syllogism, is it intended to prove that his bodily maintenance is preceded by mere food in general, or that it is preceded by solid food (kavalāhāra)? In the first case, it is said that one is proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
In the second alternative, however, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the gods (tridaśa) and others, since their bodily maintenance is possible even in the absence of solid food (kavalāhāra).

If it is specified that [the reason] is "because of the maintenance of a gross body" (audārika-śarīra-sthititvāt), then there is no deviation; yet that is not correct. This is because the maintenance of their gross body consists in a form of maintenance that is supremely gross, and is thus distinct from the maintenance of a gross body such as ours;
and just as in the state of a Kevalin there is an absence of the growth of hair and so forth, the absence of eating in that state is likewise entirely uncontradicted.
Because of its unique state,
it should be known as the physical body of the Worthy One (Arhat), possessing all such qualities, endowed with every excellence, and emitting a sublime fragrance.
—Bodhaprābhṛta-gāthā 39:

That body of the Blessed One is not gross, but rather supremely sublime; a form consisting of the essence of light, resembling pure crystal, arises for him whose defects are exhausted and who is devoid of the seven constituents.
—Pravacanasaṃgrahaṭīkā, p. 28: "While remaining in a most gross body, [there is] the growth of hair and so forth"—Śrī., Ba.

Now, if it is argued that the absence of growth in those [hair and nails] is brought about by divine intervention (*devopanīta*) and not born from the destruction of the destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*), such that the absence of their consumption in the state of omniscience (*kevalyavasthā*) might likewise be established—just as Indra, immediately after plucking out the hair of a child, whirls his thunderbolt (*vajra*) around the Blessed One’s nails and hair, and thus there is no growth in them—that is incorrect. For, due to the power of the thunderbolt, it would follow that they could not even sprout from the root, and it would further follow that all Tīrthaṅkaras would be perceived as having identical hair and so forth. But this is not the case, because the mass of hair of Tīrthaṅkaras such as Ṛṣabha is observed to be distinct in its relative weight (*gurulaghubhāva*).

Therefore, since at the stage of the destruction of the destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*) only as many nails and hairs as one possesses remain, there exists in the state of omniscience (*kevalitva*) a specific excellence born from that destruction characterized by the absence of growth in the hair and so forth for the duration of that body; likewise, let there also exist an excellence characterized by the absence of eating, as there is no distinction between them.

Furthermore, if eating were admitted for this [omniscient being] as it was during the stage of the obscured state (*chadmastha*), then the presence of eyelashes, blinking, the growth of nails and hair, and so forth would also have to be admitted.
Or, if one accepts the excellence of the absence of that [eating], then the excellence of the absence of eating must also be accepted, as there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Furthermore, because of the power of austerity (*tapas*), there is no contradiction whatsoever in the maintenance of the body even when preceded by non-eating—just as in the case of having four faces and so forth.

For it is observed that the state of the body for one who eats five times [a day] is exactly the same as that of one who eats four, three, two, or once [a day], provided they are endowed with the cultivation of the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*). Likewise, the state of the body for one who eats every day is exactly the same as that of one who eats with intervals of one, two, or more days.
Furthermore, it is heard that even when there was a deficiency of food for as long as a year, the bodily stability of Bāhubalin and others remained exceptional;
for indeed, the primary cause of such stability is the very karma of lifespan (*āyuḥ-karma*), while eating and so forth are merely auxiliary factors.

Moreover, the nourishment of their bodies is possible because, through the destruction of the obstacle to gain (*lābhāntarāya*), they obtain divine atoms (*paramāṇu*) at every moment which serve as the cause for that nourishment.
The absence of growth of hair and so forth; "the hair of the head, beard, and body hairs remain as they were" (Āyāraṅga-sutta 34); "faults have been removed" (Bṛhatkalpa-bhāṣya).
arising from the destruction of the substrate (dhātikṣayaja), immediately after the arising of the noble [path] (āryotpādānantara),
exclusively (kevala).
—ṇātiśa— [Variant:
śra°] In the case of the admission of eating by a Kevalin, [variant: ba°].

—If it is accepted that [he possesses] a pre-eminence [of power] due to the greatness of his asceticism, just as [the Lord Brahmā possesses] four faces and so forth, then what contradiction is there in his not eating beforehand? —*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
302. —[He] eats food during the day. —*Ba*.
—The "gain" (lābha) is also to be understood as described in the Śrāvakabhūmi (p.

Because of the complete elimination of all obstacles to gain, those Kevalins who have abandoned the act of taking morsel food (*kavalāhāra*) come into contact at every moment with infinite, supremely pure, subtle *pudgala* particles that are not shared by other humans and which serve as the cause for sustaining the strength of their bodies; this is the "gain" resulting from destruction (*kṣāyika*).

Therefore, that statement— asking how the existence of a coarse body for nearly a hundred thousand years prior to its limit could possibly occur without the consumption of solid food— is understood to be the work of one who is unlearned. (Rājavārttika 2.4)

The cause for the maintenance of an extremely gross body—characterized by the acquisition of gain from a supremely virtuous person through the exhaustion of obstacles to gain—is [the result of] that [merit].
(*Tattvārthaśloka*, p. 314; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

If it is argued that even in the absence of [food] for a month or a year, its continued existence does not constitute an untimely state, because one perceives the resumption of activity toward that food once again—then from what source is this non-perception of an untimely state during its existence? Is it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through inference (*anumāna*)? If it were through direct perception, then a funeral libation (*jalāñjali*) has been offered to the omniscient and dispassionate ones, since there is no distinction between them and others in the non-perception of such [untimely states]. If its establishment is through inference, then that is no different in other cases as well.

For just as the excellence of knowledge and the removal of the veil of defects reach a supreme limit somewhere because they are being perfected, like [the limit of] measurement, so too let it be said that for those who fast for one, two, or more days, the excellence of bodily maintenance preceded by fasting reaches a supreme peak somewhere because it is such [a perfection], just like that [excellence of knowledge], since there is no difference [in the reasoning]. Therefore, even regarding the maintenance of the body, it cannot be maintained that the Blessed One experiences the arising of hunger capable of necessitating the consumption of solid food due to the arising of the *vedanā* (sensation) and other [mental factors].
Those bodies remain for a month or even a year by virtue of that which was consumed; they do not perish before their time, nor otherwise. (From *Bhukti-kevalibhukti*, verse 22).
*Syādvādamañjarī*, folio 480—wherein it says: "How could there be [a state] remaining therein? (*kutastatrasthi*)—Ā. (Commentary).

Therefore, since the excellence of the abandonment of passion and other defilements is observed through the power of cultivating their opposites (*vipakṣabhāvanā*), and since this establishes that such a supreme degree [of abandonment] exists in the Kevalin (the Omniscient One), why should the supreme degree of the absence of eating not also exist there, given that the possibility of being free from passion is established? For there is no difference in observing an excellence of abandonment even regarding eating and so forth due to that cultivation;

for instance, one who eats many times in a single day might, through the power of cultivating the opposite, eat only once, while another might skip a meal by intervals of one day or more, and yet another might skip meals with intervals of a fortnight, a month, or a year.
—*Ratnakaṇikā-ṭīkā*, p. 6; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 302.

Furthermore, the state of having all causes complete is unestablished for hunger; for it is only when karma such as that to be experienced (*vedya*) is assisted by deluding karma (*mohanīya*) that it possesses the full capacity to produce effects such as hunger, and not otherwise, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For just as an army becomes powerless when its commander has fallen, so too do the non-obscuring (*aghāti*) karmas become powerless when deluding (*mohanīya*) karma is destroyed. And just as poison, once rendered neutral by a physician, is unable to cause burning, fainting, or other such effects even when administered, so too are the karmas of feeling (*vedya*) and so forth, as well as hunger and the like, incapable of producing their effects when the rise of delusion has been consumed by the fire of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Hunger does not exist in the Blessed One, because of the absence of its cause, which is delusion; for wherever there is an absence of a cause, its effect does not occur, just as there is no smoke in a place where there is no fire; and in the Arhat, delusion is absent.
Just as hunger destroys [the body], so too does the *vedanīya* [karma] destroy the soul by the power of *moha*;
for it is only when aided by *mohanīya* karma that *vedanīya* has the capacity to produce hunger. (Jīva-go. Karma-kā. Gā. 19)
—*Ratnakaṇikā-ṭīkā*, p. 6; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 303:

Just as a seed of rice or similar grain, when accompanied by the auxiliary cause of water, produces its effect such as a sprout, even so does the karma of non-pleasurable experience (*asadvedya-karman*), when accompanied by the auxiliary cause of delusion (*mohanīya*), produce effects such as hunger.
—Pravacana-ṭīkā, p. 28—[reading "ghātikarma" in manuscript *ba* and *ā*; reading "upabhujyamāna" in manuscript *ba*]

Furthermore, O Ācārya, O Śrāvaka, if the rising (*udaya*) of *karmas* were to produce its effect independently [of other factors], then since the rising of the three types of *vedanās* or *kaṣāyas* exists among those who are negligent (*pramatta*) and so forth, sexual intercourse, frowning, and the like would occur. Consequently, due to the agitation of the mind, how could there be the attainment of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*) or the ascent of the ladder of destruction (*kṣapakaśreṇī*), from which the destruction of *karmas* would result? [Objection: "In that case, even the rising of the *nāma-karma* and other [auspicious] *karmas* would not perform its own function there [in the higher stages]. [Reply: This is incorrect; for it is logically consistent that auspicious (*śubha*) dispositions perform their own functions there, as they are unobstructed.

For just as when a powerful king who follows his own path has gained control over a region, even wicked people living there cannot commit their wicked deeds [with impunity], whereas good people, by virtue of being unimpeded, can carry out their own tasks; so too, in this case, why is it that only unwholesome (*aśubha*) dispositions (*prakṛti*) deserve to have their capacity obstructed by the Arhat, and not wholesome (*śubha*) dispositions? It is said in reply: the Arhat destroys the intensity (*anubhāga*) of unwholesome dispositions, but not that of wholesome ones; for punishment is meted out to those who destroy virtues, not to those who are without fault.

If [it is argued that] even in the absence of delusion (moha) it produces the afflictions (parīṣaha) such as hunger, then it should also produce the afflictions such as deafness and disease; but it does not do so—[see] *Pravacana-ṭīkā* p. 28, *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* p. 303.
And [it is said] by Śrī Kṣapaṇaśreṣṭhin:
"Because auspicious natures (śubhaprakṛti) are not obstructed therein"—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 303.
—by means of [their] nature as [such], the good people... bound by a firm agreement... (Baṣa) ...sujanas...
bound by a firm agreement... (Baṣa)

Furthermore, if even that which has its capacity obstructed (*pratibaddhasāmarthya*) were to produce its own effect—such as unpleasant feeling (*asātāvedanīya*)—then the Blessed One’s arrangement of the *daṇḍaka* and *kapāṭa* [mechanisms] would be futile. For those mechanisms are established so that when a short lifespan or other such [karmic result] becomes associated with a longer duration, the karmas may be brought to an equal duration; yet it is impossible to alter a karma capable of yielding its fruit through its long duration by even a hundred means. Thus, no one at all would ever be liberated.

Now, if by the power of austerity (*tapas*) karma equal to life-span (*āyuḥkarma*)—which has been worn away and is incapable of yielding its fruit due to its excessive duration—is transformed [into another form], then likewise let the experienceable karma (*vedya*) also be so transformed, as there is no distinction between them.

Nor does the production of an effect occur merely because there is no cause for it; otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the effects of the sense organs and so forth arising, and even the Lord’s sensory cognition (*mati-jñāna*) and passions (*rāga*, etc. would follow as consequences.

If it is argued that the sense organs and so forth do not perform their own functions due to the absence of auxiliary causes, namely the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil and the deluding karma (*mohanīya-karma*), then for this very reason, the experienceable karma (*vedanīya*) would also [not produce its effect] due to the lack of such auxiliaries, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Because the act of striking (in *daṇḍapratarādi*) is a movement, there is an outward emergence of the soul's spatial units (*ātmapradeśa*) collectively; this is "total projection" (*samuddhāta*).

Since the karma to be experienced (*vedanīya*) is abundant while the life-span (*āyus*) is meager, for the purpose of equalizing the life-span without prior volition—due to its inherent nature as a substance, like the subsiding of the foam, force, and bubbles of a liquid such as wine—the total projection of the soul's spatial units residing within the body from the outside is the "Kevali-total-projection" (*kevalisamuddhāta*).
—Rājavārtika, p. 53:
"Leaving behind the original body, the emergence of the living aggregate of the subsequent body from the [original] body is what is called *samudghāta*."
— Jīvaka, Gāthā 667—
The life-span karma (*āyu-karma*) of one whose duration has been exhausted is performed, Śrāmaṇa.
For this very reason, Śrī [Siddhasena Divākara] says:

"And this hunger is not the effect of *vedanīya* alone, independent of *mohanīya*, such that it would occur even when delusion (*moha*) is completely destroyed. To explain: hunger is not the effect of *vedanīya* independent of *mohanīya*, because it is a form of desire, like the desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*).

For hunger is indeed the desire to eat; how then could it be the effect of *vedanīya* alone? Otherwise, the desire to take pleasure in wombs and so forth—namely, *riraṃsā*—would also be its effect. And in that case, just as with solid food, there would be the undesirable consequence of [such desire] occurring even toward women and the like; thus, there would be no distinction between this [hunger] and the Lord (*Īśvara*)."
And just as the desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*) ceases through the cultivation of its antidote, so too does hunger cease;

the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the longing for food ceases through the cultivation of its antidote, because it is a form of longing, like the longing for women and the like. [Objection: Granted that there may be its cessation at the time of that cultivation, but in its absence, activity would surely occur again. This is the same even in the case of longing for women and the like.

Just as there is the absolute cessation of this mind because it consists of the cultivation of its antidote, so too is there the cessation of the desire for food. And just as the desire for women and the like is incompatible with the state of being free from delusion (*nirmoha*), so too is hunger incompatible with it. Thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The Kevalin does not possess hunger, because he is endowed with a nature characterized by freedom from delusion which is opposed to it; for whatever is endowed with a nature opposed to something else does not possess that thing—just as a certain region endowed with the nature of a hot touch does not possess a cold touch—and the Kevalin is endowed with a nature characterized by freedom from delusion which is opposed to hunger. [This concludes the section on] independence from the *mohanīya* karma. (*ba*)

For instance, [the commentary on the *Ratnakaraṇḍa* states]: "Hunger (*bubhukṣā*) is indeed the desire to eat; since that is an effect of deluding karma (*mohanīya*), how could it exist in the Blessed One, whose delusion has been destroyed? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a desire for sexual pleasure (*rirasā*) also existing in him.
(*Ratnakaraṇḍa-ṭīkā*, p. 6)
There would be activity [toward the object of cognition]. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 304; Śrāmaṇya)

By this, the following is also refuted: that if hunger were ceased through the cultivation of its antidote (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), then for the sake of counteracting the sensation of hunger, the scripture would teach that very cultivation and not the seeking of alms (*piṇḍaiṣaṇā*), and so forth. For as long as the mind has not yet achieved the state of being constituted by the cultivation of the antidote, there is the teaching on the seeking of alms; but once that state is established, just as the sensation of desire ceases, the cessation of the sensation of hunger is established in its entirety—so why would there be any need for the seeking of other substances to counteract that sensation? Now, if it is argued that hunger is not of the nature of longing (*ākāṅkṣā*), and therefore its occurrence is possible even in one who is free from delusion (*vītamoha*), then how could the desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*)—which is likewise not of the nature of longing—not also be possible there? If it is argued that its lack of the nature of longing contradicts experience, then the same applies to hunger.

Or, even if this [hunger] were of the nature of non-desire, it would still be impossible in the Blessed One because it is of the nature of suffering; for that which is of the nature of suffering cannot exist in Him, just as the torment of desire and so forth [cannot]. And hunger is of the nature of suffering;
where there is infinite bliss, not even a trace of suffering exists, as in the case of the Siddhas. And the Arhat possesses infinite bliss.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that what is intended [by you] is that infinite bliss which consists in the cessation of all afflictions? That is unproven, because hunger-affliction is admitted [to exist]. For such [bliss] belongs only to the *siddhas* who are liberated from all karma, and not to the *arhats*, since the arising of the *vedanīya* (feeling-producing) karma is possible for them. [Reply: This is incorrect; for it has been established on page 853, line 15 that the arising of that [karma] does not serve as a cause of affliction in that state.
Furthermore, [the text continues with] "now, in the form of a crow... (*atha kākṣārūpā*).
Its non-existence [is established] in the Kevalin, O Śrī, because of the absence of the nature of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).
How could there be for him, who is named Ananta (the Infinite), the affliction of hunger or thirst, since he possesses mastery over the four infinities?
— *Ratnakaraṇḍa-ṭīkā*, p. 6.

If there is the affliction of hunger, then for one whose power is exhausted by hunger, infinite vigor (*anantavīrya*) does not exist; likewise, for one suffering from hunger, even infinite bliss (*anantasukha*) does not exist—*Pravacanaprameyakamalamārtaṇḍa-ṭīkā*, p. 28, p. 299.
When [the goal] is accomplished, there is infinite bliss (śrī) which is absolute; because of the infinite [nature of] the removal of karma (ābhāsa), [there is] the destruction of bondage (ba).
Furthermore, regarding the arising of that which is to be experienced:

the Arhat possesses infinite bliss that pervades all parts and remains unimpeded, because it is non-localized; and since pleasure and pain are contradictory and cannot coexist in the same place at the same time, how could even a trace of the suffering of hunger be possible there? Otherwise, like the pleasure of those such as ourselves, that bliss would be merely localized.
Therefore, such bliss, when present in the Blessed One, removes its own opposite, suffering—just as fire removes cold.

And upon the cessation of that [suffering], there is the cessation of hunger, which is pervaded by it; for when the pervader ceases, the pervaded necessarily ceases, just as a *śiṃśapā* tree ceases when the tree ceases. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: where there exists a powerful contrary factor, even its fully arisen cause does not occur there, just as cold does not exist in an extremely hot region; and in the *kevalin*, there exists infinite bliss, which is a powerful contrary to the suffering of hunger.

Likewise, when something exists in a place that is incompatible with and cannot be removed by its effect, it does not produce its own effect there even if it is present in its entirety. For example, in a person afflicted by an incurable bile disorder (pitta-vikāra) that is contrary to phlegm (śleṣman) and the like, curds and such do not produce phlegm and the like. And since bliss—which is incompatible with and cannot be removed by the fruit of [ordinary] objects of knowledge—is present in the Blessed One, this [objection] is refuted: namely, that "there is no increase in hunger despite the decrease in knowledge and so forth in children and others"; for it is established that only those qualities such as knowledge which coexist with infinite bliss are antagonistic to hunger. —Śikam iva Ā. (Āgama-prāmāṇya).
Such pleasure— that is,
infinite pleasure pervading all parts—
does not exist [in others], whereas it exists in the Kevalin; for there is no suffering of hunger in him, because of the presence of infinite pleasure which is its powerful opposite.
Wherever there is that which is opposed to a given object of knowledge—just as in the case of the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti* (p. 305), manuscript *ba*:

in the Kevalin, the *vedanīya* karma does not produce its own effect, namely the suffering of hunger, because of the presence of infinite bliss which is opposed to and incapable of being set aside by that effect.

As for what was stated—that "it cannot be apprehended by those of limited vision that the knowledge of the Kevalins and so forth do not oppose hunger, because these [states] are beyond the senses," and so on—that too is mere words. For if, due to their being beyond the senses, one cannot apprehend their opposition [to hunger], it would follow that one could likewise not apprehend their omniscience and other such qualities. Indeed, just as it cannot be apprehended by those of limited vision that hunger does not occur in the presence of those [Kevalins] because they are beyond the senses, so too [it cannot be apprehended] that "these [beings] are omniscient."

If it is argued that their state of directly perceiving [the objects] is understood through inference, then what offense has been committed against that [inference], such that this [direct perception] would not be understood from that inference? Furthermore, the inference regarding its opposition to hunger was established previously; therefore, enough of this digression.
Moreover, due to the Blessed One’s omniscience, there is an absence of hunger; for if hunger were admitted, his omniscience would be lost due to that impairment, and he would become powerless.

For it is well-attested in our own experience that when one is overcome by the affliction arising from hunger, there is an absence of knowledge and so forth; this is evident from the cognition: "Afflicted by hunger, I know nothing, I see nothing, and I am not even able to stand up" (pṛ.
853, l. 2). [This applies] to the case of perfect knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) and the rest.
The state of being opposed to hunger is perceived;
[the readings] *kṣudaviro-* (Ā) and *kṣudvittvānumā-* (Ba) are incorrect.

As for what was also stated—that [hunger] is based on the arising of karma such as knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) and that its destruction [results from their destruction], etc.—that too is incorrect; for just as there is no destruction of knowledge and so forth in the Blessed One whose obscurations have been entirely destroyed, so too it is impossible for even a trace of the affliction of hunger to exist in one whose delusion (moha) has been entirely destroyed.
This is because it was previously established in detail (pp. 854, l. 4) that "the *vedanīya* [karma], when assisted by *mohanīya*, is capable of producing hunger."

The scriptural authority (āgama) stating "there are eleven [afflictions] in the Jina" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 9.11) must also be understood as being intended to exclude the eleven afflictions such as hunger; for the etymology of "eleven" is "ten plus one.

The eleven afflictions, beginning with hunger, are the effects of the *vedanīya* karma when assisted by the *mohanīya* karma; however, in the case of the Arhat, because of the absolute destruction of its assistant (*mohanīya*), those [afflictions] do not exist there merely due to the arising of the *vedanīya* karma. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the afflictions such as disease also existing there, since in people like us, diseases and the like are perceived just as hunger and thirst are upon the arising of that [karma].

Since diseases and the like do not occur even when those [karmas] arise in the case of non-omniscient Jinas and those born in the *bhogabhūmi* (land of enjoyment), there is a deviation [of the rule]; let there likewise be a deviation regarding solid food (*kavalāhāra*), because it is absent even when those [karmas] arise in the case of gods and others.
Alternatively, one should supply the remainder of the sentence as "the eleven [types of karma] do not exist in a Jina," because sūtras possess an implicit completion (*sopaskāratva*).
— *Sarvārthasiddhi* 9.11.207.
Alternatively, this is not a supplementary statement [implying] that "eleven [pariṣahas] are postulated for the Jina by some"; what then? It is because they exist as eleven.

How so? By way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Just as there is the metaphorical designation of "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) for one whose knowledge-obscuring karma has been entirely eliminated and whose knowledge is perfect—even in the absence of the cessation of one-pointed thought—because the fruit of shaking off the dust of karma is possible; likewise, even though the afflictions (*parīṣaha*) consisting of hunger and other sensations are absent, since the existence of the material afflictions (*dravya-parīṣaha*) resulting from the emergence of karma to be experienced (*vedanīya-karma*) is present, it is appropriate to apply the metaphorical designation that "the eleven [afflictions] exist in the Jina."
—*Rājavārttika* 9.11:

In the Kevalin, there exist only eleven *parīṣahas* by way of potentiality (*śakti*) and not by way of manifestation (*vyakti*), because hunger and the rest do not manifest from the *kevala* [state] of the *vedanīya* karma; thus, they are to be understood as present there only figuratively (*upacārataḥ*).
"Therefore, for the Supreme Jinas, there are no afflictions caused by suffering"—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p. 492; "For them, there are no afflictions caused by suffering"—*Karmakāṇḍa*, gāthā 275.
Since hunger, thirst, and so forth are not capable of destroying delusion because they depend upon material karma, their existence is merely figurative. — *Bhāvasaṃgraha*, verse 234.

Furthermore, as for the claim that even by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) eleven afflictions (*parīṣaha*) are not possible for him [the Jina], that is because the Sūtra is intended to exclude them; for the etymological derivation is "there are not ten afflictions plus one in the Jina" (i.e., *ekādhikā na daśa parīṣahā jine*), meaning "eleven afflictions are not in the Jina. [Thus, they do not exist there. (*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 307). [The manuscript reading *śra* is incorrect.]

Furthermore, as for that which was stated regarding the arising of [karmic] experience— that one dwells for up to slightly less than ten million *pūrva*s, and so forth— that too is not tenable, because the duration of the body is established as being caused solely by the *āyus-karma* (life-span karma), and because its persistence until the end of time has been demonstrated even in the absence of [further] consumption [of karma].
(Page 854, Line 8)

As for what was also stated—that because eating is of the nature of a fault (*doṣa*), its impossibility in the Blessed One would entail the impossibility of speech and so forth—that too is a mere assertion. This is because speech and the like are produced by the rising of the karma of being a Tīrthaṅkara and cannot possibly be of the nature of a fault; for speech is not recited among the eighteen faults in the same way that hunger and the rest are.

Furthermore, the argument that "eating must exist there because it is produced by the rising of the karma of feeling (*vedanīya-karma*)" is also inconsistent, since it is established that this [karma] has the capacity to produce [eating] only when accompanied by the presence of delusion (*moha*).

For just as the state of being a Tīrthaṅkara, accompanied by the destruction of delusion (moha), is capable of producing distinguished speech and so forth, so too the karmic matter to be experienced (vedya), accompanied by the presence of delusion,

is capable of producing experiences such as eating; and because it is impossible [to claim] that even in the case of eating there is "going" (gati) since it is produced by the rise of the karma to be experienced (vedanīya)— for [the number of karmas] is not eighteen— [Āvaśyaka-niryukti 854, verse 15].
Because of the arising of defects— namely hunger, thirst, old age, disease, birth, death, fear, and pride—
and because of the word "and" (*ca*), anxiety, discontent, sleep, wonder, intoxication, perspiration, and dejection are also included. Furthermore, passion, hatred, and delusion [are also excluded].
These are the eighteen defects—*Ratnakaṇikā*, Ṭīkā 1.6:
*vedanīyopādi* (variant: *vedanīyopādāna*).

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that just like one possessing avadhijñāna, there is no possibility of obstruction even for an omniscient being who perceives the entire world, and so forth—that too is untenable; because that knowledge is functional, it is possible for it to directly perceive all objects within its own domain at that very moment.

For at the very moment an omniscient with limited knowledge (avadhijñānin) applies the attention (upayoga) of limited knowledge, he perceives every single object that constitutes its domain and nothing else; thus, if he were to apply such attention at the time of eating, there would certainly be an obstruction. However, this situation is not possible in the case of perfect knowledge (kevalajñāna), because it is always attentive (upayukta).
(Page 855, Line 1:
Regarding limited knowledge)
At the time of the operation [of knowledge],
there is always a connection with impurity for kevalajñāna— Śrā.

As for what was also stated—that sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) does not arise merely through the connection between the sense organ and its object—that too is unsound; for if the knowledge produced when there is a relationship between the object and the subject were not sensory cognition, it would follow that the very discourse on sensory cognition is cut off. If it is argued that the sense organs do not manifest their own effect even when connected to their respective objects because of the absence of the auxiliary condition (*sahakārin*), namely the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of sensory cognition (*matijñānāvaraṇa*), then [we reply: due to the absence of the auxiliary condition of deluding karma (*mohanīya*), the karma to be experienced (*vedya*) would likewise not produce its own effect. Thus it has been said (p. 855, l. 4).

Furthermore, for what purpose does he eat—is it for the sake of nourishing the body, for the sake of preventing the depletion of knowledge, vision, vigor, and so forth, for the sake of countering the sensation of hunger, for the sake of preventing the premature shortening (*apavartana*) of a lifespan that has not yet attained liberation, for the sake of pacifying greed for flavors, or for the sake of favoring the world? It is certainly not for the sake of nourishing the body, because that is accomplished simply by the acquisition of specific atoms at every moment due to the destruction of the obstacle to gain (*lābhāntarāya*); moreover, if he were to take food for that purpose, how could he be considered "naked" (*nirgrantha*), since the possibility of bodily attachment (*śarīrasammūrcchā*) would arise, just as in the case of an ordinary man?
Nor is it for the purpose of preventing the exhaustion of knowledge and so forth; for the non-exhaustion of those [faculties] is established precisely because there is no cause for their exhaustion.

Indeed, the cause of the exhaustion of knowledge and so forth is the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veils of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and the rest; since that [exhaustion] is perceived when there is an absence of food and such, and since that [cause] does not exist in the Blessed One whose veils have been entirely destroyed, how could there even be a suspicion of such exhaustion from which eating would follow? Nor is it for the sake of counteracting the sensation of hunger, because it has already been stated that this [sensation] is impossible in the Blessed One, who possesses infinite bliss and vigor.

Nor is it for the purpose of preventing the reduction (*apavartana*) of a lifespan that has not yet achieved liberation; for since those in their final and supreme bodies possess a lifespan that cannot be reduced, such a reduction is impossible for him.
Nor is it for the purpose of quelling greed for flavors; for in one who is free from delusion (*vītamoha*), greed for flavors is itself impossible.

Nor is it for the purpose of favoring the world; for one of infinite power (*anantavīrya*), due to the absence of any cause for the exhaustion of power, is capable of favoring the world even without eating.

Comparison— [The practitioner] consumes [food] neither for the sake of strength or exertion, nor for the sake of the body's growth, nor for the sake of radiance, nor for the sake of knowledge, nor for the sake of self-restraint, nor even for the sake of meditation.
62 *Pravacanaprameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 29; *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 306.
For the sake of the non-emergence of liberation from life and for the purpose of the nourishment of the body,
there is the absorption of the body (*śarīramūrcchā*).

Due to the very absence of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇīya-karman*), there is no reduction of lifespan; [this applies to] those born by spontaneous generation (*aupapāduka*), those in their final and supreme bodies, and those with an incalculable lifespan (*asaṃkhyeya-varṣāyus*), whose lifespans are non-reducible (*anapavartya*).
—Tattvārthasūtra 2.53:

Those whose final body is supreme are "those with a final and supreme body" (caramottamadeha); the meaning is that they have reversed the cycle of saṃsāra and are worthy of attaining nirvāṇa in that very birth.
—*Sarvārthasiddhi*:

"Those in their final body" means those in their last physical existence; they attain perfection in that very body. These are the supreme persons: the Tīrthaṅkaras, Cakravartins, and Ardhacakravartins. —*Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra*:
"Devas, hell-beings, and subhuman beings and humans have an infinite lifespan."
And likewise, for supreme beings (*uttamapuruṣa*) and those in their final body (*caramaśarīra*), there is no premature death (*nirupakrama*);
[as stated in the *Sthānāṅga*], the reduction of lifespan due to external conditions is an "apavartana" (premature exhaustion).
— Rājavārttika 2.53;
liberation— Śra.

As for what was said—that he goes to the *devacchandaka* and remains there at ease, and so forth—that too is mere words. For why would the Blessed One leave the *samavasaraṇa* and go there? Is it for the sake of achieving meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by avoiding mental distraction, or for the sake of remaining at ease because of an inability to maintain suppression [of the senses], or for the sake of performing secret activities? Regarding these, the first position is untenable; for since the Blessed One is mindless (*amanaska*), mental distraction is impossible, and furthermore, "meditative absorption" is applied there only figuratively due to the presence of the cessation of yoga (*yoganirodha*).
The second position is also untenable, because it is impossible for one who possesses infinite power to be incapable of cessation,
and since there is not even a trace of suffering in infinite bliss, the expression "according to pleasure" (yathāsukha) would also be difficult to justify.
(Page 558, Line 10)
Regarding that, as for the first position:

when the body is situated on a single seat, is the cessation of its movement and the performance of secret acts blameworthy or not? It cannot be blameworthy; for it is contradictory for one whose defects have been entirely exhausted to perform an act that is blameworthy.
Now, as for that which is irreproachable: is it eating, or is it the exhaustion of karma? It cannot be eating, because that is prohibited for the Blessed One who is free from delusion;

or, if it were not prohibited, why would he go to a secluded place to eat—out of fear of a flaw in his vision, fear of beggars, or because it is an improper practice? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because the Blessed One is beyond the scope of any flaw in his vision.

For how could he whose very name brings about the pacification of the defects of vision and so forth in others be himself within the scope of such defects? As for the second alternative, it proclaims a great meanness on the part of the Blessed One;

indeed, it is not fitting for a Great Being to go off alone for food, leaving behind his disciples who are clinging to him and tormented by hunger, just as it would be improper for a father to leave his son.
Furthermore, if this were an inappropriate practice, then it would not be wise to even imagine it, just as one would not imagine the service of women and the like.

O Vachaka, does the Arhat perform the destruction (*kṣapaṇa*) of even those karmas—whether previously acquired or acquired at the time of eating? If it is of those previously acquired, are they the destructive (*ghāti*) or the non-destructive (*aghāti*)? First, it cannot be the destructive ones, because they have already been destroyed prior [to that state];

nor can it be the non-destructive ones, because they will be destroyed in due course, and because he is capable of completely burning away the heap of fuel that is karma through the constant fire of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*).

It is not reasonable to maintain that the fire of the Blessed One’s white meditation blazes only in the Devacchandaka and not in the assembly hall (*samavaśaraṇa*) and other such places; for if that were so, it would follow that he would enter another state of meditation while remaining there [in the assembly hall].
[The text reads: "blazing in solitude" (*ekānte prajvalitaḥ*, *jvalati*).

Regarding the Blessed One who resides in the assembly hall (*samavasaraṇa*), how can there be the destruction of karma acquired at the time of eating? If it is argued that this occurs through *pratikramaṇa* (confession), let it be so; however, the Blessed One’s faultlessness would be difficult to maintain, for one who performs *pratikramaṇa* is not faultless—just like ourselves and others—and yet the Blessed One performs *pratikramaṇa*.

For *pratikramaṇa* is indeed the removal of committed faults; how could one who performs it be faultless? Or, if he does not perform it, how could he remove the fault produced by the act of eating? For even by the mere mention of food, a monk who is previously heedful becomes heedless, whereas the Arhat does not, even while eating—this is truly a great marvel. Furthermore, if he were possessed of faults, he would have fallen from his spiritual stage (*śreṇī*) and thus would not possess the state of a Kevalin (one with perfect knowledge). Moreover, [the Blessed One...]
Comparison: Furthermore, does he perform the *pratikramaṇa* (confession) and so forth after eating, or not?—*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.
306. "Confession (*pratikramaṇa*) is the manifestation of a counter-action through the utterance of 'false, it was a transgression' (*mithyā-duṣkṛta*)"—*Sarvārthasiddhi*, 9.
22. To whom does the *pratikramaṇa* belong?
"O Bhakti!

It is indeed a great marvel that a virtuous person, even when merely engaged in talk about food, remains vigilant, whereas an Arhat does not become negligent even while eating"—*Ratnakaranda-śrāvakācāra-ṭīkā*, p. 864.
Just as in the case of the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* (p.

306), where, despite the absence of the cessation of thought (*cintānirodha*), there is a metaphorical designation of "meditation" (*dhyānopacāra*) with respect to the fruit of that [cessation], namely the removal of karma—so too it is here: in the excellence of *kevalajñāna*, which has completely eliminated all knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and simultaneously illuminates all objects, even though there is no cessation of thought, [the term is applied] with respect to the fruit of that [cessation], which is the removal of karma.
(*Sarvārthasiddhi* 9)

As for what was also stated—that while he is eating, he is not seen even by the Gaṇadhara deities, and so forth—in that regard, what is the cause of his invisibility? Is it being covered by a thick veil of darkness, being veiled by a curtain or the like, his own concealment through a specific supernatural power (*vidyā*), or a particular excellence of majesty that surpasses other people? Among these, the first position is untenable, because the veil of darkness has been utterly eradicated by the radiance of his body.

Furthermore, how could alms be given to one who is covered by a screen or similar object? Moreover, if a specific supernatural power (*vidyā*) were admitted for him, it would contradict his status as a *nirgrantha* (one free from attachments), just like the case of the *vidyādharas* and others.

If it is claimed that he possesses some particular excellence of greatness surpassing other people—by virtue of which he is not seen while eating—then let it be granted that his excellence surpassing other people consists precisely in the absence of eating, since that alone is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, by one who desires for the Blessed One liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), characterized by the attainment of the four infinities, infinite bliss must be admitted.
And in that [state of liberation] being desired, the absence of experience must be accepted, because it has been established that without that [absence], infinite bliss is impossible (pṛ.

In that regard, the reasons for eating in concealment are: resorting to solitude because of associating with the improper; eating while situated in thick darkness; or concealing oneself by means of a specific magical power (*vidyā*)? — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

307. Furthermore, in the case of eating in secret, there is the ground of deceit (*māyāsthāna*), the practice of wretchedness (*dainyavṛtti*), and many other faults mentioned in the context of the purity of alms-food (*piṇḍaśuddhi*). — *Pravacanasāroddhāra-ṭīkā*, p. 29.
— The state of being covered by a film is granted;
and because of his acceptance of this, Ba.
In that case, since there is no consumption [of food] due to having an extremely gross body, why does this very distinction not exist? (Pramāṇavārttika-ṭīkā, p.

29). Furthermore, liberation characterized by that [absence of consumption] belongs only to a man and not to a woman, because she—like a eunuch—is unfit for it, and because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish her liberation.
In the debate concerning the liberation of women (*strī-nirvāṇa-vāda*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the White-robed ones (*Sitapaṭa*) and Śākaṭāyana is as follows:
"Indeed, there exists this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing that [liberation]: women possess liberation because they possess the complete causes, just like men.
For the cause of liberation is the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*); right view, knowledge, and conduct (*samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritra*) constitute the path to liberation" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 1.1).

Because this has been so stated, and because that [set of jewels] exists in women; for instance—right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is faith that the things spoken by the Omniscient One are exactly thus; right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is understanding them as they truly are; and right conduct (*samyakcāritra*) is the proper performance of the vows prescribed by Him. This triad of jewels, when perfected in women, accomplishes liberation characterized by the total release from all karma.

For there is no contradiction whatsoever between women and the Three Jewels, by which the non-deficiency of the cause [of liberation] would be unestablished. Women possess the possibility of attaining *nirvāṇa* just like men; indeed, the perfection of the Three Jewels, which is the cause of *nirvāṇa*, is not incompatible with women.
For this purpose, the Pāiya-ṭīkā on the *Uttarādhyayana* should also be consulted (*Strīmukti*, verse 2, *Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 752).

Regarding those perfected through female gender (*itthīliṅgasiddha*): right vision and the other [qualities] are seen to be complete in women just as they are in men; for instance—*Prajñāpanā*, Malaya, fol.
20A; *Nandīsūtra*, Malaya, fol. 131B;
*Ratnākarāvatārikā*, 7.
*Bṛhat-Ṣaḍdarśana-samuccaya*, verse 52.

As it is stated in the *Yāpanīya-tantra*: "A woman is certainly not insentient (*ajīva*), nor is she incapable of liberation (*abhavyā*), nor is she an adversary to right view (*darśana-virohinī*). She is not non-human, nor is she born of an ignoble lineage (*anārya-utpatti*), nor does she have an infinite lifespan (*asakhyeya-āyuṣ*). She is not of an excessively cruel nature, nor is her delusion (*moha*) unabated; she is not of impure conduct, nor is her body impure. She is not devoid of resolve (*vyavasāya*), nor is she an adversary to the unprecedented effort (*apūrva-karaṇa*); she is not lacking the nine stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthāna*), nor is she incapable of attaining the state of yoga (*ayoga-labdhi*). Since she is not a vessel for misfortune, how could she not be capable of accomplishing the supreme Dharma?"
–Lalitavi. fol. 57B; Śāstravārtāsamuccaya, Yaśovijaya, fol. 429B. *yathārthāvagamaḥ* (b).

The liberation— that is, the release— from that which was thus described according to its true nature is now stated: women are opposed to the Three Jewels because they are other than men, just like gods and so forth.

"It is well known that for men born in the realms of experience of gods, hell-beings, or animals, there is a contradiction with the Three Jewels by virtue of their being gods and so forth; likewise, it is established that for women, there is a contradiction with these [Jewels] precisely by virtue of their being women. This is an unexamined statement, because the understanding of a contradiction occurs when one thing, whose causes are complete, fails to exist upon the presence of another.

And would this absence of the Three Jewels when womanhood is present be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)? It cannot be through direct perception, because the Three Jewels are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Nor can it be established through inference, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with its absence;
nor can it be established through scripture (*āgama*), because such a scripture that makes known its absence is impossible in that case—
just as in the case of gods or hell-beings— for there exists no statement of the sacred teaching (*pravacana*) that establishes its absence there.

Now, let it be granted that there is merely the Three Jewels (*triratna*) therein; we do not deny that, for that alone does not establish liberation. As for the claim that liberation is absent because the [Three Jewels] that establish liberation—having reached the limit of excellence—are absent there, that is incorrect; for it is impossible to perceive a contradiction in what is unperceived.

Indeed, the Three Jewels having reached the limit of excellence are not perceived by us, and a contradiction cannot be established regarding what is unperceived, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, for one who has not yet realized the contradiction, it is impossible to apprehend the absence of that [contradiction] therein, precisely because of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
just as [one cannot apprehend the absence of] being a woman who contradicts the Three Jewels by means of [the presence of] being a god or the like;
thus, mere words here are no authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) nor any other valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The noble nun who understands the words of the Jina, has faith in them, and practices accordingly,
possesses no impurity; there is no possibility of such a state for her, nor does she fall into a contradiction with what has been seen—
*Strīmukti*, verse 3–4.

Now, if it is argued that they lack the capacity for the destruction of those [defilements] simply because of their femininity, we say no; for there is no established contradiction between femininity and the capacity for the destruction of those [defilements].

Indeed, nowhere has it been ascertained that the capacity for the destruction of those [defilements], when its causes are unimpaired, is absent due to the presence of femininity—such that a contradiction of mutual exclusion (sahānavasthāna) could be established between the two, as is the case with fire and cold. (*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 752)
Prajñāmalaya, folio 20A;
Nandimalaya, folio 132B.
Their distinctness from the person [is established] by scripture (śruti).
The Three Jewels are recognized among women through hearing.
—only that much is the tantra, not... —only that much is the tantra, not liberation-grace...
that which is the grace produced by the means of valid cognition...
It is logical that there is no contradiction regarding what is perceived;
as for what is unperceived, [there is no contradiction] with respect to the Three Jewels.

Now, if it is thought that because the absence of *nirvāṇa* for women is understood through inference, it is not logical to accept its existence therein—specifically, that "women have no *nirvāṇa* because they do not go to the seventh earth, like those born by spontaneous generation (*sammūrcchima*) and so forth"—that is incorrect; for the negative pervasion (*viparyaya-vyāpti*) is unestablished, as the absence of going to that [seventh earth] is not pervaded by the absence of *nirvāṇa*.

In this context, it is observed that when something is restricted to a certain locus, there is a restriction based on the pervasion of its opposite by the reverse of that [locus]; for example, when smoke is pervaded by fire, the absence of fire is pervaded by the absence of smoke, and when the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is pervaded by the state of being a tree, the absence of the state of being a *śiṃśapā* is pervaded by the absence of the state of being a tree. However, such a pervasion of the reverse does not exist here. Furthermore, the absence of that [pervasion] is established because going to the seventh earth and so forth are neither causes nor non-causes for *nirvāṇa*, and because they are not pervasive.

For it is not established that going to the seventh earth is a cause of nirvāṇa—like the Three Jewels—or a pervader—like the eight qualities—such that in its absence there would be an absence of nirvāṇa. Nor does the cessation of a non-cause or a non-pervader entail the cessation of a non-effect or a non-pervaded, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, this proof has a doubtful exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*), and its deviation is certain in the case of those in their final bodies; for they attain liberation in that very birth and do not go to the seventh earth, yet they are nonetheless liberated.
They consider the absence of going to the seventh earth and so forth to be non-pervasive;
those with their final bodies do not go there because of the absence of [further] nirvāṇa—
*Strīmukha*, verse 5.
Sanmati-ṭīkā, folio 753; Prajñāpanā-malaya-vṛtti, folio 20B;
Nandī-malaya-vṛtti, folio 132B.
Ratnākara, verse 7.57;
Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, Bṛhatī, verse 52.
*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, Yaśovijaya, folio 428A;
*Vyaktiprakaraṇa*, folio 115—
"Because of pervasion" (*vyāpteḥ*), here [in the Śrāvaka school].

Furthermore, even those moving in an irregular manner proceed equally downwards, upwards, and transversely as far as the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*); therefore, their downward movement is not deficient. This is because [their movement] pervades the substance possessing the eight qualities (*guṇāṣṭakavat-dravya*), and there is no cessation of that which is pervaded.
Moreover, even those with irregular motion go equally below, above, and transversely up to the *sahasrāra*; thus, the deficiency of their downward motion is not a valid reason.

Since there is no inequality in the capacity of women and men regarding rebirth in lower realms, it is logical that there is likewise no inequality regarding rebirth in happy states; for an unwholesome transformation cannot serve as the cause for a wholesome transformation.

To explain: for serpents, birds, quadrupeds, snakes, and aquatic creatures, downward movement is uneven. This is because serpents—known as *saṃnāma*—are born in the first [hell], birds in the third, quadrupeds in the fifth, snakes in the sixth, and aquatic creatures in the seventh lowest level. However, their upward movement is uniform for all of them, since it is possible for them to be born above up to the Sahasrāra heaven.
Furthermore, even those with uneven movement travel equally upward from below up to the Sahasrāra;
thus, there is no cause for any deficiency in their downward movement when moving horizontally.
—*Strīmukha*, verse 6.

Furthermore, reptiles (*bhujaparisarpa*) travel only as far as the second earth (*pṛthivī*) and not beyond, because they lack the transformation of mental energy (*manovīrya*) of such a nature that would serve as the cause for traveling to higher earths. Birds travel as far as the third earth, quadrupeds as far as the fourth, and serpents (*uraga*) as far as the fifth; yet all of them, at most, travel upward as far as the *Sahasrāra* heaven. This is because, while a disparity in the transformation of mental energy is observed regarding downward movement, no such disparity exists regarding upward movement.
—*Prajñāmalaya*, folio 21A;
*Nandimalaya*, folio 133A;
*Ṣaḍdarśanabṛhatī*, verse 52.
*Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, Yaśovijaya edition, p.
428B; *Yuktiprayoga*, p. 115:
"The state of being a cause is not [the case]; the deficiency of the state of being a cause is not the cause."
—*Ratulyasāma*— Āryaśubhagata also says:

"In the first [dhyāna], those without consciousness (*asaṃjñin*) are born; in the first and second [dhyānas], reptiles; in three, birds; in four, wild beasts; in five, lions; in six, women; in seven, fish and humans. —*Rājavārttika*, p. 118.

The birth of humans, those similar to humans, birds, serpents, lions, women, fish, and animals occurs for the first time and so forth from the Aḍavāra hell; it happens two times—meaning twice—for each of these categories.
— *Trilokasāra*, Gāthā 205.
The first [hell] is indeed for those without consciousness; the second for reptiles; the third for birds;
lions go to the fourth; serpents, however, to the fifth earth; females, fish, and humans go to the sixth; and the seventh earth is for [certain] men.
This should be understood as the ultimate rebirth in the hellish realms—
Bṛhat-saṃgrahaṇī-gāthā 284–85; Trailokya-dīpikā-gāthā 253.

In the first [division] of the *bhujaga*s, Ā; in the first of the conscious (*saṃjñin*) *bhujaga*s, Ba; in the first of the *pūrvatra* manuscript, the second of the conscious ones; in the third of the *khaga*s, the fourth of the *bhujaga*s, the fifth of the quadrupeds (*catuṣpada*), the sixth of women, and the seventh of the aquatic creatures, Ba; in the first of the *khaga*s, the third of the quadrupeds, the fifth of the serpents (*sarpa*), and the sixth of the aquatic creatures, according to the *truṭita* *pūrva* manuscript.

Among the animals, those who are non-cognitive (asaṃjñin), fully developed (paryāpta), five-sensed, and have an immeasurable lifespan, experience the binding of merit by virtue of a small amount of wholesome transformation and are born among the Bhavanavāsins and Vyantaras.

Those same beings, when they possess cognition (saṃjñin) but hold wrong views (mithyādṛṣṭi) or are of the "falling-away" right view (sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi), are born up to the Sahasrāra heaven. Those same beings, when they hold right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), are born in the heavens beginning with Saudharma and ending with Acyuta.
— *Rājavārtika*, p. 169.
The maximum [life-span] for five-sensed animals at rebirth is in Sahasrāra [heaven]—*Bṛhatsaṃgrahaṇī*, verse 164.

Furthermore, there is no absence of liberation for them simply because they lack the attainment of powers such as debate (*vāda-labdhi*) and so forth; for there is no fixed rule that liberation occurs only in such a manner.

Indeed, it is heard that there are infinite beings who attained perfection through mere *sāmāyika* [equanimity] (*Tattvārthabhāṣya*, *Sambandhakārikā* 27). Furthermore, if women were unable to possess such spiritual excellences as eloquence and the like—which arise from the power of austerity—then liberation would likewise not be possible for them. In that case, just as those excellences are absent in the scriptures, the absence of liberation would also have been stated; for we see no other reason for excluding them, since they are heard to lack the attainments of eloquence, miraculous transformations, and so forth, and are of lesser stature.
Even in the absence of the *paryāya* (modes of conduct) characteristic of the *jinakalpa*, there is no lack of spiritual perfection (*siddhi*),

just as there is no lack of perfection despite the absence of the attainments (*labdhi*) such as debate (*vāda*) and so forth; for if there were indeed an absence of perfection for them, it would have been prevented, just as it was in the case of the Jambū-yuga and those prior to it.
—*Strīmukha*, verse 7–8;
*Prajñāmalaya*, folio 21A;
*Ratnākarāvatāra*, 7.
Nor [is it defined] by the absence of attainment such as victory in debate and so forth, because of the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the silent kevalins—
*Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya-bṛhadvṛtti*, verse 52.

For it is heard [in the scriptures] that even in the absence of self-restraint (*saṃyama*), which is the cause for specific acquisitions (*labdhi*) such as the power to digest black gram and husks, there is a cause for liberation; and because the acquisition that is purely destructive (*kṣāyika*) remains unimpeded even in the absence of the acquisition resulting from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣāyopaśamika*).
(Śāstravārttāsamuccaya, Yaśovijaya, p. 427b).
Indeed, it is so heard in the Bhaṭṭāraka and Śrāvaka traditions.
"Only those who have attained equanimity"—
it is heard that there are infinite [beings] who have attained perfection through the state of mere equanimity (*sāmāyika*), because of the statement in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya*:
"There are infinite who have attained perfection through mere equanimity," and because of the *Rājavārttika*, page 10.

[Objection: There are none [who attain liberation], because for women there exists the possession of clothing as a characteristic mark; therefore, there is no liberation. [Response: Then, since they desire liberation, why do they not renounce that? Indeed, clothing is not the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and even those are renounced by one seeking liberation—how much more so clothing? [Objection: But if she were to renounce it, there would be a contradiction with the scripture (*āgama*) which states: "It is not permitted for a nun to be naked" (Kalpasūtra 5.20). [Response: In that case, like the ritual inspection (*pratilekhana*), that [renunciation of clothing] would simply be a limb of liberation.

For just as the sweeping (pratilekhana) taught by the omniscient ones—the guides on the path to liberation—is a limb of liberation, whereas possession (parigraha) is not, so too is clothing, without distinction. Furthermore, if those things prescribed by the scriptures that are means for the Dharma were considered possessions, then alms-food, medicine, bedding, and so forth would also be possessions, just like clothing; and in that case, there would be no liberation for those who employ such means. If it is asked: "Even though they possess clothing, why is there no liberation for householders?"—it is because of the existence of the sense of "mine-ness" (mamatva).
For a householder is not one who is devoid of the sense of "mine" regarding his clothes;
indeed, the sense of "mine" itself constitutes possession,
for when the sense of "mine" exists, even a naked man is considered to possess property.
And because the noble nun has no sense of "mine," she is without possessions, like the sky which is seemingly attached to clouds and other phenomena.

For even when an ascetic enters a village or a house and takes up karmic matter (*karma*) and quasi-karmic matter (*nokarma*), there is no refuge for his state of non-possession other than the absence of the sense of "mine."—[This refers to] the garments of the [nuns]. (Śrāvakabhūmi)

If there is no liberation from the garment and so forth, one should discard it; however, if it is not permissible to abandon it, then it should be handled like the inspection of the lap-cloth (*utsaṅga-pratyupekṣaṇa*). Otherwise, the teacher would be defamed.
It was thus instructed that in the case of discarding [the garment], there is total abandonment, whereas in the case of retaining it, the fault is slight.
Clothing and even the possession of requisites for the noble ones by a teacher—whatever serves to support self-restraint during cold weather and so forth—is declared to be an "accessory" (upakaraṇa).
For that is the means for Dharma; anything other than that is called an "object of dispute" (adhikaraṇa) according to the Arhat.
— *Strīmuktāvalī*, verses 10–12; *Ratnākarāvatārikā*, 7.57.
In the *Bṛhat-Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya*, verse 52, it says:
"Clothing and even the vital breaths..."
Furthermore, there is no garment; Śraṃ kampadi baṃ,
Śraṃ hotāe baṃ, Śraṃ.
It is not permitted for a *nirgranthī* to be naked (*acelā*)—as stated in the *Kalpasūtra*: "It is not appropriate for a *nirgranthī* to be without clothing;
for it has been prescribed in the Scripture that one should wear a garment for three reasons."

Therefore, that very [restraint] must necessarily be maintained by one who is free from attachment; for those unfit for the *jinakalpa* (the mode of conduct of the Jina), the conquest of the hardships of nudity and modesty is essential, and thus that restraint is specifically intended for that purpose.
—*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, Gāthās 2602–3;
*Sanmati-ṭīkā*, p. 748, § [The reading contained within this is not found in Śrā].

[Objection: Since there is no physical body for one who is "clothed in space" (ambaramavigraha), and because injury (*hiṃsā*) exists due to the birth of living beings within clothing, conduct (*cāritra*) itself is impossible; how, then, can liberation be attained? [Response: That is not so, because injury is untenable in the absence of negligence (*pramāda*), for negligence is indeed injury.
For it is stated in the *Tattvārthasūtra* (7.13): "Harm is the depriving of life through negligent yoga (*pramattayoga*).
Otherwise, even an ascetic would be a perpetrator of harm when [engaging in activities] such as consuming food, using medicinal herbs, or occupying a bed.

Since he practices with the diligence prescribed by the Arhat, there is an absence of negligence; therefore, even though the location of the Āryikā is unknown, she too must be non-violent (*ahiṃsaka*), as there is no distinction [between them] in this regard.
As it has been said:
"Even when contact occurs, the Noble One avoids it through the exertion enjoined [by the scriptures]."

For [a woman] is not like a man in a world crowded with multitudes of living beings because of her lack of the disposition toward the destruction of life—*Strīmukti*, verse 15; *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya*, Yaśovijaya, p. 427B.
For it is thus:
by the effort spoken by the Arhat,
[the same applies] even to the noble nun.
Delusion is grasping— Tattvārthasūtra 7.17; delusion is said to be grasping— Daśavaikālika 6.21.
Whether the living being dies or lives, for one of improper conduct there is certainly violence;
whether the living being dies or lives— *Pravacanasāra*.
This is cited from the *Sarvārthasiddhi* (7.13):
"Whether the living being dies or lives, for one of unrestrained conduct, violence is certain."
For one who is self-restrained, there is no bondage through mere injury; for one who is tranquil and composed, there is no bondage through mere injury. (Pravacanasāra 3.17) Fault... bondage.

—Nor is there an absence of liberation for women simply because they are not worshipped by men, since this would lead to a logical fallacy (vyabhicāra) in the case of the Gaṇadharas and others; for they are indeed not worshipped by the Arhats and others, yet they are liberated.
Therefore, it is the Three Jewels alone that are the cause of liberation, and neither being worshipped nor not being worshipped.

If you argue that women cannot be established as members of the restrained order because they lack the capacity for debate, then let them pay homage; if you do not concede their inferiority, consider that there are women who are inferior to men who act as reciters of the Smṛtis, wandering bards, and the like.

The Arhat does not pay homage to those who resemble Tīrthaṅkaras, nor to those following the *jinakalpa* and other such observances, such as the *gaṇadharas*; yet by this much, there is no failure in his status, because liberation has been attained. Otherwise, the state of liberation is equal for both women and men.

—*Strīmukti*, verses 24–26: Now, if it is argued that because women are not objects of veneration for men established in the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*), they do not attain liberation; then, by the same logic, even the *gaṇadharas* and others would not attain liberation, since they too are not objects of veneration for the Arhats.
—*Sanmatitarka-ṭīkā*, p. 754.
Ratnākara-ava° 7.57;
Ṣaḍdarśana-bṛhatī śloka 52.
Śāstravārtāsamuccaya, Yaśovijaya’s commentary, folio 429A;
Yuktiprayoga, page 114;
now, "mucya" [is read as] "mucya" in the manuscript (śra).
Nor does their lack of liberation follow from the abundance of illusion (māyā), for men also possess that same abundance;
indeed, the arising of delusion is its cause, and that is no different for both.
Furthermore, illusion and the like are well-established as states such as hatred and so forth even in the case of persons (puruṣa).
The six types of configuration are equal for all three castes— *Strīmuktāvalī*, verse 28;
*Ratnākarāvatārikā*, section 7.

57. [This is because] even for those possessing their final bodies, such as Nārada and others, there is scriptural testimony regarding their possession of excellence in respect to *māyā* and other powers (see *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, Chapter 6, Verse 52).

Nor should it be asserted that women do not attain nirvāṇa because they are of inferior nature (*hīnasattva*); for in this context, "nature" (*sattva*) must be understood as being characterized by austerity and virtue (*tapaḥ-śīla-sādhāraṇa*), and nothing else, since [the latter] is not a factor for nirvāṇa. And this [characterization] is well-established among the noble women (*āryā*).
And it has been said:
"A woman is indeed of weak resolve; she is merely a vessel for the lap [of her husband]. Therefore, how could there not be vast fluctuations here, for these are the waves of the ocean of character."
Brāhmīsundarī, Āryā, Rājīmatī, Candanā, and other female holders of the Gaṇadhara rank, honored by gods and men, were renowned for their virtue and courage— Strīmuktiśataka, verses 29–30.
In the *Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya*, verse 52,
it is stated that for one who is devoid of austerity and virtuous conduct,
[the attainment] among noble women is indeed already established.

Even in the life of a householder, there are those of excellent character who are renowned in the world for their virtue as the most virtuous in the world; yet there are others who, though devoted to asceticism, lack true character and are devoid of virtue.

—How could women such as Sītā and others be unvirtuous and lacking in fortitude in their asceticism? (Strīmukti, verse 31). Likewise: "The liberation of men has been declared to occur at one and the same time, numbering fifty-eight. (Strīmukti, verse 32).
"By means of the female gender, twenty [attain liberation]; the rest should be known as groups of ten," and so forth;
such scriptural authority (*āgama*) is proof for the liberation of women. Furthermore, it is declared: "In a single moment, one hundred and fifty men attain liberation."
*Aṭṭhasamaya*—Śrī., *addhasaya*—Bā.

Regarding this very point, there are inserted verses (*prakṣepagāthā*) that explain further particulars: "One hundred and eight men attain perfection simultaneously; ten neuter beings likewise; beyond that, there is a prohibition for each subsequent moment."
At one time, at the maximum, twenty women attain accomplishment,
and eight hundred and eight men;
likewise, in a single moment, exactly ten neuter persons attain accomplishment.

In all cases beyond the number mentioned, there is a prohibition—*Bṛhatsaṃhitā*, *Malayagiri* commentary, verse 347: "The first appearance of men occurs in groups of one hundred and eight at a single time; they say that perfection (*siddhi*) is established in the scripture. This is established.

In the case of women, there is no secondary meaning in their union with humans, nor is there any abandonment of the primary sense—[as stated in] Strīmukha, verse 35: "equal-eating" (samadā) [variant: *samakhādā*].
By means of the female gender there are twenty; the remaining [categories] should be known as groups of ten— this is the tradition (āgama), as stated in the *Kaṃtisūtra*.

Now, if by the word "woman" (*strī*) here the female inclination (*strīveda*) is meant, how can there still be a denial of *nirvāṇa* for women? For just as attainment (*siddhi*) occurs for a man through the female inclination, so too it should occur for women; for the internal state (*bhāva*) is the cause of attainment. Furthermore, just as one who is a man in substance (*dravyataḥ*) attains *nirvāṇa* after becoming female in disposition (*bhāvataḥ*), why does a woman in substance not likewise attain *nirvāṇa* after becoming male in disposition? There is no distinction between the two cases. Moreover, the sexual inclination (*veda*) cannot coexist with one who is attaining [liberation], because it is exhausted precisely at the stage of the "subtle passion" (*anivṛtti-bādara-sāmparāya*).

Now, according to the course of past events, he is said to be "liberated" by that same cognition through which he ascends the ladder of the destroyer (*kṣapakaśreṇī*); [the opponent asks: "But why this figurative expression? Let liberation belong to the woman herself, who possesses the characteristics of breasts, procreation, and so forth. — [This is the view of] Bādarasaparāya. Ācārya.
Regarding the Vedas' refutation of the attainment of nirvāṇa through material things and women—
herein it is answered.

As for what was stated—“because the causes are unimpaired,” and so forth—in that regard, the state of having unimpaired causes is unestablished. For its cause is the Three Jewels; would that be the cause as something that has reached the highest excellence, or merely as itself? If it were merely as itself, then there would be the undesirable consequence of even householders attaining *nirvāṇa*.

If, on the other hand, it is as something that has reached the highest excellence, that is not the case, because it is impossible for that [Three Jewels] to have reached the highest excellence therein.

For instance—the supreme excellence of the knowledge and other qualities that cause nirvāṇa does not exist in women, because it is a supreme excellence, like the supreme excellence of demerit (apuṇya) which causes descent to the seventh earth. But this is incorrect, because it is impossible to perceive a contradiction regarding something unperceived; for a contradiction of an unobservable object cannot be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor even through inference (*anumāna*) and so forth. Otherwise, how could there be an apprehension of contradiction even in the case of the supreme excellence of demerit that causes descent to the seventh earth?
"tadā nāsti" does not exist in Ā and Śrī; [it occurs] in the feminine forms.

"Because of the realization of the supreme excellence of knowledge and so forth, which are the causes of liberation"—thus begins the passage from the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 328, line 10. (Note: The term "ityādi" indicates that this is the beginning of a longer citation.)

As for what was also stated regarding the invisible object—that the absence of going to the seventh earth is not pervaded by the absence of *nirvāṇa*, and so forth—that too is incorrect; for we observe the cognition of the rising of the constellation Śakaṭa from the rising of Kṛttikā even when there is no causal relationship.

Indeed, inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is the basis for the relationship between the signified and the signifier, not causality and the like; and that [inseparable connection] certainly exists here.

Indeed, it is not the case that the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is restricted solely to identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), for otherwise it would follow that the rising of the Kṛttikā star and the like could not serve as a probans for the rising of the Pleiades (*śakaṭa*).
This has been explained in detail during the investigation into the Buddhist-conceived notion of pervasion (*vyāpti*);
therefore, [the objection] that going to the seventh earth and so forth cannot be a cause for *nirvāṇa* because they are neither its cause nor its pervader, and so on, is thereby refuted.
