And how could the absence of the further part (*parabhāga*) be ascertained from the absence of the near part (*arvāgbhāga*) for one who speaks thus, given that no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) exists between these two? If it is argued that there is a relation of inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) here, and therefore the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamakabhāva*) will exist between them—surely this is the view of the Naiyāyika, not of the Śvetāmbara; for indeed, if inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished, the establishment of inherence in a single substrate is not possible, since the latter presupposes the former.

Or, let its establishment be granted; nevertheless, since there exists a relationship of the signified and the signifier between those two, let that same relationship exist between the two under discussion as well, because there is likewise a co-inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*). For it is in the very same self (*ātman*) that the capacity for going to the seventh earth is inherent, that in which the capacity for going to liberation is also inherent.

Nor is it intended to prove the denial of *nirvāṇa* for women on the grounds that they do not go to the seventh earth— which would entail the aforementioned fault— but rather, because of the reason of "being at the ultimate limit," which has a proven pervasion with the probandum in the example, the absence of the causes of *nirvāṇa* is what is intended to be proved there;
and from that absence, the absence of *nirvāṇa* will be established there of its own accord,
for indeed, the production of an effect without a cause does not occur, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, what was stated is incorrect—that going to the seventh earth is not a cause for nirvāṇa, like the Three Jewels, and so forth (p. 866, l.
15)—because there is an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).
On page 446:

Since the absence of the near-side part and the absence of the far-side part both inhere in the very same composite whole called a "wall"— namely, in the two parts called the near-side and the far-side— there indeed exists between them a mutual inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*).

Furthermore, there is no proof or logical reason for the arising of female inclination (*strīveda*) in a male body; nor is there proof for the existence of a male [inclination] in a woman. Even for a man, [male inclination] is not established [as inherent], for when ascending the ladder of destruction (*kṣapakaśreṇi*), it is said by the scripture that one is [free] from inclination through the previous [male] inclination.
The term "woman" (strī) is more appropriately applied to the primary sense than to any other—
[as stated in] *Strīmukha*, verses 39–40—
for in that system, it is accepted that the part and the whole possess some degree of identity (*tādātmya*).
For the Śvetāmbara,
because of the establishment of inherence in a single object,
[the probans exists] due to inherence in a single object.

In women, there is the presence of both the capacity to go to the seventh earth and the capacity to attain liberation; yet, it is not the case that the incapacity to attain liberation is likewise present in them.
And because there is no cause for nirvāṇa, an effect would be without a cause; therefore, what was stated [by you] is logical. Śrī. Therefore, it was rightly said by Ba.

As for what was stated [on page 866, line 20]: "That which has its deviation determined by those in their final bodies," etc.—that too is incorrect; because the absence of going to the seventh earth is the absence of the capacity to acquire karma capable of producing that [rebirth], and that [absence] exists only among women, not among those in their final bodies.

For it is heard that even for universal monarchs such as Bharata and others, who were in their final bodies, there was the accumulation of karma capable of leading them to the seventh earth at the time of their departure; however, at the time of worshipping the gods, this occurs in the Sarvārthasiddha heaven. Indeed, an excellent auspicious or inauspicious transformation initiates, respectively, the karma that serves as the cause for an excellent auspicious rebirth or an inauspicious rebirth; and regarding the initiation of that transformation, the capacity belongs to the man alone, not to the woman.
For just as she lacks the capacity for an extremely intense impure transformation, so too does she lack it for an excellent pure transformation;
and liberation is attained through an excellent pure transformation. (Page 867, Line 2)
— in the bodies, [variant] ba, śra;
at the time of the expedition for world conquest,
[variant] ṇām aprāpte ca, ba.

By this, the argument that "those who have gone astray [cannot attain liberation] even from below," and so forth, is also refuted; for it is only one who is capable of acquiring the karma that serves as the cause for initiating an excellent state of existence that possesses the fitness for liberation, not one who is the opposite of that.

For it is heard that, due to the force of specific karma initiating particular intermediate states of existence, even for hell-beings whose karma has been exhausted—though they belong to specific places of birth—there is necessarily rebirth among all types of five-sensed rational animals and among humans within the world of animals (*tiryagloka*). Likewise, due to such karma, for gods who have arisen in specific places of rebirth, there is necessarily rebirth only within the world of animals and among one-sensed beings.

Furthermore, the capacity for liberation cannot arise through the power of accumulating such [extreme] karma; thus, at the stage of investigating the fitness for liberation, there is no purpose whatsoever served by this [argument].

However, that which possesses the capacity to accomplish an excellent auspicious rebirth in the higher state must also possess that same capacity to accomplish an excellent inauspicious rebirth in the lower state—just as in the case of a man. Therefore, one who accepts the capacity of women to attain an excellent auspicious rebirth must likewise accept it for them in respect to an excellent inauspicious rebirth.
And thus, there is a contradiction with your own scripture (bhavadīyāgama), which states: "Likewise, females do not arise as the sixth [in the womb]," and so forth (pṛ. 867, l. 4); [and]:
"Having emerged from hell, [one is born] among humans and animals when the karma-complexion is perfected."

"One is born in the state of a womb-birth in the seventh earth or among the animals" — *Trilokasāra* Gāthā 203. "The movement of hell-beings [occurs] through the completion of karma by those with consciousness, as animals or humans."
Having crossed the four final [oceans], one is indeed in the seventh intermediate state—
*Karmakāṇḍa*, verse 538;
as it is described in the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti*.

—Having a fixed place of birth (niyatasthāna)—[variant: having a fixed place of arising (niyatotpādasthāna)]—among five-sensed beings with consciousness, among animals, and among humans; [the state of] being subject to nutriment exists among gods, and for gods, it occurs through proximity to [other] gods, animals, and humans.
In the case of fully developed (*paryāpta*) coarse (*bādara*) individual earth and air beings, their movement and rebirth occur only among the gods of the three classes of *bhavana-pati*,
humans, and tīrthaṅkaras; likewise, many from Īśāna and above are born among the two types of gods, humans, and the non-sentient (*asaṃjñin*).
—*Karmakāṇḍa-gāthās* 542–43 —On the means of attaining [the higher] states—Ācārya:
"Women [attain up to] the sixth; below that, no. —Bhaṭṭāraka.

As for the other statement—that there is no absence of liberation for them simply because they lack attainments such as the power of debate (*vāda*) and so forth—that too is mere words. For how could any wise person believe that where even the cause for attainments such as worldly debate, transformation (*vikriyā*), and movement (*cāraṇa*) does not exist due to a particular lack of self-restraint (*saṃyama*), that same [lack] will become a cause for liberation? Indeed, the attainment of debate is the capacity to establish one's own doctrine by avoiding quibbles (*chala*) and futile rejoinders (*jāti*), even when obstacles such as Bṛhaspati and others are present in the assemblies of Indra and the like;
while the attainment of transformation is the power to assume the form of Indra and others.
The attainment of the power of movement (cāraṇalabdhi), which is the capacity for traveling through the sky,
and by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of attainments such as the inexhaustible great storehouse (akṣīṇamahānasa) and so forth,
as well as the specific restraint (saṃyamaviśeṣa) that is their cause, is not taught regarding women in the Scripture.
Page 867, line 10:

"The restraint of women is not a cause of liberation, because it necessarily does not serve as a cause for specific supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), as otherwise [liberation] would be untenable. — *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, page 330.
Since there is no [opponent] (ba),

even when Śakra and others who are capable of obstruction are present, the state of being a debater consists in speaking without impediment and without superior, as well as observing the vulnerabilities of the opponent.
—*Rājavārtika*, p. 144:

Because alms are given by people to ascetics who have attained the excellence of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of obstacles to gain, even if the entire retinue of the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) were to eat from that vessel on that day, the food would not be exhausted; therefore, they are called "those whose great kitchen is inexhaustible" (*akṣīṇamahānasa*).
—*Rājavārtika*, p. 145.

As for what was also stated—that in the scripture (āgama) the absence of liberation might be asserted just as there is an absence of excellence in the attainment of powers such as debate (*vāda*) and so forth—that too is a mere assertion; for it is well known in the scripture that the absence of those [powers] in women is established precisely because of the prohibition of specific forms of self-restraint (*saṃyama*).

Indeed, in the scripture, the injunction for men regarding specific forms of self-restraint, such as nakedness (*ācelakya*), which are causes for liberation, is well-established, whereas for women there is a prohibition.
And an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
However, even if these [restraints] exist in them to a mere degree, they are not a cause for liberation, just like the restraints of animals, householders,
and so forth; thus, there is no liberation for women because they possess possessions, like householders (pṛ॰ 868, pa॰ 3).
One who desires the [true] mark (liṅga) eats alms-food at this very time;
even an elder nun (ajjikā) eats while covered by a single garment.
One who wears clothing does not attain perfection in the Jina’s teaching, even if he becomes a Tīrthaṅkara.
The path of liberation is nakedness; all else is a wrong path.
Regarding the female gender, since a subtle body is said to exist between the breasts, at the navel, and in the region of the armpits, how can there be renunciation for them?

If they are pure through right vision and endowed with the path, even those who practice severe conduct are said not to be sinners regarding women; for their minds are purified, and they lack laxity in disposition by their very nature.
For them, meditation upon women has been forbidden for eight months;
from the definitive standpoint (*niścaya*), the attainment of perfection (*siddhi*) by women has never been seen since that birth.
Therefore, the mark (liṅga) differentiated as corresponding to that [male state]— the sign described as distinct from the mark of the Nirgranthas, including the covering garment— belongs to women;
thus [it is stated in] the *Pravacana-ṭīkā*, folio 302.
—like a pillar and so forth, Ārya, Bhaṭṭa.

As for what was also said—that clothing is indeed a limb of liberation, just like the practice of inspection (*pratilekhana*)—that too is not tenable. For, while the practice of inspection was taught by the Blessed One for the sake of maintaining self-restraint (*saṃyama*), for what purpose was clothing taught? If you say that it too is for the sake of maintaining that [restraint], then consider this: women whose limbs and minor parts are exposed are generally overcome by men through the agitation of their minds caused by the sight of those limbs, just as a mare is overcome by stallions. In that case, one must explain why they are overcome by them and not vice versa, given that there is no difference in the fact that both are unclothed. If you argue that it is because they are overcome due to possessing little strength of character (*alpasattva*), then this distinction is well-known in the case of cows, horses, and so forth: the female nature is the object of being overcome, while the male nature is the overcomer. But this is merely the manifestation of great delusion (*mahāmoha*): how can those whose strength of character is so utterly meager that they are overcome even by mere living beings, achieve liberation—which is characterized by the destruction of the entire mass of karma that overcomes the three worlds and which is accomplished only by those of great strength of character?
pṛ॰ 868 paṃ॰ 8 women and men
— one must say "by the qualification" (viśeṣaṇena); "the person to be realized" (puruṣabhāvyaḥ),
[variant] "the destruction of the heap" (rāśikṣayaḥ), [variant] "the characteristic of the exhaustion of the heap" (rāśiprakṣayalakṣaṇam).

As for what was also stated—"If clothing were to be an acquisition of the means for accomplishing *dharma*," and so forth—what is this *dharma* such that clothing could be its means: a specific merit (*puṇya*) or a specific restraint (*saṃyama*)? In the first case, how could it be a cause for liberation? For when it is acquired according to the rules prescribed by scripture, it is a cause of merit alone, just as in the case of a householder;
and if that which is a cause of merit were also a cause of liberation, it would follow that even acts such as giving (*dāna*) would be causes of liberation.

However, its being the cause of a specific form of self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is difficult to establish; for self-restraint consists in the renunciation of external and internal possessions. And how could that [self-restraint] exist when a garment—which causes mental agitation through begging, sewing, washing, drying, storing, taking up, or being stolen by thieves—is accepted? On the contrary, this [acceptance of a garment] is actually a destroyer of self-restraint, because it stands in opposition to both external and internal non-attachment (*nairgranthyam*). (Page 868, Line 10)
If he takes up a piece of cloth or a bowl because it is necessary here in this Sūtra,
how can he be one who has abandoned [worldly things], or how can there be non-involvement in worldly activity?
He takes the broken potsherds, the milk-vessel, and other things;
he certainly engages in the injury of living beings. Distraction arises in his mind as he picks up, shakes, washes, and dries the alms-food when it has been placed in the sun.

Furthermore, how can there be no attachment for one who tears apart a piece of cloth belonging to another and yet protects it? For him, there is exertion and lack of self-restraint; thus, being intent on the property of another, how can he purify himself?
— *Pravacanasāroddhāra-ṭīkā*, p. 297;
*Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p.

331: "But if this were so, since even lumps of food, medicinal herbs, and the like would entail the status of being 'possessions' (*parigraha*), how could there be liberation even for those who take them? This objection is also without merit; for when these are accepted after avoiding defects such as those arising from their production (*udgama-doṣa*), they serve as causes for the strengthening of the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*).

For those [robes], when accepted according to the rules prescribed by our own tenets, do not act as obstacles to liberation; whereas, if they were not accepted, one would become a self-destroyer due to the onset of calamity even before the [proper] time was reached. However, this fault does not apply to clothing, for seekers of liberation abandon even food and other requisites through the sequence of the sixth, eighth, and so forth stages, and those who have attained supreme nudity also perform the inspection of their [very body]; but women never [abandon] clothing.

Nor should it be argued that even when a garment has been taken up, there is no state of non-possession because the sense of "this is mine" is absent; for this would be contradictory. For it is impossible for one who intentionally takes a fallen garment with her hand and puts it on to be free from attachment (*mūrchā*). Wherever something is intentionally taken up even if it has fallen—such as gold and the like—there is no absence of attachment. And so too is the garment taken up by women; for she intentionally takes the fallen garment with her hand. (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 333). Thus, [it is] intentional. (Śrāvakabhūmi).

By this, [the objection] beginning with "the sky appears as if covered by clouds and so forth, yet it is without possession" is refuted; for when a garment covered by clouds and the like falls, its intentional grasping is impossible,
and thus an ascetic who has taken up his robes would not be released even in cases such as hemorrhoids or fistula, or when the robes are lost during a calamity, or when they are stolen.

—*Strīmukha*, verse 17—[The opponent says: "It has been stated that [the practice] is attached since the beginning of creation. Now it is argued: if the abandonment of clothing were accepted for women, then because noble women (*kulastrī*) are characterized by an abundance of modesty (*lajjā*), they would not even undertake initiation (*dīkṣā*). However, if clothing exists, the mere wearing of it is a defect, whereas the preservation of the entire code of conduct (*śīla*) is a virtue. Thus, by determining the relative weight of virtues and defects regarding abandonment and acceptance, the Blessed One taught clothing for them. This is precisely what we desire; we do not disagree on this point, for our disagreement concerns liberation alone."
Furthermore, that discipline (*śīla*) is not capable of accomplishing liberation because it is dependent on possession (*parigraha*), just like the discipline of a householder.

Indeed, even though the discipline of a householder was taught by the Blessed One after examining the merits and faults, and the relative scarcity or abundance of [the virtues of] renunciation and acquisition, it is not capable of accomplishing liberation. The same applies to the subject at hand as well; for if it is argued that this discipline is not capable of accomplishing it because it is mixed with violence (*hiṃsā*), that is equally true for the other case as well.

Indeed, the moral conduct (*śīla*) pertaining to women is not defiled by violence (*hiṃsā*), because it involves clothing that serves as a locus for the spontaneous generation (*sammūrcchana*) of numerous creatures such as lice and nits—just like the conduct of a householder.
Furthermore, if the clothing that serves as the locus for such generation were not a constituent part of violence, then the removal of hair (*mūrdhaja*) would be purposeless;
[this is] the fault in this matter, O Brahmin. (Bhagavatī Ārādhanā)
— having perfected it for the sake of [liberation]—
it indeed becomes the natural conduct (*prakṛta-gṛhastha-śīla*) of a householder.

Regarding what was stated [by the opponent]—"For in the absence of negligence (*pramāda*), their violence is impossible," and so forth—that too is unsound. For when there is a transformation (*pariṇati*) of the passion of greed (*lobha-kaṣāya*), their state of non-negligence (*apramatta*) is impossible, because that very transformation is itself negligence.
As it has been said: "Distracted talk, as well as passions, the senses, sleep, and attachment to worldly objects..."
There are five types of negligence (*pramāda*), and these indeed become fifteen when multiplied by five.

The transformation of the impurity of greed (*lobha-kaṣāya*) exists in women, as is determined by their intentional acceptance of clothing; otherwise, even if they were free from passion (*vītarāga*), the acceptance of it might occur for the sake of removing shame, and thus the proof of that transformation would not be established for them. [Objection: If this were so, why would these women not also accept lovers and the like for the sake of removing the affliction of desire, since there is no difference [in the logic]? [Response: If the existence of that affliction implies that they are not free from passion, then this is the same even in the case of the existence of shame.
Indeed, shame does not arise in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), because shame consists in the desire to conceal loathsome limbs;
he who is free from passion is not possessed of shame, just like a child, and yet the noble lady (*āryikā*) is intended by you to be free from passion—pṛ॰ 868, l. 17.
Regarding their names:
because their livelihood is said to consist of negligence (*pramāda*), they are called *pamadā*;
therefore, they are designated as *pamadā* because they abound in negligence.
In women, there exist fickleness, delusion, malice, fear, and disgust;
and because of their various deceptions, they do not possess Nirvana—*Pravacana-sāra-ṭīkā*, p.
Abounding in illusion and delusion, there is constant falling away from those [reflections]; for one who is full of craving for rebirth, there is no burning of the mind—this is the state of being.
(Bhāvasaṅgraha-gāthā 93)
Idle talk, the passions, the senses, sleep, and likewise attachment— these four, four, five, and one respectively constitute the fifteen types of negligence (pramāda).

This verse also occurs in the *Jīvakāṇḍa* (34), where it is cited as follows: "Four times four, and five—these indeed become the fifteen types of negligence" (*pañcasaṃgraha* 1.15). It is also quoted in the *Dhavalāṭīkā*, page 178.
If clothing and other such items are accepted for the purpose of warding off the pain of cold and shame, it is [an act] preceded by conscious intent (buddhipūrvaka).
Why then is a beloved woman and the like not used for the sake of pacifying the affliction of desire? (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, p. 331; Śrāvakabhūmi, etc.)

If the affliction of desire and modesty belong to men, and nakedness is the cause of liberation for them while the wearing of clothes is the cause for women, then, due to this difference in causes, a distinction must necessarily follow even in liberation itself.

That restraint which is absolutely distinct is the initiator of an absolutely distinct result, just as the restraint of an ascetic and a householder initiates absolutely distinct results such as heaven and the like. Furthermore, the restraint of an Ārya and an Āryikā—consisting respectively of being clothed and unclothed—is intended as a cause for liberation;
yet there is no difference in liberation between these two, since you both admit that liberation, characterized by the destruction of all karma, is identical for both.
If that is so, then a distinction in liberation would necessarily follow from the distinction in its causes, just as in the case of heaven and the like.
Furthermore, regarding the Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, page 330:

Moreover, if the restraint of being clothed were the cause of liberation, then for those seeking liberation, the abandonment of clothing and such would not be taught as something to be done; yet it is so taught for them. Therefore, the status of clothing and such as a limb of liberation is untenable.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: clothing is not a limb (*aṅga*) of liberation, because its abandonment is taught as something to be performed by those seeking liberation; that which is taught as something to be performed by those seeking liberation is not a limb of liberation, just like false view (*mithyādarśana*) and so forth; and the abandonment of clothing is indeed taught as something to be performed by them. Furthermore, that which is a limb of liberation is not taught as something to be abandoned by those seeking it, just like right view (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth;
yet the abandonment of clothing is taught as something to be performed by those seeking liberation.

As for the other point that was stated—that there is an inconsistency [in the argument] regarding the fact that they are not to be venerated by ordinary persons, because of the case of the *gaṇadharas*—that too is incorrect. This is because the Arhats, by virtue of the excellence of their merit consisting of the name "Tīrthaṅkara," have attained the state of supreme greatness; thus, they are indeed to be venerated by all people, but they are not themselves veneration-givers.

For there is no one in the world worthy of a station higher than theirs who could become their venerator. However, because the *gaṇadharas* lack such merit and consequently do not attain that station, they do not possess that same quality of being objects of universal veneration.
However, the collection of factors for liberation does not differ for those who achieve it among non-Jain ascetics;
yet for an Āryikā, that collection is distinct because she lacks the three jewels (ratnatraya) which are its cause.
Thus, women do not attain the state of Nirvāṇa, because they are unfit for the status of being venerated by ascetics, householders, and gods, just like eunuchs and others.
For the state of those who strive (yatis) is twofold and worthy of veneration: the higher and the lower.
Therein, the higher is characterized by the status of a Tīrthaṅkara, while the lower is characterized by the status of an Ācārya and so forth.
Both of these are taught for men alone, not for women;
likewise, the state worthy of veneration for householders and gods is twofold, distinguished as supreme (para) and non-supreme (apara).
Among these, their supreme state worthy of veneration is the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and the status of Indra.
Furthermore, [titles] such as Great Provincial Governor (mahāmāṇḍalika) and so forth, as well as those of the Sāmānika class and so forth,
are heard of only among men, not among women;
and sovereignty over each household belongs only to men, not to women.
Likewise, whether the father exists or not, it is only the son—even if he is young or deformed—who has the authority in every matter, and not the daughters, even if they are grown or beautiful;
therefore, what a great marvel it would be if those who have no authority even over worldly prosperity were to have authority over the glory of liberation!
(Page 869, Line 4)
And by the power of his merit, he will become a Tīrthakara and a worshipper; [by the power] of that merit, he will attain that state.
The state of being that [is] the word "bhāva"—
that is, upon attaining the state of supreme greatness, there is the quality of being worthy of veneration. (Śrī., Bā.)
Like the Tīrthaṅkaras, they possess the state of being worthy of veneration by the entire world—
this [is established] for them in the Śramaṇas and that for the Āryikās in the Brāhmaṇas.
The state of being a universal monarch and so forth, which is a position to be honored even by an adversary.

Now, if it is argued that because they are unworthy of great glory, those [goddesses] cannot attain liberation, then the Gaṇadharas and others would likewise not attain liberation, since there is no difference in their being unworthy of the great glory of Tīrthaṅkara-hood; this too is incorrect, because in this context, the distinction between individual instances is not a factor in the application of injunctions or prohibitions.

For it is the class of men, not the class of women, who are authorized for great sovereignty; therefore, liberation must be accepted as belonging to that [class] alone by excluding the other. Furthermore, it is not proper to establish the equality of women with respect to liberation by raising the objection of deviation (vyabhicāra) on the grounds that liberation is observed even when such sovereignty is impossible in some individual instance.

Indeed, it is not logical that when one prince attains the kingdom, his other sons—despite being inferior to him because they do not attain it—should be equal to a daughter; for in all worldly transactions, the class of daughters is universally recognized in the world as being entirely distinct from the class of sons.
Therefore, women have no liberation because they are inferior to men, like eunuchs and the like;
nor is their inferiority to them unestablished, since this has just been demonstrated immediately prior.
There would be a distinction between individuals regarding the glory of the status of a Tīrthaṅkara, [attained] by means of the injunction for the avoidance of the female sex.

Furthermore, that is established by its attainment, because men perform the acts of inciting, restraining, and exhorting women, whereas women do not perform them for men; and men, assuming the form of the Tīrthaṅkaras, appear as such, while women do not.
And it has been said:

*Sāraṇā* (remembrance) is characterized by the recollection of what is beneficial (*hita*) or by the recollection of duties (*kṛtya*). By way of implication, *vāraṇā* (prevention) is characterized by the warding off of what is harmful (*ahita*). *Coyaṇā* (reproof) is the urging [of a disciple] through such words as, "It is not fitting for one like you to commit such a lapse in the application of self-restraint. *Praticodanā* (repeated reproof) is the urging in that same manner again and again.
— *Gacchācāra-vṛtti-gāthā* 17.
In the *Odhani-ṭīkā*, verse 448:
"Men perform the acts of reminding, restraining, and exhorting; women do not perform reminding or restraining.
— Āvaśyaka-niryukti.
Ichi-āḥ!

Now, it might be argued that inferiority or superiority is not a factor for liberation; rather, it is the Three Jewels [that matter], as in the case of disciples and teachers. For instance, disciples are inferior to teachers, while teachers are superior to them, yet both attain liberation. Similarly, it will be so for noble men (āryas) and noble women (āryikās). But this is mere faith, because even if there were inferiority and superiority as between disciples and teachers, the liberation of women and men would still be without distinction, provided that for them too the Three Jewels—which are the cause of liberation—were present without distinction. However, those [Three Jewels] do not exist in women, since they have already been extensively refuted in their case as being the causes for such [attainment].
However, even though the Three Jewels alone exist there, they are not its cause, because it would follow that even householders and others could attain liberation;
for the capacity of a lamp to accomplish a task that can only be achieved by the fierce sun is not perceived even in a dream—so too [it has been said] by the Teachers (Ācāryas). Śrā. [1.1.2]

Just as the case of the disciple and the teacher is [treated], so too is the claim regarding the noble man (*ārya*) and the noble woman (*āryikā*)—namely, that "even in the state of a householder, there are those of excellent character" (*susattva*), and so forth—which is charming only when left unexamined. For, while among men a "great being" (*mahāsattva*) is well-known for his capacity to uproot all karma through his endurance of many difficult hardships (*parīṣaha*), such a quality does not exist even in a dream for women; rather, it is only in comparison with the female sex that Sītā and others are called "great beings" due to the excellence of their character.
For women do not possess an abundance of *sattva* (courage/virtue) in any undertaking as men do;
and for those who are thus deficient in such *sattva*, how could there be the completeness of the Three Jewels—the cause of liberation to be accomplished by Great Beings (*mahāsattva*)?

For instance: a female body is not a substratum for the completeness of the Three Jewels which is the cause of liberation, because it is produced by great demerit, like the bodies of hell-beings and the like.
Furthermore, because it is the cause for the commencement of the destruction of all karma, its status as their substratum is established.

(Page 869, Line 11) — [The reading] *adhikyam api* [is found] in some places; moreover, in Ā [the manuscript], it is *kiñca*. And since it is the cause for the commencement of the exhaustion of all karma, its being the locus of that [karma] is logical.
Furthermore, it is not logically tenable that the female body can be the cause for the commencement of that [liberation];

for instance, the female body is not the cause for the commencement of the destruction of all karma, because it is acquired through great sin aided by false view (*mithyātva*), just like the bodies of hell-beings and others.
Indeed, the karma that produces a female body is great sin, and it cannot be acquired by anyone other than one with false views.

Although even one with right vision who is in the state of "attaining" (sāsādana-samyagdṛṣṭi) acquires that [right vision], nevertheless, because he is undermining right vision, he is indeed a person of wrong vision; for one who is oriented toward wrong vision is designated by that very wrong vision.

Indeed, even one with mixed right-and-wrong vision does not acquire that much [right vision]; how much less, then, can one with right vision? Even a living being being born as a female is born only while transformed by wrong vision;
as it has been said:
The cause of liberation for the body is its being supported by a self endowed with the completeness of the Three Jewels;
and [this does not belong] to the body.
"O mind, you are lax and prone to stumbling;
therefore, there is suddenly the arising of those [passions] among gods and humans.
— *Pravacana-ṭīkā*, p. 303.

For human females who have attained a pleasant birth, conception occurs constantly in the vulva, the navel, and the armpits, as well as in other parts of the body; therefore, for those women, there is no twofold restraint (saṃyama) that can remove [the embryo].
Without the wearing of the vow of self-restraint, there is truly no liberation in that birth— *Bhāvasaṃgraha*, Gāthā 94–95.
Impurity always exists in the womb due to its being the locus of flowing impurities.
A monthly lapse occurs for these women; minute, incomplete mortals are constantly produced in the wombs of women and in the joints of the armpits and other parts, due to the very nature of that body.
Their nature is contemptible and their characteristic mark is exceedingly contemptible;
therefore, the twofold self-contemplation is not directly attained.
Except for superior self-restraint, there is no fitness for white meditation (śukladhyāna).
Without that [first type of body], there is no liberation; therefore, for them, liberation is exceedingly remote.
Since they lack the first type of skeletal structure (saṃhanana), how could liberation possibly belong to those who do not even possess the power to go to the seventh hell?
If there exist anywhere established images of the Lord of the Tīrtha in the form of a woman, adorned with his liṅga as breasts, let them be proclaimed;
if they do not exist, then my opinion is that they do not exist, for if they did, they would be a source of mockery.
Thus, due to the non-attachment to these two faults, liberation is not possible for a woman— *Strībhāvasaṃgraha*, verses 244–50— [one] should cause [her] to abandon... *mi*— *Āgamahṛdaya*.
One who has lost right conviction by facing toward the level ground of wrong belief from the peak of the mountain of the jewel of right conviction should be known as a "nominal" (sāsana) ascetic—
Jīvakā° Gā° 20.

If it is argued that because of its adherence to the perverted [view] and its being a false view (*asaddṛṣṭi*), this [state] must therefore be a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and should not be designated as "falling away" (*sāsādana*), we say no. For while there is indeed a wrong view in that state—produced by the rise of the "infinite-bondage" (*anantānubandhi*) passions which obstruct right vision and conduct—nevertheless, because the perverse adherence generated by the rise of the delusion-karma (*mithyātva-karma*) is absent, it is not designated as a wrong view; rather, it is designated as "falling away"—*Dhavalā-ṭīkā*, p.
— Even that much is not the cause,
O Śrāmaṇa; how much less so, O Śrāmaṇa— arising precisely from non-existence, O Bāhuka.

In the six lower earths, among the celestial, forest, and residential [beings], and among all women, there is no rebirth for one with right view (sammādiṭṭhi) who holds the twelvefold wrong path; rather, a living being with right view arises only within the five [auspicious] conditions—*Pañcasaṃgraha-nirdeśa*, *Dhavalā-ṭīkā*, p. 209.

In the six lower earths, among the celestial beings, the forest-dwellers, and the inhabitants of the hells, there is no female, nor any follower of the teaching, nor any hell-being who is full [of merit]. — Jīvakā° Gā° 127.

The meaning is that those with right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are not reborn in the six lower hells, among the celestial beings of light (*jyotiṣka*), the intermediate gods (*vyantara*), or the residents of the celestial abodes (*bhavanavāsin*), nor among the females of animals, humans, or gods—in these twelve places of rebirth for the false view (*mithyātva*). "In the twelve places of rebirth for the false view, one with right vision is not reborn. (Pañcasaṃgraha 1.193). [Cited from] Ācārya Śrāmaṇya.
"—in the debate, women are not [qualified].

Even for those who have attained the state of gods with the most excellent lifespan, there is no attainment of the state of liberation (mokṣa); what great skill in logic this is! As for what was also said—that the scripture beginning with 'In the eighth samaya, at the ninth samaya,' etc., is an authority for the liberation of women—this too is the manifestation of no small darkness; for this scripture is not an authority for us, and its lack of authority is well-established because it teaches matters that are sublated by valid means of knowledge."
And just as the matter characterized by the nirvāṇa of women is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so it has already been explained in detail previously [at page 869,
line 13]. (Addhasaya— Ā.)
Śrī Jinabhadra says in response: "Indeed, those men who have known the Vedas and have ascended the ladder of destruction (kṣapaka-śreṇi),
even while the remaining [karmas] are arising, and who are likewise engaged in meditation— they attain liberation."

Furthermore, since there exists authoritative scripture such as *Prāk-siddhabhavya-gāthā* 6 and others which establishes that [attainment of] nirvāṇa, how could the earlier scripture convey a meaning sublated by valid cognition, or how could the attainment of nirvāṇa by women be unestablished on the basis of scripture? Such [objections] are mere wishful thinking, because that [earlier scripture] cannot possibly indicate their [women’s] attainment of nirvāṇa; for that [text] indicates liberation only for men—just as the arising of male-vedanā [indicates liberation for men]—due to the connection with the word "men" (*puruṣāḥ*) in both instances.

"Veda" is defined as a mental modification in the form of desire, arising from the activation (*udaya*) of the deluding (*mohanīya*) karma; and this activation pertains only to the state (*bhāva*), not to the substance (*dravya*).

"Those men who possess the male-veda (*puṃveda*) and have ascended the ladder of destruction (*kṣapaka-śreṇi*), even while other [karmas] are still active, likewise remain engaged in meditation and attain liberation."

Those persons who, while experiencing the *bhāva-puveda* (psychic male gender), have ascended the *kṣapaka-śreṇī* (the ladder of destruction), do so not only by means of the *bhāva-puveda* alone, but also through the arising of the remaining [genders]—that is, likewise through the arising of the *bhāva-strīveda* and *bhāva-napuṃsakaveda* in the form of desire—and being endowed with meditation (*jhāṇuvajuttā*) in the manner of those who have ascended the *kṣapaka-śreṇī*, namely, being engaged in *śukla-dhyāna* (pure meditation), they, though possessing *dravya-puveda* (physical male gender), attain perfection; that is, they become perfected beings (*sijjhati*). [Note on variants: Regarding "attain perfection" (*sijjhati*), there are also the readings *siddhibhavaṃ* (Śrī manuscript) and *ṇasiddhir vā* or *ṇāsiddhir iti* (Ba manuscript). The Ba manuscript reads *ṇāsiddhir iti*. The meaning is the same. The *ṇa* is a particle used for emphasis. Thus, it is said: "They indeed attain perfection. —[The word] *tra* [is used] because of that nirvāṇa—*ba*; —[the word] *strī* [is used] because of the nirvāṇa of women—*śra*.

Regarding the statement in the Āgama, “the state of being a Veda (*vedatā*) is the male Veda (*puveda*),” this is due to its being non-Vedic (*avedatva*). Or rather, accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises from the three Vedas in terms of existence (*bhāva*), but not in terms of substance (*dravya*); in terms of substance, it occurs only through the masculine gender.
— Sarvārthasiddhi 10.9:
With respect to the perspective of the objects of the past, attainment occurs from all three Vedas without distinction in terms of *bhāva* (disposition), but not in terms of *dravya* (substance).
However, with respect to substance, its establishment is by means of the masculine gender alone—*Rājavārttika*, p.
366; "but by means of the masculine gender alone, directly as substance"—*Tattvārtha-ślokavārttika*, 10.

Regarding the statement "for it is the transformation that is denoted," and also what was said—"substantially [they are] persons" (*dravyataḥ puruṣāḥ*), etc.—that too is an unexamined assertion. Since it has been established that, substantially, female gender lacks the capacity for accomplishing liberation, how could even a woman, having become a man in terms of disposition (*bhāvataḥ*), attain nirvāṇa? For that which is incapable of accomplishing liberation substantially is also incapable of accomplishing it dispositionally, just like animals and so forth; and a woman is incapable of accomplishing liberation substantially.

Therefore, it must be admitted—just as in the case of the world—that the person alone, when established in some way within the Veda through its actual being, possesses the capacity to completely conquer all enemies in the form of karma.

For just as it is well known among the common people that a man endowed with great strength, having mounted an elephant, horse, or the like anywhere at all, and taking up some divine weapon, experiences supreme sovereignty while uprooting the entire host of enemies on the field of battle—but he is not [merely] a weak woman who bears her name according to its literal meaning—so too, in substance, it is the man himself who, having ascended any one of the three Vedas in essence and taking up the incomparable weapon of white meditation (*śukladhyāna*), experiences supreme sovereignty while uprooting the host of enemies that are the *karma*s.
(Page 870, Line 3: *mokṣasādhana*)—Ba.
—O All-pervading One!
Among all people, [I am] the child. O Śrī!

As for what was stated—"Nor is the Veda established," and so forth—that is indeed true; for we do not maintain that liberation [comes] from the Veda, since we accept the higher and lower liberation as resulting from the fire of intense white meditation (*śukladhyāna*), which is capable of incinerating the accumulation of karma (pṛ.
Now, the author of the treatise, explaining the purpose of studying the scripture, says:
A worthy person (bhavya), having propitiated the five teachers with stainless austerities and having understood the scripture,
studies its meaning from those [teachers] by means of words that are subject to corruption, yet refer to that meaning.

Having attained the stainless state from that which is further removed from the self, the Jina—the Victorious One, whose wisdom possesses the power to perceive the entire range of the world—would himself become [the Awakened One]. 77.
*syāt* means "he would be."

Who is the *bhavya* (the one capable of liberation)? It is that which will become or transform into the cause of liberation in the form of the Three Jewels. Why is it called *bhavya*? Because one who is not *bhavya* (*abhavya*) lacks the qualification for liberation.
Of what nature would such a one be? He would be a *Jina*.

Furthermore, of what character is he? He possesses the power and wisdom to perceive the divisions of both the world and the non-world. The world (*loka*) is the collection of the six substances; beyond that is the non-world (*aloka*), which consists of pure space (*kevalākāśa*). The "divisions" (*kalā*) refer to the distinct parts of these two.

Alternatively, "loka" means the world, "aloka" means the non-world, and "kalā" refers to categories such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and other ontological principles; he in whom there exists the power, capacity, wisdom, and supreme knowledge for the observation of these is so described. How [does he observe]? "By himself," meaning by his own self and not by the assistance of the senses and so forth.
Furthermore, what is he characterized by? What has he attained? A "pada," meaning a state or station.
Of what nature is it? It is "stainless" (ākalaṅka), meaning this state of Arhatship belongs to those who are free from stain.
Having done what does the knower [attain it]? Having practiced, that is, having contemplated it again and again.

What? For that purpose; having made the meaning of that scripture—the reality of the soul and so forth—the primary object. Having understood, studied, and known what? The scripture, which is the Śruta.
From whom? From those five teachers.
From what as a limiting point? From the word.
Of what kind? Having the meaning as its object.

Furthermore, from what kind [of speech]? From that which is free from *apabhraṃśa*—that is, free from the defects of grammatical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-doṣa*). Having done what prior to that? Having propitiated the gurus, such as the Arhats and others;
how many? Five.

By what qualities? By means of external and internal austerities, by the restraint of desires that are stainless—free from impurities such as false belief—and by having practiced the words of the sacred teachings, their meanings being thoroughly mastered therein. (Laghu-tattva-vṛtti, p. 100)
Thus certain—
having repeatedly awakened from the burning of non-awakening, the wise one, with doubts destroyed,
easily takes refuge in the state of the stainless Blessed Ones.
May he tell you the auspicious path to the station of the great-souled ones.
Who shall tell it? Who shall establish it? The wise one, the knower.
Whom? The path; what kind of means for attaining the way? Auspicious; of what? Of the state, that is, the station.
Of whom? Of the great-souled ones.
To whom should he speak? To you, the disciples.
By what means? By ease, through the absence of the hardship involved in the movement of the palate and lips.
Being qualified by what? Having attained (*samāśrita*)—what? A station (*sthāna*), that is, an abiding; not one subject to momentary destruction, because there is no teaching [of such] therein.
Qualified by what? By the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), who is worthy of worship by the three worlds.
Of whom is this the place? It means the place of the stainless Arhats. Being of what nature? Having destroyed all doubt.
Having done what? Having understood—that is, having ascertained.
How? Having meditated repeatedly, again and again, upon what objects? Upon the principles (tattvas) such as the soul (jīva) and so forth;
of what nature are they? They are thoroughly established and firmly settled.
Where [is it]? In those words of the teaching.
Why? From awakening.
Of what kind? From a radiant, blazing one; that is to say, from one that shines forth through mutual competition (*ahamahamikā*), being free from confusion and intermixture.
Having done what?
Having practiced and reflected;
that is to say, having applied oneself again and again.
Which [words]? The words of the sacred teaching (*pravacanapada*).

The intention of the gods is: "May he, having attained omniscience—his stains of both substantial and dispositional nature having been consumed by the fire of white meditation (*śukladhyāna*) through the transformation of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) resulting from the practice of the supreme scriptures (*paramāgama*)—strive for the sake of others by instructing in the path to liberation.
(Laghīyastrayāvatārikā, p. 101)

Commentary: When the scripture (*āgama*)—which consists of the discourse on reasons (*hetuvāda*) and which precisely elucidates the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the viewpoints (*naya*), and the categories (*nikṣepa*), all endowed with their definitions, enumerations, objects, and fruits—is correctly understood through the lineage of teachers' instructions and practiced to the highest degree, the perfection of one's own goal (*svārtha-sampatti*) characterized by the attainment of the state of a Jina Lord occurs.
And when that is accomplished, he strives for the perfection of the goals of others (*parārtha-sampatti*) by means of instructing those seeking liberation in the path to liberation. Thus it is said.
For in its own nature,
it is indeed the accomplishment of the welfare of others; thus it is intended.
Thus ends the *Pravacanapraveśa* as remembered by the illustrious Bhaṭṭākalaṅkaśaśāṅka. [Cha] Thus the work is completed. Ba.

My understanding is not of such a kind, nor has Sarasvatī granted me a boon; furthermore, there is no assistance from anyone, even by word, in the production of this work. Whatever merit has been generated through devotion to the Lord Jina, by that [merit], this most wonderful work—supreme and produced through the grace of the virtuous—has arisen as an abode for the awakening to all meanings. (1) May this supreme work remain for a long time—a dwelling of auspiciousness, fashioned like gold, served by Vidyādharas, lofty in form, beloved by the wise, possessing manifold splendor, and resembling the king of mountains; whose state was not attained even by the wandering Bṛhaspati and others, and which churns the ocean of logic. (2) May the tree of the Jaina doctrine flourish here, bearing excellent fruits such as heaven and other realms: its root is supreme, stainless knowledge regarding all things; its base is the entire great, corroborative means of valid cognition established in worldly practice; its branches are all the *nayas*; its mass of leaves is the pure series of *nikṣepas*; and it is laden with good fruit in the form of heaven and so forth. (3) From the Lord Padmanandin—the sun to the lotuses of the *bhavyas*, a treasury of virtues, an ornament of the world, and an ocean of all scriptures beginning with the Siddhānta—there arose his disciple Prabhācandra, who is devoted to the stainless path. From him, the entire path of Nyāya, composed of incomparable objects of knowledge, became clearly manifest. (4) Having overcome his own adversaries, the illuminator of all systems of thought, an ocean of virtues, may the Sun-like Jinendra Prabhācandra, the author of this auspicious work, be victorious! (5)
My intellect is not of such a kind, nor has Sarasvatī granted me a boon; furthermore,
there is no assistance from anyone, even by word, for the production of this literary work.
Whatever merit has been produced by [this] composition of the *Nyāyakumudacandra* and so forth, born from devotion to the Lord Jina, by that may this most wonderful [work]...
Through the grace of the virtuous, there has arisen the Nyāyakumudacandra, a supreme abode for the awakening of all meanings,
a golden temple of auspiciousness frequented by the Vidyādharas. 1.
With lofty limbs, beloved by the wise, possessing manifold splendor, and resembling the lord of mountains—
he whose state was not attained even by Bṛhaspati and others as they wandered about.
May this supreme treatise, which churns the ocean of Nyāya, endure for a long time. (2) [Variants:
*nyāyāmbhodhinibandhana* (Ā), *nyāyāmbhonidhimanthanaḥ* (Śra);
*Nyāyakumudacandra*]

The root of which is supreme, stainless knowledge whose object is all things; its trunk is the entire great, concordant means of valid cognition established by worldly convention; its branches are all the *nayas*; and its multitude of leaves is the pure series of *nikṣepas*.

May the venerable Lord Padmanandin— the sun to the lotuses of the *bhavyas*, a treasury of virtues, an ocean of all scriptures such as the Siddhānta, and an ornament of the world— be victorious here, his feet having borne the excellent fruits of heaven and other realms. 3.

From his disciple Prabhācandra— who was devoted to the stainless path— the entire path of logic (*nyāya*) arose, clearly elucidated by that logician and composed of incomparable objects of knowledge. 4.

May the Lord of Jinas, Prabhācandra, the ocean of virtues and the sun that illuminates all systems of thought, be victorious—he who has overcome his own adversaries and composed this auspicious treatise.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, an ornament to the *Laghīyastraya*, composed by Prabhācandra. [End of Volume]

Thus ends the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, an ornament to the *Laghīyastraya*, composed by the illustrious Paṇḍita Pramācandra, a resident of the glorious Dhārā during the reign of the illustrious King Jayasiṃhadeva, who—having acquired stainless merit through prostrations to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) who is both transcendent and immanent—has dispelled the entire mass of impurities and stains. May there be auspiciousness!
Homage to the illustrious Candranātha!
Homage to the venerable Śrī Vijayakīrti Muni.

There was one named Nandin, a crest-jewel among those who know the causes of worldly existence, who was a lamp for the jewel-like temple of the lineage of Śrī Nandiṣeṇa; he was a knower of all omens, beginning with the *cūḍāmaṇi*. (1) His disciple was Saubhāgyanandin, a treasury of austerity, a treasury of tranquility, a treasury of knowledge, and a treasury of wisdom; his heart gladdened the hearts of the fortunate through his character, and he alone found delight in true happiness. Having boarded the ship of the quality of eloquence (*pratibhā*), which carried the jewels of right understanding, he beheld the supreme, boundless shore of the great ocean of the True Doctrine (*siddhānta*). (2) He became the disciple of that sage [Saubhāgyanandin], namely Devanandin, who was a vessel of the essence of asceticism through his blazing and intense penance; who was like a god to be saluted by the community of monks of the four orders; and who was called "Nandin" because of his union with supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). (3) From this mountain of sunrise, by the power of destiny and through the play of his rising, the illustrious Bhāskaranandin illuminated the ten directions with his splendors. The entire circle of stars of the learned, which had been obscured on all sides by the darkness of falsehood, was covered by the mass of rays of his words that revealed the truth. (4) Even the formal debate (*vādakathā*) was abandoned by the hosts of disputants, and not even the slightest frivolous talk (*jalpa*) was made. Out of shame, the chatterers, heretics, and cavillers (*vaitaṇḍika*) did not speak at all. They served only the pair of lotus-feet of the illustrious scholar-lord Bhāskaranandin, whose wisdom was sharpened on the whetstone of the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the six systems of logic (*ṣaṭtarka*). Thus ends the *Nyāyakumudacandra-vṛtti-tarka*. Total number of verses: 16,000. [Year] 1520. May there be auspiciousness! Śrī.
The lamp-jewel for the temple of the illustrious Nandisaṃdha lineage was one named Ānandin, the crest-ornament of the foremost Siddhāntins; this eulogy is found only in [the work of] Ācārya Pratāpa.
Cūḍāmaṇi, a knower of all omens beginning with the *cūḍāmaṇi*, became the preeminent among those who know the signs of worldly existence. 1.

His disciple was Saubhāgyanandin, a treasure-house of asceticism, a treasure-house of tranquility, a treasure-house of knowledge, and a treasure-house of wisdom; he delighted the hearts of fortunate beings with his virtue and, having embarked upon the ship of the quality of eloquence which carries the jewels of true enlightenment, became a treasury of the wealth of learning.
He saw the furthermost shore of the boundless great ocean of the six philosophical systems.
He became the disciple of that sage, Devanandin,
who was the very abode of truth through his intensely blazing and fervent asceticism.
He was worthy of being saluted like a god by the assemblies of śramaṇas from the four castes;
and because of his union with supreme bliss, he became Nandi, a god.
From this mountain of sunrise, by the power of destiny and through the emergence of his divine play, [he arose] on all sides.

By the illustrious Bhāskararāya Nandin, the ten directions have been illuminated with his splendors; the entire circle of the stars of the learned has been entirely covered on all sides by the mass of rays from the words that dispel the darkness of falsehood and reveal the truth. || 4 ||
Even formal debate has been abandoned by the hosts of disputants, and not even the slightest frivolous talk has been uttered; out of shame, the boastful heretics and sophists have said nothing,
for they serve one whose wisdom is sharpened on the whetstone of the Upanishads of the six systems of logic.
The pair of lotus-feet of the illustrious Bhāskararāya Nandapaṇḍitapati [is my refuge].
Thus ends the *Nyāyakumudacandra-vṛtti-tarka*. [End. The total number of verses (*granthāgra*) is 16,000. [Year] 1520. May there be auspiciousness. Glory!
This work is completed. The eulogy of the editor of the *Nyāyakumudacandra*:
While the circle of the ocean flourishes with the hooves of the virtuous in the city of Vikasatpura, during this formidable [age],...
From Suparavārajabāharalāl, the son of Mahendra was born.
In the city called Vīnā, which is the refuge of poets, he received his Sanskrit education from Dharmadāsa at the Nābhinandana school of true learning.
Beginning with his initial studies and desiring to attain excellence, he reached the Induravidyālaya, which is beautiful to the learned.
Having diligently studied Dharma from Vaṃśīdhara and Tarka with great acumen from Jīvaṃdhara, [he attained proficiency].
Having arrived at the Syādvāda Vidyālaya, I labored there for a long time without weariness. While continuously teaching Nyāya to my students,
I subsequently attained the rank of Nyāyācārya in the highest class.

Having written this commentary, history, and critical comparison here with a mind full of inquiry through much effort, the wise should correct any errors resulting from lack of attention; thus, [such flaws] are overlooked.
[This was composed] in the year of Vīranirvāṇa equal to six flavors (rasa) and two pairs of eyes (netra).
This work reached completion for me on the ninth day of the first fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, conjoined with Tuesday,
through the flood of grace from the feet of my Guru, and without any obstacle. 7.
